### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be viewed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture. An extremely accurate edition, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library gathers together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

# The Complete Works of Gregory

[Column 0009]

## The Books of Morals of Saint Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff, or Exposition of the Book of Blessed Job

### Continuation

#### Part Four, Containing Six Books

## Book Seventeen

Explains what remains from chapter 24, beginning at the half verse 20, together with chapters 25 and 26 in full, chiefly in the moral sense.

# Chapter One

[Column 0009A]

### 533. The Doctor’s purpose is to explain Job’s history typologically and in the mystical sense

Whenever, in the history of a holy man, we undertake to unfold a mystery through a new volume of typological exposition, it is necessary that we first draw out the mystical meaning chiefly from either the name or the suffering of that same man, so that, after the manner of dwellings, when we place the inscription of the title at the front of the door itself, the house may be recognized as belonging to whom it does, and one may enter with greater security.

[Note: Uticensis and Gemeticensis read, “which, mutilated in many preceding books, we resume here,” concerning the typological expression. The following books are lacking in the Lyrensis and Bigotian codices. Their place will, however, be supplied by the Pratellensis, another Ebroicensis, two manuscripts of the Church of Laon, the Germanensis, Corbeiensis Germanensis, etc.]

[Note: One Laon manuscript reads, “on the very face of the post.”]

I remember having often said that blessed Job signified the sufferings of our Redeemer and of his body, that is, holy Church, both by his own suffering and by his name.

[Note: Vindocensis reads, “how blessed Job.”] For *Job* is interpreted as “suffering.” And who else is represented in this suffering man except the one of whom it is written: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4)? Of him it is said again: “By his bruise we were healed” (ibid., 5).

But his friends represent the type of heretics, who, as we have often already said, offend God while striving to defend him.

[Note: The first Laon manuscript and Corbeiensis Germanensis read, “while they defend God, they offend him.”]

Thus the holy man speaks through his wounds and words in such a way that he also signifies our wounds and words; very often, through the spirit of prophecy, he tells of things to come and transcends the present, while at other times he discusses present matters in such a way that he remains silent about the future.

Once this rule of discernment is understood, our own understanding should alternate along with the alteration of his voice, so that it may correspond all the more truly to his meanings the more it changes together with his words.

In the preceding words, therefore, the holy man, by clear statements fashioned with the skill of prudence, brought forward the guilt of every kind of wicked person and expressed how deserving of condemnation his conduct is. He immediately adds what follows concerning his punishment, saying:

# Chapter Two [Second Recension]

## Verse 20

> “Let him not be remembered, but let him be crushed like an unfruitful tree.”

### 2. The punishment of the wicked is to be erased from God’s memory

For whoever remains enslaved to vices until the end of life is not brought into the memory of the Creator. If the memory of heavenly regard touched such a person, it would doubtless recall him from wickedness. His merits demand that he be utterly erased from the memory of the Author.

It must be understood, however, that God is by no means properly said to remember. For one who cannot forget, how can he remember? But because we embrace those whom we remember, while we withdraw from those whom we forget, God is said, in human usage, both to remember when he bestows gifts and to forget when he abandons someone in guilt.

Yet because he weighs all things and considers all things without any interruption or alternation, he remembers the good, whom nevertheless he never forgets; and he does not remember the evil, whom nevertheless he always regards in judgment.

It is as though he returns to the memory of the good, though he never abandoned it; and as though he does not look upon the wicked, though he considers their deeds, reserving judgment of condemnation against them at the end.

Hence it is written: “The eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked” (Proverbs 15:3). Hence the Psalmist says:

> “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm 33:17).

[Note: Ebroicensis, Gemetensis, and other Norman manuscripts read, “but the face of the Lord.”]

He therefore considers those whom he punishes, but he did not previously see those whom he does not know. For to some he will say at the end:

> “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7:23; Luke 13:27).

In a wondrous way, therefore, he both regards and forgets the life of the wicked, because those whom he judges with the rigor of his sentence he ignores, insofar as concerns the memory of mercy.

### 3. They will be crushed like an unfruitful tree

Because they do not enter into his memory, they are like an unfruitful tree, crushed by his judgment. The earth nourished them with temporal sustenance, and from above drenched them with the rain of preaching. But because their life produced no fruit of good works, the angry farmer cut it down, so that, according to the sentence of Truth, it would not occupy a place which another could hold profitably (Luke 13:7).

[Note: Gemeticensis and other Norman manuscripts read, “cuts it down.”]

John speaks of this unfruitful tree:

> “The axe is already placed at the root of the tree. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10; Luke 3:9).

[Note: Two Laon manuscripts read, “of the trees.”]

Here, however, to designate the eternal punishments of the reprobate, the tree is not said to be cut off but crushed.

[Note: The two Laon manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others commonly have *abscidi* and *abscidit*, etc., in place of *abscindi* and *abscindit*.] For death of the flesh cuts off the reprobate, but the punishment that follows crushes them. It is cut down here, as it were, when it is separated from the present life; but it is crushed in Gehenna when it is tormented by everlasting condemnation.

Since the holy man has expressed the severe punishment of the perverse, he immediately returns to the guilt, so that from the enormity of the injustice he may teach that such great condemnation is not unjust. It follows:

# Chapter Three [Third Recension]

## Verse 21

> “For he fed the barren woman, and the one who does not bear, and he did not do good to the widow.”

### 4. The wicked person feeds the barren flesh and abandons care of the soul

Who is called “the barren woman” here except the flesh? While it seeks only present things, it does not know how to give birth to good thoughts.

And who is called “the widow” except the soul? Since the Creator wished to join it to himself, he came to the chamber of the bodily womb, as the Psalmist testifies:

> “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm 18:6).

It is rightly called a widow, because its husband endured death for it and now, hidden from its eyes in the inner courts of heaven, lives, as it were, in another region.

[Note: All Norman manuscripts, two Laon manuscripts, Germanensis, Corbeiensis Germanensis, and others have this reading. The printed edition reads “of the virginal womb.”]

[Old Second Version.]

The wicked person therefore feeds the barren woman and neglects to do good to the widow, because, serving the desires of the flesh, he despises the care and life of the soul.

With his whole intention and every effort he considers how the flesh, though destined to die, may continue without any necessities, while he disdains to care for the life of the soul, which will undoubtedly live forever either in death or in blessedness.

[Note: The Norman manuscripts read, “neglects.”]

When it is said, “He fed the barren woman,” it is rightly added immediately, “and the one who does not bear.” For from sacred history we know certain women who were barren but nevertheless bore children at the final time. The flesh, however, is called not only barren but also “the one who does not bear,” because by its own understanding it is unable to produce good thoughts even at the end.

It has already lost its own vigor, yet it does not cease to desire transitory things.

[Note: Vindocensis reads, “labor”; Uticensis, with this word left incomplete, reads “strength.”] Exhausted now of its former strength, it is almost driven away from the world it loves, yet it still strives with wicked effort to obtain temporal things. It no longer has sufficient strength to carry out perverse deeds, yet it does not cease to think even about what it does not do.

It is rightly called not only barren but also non-bearing, since, as we have said, it does not conceive the offspring of good thought even when it has become weakened.

### 5. The labors of heretics are barren

This may also be understood of heretical preachers. Every preacher of error, while teaching a people placed outside the unity of the Church, certainly feeds one who is barren and unable to bear, because he expends the labor of his work upon one who yields no spiritual fruits.

But he does not do good to the widow, because he scorns to live for and serve the holy universal Church, whose husband endured the adversities of death.

To do good to the widow is to labor for the consolation of one who is crushed by love for her dead husband.

[Note: The first Laon manuscript reads, “to raise her by consolation, and by a second hand to labor in consolation.”] Hence this same widow, namely holy Church, complains in the voice of the Psalmist:

> “I sought one who would comfort me, and I found none” (Psalm 68:21).

She finds a comforter only when she sees many within herself rising to life from the death endured by her husband.

Often, moreover, the preacher of error joins himself to the rich of this world. Because they are occupied with earthly concerns, they do not know how to detect the subtleties of his words; and while they seek outward power, they are caught without difficulty in the snare of perverse preaching. Hence it is added:

# Chapter Four

## Verse 22

> “He has dragged down the strong in his strength.”

### 6.

In the strength of his wickedness he drags down the strong when, through the cunning of his error, he seizes the powerful of this world.

Paul says of them:

> “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

[Note: Vindocensis adds, “so that he might confound all the strong things.”]

The strength of the perverse preacher is the arrogant learning of his speech. Inflated by it, he despises others and, in contempt of all, swells with the conceit of being uniquely learned in his own eyes.

Thinking highly of himself but knowing nothing true about the Lord, he is separated far from knowledge of the faith, yet he strives to appear a preacher of the faith. Hence it is further added:

# Chapter Five [Old Third Version]

## The Same Passage

> “And when he stands, he will not believe in his own life.”

[Note: A second Laon manuscript, Uticensis, and other Norman manuscripts read, “he does not believe.”]

### 7. Every sinner is guilty of unbelief

Every perverse preacher stands in this world as long as he lives in an earthly body. But he refuses to believe in his own life because he disdains to know the truth about God.

He would believe in his own life if he thought rightly about the substance of his Creator.

We were speaking above of these matters concerning any wicked person, but suddenly we have turned to an interpretation concerning the preacher of error.

[Note: After this word the printed edition inserted: “how the sinner is tolerated for a long time.” We removed these words because they are unknown in our manuscripts and do not fit either the preceding or the following context.]

It must therefore be understood that we are led from the general to the particular in such a way that we are nevertheless not entirely torn away from the general category.

For every perverse person, even if he appears to hold the right faith in the bosom of the universal Church, stands and does not believe in his own life. For the things he understands about the Creator through faith are indeed right, but he scorns to maintain the works of faith; and he is convicted of unbelief because, by his manner of life, he rejects what he shows himself to believe.

Hence John says:

> “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

Paul says:

> “They profess that they know God, but they deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16).

James says:

> “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:20, 26).

Yet amid these things the Creator, by a wondrous dispensation of his counsel, both regards sins and grants time for living, so that the longer periods of temporal life may become either an aid to the gift of conversion or, for one who does not convert, an increase of condemnation. Hence it is further added:

# Chapter Six [Fourth Recension]

## Verse 23

> “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride.”

### 8. Mercy bestowed on and neglected by the sinner becomes punishment

Whoever sins and continues to live is tolerated by divine providence in his iniquity so that he may be restrained from iniquity.

[Note: The German, English, Norman, Laon, Vindocian, and other manuscripts give this reading; later editions read, “tolerates him in equity.”] But whoever is tolerated longer and nevertheless is not restrained from iniquity receives the gift of heavenly patience, yet by the bonds of his guilt he binds himself more tightly through that very gift.

Because he turns the time granted for repentance toward guilt, the strict Judge at the end turns the means of mercy bestowed upon him toward punishment.

Hence Paul says:

> “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5).

[Note: Most Norman manuscripts read, “or do you not know?”]

[Column 0014A]

Isaiah says:

> “The child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isaiah 65:20).

[Note: Vindocensis adds, “as though he were saying: life.”]

As though he were openly warning us, he says: The life of the child is prolonged so that he may be corrected from childish deeds; but if he is not restrained from the perpetration of sin even by the length of time, that very length of life, which he received through mercy, increases for him the accumulation of his curse.

Therefore, when we see that we are being awaited for a long time, we must fear the very periods of mercy granted to us as proofs of condemnation, lest the punishment of the sinner increase through the clemency of the Judge, and lest the very means by which someone could have been snatched from death become the means by which he advances more grievously toward death.

This usually happens because the eye of the mind is not separated from present things. The sinner neglects to consider the ways of the Redeemer and therefore grows old without ceasing in his own paths. Hence it is added:

# Chapter Seven [Old Fourth Version, Fifth Recension]

## The Same Passage

> “For his eyes are upon his ways.”

### 9. Having abandoned the ways of the Lord, the sinner delights in his own ways, that is, in vices

The sinner observes his own ways because he strives to think about and see only those things that serve his temporal advantage.

[Note: Vindocensis reads, “he strives to think about and pursue only.”]

Hence Paul says:

> “They all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21).

The way of the proud is pride; the way of the robber is greed; the way of the licentious person is carnal desire.

[Note: Gemeticensis reads, “conscience.”]

Every wicked person therefore lowers his eyes upon his own ways, because he attends only to vices, so that through them he may satisfy his soul.

Hence Solomon says:

> “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” (Proverbs 17:34),

because with the whole intention of their heart they see only that by which they may be led to the goal of earthly desire.

The sinner would never fix the gaze of his consideration upon the earth if he lifted the eyes of his mind to the holy paths of his Redeemer.

Hence Solomon says again:

> “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14),

because every wise person considers with his whole intention the one whose member he reckons himself to be through faith.

The one who said the following had disdained to look upon these ways of human conduct:

> “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways” (Psalm 118:15).

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanensis, Turonensis, the Norman manuscripts, and others read “I will exercise myself”; the printed editions read “I shall be exercised.”]

Thus he openly promises, saying: I now refuse to look upon what is mine, because I burn to proceed along the way of your imitation with the steps of a transformed life.

[Note: Vindocensis reads, “to see.”]

Whoever now contradicts the present world continually sets the ways of his Redeemer before the eyes of his heart through the exercise of love, so that his mind may flee prosperity and prepare itself for adversity;

[Note: The older printed editions, with the English, Norman, Vindocian, and other manuscripts, read “with the steps of a manner of life”; later editions read “of conversion.” Turonensis and one Laon manuscript read, “through the exercise of love.”] may desire nothing that charms it and fear nothing that is believed to deter it; may count sorrow as joy; may weigh the joys of the present life as losses of sorrow; and may not fear the losses of humiliation, but seek through them a place in abiding glory.

Truth displayed these ways to the eyes of those who follow them when he said:

> “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26).

He recalled to these ways the swelling hearts of the disciples when they were already seeking a place of glory but did not know the path to that same glory, saying:

> “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matthew 20:22).

[Note: The printed edition erroneously inserted “of confession” in place of “of session,” which is read in Corbeiensis Germanensis, Laon, Germanensis, and other manuscripts.]

They had sought the height of that session at his right and left, but they did not see how narrow the path to it would be. Hence the cup of the Passion, which they were to imitate, was immediately set before their eyes, so that, if they were striving toward the joys of exaltation, they might first find the way of humility.

Since the sinner therefore neglects to consider the ways of God and attends only to those in which he takes carnal delight, it is rightly said here:

> “For his eyes are upon his ways.”

It follows:

# Chapter Eight

## Verse 24

> “They are exalted for a little while, and they will not endure.”

### 10. One exalted by empty glory falls after a little while

Although the glory of the wicked often extends over a multitude of years, it is thought by weak minds to be long and almost stable. But when a sudden end cuts it off, it clearly proves that it was brief, since the end that brings it to completion makes known that what could pass away was only for a little while.

[Note: The Laon manuscript and Corbeiensis Germanensis read, “cuts it short.” The word “end” has been added from the Norman and English manuscripts and the older printed editions; it was absent from the recent editions.]

They are therefore exalted for a little while and do not endure, because by the very fact that they desire to appear lofty, they become far removed through pride from the true being of God.

They cannot endure because they are divided from the solidity of eternal being, and they suffer this first ruin because through private glory they fall within themselves.

Hence the Psalmist says:

> “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Psalm 72:18),

because they fall inwardly in the very measure by which they rise wrongly outwardly.

[Old Fifth Version.]

Observing this brevity of temporal glory, he says again:

> “I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Psalm 36:35).

[Note: Vindocensis, the Norman manuscripts, and most others have this reading; the old editions agree. Recent editions read “like the cedars.”]

Again he says:

> “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be” (ibid., 10).

[Note: Two Laon manuscripts read, “and he was not.”]

James says:

> “For what is your life? It is vapor appearing for a little while” (James 4:15).

[Note: First Laon manuscript adds, “our.”]

The prophet, weighing the brevity of carnal glory, declares:

> “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

The power of the wicked is compared to the flower of grass, because carnal glory, while it shines, falls; while it exalts itself in its own eyes, it is cut short and ended by a sudden death.

Thus a stalk is carried high by the breath of the winds but is quickly brought back down by its fall. Thus smoke rises to the clouds but suddenly, swelling, is scattered into nothing. Thus mist lifts itself from the depths as it thickens, but the sun’s ray rises and wipes it away as though it had not been. Thus the moisture of night dew is sprinkled upon the surface of the grasses, but it is dried by the sudden heat of daylight. Thus the foaming bubbles of water, stirred up by rains beginning, emerge eagerly from the depths, but burst and perish all the more quickly the higher they are stretched by their inflation. As they grow so as to appear, by growing they bring about the fact that they do not endure.

Of the wicked, therefore, swollen with the exaltation of temporal glory but lasting nevertheless in no solidity, it is rightly said:

> “They are exalted for a little while, and they will not endure.”

Of them it is further added:

# Chapter Nine

[Column 0016B]

## The Same Passage

> “And they will be humbled like all things, and they will be taken away.”

### 11. The earth will always remain in its essence, although it continually passes away in appearance

The progress of contemplation should be such that it is carried from a few things to many, and from many to the consideration of all, so that, advancing by degrees, it may grow by comprehending all transitory things, almost incomprehensibly expanding itself.

[Note: The printed editions and some manuscripts read: “and, by comprehending and judging all transitory things, it itself almost incomprehensibly expands.” Since this can scarcely be understood, we have restored this obscure and corrupt passage chiefly from two Laon manuscripts.]

Therefore, when the holy man was discussing the glory and downfall of the wicked, he immediately extended the eye of his mind to all things, saying:

> “They will be humbled like all things, and they will be taken away.”

All earthly things, certainly. As though he were openly saying: They cannot stand in any way, because the very things upon which they rely are themselves fleeing; and while they love temporal things, they pass away with them through the changing course of time.

But one may ask: Since Solomon says, “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4), why does blessed Job assert that all things are humbled and taken away?

We can easily resolve this if we distinguish how earth and heaven pass away and how they remain. Both pass away in the form that they now possess, yet in essence they subsist without end.

Hence Paul says:

> “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31).

The Truth himself says:

> “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

[Note: Recent editions incorrectly read, “hence through John.”]

In an angelic voice it is said to John:

> “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:4).

These are not other things that are to be created, but these same things are renewed.

Heaven and earth therefore both pass away and will be, because they are cleansed by fire from the appearance they now possess, while they are nevertheless preserved always in their own nature.

Hence the Psalmist says:

> “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101:27).

They now announce this final change of themselves to us through the very alternations by which they continually vary for our uses.

For the earth loses its winter appearance through dryness and grows green through the moisture of spring. Heaven is daily covered with the darkness of night and renewed by the brightness of day.

From this, therefore, every faithful person should gather that these things both perish and yet are restored through renewal, since it is clear that they are now continually repaired as though from decay.

[Old and Sixth Recension.]

Amid these things, therefore, when the holy man observes the course of the wicked, it becomes evident with what punishment they will one day perish, as he immediately adds:

# Chapter Ten

## The Same Passage

> “And they will be crushed like the tops of ears of grain.”

### 12. Although wicked rich people agree in oppressing the just, they are separated from one another by their desires

The tops of ears of grain are the awns. The awns emerge joined together in the ear, but as they grow little by little, they become separated from one another, bristling and rigid.

Thus wicked rich people rise toward the glory of this world. They are joined to one another by the commonality of nature, but as they grow against one another, they are divided.

One despises another, and one burns against another with the fires of envy. Those who separate themselves from the unity of charity through the swelling of their minds stand rigidly against one another, like awns.

What, then, should I call the wicked rich of this world except certain awns of the human race? While they are proud against one another but unanimously afflict the life of the good, they are divided among themselves, yet in agreement they press the grains downward.

### 13. The reprobate now rise like awns; the elect lie hidden like grains

Now the awns thrust themselves upward, while the grains remain hidden, because the power of the reprobate stands out, whereas the glory of the elect is not apparent.

[Note: The Norman manuscripts and others read, “shoot upward.”]

[Note: The first Laon manuscript reads, “that one displays himself by the deeds of the good”; Vindocensis, “those display themselves by honors”; Gilot, “by the insignia of honors.”]

The former display themselves through the pomp of honors; the latter humble themselves in lowliness.

But the time of threshing will come, which will break the rigidity of the awns and not crush the solid grains. Then the pride of the wicked will be shattered; then it will be revealed with what integrity the life of the elect shines, because, when the unjust perish, the very crushing of the awns brings about the appearance of the grains that had lain hidden.

When the awns are broken, the whiteness of the grains is displayed, because, when the wicked fall into eternal punishments, it is shown with what truth the justice of the saints shines.

Hence John also rightly says:

> “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather the wheat into his granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17).

[Note: Vindocensis reads, “and will cleanse.” Turonensis, the two Laon manuscripts, and almost all others, with the older printed editions, read “into his granary”; recent editions read “into his granaries.”]

Blessed Job, therefore, seeing with what punishment the exaltation of the wicked is broken, compares them to awns that perish and says:

> “Like the tops of ears of grain they will be crushed,”

because the rigidity of the proud is broken by the force of the final threshing, which now rises in contempt of the life of the elect.

It follows:

# Chapter Eleven [Seventh Recension]

## Verse 25

> “But if it is not so, who can convict me of having lied and set my words before God?”

### 14. If the just should sin, they are nevertheless not to be corrected by the wicked

If things are not as he says, everyone can certainly accuse him of falsehood. Why, then, is it said:

> “If it is not so, who can convict me of having lied,”

when we know that anyone may rightly rebuke a liar?

But if we examine the speaker’s meaning through careful questioning, we quickly find how correct are the things he has brought forward.

For even if the just person ever speaks while committing some fault, it is not fitting for him to be judged by the unjust and those who live wickedly.

Thus the holy man, suppressing the pride of his friends, is confident that he cannot be reproached whether what he has said is so or not, because those who do not know how to act falsely are the ones who can rightly rebuke falsehood.

Those who still live deceitfully lose the boldness to correct deceit. He therefore says:

> “If it is not so, who can convict me of having lied?”

As though he were openly saying: Everything is as I have stated. Yet even if it were not so, you could not rebuke me, because, while you yourselves still succumb to your own faults, you are unable to criticize the falsehood of another.

### 15. Our judgments must be weighed before the supreme Judge

He aptly adds:

> “And set my words before God.”

For whoever truthfully rebukes false words, reflecting upon what he has heard and weighing it according to the rule of truth, sets the words before God, because he examines within himself, in the presence of Truth, what judgment he should pronounce outwardly against falsehood.

[Note: The first Laon manuscript reads, “words of falsehood”; two Ebroicensis manuscripts and Germanensis read, “the falsehood that has been spoken.”]

To set words before God is, after considering the inner Judge, to weigh outward speech.

The holy man therefore does not think that his words can be set before God by his proud friends. As though he were openly saying: You cannot bring what I say before the Judge because, while you are sinning, you hide his face from yourselves.

This may also appropriately be understood according to the type of holy Church. When she is reproached for her weak members by the mockery of heretics, she disdains the cunning of their mockery, because it is more acceptable to God that someone lie in weakness and ignorance with humility than that he grasp lofty things with pride.

But since the holy man has said many things against those who are proud of fleeting power and puffed up by empty honors, Baldad the Shuhite, profiting from his correction, recognizes with whom true power lies and says:

# Chapter Twelve [Old Seventh Version, Eighth Recension]

[Column 0018D]

## Chapter 25, Verse 2

> “Power and terror are with him, who makes peace in his high places.”

### 16. God alone is powerful and to be feared

As though he were openly saying: He alone truly strikes mortal hearts with terror who truly possesses them through the power of his divinity.

For what terror does human power inspire, when it does not know how long it will lack the right to that same power?

It is rightly said:

> “Who makes peace in his high places,”

because many things below disagree among themselves, yet they move toward the harmonious fullness of the heavenly realm; and through the cause of inward peace it comes about that things outwardly are often arranged without peace.

For almighty God advances the good toward merit when he permits the wicked to rage against their life.

The highest things are brought into harmony while the lowest things are confounded, because from the very place where, in the heavens, he joins his elect to the choirs of angels, he bears on earth and in the lowest places the conduct of the reprobate, which resists his commands.

[Note: Recent editions read “minds,” contrary to the manuscripts and older printed editions. A little below we read, “the conduct of subjects ... the help of a ruler’s spirit.”]

17. How angels who are supremely harmonious among themselves are said to contend. — But amid these considerations it is worth asking: if supreme peace is maintained in the heights, what does it mean that the angel says to Daniel: “I came because of your words; but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. X, 13). And shortly afterward: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. When I was departing, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid., 20). Whom else, then, does he call the princes of the nations except angels, who could have resisted him as he departed? How, therefore, can there be peace in the heights if even among the angelic spirits themselves there is a contest of battle, though they always stand before the sight of Truth?

But because particular angelic ministries have been assigned for governing each of the nations, when the conduct of their subjects merits in turn the assistance of the spirits set over them against one another, the spirits who preside over them are said to come against one another. For that angel who spoke to Daniel is understood to have been set over the captives of the Israelite people who were living in Persia. Michael, however, is found to have been appointed over those from the same people who had remained in the land of Judaea. Hence, shortly afterward, this same angel says to Daniel: “There is no one who helps me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (ibid., 21). Of him also he says what we have already quoted: “And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (ibid., 13). Since he is said not to be with him but to come to his aid, he is plainly recognized as set over that people which was being held captive in another region.

What does the angel mean by saying, “I came because of your words, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me” (ibid., 13), except that he announces to his subjects the work he has undertaken? It is as though he openly said: “The merits of your prayers indeed demand that the Israelite people be released from the yoke of its captivity, but there is still something in that people that must be purged under Persian rule, so that the prince of Persia rightly opposes my effort to free it, although the tears also of those who have remained in Judaea assist your prayers.” Hence he adds what we have mentioned: “Michael, your prince, came to help me.” And when he goes out to fight against the prince of Persia, the prince of the Greeks appears, coming against him. From this it is indicated that Judaea had also committed some offense against the Greeks, whose cause plainly resisted its release.

The angel therefore hears the prophet’s prayers, but the prince of Persia resists, because although the life of the righteous man praying already demands the people’s release, the life of that same people still opposes it, so that, since those who had been led into captivity had not yet been fully purged, the Persians might still rightly rule over them. Michael helps, but the prince of the Greeks comes to battle, because the long captivity of the oppressed could indeed have merited pardon, but the benefit of their release was obstructed by what they had also done against the Greeks.

It is rightly said, therefore, that the angels come against one another, because the merits of the nations subject to them in turn contradict one another. For the exalted spirits who rule those same nations do not contend on behalf of those acting unjustly; rather, they examine their deeds and judge them justly. When the guilt or righteousness of each nation is brought before the council of the heavenly court, the prince appointed over that nation is said either to have prevailed in the contest or not to have prevailed. Yet the single victory of them all is the supreme will of their Maker, who is above them; as they always behold that will, they never desire to obtain what they cannot obtain. Thus it is rightly said: “Who makes peace in his heights.” It continues:

CAPUT XIII [Rec. IX].

VERSE 3. — “Is there any number to his troops?”

18. The number of angels, though finite for God, is infinite for human beings. — Within the knowledge of human reason there is no number for the spirits above, because no one knows how great is the multitude of that invisible army. Of it Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII, 10). The number of the citizens above is expressed as both infinite and definite, so that what is countable for God may be shown to be innumerable for human beings. Yet standing before him is one thing, and ministering is another. Those powers undoubtedly stand before him who do not go out to announce certain matters to human beings. Those minister who come to carry out the tasks of messengers, though they too do not withdraw from inward contemplation.

And because those who minister are more numerous than those who principally stand before him, the number of those standing is shown as if definite, whereas the number of those ministering is shown as indefinite.

[Old Recension VIII]

19. Why God’s soldiers are so called. — We rightly call the angelic spirits God’s soldiers, because we know that they battle against the powers of the air. Yet they carry on these contests not by labor but by command, because whatever they desire to accomplish against unclean spirits, they can do through the help of the One who governs all things. Concerning this army, at the birth of our King it is written: “Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army” (Luke II, 13).

The number of the elect among human beings is also joined to this army: those who, through the sublime desire of their minds, are freed from the bondage of earthly conduct. Of them Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (II Tim. II, 4). Although they now appear few, in the invisible homeland they reign innumerably. For even if they are few in comparison with the wicked, they cannot be measured by the multitude of their own assembly.

But because the strength of these soldiers is reinforced not by their own powers but by the infusion of heavenly grace, it is rightly added:

CAPUT XIV.

IBID. — “And over whom does his light not rise?”

20. They are strong not by their own powers but by the gift of grace. — The light of God is prevenient grace. If it did not arise freely in our hearts, our mind would certainly remain obscure in the darkness of its sins. Hence it is added:

CAPUT XV [Rec. X].

VERSE 4. — “Can man be justified when compared with God, or can one born of a woman appear clean?”

21. No one is righteous except through God’s illumination, not by comparison with him. — This verse was spoken earlier by blessed Job, and now it is repeated in rebuke of him. Every righteous person is righteous through God’s illumination, not by comparison with him. Human righteousness, when compared with its Creator, is unrighteousness, because even if a human being had remained in the very condition of his creation, the creature could not be made equal to the Creator (Job IX, 2).

To this heavier burden of weakness was added guilt, which the lurking serpent introduced and the weakened woman persuaded him to accept (Gen. III, 6). Thus, because a human being is born through a woman subject to guilt, the liability of the first weakness is propagated in the offspring. And because the branch of the human race rotted at its root, it does not at all remain verdant in the freshness of its created condition.

Hence it is rightly said now: “Can man be justified when compared with God, or can one born of a woman appear clean?” It is as though he openly said: “So that a human being may not grow proud against his Creator, let him consider from where he has come here and understand what he is.”

But behold, some, helped by the gift of the Spirit, rise up against the weakness of their flesh; they shine with virtues and even sparkle with miracles. Nevertheless, no one passes through life without guilt so long as he bears corruptible flesh. Hence it is further added:

CAPUT XVI.

[Col. 0021D] VERSE 5. — “Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight.”

22. No one is so righteous that, in corruptible flesh, he is free from every sin. — What is signified by the moon except the Church as a whole, and by the stars except the souls of individuals who live well? Amid the conduct of wicked people, while they stand out through great virtues, they shine as if in the darkness of night. Hence Paul also says to his disciples: “Among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15).

That the holy Church is expressed by the designation “moon,” the prophet testifies when he says: “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. III, 11). For when the sun has been raised up, the moon is established in its order, because, when the Lord ascended into heaven, the holy Church was immediately strengthened in the authority of its preaching. And because the elect are signified by the name “stars,” Paul again declares: “Star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV, 41) [Old Recension IX].

The moon therefore does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight, because the holy Church does not shine with so many miracles by its own virtue unless the gifts of prevenient grace pour over it; nor are the minds of individuals who live well clean of the stains of sin if they are judged apart from mercy, because, in the eyes of the strict Judge, each person’s own corruptibility defiles him unless daily grace wipes it away.

The mind of the elect strives to advance into the freedom of righteousness, but it is still held by the fetter of weakness. It earnestly desires to subdue its faults perfectly, but so long as it is bound by the corruption of the flesh, it is tied by those bonds even when it does not wish to be. From this let us infer under how great a weight of sins those are pressed who neglect to struggle against them, if even those who fight against sin courageously do not wholly overcome it.

Therefore, after it was said, “Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight,” it is immediately added:

CAPUT XVII.

VERSE 6. — “How much more is man rottenness, and the son of man a worm?”

23. If even the holier are not free from stain, how filthy are those immersed in the impurities of the flesh. — It is as though he openly said: “If even those who shine amid the darkness of the present life through their virtues cannot be without contamination, how great is the guilt by which those are bound who still live according to the flesh? If those who already conduct themselves according to heavenly desires cannot be free from sin, what burdens of sin do those endure who, devoted to the pleasures of their flesh, still carry the yoke of rottenness?”

Peter says: “If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (I Pet. IV, 18). Through Isaiah it is said: “Upon the soil of my people thorns and briars will rise; how much more upon every house of joy of the exultant city?” (Isa. XXXII, 13). The Lord calls the mind of all the elect the soil of his people; he says that thorns and briars rise upon it because he sees that not even it is without the prickings of vices.

The house of joy of the exultant city is the mind of the wicked, which, because it neglects to contemplate the punishments to come, abandons itself to the pleasure of the flesh and rejoices vainly. Thus he says: “Upon the soil of my people thorns and briars will rise; how much more upon every house of joy of the exultant city?” It is as though he openly said: “If vices oppress the minds even of those who afflict themselves out of desire for the heavenly homeland, beneath what sins are those prostrate who abandon themselves to the pleasure of the flesh without any fear?”

24. The first man is rottenness, whose sons are worms. — It should be noted how carefully Baldad observed in his speech the order of our creation and birth: he calls man not a worm but rottenness, and the son of man a worm. The first parent of the human race was man, not the son of man; whoever came forth from him was not only man but also the son of man. Therefore, just as the son of man comes from man, so the worm is born from rottenness.

Thus man is rightly called rottenness, and the son of man a worm. The first man is rottenness, not a worm, because although he rotted through death, he did not come from rottenness by birth. But he who is the son of man is called a worm because he is already propagated from the corruption of mortal bodies.

25. Since, then, the words of the friends have ended, blessed Job takes up his argument with deeper sharpness. His words are as forceful as they are final, because it is customary among jurists to reserve for the conclusion of their argument the proof by which they foresee that they will rise above their opponents. It continues:

CAPUT XVIII [Old X, Rec. XI].

CHAPTER XXVI, VERSES 1–2. — “But Job answered and said: Whose helper are you? Surely [you are the helper] of the weak? And do you sustain the arm of one who is not strong?”

26. To wish to help the weak is charity; to wish to help the powerful is arrogance. — To help the weak is charity; to wish to help the powerful is arrogance. Since his friends, representing the type of heretics, were attempting, as if helping God, to display their own wisdom, Baldad is rightly rebuked by the words: “Whose helper are you? Is it perhaps the helper of the weak? And do you sustain the arm of one who is not strong?”

It is as though he openly said: “While you strive to help him beneath whose greatness you collapse, all the assistance you offer proceeds from ostentation, not from compassion.”

27. In what sense we are said to help God. — Yet amid these matters it should be understood that, even with regard to God, who is certainly not weak, we often help him by acting humbly. Hence Paul says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (I Cor. III, 9). When, by the voice of exhortation, we join with one whom God himself fills by inward grace, we outwardly assist by our ministry what he inwardly accomplishes through the Spirit; and only then is our exhortation brought to perfection, when God is present in the heart as the one who gives help.

Hence elsewhere he says: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (ibid., 7). To plant and to water is to help. Both forms of ministry, however, will be empty if God does not give the increase in the heart.

But those who think differently according to their own understanding do not wish to be humble helpers of God. For when they consider themselves useful to God, they exclude themselves from the fruit of usefulness. Hence the voice of Truth says to the disciples: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were bound to do’” (Luke XVII, 10). It continues:

CAPUT XIX.

VERSE 3. — “To whom did you give counsel? Perhaps to one who does not have wisdom?”

28. To give counsel to a fool is charity; to give it to the wise is ostentation; to give counsel to Wisdom itself is perversity. — To give counsel to a fool is charity; to give it to the wise is ostentation; but to give counsel to Wisdom itself is perversity. And because those whom we have said to represent the type of heretics served ostentation rather than usefulness through their speech, it is rightly added against Baldad:

[Col. 0024B] IBID. — “And you have displayed your abundant prudence.”

Everyone whose prudence is sound does not possess it in excess, because, in Paul’s words, he does not desire to be wise beyond what he ought to be wise (Rom. XII, 3). But whoever possesses it in excess does not possess sound prudence, because, when it is extended beyond measure, one declines into fault on some side or other.

Those who desire to appear wiser than others display their prudence in excess. Hence it often happens that, because they do not know how to think with moderation, they even speak foolishly. For this reason the excess of prudence is further stated:

CAPUT XX.

VERSE 4. — “Whom did you wish to teach? Was it not the one who made the breath of life?”

29. Baldad’s folly in preferring his own wisdom to divine wisdom. — We live through the breath of life; through prudence we are wise. But living comes before wisdom, because, in order for us to be wise, it is first brought about that we exist. Therefore, the one who gave life undoubtedly also conferred prudence.

Baldad, however, because he believed that blessed Job had been scourged on account of guilt, tried through proud rashness to penetrate the hidden judgment of God, which he ought humbly to have revered. Thus he preferred himself in prudence to the One whose judgment he judged without understanding it. He preferred himself in prudence to the One from whom he had received the breath of life—as though he were wiser than the One from whom he had received his existence.

But because blessed Job, bearing the figure of the holy Church, had said little in correcting the proud, whom he knew to represent the type of heretics, he now rises suddenly to instruction and expands the breadth of his knowledge in a series of pronouncements against the ignorance of the arrogant, saying:

CAPUT XXI [Old XI, Rec. XII].

VERSE 5. — “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.”

30. Proud angels and human beings are enveloped in the abyss of ignorance. — It was fitting first to blunt, through rebuke, the swelling of earthly wisdom, and afterward to pass through instruction to words full of mysteries. There is no obstacle to understanding by “giants” either apostate angels or any proud human beings.

Hence the prophet says: “The dead will not live; the giants will not rise again” (Isa. XXVI, 14). Whom does he call the dead except sinners? And whom does he call giants except those who even grow proud of their sin? The former do not live because, by sinning, they have lost the life of righteousness. The latter cannot rise again after death because, after their guilt, inflated by pride, they do not return to the remedies of repentance.

Again it is written: “The man who has strayed from the way of instruction will dwell in the assembly of giants” (Prov. XXI, 16), because whoever abandons the path of uprightness joins himself to none other than the number of proud spirits.

It is rightly said against the arrogant: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.” It is as though he openly said: “Why should a human being grow proud of knowledge, when the abyss of ignorance weighs down even the most exalted spirits among the angels?”

31. Those who desire to preside over others are placed beneath those same others. — If, however, by the name “giants” the powerful of this world are signified, peoples may be represented by the waters, as John testifies when he says: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. XVII, 15).

It is rightly said against the proud: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters,” because all the arrogant, while in this life they desire to attain the heights of honors, groan beneath the burdens of peoples. For the more someone is elevated above another here, the more he is burdened with heavier cares; and in mind and thought he is placed beneath those very peoples above whom he is placed in rank.

These words also aptly indicate briefly that all pride lies at the very depth to which it rises on high, so that it is placed beneath everyone precisely from the point at which it seeks to be above everyone. A person raised to an exalted position supports above himself as many people as he governs beneath him. Those who associate themselves with such people are also weighed down by sharing in their labors. For they endure the burden of the labor together with them, since they pursue the glory of honor together.

Hence, when he had said, “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters,” he immediately added:

CAPUT XXII.

IBID. — “And those who dwell with them.”

32. Greater responsibilities open an easier path to vices. Desired dignities cannot be administered without sin. — It is as though he said: “Those who join themselves to their glory with delight groan together with them.”

The very occupation of secular dignities is oppressed by vices made all the more accessible because it is burdened with greater cares. Would that the human mind could see and avoid sins even when at rest!

Since, therefore, he saw that the desired heights of worldly affairs could not be administered without sins, and since nothing unlawful is hidden from divine wrath, he appropriately added:

CAPUT XXIII.

VERSE 6. — “Hell is naked before him, and there is no covering for destruction.”

33. No sin is hidden from divine wrath. — The Apostle Paul also says: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13).

By the name “hell” and “destruction” he signified the devil and all his companions in damnation. But who is the one before whom hell is naked? He continues:

CAPUT XXIV [Rec. XIII].

VERSE 7. — “He stretches out the north over emptiness.”

34. The devil fills hearts empty of divine love. — In sacred speech the devil is usually called by the name “north,” because, in order to bind the hearts of the nations with the cold of sluggishness, he said: “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV, 13).

He is stretched out over emptiness because he possesses those hearts that are not filled with the grace of divine love. Yet the omnipotent God is able, by the gift of his grace, to fill even the devil’s vessels, empty of every virtue, and to place in them the firmness of divine fear, though he sees them strengthened by no act of righteousness. Hence it is aptly added:

CAPUT XXV.

IBID. — “And he hangs the earth upon nothing.”

35. The Church is founded upon the Gentiles and Jews reduced to nothing through sin. — What is designated by the name “earth” except the holy Church, which, when it receives the words of preaching, produces the fruit of good works? Concerning it Moses says: “Let the earth hear the words from my mouth; let my speech be awaited like rain” (Deut. XXXII, 2).

And what is designated by “nothing” except the Gentile peoples? Of them the prophet says: “All the nations are regarded as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. XL, 17).

The earth, therefore, is suspended upon that nothing which had previously been held by the north as emptiness, because the hearts of the Gentiles, previously oppressed by the devil’s torpor, have been filled with the love of God.

It is also possible that by “emptiness” the unbelief of Judaea is signified, and by “earth,” as we have said, the fruitfulness of the holy Church. Let the holy man, then, behold the fall of perishing Judaea and the merit of the Gentiles returning to pardon, and let him say: “He stretches out the north over emptiness, and hangs the earth upon nothing.”

For because the hearts of the Jews, empty of faith, are subject to the devil, he stretches out the north over emptiness. But because, with no prior merits existing, as it is said, “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. LV, 8), the Lord founded his Church among the Gentiles, who have been called “nothing” by the prophet, he appropriately adds: “He hangs the earth upon nothing.”

He then connects what follows by a marvelous exposition of the order in which this occurred. For he says:

CAPUT XXVI [Rec. XIV].

VERSE 8. — “He binds the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth together below.”

36. The Apostles and preachers are designated by the name of clouds. — What does he call water in this passage except knowledge, and what does he call clouds except preachers? For we have learned, with Solomon as witness, that in sacred speech water is sometimes called knowledge: “Deep waters are the words from a man’s mouth, and a flowing stream is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII, 4).

The prophet David testifies that water signifies knowledge when he says: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII, 12)—that is, hidden knowledge is in the prophets. Before the Lord’s coming, while they carried immense mysteries, pregnant with hidden sacraments, their understanding was obscured from the eyes of those who looked upon them.

But what else are designated in this passage by the name “clouds” except holy preachers, that is, the apostles, who were sent throughout the regions of the world and knew both how to rain through their words and to flash through their miracles? Isaiah the prophet, seeing them long beforehand, said: “Who are these who fly like clouds?”

Since, therefore, this man, filled with the prophetic spirit, desires in this statement to begin the praise of God with the origins of the nascent Church, he endeavors to recount its order beginning with the preaching of the apostles. They took the greatest care to preach to unformed peoples what was plain and comprehensible, not what was lofty and difficult.

For if they had poured out the holy knowledge, here signified by the name “water,” from their mouths as abundantly as they drank it in their hearts, they would have overwhelmed their hearers by its immensity rather than watered them. Therefore, with knowledge bound inwardly so that it would not burst forth all at once below, that cloud spoke, nourishing its hearers by the gradual distillation of words: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 1–2).

Who could have endured it if Paul, caught up to the third heaven and caught up into paradise, had also opened the immense depths of heavenly knowledge while hearing secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (II Cor. XII, 2)? Or whose strength as a hearer would not have been overwhelmed if the immensity of that water, which he could drink inwardly, had flowed outwardly as far as the tongue of the flesh was able to contain it?

37. Inexperienced hearers must be watered not by a flood but by the distillation of knowledge. — So that inexperienced hearers may be nourished not by a flood of knowledge but by the measured distillation of preaching, God binds the waters in the clouds so that they do not burst forth together below. He moderates the preaching of teachers so that the weakness of their hearers may grow strong, nourished by the dew of their words.

This is aptly related in the Gospel through a mystical description, when it is said: “Jesus got into Peter’s boat and asked him to put out a little from the land; and sitting down, he taught the crowds” (Luke V, 3).

What else is signified by Peter’s boat except the Church entrusted to Peter? So that the Lord might preach from it to the crowds flocking together, he ordered it to be put out a little from the land. He commands it neither to be taken into the deep nor to remain on the land, plainly signifying that his preachers ought to preach to inexperienced peoples neither things too lofty from heaven nor merely earthly things.

The water is therefore bound in the clouds, because the knowledge of preachers, speaking to the minds of the weak, is restrained from teaching them more than they are able to understand.

[Old Recension XIII]

38. Higher knowledge must be veiled from weak minds. — For often, if the heart of the hearers is corrupted by the immensity of the word, the tongue of the teachers is punished for its lack of discretion. Hence it is written: “If someone opens a cistern and digs it, and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals” (Exod. XXI, 33).

What does it mean to open a cistern except to penetrate the secrets of Holy Scripture with a strong understanding? And what is signified by the ox and the donkey, that is, the clean and unclean animal, except the faithful and the unbeliever?

Therefore, whoever digs a cistern should cover it, lest the ox or donkey fall into it—that is, whoever already understands lofty matters in sacred speech should cover sublime meanings in silence before those unable to receive them, lest through the scandal of their minds he destroy either a faithful little one or an unbeliever who might have been able to believe.

He must pay the price for the death of the animals because he is proved to have committed the deed for which he is held guilty and bound to do penance. [A later editorial addition, absent from the manuscripts, appears in some printed editions: “For whoever, reaching the lofty streams of knowledge, does not conceal these things from the hearts of brutish hearers becomes liable to punishment if, through his words, either a clean or an unclean mind is caught in scandal.”]

The cistern must therefore be covered, because higher knowledge must be read before immature minds, lest, by the means through which the heart of the teachers is lifted toward the heights, the weakness of the hearers fall into the depths.

Let it rightly be said, then: “He binds the waters in the clouds, so that they do not burst forth together below.” The waters would burst forth together if, before weak hearers, as much knowledge as there is flowed from the mouth of the speaker—if the whole fullness of preaching poured itself out at once and reserved nothing for those who were making progress.

It is fitting that the one who preaches should consider the capacity of the hearer, so that the preaching itself may grow along with the hearer’s growth. Every preacher should act as God acts toward him: he should not disclose everything he understands to the weak, because, so long as he himself is weak in mortal flesh, he does not understand everything that is above.

A preacher, therefore, ought not to preach to the inexperienced as much as he knows, because he himself cannot know how great are all the mysteries above. For this reason the Apostle Paul, after having entered into heavenly mysteries, says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12). Hence it immediately follows:

CAPUT XXVII [Rec. XV].

VERSE 9. — “He holds the face of his throne and spreads his cloud over it.”

39. In this life the glory of God is known only in part. — Knowledge is usually signified by the face. Therefore, the face of his throne is held because in this life the glory of his kingdom is not recognized by us as fully as it exists inwardly.

It is rightly said that a cloud is spread over it, because the glory of the heavenly kingdom as it truly is cannot be seen. “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15). We are therefore sprinkled with a cloud that prevents us from seeing him, because we are darkened by the very obscurity of our ignorance.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Darkness is beneath his feet; he mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds, and he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 10).

Darkness is beneath his feet because he is not seen by those below with the clarity with which he rules above. “He mounted upon the cherubim, and he flew.” Cherubim means “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore he is said to have mounted above the fullness of knowledge and to have flown, because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty.

He flew, therefore, because he carried himself far aloft beyond our understanding. He flew upon the wings of the winds because he transcends the knowledge of souls. He made darkness his hiding place because, while we are obscured by the darkness of our weakness, he is hidden from us through our ignorance, lest we see him now in eternal and inward clarity.

Hence the bride says to him in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved, flee” (Song VIII, 14) [Old Recension XIV]. We say that something flees from us whenever what we wish to remember does not come before our mind. We say that it flees from us when we cannot retain in memory what we wish to retain.

Thus the holy Church, after describing the Lord’s death, resurrection, and ascension, cries out to him, filled with the prophetic spirit: “Flee, my beloved, flee.” It is as though she said: “You who became comprehensible through the flesh, transcend through your divinity the understanding of our senses, and remain in yourself incomprehensible to us.”

He therefore holds the face of his throne because he conceals the power of his majesty from mortals.

[Textual and editorial notes: At Dan. X, 20, 2 Laudunensis and Bellovacensis read “against the prince of the lands,” rather than “against the prince of Persia.” At “the yoke of its captivity,” most Norman manuscripts read “of slavery.” Pratellensis and other Norman manuscripts read “but there is still something in that people which ought to be purged under Persian rule,” a reading judged better than “whence the deliverance,” found in later printed editions; *iure* (“rightly”) is absent in 1 Laudunensis. At the invisible army, 1 Laudunensis reads “the spirit does not know”; it simply calls the number of the heavenly citizens “infinite”; and the manuscripts read “as if definite” for the number standing before God, rather than the Vulgate’s “infinite.” Gemeticensis, Uticensis, and others read “For behold” at the opening of verse 5 and below. 2 Laudunensis reads “righteousness is not righteousness”; “in the offspring” is absent in 1 Laudunensis. Other editions read “let them infer,” against the manuscripts’ “let him infer”; Gilot and Gussanville read “unless him,” whereas the manuscripts and other editions more correctly read “unless it,” namely, corruptibility. “Every” is absent in Gemeticensis; Vindocinensis reads “by what sins they are struck down”; and 1 Laudunensis reads “of jurists and legal experts.” Two Laudunensis manuscripts read “Surely [you are the helper] of the weak?” In Gilot, the Vatican edition, and some others, *expands* is corruptly printed as *weighs out*. Gilot, following the Vulgate, reads “will not live … will not rise again.” German and Norman witnesses read “the height of honor”; 2 Laudunensis reads “from affection” rather than “from delight.” German, Corbie German, and 2 Laudunensis read “hell” rather than “destruction.” Uticensis and most witnesses add “indeed” in Heb. IV, 13; 2 Laudunensis has “the name of hell and destruction.” Older editions and nearly all witnesses read “the firmness of divine love,” against the manuscript reading “the firmness of divine fear.” Norman witnesses read “upon a nothing”; Pratellensis, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts add “with no preceding merits.” German and Norman witnesses omit “his” in “his clouds”; 1 Laudunensis reads “chief matters” rather than “comprehensible matters.” Later editions corrupt “nourished by the dew of their sayings” to “by the dew of teachers”; all Norman witnesses read “the penalty of fault.” Vindocinensis, as also two Laudunensis manuscripts and German witnesses, reads “is proved to have lost [it]” rather than “to have committed [it].” The long paragraph quoted above as a later editorial addition is explicitly reported in the source as absent from all its manuscripts and from the Paris editions of 1495 and earlier; in other editions it passed from the margin into the text. 1 Laudunensis reads “and reserves nothing for those making progress.” German and Corbie German witnesses read “not with that clarity.” The source’s editor restores the two statements that something ‘flees from us’ from all manuscripts; earlier editions had a corrupt wording involving memory.]

40. The ministries of the angels are scarcely known.—But if by his throne we understand the angelic powers—for he presides over them as over a royal seat—he keeps from us the face of his throne, because, so long as we remain in this mortal flesh, we do not see what and how great are the ministries of those angels. And he spreads his cloud over it, because without doubt he both raises our heart toward inquiry and yet, by a hidden moderation, restrains it, so that it is checked by the very immensity of its investigation. Hence it is written: “The abyss uttered its voice, from the height of its imagination” (Hab. III, 10). For the human mind is compelled to cry out in wonder when, in the height of contemplation, it is narrowed by its inquiries precisely as it extends itself more widely. Or certainly, because we ourselves are God’s throne, he is rightly said to keep from us the face of his throne when our knowledge is prevented from advancing to higher things. God is said to sprinkle his cloud over this throne because, while remaining invisible, he exercises hidden judgments over us: what we can see is accomplished openly, yet the origin of the deed remains concealed, so that we must not know why it is done. Thus it is appropriately added:

[Note: 1 Laud., “because he thus governs the knowledge of the human race.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Rec. XVI]

**VERSE 10.—He surrounded it with waters as with a boundary, until light and darkness come to an end.**

41. Perfect knowledge of eternity is granted to no one while we live.—Because, as we have said above, sacred Scripture often designates peoples by the name “waters,” the Lord surrounds the waters with a boundary, because he so regulates the knowledge of the human race that, until the alternating changes of time have passed away, it does not attain perfectly to knowledge of the innermost brightness. But if by “light” we understand the righteous and by “darkness” sinners—whence Paul also says, “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8)—there is no obstacle to understanding the passage in the sense already stated, since perfect knowledge of eternity is granted to no one until the course of the righteous and the wicked has come to an end. But since it is not surprising that earthly peoples should not know heavenly things, the holy man raises himself in wonder at that same divine power and observes that it surpasses even the knowledge of angels and of perfect human beings, saying:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Rec. XVII]

**[Col. 0030C] VERSE 11.—The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command.**

42. The pillars of heaven are either angels, or the supreme preachers of the Church, or the Churches themselves.—What else does he call the pillars of heaven except either the holy angels or the supreme preachers of the Church? Upon them, as the whole structure of the spiritual edifice grew in the heavenly places, its entire fabric arose, as holy Scripture elsewhere also testifies, saying: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev. III, 12). For whoever is established with upright intention in God’s work is raised as a pillar in the structure of the spiritual edifice, so that, placed in this temple—which is the Church—he may be both useful and beautiful.

Job calls those whom the Apostle calls pillars of the Church “the pillars of heaven,” saying: “Peter, James, and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me the right hand” (Gal. II, 9).

43. We may also appropriately understand the pillars of heaven as the Churches themselves, which are many but make one catholic Church spread throughout the whole world. Hence the apostle John writes to seven Churches, so that he might designate one catholic Church filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit (Rev. I, 4; II, 29). We also know that Solomon said of the Lord: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1).

To make it known that he was speaking of the seven Churches, he carefully inserted the mysteries themselves as well, saying: “She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set out her table; she sent her maidens to call to the citadel and the walls of the city: Whoever is little, let him come to me” (ibid.).

[Note: 1 Laud., “that she might call.”]

The Lord sacrificed victims by offering himself for us. He mixed wine by blending the cup of his commandments from historical narrative and spiritual understanding. Hence it is said elsewhere: “The cup in the Lord’s hand is full of mixed wine” (Ps. LXXIV, 9).

[Note: Many manuscripts lack the verb “is.”]

[Note: Norm., “and set out her table,” which reproduces the sacred text exactly.]

And he set out a table—that is, sacred Scripture—which refreshes those who are weary and come to it from the burdens of the world with the bread of the word, and strengthens us by its nourishment against adversaries. Hence the Church also says elsewhere: “You have set a table before me, against those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII, 5).

He sent his maidens, namely the souls of the apostles, weak at the very beginning, to call to the citadel and the walls of the city, because, while announcing the inner life, they raise us to the lofty walls of the heavenly city; and surely only the humble ascend those walls.

Hence Wisdom adds there: “Whoever is little, let him come to me” (Prov. IX, 4). It is as though she openly said: Whoever considers himself great in his own estimation narrows the entrance to my approach, because each person reaches me the higher, the more deeply his mind is humbled within himself.

[Note: The printed editions read “since he makes eternal life known”; the manuscripts—Turon., Laud., Germ., Corb. Grem., Norm., and others—have “since he makes the inner life known.”]

[Vet. XV.] 44. No one can investigate the judgments of God.—But however much anyone may advance in virtue and however much he may grow in knowledge, he is not sufficient to penetrate by what disposition of judgments our Creator governs us. Let him therefore say: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are terrified at his command,” because in many matters even those who see him announcing the rewards of that will cannot themselves attain to the height of his will.

As we said above, there is no obstacle to understanding this also of the holy angels, since even the heavenly powers themselves, which behold him without ceasing, tremble in that very contemplation. Their trembling, however, is not fear, lest it be punitive for them, but wonder. And because he has shown how great is the terror produced by his wonder, he now relates the order of our salvation. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXX [Rec. XVIII]

**VERSE 12.—By his power the seas were suddenly gathered together, and by his wisdom he struck down the proud one.**

45. Through the Lord’s incarnation the world was subdued, its swelling pressed down.—What else is designated by the name “sea” except the present age, in which the hearts of people who seek earthly things swell with various waves of thought? Stirred by the elation of pride, they strike against one another in opposing intention, as though waves colliding against one another.

But now “by his power the seas were gathered together,” because, when the Lord became incarnate, the discordant hearts of worldly people believe in harmony. Now Peter walks upon the sea, because those hearts, once swollen with pride, have been subdued by humble obedience to the preachers of Christ. The Gospel rightly portrayed the gentleness of this world when the stormy water of the sea was trodden beneath the Lord’s feet, its swelling pressed down.

But how this was accomplished is disclosed when it is said: “And by his wisdom he struck down the proud one.”

46. God preferred to strike the devil by wisdom rather than by power. The economy of the Incarnation.—Who else is called “the proud one” here except him who said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14)? And of whom God’s voice says: “He was made so as to fear nothing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25).

[Note: Utic. and others, “over all.”]

The prophet David also agrees with this statement, saying: “You humbled the proud one as though wounded” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 11).

Although, because of the simplicity of the divine nature, being and knowing are not different, nor knowing and being strong—for the very power of God is wisdom, and his wisdom is the essence of divinity—I nevertheless think that we should attentively consider why this man, filled with the prophetic Spirit, preferred to say that the proud devil was struck by God’s wisdom rather than by his power.

He does not say “his power,” but “his wisdom struck the proud one.” For although, as has been said, because of the simplicity of God’s nature his power is wisdom, the Lord nevertheless, as far as outward appearance is concerned, overcame the devil not by force but by reason.

The devil, having overthrown us in the root of our first parent, held the human race under his captivity as though justly: humanity, created with free choice, had consented to him when he urged what was unjust.
