Created for life in the freedom of its own will, it had voluntarily made itself a debtor to death.

Such guilt therefore had to be destroyed; but it could not be destroyed except by sacrifice. A sacrifice had to be sought; but what sort of sacrifice could be found for the acquittal of human beings? It was not just that victims of irrational animals should be slaughtered on behalf of rational humanity. Hence the Apostle says: “It was necessary that the models of heavenly things should be cleansed by these, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these” (Heb. IX, 23).

Therefore, if irrational animals were not worthy victims for the sake of a rational creature—that is, for the sake of a human being—a human being had to be sought who could be offered on behalf of human beings, so that a rational victim might be slaughtered for rational sinners.

But what of the fact that a human being without sin could not be found? When the victim offered for us could it have cleansed us from sin if that victim itself had not been free from the contagion of sin? What was defiled could not cleanse the defiled.

[Note: All our manuscripts, especially Corb. Germ., German., three Regii, Belvac., two Laud., Norm., and others, read “the contagion of sin”; the old editions have “by the contagion of sin,” from which Gussanville’s corrupt reading “the thought of sin” entered.]

[Note: This note appears at the foot of column 33, but its callout number was not printed in the text.]

[Note: The printed editions add a clause which, against the authority of the manuscripts, reads “while the sense elsewhere remains intact.”]

Therefore, for the victim to be rational, a human being had to be offered; but for that human being to cleanse humanity from sins, he had to be both human and without sin. Yet who could be a human being without sin if he descended through the mingling of sin?

Accordingly, for our sake the Son of God came into a virgin’s womb and there became human for us. He assumed from her a nature, not guilt. He made a sacrifice for us: he presented his body on behalf of sinners as a victim without sin, one that could die through its humanity and cleanse through its righteousness.

[Note: Gemet., “should cleanse.”]

[Vet. XVI.] When the ancient enemy saw him after his baptism, he immediately attacked him with temptations and, attempting to creep through various entrances into his inward being, was defeated and overthrown by the very unconquerable integrity of his mind (Matt. IV, 1 ff.).

[Note: Vindoc. and 1 Laud., “to burst in.”]

[Note: Gemet. and others, “unconquerable.”]

47. After having vainly tempted Christ inwardly, the devil attacked him outwardly.—But when he could not reach his inward being, he turned to his outward being, so that, since he had been defeated by the strength of his mind, he might at least appear to overcome by the death of his flesh the one whom he had been unable to deceive by temptation. As was said earlier, he was permitted to act against that which the Mediator had received from us mortals.

But where he was able to do something, there he was defeated on every side; and from the place where he received outward power to kill the Lord’s flesh, the inward power by which he held us was itself killed. He was defeated inwardly precisely when he seemed to conquer outwardly.

He who had held us as debtors to death by right lost the right of death over us by right, because through his agents he sought to destroy the flesh of the one in whom he found nothing owed on account of guilt.

Our Lord therefore paid on our behalf an undeserved death, so that our deserved death might not harm us.

It was rightly said: “His wisdom struck the proud one,” because the ancient enemy, through the excess of his presumption, lost even the one whom he had possessed by the law of an unjust persuasion. When he boldly attacked one over whom he had no claim, he justly lost the one whom he had held as though justly.

He was struck by wisdom, not by power, because, when permission was given him to tempt God, he was restrained from possessing humanity. Thus he lost the one who was beneath him precisely because he had presumed to fight with the one who is above him.

After the Lord’s flesh had been killed, what glory of virtue followed his preachers is related when it is added:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Rec. XIX]

**VERSE 13.—His Spirit adorned the heavens.**

[Col. 0033D] 48. The weakness of the apostles and of their leader before receiving the Holy Spirit.—Which heavens are meant except those of whom it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 1)? The Spirit adorned them when he filled them.

We learn this from Luke’s account, where he says: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent wind arriving, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II, 2 ff.).

[Note: Most manuscripts, “upon each one.”]

From that moment, therefore, they received the ornaments of virtue—those whom previously immense ugliness of fear had possessed.

We know that the first of the apostles, that is, of the heavens, before receiving the grace of this Spirit, denied life whenever he feared dying. He was overthrown not by punishments, afflictions, or the terrifying power of anyone, but by the single question of a servant.

[Note: Norm., “And indeed, lest the servant’s sex should show itself stronger,” etc.]

[Note: 1 Laud., “they began.”]

And indeed, lest the servant’s sex should appear stronger and more terrifying, he was tested by a maidservant’s question (Matt. XXVI, 70). Again, so that the weakness of that sex might be made still more contemptible by the lowliness of its office, he was questioned not merely by a maidservant but by a maidservant who was a doorkeeper (John XVIII, 25).

Behold how insignificant was the person selected to test him, so that it might plainly be revealed how greatly the weakness of fear possessed him—he who could not stand even before the voice of a maidservant who was a doorkeeper.

[Vet. XVII.] 49. Peter’s strength after receiving it.—But let us now see what this man, timid shortly before, became after the Spirit’s arrival. Certainly, as Luke testifies, we know with what authority he preached the Lord before priests and rulers.

After a miracle had been performed and a dispute had arisen (Acts IV, 14), the chief priests, elders, and scribes gathered to persecute the apostles. Having set them in their midst, they asked by what power they had performed the miracle.

[Note: 1 Laud., “they began.”]

Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: “Rulers of the people and elders, if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a sick man, by which this man has been saved, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you healed” (ibid., 8).

[Note: Two Laud. manuscripts, “elders.”]

When the fury of the persecutors increased and the priests and rulers forbade them to preach Jesus, the authority with which Peter rose up against the rulers’ anger is shown when the text immediately adds: “But Peter and the apostles said: We must obey God rather than human beings” (ibid., V, 29).

When the commands of those who resisted could not suppress the authority of the preachers, they proceeded to scourging. For it is added: “Then the rulers of the priests, after scourging them, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and dismissed them” (ibid., V, 40).

But because even scourging could not suppress the apostles’ strength, this is plainly shown when it immediately follows: “And they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (ibid., 41).

Soon, after the joy of the scourging, what they did is also indicated: “Every day in the temple and around the houses they did not cease teaching and preaching Christ Jesus.”

Behold: the man who shortly before was timid now speaks in tongues, shines with miracles, openly rebukes the unbelief of priests and rulers, and gives the others an example of authority in preaching Jesus. He is forbidden by beatings to speak in his name, yet he is not restrained.

He despises the scourging of those who beat him, though shortly before he had feared the words of those who questioned him. The man who, when questioned by a maidservant, trembled at her power now, after being beaten, overcomes the power of rulers.

Already strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, he pressed down the heights of this world beneath the foot of freedom, so that he might see that whatever swelled loftily against the grace of the Creator was in the lowest place.

[Note: The manuscripts Germ., Corb. Germ., Anglic., Norm., Laud., and others have this reading; the printed editions read “he might determine.”]

[Note: Anglic., “glory.”]

[Vet. XVIII.] 50. With what gifts and virtues the apostles shone when the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them.—These are the adornments of the heavens; these are the gifts of the Spirit, which customarily become manifest through various virtues. Paul enumerates them as divided by the gift of hidden providence, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Cor. XII, 8–10).

Concluding these gifts shortly afterward with a general definition, he says: “But all these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, dividing them among individuals as he wills.”

The psalm also speaks of these heavens: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII, 6). Of these spiritual adornments it adds: “And by the breath of his mouth all their power.”

It is rightly said: “His Spirit adorned the heavens,” because, unless the holy preachers had received the promised gifts of the Paraclete, they would not have shone with any beauty of strength.

But since, once the holy apostles had been adorned with the grace of virtues, their preaching of life grew strong against the hearts of unbelievers, and the ancient enemy, expelled by the voices of the preachers, left the minds of unbelievers whom he had occupied, it is appropriately added after the adornment of the heavens:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Rec. XX]

**Ibid.—And by his midwife-hand the twisted serpent was brought out.**

51. The ancient serpent was expelled from the hearts of sinners, as from his caves, by God’s hand.—Who else is called by the name of the serpent except the ancient enemy, slippery and twisted, who spoke to the human being through the serpent’s mouth in order to deceive him? Of him the prophet says: “Leviathan the bar-serpent, Leviathan the twisted serpent” (Isa. XXVII, 1).

[Note: 2 Laud., “Leviathan, the bar-serpent; Leviathan, the twisted serpent.”]

For this reason he was permitted to speak through the serpent’s mouth, so that from the very vessel he used humanity might learn what he was who dwelt within it. The serpent is not only twisted but also slippery. Therefore, because he did not stand in the straightness of truth, he entered a twisted animal.

And because, if his suggestion is not resisted at the first moment, he suddenly slips wholly into the heart’s interior while remaining unnoticed, he spoke to humanity through a slippery animal.

[Note: The printed editions read, “if it is not resisted at first.”]

The caves of this serpent were the hearts of the wicked. Because he drew them toward his own perversity, he rested as though in their habitation.

But by the Lord’s midwife-hand the twisted serpent was expelled from his own caves, because, while divine grace heals us, the ancient enemy who had held us is driven away from us. As incarnate Truth says: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John XII, 31).

Hence now he does not possess all the saints by holding them, but persecutes them by tempting them.

[Note: The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions read “holy people.”] Since he does not reign inwardly in them, he fights against them outwardly; and because he has lost dominion within, he prepares wars outside.

He expelled him from the carnal hearts of human beings who came in the flesh for the sake of human beings. While the ancient enemy held the hearts of unbelievers, the Lord, as it were, stretched his hand toward the serpent’s hiding places.

Hence the prophet rightly says: “The infant shall delight over the hole of the asp; and in the cave of the basilisk the weaned child shall put his hand. They shall not harm, and they shall not kill, throughout all my holy mountain” (Isa. XI, 8).

[Note: Pratell., Utic., and several Norman manuscripts: “over the hole … and into the cave ….”]

[Note: Gemet., “the one who has been weaned … they shall not harm or kill.” Laud has the same.]

Who does he call the infant at the breast, or the one who has been weaned, except the Lord?

[Note: All printed editions read “except God,” against the manuscripts.]

What else did he signify by the hole of the asp and the caves of the basilisk except the hearts of the wicked? Because the ancient enemy, while bringing his whole self into their consent, gathered himself together like a twisted serpent in its own hole, collecting and coiling the folds of its cunning.

He calls him by the name “asp” as one who rages secretly, and by the name “basilisk” as one who strikes openly.

The Lord therefore put his hand into the hole of the basilisk and of the asp when by divine power he took possession of the hearts of the wicked. He then seized and drew out the asp or basilisk—that is, the devil held captive—so that in his holy mountain, which is the Church, he might not harm the chosen faithful.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way, together with Laud., Norm., and almost all the old manuscripts. The more recent editors preferred the reading “which is the Church.”]

52. The devil compared with a lion.—Hence, when the bridegroom comes, it is said in the Song of Songs: “You shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions” (Cant. IV, 8).

What else are designated by the name of lions except demons, which rage against us with the most savage cruelty? And because sinners were called to the faith—those whose hearts had once been dens of lions—the Lord is believed to have conquered death by their confession and is, as it were, crowned from the dens of lions.

For the reward of victory is a crown. The faithful therefore offer him a crown as often as they confess, on the basis of the resurrection, that he conquered death.

The lion is driven from his dens because, by the Lord’s midwife-hand, the twisted serpent is forbidden to dwell in the caves he had held. Defeated, he departed from the hearts of the faithful, though previously he had reigned over them with the scepter of unbelief.

53. Christ’s first coming in humility, his second in terror.—Behold: in a few brief statements the holy man has related the order of the Lord’s coming, expressed its weight, and narrated with wonder what could be accomplished through his incarnation.

[Vet. XIX, Rec. XXI.]

But although he did marvelous things when he came in humility, it cannot be considered with what terror he will come, appearing in the strength of his majesty.

The order of his first coming could be weighed and observed only insofar as, coming to redeem earthly people, he moderated the greatness of his divinity to their carnal eyes.

But who could endure the terror of his exaltedness when, at his second coming, his power will exercise judgment through fire and he will blaze in the majesty of his authority?

Hence the holy man first relates his coming, but grows weary when he reaches the second, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**[Col. 0037B] VERSE 14.—Behold, these things have been spoken in part of his ways; and when we have scarcely heard a small drop of his words, who will be able to contemplate the thunder of his greatness?**

54. A description of God’s terrible judgment.—What else does he call “ways” here except the Lord’s actions? Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “My ways are not like your ways” (Isa. LV, 8).

In relating the Lord’s coming, therefore, he had recounted God’s ways in part, because one was the action by which he created us and another that by which he redeemed us.

Comparing what he had said about the Lord’s action with the final judgment and diminishing its apparent weight, he says: “Behold, these things have been spoken in part of his ways.”

He also calls it “a small drop of his words,” because whatever is lofty and whatever is terrible that we, placed in this life, perceive in contemplating him flows down to us from the immensity of heavenly secrets like a thin drop of liquid from above.

“And who will be able to contemplate the thunder of his greatness?” It is as though he openly said: If we scarcely endure the things of his humility that are worthy of wonder, by what strength shall we endure the sounding and terrible coming of his majesty?

This thunder of his coming the Psalmist also sounds forth, saying:

[Note: Old and recent printed editions read “dreadful”; later, only the recent editions read “makes known” in place of “sounds forth,” the reading of the Anglic., Norm., Laud., Bellovac., and other manuscripts.] “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not keep silence; fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. XLIX, 3).

The prophet Zephaniah declares the same, saying: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and comes very swiftly. The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and shouting” (Zeph. I, 14).

[Note: This passage appears somewhat differently in the earlier Vulgate editions; we have restored it from almost all the manuscripts.]

The terror of the strict judgment, which Zephaniah calls a trumpet and blessed Job a thunder, the prophet Joel likewise contemplates and says: “Let all the inhabitants of the earth be troubled, because the day of the Lord is coming, because the day of darkness and gloom is near, a day of cloud and storm; for the day of the Lord is great and exceedingly terrible, and who will endure it?” (Joel II, 1).

But how incomprehensible and unobservable is that greatness with which he will come at his second manifestation, we can to some extent weigh if we carefully consider the weight of his first coming.

Certainly, in order to redeem us from death, the Lord came to die, and in his body he endured the weakness of our flesh and its punishments.

Before he reached the gibbet of the cross, he allowed himself to be seized, spat upon, mocked, and struck with blows.

Behold to what insults he consented to come for our sake; and yet, before he allowed himself to be seized, he questioned his persecutors, saying: “Whom do you seek?” (John XVIII, 4). They immediately answered him: “Jesus of Nazareth.”

When he suddenly said to them, “I am he,” he uttered only the voice of his most gentle reply, and immediately struck his armed persecutors to the ground.

What then will he do when he comes to judge, who, even when he came to be judged, struck down his enemies with a single voice?

What is that judgment which the immortal one exercises, who, when destined to die, could not be endured in a single utterance?

Who could endure his anger when even his gentleness could not be endured?

Let the holy man therefore consider and say: “When we have scarcely heard a small drop of his words, who will be able to contemplate the thunder of his greatness?”

# BOOK EIGHTEEN

*(Contains the exposition of chapter XXVIII of the Book of Job up to halfway through verse 21, according to its multiple senses.)*

[Col. 0037]

[Col. 0037D] [Rec. I.] 1. The obscurity of sacred Scripture moves us to investigate its higher meaning.—Often in sacred discourse certain mysteries are described in such a way that they nevertheless appear to have been set forth according to historical narrative. But such statements are frequently interwoven with that same historical narrative in ways that cancel the entire surface of the history: since they convey nothing historical, they compel the reader to seek something else in them.

When, among the things we believe to be clear, we encounter something obscurely inserted, we are pricked, as it were, by certain goads, so that we may keep watch in order to understand some things more deeply and may perceive more obscurely expressed meanings, including those that we thought had been stated openly.

Therefore, when blessed Job was speaking of the Lord’s speech and of the greatness of the thunder, the following is immediately added in the same words:

## CHAPTER ONE [Vet. I, Rec. II]

**CHAPTER XXVII, VERSE 1.—Job also continued, taking up his parable, and said.**

2. Job’s mode of speaking is parabolic and mystical.—This verse plainly shows how mystically the words of this most holy man were expressed, since a parable—that is, a likeness—is said to have been taken up by one who says nothing inferior by comparison or likeness.

Let us not suppose that “parable” here refers to a musical instrument. For it is not right to believe that he used musical instruments amid the affliction of his punishments, since Truth says through Scripture: “Music in mourning is an untimely account” (Sir. XXII, 6).

With the parable named, behold, we already learn from the text itself speaking, lest we consider only the words of the text according to their literal sense. Everything must therefore be drawn toward that likeness by which the Church is figuratively designated.

At the very beginning of his speech the words are stated openly, but they are entangled with what follows, which is more obscure. For, as usual, he begins in plain speech but brings his words to completion in a narrative laden with mystical meanings.

Thus he says:

[Note: We know of no musical instrument that is or was called by this name. Nevertheless, something of the sort may be conjectured because of the parabolic figure, evidently described by a parabolic line.]

[Note: Recent editions read “from the text,” departing from the older printed editions and manuscripts. Germ. has, “Thus, taking up the parable, we now learn from the text itself speaking.”]

## CHAPTER TWO [Rec. III]

**[Col. 0039B] VERSE 2.—As God lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul into bitterness.**

3. Against the words of detractors wisdom is necessary; against the swords of persecutors, patience.—By these words blessed Job both recounts his own experience and signifies the afflicted times of the holy Church, in which it is oppressed by the manifest obstinacy of unbelievers and disturbed by the bitterness of persecution.

The Church is usually tested by adversaries in two ways: it suffers persecution either through words or through swords. The holy Church strives above all to possess wisdom and patience.

[Note: 2 Laud., “strives to possess wisdom and knowledge.”]

Its wisdom is exercised when it is tested by words; its patience is exercised when it is tested by swords.

Here, however, he speaks of that persecution in which it is assailed not by swords but by false assertions.

We know many people who, when they suffer some adversity in this life, believe that God exists. Others believe that God exists but think that he scarcely cares for human affairs.

Of the former David says: “The fool said in his heart, There is no God” (Ps. XIII, 1). The latter say to him: “How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High?” (Ps. LXXII, 11). And again: “They said, The Lord shall not see, nor shall the God of Jacob understand” (Ps. LXXXXIII, 7).

This man, bearing the type of the holy Church and established in the bitterness of his affliction, answered both groups.

To confess that God possesses the essence of life, whereas death does not, he said: “God lives.” To affirm that he cares for human affairs, he added: “Who has taken away my judgment, and brought my soul into bitterness.”

He testifies that what he suffers does not happen by chance but by God’s ordering of all things. Nor does he grant his tempter authority over his bitterness, but rather to its author.

[Note: Possibly “before the Psalmist.” The printed editions read “before himself,” but “before him” should be read on the basis of manuscripts Norm., Laud., Turon., Germ., Corb. Germ., and others.]

4. The devil has no power to tempt unless God permits it.—For he knows that, although the devil always desires to afflict the righteous, nevertheless, if he does not receive power from our Creator, he cannot in any way proceed to the moment of temptation.

Thus every desire of the devil is unjust, yet, when God permits it, all his power is just. Of himself he unjustly desires to tempt anyone; but God justly permits those who are to be tempted to be tempted in the manner in which they are to be tempted.

[Vet. II.]

Hence it is also written in the Books of Kings concerning the devil: “Because an evil spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Kings XVIII, 10).

Here the question is rightly raised: if it is “of the Lord,” why is it evil; and if it is evil, why is it called “of the Lord”?

But these two words comprise both the just power in the devil and his unjust will.

For he is called an evil spirit because of his most wicked will, and the spirit of the Lord because of the supremely just power he received.

It is therefore rightly said: “As God lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul into bitterness,” because although the enemy rages and desires to strike, it is nevertheless the Creator who permits him to prevail for some purpose.

[Note: Vindoc., “the power is just from the Lord, and the will in the devil is unjust.”]

[Note: 1 Laud., “to prevail to some extent.”]

But because the holy man has bound himself by invoking the life of God for a purpose, let us hear what he adds as he binds himself. It follows:

## CHAPTER THREE [Rec. IV]

**VERSE 34.—For as long as breath remains in me, and the Spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue meditate falsehood.**
### 5. Since all falsehood is iniquity, it is not even permissible to defend anyone’s life by a lie

[Col. 0040C] What he first called “iniquity,” he subsequently repeats by calling it “falsehood.” For every falsehood is iniquity, and every iniquity is falsehood, since plainly whatever disagrees with truth departs from equity. [Note: Vindoc. reads, “does not differ from iniquity.”] Yet there is a great difference between what he says—“to speak”—and what he adds afterward—“to meditate.” For sometimes it is worse to meditate a lie than to speak one. Speaking is often a matter of haste, whereas meditation is deliberate perversity. And who does not know how greatly guilt differs according as someone lies impulsively or deliberately? [Note: 1 Laud. reads, “whether by a distinction.”] But the holy man, in order to adhere perfectly to the truth, declares that he neither lies deliberately nor through haste.

[Col. 0040D] Every falsehood must be avoided with the utmost care, although sometimes a certain kind of falsehood is a lesser fault, if someone lies while doing good. [Note: All printed editions read *vitam praestando*, “by preserving life.” But the manuscripts Corb., Germ., Turon., Laudun., Germ., Norm., and others lack *vitam*; thus *praestare* here means “to do good.” It is used in the same sense by Isidore, Gregory’s near contemporary, in *Synonyms*, chapter 10, concerning falsehood: “Do not speak what is false either by accident or deliberately, nor strive to lie in order to do good.” This passage is likewise cited in *Causa* 22, question 2, canon 16: “every kind [of falsehood].”] But since it is written, “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), and, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5:7), [Note: Two Laud. read, “You will destroy them.”] the perfect also utterly avoid this kind of falsehood, so that no one’s life may be preserved through their deception, lest they harm their own souls while attempting to preserve another’s bodily life. [Col. 0041A] [Note: Norm. reads, “lest they harm their own life while attempting to benefit another’s flesh.” Germ. reads, “lest they harm their own soul while attempting to benefit another’s flesh.”]

Nevertheless, we readily believe that this very kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is ordinarily cleansed by a subsequent pious action (22, q. 2, c. 20), how much more easily is this fault wiped away, when piety itself, the mother of good works, accompanies it?

### 6. Reply to the objection drawn from the lie of the Egyptian midwives

[Col. 0041B] Some, however, attempt to assert from the deception of the midwives that this kind of falsehood is not a sin, especially because Scripture says of them, when they lied, “The Lord built houses for them” (Exod. 1:21). Yet in this very recompense one can better understand what the fault of falsehood deserves. The reward of their kindness—which could have been repaid to them in eternal life—was, on account of the fault of falsehood that had been added to it, diverted into an earthly recompense, so that in their present life they received the good things they had done while lying to preserve life, [Col. 0042D] and did not receive thereafter the reward they might have expected. [Note: 2 Laud. reads, “and that thereafter, etc.”] [Note: Germ., Laudun., Norm., Turon., Corb., and others read *pro admissa*, “for the fault admitted.” The printed editions read *pro admista*, “for the fault added.”] For if the matter is carefully weighed, they lied out of love for the present life, not with the intention of obtaining a reward. By showing mercy they tried to conceal the infants’ lives; by lying, their own.

### 7. In the Old Testament falsehood was a lesser fault than in the New

[Col. 0041C] Although some such examples may be found in the Old Testament, a diligent reader will nevertheless find that almost never was this or any similar kind of falsehood committed by the perfect. Falsehood may indeed seem to retain some likeness to truth, and perhaps under the Old Testament it could have been a lesser fault, since in the sacrifices of bulls and goats the sacrifice was not truth itself but a shadow of truth. For in the New Testament we advance through the higher commandments, with Truth manifested in the flesh; and it is just that we abandon certain practices that served the shadow of truth among that people. [Vet. III.]

[Col. 0041D] If someone wishes to defend his own falsehood by appeal to the Old Testament (22, q. 2, c. 19), arguing that because certain things there may perhaps have caused less harm, he ought to say that the seizure of another’s property and the repayment of injury—things permitted there to the weak—cannot harm him. Yet it is clear to all with what severity Truth pursues all these matters. Now that the shadow of its meaning has been set aside, Truth is revealed to us in true flesh.

But because the holy man promises neither to speak nor to meditate falsehood, he adds the things in which he accords with truth by carrying out his promise. [Note: 1 Laud. reads, “and by following, he joins himself.”]

### CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 5.**—[Col. 0042A] “Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I fail, I will not depart from my innocence.”

### 8. How harmful it is to flatter sinners

[Col. 0042B] He would indeed depart from innocence if he judged the wicked to be good, as Solomon testifies when he says: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both abominable before God” (Prov. 17:15).

There are some who, by exalting people’s evil deeds with praise, increase what they ought to rebuke (Dist. 46, c. 2). Hence the prophet says: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow and make pillows under the heads of people of every age” (Ezek. 13:18). A cushion is placed so that one may rest more comfortably. Therefore whoever flatters those who do evil places a cushion beneath the head or elbow of one who is lying down, so that the person who ought to have been corrected for his fault may rest comfortably, supported by praise.

[Col. 0042C] Again it is written: “He was building the wall, while they were plastering it” (ibid. 13:10). By the name “wall” the hardness of sin is signified. To build a wall, therefore, is to construct against oneself barriers of sin. But they plaster the wall who flatter those committing sins, so that what the sinners build perversely, the flatterers themselves may make appear, as it were, smooth and attractive.

But just as the holy man does not judge the good to be evil, so he refuses to judge the wicked to be good, saying: “Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I fail, I will not depart from my innocence.” [Col. 0042D] He immediately adds:

**VERSE 6.**—“I will not abandon my justification, which I have begun to hold.”

He would abandon the justification he had begun if he turned toward praising sinners. But because we then more truly abstain from the sins of others when we first guard ourselves from our own, he explains why he fears sinning concerning them when he adds:

### CHAPTER V [Rec. V]

**THE SAME PLACE.**—[Col. 0042C] “For my heart does not reproach me in all my way.”

### 9. He reproves those who hear the divine commandments but do not fulfill them

It is as though he plainly said: “I ought not to be drawn into guilt on your account, since I was afraid to sin in my own affairs.”

It should be understood that whenever anyone departs from the Lord’s commandments in conduct, each time he hears them he is reproved and confounded by his own heart, because he is reminded of what he has not done. For in the matter in which he recognizes that he has gone astray, his own conscience silently accuses him.

Hence the prophet David prays, saying: “Then I shall not be confounded, when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. 118:6). [Note: The word *in* is absent from the printed editions but appears in the manuscripts Germ., Norm., two Laud., Turon., and Corb. Germ.] For each person is profoundly confounded when, whether by reading or hearing, he regards God’s commandments, which he has despised in his life.

[Col. 0042D] Thus John says: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence before God; and whatever we ask from him, we shall receive” (1 John 3:21). It is as though he said: “If we do what he commands, we shall obtain what we ask.”

### 10. Prayer must be supported by action, and action by prayer

[Col. 0043A] These two things necessarily agree with one another before God: action must support prayer, and prayer must support action. Hence Jeremiah says: “Let us examine our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord. Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lam. 3:40).

To examine our ways is to investigate the inner movements of our thoughts. He lifts his heart with his hands who strengthens his prayer by his works. For whoever prays but refuses to act lifts his heart but does not lift his hands. Whoever acts but does not pray lifts his hands but does not lift his heart.

Accordingly, in John’s words, the heart receives confidence in prayer when no perversity of life contradicts it. Of this confidence the holy man rightly says here: “My heart does not reproach me in all my way.” It is as though he plainly said: “My heart does not remember that I have done anything for which I should be confounded in my prayers.” [Vet. IV.]

Yet one may ask how he can deny that his heart reproves him when earlier he accuses himself of having sinned, saying: “I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O watcher of humanity?” (Job 7:20); or: “If I should wish to justify myself, my mouth would condemn me” (Job 9:20).

### 11. Certain sins cannot be avoided

[Col. 0043B] It should be understood that there are sins which the righteous can avoid, and there are some which even the righteous cannot avoid. For whose heart, while it remains in this corruptible flesh, does not slip into an evil thought, even if it is not plunged as far as the pit of consent? [Note: Vindoc. reads, “For who in this corruptible flesh…”]

Yet even to think these evil things is sin. But when resistance is offered to the thought, the mind is freed from the shame belonging to it. The minds of the righteous, therefore, although free from perverse action, sometimes nevertheless fall into perverse thought. [Note: The following words, through “and yet from which,” are absent from Bellov.]

Thus he slips into sin, because he deviates at least in thought; yet he has no occasion afterward to reproach himself with tears, because he repairs himself before he falls through consent.

Rightly, therefore, the man who confessed himself a sinner does not at all confess that his heart reproves him, because, even if by thinking something unlawful he may perhaps ever have fallen short of rectitude, he nevertheless resisted the thought through a strong struggle of mind. [Note: Ebroic., Prat., and Germ. read *nonnunquam*, “sometimes.”] The text continues:

### CHAPTER VI [Rec. VI]

**VERSE 7.**—[Col. 0043C] “Like a wicked man is my enemy, and my adversary like an unrighteous man.”

### 12. The Church regards as an unbeliever the person whom it sees living within her with evil morals

In sacred speech, *sicut* (“as”) and *quasi* (“like”) are sometimes used not to express similarity but truth itself. Thus: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14). Here also, therefore, *sicut* and *quasi* seem to have been said more as affirmation than as comparison.

There is sometimes this difference between “wicked” and “unrighteous”: every wicked person is unrighteous, but not every unrighteous person is wicked. “Wicked” (*impius*) is used for an unbeliever, that is, one alienated from religious devotion; “unrighteous” (*iniquus*) is one who departs from equity by the perversity of his conduct, even if he bears the name of the Christian faith.

Thus, in the typical voice of blessed Job, holy Church—which tolerates some who contradict the right faith—confesses that she has the wicked as an enemy. But because she suffers others, placed within her under the pretext of faith, to live in evil works, she detests the unrighteous as her adversary. [Col. 0043D]

If, however, we should understand *sicut* and *quasi* as expressing similarity, holy Church marks as resembling the wicked those whom she tolerates within herself while they live according to the flesh. Her enemy within is the one who affirms himself faithful in words but denies it in conduct. And because she regards him as unbelieving, since while placed within her outwardly he attacks her by his evil action, she rightly says: “Like a wicked man is my enemy, and my adversary like an unrighteous man.” [Note: The second Laud. reads, “like a faithful man, but evil.”] [Note: The words from here through “the text continues” are absent from Vindoc.]

It is as though she plainly said: “Even in faith he differs from me who does not agree with me in conduct.” The text continues:

### CHAPTER VII [Rec. VII]

**VERSE 8.**—[Col. 0044A] “For what hope does the hypocrite have, if he greedily seizes, and God does not deliver his soul?”

### 13. The hypocrite is greedy and rapacious

A hypocrite, who in Latin is called a *simulator*, does not desire to be righteous but to appear righteous. For this reason he is greedy and rapacious: while acting unjustly, he desires to be honored for holiness, and so he seizes the praise belonging to another’s life.

It is characteristic of hypocrites both to conceal what they are and to make known to people that they are what they are not, so that they may surpass their true measure in others’ estimation and display themselves as superior to the rest in the name of their conduct. They shrink from being seen as they are and clothe themselves before human eyes with a kind of superimposed appearance of innocence.

[Col. 0044B] Hence our Redeemer rightly reproves them through the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you have become like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but within you are full of greed and iniquity” (Matt. 23:27; Luke 11:39). [Note: In Norm., Germ., and most manuscripts, *a* is absent, giving: “which outwardly appear beautiful to people.”]

[Col. 0044C] In contrast, all who are truly holy not only do not desire glory beyond their measure, but even avoid appearing to be what they have deserved to become. Hence that distinguished preacher of truth, speaking against the false apostles, recounted the extraordinary virtues of his ministry for the instruction of his disciples (2 Cor. 11:13 ff.). He described how he had endured so many dangers amid accumulated persecutions, and afterward remembered that he had been caught up to the third heaven and again into paradise, where he could have learned things so great that he could not possibly speak of them (ibid. 12:2).

He might perhaps have gone on to say even more remarkable things about himself, but restraining himself through profound consideration from human praise, he adds: “But I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me” (ibid. 12:6). [Col. 0044D] [Note: Gemet., Utic., and others read *de me*, “about me,” rather than *ex me*, “from me.”]

He therefore had something more to say about himself, since he refrained from saying it. Yet the distinguished teacher accomplished both things: by speaking of what he had done, he instructed his disciples; by remaining silent, he guarded himself within the bounds of humility. He would have been excessively ungrateful if he had concealed everything about himself from his disciples, and perhaps excessively careless if he had revealed everything about himself even to his disciples. But, wonderfully, as has been said, he accomplished both: by speaking he instructed the life of his hearers, and by remaining silent he guarded his own.

### 14. The saints sometimes praise themselves harmlessly

[Col. 0045A] It should be understood that whenever holy men make something about themselves known to their followers, they imitate the practice of their Creator. God forbids us to praise ourselves with our own mouths, yet through sacred Scripture he speaks his own praises—not because he needs them, since praise cannot make him advance, but because, while recounting his greatness to us, he lifts our ignorance toward himself. By speaking of his goodness he teaches us about the one whom no human being would know if he had wished to remain silent about himself.

Therefore he makes his praises known so that, by hearing him, we may be able to know him; by knowing him, love him; by loving him, follow him; by following him, attain him; and, having attained him, enjoy his vision.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He will proclaim the power of his works to his people, that he may give them the inheritance of the nations” (Ps. 110:6). [Col. 0045B] [Note: Germ., two Laud., and Corb. Germ. read *annuntiavit*, “he proclaimed.”] It is as though he plainly said: “For this reason he makes known the strength of his work, so that the one who hears it may be enriched by his gifts.” [Note: Another reading has, “so that the one who hears him may be enriched by his gifts.” Our manuscripts read *eam*, “it,” not *eum*, “him.”]

Holy men, therefore, imitating the practice of their Creator, sometimes reveal certain things about themselves—not so that they themselves may advance, but so that their hearers may be instructed. Yet even in this they carefully guard themselves, lest, while raising others from earthly concerns, they themselves sink into the desire for earthly praise.

[Col. 0045C] Hypocrites often imitate their words, but they utterly fail to understand the meaning of what they say. [Note: Pratel. and Gemet. read *mirantur*, “they admire,” rather than “they imitate.”] What the righteous do for the benefit of their neighbor, they do to enlarge their own reputation.

The holy man, observing hypocrites, says that they do not desire future glory but seek to hold on to the present: “For what hope does the hypocrite have?” Since he loves present things, he has no hope for the future. For it is written: “What does a person hope for from what he sees?” (Rom. 8:24). The hypocrite therefore does not reach toward eternal rewards through hope, because what ought to have been sought elsewhere he boasts that he already possesses. [Col. 0045D]

Since his fault has been exposed, his punishment is also added, as the text immediately continues:

### CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 9.**—[Col. 0046A] “Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?”

### 15. Whoever does not hear God speaking in the Law will not be heard by God when he prays in extremity

God does not hear his cry in the time of distress because, in the time of tranquility, he himself did not hear the Lord crying out in his commandments. For it is written: “He who turns his ear away so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9).

The holy man, therefore, observing that all who now disdain to do what is right turn to words of petition only at the final hour, says: “Will God hear his cry?” [Col. 0045D] In these words he follows the voice of our Redeemer, who says that at the end the foolish virgins also come, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” And the answer is given to them: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:11). [Note: Becc. and Gemet. read *venient*, “they will come.”] For at that time severity is exercised in proportion to the great mercy that is now extended; [Note: Some read *quia tanta tamque magna tunc*, “because then such great and so very great [severity]…”] and then strict judgment is brought against those who have not been corrected, by the one who now patiently offers mercy to sinners. [Note: Two Laud. and Germ. read *praerogatur*, “is granted beforehand.”]

Hence the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6). [Col. 0046B] [Note: The Roman edition of Sixtus V and the edition of Gilot omit *modo enim non videtur et prope est*, “now he is not seen and is near,” although it is found in all our manuscripts.]

Now he is not seen, yet he is near; then he will be seen, but he will not be near. He has not yet appeared in judgment, and if he is sought, he is found. For wonderfully, when he appears in judgment and can be seen, he can no longer be found. [Vet. VI.]

Hence Solomon describes Wisdom as both sweetly inviting and terrifyingly judging, saying: “Wisdom cries aloud outside; in the streets she raises her voice” (Prov. 1:20). He also conveys her words, adding: “How long, little ones, will you love childishness, and fools desire what is harmful to them, and the imprudent hate knowledge?” (ibid. 1:22). [Note: Becc. and other Norm. manuscripts read, “desire what is harmful and hate knowledge.”] “Turn back at my rebuke; behold, I will pour out my spirit upon you, and I will show you my words” (ibid. 1:23).

Behold the sweetness of the one who calls, expressed in such words. Let us now see the manner in which the severity of the one who rebukes is conveyed, so that at the end the strictness of the one who punishes may finally be exercised.

“Because I called,” he says, “and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes” (ibid. 1:24). [Note: Germ. and the second Laud. once read *dispexistis*, “you looked down upon,” instead of *despexistis*, “you despised.”]

Let him now say how he strikes those whom, though they do not return to him at all, he sustains with such patience: “I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you when what you feared comes upon you, when sudden calamity falls upon you and destruction rushes upon you like a storm, when tribulation and distress come upon you. Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and they will not find me” (ibid. 1:26). [Col. 0046C] [Note: Pratel., Gemet., and others add: “when sudden calamity comes upon them,” and so forth.]

Through the mouth of the wisest Solomon, therefore, everything concerning the heavenly judgment has been carefully expressed: first it calls sweetly, afterward it rebukes terrifyingly, and finally it condemns irrevocably.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?” For no hypocrite finds a remedy then in his cry, because he now wastes the fitting time for crying out. His perversity is further described:

### CHAPTER IX [Rec. VIII]

**VERSE 10.**—[Col. 0046D] “Or can he delight in the Almighty?”

### 16. Love of God and love of the world cannot both be contained in one heart

Whoever is overcome by love of earthly things cannot delight in God at all. The soul cannot exist without delight, for it delights either in what is low or in what is highest. The more ardently it applies itself to what is highest, the more deeply it grows weary of what is low; and the more fiercely it burns with concern for what is low, the more culpably it grows cold toward what is highest. Both cannot be loved simultaneously and equally.

[Col. 0047A] Thus the apostle John, knowing that the harvest of heavenly love cannot sprout among the thorns of worldly loves, first uproots from the hearts of his hearers, with the holy hand of the word, the thorns of worldly love before bringing forth the seeds of eternal love. He says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). Immediately he adds: “For if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

It is as though he plainly said: “The two loves cannot contain one another in a single heart; nor does the crop of heavenly love spring up in one in whom the thorns of lowly pleasure kill it.”

He then enumerates the pricks arising from this lowly pleasure, saying: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire” (ibid. 2:16).

[Col. 0047B] The hypocrite therefore cannot delight in God, because heavenly desires do not arise in his mind, which the thorns of earthly love press down. Concerning him the text appropriately adds:

### CHAPTER X

**THE SAME PLACE.**—“And to call upon God at all times?”

### 17. The hypocrite does not call upon God except when he is placed in distress

The hypocrite calls upon God only when tribulation from earthly things constrains him. When he has found in this world the fulfillment of the happiness he sought, he does not seek the author who granted that very happiness.

[Col. 0047C] As we have said, it ought to be the practice of teachers first to labor to destroy perversity in the minds of their hearers and afterward to proclaim what is right, lest hearts full of evil fail to receive the good seed of holy preaching. Hence it is said to Jeremiah: “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1:10). He is first commanded to destroy and afterward to build; first to uproot and afterward to plant, because the foundation of right truth is never laid unless the structure of error has first been destroyed.

After blessed Job had answered the arguments of his friends concerning the universal Church, as though replying to the words of heretics, and had destroyed their pride through many responses, he now presents himself as teaching, so that it may plainly appear that in what follows he plants what is right, while in what preceded he uprooted what was perverse. The text continues:

### CHAPTER XI [Rec. IX]

**VERSE 11.**—[Col. 0047D] “I will teach you by the hand of God what the Almighty possesses; I will not hide it.”

### 18. The saints attribute their wisdom to God; the proud attribute it to themselves

Blessed Job speaks in his own words in such a way that he signifies something concerning us. For holy Church, teaching as much as it is useful to know, hides nothing of the truth.

Because the Son is called the hand of God—for “all things were made through him” (John 1:3)—he says that he will teach by the hand of God those whom he sees foolishly remaining in their own wisdom. It is as though he plainly said: “I know nothing from myself; whatever I understand concerning truth, I grasp through the generosity of Truth itself.”

[Col. 0048A] You do not understand what is right because you attribute this same wisdom of yours not to the hand of God but to yourselves. For the enemies of holy Church, if they sometimes perceive something true, attribute it to their own powers. And the more they wish to possess heavenly wisdom as though it came from their own ingenuity, the more they deprive themselves of it.

Sometimes they are given, for their own judgment, to know certain things correctly, so that through this very knowledge they become more tightly bound for punishment. [Note: Norm. and Corb. Germ. read, “so that they may indeed know certain correct things…”] Hence the text appropriately adds:

### CHAPTER XII [Vet. VII]

**VERSE 12.**—[Col. 0048B] “Behold, you all know; and why do you speak vainly without cause?”

### 19. Some are given the knowledge of certain right things for their own judgment

It is written: “The servant who knew his master’s will, but did not prepare himself and did not act according to his will, will be beaten with many blows. But the one who did not know, and did things deserving blows, will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48). [Note: All manuscripts have the reading given here. Vindoc. nevertheless reads, “prepared himself.” The printed editions read: “And did not obey, and did not act according to his will, he will be beaten with many blows. But the one who did not know and did things deserving blows will be beaten with few.” Our reading agrees with the Vulgate. Germ. has: “and did things deserving blows, he will be beaten.”]

Again it is written: “Therefore, for one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4:17). [Note: The word “to do” is absent from the second Laud.] Holy Church therefore says that her enemies, to the increase of their guilt, both know what they ought to follow and refuse to follow what they know.

Elsewhere it is said of them: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Ps. 54:16). Those who understand what is happening to them are alive; the dead neither know nor feel anything at all. Thus “dead” is ordinarily used for those who do not perceive, that is, the ignorant, while “living” is used for those who perceive, that is, the knowing. To descend alive into hell, therefore, is to sin knowingly and consciously.

[Rec. X.] The text continues:

**VERSE 13.**—[Col. 0048C] “This is the portion of the wicked man with God, and the inheritance of the violent, which they will receive from the Almighty.” [Note: Becc. and other Norm. manuscripts read *suscipiunt*, “they receive.”]

He immediately explains what this portion and inheritance are when he adds:

### CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 14.**—[Col. 0048D] “If his sons are multiplied, they will be by the sword, and his descendants will not be satisfied with bread.”

### 20. Heretics, who do violence to sacred Scripture, are destined to be struck down by God

It is not inappropriate that heretics are called “wicked,” since through the error of their perverse doctrine they are alienated from knowledge of the truth. The following word also calls them “violent,” because they attempt forcibly to bend the statements of sacred Scripture, which contain correct doctrines, toward a perverse understanding.

They are therefore violent—not, perhaps, in human affairs, but certainly in the meanings of the commandments. [Note: Ebroic. and other Norm. manuscripts read, “certainly in their interpretations.”]

[Col. 0049A] The sons of the violent are the followers of heretics, who, by consenting to their error, are born, as it were, from their preaching. But when multiplied, they will be by the sword, because, although for the moment they grow in immense numbers in their lost freedom, they will nevertheless be struck by the sentence of the coming Judge.

Hence the Lord says through Moses: “My sword will devour flesh” (Deut. 32:42). The sword of God eats flesh because, at the final judgment, his sentence kills those who think according to the flesh. [Note: Vind. reads *devorat*, “devours.”]

In this matter one must ask why it is said that the wicked receive this portion and inheritance from the Almighty. Yet it is clear to those who consider rightly: although they obtained from themselves the power to act unjustly, the equity above has the authority to judge their unjust actions justly, so that the divine sentence orders into punishment those whom their disordered action drew into guilt.

The text appropriately adds: “And his descendants will not be satisfied with bread.”

### 21. They fast from knowledge of the truth when they read Scripture for disputation rather than nourishment

[Col. 0049B] The descendants of heretics are those who are born from the preaching of erring sons. Bread does not satisfy them, because, while in the nourishment of the sacred word they seek to understand more than they are capable of grasping, they remain perpetually hungry for knowledge of the truth. [Note: The first Laud. reads, “more than they understand.”] They seek the propositions of doctrine for disputation, yet are unable to possess them for nourishment.

Because holy Church gathers some of these heretics while leaving others obstinate in their wickedness, the text immediately adds:

### CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 15.**—[Col. 0049C] “Those who remain of him will be buried in destruction.”

### 22. The punishment of those who die in error

Those left behind from the people of heretics are buried in destruction, because, since they do not return to the light of truth, they are utterly weighed down by earthly understanding in everlasting punishment.

And because sometimes, when the leader of an erring multitude is taken away to punishment, the deceived multitudes are reformed into knowledge of the truth, and the subjects return to true understanding when those who had been wicked leaders arrive at eternal punishments, [Col. 0049D] the text appropriately adds:

**THE SAME PLACE.**—“And his widows will not weep.”

### 23. When teachers of error are taken away to punishment, the deceived multitudes often recover their senses

Whom do we understand as his widows except the subject multitudes, happily deprived of him by his death? For often, as has been said, while the preacher of error is carried away to eternal punishment, the multitudes subject to him return to the grace of true understanding.

The perverse preacher presided over these multitudes as a husband, because, joined to them in evil, he had clung to them as a corrupter of their minds. The widows therefore do not weep, because through the death of the wicked teacher they find the way of truth, even though they might have seemed capable of being distressed by his destruction.

Or certainly the widows do not weep because, remaining in their error, they think their preacher was holy and comfort themselves with a false hope so as not to mourn.

The text continues:

### CHAPTER XVI [Vet. VIII, Rec. XI]

**VERSES 16–17.**—[Col. 0050A] “If he should heap up silver like earth and prepare garments like clay, he will indeed prepare them, but the righteous will clothe himself with them, and the innocent will divide the silver.” [Note: The second Laud. reads, “like earth.” Most manuscripts read *praeparavit*, “he prepared,” repeated below. Laud. reads *dividit*, “divides.”]

### 24. Catholics defeat heretics by the same testimonies of sacred Scripture that the heretics produce

[Col. 0050B] “Silver” commonly signifies the brightness of sacred speech, as it is said elsewhere: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested in fire” (Ps. 11:7).

Because some desire to possess God’s word not inwardly through putting it into practice but outwardly through displaying it, the prophet says: “All have perished who are wrapped in silver” (Zeph. 1:11). These are the people who do not fill themselves with God’s word through inward nourishment but clothe themselves with it through outward display.

Thus their silver—that is, the speech of heretics—is compared with earth, because they labor over sacred Scripture to know something from it out of a desire for earthly praise.

They also prepare garments like clay, because they weave together the testimonies of sacred Scripture with which they wish to defend themselves in a loose and defiled manner. He will indeed prepare them, but the righteous will clothe himself with them, because the man full of right faith—which is customarily credited to the saints as righteousness—takes up the very testimonies of sacred Scripture that the heretic produces and uses them to refute his obstinacy in error.

When they bring against us testimonies of sacred law, they bring with them the means by which they may be defeated. Thus David, signifying the Lord, and Goliath, signifying the pride of heretics, spoke through events what we express in words.

[Col. 0050C] Goliath came to battle with a sword, while David came with a shepherd’s bag. But David overcame Goliath and killed him with his own sword. This is also what we do, since by his gracious condescension we have been deemed worthy to become members of the promised David. [Col. 0050D] [Note: Germ. and later printed editions read *promissi David*, “of the promised David.” Other manuscripts and old printed editions read *promissa David*, “the promises of David,” that is, the members of Christ.]

For when heretics come in their pride, bringing forth statements from sacred Scripture, [Note: Vindoc. reads, “bringing forward statements from the words of sacred Scripture.”] we defeat them by the very words and statements they produce—just as we cut down the exalted Goliath with his own sword. The righteous, therefore, clothes himself with the garments prepared by the unrighteous, because the holy man uses for the truth the very statements by which the perverse person attempts to display himself as learned against the truth.

### 25. The word of God must be expounded discerningly and fitted to each person: “And the innocent will divide the silver”

[Col. 0050D] To divide the innocent silver is to expound the words of the Lord minutely and discerningly, and to fit to each person what appropriately corresponds to him. [Note: The second Laud. reads, “It is to expound the words of the Lord in small portions” (*minuta*; in the margin, *munita*, “fortified”) “discerningly.”]

The word of the Lord, which here is called silver or garments, is elsewhere called spoils. The Psalmist also attests to this by comparison, saying: “I will rejoice over your words, like one who finds great spoils” (Ps. 118:162).

They are called spoils because, when the Gentiles pass over to the faith of the Lord, the Jews are stripped of the sacred words with which they had been clothed. [Vet. IX.]

[Col. 0051A] Elsewhere, too, this division of silver or spoils is described: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will devour the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. 49:27). [Note: Laudun. reads, “in the morning he ate … he divides.”] These words designate the apostle Paul, descended from the tribe of Benjamin. In the morning he devoured the prey, because at the beginning of his life he seized as many believers as he could and satisfied his own cruelty. In the evening he divided the spoils, because later, having become faithful, he distributed the sacred words by expounding them.

### 26. What has been said beneficially by heretics must be discerned

Although this “silver which the innocent man divides” may also be understood otherwise. For heretics, so that they may easily persuade people of perverse things, mix certain correct statements into their words, so that they may draw their hearers on through the correct ideas and strike them through the perverse ones. Because, with respect to God’s commandments, they alternate between sound and unsound speech, they are fittingly represented in the Gospel by the ten lepers (Luke 17:12): when diseased whiteness is spread over their healthy color, they are disfigured by this excessive whiteness. Hence we are warned not to think more highly than we ought to think, but to think with sober judgment (Romans 12:3). Moreover, because they do not yet love God, about whom they think wrongly, nor their neighbor, from whom they are divided, they are opposed to the commandments of the Decalogue, and therefore come as ten to entreat the Lord. Because they have mixed the unsound with the sound, they differ in the diversity of their color. But because they have offended against his commandments, they call him by the very title through which they offended, saying, “Jesus, Master” (Luke 17:13); and thus they immediately deserved to be healed. Therefore, because the catholic man understands which things they hold correctly and which incorrectly, he divides the innocent silver—that is, he discerns which things they have said beneficially and which destructively. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 18.—He built his house as a moth.**

### 27. The teachers of heresies corrupt the minds they occupy

A moth builds a house for itself by corrupting it. No better comparison could be made for a heretic, who establishes the place of his faithlessness only in minds that he has corrupted, and who also promises his followers freedom from eternal fire. He promises them, indeed, the refreshment of eternal rest; but his words have no solidity, because they lack the fullness of truth. Hence it follows: “And as a keeper he made a shelter.” The keeper’s shelter is supported by no foundation, but is soon destroyed as time passes. So too the rest promised by heretics is destroyed with time, since it is not found at all after this life.

And because heretics are often supported, in their contempt for the universal Church, by the patronage of the powerful of this world, and because the rich do not cease to assist them with protection and administration as far as they are able [German and Norman manuscripts: “any rich man”], every person who grows arrogant through temporal possessions against his Creator is also now touched by the holy man’s judgment; and the discourse passes from the particular destruction of heretics to a general definition of all the arrogant, when he adds:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 19.—When the rich man sleeps, he will carry nothing away with him; he will open his eyes and find nothing.**

### 28. We lose temporal goods by preserving them for ourselves; by distributing them to the poor, we preserve them

In agreement with this judgment, the Psalmist says: “All the foolish in heart were troubled; they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Psalm 75:6) [Gemetensis: “they slumbered”]. For the rich to find something in their hands after death, they are told before death into whose hands they should place their riches: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

“When the rich man sleeps, he will carry nothing away with him” [Recension XII]. He would carry his possessions away with him when he died if, while he lived, he had taken them to himself at the request of the one who asked. For all earthly things that we lose by preserving them, we preserve by giving them away; our patrimony, when retained, is lost, but what has been distributed remains [First Laudunensis: “is weighed out” (*penditur*)]. We cannot long endure together with our possessions, since either we abandon them by dying, or they, perishing, seem to abandon us while we are alive. Therefore we must act so that things destined plainly to perish may pass into a reward that does not perish.

*[Old recension X.]*

### 29. Death opens the sinner’s eyes, so that he sees temporal goods fleeing from him and punishment succeeding them

But it is very remarkable that it says: “When he sleeps, he will open his eyes and find nothing.” To sleep, we close our eyes, and on waking we open them. But here, because a human being consists of soul and body, when the sleep of one is mentioned, the waking of the other is indicated: when the body falls asleep in death, then the soul awakens to true knowledge [Ebroicensis: “thought”]. Thus the rich man sleeps and opens his eyes, because when he dies in the flesh, his soul is compelled to see what it had scorned to provide for. Then he truly awakens to knowledge; then he sees that what he possessed is nothing. Then he finds himself empty, though he had rejoiced that he was fuller than other people in possessions [Most manuscripts: “he who was full finds himself empty,” and indeed with excellent meaning].

He sleeps and carries nothing away with him—certainly nothing of the possessions he held. For the guilt of those possessions is carried away with him, although all the things for which the guilt was committed are left here. Let him go now, then, and swell with the possessions he has received; let him exalt himself above others and glory in having what his neighbor does not have. The time will come when he will awaken, and then he will recognize how empty was what he had held in sleep.

It often happens that a poor person, while asleep, sees himself rich in a dream, and is elated by the same possessions; he rejoices that he has what he did not have, and now seeks to scorn those by whom he grieved to have been scorned. But suddenly waking, he grieves that he has awakened, though meanwhile, even while sleeping, he had held the image of riches. Immediately he groans under the weight of poverty and is oppressed by the straits of his want—and all the more grievously because for the briefest time he was rich in an empty dream.

Such, surely, are the rich of this world, who swell with the possessions they have received. They do not know how to do good with their abundance; they are like rich people asleep. But when awake they find their poverty, because they carry nothing with them to that judgment that will endure. And the more exalted they have now been for a brief time, the more heavily they will groan against themselves forever.

Let him therefore say, “He will open his eyes and find nothing,” because there he opens the eyes that here he kept closed to mercy, for punishment. He opens his eyes and finds no fruit of compassion, because here he kept them closed when he found it [Bellovacensis, Normannus, and the old edition: “while he lived”]. Those who, according to Wisdom, are reported as saying at the time of their condemnation open their eyes late: “What did our pride profit us? What did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things have passed like a shadow and like a messenger running by” (Wisdom 5:8). They now recognize that what they had held was worthless and fleeting, although, as long as those things were present, they seemed both great and lasting to their foolish hearts.

The rich man opened his eyes too late (Luke 16:23), when he saw Lazarus resting, whom he had scorned to see lying before his door. There he understood what he had refused to do here; in his condemnation he was compelled to learn what he had lost when he had not acknowledged his needy neighbor. Of this it further says:

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 20.—Poverty will seize him like water; a tempest will overwhelm him by night.**

### 30. The astonishing poverty of the wicked rich man after death

Let us now consider the poverty of the rich man burning in the flames, whose abundance had been so great when he feasted. For he says: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am suffering in this flame” (Luke 16:24) [Second Laudunensis: “that he may refresh”].

These words do not make known to us that there, amid such great heat, a single drop of water is required as sufficient refreshment, but that the one who sinned through abundance is there burned by an extreme poverty. We see in the rich man’s words, through the most subtle judgment of God, how fitting a punishment answered such guilt. Driven by poverty, he was compelled there to ask even for the smallest thing [Uticensis: “even to that point”], whereas here, driven by stinginess, he had gone so far as to deny even the smallest thing. What could be repaid more subtly, or more strictly? He asks for a drop of water who denied crumbs of bread.

Thus poverty seized him like water. Not without reason is that poverty then compared with water, because it torments in hell, which is accustomed to be called a lake because it absorbs those whom it receives into its depths [Pratellensis and the other Norman manuscripts: “which torments in hell and absorbs those whom it receives …”]. Hence the prophet also says in the voice of the human race: “My life has fallen into a pit” (Lamentations 3:53). But in the exultation of those who have been rescued it is sung: “Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me; Lord, you drew my soul out of hell, you saved me from those descending into the pit” (Psalm 30:3) [Germanus, Laudunensis, Bellovacensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, Normannus, and others; the printed editions read, “and saved me”].

*[Old recension XI.]*

### 31. The whirlwind of divine judgment will overwhelm him at an hour he does not expect, and therefore by night

“A tempest will overwhelm him by night” [Uticensis, Pratellensis, and others: “what here?”]. What else does he call “night” here but the hidden time of a sudden departure? By the name “tempest” he signifies the whirlwind of judgment. The Psalmist also attests this, saying: “God will come openly; our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him [Gemetensis and many others: “will blaze”], and a mighty tempest around him” (Psalm 50:3) [First Laudunensis: “God is manifest”].

Wisdom also speaks through Solomon of this tempest: “I too will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you, when sudden calamity falls upon you and destruction rushes upon you like a tempest” (Proverbs 1:26). And because the ignorance of the coming departure itself is called night, “a tempest will overwhelm him by night”—that is, the whirlwind of divine judgment will seize him while he is unaware.

Hence Truth itself says: “If the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour when you do not expect him” (Matthew 24:43). Hence also it is said against the wicked servant: “But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to strike his fellow servants, while eating and drinking with the drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know” (ibid., 48).

Hence Paul says to the disciples: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5:4). Here the voice of God says to the rich man who was growing proud: “Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

He is said to return his soul by night who, not foreseeing death, is dragged away in the darkness of his heart. Therefore he says: “A tempest will overwhelm him by night.” Because he does not wish to do the good things he sees, he is caught in the tempest of his destruction, which he does not see. Of this it further says:

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 21.—A burning wind will carry him off and sweep him away.**

### 32. He will be carried away by the devil, who is rightly called a burning wind

Who is called “a burning wind” here if not the evil spirit, who kindles the flames of desires in the heart so that he may draw it toward eternal punishments? Thus it is said that a burning wind carries off any perverse person, because the treacherous evil spirit, who inflames every living person toward vices, drags the dying person toward torments.

Since a burning wind is usually understood as the unclean spirit, who by the breath of evil suggestion inflames the hearts of the wicked toward earthly desires, the prophet Jeremiah testifies, saying: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jeremiah 1:13). The boiling pot is the human heart, fervent with the fires of worldly cares and the anxieties of desires. It is kindled from the face of the north—that is, it is inflamed by the devil’s suggestions. For he is accustomed to be called by the name “north,” who said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds” (Isaiah 14:13).

The mind of each of the elect is therefore tempered by the burning of this burning wind when the heat of vices is extinguished in it and the flame of carnal desires grows cold. Hence the holy Church joyfully cries in praise of her Bridegroom: “I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song of Songs 2:3) [Germanus and many others: “whom I had desired”].

Through Isaiah the Lord promises her this moderation of burning: “In place of the bramble shall the fir tree ascend, and in place of the nettle the myrtle shall grow” (Isaiah 55:13) [Germanus and two Laudunensis manuscripts: “the fir tree ascends … the myrtle grows”]. In place of the bramble, the fir tree ascends in her when, in the hearts of the saints, the height of heavenly contemplation rises in place of the lowliness of earthly thought. The nettle is entirely of a fiery nature. But the myrtle is said to possess a tempering power [Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, Normannus, and many others: “the myrtle, they say, always bears …”; the old edition: “For the myrtle is always said to be of a virtuous nature”]. Therefore the myrtle grows in place of the nettle when the minds of the righteous pass from the itching and heat of vices to the moderation and tranquility of their thoughts—when they no longer desire earthly things and extinguish the flames of the flesh with heavenly desires.

*[Old recension XII.]*

### 33. Refreshment of mind was given to Mary

For this reason, too, the refreshment of mind given from heaven to Mary is expressed in the words: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Yet in this passage the two natures of the incarnate God could also be signified by the term “overshadowing.” For a shadow is formed by light and a body.
