The Lord, however, is light through his divinity; through an intervening soul, he deigned to become a body in her womb through his humanity. Since therefore incorporeal light was to become embodied in her womb, it is said to her who conceived the incorporeal one in bodily form: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you”—that is, the incorporeal light of divinity will receive in you a body of humanity.

But let us now complete what we began concerning any wicked person. The burning wind therefore carries him off, because the evil spirit, having now kindled him with the fire of perverse desire, later snatches him away to the flames of Gehenna. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXI

**THE SAME.—And like a whirlwind it will snatch him from his place.**

### 34. What is the place of the wicked

The place of the perverse is the delight of temporal life and the pleasure of the flesh. Each person is therefore snatched away from his place as if by a whirlwind when, terrified by the final day, he is separated from all his pleasures. Of that final day it suitably says immediately:

## CHAPTER XXII [Recension XIII]

**VERSE 22.—He will send against him, and will not spare.**

*[Laudunensis here and below: “he sends … he spares.” In the second Laudunensis manuscript both readings are noted: “he sends … he spares.”]*

### 35. God scourges the elect here in order to spare them, but the reprobate in order to begin punishing them. Every divine blow is either a cleansing of the present life or the beginning of the punishment to come

Whenever God corrects a sinner by striking him, he sends the scourge for this purpose: to spare him. But when, by striking him, he brings his life—which persists in sin—to an end, he sends the scourge, but by no means spares him. For he who sent the scourge in order to spare him sometimes sends it for this purpose: that he may not spare him.

In this life the Lord is more concerned to spare people the more he scourges them through waiting, as he himself says by the voice of the angel to John: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline” (Revelation 3:19). And elsewhere it is said: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

Conversely, concerning the scourge of condemnation it is written: “The sinner is caught in the works of his hands” (Psalm 9:17). Concerning this the Lord says through Jeremiah, when he sees peoples sinning incorrigibly—whom he now regards not as sons under discipline but as enemies under strict punishment [Normannus: “he regards as enemies”; Corbeiensis Germanus and Germanus: “he regards as foes”]: “The blow of an enemy I have struck you, with cruel chastisement” (Jeremiah 30:14). And what is said here, “He will not spare,” is also declared there in other words: “Why do you cry over your wound? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., 15) [Normannus: “Why do you cry to me over your wound?”].

Therefore the elect always take care that they return to righteousness before the judge’s anger is kindled unquenchably, lest, caught by the final scourge [Thus in both Laudunensis manuscripts, Normannus, and others, as well as in the old edition. Later editions read: “lest, when caught by the final scourge, their life should end together with their guilt”], their life should end together with their guilt. For the scourge then wipes away guilt when it changes the life. It does not expiate the actions of one whose conduct it does not change.

Every divine blow, therefore, is either a cleansing of the present life in us or the beginning of the punishment to come. For those who profit from the scourge it was said: “You who fashion pain through instruction” (Psalm 93:26) [Vindocinus: “who fashion labor or grief”]. When the wicked person is scourged and corrected [Vindocinus: “and is not corrected”], he who refused to hear the commandment hears pain. Pain is therefore fashioned through instruction for the one who is restrained from evil deeds by pain, as though pain had taken the place of a commandment.

But of those whom scourges condemn and do not free it is said: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to receive discipline” (Jeremiah 5:3). For such people the scourges begin in this life and continue in the eternal striking. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “A fire has been kindled by my anger, and it will burn down to the depths below” (Deuteronomy 32:22) [Beccensis and other Normanni: “to the underworld”].

With regard to the present striking, therefore, it is rightly said: “A fire has been kindled by my anger” [Vindocinus: “in my anger”] (*On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter 43). But with regard to eternal condemnation it is suitably added immediately: “And it will burn down to the depths below.”

Although some are accustomed to say what is written, “God does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1:9) [Beccensis and other Normanni: “does not judge”], they nevertheless do not attend to what is said through the prophet concerning the wicked: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jeremiah 17:18) [Laudunensis, Bellovacensis, Normannus, Corbeiensis Germanus, Germanus: “with a double destruction”; the printed editions have “with a double contrition”]. And elsewhere it is written: “Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

Yet if we grant them this—that no guilt can be struck twice—it should be understood of those who are struck by sin and die in their sin [Vindocinus: “that is, in their sin”], because their striking, begun here, is completed there. Thus for those who refuse entirely to be corrected, there is one scourge: it begins temporally but is completed in eternal punishments, so that for those who altogether refuse correction, the striking of present scourges becomes the beginning of subsequent torments.

“He will send against him, and will not spare.” It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Old recension XIII]

**THE SAME.—Fleeing from his hand, he will flee.**

### 36. We escape the hand of the one who strikes only through amendment

He flees from the hand of the one who strikes who corrects the perversity of his action. Or certainly, because in sacred speech “hand” usually signifies action, the one who sees the destruction of the perverse flees from the hand of the stricken man when he abandons the ways of perversity. Hence it further says:

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 23.—He will clench his hands against him.**

*[Laudunensis and Normannus: “he grasps.”]*

### 37. In the punishment of others we see what we must fear

To clench the hands is to establish the works of one’s life in rectitude. Hence Paul also says: “Raise up your slackened hands and weakened knees” (Hebrews 12:12).

When people therefore see another’s destruction, they are recalled to their own hearts so that they may reflect upon their own selves; and from the place where one person is led to torments, another is freed from torment. He therefore clenches his hands against him because he sees in another’s punishment what he must fear; and while he sees the delinquent struck in this way, he constrains his own weakened works with the strength of righteousness.

Thus it happens that one who, while living wickedly, had drawn many toward guilt through the delight of sin, by dying recalls some from guilt through fear of torment. The Psalmist also testifies that this occurs to the good, saying: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance upon the wicked; he will wash his hands in the blood of sinners” (Psalm 58:11). The hands of the righteous are washed in the blood of dying sinners because, when their punishment is observed, the life of the observer is cleansed. It follows.

## CHAPTER XXV

**THE SAME.—And he will hiss at him, observing his place.**

### 38. In this way we are restrained from sin

What is expressed in a hiss if not the force of astonishment? But if some other meaning is perhaps sought in the hiss at the sinner’s death, those who observe his destruction purse their lips in a hiss when they turn toward the spiritual words that they had scorned, so that they now begin to believe and preach what previously they did not believe when they saw the wicked flourishing.

For it often happens that the mind of the weak is more fearful of hearing the truth the more it sees the despisers of truth flourishing [Vindocinus: “of the boldness of truth”]. But when just vengeance removes the unjust, it restrains others from perversity. Hence Solomon says: “When the pestilent man is punished, the simple will become wiser” (Proverbs 21:11).

After the holy man had sufficiently completed his account of the punishments of the powerful who are exalted in this world, he again turns his words to the pride of heretics, who are exalted in speech. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Old recension and Recension XIV]

**CHAPTER 28, VERSE 1.—Silver has the beginnings of its veins, and gold has a place in which it is smelted.**

### 39. Heretics must be directed to the sacred pages and the books of the ancient fathers

Silver ordinarily signifies speech, and gold the splendor of life or wisdom. Because heretics so pride themselves on the brilliance of their speech that they are supported by no authority of the sacred books—and those books are, as it were, veins of silver for our speaking, since from them we draw the origin of our speech—he recalls them to the pages of sacred authority, so that, if they truly desire to speak, they may take from there what they ought to say.

And he says: “Silver has the beginnings of its veins.” As if he were saying openly: Whoever prepares himself for the words of true preaching must take the origins of his subjects from the sacred pages, so that he may refer everything he says to the foundation of divine authority and establish the structure of his speech upon it.

As we have said before, heretics often, while striving to establish their own perverse opinions, bring forward things that certainly are not contained in the pages of the sacred books. Hence the excellent preacher admonishes his disciple, saying: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words” (1 Timothy 6:20). For while heretics desire to be praised as though for exceptional talent, they bring forward certain novelties that are not contained in the old books of the ancient Fathers; and so, while they desire to appear wise, they scatter seeds of folly among their wretched hearers.

### 40. Only the catholic Church has martyrs

It is rightly added: “And gold has a place in which it is smelted.” As if he were saying openly: The true wisdom of the faithful, for which the universal Church is the place, suffers tribulation when you persecute it, but is cleansed from every stain of sin by the fire of your persecution.

Hence it is written: “Gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Sirach 2:5) [Germanus, Corbeiensis Germanus, Gemetensis, and other Normanni: “acceptable”; and indeed we say *acceptabiles*, not *acceptibiles*].

This passage can also appropriately be understood as rebuking the foolish passion of heretics. For they often suffer much for the name of Jesus Christ our Lord and Redeemer, and hope through those sufferings to become his martyrs. To them the holy man now says: “Gold has a place in which it is smelted.”

According to what has already been said before us [by Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, and elsewhere], whoever suffers outside the unity of the Church may suffer punishments, but cannot become a martyr, because gold has a place in which it is smelted.

What do you say to this, heretics? You wish to be smelted through bodily affliction, or even through martyrdom, but you do not know the place in which you ought to be smelted. Hear what is said by the voice of the holy preacher: “Gold has a place in which it is smelted.” Seek, therefore, this place of smelting; find this furnace in which gold can properly be purified.

### 41. Whatever is endured outside the Church torments but does not cleanse

There is one Church in which anyone who is able to be smelted can also be cleansed from every stain of sin [The printed editions read, “who wishes to be smelted.” In the manuscripts Germanus, Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, and others, *valuerit* is consistently read. As above, “in which gold can properly be purified”]. If, while placed outside this Church, you endure any bitterness or tribulation for God, you can only be burned, not purified.

Let Jeremiah say it; let him say how entirely empty of virtue the fire of your smelting is: “The smelter smelted in vain, for their wickednesses were not consumed” (Jeremiah 6:29). Behold the external fire smelting and imposing the punishment of harsh suffering, yet it does not burn away the guilt of error; it inflicts the torments of cruel punishments but produces no increase of merits.

The Apostle Paul also indicates how devoid of any virtue is this fire of smelting endured outside the catholic Church, saying: “If I hand over my body so that it may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 12:3) [Germanus, Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, Normannus, and other manuscripts here and below: “so that it may burn”; the printed editions read, “if I burn”]. Some think wrongly about God; others hold correct beliefs about the Creator, but do not maintain unity with their brothers. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by the commission of schism.

Thus, in the very first part of the Decalogue, the guilt of both groups is restrained when the divine voice says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5). And immediately it adds: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” For whoever thinks perversely about God clearly does not love God. But whoever thinks correctly about God while divided from the unity of the holy Church plainly does not love his neighbor, whom he refuses to have as a companion.

### 43. Charity is lacking both to schismatics and to heretics

Whoever, therefore, is divided from this unity of mother Church—whether by thinking perversely about God through heresy, or by failing to love his neighbor through the error of schism—is deprived of this grace of charity, concerning which Paul says what we quoted above: “If I hand over my body so that it may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

As if he were saying openly: Outside the place of its smelting, fire applied to me torments me with punishment but does not cleanse me. All lovers of holy peace seek this place with the utmost zeal; seeking it, they find it; finding it, they hold it, knowing where, when, and to whom the remission of sins is given.

Where, indeed, if not in the bosom of the catholic mother [Germanus, Bellovacensis, Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, Normannus, and others; the printed editions read, “in the bosom of mother Church”]? When, if not before the day of the coming departure? For “behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). And: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6).

To whom, if not to those who have been converted, who, in imitation of little children, are formed with humility as their teacher [Laudunensis: “are strengthened”]? To them it is said: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19:14). And: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3) [Recension XV].

Therefore, since true martyrs are made only in the catholic Church, it is rightly said: “Gold has a place in which it is smelted,” because the soul will not shine in the radiance of eternal beauty unless, so to speak, it has first burned here in the workshop of charity.

### 43. God saves some through innocence and others through repentance

It should also be considered that, by a hidden plan, almighty God guards some as innocent from their very beginnings and advances them to the height of virtues, so that, as their age increases, both the number of their years and the elevation of their merits may grow together [Corbeiensis Germanus, Bellovacensis, Germanus, Vindocinus, Laudunensis, Gemetensis, and other Normanni: “to the summit of virtues,” or “to the summit of virtue.” All the printed editions nevertheless read, “to the height of virtue”].

But he abandons others at their beginnings and permits them, through their vices bubbling forth, to proceed along precipitous paths. Yet often he also regards these people and kindles them with the fire of holy love to follow him; he turns the long-established itchings of vice in their hearts into the fervor of virtue. They burn all the more intensely with the desire to seek God’s mercy the more deeply they blush at the memory of their iniquity.

It often happens, for example, that in the struggle of battle a soldier standing before the eyes of his commander disgracefully yields to the enemy’s strength and, weakly presenting his back, is struck. Yet, ashamed of what he has done so disgracefully, he draws greater strength from that very shame before the eyes of his commander, and afterward performs deeds of courage in proportion both as he achieves the present glory of virtue and as he covers the former disgrace of weakness [Germanus, Ebroicensis, and other Normanni: “and afterward performs deeds of courage in such measure as to achieve the glory of present virtue”; Corbeiensis Germanus: “and [to cover] the former disgrace of weakness”].

Thus some people are occasionally strengthened more vigorously in God’s service by their past weakness; desire for the future draws them to keep the commandments, while memory of the past drives them on, so that love summons them from one side toward what lies ahead, and shame urges them from the other concerning what lies behind [Vindocinus: “are strengthened more intensely in God’s service from their former and past weakness”].

*[Old recension XVI.]*

When the enemies of the Church see such people endowed with the highest virtues, and cannot find anything in their present life by which to disparage them, they attempt to accuse them concerning the past. Thus the Manichaean attacks our Moses, attempting to defile in him the grace of his subsequent virtues with the guilt of his former murder. He does not consider how patient Moses afterward became in enduring, but how rash he had previously been in striking.

Against such adversaries, therefore, blessed Job responds with the most subtle consideration. After saying, “Silver has the beginnings of its veins, and gold has a place in which it is smelted,” he suitably adds:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Recension XVI]

**VERSE 2.—Iron is taken from the earth.**

### 44. We must not consider what the teachers of the Church are in themselves, but what they have become through grace

Heretics commonly glory in their proud confidence in their own righteousness against us, and boast of their works with the inflation of ostentation; as we have said, they accuse us of either being or having been wicked.

Therefore the holy man speaks against them through a most humble confession and truthful defense, saying: “Iron is taken from the earth.” As if he were saying openly: Strong men, who become iron through the sharpest swords of their tongues in this battle for the defense of the faith, were at one time earth in base actions.

For it was said to the sinful human being: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). But iron is taken from the earth [Distinction 50, chapter 18] when a strong defender of the Church is separated from the earthly action that he previously held. Therefore one must not despise in him whatever he was, since he has already begun to be what he was not.

Was Matthew not found in the earth, entangled in earthly business and serving the operations of the tax office (Matthew 9:9) [Germanus, first Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus: “tax office”]? But, lifted from the earth [First Laudunensis, Germanus, Corbeiensis Germanus: *tultus*; concerning this word, see book 3, number 22], he grew strong as iron. With his tongue, like an exceedingly sharp sword, the Lord pierced the hearts of unbelievers through the ministry of the Gospel. Though previously weak and despised because of earthly business, he afterward became strong for heavenly preaching. Hence it further says:

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Recension XVII]

**THE SAME.—And the stone, loosened by heat, is changed into bronze.**
## 45. By the infusion of grace the heart is softened for love and strengthened for action

Then the stone is dissolved by heat, when a hard heart, cold from the fire of divine love, is touched by that same fire of divine love and is melted in the fervor of the spirit, so that it burns with the heat of desires for the life to come, whereas previously, even when hearing of it, it remained insensible. [Old recension XVII.]

From this ardor it is both softened for love and strengthened for action, so that, just as it had previously been hard in its love of the world, it may afterward display itself as strong in the love of God; and what before it refused to hear, it may now begin both to believe and to preach. Thus the stone, dissolved by heat, is changed into bronze, because a hard mind, melted by the fire of heavenly love, is transformed into true strength, so that the sinner who previously had been insensible afterward becomes both strong in authority and eloquent in preaching. [Note: Bellovacensis and 1 Laudunensis read *sonorus*, “resounding” or “eloquent.”]

This is aptly said through Isaiah: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength” (Isaiah 40:31). We change our strength when, after our conversion, we flee the present world with as much vigor as we previously sought it.

[Note: Beccensis reads “because evil things,” or possibly “because, however, evil things.”]

But because the life previously conducted by the adversaries of Catholics is rightly judged evil, the text appropriately continues:

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Column 0061D] **VERSE 3.**—“He appointed a time for darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things.”

### 46. God regards the end of the elect and of the reprobate. He does and orders good things; he does not do evil things, but orders them

“He himself appointed a time for darkness,” namely, for the wicked, a limit by which the wicked may cease to be wicked. Hence the Apostle says to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” As the same outstanding teacher also says to other disciples: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Ephesians 5:8; Romans 13:12). [Note: Laudunensis and Normanus read *et induamur arma*, “and let us put on the armor.”]

Hence also, when the Church comes, it is said in the Song of Songs: [Note: 1 Laudunensis reads “to the Church coming.”] “Who is this that comes forth like the dawn, rising?” (Song of Songs 6:9). The Church is aptly compared with the dawn, because through knowledge of the faith she is changed from the darkness of her sins into the clear light of righteousness. [Note: 1 Laudunensis reads *cogitationem*, “thought,” for *cognitionem*, “knowledge.”]

“He therefore appointed a time for darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things.” By “all things” he intended both the elect and the reprobate to be included. For God, who does and orders good things, but does not do evil things, himself arranging that the things done by the wicked should not occur without order, considers the end of all things. He patiently tolerates everything and regards the end of the elect: that they may be changed from evil to good. [Note: Normanus reads *veniant*, “may come,” for *eveniant*, “may occur.”]

He also regards the end of the reprobate: that from an evil deed they may draw themselves toward the punishment they deserve. [Note: 2 Laudunensis reads *dignum retrahantur ad supplicium*, “that they may be drawn back to the punishment they deserve”; Primus reads *dignum se trahunt ad supplicium*, “they draw themselves to the punishment they deserve.”] He saw the end of Saul the persecutor, when, struck down, he would say: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). [Note: Two Laudunensis manuscripts read: “Lord, what do you command me to do?”] He saw the end of the disciple who appeared to be obedient: because of the crime he had committed, he would constrict his throat with a noose, thereby punishing himself for his sin and, by punishing himself more severely, deceiving himself.

He saw the Ninevites committing sin, but he considered the end of those sinners: the repentance of those who were corrected. [Note: This is the reading of Corbeiensis Germanicus, Laudunensis, Normanus, and others; the old editions read *poenitentia*, “repentance,” where later editions differ.] He also saw Sodom committing sin, but he considered the end of the heat of lust: the fire of Gehenna. He saw the end of paganism: that, although possessed by the darkness of iniquities, it would eventually shine with the light of faith. He also saw the end of Judea: that, from the light of faith which she possessed, she would blind herself with the darkness of hardened unbelief. Hence the text suitably continues:

## CHAPTER XXX [Revised recension XVIII]

[Column 0062B] **IBID., VERSE 4.**—“The stone of darkness and the shadow of death the torrent divides from the wandering people.”

### 47. At the final judgment fire will divide the good from the wicked

What else was that hard people of the Jews, hardened by unbelief, who refused to see through faith the author of life whom they had foretold through prophecy, but a stone of darkness? For it was both hard through cruelty and clouded through unbelief. It is also called by another name, “the shadow of death.”

A shadow is expressed according to the features of the thing from which it is cast. But who is called by the name “death” except the devil? Concerning him it is said, through a certain indication of the function of his servant: “And his name was Death” (Revelation 6:8). [Note: The reading in Gemetensis may perhaps be more correct: “through a certain indication of his ministry.” The devil’s ministry is to inflict death. In the old edition, instead of *ministri*, “servant,” *mysterii*, “mystery,” is read.]

That people became his shadow because, following his iniquity, it expressed his image in itself.

But what is called by the name “torrent” except that fire which proceeds from the sight of the dreadful Judge through the final examination and divides the elect from the reprobate? Hence the prophet says: “A stream of fire, swift-flowing, came forth from before him” (Daniel 7:10).

[Old recension XVIII; revised recension XIX.]

### 48. All the elect are strangers in this world

What people wander in this world except those who, hastening toward the lot of the elect, know that they have a homeland in heaven? They hope to find themselves there all the more truly at home because here they regard as alien everything that passes away.

The wandering people, then, are the entire number of the elect. They regard this life as a kind of exile for themselves and sigh toward their heavenly homeland with the full intention of their hearts. Of them Paul says: “They confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). For those who say this show that they are seeking a homeland.

The same Apostle also endured this pilgrimage when he said: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:6). He sought to escape the hardships of this pilgrimage when he said: “I have the desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). And again: “For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid. 1:21).

The Psalmist felt the heavy burden of this pilgrimage when he said: “Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Psalm 119:5). He longed to be rescued from it as quickly as possible when, burning with heavenly desires, he said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3).

But those who fix their hearts on earthly pleasures do not know this desire. For while they love only visible things, even if they believe that invisible things exist, they do not love them; because, while they follow outward things too closely, they also become carnal in mind.

Both peoples run together in this life, but they do not arrive together at eternity, because “the torrent divides the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the wandering people.” As though he were saying openly: The river of flames, proceeding from the sight of the eternal Judge, separates from the people of the elect those whom either unbelief now blinds or cruelty hardens, so that the fire of severe judgment then divides from the good those whom the darkness of vices now blinds amid their desires.

### 49. The irrigation of preaching, like a torrent, divides the good from the wicked

Perhaps the very irrigation of holy preaching may be understood by the name “torrent,” in accordance with what Solomon says: “Let the ravens of the torrents dig out the eye that mocks his father and despises the offspring of his mother” (Proverbs 30:17).

The perverse, when they criticize divine judgments, mock their father. And when heretics ridicule and despise the preaching and fruitfulness of holy Church, what else do they do but despise the offspring of their mother? We rightly call her their mother also, because those who speak against her come forth from her, as John attests when he says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

Ravens come from the torrents when true preachers proceed, for the defense of holy Church, from the streams of the sacred books. They are rightly called ravens also because they do not grow proud of the light of their righteousness, but through the grace of humility confess in themselves the blackness of their sins. Hence the Church of the elect says: “I am black, but beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:4). And John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

These ravens dig out the eye of the mocker because they overcome the purpose of wicked and stubborn people. If, then, the torrent here too is to be understood as preaching, “the torrent divides the stone of darkness and the shadow of death from the wandering people”: the preaching of the saints abandons the hardened minds of the reprobate and turns toward the devout hearts of the humble.

Hence the text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Old recension XIX]

[Column 0064B] **VERSE 4.**—“Those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, those who are pathless.”

### 50. Having left the Jews, he flowed toward the Gentiles

Who else is understood here by the “needy man” except he of whom Paul says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9)? [Note: Two Laudunensis manuscripts and Corbeiensis Germanicus read “for your sake.”]

The feet of this needy man were the holy preachers, through whose presence he went around among the Gentiles and traversed the whole world. Of them the prophet says: “And I will walk among them” (Leviticus 26:12; 2 Corinthians 6:16). [Note: Gemeticensis reads “and I will walk.”] Was he not his foot who, held in fetters, said: “For whose sake I am acting as an ambassador in chains” (Ephesians 6:20)?

But the foot of the needy man forgot those who had been the shadow of death and the stone of darkness, because, at the very beginning of the nascent Church, when the holy apostles wished to preach the kingdom of heaven to Judea, they saw that they were accomplishing nothing at all there and turned aside to preach to the Gentiles. [Note: Two Laudunensis manuscripts and Corbeiensis Germanicus read *deflexerunt*, “they turned aside,” for *defluxerunt*, “they flowed aside.”] They themselves say this in the Acts: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Of them the Psalmist also says: “The mountains will be transferred into the heart of the sea” (Psalm 45:3), because the apostles, rejected by Judea, were transferred into this Gentile world. [Note: A more elegant reading in recent editions is “into this sea of paganism”; but the German, Tours, two Laudunensis manuscripts, Corbeiensis Germanicus, Normanus, and others read *saeculum* or *saeculo*, “world” or “into the world”; the old Paris edition has *solo*, “soil,” and the Basel edition *populo*, “people.”]

Who, then, are those who, through the immense hardness arising from the obscurity of their hearts—like a stone of darkness and a shadow of death—are divided from the wandering people of the saints, except those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten? That is, those whom the Lord’s preachers, through the poverty of his humanity, abandoned because of their swelling pride, [Note: The manuscripts read *per humanitatem*, “through the humanity”; all editions read *per humilitatem*, “through humility.”] and whom they entirely forgot when they transferred the seeds of their preaching to the sole fruitfulness of the Gentiles.

He rightly also calls them “inaccessible,” because, hardened in their unbelief, they refused to provide a way for the words of life to reach their hearts. But let us hear what this Judea, which became so hardened, had once been and what she afterward suffered. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Column 0065A] **VERSE 5.**—“The land from which bread arose was overturned by fire in its place.”

### 51. The synagogue, which supplied the bread of the Law and the Scriptures, was consumed by envy and destroyed

Judea used to give bread, for she brought forth the words of the Law. Because the wicked could no longer understand or explain that Law, the prophet Jeremiah laments it in the Lamentations, saying: “The little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations 4:4).

But this land was overturned by fire in its place, because, seeing the signs of the faithful, she burned herself with the flame of envy. Since envy usually arises from pride, she perished by fire in her own place: she burned with envy because she did not abandon pride. [Note: 2 Laudunensis reads “often” for “always.”]

The land that had previously possessed bread was afterward overturned by fire, because the synagogue, which had brought forth the commandments of God through the Law, consumed itself with the fire of envy while persecuting the Church at her birth.

Was she not burning with the flames of her jealousy when, seeing the signs of our Redeemer, some of her people said: “What are we doing, because this man performs many signs?” Or certainly: “You see that we accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 11:47).

They saw the things from which they ought to have been converted, and by those very things became more perverse. They sought to extinguish the one whom they saw bringing the dead to life. They held the Law in their mouths, but persecuted the author of the Law.

Thus “the land from which bread arose was overturned by fire in its place,” because Judea first possessed within herself the Law that would nourish her, and afterward the envy that would consume her. Concerning her description the text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Column 0065D] **VERSE 6.**—“Her stones are the place of sapphire, and her clods are gold.”

### 52. The abundance of the gifts and graces with which the Jews were formerly adorned increases the gravity of their fall

The glory of the preceding state increases the guilt of the sin that follows. For everyone’s fall involves a crime all the greater in proportion to the greater virtue he could have possessed before falling.

Let Judea be described; let it be said what she was, so that the magnitude of her former virtues may increase the accumulation of her subsequent sins.

“Her stones are the place of sapphire, and her clods are gold.” What do we understand by “stones” here except the minds of the holy and strong? [Old recension XX.]

In sacred Scripture, stones are sometimes understood in an evil sense and sometimes in a good one. When a stone signifies insensibility, hard hearts are represented by stones. Hence John says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9). By the name “stones” he designates the hearts of the Gentiles, which at that time were hard and insensible through unbelief.

And through the prophet the Lord promises, saying: “I will take the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19).

Again, stones commonly designate the minds of the strong. Hence Peter says to the saints: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses” (1 Peter 2:5). [Note: Normanus and most manuscripts read “into spiritual houses.”] And through the prophet the Lord promises the coming Church, saying: “Behold, I will arrange your stones in order, and I will lay your foundations in sapphires; I will set jasper as your fortifications and your gates in carved stones; and all your boundaries in precious stones, all your children taught by the Lord” (Isaiah 54:11–12).

He arranged stones in her in order because he distinguished holy souls within her by the diversity of their merits. He founded her upon sapphires, stones of an airy color that bear in themselves a likeness to the heavens, because the strength of the Church is established in souls that seek heavenly things.

And because jasper is green in color, he set jasper as her fortifications: those who, green with inward desires, are placed against the adversaries for the defense of holy Church and do not wither through the aridity of the wicked person’s tepidity. [Note: 1 Laudunensis has “no aridity of the time of the wicked person”; most editors partly follow that reading. Our reading, however, is found in nearly all manuscripts and is greatly preferable.]

He set her gates in carved stones. [Note: Laudunensis reads *scalptos*, “carved,” and below *scalpti lapides*, “carved stones.”] These are the gates of the Church, through whose life and teaching the multitude of believers enters her. Because they excel in great works and show by their lives what they affirm in speech, they are said to be not unworked but carved stones. In their lives right action is visible; it is as though what they have done were engraved in those very stones.

There, concluding the whole number of the saints in a general summation, he adds: “All your boundaries in precious stones” (ibid. 54:12). And, as though we who heard these things were asking him to identify the stones of which he spoke, he added: “All your children taught by the Lord.”

Since holy souls who lived a heavenly life were never lacking in Judea, it is said: “Her stones are the place of sapphire.” And because she shone through faith with the great splendor of life and wisdom, it is added: “And her clods are gold.”

What are designated by “clods” except collections of the various orders and multitudes of individuals? Clods are bound together from moisture and dust. Thus all those who, infused with the dew of grace, confessed through true knowledge that they were dust because of their debt of death, while shining through the virtue of their life, lay there like golden clods.

That land had clods in the prophets, clods in the teachers, clods in the ancient Fathers, who, through the great infusion of grace, held together in unanimity of profession and action.

Let it therefore say: “And her clods are gold,” because in her the multitude of spiritual people shone with a virtue all the greater as they bound themselves together in greater unanimity toward God and neighbor. [Note: Vindocensis reads “bound together in greater unity”; 1 Laudunensis has *construxit*, “built,” instead of *constrinxit*, “bound.”]

### 53. The gold with which they shone was darkened by the gloom of unbelief

But this gold was afterward darkened by the gloom of unbelief. The prophet Jeremiah, contemplating its blackness, laments, saying: “How the gold has been darkened; the excellent color has been changed” (Lamentations 4:1).

The gold was darkened because, when unbelief broke in, that ancient splendor of faith and innocence among them stained itself with the night of wickedness.

Since we have heard what she was—namely, “the place of sapphire stones, and her clods gold”—let us now hear why that people, beloved by God, lost such great blessings. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Old recension XXI]

[Column 0067B] **VERSE 7.**—“The bird did not know the path, nor did the vulture’s eye behold it.”

### 54. Because they did not know the ways of Christ’s humility, they lost the fruit of his death

Who is signified here by the name “bird” except he who, ascending into the heavens, carried upward the fleshly body he had assumed? He is aptly expressed also by the name “vulture.”

When a vulture flies and sees a corpse lying below, it descends to feed upon the corpse; and often it is caught in death in this way, coming down from the heights to a dead animal.

Thus the mediator between God and human beings, our Redeemer, is rightly signified by the name “vulture.” Remaining in the height of his divinity, he saw, as if from a lofty flight, the corpse of our mortality in the depths, and lowered himself from heavenly things to things below. [Note: This is the reading of 1 Laudunensis, Normanus, and most manuscripts. All printed editions omit *a*, “from.”]

For our sake he deigned to become human; and when he sought the dead animal, he found death among us, although he was immortal in himself.

But the eye of this vulture was the very intention of our resurrection, because, having died for three days, he freed us from eternal death.

That faithless people of Judea therefore saw the mortal man, but paid no attention to how, by his death, he would destroy our death. [Note: Most manuscripts read: “but did not attend to how by death …”] It saw the vulture, but did not regard the vulture’s eye.

Because it refused to consider the ways of his humility by which he raised us to the heights, it did not know the bird’s path. It did not take pains to consider that his humility would raise us to heavenly things and that the purpose of his death would restore us to life.

Thus “the bird did not know the path, nor did the vulture’s eye behold it,” because, although it saw him whom it held in death, it did not wish to see how much glory for our life would follow from his death. [Note: Germanus, Corbeiensis Germanicus, Normanus, and others read “how great a glory of our life.”]

Hence it also burned with the cruelty of persecution. It refused to receive the words of life and drove away the preachers of the kingdom of heaven by prohibiting, raging against, and striking them.

After being driven away, they abandoned Judea, to which they had been sent, and were scattered into the gathering of the Gentiles. Hence the text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Revised recension XX]

[Column 0068A] **VERSE 8.**—“The sons of the merchants did not tread it, nor did the lioness pass through it.”

### 55. The apostles and their successors abandoned Judea and labored for the conversion of the Gentiles

[Note: We have restored this passage, which is extremely corrupt in the editions, from the manuscripts of Corbeiensis Germanicus, Anglicus, Normanus, Parisinus, Laudunensis, Bellovacensis, and others. Previously we found *institores*, “merchants,” in all Latin manuscripts. In the Greek texts, however, we find *negotiatores*, also “merchants.” From this I concluded that in this passage scribes, through ignorance, had written *institores* for *institutores*, “instructors.” How could they have erred by writing *institores* for *negotiatores*, when both words have the same sense? But we should read *institutores*, as it was corruptly read at that time in the Latin manuscripts of the Book of Job. That Gregory read this way is clear both from the agreement of the manuscripts—with the exception of Germanus, in which the middle syllable *tu* has everywhere been deleted—and from these words: “All who instruct the conduct of the faithful,” and so forth.]

In all Latin manuscripts we find *institutores*, “instructors”; in the Greek texts we find *negotiatores*, “merchants.” From this it can be inferred that in this passage scribes, through ignorance, wrote *institutores* for *institores*. For we call *institores* “merchants” because they devote themselves persistently to their work.

Although the two expressions differ in sound, they do not differ in meaning, because all who instruct the conduct of the faithful conduct a spiritual business: when they provide preaching to their hearers, they receive faith and right works from them. Thus it is written of holy Church: “She made and sold a linen garment” (Proverbs 31:24); and shortly afterward it is said of her: “She saw that her business was good” (ibid. 31:18).

Who are the “instructors” mentioned here except the holy prophets, who took care through prophecy to instruct the synagogue’s conduct toward faith? Their sons are called the holy apostles, who, in order to believe that God had become human, were generated for that same faith through their preaching.

Of them it is said to the Church through the Psalmist: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17).

But because the apostles, rejected by the synagogue, went forth from its boundaries, it is rightly said now: “The sons of the merchants did not tread it.” The sons of the merchants would tread it if holy preachers were pressing down the vices of that same synagogue with the foot of virtue.

If, however, we understand the merchants as the preachers of holy Church, [Note: Gemeticensis and others read “the preachers of that same holy Church.”] it is also reasonable to understand the sons of the merchants as pastors and teachers who followed the way of the apostles. [Note: Laudunensis, Vindocinensis, Corbeiensis Germanicus, and Normanus read *viam*, “way”; the editions with Germanus read *vitam*, “life.”] They did not tread the synagogue because, when their fathers—that is, the apostles—were rejected by it, they too ceased from its calling.

[Old recension XXII.]

### 56. After abandoning the synagogue, the Church devoted herself to gathering the Gentiles

The lioness did not pass through that synagogue, because holy Church, devoted to the gathering of the Gentiles, no longer occupied herself with the Jewish people.

The Church is rightly called a lioness, because through the mouth of holy preaching she kills those who live wickedly in vices. Hence it is said to the first pastor himself, as though to the mouth of this lioness: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

What is killed is killed to its former life; what is eaten is changed into the body of the one eating. Thus “kill and eat” means: Kill them with respect to the sin in which they live, and convert them from themselves into your members.

And because this Church is the body of the Lord, the Lord himself is also called a lion in the words of Jacob; in relation to himself he is called a lion, and in relation to his body he is called a lioness, when it is said to him under the figure of Judah: “You have gone up to the prey, my son; you have lain down and rested like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9). [Note: Two Laudunensis manuscripts and others read: “Who has roused him?”]

This lioness, therefore, is not said never to have passed through Judea, but not to have passed all the way through it. When the apostles preached, three thousand first believed from it, and afterward five thousand. Thus the Church passed through the synagogue, but did not pass through it completely: from it she snatched a few into the faith, but did not entirely destroy that unbelieving people in its unbelief. [Note: 2 Laudunensis, Bellovacensis, Ebroicensis, Pratellensis, and others preserve the crucial *non*: the Church passed through Judea, but did not pass all the way through it. The printed editions and Germanus omit it, to serious detriment of the sense. Gregory distinguishes *transire*, “to pass through,” from *pertransire*, “to pass all the way through.”]

But, as we have often said, after being rejected by the unbelief of the Jews, she turned aside to the calling of the Gentiles. Hence the same lioness is further described:

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Column 0069B] **VERSE 9.**—“She stretched out her hand to the flint; she overturned the mountains from their roots.”

### 57. She softened their hardness and laid low their pride

She stretched out her hand to the flint because she sent the arm of her preaching against the hardness of the Gentiles.

Hence blessed Job, foreseeing that the history of his passion would be made known to the Gentiles, says: “Let these things be written with an iron stylus on a leaden tablet, or certainly let them be carved in flint” (Job 19:24). [Note: The editions read “or with a chisel.” We follow the manuscripts Anglicus, Normanus, and Gallicus. See what we observed in Book XIV, chapter 53, section 61.]

But whom do we understand by “mountains” in this passage except the powerful people of this world, who swell upward because of their earthly wealth? [Note: Bellovacensis, Laudunensis, Normanus, and others read *altum*, “high”; the editions read *in altum*, “on high.”] Of them the Psalmist says: “Touch the mountains, and they will smoke” (Psalm 143:5). But the mountains were overturned from their roots because, when holy Church preached, the highest powers of this world fell from their innermost thoughts into the worship of almighty God. [Note: 2 Laudunensis records the variant *transierunt*, “passed over.”] The roots of the mountains are the innermost thoughts of the proud.

The mountains fall from their roots because the powers of the world are thrown down from their deepest thoughts in order to worship God. A hidden thought is rightly signified by a root, because what is not seen within bursts forth into visibility outside.

Hence, in a good sense, the prophet says: “He will send out what has been saved from the house of Judah, and what remains will send its root downward and produce fruit upward” (Isaiah 37:31). [Note: Gemeticensis, Germanus, Corbeiensis Germanicus, and others read *et mittet*, “and will send.”] As though he were saying openly: Thought is born in the depths so that reward may be given in the heights.

Let it therefore say: “She stretched out her hand to the flint; she overturned the mountains from their roots,” because, when holy preaching attacked the hardness of the Gentiles, it utterly laid low the height of the proud.

But because she fills with heavenly gifts those whom she empties of earthly thoughts, and waters with heavenly streams those whom she drains of lowly concerns, the text immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Column 0070A] **VERSE 10.**—“In the rocks he cut out channels.”

### 58. In the stony hearts of the Gentiles God opened rivers of preaching

That is, in the hard hearts of the Gentiles he opened rivers of preaching, as the prophet also says concerning the watering of the barrenness of the Gentiles: “He made the desert into a pool of waters, and the waterless land into outlets of waters” (Psalm 106:35). [Note: Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanicus, and Normanus read *aquae*, “of water.”] And in the Gospel the Lord promises, saying: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

What was then heard as a promise we now see fulfilled. For behold, in the holy preachers—not sprung from Judea—streams of heavenly commandments flow abundantly from Gentile mouths throughout the whole Church spread across the world.

Because he opened channels in the rocks, a river of holy preaching also flowed from hard hearts. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Column 0070B] **IBID.**—“And his eye saw every precious thing.”

### 59. The world is vile to God, but the souls he chose are precious

It must be understood with the greatest care that each soul becomes more precious before the eyes of God in proportion as, through love of the truth, it is more contemptible in its own eyes.

Hence it is said to Saul: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17). As though he were saying openly: You were great to me because you were contemptible to yourself; but now, because you are great to yourself, you have become contemptible to me.

Hence the prophet also says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). Thus each person becomes more vile to God the more precious he is to himself, and more precious to God the more vile he is to himself, because “he regards the humble, but knows the proud from afar” (Psalm 137:6). [Old recension XXIII.]

“His eye therefore saw every precious thing.” In sacred Scripture, God’s seeing is sometimes used to mean choosing, as it is written in the Gospel: [Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus, Normanus, 1 Laudunensis, and Germanus read “is sometimes used for choosing” instead of “for rejecting.”] “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48)—that is, “I chose you while you were placed under the shadow of the Law.”

He saw the precious because he chose the humble: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27). He saw the precious when, by the illumination of his grace, he looked upon the human soul that had been wise in its own abasement.

Concerning this soul the prophet says: [Note: Germanus, two Laudunensis manuscripts, Normanus, and others read “the prophet says.”] “If you separate the precious from the vile, you will be like my mouth” (Jeremiah 15:19). The present world is vile to God, but the human soul is precious to him.

Whoever therefore separates the precious from the vile is called like the mouth of the Lord, because through him God utters his words: by speaking whatever he can, he tears the human soul away from love of the present world.

And because the teachers of the New Testament have been led to the point of probing even the hidden obscurities of allegories in the Old Testament, the text rightly continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Revised recension XXI]

[Column 0071A] **VERSE 11.**—“He also searched out the depths of the rivers and brought hidden things into the light.”

60. God has revealed to the sacred teachers the deep and hidden things of the Law and the Prophets. — What else, then, are the rivers named here except the sayings of the ancient Fathers? Who could sufficiently reckon how mighty a river burst from Moses’ breast when he established the Law; [Note: 1 Laudensis: “burst from Moses’ breast.”] how mighty a river flowed from David’s heart; how many streams of rivers poured forth from Solomon’s mouth and from the mouths of all the prophets? But Judaea retained the outward appearance of these rivers, preserving the surface of the letter while failing to know their depths. We, however, who, with the Lord’s coming, seek their inward spiritual meaning, search out their depths. This is said to be done by the Lord himself, because we are able to do it through his gift. Through us, therefore, who follow not the letter that kills but the spirit that gives life, the Lord searches the depths of the rivers and brings hidden things into the light, because spiritual exposition now illuminates the sayings of the Law, which a very obscure historical account had concealed.

Hence Truth, speaking in parables through the Gospel, also commanded the disciples, saying: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27). [Note: Corb., Germ., Beccensis, Uticensis, and others: “for things made manifest,” [Col. 0072D].] For the statements of those who explain them openly have now made the judgments of the ancient Fathers plainly visible to us. Hence the prophet Isaiah, contemplating the clear words of the holy Church’s exposition, no longer obscured by the darkness of allegories, exclaimed: “The place of rivers, streams very broad and open” (Isa. 33:21). The sayings of the Old Testament had been like narrow and enclosed streams, constraining the immense judgments of their knowledge within a most obscure gathering. But the teaching of the holy Church consists of broad and open streams, because its sayings are abundant for those who find them and clear for those who seek them.

He therefore says: “He searched the depths of the rivers and brought hidden things into the light.” For when he infused the spirit of understanding into his interpreters, he opened the ancient obscurities of the prophets. [Note: Germ. and Norm.: “of the prophets.”] And now the holy Church recognizes through the Spirit what the Synagogue had previously been wholly unable to understand through the letter. Hence, when Moses spoke with the people (Exod. 34:33), he veiled his face, signifying that the Jewish people would know the words of the Law but would in no way see the Law’s radiance. Hence Paul rightly says: “For to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their *eor eorum*” (2 Cor. 3:15). [The printed text reads *eor eorum*; the wording is evidently corrupt.]

But since the sayings of God cannot in any way be penetrated without his wisdom—for unless one has received his Spirit, one cannot know his words at all—the holy man adds words concerning the investigation of this same divine wisdom, saying:

## CHAPTER XL [Ancient XXIV, Revised XXII]

### VERSES 12–15

“But where is wisdom found, and where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly. The abyss says, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’ Refined gold shall not be given for it, nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.”

61. The place and price of God’s wisdom cannot be assigned. — It must first be noted that he set forth two questions and then answered both. [Note: Vindocensis: “two there.”] To the earlier question, “Where is wisdom found, and where is the place of understanding?” he replied in this verse: “The abyss says, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’” To the other statement, “Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly,” he supplied the later answer: “Refined gold shall not be given for it, nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.”

He answered both questions, therefore, but by enlarging upon what had been proposed rather than resolving it. When he was asking where wisdom was located and then replied below, “The abyss says, ‘It is not in me,’” he indicated not where it was but where it was not. Again, when he said that its price was unknown to man and then answered, “Refined gold shall not be given for it,” he showed not what its price was but what it was not.

It is clear to everyone that neither this human wisdom can be contained in a place nor purchased with riches. But the holy man, filled with mystical meanings, directs us toward other things to be understood, so that we may seek not created wisdom but the wisdom that creates. For unless we search out the secrets of allegories in these words, what follows would plainly deserve contempt if considered only according to the historical narrative. A little later he says: “Gold or glass shall not be compared with it.” Since, as we know, glass is far inferior and dissimilar to gold, why, after naming gold—a precious metal—does he also say, to wisdom’s immense praise, that glass is not equal to it? The very difficulty of the letter therefore compels us to attend to the mystical meanings of these words.

What wisdom, then, does the holy man contemplate except that of which the apostle Paul says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24)? Of this it is written through Solomon: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1); and of it the Psalmist says: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). Man does not know the price of this wisdom, because he finds nothing worthy of its valuation. [Note: 1 Laudensis: “and not know, but for that reason not know.”] Yet it is not said that the price of wisdom both exists and is unknown; rather, it is unknown because it is absent. This is a manner of speaking by which anyone caught in difficulties, when he finds no remedy or assistance, is accustomed to confess that he does not know what to do.

62. It is owed by the merit of no good work. — Not to know the price of this wisdom is to find no worthy work by which one might deserve to receive it. We give a price in order that we may possess in exchange the thing we desire. But what have we given so that we might deserve to receive this wisdom, which is Christ (Rom. 11:6)? We were redeemed by grace. For by living wickedly we gave only those works for which, if a just recompense had been preserved, we would have received not Christ but punishments.

But man deserved one thing by justice and received another by grace. [Note: Laudensis, Normannicus, and others have this more elegant wording, rather than the reading attested in the edition.] Let Paul testify what thorns of error had oppressed him before his mind received the seed of gratuitous truth: “I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13). Let him testify for what sort of people Christ deigned to die: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly at the appointed time” (Rom. 5:8). Since, therefore, when wisdom came we were found ungodly, what good work did we give by which we might deserve to receive that same wisdom?

Man does not know the price of this wisdom, because whoever is distinguished from brute animals by rational understanding recognizes that he was not saved by his own merits and acknowledges that he gave no good work by which he came to faith. To give a price for receiving wisdom is, as it were, to suppose that one can reach knowledge of God by the payment of one’s own action. [Note: Vindocensis: “to reach it through the reward of his action”; 2 Laud.: “to anticipate the reward.”]

63. Grace is given freely, not on the basis of merits. — He had recognized that this wisdom has no price who said: [Note: Laudensis: “Who first gave to him?”] “Who first gave to him, that he might be repaid?” (Rom. 11:35). Again it is written: [Note: Laudensis: “saved freely”; Vindocensis: “For by grace you have been saved.”] “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8). Again he speaks of himself, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). Because, through the inspiration of this grace, works of virtue are immediately generated in the heart, so that action may also follow from free choice, to which eternal recompense may respond after this life, he immediately adds: “And his grace toward me was not empty” (ibid. 15:10).

[Ancient XXV.] But there are some who boast that they are sound through their own powers and glory that they have been redeemed through their preceding merits. [Note: Vindocensis, Corb. Germanicus, Turonensis, and Normannicus read thus. The edition has “who save themselves”; Laudensis instead reads “because they know by their own powers,” etc.—an error of copyists who formed *quia nosse* from *quia sanos se*.] Their assertion is plainly self-contradictory, because while they claim both to be innocent and to be redeemed, they thereby empty the very name of redemption in themselves. Everyone who is redeemed is undoubtedly freed from some captivity. How, then, has such a person been redeemed if he was not previously captive under guilt?

It is therefore clear that anyone who thinks such things is greatly foolish. Heavenly grace does not find human merit in order to come, but creates it after it has come. God comes even to an unworthy mind and, by coming, makes it worthy of himself; and he creates in it the merit that he will reward, although he had found in it only what he could punish.

[Ret. XXIII.] 64. An example of gratuitous predestination in the thief who obtained salvation. — In the midst of these matters, it is pleasing to turn the eyes of the mind toward that thief who climbed from the devil’s throat to the cross, and from the cross to paradise. [Note: The editors supplied “the devil’s,” found in Vindocensis and 2 Laudensis; Uticensis had over the words “from the throat” the reading “from judgment.”] Let us consider what sort of man he came to the gallows as, and what sort he departed from the gallows as.

He came guilty of a brother’s blood; he came bloodstained, but inward grace changed him on the cross. The man who had inflicted death on his brother proclaimed the life of the dying Lord, saying: “Remember me, [Note: “Lord” is absent from most witnesses and likewise below.] Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). [Note: Laudensis and Bellovacensis: “he cried out on the cross.”]

Nails had bound his hands and feet to the cross, and nothing in him remained free from punishment except his heart and tongue. Inspired by God, he offered him everything that he found free within himself, so that, in accordance with what is written, “he might believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

The Apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful, saying: “But now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity” (1 Cor. 13:13). Filled suddenly with grace, the thief both received all of them and preserved them on the cross. He had faith, for he believed that the Lord would reign, though he saw him dying alongside him. He had hope, for he asked for entrance into his kingdom, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). He also held charity vigorously in his death, for he rebuked his fellow thief, dying for a similar crime and in his wickedness, and proclaimed to him the life he himself had come to know, saying: [Note: The Vulgate reads “the life which he had not known”; the negation is absent from Corb. Germ., Vindocensis, Bellovacensis, Laudensis, Normannicus, and other manuscripts.] “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing evil” (ibid. 23:40–41). [Note: Bellovacensis: “he did nothing wrong.”]

He who came to the cross as such a man through guilt—behold what sort of man he departed from the cross through grace. He confessed the Lord whom he saw dying beside him in human weakness, at the very time when the apostles were denying the one whom they had seen performing miracles by divine power. [Note: Gemetensis and others: “God.”]

[Ancient XXVI.] 65. The error of those who assert that man is saved by his own powers. — But those who assert that man is saved by his own powers suppose that this same confession by the man came from human strength itself. If that were so, the Psalmist would not say in praise of God: “Confession and magnificence are his work” (Ps. 110:3). We therefore receive the ability to confess rightly from the one from whom we also receive the ability to perform great things. [Note: In Germ., Corb. Germ., and the editions: “and great things are given to be done.” The English and certain other manuscripts read “great things is given.”]

Since, therefore, we gave no good work by which we might deserve to receive this wisdom, it is rightly said: “Man does not know its price.” For the more deeply anyone who now uses reason despises himself under the understanding of this wisdom, the more truly he recognizes its inward realities, so that he sees himself as unworthy to have reached this wisdom, through which he is freely made worthy. Concerning it, the text rightly adds:

## CHAPTER XLI [Revised XXIV]

### VERSE 13

“Nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly.”

66. Whoever is nourished by the pleasures of this life is separated from understanding eternal wisdom. — What is signified here by the name “land” except the human soul? Of it the Psalmist says: “My soul is like land without water to you” (Ps. 142:6). This wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because whoever is still nourished by the pleasures of this life is separated from understanding eternal wisdom.

For if he truly were wise, expelled from inward joys he would mourn, in the blindness of his exile, over the place into which he had fallen. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18), because the more a person begins to know what he has lost, the more he begins to mourn the sentence of his corruption that he has encountered.

He considers from where and to where he has fallen: from the joys of paradise to the hardships of the present life; from the fellowship of angels to the cares of necessities. He weighs how many dangers now beset him who previously scorned standing without danger. He mourns the exile he endures under condemnation and longs for the state of heavenly glory, which he could securely enjoy if he had not wished to sin.

Considering this well, the Psalmist says: “I said in my fear: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Ps. 30:23). Contemplating the inward joys of the vision of God and the fellowship of the angels who persevere, he turned his eyes downward and saw where he lay—he who had been created so that he might have stood in heavenly places. He considered where he was and groaned over where he ought to have been; he grieved that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes, because, in comparison with the inner light, he had felt more heavily the darkness of his exile, which he endured.

[Ancient XXVII.] Hence he admits no consolation of any grace to his soul from the present life, saying: “I refused to let my soul be comforted” (Ps. 76:3). [Note: Laudensis and Bellovacensis: “no consolation of any grace.”]

For the rich of this world, when afflicted by weariness of mind, often look upon the temporal goods they have received and soothe their sadness. When they feel themselves touched by some sorrow, they look at their horses, contemplate their vessels of gold and silver, and travel around their estates. When they willingly draw their eyes through these temporal things, they overcome the grief that has arisen in the soul. Hence Truth says to them in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation here” (Luke 6:24).

But the holy man, who mourns because he has fallen from eternal joys, does not accept consolation from temporal things, saying: “I refused to let my soul be comforted.” As if he said openly: “Since I do not mourn the loss of temporal things, I cannot at all be comforted by an abundance of temporal things.”

And as though we who heard this might say to him, “What, then, do you seek, since you refuse to be comforted by the things of the world?” he immediately adds: “I remembered God, and I was delighted” (Ps. 76:4). As if he said openly: “Neither the abundance of earthly things refreshes me, nor does their loss distress me; but the memory alone of my Creator, whom I am not yet able to see, delights me.” This, then, is the bitterness of wisdom: while those who are raised on high by hope do not lay their souls down in any joys here below.

Hence it is written: “The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy” (Eccl. 7:5). Hence James says: “Be miserable, mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (Jas. 4:9). Hence Truth itself bears witness, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

Wisdom, therefore, cannot be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because they are more truly foolish the more they rejoice in small things while losing greater ones. Hence Peter rebukes the same folly of the wicked, saying: “Esteeming the delights of the day to be pleasure, [Note: Beccensis and Uticensis give a double reading: “pleasure” and “will.”] [they are] stains and blemishes of defilement” (2 Pet. 2:13). [Note: Germ.: “considering the will of God, delights of defilement”; Corb. Germ.: “considering the will of the day, delights of defilement”; Bellovacensis: “offenses of defilement,” according to the Greek text, “defilements.”]

Hence Solomon says: “I counted laughter error, and I said of joy: Why are you deceived in vain?” (Eccl. 2:2). Let the holy man therefore say of wisdom: “Nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly,” because those who live pleasantly in this world are still so foolish that they do not even know from what they have fallen. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XLII [Revised XXV]

### VERSE 14

“The abyss says, ‘It is not in me.’”

[Col. 0076D] 67. Those who think according to the flesh and according to the world are alienated from God’s wisdom. — What else does he call the abyss here except the hearts of men? They are fluid through their fall and dark through the obscurity of duplicity. This abyss professes that wisdom is not in it, because when an unrighteous mind desires to be wise according to the flesh, it shows itself foolish with respect to spiritual things.

For, as Paul testifies, “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19). Each person becomes inwardly more foolish the more he strives to appear outwardly wise. Of this abyss John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might deceive the nations no longer, until the thousand years were completed” (Rev. 20:1–3).

By the number one thousand he signified not a quantity of time but the totality in which the Church reigns. The ancient serpent, bound with a chain, is cast into the abyss because, bound away from the hearts of the good and confined within the minds of the reprobate, he exercises a more savage dominion over them. A little later he is also described as being brought up from the well of the abyss, because from the hearts of the wicked, where he now rages secretly, he will then, having received power against the Church, burst forth into open persecution. [Note: Normannicus: “because he is banished.” All printed editions, with other manuscripts, read “bound again.”] This abyss, therefore, in which the devil is now kept hidden, says that wisdom is not in it, because through wicked deeds it shows itself alien to true wisdom.

For when a person conceals malice in his heart but displays flatteries with his mouth; when he clouds his thoughts with duplicity; when he avoids words of purity as though they were foolishness; when he shuns the straightforward paths of innocence; the abyss, as it were, refuses to possess the wisdom of God. [Note: Another reading, with Germ. and Corb. Germ.: “while [he avoids] the simple paths of innocence.”]

And because minds devoted to this world are disturbed by the cares and anxieties of the present life, and therefore can in no way enjoy the tranquility of this wisdom, the text rightly adds:

## CHAPTER XLIII

### THE SAME PASSAGE

“And the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’”

68. Those distracted by earthly cares do not enjoy it. — What else is signified by the name “sea” except the bitter restlessness of worldly minds? [Note: 2 Laudensis: “the bitterness of minds is signified.”] As they attack one another with mutual hostilities, they collide like opposing waves. The life of worldly people is rightly called a sea, because, stirred by the stormy movements of their actions, it is separated from the repose and stability of inward wisdom.

In contrast, the prophet rightly says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). The spirit flees earthly minds all the farther because it finds no rest among them. Hence the Psalmist says of certain people: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. 13:3).

From this destruction of disturbance the Lord calls us back, saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29). What is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is quieter here than to desire nothing of this world?

[Ancient XXVIII.] Hence the Israelite people received the observance of the Sabbath as a gift (Exod. 16:29); hence, in contrast, Egypt was struck by a multitude of flies (Exod. 8:21). The people who follow God receive the Sabbath—that is, rest of mind—so that they are not wearied in this life by any appetite for carnal desires. Egypt, however, which bears the figure of this world, is struck by flies. A fly is an exceedingly insolent and restless creature. What else, then, is signified by it except the insolent cares of carnal desires?

Hence it is said elsewhere: “Dead flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccl. 10:1), because superfluous thoughts, which are continually both arising and fading in a mind that thinks carnally, destroy the sweetness with which each person is inwardly anointed through the Spirit. [Note: 2 Laudensis: “which each person who is anointed possesses”; these thoughts “destroy” it.] They do not permit him to enjoy its integrity.

Egypt, therefore, is struck by flies because the hearts of those who love earthly life, while being struck by the restlessness of their desires, [Note: *while* is absent from Normannicus, Germ., 2 Laudensis, and Corb. Germ.] are pressed downward by crowds of carnal thoughts, so that they are not lifted toward the desire for inward rest. Thus, when Truth comes to the heart by a wondrous work of mercy, it first drives from it the heat of carnal thoughts and afterward arranges within it the gifts of virtue.

The sacred Gospel history indicates this well. When the Lord was summoned and led to raise the ruler’s daughter, it immediately adds: “When the crowd had been put outside, he entered, took her by the hand, and the girl arose” (Matt. 9:25). The crowd is therefore cast out so that the girl may be raised, because unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the heart’s inner chambers, the soul lying dead within does not rise again. For while it scatters itself through countless thoughts of earthly desires, it cannot collect itself at all for self-consideration.

Knowing, therefore, that wisdom cannot dwell amid these waves of unrest, he says: “And the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’” No one fully receives it except one who strives to withdraw from every fluctuation of carnal activity.
