Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Write wisdom in a time of leisure, and whoever is less occupied with activity will receive it” (Ecclus. 38:25). And again: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. 55:11). [Note: Normannicus and others: “for I am the Lord.”]

[Ancient XXIX.] 69. Unless they serve them without earthly devotion. — But what of the fact that we know many of the ancient Fathers both to have held this wisdom vigorously within and to have regularly administered worldly cares outwardly (Gen. 42:43, etc.)? Shall we say that Joseph was deprived of the perception of this wisdom, although, when famine came, he undertook the administration of all Egypt and not only supplied food to the Egyptians but also preserved the lives of foreigners who came there through the skill of his service? Or was Daniel alien to this wisdom, who, having been made chief of the magistrates in Babylonia by the Chaldean king, was occupied with all the greater cares because he was preferred to everyone in a higher dignity (Dan. 2:48)?

Since it is clear that even good people are often entangled in earthly cares without earthly devotion, we plainly recognize that sometimes citizens of Jerusalem pay forced labor to Babylon, just as citizens of Babylon often pay forced labor to Jerusalem. For some preach the word of life solely for the display of wisdom and provide the assistance of almsgiving out of an appetite for empty glory. What they do appears to belong to Jerusalem, but they are nevertheless citizens of Babylon.

70. One should desire to be free for God alone and serve external cares according to God’s will. — It therefore sometimes happens that those who love only the heavenly homeland seem subject to the cares of their earthly homeland. Yet their service is generally distinguished from the works of the wicked in action, and sometimes before the heavenly Judge in thought alone.

Filled with heavenly wisdom, they discern how they ought to be free inwardly for one thing and occupied outwardly with another: [Note: Turonensis and Normannicus read: “and to perform one thing outwardly and be free for another inwardly.”] if, perhaps through God’s hidden ordinance, some concern of this world is imposed upon them against their desire, they yield to the God whom they love and, because of their love, desire inwardly only his vision; but because of fear of him, they humbly carry out the external task imposed upon them, [Note: Two manuscripts of Ebroicensis and Pratensis: “let them perform it.”] so that they desire to be free for God through the grace of love and, in turn, fulfill the cares imposed upon them through the condition of servitude.

When external occupations resound around them, inwardly they retain the most peaceful rest of love. [Note: Turonensis, Bellovacensis, Laudensis, Vindocensis, Normannicus, and others read “and the tumult of occupations resounding outwardly”; Germ. reads “and the occupation resounding outwardly”; the printed editions read “and the tumult of occupation resounding outwardly.”] The reason presiding within, like a judge, manages the tumult of occupations resounding outwardly and, with tranquil moderation, orders the matters around it that are less tranquil. For just as the vigor of the mind presides over the restraint of the movements of the flesh, so the love of rest often governs well the tumults of occupation imposed upon it. External cares, if they are not desired with perverse love, can be administered by an orderly rather than confused mind.

Holy men do not desire these cares at all; rather, they grieve that they have been imposed upon them by a hidden order. Although they flee them through a better intention, they nevertheless bear them through a submissive mind. If permitted, they hasten above all to avoid them; but, fearing God’s hidden dispensations, they hold what they flee and perform what they avoid.

They enter into their own hearts and consult there what God’s hidden will desires. Recognizing that they must be subject to the highest ordinances, they bow the neck of their hearts beneath the yoke of divine dispensation. Whoever is such a person, whatever tumult may be stirring outwardly, it never reaches his inward parts. Thus one thing is held inwardly as a desire and another outwardly as a duty; and this wisdom fills tranquil rather than turbulent and confused hearts.

The text therefore rightly says of it: “The abyss says, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’” As if it said openly: The disturbed minds of worldly people cry out by this very fact—that they are not at peace—that they are far separated from true wisdom.

But because this wisdom of God, remaining with the Father before the ages, was to be incarnated at the end of the ages, so that, for the redemption of the human race, he might send neither holy angels nor righteous men but come himself in the manifestation of his vision, the text rightly adds:

## CHAPTER XLIV [Revised XXVI]

### VERSE 15

“Refined gold shall not be given for it.”

[Col. 0080B] 71. Angels are free from every stain of the world, but not human beings. — What else is signified by refined gold except the holy angels? They are rightly called both gold and refined gold: gold because they shine with the radiance of righteousness; refined gold because they have never had any contamination of guilt.

Righteous human beings, however, as long as they live mortally in this corruptible flesh, can indeed be gold, but they cannot at all be refined gold, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15). [Note: The column numbering advances to 591 in the source.] For although in this life they shine with great radiance of righteousness, they are nevertheless not entirely free from the filth of sins, as the apostle John bears witness, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). James likewise affirms, saying: “For in many things we all offend” (Jas. 3:2). The prophet also prays: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

Those are called refined gold who, remaining in the innocence in which they were created, shine with the radiance of righteousness and are stained by no, not even the smallest, filth of guilt.

[Ancient XXX.] 72. Nevertheless, none of the angels was sent or sufficient to redeem man. — But because no angel was to be sent as redeemer of the human race in place of this wisdom, lest anyone place hope in those angels whom we have often learned appeared to assist human beings, it is said: “Refined gold shall not be given for it.” As if it said openly: Wisdom will be manifested by itself, so that the human race may be redeemed from guilt. No angel is sent in its place, because it is necessary that the creature be liberated by the Creator.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36). [Note: 2 Laudensis: “but a man in the Spirit”; Gemetensis and others have “full” in place of “filled”; “holy” is absent.] But the holy man, filled with the Spirit of this same wisdom, foresaw that some in Judaea would not be lacking who would place their hope in the lawgiver and think Moses the author of their salvation, just as they say while cursing a man who had been healed: “You be his disciple; we are disciples of Moses” (John 9:28). [Note: “healed” is absent in Pratensis, Beccensis, and Uticensis. In 2 Laudensis, *healed* is accompanied by “the blind man,” as an explanatory addition.]

Hence the text appropriately continues:

## CHAPTER XLV

### THE SAME PASSAGE

“Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.”

73. The madness of those who think Moses or any saint the author of their salvation. — Since divine utterances are often signified by silver, the writers of those utterances may also be understood by the word “silver”—those whose lives shone among human crowds with the light of virtues. But because the Law could point out sins, not remove them, neither any of the ancient Fathers nor Moses the lawgiver became the redeemer of the human race.

Silver, therefore, is not weighed in exchange for this wisdom, because however holy they could be, in comparison with the only-begotten Son of God they are reckoned to have no merit. They would never have been holy unless they had recognized themselves as servants of this wisdom. They were sent for this purpose: by preaching, to prepare a way for this wisdom in human hearts, not to take its place, but through it to govern the peoples entrusted to them.

Because it was certain that, as the failing age advanced, the infirmities of the world would increase, it was arranged that the eternal wisdom of God would come at the end of the ages by itself to this great and exceedingly sick patient—that is, to the human race, lying languid throughout the world—so that, after preachers had first been sent as certain visitors, the power of the physician would afterward come all the greater as the illness of the patient had grown. [Note: In the manuscripts of Bellovacensis, Corb. Germanicus, Germ., Laudensis, Normannicus, and others, as well as in the old edition, this is the reading. Germ. and later editions read “it would become,” but incorrectly. It could not properly be said that the physicians of God would become greater in power, since that power is infinite and admits neither greater nor lesser.]

Because no one is sent in his place to save us, it is rightly said: “Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it,” since however brightly the life of righteous preachers may shine with the light of holiness, it does not substitute for us the coming of heavenly wisdom through its own presence.

But there were many gentiles who, devoted to the disciplines of the world’s wise men, observed what was honorable among human beings and believed that they would be saved by having preserved that honor; they no longer sought the Mediator between God and human beings, since they possessed what they regarded as a sufficient teaching of philosophers. In their contempt the text immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XLVI [Revised XXVII]

### VERSE 16

“It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India.”

[Col. 0081D] **74. How far the wisdom of God surpasses the philosophy of counterfeit verbal brilliance.**—What else is signified by Ethiopia, which sends forth a black people, than this world, in which human life is generated darkened by sin? The dyed colors of Ethiopia are the wise men of this world. Although through unbelief, and often through their conduct, they are foul, nevertheless in the eyes of men they are made up with the color of a superimposed respectability.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Turon. reads *fuscantur* (“are darkened”). 2 Laud. has both *fuscantur* and *fucantur*. Germ. has *fuscantur*, *fuscatio* (“darkening”); the same occurs several times below.]

But the coeternal wisdom of God is not compared with the dyed colors of Ethiopia, because whoever truly understands it recognizes how far he stands from those men whom the world honors as wise. The very words of its commandments differ from the wise men of this world. While they devote themselves to eloquence, their sayings appear outwardly beautiful, as though adorned with the beauty and coloring of dye; and because they lack the power of the realities themselves, they falsely represent themselves, through verbal compositions as though through superimposed colors, as something other than they are.

By contrast, the teaching and preaching of wisdom is beautiful and conspicuous in pure truth.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Turon. reads: “and conspicuous in purity.”]

It does not deceitfully present one thing outwardly while reserving another inwardly. Nor does it seek to appear beautiful in its utterances through verbal brilliance, but through the integrity of truth. In its commandments, therefore, the wisdom of God is not compared with the dyed colors of Ethiopia, because, lacking the counterfeit ornaments of eloquence, it pleases like a garment without dye.

Paul had rightly despised this counterfeit coloring of dye when he said: “The things which we speak are not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit” (1 Cor. II, 13). He preferred to display this wisdom through the single purity of truth, rather than to counterfeit it through the coloring of eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Norm. reads *fuscare* (“to darken/counterfeit”).]

It continues:

## CHAPTER XLVII

[Col. 0082C]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—Nor with the most precious sardonyx stone, or sapphire.**

**75. No human being or angel is to be compared with Christ.**—Who does not know that sardonyx and sapphire are precious stones? And since many other stones are precious, which far surpass these in the estimation of their size, why is sapphire or sardonyx specifically called precious, when each of these stones is extremely cheap in comparison with other stones? Unless it is so that, when we recognize that the stones described as precious are not precious, we may seek something else in their meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] We add *non* (“not”), from the manuscripts Germ., Corb., Norm., Laud., and others. The addition of the negation is confirmed by the entire context, in which Saint Gregory’s purpose is to show that sardonyx and sapphire are not precious stones but, as he himself says, very cheap when compared with other precious stones. His meaning is made clear by these words: “when we recognize that sardonyx and sapphire are not precious.” Nevertheless, the negation is absent from all editions except the Paris edition of 1495 and perhaps some older ones.]

Sardonyx bears the likeness of red earth, whereas sapphire has an airy appearance.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] In 2 Laud., Germ., Corb., Germ., and others, the usual reading is *aeriam* (“airy”), and so below.]

Thus, by red earth in sardonyx human beings can be signified, while in sapphire, through its airy appearance, angels can be signified.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] Turon. reads: “in sapphire, which has the appearance of air, the vision of an angel can be signified.”]

Since the sardonyx stone has the appearance of red earth, it appropriately signifies a human being, because Adam, who was created first, is called “red earth” in the Latin language. What, then, does it mean that this wisdom is not compared with sardonyx or sapphire, except that he who is the power and wisdom of God—the mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus as man—surpasses all things by such greatness that neither the first human beings on earth nor the angels in heaven can be compared with him? Hence the Psalmist says: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 7).

**[Vet. XXXI.] 76. How the celibate apostles surpass the married fathers of the Old Testament.**—The fathers of the Old Testament can be expressed through the sardonyx stone, and the preachers of the New Testament through sapphire. Although the former possessed a life of great righteousness, they nevertheless served carnal propagation. Since it is evident that they engaged in certain earthly things, they are appropriately signified by the sardonyx stone, which, as we said above, bears the appearance of red earth.

Through sapphire, however, which is of an ethereal color, we appropriately understand the preachers of the New Testament, who, setting aside the desires of carnal procreation, pursued heavenly things alone. Hence the prophet, seeing the holy apostles transcend all the desires of the flesh through spiritual fervor, exclaimed in wonder: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX, 8). It is as though he plainly said: We walk upon the earth, because we are still entangled in marriages and devote the work of the flesh to the propagation of offspring; but these do not walk upon the earth—they fly like clouds, because, while they desire heavenly things, they touch nothing of earthly desires.

He therefore says that the wisdom of God is not compared with the stone sardonyx or sapphire, as though he were plainly indicating: No one who is seen as a human being among human beings—not among the ancient fathers nor among the new—can be equal to him, because from his divinity he possesses what no one in his humanity possesses as his equal.

Hence it is further said:

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**Verse 17.—Gold or glass shall not be compared with it.**

**77. The blessed will shine in heaven like gold and will be translucent like glass.**—Who, possessing sound understanding, would deign to interpret this according to the literal sense? Glass, as we said above, is far cheaper than gold; and after it has been said that gold is not equal to this wisdom, the statement is added, as though by increasing the comparison, that even glass cannot be equal to it. But the letter itself, failing to yield a historical meaning, sends us to investigate the mystery of the allegory.

We know that the metal gold shines with greater brilliance than all other metals.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] We have restored this from two Laud., Germ., Norm., and others. Previously it read: “But the nature of glass is that, pure in external appearance, it shines inwardly through transparency.”]

The nature of glass, however, is that what is seen externally shines inwardly with pure transparency. In another metal, whatever is contained within is hidden; in glass, whatever liquid is held inside is displayed outwardly in the same condition, and, so to speak, every liquid enclosed in a glass vessel is visible.

What else, then, do we understand by gold or glass except that heavenly homeland, that society of blessed citizens whose hearts shine toward one another in brightness and are mutually transparent in purity? John had seen this in the Apocalypse when he said: “The structure of its wall was of jasper; and the city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. XXI, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0083D] Thus the corrected edition reads; Germ., Gemet., Prat., 2 Laud., and many other manuscripts have: “like pure gold,” etc. Corb. and Germ. have: “like pure gold,” etc. The older editions read: “like pure gold,” etc.]

Because all the saints will shine there with the supreme brightness of blessedness, it is said to be “constructed of gold.”

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Vindoc. reads *constructa* (“constructed”). 2 Laud., Gemet., and Bartholomew’s edition of the year 14[.....]4 have *instructura auro* (“furnished with gold”).]

**78. In their faces the inmost movements of their souls will be seen.**—And because their brightness will be mutually visible in one another’s hearts, and when each person’s face is observed his conscience will at the same time be penetrated, this is why the gold is said to be like pure glass.

[Col. 0084B] There, the bodily substance of the limbs will not hide each person’s mind from the eyes of another; rather, the soul will be manifest. The harmony of the body itself will also be visible to bodily eyes, and thus each person will then be perceptible to another as he is now unable to be perceptible even to himself.

[**Vet. XXXII.**] But now, as long as we are in this life, our hearts cannot be seen by one person within another. They are enclosed not in glass vessels but in vessels of clay. The Prophet feared to cling to this clay through the passion of his mind when he said: “Deliver me from the clay, that I may not cling to it” (Ps. LXVIII, 15).

[Col. 0084C]

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Turon. reads *habitaculum corporeum* (“bodily dwelling”).]

Paul calls this dwelling of bodies an earthly house, saying: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. V, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Germ. reads: “if our earthly house of habitation”; 2 Laud. reads: “of our earthly habitation.”]

As long, therefore, as we live in this earthly house, we cannot in any way penetrate the wall of our corruption with the eyes of the mind, nor can we see hidden things in others. Hence the holy Church, desiring to see the form of her Bridegroom in his divinity but unable to do so—for the humanity he assumed concealed from her eyes the form of his eternity, which she longed to behold—says mournfully in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song II, 9).

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Vindoc. reads: “Hence the bride, desiring to see the Lord in his divinity …”]

As though she were plainly saying: I already desire to see him in the form of his divinity, but I am still excluded from his vision by the wall of the flesh he assumed. As long, therefore, as we live in this corruptible flesh, we do not see one another’s thoughts.

Hence again Paul says: “Who among human beings knows the things of a human being, except the spirit of the human being which is in him?” (1 Cor. II, 11). And again: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. IV, 5).

That city, therefore, which makes the hearts of its individual citizens mutually manifest is said to be like pure glass made of gold, so that it may be signified as bright like gold and transparent like glass.

**79. In what way the saints are like God and unlike him.**—Although all the saints there shine with such brightness and are so transparent, they nevertheless cannot be equal to that wisdom from whose image they possess all that they are. It is therefore rightly said: “Gold or glass shall not be compared with it.”

For all the saints reach those eternal joys so that they may be like God, as it is written: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III, 2). Yet it is written: “Lord God of hosts, who is like you?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 9). And again: “Who shall be like God among the sons of God?”

How, then, are they like him, and how are they not like him? They will be like this wisdom according to its image, yet they will not be like it according to equality. By contemplating the eternity of God, they become eternal; and while they receive the gift of his vision, through the reception of blessedness they imitate what they see. Thus they are like him because they become blessed; yet they are not like the Creator, because they are creatures. They possess a certain likeness to God because they have no end; yet they do not possess the equality of the uncircumscribed one, because they are circumscribed.

Let it therefore rightly be said: “Gold or glass shall not be compared with it,” because however greatly the saints may shine in brightness and transparency, it is one thing for human beings to be wise in God and another thing for a human being to be the wisdom of God.

That wisdom was truly recognized by the one who did not presume to compare any of the saints with the mediator between God and human beings. Hence it is further said:

## CHAPTER XLIX [Vet. XXXIII]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—Nor shall lofty and eminent vessels of gold be exchanged for it.**

**80. All the saints must be passed beyond in order to arrive at Christ, God and man.**—Elijah was a lofty vessel of gold; Jeremiah was a lofty vessel of gold; the earlier fathers were lofty and eminent vessels of gold. But this wisdom of God appeared in the flesh in order to redeem us from a carnal way of life. Whoever did not truly recognize it thought that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, was one of the prophets, although the eyes of the elect held him by faith as God when they saw him as man.

Hence he says to his holy disciples: “Who do human beings say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI, 13).

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Germ. and 1 Laud. read: “Who do human beings say that he is?”]

When they immediately replied, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah,”

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Most copies read: “others, however, Elijah.”]

“and others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets” (ibid., 14), he then asked them about their own judgment: “But who do you say that I am?” (ibid., 15). Peter immediately answered in the voice of the whole Church: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16).

Since, according to Paul’s words, we know Christ to be “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I, 18, 30), Peter did not wish to exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this wisdom, because he understood it to be nothing other than what it was.

John was, as has been said, a great vessel of gold; Elijah or Jeremiah was a great vessel of gold. But whoever believed that any one of them was the same God exchanged a lofty and eminent vessel of gold for wisdom. The Church, however, does not exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this wisdom, because she believes Christ the Son of God to be not one of the prophets but the Lord of the prophets.

Seeing that this wisdom itself had come to her, she did not wish to fix herself in those golden vessels but strove to pass beyond them with the firmest faith. Hence she says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” A little while after I had passed beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song III, 3–4).

For whom do we understand by the watchmen who guard the city except the earlier fathers or prophets, who strove to keep watch for our protection through the voice of holy preaching? But when the Church was seeking her Redeemer, she did not wish to place her hope in those ancient preachers. She says: “A little while after I had passed beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves” (ibid., III, 4). She could not have found him if she had not wished to pass beyond them.

The unbelievers had fixed themselves upon these watchmen, believing Christ the Son of God to be one or another of them. Therefore, through Peter’s voice and faith, the holy Church passed beyond the watchmen she had found; she refused to believe the Lord of the prophets to be merely one of the prophets.

Let it therefore be said: “Nor shall lofty and eminent vessels of gold be exchanged for it,” because each of the elect both venerates the life of the saints for its sublimity and yet does not accept them in error.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] Norm. reads: “and yet does not look up to them.” Vindoc. reads: “and yet does not suspect them.”]

For those whom they know to be merely human beings they do not at all compare with the God-man.

Hence it is further said:

## CHAPTER L

**Verse 18.—Nor shall they be mentioned in comparison with it.**

**81. All the holy and righteous citizens of heaven are so through participation in divine wisdom, not through comparison with it.**—All the elect of the heavenly homeland are indeed holy and righteous, but through participation in wisdom, not through comparison with it. What are human beings when compared with God?

Wisdom is called light, and the servants of wisdom are also accustomed to be called light. But wisdom is illuminating light, while they are illuminated light, as it is written: “He was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9). To them, however, it is said only: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14).

Wisdom is also righteousness, and the servants of wisdom are likewise called righteousness. But wisdom is justifying righteousness, whereas they are justified righteousness. Of God, who is wisdom, it is said: “So that he himself may be just and the one who justifies” (Rom. III, 26). They, however, say: “So that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. V, 21).

[Col. 0087A] Illuminating light must therefore be honored in one way, illuminated light in another; justifying righteousness in one way, justified righteousness in another.

[**Vet. XXXIV.**] Wisdom both is and is wise; it does not have being as one thing and being wise as another. The servants of wisdom, however, can indeed be wise, yet being wise is not identical with their being; for they can exist without being wise.

Wisdom has life, but it does not have one thing and then another thing as its being, since for it being and living are the same. But the servants of wisdom, when they possess life, are one thing and possess another, since for them being and living are not the same; for they can exist in some respect without living.

Their being is one thing and their living another, because in the first parent they received essence at the beginning and life subsequently. First, the human being was made from earth; afterward, as it is written, “He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. II, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Another reading: “They possessed being at the beginning.”]

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Germ., 2 Laud., Corb. Germ., Beccens., and others add: “and afterward it is written: ‘He breathed into his face … and he became,’” etc.]

Wisdom, however, possesses essence and life, but it itself is what it possesses. Therefore it lives immutably, because it lives essentially, not accidentally. It alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, truly is; compared with its essence, our being is non-being.

If we are joined to it, we exist, live, and possess wisdom; if we are compared with it, we neither possess wisdom nor live nor exist at all.

**82. The more the saints know God, the more worthless they regard themselves.**—This is why all the saints, when they advance in the vision of God, recognize themselves as nothing the more they behold the inner things of the divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Laud. reads *in terra* (“on earth”); Corb. Germ. reads *aeterna* (“eternal things”).]

Nowhere, indeed, do we read that Abraham professed himself to be “dust and ashes” except when he was granted a conversation with God. For he says: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27). He might perhaps have believed himself to be something if he had not perceived the true essence which is above him. But when he was raised above himself to contemplate the immutable one, filled with such power of contemplation, as he saw him he saw himself to be nothing but dust.

Hence the Prophet, filled with the same wisdom, also exclaims: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. CII, 15). Then, contemplating the immutability of that same essence, he says: “All things will grow old like a garment, and you will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 27–28).

[Note: [Col. 0087D] The editions read *Omnes . . . veterascent . . . mutabis ea* (“All [persons] will grow old … you will change them”); Corb. Germ. reads *omnia veterascent . . . mutabis eos* (“all things will grow old … you will change them”).]

To Moses it is said: “I am who I am”; and: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14–15). For he alone truly is who alone remains immutable. Whatever is now one way and now another is, in a certain respect, non-being, because it cannot remain in its own state. In some way it moves toward non-being, since from what it was it is continually led toward something else through the moments of time.

Therefore, if we are to be something through participation in that essence, let us recognize ourselves, because we are almost nothing. It is rightly said, then: “Nor shall they be mentioned in comparison with it,” because the lofty and eminent vessels of gold, which are worthy of our veneration through their participation in wisdom, are not even worthy of mention when compared with wisdom.

Because this wisdom is secretly infused into human hearts, as it is also said of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John III, 8), it is therefore added:

## CHAPTER LI

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—For wisdom is drawn from hidden places.**

**83. The wisdom of God revealed from hidden places. The Church, when open enemies were lacking, began to be tested by her own members.**—Wisdom is drawn from hidden places because, since it is invisible, it is found only invisibly. It is rightly also said to be drawn, because just as we draw in breath so that the body may live, so the spirit is led from the innermost depths of wisdom so that the soul may endure unto life. Hence the Psalmist says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII, 131).

This wisdom, having assumed human flesh together with a rational soul, appeared openly from the hidden depths. Since this world could not see its invisible creator, when it saw him as a visible human being it also recognized him as invisible God.

The proud Gentile world was turned from the darkness of its unbelief; faith grew when signs and wonders were displayed; and as faith spread, the summit of the holy Church shone forth in the veneration of all. But when open adversaries were lacking, she began to be tested by her own members. For many heresies also arose within her and prepared wars of harsh conflict against her. She must be exercised through labor in the present time, since she is destined for reward in the age to come.

As a result, some appeared within her who said that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, was a mere human being created by God but deified by grace. They attributed to him only as much holiness as they recognized in the other saints, his servants. Blessed Job, inspired by the spirit of prophecy, refuted them by the definition of his judgment, saying:

## CHAPTER LII [Vet. XXXV]

**Verse 19.—Ethiopian topaz shall not be compared with it.**

[Col. 0088D]

**84. Those who teach that Christ, as a mere human being, is like the other saints are refuted.**—What else do we understand by Ethiopia except the present world? By the blackness of its color it signifies the sinful people, foul with their merits.

At times, however, the name Ethiopia is used particularly to signify the Gentiles, previously black with the sins of unbelief. When the Lord came, the prophet Habakkuk saw Ethiopia terrified with fear and said: “The tents of Ethiopia tremble, the tents of the land of Midian” (Hab. III, 7).

The prophet David also, seeing that the Lord would come to redeem Judea, but that the Gentiles would believe first and Judea would follow afterward, as it is written, “until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25), says: “Ethiopia shall offer its hands to God in advance” (Ps. LVII, 32). That is, before Judea believes, the Gentiles, black with sins, offer themselves to almighty God for salvation.

Topaz is a precious stone; and because in Greek *pan* (πᾶν) means “all,” it is called *topazium*, as though *topantium*, because it shines with every color.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] 1 Laud., Germ., and Corb. Germ. have a form resembling *topandium*. 2 Laud. has a form resembling *topanzium*.]

When the Gentiles were converted and believed in God, many among them were enriched by the gift of his Spirit, so that they shone, as it were, with many colors—that is, with many virtues. But lest anyone become proud of the virtues he has received, the holy man now says: “Ethiopian topaz shall not be compared with it.”

As though he plainly said: No saint, however full of virtues, gathered though he is from the blackness of this world,

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Vindoc. reads *infactus*; the reading is uncertain.]

can be equal to him of whom it is written: “That which shall be born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

[Note: [Col. 0089D] 2 Laud. omits “of you.”]

Although we are made holy, we are not born holy, because we are constrained by the condition of corruptible nature itself, so that we say with the Prophet: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth” (Ps. L, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0089D] 2 Laud. reads: “and in pleasures.”]

But he alone was truly born holy who, in order to overcome the condition of corruptible nature itself, was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse.

**85. Nestorius’s madness against Christ: he taught that Christ, although a mere human being, attained through merits the status of God. He is refuted. The manner of the Incarnation of the Word. Christ is one thing from the Father and another from his mother, but he is not one person from the Father and another from his mother.**—A certain heresiarch wished to make himself equal to this wisdom, as though he were a kind of Ethiopian topaz, when he said: “I do not envy Christ because he was made God; for, if I wish, I too can become one.”

He thought that Jesus Christ our Lord became God not through the mystery of his conception but through an advancement in grace. By a perverse argument he asserted that Christ was born a mere human being but advanced through merit so as to be God. Consequently, he supposed that he and any others could be made equal to Christ, since they become children of God by grace. He did not understand, did not consider, that “Ethiopian topaz shall not be compared with it.”

For it is one thing for human beings, once born, to receive the grace of adoption, and another for one uniquely to come forth as God from conception itself through the power of divinity. Glory possessed by the Only-Begotten through nature cannot be equaled by glory received through grace.

For the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. II, 5), is not, as this heretic foolishly claims, one in his humanity and another in his divinity.

[**Vet. XXXVI.**] He was not conceived and born as a mere human being and afterward received, through merit, the status of God. Rather, when the angel announced it and the Spirit came upon her, immediately the Word was in the womb; immediately within the womb the Word was flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Vind. reads: “and when the Holy Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb; immediately within the womb the Word was flesh.”]

While the essence remained immutable—the essence he shares coeternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit—he assumed within the Virgin’s womb that by which the impassible could suffer, the immortal could die, and the eternal, existing before the ages, could become temporal at the end of the ages. Thus, through an ineffable sacrament, by holy conception and inviolate birth, according to the truth of both natures, the same virgin was both the handmaid of the Lord and his mother.

Thus Elizabeth says to her: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke I, 43). And the Virgin herself, conceiving, said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid., I, 38).

Although he is one thing from the Father and another from the Virgin, he is not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin. Rather, he himself is eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; he himself is the one who made and the one who was made; he himself is beautiful in form above the sons of human beings through his divinity, and he himself is the one of whom it was said: “We saw him, and there was no appearance, nor was there beauty or comeliness in him” (Isa. LIII, 2), through his humanity.

He himself existed before the ages from the Father without a mother; he himself, at the end of the ages, came from his mother without a father.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] In Germ. and the later editions: “he himself the temple of the Creator.” *Of the Creator* is not read in Corb. Germ., Turon., two Laud., Norm., and others, nor in the older editions, but only in later ones.]

He himself is the temple; he himself is the creator of the temple. He himself is the author of the work; he himself is the work of the author. Remaining one from and in both natures, he is neither confused through the union of the natures nor divided into two through their distinction.

But since we have not undertaken to discuss these matters, let us return to the order of exposition.

[Col. 0090C]

**86. Recapitulation of what has been said above.**—We must note that the holy man, in order to show that the angels are far inferior to this wisdom, says: “Gold of Ophir shall not be given for it.” To show that he also regarded the ancient fathers, interpreters of sacred eloquence, as inferior, he added: “Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.” To show that the wisdom of philosophers also lies far beneath it, he continued: “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of Ethiopia.” Then he added: “Nor with the most precious sardonyx stone, or sapphire.” To demonstrate that in that heavenly city as well no one can attain equality with the Only-Begotten, he added: “Gold or glass shall not be compared with it.” To show that the prophets also are subordinate to him, he added: “Nor shall lofty and eminent vessels of gold be exchanged for it, nor shall they be mentioned in comparison with it. For wisdom is drawn from hidden places.”

Finally, to rebuke those heretics within the Church who, coming from the error of paganism, divide through pride the faith they receive, he added: “Ethiopian topaz shall not be compared with it.”

As though he plainly indicated: Those who come to conversion from the blackness of sin cannot be made equal to the God-man,

[Note: [Col. 0090D] The editions read “be made wholly equal to God,” instead of “to the man,” as found in two Royal manuscripts, two Sangerman manuscripts, two Laud manuscripts, Bellovac., and Norm. Saint Gregory is clearly speaking of wisdom clothed in flesh, or of God as man.]

although they may appear to shine with the many colors of virtues.

[Col. 0091A]

To refute their pride, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER LIII

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—Nor shall they be matched with the purest dye.**

**87. Those are truly humble and holy who attribute nothing to their own merits.**—Those who are truly humble and truly holy are called “the purest dye.” They know that of themselves they do not possess the appearance of virtue, but that they hold it from the gift of grace that has come upon them. They would not be dyed if they had possessed holiness by nature. But they are the purest dye because they humbly preserve within themselves the grace of virtue that has come upon them and that they have received.

Hence the voice of the Bridegroom says of the holy Church: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song VI, 9; III, 6). Because the holy Church does not possess the heavenly life by nature, but is adorned with the beauty of gifts when the Spirit comes upon her, she is said not to be white but to be made white.

It should be noted that earlier, when he had said, “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of Ethiopia,” he did not call those same colors pure. Here, however, in order to distinguish the dye of genuine virtues from the counterfeit coloring of philosophers, he says “dyes” and adds “purest.”

Those are rightly called the purest dyes who were previously foul through evil works but, when the Spirit came upon them, were clothed with the splendor of grace, so that they appeared to be something entirely different from what they had been.

Hence our descent into the water itself is called baptism—that is, “dyeing” or “immersion.”

[Note: [Col. 0091D] The manuscripts read *tinguimur* (“we are dyed/immersed”).]

We are dyed, as it were; and those who were previously disfigured by the deformity of vices are made beautiful by the grace and adornment of virtues after receiving faith.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] Vindoc. adds: “and by the adornments of all virtues.”]

[Col. 0091C] It continues:

## CHAPTER LIV [Rec. XXVIII]

**Verses 20–21.—Whence, then, does wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living beings.**
88. As long as we live in mortal flesh, we see God not in his own nature but through certain images, unless we first die to bodily life by completely extinguishing our love for it.—We must carefully consider what the holy man is asking when he inquires from where wisdom comes. For it comes from the one from whom it originated. But because it is born from the invisible and coeternal Father, its way is hidden. [Note: [Col. 0092D] See, “its life.”] Hence the prophet also says: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8). Its place, however, is the human mind; when the wisdom of God fills that mind, it makes it holy. Since, therefore, the one from whom it proceeded is invisible, and it is uncertain in whose mind it comes to rest when understood, it is rightly said here: “From where, then, does wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding?” [Ancient recension XXXVII.]

But what immediately follows is very surprising: “It is hidden from the eyes of all the living.” For if Wisdom, who is God, were hidden from the eyes of all living beings, surely none of the saints would have seen her. Yet I hear John agreeing with this statement when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John IV, 12). Again, when I consider the fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many of them saw God, as the history of sacred Scripture itself bears witness.

Jacob saw the Lord, saying: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved” (Gen. XXXII, 30). Moses saw God, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exod. XXXIII, 11). Job also saw the Lord, saying: “I have heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job XLII, 5). Isaiah saw the Lord, saying: “In the year when King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI, 1). Micaiah saw the Lord, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and the whole army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left” (1 Kings XXII, 19).

What, then, does it mean that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while it is said of this Wisdom, who is God, “She is hidden from the eyes of all the living,” and John says, “No one has ever seen God” (1 John IV, 12)? Surely the evident meaning is that, as long as one lives mortally in this world, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the very form of his nature: the soul, breathed upon by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain representations, but does not reach the very power of his essence.

This is why Jacob, who testified that he had seen God, saw him only in an angel (Exod. XXXIII, 11). [Col. 0092C] This is why Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks with his friend, says to him in the very course of his speech: “If I have found grace in your sight, show yourself clearly to me, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). [Note: [Col. 0092D] Norm. and Corb. Germ.: “speaks … with his friend; to him, in the very words, his radiance” [the reading is materially uncertain]. Germ.: “speaks … to him in the very words.”]

Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not “Show yourself to me.” But if it was God with whom he spoke face to face, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing? His request makes clear that he thirsted to behold, through the unbounded radiance of God’s nature, the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images. He desired that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, so that no created image might temporally intervene between him and the vision of eternity.

Thus the fathers of the Old Testament saw the Lord and yet, in accordance with John’s statement, “No one has ever seen God” (John IV, 12); and, in accordance with blessed Job’s saying, Wisdom, who is God, is hidden from the eyes of all the living. For those who remain in mortal flesh could see God through certain bounded images, but could not see him through the unbounded light of eternity.

[Ancient recension XXXVIII.]

89. But if the eternal brightness of God can still be seen in this corruptible flesh by some who are living in it, yet growing through immeasurable virtue, with a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with blessed Job’s statement: “She is hidden from the eyes of all the living.” For whoever sees Wisdom, who is God, dies completely to this life, so that he is no longer held by love for it.

No one has seen her who still lives bodily, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever sees God dies by that very fact, insofar as, either in the intention of his heart or in the effect of his works, he separates himself entirely from the pleasures of this life.

Hence it is said again to this same Moses: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 21). [Col. 0093B] It is as though he said openly: No one ever sees God spiritually while living carnally in the world.

Thus the apostle Paul, who, as he himself testifies, had still understood the invisible things of God only in part (1 Cor. XIII, 12), declared that he had already died entirely to this world, saying: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

As we said much earlier, it would not have been enough for him to say, “I have been crucified to the world,” unless he had also prefaced it with, “The world has been crucified to me.” In this way he testified not only that he was dead to the world, but also that the world was dead to him, so that he no longer desired the world, nor the world him.

For if, in one place, there were two persons, one alive and the other dead, even though the dead person does not see the living, the living person nevertheless sees the dead. But the preacher of God wished to show that, through the rejection by which he had humbled and cast himself down, he had become such that neither he desired the world nor the world desired him.

Therefore he said not only that he had been crucified to the world, so that, like a dead man, he would not see the glory of the world that he might otherwise desire; he also asserted that the world had been crucified to him. He had cast himself down in such profound humility that the world itself, as though dead to him, could no longer see Paul in his humility and contempt.

90. Those who assert that the blessed see God only in his glory and not in his nature are refuted.—It must be understood that there were some who said that, even in that region of blessedness, God is indeed seen in his glory, but cannot be seen in his nature. They were misled by an insufficiently subtle inquiry.

For in that simple and unchangeable essence, glory is not one thing and nature another. Rather, his very nature is his glory, and his very glory is his nature.

Because this Wisdom of God would one day reveal herself to those who love her, she herself promises it, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John XIV, 21). It is as though she plainly said: You who see me in your own nature must finally see me in my nature.

Again she says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). Hence Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. XIII, 12).

[Ancient recension XXXIX.]

91. Those who imagine that angels are deprived of the divine vision are likewise refuted.—Since the first preacher of the Church says of God, “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. I, 12), there are some who suppose that even the angels do not see God. Yet we know that Truth itself says: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10). Does Truth, then, proclaim one thing and the preacher of Truth another?

But if both statements are compared, it is recognized that they in no way disagree. Angels both see God and desire to see him; they thirst to behold him, and they behold him.

If they desired to see him in such a way that they could not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, desire without fruition would bring anxiety, and anxiety would bring punishment. But the blessed angels are far removed from every punishment of anxiety, because punishment and blessedness never coexist.

Again, when we say that they are satisfied with the vision of God, since the Psalmist also says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI, 15), we must consider that satiety is usually followed by weariness. For the two statements to agree properly, let Truth say, “They always see,” and let the distinguished preacher say, “They always desire to see.”

To prevent desire from becoming anxiety, those who desire are satisfied; but to prevent satisfaction from becoming weariness, those who are satisfied continue to desire. Thus they desire without labor, because desire is accompanied by satisfaction; and they are satisfied without weariness, because satisfaction itself is continually kindled by desire.

So shall we also be when we come to the very fountain of life. Thirst and satisfaction will be delightfully impressed upon us at the same time. Yet necessity will be far from this thirst, and weariness far from this satisfaction, because we shall be satisfied while thirsting, and thirst while satisfied.

[Note: Norm., “We shall therefore see God himself, and he himself will be the reward of our labor.” Two Laud., “God himself, which will be the reward.”]

We shall therefore see God, and he himself will be the reward of our labor, so that, after the darkness of this mortality, we may rejoice in the light kindled by him. [Note: 1 Laud., “having been set alight.”]

92. In what sense God dwells in inaccessible light.—But when we say that his light is accessible [Note: The same manuscript, “kindled.”], what Paul says resists this thought: “He dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (1 Tim. VI, 16). Again I hear the Psalmist say: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6).

How, then, are we enlightened by drawing near, if we do not see the very light by which we can be enlightened? But if, by drawing near to him, we see the light by which we are enlightened, how is it said to be inaccessible?

In this matter we must consider that the one who said “inaccessible” meant inaccessible to every person wise according to human standards. [Note: Germ., “but to every human being”; “but human.” Norm. and Corb. Germ., “but to a human being; to a human being, but one wise according to human standards.” 1 Laud., “but to a human being wise according to human standards.”]

Sacred Scripture usually designates all followers of bodily things by the term “humanity.” Thus the same apostle says to certain people who were quarreling: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to human standards?” (1 Cor. III, 3–4). Shortly afterward he adds: “Are you not human beings?”

Elsewhere he gave this testimony: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II, 9). And after saying that this was hidden from human beings, he immediately added: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (ibid.). [Note: 1 Laud., “but to you.”] In this way he distinguished himself from the designation “human,” since one who had been caught up above humanity already understood divine things.

So too in this passage, when he declared that the light of God is inaccessible, he added, in order to show to whom it is inaccessible: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see.” In his customary manner, he calls all who understand according to human standards “human beings,” because those who understand divine things are, so to speak, above humanity.

We shall therefore see God, if by a heavenly manner of life we deserve to be above humanity. Yet we shall not see him in the same way that he sees himself. For the Creator sees himself in a manner vastly different from that in which the creature sees the Creator. As far as the immensity of God is concerned, a certain limit is imposed upon our contemplation, because we are circumscribed by the very condition of being creatures.

[Ancient recension XL.]

93. We do not see God as he sees himself.—Certainly we do not see God as he sees himself, just as we do not rest in God as he rests in himself. Our vision and rest will be in some way similar to his vision and rest, but they will not be equal to them.

So that we do not, so to speak, lie inert within ourselves, the wing of contemplation lifts us up; we are raised from ourselves to behold him. Carried away by the intention of the heart and the sweetness of contemplation, we go forth from ourselves in some manner into him. Yet this very going forth of ours is less than resting, and nevertheless to go forth in this way is perfect rest.

Perfect rest therefore exists because God is seen. [Note: Thus the manuscripts Norm., Corb. Germ., and many others read, and the ancient editions follow them. In the later printed editions, with Germ., “where God is seen” (qua Deus cernitur) is read instead of “because God is seen” (quia Deus cernitur), and below, “where not from himself” (qua non a se). The old printed editions also have here “because not from himself” (quia non a se).]

Yet it must not be made equal to the rest of the one who does not pass from himself into another in order to rest. There is therefore a rest, so to speak, both similar and dissimilar, because what is rest in him is imitated by our rest.

In order that we may be blessed and eternal forever, we imitate the Eternal. For us, eternity is great: it is the imitation of eternity. Nor are we excluded from the one whom we are able to imitate, because by seeing him we participate in him, and by participating in him we imitate him. [Note: Plural manuscripts, “we participate.”]

This vision begins now through faith, but then it is perfected in direct perception, when we drink at the very source the Wisdom coeternal with God, which now we receive through the mouths of preachers as though through flowing rivers.

## BOOK NINETEEN

The exposition proceeds from the final part of verse 21 of chapter XXVIII up to, but excluding, verse 21 of the following chapter; various meanings are disclosed no less learnedly than devoutly, especially concerning Christ and the Church.

[Col. 0095]

[Ancient and Recent recensions I]

1. Why should it be surprising that the eternal Wisdom of God cannot be seen, when even the invisible things created through it cannot be grasped by human eyes? In created things, therefore, we learn with what humility we must revere the Creator of all things, so that in this life the human mind may dare to claim nothing for itself concerning the form of almighty God—a privilege he reserves as a reward for his chosen ones in the recompense that follows.

Thus, after it has been said, “She is hidden from the eyes of all the living,” it is immediately added:

## CHAPTER ONE

**CHAPTER XXVIII, VERSE 21.**—“It is hidden even from the birds of the sky.”

2. In Scripture, the birds of the sky are sometimes understood in a bad sense and sometimes in a good sense.—In sacred Scripture, birds are sometimes presented as signifying evil and sometimes good.

By birds, powers of the air opposed to the efforts of the good are sometimes designated. Hence Truth says: “When the seed fell beside the way, the birds came and devoured it” (Matt. XIII, 4; Luke VIII, 5). For malignant spirits, besieging human minds and injecting harmful thoughts, tear the word of life from the memory.

Again, to a certain rich man who was wise in a proud manner it is said: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII, 20; Luke IX, 58).

Foxes are exceedingly deceitful animals. They hide in pits or caves, and when they appear, they never run along straight paths but through winding turns. Birds, as we know, raise themselves into the air on high flight. Therefore, under the name of foxes, deceitful and fraudulent beings are designated; under the name of birds, these same proud demons are designated.

It is as though he said: Deceitful and exalted demons find their dwelling in your heart, that is, in your proud thoughts; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, meaning that my humility finds no rest in your proud mind.

For that first bird, as though by a certain flight, lifted itself up when it said through an exalted thought: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13–14). See how high it sought to rise by flying proudly.

It also persuaded the first human beings to make this flight. They too tried, as though by flying, to rise above themselves when they were told to taste and be like gods (Gen. III, 5, 19). And when they desired the likeness of divinity, they lost the gifts of immortality (ibid., 19). They would not have gone down into the earth by dying if they had been willing to stand humbly upon the earth.

3. On the other hand, birds are accustomed to be placed in a good sense. Thus, when the Lord announced the likeness of the kingdom of heaven by means of a mustard seed, he said: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a mustard seed, which a man took and cast into his garden; it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of the sky rested in its branches” (Matt. XIII, 31). [Note: Norm., “mustard,” and likewise below.]

He himself is the mustard seed, which, planted in the burial-place of the garden, rose as a great tree. He was a seed when he died, a tree when he rose again: a seed through the humility of the flesh, a tree through the power of majesty. A seed, because “we saw him, and there was no appearance in him” (Isa. LIII, 2); a tree, because he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3). [Note: Turon., “which … was planted.” Another manuscript, “through the omnipotence of majesty.”]

[Ancient recension II.] The branches of this tree are the holy preachers. Let us see how widely they are extended. What is said of them? “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

In these branches the birds rest, because holy souls, raising themselves from earthly thoughts on certain wings of virtue, breathe again from the weariness of this life in the words and consolations of the preachers.

Therefore, after it has been said of Wisdom, “She is hidden from the eyes of all the living,” it is rightly added: “It is hidden even from the birds of the sky.” For those established in this corruptible flesh do not penetrate the power of her nature even by seeing her—those who already fly by the merit of holy contemplation.

Here it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER TWO [Recent recension II]

**VERSE 22.**—“Destruction and death said: With our ears we have heard the report of her.”

4. The proud angels, because they do not enjoy divine Wisdom, do not see her.—Who are signified by the names “destruction” and “death” except malignant spirits, who became the inventors of death and destruction? Concerning their prince himself, under the figure of his minister, John says: “His name was Death” (Rev. VI, 8).

All the spirits of pride subject to him say of this Wisdom, who is God: “With our ears we have heard the report of her,” because they were unable to possess her vision in complete blessedness. For to see the Wisdom coeternal with God perfectly is the same as to possess her.

Hence it is said to John concerning the reward of the one who conquers: “I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Rev. II, 17).

In this life we can know or see even what we have not received. But to possess the new name written on the stone means to know, in the eternal reward, a knowledge of God unfamiliar to human senses; no one can know it except the one who receives it and possesses it. [Note: This passage is badly corrupt in the printed editions and in most manuscripts. We have restored it with the aid of the manuscripts Norm., namely the two from Évreux, Gemet., Pratell., Beccens., Utic., and Sag. Later editions read: “which we do not receive to possess. But the new name written on the stone—that is, the knowledge of God unfamiliar to human minds in the eternal reward—no one can know unless he has also received it to possess.” Who could explain such an Oedipus? Nearly the whole defect arises from the placement of points and commas. The manuscript Sagerm. seems to support this reading, but it is interpolated here and marked with obeli, signs of corruption. Our reading is represented exactly by the old editions of Basel and Paris 1518, except that they read “that is” instead of “is”; this difference is sufficient to overturn the sense.]

Since, then, as we have said, to see God is the same as to possess him, the wicked spirits do not see this Wisdom because, rejected through pride, they could in no way possess her. They closed the eyes of their hearts to her light, resisting when her rays were poured over them. The statement written about these same malignant spirits may be understood in this sense: “They were rebellious against the light” (Job XXIV, 13). [Note: Germ., Two Laud., and Corb. Germ., “of the light.”]

For malignant spirits to hear the report of Wisdom but not to see that same Wisdom means that they recognized her power through her might, yet refused to stand humbly beneath her. Hence Truth says of the head of the malignant spirits: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44).

It follows:

## CHAPTER THREE [Recent recension III]

**VERSE 23.**—“God understands her way, and he himself knows her place.”

5. Human beings did not know when Wisdom would come to them through the flesh, or how, appearing outwardly, she would remain invisible with the Father.—This Wisdom, coeternal with God, has a way in one sense and a place in another.

If anyone understands “place,” it must not be understood as a local place. For God cannot be held bodily. Rather, as has been said, “place” is understood nonlocally: the Father is the place of Wisdom, and Wisdom is the place of the Father. As Wisdom herself testifies: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

Wisdom therefore has a way in one sense and a place in another: a way through the passage of humanity, and a place through the breath of divinity. [Ancient recension III.] From the latter she does not pass, because she is eternal; but from the former she passes, because for our sake she appeared in time. [Note: Gemet., “from which she is coeternal.”]

Thus it is written in the Gospel: “As the Lord was leaving Jericho, he was passing by; and two blind men sitting beside the way cried out, saying, ‘Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David’” (John XIV, 10–11; Matt. XX, 29–30). At their cry, as it is written there, Jesus stopped and restored their sight.

What does it mean that he heard while passing by and restored light while standing, except that through his humanity he had mercy on us, while through the power of his divinity he expelled the darkness of our minds from us?

That he was born and suffered for us, that he rose again and ascended into heaven, is as though Jesus passes by, because these actions are temporal. But he touched and enlightened them while standing, because the eternity of the Word does not pass away as that temporal dispensation does; remaining in itself, it renews all things.

For God’s standing means arranging all mutable things in an unchanging thought. Thus he who, passing by, heard the voices of those who asked, restored light while standing: although he endured temporal things for our sake, he granted us light from that in which he knows no passage into mutability.

Since it was uncertain when he would appear to human beings through the flesh, it is rightly said here: “God understands her way, and he himself knows her place.” It is as though it were openly said: Hidden from human thought are both when Wisdom will come to human beings through the flesh and how, even when she has appeared outwardly, she will remain invisible with the Father.

6. Her coming and dwelling in human hearts are unknown.—This may also be understood in another way. For her way can appropriately be understood as the very fact that she comes into the heart and pours herself inwardly into us. Her place becomes the heart, to which she comes and in which she remains.

Of this way of hers it is said: “A voice crying in the wilderness, prepare the way for the Lord” (Matt. III, 3). [Note: Germ. and Two Laud., “the way of the Lord.”] That is: Open an entrance in your heart for Wisdom as she comes. Likewise it is said: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Ps. LXVII, 5).

To ascend above the setting means to overcome by rising again the death that he had endured. He says, therefore: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting”; that is, provide a way in your hearts through faith for the Lord who is rising again.

Hence it is said to John through the Spirit: “You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke I, 76). For whoever, by preaching, cleanses the hearts of his hearers from the filth of vices prepares a way for Wisdom as she comes.

This Wisdom therefore has a way and also has a place: a way by which she comes, and a place in which she remains, as she herself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23). The way, therefore, is by which she comes; the place is in which she remains.

But where does she come, since she is everywhere? Or is Wisdom’s coming the manifestation, through the illumination of our minds, of the presence of her majesty?

And because it is uncertain to human beings either into whose heart she comes or in whom she remains and rests after coming, it is rightly said here: “God understands her way, and he himself knows her place.” For it belongs to divine vision alone to perceive either by what means the understanding of Wisdom comes to the human heart or whose mind does not lose, through deadly thoughts, the understanding of life that it has received.

And because this same Wisdom, manifested through the grace of humanity, was destined to fill the hearts of the elect in every part of the world, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER FOUR [Ancient recension IV]

**VERSE 24.**—“For he himself beholds the ends of the world, and he sees all things that are under heaven.”

God reforms us by looking upon us through grace.—7. For God to look upon something means to restore to his grace what had been lost and ruined. Hence it is written: “The king who sits upon the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze” (Prov. XX, 8).

By looking upon us, he restrained the evils of our fickleness and granted us the great merits of maturity. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER FIVE [Recent recension IV]

**VERSE 25.**—“He who made weight for the winds,”

8. He fixes wandering souls and grants them weight.—In sacred Scripture, souls are often signified by the speed and subtlety of the winds. Thus the Psalmist says of God: “He who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. CIII, 3). [Note: Gemet., “who walks.”] That is, he surpasses the powers of souls.

He therefore “made weight for the winds,” because, when heavenly Wisdom fills souls, she makes them weighty with the maturity she bestows. [Note: 1 Laud., “makes them weighty with their customary maturity.” Another Laud., “makes them weighty with maturity either given or indicated.”]

This is not the weight of which it is said: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. IV, 3). [Note: Laud. and Germ., “heavy of heart.”] For it is one thing to be weighty through counsel and another through sin; one thing to be weighty through steadfastness and another through guilt. The former weight has the burden of virtue; the latter, the burden of a load.

Souls therefore receive weight so that they no longer leap away from attention to God with a light movement, but remain fixed in him through the weight of steadfastness. [Note: Bellov. and 1 Laud., “through the sweetness of steadfastness.”]

That people was still being lightly moved of whom the prophet says: “He went wandering in the way of his heart; I saw his way, and I left him” (Isa. LVII, 17). But the grave counsel of the heart drives out every instability of wandering.

And because there are souls that, through light movement, desire now one thing and now another, almighty God does not lightly regard the mind’s slight fluctuations; he judges their wandering by abandoning the heart to it. But when, through grace, he looks upon the wandering mind, he fixes it in the stability of counsel.

It is rightly said, therefore: “He who made weight for the winds,” because when he mercifully looks upon the mind’s light movements, he immediately forms it toward the maturity of steadfastness.

Or certainly, to make weight for the winds means to temper the glory granted here to the elect through virtues by mixing it with weakness. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER SIX

**The same passage.**—“And he weighed the waters by measure.”

9. He tempers the virtues of the elect with weakness so that they do not become proud.—In sacred Scripture, waters sometimes signify the Holy Spirit, sometimes sacred knowledge, sometimes wicked knowledge, sometimes tribulation, sometimes peoples flowing away, and sometimes the minds of those who follow the teachings of faith. [Note: Corb. Germ., Bellov., Turon., Vindoc., and 1 Laud., “the minds of those following the teachings of faith.” Norm., “the proofs of the faith of those who follow.” Germ. and the printed editions, “the proclamations of the faith of those who follow good things.”]

The infusion of the Holy Spirit is signified by water, as it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38). The Evangelist follows by adding: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive.”

Again, sacred knowledge is signified by water, as it is said: “He will give them to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Sir. XV, 3).

Wicked knowledge is also customarily called water, as in Solomon, where the woman who represents heresy flatters with cunning persuasions, saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17).

Tribulations are also sometimes understood under the name of waters, as the Psalmist says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. XLVIII, 2).

Peoples are signified by water, as John says: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. XVII, 15).

By water are signified not only the flow of peoples passing away, but also the minds of good people who follow the teachings of faith, as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow upon all waters” (Isa. XXXII, 20). The Psalmist likewise says: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters” (Ps. XXVIII, 3).

What, then, are the waters signified by this passage except the hearts of the elect, which, through understanding Wisdom, have already received the hearing of the heavenly voice? Of them it is rightly said: “And he weighed the waters by measure.” [Ancient and Recent recensions V.]

For the saints themselves, who are carried upward to the heights by the Holy Spirit lifting them, are restrained by certain temptations as long as they remain in this life, lest they become proud through exaltation. Thus they cannot advance as far as they wish, and a certain measure of virtues is present in them, lest they be lifted up by pride.

10. This is confirmed by the example of Elijah fleeing from Jezebel.—For this reason Elijah, although he had advanced to great heights through so many virtues, was held back by a certain measure when he later fled from Jezebel, even though she was a queen, yet merely a woman (1 Kings XIX, 3).

I consider this man of extraordinary virtue drawing fire from heaven, and a second time consuming captains of fifty with all their men by a sudden request [Note: In all the manuscripts—Germ., Norm., Laud., Vindoc., Corb. Germ., and others—this is the reading, not “and a second time, fifty men … by a submitted request,” as in the later printed editions. Gussanv. alone reads “fifty men” for “captains of fifty.”], closing the heavens to rain by his word and opening the heavens to rain by his word, raising the dead, and foreseeing all future things [Note: Other editions read “future things also,” a reading found in no manuscript.]. Yet once again I recall with what fear he fled before a single woman.

I consider this man, struck down by fear [Note: So all our manuscripts; not “struck by fear,” as in the Vatican and Gussanv. editions.], asking death from the hand of God but not receiving it, and fleeing death from the hand of a woman. For while fleeing he sought death, saying: “It is enough for me; take my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (ibid. XIX, 4).

From where, then, did he have such power that he could perform all those virtues? From where such weakness that he feared a woman so greatly? Surely because “the waters are weighed by measure,” so that the holy men of God may have great power through God, yet may also be moderated by a certain measure through their own weakness.

In those virtues Elijah recognized what he had received from God; in those weaknesses he recognized what he could be in himself. The former power was a virtue; the latter weakness was the guardian of virtue. [Note: Corb. Germ., Beccens., and Utic., “what might be lacking in himself”; other manuscripts have the preferable “what he could be in himself.”] [Note: Vindoc., “in those heavenly things.”] In those virtues he showed what he had received; in those weaknesses he guarded what he had received. In miracles Elijah was displayed; in weaknesses he was preserved.

## 11. And of Paul Avoiding Death, or Suffering Satan’s Temptations

Thus I see Paul enduring dangers from rivers and robbers, from cities and wildernesses, by sea and land (II Cor. XI, 26); restraining his body by fasts and vigils; enduring the hardship of cold and nakedness; diligently and pastorally applying himself to the guardianship of the churches [Note: [Col. 0102D] Recent Vulgate editions, with Germ., have *exerentem*, “exerting.” We follow the manuscripts Turon., Vind., Norm., etc., and the older printed editions]; caught up to the third heaven and again caught up into paradise (ibid. XII, 4), and hearing secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter; and yet, when the angel of Satan is permitted to tempt him (ibid. XII, 7), he prays that he may be freed, but is not heard.

When I consider the very beginnings of his conversion [Note: [Col. 0102D] Vind. has “of his preservation”], I weigh the fact that heavenly mercy opens the heavens to him, and that Jesus reveals himself to him from on high. He temporarily lost the light of his body, but received the light of his heart forever.
