He is sent to Ananias (Acts IX, 7), and is called a chosen vessel; yet he withdraws by flight from that same city which he had entered after seeing Jesus, as he himself testifies, saying: “The governor of King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and I was let down through a window in a basket over the wall, and so I escaped his hands” (II Cor. XI, 32).

To him I may freely say: “O Paul, you already behold Jesus in heaven, and on earth you still flee from a human being? You are led into paradise, you learn God’s secret words, and yet you are still tempted by Satan’s angel?”

Whence are you so strong that you are carried up to heavenly things? Whence so weak that you flee from a human being on earth and still endure adversity from Satan’s angel—unless because he who lifts you up again regulates you by the most subtle measure, so that in your miracles you may proclaim to us the power of God, and again, in your fear, make us remember our weakness?

Yet, lest this weakness drive us into despair when it strikes us, while you were asking the Lord concerning your weakness and were not heard, you also told us what you heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).

## [Vet. VI.] 12. Weakness Is the Guardian of Virtue [Note: [Col. 0102D] Most manuscripts have “openly.”]

It is therefore shown by the clear voice of God that weakness is the guardian of virtue. For we are then well guarded inwardly when, by God’s dispensation, we are tolerably tested outwardly—sometimes by vices, sometimes by afflictions. For even those whom we know to have been men of virtue were not without temptations and struggles with vices. Hence that outstanding preacher, for our consolation, deigns to disclose certain such things about himself, saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23).

The flesh drags downward, lest the spirit become exalted; [Note: [Col. 0103D] So Germ., Norm., Laud., Corb. Germ., and nearly all the others. The editions read: “and it lifts up to the heights.”] and the spirit draws upward, lest the flesh cast us down. The spirit raises us, so that we do not lie in the lowest places; the flesh weighs us down, so that we are not lifted up from the highest. If the flesh tested us without the spirit lifting us up [Note: [Col. 0103D] Vatic. and Gussanv. read “by the weight . . . of temptation,” against the manuscripts Germ., Corb. Germ., Norm., Laud., and Turon., with which other printed editions agree], it would undoubtedly cast us into the depths by the full force of its temptation. Again, if the spirit lifted us to the heights without the flesh testing us, that very exaltation would cast us down more disastrously in a fall into pride.

But a precise moderation is established, so that while each of the saints is indeed already carried inwardly toward the heights, yet is still tested outwardly, he falls neither into despair nor into elation: outward temptation does not complete guilt, because inward intention draws upward; nor does inward intention raise us into pride, because outward temptation humbles us while it weighs us down.

And thus, by a great ordering, we understand what we receive in inward progress and what we are in outward decline. In a wondrous manner it comes about that no one should be lifted up because of virtue or despair because of temptation, since, while the spirit draws upward and the flesh draws back, the soul is balanced by the most subtle regulation of inward judgment in a position between the heights and the depths. Well, therefore, is it said: “And he weighed the waters by measure.” It follows:

# CHAPTER VII

### VERSES 26, 27

“When he established a law for the rains, and a way for the sounding storms, then he saw her, and declared her, and prepared her, and searched her out.”

## 13. A Law Is Established for the Heralds of God’s Word, So That They May Fulfill in Deed What They Preach. For Those Who Keep This Law, Access to Human Hearts Lies Open

The sayings of preachers are customarily signified by rains. Hence it is said through Moses: “Let my speech be expected like rain” (Deut. XXXII, 2). Their words are rains when they gently persuade; but when they thunder forth frightening things about the coming judgment, they are sounding storms. And it should be noted that a law is established for the rains, so that a way may be opened for the sounding storms.

For a law is established for preachers themselves: by living, they must fulfill what they hasten to urge in speech. The authority of speech is lost when the voice is not supported by conduct. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds, and take my covenant upon your mouth? You have hated discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX, 16) [Note: [Col. 0104D] Gemet. reads “backward”; other Norman manuscripts, together with Germ. and Corb. Germ., retain “after you”].

A preacher casts God’s words behind him when he scorns to do what he says. When he himself rejects in deed what he preaches in speech, how will another obey his words, while he pretends not to hear what he proclaims?

Concerning this law of preaching it is written: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people so, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does and teaches so will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 19) [Note: [Col. 0104D] The word “so” is not found in our manuscripts except in Germ.].

By “the kingdom of heaven” he evidently calls the present Church, concerning which it is written: “And they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. XIII, 41). For in the heavenly kingdom above there are no scandals to be gathered out of it. Therefore, whoever breaks the commandment in deed and so teaches in speech will be least in this kingdom of heaven, and in that kingdom will not even be least.

He established a way for the sounding storms when, through his preachers, he opened access to human hearts struck with fear of the coming judgment. A law is therefore established first, so that afterward a way may be opened, because that voice penetrates the heart of the hearer which preserves in deed what it has uttered with the mouth [Note: [Col. 0104D] “With the mouth” is absent from many manuscripts].

[VET. VII.] Then, when he established a law for the rains and a way for the sounding storms, God saw this wisdom, declared it, prepared it, and searched it out. In the customary language of sacred Scripture, God is said to “see” in order to make us see, just as the Lord says to the righteous man: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. XXII, 12). And the Israelites are warned: “The Lord your God tests you, so that he may know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII, 3)—that is, so that he may make you know.

Therefore, when he established a law for the rains—that is, when he gave the preachers a commandment to be kept—he caused this incarnate Wisdom to be seen and declared by the preachers, and to be prepared and searched out by the hearers. Whoever prepares her well for himself by living well prepares her to be gracious to him on the day of judgment.

And it should be noted that four things are said concerning her. For he says: “He saw, declared, prepared, searched out.” He saw, because she is form; he declared, because she is word; he prepared, because she is remedy; he searched out, because she is hidden. But when can the eternal Wisdom of God—called the appearance of the Father and the Word—be penetrated by the human mind? Who can understand either a word without time or an appearance without limitation? Something therefore had to be said which a human being could know about her in himself. Hence it is suitably added:

# CHAPTER VIII [Rec. VI]

### VERSE 28

“And he said to the human being: Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom itself; and to depart from evil—that is understanding.”

## 14. One Who Fears God Begins to Possess His Wisdom and Recognizes in Himself What He Cannot Recognize in God’s Own Nature

As though he were speaking plainly, he said: “Return to yourself, human being; search out the secrets of your heart. If you discover that you fear God, it is certainly evident that you are full of this wisdom. If you still cannot know what she is in herself, meanwhile you already know what she is in you.”

For what is feared among the angels in God’s presence is called among you “the fear of the Lord,” because it is certain that you possess her if it is not uncertain that you fear God. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX, 10), because she begins to penetrate the heart when she disturbs it with fear of the final judgment.

The divine word therefore draws itself down to our smallness: [Note: [Col. 0105D] Germ. and the later Vulgate editions read: “just as when a father speaks with his little son . . . he babbles.” We have deleted the redundant word *cum*, following almost all the manuscripts.] just as a father speaks with a little son and willingly babbles so that he may be understood. Because we cannot penetrate the nature of wisdom—what she is in herself—we hear, through God’s condescension, what she is in us, when it is said: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom itself.”

But because the one who truly understands the force of divine fear is the one who guards himself from all evil works, it is rightly added: “And to depart from evil—that is understanding.” What follows, since it is filled with the spirit of prophecy, is attested by the very words of sacred history, when it is said:

# CHAPTER IX [Vet. VIII, Rec. VII]

### Job 29:1

“Job also continued, taking up his parable [Note: [Col. 0105D] “And he said” is absent from many manuscripts], and said.”

## 15. Job Foretells the Final Times of the Church, When She Will Suffer Carnal People and Heretics

Since “parable” means “likeness,” it is clearly evident that the one who is said to have taken up a parable speaks mysteries through the form of external words. For when he recounts his own experiences, he announces whatever things are destined to come upon the holy Church; and through what he himself suffers, he indicates what she will suffer.

Sometimes, however, he mingles the words of his history with such things that nothing allegorical sounds forth; sometimes he speaks of his own sorrows as though he were speaking with the voice of the sorrowing Church. In this final portion of his speech he designates the final time of the Church, when she is compelled to endure her adversaries—that is, all carnal people, heretics, and gentiles—as they mock her, raised up by unrestrained boasting; she now strives to suppress them by the authority of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0105D] Two Laud. have “to endure in ridicule”].

Hence it is also said in this speech: “But now those younger in age than I mock me, whose fathers I would not have deemed worthy to be placed with the dogs of my flock” (Job XXX, 1). The very order of the passage also requires that the final days of the holy Church be designated by the words of blessed Job, when, as persecution increases, she is compelled to endure the open voices of heretics, as they reveal in the voice of manifest error the movements of their hearts which they now conceal within the folds of their thoughts.

For now, as it is said through John (Rev. XX, 3), the dragon is held shut in the abyss, because diabolical malice is hidden in their deceitful hearts. But, as it is said there [Note: [Col. 0105D] The editions, against the manuscripts, read “it is written”], the dragon will be brought out of the pit of the abyss, because what is now concealed through fear will then be opened publicly against the Church: all the serpent’s venom will emerge from the hearts of the wicked [Note: [Col. 0105D] Turon. has “in the mouth of the wicked”].

For now a raging conscience conceals itself beneath a flattering tongue, and the malice of cunning covers itself, as though with a certain abyss of pretense. Now the Lord, as it is said by the voice of the Psalmist, “gathers the waters of the sea as into a wineskin” (Ps. XXXII, 7) [Note: [Col. 0105D] 2 Laud. has “into a vessel”]. The wineskin is carnal thought. The waters of the sea are gathered into a wineskin when the bitterness of a perverse mind does not burst outward into the voice of perverse freedom.

The time will certainly come when the perverse and carnal will proclaim openly against the Church what they now contrive in secret thought. The time will come when they will oppress the Catholic Church not only with unjust voices but also with cruel blows.

## 16. The Church Suffers Persecution in Two Ways: by Words and by Swords

The Church suffers persecution from her adversaries in two ways: either by words or by swords. When she endures persecution by words, her wisdom is exercised; when by swords, her patience is exercised.

But we still endure persecutions of words from heretics every day, when the heretics themselves flatter us with deceitful tongues and false humility. Persecutions by swords will follow near the end of the world, so that the grains destined to be stored in the heavenly barns may be stripped more truly from the chaff of sinners the more tightly they are afflicted [Note: [Col. 0106D] So Germ., Corb. Germ., the Laudunenses, and nearly all the manuscripts, followed by the older editions. Later editors preferred *acrius*, “more sharply,” found in Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv.].

Then all the elect who are caught up in that tribulation will remember these times in which the Church now holds the peace of faith and restrains the proud necks of heretics—not by the power of rank, but by the yoke of reason. They will remember us, who live through tranquil times of faith; and although we are pressed by the wars of the nations, we are not attacked in the words of the fathers [Note: [Col. 0106D] Vind. has “in judgments”].

Blessed Job, therefore, bearing the type of the holy Church, which will then be found in those straits, yet remembering, as I have said, our present tranquility, recounts what has passed for himself and announces what is to come for others, saying:

# CHAPTER X [Rec. VIII]

### VERSE 2

“Who will grant me that I may be as in the former months?”

## 17. Although the Church Has Already Suffered Great Things, She Will Suffer Far Greater Things

The holy Church, pressed by sorrows, will say many such things. She will be so confined by immense future tribulations that she will long with a great sigh for these times which we endure with great grief. Let her therefore say—let her say through the voice of blessed Job: “Who will grant me that I may be as in the former months?”

Since a fixed number of days is called “months,” what else does he signify by the name of “months” except gatherings of souls? When days are gathered into months, they are withdrawn; so also in this present age the holy Church, while gathering souls shining with the light of truth, hides them in secret places.

Sometimes “month” also signifies perfection, as the prophet says: “Month after month” (Isa. LXVI, 23)—that is, perfection in rest for those whose perfection is now found in labor. Let her therefore remember her former perfection, and recall how great profits she brought back through her preaching from souls gathered together [Note: [Col. 0107D] Most manuscripts, with Germ. and Corb. Germ., have “of her preaching”]. And, confined by tribulations, let her say: “Who will grant me that I may be as in the former months?” What she was in those months she proceeds to enumerate, saying:

# CHAPTER XI

### VERSES 2, 3

“According to the days in which God guarded me, when his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness.”

## 18. Then Many Weak People Will Fall, While the Strong Grieve over Their Fall

Then she sees many of the weak falling from her, compelled by persecution—those whom she now cherishes as a mother within the embrace of peace and keeps within the tranquil cradles of faith [Note: [Col. 0107D] Turon. has “in the tranquil cradle of faith”], because, mingled with the strong, they are nourished by that very tranquility of faith.

But then many such people will fall, and through the entrails of charity the mind of the perfect will grieve that it suffers whatever loss is borne on behalf of the little ones. For the losses of the weak pass into the hearts of the strong through compassion. Hence Paul says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. XI, 29). Each person is perfect to the extent that he perfectly feels the pains of others.

Therefore the holy Church, distressed when the weak then fall [Note: [Col. 0107D] Most manuscripts, with Germ. and Corb. Germ., have “confined”], will rightly say, when she recalls these times: “According to the days in which God guarded me,” because she then judges herself to be falling in those circumstances in which she now sees herself guarded [Note: [Col. 0107D] Norm. has “in which she now sees herself standing”; Laud. has “in which she now sees herself guarded.” Vindoc. has a difficult reading: “because then she judges herself to be the same in those circumstances which she now judged herself to be guarded in these”; it is certainly obscure and, in our judgment, corrupt].

Well, therefore, is it said: “When his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness.” By the name “lamp” the light of sacred Scripture is signified. Concerning it the Church’s own pastor says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (II Pet. I, 19). The Psalmist also says: “Your word is a lamp for my feet, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 105).

Since our governing faculty is the mind, the mind is called by the name “head.” Hence the Psalmist says: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Ps. XXII, 5), as though he plainly said: “You have filled my mind with the richness of charity.”

Now the lamp shines over the head of the Church, because the sacred utterances illuminate the darkness of our mind, so that in this shadowy place of the present life, while we receive the light of God’s words, we may see what ought to be done. Now she walks by its light in darkness, because the holy universal Church, although she does not penetrate the hidden thought of another—for she does not recognize a face in the night [Note: [Col. 0108D] The word “because” is omitted in two Laud.]—nevertheless sets the steps of good works in the direction of the light of heavenly speech. It follows:

# CHAPTER XII [Rec. IX]

### VERSE 4

“As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle.”

## 19. The Various Ages of the Church: Infancy, Youth, and Old Age. Yet at the End She Will Receive Many Children

The age of the holy Church is described just as the age of an individual human being. She was little when, newly born, she was unable to preach the word of life. Hence it is said concerning her: “Our sister is little, and has no breasts” (Song VIII, 8), because, before the holy Church advanced through growth in virtue, she could not provide the breasts of preaching to her weaker hearers.

The Church is called mature when, joined to God’s word and filled with the Holy Spirit, she becomes pregnant with children through the ministry of preaching [Note: [Col. 0108D] So Germ., Corb. Germ., Laud., Norm., Bellov., etc.; the printed editions read “is made fruitful”], whom she brings to birth by exhorting and bears by converting. Concerning this period of her life it is said to the Lord: “The young women have loved you” (Song I, 3). All the churches which together constitute the one Catholic Church are called young women—not already old through fault, but renewed through grace; not sterile through age, but, in the age of the mind, suited to spiritual fruitfulness.

Therefore, when in those days the Church, weakened as though by a kind of old age, is unable to bear children through preaching, she remembers her former fruitfulness, saying: “As I was in the days of my youth.” Yet after those days in which she is brought low, she will still be strengthened near the very end of time by the great power of preaching. For, once the nations have entered in to their full number, she will draw into the bosom of faith the entire Israelite people who are then found. For it is written: “Until the fullness of the nations should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

But before those times there will be days in which she will appear to be oppressed for a little while by her adversaries, as she remembers those days, saying: “As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle.”

## 20. One Who Meditates on God’s Commandments Has God Dwelling Within Him. The Saints Examine Themselves Outwardly and Inwardly [Vet. X]

What should we understand by “tabernacle” in this passage except the dwelling-place of the mind? For through everything we do by thinking, we dwell in the counsel of our heart. Whoever silently thinks upon God’s commandments has God secretly in his tabernacle.

He had seen the dwelling-place of his heart to be before God’s eyes who said: “And the meditation of my heart is always in your sight” (Ps. XVIII, 15). External works are open to human eyes, but our inward and most subtle thoughts are incomparably more open to God’s eyes. For all things, as it is written, are “naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13).

Often we fear appearing disordered in external action before human eyes, yet in inward thought we do not fear the gaze of the one whom we do not see, though he sees all things. We are much more visible inwardly to God than outwardly to human beings. Hence all the saints examine themselves outwardly and inwardly, both rebuking themselves outwardly and invisibly fearing to be seen as wicked inwardly.

This is why the living creatures seen by the prophet are said to be full of eyes all around and within (Ezek. I, 18; X, 12). Whoever arranges his outward conduct honorably but neglects his inward life has eyes all around but not within. But all the saints, because they watch over their external conduct so as to offer good examples to their brothers, and vigilantly attend to their inner life because they prepare themselves to be irreproachable before the sight of the inward Judge, are said to have eyes all around and within.

They chiefly order themselves in their inward life so as to please God, just as the Psalmist also says concerning the holy Church: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV, 14) [Note: [Col. 0109D] Corb. Germ., two Laud., Germ., all the Norman manuscripts, etc., have “daughters of kings.” In the Vulgate and the Hebrew text: “of the king”].

But because she also guards her outward conduct as irreproachable, he rightly adds concerning her: “She is clothed round about in golden fringes, adorned with variety” [Note: [Col. 0109D] So Bellov. and the praised ancient manuscripts and editions; the recent editions have “with various adornments”], so that she is beautiful inwardly to herself and outwardly to others—advancing herself through inward glory and instructing others through the external examples of her works.

Therefore blessed Job should speak from himself, and speak in the person of the universal Church: “When God was secretly in my tabernacle.” To show how much she had advanced inwardly, he declares that God was secretly in his tabernacle. To show also how greatly he guarded works of righteousness outwardly, he adds:

# CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 5

“When the Almighty was with me, and my children were around me.”

## 21. While the Saints Attend to God Within, the Wicked Seek Only What Is Outward. They Do Not Possess Religion but Pretend to It

All who fear the divine commandments become God’s tabernacle. Hence, as we have already said above (No. 6), Truth itself says concerning one who keeps his commandments: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23) [Note: [Col. 0109D] The editions add “my.” It is not found in any of our manuscripts except Germ. and Corb. Germ.].

But the perverse, because they do not desire inward things, pour themselves outward into their thoughts. Hence it is said to them through the prophet: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. XLVI, 8). And again: “Woe to those who think of useless things” (Mic. II, 1).

People fear those whom they see bodily in their actions, and do not reckon that God is present to them, whom they do not see. In contrast, it is said in praise of the righteous man, when he despised the king of Egypt and obeyed God’s commandments: “He endured as seeing the invisible one” (Heb. XI, 27). He treated the perverse earthly ruler as though he did not see him, because he cast him away from the eyes of his heart. But he endured the invisible King as though seeing him, because he did not turn away the eye of his mind from the sight of fear of him [Note: [Col. 0110D] Vindoc. has “from the sight of love”].

Thus the holy Church, caught up in great tribulations at that time, when she sees many departing from God through perverse thought, plainly sees that their dwelling-place of mind remains empty as God departs from it; and, rightly lamenting, says: “When God was secretly in my tabernacle.”

These words also not undeservedly lament religious pretense, because even now some people do not desire to be Christians but only to be seen as Christians. For such people God is in public, not in secret. But the holy Church desires to have God in secret, because she regards as truly faithful those whom she knows to remain with a full heart in the life of faith.

According to the external rectitude of her strength, she also says: “When the Almighty was with me, and my children were around me.” Those are called children who serve the heavenly commandments. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I and my children whom God has given me” (Isa. VIII, 18) [Note: [Col. 0109D] Norm. has “the Lord”]. And again in the Gospel: “Children, do you have anything to eat?” (John XXI, 5) [Note: [Col. 0109D] Turon. has “food”].

Now her children are around her, because in nearly all nations there are people who keep the heavenly commandments and obey the rules of spiritual discipline. Such children will be lacking then, when those who are found to be wicked despise her spiritual commandments. It follows:

# CHAPTER XIV [Rec. X]

### VERSE 6

“When I washed my feet with butter.”

## 22. The Lord’s Feet Are the Preachers, Whom He Anoints and Cleanses

Since we have often said that Christ and the Church are one person—Christ being the head of this body and the Church the body of that head—these words must be understood in one way according to the voice of the head and in another according to the voice of the body.

Whose feet, then, should we understand as the Lord’s feet except the holy preachers? Concerning them he says: “And I will walk in them” (Lev. XXVI, 12) [Note: [Col. 0110D] So Laud., Germ., Corb. Germ., Norm., and later editions; other witnesses read “and I will walk”]. The feet are therefore washed with butter because the holy preachers are filled with the richness of good works.

For, as we have already said above (Book I, no. 30), scarcely does preaching pass by without some fault being committed. Any preacher is drawn either to a small degree of indignation when he is despised or to a small degree of glory when he is honored by his hearers. Hence the apostles’ feet were washed, so that they might be cleansed from whatever slight contamination had been contracted in the very act of preaching, as though from dust gathered on a journey.

And blessed James says: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers” (James III, 1). And shortly afterward: “For we all offend in many things” (ibid., 2).

The feet are therefore washed with butter because the accumulated dust of the glory of preaching is moistened and cleansed by the richness of good works. Or certainly the feet are washed with butter when the holy preachers receive from their hearers the support due to them. The richness of good works displayed by their disciples refreshes those whom the labor of preaching has wearied—not because they preach in order to be fed, but because they are fed in order to preach; that is, so that they may continue preaching [Note: [Col. 0111D] One Laud. has “so that the preachers may persist”; another, “so that they may devote themselves to preaching”]. The preacher’s activity must not pass into an intention to obtain food; rather, the ministry of support must serve the usefulness of preaching [Note: [Col. 0111D] Corb. Germ., 1 Laud., and Norm. have “the activity of preaching”].

Therefore good preachers do not offer preaching for the sake of food; they receive food for the sake of preaching. And whenever necessities are provided to preachers by their hearers, they do not usually rejoice in the gift of possessions but in the reward of those who provide them [Note: [Col. 0111D] Vindoc. and 2 Laud. have “but in the reward of the confessors”].

Hence Paul says: “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. IV, 17). The gift is the thing itself that is provided; the fruit of the gift is when something is provided with a kindly mind and in the hope of a future reward. Thus we understand the gift in the thing and the fruit in the heart.

And because the Apostle was nourished more by the reward than by the gift of his disciples, he declares that he seeks not the gift but the fruit. Hence he immediately adds, saying: “I have all things and abound” (ibid., 18).

The feet are therefore washed with butter when the holy preachers, wearied by preaching itself, as we have said, are refreshed by the good works of their hearers. That man had anointed weary feet with butter who heard: “The hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother” (Philem. 7). The foot that was held in chains had been anointed with this butter when he said: “May the Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain” (I Tim. II, 16).

If, therefore, we consider these words as spoken by the voice of the head, we rightly understand the feet, as has been said, to be the preachers.

## [Vet. XII.] 23. The Feet of the Church Are the Inferior Ministers Who Attend to Earthly Matters

But if we must understand these words as spoken by the voice of the body alone, then the feet of the Church are certainly the ministers of lower works. While they carry out externally those things that are required for necessary uses, they cling to the earth like feet through their final ministry.

Those who preside and devote themselves to the study of doctrine ought, with attentive care, to seek out the hearts of those occupied with such matters and, through frequent admonition, supply them with the infusion of that richness which the teachers themselves receive in leisure [Note: [Col. 0111D] 1 Laud. has “by calling”]. For because the members of one body are concerned for one another, just as our outward extremities are supported by the ministries of those people, so it is necessary that their inward parts be filled by our exertions [Note: [Col. 0111D] Some editions have “our externals,” which better corresponds to what follows, “their interior parts”; but we follow the manuscripts and the ancient editions, rather than conjectures. Our reading is confirmed by the word “extremities,” repeated several times below].

Therefore, when the holy teachers preach the anointing of the Lord’s incarnation to certain people devoted to the lower ministries, they wash their feet with the butter of speech.

The feet are also often torn by the roughness of the journey. Hence it is altogether difficult to travel the path of this life amid earthly activities without suffering wounds from the labor of the journey. When vigilant superiors call their hearers, who are intent on external concerns, back to their hearts so that they may recognize the evils they have committed amid those very lawful activities and grieve over what they recognize, they wash their feet with butter, because they supply the wounds of those hearers with the ointments of penitential lamentation [Note: [Col. 0112D] Gemet. has “the laments of repentance”].

Let the Church, therefore, then grievously afflicted, remember how in the time of her peace she also cleansed her most remote members within herself through the word of exhortation, and let her say: “When I washed my feet with butter.”

It is delightful to consider this admirably in blessed Job, who, amid so many concerns with possessions, so many affections for his children, and so many preoccupations with sacrifices, preached the good things of the life to come to those subject to him, however lowly they might be, so that he might instruct them concerning heavenly things—those who served him in earthly works.

What do we bishops say to this, who do not take care to impart the word of life to those entrusted to us, when neither the status of a married man nor the great burden of possessions was able to keep a married man from the office of preaching? [Note: [Col. 0112D] So all the manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and the ancient editions. In 2 Laud. the phrase begins with “from the word of preaching”; in Germ., Corb. Germ., and the recent editions, with “from the butter of preaching.”]

[Rec. XI.] But, preserving the truth of the historical sense, let us return to the words of the holy Church, which speaks through blessed Job—that is, through the mouth of one of her members—of the magnitude of what she will suffer at the end of time, when she remembers what has passed, when, through the richness of the word, the life of those who serve was washed [Note: [Col. 0112D] Bellov. has “when the life of those who work passed by”]. And, pursuing more fully the vigilance of her preachers, she adds:

# CHAPTER XV

### Ibid.

“And the rock poured out streams of oil for me.”

24. In the Church, the streams of oil are either sacred doctrines or the grace of the Holy Spirit.---Because Christ is understood by the name “rock,” the outstanding preacher declares, saying: “The rock, however, was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). This rock now pours forth streams of oil for the use of the holy Church, because the Lord, speaking in it, causes the pronouncements of inward anointing to flow forth. From this rock there came a stream of oil: the book of Matthew, the book of Mark, the book of Luke, and the book of John. In the various regions of this world where it issued its pronouncements, this rock poured forth so many streams of oil through the mouths of all the apostles. Even now a stream of oil flows from this rock as often as the things said about Christ in the ancient books are explained by the Holy Spirit to the minds of hearers who are to be anointed. And they are called streams of oil because they run down and anoint. Whoever is dipped in them is anointed; whoever is anointed is inwardly enriched. [Note: So the German, Gemet., together with other Norm., the two Laud., Turon., and the old printed editions. In the later editions the first occurrence of “is anointed” is omitted. It is not worth mentioning that the manuscripts read *tinguitur*, *unquitur* for *tingitur*, *ungitur*.] Concerning this richness the Psalmist says: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62:6).

The name “oil” may also designate the anointing of the Holy Spirit, concerning which it is said through the prophet: “The yoke shall rot because of the face of the oil” (Isa. 10:27). The yoke rots before the face of the oil because, when we are anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit, we are freed from the servitude of our captivity; [Note: Utic. formerly read “captivity.”] and when the proud domination of the evil spirit is driven away, the yoke is broken by which the necks of our freedom were being oppressed. Again, concerning this oil it is written: “A vineyard was made for my beloved, on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5:1). [Note: “my” is absent in most manuscripts.] The “son of oil” is called the faithful people, who are generated for the faith of God by the inward anointing of the Holy Spirit. [Note: The second Laud.: “because faith in God is generated from the inward anointing of the Holy Spirit.”]

Therefore, when the holy Church is then weighed down by many tribulations, let it recall the gifts of the Spirit and the wondrous pronouncements it now possesses, and lament its silence, saying: “The rock poured forth streams of oil for me.” To these words it fittingly adds:

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERSES 7–10.**—“When I went forth to the gate of the city, and in the square they prepared a chair for me. Young men saw me and hid themselves, and the elders, rising, stood. Princes ceased speaking and put their finger over their mouth. Leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.”

25. Good works and the chair of teaching are the Church’s insignia.---It was the custom of the ancients for elders to stand at the gate and judge the cases of those entering, so that the people of the city might be peaceful in proportion as discordant persons were not permitted to enter it. But, honoring sacred history, we hold it certain that blessed Job did these things in defense of justice, and we are led to investigate the mysteries of allegory.

What, then, is signified by the gate of the city except every good action, through which the soul enters the assembly of the heavenly kingdom? Hence the Prophet also says: “You who raise me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15). The gates of death are wicked actions, which drag one toward destruction. Since Zion means “watchtower,” by the gates of Zion we understand good actions, through which we enter our heavenly homeland so that we may contemplate the glory of our King.

What, moreover, is signified by the chair except the authority of teaching? In Greek usage, *platea* means “breadth.” [Note: The printed editions read *lingua* (“language”), against the manuscripts.] Now the holy Church proceeds to the gate of the city because, in order to obtain entrance to the heavenly kingdom, it manifests itself in holy actions. A chair is prepared for it in the square because, in the breadth of great authority, it displays the freedom of its teaching. For it publicly proclaims what it rightly thinks, and sits, as it were, in a chair in the square, since it fears nothing from its preaching and, oppressed by no one’s terrors, does not hide itself in silence. Does it not preside publicly for teaching, supported at once by the truth of its judgment and by the power to teach? [Note: Thus Germ., Corb. Germ., 1 Laud., Bellov., Norm., etc. The Vulgate editions add *super*, which editors thought should be supplied. But, as already noted in Book I, no. 23, the ancients used *cathedram sedere* (“to sit a chair”). 2 Laud. has *cathedra sedet*; the same manuscripts shortly below have *cathedram sederet* or *cathedra sederet*.]

But when it proceeded to the gate and sat in a chair in the square, it adds what was done by the insignificant and by the great, saying:

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 8.**—“Young men saw me and hid themselves, and the elders, rising, stood.”

26. The immature fear the Church’s vigor and uprightness; the mature love them.---If we attend to the historical sense, we believe what it said; if to the allegorical sense, we see what it foretold. Those are commonly called young men who are not weighed down by any seriousness of counsel. [Note: The printed editions, together with the German, have “are supported by the seriousness of counsel,” contrary to the manuscripts Norm., Vindoc., Laud., Turon., and Corb. Germ.] The Sacred Scripture, however, does not usually call those elders who are so merely by the length of time, but those mature in the greatness of their character. Hence a certain wise man says: “For old age is honorable, not that which is of long duration, nor counted by number of years. The gray hairs of a person are understanding, and a blameless life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4:8). Hence the Lord also rightly says to Moses: “Gather to me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people” (Num. 11:16). What else is required in them than old age of heart, when those are ordered to be chosen who are known to be elders? [Note: Vindoc.: “if they are elders.”] For if bodily old age were sought in them, they could be known by as many as could see them. But when it is said, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is plainly clear that old age of mind, not of body, is being declared necessary. [Old XIV.]

Therefore, young men now see the holy Church and hide themselves, while the elders rise and stand before it, because the immature fear its vigor and uprightness, whereas the mature glorify them. [Note: Later editions, together with the German, have “every frivolous person.” Others have “every frivolous person is,” or “every frivolous person indeed is who flees.” We follow the manuscripts Norm., Laudun., Corb. Germ., and others.] Every frivolous person flees; the serious and perfect, by rising in reverence, honor it through the merits of their life. The perfect love its discipline; the imperfect criticize it. Young men therefore see it and hide themselves because they fear being exposed in their secret actions. The elders, however, rise and stand because all the perfect, out of humility, show how far they have advanced in good works.

But since it speaks of its own people, let it also tell how it is feared by outsiders:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSES 9–10.**—“Princes ceased speaking and put their finger over their mouth. Leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.”

27. Heretics were forced to be silent in the time of St. Gregory. Heretics agree in guilt but disagree in doctrines. In the Church’s adversity, heretics preach freely.---Who else can be understood here as leaders or princes except the authors of heretical wickedness? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Contention was poured out upon their princes, and they led them astray in a pathless place, and not on the way” (Ps. 106:40). For, since they do not fear perversely interpreting God’s dispensation, they drag their subject peoples not along the way that is Christ, but into a pathless place. It is rightly said that contention was poured out upon them, because they contradict one another through their own mutual arguments.

Arius, accepting three persons in the Godhead, also believed in three gods. Against him, Sabellius, accepting one God, believed there was one person. In their midst the holy Church, holding undeviatingly to the straight path of its preaching, asserts one God and three persons against Sabellius, and, asserting three persons, confesses one God against Arius.

Because Manichaeus discovered that virginity was praised in sacred eloquence, he condemned marriage. Conversely, because Jovinianus learned that marriage was permitted, he despised the purity of virginity. [Note: 1 Laud. reads *Jovianus*; Germ. reads *Jobianus*.] Thus, whenever heretics are confounded by their perverse understanding, their wickedness agrees with itself in guilt but differs in doctrine.

The holy Church, on the other hand, walks in ordered peace through the conflicts between both sides. It knows how to accept higher goods while also honoring lower ones, so that it neither equates the highest with the lowest nor despises the lowest while honoring the highest.

Now, therefore, the princes of heretical peoples, weighing the authority of the holy Church, cease speaking and place a finger over their mouth, signifying that they are restrained from false complaints not by the force of speech but by the hand of power. The leaders restrain their voice because those who strive to drag erring peoples after them now dare not speak perversely: they are checked both by the weight of authority and by the force of reason. Their tongue clings to their throat because, although they do not dare to speak perversely with a free voice, inwardly they conceal within themselves everything false that they contrive to propose against the true faith. [Note: Others, together with Corb. Germ., have “against the true faith.”]

Recalling these times, discovered through the tribulation that followed, the Church laments, saying: “When I went forth to the gate of the city, and in the square they prepared a chair for me. Young men saw me and hid themselves, and the elders, rising, stood. Princes ceased speaking and put their finger over their mouth. Leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.”

As though it openly said: “When I was permitted to preach in a public voice, everyone who was not subject to the truth was terrified by me. [Note: Most manuscripts read “with a free voice.”] At that time, when the holy Church is pressed by adversity, license to speak is granted to every wicked preacher.” [Old XV.]

Jeremiah saw this long beforehand and said: “Even the jackals uncover their breast; they nurse their young” (Lam. 4:3). What does he call jackals except heretics, who bear a human face but, through impiety, possess bestial hearts? They uncover their breast when they freely preach their error. They nurse their young when, by insinuating perversities, they strengthen the childish souls of their evil followers through nourishment in impiety.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XIX [Rec. XII]

**VERSE 11.**—“The ear that heard blessed me, and the eye that saw bore witness to me.”

28. We ought to bear witness to the Church by living well.---When blessed Job declares that he was blessed by those who heard him and that those who saw him bore witness to him, he shows what he was in speech and what he was in conduct. For he is not yet perfect in conduct if the wickedness of his tongue still contradicts him; nor is he praiseworthy in speech if he does not show by his deeds what he says. [Note: Gemet. and others read “what the mouth speaks.”] Thus, in order to testify that blessed Job possessed both qualities, having been tested by the rebukes of his friends, he makes clear that he was held in reverence both by those who heard and by those who saw him.

If we refer this to the voice of the holy Church, that person blesses its words who completes in action what he has heard. He bears witness to it who responds to its example by living well. For he truly sees the holy Church whose life testifies that he sees it. The uprightness of the good within it is discerned for this purpose: so that whoever sees it may be corrected from his own wickedness. Therefore, one who has not been corrected from evil does not yet see the good within the holy Church.

But how witness is borne to it is shown when he adds:

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSES 12–13.**—“Because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow.”

29. The Church both feeds and protects its children.---These are works of great mercy: to deliver the poor man who cries out, to provide help for the orphan, to rescue one who is perishing, and to console the widow’s heart. Earlier it was said what he offered through teaching. He said: “The ear that heard blessed me.” Now he relates what he bestowed through mercy, saying: “Because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper.” [Note: Laud. and Norm.: “who had no helper.”] His speech necessarily agrees with his works. Blessed Job both displayed these things to his subjects and signified that they were to be displayed through the holy Church. [Note: Several manuscripts: “both of which.”]

The Church now exercises both without ceasing: it feeds its children by speaking and protects them by defending them, so that it satisfies the good through words and shields them from evils through its advocacy.

It is well written: “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation, producing seed, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind” (Gen. 1:11). [Note: Norm. reads “fruit-bearing.”] This was truly accomplished in such a way that it signified something that was also truly to be done. The earth figures the Church, which refreshes us with the food of the word and guards us with the shelter of its protection; it feeds by speaking and protects by helping, so that it brings forth not only the grass of refreshment but also, with the fruit of works, the tree of protection.

[Old XVI.] 30. In the rulers of the Church, vigor must be neither rigid nor gentleness lax.---I also see that those who govern peoples must consider what was said earlier: “Young men saw me and hid themselves,” and what is now added: “I consoled the heart of the widow.” What discipline of government, that young men hide themselves before him; what gentleness of compassion, that the hearts of widows are consoled through him!

For some are so strict that they lose every kindness of gentleness, while others are so gentle that they abandon the rights of strict governance. [Distinction 45, canon *Sunt namque*.] [Note: Some manuscripts: “the kindness of gentleness.”] Therefore, all rulers must hold fast to both with the greatest care: in the vigor of discipline, they must not abandon the kindness of gentleness, nor, in gentleness, the strictness of discipline. Thus, when they correct the stubborn, they must not become hardened against compassionate pity; and when they console the weak, they must not soften the vigor of discipline. Let the vigor of discipline govern gentleness, and let gentleness adorn vigor. Let each commend the other, so that vigor is neither rigid nor gentleness lax.

31. The Church performs works of compassion bodily and spiritually.---The works of compassion mentioned above the holy Church performs bodily and does not cease to perform spiritually. It delivers the poor man who cries out when it releases the sins he has committed for the sinner who begs forgiveness. Concerning such poor people it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). The cry of such poor people is voiced by the Psalmist: “Let your mercy quickly go before us, for we have become exceedingly poor” (Ps. 78:8).

It delivers the orphan who has no helper when each person, after the ancient father—the devil—has died, runs to the bosom of the holy Church and finds in it the help of exhortation, having now fled the desires of the pursuing world. The name “orphan” may also be understood of any faithful person because of the death of a good father, deprived for a time of his sight, although not deprived of consolation.

The blessing of the perishing comes upon it when it anticipates the sinner’s destruction and, through holy exhortations, leads him back from the pit of guilt. Hence it is written: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death” [Note: 1 Laud.: “has saved.”] “and will cover a multitude of sins” [Note: German and Norm.: “and covers”] (Jas. 5:20). If it is a great reward to rescue from death flesh that will one day die, how much greater is the merit of freeing from death a soul that will live forever in the heavenly homeland?

He consoles the widow’s heart when he recounts to each faithful soul the Lord’s eternal rewards, recalling, as it were, the good things of her husband. Because the soul is spiritually joined to him, she is called a widow when he has died, but she is revived by the words of the holy Church through his resurrection. The widow’s heart therefore receives great consolation when the faithful soul learns from the Church’s words something about the coming of the one to whom it is spiritually joined.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 14.**—“I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself with it as with a garment.” [Note: German and 2 Laud.: “and it clothed me as with a garment”; the same reading occurs below.]

32. No good works exist if they are stained by certain wicked works.---When we are clothed with a garment, we are surrounded on every side. Therefore, the person who clothes himself with justice as with a garment is one who protects himself on every side with good works and leaves no part of his conduct naked before sin. For whoever is just in some actions but unjust in others has covered one side and left another bare. His works are no longer good when they are polluted by other wicked works that have arisen.

Hence Solomon says: “Whoever offends in one thing will lose many good things” (Eccl. 9:18). Hence James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all of it” (Jas. 2:10). [Note: Utic. and others read: “James says, ‘Whoever [keeps] the whole law.’”] He carefully explained this judgment of his when he added: “For he who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Now if you do not commit adultery but kill, you have become a transgressor of the law” (ibid., 11).

[Old XVII.] 33. Vigilance and protection must be applied everywhere. It is useless for the rest to be fortified when even one entrance is opened to the enemy.---With the eyes of the heart extended in every direction, we must apply vigilance everywhere. Hence Solomon rightly says: “Guard your heart with every care, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). [Note: 1 Laud. and Turon. read “he first said every care.”] For, intending to say “guard,” he first said “with every,” so that each person might carefully examine himself on every side and, as long as he is in this life, know that he is stationed in battle against spiritual enemies. He must not lose through one set of actions the reward he gathers through another; he must not close the doors to the enemy on one side and open an entrance elsewhere.

If a city were fortified against lurking enemies by a great embankment, surrounded by strong walls, and secured on every side by sleepless vigilance, but one small opening were left unguarded through negligence, the enemy would undoubtedly enter through it, though he seemed to have been excluded everywhere.

Let us hear what defenses that Pharisee employed who went up into the temple to pray: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 18:12). He began with the words: “I give thanks to you,” and certainly established great fortifications. But let us see where he left an opening unguarded for the lurking enemy: “Because I am not like this tax collector” (ibid., 11). Behold, through pride he opened the city of his heart to the lurking enemies, which he had closed in vain through fasting and almsgiving.

The rest was fortified in vain when one place, through which the enemy had an entrance, was not fortified. He gave thanks rightly, but perversely exalted himself above the tax collector. By exalting himself he betrayed the city of his heart, which he had preserved by abstaining and giving. By abstinence he conquered gluttony; by generosity he overcame stinginess and suppressed greed. Through what labors do we believe this was accomplished? Yet how many labors fell, struck down by one vice; how many good things were killed by the sword of a single fault!

Therefore, we must diligently perform good works and also carefully guard ourselves in our thoughts from those very good works, lest, if they raise the mind, they cease to be good—not serving their author but serving pride.

[Rec. XIII.] 34. Pride must be avoided above all.---On this matter we do not act improperly if we produce testimony from books that, although not canonical, were nevertheless published for the edification of the Church. [Note: That is, books not included in the Hebrew canon because they were not written in Hebrew; on this matter see the general preface, where the teaching of St. Gregory is discussed.] Eleazar struck an elephant in battle and felled it, but he died beneath the one he had destroyed (1 Macc. 6:46). Whom, then, does this man signify, whom his own victory crushed, except those who overcome vices but, by becoming proud, succumb beneath the very things they subdue? For he dies beneath the enemy he has cast down who is lifted up by the guilt he has overcome.

We must therefore consider most carefully that good things cannot benefit us if we do not guard against the evils that creep in. Everything done is lost if it is not carefully preserved in humility. Hence it is well said of our first parent: “The Lord placed him in the paradise of delight, to work and to guard it” (Gen. 2:15). He works who does the good that is commanded, but he does not guard what he has worked when what is forbidden creeps in upon him.

Blessed Job, therefore, because he had covered himself on every side with good works, says: “I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself with it as with a garment.” Immediately it is added:

## CHAPTER XXII [Old XVIII]

**IBID.**—“And with my judgment as with a diadem.”

35. The just carefully consider what they owe to God and to their neighbor.---The judgments of the just are rightly compared to a diadem because, through the glory of great works, they lead to the crown of recompense. These judgments they conduct inwardly with themselves every day: they carefully examine what they owe to God and to their neighbor, strongly kindle themselves to do good, and strictly rebuke themselves for the evils they have committed.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “The thoughts of the just are judgments” (Prov. 12:5). [Note: German, Norm., Laud., Turon., and others have this reading; in the printed editions, “the just” or “these” is read instead of “inwardly.”] Within, they return from all worldly commotion to their hearts; there they ascend the tribunal of the mind, set themselves and their neighbor before their eyes, and bring forward the rule of the Testament, which says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12). [Note: Some editions translate: “They transfer the person of their neighbor to themselves.”]

They transfer the person of their neighbor into themselves and carefully consider what they would justly want done or not done to them if they were in that person’s place. Thus, by strict law and judgment, they examine their own case and that of their neighbor in the court of the heart according to the tablets of divine law.

It is rightly said, therefore: “The thoughts of the just are judgments,” because the innermost movement of their heart is like a certain scale of judicial power. When these judgments have been completed, since they do not seek recompense below, their judgments are rightly compared to a diadem. A diadem is placed on the upper part of the body. The judgment of the just is therefore called a diadem because through it they desire to be rewarded not in earthly and lowly things but above.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Rec. XIV]

**VERSES 15–16.**—“I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know.”

36. Good works, though to be hidden through humility, must sometimes be made public out of necessity.---The reader’s mind may perhaps ask why blessed Job enumerates his virtues so carefully. It is characteristic of holy men to conceal the good things they have done, lest they fall into the snare of pride. Hence Truth itself says: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1).

For this reason, when he illuminated two blind men sitting beside the road, he commanded them: “See that no one knows” (Matt. 9:30). Immediately afterward it is written that, when they departed, they spread his fame throughout that whole region.

But we must ask what this means: the Omnipotent, for whom willing and being able are the same, both wished his virtues to be kept silent and yet was reported by those who had been illuminated, as though against his will. It means that he gave an example to his servants who follow him: they should desire their virtues to be hidden, yet, so that others may progress through their example, their virtues should be disclosed against their will. By concealing their deeds they should guard themselves; but when they are unwillingly disclosed, they should transmit good examples to their neighbors.

Let them therefore be hidden by deliberate intention and made public by necessity. Let their concealment be their own protection, and their publication the benefit of others.

Again, it is written: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a measure, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. [Note: 2 Laud. reads “under the measure.”] Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:15–16).

Sometimes holy men are compelled to do good before others or to recount their own deeds to others. But they refer everything to this end: not they themselves through those works, but their Father who is in heaven, should be glorified. When they preach holy things, their preaching may perhaps be despised because their life is unknown. Therefore, they are compelled to speak of their life so that they may be able to change the lives of their hearers. They recount their deeds so that they may be held in reverence; they seek to be revered so that they may be heard with respect.

For it is written: “When the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels also rose at the same time” (Ezek. 1:19), because, when the minds of hearers receive the life of preachers, they necessarily also admire the force of their preaching. [Note: German, Laud., Norm., Corb. Germ., and most of the old editions: “when they receive the life.”]

[Old XIX.] 37. Saint Paul confirmed this by his own example. Those who imitate him do not serve pride but humility.---This is why good preachers both flee honor on account of pride and nevertheless wish to be honored for the sake of imitation. Thus the apostle Paul, speaking to his disciples, both fled honor and showed how much honor he deserved.

For when he said to the Thessalonians: “For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with an opportunity for greed—God is witness” (1 Thess. 2:5), he continued: “Nor seeking glory from people, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ, but we became little ones in your midst” (ibid., 6–7). [Note: Norm., Corb. Germ., and many others: “nor seeking.”] [Note: Beccens., Utic., Prat., and Corb. Germ. have “to be held in honor,” as is also read in many printed editions. In the Vulgate we read “to be a burden,” to which the Greek text also corresponds, although not wholly contrary to the other reading; for the Greek word *baros* (βάρος) means not only “burden” or “weight,” but also “gravity” or “authority.” Erasmus translates: “although we could have been in a position of authority.”]

Again, to the Corinthians, fleeing honor, he says: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5). Yet, when he saw them deviating from the path of true faith through the persuasion of false apostles, he showed them with the greatest emphasis how worthy of honor he was, saying: “In whatever anyone dares—in folly I speak—I also dare. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? As one less wise I speak: I more” (2 Cor. 11:21–23).

He also adds that the secrets of the third heaven had been opened to him and that, having been caught up, he had entered the mysteries of paradise.

Behold: fleeing honor, he proclaims himself the servant of his disciples. Behold: seeking honor for the benefit of his hearers, he places the merits of his life above the false apostles. The outstanding teacher acted so that, when his own character was recognized, both the life and the speech of the wicked preachers might become contemptible by comparison. He would have commended them if he had hidden himself; and, by not showing himself, he would have given error an opportunity.

In a wondrous manner, therefore, he both displays the grace of humility and seeks an increase of usefulness: he proclaims himself the servant of his disciples and shows himself superior to his adversaries. He shows the disciples what humility he has received; he shows his adversaries what sublimity he possesses. [Note: Other witnesses read “is shown” in place of “is recognized.”]

He makes known to his adversaries what they possess from a gift; he makes known to his disciples what he remains like within in thought; he makes known to his adversaries what he appears like outwardly in action. [Note: Thus Laud., Bellov., Turon., Corb. Germ., and Vindoc., followed by the old Paris edition of 1495 and the Basel edition of 1514. In Paris 1518 it reads: “It becomes known to the adversaries how strong he appears in action; it becomes known to the disciples what he possesses by birth, which is vicious.” In the recent editions, more suitably: “It becomes known to the disciples what he remains like within in thought; it becomes known to the adversaries what he appears like outwardly in action.” This reading is found in German, Utic., and other Norman manuscripts.]

Holy men, therefore, when they are compelled to recount the good things they do, do not serve pride but usefulness. Hence blessed Job opens his deeds to his friends, who were unjustly rebuking him and therefore did not know his good works, so that they might learn not to rise up by rebuking his life, but silently to imitate it. Yet, as we have already said, the despair introduced by their rebukes compelled him to recall his deeds to mind. For amid so many pains from his wounds and words of despair, when he recounts the good things he has done, he reforms his spirit, which had collapsed under words and blows, toward hope.

Let him therefore declare the good things he has done, so that amid all the evils he hears he may not be forced to despair of himself: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.”

38. Works of justice must precede works of mercy. Whoever gives alms but does not abstain from sin gives his property to God and himself to sin.---When we consider examples of holy conduct, we must first observe the proper order of narration, so that works of justice are described before works of mercy. For the person who does good and compassionate things acts well when he knows first to preserve what is just, so that the stream of mercy poured upon his neighbors may be drawn from the fountain of justice. [Old XX.]

Many people bestow what seem to be works of mercy upon their neighbors but do not abandon their practices of injustice. If they truly desired to show mercy to their neighbors, they should first have shown mercy to themselves by living justly. Hence it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24). Whoever wishes to show mercy to his neighbor must necessarily draw the beginning of mercy from himself. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:19). How, then, is a person compassionate toward another when, by continuing to live unjustly, he is still impious toward himself?

Hence a certain wise man says: “Whoever is wicked toward himself, to whom will he be good?” (Sir. 14:5).

For mercy to be fully extended outwardly to those in need, two things are necessary: a person to provide it and a possession to be provided. But a person is incomparably better than a possession. Therefore, whoever gives external property to a needy neighbor but does not guard his own life from wickedness gives his property to God and himself to sin. He offers the lesser thing to the Creator and preserves the greater thing for iniquity.

Accordingly, blessed Job first rightly says: “I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself with it as with a garment; and with my judgment as with a diadem.” [Note: 1 Laud.: “and it clothed me as with a garment.” In Bellov.: “and I dressed myself.”] Then he adds: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.” For an offering of true uprightness is presented to God when branches of compassion grow from the root of justice.

But since, in the work of mercy itself, the inner disposition is usually weighed more than the deed by the inward Judge, it should be noted that he asserts he was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. [Note: German, Bellov., and Norm.: “an eye to the blind … a foot to the lame.”] By saying this, he clearly indicates that he had personally extended his hand to the one and supported the other by carrying him. From this it is inferred how greatly the compassion of his heart poured itself out over the needy and the weak. Hence he adds: “I was a father to the poor.”

[Col. 0123B] **39. The Church gives sight to the blind and supports the lame.**—If we refer these words, by a typological interpretation, to the voice of the holy Church, she herself is the eye of the blind, because she shines through the word; she herself is the foot of the lame, because she supports through assistance. By preaching she gives light to the blind, while by helping she sustains the lame. For the blind person is one who still does not see where he should go; the lame person, however, is one who cannot go where he sees. Sin is frequently committed either through ignorance or through weakness, so that a person either does not know what he ought to will, or cannot accomplish everything he wills. Against this it is rightly said through the Psalmist: “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Ps. XXVI, 1). Because the Lord supplies both knowledge and strength, he is called “light” against ignorance and “salvation” against weakness. Hence it is also said of the wicked: “Let their ways become darkness and slippery ground” (Ps. XXXIV, 6), so that through the darkness they may not see where they ought to go, and, even if they should see what is right, they may nevertheless be unable to stand in it because of the slippery ground. [Note: Germ., 1 Laud., and Corb. Germ.: *quo* (“where/by which”); 2 Laud.: *qua* (“by which/where”), “they do not see where they ought to go, who, even if they see what is right . . . cannot stand.” Norm. likewise.] [Note: The same manuscripts, except Germ.: “this one . . . limps; that one . . . is ignorant.”] These people, therefore, stumble amid good things because of the slippery ground; those people, through the darkness, do not know which good things to pursue. Thus the holy Church, seized by extreme tribulations, remembers former times, when she was accustomed both to enlighten by teaching and to strengthen by helping, and through the mouth of that earlier member of hers speaks, saying: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.”

[Vet. XXI.] **40. The Gentiles are blind, but the Jews are lame.**—Since she gathered two peoples into herself, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, the Gentile may rightly be signified by “the blind,” and the Jewish people by “the lame.” The Gentile, as it were, had no eyes, because, having not received the law, he did not see where he ought to go. In contrast, the Jewish people, though possessing eyes, was lame, because it held to the law by knowing it, but did not extend its step in upright action. For if the Gentile people had not been blind, the prophet would not have said: “The people that sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX, 2). Again, if the Israelite people had not stumbled away from good works, the Psalmist would by no means have said in the voice of the Lord: “The foreign sons have lied to me; the foreign sons have grown old [Note: Germ., the two Laud. manuscripts, Corb. Germ. and Norm.: *inveteraverunt*, “have grown old.”] and have stumbled from their paths” (Ps. XVII, 46). This people is called lame because it did not have a sound step in its conduct, since it refused to use both feet: it received one Testament and rejected the other. When the holy Church receives this people as it comes to her, because she joins the New Testament to the Old Testament that it already possessed, she attaches, as it were, another foot in order to direct its steps.

This faithful people of the holy Church rightly adds: “I was a father to the poor,” because the humble—those who are called “poor in spirit”—are generated through her preaching. But we must weigh carefully the precise words of the history in all these matters. For he says:

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 16.—“I was a father to the poor, and the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently.”**

**41. It is better to do a good work from affection than from command.**—People frequently give much to the poor, not because they love those poor people, but because, if they do not give, they fear the anger of the heavenly Judge. If they did not fear God, they would not wish to give what they possess. And indeed, in a good work, the first step of beginners is that one who does not yet know how to love his neighbor as himself should nevertheless begin to fear the heavenly judgments. Since, therefore, it is one thing to do a good work from command and another to do it also from affection, the holy man, to make known to us the disposition of his action, says: “I was a father to the poor.” [Note: The two Laud. manuscripts, Corb. Germ. and Norm.: “therefore not.”] For he does not testify that he was a patron, or a neighbor, or a helper of the poor, but that he was their father, because by a great service of charity [Note: Gemet.: “by the duty of great charity.”] he turned the practice of mercy into the affection of nature, so that through love he regarded as sons those over whom, as a father, he presided through protection. Since the power of his mercy had imitated nature, he recalls that he was a father to the poor. Here he also adds:

## CHAPTER XXV

**SAME PLACE.—“And the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently.”**

[Col. 0124D] **42. Although no good works are to be neglected, lesser works must nevertheless be placed after more important ones.**—In these words, everything must be considered: how distinctly all things are narrated, and how no reward is omitted by him. He is just in his actions, compassionate toward the weaknesses of his neighbors, and diligent in the affairs of the poor. For one who considers the good things of eternal recompense must apply himself to every matter that will bring a future reward. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Eccl. VII, 19). Hence Paul also says: “Ready for every good work” (II Tim. II, 21).

Yet amid these things we must understand that at times lesser goods are to be passed over for the sake of the usefulness of greater ones. For who does not know that burying the dead is a meritorious good work? And yet a certain man who had asked to be released in order to bury his father was told: “Let the dead bury their dead, but you go and announce the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 60). The service of this ministry had to be placed after the office of preaching, because by the one he would bury the dead in the flesh in the earth, while by the other he would raise the dead in soul to life. Through the prophet it is also said to the leaders of the synagogue: “Seek justice, assist the oppressed” (Isa. I, 17). And yet the apostle Paul says: “Those who are contemptible in the Church, appoint them to judge” (I Cor. VI, 4). For he was arousing his hearers toward the virtue of wisdom, toward kinds of languages, and also toward investigating the mysteries of prophecy, saying: [Note: Vindoc.: “Strive after the better gifts.”] “Strive after spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (I Cor. XIV, 1). But because they would not grasp spiritual gifts if earthly affairs weighed them down, he first said: “Those who are contemptible in the Church, appoint them to judge” (I Cor. VI, 4). It is as though he openly said: Let those who are of lesser merit in the Church and do not possess the powers of great gifts judge earthly affairs, so that lesser goods may be supplied by those who cannot accomplish great things. He calls them contemptible, and yet calls them wise when he says: “Is there not among you anyone wise enough to judge between his brothers?” (Ibid., 5). What else can be inferred from this except that those who have received wisdom in external matters should examine earthly cases? But those who have been enriched with spiritual gifts should certainly not be entangled in earthly business, so that, while they are not compelled to arrange lesser goods, they may be able, through exercise, to serve higher goods.

[Vet. XXII.] **43. Those who cannot act personally are obliged to perform the duties of charity through others.**—But great care must be taken that those who excel in spiritual gifts do not altogether abandon the affairs of their weaker neighbors; rather, they should entrust these matters to others who are suitable to handle them. Thus Moses also appointed seventy men for the people in his place, so that, the more he withdrew from external affairs, the more ardently he might penetrate interior realities. In this way it comes about that great men advance more toward spiritual gifts, since lowly matters do not trample upon their minds; and again, the lesser men in the Church do not live without good works, since in external matters they find right things to do.

For the holy Church is held together by the unity of the faithful just as our body is united by the structure of its members. Some members of the body serve the purpose of looking upon the light, [Col. 0126A] [Note: Germ. and the later printed editions: “others that are not separated from earthly activity.” The manuscripts Corb., Germ., Norm., the two Laud. manuscripts, Vindoc., Turon., and the old edition confirm our reading.] while others are not separated from contact with the earth. The eye is directed toward the light and is guarded from dust so that it may not become blind. The foot, however, performs its duty properly when it does not refuse to receive the dust of the earth. Yet these members of the body are joined together by sharing their functions with one another, so that the foot runs for the eyes and the eye looks out for the foot.

**44. The members of the Church, though distinct in function, are joined by charity.**—Thus the members of the holy Church ought both to be distinct in function and to be joined in charity, so that the great men may carefully watch over the way [Note: Gemet., Utic., and Beccens.: “their life.”] of those who are occupied with earthly affairs, in order that the foot may walk, as it were, toward the light of the eyes; and again, whatever those involved in earthly business do, let them refer it to the benefit of their superiors, so that the foot whose path is watched over may walk not only for itself but also for the eyes. While, therefore, they assist one another through alternating service, it is wonderfully brought about that, because all the elect perform for one another whatever they are able to provide, even those works which they themselves cannot do become their works.

**45.
