When necessity urges, contemplation must be interrupted so that one may serve the usefulness of one’s neighbor.**—But amid these things we must understand that, when there are no suitable people to attend to the external affairs of their neighbors, even those who are filled with spiritual gifts must stoop to the weakness and earthly needs of others and, insofar as they can appropriately do so, serve them through a condescension of charity. The mind should not become weary if its understanding, always intent upon contemplating spiritual things, is sometimes bent down, as though diminished, to arrange lesser matters, since that Word through whom all created things subsist, in order to benefit human beings, by assuming humanity, willed to be made for a little while lower than the angels. [Note: In most manuscripts, “from.”] What wonder is it, then, if a human being draws himself down for the sake of another human being, when the Creator of human beings and angels assumed the form of a human being for the sake of human beings? Yet his understanding is not diminished when it is so drawn down, because he penetrates higher things all the more subtly insofar as, more humbly, for love of the Creator, he does not disdain lower things. What is unworthy or difficult for us if we guide the mind above and below, when with the same hand of the body we wash the face and put shoes on the foot?

Blessed Job, therefore, because while doing great things he did not despise lesser ones, says: [Vet. XXIII.] “And the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently.”

[Col. 0126D] **46. Let us not be hasty in judgments. Greater crimes should be believed slowly; but when recognized, they should be punished more quickly.**—In this matter I see that we must take care never to be hasty in pronouncing judgment, lest we rashly judge matters that have not been investigated, lest any evils we hear move us, and lest we indiscriminately believe statements without proof. We certainly fear committing this if we weigh more carefully the deeds of our Creator. For, in order to restrain us from issuing a hasty judgment, although all things are naked and open to his eyes, he nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay. He says: “The outcry of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave; I will descend and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII, 20). [Note: Gemet. and most Norman manuscripts: “and of Gomorrah.”]

The almighty Lord [2, q. 1, c. “Deus omnipotens”], who knows all things, why does he appear to doubt before the proof, unless to set before us an example of gravity, so that we do not presume to believe human evils before proving them? Behold, through angels he descends to learn the evils, and immediately strikes the criminals. He who is patient, he who is gentle, he of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquillity” (Wis. XII, 18), he of whom it is again written, “The Lord is patient, but he repays” (Ecclus. V, 4)—when he found them entangled in so great a crime, as though he had set aside his patience, he did not wish to await the day of the final judgment for vengeance, but anticipated the day of judgment by striking them with the fire of judgment.

Behold: when he heard the evil, he believed it, as it were, with difficulty; yet, when he discovered its truth, he struck without delay, so that he might give us an example: greater crimes should be believed slowly when they are heard, but punished more quickly when they are truly recognized.

Concerned with this diligence, blessed Job says: “And the case that I did not know I investigated most diligently.” These words can also, not inappropriately, be referred typologically to the voice of the Church. For she, through her elect, when she judges the evils of carnal people, investigates what she does not know, because she investigates through judgment, by correcting, the evils that she does not know through practice. Thus, when the holy Church has for a time been oppressed by the wickedness of the unjust, she remembers and says: “The case that I did not know I investigated most diligently.” It is as though she openly said: “The evils that I did not know by being practiced in my elect, I punished by strictly judging them in wicked people.”

And because now, by the power of her preaching, she crushes the devil and snatches from his mouth the soul of each person whom she receives, she continues, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Rec. XV]

**VERSE 17.—“I was breaking the grinders of the wicked, and I was taking prey from his teeth.”**

**47. The Church snatches prey from the devil when she recalls someone from error or sin.**—Oh, what prey she took from the devil’s mouth when, by converting Saul—the robber himself—she snatched him away, when he was still breathing threats, had received letters, and was traveling to Damascus; while by persecuting the faithful he was gathering prey for the devil, he himself, by recognizing the faith, was added to Christ (Acts IX, 2)! [Note: The English and our manuscripts, except Corb. Germ., read “was gathering prey”; the old and recent printed editions read “was gathering the people.”] As often as, by preaching, she tears a soul away from the bite of error, so often the Church takes prey from the teeth of the wicked.

For who can more truly be called “the wicked” than the devil? We break his grinders whenever, by reasoning against his snares, we reveal his hidden machinations; and we take prey from his teeth when, by converting it to the salvation of life, we recall the mind that he had already bitten and broken for sin. [Vet. XXIV.] By the grinders, his hidden snares are indicated; by the teeth, the open perpetration of sin already committed.

Of these jaws and teeth it is written through the Psalmist: “But God will crush their teeth in their mouths; the Lord will break the grinders of lions” (Ps. LVII, 7). [Note: Many manuscripts: “will crush . . . will break.”] But the holy man first asserts that he breaks the grinders, so that afterward he may take prey from his teeth, because we then truly take prey from his teeth when we first know how to break his grinders. First it is necessary to expose the hidden machinations of his counsels, so that afterward we may be able to recall our hearer’s soul from open falling.

The supreme shepherd of the Church himself broke the grinders of this wicked one by preaching when he said: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (I Pet. V, 8). Against this lion, because the holy Church sees his snares, she fortifies the sheepfolds of faith. She breaks his grinders as often as she destroys the arguments of heretics; and she snatches prey from his teeth as often as, by preaching, she converts someone from error.

And because many of the righteous will then be among those who believed that they would depart from this world during a time of ecclesiastical peace, blessed Job, while recounting his own words, also indicates the voices of the righteous who follow, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Rec. XVI]

**VERSE 18.—“And I said: In my little nest I shall die, and I shall multiply my days like the palm.”**

[Note: “In Hebrew, ‘like sand.’ Yet among certain Hebrews it is the phoenix. And because φοῖνιξ (*phoinix*) in Greek signifies ‘palm,’ interpreters translated it ‘like the palm.’ Others prefer to understand here a reference to the phoenix bird, the most famous but also the most fabulous of birds.]

**48. If her children desire to enjoy peace, let them remain in her nest and bosom.**—What is expressed in this passage by the name “nest” except the tranquil rest of faith, by which each weak person is nourished? For that multitude of good people which is found amid times of persecution believed that it would complete the days of its nourishment in a nest—that is, in a place of rest.

For unless the holy Church now nourished her weaker children in the nest of peace, the Psalmist would not say: “Indeed, the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young” (Ps. LXXXIII, 4). The sparrow has already found a house for itself, because our Redeemer has entered the eternal dwelling of heaven. And the turtledove has found a nest, because the holy Church, moved by love of the Creator, makes frequent lamentation and builds for herself, as it were, a nest—that is, the most peaceful rest of faith—in which she warms and cherishes her growing children, like fledglings growing feathers, in the lap of charity until they fly upward.

Since, therefore, there will then be those who believed that during a time of peace they would migrate to higher things—that is, fly out of the nest—their voice is anticipated by the voice of blessed Job when he says: “And I said: In my little nest I shall die.” Because they also promised themselves this leisure of peace over the length of many days, he rightly adds: “And I shall multiply my days like the palm.”

For the palm advances slowly but remains green for a long time. The holy Church came to the condition of faith through many difficulties, and, for the sake of gathering many people, desires to remain longer in the glory of that same faith. Thus she believed that she would multiply her days like the palm, but, when a sudden moment of temptation arises, she grieves that the grace of her peace, attained slowly by the faithful, is quickly intercepted by the unfaithful.

[Col. 0129B] [Vet. XXV.] **49. Why the righteous are compared with the palm.**—Nor is the life of the righteous compared with the palm without reason, because the palm is rough to the touch below and wrapped, as it were, in dry bark, but above it is beautiful to behold because of its fruits. Below it is constricted by the folds of its bark, but above it spreads out in the breadth of beautiful greenery.

Such is the life of the elect: despised below, beautiful above. Here below it is wrapped, as it were, in many layers of bark while it is constricted by innumerable tribulations; at the summit, however, it spreads out like leaves of beautiful greenery in the breadth of its reward.

The palm has another characteristic by which it differs from all kinds of trees. Every tree stands broad in its strength near the ground, but as it grows upward it narrows; and the higher it rises, the more slender it becomes. The palm, however, begins with less breadth at its base and rises with greater strength toward its branches and fruits. What begins thinly below grows broader toward the top.

What other trees, then, are found to resemble earthly minds, broad below and narrow above? All lovers of this world are strong in earthly matters [Dist. 47, c. 3] but weak in heavenly matters. They desire to toil even to death for temporal glory, but for the hope of eternity they do not endure even the smallest labor. For earthly profits they tolerate every kind of injury, but for heavenly reward they refuse to bear insults even for the sake of the slightest word. They are strong enough to attend an earthly judge throughout the whole day, but in prayer before the Lord they grow weary after even a moment of one hour.

They often endure nakedness, degradation, and hunger in order to acquire riches and honors, and torment themselves through abstinence from the very things they hasten to obtain; but they are all the more reluctant to seek heavenly things laboriously because they think their reward will be delayed. Thus they are broad below and narrow above, after the manner of other trees, because they stand strong in lower things but fail with respect to higher things.

In contrast, the quality of the palms signifies the advancing life of the righteous. They are not strong in earthly pursuits and weak in heavenly ones; rather, they show themselves more diligently and more persistently devoted to God than they remember having been to the world.

When our preacher says to some people: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh; for just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. VI, 19), he is certainly condescending to their weakness, as though he were saying more openly: “If you are no longer able to do more, at least be as you are in the fruit of good works as you once were in the practice of vices.” [Note: The manuscripts and printed editions vary greatly here. Turon has: “lest holy liberty find you weaker, whom . . .” Norm. with 1 Laud.: “lest . . . liberty of the air find you . . .” Corb. Germ.: “nor . . . liberty of the air find you . . .” Vindoc.: “lest holy liberty find you weaker than those whom earthly desire holds strong in the flesh.” The Bellov. manuscript is corrupt here. The old Paris edition: “lest . . . the holy scale of work find you . . .” Germ. and the Basel edition: “holy liberty find you heirs whom . . .” All the manuscripts read *quos*, “whom,” not *quam*, “which,” as in the Gussanville edition. Gratian likewise reads *quos*, as is clear from Dist. 47, c. “Omnes.”] Let not the holy freedom of charity find you weaker than those whom the practice of earthly pleasure held strong in the flesh.

[Vet. XXVI.] **50. Those who, after beginning well, do not persevere are not compared with the palm.**—There are some who, when they desire heavenly things and abandon the harmful deeds of this world, decline each day from their beginning through the fickleness of faintheartedness. To what trees except the remaining kinds should I compare them? They do not rise above in the manner in which they grow below. These people, when they come to conversion [Note: Germ., the two Laud. manuscripts, Gemet. and other Norman manuscripts: “coming into their manner of life.” Corb. Germ. and Prat.: “coming into conversion.”], do not persevere as they began; and, like trees, they are broad at their beginning but grow thin, because little by little, as time increases, they suffer losses in virtue.

Their heavenly desires gradually grow weak. Those who had made strong and courageous resolutions bring them to a weak and feeble completion; and, while they advance in age, they grow like pliable things. But the palm, as has been said, [Note: So the two Laud. manuscripts, Corb. Germ., Norm. and others. The reading in the printed editions is different. In the old edition, as in the Germ. manuscript, it reads: “broader at the summit than the quality with which it began from the root.” The later editions have the same, omitting *qualitatis*, which Corb. Germ. preserved.] is broader at the summit than the size with which it began at the root, because the conversion of the elect often accomplishes more in its completion than it proposes in its beginning. If it begins somewhat lukewarmly, it completes its end more fervently; it always considers itself to be beginning, and for that reason remains tireless in newness.

Observing this constancy of the righteous, the prophet says: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength; they will take up wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not faint” (Isa. XL, 31). They change their strength because they strive to be strong in spiritual work, though previously they were strong in the flesh. They take up wings like eagles because they fly through contemplation. They run and do not grow weary because they preach great things with swift speed. They walk and do not faint because they retain the quickness of their understanding in order to condescend to those who are slower.

In all the good things they receive, the more gladly they accommodate them to others, the more steadfastly they themselves continue in newness; and those who emerge thin from the root of their beginning grow strong in the perfection of their summit.

Let blessed Job speak, therefore, from his own person; let him speak from the voice of the holy Church [Note: In the recent edition we supplied the omitted particle *pro* (“for”) from the manuscripts and the old edition.] for those whom she had converted to herself during a time of peace and whom she believed would persevere in good morals: “And I said: In my little nest I shall die, and I shall multiply my days like the palm.” [Note: In Gilot, Vatic. and Gussanville, corruptly: “as though, indeed, like a palm.” Corrected from an ancient codex, whether manuscript or printed.]

For she believed that she would multiply her days like the palm because she thought that the minds of the faithful would rise stronger right to the end. When the hearts of many begin to grow soft from being wearied by persecutions, she grieves that those whom she had admired for making strong resolutions are already tending toward weakness. [Note: Gemet.: “because she always directs the mind toward spiritual knowledge,” etc. Turon: “minds,” etc.] And because she always directs her mind toward spiritual knowledge, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 19.—“My root is opened beside the waters.”**

**51. The Church is always intent upon spiritual knowledge.**—The root is opened beside the waters when the hidden thought of the mind expands itself to receive the streams of truth. As we have already said in the preceding book (Book VIII, no. 81), the name “root” in sacred eloquence usually signifies hidden thought. We open our root beside the waters when we direct the silent thought of the heart toward the inward infusion.

[Vet. XXVII.] If these words are referred to the voice of the holy Church, her root itself ought to be understood as the incarnation of the Redeemer. It was opened beside the waters when the invisible God, through the assumption of his humanity, became manifest to the sight of our vision. The Creator, who could not be seen in divinity, assumed from us that by which he might be seen by us. The root, therefore, is opened beside the waters because the author of the human race is revealed to human beings through his humanity.

Hence it is also rightly said through the Psalmist: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the streams of waters” (Ps. I, 3). The streams of waters are the daily passages of peoples who are failing. And Truth says of himself: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 51). The tree, therefore, is beside the streams of waters because the Creator appeared in the flesh, offering us the fruit and protection of his shade, in order that he might establish the human race through the resurrection, which was daily going toward death through decay.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIX

**SAME PLACE.—“And the dew will remain in my harvest.”**

**52. Her harvest is to be attributed to the dew of grace.**—Understand: “I was saying.” The harvest of the holy Church may appropriately be understood as the perfect souls withdrawn from their bodies, like ripe crops cut from the earth and migrating to the heavenly granaries. [Note: Corb. Germ. and the two Laud. manuscripts: *demigrantur*, “migrate.”] Because this occurs not through our own virtue but through the gift of heavenly grace, he rightly says: “And the dew will remain in my harvest.”

For dew falls from above, while the harvest is gathered below. Therefore the dew remains in the harvest because grace, coming from above, brings it about that we are worthy to be gathered from below. As grace itself pours into us from above, we bear the fruit of good works.

Hence it is also rightly said through Paul: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me has not been empty” (I Cor. XV, 10). If it is asked what the dew coming from above is, he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” If we observe the harvest growing under the dew, he says: “And his grace in me has not been empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXX

**VERSE 20.—“My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.”**

[Col. 0132C] **53. The Church laments the children whom she recognizes as returning to their former life.**—Understand: “I was saying.” What follows is joined to the preceding sentence, being added in continuous speech when he says: “And I said: In my little nest I shall die, and I shall multiply my days like the palm.” Then he adds: “My root is opened beside the waters, and the dew will remain in my harvest. My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.”

It is clear to all who know the truth that vices belong to the old life and virtues to the new. Hence Paul says: “Strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new” (Col. III, 9). Again he says: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Rom. VI, 6). Hence the Psalmist, speaking typologically in the person of the human race, says, when found among evil spirits: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI, 8).

For through some habit of living we grow old, as it were, either among spiritual enemies or among whatever carnal neighbors surround us, away from the fervor of the mind, and we darken the appearance of the newness we have assumed. Yet, if the practices of circumspection keep watch, we are renewed daily from this old age [Note: So the two Laud. manuscripts, Corb. Germ., Bellovac., Norm. and others, with which the old editions agree. The more recent editions preferred the reading found in Germ.: “if we diligently attend through the discipline of vigilance.”] by praying, reading, living well, and applying ourselves to holy meditations; for while our life is washed by tears, exercised in good works, and stretched toward holy meditations, it is ceaselessly restored to its newness.

Blessed Job, therefore, recounts his own affairs in such a way as to signify ours, because when the holy Church sees her faithful returning to the sins of their former life, she is compelled to weep for those whom she sees losing the newness of their minds. The excellent preacher says to his disciples: “For what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord?” (I Thess. II, 19). Thus the holy Church laments her glory as lost when she observes her faithful returning to their former life. She says: “I said: My glory will always be renewed,” because she recognizes that those whom she believed would serve in her as soldiers of the new life [Note: Vindoc.: “to serve in newness”] are serving their former desires.

[Vers. XXVIII.] **54. What things are signified in sacred Scripture by the name “bow.”**—In sacred eloquence the name “bow” sometimes signifies the snares of the wicked, sometimes the day of judgment, and sometimes the sacred eloquence itself. The snares are represented by the bow, as the Psalmist says: “They have stretched their bow, a bitter thing” (Ps. LXIII, 4). The final day of judgment is also signified by the bow, as the same Psalmist says again: “You have shown your people hard things; you have given us to drink the wine of compunction; you have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. LIX, 5).

For in a bow, the farther the string is drawn back, the more forcefully the arrow comes from it. So the day of final judgment: the longer it is delayed before it comes, the more severe the sentence will proceed from it when it comes. We are struck now by various calamities so that, corrected by them, we may then be found more ready. Hence it was said earlier: “You have shown your people hard things”—namely, the scourges of this age that go before the more grievous day of judgment that will follow. “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction,” so that earthly joys might be turned into tears. “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

It is as though he openly said: “This is the time of mercy; that will be the time of judgment.” Through the scourges of this present time, therefore, you signify how you will strike then, when you judge without sparing—since you now strike so strictly while you spare.

## 55. Holy Scripture itself is the bow of the Church

Sometimes, however, the bow also signifies Holy Scripture. For it is itself the bow of the Church; it is itself the bow of the Lord, from which sentences come to human hearts like striking arrows, and so terrify them. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “He has bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he has prepared the instruments of death; he has made his arrows for those who burn” (Ps. 7:13). The Lord has bent his bow, because through Holy Scripture he has displayed threats to all sinners. In this bow he prepares instruments of death, because according to the judgment of his utterance he condemns as reprobate those who now neglect correction. In it also he has made his arrows for those who burn, because against those whom he corrects through terror he sends forth fiery judgments of words.

Of this bow of preachers Isaiah says: “With arrows and bow they will enter there” (Isa. 7:24), because the holy apostles came with sharp points of words to strike the hardness of pagan life.

[Note: Germ., Gemet., and others read “they will enter.” Corb. Germ. reads “they enter.”]

What, then, should be understood in this passage by the name “bow” except sacred eloquence? In the string the New Testament is understood, and in the horn the Old Testament. In a bow, when the string is drawn, the horn is bent; so in this same sacred eloquence, when the New Testament is read, the hardness of the Old Testament is softened.

[Note: 1 Laud. and Corb. Germ. read “as in this same.”]

For the rigor of the letter inclines toward the spiritual and gentle commandments of the New Testament, because, when the New Testament is drawn as though by the arm of a good work, the laws of severity in the Old Testament are bent. Nor is it inappropriate to say that the string corresponds to the New Testament, which is known to have come into existence through the Lord’s incarnation. Thus the string is drawn and the horns are bent, because, while the incarnation of the Mediator is recognized in the New Testament, the rigor of the Old Testament is inclined toward spiritual understanding.

The holy man therefore says: “I said, ‘My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.’”

## 56. He uses this bow rightly who, understanding the divine utterances, fulfills them in deed

The bow in the hand is Holy Scripture in action. For he holds the bow in his hand who fulfills by his deeds the divine utterances that he knows through understanding. Thus the bow is restored in the hand when whatever is learned through study from sacred eloquence is completed in life.

Hence also Solomon, when describing strong warriors in spiritual battle, says: “All holding swords and most skilled for war” (Song 3:8). What is signified in divine Scripture by the sword Paul made clear when he said: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17).

[Old edition VI.]

Solomon did not say, “All having swords,” but “holding,” because it is not remarkable merely to know the word of God, but to do it. He has the sword but does not hold it who knows divine eloquence but neglects to live according to it. Nor can he be considered learned for battle who does not exercise the spiritual sword he possesses.

[Note: Recent editions read “would no longer wish.” The sense is inconsistent, and none of the manuscripts available to us supports it. Our reading is found in the Laud., Turon., Vindoc., Norm., and Corb. Germ. manuscripts, as well as in the old printed editions.] For he is wholly unable to resist temptations who, by living badly, puts off holding this sword of the word of God.

Therefore holy Church, which is oppressed by the persecution that follows, considering the abundance of the wicked and the scarcity of the good, foretells her own losses in the words of blessed Job, saying:

[Note: Vindoc. reads “tribulation.”] “And I said, ‘In my nest I shall die, and like the palm I shall multiply my days. My root is open beside the waters, and dew will remain on my harvest. My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.’”

Considering all these things, she was by no means deceived by an empty hope.

[Note: 1 Laud. reads, “nor was she deceived into thinking that she had sinned.”]

For all the perfected now see many helpers belonging to her, but without doubt they consider that, when the moment of persecution emerges, many of those who appear to be her citizens in time of peace will become her enemies.

[Note: Two Laud. manuscripts read “hearers”; this was formerly written in Utic. The old editions likewise have this reading.]

They do not despair in this way concerning everyone, yet it often happens that those from whom they had held a greater confidence of faith themselves become more savage enemies of that same faith.

[Note: Pratel., Gemet., and several others read *majorem spei fid.* (“a greater confidence of hope”). But *fidei* (“of faith”) seems to be the reading, since shortly afterward occurs “of the same faith.”]

[Note: Vindoc. reads “more ferocious.”]

Then they see them acting against the sacred utterances, although from their works they had believed that these same sacred utterances would be restored to the grace of preaching.

Yet we groan that these times have already begun, when we see many placed within the Church who either do not wish to do what they understand or even disdain to understand and know this very sacred eloquence. For, turning their hearing away from the truth, they turn to fables, while all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21). The writings of God are found everywhere and placed before people’s eyes, but people disdain to know them. Almost no one seeks to know what he has believed.

Therefore let the multitude of the former good grieve that its bow is being destroyed, since it had always believed that sacred eloquence would be restored through the zeal of those who followed.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and old editions; recent editions read “grieved.”]

# BOOK TWENTY

A fuller explanation of the five final verses of chapter 29 of the Book of Job, together with the whole of chapter 30, chiefly concerning heretics and carnal people who afflict the Church.

[Col. 0135]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0135B]

## 1. Holy Scripture must be preferred to all other books

Although Holy Scripture surpasses every kind of knowledge and instruction beyond comparison—to say nothing of the fact that it proclaims the truth, calls us to the heavenly homeland, and changes the heart of the reader from earthly desires to the embrace of things above; that through more obscure statements it exercises the strong and by humble speech caresses the little ones; that it is neither so closed that it ought to be feared nor so open that it becomes worthless; that use removes weariness and it is loved more the more it is meditated upon; that it supports the reader’s spirit with humble words and lifts it with sublime meanings; that in some way it grows together with its readers; that it is almost recognized by inexperienced readers and yet is always found new by the learned—to say nothing, then, of the weight of its subject matter, it surpasses all sciences and teachings even by the manner of its speech.

For in one and the same discourse, while it narrates the text, it reveals the mystery; and it knows how to speak of past things in such a way that by that very act it proclaims the future. Without altering the order of its expression, it knows in the same words how both to describe what has already happened and to announce what must happen.

[Note: Germ., Corb. Germ., and the manuscript of Vallis Clara, with which we corrected the following books of the *Moralia*, and others read “and what has been done.” We shall henceforth designate the cited manuscript by the note “Val. Clar.”]

Such are these same words of blessed Job: while he speaks of his own affairs, he foretells ours; and while he expresses his personal laments in speech, he sounds forth in understanding the circumstances of holy Church. For he says:

# CHAPTER TWO

## Job 29:21–23

“They who heard me waited for a sentence, and, attentive, they kept silence for my counsel. They did not dare add anything to my words, and my utterance dripped upon them. They waited for me as for rain, and they opened their mouths as for the late rain.”

## 2. The faithful hear the Church teaching, intending to follow her words, not to judge them

We undoubtedly believe that such was the reverence of those subject to blessed Job. But, as we have often said, holy Church, pressed by the tribulations of heretics or carnal people, recalls the former times in which everything said by her was heard by the faithful with fear. Lamenting the insolence of her adversaries, she says:

[Rec. II.]

“They who heard me waited for a sentence, and, attentive, they kept silence for my counsel.”

As though she were openly saying: “Not like these insolent and arrogant people, who, while they refuse to receive the words of truth, anticipate the judgments of my preaching as though they were teaching.” Her disciples now keep silence, attentive to her counsel, because they do not dare to oppose her words but to believe them. In order to profit from them, they certainly hear them not to judge them, but to follow them.

## 3. They add nothing to her doctrine; heretics do otherwise

Concerning these people it is rightly added: “They did not dare add anything to my words.” For at that time heretics, when they have been unrestrained by a most wicked liberty against her, presume to add something to her words, when they attempt, as though correcting them, to amend the rectitude of her teachings.

Of good hearers he adds further: “And my utterance dripped upon them.”

## 4. Preachers ought to adapt themselves to the capacity of their hearers

What else is understood by this dripping of speech except the measured delivery of holy preaching? For the grace of exhortation must be imparted to each person according to the capacity of his understanding.

Thus, by the statement “They did not dare add anything to my words,” the reverence of the hearers is praised. By what follows—“And my utterance dripped upon them”—the administration of teachers is indicated. The one who teaches must carefully discern that he not strive to preach more than the hearer can grasp. He must descend by contracting himself to the weakness of his hearers, lest, while speaking sublime things to the little ones—and therefore things that will not profit them—he take greater care to display himself than to benefit his hearers.

[Old edition II.]

At the Lord’s command, not only bowls for the table of the tabernacle but also cups were prepared (Exod. 37:16). For what is signified by bowls except abundant preaching, and what by cups except slight and limited speech about God? On the Lord’s table, therefore, both bowls and cups are prepared, because in the teaching of sacred eloquence one must present not only great and mysterious things that intoxicate, but also small and subtle things that provide knowledge as though by tasting.

Let holy Church, then, pressed by the final times, remember this most discerning administration of hers and say: “My utterance dripped upon them.”

## 5. The humble open their mouths to receive their doctrine like the late rain

Here it is appropriately added: “They waited for me as for rain, and they opened their mouths as for the late rain.”

We receive the words of holy preaching as rain when, with true humility, we acknowledge the dryness of our heart, so that we may be watered by the drink of holy preaching. Hence the Psalmist rightly says to God: “My soul is like land without water to you” (Ps. 142:6). The prophet urges us to be filled with these streams of doctrine, saying: “You who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55:1).

When, at the final period of the world, we receive the words of holy preaching, we open the mouth of our heart as for the late rain. For if there were no mouth in the heart, the Psalmist would not say: “Deceitful lips in the heart, and with the heart they spoke evil” (Ps. 11:3). Since, then, we attend with the mouth of the heart to the words of the final preaching, we open it, as it were, to these late streams.

This preaching proceeded to us from the sacrifice of the one who says through the Psalmist: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2). Because our Redeemer endured the force of his persecutors near the end of the world, he offered himself for us as an evening sacrifice.

Of this late rain it is written elsewhere: “I will give you the early and the late rain” (Jer. 5:24).

[Note: Although this word may seem barbarous, we have not judged that it should be avoided, because it is found in all the manuscripts—Corb. Germ., Norm., Laud., Turon., Vindoc., and others. In its place Germ. and the editions read *temporaneam*, and the old edition, Barthol. and Basil., *temperaneam*.]

He gave the early rain because in the former period he granted his chosen ones understanding of the Law. He also bestowed the late rain because he caused the mystery of his incarnation to be preached in the last days.

Because holy Church does not cease to proclaim this every day, she fills the mouths of her hearers’ hearts, as it were, from the late rain. It follows:

# CHAPTER THREE [Rec. III]

## Job 29:24

“If I ever laughed at them, they did not believe it, and the light of my face did not fall upon the ground.”

## 6. A superior should show himself grave without being hateful, cheerful without becoming contemptible

If we understand this according to the words of the historical account, we must believe that the holy man presented himself to his subjects in such a way that even when he laughed he could be feared. But since above he declares that he had been a father to the poor and a consoler of widows, the matter requires very careful discernment: how, amid such great terror of governance, there could also have been such great gentleness and meekness of compassion.

This could not have existed without great gentleness of kindness, since he says that he was a father to the poor and a consoler of widows. Yet again, without great severity he could not have been feared even while laughing.

What else are we taught by this except that the administration of authority must be such that the one who presides moderates himself toward his subjects with such measure that he is to be feared when smiling and loved when angry? Neither should excessive cheerfulness make him contemptible nor immoderate severity hateful.

For we often break our subjects when we hold the force of justice more tightly than is right.

[Note: Turon., Ebroic. and other Norm. manuscripts read “rigor”; below, “rigor is already present.”]

That force will no longer be the force of justice if it does not preserve itself under just moderation. And often we release subjects from the fear of discipline if we loosen the reins of cheerfulness in our governance, because when they see us cheerful as though without restraint, they themselves boldly give way to unlawful things.

[Old edition III.]

But if the ruler’s face ought to be feared even when cheerful, he must himself constantly fear the face of his Creator. For it is difficult to believe that mind cheerful which is known by its subjects to afflict itself continually for love of the Lord. When someone seeks the things above with the unceasing heat of spiritual desire, it becomes very doubtful that he should at times appear cheerful before human beings.

[Note: Gemet., Utic. and other manuscripts read this way. The editions have *valde de ea*; Corb. Germ. has “For she who … very much concerning her.”]

Hence blessed Job himself will say not long afterward: “For I always feared God as though waves swelling over me” (Job 31:23). He feared his judge as though the attacks of waves were already rushing upon him, on the point of death.

[Note: Some editions read “as though swelling.” Others read “as though threatening.” All the manuscripts available to us support our reading.]

Since sorrow from divine fear had filled his mind, his subjects rightly did not believe in his cheerfulness, because they were compelled not to believe the laughter of one whose heart they knew was continually held by sorrow in fear of the Creator.

[Note: Germ., Corb. Germ., and Gemet. read *ita mentem moeror* (“thus sorrow [filled] the mind”).]

## 7. Our light falls to the ground when we desire earthly things

According to the historical account, what immediately follows can also appropriately be understood: “And the light of my face did not fall upon the ground.”

For it is written: “The eyes of fools are on the ends of the earth” (Prov. 17:24). Again, through the same Solomon it is said: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). Paul also says: “The head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3).

The eyes of the wise man are therefore in his head when he constantly contemplates the works of his Redeemer, which he ought to imitate. The light of his face did not fall upon the ground because he did not look upon earthly things through desire.

## 8. The saints are never secure; careless security is a grave danger

But since we have briefly examined the surface of the historical account, let us consider what mystical meaning lies hidden in these words.

We have often said that Christ and the Church are generally one person, and that frequently the voice of the head passes into the voice of the body, and the voice of the body into the voice of the head. Since those who are in one flesh may also agree in one voice, let Christ speak from the voice of his chosen ones; let the Church say:

“If I ever laughed at them, they did not believe it.”

For God’s laughing means that the ways of the saints are attended by the favorable prosperity of God, as is also said in ordinary speech concerning those whom the comforts of happiness accompany in this world: “The time smiled upon them.”

Conversely, the anger of the Lord is called the weakening of good actions, as it is written: “Lest the Lord become angry, and you perish from the just way” (Ps. 2:12). If the Lord is said to become angry when people lose the way of justice, the Lord is rightly said to smile when the favor of heavenly grace accompanies our good works.

[Res. V.]

Yet all the elect, as long as they are in this life, do not promise themselves confidence in security. At every hour they fear the ambushes of the hidden enemy, suspicious of temptations; even when temptation has ceased, they are disturbed by mere suspicion.

[Note: Norm. reads: “who, even if temptations cease, are disturbed by suspicion.” Our manuscripts everywhere have *suspectio*, *suspectionem*, for *suspicio*, *suspicionem*. But what Saint Gregory teaches here about vigilance he explains elsewhere, especially in book 6, letter 22, according to the ancient order of the letters.]

For careless security has often been a grave danger to many, so that they recognized the ambushes of the crafty enemy only after they had not been tested but already overthrown.

One must always keep watch, so that the mind, continually attentive, never relax its upward intention. Otherwise, abandoning what requires labor, it may lie in loose thoughts as though on soft bedding, and, having become relaxed, surrender itself to the approaching corrupter, the devil.

The spirit must always be raised for battle against the adversary; vigilance must always be provided against hidden ambushes.

Hence the prophet Habakkuk says: “I will stand upon my watch” (Hab. 2:1). Again it is written: “Appoint a watchtower for yourself; set bitterness for yourself, you who proclaim good news to Zion” (Jer. 31:21). Through Solomon it is said: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. 28:14). Again he says: “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh, because of nighttime fears” (Song 3:8).

Nighttime fears are the ambushes of hidden temptation. The sword upon the thigh is vigilant watchfulness, pressing down the allurements of the flesh. Therefore, lest nighttime fear—that is, hidden and sudden temptation—creep in, it is always necessary that the sword of watchfulness, laid upon our thigh, continually press it down.

[Old edition IV.]

Holy men are so certain of hope that they nevertheless are always suspicious of temptation. For they are told: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11), so that rejoicing may arise from hope and trembling from suspicion.

Again the Psalmist speaks in their voice: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. 85:11).

[Note: Corb. Germ., Bellov., Germ. and Norm. read “and it should be noted that.” Two Laud. manuscripts read “where it should be noted.”]

Here it should be noted that he does not say, “Let it rejoice so that it may be secure,” but, “Let it rejoice so that it may fear.” For although their action prospers, they remember that they are still in this life, concerning which the same Job says: “Human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1).

They also remember what is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

They remember and fear, and do not presume to promise themselves certainty within themselves. Placed between the joy of hope and the fear of temptation, they trust and fear; they are strengthened and stumble; they are reassured and remain suspicious.

[Note: Germ., Turon., Vind., Corb. Germ., two Laud., Val. Cl., and all Norm. manuscripts read *non certificantur* (“they are not made certain”), whereas the editions read *certiorantur* (“they are made certain”).]

Therefore it is rightly said through the voice of the elect member under the figure of our head: “If I ever laughed at them, they did not believe it.” We do not believe our Redeemer as though he were smiling upon us when, although many gifts of his already testify to it and we receive the grace of his favor, we nevertheless still tremble under his judgment because of our weakness.

## 9. Saint Paul, although carried up to the third heaven, was not free from fear

Let us see how grace from above already smiles upon Paul, while he himself still seems not to believe because of the fear of suspicion.

The Lord had already spoken to him from heaven, opening the eyes within him and closing those without, and had displayed the power of his majesty (Acts 9:4). He had already said concerning him to Ananias: “He is a vessel of election for me” (ibid. 9:15). He had already been carried above himself to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2); he had already been led into paradise and heard secret words that he could not utter.

Yet he still says fearfully: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27).

[Note: Two Laud. manuscripts read “and I reduce it to servitude.”]

Behold: toward divine grace, which is already smiling upon him, he believes through hope, but he does not yet believe through security.

That these words appropriately correspond to the voice of our Redeemer is also shown by what follows: “And the light of my face did not fall upon the ground.”

For what is called “earth” except the sinner, to whom the first sentence was spoken: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19)? The light of the Lord’s face does not fall upon the earth, because the brightness of his vision does not appear to sinners.

For it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10). The light would fall upon the earth if, coming in the final judgment, he were to reveal the brightness of his majesty to sinners.

[Note: Others read “the majesty of his brightness.”]

## 10. Strong things must not be preached to the weak

If we receive these words from the voice of holy Church, we can appropriately understand that the light of her face does not fall upon the earth because she forbids the mysteries of her highest contemplation to be preached to those occupied with earthly actions.

[Note: Norm. reads “she avoids the highest things.” Germ. and 2 Laud. likewise.]

She forbids strong things to be spoken to the weak, lest, when they hear what they cannot receive, they be crushed by the words of preaching through which they ought to have been raised.

[Note: 1 Laud. reads “to the lowest.”]

The bodily light itself, which illuminates healthy eyes, obscures weak ones; and when inflamed eyes gaze at the sun’s brightness, blindness is often produced in them by the light.

Therefore holy Church, oppressed in the time of persecution but remembering her former discernment, says: “The light of my face did not fall upon the earth.”

But since we have begun to understand these words from her head, let us continue with what follows in him. For it is added:

# CHAPTER FOUR [Rec. VI]

## Job 29:25

“If I wished to go to them, I would sit first.”

## 11. In the heart of the carnal Christ sits last; in the heart of the just, first

Because in the heart of the reprobate the actions of the flesh occupy the first place and the actions of the soul the last, Christ undoubtedly sits not first but last in their thoughts.

But the elect, because they think above all about eternal things and arrange temporal matters, if any exist, with secondary and lesser care—and to them the magisterial voice of Truth says, “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33)—have the Lord sitting first in their heart.

The statement “If I wished to go to them” appropriately precedes this. Since, as it is written, he works all things according to the counsel of his will (Eph. 1:5), the Lord enlightens us by his visitation not according to our merit but because he himself wills it.

Thus he comes when he wills; and when he comes, he sits first, because his arrival in our heart is gratuitous, and the desire for him is not equal in our thought to the other desires.

It follows:

# CHAPTER FIVE [Rec. VII]

## Ibid.

“And when I sat like a king with an army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a consoler of the sorrowful.”

## 12. Christ, sitting in us as king, consoles the sorrowful; the Church does the same

The Lord sits as king in the heart because he rules the movements of our souls that resound around us in our thought.

In the mind he inhabits, he awakens what is sluggish, restrains what is restless, kindles what is cold, moderates what is kindled, softens what is rigid, and constrains what is unstable. From this diversity of thoughts, a kind of army surrounds him.

Or certainly he sits as king with an army surrounding him because a multitude of virtues surrounds him as he presides over the minds of the elect.

He is also a consoler of the sorrowful, in accordance with the promise in which he says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). Again: “I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

What we have said concerning the head of holy Church may also appropriately be referred to the voice of the Church herself. In her, the order of teachers presides like a king, surrounded by the multitude of the faithful.

This multitude of the faithful is rightly also called an army, because every day it is continually prepared in the ranks of good works for the battles against temptations.

[Old edition V.]

Holy Church also consoles the hearts of the sorrowful when she considers the minds of the elect afflicted by the hardship of the present pilgrimage and makes them rejoice through the promise of the eternal homeland.

[Note: Laud., Germ. and Norm. read “while through the hardship of the present pilgrimage.” Corb. Germ. reads “while in the hardship of the present pilgrimage.”]

She also considers that the thoughts of the faithful have been struck by divine fear; and those whom she sees to have heard severe things about God, so that they may fear, she causes also to hear of his compassionate gentleness, so that they may presume.

## 13. She mingles hope and fear, lest we either trust carelessly in mercy or fear justice despairingly

Thus holy Church, in the course of her preaching, mingles hope and fear for her faithful concerning the mercy and justice of the Redeemer, so that they neither trust carelessly in mercy nor fear justice despairingly.

With the words of her head she refreshes those who fear, saying: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). Again she terrifies those who presume when she says: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38).

Again she refreshes those who fear, saying: “Rejoice because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). But she terrifies those who presume in themselves when she says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (ibid. 10:18).

She refreshes those who fear when she says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (John 10:27). But she terrifies those who presume in themselves, saying: “They will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error” (Matt. 24:24).

She refreshes those who fear, saying: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (ibid. 24:13). She terrifies those who presume, saying: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

[Note: The same manuscript, together with two Laud. manuscripts, Val. Cl. and Norm., reads: “the one who fears is relieved … the one who presumes is terrified.” Corb. Germ. and Germ. read: “the one who fears is refreshed … the one who presumes is terrified.”]

She refreshes those who fear when he says to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). But she terrifies those who presume when Judas falls from the glory of apostleship into hell. Concerning him it is declared by a definitive sentence: “I chose you twelve, and one of you is a devil” (John 6:70).

She refreshes the one who fears when she says: “If a man sends away his wife, and she departs from him and marries another man, will she return to him again? Will not that woman be defiled and polluted? Yet you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3:1).

[Note: “To him” is absent in 1 Laud., Corb. Germ., Norm. and others.]

But she terrifies the one who presumes when she says: “Why do you cry out over your affliction? Your pain is incurable” (Jer. 30:12).

She refreshes the one who fears, saying: “At least from now on call me, ‘My father, you are the guide of my virginity’” (Jer. 3:4). But she terrifies the one who presumes, saying: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16:3).

[Note: Germ., Utic., Beccensis and Corb. Germ. read “Cethaea.”]

She refreshes the one who fears when she says: “Return, rebellious Israel, and I will not turn my face from you, because I am holy, says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever” (Jer. 3:12). But she terrifies the one who presumes when she forbids her prophet to intercede, saying: “Do not take up praise and prayer for them, because I will not hear at the time of their cry to me in the time of their affliction. Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people” (Jer. 7:16).

[Note: In the Vulgate editions: “because I will not hear their cry in time.” We have followed the manuscripts—Turon., Vindoc., Bellov., two Laud., all Norm., Germ. and Corb. Germ.]

[Rec. VIII.]

Holy Church therefore both raises the minds of her hearers through the kindness of mercy and disturbs them through the severity of judgment, so that, while she rightly mingles both in her preaching, her elect neither presume because of the justice they have displayed nor despair because of their former iniquity.

## 14. In good shepherds kindness and authority, mercy and discipline are joined

But concerning what he says, “When I sat as a king with the army surrounding me, yet I was a comforter of the mourners,” we should understand that this can greatly edify the reader even according to the historical sense, if he considers how, in good rulers, the authority of governing is combined with the kindness of consoling. For he says: “When I sat as a king with the army surrounding me”—behold the authority of governance: “Yet I was a comforter of the mourners”—behold the ministry of compassion. [Note: In the German and Tours manuscripts: “behold the mystery.” The second Laon manuscript has both readings.]

Discipline—or mercy—is greatly weakened if one is maintained without the other. But toward their subjects rulers ought to possess both mercifully and justly consoling mercy, and piously severe discipline. [Note: In two German manuscripts, two Laon manuscripts, Vendôme, Tours, and the Norman manuscripts: “and justly providing care.”]

This is why, for the wounds of that half-dead man who was brought by the Samaritan to the inn, both wine and oil are applied (Luke 10:33–34): so that the wounds may be made to smart by the wine and soothed by the oil. Thus everyone who is responsible for healing wounds should apply, in the wine, the bite of strictness, and, in the oil, the gentleness of compassion; by the wine, putrefying things should be cleansed, and by the oil, things requiring healing should be soothed. [Note: He writes nearly the same thing in Letter 25, Book I.]

Gentleness must therefore be mingled with severity, and a certain tempering must be made from both, so that subjects are neither ulcerated by excessive harshness nor dissolved by excessive kindness. This is clearly signified by the ark of the tabernacle, in which the tablets, the rod, and the manna are together (Hebrews 9:4), because when knowledge of Holy Scripture is in the heart of a good ruler, there should be both the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness.

Hence David also says: “Your rod and your staff—they themselves have comforted me” (Psalm 22:4). For we are struck by the rod and supported by the staff. If, then, there is the strictness of the rod that strikes, let there also be the consolation of the staff that supports.

Let there therefore be love, but not one that makes soft; [Note: Another reading: “let there be rigor.” In the German, Beauvais, Corbie German, Tours, Vendôme, and other manuscripts, the reading is “let there be vigor.”] let there be vigor, but not one that provokes; let there be zeal, but not one that rages immoderately; let there be compassion, but not one that spares more than is expedient.

It is a pleasure to contemplate in Moses’ heart mercy joined with severity. Let us see him loving with compassion and raging with strictness. Certainly, when the Israelite people had incurred before God’s eyes an offense almost beyond remedy, so that its ruler heard: “Go down; your people have sinned” (Exodus 32:7)—as though the divine voice were immediately saying to him, “He who has fallen into such a sin is no longer mine,” and adding, “Let me alone, so that my fury may rage against them and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation”—he, once and again placing himself in the way of God’s angry assault on behalf of the people over whom he ruled, said: “Either forgive them this offense; or, if you will not, erase me from the book that you have written” (ibid., 32:32).

Let us consider, then, with what inward affection he loved that people, for whose life he asked to be erased from the book of life. Yet let us also consider how greatly this man, who was bound by such love for that people, was inflamed against its sins by zeal for righteousness.

For immediately, [Note: The words “immediately, as soon as” are absent from the German, two Laon manuscripts, Corbie German, and several others.] after he had obtained pardon for the offense through his first petition, so that they would not be destroyed, he came to that same people and said: “Let each man put his sword [Note: “His” is absent from the German, Corbie German, and most other manuscripts.] upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” And on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell (ibid., 32:27).

Behold: he who had sought the life of all, even at the cost of his own death, extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Within, he burned with the fire of love; without, he was kindled by the zeal of severity. His compassion was so great that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord on their behalf; his severity was so great that those whom he had feared would be struck by divine judgment, he himself struck with the sword of judgment.

He loved those over whom he ruled so much that he did not spare himself for them; yet he pursued those whom he loved when they sinned so severely that, even while the Lord spared them, he overthrew them. In both respects he was a strong ambassador; in both respects an admirable mediator. By prayers he pleaded the people’s cause before God, and by swords God’s cause before the people. Within, loving, he resisted the divine anger by his supplication; without, raging, he brought sin to an end by striking it.

He hastened to aid all by displaying the death of a few. And therefore almighty God more quickly heard his faithful servant acting on behalf of the people, because he saw what he himself would do for God against the people.

Thus, in governing the people, Moses combined both qualities, so that neither discipline was lacking in mercy nor mercy in discipline. Hence here too, according to both virtues, it is said: “When I sat as a king with the army surrounding me, yet I was a comforter of the mourners.” To sit with an army surrounding one is the vigor and discipline of governance; to console the hearts of mourners is the ministry of compassion.

But since amid these things the discourse of exposition must return to spiritual understanding, the holy Church, pressed by its adversaries in the final times, remembers the rights of governance it once exercised; it also remembers how many benefits of compassion it bestowed upon the afflicted. Its discipline and mercy are then mocked by the frivolous. Hence it continues:

## CHAPTER VI [Old recension VII, New recension IX]

### Chapter 30, verse 1

> “But now the younger in age mock me.”

## 15. All heretics are younger than the Church

All heretics, when compared with the age of the universal Church, are fittingly called younger in time, because they went out from her, whereas she did not go out from them. Hence it is rightly said through John: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

The younger in time therefore mock the holy Church when those who went out from her despise the words of her teaching. Concerning them it is further said:

> “Whose fathers I would not place with the dogs of my flock.”

[Note: In the Tours manuscript: “What does ‘flock’ mean?”]

What is the flock of the holy Church except the multitude of the faithful? [Note: Or who else are called the dogs of this flock except the holy preachers, who became guardians of those same faithful and, so to speak, uttered great barking?] Or who else are called the dogs of this flock except the holy teachers, who became guardians of those same faithful? While devoting themselves to watches for their Lord by day and by night, they cried out and gave, so to speak, great barks of preaching.

Concerning them it is said to that same Church through the Psalmist:

> “The tongue of your dogs—from the enemies, by him [Note: “By him” is omitted in the Beauvais, Corbie German, and many others.]” (Psalm 67:24).

For some, recalled from the worship of idols, became preachers of God. Thus the tongue of the Church’s dogs comes forth from enemies, because the Lord also makes converted Gentiles into preachers.

Hence the sluggishness of the Jews, who were unwilling to speak for God, is reproved by the rebuking prophet, who says:

> “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10).

## 16. Their leaders are rejected even in those things that appear to have been well done

By the fathers of heretics we mean those whom we call heresiarchs, from whose perverse preaching—that is, from the seed of their speech—peoples have been generated in error.

The holy Church therefore disdains to place the fathers of heretics with the dogs of her flock, because, by judging them, it rejects the inventors of errors and refuses to count them among true fathers. Even if some of them appeared to have recalled certain people from the error of paganism or to have taught certain people to perform honorable deeds, nevertheless, because they did not think rightly about God, [Note: Another reading: “about the Lord.”] she does not place them with the dogs of her flock; that is, she does not reckon them with the upright preachers.

It is clear that Arius, Photinus, Macedonius, Nestorius, [Note: The German manuscript has “Eutycius”; Corbie German, “Euthices”; Gembloux, Utrecht, Béthune, Pratelles, and other Norman manuscripts, as well as the Vallicellian manuscript, “Eutychius.” We believe this is how it is found in most manuscripts; yet a few collators observed this variant reading, considering it of little importance.] Eutyches, Dioscorus, Severus, and many like them attempted, by teaching and persuasion, to appear as fathers. But the holy universal Church, judging them with strict severity, [Note: Corbie German, two Laon manuscripts, and Tours: “with severe truth.” Beauvais: “with severe virtue.”] does not number among the guardians of her flock those whom she condemns for scattering the unity of that same flock.

Concerning them Paul says to the Ephesians:

> “I know that after my departure savage wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock” (Acts 20:29).

[Note: Beauvais has “savage she-wolves,” perhaps because *gravis* was thought to mean “pregnant” or “bearing young.” Properly speaking, however, not wolves but she-wolves are *graves* in this sense. In Greek the word is βαρεῖς (*bareis*), with another meaning.]

And because heretics sometimes, the further they slip into the error of faithlessness, guard themselves all the more carefully in outward conduct, [Note: In Gembloux, two Laon manuscripts, and Corbie German: “as though the more.”] so that they may appear to act more impressively than others, the holy universal Church despises all their works, since it recognizes that they do not proceed from the authority of faith.

Hence blessed Job’s voice rightly continues:

## CHAPTER VII

### Verse 2

> “The strength of whose hands was regarded by me as nothing, and they were thought unworthy even of life.”

## 17. Because they abandoned love of God and neighbor. Some heretics performed miracles. Heretics are unworthy of life because, under Christ’s name, they fight against Christ

Strength in the hand means greatness in action. But the strength of the heretics’ hands is regarded by the holy Church as nothing, because, once true faith has been lost, she sees no merit in whatever they do.

They abandon love of God and neighbor: they think falsely about God and separate themselves from their neighbors by quarrelling. But the outstanding preacher testifies that strength of hands is worthless without love, saying:

> “If I distribute all my possessions for feeding the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, [Note: The Norman manuscripts, Corbie German, two Laon manuscripts, and others have “so that it may burn.” The Greek text and the Vulgate more appropriately have “so that I may burn,” or “so that I may be burned.”] but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

[Old recension VIII.]

Sometimes, however, heretics also perform signs and miracles, but so that they may receive rewards for their affliction and abstinence—namely, the praises they seek. Hence the Redeemer’s voice says:

> “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘I have never known you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.’”

[Note: The printed edition has “because I do not know you.” This is found in none of our manuscripts.]

What else is conveyed by this judgment except that people ought to honor the humility of love, not the signs of miraculous powers? Hence now the holy Church despises even whatever miracles are performed by heretics, because she recognizes that these are not evidence of holiness. [Note: The German, Béthune, Utrecht, Corbie German, and many others have “not an appearance of holiness.”]

The proof of holiness is not to perform signs, but to love each person as oneself, to think truly about God, and to think better of one’s neighbor than of oneself. Since true virtue lies in love and not in the display of miracles, the Truth demonstrates this when he says:

> “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

For he did not say, “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you perform signs,” but said, “If you have love for one another.” He plainly indicates that God’s true servants are proved not by miracles but by love alone.

The gift of brotherly love is therefore testimony to heavenly discipleship. Since all heretics refuse to possess this love, separating themselves from the unity of the universal Church, it is rightly said of them:

> “The strength of whose hands was regarded by me as nothing.”

And because they do not agree in humility with the very signs they display, it is rightly added:

> “And they were thought unworthy even of life.”

Or certainly, the holy Church declares all heretics unworthy even of life, because under Christ’s name they fight against the name of Christ. Concerning them it further says:

## CHAPTER VIII [New recension X]

### Verse 3

> “Sterile through want and hunger.”

## 18. By searching curiously into divine matters, they suffer want and barrenness

All heretics, while striving to investigate the secrets of God in sacred discourse more than they are capable of grasping, become barren through their hunger. For they do not seek those things from which they might educate themselves in humility, order their conduct in tranquility, maintain patience, or exhibit perseverance. They seek only those things that may show them to be learned and eloquent; they desire to know those matters by which they may appear uniquely instructed.

For the most part they boldly discuss the nature of divinity while, in their misery, they do not know themselves. Thus they become barren through their want and hunger, because they desire to investigate matters from which they produce no shoots of a good life. What they investigate lies beyond them; and while they strive toward what they cannot comprehend, they neglect to learn those things from which they could have been instructed.

How well the outstanding preacher restrains their boldness when he says:

> “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3).

Hence Solomon says:

> “Put a limit to your wisdom” (Proverbs 23:4).

Again he says:

> “If you have found honey, eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are filled, you vomit it up” (Proverbs 25:16).

Whoever desires to eat the sweetness of spiritual understanding beyond what he can contain also vomits up what he had eaten, because, while seeking to understand sublime matters beyond his strength, he loses even what he had understood well. Hence again he says:

> “As it is not good for someone who eats much honey, so whoever is an investigator of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (ibid., 25:27).

The glory of the invisible Creator, when investigated moderately, lifts us up; when searched beyond our strength, it crushes us.

Thus, because heretics desire to be filled ever more with lofty understanding, they become ever more empty. It is rightly said of them:

> “Sterile through want and hunger.”

For the more they pursue, with immoderate daring, knowledge of heavenly matters, the more they lose it.

[Old recension IX.]

## 19. The humble understand heavenly things, or reverence what they do not understand

By contrast, those who are truly humble and truly learned in the holy Church know both to understand certain heavenly secrets after considering them and to reverence others that they do not understand. Thus they hold reverently what they understand and humbly await what they do not yet understand.

Hence it is said to us through Moses:

> “While eating the lamb, whatever remains of it we shall burn with fire” (Exodus 12:10).

We eat the lamb when, by understanding, we store much of the Lord’s humanity within the belly of the mind. Some things remain from it that cannot be eaten, because much still remains concerning him that cannot in any way be understood. Yet these things must be burned with fire, because what we cannot grasp concerning him we humbly reserve for the Holy Spirit.

Often this humility even discloses to the minds of the elect things that had seemed impossible to understand. But the perverse minds of heretics, arrogantly attributing understanding to themselves, presume to give supposedly certain judgments even concerning unknown things. The result is that the very pride that raises them up within themselves drives them away from the truth outside; and those who thought themselves uniquely to have penetrated spiritual secrets scarcely grasp even the outward matters in God’s words.

Hence here too it continues:

## CHAPTER IX [New recension XI]

### Verses 3–4

> “They gnawed in the wilderness, filthy with calamity and misery; and they ate herbs and the bark of trees.”

## 20. Heretics do not eat the marrow of Holy Scripture but gnaw its bark

What cannot be eaten is usually gnawed. Heretics, because they attempt to understand Holy Scripture by their own power, are plainly unable to grasp it. Since they do not understand it, they are as though they do not eat it. And because, without the help of heavenly grace, they cannot eat it, they gnaw it, as it were, with certain efforts.

Outwardly they handle it, since they make an attempt, but they do not reach its inner parts. [Note: The same manuscripts and the German manuscript read “while they grasp something.” Ancient editions have variously “while they grasp certain things,” “while something is grasped,” or “while certain people grasp.”]

Because they are separated from the fellowship of the universal Church, they are said to gnaw not anywhere at all but in the wilderness. Since false preachers would draw their followers into this wilderness, the Truth warned long beforehand, saying:

> “If they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out” (Matthew 24:26).

They are rightly described as filthy with calamity and misery, because they are despised both for the ruin of their conduct and for the perversity of their understanding.

They also eat herbs and the bark of trees, because, repelled by the barrier of their pride, they cannot perceive great and inward things in sacred discourse; they scarcely recognize certain tender and outward matters in it.

By herbs are signified plainer sayings; by the bark of trees, the outward words of the Fathers. Those who seek to know things by which they will not truly become learned but only appear to be learned, while they do not search to the marrow of sacred writings for the force of love toward God and neighbor, feed, as it were, on herbs and bark. For what nourishes the minds of the proud is either low or outward.

Or, certainly, to eat herbs means to observe the lesser commandments of Holy Scripture while despising the greater. The Truth rightly rebukes such people, saying:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill [Note: Gembloux and Tours have “and cumin,” followed by the old editions. Two Laon manuscripts and Corbie German have *cyminum*, another spelling of “cumin.”] and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law” (Matthew 23:23).

They also eat the bark of trees, because there are some who venerate only the surface of the letter in the sacred writings and preserve nothing of spiritual understanding. They suppose that nothing more exists in the words of God than what they have heard outwardly.

Yet throughout all their errors they are possessed by the desire for empty glory, and the ambition for honor holds them captive. Often, through the very things they say, they seek nothing other than earthly profits. Concerning them Paul says:

> “For such people do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly” (Romans 16:18).

Hence it rightly continues:

## CHAPTER X [New recension XII]

### Verse 4

> “And the root of junipers was their food.”

## 21. They seek only temporal profits

The juniper tree has prickles instead of leaves. What it produces is so bristling that it can pierce someone who handles it, like thorns. A thorn is every sin, because, while it draws the mind toward pleasure, it tears the mind as though by pricking it.

Hence the voice of the righteous and penitent says:

> “I turned to sorrow when the thorn was broken” (Psalm 31:4),

because the mind is turned toward lamentation so that the prick of sin may be broken through repentance.

In another translation, the thorn is said not to be broken but fixed, which does not differ from the same meaning, because the penitent’s spirit is led to mourning while the committed fault is retained, fixed in memory.

What, then, is signified by the root of the juniper except avarice, from which the thorns of all sins grow? Paul says concerning it:

> “The root of all evils is greed” (1 Timothy 6:10).

It secretly arises in the mind, but openly produces the prickings of all sins in action. The outstanding preacher immediately indicates these prickings arising from that root when he adds:

> “By desiring it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains” (ibid., 6:10).

By speaking of many pains, he made known that the prickings are born from this root.

In the junipers, therefore, we understand sins; in the root of the junipers, what else but avarice—that is, the material of sins?

Since heretics often pursue only outward profits in their words, and do not fail to know that they are asserting perverse things, yet do not abandon their proclamation of error, while they wish to receive payment as though they were teachers, [Note: The German, Béthune, and most Norman manuscripts have “as though they were teachers.”] it is rightly said of them here, in the voice of the holy men:

> “And the root of junipers was their food,”

because, while they think of avarice with every faculty of their minds, they feed, as it were, on the nourishment from which the prickings of subsequent sins unquestionably tend to arise.

Whenever they find in sacred discourse something that they regard as clever, and, because they do not understand it, suppose it to support their own assertions, they immediately scatter it, shouting it out to their wretched hearers, whose possessions—not their souls—they desire.
