Hence it fittingly follows:

## CHAPTER XI [New recension XIII]

### Verse 5

> “They snatched these things from the valleys; whenever they found something, they ran to it with a shout.”

## 22. They twist and drag obscure statements of Holy Scripture and of the Fathers toward themselves

They snatch these things from the valleys because they gather them, with a proud spirit, from the humble sayings of the Fathers.

When they boast that they have found these things in support of their own party, they run to them with shouts, because, driven by a desire for praise, they try to spread among human ears everything they think.

[Note: Corruptly in the editions of Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville: “for their own fathers”; otherwise one would have to read *whom*, not *which*. Anyone consulting the manuscript codices will have no doubt about the reading.]

It continues:

## CHAPTER XII

### Verse 6

> “They lived in the deserts of torrents, and in caves of the earth, or upon gravel.”

## 23. Heretics are distinguished by hiding places and instability

We call torrents streams that are gathered from winter waters and that also dry up at appointed times. Thus the inventors of perverse doctrines are rightly called torrents, because they are cold from the heat of love and swell, as it were, in the torpor of winter. They do not flow with perpetual fullness but are dried up by the arguments of Catholics, as though by summer suns. [Note: Another reading: “as though by the heat of the sun.”]

Indeed, the inventors of perverse doctrines who arose against the holy Church have already been extinguished in the fervor of truth. Yet their disciples do not cease to hold and defend what those men taught. [Note: Gembloux: “they attempt to hold and defend.”]

Those, therefore, who follow their errors live in the deserts of torrents—that is, they trust in the preaching of those whose words have already been dried up by the replies and reasoning of Catholics.

[Old recension XI.]

What else should we understand by caves of the earth except the hidden preachings of heretics? Heretics meet secretly among themselves in clandestine gatherings, so that they may give their error the reverence they cannot obtain through reason by means of concealment. To weak souls, a statement of perversity appears so much more worthy of reverence the more secret it is.

Hence in Solomon a woman, representing heresy, urges people, saying:

> “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Proverbs 9:17).

The Truth condemns such hidden proclamations, saying:

> “If anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There he is,’ do not believe it.”

And again:

> “If they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. For just as lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:23, 26).

What is there called “in the inner rooms” is here called “in caves.” Heretics therefore live in caves, because they often conceal their error in secret preachings, so that the less they reveal themselves to the more learned and prudent, the more vigorously they draw the inexperienced to themselves.

Hence it is also appropriately added:

> “Or upon gravel.”

We call gravel those very small stones that flowing water carries. [Note: The printed editions have “which rainwater carries.” The Vendôme, German, Tours, Laon, Norman, and other manuscripts read “which river water carries.”]

The teachers of perverse doctrines therefore live upon gravel because they draw along those human minds that are not solidified by any stability of gravity, but are led, as though from place to place, by the rivers of error.

Hence the outstanding preacher, wishing his hearers not to be led temporally but to be established with firm gravity, admonished them, saying:

> “So that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14).

Thus the holy Church, temporarily depressed by her adversaries, when she sees the bold minds of the erring insulting her, recalls what their way of life had been and says:

> “They lived in the deserts of torrents, and in caves of the earth, or upon gravel.”

Because their perverse preaching, having lost the fire of love, grew strong through the coldness of the mind, it plainly lived in the deserts of torrents. Because it was neither open nor free, it lay hidden in caves. Because it held the people not fixed but unstable, it remained not upon rock but upon gravel.

Concerning them it further says:

## CHAPTER XIII [New recension XIV]

### Verse 7

> “They rejoiced among such things and considered it a delight to be beneath thorns.”

## 24. They exult and delight in the worst things

What should we understand by thorns except those prickings of sins that we mentioned above? [§ 21 above in this book.]

Because perverse minds rejoice in the iniquities over which they ought to have wept, all heretics raise themselves up in such empty joy the more they grow strong in worse things. They consider it a delight to be beneath thorns, because they lift their perverse minds toward joy from the very place where they bear the thorns of sins.

For whenever they have managed to draw someone into their error, they boast with delight. From the very source by which they gather sins for themselves each day, even by destroying others, they exult as though they were guides to righteousness.

It is therefore rightly said:

> “They rejoiced among such things and considered it a delight to be beneath thorns.”

They draw to their own destruction those whom they can, and they believe that, by being under sins—or by adding sins to sins—they are amassing an abundance of virtues. [Note: This passage has been restored with the aid of manuscripts and old editions. In the German manuscripts and in Gilot’s edition and those following it, the reading is: “And they do not believe themselves to be under sins … but that they are accumulating an abundance of virtues,” a meaning plainly contrary to that found in the English, Norman, Laon, Tours, and other manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XIV [New recension XV]

### Verse 8

> “Sons of fools and of men without honor, and not reckoned at all among the earth.”

## 25. The fathers of heretics are foolish and without honor

These are the sons of those who were teachers of errors. They are called sons not because they were generated from their seed but because they were generated through imitation. By teaching perverse things, those fathers were foolish through ignorance; by living wickedly, they were without honor in their conduct. Such sons are joined to our Redeemer by no kinship of wisdom or of life.

Of him Solomon says in praise of the holy Church:

> “Her husband is noble at the gates” (Proverbs 31:23).

Because these people followed the perverse examples of the erring, they are remembered as sons of fools and of men without honor.

It is rightly added:

> “And not reckoned at all among the earth,”

because, while they desire to be regarded here as something, they are plainly deprived of a share in the land of the living.

## 26. The same things can be said of the carnal as of heretics

What we have said under the figure of heretics in no way prevents us from understanding it also of the perverse and carnal, even when they stand within the true faith.

For the holy Church of the elect does not count as her adversaries only those who dissent from her faith while standing outside it; it also counts those who, by living badly, oppress her life from within.

Let her, therefore, afflicted by the misery of invading adversity, contemplate how, in the time of her prosperity, she was weighed down by the wickedness of those who lived within her. Let her contemplate how, as certain people deserved, the life of all was not unjustly disturbed, and let her say:

> “They gnawed in the wilderness, filthy with calamity and misery.”

As I stated at the beginning of this work, the wilderness of the mind can sometimes be understood through the power of contemplation. But here, when wilderness is mentioned as a reproach, what else does it demonstrate except the abandonment of goodness?

Hence Jeremiah also, under the figure of Judea, laments the soul of the sinner, saying:

> “How solitary sits the city that was full of people!” (Lamentations 1:1).

But when blessed Job says concerning the wicked, “They gnawed in the wilderness,” it is pleasing to consider also what is said through the Psalmist:

> “His enemies shall lick the earth” (Psalm 72:9).

## 27. Some pursue avarice through flattery, others through open force

[Old recension XII.]

There are two kinds of people who serve their ambition. One always uses the tongue’s flattery for avarice; the other applies himself to plunder by open force.

For we gnaw when we wear away something outwardly by vigorous effort. Something is licked when what cannot easily be eaten is tasted through the gentleness of a pressing tongue.

Thus all who live perversely even under the appearance of faith, who desire what belongs to others but cannot seize what they desire, and who attempt to draw it away through flattering words and a kind of sweet gentleness—what else do they do but lick the earth? For what they cannot take away by force, they strive to obtain through the gentleness of the tongue.

But those who are supported by some power in this world and desire what belongs to others, who disdain to flatter deceitfully because they can fulfill their wishes even by unjust strength—these do not lick what they desire but gnaw it, since by the strength of their power they demolish the lives of their neighbors as though with the effort of their teeth.

Let the holy Church therefore contemplate the true riches of the eternal homeland, the multitude of the heavenly citizens, the cultivation of the mind in her elect, [Note: Many manuscripts read: “of eternal glory.”] and the innumerable goods of the virtues. Let her turn her mind’s eye from them to the life of the wicked, which is deprived of every good, and, by comparing the two, see how empty the latter is of all virtues, because it has abandoned heavenly things and desired earthly ones.

Let her see how, whenever possible, such a person even violently seizes what he desires. Let her see that she has long tolerated such people as though they were placed within her, and that through their sins the danger and loss even of the good have been reached. Let her say:

> “They gnawed in the wilderness.”

As though she were openly complaining:

> “They would not gnaw by violently seizing what belongs to others unless they themselves had first remained solitary and empty within, without the cultivation of virtue.”

He also aptly explains their condition, saying:

> “Filthy with calamity and misery.”

For when sick flesh is neglected instead of being diligently cared for, it is made worse in its illness by the filth drawn over it from above. And when the misery of negligence is added to the calamity of sickness, a heavier suffering is endured because filth has arisen.

## 28. By serving the necessities of nature beyond due measure, we increase its infirmities

Human nature, therefore, created good but having fallen through the fault of its own will into infirmity, fell into calamity, because, oppressed by innumerable necessities, it found in this life nothing except occasions of affliction. But when we generally serve these necessities of our nature more than is fitting, and neglect the care of the mind,

[Note: Sag., Gemeticensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “more than necessary.”]
 we add to our infirmity, through the misery of negligence, the squalor of sin. Natural necessities ordinarily have this especially dangerous feature: it is often not at all discerned what is done in relation to them out of a concern for usefulness and what out of the vice of pleasure. For, when an occasion for seduction is frequently discovered, while we render what is owed to necessity, we serve the vice of pleasure; and the excuse of infirmity cloaks itself before the eyes of discernment and, as though under the protection of fulfilling what is useful, conceals itself.

To relax the infirmity of our nature through negligence is nothing other than to add misery to calamity and to multiply the squalor of vices from that same misery. Therefore holy men distinguish everything they do with the most diligent intention, lest the infirmity of their nature demand more from them than is due, and lest, under the cover of necessity, the vice of pleasure grow within them. They endure one thing from infirmity and another from the suggestion of temptation; and, stationed like most upright arbiters between necessity and pleasure, they alleviate the former by consoling it and restrain the latter by repressing it.

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus, two Laudunenses, and Germanus read *arbitres* (“arbiters”); we have sometimes found this in other old manuscripts in place of *arbitri*.]

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus and Laudunensis read *hanc consulendo* (“by attending to this”); Vindocinensis reads *hanc solvendo sublevant* (“they relieve this by loosening it”).]

Thus it happens that, although they endure the calamity of their infirmity, they nevertheless do not descend through negligence into the squalor of misery. For to be in calamity itself is to endure the necessities of nature because of the infirmity of still-corruptible flesh. These necessities the one who said, “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm 24:17), desired to escape. For he knew that the sins of pleasure often burst forth from the occasion of necessities; and, lest he willingly admit anything unlawful, he sought to have removed precisely that which he unwillingly endured at its root.

## 29. While the carnal appear to serve necessity, they serve pleasure. Would that their own death alone were enough for the wicked

But, on the contrary, the wicked rejoice in the necessities of their corruption, because they turn them toward the use of pleasures. When they serve nature by restoring their bodies with food, through the delight of the appetite they stretch themselves out in the excess of pleasure. When they seek clothing to cover their limbs, they desire not only garments that cover them, but also those that make them conspicuous; and, against the numbness of cold, not only those that protect them by their thickness, but also those that delight them by their softness—not only those that soothe the touch by their softness, but also those that seduce the eyes by their color.

To turn the cause of necessity, then, into the use of pleasure—what is this other than to join the squalor of misery to one’s own calamity?

[Note: Gemeticensis, other Norman manuscripts, and one Laudunensis read “to the misery of his calamity.”]

Therefore, when the Church is pressed by the time of adversity, let it remember those through whose merits it endures such things, and say: “Those who gnawed in the wilderness, squalid with calamity and misery.” They would not be squalid with calamity if they did not add the misery of pleasures to the necessities implanted in them.

[Note: The Received Edition has “if in these”; the manuscripts of Bellovacensis, Turonensis, all the Norman witnesses, Vallis Clara, and others read *insitis* (“implanted”), which we follow along with the ancient printed editions. Germanus reads “if in the necessities of nature”; Corbeiensis Germanicus reads “if in unusual necessities.”]

These necessities we deserved because of the guilt of our first parent. But those who add misery to their calamity proceed from the torment of punishment to the increase of guilt. Would that such people, when they disdain to be changed for the better, acted perversely in such a way that they did not also offer those things to others. Would that their own death alone were enough for them, and that they did not also kill the lives of others by poisonous persuasion. For they begrudge others being what they are not, and grieve that others obtain what they themselves are losing. If they happen to see some good arising in the conduct of others, they immediately tear it out with the destructive hand of reproach.

Hence it follows [Ancient Edition XIII]: “And they gnawed herbs and the bark of trees.”

## 30. They attempt to pervert those who are beginning and advancing in the good

What is signified by “herbs,” then, except the tender life of those who are beginning well, close to the earth; and what by “the bark of trees,” except the outward works of those who already aspire to higher things? For when the wicked see people beginning what is right, they contradict them either by mockery or as though by giving advice. But when they already judge some to be advancing toward the heights, because they cannot utterly destroy their progress, they turn them away from some of their works.

Thus, for them to gnaw herbs and the bark of trees is, through poisonous persuasion—as though with certain teeth of their malice—to destroy either the endeavors of those beginning well or the works of some who, already like trees, are reaching toward higher things. The reprobate gnaw herbs when they consume the beginnings of the weak by mocking them. They also gnaw the bark of trees when, by the hand of perverse counsel, they remove the covering of good works from the life of those who are growing rightly.

[Note: Gilotius and other more recent editions read “of those who rightly believe,” against all the English and our manuscripts, except Germanus.]

They strip some of their works as though they were trees; others, like herbs, they drag down in contempt and devour as though they were trampling them. They partially demolish the strength of some that is already rising on high, while they utterly crush the tender growth of others still placed below. Let him therefore say: “They gnawed herbs and the bark of trees,” because by wicked mockery they destroyed outward works in some and hearts verdant with hope in others.

[Note: Gemeticensis and Uticensis read “outward goods.”]

## 31. Some feed only on the appearance of virtue, as though on bark

Or, certainly, “to gnaw herbs” means to imitate certain light and tender things from the ancient fathers. But “to eat the bark of trees” means to perform their works only outwardly, while not maintaining a right intention in those same works. There are some who, because they cannot obtain the glory of the present world through the activities of that world, desire the appearance of holiness, assume the habit of reverence, and long to appear imitators of the ancient fathers. They perform certain small and easy deeds, but disdain to imitate their courageous works—those that proceed from the root of charity alone.

These people eat herbs, because they neglect great things and are satisfied with what is worthless. Yet they often perform certain works that seem more robust, but they do not maintain a right intention in those same works. For them, to gnaw the bark of trees is to assume the outward acts of the elect while not possessing a good intention in good deeds. While they seek righteous works for human praise but neglect to imitate the heart of those who act rightly, they are filled only with the bark of trees. For with their whole desire they seek the glory or abundance of the present life. Hence it is rightly added: “And the root of junipers was their food.”

## 32. A wrongful act that delights in guilt pricks in punishment

Although they are placed inwardly through faith, when they commonly serve the thoughts of avarice, they eat, as it were, that from which, at the end of life, the harshness of punishments is brought forth. Since they do not desire the fruit of divine utterance but serve the pursuit of temporal things, they are satisfied not with wheat bread but with the root of juniper. For what arises from the lowest and most base things occupies them; later, like juniper, it will prick them through the hardness of retribution, as though through the roughness of its leaves.

[Note: So read the manuscripts of Corbeiensis Germanicus, the Norman witnesses, Laudunensis, Turonensis, Vallis Clara, and the old edition. Recent editors changed *retributionum* (“of retributions”) to *tribulationum* (“of tribulations”), which they considered more suitable.]

While they despise God here, they scarcely perceive how great is the evil they do. They still eat the root of juniper, but they do not consider how rough are the branches of this root, because a wrongful act now delights like a root in guilt, but later pricks like branches in punishment. Hence it is rightly added: “Those who, snatching these things from the valleys, whenever they found anything, ran to them with a shout.”

## 33. In the valley of the present life, people often quarrel with a great shout over a worthless wage

In comparison with the things above, all the present life is a valley. But because these people cannot contemplate the heights of the mountains—that is, the courageous deeds of the saints—they always dwell in lowly pleasures as though in valleys; and whenever they find any gain, even a small payment, they run with a shout, because they strive to seize it even by quarrelling.

To run with a shout to each thing found in the valley is to quarrel even over a small payment when occasions for disputes arise. Often, however, an action that displays a person as holy is tested when an opportunity for earthly advantage arises. You may see some already doing lofty things, already following the examples of earlier fathers in works of abstinence and instruction; but when suddenly they find the gain of the present life, like the fruit of a valley, they run to it with a shout, because, breaking the tranquility of the holiness they had assumed, they leap out toward it.

## 34. Many seek the reward of virtue, not virtue itself

[Ancient Edition XIV.] Through “herbs” and “the bark of trees” one may understand not only, as was said above, the works of the good, but also the consolations and prosperities of this life. For often almighty God enriches his elect with inward gifts and also supports them with outward honors. When he makes them honorable by preferring them to others, he displays them more broadly as objects of imitation. Yet sometimes the wicked despise their way of life while longing to attain their happiness in this world.

Because they seek here the flatteries of passing consolation, they eat herbs: in their thoughts they meditate on the outward glory of such people, and so they gnaw the bark of trees. And because in all these things they serve avarice with their entire intention, they are filled with the root of juniper. They snatch all these things from the valleys, because they burn with immense desires out of love for this lowly and corruptible life.

[Note: The edition has corruptly “and when they snatch each thing.” The text of Job recommends reading “when they find each thing,” as do the manuscripts of Germanus, Turonensis, Laudunensis, the Norman witnesses, Corbeiensis Germanicus, and others.]

And when they find each thing, they run to it with shouts, because they strive to seize the places and offices of the holy fathers, whose merits they do not seek to acquire; and when they generally cannot attain these things peacefully, they attempt to obtain them even by breaking the peace of concord.

## 35. What the righteous despise, they desire most intensely

Because they are separated far from the conduct of the fathers who came before them, it is rightly added: “They dwelt in the deserts of torrents, and in caves of the earth, or upon gravel.”

In the good sense, we rightly understand “torrents” as holy preachers, who, while they flow into us through divine utterances in the present life, are gathered like a multitude of waters in winter. They withdraw when the summer sun arrives, because when the light of the eternal homeland shines forth, they will cease to preach. The comforts of temporal life are the deserts of these torrents. They abandon them and turn themselves toward acquiring heavenly gains.

[Note: Turonensis reads *appetenda* (“to be sought”) for *adipiscenda* (“to be acquired”).]

That torrent had left all these things behind—the one who said: “For whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things and consider them as refuse” (Philippians 3:8).

But because the minds of the wicked desire to attain in this life those things which the righteous leave behind in contempt, they are said to dwell in the deserts of torrents. For they greatly desire to receive what is unworthy of the saints. The caves of the earth are wicked thoughts, in which they hide themselves from human eyes. The wicked flee being seen by others as they are; and while they pretend to be something other than they are, they conceal themselves in the hiding places of their conscience as though in caves of the earth.

[Note: Most editions omit *terrae* (“of the earth”), but it is found in the English and our manuscripts, as well as in the old Paris edition of 1495; it is not redundant, since the hiding places of conscience are compared with caves of the earth.]

They would not do all these things unless they despaired of eternal and enduring life, unless they fixed their minds upon the uncertainty of temporality. Hence it is rightly added: “Or upon gravel.”

## 36. Clinging to things that flow away, they roll down to the depths

Gravel is the present life, which is ceaselessly carried toward its end by the very failure of its mutability, as though by the force of a river. To dwell upon gravel, then, is to cling to the flow of the present life and to place one’s intention where one cannot make one’s step firm by standing steadily.

There is another feature of gravel that should by no means be passed over in silence: when the foot is placed upon its surface, it slips because of the gravel’s very instability and rolls down to the depths.

[Note: Two Laudunenses read “is devoured”; but, as we think, this is corrupt. We sometimes record the errors of manuscripts so that their character may be evident and they may not be believed immune from every mistake. Corbeiensis Germanicus gives both readings.]

In this respect the life of the wicked differs in no way. When, out of love for the world, they take pains to do certain lawful and respectable things, they place their foot as though upon a level surface; but suddenly the foot slips toward the depths, because, while their activity continually desires more, it descends all the way to what is unjust and unlawful.

Therefore, when the holy Church endures the adversities of this time, let it return in memory to the life of the carnal, whom it has endured as its adversaries even amid prosperity, and let it recognize that it suffers these things because of their merits, saying: “They dwelt in the deserts of torrents, and in caves of the earth, or upon gravel.” Because they are deprived of the teaching of the fathers, they are said to dwell in the deserts of torrents; because they cover themselves in hidden thoughts, in caves of the earth; and because they desire to fix their intention upon the instability of the present age, upon gravel.

Would that such people, since they do not wish to fight the sins that tempt them, would at least wipe away by weeping the sins they have committed! Would that they would recognize their accomplished evils and apply to the sterile fig tree the basket of manure—that is, the nourishment of lamentation to the unfruitful mind!

## 37. The evil we do places a barrier before the eye of the mind

[Ancient Edition XV.] The human mind generally has this characteristic: as soon as it slips into guilt, it is separated still farther from knowledge of itself. For the very evil it does inserts a barrier before the eye of reason in the mind. Thus it happens that the soul, first besieged by voluntary darkness, afterward no longer recognizes even the good it should seek.

For the more closely it clings to evils, the less it understands the good it is losing.

[Note: The editions read *districtus judex* (“the strict Judge”); although the difference is not of great importance, we judge that it should be changed because of the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.]

The light of truth examines the faults of the reprobate with subtlety; and the more it is neglected when possessed, the more strictly it judges, the more it permits that what has been lost is not even sought. When it is driven away from action, the light flees from awareness, so that, although its face was despised in action, its back is no longer seen even in recollection.

Hence it is that the reprobate rejoice in the crimes that ought to be wept over, of whom Solomon says: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2:14). Hence they carry out the causes of their tears in triumph; hence they execute the business of their own death while laughing. Therefore here too it is appropriately added:

# CHAPTER XV [Received Edition XVI]

### Verse 7

“Those who rejoiced among such things and considered it a delight to be beneath thorns.”

## 38. Rejoicing in transitory things, they are afflicted by heavy cares

They rejoice “among such things” because they attend to the transitory things they receive and neglect to look upon the permanent goods they are losing. While they burn with love of temporal things, they willingly remain ignorant of true joy. If they earnestly sought to know it, they would see how worthy of tears are the joys they desire. But while they disdain to know better things, they choose for themselves as though they were supreme those things that visibly flatter the eyes with fleeting seduction.

Following visible things, they fix their hearts upon them; and they rejoice outwardly all the more because inwardly they have no recollection of themselves.

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus, Bellovacensis, Laudunensis, and Germanus perhaps more correctly read “they flee the heart.” We have retained the earlier reading, which is also supported by the Norman manuscripts and most others. Vallis Clara reads “they flee from the heart.”]

Yet their joys are often mixed with tribulations, and they are scourged by the very things in which they take pride. For without the heavy distress of cares they cannot seek the temporal things they desire when they do not possess them, preserve what they have sought, pursue greater glory among their equals, demand more reverence than is fitting from their inferiors, and show less of the same reverence than they owe to their superiors; often display power through powerlessness;

[Note: The editions read “through injustice”; our manuscripts read more elegantly “through powerlessness.”]

and continually act wickedly while anxiously guarding themselves against acquiring a reputation for wickedness.

All these things certainly prick the miserable, but, conquered by their love of temporal things, they do not feel those very prickings. Hence it is rightly said: “And they considered it a delight to be beneath thorns,” because, pressed by the pleasures of sins, they do not recognize, through their affection for the present life, how harsh are the things they endure.

## 39. They regard remaining beneath thorns as a delight

They rejoice, then, but beneath thorns, because they enjoy temporal things; yet, since they cannot manage those temporal things without tribulation, the miserable are pricked by the care that weighs upon them. They remain beneath thorns and consider this itself a delight, because they endure hard things out of love for the present life, and yet, bound by an excessive desire, they regard the labor of that endurance as pleasure.

Hence Jeremiah, rightly taking upon himself the figure of the whole human condition, complains in lamentation, saying: “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lamentations 3:15). For, as we stated earlier in the seventh book, no one who is drunk knows what he is suffering. But one who is drunk with wormwood finds what he has taken bitter, yet does not understand the bitterness with which he is filled.

Thus the human race, by the just judgment of God abandoned to its own pleasures and through those same pleasures handed over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood:

[Note: Gemeticensis reads *voluntates* (“wills”) for *voluptates* (“pleasures”), here and below.]

 what it endures for love of this life is bitter, yet, through the blindness of desire—as though through the insensibility of drunkenness—it does not recognize that same bitterness. While thirsting for the glory of the world, it encounters many tribulations on its account; what it drinks is bitter. But because it has taken it with excessive eagerness, it is no longer able, because of its very drunkenness, to discern the evil of that bitterness.

[Ancient Edition XVI.] Perverse people love even tribulations for the glory of this world; they willingly serve every sweat endured for it and most devotedly submit their necks to the yoke of heavy labors. This is well described under the figure of Ephraim when the prophet Hosea says: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hosea 10:11). A heifer accustomed to the labor of threshing often returns to the same labor even when released and not compelled.

So the mind of the wicked, devoted to the services of this world and accustomed to the fatigue of temporal things, hastens to remain subject to earthly labors even when it is permitted to rest freely. It seeks the practice of a miserable way of life as the threshing of labor, so that it does not wish to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude even when it is permitted to do so.

[Note: So read the manuscripts. Two German manuscripts and the editions have “earthly sweats … and the use of misery.”]

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus and the Vulgate read “was lifting [it] from the neck of the disciples”; we follow the other manuscripts.]

The Lord was loosening this yoke from the necks of his disciples when he said: “Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). He immediately added: “And with the cares of this life; and that day come upon you suddenly.” Again: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:28).

[Note: The editions read “for what is it to say that the Lord …” The Gregorian style is better preserved in the reading “for what is it to say … to the Lord,” found in two Laudunenses, Germanus, the Norman witnesses, and others.]

For what is it to say in his teaching that the Lord is gentle and humble, except that, after abandoning the difficult paths of practicing pride, he demonstrates certain level paths of living well? But because the minds of the wicked take greater pleasure in the harshness of pride than in the gentle things of humility and meekness, they consider it a delight to be beneath thorns. For, out of love for the world, they are prepared to bear hard things as though they were soft and pleasurable, while they strive to seize the heights of worldly affairs in this life.

## 40. They take greater pleasure in the harshness of labor than in the sweetness of rest

The Lord commands cessation from the labors of the world and commends the sweetness of holy rest; yet the mad mind of the wicked rejoices more in attaining harsh things carnally than in possessing gentle things spiritually. It feeds more on the bitterness of weariness than on the sweetness of rest.

The Israelite people plainly displayed this in themselves (Exodus 16:3). While receiving the refreshment of manna from above, they desired the pots of meat, the melons, the leeks, and the onions of Egypt.

What is signified by manna except the food of grace, sweet in taste, given from above for the refreshment of the interior life to those who devote themselves well to rest? And what by the pots of meat except carnal works, scarcely cooked through the labors of tribulations as through fires?

[Note: The Roman edition of Sixtus V reads “except the carnal burdens of life,” as does Gilotius. The English and our manuscripts have *vix* (“scarcely”), which is more fitting.]

What by melons except earthly sweetness? What is expressed by leeks and onions, which generally make those who eat them shed tears, except the difficulty of the present life, which is carried on by those who love it not without lamentation and yet is loved with tears?

Therefore, abandoning manna, they sought leeks and onions along with melons and meats, because perverse minds despise the sweet gifts of rest through grace and desire the laborious paths of this life, even though filled with tears. They disdain having a place where they may rejoice spiritually and eagerly desire a place where they may groan carnally.

Let truthful Job rebuke their foolishness, because in perverse judgment they prefer disturbance to tranquility, harsh things to gentle, rough things to mild, transitory things to eternal, and dangerous things to secure.

[Note: Norman manuscripts read “their foolishness.”]

Let the holy Church remember the foolishness of these people when it is pressed outwardly by savage adversities—people whom it contained within itself as though they were faithful, but whose life hostile to the faith it endured for a long time—and let it say: “Those who rejoiced among such things and considered it a delight to be beneath thorns,” because they learned the evils they practice from the perversity of their wicked predecessors. Hence it is rightly added:

# CHAPTER XVI [Ancient Edition XVII]

### Verse 8

“Sons of fools and ignoble men.”

## 41. There are two kinds of foolishness; one is joined to the highest nobility

We must understand that some within the holy Church are called foolish but are nevertheless noble, while others are both foolish and ignoble. They are called foolish but cannot be ignoble who, despising the prudence of the flesh, seek the foolishness that benefits them and are raised to the nobility of an inward offspring by virtue.

[Note: Germanus and the editions read “and to nobility,” against all our other manuscripts.] They despise the foolish wisdom of the world and desire the wise foolishness of God.

For it is written: “What is foolish of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25). Paul urges us to grasp this foolishness when he says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (ibid. 3:18).

Those who followed this foolishness perfectly deserved to hear the voice of Wisdom: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

[Note: Most Norman manuscripts, as well as Pratensis, Beccensis, and Uticensis, read “upon twelve seats.”]

Behold: by abandoning temporal things, they purchased the glory of eternal power. What, then, is more foolish in this world than to abandon one’s possessions? And what is nobler in eternity than to come as judges with God?

The nobility of these judges is recalled with Solomon as witness, when it is said:

[Note: Gemeticensis, Ebroicensis, and the first hand of Germanus read “when [he was joined] to the knowledge [of the Creator]” for “to the kinship [of the Creator].]

 “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Proverbs 31:23). For he considers them very noble whom he calls elders. Paul had perceived this nobility in himself when, joined by the Spirit to the kinship of his Creator, he said: “Since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold, silver, or stone, the sculpture of art and the imagination of a human being” (Acts 17:29).

[Note: One Laudunensis and Vallis Clara read “or stones.”]

We are called the offspring of God not because we are born from his nature, but because we are created by his Spirit and voluntarily fashioned and renewed by adoption. Therefore each person is raised to this nobility in proportion as, through the image he has received, he is renewed into his likeness by imitation.

## 42. Another kind is ignoble, because it abandons heavenly wisdom

But, on the contrary, there are foolish and ignoble people who, while fleeing heavenly wisdom by following themselves, are lulled in their ignorance as though in the baseness of a rejected offspring. Because they do not understand the purpose for which they were created, they also lose the kinship of the nobility received through the image.

[Note: Vallis Clara reads “the kinship received.” Most Norman manuscripts read “the knowledge received.” Germanus first reads “kinship,” but changes it to “knowledge.”]

They are foolish and ignoble, then, whom the slavery of the mind excludes from fellowship in the eternal inheritance. For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). And the distinguished preacher says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness before God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). Those who, while savoring earthly things, have been excluded from inward nobility were therefore both foolish and ignoble.

When many imitate their deeds, they become sons of fools and ignoble men; while they follow them in understanding and conduct, they are foolish because they do not understand true wisdom, and ignoble because they are not renewed by any freedom of the Spirit. Although these people often practice the deeds of the wicked, they nevertheless occupy in this life the places of the righteous and consider themselves the sons of those whose offices they administer outwardly through their desire for honor.

[Note: The editions read “whom holy Church [recalls] through correction to …”; we follow two German manuscripts, the Norman witnesses, Laudunensis, Vallis Clara, and others. Some editions read “and from thought.”]

Holy correction recalls them to knowledge of themselves, so that, being placed in wicked desires, they may recognize whose sons they are. For they are not the sons of those whose places they occupy, but of those whose works they perform. Let it rightly be said, therefore: “Sons of fools and ignoble men.” Here it is appropriately added:

# CHAPTER XVII

### The same verse

“And who do not appear at all upon the earth.”

## 43. They are foolish and ignoble whom God professes not to know. Many press upon the truth by knowing it, but do not touch it

Just as many are upon the earth and are hidden from human knowledge by the obscuring veil of their lowliness, so there are some in the Church who, while submitting themselves to the degradation of wicked works, are not known to the divine sight. To them it will eventually be said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12).

To be upon the earth and to appear is to display the nobility of the mind through the virtue of one’s works in the true faith. But to be upon the earth and not to appear at all is to stand within the Church in faith while demonstrating nothing worthy of faith in one’s works.

Thus, within the holy Church, these people are both seen by the eyes of the divinity through judgment and yet are not seen through the merit of a good life, because they do not exhibit in living what they hold in confession. Paul says of them: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

Within the holy Church they suppress rather than venerate the faith they claim to hold, since they desire to acquire their own gains in its name more than to attain the faith itself.

[Ancient Edition XVIII.] But the elect, while taking care to preserve the merit of faith through righteous works, draw near to knowledge of their Creator even amid the tumult of the reprobate. This was well signified in the Gospel by the woman suffering from a flow of blood. When the Lord said of her, “Who touched me?” (Luke 8:45), Peter replied by reasoning: “The crowds press upon you and oppress you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”

[Note: Gemeticensis reads “by reasoning.”]

[Note: Vallis Clara reads “to hear the reason.”]

But he deserved to hear the explanation of the true reason when the Lord said to him: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me.”

Behold, the crowds were pressing upon the Lord, but only the woman touched him who came to him humbly, because many even in the holy Church press upon the truth by knowing it, while they neglect to touch it by living well. They press upon it and are far away, because they follow divine knowledge in their professions but flee from it in their conduct.

[Note: Gemeticensis reads “they establish [it] by professions”; Germanus reads “having professed divine knowledge, they follow [it] with their voices.”] They press upon it, I say, but are far away, because by their actions they contradict the very faith that they affirm in speech.

[Note: Later editions read “by doing evil”; *evil* is absent from all our manuscripts.]

Just as this testimony teaches us that some do not touch the Lord by touching him, so some are not seen by the Lord even when they appear to be seen, because before his hidden gaze they appear for the punishment of condemnation but do not appear for the merit of election.

[Note: The editions read, “so some appear to be seen by the Lord even when they are not seen.” We have followed the manuscripts of Laudunensis, Vallis Clara, Germanus, the Norman witnesses, and Corbeiensis Germanicus.]

Let it rightly be said, then: “And who do not appear at all upon the earth,” because although the Church held them outwardly, the Creator did not see them within it, as though he did not know them.

They hold the faith in words alone during a time of tranquility because they see that the same faith flourishes generally. But when a sudden storm of adversity arises against it, they are immediately separated from it by public denial, and they afterward fight against whatever they had previously held as though venerating it. Hence it is appropriately added:

# CHAPTER XVIII [Received Edition XVII]

### Verse 9

“Now I have become their song, and I have become their proverb.”

## 44. As the wicked increase, faith will become a reproach and truth a crime

These words express that time of the holy Church when it is publicly mocked by the reprobate—when, as the wicked increase, faith will become a reproach and truth a crime. Each person will be held in greater contempt in proportion as he has been able to be more righteous; he will be more abominable in proportion as he has been more praiseworthy.

Thus, in a time of affliction, the holy Church of the elect becomes a proverb to the wicked. When they see the good dying under torments, they take from them an occasion for a curse. The more they see transitory death but do not see abiding life, the more, in mockery, they make present evils their object of flight, because inwardly, through understanding, they do not attain permanent goods.

[Note: The Norman manuscripts read “the things set forth” for “the things that follow.”]

But since the things that follow are not entangled in more obscure statements, we should pass over them briefly, so that we may arrive more quickly at those requiring labor. It follows:

# CHAPTER XIX

### Verse 10

“They abhor me, and flee far from me, and are not afraid to spit in my face.”

45. The Church is not cast down by the mockery of the wicked, but is raised up and grows.---All the wicked flee far from the holy Church, not in the steps of their feet but in the qualities of their conduct; they flee far, not in place but in merit, while, as pride increases, they despise her with open reproach. For to spit in her face is not merely to slander the good in their absence, but also to refute every righteous person in his presence. When the wicked openly scorn them, they pour forth in their insults slippery words, as though spitting out streams of saliva.

[Note: [Col. 0164D] In Germ., Utic., and Turon., “they become far away.” Both readings occur in Corb. Germ., where “they flee” is nevertheless preferred.]

[The old XIX.] But the holy Church knows how to grow through sufferings and to maintain an honorable life amid reproaches. She knows neither to be cast down by adversity nor to glory in prosperity; she knows how, in opposition to prosperity, to lay her mind low in humiliation, and, in opposition to adversity, to raise her spirit toward hope of the heavenly summit. She knows how to attribute her good works to the mercy of the Redeemer and her evil to the justice of the Judge: that she possesses the good because he bestows it, and suffers the evil because he permits it. Thus she immediately continues concerning the Lord, saying:

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0164D] VERSE 11.—For he opened his quiver and afflicted me.

46. She knows that, by God’s permission, though through a hidden judgment, she suffers evil.---What is signified by God’s quiver, if not a hidden plan? The Lord shoots an arrow from the quiver when he brings forth an open sentence from his hidden plan. We know that someone is scourged, but we do not know for what reason the scourging comes. When correction of life follows the scourges, the power of the plan itself is also revealed. The closed quiver, therefore, is the hidden plan. But we are afflicted by an opened quiver when, through what follows the scourging, we see the plan according to which we are scourged.

When the Lord sees sins and yet does not move his hand to punishment, he holds, as it were, a closed quiver; but by striking he shows how greatly displeasing to him was that which he had long tolerated while observing it. Thus the holy Church of the elect, pressed by tribulations, says: “For he opened his quiver and afflicted me.” While enduring the insolent voices of her adversaries, she sees that her preaching is not accepted and, abandoning the hardness of certain people, moderates the words of her preaching. For, perceiving that her persecutors become worse at the sound of her exhortation, she chooses rather to remain silent. When she sees that those who hear are unworthy, she restrains her preaching by imposing silence. Hence she appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XXI

IBID.—And he placed a bridle in my mouth.

47. Preaching must be restrained when those who receive God’s word become worse through it.---Those who said, “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46), recognized that a bridle had been placed upon them among certain people.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] Gemet., Germ., and several others read: “but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy.”]

Holy men see the bridle of silence imposed upon them before the hard hearts of the wicked, when they say through the Prophet: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136:4). Paul also taught that a bridle should be applied when he instructed his disciple, saying: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Tit. 3:10).

For holy teachers often perceive, with deep consideration, the hearts of those who resist; and when they see that these have been abandoned by God, they fall silent, afflicted and groaning. Does Solomon not at times impose a bridle upon teachers when he says: “Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Prov. 9:8)? But if we remain silent about rebuke because we fear that the scoffer’s hatred will rise against us, then we seek not God’s gains but our own.

Here it must be understood that sometimes the wicked become worse when they are rebuked. We therefore do not spare them—and not ourselves—if, out of love for them, we cease rebuking them. Hence it is necessary sometimes to tolerate in silence what they are, so that they may learn by seeing our good conduct what they themselves are not.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] So most manuscripts and the old edition; the reading is contradicted by Germ. and the later editions, which omit the negation.]

[Note: [Col. 0165D] Corb. Germ. and the editions read “may learn by seeing.” Gillot, however, noted our reading in the margin; it occurs both in the English manuscripts and in others of ours.]

Because the holy Church, which always brings forth her words through charity, sometimes also restrains them out of charity, let her say: “He placed a bridle in my mouth.” As though she openly confessed, saying: “Because I saw no progress from my preaching among certain people, I restrained my impulse toward them, so that at least through my patience they might learn my way of life, since they did not wish to accept my words when preaching was offered to them.”

[The old XX.] Yet amid tribulations we are often pained most by the fact that we suffer them from those in whom we trusted with brotherly love. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXII [Rec. XVII]

VERSE 12.—At the right hand of the Rising One my calamities immediately arose.

48. The Gentiles are to be understood by the left, and the Jews by the right.---Calamities would arise on the left if he suffered the adversity of persecution from people placed outside the religion and openly denying Christ. But when he suffers the torment of temptation from those who seem to be faithful, his calamities arise, as it were, on the right, because those who serve under Christ’s name attack Christ’s name in him.

In ordinary speech we call something “right” that we value highly, and “left” what we despise. Zechariah clearly indicates this when he says: “And he showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. 3:1). To make clearer what he had said, he added: “And the Lord said to Satan: ‘The Lord rebuke you, Satan, the Lord who chose Jerusalem. Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?’ And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” (ibid., 2).

[Note: [Col. 0166D] The same manuscripts say “clothed.”]

Jesus was clothed in filthy garments because, although foreign to every sin, he came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Satan stood at his right hand when he came. For the Lord seemed to regard the Jewish people as something great and the Gentiles as nothing. But after he appeared incarnate, the Gentiles, who had been regarded as the left, believed, while the Jewish people turned toward unbelief.

Satan therefore stood at his right hand because he snatched from him the people who had formerly been beloved. But because that Jewish people, now lost, will at the end eventually believe, as the Prophet testifies: “A remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10:21), the Lord removes Satan from his right hand, saying: “The Lord rebuke you, Satan” (Zech. 3:1). Indicating the liberation of that people, he adds: “For he has chosen Jerusalem” (ibid., 2). Since that people, led by unbelief, was flowing down toward the fires of Gehenna, but, when restored to faith, is freed from the same fire of eternity, it is immediately said of it there: “Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?”

49. The people who follow the faith of the Church, from whom she herself at times suffers violence.---As the Jewish people there signifies the right, so here the faithful people of the holy Church is designated by the word “right.” Hence the coming Judge will place the goats on the left and the sheep on the right (Matt. 25:33).

But when, in a time of adversity, even those who seemed to be faithful attack the holy Church, her calamities undoubtedly arise on the right.

[The old XXI.] This very right is appropriately called the right of the Rising One. For it is written concerning that Church’s very head: “The Rising One is his name” (Zech. 6:12). Since light rises from the east, he is rightly called “the Rising One,” by whose light of righteousness the night of our unrighteousness is illumined.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The recent editions read “by whose righteousness the night of our righteousness is illumined.” The reading followed here is found in the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Anglic., with only one exception, and in all the Norman manuscripts, Turon., Germ., and several others, on which all the old editions were based. Utic. has “is illuminated” instead of “is illumined.”]

Thus calamities arise at the right of the Rising One because even those who were believed to be chosen members of our Redeemer rush forth to persecute.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The same later editions read “in accordance with which, namely, the calamities.” Our reading is found in the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Turon., and the others cited above, with which the ancient printed editions agree.]

He rightly asserts that these calamities arise immediately, because, since those who persecute are not outsiders, evils are suddenly and immediately inflicted by them. But if “the right” refers to those who are truly faithful, calamities arise at the right of the Rising One because, when the moment of persecution breaks out, the righteous suffer the cruel attacks of the wicked.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Rec. XIX]

[Col. 0167B] IBID.—They overturned my feet and overwhelmed them as with the waves of their paths.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] Turon. and several Norman manuscripts read “my paths,” but incorrectly.]

50. The Church’s lowest members are sometimes overturned like feet.---What is signified by the feet of the Church, if not her lowest members? Since they are devoted to earthly works, they can be deceived by adversaries all the more quickly because they understand lofty matters less.

The adversaries overturn these feet when they draw her lowest members into the error of their own doctrine. Overturned feet cannot keep to the road, when the weak, persuaded by the promises of their persecutors, frightened by their threats, or broken by their tortures, stray from the right path.

The paths of the adversaries are appropriately compared with waves when it is said: “And they overwhelmed them as with the waves of their paths,” because the life of the wicked, troublesome through insolent unrest, pours in like a storm to engulf, so to speak, the ship of the heart. Concerning this storm Solomon says: “As a storm passing by, so the wicked shall not be” (Prov. 10:25).

When a weak person sees the wicked flourishing, the wave of wretched imitation plunges him into the sea of perversity.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV

VERSE 13.—They destroyed my paths, they lay in wait for me, they prevailed, and there was no one to bring help.

51. His ways are destroyed by the hidden ambushes of enemies, while God usefully abandons him for a time.---Let blessed Job speak these words concerning the evil spirits, his hidden enemies; let the universal Church speak them concerning wicked persecutors, her open adversaries.

They destroy her paths when, through crafty persuasion, they disturb the ways of truth in the minds of certain weak people. They prevail while lying in wait when they corrupt those whom they cannot openly draw into evil by pretending to be good.

But it is very surprising that he adds: “There was no one to bring help,” when the Psalmist cries concerning divine aid: “A helper in times of trouble and tribulation” (Ps. 9:10); and: “Let all who know your name hope in you, for you, Lord, have not abandoned those who seek you” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Val. Cl., Germ., Norm., Corb. Germ., and several others read: “in you, all who.”]

And since it is written again: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame? Who has persevered in his commandments and been forsaken? And who has called upon him and he despised him?” (Ecclus. 2:11–12), for what reason is it now said: “There was no one to bring help”? Only because almighty God sometimes abandons for a time those whom he loves eternally.

Hence it is written: “For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while, but with everlasting mercy I have had mercy on you” (Isa. 54:7).

For this reason the Psalmist also prayed: “Do not abandon me utterly” (Ps. 118:8). He knew, therefore, that it could be useful for him to be abandoned for a little while, since he asked not to be abandoned utterly.

The Lord helps his saints by coming to them and tests them by abandoning them; he strengthens them with gifts and tests them through tribulations. Hence a certain wise man rightly says: “At first he chose him; he will bring fear, dread, and testing upon him, and he will torment him with the tribulation of his discipline until he tests him in his thoughts” (Ecclus. 4:18).

Grace calls the soul of the righteous, and temptation questions it. Almighty God also permits the adversaries of his elect to increase for a time, so that the life of the good may be purified through the savagery of the wicked.

52. The power of the wicked also serves the advantage of the righteous.---The Lord would never permit adversaries to be against the good unless he also saw how much they would benefit them. For while the unjust rage, the just are purified; and the life of the wicked serves the advantage of the innocent, since by pressing down the latter’s life it humbles it, and by humbling it continually forms it for the better.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “The fool shall serve the wise” (Prov. 11:29). Yet we often see the wise subject to the foolish, while fools hold the citadel of domination; the wise obey in servile fashion, while fools rule with tyrannical arrogance.

How, then, does the fool serve the wise according to the definition of the divine sentence, when he often suppresses him by the right of temporal domination?

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Ebroic., Gemet., and others read “of divine wisdom.”]

It must be understood that when a foolish person in a position of superiority exercises the terror of power against the life of the wise, when he exhausts him with labors and tears him with insults, he thereby purifies him by burning away all the rust of vice. The fool, therefore, serves the wise even while dominating him, because by pressing him down he advances him toward a better condition.

Thus sometimes servants preside over orphaned masters for the sake of discipline: they frighten, oppress, and strike them, yet in no way cease to be servants, because they were appointed for this very purpose, that by striking they might serve masters who are making progress.

Because the evils of the wicked purify the good while tormenting them, the power of the wicked also serves the advantage of the righteous. But often the righteous, caught in tribulation, consider the hand of their helper slow when the cruelty of their persecutors confines them somewhat longer.

The remedies of the deliverer are indeed swift, but what the deliverer accomplishes quickly seems slow to the person in pain. When help is sought in response to prayer, if it does not immediately follow the voice, it is thought to be absent. Hence it is now said: “And there was no one to bring help.”

In this utterance the force of the suffering itself is expressed: heavenly help is present insofar as it belongs to the ordered providence of the protector, yet it is believed absent insofar as it does not answer the sufferer’s urgent desires.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXV [Old XXII, Rec. XX]

VERSE 14.—As through a breached wall and an open door they rushed upon me, and they rolled down upon my miseries.

53. The state of the soul is to be mourned when enemies rush into it after the wall of faith has been breached or the structure of discipline destroyed.---What else is called a wall in this passage but the Redeemer of the human race? Concerning him, for the building of the holy Church, the Prophet says: “A wall and an outer wall shall be placed in it” (Isa. 26:1).

He himself is our wall, who prevents the advance of evil spirits from reaching our hearts. He also placed an outer wall of our faith, because before he manifested himself in the flesh he sent prophets as preachers of his mystery. They are rightly called an outer wall because, while they proclaimed the Lord who was to follow, they stood, as it were, before the wall.

The wall is breached when the faith that is in our Redeemer is scattered in the hearts of certain people through the persuasions of the wicked. And when power is granted to the perverse in this life, what else is opened than a door of error?

Thus, as through a breached wall and an open door, the wicked rush upon the good when, having received temporal power, the perverse also try to destroy the defenses of faith in the hearts of certain people.

Of these it is appropriately said: “And they rolled down upon my miseries,” because they first fell into their own miseries. For unless they had first fallen into their own miseries by living perversely, they would never afterward have persuaded others to fall into them. But after their own fall, the wicked roll down upon our miseries as well when they draw some who are united with us into the evils in which they themselves are already entangled.

54. The word “wall” can also be understood as the fortification of discipline, as Solomon attests when he says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, nettles had entirely filled it, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. 24:30).

To pass by the field of a lazy man and the vineyard of a foolish man is to inspect the life of someone who is negligent and to consider his works.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Gemet. reads “more negligently.”]

Nettles and thorns fill it because in the heart of the negligent, earthly desires that cause itching and the pricks of vices spring up, since it is written: “Every idle person is in his desires” (Prov. 28:19, according to the Septuagint).

The stone wall had been destroyed—that is, the discipline of the fathers had been dissolved from his heart.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] So Germ., Bellov., Turon., Laud., Val. Cl., Corb. Germ., and Norm. The earlier editions read: “For because he saw the stone wall destroyed and the discipline dissolved,” and so forth.]

When he saw that the stone wall had been destroyed and the discipline dissolved, he immediately added: “When I had seen this, I placed it in my heart and learned discipline from the example” (Prov. 24:32).

Thus the enemy enters as through a breached wall when, through the crafty persuasion either of evil spirits or of wicked people, the defenses of discipline are scattered in the heart. But when the vigor of that discipline is dissolved in the hearts of the wicked, all honorable works are held in contempt before their eyes, and they consider worthless whatever virtues they see in the elect.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXVI

VERSE 15.—I have been reduced to nothing.

55. When the true goods are despised, they rely upon fleeting carnal goods, with which they perish.---In the estimation of the wicked we are reduced to nothing when we do not possess the temporal goods that they themselves cherish as supreme. Having despised the heavenly promises, they desire earthly things; and if some desire for eternity arises in their minds, it is quickly scattered by an immediately arising transient pleasure.

Hence it follows at once:

IBID.—You have taken away my desire like the wind.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The recent editions read “he has taken away,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts, the old editions, and also the Hebrew text and the Vulgate.]

The faithful people declare that they suffer what they grieve that those whom they love suffer. The wind takes away desire when any transient reality destroys the longing for eternity.

Hence it fittingly continues:

IBID.—And my salvation passed away like a cloud.

A cloud rises high, but the wind drives it along its course. Such, surely, are the temporal goods of the wicked. They seem to dwell high, as it were, through the loftiness of honor; yet they are driven daily toward the course of life by the gusts, so to speak, of their mortality.

Salvation therefore passes like a cloud, because the glory of the perverse, however high it is, is not fixed.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The edition reads “which is high,” but the manuscripts we have followed more elegantly read “however high it is.” Germ. reads “however suitable it is.”]

But once the desires and deeds of the weak have been completed, the discourse turns to the voice of the elect, when it immediately continues:

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0171A] VERSE 16.—But now my soul withers within me, and days of affliction possess me.

56. Now the elect wither in themselves, but flourish in God.---The soul of the elect now withers because afterward it will become green with eternal rejoicing. The days of affliction possess them now because days of joy follow afterward.

For it is written: “It will be well with one who fears God at the end” (Ecclus. 1:13, 19). And again it is said of the Church: “She will laugh on the last day” (Prov. 31:25).

Now is the time of affliction for the good, so that rejoicing without end may eventually follow them. Elsewhere they say: “You humbled us in a place of affliction” (Ps. 43:20). The present life is the place of affliction. The righteous, therefore, have been humbled here, that is, in the place of affliction, because in eternal life, the place of joy, they are exalted.

When he said that the soul withers, he rightly also prefaced it with “within me,” because within ourselves we are afflicted, but in God our mind is refreshed; and it is the farther from the greenness of joy insofar as, still repelled from the light of its Creator, it turns back upon itself.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] So Prat., Corb., Germ., Gemet., Turon., Val. Cl., and Germ. In Laud., “is afflicted.” The old editions read “we are affected”; later editions, “we are afflicted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0171D] So the manuscripts and the old printed editions. The recent editions read “returns to itself.”]

It reaches the greenness of true joy when, raised up through the grace of eternal contemplation, it passes beyond even itself.

But although we have briefly passed over these matters by allegorical investigation, we must also hold them in every respect according to the historical sense. I pass over that sense here because I do not fail to recognize that it is clear to readers.

During the days of the final persecution, however, because many perish and few are saved—

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Some read: “many who perish, few are,” and so forth.]

—the holy man therefore speaks, in the time of his passion, a little about the good and much about the perverse. Hence he immediately turns his words to the person of those who fall, and thus presents his own words so that what he narrates may suitably apply to those who are falling.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The editions read “so that they may be suitable for those who hear.” Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Turon., Germ., Laud., Val. Cl., and Norm. support our reading, which Gillot noted in the margin.]

For it follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Rec. XXI, Old XXIII]

VERSE 17.—At night my bone is pierced with pains, and those who consume me do not sleep.

57. When persecution rages, the strong, who are the bones in the body of the Church, fail.---If we attend to the historical sense, the reason is evident: a multitude of worms, flowing from the openings of his ulcers, tore the body of the holy man.

But if we examine the mystery of the allegory, what are signified by bones if not the strong members in the body of the holy Church? They contain the members, as it were, by their own strength, while they steadily bear the conduct of the weak.

But when the fervor of the final tribulation grows against her, her bone is pierced with pains in the night, because sometimes even those who seemed to uphold others in faith fall away into unbelief, overcome by torments.

He therefore says: “At night my bone is pierced with pains.” As though he openly said: “Pressed by the darkness of tribulation, they are so pierced by affliction that even those who possessed strength and vigor in me now have, as it were, a certain opening of fear.””

[Note: [Col. 0171D] So Anglic., Val. Cl., Pratell., and many others. This is clearly the correct reading, both from the passage in Job being explained—“my bone is pierced”—and from the words that follow: “as though they already had a certain opening of fear.” Saint Gregory is evidently alluding to the preceding expression “is bored through” or “is pierced.” The editions Barthol. 1494, Paris. 1495, Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv. read “are darkened.” Paris. 1518 and Basil. 1514, through a crasser error, read “are terrified.” Germ. and Corb. Germ. read “are darkened.”]

It is rightly said: “And those who consume me do not sleep,” because the evil spirits who consume the carnal among the Church cannot cease from temptation all the more because they are burdened by no weight of flesh.

But because the persecutors of the holy Church are exceedingly perverse, would that they were few.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Rec. XXII]

VERSE 18.—In their multitude my garment is consumed, and they girded me like the collar of a tunic.

58. Those who cling to the Church like a garment are sometimes separated from her by the force of torments.---If we attend to the historical sense, what else should we understand as blessed Job’s garment than his body? His garment is consumed when his flesh is tortured.

According to the mystery of the allegory, however, the garment of the holy Church is the life of the faithful. For just as the whole Church together is the garment of Christ, so each of the faithful is regarded as a garment of that same Church.

If the holy Church were not Christ’s garment, Paul certainly would not say: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27)—that is, neither having a spot through sin nor a wrinkle through duplicity, because she is clean through righteousness and stretched smooth through single-mindedness.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] Some read “or wrinkle.”]

She has therefore been washed so that she may have no spot, and stretched so that she may have no wrinkle: she is certainly a garment.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] This is read not only in the manuscripts but also in the old edition. Others have “cleansed,” incorrectly, as is evident from the following words: “which has therefore been washed so that it may have no spot, stretched so that it may have no wrinkle”; the term “cleansed” does not fit.]

Just as the whole Church in general is called Christ’s clothing, so the souls of individuals are the clothing of the Church. Converted from error, they surround that same Church by believing and faithfully clinging to her.

Concerning them the Lord says to that Church through the Prophet: “As I live, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. 49:18).

But when the storm of fierce persecution arises, many of the faithful are separated from the love of the Church, although they had seemed to cling to her diligently. Let her therefore say: “In their multitude my garment is consumed,” because while many are inflicting torments, very many who had clung to her through the bond of love are destroyed.

59. The wicked try to extinguish within the Church the life of faith and the voice of preaching.---It is rightly added: “And they girded me like the collar of a tunic.” The collar of a tunic surrounds the neck of the person wearing it. When the neck is constricted, the use of the voice and the vital breath are strangled.

The wicked therefore constrict the holy Church like the collar of a tunic, because through their persecutions they try to extinguish within her the life of faith and the voice of preaching. This is what her persecutors especially seek: first of all, to remove from her the word of preaching.

Hence those who resisted the beginnings of the holy faith, after having beaten the Apostles, declared: “We strictly commanded you not to teach in this name, and behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching” (Acts 5:28).

They had girded the body of the holy Church as with the collar of a tunic: by binding the preachers, they wished, as though pressing upon her neck, to close the passage of her voice within her.

But at the time of their persecution, all the elect are more ready to die than to remain silent. When they fall bodily in death, they are regarded by the foolish and carnal as despised and worthless, because, unable to see the spiritual good that the elect possess, the wretched consider those whom they see extinguished bodily to be unfortunate.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXX

VERSE 19.—I have been compared with mud and made like ashes and dust.

60. They trample her as though she were mud, ashes, and dust.---In the judgment of the wicked, the holy Church of the elect is compared with mud because, trampled down temporally, she is despised. She is made like ashes and dust because, since they do not see her inward goods, they suppose that she has been reduced to the evils alone that they see displayed bodily in her.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] The manuscripts read this better than the editions, which have “nevertheless faithful.”]

But the faithful people of the elect, when they see many falling away from among them, wish, if they could obtain it, that the times of their adversity might be changed. Because this prayer is delayed, the groaning increases.

Hence it continues:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Old XXIV]

VERSE 20.—I will cry to you, and you will not hear; I will stand, and you will not look upon me.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] The recent edition reads “I cry … and you do not hear.” We follow the manuscripts Germ., Bellov., Laud., Val. Cl., Norm., Corb. Germ., and the oldest editions.]

61. The prayer of the Church asking for deliverance is not immediately heard. For what reason?---The holy Church stands by faith and cries out in longing during the time of her persecution. She grieves that she is not looked upon, as it were, when she sees her prayers delayed amid tribulations.

By a profound plan, almighty God, when his saints are oppressed by the persecutions of their adversaries and cry out to him continually in their appeals for deliverance, usually delays the voices of those who ask, so that the merits of those who suffer may increase. Thus they are heard all the more according to merit the more promptly they are not heard according to their desire.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “My God, I will cry by day, and you will not hear, and by night” (Ps. 21:3). The benefit itself of delay in being heard is immediately added there: “And not for my foolishness” (ibid.).

For what was requested to be received slowly contributes to the multiplication of the saints’ wisdom, so that from delay desire grows, and from desire understanding increases. When understanding is intensified, a more ardent affection toward God is revealed. Affection becomes capable of attaining heavenly things in proportion as it becomes patient through waiting.

Yet amid these things pain presses the patience of the saints toward speech. As they advance through delay, they fear that, their strength failing, they may be despised and rejected.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Rec. XXIII]

VERSE 21.—You have become cruel toward me, and in the hardness of your hand you oppose me.
