62. We can say or think nothing about God that is worthy of him.---The old translation differs greatly from this sentence, because what is said here concerning God is remembered there concerning adversaries and persecutors.

Nevertheless, since this recent translation is said to have transferred everything more faithfully from the Hebrew and Arabic languages, we must believe whatever is said in it, and our exposition must carefully examine its words. It says: “You have become cruel toward me, and in the hardness of your hand you oppose me.”

[Note: [Col. 0173D] From this it is clear that, in the view of Saint Gregory, who was living among the Arabs, the Book of Job had first been written in Arabic. It is otherwise certain that Job lived in Arabia; hence the neighboring Sabaeans invaded his house (Job 1:15). Moses, moreover, having spent a long time among the Midianites, who are counted among the Arabs, learned the whole history. See below, book XXXV, formerly chapter 13, now no. 43.]

In Holy Scripture, when something unworthy is said concerning God, the reader’s mind is disturbed, as though something worthy of God were sometimes being said of him. Nearly everything said about God is already unworthy by the very fact that it could be said. For when will a speaking tongue suffice for the praise of one whose greatness an astonished conscience cannot sufficiently contemplate?

[Note: [Col. 0174D] The conjunction is omitted in several copies, which read “the supreme divine things.” Germ. reads “the supreme divine words,” and sometimes uses such expressions concerning God.]

The Holy Spirit, insinuating this very point to understanding human beings—that the highest and divine things are unspeakable—sometimes uses concerning God even words that are considered faults among human beings. Thus, from things that seem unworthy to human beings and yet are said concerning God, people may be warned to understand that even those things are not worthy of God which, because they are regarded as worthy among human beings, are thought worthy of God.

[Note: [Col. 0174D] We have restored this passage from the manuscripts Anglic., Norm., Laud., Bellov., and others. In Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv. it previously read “something unworthy.” Germ. and Corb. Germ. nevertheless have that reading. Our reading is confirmed by the entire context, from which it is clear that the holy Doctor’s intention is to show that mortals can neither think nor speak anything worthy of God’s majesty.]

### 63. In what sense God is said to be jealous, angry, repentant, merciful, and foreknowing. Nothing is past or future to God. Things are not seen by God because they exist; rather, they exist because they are seen.

For God is called jealous, as it is written: “The Lord: ‘Jealous’ is his name” (Exod. 34:14). He is called angry, whence it is written: “The Lord was angry against Israel” (Num. 32:13). God is called repentant, as it is written: “It repents me that I made man [Col. 0174D] upon the earth” (Gen. 6:7).

[Note: Gembloux and most manuscripts lack “upon the earth” in the preceding quotation.]

And again: “It repents me that I appointed Saul [Col. 0175A] king in Israel” (1 Sam. 15:11).

[Note: Lauda reads “king of Israel.”]

He is called merciful, as it is written: “The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful” (Ps. 85:15). He is called foreknowing, as the Apostle says of him: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29), although neither jealousy, nor anger, nor repentance, nor properly mercy, nor foreknowledge can exist in God.

All these expressions have been drawn from human qualities and applied to him, since he descends to the language of our weakness, so that, as though certain steps had been made for us and placed beside us, we may eventually ascend through those things that we see as near to us toward his heights.

[Note: Later editions, together with the German manuscript, read *zelare* (“to be jealous”).]

A man is called jealous when, with anguish of mind, he guards his wife’s chastity. A man is called angry when he is inflamed by fervor of spirit against a vice that must be punished. A man is called repentant when he is displeased with what he has done and, by changing something, does something else instead. A man is called merciful when he is moved by compassion toward his neighbor.

Now *mercy* is so called from “a wretched heart” (*misero corde*), because when someone observes another person in misery and, moved by compassion, is touched by the pain of his spirit, he makes his own heart wretched in order to free the one to whom he has directed his attention from misery. A man is called foreknowing when he sees each thing before it comes and foresees what is future before it becomes present.

How, then, is God jealous, when he is touched by no anguish of mind in guarding our chastity? How is he angry, when he is moved by no disturbance of spirit in avenging our vices? How is he repentant, when he never grieves that he has done what he once did? How does he have mercy, when he never has a wretched heart? How is he foreknowing, since only things that are future can be foreknown?

And we know that nothing is future for God: before whose eyes no past things are absent, present things do not pass away, and future things do not arrive, since everything that was and will be for us is present in his sight; and everything that is present can be known rather than foreknown.

[Note: Lauda reads, “can be known rather than foreknown.” I would follow this reading if it occurred in more manuscripts.]

And yet he is called jealous, angry, repentant, merciful, and foreknowing, so that, because he guards the chastity of each soul, he may be called jealous in human fashion, although he is not touched by anguish of mind. And because he strikes down sins, he is said to be angry, although he is moved by no disturbance of spirit. And because, being himself immutable, he changes what he wills, he is called repentant, although he changes the thing, not his counsel. And when he comes to the aid of our misery, he is called merciful, although he helps the miserable and never has a wretched heart. And because he sees those things that are future for us, though they are always present to him, he is called foreknowing, although he does not in any way foresee what is future, since he sees it as present.

For even things that exist are not seen in his eternity because they exist; rather, they exist because they are seen.

[Note: Thus read in the Corbie, German, Vincennes, and Val-Clair manuscripts. The Paris edition of 1495 agrees. Other copies read “from eternity,” as do the German, Utica, and other Norman manuscripts.]

When, therefore, he descends to the language of our mutability, let whoever can ascend by means of certain steps made from these expressions to the immutability of God, so that he may see one who is jealous without jealousy, angry without anger, repentant without grief and repentance, merciful without a wretched heart, and foreknowing without foreknowledge.

[Note: The Gembloux, Corbie German, Lauda, and other manuscripts read “without foresight.”]

For neither past nor future can be found in him; rather, all mutable things endure immutably, and those things that cannot exist together in themselves are all present together to him.

[Note: Vincennes reads “from themselves.”]

Nothing passes away in him as it passes away, because in his eternity, in an incomprehensible manner, all the passing ages remain; what runs stands still.

[667]

### [Old XXV.] 64. God appears cruel when, although he strikes justly, he does not spare.

Just as, then, we understand one who is jealous without jealousy and angry without anger, so it could also be said by the holy man that he is cruel without cruelty. A man is called cruel when, striking with severity, he does not spare; thus, in this passage, “cruel” can be understood as one who strikes severely and does not spare the guilt that must be avenged.

Hence Isaiah too, when he saw that the day of the final judgment would come not now with pardon but with severity, said: “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, cruel, full of indignation, wrath, and fury, to make the earth a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it” (Isa. 13:9).

[Note: The German, Utica, and other Norman manuscripts read: “and full of indignation.”]

[Note: The German, Vincennes, Pratel, and many others read: “into desolation.”]

Therefore, wishing to assert that this same cruelty could be attributed to himself rather than to God, the holy man says: “You have changed into cruelty toward me.” As though he were openly saying: “Although there is nothing cruel in yourself, you appear cruel to me, whom you do not allow to recover breath from your blows.”

[Note: The printed editions read “from persecution,” which sounds harsher when spoken of God and is not found in our parchment manuscripts.]

For God cannot be cruel any more than he can in any way be changed. But since neither cruelty nor mutability ever enters into God, when he says “to me,” he shows that he perceives God in himself as neither cruel nor mutable. For when certain favorable and adverse circumstances vary around us, we suppose, as though he had changed, that his attitude toward us has changed. Yet he himself remains immutable in himself and is perceived differently by human beings according to the quality of their merits.

The light of the sun, for example, although it is not at all unlike itself, appears harsh to the weak and gentle to healthy eyes—not because of any change in itself, but because of a change in them. Thus, as we have said, when he says, “You have changed,” he adds, “toward me,” so that this very cruelty and change may be understood to exist not in the character of the judge but in the mind of the one who suffers.

He makes the same point in other words, saying: “And in the hardness of your hand you oppose me.”

[Note: Vincennes reads: “For the hand of God, the anger of God.”]

The hand of God is believed to be hard when, contrary to our will, he pursues with blows what displeases him in us and multiplies his scourges while the grieving soul awaits mercy. Yet these words also fit well, in the mystery of allegory, the voice of holy Church speaking through the infirm, who often think they are struck more than they deserve and regard the judge’s severity as cruelty, even though the incision is entirely just. For when a sick person’s wound is cut with a medical instrument, the physician is called cruel; nevertheless, through the hardness of the hand that cuts, he opposes the wound but agrees with the patient’s recovery.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Rec. XXIV]

**Verse 22.—“You have lifted me up and, placing me as though upon the wind, you have struck me down violently.”**

### 65. He sits upon the wind who rejoices in transitory successes. Adversity does not cast down the one whom prosperity does not corrupt.

Because the glory of the present life appears to be in a high place but is established with no stability, the one who rejoices in transitory prosperity is placed as though lifted upon the wind. The fleeting breeze of happiness raises him only for this purpose: to lay him suddenly and more disastrously low.

[Note: The recent editions preferred *quando* (“when”), against the German manuscripts, which read *quoniam ad hoc solum hunc* (“because for this purpose alone him”), and so forth.]

Because holy Church is held in honor by all, do not those within her who rejoice in transitory successes appear lifted up as though placed upon the wind?

[Note: Tours, the German and Norman manuscripts read *successionibus* (“successions”) in place of *successibus* (“successes”); the former was also written by a second hand in Corbie German, where *successionibus* was first read.]

When the time of persecution follows and the breeze of prosperity passes away, their elevation immediately collapses; suddenly falling, they learn that, having first been lifted up, they had sat upon the wind.

[Note: Another reading is “they sat in the wind.” Gilot and many printed editions read “they gave themselves to the wind.”]

These words also apply especially to the person of the holy man—not according to what he was, but according to what he appeared to be. For fleeting prosperity had not lifted his mind, since, amid such abundance of possessions, the extraordinary weight of his virtue always pressed him down. Yet according to what could be seen outwardly, he who was humble in himself but exalted in the eyes of others, and who was placed as though upon the wind, was struck down violently, because, supported by external circumstances, he appeared to have fallen from the place from which he was thought to rise.

The holy man did not endure this fall in his mind, because no adversity casts down the one whom no prosperity corrupts. Whoever clings to truth does not in any way succumb to vanity, because when he has fixed the intention of his thought firmly within, whatever is enacted changeably outside does not reach the citadel of his mind.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Old XXVI, Rec. XXV]

**Verse 23.—“I know that you will deliver me to death, where the house appointed for every living thing is.”**

[Note: The German, Lauda, and Val-Clair manuscripts read, “you will deliver me to death,” and this form is consistently quoted in what follows.]

### 66. No one escapes death; few escape the pit and destruction of pleasures. Elijah postponed death; he did not escape it.

Earlier in this work it was discussed that, before the Lord’s coming, even the just descended to the dwellings of hell, although they were kept there not in punishments but in rest (above, Book XII, chapter 6, in the new edition of Gussanville, no. 13). We do not now take the trouble to establish this by testimony, because we think it has already been sufficiently proved there.

Accordingly, what is said here—“I know that you will deliver me to death, where the house appointed for every living thing is”—properly fits blessed Job even according to the historical sense, since it is clear that before the grace of the Redeemer even the just were led to the confines of hell.

[Note: The printed editions, together with the German manuscript, read “would descend,” which has the same meaning. We have judged that “would be led” should be restored in its place because of the agreement of the manuscripts and early editions.]

That reception in hell is called the house of all the living because no one comes here who, before the Mediator’s coming, did not pass there by the very condition of his corruption; no one comes here who did not proceed toward the death of the flesh by the steps of that same corruption. Concerning this death the Psalmist says: “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” (Ps. 88:49).

Even if Elijah is said to have been taken up into heaven, he postponed death; he did not escape it. For Truth himself says of him: “Elijah indeed will come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. 17:11). He will come to restore all things because he is restored to this world precisely so that he may fulfill the ministry of preaching and pay the debt of the flesh.

Yet this saying of the holy man also corresponds, according to the mystery of allegory, to the voice of holy Church speaking through the infirm, who hold the faith in words but serve their own desires against the precepts of faith. For she says: “I know that you will deliver me to death, where the house appointed for every living thing is.”

Because she sees many people devoted to pleasures within herself and already foresees their destruction,

[Note: The recent printed editions omit “within herself.” It has been supplied from the Corbie German, Lauda, Beauvais, and Norman manuscripts, with which the old printed editions agree.]

she considers that, while on the road of the present life they serve their own desires, all who live carnally in it nevertheless reach the house of death. There are, however, some who fall into the pit of their pleasures but, through the lamentations of repentance, quickly draw their foot back from the depths; the blows of heavenly chastisement cut them for instruction rather than for destruction.

The following words appropriately continue:

## CHAPTER XXXV

**Verse 24.—“Yet you do not send out your hand for their destruction; and if they fall, you yourself will save them.”**

### 67. Some who are struck by God are freed from sin for instruction, not for destruction.

In these words we must carefully understand that blessed Job, while recounting his own affairs, represents others in himself. He seemed to speak especially of himself when he said: “You have lifted me up and, placing me as though upon the wind, you have struck me down violently; I know that you will deliver me to death, where the house appointed for every living thing is.”

[Note: Most Norman manuscripts omit *quasi* (“as though”).]

Yet he then adds, not about himself but about others: “Yet you do not send out your hand for their destruction.”

For when, while speaking about himself, he reasons and adds causes concerning others, he shows how many persons he signifies in himself.

[Note: Another reading is “because [he signifies] many persons.”]

The Lord does not send out his hand for the destruction of sinners when, by striking, he corrects them from their sins and saves those who fall. He wounds those who fall into guilt for the salvation of their bodies, so that, cast down outwardly, they may rise inwardly; so that, lying prostrate in body, they may return to their interior state, those who, standing outwardly, were lying fallen from the state of their mind.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Rec. XXVI]

**Verse 25.—“I once wept over him who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”**

### 68. Almsgiving must chiefly be judged by the disposition of mind with which it is done. Let compassion, not abundance of possessions, make the giver.

Although true compassion is to join oneself through generosity to the suffering of one’s neighbor, sometimes, when external goods are abundantly available for giving, the giver’s hand finds the act of giving more quickly than the soul finds sorrow. Therefore, we must know that the one gives perfectly who, together with what he offers to the afflicted, also takes the afflicted person’s disposition into himself, first transferring into himself the suffering of the one who grieves and then confronting that suffering through his service.

For often, as we have said, abundance of possessions makes someone generous in gifts, and not the virtue of compassion. Whoever perfectly sympathizes with the afflicted often gives the needy something that would cause him distress if he himself were to give it.

[Note: The German manuscript and printed editions read: “in which the one who has given is himself distressed.” We have changed *qui* (“who”) to *si* (“if”), following the consensus of the other manuscripts.]

Our compassion is complete when we do not fear to take upon ourselves the harm of poverty for the sake of our neighbor, in order to free him from suffering.

### 69. Christ gave us the model of compassion, and Paul taught it.

The Mediator of God and human beings gave us this model of compassion. Although he could have come to our aid without dying, he nevertheless wished to help human beings by dying, because he would have loved us less if he had not also taken our wounds upon himself; nor would he have shown us the power of his love unless he himself had endured for a time what he was taking away from us.

[Note: The German, Gembloux, and other Norman manuscripts read *infunderet* (“might instill”).]

He found us mortal and subject to suffering; and he who created us from nothing could have recalled us from suffering even without his death. But in order to show how great the power of compassion is, he deigned to become for us what he did not wish us to be, so that in himself he might temporarily undergo the death that he would drive away from us forever.

[Note: The Vatican and other recent editions read: “what he wished us to be.” The manuscripts object to this, as does the thought of Saint Gregory: he says that Christ took death upon himself so that we might escape it, that is, he wished to become what he did not wish us to be. Our reading is also found in many early editions.]

Could he not, remaining invisible in the riches of his divinity, have enriched us with wondrous powers?

[Old XXVII.]

But in order that the human being might return to inward riches, God deigned to appear outwardly as poor.

Hence the distinguished preacher, in order to kindle our inner being with compassion for the grace of generosity, said: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). He also says: “Not so that there may be relief for others and tribulation for you” (ibid., 13).

He certainly said this by accommodating himself to the infirm, because for some who are unable to bear poverty, it is more tolerable to give less than, after their generosity, to grumble because of the distress of poverty. But in order to kindle his hearers’ minds to great eagerness for giving, he shortly afterward added: “This I say: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6).

We sometimes say that compassion from the heart is greater than giving, because whoever perfectly sympathizes with the needy considers everything he gives of little account. If the giver’s good will did not prevail, the same distinguished preacher would not have said to his disciples: “You began not only to do, but also to wish, from the previous year” (2 Cor. 8:10).

It is easy to obey in a good work even against one’s will.

[Note: The printed editions also read “the one who is willing.” The Corbie German, English, Norman, Lauda, German, Val-Clair, and Beauvais manuscripts read “the one who is unwilling.” The following words support this reading: “But this great virtue had appeared in the disciples: that they had first wished to do the good thing that had been commanded them.”]

But this great virtue had appeared in the disciples: that they had first wished to do the good thing that had been commanded them.

### 70. One who gives external things gives something of what he possesses; one who offers compassion gives something of himself.

Since the holy man knew that before almighty God the gift of the mind is sometimes greater than the gift itself, let him say: “I once wept over him who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”

The one who gives external goods offers something outside himself. But whoever gives tears and compassion to his neighbor gives him something also from himself.

[Note: Val-Clair reads: “he gave something of himself, as the grace of charity breathed upon him.”]

We therefore say that compassion is greater than the gift because anyone may give a material thing without compassion, but one who truly has compassion never refuses what he sees to be necessary for his neighbor.

### 71. Church, having compassion for her penitent children, joins tears to prayers.

This saying also corresponds well to the voice of holy Church. When she sees the afflicted through the lamentations of repentance, she joins her own tears to them through continual prayer and has compassion on the needy as often as she helps, through the prayers of her intercession, a mind stripped of virtues.

[Note: Many manuscripts read “she joins her own tears to them,” which Gilot also noted in the margin.]

We weep in compassion over the afflicted when we count the losses of others as our own and strive to cleanse the sins of those who have sinned with our tears. In doing this, we often help ourselves more than those for whom we act, because before the innermost Judge, with the grace of charity breathing upon him, one who purely laments the sins of others perfectly washes away all his own offenses.

[Note: The Corbie German, Lauda, and German manuscripts read “before the innermost judge.” Val-Clair reads “before the most merciful judge.” In the Basel edition of 1514, “judge” is noted in the margin.]

When holy Church, seized by the tribulation of the final persecution, recalls the good things she did in a time of peace, let her say: “I once wept over him who was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor.”

Desiring the eternal joys of inward light, yet still delayed from them because she is pressed by external evils, she joins to the words of the holy man:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Rec. XXVII]

**Verse 26.—“I expected good things, and evils came to me; I awaited light, and darkness burst upon me.”**

### 72. The sorrow of the elect and of the Church, who even in a time of peace endure persecution from their own.

The faithful people expect good things but receive evils; they await light and encounter darkness, because they hope that, through the reward of recompense, they will presently share in the joys of the angels, yet, being delayed here for a longer time, they endure the hands of persecutors. They believe that they will soon enjoy the recompense of eternal light, yet here they are still compelled to suffer the darkness of their persecutors.

These evils inflicted by persecutors would grieve them less if they arose from unbelievers and enemies. But they torment the minds of the elect more severely because they come from those from whom they expected good things. Hence it is added:

**Verse 27.—“My inward parts boiled without any rest.”**

For the inward parts of holy Church boil when, in the violence of persecution, she must endure even those whom she had previously carried as her own inward parts through the love of faith. The more they know her secrets and understand where she is most vulnerable, the more grievously they afflict her and refuse to let her rest.

Yet she also bears them heavily in a time of peace, because through her preaching she recognizes that their conduct is contrary to her own. She groans when she sees that their life is unlike hers. Concerning them it is appropriately added:

**Ibid.—“The days of affliction have overtaken me.”**

For holy Church of the elect knows that she will suffer many evils in the final persecution. But the days of her affliction overtake her beforehand, because even in a time of peace she bears within herself, with great sorrow, the life of the wicked. Although the open persecution of unbelievers will follow in the last days, those who are nominally faithful within her run ahead of it through their wicked conduct even before it appears.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Rec. XXVIII]

**Verse 28.—“Mourning, I walked about; without anger I rose up; in the assembly I cried out.”**

### 73. The saints preserve humility at the height of honor and sorrow amid joyful circumstances. They struggle inwardly against prosperity. Everything that abounds without the vision of God is poverty.

I carefully observe, according to the historical sense, that the holy man who shortly before said, “You have lifted me up,” adds here, “Mourning, I walked about.” In a wondrous order, at one and the same time the height of outward honor and the sorrow of inward humility are usually found together in the actions of the good.

[Note: This reading agrees with the Corbie German, Tours, Gembloux, other Norman manuscripts, and early editions. Recent editions read instead: “the afflicted sorrow.”]

Thus the holy man, though elevated by possessions and honors, walked about mourning. Although the glory of power had shown him as exalted among human beings, inwardly he offered the Lord, through his sorrow, the secret sacrifice of a contrite heart. “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. 50:19).

The elect know, through deep reflection, how to struggle against the temptations of outward excellence. If they were to set their heart upon their external happiness, they would certainly not be just. But because the human heart cannot, amid the very prosperity of circumstances, avoid being tempted by some degree of glory, the holy men struggle inwardly against their prosperity—not, I say, merely so that they do not become elated, but so that they do not even succumb to love of it. To succumb to it completely is to submit the captive mind to its desires.

Who, thinking in earthly terms and embracing temporal things, would not believe that blessed Job was joyful amid such prosperity, when he possessed bodily health, the lives of his children, the safety of his household, and the soundness of his flocks? Yet he himself testifies that he did not rejoice in all these things when he says: “Mourning, I walked about.”

For the holy man, while still placed in this pilgrimage, everything that abounds without the vision of God is poverty. When the elect see that everything is present to them, they groan because they do not see the author of everything. All this is less for them because the appearance of the One is still lacking. Thus the grace of heavenly dispensation exalts them outwardly, while inwardly the sorrow of charity, their teacher, keeps them under discipline.

Through this sorrow they learn, because of what they receive outwardly, to humble themselves ever more deeply within themselves, to keep their minds beneath the yoke of discipline, and never to burst into impatience through the license of power. Hence it is appropriately added: “Without anger I rose up; in the assembly I cried out.”

For the tumult of seditious people often provokes the minds of their superiors, and through disordered movements they exceed the limits of their rank.

### 74. Impatience is almost always the companion of power, but the good overcome it.

Often those who preside, unless they are held in check by the bridle of the Holy Spirit at the mouth of their heart, leap into the cruelty of angry retaliation. The more they are able to do, the more they think they are permitted to do against their subjects.

Impatience is almost always the companion of power; it commands even power when that power is evil and subject to it, because power carries out what impatience feels. But holy men subject themselves inwardly to the yoke of patience more than they preside outwardly over human beings. They display a truer rule outwardly to the degree that they maintain a more humble service to God inwardly.

For this reason, the more they are able to avenge themselves upon certain people, the more they often tolerate them; and lest they ever proceed to unlawful acts, they often refuse to carry out on their own behalf even what is lawful. They endure the clamor of their subjects and rebuke through love those whom they bear with gentleness.

Thus it is rightly said here: “Without anger I rose up; in the assembly I cried out,” because the good raise a cry against the tumult of the insolent without possessing anger, since they do not cease to teach those whom they mercifully tolerate.

What we have said according to the historical sense about one person must, according to the allegorical sense, be understood of the various elect of the Church. She herself walks mourning in her elect even amid prosperity, because she counts nothing truly prosperous for herself until she has seized the good that she uniquely seeks.

Her faithful enjoy temporal peace, yet sigh perpetually; they are honored and afflicted, because they often appear to be at the summit where they are not citizens.

She also rises without anger in the assembly and cries out, because she pursues the life of the wicked with the zeal of right emulation, not with the madness of fury. She is angry and loving, fierce and tranquil, so that she may correct her infirm members through emulation and favor them through compassion.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Rec. XXIX]

**Verse 29.—“I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches.”**

### 75. There is no true holiness except that which has been tested among the wicked.

What is signified by the name “dragons” except the life of malicious people? Concerning them the prophet says: “They drew in the wind like dragons” (Jer. 14:6). The perverse draw in the wind like dragons when they are puffed up with malicious pride.

Who are understood by the name “ostriches” except hypocrites? The ostrich has feathers but cannot fly, because hypocrites possess the appearance of holiness but do not possess the power of holiness. The spectacle of good action adorns them, but the feather of virtue does not lift them from the earth.

Therefore, because the elect people of holy Church endure within themselves certain malicious and hypocritical people in a time of peace, let them say: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches.”

This also applies especially to blessed Job, who was good among the wicked and reached the summit of great strength.

[Old XXIX.]

No one is perfect who is not patient amid the evils of those around him. Whoever does not tolerate the evils of others with equanimity is himself a witness, through his impatience, that he is far from the fullness of goodness.

[Note: Vincennes reads: “because he is far from the entire fullness of the law.” The German manuscript reads: “because he is far from all fullness.”]

He refuses to be Abel if Cain’s wickedness does not exercise him (Gen. 4:3 ff.; 7, q. 1, c. “Adversity,” § 3, under “Abel”).

### 76. Why are the wicked mixed here among the good?

Thus, on the threshing floor, grains are pressed beneath chaff; thus flowers emerge among thorns, and the fragrant rose grows together with the thorn that pricks.

The first man had two sons, but one was elect and the other reprobate (Gen. 4:1–2). Noah’s ark contained three sons, but while two persisted in humility, one fell into mocking his father (ibid. 9:18). Abraham had two sons, but one was innocent and the other persecuted his brother (ibid. 16:15; 21:9).

Isaac also had two sons: one was preserved in humility, while the other was rejected even before he was born (ibid. 25:24 ff.). Jacob fathered twelve sons, but one was sold because of his innocence, while the others became sellers of their brother through wickedness (ibid. 37:27).

Twelve apostles were chosen in holy Church, but one was mingled with them so that, by persecuting them, he might test them, lest they remain unproved. Thus the sinner is joined to the just with wickedness, just as in a furnace chaff is joined to gold with fire, so that as the chaff burns, the gold may be purified.

Those, then, are truly good who are able to persist in goodness even among the wicked. Hence, in the voice of the Bridegroom, it is said of holy Church: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2:2).

Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions” (Ezek. 2:6).

Hence Peter glorifies the life of blessed Lot, saying: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the injurious conduct of the wicked” (2 Pet. 2:7).

[Note: Thus read in the Norman, Beauvais, Corbie German, Lauda, and Val-Clair manuscripts. In Vincennes: “from an unjust way of life.” The printed editions, together with the German manuscript, read: “from an unjust conduct.”]

He was righteous in what he saw and heard, dwelling among those who day after day tormented the soul of the righteous man with wicked deeds.

Hence Paul glorifies the life of the disciples and, by glorifying it, confirms it, saying: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. 2:15).

[Note: A recent edition reads: “Hence John, through the angel of the church of Pergamum.” In the Tours, Beauvais, Lauda, Corbie German, German, and other manuscripts, it is not “John through the angel,” but “the angel speaks through John”; this agrees better with the sacred text and with the argument.]

Therefore blessed Job, to show what strength he possessed, indicates with whom he lived when he says: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches.”

[Note: Many Norman manuscripts read: “because the good things he himself did would be less significant.”]

For what he himself did well would be of less account unless, to increase the sum of his goodness, he also endured the evils of others.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XL [Rec. XXX]

**Verse 30.—“My skin has grown black upon me, and my bones have dried up from the heat.”**
77. Because of the fall of the weak, the strong are scorched by the fire of their zeal.

We neglect to weigh these words according to the historical sense, since the force of the passage is evident from the punishment of suffering. But because, as we have often said, blessed Job frequently narrates events in such a way as to foretell what must be done, this accords well with the voice of holy Church, which keenly feels the pain of the final persecution in the weak. And when some perish from among her, all the stronger members are tortured by grief.

Her exterior cause is earthly administration, but her interior concern is heavenly. By the name “skin,” therefore, those weak members are signified who now serve her external usefulness. By the “bones,” however, her strong members are represented, for in them the whole structure of her body is made firm.

Since, then, whether enticed by gifts or afflicted by persecutions, many weak members fall from the stability of faith within her, and after falling persecute the very Church to which they belonged, what else does she suffer than the blackness of her skin, so that she afterward appears shameful in those in whom she had previously appeared beautiful? For when those who formerly were accustomed to administer external matters well later rage against God’s elect, it is as though the skin of the Church has lost the color of her former righteousness and has come to the blackness of iniquity.

Jeremiah also laments this under the image of a precious metal, saying: “How the gold has become darkened, how the finest color has been changed” (Lam. IV, 1).

Thus, when the perverse depart from her sacraments, they often take a place of honor among the reprobate, so that those who, as though possessing knowledge, despise the holy Church may themselves rage against her with authority. Hence, after saying, “My skin has become black,” he added, “upon me,” because she now bears as black those whom she formerly possessed as white, as it were, for the adornment of righteousness.

But when the skin is turned black, the strong members within her waste away through zeal. Therefore he appropriately adds:

“And my bones have dried up because of the heat.”

So also, at an earlier time, Paul, the strongest bone of the holy Church, was burning with a certain dryness of weariness when, as some were falling, he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (II Cor. XI, 29).

Thus the skin is blackened and the bones dry up from the heat, because while the weak rush into iniquity, the strong are tortured by the fire of their zeal. It follows:

## CHAPTER XLI [Formerly XXX, in the Received Text XXXI]

### Verse 31

“My harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”

78. When the ministers of the divine word are despised, let them be silent and flee to the mourning of repentance. Let moderation govern abstinence. Let the vices of the flesh be extinguished, not the flesh itself.

Because an organ sounds through pipes and a harp through strings, the harp may signify right action, while the organ may signify holy preaching. For the pipes of the organ can appropriately be understood as the mouths of preachers, and the strings of the harp as the intention of those who live rightly.

When this intention is directed toward the next life through the affliction of the flesh, it sounds, like a string stretched thin, through the admiration of those who behold it.

For a string is dried so that it may produce a fitting sound on the harp, because holy men chastise their bodies and bring them into servitude (I Cor. IX, 27), and are stretched from lower things toward higher ones.

It should also be considered that a string on a harp, if it is insufficiently tightened, makes no sound; but if it is tightened too much, it produces a harsh sound. The virtue of abstinence is entirely absent if a person does not subdue the body as much as he is able; but it is very disordered if he afflicts the body more than he is able to bear.

Through abstinence, the vices of the flesh are to be extinguished, not the flesh itself. Each person ought to govern himself with such moderation that the flesh neither grows proud into sin nor ceases to serve the work of righteousness.

In this connection it is pleasing to observe the outstanding preacher, and with what skill he manages the souls of the faithful, as though they were strings stretched upon a harp: some he makes thinner by tightening them further, while others he preserves by loosening their tension.

To some he says: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in sleeping chambers and impurities” (Rom. XIII, 13). Again he says: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. III, 5). Yet to his beloved fellow preacher he writes: “Do not continue to drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (I Tim. V, 23).

Thus, by making those strings thinner, he tightens them, lest, being entirely slack, they make no sound; but he moderates the tension of this other string, lest, when tightened too much, it sound less effectively.

79. There are two kinds of exhortation: one by words, the other by deeds.

Whether holy preachers in the Church or any simple and abstinent persons, according to the strength they receive, render to their neighbors within her a song of good exhortation. The prudent diligently devote themselves to the fruit of preaching and labor with the sound of great persuasion to draw others toward life. Those who appear slower in understanding take from the merit of their own lives, insofar as they recognize that they are able, the authority to exhort others, and do not cease to draw those whom they can toward the heavenly homeland.

But when the holy Church, pressed by the final persecutions, sees that her words are despised by the reprobate, she turns the grace of her love toward lamentation alone, since she mourns for those whom she cannot draw by exhortation. Therefore let her say:

“My harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”

As though she openly confessed, saying: “In the time of my peace, through some I preached little things in the manner of a harp, and through others great and resounding things in the manner of an organ. But now the harp has been turned into mourning and the organ into the voice of those who weep, because, seeing myself despised, I lament those who do not hear the song of preaching.”

The holy Church will do this through some at the end; she has done it through some at her very beginnings. The first martyr, Stephen, tried by preaching to benefit the Jews who were persecuting him. But when, after his words of preaching, he saw them rush to throw stones, he prayed on bended knees, saying: “Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII, 59).

What else, then, had happened to this man, who had long recounted both small and great things, except that the song of his harp and organ had already fallen silent and been turned into mourning? For those whom he had not drawn by preaching, he wept over in love.

The holy Church does not cease to do this daily. She now sees that the word of preaching has fallen silent almost everywhere. Some avoid speaking; others refuse to hear what is right. But when the minds of the elect see the song of preaching fall silent, they return, grieving and silently, to weeping.

Therefore let her say:

“My harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep,”

because the more the voice of holy preaching has fallen silent, the more grievously each of the elect laments the losses of the Church.

Thus far blessed Job has described the evils that he endured. From this point, however, he begins to recount more carefully the good things that he did. We have passed rapidly over the words of his suffering according to both the historical and allegorical exposition; but, for the most part, we retain the deeds of his virtues according to the historical text alone, lest, if we draw them toward the investigation of mysteries, we seem perhaps to empty the truth of his actions.

# BOOK TWENTY-ONE

An exposition of Job, chapter XXXI, up to but not including verse 24; after first praising chastity, humility, and mercy, it teaches above all many things about avoiding occasions of sin.

[Col. 0187]

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. In explaining Holy Scripture, one must follow neither the historical sense alone nor always the allegorical sense.

The meaning of sacred speech must be weighed with such balance between the text and the mystery that, with the scales of both sides properly regulated, neither is it depressed by the weight of excessive analysis nor left empty by the torpor of negligence.

Many of its statements are so pregnant with allegorical meanings that anyone who tries to hold them solely according to the historical sense is deprived, through his own negligence, of knowledge of them. Others, however, serve external precepts in such a way that if someone desires to penetrate them more subtly, he finds nothing within, but also conceals from himself what they say outwardly.

### 2. The first proposition is proved.

Therefore it is also well said in a historical narrative through signification:

“Jacob took green poplar rods, almond rods, and rods from plane trees; he partly stripped them, and when the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in those places that had been stripped, while those that remained whole stayed green; and in this way the color became varied” (Gen. XXX, 37).

Then it is added:

“He placed them in the channels where the water was poured, so that when the flocks came to drink, they would have the rods before their eyes and conceive at the sight of them. And it happened that, in the heat of mating, the sheep looked at the rods and gave birth to spotted and variegated young, marked with different colors” (ibid., vv. 38–39).

What does it mean to place green, almond, and plane-tree rods before the eyes of the flocks, except to offer the lives and teachings of the ancient Fathers to peoples as examples through the sequence of sacred Scripture? Since these are straight according to the examination of reason, they are called rods.

Jacob partly removes their bark, so that their innermost whiteness may appear in what is stripped; and he partly preserves the bark, so that what was outwardly present may remain green. The color of the rods becomes varied when the bark is partly removed and partly retained.

For the teachings of the Fathers who preceded us are set before the eyes of our consideration like varied rods. When we frequently depart from the literal meaning, we remove the bark, as it were; when we frequently follow the literal meaning, we preserve the bark, as it were. When the bark of the letter is taken away from them, the inner whiteness of allegory is revealed; and when the bark is left, the vigorous examples of outward understanding are displayed.

Jacob rightly placed them in channels of water, because our Redeemer fixed them in the books of sacred knowledge by which we are inwardly infused.

The rams mate with the ewes while looking at them, because our rational spirits, when fixed upon their meaning, are mingled with each of our actions, so that they produce offspring of deeds corresponding to the examples of those who preceded us, which they see in the words of the commandments. The offspring has a varied color of good works, because sometimes, after the bark of the letter has been removed, it considers inward things more sharply, while at other times, with the covering of the historical sense retained, it shapes itself well in outward matters.

### 3. The second proposition is proved.

Because divine teachings must at times be searched out inwardly and at other times observed outwardly, Solomon also says:

“He who presses the breasts strongly to draw out milk expresses butter; and he who milks violently draws out blood” (Prov. XXX, 33).

We press the breasts strongly when we weigh the words of sacred speech with subtle understanding. By that pressure, while we seek milk, we find butter, because while we seek to be nourished even by a slight understanding, we are anointed with the richness of inward abundance.

This should not, however, be done excessively or constantly, lest, while milk is sought from the breasts, blood follow. Often, when some people examine the words of sacred speech more than they ought, they fall into a carnal understanding. He draws out blood who milks violently, because what is perceived through excessive scrutiny of the spirit becomes carnal.

Therefore it is necessary that we examine the deeds of blessed Job—which he recounts amid the words of his reproaching friends precisely so that his afflicted mind might not fail in despair—according to the weight of the historical sense. Otherwise, if the mind investigates these matters spiritually more than is necessary, blood may answer us from his breasts of words instead of milk.

Whenever he mixes certain mystical matters into his account of his deeds, the mind must return to those matters toward which the order of his speech itself, as may be understood, summons it.

For after the holy man had narrated the things inflicted upon him by the Lord’s scourge, he now makes known, by enumerating his virtues in order, what sort of man he had been before the scourge. Thus he weaves the history of his life, inserting only very rarely something that may be understood allegorically, so that most of what he relates is historical, while at times through these same things he rises toward spiritual understanding.

He indicates with what strength he had bound his outward conduct against every fall by the discipline of inward watchfulness, saying:

## CHAPTER II

### Job XXXI, verse 1

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.”

### 4. So that the mind may not desire what is illicit, the outward senses, which are the entrances of the mind, must be restrained. It is not fitting to look upon what one may not desire.

Although the soul is invisible, it is touched by the pleasure of bodily things only because, being joined to the body, it possesses in that body certain openings through which it may go forth. Sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are like certain paths of the mind by which it comes outside and desires what lies beyond its substance.

Through these bodily senses, as through certain windows, the soul looks upon external things and, looking, desires them. Hence Jeremiah says:

“Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses” (Jer. IX, 21).

Death climbs through the windows and enters the house when desire, coming through the bodily senses, enters the dwelling place of the mind.

By contrast, Isaiah says of the just, in opposition to what we have often stated:

“Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX, 8).

The just are said to fly like clouds because they are lifted above earthly contaminations. They are like doves at their windows because, through the bodily senses, they do not look upon external things with predatory intent, nor does carnal desire carry them outward.

Whoever looks carelessly outward through these bodily windows often falls into the pleasure of sin even against his will. Bound by desires, he begins to will what he did not will before. For the soul, rushing headlong because it did not previously take care lest it see carelessly what it might desire, later begins blindly to desire what it has seen.

Thus the prophet’s mind, which had often been raised up and present amid inward mysteries, because he carelessly saw another man’s wife, afterward became darkened and unlawfully joined himself to her (II Sam. XI, 2).

But the holy man, who, having received the bodily senses as subordinate servants, presides over them like a perfectly just judge, perceives faults before they arrive and, as against an enemy lying in wait, closes the windows of the body, saying:

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.”

For in order to preserve the thoughts of his heart chastely, he made a covenant with his eyes, so that he would not first look carelessly upon what he would afterward love against his will.

It is a very serious matter that the flesh drags downward, and once the appearance of a form has been fastened to the heart through the eyes, it is scarcely released except by the effort of a great struggle.

Therefore, so that we may not turn over slippery things in our thoughts, we must take precautions, because it is not fitting to look upon what it is not lawful to desire. To keep the mind clean from wantonness in its thoughts, the eyes—which are in a sense plunderers leading to sin—must be lowered from the pleasure of their will.

For Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree unless she had first looked upon it carelessly. It is written:

“The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing to behold; and she took of its fruit and ate” (Gen. III, 6).

From this we must consider with what restraint we ought to restrict our sight from unlawful things while living a mortal life, if even the mother of the living came through her eyes to death.

Again, under the voice of Judea, which, desiring external things by seeing them, had lost inward goods, the prophet says:

“My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. III, 51).

By desiring visible things, she lost invisible virtues. She who lost inward fruit through outward sight suffered, through the bodily eye, the plundering of her heart.

Therefore, to guard the purity of the heart, we must also maintain discipline over the outward senses. For however greatly the mind may possess virtue, however firmly it may stand in seriousness, the carnal senses nevertheless make a childish disturbance outwardly; and unless they are restrained by the weight of inward seriousness and by a kind of youthful vigor, they drag the weakened mind toward everything unstable and frivolous.

### 5. Job’s example in restraining not only the luxury of the flesh but also that of the heart and mind. What was committed through Moses is condemned even when merely conceived by Christ. Whoever is a citizen of heaven must abandon luxury, not from fear but from love.

Let us see, then, how blessed Job restrained with the youthful vigor of wisdom whatever might have been loose and childish in the flesh. He says:

“I made a covenant with my eyes.”

And because he extinguished in himself not only the action but also the thought of lust, he immediately added:

“That I would not even think about a virgin.”

He knew that lust must be restrained in the heart. He knew, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, that our Redeemer, when he came, would transcend the precepts of the law and abolish in his elect not only lust of the flesh but also lust of the heart, saying:

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 27).

Through Moses, lust committed in deed is condemned; by the author of purity, lust conceived in thought is condemned.

Hence the first pastor of the Church says to the disciples:

“Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace offered to you” (I Pet. I, 13).

To gird the loins of the flesh is to restrain lust from being carried into effect. To gird the loins of the mind is to restrain it even from thought.

Hence the angel who speaks to John is said to be girded with a golden sash across his breast (Rev. I, 13). Because the purity of the New Testament also restrains lust of the heart, the angel who appeared in it came girded across the chest. A golden sash properly binds him, because whoever is a citizen of the heavenly homeland abandons impurity no longer from fear of punishment but from love of charity.

The evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. For our crafty enemy, when driven out from the effect of the deed, tries to pollute the secret places of thought.

Hence the Lord says to the serpent:

“You shall crawl upon your breast and belly” (Gen. III, 14).

The serpent crawls upon its belly when the slippery enemy, through human members subjected to him, exercises lust all the way to the completion of the deed. The serpent crawls upon its breast when it pollutes in thought those whom it cannot pollute in the act of lust.

One person is already committing lust in deed: for him the serpent crawls from the belly. Another turns over the lust he is about to commit in his mind: for him the serpent crawls from the breast. But because one reaches the completion of deeds through thought, the serpent is rightly described as crawling first upon the breast and afterward upon the belly.

Thus blessed Job, because he maintained discipline even in thought, overcame the breast and belly of the serpent with a single act of vigilance, saying:

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.”

### Formerly III

Whoever does not desire to attain this purity of heart—what else does he do than drive away from himself the author of that same purity? Therefore blessed Job immediately adds:

## CHAPTER III

### Verse 2

“For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?”

### 6. If we are to be God’s inheritance, sin must not reign in us. Neither proud chastity nor unchaste humility is of any benefit.

As though he openly said:

“If I pollute my mind in thought, I cannot possibly be the inheritance of him who is the author of purity.”

No other good qualities have value if they are not approved in the eyes of the hidden Judge by the testimony of chastity. All virtues support one another in the sight of the Creator, so that, since one virtue without another is either nothing at all or very small, they may be strengthened by their mutual union.

If humility abandons chastity, or chastity abandons humility, what can either proud chastity or polluted humility accomplish before the author of humility and purity?

Therefore, so that the holy man might deserve to be possessed by his Creator in the other good things, he guards the purity of his heart and says:

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin. For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?”

As though he openly confessed, saying:

“The Creator refuses to possess me as his property in the heights if my mind wastes away before his sight in base desires.”

### 7. An impure thought does not defile when it knocks, but when it subjugates through pleasure. In corruptible flesh it is enough that sin not reign.

But amid these matters it must be understood that one thing is what the mind suffers from the temptation of the flesh, and another is when it becomes bound by pleasures through consent.

Often it is struck by an evil thought but resists. Often, however, when it conceives something perverse, it turns it over within itself even through desire. An impure thought does not defile the mind when it knocks, but when it subjugates it through pleasure.

Hence the outstanding preacher says:

“Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (I Cor. X, 13).

Human temptation is that by which we are often touched in thought even against our will, because the fact that unlawful things sometimes come to the mind is something we possess within ourselves through the burden of corrupt human nature.

But temptation is demonic rather than human when the mind binds itself through consent to what the corruptibility of the flesh suggests.

Again he says:

“Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12).

He did not prohibit sin from existing in the mortal body, but from reigning there, because in corruptible flesh sin can fail to reign, but it cannot fail to exist. Even to be tempted by sin is itself a sin; and because we are never entirely free from this so long as we live, holy preaching, since it could not wholly expel it, took away its reign from the dwelling place of our heart. Thus, although unlawful desire often secretly inserts itself among our good thoughts like a thief, if it enters at least it does not rule.

Therefore, when the holy man says:

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin,”

he does not at all mean that guilt never touched his mind in thought, but that it never overcame him through consent.

He claims his mind as God’s completely intact possession against the plundering of the adversary, and immediately adds:

“For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?”

As though he openly said:

“Though I am subject in mortal flesh to the condition of corruption, how do I serve its author if I do not defend from the consent to sin the mind that belongs wholly to him?”

It follows:

## CHAPTER IV [Formerly and in the Received Text IV]

### Verse 3

“Is there not destruction for the unjust, and alienation for those who practice iniquity?”

### 8. The just travel to the homeland of salvation by a rugged road; the reprobate travel toward the pit through pleasant meadows.

The considered end of the wicked is a swift consolation for the good. For when they see in the destruction of the wicked the evil from which they escape, they consider light whatever adversity they suffer in this life.

Let the reprobate go now, then, and fulfill the desires of their pleasures. At the condemnation of their end they will realize that, while living badly, they loved death.

Let the elect be afflicted by a passing blow, so that the scourges may correct from wickedness those whom paternal love preserves for an inheritance. For now the just person is scourged and corrected by the blow of discipline because he is being prepared for the patrimony of the eternal inheritance.

But the unjust person is relaxed amid his pleasures, because temporal goods are supplied to him in proportion as eternal goods are denied him. The unjust person, running toward the death he deserves, indulges in unrestrained pleasures, because calves destined for slaughter are also left in unrestricted pastures.

By contrast, the just person is restrained from the delight of passing pleasure, because a calf assigned to the labor of life is kept under the yoke.

Earthly goods are denied to the elect in this life, because a physician does not grant to the sick, who have hope of living, everything they desire. Goods desired in this life are given to the reprobate, because desperate patients are not denied everything they wish for.

Let the just consider, therefore, what evils await the wicked, and let them not envy the happiness that passes away. What is there to admire in their joys, when the just themselves are traveling by a rugged road toward the homeland of salvation, while the wicked are traveling, as it were, through pleasant meadows toward the pit?

Therefore let the holy man say:

“Is there not destruction for the unjust, and alienation for those who practice iniquity?”

The word “alienation” would sound harsher if the translator had retained it in the word of its own language. What is called *alienation* among us is called *anathema* among the Hebrews. Alienation will therefore be the lot of the reprobate when they recognize that, excluded from the inheritance of the strict Judge, they are anathema, because here they despised him by their perverse conduct.

Let the wicked flourish, then, alienated from the flowering of the eternal inheritance. But let the just diligently examine themselves and fear that the Lord sees them in all their actions.

Hence he appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER V

### Verse 4

“Does he not himself consider my ways and number all my steps?”

### Editorial and textual notes

- [Col. 0184D] Turonensis: “in the person of the Passion.”
- [Col. 0184D] Gilot and many editions read *ut gerendo* (“as he does [them]”); Gussanville reads *pronuntiet* (“may declare”), which would be judged a typographical error were it not also found in the old Paris and Basel editions. The manuscripts, however, with remarkable agreement, read *praenuntiet* (“may foretell”), and the sequence of the argument proves that this is the correct reading.
- [Col. 0184D] Laudunensis reads *in infimis* (“in the lowly”), but incorrectly. Here St Gregory contrasts the weak with the strong.
- [Col. 0185D] The English and Norman manuscripts read, as though, *extenta* (“stretched”), a reading apparently demanded by the repeated words here, *tenditur, tenduntur* (“is stretched, are stretched”). But manuscripts of the best quality, especially the German, Laudunensis, and Corbie German manuscripts, read *extenuata* (“made thin”); this word should therefore be retained as more probably used by St Gregory and later changed by the learned, because *extenta chorda* (“a stretched string”) seemed to suit the passage better. Certainly, if *extenta chorda* had been read first, no one would have thought, after deleting that word, to write *extenuata chorda*. The words below support this reading: “by tightening he makes thin; by making thin he tightens.”
- [Col. 0185D] Thus Corbie German, Norman, Laudunensis, Vallicellian, and German manuscripts; the printed editions read “they stretch.”
- [Col. 0186D] Recent editions read “for the affection.” One must read “for the effect,” whether one consults reason or the manuscripts—Tours, German, Laudunensis, Norman, Corbie German, and others.
- [Col. 0186D] Tours reads “whom by praying”; Corbie German formerly read the same, but now reads “whom by exhorting.”
- [Col. 0186D] This shorter wording is found in the Tours, Beauvais, German, and Norman manuscripts than in the printed editions: “but now it has been turned into mourning,” etc. Corbie German is still shorter: “but now harp and organ have been turned into mourning.”
- [Col. 0186D] Corbie German, Norman, and German manuscripts read *canticum* (“song”); and so below, instead of *cantus*, “song.”
- [Col. 0186D] German, Beauvais, Corbie German, and many manuscripts, especially the Norman, read “the martyr Stephen,” omitting “first.”
- [Col. 0187D] Évreux, Utica, and many manuscripts read *suspensus* (“suspended”).
- [Col. 0187D] Following the Vulgate, the Corbie German, Norman, German, Laudunensis, Vallicellian, and other manuscripts, together with the old editions, read: “in those which had been stripped, whiteness appeared; those which were whole remained green.” The old Basel edition, however, has “those which were whole were green.” The Roman editors under Sixtus V and Gussanville preferred: “those which had been stripped … those which were whole … green.” Then follows: “and they gave birth to spotted and variegated young, marked with different colors.”
- [Col. 0188D] In the very ancient Laudunensis manuscript appears *cortix*, perhaps once used in place of *cortex*; hence in the oblique cases, *corticis, cortici*, etc., rather than *cortecis, corteci*.
- [Col. 0188D] Vendôme reads “our senses.”
- [Col. 0188D] German and Jumièges: “after the bark of the letter has been removed.”
- [Col. 0188D] Vendôme and the old Paris edition read *emulget*; Tours, *emulgit*; Corbie German, *emulgetur*; Laudunensis, German, and Vallicellian, *emulgitur*; Norman, *emungitur*, and so below.
- [Col. 0189D] Vallicellian: “lest, if these matters strike the mind … when investigated spiritually, blood answer from the words,” etc.
- [Col. 0189D] Norman: “so that he inserts something very rarely.”
- [Col. 0189D] German reads “through our windows.” Utica, Bec, and others read “through your windows … your houses”; Vallicellian likewise has “and enters the houses.” The reading should follow the Vulgate, the other versions, and the Hebrew text: “our windows,” etc.
- [Col. 0190D] Printed editions read “against death lying in wait.” This is supported by the Isaiah passage explained above, “Death has climbed through our windows”; but the English manuscripts and ours oppose it, reading “against an enemy lying in wait.” The German and Corbie German manuscripts, however, read “against death lying in wait.”
- [Col. 0190D] Recent editors preferred to add “serious,” although the manuscripts and earlier printed editions simply read: “For it is a great matter that …”
- [Col. 0190D] German and Norman: “ought not to look upon what it is not lawful to desire”; some printed editions have the same.
- [Col. 0190D] German, Jumièges, Utica, and Pratelles: “of its own will.”
- [Col. 0190D] Gilot gives in the margin as a variant reading *protulit* (“brought forth”), which is also found in some old editions.
- [Col. 0191D] Recent editions read: “our adversary … attempts to pollute the secret places of thought.” Our reading is found in the ancient copies, both printed and manuscript, except Corbie German, which agrees with the recent editions.
- [Col. 0192D] Thus the old editions, with Corbie German, Norman, and other manuscripts. Recent editions read “to possess in me.”
- [Col. 0192D] Recent editions added “shameful,” against the manuscripts and old printed editions.
- [Col. 0193D] We have removed from this place the words, “O what consolation for the sick, and what sorrow [or fear] for the healthy,” which are not found in the manuscripts and undoubtedly slipped into the printed text from the margin. The explanation of Job’s text begins with the words “The considered end is a swift consolation,” etc., which do not cohere with “O what …,” etc. Someone had noted that sentence in the margin, and later editors inserted it into the text too carelessly.
- [Col. 0194D] The old printed editions, following most manuscripts, read “delight.”
- [Col. 0194D] German, Corbie German, Laudunensis, Vallicellian, Tours, and Norman: “which await the wicked.”

### 9. The very smallest thoughts and the slightest words, which we regard as trivial, will not be overlooked in God’s judgment. As the degrees of guilt increase, so does the order of the condemning sentence.

What does he signify by the name “ways” except actions? Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “Make your ways and your practices good” (Jer. 7:3). What do we understand by the designation “steps” except either the movements of minds or the progress of merits? By these steps, surely, the Truth calls us to himself, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28). The Lord commands us to come to him—not, of course, by bodily steps, but by advances of the heart. For he himself says: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John 4:21). And shortly afterward: “True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth; for the Father also seeks such people to worship him” (ibid., 23). Thus he indicates that steps exist in the heart, since he both calls us to come and nevertheless declares that we are by no means to pass over to other places by bodily movement.

[Old version.] The Lord therefore considers the ways of each person and numbers his steps in such a manner that not even the very smallest thoughts or the slightest words—things that have become cheap in our ordinary usage—remain unexamined in his judgment. Hence he says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22).

[Note: The printed edition reads “an utterance of one who is indignant.” In all the English, Norman, Corbie German, Tours, Vendôme, German, Laon, and other witnesses, we read “an interjection.”]

In Hebrew speech, *Raca* is an interjection, which indeed reveals the anger of the person who is angry, but does not yet express a complete word of anger. First, therefore, anger without speech is reproved; afterward, anger with speech, but not yet formed in a complete expression; and finally, when he says “Fool,” anger is rebuked after it has been expressed through an utterance and completed by a fully formed word.

It should be noted that he declares a person guilty of anger in the judgment, of anger expressed in speech—that is, “Raca”—before the council, and of the word expressed in speech—that is, “Fool”—before the fire of Gehenna. For the order of the sentence increases according to the degrees of guilt: in the judgment the case is still being examined; in the council the decision of the case is already determined; but in the fire of Gehenna the sentence proceeding from the council is carried out.

Since, therefore, the Lord numbers the steps of human actions with such subtle scrutiny, anger without speech is delivered to judgment, anger expressed in speech to the council, and anger expressed both in speech and in a complete utterance to the fires of Gehenna.

The prophet had perceived this subtlety of his consideration when he said: “Most mighty, great and powerful Lord of hosts is your name, great in counsel and incomprehensible in thought, whose eyes are open over all the ways of the children of Adam, to repay each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his devices” (Jer. 32:18).

[Note: “Lord” is absent from recent editions, although it occurs in the manuscripts and older printed editions.]

[Note: The German witness and recent editions add “of his hands”; it is absent from the other manuscripts and older printed editions, and also from the text of Jeremiah.]

### 10. No good deed is without reward, and no evil deed without punishment.

The Lord considers these same ways with such subtle examination that in each of us he neither overlooks the good deeds he rewards nor leaves uncorrected the evils that displease him. Hence he both praises and rebukes the angel of the church at Pergamum, saying: “I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is; and you hold fast my name and did not deny my faith” (Rev. 2:13–14). And shortly afterward: “But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam.”

[Note: The printed editions omitted “of the church,” which is found in the manuscripts except in the German and Corbie German witnesses.]

To the angel of the church at Thyatira he says: “I know your works, your love, your faith, your service, and your patience, and that your last works are more numerous than the first. But I have a few things against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed to idols” (ibid., 19).

[Note: “A few” is absent from Laon, Corbie German, Utica, Bec, and other Norman witnesses.]

Behold, he mentions the good deeds, yet does not forgive the evils that must be cut away except through repentance. For he considers the ways of each person and weighs them by numbering the steps, so that with subtle examination he may determine either how far each person advances toward good or how far, turning toward evil, he opposes his own progress.

The increase of merits, which grows through devotion to a good life, is often held back by the admixture of evil; and the good that the mind builds by its actions it overturns by committing other deeds. Hence holy men restrain themselves in thought all the more carefully as they see themselves examined more strictly by the heavenly Judge. They scrutinize their minds and seek to discover whether they have left anything behind, so that they may be as irreproachable before the Judge as they daily and unceasingly reproach themselves.

Yet they do not on this account already take up the joys of security, because they realize that they are seen by one who sees in them even those things which they themselves cannot see in themselves. Blessed Job indeed maintained a life of perfection among the ancients; but because his intention, by prophetic inspiration, bursts forth toward the coming of the Redeemer in his teachings, he himself weighs how much he still lacks of perfection. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER VI  
[Old version VI, revised version V]

### Verses 5–6

“If I have walked in vanity, and my foot has hastened toward deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my simplicity.”

### 11. Let the saints take care to weigh their merits in Christ as in a balance, so that they may recognize what they lack.

[Note: Corbie German and Laon read “God’s knowing.”]

God is said to “know” when he makes us know, according to our customary manner of speaking, by which we call a day “joyful” because it happens to make us joyful. Hence the Lord says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12). The Creator of time did not learn anything from time; rather, his “knowing” means that, through the emergence of some cause, he grants us knowledge.

Who, then, is signified by the name “balance” except the Mediator between God and human beings? In him all our merits are weighed on an equal scale, and in his commandments we recognize what we lack in our life. We are weighed in this balance whenever we are called to imitate his life.

Hence it is written: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps, he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2:21).

[Note: Corbie German and Laon read “for you.” The copyist, reading “leaving you an example so that you might follow,” etc., thought that “Christ for you” ought also to have been written earlier. The Greek text reads: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that you might follow.” This wording seems to require that “leaving you” be read earlier. Consult the critics on this passage.]

[Note: Utica, Bec, and others read *non remaledicebat* (“he did not revile in return”), which corresponds to the Greek text, unless one prefers: “he did not return revilings.”]

Hence Paul says: “Let us run with patience the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Heb. 12:1).

[Note: The Norman, Corbie German, Laon, and German witnesses read *curramus propositum* (“let us run the course set before us”). Most Norman witnesses read *in auctore . . . et consummatore* (“in the author . . . and perfecter”).]

The Lord therefore appeared in the flesh for this purpose: to rouse human life by his exhortation, kindle it by his examples, redeem it by his death, and restore it by his resurrection.

Since blessed Job found nothing in himself that could rightly be reproved, he directs the eyes of his mind toward the Redeemer’s life, which surpasses everything, so that in it he may recognize what he himself lacks, saying: “If I have walked in vanity, and my foot has hastened toward deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my simplicity.”
