It is as though he were openly saying: “If I have ever done anything lightly or anything destructively, let the Mediator of God and human beings appear, so that in his life I may learn whether I have truly been simple.”

For, as we have said, he had surpassed the men of his own time, yet he sought the Mediator between God and humanity so that, when weighed against him, he might recognize whether he had truly maintained a simple life.

Let him therefore say: “Let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my simplicity.” That is: “Let him make me know.”

It is as though he were plainly confessing: “As far as the standard of human life is concerned, I now see nothing in myself deserving reproach; but unless the Mediator between God and human beings appears with the commandments of a more refined life, I do not recognize how far I still differ from true simplicity.”

[Note: Vendôme reads: “I now see that no one reproves me.”]

The order is correct when he is first said to have walked in vanity and afterward to have hastened with his foot toward deceit. Vanity pertains to frivolity, whereas deceit pertains to malice. Many people often arrive at certain malicious deeds because they do not first avoid trivial faults.

It follows:

## CHAPTER VII  
[Old version VII]

### Verse 7

“If my step has turned aside from the way.”

### 12. We turn aside from the way whenever we consent to error.

The step turns aside from the way whenever our thought abandons the path of uprightness by consenting to error. It is as though we place so many steps outside the way as we separate ourselves from delight in heavenly life through perverse desires.

As we said earlier, while we are still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, we cannot live in such a way that no delight in sin can assail us. But one thing is to be touched against one’s will; another is for a consenting mind to be destroyed.

Holy men guard themselves with more watchful vigilance because they disdain being assailed even temporarily by sinister impulses.

[Note: Tours reads “by morals, or temporarily.” So too do Val-Clos and German, though they retain the word “impulses.”]

Hence it is further added:

## CHAPTER VIII  
[Revised version VI]

### The same passage

“If my eye has followed my heart.”

### 13. The eye must refuse to serve the heart when it unlawfully desires. Temptation is sometimes drawn in through the eyes, and sometimes conceived within. Whoever uses the external eye carelessly is justly blinded in the inner eye.

Behold, he again returns from guarding inner strength to disciplining the external members, so that, if the heart should perhaps desire something unlawful, the eye, restrained by the authority of discipline, might refuse to look.

For just as temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes a temptation conceived within compels the external eyes to serve it. Frequently some object is looked upon with an innocent mind, but by the very act of looking the soul is pierced by the sword of desire.

David, for example, did not gaze intently upon Uriah’s wife because he had already desired her; rather, he desired her because he looked carelessly.

By the examination of a just recompense, it happens that whoever uses the external eye carelessly is not unjustly blinded in the inner eye.

[Note: Vendôme reads: “so that whoever looks carelessly at external things is not unjustly blinded in the inner eye.”]

Often, however, desire rules within, and the enticed mind, tyrant-like, requires the bodily senses to serve its purposes and compels the eyes to serve its pleasures. Thus, so to speak, it opens the windows of light toward the darkness of blindness.

Therefore, when holy men feel themselves assailed by a sinister delight, they restrain the very lights through which the appearance of outward forms enters the mind, under the authority of discipline, lest sight, flattering an evil thought, become its servant.

If this is ever neglected and not guarded carefully, the impurity of thought immediately passes into action. Hence it is added at once:

## CHAPTER IX  
[Revised version VII]

### The same passage

“And if a stain has clung to my hands.”

### 14. So that guilt may not emerge into action, let it be extinguished within, where it is born.

The holy man therefore knew that an evil thought often comes to the mind through the eyes, and a little earlier said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.”

He also recognized that desire sometimes arises in the mind, while the eyes perversely serve what has arisen in it, and said: “If my eye has followed my heart.”

It is as though he were openly saying: “I did not wish to look indiscriminately at what I might desire, nor did I ever follow by looking what I had desired.”

Let him therefore say: “If my eye has followed my heart,” because, even if his human mind ever conceived something unlawful, he refused, under the authority of a higher discipline, to let his eyes follow it into unlawful things or serve it.

[Note: This is found with the Norman, Tours, Laon, Val-Clos, Corbie German, and older printed editions. In these, however, the reading is “the eye, constrained,” instead of “the eyes, constrained.” Recent editions, following the German witness, altered the passage on their own authority to read: “the eye, constrained, refused to lead itself into unlawful things and serve them.”]

Let us consider our consciences in relation to this, and from the abasement of our own hearts let us see how exalted this man was.

Behold, if he ever thought of anything unlawful, he quickly extinguished it within the secret places of his heart by the sword of holy strength and did not permit it to reach his actions. Hence, as we said, he immediately adds: “And if a stain has clung to my hands.”

For when a stain is on the hands—that is, when guilt clings to actions—how could discipline’s judgment have prevented it from advancing in thought? Guilt is not permitted to emerge into action if it is extinguished within, where it is born.

But if one does not quickly resist a temptation arising in the heart, it is strengthened by the very delay through which it is nourished.

[Note: Val-Clos reads “and coming out into the open.” Corbie German, Évreux, and Prat read “and coming out into the outside.”]

Once it exists outwardly in actions, it can scarcely be conquered, because it holds the mind captive within, as though it were the mistress of the bodily members.

Since the holy man introduced all the preceding matters conditionally—“if he ever committed these things”—he binds himself by a sentence of condemnation, saying:

## CHAPTER X  
[Revised version VIII]

### Verse 8

“Let me sow, and let another eat, and let my offspring be uprooted.”

### 15. The preacher sows fasting, and another eats, when he does not practice what he teaches.

According to sacred language, we call it “sowing” when we preach words of life. Hence the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32:20).

He saw the preachers of Holy Church sowing beside all waters because they entrusted the words of life, like grains of heavenly bread, to all peoples far and wide.

[Note: Prat reads: “For Holy Church beheld the preachers . . . sowing.”]

“To eat” means to be satisfied with good works. Hence the Truth says of itself: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

If, therefore, he neglected to do what he had proclaimed, he says: “Let me sow, and let another eat.” It is as though he were openly saying: “What my mouth speaks, let another, not I, perform.”

For a preacher whose conduct differs from his words sows fasting for another to eat, because he himself is not nourished by his own seed when he is rendered idle from the uprightness of his speech by evil action.

[Old version VIII.] And because pupils often hear good things to no purpose when they are overthrown by the example of their teacher’s life, it is rightly added: “And let my offspring be uprooted.”

### 16. His offspring is uprooted because he kills by his example those whom he begets through his word.

The offspring of a teacher is uprooted when the one who is born through the word is killed through example. For the negligence of life kills the one whom a watchful tongue gives birth to.

We must not pass over with sluggish minds what is written in Solomon: a woman killed her son, whom she was accustomed to nurse while awake, when she was asleep (1 Kings 3:19). For teachers who are indeed awake in knowledge but asleep in life nourish their hearers through the vigilance of preaching, yet kill them through the sleep of lethargy when they neglect to do what they say, and by their negligence crush those whom they seemed to feed with the milk of their words.

Hence, while they themselves live reprehensibly and cannot have disciples of praiseworthy life, they try to draw others to themselves, so that by displaying good followers they may excuse the evils they do before human judgment and, as it were, conceal their deadly negligence through the life of their subordinates.

Thus the woman there, because she had killed her own son, sought someone else’s. Yet Solomon’s sword found the true mother, since the final examination of the strict Judge reveals whose offspring lives and whose dies.

There too we should carefully observe that the living child is first ordered to be divided, so that afterward he may be given to his mother alone. This is because in the present life the disciple’s life is, as it were, permitted to be divided: one person may sometimes have merit before God, while another has praise before human beings.

### 17. Having lost her own children, she begrudges life to another’s.

But the false mother does not fear having the one she did not give birth to killed, because arrogant teachers, ignorant of charity, if they cannot obtain the fullest reputation for praise from other people’s disciples, cruelly attack those disciples’ lives.

Burning with the torch of envy, they do not want those to live for others whom they see themselves unable to possess. Hence the perverse woman cries out: “Let it be neither mine nor hers” (ibid., 26).

As we have said, those whom they do not see serving them for the sake of temporal glory, they begrudge living for others in the truth.

But the true mother strives that her son may at least belong to another and live. For faithful teachers allow others to receive the honor of teaching from their disciples, provided that those disciples do not lose the integrity of their lives.

The true mother is recognized by these compassionate entrails, because every teaching office is approved by the examination of charity. She alone deserved to receive the whole because she seemed to concede the whole.

Faithful superiors, because they not only do not begrudge others praise from their good disciples but also pray that those others may profit through them, receive their children whole and alive when, at the final examination, they obtain the joys of perfect recompense from their disciples’ lives.

We have said these things briefly and by way of digression to show how the offspring of hearers is extinguished through the negligence of teachers. Whoever does not live according to what he says tears from the stability of uprightness by his actions those whom he has begotten by his word.

[Note: Val-Clos reads “through the life of teachers.”]

But blessed Job, whom he produced while awake through his preaching, did not extinguish by sleeping in his actions. Therefore he confidently says: “If I have failed to fulfill the foregoing, let me sow, and let another eat, and let my offspring be uprooted.”

Still examining himself for defilement by evil action, he adds:

## CHAPTER XI  
[Old and revised version IX]

### Verse 9

“If my heart has been deceived by a woman, and if I have lain in wait at the door of my friend.”

[Note: The German witness and recent editions corruptly read “at the door of my enemy,” here and below. The Hebrew text and all its versions read “at the door of my friend,” “companion,” or “neighbor.” The same reading occurs in all the English, Norman, Laon, Vendôme, Corbie German, Tours, Val-Clos, and older printed witnesses.]

### 18. In sacred Scripture adultery and fornication are sometimes distinguished and sometimes have the same meaning. Both are forbidden. Job abstained even from the thought of either.

Although the guilt of fornication is sometimes by no means distinct from the guilt of adultery, since the Truth says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28), nevertheless the two are often distinguished by the situation or rank of the person desiring.

[Note: Here we remedy the obscurity of the text and restore it by adding parentheses and removing the superfluous particle *quod* before *tamen plerumque*, found in the German witness and printed editions contrary to the other manuscripts. Because the Greek word *moichos* means “adulterer,” while the prohibition concerns looking not at another man’s wife but at a woman, the Truth clearly shows that even by the mere act of looking, when an unmarried woman is shamefully desired, adultery is committed.]

Nevertheless, the guilt is generally distinguished according to the circumstance or rank of the person desiring: eager desire in the sacred order defiles the one, just as the guilt of adultery defiles the other.

Yet in persons who are not unlike, the same guilt of lust is distinguished. That fornication is distinguished from adultery is attested by the tongue of the eminent preacher, who says among other things: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9).

[Note: We have also corrected this passage, which is extremely corrupt in the German and Corbie German witnesses and in the printed editions, chiefly with the aid of the Norman manuscripts. No legitimate sense could be extracted from the readings found in the common editions, whereas the meaning of our reading is clear: in the Apostle’s words fornicators and adulterers are distinguished.]

For by attaching a sentence to distinct forms of guilt, he shows how greatly they differ from one another.

Thus, by the words “If my heart has been deceived by a woman,” the holy man shows that he did not even think of the stain of fornication. By adding, “And if I have lain in wait at the door of my friend,” he plainly makes known that he was free from the guilt of adultery.

But someone might perhaps say: What is remarkable in the holy man’s claim if he preserved himself free not only from the crime of adultery but also from the pollution of fornication?

We would regard this as insignificant if we did not carefully consider the times in which he lived. The stricter discipline of revealed grace had not yet advanced to the restraint of the flesh, a discipline that reproves not only bodily but also interior lust.

The examples of the chastity of many continent people had not yet appeared for imitation, and yet blessed Job offered examples of purity that he had not received.

Even now, after God’s prohibition, many commit the impurity of the flesh. From this we must conclude how great the guilt is when grave sins are committed after the commandment, since abstaining from grave sins beforehand was worthy of such praise.

[Note: Laon, Val-Clos, and the Norman witnesses read this way; the German and Corbie German witnesses and the printed editions read: “with how great guilt … with such great …”]

If he ever committed this deed, he asks that the same guilt be turned into punishment for him, saying:

## CHAPTER XII

### Verse 10

“Let my wife be the prostitute of another, and let others bow over her.”

### 19. The crime of lust devours a person to destruction and destroys every virtue. No one in this life is without sin.

Since we often do not grasp, while committing something, how serious it is, we weigh it by suffering. Thus he reveals the force of the same crime by declaring that, if he were guilty, he ought to suffer it, saying:

### Verses 11–12

“For this is a wickedness and a very great iniquity; it is a fire devouring to destruction and uprooting all offspring.”

There is this difference between sin and crime: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime.

In this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sins. Hence the holy preacher, when describing a man worthy of priestly grace, did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” but, “If anyone is without crime” (Tit. 1:6).

Who can be without sin, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

In this distinction between sins and crimes we must consider that some sins pollute the soul, whereas crimes destroy it.

[Note: The German, Laon, Corbie German, Val-Clos, and most Norman witnesses read: “for crimes destroy them.”]

Hence blessed Job, defining the crime of lust, says: “It is a fire devouring to destruction,” because the guilt of this crime not only stains as far as pollution but devours as far as destruction.

And because, whatever other good works there may be, if the crime of lust is not washed away they are overwhelmed by the enormity of this crime, he adds: “And uprooting all offspring.”

The offspring are the soul’s good works. Yet if the flesh rules it in a perverse order, the fire of lust burns up everything well brought forth.

No works of justice or piety are clean before the eyes of almighty God when they are shown to be contaminated by corruption.

For what benefit is it if someone compassionately helps a neighbor in need, when he impiously destroys himself, the dwelling place of God?

[Note: In Corbie German, in the first hand, Tours, Laon, German, Norman, and other witnesses, the reading is “when he impiously destroys himself,” while the second hand of Corbie German and the printed editions read “when he impiously destroys God’s dwelling in himself.”]

If, therefore, the flame of lust is not extinguished through purity of heart, every virtue that arises is useless, as it is said through Moses: “A fire has been kindled by my anger, and it will burn down to the depths of the underworld; it will consume the earth and its produce” (Deut. 32:22).

[Note: Corbie German and Laon read “and its offspring,” a reading repeated below.]

The fire consumes the earth and its produce when lust consumes the flesh and, through the flesh, everything well done. For whatever emerges from the harvest of uprightness is burned by the flame of corruption.

Let him therefore say: “It is a fire devouring to destruction and uprooting all offspring,” because if the evil of corruption is not resisted, those things too undoubtedly perish that had seemed good.

Some vices, however, often bring certain people low into humility, while virtues raise them into pride of mind. [Old version I.] We must therefore ask whether blessed Job was also humble amid such purity of chastity.

But the holy man, though he possessed lofty virtues, suddenly reveals how humbly he thought of himself when he adds:

## CHAPTER XIII

### Verse 13

“If I disdained to enter judgment with my male servant and my female servant when they disputed against me.”

[Note: Utica, Bec, Gemet, and others read “with my maidservants”; this reading is consistently used in the subsequent discussion of the text.]

### 20. Job’s remarkable humility amid such innocence of life.

For he who did not refuse to be judged together with male and female servants plainly shows that he was never proud against any neighbor.

Here it is worth observing with what discretion the holy man guarded his life in every respect.

A little earlier he had said: “Young men saw me and hid themselves; old men rose and stood. Princes stopped speaking and placed their finger upon their mouths; the voices of leaders were restrained, and their tongue clung to their throat.”

[Reg. X.]

But now he says: “If I disdained to enter judgment with my male servant and my female servant when they disputed against me.”

Who could worthily consider the lofty moderation of this man’s virtues?

He possessed such authority of governance that leaders were restrained into silence, and such humility of heart that female servants were permitted to come with him as equals to judgment.

Behold, in a marvelous way he appears more powerful than princes in authority, yet equal to servants in litigation; in the assembly of princes he remembers his office of rule, and in the dispute with servants he remembers his common condition.

[Note: Laon, Corbie German, Val-Clos, Tours, Vendôme, and the Norman witnesses read *potior* (“more powerful”); the German witness and common editions instead read *Dominus potentior* (“a more powerful lord”).]

He sees himself as a servant under the true Lord and therefore does not exalt himself above servants in the height of his heart.

Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XIV

### Verse 14

“For what shall I do when God rises to judgment? And when he inquires, what shall I answer him?”

### 21. Those who rule over others should always bear in mind that they are subject to God.

Whoever thinks of the Judge who will come continually prepares the accounts of his deeds each day for improvement. Whoever looks upon the eternal Lord with trembling heart is compelled to moderate the rights of temporal dominion over his subjects.

For he considers that his temporal preeminence over others is nothing when he is subject to giving an account to the one who rules without end.

Temporal power often carries the mind away along the steep paths of pride. And because each person is exalted insofar as he sees himself above others, he ought always to look upon the one who is above him, so that fear of the one who is above all may suppress the swelling of his mind as it grows within.

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read “let him look upon”; the manuscript copies and the purpose of blessed Gregory contradict this. Since he wishes to urge us toward humility, he exhorts us to consider not those who are beneath us but the one who rules over us.]

He observes who is beneath him, but he should consider beneath whom he himself stands, so that through consideration of the true Lord the pride of false domination may diminish.

Hence blessed Job, because he fears the judgment of the one who is above all, comes to temporal judgment as an equal with his servants, saying: “If I disdained to enter judgment with my male servant and my female servant when they disputed against me. For what shall I do when God rises to judgment? And when he inquires, what shall I answer him?”

To keep his heart always bowed in humility, he does not look upon the same servants as differing from him in status, but as sharing the same nature. Hence he also adds:

## CHAPTER XV  
[Old version XI]

### Verse 15

“Did not the one who made me in the womb also make him, and did not one fashion us in the belly?”

### 22. Let them consider equality of condition, not superiority of rank; and let them strive to be more useful than preeminent.

For powerful men, humility is a great virtue when they consider the equality of condition.

All human beings are equal by nature; but through the ordered arrangement of administration it has come about that some appear to be placed over others.

If, therefore, we press down in our minds what has been added temporarily, we quickly discover what we are by nature.

The power that has been received often presents itself to the mind and deceives it with proud thoughts. The swelling of pride must therefore be pressed down by the hand of the humblest consideration.

For if the mind descends within itself from the summit of its height, it quickly finds the level ground of natural equality.

As we said earlier, nature produced all human beings equal, but by the varying order of merits a hidden dispensation places some beneath others.

This very diversity, which arose from fault, has rightly been ordered by divine judgments, so that, because every human being does not walk the path of life equally, one may be ruled by another.

When holy men preside, they attend not to the authority of rank but to the equality of condition. They do not rejoice in being preeminent over human beings but in being useful to them.

For they know that our ancient fathers are remembered as having been not so much kings of human beings as shepherds of animals.

When the Lord said to Noah and his sons, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” he added: “And let your fear and dread be upon all the animals of the earth” (Gen. 9:1, 7).

[Note: Vendôme, Val-Clos, and German add “and fill.”]

He did not say, “Let it be upon human beings who will come,” but, “Let it be upon all the animals of the earth.”

### 23. By nature, human beings are placed over irrational animals, but not over other human beings.

By nature, the human being is placed over irrational animals, but not over other human beings. For this reason he is told to be feared by animals and not by human beings, because it is contrary to nature to be proud against an equal and to wish to be feared by an equal.

Nevertheless, holy men often desire to be feared by their subjects, but only when they discover that those same subjects do not fear God at all, so that at least through human fear they may fear to sin—those who do not fear divine judgments.

Superiors therefore do not grow proud from the fear they seek in such circumstances, since they are seeking not their own glory but the righteousness of their subjects.

In demanding fear from those who live perversely, they rule, as it were, not over human beings but over brute animals, because insofar as their subjects are beastlike, they ought also to lie subjected to fear.

## 24. Without any necessity requiring the correction of a fault, superiors shun being feared and being esteemed more highly.

When there is no fault to be corrected, they rejoice not in the excellence of their power but in the equality of their condition; and they shrink not only from being feared by them, but also from being honored more than is necessary. For they do not consider it a slight loss to humility if, perhaps on account of the dignity of their rank, they are esteemed more highly by them.

Hence the first shepherd of the Church, when Cornelius worshiped him and saw honor being offered to himself, quickly returned to the equality of his condition, saying: “Rise, I myself am also a man” (Acts 10:26). For who does not know that a human being ought to prostrate himself before his Creator, not before another human being? Therefore, when he saw that his neighbor had humbled himself before him more than was fitting, he recognized himself as a man, lest his mind swell beyond the bounds of humanity; thus, by considering the equality of their condition, he broke the elation produced by the honor shown to him.

Hence, when an angel was worshiped by John, he recognized himself to be a creature, saying: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Revelation 19:10; 22:9). Hence, when the prophet is carried away to behold sublime things, he is called “son of man” (Ezekiel 3:1), so that, led to heavenly things, he might remember that he was a human being. It is as though the divine voice admonished him in clearer words, saying: “Remember what you are, lest you be lifted up by those things to which you are carried away; temper the height of revelation by remembering your condition.”

From this, therefore, we should gather how greatly the pride of earthly power ought to be pressed down in the heart by the remembrance of our common nature, since the word “humanity” is used to prevent the elation of thought from arising out of heavenly secrets.

The blessed Job always kept a good remembrance of this humanity, saying: “Did not the One who made him make me also in the womb, and did not one and the same One form us in the womb?” As though he plainly said: “Why should we not be examined equally in the judgment of any matter, since by the power of the Creator we have been made equal?”

But since we have learned of his deeds of chastity and humility, let us now learn of his works of generosity. It follows:

# CHAPTER XVI [Old XII, Revised XI]

### VERSE 16

“If I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait.”

## 25. Job’s generosity in giving to the poor according to their desire. Those who ask beyond the limits of poverty do not deserve to obtain what they seek.

By these words the holy man is shown to have served not only the poverty of the poor but also their desire to possess. But what if the poor themselves desired something that would perhaps not be expedient for them to receive? Or, since in Sacred Scripture the humble are accustomed to be called “the poor,” should only those things be considered which the poor wish to receive—those things which the humble ask for?

**Note:** Thus we read in the old edition and in the manuscripts Corbeiensis Germanicus, Turonianus, Laudunensis, Germanensis, Vallicellanus, Normannicus, and many others. More recent editors, on slight conjecture, altered this passage thus: “Only those things are to be considered which the poor ought to receive—those which the humble ask for” (*ea sola aestimanda*; Gussanvillianus, *aestimandi*).

There is no doubt that whatever is requested with true humility ought to be given without hesitation—that is, whatever is sought not from desire but from necessity. For it is already great arrogance to desire something beyond the limits of poverty. Hence it is said to those who ask arrogantly: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3).

Since, therefore, those are truly poor who are not puffed up by the spirit of pride—those whom Truth plainly describes when it says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3)—the holy man rightly says here: “If I denied the poor what they desired.” For those who desire what is clearly not expedient for them, by the very fact that they abound in the spirit of pride are no longer poor.

But when blessed Job calls the humble “the poor,” he did not deny whatever a poor person wished to receive from him, because truly humble people neither could nor wished to ask for what was not fitting.

**Note:** The editors, removing the word *oportere* (“to be fitting,” “to be necessary”), chose to substitute *obtinere* (“to obtain”), which certainly sounds better. But the manuscripts oppose this change, especially Laudunensis, Germanensis, Normannicus, and Corbeiensis Germanicus.

## 26. Job’s munificence is to be assessed not only from the gift but from the speed of giving.

But when he reveals the generosity of his mind by declaring that he hastened to fulfill the desire of the poor, we must ask whether he may have dimmed the light of mercy by delaying his gift. Hence he adds:

“And I made the eyes of the widow wait.”

He did not wish to make the widow wait while she was asking him, so that he might increase the merit of his good works not only by the gift itself but also by the speed of the gift. Hence it is written elsewhere: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give,’ when you can give immediately” (Proverbs 3:28).

But some people are accustomed to give much outwardly while, rejecting the grace of shared daily life, refusing to have the poor as companions in domestic fellowship. Therefore blessed Job, to show not only that he had provided much outwardly but also that he had received the needy into domestic fellowship with himself, immediately adds:

# CHAPTER XVII [Revised XII]

### VERSE 17

“If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it.”

## 27. The needy are to be received as guests and admitted to the table.

He considered that he would wrong piety if he alone ate what the Lord of all had created for common use. Such fellowship of life with these people ought indeed to exist within the household, so that from it they might advance toward the merits of eternal reward.

Therefore the holy man declares that he had not just anyone, but an orphan, as his companion at table.

**Note:** Normannicus has: “But nevertheless, let it be known whether these things . . . from the grace of his Creator . . .”

But let it be made known whether he possessed such great compassion of his own accord, or whether he received it by the grace of his Creator. It follows:

# CHAPTER XVIII [Revised XIII]

### VERSE 18

“For from my childhood compassion grew with me, and from my mother’s womb it came forth with me.”

## 28. The saints attribute their good qualities not to themselves but to God. Some, as they grow in age, decline from innocence.

Although compassion was within his power in the sense that it could progress along with him, it is nevertheless clear that it was not within his power to come forth with him from the womb. It is therefore evident that he attributes nothing to his own virtue, since he plainly testifies that he received this as a gift of his condition.

Thus, when he indicates that he possessed goodness by virtue of his condition, he clearly recounts it to the praise of the Creator, declaring that he received from Him the ability to be compassionate, just as he received from Him the ability to exist; for just as he was not formed in the womb by his own work, so neither was he compassionate from the womb by his own virtue.

**Note:** The printed edition has “from the Creator” (*ex conditoris*). Our reading is found in Germanensis, Normannicus, all the Turonian manuscripts, Corbeiensis Germanicus, Laudunensis, and others. Below, too, the reading is “from his condition” (*a conditione*), where the edition had “from the Creator” (*a conditore*).

But we must consider what he asserts: “It grew with me.” For some grow in age while declining from innocence. In the elect, however, while the age of the body grows outwardly, inwardly—if one may so speak—the age of virtue grows.

It follows:

# CHAPTER XIX [Old XIII, Revised XIV]

### VERSES 19–20

“If I looked down on one passing by because he had no clothing, and on the poor man without a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep.”

## 29. Mercy toward the poor must be accompanied by humility. Those who give alms after first insulting others scarcely make satisfaction for the injury they have inflicted.

By not looking down on the poor man, he displayed the virtue of humility; by covering him, he displayed piety.

These two virtues ought to be so joined to one another that they always support each other by reciprocal action: humility, when it honors one’s neighbor, must not abandon the grace of generosity; and piety, when it gives, must not become swollen with pride.

Thus, in the face of a neighbor’s need, piety should support humility and humility piety, so that, when you see someone sharing your nature in need of necessities, you neither cease to cover him through impiety nor neglect to honor him through pride as you cover him.

For there are some who, as soon as necessary things have been requested from them by needy brothers, first hurl insulting words at them and only afterward give their gifts. Although they complete the service of piety by their material possessions, by their words they lose the grace of humility. It often seems that, when they give gifts after their insults, they are making satisfaction for the injury they have already inflicted.

What they give in response to the request is not a great work, because by the very gift they give they scarcely cover over the excess of their speech. To such people the book of Ecclesiasticus rightly says: “With every gift do not cause the sadness of an evil word” (Ecclesiasticus 18:16). And again: “Behold, a word above a good gift, and both are with a justified person” (ibid., 17)—that is, a gift should be offered through piety, and a good word should be given through humility.

**Note:** Gilot and other more recent editions add the word “add” (*adde verbum*). The older editions agree with the manuscripts and have: “Behold, a word above a good gift.”

On the other hand, there are others who do not take care to support needy brothers with material things, although they are able to do so, but seek only to warm them with flattering words. Holy James’ preaching severely reproves such people, saying: “If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ but you do not give them what is necessary for the body, what good will it do you?” (James 2:15–16).

**Note:** Normannicus has “which John”; Germanensis has “to whom John says.”

The Apostle John also admonishes them, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:13). Our love must always be displayed both through the reverence of speech and through the service of generosity.

### [Old XIV] Giving alms to the poor, we offer gifts to patrons. We sow what we shall later reap with great interest.

It greatly helps to tame the pride of the giver if, when he gives earthly things, he carefully considers the words of the heavenly Teacher, who says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

If we acquire eternal dwellings through their friendship, then without doubt, when we give, we ought to consider that we are offering gifts to patrons rather than bestowing presents upon the needy. Hence Paul says: “Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also be the supply of your need” (2 Corinthians 8:14).

We should carefully reflect that those whom we now see in need we shall one day see in abundance; and that we who are seen to abound, if we neglect to give generously, shall one day be in need.

Therefore, whoever now gives temporal assistance to the poor, expecting later to receive from him what is everlasting, cultivates, so to speak, the earth for its fruit: what it has received, it returns more abundantly.

It remains, then, that pride should never arise from the gift, since the rich person, by giving to the poor, acts so that the poor person may not remain poor forever.

Thus blessed Job, wishing carefully to show how greatly humility and mercy were joined together in him by thoughtful consideration, says: “If I looked down on one passing by because he had no clothing, and on the poor man without a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep.”

As though he plainly said: “In love of my neighbor, suppressing both the vice of pride and the vice of impiety in the same manner, I neither looked down on someone passing by while regarding him humbly, nor did I fail to warm him mercifully.”

For whoever exalts himself in arrogance over the person to whom he gives something commits a greater fault inwardly through pride than he earns merit outwardly through generosity. He makes himself naked of inward goods while looking down on the naked person whom he clothes; and he acts so as to become worse than himself, insofar as he considers himself better than his needy neighbor.

The needy person who lacks clothing is less needy than the one who lacks humility. Therefore, when we see those who share our nature lacking external things, we must consider how many inward goods are lacking in us, so that our thought may not lift itself above the poor when it carefully sees that we are more truly needy, because we are needy inwardly as well.

## 31. Alms should also be given to those who are unknown to us.

Since there are some who do not know how to extend their compassion even to strangers, but show mercy only to those whom they have come to know through constant association—among whom familiarity evidently counts for more than nature, since they give necessities to certain people not because they are human beings but because they are known—it is rightly said here through blessed Job:

“If I looked down on one passing by because he had no clothing.”

He indicates that he had shown mercy to an unknown neighbor by calling him “one passing by,” because in a compassionate mind nature counts for more than acquaintance. Indeed, everyone who is in need is already no stranger to us by the very fact that he is a human being.

It follows:

# CHAPTER XX [Revised XV]

### VERSE 21

“If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate.”

**Note:** This is also absent from Laudunensis and from many Normannican manuscripts.

## 32. The saints willingly suffer injury and are especially cautious about exacting what is owed to them.

It was the custom among the ancients for elders to sit at the gate and distinguish the disputes of those engaged in conflict by judicial examination, so that people who ought to live together in concord would not enter the city while still divided by discord.

Hence the Lord also says through the prophet: “Establish judgment in the gate” (Amos 5:15).

What, then, is expressed here by the word “gate,” except what was conducted at the gate? Just as we say “to fight camps,” meaning that fighting takes place from the camps—

**Note:** Normannicus has “in the camps” (*in castris*)—

so the judgment that was customarily conducted at the gate is called “the gate.”

Therefore, he sees himself superior in the gate who recognizes, by the merit of justice, that he belongs to the better side in judgment.

Blessed Job, then, because he did not even at that time raise his hand against the orphan when he saw himself superior even by the merit of justice, gives us a rule of fear, saying: “If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate.”

**Note:** Corbeiensis Germanicus, Laudunensis, and many Normannican manuscripts have “raised his hand” (*manum exercuit*), whereas the editions, together with Germanensis, have this reading. Shortly afterward they have *potentiorem* (“more powerful”) instead of *potiorem* (“superior”), which is the reading found throughout the manuscripts, especially Corbeiensis Germanicus, Normannicus, Turonianus, Germanensis, Laudunensis, and Vallicellanus.

As though he plainly said: “I did not wish to pursue the affairs of my own advantage by force against the orphan even then, when in judgment I saw myself superior also by justice.”

### [Old XV]

When holy men enter into disputes with persons inferior to them, they fear burdening them even in the smallest matters; and they do not refuse to be burdened themselves, even against justice. For they know that all human justice is judged to be injustice if it is examined strictly by God.

Therefore, they are extremely cautious about demanding what belongs to them, lest their actions be subjected to a subtle examination of the highest rectitude. But so that they may be found just in the divine judgment, they often allow themselves to be burdened and unjustly treated in human courts.

Blessed Job, while recounting the height of his life, has said many remarkable things. But because the human mind often refuses to believe good qualities which it does not know how to practice, he immediately adds a sentence of condemnation upon himself if he has failed to fulfill in action any of the things he has mentioned, saying:

# CHAPTER XXI [Revised XVI]

### VERSE 22

“Let my shoulder fall from its joint, and let my arm be crushed together with its bones.”

## 33. Concord in society cannot endure without perseverance in patience.

Since bodily action is performed through the shoulder and arm, if he failed to fulfill in action the good things he had expressed with his mouth, he desires that his shoulder fall and his arm be crushed.

As though he plainly said: “If I refused to practice what I have said, let me lose the very bodily member that was given to me for acting, so that what I refused to exercise for usefulness may fall away from the body.”

**Note:** Ebroicensis, Gemeticensis, and other Normannican manuscripts have “If I refused to practice the good things which . . .”; Laudunensis here has “that very thing which is mine” (*ipsud quod mihi*) instead of *ipsum* (“the very thing”).

If this sentence of condemnation is to be referred to a spiritual meaning, it is clear that the arm is joined to the body through the shoulder. Just as the arm signifies good action, so the shoulder signifies the joining of social life.

Therefore the prophet, looking upon the peoples of the universal Church who would serve God in concord, says: “And they shall serve him with one shoulder” (Zephaniah 3:9).

In saying, “If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate,” he asserts that he preserved the remarkable virtue of patience: he did not avoid being burdened by persons of little importance, nor did he resist what might justly have belonged to him.

But if he had not done this, he adds: “Let my shoulder fall from its joint.” For whoever refuses to preserve patience soon abandons social life through impatience.

The shoulder falls from its joint when the mind, unable to endure some adversity, abandons fraternal concord; and, like a limb separated from the body, one who could practice good is cut off from the community of all good.

For concord can never be preserved except through patience alone. In human affairs, occasions frequently arise by which people’s minds are separated from one another’s unity and affection.

**Note:** Gemeticensis has “from gentleness” (*a suavitate*).

Unless the mind prepares itself to endure adversity, the shoulder certainly does not remain attached to the body. Hence Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Hence Truth itself says: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

### [Old XVI] 34. Without patience joined to charity, good works perish.

Rightly, after the shoulder falls, he adds: “And let my arm be crushed together with its bones,” because all our activity, even when it appears to be accompanied by virtues of every kind, is undone unless patience is preserved through the bond of charity.

**Note:** The editions added “supported” (*fulta*), which is absent from the manuscripts. Germanensis has “joined to the virtues”; Corbeiensis Germanicus has “full of virtues.”

Whoever refuses to endure the evils of others loses the ability to practice his own good works.

**Note:** Gussanvillianus, Vaticanus, and other recent witnesses read: “continues to practice his own good works” (*pergit operari*). But this is contrary to the mind of Saint Gregory, who teaches that the person who refuses to suffer what belongs to others ceases to practice good works, and contrary to the testimony of the English and Norman manuscripts, as well as Corbeiensis Germanicus, Turonianus, Germanensis, Laudunensis, and others, which agree with the older edition.

For when someone is wounded by the heat of an angry spirit, he recoils from love; and when he cannot tolerate being burdened outwardly, he darkens himself inwardly by losing the light of charity.

**Note:** Vallicellanus has “the light of clarity” (*lumen claritatis*).

He no longer sees where to direct the step of good action when he has lost the eye of love.

But the shoulder of holy men does not fall from its joint, because their love does not withdraw through impatience from the concord of social life. Their arm is not broken, because all their action is guarded in the shoulder’s joining—that is, in the bond of charity.

But by what consideration he performed such great good works and abstained from all evils, he adds, saying:

# CHAPTER XXII [Revised XVII]

### VERSE 23

“For I always feared God, as though waves were swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight.”

## 35. The great force of the fear of God in persuading us to despise all things. Preliminary signs of the final judgment.

If we can, let us measure from this fearful comparison how great was the force of fear in the holy man.

When swelling waves threaten from above and menace the death they carry, those sailing have no concern for temporal things, and no bodily pleasure returns to the mind. They even throw out of the ship the very things for which they undertook long voyages. All possessions come to the mind’s contempt through the love of remaining alive.

Therefore, he fears God as though waves were swelling over him who, desiring true life, despises everything he carries while possessing it here. For just as those caught in a storm throw off the ship’s weight, so we remove earthly desires from a mind oppressed by them.

The ship that was sinking beneath its load rises and floats when it has been lightened, because the cares that weigh down the mind in this life drag it into the depths. The mind is lifted all the higher amid the waves of temptation the more carefully it is emptied of the thoughts of this age.

There is also another matter concerning the disturbance of the sea that should be carefully observed. When a storm arises, gentle waves are stirred first, then larger masses; finally, the waves rise high and overturn the sailors by their very height.

Thus, surely, that final storm is hastening which will overthrow the whole world. For now it shows us its beginnings through wars and disasters, as through certain waves; and the nearer we come to the end each day, the more we see greater masses of tribulation rushing upon us.

Finally, when all the elements have been shaken, the heavenly Judge comes and brings the end of everything, since then the storm raises its waves to heaven. Hence it is said: “Yet a little while, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Haggai 2:7).

Because holy men watch for this storm attentively, they fear every day as though swelling waves were threatening over them; and from the tribulations that strike the world they foresee what will follow.

**Note:** Vallicellanus has “which have not yet struck” (*quae nondum feriunt*).

## 36. The saints fear the final judgment; how much more should sinners tremble.

It is rightly added: “And I could not bear his weight,” because whoever considers the coming of the final judgment with an attentive mind sees that such terror threatens that he fears not only what he will see then, but even what he now foresees.

The mind trembles with fear when it considers such great terror; lowering the eyes of its attention, it refuses to look upon what it foresees. Therefore it is rightly said: “And I could not bear his weight,” because when the mind tries, by reflection, to investigate the power of the heavenly Majesty coming to judgment and the terror of such a great examination, it immediately flees back into itself and is terrified to discover what it has found within itself.

But amid these things we must consider that blessed Job speaks thus of himself both when praised and when scourged. If, then, one who feared in this way was struck at least for the advancement of his merits, how shall the one who despises be struck? How will God’s judgments crush those who exalt themselves, if they temporarily crush even those who always fear them in humility? How will one who despises be able to bear God’s weight, if even the man who foresaw it through fear endured it under the rod?

Therefore we must fear above all that examination of such strictness. It is clear, however, that in this life, when God strikes and correction follows the blow, it is the discipline of a father, not the anger of a judge; it is the love of one who corrects, not the severity of one who punishes.

From the present blow, therefore, we must consider the eternal judgments. Hence we must carefully reflect how that judgment which condemns will be endured, if the anger that purifies can scarcely be endured now.

# BOOK TWENTY-TWO

The remainder of chapter 31 of the Book of Job is explained, with particular commendation of humility and moderation of spirit, patience, charity, and concern for those subject to one’s authority.

# CHAPTER ONE

## 1. To avoid despair, it is permissible to remember what one has done rightly.

What I have often already said is not burdensome for me to repeat frequently, since the excellent preacher also says: “For me to write the same things to you is not burdensome, but for you it is necessary” (Philippians 3:1).

Blessed Job recounts the virtues he has practiced because, caught amid words of reproach and blows of affliction, he sees that his mind may be shaken from confidence in hope. He had heard from his reproving friends that he had done many evil things; and lest his mind, pressed equally by words and scourges, fall into despair, he restores it to hope through the memory of his virtues, so that it should not be cast down in calamity, since it remembered having done such sublime things in a time of tranquility.

Since, then, we have explained the reason for his intention, it remains for us to weigh carefully the virtues we have heard him recount.

**Note:** More recent editions have “which I said earlier many times” (*quod ante saepe*). We follow the manuscripts and the older edition.

The distinguished preacher says: “For me to write the same things to you is not burdensome, but for you it is necessary” (Philippians 3:1).

**Note:** The Pratellian manuscript, exceedingly elegant and carefully corrected, together with the excellent manuscripts Uticensis and Beccensis, has *non piguum*, derived from *piget* (“it is burdensome”), rather than the usual reading.

## 2. One virtue without the others is either nothing or very little.

This must first be understood: whoever is believed to excel in some virtue truly excels only when he is not subject to vices on another side. For if he is subject to vices elsewhere, that quality is not solid in which he was thought to stand.

Each virtue is smaller to the extent that the others are lacking. We have often encountered some people who were indeed chaste but not humble; others who seemed humble but were not merciful; others who seemed merciful but were in no way just; and others who seemed just but trusted in themselves rather than in the Lord.

It is certain that chastity is not true in the heart of one who lacks humility, since, when pride inwardly corrupts him, he commits fornication by loving himself and withdrawing from divine love.

**Note:** The manuscripts differ here. Turonianus and Germanensis read: “because, with pride corrupting him inwardly, he commits fornication, loving himself and separating himself from divine fear.” Vallicellanus has: “he commits fornication, dividing himself from divine love.” Vindocinus, the Normannican manuscripts, and Corbeiensis Germanicus have: “loving himself, he commits fornication by separating himself from divine love.”

Nor is humility true when it is not joined to mercy, because humility should not be called humility if it does not know how to incline toward compassion for a brother’s misery.

Nor is mercy true when it is alien to the rectitude of justice, because whoever can be polluted through injustice clearly does not know how to show mercy even to himself.

Nor is justice true when it places its confidence not in the Creator of all things but perhaps in itself or in created things, because, when it withdraws hope from the Creator, it perverts within itself the order of principal justice.

Thus one virtue without the others is either altogether nothing or imperfect. To speak, as some have thought, of the first four virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—each is perfect to the extent that they are joined together in mutual relation.

**Note:** Corbeiensis Germanicus, Normannicus, and many others, together with the old edition, have: “prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice are each so much more perfect.”

Separated from one another, they can in no way be perfect. Prudence is not true if it is not just, temperate, and strong; temperance is not perfect if it is not strong, just, and prudent; fortitude is not complete if it is not prudent, temperate, and just; and justice is not true if it is not prudent, strong, and temperate.

# 3. All these virtues came together in Job.

Blessed Job makes known that he possessed virtues joined together in himself, not one without the others, by enumerating them individually.

To indicate the goodness of chastity, he says: “If my heart was deceived concerning a woman” (chapter 31:9). And to show that the grace of humility was in no way absent from that same chastity, he adds afterward: “If I disdained to enter into judgment with my servant” (verse 13).

To show that mercy was joined to his humility, he says shortly afterward: “If I denied the poor what they desired” (verse 16). And to show that his mercy descended from the root of justice, he had prefaced this somewhat earlier, saying: “If I walked in vanity, and my foot hastened toward deceit” (verse 5).

To show how fearful and watchful he was in every matter, he asserts below: “For I always feared the Lord as though waves were swelling over me” (verse 25).

If, placed in prosperity and supported by an abundance of possessions, he had placed his hope either in his own deeds or in the things surrounding him, he would certainly not have been just. But when did this holy man place his hope in himself, who plainly says: “Behold, there is no help for me in myself” (Job 6:13)?

### [Old and Revised II]

What, then, remains except to make known with what disposition of mind he possessed even his riches? For he says:

### CHAPTER 31, VERSE 24

“If I thought gold was my strength, and said to refined gold, ‘My confidence.’”

# CHAPTER TWO

## 4. Confidence must be placed not in passing riches but in God alone.

We call *obryzum* “raw gold.”

**Note:** Turonianus, Laudunensis, Vallicellanus, and the Normannican manuscripts have “raw gold” or “a mass of raw gold.”

The holy man therefore did not consider gold to be his strength, nor refined gold—that is, a mass of raw gold—to be his confidence, because, fixing his hope and delight in the grace of the Creator alone, he neither sinned through the quantity of his gold nor through its appearance.

To despair of the Creator would have been to place hope in a creature.

That rich man had fixed his hope in uncertain things who said: “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.” But a heavenly voice rebukes him, saying: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12:19–20).

On that same night he was taken away—the man who had expected many years from the abundance of his possessions—so that he who had prudently gathered provisions for a long future could not see even one following day.

It is like laying a foundation on flowing waters when someone wishes to make the confidence of hope firm in passing things. For while God remains forever, everything passes.

**Note:** Normannicus, Corbeiensis Germanicus, and Germanensis have: “What, then, is fleeing from the One who stands, if not clinging to things that pass?”

What, then, is fleeing from the One who stands, if not clinging to passing things? Could anyone ever be swept away by the swollen whirlpools of rushing rivers and remain fixed while the water flowed downward?

Therefore, whoever avoids flowing away must flee what is flowing away, lest through what he loves he be compelled to arrive at what he avoids.

**Note:** Vindocinus has: “what harms.”

For whoever clings to passing things is dragged toward the place where what he holds is moving. First, therefore, one must take care not to love temporal things; then one must take care not to place confidence in those same temporal things which one retains not for pleasure but for use, because a mind joined to what is rushing away soon loses its stability.

The current of the present life drags along the one whom it raises, and it is exceedingly foolish to be rolled about upon a wave while trying to plant one’s feet.

But there are many who, although they place no confidence in passing things, nevertheless rejoice silently in their minds when they have an abundant supply of what is necessary for their use.

There is no doubt that a person grieves less over the absence of eternal things to the extent that he rejoices more in the presence of temporal things; and the one who grieves less over the absence of temporal things more certainly awaits the presence of eternal things.

Blessed Job, testifying that he had not possessed this kind of joy over earthly things, adds:

# CHAPTER THREE [Old III]

### VERSE 25

“If I rejoiced over my many riches, and because my hand found very much.”

## 5. Holy men either distribute the burden of temporal goods by giving them away or lay it down entirely by despising it.

In the hardship of this pilgrimage, holy men are not yet permitted to contemplate the sight of their Creator, which they desire. Therefore they count all the abundance of the present life as poverty, because nothing outside God is sufficient for the mind that truly seeks God.

Often their very abundance becomes exceedingly burdensome to them, because they bear heavily the fact that, while hastening toward their homeland, they carry many things along the road.

Thus they devote themselves to sharing these things with needy neighbors, so that while one takes what he does not have, the other lays down what he had in excess; neither fellow traveler walks empty-handed, nor does an excessive burden weigh down the one whom it could have delayed on the way.

The elect therefore do not rejoice in great abundance, which, for love of their heavenly inheritance, they either scatter by giving or abandon by despising.

It follows:

# CHAPTER FOUR

### VERSES 26–28

“If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly; and my heart secretly rejoiced, and I kissed my hand with my mouth—which is the greatest iniquity and a denial against the Most High God.”

[Col. 0214D] **6. They restrain their senses and continually gather themselves within their own minds.**—It is not uncertain that both of these lights, assigned to human service, are called the army of heaven. We know from Scripture that many have fallen into their worship, as it is written: “They worshiped the whole army of heaven” (2 Kings 17:16). And because the sun and moon are seen in one way for use and in another for veneration, blessed Job declares that he by no means saw the sun and moon in the manner in which their worshipers customarily venerate them; nor did his heart rejoice, nor did he kiss his hand with his mouth. What else, indeed, is expressed by that kissing than the grace of veneration? If he had ever done this, he calls it “the greatest iniquity” and a denial of God.

But after he has recounted such lofty summits of virtue concerning himself in the preceding passages, what is surprising if he now declares that he did not worship the sun and moon? We must therefore consider that, after testifying that he had not placed his trust in gold and had not rejoiced in abundant riches, he is still led to higher things, so that he may instruct us all the more profoundly by recounting certain matters about himself with greater subtlety.

For he says: “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly, and my heart rejoiced in secret.” What is meant here by “seeing,” unless looking upon something with desire? Hence the Psalmist says: “If I regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear” (Psalm 65:18).

[Note: Pratensis and other Norman witnesses read, “If I looked upon … God will not hear.”]

That iniquity could not be expressed by the mouth if it were not first seen in the heart. But there is one kind of seeing through judgment and another through desire. Blessed Job therefore declares that he did not see the shining sun or the brightly moving moon, in order to show that he did not desire the appearance of the present light. It is as though, after openly despising his earthly abundance, he were saying: “What shall I say? I certainly did not rejoice in gold, since I did not delight even in this bodily light.”

For holy men, after despising all the pleasures of the present life, turn their minds away from this external light as though from darkness, because of the sweetness of that inner light. They struggle greatly within themselves lest they be carried away by delight in this light which shines outwardly. Visible light, if loved without caution, blinds the heart to invisible light; for the more the longing mind pours itself outward, the more it is struck back from inward vision.

Therefore all who are diligent, lest they slip too far outward through bodily senses, continually gather themselves within their minds by the hidden discipline of watchfulness, so that they may be found inwardly all the more whole the less they are scattered outwardly. By this strength of discipline he had confined himself within the secrets of his mind when, fleeing desire for outward life, he said: “I have not desired the day of man—you know” (Jeremiah 17:16). What is said by the prophet, “I have not desired the day of man—you know,” blessed Job asserts of himself in other words: he did not see the shining sun or the brightly moving moon, nor did he rejoice over them in the recesses of his heart, because he could not rejoice in what he did not see through the desire of delight.

[Note: In Laudunensis, “which he is now clearly recalling.”]

**[Old IV.] 7. They take care not to rely upon their own prudence.**—But if we examine through the mysteries of allegory all that we have discussed in accordance with the historical sense, what do we understand gold to mean here except the talent of an excellent intellect? And what does *obryzum* mean except the mind, which, when refined by the fire of love, continually preserves within itself the brightness of beauty through the daily renewal of fervor?

A mind that strives always to begin anew through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness.

[Note: In Germanus, Laudunensis, and Corbeiensis Germanus, “to grow old.”]

Hence Paul says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23). Hence the Psalmist, who had already reached the summit of perfection, spoke as though beginning: “I said, ‘Now I begin’” (Psalm 76:11). For if we do not wish to grow weary of the good things we have begun, it is very necessary that we believe we must begin anew every day.

Nor is it contrary to the order of reason to say that gold signifies intellect. Just as gold is placed in an ornament so that an arrangement of gems may be set above it, so the bright intellects of holy people are humbly subordinated to divine gifts and receive above themselves the ordered gifts of grace.

And unless some such thing as gold existed together with wisdom, a certain wise man would never have said: “Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure—what use is there in either of them?” (Sirach 20:32; 41:17). Holy men, however, do not regard their strength as gold, because, however brilliantly they may shine in intellect, they consider themselves nothing through their own powers.

And although they are able to perceive everything with strength, they first desire to understand themselves, so that the light of intellect, like the sun, may first illuminate the place in which it rises, and afterward the other things toward which it extends as it proceeds. Otherwise, if they devote themselves to knowing others while failing to know themselves, the sun’s ray becomes darkened precisely where it rises.

They therefore direct the power of their intellect toward recognizing their own weakness, and through a better knowledge of their weakness they grow strong. Gold is not believed to be strength if no trust is placed in the intellect that has been received. Solomon rightly admonishes this, saying: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own prudence” (Proverbs 3:3).

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanus, Laudunensis, Germanus, and most witnesses read, “with your whole heart.”]

Let him therefore say: “If I thought gold were my strength, and said to fine gold, ‘You are my confidence.’” As though he were openly admitting: “I did not attribute even what I truly understood to my own intellect; nor, if it happened that I did any good, did I principally credit my own mind with it.”

Still more subtly conveying to us the humility of his heart, he adds:

## CHAPTER V [Rec. III]

**Verse 25.—“If I rejoiced over my many riches, and because my hand found very much.”**

**8. It is dangerous to understand much in the sacred writings unless what is understood is guarded.**—What do we believe is figuratively signified by “many riches,” except an abundance of insights into counsels?

[Note: Vindocinus reads, “we say.”]

The hand of the seeker finds these when the thought of one who reflects brings them forth. Contemplating these riches of wisdom, Solomon says: “The riches of the wise are their crown” (Proverbs 14:24). Since he calls riches not earthly metals but prudence, he immediately adds by contrast: “The imprudence of fools is folly” (ibid., 14:24). For if he had called earthly riches the crown of the wise, without doubt he would have described the poverty of fools rather than their imprudence as folly. But by adding “the imprudence of fools” to “folly,” he showed that he called the riches of the wise prudence.

Contemplating the riches of knowledge within himself, and humbling his contemplation by considering human weakness, Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Thus we find many riches within ourselves when, by investigating the sacred words, we receive gifts of abundant understanding and perceive many things in them that are nevertheless not mutually contradictory.

Yet in the divine writings it is not a secure cause for rejoicing to know strong or numerous things, but to guard what has been understood. For one who understands rightly recognizes what he ought to do by understanding.

[Note: The printed editions read, “what he ought to do by understanding.” The word “to do” is absent from Turonensis, Germanus, Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, Vallicellianus, and all the Norman witnesses; the sense remains complete without it.]

The farther understanding extends, the more earnestly it is bound to accomplish works.

[Note: Pratensis and several Norman witnesses read, “for the farther understanding extends.”]

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from him to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more” (Luke 12:48).

[Note: Laudunensis reads, “more will be sought from him … they will demand more.” The same reading occurs in Vallicellianus and the Norman witnesses, except that where they have “more,” one Norman witness reads “much.”]

**[Old V.] 9. The understanding that has been given is like money received on loan, to be repaid with interest.**—Let us therefore regard the understanding that has been given as money received on loan, because the more that is credited to us through kindness, the more we are bound as debtors in our works. And often this same money of understanding that has been received is lost when it is lent out at interest to hearers, unless it is distributed cautiously.

For we must not carelessly overlook what is read in the Book of Kings: when the sons of the prophets were cutting wood in the Jordan, the axhead of one of them slipped from its handle and disappeared into the depths (2 Kings 6). The iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart. Cutting wood with it means rebuking those who act wickedly.

Sometimes, when this is done carelessly, when the fall of empty glory is not avoided in the knowledge that has been received, the iron is lost in the water, because through undisciplined action understanding becomes foolish.

[Note: More recent editions read “wisdom,” contrary to the manuscripts and the authority of the older printed editions.]

We know that this understanding is given for the purpose of being restored through good action before the eyes of the giver. Hence the one who had lost the iron rightly cried out: “Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And this one I had received on loan” (2 Kings 6:5).

[Note: Laudunensis, Corbeiensis Germanus, and Germanus read, “I had borrowed this one.”]

The elect have this distinctive quality: if the guilt of empty glory secretly steals upon them in their knowledge, they quickly return to their hearts and pursue with tears whatever they find in themselves condemnable before the eyes of the strict Judge.

[Note: The Norman witnesses read, “the stealthy fault of empty glory slips in”; Germanus, Corbeiensis Germanus, Vallicellianus, and Laudunensis likewise read *furtiva* (“stealthy”) in place of *furtive* (“stealthily”).]

In their weeping they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed, but also the good things they ought to have returned from the gift they received.

[Note: Germanus and the Norman witnesses add after “ought to have returned,” “they attend to this, because …”]

For they feel themselves to be all the more sinners insofar as they are held debtor for the good things they neglected, although they were able to perform them.

The one who lost the iron therefore rightly cried out: “Alas, alas, alas! And this one I had received on loan.” As though he were saying: “Through the dissolution of negligence I lost what I had received by the grace of the creditor in order to repay it through good works.”

[Note: The printed editions read “of the Creator”; this is also found in some manuscripts. Vindocinus, Corbeiensis Germanus, Laudunensis, and Vallicellianus read “of the creditor,” a variant noted by Gilot.]

Yet God never abandons a mind that truly recognizes itself in sins. Hence Elisha immediately comes, casts a piece of wood downward, and raises the iron to the surface. For our Redeemer, looking upon us in mercy, humbles the sinner’s heart and restores to him the understanding he had lost. He sinks the wood and raises the iron: he afflicts the heart and restores knowledge.

Hence another translation rightly says that he broke the wood and threw it in, and thus lifted up the iron. To break the wood is to crush the heart’s pride. To throw the wood down to the depths is to humble the exalted heart through knowledge of its own weakness, as we have said. Immediately the iron returns to the surface, because understanding returns to its former use in practice.

[Col. 0218B] **10. For this reason the righteous fear more than they rejoice over the gift entrusted to them.**—Since the gift of understanding that is received is scarcely guarded amid so many difficulties—for care must be taken lest it grow sluggish through idleness, and care must also be taken lest it vanish through the fault of pride in the practice of work—holy men do not rejoice merely when they recognize what they ought to do, but when they do what they have recognized.

And if they rejoice together with the gift of the giver when they understand, they nevertheless consider with sorrow the obligation of work, so that by their action they may repay what has been advanced to them in knowledge.

A debtor is foolish who joyfully receives borrowed money but does not consider the time when he must repay it. The joy of receiving is moderated when the appointed time for repayment is also considered with careful foresight.

Since righteous men are not lifted up by secure joy in what they understand with vigilance, it is rightly said: “If I rejoiced over my many riches, and because my hand found very much.” As though it were openly said: “I did not consider myself enriched in righteousness because I understood many right things that I ought to do; nor did understanding lift up my heart, because consideration of the duty of action weighed upon it.”

**[Old VI.]** It must be understood, however, that it often happens that, when the height of understanding is perceived, a mind very anxious about itself is restrained from the fall of pride.

[Note: Vindocinus reads, “when understanding lifts up the heart, height is perceived.”]

But when it also begins to do the marvelous things it understands, it sometimes falls precisely by being displayed outwardly and boasts that it surpasses others in its actions.

Blessed Job therefore did not exalt the gold of understanding in himself, nor did he raise before human eyes the light of marvelous action. Hence he appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER VI [Rec. IV]

**Verse 26.—“If I saw the sun when it shone.”**

**11. They do not exult in the splendor of their good works. A debtor is not acquitted who repays much, but one who repays everything.**—The sun in its radiance is a good work in its manifestation. For it is written: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). And again: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:33).

What is signified here by the shining sun is signified in the Gospel by burning lamps. When a good work shines among unbelievers, a lamp burns in the night; but when it shines within the Church, the sun shines in the day.

A good work, if it is still such that only the wicked admire it, is a lamp in the night. But if it progresses so far that good and more perfect people can admire it, it is truly the sun in the day.

When a good work shines through the bodily life of active conduct, light gleams from an earthen vessel as from a lamp.

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanus, the Norman witnesses, Turonensis, Germanus, and Laudunensis read “shines in bodies”; the older printed editions retain the manuscript reading.]

But when it is raised through the mind’s virtue alone in contemplation, it appears as light coming from heaven in the manner of the sun.

Since blessed Job had recounted many good works of hospitality and mercy concerning himself—works that were still all the more elementary because he knew they had been performed bodily—he recalled the eye of his mind to the summit of spiritual virtues, remembered his perfection, and called the light of his examples, which he had offered to others, the sun.

**[Reg. V.]** There are some who, when they do any good things, immediately forget their sins and fix the eye of their heart upon consideration of the good works they have displayed. They already consider themselves holy precisely because, amid the good things they do, they avoid remembering their sins, in which they may perhaps still be entangled.

If they attentively considered the strictness of the Judge, they would fear their evils more than they would exult over their imperfect goods. They would look more closely at the fact that they remain debtors for the things still to be done than at the fact that, by performing certain works, they have already paid part of their debt.

For a debtor is not acquitted who repays much, but one who repays everything. Nor does the runner reach the prize of victory if he runs swiftly through a large part of the contest but fails at the finish line in what remains.

[Note: Vallicellianus reads, “but [he who fails] when he comes to the finishing posts,” a reading also found in Corbeiensis Germanus, the Norman witnesses, and Germanus, with *who* omitted.]

Nor does it help travelers headed toward their appointed destinations to begin and cover a long journey if they are unable to complete it entirely. Therefore, when we seek eternal life, what are we doing other than traveling along certain roads by which we hasten toward our homeland?
