But what does it profit us to cover so much if we neglect what remains to be done in order to arrive?

**12. We should not consider how much of the journey has already been completed, but what remains to be accomplished.**—In the manner of travelers, we must by no means look at how much of the road we have already traveled, but how much remains for us to complete, so that what is constantly and anxiously still regarded as future may, little by little, become past.

[Note: Vallicellianus and Laudunensis read, “so that we may proceed.”]

We ought therefore to inspect more closely the good things we have not yet done than those we rejoice to have already done.

But human weakness has this characteristic: it prefers to look at what pleases it in itself rather than at what displeases it in itself. The sick eye of the heart, fearing the effort of self-examination, seeks in the mind a kind of bed of pleasure on which it may lie softly. Therefore it understands what benefits it has gained from completed good works, but does not know what losses it suffers from neglected ones.

[Note: Turonensis reads, “what losses it suffers from negligences.”]

Even the elect are often tested by this fault. Their hearts are often prompted to recall the good things they have done and to exult in the joy of security. But if they are truly elect, they turn the eyes of their minds away from what pleases them. They suppress within themselves all joy over completed good works, seek sorrow over what they understand themselves to have done less well, and consider themselves unworthy.

They are almost the only ones who do not see their own good works, even though they offer themselves to everyone else as examples in which those works may be seen.

Hence Paul, setting aside the good things already accomplished in himself and thinking only of what still remained to be completed, said: “I do not consider that I have apprehended” (Philippians 3:13). Hence, in order to humble himself regarding the good things he was doing, he strove to bring his former evils back to mind, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Timothy 1:13).

**[Old VII.] 13. When it is permissible to recall or recount the good things one has done.**—Did he not at some point also say: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7)?

We must consider very carefully that he said this at the time when he knew he was about to depart from the body. For he had prefaced it by saying: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand” (ibid., 6).

At that point, therefore, he brought the perfection of his work back to memory, when he already foresaw that no time remained for him to continue laboring in the space of divine generosity.

Just as, while we live, we must drive our good works from our memory lest they lift us up, so, when the end approaches, we often bring them back to memory so that they may provide confidence and press down the fear of despair.

[Note: The printed editions, together with Corbeiensis Germanus, read “we rightly recall.” Germanus removes the adverb; the English manuscripts and other witnesses read “we recall again,” which gives an excellent sense.]

And when he recounted his good works to the Corinthians, he sought to strengthen them, not to display himself. For he showed that he did not regard those same good works as belonging to himself but to the Lord. When he had disclosed the tribulation of his own temptation, he added: “Therefore I am pleased with my weaknesses” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

[Note: Turonensis reads, “so that he might regard these not in himself but in the Lord.”]

Thus, in order to instruct his disciples, he reported the greatness of his own achievements; but in order to preserve himself in humility, he fixed the eye of his consideration not upon his virtues but upon his weaknesses.

Holy men therefore have this characteristic: they see the good things they do, yet, when they have completed them, they turn their eyes away from remembering them.

Hence it is rightly said through blessed Job: “If I saw the sun when it shone.” As though he were openly saying: “Even when my work gave others the light of examples, I did not attend to it for the sake of presumption, because, fearing that I might be lifted up by it, I turned my eyes away from looking upon it.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER VII

**The same passage.—“And the moon proceeding brightly.”**

**14. One must not hunt after reputation gained from good works.**—After mentioning the sun, he appropriately added the brightly moving moon, because after a good work comes a praiseworthy reputation, through which a celebrated name is possessed in the night of the present life.

If it is true, as some think, that the moon receives its illumination through an invisible circuit from the sun’s ray, so that it can display light during its nocturnal courses, this interpretation also accords with the order of the symbolism.

For reputation receives strength from a good work and pours out the grace of approval like the brightness of light.

[Note: Vindocinus adds, “and the grace of splendor.”]

There is also another feature of the moon that suits, by comparison, a reputation that scatters good things. Its light shows the way to travelers even during the darkness, because when the light of praise shines forth from another’s life, it illuminates others for the practice of good works. When that person’s reputation is recognized as bright, the light of example is provided to someone proceeding along the road.

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanus, the Norman witnesses, Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, and the older editions have the wording translated above; more recent editions read, “for the performance of good works.” Germanus abbreviates the whole passage: “for when the light from another’s life, which is known to be bright by that person’s reputation, is shown, it supplies, as it were, to one traveling from the road …”]

But sometimes a work derived from another’s reputation is formed in the mind with an impure desire. Weak minds, when they hear good things about others, sometimes kindle themselves to right action not through love of virtue but through delight in praise.

It is clearly evident that, just as it is the nature of the sun to kindle and dry whatever it touches, it is characteristic of lunar fire to burn whatever it touches, but in burning to make it moist.

[Note: The more recent witnesses read, “it is the nature of the sun,” contrary to the manuscripts and ancient editions.]

Some are inflamed toward a good life by the love of right action for God’s sake; others are inflamed by love of praise.

[Note: Turonensis, Germanus, Corbeiensis Germanus, and most Norman witnesses read, “through love.”]

When we are kindled by love of right action, we are dried, as it were by the sun’s fire, from the moisture of vices.

But the one whom love of praise provokes to good work is touched by the desired reputation like the moon: it both kindles and dissolves his mind. It kindles him for the practice of the work, but dissolves him into the desire for approval.

Often, nevertheless, the examples of others usefully persuade us to practice good works. When with humble minds we receive the good of another’s reputation, we either bring our own good works to greater perfection or change our evil works into good.

And when the splendor of our neighbor’s life shines upon us, our mind, as we said, directs itself toward attaining the path of virtue and sets its steps, as it were, in the moonlight.

[Note: Vindocinus reads, “which directs itself in this way toward attaining the virtues.”]

But just as we progress through another’s reputation, so, if we hunger after praise for our own reputation, we are often emptied of virtue.

[Note: Almost all printed editions read, “if we hunger after the praises of our reputation.” We have followed the manuscripts—Corbeiensis Germanus, Turonensis, Laudunensis, Germanus, Vindocinus, the Norman witnesses, and the Paris edition of 1495—which read “if we attend to the praises of our reputation.”]

For when the mind takes delight in what it considers to be thought of it outwardly, it forgets what it was inwardly longing for.

**[Old VIII.] 15. Understanding, good works, and praise did not harm Job’s humility—a rare occurrence.**—Since the holy man was not corrupted by the understanding of knowledge, he refused to rejoice over many riches. Since the greatness of his work did not inflate him, he did not see the shining sun. And since the fame of praise did not exalt him, he paid no attention to the brightly moving moon.

[Note: Corbeiensis Germanus, Vallicellianus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman and German witnesses add, “nor did a praiseworthy reputation.”]

There are some who fall into pride precisely through subtle understanding, because they recognize good things that they themselves do not do. These rejoice over many riches when they discover lofty matters through understanding, and they are corrupted by those very discoveries through pride.

There are others whom understanding does not lift up, but whose performed work exalts them. When they look upon their actions, they disdainfully place others below themselves in their own minds. These, although they do not rejoice over many riches, nevertheless see the shining sun, because they swell with pride over the mere greatness of their good work, as though despising others.

[Note: The words from “these, although…” through “they swell with pride by despising” are absent from Germanus, Vindocinus, Corbeiensis Germanus, and the Norman witnesses.]

There are still others whom their own work does not exalt; but when people begin to praise them for this same good work, conquered by human approval, they picture themselves in their thoughts as great people and are loosened from the guardianship of the heart.

These, although they did not wish to see the shining sun, nevertheless look upon the brightly moving moon. Amid the darkness of this life, they fix their minds upon the brightness of their own reputation and thereby lose the grace of humility as though from nocturnal light. Looking at the moon, they do not see themselves, because they begin not to know themselves when they fix the eyes of their minds upon passing approval.

**16. Various advances and stages in virtue; what must be feared at each stage.**—Human progress is like the growth we observe in trees. The power of the future tree is first in the seed, afterward in the shoot, and finally it is extended into branches. Thus the virtue of each person who acts gradually grows.

It is sown in understanding, rises in action, and finally grows strong until it reaches the breadth of great progress.

But when someone’s understanding lifts him up, the tree that could have arisen in the seed rots. When, after good action, it is corrupted by the plague of pride, it dries up as though already grown. But when neither understanding nor action corrupts it, but, as its greatness increases, the favor of those who praise follows and overturns the mind of the one who acts well from its proper position, the tree endures the winds of tongues, and the storm of reputation tears up by the roots everything that had grown strong in it.

[Note: The Norman witnesses read, “but as greatness increases, powerful favor”; the reading printed here was formerly found in Uticensis and Beccensis. The older editions read, “but while favor follows increasing greatness …”]

For the higher a tree has risen toward the heights, the more forcefully it feels the power of the winds; so the more someone is lifted up through good works, the more he is wearied by the stronger breath of those who praise him.

If the tree is still in the seed, we must fear that it may rot through the very knowledge of learning. If it has already emerged as a shoot, we must take care that the hand of pride does not touch it and dry it from the greenness of its action. But if, already possessing vigorous strength, it raises itself toward the heights, we must greatly fear that a heavier wind of praise may strike it and tear it up by the roots.

**[Old IX.] 17. Because of the danger arising from reputation and human praise, God permits detraction to be set against it.**—Amid all this, we must understand that, lest we be carried away by excessive praise, by the marvelous governance of our ruler we are often permitted to be torn apart even by detraction.

Thus, when the voice of one who praises lifts us up, the tongue of one who detracts may humble us. A tree is often driven by the force of one wind so violently that it seems almost capable of being uprooted, yet it is raised upright by the breath of another wind coming from the opposite direction; and although it has suffered bending on one side, it returns to its position from the other.

[Note: The edition reads *eruamur*, “we may be uprooted,” whereas one edition has *erigamur*, “we may be raised up.” Perhaps an unskilled copyist, thinking that *eruere* meant only “to snatch away,” changed *eruamur* into *erigamur*. The first reading occurs in Turonensis, Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, Vindocinus, the Norman witnesses, and the two Sangerman witnesses, Germanus and Corbeiensis Germanus.]

That tree, deeply rooted and standing firm amid opposing winds, was the one that said: “Through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute” (2 Corinthians 6:8).

Often, praise improperly brought to the ears of one who acts well, while it resounds outwardly in words, generates within the mind a certain silent storm of pride.

[Note: This is the reading of the two Sangermanensis witnesses, the Norman witnesses, Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, and many others; the Paris edition of 1495 joins them, reading, “through a silent storm of pride.” In the remaining witnesses, with *per* omitted, the text reads, “it generates a silent storm of pride.”]

Thus it happens that the mind does not readily reveal outwardly that it rejoices in human approval, yet inwardly it feels the force of corruption keenly.

There are some whom praise inflates so much that it draws them into words of pride. Others, as we said, are ashamed to reveal that they are being lifted up. They are nevertheless exalted when they hear their praises, but they do not go so far as to utter words of pride, nor do they show that they rejoice in such things.

Blessed Job, therefore, because he knew that he had not been arrogant not only in words but even in silent thought, after saying, “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly,” immediately added:

## CHAPTER VIII

**Verse 27.—“And my heart rejoiced in secret.”**

[Col. 0223D] **18. It is forbidden to rejoice even secretly over one’s own praises.**—What is conveyed to us by this testimony except that great fear and vigilance are necessary lest our mind ever rejoice, even silently, over its own praises?

For whoever regards the greatness of his reputation as though it were the brightness of the moon, and secretly creates joy for himself in the hidden place of his mind, has preferred himself to whom other than the author from whom he received the gift of acting well, while nevertheless becoming cheerful over the praise of his own grace?

By despising the honor of the Creator, he is shown to love himself more, since he rejoices in his own praises.

Sometimes, however, holy men also rejoice over a good reputation; but when they consider that through it those who hear of them may progress toward better things, they no longer rejoice over their own reputation but over the benefit of their neighbors. For it is one thing to seek approval, and another to rejoice in another’s progress.

In this matter it is necessary that, when a praiseworthy reputation does not benefit those who hear of it, it should not lift up our mind but burden it.

When we are praised by the testimony of human speech, we are secretly tested as to what we think about ourselves.

[Note: Turonensis reads, “by a hidden dispensation.” In Gemeticensis, read “we test” (*requirimus*) in place of “we are tested” (*requirimur*).]

For a proud mind rejoices even when false good things are said about it, because it considers not how it lives before God but how it may become known among human beings. It despises the judgment of almighty God concerning itself, seeks only the judgment of people, and is lifted up amid praises it has heard. It rejoices as though it had received the prize of its work, although this was the only thing it had sought.

By contrast, if the heart is truly humble, it either does not recognize the good things it hears said about itself and fears that they are false, or, if it knows that those good things truly belong to it, it fears precisely because it considers them to have been made known to people. It is greatly afraid that the hope of a future reward may be exchanged for the payment of passing approval.

## 19. The saints are tormented by their own praises

From this it follows that the minds of the elect are tormented by the great fire of their praises and are refined by the sorrow of reflection from every rust of their sluggishness. For, with cautious consideration, a person trembles lest either he find God’s judgment greater than the things for which he is praised and which are not truly present, or, because the things for which he is praised are present, he lose the fitting reward for them. Hence it often happens that, just as an unjust person is polluted by his praise, so a just man is purified when he hears his praise. For when he recognizes that the good things he has done are proclaimed by others, he fears the subtle examination of the final judgment, as has been said; and, trembling, he returns to his conscience and corrects whatever reprehensible thing is found there. For when he fears that his good deeds have become known, dreading the subtlety of the examination to come, he cuts away whatever hidden evils there are in him. He is afraid that he may not appear to God to be at least what he is thought to be by human beings; nor is he content that he should remain in the condition in which he has been able to become known. For he already considers that he has received a recompense for his good deeds unless he adds to them other deeds unknown to human beings. Hence Solomon rightly says: “As silver is tested in the crucible and gold in the furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of one who praises” (Prov. 27:21).

Silver or gold, if it is base, is consumed by fire; but if it is genuine, it is revealed by fire. So also it is with the disposition of the person who acts: what sort of person he is is shown in the thing for which he is praised. For if he exalts himself at hearing his praises, what else was he than base gold or silver—the furnace of the tongue has consumed him? But if, hearing his praises, he returns to consideration of the heavenly judgment and fears that he may be burdened before the hidden Judge, then, as though through the fire of purification, he grows toward the greatness of brightness; and from the very source where he endures the blaze of trembling, he shines more brightly.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Laud., two Sangerm. manuscripts, and Val. Cl. read “the hidden Judge”; as we have already observed more than once.]

Blessed Job, therefore, because he did not in any way put himself forward on account of his actions, says confidently: “If I looked upon the sun when it shone.” But because this praiseworthy reputation did not turn him away from the contemplation of the inner Judge, he adds: “And the moon proceeding in brightness.”

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Val. Cl. reads “from the contemplation of the inner Judge.” Vindoc. reads: “because this praiseworthy reputation [did not turn him away] from the contemplation of the inner hearing.”] And because he did not allow his mind to be bound by the favor of his reputation, not even in silent thought, he immediately adds: “And if my heart rejoiced in secret.” [Vet. X.]

And because an unreflective mind, when it does not resist passing favor, is often dragged to the point that it praises what it itself does, the condition stated above is appropriately followed by:

## CHAPTER IX

**Ibid.—“And I kissed my hand with my mouth.”**

### 20. They attribute their good works to God, not to themselves. Preventing grace

By the hand, action is signified; by the mouth, speech—as Solomon says: “The lazy person hides his hand beneath his armpit and is weary if he brings it to his mouth” (Prov. 19:24).

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Laud., Norm., the two Sangerman manuscripts, and many others read “beneath his armpit,” a reading found in the older editions.] For the lazy person it is labor to bring his hand to his mouth, because every idle preacher is unwilling to do what he says. To bring one’s hand to one’s mouth is to make one’s action agree with one’s speech. Therefore he kisses his hand with his mouth who praises what he does and, by the testimony of his own speech, attributes the virtue of the work to himself.

But in this matter, whom does he despise except the one who grants the very gifts of action? Hence the eminent preacher rightly says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

But holy men know that, after the fall of our first parent, they were born from a corruptible stock and were changed toward better desires or works not by their own virtue but by prevenient heavenly grace. Whatever evil they recognize to be in themselves, they understand as the due of mortal descent; whatever good they discern in themselves, they recognize as the gift of immortal grace. Thus they become debtors to the one who, by going before them, gave them the good will that they did not possess, and who, by following after them, granted them the ability to do the good they desire.

Hence John rightly says: “They worshiped the one who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne of the Lord” (Rev. 4:10). To cast their crowns before the throne of the Lord is not to attribute the victories of their struggles to themselves but to their author, so that they refer the glory of praise to the one from whom they know they received the strength for the struggle.

Blessed Job, therefore, because he recounts the good things he has done in such a way that he does not attribute them to his own action but returns to the praise of their author, denies that he kissed his hand with his mouth. It is as though he plainly said: “I do not present my works as my own, for whoever attributes to himself what he does is convicted of denying the grace of its author.”

Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER X

**Verse 28.—“Which is a very great iniquity and a denial against the most high God.”**

### 21. Whoever presumes on his own strength denies God

For it is clear that he denies the one whose grace he has despised and to whom he arrogates the strength for a good work. This is rightly also called “a very great iniquity,” because every sin that arises from weakness does not wholly destroy hope, since it seeks pardon from the heavenly Judge. But presumption in one’s own virtue is all the more serious in its desperation the farther it is from humility. When a person attributes the strength of his work to himself and does not return to the help of its author, the result is that the sinner perishes more grievously because he is unaware even of the fact that he is a sinner.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XI [Rec. VI]

**Verse 29.—“If I rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me and exulted because evil had overtaken him.”**

### 22. Only love makes us disciples of God. The proofs and signs of love

Only the keeping of love proves that we are disciples of almighty God. Hence Truth itself says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

This love, if it truly fills our heart, is usually shown in two ways: namely, if we love our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake. But we should know that love of an enemy is truly maintained when we are neither saddened by his advancement nor rejoice at his downfall. For often the mind deceives itself under the appearance of love toward an enemy and thinks that it loves him if it does not actively oppose his life. But the force of love is secretly and truly tested either by the enemy’s advancement or by his fall.

[Note: [Col. 0226D] The two Sangerman manuscripts and the Norman manuscripts regularly read *provectus*, *provectu*, and related forms where the printed editions read *profectus*, *profectu*, even where the opposition to *defectus* seemed to favor *profectus*: “to have changed the manner of his state in decline or advancement.” Below likewise: “neither his decline nor his advancement makes [the mind] subject.”]

In this matter, the human mind does not fully know itself unless it finds that the person whom it believes to be its adversary has changed the condition of his life either for the worse or for the better. For if it is saddened by his prosperity and rejoices at the misfortune of the one who hates it, it is clear that it does not love the person whom it does not wish to become better; and, while he stands, it persecutes him in its desire—the very person whose fall it celebrates.

[Col. 0226D] [Vet. XI] [709]

### 23. How can we rejoice at an enemy’s downfall or grieve at his glory without violating love? What must be guarded against in this matter

But in this connection we should know that it often happens that, without losing love, we are made glad by the downfall of an enemy and, again, are saddened by his glory without any fault of envy: when we believe that, as he falls, certain people are rightly raised up, and when we fear that, as he advances, many are unjustly oppressed.

In this matter our mind is neither raised up by his downfall nor made subject to his advancement if our right thought attends not to what is in him but to what is being done concerning him for the benefit or harm of others.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] The word *erigit*—“raises up”—is omitted in the Norman manuscripts. They read as expressed in the preceding note, and with excellent sense: the holy Teacher means that our mind is at times subject to no guilt or servitude if, when an enemy declines or advances, we rejoice or grieve. Older editions read *afficit*—“affects”—instead of *addicit*. We have already discussed what *addicit* and *addicere* mean in Gregory and other authors; see Book II, chapter 9, number 15. See also Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 74, and Ennodius, *Dicta* 22.]

Yet, to preserve these dispositions, the examination of the most subtle discernment is greatly necessary, lest, while we carry out our hatred, we be deceived under the appearance of another’s advantage.

For if one ought never to rejoice at the death of an enemy, the Psalmist would not say: “The just person will rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked” (Ps. 57:11). But enduring an impious person is one thing, and enduring an enemy another. For there are many enemies who are not impious, and there are some impious people who do not appear to be our particular enemies.

The human mind, however, considers everyone whom it endures as an enemy to be impious and wicked as well, because spiteful hostility magnifies his faults before its own thoughts. However burdened another person may be by whatever crimes, he is considered less wicked if he is not perceived as an adversary.

In this matter we must distinguish between the harm our enemy does to us and the harm he does to himself and to others. For if he is good to others, perhaps he cannot be bad to us without some fault of our own; and we should not at all rejoice at the downfall of one whose adversity we alone have certainly endured.

But when our enemy and the enemy of many is destroyed, the mind must rejoice more at the deliverance of those close to us than at the death of the enemy.

### 24. We should grieve over the misery of the one who perishes and rejoice in the justice of the Judge

For when an adversary perishes, we ought carefully to weigh what we owe to the sinner’s downfall and what we owe to the justice of the one who strikes. When almighty God strikes a perverse person, we must both grieve over the misery of the one who perishes and rejoice in the justice of the Judge, so that the punishment of our neighbor who dies may be a cause of mourning for us, while the equity displayed by God in judging may again become a cause of joy. Thus we will neither be adversaries to the person who perishes nor be found ungrateful to the God who judges.

Blessed Job, therefore, because he completely trampled down every hatred in adversity, says: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me and exulted because evil had overtaken him.” For, loving his enemy, he grieved over his falling adversary; and in his enemy’s misfortunes he himself grew toward the good, so that he might grow in kindness from the very circumstance in which the evils he deserved had overtaken the other.

Since, however, many people often strike those whom they consider their adversaries with curses because they cannot strike them by force—for it plainly appears what evils they would do if they could, when they do not cease to invoke those evils which they are unable to inflict—blessed Job, showing that he was free even from the guilt of cursing, continued:

## CHAPTER XII

**Verse 30.—“For I did not give my throat to sin, to seek the death of his soul by cursing.”**

### 25. We must abstain from curses

He would sin if he wished God to do what he himself either could not do at all or, if he could, ought not to do. For those who attack an enemy with curses—what else do they wish God to do to him except what they themselves are either unable or ashamed to do? They wish death upon their adversary, which, even if they can inflict it, they fear to do, lest they be held guilty of murder or appear wicked even while they are wicked.

What, then, is it to say to God, “Kill the one I hate,” except to cry out to him in explicit words: “Do to my adversary what it is not fitting for me, a sinner, to do to him”?

In these words we should carefully consider where this man had read: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:27, 35); where he had read: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14); and again: “Not repaying evil for evil or abuse for abuse” (1 Pet. 3:9). Yet he observed the commandments of heavenly grace without hearing them outwardly, because the inspiration of the Holy Spirit was writing them in his mind.

Still, it would have been too little for him to love those who were outside unless he also endured as adversaries those living within and conversing with him daily—his own household and intimates. Hence he adds:

## CHAPTER XIII [Rec. VII]

**Verse 31.—“If the men of my tent did not say: ‘Who will give us some of his flesh, that we may be filled?’”**

### 26. We must patiently endure those of our household and our intimates who oppose us. The sacrifice of the altar. Adversity must be endured outwardly with strength and inwardly with mercy

This sentence can also be understood mystically as spoken by the voice of the Redeemer. The men of his tent desired to be filled with his flesh—whether the persecuting Jews or the believing Gentiles. For the former plotted to destroy his body, as though by consuming it; the latter desire to satisfy their hungry minds with his flesh through the daily sacrifice of immolation.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] All our manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “through the sacrifice of daily immolation.”]

But now, following only the force of the historical sense, let us consider with what great strength the mind of the holy man, vigilant both outwardly and inwardly, bears its share in all things.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] The recent Paris and Basel editions and others read *paratur*—“is prepared”; this reading must be rejected on the authority of the two Sangerman manuscripts, Tours, Vindoc., all the Norman manuscripts, Laud., Val. Cl., and others, which read *partitur*. Here *partitur* is passive, for the active is *partio*, whose passive is *partior*. The edition of Bartholomew reads *patitur*—“endures.”] If he had ever yielded to those acting unjustly, either through silence or by failing to oppose them with righteousness, he would certainly not have had adversaries. But because he held to the ways of life, he found people desiring his death. He endured adversaries who were openly outside and those who were hidden within.

It is a lesser virtue in the struggle to see outside oneself someone whose evil one can overcome while having nothing within to endure. But the praise of perfect greatness is to endure adversity outwardly with strength and inwardly with mercy.

For there are some things that cannot be corrected even in the interaction of one’s own household without fault on the part of the one correcting. Therefore, when such things either stain the one who corrects or burden the one who does not engage in them at all, they must be concealed and endured with great skill in teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] In recent editions the opposite meaning is given, “or in every way,” but the old editions and the manuscripts, both English and our own, oppose that reading.]

We more quickly release from our heart what is inflicted against us when we recognize our own errors toward our neighbors. Hence Solomon also rightly says: “Do not apply your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you. For your conscience knows that you yourself have often cursed others” (Eccl. 7:22–23).

For when we consider what sort of people we have been toward others, we are less distressed that others are such toward us, because another person’s injustice exacts from us what our conscience justly accuses in itself.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIV [Rec. VIII]

**Verse 32.—“The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler.”**

### 27. Mercy in sparing should be followed by mercy in giving

Because, as Paul testifies, love is described as patient and kind (1 Cor. 13:4), through patience it bears the evils of others with equanimity, and through kindness it mercifully supplies its own good things. Hence blessed Job both patiently endured members of his household who cursed him and kindly welcomed travelers and strangers: to the former he offered examples of conduct, while to the latter he supplied outward assistance; toward the former he was not quick to anger through gentleness, and toward the latter he was ready to help through mercy.

For the holy man, contemplating the Redeemer of the human race through the spirit of prophecy, also observed in his conduct the precepts he gives us, saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37).

[Note: [Col. 0229D] In the same printed editions: “For giving pertains to things.” We add “our own,” following almost all our manuscripts and the older printed editions.]

Our giving pertains to the things we possess outwardly; forgiving, however, pertains to releasing the pain that we have inwardly contracted from another’s fault. But we should know that one who forgives and does not give, although he has not acted fully, has nevertheless retained the better part of mercy. But one who gives and does not forgive performs no mercy at all, because almighty God does not receive from the hand a gift that is offered by a heart bound in malice.

### 28. The conditions that make almsgiving meritorious

The mind of the person who offers alms must first be cleansed, because everything that is given to God is assessed according to the mind of the giver. Therefore every stain of malice must be wiped from our inner person by a change of thought, because an offering does not know how to appease the Judge unless the purity of the one offering makes it pleasing.

Hence it is written: “God looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look” (Gen. 4:4–5). For sacred Scripture does not say, “He looked upon Abel’s offerings, but he did not look upon Cain’s offerings”; rather, it first says that he looked upon Abel and then adds, “and upon his offerings.” Again it says that he did not look upon Cain and then adds, “nor upon his offerings.”

What is given is received from the heart of the giver. Therefore the offerings pleased not Abel because of the gifts, but the gifts pleased because of Abel. For the Lord is read to have looked first upon the one who gave and then upon what he gave.

Hence, when blessed Job was about to tell us of his generosity in hospitality, he first set forth his patience and kindness toward adversaries: that he did not rejoice at the downfall of his enemy, that he did not attack his persecutors with words of cursing, that he patiently endured those raging inwardly; and only then did he set forth his generosity in hospitality.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Laud., Corb. Germ., Norm., and several others read: “that he did not rejoice at the enemy’s downfall.” The German manuscript, in a second hand, reads: “that he did not rejoice in the downfall.”]

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Most copies read *narrationis suae*—“of his account”—perhaps contrary to the rules of the grammarians. Yet it is clear that Gregory did not scrupulously observe such rules. The two Sangerman manuscripts have no pronoun added.]

Thus, when the order of his account has been heard, we learn that outward gifts are made worthy by the inward purity of the heart, so that the interweaving of his virtues may teach the reader what sort of person he ought to be when he supplies outward goods to others.

### 29. Pride must be avoided in good works

But who would not think himself holy amid such heights of virtue? Who would not, in some way, be tempted by so many merits, so that, if at any time he sinned as a human being, he would be unwilling for his sin to become known to others, would consider it a small matter if he sinned in minor things, and would prefer to conceal his fault in silence rather than disclose it by a spoken confession?

For it often happens that a mind lifted up by virtues, when it learns that many good things are being spread about it in the estimation of its neighbors, does not wish anything reprehensible that it does to be recognized.

The mind endures these shadows of error because swelling pride weighs down the eye of the heart. Hence blessed Job, amid so many outstanding deeds of virtue, who was so exalted in action that he demonstrated how humble he was in mind, immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XV [Vet. XIII, Rec. IX]

**Verse 33.—“If, like a human being, I hid my sin and concealed my iniquity in my bosom.”**

### 30. Confessing one’s fault is an evidence of humility; excusing it is an evidence of pride. By excusing our sins, we make them more serious

These are the marks of true humility: for each person to recognize his iniquity and to disclose what he has recognized by an audible confession. In contrast, it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin while concealing it, and to hide what has been committed by denying it, and to multiply what has been exposed by defending it.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Here the manuscripts remarkably disagree. Germ., Tours, and Corb. Germ. in the first hand read *et libendo peccatum*—“and to commit sin at pleasure”; this is also found in all the Norman manuscripts save one from Évreux, which reads *et ad libitum peccatum committere*. Laud., Corb. Germ. in the second hand, and Val. Cl. read *et labendo peccatum*—“and to commit sin by slipping/falling”; this reading is followed by the older editions of Bartholomew, Paris, and Basel. Vindoc. reads *et blande peccatum committere*—“and to commit sin smoothly/softly.”]

From the fall of the first human being we derive these increases of wickedness, because from that fall we drew the very root of guilt. For when he had touched the forbidden tree, he hid himself from the face of the Lord among the trees of paradise. In this hiding—since he could not escape God’s notice—the effect of concealment is not described, but his disposition is indicated.

When the Lord accused him of having touched the forbidden tree, he immediately replied: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). The woman, when questioned, likewise replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid., 13).

They had been questioned so that, by confessing, they might erase the sin they had committed by transgression. Hence that serpent, the persuader who was not to be recalled to forgiveness, was not questioned about his guilt.

The man was therefore asked where he was, so that he might look upon the guilt he had perpetrated and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the face of his Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Val. Cl. reads “had departed.”]

But each of them chose the support of a defense rather than of a confession. When the man sought to excuse the sin through the woman and the woman through the serpent, they increased the guilt they had tried to defend: Adam obliquely implicated the Lord, since he had made the woman; and Eve referred the guilt to the Lord, who had placed the serpent in paradise.

For when they had heard from the mouth of the deceiving devil, “You will be like gods” (ibid., 5), and could not become like God in divinity, they attempted, as an addition to their error, to make God like themselves in guilt.

Thus, while they sought to defend their offense, they made their guilt more atrocious when examined than it had been when committed.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Gussanville reads *notati sunt*—“they were marked,” a reading found in none of the manuscripts or old editions and otherwise contrary to the sense. Yet it is not a typographical error, for the true reading, *conati sunt*—“they attempted,” appears rejected into the margin at the same place.]

### 31. Many imitate Adam, thinking to hide sin with the leaves of trees. The sinner emerges from the tomb through confession

Hence even now the branches of the human race draw bitterness from this same root, so that, when someone is accused of his fault, he hides himself beneath words of defense as beneath certain leaves of trees and flees with his face from the Creator into the shadowy recesses of his excuses, because he does not wish what he has done to be known.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Val. Cl. reads “beneath the word of defenses, as beneath a certain leaf of trees.” Most Norman manuscripts read “beneath words of defenses, as beneath certain leaves of trees.”]

In this concealment he hides not himself from the Lord but the Lord from himself. He acts so that he may not see the one who sees everything, not so that he himself may not be seen.

By contrast, for every sinner the beginning of illumination is the humility of confession, because one who is not ashamed to confess the evil he has done has ceased to spare himself; and one who could have been accused by defending himself defends himself most quickly by accusing himself.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] The same manuscripts read: “to accuse … by accusing himself he most swiftly defends himself.”]

Hence, when Lazarus was dead and weighed down by a great mass, it is not said, “Come back to life,” but, “Come out” (John 11:43). In this resurrection, which took place in his body, it is signified how we are raised in the heart: when the dead man is told, “Come out,” the human being who is dead in his sin and already buried beneath the weight of evil habit—lying hidden within his conscience because of wickedness—may come out from himself through confession.

“Come out” is said to the dead man so that he may be summoned from excusing and concealing his sin to accusing himself with his own mouth. Hence the prophet David, coming back to life from the death of so great a crime, came out, as it were, at the Lord’s voice when, rebuked by Nathan, he accused himself of what he had done (2 Sam. 12:13).

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Except for Bartholomew, the editions read “from the burden of so great a crime”; the manuscripts oblige us to reject that reading.]

### 32. The guilt of concealing sin has grown exceedingly great

Since, therefore, this fault of concealment has grown exceedingly great in the human race, blessed Job rightly inserted “like a human being” when he said, “If I hid my sin.” For he sees that what derives from the imitation of our former parent is characteristic of humanity.

He appropriately adds: “And I concealed my iniquity in my bosom.”

[Vet. XIV, Rec. X.]

Sacred Scripture often uses “bosom” for “mind,” as the Psalmist says concerning our persecutors, who are related to us by nature but separated from us by their way of life: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom” (Ps. 78:12). It is as though he plainly said: “Let them receive in their mind what they inflict while raging against our bodies, so that, while they punish us outwardly in part, they themselves may be perfectly punished inwardly.”

Since, therefore, the bosom signifies the secret place of the mind, to conceal iniquity in one’s bosom is to hide it in the recesses of one’s conscience and not disclose it through confession, but veil it through defense.

In contrast, James says: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Solomon also says: “Whoever conceals his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13).

### 33. Confession of sin without humility is feigned. The marks of sincere confession

But in this matter we should know that people often confess their faults and yet are not humble. We know many who, when no one accuses them, confess that they are sinners; but when they have perhaps been corrected concerning their fault, they seek the protection of a defense so that they may not appear to be sinners.

If, when they voluntarily say this, they recognized in truthful humility that they are sinners, then, when accused by others, they would not deny that they are what they had confessed themselves to be.

In this matter, the marks of true confession are present if, when someone calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same thing about him. For since it is written, “The just person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. 18:17), a person who confesses himself a sinner when no one accuses him desires to appear not a sinner but just; yet the truth of his confession is proved when another reproves the evil we have done.

If we defend ourselves arrogantly, it is clear that we were hypocritically calling ourselves sinners. Therefore we must take the greatest care both to confess voluntarily the evils we have done and not to deny them when others accuse us of them.

[Col. 0233A] For it is a vice of pride that what someone deigns to confess about himself, as though voluntarily, he disdains to have said about him by others.

### 34. Job’s humility in confessing sin. It is often a more serious struggle to confess sins than to avoid them

Blessed Job therefore showed how humble he was: he knew that he lived even among adversaries, yet he was not afraid to disclose his faults in a spoken confession.

But we should note that above he speaks of his virtues, while below he confesses sin. By this he clearly demonstrates how true his statements about his good deeds were, since he did not remain silent about his evils. Now he indicates his virtues, now his fault; thus he shows both that he committed sin and that he did not keep silent about it.

From this it most certainly appears how pure he was in the eyes of almighty God: he both avoided evil so as not to commit it and did not hide from human beings what he happened to commit. Thus the glory of righteousness belonged to him for turning away from sin, and the safeguard of righteousness for exposing what he could not turn away from.

Let this man appear great to anyone in his virtues; to me, certainly, he appears exalted even in his sins. Let those who wish marvel at his continence of chastity; let them marvel at the integrity of his justice; let them marvel at the depths of his compassion. I admire in him no less his most humble confession of sins than all those exalted deeds of virtue.

For I know that, because of the shamefulness of weakness, it is often a more serious struggle to disclose sins that have been committed than to avoid sins that have not been committed; and although each evil may be avoided with greater strength, it is nevertheless disclosed with greater humility.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] The same manuscripts read: “for each evil.”]

Blessed Job, therefore, supported by so many great works, was not ashamed to confess his fault and showed how humble he was in his virtues.

But because secure authority always arises from true humility—so that a person fears nothing outwardly to the extent that his mind does not pant after the heights of worldly things through a desire for exaltation—after his explicit confession of sin it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XVI

**Verse 34.—“If I feared the great multitude and the contempt of relatives terrified me; and I did not remain silent, nor did I go out through the door.”**

### 35. The remarkable security of a heart free from desire for earthly things. Yet this does not exempt it from the discipline of vigilance

Great is the security of a heart that possesses no worldly desire. For if the heart longs to attain earthly things, it can in no way be secure and tranquil: it either desires what it does not possess in order to possess it, or fears, once it has acquired it, that it may lose it. While it hopes for prosperity amid adversity, it fears adversity amid prosperity; it is rolled about as though by certain waves, and is tossed about in various ways by the changing instability of alternating circumstances.

But if the mind is once firmly established in the pursuit of its heavenly homeland, it is less troubled by the disturbance of temporal things. It withdraws its single purpose from all outward movements as into a most secret retreat; and, clinging there to the unchanging one and transcending all changeable things, it is already, in the very tranquility of its rest, in the world and yet beyond the world.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] This is the reading of Norm., the two Sangerman manuscripts, Laud., Val. Cl., and others; it is followed by the edition of Bartholomew of 1494 and the Paris edition of 1495. In the Basel edition of 1514 and those that follow, we read “clinging immutably.” This reading of the editors seems doubtful to me: for even the holiest people who cling to the unchanging God cannot be said in this life to cling immutably to God. See above, Book V, numbers 57, 58, and 60, and Book VIII, numbers 49 and 50.]

It certainly rises above all that is lowly through its orientation toward the heights, and it feels itself superior, by a kind of freedom, to all the things it does not desire. It does not endure inwardly the storms of temporal affairs that it observes outwardly, because all earthly things that, when desired, could oppress the mind lie beneath it, despised.

Hence the prophet rightly says: “Set up a watchtower for yourself” (Jer. 31:21), so that, while each person watches the things above, he may rise above the lowest things. Habakkuk also says: “I will stand upon my watch” (Hab. 2:1).

For a person stands upon his watch when, through the diligence of discipline, he does not succumb to earthly desires but rises above them, so that, while he continually seeks the eternity that stands forever, everything that passes may be beneath him.

### 36. Because he does not exclude the infirmities and disturbances of the flesh. The saints, though rendered undisturbed by God’s gift, remain subject to disturbances through their own weakness

Yet although a holy man may advance in however great a virtue, as long as he is placed in this life the infirmity of the flesh still presses upon him outwardly, as it is written: “Although man walks in the image of God, yet he is troubled in vain” (Psalm 38:7). It often happens, therefore, that he is disturbed outwardly while remaining inwardly undisturbed, and that whatever can be troubled in vain proceeds from the infirmity of the flesh, whereas his walking in the image of God proceeds from the virtue of the mind—so that he is strengthened within by divine assistance and yet is still burdened outwardly by human weakness.

Hence Habakkuk aptly expresses one statement that serves both purposes. [Note: Vindoc. reads “the following” (sequentem).] For he says: “And trembling entered into my bones, and beneath me my strength was troubled” (Habakkuk 3:16). It is as though he were saying: “The strength in which, having been caught up above [Note: Anglic. reads ‘having been caught’ (captus).], I remain undisturbed is not my strength [Note: The editions read ‘but it is of my weakness.’ Our reading is that of the Anglic., Norm., Laud., Val. Cl., and two Sangerm. manuscripts.]; but the strength in which I am troubled below is my strength.” Thus he is undisturbed above himself and capable of disturbance beneath himself: above himself, because he had ascended insofar as he was carried away to the heights; beneath himself, because he was still beneath himself insofar as he continued to bear remnants of himself in the depths.

He is undisturbed above himself because he had already passed into the contemplation of God; he is capable of disturbance beneath himself because beneath himself he remained a weak human being.

In harmony with this statement, the prophet David says: “I said in the excess of my mind: Every man is a liar” (Psalm 115:2). One might answer him: “If every man is a liar, then you are one too, and the statement you have uttered as a liar will already be false. But if you yourself are not a liar, the statement will no longer be true, since, while you are truthful, not every man is recognized as a liar.” Yet we must note what precedes: “I said in the excess of my mind.” Through the excess of his mind, then, he passed even beyond himself when he pronounced judgment concerning the condition of humanity. It is as though he plainly said: “I uttered a true statement about the falsity of all human beings from the place where I myself was above humanity.” Yet he too is a liar insofar as he is human, but is altogether not a liar insofar as, through the excess of his mind, he is above humanity.

### 37. These things do not hinder inward peace and contemplation

Thus all the perfect, although they still endure something turbulent because of the infirmity of the flesh, nevertheless already enjoy inwardly, in the most tranquil seclusion, the repose of contemplation, so that whatever happens outwardly does not disturb them inwardly in any respect.

Therefore blessed Job, showing the security of a holy mind, after he had proclaimed so many virtues concerning himself, added the following, continuing what we quoted earlier. [Note: The edition reads “showing that security of mind is in him”; we read “the security of a holy mind,” as in Vindoc., Laudun., Val. Cl., and all the Norm. manuscripts, as well as two Sangerm. manuscripts.]

### [Older recension XVI, later recension XI.]

“If I was afraid at a very great multitude, and the contempt of my relatives terrified me; and I did not rather keep silent, nor go out of the door.”

It is as though he were saying more plainly: “When others were outwardly disturbed against me, I myself remained inwardly undisturbed within myself.” For what else should we understand the “door” in this passage to mean except the mouth? Through it we seem to go out when, by the words available to us, we disclose the secrets of our heart; and whatever we remain inwardly in our conscience, such we go forth outwardly through the tongue. [Note: Recent editions, abandoning this reading—which is found in the manuscripts and older editions—have “through the mouth.”]

### 38. The saints are silent in times of agitation; others behave differently. We must remain silent unless we can benefit others by speaking

There are some who are utterly afraid of being despised and, lest they perhaps be judged worthless, desire to appear wise. Such people are compelled to go out through the door, because, when struck by insults, they reveal by speaking how great they secretly consider themselves. When, overcome by impatience, they disclose things about themselves that had not been known, they go out, as it were, through the door of the mouth.

Hence blessed Job, about to say that he had not gone out through the door of his mouth, rightly first said: “I was silent.” For, plainly, if he had not known how to keep silent, he would have gone out from the house of his conscience, disturbed by impatience.

### [Later recension XII.]

For holy men, when tested by the temptation of agitation, utterly avoid displaying themselves; and when they cannot benefit their hearers, they willingly remain silent even while being despised, lest they glory in displaying their wisdom. When they say something prudently, they do not seek their own glory but the life of their hearers. When they see that they cannot gain the life of their hearers by speaking, they hide their knowledge by remaining silent. [Note: Thus Turon., Vindoc., Laud., all the Norm. manuscripts, and two Sangerm. manuscripts. The editions read “ad imitandum quippe viam” (“for indeed the way is to be imitated”).]

For, in order to imitate the Lord’s life, we run, as it were, toward a certain sign set before us. When the Lord saw that Herod was not seeking improvement but wished to marvel at signs or knowledge, he remained silent when questioned by him; and because he steadfastly remained silent, he was mocked by him and departed.

For it is written: “When Herod had seen Jesus, he rejoiced greatly” [Note: “Greatly” is absent in several copies.]—“for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him, and he hoped to see some sign performed by him” (Luke 23:8). It then continues: “He questioned him with many words, but he answered him nothing.” [Note: Others read “he replied to him.”]

The Lord’s silence is shown to have been despised when it immediately follows: “Herod, with his soldiers, despised him and mocked him.” [Note: Gemet. and two Sangerm. manuscripts read “but he despised him.”]

We who hear this deed ought to learn from it that whenever our hearers wish to know what belongs to us as though it were worthy of praise, but do not wish to change their own perverse ways, we should remain altogether silent. Otherwise, if we speak the word of God out of a desire for display, their fault—which already existed—will not cease to exist, and our fault—which did not exist—will come into being.

### [Older recension XVII.] 39. How it can be known whether hearers are making progress through the teaching of preachers. What it means to speak from God and before God

Someone may perhaps say: “How do we know with what disposition someone listens?” Yet there are many things that reveal the mind of the hearer, especially if our hearers always praise what they hear but never follow what they praise.

The excellent preacher had avoided this empty glory of speaking when he said: “For we are not like so many, adulterating the word of God; but from sincerity, as from God, before God, we speak in Christ.” To adulterate the word of God means either to think about it otherwise than it is, or to seek from it not spiritual fruits but adulterous offspring—human praise. To speak from sincerity means to seek nothing in one’s speech beyond what is appropriate.

He speaks from God who knows that he does not possess from himself what he says, but has received from God what he says. He speaks before God who, in everything he says, does not seek human favor but directs his attention to the presence of almighty God; he seeks not his own glory but the glory of the author.

But one who knows that he has received from God what he says and yet seeks his own glory by speaking speaks from God, but not before God. For when he preaches, he regards as absent the one whom he does not set before his heart.

Holy men, however, speak both from God and before God, because they know that they have from him what they say and consider him to be present as judge and hearer of their words. [Note: The editions read “as helper also”; the Anglic., Norm., Laud., and two Sangerm. manuscripts have the reading preferred here.] Hence, when they recognize that they are despised by those close to them and that their words are not benefiting the lives of their hearers, they conceal how great their virtue is, lest, if a word uselessly uttered should disclose the secret of their heart, it break forth into empty glory.

### 40. Neither pride nor impatience compelled Job to recount his virtues

Blessed Job, therefore, not desiring to become renowned among obstinate minds through the disclosure of his virtue, says: “If the contempt of my relatives terrified me, and I did not rather keep silent, nor go out of the door.”

He who was made steadfast through humility and in no way feared being despised was not overcome by impatience so that his tongue might cast him outward. It is rightly prefaced: “If I was afraid at a very great multitude,” so that the constancy of the man might be recognized: outwardly, the number of people in no way terrifies one whom inwardly the crowd of vices does not devastate.

In this life, whoever desires no prosperity undoubtedly fears no adversity.

### 41. What Job recounts about himself is to be understood of Christ

If we draw these words toward their mystical meaning, we quickly find in them the work of our Redeemer. He was not afraid of a very great multitude, for he struck his persecutors, who came with swords and clubs, with one reply alone, saying: “I am he” (John 18:6).

He was not terrified by the contempt of his relatives, for, freeing us from eternal punishments, he received blows upon his face with equanimity. He kept silent and did not go out through the door: while enduring the weakness of his humanity at the very hour of his Passion, he did not wish to exercise the power of his divinity. [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl. read “he did not wish to exercise it.”]

For it would have been as though the Mediator of God and humanity had gone out through the door if, while being held as a human being, he had wished to display the power of his majesty [Note: Gemet. reads “the majesty of his power.”] and, through the greatness of his divinity, pass beyond the weakness of the flesh he had assumed. In order that he might die as an openly manifested human being, God remained hidden: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

He therefore did not go out through the door: when questioned by Pilate, he remained silent; among the hands of his persecutors he offered his body to suffering, the body he had assumed for the elect, and he did not wish to demonstrate to those resisting him what he was.

Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: “They made me an abomination to themselves; I was handed over, and I did not go out” (Psalm 87:9). When he was despised because he appeared to be human, he would have gone out if he had wished to display his hidden majesty. But because he revealed his weakness, he concealed his power; in remaining unknown to his persecutors, he did not go out to them at all.

Yet he goes out to the elect, because he reveals to those who seek it the sweetness of his divinity. Hence it is said to him through the prophet: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Habakkuk 3:13).

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVII [Older recension XVIII, later recension XIII]

### Verse 35

“Who will grant me a helper, so that the Almighty may hear my desire?”

### 42. No one should rely on his own merits. A helper and Mediator—Christ—must be sought

After the holy man had recounted so many lofty deeds of his virtues, knowing that he could not reach the heights by his own merits, he seeks a helper. And whom does he contemplate, surely, except the only-begotten Son of God, who, by assuming human nature laboring in this mortality, helped it?

He helped humanity by becoming human, so that, because a way of returning to God was not open to a mere human being, the way of return might be made available through the human God. We, mortal and unjust, were far separated from the just and immortal one.

But between the immortal and just one and us, mortal and unjust, there appeared the Mediator between God and humanity, mortal and just: he possessed death with humanity and justice with God, so that, because through our lowliness we were far separated from the heights, he might in himself join the lowly to the exalted, and through him the way of return to God might be made for us, by which he united our lowliness to his heights.

Thus blessed Job, speaking as a figure of the whole Church, seeks the Mediator. When he had said, “Who will grant me a helper?” he fittingly added: “So that the Almighty may hear my desire.” For he knew that human prayers could not be heard for the rest of eternal deliverance except through their advocate.

Of him the apostle John says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

Of him the apostle Paul says: “Christ Jesus, who died for us—indeed, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34). [Note: Norm. reads “at the right hand of God.”]

For the only-begotten Son to intercede for humanity means that he presents himself as human before the coeternal Father; and to ask for humanity means that he has assumed that same nature in the exalted state of his divinity.

The Lord therefore intercedes for us not by speech but by mercy, because, by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the elect, he set it free. A helper is therefore sought so that the desire may be heard, because unless the intercession of the Mediator intervened for us, the voices of our prayers would undoubtedly be silent far from the ear of God.

### 43. God hears not words but the desires of the heart

It should also be noted that he does not say “may the Almighty hear my prayers,” but “may the Almighty hear my desire.” For true petition lies not in the voices of the mouth but in the thoughts of the heart.

Our words do not make the stronger voices before the most secret ears of God; our desires do. If we ask for eternal life with our mouth but do not desire it in our heart, then, though we cry out, we are silent. But if we desire it from the heart, then even when we are silent with our mouth, we cry out while remaining silent.

Hence the people in the wilderness resound with voices, while Moses is silent amid the clamor of words; yet, though silent, he is heard by the ear of divine mercy when it is said: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus 14:15).

Within desire, therefore, there is a hidden cry that does not reach human ears and yet fills the hearing of the Creator. Hence Anna, going to the Temple, was silent with her mouth, yet uttered so many voices of her desire (1 Samuel 1:13).

Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Enter into your room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6:6). [Note: “Your” is absent in several copies and appears redundant. Laud. reads “in secret.”]

One prays in a room with the door shut when, while the mouth is silent, one pours out the affection of the mind in the sight of divine mercy. A voice is heard in secret when one silently cries out through holy desires.

Hence it is rightly said through the Psalmist: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Psalm 19:17). [Note: Two Sangerm. manuscripts, Laud., Val. Cl., Norm., and the old Paris edition read “the desires.”]

But blessed Job reveals in the words that follow whom he seeks as his helper in having his desire heard, saying:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Older recension XIX]

### The same passage

“And let the one who judges write the book himself.”

### 44. Christ, who is legislator and judge, must be sought as helper. Ezekiel’s prophecy concerning him

Because the Law was transmitted to the still-fearing people through a servant, whereas the grace of the Gospel was bestowed upon those who love as sons through the Lord—and because, coming for our redemption, he established for us a new covenant, but will also come as judge when he examines us according to the command of that same covenant—it is unnecessary to make clear through exposition that the one who judges himself writes the book.

For Truth itself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). The author of judgment, then, will be the one who is now the creator of the book, so that then he may exact sternly what he now commands gently.

We see this daily in the case of teachers: they kindly impose the first elements of letters upon children, but later demand these from them harshly; what they give with gentleness, they require with blows. The commands of divine speech now sound gentle, but they will be experienced as harsh in their enforcement. The admonition of the one calling is gentle now, but then the justice of the judge will come with severity, since it is certain that not even the smallest command will pass without examination. [Note: Germ. and most Norm. manuscripts read “will pass without being examined”; Laud. and Corb. G. read “will pass in the examination.”]

Thus it is clear that the one who judges wrote the book himself. That this book is the New Testament, which the Redeemer of the human race himself would establish at the end, the prophet Ezekiel aptly announces, saying:

“Behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate, which faces toward the north, and each had the vessel of destruction in his hand. One man among them was clothed in linen, and he had a writer’s inkhorn at his loins” (Ezekiel 9:2).

What else is signified by the six men who come except the six ages of the human race? They come from the way of the upper gate because, from the creation of paradise—as from the entrance into the world—they unfold from the earlier generations. [Note: Norm. and Laud. read “who come from the way.”]

The gate faces toward the north because, plainly, if the mind of the human race, opened to vices, had not abandoned the warmth of charity and sought the torpor of the mind, it would not have emerged into this expanse of mortality.

Each one has the vessel of destruction in his hand because each generation, unfolding through its respective age, possessed before the Redeemer’s coming in its own actions the means by which it incurred the punishment of condemnation.

There is also one man in their midst clothed in linen, because our Redeemer, who was pleased to have parents according to the flesh even from a priestly tribe, is said to come clothed in linen. Or certainly, because linen arises from the earth, whereas wool arises from corruptible flesh, he came to us clothed in linen: he received the garment of his body from a virgin mother, not from the corruption of intercourse.

“And he had a writer’s inkhorn at his loins.” The loins are the body’s posterior region. Since the Lord himself, after dying for us, rising again, and ascending into heaven, then wrote the New Testament through the apostles, this man had the inkhorn at his loins. He who established the writing of the New Testament after he had departed carried the inkhorn, as it were, behind him. [Note: Vindoc. reads “the inkhorn, as it were, at his loins.”]

The one who says, “Let the one who judges write the book himself,” therefore sees this inkhorn clinging to the man clothed in linen.

But why, blessed Job, do you desire the book to be written by the one who is judge? The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIX [Older recension XX, later recension XIV]

### Verse 36

“That I may carry it on my shoulder and surround myself with it like a crown.”

### 45. Scripture must be carried on the shoulder through action, so that it may surround us like a crown through reward

To carry the book on the shoulder means to fulfill Holy Scripture by putting it into practice. We should note the order in which this is described: first it is carried on the shoulder, and afterward it surrounds one like a crown. For the commands of sacred speech, if they are now carried well in one’s works, afterward present us with the crown of victory in recompense. [Note: Germ. and Corb. Germ. (in the first hand), as well as even the older editions, read “to carry” (portare), an evident error; despite the opposition of the other manuscripts, it was propagated in all the more recent editions.]

But why does blessed Job ask that the book be written by the judge, when he could not reach the times of the New Testament? As has often already been said, he uses the voices of the elect and, in their figure, asks for what he foresaw would benefit them in every way. Through the Spirit he already held this book long ago; through the grace of inspiration he had received it, both to know it by living and to announce it by foreseeing.

Yet amid these things we must understand that, when we ponder the precepts of the same sacred speech and turn the mind away from love of corruptible life, we hurry toward inward things as though by certain steps of the heart. No one abandons the lowest things and suddenly becomes the highest. To obtain the merit of perfection, as the mind is daily led upward, one undoubtedly reaches it by certain steps resembling an ascent. Hence this too is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XX

### Verse 37

“I will proclaim it through each of my steps.”

### 46. There are various steps toward perfection. To advance toward God, we must decline from ourselves

The Psalmist speaks of these steps of merit: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83:8). Again, contemplating the holy Church, he says: “God is recognized in her steps, when he receives her” (Psalm 47:4). [Note: Turon. reads “having contemplated the holy Church, he says.”] For, as has been said, one does not suddenly reach the heights; the mind is led to the loftiness of virtues by gradual growth.

Hence the same prophet says again: “I have been exercised, and my spirit failed for a little while” (Psalm 76:4). What does he mean by “my spirit” except the spirit of the human being—that is, the spirit of pride? Since, through hidden grace, we advance toward the love of God by a measure tempered from above, the more the virtue of God’s Spirit grows in us daily, the more our own spirit diminishes.

Because this spirit of error is not suddenly cut off from us altogether, it is rightly said to have failed “for a little while.” We truly advance fully in God when we have utterly failed in ourselves.

These measures of growing virtues are called steps by the words of the holy man. Every elect person begins first from the tender weakness of his beginnings and afterward grows strong in what is robust and powerful.

Truth clearly demonstrates this in the Gospel, saying: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground, and sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow, while he does not know it” (Mark 4:26).

In announcing the growth of this seed, he adds: “For the earth produces fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” [Note: Others read “ears” (spicas), here and below.] He also adds its final development, saying: “And when the fruit has been produced, immediately he sends the sickle, because the harvest has come.” [Note: Val. Cl., most Norm. manuscripts, and Sangerm. manuscripts read “when the fruit has developed.”]

Behold: in the words of Truth, the growth of merits is distinguished according to the stages of crops. He says: “First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”

Was Peter not still a blade when, at the sudden breath of a single sentence from a servant girl, he was bent back? He was already green through devotion, but still tender through weakness. He was found to be full grain in the ear when he resisted the rulers who persecuted him, saying: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

He was found to be full grain in the ear when, in the threshing of persecution, he endured so many blows and yet was not diminished like chaff, but remained a whole grain. [Note: “In the ear” is absent in Utic. and several other manuscripts.] [Note: Val. Cl. reads “in torture.”]

For a little while, as it were, the moisture of inward grace overflows in each soul, so that the blade may grow into grain. Let no one, therefore, despair of grain when he still sees only a neighbor’s blade. The grains of crops that rise are strengthened by the leaves of the blades, which gently bend this way and that.

### [Older recension XXI.] 47. The various stages of progress expressed through Daniel

The prophet Daniel, while the Lord was speaking to him, aptly signified these increases of merit when he sought to disclose to us the position of his body. For he says:

“I heard the voice of his words, and, hearing, I lay terrified upon my face, and my face clung to the ground. And behold, a hand touched me and raised me upon my knees and upon the joints of my hands, and he said to me: ‘Daniel, man of desires, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand in your position; for now I have been sent to you.’ And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood trembling, and he said to me: ‘Do not fear’” (Daniel 10:9). [Note: “His” is absent in Utic., Becc., Prat., and Sangerm.]

He would not have expressed the position of his body with such care while hearing the words of the one speaking inwardly if he had known it to be devoid of mysteries. In Holy Scripture, not only what righteous men say is prophecy; often what they do is as well.

The holy man, therefore, full of inward mysteries, expresses the power of the voice even through the position of his body. By first lying prostrate on the ground, then raising himself upon the joints of his hands and upon his knees, and finally standing erect but trembling, he makes known in himself the whole order of our progress.

We hear the words of God while lying on the ground when, placed in sins and joined to earthly pollution, we learn spiritual precepts through the voice of the saints. [Note: Corb. Germ., Val. Cl., and most Norm. manuscripts read “when joined to earthly pollution.”] [Note: Turon. and Corb. Germ. read “to his precepts.”]

We are raised to these precepts as if upon our knees and upon the joints of our hands when, withdrawing from earthly contamination, we already lift up our minds from the lowest things. [Note: German., Corb. Germ., Regio, and others read “we lift up the belly.” The older printed editions also have this reading. We have preferred the alternative reading, “we lift up the mind,” found in the Anglic. and Norm. manuscripts.]

Just as one who lies terrified is wholly attached to the earth, so one who bends upon his knees and the joints of his hands is, as progress begins, already suspended from the earth to a great extent.

Finally, we stand upright but trembling when raised by the Lord’s voice, because, lifted perfectly above earthly desires, we fear God’s words more deeply the more fully we understand them.
