He still lies, as it were, on the ground who neglects to be raised to heavenly things because of earthly desires. He still rests upon his hands and knees, as though partially lifted up, who abandons certain contaminations but does not yet oppose certain earthly deeds. But he stands upright at the words of God who perfectly raises his mind to sublime things and refuses to be bent by impure desires.

### 48. We must proceed from fear to love and charity

He rightly indicates that he stood trembling, because the more one advances toward that inward examination of subtlety, the more one fears it. The divine voice aptly adds: “Do not fear.” For the more we recognize what we ought to fear, the more that which we are to love is poured into us by God through inward grace.

Thus our contempt gradually passes into fear, and fear passes into charity: because we resist God, who seeks us, through contempt; we flee through fear; and, eventually setting aside both contempt and fear, we are joined to him by love alone.

For a little while we even learn to fear him to whose love alone we cling. [Note: Corb. Germ. and Vindoc. read “we have learned even to fear, and we cling to him by the force of love alone.” Laud., Val. Cl., and Turon. likewise change the past “we have learned” to the present “we learn.” Norm. reads “when we have departed from fear, and cling to him,” etc.]

When, therefore, we set before ourselves certain steps of progress, we first place the foot of the mind at the lowest point through fear, and afterward raise it to the heights of love through charity, so that we may be restrained from what makes us swell with pride in order that we may fear, and may be lifted from what we already fear so that we may have confidence. [Note: Val. Cl. reads “so that from what one feels to be at rest one may also be restrained.”]

It is not difficult to grasp these steps of virtue when one passes from one to another. [Note: Norm., Vindoc., and Val. Cl. read “it is to weigh”; Corb. Germ. and Laud. read “it is to hang.”]

### 49. The stages of individual virtues are various. The growth of faith

The matter requires very subtle consideration when the mind attempts to weigh by what stages of progress it is raised within one and the same virtue.

To speak of the first elements of the virtues—faith and wisdom—each cannot be possessed perfectly unless we ascend to them by distinct and orderly means, as by certain steps. Faith itself, which trains us to grasp other good things perfectly, is often both wavering and firm in its beginnings; it is already held with the greatest certainty, yet one still trembles in uncertainty concerning confidence in it. A part of it is first received so that it may afterward be completed perfectly in us.

For if faith did not advance by a definite step in the mind of the believer, the father of the boy to be healed would not have said when questioned in the Gospel: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:23). He was still ascending toward the faith he had already received: at one and the same time he cried out that he already believed and that he still doubted because of unbelief.

Hence the disciples also say to our Redeemer: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5), so that what had already been received in its beginning might come to perfection through successive increases of its steps.

### [Older recension XXII.] 50. Wisdom, the teacher of good works, is bestowed through growth. Its various stages

Wisdom itself, which is accustomed to be the teacher of good works, is bestowed upon the longing mind through growth, so that one undoubtedly ascends to it by stages of great moderation.

The prophet Ezekiel aptly announces this in a figurative account. He speaks of the man whom he had seen on a high mountain, saying:

“He measured a thousand cubits, and led me through the water up to the ankles. Again he measured a thousand, and led me through the water up to the knees. And he measured a thousand, and led me through the water up to the loins. And he measured a thousand—a torrent—which I could not cross, because the deep waters of the torrent had swelled, and it could not be forded” (Ezekiel 47:3–4). [Note: Val. Cl. and Gemet. read “and I could not cross the torrent.”]

What else is signified by the number one thousand except the fullness of the gift bestowed?

The man who appeared measures a thousand cubits, and the prophet is led through the waters up to the ankles, because when our Redeemer grants those who have turned toward him the fullness of a good beginning, he pours into our first steps in action the gift of spiritual wisdom.

For the water reaching the ankles means that, through the wisdom we have received, we already hold the steps of the righteousness we desire. Again he measures a thousand, and the prophet is led through the water up to the knees, because when the fullness of good work is bestowed, our wisdom is increased to the point that it is no longer bent toward wicked deeds.

Hence Paul says: “Raise up the drooping hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Hebrews 12:12). The water reaches the knees when the wisdom we have received binds us perfectly to the uprightness of good work.

Again he measures a thousand, and the prophet is led through the water up to the loins, because the fullness of work grows in us when the wisdom we have received extinguishes, insofar as possible, every pleasure of the flesh. If the pleasure of the flesh were not in the loins, the Psalmist would not have said: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Psalm 25:2).

The water therefore reaches the loins when the sweetness of wisdom also destroys the incentives of the flesh, so that the fires of pleasure that could burn the mind grow cold. [Note: Val. Cl. reads “so that the fires of pleasure that used to oppress the manly mind may grow cold.”]

He then measures another thousand—the torrent that the prophet could not cross—of which he also says: “Because the deep waters of the torrent have swollen, and it cannot be forded.”

After the perfection of work has been received, one comes to contemplation. As the mind is led upward in contemplation, it sees in God, having been lifted up, that it cannot penetrate what it sees. It touches, as it were, the water of the torrent which it cannot cross: it sees through contemplation what delights it, yet it cannot fully contemplate even that which it delights to see.

The prophet therefore eventually reaches water that he does not cross, because, when we are finally led to the contemplation of wisdom, its very immensity—which lifts the human being up from itself—denies the human mind complete knowledge of it. Thus one loves it by touching it, yet cannot penetrate it by passing through it.

### 51. After these stages have been traversed, one reaches contemplation

Because blessed Job saw that these increases of virtue were distinctly bestowed upon human beings by a heavenly gift, he called them steps, since by them one ascends in order to reach the possession of heavenly things.

In making mention of the sacred books—that is, divine speech—he says: “I will proclaim it through each of my steps.” For the one who truly ascends to the teaching of God is the one who has broken through to obtain it by the steps of holy action.

He proclaims the book through each of his steps, as it were, who demonstrates that he has received its knowledge not merely through words but also through works. Hence he adds:

### Verse 37

“And I will offer it as to a prince.”

For everything we offer we hold in our hands. To offer the book to the prince who comes to judgment is therefore to hold the words of his precepts in action.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXI [Older recension XXIII, later recension XV]

### Verses 38–40

“If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it; if I have eaten its fruits without payment, and have afflicted the life of its farmers; let the thistle arise for me instead of wheat, and the thorn instead of barley.”

### 52. Concerning the injustice and errors of rulers: the less perfect complain but do not grieve; the perfect, however, are silent and mourn. The more perfect grieve over others’ losses in proportion as they grieve less over their own.

What does it mean to have the earth cry out, the furrows lament, and to eat one’s own produce after buying it? Who has ever needed to buy what is his own? Who has heard the earth crying out? Who has seen furrows lamenting? And since the furrows of the earth are always made from the earth, what does it mean that, in distinct wording, the earth is said to have cried out and its furrows to have lamented with it? Since the literal sequence offers no further explanation, the mystical meaning presents itself to us as though the doors had already been opened. It is as if it plainly cried out:

“Since you recognize that the literal meaning has failed, it surely remains for you to return to me without hesitation.”

For anyone who either governs a household by private right or presides over faithful communities for the common good—since he possesses the rights of government over those entrusted to him—what else does he hold than earth to be cultivated? For by divine dispensation each person is placed over others so that the mind of those subject to him may be made fruitful, like cultivated earth, by the seed of his preaching.

[Note: Corbie, Germanicus, Normannicus, Germanicus, and Laudianus: “the earth laid beneath.”]

But the earth cries out against its possessor when either a private household or the holy Church murmurs against the one who presides over it because of some just grievance.

[Note: The printed editions read “something unjust,” contrary to Saint Gregory’s meaning: the holy Doctor is speaking of just complaints against the injustice of superiors, as is plain from what follows. Our reading is supported by the Anglican, Normannic, Laudian, and Saint-Germain manuscripts.] To have the earth cry out is rationally to grieve over the ruler’s injustice. Accordingly, it is rightly added: “And with it its furrows lament.”

The earth, even when cultivated by no labor, generally produces some nourishment for human use; when ploughed, however, it yields crops in abundance. There are some who have been cut by neither the ploughshare of reading nor that of exhortation and nevertheless produce certain good things, however slight, from themselves, like earth not yet ploughed. Others, always intent on hearing and retaining holy preaching and meditation, are cut away from the former hardness of their minds, as by a ploughshare of the tongue, and receive the seeds of exhortation; through the furrows of voluntary affliction they return the harvest of good works.  
[Note: In Uticensis, *scissa* (“cut”) is read; this was also formerly read in Beccensis. *Scissa* may refer to the hardness of mind mentioned above.]

[Note: Vallicellianus reads “by the plough of action”; Laudianus, “by the plough of furrowing.”]

Often, however, those who preside do something unjust, so that the very people who ought to benefit their subjects harm them instead. When the inexperienced see this, they are stirred to murmur against the ruler, yet they do not grieve deeply for their neighbors out of compassion. But when those who have already been worn down by the plough of reading and cultivated for the harvest of good works see the innocent burdened even in small matters, they immediately turn, through compassion, to lamentation, because they mourn as their own the things that their neighbors suffer unjustly.

The perfect, since they are always moved by spiritual concerns, know how to groan over the bodily losses of others in proportion as they have learned not to grieve over their own.  
[Note: Vallicellianus: “Since they are never moved by bodily afflictions, they know all the more how to groan over others’ losses.” Laudianus: “Since they are not moved by bodily matters, they know all the more,” and so forth.]

Therefore, whenever one who presides exercises perverse conduct toward his subjects, the earth cries out against him and the furrows lament. The inexperienced indeed break out against his injustice in murmuring voices, but the perfect afflict themselves with tears because of his evil conduct. What the unskilled cry out and do not grieve over, those subject to them who lead a more approved life lament and keep silent.  
[Note: This passage is corrupted in Germanicus and in the recent editions, especially through the omission of the negative particle, which we have supplied from our manuscripts and from the Anglican manuscript. Without *non*, the antithesis and the rhetorical force disappear. In the old printed editions one reads *non deflent* (“do not lament”) instead of *non dolent* (“do not grieve”).]

Thus, when the earth cries out, for the furrows to lament means that, through the complaint by which the multitude of the faithful justly protests against its ruler, people of more fruitful life are brought to lamentation. The furrows, therefore, are both from the earth and yet distinguished from the name “earth,” because those in the holy Church who cultivate their minds through the labor of holy meditation are better than the other faithful in proportion as, having received the seeds, they return more fruitful works.

[Note: Another reading: “distinguished from the earth.”]

There are also some who, placed over holy communities, receive the support of life from the generosity of the Church but do not provide the ministry of exhortation owed to it.  
[Note: Laudianus: “the exercise” (instead of “the ministry”).]

Against such people the example of the holy man is rightly continued, when it is immediately added:

### CHAPTER XXII [Recension XVI]

**Verse 39.** “If I have eaten its produce without money.”

### 53. How greatly rulers sin when they silently consume ecclesiastical goods. What solicitude those who preside owe to their subjects.

To eat the produce of the earth without money is to receive provisions from the Church but not to offer the Church the price of preaching.

[Note: Laudianus: “the fruit of preaching.”] Concerning this preaching the author’s voice says: “You ought therefore to have put my money with the money-changers, and when I came I would certainly have received what was mine with interest” (Matthew 25:27).

Thus the person who eats the earth’s produce without money receives ecclesiastical benefits for the use of his body but does not provide the people with the ministry of exhortation. What shall we pastors say to this? We anticipate the coming of the strict Judge, we undertake the office of herald, yet we silently consume ecclesiastical provisions. We demand what is owed to our bodies, but we do not provide what we owe to the hearts of our subjects.

Behold, the holy man, bound by so many obligations in this world, remained free amid countless occupations for the study of preaching. He never ate the produce of the earth without money, because he returned to his subjects the word of good admonition, from whom he received the fruit of bodily service. This is what everyone who presides over a people owes to almighty God; this is what the one who presides over many owes; this is what the one who presides over fewer owes: he should demand the services owed by his subjects in such a way that he himself also attends carefully to what admonition he must always give.

For all of us who, under the administration of the Creator, are joined to one another in a vicarious ministry under one true Lord—what else are we but servants of one another? When the subordinate serves in obedience, it undoubtedly remains that the superior should serve through the word. When the subordinate obeys commands, the superior must offer care and compassion.

Thus it happens that, while we now diligently strive to serve one another through charity, one day we shall rule together with the true Lord in common rejoicing.  
[Old recension XXIV.]

There are, however, some who, while displaying the office of preaching, envy others the good they possess and therefore no longer truly possess it. To such people James rightly says: “But if you have bitter jealousy among yourselves and there are quarrels in your hearts, this is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic” (James 3:14).

Hence here too, when it has been said, “If I have eaten its produce without money,” it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXIII

**In the same passage.** “And I have afflicted the souls of its farmers.”

### 54. Let the ruler of a church not envy those who cooperate with him in preaching.

The farmers of this earth are those who, placed in a lesser position, cooperate in the grace of preaching for the instruction of the holy Church, with whatever zeal they can and with as much labor as they are able. Not to afflict these farmers of the earth means not to envy their labors, lest the ruler of the Church, while claiming the right of preaching for himself alone, oppose others who preach rightly, bitten by envy.

The devout mind of pastors seeks not its own glory but that of the author, and therefore wishes what it does to be aided by everyone. The faithful preacher hopes, if it could be achieved, that the mouths of all would proclaim the truth which he alone is not sufficient to speak. Thus, when Joshua wished to oppose the two men who had remained in the camp and were prophesying, Moses rightly said to him: “Are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his spirit!” (Numbers 11:29).

He wished all to prophesy who did not envy others the good that he himself possessed. Since blessed Job therefore brought forward all these matters conditionally, binding himself by a sentence of malediction if he had not done them, it follows:

### CHAPTER XXIV [Recension XVII]

**Verse 40.** “Let a thornbush grow for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley.”

### 55. For rulers who misuse their authority, a thornbush grows instead of wheat and a thorn instead of barley.

It is as though he plainly said: “If I have acted unjustly toward my subjects; if I demanded what was owed and did not myself provide what I owed; if I envied others the exercise of good works, then in judgment let evils that pierce be repaid to me instead of the good things that restore forever.”

A thornbush grows instead of wheat and a thorn instead of barley when, at the final recompense, where the reward of labor is sought, the pricking of pain is found. It should be noted that, just as barley differs from wheat although both provide nourishment, so a thornbush differs from a thorn although both prick: the thornbush is softer, whereas the thorn is always harder for pricking.

He therefore says: “Let a thornbush grow for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley.” It is as if he plainly said: “I know that I have done both great and small good things; but if this is not so, let small evils answer me for great goods, and greater evils for small goods.”

This may also be understood in another way. In wheat is figured spiritual work, which nourishes the mind; in barley, the administration of earthly affairs. In this administration we are often compelled to serve the weak and carnal, as though preparing their appropriate nourishment for animals; and the very use of our works, like barley, contains something mixed with straw.  
[Note: Laudianus: “as though preparing pleasant nourishment for the mind.”]

It often happens that the ruler who presides, while exercising injustice against his subjects, while refreshing no good people with any kindness, and—what is more serious—while afflicting out of envy all who work well, nevertheless sometimes does certain good things. It is as though he sowed wheat and, in administering earthly affairs, sometimes mixed them not out of avarice but for the benefit of carnal people, then expected the fruit of the same labor like a harvest of barley.  
[Note: Through the omission of the two little words *non* and *sed*, this passage had been distorted in earlier editions. The Anglican and our manuscripts, as well as the old Paris and Basel editions, indicated the error.]

Yet the subjects cannot rejoice in his minor good deeds because they are burdened by him in matters of greater importance. For the work which the injustice of another work has polluted does not please God, nor is the administration of earthly affairs believed to have been undertaken for the benefit of subjects when the ruler appears to be driven by avarice.

[Note: Normannicus and Laudianus: “because the work does not please when it is [the work] of another work.”] Consequently, even for the few good things they observe amid many evils, they return not praise but groans; and, while they recognize that what they see is not the work of a pure heart, they murmur in their weakness.

He therefore says: “If my earth cries out against me, and its furrows lament with it; if I have eaten its produce without money and afflicted the souls of its farmers; let a thornbush grow for me instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley.”

It is as if he plainly said: “If I have not carefully done the great things I owed, I shall receive from my subjects the pricks of murmuring, even because of the good I have done. If I have neglected to provide what gives nourishment, their tongue, rightly breaking out into complaint, shall prick me.”

### 56. Let rulers beware of providing evil examples, and subjects of rash judgments.

Here one must always weigh the matter with careful consideration, lest either those who preside provide their subjects with examples of evil conduct and destroy their lives with the sword of their own wickedness, or those who are subject to another’s rule dare too readily to judge the deeds of their rulers. By murmuring against those placed over them, they would then oppose not a human order but the divine order of the One who arranges all things.

To the rulers it is said: “My sheep fed upon what had been trampled by your feet, and they drank what your feet had disturbed” (Ezekiel 34:19). The sheep drink what has been disturbed by feet when subjects seek as an example for their way of life the things that their rulers have corrupted by evil conduct.

Conversely, those under them hear the rulers say: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exodus 16:8). For whoever murmurs against the authority placed over him clearly reproves the One who gave that authority to a human being.

At last, by God’s generosity, we have arranged in order the sentences of blessed Job, full of mystical power, in which he replied to the words of his friends. Now it remains for us to come to the words of Eliu, which must be weighed with the more serious vigilance because they are spoken with a more fervent spirit through the boldness of youth.

## Part Five, Containing Six Books

## The Twenty-Third Book

Chapters 32 and 33 are expounded up to verse 22, where Eliu the younger, while Job is silent, sets forth many things that are right and sound, but not with a right or sound intention.

[Column 0249]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Column 0249B]

### 729. By what purpose of God and by what means Job was tested.

I must necessarily repeat the preface to this work as often as I bring my speech to a pause at the division of the volumes, so that, whenever the beginning of the reading is taken up, the memory of the reading itself may first be renewed, and the edifice of doctrine may rise with greater strength in proportion as its foundation is more diligently laid in the mind through consideration of its origin.

[Note: These words show a division of the whole work neglected in the earlier editions, though traces of it remain in old editions, which prefix to this book either “The fifth part of the Morals begins” or “The fifth part of the whole work.” The old Basel edition reads: “as often as I come to this point, at the division of the volumes, in a pause of my discourse.” In the Colbertinus, formerly of the monastery of Saint Dionysius and written about eight hundred years ago: “as often as I come to this division . . .” The Germanicus manuscript is lacking up to section 31, and Corbie Germanicus up to section 28, exclusive.]

Blessed Job, known only to God and to himself, was touched by a blow while at peace, so that he might be brought to our knowledge and spread the fragrance of his strength more widely, in proportion as he gave off a better scent through burning, like aromatic substances.  
[Note: Vindocensis and Normannicus: “so much more abundantly.” Colbertinus has *flagraret* (“burn”) instead of *fragraret* (“give off fragrance”).]

He knew how to rule his subjects devoutly in prosperity and to guard himself strictly from evil. He knew how to use the possessions he had, but we did not know whether he would remain patient when they were taken away. He knew how to offer daily sacrifices to God for the health of those entrusted to him, but it was uncertain whether, deprived of them, he would also offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving. Therefore, lest prosperity conceal some defect, it was fitting that suffering should reveal it.

Permission was therefore given to the crafty enemy to test the holy man. While seeking to destroy his good qualities, known to many, he also brought to light the good of patience that had been hidden. He thought that he was constricting the man whom he persecuted, but through his blows he enlarged him and made him an example.

Nor did he exercise the permission he had received without grave skill. He burned the flocks, destroyed the households, overwhelmed the heirs, struck the health of the body, and, in order to hurl the dart of a still heavier temptation, preserved the tongue of his wife (Job 1, 2, 9, and elsewhere), so that he might overthrow the strong and solid heart of the holy man through grief at the loss of possessions and pierce it through the words of his wife with a curse.

But as many wounds as the raging enemy inflicted, so many victories, unknowingly, did he provide the holy man. For the faithful servant of God, caught at one and the same time among wounds and words, endured his suffering flesh with equanimity and wisely rebuked his foolish wife.

Therefore, when the ancient enemy grieved that he had been defeated in domestic matters, he immediately sought external weapons. He stirred up Job’s friends from their various places, as though to exercise charity, and opened their mouths under the appearance of consolation; but through them he hurled darts of reproach, which pierced the secure heart of the one listening all the more harshly because they wounded him unexpectedly amid the darkness of a displayed but unfulfilled charity.  
[Note: Turonensis and Normannicus: “they wounded him unexpectedly.”]

After these, Eliu the younger too is stirred up to insults, so that the light-mindedness of an age that disdained such great gentleness might at least disturb its tranquility. But against all the engines of the ancient enemy stood unconquered steadfastness and unbroken equanimity. At one and the same time he opposed prudence to hostile words and a life of virtue to hostile deeds.

Therefore, although it is plainly written of the holy man after the blows, “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips” (Job 2:10), let no one suppose that he later sinned in words during his dispute with his friends. Satan sought his temptation; but God, who had praised him, took upon himself the purpose of the contest. Whoever therefore complains that blessed Job sinned in his speeches—what else does he confess than that God, who undertook the cause on his behalf, was defeated?  
[Note: Turonensis: “that he had sinned.”]

### 2. The ancient Fathers are like fruitful trees. Their fruit was to signify Christ and the Church.

Since the ancient Fathers resemble fruitful trees, beautiful not only in appearance but also useful in abundance, their life should be evaluated in such a way that, while we admire the greenness found in the historical account, we also discover how great is the abundance found in allegory. Thus, while we delight in what exhales a pleasant fragrance from the leaves, we may also recognize how sweet is what tastes good in the fruit.

No one received the grace of heavenly adoption except the one who received it through knowledge of the Only-Begotten. It is therefore fitting that the one who illuminates them so that they may deserve to shine should himself shine forth in their life and speech. For when the light of a lamp is kindled in darkness, the lamp itself, which makes other things visible, is seen first.

Therefore, if we truly intend to see illuminated things, we must strive to open the eyes of our mind to the light that illuminates them. This also flashes through the speeches of blessed Job himself, even when the shadows of allegory are removed, as though the darkness of deep night had been pressed down, like a flash passing through, when he says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:25).

Paul had found this light in the night of history when he said: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:2).

If the rock therefore bore the figure of the Redeemer, why should blessed Job not suggest his figure, since he both proclaimed by his voice the one whom he also signified by his suffering? Hence Job is not inappropriately called one who suffers, because he expresses in himself the image of the one of whom Isaiah announced long beforehand that he himself bore our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4).

It must also be understood that our Redeemer presented himself as one person with the holy Church whom he assumed. Of him it is said: “in him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Again, of his Church it is written: “The body of Christ, which is the Church” (Colossians 1:24).

Blessed Job, therefore, who bore the type of the Mediator all the more truly because he prophesied his suffering not only by speaking but also by suffering, sometimes passes, when his words and deeds rest upon an expression of the Redeemer, into the signification of his body. Thus, what we believe about Christ and the Church as one person, we may also see signified through the actions of one person.

### 3. Job’s wife prefigures carnal people within the Church; his friends prefigure heretics.

His wife, who urges him to curse, signifies nothing other than the wickedness of carnal people. Placed within the holy Church with unreformed morals, they press upon the life of the faithful more harshly the nearer they are; for, since they cannot be avoided by the faithful as though they were outsiders, they are endured all the more grievously because they are endured within.

[Old recension II.] His friends, however, who attack him as though offering counsel, express the figure of heretics, who under the appearance of giving advice conduct the business of seduction. Thus, while they speak on behalf of the Lord to blessed Job, they are rejected by the Lord, because all heretics, while attempting to defend God, offend him.

Hence the holy man appropriately says to them: “I desire to argue with God, first showing you to be fabricators of lies and worshipers of perverse doctrines” (Job 13:3–4). It is therefore clear that they bear the type of heretics whom the holy man rebukes for serving the worship of perverse doctrines.

Since Job is interpreted as “one who suffers,” and through this suffering either the passion of the Mediator or the labor of the holy Church is expressed—the Church tormented by the manifold weariness of the present life—his friends too indicate through the meaning of their names the character of their activity.

Eliphaz, in the Latin tongue, means “contempt of God.”

[Note: The Baluzian fragments, not much later than Saint Gregory, together with Colbertinus, Vindocensis, and Normannicus, read “contempt of the Lord.”] What else do heretics do except, while holding false opinions about God, despise him through their pride? Baldad is interpreted as “mere old age.” All heretics are rightly called “mere old age” in what they say about the Lord, because they seek to appear as preachers not with right intention but out of desire for temporal glory. They are stirred to speak not by the zeal of the new person but by the wickedness of the old life.

Sophar, likewise, in Latin speech means “the dispersal of the watchtower,” or “the one dispersing the watchtower.”  
[Note: Vindocensis, Pratellensis, and others: “the one who disperses the watchtower.”]

The minds of the faithful raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things. But when heretics seek to corrupt those who contemplate what is right, they attempt to disperse the watchtower.

Thus, in the three names of Job’s friends, three falls into destruction among heretics are expressed. If they did not despise God, they would never think perversely about him; and if they did not contract old age, they would not err in understanding the new life; and if they did not destroy the watchtower of good things, the heavenly judgments would not condemn them with such strict examination for the fault of their words.

By despising God, therefore, they remain in old age; but by remaining in old age, they injure, through their perverse speeches, the contemplation of the upright.

[Note: What is said here of heretics occurs in almost the same words in Saint Gregory’s general preface, chapter 7.]

### 4. Eliu represents faithful but proud teachers.

After these, Eliu the younger is introduced in reproach of blessed Job. In his person the character of certain faithful but arrogant teachers is signified. We do not easily understand his words unless we assess them in light of the Lord’s subsequent rebuke.

For the Lord says of him: “Who is this who wraps up judgments in ignorant speeches?” (Job 38:2). When he says “judgments” but does not immediately add what kind, he undoubtedly wishes good judgments to be understood. For when judgments are mentioned, unless they are also called evil, they cannot be understood as evil. We always take judgments in the good sense when they are stated without an addition of condemnation, as it is written: “The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who speak judgments” (Proverbs 26:16).

[Note: The printed editions read “are called evil,” but erroneously. Saint Gregory’s point is that *sententiae* must always be understood favorably unless something is added to condemn them.]

But when it is said that his judgments are wrapped in ignorant speeches, it is shown above all that he utters them with the foolishness of pride. There is great ignorance in him: he does not know how to say humbly that he does not know what he is saying, and he mixes words of pride with the perceptions of truth.

### [Old recension III.] 5. Sometimes evil things are spoken well, and good things badly.

Everything that is said can be distinguished according to four qualities: whether evil things are spoken badly, good things well, evil things well, or good things badly.

Evil is spoken badly when something perverse is recommended, as it is written: “Bless God and die” (Job 2:9).

Good is spoken well when right things are proclaimed rightly, as John says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2).

Evil is spoken well when a fault is expressed through the speaker’s mouth for the purpose of condemning it, as Paul says: “Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature” (Romans 1:26). In that passage he also added the detestable crimes of men; but he narrated indecent things honorably, so that by narrating indecent things he might recall many to the pattern of uprightness.

Good is spoken badly when something right is not brought forward with a right intention, as the Pharisees are reported to have said to the man enlightened from blindness: “You be his disciple” (John 9:28). They said this as a curse, not as a prayerful wish.

Or as Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, so that the whole nation may not perish” (John 11:50). He spoke something good, but not well, because while he desired the cruelty of death, he prophesied the grace of redemption.  
[Note: The word *hominem* (“man”) is absent from three Normannic manuscripts, from Baluzianus, and from Colbertinus.]

In this way Eliu too is censured for saying good things badly, because in the things he speaks truthfully he is puffed up arrogantly. He represents the character of the arrogant in that, through the sense of what is right, he raises himself into words of pride.

### 733. 6. In the reconciliation of Job’s friends, the conversion of heretics must be recognized. Their sacrifices do not please God, but those offered by the Church do.

Why does the divine voice command the three friends to be reconciled through seven sacrifices, but leave Eliu under the rebuke of only one sentence? It is because sometimes heretics, drenched in the abundance of divine grace, return to the unity of the holy Church.

This is well signified by the reconciliation of the friends, for whom blessed Job is nevertheless commanded to pray. The sacrifices of heretics cannot be acceptable to God unless they are offered on their behalf by the hands of the universal Church, so that they may find the remedy of salvation through the merits of the Church which they attacked with the darts of their words.

Hence seven sacrifices are said to have been offered for them, because when they confess and receive the sevenfold Spirit of grace, they are cleansed, as it were, by seven offerings. For this reason, in the Apocalypse of John the universal Church is signified by the number seven, through the seven churches (Revelation 1:11). For this reason Solomon says of wisdom: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1).

The number of the sacrifices by which the heretics were reconciled therefore expresses what they had formerly been: they are joined to the perfection of sevenfold grace only by returning.

They are also rightly described as offering bulls and rams for themselves. In the bull, the neck of pride is signified; in the ram, the leadership of flocks that follow. What, then, is it to slaughter bulls and rams for them except to kill their proud leadership, so that they may think humbly about themselves and no longer lead the hearts of the innocent astray after them?

With swollen necks they had withdrawn from the universality of the Church and dragged weak peoples after them like following flocks. Let them therefore come to blessed Job—that is, let them return to the Church—and offer bulls and rams to be slaughtered through a sevenfold sacrifice. In order to be joined to the universal Church, let them, with humility intervening, kill whatever they had previously conceived in their proud leadership.  
[Note: In all printed editions and in some manuscripts the sense was corrupted by changing *qui* into *quia*. The reading should be *qui*, not *quia*, as in the preface of Saint Gregory, section 18.]

### [Old recension IV.] 7. Those who preach rightly but serve empty glory are not reconciled; they are very often condemned.

Eliu represents lovers of empty glory who are established within the holy Church and disdain to express humbly what they rightly understand. They are not commanded to be reconciled through sacrifice, because arrogant yet faithful people, since they are already within, cannot be recalled by seven sacrifices.

Nevertheless, under the figure of Eliu, the divine sentence rebukes them and condemns in them not the judgments of truth but the mind and words of pride.

[Note: The printed editions add “swollen,” but the manuscripts do not; the sense remains the same.] What else does this rebuke signify except that, while they remain within, the correction of heavenly severity either chastises them through scourging or leaves them to themselves through just judgment?

Such people preach what is right within the holy Church, yet under God’s judgment they deserve to hear adverse things, because through the good things they proclaim without making them their own, they seek not the glory of their author but their own praise.

This too must be carefully considered: the divine voice says of Eliu, “Who is this?” (Job 38:2). Such a question is the first form of reproach. We do not say “Who is this?” except of someone whom we do not know. Not to know is to reject in God’s judgment. Hence at the end he will say to certain people whom he rejects: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27).

What, then, does it mean to ask concerning this arrogant man, “Who is this?” except plainly to say: “I do not know the arrogant”—that is, I do not approve their life in the power of my wisdom, because, while they are puffed up by human praise, they are emptied of the true glory of eternal recompense.

By not rejecting his judgments, yet reproving the man who uttered them, God seems to say plainly: “I know what he says, but I do not know who says it. I approve what is spoken truthfully, but I do not recognize the man who exalts himself over the good things he proclaims.”

### 8. The outstanding image of the ideal preacher. Good things are scarcely made known without danger. Whoever is wise should strive to be wise, not to appear wise.

To show more clearly how disgracefully Eliu declines into the boastfulness of pride, we must first display the form of a good preacher, so that from the state of this uprightness the crookedness of that perverse bending may be plainly revealed.

Each spiritual preacher of the holy universal Church examines himself with careful diligence in everything he says: lest, while preaching what is right, he raise himself up through the fault of pride; lest his life disagree with his tongue; lest he lose within himself the peace he proclaims in the Church by speaking well but living badly.

[Note: Turonensis reads “carefully considers with diligent concern.”]

He strives above all, against the malicious rumors of his opponents, both to defend by speaking what he lives and to adorn by living what he says. In all this he seeks not his own glory but that of the author. He does not consider that he received the whole grace of wisdom, which he received in order to speak, through his own merits, but through the intercession of those for whom he speaks.  
[Note: Vindocensis, Ebroicensis, and other Normannic manuscripts: “the glory of wisdom.”]

Thus, while he casts himself down below, he rises above, because it greatly advances his own reward that he attributes to the merits of others the good works he is able to perform. He considers himself unworthy of everyone, even when he lives more worthily than all.

He knows that the good things made known to human beings can scarcely exist without danger. And although he feels himself to be wise, he would nevertheless rather be wise than appear wise; he fears above all what is revealed by his speaking. If permitted, he desires to be silent, since he sees that silence is safer for many and considers those happier whom a lower position within the holy Church keeps hidden through silence. Yet, in order to defend the holy Church, because the force of charity urges him to speak, he accepts the office of speech out of necessity but seeks the leisure of silence out of great desire. He preserves the former as his wish and practices the latter as his ministry.  
[Note: Baluzianus, Colbertinus, the Normannic manuscripts, and the old Paris and Basel editions read “safer”; recent editions read “much safer.” The same Normannic manuscripts, Vindocensis, and others read “and considers them happier,” whereas the printed editions read “and considers themselves happier.” Baluzianus and Colbertinus read “silence.”]

The arrogant do not know this rule of speech. They do not speak because occasions arise; they desire occasions to arise so that they may speak. Eliu now represents them, for in his speech he raises himself up with the immense fault of pride.

When the speeches of blessed Job had ended, it follows:

**Chapter 32, verse 7:** “These three men ceased to answer Job, because he seemed righteous to himself.”

[Col. 0256A] [Old Version V, Revised Version II.] Regarding the statement about him, “because he seemed righteous to himself,” the sacred writer of this history referred it to the judgment of the friends, and did not thereby condemn blessed Job for the swelling of pride. It follows:

## CHAPTER II

**Verse 2.**—Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram, was angry and indignant.

### 9. By Elihu, his father, and his kindred are signified the proud who hold fast to the true faith.

The names themselves—whether of the man, his father, the place, or the kindred—aptly express the character of their action. Elihu, when interpreted, means “This is my God,” or “God the Lord.” Through him, as we said above (No. 7), is signified the correct faith of the arrogant who are placed within the Church [Note: One manuscript from Ebroic reads “against the holy Church”; Vindoc. and other Norman manuscripts read “within the holy Church.”]. Thus this very name also suits them. For although they do not live according to the Lord’s commandments, they nevertheless acknowledge that God is Lord, because they recognize the form of the Godhead in the truth of the flesh, as the Prophet says: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Psalm 99:3).

Barachel, however, is said by interpretation to mean “blessing of God” [Note: Vindoc. and most Norman manuscripts read “the Lord’s blessing.”], while Buzite means “contemptible.” Both meanings aptly correspond to those who preach arrogantly: in the eloquence of their preaching they receive, indeed, the blessing of divine grace, but by their exalted conduct they show that this blessing is contemptible. The very good things they have received they make despicable because they do not know how to use them properly.

It is also fittingly said that he was of the kindred of Ram. Ram means “exalted.” Exalted, indeed, is the people of the faithful, who despise the lowly and rejected things of this life. They are exalted who know how to say with Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20) [Note: Vindoc. reads “but our citizenship.”].

Elihu, therefore, is said to be of the kindred of Ram because every arrogant preacher placed within the universal Church is joined to holy peoples by the truth of faith, although by the perversity of pride he is separated from their way of life. It follows:

## CHAPTER III [Revised Version III]

**Verses 2–3.**—But he was angry with Job because he said that he was righteous before God. He was also indignant with his friends because they had not found a reasonable answer, but had merely condemned Job.

### 10. These men rightly oppress heretics by their preaching, but by their pride they oppress the Church.

We must carefully observe that Elihu reproved blessed Job because he had said that he was righteous before God, but reproved Job’s friends because, while condemning him, they had not offered a reasonable reply against him. From these indications it is plainly gathered that the type of lovers of vainglory is represented by Elihu. He reproved Job for his presumed righteousness, but Job’s friends for their foolish answer.

All followers of vainglory, while putting themselves before everyone else, reproach some for foolish opinions and others for unworthy conduct; that is, they judge some to know nothing and others not to live well. Although they justly reproach all those placed outside the Church for thinking perversely, they nevertheless despise even those who are within because of the contemptible quality of their lives. Against the former they grow proud, as though because of the greatness of their right thinking; against the latter, as though because of the merit of living well.

[Old Version VI.] Elihu is rightly said now to rebuke blessed Job and now his friends, because lovers of vainglory, when established within the holy Church, sometimes oppress its adversaries by preaching the truth, and contradict the conduct of that same holy Church while boasting about their preaching. [Col. 0257B] They oppress the adversaries by the force of their speech; they oppress the holy Church by the character of their discourse. They attack the former by preaching the truth, and the latter by the vice of pride. It follows:

**Verses 4–5.**—Elihu therefore waited while Job was speaking, because those who were speaking were older. But when he saw that the three could not answer, he became exceedingly angry [Note: Baluz., Colbert, and Pratel read “because they could not answer”; “the three” is omitted].

### 11. Acute reasoning and a more intricate investigation of words arose only after the conflicts with heretics.

Although the holy Church is undoubtedly older than its adversaries—for they came from it, whereas it did not come from them, as John says of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19)—Elihu is nevertheless rightly described as younger than those same adversaries. For after the wars of the heretics had arisen [Note: One manuscript reads “after the wars of the enemies had arisen.” The sequence of the passage requires “heretics,” not “enemies”], arrogant men, inflated by the pride of knowledge, began to appear within the holy Church.

When the more serious battles with the enemy emerged, subtler weapons of reasoning were certainly required; then obstacles of argument, then a more intricate investigation of words. Often, when men fervent in intellect find these things appropriately, they swell with pride; and—as commonly happens through the vice of arrogance—they are struck down by the same sharp understandings with which they strike the enemy, when in the things they rightly think about God they seek not God’s glory but their own.

Thus Elihu also speaks many things correctly, yet is rebuked by the divine voice as though he had spoken perversely. When it is said that Elihu waited for Job to speak because those who were speaking were older, it is plainly shown that he reserved honor for blessed Job not on account of Job himself but out of reverence for his friends. For arrogant men placed within the Church despise that same holy Church which they defend. It often happens that they honor the intellects of those who think badly more than the simple life of the innocent, and reserve more respect for the tongues of those speaking outside than for the merits of those placed within, although they oppose both in different ways, disagreeing with the former because of the correctness of their opinions and with the holy Church because of the perversity of their conduct. It follows:

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0258A]

**Verses 6–7.**—And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: I am younger in age, but you are older; therefore, lowering my head, I was afraid to declare my opinion to you. For I hoped that greater age would speak, and that the multitude of years would teach wisdom.

### 12. To be silent is often to be wise.

All these things, which he utters through the swelling of pride, should be touched on briefly rather than explained at length. What lacks substantial gravity does not require the subtlety of exposition. I think, however, that this alone should be briefly made clear: as long as Elihu remained silent out of regard for his age, he was wiser; but when, preferring himself to others, he despises the multitude of their years, he shows how childishly foolish he is.

For contrary to his opinion, greater age does speak, and wisdom is taught through the multitude of years, because although longevity does not by itself provide understanding, it nevertheless greatly exercises one through experience [Note: The printed editions read “yet exercises through use”; the manuscripts have “yet through experience,” which is better]. It follows:

## CHAPTER VI [Revised Version IV]

**Verse 8.**—But, as I see, there is a spirit in human beings, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding.

### 13. Four forms of swelling among the arrogant: first, to believe that one possesses good from oneself; second, to believe that it was given to oneself on account of one’s merits. Grace is not given for merits. Third, falsely to attribute some good to oneself; fourth, to claim it for oneself alone while despising others.

He would say this correctly if he did not arrogate that same understanding to himself above others. It is not a wrongful condemnation to boast privately of a good that is given commonly: to know from whom one has received the good, yet not to know how one ought to use the good one has received.

[Old Version VII.] There are four forms by which every swelling of the arrogant is revealed: they think either that they possess good from themselves; or, if they believe it was given to them from above, they suppose that they received it on account of their own merits; or they boast that they possess what they do not possess; or, despising everyone else, they wish to appear uniquely to possess what they have.

He boasted that he possessed good from himself to whom the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Again, lest we believe that the good of grace is given to us on account of preceding merits, the same Apostle admonishes us, saying: “You have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8) [Note: Vindoc. omits “but”; “for it is the gift of God.” The word is also absent from the Norman, Baluz, and Colbert manuscripts].

He also says of himself: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). By these words he plainly declares that grace is not given for merits [Note: The Norman and Vindoc. manuscripts read “is not attributed to merits.” Both forms reflect the Augustinian meaning], since he himself taught both what he deserved because of his wickedness and what he received because of divine benevolence.

Again, some boast that they possess what they do not possess, as the divine voice says through the Prophet concerning Moab: “I know his pride and his arrogance, and that his strength is not according to it” (Jeremiah 48:29) [Note: Most manuscripts read “the pride of Moab.” The older printed editions also read “according to him”; Vindoc., Baluz., Colbert, and Norman manuscripts read “according to it,” referring to pride and arrogance. The Vulgate likewise reads “according to it,” following the Hebrew text].

And to the angel of the church of Laodicea it is said: “Because you say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17) [Note: The Norman manuscripts read “Laudicia”; the old editions read “Laodicea.”]

Again, some, despising everyone else, wish to appear uniquely to possess the good they have. Thus the Pharisee descended from the temple without justification (Luke 18:14), because, attributing the merits of good works to himself as though they were uniquely his, he placed himself above the praying tax collector.

The holy apostles too are recalled from this vice of pride. Returning from preaching, they said in their elation: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10:17). So that they would not rejoice in this uniqueness of miracles, the Lord immediately answered them: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18).

He himself, exalted in his uniqueness, had said: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13). Wonderfully, therefore, the Lord, in order to suppress pride in the hearts of the disciples, immediately recalled the judgment of the fall which the teacher of pride had received, so that in the author of pride they might learn what they should fear in the vice of exaltation.

In this fourth form of arrogance the human mind frequently falls: it boasts that what it possesses, it possesses uniquely. Yet in this it approaches the likeness of the devil more closely, because whoever rejoices in possessing good uniquely, whoever seeks to appear superior to others, imitates him who, despising the good of the fellowship of the angels, placed his seat in the north and proudly sought the likeness of the Most High, striving through an iniquitous desire to burst forth toward a certain summit of uniqueness.

Elihu, therefore, although he confesses that wisdom is given by the Lord, falls into this form of pride, rejoicing that he is wiser than others and foolishly exalting himself as though because of a unique good. He indicates this in the words that follow:

## CHAPTER VII

**Verses 9–12.**—The long-lived are not wise, nor do the elders understand judgment. Therefore I shall speak: Listen to me; I also shall show my wisdom. For I waited for your words; I listened to your prudence until you had disputed with words. And while I thought that you were saying something, I considered it [Note: Pratel reads “I also”; Baluz. and Corb. read “my knowledge.” Those manuscripts read below “until you disputed” rather than “until you had disputed”].

### 14. Some remain silent arrogantly; and the elders listen, not in order to learn, but in order to judge.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, Elihu’s speech indicates how proudly he remained silent. When he says, “I waited for your words, and I thought that you were saying something,” he plainly declares that he remained silent in order to judge the words of the elders, not from a desire to learn.

Yet these words more aptly represent the life of the arrogant, who, when placed within the holy Church and seeing the adversaries of that same holy Church, customarily weigh not the length of their years but the intention of their words. However much older the heretics may be than these arrogant men, the latter boldly suppress them when they detect perverse doctrines in their speech. It follows:

## CHAPTER VIII [Old Version VIII]

**Verses 12–13.**—But, as I see, there is no one who can rebuke Job or answer his words among you. Lest you should perhaps say: “We have found wisdom; God has overthrown him, not man.”

### 15. In this life God sometimes grants consolations without any loss to eternal life.

Heretics, because they are often despised even by human beings, frequently strive to tear apart the reputation of the holy Church by whatever reproaches they can, when they see it honored by nearly all peoples. They say: “Temporal goods are supplied to it for this reason: because it is deprived of the rewards of eternal gifts.”

Elihu counters their words, saying: “Lest you should say, ‘We have found wisdom; God has overthrown him, not man.’” It is as though the arrogant who are within the holy Church, yet faithful, were saying against the heretics: “Because you see the holy Church flourishing temporarily in human honor, do not believe that it has been overthrown by the Lord. Its Redeemer knows both how to grant consolation to it as it travels along this journey and how to reserve heavenly rewards for it when it reaches its eternal homeland.”

You say in vain that God, and not man, has overthrown it, when you see it honored by nearly all human beings. For earthly assistance is granted to it in such a way that through this it is carried more abundantly toward heavenly things. It follows:

## CHAPTER IX

**Verse 14.**—He has said nothing to me, and I shall not answer him according to your words.

### 16. When the proud are rebuked, they do not listen or they pretend not to hear.

What does he mean by saying, “He has said nothing to me”? Does the holy Church, through righteous preachers, fail to instruct and rebuke the arrogant whom it sees within itself? It does these things, and does not cease to do them daily.

But Elihu, who had heard blessed Job speaking publicly, says, “He has said nothing to me,” because all arrogant people hear the voices of the holy Church but pretend that those voices are not addressed to them when they disdain to correct the vice of pride. They do not think that they are being rebuked for pride, because they consider themselves humble; indeed, they despise being rebuked because they judge themselves wiser even than those who rebuke them.

As for what he says, “I shall not answer him according to your words,” he rightly says that he will not answer blessed Job according to their words. For the arrogant placed within the holy Church answer against it, but not as do the heretics placed outside. They do not contradict it by preaching perversely, but by living perversely. They do not, like heretics, hold unworthy opinions about God; rather, they think more highly of themselves than is necessary. It follows:

**Verse 15.**—They were terrified and answered no more; they withdrew speech from themselves.

[Old Version IX.] The friends of Job are rightly said to have been terrified at Elihu’s words, because sometimes the arrogant defenders of the Church, although they do not maintain the proper order of speaking, nevertheless disturb their adversaries by the very force of what they say. It follows:

## CHAPTER X

**Verse 16.**—Since I waited and they did not speak, they stood and answered no more.

### 17. When they rebuke those who err, they desire only to display their own wisdom, not to benefit others. Good preachers act otherwise.

It is ordinarily the mark of the wise in speech to speak only so far as to impose silence upon their adversaries. They do not wish to display themselves, but to restrain those who teach perversely.

After it had been said of Job’s friends, “They were terrified and answered no more; they withdrew speech from themselves,” Elihu adds: “I waited, and they did not speak; they stood and answered no more.” Although they are already silent, he multiplies his words, because the arrogant man, presenting in himself the form of the arrogant, hastens not to surpass the words of his adversaries but to display his own wisdom. Hence it follows:

**Verse 17.**—I too shall answer for my part, and I shall show my knowledge.

Every arrogant person considers this his portion: not so much to possess knowledge as to display it. For all the exalted do not desire to have knowledge but to exhibit it.

In contrast, Moses rightly says: “A vessel that has no covering or binding above it shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:15). The covering or binding of the lid is the discipline of restraint. Whoever is not restrained by it is rejected as an unclean and polluted vessel.

Was Elihu not a vessel without a covering, since he considered this his portion: to display the knowledge he possessed? Just as a vessel without a lid or binding is polluted, so the person who stands open through eagerness for display, covered by no veil of silence, is polluted.

[Old Version X.] Holy preachers, however, regard it as their portion if they themselves rejoice inwardly in their wisdom, while outwardly restraining others from error. They do not leave themselves through speaking in such a way that they place the joy of their mind in the display of eloquent speech. Rather, they meditate upon the good of knowledge in the secrecy of the heart, and rejoice where they receive it, not where they are compelled to become known amid so many snares of temptation. When the good they have received becomes known, they rejoice through the benefit of their hearers, with charity intervening, and not through their own display.

For when arrogant people receive knowledge, they think they have received nothing if they happen to keep it hidden. They place their joy nowhere except in the mouths of men. Thus the foolish virgins are said not to have taken oil in their vessels (Matthew 25:3), because arrogant people, even when they perhaps restrain themselves from certain vices, cannot possess the good of glory within their consciences.

Paul had taken oil in his own vessel when he said: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). To carry an empty little vessel, therefore, is to seek the judgment of the human mouth with an empty heart within [Note: The Vulgate editions read “of human favor.” Our reading is found in the Vindoc., Norman, and other manuscripts. Baluz. and Colbert read “in the human mouth.”].

Since Elihu seeks glory outwardly and therefore has no oil within the vessel, he says: “I too shall answer for my part, and I shall show my knowledge.” Hence he also reveals in the following words what he suffers inwardly from the fervor of vainglory:

## CHAPTER XI [Revised Version V]

**Verses 18–20.**—I am full of words, and the spirit of my inward being constrains me. Behold, my belly is like new wine without an opening, which bursts new wineskins. I shall speak, and shall breathe for a little; I shall open my lips, and shall answer.

### 18. The proud imitate the loftiness of such men’s speech, not their intention of usefulness.

Sometimes arrogant men, when they see holy preachers uttering great things and being honored for their speech, imitate the loftiness of their speech rather than the usefulness of their intention. They do not love what the preachers seek; instead, they desire above all to appear distinguished in the eyes of men.

Often wise men, when they see that they are not being heard, impose silence upon their mouths [Note: The verb *addicere* is used here in the sense of simply condemning or silencing. We have previously noted its use in Book II, No. 15, and elsewhere. Among the cited authors we added Peter Chrysologus, who says in Sermon 74: “Death is assigned, which advances against us and rushes upon the judge.” We also added Ennodius, who says in Discourse 22: “That he may support the enemy, he assigns his companions …”]. But frequently, when they see the crimes of the wicked increasing while they themselves remain silent and do not rebuke them, they endure a certain pressure of spirit, so that they burst forth into open speech of correction.

Thus the Prophet Jeremiah, when he had imposed silence upon himself in preaching, saying, “I will not remember him, nor speak any longer in his name,” immediately added: “And there was in my heart as it were a burning fire, enclosed in my bones; and I grew weary, unable to endure it, for I heard the insults of many” (Jeremiah 20:9).

Because he saw that he was not being heard, he desired silence; but when he saw evils increasing, he did not remain in that silence. Since he was silent outwardly, through weariness of speaking he endured inwardly the fire of zeal for charity.

The hearts of the righteous are inflamed when they see the deeds of the wicked increasing without correction, and when they believe themselves participants in the guilt of those whom, by remaining silent, they allow to increase in iniquity.

After the Prophet David had imposed silence upon himself, saying, “I set a guard upon my mouth while the sinner stood against me; I was silent and humbled myself, and kept silence from good things” (Psalm 38:2), he burned with this same zeal for charity in his very silence. He immediately added: “My pain was renewed; my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire burned” (Psalm 38:3).

His heart therefore grew hot within, because the ardor of love refused to flow outward through an admonishing word. The fire burned in the meditation of his heart because the rebuke of sinners had cooled through the restraint of his mouth. The zeal of charity regulates itself by increasing through a wonderful consolation when it flows forth in a voice of correction against the deeds of the wicked, so that it does not cease to rebuke what it cannot correct, lest through the consent of silence it condemn itself as a participant in the guilt of sinners.

[Old Version XI.] 19. Some vices imitate virtues.

But since certain vices often pretend to be virtues—for dissipation sometimes wishes to appear mercy, stinginess sometimes frugality, and cruelty sometimes justice—so the anxiety of vainglory, unable to contain itself within silence, often inflames the mind toward an impulse to speak as though it were zeal for charity. The force of the desired display drives it toward uncontrolled speech, and the desire to appear breaks out as though under the pretext of offering counsel.

Such a person does not care, in speaking, what may be useful, but what may appear impressive. He does not strive to correct the evil he sees, but to display the good he feels.

Thus Elihu too, stretched out by the spirit of pride and unable to contain himself within the confines of silence, says: “I am full of words, and the spirit of my inward being constrains me. Behold, my belly is like new wine without an opening, which bursts new wineskins.”

### 20. The inflation of pride sometimes imitates zeal arising from the breath of the Holy Spirit.

If we ought to understand this spiritually, he calls the belly here the recess of the heart. By “new wine,” however, we understand the fervor of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “They put new wine into new wineskins” (Matthew 9:17).

When the apostles were suddenly filled with it (Acts 2:4), and spoke in every language, the Jews, ignorant of what was happening but nevertheless bearing true witness, said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13).

By the frail wineskins we may appropriately understand human consciences, or certainly these earthly vessels of the body, concerning which the Apostle Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

But Elihu, because, as we said above, he is stretched by the inflation of pride as though he were kindled to speak by the grace of charity through the ardor of the Holy Spirit, compared the spirit of his thought, which he kept silent about, to new wine without an opening [Note: Baluz. and Colbert read “which he taught,” evidently in error].

And he rightly says, “which bursts new wineskins,” because the fervor of the Holy Spirit is scarcely contained not only by an old life but even by a new one. New wine bursts new wineskins because the power of its fervor surpasses even spiritual hearts.

“I shall speak, and shall breathe for a little; I shall open my lips, and shall answer.” He rightly says, “I shall breathe,” because just as it is the labor of the righteous to see evil and not correct it, so it is a heavy labor for the arrogant if they do not display what they know. They can scarcely bear the force boiling within them if everything they think is revealed only a little later.

Therefore, whenever a good deed is being done, its exaltation must first be conquered in the heart, lest, if it proceeds from the root of a wretched intention, it produce the bitter fruits of wickedness.

[Old Version XII, Revised Version VI.] 21. Those who are still subject to vices should not presume to govern others.

Those who are still subject to the battle of vices ought by no means, through the practice of preaching, to preside over the instruction of others (Distinction 44, chapter “It is not permitted”).

For this reason, according to the voice of divine dispensation, the Levites serve at the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, but from their fiftieth they become guardians of the vessels [Note: Turon., Colbert, and Norman manuscripts read “from the fiftieth year.” Below they likewise read “through the fiftieth year.” The old Paris and Basel editions also have this reading, and shortly afterward: “And from the fiftieth year they become guardians,” etc.].

What is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth appears, except the very battles against each vice? And what is signified by the fiftieth year, in which the rest of the jubilee is included, except the inward rest that follows when the battle of the mind has been subdued?

What, moreover, are signified by the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of the faithful? The Levites therefore serve at the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, and become guardians of the vessels from their fiftieth, so that those who still endure the conflicts of attacking vices through consenting delight do not presume to take charge of others. But when they have subdued the battles of temptation, and are already secure in themselves because of inward tranquility, they may receive charge of souls.

Yet who can perfectly subdue these battles of temptation, when Paul says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Romans 7:23)?

But it is one thing to endure battles courageously, and another to be weakly overcome by battles. In the former, virtue is exercised so that it should not be lifted up; in the latter, it is utterly extinguished so that it cannot remain.

Whoever, therefore, knows how to endure the temptation of battle courageously, and, while shaken by temptation, sits in the high fortress of tranquility, is content to remain beneath himself, because even within himself he sees the conflicts of vices beneath him, and consents to none of them, broken by delight. It follows:

## CHAPTER XII

**Verses 21–22.**—I shall not accept the person of man, nor equate God with man. For I do not know how long I shall endure, or whether my Maker will take me away after a little while.

### 22. The time of the present life is brief because it does not endure.

It is a correct consideration that he does not equate God with man because he does not know how long he will remain here or when he will be taken to God’s judgment. He rightly says: “My Maker will take me away after a little while,” because however long the time of the present life may be, it is brief precisely because it does not endure. Whatever is bounded by an end cannot rightly be judged lasting.

Yet amid these statements, which he puts forward as solid because they are true, he again bursts into words of pride, saying:

## CHAPTER XIII [Revised Version VII]

[Col. 0265A]

**Job 33:12.**—Therefore, Job, hear my speeches, and listen to all my words. Behold, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat.

### 23. The proud do not preach sound doctrine soundly, because they become insolent.

Let us consider from what pride he descends when he admonishes blessed Job to hear him, declares that he has opened his mouth, and promises that his tongue will speak in his throat [Note: Colbert, Vindoc., and Norman manuscripts read “in his own throat”].

This is characteristic of the doctrine of the arrogant (Distinction 46, chapter “This is characteristic”): they do not know how to present what they teach humbly, nor can they rightly administer the truths they understand. Their words reveal that, when they teach, they seem to themselves to sit upon a certain summit of superiority, and they look down upon those whom they teach as though they were placed far below them. They do not deign to speak to them by offering counsel, but as though scarcely deigning to rule over them.

The Lord rightly says to such people through the Prophet: “You ruled over them with harshness and with power” (Ezekiel 34:4). They rule with harshness and power when they hasten not to correct their subjects by calm reasoning but to bend them harshly through domination.

[Old Version XIII.] 24. True doctrine avoids pride.

True doctrine, by contrast, flees this vice of pride all the more intensely in its thinking as it pursues the very teacher of pride more ardently with the arrows of its words. It takes care not to preach with exalted conduct the one whom it attacks with sacred words in the hearts of its hearers.

It strives both to speak humility and to display it by living, because humility is the teacher and mother of all virtues. Thus it may express humility to the disciples of truth more by conduct than by words.

Hence Paul, speaking to the Thessalonians and seeming to forget the summit of his own apostleship, says: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

The Apostle Peter, when he said, “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15), asserted that a manner of teaching must be preserved even in the knowledge of doctrine, adding: “But with gentleness and fear, having a good conscience” (1 Peter 3:16).

When Paul says to his disciple, “Command and teach these things with all authority” (1 Timothy 4:11; Titus 2:15), he recommends not domination by power but the authority of one’s life [Note: Vindoc., Norman, and others read “with every kind of authority”]. One teaches with authority when one first does what one teaches.

For doctrine loses confidence when conscience hinders the tongue. Paul therefore did not convey power for elevated speech, but confidence arising from good action.

Thus it is also written of the Lord: “He was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees” (Matthew 7:29). He alone, uniquely and principally [Note: “alone” is absent from the Norman manuscript], spoke with the authority of goodness, because he committed no evil through weakness. From the power of his divinity he possessed what he ministered to us through the innocence of his humanity.

[Old Version XIV, Revised Version VIII.] 25. What preachers should consider in order to avoid pride.

We, because we are weak human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, must first remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider by what manner of teaching we should assist our weak brothers [Note: Vindoc. and most Norman manuscripts read “know”].

Let us therefore consider whether we are now what some of those whom we correct are; or whether we once were such, even though through the working of divine grace we are no longer so. We should correct with a humble heart all the more gently as we recognize ourselves more truly in those whom we correct.

But if we are neither now nor ever were what those whom we seek to correct still are, let us recall before our eyes their other good qualities, lest our heart perhaps grow proud and fall more grievously because of that very innocence by which we correct their faults.

If they have no good qualities at all, let us turn back to the hidden judgments of God. For just as we received the very good that we possess without any merits of our own, so grace may also pour into them the power from above, so that, awakened later, they may even surpass the good things that we received earlier.

Who would have believed that Saul would one day surpass the stoned Stephen in the merit of apostleship (Acts 7:57), when at Stephen’s death he was guarding the garments of those who were stoning him?

By these thoughts, therefore, the heart must first be humbled, and only then should the iniquity of sinners be rebuked.

But Elihu is shown, as has often been said, to be ignorant of this manner of speaking. In his discourse he is inflated by the swelling of pride, as though by the force of some authority, when he says: “Therefore, Job, hear my speeches, and listen to all my words. Behold, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat” [Note: Baluz., Colbert, Norman, and the old Paris and Basel editions read *typo*; others have *typho*.
