Mabillon observes, in his note on Letter 247 of Saint Bernard, that *typum* is often read for *typho* in manuscripts. This occurs frequently in handwritten copies of Gregory. In chapter 31 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, where the text reads “without pride or delay,” Hildemar reads “without *typho*,” that is, without haughtiness or arrogance. Augustine, on Psalm 55: “You find a proud man, swollen with the most arrogant *typhus*”; and in *The City of God*, Book II, final chapter: “one rejoicing in God, the other swollen with *typhus*.”].

### 26. Some merely feign modesty

To speak in the throat means to speak quietly, not to shout loudly. By these words he indicates the arrogant who are placed within holy Church. They are said to speak “in the throat” when they do not cry out against adversaries living outside, but reproach certain people within the bosom of holy Church, as though they were neighbors and close at hand. Often, however, the arrogant pretend to flee the very arrogance they possess; and while they do everything in such a way that no one remains unaware of them, they privately tell these things to individuals, as though secretly, so that they may boast

**[Note:]** Most manuscripts read *silenter*, “quietly.” not only of the soundness of their understanding but also of their contempt for arrogance in the eyes of others. Hence it is now said: “Let my tongue speak in my throat.” As though he were saying openly: “What I prudently think against you, behold, I relate quietly.”

Sometimes, however, they rush into such shameless arrogance that, while others are silent,

**[Note:]** Vindocensis reads: “into such shameless exaltation of pride.” they themselves are accustomed to praise what they say. Hence he adds:

### CHAPTER XIV

**Verse 3.** “My words are from a simple heart, and my lips shall speak a pure judgment.”

**[Note:]** *Meo* (“my”) is absent in the Norman manuscripts.

### 27. They falsely boast of simplicity

Simplicity of speech is the praise of a great virtue. Because the arrogant do not possess it, they earnestly assert that they do, so that they may be heard with greater security. They announce that they will speak purely because they fear that the malice of their duplicity may be exposed. Often they also mix truths with falsehoods, so that their lie may more readily be believed because they are recognized to contain an assertion of truth.

Since, therefore, Eliu both affirmed that he would speak purely and anticipated approval by calling his statements “judgments,” he now adds the very judgment he had promised, saying:

### CHAPTER XV [Old XV, Revised IX]

**Verse 4.** “The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.”

### 28. Doctrine uttered without order becomes sterile and disfigured

He was about to speak truths, but first he had uttered proud words; and before making known what he rightly understood, he had already revealed how greatly he was swollen with pride. Thus, indeed, thus do the minds of the arrogant rave: even in the things they rightly perceive, they are distorted by the crookedness of their pride. Consequently, even their correct statements do not instruct their hearers at all, because through the things they arrogantly perceive they summon them not to reverence but to contempt. When words of wisdom are mixed with words of folly, folly is despised by the hearer, and wisdom too is not retained.

Hence it is said through Moses: “The man who suffers an emission of semen shall be unclean” (Leviticus 15:10). For what is speech except semen? When it is emitted in an orderly way, the mind of the hearer, like a womb conceiving, becomes fertile with the offspring of good works. But if it flows out inopportunely, polluting the one who emits it, it loses the power of generation.

**[Note:]** Here Gussanvilleus advises that, in the Vatican manuscripts, after the words “it loses the power of generation,” the following should be appended: “For if speech were not semen, the Athenians would never have said of the preaching Paul: ‘What does this babbler [literally, “seed-sower of words”] intend to say?’ (Acts 17:18).” The added words are: “For in the minds of the hearers, speech is the seed of the thought that will follow; the equality of expression having been added, because when speech is conceived through the ear, thought is generated in the mind.” What “the equality of expression having been added” signifies is entirely unclear to me. This addition is found neither in our manuscripts nor in the printed editions, nor even in the Roman edition of Sixtus V, which was prepared especially from the Vatican manuscripts.

For if speech were not semen, the Athenians would never have said of the preaching Paul: “What does this babbler intend to say?” (Acts 17:18). Luke also says of him: “For he was the leader of the word” (Acts 14:11). Thus semen devoted to the use of propagation, when it flows improperly, pollutes the other members; so speech, through which knowledge ought to be born in the minds of hearers, if it proceeds without order, disfigures even the things it has rightly understood.

Eliu therefore also stains whatever he is able to understand rightly, because he does not know to whom or what he should speak; and he is like one suffering an emission of semen when he moves a tongue suited to usefulness through words of empty speech.

**[Note:]** Vindocensis reads *qui linguam* (“who [moves] a tongue”); Ebroicensis, Baluze, and Colbertinus likewise. Most Norman manuscripts read *cui linguam* (“to whom [he moves] a tongue”).

Yet he asserts both that he was made in good order and that he was given life. He says that he was made through the Spirit and given life through the breath. For after Adam had been made, it is written: “He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). But let us hear whether he rightly develops what he rightly asserts. It follows:

### CHAPTER XVI

**Verse 5.** “If you can, answer me and stand against my face.”

### 29. The foolish boasting of the arrogant, excessive beyond measure

Behold: while he recounts the order of true creation, he suddenly breaks out into the pomp of proud exaltation and repeats the same thing in other words, saying:

**Verses 6–7.** “Behold, God made me as he made you, and I too was formed from the same clay. Nevertheless, let my marvel not terrify you, and let my eloquence not be burdensome to you.”

What does it mean that Eliu acknowledges the order of true creation but does not understand the proper manner of speaking? What does it mean that he equates himself with blessed Job as one who has been created, yet exalts himself as one who is about to speak, except that all arrogant people remember that they were created equally with all human beings, but through the conceit of knowledge disdain either to be or to believe that their hearers are equal to them? They compare themselves with others by the condition of nature, but place themselves above them through the swelling of knowledge. They judge themselves to have been equal at birth, but not to have remained equal in life.

**[Note:]** Ebroicensis reads, with a lacuna in the reported reading: “and therefore that they are equal … are already.” Thus, in the fact that they are, as it were, no longer equal through living, they refer to the greater marvel the fact that they were equal at birth.

Accordingly, the inflated Eliu says: “Behold, God made me as he made you, and I too was formed from the same clay. Nevertheless, let my marvel not terrify you, and let my eloquence not be burdensome to you” [Old XVI]. The arrogant also have this characteristic: before they speak, they always imagine that they are about to say marvelous things, and they forestall their speech with admiration, because, even in their sharp perceptions, they do not know how great their pride itself is in its folly.

It should also be noted that Paul, when he was wonderfully admonishing the Hebrews, added: “I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation; for I have written to you only briefly” (Hebrews 13:22). Eliu, however, uttered empty words and, as though offering consolation, added: “Let my marvel not terrify you, and let my eloquence not be burdensome to you.” Paul calls his statements “a word of consolation”; Eliu calls his “eloquence” and “a marvel.” Behold how different are the flavors produced by the fruits of different roots of thought. The former thinks humbly of great things; the latter emptily exalts himself over trifles.

What, then, is to be carefully observed here except this: those who are about to ascend consider themselves to be at the bottom, while those who are about to fall always stand on a precipice?

**[Note:]** Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts read: “that both those who are about to rise … and those who are about to fall.” Baluze reads “those who are about to rise … and the dearer always stand in precepts,” with a corrupt and contrary sense. Colbertinus reads “those who are about to rise … and those who are about to fall always stand in steep places,” perhaps *praecipitiis* (“precipices”).

Solomon testifies to this when he says: “Before ruin the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Proverbs 16:18). It follows:

**Verses 8–11.** “You have spoken, therefore, in my ears, and I have heard the voice of your words.”

**[Note:]** *Tuorum* (“your”) is absent from Baluze, Colbertinus, and many other witnesses.

**[Revised X.]** Adding the same voice, he says: “I am pure and without fault, blameless, and there is no iniquity in me. Because he found complaints against me, he considered me his enemy. He put my feet in the stocks; he watched all my paths.”

Then, immediately presenting his judgment against these words which he claimed blessed Job had spoken, he says:

### CHAPTER XVII

**Verse 12.** “This, then, is the matter in which you are not justified.”

### 30. They strive more to rebuke than to console

Blessed Job had truly said that he had been scourged without guilt. He said of himself what the Lord said concerning him to the devil: “You have moved me against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3). But Eliu did not believe that, when guilt had ceased, Job could nevertheless have been scourged for the sake of grace. He did not know that the scourges did not erase Job’s fault but increased his merit. Because Job had said that he had been scourged without guilt, Eliu rebukes him with this judgment, saying: “This, then, is the matter in which you are not justified.”

The arrogant have this characteristic: they desire more to rebuke than to console, and they suppose that whatever happens to people has arisen solely from their iniquities. They do not know how to investigate the hidden judgments subtly or to examine humbly what they do not understand, because the very pride of their knowledge often casts them down from the secret investigations of God’s judgments even as it exalts them.

### 31. The swelling of the mind is an obstacle to truth. The effects of true knowledge

The swelling of the mind is an obstacle to truth, because while it inflates, it obscures. Even when such people appear to acquire knowledge, they feed, as it were, on a kind of outer shell of things, not on the marrow of hidden sweetness. With minds that sparkle, they often touch only external matters, but remain ignorant of the taste within: sharp on the outside, but blind within.

They do not perceive of God that he has an inward sweetness, but only what, when struck externally, makes a sound. Even if they grasp certain hidden things through understanding, they cannot experience their sweetness; and if they know what these things are, they do not know, as I have said, how they taste [Old XVII]. It often happens that they speak forcefully but do not know how to live according to what they say.

Thus a certain wise man rightly said: “May God grant me to speak according to judgment” (Wisdom 7:15). “Judgment” derives its name from “sense” or “perception.” Whoever desires to speak rightly of what he understands seeks to speak not from knowledge alone but also from inward perception; he wishes not merely to speak by knowing but to experience through feeling what he says.

The mind of the arrogant, however, does not penetrate the sense of its own words, because, by a just judgment, it is dashed away from inward taste against those human favors to which it yearns, as against a reef.

**[Note:]** The printed editions read, “is reduced to those favors.” Since the clearer manuscripts—English, Norman, Baluzean, Colbertine, and others—support it, we have changed *redigitur* to *reliditur*, “is dashed against,” from which a more refined sense follows. The meaning is that the mind of the arrogant is dashed against the human favors for which it yearns, like a ship against a reef.

True knowledge, however, affects rather than exalts; and those whom it fills it makes not proud but grieving. When someone has been filled with it, he first desires to know himself; and once conscious of himself, he possesses wisdom all the more robustly through it the more truly he recognizes himself as weak. His humility itself opens a broader path to this knowledge. When he perceives his weakness, the knowledge of sublime secrets opens hidden recesses to him; and under the pressure of that knowledge he becomes more subtle, so that he may be drawn up to hidden things.

**[Note:]** Vindocensis, Baluze, Colbert, and many Norman manuscripts read: “so that he may be seized for the hidden things.” The reading is obscure, perhaps even meaningless.

Eliu therefore did not discover a true explanation in the scourges of blessed Job because he did not know how to seek it humbly. More ready to rebuke than to console, he says: “This, then, is the matter in which you are not justified.”

### 32. The proud often lie when rebuking others

It should also be noted that blessed Job said that his foot had been placed in the stocks, but he did not at all claim that he was pure in the manner Eliu alleges: without sin, blameless, and free from iniquity. Eliu, while harshly striving to rebuke what had been said, falsely added what had not been said.

Those who always desire to rebuke and never to encourage often tell many lies in the very act of rebuking. In order to appear learned in their accusations, they sometimes invent things to condemn. While they themselves, like horses, burn to run in the course of their own self-display, they prepare a field for their attacks upon their subjects out of fabricated iniquities.

Moreover, as I said above (section 31), it must be understood that arrogant men often mix forceful statements with their inflated words; they do not sometimes consider how they live, but carefully weigh what they teach.

**[Note:]** A recent edition reads, “what use there is in what lacks sense.” The manuscripts—English, Norman, Vindocensian, Baluzean, and others—more correctly read, “how they live,” that is, by what manner they shape and order their life; the old edition also has this reading.

Eliu now represents this type: he does not seek to live rightly, but to teach. Since, therefore, he speaks as one who knows but is arrogant, let us now leave aside how he lives in pride and listen to what he says that is solid. After so many words of exaltation, he finally begins to display his knowledge and says:

### CHAPTER XVIII

**Verse 12.** “I shall answer you that God is greater than man.”

### 33. Whatever we suffer from God, who is better than we are, let us believe to be just

Someone may perhaps say: “Who does not know this, even without hearing it?” Yet this statement is plainly considered trivial if it is not weighed from the very root of its intention.

He was speaking to one who had been scourged, who had received the blows of punishment but did not know their causes. He therefore continued: “I shall answer you that God is greater than man,” so that the scourged man, considering that God is greater than he, might submit himself in everything he suffered to God’s judgment, since he did not doubt that God was greater than he; and whatever he suffered from one who was better, he might believe to be just, even if he did not understand the reasons for that justice.

**[Note:]** This is the preferable manuscript reading, rather than the printed reading *cui se minorem* (“than whom he knows himself to be lesser”).

Whoever is struck even for sin begins already to be just, unless he resists by murmuring, precisely when he does not accuse the justice of the one who strikes. Human beings were created under God, and they return to the order of their creation when they place before themselves the equity of their judge, even an equity they do not understand.

It is therefore rightly said: “I shall answer you that God is greater than man,” so that, when the Creator’s power is considered, the swelling of the mind may subside through remembrance of creation. Hence the prophet David, when the weight of punishment forced him to break out into an excess of speech, gathered himself back to consideration of his created condition and said: “I was silent and did not open my mouth, because you made me” (Psalm 38:3).

He weighed the order of his created condition and found justice in his punishment, because the one who had kindly created him when he did not exist would surely have struck him justly when he did exist. It follows:

### CHAPTER XIX [Revised XI]

**Verses 13–14.** “You contend against him because he has not answered you concerning all your words. God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time.”

**[Note:]** This reading is to be adopted from the English manuscripts and ours. The printed editions read: “He speaks once … he does not repeat.” Our reading seems to agree more closely with the Hebrew text, in which the future *iedabber* is used. Jerome nevertheless translates, “He speaks once.” That Gregory read *loquetur* (“he will speak”) is clear from section 35 below, where he observes that the text says not *locutus est* (“he spoke”) but *loquetur* (“he will speak”), using the future rather than the past tense.

### 34. In Holy Scripture God teaches us whatever it is right for us to know

It is characteristic of an afflicted heart that, whenever it desires something yet encounters an order of things contrary to its desire, it wishes, if possible, to be answered by divine voices as to why things are or are not so. It wishes to consult God about every controversy concerning events and, once the reason for his answer is known, to rest.

Eliu, however, foresaw that the Lord would establish Holy Scripture so that it might answer all questions, both public and hidden. He says: “You contend against him because he has not answered you concerning all your words. God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time.” As though he were saying: “God does not answer the hearts of individuals with private voices; rather, he constructs such an utterance as will satisfy the questions of all.”

If each of us seeks our own causes in the utterance of his Scripture, we find them there. There is no need for each person to seek a special divine voice answering specifically what he suffers. In Scripture, all of us receive a common answer concerning what each of us suffers individually. There the life of those who went before becomes a pattern for those who follow.

To offer one example: when we are afflicted by some illness or bodily trouble, we may wish to know the hidden causes of that illness or trouble, so that we may be consoled in what we suffer by knowledge of its causes. But because no special answer is given individually to each of us concerning our particular temptations, we turn to Holy Scripture.

There we find that Paul, who was tempted by bodily weakness, heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). This was said to him in his own weakness so that it would not have to be said individually to all of us.

Thus, in Holy Scripture, we have heard the voice of God speaking to afflicted Paul, so that, when we ourselves are perhaps afflicted, we would not each seek to hear it privately as a personal consolation. The Lord therefore does not answer us concerning every word, because he speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time. That is, through what he set forth in Holy Scripture for our fathers, he has taken care to instruct us.

Let the teachers of holy Church say this; let the arrogant say it too, when they see some people laboring within the Church through faintheartedness: God does not answer us concerning every word, because he speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time. That is, he no longer satisfies the thoughts or temptations of individuals everywhere through the voices of prophets or through angelic ministries, because he has included in Holy Scripture whatever can happen to individuals and has taken care, through the examples of those who went before, to shape the life of those who follow.

**[Note:]** The Paris old edition, with Colbertinus, Turonensis, and Norman manuscripts, reads: “Let the holy doctors of the Church, therefore, say; let the arrogant also say, when they see some laboring within it through faintheartedness.” Other editions read instead: “Let the holy doctors of the Church learn; let the arrogant also learn, when [they see] some laboring within it.”

### 35. For God to speak is to beget the Word

Although the statement, “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time,” can be understood more subtly in this way: the Father begot the only-begotten Son, consubstantial with himself. For God’s speaking is the begetting of the Word. God’s speaking once means

**[Note:]** *Dei* (“of God”) is absent in Uticensis and most Norman manuscripts.

 that he has no Word other than the only-begotten. Hence it is appropriately added: “And he does not repeat the same thing a second time,” because he begot this very Word—that is, the Son—as the only one.

The text does not say, “He spoke,” but “He shall speak,” placing not the past but the future tense. It is clear to all that neither past nor future time properly belongs to God. Any tense may therefore be freely assigned to him precisely because none truly belongs to him. Nor could any tense be assigned freely if even one were assigned properly. Thus we may boldly speak of time in God in any manner because no time may properly be spoken of in him. The Father begot the Word without time.

### 36. We ought to marvel at this generation, not investigate it

Who could worthily express that ineffable birth: that the one born from the eternal is co-eternal; that the one existing before the ages begot an equal; that the one born after the begetter is not later? We can marvel at this, but we cannot in any way behold it. To be able already to marvel somewhat at the power of that birth is itself a kind of seeing. But how do we see what we do not comprehend?

There is something here that we must transfer from bodily experience to spiritual understanding. If someone were lying in darkness with his eyes closed, and the sudden light of a lamp burst forth before him, his closed eyes would be struck by the arrival of the light and would open. Why, then, would they be disturbed if, while closed, they saw nothing? Yet what they could see while closed was not complete. For if they had seen everything perfectly, why would they open and seek what they might see?

So, precisely so, we are when we try to behold something of the incomprehensible birth. The mind is struck by the wonder of the radiance itself and, as though seeing what cannot be seen, beholds through closed eyes, as one placed in darkness, the power of the light.

**[Note:]** In the printed editions, after “as though seeing what cannot be seen,” the following is added: “For Eliu says: ‘God speaks once.’ But David, contemplating the birth of the only-begotten Word, says: ‘God spoke once.’ Because the only-begotten Son, the very Word of the Father, is said to have been born in perfection and is also said, on account of his eternity, always to be born, Holy Scripture freely customarily says of God both that he has spoken and that he speaks. In that he begot the perfect Word, the Father has spoken; in that he always begets him, he speaks, although we do not properly call that which we have called perfect so. For what has not been made is not properly called perfect; rather, we express its fullness through a certain limitation of our speech, just as the Lord also says concerning the Father: ‘Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.’”

This addition is missing from all the Norman, Turonian, Vindocensian, Colbertine, and Baluzean manuscripts. This codex is worn away or mutilated in many places. I am persuaded that the addition is not genuine not only by the silence of the manuscripts but also by the sequence of the discourse, which appears to be interrupted by this long parenthesis. Indeed, after the words “the mind is struck by the wonder of the radiance,” the following ought to follow immediately: “Because the wonder of these secrets of the divine nature ….”

Because the wonder of these secrets of the divine nature is not easily perceived by minds occupied with earthly desires, Eliu appropriately indicates how God’s speech comes to us, saying:

### CHAPTER XX [Old XX, Revised XII]

**Verse 15.** “In a dream, in a night vision, when sleep falls upon people and they sleep in their beds.”

### 37. God’s voice is heard when one rests from worldly works with a tranquil mind

What does it mean that the speech of divinity becomes known to us through a dream, except that we do not know God’s secrets if we remain awake in earthly desires? In a dream, the external senses sleep, and inward things are seen. If, therefore, we wish to contemplate what is within, let us sleep to external involvement.

The voice of God is heard, as it were, through a dream when the mind rests tranquilly from the activity of this world and, in the silence of the mind itself, weighs the divine commands. When the mind is lulled to sleep with regard to external activities, then the weight of God’s commandments is more fully recognized. The mind penetrates God’s words more vividly when it refuses to admit the tumult of worldly cares.

A person is badly awake when the heat of worldly affairs disturbs him arrogantly. The multitude of earthly thoughts closes the ear of the heart by its din; and in the inner chamber of the mind, the less the sound of turbulent cares is restrained, the less the voice of the presiding judge is heard. A person divided between both does not suffice perfectly for either. While he wishes to be instructed inwardly in such a way that he nevertheless remains entangled outwardly, from the place where he opens himself to outward hearing, he becomes deaf inwardly.

Moses, mingling with the Egyptians, was, as it were, awake, and for that reason, while he remained in Egypt, he did not hear the Lord’s voice (Exodus 2:11–12 and following). But after he had killed the Egyptian and fled into the desert, where he spent forty years, he fell, as it were, asleep to the tumult of restless earthly desires. For that reason he deserved to perceive the divine voice: through heavenly grace, the more he became torpid toward external things that might be desired, the more truly he remained awake to the knowledge of what was within.

Again, when he was placed over the crowds of the Israelite people in order to receive the precepts of the law, he was led up the mountain; and, in order to penetrate inward things, he was hidden from external tumult (Exodus 19:3).

### 38. Those who serve in external ministries should diligently withdraw into the secrets of the heart

Hence holy men who, compelled by the necessity of their office, must serve in external ministries always diligently withdraw into the secrets of the heart. There they ascend to the summit of their deepest thought and receive the law, as it were, upon the mountains, when, having set aside the tumult of temporal actions, they investigate the judgment of the heavenly will at the summit of their contemplation.

This is why Moses repeatedly returned to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters. There, in secret, he consulted the Lord and recognized what certain decision he should make.

**[Note:]** The Norman and Colbertine manuscripts read: “what was more certain.”

To leave the crowds and return to the tabernacle means, after setting aside the tumult of external things, to enter the secret place of the mind. There the Lord is consulted, and what must be done publicly outside is heard silently within.

Good rulers do this every day. When they recognize that they cannot discern doubtful matters, they return to the secret place of the mind as though to a certain tabernacle. Having examined the divine law, they consult the Lord as though the ark were set before them; and what they first hear inwardly in silence, they later make known outwardly by their actions.

To serve external duties without stumbling, they take constant care to return to the secrets of the heart. Thus they hear the voice of God, as it were, through a dream, when in the meditation of the mind they are withdrawn from carnal movements.

**[Note:]** Some witnesses read “from carnal senses” (*a carnalibus sensibus*) rather than “from carnal movements” (*a carnalibus motibus*); Vindocensis, the Norman manuscripts, and others have the former reading.

This is why the bride in the Song of Songs had heard the bridegroom’s voice as though through a dream. She said: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). As though she were saying: “While I lull my external senses to sleep from the anxieties of this life, with my mind at leisure I perceive inward things more vividly. Outside I sleep, but within my heart is awake, because while I seem not to sense external things, I grasp inward things attentively.”

### 39. We contemplate divine and inward things only obscurely and as though in a night vision

Eliu therefore rightly says that God speaks through a dream, and appropriately adds: “In a night vision.” A night vision usually appears in the contemplation of the mind under certain images. In daylight we see with greater certainty; in a night vision we see hesitantly.

All the saints, so long as they are in this life, behold the secrets of the divine nature as though under a certain image, because they do not yet contemplate them with the clarity with which they exist. Eliu therefore rightly says, after stating that God speaks to us through a dream: “In a night vision.”

The present life is night. So long as we remain in it, whenever we behold inward things, we are shrouded in uncertain imagination. The prophet, feeling himself pressed by a certain darkness while seeking to see the Lord, said: “My soul desired you in the night” (Isaiah 26:9). As though he were saying: “In the obscurity of this present life I desire to see you, but I am still enclosed by the cloud of weakness.”

David too, avoiding the darkness of this night and awaiting the brightness of the true light, said: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall see” (Psalm 5:5). Whoever longs for the future morning in order to see God recognizes that he sees less clearly while still in the night.

Since, as we have said, to cease from external action is to sleep, Eliu appropriately adds: “When sleep falls upon people.” And since holy men, when they do not serve in external activity, rest within the chambers of the mind, he suitably continues: “And they sleep in their beds.”

**[Note:]** Ebroicensis reads *cubicula* (“chambers”).

For holy men, to sleep in a bed means to rest within the chamber of their mind. Hence it is written: “The saints shall rejoice in glory; they shall exult upon their beds” (Psalm 149:5).

Let it therefore be said that God speaks to us once through a dream, in a night vision, when sleep falls upon people and they sleep in their beds, because we recognize the secrets of divinity precisely when we are separated from the tumultuous desire of this world within the chambers of our mind.

Since, as we have often said, the tumult of worldly affairs closes the ear of the heart, while the quiet of secret reflection opens it, he appropriately adds:

**Verse 16.** “Then he opens the ears of men, and, instructing them, teaches them discipline.”

### 40. Those who cease from external works are instructed in compunction

When they are lulled to sleep with regard to external activities, they hear, with the inner ear opened, the causes of the inward examination. While they attentively consider either public scourges or hidden judgments, they do not cease to afflict themselves with tears.

**[Revised XIII.]** Hence it is rightly said: “And, instructing them, he teaches them discipline,” because, for the mind that reflects and tears itself through repentance, the lamentations of compunction are like certain wounds inflicted by blows.

Solomon therefore rightly joins together the force of both kinds of blows when he says: “The bruise of a wound cleanses away evil, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Proverbs 20:30). By “the bruise of a wound” he signifies the discipline of bodily punishment. The “blows in the innermost parts of the belly” are the inward wounds of the mind produced by compunction.

For just as a belly is enlarged when filled with food, so the mind, enlarged by evil thoughts, is lifted up. Both the bruise of a wound and the blows in the innermost parts of the belly therefore cleanse away evil, because external discipline washes away faults, while compunction pierces the expanded mind with the punishment of repentance.

But the two differ in this respect: the wounds of blows cause pain, whereas the lamentations of compunction bring savor. Those afflict and torment while they wound; these restore while they afflict. Through the former there is sorrow in affliction; through the latter there is joy in sorrow. Nevertheless, because compunction itself wounds the mind, he not inappropriately calls compunction “discipline.”

### 41. The righteous are affected by compunction in four ways, as is shown by the examples of Paul and David

There are four qualities by which the soul of righteous men is powerfully affected in compunction. It is affected when they remember their sins and consider where they were; when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments and asking themselves where they will be, they reflect; when, attentively considering the evils of the present life, they sorrowfully recognize where they are; or when, contemplating the good things of the heavenly homeland, they grieve because they have not yet attained them and perceive where they are not.

Paul remembered his sins and afflicted himself over the state in which he had been when he said: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

Again, carefully weighing the divine judgment, he feared that he would be in an evil state in the future, saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

He also considered the evils of the present life when he said: “While we are in this body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6).

**[Note:]** *Hoc* (“this”) is absent in the Norman manuscripts and Colbertinus. And: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:23).

Again, he considered the good things of the eternal homeland when he said: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know just as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

Contemplating the good things of this house, he says to the Ephesians: “That you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe” (Ephesians 1:18).

Blessed Job, considering the evils of the present life, says: “Human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 6:1).

**[Note:]** Colbertinus, Uticensis, and other witnesses read *vita hominis* (“the life of man”). Hence David also says: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6). And although man walks in the image of God, yet he will be troubled in vain.

Again, contemplating the eternal homeland, weighing the evils in which he was and considering the good things in which he was not yet, David said: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Psalm 120:5). And: “I said in my alarm: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Psalm 30:23).

Raised up in ecstasy—which our translators properly called “alarm”—he saw that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes.

**[Note:]** The printed editions add *non* (“not”), which is omitted in the English manuscripts and ours.

After the vision of the inner light, which had flashed into his soul through the grace of contemplation with a ray of brightness, he returned to himself. Through the knowledge he had received, he discovered either what good things he lacked there or what evils he still possessed here.

For no one can fully behold the evils of the present life as they are unless he is already able to touch the good things of the eternal homeland through the taste of contemplation. Hence he recognized that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes. Raised up, he saw what, returning to himself, he lamented that he could not see here about himself.

### 42. The Effect of Compunction in the Perfect

This compunction is accustomed to affect the perfect soul in a more intimate way: it shakes off all bodily images that intrusively present themselves to it [Note: Vindoc. and Norm.: “strikes down”], and directs the eye of the heart to fix itself upon the very ray of the boundless light. For through the weakness of the body it has drawn these forms of bodily images inward to itself. But when perfectly compunct, it watches with the greatest care lest, while seeking the truth, imagination should deceive it with a circumscribed vision; and it rejects all images that confront it. Because it fell below itself through those images, it strives to rise above itself without them. And after being improperly scattered among many things, it endeavors to gather itself into one, so that, if it prevails by the great power of love, it may contemplate that which is one and incorporeal.

### 43. The Taste of Contemplation Affects the Mind Only in a Sudden Rapture; Hence Pious Groanings, Though Without the Fullness of Delight

For at times the soul is admitted to a certain unfamiliar sweetness of inward savor and, somehow suddenly breathed upon by an ardent spirit, is renewed. The more it tastes what it loves, the more eagerly it longs for it. [Note: Ebroic. and Vindoc.: “and longs to enter into this.”] It longs within itself for that which it inwardly perceives to taste sweet, because through love of that sweetness it has become despicable to itself in its own presence. And after it has been able, in whatever measure, to perceive it [Note: The same manuscripts, together with Utic., Pratel., and Becc.: “to receive it”], it discovers what it had been without it for so long.

It strives to cling to it, but its continuing weakness drives it back from its strength. And because it cannot contemplate its purity [Note: Thus Norm., with Vindoc., Colb., and others; the printed editions have “because it cannot be conformed to its purity”], it finds sweetness in weeping and in spreading out before itself the tears of its weakness as it falls back upon itself. For it cannot fix the eye of the mind upon that which it has briefly glimpsed within itself, because the very habit of its old condition compels it to go downward.

Meanwhile it pants and burns; it strives to rise above itself, but, overcome by weariness, falls back into its familiar darkness. Since, therefore, the soul in such a condition endures a severe struggle against itself [Note: We have restored *semetipsam* (“against itself”) here; the word had dropped out of the printed editions, although its omission makes for a more polished sense], and since all this controversy within us, when it affects us [Note: Recent editions read “when it afflicts us.” Not only is *afflicts* redundant, but it also destroys the sense; we have deleted it, following the Colbert, Norman, Vindoc., and other manuscripts], produces no slight pain—even though mixed with delight—Elihu, after saying that God speaks to us through a dream and that by his speech our ears are opened, rightly calls this same opening of the ears “discipline.” For the more deeply he affects and chastens us, the more the sound of inward understanding breaks forth to us through the hidden grace of his inspiration.

No one would weep outwardly over what he is, if inwardly he had not been able to perceive what he is not yet. For when we look upon ourselves as well fashioned, but deceived by a destructive consent into accepting the devil’s persuasion, we recognize within ourselves that one thing is what we have done and another what we have become: whole by our creation, but corrupted by guilt.

Therefore, once compunct, we desire to avoid what we have done, so that we may be restored to what we were made to be. Hence it appropriately follows:

## CHAPTER XXII [Al. XXII]

**VERSE 17.—“That he may turn a man away from the things he has done and free him from pride.”**

### 44. Through Compunction We Are Turned Away from Previously Committed Sins and Freed from Pride

For what has a human being done of himself except sin? [Note: Ebroic. and other Norm. manuscripts: “of his own property.”] And it is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10:15). It is therefore rightly said that when a person is turned away from the things he has done, he is freed from pride.

To grow proud against the Creator is to transgress his commandments by sinning, because such a person, as though shaking off the yoke of his dominion, refuses to remain subject to him through obedience. [Note: Thus Vindoc., Colbert., and others, as well as the old edition; recent editions have: “to whom he refuses to remain subject through disobedience.”]

But whoever desires to avoid what he has done recognizes what he was made by God and humbly returns to the order of his creation. Fleeing his own works, he loves himself as one made by God. [Note: The printed editions add “to be,” which we have deleted in accordance with the manuscripts.] Since eternal glory is received through this understanding and eternal punishments are avoided, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Rec. XIV]

**VERSE 18.—“Delivering his soul from corruption, and his life, so that it may not pass into the sword.”**

### 45. Thus the Soul Is Delivered from Corruption and from the Sword of Divine Judgment

Every sinner is compelled to pass from the corruption of vices here to the sword of punishments there, so that he may justly be tormented there by the very thing in which he wickedly delighted here.

It must therefore be noted that when God speaks to us through a dream, he first frees us from corruption and afterward from the sword. For he rescues from the vengeance of punishment there the life of the one whose mind here he withdraws from the pleasure of sin. Whoever, after being corrected here, has not been corrupted by the pollution of guilt need not fear there the sword of judgment.

It is therefore rightly said: “Delivering his soul from corruption, and his life, so that it may not pass into the sword.” To pass from corruption into the sword is to arrive, after sins have been committed, at the punishments that must be endured.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Vet. XXIII, Rec. XV]

**VERSE 19.—“He also rebukes him through pain upon his bed, and makes all his bones wither.”**

### 46. In the Present Life, Every Rest We Prepare for Ourselves Is Disturbed by Temptations; We Cannot Live in Any Retreat Without Temptations

In Sacred Scripture a bed, couch, or resting-place is sometimes understood as the pleasure of the flesh, sometimes as repose in good works, and sometimes as temporal rest. [Note: Norman manuscripts read “or a resting-place,” and so below.] For what else does the Lord say in the Gospel to a certain man who had been healed, “Rise, take up your pallet and go to your house” (John 5:8), except that the pallet signifies bodily pleasure?

He commands the man, once healed, to carry what he had lain upon when sick, because everyone who is still delighted by vices lies sick in the pleasures of the flesh. But once healed, he carries this where he had lain when sick [Note: The word “sick” is absent in Pratel., Becc., Utic., and other manuscripts], because, rescued from vices by divine assistance, he afterward endures the insults of that same flesh in whose desires he had previously rested.

Again, a bed or resting-place signifies repose in good works. Hence the Apostle Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Aeneas, may Jesus Christ heal you; rise and make your bed” (Acts 9:34). What does “Rise” mean except: “Abandon the evils you have committed”? And what does “Make your bed” mean except: “Perform works that will earn the reward in which you ought to rest”? Thus by rising he abandons what he has done, and by making his bed he finds what he may do.

The Prophet briefly embraces both points when he says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). To turn away from evil is to rise from the place where one lay; to do good is to prepare works of reward in which one ought to rest. Whoever turns away from evil but does not yet do good has indeed risen from the place where he lay, but has not yet prepared the place in which he ought to rest.

Again, a bed or resting-place is understood as temporal rest, as it is written: “You have turned his entire bed in his sickness” (Ps. 40:4). When someone, wearied by worldly cares, is moved by divine grace to abandon the laborious roads of this world, he begins to consider how he may escape the desires of the present life and rest from its labors. He then seeks for himself an order of the desired quiet and longs to find, as it were, a resting-place where he may cease from all his labors.

But because, while still placed in this life, a human being cannot live without temptations in any station or in any secluded retreat [Note: The same manuscripts read: “in any retreat to live without temptation”], often greater pain from temptation is found precisely in what is built for rest. Hence the Prophet rightly says: “You have turned his entire bed in his sickness.” It is as though he said: “Everything he prepared here for his rest, by a hidden judgment you have changed into a source of disturbance.” This is done by the gracious counsel of God [Note: *God* is omitted in Pratel.], so that during the time of this pilgrimage the life of the elect may be disturbed.

### [Vet. XXIV] 47. Here We Are Afflicted by God’s Excellent Counsel, Lest We Love the Way Instead of Our Homeland

The present life is the way by which we journey toward our homeland. Therefore here we are worn down by frequent disturbances through a hidden judgment, lest we love the way instead of our homeland.

Some travelers, when they happen to see pleasant meadows along the road, commonly delay their journey and turn aside from the straight path they had begun. The beauty of the journey slows their steps because it delights them.

Thus, for his elect who are journeying toward him, the Lord makes the road of this world harsh, lest, while someone is nourished by the rest of the present life as though by the pleasantness of the way, he should prefer to travel for a long time rather than arrive more quickly; lest, while delighted by the road, he forget what he desired in his homeland.

Since, therefore, all the rest we may have prepared for ourselves in this life is disturbed, it is rightly said: “He also rebukes him through pain upon his bed”—that is, in the rest of the present life he disturbs us either by the goads of temptation or by the affliction of the scourge.

Often, when the human mind has remained for even a short time without temptation in good pursuits, it is soon lifted up by those very pursuits in which it rests while exerting itself, and by the very virtues through which it strives to grow, as it feels itself making progress. Therefore, by the loving moderation of our Ruler, it is afflicted by the impulse of temptation, so that the pride arising from its progress may itself be restrained.

For this reason, after saying, “He also rebukes him through pain upon his bed,” he appropriately added [Rec. XVI]: “And makes all his bones wither.”

### 48. Through Temptation We Learn What We Can Do by Our Own Strength and What We Can Do by Divine Gift

In Sacred Scripture we understand “bones” as virtues, as it is written: “The Lord preserves all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. 33:21). This is not said of bodily bones, [Note: Ebroic. and Vindoc.: “but of virtues,”] but of the powers of the mind.

For certainly we know that the bodily bones of many martyrs were broken, and that the persecutors of the Lord broke the legs of the thief to whom it was said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), just as they did those of the other thief on the cross.

When, therefore, he rebukes through pain upon the bed and makes all the bones wither, this means that when we are afflicted by the scourge of temptation in the rest we prepare for ourselves from this world, we who may perhaps have become inflated by our virtues are weakened by weariness from the knowledge of our weakness.

When we progress toward God as we desire, if no temptation assailed our progress, we would believe ourselves to possess some great strength. But by the dispensation of heaven it is brought about that, because in our progress we forget our weakness, we recall it when tempted. In our progress we learn what we are through divine gift; in temptation we learn what we are through our own strength.

Yet this temptation would carry us away completely if heavenly protection did not preserve us. It strikes but does not break; it pushes but does not move; it shakes but does not overthrow. Thus we learn that the fact that we are shaken comes from our weakness, while the fact that we stand comes from divine gift. [Note: Norman and Vindoc. manuscripts read “that which we suffer” in place of “that we are shaken.”]

And because the soul, conscious of some good, often feeds upon a certain delight when it recalls its virtues to mind and, as though rejoicing in its own fullness, grows fat, it is rightly said that the bones wither when temptation strikes. For when our own weakness is recognized through the questioning of temptation, all that fat and flourishing rejoicing in our powers is suddenly dried up by the sorrow of anxiety. We who, by reflecting on our good deeds, believed ourselves to be of some importance begin, when struck, to fear that we are about to perish at any moment.

Then all the joy of our good deeds is turned into fear of punishments. Then we discover that we are wicked, though shortly before we believed ourselves holy. The mind wastes away; the eyes are stunned; everything that previously smiled upon us in prosperity vanishes. Even light becomes distasteful, and only the darkness of sorrow pours through the soul. Nothing that gives pleasure is seen; whatever presents itself is sad.

Hence it appropriately follows:

## CHAPTER XXV [Rec. XVII]

**VERSE 20.—“Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and food formerly desirable to his soul.”**  
[Note: Vindoc.: “was abominable to him.”]

### 49. In Sacred Scripture Bread Signifies Many Things: (1) Christ; (2) Grace; (3) Sacred Doctrine; (4) the Preaching of Heretics; (5) Support for the Present Life; (6) the Delight of Human Pleasure

It is as though he openly says: “The afflicted mind perceives that whatever previously satisfied it gently and willingly has been turned into bitterness.”

In Sacred Scripture “bread” is sometimes understood as the Lord himself, sometimes as spiritual grace, sometimes as instruction in divine doctrine, sometimes as the preaching of heretics, sometimes as support for the present life, and sometimes as the delight of human pleasure. [Note: In the Gussanville edition there is here a large lacuna, which we have recognized with the help of manuscripts and old editions.]

Bread signifies the Lord, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

Again, bread signifies the grace of a spiritual gift, as it is said through the Prophet: “He who stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed and closes his eyes so as not to see evil—he shall dwell on high; the heights of the rocky strongholds are his refuge; bread shall be given him” (Isa. 33:15).

What does it mean to stop one’s ears so as not to hear of bloodshed except not to consent to sins prompted by the passions, which arise from blood and flesh? And what does it mean to close one’s eyes so as not to see evil except not to approve whatever is opposed to uprightness?

“He shall dwell on high,” because although the flesh still holds him below, he has already fixed his mind on things above. “The heights of the rocky strongholds are his refuge,” because whoever tramples underfoot the base desires of earthly conduct raises himself toward the heavenly homeland through the examples of the fathers who preceded him. [Note: All printed editions have, erroneously, “things set before him.”]

And because he is satisfied with spiritual grace through the gift of contemplation, it is appropriately added: “Bread shall be given him”—that is, he receives the refreshment of spiritual grace because, by hoping for heavenly things, he suspends himself from things below.

Hence the Lord says through David concerning the holy Church: “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. 131:15), because in her the minds of the humble are filled with the refreshment of spiritual gifts.

Again, bread signifies instruction in divine doctrine, as it is said through the Prophet: “You who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread” (Isa. 21:14).

Those who dwell in the land of the south are those who, placed in the holy Church, are breathed upon by the love of the heavenly Spirit. The fugitive is one who desires to escape the evils of this world.

Therefore let the one who dwells in the land of the south meet the fugitive with bread—that is, let the one who is already filled with the Holy Spirit within the Church console, through instruction and speech, the person striving to escape his evils. To meet the fugitive with bread means to offer the food of sacred doctrine to one who fears eternal punishments, at one time restraining his pride through fear and at another reviving his fear through encouragement.

Since the refreshment of Scripture is appropriately understood as bread, the same Prophet says to the Jews who cling only to the letter: “Why do you weigh out silver and not for bread?” (Isa. 55:2). It is as though he said: “You weigh the sacred words, but not for refreshment, because while you preserve only the outward form of the letter, you lose the richness of inward refreshment from spiritual understanding.” Hence he appropriately adds there: “And your labor not for satiety” (ibid.).

### [Vet. XXVI]

Again, bread signifies the preaching of heretics, as Solomon’s woman who bears the figure of a heretical church and summons the foolish says: “Eat gladly the hidden breads” (Prov. 9:17). Or, as it is written in our translation: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasing.”

There are some heresies that are afraid to preach openly what they believe. Among the minds of the weak, they season their words all the more heavily the more reverently they seem to hide them. [Note: Turon. reads *condunt* (“hide”) in place of “season.”] Hence it is not without reason that it is said: “Eat gladly the hidden breads.” For hidden words of heretics taste all the better to wretched hearts because they are not held in common with the rest.

Again, bread signifies support for the present life, as Jacob, when departing for Laban, says: “Lord God, if you give me bread to eat and clothing to wear” (Gen. 28:20). Likewise, in the Gospel the Lord says to the crowds following him: “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled” (John 6:26).

They had been filled with seven loaves. Through their person the Lord condemns those within the holy Church who, drawing near to the Lord through sacred orders, seek in those same orders not the merits of virtues but the supports of the present life. They do not consider what they ought to imitate by living, but what advantages will satisfy them when received.

To follow the Lord after being filled with bread is to have taken temporal nourishment from the holy Church. It is not to seek the Lord for the sake of signs, but to seek him for the sake of bread—to cling to the office of religion not for the increase of virtues but for the pursuit of material support. [Note: Most Norm. manuscripts: “it is to seek the Lord not for signs but for bread, for the office of religion.”]

Again, bread signifies the delight of human pleasure. Thus the Prophet Jeremiah, lamenting the degraded conduct of the synagogue, says: “All her people groan, seeking bread; they have given their precious things for food to restore the soul” (Lam. 1:11).

The people groan while seeking bread when the wicked multitude is afflicted because it is not satisfied according to its desire with the delight of the present life. It gives all its precious things for food because it inclines the virtues of the mind toward the appetite for passing pleasure. It strives to restore the soul because it attempts to satisfy its perverse desires.

Therefore, immediately afterward, from the voice of that elect multitude, he appropriately adds: “See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become contemptible” (Lam. 1:11). The people of God become contemptible when, as the number of the wicked increases, they pursue in them not what is sublime and heavenly but what is rejected and earthly.

### [Vet. XXVII] 50. Whatever Gives Pleasure Is Made Bitter by the Force of Temptation

What else, then, does Elihu call bread except the delight of the present life? After expressing the force of temptation, he immediately adds: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and food formerly desirable to his soul,” because everything that previously tasted sweet from the prosperity of life afterward becomes bitter through the force of temptation.

Sometimes whatever joy or virtue seemed to support us is suddenly lost in the fear of temptation, and, as though emptied of those same virtues, the sorrowful mind is possessed by grief alone. When it is affected by the impulse of temptation with somewhat greater force, it cannot exercise the strength customary to it. It grieves as though that strength had already been lost; and, sensing itself empty of itself, it recognizes its weakness in its very emptiness. [Note: The Roman edition of Sixtus V has “from its own vanity.” The English and our manuscripts have “from its own emptiness.”]

Thus it is immediately broken away from every delight. Rejecting the food of its former joy, it is satisfied by the grief that alone it willingly seeks.

When prosperity in living smiles upon a person, everyone grows cheerful, and cheerfulness itself refreshes the mind like desirable food. But when the person is struck by a temptation that presses somewhat more heavily, all joy is rejected from the mind through the disgust of sorrow—the mind that had previously rejoiced as though satisfied by that same joy.

Since, therefore, a tempted person rejects every food of delight from the mouth of the heart, and is pleased to do nothing but recognize and lament himself [Note: Thus Ebroic., Vindoc., and others; the printed editions have: “and nothing else pleases him”], it is rightly said: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and food formerly desirable to his soul.”

### 51. The Usefulness of Temptations and Scourgings

But, as we said above (no. 48), we are permitted to be tempted by the governance of a hidden dispensation so that, while we progress in virtue through divine gift, we may also remember what we are through our own weakness; and while we produce works of virtue through receiving the gift, we may offer the sacrifice of humility through remembering our weakness.

Sometimes, after our strength has advanced, not only do vices tempt us, but scourgings also chastise us. When we are tempted by vices, God deals with us through a loving dispensation so that we may not be lifted up by the virtues through which we progress. But when we are worn down by scourgings, we are warned by afflictions that rebuke us not to be deceived by the flattering world.

Vices, when they tempt us, humble us as we make progress in virtue; scourgings, when they tempt us, uproot the pleasures of this world rising in the heart. Through tempting vices we learn what we are; through striking scourgings we learn what we must flee in this world. [Note: Norman manuscripts read: “what we are of ourselves; through striking scourgings, what we should think of this world.”] By the former we are restrained lest we be lifted up inwardly; by the latter we are compressed lest we desire anything outwardly.

While we are therefore in this life, it is necessary that we be worn down by scourgings and at times tempted by vices. Whether in the labor of scourgings or in the struggle against vices, not only does our weakness become known to us, but we also recognize how greatly we have advanced in virtue.

### [Rec. XVIII]

No one recognizes his strength in peace. If wars are absent, the tests of virtue do not appear. The soldier who boasts that he is strong in peace is unprepared.

### [Vet. XXVIII]

Since, therefore, the merits of strength are often revealed through the adversities of scourgings, Elihu appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 21.—“His flesh shall be consumed, and the bones that were covered shall be laid bare.”**

### 52. No One Knows How Far He Has Advanced Except amid Adversity

When every outward pleasure is worn down beneath pressing scourgings, the bones of inward strength are laid bare. What else is meant here by “flesh” except carnal pleasure? And what else is signified by “bones” except the virtues of the soul?

Thus the flesh is consumed and the bones are laid bare, because when carnal pleasure is weakened by rebuking scourgings, the strong virtues that had previously lain hidden, as it were, beneath the flesh are revealed.

No one knows how far he has advanced except amid adversity. When prosperity is present, the proofs of strength cannot be seen. [Note: Vindoc. and most Norm. manuscripts: “the proofs of virtue cannot be discerned.”] Hence it is written elsewhere: “In the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and at night he declared it” (Ps. 41:9). For each person receives the grace of a heavenly gift in the tranquility of rest, but shows how much he has received in the adversity of disturbance.

Let the flesh therefore be consumed, so that the bones may be laid bare. [Note: Most manuscripts add, “and let them be laid bare.”] Let us be struck by paternal corrections [Note: The printed editions read “by paternal disturbances,” a reading found in no manuscript], so that we may recognize how far we have advanced. Through the Lord’s scourgings the fatness of carnal pleasure is worn down, but the bones of our virtues are revealed. Our outward beauty is disfigured by the adversity of this world, but what lay hidden within us is shown.

After the Apostles had been beaten, they were ordered not to speak any longer in the name of Jesus. Yet they rejoiced with great exultation that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus [Note: Turon. and Norm.: “to suffer insults on account of his name”], and they answered their adversaries with confidence: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29).

Behold: amid adversity the strength of faith shone forth more powerfully. Behold: the integrity of their flesh was cut, but the bones of their virtues were revealed.

Hence Wisdom says of them: “God tested them and found them worthy of himself” (Wis. 3:5). [Note: Vindoc.: “They were tested … in the adversity of blows, but they were found worthy in the exposure of their bones.” Baluz. and Colb.: “of the bones.”] They were tested by the adversity of blows, but were found worthy through the exposure of their bones.

That this was the testing applied to them through scourgings is openly declared there when it continues: “As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as a sacrificial burnt offering he accepted them” (Wis. 3:6).

Since, therefore, everyone’s strength is revealed only through adversity, it is rightly said: “His flesh shall be consumed, and the bones that were covered shall be laid bare.” The flesh is consumed when everything weak and transient is worn down by scourgings. The bones are laid bare when through these things even what is strong but hidden within us is revealed.

But, as was also said above, in the adversity of temptation not only is the strength of fortitude uncovered, but human weakness is also recognized. The person who is tempted indeed shows how far he has advanced through God, but in the affliction of the scourgings he also recognizes how weak he is in himself. For not only are the bones laid bare, but the flesh is also consumed. Therefore it appropriately follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Rec. XIX]

**VERSE 22.—“His soul shall draw near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.”**  
[Note: Baluz., Utic., and other Norm. manuscripts: “shall draw near”; likewise below.]

### 53. When Corruption Seems to Draw Near More Closely in Temptation, We Are Delivered from It

The soul of each just person who is tempted is said to draw near to corruption when, lest virtue should lift it up, it is compelled through scourgings to feel what it is from its own weakness. [Note: Vindoc. and most manuscripts read “to know” instead of “to feel.”]

It draws near to corruption because it recognizes that, by its own strength, it is close to destruction [Note: Ebroic. and Vindoc. read “close to corruption”], so that it may attribute to the Lord, not to itself, the fact that it remains far from destruction. It draws near to things that bring death because, from the weakness of the flesh, it sees itself close to sins that bring death. Through divine gift it is made farther from them precisely in proportion as, by its own merits, it discovers itself to be near them.

David had drawn near to corruption through contemplation of his condition when he said: “Remember, O Lord, that we are dust; human beings are like grass, their days” (Ps. 102:15).

Paul had likewise drawn near to things that bring death through contemplation of his own weakness when he said: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:23).

To draw near, therefore, to corruption and to things that bring death [Note: Some witnesses read “or to things that bring death”] means, after considering the weakness of one’s humanity, to see oneself as a sinner by one’s own merits and to possess no arrogance concerning one’s own strength.

For what are we if we are abandoned by the protection of our Creator? This protection is considered less necessary if it is always possessed. Yet it is often usefully withdrawn, so that a person may be shown how utterly he is without it.

The hand of God therefore sometimes makes us known to ourselves through adversity—the hand that also, without our knowing it, carries us in prosperity. When deprived of it, we begin to fall, yet while being helped we are held back. Thus our trembling in the fall becomes instruction, and our remaining upright becomes protection.

### 54. We Must Never Presume upon Our Own Strength

Let no one, therefore, consider himself possessed of any virtue, even when he is able to act bravely. For if divine protection abandons him, he is suddenly overwhelmed in weakness precisely where he had boasted of standing firmly.

What else is the meaning of the man of God who was sent to prophesy against the altar of Samaria? In the presence of the king he exercised the authority of a free voice, and miraculously stiffened the king’s outstretched arm into rigidity [Note: Most printed editions have “miserably.” But the manuscripts Baluz., Colb., Turon., Vindoc., Norm., English, and the old Basel edition have “miraculously”], though soon afterward he mercifully restored it to health (1 Kings 13:4). In the house of the king he had refused the invitation to eat, because he had obeyed the Lord’s command not to eat on the way.

Yet on that same journey he was both deceived into eating and, after eating, perished. What do we gather from this by careful reflection—or, so to speak, what should we suspect with fear—except that perhaps he was silently boasting within himself that he had despised the king for the sake of the divine commands? [Note: We have restored “therefore” from the manuscripts; its omission leaves the sense mutilated in other editions.]

Thus he was immediately shaken from his inward firmness, and the fault slipped into his action from the same source from which pride had arisen in his heart. Deceived by the words of the false prophet, he learned that what had enabled him to resist the king’s words had not been his own strength.

It was fitting that he received the sentence of death from the mouth of the one whose deception caused him to depart from the command of life, so that he might truly receive punishment from the same source through which he had carelessly incurred guilt.

Since, therefore, divine grace guards each of its elect more carefully by educating him precisely when it seems to abandon him by striking him, it is rightly said: “His soul shall draw near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.” The more a person sees through adversity that he is near death by his own strength, the more firmly he lives in all that he does bravely by fleeing to the stronghold of divine hope.

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

The eleven concluding verses of chapter 33 and the first eighteen verses of chapter 34 are expounded; excellent teachings are given concerning Christ the mediator, contemplation, the order of conversion, and the pastoral office.

[Col. 0287]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0287A]

### 1. All People, Even the Elect, Are Subject to Temptations

Elihu, indicating the force of the heavenly dispensation, introduced the striking of each elect person by saying: “His soul shall draw near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.” [Note: Colb. and Baluz.: “the exalted one”; this is evidently an error.]

While he presents one tempted human being, he shows the temptation in which the whole human race is placed. While he recounts what happens specifically in individuals, he clearly reveals what happens generally in everyone. He expressed the temptation of certain people—of individuals in particular—in such a way that it may also be understood universally of all.

For the entire race of the elect is afflicted in this life by weariness with its labor. Therefore, immediately afterward, he adds a universal remedy for this universal affliction, saying:

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0287B]

**CHAPTER 33, VERSES 23–24.—“If there is for him an angel speaking, one among the similar ones, to announce a person’s uprightness, he will have mercy on him.”**
[Rec. II.] **2. Christ, God and man, intercedes with God for human beings. The economy of the Incarnation.**—For who is this angel, if not the one of whom it is said through the prophet: “Angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9:6, according to the Septuagint)? Since in the Greek language *to evangelize* means “to announce,” the Lord is called an angel because he announces himself to us. And he rightly says: “If there is for him an angel speaking,” because, as the Apostle says, he “also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). But let us hear what he speaks for us: “One of the similar ones.”

It is the practice of medicine sometimes to cure like with like, and sometimes opposites with opposites. [Col. 0287C] [Note: [Col. 0287D] Utic., Pratell., the old Paris and Basel editions: “for often hot things with hot, but often cold things with hot,” etc.] For often it is accustomed to heal hot things with hot, cold things with cold; but often cold things with hot, and hot things with cold. Therefore, when our physician came to us from above and found us oppressed by such great illnesses, he applied to us something similar and something contrary. He came to human beings as a human being, but to sinners as a righteous man. He agreed with us in the truth of nature, but differed from us [Note: [Col. 0287D] Thus Vindoc., Baluz., Colb., and Norm.; the editions have *pro rigore*, “in strictness,” [Col. 0288D].] in the strength of righteousness.

For a vicious human being could not be corrected except by God. Yet the one who corrected him had to be seen, so that, by offering a model for imitation, he might change his former wickedness. But God could not be seen by a human being; therefore he became human, so that he could be seen, and people might change the life of their former wickedness. [Vet. II.] Thus the just and invisible God appeared as a visible human being like us, so that, while he healed through righteousness by being seen in what was similar, [Col. 0287D] and while he agreed with our condition in the truth of our kind, he might oppose our sickness by the power of his art.

**3. When the Lord came in the flesh, he assumed neither guilt from vice nor punishment from necessity.**—Since, therefore, when the Lord came in the flesh, he did not assume our guilt from vice or punishment from necessity—for, being polluted by no stain of sin, he could not be held by the condition of our guilt, and therefore, having trampled down every necessity of our death, he freely accepted it when he wished—it is rightly said that this angel speaks for the tempted human being “one of the similar ones,” because he was neither born as the rest are born, nor died as they die, nor was raised as they are raised.

For he was conceived not through sexual union but through the coming of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:33). In his birth, his mother’s womb was both fruitful and remained undefiled. Again, all of us die unwillingly, because the condition of our guilt constrains us to pay the debt of punishment; but he, because he was joined to no guilt, was compelled to submit to no punishment. Yet because he subjected our guilt by ruling over it [Note: [Col. 0288D] Turon.: “by condemning it.”], he assumed our punishment by showing mercy, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). He also said beforehand: [Note: [Col. 0288D] Pratell. and other Norman witnesses: “No one will take it away.”] “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.”

Again, he was not raised as the rest are, because our resurrection has been postponed until the end of the age, whereas his was celebrated on the third day. We rise through him, but he rose through himself. For he who was God did not, like us, need another by whom he might be raised. His resurrection therefore differs from ours in this respect: we do not rise through ourselves, as he did. Because we are simply human beings, we need assistance from above in order to rise; but he, as God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, manifested the power of that resurrection, although he alone experienced it in his humanity. [Col. 0288C]

[Vet. III.] Since, therefore, the Lord was truly born, truly died, and truly raised, yet in all things differs from us by the greatness of his power, while agreeing with us only in the truth of his nature, it is rightly said that this angel speaks for us “one of the similar ones.” For although in all his works he surpasses us by immeasurable power, in one respect—namely, in the truth of his form—he does not differ from us.

**4. He speaks to the Father for us when he shows himself to be like us.**—He speaks to the Father for us by showing himself to be like us. For his speaking, or interceding, consists in demonstrating that he himself is human for human beings. And after saying, “He speaks one of the similar ones,” he immediately adds: “To announce the righteousness of the human being.” [Note: [Col. 0288D] Vindoc. and Norm.: “speaking.”] For unless he became like human beings, a righteous human being would not appear before God. From the point at which he deigned to assume our weakness, he announces our righteousness. [Col. 0288D]

That hostile persuasion had polluted all of us from the very root in the contagion of guilt (Gen. 3:5), and there was no one who, speaking before God for sinners, could appear free from sin, because the same guilt equally enveloped all who had been born from the same mass (Rom. 5:12). Therefore the Father’s Only-Begotten came to us and assumed from us a nature without committing guilt. He had to be without sin if he was to intercede for sinners, because he would not cleanse the contagion of another’s pollution if he himself bore his own.

It is therefore rightly said that, in the fact that he appeared like us, [Note: [Col. 0289D] We have supplied from the English and our manuscripts the word *nobis*, “to us,” absent from the editions.] he announced righteousness to human beings. By interceding for sinners, he showed himself to be a righteous human being who could obtain mercy for others. The text continues:

## CHAPTER III [Rec. III]

[Col. 0289B] **VERSE 24.—“He will have mercy on him and will say: Deliver him, so that he may not descend into corruption; I have found one in whom I may be propitious.”**

**5. Christ alone delivered us and made God propitious. Strength arising from humility.**—The mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, has mercy on a human being in that he assumed the form of a human being (1 Tim. 2:5; Phil. 2:7). In this mercy he says to the Father on behalf of the redeemed human being: “Deliver him, so that he may not descend into corruption.” As we have already said, [Note: [Col. 0289D] This passage appears in later editions as follows: “His saying is to deliver the human being, to demonstrate the human being’s free nature.” Nothing could be more obscure than this. With the help of manuscripts and the old editions, we have restored the text in such a way that everything is clear: the meaning is that Christ said to the Father concerning fallen humanity, “Deliver him,” when, by assuming human nature, he demonstrated it to be free.] his saying is “Deliver the human being”: by assuming human nature, he demonstrated it to be free. From the flesh he assumed, he also showed that flesh free which he redeemed.
