That redeemed flesh is, of course, what we are, who are bound by knowledge of our guilt. [Note: [Col. 0289D] Thus in Colb., Ebroic., and the other Norman witnesses and old editions; where the more recent editions read *qui conditione*, “who by condition.” Baluz. has *cogitatione*, “by thought,” instead of *cognitione*, “by knowledge.”] But we are freed by the righteousness of so great a Mediator, as he himself says: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

And it is rightly said on behalf of this redeemed human being: “He may not descend into corruption.” [Vet. IV.] Earlier it had been said: “His soul will draw near to corruption”; afterward it is said: “He may not descend into corruption.” It is as though he were saying: Since, by recognizing his weakness, he does not fail to understand that he is near corruption, for that reason let him not descend into the destruction of corruption. He would rightly descend into corruption if he judged himself to be far from corruption by his own strength. But because he has humbly approached corruption, he ought to be mercifully delivered from it, so that he may be strong against the vices that attack him precisely because he recognizes himself to be weak by his own merits.

For whoever exalts himself above himself is weighed down by the very burden of his pride; and he plunges himself into the depths to the degree that, rushing into the vice of pride, he has distanced himself from the one who is truly exalted. He desires the lowest things all the more because he has judged himself joined to the highest, as it is said through the prophet to the soul that exalts itself: “The more beautiful you are, descend and lie with the uncircumcised” (Ezek. 32:19). For everyone who neglects to consider the ugliness of his weakness but, through the arrogance of pride, attends to the glory of his virtue descends from the very place where he is more beautiful. By exalting himself on account of his merits, he falls into the depths of destruction from the place where he judged himself glorious. [Note: [Col. 0290D] The editions read “more grievously into the depths”; Colb. has “more inwardly into one [depth].” We follow the Baluz., Vindoc., and Norman manuscripts.] Descending, he sleeps with the uncircumcised, because in eternal death he perishes with the other sinners.

Since, therefore, this human being humbly recognized himself to be near corruption, it is rightly said of him: “Deliver him, so that he may not descend into corruption,” so that he may escape punishment all the more because he did not turn his eyes toward guilt. [Note: [Col. 0290D] The editions read: “does not turn away from guilt,” which is nonsensical and more foreign to the holy Doctor’s thought. Our reading is found in the English and Gallican manuscripts.]

Since there was no one whose merits could have made the Lord propitious to us, the Father’s Only-Begotten, assuming the form of our weakness, appeared alone as righteous, so that he might intercede for sinners. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Vindoc., Pratel., and others: “interceding.”] [Col. 0289B]

**6. No human being appeared before God as a righteous intercessor for human beings.**—And the angel, speaking on behalf of this redeemed human being, rightly says: “I have found one in whom I may be propitious to him.” It is as though the mediator of God and human beings were openly saying: Since there was no human being who could appear before God as a righteous intercessor for human beings, I made myself human in order to make God propitious to human beings; and, by presenting myself as a human being, I found one in whom I might justly make God propitious to human beings. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Ebroic.: “in which righteous human being I might make him propitious to human beings, I have found.”]

And because, by assuming weakness, the Lord endured our punishment in dying and changed our corruption in rising again, this angel rightly adds the scourges of our mortality and has mercy on them, saying:

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0290C] **VERSE 25.—“His flesh is consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth.”**

**7. When we departed from God, we found nothing except what would afflict us.**—When the first human being departed from God, we were driven away from the joys of paradise and fell into the misery of this mortal life. We committed a grave guilt through the serpent’s persuasion (Gen. 3:23), and we experience the punishment of our retribution. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Pratel.: “we experience the punishment of our retribution.”] Having fallen here, we found nothing apart from God except what would afflict us.

And because we followed the flesh through the sight of our eyes, we are scourged by that very flesh which we placed before the commands of God. In it we daily endure groaning, in it torment, in it death, so that by a wonderful ordering the Lord might turn into punishment for us the very thing by which we committed guilt. The administration of punishment would not arise from anywhere other than the source of sin, [Note: [Col. 0290D] Vindoc., Norman, and other witnesses: “by a wonderful dispensation.”] so that by the bitterness of that flesh the human being might be instructed unto life—the flesh whose delight led him through pride to death. [Col. 0290D]

**8. Christ delivered us from the punishments of carnal life and renewed us.**—Since, therefore, the human race was oppressed by innumerable punishments of carnal life, but with the coming of our Redeemer both the vices of our corruption and its torments were destroyed, let it be said of the redeemed human being: [Vet. V, Rec. IV.] “His flesh is consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth.”

It is as though he were saying: He has been cast down by the punishment of his mortality into a certain old age of his former state; “let him return to the days of his youth,” that is, let him be renewed in the integrity of his former life, [Note: [Col. 0291D] The more recent editions: “so that he may not remain where he”; we have followed Vindoc., Turon., Ebroic., and the other Norman witnesses.] so that he may not remain where he fell, but, having been redeemed, may return to that for the attainment of which he was created.

Sacred Scripture often uses “youth” for newness of life. Hence it is said to the coming bridegroom: “Young women have loved you” (Song 1:3); that is, the souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism, who do not waste away in the practices of the old life but are adorned by the conduct of the new human being. That old age of the former human being, wasting away amid vices, was mourned by the one who said: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:7). Conversely, another, urging rejoicing in virtues, says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccl. 11:9). It is as though he were saying: Let every strong person rejoice in his renewal; that is, let him establish his joy not in the pleasure of the old life but in the virtue of a new way of life.

Since we are recalled to this strength of newness not by our own powers but through the intervention of the Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0291D] Vindoc., Ebroic., and several others: “but we are renewed through the intervention of the Mediator.”], let the angel pray for this scourged human being: “Let him return to the days of his youth.” And because, when our Redeemer intercedes with the Father for us, we too, having shaken off the torpor of our former life [Note: [Col. 0291D] Pratel. and Vindoc.: “of the old life.”], are kindled with a thirst for prayer [Note: [Col. 0292D] Ebroic., Vindoc., and several others: “to the state of prayer.”], it is fittingly added concerning this redeemed human being: [Col. 0291C]

## CHAPTER V

**VERSE 26.—“He will entreat God, and he will be favorable to him.”**

**9. By praying for us, Christ kindles us to pray.**—He first speaks of the angel’s request and afterward of the human being’s, because unless the Lord himself, interceding with the Father through his Incarnation, first sought life for us, our insensibility would never rouse itself to ask for those things that are eternal. His prayer in the Incarnation came first, so that the awakening of our torpor might follow.

[Vet. VI, Rec. V.] Since, after temptations, and often after immense bitterness, the light of truth breaks forth within our mind in hidden joy, it is rightly added concerning this tempted and praying human being:

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0291D]

**THE SAME.—“And he will see his face in jubilation.”**

**10. Two kinds of compunction: one of sorrow, the other of joy, bringing forth tears. From this arises ineffable joy.**—It was said above (Book XXIII, no. 40 and following) how God afflicts us by making himself known; now it is said how, while making himself known, he gladdens us. A person is moved to compunction in one way when, looking inward, he is terrified by fear of his evils; but in another way when, beholding heavenly joys [Note: [Col. 0292D] Vindoc.: “when he beholds eternal joys.”], he is strengthened by a certain hope and security. The former compunction brings forth sorrowful tears, while the latter brings forth joyful tears.

For “jubilation” is said to occur when the mind conceives an ineffable joy that can neither be hidden nor disclosed in words, yet is revealed through certain movements, although it cannot be expressed in any precise form. Hence the prophet David, observing that the souls of the elect conceive such great joy in their minds that they cannot disclose it in speech, says: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88:16). He does not say, “that speaks,” but “that knows,” because jubilation can indeed be known by understanding, [Note: [Col. 0292D] Vindoc.: “but expressed”; *sed*, “but,” is absent from Colb. and Baluz.] but cannot be expressed in words.

Through it one experiences what lies beyond experience. And when the consciousness of the one experiencing it scarcely suffices to contemplate this, how could the tongue of the one speaking suffice to express it? Since, therefore, the light of truth insinuating itself into our hearts sometimes makes us sorrowful by displaying strict justice, and sometimes makes us joyful by opening inner delights, after the bitterness of temptations and the mourning of tribulations it is fittingly added: “He will see his face in jubilation.”

**11. One does not reach that state unless the mind has first been purified by the fire of tribulation.**—The fire of tribulation is first sent into our mind because of its consideration of its own blindness, so that every rust of vices may be burned away. Then, when the eyes of the heart have been cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened to them, so that we first purge by mourning what we have done and afterward contemplate more clearly, through joy, what we seek.

First, the darkness of evils is wiped away from the mind’s sharp vision by the intervening burning of sorrow; then the heart is suddenly illuminated by the flashing radiance of the boundless light. Having caught some glimpse of it, the mind is swallowed up in the joy of a certain security. [Note: [Col. 0292D] The Roman edition of Sixtus V has *severitatis*, “severity”; the English and our manuscripts have *securitatis*, “security.”] As though carried beyond the end of the present life and snatched above itself, it is somehow restored in a certain newness.

There the mind is sprinkled by an infusion of heavenly dew from an immense fountain; there it perceives that it is insufficient to contemplate that to which it has been snatched, and, while experiencing the truth, it sees that it does not see how great the truth itself is. It considers itself farther from that truth the more closely it approaches it, because unless it saw it in some fashion, it would in no way feel that it was unable to see it.

**12. In contemplation, the soul, struck back by divine light, slips back to itself. Contemplation is not a solid and abiding vision.**—When the effort of the soul is directed toward that vision, it is struck back by the flashing immensity surrounding it. For that immensity itself fills all things and surrounds all things. Therefore our mind cannot expand sufficiently to comprehend the boundless surrounding, because the narrowness of its own limitation constricts it. Thus it more quickly slips back to itself and, having caught sight, as it were, of certain traces of truth, is recalled to its own depths.

This vision, brought about through contemplation, is nevertheless not solid and abiding but, so to speak, something like an imitation of vision; it is called the face of God. [Col. 0293A] [Vet. VII.] Since we recognize anyone through his face, we appropriately call the knowledge of God his face. Hence, after Jacob had wrestled with the angel [Note: [Col. 0293D] Baluz. and Colb.: “had spoken.”], he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face” (Gen. 32:30). It is as though he were saying: “I have come to know the Lord, because he himself deigned to know me.” Paul testifies that this knowledge will be made complete at the end, saying: “Then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Since, therefore, after struggles of labor and after the waves of temptations, the soul is often suspended in ecstasy so that it may contemplate the knowledge of the divine presence—a presence it can indeed sense but cannot contain—it is rightly said after so many labors concerning this tempted human being: “He will see his face in jubilation.”

Since, however, the more each person contemplates heavenly things, the more he is corrected in his earthly activity, after the grace of contemplation the righteousness of action is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER VII

**THE SAME. “And he will restore to the human being his righteousness.”**

**13. In what sense our righteousness is called ours.**—Our righteousness is called ours, not because it originates from us as ours, but because it becomes ours through divine generosity, just as we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6:11; Luke 11:3). Behold, we call it ours, and yet we pray that it may be given. It becomes ours when it is received, yet it is God’s because it is given by him. Thus it is God’s by gift and truly becomes ours through reception.

In this passage, therefore, the Lord restores to the human being his righteousness—not one that he possessed from himself, but one that he received when he was created in order to possess it, and in which he did not wish to persevere after his fall. God will therefore restore to the human being that righteousness for which he was created: that he might delight in cleaving to God, fear his threatening judgment, and no longer believe the crafty serpent’s flattering promises.

**14. Every day the devil attempts to tear God’s words from human hearts.**—For what he did in paradise (Gen. 3:5), the ancient enemy does not cease to do every day. He strives to tear God’s words from human hearts and to plant in them the flattering deceptions of his fictitious promises. Every day he makes light of what God threatens and invites people to believe what he falsely promises.

For he falsely promises temporal things in order to make light in human minds of the punishments that God threatens as eternal. When he promises the glory of the present life, what else does he say than: “Taste, and you will be like gods”? [Vet. VIII.] It is as though he were openly saying: “Touch temporal desire, and appear exalted in this world.”

And when he tries to remove fear of the divine judgment, what else does he say than what he said to the first human beings: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” (Gen. 3:1). But because the human being, redeemed by divine generosity, received back the righteousness that he lost when he was first created, he now exercises himself with greater strength against the flatteries of crafty persuasion, because experience has taught him how much he ought to obey the command.

The one whom guilt once led to punishment is now restrained from guilt by his own punishment, so that he fears sinning all the more because, compelled by punishment, he himself now also condemns what he has done. Hence it continues:

## CHAPTER VIII [Rec. VI]

**VERSE 27.—“He will look upon human beings and will say: I have sinned.”**

**15. Whoever looks upon the examples of the holy Fathers understands that he is a sinner, which is the beginning of righteousness.**—He would not recognize himself as a sinner if he did not possess righteousness. For no one detects his crookedness unless he has begun to become upright. The person who is wholly perverse cannot even see what he is. But whoever understands that he is a sinner has already begun to be righteous in some measure, and he accuses what he did as an unrighteous person from the standpoint of whatever righteousness he possesses.

Through this accusation he begins to cling to God, condemning in himself what he perceives to displease God, while pronouncing a right judgment against himself. Having received his righteousness, therefore, this human being says: “I have sinned.”

It should be noted that the text first says: “He looks upon human beings,” and then adds: “And he will say: I have sinned.” Some people do not know that they have sinned because they do not pay attention to human beings. For if they considered human beings, they would more quickly recognize how far below human dignity they had fallen through sinning.

Although sacred Scripture sometimes uses “human beings” for those who think in a merely human way, as the Apostle says: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal?” (1 Cor. 3:3), and shortly afterward adds: “Are you not human beings?” nevertheless, it sometimes calls “human beings” those whom reason distinguishes from beasts, [Note: [Col. 0293D] Colbert. and Baluz.: “distinguishes by reason.”] that is, those whom it shows not to be worn down by the bestial movement of passions.

Through the prophet the Lord says to these: “You are human beings, and you are the flocks of my pasture” (Ezek. 34:31), because the Lord feeds those whom carnal pleasure does not affect in the manner of beasts. In contrast, those who succumb to carnal feeling are called not human beings but beasts. Thus it is said through the prophet concerning some who die in their sin: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). For beasts rotting in their dung means carnal human beings ending their life in the stench of lust.

They are shown not to be human beings but beasts, those of whom it is said through the prophet: “Each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5:8). And another prophet says of them: “Their flesh was like the flesh of asses, and their discharge like the discharge of horses” (Ezek. 23:20). Hence David says: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Since those supported by the rationality of righteousness are called human beings, while those who serve carnal pleasure are called irrational beasts, it is rightly said of this penitent: “He will look upon human beings and will say: I have sinned.” [Vet. IX.] It is as though it were said: He sees the examples of holy men and, weighing himself against them, discovers that he is unrighteous.

Whoever desires to understand fully what he is must look upon those who are what he is not, so that from the form of the good he may measure how deformed he is through abandoning the good. From those in whom goodness is fully present, he perceives what is lacking in himself; in their beauty he sees his own ugliness, which he can both endure and fail to perceive in himself.

One who wishes to judge darkness must look upon light, so that in the light he may see what he should think about the darkness that prevents him from seeing. For if a sinner, knowing nothing of the life of the righteous, looks only at himself, he cannot in any way understand that he is a sinner. He cannot see himself because, not knowing the brilliance of light, when he looks at himself he sees nothing but darkness.

We ought therefore to look upon the life of the righteous in order to discern our own with subtlety. Their appearance is set before us as a kind of model for imitation.

**16. The righteous are books from which we shall be judged.**—[Note: [Col. 0295D] Baluz., Colb., Norm. read thus. The editions, after “is set before us,” add: “because the living reading is the life of the good; hence.” The sense becomes more obscure through the addition of *quia*, “because,” and the altered punctuation. Necessity will sometimes compel the use of this expression—although it is less customary, or even recently coined—so that circumlocution may be avoided.] The life of the good is a living reading. Therefore, not without reason, these same righteous people are called books in sacred speech, as it is written: “The books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life, and the dead were judged from what was written in the books” (Rev. 20:12).

The book of life is the very vision of the Judge who is to come. In it, as though written down, is every commandment, because whoever sees him immediately understands, with conscience as witness, whatever he has not done.

The books are also said to be opened because the life of the righteous will then be seen, in whom the heavenly commandments are discerned as impressed by their works. “And the dead were judged from what was written in the books,” because, in the life of the righteous displayed before them, as though in the opening of books, they read the good that they themselves refused to do and are condemned by comparison with those who did it.

Therefore, lest anyone then mourn upon seeing in them what he did not do, let him now attend to what he may imitate in them. The elect indeed never cease to do this. [Note: [Col. 0296D] The editions, against the manuscripts, read “the better”;] They consider the life of those who are better and change the conduct of their inferior way of life.

[Vet. X.] **17. And the lilies among which we must feed.**—Hence, in the Song of Songs, the voice of the bridegroom says to the holy Church: “Your two breasts are like two young roes, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song 4:5).

What are the two breasts except the two peoples coming from the Jews and the Gentiles, who, in the body of the holy Church, are fixed through the pursuit of wisdom in the secret place of the heart? Those among these peoples who are elect are compared to young roes because, in humility, they understand themselves to be small and sinful; but when they run through charity, if any obstacles arising from temporality confront them, they cross over them, and by leaps of contemplation they climb to heavenly things.

To do this, they look upon the examples of the saints who went before them. Hence they are said to feed among the lilies. For what is signified by lilies except the life of those who truly say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (2 Cor. 2:15)? [Note: [Col. 0296D] Turon.: “unless their life is compared.”]

The elect, therefore, in order to attain the highest things, are nourished by seeing the fragrant and radiant life of the righteous. They already thirst to see the Lord; already they burn with the heat of charity to be satisfied by contemplation of him. But because, while placed in this life, they are not yet able to do so, they are meanwhile fed by the examples of the Fathers who preceded them.

Thus the time of this feeding among the lilies is fittingly defined when it says: “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” We need to be refreshed by the examples of the righteous only until, when the eternal day breathes upon us, we pass beyond the shadows of our present mortality. When the shadow of this temporal existence has inclined, after this mortality has passed, because we see the inner light of that day itself, we will no longer desire to be inflamed toward its love through the examples of others.

But now, because we cannot yet look upon him, it is supremely necessary that, by seeing the actions of those who followed him perfectly, we be stirred to imitate them. [Note: [Col. 0296D] Turon.: “let us imitate.”] Let us therefore behold how beautiful is the agility of those who follow, and see how ugly is the sluggishness of the idle. As soon as we look upon the deeds of those who act well, we judge ourselves, with intimate shame taking its revenge upon us. Shame immediately shakes the mind; guilt, rightly raging, immediately condemns it; and we are also deeply displeased that we may perhaps still take shameful pleasure in what is wrong.

**18. The righteous person is the temple of God; from seeing him we are confounded by our sins.**—Hence it is rightly said through Ezekiel: “Son of man, show the house of Israel the temple, so that they may be confounded by their iniquities, and measure its structure, and be ashamed of all that they have done” (Ezek. 43:10).

The temple of God is shown to the children of Israel for their confusion when the soul of each righteous person, which God inhabits by breathing into it, is displayed to sinners for their confusion in the brilliance of its holiness, so that in it they may see the good they neglect and in themselves blush at the evil they commit.

To measure the structure is to weigh the life of the righteous with careful attention. But while the structure is measured, it is necessary that we be ashamed of everything we have done, because the more carefully we examine the life of the good, the more severely we reject in ourselves everything that has been done wickedly.

The prophet is rightly told to show the temple. Since the sinner dissimulates in considering the uprightness of the righteous, let him at least recognize it through the voice of the preacher. To show the temple to sinners is to recount the works of the upright to those who are unwilling to consider them of their own accord.

Those who, as we have said, desire to be led to the highest things must always attend to the progress of those who are better, so that they may judge their own faults with greater strictness the more deeply they see in others what they ought to admire.

**19. The righteous themselves progress through considering other saints.**—But why should we say this about sinners, when we see that even those who practice righteousness are advanced by such a great dispensation (1 Cor. 12:8–11)?

One person receives the gift of knowledge, yet does not attain the virtue of remarkable abstinence. Another is girded with great virtue in abstinence, yet does not expand into the highest contemplation of knowledge. One person is able, through the spirit of prophecy, to know beforehand everything that will happen, yet through the grace of healing cannot relieve the evils of present affliction. Another, through the grace of healing, relieves the evils of present affliction, yet, because he does not possess the spirit of prophecy, does not know what will follow.

One person is already able to distribute many of his own possessions to those in need, yet cannot freely oppose those who act unjustly. Another boldly opposes those who act unjustly for God’s sake, yet refuses to give to the needy everything he possesses. One person, already restraining himself from idle speech, overcomes the wantonness of his tongue, yet does not perfectly trample down the goads of rising anger. Another has already perfectly subdued rising anger, yet still loosens his tongue into merriment.

What is this—that one person needs the good in which another excels, while the latter, though excelling in many things, sees that another possesses abundantly the good whose absence in himself he laments—except that, by a marvelous dispensation, it is arranged among us that, through what one person has and the other does not, one may be shown better than another [Note: [Col. 0297D] Ebroic. and others: “one better than the other.”], so that each may advance toward humility with greater fervor to the degree that he considers himself inferior to those who possess the good he lacks? Thus, while one person sees in another what he should admire, and the other in the first, distinct goods both restrain them from the height of pride and kindle them to pursue progress.

We gird ourselves with great concern for the care of our improvement when we see in others a virtue that we do not possess. Hence the prophet Ezekiel, after describing the flying creatures, added: “And I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion: Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his holy place, and the sound of the wings of the creatures striking one against another” (Ezek. 3:12). [Note: [Col. 0297D] Vindoc. and Baluz.: “from his place.”]

For what should we understand by the wings of the creatures except the virtues of the saints? While they despise earthly things, they are lifted up by flying toward heavenly things. [Vet. XI.] Hence it is rightly said through Isaiah: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength; they will take wings like eagles” (Isa. 40:31).

The flying creatures therefore strike one another with their wings, because the minds of the saints, in their desire for heavenly things, are stirred by considering one another’s alternating virtues. His wing strikes me who, by the example of his holiness, kindles me toward what is better. And I strike the neighboring creature with my wing if I sometimes show another a good work for imitation.

### 20. Confirmed by the example of the holy apostles Paul and Peter

But since we have said that the life of the saints is signified by these living creatures, let us raise the eyes of our mind to the creatures’ very flight and carefully consider how they rouse one another by the striking of their wings.

For Paul, when by laboring more vigorously in preaching he surpassed the concern of the other saints, so that he might restrain himself from elation [Col. 0298A] and nourish his strength in the lap of humility, mindful of his former cruelty and contemplating the innocence of all the apostles, said: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

And yet Peter, first among all those apostles, as though forgetting the primacy he had received and as though he himself possessed less understanding, marvels at Paul’s wisdom, saying: “As also our most beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as also in all his letters, speaking in them about these matters, among which there are some things difficult to understand” (2 Pet. 3:15).

Behold: Paul marvels at the apostles’ innocence; behold: the prince of the apostles marvels at Paul’s wisdom. [Old version XII.] What does this mean except that holy men, while each in turn places others before himself when considering their virtues, touch one another with the striking of their wings, so that they are raised to a higher flight precisely insofar as each more humbly sees in the other something to admire?

From this, then, we must gather how diligently we ought to contemplate the life of our superiors, who lie in the lowest places, if even those who have already been raised to such heights of holiness that they advance to greater things by the steps of humility still seek in others something to admire and imitate.

### 21. The reprobate always turn to examples of what is worse

But the reprobate do not know this, because they always press the eyes of their mind down toward the lowest things. Even if they sometimes enter the way of the Lord, they turn not to contemplate the footsteps of their superiors, but always to observe examples of those who are worse. They do not consider the lives of those before whom they might place themselves by humbling themselves [Col. 0298C], but of those over whom they might exalt themselves by their pride.

They look upon those who are worse, boasting that they themselves are better; and for this reason they cannot advance to better things, because they judge it sufficient for themselves that they surpass the worst. O wretched people! They proceed along the road while looking backward. By hope, indeed, they seem to put one foot forward; but by contemplating wicked people they stretch their eyes behind them.

They desire to appear upright, but they take a crooked rule for finding themselves. If they desire to know what they themselves are like, they ought not to have looked at those who were worse, but at the examples of those who were better. Thus they do not understand that they are sinners, because they do not attend to other human beings. For if they attended to human beings, they would discover how far they are separated from good people by their sins.

Concerning the penitent who therefore considers the examples of the good so that he may recognize how far he has withdrawn from goodness, it is rightly said:

## CHAPTER IX

**Verse 27.**—“He will look upon human beings and say: ‘I have sinned and truly transgressed, and I have not received what I deserved.’”  
[Note: [Col. 0297D] Pratel and others read “I have sinned,” followed by “and truly transgressed.”]

### 22. When they falsely confess themselves sinners, they wish to be adorned by the confession of sin, not humbled

[Note: [Col. 0298D] Pratel, Vindoc., and Turon.: “Even those who do not believe that they have sinned confess themselves sinners.”]

Even those who do not believe that they have sinned often confess themselves sinners. For it frequently happens that people openly admit that they are wicked, but when they hear others truly reproving their sins [Col. 0299A], they defend themselves with all their strength and try to appear innocent.

Therefore, whenever someone is like this, if he says that he has transgressed, he does not truly say it, since he asserts that he is a sinner not from the depths of his heart, but only in words. Because it is written, “The just person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. 18:17), this man wished to be adorned by the confession of sin, not humbled; by accusing himself, he sought to appear humble, not to be humble.

For if, by confessing his sin, he genuinely desired to be humble, he would not attack those who reproved him for committing the sin. Thus the just person, judging his own life by the examples of those who are better, recognizes from the depths of his heart that he is what he says. For he says: “I have sinned, and truly transgressed.” And concerning the very punishment he endures he adds: “And I have not received what I deserved” [Col. 0299B].

### 23. Whoever is scourged for his sins should recognize that he has been struck less than he deserves. Punishment asks us whether we truly acknowledge our guilt

For everyone who is placed under the scourge still considers his sins insufficiently if he thinks that he has been struck either as much as or more than he deserved. But this man, the more he considers the examples of those who are greater, the more strictly he examines himself; he recognizes that he has been struck less than he deserved, because in their righteousness he sees how serious his guilt was in going astray.

For this reason he does not regard what he suffers as severe, because he knows how strictly to weigh what he has done. It is very easy, however, for anyone to confess himself a sinner when he suffers nothing for his sin. We call ourselves wicked with confidence when we feel no punishment for our wickedness. In tranquillity we indeed call ourselves sinners, but when we are corrected for those very sins by the intervention of the scourge, we grumble.

Punishment therefore asks us whether we truly acknowledge our guilt. Thus the just man, because he considers his guilt strictly, should say even when placed under the scourge: “And I have not received what I deserved.” It follows:

## CHAPTER X

**Verse 28.**—“For he delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction.”

### 24. The harmony of prevenient grace and subsequent free will

Because our free will follows divine grace when it precedes us in a good action [Note: In the Vatican edition, Gilot, and most of the older editions, the reading is “we follow our free will.” But in the manuscripts of Turon., Norm., and others, we read “it follows.”], we are said to deliver ourselves when we consent to the Lord who delivers us.

Thus Paul, when he said, “I labored more abundantly than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10), immediately added, lest he seem to attribute his labors to himself: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

Because he had followed God’s prevenient grace in himself by free will [Note: The printed editions read, “even he himself by free will.” The manuscripts of Anglic. and Gallic., from which we take our reading, contradict this.], he appropriately adds, “with me,” so that he would neither be ungrateful for the divine gift nor remain unrelated to the merit of free will.

Concerning the person who, by recognizing his deliverer, consented to him, it is rightly said: “He delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction.” It follows:

**The same passage.**—“But, while living, he would see the light.”

The light, namely, of truth, which one dead in heart could not see. Or certainly, because the Lord said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), even the dead will see the light when all the unjust behold him coming to judgment in the form of his humanity.

But the person who, while living, looks upon the light is the one who, with the free eyes of his heart, contemplates him in the form of his divinity. It follows:

## CHAPTER XI [Recension VII]

**Verse 29.**—“God does all these things three times for each person.”

### 25. The elect are accustomed first to be affected by sorrow and afterward by joy, three times

Concerning this man who was tested and scourged, it had earlier been said: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life; his soul draws near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.” But later it was added: “He will entreat God, and he will be gracious to him; he will see his face with rejoicing, and he delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction, but, while living, would see the light.”

Thus, when these statements have already been collected and heaped together—above, the sorrow of bitterness, and below [Note: Vindoc. and most of the Norman manuscripts: “has been set below.”], the joy of security—immediately afterward it is said: “God does all these things three times for each person.”

It is as though he were saying: “What I have said once about one person is enacted three times for each person.” But we must carefully observe what these three occasions are on which each person is afflicted with anxiety and sorrow and immediately afterward recalled from sorrow to the security of joy.

For, as I have already said, the earlier passage narrated that a grievous sorrow first afflicts him and that afterward great joy raises him up. Therefore, if we pay close attention, we find these three occasions of sorrow and joy alternating in the mind of each of the elect in the following ways: conversion, testing, and death.

### 26. 1. In conversion, when the spirit calls from one side and the flesh recalls from the other

In the first of the occasions we have called conversion, there is grievous sorrow. Each person, considering his sins, wishes to break the chains of worldly cares, walk along the way of God through the expanse of a secure manner of life, cast off the heavy burden of temporal desires, and carry the light yoke of the Lord in free service [Note: Others read “gentle” (lene)].

But when he is considering these things, his familiar carnal pleasure comes before him—that pleasure which, having long grown old, binds him all the more tightly the longer it has held him and permits him to depart from it only with greater difficulty.

What sorrow and anxiety of heart there are when the spirit calls from one side and the flesh recalls from the other; when love of a new manner of life invites from one side and the habit of an old perversity attacks from the other; when from one side he burns with desire for the heavenly homeland, while from the other he endures within himself a carnal desire that delights him in some measure even against his will! [Col. 0301A]

It can rightly be said of this embittered man: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life; his soul draws near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.”

But because divine grace does not permit us to be afflicted by these difficulties for long, it quickly leads us, by consoling us, to the freedom of a new manner of life after the bonds of our sins have been broken. The joy that follows refreshes the preceding sadness, so that the mind of each convert rejoices all the more in reaching its desire, the more it remembers having sorrowfully labored for it.

Immense joy arises in the heart, because through the hope of security it already draws near to the one whom it desires. Thus it should rightly be said of this person: “He will entreat God, and he will be gracious to him; he will see his face with rejoicing.” Or certainly: “He delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction, but, while living, would see the light” [Col. 0301B].

### 27. 2. In the exercise of temptations. The goads of temptation are sharper after conversion

But lest anyone who has been converted should already believe himself holy, and lest security itself should afterward overthrow the person whom the struggle of sorrow was unable to overcome, God’s dispensation permits him to be wearied by the goads of temptations after his conversion.

By conversion we have indeed already passed through the Red Sea; but in the wilderness of the present life enemies still meet us face to face. We already leave behind us our former sins like Egyptians who have been destroyed; but harmful vices, like other enemies, still confront us, so that they may obstruct the journey we have begun toward the promised land.

Our former faults, like pursuing adversaries, have been struck down by divine power alone; but the goads of temptations, like other enemies [Note: Ebroic. and Vindoc.: “come before the face.”], come against us face to face, and they must be overcome with our labor.

Conversion produces security, but security is usually the mother of negligence. Therefore, lest security produce negligence, it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2:1). He does not say “for rest,” but “for temptation,” because while our enemy sees us still placed in this life, the more he sees us rebelling against him, the more he strives to conquer us.

He neglects to attack those whom he feels he possesses by an undisturbed right. But against us he is stirred all the more violently the more he is expelled from our heart as though from the right of his own dwelling.

The Lord himself represented this in a certain dispensation [Col. 0301D] (Matt. 4:1): he allowed the devil to tempt him only after baptism, so that he might indicate to us a sign of the conversion to come—namely, that after his members had advanced toward God, they would endure more violent ambushes of temptation.

After the first occasion of sorrow and joy, then, which each person recognizes through the discipline of conversion, this second one arises: lest he be made lax through the negligence born of security, he is afflicted by the assault of temptation.

And indeed, at the very beginning of conversion, each person is often received with great sweetness of consolation [Col. 0302A], but afterward experiences the hard labor of testing [Note: Most manuscripts: “experiences the testing of temptation.”].

[Old version XIII.] ### 28. Three stages of conversion

There are three modes of those who are converted: beginning, middle, and perfection. At the beginning they find the caresses of sweetness; in the middle period, the struggles of temptation; and finally, perfection in its fullness.

At first, therefore, sweet things receive and console them; afterward, bitter things exercise them; and at last, pleasant and exalted things strengthen them. For every husband first cherishes his bride with sweet caresses, but after she has been joined to him he tests her with harsh reprimands, and once tested, possesses her in secure affection.

Thus the Israelite people, when God, having betrothed it to himself, called it from Egypt to the sacred marriage of the mind, first received, as though in place of a pledge, the caresses of signs. Once joined to him, it was exercised by trials in the wilderness; once tested, it was strengthened in the promised land by the fullness of virtue.

First, therefore, it tasted in miracles what it was to desire; afterward it was tested by labor to see whether it knew how to preserve what it had tasted; and finally it deserved to receive more fully what, having been tested by labors, it had preserved.

Thus the life of each convert is touched by the gentleness of its beginning, tested by the harshness of its middle period, and strengthened by the fullness that follows perfection.

### 29. Grave temptations often follow the most peaceful beginnings of conversion

For converts often receive, while still at the very entrance of their beginning, either an exceedingly peaceful tranquillity of the flesh, or gifts of prophecy, or expressions of teaching [Col. 0302C], or miracles of signs, or the grace of healing (1 Cor. 12:10). After this, however, they are wearied by the harsh tests of temptations—temptations from which, when they were beginning, they had believed themselves entirely free.

This occurs by the dispensation of divine grace, lest at their beginning they be touched by the harshness of temptations [Note: Most printed editions read, “be broken by adversity.” This is excellent in meaning. Nevertheless, we have been compelled to abandon that reading by the common agreement of the manuscripts Norm., Vindoc., Baluz., Colb., and others, which are followed by the old Paris edition.]. For if the bitterness of temptation confronted their beginnings, they would return just as readily to what they had left behind as though they had not gone far away; for, having first despised their vices, they would be entangled with them again as though with things lying close at hand [That is, “re-entangled,” or “entangled once more.”].

Thus it is written: “When Pharaoh had sent out the people, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is nearby, thinking that they might perhaps repent if they saw wars arising against them and return to Egypt” (Exod. 13:17).

Those leaving Egypt are therefore kept from nearby warfare, because those abandoning the world are first shown a certain tranquillity, lest, disturbed in their very tenderness and beginning, they be frightened and return to what they escaped [Note: Turon.: “what they overcame.”]

First, therefore, they feel the sweetness of security; first they are nourished by the quiet of peace. After they have come to know sweetness, they endure the struggles of temptations more tolerably, the more deeply they have come to know in God what they love.

Thus Peter is first led up the mountain; first he contemplates the glory of the Lord’s transfiguration (Mark 9:1); and only then is he permitted to be tested when the servant girl questions him (Matt. 26:70). In this way, having become conscious of his weakness through temptation, he might return with tears and love to what he had seen.

And when the wave of fear carried him into the sea of sin (Matt. 14:24), there would be an anchor of his earlier sweetness to hold him fast.

Often the struggles of temptations are as long as the caresses of the beginnings had been. Often greater sweetness is given at the beginning, but less in the labor of testing. Often less sweetness is given at the beginning, but greater labor in testing. Yet labor in temptation is never followed by a disproportionate perfection of steadfastness, because each person is rewarded with the fullness of perfection according to the measure of the struggle.

Very often, however, a convert falls into this error: having been received with the sweetness of a beginning through certain gifts of grace, he supposes that he has received confirmation in perfection and considers it the completion of fullness, not realizing that these are still merely the caresses of a beginning.

Consequently, when he is touched by the sudden storm of temptation, he suspects that he has been despised and abandoned by God. If he did not immediately trust his beginning, he would, while still placed in prosperity, prepare his mind for adversity and would afterward resist the approaching vices more firmly because he had foreseen them more shrewdly.

Whatever one foresees, one endures more calmly. Nevertheless, even if he foresees these struggles, he does not avoid them altogether [Note: The same manuscript, together with Baluz. and Colb., reads: “which is the customary course of our journey” (qui usus nostri itineris)], because the course of our journey is by no means completed without the dust of temptation.

### 30. Why temptations appear sharper after conversion than before

Often each convert is agitated by such goads of temptation as he remembers never having experienced before the grace of conversion—not because that same root of temptation was absent then, but because it was not visible.

For the human mind, occupied by many thoughts, often remains in some way unknown to itself, so that it does not know at all what it endures. While it is scattered among many things, it is removed from inward self-knowledge.

But if it desires to be free for God and cuts off the branches of its many kinds of thought, then it clearly sees what proceeds from the innermost root of the flesh.

For if a thornbush grows in a road, it is worn down by the feet of travelers [Note: Vindoc. and Norm.: “is trampled underfoot”], and by the continual passage of those who go by its surface is rubbed away so that it does not appear [Note: Norm., Vindoc., Turon., Baluz., and Colb. read “is rubbed away”; the printed editions have “is broken,” for no other reason than that it seems to fit this passage better.].

Although the branches of its thorns are not visible above, its hidden root nevertheless remains below. But if the feet of passersby cease to rub and trample it, it soon rises to the surface and emerges as a thorn into the open whatever had remained alive but hidden in the root.

So too, in the hearts of worldly people, a certain hidden root of temptations often does not readily appear, because, situated as though in the road of activity, it is trampled by the foot of thought and pressed down by countless cares as by countless travelers, so that it is not seen.

But if, through the grace of conversion, the crowd of cares is removed from the road of the heart, so that no insolence of action crushes it and no tumult of thoughts presses upon it, then what was hidden is recognized; then the thorn of temptations freely pricks from the root of vices.

Against this, the hand of one who lives well works so that, insofar as possible, what is hidden is not covered over but uprooted. Until this happens, the thorn so disturbs the mind of each convert that he often feels almost overcome by its sudden prick and dreads the wound inflicted to the marrow as deadly.

[Old version XV.] ### 31. Temptations become dangerous when they are despised because of their persistence. God tests us by temptations; he does not reject us

Often the goads of temptations themselves, when they become habitual, spread out and are not sharper but longer-lasting. They cause less pain but infect more deeply, because, while they cling to the mind longer, they become less frightening insofar as they become more familiar.

[Note: Baluz., Colb., Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts, followed by the old Paris and Basel editions, read “caught” (deprehensa); recent editions read “depressed” (depressa).]

Meanwhile, the mind caught among them is stretched this way and that and scattered by the various waves of temptations. Often provoked from every side, it does not know which vice to confront or which one to attack first.

Hence it often happens that, while the excessively rising vices torment him and again and again incline the mind that resists them almost toward the fall of despair, each convert becomes afraid of this very lofty way that he has chosen as a remedy. He totters as though led out onto a summit, though he had stood more securely below.

He is so constricted by the surrounding roar of temptations [Col. 0304C] that it may rightly be said of him: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and the food formerly desired by his soul.” Or certainly: “His soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.”

But because the merciful God permits us to be tested by temptations, not rejected, as it is written, “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13) [Note: Baluz., Colb., Pratel.: “beyond what you are able to bear.” Vindoc.: “But God is faithful.”], he quickly comes to our aid with the help of consolation, calms the rising goads of temptations, and stills with inward peace the movements of thoughts that attack him.

Immediately the soul receives immense joy from heavenly hope when it sees the evil it endured overcome. Thus it may rightly be said of this tested and delivered man: “He will see his face with rejoicing; and he delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction, but, while living, would see the light.”

After these two occasions—conversion and testing—have been passed through sorrow and joy, a third remains, in which he still endures sorrow but also attains joys.

[Old version XVI.] ### 32. On the third occasion the just are assisted by fear of death and dread of the final judgment

After the struggles of conversion and the distress of testing, a harsh temptation still remains, because no one can come to the joys of freedom fully attained unless he has first paid the debt owed by human condition.

Each convert, carefully concerned for himself, does not cease silently to consider within himself how strict the eternal Judge will be when he comes. Every day he looks toward his end and considers what account of his life he will have to render before the severity of such justice.

Even if he has avoided all the wicked deeds he was able to recognize, nevertheless, when he is about to come before the strict Judge, he fears more those things within himself that he does not recognize. For who can consider how many evils we commit at every moment of time through the very unstable movements of our thoughts? [Note: Vindoc.: “It is easy to avoid works arising from perverse vanity, but it is exceedingly difficult to guard the heart from unlawful thought.”]

It is easy to avoid wicked actions, but exceedingly difficult to cleanse the heart from unlawful thought. And yet it is written: “Woe to you who think of useless things” (Mic. 2:1). And again: “On the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Rom. 2:16). He also said beforehand: “Their mutually accusing or even defending thoughts” (ibid., 15). And again: “They spoke deceitful lips and evil things in the heart” (Ps. 11:3) [Note: Pratel. and others read, “Deceitful lips have spoken in the heart.” In Vindoc. this verse is omitted here: “deceitful lips,” and so forth.]. And again: “For in your heart you work iniquities upon the earth” (Ps. 57:3).

Now the human soul, having once abandoned the condition of eternity and fallen into the flux of temporality, must endure against its will, when it strives to rise, this mutability of alternating movements which, when it fell, it willingly desired.

It was punished precisely where it took delight, because from the place where, in its perversity, it sought the joy of pleasure, it now has, in its conversion, the labor of struggle.

Often, therefore, something that the elect do not want slips into their thoughts. They carefully examine it within themselves and consider before God how great its guilt is. Although they always dread strict judgments concerning all these things, they fear them especially when, coming to pay the debt of human condition, they see themselves drawing near to the strict Judge [Note: Another manuscript: “to the Judge of strict judgment.”].

And fear becomes sharper in proportion as eternal recompense draws nearer. At that time nothing empty from the phantasm of thought passes before the eyes of the heart, because, with everything else removed from their midst, they consider only themselves and the one to whom they are drawing near.

Dread grows as the recompense of justice approaches; and as the payment demanded by the flesh presses upon them, the more the strict judgment is already, so to speak, touched, the more intensely it is feared.

Even if they remember never having omitted the things they know, they nevertheless fear the things they do not know, because they are entirely unable to judge and comprehend themselves. As the end presses upon them, they are terrified by a subtler fear.

Thus our Redeemer, approaching the dissolution of the flesh and preserving in himself the form of his members, “being in agony, began to pray more earnestly” (Luke 22:44). For what could he ask for himself while in agony, he who, placed on earth, bestowed heavenly things with power? But as death approached, he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind: the force of terror and fear that we suffer when, through the dissolution of the flesh, we draw near to eternal judgment.

For it is not without reason that anyone’s soul is then terrified, when shortly afterward it finds what it cannot change for eternity.

[Old version XVII.] ### 33. What must be feared when death is imminent

We consider that we have by no means been able to pass through the road of the present life without guilt. We also consider that even what we have done laudably is not without some guilt of our own if we are judged apart from mercy.

For who among us could either surpass or equal the life of our forefathers? And yet David says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

When Paul said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” he cautiously added: “But I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). James says: “For we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:2). John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

What, then, will the boards do if the columns tremble? Or how will the motionless shrubs stand if even the cedars are shaken by the whirlwind of this fear? [Note: Vindoc.: “unshaken branches.”]

As the dissolution of the flesh approaches, therefore, the soul even of the just is sometimes disturbed by terror of punishment. If it was able to experience anything tranquil in this life, the arrival of the moment of death shakes it, so that it may rightly be said: “Bread becomes abominable to him in his life, and the food formerly desired by his soul.” Or certainly, because of the punishment of fear, what follows there: “His soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.”

[Old version XVIII.] ### 34. By this fear the souls of the just are cleansed from lesser faults

But because the souls of the just are often cleansed from every lesser contagion by the very fear of death, and from the dissolution of the flesh already begin to receive the joys of eternal recompense, they often become joyful through some contemplation of inward recompense even before they are stripped of the flesh.

While they pay the debt of their old condition, they enjoy the joy of a new gift. Thus it is rightly said: “He will see his face with rejoicing.” Or certainly: “He delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction, but, while living, would see the light.”

The soul of the just therefore beholds God’s face in rejoicing, because it receives as much inward joy as it could scarcely receive even when it has been assumed into that joy. There it sees the light while living, because it fixes its spiritual eye upon the rays of the eternal sun.

There it sees the light while living, because, having trampled down every alternation and shadow of mutability, it clings to the truth of eternity. By clinging to the one whom it sees, it rises toward the likeness of his unchangeableness; and while it gazes upon the unchangeable form of its Creator, it assumes that form within itself.

For the soul that by itself fell into mutability is shaped into the state of unchangeableness by seeing unchangeableness [Note: The same manuscript: “is shaped by living.”]

Thus Elihu, concerning this afflicted and delivered man, because he expressed first the bitterness of sorrow and afterward the joys of consolation, appropriately added: “God does all these things three times for each person”—namely, in conversion, testing, and death—because through these three occasions he is first afflicted by harsh goads of sorrow and afterward refreshed by the great joys of security.

And because the mind of each of the elect is worn down by these same three occasions—either by the labor of conversion, the temptation of testing, or the fear of dissolution—and is freed after being purified by that very wearing down, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XII [Old version XIX]

**Verse 30.**—“To recall their souls from corruption and illuminate them with the light of the living.”

### 35. The present light belongs to the dying; eternal light belongs to the living

The light that we see with bodily eyes belongs to the dying. Those who still live for this world are darkened by the light of the dying. But those are illuminated by the light of the living who, despising temporal light, turn back to the splendor of inward clarity [Col. 0307B], so that they may live there where, by perceiving the true light, they may see; where there is not one light and another life, but where the light itself is life; where the light so surrounds us outwardly that it fills us inwardly, and fills us inwardly in such a way that, though unbounded, it surrounds us outwardly.

They are therefore illuminated by this light of the living, which they then behold more subtly in proportion as they now live more purely toward it.

### 36. The proud habitually mix empty and inflated things with what is true and mystical

Elihu brought forth great and very powerful things, but this is something each arrogant person customarily possesses: while speaking what is true and mystical, he suddenly mixes in certain empty and proud things through the swelling of his heart.

Outwardly he desires to please in what he genuinely understands; and from the very point where he withdraws from inward truth through the appearance of elation [Note: Baluz., Colbert., and others: “through the swelling of pride.”] [Col. 0307C], he immediately becomes empty.

Because, though instructed, he seeks approval outwardly, he loses inwardly the fullness by which he was being taught. Thus Elihu, whom we have already often said represents the type of arrogant people, after setting forth many profound matters of wisdom, suddenly raises himself up in pride, inflated by the conceit of knowledge, after those same true and mystical statements.

As a result of this inflation, his thought immediately turns toward empty words. For he added, saying:

## CHAPTER XIII

**Verses 31–33.**—“Pay attention, Job, and listen to me, and be silent while I speak. But if you have something to say, answer me; speak, for I wish you to appear just. But if you do not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”

### 37. When they speak with some humility, they do not persevere long in the appearance of that same humility

What he thinks of himself he reveals in this speech, when he says: “Pay attention, Job, and listen to me, and be silent while I speak.” For it is immense arrogance to demand reverence from one’s elder and to command silence from someone better than oneself. [Vet. XX.]

Since righteous preachers, whenever they correct anyone, often return through the grace of humility to the depths of their own thoughts, and, even in the very matter for which they are correcting others, inquire lest they themselves perhaps be mistaken, they grant those whom they have corrected permission to acknowledge whatever they may think more just on their own behalf. [Note: The Basel edition of 1514, the Vatican, and Gilot read “to the knowledge of their own”; our reading is drawn from the English, Norman, Tours, and other manuscripts.] [Note: The English, Norman, and other manuscripts read: “so that, if they themselves think anything more just on their own behalf …”] Arrogant men sometimes desire to imitate this. For a little while, setting aside their language of self-exaltation, they seem to seek the justice of those whom they correct, if perhaps they can discover it—not because they truly think this way, but because they desire to adorn themselves with the appearance of humility. [Note: Other witnesses read: “if perhaps it can be found.”] They are afraid that, because they are proud and swollen, they may be seen to be so. [Note: Tours reads: “lest, swollen with pride, they be seen to be so.”] Hence Eliu immediately adds:

“If, however, you have something to say, answer me; speak, for I wish you to appear just.”

But because he did not utter these words from his heart, he did not wait to hear what he had requested. For he immediately adds:

“But if you do not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”

Those who truly seek to hear what is just patiently await what they seek to hear. Eliu, however, because he did not sincerely utter the words of inquiry, did not allow what he had sought to be said. Instead, what he inwardly harbored burst forth at once, and he revealed what he was in his own eyes, saying: “Be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”

For arrogant men, whenever they give voice to something humbly, do not long persist in the appearance of that same humility. When they perhaps ask to hear, they immediately interrupt by speaking, so that they may not be taught; for the intention of self-display, which rises from the root of the heart, quickly suppresses the outward appearance of the voice they had produced. [Note: Baluz and Colbert read “corrupts.”] That form of humility, assumed only in appearance, is exposed all the more quickly because it is foreign to them, and they cannot maintain it for long.

Behold: when Eliu asks to learn justice, he promises that he will teach. Behold: as though seeking what is just, his tongue had uttered something plain; but he could not immediately conceal what was swollen with inward pride. For suddenly he adds: “Be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”

Since all arrogant men are inflated with the swelling of pride in what they say, and, as though placed on high, assume the appearance of teachers—as if their words were poured down from heaven by some act of condescension upon unworthy people—the author of this history appropriately inserts a verse, saying:

## CHAPTER XIV

**Chapter 34, verse 1.**—“Eliu also continued speaking and said these things.”

[Note: Thus in the manuscripts generally and in the old edition. In the more recent editions one reads: “and so, beginning his pronouncement.”]

### 38. The just speak from the root of humility; it is otherwise with the wicked

What else is indicated by the word “pronouncement” than an inflation of self-exaltation, so that words which came from the lofty root of pride proceed with a certain appearance of elevation and distinction? Is this not how all arrogant men habitually preach? With a certain disdain they utter what they believe they alone have understood; and perhaps they preach humility precisely when, through the swelling of pride, they display examples of arrogance.

Thus their preaching cannot remain consistent with itself, because what they sow while speaking correctly they attack by swelling perversely. They do not accommodate their words to humble hearers; rather, they scarcely deign to bestow them. They think themselves placed far above others, and, as though preceding their hearers, scarcely deign from their height to bend their regard toward instruction. [Note: The passage is somewhat obscure in the printed editions, and no clearer in the Évreux and other manuscripts, which read *quasi procedentis doctrinae respectum* (“as though [of] advancing instruction, a regard”), etc.]

But the words of the just come from the root of humility, so that they may be able to bear the fruit of devotion. Whatever salutary thing they can provide, they supply not by swelling with pride but by sharing compassionately. [Note: The manuscripts of Évreux and Vendôme read, “through the force of charity”; the manuscript of Tours, “through the way of charity.”]

Through words of charity they so transform either themselves into their hearers or their hearers into themselves that it is as though the hearers, through the preachers, teach what they hear, and the preachers, through the hearers, learn what they utter in teaching.

Eliu, therefore, bearing the character of arrogant men and beginning with the ostentation of a formal pronouncement, let us hear what he says. [Note: Pratel reads: “beginning with a pronouncement.”] It follows:

## CHAPTER XV

**Verses 2–3.**—“Hear my words, you wise men, and listen to me, you learned ones. For the ear tests words, and the throat distinguishes foods by taste.”

### 39. Proud teachers do not seek to make their hearers wise, but to display their own wisdom

It is as though he said: Just as neither the ear recognizes foods nor the throat words, so no fool can understand the judgment of a wise person. Therefore, you wise and learned people, hear what I say—you who are able to recognize whatever may be said.

Let us see, then, how greatly he swells with pride, since he considers it fitting that his words be heard only by the wise. The true preacher of wisdom, however, says: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1:14). The arrogant man, by contrast, expects in his preaching only the ears of the wise, because he does not preach in order to make just anyone wise; rather, he seeks the wise so that he may display, in his pride, what he has understood.

As was said above, he does not desire to instruct them but to display himself. Nor does he consider how just those who hear him may become, but how learned he himself may appear when he is heard by the learned. [Note: This was omitted by the learned editors in the Roman edition and others; we supplied it from the English, Norman, Vendôme, Colbert, and Baluz manuscripts.] [Page 779; Vet. XXII.]

Since no one would accept the preaching of arrogant men if they did not mingle with it something resembling humility, Eliu, after exalting himself through swollen words, appropriately descends again, as though toward harmony among equals, saying:

## CHAPTER XVI

**Verse 4.**—“Let us choose judgment for ourselves, and let us see among ourselves what is better.”

### 40. They sometimes display humility, but it is feigned

Whether he sought this judgment from a humble heart can easily be recognized if we consider his following words. It continues:

**Verses 5–6.**—“For Job said: ‘I am just, and God has overturned my judgment. For in judging me there is falsehood; and my arrow is violent, without any sin.’”

#### They accuse the just of false crimes

He complains that blessed Job said these things, although the words of sacred history, when examined, testify that he certainly did not say them. But the man who had sought judgment fairly immediately pronounces sentence on the basis of a fault he has fabricated. For it follows:

**Verses 7–8.**—“What man is like Job, who drinks mockery like water, who walks with those who practice iniquity, and goes about with wicked men?”

[Rec. IX.]

Behold: while seeking judgment, he has pronounced judgment; and, after making his accusation, without awaiting any response from blessed Job, he judged him worthy of condemnation on the basis of association with the reprobate. For he says: “What man is like Job?”—so that we should understand, “No one.” And he adds: “Who drinks mockery like water.”

When water is drunk, it is taken in so fluidly that nothing in its thickness delays it from being swallowed. To drink mockery like water, however, is to ridicule God without any obstacle in one’s thoughts, so that neither the tongue nor the conscience, in its pride, is checked by any hesitation.

How far this judgment of his against blessed Job departs from the path of truth we learn from that testimony of the Lord in which he says to the devil: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?” (Job 1:8). Behold: the Truth calls the one whom Eliu declares to be, without comparison, a sinner righteous without comparison.

[Note: In the Vendôme manuscript “without comparison” is absent, but wrongly so and contrary to the mind of Saint Gregory, whose purpose is to say that the same Job whom God preferred to all the just was judged by Eliu to be the most wicked of all the unjust.]

This is characteristic of arrogant preachers: they desire to rebuke their afflicted hearers more severely than to comfort them gently. They take greater care to denounce evils by reprimanding than to strengthen good things by praising. They desire to appear superior, and rejoice more when anger elevates their own spirit than when charity makes them equal. [Note: The Norman, Vendôme, and other manuscripts read, “if they desire to appear superior.”] They always seek something that they can strike harshly by rebuking. Hence it is written: “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride” (Proverbs 14:3), because he knows how to strike harshly but does not know how to share compassion humbly. [Note: In the Roman edition and others, incorrectly, “so anger elevates it.”]

### 41. When holy preachers are about to correct others, they first offer words of kindness. Like skilled physicians, they first touch gently and afterward strike

[Note: This section is omitted by Baluz.]

Righteous preachers too habitually correct their hearers by rebuking them, and habitually attack their vices with stern denunciation. Hence it is written: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Their words are rightly called nails, because they do not know how to stroke the faults of sinners but to pierce them.

Were John’s words not nails when he said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3:7). Were Stephen’s words not nails when he said: “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51). Were Paul’s words not nails when he said: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Galatians 3:1). And again, when he said to the Corinthians: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to human ways?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

But we must carefully observe that righteous preachers, even in those whom they correct, when on another side they perhaps find something of good conduct, descend to these same words of rebuke with the greatest prudence.

Behold Paul, teaching the Corinthians and seeing them at fault because of division, begins by saying: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him” (1 Corinthians 1:4). He greatly praised those whom he called enriched in everything in Christ.

And behold, he multiplies his words of kindness, saying: “In every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you” (ibid., 5). He said, “The testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you,” as though they had accomplished in their works what they had learned in teaching.

Then, completing his praise, he added: “So that nothing is lacking to you in any grace, as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Tell me, Paul, after all these expressions of favor, where you are heading. And behold, shortly afterward it follows: “But I appeal to you, brothers, through the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe’s household, that there are quarrels among you” (ibid., 10).

A little later he adds concerning these quarrels: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to human ways?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). [Note: The Vendôme, Pratel, and other manuscripts read: “Behold how, through praise, he descends to explicit words of correction.” This is omitted by Baluz and Colbert.]

Behold by what praises he descended to explicit words of correction. Behold how, in the hearts of his hearers, he opened the way for stern rebuke with the gentle hand of favor. First he worked to bind the arms of the proud with the bonds of kind words, so that afterward he might cut into the wound of pride with the knife of correction.

There were surely in the Corinthians things that ought to be praised, and things that ought to be reproved. The skilled physician therefore first gently touched, by praising them, the healthy limbs surrounding the wound, and afterward pierced the rotten cavity of the wound by striking it.

Thus the rule of teaching has its proper weight in both respects among holy preachers: they nourish what is upright by encouraging it, and cut away what is perverse by taking notice of it. [Note: The printed editions read incorrectly, “they nourish those who do right.” All the manuscripts have “they nourish those who favor or foster what is right.”]

[**Vet. XXIV, Rec. X.**]

### 42. It is one thing to strike when justice urges it, and another when pride inflates. The measure to be observed in correction. The proud do not know it

Sometimes righteous preachers also strike sternly. But it is one thing when justice urges them, and another when pride inflates them. When the just correct severely, they do not lose the grace of inward sweetness. Often, to restrain the restlessness of the wicked, they assume the severity of strict discipline, but inwardly they are melted by the fire of charity and burn with love for those against whom they rage with harsh correction. In the secret of their hearts they humble themselves even before those whom outwardly they chastise with the hard goads of their judgments, as though despising them.

Often they despise without despising, and despair without despairing, so that they may make those people fear and recoil from their fault all the more quickly by showing them, as it were, the pit of death already near. [Note: The editors chose to replace *pavescere* (“make them fear”), the reading of Baluz, Colbert, Évreux, Vendôme, Tours, and other manuscripts, with *reviviscere* (“make them revive”).]

They also frequently disclose their own faults before their disciples with a fitting moderation, so that those who hear may learn how to criticize themselves subtly for their own actions.
