They regulate themselves with such great prudence that, when they raise themselves, they are not inwardly harsh, and, when they humble themselves, they are not outwardly lax; for they preserve humility in discipline and discipline in humility.

Paul maintained discipline when he said to the Corinthians: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to human ways?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). Yet he did not lose humility within his discipline, because he prefaced his words with an appeal, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, through the mercy of God, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you” (1 Corinthians 1:10). [Note: Vendôme and most Norman manuscripts read, “But I appeal to you.”]

Again, he maintained humility when, speaking to the same Corinthians, he perhaps went on at greater length than he had wished and criticized himself, saying: “I have become foolish” (2 Corinthians 12:11). Yet he did not lose discipline in this humility, because he immediately added: “You compelled me.”

He displayed a great example of humility when he said to his disciples: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5). Yet he did not lose the justice of discipline in this humility, for he says to those same offenders: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Corinthians 4:21), and so forth. [Note: Another manuscript reads, “the discipline of justice.”]

Holy preachers therefore know how to temper the art of teaching with both forms of moderation. When they find the guilt of sinners, they know how to correct severely at one time and to appeal humbly at another.

But when arrogant men desire to imitate them, they take from them the harsh words of correction, while they do not know how truly to take from them the prayers of humility. They can be more terrifying than gentle. [Note: Thus in Évreux and other Norman manuscripts, Vendôme, Baluz, and Colbert. The Paris edition of 1495 reads: “For they desire, if they can, to be more terrifying than gentle.” The wording is best left as the manuscripts have it. The Basil edition of 1514 and Paris edition of 1518 corrupt the passage as: “They desire to be terrifying whom they can,” etc. Other printed editions read: “They desire to be terrifying rather than gentle.”]

For this reason they learn how to exalt themselves, and neglect to learn how to submit their spirit. Since they do not know how to admonish sinners calmly, through excessive severity they become unrestrained in the anger of denunciation, even against those who act rightly.

Eliu, therefore, bearing the character of such men, does not comfort blessed Job but rebukes him, saying:

“What man is like Job, who drinks mockery like water, who walks with those who practice iniquity, and goes about with wicked men?” [Vet. XXV.]

And because pride is always foreign to truth, he immediately breaks out into falsehood as well, saying:

## CHAPTER XVII

**Verse 9.**—“For he said: ‘A man will not please God, even if he has run with him.’”

### 43. Pride is always foreign to truth

That blessed Job certainly did not say this, anyone who reads his words recognizes. But the man who speaks in order to become proud by displaying himself—why should it be surprising if he invents in another what he may criticize? For how can someone whose inward swelling separates him far from the truth within himself remain joined to truth in words of correction?

It follows:

**Verse 10.**—“Therefore, men of understanding, listen to me.”

Behold, again inflated by the arrogance of pride, he seeks only those who, as though capable of following him through worthy understanding, might attain him; and thus what he thinks bursts forth in his words, as he says:

## CHAPTER XVIII

**Verses 10–11.**—“Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will repay a man according to his work, and according to the ways of each he will restore to them.”

[Page 782]

### 44. In this life God does not always repay each person according to his works

He spoke well in saying that there is no iniquity or impiety in almighty God. But in this life what he adds does not always occur: that he repays each person according to his work and according to his own ways.

For he freely anticipates many who commit unlawful and perverse deeds and turns them toward holy works. He also chastises some devoted to upright actions by intervening affliction and, as though they displeased him, afflicts those who please him, as Solomon testifies when he says: [Note: The printed editions wrongly read *ac si* (“as if”) for *ac sic* (“and thus”).] “There are just people to whom much happens as though they had done the works of the wicked, and there are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the just” (Ecclesiastes 8:14).

Almighty God arranges this with immeasurable compassion so that scourges may torment the just, lest they exalt themselves over their works, while the unjust may at least pass this life without punishment, since by doing evil they hasten toward torments without end.

That the just are sometimes not chastised according to their works is shown by this very history that we are interpreting. For blessed Job had not been scourged on account of guilt; before the scourge, he had been praised by the testimony of the Judge himself.

Eliu would therefore have spoken more truly if he had said: “Because there is no impiety or iniquity in almighty God, even when he does not appear to repay people according to their own ways.” For what we do not understand proceeds from the not-unjust balance of hidden judgment.

Since arrogant preachers, while scattering many empty things, also often utter true and solid ones, Eliu appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XIX [Vet. XXVI]

**Verse 12.**—“For truly God will not condemn without cause, nor will the Almighty overturn judgment.”

### 45. God’s judgments are just, even when hidden

The Lord says to the devil: “You moved me against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3). Eliu, however, says: “The Lord will not condemn without cause.” This seems to conflict with the words of Truth unless it is weighed with careful consideration. For it is one thing to condemn and another to afflict.

He may therefore afflict someone in some respect without cause, but he does not condemn without cause. Did he not afflict Job in some respect without cause, when his guilt was not being removed but his merit was being increased? [Note: Most Norman and Vendôme manuscripts read, “for he was not removing a fault but increasing merit.” In Baluz this is corrupt: “which did not remove … but increased.” Colbert agrees with it, although we might have thought it copied from the former manuscript, were it not that it differs in a few small details.]

He cannot condemn without cause, because condemnation cannot be made only in part or with respect to some particular thing; rather, at the end it punishes everything that each person has committed wickedly here.

Nor does the Almighty overturn judgment, because even if the things we suffer seem less than just, they are nevertheless rightly decreed in a hidden tribunal. It follows:

## CHAPTER XX [Rec. XI]

**Verse 13.**—“Who appointed another over the earth, or whom did he set over the world that he fashioned?”

### 46. He who created the world by himself also governs it by himself

That is, you should understand, “No one.” He governs by himself the world that he created by himself; and he does not need another’s assistance to govern, since he did not need it to create.

These points are gathered for this reason: to show clearly that, if almighty God does not neglect to govern by himself what he created, then he certainly governs well what he created well. For he who created it in goodness does not administer it wickedly; and he who cared for things not yet made so that they might exist does not abandon the things that have been made.

Since the one who was the author of creation is present in its governance, he does not pass over our care. Hence he aptly adds:

## CHAPTER XXI

**Verse 14.**—“If he directs his heart toward him, he will draw his spirit and breath toward himself.”

[Page 783]

### 47. When he wills, he directs the crooked hearts of human beings by raising them toward himself

The heart is crooked when it seeks what is below; it is directed when it is lifted toward what is above.

If, therefore, a person directs his heart toward the Lord, the Lord draws his spirit and breath toward himself. He uses “spirit” for inward thoughts and “breath,” which is drawn through the body, for outward actions. [Note: The Roman edition has incorrectly, “for eternal actions.”]

For God to draw a person’s spirit and breath toward himself means that he changes both our inner and outer life toward conversion to himself, so that nothing external may now please the mind, and the flesh may neither seek nor strive to obtain anything below. Rather, everything that the human being is should burn inwardly with desire for him from whom it comes, and outwardly restrain itself by mastering itself; nothing external should please the mind, nor anything below the flesh—or, if it desires it, should it strive to obtain it.

Hence he aptly adds:

## CHAPTER XXII [Rec. XII]

**Verse 15.**—“All flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.”

### 48. Then the flesh will fail, and through humility man returns to ashes

All flesh fails together when it no longer serves any of its own impulses, because the spirit presiding over it restrains all its instability and, with the sword of its discipline, kills whatever was living wickedly within it.

Jeremiah had killed himself with this sword of discipline when he said: “After you converted me, I repented; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jeremiah 31:19). For what is understood by the thigh except the pleasure of the flesh? And what does he mean by saying, “After you showed me, I struck my thigh,” except that, after he had spiritually seen what is above, he extinguished whatever lived carnally below within him, so that the more fully the highest things became clear, the less the lower things he had held delighted him?

For the more one begins to live above, the more one also begins to die below. In accordance with the inclination toward carnal activity, all Paul’s flesh had died together when he said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

### 49. The sinner forgets his mortality; the just person does not

Eliu also rightly adds here: “And man will return to ashes.” For anyone placed in sin forgets his mortality and does not remember that he is earth, while he is still inflated by pride.

After the grace of his conversion, however, when he is touched by the spirit of humility, what else does he remember himself to be than ashes? David had already returned to ashes when he said: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Psalm 102:15). Abraham had returned to ashes when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27).

Even if death had not yet dissolved their living flesh into earth, inwardly they were already what they foresaw without doubt that they would become. Hence it is said elsewhere: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Psalm 103:29).

What spirit is meant except the spirit of pride? Let their spirit, then, be taken away so that they may fail—that is, once the spirit of pride has been withdrawn, let them recognize that of themselves they are nothing. And let them return to dust—that is, let them be humbled by the weakness of their condition.

Because of this dust, to the memory of which those who examine themselves are recalled, Wisdom says: “The just will shine, and like sparks they will run through the stubble” (Wisdom 3:7). For holy men, when they are mingled among sinners, set them aflame with the fire of their example and reduce all that shines in them to ashes. [Note: Here, following the Colbert, Baluz, Vendôme, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts, the printed text has been corrected; it read: “through everything in which they shine, they return to ashes.”] Consumed by the flame of devotion, when they behold the weakness of their condition, they recognize themselves to be nothing other than ash, so that, released from the hardness of their pride, they may say in repentance what we quoted above: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Psalm 102:15).

It is therefore rightly said that, when the Lord draws a person’s spirit toward himself, “all flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.”

[Rec. XIII.]

These things that Eliu says are both true and great. But because he immediately became swollen with pride on account of what he had rightly understood, he exposes himself in the following words, saying:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Vet. XXVIII]

**Verse 16.**—“If, therefore, you have understanding, hear what is said, and listen to the voice of my eloquence.”

### 50. The proud become more blind the more they see. The more we suffer from the vice of pride, the less we see

All arrogant men have this characteristic: when they perhaps perceive something acute, they immediately break out from it into the vice of self-exaltation; they despise everyone’s understanding in comparison with their own and, in their own judgment, place themselves before the merits of others.

These wretched people become darker the more they see, because, while they attend to subtle matters, they do not know how to look at themselves. The more sharply they perceive understanding, the worse they fall through pride. They would indeed perceive subtle things well if they could see themselves in what they utter. [Note: Tours reads, “the more cautiously they perceive.”]

Earlier Eliu had said: “If you have something to say, answer me; speak, for I wish you to appear just” (Job 33:32). But now he says: “If you have understanding, hear what is said.”

Behold how exaltation progresses little by little through the growth of his words. Earlier he doubted whether blessed Job could utter what was just; now he questions whether he can even hear what is said.

There he said: “If you have something to say, answer me,” as though he were saying: “Say something—if, that is, you can prove worthy to say it.” Here, however, he says: “If you have understanding, hear what is said,” as though he were openly saying: “Hear me—if, that is, you can prove worthy to hear.”

These are the daily declines that occur in the hearts of the reprobate, by which they continually descend to worse things. While they carelessly neglect lesser matters, they dangerously break out into greater ones.

It had already been pride that he doubted whether blessed Job could speak what was just. But by neglecting to consider this in himself, he proceeded to worse things: he not only doubted that Job could say what was just, but also despaired that Job could understand him when he spoke justly.

Therefore the vice of pride must be cut off from its very root, so that, when it secretly arises, it may then be cut away watchfully, lest it grow strong through advancement and become strengthened through use.

No one easily detects pride that has become entrenched in himself, because the more we suffer from this vice, the less we see it. Pride is generated in the mind just as darkness is generated in the eyes. The more widely it spreads, the more severely it constricts the light.

Exaltation therefore grows for a little while in the heart; and when it has extended itself more broadly, it completely closes the eye of the oppressed mind, so that the captive spirit can both suffer the character of self-exaltation and yet be unable to see what it suffers.

But since arrogant men sometimes, as we have said, do not rightly think about right things, and know how to discover good things but disdain expressing them properly, after adopting the character of exaltation in the words, “If you have understanding, hear what is said,” Eliu adds:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Vet. XXIX]

**Verse 17.**—“Can one who does not love judgment be healed? How then do you condemn him who is just?”

### 51. In everything we say, we must consider what is said, to whom, when, and how

He uttered a good judgment, but it ought not to have been uttered to blessed Job. In everything that is said, we must look with the greatest care at what is said, to whom it is said, when it is said, and how it is said.

Eliu considered what he should say, but he did not consider to whom he should say it. Blessed Job did love judgment, for he knew how to weigh his cases carefully with the Lord. He had not condemned the one who is just; rather, while placed in suffering, he humbly sought why he had been struck without sin.

Whoever carefully examines his ways loves judgment. Entering into the secret place of the heart, he weighs what the Lord grants him and what he himself owes the Lord.

How could blessed Job not have done this, when he offered such frequent sacrifices for the cleansing of his children, even for their thoughts? [Note: Another manuscript reads, “for expiation.”]

Since Eliu had said that the one who does not love judgment cannot be healed, accusing blessed Job of not loving judgment and of having condemned the one who is just, he immediately adds the justice of that same just one, namely, the Lord, saying:

## CHAPTER XXV [Rec. XIV]

**Verse 18.**—“Who says to the king, ‘Apostate’; who calls rulers wicked.”

### 52. He is an apostate who presides over others not to benefit them but to dominate them

We often know that many who preside over others demand from their subjects a disordered fear of themselves, and wish to be revered not so much for the Lord’s sake as in place of the Lord.

Within, they exalt themselves through the swelling of their hearts, and despise all their subjects in comparison with themselves. They do not assist them by condescending to them; rather, they oppress them by domination, because they raise themselves up in the loftiness of their thoughts and do not recognize themselves as equal to those whom they happen to govern. [Note: Tours reads, “they comfort them.”] [Note: Baluz and Colbert read, “they presume to rule them.”]

Against this swelling, the book of Ecclesiasticus says: “They appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1).

The Lord rebukes this swelling among shepherds through the prophet, saying: “But you ruled them with harshness and with power” (Ezekiel 34:4). They utter even the good things they say to their subjects by dominating rather than by advising, because they imagine that they have lowered themselves by saying anything to them as equals. They rejoice in the singularity of their eminence and not in the equality of their condition.

But because the Lord carefully weighs these swelling hearts of rulers, it is rightly said against them: “Who says to the king, ‘Apostate.’”

Every proud ruler falls into the guilt of apostasy as often as, delighting in presiding over people, he rejoices in the singularity of his honor. He does not consider under whom he stands, and he exults as though he were not equal to those who are his equals.

From where does this root of vices sprout in the heart of rulers, unless from imitation of him who, despising the fellowship of the angels, said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14)?

Therefore, whenever a ruler exalts himself in ruling others, he is separated through the fall of pride from the service of the supreme Ruler. And when he despises subjects equal to himself, he does not acknowledge the dominion over him of the one under whom all are equal. Thus it is rightly said: “Who says to the king, ‘Apostate.’”

[**Vet. XXX.**]

### 53. He is wicked if, by the example of his own pride, he drags his subjects headlong

Since those who preside by domination draw their subjects toward wickedness through the example of their own pride, it is appropriately added: “Who calls rulers wicked.”

They would lead them along the way of devotion if they displayed examples of humility before the eyes of their subjects.

A ruler is wicked if he strays from the path of truth; and, while he himself rushes headlong, he invites those who follow him toward the precipice. A ruler is wicked if, through examples of swelling pride, he shows the way of error.

Paul feared becoming a leader into wickedness when he restrained the loftiness of his authority, saying: “Nor seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ; but we became little ones in your midst” (1 Thessalonians 2:6). [Note: Pratel reads: “although we could have been.”]

He had become little in their midst because he feared that, if he claimed for himself the honor of his loftiness among his disciples, he would display examples of exaltation. He feared, surely, that while he sought for himself the power of pastoral authority, the subordinate flock might follow him toward the precipice, and that the one who had undertaken the office of devotion might lead his followers into wickedness.

54. Let him shine before those subject to him with the splendor of his virtues. Let him correct their faults prudently and humbly.—Hence it is necessary that the person in authority carefully consider what examples he offers to those subject to him; and let him know that he must live in proportion to the number of those over whom he presides, [Note: Thus Baluz., Colb., and Norm., followed by the old editions. More recent editors preferred, “over how many he presides.”] and vigilantly ensure that he does not become swollen with pride in the office to which he has been appointed; that he does not demand the rights of his due authority immoderately; that the right of discipline is not changed into the harshness of pride; and that, by the very means through which he could restrain his subjects from perversity, he does not rather corrupt the hearts of those who observe him; [Col. 0318C] lest, as has been said, he become a leader of impiety through the exercise of an office of piety.

He ought not to undertake the leadership of men who does not know how to go before men by living well, lest the one chosen for the purpose of correcting the faults of others himself commit what he ought to cut away. Therefore let those in authority look carefully around themselves in every direction, [Note: Others: “let them look around themselves.”] so that they may live both for themselves and for their subjects; so that the good they do they may both conceal within the bosom of their minds and nevertheless, from it, offer examples of right action for the advancement of those who follow them; so that, observing the faults of their subjects, they may correct them, yet not become swollen with pride through the force of that same correction; so that they may patiently tolerate certain matters corrected gently, yet not dissolve the bonds of discipline through that same gentleness; so that they may overlook certain matters by tolerating them, yet not, by overlooking them, permit them to grow.

These things are laborious, and unless divine grace supports them, difficult to maintain. Rightly, concerning the coming of the strict Judge, it is said through the Book of Wisdom: “He will appear terribly and swiftly, for a very severe judgment will be made upon those who are in authority” (Wis. VI, 6). Since, therefore, through the power of governance one often bursts forth into the fault of pride, and since before the strict Judge that very pride is judged impiety, Elihu rightly says concerning the Lord: “Who calls leaders impious.” For, while they grow proud of their very leadership, they draw their subjects toward impiety by their example.

[Col. 0319A] 55. In judging others, let him constantly present himself before the heavenly Judge. Let authority received be regarded not as an honor but as a burden. The pursuit of office brings innumerable evils. Pastoral care must be embraced neither from ambition nor abandoned through fear.—Therefore the greatest care must be taken that the one placed over the governance of men preside within himself, in the secret chamber of his mind, upon the throne of humility. And while others attend him outwardly as he judges, let him look unceasingly with watchful eyes upon the Judge before whom he himself will one day stand to be judged concerning these matters; so that the more anxiously he now trembles before the one whom he does not see, the more securely he may behold him when he does see him. [Note: The words “outwardly” are absent in the same manuscripts.]

[Rec. XVI.] Let the one who has perhaps scarcely enough strength to render an account of his own soul before the strict Judge reckon that, since he presides over as many subjects as he governs, at the time when an account must be rendered before that Judge he has, so to speak, that many souls alone. [Note: Anglic., Pratel., and other Norm.: “he alone has so many souls.”] This thought, if it continually torments the mind, suppresses every swelling of pride. And a prudent ruler will then neither be called an apostate king nor an impious leader, in proportion as, through anxious reflection, he regards the authority he has received not as an honor but as a burden.

For whoever now delights to be a judge will then dislike seeing the Judge. The faults committed out of love for possessing authority cannot be counted. Authority is administered well only when it is retained not through love but through fear. For it to be exercised properly, it must first be imposed by necessity, not by ambition. Once received, it must not be abandoned through fear, nor embraced out of desire; otherwise a person may grow worse in pride under the appearance of humility, if by fleeing he despises the order of divine dispensation, or may cast off the yoke of the heavenly Ruler because he delights in private governance over others.

Therefore, when authority is received, it must not be loved out of desire, [Col. 0320B] but endured with patience, so that at that time it may be beneficially light for judgment, whereas now it is known to be patiently heavy for ministry. [Note: In the Gussanville edition: “beneficially gentle,” which we believe to be a typographical error. All manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, read—and should read—“light,” in contrast with “heavy.”]

# BOOK TWENTY-FIVE

In the exposition of chapter 34, verses 19–30, concerning the punishment of the reprobate and the hidden judgments of God.

[Col. 0319]

# CHAPTER ONE

1. The error of those who attend to what people possess rather than to what they are.—The very condition of human nature shows how far it surpasses other things. For the reason bestowed upon humanity declares how greatly rational nature surpasses everything that lacks either life, sensation, or reason. Yet, because we close our eyes to what is inward and invisible and feed them upon visible things, we often honor a person not for what he is himself but for what surrounds him. And when we do not consider what he is, but what power he has in the acceptance of persons, we are guided not by the persons themselves but by the things adjacent to them. Thus it happens that even one who is honored outwardly comes to be despised inwardly among us, because, while he is regarded as honorable on account of what surrounds him, in our judgment he is ranked below his possessions.

But almighty God examines human life solely according to the quality of its merits; and often he punishes a person more on account of what he has here contributed in greater measure for service, as the Truth bears witness, saying: “From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke XII, 48). Hence Elihu rightly says here:

# CHAPTER TWO

## CHAPTER 34, VERSE 19

“He does not accept the person of princes, nor recognize the tyrant when he contends against the poor.”

2. There is no acceptance of persons with God.—A proud person may be understood by “prince” or “tyrant,” while the humble person is designated by “poor.” Therefore he does not recognize the tyrant contending against the poor, because he declares that in the judgment he will not acknowledge all the proud who now oppress the life of the humble, saying: “I do not know where you are from” (Luke XIII, 25). And because he destroys powerfully whenever he wills, just as he powerfully created when he willed, the argument appropriately continues:

## THE SAME PLACE

“For all are the work of his hands.”

[Rec. II.] And immediately it continues:

# CHAPTER THREE

## VERSE 20

“They will die suddenly, and in the middle of the night the peoples will be bowed down and pass away.”

3. The death of all the wicked is sudden because it is not foreseen.—However late the wicked are taken from this life, they are taken suddenly and unexpectedly, because they do not know how to foresee their end by reflecting upon it. What a person could not think about beforehand is sudden for him.

Suddenly that rich man was taken away who abandoned the barns he had prepared and found the place of hell that he had not foreseen. [Note: Vindoc. and Pratel.: “that rich man was taken away”; the old edition and others: “that rich man was snatched away.” Colb. has: “that foolish man was snatched away.” Recent editions have: “that rich foolish man was snatched away.” The editors evidently read *stultus* (“foolish”) in the manuscripts instead of *tultus*, whose meaning they perhaps did not understand. The reading nevertheless appears in Baluz. We have already discussed this word in Book III, no. 22.]

By thought he was training his soul for one thing, but by sentence he sent it forth to another; while he lived he contemplated one thing, while he died he experienced another. He left behind temporal matters long considered and found eternal things he had not expected. Therefore, because of this ignorance of his blindness, the divine sentence rightly says to him: “This night they demand your soul from you” (Luke XII, 20).

It was taken away in the night, for it was lost in the darkness of the heart. It was taken away in the night, because it did not wish to have the light of reflection by which it might foresee what it could suffer. Hence the Apostle Paul rightly says to the disciples who were considering future things: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or of darkness” (I Thess. V, 4).

The day of departure overtakes like a thief in the night when it drives out the souls of fools who do not foresee the future. Hence it is appropriately added here: “And in the middle of the night the peoples will be shaken and pass away.” They pass away, bowed down in the middle of the night, who are humbled and snatched away in the darkness of their negligence. [Note: Vindoc.: “who are snatched away in darkness.”] Then they will be shaken by the sentence of the Judge, those who now neglect to be humbled through humility of heart. But so that the elect may not be unwillingly humbled in death, they voluntarily humble themselves in humility. Hence it is said to the holy Church concerning the converted offspring of persecutors: “The sons of those who humbled you will come to you, bent low” (Isa. LX, 14).

4. Human life after sin is a passage; it was otherwise before sin.—And rightly, speaking of dying peoples, he did not say, “They will pass,” but “They will pass away,” because even while living temporally we advance daily toward our end, and by traversing the present life as though it were a road, we pass through it. For this very act of living while destined to die is to go toward death. And as we complete each day of life, we draw nearer to the appointed place by as many steps as the days contain.

The very increases of time are losses, because as the spans of our life begin to become greater, they already begin to cease to exist. [Note: Turon.: “living while destined to die.”]

The first man, however, was created in such a way that time would pass while he remained, so that he himself would not pass away with time. He stood while moments ran on, because he did not tend toward the end of life through the increase of days. He stood more firmly insofar as he clung more closely to the One who always stands. [Note: Turon., Vindoc., Baluz., Colb., and many Norm. manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions changed “more closely” to “more ardently.”]

But when he touched what was forbidden, immediately, having offended the Creator, he began to go along with time. Having lost the state of immortality, he was swallowed up by the course of mortality (Gen. III, 4). And as he was drawn from youth to old age and from old age to death, by passing away he learned what he had been by standing.

Because we are born from his stock, we retain the bitterness of the root as though in a young shoot. For since we derive our origin from him, by being born we receive his course, so that in the very daily moment in which we live we unceasingly pass away from life, and the span of life which is thought to increase for us decreases from that same source.

Since, therefore, through the increase of living we daily advance toward the end of dying, it is rightly said of those who die not that they will pass but that they will pass away: they pass even while they live, but they pass away when they die. It follows:

# CHAPTER FOUR [Rec. III]

## THE SAME PLACE

“And they will take away the violent man without a hand.”

5. The hand of God, unseen because it is not foreseen, snatches the wicked away for punishment.—You should understand: “the divine judgments.” “Without a hand” means that they will take away the one who was violent by hand. They will take him away without a hand because, under the pressure of a sudden departure, the one who visibly snatched others is invisibly carried away. He saw those whom he snatched away, but he does not see who snatches him away in death. Thus the violent man is taken away without a hand: he does not behold his snatcher, yet he is led away.

A stricter sentence follows him in proportion as the patience extended toward his sin has been great, because divine severity punishes the wicked more harshly the longer it has endured him. [Note: Baluz., Colb., Ebroic., and Prat.: “the patience extended beforehand.”] Often, while heavenly mercy waits for sinners, they leap into a greater blindness of heart. Hence it is written: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Rom. II, 4).

And behold: while each violent man snatches away whomever he can, while he oppresses the weak, and while for a long time he practices everything he wickedly desires, because he is not struck suddenly but his punishment is deferred until the end, he thinks that his most wicked action is not seen by God. Hence, after narrating his destruction, the text immediately adds concerning the Lord:

# CHAPTER FIVE

[Col. 0322C]

## VERSE 21

“For his eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps.”

6. The sinner foolishly and impiously reasons from God’s patience that his crimes are either not seen by God or approved by him. Punishment will open the eyes that guilt closed.—He was then thought not to consider matters at all, when this violent man perpetrated every evil he could with impunity. God was judged not to see the deeds of the wicked, because he delayed condemning them justly; and his great patience was regarded as a kind of negligence. [Note: Thus Turon., Baluz., Colb., Vindoc., Longip., and the Norman manuscripts; the printed editions read “things done unjustly.”]

The wicked man himself likewise believed that he was not seen by God as often as he sinned with impunity. A certain wise man says to him: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’” (Ecclus. V, 4). He does not wish to amend the wickedness for which he has not yet suffered a fitting punishment; and insofar as he has been mercifully awaited, he has been provoked to sin more wickedly. Despising the long-suffering of heavenly patience, he has accumulated guilt from the very source from which he ought to have corrected it, as is said through the same Job: [Note: Others, as in Baluz. and Colb.: “and despising the patience of heavenly long-suffering.”] “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it in pride” (Job XXIV, 23). Often, too, because he does not suddenly receive the punishment he deserves, he does not judge that what he is doing displeases God.

Let him go, then, and burst forth presumptuously into every kind of blasphemy; let him fulfill the wickedness of his desires, seize what belongs to others, and glut himself upon the oppression of the innocent; and, because he has not yet been struck, let him think that his ways are either not seen by the Lord or, worse, approved by him! [Note: Pratel.: “and rush into every blasphemy”; the phrase “of his desires” appears in Turon., and likewise in Baluz. and Colb.]

The eternal and sudden blow will surely come, will surely come; and then he will know that all things are seen by God, when he sees himself condemned by an unforeseen departure in requital for all his deeds. Then in his punishment he will open the eyes he long kept closed in guilt. Then he will perceive that the true Judge has considered everything, when, by experiencing it, he can no longer escape the desert of his evils. Therefore the wicked man who was long awaited was suddenly taken away because the eyes of the Lord are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps.

It is as though he said: “Because he does not forever leave unpunished the things he patiently observes for a long time. For behold, he suddenly snatched away the violent man and, by judging them, cut off the evils he had endured while awaiting them.” [Note: Pratel. has “and then he recognizes”; below, “he opens” and “he perceives,” readings also found in Baluz. and Colb.]

Let no one therefore say that God does not see human deeds when he observes some wicked person freely piling up his iniquities. He is suddenly taken away who is long tolerated.

7. What are the steps of human beings that God considers?—By “the steps of men” he means either the individual actions upon which we rely or the alternating movements of inward thought by which, as though by steps, we either withdraw far from the Lord or draw near to him in piety. For the mind approaches God by as many steps as it advances through good movements. Conversely, it becomes distant by as many steps as it is worn away by evil thoughts. [Note: Baluz., Colb., the Norman manuscripts, etc., support *deterescit* (“is worn away”), rather than *decrescit* (“decreases”), found in the printed editions. Baluz. and Colb. omit “the mind.”]

Hence it often happens that the movement of the mind has not yet advanced into action, and yet guilt is already complete through the very culpability of thought, as it is written: “The wicked will not be innocent when hand is joined to hand” (Prov. XI, 21). [Note: Vindoc. and Prat.: “when hand is joined to hand.”] The hand is usually joined to the hand when it rests in idleness and no use of labor exercises it. Therefore, “The wicked will not be innocent when hand is joined to hand.” It is as though he said: “Even when the hand refrains from wicked action, the wicked person is nevertheless not innocent through thought.”

Since we know, therefore, that all things are strictly weighed—not only deeds, but at least thoughts—what will become of the movement of evil action, if God judges so minutely the steps of the heart? Behold, no human being sees the hidden paths of our minds, yet before God’s eyes we place as many steps as the affections we set in motion. [Vet. IV.] As often as we limp with the weak foot of thought from the right path, so often we fall before him. For unless this continual falling of our minds increased in his sight, he would not cry out through the prophet: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. I, 16).

By saying this, he testifies that he cannot, as it were, bear the force of our concealed wickedness. It cannot be concealed from him, because whatever is illicitly thought by us in secret is thrust importunately into his sight. [Col. 0324A] For, as it is written, “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13). Hence it is appropriately added here:

# CHAPTER SIX [Rec. IV]

## VERSE 22

“There are no darknesses, and there is no shadow of death in which those who practice iniquity may be hidden.”

8. No one is hidden from God’s judgment, which neither forgets nor fails to know anything.—What did he intend to designate by “darkness” if not ignorance, and by “the shadow of death” if not forgetfulness? Of the ignorance of certain people it is said: “Having their understanding darkened” (Eph. IV, 18). And again, concerning the forgetfulness that occurs in death, it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. CXLV, 4). Since, therefore, through death everything conceived while living is utterly handed over to forgetfulness, forgetfulness is, as it were, a certain shadow of death. For just as death intervenes and makes what existed in life no longer exist, so forgetfulness intervenes and makes what existed in memory no longer exist. It is rightly called its shadow, because it is, as it were, drawn from death itself while imitating its force by putting the senses to sleep.

But since God neither fails to know the evils of human beings when they are merely conceived nor forgets them once perpetrated—unless they are erased from his eyes through repentance—it is appropriately said: “There are no darknesses, and there is no shadow of death in which those who practice iniquity may be hidden.” It is as though he said: “No one is hidden from his judgment, because he can in no way either fail to see what we do or forget what he sees.”

9. God is free from every mutability; neither human beings nor angels are.—Yet “darkness” and “the shadow of death” may also be understood in another way. [Note: Prat.: “his darkness.”] Every change is, as it were, an imitation of death. For that which changes something kills it, as it were, with respect to what it was, so that it ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not.

Therefore the true light, our Creator, because he is not darkened by any changeable succession and is not overshadowed by any defects of his nature, but for him to exist is to shine without mutability, is said to have neither darkness nor the shadow of death. Hence it is written elsewhere: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jas. I, 17). And again the Apostle Paul says: “Who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. VI, 16).

[Vet. V.] But since we all know that the human soul and angelic spirits were created immortal, why is God alone said by the Apostle to possess immortality, unless because God alone truly does not die, since he alone never changes?

10. The human soul would not fall if it were not mutable.—The human soul would not fall into ruin if it had not been mutable. Having been expelled even from the joys of paradise, it would never return to life if it were not mutable. [Note: Vindoc., Baluz., and Colb.: “would in no way return.”] In the very fact that it strives to return to life, it is compelled to endure its defects through alternating mutability.

Since it was created from nothing, it tends by itself toward what is beneath it, unless it is held by the hand of its Maker in the state of desire for the good. Because it is a creature, it is inclined to go downward. By its own strength it recognizes that it can go headlong, but by the hand of love it holds itself to its Creator, lest it fall, until it passes into immutability and lives truly immortally because it lives immutably.

11. The angelic spirits too were created mutable by nature, so that they might either fall by their own will or stand by their own choice.—But because they humbly chose to cling to the one by whom they were created, they have already overcome this mutability in themselves through the immutability of their standing, so that they have thereby meritoriously transcended the fact that, according to the order of their nature, they could have been subject to mutability.

[Note: Here Gussanville notes that the following is added in Vatican Manuscript 1: “They received from the vision of their Ruler the ability to persist without defect within themselves. From this, however, a wondrous art of standing is formed in them: while they know what they can do from their own position, they consider what they owe to the governance of their Ruler. And the more readily they perceive that they can fall through mutability, the more tightly they bind themselves to the love of their Ruler lest they fall. They recognize that by their own position they can go headlong, but by the hand of love they hold themselves to their Creator, lest they fall. This very…” Although this addition is not inconsistent with Gregory’s style, it appears in no manuscripts, either handwritten or printed—not even in the Roman editions.]

Since, therefore, it belongs to the divine nature alone not to endure the shadows of ignorance and mutability, let it rightly be said: “There are no darknesses, and there is no shadow of death in which those who practice iniquity may be hidden.”

[Vet. VI.] For the eternal Light, which is God, shines with such penetrating vision in proportion as it shines immutably; he neither fails to know hidden things, because he penetrates all things, nor forgets what he has penetrated, because he endures unchangeably.

Therefore, whenever we conceive anything unworthy in our hearts, we sin in the light, because that light is present to us, not to itself, and we stumble against it by walking perversely, although we are far from it by our merits. When we do not believe that we are seen, we keep our eyes closed in the sun. We hide him from ourselves, not ourselves from him.

Now, therefore, while we can, let us erase from the sight of the eternal Judge both the things we have thought wrongly and, worse, the things we have perpetrated. Let us recall before the eyes of our hearts everything we have done perversely through the wickedness of presumption. Let our weakness flatter itself in nothing, nor gently caress itself in recalling these things. Rather, in proportion as it is conscious of its evil, let it be more kindly severe toward itself; let it set the future judgment against itself, and whatever it perceives in itself will be strictly punished by the Judge’s sentence, let it piously punish in itself through the repentance of conversion.

Hence, after the punishment of this violent man has been described, it follows:

# CHAPTER SEVEN [Rec. V]

## VERSE 23

“For it is no longer in a man’s power to come before God in judgment.”

[Col. 0325D] 12. We must anticipate God’s judgment by judging ourselves.—This verse requires the greater discussion because, if what it says is neglected, it causes the sharper pain. Here the reference is not to the judgment that punishes through eternal retribution, but to the judgment that dissolves what has been conceived in the mind through conversion. [Note: Pratel. and others, as also in the old Paris and Basel editions, read “through conversion” rather than “through conduct.”] For no one wishes to come to that judgment if he fears being condemned by it.

When it is said, “It is no longer in a man’s power to come before God in judgment,” it plainly shows that there is a certain judgment which even the condemned and reprobate may one day desire. And what is that judgment except the one of which the Apostle Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI, 31)? It is also the judgment of which the prophet says: “There is no judgment in their steps” (Isa. LIX, 8), and of which David says: “The honor of the king loves judgment” (Ps. XCVIII, 4)—that is, the one who already honors God by faith should carefully judge what he owes him in action.

Hence it is written again: “Judge before the Lord, and wait for him” (Job XXXV, 14). The person is judged before the Lord who beholds the Lord in his heart and, in his presence, discerns his actions through careful examination. The more securely he awaits him, the more suspiciously he examines his life each day. [Note: Baluz. reads, “the more securely he awaits”; other manuscripts read “the more securely.”] For the one who comes to his final judgment is judged no longer before him but by him.

Concerning this judgment of the mind, the Lord says through the prophet to the forgetful soul: “Recall me, so that we may be judged together; tell me if you have anything, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 26).

[Rec. VI.] 13. The order of this judgment: conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, and sorrow tortures.—Each person’s mind must carefully examine before the Lord both its own case and the Lord’s case against it; it must cautiously weigh either the good things it has received from him or the evil things by which, through perverse living, it has answered his good things. [Note: Turon.: “examine”; the proper sense is “weigh.”]

The elect never cease doing this each day. Hence Solomon rightly says: “The thoughts of the just are judgments” (Prov. XII, 5). For they enter the Judge’s secret chamber within the bosom of the heart. They consider how strictly the one who waits patiently for a long time will one day strike. They fear the things they remember having done, and by weeping they punish what they understand themselves to have perpetrated. They fear God’s subtle judgments even concerning things they perhaps cannot understand within themselves.

They see divinely that which they themselves do not see in themselves through human weakness. They behold the strict Judge, who, the later he comes, strikes the more severely. They also contemplate the assembly of the holy fathers sitting with him, and they reproach themselves for having despised either their examples or their words. In this secret judgment of the interior, constrained by the very execution of their own minds, they strike through repentance what they committed through pride.

There, they enumerate whatever attacks them against themselves; there, they heap before their own eyes everything for which they should mourn; there, they behold whatever could be decreed through the anger of the strict Judge; there, they suffer as many punishments as they fear suffering. Nor is any means of punishment lacking in this judgment conceived in the mind, which should more fully punish the guilty. For conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, and sorrow tortures.

This judgment punishes all the more certainly insofar as it rages more inwardly, because it does not come from external things. When each person begins to bring his own case into this examination against himself, he is himself the plaintiff who brings the case, and himself the defendant against whom it is brought. [Note: Through a copyist’s error Turon. reads *auctor*; *actor* (“plaintiff”), which is opposed to *reus* (“defendant”), must be read.] He hates himself as he remembers having been; and the person he is pursues through himself the person he was. Thus, within the soul, a kind of conflict arises between the person and himself, giving birth to peace with God.

The Lord was seeking this conflict of the heart when he said through the prophet: “I paid attention and listened: no one speaks what is good; there is no one who repents of his sin, saying, ‘What have I done?’” (Jer. VIII, 6). God was appeased by this conflict of the human heart when he spoke through his prophet concerning King Ahab, who reproved himself, saying: “Have you seen Ahab humbled before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days” (III Kings XXI, 29). [Note: Ebroic., Pratel., Utic., Turon., Baluz., and Colb. read “this conflict of the heart was not appeased,” as do all the printed editions except one older Paris edition. Careful consideration of the context shows that the printed reading is corrupt.]

14. This judgment, which the wicked avoid, the just always practice; how beneficially we should undergo it.—Since it is now in our power to undergo within our minds this judgment against ourselves, let us accuse ourselves by recognizing our faults and torment ourselves through repentance for what we have been. Let us not cease, while it is permitted, to judge what we have done; let us carefully heed what is said: “It is no longer in a man’s power to come before God in judgment.”

It is usually characteristic of the reprobate always to do what is wrong and never reconsider what they have done. For they pass over everything they do with a blinded mind and do not recognize their deed until they have been punished. But it belongs to the elect to examine their actions daily from the very source of thought and dry up everything turbid that flows forth from within.

[Vet. VII.] Just as we do not perceive how our limbs grow, how the body develops, or how our appearance changes, how the blackness of our hair becomes gray—since all these things happen in us without our knowledge—so our mind is changed from moment to moment by the very practice of the cares of life. We do not recognize this unless, by vigilant guardianship, we sit within ourselves and daily weigh our progress and our defects.

For to remain in this mortal life is, as it were, to proceed toward old age; and when the mind is left unexamined, it is lulled into a certain old age of torpor. Neglecting itself and imperceptibly losing the strength of its purpose, it grows old without knowing it, moving away from the form of its former strength. Hence it is said through the prophet under the figure of Ephraim: “Strangers have consumed his strength, and he did not know it; gray hairs have also been scattered upon him, and he did not know” (Oseae II, 9). [Note: Turon. and others seen by Gussanville: “had grown cold.”]

But when the mind seeks itself and examines itself carefully through repentance, it is washed of this very old age by tears and kindled by sorrow; and what had almost grown old and cold becomes warm again through the supplied efforts of inward love. Hence the Apostle Paul admonishes disciples growing old through the practice of mortal life, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. IV, 23).

[Rec. VII.] 15. The examples of the holy fathers and the divine precepts exhort us to do this.—The examples of the fathers and the precepts of sacred Scripture greatly assist us in doing these things. For if we look upon the works of the saints and lend our ears to the divine commands, some things we contemplate and others we hear set us aflame; and our heart is not confined by torpor while it is stirred to imitation.

Hence it is rightly said to Moses: “The fire on the altar shall always burn, and the priest shall feed it, placing wood beneath it every morning, day by day” (Lev. VI, 12). The altar of God is our heart, on which the fire is commanded always to burn, because it is necessary that a flame of love continually rise from it to the Lord. The priest should place wood beneath it each day, lest it be extinguished.

For every member endowed with faith in Christ has certainly been made a member of the high priest, just as the Apostle Peter says to all the faithful: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II, 9). And as the Apostle John says: “You have made us a kingdom and priests for our God” (Apoc. II, 6). [Note: Some editions add “and a priesthood.”]

Therefore the priest who feeds the fire on the altar should place wood beneath it daily—that is, each faithful person, lest the flame of love fail within him, should not cease gathering in his heart both the examples of those who preceded him and the testimonies of sacred Scripture. [Note: Pratel. and Vindoc.: “gather.”] For supplying the fire with fuel, as it were, is to provide, for the kindling of love, either the examples of the fathers or the Lord’s commands. [Note: Ebroic. and Pratel.: “for the exercise” of love.]

Since our inward newness grows old each day through the very conduct of this life, this fire must be nourished by the addition of wood, so that, while it is weakened through the use of our old nature, it may revive through the testimonies and examples of the fathers.

And rightly it is commanded there that wood be gathered each morning, day by day. For these things do not happen unless the night of blindness is extinguished. Or certainly, because morning is the first part of the day, after setting aside thoughts of the present life, each of the faithful should first consider how he may kindle by whatever efforts he can the zeal of love that is already failing within him.

For this fire on the Lord’s altar—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is carefully restored through the examples of the fathers and the testimonies of the Lord.

### 16. Thus set ablaze with the fire of charity, we are a holocaust to God.

Well is it added there:

> “And when the holocaust has been placed upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings” (Leviticus 6:12).

For whoever kindles this fire of charity within himself places himself as a holocaust upon the altar, since he burns away every vice that was living wickedly within him. When he examines the inner things of his thoughts and, by the sword of transformation, sacrifices his depraved life, he has placed himself upon the altar of his heart and kindled himself with the fire of charity. The fat of the peace offering gives off its fragrance from this sacrifice [Note: Norm. and Vindoc. read, “because it is the inward enrichment of the new life.” Vindoc. nevertheless reads *impugnatio*, “assault,” through an obvious scribal error], because the inward enrichment of new charity, which makes peace between us and God, sends forth from us the sweetest odor.

And because this same charity remains unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is appropriately added there:

> “This is the perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar” (ibid., 13).

Certainly this fire shall never fail from their altar, because even after this life the ardor of charity increases in their minds. For through eternal contemplation it comes about that the more the almighty God is seen, the more greatly he is loved.

### [Old Version VIII.] 17. Aided by the divine commandments and the examples of the saints, we attain freedom.

That we are rescued from the depths of this life when aided by divine admonitions and the examples of those who preceded us is also well signified by the prophet Jeremiah, who was cast into a pit. When he is to be lifted from the pit, ropes and old rags are lowered to him (Jeremiah 38:11).

For what are signified by the ropes if not the Lord’s commandments? [Note: Vindoc. and Norm., “which, as it were, us.”] Since they both convict us when we are placed in evil conduct and rescue us [Note: All the printed editions we have consulted read *et convincunt*, “and they convict,” through a gross error. It cannot be doubtful to anyone attending to the comparison instituted by Saint Gregory that one must read *et convinc[i]unt*, “and they rescue,” as it appears in the manuscripts of Utic. and Pratel.], they bind and draw us, constrain and lift us, as it were.

But lest someone bound by these ropes be injured while being drawn, old rags are lowered at the same time. For, so that the divine commandments may not terrify us, the examples of the ancient fathers strengthen us; and by comparison with them we presume that we can do what we fear on account of our weakness.

If, then, we hasten to be lifted from this depth, let us be bound with ropes—that is, let us be held fast by the Lord’s commandments. Let old rags also be present, by which the ropes may be held more securely: that is, let us be strengthened by the examples of those who preceded us, lest the lofty commandments wound us, weak and fearful as we are, while they lift us.

The apostle Paul added certain old rags of this kind when, in lifting his disciples by spiritual commandments, he supplied them with the examples of the ancients [Note: Ebroic. and other Norm. manuscripts read “commended”], saying:

> “The just experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were cut in pieces, they were tested; they died by the slaughter of the sword” (Hebrews 11:36).

[Col. 0329D] And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses placed over us, laying aside every burden and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience the contest set before us” (Hebrews 12:1).

And again:

> “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; observing the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7).

Earlier, then, while he was speaking spiritual commandments, he had, as it were, sent down ropes; afterward, when recalling the examples of the elders, he brought in, as it were, old rags.

### 18. We must return from external matters to the heart.

Therefore, awakened by so many voices of commandments and aided by so many comparisons with examples, let us return to our hearts. Let us examine everything we do, and let us accuse whatever within us offends the rule of divine uprightness, so that this very accusation may excuse us before the strict Judge.

For in this judgment of our mind, we are acquitted all the more quickly the more strictly we hold ourselves guilty. Nor should the times in which we are free be set aside for doing these things [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norm. manuscripts read *perdenda sunt*, “must be lost”]. For after the times of this life there is no opportunity to do them. It is not said without reason:

> “For it is no longer in a man’s power to come to judgment with God” [Col. 0330B].

For this reason we are reminded of what we shall then be unable to do, lest we neglect now what we can do.

But behold, occupations take possession of us. Constantly imposed upon us, they turn the eye of our mind away from considering ourselves. For amid these visible things at which it gazes, our heart is scattered outside itself, and, while occupied externally, it forgets what is taking place within.

The divine voice, however, pierces it with its terrible sentences like so many nails, so that it may awaken, and so that a person, at least struck by terror, may fear the hidden judgments hanging over him which, weighed down by torpor, he neglects.

As we said above, by the very habit of its former life the mind, badly accustomed, is weighed down [Note: Ebroic. and Pratel., followed by the old Paris and Basel editions, read *et in his quae exspectat*, “and in the things which it expects”; this word is frequently used in manuscripts for *spectat*, “looks at.” In Baluz. and Colb. one reads, “so that it may expect these things”]. And in the things at which it looks outwardly it is lulled into sleep, as it were. Once it has poured itself outward toward visible things that it desires, it vanishes inwardly from contemplation of invisible things.

Hence it is now necessary that what is scattered among visible things should be struck by invisible judgments; and because it has thrown itself down through its evil delight in external things, let it at least, when struck, seek again what it abandoned.

Behold, therefore, Holy Scripture pierces torpid hearts with a certain terror, lest they cling to things that pass away externally, but rather recover inwardly the eternal things they have lost. It indicates what hidden judgment is being decreed, lest we think excessively about these public affairs. It declares what is being done concerning us and within us, so that from this public temporality we may gather the eye of the heart into the secrecy of the inward disposition.

### [Old Version IX.] For after many things had been related about the punishment of the wicked, a hidden judgment is suddenly introduced: how some lose what they seemed to possess, while others receive what others lose through their merits. He says:

## CHAPTER VIII

### Verse 24

> “He shall crush many and innumerable people, and shall make others stand in their place.”

### 19. Some lose what they seemed to possess; others recover what they had previously lost. To be thrust toward external things is a sign of rejection; to be drawn toward inward things is a sign of predestination.

This happens every day. But because the final outcome of both groups is not yet visible, it is feared less. For the rejected never recognize their guilt except in punishment. And because punishment is delayed, guilt is despised.

Some slip from the state of righteousness, and, when they fall, others receive the place of life. Yet they neglect their fall because they do not consider the destruction that remains for them eternally. If they would turn their eyes toward what they will suffer there, they would fear what they do here [Note: The Roman edition of Sixtus V has, erroneously, “what they flee here”].

It is clear to all that at that final reckoning the almighty God will conduct a public examination, abandoning some to torments and admitting others to participation in the heavenly kingdom. But what is then displayed publicly is now carried out daily by a hidden judgment [Note: A recent edition reads “by a public judgment.” We have removed *in*, “in,” at the urging of the manuscripts and the old printed editions; thus this clause corresponds more elegantly to the other: “by this hidden judgment now”].

For, justly and mercifully examining or ordering the hearts of individuals, he thrusts some toward external things and draws others toward the things within. He kindles in these a desire for inward things; he abandons those, on account of their pleasures, to think about external things. He raises the minds of these toward heavenly things, while he plunges the pride of those into the lowest desires [Note: The same printed editions read, “he plunges their pride through pride.” *Per*, “through,” is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts of Vindoc., Norm., and others, as well as from the old printed editions].

But the hearts of others are closed to human eyes, and it is not known who is being rejected, because what each person is thinking cannot be penetrated [Note: The printed editions read, “because they cannot penetrate what lacks sensation.” It should be read, as in the manuscripts of Vindoc., Utic., Pratel., and others, “because what is thought by each person cannot be penetrated”].

For often, in a perverse heart, the deliberation of a thought has not yet advanced to the accomplishment of an act, and perhaps it is still held inwardly by habit, although it already wanders outwardly in the mind. But such a person has fallen before the eyes of the inward Judge at the moment when, through desire, he departed from the things that should be desired inwardly.

Sometimes, however, others revive suddenly with love for heavenly hope after practicing evil deeds. Those who had scattered themselves in perverse action gather themselves back into the bosom of inward reconsideration by reproving themselves.

People who still look upon them, knowing what they once were in their conduct, think them to be the same. But they themselves, through the examination of strict reflection [Note: Ebroic. and others, “of strict conduct”], recall and pursue what their life had been; what they were is known, but what they have now begun to be is unknown.

In both groups of people, therefore, it often happens that those who appear to stand according to human judgment are already lying before the sight of the eternal Judge, while those who still lie before human beings are already standing in the sight of the eternal Judge.

Who could have judged that Judas would lose the lot of life even after his apostolic ministry (Luke 23:40)? And who, on the other hand, would have believed that the thief would find the claim to life at the very moment of death?

But the hidden Judge, presiding and discerning the hearts of both, mercifully established one and justly crushed the other. He strictly rejected the former outwardly and mercifully drew the latter inwardly.

Therefore the prophet also appropriately announces that, at the time of his passion, some would fall and others rise, saying:

> “I mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10).

Drink is drawn inward from external things, while weeping flows outward from inward things. To mingle one’s drink with weeping before the Lord, therefore, is to draw some inward from external things and to reject others from inward things toward the exterior.

### [Old Version X, Revised Version VIII.] “He shall crush many and innumerable people, and shall make others stand in their place.”

### 20. Rejection is first carried out inwardly and afterward displayed outwardly. The number of the elect is fixed and definite.

As we said above, this crushing is first carried out inwardly, so that afterward it may be displayed outwardly. Through this crushing, the exterior aspects of some may still appear sound, while their interior has already rotted.

For it is written:

> “Before ruin, the heart is exalted” (Proverbs 16:18).

They are therefore struck in the very place where they grow proud. Hence it is written:

> “I crushed their adulterous heart, which departed from me” (Ezekiel 6:9).

To commit adultery inwardly is to delight outwardly in forbidden things. But this same exaltation of the proud is a great crushing of the heart. For by the very thing through which it swells with the boasting of some virtue, the heart falls from the integrity of salvation.

The proud despise God and, abandoning the glory of their Creator, seek their own. For them, this very falling consists in coming into themselves after losing the power of the One above them. They are also crushed because, abandoning heavenly things, they seek earthly things.

What greater crushing could there be than to seek the creature after abandoning the Creator, to yearn for the lowest things after abandoning the joys above? Hence the Prophet rightly says:

> “But he humbles sinners down to the earth” (Psalm 146:6).

After heavenly things are lost, everything they thirst for is earthly [Note: Longip. reads, “what they feel”]; and while they strive to appear greater, what they desire is lesser.

Of such people it is rightly said through Jeremiah:

> “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jeremiah 17:13).

But of the elect it is said:

> “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

This crushing, therefore, first creeps into the mind and afterward proceeds into action. It first shakes the foundations of thought and afterward casts down the structure of conduct. Hence the utmost care must be taken to avoid it there, where it arises.

For it is written:

> “With all vigilance guard your heart, because from it proceeds life” (Proverbs 4:23).

And again it is written:

> “From the heart come evil thoughts” (Matthew 15:18).

We must therefore keep watch inwardly, lest the mind fall while it is being exalted. Let us guard inwardly everything we do outwardly. For if the rottenness of elation once consumes the marrow of the heart, the empty shell of outward appearance quickly collapses.

It should also be noted that, while some fall, others are said to be strengthened in order to stand; thus the number of the elect is shown to be fixed and definite. Hence it is also said to the Church of Philadelphia through the angel:

> “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Revelation 3:11).

### [Old Version XI.] 21. The Church’s teaching concerning predestination and rejection nourishes the hope of the humble and suppresses the pride of the arrogant. The rejected are innumerable.

By this sentence, then, which tells of some being raised up and others being crushed in their life, the hope of the humble is nourished and the pride of the arrogant is suppressed: the former may lose the good things of which they are proud, while the latter may receive those things which they are despised for not possessing.

Let us therefore fear in regard to what we have received, and let us not despair of those who have not yet attained it [Note: Thus Baluz., Colb., Longip., Norm., and the old editions. Recent editions read *despiciamus*, “let us despise.” Gussanvillaeus presents this variant reading, though we do not know where he obtained it: “nor let us despair of those who have not yet attained it”].

We know what we are today, but we do not know what we may shortly become. Those whom we perhaps despise may begin late, yet nevertheless surpass our life through more fervent devotion.

It must therefore be feared lest, as we fall, one may rise whom we mocked while we stood. Yet one who knows how to mock a person who does not stand no longer knows how to stand.

The apostle Paul instilled this fear of heavenly judgments into the hearts of his disciples when he said:

> “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

When he said, “He shall crush many,” and immediately added, “innumerable,” he either wished to express the multitude of the rejected, which surpasses the capacity of human reckoning, or certainly wished to indicate that all who perish are not included within the number of the elect, so that they are innumerable because they run outside that number.

Hence the Prophet, observing that so many in the time of the Church appear outwardly to believe—so many, indeed, that they plainly exceed the fixed number and total of the elect—says:

> “They have been multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 39:6).

It is as though he said: Since many enter the Church, even those come to the faith in outward appearance who are excluded from the number of the heavenly kingdom, because by their multitude they surpass the total of the elect [Note: Vindoc. reads, “by their multitude”].

Hence it is also said through the prophet Jeremiah:

> “The city shall be built for the Lord, from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate, and it shall extend beyond the rule of measurement” (Jeremiah 31:38).

No one is unaware that the holy Church is the city of the Lord. Hananel is interpreted as “the grace of God.” At a corner, two walls are joined. The city of the Lord is therefore said to be built from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate because the holy Church, beginning from the height of heavenly grace, is built up to the entrance and reception of both peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile.

But because, as its multitude increases, the rejected are also gathered into it, it is appropriately added:

> “And it shall extend beyond the rule of measurement,”

because it reaches even to those who, passing beyond the rule of righteousness, are not held within the number of heavenly measure [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norm. manuscripts read, “are not held”].

Hence it is also said to the same Church through Isaiah:

> “For you shall spread out to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations” (Isaiah 54:3).

For amid such a multitude of nations, it extends to the right when it receives some who are to be justified. It also expands to the left when it admits to itself some who will remain in iniquity [Note: Tur., Longip., Norm., “for when the multitude enters”].

Because of this multitude, which lies outside the number of the elect, the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Many are called, but few are elect” (Matthew 20:16).

But because the fact that some of the elect are crushed while others are raised up arises from the merit of the one who suffers, not from the iniquity of the one who punishes, it is appropriately added:

> “For God is not unjust, who inflicts wrath” (Romans 3:5).

## CHAPTER IX [Revised Version IX]

### Verse 25

> “For he knows their works, and therefore he will bring on night, and they shall be crushed.”

### 22. God sometimes punishes the sinner with blindness.

It must be understood with the greatest care that every wicked person is crushed in night in two ways: either when he is struck by the tribulation of an external punishment, or when, by a hidden judgment, he is blinded inwardly.

He falls in night when, at the final judgment, he loses forever the light of life. Hence it is written:

> “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:13).

Then he is compelled to be cast into outer darkness because now he is voluntarily blinded in his inner being.

Again, the wicked person is crushed in night when, condemned through the confusion of his preceding sins, he does not find the light of truth and does not recognize what he ought to do thereafter.

### [Old Version XII.]

Every sin which is not quickly wiped away by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin. A sin that repentance does not wash away soon draws a person onward to another sin by its own weight. Thus it comes about that it is not only sin, but sin and the cause of sin.

For a subsequent fault arises from that vice by which the blinded mind is led to become entangled more grievously in another [Note: Longip. reads, “from which the mind, having been provoked,” or “aroused,” is led].

But the sin that arises from sin is no longer merely sin; it is sin and also the punishment of sin. For by a just judgment the almighty God darkens the heart of the sinner, so that, through the desert of his preceding sin, he may also fall into other sins.

The One whom he did not wish to free struck him by abandoning him. Therefore it is not without reason called the punishment of sin: what is perpetrated through a justly inflicted blindness from above is the vengeance for a preceding sin.

This is carried out according to a disposition ordered above, but confused below through iniquity, so that the preceding fault is both the cause of the subsequent sin, and the subsequent fault in turn is the punishment of the preceding one [Note: Vindoc. reads, “so that it is the cause of the subsequent sin”].

Paul had well observed this as a kind of seed of error in unbelievers and the morally unrestrained when he said:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; rather, they became futile in their thoughts” (Romans 1:21).

But he immediately adds what sprang up from the seed of this error, saying:

> “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity” [Note: Another reading has, “to uncleanness”], “so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves” (ibid., 24).

Because, although they knew God, they committed the sin of pride through their understanding, they are also blinded so that they do not understand what they are committing. Those who refuse to follow their understanding lose, in sin and as the cause of sin, the very light of understanding in sin and as the punishment of sin.

Thus, through the merit of the earlier sin, the pit of subsequent sins is covered over, so that the one who knowingly commits evil may thereafter justly fall into other things even unknowingly.
