### 23. Sins are punished by sins, so that punishments increase along with the growth of vices.

This is brought about so that sins may be struck by sins, so that the very increase of vices may become the punishment of sinners. For because the almighty God grants time for repentance, but human wickedness twists that time toward the practice of iniquity, the guilt is permitted to increase by God’s just judgment, so that it may eventually be heaped up for a deeper blow.

Hence the apostle Paul again says of certain people:

> “So as always to fill up their sins” (1 Thessalonians 2:16).

Hence the angel says to John:

> “Let the one who does harm do harm still; and let the one who is in filth become filthy still” (Revelation 22:11) [Note: Vindoc. reads, “Hence, by an angelic voice in the Apocalypse of John, it is said”].

Hence David says:

> “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, so that they may not enter into your righteousness” (Psalm 68:28).

Hence again the same Psalmist says of the Lord:

> “Through evil angels he made a path for the way of his wrath” (Psalm 77:49).

The Lord justly permits a heart weighed down by its earlier deserts to be deceived also by the subsequent persuasions of evil spirits. When it is deservedly dragged into guilt, its liability is increased in punishment. Hence the Lord is said to have made a way for his wrath out of a path.

For a way is broader than a path. To make a way for his wrath out of a path is to enlarge the causes of wrath through strict judgment, so that those who, after being enlightened, refused to act rightly may, once justly blinded, still do things by which they deserve to be punished more severely.

Hence it is said through Moses:

> “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed” (Genesis 15:16).

Hence the Lord says through the same Moses:

> “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their offspring from Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their clusters are bitter to them. The wine of dragons is their wine, and the fury of asps is incurable. Are not all these things gathered up with me and sealed in my treasuries? On the day of vengeance I shall repay them” (Deuteronomy 32:32–34) [Note: *omnia*, “all,” is absent in Pratel., Colb., and Baluz.].

He recounted how many were their evils, and yet immediately added:

> “At the time when their foot shall slip” (ibid., 35).

Behold, their most atrocious crimes are described, yet a further fall is still awaited for the day of vengeance, by which their sins may be heaped up. They already have grounds for deserving to be struck; nevertheless, sin is still allowed to grow, so that a more atrocious punishment may eventually torment the sinners.

Sin already deserves punishment and is already the cause of sin; yet it is still awaited that an increase of punishment may introduce further sin and the punishment of sin.

### 24. The same sin is sometimes both the punishment and the cause of sin. God blinds by not freeing a person from blindness.

Very often one and the same sin is both sin itself and the punishment and cause of sin. We shall show this more clearly if we bring the matters themselves before us.

Unrestrained gluttony of the belly incites the fullness of the flesh toward the heat of lust. Once lust has been committed, it is often concealed by perjury or murder, lest it be punished by the vengeance of human laws.

Let us therefore place before our eyes a man who has loosened the reins of gluttony. Overcome by this gluttony, he committed adultery. When he was discovered in adultery, he secretly killed the adulteress’s husband so that he would not be brought to trial.

This adultery, then, standing between gluttony and murder—arising from the former and generating the latter—is both sin and the punishment and cause of sin. It is plainly sin in itself; it is the punishment of sin because it increased the guilt of gluttony; and it is the cause of sin because it generated the subsequent murder.

One and the same sin is therefore both the punishment of the preceding sin and the cause of the subsequent guilt, because, while it increases and condemns what has already happened, it also sows what will follow and must be condemned.

Since, therefore, the eye of the heart is blinded by preceding sins, the blindness itself which confuses the sinner’s mind through the condemnation of his former guilt is rightly called night, because through it the light of truth is hidden from the eyes of the offender.

It is therefore rightly said:

> “For he knows their works, and therefore he will bring on night, and they shall be crushed,”

because, as has often been said, preceding evils cause them to be enveloped again in the darkness that follows, so that they can no longer see the light of righteousness precisely because, when they could see it, they refused to do so.

The Lord is said to bring on night, not because he himself introduces darkness, but because he mercifully does not illuminate the darkened hearts of sinners. Thus, to blind them in night means that he has refused to free them from the darkness of blindness.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER X [Revised Version X]

### Verse 26

> “As the wicked he struck them in the place of those who see.”

### 25. Those who live wickedly within the bosom of the Church are struck by divine vengeance as though they were wicked. The meaning of “as” in Scripture. The Church is the place of those who see.

In Holy Scripture, *as* is sometimes customarily used for resemblance and sometimes for truth. It is used for resemblance when the Apostle says:

> “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10).

It is used for truth when John says:

> “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

In this passage it makes no difference whether it is used for resemblance or for truth, because in either construction the depraved life of the wicked is plainly signified.

Holy Scripture properly calls unbelievers “the wicked.” For sinners are distinguished from the wicked by this difference: although every wicked person is a sinner, not every sinner is wicked. Even one who is devout in faith can be called a sinner. Hence John says:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

But one who is separated from the piety of religion is properly called wicked. Of such people the Prophet says:

> “The wicked shall not rise in the judgment” (Psalm 1:5).

The place of those who see is called the holy Church. In it one rightly stands so that the true light, which is God, may be seen.

Hence it is said to Moses:

> “There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock when my majesty passes by” [Note: Vindoc. and Pratel., “when it passes by”; Baluz., “when I pass by”] (Exodus 33:21).

And shortly afterward:

> “I shall remove my hand, and you shall see my back” (ibid., 23).

The Church is signified by the place, the Lord by the rock, and the multitude of the Israelite people by Moses, since Israel did not believe in the Lord while he was preaching on earth.

It therefore stood upon the rock, looking at the back of the passing Lord, because, after the Lord’s Passion and Ascension, having been brought within the holy Church, it deserved to receive the faith of Christ. It did not see his presence, but it came to know his back.

Let it therefore be said of those whom divine vengeance finds persisting in iniquity within the holy Church—let it be said of those whose life the apostle Paul condemns:

> “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16):

> “As the wicked he struck them in the place of those who see.”

For they stood there where they appeared to see God. There they loved darkness where the light of truth is seen. Although they kept their eyes open in faith, they nevertheless kept them closed in their conduct.

Hence it is rightly said of Judaea:

> “Its watchmen are blind” (Isaiah 56:10),

because they did not see in their conduct what they perceived in their profession.

Hence it is also written of Balaam:

> “Falling, he has his eyes open” (Numbers 24:16).

For, falling in conduct, he kept his eyes open in contemplation.

Thus these people also opened their eyes in faith but did not see in their conduct. Placed within the Church under a pious appearance, they were found outside the Church in their impious way of life.

Of them it is elsewhere well written:

> “I saw the wicked buried, who, while they still lived [Note: Thus the manuscripts of Baluz., Colb., Pratel., and others. The printed editions have “while they were still alive.” *Advivo* means the same as simply *vivo*, “to live,” but is used more rarely], were in the holy place and were praised in the city as though for the works of the just” (Ecclesiastes 8:10).

### 26. The peace of the Church conceals many false Christians. Some seek glory from professing the Christian religion.

For ecclesiastical tranquility and peace conceal many who are afflicted by the plague of their own depravity under the Christian name. Yet if even a slight breeze of persecution strikes them, it immediately carries them outside the threshing floor like chaff.

### [Old Version XV.]

Some, however, are marked by the Christian calling for this reason: because the name of Christ has been exalted so highly, almost everyone now appears to be regarded as faithful. Since they see others being called by this name, they are ashamed not to appear faithful, but they neglect to be what they glory in being called.

They take the reality of inward virtue as an adornment of outward appearance. Though they stand naked before the heavenly Judge in the unbelief of their conscience, they cloak themselves before human eyes with a holy profession in words alone.

### 27. The faithful who live wickedly often suffer the loss of faith through divine judgment. Many die without faith in the house of faith. For them, the fellowship of the faithful becomes an increase of punishment.

Some hold the faith profoundly, but take no care at all to live faithfully. They do not follow in their conduct what they venerate by belief. It often happens to such people, by divine judgment, that through living wickedly they lose even what they rightly believe.

They continually defile themselves with evil actions, yet doubt that the vengeance of just judgment can be repaid for them. Often, when they neglect to live well, they slide into faithlessness even though no one is persecuting them.

For those who do not believe that strict judgment is imminent, who suppose that they may sin without punishment—how can they either be or be called faithful? To have lost the faith is not to believe that fitting punishments can be repaid for uncorrected evil deeds.

Since they scorn preserving works worthy of faith, they also lose the faith which they appeared to possess. Concerning them, words are appropriately recalled under the image of enemies destroying Jerusalem:

> “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations” (Psalm 136:7).

For Paul says:

> “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” [Note: Utic. and Pratel., “which is Christ Jesus”] (1 Corinthians 3:11).

The enemies destroying Jerusalem lay it bare down to its foundation when perverse spirits, first destroying the structure of good works in the hearts of the faithful, also drain away the solidity of their religion. For just as a building is constructed upon its foundation, so works are constructed upon faith.

To lay it bare down to its foundation, therefore, is, after overturning the work of living well, also to dissipate the strength of faith.

Hence it is also said to Judaea through Jeremiah:

> “The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you to the crown of your head” (Jeremiah 2:16) [Note: Vindoc. and Norm., “and of Tahpanhes”; Baluz. and Colb., “and of Taphnis”].

To be violated to the crown of the head means that, after practicing evil, one is corrupted even in the very height of faith. When the most wicked spirits entangle a person’s soul in evil works but cannot corrupt the integrity of faith, they pollute, as it were, the lower limbs but do not reach the crown.

Whoever is corrupted in faith, however, is violated even to the crown. For the evil spirit reaches from the lower limbs to the highest parts when, after polluting the active life, it corrupts the chaste height of faith with the disease of distrust.

Since all these things are hidden from human eyes but lie open to divine sight, and since many die without faith in this house of faith, it is rightly said:

> “As the wicked he struck them in the place of those who see.”

They display themselves as pious to human beings in the Church, but because divine judgments cannot be hidden, they are struck as wicked.

What increases their punishment still further is that each of them, mingled with the faithful in the Church, knowingly despises the truth of faith; and the vengeance that follows is all the more severe because, through the examples of the upright, knowledge of how to live well also accompanies them.

As many upright and faithful brothers as are now shown to them, so many witnesses will oppose them at the coming judgment. They know what they neglect to follow.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XI [Old Version XVI, Revised Version XI]

### Verse 27

> [Note: Utic. and other Norm. manuscripts read here and thereafter, “because, as though deliberately”; this wording is also found in the old editions.]

> “Who deliberately departed from him.”

### 28. Sin is committed through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate intention—the last being graver. It is one thing not to do what is good, another not even to love it, and another to hate it.

It must be understood that sin is committed in three ways (*De poenitentia*, distinction 2, canon “Sciendum”): through ignorance, through weakness, or deliberately. Sin committed through weakness is graver than that committed through ignorance, but sin committed deliberately is far graver than that committed through weakness.

Paul had sinned through ignorance when he said: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13). Peter, however, sinned through weakness when one voice—a girl’s—shook all the strength of faith that he had shown toward the Lord, and he denied with his voice the God whom he held in his heart (Luke 22:57).

But because the guilt of weakness or ignorance is more easily wiped away precisely because it is not committed deliberately, Paul corrected by knowledge what he had failed to know, and Peter, watering with tears the root of faith that had been shaken and was already, as it were, withering, made it firm again.

Those, on the other hand, of whom the Teacher himself said, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22), had sinned deliberately. And shortly afterward: “They saw me and hated both me and my Father” (ibid., 24).

It is one thing not to do good things and another to hate the teacher of good things, just as it is one thing to sin through rashness and another through deliberation. Sin is often committed rashly, yet condemned through counsel and deliberation. For it usually happens through weakness that one loves what is good but cannot fulfill it. To sin deliberately, however, is neither to do nor to love what is good.

Just as it is sometimes a graver sin to love sin than to commit it, so it is more wicked to hate righteousness than not to have practiced it. There are therefore some in the Church who not only do not perform good works but even persecute them; and what they themselves neglect to do, they detest in others.

Their sin is committed not through weakness or ignorance but through deliberate intention alone. For if they wished to fulfill good works but were unable to do so, they would at least love in others what they neglect in themselves. If they desired such things even by mere intention, they would not hate them when performed by others. But because they learn of these same good things by hearing, despise them in their lives, and persecute them when they observe them, it is rightly said: “Who deliberately withdrew from him.”

[Note: Baluz. and Colb. read: “by seeing” (*videndo*).]

Therefore it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XII

**Ibid.—“And they were unwilling to understand all his ways.”**

### 29. How seriously those sin who seek impunity for sin through their ignorance. It is one thing not to have known, another to have been unwilling to know.

For he does not say, “They do not understand through weakness,” but “They were unwilling to understand,” because they often refuse even to know what they disdain to do.

Since it is written, “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving blows shall receive few blows; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to it shall receive many blows” (Luke 12:47), they consider the impunity of sin to be a remedy for ignorance.

[Note: Utic. and Pratel. read: “and does not do things deserving [blows], he shall receive few stripes.” This reading not only departs from the Vulgate but also conflicts with the Greek text.]

They are darkened by the blindness of pride alone, and therefore do not discern that it is one thing not to have known and another to have been unwilling to know. Not to know is ignorance; to have been unwilling to know is pride.

And the less excuse they can have for not knowing, the more they are confronted—even against their will—with what they ought to recognize. Hence Solomon says: “Does not Wisdom cry out, and does not Prudence give her voice? At the highest and loftiest places, standing above the way, in the midst of the paths” (Prov. 8:1)?

Perhaps we could pass along the way of this temporal life in ignorance of it, if this same Wisdom had stood hidden in the corners of the path.

### 30. The ways of divine Wisdom are open to all through the Incarnation. What it means to understand God’s ways. Humility opens the light of understanding; pride closes it.

It would have been necessary to seek her if she had wished to remain hidden.

[Note: Baluz. and Colb. read: “It would have been necessary to seek her by searching, if she had wished to remain hidden.”]

But after he publicly displayed the mysteries of his Incarnation, after he offered examples of humility to the proud, he fixed himself before us, as it were, in the midst of the paths, so that we might stumble against the one whom we do not wish to seek and, by stumbling, touch the one whom we neglect to see as we pass by.

Let it therefore be said: “And they were unwilling to understand all his ways.”

A way, then, is every action of incarnate Wisdom that he performed temporally. His ways are the patterns of life that he laid out for those coming to him. He provided as many ways of coming to him as he showed examples of good living.

The Prophet had looked upon his ways of humility when he sighed, saying: “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways” (Ps. 118:15). Again, this is said of every righteous person who takes care to walk by the Lord’s examples: “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he greatly desires his way” (Ps. 35:23) [Old recension XVII].

Since, therefore, all proud people despise the deeds of the Lord’s humility, it is rightly said: “They were unwilling to understand his ways.” These ways are despised in what is seen but revered in what is understood. For one thing is visible in them, and another is to be hoped for.

What else did he display in this life to the eyes of those who looked upon him except abasement, spittle, mockery, and death? Yet through these lowly things one passes to the heights; through these disgraces that precede them, eternal and glorious things are promised to us.

The proud therefore saw the ways of God but were unwilling to understand them, because, while they despised the lowly things that those ways display in themselves, they lost the lofty things that they promise.

[Note: In Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses, Vindoc., Baluz., and Colbert, the reading is: “because, while they despise the lowly things that he displays in himself, they have lost the lofty things that are promised.” The older edition has: “because, while they despise the lowly things that he displays in himself, they have lost the lofty things that he promises.” Recent editions read: “they have justly lost the lofty things that he promises.”]

To understand the ways of God, therefore, is both humbly to endure transitory things and steadfastly to await what endures, so that, following the Lord’s example, one may seek coeternal glory in comparison with temporal reproaches, and may direct one’s attention not to what one endures here but to what one awaits.

The proud therefore kept their eyes closed to these things, because, while they took pride in the glory of the present life, they did not see the height of the Lord’s humility. Humility opens the light of understanding; pride conceals it.

For there is a certain sacred mystery: the more the mind swells with pride, the less it reaches it, because it is driven outside precisely in proportion to the madness with which it is puffed up.

[Note: Longip., Pratel., and other Norman witnesses read “is inflated” (*inflatur*) for “is puffed up” (*afflatur*).]

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIII [New recension XII]

**Verse 28.—“So that they might cause the cry of the needy to reach him, and that he might hear the voice of the poor.”**

### 31. When the cry of the poor reaches God. A pastor is false who, neglecting preaching, is occupied with worldly concerns. The necessity of confession.

While these men are proud, those who are oppressed by the proud cry out to God.

[Note: Pratel. reads: “those who are oppressed by them while they are proud.”]

Or certainly it is said that they caused the cry of the poor to reach God because, when these men fall, the poor—that is, those humble in spirit—are put in their place. Since this happened through their fall, they are said to have caused it, in the same manner of speech by which we say that camps fight, because fighting is carried on from them.

Or certainly, because everything said above can also be referred to ecclesiastical rulers who, abandoning the work of preaching, become entangled in earthly affairs under the pretext of governance, it is appropriately added: “So that they might cause the cry of the needy to reach him, and that he might hear the voice of the poor.”

For while they themselves, occupied with worldly concerns, abandon the office of preaching, they compel the flock entrusted to them to break out into a cry of complaint, so that each subject may, as it were, lawfully murmur against the life of the false pastor: Why does one who does not perform the office hold the place of a teacher?

Perhaps, however, it is better to understand the pride of the Jews through the arrogance of the powerful and the desires of the Gentiles through the cry of the poor, just as, according to the testimony of Truth, the Jewish people are represented by the rich man who feasted splendidly. He assumed the abundance of the Law not for the necessity of salvation but for the pomp of exaltation; in the words of the commandments he did not nourish himself in an orderly way but displayed himself boastfully.

Through Lazarus, who was wounded and whose name means “helped,” the form of the Gentile people is expressed. Divine assistance raises them up all the more as they place less confidence in the resources of their own strength.

He is described as poor and full of wounds because the Gentile people, humble in heart, opened the confessions of their sins. For just as, in a wound, poison is drawn from within to the surface of the skin, so in the confession of sin, when hidden things are disclosed publicly, evil humors, as it were, burst forth from the innermost organs.

When those men therefore sinned, the cry of the poor was heard, because, while the Jews acted proudly against God, the prayers of the Gentiles reached God.

Therefore, immediately afterward, shuddering at these immense and profound judgments, he does not undertake to examine them by reasoning but venerates them with wonder, saying:

## CHAPTER XIV [New recension XIII]

**Verse 29.—“For when he grants peace, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him?”**

### 32. No one should investigate why one person is called and drawn while another is rejected.

Let no one investigate why, while the Jewish people remained, the Gentiles had previously lain in unbelief, or why, when the Gentiles rose at the end, the Jewish people were overthrown through the guilt of unbelief.

[Note: Pratel. and some Norman witnesses read: “through the guilt of unbelief.”]

Let no one investigate why one is drawn by grace while another is rejected on the basis of merit.

If you are astonished that the Gentiles have been taken up, “When he grants peace, who can condemn?” If you are bewildered by the destruction of Judea, “When he hides his face, who can behold him?”

Thus the counsel of supreme and hidden power becomes the evident satisfaction of reason.

Therefore, when the Lord spoke in the Gospel about the cause of this matter, he said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father” (Matt. 11:25).

Immediately afterward, adding something like an explanation of this hiding and revelation, he said: “Because thus it was pleasing before you.”

By these words we receive examples of humility, so that we may not rashly presume to investigate heavenly counsels concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others. When he had introduced both matters, he did not immediately give an explanation but said that it had thus pleased God, showing by this that what pleased the just one cannot be unjust.

Hence, when he paid the laborers in the vineyard, making unequal workers equal in their reward, and the one who had labored longer demanded more pay, he said: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius? I wish to give this last one as much as I give you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?” (Matt. 20:13).

In all the things that are arranged outwardly, therefore, there is an evident cause belonging to the hidden justice of the will.

[Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses read: “which are explained outwardly.”]

Let it therefore be said: “For when he grants peace, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him?” [Old recension XIX].

And because God judges the smallest things just as he judges the greatest, and individuals just as he judges all things, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XV

**Ibid.—“Both over a nation and over all people.”**

### 33. God provides for the smallest as for the greatest, and for individuals as for all.

We are openly admonished to understand that this judgment, which is described as taking place over one nation, is also carried out over all people by an unseen examination, so that one is secretly chosen and another rejected, but no one unjustly.

What we see happening among the greatest, let us therefore fear carefully in each of ourselves. Divine judgments are directed over one soul just as over one city, over one city just as over one nation, and over one nation just as over the whole multitude of the human race.

The Lord attends to individuals as though he were free from all else, and he attends simultaneously to all as though he were free from each individual. For, while administering all things, he fills them; while filling them, he governs them. He is not absent from all when he orders one, nor absent from one when he orders all, since in the power of his nature he performs all things in tranquility.

[Note: Pratel. reads: “when he orders the universe.” Baluz. and Colb. read: “nor is he absent from the universe … when he orders the universe.”]

What is surprising, then, if he who works tranquilly is not confined when he attends to things?

Let it therefore be said that he exercises this subtle judgment both over a nation and over all people.

[New recension XIV.]

Since he has passed from the particular to the general, he now turns from the general back to the particular and shows what Judea specifically deserves, saying:

[Note: Turon. reads: “he passes to the general.”]

## CHAPTER XVI [Old recension XX]

**Verse 30.—“Who makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people.”**

### 34. Those subject to evil rulers should attribute this to their own guilt. The Antichrist will reign because of the sins of the peoples.

Judea was unwilling to have the true king reign over it, and therefore, as its merits demanded, it received a hypocrite, just as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:43).

And as Paul says: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie” (2 Thess. 2:10).

In the statement, “Who makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people,” the Antichrist himself, the head of all hypocrites, may be signified.

[Note: In Turon. the word “seducer” is absent.]

That seducer will then simulate holiness in order to draw people into iniquity. But he is permitted to reign because of the sins of the people, since those are then placed under his rule who were foreknown before the ages as worthy of his dominion; by their subsequent sins they demand to be arranged under him according to preceding judgments.

[Note: Baluz. reads “indications” (*indiciis*) for “judgments” (*judiciis*).]

That the Antichrist then reigns over the impious is therefore not the result of injustice in the judge but of guilt in those who suffer it. Indeed, many do not see his dominion and nevertheless serve it because of the condition imposed by their sins. For the one whom they do not see ruling over them, they undoubtedly venerate by living perversely.

Are they not his members—those who, through the appearance of assumed holiness, seek to seem what they are not? He is the principal bearer of hypocrisy, since, although he is a condemned human being and an evil spirit,

[Note: The Roman edition of Sixtus V reads “and by no means a spirit.” Gilot. likewise reads this, although he noted in the margin as a variant, “and an evil spirit.” This is also the reading in five English manuscripts and in our manuscripts, as well as in the Basel edition of 1503.]

he falsely claims to be God.

But undoubtedly those now proceed from his body who hide their iniquities under the covering of sacred honor, seeking by profession to appear to be what they refuse to be in their works.

Since it is written, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin,” the more freely they carry out the perverse things they desire, the more tightly they are bound to his service (John 8:34).

[Note: Gussanv. reads “the less freely,” against the manuscripts and other printed editions.]

No one who suffers such a ruler should accuse the one whom he suffers, since it was truly through his own merit that he became subject to the power of a perverse ruler. Let him accuse the guilt of his own work rather than the injustice of the one who governs.

For it is written: “I will give you kings in my anger” (Hos. 13:11). Why, then, do we despise having those rule over us whose governance over us we receive from the Lord’s anger?

If, therefore, when God is angry, we receive rulers according to our merits, we gather from their actions what we should think of our own character.

[Note: Turon., Vindoc., and the Norman witnesses read “we read” (*legimus*).]

Although often the elect are also subject to the reprobate. Thus David endured Saul for a long time (1 Sam. 18:11), but he is exposed by the subsequent guilt of adultery as having then been worthy of being oppressed by so harsh a superior.

### 35. Because of the offenses of the flock, a good pastor is sometimes corrupted.

Thus the persons of rulers are assigned according to the merits of their subjects, so that those who appear good are often changed as soon as they receive authority. Scripture made this clear concerning that same Saul, saying that he changed in heart when he received dignity.

Therefore it is written: “When you were little in your own eyes, I made you head over the tribes of Israel” (1 Sam. 15:17).

The actions of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, because of the wickedness of the flock, even the life of a truly good pastor commits an offense.

[Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses read: “because of the merit of the flock.”]

That David the prophet was praised by God and acquainted with heavenly mysteries, yet, inflated by the swelling of sudden pride, sinned by numbering the people; nevertheless, while David was sinning, the people received punishment (2 Sam. 24:9).

Why was this? Because the hearts of rulers are arranged according to the merit of the peoples. The just Judge corrected the fault of the sinner by the punishment of those whose cause had led him to sin. But because David himself, growing proud by his own will, was not free from guilt, he too received punishment for his sin.

The wrath that struck the people bodily in its fury also cast down the ruler of the people through the inward grief of his heart.

It is certain that the merits of rulers and peoples are so connected with one another that often the life of the people becomes worse through the fault of the pastors, and often the life of the pastors is changed because of the merit of the people.

[Old recension XXI.]

### 36. Subjects should tolerate even bad superiors if they can do so without endangering the faith. Humility is the teacher of righteousness.

Since rulers have their own judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of those who govern.

For it was not without reason that the Lord himself scattered the money-changers’ coins and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21:21), clearly signifying that he judges the life of the people through teachers but examines the deeds of teachers by himself.

The vices of subjects, moreover—vices that are now either concealed by their teachers or cannot be judged—are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, while the matter is conducted without danger to the faith, it is a mark of virtue to tolerate whatever belongs to one’s superior. Nevertheless, one should humbly offer advice if what is displeasing can perhaps be corrected.

But one must take the greatest care that an unregulated defense of righteousness does not turn into pride; that, while righteousness is loved carelessly, humility—the very teacher of righteousness—is not lost.

[Note: Longip. reads “is changed”; Baluz. reads, corruptly, “is loved.”]

One must not despise as a superior someone whom one happens to criticize in some action.

Against this swelling of pride, the mind of subjects is subdued for the preservation of humility if it continually attends to its own weakness. For we neglect to examine our powers truthfully, and because we believe ourselves stronger than we are, we judge strictly those who have been placed over us.

The less we know ourselves, the more we see those whom we try to criticize.

These are individual evils, often committed by subjects against superiors and by superiors against subjects. Those who rule consider all their subjects less wise than themselves; and those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers and think that, if they themselves happened to hold authority, they could act better.

[Note: The printed editions read, “These are common evils.” The reading given here is preserved by the manuscripts Vindoc., Turon., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses. It should especially be preferred because, if “common” had originally been read, it would scarcely have been changed into “individual”; the former reading appears more appropriate after the latter. A pedant, not approving “these are individual evils”—perhaps because he did not understand it—thought that “these are common evils” should be written. The earlier reading is nevertheless excellent, signifying that the vices attacked by Gregory belong to individuals. Baluz. and Colb. nevertheless have “these are common evils.”]

Hence it often happens that rulers see less wisely what ought to be done, because the cloud of exaltation itself darkens their eyes; and sometimes the one who is subject does, after becoming a superior, what he formerly criticized when he was subject, and blushes because he not only commits what he had judged but had also judged it.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care that the higher position does not exalt their hearts through an assessment of singular wisdom, so subjects must take care not to be displeased by the actions of their rulers.

[Old recension XXII.]

### 37. Bad pastors are to be honored, not imitated.

If the life of teachers is rightly criticized, subjects ought nevertheless to honor them, even when they are displeasing.

[Note: After these words Baluz. reads: “Here ends Book XXV.” Book XXVI begins only with the words “Does God require anything from you?”]

[New recension XV.]

But this must be carefully observed: do not seek to imitate someone whom you must honor, nor cease to honor someone whom you disdain to imitate.

A subtle path of righteousness and humility must be maintained, so that the reprehensible deeds of teachers displease us in such a way that the minds of subjects do not withdraw from preserving reverence for the teaching office.

This is well expressed in Noah when he was drunk: his good sons, turning away as they came, covered his exposed shame (Gen. 9:21).

We are said to turn away from what we reject. What, then, does it mean that the sons, with their backs turned, covered their father’s shame by throwing a cloak over him, except that good subjects are displeased by the faults of their superiors while nevertheless concealing them from others?

They carry the covering with their backs turned because, while judging the deed and honoring the office of teaching, they do not wish to look upon what they cover.

[New recension XVI.]

### 38. To despise pastors occupied with temporal matters is to accuse God. The authority of governance cannot be administered without attention to temporal care.

There are some who, when they begin a little of the spiritual life, observe that their rulers conduct temporal affairs and attend to earthly matters, and immediately accuse the order of heavenly providence, claiming that those placed over them were not appointed rightly to govern because they display examples of a lowly manner of life.

[Note: The older editions read: “of a weak manner of life.”]

But while these people fail to restrain themselves from criticizing their rulers, the merits demanded by their own guilt carry them as far as the criticism of the Creator himself.

[Note: Turon. reads: “go forth.”] His dispensation is recognized as more rightly ordered by the humble precisely where it is judged to be disorderly by the proud.

[Note: Gussanv. and other editions read “is not rightly judged.”]

Because the authority of governance cannot be administered without attention to temporal care, almighty God sometimes, through a marvelous dispensation of mercy, assigns the burden of governance to hard and laborious hearts, so that the tender minds of spiritual people may be separated from earthly care. In this way the latter can remain more securely hidden from the world, while the former willingly labor amid earthly concerns.

In carrying out the burden they have undertaken, they endure the harsh paths of worldly service for the benefit of their subjects as well.

[Note: Recent editions read “they are of a hard life.” The reading preferred here is found in the manuscripts Turon., Vindoc., Colb., Longip., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses, as well as in the old edition.]

### 39. How much we should value those who free us from temporal care by attending to it themselves.

Often, as has been said, merciful God hides his own people carefully from external activities precisely because he wishes to preserve them.

A master of a household often directs servants to the labor from which he keeps his delicate sons; and the sons are handsome and undefiled because the servants are soiled in the dust.

[Note: Recent editions read: “from which he keeps his sons more delicately.”]

How rightly this is accomplished divinely in the Church is signified by the very construction of the Tabernacle.

God commanded Moses that, to cover the inner Holy of Holies, curtains should be woven of fine linen, scarlet, and violet; and he ordered that, to protect the Tabernacle, curtains of goat hair and skins should be spread over it, since these would endure rain, winds, and dust (Exod. 26:1).

What, then, do we understand by the skins and goat-hair cloth with which the Tabernacle is covered except the rough minds of people who, by God’s hidden judgment, are sometimes preferred in the Church, even though they are hard?

Because they are not afraid to serve temporal concerns, they must bear the winds and rains of temptations arising from the opposition of this world.

What, moreover, is signified by the violet, scarlet, and fine linen except the tender yet radiant life of the saints?

While this is carefully hidden in the Tabernacle beneath goat hair and skins, its complete beauty is preserved. For fine linen may shine within the Tabernacle, scarlet may glitter, and violet may gleam with its blue color because above them the skins and goat hair bear the rain, wind, and dust.

Those who advance in great virtues within the bosom of the holy Church should not therefore despise the life of their superiors when they see them occupied with external affairs. Their own secure penetration into the interior depends upon the assistance of those who labor outwardly against the storms of this age.

What grace of its whiteness would fine linen retain if rain touched it? Or what brightness and radiance would scarlet or violet display if the dust that they received defiled them?

Let there therefore be, above, a goat-hair fabric strong against dust; let there be, beneath, a violet color suited to beauty. Let those who devote themselves solely to spiritual matters adorn the Church; let those whom the labor of bodily affairs does not burden cover the Church.

Let no one who already shines spiritually within the holy Church murmur against a ruler engaged in external affairs. If you shine securely within like scarlet, why do you accuse the goat hair by which you are protected?

[Old recension XXIII.]

### 40. God arranges the wicked examples of superiors as punishment for proud subjects. When prophets seem to curse, they are foretelling.

Some complain that, while rulers devote themselves excessively to temporal concerns at least for the benefit of their subjects, many in the Church grow cold through their example.

[Note: Perhaps *queritur* should be read, used passively: Gregory frequently uses deponent verbs in this way, for example *meditari* at the beginning of Book XX and *intueri* in Book XXI, §35. Thus “it is complained by some” may perhaps mean “some complain.”]

Who could deny that this is often true, when he sees pastors caring more anxiously for earthly things than for heavenly ones?

Yet these things are not unjust if, as we said above, the affairs of those who preside are arranged according to the merits of their subjects.

Secretly committed sins, committed willingly, demand that corrupt examples be offered even by pastors, so that, by a just judgment, the one who proudly strays from the way of God may stumble on the very path along which he walks, even through the guidance of his pastor.

Hence, through the prophet’s intention to foretell, not through a desire to curse, it is said: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs forever” (Ps. 68:24).

It is as though he said: Let those who preside over the actions of human life, as though they were foreseeing its paths, lack the light of truth, so that their subjects, who follow them, may be bent beneath the burdens of their iniquities and lose every upright posture.

We undoubtedly know that this happened in Judea. At the very coming of our Redeemer, the crowd of Pharisees and priests closed the eyes of their minds to the true light, and the people, walking according to the examples of their superiors, wandered in the darkness of unbelief.

[Note: Longip. reads “at the sight” rather than “at the coming.”]

### 41. In what sense God makes a hypocrite reign.

It may reasonably be asked how this passage says that the Lord makes a hypocrite reign, when elsewhere the prophet expressly complains about this matter, saying: “They have made kings, but not through me; they have appointed princes, and I did not know it” (Hos. 8:4).

Who, thinking rightly, would say that the Lord does what he does not know?

But because God’s knowing means approving and his not knowing means rejecting—for to those whom he rejects he says, “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:25)—and because God is sometimes said to do what he forbids by permitting it in anger, as he is said to have hardened the heart of the king of Egypt (Exod. 4:21), since he permitted it to be hardened, the Lord in a marvelous way both makes hypocrites reign and does not know them: he makes them reign by permitting it, and does not know them by rejecting them.

It is therefore necessary that, regarding everything desired in this life, the inner will first be sought.

[Note: Turon. reads “is regarded” (*respicitur*) for “is desired” (*concupiscitur*).] When the ear of the human heart seeks to perceive that will, it should know that it sounds not in words but in deeds.

When a position of governance is offered to someone who is to govern, each person must first examine himself to see whether his life corresponds to the position and whether his conduct does not conflict with the honor. Otherwise, afterward, in tribulation, the just ruler of all may not hear his prayers because he ignored the very beginnings of the honor from which that tribulation arose.

# BOOK TWENTY-SIX

The holy Doctor explains the final seven verses of chapter 34, chapter 35 in its entirety, and the first twenty-one verses of chapter 36, extending at great length into both allegorical and moral interpretations.

[Column 0347]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Signs of feigned and genuine humility.

Among the characteristics that arrogant men commonly display in their speech is this: they ask their listeners whether they may perhaps have said something disorderly precisely when they know that they have said something praiseworthy.

They do this not because they are uncertain about their own words but because they seek approval from the judgment of their hearers. Their state of mind can easily be discovered if, when someone praises their good qualities, he also criticizes their faults.

For it is certain that just as they swell with praise, so they flare up at correction; and when they see themselves criticized—even justly—by anyone, they immediately seek fuel for defending their faults.

[Note: The printed editions read, “and when they see themselves criticized by anyone, even justly, they despise it.” The manuscripts Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses provide the much better reading translated here.]

How, then, do they humbly question their good qualities when they perversely attempt even to defend their faults?

The truly humble person in good things is the one who is not a defender of evil. For when someone is reproved for his faults and becomes inflamed against the words of the reprover, then, when he hesitates over his good qualities as though humbly, he wishes to adorn himself through the language of humility, not to be taught.

Thus Elihu, representing the life of arrogant people, after introducing many profound and lofty matters, assumes the appearance of humility in his words. With a proposal of fairness and under the guise of discipleship, he addresses blessed Job, saying:

## CHAPTER II

**Chapter 34, verses 31–32.—“Because I have spoken to God, I will not forbid you either. If I have erred, teach me; if I have spoken iniquity, I will not add more.”**

[Note: Vindoc. reads “because therefore I”; Colb. reads “because therefore I have spoken.”]

[Note: Pratel. reads “I do not forbid you.” Colb. has the same reading.]

### 3. The Mask of Humility Is Quickly Cast Off

As it often happens that even the wicked speak good things, Eliu remembered that shortly before he had said many forceful things, and therefore, secure in himself, he was asking whether perhaps he had gone wrong. For he would not have asked this if he had believed that he had erred. It is, as I have said, a characteristic deceit of the arrogant that they then make a point of asking about their error when they know that they have not erred. But when they truly recognize that they have gone wrong, they disdain either to ask about the error or to be reproved for it. They do not desire to be humble, but to appear humble; and then they assume the appearance of humility by asking when they are praised more for the very act of asking.

But because it is altogether difficult for the arrogance that reigns in the heart not to burst forth in speech, if the hearers of the arrogant silently wait for a little while and consider their words, the subsequent words more quickly reveal their hearts. For they cannot long remain in the very appearance of humility which they assume only outwardly. Humility is a high place for proud minds, and when they strive to climb into its form, their weary steps of spirit slip away, as though from steep and rugged paths. What they desire to appear is foreign to them, and therefore they can by no means cling long to its image. They regard it as a heavy burden when they carry it even outwardly, and until they cast it off they suffer a kind of constraint in their hearts, because they serve the tyranny of arrogance, which has come to dominate them badly, and by its command they are compelled to reveal themselves as they are, lest they should long appear to be what they are not.

Accordingly, after Eliu had asked to be taught about his error, and had promised that he would not speak iniquity any longer, he suddenly leapt from the appearance of humility into words of swollen excuse. [Note: The editions read “of swollen excuse”; the reading followed is that of the English, Norman, Vendôme, Colbert, and other manuscripts consulted by Gussanville.] For he added:

### CHAPTER III

**Verse 33.** “Does God require it from you because it displeased you?”

As if he were saying: “I shall have to give an account before the Lord of why my iniquity is now reproved by you, although it is clear that it will not be demanded from you at the judgment.” Upright men, when they are unjustly attacked by human beings, appeal to the heavenly judgment.

[Ancient and Revised Recensions II.] [Note: This is how the old manuscripts and the older editions read most correctly. In Gilot 1571 and the editions following it, including Gussanville’s, a very serious error appears: “And therefore it is said by the same one to blessed Job: ‘Behold, in heaven …’” Those words belong to Job himself.]

Thus blessed Job is also made to say by the same one: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and my conscience is on high” (Job 16:19). And because they desire above all to please him, they seek the testimony of him alone.

The perverse, too, because they abandon the life of the righteous but sometimes follow their words, when they are reproved for their evil deeds, take as an argument for their defense what the righteous put forward as testimony to their innocence. [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and older editions; more recent editors altered it to “as testimony to innocence,” which does not correspond at all to the other member.] Hence it has already become their practice that, if anyone reproves them for their deeds, they seek God’s judgment rather than that of human beings. For even when they know that they will be condemned by God, they do not fear being judged by him, while they are ashamed to be judged by human beings. Thus they propose the greater judgment, which they do not fear, in order to evade the lesser judgment, of which they are ashamed.

For it is written: “Each of us will give an account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12). Since, then, the condemnation of each person is manifest at that time, the wicked infer from this that each person’s action is now safe even when perverse, lest any righteous person, by reproving it now, examine an action that is clearly destined to be alien to him at the judgment.

By contrast, the consciences of the godly believe that a great reward is conferred on them when they are now reproved for certain unlawful actions of theirs. [Note: Most Norman manuscripts read “they reckon it gain.”] For they set before the eyes of their hearts that the strict judgment of God will then be softened over them all the more truly in proportion as it is forestalled now by a human being’s sharper reproof; and they count temporal anger toward themselves as gain, since they know that through it they may escape eternal anger.

Eliu, therefore, representing all the arrogant and preferring to be struck by eternal denunciation rather than reproved temporarily, says: “Does God require it from you because it displeased you?” But because those who begin to speak contentiously are usually more blameworthy than those who answer them, he added:

### CHAPTER IV

**The same passage.** “For you began to speak, and not I.”

### 4. Those who are attacked and answer harshly falsely consider themselves innocent

He considered himself innocent precisely because, when attacked, he burst forth—plainly unaware that innocence is not defended by timing but by reason. For what support does his defense gain from the fact that, although he had introduced nothing against one who was silent, he nevertheless gave a wrong answer to one who had rightly begun? [Note: Pratel has “is extended”; but “is shown” must be read, because of the antithesis with the other verb, “is cloaked.”] Once he is shown in words of arrogance, behold, again he is cloaked under the appearance of inquiry, and he continues:

**The same passage.** “But if you know anything better, speak.”

Although, by not saying, “Because you know better,” but rather, “If you know anything better, speak,” he displayed excessive pride in doubting whether the other possessed superior knowledge. Nevertheless, by granting blessed Job an opportunity to speak, he indicated that he had displayed humility. [Note: The more recent editions, against the manuscripts, read “judged that he had displayed.”] But, as was said above, because in the conduct of the arrogant everything concealed beneath elaborate speech is exposed again when the intention of arrogance breaks through, Eliu soon made known with what state of mind he had asked blessed Job to speak. For it follows:

### CHAPTER V [Revised Recension III]

**Verses 34–35.** “Let men of understanding speak to me, and let the wise man hear me. But Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not sound of discipline.”

### 5. One may not lie for the sake of humility

Behold: while he seemingly humbly grants blessed Job the right to speak, he reveals what he was harboring inwardly, saying: “Let men of understanding speak to me”—plainly disdaining that blessed Job should presume to speak, as though he could not understand his words. And because he judged blessed Job unworthy not only of speaking but also of listening, he immediately added: “Let the wise man hear me.” As if he were saying: “This man is unjustly permitted to speak, although he does not even deserve to hear the words of the wise.”

Then he openly reveals how contemptuously he thinks of him, saying: “But Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not sound of discipline.” He believed that blessed Job had spoken without discipline because Job had declared that he had been righteous in his deeds. But perhaps Eliu would have said this if he had not thought that the very things blessed Job had related about himself came from an author of discipline. Job had innocently asserted that he had been scourged, and God himself testified that he had been struck without cause (Job 2:3). What, then, was proud in the voice of one who had been struck, when it in no way differed from the sentence of the one who struck him?

[Note: This is how our manuscripts and nearly all the editions read. In Gussanville, “the humble are incautious.” Gratian, at the cited place, gives two readings: “the humble are incautious” and “men are incautious.”]

“The humble are incautious” (22, question 2, chapter *Incaute*): they entangle themselves in falsehood while avoiding arrogance; indeed, by lying they become proud, because they rise up against the truth, which they abandon. For whoever, compelled by necessity, speaks true good things about himself is joined to humility all the more closely because he is also joined to truth. Was Paul not humble when, out of zeal for the truth, he related to the disciples so many great things he had done against false apostles (1 Timothy 2:7; Acts 20:18–19)? He would plainly have been an enemy of the truth if, by concealing his own virtues, he had allowed preachers of error to prevail.

But because arrogant men, in proudly examining the words of the good, weigh the surface of words more than the order of realities, Eliu believed that blessed Job’s statements had not sounded of discipline. [Note: Vindoc, Baluz, Colbert, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts read “the order of realities,” rather than the printed editions’ “the hinge of realities.”]

[Ancient Recension III.] Since the harshness of the proud often extends even to the hardness of cursing, he immediately adds words against blessed Job, as though speaking to God:

### CHAPTER VI [Revised Recension IV]

**Verse 36.** “My Father, let Job be tested to the end.”

### 6. The proud do not know how to sympathize with the afflicted. In correction, swollen things must be pressed down in such a way that wounded things are cherished

Behold: what he had conceived from the swelling of arrogance, he exalts even in words of cursing.

[Note: Pratel: “which was, as it were, from arrogance.”]

But perhaps he would have desired the force of a benevolent test if he had judged that Job had stood firm in the testing. Thus, so that his evil may be clearly recognized as cruelty, he asks that the one whom he already complains has fallen amid the blows be tested still further by blows. He first stated what he perceived, so that what he desired might be known more openly. He asks that the one whom he accuses of having sinned under the hand of the striker be struck still more.

These are the characteristic wishes of the arrogant: they ask that the life of the suffering be examined more harshly, because the more righteous they consider themselves, the harsher they are toward the sufferings of others. They do not know how to draw into themselves the pain of another’s weakness and to show compassion for their neighbor’s infirmity as for their own. Because they think highly of themselves, they in no way condescend to the humble. Eliu believes that blessed Job was struck because of guilt and therefore did not think that he owed him any bowels of compassion amid so many sufferings.

But truly holy men, when they recognize that someone is being scourged even for guilt, although they correct certain disorders in him, nevertheless sympathize with him in certain things that cause pain; and they know how to press down swollen things in such a way that they also know how to cherish wounded things, so that, while hard things are softened in them, the weak may be strengthened.

[Note: Turon, Baluz, Colbert, and most of the Norman manuscripts: “while they soften hard things in them.” The old Paris and Basel editions read: “so that hard things may be softened in them and weak things strengthened.”]

By contrast, because arrogant men do not possess the bowels of charity, they not only fail to sympathize with righteous people who are suffering, but even afflict them under the appearance of righteous correction; either they magnify whatever small evils may be in them, or, by interpreting what is truly good in them badly, they transform it.

### 7. Holy teachers often exaggerate the faults of sinners. What it means to dig through the wall of the heart

Nevertheless, chaste teachers often do exaggerate the faults of sinners and investigate hidden things from certain public signs, so that they may discern greater things from the smallest indications.

[Note: This is how it is read in the manuscripts of Baluz, Colbert, Vindoc, Turon, and the Normans, followed by the earlier editions. Later editors thought that *sancti* (“holy”) was sufficient in place of *casti* (“chaste”). Teachers may indeed be called chaste when they do not adulterate the chaste words of God.]

Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezekiel 8:8). He immediately added: “And when I had dug through the wall, one door appeared,” [Note: Another reading is “and when I had pierced through it.”] and he said to me: “Enter and see the most detestable abominations that these people commit here. And I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of reptiles, the abomination of animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel had been painted on the wall” (ibid. 9–10).

Through Ezekiel, the person of rulers is signified; through the wall, the hardness of subjects. And what is it to dig through the wall except to open the hardness of the heart by harsh corrections? When he had dug through it, a door appeared, because when the hardness of the heart is opened by harsh corrections, a kind of door is revealed through which all the inner thoughts of the one being corrected may be seen.

Hence it appropriately follows there: “And he said to me: Enter and see the most detestable abominations that these people commit here.” The one who, after examining certain outwardly visible signs, penetrates the hearts of his subjects so that everything they think inwardly becomes known to him, is as though entering in order to see abominations. Hence he adds: “And I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of reptiles, and the abomination of animals.”

In reptiles, wholly earthly thoughts are signified; in animals, thoughts already somewhat raised above the earth but still seeking the rewards of earthly payment. Reptiles cling to the earth with their entire bodies; animals, though suspended above the earth by their bellies, are nevertheless always inclined toward the earth by their appetite for food.

Thus there are reptiles within the wall when thoughts turn over in the mind that are never lifted up from earthly desires. There are also animals within the wall when, although certain just and honorable things are already being thought, they nevertheless serve the pursuit of temporal profits and honors. By themselves they are already, as it were, raised above the earth, but through ambition, as through the desire of the belly, they still lower themselves toward the depths.

Hence it is rightly added: “And all the idols of the house of Israel had been painted on the wall.” For it is written: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3:5). Therefore idols are rightly described after animals, because although people raise themselves from the earth through honorable action, they nevertheless lower themselves to the earth through dishonorable ambition.

It is also rightly said: “They had been painted,” because when the forms of external things are drawn inward, whatever is imagined through fictitious images is, as it were, painted in the heart.

[Ancient Recension V.]

### 8. The compassionate severity of the ruler of souls in investigating the sins of the heart. Let one who refrains from correction fear condemnation

It should therefore be noted that first an opening in the wall is seen, then a door, and finally the hidden abomination is revealed. For, plainly, with every sin signs are first shown outwardly, then the door of open iniquity, and finally all the evil hidden within is disclosed.

[Note: This is how the manuscripts of Anglic, the Normans, Baluz, Colbert, Vindoc, Turon, and others read. The old Paris edition has: “so that they may reach the utmost errors.” More recent editions have: “so that they may reach external errors.” The manuscript reading is preferable, since it seems to allude to what preceded: “It should therefore be noted that first the opening …”]

For this reason holy teachers also commonly examine small matters with seriousness, so that they may proceed from the extreme outward signs to greater hidden things. Words of harsh reproof stir people up so that they may uproot the thorns of deadly thought; and when they do this, they rage out of love of charity, not swell with the pride of arrogance. They are ready to die for those whom, as though raging against them even unto death, they afflict. In their thoughts they preserve what they love; in outward appearance they take on what they persecute. They commend good things by preaching and foretell evils to be avoided; they do not, like Eliu, desire and pray for them.

Toward those entrusted to them they sometimes burn so fiercely in correction that they seem to possess no tranquility; yet they are so tranquil in love that they seem untouched by any fervor. For they greatly fear that, if they cease correcting the wicked, they themselves will be punished for the wicked’s condemnation. And when they are inflamed toward words of denunciation, they come to these unwillingly, yet by them they prepare a defense for themselves before the strict Judge.

[Note: Vindoc and Pratel: “they inflame themselves.”]

### 9. The order of correcting those who must be reproved and instructing sinners toward repentance and piety

Hence it is said again to the same Ezekiel:

[Note: In Turon and some ancient manuscripts, “to Jezechiel.” Below also, “Jezechiel.”]

“Son of man, take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem; and arrange a siege against it, and build fortifications, and heap up a rampart, and set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it. And you, take an iron pan for yourself, and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city” (Ezekiel 4:1ff.).

For whom does Ezekiel represent the figure except teachers? To him it is said: “Take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem.” Holy teachers take a brick for themselves when, in order to teach, they grasp the earthly heart of their hearers. They place the brick before them because they guard it with the whole attention of their concern. They are commanded to draw the city of Jerusalem upon it because, by preaching to earthly hearts, they take the greatest care to show how great is the vision of heavenly peace.

To it he is also rightly told: “And arrange a siege against it, and build fortifications.” Holy preachers arrange a siege around the brick on which the city of Jerusalem has been drawn when they show an earthly mind—already seeking the heavenly homeland—how greatly the adversity of vices attacks it during the present life. When it is shown how each sin lies in wait for the mind, a siege around the city of Jerusalem is, as it were, arranged by the preacher’s voice.

But because they not only explain how the vices lying in wait assault the mind, but also how guarded virtues strengthen it, it is rightly added: “And you shall build fortifications.” The holy preacher builds fortifications when he never ceases to indicate which virtues oppose which vices.

And because, as virtues increase, the battles of temptation often increase, it is rightly added: “And you shall heap up a rampart, and set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it.” Each preacher heaps up a rampart when he points out the mass of a growing temptation. He raises camps against Jerusalem when he announces to the upright intention of his hearers the attacks of a crafty enemy as though they were incomprehensible ambushes.

[Note: Here the manuscripts diverge. Longipont has: “watching for crafty enemies, as it were, and so forth.” Turon: “when he discloses to the upright intention of his hearers, and foretells, as it were, incomprehensible ambushes.” Baluz, Colbert, and the Normans: “watching for the crafty enemy and for, as it were, incomprehensible …” The old Paris and Basel editions: “unwatchful and, as it were …”]

And he places battering rams around it when he makes known the goads of temptations that surround us on every side in this life and pierce the wall of the virtues.

### 10. What and how great zeal is necessary for this

Here it is rightly added: “And you, take an iron pan for yourself, and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city” (Ezekiel 4:3). By the pan, frying is signified; by iron, strength. But what so fries and tortures the mind of a teacher and master as zeal for the Lord? Hence Paul was inflamed by the burning of this pan when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

And because whoever is inflamed with zeal for God against sinners is forever fortified by a strong guard, lest he be condemned for neglecting the care of preaching and governance, it is rightly said: “You shall place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city” (Ezekiel 4:3). The iron pan is placed as an iron wall between the prophet and the city because, when teachers now display strong zeal, that same zeal later serves as a strong defense between them and their hearers, lest they then be left without protection for punishment if they have now grown lax in correction.

The prophet heard of this pan, so that he might take it as a wall between himself and his hearers, when the divine voice first said to him: “If you announce to the wicked man, and he is not converted from his wickedness and from his wicked way, he himself will die in his wickedness, but you have delivered your own soul” (Ezekiel 3:19).

[Note: This is how Vindoc, Baluz, Colbert, and the Normans read. The printed editions have “in his iniquity.”]

Paul had placed this pan as a wall between himself and his disciples when he said: “I am clean from the blood of you all; for I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26).

Thus teachers must now desire to be heated by the ardors of zeal,

[Note: Vindoc, Ebroic, and other Norman manuscripts: “by the fervors of zeal.”]

lest afterward they be compelled to be tortured by the fire of Gehenna because of the torpor of negligence.

[Ancient Recension VI.]

### 11. With what discernment it must be practiced. It must not arise from hidden hatred

But one duty is owed to the unjust and subject, and another to the just and non-subject.

[Note: Turon: “one duty to the unjust and subject … another to the just and non-subject.”]

Fear should impel us to correct the former and to guard them, since we shall have to render an account for them; but toward the latter a considered equity itself should incline us to reverence.

[Note: Vindoc, Pratel, and most of the Normans: “but toward the reverence of the latter.”]

But arrogant men, because they do not know the form of this discernment, show toward the just and non-subject what they see good preachers doing toward the unjust and subject. When they rush unjustly into the heat of denunciation, they also go beyond the limits of speech into words of cursing. Because they do not love their neighbors as themselves, they do not cease wishing for their neighbors what they themselves fear happening to them.

[Note: Colbert, Pratel, and others cited by Gussanville read this way. Gussanville himself, together with the more recent editions, preferred the reading: “they fear that he himself may find.”]

Thus Eliu, sweating forth hidden hatred in the revelation of his curse, says: “My Father, let Job be tested to the end; do not cease from the man of iniquity.” He calls him a man of iniquity whom God, by heavenly testimony, declares to be righteous above all others.

And because many further things are added under this lack of discernment, I think they should be passed over briefly. Statements lacking weight do not require concentrated exposition. It follows:

### CHAPTER VII [Revised Recension VI]

**Verse 37.** “He has added blasphemy to his sins.”

### 12. Eliu represents those who, although they seem to speak for the truth, are alien from the truth

He accuses Job both of having deserved blows for his sins and of having sinned after the blows. But the Lord judges quite otherwise: he indicates that Job was struck without cause and restores double goods to him after the blows (Job 2:3; 42:10). Punishment is owed to guilt, not reward. Blessed Job is therefore shown to have spoken without guilt, since rewards follow after his speech (Job 42:10).

Eliu, then, while speaking in defense of the Lord, thinks something different about blessed Job from what the Lord thinks; thus, while multiplying words as though on behalf of the truth, he disagrees with the truth. It follows:

### CHAPTER VIII

**The same passage.** “Let him meanwhile be bound among us, and then let him challenge God to judgment with his words.”

### 13. They strive not only to say foolish things but also to say many things

As if he were saying: “Let him learn from our assertion that he is in no way equal to divine examination.” And because arrogant men strive not only to say foolish things but also to say many things, the verse that follows is appropriately brought forward concerning him repeatedly.

### CHAPTER IX [Ancient and Revised Recension VII]

**Chapter 35, verse 1.** “Therefore Eliu again spoke these things.”

### 14. The boundless talkativeness of the proud

Everyone who speaks much always strives to begin again in his speech, so that by the very beginning he may keep his hearers suspended and make them listen more attentively because they are expecting to hear something apparently new. Eliu, however, constantly finishes one subject and begins another, so that boundless talkativeness may continually be prolonged through the successive beginnings. It follows:

### CHAPTER X

**Verse 2.** “Does your thought seem right to you, when you say: ‘I am more righteous than God’?”

### 15. How unjustly they are accustomed to accuse the innocent

Everyone who reads the text of the story recognizes that blessed Job did not say that he was more righteous than God, but he did say: “Let him set forth equity against me, and my judgment will reach victory” (Job 23:7).

Weighing his life, plainly, and ignorant of the reasons for his being struck, as has often already been said, he believed that he was being scourged for the cleansing of sins and not for the increase of merits. Therefore he was confident that his judgment would reach victory, because he did not find in himself the guilt for which he ought to have been struck.

The Lord also said this concerning him to the devil: “You moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3). What, then, did he do wrong by saying this, when, even unknowingly, his words agreed with the divine and hidden judgment concerning him?

Or what harm is there if our words outwardly differ, in appearance before human judgment, from the uprightness of truth, when inwardly, at the core of the heart, they are joined and harmonized with it? Human ears judge our words according to what they sound like outwardly (22, question 5, chapter *Humanae*); divine judgments hear them according to what they issue from within. Among human beings the heart is weighed from the words, but before God the words are weighed from the heart.

Therefore, when blessed Job said outwardly what the Lord had said inwardly, everything he spoke was all the more justly expressed outwardly because he had not departed in piety from the inward judgment.

Although, filled with the prophetic Spirit, when he said, “Let him set forth equity against me, and my judgment will reach victory” (Job 23:7), he may also have perceived the presence of our Redeemer. For he himself is the power and wisdom of the Father, and he may not improperly be understood as that very equity. Hence it is written: “He was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

When God, by showing that equity incarnate had been set against the wicked who were fleeing from him, he immediately recalled them from iniquity; and in that judgment the ancient adversary was defeated, when he found God’s equity opposing his own ways. It follows:

### CHAPTER XI

**Verse 3.** “For you have said: ‘What is right does not please you,’ or, ‘What benefit will it be to you if I sin?’”

### 16. They either speak falsely or, if they speak truly, they speak things that do not fit

If the whole sequence of the book is considered, blessed Job is shown to have said none of these things. But arrogant men, as we said above, commonly possess this characteristic: when they advance in excessive denunciation, they also lie while denouncing; and when they cannot justly reprove what exists, they reprove by lying about what does not exist. It follows:

**Verse 4.** “Therefore I will answer your words and your companions with you.”

By the preceding words he had represented the words of blessed Job as blameworthy and proposed them as material for his own speech. But in the words that follow he sharply exposes what he had deceitfully fashioned for himself as material for speaking. The statements that follow are indeed forceful, but they do not fit the person of blessed Job; and the darts of this denunciation strike him all the less because they are directed unjustly against him. It follows:

### CHAPTER XII [Revised Recension VIII]

**Verses 5–7.** “Look up at heaven, and behold; contemplate the sky, which is higher than you. If you sin, what harm will you do to him? And if your iniquities have multiplied, what will you do against him? Moreover, if you act justly, what will you give him, or what will he receive from your hand?”

### 17. Creatures are the footprints of God

Although these things ought not to have been said to blessed Job, who knew greater things, nevertheless what is said is true: our sins do not harm God, nor do our good deeds contribute anything to him. Hence he continues:

**Verse 8.** “Your wickedness will harm a man who is like you, and your righteousness will help a son of man.”

But among these words we should carefully observe what he says: “Look up at heaven, and behold; contemplate the sky, which is higher than you.” By saying this, he plainly infers that one should consider how much less one’s action can benefit or harm God, since one cannot benefit or harm the height of heaven and the sky.
