Although by heaven or sky we may understand the heavenly powers, which always cling to the divine gaze, so that, when we see angelic spirits still far above us, we may recognize how far beneath the Creator and Ruler of spirits we are, nevertheless there is no obstacle to understanding here the bodily matter of heaven and sky.

[Ancient Recension VIII.]

For if we watchfully contemplate outward things, through them we are recalled to inward things. The marvelous works of visible creation are the footprints of our Creator. We cannot yet see him himself, but we are already moving toward the vision of him if we admire him in the things he has made. We therefore call creation his footprints because, by following through the things that come from him, we go toward him.

Hence Paul says: “His invisible things are understood and seen through the things that have been made, and his eternal power and divinity also” (Romans 1:20). It is also written in the Book of Wisdom: “Through the greatness and beauty of creation the Creator can be seen intelligibly” (Wisdom 13:5).

Our mind, scattered outwardly by its own sin, does not yet know God inwardly as he is. But while he sets the beauty of his work before us outwardly, he hints to us, as it were, by certain signs and shows us what we should pursue within; [Note: More recent editions read “hints himself to us”; *himself* is absent from the Colbert, Pratel, and other manuscripts.] and, in a marvelous way, through those outward forms themselves he leads us inward. By showing outwardly these marvelous things, which he is not, he suggests with immense wonder what he is.

Hence it is written of Wisdom: “She shows herself to them cheerfully in her ways, and meets them with every providence” (Wisdom 6:17).

### 18. The ways to the Creator. We withdrew from God through visible things; through those same things we must return to God

The works of creation, when contemplated, are the ways to the Creator.

[Note: More recent editions: “the works of the Creator, when contemplated,” against the manuscripts of Colbert, Turon, Ebroic, and others, as well as the old editions.]

When we see that these things have been made, we marvel at the power of their Maker. In these ways Wisdom meets us with every providence, because in everything that appears to have been wonderfully made, the Maker’s power is presented for our investigation. Wherever the soul turns, if it attends watchfully, it finds God in the very things through which it departed from him; and from considering again those things whose love caused it to desert him, it recognizes his power. Through the things by which it fell perversely, it is recalled when converted.

Where we fell, there we strive to rise; and, as though rising there, we fix the hand of our consideration where, by the foot of slippery love, we fell and lay neglected. Because we fell from invisible things through visible things, it is fitting that we should again lean upon visible things to reach the invisible, so that by the same step through which the soul came to the depths, it may return to the heights; and by the same steps through which it fell, it may rise, since, as has been said, those things that wrongly chosen divided us from God recall us to him when rightly considered.

Thus Eliu, in order to apply the force of consideration and to show from bodily things how much higher God is than a human being, rightly added: “Look up at heaven, and behold; contemplate the sky, which is higher than you.” From created and bodily things themselves we recognize how far we stand below the sublimity of our Creator, because everything we see reminds us to be humble, so that contemplated creation may be, as it were, a kind of reading for our mind.

[Note: Another manuscript has “the appearance of our mind.”]

Let him therefore say: “Look up at heaven; and behold, and contemplate the sky, which is higher than you. If you sin, what harm will you do to him? And if your iniquities have multiplied, what will you do against him? Moreover, if you act justly, what will you give him, or what will he receive from your hand?”

As if he were saying: “From the very creatures that you see to be bodily higher than you, understand how far you are separated from the sublimity of divine power; and from this consideration of yourself conclude that you neither help God by living well nor burden him by evil actions.”

### 19. We are inferior to angels, and therefore all the more to God

But if, as we said above, we understand the heavenly powers by heaven or sky, Eliu’s words admonish us to consider that, since those angelic spirits cannot fully contemplate the power of our Creator, although it is certain that they are higher than we are precisely because they have not fallen into the depths, we should infer how much lower we are than God, since we are subject even to exalted creatures who are nevertheless far below him.

As if he were saying: “See how far you are separated from the divine height, before whose power even those powers tremble in their humility, although they surpass you by immeasurable sublimity; and see how far you yourself are below the Highest, since you discover that you are lower even than those who are lower than he.”

[Note: Longipont, Pratel, and other Normans, supported by the old Basel edition: “those humbled powers tremble.”]

By showing the highest things, he then brings the discussion back to equals, and says:

### CHAPTER XIII

**Verse 8.** “Your wickedness will harm a man who is like you, and your righteousness will help a son of man.”

### 20. A human being can harm or benefit another human being, but not angels. (1, question 4, canon “To a human being.”)

Human impiety harms the one whom it pollutes by corrupting him. Conversely, our righteousness helps the one whom it turns away from wicked actions. For those things cannot harm or help which are unable either to corrupt someone from the good or to change someone from evil. Therefore the powers above cannot be harmed or helped in the manner in which they have already been established as immutable. But those entangled in earthly desires cannot consider these matters. For minds scattered outwardly find it difficult to return to themselves, because corrupt paths, once they have been entered, hold them with all the greater pleasure insofar as everything one desires is permitted in them. No wall of discipline stands in the way to restrain them; no punishment of retribution is foreseen to frighten them. Rather, with the eyes of the heart closed, the soul is hurled down into the depths precisely as it is darkened with respect to things above; and it perpetrates temporal evils all the more securely as it despairs more stubbornly of eternal goods.

> **Note:** Pratel. and other Norman witnesses: “once they have been seized.”

### [Older and Revised Recensions IX.] 21. The wicked purify the good by pressing them down.

But the wickedness of the reprobate, like a threshing floor separating the life of the elect as grain from chaff, presses it down in order to purify it.

> **Note:** Ebroic. and other witnesses: “presses and purifies.”

For the wicked free the good more thoroughly from the desires of this world while they afflict them, because, by inflicting many forms of violence upon them here, they compel them to hasten toward what is above. This was aptly signified concerning the Israelite people when Moses was calling and King Pharaoh was raging (Exod. 3:7). Moses was sent to summon them precisely when Pharaoh had already been stirred up to oppress them with harsh labor, so that the minds of the Israelites, disgracefully attached to Egypt, might be moved: one, by calling them, as though drawing them; the other, by raging, as though driving them forward. Thus the people, shamefully fixed in servitude, would be moved either by the attraction of good things or by the impulse of evils.

This happens daily, when the reprobate are permitted to rage against the elect while heavenly rewards are preached, so that, if we neglect to leave when called to the land of promise, we may at least be driven onward by the pressures of raging persecution. In this way Egypt—that is, the present life—which oppressed us while flattering us, may help us by pressing us; and what, while cherishing us, crushed us beneath the yoke of servitude, may show us the way of freedom while tormenting us.

> **Note:** Many Norman witnesses: “This, then, is the reason.”

This, certainly, is why the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust: so that, while they hear of future goods which they may desire, they may also suffer present evils which they dread; and so that, while love urges them toward an easier departure, suffering may drive them onward. Thus Elihu, continuing his account of the same labors of the elect under the oppression of the reprobate, says:

## CHAPTER XIV [Revised Recension X]

**821 Verse 9.**—“Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out, and they will lament because of the violence of tyrants.”

> **Note:** In Sacred Scripture and in ecclesiastical writers, *calumniator* often means not one who brings a false charge, but one who harasses and oppresses others. Isaiah 42:4: “Assyria oppressed him without any cause,” that is, “vexed him unjustly.” Luke 3:14: “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages.” Victor of Utica, *The Persecution of the Vandals*, book 2: “He burdened the provinces of his kingdom with various exactions and levies”; p. 22 of the new edition. See also pp. 38 and 40.

### 22. Those who deprive us of virtues by wicked examples are worse than those who deprive us of external goods.

We may rightly call all the wicked “oppressors,” not only those who seize external goods, but also those who strive to scatter what is within us through their evil conduct and the example of a reprobate life. The former seek to invade what is external to us, whereas the latter seek to plunder us inwardly. The former never cease raging out of love for possessions; the latter, out of hatred for the virtues. The former envy what we possess; the latter, how we live. The former endeavor to seize external goods because they please them; the latter strive to destroy internal goods because those goods displease them.

Therefore, just as a life of moral conduct is more valuable than the substance of possessions, so much more grievous an oppressor is the one who, by living wickedly, inflicts violence upon our morals than the one who, by violently oppressing us, brings loss upon our possessions. The latter has taken nothing away from our sustenance, but has set before us examples of destruction. He has therefore inflicted a more grievous oppression insofar as he has disturbed a peaceful heart in temptation. Even if he has not at all persuaded us by the deeds of his conduct, he has nevertheless introduced the battle of temptation.

Thus we suffer a grievous oppression because of his life, since we certainly suffer inwardly what we must overcome with labor. And because the life of the wicked, which torments, abounds in this world, it is rightly said: “Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out.”

### 23. Some persuade us to vices by their example; others command them and compel us to them by tyrannical force.

Because those things which they cannot persuade by words they sometimes also strive to extort by unrestrained force, the text appropriately adds: “And they will lament because of the violence of tyrants.” Whoever compels us to live wickedly by his example is still using the voice of an oppressor against us; but whoever, while persuading us to sin, also seeks to frighten us is already raging against us with the arm of tyranny. For it is one thing to persuade us to vices by living in a certain way, and another to command them by frightening us. When, therefore, we observe examples of evil conduct, we seem still to hear the clamor of an oppressor; but when we are compelled by force to sin, we already endure a tyrant in our heart.

### 24. Nevertheless, the minds of the elect resist their efforts. One must go to God not only through gentle paths but also through rough ones.

But the minds of the strong, firmly fixed in God, despise these things all the more insofar as they see that they grow up against the commands of the Creator. For, awaiting the rewards of eternity, they draw strength from adversities, because they have no doubt that, as the struggle increases, a more glorious victory awaits them.

Thus the desires of the elect, while being pressed down, advance through adversity, just as fire is pressed by the action of air so that it may grow; and from the point where it appears almost to be extinguished, it gains strength. We show how ardently we burn with desire for the Lord when we proceed toward him not only through calm and gentle circumstances, but also through rough and harsh ones.

Hence the Prophet says: “He made my feet like those of a stag” (Ps. 17:34). For when a stag climbs the ridges of the mountains, it leaps over every roughness it sees and every obstacle lying in its path, entangled with thorns, and rises to higher places without any impediment to its course.

> **Note:** Turon.: “if whatever rough things present themselves”; Pratel. and other Norman witnesses: “whatever rough things, whatever things present themselves.” Baluze and Colbert likewise.

In the same way, the minds of the elect leap over whatever they see opposing and obstructing them in this world by a leap of contemplation; and, like stags, despising the thorns of earthly things, they raise themselves to what is above. Again he says: “And in my God I will leap over a wall” (ibid., 30).

A wall is everything placed in the way of our journey so that we may not pass to the one whom we love. But we leap over the wall when, out of love for our heavenly homeland, we trample upon whatever has been placed in our way in this world.

Again, through the same Prophet, the Lord says to the struggling soul: “I heard you in the hiding-place of the storm; I tested you at the waters of contradiction” (Ps. 80:8). The hiding-place of the storm is when, in a contrite heart, the waves of tempting thoughts swell, and when the tumult of worldly cares crashes against the pursuits of holy love. One is therefore heard in the hiding-place of the storm, because this very fluctuation of tribulation is the cry of the one who prays.

Since there are certainly those who contrive to persuade seekers of good things to pursue what is perverse, “the waters of contradiction” are the resisting peoples. And because desire is tested when some adversity resists it, it is rightly said: “I tested you at the waters of contradiction.”

Through these struggles for virtue, therefore, the strong advance by means of adversity. But the weak often grow faint in their desires when something is set against them; and when they are struck by severe tribulation, they fail through cowardice. Thus Elihu, reproaching blessed Job with cowardice and having first described the oppression of the wicked, immediately proceeds to set forth the cowardice of the weak, saying:

## CHAPTER XV [Revised Recension XI]

**Verse 10.**—“And he did not say, ‘Where is God who made me?’”

### 25. Whoever is broken by temptation does not seriously consider God’s providence.

It is the custom of Sacred Scripture suddenly to pass from the singular number to the plural, and often from the plural to the singular. Thus, when Elihu had said, “They will cry out, and they will lament,” he did not add, “They did not say, ‘Where is God?’” but rather, “He did not say, ‘Where is God?’” Passing from the plural number to the singular, he suddenly turned to the person of each individual who is weak—perhaps because whatever is said about them in the singular is more readily recognized by individuals, so that each person may return to his own heart and condemn in himself what is said about each one.

> **Note:** Baluze, Colbert, Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses read *dici* (“said”); it is absent from the printed editions.

He therefore maintained the singular number, saying: “He did not say, ‘Where is God who made me?’” For whoever is broken by the tribulation of adversities does not contemplate the one by whom he was made. The one who made what did not exist does not abandon what has been made without governance; and the one who kindly created the human being certainly does not permit him to be tortured unjustly. Nor does he allow what exists to perish through neglect, since he created even what did not exist so that it might exist.

> **Note:** Pratel. and some Norman witnesses: “took care that it might exist.”

When, therefore, we seek the cause of our tribulation and perhaps find it only slowly, this consideration remains: that we suffer nothing unjustly.

> **Note:** Pratel.: “this is a ready explanation”; the same reading occurs in Utic., Baluze, and Colbert. For if, by God’s authorship, we exist who once did not exist, then, under God’s governance, we who exist are not afflicted unjustly.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVI [Older Recension XI, Revised Recension XII]

**[Col. 0362D] The same passage.**—“Who gave songs in the night.”

### 26. So that we may not be overcome, God tempers tribulations with consolation.

A song in the night is joy in tribulation. For although we are afflicted by the pressures of temporal existence, we already rejoice in hope because of eternity. Paul proclaimed songs in the night when he said: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12).

David had taken up a song in the night when he said: “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounded me; my joy, deliver me from those surrounding me” (Ps. 31:7).

> **Note:** Vindoc.: “Behold, he calls the distress ‘night.’”

Behold: he calls the distress “night,” and yet amid his straits he calls his liberator his joy. Outwardly there was night in the surrounding distress, but inwardly songs resounded from the consolation of joy.

> **Note:** Turon.: “from the consolation of righteousness.”

Since we cannot return to eternal joys except through temporal losses, the whole intention of Sacred Scripture is that the hope of abiding joy should strengthen us amid these passing adversities.

> **Note:** Another reading: “so that the hope of what endures,” as Colbert has it.

Hence the prophet Ezekiel also testifies that he received a book in which were written “lamentation, song, and woe” (Ezek. 2:9). What else is signified by this book except the divine utterances? Since they command us to shed tears and mourn, lamentations are said to have been written in it. It also contains song and woe, because it proclaims joy concerning hope in such a way that it nevertheless instills present pressures and straits.

> **Note:** Vindoc.: “so that present pressures nevertheless…”

It contains song and woe because, although we desire sweet things there, it is first necessary that we endure bitter things here. The Lord proclaimed song and woe to his disciples when he said: “I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace; in the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33). As though he were saying openly: “Let there be within you something from me that may restore you through consolation, because outwardly there will be something from the world that will oppress you severely through its violence.”

Since, therefore, when a weak person is oppressed, he is exhausted by excessive cowardice and loses hope of joy, and while enduring adversities outwardly forgets inwardly what he was rejoicing in, it is rightly said: “He did not say, ‘Where is God who made me, who gave songs in the night?’” If he had said this, he would have tempered the force of what he suffers; and by seeking within himself what would remain, he would not have judged intolerable what he endures outwardly as something passing.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVII [Revised Recension XIII]

**Verse 11.**—“Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and instructs us above the birds of heaven.”

### 27. God teaches us to avoid the pleasures of the flesh and the exaltation of the spirit.

The beasts of the earth signify those who, by the habit of a carnal life, seek what is below; the birds of heaven signify those who, out of an eagerness for proud curiosity, investigate what is lofty. The former lower themselves by living beneath what they are; the latter raise themselves by inquiry above what they can attain.

> **Note:** Pratel. and others: “pleasure casts them into the depths… desire for curiosity raises these as though to higher places.”

The former are cast down into the depths by the pleasure of the flesh; the latter are lifted, as though to higher places, by the desire of curiosity. To the former Sacred Scripture says: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9). The proud labor of the latter is rebuked when it says: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not investigate what is stronger than you” (Sir. 3:22).

> **Note:** Vindoc.: “the pride of the latter is rebuked.”

To the former it says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire” (Col. 3:5). To the latter it says: “Let no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. 2:8).

God therefore teaches us above the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven, because, when we recognize what we are, neither the weakness of the flesh casts us down nor the spirit of pride lifts us up. We are neither subjected by sinking into the depths nor inflamed by pride concerning lofty things. Whoever slips through the flesh is overthrown by the appetite of beasts; whoever is lifted up in mind is raised, as though on the wing of lightness, after the manner of birds.

### [Older Recension XII.] 28. Pride is the seedbed of lust. The flesh plunges down those whom proud knowledge raises. The mind justly loses mastery over the flesh if it refuses to serve God.

But if one attends vigilantly so as to retain both humility of mind and chastity of the flesh, one quickly understands that each is guarded through the other. For pride has often been a seedbed of lust for many: while the spirit raised them as though on high, the flesh plunged them into the depths.

> **Note:** Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “into the depths.”

Such people are first secretly lifted up, but afterward fall publicly, because while they swell through hidden movements of the heart, they fall through open lapses of the body. Thus, indeed, those who were lifted up were rightly struck by a just retribution: because they place themselves above human beings through pride, they are brought down through lust to the likeness of beasts.

For “when the human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). As though by the wing of knowledge, a certain knowledge had raised these people on high. Paul spoke of them in the passage cited above: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21).

How they fell into the pleasure of beasts, or even into something worse than the pleasure of beasts, he added by saying: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness” (ibid., 24).

> **Note:** Pratel., Baluze, Colbert: “of their hearts.” The printed editions read: “of their mind.”

Behold: the flesh plunged down those whom proud knowledge had raised, and they fell from the flight of birds beyond it, into the appetite of beasts; and they were cast down beneath themselves precisely from the place where they seemed to be going above themselves.

Therefore the mind must be guarded with care and by every means from the swelling of pride. Our thoughts do not fly past God’s eyes empty, nor do any moments of time pass through the mind without a condition of retribution. God therefore sees inwardly what lifts up the mind, and for that reason permits outwardly what brings it down to grow strong. What is afterward struck by the corruption of lust is first raised up inwardly. A hidden fault is followed by an open blow, so that the inner realities may be punished by outward evils, and the heart may collapse publicly after swelling secretly.

Hence, through Hosea, the following is said against the Israelites: “The spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord” (Hos. 5:4). To show that the cause of lust had burst forth from the fault of exaltation, he immediately added: “And the arrogance of Israel will answer to his face” (ibid., 5). As though he were saying: “The fault that lay hidden in the exaltation of the mind has answered openly through the lust of the flesh.”

Therefore purity of chastity must be preserved through the guardianship of humility. For if the spirit is devoutly held beneath God, the flesh is not illicitly raised above the spirit. The spirit has been entrusted with mastery over the flesh, provided that it recognizes under the Lord the rights of legitimate servitude. But if, through pride, it scorns its Creator, it rightly receives conflict from the flesh subjected to it.

Hence the first disobedient human being, as soon as he sinned through pride, covered his shameful parts (Gen. 3:7). Because he had inflicted an insult upon God through the spirit, he immediately encountered an insult through the flesh. And because he refused to be subject to his Creator, he justly lost control over the subjected flesh that he governed, so that the shame of his disobedience might rebound upon him and, once overcome, he might learn what he had lost through exaltation.

### [Older Recension XIII.] 29. If we neglect humility of heart, God despises integrity of the flesh.

Therefore, after beginning to seek what is above, no one should judge himself conquered only when he is openly overcome by the pleasure of the flesh.

> **Note:** Vindoc.: “then let him judge himself righteous.” This reading is excellent on the surface. The other reading, however, is preferable. Its meaning is that those who are overthrown by the pleasure of the flesh did not begin to be conquered only when they were defeated by an open fall; rather, they had already been cast down by the exaltation of the mind, which is the root of lust. Not understanding this, some superficial scholar considered it absurd—even impious—to say that someone who falls into lust should not be regarded as conquered at that point, and therefore thought the text should read: “Let no one… then judge himself righteous,” with the word “conquered” deleted.

For if the poison of lust usually arises from the root of exaltation, the flesh conquered when the spirit secretly swelled with pride. The soul had already fallen, through the origin of its fault, into the wantonness of beasts when, by exalting itself, it flew, after the manner of birds, beyond what it ought.

This is why prolonged continence is suddenly broken; this is why virginity, often preserved even into old age, is violated. Because humility of heart is neglected, the just Judge also despises bodily integrity; and eventually, through an open evil, he declares reprobate those whom he had long tolerated secretly as reprobate.

For whoever suddenly lost a good preserved for a long time had inwardly harbored another evil, from which the other suddenly burst forth. Through that evil he had already stood alienated from Almighty God, even when he appeared to cling to him through bodily purity.

> **Note:** Vindoc.: “from which came the other.”

Since, therefore, exaltation of mind drags the flesh toward pollution, the heart of the reprobate is plunged from the flight of birds into the wantonness of beasts. Holy men, however, lest they fall through a bestial appetite into the abyss of lust, carefully guard the thoughts of their minds from the flight of pride; and, lest they fall through folly into the depths, they humbly press down everything they understand in a lofty way.

It is therefore rightly said: “Who teaches us above the beasts of the earth, and instructs us above the birds of heaven.” The unspoken sense is: “He did not say this either.”

### 30. We fail in adversity because we do not know how to use prosperity with moderation.

He does not say that the one who surpasses beasts and birds remembers this in tribulation. As though he were saying: “The weak person does not strengthen himself at all in disturbance because he does not exercise restraint in tranquility; and for that reason he does not know how to endure adversity, because, placed in prosperity, he does not know how to press himself down in thought from the flight of birds, nor to lift his carnal impulses above the voraciousness of beasts.”

But this is said so incongruously of blessed Job, since his life was wonderfully balanced between what is lofty and what is lowly.

It can also be understood in another way: “Who teaches us above the beasts of the earth, and instructs us above the birds of heaven.” For just as the term “beasts” signifies the life of human beings still subject to the impulses of the flesh, so the designation “birds” represents the exaltation of proud spirits. Thus “beasts” signify earthly human beings, while “birds” signify demons.

Hence, when the Lord said that the seeds had fallen beside the road, he added: “The birds of heaven came and ate them” (Matt. 13:4), clearly signifying by the birds the powers of the air.

### 31. While submitting themselves to God, the saints rise above and despise all passing things.

Holy men, because they neither pursue the low examples of human beings nor are deceived by demonic subtlety, grow through the virtue of instruction above both the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven.

They have been taught above the beasts of the earth because they despise whatever can be sought in the depths. They have also been instructed above the birds of heaven because they understand all the snares of unclean spirits.

> **Note:** Pratel. and other Norman witnesses: “the snares of wicked spirits.” Some perhaps preferred to write “wicked” rather than “unclean,” since it is more fitting to say that wicked spirits lay snares than unclean spirits.

They have been taught above the beasts of the earth because they seek nothing in this life that passes away. They have been instructed above the birds of heaven because they already trample by the merits of their life the aerial powers which they still endure through the weakness of the flesh.

Paul had already been taught above the beasts of the earth when he said: “For many walk…” And shortly afterward: “Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they think about earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:18–19).

Again, he knew himself to have been instructed above the birds of heaven when he said: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

He saw beasts beneath him, because, although still placed on earth, he trampled the ways of those who live in the depths.

> **Note:** Vindoc., Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “he trampled the minds.”

Again, he had surpassed the flight of birds by the dignity of his merits, because, about to enter the heavenly realm, he knew that he would judge angels. In the former he trampled the depths of the unclean; in the latter, the heights of the proud.

The minds of the saints despise all passing things and contemplate beneath themselves whatever is proud and whatever passes away. Established, as it were, at a certain summit of realities, they see all things subjected to them to the extent that they more truly subject themselves to the Author of all things. And from the very place where they prostrate themselves in true humility before the Creator of all, they transcend everything.

Let him therefore say: “Who teaches us above the beasts of the earth, and instructs us above the birds of heaven.” As though he were saying: “The weak person, overcome by cowardice, did not say these things, and therefore the adversity of temptation struck him, because in the time of tranquility he did not surpass all these passing things through any perfection.”

He would not dread the adversities of this life if, by the merit of perfection, he had also trampled upon its prosperities.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Revised Recension IV]

**[Col. 0367A] Verse 12.**—“There they will cry out, and he will not answer because of the pride of the wicked.”

### 32. The just are permitted to be oppressed so that they may be purified and so that the wickedness of their oppressors may be brought to completion.

“There,” that is, in tribulation, just as it is written conversely concerning joy: “The children of your servants will dwell there” (Ps. 101:29).

But it seems uncertain whether the text means, “He will not answer because of the pride of the wicked,” or, “Because of the pride of the wicked they will cry out.” It can be understood better if they are said not to be heard because of the pride of the wicked rather than to cry out because of it.

For that they cry out because of the pride of the wicked was already stated above, in the verse that says: “Because of the multitude of violent men they will cry out.”

> **Note:** In the earlier passage where this place in Job is expounded, the reading is “oppressors.” The Hebrew text permits both interpretations. Some versions have “because of power” or “because of violence.”

Something, therefore, is hinted at in this verse that should be considered with greater subtlety. Often, when certain oppressed people have cried out, they deserve to be heard on their own account, yet their desires are delayed because of the pride of those who oppress them.

For God is just: he permits his own to be oppressed temporarily and allows the wickedness of the violent to increase wickedly, so that, while the life of the former is worn away in purification, the wickedness of the latter may be brought to completion.

> **[Older Recension XV.]**

Often, however, it happens that the just, caught in tribulation, receive heavenly consolation even temporarily, although they do not implore it for temporal purposes. They desire to be saved not for their own sake but for the salvation of their adversaries, so that, when Almighty God frees them from immense dangers through some miracle, he may make his power known even to their persecutors. In this way he may redeem the adversaries for eternity through the very means by which he saves his own temporarily.

Thus the Prophet, taking up the voice of the martyrs, says: “For the sake of my enemies, deliver me” (Ps. 68:19). As though he were saying: “I do not seek to be delivered from temporal tribulation for my own sake, but I desire to be delivered for the sake of my adversaries, so that, when my life is seen to be saved miraculously, the hardness of my enemies may be converted by the very sight of the miracles.”

Just as the Lord often rescues the life of his own temporarily for the conversion of his enemies, so he often does not answer the voices of his own for the condemnation of their persecutors, so that they may heap up their guilt precisely through the means by which they wickedly rejoice that they have prevailed.

For those who despise invisible things can sometimes be moved by visible miracles. But visible wonders are often not performed for the just because their adversaries do not deserve to be illumined invisibly.

Let it therefore be said: “There they cried out, and he will not answer because of the pride of the wicked.” As though he were saying: “The guilt of the oppressors prevents him from hearing the voices of the oppressed.”

> **Note:** Another reading: “to be heard.”

Nor are the just visibly rescued, because the unjust do not deserve to be saved invisibly.

> **Note:** The Roman edition of Sixtus V and some others read, incorrectly: “because they do not deserve to be saved visibly.” The English, Norman, Vindoc. and other manuscripts, as well as the older editions, have: “invisibly.”

Hence again the Prophet says: “When he sees the wise dying, together the foolish and the senseless will perish” (Ps. 48:11). Those who see them dying visibly do not believe that they can live invisibly; and they thereby heap up the guilt of their unbelief, insofar as, seeing the death of the faithful, they despair of eternity.

Therefore all the violent grow worse inwardly precisely through the means by which they grow stronger outwardly against the life of the innocent. The more they are permitted temporarily to accomplish what they wish against God’s own, the more completely the innermost Truth casts them out from himself.

### 33. The prosperity of the wicked is a more severe punishment. It is a clear sign of rejection.

Whoever persecutes the life of the good is condemned by a worse vengeance when he encounters no adversity; and he lies exposed to the dangers of a stronger anger when he successfully accomplishes what he wickedly desires. For the vengeance of the heavenly judgment, by reserving him for future punishments, has abandoned the one whom it has refused to oppose here in his evil.

Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “I sent them away according to the desires of their hearts, and they will go in their own wills” (Ps. 80:13).

> **Note:** Vindoc., Baluze, Colbert and most Norman witnesses: “and they will go in their pleasures.” The earlier reading accords better with the Hebrew text and the Vulgate: “in their inventions.”

Again it is said: “The rod of God is not upon them” (Job 21:9). Again, concerning their very leader, it is written: “He will act and prosper” (Dan. 8:12). Again, concerning the same one, it is said: “And deceit will be directed in his hand” (Dan. 8:25).

> **Note:** Baluze, Colbert, Ebroic. and other Norman witnesses: “in his hand.” The recent editions omit *in*.

Deceit is directed in the hand of Antichrist because, in whatever he proposes against the good, he is hindered by no temporal adversity from carrying it out.

Again, through Solomon, it is said: “The prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32).

> **[Older Recension XVI.]**

It is therefore a clear sign of destruction when the outcome that follows upon desired wickedness favors it, and no opposition hinders what a perverse mind has conceived. Often, when the desires of wicked people are delayed, they are changed; and when they experience the difficulty of carrying them out, they acknowledge the guilt of their evil action. Those who were previously opposed against their will may afterward, willingly, oppose what they had conceived.

Since, therefore, when the Lord abandons the wicked, he permits them to prevail, and since the wickedness of the proud is completed through the very means by which the endurance of the humble is perfected, it is rightly said: “There they will cry out, and he will not answer because of the pride of the wicked.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIX [Revised Recension XV]

**Verse 13.**—“For God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will regard the causes of individuals.”

### 34. The desires of the saints are heard more abundantly the longer they are delayed.

It should be noted that two things are said: he hears the one who cries out not in vain, and yet, while observing what he suffers, he appears not to hear his voice; he is not ignorant of what each person endures.

Therefore no one who is heard only after a delay should believe that he is neglected by heavenly care. Often our desires are heard precisely because they are not immediately fulfilled; and what we ask to be accomplished quickly is made more beneficial by the very delay.

Often our voice is perfected through being deferred; and when our petition seems to be neglected on the surface, our desires are fulfilled more deeply at the root of our thoughts. So too seeds of crops are strengthened when pressed by frost; and the more slowly they emerge to the surface, the more abundantly they rise toward fruit.

Our desires are therefore extended by delay so that they may advance; they advance so that they may grow strong for what they are going to receive; they are exercised in struggle so that they may be increased by greater rewards in recompense. The labor of the battle is prolonged so that the crown of victory may grow.

When the Lord does not hear his own swiftly, he draws them when he is thought to be driving them away. He is an inward physician, and he cuts away the infections of sin within us which he condemns as being rooted in our marrow; he removes the poison of corruption with the instrument of tribulation. And the more he seems not to hear the voice of the sick person, the more he works to bring the illness to an end.

Hence the Prophet says: “My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, yet not to my folly” (Ps. 21:3). As though he were saying: “It does not at all contribute to my folly that you continually do not hear me crying out day and night, because, insofar as you seem to abandon me in temporal tribulation, you instruct me more deeply in eternal wisdom.”

Again he says: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation” (Ps. 9:10). In speaking of tribulation, he first mentioned “times of opportunity,” because often we are crushed by tribulation, and yet the opportune time has not arrived for us to be helped according to our desire for deliverance.

> **Note:** The editions read: “so that we may be helped according to our desire for deliverance.” The manuscripts of Turon., Vindoc., Colbert and the Norman witnesses more correctly have: “so that we may be helped toward desire,” that is, “so that we may be helped in accordance with our desire.”

Let it therefore be said: “For God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will regard the causes of individuals.”

> **[Older Recension XVII.]**

But since many are often broken even by the delay of assistance, he appropriately adds:

## CHAPTER XX [Revised Recension XVI]

**Verse 14.**—“Even when you say, ‘He does not consider it,’ judge before him, and wait for him.”

Source preparation: Canonical supplied local source used directly; all textual notes, source fragments, and printed citations retained in translation.

### 35. When the storm of despair breaks in, God’s benefits must be recalled

For perhaps, while our cry seems to be disregarded, the hope that was in our heart grows weak; and we believe that heavenly help will fail us because we obtain it more slowly. We almost groan that the things we endure unavenged have been almost overlooked by God. But when this storm of despair disturbs us, the shaken mind more quickly places itself in the harbor of hope if it carefully weighs its case with the Lord; if it recalls His benefits [Col. 0369D]; if it does not cunningly excuse before itself the evils it has repaid for His benefits; if it considers what it has justly deserved from Him and what it has mercifully received; if it vigorously examines its life; if, examining before God’s eyes everything it does, it does not hide itself from itself; if it remembers that it was made when it did not exist [Col. 0370A]; if it recognizes that it was enlightened and raised up when it lay in darkness.

Gathering all these things together within itself, when it considers the benefits it has received, it does not accuse the adversities it endures. Nor is it broken by despair, since it is strengthened by the consolation of so many gifts; for it recovers hope for the future while it recognizes the benefits of the past.

Let it therefore say:

> “Even when you say: ‘He does not consider,’ judge yourself before Him, and wait for Him.”

As though he were saying: Since God is believed not to consider your case because He shows mercy slowly, enter into the depths of your thought and there submit your case to judgment before His eyes. Discern what grounds you yourself have supplied Him by your life, and what you have received from Him mercifully; then you return to confidence in hope, while you blush at the goodness of so great a kindness, so that amid adversities you may confidently await Him whom, even after your sins, you remember to be propitious [Col. 0370B].

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Longip.: “what cause you yourself have brought upon Him by your manner of life, or what …”]

Heavenly help ought indeed to have been hoped for even if no benefits had preceded it. And it must be known that God does not unjustly reject the human being whom He mercifully created.

### 36. Whoever considers past gifts should not despair of future ones

We must therefore consider how great a danger it is to see the gifts of the past and despair of those to come; how great a danger it is if, in this storm of tribulations, we are broken by the shipwreck of despair, though we are bound to the harbor of hope as if by immense cables—the gifts of the past.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Vindoc.: “if in this life’s storm of tribulations.”]

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Vindoc., Ebroic., and others: “who are bound to the harbor of faith.” Baluz. and Colb.: “because we are bound to the harbor.”]

It is rightly said:

> “Judge yourself before Him, and wait for Him.”

For whoever does not judge himself before God does not wait for Him when he is afflicted. Whoever pretends not to notice that benefits have preceded him despairs that help can follow; and when he forgets what came before, he is deprived even of the abundance that follows [Col. 0370C].

But behold: while we are afflicted, while we patiently endure the grace of consolation, the wicked rush on to worse things and advance in the aggravation of their iniquity precisely because they are left without punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Vindoc. and Pratel.: “while we longanimously await the grace of consolation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0370D] Here the manuscripts and editions vary. Some have *aggregatione* (“increase”), as in Turon. and the old Paris and Basel editions, and as most copies agree; others have *exaggeratione* (“aggravation”), as in Vindoc., Longip., Baluz., Colb., Ebroic., the other Norman copies, and the Paris edition of 1605.]

And yet the Almighty mercifully waits for sinners. He grants time for repentance, which He turns into evidence of a heavier guilt against those who do not reform. He patiently restrains the anger that He will one day pour out irreversibly.

Hence it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XXI [Old XVIII, Revised XVII]

### Verse 15

> “For now He does not bring on His fury, nor does He greatly punish crime.”

### 37. God long tolerates those whom He will condemn forever

God long tolerates the one whom He condemns forever [Col. 0370D]; and He now refrains from bringing on His fury because He reserves it to be poured out without end in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0370D] The Vatican edition of 1589 has corrupted the order of two words here, reading: “For God tolerates for a long time because He condemns forever; and He conceals the fury … which,” and so forth.]

It belongs to the elect to be crushed here, so that they may be taught toward the rewards of an eternal inheritance. It is ours to receive scourges here by which we are preserved to rejoice in eternity.

For it is written:

> “He scourges every son whom He receives” (Hebrews 12:6) [Col. 0371A].

To John it is said:

> “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline” (Revelation 3:19).

Peter says:

> “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God” (1 Peter 4:17).

Immediately he adds with wonder:

> “And if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe God’s gospel?” (ibid., 17).

Divine severity does not allow sins to remain unpunished. Rather, the anger of judgment begins here with our correction, so that it may come to rest in the condemnation of the reprobate.

Let the reprobate now go on and consume the desires of their pleasures in unpunished iniquity; let them fail to experience temporal scourges precisely because eternal punishments await them.

Their unpunished wickedness was well represented when Ham sinned. His father said to him:

> “Canaan is cursed; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Genesis 9:25).

Canaan was, of course, Ham’s son [Col. 0371B]. Why, when Ham sinned, does Canaan, his son, receive the sentence of punishment? Why is he struck not in Ham himself but in his posterity? Is it not because the wickedness of the reprobate advances here without punishment, but is struck in the future?

Let it therefore be said:

> “For now He does not bring on His fury, nor does He greatly punish crime.”

### 38. Nevertheless, He sometimes begins to strike them in this life

It must be noted that he added the word “greatly.” For although He tolerates certain things patiently, He nevertheless scourges certain things even in this life, and sometimes begins here to strike what He completes through eternal damnation.

Therefore He strikes some things and leaves others unpunished. For if He cut off nothing, who would believe that God cares for human affairs? And again, if He struck everything here, what would remain for the final judgment [Col. 0371C]?

Some things, then, are struck so that we may fear the solicitude of our Ruler over us; others are preserved unpunished so that we may perceive that judgment still remains.

It is therefore rightly said:

> “Nor does He greatly punish crime,”

because, while some small part of iniquity is struck, the sentence of eternal judgment is already announced to unconverted minds.

### 39. It is one thing to say what is right, another to say it rightly

All this, then, is rightly said by Elihu—if it were said rightly. He knows what he ought to say, but does not know to whom he is speaking. What he said is true, but it does not apply to the rebukes directed at blessed Job, because Job needed such correction no more than he sinned through any faintheartedness.

[Old XIX.] But because the arrogance of the proud often becomes an occasion of virtue for righteous men, blessed Job is dealt with by a hidden judgment, so that, after the scourges of punishment, he may also grow through the words of the arrogant [Col. 0371D].

For behold, the more he is despised by the minister of pride, the more he is inwardly refreshed by the teacher who is truth.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] We have restored this passage, which was interpolated in the editions and in some manuscripts, with the aid of Cod. Colb., Baluz., Vindoc., Ebroic., Pratel., Utic., and other Norman copies. The editions read: “the more he is inwardly refreshed by the truth,” with *quanto a veritate intrinsecus*, that is, “by the teacher of humility.” The words “that is, the teacher of humility” seem to have been added for explanation. In the Turon. manuscript the wording is corrupt: “the more he is inwardly refreshed by authority.” The copyist was mistaken in reading, or perhaps in taking down from dictation, what he later wrote—*auctoritate* (“by authority”) instead of *a veritate* (“by truth”) [Col. 0372D].]

For after Elihu recognized that he had said so many forceful things, he revealed what pride he was carrying. He looked down on blessed Job because of his lofty opinion of himself [Col. 0372A], saying:

## CHAPTER XXII

### Verse 16

> “Therefore Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge.”

### 40. Loquacity and impatience in listening are vices of the proud

By saying this, he asserts that blessed Job knew nothing and had said much; yet although he himself speaks at length about what he thinks, he accuses Job of the vice of loquacity.

But this too is commonly a characteristic vice of the arrogant: they regard as little whatever they themselves have said at length, and as much whatever is said to them briefly. Because they always wish to speak their own words, they cannot listen to those of others. They consider themselves subjected to violence if they do not pour forth even more immoderately what they feel immoderately.

Although blessed Job remained silent before his words, Elihu found in Job’s speech, by which he had answered his friends, an occasion for attack [Col. 0372B]. He did so in order to make Job’s silence serve him at greater length and, so that he himself might answer much, to assert that Job had multiplied words.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] The passage is obscure both in the manuscripts and in the printed editions. The handwritten copies read *posset* where the editions have *possit*.]

For immediately he begins the opening of a lengthy speech, and, as though he had said nothing yet, attempts to begin.

Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Old XX, Revised XVIII]

### Chapter 36, verses 1–2

> “Elihu continued and said these things as well: ‘Bear with me a little, and I will show you.’”

### 41. They measure their teaching by their abundance of speech; while displaying themselves, they pretend to speak for God

He had already said much, and still hoped to be tolerated for a little while, because the arrogant judge that they suffer serious loss if they restrain their knowledge by brevity of speech.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Turon., Vindoc., Baluz., Colb., Ebroic., other Norman manuscripts, and the old Paris edition read *sperat* (“hopes”) in place of *postulat* (“demands”), found in most printed editions. The old Basel edition has *imperat* (“commands”) for *sperat*, apparently through a hasty printer’s misreading.]

They believe they show themselves more learned in proportion as they can reveal themselves through the multiplicity of their loquacity.

But because they often perceive that the reverence due to silence is not granted them, they sometimes indicate the power of the Lord about whom they appear to speak, and under His pretext demand for themselves a silence they do not deserve. While they mention God outwardly, they seek, by demanding that they be listened to out of reverence for Him, to display themselves more than to proclaim His works [Col. 0372C].

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Pratel.: “they rather strive to display themselves.”]

Hence Elihu adds:

> “For I still have something to say on God’s behalf.”

831

But because holy teachers sometimes repeat what they have said obscurely, so that by the sound of repetition they may impress what they proclaim secretly upon the hearts of their hearers, the arrogant often also try to imitate this [Col. 0372D]. They repeat insolently what they have said—not because they desire to impress the matter upon the hearts of their hearers, but because they wish to appear eloquent in their judgment.

Hence Elihu adds:

### Verse 3

> “I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning.”

But since, when knowledge was mentioned, the swelling of his heart had become clear in his voice, the arrogant man is openly recognized—unless he is quickly covered by some veil.

Therefore, immediately introducing the justice of the Lord as a concealment of his arrogance, he says:

> “And I will prove my Maker just” [Col. 0373A].

Thus, while he appears to speak on behalf of God’s justice, he excuses before human judgments whatever flows forth arrogantly.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Verse 4

> “For truly my words are without falsehood.”

### 42. Those who have no testimony from God seek it from human beings

When they see that they cannot be understood by weak hearers, even righteous people often customarily praise the good things they say—not because they delight in their own praise, but so that they may awaken their hearers’ attentiveness to listening. Thus, when the words are spoken by their voice, the hearers may be seized by them with more ardent affection.

Hence Paul, after saying many remarkable things to the Corinthians, added:

> “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6:11) [Col. 0373B].

But the arrogant, because they do not know the heart of the good and sometimes imitate only their words, exalt in praising what they say—not because the sluggishness of their hearers displeases them, but because they themselves greedily delight in their own praise.

They imitate the voice of the righteous but do not understand its force. They see what the righteous utter but do not know what they seek.

For when holy teachers exalt the praise of preaching,

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Vindoc., Utic., and other Norman manuscripts: “holy preachers.”]

they raise the hearts of their hearers from their low thoughts as if with the hand of their voice, so that, quickly shaken awake by the following words, they may meet them as travelers on a road and embrace them with as much understanding as they had already loved them in the voice of the one praising them, almost before they saw them [Col. 0373C].

But, as I have said, the arrogant do not know these things. Since what they seek is external, they cannot sense what is desirable within.

Of the Church of the elect it is written:

> “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44:14).

And the wise virgins are said to carry oil in their vessels (Matthew 25:4).

Hence the voice of the saints says:

> “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

But the arrogant, because they do not possess the testimony of their conscience before God, seek before human beings the testimony of another’s voice. When they find it only slowly, they themselves break out into shameless self-praise.

For if they do not find the voices of human beings that they greedily await, they proclaim their own knowledge while praising themselves.

Hence Elihu adds:

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0373D]

### Verse 4

> “And perfect knowledge will be demonstrated to you.”

### 43. The elevation of the heart, though hidden, is inexcusable; how much more so when it bursts forth in words

He sensed that he was about to say great things, but, with his heart swollen, he could not keep silent about what he had loftily judged concerning himself. Therefore he anticipated what he regarded as right by praising it, because he would already have been guilty before divine judgment if he had merely thought great things about himself, even while remaining silent.

Before the subtle examination of truth we are never entirely secure, even if, in human judgment, we have nothing that ought to be reproved in us [Col. 0374A]. For often, while thinking carelessly, we are struck by pride, which we nevertheless suppress by silence.

But unless, through reconsideration, the hidden swelling is quickly suffocated in the very chamber of the heart where it arises, every merit of our action is extinguished before the strict Judge.

From this, then, we must consider with what severity that elevation of the heart will be condemned which is nourished even to boldness of speech, since the elevation that secretly arises in the heart is itself inexcusable.

We must also consider what sort of inward pride rules when it is preserved so far that it is not ashamed even to burst outward.

Elihu, then, because he had conceived great thoughts, did not know how to restrain himself humbly. He grasped the loftiness of knowledge but rejected the grace of humility. While pursuing the good which he desired in order to speak well, he lost the good by which he could have lived well [Col. 0374B].

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Pratel.: “the good which he desires in order to speak well.”]

> “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1).

But now let him say what is right, though he does not know how to say it rightly. After exhaling the inflated thoughts of his mind through words of pride, he added a forceful judgment, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVI [Old XXI, Revised XIX]

### Verse 5

> “God does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is mighty.”

### 44. Temporal power, even when good, is exposed to the temptation of pride. Whoever sees that he can do more than others easily believes that he knows more. In this he resembles Satan

In the conduct of mortal life, some things are harmful in themselves, while others harm us because of what surrounds them.

Some things are harmful in themselves, such as sins and crimes. Other things sometimes harm us because of what surrounds them, such as temporal power or the marriage bond.

Marriage is indeed good, but the things that grow up around it from worldly concern are evil. Hence Paul says:

> “But the married man is concerned about worldly things, how he may please his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:33).

And, persuading certain people to what is better, he recalls them from marriage, saying:

> “But I say this, not to cast a snare upon you, but with a view to what is honorable and what affords opportunity to beseech the Lord without hindrance” (ibid., 35).

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Turon.: “to serve the Lord.” Pratel. and Utic.: [Col. 0374D] “to observe the Lord”; in the margin, “to beseech the Lord.” Colb. has both readings.]

Thus, although what does not harm is retained, what harms is often committed through things placed beside it [Col. 0374C]. It is as when we travel along a straight and clean road, yet thorns growing beside the road catch us by our clothing [Col. 0374D]. We do not stumble on the clean road, but something grows at its side by which we are pricked.

Temporal power too is great. It has its own merit before God when authority is administered well. Yet sometimes, precisely because it surpasses others, it swells with the pride of thought; everything lies ready for its use.

[Note: [Col. 0374D] Turon.: “and while all things lie ready for use.”]

Commands are quickly fulfilled at its desire; all subjects exalt whatever has been done well in praise and, through lack of authority, do not contradict what has been done badly. Often they even praise what they ought to have rebuked.

Deceived by the things that are supplied below, the mind is lifted above itself.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] The editions read “by the things that are supplied within.” We have corrected this from the manuscripts Longip., Vindoc., Baluz., Colb., Pratel., and other Norman copies. Gilot nevertheless noted in the margin “below,” while retaining *intra* in the text.]

While it is surrounded outwardly by immense favor, inwardly it is emptied of truth. Forgetting itself, it scatters itself into the voices of others. It believes itself to be what it hears outwardly, not what it ought to discern inwardly. It despises its subjects and does not recognize them as equal to itself by the order of nature. Those whom it has surpassed by the lot of power, it believes it has also surpassed in the merits of life. It considers itself wiser than all those whom it sees it can command more fully [Col. 0375A].

It establishes itself, in its own estimation, on a kind of summit. Though bound together with others by the same condition of nature, it disdains to regard others as equals. Thus it is led to resemble the one of whom it is written:

> “He beholds every high thing; he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25) [Col. 0375B].

And of whose body it is said:

> “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and whose eyelids are lifted up” (Proverbs 30:13).

It is led to resemble the one who, desiring a solitary summit and despising the shared life of the angels, said:

> “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14).

Thus, by a marvelous judgment, it discovers within itself a pit of humiliation while outwardly exalting itself on the summit of power.

It becomes like the apostate angel when it disdains to be like other human beings. So Saul grew from the merit of humility into the swelling of pride through the height of power. Through humility he was promoted; through pride he was rejected, as the Lord testified when He said:

> “When you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17) [Col. 0375C].

Before receiving power he had seen himself as little; but, supported by temporal power, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself in comparison with others, he judged himself great in his own estimation.

In a marvelous way, when he was little in his own eyes, he was great before the Lord; but when he was great in his own eyes, he was little before the Lord.

Through the prophet the Lord forbids us to be great in our own eyes, saying:

> “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight” (Isaiah 5:21).

Paul admonishes us not to be great in our own estimation:

> “Do not be wise in your own sight” (Romans 12:15).

Often, then, when the mind is inflated by the abundance of those subject to it, it is corrupted into the luxury of pride, with the very summit of power acting as its seductress.

### 45. Legitimate power is raised above faults, not above people. The examples of Saint Peter and Saint Paul [Col. 0375D]

But it is one thing for any good not to exist, and another not to know how to possess good things well. Power is good in its proper order, but it requires the cautious life of the one who governs.

Therefore he exercises power well who knows both how to retain it and how to oppose it. He exercises it well who knows how to rise above faults through it and how to be joined to others in equality while possessing it.

The human mind is often lifted up even when it is supported by no power. How much more does it raise itself when power is added to it? And yet it is prepared by suitable execution to correct the faults of others. Hence Paul says:

> “For he is God’s minister, an avenger unto wrath upon the one who does evil” (Romans 13:4).

[Old XXII.] Therefore, when the ministry of temporal power is undertaken, one must watch with the greatest care, so that each person may know how to take from it what helps and overcome what tempts; how to see himself as equal to others along with it and yet to place himself above sinners through zeal for punishment.

We understand this distinction more fully if we also observe examples of ecclesiastical power.

Peter, by God’s authority holding the primacy of the Church, refused to accept excessive veneration from the good Cornelius, who humbly prostrated himself before him. He recognized himself as Cornelius’s equal, saying:

> “Rise; do not do this. I too am a human being” (Acts 10:26) [Col. 0376A].

But when he discovered the sin of Ananias and Sapphira, he immediately showed how greatly he had risen above others in power (Acts 5:5 and following). By his word he struck their life, which he had detected through the searching of the Spirit; and he remembered himself as supreme within the Church against sins, a position he did not acknowledge before brothers who were acting well, despite the great honor shown him [Col. 0376B].

There the holiness of action earned communion in equality; here the zeal of punishment revealed the right of power.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] Baluz.: “the right of power appeared.”]

Paul did not know himself to be superior to brothers who were acting well when he said:

> “Not because we lord it over your faith, but because we are helpers of your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:23).

And immediately he added:

> “For you stand firm in faith.”

As though he were saying: We do not lord it over your faith because you stand firm in faith. We are equal to you where we recognize that you stand.

He likewise did not know himself to be superior to his brothers [Col. 0376C] when he said:

> “We became little ones in your midst” (1 Thessalonians 2:7),

and:

> “But we [are] your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

But when he found a fault that ought to be corrected, he immediately remembered that he was a teacher, saying:

> “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

### 46. When superiors punish faults by right of power, they should recognize themselves as equals of those corrected through the preservation of humility—and even place themselves beneath them

The highest position is well governed when the one who presides dominates faults rather than brothers.

Nature created all people equal. But when some are entrusted with governing others, it is not nature but fault that places the latter beneath them.

Therefore rulers ought to raise themselves above faults, for whose sake they are placed above others. And when they correct offenders, they must carefully see to it that, through discipline, they strike faults by right of power, but, through preserving humility, recognize themselves as equal to the brothers whom they correct [Col. 0376D].

[Note: [Col. 0376D] Others have “the brothers whom they correct.”]

Yet often it is also fitting that we prefer, in silent thought, those whom we correct. Their faults are struck through us by the force of discipline;

[Note: [Col. 0376D] The Norman manuscripts, Baluz., and others read *vigore* (“by the force”); the old edition has *vigore*, while the more recent edition reads *in vigore* (“in the force”).]

but in the faults we ourselves commit, we are not wounded by anyone’s verbal attack.

We are therefore under greater obligation before the Lord in proportion as we sin without punishment before human beings.

[Old XXIII.] Our discipline makes our subjects all the freer before divine judgment, since here it does not leave their faults without punishment [Col. 0377A].

Humility must therefore be preserved in the heart and discipline in action. In the midst of these things we must carefully watch lest, while the virtue of humility is preserved beyond measure, the rights of governance be dissolved; and lest, while some superior casts himself down more than is fitting, he becomes unable to restrain the life of his subjects under the bond of discipline.

Let us hold outwardly what we undertake for the benefit of others; let us hold inwardly what we think about our own worth. Yet, through certain signs appropriately allowed to emerge, even those entrusted to us should know what we are in our own estimation, so that they may see in our authority what they should fear and in our humility what they should imitate [Col. 0377B].

While preserving the authority of governance, let us return continually to our heart and constantly consider that we were created equal with others, not that we have been placed above others temporarily.

For the more power stands out outwardly, the more it must be pressed down inwardly, lest it conquer the thought; lest it carry the mind away into delight in itself; lest the mind become unable to rule beneath itself the power to which it has submitted through the desire to dominate.

### 47. An example of power administered humbly in David

David knew well how to govern the power of his kingdom. He conquered the pride of that power by restraining himself, saying:

> “Lord, my heart is not exalted” (Psalm 130:1).

To increase the expression of his humility, he added:

> “Nor are my eyes lifted up.”

And he continued:

> “Nor have I walked in great things.”

Still examining himself through the most subtle inquiry, he said:

> “Nor in things too wonderful for me.”

And, drawing out all his thoughts from the depths of his heart, he added:

> “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul” [Col. 0377C].

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Turon.: “if I exalted.”]

Behold, he repeats again and again the sacrifice of humility offered from the depths of his heart. By confessing repeatedly, he does not cease to offer it; speaking of it in many ways, he displays it before the eyes of his Judge.

What is this? How had he learned that this sacrifice pleased God, which he offered before Him through such repeated speech? It is because pride is usually near to those who possess power, and elevation is almost always joined to abundant circumstances, just as an abundance of moisture often produces the hardness of swelling [Col. 0377D].

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Jamezius corrects this passage from English manuscripts, in which he read “did not know how to please.” In our Norman manuscripts and others, as well as in the older and more recent printed editions, the reading is the one we have given.]

[Old XXIV.]

### 48. The rare combination of humility and power

It is exceedingly remarkable when humility of character reigns in the hearts of the exalted.

From this we must understand that powerful people, when they think humbly, attain the summit of a virtue foreign to them and seemingly far removed. Through this virtue they rightly please the Lord more quickly, because they humbly offer Him the sacrifice that the powerful can scarcely find.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Turon., Pratel., and Utic.: “the sacrifice which the powerful offer.”]

The most subtle art of living is to hold the summit while suppressing glory; to be powerful but not know oneself to be powerful; to recognize oneself as powerful for giving benefits, but to disregard whatever one is powerful enough to inflict as harm [Col. 0378A].

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Turon., Pratel., Utic.: “for repaying harms.”]

It is therefore rightly said of such people:

> “God does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is mighty.”

The person who administers the summit of power with attention to the usefulness of others, not inflated by his own praises, desires to imitate God. He who has been placed above others desires to benefit them, not to dominate them.

The swelling of pride, not the order of power, is the fault. God grants power; the wickedness of our mind discovers the pride of power.

Let us remove what we have added from ourselves, and the things we possess by God’s generosity are good.

Because it is not just power but wrongful action that is condemned, it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER XXVII [Revised XX]

[Col. 0378B]

### Verse 6

> “But He does not save the impious, and gives judgment to the poor.”

### 49. God condemns the pride of power, not the height of power

Sacred Scripture commonly calls the humble “poor.” Hence, when the addition “in spirit” is made in the Gospel, they are called:

> “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

[Note: [Col. 0378D] So also Baluz., Colb., Ebroic., and others among the older editions. The revised edition reads: “For those who …”]

Because riches visibly display people as powerful, those who are not lifted up in their own consciences are poor in themselves.

He calls impious those who are either separated from the devotion of faith or contradict by evil conduct what they faithfully believe.

Therefore, because Almighty God condemns the pride of wickedness, not the height of power, after it has been said:

> “God does not reject the mighty, since He Himself is mighty,”

it is rightly added:

> “But He does not save the impious, and gives judgment to the poor” [Col. 0378C].

That is: He destroys the proud but sets the humble free through judgment.

Or certainly, He gives judgment to the poor because those who are now wickedly oppressed will then come as judges over their oppressors.

### 50. Among the reprobate, some are judged and others are not judged

There are two groups, namely the elect and the reprobate. But each of these groups contains two orders: some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish. Some are judged and reign; others are not judged and reign.

Those are judged and perish to whom the Lord’s proclamation says:

[Note: [Col. 0378D] We follow Baluz., Colb., Vindoc., Utic., and other manuscripts rather than the printed editions, which read “by the Lord’s voice in condemnation.”]

> “I was hungry, and you did not give Me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give Me drink [Col. 0378D]; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome Me; naked, and you did not clothe Me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit Me” (Matthew 25:42–43).

It is said beforehand to them:

> “Depart from Me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

But others are not judged at the final judgment and perish. Of them the Prophet says:

> “The impious will not rise in judgment” (Psalm 1:5).

[Note: [Col. 0378D] The cited manuscripts and old editions read “will not rise”; more recent editions prefer “will not rise again.”]

And the Lord says of them:

> “Whoever does not believe is already condemned” (John 3:18).

And Paul says:

> “Those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Romans 2:12).

All unbelievers therefore rise, but for punishment, not for judgment. Their case is not examined then, because they approach the presence of the strict Judge already carrying the condemnation of their unbelief [Col. 0379A].

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Some witnesses read “who approach the presence.”]

Those who retain the profession of faith but do not possess the works of that profession are rebuked so that they may perish. But those who have not even retained the sacraments of faith do not hear the Judge’s rebuke in the final examination. Prejudged by the darkness of their unbelief, they are not deemed worthy to be rebuked by the reproach of the One they had despised.

The former at least hear the words of the Judge because they at least retained the words of His faith. The latter, in their condemnation, do not even hear the words of the eternal Judge, because they did not wish to preserve His reverence even in words [Col. 0379B].

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Vindoc., Pratel., and other Norman manuscripts: “they preferred to preserve.”]

The former perish according to the law because, placed under the law, they sinned. To the latter, in their destruction, nothing is said from the law because they made no attempt to possess anything belonging to the law.

[Old XXV.] A prince governing an earthly commonwealth punishes differently a citizen who sins within the state and an external enemy who rebels. In the citizen he upholds his own laws and condemns him under words of deserved reproach. Against the enemy, however, he wages war, employs instruments of destruction, and repays his wickedness with punishments worthy of it; he does not inquire what the law provides concerning the enemy’s evil [Col. 0379C].

For it is not necessary to kill by the law one who could never have been held by the law.

Thus, at the final judgment, legal reproach strikes the person who turned aside in action from what he held in profession; but the one who is not bound by the law of faith is destroyed without judicial reproach.

### 51. Some of the elect also undergo judgment, while others do not, but sit as judges

Among the elect, some are judged and reign: those who wipe away the stains of their lives with tears, redeeming their former evils by subsequent deeds, and covering whatever unlawful things they have at any time done from the Judge’s eyes by the superimposition of almsgiving. To these, when the Judge comes, standing at his right hand, he says:

“I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25:35).

To them he first says:

“Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

But others are not judged and reign—those who surpass even the commandments of the law by the perfection of their virtues [Note: Some copies read, “by the virtue of perfection.”]—because they are by no means content merely to fulfill what the divine law commands all alike, but in their more excellent desire they seek to offer more than they could hear in the general commandments.

To these the Lord’s voice says [Note: Tours reads, “you have left all your possessions.” Pratel, Utic, and many Norman witnesses read, “you have left your possessions.”]:

“You who have left everything and followed me, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).
