And of these the prophet says:

“The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14).

And concerning these Solomon, speaking of the Bridegroom of Holy Church, says [Note: Gussanville, Paris 1605, and Gilot corruptly read, “when speaking of the bride of Holy Church.” Ebroic and the other Norman witnesses, Tours, and the older Paris and Basel editions correctly read, “the Bridegroom.”]:

“Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31:23).

These, therefore, at the final judgment are not judged but reign, because they come as judges together with their Creator. For, leaving everything, they have carried out with more ready devotion what they heard commanded [Col. 0380B] generally than what was generally ordered [Note: So read the manuscripts of Longipontus, Pratel, and other Norman witnesses, as well as the old Paris editions of 1495 and 1518 and the Basel edition of 1514. In Gilot 1571, Vatican 1589, and Gussanville, the text is corrupt: “than what he commanded.”].

For by a special command, addressed to a few who were more perfect and not generally to all, the rich young man heard:

“Go and sell everything that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21) [Note: Pratel reads, “Sell what you have.” Baluz and Colbert read, “Go, sell … and come, follow me.”].

If a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be sinful for us to possess anything from this world [Note: The same witness reads, “it would certainly be a fault.”]. But one thing is what Holy Scripture commands all generally, and another what it specially enjoins upon the more perfect.

These, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment, because by their manner of life they have surpassed even the general commandments [Note: Some copies add, “because they have also surpassed the commandments.”]. For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, despise being held by the law are not judged but perish [Note: So read Vindoc, the Norman witnesses, Baluz, Colbert, and the old editions. Other copies read, “to hold the law.”], so those who, persuaded by devotion, advance even beyond the general precepts of the divine law [Col. 0380C] are not judged but reign [Note: The Vatican edition of 1589, Gilot 1571, and some others read, “beyond the general precepts of the divine law.” We have preferred the reading “beyond the generalities,” found in the English, Norman, and Tours manuscripts and in the older Paris and Basel editions.].

This is why Paul, surpassing even the special commandments, offered more in deed than he had received by the instruction of permission (1 Thess. 2:7). For although he had received permission to live from the Gospel while preaching the Gospel, he both brought the Gospel to his hearers and nevertheless refused to be supported by the Gospel’s provisions.

Why, then, should he be judged so as to reign—he who received a lesser obligation to observe, but found a greater one by which to live?

Let it rightly be said, then:

“He grants judgment to the poor,”

because, the more they were despised in this world with great humility, the more they will then grow in the height of their power after receiving their seats.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Rec. XXI]

### Verse 7

“He will not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, and he sets kings upon a throne forever, and there they are raised up.”

### 52. God looks more attentively upon the righteous when they are unjustly afflicted

The Lord is perhaps thought to have withdrawn his eyes from the righteous because here they are torn apart by the cruelty of the wicked without receiving vengeance. Yet he looks more attentively upon his servants when the wickedness of their persecutor unjustly afflicts them. For when he sees what they humbly endure here, he surely already foresees what he will mercifully repay them there.

He does not, therefore, withdraw his eyes from the righteous. Behold: one humbly groans, while another grows proud and prospers wickedly. One crushes his heart, while another exalts himself through the glory of iniquity. Which of these, then, is farther from the divine gaze: the one who endured injustice, or the one who inflicted it upon those who suffered; the one who preserved heavenly grace amid the darkness of sorrow, or the one who amid outward joys inwardly lost the light of justice?

### 53. Why the saints are called kings in Holy Scripture; sitting with Christ on a throne means judging by his power

The holy men are rightly called kings in the testimony of Holy Scripture, because, placed above all the movements of the flesh, they sometimes restrain the appetite for lust, sometimes moderate the heat of avarice, sometimes bend the glory of pride, sometimes suppress the prompting of envy, and sometimes extinguish the fire of anger.

They are therefore kings because they know how not to succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to rule over them and preside over them. Since, then, they pass from this power of governing to the power of recompense, it is rightly said:

“He sets kings upon a throne forever.”

By governing themselves they were wearied for a time, but they are placed forever upon the throne of the eternal establishment of the kingdom. There they receive the power to judge others worthily in the same measure in which here they do not know how to spare themselves wickedly.

Hence it is said elsewhere:

“Until justice is turned into judgment” (Ps. 93:15).

Paul says of himself and his companions:

“So that we might become the justice of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21).

Justice, therefore, is turned into judgment, because those who now live justly and irreproachably then obtain the power to judge [Note: Longipontus reads, “then exercise the power of judging.”].

For this reason the Lord says to the Church of Laodicea:

“Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3:21).

The conquering Lord declares that he sat on the throne with the Father because, after the struggles of his Passion and the triumph of his resurrection, he showed more clearly to all that he was equal in power to the Father; having trampled the sting of death, he made it known that he was not unequal to him.

Thus, to Mary, who did not yet believe him equal to the Father, he says:

“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:17).

For us, to sit on the Son’s throne means to judge by the power of that same Son. Because we receive the primacy of judgment from his power, we sit, as it were, upon his throne.

Nor is it contrary to the truth that elsewhere he testifies that the disciples will come upon twelve thrones [Note: Vindoc and the Norman witnesses read, “will sit.”] (Matt. 19:28), while here he says that they will sit upon his throne. For through the twelve thrones the universal judgment is shown, while through the one throne of the Son the singular summit of judicial power is shown.

What is signified by the twelve thrones is therefore signified by the one throne of the Son, because the universal judgment is received through the intervention of our Mediator.

Let it therefore be said:

“He sets kings upon a throne forever.”

### 54. The seat of the saints is eternal; first humbled, they will be raised up

By adding “forever,” he appropriately makes clear what he means. If he were speaking of the throne of an earthly kingdom, he would certainly not have added “forever” [Note: Ebroic and other Norman witnesses read, “because whoever seizes it …”], because those who seize such a throne are placed upon it not forever but for a time.

He rightly adds:

“And there they are raised up.”

As though he were indicating to the hearer’s understanding:

“Because they have been humbled here, they are raised up there.”

For this place is one of humility for holy men, so that the other may be one of exaltation. Hence it is written elsewhere:

“You humbled them in the place of affliction” (Ps. 43:20) [Note: Pratel and Utic read, “You humbled us.”].

The present life is the place of affliction. Therefore those who are journeying toward the eternal homeland now despise themselves temporarily in the place of affliction, so that they may then truly be exalted in the place of joy.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXIX [Rec. XXII]

### Verses 8–9

“And if they are in chains and are bound with the cords of poverty, he will declare to them their works and their crimes, because they have been violent” [Note: Baluz, Colbert, Pratel, and Utic here and below read “he declared.” The interchange of *b* and *v* is easy and frequent.].

### 55. The saints consider themselves bound in chains as long as they live here

The chains of bondage are the continued confinement of our pilgrimage. Paul saw himself bound by these chains when he said:

“Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

He perceived himself bound by the cords of poverty when, contemplating the true riches, he also entreated his disciples concerning them, saying:

“That you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints” (Eph. 1:18) [Note: This is better read in Tours, Vindoc, Pratel, Utic, Colbert, and Baluz than in the printed editions, which have “he explained to them.”].

It is rightly added after this:

“He will declare to them their works and their crimes, because they have been violent.”

For when, by loving heavenly glory more deeply, we come to know it, then we feel that the evils we have committed were more serious. Hence Paul, after receiving the grace of heavenly things, recognized that the practices of virtue he had formerly believed to be in himself had actually been crimes, saying:

“Who formerly was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent; but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13).

Or certainly:

“But whatever things were gain to me, these I counted as loss for Christ” (Phil. 3:7).

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXX

### Verse 10

“He will also reveal their ear, to correct them, and he will speak so that they may return from iniquity” [Note: Utic and Pratel read, “He revealed … he speaks”; Colbert and Baluz also have this reading.].

### 56. Through love of heavenly glory, sins formerly committed become more grievous

To reveal the ear from iniquity is to open the understanding to knowledge. Once the ear has been opened, each person is corrected when inwardly he perceives the desire for eternal goods and recognizes the evils he has committed outwardly.

The phrase may also be understood as referring to the temporal affliction of punishment. For often those who do not heed the words of the one who commands are admonished by the blows of the one who strikes [Note: The printed editions read, “so that they may be drawn to eternal goods.” We follow the manuscripts of Baluz, Colbert, Vindoc, Tours, Ebroic, and other Norman witnesses.], so that at least punishment may draw toward good desires those whom rewards do not invite.

Hence the prophet says:

“With bit and bridle bind their jaws” [Note: Pratel and Utic read, “you will bind”], “who do not come near you” (Ps. 31:9).

But if they also despise scourges, it is plainly evident that there they will feel punishments of more grievous vengeance in proportion as here they trample upon the grace of greater providence.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI

### Verses 11–12

“If they hear and observe, they will complete their days in goodness and their years in glory. But if they do not hear, they will pass through the sword and be consumed by folly.”

### 57. How severely those must be punished who are not restrained from their ruined ways even by scourges

“Goodness” signifies right action, while “glory” signifies heavenly recompense. Those, therefore, who strive to obey the heavenly commandments complete their days in goodness and their years in glory, because they both carry out the course of the present time in right conduct and bring their end to completion through a blessed recompense.

But if they do not hear, they will pass through the sword and be consumed by folly, because vengeance strikes them in tribulation and their end concludes in foolishness.

There are some whom not even torments restrain from their ruined ways. Of them the prophet says:

“You struck them, and they did not grieve; you scourged them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5:3).

And of them it is said under the figure of Babylon:

“We healed Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9).

Again it is said of them:

“I struck and destroyed my people, and yet they did not return from their ways” (Jer. 15:7).

Such people sometimes become worse through the blow, because, assailed by pains, they either become harder through stubborn obstinacy [Note: Some copies read, “or through the obstinacy of stubbornness,” as does Baluz], or, what is worse, rush into an intensification of blasphemy.

It is therefore rightly said that they pass through the sword and are consumed by folly, because they increase by scourges the sins that they ought to have corrected by scourges. Here they already feel the punishments of being struck, and there they do not escape the penalties of just recompense.

For the foolishness of folly is that iniquity binds them so tightly that punishment does not restrain them from guilt.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Rec. XXIII]

### Verse 13

“Hypocrites and the crafty provoke the anger of God.”

### 58. The likeness of a crafty hypocrite

When he says “hypocrites,” he appropriately adds “crafty,” because unless they are skillful by their intelligence, they cannot suitably pretend to be what they desire to appear.

There are some vices that even those of slower understanding easily commit. Anyone, however dull his perceptions, can swell with pride, pant after the heats of avarice, or succumb to the assaults of lust. But no one can carry out the falsehood of hypocrisy unless he possesses a subtler intelligence.

Whoever is such a person is divided, as it were, between two tasks requiring continual vigilance: he must know how craftily both to conceal what is and to display what is not; both to suppress true evils and to show false goods [Note: Vindoc, Pratel, and Utic add, “and to conceal true evils badly”]; neither openly to exalt himself in what he appears to be, nor, in order to retain greater glory, often to pretend to avoid glory [Note: The printed editions read, “he often pretends.” Tours has “in place of pretending,” and reads “to demonstrate.”].

Because he cannot grasp glory by pursuing it openly before human eyes, he generally strives to retain it by fleeing from it. These things do not at all belong to the simple, for if they did belong to them, they would no longer be simple.

### 59. The hypocrite not only deserves God’s anger but provokes it

When he says “hypocrites and the crafty,” he rightly does not add “they deserve” God’s anger, but “they provoke” it.

To deserve God’s anger is also to sin without knowing it. To provoke it, however, is knowingly to oppose his commandments: to know the good but despise it; to be able to do it but not wish to.

Such people grow inwardly dark through the perpetration of wickedness, while on the surface they are whitened by the display of righteousness. To them the Lord’s voice says:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones and every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23:27).

Outwardly, therefore, they display what they attack inwardly by their manner of life. Inwardly, by thinking evil thoughts, they intensify what they conceal outwardly by superimposing something else upon it.

Before the strict Judge they can no longer have the excuse of ignorance, because, while they display every appearance of holiness before human eyes, they themselves bear witness that they are not ignorant of how to live well.

Let it rightly be said, then:

“Hypocrites and the crafty provoke the anger of God.”

What follows them at the end he adds, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### The same passage

“Nor will they cry out when they have been bound.”

### 60. Even when struck, the sinner is ashamed to confess his sins

Every wicked person who, although wicked, does not seek to appear holy, when caught by the blow of the scourge, is not ashamed to confess that he is wicked.

But one who does evil while intercepting human judgments concerning himself under the appearance of holiness, even when struck by the scourge, avoids exposing himself as wicked because he is accustomed to appear holy. When he is severely constrained, he scarcely confesses himself wicked even outwardly, because he is ashamed to disclose his inner state through a true confession.

We are, as it were, free when we are chastised by no correction [Note: Ebroic and other Norman witnesses read, “but we are conquered,” which better corresponds to the other member: “as it were, free, but conquered when we are bound by the blow of the scourge.”]; but we are conquered when we are bound by the blow of the scourge.

The more truly we confess our sins when placed under the blow, the more loudly we cry out when bound. For devoted confession is a powerful voice in the ears of God.

Since, therefore, scourges, even when they strike hypocrites, do not bring them to simple confession—for they shrink from being known as sinners, since they were regarded by everyone as holy—although the scourges already strike them at the end, and although they know that they are being led to eternal punishments, they nevertheless desire to remain in human judgment as they had always striven to appear.

Thus, even when detected by the scourge of the final blow, because they neglect to utter a pure confession despite their affliction, they refuse, as it were, to cry out when bound.

It is rightly said:

“Nor will they cry out when they have been bound.”

### 61. Hypocrites consider themselves holy not because they are holy, but because they are called holy. Deceived by empty hope, they do not flee to the remedy of confession even at the end. A person’s heart is often far from the person himself

The passage can also be understood in another way. Anyone who, although wicked, does not fear being called holy by people, even if he silently reproves himself in thought for being wicked, nevertheless, once he has often begun to hear himself called holy, loses what he had inwardly retained about himself.

He pours out his heart outwardly, and because he willingly receives a false testimony about himself from outside, he does not ask what sort of person he is within. Thus it happens that he seeks even the nourishment of empty praise when it is absent, and, forgetting what he is, desires to appear what he is not.

Therefore, when such people pretend to be righteous before human judgments and display their actions as worthy of praise to the eyes of those who see them, judgment is secretly carried out upon them. Insofar as they strive outwardly to deceive others, they are inwardly deceived even about themselves.

For they lose every eye of careful investigation directed toward themselves. They pretend not to examine and scrutinize their lives, but consider themselves to be what they hear themselves called. They believe themselves holy not because they live in that way, but because they are called that.

The judgment of God is subtle, and they neglect to look upon themselves because they place confidence in the testimony of their own merit on the lips of others.

When they are struck by a sudden blow, they are entirely unable either truly to confess themselves wicked or to recognize themselves as they are, because they have believed themselves holy on the basis of human affirmation.

It is rightly said:

“Nor will they cry out when they have been bound.”

Such people trust, through an empty hope, that they will come before the heavenly Judge as they know they have become known to human beings. Miserable as they are, they do not discover themselves even amid torments, and, while they regard the testimony of false praise, they lose the remedy of true confession.

They are led away bound, yet do not cry out, because, overcome by the importunity of human praise, the wretches think themselves holy even when they die in their sins.

To them the prophet rightly says:

“Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 46:8) [Note: Vindoc, Ebroic, and other Norman witnesses read, “they would not scatter themselves through words of outward testimony.”].

For if they returned to the heart, they would not pour themselves out through words of outward testimony. What is nearer to us than our own heart? What is nearer to us than that which is within us?

Yet when our heart is scattered through perverse thoughts, it wanders farther from us. The prophet therefore sends the transgressor far away when he compels him to return to his own heart, because, having poured himself out outwardly, he scarcely finds a way back to himself.

Since the mind of hypocrites, being divided from the single purpose of eternity, is devastated by the flood of manifold thoughts, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### Verse 14

“Their soul will die in the storm” [The printed text reads *amma ecrum*, evidently a corrupt form of *anima eorum* (“their soul”); the translation follows the evident sense while marking the textual uncertainty.].

### 62. Hypocrites die in a sudden storm

They seemed to live peacefully because they took delight in enjoying the praise of holiness. But their soul dies in a sudden storm—the soul that had rejoiced in the wretched tranquility of human praise.

Often a sudden and unexpected storm changes everything that the clear sky flatters [Note: Pratel and Utic omit “clear”; the printed editions read “the clear sky.”]; and danger cannot be avoided precisely because it could not be foreseen. Hence hypocrites, who neglect the guardianship of their lives, are said to die in a storm.

A sudden whirlwind casts out those whom the arrogance of external favor exalts; and while they embrace in praise what they are not, they suddenly find in punishment what they are.

Solomon rightly says:

“As silver is tested in the crucible and gold in the furnace, so a person is tested by the mouth of the one who praises” (Prov. 27:21).

Praise torments the righteous but exalts the wicked. It purifies the righteous when it torments them, but when it delights the wicked, it shows them to be reprobate.

The latter feed upon their own praise because they do not seek the glory of their Creator. But those who seek their Creator’s glory are tormented by their own praise, lest what is said outwardly not exist inwardly; and lest, even if what is said does exist, it be emptied before God’s eyes by those very favors; lest human praise soften the strength of the mind and overthrow it in its own delight; and lest what ought to be an aid toward increasing one’s work already become the recompense for one’s labor.

When they perceive that their praises are directed toward God’s praise, they embrace them also with desire. For it is written:

“Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

They make themselves a way for human beings whenever they display in themselves something by which God may be known, because they do not strive to fix human praise upon themselves [Note: Tours reads, “to make it become [fixed]”], but seek to let it pass through them toward the glory of their Creator [Note: Longipontus reads, “but seek to let it pass more effectively through them toward the glory of their Creator.” Utic, Pratel, and Ebroic read, “to pass through them toward the author of glory.” Colbert and Baluz agree.].

But the arrogant prostitute their tender hearts to human praises because they are corrupted by love of themselves. Of them it is said elsewhere:

“People will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2).

Their corruption is appropriately added here:

## CHAPTER XXXV

### The same passage

“And their life is among the effeminate.”

### 63. Those who are corrupted by human praise are effeminate

If they lived manfully, passing praise would corrupt them in no way. Hence the prophet exhorts the elect, saying:

“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 30:25).

In saying “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened,” he immediately added this as though he were concerned to fortify the gender of the heart [Note: Vindoc reads, “luxuriously.”].

The mind of the luxurious is corrupted if it delights in transitory things. Thus the life of hypocrites dies among the effeminate, because it is found corrupted by the luxury of praise.

The Septuagint translators, however, do not have “their life is among the effeminate,” but rather “their life will be wounded by angels.” The Greek reads:

ἐν χερι ἀγγέλων

—that is, “in the hand of angels,” namely, of the saints. This may perhaps arise from the similarity between the Hebrew words *kadosch* and *kadesch*, one of which means “holy” and the other “effeminate” or “catamite.”

Although the two translations differ in wording, they agree in meaning. For angels wound the life of the effeminate when the messengers of truth assault it with the arrows of holy preaching.

Since, then, we have heard what happens concerning the damnation of the reprobate, let us hear what follows concerning the deliverance of the humble.

### Verse 15

“He will deliver the poor from his distress.”

### 64. The humble are freed from distress when they die

The poor person is delivered from his distress when each humble person is freed from the affliction of his pilgrimage. Here he is pressed by continual tribulation so that he may be summoned to seek the joy of true consolation.

Hence it follows:

### The same passage

“And in tribulation he will reveal his ear.”

To reveal the ear in tribulation is to open the hearing of the heart through the blows of scourges. When we despise the commandments, we are dealt with by a loving severity so that we may fear the scourges.

Tribulation therefore opens the ear of the heart, which the prosperity of this world often closes. Solomon says:

“The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Rec. XXIV]

### Verse 16

“Therefore he will save you from a narrow mouth into a very broad place.”

### 65. The habit of sin is a very narrow pit, from which only grace can draw us

Everyone who abandons the way of life and casts himself into the darkness of sins plunges himself, as it were, into a pit or ditch. But if, through long persistence, he is also oppressed by the habit of iniquity, so that he can no longer rise to higher things, he is constrained as though by the narrow mouth of a pit.

Hence the prophet David, speaking in the guise of sinners, entreats:

“Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16).

The iniquity of an evil deed has shaken one from the stability of the good, as a storm of water has swept him away; but if it has not yet prevailed through a long habit, it has not drowned him.

He has fallen into the pit who has committed what the divine law forbids. But if a long habit has not yet crushed him, the pit has by no means narrowed its mouth over him. The less firmly he is constrained by habit, the more easily he rises out.

Therefore the prophet Jeremiah, seeing that Judah had been overwhelmed by iniquities through long habit, laments himself in his Lamentations under Judah’s figure, saying:

“My life has fallen into the pit, and they have placed a stone over me” (Lam. 3:53).

Life slips into a pit when it is stained by the pollution of iniquity. A stone is placed over it when the mind is also swallowed up by a hard habit of sin, so that even if it wishes to rise, it can no longer do so in any way, because the mass of evil habit presses down from above.

But because he is subject to divine power, and after the narrowness of a perverse habit is recalled to the breadth of good action [Note: Ebroic, Vindoc, and others read, “he deserves to be recalled.” Baluz and Colbert read, “therefore he is said to be recalled.”], it is said:

“He will save you from a narrow mouth into a very broad place.”

He is saved into a very broad place from a narrow mouth when, after the yoke of iniquity, he is brought back through repentance to the freedom of good works.

### 66. What distress it is to wish to rise from an oppressive evil habit but be unable to do so

There is a kind of distress, like that of a closed mouth, in wishing to rise from an oppressive evil habit but being unable to do so [Note: Some printed editions read, “as though the narrowness of a confined mouth.”]. One already tends toward heavenly things by desire, but remains below in action; he goes ahead in his heart but cannot follow in his deeds, and suffers contradiction within himself [Note: Longipontus reads, “from the evil habit of the guilt that oppresses him.”].

But when the soul thus striving is helped by the hand of uplifting grace, it passes from a narrow mouth into spaciousness, because, after its difficulties have been overcome, it accomplishes the good works it desires.

The prophet David had seen the confinement of a narrow mouth when he said:

“You saved my soul from distress, and did not shut me into the hands of the enemy” (Ps. 30:9).

He knew that he had been saved into a very broad place when he added:

“You set my feet in a spacious place” (ibid.).

The feet are established in a spacious place when we both strive toward fitting good things and are hindered by no difficulty. We go wherever we wish, as though through a broad place, because no opposing difficulties constrict us.

### 67. Job was wrongly believed to have fallen into this pit

Elihu would have spoken rightly about these matters if his opinion had applied to blessed Job. He believed that Job had been scourged because of guilt, and therefore judged that he had fallen into a narrow mouth.

The more he saw Job afflicted by powerful blows, the worse he believed his iniquities to be pressing upon him, plainly unaware that his scourges were an increase of merit, not punishment for sin.

When he admits that Job had fallen into a narrow mouth, he continues as though explaining more fully the depth in which Job was held, saying:

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Old Rec. XXXII]

### The same passage

“And without a foundation beneath it.”

### 68. Whomever the narrow pit of evil habit confines is swallowed by hell and by the abyss of despair

No sin has a foundation, because it does not subsist from its own nature. Evil is without substance. Yet, in whatever way it exists, it is joined to the nature of the good [Note: The old edition reads, “does not coalesce in nature.” But this conflicts with the thought of the holy Doctor: evil arises from the good and subsists in the good, as Saint Augustine teaches in *Enchiridion*, chapter 14, from whom Gregory scarcely ever departs. The negative particle is absent from all the manuscripts we consulted—Baluz, Colbert, Pratel, Utic, Tours, and others.].

Thus the narrow mouth is said to have no foundation beneath it because the pollution of sin has no proper right of subsistence [Note: Longipontus reads, “the use of subsisting.”].

Since the word “foundation” derives from “bottom,” we may also suitably understand “foundation” as standing for “bottom,” just as “hearing” derives from “ear,” yet the ear itself is often designated by the word “hearing.”

When, therefore, he said “a narrow mouth,” wishing to express the depth of the abyss, he added:

“And without a foundation beneath it.”

For whoever is seized by iniquity is swallowed by hell. Hell is rightly believed to have no bottom, because whoever is seized by it is devoured in an immeasurable depth.

Desiring to express its immense breadth, the prophet says:

“Hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit” (Isa. 5:14).

Just as one who draws many to himself is said to have been enlarged without limit, so he is not unfittingly believed to be deep without a bottom, because he swallows those whom he receives into himself as though into a certain abyss of his immensity [Note: Pratel and Utic read, “he is not unfittingly said.”].

Therefore, when he said:

“He will save you from a narrow mouth into a very broad place,”

he appropriately added:

“And without a foundation beneath it.”

As though he were saying:

“He will save from the narrow mouth which has no bottom beneath it, because through sin one moves toward hell. Whoever he saves from sin, he frees from the narrow mouth; and whoever he snatches from the narrow mouth, he draws away from the depth of hell.”

### 69. Another interpretation

It can also be understood in another way. Just as one who is plunged into a pit is held in the depth of the pit [Note: Vindoc reads, “at the bottom of the pit”], so the soul that falls, as though it had settled in a certain place of the bottom, would remain there if, once fallen into some measure of sin, the mind restrained itself within it.

But because it cannot be content with the sin into which it has fallen, and is cast daily into worse things, it finds no bottom in the pit into which it has fallen by which it can be fixed.

There would be a bottom to the pit if there were a measure of sin. Hence it is rightly said elsewhere:

“When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

He neglects to return because he despairs of being able to receive mercy. But when, through despair, he sins more, he removes the bottom from his own pit, so that he finds nowhere in which he can be held.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### The same passage

“And the rest of your table will be full of richness.”

### 70. Grace fills with the delight of inward satisfaction the person whom it rescues

The rest of the table is the refreshment of inward satisfaction. It is said to be full of richness because it is prepared in the delight of eternal pleasure [Note: Ebroic reads, “because it is in inward [pleasure].”].

The prophet hungered for the feasts of this table when he said:

“I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15).

He thirsted for the cups of this table when he said:

“My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 42:3) [Note: Vindoc, Pratel, and Utic read, “to God, the living fountain … and I shall appear.” Baluz also has “I shall appear.”].

Thus Elihu, wishing to console blessed Job’s temporal blows with the eternal recompense that was owed him by his merits, promises it as though gratuitously from himself, saying:

“And the rest of your table will be full of richness.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Rec. XXV]

### Verse 17

“Your cause has been judged as that of an impious man; you will receive cause and judgment.”

### 71. The righteous are scourged so that they may be instructed toward greater vigilance

The cause of the good is righteousness. Their cause is judged as though it were that of the wicked, because here their righteousness is wearied by a fatherly scourging [Note: Turon., “is chastised by a fatherly scourge”], so that they may be instructed toward greater vigilance not only by the commandment of precepts but also by the blows of scourges. Yet they receive both their cause and their judgment, because from the righteousness by which they now live they then shine forth at the summit of judicial authority, so that they may judge all things with greater power then, in proportion as all things are now more subtly judged in them.

Eliu introduced these matters as though promising something new, although blessed Job had always held them firmly by faith. [Vet. XXXIII.] All the arrogant certainly have this characteristic: they exaggerate whatever evil they say about others, and if they happen to mention something good, they present it as though it were unfamiliar. Hence they even dare to teach those who are more learned than themselves, evidently because they think that they alone know such things. But when they turn to words of consolation, they immediately think that they have become contemptible, and through the harshness of an inflated rebuke they fashion for themselves a kind of cleverness, so that those who appeared to have stooped down in flattering condescension may be feared when a rebuke suddenly arises [Note: Recent Vulgate, “as though those who had climbed up by flatteries”; we follow the manuscripts Turon., Vindoc., Norm., Longipont., etc., and also the early printed editions]. Hence Eliu immediately added, saying:

## CHAPTER XL [Rec. XXVI]

### Verses 18–21

“Therefore let anger not overcome you, so that you oppress anyone; nor let the multitude of places incline you. Lay down your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength. Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may ascend in their place. Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity; for you began to follow it after misery.”

### 72. The proud criticize whatever is rightly done by others

In most manuscripts we find *donorum* (“of gifts”); in a few, but older ones, we find *locorum* (“of places”). [Note: In certain biblical manuscripts *vel locorum* is noted as a variant reading. In the Bibles of Robert Estienne, which were revised against the most ancient manuscripts, the margin reads *vel villarum* (“or of villages”). Nothing similar is found either in the Hebrew text, in the translation of the Septuagint interpreters, or in the other ancient versions.]

But since the statement “Nor let the multitude of gifts incline you” requires no explanation, it seemed preferable to explain the reading that appears somewhat difficult to open up. The degree of arrogance contained in these words is shown by the very swelling of the one who formed them.

But since we have said that Eliu represents the arrogant and blessed Job the elect, if we distinguish these matters more carefully, we shall show how they apply even now within the Church to the arrogant. Holy men marvel even at the small works of others, while they despise even their own great works. The arrogant, on the contrary, despise even the great works of others, while they admire their own, even when they are small; and they frequently judge their own evils to be good, while they do not cease to regard the good of others as evil.

For while they seek their own glory, they perniciously strive to have whatever virtue is practiced by others torn apart by the charge of iniquity, and they turn the weight of a good action into a stain of crime. Often, when they see the wicked strictly corrected by the Church, they complain as though the innocent were being unjustly afflicted [Note: The early edition of Gilot and the Vatican edition read “the guilty.” The reading is corrected from the English, Norman, Turon., and Longip. manuscripts], and they change the radiance of her discipline into the name of wickedness.

Thus Eliu, retaining the figure of the arrogant and speaking as though admonishing blessed Job, says:

“Therefore let anger not overcome you, so that you oppress anyone.”

[Vet. XXXIV.] The arrogant count as a movement of anger whatever is done by the holy Church under the authority of discipline [Note: Recent editions: “whatever comes from the saints.” We follow the manuscripts Turon., Longip., Ebroic., Pratell., and other Norman manuscripts]. And because, through their appetite for human praise, they always strive to appear benevolent, they think that no one should be corrected by strict severity [Note: Vindoc., “And because through the desire for human praise…”]. Hence, as was said above, they consider those to be oppressed by good rulers whom they see being restrained from their vices against their will.

### 73. The Church’s temporal power in all parts of the world; the enemies of the Church unjustly reproach her for it, although some within her bosom become proud of her glory

By the Lord’s agency, the holy Church has grown in the summit of religion throughout all parts of the world. They maliciously distort this very temporal power, which she uses well, into the vice of pride. [Rec. XXVII.] Hence Eliu continues, saying:

“Nor let the multitude of places incline you.”

As though this were said in the voice of the arrogant to the same holy Church, which preserves humility more greatly amid prosperity: “Because you are honored everywhere with reverence for the faith, beware lest you be exalted by the burdens of that same reverence” [Note: Vindoc., Pratel., and Utic. have *reverentiae fastibus* (“by the pomps of reverence”), which is indeed more elegant than the reading in the Vulgate editions].

They observe certain people who swell with the vice of pride under the pretext of religion, and they unjustly extend to the charge of all what they rightly censure in some. They do not at all consider that there are within her those who know both how to govern temporal affairs perfectly while despising them, and how to await eternal things with full desire; who carry out the administration of the power they have received while preserving the ministry of their innate humility. Thus they neither neglect the care of the government entrusted to them under the pretext of humility, nor, again, allow humility to swell within them on the occasion of government.

Even if there are perhaps some within her who, under the pretext of religion, serve not God’s glory but their own, she nevertheless strives either to correct them strictly, if she is able, or to tolerate them with equanimity, if she is not. By correcting them she embraces them as sons; by tolerating them she is exercised as by enemies.

For she knows that the life of the righteous is torn apart by their pride; she knows that whatever is sinned through the wickedness of such people is extended into a charge against her. Yet she fears bearing the mark of another’s crime all the less because she knows that her Head also endured such things. Of him it is written: “And he was counted among the wicked” (Mark 15:28). Again it is said of him: “He himself took our weaknesses, and he himself bore our pains” (Isaiah 53:4) [Note: *ipse* (“himself”) is omitted in Pratel. and Utic.].

Let the arrogant go, then, and in their estimation of the wicked bite at the lives of the innocent. The Church of the elect knows how to endure both the deeds of the wicked and the words of the good [Note: Longip., “and the words of the good”]; she knows how, by enduring them, to convert the minds of the wicked. Even if they cannot be converted, she nevertheless bears their disgrace with equanimity. For she perceives that what is despised outwardly because of the merits of those whose life is torn apart inwardly contributes to her double reward.

### 74. Whoever is exalted temporally falls

It should be noted that he does not say, “Nor let the multitude of places exalt you,” but, “Nor let the multitude of places incline you.” For everyone who is exalted temporally is, by that very exaltation, inclined downward: when he raises himself outwardly, he falls inwardly.

Eliu, therefore, observing the fall of the heart in pride, says:

“Nor let the multitude of places incline you.”

As though this were said in the voice of the arrogant to the holy Church [Note: Some manuscripts add *diceret*, “would say”]: “Beware lest, if you are exalted by the reverence of the whole world, you be bent away from your inward purpose.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XLI [Rec. XXVIII]

### Verse 19

“Lay down your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength.”

### 75. When the apostles and the strong of the Church were called to rewards, God strengthened the weak in their place for the contest

Whom else should we understand as the strong of the holy Church except those who grow strong in overcoming the desires of this world, both through lofty beginnings and through completed progress? Her greatness therefore consists in the life of her strong members, because she is rendered more glorious when her elect contend with steadfast courage even unto death for the defense of truth [Note: Colb., “with unwavering courage”].

The arrogant, therefore, seeing that the apostles have been taken from this world and the martyrs have been taken to the heavenly realm, and perhaps perceiving that learned and capable rulers are altogether lacking [Note: Baluz. and Colb. read *abunde esse*, “to be abundant,” which is faulty, although “to be abundantly lacking” can scarcely be said; nevertheless this is how it is read in the manuscripts Pratel., Utic., and others, as well as in all the printed editions], suspect that they alone remain within the Church. Hence, while they put themselves forward, they mock her as though offering counsel, saying:

“Lay down your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength.”

As though they were openly reproaching her: “Do not at all trust that you possess greatness, for once the former leaders have been removed, you no longer have fathers whose lives you may glorify.”

They say this, of course, not knowing that almighty God does not abandon his Church without a fitting administration. For when he calls the strong to their reward, he strengthens the weak in their place for the contest; when he receives and rewards the former, he supplies the latter with the strength for labors that he will reward.

Of these it is said to the same holy Church: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17). Those who are later appointed take the place of the virtue of the ancient fathers, just as, when aged trees are cut down, tender shoots grow up into their strength. But arrogant men do not believe that those whom they once knew as weak can grow strong; and they disdain to honor those whom they remember to have been contemptible after they have been transformed.

[Vet. XXXV.]

### 76. There are far fewer righteous than wicked in the Church. Proud pastors reap in exultation what their fathers sowed by dying

Because they see few who are more righteous in her and many who are wicked—just as on the threshing floor the quantity of chaff is greater than that of grain—they despise even the life of the righteous according to their estimation of the wicked.

They see that some of her rulers, supported by temporal power, are nourished by the pride of that same power. They see that these men reap by exulting in earthly joys the reverence of religion which the fathers preserved for this world by dying [Note: Turon., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts, Colbert, etc., together with the early editions, read *servaverunt* (“preserved”). The more recent editions preferred *severunt* (“sowed”), evidently because of the antithesis with the other verb, *metunt* (“they reap”). Vindoc. and Turon. instead read *metuunt* (“they fear”)].

They perceive indeed that these men are strong, but not with strength. For while they are supported by temporal power, they are strengthened by a kind of weakness. The stronger they are outwardly, the more completely they are emptied inwardly of every power of strength.

Therefore the arrogant say to her:

“Lay down the strong in strength.”

As though it were said openly: “Those who truly clung to you were strong, because they preserved in their lives what they had proclaimed while teaching. But now those who preside over you are strong in appearance, not in strength, because they do not cease to display themselves as honorable, yet they are all the weaker and more contemptible in proportion as they fear that the glory of their honor should be despised for the sake of truth” [Note: Vindoc., “May the strong truly cling to you”].

What the arrogant think about many people is indeed true, but they fall into the vice of pride by judging all those whom they see presiding to be such. For the evil of many must not be extended into an estimation of all; for even if those whom they recognize and judge are wicked, there are nevertheless some holy people whom they do not know.

It is the season of threshing [Note: Turon., “and if there are still grains”], and grain still lies hidden beneath the chaff. No fruit, therefore, should be expected from the threshing floor if it is believed that it contains only what appears on the surface.

Since, then, they despise those whom they see and disdain those whom they know to have been substituted into the ranks of the ancient fathers, it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER XLII

### Verse 20

“Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may ascend in their place.”

### 77. It is night for the Church when the unlearned and weak occupy the places of teachers and the strong

As though the arrogant were saying openly: “Do not act in the darkness of your ignorance so as to substitute a multitude of weak people for the strong.”

The people are designated by the word *peoples*, because, as though devoted to ordinary custom, they live indiscriminately in all that they desire. To prolong the night is to allow peoples to ascend in place of the strong, if negligence causes the places of teachers and the strong to be obtained by the unlearned and weak.

Peoples ascend in place of the strong when those who have learned to live wickedly receive the places of pastors. This could indeed have been said rightly if it had been said humbly. For the arrogant, even when they offer good admonition, exercise the vice of their superstition. As was said above, they seek more to wound by rebuking [Note: Ebroic., Pratell., Utic., Vindoc., “than to counsel”] than to restore by consolation.

Hence it is immediately added:

### Verse 21

“Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity; for you began to follow it after misery.”

[Note: In the more recent editions, *Cave* (“beware”) is absent. It is absent from the manuscripts Baluz., Colb., Norm., and from the early printed editions.]

The arrogant certainly call the Church’s misery the fact that they suppose her multitude to be despised by God; and they despise her with all the greater pride because they suppose her to be utterly despised by God.

Having passed through these figurative interpretations, we must now set forth what is understood morally, so that, once the figure of the Church—which we generally believe to have been expressed—has been recognized, we may also hear what can be gathered from these words in their particular applications.

He therefore says:

## CHAPTER XLIII [Vet. XXXVI]

### Chapter 36, verse 18

“Therefore let anger not overcome you, so that you oppress anyone.”

### 78. MORAL MEANING: In correction, anger should be subordinate, not dominant

Anyone through whom it is necessary to correct the vices of others ought first to examine himself carefully, lest, while he avenges the faults of others, he himself be overcome by the fury of vengeance.

Very often the enormity of anger devastates the mind under the pretext of justice; and while it appears to rage with zeal for uprightness, it satisfies the madness of fury, and whatever anger wickedly dictates it considers just. Hence it often exceeds the proper measure of vengeance, because it is not restrained by the measure of justice.

It is fitting, then, that when we correct the faults of others, we first measure our own, so that the mind may first cool from its own burning, and first compose within itself the impulse of its zeal with calm equity. Otherwise, if we are dragged by abrupt fury to punish vices, we sin by correcting sin, and, while pursuing guilt through judgment, we act with immoderate violence [Note: This more elegant reading is found in the manuscripts Colb., Baluz., Turon., Vindoc., one Ebroic., Pratel., Utic., and in the early Paris edition. Other editions read, “we rage by striking”].

Correction of the delinquent no longer follows, but rather oppression, if anger is extended in punishment beyond what the fault deserves. In the correction of vices, anger should be subordinate to the mind, not dominant, so that it does not anticipate the execution of justice by ruling, but follows it by serving; and so that, when held in subjection, it fulfills the known judgment, rather than, when it holds sway, running ahead of it [Note: Baluz. and Pratel., “and, possessing the known judgment, fulfills it; it does not anticipate it.” The same reading is found in the early Paris and Basel editions].

Thus it is rightly said:

“Therefore let anger not overcome you, so that you oppress anyone.”

For if the one who strives to correct is overcome by anger, he oppresses before he corrects. For when he is inflamed more than he ought to be, under the pretext of just vengeance he is unrestrainedly driven toward the savagery of cruelty.

This generally happens because the hearts of rulers are insufficiently intent upon the love of the Creator alone. While they desire many things in this life, they are scattered among innumerable thoughts [Note: Pratel., “among countless thoughts”]; and when they suddenly encounter the faults of their subjects, they cannot judge them rightly with God, because they cannot suddenly gather their hearts, dispersed among transient concerns, to the summit of strict discernment [Note: We follow Baluz., Colb., Vindoc., Pratel., Utic., and other Norman manuscripts, rather than the printed editions, which read “toward discernment”].

Therefore, the more they are moved to punish sins, the less they discover the balance of equity, because they do not seek it in a time of tranquility.

Hence, when Eliu said, “Let anger not overcome you, so that you oppress anyone,” expressing the same causes of injustice and of anger’s domination, he immediately added:

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 0395B]

### The same passage

“Nor let the multitude of places incline you.”

### 79. From original sin arises man’s restless mutability. Unable to be satisfied by the quality of things, he seeks satisfaction at least through variety

We are inclined in as many places as we are extended among unnecessary cares. For just as a place is a bodily space belonging to a body, so a place is each individual intention of the mind. When that intention is driven here and there, if it is willingly occupied by some pleasure of thought, it is placed, as it were, in a certain location so that it may rest.

For whenever, overcome by weariness, we are led from one thought to another, we migrate, as it were, with a tired mind from place to place. Thus as many places incline the summit of the mind as arising thoughts dissipate the unity of a good intention.

A right mind would stand firm if it always clung to the one thought to which it ought to cling. A right mind would stand firm if it did not overthrow itself through unstable mutability in countless movements. But while it now considers one matter and then slips away to another, it is inclined from the state of its uprightness, as though through a multitude of places; and while it extends itself through many things, it casts itself down from the one intention to which it ought to have clung.

This habit of mutability, however, has now come, as it were, into nature from the fault of the first transgression. For when the mind strives to stand within itself, it is in some way drawn away from itself, even without knowing it.

The human soul is removed from each thing to which it gives attention by the impulse of weariness. But while it eagerly desires things to be thought about and suddenly grows weary of what it has thought, it shows that it depends elsewhere, since it does not rest when placed in any one thing.

It is suspended from the One by whom it was formed. And because it was made to desire God alone, while everything below God is lesser, what is not God rightly does not suffice for it.

Hence it is scattered here and there, and, as we have said, it is removed from each thing by the impulse of weariness. Greedy for pleasure, it seeks a place where it may rest, but it has lost the One whom it could have possessed sufficiently. Hence it is led through many things, so that, unable to be satisfied by the quality of things, it may at least be satisfied by variety.

[Vet. XXXVII.]

### 80. By clinging to God, the saints heal this anxiety

The holy men guard themselves with cautious discipline [Note: The printed editions read, “the holy men, because they guard themselves with careful watchfulness.” *Quia* (“because”) is redundant and is omitted in the manuscripts Pratel., Utic., and others. Baluz. and Colb. read *casta se* (“with purity”)], lest they be loosened by mutability from their intention; and because they desire to remain the same, they diligently bind themselves to the thought by which they love God.

In contemplation of the Creator they will receive this gift: always to enjoy a single stability of mind. No mutability will then scatter them, because their thought will always remain undivided from itself.

With labor they now strive to imitate what they will afterward receive with joy as a gift. The Prophet had bound himself to this immutability by the power of love when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Psalm 26:4).

Paul adhered to this unity by his intention, saying: “But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ” (Philippians 3:13) [Note: Pratel. and Utic., “of the heavenly calling of Christ.” This agrees with Baluz. and Colb.].

For if anything humanly dissipates in their hearts, severe examination immediately restrains it; and when their thought slips like a child, it is immediately curbed by youthful discipline. Thus they continually gather their scattered mind and compose it, as far as they can, into a single thought.

Since, therefore, the mind’s stability is bent by the mutability of thoughts, Eliu rightly says:

“Nor let the multitude of places incline you.”

### 81. Those who devote themselves to God must beware of pride

But often, while the mind of righteous men remains at the very summit of its intention, while it gathers itself from every scattering of mutability, and while it suppresses whatever arises in it superfluously, it is touched by the glory of its own uprightness and raised up in the swelling of its own presumption.

For whoever does great things, even if he thinks humbly of himself, nevertheless knows that what he does is great. If he does not know that they are great, he certainly does not guard them sufficiently. When he neglects to guard them, he either makes less progress in them or loses them completely.

Thus, while it is necessary for us to know our good works in order to guard them, from that very knowledge a path to pride is opened, and the hand of guilt is admitted to the heart of the worker, so that it may be seized and laid waste by the devastation it causes.

Yet by a marvelous dispensation our Creator permits a mind lifted up by prosperity to be shaken by a sudden temptation, so that it may see itself more truly in weakness and, now better than before, descend from the haughty elevation that it had drawn from its virtues.

Hence it is well added here:

## CHAPTER XLV

### Verse 19

“Lay down your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength.”

### 82. So that we may not presume upon ourselves, God allows us to be struck by temptation

The movements of the heart are strong when they perceive nothing except what belongs to virtue. But we lay down greatness and strong movements when, as vice strikes us, we are forced to consider what we are.

We lay down strong movements when we are no longer lifted up by virtue, but, by consenting to guilt, we fear being overwhelmed by the very weakness by which we are shaken [Note: Most editions read, “which we suffer”].

The mind has great confidence in itself when it sees that it possesses strength sufficient to fulfill its desires. It now arrogates to itself the confidence of holiness; it thinks itself capable even of all the heights of virtue that it has conceived by thought alone.

But when sudden temptation pierces it, it utterly disturbs the lofty thoughts that had arisen from virtue. An unexpected enemy enters a secure city, as it were, and the necks of its proud citizens are struck by a sudden sword.

Then nothing is done except continual mourning, while the captured city of the soul is emptied by slaughter of the glory of its great men [Note: Turon. and Colb., “while the captured city is emptied by the slaughter of its great men.” In the Norman text *magnatorum* also occurs; several lines are omitted in Baluz.].

Hence it is now said:

“Lay down your greatness without tribulation, and all the strong in strength.”

As though it were said openly: “Suppress everything that had swelled inwardly from a good action [Note: Some manuscripts read, “that had swelled,” as in Pratell.], and lay down the movements of the heart that had been made strong by upright conduct, because in this very temptation of adversity you now see how vainly you had previously been elated by great thoughts of yourself.”

This greatness is said to be laid down without tribulation because, when humility advances through temptation, the adversity itself is prosperous: it guards the mind from pride.

[Vet. XXXVIII.] Yet this does not occur without great tribulation, since a tranquil mind is disturbed by the irruption of temptation, as by a sudden enemy. For the adversity of temptation, when it inserts itself into the mind, produces a kind of darkness within it and disturbs it with the obscurity of its bitterness, although the mind had previously shone brightly through the sweetness of its virtues.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XLVI

### Verse 20

“Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may ascend in their place.”

### 83. Temptation produces darkness and raises storms

The night is prolonged when the sadness arising from temptation is not quickly ended by consolation. The night is prolonged because the mind’s grief is extended through confused thoughts.

For when the mind placed in temptation considers that it is being driven away from the former firmness of its virtue, it is blinded by sorrows spread over it as by darkness; the eye of its joy is closed to every light, while it anxiously trembles lest it completely lose what it had long ago begun to be.

Hence it is rightly said that in this night peoples ascend in place of the strong, because in the sorrow of temptation unworthy and manifold thoughts leap up in the heart in place of strong movements.

For when the mind sees that it has almost lost what it was [Note: Longip., “believing that it had almost lost what it had been, it gathers waves…”], it piles up innumerable waves and tumults within itself. At one moment it grieves because it has lost its tranquility; at another it fears falling into wicked deeds; at another it remembers the height at which it had stood; at another it considers the depth of vices in which it lies through pleasure; at another it prepares to recover its strength; at another, as though already defeated and broken, it despairs of being able to recover it.

### 84. In this night, manifold thoughts press upon the mind like tumultuous peoples

When such manifold thoughts arise over the mind that has been given over [to temptation] [Note: The printed editions read “over the aforesaid mind.” We have corrected this from the manuscripts Baluz., Colb., Utic., Pratel., etc. We have already discussed this word, familiar to Gregory, in Book II, chapter 9, section 15], they press upon it as though peoples were rising in the night.

The Prophet had presumed that he could subdue these peoples not by his own power but through the help of divine protection, when he said: “My protector, and in him I will hope, who subjects peoples beneath me” (Psalm 143:2).

Peoples are subdued in holy minds when foolish thoughts leap away from them through the presence of strict severity, so that they do not carry the mind away over the precipices of fantasies, but, subjected to reason, rest humbly in the heart.

Since, therefore, the mind placed in temptation, which in prosperity had presumed great things of itself, endures the tumult of hope and despair, it is rightly said:

“Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may ascend in their place.”

As though it were said openly: “Caught in temptation, cut short the darkness of sorrow more quickly, lest you who thought highly of yourself in tranquility should also confound yourself more disastrously in disturbance through the darkness of your thoughts.”

Eliu would rightly have said this, if he had known to whom he was saying it. For these things apply all the less to blessed Job, inasmuch as he understood everything at a higher level.

But because, as we have often said, the arrogant, while presuming to teach those whom they ought not to teach, descend even to insulting words of rebuke, it is added:

## CHAPTER XLVII [Rec. XXIX]

### Verse 21

“Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity; for you began to follow it after misery.”

### 85. Impatience must then be avoided, though it is unjustly charged against Job

He follows iniquity after misery who, after enduring evils for the sake of correction [Note: Vindoc., “which he endures for the sake of corruption”], inflames himself with the torches of impatience in a heated heart.

Eliu believed that blessed Job had done this, because he heard him speak freely while placed amid scourges. He did not know that everything Job said proceeded not from the iniquity of impatience but from the virtue of truth, and that he did not err even when he justified himself before the judgment of the inner Judge.

[Vet. XXXIX.] Yet it must be carefully considered how, when Eliu said, “Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity,” he immediately added of that same iniquity:

“For you began to follow it after misery.”

### 86. The proud do not know how to observe moderation in accusation

What does this mean? While he forbids turning aside to it, he immediately condemns him as though he had already turned aside to it [Note: Utic. and Pratell., “to turn aside”]. It means that arrogant men wish to appear more as judges than as comforters.

Hence they sometimes strike with strict judgments things they merely imagine to have arisen in the heart; before the fault of the guilty is certain, a strict denunciation of words is produced; and someone is struck by a sentence before the thing to be struck has emerged.

### 87. The discernment of the saints in correction

Righteous men also often confront wicked and hidden thoughts through admonition. But when certain preceding actions reveal those thoughts, they frequently root out from the hearts of their hearers, by the hand of correction, vices that have not yet been expressed; they recognize that these are already following from other things that have preceded them.

Just as bodily physicians discover that some illnesses have already arrived, while they treat others so that they may not arrive [Note: Vindoc., Pratell., and others: “but they treat certain illnesses so that they may not come.” Colb., “they treat them so that they may not come”], so holy teachers sometimes restore wounds that have been found to health, while at other times they act within minds so that they may not be wounded.

In these matters it must be carefully observed that just as they generally rebuke certain things with severity when they are certain, so they oppose uncertain vices with tranquility. They rebuke by striking what is certain; they avoid what is uncertain by guarding against it.

But because arrogant men do not know this rule of discernment, with the darts of their sentences they pierce what is known and what is unknown alike, what is certain and what is uncertain alike.

Hence Eliu now says:

“Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity; for you began to follow it after misery.”

But because the matters that follow are extended through a longer argument, we bring this little book to a close here, lest it be extended beyond measure.

# THE TWENTY-SEVENTH BOOK

The final twelve verses of chapter 36 are expounded, together with the whole of chapter 37, through ingenious investigations intended to establish both Christian doctrine and Christian ethics.

[Col. 0399]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. From the correct statements of the proud, one should take what is useful and reject what is harmful

Whoever strives to draw knowledge from the grand statements of the arrogant must carefully take precautions lest he imitate the lofty swelling of their knowledge; lest, together with words about virtues, he gather vices of conduct [Note: The early Basel, Gilot, Gussanville, and many other editions read, “lest, together with the flower of virtues.” For *flore* (“flower”), all our manuscripts and the early Paris edition read *verbis* (“words”)] and, while acquiring knowledge of speech, make himself unskilled in living.

For when we hear them say powerful things, yet observe that they swell with pride over their powerful statements, we enter, as it were, a garden of doctrine and pluck roses from thorns.

We therefore need discreet vigilance both to pluck what gives off fragrance and to avoid what pricks, lest, if the flower of their words is read carelessly, the unwary reader’s hand be torn by the thorn of their character [Note: Some editions read “for unwary readers,” as in Gilot., Gussanville, and many others. Our reading is found in the manuscripts Turon., Colb., Longip., Ebroic., other Norman manuscripts, and the early Paris and Basel editions].

Eliu, therefore, learned and arrogant, sometimes brings forth what is fragrant and sometimes what pricks. Thus one should take from his teaching what gives off fragrance, while carefully avoiding the pride that wounds.

Above he introduced many moral interpretations, but in the words that follow he raised himself to the highest secrets of prophecy alone [Note: Longip., “he raises himself to the secrets”; *sustollit* (“raises”) is also read in Pratel. and others]. He abandons the depths of morality and climbs to the heights of prophecy.

### 2. The proud are sometimes filled with the spirit of prophecy

Nor is it surprising that an arrogant man could be filled with the prophetic spirit, since Saul too was among the prophets (1 Samuel 10:6).

But why do we say this about Saul, when we know that even a donkey received rational words from the vision of an angel (Numbers 22:28)? Yet just as an irrational animal uttered words of reason without approaching a transformation of its rational nature, so often an unworthy person receives holy words through the spirit of prophecy, yet does not attain the glory of holiness that merits divine favor. Thus he rises above himself in speech while remaining sluggish beneath himself in life.

Hence Eliu now sees the humble advent of our Redeemer without being humble himself, and proclaims him prophetically whom he attacks through his proud character, saying:

## CHAPTER II

### Chapter 36, verse 22

“Behold, God is exalted in his strength, and none is like him among legislators.”

### 3. Christ, at once humble in weakness and exalted in strength, far surpasses the other lawgivers

As if he were plainly saying: “He who will appear humble in weakness remains exalted in strength,” as Paul also testifies, saying: “For although he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4). Concerning him it is rightly added: “And none is like him among the lawgivers.”

Moses was a lawgiver, Joshua a lawgiver, and the prophets also were lawgivers. We may call all those lawgivers whom we know to have admonished the people concerning what is right according to the law. But among the lawgivers none is like this Mediator, because they, called freely from sins, return to innocence, and by preaching lead others back from the things they themselves have experienced. Our Redeemer, however, is a human being without sin, a son without adoption; he never committed what he rebuked, and he speaks to the world according to his humanity while nevertheless ruling the same world, before the ages, according to his divinity.

Some thought that this Mediator was like the lawgivers. For when the disciples were asked, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” they answered: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets” (Matt. 16:13).

> **Note [Col. 0400D]:** In the editions of Gilot, Gussanville, and some others the passage is very corrupt: “[Col. 0401D] but surely Peter appeared how exalted he was in strength.” There the strength is attributed to Peter, whereas the holy Doctor commends Christ’s divinity, alluding to this passage in Job: “Behold, God is exalted in strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers.” In the old Basel and Paris edition of 1518, and in some others, one reads: “He revealed how exalted Peter was in strength (Christ).” This is indeed the best sense; later editors, reading carelessly, corrupted *aperuit* (“revealed”) into *apparuit* (“appeared”). We follow the manuscripts Baluze, Colbert, Tours, Vendôme, Normandy, and others.

But he revealed to Peter how exalted he was in strength when Peter, looking upon him truthfully, distinguished him from the equality of the lawgivers by saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16).

Hence the bride rightly says of him in the Song of Songs: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him” (Song 3:1). And shortly afterward: “The watchmen who guard the city found me.” Concerning them she again says: “They wounded me; they took away my cloak.” Again she asks them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” “A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:3).

### 4. He is sought at night, but is found only after the prophets and patriarchs have been surpassed

The beloved is sought by night upon the bed because, amid spiritual tribulation, he is desired within the secret chambers of the heart. Yet the bride does not find him while seeking, because every chosen soul already burns with the flames of his love,

> **Note [Col. 0402D]:** Longipontanus: “but his appearance is still being sought.”

but the appearance for which it searches is still denied, so that the lover’s desire may increase. As water is withheld from one who is thirsty, so that the heat of thirst may grow, the longer one thirsts for it, the more eagerly one eventually drinks it when it is found.

But while she is seeking, the watchmen find her, wound her, and take away her cloak, because whenever vigilant teachers find a soul already seeking the appearance of its Redeemer, they wound it with the arrows of heavenly love through the word of preaching.

> **Note [Col. 0402D]:** Vendôme, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts: “they pierce her with arrows.”

And if some covering from its former manner of life still remains, they remove it, so that, the more completely it is stripped of the burden of this world, the more quickly the one whom it seeks may be found by it.

It is rightly added: “A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” For unless the mind eager for his vision passed beyond the estimation of the prophets, beyond the greatness of the patriarchs, and beyond the measure of all human beings, it would not find him who is above human beings.

To pass beyond the watchmen, therefore, is to place even those whom the soul admires below him in comparison.

> **Note [Col. 0402D]:** The more recent editions omit *anima* (“soul”); we have restored it from the manuscripts Baluze, Colbert, Évreux, and others.

Then the one who was sought is perceived, if he is believed to be human, yet nevertheless beyond human measures. Hence it is rightly said here: “None is like him among the lawgivers.”

Appearing to our eyes through the weakness of the flesh, he displayed marvelous judgments while rejecting some and calling others—judgments that we can think about, but cannot comprehend. For he says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). And again: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

In these judgments, Judea is rejected and the Gentiles are gathered in. We can marvel at what was done, but we cannot investigate it fully. Hence Elihu rightly adds:

## Chapter III

### Verse 23

> “Who can search out his ways? Or who dares say to him, ‘You have acted unjustly’?”

### 5. We ought neither to search out his judgments nor, still less, to criticize them

As if he were saying: “If no one can investigate his action, how can anyone criticize it?” For no one judges rightly what he does not know.

We ought therefore to remain silent and rest beneath his judgments all the more because we see that we do not perceive their rationale. Hence it is rightly added:

## Chapter IV [Old and Revised II]

### Verse 24

> “Remember that you do not know his work, concerning which men have sung.”

### 6. Angels and teachers praise these things, yet do not fully know them

In sacred Scripture, “men” sometimes refers to angels and sometimes to human beings of perfected life. That an angel is sometimes called a man is testified by the prophet Daniel, who says: “Behold, the man Gabriel” (Dan. 9:21). Again, that people of perfected life are designated by the name “men” is expressed in Proverbs, where Wisdom says: “O men, to you I call” (Prov. 8:4).

Men therefore sing of the Lord when either heavenly spirits or perfected teachers make his power known to us. Yet his work remains unknown, because even those who proclaim him reverently acknowledge his judgments as impenetrable.

They know, then, the one whom they proclaim, and yet they do not know his works. They know him by grace as the one by whom they were made, but they cannot comprehend his judgments, which are enacted by him even upon them.

That the almighty God is not clearly perceived in his action is testified by the Psalmist, who says: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12). Again: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 36:7). And once more: “The abyss like a garment is his clothing” (Ps. 104:6).

Hence Solomon also rightly says: “Just as you do not know the way of the spirit, or how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who makes everything” (Eccl. 11:5).

### 7. An example of God’s hidden judgments in children who die without baptism or after baptism

To speak of one case among many: two children come into this light, but one is granted return to redemption through baptism, while the other is taken away before the water that regenerates him has washed him. Often the child of believers is taken away without faith, while the child of unbelievers is renewed through the sacrament of faith that has been granted.

Perhaps someone will say that God knew that the first would act wickedly even after baptism and therefore did not bring him to the grace of baptism. But if this is so, the sins of some are punished before they have been committed.
