And who, thinking rightly, would say that the almighty God, who frees some from crimes already committed, condemns in others crimes not yet committed?

His judgments are therefore hidden; and just as they cannot be seen because of their great obscurity, so they ought to be revered with great humility.

Let him therefore say: “Remember that you do not know his work, concerning which men have sung.” As if he were plainly saying: “The works of the one about whom all the strong have spoken are hidden from the eyes of your mind, because they exceed the measure of your knowledge precisely insofar as you are confined by your humanity.”

The text continues:

## Chapter V [Revised III]

### Verse 25

> “All people see him; each one beholds him from afar.”

### 8. God is seen only from afar, even by the elect

Every human being, by the very fact of having been created rational, ought to infer from reason that the one who created him is God. To see him already means to perceive his divinity by reasoning.

> **Note [Col. 0403D]:** *Ratiocinando* (“by reasoning”) is absent from Baluze, Uzès, Pratel, and other Norman manuscripts.

Since it is said, “All people see him,” it is rightly added: “Each one beholds him from afar.”

To behold him from afar means not yet to see him in his appearance, but still to estimate him solely from admiration for his works. Even the elect see him here from afar, because they do not yet apprehend his glory through the penetrating power of inward vision.

> **Note [Col. 0403D]:** Évreux and many others: “through the keenness of his inner vision.”

Although they are already near him through love, they are still separated from him by the burden of their earthly dwelling. Even though they cling to him by living well, they sigh that they are far from the appearance of his contemplation.

The reprobate also behold him from afar when they see him coming to judgment, because they see him not in the form of his divinity but only in the humanity by which he could also be grasped. Their eyes are then struck by the memory of the evil things they have done; and while they see his humanity without seeing the glory of his divinity, they are strangely made far from the vision of the one whom they behold.

[Old III.] But when it says, “Remember that you do not know his work,” and then adds, “All people see him,” and when, as we said, to see him means to infer by reason his essence, which transcends all things, it is very remarkable that we both perceive him and do not know his work.

We are not uncertain about his essence, yet we remain uncertain about his judgments. What is highest is evident to us; what is least is hidden. His works are less than he is. We see the one who acts, but we are blind in regard to the action, because it is uncertain why something is done, whereas it is not uncertain who does these uncertain things.

Let him therefore say: “Remember that you do not know his work, concerning which men have sung: All people see him; each one beholds him from afar.” For we see by reason that he exists whose judgments we scarcely comprehend.

> **Note [Col. 0403D]:** The old Paris and Basel editions, and other later editions, read: “whom we still see from so far away as we are from his strength.” Our reading, which Gussanville noted in the margin, is supplied by the manuscripts Baluze, Colbert, Vendôme, Longipontanus, Évreux, and others from Normandy.

Yet we still see him from afar, because a cloud of our weakness separates us from his strength.

The text continues:

## Chapter VI [Revised IV]

### Verse 26

> “Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge.”

### 9. We begin to understand something of God only when we realize that we cannot know him worthily

Earlier he had said: “Behold, God is exalted”; now he again says: “Behold, God is great.” Why, when speaking of God, does he say “behold” and repeat “behold,” unless we say “behold” of something that we display as present? And because God is present everywhere, when “behold” is said of him, his presence is recalled even to those who do not see him.

He rightly says that he surpasses our knowledge, after having said that he is seen by all, because although he is perceived by reason, his greatness cannot be penetrated by any subtlety of our understanding.

Whatever we know of the radiance of his greatness is beneath him; and the more we suppose that we have comprehended his power, the farther we are driven from knowledge of him. For although our mind is carried upward, it is nevertheless surpassed by the immensity of his greatness.

We know something of him as though only in part when we realize that we cannot know him worthily.

The text continues:

## Chapter VII

### Same passage

> “The number of his years is beyond reckoning.”

### 10. God is immeasurable, without temporal extension, and eternal without beginning or end

He wished in some way to speak of eternity, and he called the length of eternity “years.” For when we wish to extend a brief period of time, we expand moments into hours, hours into days, days into months, and months into years.

Because, therefore, he wished to express something exceedingly vast but found nothing broader to say,

> **Note [Col. 0404D]:** The printed editions read *ideo annos* (“therefore years”) instead of *in Deo* (“in God”). The manuscripts Colbert, Baluze, English, and Norman, as well as the codices consulted by Gussanville, persuaded us that *in Deo* is correct; he placed this reading in the margin.

he multiplied years in God beyond any reckoning, saying: “The number of his years is beyond reckoning.” Thus, by multiplying the things that are extended in relation to him, human weakness may recognize that it cannot measure the length of eternity.

Stretch your eye toward eternity, so that you may see God—either when he began to exist or how far he extends.

> **Note [Col. 0404D]:** Longipontanus: “and nowhere is the higher end found.”

There is nowhere an upper end, because he does not begin to exist; nowhere a lower end, because he does not cease to exist. Everything is compressed within him, while he extends around everything without spatial limitation and expands without location.

Behold, all created things are enclosed by an upper and lower limit, according to the very limitation by which they were created. For Scripture teaches that, since they begin from non-being, they hasten toward non-being.

> **Note [Col. 0404D]:** The old editions read “because, when they begin to exist”; Gilot and later editions read “because they precede beginning to exist.” We have corrected this corrupt passage with the help especially of the manuscripts Vendôme, Évreux, and others from Normandy.

### 11. Some things will be eternal in the future, although they did not always exist

Yet certain things have wondrously received this quality: although their upper end gives them a beginning, their lower end does not confine them; and although they begin to exist, they do not cease to exist forever.

Their eternity is unlike the supreme eternity for this reason: they began to be eternal. When we look toward their extremities, we do not comprehend their end, which is entirely absent; yet we perceive their beginnings when we draw our mind backward. As we direct our mind through them, both below and above, we do not understand how far they extend, but we see from when they began.

God, however, is eternal in such a way that in him there is something extended throughout eternity which neither arises from a beginning nor is terminated by an end; in him there is neither a “from when” nor a “how far.” Let it therefore be said: “The number of his years is beyond reckoning.”

By saying that the number of his years is spoken of, the duration of his being is shown. By saying that this number is beyond reckoning, that very being is shown to be infinite and incomprehensible.

But since we have learned how he is made known to human minds—when all people see him—and since we perceive his greatness by marveling at him, when the number of his years is regarded as beyond reckoning, it remains for us now to hear what he does.

The text continues:

## Chapter VIII [Old IV, Revised V]

### Verse 27

> “He removes the stars of rain and pours down showers like torrents.”

> **Note [Col. 0405D]:** See column 295, among the numbers printed in heavier type, in the notes.

### 12. The holy patriarchs and prophets were stars producing rain

There are two kinds of righteous people in this life: one consists of those who live well but teach no one; the other of those who live rightly and teach that same righteousness, just as in the sky some stars appear that are followed by no rain, while others appear that pour abundant showers upon the parched earth.

Therefore, whenever some people live rightly in the holy Church but do not know how to preach that same righteousness, they are indeed stars, but stars born in dry air. Through the example of good living they can shine upon others, but through the word of preaching they cannot rain.

When, however, some both live rightly and pour that same righteousness into others through the words of preaching, stars are brought forth in the sky as though to produce rain. They shine through the merits of their life and also rain through the discourse of preaching.

Was Moses not a star of rain in this sky? When he shone forth from above, did he not water the hearts of sinners—like parched earth below—with the rain of holy exhortation, making them fertile for sprouting?

Was Isaiah not shown as a star of rain? By holding before him the light of truth, did he not water the dryness of unbelievers by announcing it through prophecy?

Were Jeremiah and the other prophets not stars of rain, set as it were in the sky? Raised to the height of preaching, when they dared freely to rebuke the wickedness of sinners, did they not restrain the dust of human blindness by watering it with drops of words?

When the souls of these men, taken from corruptible flesh, are removed from the present life by heavenly judgments, they are like stars of rain withdrawn from the face of the sky; the stars return to concealment when, having completed their courses, the souls of the saints are stored in the treasuries of the inner ordering.

### 13. After these stars have been removed, the apostles were sent, pouring down showers like torrents

But because the earth would dry up if, once the stars of rain had been withdrawn, the heavenly streams ceased altogether, it is rightly said: “He removes the stars of rain and pours down showers like torrents.”

For when he removed the prophets, the Lord sent apostles in their place, so that they might rain like torrents after the ancient Fathers had fallen silent concerning the outward proclamations of the law.

He hid the stars of rain and poured down showers like torrents because, when he brought the preachers of the law into hidden and inward realities, a richer force of preaching flowed forth through the words of those who followed.

[Old V.] ### 14. After the apostles, the holy Fathers increased sacred doctrine

The apostles may also be signified by the stars of rain, concerning whom Jeremiah says of rejected Judea: “The stars of rain were withheld,”

> **Note [Col. 0405D]:** Same reference.

“and the late rain did not come” (Jer. 3:3).

> **Note [Col. 0405D]:** Some printed editions: “the rain did not fall.”

The Lord therefore withdrew the stars of rain and poured down showers like torrents, because when he removed the apostles who preached in Judea, the teaching of the new grace watered the world.

Both events can appropriately be understood as having taken place in the Church. When he brought the souls of the apostles, their bodies having been released, into the secret recesses of heaven, he hid the stars of rain, as it were, from the face of the sky.

But after removing the stars of rain, he gave showers in the manner of torrents,

> **Note [Col. 0406D]:** Évreux and others: “he poured down showers.”

because even after the apostles had been taken up to heaven, through the tongues of later interpreters he revealed the streams of divine knowledge, long hidden, in a more abundant outpouring.

For what the apostles said briefly, these interpreters multiplied through exposition. Hence the preaching of the interpreters is not inappropriately compared to torrents: while they gather together the sayings of many predecessors, they themselves expand more deeply in what they establish.

By joining testimony to testimony, they make torrents, as it were, out of drops. As the Gentiles are taught daily through their words, and the mind of the sinner receives heavenly knowledge, the torrents display themselves like water standing upon the earth.

Yet interpreters must never place themselves above the apostles in knowledge merely because they speak at greater length in their explanations. They must constantly remember through whom they received the discoveries of that same knowledge.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## Chapter IX

### Verse 28

> “Which flow from the clouds.”

### 15. Yet they must not be preferred to the apostles, the first transmitters of this doctrine

These torrents flow from the clouds because, if the force of understanding did not begin from the holy apostles, it would never flow more abundantly through the mouths of teachers.

In sacred Scripture, clouds sometimes signify people of changeable character, sometimes prophets, and sometimes apostles.

Human instability of mind is expressed by clouds, as Solomon says: “He who watches the wind does not sow, and he who considers the clouds never reaps” (Eccl. 11:4).

He plainly calls the unclean spirit “wind” and the people subject to it “clouds,” because the spirit drives them and calls them back here and there whenever its temptations alternate through the breath of suggestions in their hearts.

Therefore, he who watches the wind does not sow, because one who fears coming temptations does not resolve to devote his heart to good works. And he who considers the clouds does not reap, because one who trembles before the terror of human mutability deprives himself of the reward of eternal recompense.

> **Note [Col. 0406D]:** Pratel, Uzès, and others: “of the reward of eternal recompense.”

Prophets are represented by clouds, as the Psalmist says: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 18:12)—that is, hidden knowledge is in the prophets.

[Old VI.] Apostles too are represented by clouds, as Isaiah says: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

They themselves are stars, because they shine through the merits of their life; they themselves are clouds, because they water the parched earth of our hearts with streams of heavenly understanding.

If they were not clouds, the prophet, looking upon them, would never have said: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8).

The torrents of showers therefore flow from the clouds because the deep teachings of those who came later received their origin from the holy apostles.

Concerning these clouds it is appropriately added:

## Chapter X

### Same passage

> “Which cover everything above.”

### 16. Why the apostles are called clouds

When clouds cover the air above, if we raise our eyes to heaven, we see not heaven but the clouds themselves. Our sight does not penetrate the regions of the ether, because the clouds conceal them from us through our own weakness. And when the sun shines from heaven, the air interposed before it is illuminated first, so that afterward we may contemplate the sun’s rays in the sky.

Because we are carnal human beings, when we strive to seek what is above, we raise our eyes as though toward heaven and direct our gaze as though toward heaven, because, weighed down by our habitual concern with bodily things, we attempt to teach spiritual realities.

But because our understanding is not permitted to pass over into divine things unless it is first shaped by the examples of the holy ones who preceded us, our eye receives, as it were, the sky, but sees clouds. It desires to grasp the things of God, but can scarcely admire what has been granted to human beings.

> **Note [Col. 0407D]:** The same manuscripts: “because it is able to apprehend.”

Hence it is said elsewhere: “You illuminate wondrously from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. 76:5). One who cannot contemplate the rising sun looks upon the mountains illuminated by it and realizes that the sun has risen.

God therefore illuminates us from the everlasting mountains, because through the life of the preceding Fathers, which we admire, he enlightens us with a ray of his own brightness.

Behold, we are kindled with zeal for devotion to the Lord and for charity, but in this devotion and charity we are formed more perfectly by contemplating these clouds.

For who was more devoted than Peter (Matt. 14:29)? Who more full of love than John (John 13:23)? The one, through devotion, did not fear to tread upon the yielding surface of the sea; the other, through love, rested upon the breast of our Creator. He who had come for the nourishment of a bodily meal received spiritual food from the bosom of the Redeemer.

[Revised VII.] ### 17. Why the prophets and ancient Fathers are also called clouds

Abraham teaches us obedience; Isaac, patience; Jacob, a life of labor; Joseph, chastity; Moses, gentleness; Joshua, steadfastness; Samuel, kindness; David, piety and humility.

But since we have said that prophets too are represented by clouds, we must now bring forward further examples from the ancient Fathers.

Behold, when we desire to submit to heavenly commands through obedience, we are helped by considering the footprints of the ancient Fathers. For who was more obedient than Abraham? At a single divine command he left relatives and homeland, and, in order to obtain an eternal inheritance, did not hesitate to strike the very one whom, already old and almost at the point of death, he had received as his heir (Gen. 12:4).

When we try to seize the virtue of patience, we look upon the examples of those who preceded us. For who was more patient than Isaac? He carried the wood, asked about the burnt offering, and shortly afterward was bound without speaking; he was placed upon the altar and did not resist (Gen. 22:7).

What can be said to be more patient than this man? He is led as though for consolation, and he asks questions; he is bound for slaughter, and he falls silent; he asks while he is about to offer the burnt offering, and he is silent when he is about to be offered as the burnt offering.

When we strive to gird ourselves for endurance of labor, we are strengthened by the examples of those who preceded us.

> **Note [Col. 0407D]:** Some manuscripts and editions read “we are formed.” We follow the manuscripts Baluze and Colbert.

For who was more laborious than Jacob? Although related to Laban by kinship, he worked for so long in the condition of a servant, performing the duties of a slave, in order to enjoy the rewards of an heir (Gen. 30:26).

When we strive to climb the citadel of continence and chastity, we are strengthened by the examples of those who preceded us. For who was more chaste than Joseph? Even as a captive, he could not be crushed beneath the yoke of lust by the desire of a wanton mistress. He was indeed a servant to human beings, but against the ruling power of wickedness he remained free even in servitude (Gen. 39:12).

When we desire to be filled with gentleness, we are helped by the examples of those who preceded us. For who was gentler than Moses? He endured the rebellion of the people entrusted to him and yet pleaded with the Lord, who was angry, on behalf of those same persecutors. He exposed himself to divine fury for their sake, because in his holy heart love was inflamed even by persecution (Exod. 32:32).

When we strive to form steadfastness of mind against the adversities of the world, we are supported by considering those who preceded us.

> **Note [Col. 0407D]:** Thus Tours, Vendôme, Baluze, Colbert, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts read. The old edition and Gilot have “to strengthen the mind through steadfastness.” Others read “to strengthen the steadfastness of the mind.”

For who was more steadfast than Joshua? Sent to investigate the character of the nations, he was not terrified either by their great stature or by the multitude of their numbers. Thus the very nations whom he did not fear when investigating them he also struck down in battle (Josh. 10:7).

When we strive to attain the summit of kindness, we are instructed by the examples of those who preceded us. For who was kinder than Samuel? Removed from the office of governing the people, he humbly sought a successor for himself; when he found him, he anointed him king, and immediately endured the one whom he had anointed as his persecutor.

> **Note [Col. 0408D]:** Thus Vendôme, Pratel, and other Norman manuscripts, the old editions, and Gussanville read: “he endures the persecutor.”

He feared that Saul might kill him, yet he pleaded that the Lord not become angry with Saul. For when he was sent, he said: “Saul will hear, and he will kill me” (1 Sam. 16:2). And Truth itself said to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (ibid., 1).

What, then, can be said to be kinder than this man, who did not want the one by whom he feared being killed to be struck down by God?

When we strive toward the height of piety and humility, we are lifted up by the examples of those who preceded us. For who can be called more merciful or more humble than David? He received insults from a rejected king in return for his victories; he bravely rescued the Israelite people from the hand of the enemy, yet he fled like a weak man lest he himself be killed (1 Sam. 17:18–19).

He recognized both that he had been chosen by divine judgment and that his persecutor had been rejected, yet he subjected himself to that same persecutor through repeated acts of humble submission. He took the persecutor’s spear, cut off the edge of his cloak, and immediately hastened to the top of the mountain. At one and the same time he displayed that he had possessed the power to kill him and pleaded that he himself not be killed.

### 18. We read that the life of those holy men was stretched over us in the manner of clouds

Since, then, we are formed by the examples of those who preceded us in all that we spiritually desire, it is rightly said of these clouds: “Which cover everything above.”

The life of the Fathers, extended over us in the manner of clouds, covers us, so that we may be watered for the fruit of fertile growth. When we look toward heaven, we first see clouds, because we first admire the deeds of the good and afterward penetrate, through experience, the things that are heavenly.

But the life and virtue of these clouds—that is, the ancient Fathers—would never be revealed to us unless other clouds, namely the holy apostles, opened them to the light of their preaching. Let the discourse therefore return to these clouds, which travel throughout the world by preaching, and show what the Lord accomplished in the world through them.

The text continues:

## Chapter XI [Revised VI]

### Verses 29–30

> “If he wills to spread out the clouds as his tent and to flash with his light from above, he will also cover the farthest boundaries of the sea.”

### 19. The saints of God are tents in which he dwells and walks among us. When Paul was traveling to Rome, God went hidden in his breast as though beneath a tent

The Lord spreads out the clouds when, opening the way of preaching to his ministers, he diffuses them in every direction throughout the breadth of the world.

It is rightly said: “As his tent.” A tent is ordinarily set up during a journey. And when holy preachers are sent into the world, they make a road for God.

Hence it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Mal. 3:1).

> **Note [Col. 0409D]:** In Vendôme, Colbert, and Baluze, *ante te* (“before you”) is omitted.

And again the Psalmist says: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting sun” (Ps. 68:5). And again: “O God, when you went out before your people, when you passed through the wilderness, the earth was shaken” (ibid., 8).

God, who is everywhere not locally in himself, walks locally through the regions of the world by means of his preachers. Hence it is also said through the prophet: “And I will walk among them” (Lev. 26:12; 2 Cor. 6:16).

He makes a road through them when he pours himself into human hearts through their speech. In this journey, the hearts of the saints are God’s tents: he is covered in them as though resting on the road, while, coming through them to the minds of human beings, he accomplishes what he has ordained and remains unseen.

[Old VIII.] Hence the whole synagogue is called a tent when the Lord complains through Jeremiah that the priests have ceased preaching, saying: “There is no one who will extend my tent any further and raise up my skins” (Jer. 10:20).

Again, concerning its destruction, it is said: “He has destroyed his tent like a garden; he has demolished his tabernacle” (Lam. 2:6).

> **Note [Col. 0409D]:** Longipontanus: “because at that time the Lord walked among human beings in the worship of that people.”

Because the Lord at that time was hidden among human beings in the worship of one people, he called that same people his tent.

Hence these clouds are also rightly called his tent, because when God comes to us by grace, he is covered within the minds of his preachers.

Was Paul not his tent when, traveling from Jerusalem and throughout the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum, the Lord came to the hearts of mortals and rested in Paul’s mind (Rom. 15:19)?

He was a cloud to human beings and a tent to God, because the one whom he poured into his hearers through preaching he retained invisibly in his mind.

Again, when Paul, bound in chains, was traveling to Rome to take possession of the world, God went hidden in his breast as though beneath a tent (Acts 28:15).

For he was hidden and could not be seen, yet, revealed through the words of preaching, he continued without interruption the journey of the grace that had begun.

Moses was his cloud when, before giving leadership to the Israelite people, he remained in the wilderness for forty years, aspiring to higher things and living apart from the society of the people.

He became God’s tent when he went forth, sent to bring the people back from Egypt (Exod. 3:10), carrying invisible truth in his heart. The almighty God was revealed in his work but hidden in his heart.

Present everywhere and containing all things, God made a journey into Egypt in his servant. Hence it is written: “God went into Egypt to redeem a people for himself” (Exod. 15:13, according to the Septuagint).

Behold, he is said to go, although all things are contained by his uncircumscribed presence, because he who is everywhere in majesty places his steps, as it were, upon a road through preaching.

### 20. God flashes through the saints when he performs miracles. Such miracles are necessary in preachers

Yet words alone are by no means sufficient for those same holy preachers to persuade unless miracles are also added.

Therefore, after it has been said, “If he wills to spread out the clouds as his tent,” it is rightly added: “And to flash with his light from above.”

What else should we understand by flashes of lightning than miracles? Concerning them the Psalmist says: “You will multiply flashes of lightning and trouble them” (Ps. 144:6, according to the Septuagint).

Through these clouds he flashes with his light from above, because through holy preachers he illuminates, even by miracles, the darkness of our insensibility.

### 21. The Conversion of the Furthermost Regions of the World. Britain Subjugated to the Faith

And when these clouds rain with words, and when they reveal the power of flashing light through miracles, they also convert the furthermost regions of the world to divine love. Hence it is rightly added: “He will also cover the farthest limits of the sea.” [Note: Vindoc., Pratel., and others have the future tense.]

We have indeed heard from Elihu’s words that this was to be done, but we now see that it has already been accomplished by God as its author. For the omnipotent Lord covered the farthest limits of the sea with flashing clouds, because, through the miracles of preachers shining forth, he brought even the ends of the world to the faith.

Behold, he has now penetrated the hearts of nearly all nations; behold, in one faith he has joined the boundary of the East to that of the West; behold, the tongue of Britain, which had known nothing except to roar barbarously, has long since begun to resound with the Hebrew “Alleluia” in divine praises. Behold, the once-swollen Ocean now lies subdued and serves at the feet of the saints; and its barbarous movements, which earthly rulers could not tame with the sword, priests restrain by simple words because of divine fear. The Ocean that, while unbelieving, had not feared troops of warriors now, as a believer, fears the tongues of the humble.

For when heavenly words have been received and miracles have also shone forth, the power of divine knowledge is poured into it; it is restrained by fear of that same divinity, so that it fears to do evil and longs with all its desires to attain the grace of eternity. Hence it is suitably added here also:

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 31.**—“For by these he judges the peoples, and gives food to many mortals.”

### 22. Through the same preachers signified by the clouds, terror is inflicted and food is given

By these words of the preachers—namely, by the drops of the clouds—and by these flashes of miracles, God judges the peoples, because he calls their terrified hearts to repentance. For when they hear heavenly things and attend to wondrous works, they immediately return to their hearts; and, grieving over their former wickedness, they fear eternal punishments.

But through the same clouds by which terror is inflicted, food is also given, because it is the great duty of preachers to know how to afflict the minds of the proud in such a way that they also know how to nourish the afflicted with the language of consolation. Thus they terrify sinners concerning eternal punishments and feed penitents concerning the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

Hence the order of this dispensation has been appropriately preserved, so that Elihu says in sequence that through these clouds he first judges the peoples and afterward provides food. For the omnipotent God first shakes us through his preachers by reproving us for wicked action, and afterward nourishes us by consoling us with hope.

If divine providence did not now exercise judgment through these clouds, he would never have said to the same clouds: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22). And again, if through them he did not feed our fasting hearts, the Lord would never have said to the disciples concerning the hungry crowds: “You give them something to eat” (Matthew 14:16).

We believe that this was then accomplished by their hands in such a way that we now see it accomplished daily without ceasing through their words. What does Peter do when he speaks through his letters, except satisfy our evil hunger with the nourishment of the word? What do Paul and John accomplish when they speak through their letters, except that our minds receive heavenly food and overcome the disgust of their hunger by which they were dying?

Let it therefore be said: “If he wishes to stretch out the clouds like his tent, and to flash with his light from above, he will also cover the farthest limits of the sea. For by these he judges the peoples, and gives food to many mortals.” It is as though he were saying plainly: If he stretches out his saints for the ministry of preaching and supports their words with miracles, he calls the boundaries of the whole world to the faith; through this he first judges the proud [Note: Gussanv. omits *per* (“through”).] and afterward strengthens the humble in hope by nourishing them with the word of consolation.

*[Old recension IX.]*

### 23. Faith is not given to everyone

But when he said that he gives food to mortals, it should be noted that he did not say “to everyone,” but “to many,” since it is written: “Faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thessalonians 3:2). And to some it is said: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47). Again: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). And again: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

Thus, even within the holy Church, many hold the faith but do not hold the life of faith; they receive the mysteries of the Lord’s humility but disdain to humble themselves in imitation of the Lord; they share in the appealing teachings of divine eloquence but remain monstrous among themselves in their swelling pride. Hence, after the breadth of the Church gathered from the farthest limits of the sea has been indicated, it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER XIII [Recension VII]

**VERSE 32.**—[Note: Gregory reads thus, although in the Hebrew source, the Vulgate, and other versions one finds “in the hands,” or something similar—for example, “in the palms,” namely of the hands, or metaphorically of the clouds. The Hebrew word *chappaim* properly means “hands.” Lyranus follows this defective reading of Saint Gregory.] “He hides the light from the monstrous.”

### 24. Knowledge of the truth is denied to the proud

Those are monstrous who exalt themselves with lofty thoughts. Against them Isaiah says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). Paul also says against them: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Romans 12:16).

But the light is hidden from these monstrous persons, because knowledge of the truth is denied to the proud. Hence the Truth himself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:25). By “wise and prudent” he evidently means the proud. For by not adding, “You have revealed them to the foolish,” but “to little ones,” he made it clear that he condemned arrogance, not intelligence.

Hence it is also said elsewhere: “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Psalm 114:6). And to show what this littleness is called, it is added: “I was humbled, and he delivered me” (ibid., 6).

Since, therefore, there are many in the Church who disdain to be little ones, they do not cease to be monstrous in their own estimation even in the place of humility. You will often see such people lifted up by honors, enjoying pleasures, and expanding through an abundance of possessions. They frequently desire nothing so much as to preside over others; they rejoice to be feared by many; they neglect to live rightly but desire to possess the reputation of right living; they seek flattery and swell with approval.

And because they are ready for the things abundantly present to them, they do not seek future joys. When various activities occupy them, they show themselves to be alien even to themselves. *[Old recension X.]* Yet if some trial of faith arises, because at least outwardly they are contained within it, they defend it with words and labors, and claim the heavenly homeland, although they do not love it.

### 25. Many fight for the promised land, although they scarcely love it. The example of the Gadites and Reubenites

The sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh fittingly represent such people in Moses’ writings. Possessing many flocks and cattle, and desiring outside the Jordan the plains they had seen, they refused to have an inheritance in the promised land, saying:

“The land that the Lord struck down before the children of Israel [Note: Thus Turon., Baluz., and Colb. Pratel. and some others have “a very fertile region.” The printed editions follow them.] is exceedingly fertile for feeding animals; and we, your servants, have very many cattle, and we ask, if we have found [Note: Turon. has “your favor.”] favor before you, that you give it to us, your servants, as a possession, and do not make us cross the Jordan” (Numbers 32:4).

Those who therefore possess very many cattle refuse to cross the Jordan, because those whom many entanglements of the world occupy do not seek a dwelling in the heavenly homeland. Yet the faith that they hold, at least outwardly, rebukes them, lest they grow sluggish through the enjoyment of leisure and by their example break others’ endurance of labor and devotion to perseverance.

Hence Moses says to them: “Will your brothers go to war, while you sit here? Why do you overturn [Note: Vindoc., Pratel., and others have “the hearts of the children of Israel.”] the minds of the children of Israel?” (ibid., 7).

But because they are ashamed not to defend what they confess, they hasten to battle for the same faith they professed; they claim it not for themselves but for their neighbors. Hence they say to Moses: “We will build sheepfolds and stalls for the cattle, and fortified cities for our little ones; but we ourselves, armed and girded, will go forth to battle before the children of Israel” (ibid., 16).

They soon come forward bravely on behalf of others, free the promised land from its enemies, and leave it; then they return beyond the Jordan to feed their herds. Many, although faithful, occupied with present concerns, feed their herds, as it were, beyond the Jordan [Note: Turon. has “because of the faith of baptism.”], because with all their mind and every desire they serve perishable things against the faith of baptism.

Nevertheless, as we have said, when a trial of faith arises, they gird themselves with the weapons of defense. They slaughter the enemies of the faith by overcoming them, but they do not love the inheritance of the promised land—that is, the fruit of faith. Thus they fight for it, yet leave their own dependents outside it. Because they have little ones outside, they have no affection for dwelling in it.

Hence they return to the plains, because they slide down from the high peaks of the mountains, as from hope in heavenly things, in order to nourish irrational animals outside the promised land. They labor to feed [Note: Ebroic., Utic., and others have “with empty desires.”] irrational movements of the soul with various desires, because those who are blinded by transient occupations do not know the greatness of the brightness of eternal light. And while they grow proud over earthly things, they close for themselves the entrance to heavenly light.

*[Old recension XI.]* Hence it is rightly said now: “He hides the light from the monstrous.”

Yet sometimes heavenly grace looks upon these monstrous persons, afflicts them amid the very occupations produced by their abundance, and inserts adverse but useful tribulations into their prosperity, so that, having been saddened, they return to their hearts and recognize how vainly they are occupied with perishable things. Hence, after the light is said to have been withdrawn, it is suitably added:

## CHAPTER XIV

**The same passage.**—“And he commands it to come again.”

### 26. The light of truth, hidden from exalted and occupied minds, is revealed to the afflicted and humbled

The light of truth, which is hidden from exalted and occupied minds, is revealed to the afflicted and humbled. The light comes when the afflicted mind recognizes the very darkness of tribulations that it endures because of perishable things. For unless it received something from the inner light, it would not see even that it had lost the light.

This can also be understood specifically of the Jews, who dared to oppose our Redeemer when he came in the flesh because they were monstrous in their own estimation. The light was hidden from these monstrous persons, because, while the proud persecuted the light of truth, they lost it.

But because they are to be received into the faith at the end of the world, it is rightly added: “And he commands it to come again.” Hence Isaiah also says: “Although the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 10:22). Then the light returns to them when they themselves return to confessing the power of our Redeemer. [Note: Ebroic. and many others have “are converted.”]

### 27. God hides or reveals the light as he wills

But if we take “in the hands” not as one noun in the dative case but as two parts of speech, it can be understood that the light is hidden in the hands when the wicked are blinded in their own works before the righteous Judge.

Yet it is commanded to come again, because when sinners recognize that they cannot be saved by their own strength, they receive the light of grace and are illuminated by the rays of inward protection, so that afterward they may love the heavenly homeland with greater ardor than formerly they burned with earthly pleasure.

But when, in speaking of the heavenly homeland, we hear that hosts of angels endowed with wondrous brightness dwell there; when we hear that the Creator of all things presides over it, fills it by refreshing it with his vision, and that true inheritance is light, with no failure of that light—then we bring our minds back to ourselves and consider that we bear earthly members.

We reflect that, born in darkness and alienated from the rays of inward light, we have lived so much more wickedly the more, devoted to bodily things, we dwelt far from spiritual things. Moved by this consideration, the heart, conscious of its evil, trembles and despairs of being able to become a citizen of that homeland it hears about.

Hence, so that the fearful mind may be brought back to confidence, it is suitably added here. For concerning this light he immediately says:

## CHAPTER XV [Recension VIII]

**VERSE 33.**—“He announces concerning it to his friend that it is his possession, and that he can ascend to it.”

### 28. God promises heavenly glory to human beings who are almost despairing

A friend of the truth is one who loves right action. Hence the Truth himself says to the disciples: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). A friend is called the guardian of the soul. Therefore, not without reason, the one who strives to keep God’s will in his commandments is called his friend.

Hence the Truth again says to the same disciples: “I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (ibid., 15).

Concerning this light of the eternal homeland, therefore, God announces to his friend that it is his possession [Note: Thus Utic., Pratel., Colb., and Baluz. This is a manner of expression not uncommon in Gregory; shortly below, in section 30, we read, “Let him not, therefore, despair of himself.”], so that he may not despair because of the weakness of his frailty, nor consider what he was when created, but what he has become when recreated. Let him know with greater certainty that he will possess the brightness of that light the more truly he now tramples beneath his feet the darkness of the vices that assail him.

The promise appropriately adds: “And that he can ascend to it.” For what is more difficult than for a human being, born on earth and bearing earthly and fragile limbs, to climb to the heights of heaven and penetrate the secrets of the heavenly spirits?

### 29. Christ established peace between angels and human beings. He made us equal to the angels

But the Creator of those spirits came to us and displayed himself as a human being even beneath them, as the Prophet says to the Father concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6).

And because he found between us and those spirits the scandal of a life at odds with them, by wondrous power and still more wondrous mercy, creating what is highest, he joined the lowest to the highest by taking up the lowest. [Note: Most Norman manuscripts have “receiving the lowest, he joined it to the highest.”]

Hence, when that same King was born, choirs of angels came forth to announce him and sang a hymn. With the discord of wicked life overcome, they acknowledged as fellow citizens those whom they had formerly despised, proclaiming with harmonious voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

It is as though they said plainly: “Those whom wickedness had separated from us, let goodness now born on earth unite.”

Hence before his incarnation a human being is read to have worshiped an angel in the Old Testament, without being forbidden to worship him (Genesis 18:2). But after the Mediator’s coming, when John had fallen down in worship before an angel, he heard: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” (Revelation 19:10; 22:9).

What does it mean that previously they allowed themselves to be worshiped without objection, but afterward angels refuse worship from a human being, except that formerly they justly despised human beings, whom they knew to be more degraded because they were devoted to carnal corruptions and had not been redeemed from those corruptions; but afterward they could no longer hold human nature in such subjection, because they saw it in its author raised even above themselves?

For that which had been subjected in the members ought no longer to be despised, since in the very Head of the members it had merited being exalted and honored. [Note: We have supplied *iam* (“now”), a particle lacking in the printed edition.] [Note: Here *prae­lata* is taken in a passive sense, as though he were saying: “human nature, assumed by Christ, merited being honored.” It is often used passively, for example in Book XVIII, section 13, and Book XIX, section 36.]

He, therefore, who for our sake became lower than the angels made us equal to the angels through the power of his humbling. Hence, by dying he taught us not to fear death; by rising, to trust in life; and by ascending, to glory in the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, so that the members might rejoice to follow where they see the Head go before.

Hence our same Head rightly says: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 24:28). Peter says: “Into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven” (1 Peter 1:4). Paul says: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

### 30. Christ alone ascended into heaven, which is open only to his members

But if we too, who were born on earth, ascend into heaven, where is what the Truth says again: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13)?

The same Truth immediately answers this statement by saying: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). His words do not disagree with one another; rather, they kindle the effort of our minds to investigate what appears discordant.

For all of us who have been born in his faith are undoubtedly his body. Since, therefore, through a wondrous dispensation of mercy the Lord has become the Head of his members, and the multitude of the rejected has been cast away, he alone is also with us.

“No one therefore ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13), because, since we have already become one with him, where he alone came in himself, there he alone returns also in us. And he who is always in heaven ascends daily to heaven, because he who remains above all things in divinity daily draws himself to heaven through the structure of his humanity. [Note: The printed editions have “therefore, if he despairs.” Our reading, found in the manuscripts Baluz., Colb., Vindoc., Longip., Norman., was rejected to the margin by Gussanvillaeus. See above, section 28.]

Let human frailty not despair of itself, therefore. Let it consider the blood of the Only-begotten and see in its price how great is that which is worth so much. Let it carefully ponder where the Head has gone before; and let what is bound by commandments for living be strengthened by the example for hoping. Let it trust in the heavens, hope for the heavenly homeland, know itself to be the companion of angels, and rejoice that in its Head it has been exalted even above the angels.

Let it therefore rightly be said concerning this light of the eternal homeland: “He announces concerning it to his friend that it is his possession, and that he can ascend to it.”

*[Old recension XII.]*

These things are exceedingly wondrous, exceedingly terrifying: that a human being born on earth, condemned far from the heavenly homeland by the demands of his merits, is not merely restored to the condition of his creation but is exalted still more gloriously, so that the one who lost paradise receives heaven; and that not only does the guilt owed by him fail to hold him back after his fault, but gifts increase for him all the more abundantly after his sin, so that the despiser of God, the imitator of the devil, if he returns to the fruit of repentance, may ascend to the height of contemplating the innermost light.

Whose heart would not leap in wonder at such mercy? Whose sluggishness would not tremble at the elevation brought about by such a contemplation? Hence it is suitably added:

## CHAPTER XVI [Recension IX]

**Chapter 37, verse 1.**—“At this my heart trembled, and it was moved from its place.”

### 31. Having considered the light of the eternal homeland, the mind is carried into ecstasy

Because fear, when it strikes the mind, makes it alienated from itself, Latin interpreters sometimes call ecstasy *fear*, as it is said through the Psalmist: “I said in my fear, I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Psalm 30:23). There, evidently, “excess” could have been said instead of “fear”; but “fear” is used for “excess,” because the mind is alienated in fear just as it is in ecstasy.

Hence here also, after considering the light of the eternal homeland, it is rightly added: “At this my heart trembled.” It is as though he said: “It passed over into an excess of wonder; and because the mind was filled with the spirit of a new hope, it left behind the condition in which it had been in its former way of thinking.”

### 32. Having despised earthly things, the heart sighs for heavenly things alone

It is rightly said: “And it was moved from its place.” The place of the human heart is the pleasure of the present life. But when the place of our heart is touched by divine inspiration, it becomes love of eternity.

Through consideration of the eternal homeland, therefore, the mind is moved from its place, because, after abandoning lowly things, it is placed in heavenly thoughts. Formerly it did not know what eternal things were; it had grown sluggish in the pleasure of present things; and, while itself passing away, it clung in love to passing things.

But after it learned what eternal things were, after it touched the rays of heavenly light by a fleeting contemplation, it raised itself from lowly things through wonder at what is above. [Note: Pratel., Utic., and others have “by wonder itself.”] Thus nothing now pleases it except what is eternal; and, despising transient things, it seeks only what endures.

It is therefore rightly said: “At this my heart trembled, and it was moved from its place,” because the sluggish heart, formerly devoted to earthly thoughts, when suddenly it raised itself through ecstasy to the heights [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and others have “raised itself to heavenly things.”], changed the place of its lowly thinking.

But because the mind, lying prostrate in love of the present age, sleeps through its own nature, and, unless it is struck by the inspiration of divine grace, grows cold and insensible in its pleasures, it is necessary to add how it is touched by inward thought and in what way it is made sensitive to spiritual things. [Note: Baluz. and Colb. have “may be signified.”] It continues:

## CHAPTER XVII [Old recension XIII; Recension X]

**VERSE 2.**—“He will hear the hearing in the terror of his voice, and the sound proceeding from his mouth.”

### 33. God first chastises us through fear of judgment, then restores us through the consolation of heavenly sweetness

It is the custom of sacred eloquence, when it conveys something to hearing, to speak of the hearing itself as being heard, just as Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard your hearing, and I was afraid” (Habakkuk 3:1).

Hence here also it is said: “He will hear the hearing in the terror of his voice.” It should be noted that the voice of God is said to be heard not in joy but in terror, because when a sinner thinks only of earthly things, when he carries a heart oppressed by lowly thoughts, if he is suddenly touched by the inspiration of divine grace, he understands above all that everything he does will be punished by the strict judgment of the eternal Judge.

The hearing of God’s voice therefore first occurs in terror, so that afterward it may be changed into sweetness. For he first chastises us through fear of strict judgment, so that, once chastised, he may restore us through the consolation of heavenly sweetness.

When violent pleasure in temporal things possesses us and presses the eyes of our mind in the sleep of sluggishness, if we are suddenly awakened by the hand of heavenly regard [Note: Pratel. and some others have “if we are suddenly awakened by a hand.”], we immediately open those long-closed eyes of the mind to the light of truth. We remember the evils we have done; we see how the strict Judge will come against them; the greatness of that Judge’s coming turns over in the mind [Note: Longip. has “we turn over in the mind.” Baluz. and Colb., instead of “of the judge,” have “of the judgment.”]; we consider what the gathering of human beings and angels will then be, how fiercely the burning elements will fight against the rejected, and how terribly the eternal sentence will proceed from the mouth of the strict Judge, by which he says to the rejected: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). The punishment of those rejected is revolved before the eyes, and the darkness of Gehenna is weighed with the grievous obscurity of bitterness.

Since, therefore, the proud heart is first shaken by terror so that, once shaken, it may be made firm in love, it is rightly said now: “He will hear the hearing in the terror of his voice.” And it is suitably added: “And the sound proceeding from his mouth.”

### 34. The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Lord’s mouth, provides both things

The sound from God’s mouth is the force of fear rushing upon us through heavenly inspiration, because when the Lord fills us by inspiring us with what is to come, he undoubtedly terrifies us concerning the evils of the past.

The mouth of God can also signify the Only-begotten Son, who is called his arm because through him the Father accomplishes all things, as the Prophet says: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). John says of him: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). In the same way he is also called the mouth.

Hence the Prophet says: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isaiah 58:14). Through him he speaks everything to us; and by the name “mouth,” the Word is plainly indicated, just as we too are accustomed to use “tongue” for words when, speaking of the Greek or Latin tongue, we mean Greek or Latin words.

We therefore rightly understand the mouth of the Lord to be the Son himself. Hence the Bride says to him in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1). It is as though she said: “Let him touch me with the sweetness of the presence of the Only-begotten Son, my Redeemer.”

*[Old recension XIV.]*

By the sound of the mouth, however, the Holy Spirit of the same Lord can be signified. Hence elsewhere, in reference to this same Spirit, it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind” (Acts 2:2).

The sound therefore proceeds from the mouth of the Lord when the Spirit consubstantial with him, coming to us through the Son, breaks through the deafness of our insensibility, just as the mouth of the Lord speaks concerning this same sound, uncircumscribed and incorporeal, saying: “He will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:15).

The force of fear can therefore be understood through the terror of the voice, and the sweetness of consolation through the sound of the mouth. For those whom the Holy Spirit fills, he first terrifies concerning earthly action and afterward consoles with hope of heavenly things, so that afterward they may rejoice in rewards with as much confidence as previously they feared when they saw only punishments. [Note: Thus Baluz., Colb., Longipont., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts; the printed editions have *confitendo* (“by confessing”) instead. Gussanvillaeus noted *confidendo* (“by trusting”) in the margin as a variant reading but did not indicate the manuscripts from which it was taken.]

Hence Paul speaks of the Spirit of the Only-begotten, as of this sound of the mouth: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

Hence the Truth himself says: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22). Behold, the terror of converts is changed into power, because when they punish their own evils through repentance, they rise even to the exercise of judgment. Thus they receive from God the power over what they formerly feared from God.

They become judges who have perfectly feared the heavenly judgment; and they begin to forgive the sins of others, who formerly had feared that their own might be retained.

But because this judgment, which is now exercised spiritually, is not seen by carnal people, there are some who do not think that God cares for human affairs and suppose that they are carried along by chance movements. Against them it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Recension XI]

**VERSE 3.**—“He himself considers beneath all the heavens, and his light is over the ends of the earth.”

### 35. God’s providence over the highest and the lowest

It is as though he were saying plainly: He who governs the highest does not abandon the lowest, because he attends to the greatest in such a way that this same care of governance is not hindered by small things.

For he who is present everywhere and equal everywhere is not unlike himself even in dissimilar things. He therefore regards all things equally and orders all things equally; present in every place, he is neither confined locally [Note: Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts and Longip. have “nor extended locatively.”] nor changed by caring for different things.

But if we understand the heavens as holy preachers, with the Prophet bearing witness when he says, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1), then, after the coming of the Holy Spirit has been signified through the sound of the mouth, it is rightly added: “He himself considers beneath all the heavens, and his light is over the ends of the earth.”

### 36. Why miracles were granted at the beginnings of the Church

There are some who, when they hear of the wondrous works of the apostles—that after receiving the Holy Spirit they raised the dead by a word, drove demons from the possessed, removed illnesses by their shadow (Acts 5:12 ff.), foretold future events by prophecy, and preached the Only-begotten Word of God while speaking in the languages of all nations (Acts 2:4)—because they do not now see these powers in the Church, suspect that heavenly grace has already been withdrawn from the Church.

They do not know how to consider what is written: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation” (Psalm 9:10). The holy Church needed the assistance of miracles when the tribulation of persecution pressed upon it. For after it had subdued the pride of unbelief, it no longer required signs of power but only the merits of works, although even now it displays those signs through many whenever necessity demands.

For it is written: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14:22). Where, then, all are believers, what need requires that signs be displayed? We may perhaps satisfy the question more readily if we recall something concerning the apostolic dispensation itself.

### 37. Signs were given not to believers but to unbelievers

When the outstanding preacher Paul came to Melite [Note: Baluz. and Colb. have *Melitene*. Vindoc., Pratel., Utic., the old Basel editions of 1503 and 1514, and the Paris edition of 1518 have *Mitilenem* or *Mitilens*; Paris 1488 has *Miletum*, an error no less serious.], and knew that the island was full of unbelievers, he saved Publius’s father, who was afflicted with dysentery and fevers, by praying (Acts 28:8). Yet, when Timothy was ill, he instructed him, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5:23).

What does this mean, Paul? You restore a sick unbeliever to health by prayer, yet you care for so great a helper of the Gospel, as a physician would, through nourishment. What else does it mean except that external miracles are performed so that the minds of human beings may be led to inward things, so that through what is visibly displayed as wondrous, invisible things still more wondrous may be believed?

Publius’s father had to be healed by a sign of power so that he might revive inwardly while being restored to health through the miracle. But Timothy did not require an external miracle, because he was already wholly alive inwardly.

What is surprising, then, if miracles do not frequently occur after the faith has spread, when the apostles themselves did not perform them among certain believers?

*[Old recension XV.]*

With the heavens therefore lifted up, the Lord considers what is below, because, even when the highest preachers have been taken away, he continually cares for the lowest aspects of our weakness. And, as though beneath the heavens, his light looks upon the ends of the earth, because, after the exalted life of those who went before, it also embraces the habits and deeds of sinners by the illumination of his grace.

Although he does not now frequently manifest signs of power through the life of the faithful, he nevertheless never departs from those same faithful through the power of their works. The statement “his light is over the ends of the earth” can also be understood in this way: when the preaching of heavenly grace gathers the nations to the faith, it encloses within itself the boundaries of the world.

### 38. The miracle of divine grace in the conversion of sinners placed at the point of death

—or certainly, “the ends of the earth” are the ends of sinful human beings. It often happens that many abandon God and spend the years of their life in carnal desires; yet, visited by heavenly grace, they return to God at the end of their lives, [Col. 0421B] recognize what the eternal judgments will be, punish with tears all that they remember themselves to have done perversely, and show by their upright deeds that these things truly pursue them. When justice follows, everything they previously did wrong is certainly forgiven them.

Hence Anna says through the spirit of prophecy: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth” (1 Samuel 2:10), because God does not judge the former life when, through regard for his heavenly mercy, he illumines what comes afterward. Hence Moses says: “You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep” (Exodus 13:13). The donkey signifies uncleanness, whereas the sheep signifies innocence. Therefore, to exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life into the simplicity of innocence, so that, after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now produce, by doing other things, what he can place upon God’s altar.

Because, then, the sinner is converted after wicked deeds and is at some point recalled from the darkness of his actions near the end of his life, it is rightly said here: “And his light is upon the ends of the earth.” But the same grace that fills the mind after its crimes also afflicts it with profound grief. For it recalls evil deeds to memory and shows a person how justly he ought to be condemned. Thus it happens that he pursues with daily tears every sin he remembers having committed; and the more he is now able to see what is just, the more ardently he desires to punish himself with groans for having pursued what was unjust. Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XIX [Rec. XII]

**VERSE 4.—“After him a sound will roar.”**

### 39. When grace breathes upon and illumines a person, the groans and roarings of repentance are heard

Whoever the Lord has filled by illumining him, he undoubtedly turns that person’s life into lamentation. The more he discloses eternal punishments to an illumined mind, the more harshly he burdens it with groans over its past wickedness. [Note: Longipontanus has *clarius*, “more clearly.”] A person grieves over what he was, because he begins already to see the good that he was not; he hates the person he remembers having been and loves the person he recognizes he ought to have been. He now delights only in the bitterness of repentance, because he carefully considers in how many pleasures he sinned through his own delight.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “After him a sound will roar,” because when God enters the mind, it undoubtedly follows at once that the groans of repentance arise, so that the person may now find it salutary to weep over those iniquities in whose lamentable delight he formerly rejoiced. [Vet. XVI.] But the more abundantly guilt is wept over, [Note: Pratellianus has “the higher.”] the more deeply the knowledge of truth is reached, because, in order to see the inner light, a conscience once defiled is renewed after being baptized by tears. Hence, after the roaring of repentance, it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XX [Rec. XIII]

**THE SAME.—“He will thunder with the voice of his greatness.”**

### 40. The voice of God, like thunder, awakens the sluggish sinner

God thunders with the voice of his greatness when he reveals to us, now well prepared through lamentation, how great he is in the heavens. For thunder seems to proceed from heaven when the visitation of grace suddenly strikes us, sluggish with carelessness and negligence, with fear; and, placed upon the earth, we hear a sound from above, because, occupied with earthly thoughts, we suddenly fear the sentence of heavenly terror. The mind, now rightly concerned with higher things, trembles, though previously it had lain sluggishly and wrongly secure amid lower things. [Note: Baluzianus, Colbertinus, and Longipontanus have “the visitation of heavenly grace.”]

But the terror of this hidden visitation, by what means it makes itself known to us, is not understood; nor is it grasped by the mind’s own vision, whose intention is changed toward what is better. [Note: Vindocinus, Pratellianus, and others have “but this terror.”] Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XXI

**THE SAME.—“And it will not be investigated when his voice has been heard.”**

### 41. The ways in which this voice makes itself known to the ears of the heart are unknown

The Lord’s voice is heard when the inspiration of his grace is conceived in the mind, when the insensibility of hidden deafness is broken, and the heart is roused to the pursuit of supreme love, penetrated by the cry of inner virtue. Yet even the mind itself, once illumined by this voice of the Spirit who comes upon it and makes himself known to the ears of the heart, does not investigate it. Invisible power cannot weigh by what channels it flows into us, by what means it comes to us, or by what means it departs.

Hence it is rightly said through John: [Note: Pratellianus has “For the Spirit breathes where he wills,” and so forth.] “The Spirit breathes where he wills; you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going” (John 3:8). To hear the voice of the Spirit is to rise, through the force of inner compunction, into love of the invisible Creator. But no one knows where it comes from, because it is unknown through what opportunities he pours himself upon us through the mouths of preachers. And no one knows where it is going, because when many hear one and the same preaching, it certainly cannot be known whom he abandons and casts away, or in whose heart he enters and takes up his rest.

One thing is done outwardly, but it does not penetrate the hearts of those who behold it in one and the same way, because he who invisibly orders visible things plants, incomprehensibly, the seeds of causes in human hearts. Hence, when Lazarus had been raised, [Note: Vindocinus, Pratellianus, Uticensis, and others read *quidam*, “some,” which signifies less than *multi*, “many”; this is the editors’ reading.] some believed, but nevertheless many of the Jews were stirred by that very resurrection to a zeal for persecution (John 11:45). The one and the same miracle that gave the light of faith to some blinded others to the light of the mind through the darkness of envy.

Hence each of the two thieves saw the same death of the Redeemer, a death like his own death (Luke 23:39). [Note: Longipontanus has “a death like his own deaths.” Turonensis likewise has this, except that *suis moribus*, “like his own character,” is read corruptly instead of *suis mortibus*, “like his own deaths.”] [Note: Pratellianus reads: “but one did not fear, through pride, to assail him with insults, whereas the other honored him through fear,” etc.] Yet one did not fear to assail him with insults through pride, whereas the other honored him through fear. Their thought was not the same in the one matter, because the inner Judge invisibly distinguished it by directing it.

[Note: *Quia* (“because”) is omitted in Pratellianus, Uticensis, and other witnesses.] But because these modes of hidden inspiration cannot be grasped by our thinking, the traces of the divine voice are naturally unknown. Rightly, therefore, it is said: “And it will not be investigated when his voice has been heard.” Hence it is further added:

### CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 5.—“God will thunder wondrously with his voice.”**

### 42. God sounds wondrously because, silently and by a hidden heavenly power, he refreshes the soul with food

God thunders wondrously with his voice because, by a hidden power, he incomprehensibly penetrates our hearts. While he presses them into fear through hidden movements and forms them in love, he silently proclaims, in some fashion, with what ardor he ought to be followed; and there is an excess of impulse in the mind when nothing sounds in the voice. This resounds among us with greater force insofar as it causes the ear of our heart to become deaf to every outward clamor.

[Vet. XVII.] Hence the soul, immediately gathered into itself by this inner cry, wonders at what it hears, because it perceives the force of an unknown compunction. This very wonder is well signified by the manna that came down from above in the case of Moses (Exodus 16:15). For the sweet food received from above is called *manhu*. *Manhu* means “What is this?” And we say “What is this?” when, not understanding what we see, we marvel at it.

The soul therefore perceives heavenly manna when, lifted up by the voice of compunction, it is astonished at the new form of inner refreshment, so that, filled with divine sweetness, it rightly answers, “What is this?” For, suspended from lowly thought, it marvels unusually at what it sees from above.

And because, when this voice is heard, the deafness of our sluggishness is broken and [Note: Pratellianus and others read, “the practice of the old life is immediately changed.”] the practice of our former life is immediately changed, so that the soul, breathed upon by the heavenly Spirit, desires above what it had despised and despises below what it had desired, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXIII

**THE SAME.—“Who does great and inscrutable things.”**

### 43. God works marvelous and astonishing things in the conversion of the sinner

When a person devoted to earthly occupations and oppressed by wicked desires suddenly burns with eagerness for new things, grows cold toward what was customary, renounces outward concerns, and longs for inner contemplation, who could adequately consider this power of the heavenly voice? Who could comprehend it by considering it?

The things the Lord does through his voice are great, but they would be less great if they could be investigated. He therefore does great and inscrutable things, because he displays the perfection of the work outwardly, while the very quality of the operation remains hidden within.

Through the apostles he also resounds outwardly with his voice, but inwardly he himself illumines the hearts of those who hear, as Paul bears witness when he says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Although, therefore, the apostles themselves do not give our minds the hearing of the heavenly voice, they have nevertheless been sent to accommodate themselves to us through outward words. Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XXIV [Rec. XIV]

**VERSE 6.—“Who commands the snow to descend upon the earth, and the winter rains, and the rain of his strength.”**

### 44. Holy preachers, whose way of life is in heaven, nevertheless accommodate themselves to their weaker brothers

Since the Psalmist says, “You will wash me, and I will be made whiter than snow” (Psalm 50:8), what are we to understand by snow in this passage except the hearts of the saints, made white by the light of righteousness?

Water drawn upward is compacted in the heights so that it becomes snow. But when this same snow comes down to earth, it is again turned into flowing water. The minds of preachers, therefore, are waters: when they raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things, they are solidified by a higher understanding. When they are carried away in sublime contemplation, they receive the strength of firm virtue. [Note: Vindocinus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts have “confirmations of virtues.”]

But because they are still held upon earth by fraternal love, they moderate themselves from their lofty understanding and, preaching humbly to the weak, water dry hearts in the manner of snow melted. [Note: Ebroicensis, Pratellianus, and several others have “the hearts of the parched.”] Snow therefore comes down from heaven to earth when the sublime hearts of the saints, already nourished by solid contemplation, descend for the sake of fraternal love to the humble words of preaching. [Note: Turonensis has “descend in the word to the humility of preaching.”]

[Vet. XVIII.] For just as snow covers the earth when it lies upon it, but waters it when it melts, so the virtue of the saints both protects the lives of sinners before God through its steadfastness and, through its condescension, pours itself out like melted snow upon the parched earth so that it may produce fruit.

And because water is first drawn up from below so that afterward it may be scattered and returned from above, all the saints, even when they stand upon the summit of virtues, consider from what lowliness they were raised, lest they despise the weakness of others as beneath them. Thus the righteous return like water to the lands from which they were raised when, in their condescension, they do not cease to remember what they themselves once were.

Certainly Paul was still water upon the earth when he understood the law carnally; but when he was led to heavenly things, he was changed into snow, because what he had previously understood weakly he changed into the solidity of true understanding. Yet, condescending to his brothers, he returned to the low places like snow, since even after the heights of virtue he recognized how unworthy he had been, saying: “Who previously was a blasphemer” [Note: Vindocinus has “and a persecutor and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.”] “and a persecutor” (1 Timothy 1:13), and so forth.

See how gently he recalls his own weakness, so that he may endure the weaknesses of others with equanimity. For, as it were, water returned after heaven to the earth from which it had been taken, when Paul, after so many secrets of contemplation, remembered that he was a sinner, so that he might humbly benefit sinners.

Let us therefore see how this water, destined to be changed into the solidity of snow, is drawn upward. He says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Corinthians 5:13). Let us see how the snow returns to the low places, so that, while melting, it may pour itself out. He says: “Whether we are sober, it is for you” (ibid.). Let us see by what hand it is drawn, so that both what lies low may be raised and what has been raised may be recalled. He says: “For the love of Christ urges us” (ibid., 14).

Because, then, the love of Christ, which raises the minds of the saints to heavenly things, also shapes them through its gracious moderation for fraternal love toward the humility of condescension, it is rightly said: “Who commands the snow to descend upon the earth.” Here it is aptly added: “And the winter rains and the rain of his strength.”

### 45. Winter is the present life, in which the rains of holy preachers abound

Winter is the present life, in which, although hope already raises us toward heavenly things, the cold sluggishness of our mortality still binds us, because it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

This winter has rains, namely, the preaching of the righteous. Concerning these rains Moses says: “Let my speech be expected like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2). These rains certainly suit winter and will cease in summer, because, while heavenly life is now hidden from the eyes of carnal people, it is necessary that it be sprinkled upon us through the preaching of the saints. [Note: Longipontanus has “be made manifest.”]

But when the heat of the eternal judgment has grown hot, no one will then need the words of preachers, because, when the Judge comes, each person is brought back to his own heart, so that he may feel the holiness he can no longer practice and may learn, through the punishment of his crookedness, what righteousness he ought to have followed.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them on the day of slaughter” (Jeremiah 12:3).
