On the day of slaughter the reprobate are sanctified, because then they perceive the holy things they ought to have done, when they can no longer avoid the punishments deserved by their wickedness.

Since holy preaching will cease with the present life—that is, the rains will cease with winter—it is rightly said by the bridegroom’s encouraging voice to the soul that is departing and [Note: The Ebroicensian and other Norman witnesses, with Vindocinus, read “hastening toward the eternal summer.”] hastening toward the summer of eternal happiness: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come; for winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed” (Song of Songs 2:10).

When winter passes, the rain withdraws, because, when the present life in which the cloud of ignorance and the sluggishness of corruptible flesh had bound us has been completed, every ministry of preaching ceases. Then we shall see more clearly through ourselves what we now hear more obscurely through the voices of the saints.

The Lord therefore commands the snow, the winter rains, and the rain to descend upon the earth when, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he humbles the hearts of the saints for the ministry of preaching, so that sinners may be corrected. Here it is rightly added: “And the rain of his strength.”

### [Rec. XV.] 46. The rain of strength is the preaching of divinity; the rain of weakness is the preaching of Christ’s humanity

The rain of God’s strength is the preaching of his divinity. The rain of weakness is the preaching of his incarnation, of which Paul says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25). And again: “Although he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

The holy men preach the weaknesses of his humanity in such a way that they also pour the strength of his divinity into the hearts of their hearers. Let us hear, through the thunder of the cloud, the rain of strength: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Let us also hear the rain of weakness: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

Let us hear the rain of strength: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made, in him was life” (ibid., 3). Let us also hear the rain of weakness: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (ibid., 11).

He therefore commands the rain of his strength to descend upon the earth because, through the voices of his saints, he preaches to us the weaknesses of his humanity in such a way that the wondrous and mighty things of his divinity are also made known to us.

But when we hear of the power of our Creator, we are immediately brought back to our hearts under the compulsion of fear. [Note: Recentior Vulgata has “with strength compelling”; the older Paris and Basel editions read, as do the manuscripts of Vindocinus, Longipontanus, Ebroicensis, and others of Normandy, “with fear compelling.”] Considering the Judge above us, we weigh what things we have done worthily and what things unworthily. [Note: Pratellianus and other Norman witnesses have “the things we have done unworthily,” omitting the *τὸ*—“the things”—that is, “the things we have done worthily.” Not without reason: when fear of the final judgment presses upon the mind, evil deeds rather than rightly performed deeds come to mind. Nevertheless, we have retained the reading found in all the printed editions.] Hence it is also rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXV [Rec. XVI]

**VERSE 7.—“He seals in the hand of every person, so that each may know his own works.”**

### 47. By knowing God we come to know ourselves and judge ourselves more severely

People do not care to weigh the evils they commit. But when they hear of the power of heavenly strictness, they recognize the burden of their evil works that weighs them down. Struck by the words of preaching, they awaken so that they may consider toward what punishments the merit of their former actions is dragging them.

When, therefore, the rain of strength descends upon the earth, it is sealed in the hand of each person, so that he may know his works; for, when the incomprehensible power of majesty is recognized, everyone examines his life more carefully.

### 48. Through natural light, as through a law of the mind, wrong and right are made known

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. The omnipotent Creator made the rational creature, the human being, distinct from all insensible and irrational creatures, [Note: This is the reading of Turonensis and most older manuscripts and printed editions. Recent editions, with Uticensis and Pratellianus, read *distinctam*, “distinct.”] so that he could not be ignorant of what he had done. By the law of nature he is compelled to know whether what he does is wrong or right. For why does he come to judgment for his actions if he could have been unaware of what he did?

Even those who disdain instruction through the Lord’s commandments know whether what they do is good or evil. For if they do not know that they are doing good, why do they boast publicly about certain deeds? Again, if they are ignorant that they do evil, why do they avoid the eyes of others in those same deeds? They themselves are witnesses to themselves, because they know that what they do is evil and fear that it may be seen by others. If they did not truly believe it to be evil, they would certainly not fear that others might see it.

Hence it is rightly said by a certain wise man: “Since wickedness is timid, it gives testimony to its condemnation” (Wisdom 17:10). [Note: Turonensis has “the fear that strikes the conscience through the deed.”] When fear, striking the conscience because of its deed, rebukes it, it itself bears witness that what it does is deserving of condemnation.

By contrast, John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God” (1 John 3:21). Let the wicked therefore flee human eyes; they certainly cannot flee themselves. Because they know that what they do is evil, they have conscience as a witness and their own reason as judge. In the sin they commit, therefore, they first encounter the judgment of their own reason against themselves, and afterward they are brought to the strict examination of the eternal judgment.

Perhaps this is what is said through the Psalmist: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Psalm 41:8). For, by the wondrous order of a hidden disposition, what is done is not permitted to remain unknown; the sinner already condemns himself by his own judgment in conscience, and after his own condemnation hastens to the sentence of the eternal Judge. [Note: Ebroicensis and other Norman witnesses have: “Therefore, to call deep to deep is to pass from judgment to judgment,” and so forth.]

To call deep to deep, then, is to pass from one judgment to another. Let the holy preachers go forth and rebuke the deeds of sinners; let wicked hearers despise the words of the righteous; let them defend their wickednesses as much as they wish, and, by defending shamelessly what they have done, multiply them even more shamelessly. Certainly they themselves are witnesses against themselves in conscience, because they are not excusable. By the very fact that God made the human being a rational creature, he “seals in the hand of every person, so that each may know his own works.”

876 But because Elihu had pronounced judgment concerning the wickedness of individuals, he immediately turns the eyes of his mind toward the author of that wickedness, through whom every evil arises. Since in this verse he had briefly touched upon the members of the wicked head, he now briefly describes the head itself.

Or, because above [No. XIX] he had introduced the powers of God’s clouds, [Note: Longipontanus has “the virtues of God’s snow,” perhaps in place of “the snow of God,” that is, the apostles, whom he compared to snow when explaining this passage of Job: “who commands the snow to descend upon the earth.”] he now acts so that the attacks of the adversary against the life of the good may also be made known. For it follows:

### CHAPTER XXVI [Vet. XIX, Rec. XVII]

**VERSE 8.—“The beast will enter its hiding place, and will remain in its den.”**

### 49. The Antichrist and all the reprobate are the devil’s den

Who else is understood by the name “beast” except the ancient enemy, who savagely assailed the first human being by deception and tore apart the integrity of his life through evil counsel? Concerning him, it is promised through the voices of the prophets that the holy Church of the elect will be restored to its former state: “The evil beast will not pass through it” (Isaiah 35:9).

But when, after the coming of the Redeemer and after the voices of the preachers—like the thunder of the clouds—this beast has attacked, at the end of the world, that condemned man who is called the Antichrist, what else does it do than enter its hiding place, [Note: The words “after the Redeemer’s coming” are omitted in Vindocinus.] so that it may remain in its own den? That vessel is the devil’s den and the beast’s hiding place, so that, lying in wait for human beings as they travel along the way of this life, it may hide in him through signs and kill through wickedness.

Yet even now, before it appears openly, it possesses the hearts of all the reprobate; it holds them as its own den through hidden wickedness and hides itself in their obscure minds for every harm it desires to inflict on the good. [Note: Vindocinus reads “with which to harm.”]

Were not the hearts of the persecuting Jews the den of this beast, in whose counsels it lay hidden for a long time but suddenly burst forth in the cries: “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6)? And because, by tempting, it could not reach the wounding of the mind in our Redeemer (Matthew 4:3), it yearned for the death of his flesh.

This beast certainly possessed many hearts even of the elect, [Note: Pratellianus, Uticensis, Ebroicensis, and others read *multa et electorum*, “many [hearts] also of the elect,” which is stronger; there *et* also means “even.”] but the Lamb, by dying, drove it out from them. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). By a wondrous and righteous judgment, while he illumined and accepted the confessions of the humble, he abandoned and blinded the eyes of the proud.

Hence the Psalmist says to him: “You set darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forests will pass through, the young lions roaring to seize prey and seek their food from God” (Psalm 103:20–21). The Lord sets darkness when, repaying sins with judgments, he withdraws the light of his understanding. It becomes night because the mind of the wicked is blinded by the errors of its ignorance.

In that night all the beasts of the forest pass through, as evil spirits, lying hidden under the shadow of deception, pass through the hearts of the reprobate by fulfilling their wickednesses. In it the young lions roar, because ministering spirits of exceedingly wicked yet powerful authorities rise up with persistent temptations. Yet they seek food from God, because they cannot seize souls unless they are divinely permitted to prevail by a just judgment.

Here it is aptly added: “The sun rose, and they were gathered together, and they lay down in their dens” (Psalm 103:20). When the light of truth appeared through the flesh, they were driven from the minds of the faithful and returned, as it were, to their dens, since they held only the hearts of unbelievers. Thus what is there called the lions’ den is here called the beast’s den.

### 50. The devil sometimes enters the minds of the good, but does not remain in them

I consider it especially important to note that this beast is said not only to enter its den but also to remain in it. Sometimes it even enters the minds of the good, [Note: Vindocinus, Ebroicensis, and others read “even [the minds] of the elect.”] suggests unlawful things, fatigues them with temptations, tries to turn the uprightness of the spirit toward the pleasure of the flesh, and strives to bring pleasure to consent. Yet, because heavenly help resists, it is prevented from prevailing. It can therefore enter the minds of the good, but it cannot remain in them, because the heart of a righteous person is not this beast’s den.

Those whom it possesses as its own den it undoubtedly holds by remaining in their minds, because it first leads their thoughts to unlawful desires and afterward leads their unlawful desires to the most wicked deeds. The reprobate do not strive to repel its suggestions with the hand of right judgment, [Note: So the highly praised manuscripts read. The sense is excellent. The older Paris editions of 1488, 1495, and 1518, Basel 1503 and 1514, Gilot 1571, Gussanville, and others, however, have “whose pleasures they desire to serve with submissive delight.”] since they desire to serve its wishes with willing delight.

When something wicked arises in their hearts, it is immediately nourished through the pursuit of pleasure; when it is not resisted at all, it is immediately strengthened by consent; consent is at once carried into action, and action is further burdened by habit. Rightly, therefore, this beast is said to remain in its den: it holds the thoughts of the reprobate until it also pierces their lives with the sting of wicked action.

Hence the Lord rightly says to Judea through the prophet: “How long will harmful thoughts remain in you?” (Jeremiah 4:14). For he does not rebuke them because they come, but because they remain. Unlawful thoughts also come into good hearts, but they are prevented from remaining, because all who are upright, lest they offer the house of their conscience to captivity, drive the enemy away from the very threshold of the heart. Even if he sometimes steals forward through sudden suggestions as far as the first vestibule, he does not reach the door of consent.

Overcome by the impulse of sudden fear, Peter opened the door of his heart to this beast by denying the Lord; but, recognizing him more quickly, he resisted and closed it by weeping (Matthew 26:70). [Vet. XX.] Since, however, the ancient enemy not only entered the hearts of the persecutors but also possessed them by holding them, it is rightly said: “The beast will enter its hiding place, and will remain in its den.”

We learn how long it remained in the minds of the Jews when we hear, in the testimony of the Gospel narrative, of their counsels. There it is described with what anxious cruelty they raged toward the death of our Redeemer when they saw him bringing the dead to life; how ardently they wished to fulfill their wicked desires against him, yet feared the people (John 11:24, 49); how many opportunities they sought to kill him but could not find them (Matthew 26:3–4); and how often they used the hands of foreigners to fulfill their savagery, because they handed over to the Gentiles for execution the one whom they themselves could not legally kill, so that the Roman governor might carry out by his authority what they themselves, in their sheer malice, longed to have done (John 18:28). Hence it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XXVII [Rec. XVIII]

**VERSE 9.—“From the inner parts the storm will come forth, and from Arcturus the cold.”**

### 51. Christ suffered persecution from the Jews and the Gentiles

When Sacred Scripture mentions “the inner parts” in opposition to Arcturus, it designates a region of the South different from the parts of the North. Hence it is written in this same book: “He makes Arcturus, Orion, and the inner parts of the South” (Job 9:9).

Because the inner parts of the South are held by the hotter sun, whereas Arcturus has no course there at all, [Note: Pratellianus reads “in Arcturus.”] by “the inner parts” the Jewish people are expressed, while by the name “Arcturus” the Gentile people are signified in this passage. Those who knew the one invisible God and at least served his law carnally were held, as if beneath the southern sun, burning with the warmth of faith. But the Gentiles, because they had attained no knowledge of heavenly understanding, remained cold under the North, as though without the sun.

Because a storm drives, whereas cold oppresses through torpor, it is rightly said here: “From the inner parts the storm will come forth, and from Arcturus the cold.” It is as though he openly said: “From the Jews arises persecuting wickedness, and from the Gentiles comes oppressive power.”

For the commandments of the law had not forbidden miracles to be performed, yet the Jews sought to kill the Redeemer of the human race because of those miracles (John 11:48). Unable to accomplish what they had begun, they therefore hurried to Pilate’s praetorium, so that he might kill the one whom no law restrained from killing unjustly. [Note: Recentior has *perimere*, “to kill,” changing the reading found both in the manuscripts and in the older printed editions.]

The storm therefore came forth from the inner parts, and the cold from Arcturus, when what Judea sought through envy the Gentile judge accomplished through Roman authority. Hence, against this same envy, it is further added:

### CHAPTER XXVIII [Vet. XXI]

**VERSE 10.—“When God breathes, frost is formed.”**

### 52. The hearts of the Jews had been hardened by the frost of envy

The more the Holy Spirit breathed upon the hearts of the faithful and bestowed greater miracles of virtues, the more severe grew the torpor of envy in the minds of unbelievers. Thus the unbelieving people hardened themselves against God precisely where the humble people softened the former hardness with which they had bound themselves. [Note: The particle *in* is absent from the printed editions but present in the manuscripts.]

By God’s breathing they had been changed into frost when, seeing the miracles, they envied them and said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19). They observed the signs and saw miracles performed through his ministers; they foresaw that the whole world would now follow the teachings of the faith. Yet, to the degree that the Holy Spirit had filled the world (Wisdom 1:7), he bound their minds more tightly with the wickedness of envy.

The water had therefore been changed into frost when, while the world followed God, Judea remained sluggish in envy. But because heavenly power was also able to dissolve the hardness of such great cruelty and melt the hearts of unbelievers into love for God, after this frost it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXIX

**THE SAME.—“And again very broad waters are poured out.”**

### 53. Some hearts were afterward softened and melted into rain

After the frost the Lord poured out very broad waters, because, after enduring the savagery of the Jews even unto death, he immediately melted their hearts from the hardness of unbelief through the inspiration of his love. Thus they ran all the more desirably to obedience afterward because they had previously resisted his commandments with greater obstinacy.

Hence it is rightly said by a certain wise man: “As ice in fine weather, so your sins will be dissolved” (Sirach 3:17). The Prophet had desired to be released from this frost of cold torpor when he said: “Turn our captivity, O Lord, like a stream in the South” (Psalm 125:4).

Of these waters—that is, of peoples running to God—it is said again: “He will send his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” (Psalm 147:18). [Note: The same manuscripts have *flavit*, “he blew.”]

The waters run from frost because many who were harsh persecutors become great preachers. Frost is therefore melted into water when the torpor of inner cold is turned into the watering of preaching.

Was Paul not frost when, having received letters and traveling to Damascus (Acts 9:2), he sought to restrain the seeds of God’s word, cast upon the hearts of the faithful as upon earth, lest they rise to the perfection of works? But this frost returned to water, because those whom he had previously endeavored to oppress by persecution he afterward watered with streams of holy exhortation. Thus the harvest of the elect might rise all the more abundantly because God’s rain also watered it from the mouth of a persecutor.

Hence it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXX [Vet. XXII, Rec. XIX]

**VERSE 11.—“The cloud desires grain.”**
54. The elect are grain, for which the rain of the divine Word is necessary. — For what are the elect, each and every one, except God’s grain to be stored in the heavenly granaries? At present they endure the chaff on the threshing-floor, because in this purification of holy Church they bear the contrary conduct of the reprobate, until the inner farmer separates these by the winnowing-fan of judgment and, receiving his elect into the heavenly dwellings as already-clean grain, consigns the chaff to eternal fires. Hence John rightly says: “Whose winnowing-fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing-floor, and will gather the wheat into his granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:12).

[Note: Gilot., Vatic., Gussanv.: “until he separates this Church,” namely, the Church. The older editions, following the manuscripts, especially Turon., Vindoc., Pratel., Utic.: “until he separates this,” namely, the grain.]

But until this grain comes to the perfection of its fruits, it awaits the rains of the clouds in order to grow, because the mind of the good is watered by the words of preachers, lest it be dried by the sun of carnal desires and deprived of the moisture of charity. The heavenly farmer saw this grain rising in the world and desiring the clouds when he said: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. 9:37–38). What is called grain here is called harvest there; and what is called clouds here is called laborers there, because holy preachers are both clouds and laborers: clouds through their teaching, laborers through their life; clouds because they pour down through their words, laborers because they do not cease to do what they say. Hence it is added:

CHAPTER XXXI.

THE SAME, 6. — And the clouds scatter their light.

55. The holy preachers are clouds. —

[Note: Nearly the same material is found below, at the verse, “Do you know when God commanded the rains?” no. 60.]

To scatter light is for holy preachers to spread abroad the examples of their life, both by speaking and by acting. Yet although they scatter the light of inward proclamation, they do not reach the conversion of all the hearts they desire. For it follows:

CHAPTER XXXII.

VERSE 12. — Which illuminate all things around, wherever the will of the governor leads them.

56. They illuminate all things, while God governs their course. — Often holy preachers wish to exhort certain people, but cannot. Often they desire to avoid certain others, yet by the impulse of an inward prompting they are compelled to exhort them with the greatest urgency. Let us see how God’s cloud is guided by the hand of its governor even toward what it does not desire, and how it is again restrained from its impulse by the hand of the governor.

Certainly, when Paul wished to leave the Corinthians, shaking out his garments, he heard: “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent, because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city” (Acts 18:9–10).

[Note: Pratel.: “because I am with you.”]

Again, when he wished to go to the Thessalonians, he was held back, saying: “I, Paul, wished to come to you once and again, but Satan hindered me” (1 Thess. 2:18).

[Note: Vindoc., Pratel. and other Norman manuscripts: “we wished.”]

For Satan could not by himself obstruct the ways of so great an apostle; rather, while opposing him, he unknowingly served the purposes of a hidden dispensation, so that, while Paul wished to approach some but was unable to do so, he might benefit more fittingly those from whom he could not depart. God’s clouds, therefore, illuminate all things around, because by the light of preaching they illumine the ends of the world. But because, being subject to divine commands, they cannot accomplish what they wish, they cannot go except where the will of their governor leads them. Hence it is further added:

CHAPTER XXXIII.

[Col. 0433A]

THE SAME. — Toward everything that he commands them upon the face of the earth.

57. While he also governs their inward movements. — Often, when they are led by the will of their governor, they desire to act in one way but are directed in another. Frequently they strive to correct certain hearers gently, yet their speech is led into harshness. Frequently they wish to cut down certain people harshly, yet their vigor is restrained by the spirit of gentleness.

[Note: Thus Turon., Vindoc., Pratel. and other manuscripts. The printed editions read rigor (“severity”).]

Just as they cannot go where they wish, so they cannot act as they wish. For since the inward judge holds them when he sends them, he also receives them, regulating them, when he brings them to their destination, so that at times they plan one thing in thought but accomplish another in action; at times they begin in one way but finish in another. Since, therefore, they serve according to what is commanded them, it is rightly said: “Wherever the will of their governor leads them, toward everything that he commands them upon the face of the earth.” They find a more open path of preaching precisely when they are led to it not by their own but by their teacher’s commands. Hence it is further added:

CHAPTER XXXIV [Rec. XX].

VERSE 13. — Whether in one tribe, or in his land, or in whatever place of his mercy he commands them to be found.

58. The preaching of the Gospel has been granted not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles. — By “one tribe” Judah is plainly understood, which in Sacred Scripture is mentioned as distinguished and multifaceted above the others. In that it produced from itself the flesh of our Redeemer, it received a special gift above all others.

The whole of Judaea is likewise called God’s land, because it was the land that then produced the fruit of faith for him, when the world, with the nations having fallen wholly into the worship of idols, was wandering astray.

The place of God’s mercy is the Gentile world itself; if the strict judge had dealt with its faults according to justice, it would never have come to reconciliation with grace.

[Note: Pratel. and Utic.: “and which, when it had no [merits] at all.”]

Although it had no merits before God, it nevertheless received the grace of reconciliation solely from mercy. Hence Paul rightly says: “But the Gentiles are to glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. 15:9). Again it is written: “Those who once had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1 Pet. 2:10).

[Note: The same manuscripts: “and which … did not obtain mercy, but now … obtained it.” The old editions agree. Our reading agrees more closely with the Greek text and the Vulgate.]

God therefore leads his clouds, whether in one tribe, or in his land, or in whatever place of his mercy he commands them to be found, because at one time he granted the preachers of the Old and New Testaments to the tribe of Judah alone, and rejected nearly all Israel because of the wicked rule of its kings. At another time he makes these clouds rain upon his land, because after correction and captivity he restored the same Israelite people to its former grace.

[Note: Vindoc.: “after corruption.”]

[Note: Pratel.: In this passage *de* is absent from “at one time”; this alters the sense.]

At another time he wished them to shine forth from the place of his mercy, because through holy preachers he also displayed to the Gentiles miracles of virtue, in order that by mercy alone he might release from the yoke of error those whom the anger of their innate unbelief was oppressing.

[Vet. XXIII.]

But behold: because Elihu perceived future things through the prophetic spirit and uttered many lofty statements, the arrogant man, wearied by the weight of his own pride, is unable to bear what he says. For he immediately adds boastfully:

CHAPTER XXXV.

VERSE 14. — Listen to this, Job; stand and consider the wonders of God.

59. What it means to consider God’s wonders while standing, and what it means while lying down. — It is as though he saw the blessed Job lying in comparison with himself, and admonished him to stand for words of such great preaching. Yet by saying “Listen,” he also inflicts a grave insult upon blessed Job, because, as we have already said above concerning him—and often afterward (Book XII, no. 38)—the arrogance of an inferior is displayed in wanting to extort a hearing for himself from a superior.

But although Elihu does not know how to weigh the good things he says or to whom he says them, we who seek to be instructed by everyone ought carefully to investigate the words of his teaching. For perhaps with great skill in virtue it is said: “Stand and consider the wonders of God.” There are some who consider God’s wonders while lying down, because they admire the power of his work without following it. To stand means to act rightly. Hence Paul says: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

Often they admire heavenly judgments, delight in the proclamations of the heavenly homeland when they hear them, and are astonished by the wondrous works of the inner dispensation; nevertheless, through love and conduct they neglect to rise toward these same works. They therefore consider God’s wonders while lying down who weigh his power by knowing it but do not love it by living accordingly. Through contemplation they direct their eyes toward consideration, yet through their intention they do not raise themselves from the earth.

Hence Balaam is rightly reproached: “Who, falling, has his eyes open” (Num. 24:4). He had said many things about the coming of the Redeemer and had foreseen what would occur in the last times, yet by living rightly he did not wish to rise toward the one whom he proclaimed by foreseeing him. He had his eyes open while lying down, since prophecy lifted his mind toward heavenly things while avarice held him on earth. He had his eyes open while lying down, because he could see from above the one whom, prostrate in the depths, he did not love.

Elihu, therefore, who certainly did not believe that blessed Job had retained in his life what he had said, speaks as though admonishing him: “Stand and consider the wonders of God.” He then examines him further concerning future things and, as though humiliating him for ignorance, adds:

CHAPTER XXXVI [Rec. XXI].

THE SAME, 15. — Do you know when God commanded the rains, so that they might reveal the light of his clouds?

60. Preachers inspired by God water and shine. — If the holy preachers are clouds, the rains of the clouds are the words of preaching. But when clouds fly through the air, unless rains come down, it is not known how great a mass of waters they carry.

[Note: Pratel.: “unless rain … comes down.”] Unless the bright sun breaks forth among the rains, it cannot be understood what brightness is also hidden within them. For clearly, if holy preachers remain silent and do not show by speaking how great is the brightness of heavenly hope that they carry in their hearts, they appear either like other people or far more contemptible than they.

But when they begin, through preaching, to disclose the reward of the heavenly homeland that they hold within; when, pressed by persecution, they make known in what stronghold of virtue they have advanced; when, despised in appearance, they reveal by speaking the source of the fear they inspire—then the rains that flow from the clouds themselves show us the light of those clouds.

[Note: Utic. and other Norman manuscripts: “to what stronghold of virtue.”] For through the preachers’ words we recognize the brightness of life they desire, so that we may venerate it with great humility.

Paul was showing this light to his disciples when he said: “That you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe” (Eph. 1:18–19).

The Corinthians had recognized this light through the words of his writings, as though through drops of rain, when they said: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Cor. 10:10).

But often holy preachers wish to display themselves so as to benefit others, yet cannot; often they desire to remain hidden so that they may be at rest, yet are not permitted. No one therefore knows when the rains reveal the light of the clouds, because no one comprehends when God grants the power of preaching so that the glory of the preachers may shine forth.

He therefore says: “Do you know when God commanded the rains to reveal the light of his clouds?” As though he plainly said: “Do you, who already see preachers destined to come into the world, comprehend when the Lord will impel them to preach by the fullness of the Holy Spirit, and by what means he will make the brightness of their life known to the world?” Hence he appropriately adds:

CHAPTER XXXVII [Rec. XIII].

VERSE 16. — Do you know the great paths of the clouds, and perfect forms of knowledge?

61. The strict discipline of right living is not a broad road but a path. — These clouds have exceedingly narrow paths, namely, the ways of holy preaching. For narrow is the gate that leads to life (Matt. 7:14). They constrain people along paths when those people do not wander out from the track of their intention through the broad desires of the world.

The strict discipline of right living is not a broad road but a path, in which every preacher is carefully constrained, being diligently narrowed under the guardianship of the commandments. Is it not a kind of narrowness of the journey to live in this world but possess nothing of this world’s desire; not to desire what belongs to others, not to cling to what is one’s own; to despise the world’s praises and love reproaches for God; to flee glory and pursue contempt; to despise flatterers and honor those who despise; to dismiss from the heart the evils of those who harm us, and to retain immovable in the heart toward them the grace of love?

All these are paths, yet great ones, because the narrower they are in the present life for the very discipline of living, the more widely they are expanded in eternal recompense.

[Note: Pratel.: “into eternal recompense.”]

Hence it is rightly added: “And perfect forms of knowledge.”

62. Perfect knowledge is knowing that one is nothing. — Perfect knowledge is both to do all these things carefully and to know that one is nothing on account of one’s own merits. Hence even the clouds are taught this perfect knowledge when the Voice of Truth says to them: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are useless servants” (Luke 17:10).

Perfect knowledge is to know everything and yet, in a certain sense, not to know oneself to be knowledgeable. For although we now know God’s commandments, although we now weigh his words with attentive consideration, and although we now do what we believe we have understood, nevertheless we still do not know with what strictness of examination the deeds we have done must be scrutinized. We do not yet see God’s face.

[Note: Turon.: “not yet [the] narrow …”]

We do not yet see his hidden counsels. How great, then, is our knowledge, which, as long as it is weighed down by mortality, is blinded by the very cloud of its uncertainty? Concerning this Paul rightly says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2).

While we live in this world, therefore, we know perfectly what must be known when, progressing in understanding, we recognize that we know nothing perfectly. He therefore says: “Do you know the great paths of the clouds and perfect forms of knowledge?” As though he plainly said: “Do you now see the lofty deeds of the preachers, who, after rising to high things through knowledge, humbly incline themselves downward through recognition of their own ignorance?”

Because this occurs through the gift of the Holy Spirit alone, so that the human heart may be perfectly taught not only about knowledge but also about its own ignorance, and may burn toward heavenly things with the warmth of love while considering in the depths that what it has learned is less than the highest, it is rightly added:

CHAPTER XXXVIII [Rec. XXIII].

VERSE 17. — Are your garments not warm when the earth has been blown through by the south wind?

63. Those who cling to the Church grow warm through the breath of the Holy Spirit. — We have often said that blessed Job represents the figure of holy Church. The garments of the Church are all those who are joined to her in the unity of faith. Concerning them the Lord says to the same Church through the prophet: “As I live, you will be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. 49:18).

By the South, which is clearly a warm wind, the Holy Spirit is rightly signified, by whom each person, when touched, is released from the torpor of his iniquity. Hence it is rightly said in the Song of Songs: “Rise, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16).

The North is commanded to rise so that the hostile spirit that constricts the hearts of mortals may flee. The South comes and blows through the garden so that its spices may flow, because through the coming of the Holy Spirit, while the human mind is filled, the reputation of its virtues is immediately scattered from it. Thus the tongue of the saints, like a garden blown through by the South, rightly says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

The garments of holy Church are therefore warm when the earth is blown through by the South, because those who cling to her by faith burn with the fervent zeal of charity while their minds are flooded by the breath of the Holy Spirit. Nothing prevents this from also being understood of blessed Job himself, because although we speak of these things generally in holy Church, we nevertheless hold them specially through each of her members.

64. Through the concord of teachers and hearers, charity burns mutually within them. — Everyone who lives rightly and is accustomed to teach this to others has, as it were, as many garments as he has hearers clinging to him in concord.

The nature of garments is that they cannot become warm by themselves. But when joined to a living body, while they cover the pores exhaling from the limbs, they retain the heat issuing from within; by this heat the same garments are warmed, and once warmed they return to the body the heat they have received by retaining it.

What, then, is signified by garments clinging to a living body except the life of disciples joined to teachers who live well? The disciple receives heat, as through pores, because he is kindled toward the love of God both by the example of action and by the force of exhortation. He expels his former coldness by departing from his former iniquity; he retains the heat he has received because he grows strong in the fervor he has taken in through preaching.

[Note: Vindoc. and Pratel.: “rejects it.”]

[Note: The same manuscripts and Ebroic.: “in which he has grown strong through preaching.”]

Holy teachers, meanwhile, when they perceive their hearers progressing in the love of God, themselves grow more fervent in the virtue of teaching. Because they see their hearers becoming ardent and fervent toward the highest things, they are kindled more powerfully to proclaim the good things of the heavenly homeland.

And if at times, because they still live the corruptible life of human weakness, they are tempted by some fault—however slight—in action, speech, or thought, they see the progress of their disciples and blush to be blameworthy even in the smallest matters, lest they perhaps provide examples of crookedness to those whom, by the voice of preaching, they call to the rule of inward rectitude.

Thus, while hearers are kindled by the teachers’ word, the garments are warmed as though by a living body. But while the life of the teachers also advances through the progress of their hearers, heat returns to the body as though from warmed garments.

Yet teachers must not attribute to themselves the fact that they see their hearers progressing toward the highest things through their exhortation. Unless the Holy Spirit fills their hearts, the voice of teachers sounds uselessly in bodily ears. They can form the teacher’s voice outwardly, but they cannot impress it inwardly. “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Let it therefore be said: “Are your garments not warm when the earth has been blown through by the South?” For then hearers who already cling to teachers living well receive the warmth of heavenly love, when they are stirred by the breath of the Holy Spirit—as though he plainly said to blessed Job:

“You attribute it to yourself in vain if you contemplate some whom you believe to have progressed in virtue through you. For those whom you think have grown warm through you would remain cold in their insensibility unless the fervor of the Holy Spirit touched them.”

After he had spoken these weighty words, he was lightly stirred by arrogance and immediately added words of mockery, saying:

CHAPTER XXXIX [Rec. XXIV].

VERSE 18. — Perhaps you fashioned the heavens with him, which are cast as though from bronze, exceedingly solid.

65. By the heavens cast as though from bronze, the holy angels and the minds of the elect are signified. — By “heavens” may be signified the angelic spirits who were created in the heavenly realms. Hence we are instructed by the Voice of Truth to say in our prayer: “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.” That is, just as God’s will is done by the higher creature, so it may also be observed in all things by human weakness.

Concerning these it is rightly said: “Which are exceedingly solid, as though cast from bronze” (Matt. 6:10). The nature of bronze is that it is difficult to consume with rust. The angelic virtues, which remained fixed in divine love, received this as a gift of recompense when the proud angels fell: that they should no longer be gnawed by any rust of creeping fault, but should remain in contemplation of their Creator without end to their blessedness and persist in eternal stability in the state in which they were created.

The very words of the history of the world’s origin in Moses bear witness to this (Gen. 1:6), when heaven is first said to have been made and afterward called the firmament. For the angelic nature was first created more subtly in the heights, and afterward, so that it could never fall, was more wondrously confirmed.

[Note: Pratel.: “It is subtle … created.”]

The heavens may also, as we have often said, express the minds of the elect, lifted above every earthly contamination by inward love. Although they live bodily in the lowest places, because in heart they already cling to the highest, they truly say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). They are exceedingly solid, as though cast from bronze, because no rust of change consumes them from the integrity of the strength they began with.

To those who endure adversity courageously, the voice of their Author says: “You are my friends, who have remained with me in my temptations.” But although the learned and arrogant, when he tries to mock the holy man, mixes forceful statements into his mockery, he nevertheless continually falls back from strong words into empty ones. For again, mocking him, he adds:

VERSE 19. — Show us what we should say to him, for we are indeed wrapped in darkness.

And as though he said: “You, who already enjoy the great light of understanding, ought to teach us, who are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance.”

He then immediately recoils from mockery and adds contemptuously:

VERSE 20. — Who will tell him what I speak?

As though he plainly said: “Who can recount to him the things that I, acutely discerning his praises, speak of him—things unheard of?” Who can recount these things even after hearing them?

But because teaching and arrogance clash within the dwelling of a single mind, the speaker’s mouth gives forth not only the levity of conduct but also the gravity of thought. After Elihu had swollen slightly through arrogance, saying, “Who will tell him what I speak?”, he immediately added by way of instruction:

CHAPTER XL [Vet. XXVI, Rec. XXV].

THE SAME. — Even if a human being speaks, he will be swallowed up.

67. For a human being to speak about God is for a blind man to discourse about light. — Everything that swallows something draws it inward, hides it from the eyes of those looking on, and carries into the depths what could be seen on the surface.

When a human being is silent about God, he appears to be something through the reason in which he was created. But if he begins to speak about God, it is immediately shown how much he is nothing, because he is swallowed up by the immensity of God’s greatness and, as though carried into the depths, is hidden. In desiring to speak the ineffable, he is engulfed by the very narrowness of his ignorance.

Flesh speaks about spirit; a circumscribed spirit about the uncircumscribed; a creature about the Creator; the temporal about the eternal; the mutable about the immutable; the mortal about the one who gives life. And when, placed in darkness, a human being does not know the inward light as it is, a person desiring to discourse about eternity speaks about light like a blind man.

If a human being speaks, therefore, he will be swallowed up, because if a human being desires to utter eternity as it is, he even loses what he silently apprehends of it.

Yet behold: eternity truly became known to human beings when it revealed itself to them by assuming humanity. Since it had not yet been revealed, it is rightly added concerning those same human beings:

CHAPTER XLI.

[Col. 0439C]

VERSE 21. — But now they do not see the light.

68. Through Christ, light shone upon human beings. — Concerning this light the prophet also says: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light” (Matt. 4:16; Isa. 9:2).

[Note: Basel edition of 1514: “who was walking”; the other editions: “who walks.”]

But he indicates how this same light is seen by human beings when he immediately adds:

THE SAME. — Suddenly the air will be condensed into clouds.

The air is so dispersed by its very thinness that it is solidified by no firmness. Clouds, however, are firmer in proportion as they are denser. What, then, is signified by air except the minds of worldly people, who, devoted to the countless desires of this life, are scattered here and there like fluid air?

But the air is condensed into clouds when minds that were flowing away are strengthened by the grace of heavenly regard with the solidity of virtue, so that, thinking rightly, they gather themselves within the bosom of the heart and do not dissolve in vain thoughts.

69. Peter and the other apostles were made solid into clouds through grace. — Peter had been air when, scattered through earthly desires, the concern of fishing drove him about like a passing breeze for the sake of bodily life (Matt. 4:18). All the apostles had likewise been air: they had already learned lofty things through the Law, but had not yet acquired firm understanding through faith.

Suddenly, however, the air was condensed into clouds, because through the regard of heavenly grace the fluid hearts of fishermen were transformed into the solidity of preachers. Their weak thoughts grew dense by thinking strong thoughts; like clouds, they received the waters of knowledge and irrigated the earth lying beneath them with the words of preaching. When this ministry had been accomplished, they returned to the secrets of heaven and, their labor finished, reached eternal rest.

Hence it is also rightly added:

CHAPTER XLII.

THE SAME. — And a passing wind will drive them away.

70. After the world had been watered by the preaching of the Gospel, those clouds were driven from our eyes. — The passing wind is the present life. The passing wind therefore drives away the clouds because mortal life, running its course, hides the holy preachers bodily from our eyes.

The passing wind drives away the clouds because the course of temporal life removes the apostles from the flesh and hides them from the surface of the earth in secret repose, as though in the hinge of the heavens.

But because they do not cease preaching until death, and, like clouds, pass through the span of the present life with the rain of their words, he adds what their labors accomplish in holy Church when he immediately says:

CHAPTER XLIII [Rec. XXVI].

VERSE 22. — From the North gold will come.

71. The Christian religion was propagated chiefly from the Gentiles. — What is signified by the North except the Gentile world, bound by the cold of sin? The one who held it under the yoke of his tyranny, growing proud, said: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14).

What, moreover, is expressed by the name of gold except faithful souls? Concerning them Jeremiah says: “How the gold has grown dim; how the finest color has been changed” (Lam. 4:1). He mourned that the gold had grown dim because in certain people he saw the brightness of innocence turned into the blackness of guilt.

Gold is therefore said to come from the North because, through the regard of the Redeemer’s grace, the precious life of the faithful is multiplied within holy Church from the Gentile world, once cold with the torpor of unbelief. Gold comes from the North when true faith in the Lord shines forth from the very worshipers of idols.

But when the Gentiles are converted to the faith, Judaea objects and disdains to receive into the heavenly recompense of rewards those who had formerly been worshipers of idols. Hence after the conversion of the Gentiles Peter is asked: “Why did you enter men who had foreskins, and eat with them?” (Acts 11:3).

In opposition to this the Lord rightly says through Isaiah: “I will say to the North: Give; and to the South: Do not forbid” (Isa. 43:6). For just as the North signifies the Gentile world, so the South signifies Judaea, which grew warm like the midday sun because, when the Redeemer appeared in the flesh, it first received the warmth of faith.

“Give to the North” is said when the Gentile world is commanded to offer God the gifts of its faith. The South is commanded not to forbid because the Hebrews established in the faith are instructed not to reject or condemn the life of the Gentiles.

[Note: Vindoc.: “lest by rejecting the life of the Gentiles they despise it.”]

Hence here also, because it was said, “From the North gold will come,” it is appropriately added:

THE SAME. — And from God comes fearful praise.

72. Concerning the conversion of the Gentiles, the apostles and other believers from the circumcision praised God. — “Fearful praise” is said to come from God, as though it were said to come from those who belong to God—that is, from the faithful.

[Note: Vindoc. lacks “to come.”]

[Note: Pratel., Utic. and Vindoc. omit “to come.”]

When gold therefore came from the North, fearful praise came forth from God, because, when the Gentile world offered the brightness of its faith, the multitude of faithful Hebrews praised God while fearing his judgments.

But how gold comes from the North, and how fearful praise bursts forth from those who are under God, the very history of sacred eloquence shows us. For it is written:

“Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called the Italian, devout and fearing God with all his household, giving many alms to the people and always praying to God, saw clearly in a vision, about the ninth hour of the day, an angel of God entering to him and saying: Cornelius. But he, looking at him, seized with fear, said: Who are you, Lord? And he said to him: Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial in the sight of God” (Acts 10:1–4).

[Note: Vindoc.: “looking at him.”]

Gold therefore comes from the North when, from the Gentiles, prayer ascends before God together with alms.

When Peter had reported this to the brothers—how Cornelius had seen the angel, and how he himself had seen a sheet sent down to him from heaven containing beasts, reptiles, and birds, and how the Holy Spirit had also flooded the hearts of the Gentiles before baptism, although he had never come into the minds of Jews except after the water of baptism—it is immediately written:

“When they had heard these things, they were silent and glorified God, saying: Then God has also granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles” (Acts 11:18).

The multitude of the faithful therefore offered fearful praise to God; when the Gentiles had been saved, they restrained their own murmuring in wonder at the gifts of heavenly grace.

[Note: Gussanvil.: “fearful praise of God.” The error is evident not only from the manuscripts and from other copies, but also from the unmistakable sequence of the discourse.]

Hence Peter himself also marvels, saying: “In truth I have found that God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34).

73. And they feared concerning the rejection of the Jews. — But when the Gentiles receive the faith, why is fearful praise said to come from those who are already faithful, when it ought rather to have come joyfully than fearfully?

For this reason fearful praise arose from the Hebrews who were already faithful when the Gentiles were converted: Judaea was justly rejected while the Gentile world was mercifully called, and Judaea feared the losses of its rejection when it saw the gains of another’s calling.

Thus we too each day, when we suddenly see certain wicked people raised to an unexpected height of life, rejoice with fear under God’s hidden judgments, lest through hidden judgments God abandon some whom he is thought to regard as worthy, while through these same judgments he calls to himself those thought unworthy.

It follows:

CHAPTER XLV.

VERSE 23. — We cannot find him worthily.

74. We cannot think worthily of God, who is great in strength, judgment, and justice. — Even if we can now find him, we cannot find him worthily, because whatever we think about him is from faith, not from sight.

[Note: Vindoc.: “now God.”]

[Note: Pratel. and Vindoc.: “not yet from sight.”]

Yet he adds what he now considers himself to have found, saying:

THE SAME. — Great in strength, judgment, and justice, and he cannot be described.

He is great in strength because he overcomes the strong adversary and, taking the vessels of dishonor from his house, transforms them into vessels of mercy. He is great in judgment because, although here he humbles his elect through adversities, he will one day raise them up in the glory of eternal prosperity. He is great in justice because, although he tolerates the reprobate for a long time, he nevertheless condemns them without end when the time comes.

It is rightly added: “And he cannot be described.” For if he cannot be worthily apprehended, how much less can he be spoken of? Yet we speak of him better, in some fashion, if in awe at his consideration we remain silent in wonder.

It follows:

CHAPTER XLVI [Rec. XXVII].

VERSE 24. — Therefore men will fear him, and all who seem wise in their own eyes will not dare to contemplate him.

75. Those who preach rightly but do not live rightly become heralds of their own condemnation.—Here Elihu calls “men” those who are strong in understanding. It should be noted that he does not say, “And the wise will not dare to contemplate him,” but rather, “All who seem wise in their own eyes.” By these words he indicates people who are indeed learned, but arrogant. Thus, while Elihu expresses many things forcefully, at the end of his speech he has touched upon himself. For arrogant and learned men, when they do not live rightly but are nevertheless compelled by the impulses of their teaching to speak rightly, become in some way heralds of their own condemnation: while proclaiming what they refuse to do, they loudly declare by their own voices that they are condemned. Of such men the Psalmist rightly says: “They have turned themselves into a crooked bow” (Ps. LXXVII, 57). A crooked bow strikes the very person who bends it. In their words, the tongues of the arrogant resemble a crooked bow, because while they speak against pride, they plant arrows in their own authors. Therefore we must take the greatest care lest received wisdom, while it illuminates the darkness of ignorance, remove the light of humility, so that it can no longer be wisdom. For although it may shine through the power of speech, it obscures the speaker’s heart beneath a veil of pride.

[Col. 0442C]  
[Note: [Col. 0442D] Turin, “condemning themselves by their own voices.”]

76. Some goods are supreme, others intermediate.—Some things are supreme goods, and others intermediate goods. The supreme goods are faith, hope, and charity. When these are possessed truly, they cannot be turned toward evil. The intermediate goods are prophecy, teaching, the power of healing, and the other gifts (1 Cor. XII, 10). They are placed between the two alternatives in such a way that through them alone one may sometimes seek the heavenly homeland, and at other times earthly glory. We therefore call these virtues “intermediate,” because we incline them toward whatever the mind desires. Once received, the mind can use them just as it can earthly riches. Through earthly riches some grow proud in displaying their glory, while others perform works of mercy for the needs of their neighbors. When external praise is sought through teaching and prophecy, the summit of earthly glory is pursued as through bodily riches. But when teaching and prophecy are devoted to winning souls, the riches received are distributed to needy brothers.

[Col. 0442D]  
[Note: [Col. 0443D] Turin, “through the very teaching by which.”]

Because the unwary mind often distances itself from the hand of the giver through the very gifts whose reception makes it rejoice, we must take vigilant care that vices are first subdued and that afterward the gifts are held with circumspection. For if the mind carelessly abandons itself in these things, it is not lifted up with their help; rather, as though rewarded for its past labors, it is rejected. Hence it also happens that a received virtue, when employed in the service of passing praise, is not a virtue, because it serves vice. Since humility is the origin of virtue, that virtue truly grows in us which endures in its proper root, namely, humility. When it is cut off from that root, it withers, because it loses the charity-giving moisture that gives it life in the depths.

[Col. 0443A–B]  
[Col. 0443]

77. David’s remarkable humility amid supreme achievements: by fighting he conquered his enemies; by pursuing humility he conquered himself.—Since Elihu’s words, “All who seem wise in their own eyes will not dare to contemplate him,” condemn hidden pride of heart, it is worthwhile to consider how many gifts of virtue David had received, and with what strong humility he preserved himself amid them all (1 Sam. XVII, 36; XVIII, 25). What would not have exalted the man who had broken the jaws of lions, torn apart the arms of bears, been chosen over his elder brothers, been anointed to govern the kingdom after the rejected king, felled the fearsome Goliath with one stone, brought back from the slain Philistines the numerous foreskins demanded by the king, finally received the promised kingdom, and possessed the entire Israelite people without any opposition (2 Sam. III, 18)?

And yet, when he brought the ark of God back to Jerusalem (ibid., VI, 14), as though forgetting that he had been placed above all others, he danced before the ark amid the people. And because dancing before the ark was, as is believed, the custom of the common people, the king whirled about in the service of God by dancing. Behold the man whom the Lord had uniquely preferred to all others: under the Lord, he despises himself by making himself equal to the least and by presenting himself as lowly. He does not recall the power of the kingdom; he does not fear becoming contemptible in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; he does not recognize himself as superior in honor to others before the ark of the one who had granted him that honor. Before God he performed lowly and even contemptible acts, in order by humility to make firm what he had done bravely before human beings.

[Col. 0443C–D]  
[Note: [Col. 0443D] Vindoc. and Pratel.: “he performed weak deeds.” The old Paris edition also reads this way.]

I do not know what others think of his actions; I am more astonished by David dancing than by David fighting. By fighting he subdued enemies, but by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself. When Michal, the daughter of Saul, still insane with the pride of royal lineage, looked down upon him in his humiliation and said, “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and being naked as one of the buffoons is naked” (ibid., 20), she immediately heard him reply: “As the Lord lives, I will play before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.” A little later he said: “I will play, and I will make myself even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (ibid., 22). It is as though he openly said: “I desire to become contemptible before human beings, because through humility I seek to preserve my nobility before the Lord.”

[Col. 0444A]  
[Note: [Col. 0443D] Vindoc., Pratel., Utic.: “to preserve my character before God.” The old Paris and Basel editions: “to preserve my dignity before God.” The Longipont manuscript: “because I seek that the kingdom be preserved for me before the Lord.”]

78. Some fear being despised even while thinking humbly of themselves; others grow proud of their humility by desiring to be despised.—There are some who think humbly of themselves because, placed in positions of honor, they consider themselves nothing but dust and ashes; yet they refuse to appear despised before human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0444D] Vindoc., Pratel. and others: “to appear contemptible.”]

Against what they inwardly think of themselves, they cover themselves outwardly with a kind of rigid beauty. There are also some who desire to appear contemptible to human beings and, by presenting themselves as degraded, despise everything they are; yet inwardly, within themselves, they swell with pride as though because of the very merit of their displayed lowliness. They are all the more elevated in heart the more they suppress outwardly the appearance of elevation.

David detected both these struggles of one and the same pride with great vigilance and overcame them with remarkable virtue. Because he indicates that, thinking humbly of himself inwardly, he does not seek honor outwardly, he says: “I will play, and I will make myself more contemptible” (ibid., 22). And because, by presenting himself as contemptible outwardly, he does not swell inwardly, he adds: “And I will be humble in my own eyes” (ibid., 22). It is as though he said: “I regard myself inwardly as the sort of person whom I display outwardly when I make myself contemptible.”

What, then, should those do whom learning elevates, if David knew that the Redeemer would come from his own flesh and announced his joys prophetically, yet nevertheless crushed the neck of his heart beneath the powerful heel of discernment, saying: “I will be humble in my own eyes”?

[Col. 0444B–C]  
[Col. 0444]

890 79. Those who seem wise in their own eyes cannot contemplate the wisdom of God. Laudable folly must be pursued.—Elihu therefore rightly says: “For this reason men will fear him, and all who seem wise in their own eyes will not dare to contemplate him.” Those who seem wise in their own eyes cannot contemplate the wisdom of God, because they are as far from its light as they are lacking in humility before themselves. For while the swelling of pride grows in their minds, it closes the eye of contemplation; and by the very thing through which they judge themselves to shine above others, they deprive themselves of the light of truth.

If, then, we truly desire to be wise and to contemplate wisdom itself, let us humbly acknowledge ourselves to be fools. Let us abandon harmful wisdom and learn laudable folly. Hence it is written: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. I, 27). Again it is said: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may be wise” (ibid., III, 18).

The words of the Gospel narrative likewise testify that Zacchaeus, when he could not see because of the crowd, climbed a sycamore tree in order to see the Lord as he passed by. [Col. 0445A] For sycamore is called “foolish fig.” Thus little Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore and saw the Lord (Luke XIX, 4 ff.), because those who humbly choose the folly of the world themselves contemplate the wisdom of God with subtle understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0444D] Pratel., Utic., Vindoc.: “the sycamore tree.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0445A] Vindoc.: “faint-heartedness.”]

The crowd hinders our smallness from seeing the Lord, because the tumult of worldly concerns weighs down the weakness of the human mind so that it does not direct its attention toward the light of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0445A] Vindoc., Pratel. and others: “so that it does not attend to the light of truth.”]

But we wisely climb the sycamore if we carefully retain in our minds the folly prescribed by God.

[Note: [Col. 0445B] In the same manuscripts: “we hold folly in mind,” omitting τὸ *mente* (“in the mind”).]

For what is more foolish in this world than not seeking what has been lost, releasing possessions to those who seize them, returning no injury for injuries received, and even offering patience in addition to these things? It is as though the Lord commands us to climb the sycamore when he says: “From the one who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke VI, 30). And again: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V, 39).

The Lord is seen passing by the sycamore, because through this wise folly the wisdom of God, although not yet seen firmly as it is, is nevertheless already perceived as though in passing through the light of contemplation. According to Elihu’s words, those who seem wise in their own eyes cannot see it, because, caught up in the proud crowd of their thoughts as they seek to behold the Lord, they have not yet found the sycamore tree.

[Col. 0446A]

The sixth and final part, comprising eight books

The twenty-eighth book. [Note: [Col. 0445D] In the first Laon manuscript this book is entitled XXIII.]

The first eleven verses of chapter XXXVIII are explained in their various senses, especially the moral sense.

[Col. 0445]

891 PREFACE

[Col. 0445B–C]

Nothing harms the soul more grievously than virtue conscious of itself, unless it is exercised by corrections. Job is greatest because he is inferior to God alone.—After the loss of his possessions, the deaths of his children, the wounds of his body, the words of his ill-advising wife, the insulting words of his comforters, and the many darts of suffering that he bravely endured, blessed Job had been worthy of praise by the judgment of the Judge because of his great virtue of steadfastness—if he had already been summoned from the present age.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] Vindoc.: “for such great steadfastness of virtue.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0445D] Corb., Germ. and Pratel.: “but if he had already been…”]

But after he is to receive double blessings here, after he is restored to his former health so that he may enjoy his restored possessions for a longer time, lest his very victory strike him down with the sword of pride, almighty God must rebuke him with strict justice—the man whom he preserves for life. For what more often kills the soul than virtue conscious of itself? While inflating the soul through self-contemplation, it empties it of the fullness of truth; and while suggesting that it is sufficient to receive rewards, it diverts it from the purpose of improvement.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] Turin: “from the better intention.”]

Job was righteous before the blows, but remained more righteous after the blows; praised earlier by God’s own voice, he afterward grew through chastisement. Clearly, like a drawn trumpet enlarged by being struck, he was raised all the higher in praise of God the more severely he was struck by correction.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] “Higher” is absent in Utic. and Pratel.]

Yet this man, who stood so firmly in virtues while prostrate beneath ulcers, had to be humbled. He had to be humbled lest the arrows of pride pierce so stout a breast, a breast that had certainly shown that the wounds inflicted upon it could not overcome it.

[Col. 0446B–C]

A human being had to be sought whose comparison could overcome him. But how could he be defeated by comparison with anyone when God himself testifies of him: “Have you seen my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth” (Job I, 8; II, 3)? By comparison with whom, then, could he be conquered, when God testifies that he could be equaled by comparison with no human being?

What, then, was to be done except that the Lord himself should recount to him, speaking in his own person, the virtues of the Lord, and say: “Do you bring forth the morning star in its time, and cause the evening star to rise over the children of earth?” And again: “Are the gates of death opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?” Or certainly: “Have you, after your birth, commanded the dawn, and shown the morning its place?” (Job XXXVIII, 32, 17, 12).

[Col. 0446D]

Who but the Lord can do these things? Yet a human being is questioned so that he may recognize that he cannot do them; thus the man who had grown through such immense virtues, and who could be conquered by no human example, is overcome by comparison with God, lest he be lifted up.

But how powerfully is he raised who is humbled so sublimely! What a great victory for a human being—to have lost by comparison with God! How much greater than other human beings is the one who is proved by testimonies to be less than God! He is very powerful who is shown by such a question not to be powerful.

But since we are being led into the discussion of matters excessively obscure, let us now come to the words of the same text.

[Col. 0447A]

CHAPTER ONE [Old and Rec. II]

Chapter XXXVIII, verse 1.—“But the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said.”

1. In how many ways and by what means God speaks to human beings.—I observe that if it were said that speech had been addressed to a healthy and unharmed man, it would by no means have been written that the Lord spoke from the whirlwind. But because he speaks to a man who has been scourged, he is described as having spoken from the whirlwind.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] The manuscripts written by scribes do not have a single reading here. The English manuscripts read: “For if he had spoken to him while he was sound and unharmed, the Lord’s speech would have been said to have come from tranquility, and it would by no means have been written that the Lord spoke from the whirlwind. But because he spoke to one who had been scourged…” In Longipont, Corb. Germ., and most manuscripts one reads: “if … he had spoken, the Lord’s speech would have been said to have come from tranquility,” as also in the printed editions. We have followed the simpler reading found in the manuscripts of Vindoc., Ebroic., Pratel., Utic., and other Norman witnesses, and have rejected the rest as additions.]

The Lord speaks to his servants in one way when he advances them inwardly through compunction, and in another when, through strictness, he presses them down lest they become proud. Through gentle speech the sweetness of the Lord, which ought to be loved, is revealed; through terrible speech his power, which ought to be feared, is displayed.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] Pratel.: “is expressed.”]

In the former, the soul is persuaded to make progress; in the latter, the soul that is making progress is restrained. Through the former it learns what it should desire; through the latter, what it should fear. Through the former he says: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst” (Zech. II, 10).

[Note: [Col. 0447D] Vindoc., Laon, Pratel., Corb. Germ., etc.: “Rejoice and be glad,” as it is read in the Vulgate.]

Through the latter it is said: “The Lord will come in the storm, and in the whirlwind are his ways” (Isa. LXVI, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0447D] “Will come” is omitted in Laon, Corb. Germ., Pratel., and Utic.]

He is gentle when he comes to dwell in our midst. But when he reveals himself through storm and whirlwind, he certainly disturbs the hearts he touches; and he rises up to tame pride when he makes himself known as powerful and terrible.

2. God speaks either through angels or through himself.—It should also be understood that divine speech is distinguished in two ways.

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Another reading: “because divine speech is distinguished in two ways.”]

Either the Lord speaks through himself, or his words are formed for us through an angelic creature. But when he speaks through himself, he is disclosed to us solely by the power of inward inspiration. When he speaks through himself, the heart is taught about his word without words and syllables, because his power is recognized through a certain inner uplifting.

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Vindoc., Laon, Pratel. and Corb. Germ.: “in the innermost [place].”]

The mind, when full, is lifted up toward it; when empty, it is weighed down. For it is a kind of weight that lifts every soul it fills.

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Laon and Longip.: “which it pleases,” for “which it lifts.” In the Basel edition of 1514, “which it washes.”]

It is incorporeal light that both fills the inner regions and, once they are filled, encompasses them outwardly. It is speech without noise, which opens the hearing yet does not know sound.

For concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each of them” (Acts II, 2). The Lord appeared through fire, but through himself he produced speech inwardly. The fire was not God, nor was that sound; rather, through what he displayed outwardly, he expressed what he accomplished inwardly.

Because he made the disciples inwardly both burning with zeal and instructed by the word, he showed fiery tongues outwardly. The elements were therefore employed as signs, so that bodies might perceive fire and sound, while hearts were instructed by invisible fire and a voice without sound. Thus the fire that appeared was outward, but the fire that gave knowledge was inward.

And when the eunuch of Queen Candace, seated in charge of the chariot and traveling along the road, had Isaiah in his hands without understanding him, the Spirit had said in Philip’s heart: “Draw near to the chariot” (Acts VIII, 29).

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Vindoc.: “the book of Isaiah.”]

And when Cornelius sent God-fearing soldiers to summon Peter, Peter undoubtedly heard inwardly from the Spirit: “Behold, three men seek you; rise, go down, and go with them” (Acts X, 19).

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Corb. Germ., Pratel., Ebroic. and others: “for it was the Spirit of God.”]

For the Spirit of God speaks to us, as it were, through words when by a hidden power he makes known what must be done, and suddenly makes a human heart ignorant of hidden things knowledgeable, without the noise and delay of speech.

Hearing does not grasp all that is spoken to it at once, since it perceives causes through words and words piecemeal through syllables. But our sight, when directed toward something, apprehends the whole of it suddenly and simultaneously. Thus God’s speech, made inwardly to us, seems to be seen rather than heard, because, while he inserts himself without the delay of speech, he illuminates the darkness of our ignorance with sudden light.

Hence Baruch, son of Neriah, when asked to explain how he had heard the words of the prophesying Jeremiah, said: “He spoke from his mouth as though reading, and I wrote” (Jer. XXXVI, 18). One who speaks while reading directs his attention to one thing but utters a word about another, because he says what he sees. Thus God’s prophets, because they see his words in their hearts rather than hear them, speak as though reading.

3. How God ordinarily speaks through angels: sometimes by words, sometimes by things, sometimes by words and things together, and sometimes by images shown to the eyes of the heart or body.—When the Lord makes his will known through an angel, he sometimes demonstrates it by words, sometimes by things, sometimes by words and things together, sometimes by images shown to the eyes of the heart, sometimes by images temporarily assumed from air and placed before the bodily eyes, sometimes through heavenly substances, sometimes through earthly substances, and sometimes through earthly and heavenly substances together. At times God also speaks through an angel to human hearts in such a way that the angel himself is presented to the mind’s vision.

4. God speaks through an angel by words when nothing is shown in an image, but words of heavenly speech are heard, as when the Lord says: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you,” and the answer immediately follows: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John XVII, 1).

God, who without time cries out by the power of inward impulse, did not utter through his substance, within time, that voice which he divided by human words and confined within time. Rather, speaking from heavenly things, he formed the words he wished human beings to hear through the ministry of a rational creature.

5. Sometimes God speaks through angels by things, when nothing is said by word, but future events are announced through an image taken from the elements. Thus Ezekiel, hearing no words, saw the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire, so that by looking at the appearance alone he might understand what would come in the last days (Ezek. I, 4).

Electrum is made by mixing the metals of gold and silver. In this mixture the silver is made brighter, yet the brilliance of the gold is moderated. What, then, is represented by electrum if not the mediator between God and human beings? By composing himself for us from a divine and human nature, he made the human nature brighter through divinity and moderated the divine nature for our sight through humanity.

Because his humanity shone with so many miracles through the power of his divinity, silver grew from gold. And because God could be known through the flesh, and through the flesh endured so many adversities, the gold was, as it were, tempered by silver.
