This is rightly also shown in the midst of fire, because the mystery of his incarnation is accompanied by the flame of the judgment that follows. For it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22).

[Col. 0449C]

[Old III.] 6. Sometimes God speaks through angels by words and things together, when by certain movements he conveys what he narrates in words.—Adam could not, after his sin, hear the Lord in the substance of his divinity; rather, he heard through an angel the words of rebuke. It is written: “When he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the breeze after midday, he hid himself among the trees of the garden” (Gen. III, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0449D] The printed editions, with Corb. Germ., read: “For Adam could not … see the Lord.” The English, Norman, and Vindoc. manuscripts read better: “hear the Lord,” as the preceding and following context clearly demonstrate.]

What does it mean that after the human being sinned the Lord no longer stands in paradise but walks, except that, when guilt intervened, he showed that he had been moved away from the human heart?

[Note: [Col. 0449D] The same manuscript: “from the heart of the human being.”]

And what does “at the breeze after midday” mean except that the more fervent light of truth had departed, and the coldness of guilt was constricting the sinful soul?

Thus he rebuked Adam while walking, so that he might disclose his wickedness to blind minds not only by words but also by things. In this way the sinful human being heard through the words what he had done; through the walking, he perceived the instability of his mutability after losing the state of eternity; through the breeze, he recognized his torpor after the fervor of charity had been driven out; and through the sun’s decline, he understood that he was drawing near to darkness.

[Col. 0450A]

[Old IV.] 7. Sometimes God speaks through angels by images shown to the eyes of the heart, as Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder resting on the heavens (Gen. XXVIII, 12); as Peter, seized in ecstasy, saw a sheet full of reptiles and four-footed animals (Acts X, 11)—for unless he had seen these things with incorporeal eyes, he would not have been in ecstasy; and as a Macedonian man appeared to Paul in a night vision (Acts XVI, 9), asking him to cross over into Macedonia.

Sometimes God speaks through angels by images temporarily assumed from air and placed before the bodily eyes, as Abraham was able not only to see three men but also to receive them into his earthly dwelling and, not merely to receive them, but to provide food for their use (Gen. XVIII, 2 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Pratel.: “to us on earth.”]

For unless angels, announcing certain inward things to us, temporarily assumed bodies from air, they would certainly not appear to our outward eyes; nor would they eat food with Abraham unless, for our sake, they carried something solid from the heavenly element.

It is not surprising that there those who were received are called at one moment angels and at another the Lord, because those who ministered outwardly are expressed by the term “angels,” while by the title “Lord” the one who inwardly presided over them is revealed. Thus through one name the authority of the one presiding is made clear, and through the other the service of those ministering.

[Col. 0450C]

[Old V.] 8. Other various ways in which God speaks to human beings.—Sometimes God speaks through angels by heavenly substances, as, when the Lord was baptized, it is written that a voice sounded from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

[Note: [Col. 0449D] In the Laon manuscript, “through angels” is absent.]  
[Note: [Col. 0450D] The same manuscript: “with whom I am well pleased.” In Corb. Germ. “well” is omitted.]

Sometimes God speaks through angels by earthly substances, as when, in rebuking Balaam, he formed human words in the mouth of a she-ass (Num. XXII, 28).

[Note: [Col. 0450D] In the same Laon manuscript, “through angels” is omitted.]

Sometimes God speaks through angels through earthly and heavenly substances together, as to Moses on the mountain, when, uttering the words of his command, he joined fire and a bush, combining one above with the other below (Exod. III, 2).

This, however, is done only when something is signified by the conjunction itself. For when he spoke to Moses through the burning bush, what else did he show except that Moses would become the leader of that people which would receive the fire of the law and nevertheless would by no means avoid the thorn of sin? Or that from that people would come one who, in the fire of divinity, would receive the sins of our flesh like thorns of a bush, while preserving the substance of our humanity unconsumed even in the flame of divinity?

[Note: [Col. 0450D] Corb. Germ., Pratel. and Utic.: “leader.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0450D] The old Paris and Basel editions and other more recent editions: “the sufferings of our flesh.” The Turon, Norman, Laon, Vindoc., Corb. and Germ. manuscripts read “sins,” not “sufferings.”]

[Col. 0451A]

[Old VI.] 9. At times prophets are inspired through angels.—Sometimes, through angels, God also infuses into human hearts the power of his inspiration by their hidden presence. Hence Zechariah says: “And the angel who was speaking in me said to me” (Zech. I, 14). By saying that the angel spoke to him but in him, he clearly shows that the one who spoke words to him was not outside him in bodily form. Hence a little later he adds: “And behold, the angel who was speaking in me was going out” (ibid., II, 3).

For often angels do not appear outwardly; but, as angelic spirits are, they make God’s will known to the senses of the prophets and lift them to higher things.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Laon and Corb. Germ.: “and thus lift them to sublime things.”]

They show future events as already present in their original causes. The human heart, weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, supports this very corporeality as an obstacle and does not penetrate inward things.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Longip.: “his own corruption.”]

It lies heavily outward because it does not have an inner hand to lift it.

Thus, as has been said, the subtlety of angelic power appears to the senses of the prophets as it truly is, and their mind is lifted as it is touched by the subtle spirit. It no longer lies sluggish and torpid in lowly things; filled with inward breathings, it ascends to higher things, and from a certain summit of reality it sees what is to come below.

But lest anyone think that in the words of Zechariah the name “angel” designates the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, if he considers the text of sacred Scripture, he will quickly correct his opinion. Scripture never calls the Father or the Holy Spirit an angel, and calls the Son an angel only in the proclamation of his incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Vindoc. and Corb. Germ.: “on account of the proclamation of his incarnation.”]

Hence it is clearly shown in the same words of Zechariah that a true angel—that is, a creature—was speaking in him, when it says: “And behold, the angel who was speaking in me was going out” (Zech. II, 3). Immediately it adds: “And another angel went out to meet him and said to him: Speak to this boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls” (ibid., II, 3).

The God who is sent is therefore not the angel who is commanded by an angel what he must say. But because angelic ministries are ordered in the sight of the Creator by a distinct arrangement of ranks, so that they may rejoice together in seeing their Maker for the common blessedness of happiness, while nevertheless some serve others according to the arrangement of dignity, an angel sends an angel to the prophet. The one whom he sees rejoicing with him in God, and who shares with him in that joy, he both teaches and directs, because he surpasses him in the power of knowledge through superior understanding and in the height of authority through a more excellent grace.

[Col. 0451D]  
[Note: [Col. 0451D] Laon: “appointed and distinguished.”]

10. How God answered Job.—These things have been said to demonstrate the ways in which God speaks to human beings. But when it is said that the Lord answered blessed Job from the whirlwind, it is uncertain whether he spoke through himself or through an angel.

For movements of the air could have been produced through an angel, and the words that follow could have been delivered to Job through him. Again, an angel could have stirred the air outwardly into a whirlwind,

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts: “into a whirlwind.”]

while inwardly the Lord himself caused the power of his judgment to resound in Job’s heart without words. Thus it may be believed that the Lord himself then uttered the words that follow, after he had already heard them without words, filled with God.

[Old VII, Rec. III.] Therefore it is said:

CHAPTER TWO

Verse 2.—“Who is this who wraps up judgments in ignorant words?”

[Col. 0452B]

11. Those who think correctly but speak arrogantly are condemned. The first folly of the angel was pride.—As we have already said in the preceding section, the first reproach is contained in the question: “Who is this?” For Elihu had spoken arrogantly. We ask, “Who is this?” only concerning someone whom we do not know. To know is to approve in God’s judgment; not to know is to reject. Hence he says to certain people whom he rejects: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII, 25, 27).

What, then, does it mean to inquire about this arrogant man, “Who is this?” except openly to say: “I do not know the arrogant”—that is, “I do not approve their lives in the citadel of my wisdom”? For while they are inflated by human praise, they are emptied of the true glory of eternal recompense.

In saying “judgments,” and not adding what kind, we understand him to mean good judgments. Yet he asserts that they are wrapped up in ignorant words, because they had been spoken with words of boasting. The fault of ignorance is not to understand what is right rightly: that is, to incline a heavenly gift toward the pursuit of earthly praise.

For just as it often happens that good things are expressed badly and bad things well, so arrogant Elihu expressed what was right wrongly, because he spoke humble judgments in defense of God without humility. Hence he not improperly represents those within the Catholic Church who strive after empty glory: while they believe themselves more learned than others, they are accused by divine judgment of ignorance. For, as the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. VIII, 2).

Because the first folly of the angel was pride of heart, true wisdom consists in a human being’s humility concerning himself. Whoever abandons this humility by thinking highly of himself becomes all the more foolish precisely because he does not know himself.

Thus Elihu uttered judgments and wrapped them in ignorant words: he knew what was right to say about God, yet the foolish pride of what he said about himself made him foolish.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Pratel., Utic., Vindoc. and Corb. Germ.: “made foolish.” Laon: “made foolishly dull.”]

Having rejected this, the speech turns to instruct Job:

CHAPTER THREE [Rec. IV]

[Col. 0453A]

Verse 3.—“Gird your loins like a man.”

## 12. Lust must be restrained not only of the flesh, but also of the proud heart

Sacred Scripture customarily calls “men” those who follow the ways of the Lord with strong and not slackened steps. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXX, 25). Hence Paul says: “Raise up the relaxed hands and the feeble knees” (Heb. XII, 12). Hence Wisdom also says in Proverbs: “O men, to you I cry” (Prov. VIII, 4). As though it plainly said: “I speak not to women, but to men, because those whose minds are lax can in no way receive my words.”

To gird one’s loins, moreover, is to restrain lust either in one’s conduct [Note: Gilot and some editions: “or in thought, to restrain the desire for praise.” Gussanville omitted this reading, although he took care to record it.] or in one’s thoughts. For the pleasure of the flesh is in the loins. Hence it is also said to holy preachers: “Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning” (Luke XII, 35). By the loins lust is signified, and by the lamps the brightness of good works. They are therefore commanded to gird their loins and to hold their lamps. As though they plainly heard: “First restrain lust within yourselves, and then display to others examples of good works from yourselves.”

But since we know that blessed Job was endowed with such great chastity, why is he told after so many scourges, “Gird your loins like a man”—that is, “as a strong man, restrain lust”—unless it is because one lust of the flesh corrupts chastity, while another lust of the heart causes us to glory in chastity? He is therefore told: “Gird your loins like a man,” so that he who had previously conquered the lust of corruption might now restrain the lust of elation, lest, growing proud of his patience or chastity, he should be inwardly more lustful before God’s eyes precisely to the degree that he appeared patient and chaste before human eyes.

Hence Moses rightly says: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts” (Deut. X, 16)—that is, “After you have extinguished lust from the flesh, cut away also the superfluity of your thoughts.” [Note: Pratel and other Norman witnesses: “cut away superfluous thought.” Corbie Germ. and Vindoc. likewise have this. But Laudun has: “cut away superfluity by thought.”]

The text continues:

## CHAPTER IV [Rec. V]

**There.**—“I will question you, and you shall answer me.”

## 13. God questions us in three ways: by scourging; by issuing difficult commands; and by concealing certain things from us

Our Creator customarily questions us in three ways: either when he strikes us with the severity of a scourge and shows how much patience is present—or lacking—in us; or when he commands certain things we do not want and reveals to us our obedience or disobedience; or when he discloses some things to us and conceals others, making known to us the measure of our humility.

He questions by a scourge when he strikes with afflictions a mind that has been peacefully subjected to him, just as Job is both praised by the testimony of the Judge and yet delivered over to the blows of the smiter (Job II, 3, 7), so that his patience might shine forth more truly in proportion as it had been more severely tested. [Note: Corbie Germ., Vindoc., Pratel, Utic, and the old editions more correctly read *et tamen ictibus conceditur* (“and yet is handed over to the blows”); the more recent Vulgate editions have *conciditur* (“is crushed”).]

He questions us by issuing difficult commands, as Abraham is ordered to leave his land and go where he did not know (Gen. XII, 1), to lead his only son to the mountain, and to sacrifice the son whom, as an old man, he had received for his consolation (Gen. XXII, 2). [Note: Laudun and Corbie Germ. read *senis* (“of an old man”) for *senex* (“an old man”).] To him, when he rightly answered the question—that is, when he obeyed the command—it is said: “Now I know that you fear God” (ibid., 12). Or, as it is written: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII, 3). For God’s testing is his questioning us with great commands; and his knowing is making us know our own obedience.

[Veteran reading VIII.] God also questions us by opening certain things to us and closing others, as it is said through the Psalmist: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. X, 6). With open eyelids we see; with closed eyelids we see nothing. [Note: The printed editions, together with Corbie Germ., read: “what, then, do we understand by the eyelids?” The *per* is absent from the Laudun and other older manuscripts, a reading more characteristic of Gregory’s phrasing.]

What, then, should we understand by the eyelids of God except his judgments? They are closed to human beings in one respect and opened in another, so that people who do not know themselves may become known to themselves. Thus, while they grasp some things by understanding but are entirely unable to know others, their hearts may secretly inquire into themselves, asking whether divine judgments, when closed, fail to rouse them, or, when opened, inflate them.

By this questioning Paul was tested. After receiving inward wisdom, after the barriers of paradise had been opened, after ascending to the third heaven, and after the mysteries of heavenly speech, he still says: “I do not consider that I have comprehended” (Phil. III, 13). And again: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV, 9). [Note: Vindoc. omits *Ego sum minimus apostolorum . . . vocari apostolus* (“I am the least of the apostles . . . to be called an apostle”).] And again: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 5).

Paul therefore answered rightly when questioned by God’s opened eyelids: he touched the secrets above, and yet stood sublimely in humility of heart. [Note: Ebroic., Pratel., Laudun., Corbie Germ., and others, as well as the Paris editions of 1488 and 1495, read *in humilitate cordis sublimiter stetit* (“he stood sublimely in humility of heart”); other printed editions read *humiliter stetit* (“he stood humbly”).] When, however, he examined the secret judgments of God concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and could not reach them, he was questioned as though by God’s closed eyelids. [Note: Another Ebroic manuscript: “but the secret was very great.”]

Yet he gave a thoroughly right answer: he knowingly bowed before God in that very ignorance of his, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. XI, 33).

Behold: questioned about hidden mysteries, as though by closed eyelids, he gave a pleasing and right answer. Knocking at the entrance to the secret, he could not be admitted within through knowledge, and so stood humbly before the doors through confession. [Note: Ebroic., Pratel., and other Norman witnesses read *humiliter stetit* (“stood humbly”).] What he could not comprehend within, he praised outside in fear.

Thus blessed Job is now examined after the questioning of blows by the questioning of speech, so that he may consider what is above. When he scarcely comprehends these things, he may return to himself and recognize how close he is to nothing in comparison with heavenly realities. Let him therefore hear: “I will question you, and you shall answer me.” As though it were said more plainly: “By my words I rouse you to consider sublime things; and while you perceive that you do not know what is above you, I make you better known to yourself. You truly answer me when you understand what you do not know.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER V [Rec. VI]

**Verses 4–6.**—“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who established its measurements, if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it? Upon what were its bases made firm?”

## 14. By the foundations of the Church the apostles should be understood; by the foundation, Christ alone

Behold, everything is woven together as a historical narrative concerning the origin of the world. Suddenly, however, there follows something that appears to have been said not about the creation of the world, but about the establishment of the Church. For it says:

“Or who released its cornerstone?”

Because this did not occur at the origin of the world, the earlier passage is also shown not to have been spoken about the origin of the world. For this reason obscure and discordant things are mingled with clear and evident ones, so that, through what differs from the literal sense, that which sounds literal may also be sought mystically. Just as we recognize some things that are closed through other things that are open, so through certain closed things we are compelled to knock with a deeper understanding at those things we had believed to be open.

Let him therefore say: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” [Veteran reading IX.] In Sacred Scripture, what else should we understand by “foundations” except preachers? When the Lord placed them first in the holy Church, the entire structure of the subsequent building rose upon them.

Hence, when the priest enters the tabernacle, he is commanded to carry twelve stones on his breast (Exod. XXVIII, 17). For our High Priest, offering himself as a sacrifice for us, displayed strong preachers at the very beginning; he carried twelve stones beneath his head, in the foremost part of his body. The holy apostles are therefore stones upon the breast as the first display of adornment, and foundations in the ground as the first solidity of the building.

Hence the prophet David, when he saw the holy Church placed and built upon the lofty minds of the apostles, said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1).

When Sacred Scripture speaks not of “foundations” but of “the foundation” in the singular, no one else but the Lord himself is designated. Through the power of his divinity the wavering hearts of our weakness are made firm. Of him Paul also says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11).

He is the foundation of foundations, because he is both the origin of those who begin and the steadfastness of those who are strong. Since, then, our foundations are those who bore the burdens of our iniquities, blessed Job is examined in the very first part of the Lord’s speech concerning the holy preachers, lest he be lifted up in pride by the power of his virtues. The more he saw them come as admirable, the more humbly he would judge himself in comparison with them.

This is described by the Lord as though already past because whatever will outwardly be future in works has already been accomplished inwardly in predestination. He is therefore told: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” As though it were plainly said: “Consider the virtue of the strong, and reflect that I was their author before the ages. When you behold as admirable those whom I created in time, weigh how greatly you ought to be subject to me, whom you recognize as the timeless author of those wonders.”

The text continues:

## CHAPTER VI

**Verses 4–5.**—“Tell me, if you have understanding: who established its measurements, if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it?”

## 15. By his will holy preachers were sent to certain regions of the world and rejected by others

Measuring lines are stretched across lands in their division, so that the equity of dimension may be maintained through the stretching of the lines. When the Lord came in the flesh to the Church, he measured the earth’s dimensions with lines, because he distinguished the boundaries of the Church by the subtlety of hidden judgment.

The hidden measurements or lines of this earth were being stretched when holy preachers, moved by the Spirit, were called to go to some parts of the world, while they were restrained from approaching others. For the apostle Paul, when he was neglecting to preach in Macedonia, saw in a vision a Macedonian man who said: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts XVI, 9).

On the other hand, as it is written: “The apostles attempted to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (ibid., 7). [Note: The printed editions, even the older ones, erroneously read “to go into Asia,” contrary to the Greek text and the Vulgate. The manuscripts of Tours, Corbie Germ., Vindoc., Laudun, Pratel, and others read “to go into Bithynia.” The error may have arisen from what follows: “and they are forbidden by Asia.” Here, however, “Asia” must be understood as Bithynia, which is part of Asia.]

When, therefore, holy preachers were both called to Macedonia and prevented from entering Asia, there the line of hidden measurements was drawn, and here it was drawn back. There it is stretched so that Macedonia may be gathered within the spaces of the holy Church; [Note: Pratel and other Norman witnesses read *hic attrahitur* (“here it is drawn inward”) for *hinc attrahitur* (“from here it is drawn inward”).] here it is drawn inward so that Asia may be left outside the boundaries of the faith. At that time there were in it those who were not to be gathered; when they had been lost according to their deserts, Asia has now, by God’s generosity, been received within the measurements of the Church.

## 16. The elect are within the measurements established by Christ; the reprobate are outside. The arrangement lies in God’s hand, not man’s

Within these measurements, then, are all the elect; outside them are all the reprobate, even if they appear to be within the boundary of the faith. Hence it is also written in the Apocalypse: “Cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it” (Rev. XI, 2). For what else does the court signify except the breadth of the present life? Those represented by the court are rightly outside the temple, and therefore are not to be measured, because “narrow is the gate that leads to life” (Matt. VII, 14), and the breadth of the life of the wicked is not admitted into the measurements and rules of the elect.

These spiritual lines were stretched by hidden judgment when someone said: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. VIII, 19), and the same teacher answered: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (ibid., 20).

These measurements and lines were stretched when someone said: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father” (Luke IX, 59), and the same teacher answered: “Let the dead bury their dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God” (ibid., 60).

Behold: one promises that he will follow, and is rejected; another asks to be released, and is held back. Why is this, unless the lines of heavenly judgments were stretched over the hidden spaces of the heart, so that incomprehensible measurements might restrain the one inwardly, while the other might justly remain outside?

But since no one is unaware that God stretches these lines of hidden judgments, why is Job told: “Tell me, if you have understanding, who established its measurements, if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it?” Is this asked so that what he knew, but might nevertheless have neglected, may be recalled to him, so that he may weigh more carefully the weight of God’s secrets—namely, that the disposition of a human being rests not on human strength but in the hand of the Creator? [Note: The printed editions read *dispensationem* (“administration” or “dispensation”), against the manuscripts’ *dispositionem* (“disposition”).] Thus, while he considers invisibly who effects these things, he may attribute nothing to his own power and no longer dare to claim anything for himself, fearing God’s hidden judgments. Rather, as he weighs the measurements and lines stretched incomprehensibly from above, let him remain all the more in humble fear, the more he sees that everything depends upon the power of the measurer.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER VII

**Verse 6.**—“Upon what were its bases made firm?”

## 17. The bases of the Church are the holy teachers and prophets

What else should we understand by the bases of this earth except the teachers of the holy Church? Upon bases columns are raised, and upon columns the weight of the entire structure. The holy teachers are therefore not improperly designated by the name “bases,” because, while they preach what is right and make their lives agree with their preaching, they support the whole weight of the Church through the firm gravity of their conduct. They endure harsh temptations from unbelievers, and by examples of their works they show to be easy whatever in God’s commandments is feared by the faithful as difficult.

Hence, when the tabernacle was being erected as a type of the Church, Moses was rightly told: “You shall make four columns, and you shall cover their bases with silver” (Exod. XXVI, 32). [Note: Laudun., Pratel., and other Norman witnesses read *et bases earum vestitas argento* (“and their bases covered with silver”).] For what else is understood by silver except the brightness of divine speech? As it is written: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, tried in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7).

The bases, therefore, covered with silver, support the four columns of the tabernacle, because the preachers of the Church, adorned with divine speech, bear in word and deed the sayings of the four evangelists, so as to provide an example to all. [Note: Corbie Germ., Vindoc., Pratel, and other Norman witnesses: “as in all things.”]

## 18. The prophets too may be signified by the bases

The prophets also may be signified by the bases. Since they were the first to speak openly about the Lord’s incarnation, we see them as certain bases rising from the foundation and supporting the burdens of the structure placed upon them.

Hence, when the Lord again commanded Moses that the boards of the tabernacle be raised, he ordered that their bases be cast in silver (Exod. XXVI, 32). For what else are the boards than the apostles, extended throughout the world by their preaching; and what else are the silver bases than the prophets? They firmly and solidly support the boards placed upon them, because the life of the apostles is instructed by the prophets’ preaching and made firm by their authority.

Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board, because, when the holy prophets agree in their words concerning the incarnation of the Mediator, the preachers who follow build the Church without doubt; and when the prophets do not differ from one another, they fix those preachers more firmly in themselves.

Nor is it without reason that the bases signifying the prophets are commanded to be cast from silver. The brightness of silver is preserved through use; without use it turns black. Before the Mediator’s coming, the words of the prophets, because they were not yet in use for spiritual understanding and could not be perceived on account of their obscurity, remained as though black. But after the Mediator came and polished them before our eyes with the hand of his incarnation, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth, and he gave the meaning of the earlier fathers for use, because he explained their words through events.

Whether, then, he signifies prophets or teachers who follow in the final times by the designation of “bases,” let him say: “Upon what were its bases made firm?” The implied answer is: “Upon what but me, who wondrously sustain all things and provide inwardly the principal origin of external goods?”

For whoever attributes to himself what is good is not a solid base. Since he does not rest upon the foundation, he is cast down to the depths by his own weight. [Note: Thus Laudun, Vindoc., and Tours, followed by the old editions. Corbie Germ., Pratel, other Norman witnesses, and many others read: “but when there is so much.”]

But since much has now been said about the construction of the holy Church, the mind wishes to hear by what power hostile nations have been joined together—that is, by what art the diverse buildings of this house agree with one another.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER VIII

**There.**—“Or who released its cornerstone?”

## 19. Christ is the cornerstone, in whom Jews and Gentiles have come together

By divine grace it is now clear to all whom Sacred Scripture calls the “cornerstone”: surely the one who, receiving into himself on one side the Jewish people and on the other the Gentile people, joins two walls together in the single structure of the Church—the one of whom it is written: “He made both one” (Eph. II, 14).

He displayed himself as the cornerstone not only in the lower realms but also in the heavenly ones. On earth he joined the nations of the Gentiles to the people of Israel, and in heaven he joined both together with the angels. At his birth the angels cried out: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II, 14). At the birth of the King they would not have offered the joys of peace to human beings as something great if they had not possessed discord.

Of this stone the prophet says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. CXVII, 22).

King Jeconiah held the type of this stone. When Matthew described the generations in groups of fourteen, he counted him twice (Matt. I, 11). He inserted the same person at the end of the second generation and again at the beginning of the third. For he was carried into Babylon with the people of Israel; and since he was led from one place to another, he is appropriately counted twice as representing the side of each wall. By the turning of this migration he signifies the cornerstone. Where a line turns away from straightness so as to go in another direction, it makes something like a corner.

He could therefore rightly be counted twice, because through both walls he displayed in himself, as it were, two sides. Thus he fittingly bore the image of the one who, born in Judea and gathering the Gentiles, came as if from Jerusalem to Babylon, and by the art of charity wove into himself this structure of faith, formerly divided through devotion to discord. [Note: Tours and Laudun: “formerly devoted to discord.” Corbie Germ., “formerly split apart through hatred of discord.”]

What has been said about the meaning of the holy Church should now be explained morally in a brief recapitulation. It is fitting that through what we recognize as having been said to blessed Job, we should be recalled to our own hearts, because the mind understands God’s words more truly when it seeks itself within them. Behold, it is said:

## CHAPTER IX

**Verse 4.**—“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?”

### Moral sense

## 20. We must always consider what we have been, lest we attribute to ourselves what we are by God’s gift

If the soul of the sinner is dust, which is lifted up on the surface and carried away by the breeze of temptation—as it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. I, 5)—nothing prevents us from understanding the earth as the soul of the righteous, of which it is written: “For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it and producing vegetation useful to those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing” (Heb. VI, 7). [Veteran reading X.] [Note: Laudun, omitting much, reads: “But the foundation of this earth is laid.”]

The foundation of this earth, however, is faith. The foundation of this earth is laid when, in the hidden places of the heart, fear of God is first breathed in as the cause of firmness.

One person does not yet believe the eternal things he hears; when faith is given to him, the foundation of the subsequent building is already laid. Another already believes eternal things, yet does not fear; he despises the terror of the coming judgment and boldly involves himself in sins of flesh and spirit. When the fear of future things is suddenly poured into him, the foundations are already being built so that the structure of a good life may arise.

Once the foundation of salutary fear has been laid, and the structure of virtues is raised upward, it is necessary that each person carefully measure his strength, so that, when he has begun to become great through divine construction, he may look continually upon himself and, humbly attending to what he was found to be by merit, claim nothing for himself of what he has become by grace. [Note: Laudun: “and as he constructs what is divine.”] [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses: “may observe.”]

Hence blessed Job is now brought back to himself by the heavenly voice. Lest he dare to glory in his virtues, he is reminded of his former life, and told: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” As though Truth plainly said to the justified sinner: “Do not attribute to yourself the virtues you have received from me; do not become proud against me because of my gift.” [Note: Pratel: “do not exalt yourself against me . . .”] “Recall where I found you, when I laid in you the first foundations of virtue through my fear. Recall where I found you, when I made you firm through my fear.” [Note: These words are absent from Laudun up to: “recall where I found you, when I made you firm through my fear.” Vindoc. and Corbie Germ. read: “recall where I found you, when I first [laid foundations] in you,” omitting “through my fear.”]

“If I am not to destroy in you what I have built, do not cease to consider what I found. For where did Truth find a person except either in shameful acts or in excesses? Yet after this we can preserve what we are if we never neglect to weigh what we were.”

Sometimes, however, hidden elation is accustomed to creep even into watchful hearts, so that the thought of good things, although subtle and restrained, when it grows greatly in virtues, forgets its own weakness and does not recall what it was in vices. Hence almighty God, seeing that weakness increases even through remedies of salvation, imposes a measure upon our very progress. He gives us certain good virtues we never sought, and makes us seek certain others without allowing us to possess them. Thus, while our mind cannot possess what it desires, it understands that it does not possess by itself even what it does possess; through what is present, it considers what is absent; and through what is profitably absent, it humbly preserves the good that is present.

Hence, rightly, in the providence of this earth—that is, of the righteous soul—the following is added: [Note: Laudun: “through the providence of this earth . . .”]

## CHAPTER X

**Verses 4–5.**—“Tell me, if you have understanding, who established its measurements, if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it?”

## 21. How wisely God distributes his gifts—not all to everyone, but each to particular persons

For who but our Creator establishes the measurements of this earth? (I Cor. XII, 8). [Note: The same codex reads *creditor noster* (“our creditor” or “benefactor”) for *conditor noster* (“our Creator”).] Through the secret governance of inward judgment, he gives one the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another full faith, another the grace of healings, another the working of miracles, another prophecy, another the discernment of spirits, another kinds of tongues, and another the interpretation of languages.

Thus, in one and the same Spirit, one person excels in the word of wisdom but is not supported by the word of knowledge—that is, by teaching—because he is sufficient to perceive and discover even what he has not grasped through diligent study. Another shines in the word of knowledge but does not grow strong in the word of wisdom, because he is sufficient to fulfill what he has learned but does not rise by himself to perceive something subtle. [Note: The same codex reads *quantum dicit*, a reading the editor suspects to be corrupt.]

One commands the elements through faith but does not cure bodily illnesses through the grace of healings. Another removes diseases through the power of prayer but does not restore rain to parched earth by a word. One recalls the dead to the present life through the working of miracles, yet, lacking the grace of prophecy, does not know what is to come. Another regards future events as though they were present, yet does not manifest himself in any working of signs.

One sees minds subtly in their deeds through the discernment of spirits, but does not know languages of different kinds. Another examines languages of different kinds, but does not consider how hearts unlike one another may be dissimilar in similar matters. Another prudently examines the weight of speech by interpreting in the one language he knows, yet patiently lacks the other good things he does not possess.

## 22. Thus provision is made for humility and charity

Our Creator and disposer orders all things in such a way that the person who could be lifted up by the gift he possesses is humbled by the virtue he does not possess. He orders all things so that, while he raises each person up through the grace he expends, he also subjects one to another through unequal gifts; each person regards the one subject to him as better in another gift, and although he recognizes that he surpasses him in some respects, he nevertheless places himself below that same person in others.

He orders all things so that, while each individual gift belongs to all through a certain bond of charity, all things become the possession of each individual. Each person possesses in another what he has not received, and so humbly supplies to another for possession what he himself has received.

Hence Peter says: “As each has received grace, ministering it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (I Pet. IV, 10). The manifold grace of God is then well administered when the gift received is believed to belong also to the one who does not have it, when it is considered to have been given to oneself for the sake of the person to whom it is expended. [Note: Laudun and Corbie Germ.: “and to the one who does not have it.” The older editions likewise read this. We follow Pratel and most others.]

Hence Paul says: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. V, 13). Charity then frees us from the yoke of guilt when, through love, it subjects us mutually to one another’s service; when we believe the goods of others to be our own and offer our own to others as though they were theirs.

Again Paul says: “For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where would be the sense of smell?” (I Cor. XII, 14 ff.). And shortly afterward: “If they were all one member, where would be the body? But now there are indeed many members, yet one body” (ibid., 19).

## 23. In the body of the Church one is an eye, another a hand, another a foot, and so forth

For what is the holy Church except the body of its heavenly Head? In it, one is an eye by seeing lofty things; another a hand by doing what is right; another a foot by running to what has been commanded; another an ear by understanding the voice of the commandments; another a nose by discerning the stench of evil things and the fragrance of good things. [Note: Laudun: “the fragrance.”]

Like bodily members, while they mutually provide the services they have received, they make one body [Note: Laudun. reads *accessa officia* (“the services that have come to them”) for *accepta officia* (“the services they have received”).] out of themselves all together. Although they perform different actions in charity, they prevent difference from existing where they are contained. But if everyone performed one and the same thing, they would not be a body composed of many members, because it would not exist as something joined together in many ways if harmonious diversity of members did not hold it together.

Since, therefore, the Lord distributes gifts of virtues among the holy members of the Church, he establishes the measurements of the earth. Hence Paul says again: “According as God has divided to each the measure of faith” (Rom. XII, 3). And again: “From whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, produces the body’s growth for its building up in charity” (Eph. IV, 16).

## 24. Let individual members perform the duties assigned to them and not usurp those of others

But since our wondrous Author and disposer gives to one what he denies to another, and denies to another what he gives to this one, whoever tries to do more than he has received strives to go beyond the measurements established for him. Thus, if someone has been given only the task of explaining the hidden things of the commandments but attempts also to shine with miracles; or if someone whom the gift of heavenly power strengthens for miracles alone strives also to expound the hidden things of divine law—[Note: The same codex reads *in praecipiti* (“on a precipice”) for *in praecipitio* (“onto a precipice”).]—he extends his foot onto a precipice, because he does not attend to the limit of his measurements.

Often he loses even what he could do, because he rashly hastens to seize what he cannot attain. We likewise use the services of our bodily members properly only when we preserve their distinct functions. We see light with our eyes, but hear a voice with our ears. If someone, reversing the order, were to apply eyes to a voice and ears to light, both would be open to him in vain. If someone wished to distinguish odors with his mouth and taste flavors with his nose, he would destroy the service of both senses by perverting them. For when these things are not adapted to their proper uses, they abandon their own functions and do not rise to foreign ones.

## 25. David and Paul kept themselves within those measurements

The prophet David had rightly kept the foot of his heart within the measurements received from divine generosity when he said: “I have not walked in great matters, nor in wonders beyond me” (Ps. CXXX, 1). He would walk in wonders beyond himself if he sought to appear greater than he was capable of being. He is raised above himself in wonders who strives to appear capable even of things for which he is insufficient.

Paul likewise rightly confined himself within these measurements, even in the breadth of his preaching, when he said: “For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me” (Rom. XV, 18).

The received measure is preserved rightly when the life of spiritual men is set before the eyes and contemplated. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XI

**Verse 5.**—“Or who stretched the measuring line over it?”

26. From the saints the rule of life must be taken.—A line is stretched over this earth when the examples of preceding fathers are displayed to each elect soul [Note: [Col. 0463D] The same author, on the rule for living supremely.], so that from their life it may consider what it should preserve in its own actions. Thus, keeping in view the path of a just boundary, it will neither fail by neglecting the smallest matters, nor extend itself beyond the greatest through pride; it will neither attempt less than is sufficient, nor seize more than it has received. Otherwise it will either not reach the measure it ought to attain, or, abandoning that same measure, fall outside the limit.

For narrow is the gate that leads to life (Matt. 7:14); and the one who enters it is carefully constrained in everything he does by the subtlety of discernment. For whoever expands himself with a secure mind according to his own desires shuts himself off from access to the narrow gate. Therefore, in order that the measure of this earth may be preserved, a line is divinely stretched over it: so that our works may either advance when they are lesser or be moderated when they are greater, the subtle life of the saints is spread before us through the sacred Scriptures, and what and how much we ought to do is defined by the discernment displayed in them.

[Vet. XII.] 27. In Peter’s examples a measure of authority and humility is proposed.—Suppose that someone, fearing either the loss of possessions or bodily affliction, dreads the threats of earthly power and does not dare to defend the truth against those who resist it. Peter, because he sees such a person hemmed in by fear, stretches him toward the breadth of virtue by displaying the line of his own examples.

Peter himself, after being scourged by the rulers of the people (Acts 5:40), saw that he was being released for the very purpose of making him cease preaching. Although he was forbidden to speak thereafter, he did not yield even for the present. For he immediately replied: “We must obey God rather than men” (ibid. 4:29). And again: “For we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” The man who had earlier been weak and fearful of immediate losses, when he contemplates such examples of courage, now follows Peter’s line in the authority of his speech; now he fears no adversity; now, even amid bodily suffering, he despises the worldly powers that resist God.

[Note: [Col. 0463D] We restore this from the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Laud., Vindoc., Pratel., and others from Normandy, from which the printed editions have departed. For they read: “but nevertheless, by suffering, he destroys the strength of his persecutors to such an extent that … he yields to no terrors. Often another …”]

Yet the more courageously he destroys the strength of his persecutors through suffering, and the more steadfastly he yields to no terrors amid adversity, the more often, even in matters he experiences while placed among the faithful, he sets himself above the others, chooses his own counsels more readily, and trusts himself rather than others. While this man, not yielding to unjust objections [Note: [Col. 0463D] Pratel. and other Norman manuscripts read “to unjust obediences”], exerts himself in virtue, he also stretches his foot beyond the limit by refusing to accept the sound counsels of others.

Peter recalls him within the line of measure. After he had pressed down the authority of the rulers by the freedom of his speech, he listened in humility of heart to Paul’s counsel concerning the Gentiles who were not to be circumcised (Acts 15:7). Thus he knew how to raise himself against adversaries by authority, yet did not trust himself in matters where he did not think rightly; by the freedom of courage he surpassed the swelling powers, while by the gentleness of humility he offered obedience in a sound counsel even to lesser brothers, and at one time opposed others by himself, at another opposed himself together with others [Note: [Col. 0464D] Laud. reads “he observed”].

Thus, in Peter’s deeds a certain line of authority and humility is stretched before our eyes, lest our mind either fail to reach the measure through fear or exceed the limit through arrogance.

28. Discretion advises that works of the same virtue sometimes be performed and sometimes omitted.—It has been said how a line is stretched lest, through the strength of one action, we pass into the fault of another [Note: [Col. 0464D] The edition of Gilot and later editions read “fear”; the older editions, together with the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Turon., Laudun., Norman., and others, read “strength”]. Let us now say how, in one and the same virtue, we abandon the line of discretion if we do not know how both to practice it at times and to set it aside at times.

The same thing is not always virtue, because the merits of actions are often changed by the moments of time. Hence it happens that, when we do something well, we often do better by ceasing from that action, and that what the mind held laudably in its proper time is more laudably abandoned for a while. For if, on account of our small good works—by performing which we advance, though we do not perish when they are interrupted—greater evils of labor threaten our neighbors, we necessarily set aside the increase of virtues, lest we generate a loss of faith in our weaker neighbors, lest what we are doing cease to be virtue precisely because, through the occasion it provides, it destroys the foundations of virtue in the hearts of others.

29. An example of this discretion in Saint Paul.—Paul stretched this line of discretion well before the eyes of those who observe it. He prohibited Gentiles coming to the freedom of faith from being circumcised (Acts 15:2), and yet, when passing through Lystra and Iconium [Note: [Col. 0464D] Vindoc. reads “and coming to Iconium”; Laud. reads “and to Iconium”], he himself circumcised Timothy, who had been born of a Gentile father (Acts 16:3).

For he saw that, unless he showed himself to be observing the commandments of the Law, he would provoke the fury of the Jews even against those who were then his companions. He therefore set aside the force of his assertion and, without harm to the faith, protected himself and his companions from the violence of persecution [Note: [Col. 0465D] The word “companions” is absent from Laud., Corb. Germ., Pratel., and other Norman manuscripts]. He did what love of the faith had forbidden to be done, but turned toward the service of faith what he had done as though not faithfully [Note: [Col. 0465D] Laudun. reads “returned”].

Often virtue is lost when it is held indiscriminately; and when it is discreetly interrupted, it is held more firmly. Nor is it surprising if we understand this in incorporeal things, since we see it also occurring in bodily matters [Note: [Col. 0465D] Laud. adds “and in bodies”]. Through practice a bow is drawn tight, so that at the proper time it may be stretched with effect. If it does not receive the relaxation of rest [Note: [Col. 0465D] Pratel. reads “for if it has no rest”], it loses its power of striking through the very use of its tension. Thus, at times virtue in its exercise is preserved when it is set aside through discretion, so that it may strike vices more vigorously afterward, in proportion as it prudently refrains from striking for a time.

Therefore a line of subtle discretion is stretched over this earth when, after the examples of preceding fathers have been shown to each soul, virtue is both usefully kindled toward action and sometimes more usefully moderated [Note: [Col. 0465D] Later editions read “therefore, through subtle discretion”].

[Vet. XIII.] 30. We must beware lest, under the name of discretion, we serve our own interests.—But when the strength of zeal is set aside for a little while [Note: [Col. 0465D] Vindoc., Pratel., and others read “from the mouth of zeal”], careful consideration is necessary, lest one cease from exercising virtue not for the counsel of the common good, but through personal fear or the pursuit of some ambition. When this is done, one no longer serves prudent dispensation but guilt.

Therefore one must carefully see to it that, when someone moderates an undertaking he has assumed by suspending the exercise of virtue, he first examines himself at the root of his heart [Note: [Col. 0466D] Laud. reads “fixes himself”], lest through this he greedily seek something for himself, and through this, fearful, spare himself alone [Note: [Col. 0466D] Longip. reads: “lest he greedily seek for himself something by which he may, fearful for himself alone, spare himself”]. What follows in the action becomes crooked to the extent that it does not arise from a right intention of thought.

Hence Truth rightly says in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness” (Matt. 6:22). For what is expressed by the eye except the intention of the heart that precedes its work? Before it exercises itself in action, it already contemplates what it desires. And what is designated by the term “body” except each action, which follows its intention as an observing eye?

The eye is therefore the lamp of the body, because the merits of an action are illuminated by the ray of a good intention. “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light,” because, if we intend rightly through simplicity of thought, a good work is accomplished even if it appears to be less good. “And if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness,” because when something right is done with a perverse intention, even if it is seen to shine before human beings, it is nevertheless darkened before the examination of the inner Judge [Note: [Col. 0466D] One manuscript from Évreux reads “of the eternal Judge”].

Hence it is rightly added [Note: [Col. 0466D] These words are absent from Vindoc. up to “if the light”]: “See therefore that the light which is in you is not darkness. If the light which is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (ibid. 23) [Note: [Col. 0466D] Laud. reads “how great are they?”]. For if we darken through a bad intention what we believe we are doing well, how great are those evils which we do not fail to recognize as evil even while committing them? And if we see nothing where we hold what is, as it were, the light of discretion, with what blindness do we stumble in those things we undertake without discretion?

Therefore, with watchful care, our intention must be weighed throughout all our works, so that it seeks nothing temporal in what it does, but fixes itself wholly upon the solidity of eternity. Otherwise, if the structure of our action is placed outside its foundation, it will be dissolved when the earth splits open. Hence it is suitably added here also:

CAPUT XII.

VERSE 6.—“Upon what were its bases made firm?”

31. The bases of the soul are its intentions.—The bases of each soul are its intentions. For just as a structure rests upon columns, and columns upon bases, so our life rests upon virtues, while the virtues rest upon the innermost intention.

And because it is written, “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11), the bases are upon the foundation when our intentions are strengthened in Christ. In vain do bases raise high buildings above themselves if they do not themselves stand upon the solidity of the foundation [Note: [Col. 0466D] Recent editions read “made firm in the foundation”]. For however lofty the works they perform, they accomplish them uselessly if the intentions of their hearts are turned aside from the certainty of eternity and do not seek the rewards of true life. They build upon themselves consequences of ruin all the heavier in proportion as they carry higher structures outside the foundation; for when they do not aim at the rewards of eternal life, the more they seem to elevate themselves in virtues, the more deeply they fall into the pit of empty glory.

We must not therefore consider what the bases support, but upon what they are supported, because God searches human hearts to discover not only what they do but what they seek in their works. Thus, when Paul was describing the strict Judge and recounting the good things of actions, saying, “He will repay each according to his works,” and then, “to these indeed, according to patience in good work, glory and incorruption” (Rom. 2:6–7)—since, by naming the patience of good work, he had spoken as though of the whole structure of elect action—he immediately and subtly sought where the bases of that structure should stand, saying: “To those seeking glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life” (ibid. 7).

It is as though he were saying openly: Even if some display patience in good work, they do not receive glory and incorruption if they do not fix the intentions of their hearts—that is, the bases of the structure—upon the foundation. For God plainly does not inhabit the structure of an honorable life which he himself does not sustain because it has been placed outside him.

32. They must be directed toward the hope of eternity.—Since, therefore, the intentions of each elect soul rest upon the hope of eternity [Note: [Col. 0467D] Pratel. reads “may look toward the hope of eternity”], the Lord’s voice rightly says of this earth: “Upon what were its bases made firm?” [Note: [Col. 0467D] Laud. reads “upon which”]. As though he were saying openly: “Unless upon me.” When each just soul directs its intention toward him, whatever it does temporally it undoubtedly builds in me in a manner that is not temporal.

Because we are strengthened more firmly upon the foundation when we both follow God’s words in outward commandments and weigh them more subtly by understanding them in our inward thoughts, it is rightly added:

CAPUT XIII [Vet. XIV].

IBID.—“Or who released its cornerstone?”

33. Christ is the cornerstone, because he joined active and contemplative life in himself.—The cornerstone is the twofold understanding of the sacred words. It is divinely released when it is not bound by the strict judgment to the darkness of its ignorance, but enjoys a certain freedom, being sufficient either to perform outward things by carrying out God’s commandments or to perceive inward things by contemplation.

Our understanding would never rise to this if our Creator himself had not come to assume our nature. He is called the cornerstone in one way because he joined two peoples in himself, and in another because he displayed in himself the examples of the two joined lives, namely the active and the contemplative.

The contemplative life is far removed from the active; but our incarnate Redeemer, coming and displaying both, joined both in himself. For when he worked miracles in the city and continually spent the night in prayer on the mountain, he gave his faithful an example, so that they would neither neglect the care of their neighbors through devotion to contemplation, nor again, being excessively bound by care for their neighbors, abandon the practices of contemplation. Rather, they should divide and unite their mind between both in such a way that love of neighbor does not impede love of God, nor love of God, because it transcends all things, cast away love of neighbor.

Since, therefore, the Mediator of God and humanity appeared to the human heart that did not know what it should do—he who by acting ordered temporal things and by contemplating showed from where all things depended—it is rightly said: “Or who released its cornerstone?” As though the Lord were saying openly: “Unless I did so, I who, having begotten the Only-Begotten without time, displayed him in time for the salvation of human beings, so that in his life they might learn that different pursuits of living do not conflict” [Note: [Col. 0467D] Évreux and other Norman manuscripts, as well as Laud., read “might discern”].

It should be noted that he says that he did not send him forth but released him, because the Son, assuming human nature, came down from the heights to the depths. Since the elect angels also marveled at the mystery of this incarnation, although they were not redeemed by that same mystery, it is rightly added:

CAPUT XIV [Rec. VII].

VERSE 7.—“When the morning stars praised me together.”

34. Why the angels are called morning stars.—Because the first nature created in time is believed to have been that of rational spirits, the angels are not improperly called morning stars. If this is so, while the earth was invisible and unformed, while darkness was over the abyss (Gen. 1:2), they anticipated by their existence the coming day of the age to follow through the light of wisdom.

We must not carelessly hear what is added: “together.” For the morning stars praise the Redeemer’s power even together with the evening stars, when the elect angels glorify the abundance of heavenly grace together with human beings redeemed at the end of the world [Note: [Col. 0467D] Pratel. and Utic. read: “For they themselves, namely the morning stars …”].

Indeed, in order to kindle us to praise the Creator, they cried out when the light mentioned above had arisen through the flesh: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). They therefore praise together, because they join their voices of exultation to our redemption. They praise together because, when they see us received, they rejoice that their own number is being completed.

Perhaps they are also called morning stars for this reason: they have often been sent to exhort human beings, and, while announcing the coming morning, they drive away the darkness of the present life from human hearts.

But behold: the angels praise the divine power, because the vision of such great brightness [Note: [Col. 0468D] We follow the manuscripts, especially Turon., Laud., Évreux, Pratel., and other Norman witnesses; the printed editions read “the vision delights.” Corb. Germ. reads “expands”] expands them. But we who are redeemed, yet are still weighed down by the corruption of the flesh—by what power do we praise the gift we receive? For how can the tongue say what our mind is not sufficient to feel? It follows:

CAPUT XV

IBID.—“And all the sons of God shouted for joy.”

35. What rejoicing is, and why it suits human beings, not angels.—“Rejoicing” [jubilatio] is said to occur when the effectiveness of the mouth does not fulfill the joy of the heart, but in certain ways gives expression to a joy which the one who rejoices can neither conceal nor fully express.

Let the angels praise, then, who already see such a height of brightness [Note: [Col. 0468D] Corb. Germ., Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts read “breadth”] in the heights. But let human beings shout for joy, who still endure the narrowness of their mouths in the lower regions. Because the Lord knew that these things would certainly occur, he does not so much announce them as things to be done as narrate them as things already done.

But what are we to make of the fact that, when the good rejoice over the mystery of their redemption, the wicked are inflamed by envy? While the elect advance, the reprobate are stirred to the madness of fury, and, because they do not wish to imitate the good things that arise, they persecute them.

Yet even amid these things, the one who redeemed them does not abandon them. For it is written: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13). Our Creator knows when to allow the storm of persecution to rise and when to suppress what has risen. He knows how, for our protection, to restrain what he permits to go forth against us for our exercise, so that the raging storm may cleanse us but not drown us. Hence it is also added:

CAPUT XVI [Vet. XV, Rec. VIII].

VERSE 8.—“Who shut in the sea with doors, when it burst forth, proceeding as though from the womb?”

36. God confined the world raging against the saints. After earthly rulers were humbled, the Lord raised the Church through them above the summit of the world.—What do we understand by the sea except the world, and by the womb except the conception of carnal thought? In this passage, the name “womb” designates the hidden and malicious thought of carnal people. This womb does not conceive the substance of a body in order to bring forth offspring, but conceives a cause of pain in order to fulfill wickedness.

Elsewhere it is said of this womb of the heart of the wicked: “He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity” (Ps. 7:15). Through this womb the wicked conceive when they think evil; through this womb they give birth when they carry out the evil they have thought.

The sea therefore burst forth as though proceeding from the womb when the waves of worldly threats, conceived from the iniquity of carnal thought, raged toward the destruction of the holy Church. But by God’s authority this sea was shut in with doors, because holy men were set like certain doors against the swelling of persecutors, so that the anger of the persecutors might be broken by their miracles and reverence.

For after humbling earthly rulers, the Lord raised the holy Church through them above the summit of the world, and, by increasing the Church’s power, restrained the surge of the raging sea.

But let us hear what the Lord did to this raging sea. It follows:

CAPUT XVII [Rec. IX].

VERSE 9.—“When I made the cloud its garment, and wrapped it in darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy.”

37. God restrained the malice of persecutors, which was like childishness.—The raging sea is clothed with a cloud because the cruelty of persecutors is clothed in the covering of its own foolishness. Since the darkness of their unbelief has been interposed, they are not capable of seeing the clear light of truth; and what they do under the impulse of cruelty they do not recognize because of the desert of their blindness.

For, as the Apostle says, “if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

This cloud commonly weighs down not only unbelievers placed outside, but also darkens some who live carnally within the Church. Hence holy men, who sympathize even with the negligence of others and consider themselves to suffer what they see others undergoing, say to God in prayer: “You have set a cloud before you, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. 3:44).

As though they were saying openly: You justly place before our mind, accustomed to earthly pleasures, the phantoms of its worldly cares [Note: [Col. 0469D] One manuscript from Évreux reads “of its worldly cares”], by which you confound it in the very intention of its prayer. You know that it is devoted to low desires [Note: [Col. 0469D] Recent editions read “to weak desires”], and rightly strike it blind so that it cannot gaze upon the clarity of your light. Thus, when it directs itself toward you, it is turned back by the very cloud of its thoughts; and because it willingly thinks constantly about earthly things, it must endure those same things in prayer when it does not wish to think about them.

Since, therefore, the wickedness of persecutors itself is restrained by a heavenly dispensation, lest it rage against holy men as much as it wishes, after saying, “When I made the cloud its garment,” he aptly added: “And wrapped it in darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy.”

The feet and arms of infants are bound in swaddling-clothes [Note: [Col. 0469D] Laud., Corb. Germ., Pratel., and Utic. read “lest they be thrown this way and that”], lest they be tossed here and there in uncontrolled freedom. Since the persecutors of the holy Church are restless through the instability of their hearts and devoted to this world, possessing not mature but childish understanding, and since they are constrained by obscurity and darkness rather than by an understanding of the heavenly judgment, so that they cannot persecute as much as they wish, they are said to be wrapped in the swaddling-clothes of infancy.

As has been said, they possess childish understanding; yet, constrained by divine dispensation, they cannot extend their arms wherever they wish. Although they desire to perpetrate all evils lightly, they are nevertheless not permitted to accomplish all that they desire. It follows:

VERSE 10.—“I surrounded it with my boundaries.”

The Lord surrounds the sea with his boundaries because he moderates the anger of persecutors by the dispensation of his judgments [Note: [Col. 0469D] Turon. and Laud. read “by the dispensation makes gentle”; [Col. 0470D] Vindoc., Corb. Germ., Évreux, and other Norman witnesses read “of a hidden disposition”], so that the swollen wave of madness may be broken upon the level shore of hidden providence. It follows:

CAPUT XVIII [Vet. XVI].

VERSES 10–11.—“And I set its bar and doors, and said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall come no farther, and here your swelling waves shall be broken.’”

38. Holy preachers, like doors set against the sea of the world raging savagely, could be battered by the waves but not broken down, because Christ strengthened them. These doors are open to the humble and closed to the proud.—What is designated by the doors except holy preachers, and by the bar except the incarnate Lord? He set these doors against the assault of the raging sea, making them all the stronger in proportion as he strengthened them by his own protection [Note: [Col. 0470D] Laud. reads “he set them in place”].

Because the doors of the holy Church were made solid by the opposition of this bar, they could indeed be battered by the waves but could not be broken down. The flood of persecution struck them externally, but it could not penetrate the interior of their hearts.

And because holy teachers are open through their preaching to those who follow it, but closed by their authority to those who resist it [Note: [Col. 0470D] Vindoc., Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts read: “they are open to those who follow their preaching, but closed to those who resist their authority”], they are not improperly called doors—that is, open to the conduct of the humble [Note: [Col. 0470D] Vindoc., Pratel., and Utic. read “open to conversion”], and closed to the terrors of the proud.

They are not improperly called doors, because they open the entrance to the faithful and, again, set themselves against the faithless so that they may not enter. Let us consider what sort of door of the Church Peter was: he received Cornelius, who was seeking faith, but rejected Simon, who was seeking miracles for a price.

To Cornelius, saying, “I truly understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34), he benevolently opened the secrets of the kingdom. To Simon, saying, “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20), he closed the entrance to the heavenly court by the sentence of strict condemnation.

What are all the apostles except doors of the holy Church, when they hear from their Redeemer: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:22–23)? As though he were saying openly to them: Through you those will enter to me to whom you open yourselves, and those from whom you close yourselves will be driven back.

Thus, while the sea rages, the Lord sets up the bar and the doors [Note: [Col. 0471D] Turon. reads “sets them in place”], because, while the storm of persecution spreads through the world from bitter and faithless hearts, God exalts the glory of his Only-Begotten and the reverence of his preachers. As the mysteries of divine power become known, he breaks the waves of fury in the wicked.

39. By divine providence the storm of persecution either surges forth or becomes calm.—It is rightly said: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall come no farther.” For it is the hidden measure of judgment [Note: [Col. 0471D] So read Vindoc., Norman, Laud., Longip., and others seen by Gussanville; he noted this reading in the margin. In the text, with the other printed editions, he has “it is the hidden measure of the divine judgment”] both when the storm of persecution surges forth and when it becomes calm, lest, if not stirred up, it fail to exercise the elect, or, if not moderated, plunge them into the depths.

When knowledge of the faith extends even to the persecutors, the swelling of the troubled sea subsides. There the sea breaks its waves, because, coming to knowledge of the truth, it is ashamed of everything it has wickedly done.

For a broken wave recoils upon itself, because conquered wickedness is accused even by the thought of its own heart; and it receives, as it were, the very force it had inflicted, because it feels the goads of its guilt arising from the wickedness it committed. Hence Paul says to certain people: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

As though it were said: How high did the waves of your wickedness rise, when now, broken within yourselves, they make you ashamed in your conversion of the very things by which they had inflated you in your perversity?

It is therefore rightly said: “And here you shall break your swelling waves.” The fact that doors are mentioned a second time in this conclusion of the sea follows the custom of sacred language, in which something once said is repeated for confirmation.

40. By the sea one may understand the world, against which God set the doors of the precepts of the Law and the New Testament.—But if in this passage we should understand by the sea not specifically the crowd of persecutors but the world generally, the Lord set doors against this sea a second time, because he first gave the human race the precepts of the Law and afterward the testament of the new grace.

By placing doors against it a second time, he closed the assault of this sea, because those whom he took up into the service of his worship he first restrained from idols by the Law he gave, and afterward corrected from carnal understanding by grace revealed.

The sea received doors a second time because God first prohibited the human race from works of iniquity, and afterward also restrained it from the guilt of thought.

Let us see how the Lord places doors upon the first swelling sea. For in the Law it is said: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20:13–14). Let us see how the Lord closes this sea with a second set of doors. In the Gospel he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27–28).

Again it is said: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy’; but I say to you, love your enemies and do good to those who hate you” (ibid. 43–44).

Thus, since he first prohibits wickedness in action and afterward drains away the guilt of the heart, he places doors twice upon the swelling sea, lest it cross the shores of justice that have been drawn around it.

[Vet. XVII.] 41. Laws were given to the world when it was still near its origin, although God had not yet shone upon it. The world was wrapped beneath the darkness of the letter as in the swaddling-clothes of infancy. First bound by fear, it later attained freedom. The Old Law was imperfect and weak.—When he rightly said, “Who shut in the sea with doors?” he immediately added the time, saying: “When it burst forth, proceeding as though from the womb.”

For he then confronted the human race with the commandments of the Law, when the world, still near its origin, was emerging from its own beginning toward the progress of a carnal life, as though from its birth. To proceed from the womb means to appear carnally in the light of present glory.

It is rightly added: “When I made the cloud its garment.” For God did not then present himself to human beings in open manifestation. While rescuing them from the error of faithlessness, he did not yet disclose to them the brightness of his light; he took them out of darkness but still clothed them in a cloud, so that they would abandon the deeds of their former perversity and yet would not clearly see the good things to come.
