Hence it is suitably added: “And wrapped it in darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy.” For when he taught immature peoples not through open preaching of the Spirit but bound them by the commandments of the letter expressed in figurative language, he wrapped them, still understanding weak things, in the darkness of his words as in the swaddling-clothes of infancy. Bound by grosser commandments, they would grow, lest, being wickedly free, they perish in their pleasures.

While not love but fear still bound them to the way of justice, divine dispensation pressed them, as it were, in order to nourish them [Note: [Col. 0472D] Laud. reads “by divine dispensation it pressed them as though”]. For when the weak people unwillingly endured the swaddling-clothes of the commandments, they reached a firmer condition through that very binding [Note: [Col. 0472D] The same manuscript reads “to the condition of the stronger”]. Because fear first restrained them from guilt, they afterward appropriately passed into the freedom of the Spirit.

The Lord himself reproved through the prophet these swaddling-clothes of infancy, which he had given to beginners, saying: “I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25). Things that are evil cease to be regarded as evil in comparison with worse things, and things that are good are not regarded as good in comparison with better things.

Thus, just as it is said to wicked Judah concerning Sodom and Samaria: “You have justified your sisters in all your abominations which you committed” (Ezek. 16:51), so, in comparison with the better commandments that followed in the New Testament, the good commandments given to the immature are described as not good.

For minds clinging to the usage of carnal life could not be lifted from low things unless they advanced through preaching conducted step by step. Hence, when they were in Egypt, their hidden desire was indulged with pious and just moderation, and they were ordered to depart after taking vessels of gold and silver from their neighbors (Exod. 3:22). When they had been led to Mount Sinai and received the Law, they immediately heard: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20:17).

Hence also, in the same Law, they are commanded to demand “an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. 21:24), yet later, when grace had been revealed, they are commanded to offer the other cheek when struck (Matt. 5:39).

Because anger in vengeance always demands more than the injury it has received, they first learned not to return evils multiplied, so that eventually they might learn willingly to endure even multiplied evils.

Hence also, he prohibited this immature people from certain practices, while preserving certain others for their former use, though he fashioned even these into a figure of the better life. In Egypt they sacrificed brute animals to idols; afterward he retained for them the slaughter of animals as a customary use but forbade the worship of idols. Thus, while they lost something from their customary practice, their weakness was consoled by the fact that they retained something of it.

By a wondrous dispensation of counsel, what the Lord retained for them from their carnal custom he more powerfully transformed into a figure of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0473D] Turon., Laudun., and Pratel. read “by a wondrous dispensation of counsel”]. For what do the sacrifices of those animals signify except the death of the Only-Begotten? What do the sacrifices of those animals signify except the extinction of our carnal life?

From the very point at which he condescends to the weakness of the immature people, he announces to them, through the shadowy forms of allegories, a greater strength of the Spirit.

It is therefore rightly said: “And wrapped it in darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy,” because from the weakness by which he bore with their tenderness he made a deep cloud of spiritual meanings [Note: [Col. 0473D] Vindoc., Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts read “from which he made another …”].

*[Old Version XVIII]* 42. The precepts of the new life, opposed to the immoderate movements of the soul, are strengthened by Christ’s examples.—Because he enclosed him within the limits of his commandments, restraining the soul’s immoderate wanderings, he rightly adds: “I surrounded it with my boundaries.” And because he curbed the movements of the human race by sending the Mediator, he appropriately continues: “And I set a bar and doors.” For he set a bar and doors because, when our Redeemer was sent against the offenses of sinners, he established the principles of the new life. Closed doors are strengthened by a bar placed against them. God therefore set up a bar because he sent the Only-Begotten against the wanton movements of the human race, and he made firm by his deeds the spiritual precepts that he taught by speaking.

Well, then, it follows: “And I said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther; and here you shall break your swelling waves.’” This sea had passed beyond the earlier doors, because the wave of human pride was leaping over the barriers of the law set against it.

[Note: Vindoc, Laon, Corbie German, and Pratel read: “was leaping.”] But after the world encountered the Only-Begotten set against it, it broke the force of its own arrogance and could not pass beyond, because by his strength it found a closed boundary for its fury.

[Note: Turin and Corbie German read: “because it found his strength.” Pratel and Corbie German have “found it closed,” not “found a closed boundary.”]

Hence it is rightly said through the Prophet: “The sea saw and fled” (Psalm 113:3). The open doors may also, without impropriety, be understood as his open sufferings. Against these he set a bar from within, because he strengthened them by his invisible divinity. The waves of the world come against them, but, broken, fly apart: the proud despise them when they see them, yet fear their power when they experience it.

[Note: Corbie German, Laon, and the manuscripts used for the Paris editions of 1495 and 1518, and for the Basel edition of 1514, read “when they see them.” Gilot and later editions read “by living,” as do the Pratel, Utica, and other Norman manuscripts.] For when the human race first mocked the sufferings of the Only-Begotten, it afterward became afraid: like the sea, coming against the doors placed before it in the manner of a wave striking its barrier, it came swollen with pride, but, broken by their power, it flew apart.

But because this is said to blessed Job so that the glory of his heart might be pressed down on account of so many virtues, lest he perhaps attribute to himself [Note: Turin and Laon read: “who does not fail to recognize that he does not stand sublimely.” Our reading, which is found in all the editors, is found also in other manuscripts, especially Corbie German, Pratel, and the other Norman manuscripts. It is confirmed by what is read at the end of this book: “Thus blessed Job, lest he attribute to himself that he stands firmly against the storms of his heart.” These words overturn the reading of the Laon and Turin manuscripts.] the fact that he does not fail to recognize how sublimely he stands, when we consider how greatly these words contribute to his edification, let us also discuss them morally. Let him therefore say:

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 8.—“Who enclosed the sea with doors?”**

43. The human heart is a seething sea, which God alone can restrain.—What is the sea except our heart, turbid with fury, bitter with quarrels, swollen with the arrogance of pride, and dark with the deceit of malice? Anyone who understands the hidden temptations of his thoughts within himself perceives how violently this sea rages.

[Note: Laon reads: “hidden thoughts.”] For behold, we now abandon perverse things, now cling to righteous desires, now cut away wicked actions outwardly; yet inwardly we are secretly wearied by the storm of the former life with which we came here. Unless the barriers of immense fear, arising from regard for judgment and dread of eternal punishment, restrained it, all the foundations of the work built up within us would have collapsed completely.

For if what rages inwardly by suggestion were to burst outward through deliberation, the structure of our life would lie utterly ruined. “In iniquity I was conceived, and in sin I was brought forth” (Psalm 50:7); we carry with us here the struggle arising from the troubles of innate corruption, and overcome it only with difficulty. Hence it is rightly said of this sea: “When it burst forth, as though proceeding from the womb.”

The womb is the adolescence of wicked thought. Concerning it the Lord says through Moses: “The sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from its adolescence” (Genesis 8:21). The evil of corruption, which each of us received from the beginning of our carnal desires, exercises itself as age advances;

[Note: Vindoc, Ebroic, and others read: “manifests itself as age advances.”] and unless the hand of divine fear quickly restrains it, sin suddenly devours in the abyss every good thing of created nature.

Let no one, then, attribute victory over his thoughts to himself, when Truth says: “Who enclosed the sea with doors, when it burst forth, as though proceeding from the womb?” For unless divine grace held back the waves of the heart from the very beginning of thought, the raging sea of temptations would undoubtedly have overwhelmed the land of the human mind, so that, drenched by its salty waves, it would dry up—that is, delighted by the destructive pleasures of the flesh, it would perish.

The Lord alone, therefore, encloses the sea with doors: he places the barriers of inspired fear against the heart’s wicked movements. But because we are forbidden to follow the things we see, because we are beaten back from delight in bodily things,

[Note: Corbie German and Vindoc read: “we now desire.”]

we desire also to raise the eyes of the mind to invisible things and to see those very things that we are commanded to pursue. But what are we to do? Those things are not yet open to our weakened sight. Behold, we are called to love them, yet restrained from seeing them; for even when we furtively and barely glimpse something, we still grope beneath an exceedingly uncertain vision.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XX [Old Version XIX]

**VERSE 9.—“When I placed a cloud as its garment, and wrapped it in darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy.”**

44. This sea is wrapped in darkness and gloom.—This tumultuous sea, namely, our heart wavering amid thoughts, is clothed with a cloud,

[Note: “Wavering” is absent in Corbie German, Pratel, and Vindoc.] because, lest it see its inward tranquility clearly, it is darkened by the confusion of its own restlessness. This sea is wrapped in darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy, because its still-tender senses are bound by the weakness that prevents it from contemplating lofty things.

Let us see Paul wrapped in a certain darkness as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy, when he says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). If he did not see himself as an infant in relation to grasping heavenly things,

[Note: Turin, Corbie German, Laon, Utica, and the other Norman manuscripts, supported by the Paris edition of 1495, read “for grasping”; other witnesses read “for contemplating.”]

 he would in no way have prefaced the comparison with his own age, saying: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child.”

Then we ascend to youthful strength when, with a strong understanding, we see the life toward which we are striving. But now, because the sharpness of our attention is blunted by its own weakness against the inner light, our mind is held bound by the swaddling-clothes of infancy.

Here it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 10.—“I surrounded it with my boundaries.”**

45. What boundaries were placed around this sea.—The Lord surrounds this sea with his boundaries because he humbles our heart, still troubled by the distress and care of its corruption, beneath the measure of contemplation, so that although it desires more, it nevertheless does not rise beyond what is permitted to it.

Or certainly, the Lord surrounds this sea with his boundaries because he calms our heart, swollen with temptations, by the hidden distribution of gifts: sometimes acting so that a wicked suggestion does not reach delight; sometimes so that wicked delight does not burst forth into consent. Thus, when he regards the unlawful movements of the heart and prevents some of them from reaching consent, while restraining others even from delight, he plainly imposes boundaries on the raging sea, so that it does not emerge into action, but the wave of temptation collides within the bosom of the mind, murmuring against itself.

Because it is then strongly restrained when it is met by delight in God and by virtues inspired by him, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSES 10, 11.—“And I set a bar and doors, and I said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther; and here you shall break your swelling waves.’”**

46. The raging sea dissipates virtues unless they are strengthened by charity.—What do we understand morally by the doors except virtues, and by the bar except the strength of charity? This sea, therefore, the sea that rages, dissipates these doors—that is, the virtues exercised in action—unless charity, opposed to it within the hidden places of the mind, binds them fast.

Every good work of virtue is easily destroyed when temptation rushes upon the heart, unless it is made firm by charity fixed in the innermost depths. Hence Paul, in his preaching, when he set certain doors of virtue against the sea of temptation, immediately added to those same doors the strength of a bar, saying: “Above all these things, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14).

Charity is called the bond of perfection because through it every good that is done is bound together, so that it does not perish. Any work is quickly torn away by the tempter if it is found loosened from the bond of charity. But if the mind is constrained by love of God and neighbor, then, whenever the movements of temptation suggest anything unjust to it, love itself opposes them and breaks the waves of wicked persuasion against the doors of virtue and the bar of inward love.

*[Old Version XX.]* Since, therefore, the Lord restrains the vices arising in the heart through the strength of inspired charity, he checks the force of the rising sea by closed barriers. Anger perhaps irritates secretly; but, lest heavenly peace be lost, the service of the tongue is withdrawn from the disturbance of the mind, so that what sounds tumultuously in the bosom of the heart does not reach the voice.

Lust is kindled in hidden thoughts; but, lest the mind lose its heavenly purity, it chastises those members that might have served the conceived impurity, so that the stench of the heart does not exhale into bodily corruption.

[Note: Corbie German, Laon, and Pratel read “is kindled.”]

Avarice stimulates; but, lest the mind be deprived of the heavenly kingdom, content with frugality, it binds itself within the barriers of moderation to its own possessions, lest it expand into wicked action and the heat of inward desire sweat outward into deeds.

[Note: Corbie German reads: “the avarice of the heart.”]

[Note: Laon reads: “content with frugality within the barriers, it is bound to its own possessions.”]

Pride inflates; but, lest one lose true exaltation, each person, considering that he is dust, humbles himself from the height of the pride he has conceived, striving that what he tolerates in the suggestion of thought may not burst forth into the practice of action.

It is therefore rightly said: “I set a bar and doors, and I said: ‘Thus far you shall come, and you shall proceed no farther; and here you shall break your swelling waves.’” For when each of the elect is tempted by vices and nevertheless resists doing what has been suggested as evil, the sea is held enclosed, as it were.

Although it strikes the mind inwardly with tumultuous waves of thought, it nevertheless does not pass beyond the shores established by good living. The sea does rise in swelling, but when it is dashed against the fixed deliberation of the heart, it returns broken.

Therefore blessed Job, lest he attribute to himself the fact that he stands firmly against the storms of his heart, should hear from the divine voice: “Who enclosed the sea with doors, when it burst forth, as though proceeding from the womb,” and so forth. It is as though he were told plainly: “You weigh yourself outwardly by your good works to no purpose if you do not consider me inwardly, the one who restrains the waves of temptation within you. For that you may be able to endure waves in action is the work of my power, since I break the waves of temptation in your heart.”

# BOOK TWENTY-NINE

Twenty-two verses of chapter 38, from verse 12 through verse 33 inclusive, are explained; many matters are taught, especially concerning Satan’s arts and snares, grace, predestination, reprobation, and the hidden judgments of God.

[Column 0477]

## CHAPTER I

[Column 0477A]

1. The Son of God, unknown to us in his eternal birth, willed to be born in time so that he might offer himself for imitation.—Our Lord God Jesus Christ, inasmuch as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before the ages (1 Corinthians 1:24); or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us say more truly that he was always born.

[Note: Vindoc reads: “nor began to be.”]

We cannot say “he is always being born,” lest he appear imperfect. But, so that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say “always born,” so that “born” may pertain to perfection and “always” to eternity; thus, in whatever manner possible, that essence which is without time may be designated by temporal speech.

Yet even by calling it perfect we depart greatly from expressing that truth, because what has not been made cannot be called perfect. Nevertheless, the Lord, accommodating himself to the words of our weakness, says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48).

In that divine birth, therefore, he could not be known by the human race. Accordingly, he came in human nature so that he might be seen; he willed to be seen so that he might be imitated. This birth in the flesh seemed contemptible to the wise of the world. For they despised the weakness of his humanity, judging such things unworthy of God. Yet man was all the more indebted to him because God accepted even what seemed unworthy for man’s sake.

“For since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). It is as though he said: Since the world could not find God, who is wisdom, through its own wisdom, it pleased God that it should recognize God made man through the foolishness of humanity, so that his wisdom might descend to our foolish things and our blindness might see the light of heavenly prudence, illuminated by the clay of his flesh.

[Note: Laon and Corbie German read: “through the foolishness of his humanity.”]

[Note: Turin, Vindoc, Laon, Corbie German, Ebroic, and the other Norman manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “to our foolishness.”]

Born from the Father without time, he deigned to be born from his mother in time, so that by enclosing his origin between beginning and end, he might open to the eyes of the human mind an origin that is neither taken from a beginning nor confined by an end.

Hence it is rightly now said to blessed Job:

## CHAPTER II [Received Version II]

[Column 0478A]

**VERSE 12.—“Did you perhaps, after your birth, command the dawn and show the morning its place?”**

2. When the Lord was born, the Church, like the dawn, was changed from darkness into light.—Supply: “as I did.” His divine birth has no “before” or “after.” Since his being is eternal, while it encompasses everything that passes away, it encloses within itself the course of times.

But his human birth, because it both began and ended, received from time the possession of a before and an after.

[Note: This reading, “after this birth,” is supported by the English and other manuscripts and by the Job passage being explained (“after your birth”). Older editions—Gilot, Vatican, Gussanville—and Corbie German read “through this birth.” The latter reading also occurs in the Basel editions of 1503 and 1514 and the Paris editions of 1488, 1495, 1518, and 1571.] Yet because, when he took upon himself the shadows of our temporality, he poured into us the light of his eternity, the morning rightly recognized its timeless place after this birth that the Creator established for himself in time.

For since dawn or morning is changed from darkness into light, the whole Church of the elect is not inappropriately designated by the name of dawn or morning. While she is led from the night of unbelief to the light of faith, she is opened to the day after darkness, like the dawn, by the splendor of heavenly brightness.

Hence it is rightly said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song of Songs 6:9). The holy Church, desiring the rewards of heavenly life, is called dawn because, while she abandons the darkness of sins, she shines with the light of righteousness.

*[Old Version II.]* 3. As long as we live, we are dawn, not the full day.—Yet there is something more subtle that we may consider by reflecting on the character of dawn or morning. Dawn or morning announces that night has passed, but does not yet display the full brightness of day. While driving away night, it receives day, and holds a light mingled with darkness.

What, then, are all of us who follow the truth in this life except dawn or morning? For we already do certain things that belong to the light, yet in some respects we are still not free from the remnants of darkness.

Through the Prophet it is said to God: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 143:2). And again it is written: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2). Paul likewise says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans 7:23).

Where, then, the law of sin contends with the law of the mind, there is surely still dawn, because the light that has already appeared has not yet completely suppressed the darkness that is passing away. There is still dawn because, while the law of the flesh strikes against the law of the mind and the law of the mind against the law of the flesh, light and shadow struggle with one another in turn.

Hence Paul, when he said, “The night has passed” (Romans 13:12), did not add, “The day has come,” but rather, “The day has drawn near.” For by saying that the day has drawn near, rather than that it has already come, after the departure of night, he plainly shows that he is still before the sun, after the darkness, in the dawn.

4. It will be day when no darkness of sin remains.—Then the holy Church of the elect will fully be day, when no shadow of sin is mingled with it. It will fully be day when it shines with the perfect fervor of inward light. It will fully be day when, tolerating no troubling memory of its evils, it hides from itself every remnant of darkness.

Hence the dawn is rightly shown as still in transition when it is said: “And you showed the morning its place.” For whatever is shown its place is plainly called from one place to another. What is the place of dawn except the perfect brightness of eternal vision?

[Note: Turin, Corbie German, Pratel, Laon, and others read: “of inward vision.”]

When it arrives there, it will have nothing of the darkness of the night that has passed. But now, while still enduring the troubles of temptation, because the Church hastens toward another state through the intention of the heart, the dawn is moving toward its place. If it did not see that place with the mind, it would remain in the night of this life.

[Note: Turin reads: “but because each day it sees its place increasing, and seeks for the sun to shine fully upon it.”]

But as it strives each day to be perfected and to grow daily into the light, it already sees its place and seeks for the sun to shine fully upon it. The dawn considers its place when the holy soul burns to contemplate the appearance of its Creator.

The dawn was striving to reach its place when David said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 42:3). Truth showed the dawn its place when, through Solomon, it said: “What more has the wise man than the fool? And what does the poor man have except that he should go there where life is?” (Ecclesiastes 6:8).

The Lord showed this very place to the fathers who preceded his incarnation, after his birth, because unless they recognized through the spirit of prophecy the King of the heavenly homeland who was to be incarnate, they would not see how desirable the good things of that homeland were.

Truth disclosed the dawn’s place when he asked the Father in the presence of his disciples, saying: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

[Note: Laon reads: “and there may they be with me.”]

He showed the dawn its place when he said: “Wherever the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 24:28).

[Note: Corbie German, Pratel, Utica, and others read: “there they will be gathered.”]

The dawn was hastening to reach this place, which it had come to know, when Paul said that he desired to depart and be with Christ: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). And again: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:4).

The dawn is rightly said to have been shown its proper place after his birth, because, before he himself became known through the body, he held the blessedness of future recompense within the understanding of a few. But when he took upon himself the weakness of human birth, he spread knowledge of the glory to come through the love of an innumerable multitude.

[Note: Laon reads: “he spread it in love among innumerable multitudes.”]

But since the mystery of the divine work is carried out by mercy in such a way that anger also accompanies it, so that the hidden Judge, looking upon some, redeems them, while abandoning others, he destroys them—because we have learned how he illuminates the elect through his incarnation, let us now hear how he condemns the reprobate. It follows:

## CHAPTER III [Received Version III]

**VERSE 13.—“Have you perhaps taken hold of the ends of the earth, shaking them, and shaken the wicked out of it?”**

5. The Lord chose the rejected and humble.—The Lord took hold of the ends of the earth because, at the end of the ages, he came to the synagogue, now destitute and subjected to foreign kings. From it he shook out the wicked because he drove away from the glory of the carnal sacrifice those who rejected the spiritual principles of faith.

Or certainly, he took hold of the ends of the earth because from Judea he chose a few who were rejected and humble (Matthew 4:18 and following). He took hold of the ends of the earth because, abandoning the teachers of the law, he assumed fishermen. While he holds its ends, he shakes the wicked out of it, because, while he strengthens the weak faithful, he condemns the strong unbelievers within it.

He rightly added “shaking,” because by his coming he moved even the hearts of the reprobate with immense terror.

[Note: Ebroic and the other Norman manuscripts read: “with immense strength.” Corbie German reads: “with immense fear.”]

They had indeed been shaken who said: “We accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19).

[Note: Laon and Corbie German read: “after him.”]

A thing that is shaken is dragged here and there and wearied. Judea, therefore, had been shaken: through some it said of Christ, “He is good” (John 7:12); through others it resisted, saying, “No, but he deceives the crowds” (ibid.); through others it said, “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (John 9:33); and finally, through others it cried out: “If he were not a malefactor, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18:30).

The reprobate were shaken but not overthrown when at one moment they looked upon his miracles in astonishment, and at another mocked him, despising the reproaches directed at his weakness. Were they not shaken when they said: “How long will you take away our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24)?

Or certainly, he shook and took hold of the ends of the earth because, when he terrified the weak hearts of the humble with pious fear, he did not abandon them by strict judgment. From the very place where the multitude of believers was humbled and trembled within itself, it stood more firmly in God.

For because God holds the one whom he shakes, the Prophet indicates this, saying: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one, and upon him who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2, according to the Septuagint).

Because he holds the one whom he shakes, this is also declared through Solomon, who says: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but whoever is hard of mind will fall into evil” (Proverbs 28:14).

Since, therefore, the Lord held the ends of Judea in the apostles and, on account of their impiety, rightly rejected from it the scribes, Pharisees, and high priests, let us hear what is further added concerning their condemnation. It follows:

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 14.—“It shall be restored as clay is to the seal, and it shall stand like a garment.”**

[Column 0481B]

6. The Jews, first freed from brickmaking, returned to bricks when they set their minds on earthly things.—What else did the Lord find the Israelite people to be except clay? He found them serving in Egypt, devoted to the service of the nations and laboring at bricks. After leading them through so many miracles to the promised land (Exodus 5 and following), after filling them with knowledge of himself when they had been brought there, after granting them so many hidden mysteries through prophecy, what else did he make them except a seal for preserving the mystery?

[Note: Corbie German, Turin, Vindoc, and one Ebroic manuscript read this way. Laon reads: “for in that very divine prophecy.” Pratel, Utica, and the other Norman manuscripts, followed by the printed editions, read: “for a long time in prophecy.”]

For divine prophecy itself held enclosed whatever Truth revealed about himself at the end. But after so many divine secrets and so many miracles received, at the coming of their Redeemer they loved earth more than truth, saying through the priests: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11:48). Thus they returned to the bricks they had abandoned in Egypt; and although they had already been made a seal of God, they bent themselves again toward what they had left behind. After the seal, they presented themselves as clay in the eyes of Truth when, through the malice of their impiety, they lost the mysteries of the word they had received and chose to set their minds only on earthly things, which defile.

7. Serving only the letter, they were unwilling to cling to God through charity.—Hence it is appropriately added: “And it shall stand like a garment.” Unpolished and coarser garments, even when they have been put on, are said to stand because, not being well fitted, they do not cling to the limbs of the person wearing them.

Judea, therefore, even when it seemed to serve in the knowledge of the truth, stood like a garment, because through external commandments it showed that it served the Lord, but did not wish to cling to him through the understanding of charity.

[Note: Another Ebroic manuscript reads: “through the indulgence of charity.”]

While it held only the letter in the commandments of God and did not unite itself inwardly to their meaning through the spirit, it did not cling to the one who had clothed it, as it were. Hence it is appropriately added:

[Note: In the Norman manuscripts this belongs to the preceding sentence, which reads: “but did not wish to cling to him through the understanding of charity” (or “the indulgence of charity”), “while it held only the letter ….” It then continues: “And it in no way joined itself …, because to him,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER V

**VERSE 15.—“The light of the wicked shall be taken away.”**

8. They lost knowledge of the law because they refused to believe the truth.—Because they refuse to believe the truth, they lose knowledge of the law forever; and because they grow proud over the law they received, they are blinded by the glory of their knowledge.

For it is written: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see” (Psalm 68:24). Again it is written: “Blind the heart of this people and weigh down its ears” (Isaiah 6:10). And again it is written: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

And because they exalted themselves through the works of the law against the Lawgiver, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER VI

**The same passage.—“And the exalted arm shall be broken.”**

9. The proud observance of the law is rejected.—The exalted arm is broken when, after the grace of faith has been proclaimed, the proud practice of the law is rejected, as it is said: “By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified” (Romans 3:20).

10. The ends of the Church, which God both holds and shakes.—Yet all these things can also be understood in another way. Sacred Scripture is accustomed to call the Church “earth.” The Lord therefore holds and shakes the ends of the earth because he permits the farthest reaches of his Church to be disturbed by the most savage persecution at the coming of Antichrist, yet does not abandon them by permitting this.

At one time the Lord holds this earth without shaking it; at another he both holds and shakes it: sometimes he possesses it in the tranquil peace of faith; sometimes he commands it to be moved by the assault of persecution.

11. In the persecutions of the Church, false Christians are shaken out like chaff.—When he said, “Have you perhaps taken hold of the ends of the earth, shaking them,” he immediately added: “And have you shaken the wicked out of it?” For, as Paul testifies, there are many in it who profess that they know God but deny him by their deeds (Titus 1:16).

The Lord therefore shakes the wicked out of it because those whom inward vices now possess will then fall into the abyss of open unbelief; and they become a heap of chaff when they are stirred by the breeze of that temptation. Although they now conceal themselves under the appearance of faith within the bosom of the threshing floor, they will then rebound outside the heap of grain when driven by the winnowing-fan of the strict examination.

*[Received Version IV.]*

12. In them the seal of faith is turned into clay.—Hence it is appropriately added: “It shall be restored as clay is to the seal.” It is as though he said openly: Those who now appear as a seal within the bosom of the Church will then, before the eyes of all, be restored as clay; that is, they will by no means deceive human judgments by their profession of religion, but will be shown to set their minds on earthly things.

[Note: Corbie German, Laon, Pratel, and the other Norman manuscripts read: “but that they set their minds on earthly things.”]

Sacred Scripture commonly uses “seal” for faith and “clay” for iniquity. For the younger son, who returned to his father after wasting his substance, received a ring as a gift (Luke 15:22). The Gentile people, who, after losing immortality, return to God through repentance, are fortified by the seal of faith.

Hence the Church is told by her Bridegroom: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song of Songs 8:6). A seal is placed on things precisely so that they may not be violated by the presumption of those who would plunder them.

The Bridegroom is placed as a seal upon the heart when the mystery of his faith is impressed in the custody of our thought, so that the unfaithful servant—namely, our adversary—when he sees hearts sealed by faith, does not presume to break into them by tempting them.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “the seal is placed upon the heart.”]

[Note: Pratel and Corbie German read: “but by clay the contamination of earthly things is shown, as the Psalmist bears witness.”]

By clay, however, earthly contaminations are shown, as the Psalmist bears witness when he says: “You brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of filth” (Psalm 39:3).

Since, therefore, many who are found in earthly contaminations are brought to the Church and marked with the sacrament of heavenly faith, yet do not withdraw from wicked deeds, and now conceal themselves under the veil of faith but, when they find the opportunity, reveal what they truly are, it is rightly said: “It shall be restored as clay is to the seal.”

Those whom we now believe to be faithful we shall then find to be enemies of the faith. Although, while untested, they may appear as a seal, once tested they will undoubtedly be clay. Hence it is also rightly said, “It shall be restored,” because the wicked life they subsequently lead proves them to have the same character as their conscience could have had before faith.

[Note: Corbie German and Laon read: “such is their wicked life afterward.”]

Concerning them it is appropriately added: “And it shall stand like a garment.”

13. The Church is now adorned with many garments, but when persecution blazes she will be stripped of them.—The holy Church is now clothed, as though with as many garments as she is adorned by the veneration of the faithful. Hence, when the Gentiles had been shown to her, the Lord says to her through the Prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49:18).

Yet she is now clothed, at least in appearance, with many who seem faithful; but when the assault of persecution strikes, she will then be stripped of them and left naked. Concerning their lot it is said here: “And it shall stand like a garment.”

To “stand” in this passage means to persist in sin. Hence it is written: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (Psalm 1:1).

Or certainly, each reprobate person is said to stand like a garment to show that he cannot stand; for just as a garment, when worn, is stretched over the body in the appearance in which it is seen, but, when removed, becomes broken and folded, so each person who then withdraws from the state of the holy Church will have been stretched out and handsome, as though while being worn, but afterward, when stripped off, will lie broken and cast away.

If, however, we understand “to stand” as “to endure,” then each reprobate person stands like a garment because he endures briefly in this life, which he loves. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “All these things shall grow old like a garment, and like a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed” (Psalm 101:28).

These matters, which he first introduced rightly under the cloud of allegories, are now made known in clearer words, when he adds:

## CHAPTER VII

[Column 0484A]

**VERSE 15.—“The light of the wicked shall be taken away.”**
### 14. The light of faith will be taken away from those who believe but live wickedly, especially at the time of the persecution of Antichrist.

For the light of God does not now illumine those who cloak the wickedness of their iniquity under the name of faith. [Old III, Rec. V.] For while they neglect to live according to the teaching of faith, yet outwardly honor that same faith, they seek the esteem of the present life in the name of religion; and this shines upon them from faith: that faith wins them favor before human beings. There are, however, some who truly believe the eternal realities they hear proclaimed, yet by living badly contradict the very faith they hold. They too have their light amid darkness [Note: Corbie Germanicus, Vindobonensis, Pratellensis, Uticensis: “among darkness”], because, while they act perversely, they nevertheless think rightly about God; thus, lest they become wholly dark, they are illumined in some measure by the radiance of light.

But when they love earthly things more than heavenly things, and what they see more than what they hear [Note: This passage is damaged by the omission of the verb “they love” in the editions of Gilot, Vaticanus, and several others. It has been restored with the help of English and Gallican manuscripts and the old Paris and Basel editions], at the onset of persecution they lose what they had seemed to believe rightly. This happens especially at that time when the very head of the wicked rises up and, in the final persecution of holy Church, attacks its strength with all the power at his disposal. Then the heart of each person is revealed, when whatever lay hidden within is brought to light. Those who are now pious in speech but impious in heart fall when their wickedness is made public, and lose the light of faith which they had possessed only outwardly.

Amid all this, each of us must return to the secret place of his heart and fear the damage caused by his conduct, lest, as our merits demand, the strict justice of God’s judgments place us among such people.

### [Rec. VI.] 15. Antichrist already lives and rages in his members.

Let no one carelessly flatter himself and therefore think himself safe from such a calamity, because he does not expect to reach the storm of that future age [Note: So Corbie Germanicus, Vindobonensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman witnesses, as well as the old Paris edition of 1488 and 1495. The Paris edition of 1518 and the Basel editions of 1503 and 1514 read simply: “consider himself a stranger to such a fall.” In more recent editions one finds *occasu* (“at the fall”) instead of *casu* (“calamity”)].

How many have not seen the time of that temptation, yet are caught up in the storm of its temptation! Cain did not see the time of Antichrist, yet by his merits he was a member of Antichrist (Genesis 4). Judas did not know the violence of that persecution, yet, urged on by greed, he succumbed to the power of its cruelty (Matthew 26:15) [Note: Corbie Germanicus, Ebroicensis, other Norman witnesses, and the old Paris edition: “and yet he succumbed to the right of its cruelty.” The Laudian manuscript reads: “and yet, by right of its cruelty, he succumbed to the greed that persuaded him.”]. Simon lived long before the times of Antichrist, yet by perversely seeking the power of miracles he joined himself to Antichrist’s pride (Acts 8:19).

Thus the wicked body is joined to its head, and members are joined to members: they may not know one another in time, yet they are united by wicked action. For Pergamum had neither known Balaam’s books nor his words, yet, following his wickedness, it heard the voice of heavenly rebuke: “You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication” (Revelation 2:14) [Note: Vindobonensis, Laudianus, Pratellensis, and others: “the voice of heavenly rebuke.”].

The church of Thyatira was separated from Jezebel in knowledge, time, and place [Note: Laudianus: “long periods of time divided them.”]; but because guilt of the same kind bound it to her, Jezebel is said to be present in it and to persist in perverse works, as the angel testifies: “I have this against you: you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols” (ibid., 20).

Behold: because people could be found who followed Jezebel’s life through wicked conduct, Jezebel is said to have been found there. For joined customs make one wicked body, even when places and times divide them. Thus it happens that every wicked person who has already passed away remains in his perverse imitators, and that the author of the wicked, who has not yet come, already appears in those who carry out his works.

Hence John says: “Now many Antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18), because all the wicked are already his members; by their wicked lives they have perversely anticipated their head. Hence Paul says: “So that he may be revealed in his own time; for the mystery of iniquity is already at work” (2 Thessalonians 2:6). It is as though he were saying: “Then Antichrist will be openly seen; for even now he secretly works his hidden deeds in the hearts of the wicked.”

To say nothing of more conspicuous crimes, one person silently envies his brother in his heart and, if he finds an opportunity, strives to overthrow him. Whose member is he, if not a member of the one of whom it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24)?

Another, thinking himself to possess great merit, places himself above everyone through the swelling of his heart and believes all others inferior to himself. Whose member is he, if not a member of the one of whom it is written: “He sees every proud thing, and he is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41:25) [Note: The same manuscript adds: “and he himself is king over all the children of pride.”]?

Another seeks the power of this world, not in order to benefit others, but so that he himself may not be subject to anyone else. Whose member is he, if not a member of the one of whom it is written: “He said: I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13)?

For the Most High alone rules over all in such a way that he cannot be subject to another. The devil perversely wished to imitate him, refusing subjection while seeking dominion. Therefore whoever desires power for this reason—that he disdains to be subject to the one placed over him by heavenly ordinance—imitates the devil.

### [Old IV.] 16. Those who deny the truth are guilty of unbelief.

There are, moreover, many things that declare certain people to be unbelievers even while they remain within the peace of the Church. I see some who show such partiality toward a powerful person that, when questioned by him, they do not hesitate, for his favor, to deny the truth in a matter concerning their neighbor.

And who is the Truth, if not the one who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)? John the Baptist did not die when questioned about confessing Christ, but when questioned about the truth of justice (Mark 6:28). Yet because Christ is the Truth, he went to his death for Christ—that is, for the Truth.

Let us place before our eyes the case of someone who, when questioned, showed partiality toward a powerful person and, to avoid suffering even an insult in words, denied the truth. What, I ask, would such a person do amid the pain of punishments, when he was ashamed of Christ amid the blows of words? Behold, even afterward he is still a Christian before human eyes; yet if the Lord has determined to judge him strictly, he is no longer one.

### 17. Those who neglect to correct when they are obliged to do so. The trials of Antichrist are not absent even in the peace of the Church.

I see others who, through the office of teaching, have been entrusted with the duties of exhorting and rebuking. They see something unlawful being committed, yet, because they fear offending the favor of certain powerful people, they do not dare to rebuke it.

Whoever this person is, what else does he do but see the wolf coming and flee (John 10:12)? He flees because he keeps silent; he keeps silent because, scorning eternal favor, he has loved temporal glory more. Behold, before the face of the powerful person he hides himself within the hiding-place of his silence, and thus gives room to concealed fear just as he would to open persecution [Note: Turonensis: “thus he secretly gave room to fear.” Laudianus: “thus, concealed, he gave room to fear.”].

It is rightly said of such people: “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John 12:43). Whoever is such a person, if these things are judged strictly, has denied Christ by his silence, even though open persecution was absent. Therefore the trials of Antichrist are not absent even in the peace of the Church. Let no one, then, fear only the final times of persecution as though they alone were dreadful.

Among the wicked, the cause of Antichrist is enacted every day, because he already works his mystery secretly in their hearts. And although many who outwardly remain within the Church pretend to be what they are not, at the coming of the Judge they will be exposed as what they are. Concerning them Solomon rightly says: “I saw the wicked buried; they had even been in the holy place while they were still alive, and they were praised in the city as though for works of the just” (Ecclesiastes 8:10).

Thus, after it had been said of the wicked, “He will be restored as clay for the seal, and he will stand like a garment, and his light will be taken away from the wicked”—which is certainly to be fulfilled in the persecution of Antichrist—God immediately consoles us concerning the destruction of that same Antichrist, saying:

### CHAPTER VIII

**Verse 15.**—“And the lofty arm will be broken.”

### 18. The pride and fall of Antichrist. The angel and the human being fell because they wished to be like God through power, not through justice.

For what else is meant by the lofty arm than the proud height of Antichrist, which rises over reprobate human minds through the arrogance of worldly glory, so that sinful man, while despising being regarded as a human being, pretends to be a god over human beings?

Hence the apostle Paul says: “So that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4). To show his swelling pride more fully, Paul first said: “Who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (ibid.).

A human being can sometimes be called “god,” as it was said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you as god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1). But a mere human being cannot be worshiped as God. Because Antichrist exalts himself both above holy human beings and above the very power of divinity, through the title of glory he claims for himself, he attempts to surpass both what is called God and what is worshiped as God.

We should note into what a pit of pride he fell, since he did not remain within the measure of the ruin by which he fell. The devil and the human being, with uplifted minds, fell from the state proper to their creation: the one saying, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:18), and the other believing when he heard, “Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Genesis 3:5).

Thus both fell because they desired to be like God, not through justice but through power. But the human being, liberated by grace—the one who had fallen by perversely desiring God’s likeness—recognizes that, in the guilt of his crime, he is utterly unlike God and cries: “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 88:8).

The devil, however, was abandoned in the fall of his crime to the justice due him and did not remain within the measure of his ruin. The longer he remained separated from the grace of the Almighty, the more he accumulated the guilt of his crime. He fell because, by a perverse ordering, he wished to be like God; yet he was brought to such a point that, coming in Antichrist, he disdains even to appear like God and, in his pride, considers inferior the one whom he could not have as his equal.

When it is said of him, as we have already noted, “Exalting himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (2 Thessalonians 2:4), it is plainly shown that, once desiring God’s likeness, he wished to raise himself up as though beside God; but, as he grew in the guilt of pride, he now exalts himself above everything that is called God and worshiped as God.

Because this pride of his will be struck down by the coming of the strict Judge, as it is written, “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the appearance of his coming” (ibid., 8), it is rightly said: “And the lofty arm will be broken.”

### 19. The power of the divine word increases the more it is ground down.

All these matters, although examined twice, can still be understood in another way. The words of God are like certain medicinal substances prepared for our help. And just as a medicinal substance grows stronger in its cup the more it is ground, so the more we grind down the divine utterances through exposition, the more we help our hearers, as though they were drinking them [Note: Gussanville and some editions read: “the more they are ground down through exposition, the more the hearers are helped.” The present reading has been corrected from English, Norman, Laudian, and Corbie Germanicus manuscripts].

[Old V.] Since merciful God tolerates human sins for a long time and, when he sees the end already near, often changes the minds of sinners, he rightly reveals the force of such great compassion when he says:

### CHAPTER IX

**Verse 13.**—“Have you held the extremities of the earth while shaking them, and shaken the wicked out of it?”

### 20. God does not abandon the human being, and at the end he purifies the elect with greater care.

By “earth” is signified the human being who thinks of lowly things; to the sinner it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). But because the gracious Creator does not abandon his creature, he tolerates human evils both through his wisdom and, at times, releases them through their conversion [Note: Vindobonensis, Ebroicensis, other Norman witnesses, Laudianus, and others read this way. The editions together with Corbie Germanicus read: “and tolerates them through his patience.” Perhaps, judging that “to tolerate” belongs more properly to patience than to wisdom, they thought this word should be changed.].

When he sees hard and insensitive minds, he terrifies them sometimes with threats, sometimes with blows, sometimes with revelations, so that those who had hardened themselves in the worst security may soften through a salutary fear, return even at the last moment, and blush at least for the fact that they were long awaited [Note: Laudianus: “had endured.”].

Thus the Lord judges the final moments of our life more strictly and therefore purifies his elect more carefully at the end. For it is written: “God will judge the ends of the earth” (1 Samuel 2:10). He watches over our final moments with all the greater diligence because he considers that the beginnings of the life to come depend upon them.

Because he does this mercifully, and because he instructs blessed Job in his justice by bringing forward his compassion, through which he receives even sinners converted at the last, he says: “Have you entered the depths of the sea and walked about in the farthest parts of the abyss?”

The sense is: “I often shake sinners in their final moments by terrifying them, hold them by converting them, and tear away from their hearts the movements of wicked thoughts.” The Lord rightly discloses to blessed Job how he converts sinners near the end. It is as though he were saying openly: “Consider the power of my mercy and restrain the pride of your justice.”

Since the final state of the human being, even when he is converted, is accompanied by the retribution for ancient guilt through the death of the flesh, he immediately makes this clear when he says:

### CHAPTER X

**Verse 14.**—“He will be restored as clay for the seal, and he will stand like a garment.”

### 21. The human being, God’s seal and image, becomes earth and ashes through death as punishment for pride.

The Lord made the human being, whom he created in his likeness, like a certain seal of his power. Yet he will be restored as clay, because although through conversion he escapes eternal punishments, he is nevertheless condemned, in retribution for his pride, to the death of the flesh.

The human being was formed from clay and, having received reason in his mind, was adorned with the likeness of the divine image. But, swelling with pride of heart, he forgot that he had been formed from lowly matter. Thus, by the wondrous justice of the Creator, because he swelled through the understanding he had received, he became earth again through death—the very earth he had refused humbly to acknowledge himself to be. And because by sinning he lost the likeness of God, while by dying he returns to the material of his clay, it is rightly said: “He will be restored as clay for the seal.”

And because, when the spirit is called away from the body, the human being is stripped of his flesh as though of a kind of covering [Col. 0489A], it is aptly added concerning the same clay: “And he will stand like a garment.”

For our clay “standing like a garment” means that, stripped and empty, it endures until the time of the resurrection. But because this punishment of pride does not pass away even for those who overcome that same pride by living humbly, he adds what the particular punishment of the proud will be, saying:

### CHAPTER XI

**Verse 15.**—“His light will be taken away from the wicked, and the lofty arm will be broken.”

### 22. The death that restores the elect to their light takes away light from the reprobate—namely, the glory of the present life.

The death of the flesh, which restores the elect to their own light, takes away their light from the reprobate. For the light of the proud person is the glory of the present life. This light is taken away from him when, through the destruction of the flesh, he is summoned to the darkness of his retribution [Note: Turonensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman witnesses, together with Laudianus, read “of their retributions.” The editions have *rationum* (“of accounts”) instead of *retributionum*. Corbie Germanicus supports the manuscript reading, though it previously had *orationum* (“of prayers”).].

There the lofty arm is broken, because the height of the heart, violently seized beyond the order of nature, is shattered by the weight of divine justice pressing it down. Thus, because it had perversely raised itself up for a short time, it recognizes that, under the weight of judgment, it has been broken forever.

None of us would know what follows death if the Creator of our life had not come even to the punishment of our death. For unless he himself had mercifully descended to the lowly places, he would not justly have recalled us, lost though we were, to the heights according to his image.

Hence it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XII [Rec. VII]

**Verse 16.**—“Have you entered the depths of the sea and walked about in the farthest parts of the abyss?”

### 23. The Lord descended for us not only into the world but also into hell.

It is as though he were saying: “I not only entered the sea—that is, the world—by assuming human flesh and a human soul, but, through that flesh and soul willingly placed in death, I also descended to the lowest parts of hell, as though to the depths of the sea.”

If, in accordance with the manner of divine speech, “sea” should be understood as the world, nothing prevents “the depths of the sea” from being understood as the prison of hell. The Lord entered these depths of the sea when he entered the lowest parts of hell to rescue the souls of his elect.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “You made a way through the depths of the sea, so that the redeemed might pass over” (Isaiah 51:10). Before the coming of the Redeemer, this depth of the sea was not a way but a prison, because it enclosed within itself even the souls of the good, although not in places of punishment.

Yet the Lord made this depth a way, because when he came there he granted his elect passage from the prison of hell to the heavenly places. Hence it is aptly said there: “So that they might pass over in freedom” (ibid., 10).

What he had called “the depth of the sea,” he repeats in other words by calling it “the farthest part of the abyss,” because just as the abyss of waters cannot be grasped by any sight of ours, so the hidden places of hell cannot be penetrated by any faculty of our understanding [Note: Laudianus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman witnesses: “by any sense of thought.”]. We see those who are taken away from here, but we do not see what retribution of punishments awaits them according to their merits.

### [Old VI.] 24. He walked about in hell because he came free among those held captive.

We should carefully consider that he declares himself to have walked about in the farthest part of the abyss [Note: Laudianus and Corbie Germanicus: “in the farthest part.”]. Walking about belongs to one who is not bound but free. Whoever is held by chains is likewise hindered in his steps.

Since the Lord bore no bonds of sin, he walked about in hell. He came free among those held captive. Hence it is written: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5).

For the Lord to walk about in the farthest parts of the abyss is for him to find nothing in the place of condemnation that could hold him, as Peter testifies: “Having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24).

Or certainly, because when we walk from place to place we are present here and there, the Lord is said to have walked about in hell to show that, by the power of his divinity, he was present among the elect souls in their various places.

Hence the spirit of wisdom is described as mobile (Wisdom 7:4), so that by this it may be shown that, because it is absent from no place, it meets us everywhere. The Lord regards this descent of his as all the more wondrous insofar as he pours it more frequently into redeemed humanity.

Repeating this descent, he adds:

### CHAPTER XIII

**Verse 17.**—“Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?”

### 25. He overcame the gates of death—that is, the hostile powers.

The gates of death are the hostile powers. The Lord opened them when he descended, because by dying he overcame their strength. They are also called “dark doors,” because, hidden by the ambushes of their concealment, they are not seen and open the way of death to deceived minds.

The Lord sees these dark doors because he both observes and restrains the deceptive wickedness of unclean spirits. If he did not see and restrain them without our knowledge, our mind would know nothing of their ambushes and, captured by those same ambushes, would perish.

We too see these dark doors when we are illumined by the rays of the heavenly light. Hence it is said through the prophet: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall see my enemies” (Psalm 117:7). He himself sees our enemies because by his gift he makes them visible to us.

Or certainly, the Lord saw the dark doors at that time when, penetrating the prison of hell, he struck the cruel spirits and, by dying, condemned the rulers of death. This is said here not of the future but already of the past because what he was going to accomplish in deed he had already accomplished in predestination.

Because the Church grew after his death and resurrection and was extended among all the nations, it is aptly added:

### CHAPTER XIV [Old VII]

**Verse 18.**—“Have you considered the breadth of the earth?”

### 26. The Church grew through Christ’s death. Like Samson, he destroyed more enemies by dying than by living.

When the Lord entered the narrow confines of death, he extended his faith among the nations and spread the holy Church into countless hearts of believers. Through the prophet it is said to her: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes, for you will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations” (Isaiah 54:2).

This breadth of the earth certainly would not have come about unless he had first disdained, by dying, the life known to us and then, by rising again, shown the life unknown to us. In his death he opened the eyes of our mind and showed what the life to follow would be.

Hence, preserving this order in the Gospel, he says to his disciples: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24:46).

For while he himself preached, only a few from the people of Israel believed; but countless peoples of the nations followed the way of life when he died. While he still lived in a passible body, he endured the proud; but, dead, he struck down many from that passible life [Note: Vindobonensis, Corbie Germanicus, Pratellensis, and Uticensis agree. Laudianus also reads this way, except that it corruptly has *mortuos* (“the dead”) instead of *mortuus* (“dead”). The editions read: “while he lived a passible life, he struck down many when he died.”].

Samson once figurally expressed this well in himself (Judges 16:30): while alive he killed only a few, but when the temple was destroyed, he killed countless enemies as he died. In the same way the Lord destroyed a few from the arrogance of pride while he lived, but many more when the temple of his body was dissolved (John 2:19); and the elect from the nations, whom he had endured while living, he struck down all together by dying.

Therefore, after he had shown that he had penetrated the regions below, he immediately added that the breadth of the earth should be considered: “Have you considered the breadth of the earth?” It is as though he were saying to the afflicted human being: “Consider what I endured, and weigh what I purchased; do not complain about your own scourging while you do not know what rewards await you in the retribution.”

Amid these words of the Creator, I think it worthwhile to turn our eyes for a little while from the common and public good and observe what he secretly accomplishes in each of us. For he says:

### CHAPTER XV [Rec. VIII]

**Verse 16.**—“Have you entered the depths of the sea?”

### 27. God enters the depths of the sea when he visits the mind of a sinner.

The sea is the human mind. God enters its depths when, through self-knowledge, the mind is disturbed from its innermost thoughts into the laments of repentance, when it recalls the wickedness of its former life and shakes its wavering spirit in confusion [Note: Ebroicensis and other Norman witnesses: “turns his spirit toward confession.” Vindobonensis likewise reads “turns.”].

God penetrates the depths of the sea when he changes even hearts that seemed beyond hope. He enters the sea when he humbles the worldly heart; he enters the depths of the sea when he does not disdain to visit minds oppressed by crimes [Note: Vindobonensis, Laudianus, Pratellensis, and others: “for thus he enters the sea.” Corbie Germanicus: “if indeed he enters.”].

Hence it is rightly added in the form of a question: “And have you walked about in the farthest parts of the abyss?” [Note: Ebroicensis and others: “For what is it?”]

For what is the abyss except the human mind? Since it cannot comprehend itself, it hides itself, in all that it is, like a dark abyss. Hence it is well said through the prophet: “The abyss gave forth its voice from the height of its imagination” (Habakkuk 3:10), because, since the human mind does not penetrate itself, from comparison with itself it praises more humbly the power of the divine nature, which it is unable to comprehend.

### 28. He walks about in the farthest parts of the abyss when he converts the hearts of the most wicked.

For God to walk about in the farthest parts of the abyss means that he converts even the hearts of the most wicked and wonderfully reforms minds that seemed beyond hope by touching them with the traces of his visitation.

When, after immense crimes, a person is pierced with remorse, what else appears to be happening than that God is walking about in the farthest parts of the abyss? God walks about as though in an abyss when, penetrating the dark heart, he treads down the invisible waves of vices.

Often we lament some past sins while being oppressed by other present ones: at one time we are exhausted by the temptation of pride, at another by anger, at another by lust, and at another by greed. But when the Lord restrains all these things in our heart through fear of his hidden visitation, what else does he do than place his steps in the abyss?

We see these steps in our mind when we consider how the gifts of his fear confront the vices rising against us. The prophet had seen these steps when he said: “Your processions have been seen, O God, the processions of my God, my King, who is in his sanctuary” (Psalm 67:25).

Whoever sees the disordered movements of his spirit being restrained within him by the memory of divine judgments sees, as it were, the steps of the Lord walking within him.

Let it therefore be said to blessed Job: “Have you entered the depths of the sea and walked about in the farthest parts of the abyss?” The implied sense is: “I, who in wondrous mercy tread down now anger, now lust, now greed, now the pride rising up in the hearts of sinners” [Note: The manuscript tradition varies: “for thus God enters the sea” / “if indeed God enters the sea.”].

It is as though he were told openly: “If you see that I alone restrain the hidden vices of the heart, you will cease to be elated over your own righteousness.”

[Old VIII.] And because, when we are visited by God, we are led to confession even concerning the hidden and unlawful movements of the mind, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XVI

**Verse 17.**—“Have the gates of death been opened to you?”

### 29. The gates of death are wicked thoughts, which we open before God through confession.

The gates of death are wicked thoughts, which we open before God when we confess them with tears in repentance. He sees them even when they are not confessed, but he enters them when they are confessed. He opens a way for himself through the gates of death when, after confession, he comes to us once our wicked thoughts have been loosed.

They are called the gates of death because the way to destruction is always opened through wicked thoughts [Note: The word “always” is absent from Pratellensis and some others. It might rightly be removed unless the discussion here concerned adults alone; for it is certain that infants dying in original sin proceed to destruction by another gate than that of wicked thoughts.].

This is repeated when it is added:

**The same passage.—“And have you seen the dark doors?”**

### 30. The dark doors are the hidden evils of the mind.

The dark doors are the hidden evils of the mind, which can be possessed inwardly but cannot be seen by another. Yet the Lord sees them when he destroys them through the hidden regard of grace.

For it is written: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze” (Proverbs 20:8).

And because every vice constricts the soul, while every virtue enlarges it, after the vices have been destroyed it is rightly added: “Have you considered the breadth of the earth?”

For unless virtue enlarged the soul, Paul would never say to the Corinthians: “You too must be enlarged, and do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:13).

We must carefully observe what is said:

### CHAPTER XVII

**Verse 18.**—“Have you considered the breadth of the earth?”

### 31. While the saints are pressed by afflictions outwardly, they are enlarged inwardly.

The breadth of interior goods cannot be grasped unless it is considered carefully [Note: Ebroicensis, other Norman witnesses, and Laudianus: “the breadth of interior goods is not at all comprehended.” Corbie Germanicus agrees, and additionally reads *ante* (“before”) instead of *caute* (“carefully”).].

Often poverty humbles such people outwardly and the torment of punishment constricts them; yet amid all this their inner strength continually expands toward the hope of heavenly things [Note: *Se* is absent from Corbie Germanicus, Pratellensis, Uticensis, and others, which therefore read: “their strength … enlarges,” just as above: “poverty humbles, torment constricts.”].

The apostles were outwardly constricted when they endured scourging, but inwardly they stood in great freedom and breadth, turning those same scourges into joy within themselves. For it is written: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

Paul found this breadth amid afflictions when he said: “I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has actually served to advance the Gospel, so that my chains have become known throughout the whole praetorium” (Philippians 1:12).

David possessed this breadth amid afflictions when he said: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Psalm 4:2) [Note: Turonensis and Laudianus read “desired.” The better reading, “possessed,” is found in Corbie Germanicus, Pratellensis, Uticensis, and most others.].

This earth—that is, the conscience of the saints—is enlarged when it is pressed outwardly by the adversities of this world. When it is driven away from the security of the present life, it is forced inward toward itself so that it may strive toward the things above. When it is not permitted to wander outward, it is recalled, as it were, into its own bosom and is enlarged.

We see what adversities good people endure, but we do not see how much they rejoice inwardly. We recognize the breadth of their minds by considering their words and deeds, but we do not know how great the extent of that breadth is [Note: Pratellensis: “we recognize it by considering it.”].

Let human wisdom therefore hear and learn that it is foolish: “Have you considered the breadth of the earth?” It is as though he were saying: “I alone fully consider the hidden joy of the just, encircled as they are by scourges, because I alone mercifully form it” [Note: So Vindobonensis, Corbie Germanicus, Laudianus, Pratellensis, and others, as well as the old edition. Recent editions read “let it say” instead of “let it learn.” The recent printed editions have *plane* (“fully”). The manuscripts Turonensis, Vindobonensis, Laudianus, Corbie Germanicus, and the older printed editions support *misericorditer* (“mercifully”); the recent editions read *firmo* (“I establish”).].

Or perhaps blessed Job is asked whether he has considered the breadth of the earth so that he may be humbled by the example of another’s breadth. It is as though he were told openly: “Consider those whom the countless evils of the present life cannot constrict, and cease to boast about the state of your heart amid blows” [Note: The editions read *inter verba* (“amid words”), but the sequence of the sermon proves that *inter verbera* (“amid blows”) should be read; this is also found in Corbie Germanicus, English, Norman, and other manuscripts.].

### CHAPTER XVII [Old and Rec. IX]

**Verses 18–20.**—“Tell me, if you know all things, in what way the light dwells, and where the place of darkness is, so that you may lead each thing to its proper boundaries and understand the paths of its house.”

### 32. By “light” righteousness is signified, and by “darkness” wickedness. We do not know who will persevere in righteousness or die in sin.

Blessed Job is examined by a grave question, so that he may be asked both where the way of light dwells and what place belongs to darkness, in order that he may lead each to its appointed boundaries and understand the paths of its house. For what is understood by the name “light” except righteousness? And what is designated by “darkness” except wickedness? Hence it is said to some who have been converted from the wickedness of sins: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). And of some who remain in sin it is recorded: “Those who sleep, sleep at night” (1 Thessalonians 5:7).

Therefore it is said to blessed Job: “Tell me, if you know all things, in what way does light dwell, and what place does darkness occupy?” As though it were said to him: If you suppose that you possess complete knowledge, say either into whose heart the innocence that is now absent may come, or in whose heart the wickedness that is now present may persist. [Note: The printed editions, with Corbiacensis Germanicus, read “in whose heart”; Vindocensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “into whose heart.”] “In what way does light dwell”—that is, whose mind is filled when righteousness comes; “and what place does darkness occupy”—that is, in whom blind wickedness continues; “so that you may lead each to its appointed boundaries”—that is, so that you may judge whether the one who is now seen to be wicked will end his life in wickedness, or whether the one who is seen to be righteous will conclude the extremity of his life with the perfection of righteousness; “and understand the paths of its house”—that is, consider and discern either to whom persevering good action grants an eternal dwelling in the kingdom, or whom evil action, binding him to his appointed end, condemns to everlasting punishment.

“House,” then, is put for dwelling, and “path” for action. The path therefore leads to the house, because action draws one toward one’s dwelling. But who among human beings, once examined in these matters, could speak thus? Who could hear them, at least, without terror? For every day we see many who shine with the light of righteousness and yet, at their end, are darkened by the obscurity of wickedness; and we observe many wrapped in the darkness of sins who nevertheless, near the end of their lives, are suddenly restored free to the light of righteousness. [Note: Corbiacensis Germanicus, Ebroicensis, and others read “restored to the light of righteousness.” So too the old Paris and Basel editions.]

We also know many who have once found the way of righteousness and kept it undefiled until death, while we have seen very many accumulate, without cessation, the sins they once began, right up to their end.

### 33. The clouds of God’s judgments are impenetrable to the rays of our mind.

Who, amid these clouds of hidden judgments, could send forth the ray of his mind so as to discern by any reflection who will persist in evil, who will persevere in good, who will be converted from the depths to the heights, or who will return from the heights to the depths?
