[Note: Pratelensis, Laudunensis, and others read “be driven back.”] These things are hidden from human understanding, and nothing concerning anyone’s end can be known, because the abyss of divine judgments cannot in any way be penetrated by the eye of the human mind.

For we see that the Gentile world, once hostile to God, has been suffused with the light of righteousness, while Judea, formerly beloved, has been blinded by the night of unbelief. We also know that the thief passed from the gallows to the kingdom (Luke 23:43), while Judas fell from the glory of apostleship into Tartarus (Matthew 27:5). Again, since sometimes the lots that have begun are not changed, we know that another thief reached punishment, while we know that the apostles received the kingdom they had desired and sought.

Who, then, could examine in what way light dwells and what place darkness occupies, so as to lead each to its appointed boundaries and understand the paths of its house? I see Paul called from the fury of persecution to the grace of apostleship (Acts 9:1 ff.), and yet he fears amid these hidden judgments so greatly that he is afraid he may be rejected even after he has been called. For he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). And again: “I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. But forgetting what lies behind and stretching myself toward what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. I pursue it, however, if I may apprehend that for which I have also been apprehended” (Philippians 3:13). [Note: Turonensis reads, “forgetting what lies behind”; Corbiacensis Germanicus, “but forgetting the things that lie behind.”]

And certainly it had already been said of him by the voice of the Lord: “He is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9:15); yet even then, chastising his body, he feared that he might be rejected.

### 34. Let fear accompany our hope rather than security. Woe even to a praiseworthy life if it is judged without mercy.

Woe to us miserable people, who have not yet learned any word of God concerning our election and already grow sluggish in idleness as though we were secure. In hope there ought certainly to be not security alone but also fear in our manner of life, so that the former may encourage those who are striving and the latter prick those who are growing sluggish. Hence the prophet rightly says: “Those who fear the Lord, hope in the Lord” (Psalm 113:11). As though he were saying openly: He presumes upon hope in vain who refuses to fear God in his works.

But why is blessed Job questioned about so profound a matter, one entirely unknown to human beings, so that he might grasp the end of the righteous and the wicked? It is so that, unable to know another’s end, he may return to his own; for just as he does not know another’s end, so also he does not know his own. Thus, being ignorant, he may fear; fearing, he may be humbled; and once humbled, he ought no longer to be lifted up by his works. Then, not puffed up, he may remain established in the citadel of grace.

Therefore let it be said to him: [Note: Vindocensis, Pratelensis, and other Norman manuscripts read, “Tell me, if you know all things,” as in the Vulgate. Nevertheless, we have retained the reading of Corbiacensis Germanicus and the printed editions because we believe that Saint Gregory adopted it, and not without reason. If he had followed the other reading, namely that of the Vulgate, what reason would there have been for scribes to alter it? On the contrary, when they observed that these words, “if you have understanding,” differed from the text of Job, they omitted them and restored “if you know all things,” as it is read in Job.]

“Tell me, if you have understanding, in what way light dwells and what place darkness occupies, so that you may lead each to its appointed boundaries.”

As though it were said: Just as you do not know who will be converted from evil to good or who will return from good to evil, so also you do not understand what will happen to you according to what your merits demand. And just as you cannot in any way comprehend another’s end, so you cannot foresee your own. You know how much you have already advanced, but you do not know what I still secretly think of you. You consider the deeds of your righteousness, but you do not know how strictly they are weighed before me.

Woe even to the praiseworthy life of human beings if it is judged without mercy, because, rigorously examined, it is overwhelmed before the eyes of the Judge by the very thing from which it supposes that it pleases him. Hence it is rightly said to God through the prophet: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2). Hence Solomon rightly says: “There are righteous and wise people, and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Ecclesiastes 9:1). Again, through the same Solomon it is said: “Who among human beings can understand his way?” (Proverbs 20:24).

Certainly a person is known to be doing good or evil by the testimony of conscience. But it is said that his way is unknown to human beings because, even if someone understands that he is performing righteous works, he nevertheless does not know, under strict examination, toward what end he is advancing.

[Old and Recent X.] After terrifying him, therefore, by consideration of his end, God returns to examine his beginning. And lest Job complain that he does not know his end, he is also reminded that he does not understand by what beginning he came here. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 21.**—“Did you know then that you would be born, and did you know the number of your days?”

### 35. No human being knows his own beginning or his end.

As though he were saying openly: What is surprising if you do not understand your end, when you do not comprehend even your beginning? And since you do not know by what beginning you came here, what is surprising if you do not know by what end you will be taken away? If it was mine to bring you forth from hidden things into the open by your beginning, it will also be mine to recall you from the open into hidden things. Why do you complain about the ordering of your life, when you are held unknowingly in the hand of the craftsman?

Therefore you ought all the more not to exalt yourself in what you do, since, enclosed within the bosom of eternity, you recognize neither by what order you came here nor when or how you will be led away.

### 36. Christ is exempt from this law.

These words may nevertheless be understood in another way: “Did you know then that you would be born, and did you know the number of your days?” The implied sense is: as I did, who knew that I would be born, because even before the birth of my humanity I always existed substantially in divinity.

Human beings begin to exist when they are born in their mothers’ wombs. Indeed, conception itself is also called birth, according to what is written: “What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20). They therefore do not know that they will be born because they do not exist before they are created.

But God, who has always existed without beginning, foreknew concerning himself that that which took its beginning in the Virgin’s womb would be so;“ [Note: Vindocensis, Laudunensis, Pratelensis, and others read “took its beginning.” The printed editions, with Corbiacensis Germanicus, read “assumed its beginning.”] and because he foreknew it, he ordained it. Because he ordained it, he certainly endured nothing in human form without his will.

Let a human being, therefore, be convicted of why he complains about his scourges, when he could not foresee his own birth, [Note: Pratelensis reads, “when he himself.”] if even he who ordained his own birth by foreknowledge prepared himself among human beings for scourges.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XX [Recent XI]

**VERSES 22–23.**—“Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or have you looked upon the storehouses of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?”

### 37. The wicked are preserved for the testing of the righteous.

What else should be understood by snow or hail except the cold and hardened hearts of the wicked? For just as charity is usually signified in sacred eloquence by heat, so malice is signified by cold. For it is written: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so malice makes the soul cold” (Jeremiah 6:7). And again: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). [Note: Laudunensis, Pratelensis, and Uticensis read *abundavit* (“has abounded”).]

What, then, can more suitably be understood in the coldness of snow or the hardness of hail than the life of the wicked, which grows cold through apathy and strikes through the malice of hardness? [Note: Pratelensis reads “through the hardness of malice.”] Yet the Lord endures their life because he preserves them for the testing of his righteous.

Hence he rightly added: “Which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war.” When our adversary, the devil, tries to tempt us, he uses their behavior against us as though they were his weapons. Through them he rages and torments us, but without knowing it he purifies us. They become scourges through our sins; while we are struck by their manner of life, we are freed from eternal death.

Thus it comes about that even the lost life of the reprobate benefits the lives of the elect; and while their destruction serves our usefulness, by a wonderful dispensation it is brought about that nothing that perishes is also lost to God’s elect.

[Old XI.] ### 38. Some of them are elect and called to the greatest things.

This may also be understood in another way, so that, because it appears joined to the preceding words, it does not differ from the exposition of the preceding verse. Since he had indicated that either the good could be converted to evil or the wicked to good, he immediately added:

“Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or have you looked upon the storehouses of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?”

In the coldness of snow or hail, or in their hardness, as has been said, we understand the hearts of the wicked. But because almighty God chose his saints from among such people, and knows how many of the elect he still has hidden amid the life of the wicked, he appropriately declares that he has storehouses in snow and hail.

The word “treasure” (*thesaurus*) is derived from ἀπὸ τῆς θέσεως (*apo tēs theseōs*), that is, “from placement.” He looks upon many who lie hidden for a long time in a cold life; when he commands, he brings them forth into the midst and displays them, made bright with the radiance of righteousness through heavenly grace. For it is written: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Psalm 50:9).

He conceals them for a long time, prepared for the day of battle and combat, within the bosom of his foreknowledge. But when he suddenly brings them forth, he strikes the resisting breasts of their adversaries with their words and reproaches as with hailstones. [Note: Turonensis and Laudunensis read “are struck.”] Hence it is written elsewhere: “Before his brightness the clouds passed by, hail and coals of fire” (Psalm 17:13).

The clouds pass before his brightness because holy preachers traverse all the spaces of the world with the brilliance of miracles. They are also called hail and coals of fire because they strike through correction and kindle through the flame of charity.

The uninhibited rebuke of the saints is also appropriately expressed by the nature of hail. Hail strikes when it falls and waters when it melts. Holy men likewise strike the hearts of their hearers by frightening them and pour themselves into them by soothing them. How they strike, the prophet testifies, saying: “They shall speak of the might of your terrible acts, and they shall tell of your greatness” (Psalm 144:6). And how they water by soothing, he adds: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they shall rejoice in your righteousness” (ibid., 7).

There are therefore storehouses in snow and hail, because many who are cold through the torpor of wickedness, taken up into heavenly grace, shine in the holy Church with the light of righteousness and batter the perverse knowledge of their adversaries with the blows of their teaching. [Note: The old Paris and Basel editions and other later editions, with Corbiacensis Germanicus, read “taken up from heavenly grace”; Turonensis, Vindocensis, Laudunensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “taken up into heavenly grace.”]

Hence it is appropriately added: “Which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war.” [Old XII.]

Saul had been snow and hail through his cold insensibility; but he became snow and hail against the breasts of his adversaries, either through the whiteness of righteousness or through the correction of stern eloquence. What a storehouse the Lord had in snow and hail when, placing him among the wicked, he secretly saw him already as his chosen one! To how many breasts of adversaries did he take this hail in his hand, through which he cast down so many hearts resisting him!

### 39. Let no one be elated; let no one despair.

Let no one therefore be elated over his works; let no one despair of those whom he still sees to be cold, because he does not see God’s storehouses in snow and hail. For who would have believed that the one who guarded the garments of all those stoning Stephen at his death would, through the grace of apostleship, precede Stephen whom he had stoned? (Acts 7:57.)

If, then, we return to these hidden gifts or judgments, let us despair of no one at all, nor prefer ourselves in our hearts to those over whom we are temporarily placed. For although we now see how far we have advanced, we do not know how far we will be surpassed when they begin to run.

Therefore it is rightly said to blessed Job: “Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or have you looked upon the storehouses of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?”

As though it were said openly: Prefer no one to yourself because of your works, since you do not know how many of those whom you see still cold through guilt I will make workers of righteousness and defenders of the true faith. [Note: Laudunensis reads “how many [I will make] through workers of righteousness.”] And because this is accomplished through the coming of the Mediator, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXI [Recent XII]

**VERSE 24.**—“By what way is light dispersed?”

### 40. Through the coming of the Mediator, light is dispersed.

He himself is the way who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Through this way, therefore, light is dispersed because through his presence the whole Gentile world is illumined.

He appropriately said “dispersed,” because through the voices of the apostles the light of preaching did not appear narrowed or confined but shone forth broadly. Since, however, once the light of conversion has been received, the force of love burns inwardly, so that past evils may be mourned anxiously and future goods desired with the greatest ardor, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0499C]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“The heat is divided over the earth.”

### 41. From this light the ardor of charity and the heat of persecution blaze forth.

When light has been dispersed, the heat is divided over the earth because, through righteousness preached openly, the anxiety of the heart is expanded into the exercise of virtue in seeking God. Thus one may shine in the word of wisdom, another in the word of knowledge; one may grow strong through the gift of healings, another through the working of virtues; and while individuals receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit differently, all, necessarily joined to one another, may be kindled with one accord (1 Corinthians 12:8).

[Old XIII.] But after it is said that light is dispersed, it may appropriately be understood that persecution is signified by heat, because as the light of preaching shone forth, the heat of persecution immediately blazed up from the hearts of the unbelieving.

For that persecution is expressed by heat, the Lord’s saying testifies concerning the seeds scattered on rocky ground: “When the sun rose, everything was scorched, and because it had no root, it withered” (Matthew 13:6). [Note: Laudunensis, Corbiacensis Germanicus, Pratelensis, and others read: “for when the light of preaching had shone forth, immediately …”; Vindocensis, Corbiacensis Germanicus, Pratelensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “upon rocky ground”; Corbiacensis Germanicus, Pratelensis, and Uticensis read *aestuaverunt omnia*, “all were scorched.”] When he explained this shortly afterward, he called the heat persecution.

Therefore, when light had been dispersed, the heat was divided over the earth, because, as the life of the faithful became bright, the cruelty of unbelievers was kindled. The heat was divided when persecution raged now in Jerusalem, now in Damascus, now in other distant regions.

For it is written: “On that day a great persecution arose against the Church that was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria” (Acts 8:1). Again it is written: “Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women belonging to this way, he might lead them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:1 ff.). [Note: Pratelensis, Uticensis, and other Norman witnesses read, “still breathing threats and slaughter.”]

Since persecution therefore increased now here, now there, those who had recognized the light of truth gasped, as it were, beneath the heat divided among them.

### 42. Light is righteousness, which is dispersed only progressively.

But since we have heard in the preceding words that blessed Job was questioned about hidden judgments, we ought to examine more subtly what is said about dispersed light and divided heat. He is still examined by a profound question, so that at least he may be taught that he does not know, and it is said to him:

“By what way is light dispersed, and the heat divided over the earth?”

For what is designated by the name “light” except righteousness? Of it it is written: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).

Everything that is dispersed, however, is scattered not continuously but with a certain interruption. Therefore light is said to be dispersed because, although we already perceive certain things as they are, we do not perceive other things as they ought to be seen.

The heart of Peter was held by dispersed light. He had shone with such great faith and such a radiance of miracles, and yet, when he imposed the burden of circumcision upon the converted Gentiles, he did not know what he ought rightly to say.

Light is therefore dispersed in this life because continuous understanding of every matter is not possessed. While we comprehend one thing as it is and remain ignorant of another, we see partly, as though by dispersed light, and partly remain in darkness. But then the light will no longer be dispersed for us, when our mind, wholly snatched up to God, shines.

### 43. We do not know by what means it is insinuated into the human heart.

And because it is unknown by what means this same light insinuates itself into the human heart, it is rightly asked: “By what way is light dispersed?” [Note: Longipontanus reads “by interrogation”; Laudunensis, “by hesitation.”] As though it were said openly: Tell me by what order I pour my righteousness into the hidden recesses of hearts, when I do not appear to come by a visible approach and yet invisibly transform the visible works of human beings; [Note: Laudunensis reads “by ascent,” incorrectly.] when I illuminate one and the same mind now with this virtue, now with that, and yet, through dispersed light, still permit it to remain partly in the darkness of temptation.

Let the human being be questioned, since he does not know by what way light is dispersed, as though it were plainly said: While I soften hard hearts, bend what is rigid, calm what is harsh, kindle what is cold, strengthen what is weak, stabilize what wanders, and confirm what wavers, observe, if you can, by what channels I illuminate them as I come incorporeally.

We see all these things accomplished, but we do not know how they are effected inwardly. That this way of light is invisible to us, the Truth shows in the Gospel, saying: “The Spirit breathes where it wills; you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8). [Note: Vindocensis, Laudunensis, and Corbiacensis Germanicus read, “but you do not know from where it comes.” Pratelensis and Uticensis agree.]

[Old XIV.] ### 44. As this light increases, temptations increase.

But because, when light is dispersed, temptations immediately increase from the hidden adversary against the shining mind, it is rightly added: “The heat is divided over the earth.”

The crafty enemy strives to inflame with unlawful desires the minds of those whom he sees shining with the light of righteousness, so that they often feel themselves more heavily pressed by temptations than when they did not see the rays of inward light.

Hence the Israelites, after they had been called, complained against Moses [Note: “And Aaron” is absent from Corbiacensis Germanicus, Vindocensis, Laudunensis, Pratelensis, and others.] and Aaron about their increasing labor, saying: “May the Lord look upon this and judge, because you have made our fragrance offensive before Pharaoh and his servants, and you have given them a sword to kill us” (Exodus 5:21).

When they wished to depart from Egypt, Pharaoh had taken away their straw, yet he still required bricks in the same quantity. [Note: Ebroicensis, other Norman manuscripts, and Vindocensis read “he required bricks.”] Thus the mind murmurs, as it were, against the law after its knowledge, bearing sharper goads of temptation; and when it sees its labors increasing, it grieves, because of what displeases the adversary, as though it had become offensive in Pharaoh’s eyes.

After light, therefore, heat follows, because after the illumination of the divine gift the struggle of temptation increases.

### 45. The enemy solicits each of us toward evil according to our individual disposition.

It is also rightly said that the heat is divided, because individuals are not wearied by every vice indiscriminately but by certain neighboring and closely related vices. The ancient adversary first observes each person’s disposition—the various dispositions of body and soul—and then lays the snares of temptation.

One person is cheerful, another sorrowful; one timid, another proud. The hidden adversary therefore prepares deceptions near to their dispositions, so that he may seize them easily.

Because the pleasure of lust lies close to cheerfulness, he proposes sexual vice to the cheerful. Because sorrow easily slips into anger, he offers the cup of discord to the sorrowful. Because the timid fear punishments, he threatens the fearful with terrors. And because he sees the proud lifted up by praise, he draws them wherever he wishes with flattering favors.

He therefore lies in wait for each person with vices suited to him. For he would not easily capture the lustful if he proposed rewards to the avaricious, or prostitutes to the greedy; nor would he assault the gluttonous with the glory of abstinence, or the abstinent with the weakness of gluttony; nor would he seek to capture the gentle through the pursuit of conflict, or the irascible through the fear of dread. [Note: The Basel edition of 1514, the Paris edition of 1518, the Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville editions read “through the favor of fear,” an obvious error, which we have corrected with the English, Norman, Corbiacensis Germanicus, Laudunensis, and other manuscripts, as well as the old Paris editions of 1488 and 1495 and the Basel edition of 1503.]

Since, therefore, in the heat of temptation he craftily lies in wait for each person and hides snares suited to his character, it is rightly said: “The heat is divided over the earth.”

### 46. God regulates temptations, so that they are neither too numerous nor excessive.

When the words “By what way is light dispersed?” are placed first and “The heat is divided over the earth” immediately follows, it is plainly indicated that the heat is divided by the same way through which light is dispersed.

For when the profound and incomprehensible grace of the Holy Spirit illuminates our minds with its light, it also regulates the adversary’s temptations by its dispensation, so that many do not come at once, or so that only those which can be endured touch the soul already illumined by God. Thus, although they torment us with the heat of their contact, they do not consume us in the fire of perfection.

Paul testifies to this when he says: “God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide an escape, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13). [Note: Laudunensis and Corbiacensis Germanicus read, “above what you can bear.”] [Note: Vindocensis, Pratelensis, and other Norman witnesses read “also an outcome,” or “a progress.” In Greek, ἔκβασιν, “an escape” or “way out.”]

The crafty deceiver divides this heat in one way, while the merciful Creator divides it in another. The former divides it so that it may kill more quickly through it; the latter so that he may make it bearable.

And because, when we are wearied by temptation, we are instructed not only by God’s inward Spirit but also helped by the outward words of preachers, it is rightly added after the divided heat:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Old XV, Recent XIII]

**VERSE 25.**—“Who gave a course to the vehement rain?”

### 47. As persecution increased, so did the ardor of the apostles and holy preachers. Without grace, preaching does not reach the heart.

If, as we said above (no. 41), the name “divided heat” signifies that persecution in the regions of Judea, then, because the severity of that persecution did not restrain the holy preachers from the ministry of preaching by any fear, since they were aided by heavenly grace, he appropriately adds:

“Who gave a course to the vehement rain?”

As though he were saying: No one but me. To give a course to the vehement rain after the heat has been divided is to strengthen the force of preaching amid the very hardships of persecution, so that the power of the preachers might increase in proportion as the cruelty of their persecutors increased. Thus they might pour the drops of rain upon the parched hearts of their hearers and water more abundantly the dryness of unbelief; [Note: Laudunensis reads: “so that, as the strength of preaching increased, so … the opposing cruelty might increase.”] and although the heat of cruelty blazed against them, the voice of grace might nevertheless not be silent through them.

Paul both endured and watered this heat of persecution when he said: “I suffer hardship even to chains, as though I were a criminal; but the word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2:9).

Elsewhere it is said of this rain: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon her” (Isaiah 5:6). Of this course of rain, which takes place in the hearts of the elect, the psalmist testifies, saying: “His word runs swiftly” (Psalm 147:15).

Often, however, there is rain but it has no course, because preaching comes to the ears but, when inward grace is absent, does not pass through to the hearts of the hearers. Of the words of this preaching, for the sake of the elect, it is said: “Indeed, your arrows have pierced through” (Psalm 76:19). God’s arrows pierce through when the words of his preaching descend from the ears into the heart.

Since this occurs only through divine grace, the Lord testifies that he has given the rain its course.

### 48. The efficacy of the divine word persuades us to leave everything and endure everything.

But I observe that he calls this same rain not merely vehement but most vehement. Vehement rain is great force; most vehement rain is the immeasurable force of preaching.

The rain was vehement when the holy preachers persuaded people to believe in eternal joys. [Note: Vindocensis, the Norman manuscripts, and Corbiacensis Germanicus read *credi*, “to believe.”] But the rain was most vehement when, for the sake of that hope, they urged people to abandon what they possessed, despise all visible things for the sake of invisible realities, and endure the punishments and sufferings of the present age for the sake of joys they had heard of. [Note: Corbiacensis Germanicus, Vindocensis, Pratelensis, and others read “the punishments of the present age.”]

But when, having come to faith, so many of the elect abandoned their possessions amid the raging heat of persecution, forgot fleshly affections, and, out of joy of spirit, placed their limbs amid tortures, [Note: Corbiacensis Germanicus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “fleshly affections.”] what else did the Lord do except give a course even to the most vehement rain? Through the words of the body he watered the invisible things of the heart, even to the carrying out of the highest commands.

Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Old XVI]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And a way for the resounding thunder.”

[Note: Other editions read “and a way for the sounding thunder.” We follow the Norman manuscripts, which read “for the resounding thunder,” and this is more suitable to what precedes: “Who gave a course to the rain … and a way for the resounding thunder.” Here *tonitrui* is dative.]

### 49. The thunder is compared to this. God alone opens hearts through grace.

What else is understood by thunder except the preaching of heavenly terror? When human hearts perceive this terror, they are shaken.

Sometimes the incarnate Lord himself is represented by thunder. In accordance with the fitting prophecy of the ancient fathers, he was brought to our knowledge as though from the meeting of clouds. Appearing visibly among us, he sounded forth terrifically the things that were above us.

Hence the holy apostles themselves, generated by his grace, were called Boanerges—that is, “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17).

At other times, as has been said, thunder signifies his preaching itself, through which the terror of heavenly judgments is heard.

But although any preacher can give words to the ears, he cannot open hearts; and unless almighty God, through inward grace, invisibly grants access to the hearts of the hearers through the words of the preachers, preaching is perceived by the hearer’s ear in vain, since a deaf heart prevents it from reaching the innermost places.

The Lord therefore asserts that he gives a way to resounding thunder, because, when he grants the words of preaching, he pierces hearts through terror.

The outstanding preacher Paul, while he thundered forth the heavenly mysteries with terror, [Note: Ebroicensis and others read “when he thundered forth.”] recognized that he could not give this way from himself and instructed his disciples, saying: “Pray together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ” (Colossians 4:3).

Although he spoke the mysteries, he prayed that the Lord would open a door for those same mysteries in the hearts of the hearers. He already possessed the thunder, but he sought that a way be given to him from above.

John knew that he could not give this way, for he said: “You have no need for anyone to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about all things” (1 John 2:27). [Note: Pratelensis, Uticensis, Vindocensis, and Corbiacensis Germanicus read, “but as his anointing teaches you.” Turonensis and Laudunensis read, “but according to his instruction.” “As” should be read, in accordance with the Greek text, although it is absent from other printed editions.]

Paul again indicated who could give this way when he said: “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

Let us therefore hear what this rain and thunder accomplish once they have received their way. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXV [Recent XIV]

**VERSE 26.**—“So that it might rain upon the land where no human being dwells, in the desert where no mortal lives.”

### 50. The Gentile world is the desert, watered as by rain from heavenly grace

To rain upon the earth without a man, in the desert, is to preach the word of God to the Gentile world. Since it maintained no worship of the Divinity and displayed in itself no appearance of good works, it was plainly a desert. Because there was no lawgiver in it, nor anyone who rationally sought God, it was as though there were no human being there; and, as if occupied only by wild beasts, it stood empty of mortals. [Note: Pratel.: “of this deserted earth.”]

Of this desert earth it is elsewhere said: “He made a way in the desert” (Isa. 43:19). Of this preaching granted to the Gentile world the Psalmist bears witness, saying: “He made rivers in the desert” (Ps. 106:33).

[Col. 0504C] [Ancient recension XVII.] It should be noted that, after the heat was divided over the earth, the most violent rain received its course so that it might rain in the desert. For after the harshness of persecution had raged in Judaea—so that it not only refused to receive the faith but even attacked it with swords—each preacher sent to Israel turned aside to summon the Gentiles. Hence the holy apostles say to the persecuting Hebrews, whom they are leaving:

“It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

[Note: The same manuscript, together with Corb. Germ., reads “but since you rejected it . . . and judged yourselves.”]

Thus, when the heat has been divided, the deserted earth without a man is drenched, because, when persecution had been scattered throughout the regions of Judaea, the Gentile world—previously abandoned and, as it were, estranged from the infusion of reason—is watered by drops of preaching. That this Gentile world was still to be found by preachers is shown when it is added:

### Verse 27

“To fill the pathless and desolate land.”

What the drenched earth produced is shown when it immediately continues:

### Chapter XXVI

[Col. 0505A]

**The same passage:** “And to bring forth green herbs.”

### 51. Formerly the Gentile world was pathless; through grace it became accessible

The Gentile world was formerly pathless, since the way to the word of God was not open to it. When our Redeemer came, it received the call of grace, [p. 940] although previously it had no way of prophecy. It was also rightly called desolate, whether because it lacked the faculty of counsel or because it was deprived of the fruit of good works.

The Lord therefore gave the most violent rain its course and the resounding thunder its way, so that it might rain in the desert, fill the pathless and desolate land, and bring forth green herbs. That is, he joined inward inspiration to outward preaching, so that the parched hearts of the Gentiles might become green, what was closed might open, what was empty might be filled, and what was barren might produce.

[Col. 0505B] [Ancient recension XVIII.]

### 52. It brought forth the works and teaching of eternal life

In sacred Scripture, “green herb” sometimes signifies the glory of temporal prosperity, sometimes the devil’s nourishment, sometimes the support of preachers, sometimes good works, and sometimes the knowledge and teaching of eternal life.

Its greenness signifies temporal glory, as the Prophet says: “In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flower and pass away” (Ps. 89:6). To flower and pass away in the morning like grass means that, amid the prosperity of this age, the splendor of temporal glory quickly withers.

Grass signifies the devil’s nourishment, as the Lord says of him: “To him the mountains bear grass” (Job 40:15). It is as though he said: “While the proud and swollen exalt themselves through unlawful thoughts and actions, they feed him with their iniquities.”

Grass signifies the support of preachers when it is said: “He brings forth hay upon the mountains, and grass for the service of men” (Ps. 140:8). Hay is brought forth upon the mountains, and grass for the service of men, when the elevated ones of this age, called to knowledge of the faith, supply holy preachers with transitory nourishment on the journey of this life.

Grass signifies good works, as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth green grass” (Gen. 1:11). Although we understand this historically as having occurred at the creation of the world, we may suitably understand the earth to have prefigured the Church, which brought forth green grass when it produced fruitful works of mercy in response to the word of God.

Sometimes we understand grass as the knowledge and teaching of eternal greenness, as it is said through Jeremiah: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the wind like dragons; their eyes failed, because there was no grass” (Jer. 14:5). In these words the proud and most wicked persecution of the Jews was foretold. They are called wild asses because of their mental arrogance, and dragons because of their poisonous thoughts. They stood upon the rocks because they trusted not in God but in the highest powers of this world, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). They drew in the wind like dragons because, inflated by a spirit of arrogance, they swelled with malicious pride. Their eyes failed because their hope collapsed from that toward which their heart had been directed.

[Note: Laudun., Norman., etc., read this way. In Corb. Germ. and the old editions one finds: “Who, loving temporal things . . .” There *qui* refers to the foot of the page. Earlier, where most manuscripts have *quia scilicet spes* (“because plainly their hope”), this manuscript, with the old printed editions, gives *quia scilicet pes* (“because plainly the foot”). The recent editions corrected this well and have *quia scilicet spes*, but in a serious error retained *qui temporalia*. It should therefore read *quae*, namely “hope.”]

Their hope, loving temporal things, neglected to await eternal things, and therefore lost earthly things because it preferred them to God. For they said: “If we let him continue in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11:48). They feared that they would lose their place if the Lord were not killed, and yet they lost it when he was killed.

But why these things happened to the wretched is added: “Because there was no grass”—that is, because their hearts lacked the knowledge of eternity, and no nourishment of the teaching of inward greenness refreshed them.

[Note: Corb. Germ., Pratel., and Utic. read “the teaching of inward greenness”; Laud. reads “inward teaching.”]

What else, then, do we understand in this passage by green herbs except the knowledge of holy teaching or fitting works? The deserted earth is drenched so that it may bring forth green herbs, because, when the Gentile world received the rain of holy preaching, it brought forth the herb of works and teaching.

[Note: Turon., Ebroic., Pratel., and other Norman manuscripts read “and it brought forth the herb of teaching.” Laudun. reads “and the herb of teaching germinated.” In Corb. Germ. and all the editions, the words are “germinated.”]

This greenness is promised prophetically to the deserted earth when it is said: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, greenness of reed and rush shall arise” (Isa. 35:7). What is signified by the reed except writers—

[Note: Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts: “except writers.”]

—and by the rush, which always grows beside moisture, except the small and tender hearers of sacred eloquence? Thus greenness of reed and rush arises in the dens of dragons, because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed there accumulates both the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers.

[Col. 0506C]

[Ancient recension XIX.]

### 53. The hearts of individuals are like a desert before they are made fruitful by the rain of grace

If we carefully examine what has been said generally about the Gentile world, we see it taking place within the bosom of the holy Church in individuals. There are many who are utterly insensitive to the words of God. Although they are reckoned among the faithful, they hear the words of life with their ears but do not at all allow them to pass into the inner heart.

What else are these people than a deserted earth? That earth has no man, because their mind lacks the sense of reason. No mortal dwells in this land, because even if thoughts possessing rational judgment sometimes enter their conscience, they do not remain. Perverse desires find a dwelling in their hearts; but right desires, whenever they come, run away as though driven out.

But when merciful God deigns to give his rain its course and the way of resounding thunder, they are moved by inward grace and open the ears of their hearts to the words of life. The pathless land is filled, because, while it provides hearing to the word, it is heaped with mystery. It brings forth green herbs, because, through the grace infused by compunction, it not only gladly receives the words of preaching but also returns them abundantly. What it could not hear, it now desires to speak; and what, by failing to hear, had inwardly withered, now, by speaking holy things, feeds any who hunger with its own greenness.

Hence it is rightly said through the Prophet: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 104:30). Thus the face of the earth is changed by the power of renewal: the mind that was formerly dry is drenched when grace comes, and after its former barrenness it is clothed, as though with herbs brought forth, in the greenness of knowledge.

The grace of our Creator is commended to us still more deeply when it is added:

### Chapter XXVII [Ancient XX, Rec. XV]

### Verse 28

“Who is the father of rain? Or who begot the drops of dew?”

### 54. This rain is given freely, not according to our merits. Sometimes it falls like dew; sometimes it pours abundantly like rain

It is as though he said: “Who except I, who freely sprinkle the dry earth of the human heart with drops of knowledge?”

Of this rain it is elsewhere said: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. 68:10). The Lord sets apart voluntary rain for his inheritance because he grants it to us not according to our merits but as a gift of his goodness. For this reason he is called the father of rain in this passage: heavenly preaching is generated in us not from our merit but from his grace.

The drops of dew are the holy preachers themselves. [Note: Laud.: “who water the lofty fields of the heart.”] They pour the grace of heavenly generosity into the fields of our hearts, which are dry amid the evils of the present life, as amid the darkness of a dry night.

Of these drops it is said to rebellious Judaea: “Therefore the drops of rain were withheld, and the latter rain did not come” (Jer. 3:3). These drops of dew are the drops of rain. [Note: Gilot. reads “the stars of dew are the stars of rain,” an obvious error, partly corrected by Gussanvil., who nevertheless retained “star of rain.” It is clearly to be read “drop of rain,” as is also found in the manuscripts Vindoc., two Remigian manuscripts, Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses, and in the older editions. Corb. Germ. nevertheless reads above “here,” and below “stars of dew” and “drops of dew.”]

When they moderate their preaching according to some dispensation, they sprinkle it like gentle dew. But when they speak with the power they possess of what they understand concerning heavenly things, they pour it out like abundant rain.

Paul sprinkled dew when he said to the Corinthians: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). Again, he flowed as rain when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11).

Hence Moses, who knew that he would speak both forcefully to the strong and tenderly to the weak, said: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32:2).

But behold, we have heard by what gift the Gentile world is called; let us now hear by what strict judgment Judaea is rejected. We have heard how he cultivates the desert and waters what is dry; let us now hear how he casts away what seems to be inward. For he does not gather the elect in such a way that he does not also judge the reprobate; nor does he forgive the faults of some in such a way that he does not strike others. For it is written: “Mercy and wrath are from him” (Sirach 5:7).

[Note: Pratel.: “mercy and wrath”—with *enim* (“for”) omitted.]

Accordingly, here too, after he has bestowed so many gifts of grace, he does not conceal the judgments of his wrath. For it follows:

### Chapter XXVIII [Ancient XXI]

### Verse 29

“From whose womb did the ice come forth? And who begot the frost from heaven?”

### 55. The rejected Jews, as though cast from the womb of divine mercy, although descended from the holy patriarchs

What else are we to understand by frost or ice except the hearts of the Jews, cold and bound by the torpor of unbelief? Once, through the receiving of the Law, the keeping of the commandments, the ministries of sacrifice, and the mysteries of prophecy, they were held within the bosom of grace, as within the womb of the Creator.

But when the Lord came, they were bound by the cold of unbelief and lost the warmth of faith and charity. Cast from the secret bosom of grace, they went forth like ice from the womb of the Creator.

“And who begot the frost from heaven?” What else is heaven to be understood as here except the sublime life of the saints? To this heaven it is said: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak” (Deut. 32:1). He was not speaking to an insensible but to a rational creature.

Of this heaven the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1). Of this throne it is elsewhere written:

[Note: Perhaps Prov. 12:23, where according to the Septuagint one reads: “A prudent man is a throne of perception.” In the Syriac version: “A cautious man is a seat of knowledge.” Other conjectures will be offered in Homily 38 on the Gospels.]

“The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.”

Since God is wisdom, if heaven is the seat of God, and the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, then the soul of the righteous is certainly heaven. Abraham was heaven; Isaac was heaven; Jacob was heaven.

But because the priests of the Jews who persecuted the Lord emerged cold with the torpor of unbelief from the lineage of those fathers, frost came forth from heaven, because a cold people of unbelievers came forth from the exalted offspring of the saints.

When Caiaphas was born from Abraham, what else occurred except that frost came forth from heaven? Yet the Lord says that he himself begot this frost because he justly permitted the Jews, whom he had naturally created good, to depart from him, made cold by their own wickedness. The Lord is the author of nature, not of sin. He therefore begot, by creating them naturally, those whom he permitted to live in their wickedness by patiently enduring them.

And because those formerly tender hearts of the Jews, open to faith, later hardened in the obstinacy of unbelief, it is rightly added:

### Chapter XXIX

### Verse 30

“The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.”

[ p. 943 ]

### 56. From being sons of Abraham they became stones because of hardness of heart; and Gentiles formerly stones were turned into sons of Abraham

I remember having taught several times that waters signify peoples. [Note: Vindoc., Corb. Germ., and most Norman witnesses: “a stone . . . signifies a Gentile people.”]

By a stone, however, Gentile peoples are sometimes signified because of their hardness. They worshiped stones. Of them it is said through the Prophet: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 13:8).

Therefore John, seeing the Jews exalt themselves over the distinction of their lineage, and foreseeing the Gentiles pass by faith into the offspring of Abraham, said: “Do not say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9). By “stones” he plainly called the Gentiles, hardened by unbelief.

Because Judaea first believed in God while all the Gentiles remained obstinate in their unbelief, but afterward the hearts of the Gentiles were softened toward faith and the unbelief of the Jews was hardened, it was rightly said: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.”

It is as though he said: “The formerly soft and faith-penetrable hearts of the Jews are turned into the insensibility of the Gentiles.”

When merciful God drew the Gentiles, he rejected Judaea in anger. It came about that, just as the Gentile world had formerly been hardened against receiving faith, so afterward, once the Gentile world had received it, the people of Judaea hardened in the torpor of unbelief.

Hence the apostle Paul says to those same Gentiles: “Just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have not believed because of the mercy shown to you, so that they also may obtain mercy. For God has imprisoned all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:30).

Considering this statement carefully—first concerning the calling of the Jews and the rejection of the Gentiles, and afterward concerning the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews—and realizing that he could not comprehend God’s hidden judgments, he added in an exclamation: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

Thus here too, when the Lord says of the unbelief of the Jews, “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone,” in order to show that his judgments concerning their rejection are hidden, he appropriately adds:

### Chapter XXX [Ancient XXII]

### The same passage

“And the surface of the abyss is congealed.”

### 57. The judgments of God are a great abyss

With a certain veil of our ignorance cast over it, the incomprehensibility of divine judgment cannot be penetrated at all by the eye of the human mind.

[Note: Corb. Germ., Laud., Pratel., and other Norman witnesses: “the incomprehensibility of divine judgment cannot at all be penetrated by the eye of the human mind.”]

For it is written: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 36:6). Let no one therefore desire to investigate why one person is rejected and another chosen, or why one is chosen and another rejected. The surface of the abyss is congealed, and, as Paul testifies: “His judgments are unsearchable and his ways are untraceable” (Rom. 11:33).

[Col. 0510A]

### 58. What has been said about the hardness and rejection of the Jews can also be understood of Satan

By the words, “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven?”, there is nothing to prevent Satan also from being understood as frost and ice.

He proceeded like ice from the womb of God because, cold with the torpor of wickedness, he emerged as a teacher of iniquity from the warmth of God’s secret things. He was begotten as frost from heaven because, destined to constrict the hearts of the reprobate, he was permitted to fall from the heights to the depths.

Although well created among heavenly beings, he bound the minds of his followers in the cold of sin like frost when he fell.

[Note: I am surprised to find *dum cecinit* (“while he sang”) in Gilot., Gussanvil., and other editions, since this makes no sense and cannot cohere with what precedes or follows. The older Paris and Basel editions, together with the manuscripts, read *dum cecidit* (“when he fell”). It is enough to cite Turon., Corb. Germ., Ebroic., and the other Norman witnesses.]

[ p. 944 ]

What he did among human beings when he came to earth is completed when it is added: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.” By waters peoples are signified; by the stone, the hardness of that same Satan.

When he came down to the depths, the waters were hardened into the likeness of stone, because human beings, imitating his wickedness, lost the tender inward organs of charity.

Since his deceitful counsels cannot be detected by the people he has seduced, it is rightly added: “And the surface of the abyss is congealed.” One thing lies hidden within him, while another is displayed outwardly. For he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14), and by his crafty art of deception he often proposes things that appear praiseworthy in order to draw people toward what is unlawful.

The surface of the abyss is therefore congealed because, while the appearance of his persuasion is displayed above like solid ice, his malice hidden in the depths is not seen.

### 59. These words may also concern the proud who grow insolent because of the gifts they have received

We can nevertheless understand all these things in another way if we investigate them morally.

[Ancient XXIII.] When almighty God forms human minds in his fear, he conceives them, as it were; and when he raises them toward manifest virtues, he gives them birth. But if they become exalted because of the virtues they have received, he abandons them.

We have often known people to be moved by consideration of their sins, to burn with fear of divine judgment, and, through the beginnings of fear, to attain the summit of virtues. But when they become exalted because of those same virtues they receive, bound by the snare of empty glory, they return to their former torpor.

Therefore, when the Lord casts such people away, he rightly says: “From whose womb did the ice come forth?” For ice comes forth, as it were, from the womb of God when those who had already grown warm within become cold through the gift of virtues. From the very place where they ought to have burned more ardently in loving inward things, they become torpid and seek outward glory.

While one excels in signs, another in knowledge, one in prophecy, another in great works, and each seeks through these gifts to please human beings, everything that had previously grown warm within is turned into torpor by loving outward praise.

Thus ice comes forth from the womb when, after receiving gifts, a person is separated from the inward compassion of the heavenly womb. Are not those who seek human praise for the virtues they receive ice? And yet, when the Judge comes, recalling their gifts to him, they say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?” (Matt. 7:22).

But the Lord shows how he casts out this ice when he says: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22).

The Lord now bears this ice in the womb because he tolerates it within the bosom of the Church. But he then openly casts it out when, in the final and public judgment, he drives such people from the heavenly secrets.

What is openly accomplished by these words except that blessed Job is humbled concerning his highest virtues, lest he become cold through pride in what had made him warm by living well, and depart rejected from the womb of the Divinity if he exalts himself in the swelling of his heart?

[Ancient XXIV.]

### 60. The punishment of pride is hardening. In what sense God is said to harden

Because by a just judgment he permits proud minds to fall into sin through the virtue they have received, it is rightly added: “And who begot the frost from heaven?”

Often he grants knowledge of sacred eloquence; but when the person who receives that knowledge becomes exalted by it, the anger of the strict Judge blinds him within the sacred eloquence itself. He follows outward approval through it and no longer sees its inward meaning. Though he could have remained within and grown warm, he goes out, becomes cold, and, hardened, falls to the depths—he who had previously stood pliable in the heights for the knowledge of God.

Is sacred eloquence not heaven? It opens for us the day of understanding and illuminates us with the sun of righteousness; while the night of the present life holds us, it shines upon us with the stars of the commandments.

But because “there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19), when a proud mind is rejected from sound understanding, the frost of heaven is generated by the vengeance of the strict Judge. Thus, while sacred Scripture itself burns in the hearts of the elect, it sends away cold from itself those who arrogantly desire to know.

They err precisely where they ought to have corrected their errors. While they are cast down from the heavenly understanding of radiant eloquence, they themselves become hardened and, as deceivers of others, fall to the depths like frost and constrict others as well.

[Note: Turon. reads “and the deceivers fall”; Laud. reads “and the deceivers fall for the others.”]

Nevertheless, the Lord is said to generate this frost—not because he himself forms the minds of the wicked for sin, but because he does not free them from sin, as it is written: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 10:27). Because he did not mercifully choose to soften it, he declared, in strict judgment, that he had hardened himself.

[Note: Corb. Germ. and the editions read “to harden himself.” The manuscripts Laud., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses more correctly read “that he had hardened himself.”]

### 61. When virtue is lost, its appearance is often retained

Because, when the virtue of the fear of God that has been begun is lost, the appearance of virtue is retained for the sake of human praise, it is rightly added: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone, and the surface of the abyss is congealed.”

Through ice, waters become hard on the surface but remain fluid in their depths. What else are we to understand by waters except the unstable hearts of the reprobate? When they abandon virtue by deliberate choice, they display themselves hypocritically as strong in good works. While they flow inwardly toward vices, outwardly they pretend to imitate the holy and the strong.

“The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone, and the surface of the abyss is congealed,” because their fluid and unstable conscience is concealed from human beings by a covering appearance of holiness. Although inwardly they are shameful to themselves, before the eyes of others they are clothed in a certain long-established way of life.

### 63. God wisely restrains the untimely fruits of virtue

But lest anyone wish to understand these words of the Lord in a favorable sense, we must also establish this interpretation for those who inquire, provided that we are not judged to have neglected what needed investigation.

The preceding verse says: “Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew?” Immediately it adds: “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven?”

If the following statement is joined to the preceding words in a corresponding sense, its meaning is certainly opened to us without difficulty, even in a favorable interpretation.

[Ancient XXV.] When the earth is drenched, seeds cast into it are more fruitfully held fast. But if rain irrigates it excessively, it changes the richness and strength of the grain into a stalk. If, however, the seed cast down is pressed by frost after the rain, the more it is prevented from appearing outwardly, the more fruitfully it takes root inwardly. The more it is prevented from advancing, the more it is forced to multiply, because, when it is restrained from premature emergence, it is more abundantly filled out by the delay of its conception.

What, then, does the Lord mean by first presenting himself as the father of rain, and afterward recounting that ice comes forth from his womb and declaring that he begets frost from heaven, except that in a wondrous manner he first waters the earth of our hearts, so that it may receive the seeds of the word, through the rain of hidden grace; and afterward, lest it overflow immoderately in the virtues it has conceived, he presses it down with the discipline of inward dispensation?

Thus the rain of grace waters what has been received, while the rigor of discipline also constrains it, lest, if the virtues conceived should emerge either before they ought or more than necessary, the grain should turn into grass. Often, when a good work is displayed by beginners before the proper time, it is emptied of the grain of perfection; and often virtues exhale when they grow more luxuriantly than necessary.

Hence the Lord either refuses the desires of his elect before the time or again restrains their progress at the proper time beyond due measure, lest, if they advance either before they ought or more than they ought, they fall through the greatness of their progress into the collapse of pride.

When the heart is moved to compunction after sins, the earth that had dried out is watered by the infusion of rain. When it plans to carry out good works after abandoning iniquities, it receives seed, as it were, after the infusion.

[Note: Another reading: “and frequently.”]

Many people, when they conceive holy desires, burn to exercise the highest virtues, so that not only may sin not stain their actions, but may not even trouble their thoughts.

They are still in the body, yet they no longer wish to suffer anything from participation in the present life. In intention they desire to imitate the inward stability of the mind.

[Note: Laud., Ebroic., and other Norman witnesses: “the eternal stability of the mind.” Corb. Germ.: “through the intention of the eternal stability of the mind.”]

But they are struck back by intervening temptations, so that they may remember their weakness and not become proud because of the virtues they receive.

When this is accomplished through the wondrous restraint of discipline, what else is generated than frost from heaven over the earth that has been drenched? What else is produced than ice from the womb of God, when a dispensation emerges from the inward secret place and our wills are restrained even in good desires?

### 63. This is confirmed by the example of Saint Paul

Let us see how Paul—the earth that has been drenched—is pressed by the ice of discipline when he says: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:18).

By asserting that he possesses the will, he shows that, through the infusion of grace, the seeds hidden within him are already present. But by saying that he does not find how to accomplish the good, he plainly indicates how greatly the ice of heavenly dispensation presses him.

Had this ice not pressed the hearts of those to whom he said: “You do not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:17)? It is as though he said openly: “The hidden seeds of your heart are already seeking to emerge into fruit, but they are pressed by the frost of heavenly governance, so that they may emerge more fruitfully afterward to the degree that they patiently bear the constraining weights of divine judgment.”

[Ancient XXVI.]

### 64. From this arise serious temptations, which are overcome by the practice of upright living

Because human hearts often cannot break through to the virtues they desire, they are wearied by the goads of temptations precisely when they recoil from the perfection of their intention. Yet they restrain these same temptations in thought and, through habitual practice, shape themselves into a certain rigor of life. It is therefore rightly added: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.”

Although fluid thoughts inwardly assault them, they do not draw them all the way to consent to evil action. Under the established habit of living well, the mind conceals outwardly, as if under a certain hardness, whatever grows soft within it through the force of temptation.

Hence it is also rightly added: “And the surface of the abyss is congealed.” For although an evil thought comes as far as suggestion, it does not leap as far as consent, because the superimposed rigor of holy deliberation presses down the mind’s fluctuating movements.

[Col. 0514A]

### 65. Adversity makes the saints stronger

Frost or ice may also signify the adversity of the present life, which, while it compresses the saints with its harshness, makes them stronger.

When almighty God permits us to be exercised by troubles and advances us toward a better condition of life through the intervention of sorrow, he wondrously produces frost and ice for the future harvest. Thus each of the elect tolerates adverse winds and cold in this life as in winter and afterward displays, as in the calm of summer, the fruits he has conceived here.

Hence, in the voice of the Bridegroom, every soul hastening after the storms of this world toward the pleasant places of eternity is told: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come; for winter has passed, the rain has gone, and it has departed” (Song 2:10).

And because, if prosperity alone is present to us, we are loosened, while through adversity we are more firmly established in virtue, it is rightly added:

[Note: Much is missing here in the Gilot. and Vatican editions, where one reads: “If prosperity alone is present to us, we are made firm,” contrary to the holy Doctor’s meaning, true piety, and the evidence of the manuscripts. The reading given here is found in the Anglic., Norman, Turon., Laud., Corb. Germ., and other witnesses.]

[Ancient XXVII.] “The waters are hardened into the likeness of stone.”

Minds that had flowed softly through prosperity become hard when constricted by adversity. Water is brought into the likeness of stone when a weak person, through the endurance granted from above, imitates the sufferings of his Redeemer.

Water had hardened into the likeness of stone when Paul, formerly an impatient persecutor, later said: “I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24).

### 66. And more concerned to guard the inward gifts

And because, when they are humbled by adversity, they guard their inward gifts more diligently, it is rightly added:

“And the surface of the abyss is frozen.”

For joy commonly opens the secret places of the mind and, by opening them, causes them to be lost; but adversity, when it humbles us outwardly, makes us more cautious inwardly. Thus, after the frost or ice, the surface of the abyss is frozen, because our mind is fortified by adversities so as to preserve the deep gifts it has received.

Isaiah had frozen the surface of his abyss when he said: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isaiah 24:16). Paul too had frozen the surface of his abyss. Laboring amid so many dangers and adversities, he speaks under the guise of referring to someone else, saying: “I heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Corinthians 12:4). And again: “But I spare you, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me” (ibid., 6). Thus, while enduring adversity outwardly, he feared opening his secrets lest he perhaps should melt away in praise. What else had he done than press down the abyss of his secrets beneath its frozen surface?

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI [Rec. XVI]

### Verse 31

“Will you be able to join together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you disperse the circle of Arcturus?”

[Col. 0515A] 948

### 67. What the Pleiades and Arcturus are. By contemplating God’s omnipotence, we are reminded of our weakness

The stars called the Pleiades take their name from **ἀπὸ τοῦ πλείστου**, that is, “from plurality.” They were created both near to one another and separate, so that they are together and yet can by no means be joined: they are united by a certain nearness, but separated by contact.

Arcturus, however, illumines the nighttime hours in such a way that, placed upon the axis of heaven, it turns through various positions and yet does not set. For it does not revolve while running outside itself; rather, fixed in its place, it inclines toward all parts of the world without ever falling.

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that a human being, made from earth and placed upon earth (Genesis 2:7), is questioned about the administration of heaven? He cannot join the Pleiades, which he sees created near one another and almost joined; he cannot disperse the circle of Arcturus, which he can nevertheless see almost dispersed by its own rotation. Is it not so that, contemplating the power of the Creator in these ministries, he may remember his own weakness and consider, in the very governance of the heavenly ministries, how immeasurable is the One whom he cannot yet see in His majesty?

## MYSTICAL MEANING

### The saints are signified by the name of the Pleiades

### 68. The Pleiades signify all the saints

But why do we say these things, when the goad of reason urges us to understand that these words are pregnant with mystical meanings? What else do the shining Pleiades—which are also seven in number—indicate than all the saints, who illumine us amid the darkness of the present life with the light of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit? Sent at different times from the very beginning of the world to its end in order to prophesy, they are in some respects joined to one another and in other respects separated.

For the stars of the Pleiades, as was said above, are joined to one another by nearness and separated by contact. They are situated together, yet each pours forth the rays of its own light individually. Thus all the saints, appearing at different times for preaching, are separated in the manifestation of their lives but joined in the intention of their minds. They shine together because they preach one thing; yet they do not touch one another, because they are distributed across separate ages.

### 69. All, even those who preceded Christ, proclaim Him and the mystery of the Trinity

How differently Abel, Isaiah, and John appeared in time! They were separated in time, but not in preaching. Abel, signifying the passion of our Redeemer, offered a lamb in sacrifice (Genesis 4:4). Concerning its passion Isaiah said: “Like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). John too said of it: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold Him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Behold: sent at different times, yet agreeing in their understanding of the innocence of our Redeemer, John spoke of the same Lamb by showing Him, Isaiah by foreseeing Him, and Abel by offering Him. The One whom John held forth by his showing and Isaiah by his proclamation, Abel held in his hands by his symbolic act.

### 70. The Pleiades agree in proclaiming the unity of the Trinity

Since we have said how the stars of the Pleiades harmonize with one another concerning the humanity of the Redeemer, let us now demonstrate how they shine together in proclaiming the unity of the Trinity.

David, Isaiah, and Paul appeared in this world at different times; yet none of them held a view different from the others. Although they did not know one another face to face, they had learned one thing through divine knowledge.

David, in order to show the one God, the Creator of all, in the Trinity, said: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Psalm 66:8). And lest, by naming God three times, he should be thought to have spoken of three gods, he immediately indicated the unity of that same Trinity by adding: “And may all the ends of the earth fear Him” (ibid.). By saying not “them” but “Him,” he made known that the three things he had named are one.

Isaiah too, when he proclaimed the unity of the Trinity, uttered the voices of the Seraphim, saying: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah 6:3). And lest, by naming the Holy One three times, he should seem to divide the unity of the divine substance, he added: “The Lord God of hosts.” Since he added not “the lords gods” but “the Lord God,” he indicated that what he had called “holy” three times exists as one.

Paul likewise, in order to show the working of the holy Trinity, said: “From Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things” (Romans 11:36). And to indicate the unity of that same Trinity, he immediately added: “To Him be glory for ever and ever. Amen” (ibid.). By saying not “to them” but “to Him,” he made known one according to nature and three according to persons—the same reality which above he had named three times.

Thus the Pleiades are situated, as it were, in one place, because they agree in their understanding of God; yet they do not touch one another, because, as has been said, they are distributed throughout the different ages of this world.

### 71. All the saints are joined by unanimity in faith and virtues

The prophet Ezekiel describes this well and briefly. When he said that he saw living creatures of different kinds, he added: “And their wings were joined, each to the other” (Ezekiel 1:9).

The wings of the living creatures are joined one to another because, although the things they do are unlike, the voices and virtues of the saints are united with one another by one and the same understanding. One is a human being, acting rationally in all things; another is a lion, strong in suffering because he does not fear the adversities of the world; another is a calf, offering himself as a living sacrifice through abstinence; another is an eagle, carrying himself aloft by the flight of contemplation. Yet, while they fly, their wings touch one another, because they are joined by the unanimity both of their confession and of their virtues.

Since it is the work of divine power alone both to join together in the preaching of the faith those sent at different times and to unite by the radiance of their intention those endowed with different virtues, it is rightly said: “Will you be able to join together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” As if He were saying: “Can you do this as I can, who, being one, fill all things and join the minds of the elect by filling them with a sense of unity?”

### 72. Arcturus signifies the whole Church and teaches the necessity of faith together with good works

In Arcturus, which by its revolution illumines the nighttime spaces without setting, not the life of individual saints taken separately but the whole Church together is signified. It suffers fatigue, yet does not incline toward the collapse of its proper condition. It endures the circle of its labors, but does not hasten toward setting along with the ages.

For Arcturus is not carried down to the lowest parts of the pole with the nighttime; rather, as it itself revolves, the night comes to an end. So, while the holy Church is shaken by countless tribulations, the shadow of the present life is brought to an end. Night passes while the Church stands, because, while she persists in her safety, the life of this mortality runs its course.

There is something in Arcturus which we may observe with greater care. It revolves in seven stars. At one time it raises three to the heights and inclines four toward the depths; at another it raises four above and presses three below.

So too the holy Church, at one time preaching to unbelievers the knowledge of the Trinity and at another preaching to the faithful the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—seems by the rotation of her preaching to alter in some way the appearance of her condition.

When she removes confidence in their own labor from those who boast of their works and exalts faith in the Trinity, what else does she do than raise the three stars of Arcturus and incline the four? And when she forbids those who lack good works to presume upon faith alone, but commands them to practice more earnestly what has been enjoined, what else does Arcturus do than raise the four stars and lower the three?

Let us see how he raises three and lowers four. Through Paul it is said to those who grow proud of works against faith: “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Romans 4:2). What does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).

Let us see how he raises four and lowers three. Through James it is said to those who grow proud of faith against works: “Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (James 2:26).

Arcturus therefore revolves because the holy Church, according to the minds of her hearers, turns by the art of preaching in different directions. Arcturus revolves because she is whirled about amid the tribulations of this night.

But the Lord will one day disperse the circle of Arcturus, because He will exchange the Church’s labors for rest. Then He will also join the Pleiades more fully, when He destroys the circle of Arcturus, because then all the saints will be joined even in the appearance of vision, when, at the end of the world, the holy Church is released from the labors she now endures.

Let him therefore say: “Will you be able to join together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you disperse the circle of Arcturus?” The implied meaning is: “Can you do this as I can, who then unite the lives of the saints even in visible form, when I physically release the circle of the universal Church?”

And what human being does not know that this belongs to divine power alone? But in order that human beings may recognize what they themselves are, let them continually remember what the Lord alone can do.

### 73. Again, the Old Law is signified by Arcturus, and the grace of the New Testament by the Pleiades

We have yet another interpretation of the stars of the Pleiades and Arcturus.

The Pleiades rise in the east, whereas Arcturus rises from the region of the north. Wherever Arcturus turns in its revolution, it displays the Pleiades; and when the light of day becomes near, the arrangement of its stars is spread out.

Thus Arcturus, which rises from the region of cold, can signify the Law; while the Pleiades, which rise in the east, can signify the grace of the New Testament.

The Law had come, as it were, from the north, terrifying its subjects with such harsh rigidity. For when it commanded that some be crushed by stones on account of their sins and others punished by death from the sword, that frozen region, seemingly removed from the sun of charity, pressed down the seeds of its commandments more by cold than it nourished them by warmth.
