Peter had shrunk from the weight of this oppression when he said: “Why are you testing God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

Nor is it surprising that the Old Testament is expressed by the seven stars of Arcturus, since, through reverence for the Law, the seventh day was established as sacred, and the vows of the appointed sacrifice extended through the whole week.

The Pleiades, which likewise are seven, as we said above, indicate the grace of the New Testament all the more openly, since we all clearly see that through it the sevenfold Spirit illumines His faithful with the light of His gifts.

Wherever Arcturus turns, it displays the Pleiades, because through everything that the Old Testament says, the works of the New Testament are announced. Beneath the text of the letter it conceals the mystery of prophecy.

It is as though Arcturus inclines itself and makes the Pleiades visible, because, when the Old Testament is bent toward spiritual understanding, the light of the sevenfold grace signified by it is revealed.

And when the light of day approaches, the arrangement of its stars is spread out, because, after the Truth had become known to us through Himself, He loosened the commandments of the letter from their carnal observances.

### 74. Christ alone possessed all the operations of the Holy Spirit abiding in Him

Our Redeemer, coming in the flesh, joined the Pleiades, because He possessed all the operations of the sevenfold Spirit simultaneously and abiding in Himself.

Of Him Isaiah says: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:1).

Of Him Zechariah says: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zechariah 3:9). And again: “And on the golden lampstand are seven lamps” (ibid., 4:2).

No human being ever possessed all the operations of the Holy Spirit simultaneously except the one Mediator between God and human beings, whose Spirit is the same Spirit who proceeds from the Father before the ages.

It is therefore rightly said: “Upon one stone are seven eyes.” For this stone’s having seven eyes means retaining in operation all the power of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit at once.

One receives prophecy, another knowledge, another powers, another kinds of tongues, another interpretations of speech, according to the distribution of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:8); but no one attains all the gifts of that same Spirit.

Our Creator, however, taking upon Himself our weakness, taught that through the power of His divinity He possessed all the virtues of the Holy Spirit simultaneously. Without doubt, He joined the shining Pleiades.

By joining the Pleiades, He disperses the circle of Arcturus, because, by making known that He, having become human, possessed all the operations of the Holy Spirit, He released the labor of the letter in the Old Testament, so that every believer might now understand with freedom of spirit what he had previously served in fear amid so many dangers.

Let blessed Job therefore hear: “Will you be able to join together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” As if it were plainly said to him: “You may possess the lights of certain virtues, but are you sufficient to exercise all the operations of the Holy Spirit simultaneously? Contemplate Me, then, joining the Pleiades in all virtues, and restrain yourself from pride concerning the few that you possess.”

Hear what is said: “Or can you disperse the circle of Arcturus?” As if it were plainly said to him: “Even if you now perceive what is right, can you by your own power destroy the labor of a coarser understanding in the hearts of others?”

“Consider Me, therefore, who correct the foolishness of the carnal while revealing Myself through the foolishness of the flesh, so that you may humble all the things which you regard as powerful among your virtues all the more, since you do not even grasp the traces of My weakness.”

But because, in the very mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the light of truth is shown to some while the hearts of others are darkened through scandal, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Rec. XVII]

### Verse 32

“Will you bring forth the morning star in its time, and cause the evening to rise over the children of the earth?”

### 75. Christ is the true morning star, especially in the resurrection; the evening is the Antichrist. Those devoted to earthly things are justly subjected to him

The Father brought forth the morning star in its time, because, as it is written: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4:4).

Born of a Virgin, He appeared like the morning star amid the darkness of our night, because, having driven away the obscurity of sin, He announced to us the eternal morning.

He made Himself known as the morning star because He rose from death at dawn, and by the splendor of His light He pressed the darkness of our mortality into the earth.

To Him John rightly says: “The bright and morning star” (Revelation 22:16). Appearing alive after death, He became for us the morning star, because, by providing in Himself an example of resurrection, He showed what light would follow.

The Lord causes the evening to rise over the children of the earth because He permits the Antichrist to rule over the unbelieving hearts of the Jews, as their deserts demand.

They are justly subjected by the Lord to this evening because they themselves willingly chose to be children of the earth. Seeking earthly things and not heavenly things, they have been blinded so as not to perceive the brightness of our morning star; and, while they desire the evening to rule over them, they are plunged into the eternal night of the condemnation that follows.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come in My Father’s name, and you did not receive Me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43).

Hence Paul says: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (2 Thessalonians 2:10).

The evening would by no means rise over them if they had wished to be children of heaven. But while they desire visible things, having lost the light of their hearts, they grow dark beneath the guide of night.

### 76. The Word of God, which is the morning star to the elect, becomes evening to the reprobate

If, however, we examine this morally, we find that it happens every day: the morning star rises for the elect, while, by God’s permission, the evening rules over the reprobate.

There is one and the same word of God in the mouth of the preacher. When some hear it with joy and others with envy, they turn the brightness of the morning star into the darkness of evening for themselves.

When the former receive the voice of holy preaching humbly, they open the eyes of their hearts, as it were, to the light of the star. But when the latter envy the one who blesses them and seek not the cause of salvation but the glory of exaltation, the evening of their iniquity breaks forth, and they close their eyes in the sleep of death.

Thus, by a hidden judgment, the one who is the morning star to the elect becomes evening to reprobate hearers, because through the holy exhortation by which the good return to life, the wicked die more grievously in their guilt.

Hence Paul rightly says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some indeed an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

He therefore saw that His word is simultaneously morning star and evening to its hearers: through it He saw some raised from iniquity and, conversely, others lulled into iniquity.

Because this is accomplished through God’s hidden judgments, which human beings cannot comprehend in this life, he rightly added there: “And who is so competent for these things?” (ibid., 16).

As if he were saying: “We are indeed competent to observe that these things occur, but we are not competent to investigate why they occur.”

Here too, therefore, because the Lord had said that for some the morning star is brought forth and for others the evening rises, lest human beings dare to scrutinize God’s hidden judgments, He immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Vet. XXXII, Rec. XVIII]

### Verse 33

“Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its reasoning upon the earth?”

### 77. No one knows the causes of God’s judgments and predestination; no one should scrutinize them

To know the order of heaven is to see the hidden predestinations of heavenly dispositions. To establish its reasoning upon the earth is to reveal before human hearts the causes of such secrets.

To establish the reasoning of heaven upon earth means either to investigate, by reflection, the mysteries of heavenly judgments or to make them known by speech. No one placed in this life can do this.

To proceed from lesser matters to greater ones, who can understand what the reason of these secrets may be: that often a just man returns from judgment not only without vindication but even punished, while his wicked adversary departs not only unpunished but victorious?

Who can understand why one person lives while plotting the deaths of those near him, while another dies who would have benefited the lives of many? One attains the summit of power, although he strives only to harm; another desires only to defend those who have been harmed, yet lies there oppressed.

One longs for leisure but becomes entangled in countless affairs; another desires to be entangled in affairs but is forced into leisure. One who begins badly is drawn toward worse things until the end of his life; another who begins well advances through the long course of time toward an increase of merits.

Conversely, one who lives badly is preserved for a long time so that he may correct himself; another who seems to live well continues in this life until he breaks forth into perverse conduct.

One born in the error of unbelief dies in that error; another born in the uprightness of the Catholic faith is brought to completion in the uprightness of the Catholic faith.

Conversely, one born from the womb of a Catholic mother is swallowed up by the abyss of error near the end of life; another completes his life in Catholic devotion, though he was born in unbelief and had absorbed the venom of error with his mother’s milk.

One desires—and is able—to attain the height of living well; another neither desires nor is able. One desires but is unable; another is able but does not desire.

Who, then, can scrutinize these secrets of the heavenly judgments? Who can understand the hidden scales of concealed justice?

No one ascends to the recesses of these secret judgments in order to know them. Let it therefore be said to a human being that he should recognize that he does not know; let him recognize his ignorance so that he may fear; let him fear so that he may be humbled; let him be humbled so that he may not presume upon himself; let him not presume upon himself so that he may seek the help of his Creator. And the one who, trusting in himself, has died, may live by desiring the assistance of his Creator.

Let the just man hear—already knowing himself, but still ignorant of what is above him: “Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its reasoning upon the earth?” That is: “Do you comprehend the hidden orders of the heavenly judgments, or are you sufficient to reveal them to human ears?”

Blessed Job is therefore questioned concerning the investigation of incomprehensible judgments, as if it were plainly said to him: “You ought to endure all that you suffer with greater patience precisely because, being ignorant of the heavenly secrets, you do not know why you suffer these things.”

# BOOK THIRTY

This book contains an exposition of the last eight verses of chapter 38 and of the same number of verses of chapter 39. In it the holy Doctor discusses, with particular fullness and devout learning, the preaching of the Gospel.

[Col. 0521] [Col. 0521D] 955 [Vet. and Rec. I.]

### 1. Why Job was questioned by God about so many and such great matters

Blessed Job is questioned by the Lord whether he has done such things—things which a human being plainly cannot do—so that, when he discovers that he cannot do them, he may flee to the One whom he understands alone to be able to do them. Before the eyes of his Judge he may then appear more powerful if he more truly recognizes his own weakness.

Because it is known that these things are wonderfully done by the Lord, the divine voice questions Job about them, and says to him:

## CHAPTER ONE

### Chapter 38, verse 34

“Will you raise your voice in the cloud, and will the rush of waters cover you?”

### 2. The Word of God is scattered in a cloud when it is announced to unbelievers

The Lord raises His voice in a cloud when, through the tongues of His preachers, He forms an exhortation addressed to the darkened hearts of unbelievers; and the rush of waters covers Him when the crowd of resisting peoples oppresses His members who act rightly.

Hence it is written: “The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, speaking to all the cities of Judah, from which they come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words which I have commanded you” (Jeremiah 26:2).

A little later: “The priests and prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking, the priests and prophets and all the people seized him, saying: ‘Let him die the death! Why did he prophesy in the name of the Lord?’” (ibid., 7).

Behold: in a cloud the Lord raised His voice, because through the prophet He directly reproved the darkened minds of the proud. Behold: the rush of waters immediately covered Him, because He endured in Jeremiah everything inflicted by the peoples who rose up and were provoked by the cause of his reproach—He who had commanded the words of reproach.

The Lord also raised His voice in a cloud through Himself when, appearing visibly after assuming a body, He proclaimed many things to His persecutors under the veil of enigmatic figures.

He raised His voice in a cloud because His truth sounded, as through darkness, to unbelievers who would not follow Him.

Hence it is also well written in the Books of Kings: “The cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not minister because of the cloud” (1 Kings 8:10–11).

By reason of their deserts, when the proud priests of the Jews heard the divine mysteries through parables, they were unable to minister in the house of the Lord, as it were because of the cloud.

And now, when they disdain to investigate the mystical meanings of the Old Testament beneath the veil of the letter and amid the dark obscurities of allegories, they lose the ministry of faith owed by them because of the cloud.

To them also the Lord now uttered His voice in the cloud of His teaching, even when He related clear things about Himself. For what is clearer than: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)? What could He say more clearly than: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58)?

But because the minds of His hearers were filled with the darkness of unbelief, the intervening cloud hid the ray of the sun that had been sent forth.

### 3. The rush of waters covers the preachers of the divine Word when unbelievers rage against them

The rush of waters immediately covered Him at this raising of His voice, because a crowd of peoples soon rose up raging against Him.

For it is written: “Therefore the Jews sought to kill Him, because He not only broke the Sabbath but also called God His own Father, making Himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

Concerning this rush of waters the Prophet cries out: “They surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me together” (Psalm 87:18). And again: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Psalm 68:2).

He endured these waters in Himself before His death, and in His own members after His ascension. Hence He cries out concerning those above: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” (Acts 9:4).

Behold: He had already ascended into heaven, yet Saul still persecuted Him with the rush of the waters of unbelievers, and the more swollen wave struck Him more violently than the others.

He is the One who speaks what is right through the good; He is the One who is wounded in the suffering of the good.

Thus, to show through the wondrous unity of charity that He is the One who preaches through the mouths of His saints to unworthy hearers, the Lord said: “Will you raise your voice in a cloud?”

And to show that He is the One who suffers every adversity in His saints, He added: “And will the rush of waters cover you?” The implied meaning is: “Will it cover you as it covers Me, whom all the wicked neither understand when I speak through preaching saints nor see when I suffer through those who die?”

The Lord therefore relates what He suffers from human beings so that the pain of the afflicted human being may be eased, as if He were plainly saying to him: “Consider My suffering carefully, and regulate your own with equanimity. It is far less for you to endure human wounds than for Me.”

### 4. Even the hearts of the just are darkened before God’s hidden inspirations

We can still examine these words more subtly if we carefully weigh our hearts amid the heavenly gifts.

We are already believers; we already believe the heavenly things we hear; we already love what we believe. But while we are burdened by certain superfluous cares, we grow dark beneath the confusion that covers us. And when the Lord insinuates to such people that certain wondrous things about Him should be understood, He raises His voice, as it were, in a cloud.

When He speaks of Himself to our darkened minds, the One who cannot be seen is heard as though in a cloud.

The things we know about Him are sublime, but we still do not see Him in the secret inspiration by which we are instructed. Thus, He who grants our hearts speech while concealing His appearance forms His voice, as it were, in a cloud.

But behold: we already hear inwardly the words of God speaking of Himself; we already recognize with what continuity and zeal we ought to cling to His love. Yet from the height of inward contemplation, through the very mutability of this mortal condition, we relapse into our habitual ways and are assailed by the troublesome persistence of sins that threaten us.

Therefore, when He subtly insinuates things about Himself into our blind minds, He raises His voice in a cloud.

### [Vet. III.] 5. When the understanding of God is overwhelmed by temptations, God himself is covered, as it were, by waters. God does not abandon us even when he is rejected.

But when, through the temptation of vices, our understanding of God himself is oppressed, God is covered, as it were, by the force of waters in his utterance. For we pour so many waters over him as there are illicit thoughts that we turn over in our hearts after his grace has inspired us. Yet he does not abandon us, oppressed as we are; immediately he returns to the mind, scatters the clouds of temptations, pours in the rain of compunction, and brings back the sun of subtle understanding. Thus he shows how greatly he loves us: he does not abandon us even when he is rejected, so that, at least in this way, the human conscience, now instructed, may be ashamed to admit temptations, while its Redeemer does not cease to love it even when it wanders.

He endures this in us through himself; through his preachers he bears it daily from unbelievers. For his gift is repelled when temptation arises in us, and yet our weakness in no way prevents him from pouring his gift inwardly. His words are publicly rejected, and yet no wickedness of unbelievers restrains him from distributing the abundance of grace. When wicked people despise his teachings, he also adds miracles for them to revere.

Therefore, after the utterance has been produced and after the force of the overflowing waters, it is aptly added:

## CHAPTER II [Rec. II]

### VERSE 35

> “Will you send forth lightning-flashes, and they will go, and, returning, say to you, ‘Here we are’?”

#### 6. The holy preachers go forth from God and return to him, attributing to him alone the miracles with which they shine.

Lightning-flashes go forth from clouds, just as wondrous works are displayed through holy preachers. As we have often said, they are customarily called clouds because they flash with miracles and rain through their words. And because human hearts, once they have not been moved by preaching, are shaken by these flashes of miracles, we learn this from the testimony of the Prophet, who says:

> “You will multiply lightning-flashes, and you will trouble them” (Psalm 17:15).

It is as though he said: “When they do not hear the words of your preaching, they are troubled by the miracles of those who preach.”

Hence it is written elsewhere:

> “At the light of your arrows they will go, at the brilliance of the flash of your weapons” (Habakkuk 3:11).

The arrows of God going forth in light means that his words resound with evident truth. But because people often despise even words of life once they understand them, miracles are added as well. Hence he adds there:

> “At the brilliance of the flash of your weapons.”

The flash of weapons is the splendor of miracles. We defend ourselves with weapons and destroy hostile things with arrows. Thus weapons together with arrows signify miracles together with teachings. Holy preachers strike their adversaries with their words as with certain arrows; but with weapons—that is, with miracles—they protect themselves, so that the force of their arrows may proclaim how greatly they should be heard, and the weapons of miracles may reveal how greatly they should be revered.

[**Vet. IV.**] Thus it is said to blessed Job:

> “Will you send forth lightning-flashes, and they will go, and, returning, say to you, ‘Here we are’?”

The implied meaning is: “Here we are for me.” The lightning-flashes go when preachers shine with miracles and pierce the hearts of their hearers with heavenly reverence. They return and say, “Here we are,” when they attribute to God’s power, not to themselves, whatever they recognize themselves to have accomplished valiantly.

What, then, does it mean to say to God, “Here we are”? A certain act of service is expressed in this word. Thus, when the holy preachers return and say, “Here we are,” they attribute praise to him from whom they perceive that they received victory in the struggle, so that they do not attribute to themselves what they accomplish. Lightning-flashes can go forth by performing works, but they cannot return by becoming proud.

#### 7. Peter did this.

Let us therefore see the lightning-flash going forth. Peter says to a certain lame man:

> “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk.”

And taking him by his right hand, he raised him up, and immediately his legs and feet were strengthened; leaping up, he stood and walked (Acts 3:6).

But when a crowd of Jews had been stirred by this deed, let us now see the returning lightning-flash. Peter says:

> “Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us as though by our own virtue or power we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus” (Acts 3:12).

A little later:

> “We are witnesses of this; and in faith in his name, this man whom you see and know has been strengthened by his name, and the faith that is through him has given him this complete healing in the presence of you all.”

The lightning-flash went forth when Peter performed the miracle; it returned when he attributed what he had done not to himself but to its author. Lightning-flashes go forth when holy preachers display wondrous works, but in returning they say, “Here we are,” when, in what they do, they turn back to the power of the author.

#### 8. Preachers sent into the public sphere of activity should strive to return to the hidden place of contemplation.

This, however, can also be understood in another way. For, as was said above, holy men are sent forth like lightning-flashes and go when they leave the hidden place of contemplation for the public sphere of activity. They are sent forth and go when they spread from the secrecy of inward contemplation into the breadth of the active life. But in returning they say to God, “Here we are,” because after the external works they perform they always return to the bosom of contemplation, so that there they may renew the flame of their ardor and, as though touched by heavenly brightness, may become inflamed.

For they would quickly grow cold amid their very good external works unless, with attentive purpose, they constantly returned to the fire of contemplation. Hence Solomon rightly says:

> “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

There they are called rivers who here are called lightning-flashes. They are called rivers because they water the hearts of their hearers; they are called lightning-flashes because they kindle them.

Of these it is written elsewhere:

> “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voices” (Psalm 92:3).

And again:

> “His lightning-flashes have shone upon the world” (Psalm 96:4).

Thus the rivers return to the place from which they flow, because holy men, although they come forth from the sight of their Creator—whose brightness they strive to behold with the mind—for our sake into the ministry of the active life, nevertheless return without ceasing to the holy discipline of contemplation. Although in their preaching they pour themselves outwardly into our ears through bodily words, in the silence of their minds they always return to contemplate that very fountain of light.

Of them it is also rightly said:

> “So that they may flow again.”

For unless they returned constantly to the contemplation of God with attentive minds, inward dryness would surely dry up even the external words of their preaching. But while they thirst unceasingly to see God, rivers destined to flow outward are always born within them, so that there, by loving him, they may receive what they can pour down upon us through preaching.

Let it therefore rightly be said:

> “Will you send forth lightning-flashes, and they will go, and, returning, say to you, ‘Here we are’?”

The implied meaning is: “Here we are for me, who, whenever I wish, appoint my preachers, after the grace of contemplation, to the ministry of the active life; yet I always recall them from external good works to the inward summit of contemplation, so that now, commanded, they may go forth to perform works, and now, recalled, may live with me more familiarly in the discipline of contemplation.”

Thus, when returning, they say, “Here we are,” because although through external actions they may seem to lack something of contemplation, nevertheless, through the ardor of desire that they continually kindle in their minds, they show their presence to God in obedience. To say, “Here we are,” is to show themselves present through love.

It follows:

## CHAPTER III [Rec. III]

### VERSE 36

> “Who placed wisdom in the inmost parts of man? Or who gave understanding to the rooster?”

#### 9. The understanding given by God to preachers, represented by the rooster that announces the day by its crowing. Why the loins of this rooster are girded.

Who else are designated here by the name “roosters” except the same holy preachers, mentioned again under another figure, who amid the darkness of the present life strive to announce, as though by crowing, the light that is to come through preaching? For they say:

> “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12).

By their voices they shake off the sleep of our sluggishness, crying:

> “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13:11).

And again:

> “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15:34).

[Vet. V.] Concerning this rooster it is written again:

> “There are three things that walk well, and a fourth that proceeds successfully: the lion, strongest among beasts, fears no encounter; the rooster girded at the loins; and the ram—and there is no king who can resist him” (Proverbs 30:29–31).

Here the lion is the one of whom it is written:

> “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).

He is called strongest among beasts because in him “what is weak of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25). He fears no encounter. For he says:

> “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

“The rooster girded at the loins” signifies the holy preachers announcing the true dawn amid the darkness of this night. Their loins are girded because they restrain the flow of lust from their members. Lust is located in the loins. Hence the Lord also says to them:

> “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

“And the ram—and there is no king who can resist him.” Whom else do we understand by the ram here except the first order within the Church, the order of priests? Of them it is written:

> “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28:1).

By their example they draw the people who walk after them, like a following flock of sheep. When they live spiritually and rightly, no king at all is able to resist them, because no persecutor who confronts them can obstruct their purpose. They know how to run anxiously toward the one whom they desire and to reach him by dying.

Thus the lion is placed first, the rooster second, and the ram third. Christ appeared first, then the holy preachers, the apostles, and finally the spiritual fathers who preside over the Churches—that is, the leaders of the flocks, because they are teachers of the peoples who follow them.

#### 10. The Antichrist, raised on high, will appear foolish. In this life, not everything that is good is successful, nor is everything successful good.

But we can affirm these things still more clearly if, by explaining the remaining words of the same passage, we add what follows. For because the Antichrist will also appear after these things, the text adds this as the fourth, saying:

> “And he who appeared foolish after he had been raised on high. If he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth” (Proverbs 30:32).

He will be raised on high when he falsely claims to be God. But, raised on high, he will appear foolish, because at the very height of his elevation he will perish at the coming of the true Judge. If he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth—that is, if, when he began to grow proud, he had foreseen his punishment, he would not have been lifted up into such an ostentation of pride, though he had once been well created.

We should not be disturbed by what was said above:

> “The fourth proceeds successfully” (ibid., 29).

It said that three proceed well and the fourth successfully. For not everything that is successful is good, nor in this life is everything good successful. The lion, the rooster, and the ram proceed well, but not successfully here, because they endure the battles of persecution. The fourth proceeds successfully, but not well, because the Antichrist will walk in deception; nevertheless, for the brief period of the present life, that deception will prosper for him, as it is said of him under the figure of Antiochus through Daniel:

> “Strength was given to him against the continual sacrifice because of sins; and truth will be cast down to the ground, and he will act and prosper” (Daniel 8:12).

What Solomon calls “proceeding successfully,” Daniel calls “prospering.”

In keeping with this testimony spoken through Solomon—

> “The rooster girded at the loins” (Proverbs 30:31)—

we rightly understand the rooster here also as the holy preachers.

Therefore, referring everything back to himself, the Lord says:

> “Who placed wisdom in the inmost parts of man? Or who gave understanding to the rooster?”

It is as though he said: “Who poured the grace of heavenly wisdom into the heart of a human being who possesses human wisdom? Or who gave understanding to the holy preachers, except me, so that they might know when and to whom they ought to announce the coming dawn?”

For this reason they perceive when and what they should do: they know it because I reveal it inwardly.

It should be noted that divinely inspired wisdom is given in the inmost parts of man because, insofar as the number of the elect is concerned, it is given not only in words but also in the senses, so that, in accordance with what the tongue says, the conscience may live, and its light may shine more brightly on the surface the more truly it burns within the heart.

## [Rec. IV.] 11. How greatly the rulers of souls need discernment.

It is a matter of great labor to examine more subtly what is added:

> “Or who gave understanding to the rooster?”

The understanding of teachers must be more subtle in proportion as it exercises itself in penetrating invisible things, in proportion as it examines nothing material, and in proportion as, while speaking through the bodily voice, it passes beyond everything bodily. Such understanding would in no way befit the highest things unless the Creator of the highest things himself supplied it to the rooster—that is, to the teaching preacher who sings.

The rooster also received understanding so that it might first distinguish the hours of the night and only then utter its awakening call, because every holy preacher first considers the quality of life in his hearers and only then forms an appropriate voice of preaching for their instruction.

To distinguish the hours of the night is, as it were, to judge the merits of sinners; to distinguish the hours of the night is, as it were, to rebuke the darkness of their actions with a fitting voice of correction. Understanding, therefore, is bestowed from above upon the rooster, because the teacher of truth is divinely granted the power of discernment, so that he may know to whom, what, when, and how he should bring his message.

[**Vet. VI.**] 12. An exhortation that benefits some harms others.

For one and the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, since not everyone is bound by the same quality of character. Often what benefits some harms others. Frequently, herbs that restore one animal kill another; a gentle whistle calms horses but incites puppies; a medicine that reduces one person’s illness adds strength to another; and bread that strengthens the life of the strong kills the little ones.

The discourse of teachers must therefore be formed according to the quality of the hearers. It should suit each person individually and yet never depart from the art of common edification.

For what are the attentive minds of hearers except, as it were, certain stretched strings laid upon a lyre? The musician who knows how to touch them strikes them differently, so that they do not produce a song unlike themselves. The strings therefore give back a harmonious melody because they are struck by a single plectrum, but not with a single stroke. Thus every teacher, in order to build everyone up in the one virtue of charity, should touch the hearts of his hearers from one doctrine, but not with one identical exhortation.

### 13. Different admonitions should be given according to the character of each person.

[Note: These matters are treated at great length in the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, which the holy Doctor was already contemplating at that time, as is clear from what follows.]

Men must be admonished in one way and women in another; young people in one way and the old in another; the poor in one way and the rich in another; the joyful in one way and the sorrowful in another; subjects in one way and superiors in another; servants in one way and masters in another; those wise in the ways of this world in one way and the dull in another; the shameless in one way and the modest in another; the insolent in one way and the fainthearted in another; the impatient in one way and the patient in another; the kind in one way and the envious in another; the simple in one way and the impure in another; the healthy in one way and the sick in another; those who fear scourges and therefore live innocently in one way, and those who have grown so hardened in wickedness that even scourges do not correct them in another; the excessively silent in one way and those devoted to much speaking in another; the timid in one way and the bold in another; the lazy in one way and the rash in another; the gentle in one way and the angry in another; the humble in one way and the proud in another; the obstinate in one way and the fickle in another; those devoted to gluttony in one way and the abstinent in another; those who mercifully distribute what is theirs in one way and those who strive to seize what belongs to others in another; those who neither seize what belongs to others nor give away what is theirs in one way, and those who both give away what they possess and do not cease to seize what belongs to others in another; the discordant in one way and the peaceful in another; those who sow quarrels in one way and the peacemakers in another.

Those who do not correctly understand the words of sacred law must be admonished in one way, and those who understand them correctly but do not speak them humbly in another. Those who are capable of preaching worthy things but are afraid because of excessive humility must be admonished in one way, and those whom imperfection or age prevents from preaching but whom rashness drives forward in another. Those who prosper in the temporal things they desire must be admonished in one way, and those who indeed covet the things of the world but are worn out by the labor of adversity in another. Those bound by marriage in one way, and those free from the bonds of marriage in another; those who have experienced sexual intercourse in one way, and those who have not in another; those who lament sins of action in one way, and those who lament sins of thought in another; those who mourn the sins they have committed but do not abandon them in one way, and those who abandon them but do not mourn them in another; those who even praise the unlawful things they do in one way, and those who accuse their evil deeds but nevertheless do not avoid them in another.

Those who are overcome by sudden desire must be admonished in one way, and those who are bound to sin by deliberation in another; those who frequently do unlawful things, though they are small, in one way, and those who guard themselves from small things but sometimes plunge into grave sins in another; those who do not even begin good works in one way, and those who do not complete what they have begun in another; those who do evil secretly and good publicly in one way, and those who conceal the good they do yet allow others, through certain actions, to form a public opinion that they are evil in another.

Indeed, we ought to have set forth in detail what order of admonition is appropriate for each person, but fear of the length of the discourse holds us back. With God as author, however, my mind desires to complete this in another work, provided that some time still remains for me in this laborious life.

[**Vet. VII.**] 14. The wicked must be rebuked with loud and powerful voices; those who have withdrawn from wickedness must be admonished with gentle and soothing ones.

There is another point concerning the rooster’s understanding that we ought to consider: during the deeper hours of night it customarily produces stronger and longer songs, but when the morning hour is already approaching it forms voices that are altogether gentler and shorter.

The considered discernment of preachers shows us what the understanding of this rooster signifies. When they preach to minds that are still wicked, they proclaim the terrors of the eternal judgment in loud and powerful voices, because they cry out, as it were, amid the darkness of a deep night. But when they recognize that the light of truth has already come near to the hearts of their hearers, they turn the loudness of their cry into the gentleness of sweetness, and bring forth not so much what is terrifying about punishments as what is reassuring about rewards.

They also sing then in shorter voices, because, as morning approaches, they preach the more subtle things concerning the mysteries, so that their followers hear the finer points of heavenly matters in proportion as they draw nearer to the light of truth. Those whom the rooster’s long cry had awakened while they were asleep are delighted by its shorter call while they are awake. Thus, once corrected, each person may take pleasure in learning subtly about the kingdom, though previously he had feared the adversities of judgment.

This is well represented through Moses, when the trumpets are commanded to sound in a shortened blast for the setting out of the army. For it is written:

> “Make for yourself two silver trumpets, beaten out of one piece” (Numbers 10:2).

And shortly afterward:

> “When the shortened blast sounds the alarm, the camps shall move” (ibid., 5).

The army is led by means of two trumpets because, through the two commandments of charity, the people are called to the battle array of faith. They are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of preachers may be clear with the brightness of light and may not confuse the minds of their hearers by any obscurity of their own.

They are commanded to be beaten out because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations. It is rightly said:

> “When the shortened blast sounds the alarm, the camps shall move” (Numbers 10:5),

because when the word of preaching is delivered more subtly and precisely, the hearts of hearers are stirred more ardently for battle against temptations.

### 15. Those who exhort others by office should first exercise themselves in good works.

There is still another matter that should be carefully observed in the rooster: when it is about to sing, it first shakes its wings and strikes itself, making itself more alert.

We plainly perceive this if we watch attentively the life of the holy preachers. When they utter the words of preaching, they first exercise themselves in holy actions, lest, while sluggish in their own works, they awaken others with their voice. First they shake themselves through exalted deeds, and then they make others eager to act well.

First they strike themselves with the wings of their thoughts, because through careful examination they detect whatever uselessly lies sluggish within them and correct it through strict scrutiny. First they take care to punish their own faults with tears, and then they announce what must be punished in others.

Thus they first make their wings resound before they utter their song, because before they bring forth words of exhortation, they proclaim by their works everything they are about to say. When they are fully awake in themselves, they then call others who are sleeping to wakefulness.

### 16. Preachers and teachers receive from God what enables them to discharge their office rightly.

But where does a teacher obtain such great understanding that he can remain perfectly awake himself and call those who sleep to wakefulness through certain advances of his cry; that he can first carefully examine the darkness of sins and afterward discreetly show the light of preaching; that he can suit each person according to measure and time and at the same time show all people the things they should follow?

How can one reach such great and subtle things unless he is taught inwardly by the one by whom he was created? Since the praise for such great understanding is not the preacher’s virtue but the author’s, it is rightly said by that same author:

> “Or who gave understanding to the rooster?”

It is as though he said: “Who except me, who wondrously created the minds of teachers from nothing, has instructed them still more wondrously to understand hidden things?”

Therefore, to show that in the words of preachers he is not only the inspirer of understanding but also the author of speech, he adds:

### VERSE 37

> “Who will declare the order of the heavens?”

[**Rec. V.**] Yet because, when he reveals himself to us in his appearance, he withdraws their words, he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER IV

### THE SAME PASSAGE

> “And who will make the concert of heaven sleep?”

#### 17. When God is revealed in his majesty, preaching will cease. The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son and is coeternal with both.

In this life, the Lord has spoken to our weakness not through the open appearance of his majesty but through the voice of his preachers, so that a bodily tongue might strike hearts that are still carnal, and so that they might more easily receive unfamiliar things because they heard them through the sound of a familiar voice.

But after, through death, the flesh has been dissolved into dust and, through the resurrection, the dust has been given life, then we do not seek to hear words about God, because we already see the Word of God itself, which fills all things, in his visible appearance. It sounds to us all the more profoundly as the power of inward illumination penetrates our minds.

When the words that rise and set have been removed, the very image of inward vision becomes, as it were, a certain sound of eternal preaching. Hence the Lord rightly now says to blessed Job:

> “Who will declare the order of the heavens, and who will make the concert of heaven sleep?”

For what is understood by the order of the heavens except the heavenly power of hidden things? What is signified by the concert of heaven except the harmonious speech of preachers?

Thus, when our Creator begins to declare the order of the heavens, he makes the concert of heaven sleep, because when he is already shown to us in his visible appearance, the words of preachers are surely withdrawn.

For this reason the Lord says through Jeremiah:

> “A man will no longer teach his neighbor and his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:34).

Hence Paul says:

> “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13:8).

[Vet. VIII.] Alternatively, the order of the heavens is the life-giving power itself that forms the spirits of angels. For God is the cause of causes, the life of the living, and likewise the order of rational creatures. The Lord then declares the order of the heavens when he reveals how he presides over the elect spirits. He declares the order of the heavens when, having wiped away the darkness of our minds, he manifests himself in a clear vision.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25).

He asserts that he will announce the Father openly because he will then show, through the disclosed appearance of his majesty, how he is born from the one who begets him without being unequal to him, and how the Spirit of both proceeds, coeternal with both.

Then we shall clearly see how that which exists by being born is not subsequent to the one from whom it is born, and how the one produced through procession is not preceded by those who bring him forth. Then we shall clearly see how the one is three divisibly, and the three are one indivisibly.

The tongue of God who then speaks is the visible brightness that lifts us up. The concert of heaven will then sleep, because, when the rewarder of works appears in judgment, the words of exhortation will cease.

Thus the time of the resurrection itself is also plainly added, when it immediately says:

## CHAPTER V

### VERSE 38

> “When dust was formed upon the earth, and the clods were joined together.”

#### 18. The time of the resurrection foreseen and foretold by Job.

In its customary manner, divine speech describes things that are still future as though they had already passed, preserving in itself what is said through it:

> “He has made the things that are to come” (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

Then dust is formed upon the earth because it is restored to solid limbs. And the clods are joined together because firm bodies, gathered from dust, rise.

But having explained how these words of the Lord are to be understood concerning the future, let us now also indicate what they disclose concerning the present.

[Vet. IX.] 19. Heavenly things are hidden from the reprobate and revealed to the elect.

> “Who will declare the order of the heavens, and who will make the concert of heaven sleep?”

The Lord declares the order of the heavens when, by now revealing heavenly secrets, he illuminates the minds of his elect. He makes the concert of heaven sleep when, by a just judgment, he hides from the hearts of the reprobate the harmonious hymns of the angels and those joys of the heavenly powers.

Although this concert of heaven is inwardly awake in itself, it sleeps outwardly in the very ignorance of the reprobate. Thus the order of the heavenly secret is declared, yet the concert of heaven is permitted to sleep, because the knowledge of heavenly reward is disclosed to some through inspiration, while the sweetness of inward praise is concealed from others.

20. Visible things hinder the reprobate here, but compel the saints toward better things.—The order of the heavens is recounted because what the reward of heavenly things is is continually disclosed to the minds of the elect, so that they may advance without ceasing and, passing beyond visible things, extend themselves toward invisible realities. For every visible thing that fixes the reprobate in this life impels the elect toward other things [Note: Pratel., Utic., and others: “toward another,” namely, life. Corb. Germ.: “everyth— — — the reprobate made” (and in the margin, as though a different reading, “renews the reprobate”) — — — “impels toward another.”]. For while they look upon the good things that have been made, they burn with love for Him by whom they were made; and they love Him all the more excellently because they consider that He Himself, who created this good, surpasses it. An invisible tongue speaks inwardly to them, sounding silently in the voice of compunction [Note: Corb. Germ., Pratel., Utic., Val. Cl., Laud., etc., have this reading. Where the printed editions read, “which sounds silently.”]. They hear it inwardly all the more fully the more perfectly they turn away from the din of outward desires [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl.: “more gently.”].

Thus the song of heaven does not sleep for them, because their mind, with the ear of love applied, recognizes the sweetness of heavenly praise. Within, they hear what they desire, and by the very desire for divinity they are instructed concerning the rewards of heavenly goods. Hence they endure the present life gravely, not only when it opposes them but even when it favors them, because everything visible is burdensome to them insofar as it delays them from what they hear within. They judge everything available to them burdensome because it is not that for which they yearn; yet their mind, wearied continually by the labors of temporality, is lifted up to be restored in that heavenly joy, while the song of heaven breaks forth within the ear of the heart and they daily await fellowship with the citizens above.

This song of heavenly praise had broken forth in the ear of the one who said:

> I shall enter the place of the wondrous tabernacle, as far as the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of a festive city (Psalm 41:5).

Since, then, he had heard within the voice of exultation and confession and the sound of a festive city, what else was arousing him except the song of heaven? [Note: Gilot. and later editions: “in his voice.” The older Paris and Basel editions more appropriately read “in his ear,” which accords better with what precedes and is found in the manuscripts Norm. and others.]

21. The song of heaven is not heard by the wicked.—Yet this song sleeps for the reprobate, because it is not made known to their hearts through the voice of compunction. They do not strive to contemplate that desirable multitude of heavenly citizens; they see none of the festivals of that inward solemnity by any ray of ardor; they are not lifted up in the inmost places of contemplation on any wing. For they serve visible things alone. Therefore they hear no sweetness of heavenly things inwardly, because, as we said above, the deafening tumult of worldly cares presses upon them in the ear of the heart.

Since, then, by the hidden dispensation of judgment what is opened to some is closed to others, and what is disclosed to some is concealed from others, it is rightly said:

> Who can recount the order of the heavens, and who can make the song of heaven sleep?

This became more widely known to us when our Redeemer, appearing through the mystery of His dispensation, both granted mercy to those who were unworthy and excluded from Himself those who seemed worthy. Hence what follows here is also fitting:

## CHAPTER VI [Old X, Recension VI]

### Verse 38

> When the dust was founded upon the earth, and the clods were compacted together.

22. Sinners are like dust, carried away by every breath of temptation; they are made firm by the grace of the Holy Spirit and compacted by charity.—Whom do we understand by dust if not sinners, who, solidified by no weight of reason, are carried away by every breath of temptation? Of them it is written:

> Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth (Psalm 1:5).

Dust, therefore, is founded upon the earth when sinners who have been called are made firm by the reason of the faith entrusted to them [Note: Longip.: “so that those who were previously unstable in conscience…”], so that those who before were unstable and were lifted up by the breeze of temptation might afterward stand immovable against temptations and, clinging steadfastly to God, retain the firm weight of a good life.

Clods, however, are coagulated from moisture and dust. Thus in this earth the clods are compacted, because sinners who have been called and infused with the grace of the Holy Spirit are united in the gathering of charity [Note: Laud., Corb. Germ., and Val. Cl.: *compinctae*, from *compingo*, “I compact.” This reading is found consistently thereafter. In some editions, especially the Vatican edition, the corrupt form *compunctae* appears, “pierced” or “pricked.”].

These clods are compacted in the earth when peoples who formerly, as though scattered dust, held different opinions afterward, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, came together in that most peaceful concord of unanimity, so that, when there were three thousand or again five thousand, Scripture could testify that “there was in them one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

The Lord daily compacts these clods in the earth from one dust, though distinguished as if by different masses, because, while preserving the unity of the sacrament, He gathers into the Church faithful peoples diverse in customs and languages. The Lord already indicated these clods when He commanded people to recline for the eating of the bread and fish by fifties or by hundreds (Matthew 14:19–20).

23. There are different orders in the Church.—Yet if we consider these clods in the Church according to the diversity of merits, perhaps we can distinguish them still more subtly. For one is the order of preachers and another of hearers; one of rulers and another of subjects; one of married people, another of the continent, another of penitents, and another of virgins. It is as though one earth had produced a variety of distinct clod-forms, since within one faith and one charity the merits of those who act well are shown to be diverse.

That people signified these clods who, with one purpose, offered diverse gifts for the construction of the tabernacle. Of them it is written:

> Whatever was necessary for the service of the tabernacle [Note: *Tabernaculi*—“of the tabernacle”—is absent in Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Laud., and Val. Cl.] and for the holy vestments, men together with women supplied: bracelets and earrings, rings and armlets; every golden vessel set apart as a gift to the Lord. Whoever possessed violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, and goats’ hair (Exodus 35:22), etc.

24. Each person offers gifts to complete the worship of the Church.—Thus, in the adornment of the tabernacle, men offer gifts together with women, because in fulfilling the worship of the holy Church both the sublime deeds of the strong and the modest works of the weak are reckoned. What is signified by bracelets, which bind the arms, if not the works of those in authority who labor vigorously? And what is expressed by earrings if not the obedience of subjects?

What is signified by rings if not the seal of hidden things? Often teachers seal what they see cannot be grasped by their hearers. And what is recalled by armlets if not the ornaments of the first work [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts: “are shown.”]?

What is understood by the golden vessel set apart as a gift to the Lord if not an understanding of divinity, which is separated from love of lower things all the more insofar as it is lifted up to love only what is eternal [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl.: “from the love of the weak”?]? What is signified by violet if not hope of heavenly things? What by purple if not blood and the endurance of sufferings offered through love of the everlasting kingdom? What by twice-dyed scarlet if not charity, which is dyed twice for the sake of perfection because it is adorned by love of God and neighbor?

What is signified by fine linen if not the undefiled incorruption of the flesh? And what is indicated by goats’ hair, from which the roughness of haircloth is woven, if not the harsh affliction of penitents?

Thus, while some exercise strong teaching through bracelets and rings, others display devoted obedience and upright action through earrings and armlets; some possess, through the vessel of gold set apart, a splendid and more refined understanding of God; others, through violet, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope for, believe in, and love the heavenly things they have heard, even though they do not yet know them through a more subtle understanding; some offer the incorruption of the flesh through fine linen; others, through goats’ hair, harshly lament what they willingly committed. As though from one earth, countless clods are brought forth, because from one and equal service diverse deeds of the faithful proceed.

These clods would by no means rise, congealed from dust, unless the dust first received water and solidified itself by taking in moisture. For unless the grace of the Holy Spirit infused each sinner, the unity of charity would not hold them bound together for the works of faith.

When, therefore, the Lord recounts the order of the heavens or makes the song of heaven sleep, let Him disclose it. For He says:

> When the dust was founded upon the earth, and the clods were compacted together.

It is as though He said: “Then, through manifest calling and distinction, I first opened spiritual secrets to some, not without mercy, and closed them to others, not without justice, when I rejected some and united others within the Church in the concord of charity.”

Since this holy Church, rejected by the unbelief of the Jews, turned to seize the nations and convert them into its own body—a work accomplished not by its own strength but by the Lord’s power—it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER VII [Old XI, Recension VII]

### Verse 39

> Will you seize prey for the lioness, and fill the souls of her cubs?

25. The Church is the lioness, whose cubs were the apostles.—This is surely that lioness of which Job spoke when he saw proud Judea passed over while the Church preached:

> The children of the merchants have not trodden it, nor has the lioness passed through it (Job 28:8).

The Lord therefore seizes prey for this lioness in order to fill the souls of her cubs, because for the increase of this Church He snatched innumerable people from the nations and satisfied the hungry desires of the apostles through the gain of souls.

They were called cubs because of the tenderness of their minds and the weakness of their fear; for when the Lord had suffered, they remained behind closed doors, as it is written:

> When evening had come on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst (John 20:19).

Hence what follows here concerning these same cubs is also fitting:

## CHAPTER VIII

### Verse 40

> When they lie in dens and lie in wait in caves.

26. At first they lay in dens, from which they leapt forth into the world to seize prey.—When the holy apostles did not yet rise up against the members of the devil with the free voice of preaching, and, not yet strengthened after the Lord’s Passion by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, did not proclaim their Redeemer with firm authority, they still lay in wait against their adversaries as though in dens.

With the doors closed, their cubs lay as if in hidden caves, preparing to carry off the world, so that afterward they might boldly seize the prey of souls. It is certain that at that time they feared the assault of the world even while hiding from it themselves. With those doors closed, these cubs sought by lying in wait the death of our death, so that they might kill our guilt and destroy within us the entire life of sin.

To the first of these hungry cubs, already strong, when the nations were shown through the linen cloth as though prey had been displayed, it was said:

> Kill and eat (Acts 10:13).

To these cubs, still weak, they are commanded to lie in dens when the Lord’s voice says:

> Stay here in the city until you are clothed with power from on high (Luke 24:49).

Are they not rightly called the cubs of the lioness, who, born in the Church, seized the hostile world with their mouths?

27. The perfected teachers imitate them. He knows how to speak rightly who knows how to remain silent in due order.—We know that these things were done by the holy apostles, and we now see them done by perfected teachers [Note: Vindoc., Pratel., and Utic.: “by holy teachers.” Laud. and Val. Cl.: “by upright teachers.”]. They are indeed fathers of later peoples, but they are sons of those who came before; hence they are also not improperly called cubs. Or certainly, although they are teachers of some of the faithful, they glory in being disciples of the universal Church.

The Lord therefore seizes prey for the lioness because, by the power of His inspiration, He snatches the life of sinners from error; and He fills the souls of her cubs because, through the conversion of many, He satisfies the holy desires of teachers.

Of these cubs it is rightly added:

> When they lie in dens and lie in wait in caves.

For not every time is suitable for teaching. Often the force of words is lost if they are uttered at an unsuitable time. Frequently, however, what is said more gently is enlivened by the fitting occasion. He therefore knows how to speak rightly who also knows how to remain silent in due order.

What benefit is there in rebuking an angry person at a time when, with his mind deranged, he is scarcely able not only to understand another’s words but even to endure himself? Whoever rebukes a raging person through invective is like someone who inflicts blows on a drunkard who cannot feel them.

Therefore, if teaching is to reach the heart of the hearer, it must weigh which moments are suitable for it. Thus it is rightly said of these cubs:

> When they lie in dens and lie in wait in caves.

For holy teachers, when they observe things requiring correction but nevertheless restrain themselves in their thoughts through silence, lie hidden as though in caves and conceal themselves as though in dens, because they hide within their own hearts. But when they find the appropriate time, they suddenly leap forth, withholding nothing that ought to be said, and hold the necks of the proud with the bite of harsh reproof.

Thus, whether through the apostles or through the teachers whom He appointed in the apostles’ place, the Lord daily seizes prey for this lioness; and through those whom He has captured, He does not cease to capture others also. For this is why the righteous seize the sinners of this world: so that, through those who have been converted, others from the world may also be seized.

Hence the same gentile people, which was captured by the devout mouth of the apostles [Note: Vindoc. and Val. Cl.: “was captured by the mouth”], now hungers for others with as great a hunger as it knows itself to have been desired by the apostles. Therefore it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER IX [Old XII, Recension VIII]

### Verse 41

> Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no food?

28. The converted nations are the raven, whose young are the holy preachers.—What else is designated by the raven and its young than the nations black with sins? Of them the Prophet says:

> He gives their food to the beasts, and to the young of ravens calling upon Him (Psalm 146:9).

The beasts receive food when minds that were formerly brutish are satisfied with the nourishment of Sacred Scripture. Food is given to the young of hinds (*pullis cervorum*)—that is, to the sons of the nations—when their desire is refreshed by our manner of life [Note: Vindoc., Corb. Germ., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts: “by our conversion”; “conversation” in the main text].

This raven was food when the holy Church itself was seeking it [Note: Laud.: “while it was seeking the holy Church itself,” with excellent sense]. But now it receives food, because it itself seeks out others for conversion.

29. They know that they can accomplish nothing by their own strength.—Its young, that is, the preachers born from it, do not trust in themselves but in the strength of their Redeemer. Hence it is rightly said:

> When its young cry out to God.

They know that they can accomplish nothing by their own strength. Although they hunger with devout desires for the gain of souls, they nevertheless desire these things to be accomplished by Him who works everything inwardly. For by true faith they understand that “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

30. They burn with zeal to gain souls.—When it is said, “wandering because they have no food,” this wandering signifies nothing other than the desires of preachers who are burning with zeal. While they seek to receive peoples into the bosom of the Church, kindled by great ardor, they direct their desire now toward gathering these, now those.

The burning of thought itself is, as it were, a kind of wandering; and they pass, as though by varied signals, to different places [Note: Some editions: “while seeking to help…”], as with a hungry mind they run through countless ways and diverse directions for the sake of uniting souls [Note: Laud.: “as though it were a kind of devout wandering.”].

[Old XIII.] 31. Paul’s concern for nearly all the churches. Charity, which unites what is divided, divided Paul’s heart among many.—The young of the ravens, that is, the sons of the nations, learned this wandering from the teacher of the nations himself. He burns with such powerful charity that he changes places with such excessive wandering [Note: Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts differ: “he burns with as great a charity as with excessive…” Corb. Germ.: “he himself, whom excessive ardor of powerful charity…”], moving from place to place; he desires to pass from one place to another because the very charity that fills him impels him.

Although far away from the Romans, he writes:

> I always make mention of you in my prayers, asking whether somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you; for I desire to see you (Romans 1:9–10).

Detained at Ephesus, he writes to the Corinthians:

> Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you (2 Corinthians 12:14).

Again, while staying at Ephesus, he says to the Galatians:

> I wish I could be with you now and change my voice (Galatians 4:20).

At Rome also, shut up under guard in prison, because he is not permitted to go to the Philippians himself, he promises to send a disciple, saying:

> I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn how things are with you (Philippians 2:10).

Also bound in chains and detained at Ephesus, he writes to the Colossians:

> For although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit (Colossians 2:5).

Behold how he wanders through holy desire: here he is held bodily, there he is led in spirit. He presents the affection of paternal love to these who are present and shows it to those who are absent; he performs works for those placed before him and expresses his desires to those who hear him [Note: We suspect that the reading should be “he expresses his desires to those absent,” namely, through letters, as it is read in Laud. Nevertheless, we have judged that nothing should be changed in the text, since our manuscripts, Corb. Germ. and the Norman manuscripts of excellent quality, have *audientibus*, “to those who hear,” a reading found in all the editions we have consulted.]. He is effectively present to those with whom he was, yet not absent from those with whom he was not.

We understand his wandering better if we consider further his words to the Corinthians. He says:

> I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia. For I will pass through Macedonia; but perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter (1 Corinthians 16:5–6).

Let us consider, please, what this wandering is. Behold, he remains for the time being in one place, says that he will go to another, and promises to turn aside to yet another. What is it that divides him so anxiously among so many places [Note: Turon.: “wanders”], except that he is bound to everyone by one charity? For charity, which customarily unites what is divided, compels Paul’s one heart to be divided among many. Yet it gathers him all the more tightly in God the more widely it spreads him through holy desires.

In preaching, therefore, Paul wishes to say everything to everyone at once; in loving, he wishes to see everyone at once. By remaining in the flesh, he wishes to live for everyone; and by passing from the flesh through the sacrifice of faith, he wishes to benefit everyone.

Let the young of the ravens wander, then—that is, let the sons of the nations imitate their teacher. Let them shake off the sluggishness of mind, and, when they do not find the gain of souls, their food, let them not rest. Let them extend themselves from advancement toward further advancement, and, burning for the benefit of many, let them hunger for their nourishment as though wandering.

Since, by traveling about through the work of preaching, they do not cease to satisfy the nations with the nourishment of faith, it is rightly said:

> Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no food?

[Old XIV.] 32. The Jewish people is also signified by the raven. Having witnessed the conversion of the nations, it will one day come to its senses and blush at its folly.—The Jewish people, black through the merit of unbelief, may also be designated by the name of the raven. Its young are said to cry out to God so that food may be prepared by the Lord for that same raven, because the holy apostles, born in the flesh from the people of Israel, while pouring out prayers to the Lord for their nation, like young ravens nourished the people who was their parent according to the flesh through spiritual understanding.

Thus, while its young cry out, food is prepared for the raven, because, while the apostles pray, the people once faithless is brought to knowledge of the faith and is satisfied, as it were, by the voice of the young through the preaching of its sons.

We must carefully observe in this verse, however, that food is said to be prepared for this raven first while the young are crying and afterward while they are wandering. Food was prepared for the raven while the young were crying when, as the apostles preached, Judea heard the word of God and was spiritually satisfied, at one time in three thousand, at another in five thousand [Note: All our manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions instead read, “but when the multitude of the reprobate…”].

But when, through the multitude of the reprobate, it exercised its cruelty against those preaching and, as it were, killed the life of the young, those same young were scattered throughout all the regions of the world [Note: Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts: “throughout the whole part of the world.” Val. Cl. and Corb. Germ.: “throughout all … part.”].

Therefore, when those carnal parents resisted spiritual preaching, they said:

> It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations (Acts 13:46) [Note: Vindoc.: “It was necessary for us to speak to you first.”].

They knew, of course, that after the nations believed, Judea too would come to faith. Hence it is also written:

> Until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved (Romans 11:25) [Note: Vindoc.: “should enter.”].

Since, therefore, the holy apostles earnestly strove first to preach to those who listened and afterward to show the examples of the converted nations to those who resisted, the young, hungering for this raven, sought its food first by crying out and afterward by wandering.

For from the place to which the young wander, the raven finds food: when the Jewish people sees the nations converted to God through the labor of the preachers, it finally blushes at the folly of its unbelief. Then it understands the sayings of Sacred Scripture, when it recognizes that the nations learned them before it; and, once the young have completed their wandering, it opens the mouth of its heart to receive the sacred words. For after the apostles’ journeys throughout the world have been completed, it perceives those words spiritually, words from which it had long fasted because unbelief had bound it.

Since the power of divine omnipotence alone accomplishes all these things, it is rightly said:

> Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no food?

It is as though He said: “Who except I, who endure the unbelieving people for the sake of its children who pray, feed it through those who preach, and at the end sustain it for conversion while they wander toward other places?” [Note: Gilot., Gussanv., and some editions read “and spare it while they preach,” contrary to the testimony of all our manuscripts, which read *pasco*, “I feed.” This reading is also found in the old editions, and the passage being explained proves that it should be read: “who prepares food for the raven.”]

[Old XV.] 33. Skilled teachers withhold the food of higher teaching from disciples who do not think humbly enough of themselves.—It is possible to understand something else morally concerning the raven. After its young have been born, it is said to pretend not to provide them food fully until they become black by growing feathers, and it allows them to suffer hunger until its own likeness appears in them through the blackness of their feathers. They wander here and there in the nest and seek help for food with open mouths. But when they begin to become black, it seeks food to be provided for them with all the greater eagerness, the longer it had delayed feeding them.

The raven is plainly every learned preacher who cries out with a loud voice while carrying the memory of his sins and knowledge of his own weakness as a kind of blackness of color. Disciples are born to him in faith, but perhaps they still do not know how to consider their own weakness [Note: Recent editions, together with Corb. Germ., add “to consider the blackness of their own weakness,” a mere gloss absent from the old editions and from the other manuscripts—Laud., Val. Cl., Vindoc., Ebroic., and the other Norman manuscripts. Corb. Germ. has shortly before: “to him indeed…”]. Perhaps they turn their memory away from past sins and therefore do not display the blackness of humility that must be assumed against the glory of this world.

They open their mouths as though to receive food when they seek to be taught sublime secrets [Note: Vindoc.: “heavenly secrets.”]. But their teacher gives them the nourishment of sublime teachings all the less insofar as he recognizes that they mourn their past sins with insufficient worthiness [Note: Vindoc., Pratel., Utic.: “observes.”]. For he waits and admonishes them first to become black through the laments of repentance, away from the brightness of the present life, and only then to receive the appropriate and most subtle nourishment of preaching.

The raven observes the open, gaping mouths of its young, but first desires their bodies to be clothed in the blackness of feathers. So also the discerning teacher does not minister inward mysteries to the senses of those whom he sees have not yet cast themselves away from this world.

Therefore, the less black the disciples are outwardly through the cultivation of their present life, the less they are filled inwardly by the food of the word; and the less they empty themselves of bodily glory, the more they fast from spiritual refreshment.

34. It is otherwise if they humble themselves in confession of their sins.—But if, in confessing their past life, they bring forth groans of lament as though blackening feathers, at once the teacher, contemplating the nourishment to be brought down from sublime things, flies like a raven thinking about the feeding of its young. He recalls food to their gaping mouths when, from the understanding he has begun to possess, he supplies nourishment of life through speech to his hungry disciples. He refreshes them from above all the more ardently the more truly he recognizes that they have become black, through the lament of repentance, in relation to the brightness of the world.

35.
