The greater the humility, the greater also the hope of advancement.—When the young clothe themselves in the black color of feathers, they also promise flight, because the more humbly the disciples think of themselves, and the more they afflict themselves by despising themselves, the more they promise hope of their own advancement toward higher things.

Hence the teacher takes care to feed more eagerly those whom he already foresees, through certain indications, to be capable of benefiting others. For this reason Paul admonishes Timothy to nourish the young as though they were growing feathers, when he says:

> What you have heard from me before many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be capable of teaching others also (2 Timothy 2:2).

When this discretion in teaching is carefully guarded by the preacher, a more abundant supply of preaching is divinely granted to him. For when he knows how to sympathize through charity with afflicted disciples, and through discretion understands the appropriate time for teaching, he receives greater gifts of understanding not only for himself but also for those to whom he devotes the efforts of his labor.

Hence it is also fittingly said here:

> Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no food?

For when the young cry out to be satisfied, food is prepared for the raven, because when good hearers hunger for the word of God, greater gifts of understanding are bestowed upon teachers for their refreshment.

It follows:

## CHAPTER X [Old XVI, Recension IX]

### Chapter 39, Verse 1

> Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth upon the rocks, or have you watched the hinds in labor?

36. Why spiritual teachers are signified by wild goats and hinds. A description of the wild goats. How hinds cross rivers. What we do grows all the more before God as it diminishes through humility before ourselves.—The southern region calls *ibices* birds that inhabit the streams of the Nile. The eastern and western regions, however, call small four-footed animals *ibices*, and it is their custom to give birth upon rocks, because they know how to live nowhere but upon rocks.

If at times they fall from the lofty peaks of cliffs, they receive themselves unharmed upon their horns. For they strike their heads as they fall; when they first set out their horns, their whole body is kept from the damage of the fall [Note: Most Norman manuscripts and Vindoc.: “they place them before themselves.”].

It is the custom of hinds to kill snakes they find and to tear their bodies apart with their bites. It is also said that whenever they cross rivers, they place the burdens of their heads upon the backs of those in front, and, taking turns with one another, feel none of the burden’s labor.

What, then, is the meaning of blessed Job being questioned about the birth of wild goats and hinds, except that the person of spiritual teachers is signified by hinds and wild goats? Like wild goats, they give birth upon rocks, because in the teaching of the fathers—who are called rocks because of their firmness—they beget souls for conversion.

Like wild goats, they suffer no harm from falls, since they are caught upon their horns [Note: Laud.: “are received”]. Whatever temporal ruin may approach them, they take refuge in the testimonies of Sacred Scripture and are saved, as though caught upon their horns. For it is said of these testimonies:

> Horns are in His hands (Habakkuk 3:4).

Thus they flee for consolation to the Scriptures when they are struck by some loss from a temporal fall. Did Paul not, after the manner of wild goats, receive himself upon his horns when, falling amid the adversities of this world, he said:

> Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope (Romans 15:4)?

They are also called hinds, as it is said through Jeremiah concerning teachers who carelessly abandon the children born from them:

> The hind gave birth in the field and abandoned it (Jeremiah 14:5) [Note: *De*, “of” or “from,” is omitted in Laud.].

Like hinds, they live after destroying vices, as though after extinguishing snakes; and from that very destruction of vices they burn more intensely for the fountain of life. Hence the Psalmist says:

> As the hind longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for You, God (Psalm 41:1).

Also, while they cross the fleeting moments of this temporality as though they were rivers, they bear one another’s burdens, through compassionate charity placing their burdens upon one another, because they carefully guard what is written:

> Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2).

Since, after the Lord’s coming, spiritual teachers were scattered throughout the world, able through preaching to give birth to the souls of hearers in conversion [Note: Ebroic., Laud., Corb. Germ., Val. Cl.: “in conversion”], and since this same time of the Lord’s incarnation was not known before the voices of the prophets—although the incarnation itself, which was to come, was foreknown to all the elect—it is fitting that blessed Job should be questioned about the time of the birth of the wild goats and hinds, and that it should be said to him:

> Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth upon the rocks, or have you watched the hinds in labor?

It is as though he were told: “You think that you have accomplished something sublime because you do not yet foresee that time when spiritual teachers, sent into the world, beget children through the teaching of the ancient fathers and bring me the gain of souls through their labors. For if you were to behold their fruit as the birth of wild goats and hinds, you would think very humbly of your own virtue.”

We regard great things as though they were small when we weigh them against stronger examples. Yet what we do grows in merit before God when it diminishes through humility before ourselves.

### [Old Version XVII]

#### 37. By the hinds, teachers; by the wild goats, hearers may be understood. Examples of the saints are to be considered. [Col. 0545A] King David’s humility and patience. He regarded insulting words not as reproaches but as aids. They deserve gratitude more than anger.

Teachers may indeed be understood by the signification of the hinds, and hearers by the designation of wild goats, which are very small animals. Wild goats give birth among the rocks because they are made fruitful for performing holy works through the examples of their forefathers, so that when they perhaps hear sublime precepts and, conscious of their own weakness, despair of being able to fulfill them, they may look upon the lives of their predecessors and, considering their strength, bring forth the offspring of good works.

To speak briefly of many matters, so that the diligent reader may understand much from a little: when one is oppressed by insulting words and is unable to preserve the virtue of patience, let him recall David’s deed to mind. When so many insults from Shimei pressed him, and armed nobles sought to take revenge, he said:

> “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him be, so that he may curse; for the Lord commanded him to curse David. And who is there who would dare to say, ‘Why has he done this?’” (2 Samuel 16:10).

And a little later:

> “Let him be, so that he may curse according to the Lord’s command, if perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me good for this day’s cursing” (ibid., 12).

By these words he plainly indicates that, fleeing from the son who had risen against him because of the crime committed with Bathsheba, he brought back to mind the evil he had committed and endured with equanimity what he heard. He regarded insulting words not so much as reproaches as aids, by which he judged that he could be cleansed and receive mercy. [Col. 0545C]

We tolerate insults well when, in the secrecy of our mind, we return to the evils we have committed. For what strikes us as a light injury when inflicted upon us will seem slight when we see in our conduct that what we deserved was worse. Thus it happens that gratitude rather than anger is owed for insults, since through their intervention we trust that, with God as judge, a heavier punishment may be avoided.

### [Old Version XVIII]

#### 38. By what method Joseph conquered lust. Let us turn the grace bestowed through outward gifts of God into weapons of virtue. Let us be ashamed to fight against God by means of his benefits.

Behold another person who, while prospering through the successes of this world, feels himself tempted by the goads of lust as the joy of his heart entices him. [Note: [Col. 0545D] In the printed editions, *sed si Joseph* (“but if Joseph”). The word *si* is absent from the manuscripts Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts, Vindoc., Laud., Corb. Germ., Val. Cl., and others.] But he recalls Joseph’s deed to mind and preserves himself in the citadel of chastity. When he saw that the loss of chastity was being urged upon him by his mistress, [Note: [Col. 0545D] Val. Cl. and Laud.: *impudicitiam* (“immodesty”).] he said:

> “Behold, my master, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house; nor is there anything that is not in my power, or that he has not entrusted to me, except you, who are his wife. How then can I do this evil and sin against my master?” (Genesis 39:8). [Note: [Col. 0545D] *Vel non tradiderit mihi* (“or has not entrusted to me”) is omitted in Pratel. and Utic.]

By these words it is shown that he suddenly brought to mind the good things he had obtained and conquered the evil that was assaulting him; and [Col. 0546A] because he remembered the grace he had received, he broke the force of the impending sin. When slippery pleasure tempts us amid prosperity, those very prosperities must be set against the sting of temptation, so that we may be ashamed to commit evil precisely because we remember that we have received good things freely from God. [Note: [Col. 0545D] Other manuscripts: “gratuitous goods,” as in Pratel. and Corb. Germ.; [Col. 0546D] the latter has *in quo paulo ante quos nos* (“in which shortly before, ‘whom us’”).]

Let us turn the grace bestowed through outward gifts into weapons of virtue, so that what we have received may stand before our eyes and we may subdue the things that entice us. Since pleasure itself arises from prosperity, it must be struck down by consideration of that same prosperity, so that our enemy may die from the very source from which he arises. We must take care lest we turn a gift received into vice, lest the abyss of wickedness swallow us through the favor of this life. For we kindle the anger of the heavenly Judge against ourselves unquenchably if we fight against his kindness, even by means of his own generosity. [Col. 0546B]

#### 39. Daniel is to be imitated by one who longs for contemplation. The taste of carnal things must be restrained. When outward wandering is curbed, an inner retreat is opened.

Another person seeks the sweetness of inner knowledge but is unable to reach its secrets. He looks to Daniel’s life for imitation, [Note: [Col. 0546D] Pratel.: “for imitation.”] and attains the desired summit of knowledge. He who was later called by the angelic voice, because of his desire for inner understanding, “a man of desires” (Daniel 10:11), is first remembered as having subdued within himself the desires of the flesh in the royal court, so that he touched none of the delightful foods but preferred harder and rougher fare to sumptuous and softer foods (Daniel 1:12). Thus, by withdrawing from himself the blandishments of outward food, he might reach the delights of inward nourishment; and he might receive the taste of wisdom within all the more eagerly the more firmly he had restrained the taste of the flesh without for the sake of that same wisdom. [Col. 0546C]

For if we cut away from the flesh what pleases it, we immediately find in the spirit what gives pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Vindoc. and many Norman manuscripts: “soon find in Christ what…”] If outward wandering is closed off from the soul’s concentration, an inner retreat is opened to it. For to the extent that the mind is prevented from scattering itself outward for the sake of discipline, it can direct itself above itself through progress. [Note: [Col. 0546D] Nearly all manuscripts read *intendere* (“direct itself”); the printed editions have *tendere* (“extend itself”).] A tree, too, is forced to grow upward when it is prevented from spreading through its branches; and when we block the streams of a spring, we urge its waters to rise upward.

Therefore, whenever the diligent contemplate the lives of the saints by imitating them, the wild goats give birth among the rocks. Hence Paul urged his hearers, as wild goats giving birth among the rocks, when, after enumerating the virtues of their forebears, he said:

> “Since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin that clings closely to us, and let us run with perseverance toward the contest set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). [Note: [Col. 0546D] Pratel. and Corb. Germ.: *curramus propositum* (“let us run toward the appointed goal”), instead of *curramus ad propositum* (“let us run toward the contest set before us”).]

And again:

> “Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7).

### [Old Version XIX]

#### 40. When we conceive the divine precepts, we do not immediately give birth. [Col. 0547A]

When we conceive the divine precepts in our heart, we do not immediately give birth to them as though they had already been firmly thought through. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Corb. Germ., Ebroic., Pratel. and the Norman manuscripts: *conspicimus* (“we behold”) instead of *concipimus* (“we conceive”).] Hence blessed Job is questioned not about the birth of the wild goats but about the time of their birth. If we scarcely comprehend this time within ourselves, we know it even less in another person’s mind.

First, the seeds of heavenly fear, received in the womb of the heart, are consolidated through sustained reflection so that they may remain. Afterwards, fixed by concentrated attention, they are formed, as it were, into the distinction of limbs while they move toward the judgment of discernment. Then, strengthened by persevering practice, they come, as it were, into the solidity of bones. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Vindoc., Pratel., and Utic.: *formata* (“formed”); Ebroic.: *conformata* (“conformed”).] Finally, fortified by perfected authority, they proceed as if toward birth. No one considers these stages of the divine seeds in another’s mind except the one who creates them.

For although we recognize by the testimony of certain things that someone has already conceived the force of heavenly desire, we do not know when it will break forth into birth. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Most Norman manuscripts: *in partum* (“into birth”).]

#### 41. Some offspring are miscarried because they are premature. Human praise extinguishes tender goodness.

Often the seeds conceived in the mind cannot reach perfection because, in coming forth, they precede the proper time of birth. And because they emerge before they have been fully formed in thought, they die like miscarried offspring. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Ebroic.: “not yet fully formed in understanding.”] Good things that are still tender are often extinguished by the human tongue when it praises them as though they were already strong. They die all the more quickly because they burst forth prematurely into public notice.

Sometimes, too, our imperfect thought, not yet strengthened, is scattered by the opposition of those who resist when it is shown too quickly to others; and when it tries to appear before its time as something that exists, it acts so that it does not exist. [Note: [Col. 0547D] The printed editions, together with Corb. Germ., read: “as though it were being brought about so that it might not exist.” In some older manuscripts *quasi* (“as though”) is omitted. We follow the manuscripts Turon., Vindoc., Norm., Laud., Val. Cl.]

Holy men, however, because they strive for everything they think rightly to grow strong in secret, and first form within the womb of the mind the offspring that will later emerge, are rightly questioned by blessed Job about the time of birth—namely, the time suitable for each thing, which no one knows except the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0548D] Pratel. and Corb. Germ.: *penetrabilia cordis* (“the penetrable places of the heart”); the Paris edition of 1495 and the Basel edition of 1514 agree.] When he looks into the inner chambers of the heart, he understands when our good works ought suitably to be born into human awareness. Thus it is rightly said:

> “Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth among the rocks?”

As though he plainly said: “I, who make the offspring of the elect vigorous because I bring them forth at the time I foreknow.” [Note: [Col. 0548D] Ebroic.: *praescita* (“foreknown”). So also the old edition of Basil.]

After the offspring of the hearers has been completed, it is rightly added:

> “Or have you watched the hinds giving birth?”

To watch hinds giving birth is to weigh with careful consideration the labors of those fathers who beget spiritual children. [Col. 0547D]

#### 42. What pains and what gifts belong to preachers giving birth to souls.

One must carefully observe how watchfully this statement is impressed upon us, so that it says, “Have you watched?” For it belongs to very few to consider what labor is involved in the preaching of the fathers: with how many pains, as though in labor, they give birth to souls in faith and conduct; how carefully they surround themselves with watchfulness so that they may be strong in precepts, compassionate toward weaknesses, terrifying in threats, gentle in exhortations, humble in displaying authority, dominant in contempt for temporal things, firm in enduring adversities, and yet, because they do not attribute their strength to themselves, weak.

What pain they feel over those who fall; what fear they have for those who stand; with what fervor they seek to attain some things, and with what dread they preserve others once attained. Since so few consider all this, it is rightly said to him:

> “Or have you watched the hinds giving birth?” [Col. 0548A]

### [Old Version XX]

#### 43. Those who are fathers through the strength of discipline must be mothers through the compassion of tenderness. [Col. 0548B]

There is nothing inappropriate in God’s words concerning teachers depicting them not in the form of male deer but of hinds, because the true teachers are those who, while fathers through the strength of discipline, know how to be mothers through the compassion of tenderness. [Note: [Col. 0548D] Laud. and Val. Cl.: “those are truly teachers.”]

They endure the labors of holy conception and carry within the womb of charity the children they are to bring forth for God. For in giving birth to offspring, mothers labor more, since they sustain the conception growing within the womb for many months and do not deliver what emerges from the womb without great pains. Hence the text fittingly continues:

### CHAPTER XI [Revised Version X]

**Verse 2.**—“Have you counted the months of their conception?”

#### 44. The offspring conceived in the womb of the heart must be carried for the proper time, so that it may live. [Col. 0548C]

When holy men think about the progress of their hearers, they carry conception as though already in the womb. But when they defer certain things that must be said and seek a suitable time for their exhortations, they are prolonged, as it were, in the length of months before the birth they desire to bring about.

Often, when they do not wish to say prematurely to their hearers certain things they perceive, they are strengthened, in the very delay of expressing their judgment, by a higher counsel—whether concerning things that must be urged or things that must be rebuked. While the life of their children is being considered, and the tongue does not cast forth the mind’s counsel before its time, the offspring already conceived grows within the womb, so that the judgment of the heart may come forth into the awareness of the hearers when, brought forth profitably, it lives as though through a suitable period of gestation. [Note: [Col. 0548D] Vindoc., Norm., Laud., Val. Cl.: “as though it lived through a suitable birth.”]

And because people do not know when or how these things take place in the mind of teachers, whereas God, for the glory of recompense, considers not only the result but also marks the moments of their thoughts, it is rightly said to blessed Job:

> “Have you counted the months of their conception?”

The implied sense is: “I, who count in holy preachers not only the fruit of outward works but also their prolonged thoughts, and preserve those thoughts for recompense.” [Note: [Col. 0549D] Other manuscripts: “because I also preserve them.”]

### [Old Version XXI]

#### 45. Those who prepare themselves to preach must first renew themselves inwardly through the virtues. [Col. 0549A]

The months may also be understood as multiplied virtues, since months are accumulated days. The moon is also renewed during the months; and there is nothing inappropriate in the months signifying the new creature of regeneration. [Note: [Col. 0549D] Pratel.: “the creature of a new regeneration.”] Concerning this the apostle Paul says:

> “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Galatians 5:6; 6:15).

Therefore, when holy men prepare themselves to preach, they first renew themselves inwardly through the virtues, so that in living they may agree with what they teach by speaking. They first examine their inner selves and cleanse themselves from every stain of vice, taking the greatest care that they shine with the light of patience against anger, that against the lust of the flesh they shine with purity of heart, that against sluggishness they glow with zeal, that against the confused movements of rashness they gleam with serene gravity, that against pride they shine with true humility, and that against fear they become radiant with the rays of authority. [Col. 0549B]

Since they first gather such great efforts within themselves, the months of virtues are formed, as it were, in the conception of holy preaching. The Lord alone counts these months, because no one except the one who gave them weighs the same good things in their hearts. And because the effect of fruit follows according to the measure of the virtues, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XII

**The same passage.**—“And have you known the time of their birth?”

#### 46. The proportion of fruits follows the measure of virtues. [Col. 0549C]

The implied sense is: “I, who, while counting the months of virtues in their thoughts, know when they are able to give birth to what they seek to fulfill, because, while I see the secrets of the heart, I weigh the future outward effect of the work in the inward balance of thought.”

The text continues:

### CHAPTER XIII

**Verse 3.**—“They bow down to give birth; they bring forth, and they send out their cries.”

#### 47. Preachers cannot give spiritual birth unless they do so with tears. [Col. 0549D]

They roar when, through their bending down, they give birth to the souls of their hearers in the conduct of light, because they cannot remove us from eternal punishments except by weeping and grieving. Holy preachers now sow in tears so that later they may reap a harvest of joys. Now they are like hinds in the pain of childbirth, so that afterward they may be fruitful in spiritual offspring.

To speak of one among many, I see Paul emitting the cries of great pain like a hind in labor. For he says:

> “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you, I wish I could be with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you” (Galatians 4:19).

Behold, he wishes to change his voice in his labor, so that the speech of preaching may be turned into a cry of grief. He wishes to change his voice because those whom he had already borne through preaching he was again bearing with groaning by reforming them.

What kind of cry did this hind emit in giving birth when, as they turned back from following him, he was compelled to exclaim:

> “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? And are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being brought to completion by the flesh?” (Galatians 3:1).

Or certainly:

> “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Galatians 5:7).

What a cry there was in the labor of this hind, who bore children conceived long before with so many difficulties and at last discovered that those already born had returned to the womb of wickedness! Let us consider what grief she felt, what labor she endured: after she had been able to bring forth those conceived, she was compelled once more to raise up what had been extinguished. [Col. 0550A]

### [Old Version XXII]

#### 48. Unless they descended and bent down to our weakness, they would not beget children in the faith. They must think with sobriety. [Col. 0550B]

It must be especially noted that these hinds bend down in order to give birth, because if they stood upright they would not be able to give birth. For unless holy preachers descended from that immensity of inner contemplation which they grasp, to our weakness through very humble preaching—as through a kind of bending—they would never beget children in the faith. They could not benefit us if they persisted in the uprightness of their own height.

But let us see the hind bending herself so that she may give birth:

> “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:1).

Immediately afterward he explains the reasons for this bending, saying:

> “For you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, even now you are not able” (ibid., 2).

But let us look upon this hind, who was bent down for our sake, standing upright. He says:

> “We speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Corinthians 2:6).

And again:

> “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Corinthians 5:13).

When he is beside himself for God, we cannot comprehend his ecstasy at all. Therefore, in order to win us, he bends down to us. Hence he fittingly adds there:

> “Whether we are sober, it is for you” (ibid.).

For if holy men wished to preach to us the things they grasp when they are intoxicated by heavenly contemplation, and did not rather temper their knowledge with a certain moderation and sobriety, who could receive, in the narrow bosom of understanding, those streams of the heavenly fountain?

These hinds, bent down, are elsewhere called “heavens,” concerning which it is said:

> “Lord, bow your heavens and descend” (Psalm 143:5). [Note: [Col. 0549D] Corb. Germ., Laud., Val. Cl., Pratel.: “they are called.”]

For when the heavens are bowed down, the Lord descends, because when holy teachers draw themselves down in their preaching, they pour the knowledge of divinity into our hearts. The Lord would in no way descend to us if his preachers remained inflexible in the rigor of contemplation. Thus the heavens are bowed down so that the Lord may descend; the hinds bend down so that we may be born into the new light of faith.

These bent-down hinds are called the bride’s breasts in the Song of Songs, as it is written:

> “Your breasts are better than wine” (Song of Songs 1:1). [Note: [Col. 0550D] Pratel. and Corb. Germ.: “the bridegroom’s breasts.”]

These are the breasts fixed in the chest’s ark that give us milk to drink, because they cling to the hidden things of the highest contemplation and nourish us with subtle preaching. Thus, in order to draw us away from eternal groaning and pain, the hinds now bend down and send forth cries in childbirth.

But because those who are born through the holy preaching of the fathers sometimes surpass their teachers through suffering, so that while their teachers still remain in this life they themselves are already completed through martyrdom, the text fittingly continues:

### CHAPTER XIV [Revised Version XI]

**Verse 4.**—“Their young are separated; they go forth to pasture; they depart and do not return to them.”

#### 49. Their children go to the pasture of Sacred Scripture. The Word enlightens them from the nature of his divinity. [Col. 0551A]

Sacred Scripture calls pasture that food of eternal verdure where our refreshment will no longer wither through any dryness of want. Concerning this pasture the Psalmist says:

> “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Psalm 22:2).

And again:

> “We are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 94:7). [Note: [Col. 0551D] Pratel. and Utic.: “We are your people and the sheep of your pasture.”]

Concerning these pastures the Truth itself says:

> “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10:9).

They therefore go to pasture because, leaving their bodies, they find those pastures of inward verdure. “They depart and do not return to them,” because, having been received into that contemplation of joys, they no longer need to hear the words of teachers. Having gone forth, they do not return to them because, escaping the straits of the present life, they no longer require preaching about life from teachers.

Then what is written is fulfilled:

> “A man will no longer teach his neighbor, or a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all will know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:34). [Col. 0551C]

Then what the Truth says in the Gospel is fulfilled:

> “I will announce the Father openly to you” (John 16:25). [Note: [Col. 0551D] Laud. and Corb. Germ. do not have *meo* (“my”).]

The Son announces the Father openly because, as we said above, since he is the Word, he enlightens us from the nature of divinity. Then they do not seek the words of teachers, like little streams of human speech, when they are already drawn from the very fountain of truth. [Note: [Col. 0551D] Here we follow the manuscripts Ebroic. and others, Norm., three English manuscripts, Vindoc. The printed editions, together with Corb. Germ., have *debriantur* (“are intoxicated”) instead of *derivantur* (“flow forth”).]

After many things had been said about the virtue of teachers under the figure of the bending of the hinds, the discourse now turns to the life of those who seek the secrets of a withdrawn way of life. Since they attain even the leisure of withdrawal through divine assistance and not through their own strength, the Lord says of them: [Note: [Col. 0551D] The printed editions read *vacandi* (“of being unoccupied”) instead of *cessandi* (“of ceasing”); the manuscripts Vindoc., Corb. Germ., Laud., Val. Cl., Norman manuscripts, and others support the latter.]

### CHAPTER XV [Old Version XXIII, Revised Version XII]

**Verse 5.**—“Who sent the wild ass free, and who loosed its bonds?” [Note: [Col. 0551D] Some printed editions add *in solitudinem* (“into the wilderness”).]

#### 50. By the name of the free wild ass are understood those who, freed from the servitude of secular affairs, devote themselves to solitude. [Col. 0552A]

The implied sense is: “No one except me.” The wild ass, which dwells in solitude, appropriately signifies the life of those who live withdrawn from the crowds. [Note: [Col. 0552D] The printed editions read *saecularibus* (“secular”) for *popularibus* (“of the populace”); we follow the cited manuscripts and Turon.] It is also suitably called free, because the servitude of secular business is great: the mind is severely worn down by it, although it may sweat over such affairs voluntarily. [Note: [Col. 0552D] Val. Cl.: *desudetur* (“one sweats over it”); Corb. Germ. has both readings.]

To be free from the condition of this servitude is to desire nothing in the world any longer. Prosperity presses upon us as though with a certain yoke of servitude when it is desired, [Note: [Col. 0552D] Laud., Corb. Germ., and many others: *jugo servitii* (“yoke of service”).] and adversity presses upon us when it is feared. But if someone once shakes the neck of his mind free from the domination of temporal desires, he already enjoys a certain freedom even in this life, since he is troubled by no desire for happiness and constrained by no terror of adversity.

The Lord saw this heavy yoke of servitude impressed upon secular people’s necks when he said:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28).

For it is a harsh yoke and, as we said, a burden of severe servitude to be subject to temporal things, to pursue earthly goods, to hold on to things that pass away, to wish to stand amid things that do not stand, to desire things that are passing while refusing to pass away with them. Since everything flees contrary to our wishes, the things that earlier afflicted the mind through the desire to obtain them later press upon it through fear of losing them.

The one who, having trampled upon earthly desires, is relieved in mind from the pursuit of temporal things is therefore sent forth free. “And who loosed its bonds?” The implied sense is: “No one except me.”

#### 51. Through divine assistance the bonds of carnal desires are broken. [Col. 0552C]

Everyone’s bonds are loosed when, through divine assistance, the inward restraints of carnal desires are broken. When a devout intention calls someone to conversion but the weakness of the flesh still turns him back from that intention, the soul is hindered as though bound by certain chains.

We often see many people desire a life of holy conduct, [Note: [Col. 0552D] Val. Cl.: *viam quidem* (“indeed, the way”) instead of *vitam quidem* (“indeed, the life”).] but fear that they will be unable to attain it because sometimes sudden misfortunes arise and sometimes future adversities are feared. While they look ahead at certain evils as though cautiously, they are carelessly held fast in the bonds of their sins. They place many things before their eyes, fearing that, if these should happen to them in their way of life, they would be unable to stand. Concerning such people Solomon rightly says:

> “The way of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns” (Proverbs 15:19).

For when they desire the way of God, suspicions of their fears, placed before them like thorns of obstructing hedges, prick them. Since this does not usually hinder the elect, he rightly adds there:

> “The way of the righteous is without stumbling” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0552D] Laud.: “For these people…”]

The righteous do not stumble in their way of life, whatever adversity may meet them, because they leap over the obstacles of temporal adversity through the hope of eternity and inner contemplation. [Note: [Col. 0552D] Pratel. and Corb. Germ.: *objectacula* (“obstacles”).] Thus God looses the bonds of the wild ass when he breaks the knots of weak thoughts in the mind of each of the elect and mercifully scatters everything that had bound the ensnared mind.

The text continues:

### CHAPTER XVI

**Verse 6.**—“To whom I gave a house in the wilderness and his tents in a land of salt.”

#### 52. There are two kinds of solitude: of the heart and of the body. One is of no benefit without the other. [Col. 0553A]

Here should we understand bodily solitude or solitude of the heart? But what does bodily solitude profit if solitude of the heart is absent? Anyone who lives withdrawn in body but involves himself in the tumult of human society through thoughts of earthly desires is not in solitude. If someone is physically oppressed by crowds of people but suffers no tumult of secular cares in his heart, he is not in the city.

Therefore solitude of mind is first granted to those who live rightly, so that they may suppress the inward noise of earthly desires; so that, through the grace of heavenly love, they may restrain cares bubbling up from below; [Note: [Col. 0553D] Turon. and Val. Cl.: *ad infima* (“toward lower things”); Corb. Germ.: *ad infirma* (“toward weak things”).] so that they may drive away from the eyes of the mind all the movements of trivial thoughts obtruding themselves at the wrong time, like flying flies, with the hand of gravity; and so that they may seek within themselves a certain secret place with the Lord, where, when outward noise has ceased, they may speak silently with him through inward desires.

### [Old Version XXIV]

#### 53. The silence of contemplation cannot be perfect in this life. [Col. 0553B]

Concerning this secret of the heart it was said elsewhere:

> “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Revelation 8:1). [Col. 0553C]

Heaven is called the Church of the elect, which, while it directs itself toward eternal and sublime things through the elevation of contemplation, suppresses the tumults of thoughts arising from below and creates within itself a certain silence for God. Since this silence of contemplation cannot be perfect in this life, it is said to have lasted half an hour.

For when the tumultuous noises of thoughts intrude upon an unwilling mind, they forcibly drag the eye of the heart back to look upon earthly things, even when it is intent upon sublime matters. [Note: [Col. 0553D] Many Norman manuscripts: “For tumultuous noises of thoughts intrude upon an unwilling mind and, even when it is intent upon sublime things…”] Hence it is written:

> “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

Thus this silence is rightly described as lasting not a complete hour but half an hour, because contemplation is by no means perfected here, although it is begun ardently.

This is also suitably expressed through the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 40:5), who testifies that, as the measure of the city built upon the mountain, he saw in the hand of a man a measuring reed six cubits long and a palm. [Note: [Col. 0553D] Pratel., Utic., Laud., Val. Cl.: “and a palm.”]

The Church of the elect is situated on a mountain because it is not founded upon earthly desires. What is signified by a cubit except action? What by the number six except the perfection of action? For the Lord is also remembered to have completed all his works on the sixth day. What, then, does the palm above the six cubits signify [Note: [Col. 0554D] Laud. and Val. Cl.: “above the cubit”] except the power of contemplation, which already demonstrates the beginnings of eternal and seventh-day rest? Because the contemplation of eternal things is not completed here, the measure of the seventh cubit is not fulfilled.

The Church of the elect, because it completes all the things that must be done, shows itself as a city placed upon the mountain and extending itself through six cubits. [Note: [Col. 0554D] Vindoc.: “because it advances toward all the things that must be done, it extends itself through six cubits, placed upon the mountain.” Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts: “because it advances toward all the things …”] But because here it still perceives only the beginnings of contemplation, it touches no more than the palm of the seventh cubit. [Col. 0554A]

#### 54. The summit of contemplation is not reached unless we are freed from the oppression of outward cares. [Col. 0554B]

It must be understood that we can in no way reach the summit of contemplation unless we cease from the oppression of outward care. We cannot look upon ourselves and know that within us there is one thing that is rational and governs, and another that is animal and is governed, unless, returning to the secrecy of this silence, we are lulled away from every outward disturbance.

This silence was also well prefigured by the sleeping Adam, from whose side a woman soon proceeded (ibid.). For whoever is swept away toward understanding inward things closes his eyes to visible matters; and then within himself he distinguishes what ought manfully to rule and what can be subject, so that within him there is one thing able to rule like a man and another, like a woman, that is ruled.

In this silence of the heart, while we keep watch inwardly through contemplation, we fall asleep, as it were, outwardly. Since withdrawn men—that is, those alienated from carnal desires—inhabit this silence of mind, the Lord gave the wild ass a house in the wilderness, so that it would not be oppressed by the crowd of temporal desires. [Col. 0554C]

### [Old Version XXV]

#### 55. As long as the saints live, they burn with desire for the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0554C]

The text continues:

> “And his tents in a land of salt.”

Salt ordinarily kindles thirst. And because holy men, as long as they dwell in the tents of this life, are kindled by the daily burning of their desire for the heavenly homeland, they are said to have tents in a land of salt. They are continually kindled so that they may thirst; they thirst so that they may be satisfied, as it is written:

> “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

The text continues:

### CHAPTER XVII

**Verse 7.**—“He scorns the multitude of the city.”

#### 56. They disdain following the multitude of earthly people. [Col. 0554D]

To scorn the multitude of the city is to avoid the perverse pursuits of human society, so that one no longer wishes to imitate the depraved customs of earthly people, who are numerous because of the abundance of iniquity. They desire to enter the narrow gate with the few, and not to enter with the many by the broad roads that lead to destruction (Matthew 7:13).

They carefully consider from whom and for what purpose they were created, and, rightly contemplating the image they have received, they disdain to follow the multitude of the crowd. Hence, in the Song of Songs, the bridegroom’s voice says to the bride:

> “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women, go out and depart after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats” (Song of Songs 1:7).

The one who is fair among women knows herself when every elect soul, placed even among sinners, remembers that it was created according to the image and likeness of its Creator (Genesis 1:26) and proceeds according to the order of the likeness it has received.

If it does not know itself, it goes out, because, expelled from the secrecy of its heart, it is scattered among outward desires. Having gone out, it departs after the tracks of the flocks because, abandoning its inner self, it is led onto the broad road and follows the examples of the peoples. It no longer pastures lambs but young goats, because it aims not to nourish innocent thoughts of the mind but to nourish perverse movements of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0555D] Laud.: “because, abandoning its own things forever…”]

Since every elect and continent person disdains to go after the tracks of the flocks, it is rightly said:

> “He scorns the multitude of the city.”

To this it is fittingly added:

### CHAPTER XVIII [Revised Version XIII]

**The same passage.**—“He does not hear the shouting of the exactor.”

#### 57. They close their ears to the devil’s more violent temptations and to the cries of the belly. [Col. 0555B]

Who else can the exactor be understood to be except the devil? Once, in paradise, he gave humanity the coin of evil persuasion (Genesis 3:6 and following), and every day he seeks to exact from humanity the guilt of this debt.

The speech of this exactor is the beginning of evil suggestion. The shouting of this exactor is temptation that is no longer gentle but violent. [Note: [Col. 0555D] A recent edition, against the manuscripts, reads “not slight.” *Lenis* (“gentle”) is better, as it is opposed to violent temptation.] This exactor shouts when he tempts forcefully. Therefore, not to hear the shouting of the exactor is not to consent in the least to the violent movements of temptations. He would hear it if he did what it suggests. But when he disdains to do perverse things, it is rightly said:

> “He does not hear the shouting of the exactor.”

[Vet. XXVI.] 58. Some, however, wish the belly to be understood here by “the tax collector.” For it demands a certain debt from us, since by nature itself it seeks that the daily fruit of human labor be expended on it. Therefore abstinent men, who are represented in this passage by the term “wild asses,” while violently restraining the desires of the appetite, as it were scorn the words of the shouting tax collector. [Note: The Corbie German, Pratel, and Utrecht manuscripts read: “while [restraining] violently.”] But since a continent man has many contests of virtue available to him against countless vices, why is it said here, after the tax collector’s shout has been scorned, that he restrains and checks the belly’s impulse alone, unless because no one seizes the palm of spiritual combat who has not first conquered within himself the incitements of the flesh through the affliction of the belly’s appetite? For one does not rise to the struggle of spiritual combat unless the enemy placed within us—namely, the appetite of gluttony—has first been subdued. If we do not overthrow what is nearer to us, we surely proceed in vain against what must be fought from farther away. For battle is waged uselessly against external enemies in the field if within the very walls of the city there is a citizen lying in ambush. The mind of the combatant, too, is driven away from the engagement of spiritual warfare under the grievous disgrace of confusion when, weakened in the battle with the flesh, it is overcome after being pierced by the swords of gluttony. For when it sees itself overthrown by small things, it is ashamed to engage with greater ones.

59. Those who do not take care to subdue the appetite rashly rise to spiritual warfare.—Some, however, ignorant of the order of combat, neglect to subdue the appetite and already rise to spiritual warfare. At times they even perform many deeds requiring great strength, but when the vice of gluttony prevails, they lose through the allurements of the flesh everything they have done bravely; and while the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are simultaneously overwhelmed through the desire of the flesh. Hence it is written of Nabuchodonosor’s conquest [Note: IV Kings 25:8; Jeremiah 52:14, according to the Hebrew text and the Septuagint, where he is called “commander of the army”; the Chaldean has “chief of the cooks.”]: “The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.” For what does Scripture signify by the walls of Jerusalem except the virtues of the soul, which tends toward the vision of peace? Or whom should we understand by the chief of the cooks except the belly, which is served with the greatest care by those who cook? Therefore the chief of the cooks destroys the walls of Jerusalem, because, while the belly is not restrained, it destroys the virtues of the soul. Hence Paul took strength away from the chief of the cooks while contending against the walls of Jerusalem, when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (I Corinthians 9:27). Hence also he said earlier: “So I run, not as uncertainly; so I fight, not as one beating the air” (ibid., 26). For when we restrain the flesh, by the very blows of our abstinence we beat not the air but unclean spirits; and when we subject what is within us, we strike with our fists the adversaries placed outside. [Note: Tours, Laon, Corbie German, Val-Clos, Pratel, and others read “by the very blows of continence.” Recent printed editions read “we wage battles”; the Corbie German, Norman, Laon, Val-Clos, and other manuscripts, as well as the old Paris and Basel editions, read “we strike blows,” a reading supported by the Greek: where the Vulgate has “so I fight,” πυκτεύω properly means “I box.”] Hence, when the king of Babylon orders the furnace to be set alight (Daniel 3), he commands a heap of naphtha, tow, pitch, and pitchy firewood to be supplied; yet this fire does not consume the abstaining youths, because although the ancient enemy sets before our eyes innumerable desires for food by which the fire of lust may grow, the grace of the heavenly Spirit breathes upon good minds so that they remain unharmed amid the heats of carnal desire. Thus, even if the flame burns as far as the heart’s temptation, the temptation nevertheless does not consume them as far as consent.

[Vet. XXVII.] 60. Gluttony tempts us in five ways. It is not food but appetite that is blameworthy.—Furthermore, it must be known that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways (On Consecration, distinction 5, chapter “In Five Ways”). Sometimes it anticipates the time of need; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more luxurious foods; sometimes it demands that whatever is to be eaten be prepared with excessive care; sometimes it conforms both to the quality of the food and to the proper time, but exceeds the measure of moderate nourishment in the quantity consumed. At other times, what it desires is humbler, yet it sins more gravely through the very heat of its immense desire.

Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father’s mouth because he anticipated the appointed time for eating by tasting honey (I Samuel 14:27). And the people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more luxurious (Numbers 21:5). And the first sin of the sons of Eli arose because, at their request, the priest’s servant wished to take from the sacrifice not meat cooked according to ancient custom, but raw meat, which he could prepare more carefully (I Samuel 2:12 ff.). And when it is said to Jerusalem, “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance” (Ezekiel 16:49), it is plainly shown that it lost salvation because, together with the vice of pride, it exceeded the measure of moderate nourishment. Esau also lost the glory of the firstborn because, in the great heat of desire, he longed for a cheap food, namely lentils (Genesis 25:33); and by preferring them even to the sale of his birthright, he showed with what appetite he panted after them. For it is not food but appetite that is blameworthy. Thus we often consume more luxurious foods without guilt, while we taste humbler foods not without a guilty conscience. This Esau, whom we have mentioned, lost his primacy through lentils, whereas Elijah preserved bodily strength in the wilderness by eating meat (III Kings 17:6). [Note: The recent edition reads, “in the wilderness through the strength of the spirit.” The old Paris and Basel editions read, “in the wilderness the strength of the spirit,” and we would gladly embrace that reading as preferable if it were not opposed by the agreement of the English, Norman, Corbie German, Tours, Laon, Val-Clos, and Longpont manuscripts, in which “the strength of the body” is read. By “the strength of the body” continence and unimpaired chastity of the flesh may here be understood.]

Hence the ancient enemy, because he understands that the cause of condemnation is not food but desire for food, subjected the first man to himself not through meat but through a fruit (Genesis 3:6), and tempted the second not through meat but through bread (Matthew 4:3). Hence Adam’s sin is often committed even when humble and cheap foods are consumed. For Adam alone did not receive the command of prohibition so that he might abstain from the forbidden fruit. When God indicates that certain foods are contrary to our health, he forbids us from them, as though by a sentence. And when we touch harmful things with desire, what else are we doing but tasting what is forbidden?

61. One should eat what necessity requires, not what desire suggests. How much discernment this requires.—Therefore one must consume what the necessity of nature requires, and not what the desire for eating suggests. But great is the labor of discernment: to offer something to this tax collector and to deny him something; to restrain the appetite by withholding, and to nourish nature by giving. [Rec. XIV.] Perhaps this discernment is added when it is said: “He does not hear the shout of the tax collector.” For the speech of this tax collector is the necessary demand of nature; but his shout is the appetite of gluttony exceeding the measure of necessity. Thus this wild ass hears the speech of the tax collector but does not hear his shout, because the discerning and continent man both refreshes his belly enough to temper necessity and restrains it from pleasure.

[Vet. XXVIII.] 62. Pleasure disguises itself under the appearance of necessity.—It must be known, however, that pleasure so disguises itself under the appearance of necessity that scarcely anyone, however perfect, can discern it. While necessity demands that a debt be paid, pleasure supplies the desire to be satisfied; and it drags gluttony headlong with greater security insofar as it conceals itself under the respectable name of satisfying necessity. [Note: The editions read “and so much the more securely it drags gluttony”; our manuscripts have “gluttony” in the accusative.] Often, while one is proceeding to eat, pleasure secretly attaches itself afterward; sometimes it even tries shamelessly to go ahead of necessity. It is easy to detect when pleasure anticipates necessity, but it is very difficult to discern when it secretly joins itself to necessary eating. For because it follows the appetite that precedes nature, it appears to come later, as if from behind. At the time when the debt owed to necessity is being paid, pleasure is mingled with necessity through eating, and it is not known what necessity demands or what, as has been said, pleasure supplies. Often we do discern it; and because we know that the two are joined together, we enjoy deceiving ourselves knowingly in the fact that we are carried beyond the limits. While the mind flatters itself on the ground of necessity, it is deceived by pleasure. For it is written: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14). Therefore what is forbidden when done from desire is permitted when done from necessity.

63. The desires of the flesh, not the flesh itself, must be put to death. Care must be taken lest, while pursuing the enemy, we slaughter the citizen whom we love.—But often, while we imprudently yield to necessity, we serve desires. At other times, while we strive to resist desires too immoderately, we increase the miseries of necessity. Thus each person must hold the citadel of continence in such a way that he kills not the flesh but the vices of the flesh. [Note: Recent editions read “that he may hold the citadel”; the old Paris and Basel editions, with the Norman, Corbie German, Laon, and other manuscripts, read “that he hold,” which we follow.] For often, when the flesh is restrained more than is right, it is also weakened for the exercise of good works, so that it is not sufficient even for prayer or preaching, while it hastens to suffocate within itself completely the incitements of vice.

We have as an assistant to our inward intention this human being whom we bear outwardly; in him are both the movements of wantonness and the resources for good action. Often, while pursuing the enemy in him, we also slaughter the citizen whom we love; and often, while sparing him as though he were a fellow citizen, we nourish the enemy for battle. For vices grow strong on the same foods by which virtues, once nourished, live. And when virtue is fed, the strength of vices is often increased. But when excessive continence weakens the strength of vices, the failing virtue itself also pants.

Therefore it is necessary that the inner person, a kind of impartial judge of ours, preside between himself and the one whom he bears outwardly, so that his outward person may always be sufficient to serve him in the required service and may never resist with a proudly unrestrained neck. Nor should he be disturbed if the outward person mutters something by way of suggestion, provided that the foot of dominion set over him always presses him down. Thus it comes about that, while we permit repressed vices to resist us, we nevertheless forbid them to contend with us on equal terms: neither do vices prevail against virtue, nor does virtue collapse through the complete extinction of vices. In this matter alone the sin of pride is utterly extinguished [Note: Gussanville, together with several editions, reads, “is not utterly extinguished.” All the manuscripts and the old Paris editions of 1488, 1495, 1518, and 1571, as well as the Basel edition of 1514 and others, disagree; in them the negation is absent. Once it is removed, the best sense remains: only the sin of pride is extinguished, while temptations are not completely lulled to sleep, since vicious thoughts continually arise and stir up war. In the Corbie German manuscript, instead of “the sin of pride alone is extinguished,” one reads, “is utterly extinguished with care.”] because, although it serves victory, continual combat is nevertheless reserved for us to subdue the pride of our thoughts.

Hence, because every continent man conforms to due necessity and resists violent pleasure, the Lord’s voice rightly says here: “He does not hear the shout of the tax collector.” And because the discerning man raises himself to understand higher things insofar as he chastises within himself the incitements of the flesh, after the contempt of the tax collector’s shout there rightly follows:

CAPUT XIX [Rec. XV].

VERSE 8.—He looks around upon the mountains of his pasture.

64. He is able to ascend to understand sublime things who has chastised the incitements of the flesh.—The mountains of pasture are the lofty contemplations of inward refreshment. For the more holy men abase themselves outwardly by despising themselves, the more abundantly they are nourished inwardly by contemplating revelations. Hence it is written: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Psalm 83:6–7), because the valley of humility keeps them outwardly in weeping, while the ascent of contemplation raises them inwardly. [Note: The Laon manuscript adds: “in the place which he appointed.”] [Vet. XXIX.] The mountains of pasture are also the sublime virtues of the angels. They refresh us here by ministering and assisting us because there they grow rich through the inward dew of contemplation. Since, by God’s generosity, they protect us in every contest, they are rightly said to be looked upon. For we see that they are present to us on every side, whose protection fortifies us against adversaries from all directions.

The mountains of pasture may also be understood as the lofty sayings of sacred Scripture, of which the Psalmist says: “The high mountains are for the stags” (Psalm 103:18). For those who already know how to make leaps of contemplation ascend the lofty summits of divine sayings like the peaks of mountains. Since the weak cannot reach these peaks, it is rightly added there: “The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (ibid.), because the feeble are not exercised by sublime understanding but are humbly held in Christ by faith alone. It follows:

CAPUT XX.

IBID.—He searches out every green place.

65. After despising transitory things, one desires what will remain forever.—All things that have been created in time and are dried up from the delight of the present life by the approaching end, as by a summer sun, are dry. But those things are called green that do not wither through any temporality. Therefore, for this wild ass to search out green places means for every holy man, after despising transitory things, to desire what will remain forever.

All these things that have been said about the wild ass can also be understood in another way. We explain them by repeating the preceding verse, so that we may leave to the reader’s judgment whatever he believes should be chosen. Therefore, after the ministry of the preachers had been described under the figure of the does, so that it might be shown through whom this same virtue of preaching is given, a remembrance of the Lord’s incarnation is immediately appended, so that it may be said:

CAPUT XXI.

VERSE 5.—Who sent the wild ass forth free?

ALLEGORICAL SENSE.—66. Christ is appropriately compared with the wild ass.—Let no one judge it unworthy that the incarnate Lord can be represented by such an animal, since it is clear to everyone that in sacred Scripture even a worm and a beetle are employed symbolically, as it is written: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21:7). And as it is said by the prophet according to the Septuagint interpreters: “The beetle cried out from the wood” (Habakkuk 2:2). Since, then, he is represented by things so lowly and worthless when they are named, what is said of him insultingly, when it is clear that nothing is said of him literally? He is called a lamb, but because of his innocence. He is called a lion, but because of his power. At times he is also compared with a serpent, whether because of death or because of wisdom. [Note: Even in the older editions only “but because of wisdom” is found. We have supplied the remainder from the English, Norman, Laon, Corbie German, Val-Clos, and other manuscripts. It is excellently said that Christ is compared with a serpent because of death: the serpent raised up in the wilderness foretold him raised upon the cross.] And therefore all these things can be said figuratively of him, because nothing can be believed to exist essentially in him as any of these things. For if any one of them existed literally, he could no longer be called another. If he were literally called a lamb, he could not then be called a lion. If he were literally called a lion, he could not be represented by a serpent. But we speak of all these things in him figuratively, the more broadly the farther they are from essence.

The wild ass, therefore, can signify the incarnate Lord. For the wild ass is an animal of the fields. [Note: Most manuscripts read: “For it is an animal of the field.”] And because the incarnate Lord benefited the Gentiles more than the Jews, taking an animal body, he came as though not into a house but rather into a field. Of this field of the Gentiles the Psalmist says: “The beauty of the field is with me” (Psalm 49:11).

Thus the incarnate Lord, who in the form of God is equal to the Father, in the form of a servant is less than the Father, and in that respect is also less than himself (Philippians 2). Therefore let it be said by the Father concerning the Son according to the form of a servant: “Who sent the wild ass forth free, and who loosed his bonds?” For everyone who sins is a slave of sin (John 8:35). And because the incarnate Lord became a participant in our nature, though not in our guilt, he is said to have been sent forth free, because he is not held under the dominion of sin. Of him it is written elsewhere: “Free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5). [Note: In the Corbie German manuscript, in many editions, and in the latest edition, “Free” occurs once, followed afterward by “he is said to have been sent forth.” It is repeated in the English, Norman, Vindoc, and other manuscripts. In the Basel edition of 1514 and the Paris editions of 1495 and 1518, after the text of the Psalm, “free among the dead” is followed by: “sent forth free among the dead.”] He is said to have been sent forth free because, taking our nature upon himself, he is in no way held by the yoke of iniquity. Although the stain of our guilt did not touch him, the suffering of our mortality nevertheless bound him. Hence, after it is said that he was sent forth free, it is rightly added concerning him:

CAPUT XXII.

IBID.—And who loosed his bonds?

67. The bonds of this wild ass were loosed when the infirmities of his passion were changed into the glory of the resurrection.—His bonds were loosed when the infirmities of his passion were changed into the glory of the resurrection. The infirmities of our mortality, which we suffer deservedly because of iniquity, were like certain bonds that the Lord willingly chose to be bound by even unto death, and which he wondrously loosed through the resurrection. To hunger, thirst, grow weary, be seized, scourged, and crucified was a bond of our mortality. But when, death having been completed, the veil of the temple was torn, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and the gates of hell were thrown open, what else is shown by so many proofs of such great power except that the bonds of our weakness were being loosed? He who had come to assume the form of a servant returned free even in that form of a servant from the bonds of hell, and ascended to heaven with his members.

The apostle Peter bears witness to these bonds when he says: “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24). And because after his death and resurrection he deigned to call the Gentiles to the grace of faith, after his bonds have been said to be loosed, it is appropriately added:

CAPUT XXIII.

VERSE 6.—To whom I gave a house in the wilderness, and his tent in a land of salt.

68. A place was given to him in the wilderness and in a land of salt when the Gentiles received him.—For in the Gentile world, in which there had been no patriarch and no prophet, there was scarcely a human being who used reason to understand God. [Note: Recent editions, against the manuscripts and old printed editions, read: “there was no prophet, because there was scarcely a human being who used reason to understand God.”] Of this wilderness Isaiah says: “The desolate and impassable land shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult and blossom like a lily” (Isaiah 35:1). And again it is said of the Church: “He will make her wilderness like delights and her solitude like the garden of the Lord” (Isaiah 51:3).

The land of salt is a repetition of this same wilderness, which, before it knew the true wisdom of God, produced salt because, producing no greenness of good understanding, it savored of perversity. Therefore it received a house in the wilderness and a tent in a land of salt, because God, having become incarnate for human beings, left Judea behind and possessed the hearts of the Gentiles. [Note: The Corbie German, Pratel, Utrecht, and Val-Clos manuscripts read: “because God incarnate for human beings possessed the hearts of the Gentiles, leaving Judea behind.”] Hence the Father says to him through the prophet: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

Insofar as he is God, he gives all things with the Father; insofar as he is human, he receives among all things from the Father, as it is written: [Note: The printed editions read “received all things”; the manuscripts read “receives among all things.” This mode of expression is familiar to Gregory.] “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27). And again it is written: “Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (John 13:1). Or as he himself says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me” (John 6:37).

But if it is asked what difference there is between a house and a tent, a house is for dwelling, while a tent is for traveling. Therefore he had the hearts of the Gentiles as tents, as he came to them; but by establishing them in righteousness, he made them a house by dwelling in them. And because he scorned to imitate the life of those to whom he had come, it is rightly added:

CAPUT XXIV.

VERSE 7.—He scorns the multitude of the city.

69. He did not follow the example of the multitude but set forth his own life for imitation. The present life is not to be loved for its own sake but endured for the sake of the future.—That is, he despises the customs of human society. Although he became human among human beings, he did not wish to maintain the ways of human beings. For this reason he became human among us: not only to redeem us by the shedding of his blood, but also to transform us by the example he displayed. In our manner of life, therefore, he found one thing when he came and taught another by living.

For all those born from the proud stock of Adam strove to seek the prosperous things of the present life, avoid adversity, flee reproaches, and pursue glory. The incarnate Lord came among them seeking adversity, scorning prosperity, embracing reproaches, and fleeing glory. When the Jews wished to make him their king, he refused to become king (John 6:15). But when they plotted to kill him, he came of his own accord to the gallows of the cross (ibid., 18:4). Thus he fled what all seek and sought what all flee. [Note: The Laon and Val-Clos manuscripts read “what human beings seek,” and similarly below.] By fleeing what all seek and seeking what all flee, he did what all would marvel at: he himself rose after dying and by his death raised others from death. [Vet. XXXI.]

There are two lives for a human being existing in the body: one before death and the other after the resurrection. Everyone knew one of these by experience but did not know the other; and the human race devoted itself only to the one it knew. The Lord came through the flesh, and while he assumed one, he revealed the other. By assuming the life known to us, he displayed the one unknown to us. By dying, he lived out the life we possess; by rising, he opened the life we should seek, teaching us by his example that this life, which we lead before death, is not to be loved for its own sake but endured for the sake of the other. Therefore, because he adopted a new way of life among human beings and did not follow the customs of Babylon, it is rightly written of him: “He scorns the multitude of the city.”

70. Christ abandoned the multitude wandering along the broad way.—Or certainly, because he abandoned the many wandering along the broad way and chose the few walking along the narrow way [Note: Corbie German, Ebroic, and other Norman manuscripts add “and along the narrow way,” namely, “the way.”], to scorn the multitude of the city is to reject from his kingdom’s portion that part of the human race which enters the broad way (Matthew 7:13), which is numerous because of the abundance of iniquity. It follows:

CAPUT XXV.

IBID.—He does not hear the shout of the tax collector.

71. The shout of the tax collector, namely, the devil, was not heard.—As was said above, who can be understood as the tax collector in this passage except the devil? By evil persuasion he brought the hope of immortality, but by deception he exacts the tribute of death; by persuasion he introduced guilt, and by raging he exacts punishment. [Note: The Laon manuscript reads: “by serving he introduced punishment.”] The speech of this tax collector is his crafty persuasion before a person’s death; his shout is the violent seizure that occurs after death. Those whom he secretly intercepts before death, he violently drags after death into participation in his punishment.

But because, when coming to death, the Lord did not fear the violent assaults of this tax collector, as he himself says, “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30), it is rightly said: “He does not hear the shout of the tax collector.” For the tax collector of the human race came to him because he saw him to be human. But the human being whom he regarded with contempt because of weakness, he found by his power to be more than human.

[Rec. XVI.] 72. Laban was a type of this tax collector, Jacob of Christ, and Rachel of the Church.—Laban represented the type of this tax collector when, coming in fury, he sought his idols from Jacob (Genesis 31:1 ff.). For Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Whitening may appropriately be understood as the devil, who, though dark because of his merits, “transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Corinthians 11:14). Jacob served him—that is, the Jewish people in part, from whose flesh the incarnate Lord came.

Laban can also represent this world, which pursues Jacob with fury because it strives by persecution to oppress the elect, who are the members of our Redeemer. Jacob took away his daughter—that is, either the daughter of the world or of the devil—when Christ joined the Church from the Gentiles to himself. [Note: The Laon and Val-Clos manuscripts read: “Jacob took away his daughter, that is, the daughter of the world.”] He also drew her away from her father’s house, for through the prophet he says to her: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11).

But what is signified by the idols except avarice? Hence Paul says: “And avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3:5). Therefore Laban came to Jacob but did not find the idols, because, although the devil displayed the world’s treasures, he found no traces of earthly desire in our Redeemer. But the things Jacob did not have, Rachel covered while sitting. For Rachel, who is also called “sheep,” represents the Church. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise after you have sat” (Psalm 126:2). Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting, because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vices of earthly desire through repentance.

The Psalmist speaks through the prophet of this covering of vices: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1). Therefore that Rachel signified us: we press down the idols by sitting if we condemn the faults of avarice through repentance. Such avarice does not usually befall those who run courageously in the way of the Lord, to whom it is said: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 30:25), but chiefly those who, walking as though with a womanly step, are weakened by the blandishments of the world. Hence these words of the same Rachel occur there: “According to the custom of women, it has now happened to me” (Genesis 31:35).

Therefore Laban did not find the idols with Jacob, because the crafty tax collector found nothing to criticize in our Redeemer. Concerning this tax collector, to our Redeemer freeing the Gentiles from his dominion, the prophet says: “For you have conquered the yoke of his burden, and the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his tax collector, as in the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9:4).

When the Lord rescued the Gentiles, he conquered the yoke of their burden by freeing them through his coming from the servitude of demonic tyranny. He conquered the rod of their shoulder when he restrained from the human race, once redeemed, the blows of that tyranny which had grievously oppressed it through perverse works. [Note: Some editions read, “when he restrained persecution”; Gilot and other editions read “the Redeemer” for “the human race, once redeemed.”] He conquered the scepter of their tax collector when he destroyed in the hearts of the faithful the kingdom of that devil who, because of the pestilential perpetration of vices, had been accustomed to exact the due tribute of punishments.

[Vet. XXXII, Rec. XVII.] 73. Gideon’s extraordinary battle against the Midianites prefigured Christ’s combat.—But let us hear how these things came about. It is immediately added: “As in the day of Midian.” I do not think it irrelevant if we discuss at greater length at some point this battle of the Midianites, which the prophet vigilantly introduced in comparison with the Lord’s coming. For in the Book of Judges (Judges 7:1 ff.) Gideon is described as having fought against the Midianites.

When he was bringing the multitude of his army out to battle, he was divinely instructed that, when he came to the river, all those whom he saw drawing water on bent knees should be removed from the conflict of war. [Note: The Norman, Val-Clos, and some other manuscripts read: “And it happened that three hundred remained.”] And it happened that only three hundred men remained, those who had drawn water with their hands while standing. With these he proceeded to battle, and he armed them not with weapons but with trumpets, lamps, and jars (ibid., 19 ff.). For, as it is written there, they placed burning lamps inside little vessels, held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, and, coming close to their enemies, blew the trumpets and broke the little vessels; the lamps appeared. [Note: Corbie German, Gilot, Gussanville, and several editions read “they opened the lamps”; the other manuscripts and the old Paris and Basel editions read “they appeared,” which reading we have preferred.] The enemies, terrified on one side by the sound of the trumpets and on the other by the flashing of the lamps, were put to flight.

What does it mean that such a battle is brought forward by the prophet and that the victory of this battle is compared with the coming of our Redeemer? Did the prophet wish to indicate to us that the victory of that battle under Gideon’s leadership signified the coming of our Redeemer against the devil? Things were surely done there which, the more they surpass ordinary warfare, the more they do not depart from the mystery of prophecy. For who ever came to battle with jars and lamps? Who, coming against weapons, abandoned weapons? These things would certainly have seemed ridiculous to us if they had not been terrifying to the enemies. But the victory itself bears witness and teaches us not to consider these events insignificant. [Note: The editions, together with the Corbie German manuscript, read “lest these things be insignificant”; “lest they be considered insignificant,” which is found in the Norman, Vindoc, Laon, Val-Clos, and other manuscripts, is better.]

Thus Gideon, coming to battle, signifies the advent of our Redeemer, of whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23:7). [Note: Val-Clos reads, “your prince.”] This Gideon prophesied our Redeemer not only by his deed but also by his name. [Note: Some witnesses read “this Redeemer.” The rationale for the following interpretation of Gideon’s name is unknown; it has no basis in the Hebrew source. Yet Jerome’s Book of Hebrew Names, Paris 1546 and other editions, has: “Gideon: going around in the womb, or useless, or the trial of their iniquity.” The words “in the womb, or useless, or the trial of their iniquity” do not appear in the newer edition.] For Gideon is interpreted as “going around in the womb.” Our Lord, through the power of his majesty, embraces all things, and yet through the grace of his dispensation he came, taking human nature within the Virgin’s womb. [Note: “Taking human nature” is absent from the Norman, Vindoc, Val-Clos, and Corbie German manuscripts.] Who, then, is “going around in the womb” except almighty God, redeeming us through his dispensation, embracing all things in his divinity, and taking human nature within the womb?
