In that womb he was incarnate but was not confined, because he was within the womb according to the substance of weakness and outside the world according to the power of majesty. [Note: The Ebroic and Vindoc manuscripts read “outside the womb.”]

Madian, however, is interpreted as “from judgment.” The fact that his enemies had to be driven back and destroyed came not from any fault of the one driving them back but from the judgment of the one who judged justly. And for this reason they are called “from judgment”: because, alienated from the grace of the Redeemer, they bear even in the word of their name the merit of just condemnation.

### [Old recension XXXIII.] 74. What the three hundred soldiers who fought with Gideon signify

Against these [Col. 0565D] Gideon advances to battle with three hundred men. The number one hundred commonly signifies the fullness of perfection. What, then, is designated by the number one hundred multiplied three times, except the perfect knowledge of the Trinity? With these, our Lord destroys [Note: [Col. 0566D] Pratel. and Vindoc.: “has overthrown.”] the adversaries of the faith [Col. 0566A]; with these he enters the battles of preaching—those who are able to know divine things and who know how to perceive perfectly what the Trinity, which is God, is.

It should be noted that this number three hundred is contained in the letter *tau*, which has the appearance of a cross. If what projects from the cross were added to it across the transverse line, it would no longer be merely the figure of a cross but the cross itself. Since, therefore, this number three hundred is contained in the letter *tau*, and since, as we have said, the appearance of the cross is shown through the letter *tau*, those who are designated by the three hundred men following Gideon are not improperly understood to be those to whom it was said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Those who follow the Lord take up the cross more truly insofar as they subdue themselves more earnestly and are pierced by compassionate love for their neighbors.

Hence it is also said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Mark a *tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve” (Ezek. 9:4). Or certainly, in these three hundred, who are contained in the letter *tau*, this is expressed: that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.

They were led to the river to drink its water, and whoever drank the water on bent knees was removed from the purpose of warfare. Water signifies the teaching of wisdom, while the standing knee signifies right action. Those, therefore, who are said to have bent their knees while drinking the water withdrew, prohibited from the conflict of war, because Christ goes forth with those to battle against the enemies of the faith who, while drinking deeply of the streams of teaching, do not bend the uprightness of their works.

For all are said to have drunk water at that time, but not all are said to have stood with upright knees. Those who bent their knees while drinking were rejected, because, as the Apostle testifies: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” (Rom. 2:13). Since, as we have said, dissolution of works is signified by the bending of the knees themselves, Paul rightly says again: “Lift up the drooping hands and strengthen the weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12:12–13).

Those, then, advance to war under Christ as their leader [Note: [Col. 0566D] Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Norm., Laud., etc., *prodeunt*, “go forth.”] who show by their works what they proclaim with their mouths; who spiritually drink deeply of the streams of teaching, yet are not carnally bent toward evil works, because, as it is written: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9).

### 75. What the trumpets, torches, and jars with which they went to battle and defeated the enemies signify

They therefore went to battle with trumpets, torches, and jars. [Note: [Col. 0566D] The same manuscripts: “And this, as we have said, was the order of battle.”] This was, as we have said, an unusual order of battle [Col. 0567A]. They sounded the trumpets, and they held the jars in their left hands; inside the jars torches had been placed. When the jars were broken, the torches were revealed, and by their flashing light the enemies were terrified and put to flight.

Thus the trumpets signify the cry of preachers, the torches the brightness of miracles, and the jars the fragility of bodies. Such were the companions our leader brought with him to the battle of preaching: men who, scorning the preservation of their bodies, would overthrow their enemies by dying and overcome their swords not with weapons or swords but with patience.

Our martyrs came armed to battle under their leader—but with trumpets, jars, and torches. They sounded the trumpets while preaching; they broke the jars when they exposed their bodies, which were to be dissolved in suffering, to hostile swords [Note: [Col. 0567D] So Turon., Vindoc., Laudun., Corb. Germ., Val. Cl., and the old edition. More recent editors preferred *supponunt*, “place beneath.”]; and they shone with the torches when, after the dissolution of their bodies [Col. 0567B], they flashed forth through miracles.

The enemies were immediately put to flight, because when they saw the bodies of the dead martyrs shining with miracles, they were shattered by the light of truth and believed what they had attacked.

They sounded the trumpets, therefore, so that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken so that the torches might appear; the torches appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight. That is: the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine through miracles; they shone through miracles so that by the divine light they might overthrow their enemies, so that those enemies would no longer resist God with raised heads but, subjected, would fear him.

### 76. The preachers of the faith accomplished more by their death than by their preaching

It should be noted that the enemies stood before the jars but fled before the torches [Col. 0567C]. The persecutors of the holy Church resisted the preachers of the faith while they were still in the body; but after the dissolution of their bodies, when miracles appeared, they were put to flight, because, crushed by fear, they ceased persecuting the faithful. They feared at the sight of the torches of miracles: the trumpets had preached, and the jars of their bodies had been broken.

### [Old recension XXXIV.] 77. Whoever cares more for the body than for preaching must fear rejection

It must also be observed that it is written there that they held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left. We are said to regard as “right” whatever we esteem greatly; as “left,” whatever we consider of no account.

It is therefore rightly written there that they held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left, because the martyrs of Christ regard the grace of preaching as something of great worth, but the preservation of their bodies as something of little worth. Whoever values the usefulness of the body more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in his left hand and the jar in his right.

For if the grace of preaching is placed first and the usefulness of the body second, it is certain [Note: [Col. 0567D] Vindoc., Pratel., Val. Cl.: “because the trumpets are on the right … and the jars on the left.”] that the trumpets are held on the right and the jars on the left.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand” (Matt. 5:15). The bushel signifies temporal advantage, while the lamp signifies the light of preaching. To put the lamp under a bushel [Note: [Col. 0568D] Val. Cl.: “to keep.”] is to conceal the grace of preaching for the sake of temporal advantage—something none of the elect does.

And rightly it is added: “But on a lampstand.” [Note: [Col. 0568D] Vindoc.: “But above the lampstand.”] In the lampstand the condition of the body is signified; the lamp is placed upon it when care for preaching is preferred to the body itself.

It was therefore rightly said through the Prophet: “You have broken the rod of his oppressor, as on the day of Midian” (Isa. 9:4). But since, for the sake of explaining the prophetic testimony, we have digressed at length, let us return to the order of our work.

After it had been said, “He did not hear the cry of the oppressor”—because, clearly, the Lord, manifested in the flesh, despised the snares of the ancient enemy—he rightly adds what he did concerning his elect, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Verse 8.—He surveys the mountains of his pasture

### 78. Christ also transformed the proud into members of his own body. He converts those whom he surveys

We understand the mountains to be all the exalted people of this age who have swollen with earthly height in their hearts. But because the Lord also incorporates such people, once converted, into the body of his Church, changing them from their former pride and transforming them into his members, these mountains are his pastures. For he is satisfied by the conversion of the erring and by the humility of the proud, as he himself says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

And he commanded the apostles, sent out to preach: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life” (John 6:27).

Of these mountains it is said through the Prophet: “The Lord will not reject his people, for all the ends of the earth are in his hand, and he beholds the heights of the mountains” (Ps. 94:4). The heights of the mountains are certainly the pride of the proud. The Lord is said to behold them—that is, to change them from their wickedness for the better.

For the Lord converts the one whom he beholds. Hence it is written: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, as he had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times’; and he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61–62).

And as Solomon says: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze” (Prov. 20:8).

Of this surveying of the mountains it is again said through the Prophet: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 96:5), because, after the hardness of their wickedness, melted by divine fear, they were brought down from that former rigid swelling. [Note: [Col. 0568D] The recent Vulgate editions read *subtracti sunt*, “they were removed,” disregarding the manuscripts and old editions.]

### 79. He feeds upon the good works of the converted. Matthew prepared a great banquet for Christ—or rather, he himself was one

It should also be observed that he does not say “he looks upon,” but “he surveys the mountains of his pasture.” The Lord was incarnate in Judea, which lay in the midst of the nations. [Note: [Col. 0568D] So Laud., Val. Cl., Vindoc., Norm., and the old edition. In recent editions, together with Corb. Germ.: “And from there.”] Therefore he surveyed the mountains because he gathered from the whole Gentile world those who had been placed all around, exalted in this age [Col. 0569A].

He feeds upon these mountains because he is satisfied by the good works of the converted as by verdant grasses. Hence the bride’s voice says to him in the Song of Songs: “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie at midday” (Song 1:6). The Lord feeds when he takes delight in our good deeds. He lies at midday when, among the hearts of his elect, he finds the refreshment of good thought amid the hearts of the reprobate burning with carnal desires.

Matthew had been a certain mountain when he was swollen with the profits of the tax office. Of him it is written that, after he believed, he invited the Lord into his house and prepared a great banquet (Luke 5:29).

This mountain therefore produced for this wild ass the grasses of a verdant pasture [Note: [Col. 0569D] Laud. and Val. Cl.: “verdant.”], because he fed him outwardly with a banquet and inwardly with the feasts of virtue.

This is still more fully explained when it follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII

### The same.—He seeks out every green thing [Note: [Col. 0569D] Pratel. and Vindoc.: “And every green thing.”]

### 80. Christ abandons dry hearts and seeks those that are green with faith and hope

He abandons what is dry and seeks out everything that is green. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Laud. and Val. Cl.: “they are dry … in heart.”]

Dry hearts are the hearts of people planted in the hope of this age, which is destined to perish, and which have no confidence in eternity. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Ebroic. and other Norm., Vindoc., and Corb. Germ.: “but they are green.”]

Those are green who cling to the inheritance of which the Apostle Peter says: “Into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Pet. 1:4). Each person is more truly green insofar as he fixes the root of his thought in the lot of the unfading inheritance. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Another reading: “of the incorruptible.”]

Whoever fears becoming dry within should flee the dry desires of this world without. Whoever desires to be sought by the Lord should grow green in the inward planting of his heart, desiring his eternal homeland.

### 81. Saint Gregory’s modesty and humility

Let these things, expounded concerning the wild ass under a twofold interpretation [Note: [Col. 0569D] Val. Cl.: “may be profitable.”], suffice. It should be left to the judgment of the reader to decide which interpretation he ought to prefer. And if he should perhaps reject the understanding of either interpretation, I myself will gladly follow my reader, who thinks more subtly and truly, as a disciple follows his teacher [Note: [Col. 0570D] Corb. Germ., Laud., and Val. Cl.: “I follow.”], because I believe that whatever I recognize him to understand better than I do has been given to me personally.

### [Old recension XXXV.]

For all who, filled with faith, strive to utter something concerning God are organs of the truth; and it lies within the power of that same truth whether it sounds through me to another or through another to me. For truth itself, present among us, is equitable even when not all live equally [Note: [Col. 0570D] Pratel. and Val. Cl.: “is equally”]; and often it touches one person so that he may hear well what it has sounded through another, while often it touches another so that he may sound well what is heard from others.

### 82. A word is sometimes attributed to a teacher because of the merit of the hearer, or withheld because of his fault

Often a word is granted to a teacher because of the hearer’s merit, and often the teacher’s speech is withheld because of the hearer’s fault. Therefore, in what the teacher proclaims abundantly, let him not exalt himself, lest perhaps his tongue is filled not for his own sake but for the hearer’s benefit. And in what the teacher says barrenly, let the hearer not grow angry, lest perhaps the teacher’s tongue grows sluggish not for his own sake but because of the hearer’s rejection.

[Note: [Col. 0570D] So Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norm., and many manuscripts, although the editions and Corb. Germ. read: “for the hearer’s benefit, a good word is given.”]

For the hearer’s benefit, good speech is given even to evil teachers, just as words of preaching could be supplied to the Pharisees, of whom it is written: “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:3).

But because of the rejection of hearers, speech is withheld even from good teachers, as is said to Ezekiel against Israel: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, unable to rebuke them as a man who rebukes, because they are a rebellious house” (Ezek. 3:26).

### 83. Sometimes speech is given or withheld because of the merit or fault of both teacher and hearers. No one should become proud of what he receives. Fear must accompany hope

Sometimes the word of preaching is given because of both teacher and hearers; sometimes it is withheld because of both. It is given because of both, as the divine voice says to Paul at Corinth: “Do not be afraid, but speak” (Acts 18:9), and shortly afterward: “For I have many people in this city” (ibid. 10).

It is withheld because of both, as when Eli the priest knew of the evil conduct of his sons but did not exercise a fitting voice of rebuke. It would certainly come to pass that the punishment of death would strike them for their crime and him for his silence (1 Sam. 3:12 ff.).

Since, then, we do not know either for whom speech is given or because of whom it is withheld, one remedy alone is salutary: we must neither exalt ourselves over what we have received more abundantly than others [Note: [Col. 0570D] Pratel.: “which [are] to them” (*quae illis*; reading uncertain)], nor mock another because he has received less. Rather, with the foot of humility firmly planted, we must walk gravely and steadfastly, because in this life we are more truly instructed insofar as we recognize that we cannot obtain instruction from ourselves.

Why, then, should anyone be proud of his teaching, when he does not know by the hidden judgment of whom, or when, it is given, nor when, or to whom, it is withheld? Although fear may always seem far removed from security, nothing is safer for us than to fear always under hope, lest an incautious mind either fall into vices [Note: [Col. 0570D] Vindoc. and Norm.: “into vices.”] through despair or fall through exalting itself over its gifts. Before the eyes of the strict yet loving Judge, the more humbly one trembles concerning oneself under hope, the more firmly one stands in him.

# BOOK THIRTY-ONE

The ninth verse is explained together with the remaining verses of chapter 39, omitting only the final three; and the efficacy of divine grace is demonstrated especially in the preaching of the Gospel and the conversion of sinners.

[Col. 0571]

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. The wound inflicted on humanity by the proud devil was healed by God’s humility

In paradise, when humanity was still sound, the devil, envious, inflicted the wound of pride, so that the one who had not received death when created might, through exaltation, deserve it (Gen. 3). [Note: [Col. 0571D] Recent editions together with Germ. read *moreretur*, “might die.” The Laud. manuscript also has this. But Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norm., as well as the old Paris and Basel editions, more correctly read *mereretur*, “might deserve it.”]

But since it belongs to divine power not only to make good things from nothing but also to restore from evils the things the devil had brought about, against this wound inflicted by the proud devil the humility of God appeared among humanity as a remedy. Thus, by the example of the Creator, those who had fallen through imitating the enemy’s pride might rise after being humbled.

Against the proud devil, therefore, God appeared among humanity as a humble human being. The powerful of this age—that is, the members of the proud devil—considered him contemptible precisely because they saw him humble. The more the wound of their hearts swelled, the more they despised the gentle medicine [Col. 0571B]. [Note: [Col. 0571D] The editions read “the medicine of life.” We have followed the English, Norman, Vindoc., two German, and Laud. manuscripts. Turon. and Val. Cl. read “the medicine of the mind,” evidently changing *mite* (“gentle”) by confusion into *mente* (“mind”).]

Thus, when the medicine was rejected by the wound of the proud, it reached the wound of the humble: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). What happened among the poor was afterward something that the rich [reading uncertain] would marvel at. For when they saw new virtues in them, they later stood amazed at the miracles of those whose lives they had previously despised.

Then, returning fearfully to their own hearts, they began to dread in the miracles the holiness they had despised in the commandments. Thus the strong were confounded through the weak, because, when the life of the humble rose into veneration, the pride of the arrogant fell.

Since blessed Job bears the figure of the holy Church, and since almighty God foresaw that, at the beginning of the nascent Church, the powerful of this age would refuse to take up her light yoke with their thick-necked hearts, let him say:

## CHAPTER IX

### Chapter 39, verse 9.—Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you? [Note: [Col. 0571D] Laud. and Val. Cl. read “rhinoceros,” and likewise below.]

### 2. By the rhinoceros are understood the proud and powerful, subdued by Christ and compelled to serve the Church. He broke their pride through miracles

The rhinoceros is entirely of an untamable nature, so that, if ever captured, it cannot in any way be held. For, as is said, it is so impatient that it immediately dies. Its name, interpreted in Latin, means “with a horn in the nose.”

What else is signified by the nose except foolishness, and by the horn except pride? For we have learned, with Solomon as witness, that foolishness is commonly understood by the nose. He says: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful but foolish woman” (Prov. 11:22). He saw heretical teaching shining with the brilliance of eloquence, yet not corresponding to a fitting understanding of wisdom, and said: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout”—that is, beautiful [Note: [Col. 0571D] Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Ebroic., Pratel., and other Norm.: “and intricately woven.”] and elaborate speech in the thoughts of a foolish mind, from whose eloquence gold hangs, but which, because of the weight of its earthly intention, does not look upward, like a pig.

He then explained this by saying: “A beautiful but foolish woman”—that is, heretical doctrine: beautiful in its wording, foolish in its understanding.

In the horn, however, pride is frequently understood [Note: [Col. 0572D] Germ., Vindoc., most Norman manuscripts, Laud., Corb. Germ., and Val. Cl.: “because pride is frequently [understood].”], as we have learned from the testimony of the Prophet, who says: “I said to the wicked, ‘Do not act wickedly,’ and to the sinners, ‘Do not lift up your horn’” (Ps. 75:5). What, then, are designated by this rhinoceros except the powerful of this age, or the highest authorities of governments themselves? Inflated by the boastfulness of foolish display, they are puffed up outwardly by false honors but inwardly emptied by true miseries.

To them it is rightly said: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9). [Note: [Col. 0572D] Germ., Vindoc., Laud., Val. Cl., and Corb. Germ.: “Why does he become proud?”]

At the very beginnings of the nascent Church, while the power of the rich rose against her and breathed with such immense cruelty toward her destruction, while she, distressed by so many tortures and oppressed by so many persecutions, was collapsing, who at that time could have believed [Note: [Col. 0572D] Germ., Corb. Germ., Ebroic., and other Norm.: “that she, standing upright …”] that she would subject the erect and harsh necks of the proud to herself and, having been tamed by the yoke of holy fear, bind them with the gentle reins of faith?

For a long time, the horn of this rhinoceros tossed her about at her beginnings, and, as though she were to be destroyed utterly, struck her down [Col. 0572C]. But by the dispensation of divine grace, she was strengthened by dying and being brought to life, while this rhinoceros, wearied by striking, bent down its horn [Note: [Col. 0572D] Val. Cl.: “having been brought to life, it recovered its strength.”] What was impossible for human beings was not difficult for God, who broke the rigid powers of this world not with words but with miracles.

For we now recognize rhinoceroses serving every day [Note: [Col. 0572D] Another reading: “rhinoceroses,” as in Germ., Vindoc., and Laud.], when we see the powerful of this world—those who once foolishly trusted in their own strength—already subjected to God.

The Lord was speaking of a certain untamable rhinoceros when he said: “It is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:23). When he was asked, “Who then can be saved?” he immediately added: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (ibid. 26). As though he were saying: This rhinoceros cannot be tamed by human strength, but it can be subjected by divine miracles.

Hence it is also appropriately said to blessed Job, who bears the figure of the holy Church: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” [Recension II.] The implied meaning is: “As he serves me, for I long endured his resistance to human admonitions, yet suddenly, when I wished, I struck him down through miracles.”

Or, more openly: “Will those who pride themselves in foolish exaltation submit to your preaching without my assistance?” Consider through whom you prevail, and bend the thought of pride in everything in which you prevail.

Alternatively, this is brought to the notice of blessed Job in order to humble his virtue: what great things would one day be accomplished through the apostles, who subject the world to God and bend to him the pride of the powerful of this age, once it has been tamed. Thus blessed Job may think less of himself insofar as he sees that such difficult souls are gathered to God through others.

Let him therefore say: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” The implied meaning is: “As he will serve me through those whom I send.” It follows:

## CHAPTER III [Old recension II]

### 997 The same.—Or will he remain at your manger?

### 3. Christ feeds these rhinoceroses with the nourishment of Holy Scripture

The manger in this passage may suitably be understood as Holy Scripture itself, in which holy creatures are satisfied with the nourishment of the word. Of them it is said through the Prophet: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Ps. 68:11).

Hence also the Lord, when born, is found by the shepherds in a manger (Luke 2:16), because his incarnation is recognized in the Scripture of the Prophets, through which we are nourished [Note: [Col. 0573D] Pratel. and other Norm.: “in those writings of the Prophets by which he nourishes us.”].

This rhinoceros, therefore—that is, every proud person at the beginning of the nascent Church—when he heard the sayings of the patriarchs, the mysteries of the prophets, and the secrets of the Gospel, mocked them, because he disdained to be enclosed and fed at the manger of the preachers, insofar as, released into his own pleasures, he occupied the field of his despair [Note: [Col. 0573D] Vindoc.: “in his desires.”].

Paul aptly indicates this field of the proud when he says: “Having become desperate, they gave themselves over to shamelessness for the practice of every uncleanness, in greed” (Eph. 4:19). For each person gives himself more freely to present evils insofar as he despairs of attaining eternal goods after this life.

But almighty God long tolerated this rhinoceros wandering through the field of perverse pleasure [Note: [Col. 0573D] Pratel. and Val. Cl.: “will.”]; nevertheless, when he wished, he suddenly tied him to his manger, so that, properly enclosed, he might receive the nourishment of life, lest, being wickedly free, he lose life altogether.

For we already see that the powerful of this age and its rulers gladly listen to the Lord’s teachings, read them steadfastly, and do not depart from the manger [Note: [Col. 0574D] So Turon., two German manuscripts, Vindoc., Laudun., Val. Cl., Norman manuscripts, etc., although the editions read “and, having been fed …”], because they do not transgress in their conduct the commandments of God—which they come to know either by reading or by hearing. Rather, they tolerate standing peacefully at the nourishment of the word, as though enclosed, so that by eating and remaining they may grow fat.

When we observe this being brought about by God, what else do we see but this rhinoceros remaining at the manger? But because, after receiving the nourishment of preaching, this rhinoceros ought to display the fruit of works, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER IV [Old and Second Recension III]

### Verse 10.—Will you bind the rhinoceros to plow with your rope?

### 4. The rulers of the world proclaim the divine commandments by which they are bound and take care that they are observed

The ropes are the Church’s commandments of discipline. To plow is to cut into the soil of the human heart with the plowshare of the tongue through the labor of preaching.

This rhinoceros, therefore, once proud and rigid, is now held bound by the ropes of faith and led from the manger to plow, because he strives to make known to others the preaching by which he himself was nourished.

We know how cruelly this rhinoceros—that is, the earthly ruler—formerly raged against the Lord, and now, with the Lord acting, we see how humbly he submits to him. This rhinoceros is not merely bound but bound for plowing, because, fastened by the ropes of discipline, he not only restrains himself from evil works but also exercises himself in the preaching of the holy faith.

For behold, as was said above, when we see the rulers and princes of human affairs fearing God in their actions, what else do we see but them bound by ropes? And when they do not cease to proclaim through laws the faith that they formerly attacked by persecution [Note: [Col. 0574D] Some editions, incorrectly: “had enriched.”], what else are they doing except sweating over the labors of the plow?

### 5. The wondrous harmony between secular power and Christian humility

It is pleasing to observe this rhinoceros—that is, the ruler of the earth—bound by the ropes of faith: how he carries his horn through worldly power and bears the yoke of faith through love of God.

This rhinoceros could be greatly feared if he were not bound. He has a horn, but he is bound. Thus, in his ropes, the humble have something to love; in his horn, the proud have something to fear.

Tightly bound by ropes, he preserves the piety of gentleness; supported by the horn of earthly glory, he exercises the dominion of power. Often, when anger demands that he be carried away to strike, he is recalled by the fear of God. Through his exasperated power he raises himself in fury; but because he remembers the eternal Judge, he bends his bound horn.

I myself often remember seeing that, when this rhinoceros was fiercely inflamed to strike, and, as though with his horn raised, threatened the smallest creatures with death, exile, and condemnation, imposing immense terror upon his subjects, he suddenly stamped the sign of the cross upon his forehead, extinguished all the fire of fury within himself, and, turning aside, laid down his threats. Since he could not proceed to deliberate acts, he recognized that he was bound.

And he not only subdues his own anger but also hastens to implant everything upright in the minds of his subjects, so that, because all venerate the holy Church from their inmost thoughts, he himself may demonstrate this by the example of his humility.

Let it therefore be said to blessed Job: “Will you bind the rhinoceros to plow with your rope?” As though it said openly: “Do you direct the powerful of this age, who trust in their foolish exaltation, to the labor of preaching, and restrain them under the bonds of discipline?” The implied meaning is: “As I did this when I wished—making those who had formerly persecuted me, whom I had endured as enemies, afterward defenders of the true faith.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER V [Old recension IV]

### The same.—Or will he break up the clods of the valleys behind you?

### 6. Those who were formerly persecutors of the faith later became preachers and defenders of it

Clods lying upon cultivated soil commonly press down the scattered seeds and suffocate what is growing. By these clods are signified those who, through their hardness and destructive life, neither receive the seeds of the word themselves nor allow the fruit of the seeds they have received to be borne by others.

Every holy preacher, coming into the world and evangelizing the poor, had plowed the soft soil of the valleys, as it were. But because the Church was unable to break the hardness of certain exalted people [Note: [Col. 0575D] Ebroic., Pratel., two German manuscripts, followed by the old Paris and Basel editions, read “of the elect,” which we have no doubt is faulty], it endured them as clods lying upon and weighing down its labor.

Many, trusting in the very unbelief of earthly rulers, weighed down the rising Church by the burden of evil living, destroying those whom they could for a long time—sometimes by damnable examples, sometimes by threats, sometimes by flatteries [Note: [Col. 0575D] Val. Cl. and Laud.: “while for a long time, in whatever way they could …”]—so that the soil of the hearers’ hearts might not come to cultivation for the fruit of the spiritual seed.

But when almighty God subjected this rhinoceros to his ropes [Note: [Col. 0575D] Val. Cl.: “this rhinoceros … subjected him, breaking the hard hearts of persecutors,” omitting everything else. Corb. Germ.: “the rhinoceros.” Germ.: “the rhinoceros.”], through him he immediately broke the hardness of the clods.

For he quickly subjected earthly rule to his faith and crushed the hard hearts of the persecutors, so that, like broken clods, they no longer pressed down the soil in their hardness but, loosened to receive the seeds of the word, might germinate.

Hence he now rightly says: “Or will he break up the clods of the valleys behind you?” As though he said: “As I do after myself: once I enter the mind of any exalted power, I not only make it subject to me but also employ it to crush the enemies of the faith” [Note: [Col. 0576D] Val. Cl.: “I exercise it”], so that the powerful of this age, bound by the ropes of my fear, may not only remain believers in me but, zealous on my behalf, break the hardness of other hearts.

### 7. The Church has many enemies in her own bosom, against whom she seeks the assistance of earthly rulers

What we have said concerning unbelievers we also see in many who are counted among the faithful. Many, placed among humble brothers, hold the faith in words alone; but because they do not abandon the pride of exaltation, because they oppress those whom they can with inflicted violence, because, while others bear fruit, they themselves do not receive the seeds of the word but turn the ear of their heart away from the voice of the one exhorting them, what else are they but hardened clods lying in plowed valleys?

They are all the worse because they neither produce the fruit of humility themselves nor, more grievously, oppress those who do produce it.

To dissolve their hardness, the holy Church sometimes, because she is not sufficient by her own strength, seeks the aid of this rhinoceros—that is, of the earthly ruler—so that he may crush the clods lying above, which the humility of the churches bears like the level ground of valleys.

This rhinoceros presses and pulverizes these clods with his foot, because the religious authority of a ruler dissolves, through its power, the hardness of wicked and powerful people, which ecclesiastical humility cannot resist.

Because this is accomplished solely by divine power, so that the heights of earthly rule may incline toward the advancement [Note: [Col. 0576D] Gilot., Vatic., Gussanv., and others, together with the German edition manuscripts, read “for the advancement”; the Corb. Germ., English, Norman, and other manuscripts read “for the promotion”] of the heavenly kingdom, it is rightly now said: “Or will he break up the clods of the valleys behind you?”

But so that blessed Job may think humbly of his own virtues and may still understand exalted things concerning the powers of this world under the name of the rhinoceros, it follows:

## CHAPTER VI

### Verse 11.—Will you trust in his great strength and leave your labors to him?

[Note: [Col. 0576D] Laudun.: “Will you have great confidence in his strength?” Val. Cl.: “Will you have faith in his powerful greatness?”]

8. Christ compels the power of the temporal ruler to serve him, and entrusted and commended his Church to him. — The Lord declares that he has confidence in the strength of the rhinoceros, because he has turned toward the worship of his veneration the powers that he temporarily bestowed upon an earthly ruler, so that, through the power he received—by which he had formerly swollen up against God—he may now render religious service to God. [Col. 0576C] For the more power he has in the world, the more he prevails for the world’s Author. Since he himself is feared by his subjects, he persuades all the more easily, inasmuch as, together with his authority, he indicates who is truly to be feared. Let it therefore be said: “Will you have confidence in his great strength?” As if it were said: “As I behold the strength of earthly rulers destined to serve my worship, so much the less do I value what you are now doing, the more clearly I already foresee that I shall bend even the greater powers of this world to myself.”

[Note: [Col. 0576D] Two German manuscripts, Laudunensis, and several Norman manuscripts read “therefore so much.”]

It is rightly added: “And will you leave your labors to him?” For the Lord left his labors to this rhinoceros because, after the earthly ruler had been converted, he entrusted to him the Church that he had purchased by his death; that is, he committed to his care the peace of the faith, to be guarded with how great solicitude. It follows:

## CHAPTER VII [Ancient version V, Revised version IV]

**VERSE 12.** — “Will you believe him that he will return seed to you and gather your threshing floor?”

9. He promulgates laws on behalf of the Church—the one who formerly raged against her. — What other seed is meant except the word of preaching? As the Truth says in the Gospel: “The sower went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3); and as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isaiah 32:20). What else should the threshing floor be understood as except the Church, of which the Forerunner’s voice says: “And he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matthew 3:12)?

Who, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, would have believed that, while that untamed earthly authority raged against her with so many threats and tortures, this rhinoceros would return seed to God—that is, would repay with his works the word of preaching he had received? Who could then have believed, among the weak, that he would gather his threshing floor? Behold, now the one who formerly raged against her through various tortures promulgates laws on behalf of the Church. Behold, he persuades whatever nations he can seize and leads them to the grace of faith; and to those whom he has taken captive he announces eternal life while preserving their present life. Why is this? Because he now gathers the threshing floor that he once scattered and winnowed with his proud horn. [Col. 0577A–B]

Let blessed Job therefore hear what the rulers of the Gentiles do, and let him not exalt himself in his own eyes because of the glory of such great virtue. Let the powerful king also hear with what devotion the more powerful kings of this world serve God, and let him not drag his own strength, as though it were unique, into the vice of pride. He has an example in others: even if at that time the Lord saw no one like him, he nevertheless foresaw many through whom he would blunt his glory.

10. Those who, out of fear of earthly rulers, do not dare to harass the Church openly turn to various devices of deceit. The Church cannot be without an enemy. — Since earthly rulers therefore humble themselves before God with great humility, wicked men who, formerly placed in unbelief, raged against the Church with open hostility now turn to other devices of deceit. For when they see those rulers venerating religion, they themselves adopt the worship of religion, and under despised clothing they oppress the life of the good by wicked conduct. They are lovers of the world, and they show in themselves what human beings venerate; they join themselves, not in mind but in clothing, to those who truly despise themselves. Since they cannot attain the present glory they love, they follow it as though they despised it. If they found a time suited to their wickedness, they would show what they think against the good. [Col. 0577B–C]

[Ancient version VI.] Yet these devices of the wicked also contribute to the purification of the elect.

[Note: Longipontanus, Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “for the increase of the elect.” Turonensis reads “for the arguments of the elect.” We have followed Ebroicensis and other Norman and Vindocin manuscripts. The printed editions have “for the salvation of the elect.”]

For the holy Church cannot pass through the periods of her pilgrimage without the labor of temptation. Even if she does not have open enemies outside, she nevertheless tolerates false brothers within. She is always in battle against vices, and even in time of peace she has her own war; perhaps she is afflicted more grievously when she is attacked not by the blows of outsiders but by the conduct of her own people. Whether in that time or in this, she is nevertheless always in labor. During the persecution of rulers, she fears lest the good lose what they are; during the conversion of rulers, she endures the fact that the wicked pretend to be good, although they are not. [Col. 0577C–578A]

Therefore, because almighty God said that this rhinoceros was bound with reins, he immediately added the hypocrisy of the wicked, saying:

[Note: Laudunensis reads “led.”]

## CHAPTER VIII [Revised version V]

**VERSE 13.** — “The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron and the hawk.”

11. Hypocrites are like the ostrich, which has wings but no flight. — Who does not know how greatly the heron and the hawk surpass the other birds in the speed of their flight? The ostrich, however, has the appearance of their feathers but does not have the speed of their flight. It cannot rise from the earth; it raises its wings, as though for flight, merely in appearance, but it never lifts itself from the earth by flying. [Col. 0578A–B]

So indeed are all hypocrites: while they imitate the life of the good, they possess the appearance of holiness but do not possess the truth of holy action.

[Note: Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts, Vindocinensis, two German manuscripts, Laudunensis, Longipontanus, Valentinus Cluniacensis, and the old Paris edition read “holy appearance”; other witnesses read “holy conduct,” apparently with a better sense. Here *appearance* may mean outward semblance, as below: “the hypocrite is clothed in the appearance of religion.”]

They have wings for flying in outward appearance, but in their conduct they crawl upon the earth, because they extend wings in the guise of holiness but, weighed down by the burden of worldly cares, are in no way lifted from the earth.

[Note: Vindocinensis reads “display.”]

In rejecting the appearance of the Pharisees, the Lord rebuked, as it were, the ostrich’s wing, which practiced one thing in its works and displayed another in its outward color, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead; so you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of greed and wickedness” (Matthew 23:27). As if he were saying: “The appearance of a wing seems to lift you up, but the burden of your life presses you down into the lowest places.”

The prophet speaks of this burden: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3).

[Note: Laudunensis, Valentinus Cluniacensis, Pratellensis, and most others read “heavy-hearted,” instead of “with a heavy heart,” which is found in two German manuscripts and in all the editions.]

The Lord promises that he will convert the hypocrisy of this ostrich when he says through the prophet: “The beasts of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches” (Isaiah 43:20).

[Note: Vindocinensis, two German manuscripts, and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “The beast will glorify me,” and below, “or certainly the beast of the field.”]

For what are minds of malice openly expressed under the name of dragons, except those that always crawl upon the earth in lowly thoughts? What are designated by the name of ostriches except those who pretend to be good, who retain the life of holiness as though it were a wing of flight in outward appearance, but do not practice it in their works? The Lord therefore asserts that he is glorified by the dragon or the ostrich, because he often turns both those who are openly wicked and those who are hypocritically good to his service from the depths of their thoughts.

Or certainly the beasts of the field—that is, dragons and ostriches—glorify the Lord when the Gentiles, who were formerly a member of the devil in this world, exalt the faith that is in him. He reproaches them under the name of dragons because of their malice, and marks them under the name of ostriches because of their hypocrisy.

[Note: Most of the Vulgate manuscripts read “he calls by the name”; the old Paris and Basel editions, together with the manuscripts, read “he marks by the name.”]

For the Gentiles, as it were, received wings but could not fly: they possessed the nature of reason but did not know the practice of reason. [Col. 0578C–579A]

12. The elect have few things here that weigh them down and many that lift them upward; the reprobate are the opposite. — We must still examine more carefully, in considering this ostrich, what is meant by the hawk and the heron. The bodies of the hawk and the heron are small, but they are supported by denser feathers. Therefore they fly swiftly, because they contain little that weighs them down and much that lifts them up.

[Note: In Pratellensis and other Norman manuscripts, here and elsewhere, *parvum* is often read instead of *parum*.]

The ostrich, by contrast, is clothed with sparse feathers and burdened by an enormous body. Even if it desires to fly, the very scarcity of its feathers cannot suspend such a great mass in the air. Thus the person of the elect is rightly signified in the heron and the hawk. As long as they live in this life, they cannot be without some contamination of fault, however slight. Yet they possess little that weighs them down, while much virtue of good action supports them and lifts them to the heights. [Col. 0579A–B]

The hypocrite, on the other hand, even if he does a few things that lift him up, commits many things that weigh him down. The hypocrite does not perform no good deeds; rather, he commits many perverse deeds by which he himself suppresses those good deeds. The ostrich’s few feathers therefore do not lift its body, because the hypocrite’s small amount of goodness is weighed down by the multitude of his wicked actions.

This ostrich feather also resembles the feathers of the heron and the hawk in color, but it does not resemble them in strength. Their feathers are closed and more firmly joined, and by the strength of their solidity they can press against the air in flight. The ostrich’s feathers, by contrast, are loose and therefore cannot take flight; they are overtaken by the very air against which they ought to press. [Col. 0579B–C]

What, then, do we see in these things except that the virtues of the elect fly forth in solidity, so that they press down the winds of human favor? The hypocrite’s action, however upright it may appear, is not sufficient for flight, because the breeze of human praise passes through the feather of his unstable virtue.

1002 [Ancient version VII]. 13. True Christians are distinguished from false ones by their fruits. — But behold: when we see one and the same outward habit among the good and the wicked, when we observe the same appearance of profession in the elect and the reprobate, where can our understanding find a means by which, through discernment, it may distinguish the elect from the reprobate and the true from the false?

We recognize this more quickly if we recall and firmly fix in our memory the words of our teacher, who said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:20).

[Note: Laudunensis reads “death.” We follow Vindocinensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts here. Turonensis reads “if inward things,” and the Corbie German manuscript has “inward things in memory.” Older printed editions with the German manuscripts read “if undefiled things.”]

For we must not weigh what they display in appearance, but what they preserve in their conduct. Therefore, after he had introduced the appearance of this ostrich, he immediately adds its deeds, saying:

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 14.** — “She leaves her eggs on the ground.”

14. Hypocrites neglect to foster and nourish those whom they beget through good examples. — What is expressed by eggs except tender offspring, which must be warmed for a long time so that they may develop into living birds?

[Note: The English and Norman manuscripts, with the German manuscripts, read “except earthly offspring.”]

Eggs are insensible in themselves, but when warmed they are changed into living birds. So it is certain that little hearers and children remain cold and insensible unless they are warmed by the diligent exhortation of their teacher. Therefore, lest those who are abandoned grow numb in their insensibility, they must be warmed by the continual voice of teachers until they are able both to live through understanding and to fly through contemplation.

Although hypocrites always practice perversity, they nevertheless do not cease to speak correctly. By speaking well they beget children in faith or conduct, but they cannot nourish them by living well. Thus it is rightly said of this ostrich: “She leaves her eggs on the ground.”

The hypocrite neglects care for his children because he subjects himself to external things out of inward love; and the more he is exalted in them, the less he is troubled by the deficiency of his offspring. To leave eggs on the ground, therefore, is to fail to lift children begotten through conversion above earthly actions by interposing the nest of exhortation. To leave eggs on the ground is to provide no example of heavenly life for one’s children.

Because hypocrites are not warmed by the inward organs of charity, they do not grieve over the torpor of the offspring they have produced—that is, over the coldness of their eggs. The more eagerly they insert themselves into earthly actions, the more carelessly they allow those whom they beget to engage in earthly things.

[Note: The German, Pratellensis, and other manuscripts read “whom they had begotten.”]

But because heavenly care does not abandon the children of hypocrites, and because it warms some among them who have been foreknown through an inward election by the regard of the grace bestowed upon them, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER X [Revised version VI]

**SAME PASSAGE.** — “Will you perhaps warm them in the dust?”

15. The grace of God warms the children both of wicked and of good teachers. — As if he were saying: “I am the one who warms them in the dust, because I set the souls of little ones, situated in the midst of sinners, aflame with the fire of my love.”

What is understood by dust except the sinner? Hence that enemy is satisfied by the sinner’s destruction, of whom the prophet says: “Dust shall be the serpent’s bread” (Isaiah 65:25). What is demonstrated by dust except the instability of the wicked? David says of it: “Not so the wicked, not so, but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4).

The Lord therefore warms the eggs abandoned in the dust, because he sets the souls of little ones, deprived of the solicitude of their preachers and placed even in the midst of sinners, aflame with the fire of his love. Hence we see many people living in the midst of the crowds and yet not adopting the life of that sluggish crowd. Hence we see many who do not flee the throngs of the wicked and yet burn with heavenly ardor. Hence we see many, so to speak, warm in the cold.

For why do some, placed amid the torpor of earthly people, burn with desires for heavenly hope? Why are some kindled among cold hearts? It is because almighty God knows how to warm even abandoned eggs in the dust. Having dispelled the insensibility of their former coldness, he brings them to life through the awareness of the living Spirit, so that they do not lie numb in the lowest places; rather, changed into living birds, they lift themselves toward heavenly things by contemplating—that is, by flying. [Col. 0580C–581A]

It must be noted that in these words not only is the perverse conduct of hypocrites condemned, but any pride that may perhaps creep into good teachers is also restrained. For when the Lord says of himself that he warms the abandoned eggs in the dust, he plainly indicates that he works inwardly through the words of the teacher; and without the words of any human being, he warms whom he wishes in the coldness of the dust.

As if he were saying openly to teachers: “So that you may know that I am the one who works through you as you speak, behold, whenever I wish, I speak even to the hearts of human beings without you.”

[Ancient version VIII.] With the teachers’ thoughts thus humbled, the discourse turns to portray the hypocrite, and under the deed of the ostrich it indicates more fully the folly in which he grows numb. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XI [Revised version VII]

**VERSE 15.** — “She forgets that the foot may trample them, or that the beast of the field may crush them.”

16. Wicked teachers are not concerned for their offspring; good teachers are. — What is understood by the foot except the course of action? What is signified by the field except this world? In the Gospel the Lord says: “The field is the world” (Matthew 13:38).

[Note: Vindocinensis, the Norman manuscripts, and most others read “is this world.”]

What is expressed by the beast except the ancient enemy, who lies in wait for the plunder of this world and is daily satisfied with human death? Concerning him the Lord promises through the prophet: “The evil beast shall not pass through it” (Isaiah 35:9).

The ostrich, therefore, abandoning her eggs, forgets that the foot may trample them, because hypocrites abandon those whom they beget as children in their way of life and take no care at all lest, deprived either of the diligence of exhortation or of the protection of discipline, they be perverted by examples of wicked works.

[Note: Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts, Vindocinensis, and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “in conversion,” or “at conversion.”]

If they loved the eggs they had produced, they would surely fear that someone might trample them by displaying perverse actions.

Paul feared this foot for his weak disciples, as for the eggs he had laid, when he said: “Many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ” (Philippians 3:18). Again: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (ibid., 3:2). Again: “We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that they received from us” (2 Thessalonians 3:6).

John feared this foot for Gaius. After Diotrephes had committed many evils, he added: “Beloved, do not imitate evil, but what is good” (3 John 11).

[Note: Two German manuscripts and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “Diotrephes.”]

The leader of the synagogue himself feared this foot for his weak flock when he said: “When you enter the land that the Lord your God will give you, beware that you do not wish to imitate the abominations of those nations” (Deuteronomy 18:9).

She also forgets that the beast of the field may crush them, because if the devil, raging in this world, seizes the children born into a good way of life, the hypocrite is entirely unconcerned.

[Note: Vindocinensis, Ebroicensis, and the Norman manuscripts read “children born in the good part of conduct”; most printed editions read “in good conversion.”]

Paul feared this beast of the field for the eggs he had laid, saying: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the charity that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 11:3).

[Note: Two German manuscripts and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “from chastity.”]

Peter feared this beast of the field for his disciples when he said: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5:8).

True teachers therefore possess, through the virtue of charity, the inward organs of fear on behalf of their disciples. Hypocrites, however, fear those entrusted to them all the less because they do not recognize what they themselves ought to fear. And because they live with hardened hearts, they do not recognize even the children they beget with any affection of due love. Hence, still under the likeness of the ostrich, it is added:

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 16.** — “She is hardened toward her young, as though they were not hers.”

17. The former burn with charity toward their children; the latter do not. — Whoever is not infused with the grace of charity regards even his neighbor—although he himself may have begotten that neighbor for God—as a stranger.

[Note: Valentinus Cluniacensis reads “as an outsider.”]

Such indeed are all hypocrites: while their minds always desire external things, they become inwardly insensible; and in everything they do, while they always seek their own interests, they do not become gentle toward the affection of their neighbor through any compassion of charity.

How tender were Paul’s inward organs when he yearned for his children with such ardor of love, saying: “We live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 3:8).

[Note: The Corbie German manuscript, Vindocinensis, the Norman manuscripts, and most others read “now we live,” as found both in the Greek text and in the Vulgate.]

And: “God is my witness, how I long for you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:8). He also says to the Romans: “God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make remembrance of you always in my prayers, asking whether somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey, by the will of God, to come to you; for I desire to see you” (Romans 1:9–10 and following).

He also says to Timothy: “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve with a pure conscience from my forefathers, because I have an unceasing remembrance of you in my prayers, longing to see you night and day” (2 Timothy 1:3).

[Note: Two German manuscripts and Pratellensis read “which I have without ceasing.”]

Indicating his love to the Thessalonians, he says: “But we, brothers, having been separated from you for a short time, in presence but not in heart, hastened all the more eagerly to see your face with great longing” (1 Thessalonians 2:17).

[Note: Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “for a time, in face and sight.”]

[Note: Laudunensis, the Corbie German manuscript, Pratellensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “we hastened.”]

Pressed by severe persecutions and yet concerned for the salvation of his children, he added: “We sent Timothy our brother and minister of God in the Gospel of Christ, to strengthen you and exhort you concerning your faith, so that no one may be shaken by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this” (1 Thessalonians 3:2–3).

He also says to the Ephesians: “I ask that you not grow weary in my tribulations for you, which are your glory” (Ephesians 3:13). Behold, while placed in tribulation, he exhorts others; and by what he himself endures, he strengthens others. He had not forgotten his children in the manner of the ostrich. Rather, he feared greatly lest his disciples, seeing in their preacher the disgrace of so many persecutions, should despise the faith in him, against which the countless insults of sufferings might prevail.

Therefore he felt less grief in his own torments, but feared more for his children because of the temptation caused by his torments. He regarded the wounds of his body as little, while he feared wounds of the heart in his children. He himself received wounds through suffering, but by consoling his children he healed the wounds of their hearts.

Let us therefore consider what charity it was to fear for others amid his own pains; what charity it was to seek the salvation of his children amid his own losses; and to guard the condition of their minds in their neighbors even through his own humiliation. [Col. 0582C–583B]

1005 [Ancient version IX]. 18. They are driven outward by desire; a mind that is not wholly with itself cannot think of itself. — Hypocrites do not know these inward organs of charity, because the more their mind is loosened outwardly through desire for the world, the more it is hardened inwardly through its lack of affection. It grows cold within through an insensible torpor, because it becomes soft without through a damnable love; and it cannot consider itself because it makes no effort to think of itself.

A mind cannot think of itself when it is not wholly with itself. It does not suffice for it to be wholly with itself, because, through however many desires it is carried away, through that many forms it is dispersed from itself, and, scattered among the lowest things, it lies there—although, if it wished, once gathered together it could rise to the highest.

[Note: The recent Vulgate editions read “through how many desires.” Two German manuscripts, Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts, Laudunensis, Longipontanus, Valentinus Cluniacensis, and others read “through desires,” as is also found in the old Paris and Basel editions, and indeed more correctly. For just as below it says “through so many appearances,” so above one should read “through how many desires.”]

19. The remarkable insight of the righteous who are gathered within themselves. — Hence the mind of the righteous, because it is restrained from the flowing desire for all visible things through vigilant discipline, is gathered within itself and inwardly made whole. It fully perceives what it ought to be toward God and neighbor, because it leaves nothing of itself outside; and the more it is withdrawn and restrained from external things, the more it is inflamed and strengthened inwardly. The more it burns, the more brightly it shines for detecting vices.

[Note: Laudunensis and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “is seen.” Vindocinensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “sees more clearly.”]

For this reason, when holy men gather themselves within themselves, they detect even the hidden sins of others with a marvelous and penetrating acuity. Hence it is well said through the prophet Ezekiel: “The likeness of a hand sent forth took hold of me by a lock of the hair of my head, and the spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me to Jerusalem in the vision of God, beside the inner gate that looked toward the north, where there was set up the idol of jealousy, to provoke jealousy” (Ezekiel 8:3).

For what is the lock of the head except the gathered thoughts of the mind, so that they do not flow away scattered but remain bound together through discipline? A hand is therefore sent down from above, and the prophet is lifted by the lock of his head, because when our mind gathers itself through watchfulness, heavenly power draws us upward from the lowest places.

He rightly says that he was lifted between earth and heaven, because every holy person placed in mortal flesh has not yet fully reached the heights, but nevertheless already abandons the lowest things.

[Note: These same manuscripts, with the Corbie German manuscript and Valentinus Cluniacensis, read “raised up.”]

He is led to Jerusalem in the vision of God, because each person who progresses through the zeal of charity contemplates what the Church ought to be.

It is also rightly added: “Beside the inner gate that looked toward the north,” because holy men, when they look through the entrance of inward contemplation, perceive that more wicked things are done within the Church than righteous ones.

[Note: The edition with two German manuscripts reads: “because he was led beside the inner gate, which looked toward the north.”]

They turn their eyes, as it were, toward the region of the north—that is, toward the left side of the sun—because against the coldness of vices they kindle themselves with the goads of charity.

And it is rightly added there: “For there was set up the idol of jealousy, to provoke jealousy.” When they observe that some within the holy Church, under the mere appearance of faithfulness, commit acts of robbery and vice, what else do they see than an idol in Jerusalem? It is called the idol of jealousy because through it heavenly jealousy is provoked against us, and the more dearly the Redeemer loves us, the more strictly he strikes those who sin.

[Note: Turonensis reads “the Redeemer of the flesh.”]

[Ancient version X.] 20. Hypocrites are sluggish toward heavenly things and ardent toward earthly things. — Hypocrites, therefore, because they do not gather the thoughts of their minds, are not held by the lock of the head. And those who do not know their own faults—how do they detect the faults of those entrusted to them? They are sluggish toward heavenly things, for which they ought to burn, and they burn anxiously for earthly things, toward which they would rightly have been sluggish.

After neglecting the care of their children, you often see them gird themselves for the dangers of immense labor, cross the seas, go to the courts, assault the authorities, break into palaces, take part in quarrels among the bands of peoples, and defend earthly patrimonies with laborious vigilance.

If they are perhaps asked, “Why do you do these things, you who have abandoned the world?” they immediately answer that they fear God, and therefore labor with such zeal to defend their patrimonies. Hence, still concerning the foolish labor of this ostrich, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XIII [Revised version VIII]

**VERSE 16.** — “She labored in vain, compelled by no fear.”

21. Having neglected the protection of her children, she drives away even lighter temporal losses through quarrels. We do not know with what disposition we possess things until they are lost. — “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm 13:5). Behold, the divine voice commands: “If someone takes your tunic and wishes to contend with you in judgment, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:40). And again: “If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6:30).

The apostle Paul, desiring his disciples to despise external things so that they might be able to preserve inward things, admonishes them, saying: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?” (1 Corinthians 6:7).

Yet the hypocrite, having assumed the habit of holy conduct, abandons the protection of his children and seeks to defend every temporal possession, even through quarrels. He does not fear losing their hearts by his example, as though through negligence, but fears losing his earthly patrimonies. A disciple falls into error, yet the hypocrite’s heart is wounded by no grief. He sees those entrusted to him going into the abyss of wickedness, and passes over it as though it were unheard of; but if he senses that some slight temporal loss has been inflicted upon him, he suddenly burns inwardly with anger for vengeance.

At once patience is broken; at once the pain of the heart runs uncontrolled through his words. By tolerating the loss of souls with equanimity, but hastening to repel the loss of temporal goods even with agitation of spirit, he reveals to all, through the disturbance of his mind, what he truly loves. There is great diligence in defense wherever the force of love is greater. The more he loves earthly things, the more vehemently he fears being deprived of them.

We are not taught with what disposition we possess something in this world except when we lose it. Whatever is possessed without love is lost without pain. But whatever we love ardently when we possess it, we deeply lament when it is taken away.

Who does not know that the Lord created earthly things for our use, but created human souls for himself? The one who neglects what belongs to God and protects what belongs to himself is therefore shown to love himself more than God.

Hypocrites do not fear losing what belongs to God—that is, human souls—but they fear losing what belongs to themselves, namely, things that pass away with the world, as though they were going to render an account of them before the strict Judge. They preserve insensible things that they have not sought, as though they might find him favorable after losing what they ought to have desired—that is, rational beings.

[Note: The conjunction “and” is absent in Laudunensis and some others.]

We want to possess something in this world, and behold, the Truth cries out: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

22. With what disposition one should litigate when necessity and charity compel it. — How, then, should the perfect Christian defend earthly possessions through quarrels, when he is not commanded to possess them?

[Note: The German manuscripts and the editions of Gilot, Vaticanus, and Gussanville read “which he is now commanded not to possess,” contrary in sense to, and at odds with, the other manuscripts and older editions.]

Therefore, when we lose our own possessions, if we follow God perfectly, we have been relieved of a great burden on the journey of this life.

[Note: Laudunensis and Valentinus Cluniacensis read “set free.”]

But when the necessity of that same journey imposes care for possessions upon us, some who seize them must simply be tolerated; others must be restrained while charity is preserved—not merely so that they do not take away what is ours, but so that, by taking what is not theirs, they do not destroy themselves.

We ought to fear for the robbers themselves more than we ought to cling eagerly to the defense of irrational things. For even if these things are not stolen, we lose them when we die; but with those robbers we are one both now according to the order of our condition and, if they strive to be corrected, after receiving the gift of grace.

Who does not know that we ought to love less the things we use and more what we are? If, then, we speak to robbers for their own benefit, we are no longer claiming only temporal things for ourselves, but also eternal things for them.

23. With what moderation one should litigate. — In this matter one must carefully observe that, through fear of necessity, desire for possessions does not creep in, and that a prohibition kindled by zeal does not, stretched out through an immoderate impulse, burst forth into the hateful disgrace of contention.

[Note: The German manuscripts, Turonensis, and most Norman manuscripts read “through a more immoderate impulse”; this is also the reading of the old edition. Gilot, Vaticanus, and Gussanville, following a German manuscript, read “as far as hateful words and disgrace.” The present reading is attested by Turonensis, the Corbie German manuscript, the Norman manuscripts, Laudunensis, Valentinus Cluniacensis, and the old edition.]

When peace with one’s neighbor is torn from the heart on account of an earthly possession, it plainly appears that the possession is loved more than the neighbor.

For if we do not possess the inward organs of charity even toward the neighbor who is a robber, we persecute ourselves worse than the robber himself and devastate ourselves more grievously than the other could. By voluntarily abandoning the good of love, we lose inwardly what we lose from ourselves, whereas he was taking away from us only external things.

But the hypocrite does not know this form of charity. Because he loves earthly things more than heavenly ones, he inflames himself inwardly with savage hatred against the one who takes away temporal goods.

[Col. 0586C] [Old XI.]

### 24. How certain people differ from hypocrites while defending temporal goods more aggressively; with what caution they are to be reproved

It must be understood that there are some whom Mother Church, nourishing them in the embrace of charity, tolerates until she brings them to the growth of spiritual maturity. They sometimes maintain the appearance of holiness but are unable to carry out the merit of perfection. They do not rise at all to spiritual gifts and therefore serve those who are attached to them in protecting earthly possessions; sometimes, in defending those possessions, they go too far in anger.

We must not believe that such people fall into the number of hypocrites, because it is one thing to sin through weakness and another to sin through malice. The difference between these people and hypocrites is this: the former, conscious of their weakness, prefer to be reproved by everyone for their fault rather than praised for feigned holiness; the latter are certain that they are doing evil, yet still swell with pride before human judgments because of the reputation of holiness.

The former do not fear displeasing wicked people even through a good action, provided that they please only the heavenly judgments; the latter never consider what they are doing, but only how they may please people by any action. The former, according to the measure of their understanding, even in worldly affairs labor for the causes of God; the latter, through the causes of God, serve the purpose of the world.

[Note: Two German manuscripts and recent editions wrongly read *illi vero* (“but the latter”) in place of *causis Dei* (“for God’s causes”). The text has been emended from the Norman, Vendôme, Laon, and other manuscripts, as well as from the old edition. The Vendôme, Laon, and Val-Clair manuscripts read *quia in ipsis quoque* (“because even in those things”); two German manuscripts read *in ipsa* (“in that very thing”).] For even in the very things by which they display themselves as performing holy works, they seek not the conversion of people but the breezes of applause.

### 25. How those who defend earthly things excessively are to be reproved without being despised

Therefore, when we see men of respectable conduct defending earthly things angrily or excessively, we ought to reprove this in them out of charity, yet we must not despise them when reproving them.

[Note: The Vendôme, Pratel, and most Norman manuscripts read *despicere* (“despise”).] For in one and the same person there are often certain visible faults deserving judgment and great qualities that remain hidden. In us, on the other hand, great qualities often appear openly, while things deserving reproach are sometimes concealed.

Our mind’s pride must therefore be humbled by this consideration:

[Note: The Vendôme and Norman manuscripts read *reprehendenda est* (“is to be reproved”) in place of *humilianda est* (“is to be humbled”).] their weaknesses are public, while ours are secret; and again, their strengths are hidden, while ours are proclaimed in public. When we reprove them for manifest weakness, we should consequently honor them in the estimation of their hidden strength; and if our mind rises because of our own manifest weakness, it should press itself down in humility by considering its hidden faults.

Often some people obey many commandments but neglect a few, while we neglect many and keep only a few. Thus it commonly happens that, because we see others neglecting what we know ourselves to keep, our mind immediately rises in pride, forgetting how much it neglects while keeping very little.

Therefore, in those matters for which we reprove others, we must bend the pride of our vigilant thought. For if our mind sees itself as higher than the rest, it is led, as though toward the precipice of isolation, and falls all the more disastrously. But why does the hypocrite, abandoning heavenly gains, labor for earthly ones? He adds this under the name of the ostrich, saying:

## CHAPTER XIV [Rec. IX]

### Verse 17. “God deprived her of wisdom, nor gave her understanding.”

#### 26. God hardens the heart, not by imparting hardness, but by failing to soften it when sins demand this

Although “to deprive” is one thing and “not to give” another, he repeats the same point by adding “nor gave,” after saying “deprived.” It is as though he were saying:

[Note: The reading in the Corbie German manuscript and in nearly all editions, “what he said,” is corrupt. I find this error in the Basel edition of 1514 and subsequently retained in the others. The Paris edition of 1495, together with the manuscripts, correctly has “what I said.” The remainder, which is obscure, should be understood as follows: “What I said—‘he deprived’—is not to be understood in the sense that God took wisdom away, for that would not be just, but in the sense that he did not give wisdom.” In the Pratel, Utica, Corbie German, and Vendôme manuscripts it reads: “he did not justly take wisdom away.” This too can be understood very well as: “I do not say that God justly took wisdom away, but that he justly withheld it.”]

“What I said—‘he deprived’—does not mean that he unjustly took wisdom away, but that he justly did not give it.”

Thus the Lord is also described as having hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not because he imparted hardness to it, but because, in accordance with Pharaoh’s deserts, he did not soften it with any perceptible infusion of fear from above.

[Note: The Norman and Vendôme manuscripts read “gift.”]

But now the hypocrite—who pretends to be holy and hides himself beneath the appearance of a good work—is oppressed by the peace of Holy Church and therefore, before our eyes, clothes himself in the appearance of religion. If any temptation to the faith breaks out, the rabid mind of the wolf immediately strips off the garment of sheep’s wool; and by persecuting, it demonstrates how savagely it rages against the good. Thus it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XV

### Verse 18. “When the time comes, she raises her wings on high; she derides the horseman and his rider.”

#### 27. The hypocrite derides not only the saints but God himself

For what are we to understand by the wings of this ostrich except the hypocrite’s thoughts, pressed down and, as it were, folded together for the present? When the time comes, she lifts them on high, because, once an opportunity has been found, she reveals them through pride. To raise wings on high is to disclose one’s thoughts through unrestrained pride.

But now, because she pretends to be holy and restrains within herself what she thinks, she folds her wings within her body through humility.
