[Col. 0588B] [Old XII.] It should be noted that he does not say, “She derides the horse and its rider,” but “the horseman and his rider.” The horse is the body of each holy soul, which knows both how to restrain itself from unlawful things by the bridle of continence and, again, how to release itself for the practice of good works under the impulse of charity.

By “horseman,” therefore, the soul of a holy man is expressed: it governs the body, its beast of burden, when that body has been well subjected. Hence the apostle John, contemplating the Lord in the Apocalypse, says: “And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses” (Rev. 19:14). He rightly calls the multitude of saints who had toiled in this battle of martyrdom an army.

[Note: The Longipontine manuscript reads: “who [were] in this world, in the battle of martyrdom.”] They are said to sit on white horses because their bodies shone both with the light of righteousness and with the whiteness of chastity.

The hypocrite therefore derides the horseman because, when he himself has broken out openly into iniquity, he despises the holiness of the elect and, raised up in pride, calls foolish those whom, while constrained by the peace of faith, he had pretended to be through crafty art.

But who else is the rider of this horseman except Almighty God, who, foreseeing what did not yet exist, created it, and, possessing what exists, governs it? He rides the horseman because he possesses the mind of each righteous man, who possesses his members well.

For this hypocrite to deride the horseman is to despise the saints; to deride the rider of the horseman is to leap forward even to an insult against the Creator.

### 28. In falls one begins with the smallest things and reaches the more serious; the Church tolerates many hidden wicked people; why the wicked are mixed with the good in the Church; the rhinoceros or unicorn signifies the Jewish people; by what art the rhinoceros is tamed

Since every fall always begins with the smallest things and, as failures increase, reaches more serious ones, the iniquity of this hypocrite is rightly distinguished by the successive stages of his deterioration:

[Note: The Laon manuscript reads *distringitur* (“is strictly examined/distinguished”).]

first, he displays himself as good when he is not; afterward, he openly despises the good; and finally he leaps even to an insult against the Creator.

No soul lies forever where it has fallen, because, once it has voluntarily fallen, it is driven by the weight of its iniquity toward worse things,

[Note: The German, Laon, and Val-Clair manuscripts read *ad pejora pondera* (“toward worse weights/burdens”); the Corbie German manuscript admits both readings.] so that, falling into the depths, it is always buried still more deeply.

Let the hypocrite therefore go on seeking his own praises now, afterward oppressing the lives of his neighbors, and at last exercising himself in derision of his Creator,

[Note: Val-Clair reads *se in irritationem* (“himself into provocation”); the German manuscript reads *se in irrisionem* (“himself into derision”).] so that the loftier the things he continually devises, the more severely he plunges himself into punishments.

Oh, how many such people Holy Church now tolerates! When the time of trial breaks out, open temptation reveals them. Because they do not presently exercise their desires against the Church, they press down, as it were, the folded wings of their thoughts.

Since this life is lived jointly by the good and the wicked, the Church is now visibly gathered from both groups, but is invisibly distinguished by God’s judgment and, at its departure, separated from the society of the reprobate. At present neither the good can exist in it without the wicked nor the wicked without the good. The two parts are necessarily joined together for this purpose: that the wicked may be changed through the examples of the good, and the good purified through the trials of the wicked.

Therefore, after the Lord had spoken at length under the figure of the ostrich about the condemnation of hypocrites, he immediately turned his words to the portion of the elect, so that those who had heard in the former what they must endure while fleeing might hear in the latter what they should love by imitating it.

It follows [Rec. X]:

“Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with neighing?”

### 29. The rhinoceros and the ostrich considered in another moral interpretation

But perhaps, before we discuss the strength and neighing of this horse, some may ask that, setting aside the moral interpretation, the strength of the rhinoceros and the foolishness of this ostrich also be explained in another way.

The word of God is manna, and whatever the will of the one who receives it desires, that is what it tastes like in the mouth of the eater (Exod. 16). The word of God is earth: the more labor it demands from the one who seeks it, the more abundantly it yields fruit. The meaning of sacred speech must therefore be sifted through repeated inquiry, because earth that is turned more often by plowing is made more suitable for a rich harvest.

What, then, we understand in another way about the rhinoceros and the ostrich, we briefly touch upon, because we are hastening to unravel matters that are more tightly bound and entangled.

[Note: The editions read “obligatory,” incorrectly; here “obligatory” should be understood as “more tightly bound and entangled.”]

This rhinoceros, which is also called a monoceros in Greek copies, is said to possess such strength that it cannot be captured by any power of hunters. But, according to those who have labored through painstaking investigation to describe the natures of animals, a virgin girl is placed before it. When it approaches her, she opens her bosom, into which the animal lays its head, abandoning all its fierceness; thus it is suddenly found by those seeking to capture it to be, as it were, unarmed.

It is also described as the color of boxwood. When it engages elephants in combat, it is said to strike the bellies of its opponents with the horn that it bears uniquely on its nose; by wounding the softer parts, it easily fells those attacking it.

Therefore, by this rhinoceros—or rather monoceros, that is, unicorn—the people may be understood who, having taken from the Law not works but only pride among all human beings, bore a solitary horn, as it were, among the other beasts.

Thus, announcing his Passion in the words of the Prophet, the Lord says: “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion, and my humility from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps. 21:22).

There were as many unicorns, or rather rhinoceroses, in that people as there were those who, relying on a singular and foolish pride, trusted in the works of the Law against the proclamations of the truth.

To blessed Job, therefore, who represents the type of Holy Church, it is said:

## CHAPTER XVI

### Chapter 39, verse 9. “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?”

#### 30. From the Jews came the fierce Saul, subdued by Christ

It is as though it were said more plainly: “Will you bend beneath the authority of your preaching that people whom you see growing proud in their foolish arrogance at the killing of the faithful?”—that is, “as I do, who see him raised up against me with his solitary horn and yet immediately subject him to myself whenever I wish.”

We demonstrate this more clearly, however, if we pass from the general to the particular. Let Paul be brought forward from this people: first outstanding in pride, and afterward an eminent witness in humility. When, in his ignorance, he exalted himself against God as though in defense of the Law, he bore a horn on his nose.

Later, inclining this very horn of the nose through humility, he says: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly” (1 Tim. 1:13).

He bore a horn on his nose because he trusted that he would please God through cruelty, as he later rebukes himself, saying: “I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Gal. 1:14).

Every hunter feared the strength of this rhinoceros because every preacher was afraid of Saul’s savagery. For it is written: “Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, approached the high priest

[Note: The Pratel and Utica manuscripts read *spirans minas et caedes* (“breathing threats and slaughters”).] and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women belonging to this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:1).

When breath is drawn in order to be expelled through the nostrils, it is called respiration; and we often detect through the sense of smell what we do not see with our eyes. This rhinoceros therefore bore a horn on its nose with which to strike, because, breathing threats and slaughter against the Lord’s disciples, after killing those present, he sought those who were absent.

But behold, every hunter hides before him—that is, every rational human being is driven away by fear of him.

To capture this rhinoceros, let the virgin—that is, Wisdom of God, herself inviolate in the flesh—open her bosom.

[Note: The Longipontine manuscript reads *involuta in carne* (“wrapped in flesh”). This reading would readily be accepted if all the consulted manuscripts and editions did not oppose it; the text here calls God’s Wisdom inviolate, and below incorrupt.]

For it is written that, as he was traveling toward Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven shone around him at midday, and a voice was made, saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” He, falling to the ground, replied: “Who are you, Lord?” Immediately he was told: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:4–5 and following).

The virgin opened her bosom to the rhinoceros when incorrupt Wisdom of God, speaking from heaven to Saul, disclosed the mystery of her incarnation. The rhinoceros lost its strength because, prostrate on the ground, it lost everything that had been swollen with pride.

When, after the light of his eyes had been removed, he was led by the hand to Ananias, it became clear by what reins of God this rhinoceros was restrained: at one and the same time he was bound by blindness, preaching, and baptism.

He also remained at God’s manger, because he did not disdain to chew the cud of the words of the Gospel. For he says: “I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me. I went up according to a revelation and conferred the Gospel with them” (Gal. 2:1–2).

And he who, while still fasting, had heard, “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5), afterward, pressed down by the wondrous power of the one who ruled him, obtained strength from the nourishment of the word and lost the heel of pride.

### 31. This rhinoceros was bound to plow the Lord’s field

The reins of God not only restrain him from fierceness; more wonderfully, they bind him to plowing, so that he not only does not attack human beings with the horn of cruelty but, serving their nourishment, also draws the plow of preaching.

He himself speaks of evangelists as plowers: “The one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of sharing in the harvest” (1 Cor. 9:10).

He who formerly inflicted torments on the faithful and afterward gladly bore scourges for the faith; who, even through written letters, preached humbly and contemptibly what he had once attacked with terror—

[Note: The Pratel and most Norman manuscripts read “more humbly and contemptibly.”]he certainly sweats well, bound beneath the plow, for the harvest, having previously lived in the field, wickedly free from fear.

Of him it is rightly said:

## CHAPTER XVII [Old XIV]

### Verse 10. “Or will he break the clods of the valleys behind you?”

[Col. 0591D]

#### 32. He broke the clods—that is, the hardness of minds

The Lord had already entered the minds of certain people who truly believed him to be the Redeemer of the human race. Yet because they did not withdraw at all from their former observance and guarded the hard commandments of the letter, the outstanding preacher said to them: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2).

When he therefore crushed, by reproving it, the hardness of the Law in the humble minds of the faithful, what else did he do than break the clods in the valley behind the Lord? This was so that the seeds, which the furrow cut by the plow of faith would receive in the heart, might not be crushed and perish under the guardianship of the letter.

Of him it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Verse 11. “Will you trust in his great strength, and leave your labors to him?”

#### 33. In what way God placed his trust in his strength

God placed his trust in the strength of this rhinoceros because, the more cruelly he endured that man’s infliction of harsh things upon himself, the more firmly he foresaw him enduring adversities on his behalf.

He also left to him the labors that he himself had endured in the flesh, because he drew him, once converted, even to imitate his own Passion. Hence it is said through this same rhinoceros: “I make up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24).

Of him it is further said:

## CHAPTER XIX

### Verse 12. “Will you believe him that he will return seed to you and gather your threshing floor?”

#### 34. He first winnowed God’s threshing floor and afterward gathered it

Let us consider who Saul was when, from his very youth, he was the assistant of those who stoned others; when he devastated other places of the Church and, having received letters, sought others to devastate; when no death of the faithful was sufficient for him, but, after some had been extinguished, he continually thirsted for the destruction of others (Acts 7).

We shall certainly recognize that at that time none of the faithful would have believed that God would bend the force of such arrogance beneath the yoke of his fear. Hence Ananias, after hearing from the Lord that he had been converted, was afraid of him and said: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem” (Acts 9:13).

Yet suddenly changed, he became a preacher from an enemy and proclaimed the name of his Redeemer throughout all the regions of the world. He endured punishments for the truth and rejoiced to suffer what he had inflicted. He called some by kindness and recalled others to the faith by terrors. To some he promised the kingdom of the heavenly homeland; to others he threatened the fire of Gehenna. He corrected some by authority, led others to the way of righteousness through humility, and in every direction bowed himself to the hand of his ruler. He gathered God’s threshing floor with as much skill as he had previously winnowed it through arrogance.

[Old XV]

### 35. Paul chastised his body through abstinence and strikes those devoted to their bellies

Nor is it inconsistent with Paul that the rhinoceros is said to be the color of boxwood and to strike the bellies of elephants with its horn. Because he was accustomed to living under the rigor of the Law, the discipline of each virtue had taken deeper root in him than in others.

[Note: The Corbie German and Tours manuscripts read: “It enclosed him more strictly than the others.”]

For what is expressed by the color of boxwood except the pallor of abstinence? He testifies that he clung firmly to this, saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Cor. 9:27).

Endowed with instruction in the divine Law, when he rebuked the gluttony of others, he struck the elephants in the belly with his horn. He had struck elephants in the belly when he said: “Many walk, of whom I often told you and now tell you even weeping, enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3:18–19).

And again: “Such people do not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly” (Rom. 16:18).

Thus this rhinoceros no longer strikes human beings with its horn but beasts, when Paul, through the strength of his teaching, attacks not the humble, who are not to be destroyed, but the proud worshipers of their bellies and kills them.

What we have learned to be written about Paul, we should consequently believe to have been accomplished in others as well. For many were converted from the arrogance of that people to the grace of humility. When the Lord subdued their savagery beneath the yoke of inspired fear, he clearly subjected to himself the strength of the rhinoceros.

But since we have heard what the wondrous power of God did among the elect, let us now hear what his wondrous patience endured among those whom he rejects:

[Note: “What [God did] among the elect” appears preferable, since it answers the other member, “among those whom he rejects.” Pratel and Utica have this reading, though the other witnesses do not. The holy Fathers were not always afforded the opportunity to write what was better and more elegant.]

## CHAPTER XX

### Verse 13. “The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron and the hawk.”

#### 36. The synagogue resembles an ostrich: it has wings but creeps upon the ground

What is signified by the name “ostrich” except the synagogue? It had the wings of the Law, but, creeping in its heart among lowly things, it never lifted itself from the earth.

What else are expressed by the heron and the hawk except the ancient fathers, who were able, by understanding, to see what they could perceive and, by living accordingly, to fly toward it?

The ostrich’s wing is therefore like the wings of the heron and the hawk, because the voice of the synagogue retained the teaching of the ancients in its speech but did not know it in its life.

Hence the Truth warns the people of that same synagogue concerning the Pharisees and scribes, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:2–3).

We could say much about the life of the heron, but because only its wing is recalled here, we are forbidden to speak about its life.

## CHAPTER XXI [Old XVI]

### Verse 14. “When she leaves her eggs on the earth, will you perhaps warm them in the dust?”

[Note: Some Norman and German manuscripts read “which abandons”; the Corbie German manuscript reads “who.”]

#### 37. She abandoned the apostles whom she had begotten; afterward the grace of Christ gave them life

In an egg, one thing is what is seen and another what is hoped for; and hope cannot be seen, as Paul attests when he says: “For who hopes for what he sees?” (Rom. 8:24).

What, then, are signified by the ostrich’s eggs except the apostles born from the flesh of the synagogue? By presenting themselves as despised and humble in the world, they teach people to hope for glory in heaven.

[Note: The Vendôme, Pratel, and other manuscripts read *sperari* (“to be hoped for”).]

Cast down and regarded by the proud as almost worthless, they lay on the earth like eggs; but inside them lay what would enable them to live, and, raised on the wings of hope, to fly toward heavenly things.

The ostrich leaves her eggs on the earth because the synagogue, refusing to listen to the apostles whom it had begotten in the flesh, abandoned them to the calling of the Gentiles.

But the Lord’s wondrous power warms these same eggs in the dust, because he raised living offspring of the apostles within that Gentile people once regarded as cast off. Those whom the synagogue had despised as senseless and lifeless now fly alive among the nations through the teaching of their doctrine and are honored.

The ostrich leaves her eggs in the dust because she does not lift from earthly desires any of those whom the synagogue has begotten through preaching. When the ancient enemy finds these desires conceived in the heart, he carries even occupied minds into crimes. Hence it is added:

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0594B]

### Verse 15. “She forgets that the foot may crush them and that the beast of the field may trample them.”

#### 38. When human hearts think about and desire earthly things, they lay themselves down to be trampled by the devil

The foot treads on the eggs and the beast of the field tramples them when they are abandoned on the earth. For human hearts, when they continually desire to think about earthly things and to do what is below, lay themselves down to be crushed by the beast of the field—that is, by the devil—so that, after being cast down for a long time in lowly thought, they may eventually be shattered by the perpetration of even greater crimes.

The synagogue therefore neglected to lift the eggs it had begotten from the earth through good living. But Almighty God found many of its children dead and cold in earthly desires, and nevertheless gave them life through the warmth of his love.

Yet the life that the synagogue did not give its children it afterward begrudged, when it attempted, through persecution, to extinguish those whom it did not remember having nurtured into good works.

Hence it is appropriately added concerning this ostrich:

### Verse 16. “She is hardened toward her young, as though they were not hers.”

#### 39. The synagogue’s cruelty toward its children

She despises them as though they were not hers when she discovers them living otherwise than she herself taught.

[Note: The same witnesses and two German manuscripts read *respicit* (“regards”) in place of *despicit* (“despises”).] As her savagery hardens, she inflicts terrors, exercises herself in their torments, and, inflamed by the fires of envy, labors to destroy those whom she did not labor to enable to live.

When she persecutes the members of the Lord, she imagines that by this she is pleasing the Lord.

[Note: The old edition, following the Corbie German, Laon, Clermont, and Tours manuscripts, reads “to appease the Lord through this.” We follow the German, Norman, and recent editions, whose reading better agrees here with the words “she supposes that she is rendering service to God.”]

Hence the Truth says to these same eggs of the ostrich: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2).

Because, when the synagogue is driven by cruelty to persecute, it supposes that it is acting under the impulse of divine fear, it is rightly added:

### The same passage: “She labored in vain, compelled by no fear.”

#### 40. In her rage she believes that she is offering service to God

In the labor of persecution, it was not fear but cruelty that compelled her to rage. But because vices are often dyed with the color of virtues and are therefore all the more wicked because they are scarcely recognized as vices, the synagogue became harsher in persecution insofar as it considered itself more religious through the deaths of the faithful.

For this reason it could not discern at all what it was doing: it had closed the light of understanding against itself through the obstruction of pride. Hence it is rightly added:

### Verse 17. “God deprived her of wisdom, nor gave her understanding.”

#### 41. Through pride she lost the light of understanding

The examination of hidden retribution is exact. Because she knowingly lost humility, she also unknowingly lost the understanding of truth.

The wounds that she inflicted on the faithful at the Redeemer’s coming are much smaller than those by which she still seeks to strike Holy Church through the coming of Antichrist. She is preparing herself for that time, so that she may crush the life of the faithful with accumulated strength. Hence it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Old XVII]

### Verse 18. “When the time comes, she raises her wings on high; she derides the horseman and his rider.”

#### 42. The synagogue first secretly, afterward openly, rises against God

The ostrich raises her wings on high when the synagogue no longer contradicts her Creator by fearing him, as before, but now openly resists him.

Passing into the members of the devil and believing the man of lies to be God, she is lifted up against the faithful all the more arrogantly insofar as she also boasts that she herself is the body of God.

Because she despises not only the Lord’s humanity but also his divinity, she derides not only the horseman but also the rider of the horseman.

With the unity of the person preserved, this can be understood as follows: the Word of God rides the horseman when he created animated flesh for himself within the Virgin’s womb. He rides the horseman when, by creating it, he subjected the human soul, ruling its own flesh, to divine worship.

The divinity assumed flesh through the mediation of the soul, and through this held the entire horseman together, because in himself he joined not only the one who was ruled but also the one who ruled.

Judea, therefore, captured by the snare of deception through the advent of the proud Antichrist, despises the fact that our Redeemer was humble among human beings and derides the horseman. But because it contradicts his divinity in all things, it likewise derides the rider.

Our Redeemer is one and the same, both the horseman and the rider of the horseman. When he came into the world, he produced strong preachers against the world; and when, at the end of the world, he endures the deception of Antichrist, he supplies strength to those who fight on his behalf.

Thus, when the ancient enemy is released into that freedom of his which will soon be ended, our faithful receive greater strength insofar as they fight against an adversary who has been released.

Therefore, when the ostrich is described as raising her wings and deriding the rider and the horseman, the memory of strong preachers is immediately brought forward, and it is said:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Old XVIII]

[Col. 0596A]

### Verse 19. “Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with neighing?”

#### 43. In sacred Scripture the horse signifies many things: the slippery life of the wicked; temporal dignity; the present age, whose extremity is pressed by the serpent Antichrist; preparation of right intention; and holy preachers

In sacred Scripture, the name “horse” sometimes expresses the slippery life of the wicked, sometimes temporal dignity, sometimes this present age itself, sometimes preparation of right intention, and sometimes a holy preacher.

The name “horse” signifies the slippery life of the wicked, as it is written: “Do not become like the horse and the mule” (Ps. 32:9). And as another prophet says: “They were lovers of horses and became stallions; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5:8).

The name “horse” signifies temporal dignity, as Solomon attests when he says: “I saw servants on horses, and princes walking like servants upon the earth” (Eccl. 10:7).

Everyone who sins is a servant of sin, and servants are on horses when sinners are exalted by the dignities of the present life. Princes walk like servants when many people filled with the dignity of virtues are raised by no honor, but here are pressed down by the greatest adversity as though they were unworthy.

Again it is said: “Those who mounted horses slumbered” (Ps. 76:7); that is, those who trusted in the honor of the present life closed the eyes of their minds in death to the light of truth.

The present age itself is designated by the name “horse,” as Jacob says: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. 49:17). We can show more clearly what the horse signifies in this passage if we explain somewhat more carefully the matters surrounding it.

Some maintain that the Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because in this passage Dan is both called a serpent and said to bite. Hence, not without reason, when the Israelite people were receiving territories in the division of the camps, Dan was the first to encamp toward the north (Num. 2:25): thereby signifying the one who had said in his heart, “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13). Of him the prophet also says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. 8:16).

He is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent. For κέρατα in Greek means “horns” in Latin, and this serpent is said to be horned. The coming of the Antichrist is therefore fittingly signified by him, because against the life of the faithful he is armed with the bite of poisonous preaching and also with the horns of power. Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus Dan becomes a serpent on the road, because in the breadth of the present life he urges those to walk whom he flatters as though sparing them; but he bites on the road because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom.

He becomes a horned serpent on the path because those whom he finds faithful, constraining themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he attacks not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also crushes with the terror of power, and [Col. 0597A] after the benefits of feigned sweetness exercises the horns of his power in the anguish of persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] The printed edition reads “in the languor of persecution.” We have preferred our manuscripts—Ebroic., other Norman manuscripts, two German manuscripts, Vindoc., Val. Cl., and others. Properly, when the Antichrist rages, persecution will not languish but rather burn fiercely.]

In this passage the horse signifies the world, which, through its pride, foams along in the course of passing time. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the world’s final extremities, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves. To bite the horse’s hooves is to touch the ends of the age by striking them.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] The English and Norman manuscripts read “to constrain by striking.” “To touch” seems better; it is also found in all printed editions, including the oldest.]

“So that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. 49:17). The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted by the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, and not on his face, as Saul is remembered to have fallen (Acts 9:4). To fall on one’s face is, in this life, for each person to recognize his own sins and mourn them in repentance. To fall backward, where one cannot see, is to depart suddenly from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led.

And because Judaea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits the Antichrist in place of Christ, Jacob is rightly turned in the same passage into the voice of the elect and says: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18)—that is, not, like unbelievers, the Antichrist, but Christ, whom I faithfully believe to be the true one who will come for our redemption.

The name “horse” signifies the preparation of a right intention, as it is written: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord grants salvation” (Prov. 21:31), because the mind indeed prepares itself against temptation, but unless it is aided, it does not fight successfully.

The name “horse” signifies every holy preacher, as the prophet testifies, saying: “You sent your horses into the sea, disturbing many waters” (Hab. 3:15). The waters had lain quiet, because human minds had long been sunk in the torpor of their vices. But the sea was disturbed by God’s horses, because, when holy preachers were sent, every heart that had grown numb through poisonous security was shaken by the impulse of salutary fear.

Thus in this passage “horse” signifies a holy preacher, when blessed Job is told:

[Ancient edition XIX; recension XI.]

“Will you give strength to the horse, or surround his neck with neighing?”

## 44. The preacher, like a horse, receives strength from God in order to act rightly, and neighing in order to teach excellently.

But what does it mean that the Lord asserts that he first gives this horse strength and afterward clothes its neck with neighing? Neighing expresses the voice of preaching. Every true preacher receives strength first and neighing afterward, because, after he has first extinguished vices within himself, he comes to the voice of preaching in order to instruct others.

[Note: [Col. 0598D] Turon. reads “for bringing out.”]

This horse has strength because it endures adversity steadfastly. It has neighing because it calls enticingly toward higher things. The Lord testifies that he gives this horse both strength and neighing, because in his preacher the power of perfection will never appear unless both life and speech agree. For it is of little benefit if someone is supported by the conduct of an exalted life, yet cannot, by speaking, rouse others to what he himself feels. Or what benefit is there in kindling others by speaking well if, by living badly, he shows himself to have grown sluggish?

Since both are necessary for perfection in the preacher, the Lord supplies his horse, together with the strength of action, with the neighing of speech, and together with the neighing of speech, with the strength of action. It should be noted why the neighing—which is drawn inward through the throat—is said to be clothed around the horse’s neck, that is, drawn outward as if in a circle. The voice of preaching flows from within, but encircles what is outside. For insofar as it arouses others to live well, it also binds the preacher’s works to right action, so that his conduct does not depart from his speech and his life does not contradict his voice.

The neighing is therefore drawn around the horse’s neck, because, lest it proceed to perverse works, the preacher’s life is also enclosed by his own words. This is why a torque is given as a reward to those fighting valiantly: since they bear the signs of virtue, they may always exercise greater virtues and fear incurring the charge of weakness, while in themselves they already possess the reward of the strength they display.

[Note: [Col. 0598D] The German, Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts read “which they may display.” The same reading is found in Corb. Germ. before it was corrected and written as “they display.”]

Hence Solomon rightly says to every hearer in praise of wisdom: “You will receive a crown of graces on your head, and a golden torque around your neck” (Prov. 1:9). It continues:

# CHAPTER XXV

[Recension XII]

## Verse 20

“Will you raise him up like locusts?”

## 45. What is to be understood by locusts: the Jewish people. They made certain leaps and immediately fell to the ground.

The name “locusts” sometimes signifies the Jewish people, sometimes the converted Gentiles, sometimes the tongue of flatterers, and sometimes, by comparison, the Lord’s resurrection or the life of preachers.

That locusts signify the Jewish people is indicated by the life of John, of whom it is written: “He ate locusts and wild honey” (Matt. 3:4). John proclaims by the kind of food he eats the one whom he declares with prophetic authority. In himself he represented the Lord, whose way he preceded. For when the Lord came for our redemption, he ate wild honey because he took up the sweetness of the unfruitful Gentiles.

But because he converted a portion of the Jewish people in his own body, he took locusts as food. The locusts signify those who make sudden leaps but immediately fall to the ground. They made leaps when they promised that they would fulfill the Lord’s commandments; but they quickly fell to the ground when, through evil works, they denied having heard them.

Let us observe in them something like a leap of locusts: “All the words that the Lord has spoken we shall do and obey” (Exod. 24:3). But let us see how quickly they fall to the ground: “Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this vast wilderness! Would that we perished, and that the Lord had not brought us into this land!” (Num. 14:3). They were therefore locusts, because their voice made a leap, while their conduct made a fall.

[Ancient edition XX.]

## 46. The Gentiles signified by locusts, and the tongues of flatterers, which destroy the fruit of good works.

The Gentiles are also designated by the name “locusts,” as Solomon testifies when he says: “The almond tree will blossom, the locust will be fattened, and the caper will be scattered” (Eccl. 12:5).

[Note: [Col. 0599D] Pratel and others read “and the caper will be scattered.”]

The almond tree displays its blossom before all other trees. And what is signified by the blossom of the almond tree if not the beginnings of the holy Church? In her preachers she opened the first blossoms of virtue and, for the production of the fruits of good works, preceded the saints who would come, like succeeding groves.

In her the locust was soon fattened, because the dry barrenness of the Gentiles was infused with the richness of heavenly grace. The caper is scattered because, when the called Gentiles attained the grace of faith, Judaea, remaining in its barrenness, lost the order of right living.

Again Solomon says: “The locust has no king, yet it advances in ordered bands” (Prov. 30:27), because the Gentiles, once abandoned, had long been strangers to divine rule; nevertheless, afterward ordered for battle against hostile spirits, they advanced to the warfare of faith.

## 47. The tongue of a flatterer is expressed by the term “locust.”

This is attested by the plague of locusts sent from heaven upon Egypt. These plagues were once inflicted bodily because of the Egyptians’ deserving, but they spiritually signified the evils that strike perverse minds every day.

For it is written: “The burning wind lifted up the locusts, which came up over the whole land of Egypt and covered the entire face of the earth, devastating everything. Thus all the grass of the land was devoured, and whatever fruit there was on the trees” (Exod. 10:13–14).

Egypt was afflicted by these plagues so that, shaken by an outward blow and suffering, it might weigh what losses of devastation it was inwardly enduring through its negligence. Thus, while it saw the smallest and most cherished things perishing outside, it might feel more grievously, through their image, what it had suffered within.

What do the locusts signify, then—creatures that harm human crops more than all other small animals—if not the tongues of flatterers? When they see the minds of earthly people producing some good, they corrupt them by praising those things beyond measure.

The fruit of the Egyptians is the work of those who pursue vainglory.

[Note: [Col. 0599D] That is, those who desire empty glory, from the Greek compound κενόδοξος.]

The locusts destroy this fruit when flattering tongues incline the heart of the worker toward seeking passing praise. Locusts eat the grass when flatterers exalt the words of speakers with popular approval. They also devour the fruit of trees when they weaken the works of certain people who are already regarded as strong, through empty praise.

## 48. The locust also signifies Christ’s resurrection and the preachers who sometimes leap toward the contemplative life and sometimes spring back.

The resurrection of our Redeemer is signified by comparison under the name “locust.” Hence he says through the prophet: “I was shaken like a locust” (Ps. 108:23).

He endured being held by persecutors even to death; but he was shaken loose like a locust, because by the leap of sudden resurrection he flew away from their hands.

## 49. This may also be referred to the number of preachers.

In them he was shaken loose like a locust, because, while Judaea raged in its persecution, they fled in different directions, making, as it were, certain leaps of withdrawal.

[Note: [Col. 0599D] Laud. reads “while they fled perversely.”]

Because that preacher is raised to the summit of perfection who is strengthened not only by the active life but also by the contemplative life, the perfection of preachers is rightly expressed by locusts. Whenever locusts attempt to raise themselves into the air, they first propel themselves upward with their legs and afterward fly with their wings.

So it is with holy men. While they seek heavenly things, they first rely upon the good works of the active life, and only then, by the leap of contemplation, suspend themselves in flight toward sublime things. They plant their legs and extend their wings, because they establish themselves by acting rightly and are lifted toward high things by living well.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] The printed editions read: “because they are strengthened by acting rightly.”]

Placed in this life, they cannot remain long in divine contemplation. Like locusts, they catch themselves on their feet after the leap they have made, when, after the heights of contemplation, they return to the necessary works of the active life. Yet they are not content to remain in that active life. As they leap eagerly back toward contemplation, they seek the air again in flight. They live their life like locusts, ascending and descending, while they constantly and supremely desire to see—

[Note: [Col. 0600D] The printed editions read “desire to see.” The manuscripts, with complete agreement, read “desire to behold.”]

—and are drawn back to themselves by the weight of corruptible nature.

## 50. In the peace of the Church they are humble; in persecution they are strong and upright.

There is still another characteristic resembling that of locusts which holy preachers possess. In the morning hours, that is, in a time of mild warmth, they scarcely lift themselves from the ground; but when the heat has blazed forth, they fly all the higher because they fly all the more eagerly.

When every holy preacher sees quiet times of faith, he appears humble and despised and, like a locust, scarcely rises from the ground. But if the heat of persecution grows hot, he immediately reveals how lofty he is, with his heart clinging to heavenly things. He is carried upward by the beating of his wings, though when at rest he seemed to have languished in the depths.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] The printed editions, together with Corb. Germ., read “blazes,” though none of our other manuscripts agrees.]

Concerning this horse, therefore—that is, his preacher—the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will you raise him up like locusts?” The implied sense is: “Like me, who lift him toward higher things by allowing him to be tormented by the more severe heat of persecution, so that a stronger virtue may awaken in him when the fiercer cruelty of unbelievers strikes against him.”

But when the holy preacher suffers many things outwardly and is tormented by the dreadful harassment of persecutors, who can discern what he sees within, since he does not feel so many outward losses? Unless the things that nourish him inwardly for salvation were marvelous, the blows inflicted outwardly would undoubtedly reach his heart as torments.

But the mind raises itself up in the fortress of hope and therefore does not fear the missiles of the siege brought against it.

[Note: [Col. 0601D] The printed editions read “the missiles of the sedition brought against it.” We have corrected this from two German manuscripts, Norman manuscripts, Vindoc., Turon., Laud., and others.]

Hence, to show how sweetly this horse already smells inwardly while suffering so many adversities outwardly, the Lord rightly adds:

# CHAPTER XXVI

## The same passage

“The glory of his nostrils is terror.”

## 51. Though they suffer so many adversities outwardly, they smell marvelous things inwardly from eternal blessedness.

In Holy Scripture, the term “nostrils” sometimes signifies folly, sometimes the instigation of the ancient enemy, and sometimes foreknowledge.

Folly is signified by the nostrils, as we learned above from Solomon, who says: “A golden ring in her nostrils is a beautiful but foolish woman” (Prov. 11:22).

[Note: [Col. 0601D] This refers to chapter 2, section 2 of this work. The Vulgate editions read “we learned” instead of “we taught,” contrary to our Corb. Germ. manuscript, which reads “we said.”]

By the term “nostrils” are understood the exhaling snares and instigation of the ancient enemy, as the Lord testifies concerning him in this same book, saying: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” (Job 41:11). It is as though he said: From his perverse instigation a most wicked darkness of thought rises in human hearts, by which the eyes of those who see are darkened.

Foreknowledge is also signified by the nostrils, as it is said through the prophet: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is considered exalted” (Isa. 2:22).

Often we grasp what we do not see by smell, so that even when certain things lie far away, the fragrance of their quality makes them known to us. As we draw breath through our nostrils, we frequently foreknow things that are not visible.

The spirit of our Redeemer is therefore said to be in his nostrils, so that his knowledge may be signified as foreknowledge. Whatever he made known that he knew in the nature of his humanity, he had certainly foreknown before the ages in his divinity.

And he immediately added through the prophet how he had the spirit in his nostrils, saying: “For he is considered exalted” (Isa. 2:22). It is as though he said: He foreknew from below what was to come from above, because he came down to the depths from heavenly places.

Holy men also, because they have believed what they heard from him, already foreknow what is to come; and while they faithfully serve his commandments, they await his coming in certain hope. Hence, in this passage, the foreknowledge and expectation of the holy preacher are signified by the nostrils of this horse. For he desires the final judgment to come, the heavenly homeland to be revealed, and rewards to be paid to the just; he draws, as it were, the breath of future things through his nostrils.

## 52. Hence the righteous rejoice, while the sinner is terrified.

“The glory of his nostrils is terror,” because the vision of the strict Judge, which the righteous ardently await, the wicked fear to come.

The righteous, considering his labors, seeks the reward of recompense; knowing the merit of his case, he longs for the Judge’s presence and desires with the greatest ardor that he come in a flame of fire, giving vengeance to the impious and bringing the vision of himself as a recompense to the devout.

[Note: [Col. 0601D] In two German manuscripts, in Gilot., Vatic., and several other editions, the corrupt reading is found: “abandoning recompense.” This passage has been restored from English, Norman, and other manuscripts. Laud. reads: “he contemplates with the most devout ardor.”]

But the one who remembers his injustice dreads coming to judgment, fears that his deeds will be examined, and knows that, if they are examined, he will be condemned.

“The glory of his nostrils is terror,” because the righteous rejoices in the very thing by which the sinner is condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0602D] The printed editions read “is assigned to punishment.” “To punishment” is redundant and is absent from the manuscripts. The verb “is assigned” and its meaning have already been discussed above, book 2, section 15, in the notes.]

Let us observe how this horse already draws through his nostrils the breath of what he does not yet see; let us observe how greatly he is exalted while awaiting what is to come. Behold, the outstanding preacher, considering his labors, says: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:6–8).

There he aptly adds: “And not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing” (ibid., 8). It is as though he said: “And to all who are conscious of good works in themselves.” They do not love the coming of the Judge except those who know that they possess the merit of righteousness in their case.

Since, therefore, the righteous rejoices in the very thing that terrifies the wicked, let it rightly be said: “The glory of his nostrils is terror.”

But while this holy preacher awaits the glory to come, while he strives to come before the Judge’s face, and while he is still deferred from receiving the reward of his labor, let us hear what he does in the meantime, placed in this life. It continues:

# CHAPTER XXVII

[Recension XIII]

## Verse 21

“The hoof digs the earth.”

## 53. It is the preacher’s duty to dig out earthly thoughts in his hearers and in himself.

The strength of labor is usually recognized in the horse’s hoof. What, then, is signified by the hoof if not the perfection of virtues in the holy preacher?

By this hoof he digs the earth when, through the example of his works, he drives earthly thoughts from the hearts of his hearers. The hoof digs the earth because he empties the hearts of his hearers of worldly cares, when the good teacher demonstrates by his conduct that the world is to be despised.

Let us see Paul dig the earth of his hearers’ hearts with the hoof of manifest virtue. He says to his disciples: “Think on these things, which you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me; do these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. 4:8–9).

And again: “Be imitators of me, brothers, as I am of Christ” (ibid., 3:17). Whoever therefore corrects others by the example of his own conduct surely digs the earth with his hoof.

[Ancient edition XXII.]

There is something else that we should consider more subtly concerning this digging with the hoof. Although holy men remain wakeful toward heavenly things with the attentive eye of the mind, although they trample with the foot of firm contempt upon everything that passes away below, nevertheless, because they are still bound to the corruption of earthly flesh, they often suffer the dust of thoughts in their hearts.

While outwardly persuading others to seek heavenly things, they continually examine themselves inwardly with subtle investigation, lest some low thought lingering in them for a long time should defile them.

This horse therefore digs the earth with his hoof when every preacher, by strong investigation, examines the earthly thoughts within himself. The horse digs the earth with his hoof when the one over whom the Lord already presides considers what mass has accumulated from his old way of thinking and does not cease to empty himself of it through tears.

Hence Isaac is rightly described as having dug wells among a foreign people (Gen. 26). By this example we learn that, placed in the misery of this pilgrimage, we must penetrate the depths of our thoughts. Until the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our investigation must not grow sluggish in emptying the earth of the heart.

But the Philistines, lying in wait, fill these wells again (ibid.), because unclean spirits, when they see us diligently digging into the heart, heap upon us thoughts of temptation.

[Note: [Col. 0603D] Many manuscripts read “emerge”; Laud. and Germ. read “submerge”; Corb. Germ. reads “immerse.”]

Therefore the mind must always be emptied and ceaselessly dug out, lest, if it is left unexamined, the earth of thoughts pile up over us until it swells into perverse works.

Hence it is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. 8:8)—that is, break the hardness of the heart with repeated blows of examination.

Hence the Lord says to Isaiah: “Enter into the rock, hide yourself in a pit in the ground, from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty” (Isa. 2:10). We enter the rock when we penetrate the hardness of our heart; and we hide ourselves in a pit in the ground from the face of the fear of the Lord when, digging out earthly thoughts, we conceal ourselves in the humility of our mind from the anger of the strict Judge.

For the more earth is thrown out by digging, the lower the floor is shown to be. Thus, if we diligently drive earthly thoughts from ourselves, we discover that we are hidden more humbly within ourselves.

## 54. Saint Gregory’s judgment concerning the day of the impending judgment.

Behold, the day of divine judgment is near; as it were, its very face of terror is already appearing. Each person must fear it all the more terribly, the more the glory of its majesty approaches.

What, then, should be done, and where should one flee? Where can anyone hide from the one who is everywhere?

But behold, we are commanded to enter the rock and hide in a pit in the ground, so that, breaking open the hardness of our heart, we may avoid the invisible anger by withdrawing within ourselves from the love of visible things. Thus, when the earth of evil thought is cast out, the mind may hide itself within itself all the more safely because it is also more humbly hidden (Deut. 23:12).

Hence the Lord commands the Israelite people through Moses that, when they go out for the necessities of nature, they should carry a peg on their belt and use it to cover with earth whatever has been excreted.

Burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, certain superfluous thoughts burst forth from the womb of our mind like the burdens of the belly.

[Note: [Col. 0604D] Turon., two German manuscripts, and Norman manuscripts read “from the womb of repentance’s pain, certain things.”]

But we must carry a peg beneath our belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have near us a sharp goad of compunction. This must incessantly pierce the earth of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceal what foulness bursts forth from us.

The excrement of the belly is covered with earth by means of the peg when the superfluity of our mind, examined by subtle reproof, is hidden from the eyes of God by the goad of its compunction.

Since holy men never cease to reprove and judge whatever useless things they think, let the Lord say concerning his horse: “The hoof digs the earth”—that is, whatever he sees moving in his mind that is earthly, he breaks apart with the hard blows of superimposed repentance.

When they judge themselves inwardly with strict subtlety, there is nothing outwardly left for them to fear. The less they tremble before present evils, the more fully they prepare themselves for future goods.

Hence it follows:

# CHAPTER XXVIII

[Ancient edition XXIII; recension XIV]

## The same passage

“He exults boldly; he goes to meet the armed.”

## 55. The holy man is neither cast down by adversity nor corrupted by prosperity. The apostles’ rejoicing amid scourging, especially Paul’s. Heretics seek the protection of secular powers. Contempt for earthly things is the mark of unbroken virtue.

“He exults boldly,” because he is not broken by adversity, just as he is not lifted up by prosperity. Adversities do not cast down the one whom no prosperity corrupts.

This horse is therefore both strong and under the bridle. So that he may not be crushed by adversity, he has the force of strength; so that he may not be lifted up by prosperity, he bears the weight of the one seated above him.

Times rush past, but for this reason they cannot drag the righteous along: they cannot lift him up. They drag along those whom they lift; in anger they cast down those whom they raise up with flattery.

But the man who is rightly subject to God knows how to stand amid passing things. He knows how to fix the step of his mind amid the falls of rushing time. He knows neither to raise himself toward what is beneath him nor to tremble before what is set against him.

Often, moreover, because he knows that he is more profitably trained by the labors of his contrition, he rejoices in adversity. While he steadfastly suffers for the truth, he rejoices that the merit of his virtue is increased.

Hence we read that the apostles exulted when they happened to endure scourging for Christ, as it is written: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

Hence, when Paul had been pressed by harsh persecutions in Macedonia, he indicates that he was not only afflicted but also gladdened, saying: “When we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest” (2 Cor. 7:5). He was plainly saying that his spirit had rest while his flesh endured the punishments of persecution for the progress of his soul.

Against this horse, therefore, the adversaries of the holy Church prepare swords from the pain of punishments and weapons from the protection of secular powers. Heretics are accustomed to cover themselves with the defenses of powerful men of the world as though with weapons; all unbelievers are accustomed to attack the preaching of the faith by stirring up even the powers of the world.

But God’s horse exults boldly and does not fear outward torments, because he seeks inward delight. He does not fear the anger of worldly powers, because through the mind’s transcendence he tramples even the desire for this present life.

Hence Solomon says: “Nothing that happens to him will grieve the righteous” (Prov. 12:21). Again it is written of him: “The righteous is confident like a lion and will be without fear” (Prov. 28:1).

A lion does not tremble at the approach of beasts because he knows that he prevails over them all. Thus the security of the righteous is rightly compared to a lion: when he sees various people rising against him, he returns to the confidence of his mind. He knows that he overcomes all adversaries because he loves only the one whom, against his will, he cannot possibly lose.

Whoever desires outward things—which are taken away even from those who do not desire them—voluntarily subjects himself to an alien fear.

Unbroken virtue is contempt for earthly desire, because the mind is placed on high when it is lifted by the judgment of hope above lowly things. It is touched by its adversaries all the less because, established in heavenly things, it is more securely fortified.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Gussanv. and many editions, together with the German manuscript, read: “It is the desire for eternal life and contempt for earthly things.” The old Paris and Basel editions agree with the English, Norman, Vindoc., Corb. Germ., Turon., Laud., and other manuscripts, which we follow.]

## 56. The righteous meets his adversaries without fear.

This horse therefore not only does not fear those who come against him but also goes to meet them. Hence it is rightly added: “He goes to meet the armed.”

Often we are left quiet and undisturbed if we do not care to oppose the wicked for the sake of justice. But if the mind has burned with desire for eternal life, if it already sees the true light inwardly, if it has kindled within itself the flame of holy fervor, then, insofar as the situation permits and the case requires, we must place ourselves forward in defense of justice and oppose the wicked when they break forth into injustice, even when they do not seek us out.

For when they strike the justice that we love in others, they wound us by that same blow, even if they seem to be showing reverence.

Since the holy man therefore sets himself against the wicked and those who act badly even when he is not sought out, it is rightly said concerning God’s horse: “He goes to meet the armed.”

## 57. Saint Paul’s example.

It is delightful to contemplate him, roused by the spurs of his rider against armed enemies, and to consider how great a fervor inflamed Paul when the flame of zeal carried him at Ephesus to break into the crowds in the theater.

For it is written: “They were filled with rage and cried out, saying, ‘Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!’ The whole city was filled with confusion, and with one accord they rushed into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions” (Acts 19:28–29).

[Note: [Col. 0606D] Turon., two German manuscripts, and Val. Cl. read “after seizing Gaius.”]

It immediately continues: “When Paul wished to enter among the people, the disciples would not permit him. Some of the officials of Asia, who were his friends, also sent to him, urging him not to give himself up to the theater” (ibid., 30–31).

In these words we recognize with what force he would have rushed against the hostile ranks, had the reins of charity not restrained him through his friends and disciples.

58. Yet danger must sometimes prudently be avoided if only slight benefit is expected from it. Paul taught this by his example.—But if we ought to confront enemies, voluntarily seek battle, and always cast ourselves into the midst of danger in the course of our zeal, what does the same outstanding preacher mean when he admits concerning himself:

> “At Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall, and so I escaped his hands” (2 Cor. 11:32–33)?

What does it mean that this horse now voluntarily attacks armed bands, and now, as though trembling, hides himself from armed enemies, except that in his skillful virtue we must learn both steadfastly at times to undertake battle with adversaries and prudently at times to avoid it? [Old XXIV.] In everything we do, we must place the matter on the scales of the mind and weigh on one side the burden, on the other the fruit of our labor. When the burden outweighs the fruit, each person may harmlessly avoid the labor, provided that he exercises himself in other matters where the fruit gained outweighs the burden of the labor. But when, according to the following measure of fruits [1024], the labor is either equal to or outweighed by the fruit, the labor cannot be avoided without grave guilt.

[Note: Vindoc., “the labor is avoided at the end with grave guilt.” Turon., “the labor is avoided without grave guilt.”]

Therefore, when the holy preacher saw that the minds of those persecuting him at Damascus were exceedingly obstinate, he did not wish to engage their opposition, because he saw both that he himself, whom he knew would benefit many, could perish and that he would benefit either no one or only a few there. He therefore withdrew from the contest and preserved himself for other battles in which he would fight more successfully. It was not virtue that was lacking in the man, but a suitable place for virtue; and therefore the strongest soldier sought the open field of battle away from the narrow confines of the siege.

But when he saw many necks of adversaries ready to be subjected to their own king, he did not fear to enter the battle even at the cost of death. Thus, when he was going to Jerusalem and the disciples tried to restrain him because they had foreseen his passion through prophecy, he bears witness concerning himself, saying:

> “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21:13).

And again:

> “For I do not make my life more precious than myself” (ibid., 20:24).

Thus, when here he fearlessly attacked hostile bands even though his passion had been foreseen, he taught that there he fled as a matter of wise dispensation, not from fear.

59. We must beware lest we flee from fear rather than from prudent dispensation.—In this matter we must consider that a person laudably avoids certain labors by a judgment of wise dispensation when he bravely endures other, greater ones for God. For often weak fear is called prudent dispensation by men; and they claim that they have prudently avoided an attack when, in shameful flight, they are struck in the back.

Therefore, when a matter of dispensation is at issue in God’s cause, fear must be weighed with the most subtle balancing of the heart, lest fear creep in through weakness and, under the appearance of dispensation, counterfeit reason, lest guilt give itself the name of prudence. Then the mind no longer returns to repentance, when it calls virtue what it has wickedly done.

Accordingly, whenever someone is caught in uncertainty and any adversity threatens, he must first fight within himself against fear and rashness, so that he neither withdraws fearfully nor confronts the danger rashly. For the person who always throws himself against adversity is exceedingly rash, and the person who always hides himself is exceedingly cowardly.

60. The experienced commander neither always advances his army against the enemy nor always withdraws it.—We learn these things better in spiritual battles if we take the pattern of warfare from bodily battles. That commander is not wise who always rashly advances his army against the enemy’s ranks; nor is that commander brave who always withdraws it cautiously from the enemy’s presence. A commander must know at one time cautiously to withdraw his army from the enemy’s attack, and at another to hem in the enemy by surrounding him with the horns of the army.

The perfect preachers carefully display this conduct: at one time, while avoiding the rage of persecution, they know how to yield wisely but not weakly; at another, while despising the attack of persecution, they know how to confront it bravely but not rashly. Since the holy man, whenever he sees it fitting, presents his breast to blows and, even when dying, blunts the arrows that come against him, it is rightly said: “He advances to meet the armed.”

Concerning this it is further rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXIX

**VERSE 22.—“He despises fear and does not yield to the sword.”**

[Col. 0607D] [1025]

61. Paul despised every fear and every hostile attack.—Let us see how he despises fear, since he tramples upon the very swords of his adversaries as he enumerates them. For he says:

> “Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution?” (Rom. 8:35).

In fear, punishment that is still to come is dreaded; in the sword, pain from a present blow is already felt. Since, therefore, the holy man does not fear future adversities, he despises fear; but since he is not overcome even when a blow falls upon him, he does not yield to swords.

Against this horse, then, there are as many swords of the enemy as there are kinds of persecution. He overcomes them all as he confronts them, because out of love for life he prepares himself for death. But since we have heard how so powerful a breast opposes itself to arrows, let us now hear what the adversaries do. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXX

**VERSE 23.—“The quiver will resound over him.”**

62. The defeated enemies resort to deceit, but in vain.—In Holy Scripture, the name “quiver” sometimes signifies God’s just and hidden counsel, and sometimes the secret plotting of the wicked.

The just and hidden counsel of God is expressed by the quiver, as the blessed Job himself testifies earlier, saying:

> “For he has opened his quiver and afflicted me” (Job 30:11).

That is: He has disclosed his hidden counsel and wounded me with a public blow. Just as arrows lie in a quiver, so judgments lie hidden in God’s secret counsel; and an arrow is drawn from the quiver when God launches an open judgment from his hidden counsel.

The name “quiver” also signifies the plotting of the wicked, as it is said through the prophet:

> “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:3).

[Old XXV.] When the wicked conceal by secret schemes the plots they devise against the good, they prepare arrows as though in a quiver. In the darkness of the present life, as though in obscurity, they strike the upright in heart, because their malicious arrows can be felt through the wound, yet cannot be detected as they approach.

Since, therefore, the horse of God is terrified by no adversity, and the more he is opposed, the more fervently he is driven against armed enemies by the force of his purpose, his persecutors—who feel that they are defeated even while striking him—confusedly return to deliberation, prepare plots, and conceal their wounds as though shooting from afar.

Thus it is rightly said now:

> “The quiver will resound over him,”

so that they may strike from a hidden scheme at a distance the one whom they approach in open conflict to no avail.

This quiver resounded over the horse of God when the forty men who had conspired to kill Paul sought to have him brought out of prison (Acts 23:16), so that by the blows of their schemes, as though by the deceit of arrows shot secretly, they might kill the man whom they could not overcome through open persecution.

The quiver therefore resounded because the plot’s purpose reached Paul.

[Note: Corb. Germ., Vindoc., Ebroic. and Norm., “as though at least.”]

63. Sometimes they conceal their devices; sometimes, to inspire terror, they display them.—If we inquire attentively, however, we find something still subtler in the sound of the quiver. Often adversaries devise plans against the good, rely upon wicked inventions, and devote themselves to contriving plots; yet they themselves arrange that the persons who ought to disclose those plots to the good should do so. They themselves secretly transmit them, so that, when preparations for punishments are made known as though furtively, they may be feared all the more, and the hearer’s mind may be disturbed more by suspected wounds than by wounds actually received.

For while the arrows lie hidden in the quiver and make a sound, they announce death even though they have not been seen. The quiver therefore makes a sound against the horse when the secret plotting of the wicked against the holy preacher makes known, with still greater deceitfulness, the plan that it deceitfully conceals. It does this so that, by previously announced threats, it may terrify him as though by the sound of a quiver, while the preacher of God does not fear open insults, like arrows striking at close range.

When he is not at all frightened by these threats, the cruelty of the persecutors soon proceeds to manifest punishments. Hence, after it is said, “The quiver will resound over him,” it is immediately added:

## CHAPTER XXXI

**THE SAME.—[Note: Val. Cl., “The spear will be brandished.” And so below. This reading is confirmed by what follows: after the quiver’s sound, the spear is brandished. Laud., “He will brandish the spear.”] He will brandish the spear.**

64. They burst forth from threats into open punishments.—The spear is brandished against the preacher of God after the sound of the quiver when, after threats have been displayed, open punishment is brought near and already strikes.

When the holy preachers undergo punishments in defense of the faith, they do not cease, even amid blows, to draw to that same faith as many as they can; and while they patiently receive wounds, they wisely return arrows of preaching against the hearts of unbelievers.

Thus it sometimes happens that those who rage in persecution grieve less that they have not softened the preacher’s heart than that through his words they are losing others as well. Since, therefore, they do not overcome him by striking him, lest others who hear him also abandon them,

[Note: Vindoc., Pratel. and many Norm., “fall into sin.”]

they immediately prepare a shield of reply against the speaker’s words. Thus, when it says, “The spear will be brandished,” it rightly adds:

**THE SAME.—“And the shield.”**

65. They also seek arguments with which to oppose him.—After the raging persecutor strikes the preacher’s body with punishment,

[Note: Laudun., “The heart of the hearers is brandished as though by a shield, but lest it be possible to hear, the shield is opposed”—a faulty reading.]

he fortifies the hearts of the hearers with the words of his disputation as though with a shield. Thus, the spear is brandished so that the holy man may be struck; but a shield is opposed so that he may not be heard.

The defenders of God have their arrows in battle, which they shoot into the hearts of their hearers all the more swiftly because they draw them from a spiritual bow—that is, from the inward tension of the heart. Paul had armed himself with these in the battle of faith when he said:

> “I suffer hardship even to chains, as a criminal; but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9).

As though he were saying: “I am struck by the spear of punishments, but I do not cease to shoot forth arrows of words. I receive the wounds of cruelty, but by speaking the truth I pierce the hearts of unbelievers.”

Let it therefore be said:

> “The quiver will resound over him; the spear will be brandished, and the shield.”

Against the horse of God the quiver resounds because the counsels of the wicked roar; the spear is brandished because open punishment is sought; and the shield is held before him because resistance is also offered through disputation.

But is he restrained from his ardor by these things? The holy man is pressed by the greater persecution, and therefore is driven all the more fiercely to preach the truth. While he patiently endures his persecutors, he eagerly hastens to draw hearers to himself.

[Note: Laud. and Val. Cl., “helpers.”]

Thus it is rightly further said of the horse of God:

## CHAPTER XXXII

**VERSE 24.—“Burning and raging, he swallows the earth and does not regard the sound of the trumpet’s clang.”**

66. Disregarding their efforts, the devoted preacher continually labors for the conversion of sinners.—To the first man after he sinned it was said:

> “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

The trumpets clang when the powers of this world terrify the saints and forbid them to speak. Since, therefore, the preacher, inflamed by zeal for the Holy Spirit and placed amid punishments, does not cease to draw sinners of every kind to himself, he undoubtedly swallows the earth while burning; and because he does not fear the threats of his persecutors at all, he does not regard the sound of the trumpet’s clang.

The trumpet, which announces the danger of battle, is nothing other than the voice of worldly powers, which, when despised by those who resist them, prepare the struggle of death.

67. The example of the Apostles, especially Saint Paul.—This trumpet sounded from the chief priests when they forbade the apostles, after scourging them, to speak about God, as it is written:

> “After having them beaten, they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:40).

But let us see how the clang of the trumpet does not terrify the horse of God. Peter says:

> “We must obey God rather than men” (ibid., 29).

To others who were also persecuting them he says:

> “We cannot refrain from speaking about what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20).

[Note: Thus read by most manuscripts.]

The horse of God therefore does not fear the clang of the trumpet, because the outstanding preacher, despising the powers of this world, fears no sound of threats.

68. Let us see how another horse of God swallows the earth and how no terror of the trumpet reaches him (Acts 14:18–21). It is written:

> “Some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing him to be dead. But when the disciples surrounded him, he rose and entered the city. On the following day he departed with Barnabas for Derbe. After they had evangelized that city and taught many, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples.”

Let us consider what threats could restrain this horse when death itself cannot prevent him from pursuing his purpose. Behold, he is buried beneath stones, yet is not removed from speaking the truth. He can be killed, but cannot be overcome. He is thrown outside the city as though dead, yet on the next day the preacher is found unharmed inside the city.

O how strong is the weakness present in this man! O how victorious the punishment! O how sovereign the patience! It is provoked to action by repulsion; it is raised up by blows to preach salvation; it is refreshed by punishment to drive away the weariness of labor. What adversity, then, could overcome the man whom punishment refreshes?

But this horse of God also despises the arrows of the quiver,

[Note: Laudun., “because he despises the counsels of an evil life.” Two German manuscripts have somewhat earlier: “but the horse of God exists and the quiver …”]

because he despises the counsels of wickedness. He overcomes the spear that has been brandished because he strengthens his breast even against the wounds of open persecution. He breaks the shield held before him because by reasoning he subdues the disputation of those who resist. He swallows the earth because by exhortation he converts sinners into his own body. He does not regard the sound of the trumpet because he tramples upon every voice of terrifying prohibition.

But what is said is still the lesser thing: that he remains strong in labors. What is greater is that he rejoices in adversities. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Rec. XVI]

**VERSE 25.—“When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Ha!’”**

69. When battle approaches, the saints may be shaken by fear of death, yet they rejoice in the future reward.—These words also show that in this passage the Lord is not speaking of an irrational horse. A brute animal cannot say “Ha!” But when the text asserts that he says what he absolutely cannot say, it indicates whom the horse represents.

“Ha!” is an expression of exultation. The horse therefore says “Ha!” when he hears the trumpet, because every brave preacher, when he considers that the struggle of passion is drawing near, exults in the exercise of virtue. He is not terrified by the danger of battle, because he rejoices in the triumph of victory.

Thus, for the horse to say “Ha!” means that the holy preacher rejoices in the passion that is to come.

[Note: Turon., many Norm., Laud., Val. Cl., two German manuscripts, “the holy preacher rejoices in the passion to come.”]

[Old XXVI.] But if the brave preacher desires the glory of passion, if he gladly seeks to undergo the danger of death for the Lord, why did Truth say to that most courageous preacher, Peter, who drew strength from a stout heart in the Name,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts Corb. Germ., Norm., Turon., Vindoc., and Laud. Germ. read “he drew [strength], ‘in the Name,’ etc.”; the printed editions read “he drew the strength of the Name.”]

> “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:12)?

How does he rejoice in passion if, girded by another, he will not wish to go where he is led? But if we consider how the mind is shaken by the approach of passion and by fear of death, yet rejoices in the reward of the kingdom that is to come, we understand how one who wishes to undergo the danger of the glorious struggle does not wish to undergo it. In death he sees what he fears while enduring it; in the fruit of death he sees what he seeks while desiring it.

70. Paul loves what he avoids, and seems to flee from what he loves.—Let us see how Paul loves what he avoids and how he avoids what he loves. For he says:

> “Having the desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

And:

> “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid., 21).

Yet he also says:
