> “We who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4).

Behold: he desires to die, yet fears to be stripped of the flesh. Why is this? Because although victory gladdens him forever, punishment itself nevertheless disturbs him for the present; and although love of the reward that follows prevails, the stroke of pain touches the mind not without sorrow.

Just as a brave man, when the battle is already near and he girds himself with weapons, both trembles and hastens, shakes and rages—appearing fearful through his pallor, yet driven forward vehemently by anger—so the holy man, when he sees himself drawing near to passion, is both shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the solidity of his hope. He trembles at the nearness of death, yet exults because by dying he will live more truly.

He cannot pass to the kingdom unless death intervenes; therefore, by trusting he seems to doubt, and by seeming to doubt he trusts. He fears while rejoicing, and rejoices while fearing, because he knows that he cannot reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

So, when we wish to drive sickness from the body, we sorrowfully drink the bitter cup of cleansing, yet rejoice because we are certain of the health that will follow. Since the body cannot otherwise attain health, we willingly take in the drink even what disgusts us. When the mind perceives life to be present in the bitterness, it grows cheerful even while troubled by sorrow.

Let it therefore be said:

> “When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Ha!’”

For the brave preacher, having learned of the coming battle, trembles as a human being at the violence of persecution, but through the certainty of hope exults in the reward that will be bestowed.

[Note: Both the old and recent printed editions, together with two German manuscripts, read “at the force of the blow”; “of persecution” is better, as found in Ebroic. and other Norm., Vindoc., Laud., etc.]

Yet he would by no means remain unshaken for this battle of passion unless he anticipated that same passion by meditating upon it with concentrated thought. The evil that is anticipated by deliberation is subjected to the mind struggling against it through reason, because each person is overcome by adversity less to the extent that he is found prepared against it by foreknowledge.

Often the heavy burden of fear is lightened by familiarity; often death itself, which disturbs when unexpected, gladdens when anticipated through deliberation. Hence it is rightly added concerning this horse:

**THE SAME.—“From afar he scents the battle.”**

71. To carry back victory, one must foresee the battle.—It is as though the text said more plainly: “He overcomes every battle for this reason: he prepares his mind for battle before the battle.”

To scent the battle from afar is to foresee through thought every adversity while it is still far off, lest it be able to overcome one by surprise. Paul urged the disciples to scent this battle from afar when he said:

> “Test yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves” (2 Cor. 13:5).

As though he were openly commanding them, he said: “Bring the struggles of persecution back to your minds, and, weighing the inner and hidden things of your hearts, discover what kind of people you will be able to remain amid punishments.”

The holy men scent this battle from afar when, placed in the peace of the universal Church, they discern either the battles of heretics or the tortures of persecution that threaten from unbelievers. While living rightly, they often receive evil in return for good and endure the insults of detraction with equanimity, so that, if an occasion for persecution arises, open enemies may find them all the stronger because the arrows of false brothers within the Church have not defeated them.

For the person who collapses from the state of patience before the wounds inflicted by tongues is himself a witness that he cannot withstand the swords of open persecution.

[Note: Thus read by the Norm. manuscripts, the Royal manuscripts, and two German manuscripts. The printed editions, even the older ones, read “the swords of manifest blows.” The preceding context persuades us that our reading is the best: “so that, if an occasion for persecution arises …”]

Since, therefore, the man of God, trained by present things for those to come and by small things for greater ones, strives onward, it is rightly said of the horse of God that he scents the battle from afar. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**THE SAME.—“The exhortation of the commanders and the howling of the army.”**

72. One must scent what the authors of error and the multitude subject to them may rage to do.—The commanders of the opposing side are the authors of error, concerning whom the Psalmist says:

> “Strife has been poured out upon their princes” [Note: From the Hebrew text and the Greek translation, “contempt” ought to be read. But because of the unanimous agreement both of the printed editions and of the handwritten manuscripts—except Corb. Germ., in which a second hand reads “contempt”—we have retained the earlier reading, which we know is otherwise used by some in the exposition of the Psalms.],
>
> “and their own vanities led them astray, and he made them wander in a pathless place and not on a road” (Ps. 106:40).

[Note: Vindoc., Laud., Corb. Germ., Val. Cl., Pratel., Utic., “they led them astray in a pathless place,” etc.]

Truth himself says concerning them:

> “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14).

[Note: Laud. and two German manuscripts, “offers guidance.”]  
[Note: Two German manuscripts and Val. Cl., “will fall.”]

These commanders are followed by a crowd of wicked people, who serve their unjust commands. It should also be noted that the text says that the commanders exhort, but that the army howls, because those who preside over unbelievers or heretics persuade them, as though by reason, to hold the wicked things they command. The crowd subject to them, because it follows their voices without judgment and roars in the madness of confusion, is said to howl with a bestial mind.

Howling properly belongs to wolves. Since the packs of the reprobate gape only with rapacity against the life and conduct of the faithful, they cry out as though by howling.

[Old XXVII.] The horse of God therefore scents from afar the exhortation of the commanders and the howling of the army, when each holy preacher considers long beforehand both what the authors of error may command against the elect and how savagely the crowd subject to them may rage.

Paul scented the exhortation of the commanders when he said:

> “By smooth words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16:18).

He scented the howling of the army when he said:

> “After my departure, fierce wolves will enter among you” (Acts 20:29).

Peter scented the exhortation of the commanders when he warned the disciples concerning certain men:

> “In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words” (2 Pet. 2:3).

He also scented the howling of the army when he added:

> “Many will follow their immoralities, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed” (ibid., 2).

[Rec. XVII.] 73. What has been said about preachers and teachers is applied to the faithful.—Since we have described what every holy preacher and commander of faith can show himself to be in the battle of persecution, let us now, under the figure of this horse, describe every soldier of Christ. Thus, even the person who considers that he has not yet reached the summit of preaching may recognize himself as expressed by this divine voice if he has already begun to live well. From this he may gather how well known he is to God if, when he reaches greater things, God does not omit to describe him distinctly even in the smallest matters.

Let us therefore go through one by one the things said about the horse and explain how the soldier of God advances from the beginning of his way of life, how he grows from small things to greater ones, and by what steps he reaches from the lowest things to those above. Let it therefore be said:

## CHAPTER XXXV

**VERSE 19.—“Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with neighing?”**

74. Faith must first arm the soldier of God.—To every soul over which the Lord mercifully presides,

[Note: Vindoc., “the Lord mercifully presiding over it.”]

he first of all gives the strength of faith, concerning which Peter says:

> “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5:8).

To this strength the neighing is joined when what is written is fulfilled:

> “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Old XXVIII]

**VERSE 20.—“Will you raise him up like the locusts?”**

75. God’s indulgence toward beginners.—Everyone who follows God is raised up like a locust at the very beginning of his course, because, although in some actions he clings to the earth with bent knees like a locust, in others he suspends himself in the air with outspread wings.

The beginnings of conversion are mixed with good and evil conduct, since something new is already being done by intention while the old life is still retained through habit. We are harmed less by these evils mingled with us for a time

[Note: Pratel., “mingled meanwhile with evils.”]

to the extent that we fight against them daily without ceasing. Nor does the fault whose wicked habit our attentive mind resists now vindicate its claim over us.

[Note: Another reading, “our anxious mind.” The earlier reading is found in Turon., Laud. and Corb. Germ.]

Thus earthly works do less harm to us beginners because they are prevented from dwelling in us for long. Since, therefore, at the very beginning of our conversion the Lord mercifully tolerates certain weaknesses in us so that he may eventually lead us to heavenly things through perfection, he raises us up like locusts at the beginning. For although he lifts us up in the flight of virtue, he does not despair of us because we fall into earthly works.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**THE SAME.—“The glory of his nostrils is terror.”**

76. Beginners are placed between hope and fear because of the struggles of the flesh, which they therefore subdue bravely.—Because something not seen is detected by smell, the name “nostrils” appropriately expresses the thoughts of our hope. Through these thoughts we foresee by hope the judgment that is to come, although we do not yet see it with our eyes.

Everyone who begins to live well rejoices when he hears that at the final judgment the just will be called to the kingdom. But because he considers that certain evils still remain in him,

[Note: Perhaps the reading in Pratel., “from what remains,” and in Germ., “from what remains,” is better. But since other manuscripts read “from the remnants,” a reading also found in all the printed editions, we have judged that nothing should be changed in the text.]

he fears the approach of the very judgment over which he begins to rejoice. He sees his life mingled with good and evil, and in some way confuses his thoughts between hope and fear.

When he hears what the joys of the kingdom are, joy immediately lifts his mind; but when he again considers what the torments of Gehenna are, fear immediately disturbs it. Thus “the glory of his nostrils is terror” is rightly said, because, placed between hope and fear, when he sees the future judgment in his mind, he fears the very thing in which he glories.

His glory itself is terror to him, because, with good works already begun, he rejoices in hope of the judgment, but because not all evils have yet been brought to an end, he is not perfectly secure. Amid these things he carefully returns to himself; refusing the storms of such great fear and arranging himself in the tranquility of peace alone, he strives with all his strength to be found free by the strict judge.

He considers it servile to fear the Lord’s presence; and, so that he may not fear the sight of his Father, he does those things by which he may recognize himself as a son. He therefore learns to love the judge with complete expectation and, so to speak, by fearing refuses to fear.

He observes that fear arises in his heart because of carnal action, and therefore, before all else, disciplines the flesh with strong mastery.

[Note: Val. Cl. and Laud., “with strong dominion.”]

Hence, after it is said, “The glory of his nostrils is terror,” it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

**VERSE 21.—“He digs the earth with his hoof.”**

77. To dig the earth with the hoof is to subdue the flesh by severe abstinence.—The more the flesh is oppressed, the more securely the mind rejoices in heavenly hope. Hence, after the dug earth, it is appropriately added:

> “He exults boldly.”

Because he vigorously suppresses what attacks him, he boldly exults in what he desires in eternal peace. The mind is better prepared to seek heavenly things the more strictly the body is subdued from unlawful desires.

Thus Solomon rightly says:

> “Diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. 24:27).

The person who first cleanses the field of the body of the thorns of vices builds the house of the mind well. Otherwise, if the brambles of desires grow in the field of the flesh, the whole structure of virtues within will be destroyed as the hunger for good works increases.

While a person is placed in the very struggle of battle, he sees the enemy’s deceit all the more subtly the more strictly he suppresses his own body as a kind of ally of the enemy. Hence, after the crushing of the body and after the joy of the heart, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Col. 0616A]

**THE SAME.—“He advances to meet the armed.”**

78. Beginners investigate the enemy’s ambushes and deceptions and anticipate them even in the hearts of others.—The armed enemies are unclean spirits, girded with countless deceits against us. When they cannot persuade us to do what is wicked, they set such things before our eyes under the appearance of virtues and conceal themselves, as it were, beneath certain weapons, so that we may not see them naked in their wickedness.

We advance to meet these armed enemies when we foresee their ambushes from far away. Thus, to advance to meet armed enemies after digging the earth is, once the pride of the flesh has been subdued, to investigate with remarkable care the deceits of unclean spirits. To advance to meet armed enemies after digging the earth is, after conquering carnal wickedness, to enter the battle against spiritual vices.

For the person who still fights weakly against himself arouses external battles against himself in vain. If someone subdues himself under carnal things, how will he resist spiritual vices? Or how can he hope to triumph in the labor of an external battle when he still succumbs within himself to the domestic battle of lust?

[Old XXIX.] 79. Or certainly, we advance to meet armed enemies when, through our zeal for exhortation, we anticipate their ambushes in another’s heart. We come, as it were, from the place where we were to another place to meet the enemies when, properly setting aside our own concerns for a time, we prevent the approach of unclean spirits into the mind of our neighbor.

It often happens that the cunning enemies test the soldier of God, already victorious in inward battle, more terribly concerning himself because they see that he has prevailed courageously against them both in himself and in another’s heart. They do this so that, when they call him back to defend himself, they may more freely invade the hearts of others that had been protected by his exhortation.

When they cannot overcome him, they at least try to occupy him, so that while the soldier of God is shaken concerning himself, not he but the person whom he had been accustomed to defend may be destroyed.

But the mind fixed immovably upon God despises the arrows of temptations and does not fear the darts of any terror.

[Note: The recent printed editions, together with Germ., read “the attack of temptations.” We have followed the majority of the manuscripts, which have “darts,” not “attack.”]

Relying upon the help of heavenly grace, he so treats the wounds of his own weakness that he does not abandon others. Hence it is rightly further said of this horse:

## CHAPTER XL

**VERSE 22.—“He despises fear and does not yield to the sword.”**
[Col. 0616D] **80. Beginners despise the threats of the enemy.**—“He despises fear,” because he is not so terrified by dread of any temptation that he becomes silent. “Nor does he yield to the sword,” because even if a violent temptation strikes him, it does not drive him away from care for his neighbor.

Thus Paul, offering us an example of unconquered conduct, both tells us what swords he receives from the enemy and shows how he does not yield to those same swords. Having already overcome every battle of carnal action, he had received from the enemy the sword of carnal temptation, when he said: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind” [Col. 0617A] “and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7:23). [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Vendôme, Laon, Valence, two German manuscripts read: “and captivating me.”]

Yet he did not yield to that same sword, which he had conquered in himself, even in the case of others, when he said to his neighbors: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body so as to obey its desires” (Romans 6:12). And again: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire” (Colossians 3:5).

A heavy sword of temptations struck him, concerning which he himself says: “In many labors, in prisons more abundantly, in blows beyond measure, in deaths often. From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck, I was in the depths of the sea night and day” (2 Corinthians 11:23), [Col. 0617B] “and so forth”—things which he himself was able to endure, while we grow weary even of enumerating them.

But how he does not yield to that same sword in love of his neighbor, he adds after many other things: “Apart from those things which are external, my daily preoccupation is my concern for all the churches” (ibid., 28).

Therefore God’s horse is struck by the sword, yet is not prevented by that blow from continuing its course: the strong soldier of spiritual combat both receives wounds from the enemy and nevertheless girds himself for the salvation of others. But against the breast of so sturdy a heavenly soldier the ancient enemy seeks sharper darts, the more robustly he sees himself despised. Hence it follows:

**CHAPTER XLI [Vet. XXX].**

**VERSE 23.—“Above him the quiver will resound; the spear and shield will flash.”**

[Col. 0617C] **81. Those who preside over the governance of others are often tried by more serious temptations from the devil: sometimes by open force, sometimes by fraud and deceit, and at times by force together with deceit.**—Because he sees the zeal of the holy mind benefiting others against him, he strives to pierce it with multiplied temptation [Note: [Col. 0617D] Two German manuscripts and the Turin manuscript read “confound.”]

Thus it often happens that those who preside over the governance of others suffer stronger battles of temptation, so that, as in bodily warfare, when the commander himself is turned to flight, the compact unanimity of the resisting army may be scattered without effort.

The crafty enemy, therefore, seeking various wounds of assault against the heavenly soldier, sometimes wounds him by ambush with an arrow from the quiver; sometimes he brandishes a spear before his face. For he conceals some vices under the appearance of virtues, while he sets others openly before his eyes as they are. Wherever he sees God’s soldier weakened, there he does not seek coverings of deceit. But wherever he considers him strong in resistance, there he undoubtedly prepares stratagems against his strength.

For when he sees someone weak in the allurements of the flesh, he openly presents to his gaze the appearance of a body capable of being desired. But if he happens to see someone strong against avarice, he insistently suggests to his thoughts the poverty of his household, so that while the mind seems to be turned piously toward providing for them, it may be secretly seduced and unjustly carried away into the pursuit of possessions.

Thus the arrow assails God’s horse [Col. 0618A] by ambush when the crafty enemy hides vice beneath virtue. The spear wounds at close quarters when manifest wickedness tempts even one who knows it.

**82.** Often both are presented to the heavenly soldier by the enemy at one and the same time, so that he may be destroyed by either single blow. For the deceitful adversary strives to strike at once, raging openly and hiding in ambush, so that while the arrow from concealment is feared, the spear before the face may be feared less; or while resistance is offered to the spear before the face, the arrow coming from concealment may not be seen.

Often he proposes the temptation of lust and then suddenly, more deceitfully ceasing from it, suggests pride over preserved chastity. There are some who, seeing many fall from the stronghold of chastity into the pit of pride, neglect the guardianship of their life and plunge into the uncleanness of lust. Others, conversely, while fleeing the uncleanness of lust, fall through the height of chastity into the abyss of pride.

Thus, as an open blow, the spear is guilt arising from vice; and, as a wound inflicted from concealment, the arrow from the quiver is guilt arising from virtue. But God’s horse overcomes the spear before its face when it tramples lust, and watches for the arrow at its side when, in the purity of chastity, it guards itself against pride.

Hence Solomon rightly says to one contending between the two: “The Lord will be at your side, and will guard your foot lest you be caught” (Proverbs 3:26). The foot moves toward what is in front. But the one who sees what is at his side does not see what is in front. Again, whoever looks ahead while anticipating the guarding of his foot abandons watchfulness at his side.

When we do something virtuous set before our face, we foresee, as it were, where the foot ought to be placed. But when guilt secretly arises from that very virtue, the side is left exposed to the arrow while we are looking ahead. Often, however, while we fear an emerging fault, we turn away from the virtue that ought to be practiced; and, as if while watching the side, we do not see how the foot should be placed in front.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “The Lord will be at your side, and will guard your foot lest you be caught,” because the soldier of God, protected by the shield of divine grace, watches attentively for what may emerge from the side [Note: [Col. 0618D] The German and Valence manuscripts read “betray,”] and does not cease to advance by carrying his step forward.

The deceitful enemy, envying him because he sees that he cannot prevail through the quiver and spear, opposes a shield [Note: [Col. 0618D] Turin: “so that, as one resisting…”], so that if he cannot pierce the breast of one who resists by striking it, he may at least block the progress of one who is advancing by certain obstacles. [Col. 0618D] For he places certain difficulties in the way of his very efforts; and when he cannot overcome him, he at least resists.

But let us hear what God’s horse does against so many strategies of war:

**CHAPTER XLII.**

**VERSE 24.—“Boiling and snorting, it swallows the earth, and does not regard the sound of the trumpet’s blast.”**

**83. Both are resisted through holy fervor and concern for progress.**—The trumpet’s blast sounds against the horse when some nearby guilt terribly tempts the mind of the elect in what it is strongly undertaking. But “boiling and snorting, it swallows the earth,” because with excessive ardor it shakes itself, and whatever earthly thing it finds in itself it consumes daily by making progress.

“And it does not regard the sound of the trumpet’s blast,” because with strong discernment it carefully avoids every vice that arises from the glory of virtue. It would regard the trumpet’s blast as sounding if, because of something else that perversely arose, it feared to undertake another right action.

Therefore, because it does not tremble before the temptations sounding in advance of strenuous deeds, it does not fear the trumpet’s blast while situated in its fervor. Often, however, while it sees itself prospering in virtues, it rejoices to be struck by temptations, lest the very prosperity of its virtues elevate it. Hence it is aptly added:

**CHAPTER XLIII.**

[Col. 0619B]

**VERSE 25.—“When it hears the trumpet, it says, ‘Ha!’”**

**84. Because prolonged peace makes many sluggish, the holy rejoice in being tempted.**—For their own prosperity has laid many low more disastrously; prolonged peace has made many sluggish. Consequently, the unexpected enemy struck them more severely because he found them negligent through long enjoyment of repose [Note: [Col. 0619D] Laon: “the unexpected enemy struck them.”]

Thus holy men, when they observe that they are making much progress through the prosperity of virtue, rejoice that, by a certain moderation of heavenly providence, they are also exercised by temptations, because they guard the glory of the virtues they have received more robustly when, shaken by the impact of temptation, they recognize their weakness more humbly.

Therefore the horse, when it hears the trumpet, says, “Ha!” For the soldier of God, when he sees the force of temptation bearing down upon him, considers the benefit of heavenly providence and gains confidence more strongly from the adversity itself.

The battles of this adversity do not overcome him for this reason: they never attack him unexpectedly. For from each circumstance he observes beforehand what battle of vice may grow from it. Hence it follows:

**CHAPTER XLIV.**

**THE SAME.—“It scents war from afar.”**

**85. Nothing unexpected tempts them; therefore nothing overcomes them.**—To scent war from afar is to recognize, from preceding causes, what battles of vices will follow. Since, as has often already been said, an unseen thing is recognized by its odor, to scent war from afar means to investigate hidden wickedness—by the breathing of the nostrils, so to speak, and by the foresight of thought.

Regarding this scent the Lord rightly says in praise of his Church: “Your nose is like the tower which is in Lebanon” (Song of Songs 7:4). By the nose we distinguish scents and stenches. And what is signified by the nose except the prudent discernment of the saints? A tower of watchfulness is set on high so that the approaching enemy may be seen from afar.

Rightly, therefore, the nose of the Church is compared to a tower in Lebanon, because the prudent discernment of the saints, carefully looking all around from its elevated position, detects guilt before it arrives and, the more vigilantly it foresees it, the more forcefully avoids it.

Hence Habakkuk says: “I will stand upon my watch” (Habakkuk 2:1). [Vet. XXXI.] Hence Jeremiah, admonishing the soul of each of the elect, says: “Set up a watchtower for yourself; place bitterness for yourself” (Jeremiah 31:21). To set up a watchtower for oneself is to foresee, through lofty consideration, the future battles of vices. The mind of the elect places bitterness for itself when, even established in the peace of virtues, it sees evils lying in wait and does not consent to rest securely [Note: [Col. 0619D] Another manuscript: “and the mind chosen for itself.”]

**86. First one must take care not to do evil, and second, not to do good carelessly. Evils often arise from good things.**—First, therefore, he considers that he must not do any evil; in the second place, that he must not do good things carelessly. After he has subdued what is wrong, he also strives to subject what is right to himself [Note: [Col. 0619D] Norman and Vendôme manuscripts: “to subject”], lest, if these things pass beyond the rule of the mind, they turn into the sin of pride.

For, as was said above, since evils often arise from good things through the fault of negligence, he watches attentively to see how arrogance may arise from instruction, cruelty from justice, laxity from piety, anger from zeal, and torpor from gentleness. When he does these good things, he sees how many enemies may rise against him through them [Note: [Col. 0620D] Laon: “how many here against him”; Valence: “how many these against him”; Cologne and German manuscripts: “how many hence against him.”]

When he labors to attain the pursuits of instruction, he carefully prepares his mind against the battle of arrogance. When he desires to punish the faults of offenders justly, he most shrewdly avoids allowing the cruelty of vengeance to exceed the measure of justice. When he strives to restrain himself through piety, he carefully watches lest he be overcome by some dissolution of discipline.

When he arouses himself with the goads of righteous zeal [Note: [Col. 0620D] Évreux: “the stimulus of upright zeal,”] he takes the greatest care lest the flame of anger kindle him more than necessary. When he moderates himself with great tranquility of gentleness, he vigilantly observes lest he grow cold through torpor.

Therefore, because every vice is seen by the thought of the spiritual soldier before it can creep in [Note: [Col. 0620D] Another manuscript: “to steal in,” as in several manuscripts], it is rightly said of God’s horse: “It scents war from afar.”

He also weighs what a multitude of iniquities might rush upon him if he permitted even a few evils to enter him. Hence it follows:

**CHAPTER XLV.**

**THE SAME.—“The exhortation of the commanders and the howl of the army.”**

**87. The commander of the devil’s army is pride, whose offspring are the seven principal vices.**—The vices that tempt us, which serve pride—the ruler over them—in its invisible war against us, go before in the manner of commanders, while others follow in the manner of an army. For not all faults occupy the heart by an equal approach.

But when greater and fewer vices forestall a negligent mind, lesser and innumerable ones pour themselves upon it in troops. For when pride itself, the queen of vices, has fully seized a conquered heart, it immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as to its commanders, to be devastated. The army follows these commanders, because from them without doubt arise the troublesome multitudes of vices.

We shall show this more clearly if, as far as we can, we set forth these commanders and the army individually by enumeration. Pride is the root of every evil; concerning it Scripture testifies: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15).

Its first offspring are the seven principal vices, produced from this poisonous root: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. Because our Redeemer grieved that we had been captured by these seven vices of pride, he came full of the sevenfold Spirit of grace for the spiritual battle of liberation.

**88. Each capital vice has its own army.**—But each of these has its own army against us. From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contentions, obstinacy, dissensions, [Col. 0621B] and presumptions of novelty.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing at the misfortune of one’s neighbor, and distress at his prosperity.

From anger proceed quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, torpor regarding the commandments, and wandering of mind toward what is illicit.

From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, acts of violence, and hardness of heart against mercy.

From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding regarding insight.

From lust are generated blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread or despair [Col. 0621C] of the future.

Therefore, because the seven principal vices produce such a multitude of vices from themselves, when they come to the heart they drag along, as it were, the troops of the army that follows. Of these seven, five are spiritual and two carnal.

**89. Each vice arises from another.**—Yet each of them is joined to the others by such kinship that one is produced only from another. The first offspring of pride is vainglory. When it has corrupted an oppressed mind, it immediately gives birth to envy, because, while it seeks the power of a famous name, it wastes away lest someone else be able to attain it.

Envy likewise generates anger, because the more the spirit is wounded by the inward injury of jealousy, the more it loses the tranquility of gentleness; and because it is touched like an aching limb, the hand of an opposing action is consequently felt as pressing it more heavily [Note: [Col. 0621D] Valence: “inward.”]

From anger, sadness also arises, because the more a troubled mind shakes itself disorderly, the more it confounds itself by condemnation; and when it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing feeds it except the grief that follows from disturbance.

Sadness also passes over into avarice, because when the confused heart has lost within itself the good of joy, it seeks outside itself something by which it may be consoled; and it desires to acquire external goods all the more because it has no joy to which it may turn inwardly.

After these, the two carnal vices remain: gluttony and lust. But it is clear to everyone that lust arises from gluttony, since in the very arrangement of the limbs the genital organs appear to be attached to the belly [Note: [Col. 0621D] German, Laon, and Valence manuscripts: “supported beneath.”] Thus, when one is improperly refreshed, the other is undoubtedly aroused to shameful acts.

[Vet. XXXII.] **90. Deceptive arguments by which the capital vices try to deceive the mind.**—They are rightly said to be commanders exhorting and an army howling, because the first vices insert themselves into the deceived mind as if with a kind of reasoning; but the innumerable vices that follow, while dragging it into every madness, confound it as if with a bestial cry.

Vainglory usually exhorts a conquered heart as though by reason, saying: “You ought to seek greater things, so that, to the degree that you surpass many in power, you may also be able to benefit many.”

Envy likewise usually exhorts a conquered heart as though by reason, saying: “In what are you inferior to this person or that? Why, then, are you not equal or superior to them? How much are you capable of that they are not? Therefore they ought not to be either superior or even equal to you.”

Anger also usually exhorts a conquered heart as though by reason, saying: “What is done against you cannot be borne with equanimity [Note: [Col. 0621D] Turin: “to be done”]; indeed, patiently to tolerate these things is a sin, because if you do not resist them with great exasperation, they will thereafter be heaped up against you without measure.”

Sadness likewise usually exhorts a conquered heart as though by reason, saying: “What have you from which you can rejoice, when you bear so many evils from your neighbors? Consider with what grief all those must be regarded who are turned against you in so much bitterness [Col. 0622C] of gall” [Note: [Col. 0621D] Pratelles and Utica manuscripts: “and not ineffectively, are involved.”]

Avarice also usually exhorts a conquered mind as though by reason, saying: “It is entirely without fault that you desire to possess certain things, because you do not seek to multiply them but fear to be in need [Note: [Col. 0621D] The manuscript of Robert Grosseteste, bishop of Lincoln: “Go on; it is without fault.”]; and what another holds badly, you yourself put to better use” [Note: [Col. 0622D] The reading “but to act” in the Gilot, Vatican, and other editions is erroneous. It is corrected from English, Norman, German, and other manuscripts, as well as from the old Vulgate.]

Gluttony likewise usually exhorts a conquered heart as though by reason, saying: “God created all things clean for eating; and whoever refuses to be satisfied with food, what else does he do but contradict a gift that has been granted?”

Lust also usually exhorts a conquered heart as though by reason, saying: “Why do you not now expand yourself in your pleasure, since you do not know what will follow you? You ought not to waste the time granted in desires, because you do not know how quickly it may pass. For if God did not wish human beings to mingle in sexual pleasure, he would not have made male and female at the very beginning of the human race” (Genesis 1:27).

This is the exhortation of the commanders. When it is incautiously admitted into the heart’s secret place, it persuades more familiarly to what is evil. The howling army follows it [Note: [Col. 0622D] Thus the Vendôme, Laon, Norman, two German, and other manuscripts. The editions read “the howl of the army”], because the unhappy soul, once captured by the principal vices, is turned to madness by multiplied iniquities and is then ravaged with savage violence.

**91. What must be done so that the vices do not harm us.**—But the soldier of God, because he strives carefully to foresee the battles of vices, scents war from afar. For, while he attentively considers what the evils going before may persuade to the mind, he detects the exhortation of the commanders through the keen sense of his nostrils. And because from afar, by foreseeing it, he sees the confusion of the iniquities that follow, he recognizes, as though by scent, the howl of the army.

Therefore, since through the account of the horse we have recognized that either a preacher of God or any soldier of spiritual combat has been described, let us now see the same person again under the sign of a bird, so that, having learned through the horse his strength, we may also learn through the bird his contemplation. For since, through the greatness attributed to the horse, we have heard how much the holy man endures through patience against the battles of vices, let us now learn through the image of birds how greatly he flies through contemplation. It follows:

**CHAPTER XLVI [Rec. XVIII].**

**VERSE 26.—“Does the hawk grow feathered by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the South?”** [Note: [Col. 0623D] Laon: “Does it extend them?” Thus the text below is rendered: “It spreads its wings toward the South.” “Wings,” therefore, etc.]

**92. By God’s grace we strip off the old person. Some noteworthy points concerning the hawk.**—Almost no one is unaware that each year the hawk casts off an old feather as a new one grows and continually becomes feathered. But this does not refer here to the time when it is clothed with down in the nest, for then, while still a nestling, it is plainly unable to spread its wings toward the South. Rather, the annual feathering is described by which, after the old feather has been loosened, it is renewed.

For domestic hawks, damp and warm places are sought so that they may grow feathered better [Note: [Col. 0623D] Turin, two German, Vendôme, Laon, and Pratelles manuscripts read “provided”; we would follow them if it did not seem absurd to say that “provided places” enable birds to grow feathered better]. For wild hawks, however, it is customary to spread their wings when the South Wind blows, so that their limbs may grow warm in the warmth of the wind and loosen the old feather.

When the wind is absent, they stretch and beat their wings against the sun’s rays, thus making warm air for themselves. In this way, with the pores opened, either the old feathers fall out or new ones grow.

What, then, is it for the hawk to become feathered in the South, except that each of the saints, warmed by the breath of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0624D] Turin: “grows strong”], casts off the practice of an old way of life and assumes the form of the new person?

Paul admonishes us to this, saying: “Strip off the old person with his acts, and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9). And again: “Although our outward person is being corrupted [Note: [Col. 0624D] Pratelles, two German, and Valence manuscripts: “is corrupted”], yet the inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

To cast off the old feather is to abandon the aged practices of deceitful action; to take up a new feather is to retain a gentle and simple disposition by living well [Note: [Col. 0624D] Corbie German, Laon, Valence, and Norman manuscripts: “of living well.”] The feather of the old way of life weighs one down, while the plumage of new transformation lifts one up, making one so much lighter for flight as one becomes newer.

[Vet. XXXIII.] **93. Confession is necessary for this renewal.**—And he rightly says: “It spreads its wings toward the South.” To spread our wings toward the South is to open our thoughts through confession at the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that we no longer wish to conceal ourselves by defending ourselves, but to make ourselves known by accusing ourselves.

Then the hawk becomes feathered when it spreads its wings toward the South, because each person clothes himself with the feathers of virtues when he lays his thoughts before the Holy Spirit in confession. Whoever does not uncover old things by confessing them produces no works of new life. Whoever does not know how to mourn what weighs him down cannot bring forth what lifts him up.

For the very force of compunction opens the pores of the heart [Col. 0624B] and pours forth feathers of virtue. When the mind diligently rebukes itself for its sluggish oldness [Note: [Col. 0624D] Vendôme and Norman manuscripts: “earnestly”], it grows young through vigorous newness.

Let it therefore be said to blessed Job: “Does the hawk grow feathered by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the South?” That is: “Have you given understanding to any of the elect, so that, when the Holy Spirit blows, he may spread the wings of his thoughts, cast off the burdens of an old way of life, and take up the feathers of virtues for the practice of a new flight?”

From this he may gather that he does not possess vigilance of understanding in himself from himself, and that he is therefore entirely unable to confer it upon others from himself.

This hawk may also signify the renewed Gentile people, as though blessed Job were plainly told: “Look upon the future feathers of virtues among the Gentiles, and cast off the old feathers of pride.”

It follows:

**CHAPTER XLVII [Rec. XIX].**

[Col. 0624C]

**VERSE 27.—“Is the eagle lifted up at your command, and does it set its nest in high places for itself?”** [Note: [Col. 0624D] Laon and Valence: “is lifted up … it sets”; and so thereafter.]

**94. What Holy Scripture signifies by the name ‘eagle’: spirits lying in wait, earthly power, the subtle understanding of the saints, or Christ’s ascension.**—In Holy Scripture, the word “eagle” sometimes signifies malignant spirits that seize souls, sometimes the powers of the present age, and sometimes either the most subtle understanding of the saints or the incarnate Lord, who swiftly traverses the depths and soon returns to the heights.

By the name of eagles, spirits lying in wait are expressed, as Jeremiah testifies when he says: “Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lamentations 4:19). Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven when wicked human beings do so much against us that, by the inventions of their malice, they seem to outstrip even the aerial powers.

Earthly power is also represented by the word “eagle.” Hence through the prophet Ezekiel it is said: “A great eagle, with great wings, long extension of limbs, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore off the top of its branches” (Ezekiel 17:3).

Who else is signified by this eagle than Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon? [Note: [Col. 0625D] The printed editions read: “who, on account of immensity … full of feathers … full of variety.” The multitude of manuscripts compelled a change of this reading. All the Norman, Vendôme, Laon, and other manuscripts present our reading. Two German manuscripts agree with the printed editions in “who, on account of immensity,” but with the other manuscripts in “full,” etc.]

He is described as having great wings because of the vastness of his army; long extension of limbs because of the duration of time; being full of feathers because of his many riches; and being full of variety because of the innumerable splendor of earthly glory.

He came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore off the top of its branches because, attacking the height of Judea, he carried away the nobility of its kingdom as the marrow of the cedar; and when he carried the tender offspring of its kings away captive from the summit of their kingdom, he tore off, as it were, the top of its branches.

**The subtle understanding of the saints, or Christ’s ascension. The eagle gazes upon the sun with fixed eyes.**—The word “eagle” expresses either the subtle understanding of the saints or the flight of the Lord’s ascension.

Thus the same prophet, when he described the four evangelists as having appeared to him under the form of animals (Ezekiel 10:1), testifies that the face of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle appeared to him among them. Without doubt he designates John by the fourth animal, the eagle, because, flying, he left the earth: through subtle understanding he penetrated the inner mysteries [Note: [Col. 0625D] Thus the Turin, Vendôme, two German, Évreux, and other Norman and Valence manuscripts read; the editions have *verbi*, “of the Word.”].

John himself, in his Revelation, does not disagree with this prophetic statement concerning himself, saying: “The first animal was like a lion, the second animal like a calf, the third animal having a face like a man, and the fourth animal like a flying eagle” (Revelation 4:7).

Although each of these rightly corresponds to one of the evangelists—one indicating the order of human birth, another the slaughter of sacrifice for the world, like the death of a calf, another the strength of power, like the roar of a lion, and another, contemplating the birth of the Word, gazing upon the eagle like the rising sun—nevertheless these four animals can also signify their own head, whose members they are.

For he himself is man, because he truly assumed our nature; he is a calf, because he patiently died for us; he is a lion, because through the strength of his divinity he broke the bond of the death he had assumed; and finally he is an eagle, because he returned to heaven, from which he had come. He was called man in being born, calf in dying, lion in rising again, and eagle in ascending to heaven.

[Vet. XXXIV.] But in this passage the name “eagle” figures the subtle understanding and lofty contemplation of the saints. The sharpness of the eagle’s sight surpasses that of all birds, so that no brilliance of its light, rebounding, shuts its eyes when they are fixed upon the sun.

Therefore the eagle is lifted up at God’s command when the life of the faithful, obeying the divine orders, is raised aloft in heavenly things. It is also said to set its nest in high places because, despising earthly desires, it is already nourished by hope of heavenly things.

It sets its nest in high places because it does not build the dwelling of its mind in a low and inferior way of life. Hence, when Balaam prophesied, it is said of the Kenite: “Your dwelling is indeed strong, but if you place your nest in the rock” (Numbers 24:21).

For “Kenite” is interpreted as “possessor.” And who are those who possess the present things except those skilled in the ingenuity of worldly wisdom? They truly build a strong dwelling for themselves if, made little in their own eyes through humility, they are nourished in Christ’s sublimity [Note: [Col. 0626D] Laon: “glory in it”]; if they recognize themselves as weak and, known in lofty humility, place the confident trust of their mind in the Redeemer for him to cherish [Note: [Col. 0626D] The readings *cogniti, redemptori fovendam*, found in Gilot, Gussanville, and elsewhere, together with a German manuscript, are corrupt. We have supplied the remedy from all our other manuscripts and the old editions]; if they do not seek what is low; if, by the flight of their heart, they transcend everything that passes away.

**95. Paul is like an eagle.**—Let us see the eagle building its nest of hope for itself in high places. He says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). And again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6).

It has its nest in high places because it fixes its purpose in the heights. It does not wish to cast its mind down to what is low, nor to dwell in the depths through the lowliness of human conduct.

Paul may perhaps have been held in prison when he testified that he was seated with Christ in the heavenly places. But he was where he had already fixed his ardent mind, not where the still sluggish flesh necessarily kept him.

**96. The elect despise all earthly things.**—This is usually the distinctive mark of the elect: they know how to travel the path of the present life in such a way that, through the certainty of hope, they know they have already reached the heights. Thus they see all passing things beneath themselves and trample, through love of eternity, everything that rises high in this world.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet to the soul that follows him: “I will lift you above the heights of the earth” (Isaiah 58:14).

There are, as it were, lower regions of the earth: losses, insults, poverty, degradation. Even lovers of the world, while they walk along the broad level of the road, do not cease to avoid and trample these things. The heights of the earth, however, are profit from possessions, the flattering favor of subjects, abundance of riches, honor, and the exalted status of dignities.

Whoever still walks through low desires considers these things high precisely because he thinks them great. But if the heart is once fixed in heavenly things, it immediately sees how low are the things that had seemed high.

For, just as one who climbs a mountain looks down upon the other things lying beneath him to the degree that he directs his steps farther toward higher places [Note: [Col. 0626D] Vendôme and Norman manuscripts: “just as when someone climbs a mountain”; two German manuscripts: “when someone climbs a mountain”], so one who strives to fix his intention in the highest things is lifted above the heights of the earth. By the very effort he discovers that there is no glory in the present life, and what he previously believed to be above him while situated in low desires, after ascending and progressing, he recognizes to be beneath him.

Thus what the Lord promises there that he will do, saying, “I will lift you above the heights of the earth” (ibid.), he testifies here to blessed Job that he alone can do, saying: “Is the eagle lifted up at your command, and does it set its nest in high places for itself?”

It is as though he said: “Does it rise at my command—I who inwardly inspire, through the grace of hidden bounty, what I command outwardly?”

It follows:

**CHAPTER XLVIII.**

**VERSE 28.—“It dwells in the rocks.”**

**97. In the rocks—that is, in the height and steadfastness of the holy fathers—they set their nests.**—When “rock” is named in the singular in sacred speech, who else is understood except Christ? Paul bears witness to this when he says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

But when “rocks” are called in the plural, his members are expressed: holy men who have been made solid by his strength. The apostle Peter calls them stones, saying: “As living stones, you are being built together into spiritual houses” (1 Peter 2:5).

This eagle, therefore, which has raised the eyes of its heart toward the rays of the true Sun [Note: [Col. 0627D] Thus our manuscripts and the old Paris and Basel editions read; many others have “draws forth”], is said to dwell in the rocks because it places the station of its mind in the sayings of the ancient and strong fathers.

It recalls to mind the lives of those whom it sees to have gone before it on the way of God [Col. 0627B] and builds for itself a nest of holy meditation by striving after the height of their strength [Note: [Col. 0627D] Thus the old manuscripts and editions read. Gilot, Vatican, Gussanville, and others have: “and by striving after the strength of their height.”]

When it silently considers their deeds and words, and reflects how low the glory of the present life is in comparison with eternal excellence, it observes, while dwelling in the rocks, that the low things of earth are beneath it.

[Old XXXV.] 98. By the name “rocks,” the powers of heaven are signified.—The lofty rocks may also be understood as the powers of the heavenly beings. These are no longer swayed here and there like trees by the wind of our mutability, because, situated like rocks in high places [Note: [Col. 0627D] Vindoc.: “in every respect.”], they are alien from every movement of mutability and, fixed in the solidity of their height, have endured through the very eternity to which they cling. Thus the holy man, when he despises earthly things, after the manner of an eagle suspends himself above higher things; and, lifted up by the spirit of contemplation, awaits the everlasting glory of the angels [Note: [Col. 0628D] The Vulgate manuscripts, with two German manuscripts, read: “and a guest in this world.”]. As a stranger in this world, by desiring what he sees, he is already fixed in the heights.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “He remains upon the rocks”; that is, in the intention of his heart he dwells among those heavenly virtues [Note: [Col. 0628D] Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts: “which through the strength of their eternity.”] which, through the strength of their eternity, are already fixed with such solidity that they are bent by no variation of mutability toward any side of sin [Col. 0627D]. Hence it appropriately follows:

CHAPTER XLIX.

SAME PASSAGE.—“And he dwells upon precipitous crags and inaccessible rocks.”

99. In Christ all things in heaven and on earth have been restored.—For what other precipitous crags are there except those very strong choirs of angels who, although not complete, nevertheless remained fixed in their own state when the devil fell with his angels? They are precipitous because one part of them fell while another remained. They stand whole [Note: [Col. 0628D] The same manuscripts: “they are.”] in the quality of their merit, but are precipitous in the quantity of their number.

The Mediator came to restore this breach, so that, when the human race had been redeemed, he might repair those angelic losses and perhaps enrich still more the measure of the heavenly homeland. Because of this breach it is said of the Father: “He purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, both those which are in heaven and those which are on earth, in him” (Eph. I, 9–10). For in him the things that are on earth are restored, when sinners are converted to righteousness. In him the things that are in heaven are restored, when humbled human beings return there from which the proud apostate angels fell.

But when he says, “Upon inaccessible rocks,” surely those that are precipitous crags are themselves inaccessible rocks [Col. 0628B]. The splendor of the angels is utterly inaccessible to the hearts of sinful human beings, because, in falling toward beautiful bodily things, the heart has closed its eyes to spiritual form. But whoever is so seized by contemplation that, lifted up by divine grace, he now inserts his intention among the choirs of angels, and, fixed in the heights, suspends himself from every lowly action [Note: [Col. 0628D] Two German manuscripts, Laud., the Norman manuscripts, and many others: “weak.”], is not satisfied to behold the glory of angelic brightness unless he can also see him who is above the angels. For his vision alone is the true refreshment of our mind.

Therefore, after saying that this eagle remains upon the rocks and dwells upon precipitous crags and inaccessible rocks, he immediately added:

CHAPTER L [Recension XX].

VERSE 29.—“From there he contemplates his food.”

[Col. 0628C] 100. The vision of God is the food of our mind.—That is, from those angelic choirs he directs the eye of his mind toward contemplating the glory of the heavenly majesty. Because he has not yet seen it, he hungers for it; once he has seen it, he is satisfied. For it is written: “Because his soul has labored, he shall see and be satisfied” (Isa. 53:11). And again: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V, 6).

What the food of our mind is, is plainly indicated when it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Ibid., 8). And because, burdened by the interposition of corruptible flesh, we cannot see God as he is, it is rightly added:

CHAPTER LI.

SAME PASSAGE.—“His eyes behold from afar.”

[Col. 0628D] 101. In this life we behold God only from afar.—However much anyone may have advanced while situated in this life, he does not yet see God in his true form, but through a mirror and in an enigma. When we look at something nearby, we see more truly; but when we extend our gaze farther away, we grow dim beneath an uncertain vision.

Since holy men therefore raise themselves into lofty contemplation, and yet cannot see God as he is, it is rightly said of this eagle: “His eyes behold from afar.” As if he were saying: “They stretch the gaze of their intention with strength, but they do not yet behold him near” [Note: [Col. 0629D] Vindoc., the German manuscripts, and most Norman manuscripts: “more closely”; Laud.: “nearby.”], whose immense brightness they are entirely unable to penetrate. For the darkness of our corruption obscures us from the incorruptible light [Note: [Col. 0629D] Pratel.: “by corruptible light.” Val. Cl.: “the darkness of our corruption is obscured.”]; and although that light can in some measure be seen, yet it cannot be seen as it is, and this shows how far away it is.

If the mind did not discern it in some fashion, it would not see that it was far away. But if it already discerned it perfectly, it would not see it, as it were, through a fog. Therefore, since it is neither wholly seen nor wholly unseen, it is rightly said that God is seen from afar.

102. Isaiah’s testimony on this subject. One ascends to the summit of contemplation by the stages of the active life.—It is useful to bring forward Isaiah’s words and to show that these statements and the others are uttered by one and the same Spirit [Col. 0629B] [Note: [Col. 0629D] The printed editions read “because [they are uttered] by one Spirit”; many printed copies also have “to investigate” instead of “to indicate.”].

When he was expressing the virtues of the active life, saying, “He who walks in righteousness and speaks the truth, who rejects avarice through oppression and shakes his hands free from every bribe, who stops his ears lest he hear of bloodshed and closes his eyes lest he see evil” (Isa. XXXIII, 15), he immediately added to what summits of contemplation one ascends by the stages of that same active life, saying: “This man shall dwell on high; the height of the fortifications of the rocks shall be his elevation; bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure. His eyes shall see the king in his beauty; they shall behold the land from afar” (Ibid., 16).

To dwell on high is to set the heart upon heavenly things. “The height of the fortifications of the rocks” is ours when we look to the commands and examples of strong fathers and separate ourselves from lowly thought [Col. 0629C]. “The height of the fortifications of the rocks” is ours when in mind we join ourselves to the heavenly choirs and camps, and, standing in the citadel of the heart, attack the malignant spirits lying in ambush, as though they had been placed beneath us.

Then bread is also given to us, because an intention raised toward the heights is refreshed by contemplation of eternity. Our waters are sure because the teaching of God gives there as a gift what it promises here through hope. The wisdom of this world is faithless, because it does not remain after death. Our waters are sure because the words of life reveal before death what they also display after death.

Our eyes behold the King in his beauty because our Redeemer will indeed be seen as a human being by the reprobate at the judgment, but only the elect are lifted up to behold the height of his divinity. To see only the servant’s form in which the King was despised by the wicked is, as it were, to see a kind of ugliness belonging to the King. But the King is seen in his beauty by the elect, because, carried beyond themselves, they fix the eyes of their hearts upon the radiance of his divinity.

And because, as long as they remain in this life, they cannot see the homeland of the living as it is, it is rightly added: “They shall behold the land from afar” (Ibid., 17).

What is said here, “The eagle shall be lifted up and shall set its nest in high places,” is said there as, “He shall dwell on high.” What is said here, “He remains upon the rocks and dwells upon precipitous crags and inaccessible rocks” [Note: [Col. 0630D] Laud.: “upon lofty rocks.”], is there expressed as, “The height of the fortifications of the rocks shall be his elevation.” What is added here, “From there he contemplates his food,” is also added there: “Bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure; his eyes shall see the King in his beauty.” And what is added here, “His eyes behold from afar,” is aptly added there: “They shall behold the land from afar.”

[Old XXXVI.] 103. How lofty an eagle Paul was.—Let us consider how lofty an eagle Paul was, for he flew up to the third heaven (II Cor. XII, 2); yet, situated in this life, he still beheld God from afar, saying: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12). And again: “I do not consider that I have apprehended it” [Note: [Col. 0630D] Val. Cl.: “grasped it.”] (Phil. III, 13).

Although he sees eternal things far less than they are, and although he knows that he cannot understand them perfectly, nevertheless he cannot pour into weak hearers by preaching those very things which he is at least able to see through a mirror and in an image. For he speaks of himself as though of another, saying: “He heard secret words which it is not permitted to a human being to speak” (II Cor. XII, 4).

Thus, although the inner realities may appear least and most remote, they are nevertheless supreme for strong preachers, while weak hearers are incapable of receiving them. Therefore holy preachers, when they see that their hearers cannot grasp the word of divinity, descend to the words of the Lord’s incarnation alone. Hence, while the eagle lifted up into high places is said to see from afar [Note: [Col. 0630D] Vindoc., Pratel., and many Norman manuscripts: “from afar.”], it is immediately added [Col. 0630C]:

CHAPTER LII [Recension XXI].

VERSE 30.—“Its young ones lick blood.”

104. We must be nourished by meditation on Christ’s Passion.—As if it were plainly said: “The eagle itself is nourished by contemplation of his divinity; but because its hearers cannot grasp the mysteries of his divinity, they are satisfied when they learn the blood of the crucified Lord.”

To lick blood is to venerate the weakness of the Lord’s Passion. Hence that same Paul, who, as we said shortly before, had flown to the secrets of the third heaven, said to his disciples: “For I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II, 2).

As if this eagle were plainly saying: “I indeed behold from afar the power of his divinity as my food, but to you, who are still little ones, I offer only the blood of his incarnation to lick.” For one who, through his preaching, teaches weak hearers only the blood of the cross, while keeping silent about the lofty divinity, what else does he provide for his young than blood?

Because, however, the soul of each holy preacher, once freed from the corruption of the flesh, is immediately led to him who willingly fell into death for us and rose from death, it is aptly added concerning this eagle:

CHAPTER LIII.

[Col. 0631A]

SAME PASSAGE.—“And wherever the carcass is, it is immediately present.”

105. Christ, reigning in heaven, gathers the elect to himself.—A carcass is so called from falling. And not without reason is the Lord’s body called a carcass because of the fall of death. [Rec. XXII.] What is said here of this eagle—“Wherever the carcass is, it is immediately present” (Matt. XXIV, 28)—the Truth promised would happen concerning departing souls, saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered.”

As if he plainly said: “I, your Redeemer, who was incarnate and preside over the heavenly throne, will also raise the souls of the elect, once I have released them from the flesh, to heavenly things.”

[Old XXXVII.] 106. Every sinner is a carcass; to it the eagles fly—namely, pious preachers hungering for the salvation of sinners. This was the reason for Paul’s flight as he traversed the world.—But what is said of this eagle—“Wherever the carcass is, it is immediately present”—may also be understood in another way.

Everyone who has fallen into the death of sin may appropriately be called a carcass. He lies as though lifeless who does not possess the life-giving spirit of righteousness. Therefore, because every holy preacher, wherever he sees sinners, flies there anxiously to show the light of life to those lying in the death of sin, it is rightly said of this eagle: “Wherever the carcass is, it is immediately present.” That is, he goes there [Note: [Col. 0631D] Laud., Val. Cl., the German manuscripts, and Vindoc.: “he tends there.”] where he foresees that preaching will be useful, so that, because he already lives spiritually, he may benefit those who lie in death. By rebuking them, he as it were devours them; but by changing them from iniquity to innocence, he converts them into his own members, as though by devouring them.

Behold Paul himself, whom we have already often brought forward as a witness: when he went now to Judea, now to Corinth, now to Ephesus, now to Rome, now to Spain, in order to announce the grace of eternal life to those lying in the death of sin, what else did he show himself to be than an eagle? Flying swiftly over all these places, it sought wherever a carcass lay, so that, when it accomplished the will of God by winning sinners, it might find its food in the carcass, as it were.

The food of the righteous is the conversion of the wicked, concerning which it is said: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John VI, 27).

Having heard, therefore, of the virtues of so many saints, blessed Job is understood to have been struck with amazement and to have fallen silent in the terror of wonder. For it follows:

CHAPTER LIV [Recension XXIII].

VERSES 31, 32.—“The Lord continued and spoke to Job: Does he who contends with God so easily become silent? Surely he who reproves God ought also to answer him.”

107. God’s rebuke of Job is pious and measured.—The holy man did not think that such severity of affliction increased his merits, but rather cut away his faults. Since he recognized no faults in himself, he believed that he had been struck unjustly; and to accuse the one who struck him is plainly to murmur about the affliction.

But the Lord, considering that Job had spoken not from the swelling of pride but from the quality of his life, piously rebukes him, saying: “Does he who contends with God so easily become silent? Surely he who reproves God ought also to answer him.”

As if he were saying more plainly: “You who have spoken so much about your conduct—why did you fall silent when you heard the life of the saints? For you accused me by doubting whether my affliction had been just. You have truly recounted your good deeds, but you did not know toward what purpose those scourges tended. For although you no longer have anything that needs correction, you still have something in which to grow.

You have learned, with me recounting it, to what a citadel of virtue I raise so many others. You considered your own height, but you did not know the height of others. Having heard, then, of the virtues of others, answer concerning your own, if you are able.”

We know, however, that the one who, while doing what is right, neglects to consider the merits of those who are better extinguishes the eye of his heart through the darkness of pride. [Col. 0632C] By contrast, he illuminates his works with a great ray of humility who carefully weighs the good deeds of others, because, when he sees outside himself and accomplished by others what he himself has done, he suppresses the swelling of pride that strives to burst forth within him from a sense of uniqueness.

Hence God’s voice says to Elijah, who thought that he alone remained: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed their knees before Baal” (III Kings XIX, 18), so that, when he recognized that he was not the only one left, he might avoid the glory of pride that could arise in him from his supposed uniqueness.

Blessed Job, therefore, is not reproved for having acted perversely; rather, he is taught about the good deeds of others [Note: [Col. 0631D] Laud., the German manuscripts, and Val. Cl.: “he is found.”], so that, when he considers that he has equals and others, he may humbly submit himself to the one who alone is supreme.

BOOK THIRTY-TWO.

After the final two verses of chapter XXXIX have been explained, the first fourteen verses of chapter XL are expounded; and much is taught both about the infinite power of God and about Satan’s harmful designs against human beings.

[Col. 0631]

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0631D]

1. The holier the saints become, the more unworthy they appear to themselves.—The more holy men advance before God in the dignity of virtue, the more subtly they discover themselves to be unworthy, because, as they draw nearer to the light, they find whatever had been hidden within them. Thus they appear all the more deformed outwardly the more exceedingly beautiful is what they see within [Note: [Col. 0631D] The older and newer printed editions read, “the less beautiful.” This is a grave error, which we corrected by attending especially to the Norman and Turonian manuscripts, Laud., two German manuscripts, and the sense intended by the holy Doctor. For he is speaking of the divine light—what could be more beautiful?].

For each person is shown to himself when illuminated by contact with the true light; and from the point at which he recognizes what righteousness is, he is instructed to see what guilt is.

Hence it often happens that, although our mind grows cold and sluggish in the activity of human conduct, although it commits faults in certain matters without knowing it, and although it considers certain sins almost nothing, yet, when it raises itself toward higher things through the compunction of prayer, awakened by the eye of its own compunction, it returns after weeping more vigilant in examining itself.

For when it abandons itself as neglected and grows numb in harmful tepidity, it considers idle words or useless thoughts to be of scarcely any guilt. But if, growing warm with the fire of compunction and touched suddenly by the breath of contemplation, it awakens from its tepidity [Note: [Col. 0633D] Thus the English and Norman manuscripts; the Vulgate manuscripts, with two German manuscripts: “from its sluggishness.”], it immediately dreads as grave and deadly the things it had shortly before considered trivial [Col. 0633B].

For it flees everything harmful, even in the smallest matters, as though it were most atrocious, because, pregnant, so to speak, with the conception of the spirit [Note: [Col. 0633D] Corb., the German manuscript, and the ancient Gemeticensis manuscript, which contains the four final books of the Moralia: “through contemplation.”], it now permits no empty thing to enter into it. From what it sees within, it perceives how dreadful are the things that rage outwardly; and the more it advances by being lifted up, the more it flees the lowly things in which, when prostrate, it had failed.

Nothing nourishes it except what it had seen within; and it bears whatever is thrust upon it from outside all the more heavily because that is not what it saw within. Rather, from those inner realities which it was able to glimpse in passing, it takes the standard by which to judge the outward things it endures.

It is carried above itself while it contemplates higher things; and, now seeing itself more freely by surpassing itself [Note: [Col. 0634D] Gemeticensis and Corb. Germanus: “by ascending.”], it understands more subtly whatever remains of itself beneath itself [Col. 0633C].

From this it comes about, in a wondrous way, that, as was said above, the more worthy a person becomes, the more unworthy he appears to himself; and he then feels himself far from righteousness when he is drawing near to it.

Hence Solomon says: “I tested all things in wisdom, and I said, ‘I shall become wise’; but it withdrew farther from me” (Eccl. VII, 24). Wisdom is said to withdraw farther when it is sought because it appears higher to one who approaches it.

Those who do not seek it, however, consider themselves all the nearer to it because they are ignorant of its rule of righteousness. Living in darkness, they do not know how to admire the brightness of the light they have never seen; and, since they are not stretched toward the form of its beauty, they willingly become more deformed in themselves each day.

For whoever is touched by its rays has his own crookedness shown to him more clearly; and the more keenly he considers the highest things, the more truly he discovers how far he is bent in vice from what is straight.

Hence blessed Job, surpassing the human race in virtues, overcame his friends in speech; but, when God spoke and he was more sublimely instructed, he fell silent as he came to know himself. He condemned them for speaking unjustly, but rightly recognized himself as guilty in the innermost meaning of the words.

Indeed, he does not know why he was scourged; yet, by his silence, he reproves himself for not having revered the scourges. For when divine judgments are unknown, they should not be examined through bold speech but revered in fearful silence. When the Creator does not disclose the reasons for his actions in affliction, he thereby indicates them to be just, inasmuch as the one who is supremely just is shown to have inflicted them.

Let the holy man, therefore, reproved first for his speech and afterward for his silence, make known what he thinks about himself. For he says:

CHAPTER II.

CHAPTER XXXIX, VERSE 34.—“Since I have spoken lightly, what can I answer?”

2. Not even the saints can excuse themselves for an idle word. But they strive to cover the faults of the tongue with the merits of their life.—As if he were saying: “I would defend my speech if I had uttered it with the weight of reason. But after my tongue has been proved to have acted frivolously, what remains except that it be restrained by silence?” It follows:

SAME PASSAGE.—“I will place my hand upon my mouth.”

According to the usage of sacred eloquence, the hand commonly signifies action, and the mouth speech. Therefore, to place the hand upon the mouth is to cover the faults of careless speech by the virtue of good works [Note: [Col. 0634D] Laud.: “to wipe away the faults.”].

Who can be found who, however perfect he may be, does not sin at least in idle speech? James bears witness, saying: “Do not become teachers in great numbers, for we all offend in many things” (James III, 1). And again: “No human being can tame the tongue” (Ibid., 8).

The Truth himself, rebuking the tongue’s faults, says: “I tell you that for every idle word which people have spoken, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII, 36).

But holy men strive before the eyes of God to cover the faults of the tongue with the merits of their life; they strive to weigh down immoderate words with the burden of good works. Hence, in holy Church, the hand is placed over the mouth when, among God’s elect, the vice of idle speech is daily covered by the virtue of good action.

For it is written: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). But again, since it is written, “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13), how can those things be covered which cannot be hidden from his eyes, to whom all things are naked?

But because we place beneath what we cover, and draw over it that with which we cover it, we are said to cover sins when we place them beneath, as it were, by renouncing them, and draw something else over them by afterward choosing the work of good action in order to set it before them.

Therefore, whoever abandons his former evils and afterward does good deeds covers the wickedness that has passed by what he adds, drawing over it the merits of good works.

Blessed Job, therefore, bearing the type of holy Church, and speaking in his own words while representing ours, may say from himself and from us: “I will place my hand upon my mouth”; that is: “What I perceive to have displeased the strict Judge in my speech, I conceal before his eyes beneath the covering of righteous action.”

It follows:

CHAPTER III.

[Col. 0635A]

VERSE 35.—“I have spoken once; would that I had not said it; and a second time, to which I will add no more.”

3. Job humbly confesses to God, who rebukes him, that he has sinned.—If we examine the past words of blessed Job, we find that he said nothing wicked. But if we bend his words, which were uttered truthfully and freely, toward some fault of pride, they will no longer be only two, for they will be many.

Yet because our human speech consists in making an inner meaning known to other human beings through words, while speech addressed to divine ears consists in displaying the movement of the mind even through the expression of action, blessed Job, weighing himself on the scale of the most subtle examination, confesses that he sinned twice in his speech.

One illicit speech consists in doing things deserving of punishment; another speech consists in murmuring even about the punishment.
