Thus the man who, before the Lord’s rebuke, had been superior to others in every work, made progress through that very lofty rebuke and recognized himself as less upright previously in his conduct and afterward less patient under the blow.

Hence he reproves himself, saying: “I have spoken once, would that I had not said it; and a second time, to which I will add no more” [Note: [Col. 0635D] Gemeticensis and the German manuscripts: “I will not add.”].

As if he were saying: “I thought myself righteous among human beings; but when you spoke, I discovered myself perverse before the scourges and unyielding after the scourges. I will add no more, because the more subtly I now understand you speaking, the more humbly I examine myself.”

[Old II, Recension IV.] 4. The objects of repentance are neglected good deeds and committed evils. The active life belongs to many; the contemplative life to few.—And because blessed Job bears the type of holy Church [Col. 0635C], these words of his can apply to all the elect, who, as they come to know the Lord, recognize that they have sinned in one way and another, because they understand that they have sinned either in thought and action or by neglecting love of God and neighbor.

They promise that they will add nothing further, because through the grace of conversion they take care by repentance to cleanse daily even what has already passed [Note: [Col. 0635D] Gemeticensis: “they hasten by repenting.”].

By the fact that blessed Job reproves himself repentantly for two things, he clearly shows that every sinner ought to have a twofold lament in repentance: namely, because he failed to do the good that he ought to have done and did the evil that he ought not to have done.

Hence Moses says concerning one who made an oath to do either evil or good and then passed over the matter itself through forgetfulness: “Let him offer a lamb from the flocks, or a she-goat, and the priest shall pray for him [Col. 0635D] and for his sin. But if he is unable to offer an animal, let him offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering” (Lev. V, 6–8).

To make an oath is to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service [Note: [Col. 0635D] Val. Cl. and Gemeticensis: “to bind ourselves to divine service.”]. When we promise good works, we pledge that we will do good. But when we vow abstinence and the mortification of our flesh, we swear that, for the present, we will do what is harsh to ourselves.

Yet no one in this life is so perfect that, however devoted he may be to God, he does not sin amid even the smallest [Note: [Col. 0635D] The recent edition reads “however great,” which seems better if the phrase refers to pious vows, but not if it refers to the avoidance of sin.] pious vows. Therefore, a lamb from the flocks or a she-goat is prescribed to be offered for sin.

For what is signified by the lamb if not the innocence of the active life? And what by the she-goat, which often feeds while hanging upon the highest and most remote crags, if not the contemplative life?

Whoever therefore sees that he has failed to fulfill what he promised and proposed should apply himself more diligently to God’s sacrifice, either through the innocence of good works or through the lofty nourishment of contemplation.

And rightly is a lamb from the flocks prescribed, while a she-goat is not prescribed from the flocks, because the active life belongs to many, but the contemplative life to few.

When we do what we see many doing and having done, we give, as it were, a lamb from the flocks. But when the strength of the one offering is insufficient for a lamb and a she-goat [Note: [Col. 0635D] Laud.: “is not sufficient to offer a lamb …”], two young pigeons or two turtledoves are added as a remedy for the penitent.

We know that young pigeons or turtledoves have lamentation as their song. What, then, is signified by two young pigeons or two turtledoves except the twofold lament of our repentance? When we do not rise to offer good works, we should bewail ourselves in two ways, because we have failed to do what was right and have practiced what was wrong.

Hence one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is so called because it is wholly burned. We offer one turtledove for sin when we give a lament for our guilt; but from the other we make a burnt offering when, for having neglected good things, we kindle ourselves completely [Note: [Col. 0636D] Others: “setting ourselves aflame.”] and burn with the fire of sorrow.

Since, therefore, a twofold lament is owed in repentance, blessed Job, advancing through the rebuke of the divine voice and growing through his own reproach, confesses in repentance that he spoke once and a second time, as if he were plainly saying: “I grew sluggish toward good things through negligence, and I rushed toward evil through presumption.”

CHAPTER XL, VERSES 1, 2.—“And the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said: Gird up your loins like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me.”

[Old III, Recension V.] What it means for the Lord to answer from the whirlwind, what it means for blessed Job to gird his loins, what it means for God to question and for a human being to answer, has already been treated in the Lord’s first speech (above, Book XXVIII, no. 1 and following). Therefore, to spare the reader’s weariness, we take the greatest care not to repeat what has already been said. It follows:

CHAPTER IV.

[Col. 0636D]

VERSE 3.—“Will you make my judgment void, and condemn me so that you may be justified?”

1049 5. Job is rightly rebuked, so that, even without knowing them, he may submit to God’s hidden judgments.—Whoever strives to defend himself against the Lord’s scourges attempts to nullify the judgment of the one who scourges him. For when he denies that he is struck because of his guilt, what else does he accuse the one who strikes him of than injustice? [Note: [Col. 0636D] Vindoc., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts, with the same sense: “since he says that he is struck not because of his own fault.”]

Blessed Job was not struck by heavenly scourges in order to extinguish faults in him, but rather to increase his merits, so that he who had shone with such holiness in a time of peace might also reveal, through the affliction, what virtue of patience lay hidden within him.

Finding no fault of his own amid the scourges, and nevertheless failing to recognize that those same scourges were the cause of an increase in merit, he believed that he was struck unjustly, since he found nothing in himself that ought to be corrected.

But lest that very innocence be inflated into the swelling of pride, he is rebuked by the divine voice. His mind, free from iniquity but pressed down by blows, is recalled to hidden judgments, so that, although the heavenly sentence is not understood, it may nevertheless not be considered unjust. Rather, he should believe everything he suffers to be just, at least because it is evident that he suffers by God’s agency.

For the just will of the Creator is a great justification of the blow. Since it is accustomed to do nothing unjust, it is recognized as just even when it remains hidden. When we are struck for the sin of injustice, if in our affliction we unite ourselves to the divine will, we are immediately freed from our injustice by that very union.

Whoever now endures the blow but is still ignorant of its causes, if, believing it just, he embraces this judgment against himself, is thereby already corrected from his injustice, because he rejoices that he has been justly struck.

For by joining himself to God in his punishment, he rises against himself; and it is already a great justice that he agrees with the will of the Judge in his penalty, though he had disagreed with it in his guilt.

The holy man, therefore, because he had not disagreed with God through any fault [Note: [Col. 0637D] Gemeticensis and Corb. Germanus: “in no fault from God.”], was, as it were, with difficulty brought into agreement with him amid punishments. For he did not believe that the scourges which usually extinguish vices increased merits alone in his case.

Hence he is now rightly rebuked, so that, even without knowing them, he may submit to hidden judgments, and it is said to him: “Will you make my judgment void and condemn me so that you may be justified?”

As if it were plainly said: “You consider your good deeds, but you do not know my hidden judgments. If, therefore, you argue against my scourges on the basis of your merits, what else do you do than hasten to accuse me of injustice by justifying yourself?” [Note: [Col. 0637D] From this passage alone the meaning of the verb *addicere* can be understood; we discussed it in Book II, no. 15, and elsewhere.]

It follows:

CHAPTER V [Old IV, Recension VI].

VERSE 4.—“Have you an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like his?”

6. Even the holiest are summoned to humility when God’s holiness is contemplated.—Because blessed Job surpassed the human race in merits, the pious Creator and Teacher summons him to consider the likeness of his own greatness, so that, once he has recognized such a great dissimilarity, he may humble himself.

### 7. God, although without a body, is compared with bodily things. The heresy of the Anthropomorphites. Why eyes and shoulders are attributed to God. In what sense “to remember” is said. What God’s wings signify.

But when a voice and an arm are spoken of in God, we must take the greatest care lest the mind suspect anything corporeal in him. For it is to fall into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites to confine within bodily outlines him who, without limitation, fills and encompasses all things. Yet almighty God, drawing us toward himself, humbles himself even to the level of our condition; and, in order to convey lofty truths, he condescends to lowly things, so that the mind of the little ones, nourished by familiar matters, may rise to seek what is unfamiliar. Thus, hearing from him who is far above it certain things that are, as it were, close to it, the mind may move toward him by successive steps. Hence, through his Scripture, he sometimes draws into himself certain wholly dissimilar likenesses from human bodies, sometimes from minds, sometimes from birds, and sometimes even from inanimate things.

Often he draws into himself a likeness from human bodies, as when the prophet says to the Israelites concerning him: “He who touches you touches the apple of his eye” (Zech. II, 8). And again, speaking through the prophet to a person who hopes in him, it is said: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders” (Ps. XC, 4). It is certainly clear that by his nature God has neither an eye nor shoulders; but because we see with the eye, while on the shoulders we bear burdens, God is said to have an eye because he sees everything, and to overshadow us with his shoulders because he tolerates us and, by that very tolerance, preserves us. For he says: “He has overshadowed you with his shoulders.” It is as though he were saying to the sinful person who, after sinning, begs for forgiveness: “The Lord protects you with the same mercy with which he has tolerated you.” He overshadows with his shoulders because, while he carries us, he defends us.

Sometimes he draws a likeness from minds, as when he says through the prophet to Israel: “I remembered you, having pity on your youth” (Jer. II, 2). [Note: Val. Cl. has “having compassion on your youth.”] And again, speaking by comparison with a bride, he says: “And even if she should forget, I nevertheless will not forget you” (Isa. XLIX, 15). For who does not know that God’s memory is neither broken by forgetfulness nor repaired by remembering? Yet when, abandoning something, he passes it over, he is said to forget in the manner of human minds; and when, after a long time, he visits what he wishes, he is called “remembering,” according to the custom of our mutability.

For how can forgetfulness dissipate the power of his divinity, with which even that praiseworthy memory itself does not essentially accord? [Note: The older Vulgate manuscripts, together with two German manuscripts, read “essentially accords with memory.” Gregory’s thought is that neither the term “forgetfulness” nor the term “memory” properly applies to God. Therefore “does not accord” should be read, as is found in all the English, Norman, Vindocian, Laudian, and other manuscripts.] Only things either past or absent are remembered. How, then, does God remember things past, when even those things which pass away in themselves always stand present before his will? Or how does he remember things absent, when everything that exists is present to him through the fact that it exists in him? If it were not present to him, it would not exist at all; for by seeing, he creates what does not exist, and by seeing, he sustains what exists. Whatever, therefore, the Creator does not see lacks the essence by which it subsists.

Sometimes, moreover, a likeness is drawn from birds, as it is said through Moses: “He spread out his wings and took them up” (Deut. XXXII, 11). [Note: Laud., Val. Cl., two German manuscripts, and most Norman manuscripts read: “and he took them up.”] And the prophet says: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVI, 9). Because, when he protects us as little ones, he nourishes us, and because, when he extends his mercies over us, he refreshes us with a protection that is not burdensome and oppressive but light and gentle, he stretches his wings over us, as birds do.

At times he even compares himself, in lofty condescension and because of our weakness, with inanimate things, as he says through the prophet: [Note: The word “lofty” (*alta*) is absent from Laud. and Val. Cl.] “Behold, I will creak over you as a wagon creaks beneath a load of hay” (Amos II, 13). For since the life of those who live according to the flesh is hay, as it is written, “All flesh is hay” (Isa. XL, 6), the Lord bears witness that, in tolerating the life of the carnal, he carries hay as a wagon does. For a wagon to creak beneath a load of hay is for him to endure, with complaint, the burdens and iniquities of sinners.

Since, then, he draws into himself wholly dissimilar likenesses, we must carefully observe that some such things are spoken of God at times with reference to the effect of his work, and at times to indicate the substance of his majesty. When an eye, shoulders, a foot, and wings are mentioned in God, the effect of his operation is indicated. [Note: The word “foot” is omitted in the edition; we have supplied it from the Vindocian, Norman, and other manuscripts. In the Corbie German manuscript, “and wings” is read as “and other things.”] But when a hand, an arm, a right hand, or a voice is spoken of in God, by these terms the Son, consubstantial with him, is demonstrated.

For he himself is the hand and the right hand, of whose ascent Moses records the Father saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand” (Deut. XXXII, 40). He is the arm of whom the prophet says: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). He is the voice, because in begetting him the Father spoke: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7). And of him it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). By this Word, David asserts, the Father made all things, saying: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII, 9).

Therefore, for God to have an arm is for him to beget the Son who acts; for him to thunder with his voice is for him to reveal to the world, with terror, the Son consubstantial with himself. Accordingly, when the Lord says to blessed Job, “If you have an arm like God, and if you thunder with a voice like his,” he exalts him while reproving him, by a wonderful dispensation of mercy: for by showing that he surpasses him through comparison with himself, he demonstrates that Job is superior to all others. To this he adds in the following statement:

### CHAPTER VI [Rec. VII]

**VERSE 5.**—“Gird yourself with beauty, and rise up to the heights, and be glorious, and clothe yourself in splendid garments.”

### 8. The angels and the Church are God’s beauty and adornment.

Understand: “as I do.” For he himself girds himself with beauty, of whom it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. XCII, 1). He himself is raised up among us when he is shown to be, in his nature, incomprehensible to our minds. He himself is glorious, because, while he enjoys himself, he has no need of praise added from elsewhere. He clothes himself in splendid garments because he has taken the choirs of the holy angels whom he created for the use of his own beauty, and he presents the Church to himself like a glorious garment, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27).

Hence it is said to him through the prophet: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed in light as with a garment” (Ps. CIII, 2). Here he puts on confession; there, beauty: for those whom here he makes confessing through repentance, there he will display shining through the beauty of righteousness. He is therefore clothed in light as with a garment, because he will be clothed in that eternal glory with all the saints to whom it was said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). Hence it is also said through the Gospel that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, his garments became white as snow (Matt. XVII, 2). What else is announced in this transfiguration than the glory of the final resurrection? On the mountain his garments became like snow because, at the summit of heavenly brightness, all the saints will cleave to him, shining with the light of righteousness.

[Vet. VI.] But because, under the name of splendid garments, he indicates how he joins the righteous to himself, he also shows how he separates the unrighteous from himself. It follows:

### CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 6.**—“Scatter the proud in your fury.”

### 9. God is angry without disturbance.

Understand: “as I do,” for I tolerate those who are united against me in a time of tranquillity, and, coming one day in severity, I scatter them in my fury. But here we must carefully observe that a grave error of unbelief is committed if anyone supposes that fury and tranquillity vary in that substance of divinity. The Creator of all is supremely immortal precisely because he is not mutable after the manner of creatures. Hence James says of him: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration” (James I, 17). Again it is written: “But you, Lord, judge with tranquillity” (Wis. XII, 18). And the prophet says: “The land has been made desolate before the face of the anger of the dove, before the face of the fury of the Lord” (Jer. XXV, 38). [Note: We have also added “for,” following the Vindocian, Gemetian, Corbie German, and several Norman manuscripts.]

What he had called the anger of the dove, he then called the fury of the Lord. The dove is a very gentle animal; and because no inequality of fury creeps into God, he called the fury of the Lord the anger of the dove. In order to show the unshaken force of divine severity, he spoke both of anger and of the dove, as though he were saying more openly: “He exercises a severe judgment without disturbance, remaining gentle while he punishes the unrighteous.” [Note: “The unrighteous” is absent from two German manuscripts, the Turonian, Laudian, and most Norman manuscripts.]

Thus, even at the final judgment, while remaining unchangeable in himself, he is not altered by any variation or mutability; yet he will not appear under the same aspect of unchangeableness to the elect and the reprobate, because he will appear tranquil to the righteous and angry to the unrighteous. Their conscience bears witness within them: they behold one and the same being, but they are not affected by him in the same way, because their former righteousness shows him as kind to some, while guilt shows him as terrible to others.

Who could describe their terror when the wretched come both to see their sins within themselves and to behold before them a just judge? This is enacted daily in the practice of our present life, so that mortal hearts may be instructed concerning the character of the coming judge. When two people go to judgment, one conscious of innocence, the other of guilt, both see the judge still silent before the sentence is pronounced; yet the one who owes a debt of guilt supposes that this very silence of the judge expresses heavy anger against him.

This anger is not announced to him by any disturbance in the judge, but by the recollection of his wrongdoing. For although the sentence does not yet cry out externally that he is guilty, his conscience nevertheless accuses him gravely within. In contrast, the friend of righteousness looks upon the face of the one who is about to decide, but within he rejoices in the testimony of a good memory; and because he has nothing within himself to fear, he sees everything concerning himself as gracious.

In this passage, therefore, the fury of the Lord does not mean disturbance in the divine substance, but the examination of just vengeance directed against sinners who are conscious of their own evil. Although they see him tranquil in judgment, nevertheless, because they do not doubt that they will be struck by him, they suppose him disturbed in their own agitations. [Note: The printed editions, together with the German manuscripts, read “in their ways” or “in his ways.” The Corbie German manuscript reads “in their deaths.” Our reading is supplied by the Turonian, Vindocian, Val-Cluse, Pratel, and several Norman manuscripts.]

It follows:

### CHAPTER VIII

**THE SAME.**—“And looking upon every arrogant person, humble him.”

### 10. Every arrogant person either recognizes guilt through repentance or experiences punishment through ruin.

As though he were saying: “as I do.” Appropriately, in the order of vengeance, the guilt of the proud is placed before the arrogant, because pride is not generated from arrogance, but arrogance is generated from pride. [The Latin distinguishes *superbia* and *arrogantia*.] Each sinner is looked upon by the Lord in two ways: either when he is converted from sin, or when he is punished because of sin.

Of the look of conversion it is said: “The Lord looked upon Peter, and Peter, remembering the word of Jesus, wept bitterly” (Luke XXII, 61). [Note: In two German manuscripts and in Gemet., “the word of Jesus” is omitted.] Of the look of retribution it is again said: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. XXXIII, 17). In both ways the arrogant person is laid low: either he recognizes his guilt through repentance, or he experiences punishment through ruin.

### CHAPTER IX [Vet. VII]

**VERSE 7.**—“Look upon all the proud, and confound them, and crush the wicked in their place.”

### 11. The proud are cast down even as they are raised up.

Understand: “as I do.” The proud are confounded by the Lord’s look, either here, when through mercy they recognize and condemn their crimes, or there, when through justice they experience punishment. The place of the wicked is pride itself, because, since it is written, “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccli. X, 15), impiety is contained where it arises, although impiety is not at all distinct from pride. For it is extreme pride to think impiously about the Creator.

The wicked person, therefore, is crushed in his own place, because the very pride by which he is lifted up is pressed down; and when he raises himself in his thoughts by exalting himself, he hides from himself the light of righteousness that he ought to have found. Often, while false glory advances outwardly against God, true misery inwardly grows empty. Hence the prophet says: “You have cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Ps. LXXII, 18). [Note: Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts read “were being raised up.”] He does not say, “You cast them down after they had been lifted up,” but “while they were being lifted up,” because this itself is the inward downfall of the proud: that false glory comes to them outwardly as elevation.

By divine judgment, their guilt here is not one thing and their punishment another; rather, their guilt is turned into punishment for them. Thus, when they are lifted up by the arrogance of pride, the very thing that appears outwardly as advancement is truly an inward fall. It follows:

### CHAPTER X

**VERSE 8.**—“Hide them in the dust, and at the same time plunge their faces into the pit.”

### 12. God permits the hearts of the proud to be oppressed by earthly affairs and desires.

As though he were saying: “as I do.” By a just judgment the Lord hides the proud and the wicked in the dust, because he permits their hearts to be oppressed by the earthly concerns they choose after scorning love of the Creator. Hence, when at the final judgment he examines their life, he does not acknowledge it, as though it were hidden from him, saying: “I do not know who you are” (Luke XIII, 27).

The life of the wicked is hidden beneath dust because it is weighed down by base and lowly desires. Whoever still desires the things of the world does not appear, as it were, before the face of the true light, because he lies hidden beneath the dust of earthly thought. The mind, oppressed by evil thoughts, endures this dust, which the wind of the most wicked temptation carries in.

[Vet. VIII.] Hence, concerning every soul weighed down by earthly desires, it is said through the prophet under the figure of Ephraim: “Ephraim has become bread baked under ashes, which is not turned” (Hos. VII, 8). By nature, an intention well formed within us is directed upward toward God; but through a way of life wickedly habituated, there is present a desire that presses us down into the present age. Bread baked under ashes is cleaner on the side it hides below and dirtier on the side where it bears the ashes above.

Whoever, therefore, neglects the intention by which he ought to have sought God presses the cleaner side downward, like bread baked under ashes; and when he willingly bears the cares of the world, he carries ashes heaped upon him. The bread baked under ashes would be turned if it cast off the ashes of carnal desires and brought upward the good intention that it had previously suppressed by despising it. But it refuses to turn when the mind, weighed down by love of worldly cares, neglects to throw off the mass of ashes placed upon it; and, because it does not desire to rise toward a good intention, it presses the cleaner side beneath.

### 13. While the proud seek higher things through pride, they are thrust back to lower things.

Appropriately it is added: “At the same time plunge their faces into the pit.” As though he were saying: “as I do.” By a just judgment the Lord plunges the faces of the proud into the pit, because he casts down the intention of their hearts, which raises itself above other human beings. For one whose face regards the pit looks toward low things.

It is rightly said of the proud that their faces are plunged into the pit, because they seek low things while, through pride, they desire higher things; and the more they raise themselves by exalting themselves, the more, by falling, they move downward. They seek earthly glory, and the things they look upon are low, while in their pride they pursue lofty things.

Thus, in a marvelous and opposite manner, matters are arranged: the humble seek heaven while casting themselves down; the proud seek low things while, by despising others, they exalt themselves as though in higher places. The former, by lowering themselves, are joined to heavenly things; the latter, by raising themselves, are separated from what is above. So, if I may put it this way, the latter lower themselves by lifting themselves up, while the former lift themselves up by lowering themselves.

The Psalmist rightly says of the proud: “But he humbles sinners down to the earth” (Ps. CXLVI, 6), because, by aspiring to what is below, they raise themselves up and, having lost heaven, what else do they seek but earth? For them, to have fallen already into the depths is precisely to have abandoned higher things and sought what is below. Their faces are therefore rightly said to be plunged into the pit, because, following low things, they move toward the abyss of hell.

It is justly ordained that those whom voluntary aversion blinds here should there be hidden from the sight of the true light by a pit worthy of their punishment. Since, therefore, the holy man was so shaken by terror of divine power that he was told, “If you have an arm like God, and if you thunder with a voice like his, scatter the proud in your fury, and, looking upon every arrogant person, humble him,” together with the other things that God can do but a human being scarcely suffices even to hear, he shows at the end of his concluding statement with what intention the Lord had prefaced all this, saying: [Note: Corbie German and Gemet. read “with what intention the Lord had [said] these things.”]

### CHAPTER XI [Vet. IX, Rec. VIII]

**VERSE 9.**—“And I will confess that your right hand can save you.”

### 14. The error of the Pelagians, who are confident that they can be saved by their own powers.

As though he were saying more openly: “If you can do these terrifying things, I attribute to you, and not to me, all the good things you have done. But if, by looking upon others who sin, you cannot destroy them, it is clear that you cannot free yourself from the guilt of wickedness by your own power.”

Behold, by the divine voice blessed Job is told that he will not be saved by his own right hand; [Note: Vindocian and Norman manuscripts read “by his own power.”] yet some people, who are far inferior to this man in strength, despise God’s help and trust that they can be saved by their own strength. For them, what else ought we to pray than that, if they have already received the gifts of good works, they may also receive this gift: that they learn from whom they received them?

Since the Lord has introduced the power of his greatness in the words just spoken, he now reveals, in what follows, the wickedness of the ancient enemy, so that the good servant, having first heard of the Lord’s virtues, might know how greatly to love him and, having afterward learned the devil’s craft, might learn how greatly to fear him.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “The lion will roar; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?” (Amos III, 8). [The supplied text has an OCR-corrupted form, “ocutus”; the sense requires “has spoken.”] Once the power of his Creator had become known to him, the adversary’s strength ought by no means to remain hidden from him, so that he might submit more humbly to his defender, the more subtly he recognized the wickedness of his enemy, and seek his protector with that much greater eagerness, the more terrible he recognized the enemy whom he was to avoid.

It is certain that the person who understands less clearly the danger from which he has been rescued loves his rescuer less, and considers the defender’s consolation of little value if he thinks his adversary’s power weak. Hence, rightly attributing his rescue to the Lord, the prophet said: “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. XVII, 1), plainly saying: “I love you all the more because, recognizing my own weakness, I know that you are my strength.”

Again he says: “Make your mercies wonderful, you who save those who hope in you” (Ps. XVI, 7), because the Lord’s mercies become truly wonderful to us who are rescued when, through those same mercies, we recognize how grave were the dangers we escaped.

### 15. The powers and frauds of our enemy are described.

Because in the preceding discourse the Lord disclosed to blessed Job the wondrous works of the saints who follow him, so that, hearing these things, Job might learn from the height of their virtues how humbly he himself ought to think, the Lord now shows him against what enemy he wages war and more subtly indicates that enemy’s powers and frauds. Thus the faithful servant, who has been brought into conversation with his Creator, may openly recognize the adversary’s devices.

In the following words the Lord discloses to his faithful servant all the schemes of the crafty enemy: everything he seizes by oppressing, everything around which he circles in ambush, everything by which he terrifies through threats, everything by which he flatters through persuasion, everything by which he breaks through despair, and everything by which he deceives through promises. He therefore begins the entire struggle of his evasions, saying:

### CHAPTER XII [Vet. X, Rec. IX]

**VERSE 10.**—“Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you.”

[Note: In Val. Cl. and two German manuscripts, *Vehemoth* is written everywhere. The same reading occurs in Gemet.]

### 16. All things were created together according to substance, but not according to form.

Whom does he indicate under the name Behemoth except the ancient enemy, who, interpreted from the Hebrew word, means “animal” in Latin? His person is clearly shown below, when his wickedness is described.

But since it is written of God that he made all things together (Eccli. XVIII, 1), why does he indicate that he made this animal with man, when it is clear that he made all things together? Again, we must ask how God created all things together, when Moses describes them as created distinctly through the changing sequence of six days (Gen. I, 32).

We recognize this more readily, however, if we investigate carefully the causes of origins. [Note: Gemet. reads “we indicate” rather than “we investigate.”] The substance of things was created together, but their forms were not formed together; and what existed together in the substance of matter did not appear together in the form of its outward shape.

When heaven and earth are described as having been made together, this indicates that spiritual and bodily things were made together, that everything arising from heaven was made together, and that everything produced from the earth was made together. The sun, moon, and stars are said to have been made in heaven on the fourth day; but what proceeded in form on the fourth day already existed on the first day in the substance of heaven by the act of creation.

The earth is said to have been created on the first day, while on the third day plants and all the earth’s vegetation are described as having been made. Yet what came forth in form on the third day had certainly been created on the first day in the substance of the earth from which it arose.

Hence Moses reported that all things were created distinctly on separate days, and yet added that they were all created together, saying: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth and every plant of the field, before it sprang up in the earth, and every herb of the region” (Gen. II, 4–5).

He who had narrated that heaven and earth, plants, and herbs were created on different days now reveals that they were made on one day, so that he might clearly show that the whole creation existed together in substance, although it did not emerge together in form.

Hence it is also written there: “God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he made them” (Gen. I, 27). Eve is not yet described as having been made, and yet the human being is already said to be male and female. But because the woman was undoubtedly destined to proceed from Adam’s side, she is already counted in him according to substance, from whom she was to be produced according to form.

We can consider this even in the smallest things, so that from small things we may weigh greater ones. When grass is created, neither its fruit nor the seed of its fruit is yet visible in it. Nevertheless, even when the fruit and seed do not appear, they are present in it, because what does not emerge together through the increments of time is nevertheless together in the substance of the root.

### 17. In what sense the angel and the human being were created together. The fallen angel lost the gifts of grace through sin, but not his nature. The two principles of the Manichaeans are rejected.

But since we say that those things were created together according to substance which we find emerging one from another, how can Behemoth be said to have been created with blessed Job, when the substance of angel and human being is not one, when the human being does not proceed from the angel, nor the angel from the human being?

If Behemoth is said to have been made with blessed Job for this reason—that every creature is undoubtedly created together by an author who is not stretched out by any delay of time in his action—why is this said specifically of Behemoth when it is generally true of all creatures?

But if we weigh the causes of things through careful examination, we recognize that the angel and the human being were made together—not, of course, by unity of time, but by rational understanding; together according to the image of wisdom they received, but not together according to the joined substance of their form.

For it is written concerning the human being: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). And through Ezekiel it is said to Satan: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12).

Thus, within the whole creation, the human being and the angel came into existence as created together, because they emerged distinct from every irrational creature. [Note: Pratel. reads “from every irrational creature by nature.”] Since, therefore, in the whole ordering of things there is no rational animal except the angel and the human being, whatever cannot use reason was not made with the human being.

Let it therefore be said to the human being; let it be said concerning the angel, who, although he lost the power of his exalted state, did not lose the subtlety of his rational nature: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you.” Thus, when the human being considers that the one who was made rational together with him has perished, he may fear the neighboring danger of pride from the destruction of the one close to him.

In these words we must also carefully observe that the wicked doctrine of Manichaeus [Note: Corbie German and Gemetian manuscripts read “Manes”; Laudian, German, and Turonian manuscripts read “Manichaeus.”] is openly condemned by the Lord’s voice. For, when he speaks of two principles, he attempts to assert that the race of darkness was not made. How, then, can that most wicked race be said not to have been made, when the Lord testifies that he himself made this Behemoth—namely, the author of wickedness—well created according to nature? [Note: Corbie German, Vindocian, Gemetian, and Laudian manuscripts read “created.”]

But since we have heard with whom this Behemoth was made, let us hear what the one who was ruined does. It follows:

### CHAPTER XIII [Rec. X]

**THE SAME.**—“He will eat hay like an ox.”

[Note: Laud., Corbie German, and Val. Cl. read “he eats.”]

### 18. The devil seeks above all to undermine the pure life of spiritual people.

If we carefully examine the words of the prophets, we find that this passage and the other were spoken by one Spirit. For when Isaiah saw the life of sinners being devoured by the ancient and insatiable enemy, he said: “The lion will eat straw like an ox” (Isa. XI, 7). [Note: Laud., Corbie German, Val. Cl., and Gemetian manuscripts read “he eats straw.”]

What else is signified by the names hay and straw except the life of those who live according to the flesh? Concerning this it is said through the prophet: “All flesh is hay” (Isa. XL, 6). Thus, here he is called Behemoth, there a lion; here hay, there straw.

But the mind strives to investigate why, both in Isaiah as a lion and here, in the Lord’s words, as Behemoth, he is compared in both passages, while eating hay or straw, not to a horse but to an ox. [Note: The same manuscripts as above read “in the eating.”] We recognize this more readily, however, if we consider the difference in the nourishment of the two animals.

Horses eat hay of any sort, however dirty, but drink only clean water. Oxen, on the other hand, drink water of any sort, however dirty, but feed only on clean hay. Why, then, is this Behemoth compared to an ox that feeds on clean fodder, except because another prophet says of this ancient enemy: “His food is choice” (Hab. I, 16)? [Note: Gemet initially reads “his food is the elect,” but later has “his food also is choice.” This manuscript is full of innumerable errors, some of which a later hand has corrected.]

For he does not rejoice in seizing those whom he sees lying voluntarily in the depths, entangled in wicked and filthy actions. He desires to eat hay like an ox because, with the tooth of his suggestion, he seeks to crush the pure life of spiritual people.

### 19. Many appear to be elect, but are not.

But I see that the question arises: how is this Behemoth said to consume the life of spiritual people by eating hay like an ox, when, as was said above, the life of those who live according to the flesh is signified by the name hay? [Note: Pratel., Val. Cl., Vindocian, and Corbie German manuscripts read “if, as.”] Nor will his food be “choice” if, by eating hay, he seizes a carnal person.

The answer quickly presents itself: some people are hay before God, yet among human beings they are counted under the name of holiness, because their life displays one thing before human eyes while their conscience intends another before divine judgments. Such people are therefore elect before human judgment, but hay before the Lord’s subtle examination.

Was Saul not hay before the divine eyes, concerning whom the prophet Samuel said to the people: “Surely you see whom the Lord has chosen” (1 Sam. X, 24), and of whom it is said shortly before: “Chosen and good”? For he whom the sinful people deserved was rejected before God, and yet, in the order of human affairs, he was chosen and good.

[Vet. XI.] Since many are hay and yet, according to human estimation, suppose themselves to be elect, Solomon rightly says: “I saw the wicked buried, who, while they were still alive, were in the holy place and were praised in the city as though for just works” (Eccl. VIII, 10).

Since many are hay, yet are surrounded by the favor of holiness, a certain wise man rightly says: “Pass by, guest, and adorn the table” (Eccli. XXIX, 33). The guest is said to adorn the table by passing by because, if someone placed at God’s altar seeks his own glory through good works, and if praise of the altar is displayed through the display of his holiness, he himself nevertheless is not counted among God’s citizens. [Note: Gemet., Val. Cl., and Corbie German read “is displayed” rather than “is extended.”] His reputation benefits others, yet he himself passes by as a stranger to God.

He adorned the table by passing by because he did not wish to remain at sacred things: in everything he strove to do, his mind ran toward human praise. Since, therefore, some people lead a clean life through diligent effort but do not seek to please God inwardly by it, Behemoth is rightly said both to have choice food and to eat hay like an ox.

It is as though clean hay lay on the ground before the mouth of this Behemoth, in the depths below, when a life is conducted as though innocent through observance of the commandments, yet the heart, amid actions that appear good, is not lifted up to seek higher things. What benefit, then, does one gain by preserving purity of life within oneself if, through a lowly intention, one leaves oneself lying on the ground to be found in the mouth of this Behemoth?

Since almighty God has revealed what our enemy does, let it now become known how he prevails, so that, the more openly the wickedness of his craft is recognized, the more easily it may be overcome. It follows:

### CHAPTER XIV [Rec. XI]

**VERSE 11.**—“His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly.”

### 20. Through lust the devil generally exercises dominion over both sexes.

The seeds of intercourse are said to be in men in the loins, but in women in the navel. Hence Truth says to the disciples: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII, 35). Hence Peter, restraining lust from the heart, admonished them, saying: “Gird up the loins of your mind” (1 Pet. I, 13).

Hence Paul, when he said that the priesthood of Melchizedek was tithed through Abraham before the time of Levi, showing where Levi was then concealed in Abraham’s body, said: “For he was still in the loins of his father” (Heb. VII, 10). [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl. read “sacrifice” for “priesthood.”]

That the seed of lust is contained in the navel of women is attested by the prophet, who, under the figure of a prostitute, rebuking the wantonness of Judea, says: “On the day of your birth your navel was not cut” (Ezek. XVI, 4). To cut the navel on the day of birth is, at the time of conversion, to cut away the lust of the flesh.

Because it is difficult to correct what has been badly begun and to reform for the better what has once been shamefully formed, Judea is reproved from her birth: although she was born in God, she retained an uncut navel because she did not sever the flowing disorder of lust.

Since, therefore, by the devil’s power both sexes are greatly subjected because of the weakness of lust, his strength is said to be in the loins against males, and his power against females in the navel.

[Vet. XII.] 21. The corruption of the flesh usually follows pride of spirit

But why, when he introduced this Behemoth as eating grass, did he append the harms of lust as the first indications of his deception, unless it is plainly evident to all that, after pride has once seized the human spirit [Note: [Col. 0648D] “Superbia” is absent in Laud., two German manuscripts, Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts; thus what is here said about pride is referred to Behemoth. Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts read “ad obrutionem” (“to crushing”) instead of “ad corruptionem” (“to corruption”).], it immediately extends itself to the corruption of the flesh? We recognize this even in the first human beings, who, when they covered their shameful members after committing pride, clearly indicated that, after they had inwardly attempted to seize lofty things in themselves, they immediately endured outwardly in the flesh what was shameful (Gen. III, 7).

This Behemoth, therefore, raging insatiably and seeking to devour the whole human being at once, sometimes raises the mind into pride, and sometimes corrupts the flesh through the pleasure of lust. Properly, however, the strength of those who are overthrown is not said to be in their loins or navel, but: “His strength is in his loins, and his power is in the navel of his belly.” It is as though it were said openly: “His strength is in his own loins, and his power in the navel of his own belly,” because those who, deceived by the blandishments of shameful suggestions, succumb to him through the fluidity of lust become, in a particular sense, his very body. It follows:

## CHAPTER XV [Rec. XII]

### VERSE 12.—“He tightens his tail like a cedar.”

22. The devil, bound by divine power, will later be released and will perform many signs through the Antichrist

Many things can be drawn from this passage for the instruction of morals; but first we shall examine the violent aspects of this Behemoth, so that afterward we may disclose his cunning more subtly. In Sacred Scripture the name “cedar” sometimes expresses the lofty excellence of heavenly glory, while at other times it signifies the rigid exaltation of the wicked.

The name “cedar” expresses the height of heavenly glory, as the Psalmist testifies: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. XCI, 13). Again, the name “cedar” signifies the proud power of the wicked, as it is said through the same Prophet: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Ps. XXVIII, 5).

But what is meant by the tail of this Behemoth except the extremity of the ancient enemy, when he enters his own particular vessel, that lost man who is specifically called the Antichrist? Because he is permitted to be raised into the swelling of power, sometimes by worldly honors and sometimes by signs and wonders of feigned holiness, the Lord’s voice rightly compares his tail to a cedar. For just as the cedar leaves the other trees behind by growing upward, so then the Antichrist, temporarily possessing the glory of the world, will surpass human measure both in the height of honor and in the power of signs.

The spirit within him is one who, created among the sublimities, did not lose the power of his nature even when cast down. His strength is therefore now displayed only minimally because, by the dispensation of divine power, it is bound [Note: [Col. 0649D] The printed editions read “by the dispensation of divine power,” a reading we would not have changed if all our manuscripts had not compelled us to do so.].

Hence it is said through John: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut him up and sealed it over him” (Rev. XX, 1–3). He is said to have been bound and cast into the abyss [Note: [Col. 0649D] “Cast” is omitted in Laud. and Val. Cl.], because, shut away in the hearts of the wicked, he is restrained by the power of the divine dispensation, lest he run uncontrolled to the extent of his ability to harm. Thus, although he secretly rages through them, he does not break out into violent ravages [Note: [Col. 0649D] In most printed editions: “pride will not break out.” This is erroneous, for the passage concerns the devil, not the vice of pride. The correction is supported by two German manuscripts, Norman manuscripts, Laud., Val. Cl., and the old Paris and Basel editions.].

But how he will be released at the end of the world is indicated there, when it says: “And after the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison [Note: [Col. 0649D] Gemet. and Corb. Germ. add: “and he will go out.”], and he will go out and deceive the nations” (ibid., 7). By the number one thousand, the entire period—whatever its length—of the holy Church is expressed according to its perfection. When it has been completed, the ancient enemy, handed over to his own powers, will be released for a short time, indeed, but with great power against us.

23. He will rage, but for a brief time

Although savagery will enlarge him for cruelty, heavenly mercy will nevertheless confine him by shortening the days. For Truth itself says: “Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be” (Matt. XXIV, 21) [Note: [Col. 0650D] Gemet. and Corb. Germ. read: “such as never was.”]. Again he says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (ibid., 22). Because the Lord sees that we are both proud and weak, he says that the days he has made exceptionally evil have mercifully been shortened—both to terrify pride through the adversity of the time and to support weakness through the brevity of the days [Note: [Col. 0650D] “Of the days” is absent in two German manuscripts, Pratel., and Utic.].

[Vet. XIII.] 24. Through the signs he will perform, he will be more fearsome than through the punishments he inflicted upon the martyrs

But it must be considered very carefully: when this Behemoth raises his tail like a cedar, in what respect will he then arise and show himself more atrociously than now? What kinds of punishments do we know whose power we do not already rejoice to have tested the martyrs? Some were struck down by a sword plunged unexpectedly into the throat; others were fastened to the cross, where death is both challenged and repelled, and, once repelled, challenged again. Others were crushed by a saw with bristling teeth; others were torn by a claw armed with iron, furrowing their flesh [Note: [Col. 0650D] Ebroic., other Norman manuscripts, Turon., Laud., Val. Cl., and Corb. Germ. read “scattered” instead of “tore.”]; others were mangled and crushed by the bites of beastlike fury; others were torn from within through the skin by the concentrated force of blows; others were buried alive in excavated earth [Note: [Col. 0650D] Corb. Germ., Pratell., and some others read: “others he shattered by a lofty precipice.”]; others, plunged into the depths, were broken by a precipice into death; others, thrown into water, were swallowed as it filled them; others were consumed by devouring flame, eaten away even to ashes.

Since, then, this Behemoth will more wickedly enlarge his tail at the end of the world, what is there that will grow more atrociously amid these torments than what Truth itself says in the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray” (Matt. XXIV, 24)? Now our faithful perform wonders while they suffer perversities; but then the followers of this Behemoth will perform wonders even while they inflict perversities.

Let us consider, therefore, what temptation that will be for the human mind, when a devout martyr subjects his body to torments and yet, before his eyes, the torturer performs miracles. Whose strength would not then be shaken from the very depths of his thoughts, when the one who torments with scourges flashes with signs? Let it rightly be said: “He tightens his tail like a cedar,” because then he will be both lofty in the veneration inspired by his wonders and hard through the cruelty of his torments.

[Vet. XIV.] 25. The Antichrist will deceive some through counterfeit powers and overcome others by force

For then he will not be raised by power alone, but will also be supported by the display of signs. Hence David says: “He lies in wait secretly, like a lion in his den” (Ps. IX, 30, or Ps. X, 9). For open power would have been sufficient if he were a lion, even without lying in wait; and, again, for secret cunning it would have been sufficient for him to steal upon his victims while lying in wait, even if he were not a lion. But because the ancient enemy is allowed to rage with all his powers, he is permitted to be unleashed against the elect in both struggle and deception: by power through might, and by deception through signs.

He is therefore rightly called both a lion and one lying in wait: lying in wait through the appearance of miracles, and a lion through worldly strength. To draw along those who are openly wicked, he displays worldly power; but in order also to deceive the righteous, he feigns holiness through signs. To the former he recommends the exaltation of greatness; the latter he deceives by displaying holiness.

Concerning this tail of Behemoth, under the figure of the dragon, it is said through John: “And its tail dragged down a third of the stars of heaven, and cast them upon the earth” (Rev. XII, 4). Heaven is the Church, which in the night of this present life shines with the stars radiating above, while it contains within itself countless virtues of the saints. But the dragon’s tail casts the stars down to earth, because that extremity of Satan, raised up through the audacity of the man he has assumed, reveals as reprobate certain people whom it finds in the Church as though they were God’s elect, by bringing them under its power. For stars falling from heaven to earth means that, under his leadership, some who had abandoned hope of heavenly things yearn for the pursuit of worldly glory.

26. He was prefigured by Antiochus

Hence Daniel speaks against this tail of the dragon under the figure of Antiochus, saying: “He cast down some of the host and of the stars and trampled upon them; and he was magnified even against the prince of the host, and from him he took away the continual sacrifice and cast down the place of his sanctuary. And strength was given him against the continual sacrifice because of sins; and truth was cast down upon the earth, and he acted and prospered” (Dan. VIII, 10–12).

He casts down some of the host and of the stars when he breaks certain people who shine with the light of righteousness and are strong in the virtue of their works. He is magnified against the prince of the host because he exalts himself against the very author of virtue. He takes away the continual sacrifice because he interrupts the Church’s devotion to holy conduct in those whom he has captured. Strength is given him against the continual sacrifice because of sins, since, unless the merits of those who perish had demanded it, the adversary could by no means have gained possession of those who were believed to be upright [Note: [Col. 0651D] Vindoc. reads: “who rightly believed.”].

Truth is cast down upon the earth because faith in heavenly realities is then bent toward the desire for temporal life. “He acted and prospered,” because then he will rage with immeasurable cruelty not only in the minds of the reprobate but also in the bodies of the elect, without any obstruction.

Again it is said through Daniel: “A king of shameless face will arise, understanding riddles, and his strength will be made firm, but not by his own strength” (Dan. VIII, 23). The strength of that man is not made firm by his own powers, because he is raised into the glory of perdition by Satan’s power. Again he says: “He will destroy the mighty and the people of the saints according to his will, and deceit will be directed by his hand” (ibid., 24–25).

He destroys the mighty when he conquers bodily those who are unconquered in mind. Or, “he destroys the mighty and the people of the saints according to his will” when he drags along at his command those who were believed to be mighty and holy. Deceit is directed in his hand because in him fraud is aided by action. What he says by deceiving, he confirms by performing wonders; for whatever his lying tongue pretends, the hand of his deeds displays as though it were true.

27. Daniel and Paul teach the same things about the Antichrist

Again he says: “He will rise up against the Prince of princes and will be broken without a hand” (ibid., 25). Hence Paul says: “So that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (II Thess. II, 4). Again he says: “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the splendor of his coming” (ibid., 8).

What was said through Daniel—“He will rise up against the Prince of princes” (Dan. VIII, 25)—is expressed through Paul as: “So that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.” And what Daniel adds—“He will be broken without a hand” (ibid., 25)—Paul expresses as: “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0651D] Gemet., Laud., Val., Cl., and two German manuscripts add: “and destroy by the splendor of his coming.”] (II Thess. II, 8).

He will be broken without a hand because, not through a battle with angels or a conflict with the saints, but through the coming of the Judge, he will be struck with eternal death by the breath of his mouth alone.

Concerning the exaltation of this Behemoth, Paul likewise says: “Who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (ibid., 4). When Daniel described him as a fourth beast supported by ten horns, he immediately added: “I was considering the horns, and behold, another little horn arose in their midst, and three of the first horns were uprooted from before it; and behold, eyes like human eyes were in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things” (Dan. VII, 8).

He is described as the eleventh horn of this beast because the power of his kingdom is strengthened by wickedness. [Vet. XV.] Every sin is “eleven,” because, by doing what is perverse, it goes beyond the commands of the Decalogue [Note: [Col. 0652D] Two German manuscripts, Laud., Pratel., and some others read: “the commandment of the Decalogue.”]. And because sin is mourned in sackcloth, eleven curtains of sackcloth are made in the tabernacle (Exod. XXVI, 7). Hence the eleventh Psalm says: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. XI, 1). Hence, fearing that the Apostles might remain at the number eleven [Note: [Col. 0652D] Gussanv. reads—perhaps through a typographical error—“the Apostle Peter, fearing that he might remain”;], Peter sought Matthias as the twelfth by casting lots (Acts I, 26). For unless he had recognized that guilt was signified by eleven, he would not have been so eager to complete the number of the Apostles with twelve.

Because transgression is expressed through eleven, the eleventh horn of this beast indicates the very author of transgression. It arises as a little horn because he is born as a mere human being; but it grows monstrously because it advances until it is joined to the power of angelic strength. It uproots the three horns that are before it because it subdues under its dominion three kingdoms that are situated near it. Its eyes are like human eyes, but its mouth speaks great things, because a human form is indeed seen in him, but by his words he raises himself above human beings.

What Paul therefore says—“Exalting himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped”—the prophet Daniel confirms by saying: “A mouth speaking great things” (II Thess. II, 4). That Daniel says he speaks great things, and Paul testifies that he exalts himself above the worship of the Deity, is what is compared in blessed Job to a cedar. Like a cedar, he strives after lofty things, prospering in every ostentation of deceit, through the strength of his power and the exaltation of his eminence.

He is rightly said to tighten his tail because all his power is gathered and concentrated in that one condemned man, so that he performs deeds of strength and wonders through him in proportion as he incites him with all his collected powers. But since we have heard what sort of person the head of the wicked is, let us now recognize what members adhere to this head. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVI [Rec. XIII]

### VERSE 12.—“The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.”

28. The arguments of the devil’s preachers are intricate. The Antichrist already has many witnesses

This Behemoth has as many witnesses as he possesses preachers of his wickedness. Are not those his testicles who corrupt human hearts by spreading the seeds of their wine-filled error through evil persuasions? It is appropriately said that the sinews of his testicles are intertwined, because the arguments of his preachers are knotted together by deceitful assertions: they pretend to be right while persuading people to what is wrong, so that the entanglement of their claims, like the intertwining of sinews, may be visible but cannot be undone.

The sinews of his testicles are intertwined because the acumen of his preachers lies hidden beneath double arguments. Often, while they infect hearts with words, they display innocence in their actions. They would not draw good people to themselves by their persuasion if they also presented themselves as perverse in their conduct. But because they are the testicles of this beast, bound by intertwined sinews, they present themselves as upright in order to remain hidden and preach what is perverse in order to corrupt, imitating their own head, who, like a lion lying in wait, rages through the power of worldly eminence and flatters through the appearance of holiness.

Would that this beast acted in such ways only then and did not even now possess these testicles of lust for corrupting the vitals of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0653D] Turon. reads: “us of lust.”]! For evil is not poured in only by speech of the mouth; it is offered even more harmfully by many through the example of their deeds.

How many have not seen the Antichrist and yet are his testicles, because by the example of their conduct they corrupt the hearts of the innocent? Whoever is lifted up in pride, whoever is tormented by the desires of greed, whoever is dissolved in the pleasures of lust, whoever burns in the scourges of unjust and immoderate anger—what else is he than a testicle of the Antichrist? By willingly entangling himself in the Antichrist’s purposes, he supplies others, through his example, with the offspring of error [Note: [Col. 0653D] Pratel. reads “the bond of error,” with another variant reading, “offspring.”].

One acts perversely; another adheres to those acting perversely and not only fails to oppose them but even favors them. What else, then, is he than a testicle of the Antichrist who, having lost the authority of the faith promised to God, bears witness to error [Note: [Col. 0653D] Val. Cl. reads: “prepares a testimony.” The printed editions read “bears witness,” a reading found in none of the manuscripts we have examined.]? Yet if anyone rebukes them, they immediately hide themselves under a kind of veil of defense, because their sinews are intertwined and badly knotted and cannot be loosened by corruption. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVII [Vet. XVI, Rec. XIV]

### VERSE 13.—“His bones are like pipes of bronze.”

29. Who are the bones of the Antichrist

In a body, bones both contain members and are themselves contained by them [Note: [Col. 0653D] The conjunction “and” is omitted in two German manuscripts, Gemet., [Col. 0654D] Pratel., Val. Cl.; the sense remains unaffected.]. This beast therefore has flesh and also bones, because some wicked people are held in error by others, while others, more wicked still, hold other people in error.

What else, then, should we understand as the bones of the Antichrist except those in his body who are more powerful than the rest? Because wickedness has become exceedingly hardened in their hearts, the entire structure of his body is sustained through them.

Many in this world appear to be rich. Because they are supported by possessions and wealth, they seem to be made solid by strength; but by distributing the very things on which they rely, they draw others into their own error. Sometimes they entice some people to become wicked by gifts; sometimes they bind others by presents so that they remain wicked. What, then, are these people except the bones of the Antichrist, who, by containing and multiplying the wicked, carry flesh within his body? [Note: [Col. 0654D] “In” is absent in a manuscript of Gemet. and other Norman manuscripts, Laud., and Val. Cl.]

Sometimes, when deceiving their hearers, they display sweetness of speech, because thorns also put forth flowers; in them what smells fragrant is indeed apparent, but what pricks remains hidden. They mix sweet things with bitter and flattering things with harmful ones; and although they seek to appear admirable through power, they cast themselves down as though humbly through unrestrained conversation, and by their speech insinuate about themselves what their conduct denies.

30. Why they are compared to pipes of bronze

Hence the bones of this Behemoth are rightly compared to pipes of bronze, because, like insensitive metal, they possess the sound of speaking well but not the sense of living well. By speaking humbly, they assert what they disdain through an exalted life. Hence Paul appropriately says: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII, 1).

For someone who speaks good things but does not follow those same good things through love produces a sound like bronze or a cymbal, because he himself does not perceive the words that he himself produces [Note: [Col. 0654D] In Gemet., before correction: “like sounding bronze, a cymbal produces a sound.”].

[Vet. XVII.] There are, however, some in the body of this beast who are not honored by rank, not supported by wealth, not adorned by the appearance of virtues, and not skilled through knowledge and cunning; yet they desire to appear to be what they are not, and therefore become more wicked against the life of the good. Concerning them it also follows:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Rec. XV]

[Col. 0655A]

### IBID.—“Its cartilage is like plates of iron.”

31. Those who are weaker in the body of the Antichrist are more wicked in carrying out evil

Cartilage indeed has the appearance of bone but does not possess the strength of bone. What, then, does it mean that its cartilage is compared to plates of iron, except that those who are weaker in him are more wicked in carrying out evil? Other metals are cut by iron, and its cartilage is said to be like iron because those who in his body are incapable of displaying virtues are inflamed more fiercely against the destruction of the faithful.

For when they realize that they cannot perform signs and wonders with him, they prove themselves his through cruelty; and because they cannot corrupt the hearts of the innocent by persuasion, they boast that, more than the others, they extinguish the bodies of the good. It is therefore rightly said: “Its cartilage is like plates of iron,” because in his body the one whom each person considers weaker [Note: [Col. 0655D] The editions read: “the more wickedly he cuts into it.” We have expressed the reading of the manuscripts—Ebroic. and other Norman manuscripts, Turon., Vindoc., German manuscripts, Laud., Val. Cl., and Corb. Germ.—in which the reading is “each person who is weak,” rather than “weaker.”] acts all the more wickedly.

They are rightly compared not merely to iron but to plates of iron, because, while they seek to spread their cruelty in every direction, they stretch themselves out as though into sheets of iron.

[Rec. XVI.] 32. A closer investigation may distinguish these same words of the Creator, which now seem to have been examined, and bring richer fruits of understanding to the instruction of morals

Since we have heard what the ancient enemy does against human beings through the man he has assumed, it remains for us now to explore what he contrives even in human beings by himself, without a human intermediary. For it is said:

## CHAPTER XIX

### VERSE 12.—“He tightens his tail like a cedar.”

33. The devil’s first suggestion is tender and easily crushed; afterward his strength becomes intolerable. Sin is admitted in three ways

The serpent’s first suggestion is soft and tender, and must easily be crushed by the foot of virtue. But if it is negligently admitted as it grows stronger, and access to the heart is freely granted to it, it magnifies itself with such power that, depressing the mind it has captured, it grows into intolerable strength.

He is therefore said to tighten his tail like a cedar because, once his temptation has been received in the heart, it dominates by a kind of right in everything he subsequently introduces. The head of this Behemoth is grass, while his tail is a cedar, because at first he humbly submits in a flattering suggestion, but, growing vehemently stronger through habit, he is fortified as the temptation reaches its end.

Everything he suggests at the beginning can be overcome; but what follows can scarcely be conquered. At first he speaks to the mind gently, as though offering advice; but once he has driven in the tooth of delight, he is afterward bound almost insolubly by force of habit. Hence he is rightly said to tighten his tail. With his tooth he wounds; with his tail he binds: by his first suggestion he strikes, but, as the temptation reaches its conclusion and grows stronger, he restrains the wounded mind so that it cannot escape.

Because sin is admitted in three ways—namely, when it is perpetrated through the serpent’s suggestion, the flesh’s delight, and the spirit’s consent—this Behemoth first puts out his tongue by suggesting what is unlawful; then, drawing the person toward delight, fixes in his tooth; and finally, possessing him through consent, tightens his tail.

For this reason some people condemn within themselves sins committed through long habit and avoid them by judgment, but are unable to evade them in practice even while struggling. Because they do not crush the head of this Behemoth, they are often bound by his tail even against their will. It has hardened against them like a cedar, because it has grown from the gentle pleasure of its beginning to the violence of retention.

Let it therefore be said: “He tightens his tail like a cedar,” so that each person may understand that he must flee the beginnings of temptation all the more urgently because he recognizes that its end cannot quickly be undone.

[Vet. XVIII.] 34. When the end of life is near, the devil suggests more grievous temptations

It must also be known that often he inflicts more grievous sins upon those whom he has captured when he recognizes that they are approaching the end of the present life; and the closer he considers himself to be to completing the temptation, the heavier the burdens of iniquity he piles upon them.

Behemoth therefore tightens his tail like a cedar, because he makes those whom he has captured through wicked beginnings worse at the end, so that his temptations may be completed with greater force the sooner they are about to cease. Because he strives to make their punishment equal to his own, he attempts more ardently before death to intensify every sin in them.

Often this Behemoth already possesses a heart wickedly subjected to him, but divine grace nevertheless drives him away and the hand of mercy casts out the one whom captive will introduced to itself. When he is expelled from the heart, he tries to drive in sharper goads of iniquity, so that the mind attacked by him may feel waves of temptations that it did not even know while he possessed it.

This is well expressed in the Gospel, where the unclean spirit is said to leave a person at the Lord’s command. For when the demon-possessed boy had been brought, it is written: “Jesus threatened the unclean spirit, saying: ‘Deaf and mute spirit, I command you, come out of him and do not enter him again.’ And crying out and greatly tearing him, it came out of him” (Mark IX, 24).

Behold, it had not torn him when it held him; it tore him as it departed, because it rends the thoughts of the mind more grievously when, compelled by divine power, it approaches the moment of its departure [Note: [Col. 0656D] Two German manuscripts read: “when it has already gone out”; the printed editions read: “when, at the end of its departure, the divine ….” We have followed the manuscripts Turon., Vindoc., Laud., Ebroic., and other Norman manuscripts.]. And the spirit that had possessed him while mute abandoned him with cries, because often, while it possesses someone, it inflicts lesser temptations; but when it is driven from the heart, it disturbs the person with a more violent assault.

It is therefore rightly said: “He tightens his tail like a cedar,” because, both while possessing the heart, he always increases in wickedness through what comes later [Note: [Col. 0656D] Laud., Corb. Germ., and Val. Cl. read: “while possessing the body.”], and, when leaving the heart, he strikes it with more vehement goads of thought.

[Rec. XVII.] The subtler arguments of this Behemoth are further disclosed by the Creator’s wondrous mercy when it is added:

## CHAPTER XX

### IBID.—“The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.”

36. Sins are so entangled that, while one is avoided, we almost always fall into another. The Church consists of three orders

The sinews of his testicles are the deadly arguments of his machinations (Dist. 13, canon 2). Through them he raises up the strength of his cunning and corrupts the fluid hearts of mortals [Note: [Col. 0657D] Thus the German, Turon., Vindoc., Laud., Norman, and other manuscripts. Corb. Germ. reads: “he exerts his strength.”]. His testicles are evil suggestions, through which he grows fervent in the corruption of the mind and begets the offspring of wicked action in the violated soul [Note: [Col. 0657D] Two German manuscripts, Laud., and Vindoc. read: “They are his testicles.”].

But the sinews of these testicles are intertwined, because the arguments of his suggestions are bound together by intricate inventions, so that they cause many people to sin in such a way that, if they perhaps desire to flee one sin, they cannot escape it without another snare of sin; they commit guilt while avoiding it, and cannot free themselves from one without consenting to be bound by another [Note: [Col. 0657D] Gratian, at the cited passage, reads: “without any other.”; and again: “to be bound.”].

We can show this more clearly if we produce some examples of this entanglement from human conduct. Since the holy Church consists of three orders—namely, the married, the continent, and those who govern—for Ezekiel saw three men delivered, namely Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV, 14ff.); and in the Gospel the Lord, when he says that some will be in the field, others in bed, and others at the mill (Luke XVII, 34–35), undoubtedly indicates three orders in the Church—we shall plainly satisfy our purpose if we examine each order in turn.

36. Temptations of those engaged in worldly affairs

Behold, someone, while seeking the friendships of this world, binds himself by oath to another person leading a similar life, promising that he will conceal that person’s secrets in complete silence. But the person to whom he swore is discovered to be committing adultery, even attempting to kill the adulteress’s husband.

The person who gave the oath returns to his own mind and is attacked by conflicting thoughts from every side. He fears remaining silent, lest by keeping silent he become a participant in both adultery and murder; and he is afraid to expose the matter, lest he bind himself by the guilt of perjury. He is therefore bound by the intertwined sinews of the testicles, because whichever way he turns, he fears that he will not be free from the contagion of transgression [Note: [Col. 0657D] Gratian, at the cited passage, reads: “contagion.”].

37. Those who desire to serve God through obedience; prelates

Another person abandons everything belonging to the world and seeks in every respect to break his own wills; he desires to submit himself to another’s rule, but through insufficiently careful investigation he fails to discern who ought to govern him before God. Perhaps, once the man chosen without sound judgment has begun to preside, he forbids the subordinate to do what belongs to God and orders him to do what belongs to the world [Note: [Col. 0657D] The same source, at the cited passage, reads: “to do.”].

The subordinate, weighing both the guilt of disobedience and the contamination of secular life, is afraid to obey and afraid not to obey: he fears that by obeying he may abandon God in the superior’s commands, or that by refusing to obey he may despise God in the superior whom he has chosen. Either, by obeying unlawful commands, he may practice against God what he sought for God’s sake, or, by refusing to obey, he may subject to his own judgment the one whom he had sought as his judge.
