This man is plainly bound by the intertwined sinews of the testicles through the fault of his lack of discernment, because whether he obeys or does not obey, he is bound in the guilt of transgression. He was striving to break his own wills, yet he takes care to strengthen them even while disregarding his superior. He resolved to abandon the world completely, yet he is compelled to return to worldly concerns by another’s will.

The sinews are therefore intertwined when the enemy’s arguments bind us in such a way that the knots of guilt, at the very point where they are sought to be loosened, bind us more tightly.

38. The peril of those who seek ecclesiastical office

Another person, neglecting to consider the burden of ecclesiastical honor, rises to a position of governance through payments. But because everything that stands out in this life is more afflicted by sorrows than it rejoices in honors, when his heart is weighed down by tribulations he is recalled to the memory of his guilt. He grieves that he reached a laborious office with guilt and recognizes, from the very difficulty of its fruit, how wrong was what he had done [Note: [Col. 0657D] Gilot., Gussanv., and others read: “from the very difficulty of the fruit.” We have restored this passage from the Norman manuscripts, Vindoc., Laud., two German manuscripts, and others, as well as from the old edition.].

Recognizing himself as guilty because of the payments he has made, he wishes to abandon the position of eminence he has acquired, but fears that it would be a graver offense to leave the care of the flock entrusted to him. He wishes to care for the flock entrusted to him, but fears that it would be a worse guilt to possess pastoral rule purchased by worldly means.

Thus, bound by his ambition for honor, he sees guilt on both sides. He perceives that he cannot be free of accusation whether the flock once entrusted to him is abandoned or whether the sacred office purchased in a worldly manner is retained. He fears in every direction and dreads every exposed side, lest, by remaining in the purchased office, he fail to mourn worthily for what he does not correct even by abandoning it [Note: [Col. 0658D] Understand this obscure passage as though he were saying: “Even if he abandons the office, he does not correct his guilt.” In Gilot. and some others it reads: “who, while correcting something else, does not even abandon it, or at least, while abandoning the office, endeavors to weep.” Nothing is clearer in those versions. Our reading is supported by the manuscripts Turon., Vindoc., two German manuscripts, Norman manuscripts, and others.]; or, while abandoning the office and trying to lament one matter, he again commits another through the very abandonment of the flock.

Because this Behemoth binds people with such inexplicable knots that, when the mind has been brought into doubt, it is often tightened more firmly in guilt precisely where it tries to free itself from guilt, it is rightly said: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.” For the arguments of his machinations are like cords that, the more they seem to be loosened so that they may release us, the more they become entangled so that they may hold us.

**[Old Version XX.] 39. Where no avenue of escape without sin appears, what should be done. Intercourse between married persons is not free from sin when undertaken to satisfy lust.**—There is, nevertheless, something that can usefully be done to destroy his deceits: when the mind is hemmed in between lesser and greater sins, and no avenue of escape without sin is entirely open, the lesser should always be chosen. For someone who is enclosed on every side by the circuit of walls so that he cannot escape throws himself into flight wherever the shorter wall is found.

When Paul observed certain incontinent persons in the Church, he permitted what was lesser so that they might avoid what was greater, saying: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife” (1 Cor. 7:2). And because spouses are without sin in intercourse only when they unite not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring, he immediately added, so as to show that even what he had permitted was not without fault, although it was a lesser fault: “But this I say by way of concession, not by command” [Col. 0659B] (ibid., 6). For what is forgiven and not commanded is not without defect. He plainly saw a sin when he foresaw that it could be forgiven [Note: Pratelensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “be forgiven” (*indulgeri*)]. But when we are constrained by doubtful alternatives, we profitably submit to the lesser, lest we sin in greater matters without pardon.

Thus the perplexity of the sinews of this Behemoth is often loosened when one passes to the greatest virtues through the commission of lesser faults. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 13.—“His bones are like pipes of bronze.”**

### 40. How great a danger threatens us through the devil’s cunning counsels

What else is signified by the bones of this Behemoth but his counsels? For just as the body’s posture and strength rest upon the bones, so all his wickedness raises itself up through fraudulent counsels. He does not crush anyone by force; rather, he kills by the crafty persuasion of his destructive influence.

Again, just as the bones, which contain the marrow, are strengthened by the marrow that moistens them, so his counsels are strengthened by the subtlety of intelligence infused through the power of a spiritual nature. His testicles differ from his bones—that is, his suggestions differ from his counsels—in this respect: through the former he openly inserts what is harmful, whereas through the latter, as though advising what is good, he draws a person into sin. Through the former he overcomes by attacking; through the latter he trips him up as though giving advice.

Hence his bones—that is, these same counsels—are rightly compared with pipes of bronze. Pipes of bronze are generally fitted for melodious songs. When they are brought near the ears and delicately sound a pleasing melody, they draw the mind’s interior faculties outward toward delight; and while what they sound to the ears is sweet, they weaken the strength of the heart in the flow of pleasure. When hearing is drawn toward delight, the mind is unmanned and loses the steadfastness of its strength.

So too his cunning counsels, while they advise as though offering a flattering provision [Note: Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts, and the old Basel edition: “with flattering persuasion”; the old edition: “with flattering promise.”], turn the heart away from firm purpose; and while they resound sweetly, incline it toward what is harmful. They are therefore like pipes of bronze: while they are willingly heard, they cast the soul down from its inward purpose into the delight of outward life.

For this Behemoth works especially hard to carry out his deception: while he presents the counsel of his perversity as though it were useful, he makes what he says sound pleasant [Col. 0660A], so that by the usefulness displayed he may charm the mind and by the wickedness concealed corrupt it.

**[Old Version XXI.] 41. This is made clear by examples: by what art he persuades people to toil at acquiring wealth**

We can show this more clearly in all cases if we briefly disclose a few examples of his counsels. Behold, someone content with his own possessions has resolved not to become entangled in any occupations of this world. He greatly fears losing the advantages of his quiet life and greatly despises accumulating profit together with sins.

The crafty enemy approaches him and, seeking to undermine his intention of good devotion, supplies counsel that seems useful, saying: “What you have [Note: Two German manuscripts and Ebroicensis with other Norman manuscripts: “the things that are”] is indeed sufficient for the present, but what will you do when these things fail? If nothing is provided afterward, you have what must presently be spent on your children [Col. 0660B], but you must nevertheless acquire what can be kept in reserve. Even what is present may soon be lacking if prudent foresight ceases to prepare what is absent. Surely it is possible both to carry on earthly activity and to avoid sin in that activity, so that it may provide external means of support without bending the inward rectitude?”

For the moment he insinuates these things with flattering words, while separately concealing the snares of sin in the earthly business he recommends. His bones, therefore, are like pipes of bronze, because his harmful counsels flatter the one who hears them with the sweetness of a voice that appears to advise.

### 42. How he turns aside one who is considering renouncing the world

Another person has resolved not only not to seek earthly advantages but also to renounce all that he possesses, so that he may devote himself to the discipleship of the heavenly Teacher [Col. 0660C] with greater freedom: the more unencumbered he becomes, the more readily he abandons and tramples underfoot whatever might weigh upon one who possesses it.

The enemy, lying in wait, addresses this person’s heart by a hidden suggestion, saying: “From where has such audacity of rashness arisen that you dare to believe you can survive after abandoning everything? The Creator made you for one condition, while you arrange yourself for another. He would have made you stronger and more robust if he had wished you to follow his footsteps amid the necessity of poverty. Do not many people refrain from abandoning their earthly inheritances and yet, through works of mercy, purchase from them the eternal goods of the heavenly inheritance?”

He makes this suggestion with flattering words, but separately places before the eyes of the person he urges to retain them the destructive pleasures concealed in those same possessions. Thus he draws the deceived heart toward outward blandishments [Note: Laudian, Turonian, and two German manuscripts: “toward flattering external things.”] and perverts it from its inward vows of perfection.

His bones, therefore, are like pipes of bronze, because his deceitful counsels, while producing a flattering sound from outward things, bring destructive loss from within.

### 43. Especially when someone is striving toward the summit of monastic perfection

Another person, having abandoned everything he possessed outwardly [Note: Laudian manuscript: “having rejected”], in order to undertake the higher form of discipleship, prepares even to break his innermost wills. By subjecting himself to the more upright wills of another, he renounces himself not only in evil desires but, for the attainment of perfection, even in good intentions; and he observes everything he must do according to another’s judgment.

The crafty enemy addresses him all the more gently the more ardently he attempts to cast him down from a lofty place [Note: So our manuscripts read. The printed editions have: “from a more exalted place.”]. Immediately, flattering him with a poisonous suggestion, he says: “O how many wondrous things you will be able to accomplish by yourself if you do not submit to another’s judgment! Why do you diminish your progress by applying yourself to improvement? Why do you break the good intention of your purpose by trying to extend it farther than necessary? What perverse things did you perpetrate when you used your own will? If you are fully sufficient for yourself in living well, why do you seek another’s judgment over you?”

He insinuates these things with flattering words, while separately preparing in the person’s own wills the grounds for exercising pride. While he praises the heart for its inward rectitude, he cunningly searches for the place where he may overthrow it in perversity.

His bones, therefore, are like pipes of bronze, because from the place where his secret counsels seem to delight the mind with flattering sweetness, they disperse it destructively from its upright purpose.

### 44. How he strives to draw people away from works of charity

Another person has almost completely broken his own wills [Note: Two English manuscripts: “almost”] and has already corrected many vices of the old self both by a changed life and by the lamentation of repentance [Note: Ebroicensis, other Norman manuscripts, Laudian, two German manuscripts, and others: “has thoroughly purged.”]. He is kindled against the sins of others with all the greater zeal because, having died completely to himself, he is not held by his own iniquities.

The crafty enemy recognizes that, through his zeal for justice, this person benefits others also. He therefore attacks him with words that seem to counsel prosperity, saying: “Why do you delay in caring for the affairs of others [Col. 0661C]? If only you could become strong enough to consider your own! Do you not understand that when you extend yourself to the affairs of others, you are found less attentive to caring for what belongs to you? And what benefit is there in wiping away the blood from another’s wound while, by neglecting your own corruption, you allow it to spread?”

While he speaks as though giving advice, he removes the zeal of charity [Note: Ebroicensis: “he loses it”] and extinguishes, with the sword of a creeping sluggishness, every good that might have proceeded from charity. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves (Matt. 19:19; 22:39), it is fitting that we burn with zeal against their vices just as we do against our own.

Because, then, while he advises sweetly, he turns the mind away from its proper purpose, it is rightly said: “His bones are like pipes of bronze.” For when, through fraudulent counsels, he sounds sweetly in the mind of the hearer, he sings as though with a pipe of bronze [Col. 0661D], so that by the very means through which he soothes, he may deceive [**[Old Version XXII.]**].

But this Behemoth brings on a much gentler struggle when he exercises himself in ambush under the pretext of weakness. He then arouses harsher temptations when he conceals the snares of iniquity before the eyes of the tempted under the appearance of virtue. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 13.—“His cartilage is like plates of iron.”**

### 45. He arouses harsher temptations when he conceals snares under the appearance of virtue

What else is understood by cartilage but his pretense? Cartilage displays the appearance of bone but does not possess the bone’s firmness. There are, in fact, certain vices that display in themselves the appearance of uprightness but arise from the weakness of perversity.

The malice of our enemy disguises itself with such great skill that it often makes faults appear as virtues before the eyes of a deceived mind, so that a person expects rewards from the very thing through which he deserves to find eternal punishments.

Often cruelty is practiced in avenging vices and is regarded as justice; immoderate anger is believed to merit righteous zeal; and when sinners should be carefully corrected from distorted behavior, they are broken by violent force. Often lax indulgence is regarded as gentleness and mercy; and when offenders are spared temporally more than is fitting, they are cruelly reserved for eternal punishments.

Sometimes extravagance is believed to be mercy; and although it is a fault to fail to preserve what has been entrusted, no fear is felt about scattering even more recklessly what has been received. Sometimes parsimony is considered moderation; and although it is a serious vice not to give, retaining what has been received is thought a virtue.

The obstinacy of the wicked is often called steadfastness; and while the mind refuses to be bent away from its perversity, it boasts as though in defense of what is right. Inconstancy is often regarded as pliability; and the less someone preserves complete fidelity toward anyone, the more he considers himself a friend to people.

At times an inappropriate fear is believed to be humility; and when someone, oppressed by temporal dread, is silent in defense of the truth [Note: The printed editions have “for the defense.” The reading in Vindocensis, Laudian, Norman, and two German manuscripts, which we follow, is “from the defense”], he thinks that he is displaying himself humbly before those more powerful than himself [Note: Turonian: “before the more powerful.”].

At times arrogance of speech is regarded as true freedom; and when truth is contradicted through pride, boldness in speaking is thought to be a defense of truth. Sloth is often regarded as the quiet of self-control; and although it is a serious fault not to perform what is right diligently, merely refraining from evil action is considered the merit of a great virtue.

Often restlessness of spirit is called watchful concern; and when someone cannot endure quiet, he thinks that by doing whatever he desires he is fulfilling the exercise proper to virtue. Careless haste toward things that ought to be done is often thought the fervor of commendable zeal; and when a desired good is corrupted by untimely action, it is judged to be done better because it is done more quickly.

The slowness of hastening toward the good is often thought to be prudence; and when one waits so that reconsideration may bring improvement, the enemy uses this delay to trip him up [Note: Pratel, Laudian, two German manuscripts, and Vallicellian: “through deliberation”; the old Paris and Basel editions: “through dragging out.”] [**[Old Version XXIII.]**].

When, therefore, a fault is regarded as a virtue, we must necessarily reflect that the mind abandons its vice all the more slowly because it is not ashamed of what it does; and the mind abandons its vice all the more slowly because, deceived by the appearance of virtue, it seeks even a reward for it.

A fault is easily corrected when it is also felt to be a fault and therefore causes shame. Since, then, error is more difficult to amend when it is believed to be virtue, it is rightly said: “His cartilage is like plates of iron.” This Behemoth, because he displays his cunning more deceitfully under the pretext of good, holds the mind more harshly in guilt.

### 46. Those who pursue the way of holiness are sometimes slow to be corrected after falling into error. They become colder than cold minds

For this reason, those who pursue the way of holiness are sometimes slow to be corrected after falling into error. They consider what they are doing to be right and join perseverance to vice just as they would to cultivated virtue. They think their conduct right and therefore serve their own judgment with greater determination.

Thus Jeremiah, after saying: “Her Nazirites were purer than snow, whiter than milk, more ruddy than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphires,” immediately added: “Their appearance has become darker than coals, and they were not recognized in the streets”; and he continued: “Their skin has clung to their bones; it has withered and become like wood” (Lam. 4:7–8).

What else is signified by the name of Nazirites but the life of those who abstain and practice self-control, which is said to be brighter than snow and whiter than milk? Snow freezes from water that comes down from above, whereas milk is pressed from flesh that is nourished below. What, then, is signified by snow but the brightness of heavenly life, and what by milk but the administration of temporal stewardship?

Because men who practice self-control in the Church often perform such remarkable works that many who have maintained heavenly life and many who have administered earthly affairs well appear to be surpassed by them, they are described as brighter than snow and whiter than milk.

And because through the fervor of the spirit they sometimes appear to surpass the life of ancient and powerful fathers, it is rightly added: “More ruddy than ancient ivory.” When the name of redness is impressed, the flame of holy desire is signified. We know that ivory is the bone of great animals [Note: Laudian manuscript: “of ivory”]. They are therefore “more ruddy than ancient ivory,” because they are often found, before human eyes, more fervent in zeal than certain fathers who preceded them [Note: Vindocensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts: “more fervent in zeal”; the German manuscripts: “more fervent in devotion.”].

To display all this together, it is added: “More beautiful than sapphires.” Sapphire is of a heavenly color. Because they appear, through heavenly conduct, to surpass many who have gone before and are striving toward higher things, they are said to have become more beautiful than sapphires.

But often, when an abundance of virtues prospers beyond what is expedient, the mind is led into a certain confidence in itself; and, deceived by its own presumption, it is suddenly darkened when sin steals upon it. Hence it is rightly added: “Their appearance has become darker than coals.”

They become black after their whiteness because, having lost God’s righteousness, they fall into sins even of which they are unaware when they presume upon themselves. And because after the fire of love they come to the coldness of sluggishness, they are compared with extinguished coals and are found colder than cold minds.

Sometimes, while they abandon the fear of God through confidence in themselves, they become even colder than cold minds. Of them it is rightly added: “They were not recognized in the streets.”

A street is called *platea* in the Greek sense of the word, from its breadth [that is, “broad way”]. What is narrower for the human mind than to break its own wills? Of this breaking the Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13). What is broader than to resist none of one’s own wills, and to spread oneself without restraint in whatever direction the impulse of one’s judgment leads?

Those who, through confidence in their holiness, set aside the judgment of their betters and follow themselves [Note: Corbeiensis Germanicus and Vindocensis: “follow their own wills”] proceed, as it were, through streets. But “they were not recognized in the streets,” because they had displayed something different in their life when, by breaking their own wills, they kept themselves on the narrow path.

It is rightly added: “Their skin has clung to their bones.” What is expressed by bone but the hardness of strength, and what by skin but the softness of weakness? Their skin is said to cling to their bones because, among those who think perversely, the weakness of vice is considered the hardness of virtue.

What they do is weak; but, deceived by confidence born of pride, they join it to things they suppose strong. The more highly they think of themselves, the more contemptuously they refuse to be corrected of their wickedness.

Hence it is rightly added: “It has withered and become like wood.” Their fault becomes all the more insensible the more it is regarded by them as praiseworthy. He rightly declares it to be withered, because it does not grow green through any reflection upon itself [Note: Two German manuscripts, Turonian, Ebroicensis, and the other Norman manuscripts: “through self-knowledge.”].

What Jeremiah calls the weakness of skin is here called, in blessed Job, the fragility of cartilage; and what is there called bones because of hardness is here called plates of iron. [**[Old Version XXIV.]**]

But let us hear what nature and condition this Behemoth has, who through his members exercises such great cunning of iniquity against God’s elect at the end of time, and who, in his own person, presents himself in such a labyrinth of ambushes to deceive minds. For he could not perform such remarkable deeds, even in wicked activity [Note: Two German, Turonian, Vindocensis, Norman, Laudian, and Vallicellian manuscripts: “could perform such great deeds”], if he did not possess a great nature. Therefore the Lord, with wondrous mercy, as though explaining the causes of such great cunning and strength, immediately added:

## CHAPTER XXIII [Recension XVIII]

**VERSE 14.—“He is the beginning of the ways of God.”**

### 47. The angel who fell was the first and noblest creature

It is as though he were saying plainly: “For this reason he is strong enough for so many things: when creating him in the substance of created things, the Creator made him first.”

For what else are the ways of God but his actions? Of these the prophet says: “For my ways are not your ways” (Isa. 55:8). Behemoth is called “the beginning of the ways of God” (On Penance, distinction 2, chapter 44) because, when he was creating all things, God formed him first and made him more eminent than the other angels.

The prophet perceives the preeminence of his primacy when he says: “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his summit; the plane trees were not equal to his branches; no tree of the paradise of God was like him or like his beauty, for he made him beautiful with many dense branches” (Ezek. 31:8–9).

What can be understood by cedars, fir trees, and plane trees [Note: Vindocensis: “What, indeed, can be understood . . . ?”] except those hosts of heavenly virtues, planted in the greenness of eternal joy, that possess lofty height? Although they were created exalted, they were neither placed above him nor made equal to him.

He is said to have been made beautiful “with many dense branches” because the beauty that placed him above the other legions made him so much more splendid, and the multitude of angels subject to him adorned him [Note: Gratian: “as great as the multitude of angels subject to him.”]. This tree in the paradise of God had as many dense branches, so to speak, as it beheld legions of heavenly spirits placed beneath it.

He was condemned without pardon when he sinned because he had been created great beyond comparison. Again, through the same prophet it is said to him: “You were the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12–13).

As he was about to speak of his greatness in many respects, the prophet gathered everything together in his first phrase. What good did he not possess if he was “the seal of the likeness of God”? From the seal of a ring an image is impressed that is like what is essentially contained in the seal itself.

Although the human being was created in the likeness of God (Gen. 1:27), the prophet, as though granting the angel something greater, does not say that he was created in the likeness of God but that he himself was “the seal of the likeness of God,” so that, insofar as he is subtler in nature, the likeness of God might be believed to have been expressed more fully in him.

**[Old Version XXV.] 48. His primacy among the nine orders of angels. What “cherub” signifies**

For this reason the same prophet, further indicating the power of his primacy, adds: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28:13).

He names nine kinds of stones [Note: Vindocensis: “the names of the stones”], because there are indeed nine orders of angels. For when the sacred writings openly mention angels, archangels, thrones, dominations, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim, they show how many distinctions there are among the heavenly citizens.

Yet this Behemoth is described as having been covered with them, because he had them as a garment for his adornment; and when he surpassed their brightness, he became brighter by comparison with them.

Concerning him the prophet further adds: “The work of your adornment was gold, and your sockets were prepared on the day when you were created” (ibid., 13).

Gold was the work of his adornment because he shone with the brightness of wisdom, which he received when he was well created. Sockets are made in stones so that, bound with gold, they may be joined together in the composition of an ornament; and those whom the gold flowing between and filling the sockets binds together do not diverge from one another.

The sockets of this stone were therefore prepared on the day of his creation because he was created capable of charity. If he had wished to be filled with it, he could have adhered to the angels who remained standing, like stones set in the ornament of a king.

For if he had made himself penetrable to the gold of charity, he would have remained, joined to the holy angels, as a stone fixed in the royal ornament, as we have said. This stone therefore had sockets, but through the vice of pride they were not filled with the gold of charity.

Since stones are bound with gold so that they may not fall, this one fell because, although pierced by the craftsman’s hand, he refused to be bound by the ties of love. Now the other stones, which had likewise been pierced like him, have been bound together as charity penetrates each of them; and when he fell, they received the gift that they would no longer be loosened by falling from the royal ornament.

The same prophet, still contemplating the height of his primacy [Note: Vindocensis, Pratelensis, and other Norman manuscripts: “the greater height of his primacy”], adds: “You were a cherub, extended and protecting, on God’s holy mountain; you walked perfect in the midst of stones of fire” (Ezek. 28:14).

“Cherub” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” This one is therefore called a cherub because he is believed to have surpassed all others in knowledge. He walked perfect in the midst of stones of fire because he stood glorious in his created splendor among the hearts of angels kindled by the fire of charity.

The prophet rightly calls him extended and protecting. Whatever we protect by extending ourselves over it, we overshadow. Because he is believed to have overshadowed the brightness of the others by comparison with his own brightness, he is said to have been extended and protecting. He covered the others, as though by overshadowing them, because he surpassed their greatness by a greater excellence.

What is there called beautiful with many branches, there called the seal of the likeness, there called a cherub, and there called protecting, is here called by the Lord’s voice “the beginning of the ways of God.”

**[Old Version XXVI.] 49. From the fall of the angel, let human beings learn not to be proud

The reason why the Lord reveals both the remarkable qualities he possessed and those he lost is to show a frightened human being what he himself will suffer if he grows proud through the fault of arrogance—if the Lord did not spare, when striking him, the one whom he had raised, by creating him, to the glory of such great splendor.

Let human beings therefore consider what they deserve when they become proud on earth, if an angel who was set above angels in heaven is cast down. Hence the prophet rightly says: “My sword has become drunk in heaven” (Isa. 34:5). It is as though he were saying plainly: “Consider with what anger I will strike the proud of earth, if I did not spare even those whom I created beside me in heaven when their pride incurred their fault.”

After hearing of so many powers of the ancient enemy and learning the greatness of his nature, who would not collapse in immense fear? Who would not yield, struck by despair?

But while the power revealed in our enemy restrains our pride, the Lord also supports our weakness by disclosing the dispensation of his grace. Therefore, when he had called him “the beginning of his ways,” he immediately added:

## CHAPTER XXIV [Recension XIX]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.—“He who made him applied his sword.”**

### 50. God restrains the power of the apostate angel

The sword of this Behemoth is the very malice by which he harms. But his sword is applied by the one who made him good by nature, because his malice is restrained by divine providence, so that he is not permitted to strike human minds as much as he desires.

Our enemy therefore has great power but strikes less than he could because the mercy of the Creator binds his sword, so that, turned back within his own consciousness, it may remain hidden and his malice may not extend itself into the deaths of human beings beyond what is justly ordained from above.

That he prevails powerfully over many things comes from the greatness of his original creation; but that he is overcome by certain people means that his sword is turned back by the Creator. This Behemoth, who is the beginning of the ways of God, when he received permission to tempt the holy man, stirred up peoples, carried away flocks, brought fire down from heaven, raised winds by disturbing the air, shook and destroyed a house, killed the children who were feasting [Col. 0667B], and exercised [Note: Vallicellian: “sharpened”] his wife’s mind through the deceit of a wicked persuasion; he pierced the flesh of her husband with inflicted wounds (Job 1:13 ff.).

Yet his sword is turned back by the Creator when it is said: “Preserve his life” (ibid., 2:6). The evangelist shows how weak he is when his sword has been turned back: he could neither remain in the possessed man nor presume to enter the brute animals again unless commanded, saying: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matt. 8:31).

The fact that his sword of malice is so turned back is shown by this: if supreme power had not granted him permission, he would not have been able even to rage among a herd of pigs [Note: Laudian, Pratel, other Norman manuscripts, and two German manuscripts: “he is not even able to rage among pigs.”]. When, then, would he dare, of his own accord, to harm human beings made in God’s image, when it is clear that without command he does not even presume to touch pigs?

[Col. 0667C] 51. The heresy of Arius is refuted

It should also be noted that when Behemoth is called “the beginning of the ways of God,” the insane doctrine of Arius is manifestly destroyed. Arius professes that the Son of God is a created being; and behold, Behemoth is shown to have been created first in the order of created things.

It remains, therefore, either for Arius not to profess that the Son was created, or, in his folly, to think that he was created after Behemoth [Note: Gussanville: “in serious error,” or “created”; the German manuscripts: “so that Arius may proclaim that the Son was created.”].

But because everything that is “applied” is brought back upon itself, Behemoth’s sword is rightly said to have been applied. His malice burns itself up when, contrary to what has been forbidden, it is not permitted to exercise itself according to its desire against the life of the elect.

He is permitted [Note: Laudian manuscript: “strives”] to strike many on account of their deserts, so that when they abandon God they may serve the condemned enemy. But he is overcome all the more powerfully by the elect insofar as they submit themselves more humbly to the sole Creator of all.

Because, then, by being called “the beginning of the ways of God” he is shown to be a formidable enemy [Note: Laudian manuscript: “because, by God’s sending, he is shown . . .”], and because by the Lord’s permission he is shown to be exceedingly intolerable, we clearly understand what a powerful enemy we are fighting.

It remains, therefore, for each of us to submit himself all the more fully to the Creator, the more truly he considers the violent forces of the adversary arrayed against him. For what are we but dust? And what is he but one of the heavenly spirits—and, what is more, their chief?

What can dust presume concerning its own strength when it fights against the prince of angels? But because the Creator of the heavenly spirits assumed an earthly body, humble dust now rightly conquers the proud angel.

By clinging to true strength, it receives the powers that the spirit who defected lost when he followed himself. It is fitting that the one who believed himself strong after abandoning the Creator should be conquered by dust, so that, overcome, he may discover that he failed when he grew proud.

He pants fiercely in his rage because, while the depths torment him, human beings ascend to the heights; because flesh, carried up into that exalted state, remains there, whereas so great a spirit himself lies cast down forever from the height.

But the order of merits has changed the places of minds. Thus, thus pride deserved to be cast down and humility to be exalted, so that the heavenly spirit, by exalting himself, might endure hell, while humble earth might reign above the heavens without end [Note: Turonian adds: “through all ages of ages. Amen.”].

# BOOK THIRTY-THREE

It presents an exposition of the fifteenth verse and the remaining verses of chapter XL, as well as the first twelve verses of chapter XLI, where the devil’s various arts are exposed, and gratuitous predestination is taught and reconciled with free will.

[Col. 0667] [Col. 0667D] 1075 [Old and Revised Version I.]

### 1. The proud serve the devil more familiarly

The proud serve the ancient enemy, who is described by the Lord’s voice under the name of Behemoth, all the more familiarly as they swell more highly in their own estimation through the successes of this life.

For when glory increases, arrogance increases with it; with arrogance comes anxiety; the mind is drawn here and there, because desires grow along with possessions. When they produce innumerable thoughts, as a field produces grass, they feed the hunger of this Behemoth with those same thoughts as with desired fodder.

Hence it is rightly said:

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0668D]

**VERSE 15.—“For him the mountains bear grass.”**
## 2. What “mountain” and “mountains” signify in Sacred Scripture

In Sacred Scripture, when *mountain* is used in the singular, it sometimes signifies the incarnate Lord, sometimes the holy Church, sometimes the testament of God, sometimes an apostate angel, and sometimes any heretic. When *mountains* are named in the plural, they sometimes express the exaltedness of the apostles and prophets, but sometimes the pride of secular powers.

A mountain designates the Lord, as it is written: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). [Col. 0669A] The incarnate Lord is indeed a mountain upon the summit of the mountains, transcending the height of the prophets.

Again, the holy Church is designated by the mountain, as it is written: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Ps. 124:1). Zion is called “watchtower” (*speculatio*), through which the Church, contemplating God, is represented.

Again, the testament of God is expressed by the mountain, as Habakkuk says: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shadowy and dense mountain” (Hab. 3:3). For he who promised in the pages of his testament that he would come seems to come from the place where he held himself, as it were, under a promise. That testament is rightly called a shadowy and dense mountain, because [Col. 0669B] it is overshadowed by the thick obscurities of allegories.

Again, an apostate angel is designated by the mountain, as, under the appearance of the king of Babylon, the preachers are told concerning the ancient enemy: “Raise a standard upon the gloomy mountain” (Isa. 13:2).

[Note: Gemetianus, two German manuscripts, Vallicellianus, and others read *caligosum* (“gloomy”); below also, “upon the gloomy mountain.”]

The holy preachers raise a standard upon the gloomy mountain when, against Satan’s pride—who often hides beneath the cloud of pretense—they exalt the power of the cross.

Again, any heretic is represented by the mountain, as the Psalmist says in the voice of the Church: “I trust in the Lord; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:1). When the faithful soul, after abandoning unity, is said to trust in the swelling doctrine of a heretical preacher, it is urged to flee from the Lord as though to a mountain.

Again, the height of the apostles and prophets is designated by *mountains*, as it is written: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7). [Col. 0669C] And Paul’s voice says: “So that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21). Or again, as the Psalmist says in the voice of the hope-filled Church: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Ps. 120:1). [1076]

Again, the pride of secular powers is expressed by *mountains*, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 96:5), because many who had previously swollen with lofty rigidity were melted by great fear through repentance when God appeared in the flesh.

Or, as the same Prophet says again: “The mountains rise up, and the plains descend” (Ps. 103:8). For many persecutors of the Lord come against him in pride, but return from him humbled. [Col. 0669D] They ascend as mountains through the swelling of power, but descend as plains, made level, that is, through recognition of their guilt.

## [Ancient recension II.] 3. By evil action, the proud nourish demons

But because some remain in the height of their pride and disdain to bend humbly to divine service, since, in accordance with the desire of the ancient enemy, they do not cease thinking and perpetrating evil, it is rightly said here concerning Behemoth: “To him the mountains bear grass.”

For the proud of this age bear grass to this Behemoth, [Col. 0670A] because they refresh him with what they wickedly do. They bear grass to Behemoth because they offer him their fleeting and slippery pleasures. “For there will be,” says the Apostle, “people who are lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2). He included their description when he said: “Lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God” (ibid., 3:4).

What, then, is the grass of the mountains, if not fleeting pleasure, which is generated from the heart of the proud? If the proud did not despise God through their pride, they would certainly not perpetrate so many slippery acts through wantonness.

[Note: The German, Laudunensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “they penetrate.”]

This Behemoth is nourished by such grass, because, hungering for the punishment of eternal death, he is filled by their ruined morals. [Col. 0670D] Laudunensis reads “hunger.” [Col. 0670B]

For although the proud of this age sometimes cease from the completion of evil works because they are hindered by the order of heavenly providence, they nevertheless multiply evil in thought: sometimes so that they may display themselves as more powerful than others through possessions and honors; sometimes so that they may exercise that same power in striving to injure another; sometimes, led by slippery impulses, so that they may dissipate themselves in frivolous deeds and pleasures.

While they continually intend to do not what is right but what is wrong with the goods divinely bestowed upon them, what else do they do except fight against God with his own gifts? Since this Behemoth therefore continually recognizes his own desires in the minds of the proud, he finds, as it were, grass in the mountains, by which he stretches his belly, refreshed for his wickedness.

It is rightly added:

## Chapter II [Recension II]

### The same passage: “All the beasts of the field shall play there”

[Note: Pratellensis and Uticensis read “shall play.”]

### 4. The demons’ play is to whirl human minds from one vice into another

What is designated by *beasts* if not unclean spirits, [Col. 0670C] and by *field* if not the present age? Hence it is said of the prince of the evil spirits, against Ephraim: “The beast of the field shall tear them” (Hos. 13:8). Or, as Isaiah says: “No evil beast shall ascend through it” (Isa. 35:9).

[Note: Vallicellianus and two German manuscripts read “shall not pass through it.”]

That the name *field* signifies the world is attested by the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13:38). The beasts of the field therefore play in the grass of the mountains, because demons, cast down from above into this world, delight in the wicked works of the proud.

[Note: Others read: “into this world.”]

The beasts play in the grass when wicked spirits drag human hearts into unlawful thoughts. Is it not play for unclean spirits to toy with minds created in the image of God—sometimes deceiving them by fabricated promises, sometimes mocking them with empty terrors, sometimes impressing upon them transient joys as though they would last, and sometimes making lasting punishments seem as though they were transient?

The Psalmist had certainly feared the illusion of these beasts when he said: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be ashamed, nor shall my enemies mock me” (Ps. 24:2).

Since the heart of the proud is therefore laid open to every vice, so that it may be prepared by evil thought for whatever wicked spirit attacks it, it is rightly said concerning the grass of the mountains: “All the beasts of the field shall play there.”

For because the proud leave no evil unconsidered in thought, there is no beast of the field that is not filled by the grass of these mountains. For even when they flee the luxury of the flesh, they commit the vice of inward luxury by boasting of their chastity. When they seize nothing outwardly through greed, they are nevertheless not free from the lure of avarice: although they seek no possessions, they try to seize human praise for their self-restraint.

To this Behemoth, therefore, the mountains bear grass, and all the beasts of the field play there, because every wicked spirit feeds all the more broadly in the heart of the proud, the more every vice is generated from pride. [Col. 0671A]

[Ancient recension III.] But since we have heard what this Behemoth eats, we must now hear where, through his wicked desire, he rests. It follows:

## Chapter III [Recension III]

### Verse 16: “He sleeps beneath the shadow, in the secret place of the reed, in wet places”

### 5. What Scripture understands by “shadow”

In sacred speech, *overshadowing* sometimes signifies the Lord’s incarnation, and sometimes the refreshment of the mind from the heat of carnal thoughts. Hence, under the name of shadow, the refreshment of the heart from heavenly protection is customarily indicated.

At other times, however, *shadow*, when charity has departed, signifies the torpor of a cold mind. That the Lord’s incarnation, while the truth of the history is preserved, is designated by the term *overshadowing* is attested by the angelic message which says to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Since a shadow is expressed only through light and body, the power of the Most High overshadowed her because incorporeal light took a body in her womb. [Col. 0671C] From this overshadowing she received in herself all refreshment of mind.

Again, refreshment of the heart from heavenly protection is expressed by *shadow*, as the Psalmist says: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:9). Or as the bride, awaiting and announcing the bridegroom’s coming in the Song of Songs, says: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I had desired” (Song 2:3).

[Note: Pratellensis reads “whom I desired”; Laudunensis, “whom I desired” with the feminine form; Vallicellianus, “whom I desired.”]

It is as though she said: “I rested from the heat of carnal desires under the protection of his coming.”

Again, when charity has departed, the torpor of a cold mind is expressed by *shadow*, as it is written concerning the sinful human being, that he followed the shadow (Gen. 3). Fleeing the warmth of charity, the human being abandoned the sun of truth and hid himself beneath the shadow of inward cold.

Hence the voice of Truth himself says: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12).

[Note: Laudunensis and Vallicellianus read: “Iniquity will abound … it will grow cold.”]

Thus the first human being, after his sin, is found hidden among the trees of paradise from the breeze after midday (Gen. 3:8). [1078] Because he had lost the midday warmth of charity, he was already torpid beneath the shadow of sin, as beneath the chill of a breeze.

### 6. Satan easily rests as beneath a shadow in those whom he makes cold; in them he lies secure

This Behemoth, therefore, because he finds a kind of rest in those whom he makes cold by withdrawing them from the warmth of the true sun, is said to sleep beneath the shadow.

Sometimes, however, *shadow*, when it is mentioned with the addition of death, signifies either the death of the flesh or any of the reprobate who, through their wicked activity, imitate the darkness of the ancient enemy. Hence the martyrs say through the Psalmist: “You humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” (Ps. 43:20).

The shadow of death covers God’s elect when the death of the flesh—which is an image of eternal death—separates them from this life, because just as eternal death separates the soul from God, so bodily death separates the body from the soul.

[Note: The printed editions, together with two German manuscripts, read “oppresses.” Below they likewise read: “the shadow of death oppresses them.” It is argued that *covers* should be read, both from the text of Sacred Scripture cited above, “and covered us,” and from the English, Norman, Vendôme, and other manuscripts.]

Or certainly the shadow of death covers them because it is written concerning the ancient enemy: “His name is Death” (Rev. 6:8).

[Note: Laudunensis and Vallicellianus read “his name.”]

All the reprobate, therefore, are the shadow of death, because they imitate the wickedness of his pride and express his image like a shadow, drawing into themselves a likeness of his malice. They cover God’s elect when they temporarily grow strong against them in the cruelty of persecution. [Col. 0672B]

But in this passage *shadow* signifies the torpor of wickedness, in which this Behemoth sleeps, because he watches anxiously against hearts warm with charity, but lies secure in cold minds.

He cannot sleep in the minds of the saints, because even if he sometimes settles in them for a brief moment, the heat of heavenly desires tires him, and he is, as it were, pricked to withdraw as often as they sigh toward eternal things with inward love. As many voices awaken him as holy thoughts cry to heaven from their minds. [Col. 0672C]

Thus, terrified by the weapons of good actions and struck by the darts of their sighs, he flees, and, returning to the cold hearts of the reprobate, seeks the shadow of wickedness which he may possess securely. Where he finds it is shown when it is immediately added: “In the secret place of the reed.”

[Ancient recension IV.]

### 7. The various meanings of “reed” and “rush” in Sacred Scripture

In sacred speech, the word *reed* or *rush* sometimes signifies the abiding Word, sometimes the skill of teachers, sometimes the instability of the mind, and sometimes the splendor of temporal glory.

By *reed*, the eternity of the Word is signified when, through the voice of the Father, the Psalmist says: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2). Since what we speak passes away but what we write remains, the Father’s tongue is called the pen of a scribe, because the Word is coeternal with him and generated without passing away. [Col. 0672D]

[Note: Turonensis, Laudunensis, the Norman and German manuscripts read “his.” Corbeiensis Germanicus reads: “because from him his Word is generated.”]

Again, the doctrine of writers is expressed by *reed*, as the prophet promises concerning the holy Church, saying: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, greenery of reed and rush shall spring up” (Isa. 35:7). As we said much earlier in this work (above, book 29, no. 51), this statement expresses by *reed* the teaching of those who write, and by *rush* the greenness of those who hear.

Again, the instability of the mind is designated by *reed*, or certainly by *rush*, as the Lord says to the crowds concerning John’s praise: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. 11:7). [1079]

[Note: The German, Laudunensis, and Vallicellianus manuscripts supply what is implicit: “John, a reed …”]

The implication is “no.” John was not a reed shaken by the wind, because no breath of tongues, blowing from different directions, bent his mind, which the Holy Spirit had made firm.

Again, the splendor of temporal glory is expressed by *reed* or *rush*, as Wisdom says concerning the righteous: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reed-bed” (Wis. 3:7). It calls the life of secular people a reed-bed because, like reeds, they seem outwardly to advance toward lofty things through temporal glory, but inwardly become empty of the solidity of truth.

Hence the kingdom of the Jews is also compared to a reed, when the prophet says, with the Lord appearing in the truth of the flesh: “He will not break the bruised reed, and he will not extinguish the smoking flax” (Isa. 42:3). [Col. 0673B]

What else is indicated by the name *reed* except the temporal kingdom of the Jewish people, outwardly bright but inwardly empty?

[Note: Another reading has “green,” as in the older editions, but not in our manuscripts.]

And because the royal line had by then failed in that people and a foreigner possessed its kingdom, it aptly calls that same kingdom a bruised reed.

What, moreover, is expressed by *flax* except its priesthood, which used linen garments? Because it had lost the warmth of charity at the Lord’s coming, it was, as though it had lost the fire of faith, not burning but smoking.

The incarnate Lord did not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax, because he did not strike with the power of judgment the kingdom of Judea, which had already been almost destroyed, or its priesthood, which did not retain the fire of faith; rather, he endured them with long-suffering patience. [Col. 0673C]

### 8. Secular minds devoted to temporal glory are like a reed

What else, then, is designated in this passage by the name *reed* except the minds of secular people devoted to temporal glory? They become inwardly empty among themselves to the same degree that they appear outwardly tall and splendid, because, while they flow outward over the surface toward external glory, they are established inwardly by no solidity.

Like a reed, they are indeed empty within through foolishness, but outwardly beautiful in appearance and display. Yet the more diligently they seek external glory, the more heavily their hearts are driven by the goads of their thoughts.

Hence this Behemoth is rightly said to sleep in the secret place of the reed, because he silently holds the hearts of those whose ambitions he stirs toward the desire for temporal splendor and eminence.

[Note: So read the manuscripts—two German, English, Norman, Vendôme, Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, and Longipontanus. The printed editions instead read: “he holds their hearts more tenaciously.”]

He sleeps there, as it were, in peace, where he does not permit those whom he possesses to rest.

While they seek to surpass others in the loftiness of goods [Note: Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and Vallicellianus read “honors”], while, like reeds, through the brilliance of outward cleanliness they outshine the appearance of the righteous, as reeds outshine the bark of solid trees, they provide this Behemoth with a place where he may rest among them, since they themselves remain inwardly empty. [Col. 0674A]

[Ancient recension V.] Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel that the spirit which goes out finds no rest in dry and waterless places, because it finds the house it had left empty and swept clean, and enters it in greater numbers (Matt. 12:43 ff.).

Because the earth that is watered becomes fluid, dry and waterless places are the hearts of the righteous, which, through the strength of discipline, are dried from every moisture of carnal desire.

Hence here too the place where this Behemoth sleeps is shown when it is immediately added: “In wet places.” [Col. 0674B] [1080]

## 9. Carnal people resemble wet places. The devil rules people through pride or lust

Wet places are the minds of earthly people, whom the moisture of carnal desire fills and therefore makes fluid. In them this Behemoth impresses the traces of his iniquity all the more deeply, inasmuch as his passage descends into those minds as into yielding earth.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “the foot of his passage.” Gussanville noted this variant reading. The following words favor it: “For the foot …”]

Wet places are indeed works of pleasure. A foot does not slip on dry ground, but when fixed on slippery ground it is scarcely held.

Those therefore make their way through wet places in the present life who cannot stand upright in it for righteousness. In these wet places Behemoth sleeps, because he rests in the slippery activity of reprobate people.

Some, however, suppose that the wet places signify the genital members. If this is so, what else is openly signified by wet places except lust, so that the glory of pride is expressed by the reed and bodily lust by the wet places?

These are the two vices that tyrannize over the human race with terrible force: one of the spirit and the other of the flesh. Pride raises up the spirit; lust corrupts the flesh.

The ancient enemy, therefore, pressing the human race chiefly through pride or lust, sleeps in the secret place of the reed and in wet places, because he holds condemned humanity under the dominion of his rule either through the pride of the spirit or through the corruption of the flesh.

He possesses some through both, because when the spirit of pride raises them up, not even the shame of corruption bends them away from the swelling of their eminence.

But do the teachers of virtue not keep watch daily and unceasingly against such people within the holy Church? Do they cease reproving base pleasures and urging the joys of the heavenly homeland?

[Note: Turonensis reads “weak pleasures”; one Ebroicensis manuscript, “lowest desires.”]

Yet the minds of the wicked listen to higher things all the more stubbornly the more tightly they have clung to lower things.

Nor is it enough for them that they themselves perish. What is worse, when they see someone being reproved and corrected, they resist the reproofs of the righteous, so that at least others may not be corrected.

Hence it is rightly added:

## Chapter IV [Recension IV]

### Verse 17: “The shadows protect his shadow”

### 10. The shadows of the devil are sinners who protect one another. When a crime is defended, it increases

The shadows of the devil are all the wicked: by serving the imitation of his iniquity, they draw from his body, as it were, the appearance of an image.

Just as the reprobate are his shadows in the plural, so, in the singular, each sinner is his shadow. But when evil people contradict the teaching of the righteous, and do not allow any wicked person to be corrected by them, the shadows of this Behemoth protect his shadow, because each sinner defends another sinner in the very matter in which he is conscious of his own wrongdoing.

The shadows protect his shadow when the more wicked defend the deeds of the utterly wicked with perverse patronage. They do this for the very purpose that, when the fault in which they themselves are bound is corrected in others, the correction may not eventually reach them.

They therefore cover themselves when they protect others, because they foresee that their own life will be attacked from the point at which they see others exposed to open correction.

Thus it happens that the sum of crimes increases when it is defended, and each person’s wickedness becomes easier to commit in proportion as it becomes more difficult to punish.

The crimes of sinners receive all the greater increase when, through the defense of the powerful, they long go unpunished.

But [1081] whether such people appear to be outside or inside the holy Church, they show themselves to be all the more open enemies of God in proportion as they are greater patrons of vices.

[Note: Vallicellianus reads “more ready.”]

For by their defenses they fight against him whose displeasure is directed at the very things that they multiply by defending.

[Note: The Vulgate and two German manuscripts read: “to whom they multiply, by defending them, the things that displease him”; this seems to us to be meaningless. In restoring this passage we have followed the Vendôme, Pratellensis, and Uticensis manuscripts.]

The Lord aptly rebuked this conduct through the prophet, speaking under the figure of Babylon: “Thorns and nettles shall spring up in its houses, and the thorn-bush in its fortifications” (Isa. 34:13).

What do we understand by nettles except the pricks of thoughts, and by thorns except the goads of vices? Nettles and thorns therefore spring up in the houses of Babylon, because in the confusion of the reprobate mind there arise both desires of thought that irritate and sins of action that prick.

But those who do these things also have other, more wicked defenders. Hence he immediately adds there: “And the thorn-bush in its fortifications.”

The thorn-bush becomes so dense with its surrounding thorns that, because of its roughness, it can scarcely be touched. Within, therefore, the nettle and thorn are born, but outwardly both are protected by the thorn-bush, because lesser sinners commit various evils, while the more wicked and powerful defend them.

Hence here too it is rightly said: “The shadows protect his shadow.” When the worse person vindicates evil, he darkens the shadow with a shadow, so that it is not illuminated by the light of truth.

It follows:

## Chapter V [Ancient recension VI, Recension V]

### The same passage: “The willows of the torrent will surround him”

### 11. The wicked are like willows: they are green, but bear no fruit

Willows are indeed fruitless trees, but they are so green that, even when cut down at the roots and cast away, they scarcely dry up.

[Note: Turonensis, two German manuscripts, Pratellensis, and several others read: “willow trees, but.”]

Hence in sacred speech, under the name of willows, the good are sometimes designated by the steadfast greenness of their life, and the reprobate at other times by their barrenness.

Unless they represented the life of the elect through the steadfastness of their greenness, the prophet would never have said concerning the sons of the holy Church: “They shall sprout among the grasses like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. 44:4). [Col. 0676B]

The sons of the holy Church sprout among the grasses like willows when, amid the withering life of carnal people, they endure both in great number and in perpetual greenness of mind.

They are rightly said to sprout beside flowing waters because each of them receives abundance for fruitfulness from the teaching of sacred speech, which passes along in time.

Again, unless the life of sinners were signified by the barrenness of willows, the Psalmist would never have said against Babylon in the voice of the preachers: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. 136:2).

Willows are described as existing in the midst of Babylon because all the fruitless, alienated from love of the heavenly homeland, are rooted with all the inward strength of their hearts in this confusion of the age.

Hence the holy preachers do not play their instruments upon these willows but hang them there, because when they behold fruitless and reprobate minds, they do not display the force of their preaching but rather remain silent in mourning. [Col. 0676C]

What else is expressed by *torrent* except the course of this mortal life? Concerning it the Prophet again says: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109:7), because our Redeemer touched the punishment of mortal life in a kind of passage and therefore did not remain long in the death to which he had willingly submitted.

Thus, on the third day, he raised up by rising the head that he had laid down by dying. [1082]

What, then, does it mean when it is said concerning this Behemoth: “The willows of the torrent will surround him,” except that those who love mortal life, alien from good works as from fruits, cling to him all the more tightly as the pleasure of passing delight pours more abundantly into them?

The torrent waters them, as it were, at the roots when the love of carnal life intoxicates them in their thoughts. Like willows, they bear no fruit but grow green in leaves, because they sometimes utter words of respectability that are not difficult to say, but display no weight of life through good works.

It is rightly said, therefore: “The willows of the torrent will surround him,” because all the fruitless, while serving the love of temporal life, obey the ancient enemy more familiarly through their wicked conduct.

[Ancient recension VII.] But since we have heard what is offered to him by his dependents, let us now hear what he himself does in them. It follows:

## Chapter VI [Recension VI]

### Verse 18: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished, and he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth”

### 12. Satan swallowed nearly all humanity before the Redeemer and afterward devoured not a few

What else is designated in this passage by the name *river* except the course of the human race, which rises by birth as though from the source of its origin but, flowing downward toward the depths, passes away through death?

Who are signified by the name *Jordan* except those who have already been imbued with the sacrament of baptism? Because our Redeemer deigned to be baptized in this river, all the baptized ought to be represented by its name, since in it this very sacrament of baptism was begun.

Since this Behemoth, therefore, from the beginning of the world, drew into himself the human race flowing downward toward the depths, with scarcely a few of the elect escaping, and continued to do so until the time of redemption, it is rightly said now: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished.” [Col. 0677B]

But because even after the Mediator’s coming he seizes some of the faithful who neglect to live rightly, it is rightly added: “And he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.”

It is as though it were said openly: “Before the Redeemer, he swallowed the world without astonishment; but, what is more grievous, even after the Redeemer’s coming he trusts that he can devour some who have been marked with the sacrament of baptism.”

He devours some who bear the name Christian because he makes them stumble through an error of faith itself. He does not turn others away from the rightness of faith, but inclines them toward wicked practice. He cannot bend others as much as he wishes into unclean action, but inwardly twists them in their own intention, so that, while they divide their minds from charity, whatever they do outwardly is not right.

They hold the faith but do not hold the life of faith, because they either openly commit unlawful acts, or, from a perverse heart, their deeds are wrong even when they appear holy.

Because some are faithful in confession but not in life, the voice of Truth says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Again he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. 1:16). John says: “Whoever says that he knows him but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

The Lord complains concerning his own first people: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark 7:6, citing Isa. 29:13). The Psalmist also says: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (Ps. 77:36).

It was not at all surprising that this Behemoth, before the water of the washing, before the heavenly sacraments, and before the bodily presence of the Redeemer, swallowed the river of the human race with the gaping mouth of profound persuasion.

But this is very surprising and very terrible: with open mouth he receives many even after they have come to know the Redeemer; after the water of the washing he pollutes them; after the heavenly sacraments he drags them into the depths of hell.

Let it therefore be said—let it be said with terror by the voice of Truth: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished, and he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.”

For the devil did not consider it a great thing to carry off unbelievers. But now he rises with all his effort toward the death of those at whose regeneration against him he wastes away with envy.

Let no one therefore trust that faith without works can suffice, since we know that it is written: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20).

[Note: Turonensis, Vendôme, Laudunensis, Pratellensis, Uticensis, and two German manuscripts read “idle.” The Greek text, *νεκρά ἐστιν* (“it is dead”), advises rejecting this reading. Perhaps *occisa* (“killed”) should be read instead of *otiosa*, as in the old Paris edition of 1518.]

Let no one imagine that he has completely escaped Behemoth’s bite through confession of faith alone. For he has indeed swallowed the river, but he still thirsts for the Jordan; and the Jordan flows into his mouth as often as any Christian descends into iniquity.

We flee his mouth because faith lifts us up, but we must take great care lest we slide into this slippery activity. If vigilance in walking is neglected, the right path is held in vain through believing, because the way of faith advances toward the heavenly homeland but does not bring there those who stumble.

### [Ancient VIII.] 13. He especially lays snares for those who excel in soundness of life; unless they exercise the utmost vigilance, they fall more disastrously from a height.

We still have something more subtle to consider in this matter. Those whom we said are represented by the Jordan can be signified by the river. For those who have already recognized the faith of the truth but neglect to live faithfully can rightly be called a river, because, evidently, they flow downward.

[Note: From the verb *yarad*, “he descended”; hence *Yardan*, in Hebrew, “Jordan.” In Jerome’s *Greek Lexicon of Hebrew Names*, in volume II of the new edition, one reads: Ἰορδάνη κατάβασις αὐτῶν, “Jordanes: their descent.” We thought this worth noting because in the biblical indexes of Hebrew names, etc., one finds only: “the Jordan, the river of judgment,” unquestionably derived from *jor*, Hebrew for “brook” or “river,” and *dan*, “judgment.”]

In Hebrew, Jordan means “their descent.” There are some who seek the way of truth, cast themselves down, and descend from the pride of their former life. When they desire eternal things, they make themselves wholly alien to this world: they not only do not desire what belongs to others, but also abandon what is their own; they not only seek no glory in it, but even despise glory when it is offered to them. Hence the Voice of Truth says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23).

[Note: The German manuscripts, Laudunensis, and Vallicellianus read, “let him deny himself to himself.”]

He denies himself who, having trampled down the fever of pride,

[Note: Vallicellianus reads *typo*. Mabillon observes, in his notes on Letter 247 of Saint Bernard, in his catalogue of barbarous words, that *typum* is often read for *typhum*. We have made the same observation in manuscripts of Saint Gregory. In chapter 31 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, where one reads *absque typo vel mora*, we think that *typhum*, “pride,” is to be understood by *typum*. Hildemar there reads not *typo* but *typho*, by which pride is signified. Augustine, on Psalm 55:6, has: “the proud man with exceedingly arrogant pride.”]

demonstrates before God that he has become alien to himself. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim” (Psalm 41:7). Jordan, as I have said, means “descent,” while Hermoniim is interpreted as “anathema,” that is, “alienation.” Therefore, from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim God is remembered by the one who, in casting himself down and existing as one alienated from himself, is recalled to the memory of his Creator.

But the ancient enemy does not consider it a great matter that he holds under the tyranny of his power those who seek earthly things. For, as the prophet bears witness, we know that “his food is choice” (Habakkuk 1:16). Nor does he consider it remarkable if he swallows those whom pride elevates, greed wastes away, pleasure expands, malice constricts, anger inflames, discord separates, envy festers, and lust, defiling them, kills.

[Note: Vallicellianus reads “pleasure delights.”]

“Therefore he will swallow the river and not be astonished,” because he does not consider it a great thing when he devours those who, through the very pursuits of their life, run downward; but he strives with all his might to snatch away those whom he sees, after despising earthly pursuits, already joined to heavenly things.

### [Ancient IX.] Hence, after the river has been swallowed, it is rightly added:

“And he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth,” because he seeks, by lying in wait, to seize those whom he recognizes as casting themselves down from the glory of the present life for love of their heavenly homeland.

Some abandon the world, leave behind the vanity of passing honors, and, seeking the lowest place of humility, surpass the customs of human society by living well. They advance to such a height of endeavor that they now perform miraculous signs. But because they neglect to conceal themselves by keeping watch over themselves, struck by the weapon of empty glory, they fall more disastrously from on high.

Hence the eternal Judge, who examines the secrets of the heart, foretells and threatens the fall of that very ruin when he says: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I shall declare to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity; I do not know who you are’” (Matthew 7:22–23).

[Note: In Laudunensis, the words “and in your name … we did” are omitted.]

Again it is said through the prophet: “The Lord called judgment to the fire, and it devoured the great abyss,

[Note: Two German manuscripts, Laudunensis, and Vallicellianus read “and it consumed.”]

and it shall consume a portion of the house

[Note: “of the Lord” is absent here and below in Vindobonensis, the German manuscripts, Turonensis, and most others.]

of the Lord” (Amos 7:4). Judgment is called to the fire when the sentence of justice is shown already destined for the punishment of eternal burning. It devours the great abyss because it burns the wicked and unfathomable minds of human beings, which now conceal themselves from others even under the appearance of miracles. But a portion of the house of the Lord is consumed because Gehenna also devours those who now boast, as though engaged in holy deeds, that they belong to the number of the elect. Thus those who are “Jordan” here are there called “a portion of the house of the Lord.” Therefore the ancient enemy trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth because sometimes, through the snares of his cunning, he kills even those who are already thought to be elect.

### [Ancient X.] But whose heart would not be shaken by these words of the Lord? Whose steadfastness of mind would not be disturbed from the deepest roots of its thoughts when our enemy is shown to possess such great strength against us? Will there be no help of consolation? Certainly there will, for it follows:

## CHAPTER VII [Revised VII]

### VERSE 19

“He will seize him before his eyes as with a hook.”

### 14. The devil, desiring to swallow Christ, was caught as with a hook.

It must be carefully observed that God, mercifully tempering the words of his Scripture, sometimes terrifies us with harsh goads and sometimes refreshes us with gentle consolations. He mixes terror with encouragement and encouragement with terror, so that, while both are wonderfully balanced around us by the art of a teacher, we may be found neither despairingly terrified nor carelessly secure.

For after he had indicated in many statements the crafty snares and unrestrained powers of Behemoth, he immediately commends the coming of his only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, and makes known by what arrangement this Behemoth is to be destroyed. Thus, having struck our heart by recounting the enemy’s power, he might quickly relieve our sorrow by declaring his destruction.

Therefore, after saying, “He will swallow the river and not be astonished, and he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth,” he immediately announces the coming of the Lord’s incarnation, saying: “He will seize him before his eyes as with a hook.”

Who does not know that bait is displayed on a hook while the barb is hidden? The bait attracts so that the barb may pierce. Our Lord, therefore, coming for the redemption of the human race, made from himself a kind of hook for the devil’s destruction. For he assumed a body so that Behemoth might desire the death of the flesh in him as his bait. When he unjustly desired that death in him, he lost us, whom he had held as though justly.

[Note: Ebroicensis and the other Norman manuscripts read: “and us also, whom he held justly.”]

He was caught on the hook of Christ’s incarnation because, while desiring the bait of the body in him, he was pierced by the barb of divinity. There was humanity to draw the devourer toward itself; there was divinity to pierce him; there was visible weakness to entice him; there was hidden power to transfix the throat of the captor. He was caught on the hook because he perished by the very thing he devoured.

Indeed, this Behemoth knew that the Son of God had become incarnate, but he did not know the manner of our redemption. He knew that the Son of God had become incarnate for our redemption, but he did not know at all that our Redeemer would pierce him by dying. Hence it is rightly said: “He will seize him before his eyes as with a hook.”

We say that we have before our eyes what we see placed in front of us. The ancient enemy saw the Redeemer of the human race placed before him; by recognizing him he confessed him, and by confessing him he feared him, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8:29).

[Note: Vindobonensis, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read: “as with a hook.”]

He was caught before his eyes as with a hook because he both recognized and bit; he first recognized whom he should fear, and yet afterward did not fear him when he hungered for the death of the flesh in him as for his own bait.

### [Ancient XI.] Since we have heard what our Head did by himself, let us now hear what he does through his members. It follows:

## CHAPTER VIII [Revised VIII]

### The same passage

“And with stakes he will pierce his nostrils.”

[Note: Vallicellianus reads “he pierced.”]

### 15. By exposing his most cunning snares, the saints pierce his nostrils as with a stake.
