What else should we understand by stakes, that is, poles, which are sharpened so that they may be driven in, except the sharp counsels of the saints? These pierce the nostrils of Behemoth when the saints both discern his most cunning snares by vigilant observation and pierce them by overcoming them.

Odor is drawn through the nostrils, and by the passage of breath a thing situated far away is perceived. Thus Behemoth’s nostrils signify his cunning snares, by which he strives with great subtlety both to discover the hidden good things in our hearts and to destroy them by his most wicked persuasion.

Therefore, in the stakes the Lord pierces his nostrils because, penetrating his cunning snares with the sharp perceptions of the saints, he renders them powerless.

Often he circles around the ways of good people with such skill in laying snares that, through what he has observed them doing well, he seeks an entrance to evil. When he sees one person giving generously, from that same fact he inflames another with the fire of discord; when he sees one showing mercy, he persuades another to become angry. Thus, by suggesting that the good was not done as a common act, he cuts concordant minds off from the good of shared grace.

Because he cannot break the minds of the righteous by persuading them to evil, he strives to sow evil among them through their good deeds. But holy men overcome these snares all the more swiftly because they also detect them more subtly.

We can show this more clearly if we call Paul, one of the many defenders of the truth, as a witness. When a certain Corinthian had committed the crime of incest, the distinguished teacher handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, for the satisfaction of repentance, so that his spirit might be preserved for the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5).

By a great art of teaching, he was handed over to the one whom he had voluntarily submitted to in guilt, but now compelled into punishment: the one who had been the author of the wickedness leading to vice was himself made the instrument of discipline.

When Paul learned that the Corinthians had already been moved to mercy toward him because of the repentance rightly carried out, he said: “Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive; for if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

Considering the grace of communion, he said: “Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive.” As if he were saying: “I do not dissent from your good action; whatever you have done, let it be mine as well.”

Then he immediately added: “And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sake.” As if he were saying: “I have added goodness to your actions; whatever I have mercifully done, I have done for your sake. Therefore my goodness is your benefit, and your goodness is my benefit.”

Then, adding the very bond of hearts in which he was thus held, he said: “In the person of Christ.”

[Note: Vindobonensis, Pratellensis, and Uticensis read: “To whom, as though we might say.”]

As though we might presume to say to him: “Why do you so carefully join yourself to your disciples? Why do you conform either yourself to their actions or them to yours with such attentive concern?” he immediately added: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan” (ibid., 11).

He indicates with what sharp perception he pierces Satan’s cunning snares by adding: “For we are not ignorant of his thoughts.” As if he were saying in other words:

[Note: Two German manuscripts, the Vatican edition reprinted at Paris, and Gussanville read “sharp,” *acuti*.]

“By the Lord’s authorship we are sharp stakes, and by carefully observing we penetrate the nostrils of this Behemoth, lest he turn what the mind has begun well toward an evil end.”

### [Ancient XII.] 16. While testing Christ’s divinity, he was pierced in the nose and captured by Christ’s words.

The sharp stakes may signify the words of his wisdom made manifest through the flesh.

[Note: Vindobonensis reads “manifest.”]

Since odor is drawn through the nostrils, the exploration of the ancient enemy may be represented by Behemoth’s nostrils. When he doubted that God had become incarnate, he sought to discover this by testing him through the miracles he demanded, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3).

Because he desired to recognize the scent of Christ’s divinity through the indications of miracles, he drew it in as breath through his nostrils. But when he was immediately answered: “Man does not live by bread alone,” and, “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (ibid., 4, 7), the truth struck down the ancient enemy’s investigation with the sharp points of its statements and pierced his nostrils, as it were, with stakes.

But because this Behemoth is stretched out through various devices of fraud, he is still designated by another name, for it follows:

## CHAPTER IX [Revised IX]

### VERSE 20

“Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?”

### 17. Divinity in the flesh pierced Satan like a hook in bait.

Leviathan is said to mean “their addition.” Whose, evidently, except human beings? He once brought upon them the guilt of transgression and extends it daily through the worst suggestions all the way to eternal death. By multiplying their guilt through the interest of sin, he undoubtedly heaps up punishments without ceasing.

Leviathan can also be called, by way of mockery, “the one who adds.” For he claimed by cunning persuasion that he would add divinity to the first man, but he took away immortality (Genesis 3:5). Thus he may be called, in mockery, “the addition of human beings,” since, while promising to add to them what they were not, he deceived them and took away even what they were.

[Note: Pratellensis reads: “because, while doing this.”]

But this Leviathan was caught by a hook because, in our Redeemer, when through his agents he bit the bait of the body, the barb of divinity pierced him. The hook held the devourer’s throat, as it were, because in Christ the bait of the flesh was visible, which the devourer desired to swallow, while divinity, which would destroy him, was hidden during the passion.

In this abyss of waters—that is, in this vast expanse of the human race—this monster, panting for the death of all and swallowing almost everyone’s life, moved here and there with open mouth. But for the death of this monster, the hook was suspended in the dark depth of these waters by a marvelous arrangement.

The line of this hook is the lineage of the ancient fathers recorded in the Gospel. For when it says, “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob” (Matthew 1:2), and when the other successors are described, with the name of Joseph inserted, down to Mary, the betrothed virgin, a kind of line is twisted, at whose end the incarnate Lord—that is, this hook—would be fastened. Hanging in these waters of the human race, he would be desired by this monster with open mouth; but after biting him through the savagery of his agents, the monster would no longer possess the strength to bite.

So that this monster, lying in wait for human deaths, might not devour whomever it wished thereafter, the hook held the captor’s throat and bit the one who was biting it.

Indicating the incarnation of the only-begotten Son to his faithful servant, God says: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” The implied words are: “As I can, for I send my only-begotten Son incarnate to destroy the captor. In him mortal flesh is seen, while the power of immortality is not seen; thus, like a hook, he destroys the devourer from the very place where he conceals the sharp point of his power that will pierce him.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER X

### The same passage

“And with a rope you will bind his tongue.”

### 18. The Lord bound his tongue by compelling its errors to be silent.

The implied words are: “As I can.”

Holy Scripture customarily signifies by a rope at one time the allotments of boundaries, at another sins, and at another faith. In reference to the allotted boundaries of an inheritance it says: “The ropes have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is very pleasing to me” (Psalm 15:6). The ropes fall in pleasant places when, through humility of life, they allot to us the portions of a better homeland.

Again, because sins are signified by a rope, the prophet says: “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isaiah 5:18). Iniquity is dragged with cords of vanity when guilt is prolonged by increase. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The ropes of sinners have entangled me” (Psalm 118:61). Because a rope is twisted by adding to it so that it grows, sin is not improperly represented by a rope, since, when defended by a perverse heart, it is often multiplied.

Again, faith is expressed by a rope, as Solomon bears witness when he says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Faith, woven from knowledge of the Trinity by the mouths of preachers, remains strong in the elect but is destroyed only in the hearts of the reprobate.

In this passage, therefore, there is no obstacle to understanding the word “rope” either as sin or as faith.

### [Ancient XIII.]

For our incarnate Lord bound Leviathan’s tongue with a rope

[Note: Others read “the Redeemer.”]

because he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemned all his teachings of error (Romans 8:3). Hence, as Paul bears witness, it is said: “And, because of sin, he condemned sin” (ibid.).

He bound his tongue with a rope because, through the likeness of sinful flesh, he destroyed from the hearts of his elect all the arguments of Leviathan’s deception.

For behold, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, Leviathan’s tongue was bound because, once his truth was recognized,

[Note: Vindobonensis, the German Corbeiensis, and many Norman manuscripts read “the doctrines of that falsehood.”]

those doctrines of falsehood fell silent.

### 19. The Academics and mathematicians refuted.

Where now is the error of the Academics, who certainly attempt to assert that nothing is certain, while with shameless boldness they demand faith from their hearers for their assertions, even though they testify that nothing is true?

Where is the superstition of the mathematicians, who, while observing the courses of the stars, suspend human lives upon the moments of the heavenly bodies? Their doctrine is openly often shattered by the birth of twins, who, although they emerge at one and the same moment of time, do not persist in the same quality of life.

Where are all the many doctrines of falsehood, which we avoid enumerating lest we depart too far from the order of our exposition? But all the teaching of error has now fallen silent because the Lord has bound Leviathan’s tongue with the rope of his incarnation.

Hence it is also rightly said through the prophet: “The Lord will lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea” (Isaiah 11:15).

[Note: The Corbeiensis, Vindobonensis, and Laudunensis manuscripts read “of Egypt”; thus also in what follows.]

The tongue of the sea is secular knowledge and teaching. The sea is rightly called Egyptian because it is darkened by the obscurity of sin.

[Note: Laudunensis reads: “Egypt is called.”]

Therefore the Lord laid waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea because, by showing himself in the flesh, he destroyed the false wisdom of this world. Leviathan’s tongue is thus bound with a rope because the preaching of the ancient sinner was bound through the likeness of sinful flesh.

### 20. When knowledge of the most holy Trinity was disseminated, secular knowledge fell silent.

But if faith is signified by a rope, the same interpretation is again suggested to us because, when faith in the Trinity became known throughout the world through holy preachers, worldly teaching ceased to erupt against the minds of the elect.

Hence it is rightly said to the Lord through the prophet: “You broke open the springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Psalm 73:15). Ethan means “strong.” And who is this strong one except the one of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3:27)?

The Lord broke open springs and torrents when he opened the streams of truth in the hearts of his apostles. Of these it is said again through another prophet: “You will draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior” (Isaiah 12:3). We go thirsting to their teaching so that we may bring back little vessels of our hearts filled with truth.

[Note: The German manuscripts, Laudunensis, Pratellensis, and many others read: “and filled with truth.”]

But when his springs poured forth, he dried up the rivers of Ethan, rendering the teaching of the strong and malicious spirit dry by displaying the radiance of his truth.

Leviathan’s tongue, therefore, is bound with a rope because, when faith in the Trinity was extended, the doctrines of error fell silent.

But since he can no longer raise himself openly, he circles around here and there and bites through his snares.

### [Ancient XIV.] The Lord watches over us against him with marvelous mercy, and defeats him even in what he contrives by fraud. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XI [Revised X]

### VERSE 21

“Will you put a ring in his nostrils?”

### 21. The ring in the devil’s nostrils is the omnipotence of divine power.

Just as the nostrils signify snares, so the ring signifies the omnipotence of divine power. When it prevents us from being seized by temptations, it holds the snares of the ancient enemy within a marvelous arrangement, enclosing them.

A ring is placed in his nostrils when the strength of heavenly protection, drawn around him, restrains his cunning.

[Note: Two German manuscripts, Laudunensis, and Vallicellianus read “his skill”; Turonensis reads “his arrow is held.”]

Thus his skill is prevented from prevailing against human weakness to the extent that, secretly investigating, it devises arguments for destruction.

The word “ring” may also signify the assistance of hidden judgment, which is placed in the nostrils of this Behemoth when he is restrained from his cunning cruelty. Hence, when the king of Babylon is forbidden to harm the Israelites, it is rightly said through the prophet: “I will put a ring in your nostrils” (Isaiah 37:29). As if it were said openly: “You sigh while devising snares, but because you cannot fulfill what you desire, you bear the ring of my omnipotence in your nostrils, so that, while you pant more ardently for the death of the good, you return empty-handed from their life.”

What is called a ring in this passage is also called a sickle by holy Scripture through John in the Apocalypse. For he says: “I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one seated like the Son of Man, having on his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle” (Revelation 14:14).

[Note: Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and Vallicellianus add: “and behold, a white cloud.”]

The power of divine judgment is called a ring because it constrains from every side; and because, cutting through everything, it encloses all things within itself, it is designated by the name “sickle.” Whatever is cut by a sickle bends in every direction and yields inward.

And because the power of heavenly judgment cannot be escaped in any way—for we are within it, no matter where we try to flee—it is rightly said, when the coming Judge is revealed, that he holds a sickle: because, powerfully meeting everything, he surrounds it by cutting.

The Prophet saw himself within the sickle of judgment when he said: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. If I take my wings before dawn

[Note: Laudunensis, Vindobonensis, and Pratellensis read “at dawn”; Vallicellianus, “before the light, at dawn.”]

and dwell at the ends of the sea,

[Note: The Corbeiensis, Laudunensis, and Gemetensis manuscripts read “at the farthest end of the sea.”]

even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:8–10).

He saw himself within a certain sickle when he recognized that no place offered him a path of escape, saying: “For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains” (Psalm 74:7)—the implied words being, “is a way of escape open.” Then, adding the complete enclosure of heavenly power itself, he said: “For God is judge.”

As if he were saying: “The way of escape is absent everywhere because the one who judges is everywhere.”

Thus divine judgments are represented by a sickle because they cut as they surround; and they are expressed by a ring because they constrain from every side.

Therefore a ring is placed by the Lord in Leviathan’s nostrils because the power of his judgment restrains him in his snares, so that he may not prevail to the extent that he wishes.

Thus it is said: “Will you put a ring in his nostrils?” The implied words are: “As I will, for I constrain his crafty snares by omnipotent judgment, so that he neither tempts as much as he desires nor captures as much as he tempts.”

It follows:

## CHAPTER XII

### The same passage

“Or will you pierce his jaw with a bracelet?”

### 22. By this he draws from his jaws many whom he had devoured.

The bracelet does not differ in meaning from the ring, because it too constrains by encircling the place where it is put. But because a bracelet extends more broadly, it signifies the more abundant protection of his hidden judgment toward us.

The Lord pierces the jaw of this Leviathan with a bracelet because, by the ineffable power of his mercy, he confronts the malice of the ancient enemy in such a way that sometimes he causes even those whom the enemy has already seized to escape. They fall, as it were, from his mouth when, after committing sins, they return to innocence.

Who could escape his jaw after once being snatched into his mouth if it had not been pierced? Did he not hold Peter in his mouth when he denied (Matthew 26:71)? Did he not hold David in his mouth when David plunged himself into so great an abyss of lust (2 Samuel 11:4)? But when both returned to life through repentance, this Leviathan lost them in some way through the openings in his jaw.

Through the opening in his jaw, therefore, those were withdrawn from his mouth who returned through repentance after committing such great wickedness.

What human being, however, can escape this Leviathan’s mouth so as to commit no forbidden act? From this we learn how greatly we are indebted to the Redeemer of the human race: he not only prevented us from entering Leviathan’s mouth, but also granted us the possibility of returning from it. He did not take hope away from the sinner; he pierced Leviathan’s jaw in order to provide a way of escape, so that at least the one who had been bitten might flee, though previously, in his carelessness, he had by no means feared being bitten.

Everywhere, therefore, heavenly medicine meets us. God gave human beings commandments so that they might not sin, yet he also gave remedies for sinning, so that they might not despair.

Accordingly, one must be extremely careful lest someone be carried away by the pleasure of sin into the mouth of this Leviathan. Yet, if someone has been seized, he must not despair, because, if he mourns his sin perfectly, he still finds an opening in Leviathan’s jaw through which he may escape.

He is already being ground by the teeth, but if he seeks a way of escape, he finds an opening in the jaw. Even one who refused to foresee his capture still has, after being captured, a way out.

Therefore, whoever has not yet been captured should flee his jaw; whoever has already been captured should seek the opening in his jaw. For our Creator is merciful and just.

### [Ancient XV.] 23. Before sin, God’s justice must be feared; after sin, his mercy must be hoped for. The fall of the great should be the caution of the small.

But let no one say: “Because he is merciful, I may sin venially.” And let no one who has sinned say: “Because he is just, I despair of the forgiveness of sin.”

[Note: Laudunensis and Vallicellianus read: “I despair of forgiveness.”]

God releases the crime that is mourned, but let everyone fear committing what he does not know whether he could mourn worthily.

Before sin, therefore, let one fear justice; after sin, nevertheless, let one presume upon mercy. Let one not fear justice so much that one fails to recover through the consolation of hope; nor let one trust in mercy so much that one neglects to apply the medicine of worthy repentance to one’s wounds.

But let the one who presumes that God will mercifully spare him always also consider that he will judge him strictly. Under his mercy, therefore, let the sinner’s hope rejoice; but under his strictness, let the penitent’s correction tremble.

Let the hope of our confidence also contain a bite of fear, so that the justice of the Judge may terrify the one whom the grace of the merciful one invites to trust in forgiveness.

Hence a certain wise man says: “Do not say, ‘The Lord’s mercies are many; he will not remember my sins’” (Ecclesiasticus 5:6). He immediately adds both God’s mercy and his justice, saying: “For mercy and wrath are with him” (ibid., 7).

Thus divine clemency, piercing the jaw of this Behemoth, comes mercifully and powerfully to the aid of the human race everywhere. It neither kept silent about the warning to avoid sin for the one who was free, nor withheld from the captive a remedy for escape.

For this reason the sins of such men—David and Peter—were recorded in holy Scripture, so that the fall of the great might be the caution of the small.

[Note: Laudunensis reads “both.”]

For this reason also the repentance and forgiveness of both are related there, so that the recovery of the lost might be the hope of those who are perishing.

Therefore, when David falls from his position, let no one become proud. When David rises after his fall, let no one despair.

Behold how marvelously holy Scripture uses the same event to strike down the proud and raise up the humble. It related one deed, but in different ways recalled the proud to fear of humility and the humble to confidence in hope.

O immeasurable medicine of a new kind, which, set forth in one and the same arrangement, dries up swollen things by pressing them down and pours itself into parched things by lifting them up! It terrified us by the fall of the great, but strengthened us by their restoration.

### 24. He hopes for mercy in vain who does not fear justice.

Thus, always thus, the mercy of divine providence both restrains us when we are proud and supports us lest we fall into despair.

### [Ancient XVI; Revised XI.]

Hence through Moses he also admonishes us, saying: “You shall not take the upper or the lower millstone as a pledge” (Deuteronomy 24:6).

We sometimes use “to take” to mean “to take away.” Thus birds that are eager to seize other birds are called *accipitres*, “hawks.” Hence the Apostle Paul says: “For you endure it if someone devours you, if someone takes from you” (2 Corinthians 11:20), as though he were saying, “if someone seizes you.”

A debtor’s pledge is a sinner’s confession. A pledge is taken from a debtor when a confession of sin is obtained from a sinner.

The upper and lower millstones are hope and fear. Hope raises one upward, while fear presses the heart downward. But the upper and lower millstones are so necessarily joined to each other

[Note: Gemetensis, two German manuscripts, Turonensis, and Laudunensis read “are joined.”]

that one is useless without the other.

Therefore, in the breast of the sinner, hope and fear must continually be joined, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear justice; and he fears justice in vain if he does not also have confidence in mercy.

The removal of either the upper or the lower millstone as a pledge is therefore forbidden because the one who preaches to a sinner must arrange his preaching with such care that, without abandoning hope, he does not remove fear, and, without removing hope, does not leave him in fear alone.

The upper or lower millstone is removed if, through the preacher’s tongue, either fear is separated from hope or hope from fear in the sinner’s breast.

### 25. Why God does not preserve the elect unharmed from carnal vices. Pride a greater sin than lust. Man makes a wound from medicine; God makes medicine from a wound.

But since, necessity requiring it, David has been brought into the discussion and we have recalled the memory of so great a crime, the reader’s mind may perhaps be moved to ask why almighty God does not preserve from bodily vices unharmed those whom he has chosen for eternity and whom he has also raised to the summit of spiritual gifts. Since we believe that a brief answer will readily satisfy this question, we shall respond briefly.

Some people, through the virtues they have received and through the grace of good works bestowed upon them, fall into the vice of pride, yet do not recognize the depth to which they have fallen. Therefore the ancient enemy, because he already rules within them, is permitted to rage against them also outwardly, so that those who have become exalted in thought may be thrown down through carnal lust. We know, however, that at times it is a lesser thing to fall into bodily corruption than to sin silently in one’s thoughts through deliberate pride; but because pride is believed to be less shameful, it is avoided less carefully. People are all the more ashamed of lust because everyone recognizes it as shameful.

Hence it often happens that some, after falling from pride into lust, become ashamed of the hidden evil of their sin because of their manifest fall; and then they correct even greater faults, when, prostrated in lesser matters, they are more grievously confounded. They see themselves guilty in lesser matters who had believed themselves free in more serious ones.

Thus, by the merciful dispensation of the Lord, this Behemoth, having sometimes been released, drags a person from one fault to another [Note: Laudunensis and others: “having been loosened … draws.”], and while striking more forcefully, loses the one whom he had seized; and by the very means through which he appears to have conquered, he is overcome. Let us consider within how secure a shelter of grace God holds us by the favor of his mercy. Behold: the one who exalts himself because of virtue returns through vice to humility.

[Old recension XVI.] Whoever is exalted by the virtues he has received is wounded not by a sword but, so to speak, by medicine. For what is virtue except medicine, and what is vice except a wound? Therefore, because we make a wound from medicine, he makes medicine from a wound, so that we who are struck by virtue may be healed by vice. We turn the gifts of virtues toward the use of vices; he takes the allurements of vices and converts them into an instrument of virtue. He strikes the condition of our salvation in order to preserve it, so that we who flee from humility when running may at least cling to it when fallen.

Yet amid these things we must understand that many people, the more they fall in many ways, are bound more tightly. When this Behemoth strikes them through one vice so that they fall, he also binds them through another so that they cannot rise again. Let a person therefore consider what sort of enemy he is fighting; and if he perceives that he has already sinned in some way, let him at least fear being dragged from one fault into another, so that he may diligently avoid the wounds by which the enemy frequently kills. For it is very rare that our enemy serves the salvation of the elect even through wounds.

### 26. Temptation is sometimes the safeguard of merit. By tempting the saints, the devil unwillingly preserves them for the kingdom.

Nevertheless, the pierced jaw of this Behemoth can also be understood in another way: he is said to hold in his mouth not those whom he has already completely entangled in sin, but those whom he still tempts through the persuasions of sin, so that “to chew” someone means to tempt him through the pleasure of sin.

He had received Paul to be chewed, but not swallowed, when, after the sublimity of so many revelations, he was harassing him with a thorn of the flesh (II Corinthians 12:7). Thus, when he received permission to tempt him, he held him in his jaw—but in a pierced jaw. The man who might have been destroyed through exaltation was tempted so that he would not perish. That temptation, therefore, was not a chasm of vices but a safeguard of merits, because this Leviathan crushed him by tiring him through affliction, but did not devour him by capturing him in guilt.

He would not have retained men exalted in holiness unless he had tempted them. For they would not be saints if they grew proud of the glory of holiness and fell under his power to the same degree that they raised themselves up in their virtues. But by a marvelous order of divine dispensation, while they are tempted they are humbled; while they are humbled, they cease to belong to him.

The pierced jaw of this Behemoth is therefore rightly mentioned, because by the very means through which he crushes God’s elect, he loses them; by the very means through which he tempts them in order to destroy them, he acts so that they do not perish. Thus the ancient enemy, serving the hidden dispensations of God, willingly tempts the souls of the saints toward destruction, but by tempting them unwillingly preserves them for the kingdom.

His jaw is therefore pierced because, when he crushes those whom he tempts—that is, chews them—as though he swallowed them, he loses them. Since this happens not through human but through divine providence, so that the craft of the ancient adversary itself may serve the advantage of the righteous, inasmuch as, when he tempts the elect, he guards them more effectively through the temptation, it is rightly said to blessed Job:

“Or will you pierce his jaw with a ring?”

The implied meaning is: “Will you pierce it as I do, who, arranging all things providentially, preserve my elect more securely in integrity by the very means through which I permit them to be shaken to some degree by the jaw of this Leviathan?” The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIII [Old recension XVIII, Revised recension XII]

**VERSE 22.** “Will he multiply prayers to you, or speak gentle words to you?”

### 27. Satan, whether through himself or through his members—that is, the reprobate—offered prayers to Christ.

The implied words are: “as he does to me.” If these words are referred to the person of the Son, he spoke gentle words to him when he said in his incarnate state: “I know that you are the Holy One of God” (Luke 4:34) [Note: Laudunensis and German manuscripts: “I know who you are.” Vallicellian: “I know who you are.” Corbeiensis and German manuscripts: “who you may be.”]

This Leviathan multiplied prayers to him when, through the legion subject to him, he said: “If you drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matthew 8:31).

It may, however, be understood more clearly [Note: Most manuscripts: “more suitably”] that he multiplies prayers to the Lord when, on the day of the final judgment, the wicked who constitute his body beg that mercy be shown to them, when his members—that is, the reprobate—cry out too late: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Luke 13:25). They are immediately told: “I do not know where you are from.”

Then also he will speak gentle words to the Lord through his members, when many from his body will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” (Matthew 7:22). They speak gentle words as they plead, repeating what they have done in his name [Note: Another Ebroicensis: “they multiply”], but when they did these things they seized them for their own praise, with hard hearts. Therefore they immediately hear: “I do not know who you are” (ibid., 23). The text continues:

## CHAPTER XIV [Revised recension XIII]

**VERSE 23.** “Will he make a covenant with you?” The implied words are: “as he makes with me.” “And will you take him as an everlasting servant?”

### 28. By tempting the saints, he serves their advantage and the will of God.

The implied words are: “as I do.” But we must observe very carefully that this Leviathan makes a covenant with the Lord so that he may be held by him as an everlasting servant. In a covenant, the will of disputing parties is fulfilled, so that each reaches its own desire and brings its quarrel to the desired conclusion.

Thus the ancient enemy, inflamed by the fire of his malice and opposed to the sincerity of divine innocence, is in conflict with it; yet even while opposed, he does not depart from its judgment. For he always maliciously desires to tempt righteous men, but the Lord permits this either mercifully or justly.

This permission to tempt is therefore called a covenant, in which the desire of the tempter is carried out, yet through it the will of the just disposer is fulfilled in a marvelous way. As we recently said, the Lord often subjects his elect, who are to be instructed, to the tempter. Thus, after the barriers of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, an angel of Satan was given to Paul, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (II Corinthians 12:7).

But, as we have already said, this very temptation is ordered so that those who might have perished through exaltation may be preserved from destruction through humility. Therefore, by the secret order of divine dispensation, where the devil’s wickedness is permitted to rage, there the goodness of God is piously brought to completion.

It is rightly said that, because of this covenant which he makes with the Lord, he is received as a servant, because by the very means through which he exercises the anger of his most wicked will, he obeys the commands of heavenly grace.

[Old recension XIX.] He is therefore a servant through the covenant who, while being permitted to fulfill his own will, is bound by the will of heavenly counsel, so that, as has been said, he willingly tempts God’s elect and, by tempting them, tests them without knowing it.

### 29. The punishment of the reprobate serves the glory of God and of his elect.

But since he serves the needs of the elect in this life only so long as he can exercise the wickedness of his malice through temptations, while here he is said by the Lord to be received not only as a servant through a covenant but as an everlasting servant, we are compelled to investigate how we may show that he serves the Lord forever even after the end of the present life.

For he is not then permitted to tempt the righteous who possess heavenly happiness, when he is consigned before their eyes to the eternal fires of Gehenna. They will not be instructed by temptations in that heavenly homeland where they are already rewarded for the labors of temptation.

But then this Leviathan, together with his body—that is, all the reprobate—is handed over to avenging flames, in which he will be tortured without end. When the righteous behold these torments, they increase in the praises of God, because in themselves they see the good with which they have been rewarded, and in those others they behold the punishment which they escaped [Note: Laudunensis and Vallicellian: “the evil.”]

Thus the universe will then be beautiful, when Gehenna justly tortures the wicked and eternal happiness justly rewards the godly. Just as black is placed beneath a painting so that the white or red laid over it may appear more beautiful, so then also God, rightly ordering the wicked, displays the joys of the blessed more fully by showing the punishments of the reprobate before their eyes.

Although their joy does not arise from the vision of the Lord in such a way that the vision itself increases it [Note: Corbeiensis, another Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts: “so that their joy increases … because the righteous, having been rewarded …”], they nevertheless feel more indebted to their Creator when they see both the good which, having been justly rewarded, they receive and the evil which, having been mercifully helped, they overcame.

[Revised recension XIV.] Therefore, if both here the temptation of this Leviathan and there his condemnation benefit the righteous, he is an everlasting servant: unknowingly he serves the praises of God, both through his just punishment there and through his unjust will here. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XV [Old recension XX]

**VERSE 24.** “Will you mock him as a bird?”

### 30. The devil is a four-footed beast through the stupidity of filthy action, a dragon through the malice of harming, and a bird through pride.

Why is our adversary first called Behemoth, then Leviathan, and now compared to a bird in the mockery of his destruction? As we have said, Behemoth means a beast. He is shown to be four-footed when he is said to eat grass like an ox. Leviathan, because he is caught with a hook, is undoubtedly recognized as a serpent in the waters. Now he is likened to a bird when it is said: “Will you mock him as a bird?”

Let us therefore investigate why he is called a beast or animal, why a dragon, and why a bird. We recognize his names more quickly if we carefully examine the cunning of his evasions. He came from heaven to earth and no longer raises himself toward the hope of heavenly things by any breath of life.

Therefore he is an irrational four-footed animal through the stupidity of filthy action; he is a dragon through the malice of harming; and he is a bird through the lightness of a subtle nature [Note: Laudunensis and German manuscripts: “a quadruped.” Gilot and Vatican manuscripts: “and fourfold.” The reading is corrected from English manuscripts and our own, as well as from the old edition.]

Because he does not understand what he is doing against himself, he is a beast in brute perception. Because he maliciously desires to harm us, he is a dragon. But because he proudly exalts himself through the subtlety of his nature, he is a bird.

Again, because in the evil he performs he is held by divine power for our benefit, he is an animal; because he bites secretly, he is a serpent; but because at times, through untamed pride, he even pretends to be an angel of light, he is a bird.

Although he assails the human race through an inscrutable art of wickedness, he tempts it especially through three vices: he subjects some to himself through lust, others through malice, and others through pride.

### 31. According to these various forms he tempts in various ways. Christ displayed bait to Satan and concealed the snare.

It is therefore not without reason that he is named from the very character of his actions, when he is called an animal, a dragon, or a bird. Among those whom he incites to the folly of lust, he is an animal; among those whom he inflames toward malicious harm, he is a dragon; and among those whom he raises into the arrogance of pride, as though they possessed lofty wisdom, he is a bird. But among those whom he pollutes simultaneously with lust, pride, and malice, he exists as animal, dragon, and bird at once.

For he enters the hearts of the deceived in as many forms as the vices in which he entangles them [Note: Gemetensis and two German manuscripts: “into the heart of those deceived.”] He is therefore called by the names of many things, because before the minds of the deceived he changes into various forms.

When he tempts someone through carnal lust but cannot overcome him, he changes his suggestion and inflames that person’s heart toward malice. Because the beast could not approach him, the dragon comes. When he cannot corrupt him with the poison of malice, he nevertheless places his good qualities before his eyes and lifts his heart into pride. Thus, when the dragon cannot creep upon him [Note: Another manuscript: “steal upon him,” as read in the manuscripts], he nonetheless brings before the eyes of his thought a phantom of empty glory, and, like a bird, flies before him.

This bird rises against us with so much the greater ferocity because it is hindered by no weakness of its nature. Since it is not weighed down by the death of the flesh and saw our Redeemer mortal in the flesh, it swelled with a loftier arrogance of pride. But when it raised the feather of its pride against its Creator, there it found the snare of its death.

For it was struck down by the death of that flesh which it had desired in its pride, and it suffered the snare from the very place where, as though it were the food of its malice, it had desired the death of the righteous.

[Old recension XXI.] Let it therefore be said: “Will you mock him as a bird?” The Lord mocked him as a bird when, in the passion of his only-begotten Son, he showed him the bait but concealed the snare. He saw what he might take with his mouth, but did not see what he would hold in his throat [Note: Most manuscripts: “what he would hold in his gullet.”]

Although he himself had confessed that Christ was the Son of God, he nevertheless believed that he would die as a mere man, and he stirred up the minds of the persecuting Jews toward his death (Matthew 8:29). But at the very time of his betrayal he is understood to have recognized too late that he himself would be punished by Christ’s death. Hence he also terrified Pilate’s wife through dreams, so that her husband would desist from persecuting the righteous man (Matthew 27:19).

But once the matter had been arranged by an inward dispensation, no machination could oppose it. For it was fitting that the death of the righteous man, who was dying unjustly, should release the death of sinners, who were dying justly.

Because this Leviathan remained ignorant of this until the time of Christ’s passion, he was mocked as a bird: while he bit the bait of Christ’s humanity, he received the snare of his divinity. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVI [Revised recension XV]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.** “Or will you bind him with your maidservants?”  
[Note: Vindocensis, Laudunensis, and the Norman manuscripts: “bind.”]

### 32. By choosing the weak things of the world, Christ conquered the devil’s strength. The house of Wisdom is Christ’s body and the Church. Those who were not capable in themselves were chosen to preach the Gospel.

The implied words are: “as I do.” Among male servants, although their condition is despised, manly strength remains vigorous; but among maidservants, both their condition and their sex are prostrate. Therefore the Lord rightly asserts that he will bind this Leviathan not with his male servants but with his maidservants, because, coming for our redemption and sending his preachers against the pride of the world, he chose the foolish instead of the wise, the weak instead of the strong, and the poor instead of the rich.

The Lord bound the strength of this Leviathan with his maidservants because, as Paul testifies: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (I Corinthians 1:27) [Note: Vallicellian: “to put the strong to shame.”]

Hence Solomon rightly says: “Wisdom built herself a house, she hewed out seven pillars, she slaughtered victims, she mixed wine, she set out a table, and she sent her maidservants to call people to the citadel and the walls of the city” (Proverbs 9:1–3).

Wisdom built herself a house when the only-begotten Son of God created for himself, within the Virgin’s womb and through the mediation of a soul, a human body. Thus the body of the Only-Begotten is called the house of God, just as it is also called a temple; in such a way, however, that the one and same Son of God and man is himself the one who dwells and the one who is inhabited.

This may also rightly be understood in another way, if the Church is called the house of Wisdom. She hewed out seven pillars for herself because she raised up minds of preachers, separated from love of the present age, to bear the structure of that same Church. Since they are supported by the virtue of perfection, they are represented by the number seven.

She slaughtered victims because she permitted the lives of preachers to be put to death in persecution. She mixed wine because she proclaimed to us together the mysteries of his divinity and humanity. She also set out a table because, by opening the nourishment of Holy Scripture to us, she prepared it for us.

She sent her maidservants to call us to the citadel and the walls of the city because she deliberately chose preachers who were weak and despised, so that they might gather faithful peoples toward the heavenly buildings of the spiritual homeland.

Hence, in the Gospel, the Lord praises Nathanael (John 1:47), yet does not number him among the company of preachers, because those who were to come to preach had to be such that they possessed nothing of their own praise. In this way it would be recognized all the more securely that what they did belonged to the truth, the more plainly it could be seen that they were not capable in themselves of doing it.

Thus, so that marvelous power might shine forth through the tongues of preachers, it was first brought about even more marvelously that those same preachers should have no merit of their own.

The Lord sent maidservants and bound the strength of this Leviathan because he displayed weak preachers to the world and restrained the powerful, who had become his body, under the bond of his fear.

This Leviathan is also bound in himself when, through weak preachers and the light of truth shining forth, the ancient enemy is not permitted to rage against the minds of the elect as much as he wishes. But lest he hold captive under unbelief all whom he desires, he is restrained by signs and virtues.

He himself therefore does these things with strength, who grants strength against him not to the strong. But since the Lord indicates whom he sends against him, he now adds what those who are sent themselves do. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVII [Old recension XXII, Revised recension XVI]

**VERSE 25.** “His friends will cut him apart; merchants will divide him.”

### 33. The devil’s members are cut apart when sinners are separated from his body in order to be joined to Christ. Preachers are merchants.

This Leviathan is cut apart as often as his members are separated from him by the sword of the divine word. When the wicked hear the word of truth and, struck by holy fear, withdraw from imitating the ancient enemy, he himself is divided in his body, since those who had perversely clung to him are taken away.

He calls them “friends” whom above he calls “maidservants”; he also calls them “merchants,” whom he had called “friends.” Holy preachers are first maidservants through fear, then friends through faith, and finally merchants through action.

To them, while they are still weak, it is said: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). Again, to them when they have grown strong, it is said: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father” (John 15:15). Finally, when they proceed to the work of their enterprise, they are commanded: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15).

In the preaching of faith a kind of business is carried on: the word is given, and faith is received from those who hear. Those who offer preaching and bring back faith from the peoples conduct a kind of business. They impart faith and immediately receive the holy life of those people [Note: Gemetensis and Corbeiensis: “they begin to impart.”]

For if the preaching of the righteous were not a business, surely the Psalmist would not say: “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine” (Psalm 80:2). On a tambourine, leather is dried so that it may sound. What then does it mean to say, “Take up the psalm and give the tambourine,” except: receive the spiritual song of the heart and return the bodily mortification of the present age?

If heavenly preaching were not a business, Solomon would never have said under the figure of the strong woman, referring to Holy Church: “She made a linen garment and sold it, and she delivered a belt to the Canaanite” (Proverbs 31:24).

For what is signified by the linen garment except the finely woven fabric of holy preaching? In it one rests softly, because in it the minds of the faithful are refreshed by heavenly hope. Hence animals are also shown to Peter in a linen cloth (Acts 10:11), because the souls of sinners, gathered together in mercy, are held within the gentle repose of faith.

The Church therefore made this linen garment and sold it, because she gave by speaking the faith that she had woven by believing, and received from unbelievers a life of upright conduct. She also delivered a belt to the Canaanite, because through the vigor of demonstrated righteousness she bound the loose works of paganism, so that what is commanded might be maintained in life: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35) [Note: Vallicellian: “through the vigor.”]

The Lord finds his preachers by seeking maidservants, makes them friends by exchanging, and displays them as merchants by enriching them. Those who had first feared the threats of the world in weakness later rise to know divine counsels. Once enriched with virtues, they are led as far as to conduct the business of faith, so that they cut apart the members of this Leviathan, reproving and persuading, with greater severity the more truly, having become friends, they join themselves to the love of truth [Note: Laudunensis: “through love”], and withdraw the souls of sinners from him all the more rapidly, the more, having become capable merchants, they display within themselves the most ample storehouses of virtues.

Because through God’s preachers the possession of Leviathan is divided in a highly praiseworthy manner, the voice of truth promises through the prophet: “And if you separate the precious from the vile, you will be like my mouth” (Jeremiah 15:19). He separates the precious from the vile who separates human minds from imitating the reprobate ancient enemy. He is rightly called the mouth of God, because through him divine utterances are undoubtedly formed. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Revised recension XVII]

**VERSE 26.** “Will you fill nets with his skin, and a fish-basket with his head?”

### 34. In the Church’s net, fishermen were caught first, and afterward rhetoricians and philosophers through them.

What is signified by nets or by a fish-basket except the communities of the faithful, which together constitute the one catholic Church? Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (Matthew 13:47).

The Church is called the kingdom of heaven because, while the Lord raises its conduct toward heavenly things, it already reigns in the Lord through a heavenly way of life. It is rightly compared to a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind because, cast into this age of paganism, it rejects no one; rather, it catches the wicked with the good, the proud with the humble, the angry with the gentle, and the foolish with the wise.

By the skin of this Leviathan we understand the foolish members of his body, and by his head the prudent. Or certainly, the skin, which is external, signifies subjects serving in these lower matters, while the head signifies those set over them.

The Lord rightly asserts, in due order, that he will fill these nets or fish-baskets—that is, his Church and the vows of the faithful—first with his skin and afterward with his head [Note: Vallicellian: “under the skin”], because, as we said above (above, chapter 16 of this book, no. 32), he first chose the weak in order afterward to confound the strong.

He chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (I Corinthians 1:27). First he gathered the unlearned and afterward philosophers. He did not teach fishermen through orators; rather, by marvelous power he subdued orators through fishermen.

He therefore says: “Will you fill nets with his skin, or a fish-basket with his head?” The implied words are: “as I do, who first gather within the Church of the faithful, as though they were the devil’s skin, those who are outwardmost and lowest [Note: Laudunensis, Pratellensis, and Vindocensis: “the weak”], and afterward subject to myself his head—that is, my prudent adversaries.”

The text continues: “Will you place your hand upon him?” That is: “as I do, who, restraining him by powerful strength, do not permit him to rage more than is expedient, and turn his rage, to the degree that I permit it, toward the advantage of my elect.”

Or certainly, to place one’s hand upon him is to overcome him by the power of virtue. Therefore blessed Job is asked:

**VERSE 27.** “Will you place your hand upon him?”

[Old recension XXIII.] It is as though it were said openly: “Will you restrain him by your own strength?” [Note: Thus the manuscripts; “you do not restrain him,” as the printed editions read.] Hence what follows is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XIX

**THE SAME PASSAGE.** “Remember the battle, and do not speak further.”

### 35. By how profound a dispensation God presses his servants either with threats or even with scourges.

The profound dispensation of God’s judgments often attacks servants who have lived well with threats, presses them with scourges, weighs them down with burdens laid upon them, or entangles them in laborious occupations, because by marvelous power he foresees that, if they remained quiet and free in tranquility, they would be unable to withstand the temptations of the adversary and would lie prostrate, wounded in mind.

Thus, when he occupies them outwardly with scourges or burdens that must be endured, he hides them from the arrows of temptation that they would otherwise receive inwardly. It is characteristic of medical treatment that the heat of the internal organs is often drawn out into an irritation of the skin; and frequently one is healed inwardly by the very means through which one is wounded outwardly.

Thus, by the medicine of divine dispensation, it sometimes happens that an internal wound is removed through external pains, and the inner corruption of vices that might have occupied the mind is driven away through the incisions of scourges.

Yet often, while people are unaware of the manifest fault within themselves and are either tormented by pains or weighed down by labors, they burst into complaint against the just and almighty Judge, clearly paying too little attention to how powerful an enemy they are fighting. If they carefully considered his intolerable strength, they would never murmur about the things they endure outwardly.

### 36. These hardships seem serious only if we fail to weigh the more serious battles of the hidden adversary. Let us fear not the father’s scourge but the enemy’s sword.

But these things seem serious to us because we do not wish to weigh the more serious battles of the hidden adversary. From many of those battles, as we have said, we are defended while being scourged and hidden while being afflicted.

Before our flesh is strengthened by the incorruption of the resurrection, if it is affected by no sorrow, it becomes unrestrained in temptations. Who does not know that it is far better to burn with the flames of fever than with the fire of vices? Yet when we are seized by fever, because we neglect to consider the heat of the vices that might have taken possession of us, we murmur about the blow.

Who does not know that it is far better to be subjected to harsh human masters than to be subjected to flattering demonic spirits? Yet when, by the deep judgment of God, we are crushed beneath the yoke of human servitude, we burst into complaint, plainly paying too little attention to the fact that, if no condition of servitude oppressed us, perhaps our mind, set free, would serve many iniquities even more wickedly.

We therefore believe the things we endure to be serious because we do not see how harsh and intolerable against us are the battles of the cunning enemy. Every burden would become light to our mind if it weighed the battles of the hidden adversary—those things that could have oppressed it.

For what if almighty God lifted the burdens we suffer, but nevertheless withdrew his assistance from us and abandoned us amid the temptations of this Leviathan? When so great an enemy is raging, where shall we go if we are defended by none of the protections of our Creator?

Because blessed Job was not conscious of guilt yet was enduring harsh scourges, lest he perhaps exceed the bounds of fault through murmuring [Note: Laudunensis and Vallicellian: “fall into”], he is reminded of what he should fear, and it is said to him: “Remember the battle, and do not speak further” [Note: Two German manuscripts and Pratellensis: “add.”]

[Revised recension XVIII.] It is as though it were said openly to him: “If you consider the battle of the hidden enemy against you, you do not accuse me for whatever you suffer. If you see the sword of the adversary attacking you, you do not dread the scourge of the Father in any way. You see with what sort of scourge I strike you, but you neglect to observe from how great an enemy I preserve you free by scourging you.

“Remember the battle, therefore, and do not speak further; that is, present yourself silently to the Father’s discipline to the same degree that you see yourself weak in the battles of the enemy. When you are struck while I correct you, recall your enemy to mind so that you may bear it calmly, and do not consider everything you suffer harsh, while through external torments you are freed from internal suffering.”

But because this Leviathan flatters himself with a false promise concerning divine mercy, after introducing the terror of his strength and stirring the spirit of blessed Job to examine him, saying, “Remember the battle, and do not speak further,” he immediately added the following in order to show the inexcusability of his guilt:

## CHAPTER XX [Old recension XXIV, Revised recension XIX]

**VERSE 28.** [Note: Pratellensis: “and his hope.”] “Behold, his hope will deceive him.”

### 37. The eternal condemnation of the devil and of all the reprobate will be proclaimed before all the elect.

This should be understood of him in such a way that it may also be referred to his body, because all the wicked who do not fear the rigor of divine justice flatter themselves in vain concerning mercy.

Then, returning immediately to our consolation, he foretells the future destruction of Leviathan at the final judgment, saying:

“And in the sight of all he will be cast down.”

He will be cast down in the sight of all because, when the eternal Judge then appears in terror, with legions of angels standing by, the entire ministry of the heavenly powers in attendance, and all the elect brought together for this spectacle, this cruel and mighty beast will be led into the midst as a captive. Together with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—he will be consigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna, when it is said: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

O what a spectacle that will be, when this most savage beast is displayed before the eyes of the elect—a beast that would have been able to terrify them greatly in the time of battle, if it could have been seen! But by the hidden and marvelous counsel of God it is brought about that, now, through his grace, it is conquered by those who fight without seeing it, and then it is seen by the joyful victors as a captive.

Then the righteous will recognize more fully how much they are indebted to divine assistance, when they see how mighty a beast they, weak as they were, have now conquered, and in the savagery of their enemy perceive how much they owe to the grace of their protector.

Our soldiers will then return from this battle bearing the trophies of their virtues. After receiving back their bodies, when at that judgment they obtain entry into the heavenly kingdom, they will first behold the immense powers of this ancient serpent, lest they consider insignificant the danger from which they escaped.

It is therefore rightly said: “And in the sight of all he will be cast down,” because his death, once seen, brings joy to those whose daily sufferings are now stirred into battle by his life, endured in their midst.

But when we hear these things, we might immediately complain and say to the Lord: “Lord, you who know that this Leviathan possesses such great strength, why do you stir him up against us in the contest of our weakness?” He immediately added:

**JOB 41:1.** “I will not stir him up cruelly.”

[Old recension XXV, Revised recension XX.] And as though we were at once asking him for the reason: “How do you not stir him up as a cruel being, when we know that you permit him to attack and devour so many?” he immediately added:

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSES 1–2.** “For who can resist my face? And who has given to me beforehand, that I should repay him?”

### 38. The grace of God is gratuitous

By these two verses he has fully set forth both the power of his might and the whole weight of the argument. For his power he said: “Who, then, can resist my face?” And to establish the reason he added: “Who has given to me beforehand, that I may repay him?” As if he were saying:

“I do not raise him up as though I were cruel, because by my power I rescue even my elect from his strength, and I justly and reasonably condemn the reprobate—not unjustly abandoning those whom I reject. That is, I can wondrously rescue those whom I graciously choose, and I do not unjustly abandon those whom I reject.”

For no one has first contributed anything to God so that divine grace might follow him. If we anticipate God by doing good, where is what the Prophet says: “His mercy will anticipate me” (Psalm 58:11)? If we have given some good work by which we deserved his grace, where is what the Apostle says: “You have been saved by faith; and this is not from yourselves, but it is the gift of God, not from works” (Ephesians 2:8)?

> **Editorial note:** Two German manuscripts, the Laudunensis, the Vallis-Clara manuscript, and the Gemeticensis read: “you have been saved.”

> **Editorial note:** The Vindocinus reads: “for it is God’s gift.”

If our love anticipated God, where is what the Apostle John says: “Not because we loved God, but because he first loved us” (1 John 4:10)?

> **Editorial note:** The Vindocinus, Pratellensis, and others read: “not because we loved him.”

Where is what the Lord says through Hosea: “I will love them freely” (Hosea 14:5)? If by our own power, without his gift, we follow God, where is what the Truth declares through the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)? Where is what he says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44)? Where is what he says again: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16)?

If at least by thinking well we anticipate, through our own power, the gifts of good works, where is what is said again through Paul so salutarily—that every human confidence in itself might be cut off from the very root of the heart—when he says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5)?

> **Editorial note:** The Laudunensis, Vindocinus, and Pratellensis read: “so subtly.” Two German manuscripts read: “where is what is said so salutarily?”

No one, then, anticipates God by merits, so as to hold him as a debtor. Yet in a wondrous manner the equitable Creator has both chosen some beforehand and justly abandoned others in their wicked ways.

> **Editorial note:** Jamezius believes that *in suis pravis moribus* (“in their wicked ways”) should be read, on the authority of the English manuscripts. The Vindocinus, Vallis-Clara manuscript, two German manuscripts, and most of our manuscripts agree with this reading.

### 39. He shows neither mercy to the elect without justice, nor justice to the reprobate without mercy

Yet he does not show his elect mercy without justice, because here he presses them with harsh afflictions. Nor does he exercise justice toward the reprobate without mercy, because here he patiently tolerates those whom he will at some time condemn eternally.

Thus, if the elect follow the grace that anticipates them, and the reprobate receive according to what they deserve, the elect find in mercy something for which to give praise, while the reprobate have nothing in justice that they can accuse. It is therefore rightly said: “Who has given to me beforehand, that I may repay him?”

As if it were said openly:

“I am compelled by no reason to spare the reprobate, because I am not held as their debtor on account of their actions. They do not receive the eternal rewards of the heavenly homeland for this reason: when they were able to merit them, they despised them through their free will.”

This free will is formed for good in the elect when, with grace breathing upon them, their minds are lifted away from earthly desires.

> **Editorial note:** Another manuscript reads: “for good.”

### 40. The good that we do belongs both to God and to us

The good that we do belongs both to God and to us: to God through prevenient grace, and to us through the free will that responds. For if it does not belong to God, why do we give him thanks forever? Again, if it does not belong to us, why do we hope that rewards will be repaid to us?

Therefore, because we rightly give thanks, we know that we are anticipated by his gift; and again, because we rightly seek recompense, we know that through the free will that responds we have chosen the good things that we should do.

> **Editorial note:** The Ebroicensis, the Gemeticensis, another Norman manuscript, and two German manuscripts read: “through the free will that follows.” This is also found in the old Basel edition and others.

It follows: “All that is under heaven is mine.” It is clear to everyone that not only the things under heaven, but also those things created above the heavens and called heavenly, serve the will of him from whom they remember that they were created. Why, then, speaking only of what is below, does he say:

### CHAPTER XXII

**Ibid.**—“All that is under heaven is mine”?

### 41. All things serve God

But because he is speaking of Leviathan, who is no longer contained in the dwelling-place of the ethereal heaven, he asserts that everything under heaven is his, so that he may teach that even the one who fell from heaven serves his power. As if he were saying:

“This Leviathan has indeed lost my blessedness, but he has not escaped my dominion, because even the powers that oppose me by their wicked actions serve me.”

It follows:

**Verse 3**—“I will not spare him with powerful words composed for entreaty.”

> **Editorial note:** Two German manuscripts, the Gemeticensis, the Pratellensis, and the Uticensis read: “with powerful words and words composed for entreaty.” The same applies in what follows.

### 42. In what sense the devil is said to entreat God

> **Editorial note:** See Book XXXII, §22.

Who, knowing that he has never read this, would suppose that the devil will ask forgiveness for his sins? Perhaps, however, that man whom this Leviathan makes his own vessel at the end of the world—whom, as Paul attests, the Lord Jesus “will kill with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8)—will be terrified by the presence of such great majesty. Since he is unable to exercise his powers, he will bend himself to prayer.

Yet this can more appropriately be understood of his body, that is, of all the wicked, who come late to words of petition because now they disdain to carry out good deeds. Hence the Truth says through the Gospel: “At last the other virgins come, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’” (Matthew 25:11). They are immediately answered: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12).

But when it is said that he composes powerful words for entreaty, this urges us all the more to understand in the present time what we have said about his body in the future.

### 43. Prayers that are not followed by a godly life are fruitless; for some, prayer becomes a form of commerce; true prayer is produced by bitter groans, not composed words

There are indeed some within the holy Church who offer lengthy prayers to the Lord but do not possess the life of those who pray. They pursue heavenly promises in their petitions but flee them in their deeds.

Sometimes they even shed tears in prayer; but when, after the time of prayer, pride strikes their minds, they immediately swell with the arrogance of self-exaltation. When greed incites them, they at once boil with the fires of covetous thought. When lust tempts them, they immediately pant after unlawful desires. When anger counsels them, the flame of madness quickly burns up the gentleness of their minds.

Thus, as we have said, they shed tears in prayer; yet, when their prayers are finished and they are struck by the suggestion of vices, they do not remember at all that they wept out of desire for the eternal kingdom.

This was made clear in Balaam, who, seeing the tents of the righteous, said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my end be like theirs” (Numbers 23:10). But when the time of compunction had passed, he gave counsel against the life of those whom he had asked to resemble even in death. When he found an opportunity through greed, he immediately forgot whatever he had wished for himself concerning innocence.

Prayer therefore has no weight of virtue when it is not held by the perseverance of continuous love. By contrast, it is rightly said of the weeping Hannah: “Her face was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Samuel 1:18). Her mind did not afterwards lose through foolish delight and dissipation what, at the time of her prayer, she had sought with the severity of groaning.

> **Editorial note:** The Laudunensis, Vallis-Clara manuscript, Pratellensis, and two German manuscripts read: “sought with rigor.”

For some, however, the labor of prayer becomes a form of commerce. Concerning them the Truth says in the Gospel: “They devour widows’ houses under the pretext of lengthy prayer. They will receive a longer judgment” (Mark 12:40).

Since, then, no mercy is shown in any way to the petitions of the wicked, who are the body of this Leviathan, when their prayers are destroyed by their conduct, it is rightly said here: “I will not spare him with powerful words composed for entreaty.”

> **Editorial note:** We have judged that this should be restored from all our manuscripts, since previously it was read: “because also through this.”

Although, by referring to powerful words composed for entreaty, the emptiness of prayer is plainly revealed. For to pray truly is to utter bitter groans in compunction, not to sound forth composed words.

### CHAPTER XXIV [Revised Recension XXII]

**Verse 14**—“Who will uncover the face of his garment?”

### 44. Satan tempts religious minds in one way and those devoted to the world in another

This Leviathan tempts the minds of human beings devoted to religion in one way, and those devoted to this world in another. He openly places before the wicked the evils they desire; but, lying in wait for the good, he deceives them under the appearance of holiness.

To the former, as to his intimates, he reveals himself more openly as wicked; to the latter, as to strangers, he cloaks himself under the pretext of a certain respectability, so that he may secretly introduce the evils he cannot openly display to them under the veil of a good action.

Therefore, when his members often cannot harm others through open wickedness, they assume the appearance of a good action; in their deeds they display what is wicked, but in appearance they pretend to be holy.

> **Editorial note:** The Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts read: “and they display themselves as wicked in their deeds, but as holy in appearance.” The Vallis-Clara manuscript reads: “and they display wicked things in deed,” omitting *se* (“themselves”).

If the wicked were openly evil, they could not be received at all by the good. But they take something from the appearance of the good, so that, while good men receive in them the appearance they love, they also unknowingly receive the poison mixed with it that they avoid.

Thus, seeing certain people serving the desires of their bellies under the guise of preaching, the Apostle Paul says: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14). What wonder, then, if his ministers are transformed as ministers of righteousness?

Joshua feared this transformation when, seeing an angel, he asked to which side he belonged, saying: “Are you ours or are you our adversaries’?” (Joshua 5:13). Thus, if he belonged to the hostile power, Joshua would recoil from the deception as soon as he recognized him as suspect.

Since this Leviathan, when he contrives a work of iniquity, often assumes the appearance of holiness—and since the garments of his deception cannot be exposed except through divine grace—it is rightly said:

> **Editorial note:** The Laudunensis reads *speciem sanctitatis induitur* (“is clothed in the appearance of holiness”), as in Psalm 92:1, *decorem indutus est* (“he has put on splendor”); excellent writers support this construction. “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” The implied answer is: “No one except me, who inspire the minds of my servants with the grace of the most subtle discernment, so that, once his wickedness has been exposed, they may see his naked face, which he conceals beneath the habit of holiness.”

And because he sometimes tries to corrupt the minds of the faithful by his appearance and sometimes by suggestion—for he acts now through deeds, now through persuasion—it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XXV

**Ibid.**—“Who will enter into the midst of his mouth?”

### 45. God reveals his cunning to the elect

The implied answer is: “No one except me, who, through the discerning minds of the elect, scrutinize the words of his suggestions and reveal that they are not what they sound like.”

They seem to promise good things, but they lead to a destructive end. To enter into the midst of his mouth is to penetrate the words of his cunning, so that one does not consider merely what they sound like, but what they intend.

Adam did not wish to enter into the midst of his mouth when he failed to weigh carefully the intention of his persuasion.

> **Editorial note:** The old and recent editions wrongly read *voluit* (“wished”); Gussanville corrected this error.

He believed that through him he would receive divinity, and he lost immortality (Genesis 3).

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis reads *super illum* (“upon him”). The Vindocinus, Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and Norman manuscripts read: “and [he lost] the grace of immortality.” Because he carelessly remained on the outside of an understanding of the devil’s words, he offered himself entirely to be devoured by his mouth.

It follows:

### CHAPTER XXVI [Revised Recension XXIII]

**Verse 5**—“Who will open the doors of his face?”

### 46. The doors of Leviathan are called false preachers; the Lord opens them by exposing the teachers of error

The doors of his face are wicked teachers. They are called the doors of his face because through them everyone enters, so that this Leviathan may appear to stand at the head of his own dominion.

Just as Holy Scripture customarily calls holy men “the gates of Zion”—for Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” and it is not unfitting that we call holy preachers the gates of Zion, because through their life and teaching we enter into the hidden things of heavenly contemplation—so also the teachers of error are signified by the gates of this Leviathan. When their perverse preaching is received, the way of perdition is opened to their wretched hearers.

These doors, however, are often open before human eyes for the purpose of admitting people, yet closed for the purpose of being recognized. They present what is right in appearance but persuade people to do what is wicked in practice. They are therefore closed for recognition because they are fortified by outward pretense, so that they cannot be known inwardly.

Yet the Lord opens them by wondrous power, because he makes the minds of hypocrites intelligible to his elect.

> **Editorial note:** The Laudunensis reads: “opens.” “Who, then, will open the doors of his face?” The implied answer is: “No one except me, who clearly reveals to my elect the teachers of error hidden under the appearance of holiness.”

And because, when the Antichrist comes, he will also seize the highest powers of this age—raging with a twofold error, attempting to draw human hearts to himself both by sending preachers and by bending the authorities— the Lord rightly added concerning this Leviathan:

### CHAPTER XXVII [Old Recension XXIX]

**Ibid.**—“Around the circuit of his teeth is terror.”

### 47. The teeth of Leviathan are likewise false teachers

By changing the name, he wished to indicate these same beings as his teeth, whom above he called doors. Perverse preachers are his doors because they open the entrance to perdition. They are his teeth because those whom they seize in error they break away from the solidity of truth.

Just as we understand the teeth of the holy Church to be those who by their preaching crush the hardness of sinners—hence it is said to her through Solomon: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep coming up from the washing” (Song of Songs 4:2)—and they are rightly compared to shorn and washed sheep because, taking up an innocent life, they have laid aside in the bath of baptism the old fleeces of their former way of life, so also the teachers of error are represented by the teeth of this Leviathan.

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis reads: “in terror.” The Laudunensis and Gemeticensis read: “like a flock.”

By biting and tearing apart the life of the reprobate, they slaughter those who have been drawn away from the integrity of truth in the sacrifice of falsehood.

> **Editorial note:** The Ebroicensis and most Norman manuscripts read: “as a sacrifice.”

Their preaching could easily have been despised by their hearers, but before human judgment the terror of secular powers added to it exalts it.

### 48. The powers of the world fortify them; some rage with words, others with swords; the snares of Antichrist arise from false miracles

It is rightly said, therefore: “Around the circuit of his teeth is terror.” That is, the wicked powers of this world protect the perverse preachers of the Antichrist. Many of the powerful strive to terrify by violence those whom the preachers seek to seduce by speech.

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis and Corbie German manuscript read: “these by themselves.”

“Therefore, around the circuit of his teeth is terror,” as if it were said openly:

“These perverse preachers crush some by persuasion because there are others around them who afflict the minds of the weak by terrifying them.”
