What will that time of persecution look like when, to pervert the devotion of the faithful, some besiege them with words and others with swords? Even the weak would despise the teeth of this Leviathan if the terror of secular authorities did not fortify them all around.

But a twofold cunning is employed against them, because what others say to them with flattering words is commanded by others who strike with swords. The action of both groups—the powerful and the speakers—is briefly expressed in the Apocalypse of John, where it is said:

> **Editorial note:** The Vallis-Clara manuscript reads: “is obtained.” Two German manuscripts, the Laudunensis, Vindocinus, and Gemeticensis read: “the talkative.” “The power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails” (Revelation 9:19).

In the mouth of the teachers is represented knowledge; in the tail, secular power. For by the tail, which is behind, the temporality of this age is signified—something that must be left behind. Concerning it the Apostle Paul says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3:13). Everything that passes is behind; everything that comes and remains is ahead.

Thus these horses—that is, the most wicked preachers, running everywhere under the impulse of the flesh—have power in their mouth and in their tail.

> **Editorial note:** *Most wicked* is absent from the Laudunensis and Vallis-Clara manuscript. They preach by persuading people to what is perverse, but, supported by temporal powers, they exalt themselves through the things that are behind.

And because they themselves may appear contemptible, they demand reverence for themselves from their wicked hearers through those whose patronage supports them. Hence it is rightly described here that “around the circuit of his teeth is terror,” because many terrors are employed so that, even if the sentence of truth is not feared in their perverse preaching, temporal power certainly is.

Thus the Psalmist rightly described this same Antichrist, saying: “Under his tongue are labor and pain; he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places” (Psalm 9:28).

There are “labor and pain under his tongue” because of his perverse doctrines. He “sits in ambush” because of the appearance of miracles. He sits “with the rich in secret places” because of the glory of secular power. Since he uses both the deception of miracles and earthly power, he is said to sit both in secret places and with the rich.

### CHAPTER XXVIII [Revised Recension XXIV]

**Verse 6**—“His body is like molten shields.”

### 49. The wicked oppose a shield of excuse to those who correct them

Holy Scripture customarily uses the name “shield” sometimes in a favorable sense and sometimes in an unfavorable one. Often the protection of a shield signifies divine protection; sometimes it signifies human resistance.

It signifies divine protection, as the Psalmist says: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Psalm 5:13).

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis, Pratellensis, Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and others read: “For it is used for divine protection, as the Psalmist says.” The Lord is said to crown us with a shield because, by protecting us, he assists us, and by rewarding us, he crowns us.

Again, the shield signifies human resistance, as the same Prophet says elsewhere: “There he broke the horns, the bow, the shield, the sword, and the battle” (Psalm 75:4). In the horns is signified the exaltation of the proud; in the bow, the ambushes of those who strike from afar; in the shield, the obstinate hardness of defensive arguments; in the sword, a blow delivered at close range; and in the battle, the mind’s very movement against the Lord.

All this is broken in the holy Church when the minds of those who resist God are subdued by the yoke of humility imposed upon them. Hence the same Psalmist says again: “He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Psalm 45:10).

The Lord breaks the bow when he dissolves the hidden schemes of those lying in wait. He shatters the weapons when he crushes the human protections raised against him. He burns the shields with fire when, by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, he kindles the minds of sinners who defend themselves with obstinate hardness to the ardor of repentance and confession.

> **Editorial note:** The Corbie German manuscript and Gemeticensis read: “to the ardor of repentance and confession.”

What is meant here by comparing the body of this Leviathan to molten shields requires investigation. A vessel that is molten is indeed hard, but when it falls it is usually fragile. If shields are molten, they are strong in receiving the blows of arrows but fragile when they fall. They are not penetrated at all by the blows of those striking them, but they break apart through their own fall.

The body of this Leviathan—that is, all the wicked—is therefore compared to molten shields because they are hard through obstinacy but fragile through their way of life. When they hear the words of preaching, they do not allow any arrows of correction to penetrate them, because in every sin they commit they oppose a shield of proud defense.

When any one of them is accused of the guilt of his wickedness, he does not immediately consider how to correct the fault, but what he can offer in defense of himself. No arrow of truth therefore penetrates him, because he receives the words of holy correction upon the shield of proud defense.

Hence Jeremiah rightly says concerning the Jews, who defended themselves proudly against the commandments of the Lord: “You will repay them, Lord, according to the works of their hands” (Lamentations 3:64). He immediately added the same repayment more explicitly: “You will give them the shield of your labor, O Lord” (Lamentations 3:65).

The Lord’s labor appearing among human beings was his passible humanity, which the Jews, thinking proudly, despised when they saw it. They refused to believe him immortal whom they saw mortal in a passible nature.

When they beheld his humility, hardened by the arrogance of pride, they exerted themselves intensely to prevent the holy words of the preachers from penetrating their minds. Thus, when the Lord repaid them according to their evil deeds, “he gave them the shield of his labor,” because by a just judgment he made them obstinately set themselves against him through the very weakness in which he had labored for us.

> **Editorial note:** The Vallis-Clara manuscript reads “humanity” in place of “humility.”

They repelled the words of the preachers because they disdained the Lord’s weakness in his sufferings. They therefore had the Lord’s labor as a shield of the heart against the Lord himself, because he appeared contemptible to those who thought proudly precisely in the respect in which he had become humble for their sake.

### 50. Adam and Eve used this shield

As we already said above, the first sinner held this shield. When the Lord asked why he had touched the forbidden tree, Adam did not attribute the fault to himself but replied that he had received it from the woman whom the Lord had given him (Genesis 3:12). Thus he indirectly threw his guilt back upon the one who had given him the woman who had offered such persuasion.

The woman also held this shield when she was questioned. She too did not attribute the fault to herself but referred it to the serpent’s persuasion, saying: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Genesis 3:13). Thus she likewise indirectly transferred her guilt back to the Creator, who had permitted the serpent to enter there and offer such persuasion.

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis, two German manuscripts, and Vallis-Clara manuscript read: “who had permitted the serpent, which would offer such persuasion, to enter there.”

The serpent, however, was no longer questioned, because his repentance was not being sought. But those whose repentance was sought brought forward the shield of the most wicked defense against the words of the most just correction (Genesis 3).

From that time down to the present, this has been drawn into the practice of sinners: when guilt is accused, it is defended; and the very means by which guilt ought to have been ended instead causes it to increase.

> **Editorial note:** The Vallis-Clara manuscript reads “to end” in place of “to have been ended.”

It is rightly said, therefore: “His body is like molten shields,” because all the wicked prepare shields of defense against the arrows of an enemy so that the words of those who correct them may not reach them.

The following further exposes this body to us:

### CHAPTER XXIX

**Ibid.**—“Compacted with scales pressing upon one another.”

### 51. Covered with scales, the reprobate resist the arrows of truth

It is said that a dragon’s body is covered with scales so that it may not quickly be pierced by a missile. Thus the entire body of the devil—that is, the multitude of the reprobate—when reproved for its wickedness, attempts to excuse itself by whatever evasions it can and presents, as it were, certain scales of defense so that it cannot be pierced by the arrow of truth.

Whoever, when reproved, desires more to excuse his sin than to mourn it is covered with scales, as he is struck by the sword of the word from holy preachers. He has scales, and therefore the arrow of the word has no path by which to pass to his inmost heart. He is repelled by carnal hardness so that the spiritual sword cannot be driven into him.

### 52. Saul’s heart, hardened by these scales, was opened to the arrows of grace

Saul had become hardened against God by carnal wisdom when no arrow of evangelical preaching could penetrate his heart. But after he had been struck by a powerful rebuke from heaven and blinded by heavenly regard—for he lost the light in order to receive the light—he came to Ananias and was illuminated.

Because in this illumination he was freed from the hardness of his defenses, it is rightly written of him: “Something like scales fell from his eyes” (Acts 9:18). The hardness of a carnal covering had pressed upon him, and for that reason he did not see the rays of the true light. But after his proud resistance had been conquered, the scales of his defenses fell away.

They fell from the eyes of his body under Ananias’s hands, but they had already fallen from the eyes of his heart under the Lord’s rebuke. For when he lay pierced by the arrow of a lofty assault, he now sought with a humble and penetrated heart, saying: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6).

The scales having been repelled, the arrow of truth had already reached the inner parts of his heart. He had laid aside the arrogance of pride, confessed as Lord the one whom he had opposed, and, not knowing what he should do, asked him.

It is pleasant to contemplate where that savage persecutor is now, where the ravenous wolf is. Behold, he has already been changed into a sheep—the one who asks which path of the shepherd he should follow.

It should also be noted that when he said, “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 22:8), the Lord did not answer him: “I am the Father’s only-begotten Son; I am the Beginning; I am the Word before the ages.”

Because Saul disdained to believe that the Lord had become incarnate and despised the weakness of his humanity, he heard from heaven what he had despised: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you persecute” (ibid., 8).

As if he were saying:

“Hear from me concerning the things above what you despise in me concerning the things below. You had despised the Creator of heaven who came to earth; from heaven, therefore, recognize the human being from earth, so that you may fear the mysteries of my weakness all the more insofar as you see that these, brought into the heavenly realm, have been raised to the excellence of power.”

Thus, prostrating you, I do not assert to you that I am God before the ages; rather, you hear from me what you disdain to believe about me. After saying “Jesus,” he added “the Nazarene,” further expressing his earthly dwelling—as if he were saying more openly:

“Receive the weakness of my humility, and cast off the scales of your pride.”

> **Editorial note:** The Vallis-Clara manuscript reads: “so that you may learn that the Author of heaven has come to earth.” The Laudunensis, Ebroicensis, Gemeticensis, Pratellensis, and two German manuscripts read *desperas* or *disperas* (“you despair” or “you scatter”) instead of *despexeras* (“you had despised”).

### 53. In hypocrites the scales are harder; malicious minds resemble hedgehogs

It must nevertheless be understood that, although these scales of defense cover almost the whole human race, they especially press upon the minds of hypocrites and cunning people. They refuse to confess their faults all the more vehemently because they are more foolishly ashamed to appear sinful before human beings.

> **Editorial note:** Apart from the German manuscripts, all our manuscripts and the old editions read *stultius* (“more foolishly”); Gilot, Uticensis, Gussanville, and the German manuscript already mentioned read *citius* (“more quickly”).

When their pretense of holiness is reproved and their hidden wickedness exposed, they cast up the scales of defense and repel the sword of truth.

Hence the Prophet rightly says concerning Judea: “There the lamia reclined and found rest there; there the hedgehog had its den” (Isaiah 34:14–15).

The lamia signifies hypocrites; the hedgehog signifies all the malicious, who cover themselves with various defenses. The lamia is said to have a human face but a beastly body. So too with all hypocrites: what they display in their first appearance is, as it were, derived from the reasonableness of holiness; but the body that follows is beastly, because the things they contrive under the appearance of good are exceedingly wicked.

The defense of malicious minds is signified by the name “hedgehog.” When a hedgehog is captured, its head is seen, its feet are visible, and its entire body can be observed. But as soon as it is seized, it gathers itself into a sphere, draws its feet inward, and hides its head. Within the hand of the person holding it, everything that had previously been visible all at once disappears.

So it is with malicious minds when they are caught in their excesses. The hedgehog’s head is visible because the beginning by which the sinner approached his guilt can be seen. The hedgehog’s feet are visible because the steps by which the wickedness was committed are recognized. Yet, when excuses are suddenly produced, the malicious mind draws its feet inward, so to speak, because it conceals all the traces of its wickedness.

It withdraws its head because, through marvelous defenses, it does not even show that it began anything wicked. It remains like a sphere in the hand of the one holding it, because the person who corrects, suddenly losing everything he had already understood, holds within his conscience a sinner who has wrapped himself up; and the one who had seen everything by recognizing it is deceived by the wicked evasion of defense and suddenly knows nothing of it at all.

The hedgehog therefore has a den among the reprobate, because the malicious mind, drawing itself together within itself, hides in the darkness of its defenses. But when the sinner excuses himself, and when by shadowy defenses he clouds the eye of the one correcting him that is fixed upon him, the divine word also shows us how such defenses are supported by their counterparts.

> **Editorial note:** Some witnesses read *caliginosis* (“murky”) for “shadowy,” including two German manuscripts, the Gemeticensis, and older codices.

It follows:

### CHAPTER XXX [Old Recension XXXIII]

**Verse 7**—“One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them.”

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis reads *inspiraculum* (“breath”), and likewise thereafter.

### 54. The wicked protect one another by mutual defenses

These scales of sinners are both hardened and joined together, so that no breath of life from the mouths of preachers may penetrate them.

> **Editorial note:** The Gemeticensis, in another sense, reads: “For those whom similar guilt joins together …”

Those whom similar guilt joins together are also bound by a perverse defense in harmonious obstinacy, so that they protect one another by mutual defense from their crimes. Each fears for himself when he sees another being admonished or corrected, and therefore they rise together against the words of those who correct them, because each protects himself in the other.

It is rightly said, therefore: “One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them,” because, while they protect one another through proud defense in their iniquities, they allow none of the breath of holy exhortation to enter them.

### CHAPTER XXXI

**Verse 8**—“One shall adhere to another, and, holding one another, they shall by no means be separated.”

> **Editorial note:** The Vulgate has *adhaerebit* (“shall adhere”). In the Hebrew source the plural is used, and the literal reading is: “a man shall adhere to his brother.”

[Col. 0708D] **55. Those who could scarcely be corrected when divided—how will they be amended when united?**—For those who could be corrected while divided persist united in the obstinacy of their iniquities, and every day become so much more separated from the knowledge of justice as they are separated from one another by no reprimand. [Note: [Col. 0708D] Gemet.: “they become from kinship …”; several manuscripts, including Corb. Germ., have “they become from thought …”] For just as the absence of unity is usually harmful among the good, so it is harmful if it is absent among the wicked. [Col. 0709A] Unity strengthens the perverse when it makes them agree, and makes them so much more incorrigible as it makes them unanimous. Concerning this unity of the reprobate, [Note: [Col. 0709D] Gemet., Pratel., Utic., Vindoc., Val. Cl., two German manuscripts, and most manuscripts: “through Solomon.” This is worth noting, since it may be inferred that Gregory attributed the Book of Ecclesiasticus to Solomon. Elsewhere, however, he often cites this book while suppressing Solomon’s name. Thus, in *Moralia* XX, no. 51: “Rightly also it is said through a certain wise man.” See Book XXVII, nos. 47 and 53, [Col. 0710D] and Book XXXIII, no. 23. The holy Doctor similarly cites the author of the Book of Wisdom, as may be seen in Book XIX, no. 26.] it is said through the Wise Man: “A gathering of sinners is a bundle of straw” (Eccli. XXI, 10). Concerning this the prophet Nahum says: “As thorns embrace one another, so is the banquet of those who drink together” (Nahum I, 10). The banquet of the reprobate is the enjoyment of temporal pleasures. At this banquet those drink together who in unison make themselves drunk with the allurements of their pleasure. Therefore, since the members of this Leviathan—that is, all the wicked, whom the word of God compares to compacted scales—are united by an equal guilt for their defense, it is rightly said: “One will cling to another, and holding fast to one another they will not be separated.” For those who hold fast to one another cannot be separated, [Col. 0709B] because they are bound together for their mutual defense precisely insofar as they remember that they are alike in every respect. Having thus described his body, the discourse returns to the head, and announces what the ancient enemy himself will do at the time of the final persecution. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XXXII [Formerly XXXIV, Recension XXV]

**VERSE 9.—The sneezing of him is the splendor of fire.**

**56. How great a disturbance will threaten from the Antichrist’s signs and powers.**—We explain this better if we first investigate how sneezing takes place. In sneezing, an inflation rises from the chest; when it finds no open pores through which to escape, it touches the brain, and, issuing through the nostrils in a concentrated rush, immediately shakes the whole head. Thus, in this body of Leviathan—[Col. 0709C] that is, either in the malignant spirits or in reprobate human beings who have clung to him through a likeness of iniquity—an inflation seems to rise from the chest when arrogance raises itself through the power of the present age. It finds no pores through which to escape, as it were, because, although it is exalted against the just, by God’s ordering it is prevented from prevailing as much as it desires. Rising up, it touches and shakes the brain, because the concentrated arrogance of Satan strikes the mind more fiercely at the end of the world [Note: [Col. 0710D] Pratel.: “more sharply”], and troubles the head when, through the one called the Antichrist, it rouses the very author of the malignant spirits more violently against the persecution of the faithful. Then the concentrated inflation issues through his nostrils, because all his iniquity of pride is displayed through the open blasts of his malice.

Because sneezing especially shakes the head, the sneezing of this Leviathan [Col. 0709D] is called that final disturbance of his by which he enters the condemned man and rules through him over the reprobate. At that time he will disturb himself with such great power that, if it can be done, he will trouble even the elect, the members of the Lord; and he will use such great signs and wonders that through the power of miracles he will seem to shine with something like the light of fire. Since, therefore, his shaken head seeks to become radiant through miracles, his sneezing is rightly called [Col. 0710A] “the splendor of fire.” For insofar as he is stirred up to persecute the just, he shines before the eyes of the reprobate through the power of signs. And because the wise men of the world cling to his tyranny, and through their counsels he carries out everything evil that he devises, it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Formerly XXXV]

**IBID.—And his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.**

**57. Why his eyes—that is, his counselors—are compared with the eyelids of dawn.**—By the eyes, which, attached to the head, serve the usefulness of sight, his counselors are appropriately signified. While they foresee through perverse schemes what ought to be done and how, they provide his evil workers with a path, as though one had been shown to their feet. They are rightly compared with the eyelids of dawn. [Col. 0710B] By the eyelids of dawn we understand the final hours of night, in which night, as it were, opens its eyes while already displaying the beginnings of the light that is to come. The wise men of this age, therefore, clinging through perverse counsels to the malice of the Antichrist, are like the eyelids of dawn, because they assert that the faith found in Christ is a kind of night of error, and promise that veneration of the Antichrist is the true morning. They promise that they will drive away darkness and announce the light of truth by shining signs, because they cannot persuade people of what they wish unless they profess to present themselves as something better.

Hence this serpent himself, speaking to the first human beings in paradise (Gen. III, 5), when he pretended to foresee something better, opened, as it were, the eyelids of dawn: he reproved the ignorance of humanity in innocent minds [Col. 0710C] and promised divine knowledge. He was driving away, as it were, the darkness of ignorance and announcing the divine morning of eternal knowledge, saying: “Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.).

Thus, when he comes in that condemned man, his eyes are compared with the eyelids of dawn, because his wise men reject the simplicity of true faith as the darkness of the night that has passed, and display his lying signs like rays of the rising sun. [Note: [Col. 0710D] Gemet.: “and his fire.”]

But since this Leviathan has not only eyes that foresee perverse things through malignant counsels, but also opens a mouth to pervert human minds—for through evil preachers he inflames the hearts of hearers to love the deception of error—it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Recension XXVI]

[Col. 0710D] **VERSE 10.—From his mouth lamps proceed.**

**58. The preachers of the Antichrist are his mouth.**—Those who foresee are called eyes, while those who preach are called mouth. But lamps come out of this mouth because they inflame the minds of their hearers to love faithlessness; and from the source by which they seem to shine through wisdom, they undoubtedly burn through wickedness. But what sort of light their wisdom is is shown when it immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXV [Formerly XXXVI]

**IBID.—Like torches of kindled fire.**

**59. They burn through malice and shine through the pretense of virtue.**—Here the hypocrisy of those whose preaching is compared with the lamps of torches is plainly described. When a torch is kindled, it has a pleasant fragrance but a murky light. So these preachers of the Antichrist, because they arrogate to themselves the appearance of holiness while practicing works of iniquity, are, as it were, pleasant in what they give off as fragrance but black in what they emit as light. They smell sweet through the pretense of righteousness, but burn darkly through the perpetration of wickedness.

John comprehended the malice of their pretense in a brief description in the Apocalypse, saying: “I saw another beast rising from the earth, having two horns like a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon” (Rev. XIII, 11). He had already described the first beast—that is, the Antichrist—in the preceding account. After him this other beast is said to have risen, because after him a multitude of his preachers boasts of earthly power. To rise from the earth is to grow proud of earthly glory.

It has two horns like those of a lamb, because through hypocrisy of holiness it falsely claims for itself both the wisdom and the life that the Lord truly possessed in himself as unique. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Laud.: “he himself”; Corb. Germ.: “who has,” shortly before, instead of “which has.”] [Note: [Col. 0711D] Ebroic.: “uniquely.”] But because under the appearance of a lamb it pours the serpent’s poison into reprobate hearers, it is rightly added there: “And it spoke like a dragon.” If this beast—that is, the multitude of preachers—spoke openly like a dragon, it would not appear like a lamb; but it assumes the appearance of a lamb in order to carry out the work of the dragon. Both aspects are expressed here through the lamps of torches: they burn darkly through the effect of malice and smell, as it were, sweetly through the pretense of life.

**60. Many preachers of the Antichrist already exist. Their life must be examined like coin; it must agree with the institutions of the ancient fathers.**—It must by no means be thought that the preachers of the Antichrist will appear only at that time, and that they are now absent from human deceptions. Now, before he appears in person, some preach him with their voices, [Note: [Col. 0711D] Gemet. and Corb. Germ.: “but most preach him by their conduct; they are preachers of that pretense who …”] while most preach him by their conduct. Or are they not preachers of that pretense who, while they hold the sacred offices of God, cling with all their desires to the world that is fleeing away; who display as virtues the things they do, although everything they do is vice? [Formerly XXXVII.]

But the more the mind of the elect clings to the inward light, the more subtly it perceives how it ought to distinguish virtues from vices. What wonder, then, if we do spiritually what we see money-changers doing bodily every day? When they receive a coin, they first examine its quality, then its image, and finally its weight, lest bronze lie hidden beneath the appearance of gold; lest what is truly gold be disfigured by the image of a debased coin; or lest what is both gold and correctly shaped be found lacking in full weight.

Therefore, when we behold the remarkable deeds of unknown people, we must sit at the scales of our mind like skilled money-changers, so that discernment may first examine the gold, lest vice conceal itself beneath virtue and what is done with a corrupt intention be masked by the appearance of right. When the quality of the intention has been approved, [Note: [Col. 0712D] German, Turon., Laud. and others: “the image of the stamped design must then be sought.”] the image of the stamped design must then be sought: whether it derives from approved minters—that is, from the ancient fathers—and whether it is in no respect corrupted by the likeness of their life.

When both the quality of the intention and the correct image through example have been recognized, it remains to investigate whether its weight is full. For a good that shines through signs and miracles, if it does not possess the perfection of its full measure, must be carefully weighed through vigilant caution, lest, when an incomplete thing is accepted as though perfect, it turn to the harm of the one who accepts it. [Note: [Col. 0712D] Val. Cl.: “as though perfect”; Turon. and two German manuscripts: “as though for something perfect.”]

How, then, do the preachers of the Antichrist possess the true quality of coin, when in what they do they do not know the force of a right intention, because through these things they seek not the heavenly homeland but the summit of temporal glory? How do they not differ from the image of the coin, when by persecuting the righteous they disagree with all the piety of the just? How do they display in themselves the weight of integrity, when they have not only failed altogether to attain the perfection of humility, but have not even touched its first door? [Col. 0712C]

From this, then, from this let the elect recognize how they should despise their signs, whose conduct clearly attacks everything that is remembered as having been done by pious fathers. Yet the elect themselves, while they behold so many signs and shudder at such great miracles performed by one who despises life, suffer a certain cloud of doubt in their hearts, because, while his malice raises itself through prodigies, the more certain sight in them is darkened to some extent. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Recension XXVII]

**VERSE 11.—From his nostrils smoke proceeds.**

**61. When they see the Antichrist’s wonders, the elect will be troubled and stagger. They cannot be completely captured in error.**—The sharpness of the eyes is injured by smoke. Smoke is therefore said to proceed from his nostrils because, through the snares of his miracles, a momentary, shadowy doubt is generated even in the heart of the elect. Smoke comes out of Leviathan’s nostrils because, through his lying prodigies, the cloud of trepidation confuses even the eyes of good minds.

Then, when the terrible signs have been seen, an obscure thought is heaped together in the hearts of the elect. Hence what we have already cited is said by the mouth of Truth through the Gospel: [Col. 0713A] “False Christs and false prophets will arise and give signs [Note: [Col. 0713D] The printed editions, together with two German manuscripts, have “great signs”; the final word is absent from the Vindoc., Norm., and other manuscripts, and is found neither in the Vulgate nor in the Greek text.] and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Mark XIII, 22).

In this matter we must carefully ask how those who are elect can be led into error, or why “if possible” is added as though from uncertainty, when the Lord, who knows all things in advance, awaits what is to happen. But because the heart of the elect is shaken by trembling thought while their steadfastness is nevertheless not moved, the Lord embraced both realities in one statement, saying: “So as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.” To stagger in thought is, as it were, already to err; but “if possible” is immediately added, because plainly it is impossible for the elect to be completely captured in error. [Note: [Col. 0713D] Another manuscript: “plainly,” as in Laud.]

The fervor of their souls is also rightly expressed in this smoke’s darkness when it immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**IBID.—Like a pot kindled and boiling.**

**62. With what zeal they will then seethe; what the devil accomplishes in human hearts through the smoke of his pestilential breath. God cannot be known except by a tranquil heart.**—For then each soul is like a boiling pot, enduring the surges of its thoughts as though they were foam from burning waves. The fire of zeal stirs these waves, while the temporal oppression itself keeps them enclosed within, after the manner of a pot.

Thus John too, when he described the signs of this beast, added: “So that he even makes fire come down from heaven” (Rev. XIII, 13). To make fire come down from heaven is to make the flames of holy zeal issue from the heavenly souls of the elect. [Formerly XXXVIII.]

But since this Leviathan is elsewhere called not only a serpent but also a *regulus*—a basilisk—because he rules over unclean spirits or reprobate human beings, as Isaiah says: “From the root of the serpent a basilisk will come forth” (Isa. XIV, 29), we must examine with the utmost care how the basilisk kills, so that from the basilisk’s operation this being’s malice may become more clearly known. For the basilisk does not kill by biting but consumes by breathing. It often infects the air with its breath and with the mere inhalation of its nostrils withers whatever it touches, even at a distance.

**63.** From this, then, we are compelled to consider what he accomplishes every day in human hearts through the smoke of his pestilential exhalation, even before he appears openly, since it is said that smoke proceeds from his nostrils. For, as we said above, since smoke weakens the sharpness of the eyes, it is rightly asserted that smoke proceeds from the nostrils of him whose harmful inspirations give birth to perverse thought in human hearts, through which the mind’s sight is dulled so that the inner light may not be seen.

As though he emitted darkness through the breath of his nostrils, he heaps the heat of manifold thoughts in the hearts of the reprobate through the aspirations of his snares, from the love of temporal life. He multiplies, as it were, globes of smoke because he piles up the most empty cares of the present life [Col. 0714A] in the minds of earthly people.

This smoke proceeding from his nostrils sometimes touches even the eyes of the elect for a time. The Prophet suffered this inward smoke when he said: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. VI, 8). He was oppressed by its flood when he said: “My heart is troubled within me, and the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII, 11). This smoke dulls the sight of the heart because, through the cloud of its darkness, it disturbs the serenity of inward quiet.

God, however, cannot be known except by a tranquil heart. Hence the same prophet says again: “Be still and see that I am [Note: [Col. 0714D] Gemet. and Corb. Germ.: “the Lord.”] God” (Ps. XLV, 11). But the mind oppressed by the floods of this smoke cannot be still, because within it the masses of earthly thoughts are heaped up through love of the present life. The light of inward peace [Note: [Col. 0714D] Norm., Vindoc., Laud., Val. Cl. and two German manuscripts: “eternal.”] is therefore lost through this smoke, because, when the eye of the heart is confused by the itch of cares, it is darkened.

**64. This smoke troubles the minds of the elect in one way and blinds the eyes of the reprobate in another.**—But this smoke troubles the souls of the good in one way and blinds the eyes of the reprobate in another. From the eyes of the good it is sprinkled by the breath of spiritual desires, lest it become dense through the prevailing of miserable thought. [Note: [Col. 0714D] Gemet., Pratel., Val. Cl. and two German manuscripts: “the minds of the wicked.”] In the minds of the reprobate, however, the more freely it gathers through foul thoughts, the more completely it removes from them the light of truth. How many unlawful desires this smoke introduces into the hearts of the reprobate, so many globes it makes swell up before them, as it were.

[Formerly XXXIX.] **65. In the carnal soul, some globes of the smoke of desire vanish above while others rise below. Vices succeed vices.**—Certainly we know how smoke forms globes: while some vanish above, others rise below. So too in carnal thought, even if some desires of depravity pass away, others succeed them. Often the miserable mind sees what has already passed away but does not see where it is still held. It rejoices that it is no longer subject to certain vices, and neglects to guard against them and lament, because others have succeeded in their place—others to which it perhaps submits more wickedly. Thus, while some vices pass away and others perpetually succeed them, the hearts of the reprobate are held without interruption by this serpent.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet Joel: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the cankerworm ate; and what the cankerworm left, the mildew ate. Awake, you drunkards, and weep” (Joel I, 4–5).

For what is signified by the caterpillar, which crawls on the earth with its whole body, except lust? It so pollutes the heart that it cannot rise to love the purity above. What is expressed by the locust, which flies up in leaps, except empty glory, which exalts itself through vain presumptions? What is figured by the cankerworm, whose entire body is almost gathered into its belly, except gluttony? What is indicated by the mildew, which burns whatever it touches, except anger?

The locust therefore eats what the caterpillar left, because often, when the vice of lust has withdrawn from the mind, empty glory succeeds it. Since the heart is no longer laid low through love of lust, it boasts of itself as holy because of its chastity. The cankerworm eats what the locust left, because often, when empty glory—which seemed to arise from holiness—is resisted, the belly or some other desire of ambition is indulged immoderately.

A mind ignorant of God is led toward any ambition all the more savagely as it is restrained by no love of human praise. The mildew consumes what the cankerworm left, because often, when gluttony is restrained through abstinence, the impatience of anger rules more fiercely. Like mildew, it consumes the harvest by burning it, because the flame of impatience [Note: [Col. 0715D] Gilot., Vatic., Gussanv.: “withers”; contradicted by the manuscripts and old editions.] withers the fruit of virtues.

Therefore, when vices succeed vices, one pest devours the field of the mind while another departs.

[Formerly XL.] **66. Those are drunk who, confused by love of this world, do not feel the evils they suffer.**—It is rightly added there: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep” (ibid.). Those are called drunk who, confused by love of this world, do not feel the evils that they suffer. What, then, does it mean to say, “Awake, you drunkards, and weep” (Joel I, 5), except: Shake off the sleep of your insensibility, and, amid the devastation of your hearts by the successive plagues of so many vices, meet them with vigilant lamentation?

Thus, through as many globes as there are plagues by which he secretly consumes the crop of the reprobate heart, smoke rises from Leviathan’s nostrils. The Lord carefully expresses the force of this smoke when he immediately adds: [Col. 0715C] “Like a pot kindled and boiling.”

A pot is kindled when the human mind is stirred by the persuasions of the malignant enemy. A pot boils when, through consent, it is already inflamed by the desires of an evil persuasion. It casts out as many waves, as it were, through boiling as the wickednesses by which it extends itself into outward actions.

The prophet had seen this boiling of the carnal conscience—that is, of the pot—coming from Leviathan’s smoke when he said: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is toward the face of the north” (Jer. I, 13). The pot of the human heart is kindled by the face of the north when, through the instigation of the adversary spirit, it is inflamed with unlawful desires.

For he who said, [Note: [Col. 0715D] German, Laud. and Val. Cl.: “I will set my seat toward the north; I will be like the Most High.”] “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV, 13), kindles the mind he has once seized through the malignant breaths of his persuasion, as though with fires placed beneath it, so that, not content with present things, it continually seethes with desires: now it longs for its own advantages, now, even to its own detriment, it opposes the advantages of others; now it satisfies the allurements of the flesh; now, as though carried to some summit by the pride of thought, it lifts itself entirely into [Note: [Col. 0715D] Turon., Gemet., Vindoc., Germ.: *typho*. Concerning this word, see note g on chapter 6 of this book, no. 13, and Book XXIII, no. 25.] arrogance, setting aside carnal concern.

Because the heart is drawn away through various desires, being inflamed by the instigations of this Leviathan, his smoke is rightly said to resemble a kindled and boiling pot. For the conscience, fanned by his temptations, raises itself through as many internal swellings as the thoughts that surge within it. [Note: [Col. 0716D] Gemet. and Corb. Germ.: “through his breath.”]

Truth explains this still more clearly in other words when it adds:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Recension XXVIII]

**VERSE 12.—His breath makes coals burn.**

**67. The carnal mind is like a coal inflamed by the devil’s breath.**—What does he call coals except the minds of reprobate people kindled in earthly desires? They burn when they desire some temporal thing, because the desires that do not allow the soul to remain tranquil and whole do indeed burn it.

Thus Leviathan’s breath kindles coals as often as his hidden suggestion draws human minds toward unlawful pleasures. He inflames some with the torches of pride, others with those of envy, others with lust, and others with avarice.

He placed the torch of pride beneath Eve’s mind when he incited her to despise the words of the Lord’s command (Gen. III, 5). He also kindled the flame of envy in Cain’s soul when he grieved over his brother’s accepted sacrifice and thereby proceeded to the crime of fratricide (Gen. IV, 8). He burned Solomon’s heart with the torches of lust, subjecting him to such love of women that, led even to the veneration of idols, he forgot reverence for the Creator while pursuing fleshly pleasure (III Kings XI, 4). He also scorched Ahab’s mind with the fire of avarice when he impelled him with impatient desires to covet another man’s vineyard and thereby dragged him into the guilt of murder (III Kings XXI).

This Leviathan therefore breathes upon coals with as great a breath as he inflames human minds toward unlawful things through the force of hidden suggestion. Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XXXIX [Formerly XLI]

**IBID.—And flame goes out from his mouth.**

**68. He will rage more fiercely through the Antichrist. He burns only wood, hay, and stubble. His flame is extinguished by tears.**—The flame of his mouth is the very instigation of hidden speech. He causes the words of evil persuasion to reach each person’s mind, but what goes out from his mouth is flame because the mind burns in its desires when it is stirred by his suggestions.

He makes these suggestions every day and does not cease suggesting them until the end of the present life. But then he expands them more wickedly when, coming through that condemned man, he displays himself more openly in the glory of this world. [Note: [Col. 0716D] That is, the Antichrist. See above, Book XXXII, no. 22, and below, Book XXXIV, nos. 1 and 29, and elsewhere.]

Then more extensive smoke proceeds from his nostrils, because a greater instigation strikes human hearts, terrified by admiration of his signs. Then his breath makes the coals burn more fiercely, because the minds of the reprobate, which he finds already hot with love of temporal glory, he sets ablaze through the blasts of his suggestion until they practice cruelty.

Then flame goes out from his mouth, because whatever he himself says, and whatever he says through his preachers, is fire by which unfruitful wood is burned. The fire of earthly desire touches the minds of those who have no desire to become precious metals.

Therefore, whoever does not wish to be touched by the flame of his mouth should, according to the judgment of the true Teacher, seek to be found not wood, hay, or stubble, but gold, silver, and precious stone (I Cor. III, 12). For the fire of his persuasion burns all the more fiercely as each person makes himself more yielding to consent.

But since no one can avoid being touched by the ardor of his persuasion while the mind is placed in this corruptible flesh, it remains that, once burned by his malignant blasts, it should turn without ceasing to the help of prayer. The flame of his suggestions is quickly extinguished by a flood of tears.

# BOOK THIRTY-FOUR

The exposition of chapter XLI, verse 13, and the following verses, especially concerning the devil’s pride and the most savage persecutions of the saints by the Antichrist.

[Col. 0717]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0717B]

**1. As the world grows old, tribulations increase with the times. The devil rages more fiercely the nearer he is to the completion of his punishment.**—Because we bear a body from this world, let us consider the end of the whole [Note: [Col. 0717D] Two German manuscripts, Laud., Gemet., and most: “from that which we ourselves …”] by that part from which we ourselves are constituted. We recognize more quickly what the end of the world will be if we carefully observe what we carry from the world.

Our age is vigorous through the strength of youthful years, but in old age it is consumed by increasing illnesses; and while it is prolonged in order to persist, it fails daily, moment by moment, in the manner of dying. So too, as the world’s time increases through the passing years, [Note: [Col. 0717D] Val. Cl.: “with evils increasing.”] it is afflicted by increasing evils; and from the source by which it receives an increase of age, it experiences a loss of well-being.

Tribulations increase for it with the times, and the weaker it becomes in the losses of life, the longer it endures as though advancing toward life. For the ancient enemy is released against it with all his strength. Although he has already perished because he lost the blessedness of his heavenly condition, he is then extinguished more completely when, deprived of the freedom to tempt, he is confined in eternal fires.

Thus he approaches the end of the world to tempt it more fiercely, because he becomes all the more ardent in savagery as he feels himself nearer to punishment. He considers that the time is near when he will lose the license of his most wicked freedom; and as he is narrowed by the brevity of time, so he expands himself through a multiplicity of cruelty, as the angelic voice says to John concerning him: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great anger, knowing that he has little time” (Rev. XII, 12).

Then he expands himself into the heat of great anger, lest he who could not remain in blessedness should fall with the few into the pit of his damnation. Then he cunningly seeks whatever he may wickedly accomplish; then he raises the neck of pride higher, and through the condemned man whom he bears wickedly displays everything by which he prevails in time. Hence it is rightly said now by the divine voice:

## CHAPTER TWO [Recension II]

[Col. 0718B]

**VERSE 13.—Strength will dwell in his neck.**

**2. The Antichrist’s pride will be joined by the power to carry out his wickedness.**—What else is signified by the neck of this Leviathan, [Note: [Col. 0717D] So Laud., Vindoc., two German manuscripts, Gemet., and others. In old and recent editions: “display.”] except the extension of exaltation by which, raising himself against God, he is lifted up with a swelling of power together with a pretense of holiness?

That pride is expressed through the neck, the prophet Isaiah testifies when he rebukes the daughters of Jerusalem, saying: “They walked with an outstretched neck” (Isa. III, 16). Strength is therefore said to dwell in the neck of this Leviathan because power joined to his exaltation also supports him. For whatever then rises proudly, whatever he cunningly devises, he also carries out with the force of secular power.

The prophet Daniel, seeing this, says: “Deceit will be directed by his hand” [Col. 0718C] (Dan. VIII, 25). Deceit in his hand is fraud joined to power, because whatever he wickedly desires, he is also able for a time to carry out forcefully. [Note: [Col. 0718D] In Laud., after these words, “but deceit,” the margin reads: “in his hand.” Other manuscripts: “therefore his deceit.”] His deceit is said to be directed because the malice of his fraud is hindered by no difficulty.

This Leviathan or his vessels commonly possess this characteristic: they are able to fulfill even more wickedly, for the increase of their iniquity, the things they wickedly desire.

**3. It is a divine gift toward the elect that they cannot perpetrate the evil they have conceived.**—For when the elect perhaps grow weak and fall into unlawful desires, they are often held back by the hand of divine grace in this respect: they find no effects for their miserable will. When strong opposition arises against their wishes, they are often corrected by the very impossibility; and, through the wondrous order of inward providence, a change of evil will follows through conversion, while perfection is denied through weakness.

Hence, under the figure of each soul, the Lord says through the prophet concerning weakened Judah, who was walking in perverse ways: “Behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will wall it in, and she shall not find her paths; and she will follow her lovers, and will not overtake them; and she will seek them, and [Note: [Col. 0718D] Laud., two German manuscripts, Vindoc., Gemet., and others in Norm.: “and she will not find them, and she will say.”] not finding them, she will say: ‘I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now’” (Hos. II, 6).

The ways of the elect are hedged with thorns when they encounter the pain of piercing in what they desire temporally. A wall placed across their ways, as it were, stands in their path when the difficulty of fulfilling their desires opposes them. [Note: [Col. 0719D] This reading is supported by both the English and our manuscripts, the old editions, and especially by the sense. Hence we are greatly surprised that *vis* [“force”] should have crept in for *viis* [“ways”] in the Gilot., Vatic., and Gussanv. editions, and that so gross an error was propagated in so many other printed editions.] [Note: [Col. 0720D] That is, the difficulty of carrying out and accomplishing their desires in action.] Their souls seek their lovers and do not find them, when, by following malignant spirits, they fail to attain the pleasures of this world that they desire.

It is rightly added that from this very difficulty she immediately says: “I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now” (Matt. XII, 44). The first husband is the Lord, who joined the chaste soul to himself through the intervening love of the Holy Spirit. The mind of each person desires him when it discovers many bitter things, like thorns, in the pleasures it desires temporally. For when the soul begins to be wounded by the adversities of the world it loves, then it understands more fully how much better it was for it with its first husband.

### 4. Those whom perverse desire corrupt, adversity often corrects

Those, therefore, whom perverse desire corrupts, adversity generally corrects. Hence it is exceedingly fearful lest prosperity follow when unjust things are desired, because an evil is corrected with greater difficulty when it is supported even by the prosperity of its accomplishment.

This Leviathan, therefore, who, together with his members, has been assigned to eternal torments—deceit is directed in his hand, and strength dwells upon his neck—because whatever he desires temporally, with a perverse will, against the good, he completes with a still more perverse power: so that the more nothing presently obstructs him through adversity, the more nothing remains for him hereafter through prosperity.

And because everyone who becomes known through his friendship by perverse conduct first loses the true riches of the mind, it is appropriately added:

## CHAPTER III [Old II, Recension III]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And poverty shall go before his face.”

### 5. The poverty of the elect is that they have lost the heavenly riches

By “face” knowledge is usually signified. Hence it is written: “And my face shall go before you” (Exodus 33:14), that is, knowledge shall provide guidance.

It should be understood, however, that in sacred language poverty is predicated of the elect in one way, and of the reprobate in another. The poverty of the elect exists when the true riches of the heavenly homeland return to their minds, and, placed in the wretched exile of the present life, they remember that they are poor.

[Note: Longipontanus: “to those riches,” namely. In Corbie Germanus, after “they remember,” there follows “of which”; the remainder is omitted.]

For they sigh without ceasing for those riches of which Paul says: “That you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:18). And because they do not yet behold them at all, meanwhile they earnestly groan in the misery of this poverty.

Jeremiah had undoubtedly perceived this poverty when he said: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation” (Lamentations 3:1). For the rod of God’s indignation is the blow of strict judgment. Man endured that indignation when, driven from paradise, he lost the true riches of inward joy (Genesis 3:24).

But because each of the elect continually perceives that he has fallen into the destitution of the present life from that innate capacity of power, it is rightly said: “I am the man who sees my poverty” (Lamentations 3:1). Whoever still desires these visible things does not understand the evil of his pilgrimage, and does not know how to see the very condition that he suffers.

The prophet David, looking upon this poverty, says: “My strength has been weakened in poverty” (Psalm 30:11). Strength is said to be weakened in poverty because the mind, fallen into this pilgrimage and battered by the troubles of its corruption, is hindered from contemplating what it has lost.

### 6. The reprobate do not know this poverty; they are emptied of the riches of the virtues, but do not understand it

The reprobate, however, cannot consider this poverty, because, while they follow what they see, they neglect to think about the invisible things that they have lost. Hence their condition is properly called poverty: while they are filled with vices, they are emptied of the riches of the virtues.

It often happens to them that, lifted up by the madness of pride, while they do not at all consider the losses caused by their ruin, they do not recognize that they are also destitute of good works. Hence, by an angelic voice, it is said to the angel of the church of Laodicea: “You say, ‘I am rich, and have become wealthy, and need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17).

He asserts himself to be rich who is exalted through arrogance over his holiness; yet he is convicted of being poor, blind, and naked. Poor, certainly, because he does not possess the riches of the virtues; blind, because he does not even see the poverty that he suffers; naked, because he has lost the first robe—and worse still, because he does not recognize that he has lost it.

Therefore, since, as we have said, the poverty of the reprobate is the deprivation of merits, it is rightly said of Leviathan: “Poverty shall go before his face.” No one is joined to his knowledge unless he has first been stripped of the riches of the virtues.

[Note: Ebroicensis: “to his thought.”]

For he first removes good thoughts, and then pours into them a clearer knowledge of his iniquity. Poverty is therefore said to precede his face because the capacity for strength is first lost, so that afterward his knowledge may be recognized, as though through familiarity.

[Note: Laudunensis: “is hindered.”]

Or certainly, because he creeps upon many so deceitfully that they cannot at all detect him, and empties their virtues in such a way that he does not reveal the malice of his cunning, poverty is said to go before his face. It is as though it were openly said: when he lies in ambush and tempts, he first strips a person before he is seen.

Hence the prophet says concerning Ephraim: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hosea 7:9). By “strangers” apostate angels are usually understood; they devour strength when, by perverting the mind, they consume its virtue. Ephraim both suffered this and did not know it, because in the temptation of evil spirits he lost the strength of his soul and did not understand that he had lost it.

Thus poverty precedes the face of Leviathan, because before the negligent person recognizes his ambush, he strips the mind by tempting it.

By the statement, “Strength shall dwell upon his neck,” therefore, the power of violence is shown. By what follows, “Poverty shall go before his face,” the subtlety of fraud is signified.

### 7. Before the coming of Antichrist, the signs of virtue will be withdrawn from the Church, or only a few will remain

Although, from our recognition that poverty goes before his face, another and even more grievous interpretation is available, we should nevertheless set it forth.

In the terrible order of a hidden dispensation, before this Leviathan appears in the condemned man whom he assumes, the signs of virtue are withdrawn from the holy Church. Prophecy is concealed, the grace of healings is removed, the virtue of prolonged abstinence is diminished, the words of doctrine fall silent, and the wonders of miracles are taken away.

The heavenly dispensation does not entirely withdraw these things; but it does not display them openly and abundantly as in former times. This is nevertheless accomplished by a wonderful dispensation, so that through one action both divine mercy and justice may be fulfilled.

For while, with the powers of the signs withdrawn, the holy Church appears as though more despised, the reward of the good increases: those who honor her for the hope of heavenly things, and not on account of present signs, are rewarded. At the same time, the mind of the wicked is more quickly exposed against her, because they neglect to follow the invisible things she promises when they are not held by visible signs.

Thus, while the humility of the faithful is seemingly deprived of the multitude and manifestation of signs, by the terrible examination of a hidden dispensation greater mercy is bestowed upon the good from the very point at which just wrath is heaped upon the wicked.

[Note: Thus two German manuscripts, Vindocinus, Longipontanus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman witnesses, where the printed editions have “mercy is bestowed.” In Paris 1495, however, “more abundant” is read; this was changed in Paris 1518, with the other editions agreeing.]

Therefore, because, before this Leviathan comes manifest and visible, the signs of virtue cease for the most part in the holy Church, it is rightly said now: “Poverty shall go before his face.”

For the riches of miracles are first withdrawn from the faithful, and then that ancient enemy is displayed against them through manifest wonders, so that, to the extent that he exalts himself through signs, he may be overcome by the faithful all the more firmly and gloriously without signs.

Nevertheless, signs will not be lacking to the faithful in his struggle; but his signs will be so great that ours will appear either few or nonexistent. Their virtue is made superior to all signs when it tramples beneath the heel of inward steadfastness everything that it sees him accomplish terribly.

[Note: Here we follow two German manuscripts, Laudunensis, Turonensis, Gemetensis, and others, as well as the older printed editions. In the more recent editions one reads: “is seen to be done … [lacuna] … presses upon the heel.”]

But the evil enemy displays himself against them with a fiercer savagery in proportion as he grieves that he is despised even when miracles are becoming manifest. He gathers his whole self for their destruction and joins all the reprobate in the slaughter of the faithful with unanimous cruelty, so that he may exercise his savagery all the more powerfully because none of the members of his body disagree among themselves concerning the things he perversely desires to do.

[Note: The same printed editions have “exercise,” contrary to two German manuscripts, Turonensis, Vindocinus, Laudunensis, Vallicellanus, Norman witnesses, and others.]

Hence it is rightly said:

## CHAPTER IV [Recension IV]

**VERSE 14.**—“The members of his flesh cling to one another.”

### 8. The harmful concord of the reprobate with Satan and among themselves

The flesh of this Leviathan consists of all the reprobate, who do not rise through desire toward an understanding of the spiritual homeland.

The members of the flesh are those who join themselves to these people acting perversely and leading others into iniquity, just as, by contrast, Paul says of the Lord’s body: “You are the body of Christ, and members of a member” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

For one thing is a member of a body, and another is a member of a member. A member of the body is a part in relation to the whole; a member of a member is a small part in relation to a larger part. A finger is a member of a member in relation to the hand, and the hand in relation to the arm; but the whole of these together is a member of the body in relation to the entire body.

Therefore, just as in the spiritual body of the Lord we call those “members of a member” who are governed by others in his Church, so in the reprobate congregation of this Leviathan those are members of the flesh who join themselves in wicked action to others more wicked than themselves.

[Note: Laudunensis: “of the carnal.”]

But because the malignant enemy agrees with himself in perverse action from first to last, the divine word speaks of the members of his flesh as clinging to one another. For the perverse think alike with such unanimity that they are not divided by any mutual dispute against one another.

No disagreement of difference then tears them apart; and for this reason they prevail so powerfully against the good, because they hold together concordantly in evil.

[Old III.] As we have already said above (Book 33, no. 55), just as it is harmful if unity is absent from the good, so it is more harmful if it is absent from the wicked. For the unity of the reprobate obstructs the way of the good all the more harshly, the more harshly it opposes it through collective force.

[Note: Recent Vulgate editions: “life,” supported by the German, Pratelian, and other Norman witnesses.]

[Note: Corbie Germanus, Ebroicensis, and many Norman witnesses: “more harshly.”]

### 9. This unity may be dissolved, following the example of Paul

Paul had perceived the harmful unity of the reprobate when, caught in the midst of the Sadducees and Pharisees, he said: “I am being judged concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead” (Acts 23:6). At this utterance, the crowd of those listening immediately turned against itself and broke apart.

When the tumultuous multitude was divided into two parties, a way of escape was opened for Paul: the united crowd of persecutors had confined him, but its division released him.

The righteous are therefore rescued when the unrighteous are divided, and the desires of the elect reach fulfillment when the armies of the reprobate are thrown into confusion through discord.

This is also well signified by the division of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21ff.). For when the water is divided into two parts, the chosen people proceed toward the promised land; so, when the unity of the wicked is split apart, good minds are brought to what they desire.

If the unity of the wicked had not been harmful, divine providence would never have scattered the tongues of the proud into such diversity (Genesis 11:8). If the unity of the wicked had not been harmful, the Prophet would not have said concerning the enemies of the holy Church: “Cast them down, Lord, and divide their tongues” (Psalm 54:10).

Therefore, because this Leviathan is then unleashed in his forces against God’s elect, he is permitted, for the increase of his malice, to have unity among the reprobate as well, so that he may exert his strength against us all the more powerfully, attacking us not only with the blow of strength but also with the mass of united forces.

But who could be sufficient against these things? What mind would not tremble from the very root of its thoughts at the weight of such pride and such a compacted force?

Therefore, because divine clemency sees that we tremble through weakness, it immediately adds what it does through itself. For it continues:

## CHAPTER V [Recension V]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“He will send lightning bolts against him, and they will not be carried elsewhere.”

### 16. They will be crushed by lightning in the judgment, while the just remain unharmed and rejoice

What is signified by the name “lightning bolts” except those terrifying sentences of the final judgment? They are called lightning bolts because they burn forever those whom they strike.

Paul had seen these lightning bolts coming upon him when he said: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the appearance of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

These lightning bolts that are sent against him are not carried elsewhere, because, while the just rejoice, they strike only the reprobate at that time.

For after the threshing of the present life, in which the wheat now groans beneath the chaff, the winnowing fan of the final judgment separates wheat and chaff in such a way that neither does the chaff pass into the granary of the wheat, nor do the grains fall into the fire of the chaff. Those lightning bolts therefore touch no other place, because by their fire they burn not the grains but the chaff.

But because punishment does not correct this Leviathan, he indicates this when he adds:

## CHAPTER VI [Recension VI]

**VERSE 15.**—“His heart will be hardened like a stone.”

### 11. Satan’s impenitence; he is rightly compared to an anvil

The heart of the ancient enemy will be hardened like a stone, because no repentance of conversion will ever soften it. And because he will be fitted only for the blows of eternal vengeance, it is rightly added at once:

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And he will be compressed like a blacksmith’s anvil.”

For the blacksmith fixes the anvil so that it may receive blows alone. The anvil is established for this purpose: to be struck by repeated blows.

This Leviathan, therefore, is compressed like a blacksmith’s anvil because he will be confined by the bonds of hell, so that he may be hammered by the continual blows of eternal punishment.

Even now he is struck, while the righteous are saved, although he remains watchful in ambush and wastes away in pains. In the anvil, other vessels are formed; but it itself, despite so many blows, is not changed into another vessel.

[Note: Namely, “the anvil”; nevertheless, all printed editions read “he himself,” but this is erroneous.]

This Leviathan is therefore rightly compared to an anvil, because while he persecutes us we are formed, whereas he himself is both perpetually struck and never changed into a useful vessel.

We leave him to eternal punishment, while we, struck in his temptation by the hand of the heavenly Craftsman, pass through him like vessels that have been formed. In him we are hammered, but so that we may come to serve the household above.

He himself is compressed like an anvil because, although he now roams through the world tempting it, once placed in hell he no longer wanders beneath the blow of the sentence.

It continues:

## CHAPTER VII [Recension VII]

[Col. 0724B]

**VERSE 16.**—“When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified.”

### 12. When the reprobate angels fell, the good were terrified and strengthened through fear

Sacred Scripture sometimes mixes past and future time, at one point using the future for the past, and at another the past for the future.

It uses the future for the past when a woman about to bear a male child, who will rule the nations with an iron rod, is shown to John (Revelation 12:5). Since this had already happened when the incarnate Lord came, a deed already accomplished was being announced.

Again, it uses the past for the future, as the Psalmist says concerning the Lord: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Psalm 21:18). In these words the appearance of the Lord’s passion is described as though it had already occurred, although it was still being announced as future, far afterward.

There is therefore no obstacle here to understanding the words “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear” as describing past events under the form of future time. Nor do we abandon sound interpretation if we believe that, when this Leviathan fell from the citadel of blessedness, the elect angels also trembled at his fall, so that, when the fall of pride expelled him from their number, fear itself strengthened them to stand more firmly.

[Old IV.] Hence it follows: “And, terrified, they will be purified.”

### 13. In what sense they were then purified: when others fell, it was granted to the rest that they could not fall

They were purified because, when he went out with the legions of the reprobate, only those who would live blessedly forever remained in the heavenly dwellings.

His fall therefore both terrified and purified them: it terrified them so that they would not proudly despise their Creator; it purified them because, when the reprobate departed, it came about that the elect alone remained.

And because God, the Maker of all, knows how to use even the evil action of the reprobate for the preservation of the good, he turned the fall of those who fell into the advancement of those who remained. From the very place where the guilt of the proud was punished, increases of merit were both found and solidified for the humble angels.

When these fell, it was granted to those others as a gift that they could not fall at all. For the holy angels, seeing in those who fell the losses suffered by their nature, now stand more cautiously and firmly in themselves.

Thus, with the Lord of all things ordering everything wonderfully, it comes about that even the losses of its own ruin benefit that homeland of the elect spirits, since it has been constructed more firmly at the very point where it had been partly destroyed.

[Note: Longipontanus: “so that that portion of the elect spirits might even profit from the loss caused by its ruin.” Laudunensis: “so that they might perceive the losses caused by its ruin.”]

### 14. Holy preachers are called angels

But because sacred Scripture often designates the preachers of the Church by the name of angels, since they announce the glory of the heavenly homeland, we can understand “angels” in this passage as referring to holy preachers.

Hence John, writing in the Apocalypse to the seven churches, speaks to the angels of the churches, that is, to the preachers of the peoples (Revelation 1:4).

Hence the prophet says: “The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isaiah 33:7).

Again, the prophet Malachi says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7).

[Note: Laudunensis, the German witnesses, and others: “will guard … will seek.”]

Hence Paul says: “Great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16).

Therefore, when he had said that the mystery of the dispensation appeared to angels, and then added that it was preached among the nations, he clearly designated holy preachers—messengers of the truth—by the name of angels.

### 15. They are terrified and purified by the fall and punishment of the reprobate

If, therefore, what is said—“When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified”—is referred to the future, then the final condemnation of this Leviathan is signified: with the strict Judge coming, he is removed from this world through the wrath of judgment, he who is now tolerated with marvelous patience and forbearance.

He is shaken out from here by such a weight of terror that even the strength of the holy preachers is disturbed. “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear,” because, when he is swept away in the storm of judgment, those who are found in bodies tremble under immense terror—even the messengers of the heavenly homeland.

[Note: Vindocinus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman witnesses: “of the Judge.”]

Although they are already strong and perfect, nevertheless, because they are still placed in the flesh, they cannot pass through the storm of such terror without being shaken by some fear.

But when this Leviathan is swept away, and all the elements are shaken at his destruction, hope of the nearness of the kingdom gladdens the holy preachers whom, as I have said, that time of judgment still finds in their bodies; while the weakness of the flesh disturbs them at the manifestation of wrath.

There will therefore be in them, in a certain sense, a joyful trembling and a secure fear, because they are certain that they will be rewarded with the heavenly kingdom, yet they tremble on account of the weakness of the flesh through fear of so great a storm.

### 16. If the just tremble, how great will be the future shaking of the reprobate

Let us consider, therefore, how the conscience of the wicked will then be shaken, when even the life of the just is disturbed.

What will those who hate the Judge’s coming do, if even those who love it are terrified by the dread of so great a judgment?

And because this fear is burned away in the holy preachers—if any rust of minor vices could have remained in them—after saying, “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear,” he appropriately added at once: “And, terrified, they will be purified.”

But since we have learned these things concerning the end of this Leviathan, let us meanwhile hear first what he does before he perishes.

It continues:

## CHAPTER VIII [Recension VIII]

**VERSE 17.**—“When the sword has seized him, he will not be able to withstand either the spear or the breastplate.”

### 17. Antichrist is rightly called the devil’s sword

In sacred Scripture, “sword” sometimes signifies holy preaching, sometimes eternal condemnation, sometimes temporal tribulation, and sometimes the anger or persuasion of the ancient enemy.

The sword is used for holy preaching, as Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17).

The name “sword” signifies eternal condemnation, as it is written concerning the heretic who preaches: “If his children are multiplied, they will be for the sword” (Job 27:14), because however great their number may be here, they are consumed by eternal condemnation.

The sword is understood as temporal tribulation, as it is said to Mary concerning the tribulations that would follow: “And a sword will pierce your own soul” (Luke 2:35).

Again, anger or the persuasion of the malignant enemy is expressed by the sword, as the Psalmist says: “You who delivered your servant David from the evil sword” (Psalm 143:10).

The sword of holy preaching is benign, for by it we are struck so that we may die to guilt. The sword of diabolical persuasion is malignant, for by it each person is wickedly struck so that he may be extinguished from the life of uprightness.

[Note: The Vatican and Gussanville editions have “so that he may be extinguished from the way.” It is better in all our manuscripts and in the old editions: “so that he may be extinguished from life.” What does it mean to be extinguished from the way?]

The sword of the ancient enemy is that condemned man, assumed for his service. He sharpens him through the malice of deceit and pierces the hearts of the weak.

[Note: Thus read from the English, Norman, Vindocine, two German, Laudunian, and other manuscripts, as well as from the old edition. Other editions have: “Therefore this Leviathan seizes the sword,” corruptly and contrary to the sense of the exposition, where the sword is not seized but seizes.]

This Leviathan’s sword therefore seizes him when his own condemned man receives him. But if anger is signified by the name “sword,” it is rightly described not as seizing the sword but as being seized by the sword.

For then he is turned toward such madness that, desiring to dominate everyone, he is in no way master of his own anger. We, when we take up anger in the service of justice, hold the sword, because by possessing it under the rule of equitable judgment we moderate it.

But he, because he is carried away through the precipices of fury, is said not to seize the sword but to be seized by the sword. He does not possess and hold anger; rather, raging with anger, he is held by it.

[Old V.] ### 18. In what sense the spear and breastplate are said to yield to this sword

It is clear to everyone that we strike an adversary with a spear, while we are protected from an adversary by a breastplate. With the spear we inflict wounds; with the breastplate we are covered so that we are not wounded.

What, then, is signified by the spear except the dart of preaching? And what by the breastplate except the strength of patience?

This Leviathan, therefore, because through the reprobate man whom he assumes he is unleashed in the anger of complete cruelty, is said to be seized by the sword. For then, by displaying immense strength, he exhibits whatever he can wickedly accomplish.

Neither spear nor breastplate will be able to withstand him, because, when he comes in Antichrist, he will appear possessed of such great power that, unless heavenly assistance is present, he will blunt the sharpness of preachers and destroy the endurance of the patient.

For unless heavenly grace strengthens the life of the just, the spear does not withstand him, because the strength of preachers is broken; the breastplate does not withstand him, because the patience of the steadfast is shattered and penetrated.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 18.**—“For he will regard iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.”

### 19. When Antichrist rages, the strength of preachers and the steadfastness of the strong will be endangered
