What he earlier called the spear he repeated below under the name of iron; and what he presented as the breastplate he again signified by the mention of bronze.

Iron is sharpened so that the adversary may be wounded; bronze, however, is scarcely consumed by rust. Iron therefore signifies the darts of preaching, while bronze signifies the steadfastness of endurance.

Hence, under the figure of Asher, Moses says of the holy Church: “Iron and bronze shall be your footwear” (Deuteronomy 33:25). In sacred Scripture footwear is understood as the protection of preaching, as it is written: “Your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6:16).

Therefore, because virtue is expressed through iron and perseverance through bronze, it is said that “iron and bronze shall be her footwear,” when her preaching is protected both by sharpness and by steadfastness.

Through iron she penetrates opposing evils; through bronze she preserves patiently the good that she has undertaken. He makes her perseverance even clearer there when he says: “As the days of her youth, so shall be her old age” (Deuteronomy 33:25).

[Recension IX.] But when this Leviathan takes up for the exercise of his iniquity that sword which sacred Scripture calls Antichrist, he will regard iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood. Unless divine grace protects them, he will consume the strength of preachers like straw by the fire of his wickedness, and reduce the steadfastness of the patient to dust like rotten wood.

Thus both the sharpness of iron and the strength of bronze fail, while through the violence of his power the meaning of preaching is blunted and the endurance of patience is scattered.

### 20. Unless God brings help, they will fail

Unless divine assistance therefore strengthens his elect, where will the weak be at that time, if the strong are regarded as straw?

What will this Leviathan do with straw if he considers iron to be straw? What will he do with rotten wood if he dissolves the strength of bronze as rotten wood?

But how many who consider themselves, by their own strength, to be iron or bronze will then discover themselves to be straw in the fire of tribulation! And how many who, through awareness of their own weakness, fear that they are straw will, supported by divine help, be strengthened with the solidity of iron and bronze, so that they are strong in God against their adversary all the more because they remember themselves to be weak in themselves!

But the higher this Behemoth raises himself against God’s elect through miracles, the more vehemently all the saints bind themselves to the words of preaching against him.

Yet he so possesses the minds of the reprobate that he does not leave them even when pierced by any dart of truth.

[Note: Laudunensis: “pierced.” Gemetensis: “confused.”]

Hence it follows:

**THE SAME PASSAGE, 19.**—“No archer will drive him away.”

### 21. Holy preaching does not drive Satan from the hearts of the reprobate

[Note: The printed editions have “for what by arrows”; we have removed “by,” since it is absent from the manuscripts and is redundant in Gregory’s style.]

What are the arrows except the words of preachers? When they are sent forth by the voice of those who live well, they pierce the hearts of those who hear.

The holy Church had been pierced by these arrows when she said: “I am wounded with love” (Song of Songs 2:5).

Of these arrows it is said by the voice of the Psalmist: “The arrows of children have become their wounds” (Psalm 63:8), because the words of the humble penetrated the minds of the proud.

Concerning these arrows it is said to the advancing champion: “Your arrows are sharp, O most powerful one; peoples shall fall beneath you in the heart” (Psalm 45:6).

The archer, therefore, is the one who, through the bow of holy intention, fixes words of right exhortation in the hearts of those who hear.

Therefore, because this Leviathan despises the words of preachers, and, when he has bitten the minds of the reprobate by evil persuasion, does not at all abandon them, hardened amid the darts, it is rightly said: “No archer will drive him away.”

It is as though it were openly said: The arrow of the holy preacher does not drive him from the hearts of the reprobate, because whoever is seized by him now scorns hearing the words of preachers.

Hence, rightly angered at preceding sins, the Lord says through the prophet concerning those whom he abandons into the hand of the ancient enemy: “I will send among you venomous serpents against which there is no incantation” (Jeremiah 8:17).

It is as though he were saying: “By a just judgment I will hand you over to such unclean spirits that they cannot be driven from you by the exhortation of preachers, as though by the speech of those who utter incantations.”

But because this Leviathan is not moved from the hearts of the reprobate by the darts of holy preaching, the contempt of holy men is also added to his account, when it is immediately said:

## CHAPTER XI [Old VI]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“The stones of the sling have become straw to him.”

### 22. Against him and Antichrist the strength of the saints appears to be straw; nevertheless, he can do nothing against their soul

What is signified by the sling except the holy Church?

For when a sling is whirled in a circle, stones come forth from it with which the breasts of adversaries are struck. Likewise, when the holy Church is carried around through the circuit of tribulations by the revolving course of time, strong men emerge from her, by whose blows, like those of stones, the hearts of the wicked are battered.

Hence the Lord says to the prophet concerning good teachers: “They shall devour and subdue with sling-stones” (Zechariah 9:15).

For the holy teachers who instruct others in virtue devour their enemies when they transform them within their own body through the power of conversion.

[Note: Two German manuscripts, Turonensis, Laudunensis, Gemetensis: “through the conduct of their way of life.” Vallicellanus: “when they transform them into their body through the power of their conduct.”]

They subject them to the stones of the sling because, when they establish strong men in the holy Church, they shatter through them the hard breasts of the proud adversaries.

Hence even the most monstrous Goliath dies by a stone from a sling (1 Samuel 17:49), because diabolical exaltation is overcome by the single stone of the holy Church.

This Leviathan, therefore, because, after assuming that condemned man, despises whichever strong men of the Church as weak and temporarily crushes their strength, is rightly said now to regard the stones of the sling as straw.

It is as though it were openly said: He reduces the strength of the saints to the softness of straw, although their tongue had previously battered his breast with hard blows.

For then, exercising the full strength of his iniquity, the more painfully he grieves that he is spiritually overcome by them, the more savagely he prevails against them bodily.

And because he realizes that he can prevail over nothing against their spirit, he completes in their flesh every device of his cruelty.

[Old VII.] But what wonder is it if he despises human strength, when he also disregards within himself the eternal torments of the heavenly judgment?

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 20.**—“He will regard the hammer as straw.”

23. He despises God’s vengeance.—As if he were saying: He also despises the weight of that punishment which, coming from above, strikes him through chastisement. In Holy Scripture, the name “hammer” sometimes denotes the devil, by whom the sins of the guilty are now struck; at other times it signifies a heavenly blow, by which either the elect feel blows from above so that they may be corrected from their wicked ways, or just wrath strikes the reprobate, showing in advance what eternal punishments they deserve.

For that the ancient enemy is expressed by the designation “hammer,” the prophet testifies when, contemplating the force of the final judgment against him, he says: “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and shattered!” (Jer. 50:23). As if he were saying: Who can comprehend with what whirlwind, when the final judgment comes, the Lord will break in eternal damnation him through whom he strikes his vessels to be fashioned for the use of ministry?

Again, a heavenly blow is expressed by the hammer, as is signified when Solomon was building the Temple: “When the house was being built, it was built of dressed and finished stones, and neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built” (1 Kings 6:7). [Note: Laudunensis reads: “But when the house had been built, and the hammer …”] For what did that house signify if not the holy Church, which the Lord inhabits in the heavenly places? For its construction the souls of the elect are brought like polished stones.

When it is built in heaven, no hammer of discipline resounds there, because we are brought there as dressed and finished stones, to be placed in locations suited to our merits. [Note: Gemeticensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus read: “that we may be placed.”] Here we are struck outwardly so that we may arrive there without reproach. Here the hammer, here the axe, here all the iron tools of striking resound. But in the house of God no blows are heard, because in the eternal homeland every noise of striking falls silent.

[Col. 0730B] The hammer does not strike there, because no punishment afflicts anyone. The axe does not cut there, because no sentence of severity casts those received within back outside. The iron tools do not clatter there, because no one thereafter feels even the slightest scourge.

[Note: Laudunensis reads: “What, then, is expressed by the hammer … except a heavenly …”] Since, therefore, the weight of a heavenly blow coming from above is expressed by the hammer, what does it mean that this Leviathan despises the hammer, except that he scorns fearing the blow of heavenly punishment? He regards the hammer as straw, because he prepares himself for the weight of just wrath as though against the lightest terrors. Hence it is more explicitly added:

CAPUT XIII [Rec. XI]

IBID.—“And he will laugh at the brandished spear.”

24. He laughs at the threat of the future judgment and is thereby made more cruel.—Against Leviathan the Lord brandishes a spear, because in his destruction he threatens a severe sentence. To brandish a spear is to prepare eternal death for him through strict punishment. But the apostate spirit, despising the author of life even in the face of his own death, laughs at the brandished spear, because he does not fear to suffer whatever grievous or dreadful things he foresees himself suffering under the strict judgment. [Note: Gemeticensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus read: “whatever dreadful thing he foresees himself suffering.”] Rather, the more clearly he sees that he cannot escape eternal torments, the more fiercely he rises to exercise wickedness.

When many of the wise men of this world observe him persisting with such obstinacy and such courage in all that he desires, they incline their hearts to serve his tyranny and bend against God whatever understanding God has granted them, turning it to the service of that enemy. [Note: Recent editions of Gilot, the Vatican, and Gussanville read “with such fear” instead of “with such courage.”] Hence it is rightly added:

CAPUT XIV [Rec. XII]

IBID. 21.—“Under him will be the rays of the sun.”

25. Some who appeared to shine in the Church through teaching or holiness are subjected to him.—In Holy Scripture, when the sun is used figuratively, it sometimes designates the Lord, sometimes persecution, sometimes the manifestation of something through visible revelation, and sometimes the understanding of the wise.

The Lord is figured by the sun, as is declared in the Book of Wisdom, where all the impious, on the day of the final judgment, recognizing their condemnation, are said to say: “We went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6). As if they were openly saying: “The ray of inward light did not shine back upon us.” Hence John says: “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet” (Rev. 12:2). In the sun is understood the illumination of truth; in the moon, which wanes through its monthly renewals, the mutability of temporal existence. Since the holy Church is protected by the splendor of heavenly light, she is clothed as though with the sun; but because she despises all temporal things, she presses the moon beneath her feet.

Again, the sun designates persecution, as Truth says in the Gospel: “When the sun had risen, the seed that had no root withered” (Matt. 13:6), because the words of life, flourishing for a temporal moment in the hearts of earthly people, dry up when the heat of persecution comes upon them.

Again, the sun designates the manifestation of something through visible revelation, as the Prophet announces the Lord appearing to the eyes of all: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18:6). As if he were saying: “He has displayed the mystery of the assumed humanity in the light of visible revelation.” Likewise, the divine voice says through Nathan to the same Prophet: “You did this in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun” (2 Sam. 12:12). For what is indicated by “before the sun” except knowledge through visible revelation?

Again, by the name “sun” the understanding of the wise is expressed, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was granted to him to scorch people with heat and fire” (Rev. 16:8). To pour the bowl upon the sun means to inflict the punishments of persecution upon men shining with the splendor of wisdom. “And it was granted to him to afflict people with heat and fire,” because when wise men, overcome by tortures, are touched by the error of evil action, the weak, persuaded by their example, burn with temporal desires. The fall of the strong provides increase for the destruction of the weak. [Note: Vindobonensis reads “arguments”; Vallicellianus reads “increases.”]

Because the sun signifies the keenness of wisdom, Solomon likewise says by comparison: “The wise man remains like the sun; the fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27:12). [Note: Laudunensis, Gemeticensis, and two German manuscripts read “will be changed.”]

[Vet. VIII.] What, then, in this passage are meant by the rays of the sun except the keenness of the wise? Since many who appeared to shine with the light of wisdom in the holy Church will then be subjected to the rebellion of this Leviathan—whether captured by persuasion, terrified by threats, or broken by tortures—it is rightly said: “Under him will be the rays of the sun.”

As if it were openly said: Those who within the holy Church appeared, through the keenness of wisdom, to scatter rays of light and to shine from above through the authority of uprightness will subject themselves by wicked action to the power of this Leviathan, so that they no longer shine from above by preaching what is right, but serve him perversely by obeying him.

The rays of the sun are therefore under him when certain learned men do not freely raise up the keenness of their wisdom through right action, but incline it to the footsteps of this Leviathan both by the perversity of their conduct and by the flattery of adulation, so that the understanding granted to them from heaven, like the sun above them, is laid beneath the feet of the ancient enemy through earthly desire.

Thus, whenever someone among the wise and learned subjects himself through the fall of flattery to earthly powers acting wickedly, for the sake of temporal advantage or glory, he lays himself down beneath the footsteps of the coming Antichrist like a ray of the sun. Behemoth, as it were, humbles the light of heaven for himself when he tramples the minds of the wise through pestilential consent.

The rays of the sun place themselves beneath the feet of this Leviathan as often as those who appear to shine with the light of teaching, through an immoderate keenness, understand what is wicked in sacred Scripture and subject themselves by perverse interpretations to his errors. For when they rise up against the faithful declarations of truth, they serve the footsteps of this Leviathan by thinking falsely.

The rays of the sun are under him as often as learned men, endowed with the light of understanding, either raise themselves up in pride while despising others; or, setting aside the highest things they know, defile themselves with sordid desires of the flesh; or, forgetting heavenly things, pursue earthly ones; or, not remembering that they are earth, glory vainly in their knowledge of heavenly things. Hence it is rightly added:

CAPUT XV [Rec. XIII]

[Col. 0732C]

IBID.—“He will spread gold beneath himself like mud.”

26. What gold signifies in Holy Scripture.—In sacred language, the name “gold” sometimes signifies the brightness of divinity, sometimes the splendor of the heavenly city, sometimes charity, sometimes the radiance of secular glory, and sometimes the beauty of holiness.

The intimate brightness of divinity itself is designated by the name “gold,” as the appearance of the bridegroom is described in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold” (Song 5:11). Since Christ’s head is God, and nothing among metals is more resplendent than gleaming gold, the bridegroom’s head is called gold because his humanity is governed for us by the brightness of his divinity.

Again, the splendor of the heavenly city is signified by the name “gold,” as John testifies that he saw it, saying: “The city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. 21:18). [Note: The German, Laudunensis, Gemeticensis, and several other witnesses read “with pure gold.” This passage is mutilated in the editions of Gilot and the Vatican, which read: “The city itself is said to be pure gold like glass,” so that also by …] The gold of which that city is composed is said to be like glass, so that by the gold its brightness and by the glass its transparency may be signified.

Again, charity is indicated by the name “gold.” The angel whom John saw speaking to him [Note: The holy Doctor calls him an angel, but John introduces him as speaking as the Son of God: “Do not be afraid; I am the first and the last, and the living one; I was dead, and behold, I am alive,” etc. (Rev. 1:17–18). That one speaking in the person of Christ was an angel is supported by what precedes: “In the midst of the seven golden lampstands, one like a son of man” (v. 13).] he saw girded around the breasts with a golden belt (Rev. 1:13), because the breasts of the heavenly citizens, no longer subject to fear of punishment and no longer released from one another by any division, are bound together solely by charity.

To have a golden belt around the breasts is to restrain all movements of changeable thoughts by the bonds of love alone.

Again, the radiance of temporal glory is expressed by the name “gold,” as the Prophet says: “Babylon is a golden cup” (Jer. 51:7). For what is designated by the name Babylon except the glory of this world? It is called a golden cup because, while displaying temporal things as beautiful, it intoxicates foolish minds with desire for it, so that they pursue visible temporal beauties and despise invisible ones. [Note: Turonensis, Germanicus, Vindobonensis, and Vallicellianus read: “with desire for itself.”]

Eve was intoxicated by this golden cup at the beginning through her own choice. The account of truth says of her that, when she desired the forbidden tree, “she saw that it was beautiful to look at and pleasing to the eyes, and she ate” (Gen. 3:6). Babylon’s cup is therefore golden because, while it displays the appearance of outward beauty, it removes the perception of inward uprightness.

Again, the splendor of holiness is understood by the name “gold,” as Jeremiah laments the Jewish people, changed from the splendor of righteousness to the darkness of wickedness: “How the gold has grown dim, the finest color has been changed!” (Lam. 4:1). As we said above, gold is darkened when the beauty of righteousness is abandoned amid the darkness of subsequent sins. The finest color is changed when the splendor of innocence is turned into the foulness of guilt. [Note: Book XVIII, no. 53; Book XX, no. 76; Book XXVII, no. 71.]

[Vet. IX.] 27. What mud signifies.—In sacred language, the name “mud” sometimes signifies the multiplicity of earthly things, sometimes doctrine that is sordid and teaches what is wicked, and sometimes the enticement of carnal desire. [Note: Gemeticensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “and sometimes the desire of carnal enticement.”]

The multiplicity of earthly things is figured by mud, as it is said through the prophet Habakkuk: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his! How long will he weigh down against himself the thick mud?” (Hab. 2:6). He weighs himself down with thick mud who, multiplying earthly possessions through greed, constricts himself beneath the burden of his sin.

Again, doctrine that is sordid and teaches what is earthly is designated by the name “mud,” as the Lord is told through the same prophet: “You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters” (Hab. 3:15). As if he were saying: “You opened a path for your preachers amid the doctrines of this age that are sordid and teach earthly things.”

The desire for sordid pleasure is also expressed by mud, as the Psalmist prays: “Deliver me from the mud, so that I may not cling to it” (Ps. 68:15). To cling to mud is to be defiled by sordid desires of carnal lust.

28. The ancient enemy deceives some under the appearance of holiness and ensnares others through foul vices.—In this passage, therefore, gold is understood as the brightness of holiness, while mud may be understood either as greed for earthly things, as the contagion of wicked doctrines, or as the filth of carnal pleasures. Since this Leviathan will subject many who appeared to shine within the holy Church with the brilliance of righteousness—whether through desire for earthly things, contagion from error, or carnal pleasures—he will undoubtedly spread gold beneath himself like mud.

To spread gold like mud is to trample the purity of life in some through unlawful desires, so that even those who previously shone against him with the splendor of virtues serve his filthy footsteps.

The ancient enemy will then deceive some under the appearance of holiness, while he will seize others through the foul vices of carnal life. Then he will rage openly through these means, but now he secretly rules the hearts of many, as the Apostle Paul says: “That he may be revealed in his own time; for the mystery of iniquity is already at work” (2 Thess. 2:6).

Even now, therefore, he spreads gold beneath himself like mud as often as he tramples the chastity of the faithful through the vices of the flesh. He treads gold like mud as often as he scatters the understanding of the self-controlled through impure desires. He will carry this out then with all the greater violence, the more unrestrainedly he perpetrates what he desires, entrusted to his lost freedom. [Note: Gussanville and several other editions read “more unbridled.”]

29. Those who are laid beneath the devil, although they appear to be gold, are mud.—Perhaps someone may wonder why the merciful God permits these things to happen: why this Leviathan, whether now through cunning suggestions or then through the condemned man whom he fills, subjects either the rays of the sun—that is, the learned and wise—or gold—that is, men shining with the brightness of holiness—beneath himself like mud by defiling them with vices.

We answer more briefly that the gold which can be spread like mud by his wicked persuasions was never gold in the sight of God. [Note: De poenitentia, distinction 2, chapter “Citius.”] Those who can at some time be seduced and never return appear to lose, in the eyes of men, a holiness that they seemed to possess; but they never possessed it in the sight of God.

Often a person is secretly entangled in many sins and appears great in one particular virtue. That virtue itself also becomes empty and fails, because, when it becomes known to people, it is certainly praised, and its praise is eagerly desired. Thus it comes about that the virtue itself is not virtue in God’s sight, since it conceals what displeases him and reveals what pleases him.

What merit, then, can such people have before God, when their evils are hidden and their good deeds are public? Frequently, as we have said, pride lies hidden while chastity becomes known. For this reason the chastity displayed for a long time is lost toward the end of life, because the pride concealed beneath it is retained uncorrected to the end.

Another devotes himself to almsgiving and distributes his possessions, yet serves many injustices or perhaps exercises his tongue in slanders. [Note: Vindobonensis, two German manuscripts, Laudunensis, Ebroicensis, Gemeticensis, and others read: “employs.”] It often happens that one who had been merciful burns, near the end of his life, with the goads of greed and cruelty. This occurs by a very just judgment, so that the one who never took care to correct what displeased God also loses before men what pleased men.

Another pursues patience; but because he does not guard against envying others and preserving malice in his heart, he eventually becomes impatient—the long-hidden sufferer revealed. [Note: Laudunensis adds: “Thus in one respect gold is also spread like mud.”]

These people, then, are gold in one respect and mud in another. That gold is spread like mud when, because hidden sins demand it, even the virtue that had shone publicly is destroyed.

But we believe it worthwhile to examine more subtly in these matters the ordering of divine providence.

[Vet. X.] 30. God tolerates the hidden evils of some so that the good they do openly may benefit the elect.—Often almighty God tolerates the hidden evils of certain people so that he may distribute the good they do openly for the benefit of his elect. For some, not wholly abandoning the world and not destined to persevere, undertake the narrow way, and by their example kindle those who will persevere to seek that narrow way.

Hence it often happens that the very life they appear to live well is lived not for themselves but rather for the elect alone, since by their example those who will persevere are summoned to the pursuit of living well by those who will not persevere. [Note: Turonensis reads: “to the practice of acting or living well.”]

Often we see some people enter a road and hurry toward a proposed destination; others, seeing them go, follow and seek the same place together. Yet it frequently happens that, when some entanglement arises, those who were leading turn back, while those who were following reach the destination.

Such, indeed, are those who will not persevere but undertake the path of holiness. They begin the road of virtue without reaching the destination so that they may show those who will reach it how to walk. [Note: Laudunensis: “those who will not persevere.”]

Their fall also serves, with no small benefit, the progress of the elect, because when the elect see their lapse, they tremble for their own standing; and the ruin that condemns the former humbles the latter. They learn to trust in the protection of heavenly assistance when they see many fall through reliance on their own strength.

When the reprobate appear to act well, they show a level path, as it were, to the elect who follow. When they fall into the collapse of wickedness, they show the elect proceeding behind them a pit of pride to be avoided.

This Leviathan, then, subjects the rays of the sun to himself and makes gold subject like mud. Almighty God knows how to use the evil of the reprobate for the consolation of his elect, since those who will reach him both advance toward him through their own merits and are often corrected by the falls of others in the very things they understand proudly.

But if this Leviathan does these things even to those whom some virtue displays as illustrious, what will he do to those whose minds have not been lifted, even in part, above earthly desires? [Note: Pratelensis and two German manuscripts read: “which nevertheless …”] Divine speech openly describes them when it continues:

CAPUT XVI [Rec. XIV]

[Col. 0736A]

VERSE 22.—“He will make the deep sea boil like a pot.”

31. In the final persecution the wrath of the reprobate will boil against the saints.—What is signified by the sea except the life of secular people, and by the deep except their lofty and hidden thoughts? This Leviathan makes that deep sea boil like a pot, because it is clear that, at the time of the final persecution, he strives to rouse the minds of the reprobate against the life of the elect through the flame of cruelty.

Then the deep sea boils like a pot when he sets the hearts of those who love the world ablaze with a powerful heat. What lay hidden, enclosed within their malice during this time of peace, then boils over into the heat of the most savage persecution and, through the unrestrained license of open cruelty, exhales the hatred of ancient resentment that they had long suppressed. [Note: The printed editions read “when he inflames the hearts of the reprobate”; our reading, “when he inflames the hearts of those who love the world,” is that of two German manuscripts, Vindobonensis, Laudunensis, Ebroicensis, Gemeticensis, other Norman manuscripts, and Vallicellianus.]

Since, however, persuaded by a pestilential error, they serve Antichrist in these matters in such a way that they then believe they are rendering more genuine service to Christ, after he has said, “He will make the deep sea boil like a pot,” he aptly adds:

CAPUT XXVII [Vet. XI]

IBID.—[Note: The Paris edition of 1495 and the Basel edition of 1514 read “it smells” instead of “he will place,” but “he will place” is found in all our manuscripts, as in the Vulgate, to which the Hebrew text corresponds.] “He will place it as when ointments boil.”

32. Those who will fight for Antichrist against the saints will believe that they are offering service to God.—When ointments boil, they give off a fragrant sweetness. Thus this Leviathan will deceive the hearts of the reprobate, so that whatever they do out of the wickedness of unbelief, they suppose they are doing for the truth of right faith; what they exercise in religious zeal therefore seems to smell good to them.

Hence Truth says to the disciples in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). [Note: Gemeticensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus read: “the hour comes, when everyone …”; Vallicellianus reads: “will think that he is rendering service.”] Thus they boil like a pot while they persecute cruelly; but to them that persecution itself smells like the fragrance of ointments, since their minds, deceived by vain suspicions, believe that they are rendering service to God.

In Holy Scripture, the opinion of virtues is commonly signified by the fragrances of ointments. Hence the bride, desiring the bridegroom, says in the Song of Songs: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). And because the Apostle Paul knew himself to give off the fragrance of virtues, he says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

Since, therefore, this Leviathan ensnares the ministers of his lost vessel in works of cruelty under the appearance of praise and the pretext of virtue, after saying, “He will make the deep sea boil like a pot,” he rightly immediately adds: “He will place it as when ointments boil.”

What the sea boiling through the fire of cruelty signifies, the judgment of those who are stirred up—under the false name of virtue—as though ointments were boiling also reveals, so that they become all the more savage in cruelty the more they believe that they deserve rewards as though acting out of religious zeal.

It is just according to divine judgment that those who neglect to discern and preserve the force of piety should be deceived by the fragrance of their own suspicion. Hence, as an increase of their delusion, signs and wonders also follow them while they perpetrate cruelties, as is rightly added:

CAPUT XVIII [Vet. XII, Rec. XV]

VERSE 23.—“After him the path will shine.”

33. Antichrist’s path will shine with miracles.—The path is said to shine after Leviathan because wherever he passes, he leaves behind immense wonder through the splendor of his miracles. Whether he comes forth by himself or through his ministers, he flashes with deceptive signs.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel, in words we have often cited: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Mark 13:22). [Note: Laudunensis, two German manuscripts, and Vallicellianus read: “great signs.”] The path after Leviathan therefore shines because he illuminates the works of those whose hearts he penetrates with miracles, so that he may hold their minds all the more deeply in the darkness of error by displaying outwardly through them what appears to be a more powerful light of miracles.

There are, however, some who retain in their memory both the prophetic words and the Gospel commandments and know both that the signs he displays are false and that the true punishments to which he subsequently draws the deceived await them. [Note: Vallicellianus reads: “subsequently.”] Since this Leviathan does not ensnare their hearts through a display of holiness, he adapts himself to them through another deception.

For he sees that some know these things but nevertheless love the present life. He immediately diminishes in their minds the punishments to come, asserts that the judgments of strictness will one day end, and craftily drags the deceived toward present pleasures. Hence it is aptly added:

CAPUT XIX [Rec. XVI]

IBID.—“He will regard the abyss as growing old.”

34. The reprobate, led astray by the devil, do not believe in the eternity of punishments. Their false arguments are answered.—That eternal and incomprehensible judgments are accustomed to be designated by the name “abyss,” the Psalmist testifies, saying: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7). Old age, however, is sometimes used to signify the nearness of an end. Hence the Apostle says: “What is becoming obsolete and growing old is near to disappearing” (Heb. 8:13).

This Leviathan, then, will regard the abyss as growing old because he so stupefies the hearts of the reprobate that he instills in them the suspicion that the coming judgment, as though it were approaching its end, will one day cease. He thinks that the abyss grows old who supposes that heavenly punishment will at some point come to an end.

Thus this ancient persuader, in his members—that is, in the minds of the wicked—lightens the future punishments, which he marks out as though bounded by a definite end, so that he may extend their sins without end; and the more their sins do not end here, the more they suppose that the punishments of sinners will end there.

35. Even now there are people who neglect to put an end to their sins for this reason: they suppose that the future judgments imposed upon them will one day have an end. [Note: Gregory teaches the same thing, very fully, in Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 44; this thoroughly refutes the story that the Emperor Trajan was liberated through the prayers of Saint Gregory.]

We answer them briefly: If the punishments of the reprobate are eventually to end, then the joys of the blessed must also eventually end. Truth itself says: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46). If, therefore, what he threatened is not true, neither is what he promised true.

But they say: “He threatened sinners with eternal punishment in order to restrain them from committing sins, because he ought to threaten his creature with eternal punishments, not inflict them.”

We answer them more quickly: If he made a false threat in order to correct people from injustice, then he also made a false promise in order to encourage them to righteousness. Who could tolerate their madness? By asserting that the punishments of the reprobate will end, they also confuse by that assertion the rewards and recompense of the elect.

Who could tolerate their madness when they attempt to establish that what Truth threatened concerning eternal fire is not true, and, while striving to present God as merciful, do not fear to preach him as deceitful?

36. It is just that sinners should be consigned to eternal punishments.—But they say: “A fault that has an end should not be punished without end. Almighty God is just, and what was not committed as an eternal sin ought not to be punished with eternal torment.”

We answer them more quickly that they would speak rightly if the just and strict Judge, when he comes, weighed not the hearts of people but their deeds. The wicked sinned with an end because they lived with an end. For they would have wished to live without end so that they might have been able to remain in wickedness without end.

Indeed, they desire sin more than life; and for this reason they wish always to live here, so that, while they live, they may never cease to sin. It therefore belongs to the justice of the strict Judge that those should never be without punishment whose minds in this life never wished to be without sin. No limit of retribution should be granted to the wicked, because, as long as he had the power, he did not wish to have an end of crime.

[Vet. XIII.] 37. When the righteous see in the torments of the wicked what punishments they have escaped, they are moved to praise God.—But they say: “No just person feeds on cruelty, and a delinquent servant is ordered by a just master to be beaten for this reason: so that he may be corrected from wickedness. He is therefore beaten for a purpose, since his master does not delight in his tortures. But to what end will the wicked, handed over to the fires of Gehenna, burn forever? And since it is certain that the pious and almighty God does not feed on the torments of the wicked, why are the wretched tortured if they are not being purified?”

We answer them more quickly that almighty God, because he is pious, does not feed on the torment of the wretched; but because he is just, he is not forever appeased by the vengeance of the wicked.

All the wicked, then, are punished with eternal suffering, and indeed by their own wickedness; yet they are burned for a purpose—namely, so that all the righteous may see in God the joys they receive and look upon in these people the punishments they have escaped. Thus they may recognize themselves as debtors to divine grace for all eternity to a greater degree, the more eternally they see those evils punished which they were able to avoid through his assistance.

38. Why the saints no longer pray for their enemies condemned to Gehenna.—But they say: “Where, then, is their holiness, if they will not pray for their enemies whom they will then see burning, when they were expressly told: ‘Pray for your enemies’ (Matt. 5:44)?”

We answer them more quickly: They pray for their enemies at the time when they can turn their hearts toward fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies except what the Apostle says: “That God may grant them repentance, and they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Tim. 2:25–26)?

And how will anyone pray for them then, when they can in no way be changed from iniquity to works of righteousness? The reason why people condemned to eternal fire are not then prayed for is therefore the same reason why prayer is not now offered for the devil and his angels, who are assigned to eternal punishment.

It is also the reason why holy people do not pray for unbelieving and ungodly human beings who have died. They know that those people have been assigned to eternal punishment, and they refuse to have the merit of their prayer annulled before the presence of the just Judge.

If even now the righteous who are living do not in the least pity the dead and unjust who have been condemned, while they themselves know that they still endure in their flesh something subject to judgment, how much more strictly will they then regard the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every fault of corruption, they will themselves cleave more closely and firmly to righteousness?

For their minds will then be so absorbed by the force of severity through their adherence to the most just Judge that they will have no pleasure whatsoever in anything that departs from the subtlety of that inward rule.

But since, when an opportunity arose, we have spoken briefly against the Origenists, let us return to the order of exposition that we had left aside. [Note: Concerning these and other errors of the Origenists, and perhaps of Origen himself, consult the most illustrious and learned Daniel Huet, Book II of the Origeniana, chapter 16 and following. There he attempts to show not only that, according to Origen’s opinion, a measure and an end will eventually be imposed on the punishments of the condemned, but also that the devil himself will eventually attain repentance and salvation. There are nevertheless some who vindicate Origen from this monstrous error. Among his more recent defenders, read the learned Tillemont, Ecclesiastical History, vol. III, under Origen, article 19.] [Note: These words and what follows up to “and I will offer a holocaust commanded by God,” Book XXXV, formerly chapter 7, are missing from Vallicellianus.]

After the merciful Lord had disclosed the crafty machinations of this Leviathan, openly proclaiming everything that oppresses the elect outwardly with violence and everything that he pours inwardly into the reprobate through flattering suggestion, he immediately indicates briefly the monstrous character of his power and adds:

CAPUT XX [Vet. XIV, Rec. XVII]

VERSE 24.—“There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him.”

39. The devil, though he lost blessedness, retained the greatness of angelic nature.—His power is declared to surpass all others upon earth because, although he fell beneath human beings through the merit of his action, he nevertheless transcends the entire human race by the condition of angelic nature.

Although he lost the blessedness of inward happiness, he did not lose the greatness of his nature. By its remaining powers he still surpasses all human things, even though, through the abasement of their merits, he is subject to holy people.

For this reason, when those same holy people contend against him, the merit of their reward increases insofar as they conquer one who, by the power of his nature, boasts that he is, as it were by right, superior to human beings. It follows:

CAPUT XXI

IBID.—“He was made so that he would fear no one.”

### 40. The first angel was created in such a way that he should reverently fear God. The freedom he desired bound him.

By nature he was indeed created in such a way that he ought to have feared his Creator chastely—that is, with a sober and secure fear; not with the fear that charity casts out, but with the fear that remains for ever and ever (1 John 4:18), that is, the fear which charity produces.

[Note: Gemetensis, two German manuscripts, and Laudensis: “with secure fear, not fear.”] For a loving wife fears her husband in one way, and a sinful maidservant fears her master in another. Thus, then, he had been created so that, with joyful fear, he would both love and fear his Maker, and both fear and love him.

But by his own perversity he became such that he feared no one. He disdained to be subject to the one by whom he had been created. For God is above all things in such a way that he himself is subject to no one. But this Leviathan, looking upon the summit of his exaltation, desired the right of perverse freedom, so that he might rule over the others and be subject to no one, saying:

[Note: Gemetensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “he perversely desired his freedom, so that …”] “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). He lost that likeness precisely by desiring arrogantly to be like him in exaltation. For he ought to have imitated his charity; instead, though subject, he sought his exaltation, and in his pride lost what he could have imitated.

He would indeed have been exalted if he had wished to cling to the one who is truly exalted. He would have been exalted if he had been content with participation in true exaltation. But while he arrogantly desired a private exaltation, he rightly lost the exaltation he had by participation. For, abandoning the Principle to whom he ought to have clung, he sought in some way to be his own principle. Abandoning the one who could truly have been sufficient for him, he judged that he could be sufficient for himself; and the more he raised himself against the glory of his Creator, the more deeply he fell beneath himself.

For the free service that exalted him was overthrown by captive freedom. By this freedom he is now driven to fear no one, yet by that very unbridledness he is gravely restrained. For, since the heavenly judgment orders all things wondrously, the freedom he desired has bound him: now, fearing no one at all, he is subject to every punishment, although he could have been superior even to the elements if he had wished to fear the one whom he ought to have feared.

[Note: Vindocensis reads *junxit*, “joined” or “bound.”]

[Note: Laudensis: “not fearing, he could even have been superior”; Corbeiensis Germanicus: “which he now.”]

He would certainly have feared one while possessing all things; now, not fearing that one, he suffers all things.

### 41. He lost the fear of God, to his own great loss.

He was therefore made such that he feared no one—no one, that is, because he feared neither God nor even what he was going to suffer. It would have been happier for him to avoid punishments by fearing than to endure them by not fearing.

Thus he turned his desire for exaltation into hardness of mind, so that he no longer perceived, through his hardness, that he had done evil, although he had sought to rule through glory. For, since he did not obtain the right of the power he had sought, he found, as it were, a remedy for his pride in the madness of insensibility; and because he could not surpass all things by advancement, he prepared himself against all things through contempt.

[Note: Vindocensis, Turonensis, the German manuscripts, and the Norman manuscripts: “that he was ill situated”; Longipontanus: “that it was ill with him”; Corbeiensis Germanicus: “into security of mind … so that … to be similar,” instead of “to have done evil.”]

[Old recension XV.] His pride is further carefully described when it immediately continues:

### CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 25.**—“He beholds every lofty thing.”

### 42. The immense pride of the devil and his members. Saul rejected because of his arrogance; David’s humility in the highest dignity.

That is, he looks upon all as though they were placed beneath him, as if from a lofty position, because, while he strives with his intention against the Creator, he disdains to consider anyone his equal. This also appropriately applies to his members, because all the wicked, raised up by the swelling of their hearts, look down with proud disdain upon everyone they see. Even if at times they show outward reverence, inwardly, in the secret of their hearts—where, in their own estimation, they are great—they place everyone’s life and merit beneath themselves, and look upon them as inferior, because by their exalted thought they have set themselves on the summit of a certain height.

To such people the prophet rightly says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). Hence Paul also says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Romans 12:16). Hence, by divine rebuke, it is said to Saul: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17). For he is little in his own eyes who, when he considers himself, judges himself inferior to the merits of others. But whoever stretches himself above the merits of others by the exaltation of his thoughts looks upon himself as great.

Saul, however, did not persevere in the good with which he had begun, because he swelled with pride at the power he had received.

[Old recension XVI.] In contrast, David, always thinking humbly of himself and placing himself beneath Saul in comparison with him, after finding an opportunity to strike and sparing that raging enemy, prostrated himself in humble confession, saying: “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog and a single flea” (1 Samuel 24:15).

And certainly he had already been anointed king; Samuel had already interceded for him and poured oil over him from the horn, and he had learned that divine grace, after Saul’s rejection, was preserving him to possess the governance of the kingdom. Yet he humbly submitted in mind to the enemy who was pursuing him, even though he knew by divine judgment that he had been placed above him. He therefore humbly placed himself beneath the one whom he knew himself to be incomparably better than by the grace of election.

Let those who do not yet know what position they hold before God learn how they ought to humble themselves before their neighbors, if even the elect humble themselves before those whom they already discover, through inward judgments, to have been placed beneath them.

[Note: Two German manuscripts, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts: “they humble themselves before them.”]

[Note: The reading *interpositos* in the Vatican and Gilot editions is erroneous. Jamezius had already corrected this passage from English manuscripts; Turonensis and other French manuscripts agree with them.]

### 43. Humility is characteristic of the elect.

This is ordinarily the distinctive mark of the elect: they always think of themselves as lower than they are. Thus David himself says: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul” (Psalm 130:2).

[Note: Laudensis and the German manuscripts: “if I exalted.”]

Hence Solomon calls the little ones to wisdom, saying: “If anyone is little, let him come to me” (Proverbs 9:4). For whoever does not yet despise himself does not grasp the humble wisdom of God.

Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:25). Again the Psalmist says: “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Psalm 114:6). Hence the teacher of the nations says: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

[Note: Laudensis, Gemetensis, and two German manuscripts: “in your midst.”]

Admonishing his disciples, he says: “Considering one another superior to yourselves” (Philippians 2:3). For because every wicked person, in his pride, considers every person whom he knows inferior to himself, the just person, by contrast, strives to regard every neighbor as superior.

And lest, while one person humbles himself before another, the former’s humility should become an occasion of exaltation to the latter, he wisely admonished both sides, saying: “Considering one another superior to yourselves”: so that in the thoughts of the heart I may prefer him to myself, and he in turn may prefer me to himself; and when the heart is pressed down from both sides, no one may be lifted up by the honor bestowed.

[Note: Turonensis, Laudensis, Longipontanus, the Norman manuscripts, and two German manuscripts: “lest one should go into exaltation.”]

### 44. The wicked do not maintain this form of humility but despise it.

But the wicked, because they are members of this Leviathan, scorn either to recognize or to maintain this form of humility, because even when they sometimes appear humble in outward appearance, they neglect to preserve the force of humility inwardly.

It often happens to them that, whenever they do some good thing, however small, they immediately turn the attention of their mind away from all their evils and constantly contemplate with complete concentration the good, however insignificant, that they have done. From this they already regard themselves as almost holy, forgetting all the evils they have committed and remembering only that one good of theirs—which perhaps they were not even able to perform perfectly.

The opposite commonly happens to the elect: though they possess the grace of many virtues, they are sorely afflicted by some very slight vice, which greatly wears them down. Thus, while they recognize that they are weakened in one respect, they do not exalt themselves at all in those virtues in which they are strong; and while they tremble because of their weakness, they preserve even their strength with greater humility.

Thus the wicked, because they carelessly contemplate their one, perhaps very small, good deed, fail to recognize the many serious evils in which they are submerged. The elect, however, because they fear being weakened by their slightest evil, are wondrously disposed not to lose the great goods to which they have advanced.

[Note: Gemetensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “being weakened.”]

### 45. Evils help the elect, while goods harm the wicked. The wicked use good badly, while the good use evil well.

[Note: Laudensis: “Thus he disposes the just …”]

The righteous and the reprobate, therefore, are ordered by the measure of a hidden judgment, so that evils help the former and goods burden the latter: the former use slight evils for the advancement of good, while the latter use the smallest goods for the increase of evil.

The former make more perfect progress in good precisely where they are tested by evil; the latter fall into greater evil precisely where they boast of good. Thus the wicked use good badly, while the good use evil well.

It often happens that one person contracts the disease of sickness from wholesome food taken without restraint, while another, using a serpent’s poison as an ingredient in a properly prepared medicine, overcomes the affliction of sickness. The one who did not know how to use wholesome food properly dies disastrously from what enables another to live healthily; while the one who carefully knew how to use serpent’s poison lives healthily from what causes others to die disastrously.

We therefore call the serpent’s poison not wickedness itself, but the suggestion of wickedness by which we are often tempted unwillingly and while resisting.

[Note: Gemetensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “always.”]

This is turned into medicine when the mind, raised up by the sight of its virtues, is humbled by the temptations directed against it.

The wicked, therefore, rejected by the approval of the inward judgment, whatever works they may perform and whatever virtues they may display, are wholly ignorant of the sense of humility, because they are members of this Leviathan, of whom the heavenly voice says:

[New recension XVIII.] “He beholds every lofty thing.”

[Note: Pratelensis and other manuscripts: “for not only.”]

For he looks down upon everyone as if from a height, not only through himself but also through the hearts of those whom he has captured.

[Old recension XVII.] ### 46. Pride reveals itself through the eyes as through certain windows.

It should be noted that this Leviathan, who is signified by a bodily beast, is described as beholding what is lofty, because pride of heart, when it extends outward as far as the body, is first indicated through the eyes.

They, swollen as if by the arrogance of pride, look down as though from a height, and the more they bring others low, the more highly they exalt themselves. For unless pride revealed itself through the eyes as through certain windows, the Psalmist would never have said to God: “You will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud” (Psalm 17:28).

Unless pride poured itself forth through the eyes, Solomon would not have said concerning the arrogance of Judea: “There is a generation whose eyes are lofty and whose eyelids are lifted up” (Proverbs 30:13).

Because, then, this Leviathan is signified by a bodily animal, and pride, coming forth as far as the body, openly rules through the eyes, the ancient enemy is described as seeing everyone as if from a height.

But since much has been brought forward to reveal the enemy of the human race, the mind greatly desires that, at the end of the divine discourse, one thing be expressed more clearly, by which his members may be shown to us in a brief designation. It follows:

### CHAPTER XXIII

**THE SAME.**—“He himself is king over all the sons of pride.”

### 47. Pride is the root of all vices and evils.

Pride alone struck down this Leviathan, so that he fell into all that has been said above. For he would not wither through so many branches of vices unless he had first rotted at the root through this one. It is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15).

Through pride he himself fell; through pride he cast down the human being who followed him. For he attacked the salvation of our immortality with the weapon by which he extinguished the life of his own blessedness.

But the Lord inserted pride at the end of his discourse so that, when after all the evils he spoke of this Leviathan’s pride, he might show what is worse than all evils. Yet by placing it at the bottom he also shows that it is the root of vices. Just as a root is hidden below while branches spread outward from it, so pride conceals itself within, but from it open vices immediately sprout.

No evils would emerge publicly unless pride secretly bound the mind. It makes the mind of this Leviathan boil like a cauldron. Hence it shakes human minds in a certain fervor of madness, but through open deeds it shows how the soul that has been shaken is overturned. For inwardly there first boils in elation what later foams outwardly in action.

[Old recension XVIII.] ### 48. Pride attacks not merely one virtue, as other vices do, but all of them.

Since occasion has been given for discussing pride, we must examine it more subtly and carefully, and demonstrate how great and of what kind it comes to human minds, and in what ways and by what means it steals upon them.

Other vices attack only those virtues by which they themselves are destroyed: anger fights against patience, gluttony against abstinence, and lust against continence. But pride, which we have called the root of vices, is by no means content with the destruction of one virtue. It rises against every member of the soul and, like a general and deadly disease, corrupts the whole body, so that whatever is done while it has taken possession—even if it appears to be a virtue—is performed not for God but only for empty glory.

For pride seizes an occupied city, as it were, like a tyrant, when it breaks into the mind; and the richer the person it captures, the more harshly it rises in domination. The more extensively a virtuous deed is performed without humility, the more broadly pride exercises its rule.

Whoever receives its tyranny within himself with a captive mind first suffers this injury: with the eye of the heart closed, he loses the fairness of judgment. [Note: We have added *vel* (“even”), from the Norman manuscripts and two German manuscripts; it adds both elegance and force to the sentence.]

Everything even done well by others displeases him, while only what he himself has done, even wrongly, pleases him. He always despises the works of others and always admires what he himself does, because he believes that whatever he has done, he alone has done it.

In what he displays, through desire for glory, he favors himself in his own thoughts; and when he believes that he surpasses everyone in all things, he walks about with himself through the broad spaces of his thoughts and silently cries out his own praises.

Sometimes the mind is led to such great exaltation that, in what swells it up, it is also driven into unrestrained speech by ostentation.

[Note: The Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville editions read “in what he fears.” The passage has been corrected from the English, Norman, Vindocensis, two German, and Longipontanus manuscripts, as well as from an old edition.]

But the more shamelessly a person exalts himself in his own estimation, the more easily ruin follows. Hence it is written: “The heart is exalted before ruin” (Daniel 4:26). Hence Daniel says:

“The king was walking in the court of Babylon, and he answered and said: ‘Is this not Babylon the great, which I have built as a royal house by the strength of my power and in the glory of my splendor?’” (Proverbs 16:18).

[Note: Laudensis: “and in glory.”]

But he immediately added how swiftly vengeance suppressed this swelling, saying:

“While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: The kingdom will pass from you, and they will drive you out from among human beings; your dwelling will be with beasts and wild animals; you will eat grass like an ox, and seven times will pass over you’” (Daniel 4:28).

Behold: because the swelling of his mind had extended as far as open words, the patience of the Judge immediately erupted into sentence; and he struck him more severely the more immoderately his pride had raised itself. And because he had enumerated the good things in which he pleased himself, he heard the evils enumerated by which he would be struck.

[Note: Pratelensis and Uticensis: “having enumerated the evils also.” The addition contributes some elegance to the wording.]

[Old recension XIX.] ### 49. Some exaltation arises from worldly things, and some from spiritual things. The pride of rulers differs from that of subjects; humility is the mother of virtues. What the proud build grows only toward ruin.

It must be understood that this very exaltation of which we are speaking possesses some people through worldly things and others through spiritual things. One swells with gold, another with eloquence; one with low and earthly matters, another with the highest and heavenly virtues. Yet before the eyes of God it is one and the same thing, although, when it comes to human hearts, it disguises itself before them under different clothing.

When someone who previously grew proud of earthly glory later becomes exalted because of holiness, exaltation has by no means left his heart. Rather, coming to him in its customary way, it has changed its clothing so that it cannot be recognized.

### 50. This temptation attacks superiors in one way and subjects in another.

It suggests to a superior in his thoughts that he has risen above others solely through the merit of his life. If he has ever done anything good, it thrusts this insistently before his mind. When it insinuates that he has pleased God in a singular way, it calls upon the reward of the authority entrusted to him as testimony to strengthen its persuasion, saying: “Unless almighty God saw that you were better than these people, he would not have placed them all under your rule.”

It then immediately elevates his mind and shows those under him to be worthless and useless, so that he no longer regards anyone as worthy to whom he might speak with equanimity. Hence the tranquility of his mind is soon turned into anger: while he despises everyone and censures the sense and life of all without restraint, he expands into anger all the more violently because he considers those entrusted to him unworthy of himself.

[Old recension XX.] ### 51. In contrast, when pride incites the heart of subjects, it strives above all to make them completely neglect consideration of their own actions and to become, in silent thoughts, perpetual judges of their ruler. While they insistently observe in him what they ought to criticize, they never see in themselves what they ought to correct.

Thus they perish more atrociously because they turn their eyes away from themselves. On the road of this life they stumble and fall while looking elsewhere.

They indeed assert that they are sinners, yet they do not consider themselves so sinful that they deserved to be placed under such a harmful person in authority.

[Note: A German manuscript adds: “they consider this only after they have been handed over.” The Norman and Vindocensis manuscripts read: “deserved to be handed over.”]

While they despise his actions and scorn his commands, they descend into such madness that they do not believe God takes care of human affairs, because they are distressed that they have been entrusted to one whom they think they may rightly criticize.

Thus, while they grow proud against their ruler, they also swell against the judgments of their Creator; and while they judge the life of their shepherd, they attack the wisdom of the one who orders all things.

Often they insolently oppose the words of their ruler and call the same pride of speech freedom. Thus exaltation presents itself as though in defense of the righteousness of freedom, just as fear often substitutes itself for humility. For just as many are silent out of fear but think they are being silent out of humility, so some speak through the impatience of pride but believe they are speaking through the freedom of righteousness.

At other times subjects do not reveal at all the insolent thoughts they have. Those whose talkativeness can scarcely be restrained sometimes become silent solely because of the bitterness of inward resentment. Withholding the words of their insolence through mental anguish, they remain silent worse than they usually speak, because when they hear something said for their correction, they indignantly suppress even the words of a reply.

When they are dealt with harshly, they often break out into complaints about that very harshness. But when their teachers approach them gently, they become even more indignant at the very humility with which they have been approached, and their minds are inflamed more widely the more carefully their weakness is judged.

[Note: Turonensis, Vindocensis, Laudensis: “is judged to be weakened.”]

These people, plainly, because they do not know humility—the mother of virtues—lose the benefit of their labor, even if they appear to perform some good deeds. The strong height of a rising structure is not fixed when it is not solidified by the strength of a foundation upon rock.

[Note: Vindocensis: “betray the use of their labor.”]

What they build therefore grows only toward ruin, because they do not first provide the foundations of humility beneath the mass of the structure. We can rightly expose them from within if we show them outwardly in a few words.

### 52. The image of a proud person.

In all who swell inwardly with proud thought there is shouting in speech, bitterness in silence, dissolution in cheerfulness, fury in sadness,

[Note: Laudensis adds “indecency in appearance, uprightness.”]

dishonesty in action, propriety in appearance, stiffness in gait, and rancor in response.

Their mind is always strong for inflicting insults but weak for enduring them; sluggish in obeying, yet importunate in provoking others; lazy in doing what they both ought to do and are capable of doing, yet ready for what they neither ought to do nor are capable of doing.

[Note: Vindocensis and the Norman manuscripts: “always ready.”]

In what it does not desire spontaneously, this mind is bent by no exhortation; but toward what it secretly desires, it seeks to be compelled. For, fearing that it might become contemptible because of its desire, it wishes to endure force against its own will.

[Old recension XXI.] ### 53. An exhortation to humility.

Since we have said that human minds are tempted in one way by carnal matters and in another by spiritual matters, let the former hear: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

Let the latter also hear what is said after miracles to some people: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27).

[Note: Gemetensis and Corbeiensis Germanicus: “to certain people who performed miracles.”]

Let the former hear: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm 61:11). Let the latter hear that the foolish virgins, who come with empty vessels, are excluded from the inner wedding feast (Matthew 25:12).

Again, because we have said that rulers are tempted in one way and subjects in another, let the former hear what is said through a certain wise man: “They have appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclesiasticus 32:1).

Let the latter hear: “Obey your superiors and be subject to them; for they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls” (Hebrews 13:17).

Let the former, when they glory in the authority they have received, hear what is said in Abraham’s words to the rich man in the flames: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime” (Luke 16:25).

Let the latter, when they break out in complaints against their rulers, hear what is answered through Moses and Aaron to the murmuring people: “Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord. For what are we?” (Exodus 16:8).

Let the former hear: “They will be shaken in the sight of the father of orphans and in the judgments of widows” (Psalm 67:5).

[Note: In the German manuscripts and in both old and recent editions: “fathers … and judges.” This reading has no basis either in the Vulgate or in the Hebrew text. Vindocensis, Pratelensis, and Uticensis read: “of the father … and of the judge.”]

Let the latter hear what is said against the stubbornness of subjects: “Whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Romans 13:2).

Let all hear together: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

Let all hear: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God” (Proverbs 16:5, according to the Hebrew text and the Septuagint).

Let all hear: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclesiasticus 10:9).

[Note: Vindocensis and two German manuscripts: “What is proud?”]

Against this disease, let us all hear what the teacher Truth teaches, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

[Old recension XXII.] ### 54. God, who is humble, teaches that a human being must not be proud.

For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our weakness; for this reason the Invisible appeared not only visible but even despised; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the disgrace of ridicule, and the tortures of suffering: so that the humble God might teach human beings not to be proud.

What, then, is the greatness of the virtue of humility, for the sake of teaching which alone the one who is immeasurably great became small even unto suffering?

Because the pride of the devil provided the beginning of our destruction,

[Note: Laudensis, Pratelensis, Gemetensis, two German manuscripts, and the old Paris and Bartholomew editions: “pride offered itself as the origin of our destruction.”]

the humility of God was found to be the instrument of our redemption. Our enemy, great among all created things, wished in his pride to appear above all things. But our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become small among all things.

[Note: This manner of expression was familiar to Gregory; see above, book 15, no. 20; book 16, no. 36; book 30, nos. 68–69.]

### 55. What the author of death teaches, and what the Creator of life teaches.

But we can better expose the cause of exaltation and disclose the foundations of humility if we briefly recall what the author of death says and what the Creator of life says.

The former says: “I will ascend into heaven” (Isaiah 14:13). The latter says through the Prophet: “My soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to the underworld” (Psalm 87:4).

The former says: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven” (Isaiah 16:13). The latter says to the human race, expelled from the seats of paradise: “Behold, I come quickly, and I will dwell in your midst” (Zechariah 2:10).

[Note: Vindocensis and Pratelensis: “Behold, I come and dwell.”]

The former says: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13). The latter says: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:7).

The former says: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14). The latter, though he was in the form of God, “did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7); and through his members he says: “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 34:10).

The former speaks through his members, saying: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not release Israel” (Exodus 5:2).

[Note: Pratelensis: “I will not let go.”]

The latter says through himself: “If I should say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar; but I do know him, and I keep his word” (John 8:55).

The former says: “My rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezekiel 29:9). The latter says: “I can do nothing from myself” (John 5:30), and again: “My Father, who dwells in me, himself does the works” (John 14:10).

The former, showing all the kingdoms, says: “I will give you authority over all these and their glory, because they have been delivered to me, and I give them to whomever I wish” (Luke 4:6). The latter says: “You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or left is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matthew 20:23).

The former says: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). The latter says: “It is not yours to know times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7).

The former, so that the divine will might be despised and his own will might be urged, says: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” (Genesis 3:1). And shortly afterward: “For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:5).

The latter says: “I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30).

The former speaks through his members, saying: “Let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; everywhere let us leave signs of our joy” (Wisdom 2:8).

The latter announces through his members: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John 16:20).

The former teaches the minds subject to him nothing other than to seek the summit of exaltation, to surpass everything equal through swelling of mind, to pass beyond the fellowship of all human beings in lofty pride, and to raise themselves even against the power of their Creator. Concerning such people the Psalmist says: “They have passed into the disposition of their heart; they have thought and spoken wickedness; they have spoken iniquity on high” (Psalm 72:6–8).

The latter, coming to spittle, blows, slaps, a crown of thorns, the cross, the lance, and death, admonishes his members, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26).

[Old recension XXIII.] ### 56. Pride is the clearest sign of rejection; humility, of election.

Since our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble, while this Leviathan is called king over the proud, we clearly recognize that pride is the most evident sign of the rejected, whereas humility is the sign of the elect.

When it becomes known what each person possesses, it is discovered under which king he serves. Each person bears, as it were, a title of his work by which he easily shows under whose ruling power he serves. Hence it is said through the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16).

Therefore, lest the members of this Leviathan deceive us by performing miracles, the Lord showed the evident sign by which they may be detected, saying: “He himself is king over all the sons of pride.”

Even when they sometimes assume a feigned appearance of humility, they cannot in any way conceal themselves completely, because their pride, unable to remain hidden for long, is exposed in one action when it is covered in another.

But those who serve under the king of humility are always fearful and watchful on every side. They fight against the arrows of exaltation and, as though against blows coming at them, chiefly guard the eye in their own body, while they especially protect humility within themselves.

### BOOK THIRTY-FIVE, AND THE LAST

In it many things already said are recalled by recapitulation, and this immense work is brought to completion through the most abject confession of human weakness.

[Col. 0749]

[Old and new recensions I.] ### 1. What is to be done in this book.

Because this is the last book of the present work, and because, after the more difficult passages have been treated, what remains is less obscure, I am pleased to pass through it with greater indulgence and relaxation.

For, as though we had traversed a great sea, we can now see the shore. Lowering the sails of our attention, we are no longer carried with the same force as before, yet we still proceed under the impulse of the former wind.

[Note: Vindocensis, Pratelensis, Uticensis, and two German manuscripts: “as if.”]

The wind of our anxiety has fallen, as it were, but its force, now calmer in itself, still drives us toward the station of the shore.

Therefore, after the Lord had shown his faithful servant how strong and cunning his enemy Leviathan is, subtly exposing his powers and his deceptions, blessed Job answered both points, saying:

### CHAPTER I [New recension II]

**CHAPTER 42, VERSE 2.**—“I know that you can do all things, and no thought is hidden from you.”

[Col. 0750C] ### 2. God’s omnipotence is set against the devil’s powers, and infinite Wisdom against his schemes.

Against his savage powers Job brought forward: “I know that you can do all things.” Against his hidden schemes he added: “And no thought is hidden from you.”

Hence Leviathan immediately reproaches him, saying:

**VERSE 3.**—“Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?”

For Leviathan hides counsel without knowledge, because although he conceals it by many deceptions against our weakness, he is revealed to us by the holy inspiration of our Protector.

[Note: The same manuscript and Vindocensis: “without wisdom.”]

He hides counsel without knowledge because, although the tempter remains hidden from those who are tempted, the Protector of those who are tempted cannot be hidden from him.

Therefore, after hearing of the devil’s strength and cunning, and also hearing of the power of our Creator, who both restrains him mightily and mercifully shields us, we ask you, blessed Job, not to conceal from us at all what you think about yourself. It follows:

### CHAPTER II

**THE SAME.**—“Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge beyond measure.”
