### 3. Whatever in created things is compared with God becomes empty and nothing.---

All human wisdom, however great its sharpness, is folly when compared with divine wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0751D] In the Basel edition of 1514 and the Gilot and Vatican editions, *comparata nec pulchra nec justa, sed insipientia est* is read: “when compared with it, it is neither beautiful nor just, but folly.” None of our manuscript codices has this reading.] For all human things—whatever is just and whatever is beautiful—when compared with God’s justice and beauty are neither just nor beautiful, and in fact are nothing. Blessed Job, therefore, would have believed that he had spoken wisely in what he had said, had he not heard the words of the higher Wisdom. In comparison with it, everything in us that possesses any semblance of wisdom is foolish. And the man who had spoken wisely to human beings recognizes, upon hearing divine judgments, that he is not wise in the truest sense.

This is why Abraham, amid the words of the Lord, saw himself as nothing but dust, saying: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27). This is why Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, after hearing the Lord speak, discovered that he was slow and impeded in speech, saying: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent; for from yesterday and the day before, from the time when you spoke to your servant, I have been slow and impeded in speech” (Exodus 4:10). This is why Isaiah, after seeing the Lord seated upon a lofty and exalted throne, after seeing the seraphim cover their faces with two wings, their feet with two, and fly with two, and after hearing one cry out to the other, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6), returning to himself, said: “Woe is me, for I was silent, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips” (ibid., 5). Immediately adding how he had recognized that uncleanness, he said: “And I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes” (ibid.).

This is also why Jeremiah, hearing the divine words, recognized that he had no words, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jeremiah 1:6). [Old II.] This is why Ezekiel, speaking of the four living creatures, says: “When there was a voice above the firmament that was above their heads, they stood and lowered their wings” (Ezekiel 1:25). For what is signified by the flight of the living creatures except the sublimity of evangelists and teachers? Or what are the wings of the living creatures except the contemplations of the saints, lifting them toward heavenly things? [Note: [Col. 0751D] Vindobonensis and the Norman manuscripts read *sublimantes*, “raising on high.”] But when a voice comes above the firmament that is over their heads, they stand and lower their wings, because when they hear the inward voice of heavenly wisdom, they lay down, as it were, the wings of their flight, since they recognize that they are less able to contemplate the very height of truth.

To lower the wings at the voice that comes from above is therefore, once heavenly power has been recognized, to humble one’s own virtues and, in contemplating the Creator, to regard oneself as nothing but lowly. Thus holy men, when they hear the judgments of divinity, recognize that the more they advance in contemplation, the more they despise what they are and understand themselves to be either nothing or almost nothing. [Note: [Col. 0751D] Laudensis, two German manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, Vindobonensis, and others, as read by Gussanville, have *divinitatis sententias*—“judgments of divinity”—although the old and recent editions read *arcana*—“secrets.”]

Let blessed Job therefore respond to the divine words and, progressing wisely, discover that he is foolish, saying: “I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge beyond measure.” Behold, he reproves himself the more strongly the more he progresses, and believes that he has exceeded his knowledge beyond measure, because in the Lord’s words he has recognized more of the secrets of divine wisdom than he had imagined. It follows:

### CHAPTER III [Recension III]

**VERSE 4.**—“Hear, and I shall speak; I shall ask you, and you answer me.”

### 4. What it means for a human being to question God, and for God to answer a human being.---

For us, hearing means turning an ear placed elsewhere toward a sound that comes from outside. In God’s case, however, for whom nothing is external, hearing properly means perceiving the desires that rise up within us beneath himself. Thus, for God, who knows even the hearts of those who remain silent, our speaking does not mean expressing what we feel with the sounds of the throat, but longing for him with ready desires.

And since a person questions in order to learn what he does not know, for a human being to question God means recognizing, in his presence, that one is ignorant. For God to answer means instructing through hidden inspirations the one who has humbly recognized his own ignorance.

Blessed Job therefore says: “Hear, and I shall speak.” It is as though he were saying: “Mercifully perceive my desires, so that, while your kindness perceives and assists them, more numerous desires may rise toward you.” For good desires multiply whenever they receive fulfillment. Hence it is written elsewhere: “I cried out, because you heard me” (Psalm 16:6). He does not say, “Because I cried out, you heard me,” but, “I cried out, because you heard me.” He who had been heard while speaking cried out, having been heard as his desires advanced.

“I shall ask you, and you answer me.” It is as though he were saying: “From the contemplation of your knowledge I recognize that I am ignorant. Answer me, then, as I question you—that is, teach me as I humbly acknowledge my own folly.” That he would question from a desire for humility and would seek God’s answer through the instruction of inspiration is made clear by the words that follow. He declares that he will question, but adds nothing in the form of a question. For, sensing only humility concerning himself and acknowledging what he had mercifully received from the Lord, he immediately adds:

### CHAPTER IV [Recension IV]

**VERSE 5.**—“With the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you.”

### 5. How greatly Job advanced through chastisements in knowledge of God and of himself.---

By these words he plainly indicates that, just as sight is superior to hearing, so what he was formerly differs from that to which he afterward advanced through the chastisements. Because he had seen the light of truth more clearly with the inward eye, he discerned more fully the darkness of his humanity. Hence it follows:

### CHAPTER V [Recension V]

**VERSE 6.**—“Therefore I reproach myself.”

### 6. The more each person sees himself, the more displeasing he becomes to himself.---

The less anyone sees himself, the less displeasing he is to himself; and the more he perceives the light of greater grace, the more he recognizes himself as blameworthy. For when he is inwardly lifted up through all that he is, he strives to conform to the rule that he sees above himself. And because human weakness still hinders him, he perceives that he differs from it in no small degree; everything in himself that does not correspond to the inward rule is burdensome to him.

Blessed Job, advancing after the chastisements, embraces this rule more fully [Note: [Col. 0753D] Turonensis, Laudensis, two German manuscripts: *inspicit*, “considers.”] and dissents from himself in a great reproach of himself, saying: “Therefore I reproach myself.” But since there is no genuine knowledge of reproach unless the laments of repentance also follow, repentance is rightly added after reproach:

### CHAPTER VI

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“And I do penance in dust and ashes.”

### 7. Knowledge of oneself is vain if repentance does not follow. What should be understood by repentance in sackcloth and ashes.---

To do penance in dust and ashes is, after contemplating the highest Being, to recognize oneself as nothing other than dust and ashes. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel to the condemned city: “If the miracles that have been performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21). In sackcloth, harshness [Note: [Col. 0753D] Gemetensis and most Norman manuscripts read *et punctio*, “and piercing,” together with Laudensis and two German manuscripts; the editions have *et compunctio*, “and compunction.”] and the piercing of sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead. For this reason both are customarily applied to repentance, so that in the piercing of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the ashes of dust may consider what we have become through judgment.

Let the vices that pierce be considered in sackcloth; let the just punishment of the vices that follows by the sentence of death be considered in ashes. Since after the sin of the flesh affronts arose, let a person see in the harshness of sackcloth what he did through pride; let him see in the ashes how far he reached by sinning. Sackcloth can also signify the piercing of grief through remembrance and repentance. For when blessed Job says, “I reproach myself,” he is pierced, as it were, by sackcloth, as he is rubbed by the harsh goads of reproach in his mind.

He does penance in ashes because he carefully considers what he became through the just judgment following the first sin, saying: “I do penance in dust and ashes.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “I do not grow proud of any gift of my Creator, because, having been taken from dust, I recognize that, through the sentence of death inflicted upon me, I must return to dust.”

[Old III.] ### 8. God’s judgment concerning Job and his friends.---

After hearing all Job’s speeches and learning the answers of his friends, we are inclined to turn the gaze of our mind toward the judgment of the inward Judge [Note: [Col. 0753D] Vindobonensis, Pratellensis, and Uticensis read *inspectionem*, “inspection”; the German manuscript reads *exspectationem*, “expectation.”] and say to him: “Behold, Lord, we have heard both parties arguing in your presence. We have learned that Job recalled the deeds of his virtue in this contest, while his friends defended the glory of your justice against him. Yet amid these things you know what our mind thinks. For we cannot censure the words of those whom we recognize as serving the defense of your cause. [Note: [Col. 0754D] Corbeiensis Germanicus, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read: “But behold, the parties stand by and await the judgment,” and so forth.]

“But behold, the parties are present and await the verdict. Bring forth, therefore, Lord, from your invisible rule the most subtle examination of your discernment, and show who has spoken more rightly in this dispute.” It follows:

**VERSE.**—“After the Lord had spoken these words to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite: My wrath is kindled against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken what is right before me, as my servant Job has.”

### 9. He is acquitted; they are condemned. Why?---

O Lord, the sentence of your judgment shows how much our blindness differs from the light of your righteousness. Behold, with you as judge, we recognize blessed Job as victorious, though we had believed that he had sinned against you in speaking. With you as judge, those who believed that they surpassed blessed Job’s merits by speaking on your behalf have been condemned.

Since we have learned from the divine sentence what we should think of the two parties, let us now weigh the words of that same sentence somewhat more subtly. How, then, is blessed Job reproved above, if, in comparison with his righteousness, his friends are said not to have spoken rightly before the Lord? Is that earlier sentence still being confirmed, in which the ancient enemy is told: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth” (Job 1:8)?

But what does it mean that he is both praised to the enemy and reproved in himself, and is reproved in himself yet nevertheless preferred to his speaking friends? It means that the holy man surpassed everyone by the virtue of his merits, but that, precisely because he was human, he could not be without reproach before God’s eyes. In a holy person who is still dwelling in this present life, the rule of divine examination still has something to judge, even though, by comparison with other human beings, it already has something to praise.

Blessed Job therefore believed that he was being chastised for guilt, not for grace; he thought that vices were being cut away from him, not that his merits were being increased. He is reproved because he suspects that the chastisement had another purpose, and yet, when opposed by his friends, he is preferred by the definition of the inward judgment.

[Old IV.] From this it is plainly gathered how great his righteousness was: in opposition to his friends’ words, he asserted the innocence of his conduct, and by divine judgment he was preferred even to those who were defending that same divine judgment.

At the beginning of this commentary [Note: [Col. 0754D] This refers not to Book XXXV, but to the whole commentary, where this text is explained in Book III, section 15.] we learned that Satan had said of him to the Lord: “Stretch out your hand, touch him, and see whether he will not bless you to your face” (Job 2:5). In response to this request, blessed Job was permitted to be touched by losses, bereavement, wounds, and the scandals of words [Note: [Col. 0754D] Laudensis reads *verberum*, “of blows.”], because the one who had praised him was certain that the holy man would in no way, as the devil asserted, fall into the guilt of cursing.

As we also said above [Note: [Col. 0755D] Often, especially in the Preface, chapter 3, near the middle.], whoever thinks that blessed Job sinned in his speech after the chastisements plainly judges that the Lord failed in his assertion [Note: [Col. 0755D] The editions read: “had erred in his assertion.” We have followed the manuscripts Corbeiensis Germanicus, Vindobonensis, Laudensis, and the Norman manuscripts. In the German manuscript: “had exposed.”].

Although, when speaking to the devil, the Lord preferred Job’s present goodness, he did not guarantee his perseverance, it must nevertheless be understood that he would never, by allowing him to be tempted, have set his righteousness before the tempter [Note: [Col. 0755D] The German manuscript and the Basel edition of 1514, followed by later editions, have *tentatori*, “to the tempter.” For the correction of this passage, the English manuscripts, Norman manuscripts, Corbeiensis Germanicus, Vindobonensis, and the old Paris edition of 1495 were consulted; the latter nevertheless reads *protulisset* in place of *praetulisset*.] if he had foreseen that he could not persevere in temptation. Since, then, the devil was divinely permitted to tempt him, whoever thinks that he succumbed in temptation accuses the one who permitted it of ignorance.

### 10. God’s judgments differ from human judgments.---

Let us therefore approve Job as truthful in his words, lest we wickedly accuse God in his providence. As far as human judgments are concerned, his friends might be thought to have said many things more correctly than he did. But Truth, bringing forth another rule from concealment, says: “You have not spoken what is right before me, as my servant Job has.”

“Before me,” he says—that is, inwardly, where the life of many often displeases, though outwardly it pleases human beings. Hence it was stated with great caution in praise of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0755D] Vindobonensis reads *castorum*, “chaste.”] married couple: “They were both righteous before God” (Luke 1:6). For it is not a secure praise to appear righteous before human beings. Human judgment often approves someone as great, as though in God; yet almighty God does not acknowledge that person, who is approved, as it were, on his own account.

This is why the Psalmist vigilantly prays, saying: “Direct my way in your sight” (Psalm 5:9). For often, in the sight of human beings, a path is believed to be straight even when it has deviated from the way of truth.

It should also be noted that it does not say, “You have not spoken what is right before me, as Job,” but, “as my servant Job,” so that, by inserting the word “servant,” while recalling him as though with a certain particular distinction, it may show that everything he had said in his defense was spoken not with obstinate pride but with humble truth. [Note: [Col. 0754D] Vindobonensis and many Norman manuscripts read: “It is now said, ‘You have not spoken what is right before me, as my servant Job,’ so that…”]

[Old V.] But because God is just and merciful, he both reproves Job’s friends strictly through justice and converts them kindly through mercy. For it follows:

### CHAPTER VIII [Recension VII]

**VERSE 8.**—“Now therefore take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job and offer a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job shall pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be charged against you.”

### 11. God reproves Job’s friends through justice and converts them through mercy.---

Behold, the just and merciful God neither leaves sins without reproof nor abandons guilt without conversion. Since he is an inward physician, he first revealed the corruption of the wound and afterward indicated the remedies by which health could be obtained. [Note: [Col. 0756D] Especially the Preface, chapter 6, section 15 and following. The 1514 edition and later editions read: “But because they often … suspect, the almighty God.” We have drawn this obscure passage out of darkness with the help of the Norman manuscripts and the old edition of 1495. In this book, which is in a certain sense a recapitulation of what precedes, Gregory very frequently recalls matters already discussed; it is not worthwhile to note where each has been treated, since they can readily be found with the aid of the index.]

We have often said that blessed Job’s friends represent heretics, who, while attempting to defend God, offend him, because in their statements they rebel against the truth, which they imagine themselves to serve by their false assertion. Since the almighty God often incorporates them into the body of the holy Church through knowledge of the truth, their conversion also, which is often brought about mercifully, is well signified by the pardon that Job’s friends receive.

### 12. Heretics cannot appease God by the sacrifice they offer themselves; they cannot be reconciled except through the Church.---

It must be especially noted that they are commanded to offer the sacrifice of their conversion to the Lord not by themselves but through Job. Clearly, when heretics return from error, they cannot by a sacrifice offered by themselves appease the Lord’s anger toward them, unless they are converted to the catholic Church, which blessed Job signifies, so that they may obtain salvation through the prayers of the one whose faith they had attacked with perverse assertions.

For he says: “My servant Job shall pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be charged against you.” [Note: [Col. 0756D] Laudensis, two German manuscripts, Pratellensis, and Uticensis read: *Job autem*, “but Job”; Laudensis reads *in stultitia*, “in folly.”] It is as though he were saying plainly to the heretics: “I do not accept your sacrifices; I do not hear the words of your petitions, except through the intercession of the one whose words of profession I recognize as truthful concerning me. Bring bulls and rams to offer as sacrifices of your conversion [Note: [Col. 0756D] Vindobonensis and most Norman manuscripts read: “by presenting sacrifices.”], but ask me for your salvation through the catholic Church, which I love. For I wish to forgive you what you have sinned against me within it, so that she may obtain your safety, she who was afflicted by your sickness.”

[Old VI.] ### 13. The prerogatives of the Church.---

She alone is the one through whom the Lord willingly accepts sacrifice (24, q. 1, c. 22, § “She alone,” *Sola quippe*); she alone confidently intercedes for those who err. Hence the Lord also gave a command concerning the sacrifice of the lamb, saying: “It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside” (Exodus 12:46). The lamb is eaten in one house because the true sacrifice of the Redeemer is offered in the one catholic Church.

The divine law prohibits taking its flesh outside, because it forbids giving what is holy to dogs (Matthew 7:6). She alone is the place in which good works are fruitfully performed; hence the reward of the denarius was received only by those who had labored within the vineyard (Matthew 20:8). She alone preserves those placed within her through the bond of strong charity. Hence the water of the flood lifted the ark to higher places, but destroyed all whom it found outside the ark (Genesis 7:20–21 and following).

She alone is the place in which we truly contemplate heavenly mysteries. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exodus 33:21). And shortly afterward: “I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back” (ibid., 23). Because truth is seen from the catholic Church alone [Note: [Col. 0757D] Longipontanus reads *in sola*, “in the Church alone.”] (Q. 1, c. 22), the Lord declares that there is a place with him from which he may be seen. Moses is placed upon the rock so that he may contemplate the form of God, because unless someone holds firm to the solidity of faith, he does not recognize the divine presence. Concerning this solidity the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

What, then, does it mean here to say to Job’s friends, “Go to Job,” except, “Ascend the rock”? [Note: [Col. 0757D] Two German manuscripts and Pratellensis read: “What does it mean to say here, ‘Go to Job,’ except ‘the rock’?”] What does “I will accept his face for you, so that your folly may not be charged against you” mean, except what is said there: “You shall see my back” (Exodus 33:23)—that is, “You shall understand the mysteries of his incarnation, which are to come afterward”?

### 14. What heretics must do in order to return to the Church.---

Because heretics disdain to stand upon the rock, they do not see the back of the passing Lord; being placed outside the Church, they do not recognize the mysteries of his incarnation as they truly are.

As we also said above [Note: [Col. 0757D] Preface, chapter 8, section 18], bulls signify the neck of pride, while rams signify leadership, which heretics exercise when they persuade the peoples, as though leading flocks astray. Of heretics who grow proud and corrupt the minds of the weak through evil persuasion [Note: [Col. 0757D] The manuscripts and the older Paris edition of 1495 read *male suadendo*, “by evil persuasion”; the 1518 and later editions, and the German manuscript, read *male consilium*, “evil counsel.”] it is said: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Psalm 67:31). And because they drag the peoples who follow them along like flocks, they are sometimes called rams. Rams lead the flock. Hence Jeremiah says in reproach: “Your princes are like rams” (Lamentations 1:6).

Since, then, when heretics return to the holy Church they abandon their proud arrogance and no longer, like those who lead following flocks, drive crowds of peoples toward destruction, Job’s friends are commanded to offer bulls and rams. To offer bulls and rams in sacrifice is to slaughter proud leadership through the humility of conversion, so that, with the neck of pride subdued, those who previously tried to lead by teaching may learn to follow through obedience. Their pride is rightly expiated by seven sacrifices, because heretics returning to the Church receive, through the sacrifice of humility, the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit of grace, so that those who had wasted away through the oldness of their arrogance may be renewed by the newness of grace.

### 15. The number seven is perfect. What does it signify? The perfection of eternity, the duration of the present life, and the universality of the Church.---

Among the wise men of this age, the number seven is considered perfect for a certain reason: it is completed from the first even number and the first odd number. The first odd number is three, and the first even number is four. Seven consists of these two numbers, and when it is multiplied by its own parts, it rises to twelve. For whether we multiply three by four or four by three, we arrive at twelve.

But because we receive the teachings of truth from a gift from above, we trample upon these physical speculations [Note: [Col. 0758D] Vindobonensis and the Norman manuscripts read *haec physica*, “these physical matters”; both old and recent editions, with two German manuscripts, differ.] by looking down on them from the fixed height of knowledge, firmly retaining this unshaken faith: that those whom the sevenfold Spirit of grace fills, it perfects; and that it grants them not only knowledge of the Trinity but also the practice of the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The Spirit is also, in a certain sense, increased in those whom he enters through his very parts: through knowledge of the Trinity, the practice of the four virtues is received; and through the practice of the four virtues, one arrives at the manifest vision of the Trinity.

For us, therefore, seven is also perfect, but in a very different way, because it rises fully and not emptily to twelve: through faith it produces works, and again through works it perfects faith. The holy apostles, who were to be filled with the Spirit of sevenfold grace, were chosen as twelve. For they were sent to make known the Trinity, which is God, in the four regions of the world. They were chosen as twelve so that, through the very structure of the number, the reason might also become clear: by means of the four lower things they were to preach the three highest.

### 16. Whether by this or perhaps by another reason, in Holy Scripture the number seven sometimes signifies the secure rest of eternity, sometimes the totality of the present age, and sometimes the universality of the holy Church.---

The perfection of eternity is suggested by the number seven when the seventh day is called sanctified for the Lord’s rest (Genesis 2:2). It is not said to have an evening, because the rest of eternal blessedness is confined by no limit. Hence, when the law was given, the seventh day was commanded to be a day of rest (Exodus 20:11), so that eternal rest might be signified through it.

Hence also, in the course of the years, the number seven multiplied seven times, with a unit added [Note: [Col. 0758D] The German, Turonensis, Laudensis, and Norman manuscripts read *monade addito*; Corbeiensis Germanicus admits both readings.], is brought to fifty, so that, signifying perpetual blessedness, the most sacred rest of the jubilee might be observed (Leviticus 25:8–9).

Hence, when the risen Lord appeared frequently [Col. 0758D] (John 21), he is described as having eaten at the final meal with seven disciples, because those who are now perfected in him are satisfied by eternal refreshment through him.

[Old VII.] ### 17. Again, through the number seven the totality of temporal existence is understood.---

The entire duration of the present life unfolds through seven days. Hence, as a figure of the holy Church—which goes around this world preaching throughout all time—the ark of the Lord, with trumpets sounding, circled the walls of Jericho for seven days and overthrew them (Joshua 6:20).

Hence the Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164). Indicating again that he had said this for the whole and entire period of his prayer, he says: “His praise is always in my mouth” (Psalm 33:1).

That the totality of the present life is signified by the number seven is shown more clearly when the number eight is added after it. When seven is followed by another number, its increase itself expresses that temporality, which must come to an end, is enclosed by eternity. Hence Solomon admonishes, saying: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11:2).

Through the number seven he expressed the present time, which is enacted through seven days; through the number eight he signified perpetual life, which the Lord revealed to us through his resurrection. For he rose on the Lord’s Day [Note: [Col. 0759D] Ebroicensis and other Norman manuscripts, Turonensis, and others read *cum dominico*, “with the Lord’s Day.”], which, following the seventh day—that is, the Sabbath—is found to be the eighth from creation.

It is fittingly said: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight, because you do not know what evil will occur upon the earth” (ibid.). It is as though he were saying plainly: “Dispose of temporal things in such a way that you do not forget to desire eternal things.” For it is necessary that you provide for the future by doing good, since you do not know how great a tribulation will follow from the coming judgment.

Hence the temple is ascended by fifteen steps, so that from this very ascent one may learn how, through seven and eight, temporal activity should be carefully administered and eternal dwelling prudently sought. Hence also, when the unit rises to ten, the Prophet sang one hundred and fifty psalms.

Because the number seven signifies temporal things and the number eight eternal things, the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the one hundred and twenty faithful who were sitting in the upper room (Acts 2). Seven and eight together make fifteen; and if, counting from one up to fifteen, we rise gradually through successive increases, we arrive at the number one hundred and twenty. Through this outpouring of the Holy Spirit they learned both to pass beyond temporal things by enduring them and to desire eternal things eagerly.

### 18. Again, the number seven signifies the universality of the holy Church.---

Hence John writes in the Apocalypse to seven churches (Revelation 1:4); but what else did he intend to be understood through them except the universal Church? Indeed, so that this universal Church might be signified as filled with the Spirit of sevenfold grace, Elisha is described as having breathed seven times upon the dead child (2 Kings 4:34). When the Lord comes upon the extinguished people, he breathes upon them, as it were, seven times [Note: [Col. 0759D] The German and the editions of Gilot, the Vatican, and Gussanville read *oscitasse*, “to have yawned.” We have preferred *inspirasse*, “to have breathed upon,” the reading of the other manuscripts and the older editions.], because he mercifully grants them the gifts of the Spirit of sevenfold grace.

Since, therefore, the universality of the holy Church is often represented by the number seven, let Job’s friends come to blessed Job and offer the burnt offering commanded by God. But let them carefully preserve the mysteries of the number seven, so that those who are outside may first join themselves to the universality of the holy Church and only then seek pardon for the guilt of their former pride.

Let them offer seven sacrifices for their guilt, because they do not receive the cleansing of their guilt [Note: [Col. 0760D] Turonensis, two German manuscripts, Vindobonensis, and the Norman manuscripts read *absolutionem*, “absolution.”] unless they are gathered by the Spirit of sevenfold grace into the universal peace from which they had been cut off.

Let it therefore be said: “Take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer a burnt offering for yourselves; and my servant Job shall pray for you; I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be charged against you.”

It is as though the following were said plainly to returning heretics: “Join yourselves through the humility of repentance to the universal Church, and obtain from me through her prayers the pardon to which you are not worthy by yourselves. When, through her, you learn to understand truthfully, you erase before me the folly of your former wisdom.” It follows:

### CHAPTER IX [Old VIII]

**VERSE 8.**—“For you have not spoken what is right before me [Note: [Col. 0760D] German and Laudensis read *recta*, “right things.”], as my servant Job has.”

### 19. The repetition of a sentence in Holy Scripture is evidence of its unchangeability.---

The Lord had already spoken these words shortly before, yet he adds the same words again by repeating them. What does this mean except that, by repeating the sentence he had once pronounced in judgment, he confirms it again? And so that blessed Job’s righteousness and his friends’ unrighteousness might be demonstrated more clearly, his praise and their reproof are expressed in repeated words, so that, once repeated outwardly, they may show how firmly they are established inwardly.

When the king of Egypt had recognized the fearful times of the coming famine in a double vision under the appearance of cattle and ears of grain, he heard from the holy interpreter: “The fact that you saw the dream a second time, as pertaining to the same matter, is an indication of its certainty” (Genesis 41:32). From this it is plainly gathered that whatever is repeated in divine speech is confirmed more firmly.

But since we have heard what the Judge decreed, let us also hear what those who have been condemned do. It follows:

### CHAPTER X

**VERSE 9.**—“So Eliphaz the Temanite, Baldad the Shuhite, and Sophar the Naamathite went away and did as the Lord had spoken to them, and the Lord accepted the face of Job.”

### 20. The order of pardon.---

We omit the interpretation of these names because we remember having discussed it at greater length at the beginning of this work. But it must be observed that the order of the pardon received is preserved with such care that, in the sacrifices, the Lord is said to have accepted not their face but the face of blessed Job.

Since, however, whoever attempts to intercede for others gains assistance for himself more truly through that very charity, it is rightly added:

### CHAPTER XI

**[Col. 0761A] VERSE 10.**—“The Lord also turned toward Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends.”

### 21. We are heard more quickly when we pray for ourselves if our prayer is seasoned with love for our neighbor, and especially for our adversary.---

Already above he is shown to have been heard for his friends, when the deed mentioned earlier is recalled: “They did as the Lord had spoken to them, and the Lord accepted the face of Job.”

But when it is immediately added, “The Lord also turned toward Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends,” it is plainly shown that, while repenting for himself, he deserved to be heard more quickly because he interceded devotedly for others. For the one who spends his prayers for others makes them more effective on his own behalf.

The sacrifice of prayer is received more willingly when, in the sight of the merciful Judge, it is seasoned with love for one’s neighbor. A person truly increases this sacrifice when he also offers it for his adversaries. Hence Truth, our teacher, says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke 6:28). Again he says: “When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25).

How much, however, the one who intervened for others obtained for himself is immediately demonstrated when it is added:

### CHAPTER XII [Recension VIII]

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“The Lord also restored to Job, double, everything that had been his.” [Note: [Col. 0761D] Pratellensis and others add *quoque*, “also.”]

22. The measure of consolation is proportioned to the weight of affliction. — He received back double everything he had lost, because, through the goodness of the merciful Judge, the support of consolations overcomes the loss occasioned by our trial. The testing causes less suffering than the reward provides consolation, so that the one who had judged from the weight of the blow that he was enduring something grievous [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the old Paris edition of 1495; later editions read “persecution.”] recognizes from the merit of the recompense that what he endured was light. Hence it is said also to afflicted Judaea: “For a brief moment, in a little while, I abandoned you, but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isa. 54:7). At times, however, the measure of consolation is proportioned to the weight of affliction. Hence it is written elsewhere: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93:19). For he indicates that he was consoled in the same measure in which he had been afflicted, who declares that he was gladdened according to the multitude of his sorrows.

The reader is not instructed only slightly if he considers the very order of the recompense. Correction follows transgression, repentance follows correction, pardon follows repentance, and gifts follow pardon. But because, struck by the permission of divine providence, he was also afflicted by the words of his friends, he must be consoled by the gifts of divine mercy and likewise refreshed by human charity, so that joys of consolation may answer him from every side, whom sorrows and adversities had wounded from every side. Hence it is also added:

## CHAPTER XIII

**Verse 11.** “And all his brothers came to him, and all his sisters, and all who had known him before; and they ate bread with him in his house, and they shook their heads over him.”

23. Not only divine consolation, but also human consolation. — What is signified by the eating of bread except charity, and what by the shaking of the head except astonishment? It is rightly added:

**The same passage.** “And they consoled him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him.”

To console one who has been struck means to rejoice with him over pardon after the blow. For the more someone is seen to rejoice over the restoration of his neighbor’s well-being, the more he shows that he had grieved over its loss.

## CHAPTER XIV [Recension IX]

**The same passage.** “And each one gave him one sheep and one gold earring.”

24. The Church will at some time receive double. — Although all these things were truly said according to the historical sense, the gifts themselves compel us to return to the mystery of allegory. For we must not accept casually that they offered a sheep, that it was one, that they offered a gold earring, and that it too was one. And although, perhaps, according to the literal sense there is nothing remarkable about why the sheep offered was one, it is nevertheless very remarkable why the earring offered was one. What connection does a sheep have with an earring, or an earring with a sheep? We are therefore compelled by the very conclusion of the gifts to investigate in the mysteries of allegory also the earlier matters that, on the surface and according to the historical sense alone, we passed over in touching upon them.

Since Christ and the Church—that is, the head and the body—are one person, we have often said that blessed Job signifies now the figure of the head, now that of the body [Old recension IX]. Therefore, while preserving the truth of the history, let us understand as enacted under a type of the holy Church what is written: “The Lord added everything that Job had, double.” For although the holy Church now loses many through the blow of temptation, at the end of this age it nevertheless receives back double what belongs to it, when, after the Gentiles have been fully received, even Judaea consents to run to the faith of the Church—all who are then found. Hence it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25). Hence Truth also says in the Gospel: “Elijah will come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. 17:11). [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl. read “will come.”] For now the Church has lost the Israelites whom it was unable to convert by preaching; but then, when Elijah preaches and gathers all whom he finds, it receives back more fully, as it were, what it lost.

25. Before the resurrection the saints receive single robes; after the resurrection, two. — Or certainly, for the holy Church to receive double at its end means that in each of us it rejoices both in the blessedness of the soul and in the incorruption of the flesh. Hence it is said through the prophet concerning the elect: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. 61:7). Hence the apostle John says concerning the saints awaiting the end of the world: “A single white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed” (Rev. 6:11).

As we said much earlier [namely, in the Preface, ch. 10, no. 20], before the resurrection the saints receive single robes because they enjoy only the blessedness of their souls; but at the end of the world they will have two, because together with blessedness of mind they will also possess the glory of the flesh.

26. The conversion of the Jews foretold for the end of the world. — But what follows more clearly confirms that it announces the conversion of the Jewish people at the end of this age. For it is added: “And all his brothers came to him, and all his sisters, and all who had known him before, and they ate bread with him in his house.”

Then his brothers and sisters come to Christ, when all who are gathered from the Jewish people are converted. For he took the substance of his flesh from that people. Thus his brothers and sisters approach him when, from that people joined to him by kinship, those who will be strong, as brothers, and those who will be weak, as sisters, hasten to him with devoted rejoicing through knowledge of the faith. [Note: Longip. reads “those who are joined to him …”] [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl. read “through kinship.”]

Then they provide him with a banquet of the most celebrated festivity, when, no longer despising him as a mere man, but remembering their kinship with him, they rejoice that they cling to his divinity. Then they eat bread in his house, when, having set aside their observance of the subordinate letter, they are nourished in the holy Church by the marrow of mystical speech, as by the substance of grain. [Old recension X] [Note: Gemet., Pratel., the two German manuscripts, and Val. Cl. read “of the superimposed [letter].”]

It is rightly added: “All who had known him before.” They had known beforehand the one whom, during his Passion, they despised as though he were unknown. For no one who had fully learned the Law was ignorant that Christ would be born. Thus King Herod, terrified by the arrival of the magi, carefully sought from the priests and rulers where they knew Christ was to be born; they immediately replied to him: “In Bethlehem of Judaea” (Matt. 2:5).

They therefore knew beforehand the one whom, at the time of his Passion, they ignored while they despised him. Their prior knowledge and subsequent ignorance are aptly and briefly represented by Isaac’s growing blindness. While he blessed Jacob, he both foresaw what would happen in the future and did not know who was standing before him (Gen. 27). Such was the people of Israel: it received the mysteries of prophecy, but nevertheless had blind eyes in contemplation, because it did not see him who was present, concerning whom it had foreseen so much in the future. It was unable to see him placed before it, whose coming it had announced long beforehand.

But behold, at the end of the world they come and recognize him whom they had previously known. Behold, they eat bread in his house, because in the holy Church they are nourished by the fruit of sacred speech, [Note: The two German manuscripts, Ebroic., and Val. Cl. read “behold, all …”] and they shake off all the former insensibility of their torpor. Hence it is added: “And they shook their heads over him.”

For what is understood by the head except the ruling principle of the mind? [Note: This is what the Greeks call τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, that is, “the ruling principle” or “the governing faculty of the soul.”] As the Psalmist says: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Ps. 22:5). It is as though he openly said: “You have watered my mind, parched in its thoughts, with the anointing of charity.”

The head is therefore shaken when the mind, touched by fear of the truth, is shaken from its insensibility. Let their relatives, then, come to the banquet and, having cast off their torpor, shake their heads—that is, let those who had been joined to our Redeemer according to the flesh eventually receive the nourishment of the word in faith and lose the former hardness of their insensibility.

Hence Habakkuk rightly says: “His feet stood firm, and the earth was shaken” (Hab. 3:5). When the Lord stands firm, the earth is undoubtedly shaken, because, when he imprints the traces of his fear upon our heart, every earthly thought within us trembles. To shake the head in this passage therefore means to cast off the mind’s immobility and to draw near to knowledge of the faith by the steps of belief.

27. How great the Church’s consolation will be from their conversion, and what the converted should offer to Christ. — But because the holy Church is now afflicted by the rejection of the Hebrews and is then relieved by their conversion, it is rightly added [Old recension XI]: “And they consoled him over all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him.”

They console Christ, and they console the Church, who recover from the error of their former unbelief and abandon the depravity of life by which they had opposed those teaching what was right. Is it not a grievous sorrow to preach fruitlessly to hardened hearts, to undertake labor in displaying the truth, yet to find no fruit of one’s labor in the conversion of the hearers? On the contrary, the subsequent progress of hearers is a great consolation to preachers. For the transformation of the one who is progressing is the relief of the one who teaches.

It should also be noted that they did not wish to console him while he was under the scourge, but came to console him after the scourge, because, at the time of his Passion, the Hebrews, despising the declarations of faith, scorned to believe that the man whom they had proved to be a man by his death was God. Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I looked for one who would grieve together with me, but there was none; I sought one who would console me, and I found none” (Ps. 68:21).

He found no one to console him in his Passion, because, in the contempt of his death, he endured even those enemies for whom he came to death. After the scourges, therefore, his relatives come for consolation, because the Lord still suffers in his members; but at the end of time all the Israelites hasten to the faith, having learned Elijah’s preaching, and return to the protection of the one whom they had fled. Then that exceptional banquet is celebrated through the manifold gathering of peoples.

Then, after the scourges, the Lord is shown healthy like Job, when, after his Passion and resurrection, those who have been converted and believe know with the certainty of faith that he lives immortal in heaven. Then Job appears as one who has been rewarded, when he is believed to be God in the power of his majesty, and those who had previously resisted are seen to be subjected to his faith.

At the end of the world, therefore, let the believing Hebrews assemble and, as though before a healthy Job, offer vows of their offerings to the Redeemer of the human race in the power of his divinity [Old recension XII]. Hence it is rightly added: “And each one gave him one sheep and one gold earring.”

What is signified by the sheep except innocence, and what by the earring except obedience? The sheep expresses a simple mind, while the earring expresses hearing adorned with the grace of humility.

## [Recension X] 28. The excellence of obedience; obedience must be preserved even unto death. — Since an opportune occasion has presented itself for displaying the virtue of obedience, I gladly examine it somewhat more attentively and earnestly and demonstrate how great its merit is.

Obedience alone is the virtue that implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted. Hence the first man received a command to keep (Gen. 2:1); if he had wished to submit himself to it in obedience, he would have reached eternal blessedness without labor.

Hence Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams; for to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to comply is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15:22).

Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices [8, q. 1, canon “Sciendum,” § “Obedientia”], because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is slaughtered. The sooner, therefore, someone appeases God, the more he sacrifices himself before his eyes, with the pride of his own will restrained by the sword of the commandment.

Conversely, disobedience is called the sin of divination, so that the greatness of obedience may be demonstrated. Thus, by its opposite, what opinion should be held of its praise is shown more clearly. If resisting is like the sin of divination, and refusing to comply like the crime of idolatry, then obedience alone possesses the merit of faith, without which anyone is proved to be unbelieving, even if he appears faithful.

Hence Solomon says in praise of obedience: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. 21:28). An obedient man speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in our hearts. [Note: Laud. reads “when we submit ourselves in the heart, we overcome ourselves.”]

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “The one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:37).

What then? If he had done his own will, would he have rejected those who come to him? Who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? But because the first man, wishing to do his own will, departed from the joy of paradise (Gen. 3:24), the second, coming for the redemption of humanity, showed that he did the Father’s will and not his own, and taught us to remain within.

When, therefore, he does not do his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because by his example he subjects us to obedience and closes for us the way of departure. Hence he says again: “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30).

Obedience is commanded us to preserve even unto death. But if he judges as he hears, then he obeys even when he comes as judge. So that obedience might not appear burdensome to us until the end of the present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as judge.

What is surprising, then, if sinful humanity submits itself to obedience during the short span of the present life [11, q. 3, canon “Quid ergo”], when the Mediator of God and humanity, who also rewards the obedient, does not abandon it? [Note: Gratian quotes this passage as follows: “when he held it … and commanded it to be held; and when he rewards the obedient.”]

## [Old recension XIII] 29. Evil must never be done through obedience, but good may sometimes be left undone through obedience. — It must be understood that evil must never be done through obedience, but that sometimes the good being done ought to be interrupted through obedience.

For the tree in paradise was not evil, which God forbade humanity to touch (Gen. 2). But so that humanity, well created, might grow better through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that it should also be prohibited from something good, so that the virtue it practiced might be more genuine, insofar as, abstaining even from something good, it humbly showed itself subject to its Creator. [Note: Gemet., Pratel., Val. Cl., and the two German manuscripts read “that he should also prohibit him from this good.”]

But it should be noted that it says there: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (ibid., 16). For the one who forbids those subject to him from one particular good must grant many others, lest the mind of the obedient perish utterly if it fasts, wholly rejected from every good. The Lord permitted the eating of all the trees of paradise while prohibiting one, so that he might more easily restrain his creature—which he did not wish to destroy but to advance—from one thing, the more freely and broadly he released it to all the others. [Note: Vindoc., Corb. Germ., and several Norman manuscripts read “more freely.”]

30. When obedience has no merit, and when it has very little. — Since we are sometimes commanded to pursue the prosperity of this world and sometimes its adversities, it must be understood with the greatest care that obedience is sometimes nothing, if it possesses something of its own; at other times it is very little, if it possesses nothing of its own. [Note: Laud. reads: “sometimes, if it has nothing of its own, it is of no account.”]

When success in this world is commanded, when a higher position is ordered, the one who obeys in order to receive these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also yearns for them from his own desire. For he does not direct himself under obedience who serves the lust of his own ambition in order to obtain the prosperity of this life.

Again, when contempt of the world is commanded, when disgrace and insults are ordered, unless the soul itself desires these things, it diminishes the merit of its obedience because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life. Obedience is led to loss when, in accepting the insults of this age, the mind is accompanied by none of its own desires.

Obedience must therefore possess something of its own in adversity, and, conversely, must possess absolutely nothing of its own in prosperity, so that in adversity it may be more glorious insofar as it joins itself to the divine order even through desire, and in prosperity it may be more genuine insofar as it completely separates from the mind the present glory it receives from God. [Note: Laud. reads “in adversity, it must in every way have something of its own.”]

31. By the examples of Moses and Paul we are taught to undertake prosperity solely at command, but adversity even from devotion. — We can display the weight of this virtue more clearly if we recall the deeds of two men of the heavenly homeland. [Note: Turon., Laud., and Val. Cl. read “heroes”; Pratel. and the German manuscripts, “men”; Corb. Germ., “true citizens.”] Moses, while tending sheep in the desert, was called by the Lord through an angel speaking in fire to preside over the whole multitude of the Israelites who were to be liberated (Exod. 3).

But because he was humble in his own mind, he immediately feared the proffered glory of so great a leadership and at once resorted to the protection of his weakness, saying: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent; from yesterday and the day before, since you began to speak to your servant, I have become slower and more impeded in tongue” (ibid. 4:10). And, putting himself aside, he asks for another, saying: “Send whom you will send” (ibid., 13).

Behold, he speaks with the Author of speech, yet, lest he assume the power of so great a leadership, he claims that he is tongue-tied.

Paul likewise had been divinely admonished that he ought to go up to Jerusalem, as he himself says to the Galatians: “Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem, taking Barnabas and Titus; I went up according to revelation” (Gal. 2:1). [Note: In Laud. “again” is absent.]

On the journey, when he encountered the prophet Agabus, he heard what adversity awaited him in Jerusalem (Acts 21). For it is written that Agabus, taking Paul’s belt and binding his own feet with it, said: “The man whose belt this is will be bound in this way in Jerusalem” (ibid., 11). Paul immediately replied: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus; for I do not consider my life more precious than myself” (ibid., 13).

Thus, going to Jerusalem at the command of the revelation, he learns of adversities and nevertheless embraces them willingly; he hears what he should fear, but he yearns for these things more ardently.

Moses, therefore, possesses nothing of his own with regard to prosperity, because he resists with prayers lest he be placed over the Israelite people. [Note: Val. Cl. reads “strives” (*nititur*).] Paul, with regard to adversity, is led even by his own desire, because he perceives the knowledge of the evils that threaten but, through devotion of spirit, burns even for more severe trials.

The one wished to avoid the glory of present power at God’s command; the other, with God arranging harsh and difficult things, prepared himself for more grievous ones. Instructed, therefore, by the unbroken virtue of both leaders, [Note: Laud. and Val. Cl. read “we are taught.”] let us strive, if we truly desire to seize the palm of obedience, to serve the prosperity of this age solely at command, but adversity also from devotion.

## [Old recension XIV] 32. Obedience is the ornament of innocence. — It should be noted that in this passage a sheep is offered with an earring, and an earring with a sheep, because the ornament of obedience is always joined to innocent minds, as the Lord testifies when he says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

No one, therefore, offered blessed Job an earring without a sheep, or a sheep without an earring, because one who is not innocent certainly does not obey his Redeemer; and one who scorns to obey cannot be innocent.

But because obedience itself must be preserved not through servile fear but through the affection of charity—not through terror of punishment but through love of righteousness—all who come to the banquet are said to have offered a golden earring, so that in the obedience they display charity may shine forth, surpassing all the other virtues as gold surpasses the other metals.

33. There can be neither innocence nor obedience except in the one true Church. — Since there can be neither innocence nor true obedience amid the numerous divisions of heretics, let those who come to knowledge of the faith offer a sheep, but one; let them offer an earring, but one—that is, let those come who remain innocent and obedient in the unity of the holy Church.

For one cannot be divided into many numbers, since this very “one” that we call one is not a number. [Note: Val. Cl. reads “into countless numbers.”] Let them offer a sheep, but one; let them offer an earring, but one—that is, coming to the holy Church with innocence and obedience, let them bring a mind that the schisms of sects do not divide.

## [Old recension XV] 34. How great the future joy in the Church from the conversion of the Jews, and the banquet that will one day be celebrated. — I wish to open the eyes of faith and contemplate that final banquet of the holy Church arising from the reception of the Israelite people.

To this banquet the great Elijah, coming as the inviter of those who will feast, is brought in; and then relatives, then acquaintances, come to him with gifts—the one whom shortly before they had despised while he was under the scourge. As the day of judgment approaches, whether through the words of the forerunner or through certain signs breaking forth, the power of the Lord who is coming already shines upon them in some manner. As they hasten to forestall his anger, they hasten the time of their conversion.

The converted come with gifts because they honor by offering works of virtue as gifts the one whom shortly before they mocked in his Passion, thereby undoubtedly fulfilling through this offering what we already see to have been accomplished in large part and still believe will be accomplished fully [Note: Even the old editions read “in large part.” Gilot noted in the margin, as a variant reading, “fully”; this is the reading to be adopted from the English manuscripts and our own, which Gussanville follows here.]: “The daughters of Tyre shall adore him with gifts” (Ps. 44:13). The daughters of Tyre then adore him more fully with gifts, when the minds of the Israelites, now subjected to the desires of this world, at last recognize him whom they denied in their pride and bring him the sacrifices of their confession.

And although, in the same period when Antichrist approaches, the life of the faithful may appear to possess somewhat less virtue; although, in the conflict with that lost man, fear may severely constrict even the hearts of the strong; nevertheless, strengthened by Elijah’s preaching, not only do all the faithful persist in the solidity of the holy Church, but, as we said above, many also among the unbelieving are converted to knowledge of the faith, so that the remnant of the Israelite nation, which had previously been utterly rejected, hastens with complete devotion to the bosom of Mother Church.

Hence it is rightly added:

## CHAPTER XV [Old recension XVI]

**Verse 12.** “But the Lord blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning.”

35. God will bless the latter days of the Church through the manifold gathering of souls. — We believe that these things happened historically; we hope that they will be accomplished mystically. Job is blessed more in his latter days than at his beginning because, insofar as this concerns the reception of the Israelite people, the Lord consoles the holy Church’s sorrow through the manifold gathering of souls as the end of the present age presses near. For it will be enriched all the more abundantly the more clearly it becomes known that the transience of the present life is pressing toward its end.

The Psalmist had seen the preachers of the holy Church being enriched by the blessing of the final age when he said: “They will still multiply in abundant old age, and they will be patient, so that they may proclaim” (Ps. 91:15). They multiply in abundant old age because, while their life is prolonged, their strength is continually extended toward what is better, and their gains in merit also increase through the passage of time. They are rightly patient so that they may proclaim, because, preaching heavenly things, they endure adversities all the more robustly as they bring back, through their endurance, richer benefits for souls.

It follows:

## CHAPTER XVI [Recension XI]

**Verses 12–13.** “And he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she-asses; and he had seven sons and three daughters.”

36. The whole assembly of the faithful is signified by Job’s doubled herds and flocks: the innocent, those formerly exulting in vices, those subjected to the yoke of the Law, and the Gentiles. — The preface of this same history shows that before the trial of the scourge he had seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she-asses; these, having been lost through the scourge, have now been restored double.

His children, however, were restored in the same number as those who had been lost. [Note: Both the old and recent printed editions read “as many as he lost.” We have followed the manuscripts scrupulously.] He had seven sons and three daughters, and is now described as having received seven sons and three daughters, so that those who had been extinguished may also be shown to live.

For when it is said, “The Lord added everything that Job had, double” (Job 1), yet sons were restored to him in the same number as those he lost, he added children twofold: he restored ten to him afterward in the flesh, while he reserved the ten who had been lost in the hidden life of souls [Old recension XVII].

If, however, anyone wishes, setting aside the stalk of the historical account, to be nourished by the grain of the mysteries—as an intellectual animal, so to speak—he must recognize what we understand. We can understand that the whole assembly of the faithful is signified by these animals.

Hence the Psalmist says to the Father concerning the Son: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, sheep and all oxen, and also the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8:8). Hence the same prophet, seeing that the holy Church is inhabited by all the simple, says: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Ps. 67:11).

37. What, then, do we understand by the sheep except the innocent; by the camels except those who pass beyond the twisted mass of the vices in which others abound [Note: The editions, including the old ones, read *exuberanti* or *extuberanti*; the German manuscripts read *extumerantium*. Our reading, *exuberantium* (“of those abounding”), is supplied by Corb. Germ., Turon., Val. Cl., and several Norman manuscripts.]; by the yoked oxen except the Israelites subjected to the Law; and by the asses except the simple minds of the Gentiles?

For that all the innocent are designated by the name of sheep the Psalmist testifies when he says: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. 94:7). Those who neglect to preserve innocence are not satisfied by that refreshment of the inner pasture.

38. Under the name of camels, sacred speech sometimes expresses the Lord and sometimes the pride of the Gentiles, as though by a twisted swelling rising above. Because the camel voluntarily humbles itself to bear burdens, it not unjustly signifies the grace of our Redeemer, who, in deigning to bear the burdens of our weakness, voluntarily descended from the height of his power.

Hence he says through the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18), and no one takes it from me. And again he says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:24).

For what is signified by the name of the rich man except anyone who is lifted up, and by the designation of the camel except voluntary condescension? The camel passed through the eye of the needle when our Redeemer entered, through the narrow passages of his Passion, even unto the acceptance of death. That Passion was like a needle because it pierced the body with pain.

It is easier, however, for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, because unless he himself, first bearing the burdens of our weakness through his Passion, showed us the opening of humility, our proud rigidity would in no way bend itself toward his humility. [Note: The manuscripts and the old editions read “the opening” (*foramen*). Gilot, the Vatican edition, and Gussanville read “the form” (*formam*), which I also read in two German manuscripts, Pratel., and Utic.]

Again, under the name of camel the twisted and vice-filled Gentile world is designated, as it is said through Moses that, when the day was already declining, Rebecca saw Isaac coming out into the field seated on a camel; immediately she descended from the camel and, ashamed at the sight of him, covered herself with a cloak (Gen. 24:64).

For what other person did Isaac signify by going out into the field when the day was already declining, except the one who comes at the end of this world, as though at the close of day, and goes forth into the field? Although invisible, he showed himself visible in this world.

Rebecca saw him while seated on a camel because the Church, coming from the Gentiles, beheld him while it still rested upon vices and had not yet adhered to spiritual but to animal impulses. But she immediately descended from the camel because she abandoned the vices by which she had previously been proudly uplifted, and she also took care to cover herself with a cloak because, having seen the Lord, she was ashamed of the weakness of her conduct. What had previously been carried freely on the camel was afterward covered, once she had descended, in modesty. Hence the apostolic voice says to the Church converted from its former pride, as to Rebecca descending from the camel and drawing a cloak over herself: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

## [Old recension XVIII] 39. In the case of oxen, sometimes the madness of the lustful, sometimes the laborious strength of preachers, and sometimes the humility of the Israelites is expressed. — That the madness of the lustful is designated by comparison under the name of an ox, Solomon indicates. Having first described the wantonness of the woman who gives evil counsel, he added: “Immediately he follows her, like an ox led to the slaughter” (Prov. 7:22).

Again, because the labor of a preacher is expressed under the name of an ox, the words of the Law testify, saying: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. 25:4). It is as though he openly said: “You shall not prevent preachers of the word from receiving their stipends.”

Again, because the people of Israel are represented under the name of an ox, the prophet asserts this when, announcing the Redeemer’s coming, he says: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. 1:3). By the ox he signifies the Israelite people, subdued by the yoke of the Law; by the ass he indicates the Gentile people, devoted to pleasures and even more brutish.

40. Under the name of asses and she-asses, sometimes the wantonness of the lustful, sometimes the gentleness of the simple [Note: Vindoc. reads “custom/habit” (*consuetudo*)], and sometimes, as we said above, the stupidity of the Gentiles is signified. That the wantonness of the lustful is expressed by comparison under the name of asses is clearly declared when the prophet says: “Their flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. 23:20).

Again, because the life of the simple is represented under the name of she-asses, our Redeemer is remembered to have sat upon a she-ass when he was going to Jerusalem. [Note: Ebroic., Vindoc., and others read “upon a she-ass.”] Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” What, then, does it signify that the Lord, seated upon a she-ass, leads her to Jerusalem, except that, while possessing simple minds by presiding over them, he leads them through his sacred sitting to the vision of peace?

Again, because the stupidity of the Gentiles is designated under the name of asses, the prophet testifies, saying: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the ass” (Isa. 32:20). To sow beside all waters is to preach the fruitful words of life to all peoples. To send forth the foot of the ox and the ass is to bind the ways of the Israelite and Gentile peoples by the bonds of heavenly commandments.

### [Old Version XIX.] 41. The letters of Sacred Scripture relate what is past and foretell what is future

With the truth of the letters thus preserved, we rightly believe that under the name of blessed Job all these animals signify the peoples of the holy Church, insofar as, through the dispensation of the Holy Spirit ordering all things wondrously, they both relate to us what has happened and proclaim what is to come.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and the old Paris and Basel editions; the revised editions of Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanville read “foretell.”]

Let us therefore recognize in the sheep the faithful and innocent peoples from Judea, formerly nourished in the pastures of the Law. Let us recognize in the camels the simple people coming from the Gentiles to the faith, who previously appeared exceedingly ugly under sacrilegious worship, as though through a certain deformity of their limbs—namely, through the foulness of their vices.

And because, as we have said, the sacred writings often take care to repeat what they affirm, the Israelites may again be understood in the oxen, as though worn down beneath the yoke of the Law; while by the asses, as has been said, the Gentile peoples may be signified, who, when they bowed themselves to the worship of stones, served every kind of idol with brute understanding, without resistance of mind, as though they had foolishly placed them upon their backs.

The holy Church, therefore, which at its beginnings, pressed by innumerable temptations, lost either the Israelite people or many from the Gentiles—namely, those whom it was unable to win—receives double at the end, because within it the number of the faithful from both nations grows more abundantly.

The yoked oxen may also signify preachers. Hence, when the Lord sent them to proclaim the Gospel, the Gospel witness (Mark 6:7) records that he sent them two by two, so that the holy preachers might recognize from the very character of their mission how greatly they ought to love the harmony of fellowship: either because there are two commandments of charity, or because fellowship cannot exist among fewer than two.

As we have said, the minds of simple people may be signified by the asses. The holy Church, however, receives both oxen and asses in duplicate, because the holy preachers who, oppressed by fear, had once kept silent during its trial, and the minds of simple people who, overcome by terrors, had feared to confess its truth, now raise their voices in confession of the truth with all the more strength because previously they had feared with such weakness.

### [Column 0772D] 42. Mysteries concealed in the different numbers and in the names of Job’s three daughters

We have briefly discussed these matters in their significance for the Church; how they serve the head of that same holy Church, we remember having explained at greater length at the beginning of this work (Preface, no. 14). Whoever therefore wishes to have fuller satisfaction concerning these matters should deign to read the second book of this work, especially no. 43.

But if we are asked also to discuss the number of the animals themselves—why a thousand yoke of oxen, or a thousand asses, six thousand camels, and fourteen thousand sheep are counted—we can briefly say that in secular learning the number one thousand is considered perfect for this reason: the square of the number ten produces a solid figure. For ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, which is already a square figure,

[Note: We have restored this passage, which is corrupt in the printed editions and in some manuscripts, with the help of two German manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and the Vindocinian manuscript. In the Tours, Laud, and Vallicellian manuscripts it reads: “but it is plane, so that it may be in height.” In the more corrupt editions of Gilot, the Vatican, and Gussanville: “But it is not plane, so that it may be in breadth.” In the old edition: “but it is not plane, so that it may be in breadth.” These readings make no sense. We must therefore read: “but it is plane,” that is, without height. Hence what follows: “so that it may rise in height.”]

but is flat. In order for it to rise in height and become solid, one hundred is multiplied by ten again, and becomes one thousand.

The number six is perfect for this reason: it is the first number completed by its own parts, namely by its sixth, third, and half—one, two, and three—which, added together, make six. No other number before six is found whose entire sum is completed when it is divided into its parts.

### [Old Version XX; Revised Version XII.] [Column 0773B]

But because through the greatness of Sacred Scripture we advance beyond all these things, there we find why six, seven, ten, and one thousand are perfect.

The number six is perfect in Sacred Scripture because, at the creation of the world, the Lord completed on the sixth day the works which he had begun on the first day (Genesis 2:2). Seven is perfect in it because every good work is accomplished through the seven virtues of the Spirit,

[Note: The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “through the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit.”]

so that both faith and works may be brought to completion.

The number ten is perfect in it because the Law is concluded in ten commandments, and every fault is restrained by no more than ten words; moreover, as the Truth recounts, the workers in the vineyard are rewarded with a denarius (Matthew 20:10–11).

For in ten, three are joined to seven. Human beings, however, who consist of soul and body, are contained in seven qualities: they are vigorous spiritually in three and bodily in four.

In the love of God, a person is spiritually stirred by three qualities, when the Law says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your mind, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matthew 22:37).

Bodily, a person is constituted by four qualities, since he is composed of hot and cold, moist and dry matter. Thus the human being, who consists of seven qualities, is said to be rewarded with a denarius, because in the reception of the heavenly homeland our seven are joined to the eternal three, so that a human being may receive the contemplation of the Trinity and, perfected as though by a denarius, live from the reward of his work.

Or certainly, because there are seven virtues in which one labors in this life, and because the contemplation of the Trinity is returned to those virtues as their reward, the life of those who labor is rewarded with a denarius. Yet every perfect person even in this life receives a denarius when he joins hope, faith, and charity to those same seven virtues.

The number one thousand is also considered perfect in sacred speech because its designation signifies totality. Hence it is written: “The word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Psalm 104:8). Since we must in no way believe that the world extends to merely one hundred generations, what else is signified by a thousand generations except the totality of generations?

Blessed Job therefore received fourteen thousand sheep. Because in the holy Church the perfection of the virtues is extended to both sexes, the number seven is doubled in it.

He received six thousand camels because those who had formerly perished through the foulness of their vices receive in it the fullness of good works.

He received a thousand yoke of oxen and a thousand asses because, after the fall of temptations, it takes Israelites and Gentiles, learned and simple alike, up to the summit of perfection.

### [Revised Version XIII.]

He also received seven sons and three daughters, because he joins hope, faith, and charity to the minds of those whom he had begotten through the seven virtues, bringing them to the sum of perfection,

[Note: Ebroic and other Norman manuscripts read: “the minds of those whom he joins with hope, faith, and charity.”]

so that he may rejoice in his offspring all the more truly because he judges that none of the virtues is lacking in his faithful.

### [Old Version XXI.]
