But because we have passed over these matters briefly, let us now turn our attention also to investigating the names of the daughters themselves. It follows:

## CHAPTER XVII

### Verse 14

“And he called the name of the one Day, and the name of the second Cassia, and the name of the third Cornustibii.”

[Note: The Laud manuscript reads “Cornutibii.” It ought to be read “Cornustibii,” in accordance with Saint Gregory’s interpretation, as the following discussion proves: although one says not *cornus* but *cornu*, and not *tibium*, the pipe of singers, but *tibia*.]

### 43.

Because these names are taken from virtues, the translator appropriately took care not to place them as they are found in the Arabic language, but to display them more clearly after turning them into Latin expression. For who does not know that *Dies* and *Casia* are Latin words?

[Note: We have corrected this variously corrupt passage in several editions on the basis chiefly of the Norman manuscript and two German manuscripts.]

But in the case of *Cornustibii*—although one says not *cornus* but *cornu*, and not *tibium*, the pipe of singers, but *tibia*—he preferred, I believe, to reveal the thing itself, although the grammatical gender of the expression was not preserved in Latin, and to retain it in the idiom of the language from which he was translating.

[Note: Jerome declares in his preface to the Book of Job that he translated it from the Hebrew and Arabic languages, and sometimes from Syriac. See the preface of the same holy Doctor to Daniel, where he also teaches that Job has a close connection with the Arabic language. Consult what we said in the first note to no. 62 of Book XX.]

Or, because he composed one word from *cornu* and *tibia*, he transferred both words into Latin through a single part of speech and licitly called them in whatever grammatical gender he wished.

### [Old Version XXII.]

What, then, does it mean that blessed Job’s first daughter is called Day, the second Cassia, and the third is recorded as having been called Cornustibii, except that the entire human race, which is chosen through the kindness of the Creator and the mercy of the same Redeemer, is designated by these names?

The human being shone like day by virtue of his creation, because his Maker sprinkled him with the splendor of innate innocence.

[Note: Gussanville’s edition reads incorrectly: “looked upon.”]

But when, of his own accord, he fell into the darkness of sin because he abandoned the light of truth, he hid himself, as it were, in the night of error, because elsewhere he is said to have followed a shadow.

Yet because our Maker’s generosity in goodness did not fail, the one whom he had first powerfully created for righteousness he later recalled from error by redeeming him with still greater power, against the darkness of our iniquity. And because, after his fall, he lacked the former firmness of his condition, God illumined him against the inner wars of opposing corruption with the manifold virtues of his gifts.

These virtues of those who make progress are perceived among other people like the fragrance of sweet odors. Hence Paul says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

Hence the holy Church, having smelled a certain fragrance of sweetness in its elect, speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “While the king was at his resting-place, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song of Songs 1:11).

As though it openly said: “While the king is hidden from my sight in his own repose, in the secret of heaven, the life of the elect is exercised in wondrous fragrances of virtues, so that, the more it does not yet see him whom it desires, the more ardently it may burn with longing.”

When the king is placed at his resting-place, nard gives forth its fragrance: while the Lord rests in his blessedness, the virtue of the saints in the Church supplies us with the grace of great sweetness.

Since the created human being shone with the light of innocence and the redeemed human race spread the fragrance of sweetness through the practice of good works, the first daughter is rightly called Day, and the second appropriately Cassia.

Cassia is rightly named because it spreads abroad in such a lofty fragrance of life. In the very origin in which the righteous human being had been created, he did not need such and so many virtues as are now necessary. For if he had wished to remain as he had been created, he could have conquered the enemy placed outside him without difficulty.

But after the adversary once entered within through the human being’s consent, he is now expelled only with greater labor—the one who, while still attacking, could previously have been driven away without effort.

### 44. We need many virtues that would not have been necessary in paradise

For now many things must be exhibited that were not necessary in paradise. Now there is need of the virtue of patience, the laborious instruction of teaching, bodily discipline, perseverance in prayer, confession of sins, and an outpouring of tears. The human being as originally created certainly needed none of these, because he received the good of salvation from his very creation.

A bitter potion is given to a sick person so that, once the illness has been removed, he may be restored to a state of health. But a healthy person is not told what he should take in order to recover; he is told instead what he should avoid so that he may not become weak.

Now, therefore, we employ greater efforts, since we do not simply preserve health that has been possessed but strive to restore what has been taken away.

And because all these efforts of our restoration are held in great esteem within the holy Church, the name of the second daughter, like cassia, gives forth a fragrance from merit: the first daughter was like day through the dignity of creation, while the second is cassia through the fragrance of strength bestowed by grace in redemption.

### [Old Version XXIII.]

Hence the Redeemer who was to come is also addressed by the Prophet: “Myrrh and drops and cassia are from your garments, from the ivory steps by which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Psalm 44:9).

What else is signified by the names of myrrh, drops, and cassia except the sweetness of virtues? What else is expressed by ivory steps except the ascent of those who make progress, shining with great strength?

When the Redeemer comes, therefore, he uses myrrh, drops, and cassia in his garment,

[Note: The Vindocinian and Pratel manuscripts read: “because in his elect.”]

because from his elect, with whom he mercifully clothes himself, he spreads the fragrance of the virtue of myrrh. In them this fragrance is led along ivory steps, because the reputation of their virtues is generated not by the display of pretense but by the ascent of true and solid works.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “by the virtue of true and solid works.”]

It is appropriately added: “By which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.” For holy souls, brought forth from the ancient fathers into knowledge of the truth, delight their Redeemer in his honor because, in what they do well, they claim nothing for their own praise.

[Note: Two German manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and the Laud edition read: “because the human race, renewed in the third order through the resurrection of the flesh, is taken up into that harmony … the third daughter, who is called Cornustibii.”]

But because the human race, renewed in the third order also through the resurrection of the flesh, is taken up into that harmony of eternal praise, the third daughter is called Cornustibii.

For what else is expressed by Cornustibii except the song of those who rejoice? There is truly fulfilled what is now said through the Prophet: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Psalm 149:1). It is truly fulfilled there, where the song of praise to God will no longer be sung from faith but from contemplated vision.

There our Maker receives from us true songs of his praises—he who made the human race Day by creating it, Cassia by redeeming it, and Cornustibii by taking it up.

For we who were created as light and are now redeemed as cassia will one day become Cornustibii, taken up into the exultation of eternal praise.

But before the bride reaches the bridal chamber, she rejects every foulness of life from herself and, preparing herself for the bridegroom’s love, adorns and equips herself with the forms of the virtues.

[Note: The Gemet, Corbie German, and two German manuscripts read “composes herself”; the Vallicellian manuscript reads “fortifies herself”; the German manuscript reads “adorns herself with the companionship of virtues.”]

For she strives to please the inward judge’s judgment,

[Note: The Laud, Vallicellian, Gemet, and two German manuscripts read *arbitris* rather than *arbitri*.]

and, lifted up by inward desires, to transcend the foul habits of human conduct.

Hence it is appropriately added concerning these same daughters of blessed Job:

## CHAPTER XVIII [Revised Version XIV]

### Verse 15

“And women as beautiful as Job’s daughters were not found in all the earth.”

### 45. The beauty of the elect

The souls of the elect surpass the entire human race, which conducts itself on earth according to human standards, by the splendor of their beauty; and the more they despise themselves outwardly by afflicting themselves, the more truly they shape themselves inwardly.

Hence it is said to the holy Church, adorned with the beauty of the elect, through the Psalmist: “The king desired your beauty” (Psalm 44:12).

A little later it is added concerning her: “All the glory of the daughter of the king is within” (ibid., 14).

[Note: The Vindocinian manuscript reads: “of the king’s daughter.”]

For if she sought glory outwardly, she would not possess inward beauty that the king could desire.

[Note: The Vatican and Gilot editions read incorrectly *haberet*, “would possess,” having removed the negation.]

### [Old Version XXIV.]

Although many in this Church shine with the beauty of virtues and surpass the merits of others through the perfection of their life, some nevertheless, because they are not capable of attaining higher things, are held within the bosom of its mercy, conscious of their weakness.

They avoid evil insofar as they are able, although they do not accomplish higher goods insofar as they desire them. Yet the Lord graciously receives them and admits them to himself according to the measure of a fitting recompense.

Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER XIX

### The same passage

“And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.”

### 46. Christ admits the weak and humble to the lot of the heavenly inheritance together with the strong and perfect

They are therefore remembered as beautiful because of the merit of the perfect; yet, as a figure of the imperfect, they also receive an inheritance among their brothers as though they were weak.

The practice of former life did not allow women to receive an inheritance by lot among males, because the severity of the Law, choosing the strong and scorning the weak, preferred to establish strict commands rather than merciful ones.

But when our merciful Redeemer came, let no one conscious of his weakness despair of receiving a share in the inheritance of the heavenly patrimony. For our Father grants women also rights of succession among the males, because he admits the weak and humble, together with the strong and perfect, to the lot of the heavenly inheritance.

Hence the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

[Note: The Laud manuscript and others add immediately: “because in that place”; these words—“with the Father”—are omitted. The German manuscript reads: “For in the house, with the Father.”]

For with the Father there are many dwelling places, because in that life of blessedness each person receives a distinct place according to distinct merit; yet no one feels the loss resulting from this inequality, because what each has received is sufficient for him.

The sisters therefore come to the inheritance with their brothers because the weak are admitted there with the strong, so that if someone is not supreme because of imperfection, he may nevertheless not be excluded from the lot of the inheritance because of humility.

Paul aptly indicates that these dwelling places are distributed to each according to merit when he says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

It follows:

## CHAPTER XX [Revised Version XV]

### Verse 16

“After these scourges Job lived one hundred and forty years; and he saw his sons and his sons’ sons, to the fourth generation; and he died old and full of days.”

[Note: The word “scourges” is not read in the two German manuscripts, the Laud manuscript, or the Gemet manuscript. It is also absent from the Vulgate. In the same Gemet manuscript, a little later, *senis* is read instead of *senex*.]

### 47. Who are called “full of days” in Sacred Scripture. Job, restored to his former condition and enriched with additional blessings, is a type of the Church

In Sacred Scripture, a person is not easily called “full of days” unless his life is praised by that same Scripture. A person is empty of days who, however long he may have lived, has spent the periods of his life in vanity.

By contrast, he is called full of days whose days do not simply pass away in perishing, but, once they have passed, are preserved with the just Judge as the daily wage of good work.

### [Old Version XXV.] 48.

But because there are people who wish to interpret these things also as a figure of the holy Church—and their wishes deserve obedience all the more because we ought to rejoice with their spiritual understanding—if we multiply fourteen by ten, we arrive at the number one hundred and forty.

The life of the holy Church is rightly reckoned as multiplied by ten and fourteen, because, preserving both Testaments and living according to both the Decalogue of the Law and the four books of the Gospel, it is extended to the summit of perfection.

Hence the apostle Paul,

[Note: Gregory here seems to admit a fifteenth Epistle of Paul, written to the Laodiceans. The Apostle himself certainly mentions an Epistle of the Laodiceans in Colossians 4:16, in these words: “When this letter has been read among you, see that it is read also in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you yourselves read the one from Laodicea.” But most learned scholars think that this Epistle is none other than the one entitled to the Ephesians, which they hold was sent not only to the Ephesians but also to the Laodiceans and other neighboring peoples whose metropolis was Ephesus—just as the Second Epistle written to the Corinthians is addressed also to all the saints who were in Achaia, whose metropolis was Corinth, as is clear from its inscription. Hence some of the holy Fathers praised the Epistle to the Ephesians under the name of the Epistle to the Laodiceans. On this matter you may consult Jerome in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, under Paul; the sacred critics, their synopsis, and other interpreters. In Hutter’s New Testament in twelve languages there is an Epistle to the Laodiceans composed in Greek, but it is rejected by everyone as spurious. Epiphanius, at the end of Heresy 42, rejects a certain Epistle to the Laodiceans praised by Marcion, which, he says, is found nowhere among the Apostle’s writings. Erasmus, instead of “and that you read the one from Laodicea,” reads: “and that you read the one written from Laodicea,” καὶ τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας.]

although he wrote fifteen Epistles, the holy Church retains no more than fourteen, so that by the number of the Epistles themselves it might show that the excellent teacher had searched out the secrets of the Law and the Gospel.

[Note: More recent editions read: “had searched out the secrets.” It will scarcely be found that Latin writers use *rimo* for *rimor*, although Priscian permits both. In the Vindocinian, Norman, and other manuscripts one finds: “had searched out the secrets.” The two German manuscripts agree with the recent edition.]

It is rightly said that blessed Job lived after the scourges, because the holy Church is first struck by the scourge of discipline and afterward strengthened by the perfection of life.

It also sees its sons and its sons’ sons to the fourth generation, because in this age, which revolves through four annual seasons, it beholds offspring being born to it daily through the mouths of preachers, even to the end of the world.

Nor is it contrary to truth when we say that periods of time are designated by generations. For what is each succession except a certain propagation of a race? When the Egyptian king’s cupbearer saw a dream in which it put forth three branches (Genesis 40:12), Joseph, skilled in interpreting dreams, declared that the three branches signified three days.

If, therefore, three days are expressed through three branches, why should four annual seasons not also be represented through four generations?

Thus the holy Church sees its sons when it beholds the first offspring of the faithful. It sees its sons’ sons when it recognizes that other sons are begotten to the faith by those same faithful.

It also dies old and full of days because, when the light that follows has been given as the reward of daily works, it is changed into the incorruption of the spiritual homeland, having laid aside the burden of corruption.

She who is full of days dies because her passing years do not pass away,

[Note: The reading should be corrected on the basis of English manuscripts and our editions, the Vatican and Gilot, in which it reads: “but immediately.”]

but are made solid by the recompense of enduring deeds. She who is full of days dies because, through these passing times, she works for what does not pass away.

Hence it is said to the apostles: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life” (John 6:27).

The holy Church therefore does not lose its days even when it leaves the present life, because it finds their light multiplied all the more abundantly in its elect the more carefully and diligently it now guards them in this life from every temptation.

The Church does not lose its days because it does not neglect to examine itself vigilantly each day in this life, and no sloth makes it grow numb in all the things it can rightly do.

Hence Solomon says of it:

[Note: The Vindocinian manuscript reads: “She considers.”]

“She considers the paths of her house, and does not eat her bread in idleness” (Proverbs 31:27).

She considers the paths of her house because she examines with subtle attention all the thoughts of her conscience. She does not eat her bread in idleness because what she has received by understanding from sacred speech she demonstrates before the eyes of the eternal Judge by exhibiting it in works.

She is said to die because, when the contemplation of eternity has absorbed her, it utterly extinguishes her from the succession of her mutability, so that nothing remains alive within her that might in any way impede the acuity of inward vision.

For she then sees inward things more truly when she more completely falls away from all outward things.

Let us therefore believe that this death and this fullness of days have occurred in blessed Job, who is one member of the Church, and let us hope that they will be accomplished in the whole Church at once, so that the truth of what happened may be preserved without annulling the prophecy of what is yet to happen.

For the good things that we know from the life of the saints, if they lack truth, are nothing; if they contain no mysteries, they are insignificant.

Thus the life of the good, described through the Holy Spirit, should shine for us through spiritual understanding, while our sense should nevertheless not depart from faith in the historical account. In this way the mind remains all the more firmly in its understanding, because it is held, as though placed in the middle, by both hope regarding the future and faith regarding the past.

### [Old Version XXVI; Revised Version XVI.] 49. Conclusion of the entire work. How greatly we must fear lest those who speak of God either say evil things carelessly or speak good things badly. The intention of human praise intrudes upon the intention of pleasing God

With this work completed, therefore, I see that I must return to myself. Even when our mind tries to speak correctly, it often scatters itself outside itself. For while words are being considered in order to determine how they should be spoken, the integrity of the soul is diminished because those words draw it inward.

We must therefore return from public speech to the council chamber of the heart,

[Note: The Laud manuscript reads: “to the care.”]

so that, as though in a council of deliberation, I may summon the thoughts of my mind to examine myself and see there whether I have said either evil things carelessly or good things badly.

For good is then spoken well when the one who speaks desires, through what he says, to please only the one from whom he received it.

And although I do not find that I have said any evil things, I nevertheless do not defend myself by claiming that I have said none at all. But if I have said anything good after receiving it from God, I confess that through my own fault I have said it less well than I should.

For when I return inwardly to myself, setting aside the leaves of words and the branches of sentences, and examine closely the very root of my intention, I recognize that I greatly desired to please God through it; yet somehow I do not know how, the intention of human praise secretly inserts itself into that same intention by which I strive to please God.

When I discern this afterward, and only belatedly, I discover that I am doing differently from how I know I began.

For this is often how the intention of human praise overtakes our intention: while our intention is begun rightly before the eyes of God, human praise secretly joins itself to it

[Note: The German manuscript reads: “secretly joined to it.”]

[Note: The Tours manuscript adds: “also.”]

and, as though catching up with it on the journey, overtakes it.

It is like food that is indeed taken out of necessity, but in the very act of eating, while gluttony secretly creeps in, the pleasure of eating becomes mingled with it. Hence it often happens that we complete for the sake of pleasure the bodily refreshment we began for the sake of health.

We must therefore confess that our right intention, which desires to please God alone, is sometimes accompanied by an intention that is less right, which seeks to please people through God’s gifts.

But if we are strictly examined by God concerning these matters, what place for salvation remains, when our evil things are purely evil and the good things we believe ourselves to possess cannot in any way be purely good?

Yet I believe that this is a worthwhile service: I openly reveal without hesitation to fraternal ears everything that I myself secretly reproach in myself. Because, in explaining, I did not conceal what I perceived, in confessing I do not hide what I suffer.

Through exposition I have made gifts manifest; through confession I uncover wounds. And because, in this great human race, there are neither lacking little ones who ought to be instructed by my words nor great ones capable of having compassion on my acknowledged weakness, through the former I contribute as much care as I can to my brothers, and from the latter I hope to receive care.

To the former I have said in exposition what they should do; to the latter I disclose in confession what they should spare. From the former I do not withhold the medicines of words; from the latter I do not conceal the tearing of wounds.

I therefore ask that whoever reads these things offer me the comfort of his prayer before the strict Judge and wash away with tears whatever he discovers to be sordid in me.

When the virtue of prayer is added to the virtue of exposition, my reader surpasses me in recompense if, while he receives words through me, he returns tears for me.

# [Homilies on Ezekiel]

## [Column 0781] Admonition concerning the following books of homilies

### [Column 0781] 1169 I.

After Saint Gregory’s exposition of the Book of Job, the order of the Holy Scriptures requires that the homilies of the same holy Doctor on the prophet Ezekiel follow. Although afflicted by illnesses, almost overwhelmed by extremely difficult affairs, and harassed by innumerable cares, he delivered them to the people.

He himself depicts the mournful condition at that time of the City and of all Italy in the sixth homily of the second book, which was formerly numbered eighteen:

“Everywhere,” he says, “we see mourning. Everywhere we hear groaning. Cities have been destroyed, camps have been overthrown, fields have been devastated, the land has been reduced to solitude [lacuna] We see some led into captivity, others mutilated, others killed.”

We omit the remaining passages in which he mourns the disasters of Rome, the Roman countryside, and all Italy.

Similar statements are read in the Preface to Book II, and especially at the end of the final homily:

“On every side,” he says, “we are surrounded by swords; on every side we fear the danger of impending death. Some return to us with their hands cut off, others as captives; others are reported to us as slain. Now I am compelled to restrain my tongue from exposition.”

Bernard, marveling at this leisure of our Gregory for interpreting Sacred Scripture amid so many and such great affairs, writes to the supreme pontiff Eugenius as follows:

“The siege of the city and the barbarian sword threatened the necks of the citizens. Yet did this frighten blessed Pope Gregory from writing wisdom in leisure? At that time—for this is clear from his own preface—he expounded the darkest and final part of Ezekiel as diligently as he did elegantly” (Book I *On Consideration*, chapter 9).

### II.

Indeed, Jerome was once compelled to decline the exceedingly difficult task of explaining this prophecy because the siege of the city of Rome had been announced to him.

“After,” he says, “the brightest light of all the lands had been extinguished—indeed, after the head of the Roman Empire had been cut off, and, to speak more truthfully, after the whole world had perished in one city—I fell silent, was humbled, and kept silence concerning good things” (*Letter to Eustochium*, which is prefixed to his commentary on Ezekiel).

Jerome gives another reason for avoiding this labor, namely, the difficulty of understanding and explaining it, which, he says, is confirmed by the tradition of the Hebrews. Unless someone among them has completed the age of priestly ministry—that is, his thirtieth year—he is not permitted to read either the beginnings of Genesis, or the Song of Songs, or the beginning and end of this book, so that the full period of human life may approach perfect knowledge and mystical understanding.

### III.

But in order that our Gregory might successfully carry out so arduous a work, he experienced the immediate presence of the divine power.

For when he was interpreting the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel, the deacon Peter, whom he used as his shorthand writer and secretary, saw the Holy Spirit resting upon Gregory’s head in the form of a white dove and placing its beak in his mouth. From this he learned, and as it were drank in, the loftiest mysteries, as Paul the Deacon relates near the end of Gregory’s Life and as John the Deacon confirms (Book IV, chapters 69 and 70).

Nor should it seem surprising that the Holy Spirit was present with Gregory in so extraordinary a manner, especially at the time when he produced the greater demonstrations of humility, since we have learned from Isaiah that the Spirit of God is the consoler and indweller of the humble (Isaiah 66:2).

Let us hear the most holy Doctor in Homily 11, no. 5, lamenting even lesser sins with the bitterest tears:

“Oh, how harsh are these things that I say, because in speaking I strike myself. My tongue neither holds the preaching as it ought, nor does my life follow my tongue to the extent that it is capable of holding it. I am often entangled in idle words, and, sluggish and negligent, I cease from the exhortation and edification of my neighbors. I have become mute and talkative in the sight of God: mute in necessary matters, talkative in idle ones.”

We pass over the rest, which displays an astonishing abasement of spirit in so great a man.

And as though something were still lacking from this humble confession, he declares himself guilty still further below (no. 26):

“But meanwhile, while I speak, I wish to turn my eyes away from myself; and behold, once again the divine word strikes me against myself, so that I may see my negligence and fear that these things I hear are being said to me. For, as I said above, whose heart, scattered among innumerable cares, gathers itself back to itself?”

## IV.

Just as the steadfastness in preaching of the most holy shepherd seems worthy of immense praise, in spite of so many cares and so many opposing difficulties, so too the Roman people’s ardent eagerness to hear Gregory and their inexhaustible hunger for the divine word deserve no ordinary commendation. For at the request of the Romans 1170 Gregory undertook an exposition of Ezekiel, as he himself states in the preface to the second book, and as John the Deacon confirms, book IV, chapter 76.

## V.

Since those homilies of which we are speaking are said to have been begun when the siege of the City was impending, and completed—or rather interrupted—when Agilulf, king of the Lombards, was already encircling the walls, we must ask at what time Rome suffered this siege. It is commonly assigned to the year 595. But in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II, chapter 4, we have shown by nearly certain and indisputable arguments that it should rather be assigned to the year 592.

## VI.

There is no controversy about the number of these homilies: twenty-two are found both in handwritten books and in printed editions. Their method of numbering, however, is not the same. In the printed editions they are counted as though they all belonged to one and the same book, so that what is the first homily of the second book is called the thirteenth in the commonly printed editions. The manuscripts proceed differently: after the twelfth homily of the first book, they call the homily that immediately follows the preface to the later book the first, and continue in this way through the tenth. We have chosen to follow their practice.

John the Deacon adopted another system of numbering. In book IV, chapter 66, he calls the homily the eighteenth which we, following the manuscript books, call the sixth of the second book. But concerning matters that seem of little or almost no importance, it is enough merely to have given this notice.

## VII.

As for the manner of speaking and writing observed by this holy Doctor, we do not claim that it is more polished or elegant; yet neither do we allow it to be despised as though it were merely humble and subdued. Certainly, in these sermons Gregory is concerned more with the substance and meaning of things than with the choice of words. Although he tries first to establish the literal sense as the foundation of all the rest, he devotes himself above all to probing the mystical senses and explaining the moral ones.

The first homily is placed before the others as a prologue, in which Gregory teaches many matters about the prophets and the Spirit of prophecy that are worthy and necessary to know. [Col. 0783] Whoever seeks more on this subject should consult the other holy Fathers who undertook to explain the prophets, and especially should read Epiphanius. At the beginning of his book *On Weights and Measures*, he discusses at length how many kinds of discourse occur among the prophets, and assigns these: teaching, contemplation, exhortation, threats, compassion, lamentation, prayers, historical narration, and prediction.

## VIII.

Throughout this work Gregory prudently consulted Jerome, who interpreted the prophecy of Ezekiel, but he did not follow him slavishly. Indeed, on occasion he refutes that same writer, though out of respect he suppresses his name. Would that some among more recent writers imitated his modesty and reverence toward Jerome—those who so freely attack the teaching of that most learned interpreter of the Sacred Scriptures!

To the more audacious pens of such writers one may oppose the testimony of the most learned Sulpicius Severus, Jerome’s contemporary, in *Dialogue* 1, chapter 4:

> “Jerome,” he says, “was a man so thoroughly trained not only in Latin and Greek letters but also in Hebrew, apart from the merit of his faith and the endowment of his virtues, that no one would dare to compare himself with him in any branch of knowledge.”

## IX.

We must now mention what this newest edition owes us.

1. In the printed editions, longer passages of Ezekiel’s text are prefixed to each homily, except the first, whereas they are absent from the handwritten books. We have removed them. But we have caused each individual verse, as it is successively explained by the holy Doctor, to be printed in separate lines, thereby coming closer to the practice of the manuscript codices, in which such verses are written either in larger characters or even painted in red or some other carefully chosen color.

2. The homilies, which had previously been read as though composed in a single continuous flow, with no clauses assigned for pauses, we have divided into various sections and added an equal number of section numbers. In notes placed below and at the foot of the columns, we have taken care to explain anything obscure that required interpretation. There too we have presented variant readings, and whenever a change of some importance was made in the text—which happened very frequently—we have identified the manuscript codices used for its correction.

To enumerate all the passages that we have healed or restored would take too long. We shall nevertheless point out a few from the earlier homilies, so that from them the usefulness—and indeed the necessity—of the new edition may be understood.

In book I, homily 2, no. 17: *de quo mox*, and so forth; homily 3, no. 5: *non tenuiter amatur*; and no. 18: *cum pes mentis*, and so forth; homily 4, no. 3: *et si simul*, and so forth; homily 5, no. 2: *vitae mortalis*, and so forth; and no. 7: *Verbum itinerantibus*, and so forth; homily 6, no. 8: *quid ergo mentes auditorum*, and so forth; and no. 13: *ligno autem*, and so forth.

Likewise, no. 18: *et humus ejus*, and so forth, where the printed editions have *et fumus ejus*. In the same place, Gussanville has *in pice ardentem* instead of *in picem ardentem*. Finally, no. 19: *terribilis quaedam*. All the editors had corrupted this passage by reading *terribilis quidem*.

We pass over many similar corruptions of the editors in order to come to a conspicuous one found in homily 8, no. 24, where the faith concerning Christ’s divinity is plainly placed in jeopardy, as will become clear from the note on that passage.

Of the remaining 1171 homilies of the first book we shall make no further selections. From the second book, however, we shall note one passage, namely homily 1—formerly numbered 13—no. 3: *et lunam sanctam Ecclesiam*, where Gussanville has *et unam sanctam Ecclesiam*.

From these few examples it can easily be understood how much correction the other passages required. This correction was supplied by the manuscript codices, which we shall now enumerate.

## X.

First must be mentioned the very ancient Corbie Codex, now in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, marked 161 and written in Merovingian letters. It is believed to surpass even the age of Charlemagne, indeed that of King Pepin, since these ancient characters gave way to Roman ones in their time. This codex contains the first book of the homilies. It will be designated by the name C. Germanensis, to distinguish it from another very ancient Corbie codex and from two other Germanensis codices, which we designate as Codices 2, 3, and 4 and cite together with the manuscripts.

The fifth is the distinguished codex of the Church of Laon, exceptionally venerable for its antiquity; it contains only the second book.

The sixth place belongs to the Gemeticensis codex, seven hundred years old, which contains both books complete.

The book of the Church of Évreux; the Uticensis, or that of the monastery of Saint-Ebrulf; the Sagiensis, namely that of the monastery of Saint Martin; the Becensis; the Lyranus; and the codex of the Rouen monastery of Blessed Mary of the Good News are believed to have been written around the eleventh century, or at least at the beginning of the twelfth. In these parchment manuscripts all the homilies mentioned above are found, except for a few leaves, either erased or torn from the Rouen exemplar. All these codices differ little from one another. The Uticensis often supplies a great many readings, written either by the same hand or by a different but ancient one.

From the celebrated library of the monastery of Saint John at Soissons we obtained for use a codex of excellent quality. Against it we also collated all those homilies, as well as against two others: one from Longpont, of the Cistercian order, and another from Clairvaux, of the same order.

Finally, we obtained the variant readings of the English codices from Thomas James, who made them public together with the other materials relating to Gregory’s works, as we have already noted. “In collating Ezekiel,” James says, “four manuscript codices assisted me.” He then lists them: two from the library of Merton College, one from the Bodleian Library, and another from the library of Balliol College.

In addition to collating so many codices, we also made use of the older Paris editions of 1502 and 1518, the Gilot edition, the Vatican edition, and finally the most recent edition of Gussanville.

## XI.

In the Soissons, Laon, and Longpont codices, we encountered a great deal of material belonging to homily 9 of the second book, formerly numbered 21. Since it is found neither in any of the printed editions nor in any other manuscripts known to us, we hesitated to insert it into the text. Nevertheless, because it is not inconsistent with Gregory’s style, we have judged that it should be recorded here. It could not easily have been contained in the very brief notes appended at the foot of the columns.

In no. 1 of the aforementioned homily, after the words “Now, therefore, when two tables are described,” the following is added in the codices mentioned:

> “And again, in the outer vestibule four tables are said to be present. It is now clearly stated that around the inner gate there were two vestibules; between them, as we have said, stood the inner gate of the north. Thus the inner gate in the inner vestibule is described as having two tables along each side, and similarly two in the outer vestibule. Four tables on this side and four on that side therefore make eight in all, since two are described on each side in the inner vestibule and two on each side in the outer one. These things, therefore,” and so forth,

up to “ignorance does not restrict,” where no. 1 ends, as in the printed editions. In the manuscripts the following is added:

> “For when one gate—that is, the inner gate—is described as standing between two vestibules, the outer gate is also silently brought to mind; within it the vestibule before the inner gate is said to be located. We must therefore no longer discuss one gate, but both. They can,” and so forth.

From the words in no. 4, “which proceeds toward the north,” the manuscript codices have the following:

> “For when he mentions an ascent, he designates the inner gate of the north, through which we have already said that the holy Church and the New Testament are symbolized. Its outer side was the Synagogue, from which faith in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ began.
>
> “And truly the faithful people found the door of understanding in the holy Church, which is said to proceed toward the north because it gathers from the Gentiles the multitude of believers out of the torpor of coldness and iniquity.
>
> “The inner gate therefore has an outer side—that is, the holy Church has the Synagogue; it has a door—that is, the understanding of the heavenly kingdom; and it proceeds toward the north because it does not despise sinners, but mercifully attends to them by receiving them into repentance.
>
> “Let it be said that there are four tables on this side and four tables on that side along the sides of the 1172 gate. For while faith and life, patience and kindness are guarded in the inner understanding, our gate has four tables in the inner vestibule. In it, while from the front side of the earlier period we behold the teaching of the Law and the prophecies, and consider in the carnal people the bonds that circumcision and sacrifice represented, four tables are likewise displayed, as it were, on the other side, outside in the vestibule. These things,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

In the Longpont codex, after the words “mercifully attends to them,” the following continues:

> “Let it rightly be said that it proceeds toward the north. For in the outer custody the letter of the Law was held. The door of the gate, however, is the historical understanding of the Law itself, which leads to the fear of the Lord.
>
> “This gate is said to proceed toward the north because that same Law, under the fear of threats, constricted the cold hearts of the Jewish people. For that people would have run, as it were, through warmth, if it had observed the Lord’s commandments out of love; but because it guarded the letter under the fear of the threatened death, it remained, as it were, in the torpor of coldness.
>
> “Hence it is said to the new peoples, who love eternal rewards rather than fear temporal punishments, and who are already burning with warmth: ‘For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, Abba, Father.’ Let it be said, then: ‘Four tables on this side,’ and so forth.”

These passages are certainly either Gregory’s own or very similar to Gregory’s. The earlier context—“and again,” and so forth—provided an opportunity for omission in the other handwritten codices, as may be inferred from the word *describuntur*, which immediately precedes it and is repeated twice within a few lines. For, having passed over the first *describuntur* together with what follows, the copyist carelessly lowered his eyes to the second occurrence and copied what came below rather than what came above.

We hesitate to preface this with anything more, lest time that could be spent more profitably in turning over and continually consulting Gregory be wasted on reading our little writings.

# THE TWO BOOKS OF HOMILIES OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, ON THE PROPHET EZEKIEL

[Note: [Col. 0785B] The most ancient C. Germanensis manuscript: “Here begins the book of the homilies of the blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome. Explanation of the holy prophet Ezekiel.” The most ancient Corbie manuscript: “On the blessed Ezekiel.” The Becensis and Lyranus have “Zezekiel.” The Rouen, Uticensis, and Gemeticensis have “Ezekiel.”] (C)

# BOOK ONE

1173

## Preface

[Col. 0785A]

To the most beloved brother, [Note: [Col. 0785B] In Gussanville’s edition, supported by the Longpont manuscript, “Marinian.” We follow the Corbie, C. Germanensis, and the other older manuscripts.] Marinian, bishop, Gregory, bishop, [Note: [Col. 0785B] In the plural the words “servant,” and so forth, are omitted. They are found in the Germanensis and other manuscripts of better quality.] servant of the servants of God.

The homilies [Note: [Col. 0785B] C. Germanensis: “The homilies which [were delivered] on the blessed prophet Ezekiel, before [the people],” omitting “as I spoke,” which almost all the manuscripts have and ought to have.] that were taken down as I spoke before the people on the blessed prophet Ezekiel I had left forgotten, overwhelmed by many cares. [Note: [Col. 0786B] Clairvaux: “in oblivion.”] But after eight years, at the request of the brothers, I took pains to seek out the scribes’ notes and, running through them with the Lord’s favor, corrected them as far as 1174 the pressures of tribulation allowed. [Col. 0786B] [Note: [Col. 0786B] Longpont: “in difficulties.”]

Your affection had asked that these be sent to you for reading. But I considered it very inappropriate that one who clearly drinks continually from the deep and lucid streams of the blessed Fathers Ambrose and Augustine should drink from contemptible water. [Col. 0785B] Yet again, when I reflect that even amid daily delicacies lower-quality foods often taste pleasant, I have sent lesser fare to one who reads better things, so that, while the coarser food is taken as though to relieve satiety, he may return more eagerly to finer banquets.

# FIRST HOMILY

*The holy Doctor, about to expound the prophet, first speaks about the times and modes of prophecy.*

[Col. 0786A]

### 1.

About to speak of the prophet Ezekiel under the inspiration of almighty God, I must first set forth the times and modes of prophecy, so that when its manner of approach has been shown, its power may be better understood.

There are three times of prophecy: past, present, and future. But it must be understood that in two of these times prophecy loses its etymology. [Note: [Col. 0786B] Évreux and the others of Normandy: “it does not possess its etymology.”] For since prophecy is so called because it foretells the future, when it speaks about the past or the present it loses the rationale of its name, [Note: [Col. 0786B] Évreux and the other Norman manuscripts: “because it does not proclaim what is to come.” Sagiensis and Germanensis: “it is not revealed.” Soissons, Longpont, Clairvaux: “it does not prophesy.” Gemeticensis and Lyranus: “it is not prophesied.”] because it does not reveal 1175 what is to come, but either recalls things that have already happened or speaks of things that are happening.

Nevertheless, we speak more accurately of these three times of prophecy [Col. 0786B] [Note: [Col. 0786B] Most manuscripts: “if these [three times] of Sacred Scripture …”] if we demonstrate them from the testimonies of Sacred Scripture.

Prophecy concerning the future is: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14).

Prophecy concerning the past is: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). For a human being spoke of that time when no human being existed.

[Col. 0787A]

Prophecy concerning the present is when the apostle Paul says: “But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all; for the secrets of his heart are made manifest, and thus, falling on his face, he will adore God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Corinthians 14:24). [Note: [Col. 0787D] Évreux and most Norman manuscripts: “and let the unbeliever enter the Church.”] [Note: [Col. 0787D] The word “for” is omitted in C. Germanensis and Soissons. It agrees with the Greek source, and so reads: “the secrets.”]

When it is said, “The secrets of his heart are made manifest,” it is plainly shown that through this mode the spirit of prophecy does not foretell what is to come, but reveals what is.

But in what sense is it called the spirit of prophecy when it indicates nothing future but relates what is present? Here we must observe that something is rightly called prophecy not because it foretells future events, but because it reveals hidden things. Just as time removes from our eyes in the future any event that is going to occur, so in the present a cause removes a thought from our eyes by hiding it in the heart.

A future event is hidden in future time, while a present thought is concealed in a hidden heart. There is also prophecy concerning the present when some matter is concealed not by the mind but by a distant place, yet is unveiled through the spirit. The mind of the prophet is present there where the body is not present. For Gehazi had withdrawn far from the prophet when he received the gifts of Naaman the Syrian; yet that same prophet said to him: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?” (2 Kings 5:26). [Note: [Col. 0787D] Corrupt in Gussanville: “from the course.”]

### 2.

It must also be understood that the times of prophecy harmonize with one another as evidence, so that sometimes the past is proved from the future and sometimes the future from the past.

Moses had said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). But who would believe that he was speaking truthfully about the past if he had not also said something about the future? For at the very end of that book whose beginning contained his statement about the past, he mingled a prophecy about future events through the voice of Jacob, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10). [Note: [Col. 0788D] Soissons and Longpont: “from his thigh.”]

Through himself also he prophesied to the people he was leading about the same one who was to be sent, saying: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him. But whoever will not listen to that prophet shall be exterminated from his people” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

Why, then, did he mix future events with past ones, unless so that, when the things he foretold about the future were fulfilled, he might also show that what he had said about the past was true?

### 3.

Since we have therefore taught how past events are proved by the prophecy of the future, it remains for us to show from the sacred utterances how, within the same spirit of prophecy, future events are proved from the past.

Certainly, when the Babylonian king had seen a dream (Daniel 2:2), he sent for the magicians and diviners and summoned all the wise men of Babylon. He asked them not only for the interpretation of the dream but also for the dream itself, so that from what had already happened he might determine whether their answers contained anything certain about the future.

Since they were wholly unable to say it, Daniel was 1176 brought forward. Asked both for the interpretation and for the account of the dream, he answered not only what he had been questioned about but also recounted the dream’s origin, saying: “You, O king, began to think on your bed what would happen after these things” (ibid., 29). A little later: “You, O king, were looking, and behold, as it were a single great statue” (ibid., 31), and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0788D] “As it were” is absent from Gemeticensis.]

As soon as he had stated the sequence of that dream, he disclosed everything that was to follow from it. Let us therefore consider the order of prophecy. From thoughts he came to the dream; from the dream he proceeded to the future. Thus, by bringing forth, so to speak, the very root of the dream, he proved from the past how true were the things he would say about the future.

Prophecy concerning the present needs the testimony neither of the past nor of the future, because when a hidden matter is disclosed through prophetic words, the matter itself that is revealed bears witness to its truth.

### 4.

Since we have discussed the times of prophecy, it remains to say something about its modes and qualities.

The spirit of prophecy touches the prophet’s mind neither always nor in the same way. Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the prophet’s mind concerning the present but does not touch it concerning the future; sometimes it touches it concerning the future but not concerning the present. Sometimes it touches it concerning both the present and the future. At other times the prophet’s mind is touched simultaneously concerning the past, the present, and the future.

Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches it concerning the past but not concerning the future; sometimes it touches it concerning the future but not concerning the past. Sometimes it touches it partly concerning the present and partly does not touch it; sometimes it touches it partly concerning the future and partly does not touch it.

Let us, if we can, demonstrate these cases from the testimonies of Sacred Scripture in the order just set out.

### 5.

The spirit of prophecy touches the prophet’s mind concerning the present but not concerning the future, as when John the Baptist, seeing the Lord coming, said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

But when he was already about to die, he sent disciples to ask: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matthew 11:3).

These words show that he knew the Redeemer had indeed come upon earth, but doubted whether he would descend by himself to open the bars of hell. He had been touched concerning the present through the spirit of prophecy: seeing the Mediator’s humanity and understanding his divinity, he confessed the Lamb who would take away the sins of the world. [Note: [Col. 0788D] Longpont: “who takes away sin.”] But he had not been touched concerning the future, because he did not know of his descent into hell.

### 6.

Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the prophet’s mind concerning the future but not concerning the present, as the history of Genesis clearly testifies when Isaac sent his son Esau out to hunt (Genesis 27:3 and following). Rebecca substituted her younger son for the blessing; dressed in goatskins, he made his brother’s body seem to his father’s touch.

Isaac gave the younger son, as though he were the elder, the blessing 1177 and foretold what would happen to him far in the future; but he could not know who it was that stood before him. [Note: [Col. 0789D] Soissons: “the father foretold future things to him.”]

The spirit of prophecy therefore touched the prophet’s mind concerning the future but did not touch it concerning the present, when the father, with clouded eyes, foretold future things but did not recognize the son who was present.

### 7.

Sometimes it touches the prophet’s mind equally concerning the present and the future. We are clearly taught this from the same book of Genesis (Genesis 48).

There it is written that, when Jacob was already approaching the end of his life, Joseph had his two sons stand before him, so that through his blessing they might obtain things far in the future. [Note: [Col. 0789D] C. Germanensis: “placing the younger on the right and the elder ... on the left,” contrary to the account of Sacred Scripture.] He placed the elder on his right and the younger on his left (ibid., 10).

Although, with his eyes dimmed by old age, he could not by ordinary sight distinguish which of his grandsons was the elder and which the younger, he crossed his arms and placed his right hand on the younger and his left hand on the elder.

When the son tried to correct him, saying, “Not so, father, for this one is the firstborn,” he heard: “I know, my son, I know. This one too shall become a people and shall be multiplied, but his younger brother shall be greater than he” (ibid., 18–19).

The spirit of prophecy therefore touched the prophet’s mind concerning both the present and the future, when Jacob foretold what was to come and, through the spirit, distinguished as standing before him those whom he could not see with his bodily eyes.

In the same way the spirit of prophecy touched the mind of the prophet Ahijah concerning both the present and the future. Although his eyes were dim, he recognized the woman who pretended to be someone else as the wife of Jeroboam, and disclosed everything that would happen to her, saying:

> “Enter, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another woman? I have been sent to you with a harsh message. Go and say to Jeroboam: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you have done evil beyond all who were before you, and have made for yourself foreign gods and molten images, provoking me to anger, while you have cast me behind your back, therefore I shall bring evils upon the house of Jeroboam” (1 Kings 14:6).

[Note: [Col. 0789D] Many of the printed editions, which the editors follow, have “Therefore the prophet’s mind was touched concerning the present.” [Col. 0790D] We adhere to the older manuscripts, C. Germanensis, Corbie, and others.]

His prophetic mind had been touched equally concerning the present and the future, since he was able to detect the woman entering and announce to her what would happen.

### 8.

Sometimes the prophet’s mind is touched simultaneously concerning the past, the present, and the future. Thus Elizabeth, seeing Mary come to her, recognized that she was carrying the incarnate Word in her womb and already called her the mother of her Lord, saying: “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

Concerning her conception, it is also said to Joseph through the angel: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20). Elizabeth said: “Blessed is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (Luke 1:45).

By saying, “Blessed is she who believed,” she plainly indicates that through the spirit she recognized the angel’s words that had been spoken to Mary. Then, by adding, “The things spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled,” she foresaw what would follow her in the future.

Thus she was touched through the spirit of prophecy concerning the past, the present, and the future at once: she recognized that Mary had believed the angel’s promises; by calling her “mother,” she understood that she was carrying the Redeemer of the human race in her womb; and by foretelling that all things would be fulfilled, she perceived what would also follow in the future.

### 9.

1178

Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the mind concerning the past but not concerning the future, as is plainly shown in the apostle Paul, who says to the disciples:

> “I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was preached by me, because it is not according to man. For I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:11).

Elsewhere too he says to the disciples: “According to revelation the mystery was made known to me” (Ephesians 3:3).

Yet, when he was going up to Jerusalem to preach this very Gospel that he had learned through revelation, he said: “And now, behold, bound by the Spirit, I go to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there” (Acts 20:22).

This is the mystery of the Gospel: that the Father’s Only-Begotten became incarnate and was made perfect man; that he was crucified, died, and was buried; that on the third day he rose again; that on the fortieth day he ascended into heaven; and that he sits at the right hand of the Father.

Paul, then, who recognized the Gospel through revelation, was touched by the spirit of prophecy concerning the past. But because he did not know what he would suffer for that Gospel, he was certainly not touched concerning the future.

For he says: “Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and tribulations await me in Jerusalem” (ibid., 23). [Note: [Col. 0790D] “In Jerusalem” is absent from C. Germanensis, Corbie, Soissons, Clairvaux, and many Norman manuscripts.]

He plainly shows that what was to happen to him had been revealed about him to others, but not to him about himself, as it is said concerning him through Agabus: “The man whose belt this is must be bound in Jerusalem” (Acts 21:11).

### 10.

Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the mind concerning the future but not concerning the past, as is shown by an act of Elisha.

When one of the sons of the prophets was cutting wood, the iron of his axe fell into the water. He cried out: “Alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing.” [Note: [Col. 0790D] Thus C. Germanensis, Corbie, Soissons, and Clairvaux. The printed editions have “I had borrowed it.”]

The man of God said: “Where did it fall?” He showed him the place. Then he cut a piece of wood, threw it there, and the iron floated (2 Kings 6:5).

From this deed of the prophet it is understood that the one who asked where the iron had fallen knew what he was going to do, but that, in asking, he clearly did not know where the iron had fallen.

The spirit of prophecy had therefore touched Elisha’s mind concerning the future but not concerning the past. He knew that he would bring the iron, sunk in the depths, back to the surface, but he had no knowledge at all of where it had fallen.

### 11.

Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the present only in part and does not touch it in part. The history of the apostle Peter bears witness to this.

When soldiers sent by Cornelius came to him, the Spirit announced them to him. For it is written: “And the Spirit said to him: Behold, three men are seeking you.” [Note: [Col. 0791D] Longpont and Soissons add: “Rise, go down, and go with them.”]

He went down to them and asked: “For what reason have you come?” (Acts 10:20).

His words show that he had not learned through the Spirit the very reason that he was asking from the soldiers. The Spirit therefore touched Peter’s mind concerning the present in part and did not touch it in part: it told him that the soldiers were present but concealed the reason for which they had come.

### 12.

Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the future in part and does not touch it in part, as when the sons of the prophets said to Elisha concerning Elijah’s being taken away:

> “Do you know that today the Lord will take away your master from you?” (2 Kings 2:3, 5).

Yet after he had been taken away, they scattered in different directions 1179 and searched for him among the rocks and valleys.

The spirit of prophecy had therefore touched their minds concerning the future in part and did not touch them in part: they knew that the one who was to be taken away would be taken away, but they sought him as though he could still be found.

They were touched in part and not touched in part because they knew that he could be taken away but did not know that he could not be found.

Elisha too was touched by the spirit of prophecy concerning the future in part and not touched in part when he said to the king of Israel: “Strike the earth with an arrow.” When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God became angry with him and said:

> “If you had struck five or six times, or seven times, you would have struck Syria to destruction; but now you shall strike it three times” (2 Kings 13:18–19). [Note: [Col. 0791D] Soissons, Longpont, Clairvaux: “until its destruction.”]

He therefore knew that he would strike Syria as many times as he struck the earth. But when he said to him, “Strike the earth,” he did not know how many times he would strike it, since he was angry that the earth had been struck a third time. [Note: [Col. 0791D] Soissons: “who certainly knew”; this would be preferable were it not that “therefore” is found in the Corbie and Germanensis manuscripts and in almost all handwritten and printed codices.]

It is therefore clear that he had been touched concerning the future in part and not touched in part: he foretold that Syria would be struck, but he wanted the earth to be struck more times.

In the same way, when Samuel was sent by the Lord to anoint David, he replied: “How shall I go? Saul will hear of it and kill me” (1 Samuel 16:2). He anointed David, and yet he was not killed by Saul. The prophet’s mind had therefore been touched concerning the future in part and not touched in part: he knew that David was to be anointed as king, but he did not know that he would not be killed by Saul. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The printed editions have “to anoint.”]

### 13.

It must also be understood that some prophets are touched concerning what is near at hand but are not touched concerning what is distant; others are touched concerning what is distant but are not touched concerning what is near; and still others are touched by the spirit of prophecy concerning both what is distant and what is near.

Some are touched concerning what is near and not concerning what is distant, as Samuel knew that the asses had been lost and announced that they had been found, and foretold that Saul would become king (1 Samuel 9:15, 20). He also announced that David would succeed him in his kingdom, but he did not foretell that David would be the father of the Eternal King (1 Samuel 16:12).

Others are touched concerning what is distant but not concerning what is near, as that same David knew that God’s Only-Begotten would become incarnate. Speaking of Judea, he said: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5). He understood that this one would ascend to heaven and sit at the right hand of the Father, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 110:1).

Yet he did not foresee many things that happened close at hand. To mention a few among many: he did not understand that the servant Ziba was lying against his master Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16:3–4). [Note: [Col. 0792D] So C. Germanensis, the Norman manuscripts, and others; the printed editions read *Sibam contra* (“Ziba against …”), Ziba being the name of Mephibosheth’s servant.]

And when he promised Amasa, he said: “May God do this to me, and add this also, if you shall not be commander of the army before me forever in place of Joab” (ibid. 19:13), plainly unaware of what would follow, since Amasa not only did not assume command of the army in place of Joab but shortly afterward ended his life at Joab’s hand (ibid. 20:10).

And when he wished to build a temple for God, not knowing what would follow close at hand, he consulted another prophet (ibid. 7:3).

14. Some are touched both from afar and from near, as Isaiah foretells far in advance things that were to come, saying: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14). Again he says of him: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (ibid. 9:6). [Note: Suession and Longip: “Who also, having been touched near at hand by the spirit of prophecy concerning King Hezekiah …” Gussanville, altering the reading of both manuscripts and editions, has “was touched because … he foretold that he would rise.”] He also, having been touched near at hand by the spirit of prophecy concerning King Hezekiah, foretold that he would recover from his illness and announced how many years he would live after his illness (ibid. 38:5).

15. Sometimes, however, the spirit of prophecy is absent from the prophets and is not always present to their minds, so that when they do not possess it, they may recognize that when they do possess it, they have it as a gift. Thus, when Elisha forbade Gehazi the servant to pull away from his feet the weeping Shunammite woman, he said: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has concealed it from me and has not told me” (2 Kings 4:27). Likewise, when Jehoshaphat asked him about future events and the spirit of prophecy was lacking in him, he had a minstrel brought in, so that the spirit of prophecy might descend upon him through the praise of psalmody and fill his mind with knowledge of what was to come (ibid. 3:11, 15). For when the voice of psalmody is produced with concentration of heart, through it a path is prepared for the omnipotent Lord to reach the heart, so that he may pour into the attentive mind either the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction. Hence it is written: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psalm 49:23). What is called *salvation* in Latin is called *Jesus* in Hebrew. In the sacrifice of praise, therefore, a way is made for the manifestation of Jesus, because while compunction is poured out through psalmody, a path is made for us in the heart, by which at the end we reach Jesus, just as he himself speaks of his manifestation, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). Hence also it is written: “Sing to the Lord, chant a psalm to his name; make a way for him who rises above the setting; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 67:5). For he rises above the setting who, by rising again, trampled down death. When we sing to him, we make a way for him to come to our heart and kindle us with the grace of his love.

[Note: C. German, Suession, Longipont, and Vallicelliana read *fit in Jesu* (“a way is made in Jesus”). The preceding words—“a way is prepared for the Lord to the heart”—and the following—“we make a way, so that he may come to our heart”—show that our reading is preferable.]

[Note: Longipont and Suession read *infunditur* (“is poured in”). We read *effunditur* (“is poured out”) in C. German and the older manuscripts.]

Since the spirit of prophecy is not always present to the prophets, this is also indicated by the man of God who, sent against Samaria, announced the evils that were to come upon it (1 Kings 13). Yet, having been forbidden by the Lord to eat on the way, he was deceived by the persuasion of a false prophet (ibid. 13:18–19). [Note: The editions, against the manuscripts, read *prophetae falsa persuasione* (“by a prophet’s false persuasion”).] A deceitful speech would not have deceived him if he had possessed the spirit of prophecy as a present gift.

16. It must also be understood that sometimes, when holy prophets are consulted, through long practice in prophesying they bring forth certain things from their own spirit and suppose that they are saying these things from the spirit of prophecy. But because they are holy, they are quickly corrected by the Holy Spirit; they hear from him what is true and reproach themselves for having spoken falsely. For who does not know that the prophet Nathan was a holy man? He openly reproved King David for his sin and announced what would come upon him because of that sin. Yet when David asked him whether he might build a temple for God, Nathan immediately replied: “Go and do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you” (2 Samuel 7:3). Concerning this, it is immediately added there: “But it happened that night, and behold, the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: Go and speak to my servant David. Thus says the Lord God: Will you build me a house to dwell in? For I have not dwelt in a house from the day when I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt until this day” (ibid. 4). A little later: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I will establish his kingdom; he shall build a house for my name” (ibid. 12–13). Behold, the prophet Nathan had first said to the king, “Go and do it”; afterward, taught by the spirit of prophecy, he declared that it could not be done and contradicted both the king’s plans and his own words, because he recognized that what he had said from his own spirit was false.

[Note: Vallicelliana, Longipont, and Lyra read *reprehendit* (“he reproached”), rather than *deprehendit* (“he discovered”).]

17. In this matter there is the following difference between true and false prophets: if true prophets ever say something from their own spirit, they promptly correct it in the minds of their hearers, having been taught by the Holy Spirit. False prophets, however, both announce falsehoods and, being alien from the Holy Spirit, persist in their falsehood.

18. Having considered, then, the times and modes of prophecy, it is pleasing to contemplate how almighty God, for the advancement of human beings, dispenses the restraints of his anger. The Israelite people had sinned against their Creator and therefore were serving the king of Babylon in captivity. Yet the prophet Ezekiel was sent into captivity with them (Ezekiel 3:11), and divine grace had made him so pleasing to God that through him God foretold all that was to come and deigned to console the mind of the afflicted people.

Let us consider, if we can, how great is the dispensation of heavenly compassion: the Lord was angry with his people, yet was not angry with them in every respect. For if he had not been angry, he would not have handed the people over to captivity; and if he had been angry in every respect, he would not have sent his elect into captivity with them. But divine mercy acts in such a way that from one and the same event—from the event by which it gives the carnal a scourge—it grants the spiritual an increase of virtue. While he purifies the former through tribulation, he stirs the latter, through their association with those in tribulation, to merit greater things. Thus he is angry with the unjust while nevertheless consoling their hearts through the fellowship of the just, lest, if he were to abandon them entirely, no one should return to pardon after his sins.

He repels by holding fast, and holds fast by repelling, when he sends into tribulation together with those whom he judges those whom he loves. Who could be sufficient to weigh the depths of such great compassion? The Lord does not leave the people’s sins without punishment, yet he does not utterly repel the sinful people from himself.

Thus, when Moses sent twelve explorers to the land of promise (Numbers 13), and ten of them afterward caused the people to despair, the same people, inflamed by the anger of their murmuring, complained that they had been led away from the Lord, so that their corpses might lie in the wilderness (ibid. 14). [Note: Vallicelliana reads “so that the corpses of those people might lie.”] The omnipotent God, angry with them, said that none of them would enter the land of promise (ibid.). Struck by this terror, they recognized that they had acted wickedly, afflicted themselves with tears, and, girded with weapons, immediately began to go up against the enemies, so that after their tears they might be able to enter the land of promise (ibid. 14:42).

Through Moses the Lord said to them: “Tell them: Do not go up, and do not fight, for I am not with you, lest you fall before your enemies” (Deuteronomy 1:42). In this matter we must consider: if he was not with them, why did he forbid them to go up lest they fall? But if he was with them, what does it mean that he said, “I am not with you”? Yet through a wondrous dispensation of discipline and mercy, he was both with them and was not with them. He was not with them so that they might conquer, but he was with them nevertheless so that they might not perish at the hands of their enemies.

O ineffable depths of compassion! He pursues sins, yet protects sinners. He shows himself angry, yet defends them from their enemies. So a mother often becomes angry with a little son who has done wrong; she reproves, scolds, and beats him. But if she sees him rushing headlong toward danger, where he is about to fall into mortal peril, she stretches out her hand and holds him back. Though she beat him in anger as if she did not love him, she holds him back in love as if she had not beaten him in anger.

[Note: Gussanville reads *retrahit* (“withdraws”), contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and to the other printed editions. A little later, the earlier editions read *diligenter* (“carefully”), whereas C. German, Corbie, Suession, Normandy, and others read *diligendo* (“by loving”).]

19. Conversing about these matters in this brief preface, we have, as it were, exercised our vessel within the harbor, so that afterward we may spread our sails toward investigating the mysteries of prophecy as though into the immensity of the sea. Yet we do not presume upon our own strength, but upon him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, because “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wisdom 1:7). For the omnipotent God is the Word of the omnipotent Father, and we who desire to speak about him shall in no way be mute in him. May the omnipotent Word, who for us became incarnate and lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, give useful words, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY II

The first five verses of the prophecy of Ezekiel are expounded according to its various senses, especially the allegorical and moral senses.

[Col. 0795C]

1183 1. It is customary in prophetic speech first to describe the person, time, and place, and afterward to begin to speak the mysteries of prophecy, so that, in order to establish the truth more firmly, it may first set down the root of the historical account and afterward bring forth the fruits of the Spirit through signs and allegories. Accordingly, Ezekiel indicates the time of his life, saying:

**Ezekiel 1:1.**—“And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month.”

Also indicating the place, he adds:

**Ibid.**—“When I was in the midst of the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.”

He also indicates the time of the captivity, adding:

[Note: Almost all the manuscripts, except the oldest C. German and Corbie manuscripts, read “he also indicates the time of the captivity.”]

**Verse 2.**—“On the fifth day of the month—which was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin.”

And, to indicate the person clearly, he also narrates his lineage, when it is added:

**Verse 3.**—“And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel the son of Buzi, the priest.”

[Col. 0796A]

2. But a first question arises for us: Why does he who had not yet said anything begin in this way, saying, “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year”? For *and* is a conjunction, and we know that a following expression is joined only to a preceding expression. Since, then, he had said nothing, why does he say, “And it came to pass,” when there is no preceding speech to which what he begins might be attached?

In this matter we must observe that just as we see bodily things, so the prophets see spiritual things; and those things that appear absent because of our ignorance are present to them. [Note: The editions read *prophetae sensu* (“by the prophet’s perception”), against the manuscripts C. German, Corbie, Ebroicensis, and others, which read *prophetae sensus* (“the perceptions of the prophets”).] Consequently, in the minds of the prophets outward things are joined to inward things, so that they see both together, and in them both the word that they hear inwardly and what they say outwardly come to be at the same time.
