The reason is therefore evident why he who had said nothing began by saying, “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year.” He joined this word, which he brought forth outwardly, to the word that he had heard inwardly. He therefore connected the words he uttered with the inner vision, and for this reason he begins by saying, “And it came to pass.” He adds what he is beginning to speak outwardly as though what he sees inwardly were also present outwardly.

3. The statement that he received the spirit of prophecy in his thirtieth year indicates something that we ought to consider: namely, that, according to the ordinary use of reason, the word of teaching is not supplied except in mature age. Hence the Lord himself, in the twelfth year of his age, wished to be found sitting among the teachers in the temple—not teaching, but asking questions (Luke 2:46). Thus, so that human beings would not dare to preach at an immature age, he who by his divinity always teaches the angels in heaven deigned, in the twelfth year of his age, to question human beings on earth.

For he himself is the Wisdom of God, and the angels live by seeing him, being satisfied with eternal blessedness.

[Note: Normandy and the Anglic manuscript read “they drink.” We have preferred the reading of C. German, Corbie, Vallicelliana, and others, which is also that of the editions: “they are satisfied with eternal blessedness.” The other reading is nevertheless supported by the phrase “they are satisfied with eternal blessedness.”]

Moses also admonishes us through the mystery of allegory, saying: “You shall not plow with the firstborn of an ox” (Deuteronomy 15:19). By the firstborn of an ox we understand the good work of our first period, when our age is immature.

[Note: Ebroicensis reads “in immaturity.”]

Yet one must not plow in that condition. For while the first periods of our adolescence or youth are passing, we must still refrain from preaching, so that the plowshare of our tongue may not dare to cleave the soil of another’s heart. For as long as we are weak, we must contain ourselves within ourselves, lest, by displaying tender virtues too soon, we lose them. Planted shrubs, too, if they have not first taken root in the earth, quickly wither when touched by a hand; but once they have firmly rooted, a hand touches them without harm, and winds drive against them without injuring them.

Walls that have been built, if pushed, collapse unless they have first been dried by their own moisture. Thus, until the mind has been thoroughly dried of the moisture of its wickedness, it must not be touched by the hand of another’s tongue, lest, before it fully receives strength, it lose its firmness; lest, when shaken, it fall; lest, like a shrub without roots, it wither while being disturbed beyond what it can endure.

Therefore, only those things that are firm should be displayed as examples. The mind must first grow strong, and afterward be shown for the benefit of its neighbors, once it can neither collapse when lifted up by praise nor wither when struck by blame. For although it is said to Timothy, “Command and teach these things; let no one despise your youth” (1 Timothy 4:11–12), it must be understood that in sacred speech youth is sometimes called adolescence.

[Note: Vallicelliana reads: “It must be understood that his adolescence was in years, not in conduct, although in sacred speech it is sometimes …” This is a gloss absent from the ancient manuscripts C. German, Corbie, Gemet, and others.]

Hence it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Ecclesiastes 11:9).

[Note: The editions, contrary to the manuscript evidence, read *profecto* (“certainly”), which destroys the sense.]

Thus the prophet is described as being of mature age, so that it may be shown what authority he possesses in preaching, and so that everything appropriate to preaching may appear to agree with him in both life and spirit.

[Col. 0797B]

4. Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and Daniel (Daniel 13:45) received the spirit of prophecy as boys, since miracles must not be taken as examples for ordinary practice. For the omnipotent God both makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21) and perfects praise from the mouths of infants and nursing children (Psalm 8:3). But one thing is what we learn from the practice and discipline of teaching, and another is what we know from a miracle.

[Note: We follow the Anglic and Vallicelliana manuscripts. In Corbie, C. German, most manuscripts, and the editions, the reading is *dicimus* (“we say”), rather than *discimus* (“we learn”).]

5. If, however, it is asked whether something mystical is also signified in the very statement of that age, it is not absurd to say that the prophet shows by the time of his own age the Lord whom he announces in words. In the thirtieth year of the prophet Ezekiel, the heavens were opened, and he saw visions of the Lord beside the river Chebar, because, as if in the thirtieth year of his age, the Lord came to the river Jordan. There the heavens were opened, because the Spirit descended in the form of a dove; and a voice also sounded from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). [Note: The editions read *Jordanis* rather than *Jordanem*; the manuscripts are preferred. C. German reads “in whom I was well pleased.”]

[Note: The Vallicelliana manuscript reads “in the form of a dove.”]

6. The Hebrew words themselves also contribute greatly to the interpretation of the mystery. For *Chebar* is interpreted as “heaviness” or “gravity”; *Ezekiel*, “strength of God”; *Buzi*, “despised” or “contempt”; and *Chaldeans*, “those who take captive,” or “as it were, demons.”

Ezekiel therefore came beside the river Chebar. Since Chebar means “heaviness” or “gravity,” what is suitably signified by the river Chebar except the human race? It flows from its origin toward death and is burdensome to itself because of the sins that it both commits and bears, since, as it is written, “iniquity sits in a talent of lead” (Zechariah 5:7).

[Note: Longipont and Vallicelliana read “in a talent.”]

Every sin is heavy, for it does not permit the soul to rise to higher things. Hence the Psalmist also says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3). [Note: Normandy and Vallicelliana read *graves* (“heavy”).]

It is written of the Lord: “He is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:18). Ezekiel therefore came beside the river Chebar, because the strength of God deigned, through the mystery of his incarnation, to draw near to the human race, which bears the weight of its sins and flows daily from its origin toward death. Of this the Psalmist says: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the running waters” (Psalm 1:3). He was planted beside the running waters because he was incarnate beside the falls of the flowing peoples.

We have said that Ezekiel means “the strength of God,” and Buzi “despised.” But Ezekiel is the son of Buzi because the Only-Begotten of God deigned to become incarnate from that people whom the Lord despised because of the guilt of its faithlessness. The strength of God, therefore, is born from what is held in contempt or despised, because our Redeemer deigned to assume humanity from a faithless and despised people.

[Note: Normandy reads “from what is held in contempt or despised.”]

He came into the land of the Chaldeans. As we have said, Chaldeans are interpreted as “those who take captive,” or “as it were, demons.” The wicked are indeed those who take captive, since they themselves commit iniquities and, by persuading others, draw them into iniquity. They are rightly also interpreted as “as it were, demons,” because those who persuade others and drag them into iniquity take upon themselves, within themselves, the service of demons for iniquity, although they are not demons by nature.

Ezekiel, the strength of God, therefore came into the land of the Chaldeans because the Only-Begotten of the Father appeared among those who had themselves flowed down into sin and were drawing others captive into sins.

[Note: This is the reading of Normandy, Corbie German, and Longipont. Corbie and Vallicelliana have “from themselves”; the Paris edition of 1518 has “who took themselves captive”; other editions have “who by themselves.”]

But now let the course of the exposition return to the person of the prophet.

**Verse 3.**—“And the hand of the Lord was upon him there.”

[Col. 0798C]

7. The hand or arm of the Lord is called the Son, because through him all things were made. Of him the Psalmist also says: “Let your hand be made to save me” (Psalm 118:173). The hand of God, which through his divinity was not made but begotten, was made through his humanity, so that it might heal the wounds of the human race. There, therefore, the prophet recognized the incarnation of the Only-Begotten, where he saw the hand of the Lord made upon him.

But what follows here is:

1186 **Verse 4.**—“And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the North.”

8. We must observe the order of speech in the prophet’s words. Earlier he had said of himself: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.” Later, as though narrating about another, he adds: “And the hand of the Lord was made upon him there.” Then, as though returning to himself, he says: “And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the North.”

What does this mean—that Ezekiel now speaks, and now speaks about Ezekiel? If he spoke throughout about himself, there would be no question. If he spoke throughout as though about another, there would likewise be no question. What, then, does it mean that prophetic speech varies in this way, so that at one moment the prophet speaks about himself and at another he seems to speak about himself as though another were speaking?

It must be understood that those who are filled with the spirit of prophecy indicate, by sometimes speaking openly about themselves and sometimes uttering words about themselves as though about others, that it is not the prophet but the Holy Spirit who speaks through the prophet. Insofar as speech comes through them, they speak about themselves; but insofar as they speak under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, that same Holy Spirit speaks through them about them, as the Truth bears witness when it says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

Hence Moses also says: “Moses was the meekest man above all the men who dwelt upon the earth” (Numbers 12:3). By not saying “I was,” but “was,” he plainly indicates that another was the one speaking through him about him.

Hence John says: “He saw that disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 21:20). And Paul, to show that it was not he who was speaking, said: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Since, therefore, in prophetic speech one person presides and another serves, when the prophet speaks about himself, the person who serves is displayed; but when the Holy Spirit speaks through the prophet about the prophet, the majesty of the one who presides is revealed.

[Note: The words “about the prophet” are absent from C. German.]

It is therefore rightly said as though about another: “And the hand of the Lord was made upon him there”; and he immediately adds about himself: “And I saw, and behold, a whirlwind was coming from the North.”

We must now examine what he means when he says: “And behold, a whirlwind was coming from the North, and a great cloud.”

9. Since the north wind contracts things with cold, the name “North” suitably signifies the torpor of the malignant spirit. The prophet Isaiah also testifies to this, declaring that the devil said: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North” (Isaiah 14:13). The malignant spirit held the mountain of the covenant because he subjected the Jewish people, who had received the law, to himself in faithlessness. When the devil holds the hearts of teachers, he presides over the mountain of the covenant. He also sits on the sides of the North because he possesses human minds that have grown cold.

Hence, in the voice of the bridegroom, it is said in the Song of Songs: “Arise, North, and come, South; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs 4:16). [Note: Suession reads *ut fluant* (“that its spices may flow”).] When, at the Lord’s command, the cold spirit departs, the warm spirit occupies the minds of the faithful. He blows through God’s garden—that is, the holy Church—so that the reputation of its virtues may flow like spices into the knowledge of many.

When the North departs—that is, the malignant spirit—the Holy Spirit fills the mind like the South. When he blows upon it by warming it, immediately the spices of virtues flow from the hearts of the faithful.

The prophet, therefore, seeing what would come at the end, saw a whirlwind coming from the North, because at the end of the world the malignant spirit will occupy human minds more severely through the cold of their torpor. Hence it is written: “Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has a short time” (Revelation 12:12). The ancient adversary has intensified the efforts of his snares more severely in human minds.

Against his growing pride the humility of the incarnate God was manifested; and, in order to heal the human race of its weakness, the physician’s power appeared great when the sick person’s illness grew.

10. It is fitting that the sending of the malignant spirit is called a whirlwind. [Note: C. German and Corbie read *malignus Spiritus ventus* (“the wind of the malignant spirit”).] For a whirlwind overturns by shaking the building that it touches. Every temptation of the ancient enemy that takes place in the mind is a whirlwind, because by shaking the mind through desires it tears it away from the state of its uprightness.

But, setting aside for the moment what will happen at the end to the human race from the cunning enemy, let us turn our words to Judea alone, from which the prophet came and whose destruction he sees in prophecy. After the Lord’s incarnation, Judea endured the whirlwind from the North all the more severely because, shaken from its uprightness and falling, it remained cold in faithlessness through the torpor of its mind.

The whirlwind therefore came from the North when the malignant spirit shook the life of the Jewish people through temptation. And rightly it is added:

**Ibid.**—“And a great cloud.”

11. For the more fiercely anyone burns with cruelty, the more he deserves to be blinded in the darkness of his ignorance. They had awaited the Redeemer of the human race, understanding him in the Law and the Prophets; yet, when they saw him, they denied him. Thus it came about that a great cloud of their ignorance covered their minds, so that afterward they would not recognize the one whom they had previously been able both to proclaim and to refuse to love.

For when they saw at one moment his mighty deeds and miracles, and at another his sufferings, a great cloud had come from the North upon the hearts of unbelievers: because of the cold of their sin, they were darkened by the weakness of his Passion even amid the signs.

What followed from that darkness of the great cloud is added when he immediately says:

**Ibid.**—“And an enveloping fire.”

12. By the name of fire, when it is used symbolically, sometimes the Holy Spirit is signified, and sometimes the wickedness of the mind. Concerning the good fire it is written: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). Fire is cast upon the earth when an earthly mind, inspired by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, is burned away from its carnal desires.

Concerning the evil fire it is said: “And now fire will consume the adversaries” (Hebrews 10:27), because a wicked heart wastes away through its own malice.

[Note: Most Norman manuscripts read “consumes.”]

[Note: C. German, Ebroicensis, and Corbie read “is afraid.”]

Just as the fire of love lifts up the mind, so the fire of malice envelops it: the Holy Spirit raises the heart that he fills, while the heat of malice always bends it toward lower things.

Judea, therefore, blinded by the cloud of its ignorance, because it soon broke out into the wickedness of persecution, was enveloped in its own fire; through that same cruelty by which it burned, it entangled itself in the bondage of wickedness.

A whirlwind was coming from the North, and a great cloud, and an enveloping fire, because, brought from the cold of its torpor into the darkness of ignorance, it broke out at last into the malice of persecution.

Hence it is also said to another prophet: “What do you see?” He immediately replied: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the North” (Jeremiah 1:13). The mind of the Jews, raging in persecution and rolling up waves of thoughts in the malice of its cruelty—what else was it but a boiling pot? Its face is said to be from the face of the North because, if it had not submitted to the hostile spirit through the torpor of its mind, it would not have burned against the good with such great malice.

The enveloping fire therefore follows the cloud, because the cruelty of persecution followed the blindness of their minds. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

But this fire burned in one place and shone in another. For it is added:

**Ibid.**—“And a brightness around it.”

13. While persecution was taking place in Judea, the holy preaching of the apostles was scattered throughout the world, as they themselves say: “The word of God had been sent to you, but since you judge yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

From the cruelty of the malice that burned up the mind of Judea, therefore, the omnipotent God scattered light among the Gentiles. For by the fact that Judea persecuted its Redeemer and his members, while the holy apostles were scattered in various directions, we who dwelt in darkness around Judea saw, by the gift of heavenly grace, the brightness of the true light.

Hence it is written: “Light has arisen for those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Isaiah 9:2).

This fire of malice, therefore, which burned from the hearts of the Jews in persecution, before it afflicted the holy apostles in its fury, exercised itself against the very author and Redeemer of the human race.

[Note: Suession and Longipont read “which burned in the Jews.” The last manuscript has *mansit* (“remained”) instead of *arsit* (“burned”).]

Hence it is also added:

**Ibid.**—“And from the midst of it there was something resembling electrum, that is, from the midst of the fire.”

14. [Note: C. German: “What is the appearance of electrum?”]

What is designated by the appearance of electrum except Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5)? Electrum is made from gold and silver. When gold and silver are mixed in electrum, the silver increases in brightness, while the gold grows pale from its own radiance. The one advances toward brightness; the other is tempered in its brightness.

Because, therefore, in the Only-Begotten Son of God the nature of our humanity was united to the nature of divinity, in this union humanity grew into the glory of majesty, while divinity tempered itself to human eyes from the power of its own radiance. [Note: The same manuscript reads *in majestatis gloria* (“in the glory of majesty”).] Through the fact that human nature was made brighter, silver grew, as it were, through gold. And because divinity was tempered to our sight from its radiance, gold grew pale for us, as it were, through silver.

That immutable nature which, while remaining in itself, renews all things—if it had wished to appear to us just as it is, its radiance would have burned us rather than renewed us. But God tempered the brightness of his greatness to our eyes, so that, while his brightness was tempered for us, our weakness might also shine through its likeness in his light and, through the grace received, so to speak, change the color of its condition.

As electrum in the fire, therefore, God became human amid persecution. It follows:

**Verse 5.**—“And in the midst of it was the likeness of four living creatures.”

1189 15. Whether “in the midst of it” is understood of the electrum or of the fire makes no difference, because these four living creatures—the holy Evangelists—were both strengthened in the power of faith through the incarnation of that same Lord and afflicted by many tribulations in the fire of persecution.

[Col. 0802B]

16. If anyone wishes to apply what we have said about the Lord’s first coming also to his second coming, he should be followed with ready agreement, because the spirit of prophecy often sees many things together in what it says as one thing.

The whirlwind comes from the North because the cause of sins requires that the shaking of the strict judgment disturb all the elements together. The terror of the final disturbance is said to come from the place where it is generated. Since the disturbance of the final judgment takes place to strike the cold minds of sinners, the whirlwind is rightly said to come from the North.

That shaking is suitably called a whirlwind because on that day the hearts of all those who are then found in mortal flesh will be moved by immense fear. [Note: C. German, Suession, Longipont, and the editions read *commoventur* (“are moved”).]

When what is written begins to be fulfilled—“The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matthew 24:29)—what human mind will not fear the sentence of the eternal Judge?

For then all sins return together before the eyes; then everything that was done with delight is recalled to memory with terror; then the darkness of wretched thought arises from the punishment of imminent damnation.

Hence it is also added: “And a great cloud.” For then the darkness of blindness, arising from the memory of sins, presses down the mind’s understanding, when the reprobate are not permitted to behold the Only-Begotten Son of God in the form of his divinity. “For they will see him whom they pierced” (John 19:37; Zechariah 12:10). And: “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26:10).

There it is also openly added: “And an enveloping fire.” For that fire of judgment, which will burn the air-filled heaven and the earth, will not permit sinners to rise in their pride; rather, it will envelop them and undoubtedly crush them in the punishment of their damnation.

17. And radiance around him. For just as lightning comes out from the East and appears as far as the West, so will be the coming of the Son of Man (Matt. XXIV, 27). Then no one is permitted to hide from judgment within his mind, because he is penetrated by the very radiance of the Judge. [Note: [Col. 0802D] Most of the Norman witnesses, with Val. Cl., read “from the judge.” Others, with C. Germ., read “from judgment.”] [Note: [Col. 0802D] Norm., Longip., and Val. Cl. read “concerning whom the Judge is mentioned immediately.” This is a gloss absent from Germ. and other older witnesses. The printed editions have the worse reading, “concerning which the day of judgment is mentioned immediately.”]

Of this it is immediately added: And in its midst there was something like the appearance of electrum, that is, from the midst of fire. For our Redeemer, who presides over all the angels, archangels, and powers, remaining like electrum, one from and in both natures—God with the Father, and mortal with human beings for our redemption—will then be seen in his terror, and the fire of judgment will serve him in the punishment of the reprobate. Hence it is written: The Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire (I Cor. III, 13). Hence the Psalmist says: God manifestly will come, our God, and he will not be silent; fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him (Ps. XLIX, 3). Hence the apostle Peter says: The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire (II Pet. III, 10). And because then all the saints who have perfectly abandoned the world come as judges, it is aptly added immediately:

18. And in its midst was the likeness of four living creatures. For what are signified by the four living creatures except the four evangelists? Nor is it without reason that the number of all the perfect is expressed through the four evangelists, since all who are now perfect in the Church have learned the rectitude of their perfection through their Gospel. In its midst was the likeness of four living creatures, because those who have now followed perfect works according to the commands of the Gospel will then be seen united to his body, joined to his majesty, and made judges with him. Hence it is said to the holy apostles themselves: You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX, 28). Hence Isaiah says: The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people (Isa. III, 14). Hence Solomon speaks of the Church, saying: Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land (Prov. XXXI, 23).

Having passed over these matters briefly, and continuing, as we began, to set forth the order of the first coming, let us return in our exposition to the persons of the Evangelists. It follows:

VERSE 5.—And this was their appearance: the likeness of a human being was in them.

19. [Note: [Col. 0803D] These words are not found in C. Germ. or in the Roman edition of Sixtus V, up to “who is described here.” They are found in four English manuscripts and all our own. In Norm., instead of “but who is this human being here,” one finds “but who is this human being?”] Since shortly afterward these holy living creatures are described separately according to their individual forms, so that one is said to resemble a human being, another a lion, another a calf, and another an eagle, what does it mean that here they are all said together to have “the likeness of a human being” in them? But who is the human being described here except the one of whom it is written: Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II, 6)? These living creatures, therefore, so that they may rise to the virtue of holiness, strive toward the likeness of this human being. They would not be holy if they did not possess the likeness of this human being, because whatever there is in them of compassionate affection, whatever of gentleness of spirit, [Col. 0804A] whatever of zeal for righteousness, [Note: [Col. 0804D] The words “whatever of zeal for righteousness” are omitted in the printed editions; we have supplied them from the English manuscripts and our C. Germ., Norm., Val. Cl., and Longip. witnesses.] whatever of vigilance in humility, and whatever of the fervor of charity, they have drawn from the very fountain of mercy, from the very root of gentleness, and from the very power of justice—that is, from the Mediator between God and human beings, the Lord God.

The outstanding preacher shows that he bears the likeness of this human being when he says: Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ (I Cor. IV, 16). He urges us to rise to his likeness when he says: The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who descended from heaven (I Cor. XV, 47). Every saint is led into the likeness of this human being to the extent that he imitates the life of his Redeemer. For to differ from his commands and works—what is that other than to withdraw far from his likeness?

Holy preachers mourn the lives of those who sin; but of our very Head it is written that he wept over Jerusalem (Luke XIX, 41). They rejoice in the good deeds of their subjects and love those who act rightly; but it is written of our Redeemer that when a certain young man said, “I have kept all these things from my youth” (Matt. XIX, 20), he loved him more. Holy preachers bear the insults inflicted upon them and return no insult to one another; but when our Redeemer was told, “You have a demon” (John VIII, 48), he did not return the insult but answered gently, saying: I do not have a demon (ibid., 49). Holy preachers burn with zeal for righteousness; but the Redeemer of all, making a whip of cords, drove the buyers and sellers from the temple, overturned the seats of those selling doves, and poured out the money-changers’ coins (Matt. XXI, 12; John II, 15). [Note: [Col. 0804D] C. Germ. and other ancient witnesses read “in everything.”]

In everything they do bravely, they preserve humility with their whole intention; but through our Redeemer it is said: Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart (Matt. XI, 29). Holy preachers love even their persecutors; but he himself, [Note: [Col. 0804D] Suess. reads “the author.”] the author and redeemer of all, while undergoing his Passion, intercedes for his persecutors, saying: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing (Luke XXIII, 34). They give their own members over to suffering for their brothers; but for the life of the elect the author of life surrendered himself even unto death.

Let it therefore be said of the holy living creatures that the likeness of a human being is in them, because whatever is holy and wondrous in them comes from the form of likeness—that is, from the virtue of imitation. [Note: [Col. 0804D] C. Germ. reads: “for our Head, after all, …”] For our Redeemer is the Head of us all. And through Solomon it is said: The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness (Eccl. II, 14). We have our eyes in the head when we behold the life of our Redeemer in silent thought, when all our intention rises toward imitation of him, lest, if the eye of the mind neglects to look upon the ways of light, it immediately falls, closed, into the darkness of error.

The Prophet hastened to rise to the likeness of this human being when he said: I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways (Ps. CXVIII, 15). Whoever silently considers the ways of the Lord in his mind and hastens to exercise himself in his commandments—what else does he reform in himself except the image of the new human being? Because this is ceaselessly brought about in the hearts of the saints, it is rightly now said of the living creatures: The likeness of a human being is in them.

20. After this likeness, which is now maintained in conduct, one day we attain the likeness of glory. Hence John says: Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when he appears, we shall be like him (I John III, 2). He immediately adds how this can happen, saying: For we shall see him just as he is (ibid.).

To be God is to remain eternal and unchangeable. For everything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not; but God’s being is never to be otherwise. Hence it is said to Moses: I am who I am. And you shall say to the children of Israel: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III, 14). James also says: With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration (Jas. I, 17).

Thus John says: We shall be like him, because we shall see him just as he is, because by beholding the essence of his nature we are freed from our mutability and fixed in eternity. We shall be changed into the one whom we shall see, because by seeing life we shall be without death; we shall transcend our mutability by seeing the immutable. [Note: [Col. 0805D] C. Germ. reads “we fix ourselves.”] [Col. 0805C] We shall be held by no corruption, seeing the incorruptible. [Note: [Col. 0805D] All manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “seeing the unchangeable.”]

21. Then, too, the likeness of a human being will exist in our bodies. Hence Paul says: Our citizenship is in heaven; from it we also await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory (Phil. III, 20). The bodies of the elect will then be conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body. Although by nature they do not possess equality with his glory, by grace they will possess the likeness of his conformity.

Since, therefore, the likeness of his life is now drawn into the conduct of the elect, and at the resurrection the likeness of eternity follows in the mind, because we shall see him just as he is; and since our bodies, too, will receive his likeness through conformity, it is rightly said of the holy living creatures: The likeness of a human being is in them.

It is sufficient that we have touched upon these matters at the beginning of our exposition, so that the power of speech, refreshed by silence, may rise stronger to investigate the mysteries that follow. For we are certain that we have as our helper the very one of whom we speak, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY III. Four verses are expounded, from the sixth through the tenth, concerning the holy preachers and their twofold life, active and contemplative.

1. The four holy living creatures, which are foreseen through the spirit of prophecy, are described in a subtle account when it is said:

EZEK. I, 6.—Each had four faces, and each had four wings.

What is expressed by the face except knowledge, and what by the wings except flight? For each person is recognized by the face, while by wings the bodies of birds are raised on high. The face, therefore, pertains to faith, and the wing to contemplation. Through faith we are known by almighty God, as he himself says of his sheep: I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and mine know me (John X, 14). Again he says: I know whom I have chosen (John XIII, 18). Through contemplation, however, because we are lifted above ourselves, we are raised as though into the air. Thus each had four faces, because if you ask what Matthew thinks about the Lord’s incarnation, he certainly thinks what Mark, Luke, and John think. If you ask what John thinks, without doubt it is what Luke, Mark, and Matthew think. If you ask what Mark thinks, it is what Matthew, John, and Luke think. If you ask what Luke thinks, it is what John, Matthew, and Mark think. Thus each had four faces, because the knowledge of faith by which they are known by God is one in each and is simultaneously present in all four. Whatever you find in one, you rightly recognize as present together in all four.

2. And each had four wings, [Note: [Col. 0806D] In C. Germ. and the ancient witnesses, pinnae pinna occurs here and elsewhere.] because all of them unanimously preach the Son of almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and, raising the eyes of their minds toward his divinity, they fly with the wing of contemplation. The faces of the Evangelists therefore pertain to the Lord’s humanity, and the wing to his divinity, because in him whom they behold as bodily [Note: [Col. 0806D] C. Germ. reads “that which is bodily.”] they fix their gaze as upon a face. But while they proclaim that, in his divinity, he is unbounded and incorporeal, they are raised as though into the air by the wing of contemplation.

Since, therefore, there is in all of them one faith in his incarnation and in each an equal contemplation of his divinity, it is rightly now said: Each had four faces, and each had four wings. But what virtue would it be if the preachers who possessed faith in and contemplation of the Lord did not also possess holy works? It follows:

VERSE 7.—And their feet were straight feet.

3. What is signified by feet except the steps of actions? The feet of the four living creatures are therefore described as straight, because the works of the holy Evangelists and of all the perfect are not turned aside toward the pursuit of iniquity. Those do not have straight feet who turn back toward the evils of the world that they abandoned. Of them it is written: A dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mud (Prov. XXVI, 11; II Pet. II, 22).

An outstanding teacher grieved over certain people because they had turned the straightness of their feet backward; he rebuked them, saying: How are you turning again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew? You observe days, [Note: [Col. 0807D] The words “and months” are absent from the C. Germ. and Norman manuscripts and from the Paris editions of 1502 and 1518. They occur in the Greek text and in all the translations.] and months, and seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain (Gal. IV, 9). He admonishes others, saying: Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet (Heb. XII, 12).

But so that gravity of life, strength, and discernment might be shown in these same holy preachers, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0807B] IBID.—The sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot.

4. That holy preachers are signified by the name of oxen is taught by the apostle Paul when he explains the testimony of the Law: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain (I Cor. IX, 9; Deut. XXV, 4).

In the holy preachers, therefore, the sole of the foot is that of a calf—one that walks with maturity, strength, and a divided hoof—because every preacher possesses reverence in maturity, strength in action, and the division of the hoof in discernment. His preaching is not readily received if he appears frivolous in his conduct. Nor will maturity be displayed if strength in action is absent against all adversities. The very strength of action attains the merit of virtue if it is discerning in understanding. [Note: [Col. 0807D] The printed editions read si discretio, “if discernment.”] For we read the sacred Scripture: if we understand everything literally, we have lost the virtue of discernment; if we reduce everything to spiritual allegory, we are likewise bound by the folly of indiscretion.

Holy preachers read the sacred writings, sometimes accepting the letter according to history, sometimes seeking the spirit through the meaning of the letter. At one time they imitate the good deeds of earlier fathers as they find them according to the letter; at another they understand spiritually certain things that are not to be imitated according to history, and they strive toward advancement. What else, then, do holy preachers do in their work except divide the hoof on their foot? Of them it is aptly added:

IBID.—And sparks were like the appearance of glowing bronze.

5. Bronze is a very sonorous metal. And rightly the voices of preachers are compared with bronze, because their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII, 5). Bronze is well called glowing, because the life of preachers both sounds and burns. It burns with desire; it sounds through the word. Glowing bronze, therefore, is preaching set aflame.

But sparks come forth from glowing bronze, because from their exhortations words aflame proceed to the ears of those who hear. The words of preachers are rightly called sparks, because they set on fire those whom they touch in the heart. It must also be considered that sparks are very fine and tenuous, because when holy preachers speak of the heavenly homeland, they cannot disclose as much by their words as they are able to burn with desire. From their tongue, therefore, sparks of a kind come to us, because in their voice scarcely anything slight can be discerned of the heavenly homeland, though it is loved by them [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Paris edition of 1502 and others, both old and recent, read “by them it is not slightly burned,” against three German manuscripts, Norm., Corb., Longip., and others, and against the sense, which resists that reading.] with no slight ardor.

For they neither suffice to see the heavenly glory as much as it is, nor are they able to speak as much as they see. Glowing bronze therefore casts out sparks when the preacher can scarcely speak even slightly of that by which he himself burns fiercely. But divine mercy brings it about that the mind of the hearer is kindled by those very faint sparks, because there are some who, while hearing little, are filled with a greater desire; and they burn perfectly with the love of God precisely from having received scarcely the faintest sparks of words.

6. The word of preaching is indeed seed in the heart of the hearer. A good hearer later brings forth a great harvest of knowledge from the place where he had first received a small seed of speech. The miracle performed by the prophet Elisha for the widow aptly corresponds to this. So that she would not lose her two sons when the creditor took them away, she obeyed the prophet’s words and poured from the little oil she possessed into empty vessels. All of them were afterward filled to the brim, and from their fullness the woman was released from her creditor’s debt (IV Kings IV, 2 ff.).

What other woman does this signify except holy [Col. 0808C] Church, the mother of two peoples—namely, the Jewish and the Gentile peoples—as of two sons? Previously, through perverse action and the persuasion of the crafty spirit, she had received from the creditor, as it were, a coin of sin, and she feared losing the two sons whom she had begotten in faith. But obeying the words of the prophet—that is, the precepts of sacred Scripture—she poured the empty vessels with the little oil she possessed. [Note: [Col. 0808D] C. Germ., Norm., and others read this way. The edition of Rembolt, 1518, followed by the Vatican and Gilot editions, has “from the little oil she possessed”; Gussanv. has “from what little oil she possessed.”] For when empty minds hear from the mouth of one teacher even a little concerning the love of the Godhead, they are filled to the brim, through grace overflowing, with the ointment of divine love.

Even now many hearts that had previously been empty little vessels are full of the ointment of the Spirit; they seemed to have been filled only from a small quantity of oil. When this is given to one person after another and faith is received by the hearers, the woman of Sarepta—namely, holy Church—is no longer held under the debt of her creditor. It follows:

VERSE 8.—And the hands of a human being were under their wings, in their four parts. [Note: [Col. 0808D] The printed editions read “in the four parts.”]

7. In this passage the four parts may be understood as the four regions of the world—namely, East, West, South, and North—because the preaching of the saints, with God as its author, has gone forth in all parts of the world.

8. We may also understand by the four principal parts the four virtues from which the remaining virtues arise: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. We truly receive these virtues when we preserve their order. Prudence is first, fortitude second, justice third, and temperance fourth.

For what good can prudence do if fortitude is absent? To know what one cannot do is punishment rather than virtue. But whoever prudently understands what he ought to do and bravely does what he has understood is already, without doubt, just. Yet temperance must follow his justice, because justice often falls into cruelty if it has no measure. Justice itself is truly justice when it moderates itself by the bridle of temperance, so that even in the zeal with which someone burns there is temperance; otherwise, if he burns too fiercely, he loses the justice whose limits he does not know how to preserve.

9. There are two lives of the holy preachers: the active and the contemplative. The active precedes the contemplative in time, because from good works [Note: [Col. 0809D] C. Germ. reads tendit, “one tends.”] one advances toward contemplation. The contemplative, however, is greater in merit than the active, because the former labors in the practice of present work, while the latter already tastes the coming rest through inward savor. [Note: [Col. 0809D] Suess. reads “of the present time.” And below, with Longip., “of inward savor.” Our reading follows other manuscripts, especially the German ones.]

What, then, is signified by the hands except the active life, and what by the wings except the contemplative life? The hands of a human being are therefore under their wings—that is, the power of action is beneath the flight of contemplation.

This is well represented in the Gospel by those two women, Martha and Mary. Martha was busy with much serving, while Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his words (Luke X, 39–40). One was therefore intent upon work, the other upon contemplation. One served the active life through outward ministry, the other the contemplative life through the suspension of her heart upon the word.

Although the active life is good, the contemplative is better, because the former fails with mortal life, while the latter grows more fully in immortal life. Hence it is said: Mary has chosen the best part, which will not be taken away from her (ibid., 42). Since the active life is less in merit than the contemplative, it is rightly now said: The hands of a human being are under their wings. For although through the active life we do something good, through the contemplative we fly toward heavenly desire. Hence among Moses’ writings the active life is called servitude, while the contemplative life is called freedom.

10. And although both lives [Note: [Col. 0809D] C. Germ., Norm., and Val. Cl. read “both lives.”] come from the gift of grace, nevertheless, as long as we live among our neighbors, one is necessary for us and the other voluntary. For who, knowing God, enters his kingdom without first acting well? Without the contemplative life, therefore, those can enter the heavenly homeland who do not neglect the good things they are able to do; but without the active life they cannot enter if they neglect to do the good things they can do. The one, therefore, is necessary; the other voluntary. The one is servitude; the other freedom.

Hence it is said to Moses: If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free without payment. With whatever garment he entered, with such let him depart. If he had a wife, his wife shall also go out with him. But if his master gives him a wife and she bears sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, while he shall go out with his garment. But if the servant says, “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,” let his master bring him before the gods, and let him be brought to the door and the doorposts; and he shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be his servant forever (Exod. XXI, 2 ff.).

We have given the testimony at somewhat greater length [Note: [Col. 0810D] Longip. reads “in order to show the strictness.”] so that we might display the distinction between servitude and freedom in both lives. But it should not be burdensome if, in explaining it, we pursue the matter by which we affirm what we have said.

11. “Hebrew” is interpreted as “one who passes over.” A Hebrew servant is bought when someone who has already passed over from this world in mind is subjected to the service of the almighty Lord. For he truly desires to serve God who has learned to pass over from this world in mind.

Thus Moses passed over in order to see the vision (Exod. III, 3). Thus David, when he saw the wicked exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon, passed over, and behold, he was no more (Ps. LXVI, 35). [Note: [Col. 0810D] Suess. and some Norman witnesses read “like cedars.” C. Germ. reads “above cedars.”] For we perhaps believe the power of the wicked to be something great unless we pass over in mind to the world that endures.

A Hebrew servant who has been bought is commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free without payment. For what is signified by the number six except the perfection of the active life, and what by seven except the contemplative life? He serves for six years and goes out free in the seventh who, through the active life that he has perfectly exhibited, passes into the freedom of the contemplative life.

It must be noted that he goes out free without payment, because those who, after doing everything, say that they are unprofitable servants (Luke XVII, 10) will undoubtedly receive the contemplative life by grace, just as the active life itself was a gift. With whatever garment he entered, with such let him depart, because it is altogether necessary that each of us persevere in what he has begun and continue to the end of the work in the intention with which he began. He passes well into the contemplative life who does not change the garment of his intention for something worse while living the active life.

There are some who, before they are joined to the service of almighty God in holy conduct, already love to do good works. [Note: [Col. 0810D] Longip. reads “love good works.”] There are others who learn good works only after they have come into the service of almighty God. Therefore, whoever took care to possess good action even before coming into God’s service is a Hebrew servant bought with a wife.

12. Often one who is such can pass into the contemplative life and yet not abandon the active life. Hence it is added there: If he has a wife, his wife shall also go out with him. For the wife goes out with him into freedom when the person who has attained contemplation does not abandon outwardly the action of good work by which he can benefit others. [Note: [Col. 0811D] C. Germ. and Corb. read “attains it and does not leave it to others.”]

But if the Lord gives him a wife and she bears sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, while he shall go out with his garment. The master gives a wife to the purchased servant when each preacher joins to good action the person whom he has handed over to the authority of almighty God. For preachers too are called masters, as it is said of the preacher of the prophet Elisha: Do you know that your master is being taken away from you? (IV Kings II, 3).

The wife of the purchased servant bears sons and daughters when good action generates strong or tender fruits. But the woman given by the master remains with that same master together with her children, while the servant goes out with his garment, because the good action, or the fruits of that good action, are reckoned to the preacher’s reward. He himself, remaining steadfast in the intention of his desire, goes out free into contemplation through heavenly grace:

But if the servant says, “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exod. XXI, 5). The servant loves his master when he carefully preserves the preacher’s words in his mind. Loving his wife and children as well, he refuses to go out free when, loving the active life and its fruits, he does not wish to pass into the contemplative life, because, considering that he possesses good works in the service he performs, [Note: [Col. 0811D] Suess. reads “to the quiet of freedom.”] he refuses to withdraw into the rest of freedom.

But let his master bring him before the gods, [Note: [Col. 0811D] Longip. reads “and bring him.”] and let him be brought to the door and the doorposts, and let him pierce his ear with an awl, so that he may be his servant forever. He who has resolved to remain in the active life is brought by his master before the gods when he is instructed by his preacher in the words of the ancient fathers, who were priests for us on the way of almighty God. He is led to the door and doorposts of the tabernacle so that he may hear something more profoundly about entering the heavenly dwelling and may carefully recognize the day of the terrible judgment, lest through the good works he performs he desire to please human beings.

Thus his ear is pierced with an awl while the subtlety of the fear of God strikes his mind. Pierced through by the sharpness of the word, he learns in everything he does always to attend to the entrance of the kingdom, and, as it were, to carry an ear pierced at the door and doorpost of the tabernacle. [Note: [Col. 0811D] C. Germ. reads “of love.”]

13. He will be a servant for the age, so that after the age he may be free. He is a servant in this world who has resolved to serve human beings through the active life, so that after the present world he may be able to reach true freedom. Of this Paul says: For creation itself will be freed from the servitude of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Then our true freedom will exist, when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God.

Now, however, not only is the active life in servitude, but contemplation itself, by which we are lifted above ourselves, does not yet possess perfect freedom of mind; it imitates it, because that innermost rest is seen in an enigma. Yet, however narrow contemplation may be, it is already far broader and higher than the active life, passing into a certain freedom of mind: it does not think about temporal things but about eternal things.

Since, therefore, the contemplative life flies toward higher things and far surpasses the active life in a certain, so to speak, dignity of its security, it is aptly now said: The hands of a human being are under their wings.

14. But if in this passage “human being” is understood as our Redeemer, the hands of a human being are under their wings because, unless God had become human and lifted the minds of the preachers toward heavenly things, those living creatures that appear would not fly. Nor is it without reason that the hands of a human being are said to be under the wings, because it is written of this same Redeemer: Since he is the radiance of his glory and the exact likeness of his substance, and upholds all things (Heb. I, 3).

His hand, therefore, carries our hearts; his hand lifts us in contemplation. For unless, as has been said, the almighty Word had become human for human beings, human hearts would not fly toward contemplating the excellence of the Word. Human minds therefore became exalted from the place where the humble God appeared among human beings.

Let it therefore be said of the holy living creatures—let it be said: The hands of a human being are under their wings. Of them it is further added:

VERSES 8, 9.—And they had faces and wings on their four sides, and their wings were joined, each to the other.

15. They have faces and wings on their four sides because, in all the regions of the world, the preachers display whatever they believe concerning the humanity and whatever concerning the divinity of our Redeemer. While they preach everywhere that God was incarnate, they display a face in the four parts of the world. And while they proclaim that he is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, everywhere they fly with the wing of contemplation.

Their wings are joined, each to the other, because all their virtue and all their wisdom, by which they surpass other human beings through the flight of their contemplation, are joined to one another in peace and unanimity. [Note: [Col. 0812D] Corb. reads “they join.”] Hence it is written: The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable (Jas. III, 17). Hence Truth says to these same preachers: Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves (Mark IX, 49).

The wing of one living creature is therefore joined to that of another because the virtue and wisdom of holy preachers are mutually united in the peace of charity and concord. The wing of one would be divided from that of another if, in soaring toward wisdom, each refused to maintain peace with the other. It follows:

VERSE 9.—They did not turn back as they went, but each proceeded straight ahead. [Note: [Col. 0812D] C. Germ. reads “each of them.” Ebroic. reads “each of them went straight ahead.”]

16. The winged creatures—namely, the holy preachers—do not turn back at all when they proceed, because they pass from earthly actions to spiritual things in such a way that they never turn back again toward what they have abandoned. For them to proceed is, as it were, to travel by a certain road, always advancing in mind toward better things. [Note: [Col. 0813D] Val. Cl. reads eos incedere, “them to proceed.”] In contrast, it is said of the reprobate that they turned back in their hearts to Egypt (Num. XIV, 3–4). And Truth says through himself: No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke IX, 62).

To put one’s hand to the plow is to open the soil of one’s heart, as though with the plowshare of compunction, in order to bring forth fruits. But he looks back after the plow who, after the beginnings of a good work, returns to the evils he abandoned. Because this does not happen at all to God’s elect, it is rightly now said through the prophet: They did not turn back as they went.

17. He indicates why they do not turn back when he adds: Each proceeded straight ahead. Eternal things are before us, temporal things behind us, because we find the former as we advance and leave the latter behind us as we withdraw. Hence that great winged creature said, having flown as far as the secrets of the third heaven: Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. III, 13–14). [Note: [Col. 0813D] C. Germ. and nearly all manuscripts read “to the things that are before”; the Vatican and Gussanv. editions read “the things that are more before.” The contrast of “behind” and “before” is superior.] He had stretched forward toward what lay ahead and forgotten what was behind, because, despising temporal things, he sought only eternal things.

The holy living creatures therefore proceed straight ahead, because they no longer look back with any desire toward what they have abandoned, and in the eternal things they desire they place the foot of good work beneath the eyes of their contemplation.

[Col. 0813C] **18.** Whoever, then, has resolved to walk before his own face must carefully consider that looking backward occurs in one way with respect to action and in another with respect to thought. For there are some who make great resolutions and, conscious of their sins, deliberate on distributing to the needy much of what they possess, so that before God’s eyes they may redeem their faults through the compassion of mercy. They begin to carry this out, but often, while they are doing so, fear of poverty shakes their minds; and, afraid that they may come to want, they become stingy toward the needy and withdraw themselves from the good work they had begun. These, plainly, have turned back while walking, because they were unwilling to walk before their own face.

Against such people Solomon rightly says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (Prov. 20:4). Whoever now neglects to do good because of fear and sluggishness of mind will beg for life when the Sun of Justice shines at the judgment as in summer, but will not receive it, because he scorned to do good on its account.

Another person, having despised the desires of the flesh, deliberates on abandoning everything and submitting himself to the service of almighty God; he resolves to restrain himself under the bridle of continence and chastity. But when he sees that others have fallen even after chastity, he fears to do what he had resolved. [Col. 0814A] Thus he returns backward in thought, although, looking toward what lies ahead, he had already been advancing mentally toward the heights. Of him Solomon fittingly says: “He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. 11:4). By “wind” is meant the evil spirit, which drives the mind about with temptations; by “cloud” is signified the sinner, who is shaken by the impulse of temptation. Whoever, therefore, watches the wind does not sow, and whoever considers the clouds never reaps, because the person who fears the temptations of the evil spirit and observes the falls of the wicked despairs of himself: he is neither now exercised in the good seed of action nor afterward refreshed by the reward of just recompense.

There are others who indeed perform the good things they know, and, while performing them, deliberate on better things; but, reconsidering the better things they had resolved upon, they change their minds. They do the good works they had begun, but succumb to the better things they had resolved upon. These seem to stand firm in action before human judgments, but before the eyes of almighty God they have fallen in their deliberation. Consequently, their good work often pleases God less, [Note: [Col. 0813D] Both the older and the more recent printed editions read “with fear of mind.” [Col. 0814D] We follow the English, French, and other manuscripts.] because when the foot of the mind is unsteadily placed on a better step of deliberation, that very instability of thought condemns it.

But because all the perfect, with great subtlety of discernment, watch themselves lest they ever slip toward what is worse either in action or in thought, they continually consider how much they advance each day. Of them it is rightly said: “They did not turn back as they walked, but each one walked before his own face.”

[Col. 0814C] **19.** In the midst of these matters, then, it is pleasing to consider who we are, and from where we have come, and to what mysteries of sacred Scripture we are lifted so as to examine them. Certainly, in our ancient ancestors, we were worshipers of idols; but behold, through the Spirit of grace we now scrutinize heavenly words. Whence is this given to us? The Redeemer of the human race fulfilled what he said through the prophet: “And strangers shall eat what has been turned from a desert into fertility” (Isa. 5:17).

These sayings of the prophets were deserts among the Jews, because they did not wish to cultivate them by seeking their mystical meaning. But for us they have been turned into fertility, because, by God’s gift, the words spoken according to the historical vision yield a spiritual savor to our minds; and now we strangers eat what the citizens of the Law refused to consume.

May there be thanksgiving to the Only-Begotten; may there be praise to eternal Wisdom, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Suess. and Longip. read “may grace be.”]

## HOMILY IV

**In the exposition, begun, of verses ten, eleven, and twelve, many moral instructions are set forth, especially concerning continual attention to God and attentiveness to oneself.**

**1.** Through the holy spirit of prophecy, the winged creatures are described with subtlety, so that the very subtlety [Col. 0815A] of the description may disclose to us that they signify the persons of the Evangelists, and so that the word of God may leave no uncertainty in our understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0814D] The printed editions incorrectly read “the subtlety of discernment,” against the C. German., Corb., Norman, and English manuscripts.]

For behold, it is said:

**VERSE 10.** “And the likeness of their faces was the face of a man; and the face of a lion on the right side of the four of them; but the face of an ox on the left side of the four of them; and the face of an eagle above the four of them.”

That these four winged creatures signify the four holy Evangelists is attested by the beginnings of each Gospel book. Since Matthew began with human generation, he is rightly represented by a man; since Mark began with a cry in the desert, he is rightly represented by a lion; since Luke began with a sacrifice, he is fittingly represented by a calf; but since John began with the divinity of the Word, he is worthily represented by an eagle. When he says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and directs his attention toward the very substance of the Godhead, he fixed the eyes of his mind upon the sun, as an eagle does.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] This is read more correctly in the manuscripts than in the printed editions, which say: “In the beginning was … while he was directing [his attention] toward it.” Gussanville adds: “who, while directing [his attention] toward it.”]

But because all the elect are members of our Redeemer, while our Redeemer himself is the head of all the elect, since his members have been represented, there is no objection if he too is signified in all these figures. For he, the Only-Begotten Son of God, truly became man; in the sacrifice of our redemption he deigned to die as a calf; through the power of his strength he rose as a lion. A lion is also said to sleep with open eyes, because in the very death in which our Redeemer could sleep according to his humanity, he remained immortal and watchful according to his divinity. After his resurrection, ascending to heaven, he was raised on high as an eagle. Thus he is all four together: by being born he became man, by dying a calf, by rising a lion, and by ascending to heaven an eagle.

But since we have already said above that through these creatures the four Evangelists—and, under their appearance, all the perfect together—are signified (Homily 3), it remains for us to show how each of the elect is expressed by these visions of the creatures.

**2.** Every elect person who is perfect in the way of God is simultaneously man, calf, lion, and eagle. A man is a rational animal. A calf is customarily slaughtered in sacrifice. A lion is a strong beast, as it is written: “The lion is strongest among beasts and will retreat before no one” (Prov. 30:30). An eagle flies up to lofty places and fixes its unblinking eyes upon the rays of the sun.

Thus everyone who is perfect in reason is a man. And because he puts himself to death with respect to the pleasures of this world, he is a calf.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Corb. reads “from the pleasure of this flesh.”]

Because, through that voluntary mortification, he possesses the strength of security against all adversities—whence it is written, “The just man, confident as a lion, will be without fear” (Prov. 28:1)—he is a lion. Because he contemplates loftily the things that are heavenly [Note: [Col. 0815D] The printed editions read “and earthly,” contrary to the manuscripts of C. German., Corb., Norm., Anglic., and others.] and eternal, he is an eagle. Therefore, since every just person becomes a man through reason, a calf through the sacrifice of his mortification, a lion through the security of his courage, and an eagle through contemplation, each perfect person can rightly be signified by these holy creatures. We say this in order to demonstrate that the things said about the four creatures also pertain to each of the perfect.

**3.** Yet a major question arises for us concerning these same Evangelists and holy preachers: why are a man and a lion said to be on the right side of the four, while a calf is on the left side of the four? For it is not without astonishment that those two are said to be on the right and this one on the left.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Here the editors read “not without remarkable reason”; perhaps “not without astonishment,” as in C. German. and most manuscripts. Corb., Val. Cl., and others read “not without admiration.”]

Again, it must be asked why the eagle is said to be not on the right or left, but above the four. We have therefore proposed two questions, which we must resolve with the Lord’s revelation.

A man and a lion, then, are said to be on the right, while a calf is on the left. On the right we have joyful things, but on the left sorrowful things. Hence we also call “left” whatever we judge to be adverse. As we have said, incarnation is signified by the man, passion by the calf, and the resurrection of our Author by the lion. All the elect rejoiced in the incarnation of the Only-Begotten Son, through which we were redeemed; but at his death the first holy apostles among the elect were saddened, and then rejoiced again at his resurrection.

Because his birth and resurrection brought joy to the disciples, while his passion saddened them, the man and the lion are described as being on his right, but the calf on his left. The holy Evangelists rejoiced in his humanity and were strengthened by his resurrection, though they had been saddened by his passion. The man and the lion are therefore on their right, because the incarnation of our Redeemer gave them life and his resurrection strengthened them. But the calf is on their left, because his death temporarily cast them down into unbelief.

The eagle’s place is rightly described as above rather than beside them, because either by signifying his ascension, or because it proclaims the Word of the Father to be God with the Father, it surpassed the other Evangelists in the power of contemplation. Although it speaks together with them about his divinity, it contemplates this more subtly than all the others.

[Note: [Col. 0816D] All the printed editions read “and together.” We have supplied “with them” from all our manuscripts; it clearly must be supplied by conjecture, since without that word the sense is defective.]

But if the eagle, joined with the other three, is said to constitute four creatures, how is it described as being above the four? This is so because John, by seeing the Word “in the beginning,” passed even beyond himself. For if he had not passed beyond himself, he would not have seen the Word in the beginning (John 1:1). Since he transcended even himself, he was not merely above three but, himself included, above four. It follows:

[Col. 0817A] **VERSE 11.** “And their faces and their wings were extended above.”

**4.** The faces and wings are described as extended above, because all the attention and contemplation of the saints reaches above themselves, so that they may attain what they desire in heaven. Whether one devotes oneself to a good work or to contemplation, what one does is truly good when one desires to please him from whom it comes.

Whoever appears to do good but desires through it to please not God but human beings presses the face of his intention downward. And whoever contemplates in sacred Scripture the things that belong to the Godhead for the purpose of being able, through what he understands, to occupy himself with disputation—because he does not desire to be satisfied with the sweetness of the blessedness he has sought, but wishes to appear learned—does not extend the wings of his understanding above. Since he occupies the vigilance of his sense in an earthly desire, he lays down below the wings that he could raise on high and by which he himself could be lifted.

Here it must be considered that every good thing that is done should always be raised toward heavenly things through intention. Whoever desires earthly glory through the good things he does presses both his wings and his face downward. Hence the prophet says of certain people: “They were bringing sacrifices into the depths” (Hos. 5:2). For what are the tears of prayer other than the sacrifices of our offering? As it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19).

There are some who afflict themselves with lamentation in prayer for the purpose either of obtaining earthly advantages or of appearing holy to human beings. [Col. 0817C] What do such people do except bring sacrifices into the depths? Because the things they seek are below, they set the sacrifice of their prayer downward.

But the elect, who desire to please almighty God in good works and, through the grace of contemplation, long already to taste eternal blessedness, extend their faces and wings above. It follows:

**IBID.** “Two wings of each were joined to one another, and two covered their bodies.”

**5.** It had been said: “Their faces and wings were extended above,” and immediately what we have quoted was added: “Two wings of each were joined.” It is clearly understood from this that two were both extended above and joined, while two covered their bodies.

But what are the *pennae* of the creatures, if not what are called wings (*alae*)? Here we must seek with careful examination what the four wings of the saints are, of which two are extended above and joined, while two cover their bodies. If we look attentively, we find four virtues that lift every winged creature from earthly actions: with respect to the future, love and hope; with respect to the past, fear and repentance.

The wings, then, are extended upward and joined to one another because love and hope lift the minds of the saints toward heavenly things. They are rightly also called joined, because the elect undoubtedly love the heavenly things they hope for and hope for the things they love.

But two cover their bodies because fear and repentance hide their past evils from the eyes of almighty God. Two wings, as has been said, are joined above when love and hope raise the hearts of the elect toward higher things and suspend them in the heavens. Two wings cover their bodies when fear and repentance conceal their past evils from the sight of the eternal Judge.

In the fact that they remember having sinned, and therefore fear and grieve, what else do they do but cover their body? They conceal their carnal deeds from strict examination by placing good works over them. For it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1). We cover sins when we place good deeds over evil acts. Whatever is covered is placed below, and that by which it is covered is brought from above. Therefore, when we reject the evils we have done and choose the good things we should do, we place, as it were, a covering over what we are ashamed to have seen.

**6.** However holy men may be in this present life, they nevertheless have something that they ought to cover before the eyes of God, because it is entirely impossible for them never to sin in action, speech, or thought. Hence blessed Job, who had spoken of perfection before human beings, but, hearing God’s voice, reproved himself for that very perfect speech, said: “I will put my hand over my mouth” (Job 39:34). In the hand is action; in the mouth is speech. To put the hand over the mouth, then, is to cover sins of speech through the power of good action.

It is pleasing, dearest brothers, to call the teacher of the nations as a witness to this matter and to observe how that holy creature relies upon four wings: with two he flies upward, while with two wings he covers his body, because he conceals the things he had done in the past.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] Norman manuscripts read, “the things he had done he hides from judgment.”]

Let us see, then, how great a love lifts him toward heavenly things: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). Let us recognize with how great a hope he is raised toward higher things: “Our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid. 3:20).

Let us see whether, placed in such great virtues, he still fears: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27). Let us recognize whether he repents of having done evil: “I am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

In his words, what else is condemned but the hardness of our mind? He mourns what he committed before baptism, while we have committed many things even after baptism and nevertheless refuse to weep. The holy creatures therefore use four wings, because through love and hope they fly toward heavenly things, and through fear and repentance they lament the unlawful deeds committed in themselves.

**7.** But since it was said, “Two wings of each were joined,” this may perhaps be understood to mean that they do not raise and join their own wings, but that the wings of one are joined to those of another, so that the raised wings agree with one another in their joining.

[Col. 0819A] A question arises here. If the two wings that lift are love and hope, while the two that cover the bodies signify fear and repentance, why are the two that are extended said to be joined, whereas the two that cover the body are not said to be joined?

[Note: [Col. 0819D] C. German. reads, “which are raised.” Above, the readings are “wings that raise” and “wings that are raised.”]

In this matter, however, an easy explanation presents itself, with the Lord granting it: the two wings of the saints that are joined are love and hope, but the two that cover their bodies—fear and repentance—are not joined to one another. David was afflicted by fearing and repenting over the fall of his flesh (2 Sam. 12:13). Peter bitterly wept over his fall into unfaithfulness (Matt. 26:75). Paul mourned in himself the cruelty of his former persecution (1 Cor. 15:9). Yet all desire one homeland and hasten to reach one Author of all things.

Thus two wings of each are joined and two are not, because through love and hope what they desire is one, but through fear and repentance what they lament is different. It follows:

**VERSE 12.** “And each one of them walked in the presence of his own face.”

**8.** Above it had been said: “Each one of them walked before his own face,” but now it is said: “Each one walked in the presence of his own face.” The same sentence therefore seems to have been repeated. But because *coram* denotes presence, we can, by more subtle inquiry, distinguish between walking before one’s face and being present to oneself.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] Several Norman manuscripts read “what else.”]

To walk before one’s face is to desire what lies ahead; to be present to oneself is not to be absent from oneself.

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Norman manuscripts read “by looking at what lies ahead”; “by looking” is absent from C. German., Corb., and others.]

Every just person who carefully watches his life and diligently considers how much he advances each day in good things—or perhaps how much he declines from them—places himself before himself and therefore walks in his own presence, since he watches attentively whether he is rising or falling.

But whoever neglects the guardianship of his life, and either disdains or does not know how to examine what he does, says, and thinks, does not walk in his own presence, because he is unaware of what he is like in his conduct and actions. Nor is the person present to himself who is not concerned to investigate and know himself each day. He truly places himself before himself and is present to himself who attends to himself in his actions as though he were another person.
