**9.** For we commit many sins, but they do not seem serious to us precisely because, loving ourselves with private affection, we flatter ourselves in our own deception with our eyes closed. Consequently, we often judge our own serious faults lightly, while judging the light faults of our neighbors severely.

It is written: “People will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2). And we know that private love greatly closes the eye of the heart. Hence what we do and do not consider serious is often done by a neighbor and appears exceedingly detestable to us.

But why does what seemed insignificant in us appear serious in our neighbor, unless it is because we do not see ourselves as we see our neighbor, nor our neighbor as we see ourselves? If we looked at ourselves as at our neighbor, we would see our blameworthy actions strictly. And again, if we looked at our neighbor as at ourselves, his action would never seem intolerable to us, since we have perhaps often done similar things and thought that we had done nothing intolerable to our neighbor.

Moses attempted to correct this wrongly divided judgment of our mind through the precept of the Law when he said that the measure should be just and the sextarius equal (Lev. 19:36). Hence Solomon says: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure, both are an abomination to God” (Prov. 20:10).

We know that in the double weight of merchants one weight is greater and another smaller. They have one weight by which they weigh for themselves, and another by which they weigh for their neighbor. They prepare lighter weights for giving and heavier ones for receiving.

Therefore everyone who weighs what belongs to his neighbor in one way and what belongs to himself in another has “a weight and a weight.” Both are an abomination to God, because if he loved his neighbor as himself, he would love him in good things as he loves himself; and if he looked at himself as he looks at his neighbor, he would judge himself in evil things as he judges his neighbor.

We ought, therefore, carefully to see ourselves as we see others, and, as has been said, place ourselves before ourselves, so that, continually imitating the winged creatures, we may not be ignorant of what we are doing and may always walk in the presence of our own face.

But the perverse, as we said a little earlier, do not walk in the presence of their own face, because they never consider what they do; they move toward destruction and rejoice in evil actions. Of them it is written: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). Often the just person who sees them weeps, but they, like madmen, are mourned while they themselves laugh.

**10.** Some give much of their own possessions to the needy, but when they find an opportunity, they oppress the needy and ravage by plunder those over whom they have gained power.

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Norman manuscripts read “those over whom they have prevailed.”]

They place before the eyes of their thought the good things they do, but do not place there the worst things they commit. These plainly do not walk in the presence of their own face, because if they were present to themselves, they would see carefully everything they do and recognize how they destroy good works through evil actions, as it is written: “And he who gathered wages put them into a pierced bag” (Hag. 1:6). From a pierced bag what is put in at one place goes out at another [Col. 0820D] (On Penance, distinction 4, chapter “Of the Pierced Bag”), because undiscerning minds do not see how the reward acquired from a good work is lost through an evil work.

Another person preserves bodily chastity and watches himself carefully so that he may not commit anything blameworthy outwardly. He is content with his own possessions and does not seize what belongs to others, yet perhaps retains hatred in his heart against his neighbor. And since it is written, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15), he considers how pure he is outwardly in action and does not weigh how cruel he is in mind.

What is this person other than absent from himself, walking in the darkness of his heart and unaware? Another no longer seizes what belongs to others, guards his body from impurity, loves his neighbor with a pure mind, and, conscious of past evils, afflicts himself with lamentation in prayer. But when prayer has ended, he cheerfully seeks things in which he may rejoice in this world, lowers his negligent mind into temporal pleasures, and does not care lest immoderate joys surpass in him the measure of his tears. Thus by excessive laughter he loses the good he gained by weeping.

This person, therefore, does not walk in the presence of his own face, because he refuses to see the losses he suffers. It is written: “The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy” (Eccl. 7:5).

In everything we do, therefore, we ought diligently to observe ourselves inwardly and outwardly, so that, following the winged creatures, we may be present to ourselves and always walk in the presence of our own face, having as our one helper Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, our Lord, who lives and reigns with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V

**On the exposition of three verses, from the twelfth through the fifteenth, in which learned discussion is given concerning the Holy Spirit and his impulse, movement, and indwelling in the saints.**

**1.** O how wondrous is the depth of the words of God! It is pleasing to direct our attention to it; it is pleasing, with grace as our guide, to penetrate its innermost parts. Whenever we examine it through understanding, what else do we do than enter the shade of forests, so that in its coolness we may be hidden from the heat of this age? [Col. 0821C] There, by reading, we pluck the greenest herbs of its meanings; by discussing them, we chew them over.

In the discourse given to you, dearest brothers, the day before yesterday, it was said how the creatures that appeared signify either our Redeemer, or his four Evangelists, or all the perfect. The power of these creatures is now expressed more subtly, so that we too, weak and contemptible though we are, may stretch ourselves toward their imitation insofar as the Lord grants.

For behold, it is said:

**VERSE 12.** “Where the impulse of the spirit was, there they went.”

**2.** There are different impulses in the elect and the reprobate: in the elect, the impulse of the spirit; in the reprobate, the impulse of the flesh. The impulse of the flesh drives the mind toward hatred, arrogance, impurity, plunder, outward glory, cruelty, faithlessness, despair, anger, quarrels, and pleasures. But the impulse of the spirit draws the mind toward love, humility, continence, generosity of mercy, inward progress, works of piety, faith in eternal things, hope of the joy to come, patience, peace, consideration [Note: [Col. 0821D] So read the manuscripts of C. German., Norm., Anglic., and others. Disregarding them, all the printed editions read “of immortal life.”] of mortal life, and tears.

It is therefore necessary that we should always consider with great care what impulse leads us in everything we do: whether our thought is driven by the impulse of the flesh or by the impulse of the spirit.

To love earthly things, to prefer temporal things to eternal, to desire outward goods not for necessary use but for pleasure, to seek vengeance on an enemy, and to rejoice at the downfall of a rival belong to the impulse of the flesh.

On the contrary, to love heavenly things, to despise earthly things, to seek transitory goods not for the fruit of pleasure but for necessary use, to grieve over the death of an enemy: these belong to the impulse of the spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] The Vatican edition reads “transient”; Suess. and Longip. read “destined to pass away.”]

And because all the perfect continually exercise themselves in these virtues, it is rightly now said of the holy creatures: “Where the impulse of the spirit was, there they went.”

**3.** We must know, however, that often the impulse of the flesh disguises itself under the covering of a spiritual impulse, and the thought itself lies to itself about doing carnally what it does, claiming that it is doing it spiritually.

Often someone, overcome by the goads of anger, is inflamed against wrongdoers by a zeal for avenging justice more than is necessary; passing beyond the limit of justice in vengeance, he acts cruelly while supposing that he is acting justly. The impulse of the flesh is therefore veiled in this person under the appearance of the spirit, since what is believed to be done justly is not held within the restraint of discernment.

Often another, devoted to excessive gentleness, sees the faults of those subject to him and refuses to correct them through the fervor of zeal; by not correcting them, he multiplies them cruelly in them. Thus his leniency becomes hostile both to himself and to those subject to him: because he considers the sluggishness of his mind patience, he distances himself from the impulse of the spirit through the spirit of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Some Norman manuscripts, with Suess. and Longip., read “through the impulse of the flesh.” We follow the ancient C. German. and Corb., with which the printed editions agree.]

Our first thought, then, must shake us into examining our heart, lest we be driven toward certain things we do by the open impulse of the flesh, [Note: [Col. 0822D] The old and recent printed editions read “lest by evil thoughts,” contrary to the manuscripts.] lest the mind, seduced by wicked pleasures, recognize that things are evil and nevertheless do them.

Our second concern must make us watchful, lest the impulse of the flesh secretly insinuate itself as though it were the impulse of the spirit and portray the faults we commit to us as virtues.

**4.** We must know that the faults that imitate virtues under an added appearance of virtue are more serious, because those that are recognized openly cast the mind into shame and draw it to repentance; but these not only fail to humble it into repentance, they even raise the mind of the one who acts, while the faults are thought to be virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Ebroic. and Lyr. read: “by raising the mind of the one who acts, they are thought to be virtues.”]

To confirm more deeply what was said above concerning the holy creatures, it is repeated:

**IBID.** “They did not turn back as they walked” (On Penance, distinction 2, chapter “They Did Not Turn Back”).

**5.** The elect strive toward good in such a way that they do not return to perpetrate evil: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). And as Solomon says: “The path of the just is like a shining light; it proceeds and increases until the perfect day” (Prov. 4:18).

In their minds, the good desire and understanding of the inner light are already part of the day. But because they advance in virtue until the end of life, they come to the perfect day when, having been led into the heavenly kingdoms, they will lack nothing of the light they desire.

It follows:

**VERSE 13.** “And the likeness of the creatures, and their appearance, was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps.”

**6.** The appearance of the creatures is compared with burning coals and lamps. Whoever touches a coal is set on fire, because whoever clings to a holy man receives from constant association with his presence, from the use of his speech, and from the example of his action the means of being kindled [Note: [Col. 0823D] Longip. reads “in the work of truth.”] with love of the truth, fleeing the darkness of his sins, burning with desire for the light, and now burning with true love [Col. 0823B] [Note: [Col. 0823D] Vatic. reads “return.” Longip. supports this reading.]—he who previously lay dead in iniquity as though he were cold.

Lamps, however, spread their light farther and, while located in one place, shine in another. Whoever is endowed with the spirit of prophecy, the word of teaching, and the grace of miracles has a reputation that shines far and wide like a lamp. All who hear of his good works, because through them they rise toward love of heavenly things, shine, by displaying themselves through good works, as though from the light of a lamp.

Because holy men kindle some who are placed near them, as though by touching them, to love their heavenly homeland, they are coals. Because they shine for some who are far away and become lamps for their journey, lest they fall into the darkness of sin, they are lamps.

The difference between coals and lamps is that coals do burn, but do not drive away the darkness of the place where they lie; lamps, however, because they shine with the great brightness of flames, dispel the darkness spread all around.

**7.** From this it should be noted that many of the saints are so simple and hidden, concealing themselves in less important places under profound silence, that their life can scarcely be recognized by others. What, then, are such people except coals? Although they possess the heat of burning through the fervor of the spirit, they do not possess the flame of example. Nor do they overcome the darkness of sins in other hearts, because they entirely avoid making their life known. They are kindled for themselves, but are not a light of example for others.

Those, however, who both offer examples of virtues and demonstrate the light of good action through life and [Note: [Col. 0823D] This is the reading required by the unanimous agreement of our manuscripts. The printed editions, departing from them, read “through word to those who err.”] word to those who journey are rightly called lamps, because through the heat of desire and the flame of the word they drive away the darkness of error from the hearts of sinners.

Whoever lives well in secret but contributes nothing to another’s progress is a coal. Whoever, placed in imitation of holiness, demonstrates to many the light of righteousness proceeding from himself is a lamp, because he burns for himself and shines for others. It follows:

**IBID.** “And this was the vision moving about in the midst of the creatures: the splendor of fire, and lightning issuing from the fire.”

8. [Note: [Col. 0823D] After the text of Job, in the Corbie manuscripts and most Norman manuscripts—which are followed by the Paris editions of 1502, 1518, and 1571, as well as the Vatican manuscript—we read: “the splendor of fire, and from the fire lightning going forth in the midst of the living creatures.” The Gussanville edition, which we follow here, agrees with manuscript C of Saint-Germain.] Fire is seen darting about in the midst of the living creatures, because unless those winged creatures received warmth from the fire of truth, they would not burn like coals and lamps. For by the name “fire” the Holy Spirit is usually signified. Concerning him the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). For when the carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, set ablaze with spiritual love it mourns the evil it has done. The earth burns when the sinner’s heart, accused by its own conscience, is scorched and consumed in the pain of repentance. Hence it is written again: “Your God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Because our Creator cleanses the mind he has filled from the rust of sins, he is called both fire and consuming.

Thus the Holy Spirit is said to dart about in the midst of the living creatures as “the splendor of fire, and lightning going forth from the fire,” because, filling the whole Church, he casts from himself flames of love into the hearts of the elect, striking them like a flash of lightning through fear and kindling their sluggish hearts to his love.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Beccensis and Lyra read: “that it may burn.”]

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Most Norman manuscripts read: “our God.”]

1209 9. But since the Holy Spirit is God, coeternal with the Father and the Son before the ages, we must ask why he is said to dart about. For everyone who darts about approaches a place where he was not and leaves the place where he was. In what sense, then, can we say that the Spirit darts about, when all things are within him and there is nowhere that he is not? As it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world” (Wisdom 1:7).

[Col. 0824C] Yet, when the praise of Wisdom was being described, it was added: “For in her is a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile” (ibid. 7:22). And shortly afterward: “Human, steadfast” (ibid. 7:23).

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Suessionensis and some others read: “a spirit of understanding, holy, unique.”]

10. In these words another great question arises for us: why is this Spirit, who fills all things, called both mobile and steadfast. But if we return to ordinary human usage, we will more quickly grasp the speaker’s meaning. A person who darts about everywhere in the region where he is undoubtedly comes everywhere to meet others, and suddenly is found where he is not expected. Thus the Almighty Spirit is called at once mobile and steadfast, so that his presence everywhere may be indicated. He is steadfast because by his nature he contains all things; but he is called mobile because he encounters all things everywhere, even those who do not know it. As the one who holds all things he is called steadfast; as the one who presents himself as present to all, he is called mobile.

Thus “the splendor of fire, and lightning going forth from the fire,” darts about among the winged creatures, because the Holy Spirit makes himself present both to each individually and to all together. He sets aflame those whom he touches and illuminates those whom he has set aflame, so that, kindled after their former coldness, they may burn and, through the fire of love they have received, return flames of example to others. For lightning going forth from this fire strikes sluggish minds, and by striking arouses and inflames them, so that afterward, burning with love, they may run both alight and radiant.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “His throne was a flame of fire, his wheels a burning fire” (Dan. 7:9). Those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the burdens of feeding the flock are not permitted to change their place. But because, established in one place, they bear within themselves the presence of divinity and burn, the throne of God is called a flame of fire. Those, however, who run about in preaching through love of the Lord are his wheels, a burning fire, because when they travel through various places out of desire for him, they themselves burn and set others ablaze.

11. Yet the darting about and mobility of the Spirit can also be understood through another consideration. In the hearts of the saints he always remains with respect to certain virtues, but with respect to others he comes in order to depart and departs in order to come. In faith, hope, and charity, and in the other good qualities without which one cannot reach the heavenly homeland—such as humility, chastity, justice, and mercy—he does not abandon the hearts of the perfect. In the virtue of prophecy, however, in eloquence of teaching, and in the display of miracles, he is sometimes present to his elect and sometimes withdraws from them. He is present so that they may be exalted, and withdraws from them so that they may be humbled. He is present to glorify them through the virtue displayed, and withdraws so that, deprived of his virtue, they may recognize themselves. He is present to show what they are through him, and withdraws to reveal who or what they remain without him.

In these virtues, therefore, without which one cannot reach life, the Holy Spirit remains in the hearts of his elect.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] This is not found in Saint-Germain or Suessionensis; immediately after “remains” they continue: “but in these.” It is found in the English and Norman manuscripts and in many others.]

Hence he is rightly declared to be steadfast. But in those virtues through which the power of holiness is displayed, he is sometimes mercifully present and sometimes mercifully withdraws.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] This passage is also absent from Saint-Germain and all the printed editions down to “darts about.” We have supplied it from all the English and Norman manuscripts.]

1210 Hence he is rightly called mobile. The Spirit is therefore said to dart about and to be mobile because he is not continually possessed, according to each person’s desire, in signs and virtues. Yet he is rightly said to dart about among the holy creatures. Darting about pertains to speed. The Spirit darts about among the perfect because, even if he withdraws from their hearts for a moment, he returns quickly.

It follows:

VERSE 14.—And the living creatures went and returned like the appearance of flashing lightning.

[Col. 0825D] 12. Since it was said above, “They did not return as they walked,” how is it now said, “The living creatures went and returned”? These statements seem completely contradictory: they went and did not return, and they went and returned. But we quickly recognize how this should be understood if we carefully distinguish two lives, namely the active and the contemplative.

In one we can remain fixed, but in the other we cannot in any way maintain an attentive mind. When we abandon our sluggishness and rouse ourselves to the pursuit of good works, where do we go except to the active life? From it we must never turn back, because whoever, after entering it, returns to the sluggishness of negligence and to the wickedness of depravity that he had abandoned plainly does not know how to be a heavenly creature.

But when we rise from the active life to the contemplative, because the mind cannot remain long in contemplation, but sees everything it perceives of eternity through a mirror and in an enigma as though furtively and in passing, the spirit, driven back by its own weakness from the immensity of such exaltedness, slips back into itself. It is necessary that it return to the active life and continually exercise itself in the practice of good works, so that, when the mind cannot rise to contemplate heavenly things, it may not refuse to do whatever good it can.

Thus it happens that, aided by its own good works, it rises again to higher things in contemplation and receives nourishment for love from the food of contemplated truth.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] *Adiuta* (“aided”) is absent from Saint-Germain; it is read in all the Norman manuscripts, Suessionensis, Longipontanus, Vallicellianus, and others.] Since its own weakness, arising from corruption, cannot keep it there for long, it returns again to good works, is nourished by the memory of God’s sweetness, and is fed outwardly by pious actions but inwardly by holy desires.

For this reason it is said of perfect men who return after their contemplation: “They shall pour forth the memory of your sweetness” (Ps. 144:7). Since, as best they can, they are able to touch by foretaste the sweetness of inner delight, as though from a flash, they strive continually to recall its memory and pour it forth in speech.

Hence the Psalmist aptly admonishes us, saying: “Light has risen for the just, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and give thanks for the memory of his holiness” (Ps. 96:11–12). Again he says: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord!” (Ps. 30:20). He could in no way know how great it was unless he had tasted it to some degree through contemplation.

Again he says: “I said in my ecstasy, ‘I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes’” (ibid. 30:23). For unless, raised up in an elevation of mind, he had known the sweetness of eternal delight, he would not, while still held in this world, have perceived how far away he lay, cast out from it.

The living creatures that have been shown, therefore, go and do not return, and go and return:

1211 the holy men neither fall from the active life they have taken up into iniquities, nor do they remain continually in the contemplative life, which they cannot perpetually sustain, but relapse from it into the active life.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] Another reading has: “do not withdraw.” We follow Saint-Germain, the Norman manuscripts, and Vallicellianus, with the Paris edition of 1502 and another of 1518. Gilot and the Vatican edition have: “do not run.”] As has been said, overcome by the weight of their weakness and driven back into themselves, they return, so that as they go they may learn what they desire, and as they return they may know where they lie. As they go, let them understand where they are not yet; as they return, what they are.

13. How these holy creatures return is shown when it is added: “Like the appearance of flashing lightning.” The returning creatures are rightly compared with flashing lightning, because when holy men fly upward to contemplate heavenly things and bind the first fruits of their spirit to the love of the heavenly homeland, yet, weighed down by the burden of human existence, return to themselves, they announce to their brothers the heavenly goods they have been able to contemplate, at least through a mirror, and kindle their minds to love of the inner brightness. They cannot see that brightness as it is, nor speak of it as they saw it.

As they speak, however, they strike and inflame the hearts of their hearers with their words. They return, therefore, like flashing lightning, because when they speak of heavenly things, the heavenly light flashes through them and inflames the minds of their hearers with love of the heavenly homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] Most printed editions read: “because, when they speak of heavenly things, the heavenly light flashes through them and kindles them to …,” contrary to the Saint-Germain, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0827D] The word “with” is absent in Lyra. In Longipontanus, “then” is read in place of “with.”]

When they strike by speaking, like flashing lightning, they scatter the fire of spiritual desire.

[Col. 0827B] 14. In another way also the holy creatures go and return. They go when they are sent to preach in order to make known the grace of the heavenly gift, and, so that they may draw unbelievers to the faith, perform wonders before them. But they return because, attributing these deeds to the power of the almighty Lord, they do not claim for themselves what they have done.

When they perform astonishing deeds, they are lightning, because they shake, terrify, illuminate, and inflame the hearts of those who behold them.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] Suessionensis reads: “Hence the prophet says.”]

Therefore it is written: “In the light your arrows shall go forth, in the brightness of the flash of your weapons” (Hab. 3:11). The Lord’s arrows are the words of the saints, which strike the hearts of sinners. But these arrows have weapons. You know, brothers, that warriors shoot arrows, but are protected by weapons. Thus, when they add miracles to their words, they protect themselves as though with weapons, lest they themselves be struck: “In the light your arrows shall go forth,” because the words of God come forth openly.

But because the deeds of miracles ought to accompany the pronouncements of holy teachers, it is rightly added:

[Note: [Col. 0827D] The Norman manuscripts read: “the judgments of their sayings.” We follow the German manuscript.] “In the brightness of the flash of your weapons,” because when you add weapons of miracles to them, the minds of their persecutors flash like lightning, so that they do not dare to persecute them.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] The printed editions read “because, when they add.” We follow Saint-Germain, Vallicellianus, Norman, and the other manuscripts, although “they add” seems to produce a better sense than “you add.”]

These creatures therefore go and return like flashing lightning, because after the saints perform wonders among men, and after they kindle the hearts of their hearers by scattering light, they return to give glory to their author, rendering praise to him through whom they know they can do such things.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] The editions printed before Gussanville corruptly read “to a certain.” We have corrected the text from both the English and the Gallican manuscripts.]

1212 15. Thus Peter, when he had performed a sign by healing a man who had been lame from his mother’s womb—a sign that greatly astonished all who knew him—said:

[Col. 0827D] “Why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us as though by our own virtue or power we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus” (Acts 3:12–13).

And shortly afterward: “By faith in his name, this man whom you see and know, his name has made strong” (ibid. 3:16).

[Note: [Col. 0828D] Other editions read “whom you see,” against the manuscripts Saint-Germain, Norman, Vallicellianus, and others.]

By performing a sign, he struck the eyes of those who looked on with the light of a miracle.

[Note: [Col. 0828D] Suessionensis reads: “with the wondrous light.”]

But by preserving humility and returning praise to its author, he returned, as it were, to the place from which he had come, because the light of the flash showed where it had originated.

Thus the holy creatures, when they come to perform signs and inwardly return to themselves in order to give glory to their author, are lightning, because both by displaying miracles and by offering examples of humility they strike and inflame the minds of those who behold them.

16. In everything they do, they always return to the praise of the Creator so that they may remain with true stability in the virtue they have received. For if they attributed anything to themselves, they could not remain in what they had received.

[Col. 0828B] Hence Solomon also says aptly: “The rivers return to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1:7).

Whether in virtues or in teaching, what else are holy men than rivers that water the dry soil of carnal hearts? But whether in the work they perform or in the words of their teaching, they would quickly dry up unless, through the intention of their hearts, they continually and carefully returned to the place from which they flow.

For if they do not return inwardly to the heart and bind themselves to the love of their Creator with the bonds of desire, the hand grows weak in what it was doing and the tongue dries up in what it was saying. But inwardly they always return through love, and what they pour forth publicly by working and speaking, they draw secretly from the spring of love. For by loving they learn what they bring forth in teaching.

[Col. 0828C] Therefore “the rivers return to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again,”

[Note: [Col. 0828D] Saint-Germain reads: “so that they may flow back.”]

[Note: [Col. 0828D] So it reads in all the old and recent manuscripts and editions except Gussanville, which has: “because the water of wisdom is drawn from the place from which it arises, lest, when it has flowed, it dry up.”]

because they always draw the water of wisdom from the place where it arises, lest, when it has flowed forth, it dry up.

In everything we do, therefore, let us return with attentive mind to the fountain of true light. Let us give thanks to our Creator for the good things we receive,

[Note: [Col. 0828D] Most Norman manuscripts read: “for the good things we do.” We follow Saint-Germain and the older manuscripts.]

and let us humbly say to him, with the prophet Isaiah: “You have performed all our works for us” (Isa. 26:12). For our good works belong to him whose compassion was not satisfied with raising us up, unless he also humbled himself for us.

If God, coeternal with the Father before the ages, had not become human in time, when would temporal humanity have understood eternal things? The descent of truth, therefore, became the ascent of our humility.

[Note: [Col. 0828D] The editions of 1502 and following read “of humanity,” against the manuscripts.]

Let us give him glory; let us give him praise—him who lives with the Father, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY VI

The verses 15, 16, and 17, together with part of verse 18, are explained, the meaning of the prophetic discourse being directed toward Holy Scripture and especially toward the commendation of the Gospel.

[Col. 0829A]

1213 1. “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12), because knowledge among the prophets is obscure. But, as Solomon’s voice bears witness, we have learned: “It is the glory of kings to conceal a word, and the glory of God to investigate a matter,” because it is an honor for human beings to conceal their secrets, while it is the glory of God to disclose the mysteries of his word (Prov. 25:2).

[Note: [Col. 0829D] This passage of Holy Scripture is read with the opposite sense in the Vulgate. Bernard followed Gregory in Sermon 65 on the Song of Songs; see note 292 in the latest edition of St Bernard, prepared by our Mabillon.]

Truth itself also says to the disciples: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light” (Matt. 10:27)—that is, explain openly what you hear in the obscurities of allegories.

The very obscurity of God’s utterances is of great benefit, because it exercises the understanding, so that it is enlarged through the labor, and the exercised mind grasps what an idle mind could not grasp. It has still another, greater advantage:

[Col. 0829B] the understanding of Holy Scripture, which would become cheap if everything in it were open, refreshes us with all the greater sweetness when discovered in its more obscure passages, the mind being wearied by the greater labor of seeking it.

For now, through the voice of the holy Ezekiel, we hear:

VERSE 15.—And when I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth.

2. What does the wheel signify except Holy Scripture, which turns toward the minds of its hearers from every side and is held back by no angle of error from the path of its preaching? It turns from every side because it proceeds rightly and humbly amid adversity and prosperity.

The circle of its precepts is now above and now below: what is said spiritually to the more perfect is suited literally to the weak; and what the little ones understand according to the letter, learned men raise on high through spiritual understanding.

For which of the little ones would not be nourished, according to the history of sacred reading, by the account of Esau and Jacob, in which one is sent out to hunt so that he may be blessed, while the other is blessed by his father through the substitution arranged by his mother (Gen. 27:3, 28)?

If one examines that history with somewhat greater subtlety, he sees that Jacob did not steal the blessing of the firstborn through fraud,

[Note: [Col. 0829D] The printed editions read *videtur* (“it seems”), with no support from any of our manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0829D] The printed editions seem to read this way, with none of our manuscripts supporting it.]

but received what was owed to him,

[Note: [Col. 0829D] In Beccensis and Rothomagensis: “but as something belonging to himself.” In the printed editions: “but so that it might belong to him.”]

which he had purchased, with his brother’s consent, by payment in lentils.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Longipontanus: “as the price of the lentils.” The editions: “by payment of lentils,” except the Vatican manuscript, which corruptly reads: “by payment of the price of the lentils.”]

3. But if someone with deeper understanding wishes to examine the deeds of both through the hidden meanings of allegory, he immediately rises from history to mystery.

For what does it mean that Isaac desires to be nourished by the hunt of his older son, except that almighty God desired to be nourished by the good works of the Jewish people? But while he delayed, Rebekah substituted the younger son, because, while the Jewish people sought good works outwardly, maternal grace instructed the Gentile people so that they might offer the almighty Father the food of good works and receive the blessing of their older brother.

The Gentile people offered these same foods from domestic animals,

[Col. 0830A] because, not seeking to please God through external sacrifices, 1214 the Gentile people say through the voice of the prophet: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will render praises to you” (Ps. 55:12).

What does it mean that Jacob covered his hands, arms, and neck with the skins of a kid, except that a kid was accustomed to be offered for sin? And the Gentile people slaughtered in themselves the sins of the flesh, but were not ashamed to confess that they were covered with carnal sins.

[Note: [Col. 0830D] In the Vatican manuscript there is inserted here: “while he is not ashamed to confess himself a sinner.” This gloss appears in none of the manuscripts known to us.]

What does it mean that he is clothed in the garments of his older brother, except that he is clothed in good works with the precepts of Holy Scripture, which had been given to the older people? And the younger uses within the house what the older, going outside, left behind, because the Gentile people hold in their minds those precepts which the Jewish people could not possess, since they paid attention only to the letter in them.

And what does it mean that Isaac does not know the same son whom he blesses, except what the Lord said through the Psalmist concerning the Gentile people: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45)?

What does it mean that he did not see the one who was present, yet saw what would come to him in the future, except that when almighty God foretold through his prophets that grace would be granted to the Gentiles,

[Note: [Col. 0830D] Vallicellianus reads: “when he proclaimed.”]

he did not see it in the present through grace, because at that time he left it in error, yet foresaw it through the grace of blessing because he was going to gather it sometime in the future?

Hence it is said in the blessing to that same Jacob, who represents the Gentile people: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord God has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). For, as Truth says in the Gospel, “The field is this world” (Matt. 13:38); and because the Gentile people, brought to the faith, spread fragrance throughout the whole world through their elect by means of their virtues, “the fragrance of the son” is the fragrance of a full field.

4. For the flower of the grapevine gives one kind of fragrance, because the virtue and reputation of preachers are great, and they intoxicate the minds of their hearers;

[Note: [Col. 0830D] Thus our manuscripts read. But the Paris edition of 1502, with others, has: “who make drunk.”]

the flower of the olive another, because the work of mercy is sweet, refreshing and shining like oil;

the flower of the rose another, because the fragrance that shines red and smells sweet from the blood of the martyrs is wondrous;

the flower of the lily another, because the white life of the flesh arises from the incorruption of virginity;

the flower of the violet another, because the virtue of the humble is great. Out of desire they occupy the lowest places, and through humility do not raise themselves from the earth to a higher position, while they preserve the purple of the heavenly kingdom in their minds.

[Note: [Col. 0830D] Saint-Germain, Ebroicensis, and other Norman manuscripts read: “in mind.”]

The ear of grain gives yet another fragrance when it is brought to maturity, because the perfection of good works is prepared to satisfy those who hunger for righteousness.

Therefore, because the Gentile people are scattered throughout the world in their elect, and through the virtues they practice fill all who understand with the fragrance of a good reputation, let it rightly be said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field.” But because it does not possess these virtues from itself, let it add: “which the Lord God has blessed.”

1215 5. And because this same people of the elect rises through some of its members into contemplation, while through others it grows rich solely in the works of the active life, it is rightly added there: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth” (Gen. 27:28).

For dew falls from above and gently. We receive the dew of heaven as often as, through the infusion of inner contemplation, we see something from above with delicate perception. But when we perform good works also through the body, we are enriched by the fatness of the earth.

6. What does it mean that Esau returns late to his father, except that the Jewish people return late to please the Lord?

[Note: [Col. 0831D] All the printed editions read: “to appease the Lord.” We prefer the unanimous reading of Saint-Germain, Suessionensis, Vallicellianus, the Norman manuscripts, and others.]

To him also it is said in the blessing: “There will come a time when the yoke will be removed from your neck” (ibid. 27:40). For the Jewish people will be freed from slavery to sin at the end, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

7. Which of the little ones would not be refreshed by the Gospel history itself in the working of the miracle in which the Lord commanded that empty jars be filled with water, and immediately changed that same water into wine (John 2:7)?

But when those more attentive in understanding hear this, they both venerate the sacred history by believing it and seek what it signifies inwardly. He who could change water into wine could also have filled the empty jars immediately with wine. But he commands that the jars first be filled with water because our hearts must first be filled through the history of sacred reading. And he changes water into wine for us when that history is transformed for us, through the mystery of allegory, into spiritual understanding.

The wheel, therefore, is drawn along as though across the earth, because it agrees with the little ones in humble speech; yet, pouring spiritual things into the great, it raises itself upward like a circle.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] Most Norman manuscripts read: “like a circle.” The printed editions agree with Saint-Germain, Suessionensis, and the others, which we follow.]

It is raised up from the very place where shortly before it seemed to touch the earth.

8. Because it builds from every side, the wheel runs as though in a circle. Hence it is also written in the Law: “You shall make a lampstand of purest gold, beaten work; its shaft and its branches, its cups, its spheres, and its lilies shall proceed from it” (Exod. 25:31; 37:17).

Who is signified by the lampstand except the Redeemer of the human race? In the nature of his humanity he shone with the light of divinity, so that he might become the lampstand of the world, in whose light every sinner might see the darkness in which he lay.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] The printed editions read: “the light shone forth.”]

Because he assumed our nature without sin, the lampstand of the tabernacle is commanded to be made of purest gold. Beaten work is produced by striking, because our Redeemer, who from conception and birth existed as perfect God and human being, endured the pains of sufferings and thus reached the glory of the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] The same editions read: “the blows of sufferings,” against all our manuscripts.]

The lampstand, therefore, was beaten from purest gold because he had no sin, yet his body advanced to immortality through the insults of the Passion. For with respect to the virtues of his soul, he had no defect through which he could have advanced by blows. But in his members, which are us, he advances daily through blows, because while we are struck and afflicted so that we may deserve to be his body, he himself advances.

Concerning this body it is written: “From him the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections, grows 1216 toward the increase of God” (Col. 2:19).

For we are all his body. The body is bound together by bonds and connections: when the chest is joined to the head, the arms to the chest, the hands to the arms, and the fingers to the hands, while the remaining members adhere to one another, the whole body is made complete.

Thus the holy apostles, because they stood close to our Redeemer, adhered to him like the chest to the head.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] The Norman manuscripts read: “were.”] Those who followed them as martyrs were like arms joined to the chest. When pastors and teachers were added to them through good works, hands adhered to arms.

This whole body of our Redeemer is supplied and constructed daily through bonds and connections in heaven, because when the souls of the elect are led there to him, his members are joined to him.

Concerning this it is rightly said: “Supplied and constructed, it grows toward the increase of God” (ibid.), because almighty God, our Redeemer, who has no need to advance in himself, nevertheless receives daily increase through his members.

Hence it is written again:

[Note: [Col. 0831D] Most Norman manuscripts read: “until we all come together.”]

“Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

The shaft of this same lampstand should be understood as the Church itself, which is his body, because it stands free amid so many adversities.

The branches that proceed from the shaft are the preachers, who have produced a sweet sound in the world, namely, a new song.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] Another reading has “proceed,” as in the printed editions.]

The cups are customarily filled with wine.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] In the Vatican manuscript and in Gussanville: “What, then, are the mouths of teachers except cups which intoxicate us with the wine of knowledge, so that we may forget the pleasures of the world that we loved?” We do not know where this reading was taken from. Our reading is found in the English, Norman, Saint-Germain, Longipontanus, Vallicellianus, and other manuscripts.]

What, then, are the minds of hearers except cups that are filled with the wine of knowledge by holy preachers?

The small spheres are nothing other than the rolling movement of preaching. For a sphere rolls in every direction. And preaching, which cannot be held back by adversity or lifted up by prosperity, is a sphere, because it is strong amid adversity and humble amid prosperity; it has neither an angle of fear nor an angle of arrogance.

It cannot be fixed in its course, because it rolls freely through everything.

[Note: [Col. 0832D] In the Norman, Longipontanus, and many other manuscripts, “sperula” is consistently written instead of “sphaerula,” and “spera” instead of “sphaera.” The Paris editions of 1502 and 1518 agree.]

9. To pursue the example we have introduced, lilies are rightly described on the lampstand after the branches, cups, and small spheres, because after the grace and rolling movement of preaching that we have mentioned comes that flourishing homeland which blooms for holy souls—that is, for eternal flowers.

The small spheres pertain to labor; the lilies to reward. Thus, just as among Moses the small sphere signifies the teaching of preaching, so here the wheel signifies Holy Scripture itself.

Therefore, when the prophet saw the holy creatures, he added: “And when I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth.”

10. In this matter we must ask why, when the wheels are described below, one wheel is first said to have appeared. The reason is that only the Old Testament was given to the ancient people, and it turned before their minds like a wheel in order to educate them.

The same wheel is rightly said to have appeared upon the earth. For it was said to sinful humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

[Col. 0833B] The wheel therefore appeared upon the earth because almighty God gave the Law upon the hearts of sinners.

But because these winged creatures, as we said earlier, signify the holy evangelists, how are the creatures seen first and the wheel afterward, when the Old Testament came first and 1217 the holy evangelists followed afterward? We can understand in this that those who excel in merit were first seen by the prophet. For just as the Holy Gospel surpasses the Old Testament, so its preachers ought to be placed first in the prophetic description.

11. There is, however, another matter that must still be considered in this description: the spirit of prophecy gathers earlier and later things together within itself in such a way that the prophet’s tongue cannot express them simultaneously. What he sees in its breadth flows out through divided utterances, and now he speaks of the last things after the first, now of the first after the last.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] The printed editions read: “from earlier utterances.”]

Hence the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of the holy universal Church, sees the glory of the evangelists through the likeness of four living creatures; yet suddenly adds things that took place in earlier times, clearly indicating that he saw simultaneously what the tongue of flesh would not suffice to say simultaneously.

But because we have said that all the perfect are also signified by the four living creatures, we must also consider that some saints existed before the Law, living strictly according to the natural law and pleasing the almighty Lord. Therefore the wheel is described after the creatures because many of the elect were perfect before the almighty Lord even before the Law.

But if we are to take the creatures, as we said, as the evangelists alone, there is still another matter we must consider.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] Corbie reads: “the saints … the evangelists.”]

The holy prophet saw that these very words, which he uttered wrapped in obscurity, would be disclosed not to the Jewish people but to the Gentiles. Therefore, speaking to us, he ought to have described the creatures first and the wheel afterward, because we who come to faith by the Lord’s gift learned not the Gospel through the Law, but the Law through the holy Gospel.

Where and what kind of wheel appeared, he adds when he says:

VERSE 15.—Beside the creatures, having four faces.

What follows is:

VERSE 16.—And the appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the appearance of the sea; and the likeness of all four was one, and their appearance and workmanship were as though a wheel were within a wheel.

12. What does it mean that, after one wheel had been mentioned, it is shortly afterward added, “as though a wheel were within a wheel,” except that the New Testament lay hidden allegorically within the letter of the Old Testament?

Hence the same wheel that appeared beside the creatures is described as having four faces, because Holy Scripture, through both Testaments, is divided into four parts. The Old Testament consists of the Law and the Prophets; the New consists of the Gospels and the Acts and sayings of the apostles.

We know that wherever we direct our face, there we see what is necessary. The wheel therefore has four faces because it first saw through the Law the evils that had to be cut away from the peoples; afterward it saw them through the Prophets; more subtly, through the Gospel; and finally, through the apostles, it perceived those things that were to be cut away from human sins.

It can also be understood that the wheel has four faces because Holy Scripture, extended through the grace of preaching, became known throughout the four parts of the world.

Hence the same wheel is rightly described as first appearing singly beside the creatures and afterward as having four faces, because, unless the Law agreed with the Gospel, it would not have become known throughout the four parts of the world. 1218
13. It follows: “And the appearance of the wheels, and their workmanship, was like the appearance of the sea.” [Note: We have deleted the conjunction “and,” added here by Gussanville contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.] Sacred utterances are rightly said to resemble the appearance of the sea, because in them there are great expanses [Col. 0834C] of sentences and heaps of meanings. Nor is Scripture called like the sea without reason, because the sentences of its speech are made firm by the sacrament of baptism. Or certainly, we should consider that we sail upon the sea in ships when we make our way toward the lands we desire. But what is there for us to desire except that land of which it is written: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Psalm 141:6)? [Note: Gussanville, most incorrectly, has *ligna autem*, “but by wood,” as he said, *evehitur quae mare transit*, “is carried across the sea.” None of these errors, however, has been recorded in the corrigenda.] By wood, as I have said, the one who crosses the sea is carried. And we know that sacred Scripture foretells the wood of the cross to us through the Law when it says: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deuteronomy 21:23). Paul attests this concerning our Redeemer when he says: “He was made a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Through the prophets also [Note: Thus the German, Suession, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts, Valeria Clara, etc. The editors preferred “is announced.”] it announces the wood when it is said: “The Lord will reign from the tree” (Psalm 96:10). And again: “Let us put wood in his bread” (Jeremiah 11:9). Through the Gospel, however, the wood of the cross is openly displayed, where the Lord’s very passion, which had been prophesied, is made clear. Through the apostles this same cross is also upheld in words and deeds, when Paul says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). And again: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 14). For us, therefore, who are making our way toward our eternal homeland, sacred Scripture is the sea through its four faces. It announces the cross because by the wood it carries us to the land of the living. If the prophet had not perceived that sacred Scripture resembles the sea, he would certainly not have said: “The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11:9). It follows:

**VERSE 16.** “And the likeness of the four was one, and their appearance and their workmanship were as if a wheel were within a wheel.”

14. The likeness of the four is one, because what the Law proclaims, the prophets also proclaim; what the prophets announce, the Gospel presents; and what the Gospel presents, the apostles preach throughout the world. Thus the likeness of the four is one, because the divine utterances, although distinguished by their times, are united in meaning.

15. “And their appearance and their workmanship were as if a wheel were within a wheel.” The wheel within the wheel is the New Testament within the Old Testament, as we have said, because what the Old Testament signified, the New Testament presented. To speak briefly of many examples: what does it mean that Eve was brought forth while Adam slept (Genesis 2:21–22), except that the Church was formed when Christ died? What does it mean that Isaac was led to be sacrificed, carried the wood, was placed upon the altar, and yet lived (Genesis 22:6), except that our Redeemer, led to his passion, himself carried the wood of his cross? Thus, in the sacrifice for us, he died in his humanity, yet remained immortal in his divinity. What does it mean that the murderer, after the death of the high priest, is released and returns to his own land (Numbers 35:25; Joshua 20:6), except that the human race, which by sinning inflicted death upon itself, is released from the bonds of its sins after the death of the true priest—that is, our Redeemer—and is restored to possession of paradise?

What does it mean that a mercy seat was commanded to be made in the tabernacle (Exodus 25:17), above which two cherubim—one from one end and the other from the other end—were placed of the purest gold, spreading their wings and covering the oracle [Note: In the Corbie, Évreux, and other Norman manuscripts: “one from one end, and the other.” The printed editions, which we follow, agree with the German and other manuscripts.] [Note: Thus the German, Suession, Norman, Valeria Clara, Longpont, and other witnesses. But the printed editions read: “what does it mean that they look at one another?”] and looking toward one another with faces turned toward the mercy seat (Exodus 25:20), except that the two Testaments so agree with one another in the Mediator between God and human beings [Note: The printed editions read “agree.”] that what one signifies, the other presents?

For what is signified by the mercy seat except the Redeemer of the human race himself? Of him Paul says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Romans 3:25). And what is signified by the two cherubim, which are said to represent the fullness of knowledge, except the two Testaments? One of them stands at one end of the mercy seat and the other at the other end, because what the Old Testament began to promise prophetically concerning the incarnation of our Redeemer, the New Testament fully relates as accomplished.

The two cherubim were made of the purest gold because the two Testaments are described with pure and simple truth. They spread their wings and cover the oracle [Col. 0836A] because we, who are the oracle of almighty God, are protected from impending sins by the edification of sacred Scripture. As we attentively contemplate its sentences, we are veiled by its wings from the error of ignorance.

The two cherubim therefore look toward one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy seat, because the two Testaments differ from one another in nothing. They hold their faces, as it were, toward one another because what one promises, the other presents, while they see the Mediator between God and human beings placed between them. The cherubim would turn their faces away from one another if what one Testament promised, the other denied. But while they speak in harmony about the Mediator between God and human beings, they look toward the mercy seat so that they may gaze upon one another.

The wheel within the wheel, therefore, is the New Testament present within the Old Testament. And, as we have often already said, what the Old Testament promised, the New presented; and what the former secretly announced, the latter openly proclaims as accomplished. The prophecy of the New Testament, therefore, is the Old Testament; and the exposition of the Old Testament is the New Testament. It follows:

**VERSE 17.** “They went toward their four parts [Note: In the Suession, Norman, and many other manuscripts: ‘going, they went.’ The word ‘going’ is absent from the German and other older manuscripts. It is nevertheless found a little below: ‘but going toward their four parts, they went.’], and they did not turn back.”

16. Where else do the divine utterances go than to human hearts? But “they went toward their four parts,” because sacred Scripture goes to human hearts through the Law by signifying the mystery. Through the prophets it goes somewhat more openly, by prophesying the Lord. Through the Gospel it goes by presenting the one whom it prophesied. Through the apostles it goes by preaching the one whom the Father presented for our redemption.

The wheels therefore have faces and ways, because the sacred utterances display knowledge of the commandments together with the performance of works. And they go toward their four parts because they speak in distinct times, as we said earlier—or certainly because they preach the incarnate Lord in all the regions of the world. Of these it is soon added explicitly:

**IBID.** “And they did not turn back when they walked.”

17. These words were spoken above concerning the living creatures, but the same things cannot be understood of the wheels as of the living creatures. We have said that the wheels signify the Testaments. The Old Testament did indeed walk, because through preaching it came to human minds; but it turned back after itself because, according to the letter, it could not be observed to the end in its commandments and sacrifices [Col. 0836D]. For it did not remain without alteration, since spiritual understanding was lacking in it.

But when our Redeemer came into the world, he caused that to be understood spiritually which he found being observed carnally. Thus, while its letter is understood spiritually, all that carnal observance in it is brought to life. The New Testament, moreover, was also called the eternal testament through the pages of the Old Testament, because its meaning is never changed.

It is therefore rightly said that the wheels went forward and did not turn back as they walked, because, while the New Testament is not abolished and while the Old, now understood spiritually, is retained, they do not return behind themselves but remain unchangeable to the end of the world. They walk but do not turn back, because they come spiritually to our hearts in such a way that their commandments and purposes are no longer altered.

It follows:

**VERSE 18.** “The stature of the wheels also, and their height, and their appearance was dreadful.” [Note: *Horribile* and *horrendum* often mean “venerable,” as in *Aeneid* VII, of the house of Picus: “Venerable for its groves and the worship of its forefathers”; that is, venerable. Here the Hebrew properly reads “terrible,” which may refer to reverential fear.]

18. What does it mean that these three things are said to be present in the utterances of sacred Scripture, so that they are remembered as having stature, height, and a dreadful—or terrifying—appearance? We must diligently inquire what is called the stature of divine Scripture, what its height is, and what its dreadful appearance is.

We must therefore understand that standing corresponds to the life of one who acts well. Hence Paul says: “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). He also says to the disciples: “Stand thus in the Lord, beloved” (Philippians 4:1). And the prophet, who saw himself standing before the Lord in life and conduct, says: “As the Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (2 Kings 3:14).

Height, however, is the promise of the heavenly kingdom. One reaches it when all the corruption of mortal life has been subdued. The dreadful appearance is the terror of Gehenna, which torments the reprobate without end and preserves them forever in torment.

The stature, therefore, consists in uprightness of command [Note: The printed editions read “in uprightness of preaching,” against the evidence of the English, Norman, German, Corbie, Suession, and other manuscripts]; the height in the loftiness of the promise from above; and the dreadful appearance in the threats and terrors of the punishment to come.

Sacred Scripture therefore has stature because it directs conduct toward standing, so that the minds of its hearers are not bent toward earthly desire. It has height because it promises the joys of eternal life in the heavenly homeland. It also has a dreadful appearance because it threatens all the reprobate with the punishments of Gehenna. Thus it displays its stature in the formation of conduct, its height in the promise of rewards, and its dreadful appearance in the terrors of punishments. It is upright in its commandments, lofty in its promises, and dreadful in its threats.

It has stature when, through the prophet, it says: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed; judge the orphan [Note: So the German and other more ancient manuscripts. The Vulgate editions have “judge the fatherless.”]; defend the widow” (Isaiah 1:17). And again: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and wandering into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise those of your own flesh” (Isaiah 58:7).

It has height when, through the same prophet, it says: “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory” (Isaiah 60:19).

It has a dreadful appearance when, describing hell, it says: “The day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion; and its streams shall be turned into pitch [Note: The 1502 edition, through a gross error, reads “and its smoke”; later editors, with no exception, propagated and adopted the reading, disregarding the manuscripts and Isaiah’s own text], and its soil into sulfur; and the land shall become burning pitch; night and day it shall not be extinguished forever” (Isaiah 34:8 and following). Blessed Job also describes it, saying: “A land that is dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death is, and no order, but everlasting horror inhabits it” (Job 10:21–22).

It has stature when the Lord, being gracious, promises through it, saying: “As the new heavens and the new earth, which I shall make stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring and your name stand” (Isaiah 66:22). For those truly stand before the Lord who do not dissipate their life in wickedness.

It has height when it immediately adds: “And it shall be month after month, and Sabbath after Sabbath, and all flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord” (ibid., 23). What is a month except the perfection of days? And what is a Sabbath except rest, in which it is not permitted to perform servile work? Thus there is “month after month,” because those who live perfectly here are brought there to the perfection of glory. There is “Sabbath after Sabbath,” because those who cease here from wicked work rest there in heavenly recompense.

It also has a dreadful appearance when it immediately adds: “And they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (ibid., 24). For what more dreadful thing can be said or imagined than to receive the wounds of condemnation and never to bring the pains of those wounds to an end?

Concerning this dreadful appearance of the wheels, Zephaniah rightly says, when the day of judgment is announced as about to come upon hardened minds: “The great day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift. The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah 1:14).

19. But since we have set forth what was said concerning the outer wheel, it remains that we should also explain the stature, height, and dreadful appearance of the inner wheel. The inner wheel has its stature when, through the holy Gospel, it forbids us to bend toward earthly desires, saying in the words of our Redeemer: “Take heed that your hearts not be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness or with the cares of this life” (Luke 21:34).

It has height when it promises concerning the same Redeemer: “But to all who believed in him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). For what can be said higher than this power, or more sublime than this height, by which each created person becomes a child of the Creator?

It has a dreadful appearance when it speaks concerning the reprobate, saying: “These shall go into eternal punishment” (Matthew 25:46).

It has stature when the Truth admonishes the disciples, saying: “Sell what you possess and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old” (Luke 12:33).

It has the height of promise when it says: “They shall come from the east and the west, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11).

It has a dreadful appearance when it adds: “But the children of the kingdom shall be cast into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 12). To them the voice of the Truth again says: “You shall die in your sins” (John 8:21, 24).

It has stature when, in the words of the first shepherd, it says: “Supply virtue in your faith, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge self-restraint, and in self-restraint endurance, and in endurance godliness, and in godliness brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love [Note: The German and Corbie manuscripts read “purity”]” (2 Peter 1:5).

It has height when it soon afterward says: “For thus an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be abundantly supplied to you” (ibid., 11). He again promises this to good shepherds, saying: “When the chief shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Peter 5:4).

It has a dreadful appearance when it says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens shall pass away with great force [Note: The printed editions read “will pass through,” although in the German, Norman, Longpont, and nearly all the manuscripts we read “will pass away”], and the elements shall be dissolved by heat” (2 Peter 3:10, 6). Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, waiting for and hastening toward the coming of the day of God [Note: Gussanville reads “through which,” departing from the manuscripts and earlier printed editions], through which the burning heavens shall be dissolved and the elements shall melt in the heat of fire?

It has stature when, through Paul, it raises us from earthly desires, saying: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3:5).

It has height when it promises, saying: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (ibid., 3).

It has a dreadful appearance when it threatens, saying: “At the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven, with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will suffer eternal punishment in destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power” (2 Thessalonians 1:7).

It has stature when it admonishes us, saying: “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:15).

It has height when it promises, saying: “If we die together, we shall also live together; if we endure, we shall also reign together” (2 Timothy 2:11). And again: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

It has a dreadful appearance when it threatens, saying: “A certain fearful expectation of judgment and the fury of fire which will consume the adversaries” (Hebrews 10:27). He says again: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (ibid., 31).

He gathers all these things together in a brief sentence, saying: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Ephesians 3:18).

Breadth belongs to love, because it embraces even the love of enemies, and through that love by which almighty God loves us broadly, he also bears with us patiently. This, therefore, is what we ought to show toward our neighbors, which we see our Creator showing toward us, though we are unworthy.

Breadth and length therefore pertain to stature, because love expands conduct so that charity may bear patiently with the faults of brothers and sisters. Height is the reward of eternal recompense, concerning whose immensity it is said: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). It therefore has height in sublimity, because the eternal joys of the saints cannot now be penetrated by any thought [Note: Longpont reads: “glory … prevails.”].

Depth is that immeasurable condemnation of punishments which plunges those whom it receives into the lowest depths. In these matters the sacred utterances have a dreadful appearance because they strike their hearers with immeasurable terror when they speak of the punishments of hell.

It is therefore rightly said: “The stature of the wheels also, and their height, and their appearance was dreadful,” because sacred Scripture in both Testaments is upright in admonition, lofty in promise, and terrifying in threat.

Let what we have said today, dearest brothers and sisters, by the Lord’s generosity, be sufficient, so that, having recovered leisure, we may return to discussing what follows, trusting in God, the Creator of all things, and in our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY VII

An exposition of verse 18 together with the five following verses, chiefly concerning the usefulness of sacred reading and the performance of works of charity with such caution that we direct our attention above all to ourselves through repentance.

1225 1. As you know, dearest brothers and sisters, it is the custom of prophecy now to look at one thing and now at another, and suddenly to carry its words from one subject to another, as the Psalmist did when speaking of the Lord: “God is a just judge, strong and long-suffering [Note: So all the manuscripts. Yet, despite their testimony, the printed editions have: ‘and patient.’]; is he angry every day? If you are not converted, he will brandish his sword, bend his bow, and prepare it; and in it he has prepared the vessels of death, he has made his arrows burning” (Psalm 7:12 and following). He suddenly adds: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity; he opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit which he made” (ibid., 15) [Note: Several Norman manuscripts read: “Behold, he brought forth injustice; he conceived, etc.”].

Behold: while he was recounting the Lord’s justice, with no apparent change of voice he suddenly introduced the sinner’s guilt. It is enough that I have mentioned this one example, because whoever is accustomed to reading the prophets knows how frequently they do this. Hence now the prophet Ezekiel, while speaking about the wheels, added:

**VERSE 18.** “And the whole body of the four was full of eyes all around them.”

2. For by saying not *ipsarum* but *ipsorum*, he clearly indicates that his speech suddenly returned from the wheels to the living creatures. Through these, as was said earlier, all the perfected are signified.

The bodies of the living creatures are therefore described as full of eyes because the action of the saints is watchful on every side: eagerly providing for what is good and carefully avoiding what is evil. This is more difficult [Note: The printed editions read “because the saints,” in place of “where the mind of the saints.”] where the mind of the saints watches intensely lest evils conceal themselves from their eyes under the appearance of good.

The life of the saints is therefore circumspect, lest it be free in such a way that it becomes proud, because pride often exceeds itself in words [Note: The Vatican, together with the Suession, reads: “and desires to be heard”], and liberty of purity seeks to be seen.

Nor should it be humble in such a way that it becomes fearful, because at times fear restrains the mind, and it does not presume to speak what is right, while nevertheless, in that very timid thought, it pretends to be humility.

Nor should it be frugal in such a way that it becomes grasping, because often stinginess seeks to be regarded as frugality, so that one may appear to hold justly and necessarily whatever one does not mercifully wish to spend on a needy neighbor.

Nor should it be merciful in such a way that it becomes wasteful, because sometimes it considers wastefulness to be mercy. For it is one thing to give necessary things to one’s neighbors out of devotion to piety, and another to scatter one’s possessions without any intention of reward.

Whatever is done, therefore, must be weighed at the root of its intention, so that we may consider with what merit it will be regarded in the judgment of the Creator.

Hence the same Creator says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke 11:34). He calls the intention the eye and the action the body. For if our intention is simple before God, our action will not be dark in his judgment.

Since holy men therefore watch carefully so that they may observe themselves on every side and guard themselves everywhere—lest they pursue evil for its own sake, or perform the same things under the appearance of good, that is, lest vices deceive them into thinking that they are virtues—they have their whole body full of eyes all around, because all their action is both filled and surrounded by the foresight of vigilance.

3. Hence it is that the apostle Paul, when he saw fit to show mercy to a certain penitent for a crime committed [Note: The German reads: “when he wished to show mercy to the Corinthians”], says: “If you have forgiven anyone anything, I also have. For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

If mercy was to be shown, why does the outstanding teacher associate himself with the will of his disciples in such humility, so that neither he himself might appear separated from the disciples nor the disciples from him in the matter of compassion? [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “why does he associate himself with the humility of so great a will?” The Corbie manuscript has this reading before correction.] It is because, with the eye of watchful foresight, he observes that often, while one person forgives, another becomes angry. And what sort of sacrifice of mercy is it when it is offered together with the discord of one’s neighbor?

Hence he rightly says: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his designs.” For he usually injects the evil of strife into one heart from the very place where he sees another has carried out an act of piety.

The good that is done without attention to whether evil may creep into it from another side is imperfect—unless, perhaps, when something cannot be done without causing someone scandal, failing to do it is itself a fault.

4. We say this, however, so that we may make known to your love that in our good work we must sometimes beware of causing scandal to our neighbor, while at other times we must disregard it as nothing [Note: The printed editions, except Gussanville, read: “as the vow of our love.” In what sense this is intended is unknown to us.].
