We learned this from our own Teacher [Note: Valeria Clara reads: “what we learned from our author himself.”], who, when the tribute was demanded of Peter, first proposed an example by which he showed that he owed nothing, saying: “From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” (Matthew 17:24–25) [Note: Several Norman manuscripts read: “the kings of the nations.”]

When Peter answered, “From strangers,” he immediately replied: “Then the sons are free.” But after he had shown that he was free, lest he should perhaps cause anyone scandal, he added: “But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea and cast a hook; and take the first fish that comes up, and when you have opened its mouth you will find a coin; take it and give it to them for me and for you” (ibid., 26).

Again, when he said that everything entering the mouth does not defile a person, the disciples approached and said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this word, were scandalized?” (Matthew 15:11 and following). But he answered: “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind and guides of the blind.”

Behold: the Truth, our teacher, gave what was not owed as tribute, so that scandal might not arise in certain hearts; and again, because he saw scandal arising in certain hearts against the truth, he permitted them to remain in their scandal.

5. From this we must consider that, insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing scandal to our neighbors. But if scandal is taken from the truth, it is more useful to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.

The bodies of the living creatures are therefore full of eyes when they carefully observe themselves on every side.

6. We must also know that often, while we attend to certain things, it happens that we neglect others; and wherever we neglect, there certainly we do not have an eye.

For we know what that Pharisee who had gone up into the temple to pray said, as the Gospel testifies. He said: “God, I give you thanks” (Luke 18:11). He rightly gave thanks to God, from whom he had received the good things he had done. He also added: “Because I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector; I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess” (ibid., 12).

Behold: the Pharisee had an eye for displaying abstinence, extending mercy, and giving thanks to God, but he did not have an eye for guarding humility.

And what does it profit that nearly the whole city is carefully guarded against the ambushes of enemies if one opening is left uncovered through which the enemies may enter? What does a guard placed almost everywhere profit when the whole city is opened to the enemies through the neglect of a single place?

The Pharisee who fasted, gave tithes, and returned thanks to God watched, as it were, almost all around in guarding his city. But because he did not pay attention to one opening of pride within himself, he suffered the enemy’s attack precisely where, through negligence, he closed his eye.

Because holy minds therefore watch themselves on every side and carry the eye of fear and concern around in all their works—lest they do anything wrong, or fail to do the right things that have been commanded, or, after completing good deeds, become puffed up in their thoughts and offend all the more grievously because they appear righteous outwardly while sinning more secretly—it is rightly said: “Their whole body was full of eyes all around.”

7. It should also be known that in the older translation one does not find: “Their whole body was full of eyes all around”; rather, it says: “Their backs were full of eyes.” 1226 This statement does not differ from the meaning that builds up. For people, even sinners, often guard those things that are before their face. But righteous men, because they also guard themselves in those things that are not seen openly and before the face, are said to have eyes in their backs.

Those, therefore, who examine what is hidden and guard themselves against the very things that lie concealed certainly have eyes in their backs. This can nevertheless also be understood in another way, because we see what is before our face, whereas another person sees our back, and we cannot see it ourselves.

Since holy men carefully examine themselves in those matters by which they may be judged by others, and see themselves strictly just as they are often strictly seen by others—men who are ignorant of nothing in themselves, not even of what could remain hidden from them [Note: The word “themselves” (*se*) is wanting in the printed editions. The manuscripts vary here: the Norman manuscripts read, “because in themselves not even those things which could lie hidden from themselves”; the Suession manuscript, “in what matter”; and the German and Longpont manuscripts, “who in themselves.”]—they carry light in their backs.

It follows:

**VERSE 19.** “And when the living creatures walked, the wheels also walked alongside them; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together with them.”

8. The living creatures walk when holy men understand in sacred Scripture how they ought to live morally. The living creatures are lifted up from the earth when holy men raise themselves into contemplation.

And because sacred Scripture itself makes progress for each saint to the extent that he has progressed in it, it is rightly said: “When the living creatures walked, the wheels also walked alongside them [Note: The words ‘alongside them’ are added in the German and Suession manuscripts]; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together with them,” because the divine utterances grow together with the reader. For each person understands them the more deeply the more deeply he attends to them.

Hence the wheels are not lifted up if the living creatures are not lifted up, because unless the minds of readers advance toward higher things, the divine words lie ununderstood, as if in the depths.

When the speech of sacred Scripture seems tepid in meaning to any reader [Note: The particle “if” is absent in the Suession, Longpont, and most Norman manuscripts. It is found in the German and several other manuscripts, as well as in the printed editions], and does not stir his mind, and no light of understanding shines forth in his thought, the wheel is both idle and upon the earth, because the living creature has not been lifted up from the earth.

But if the living creature walks—that is, if it seeks the order of good living and, by the movement of the heart, discovers how to set down the step of good action—the wheels walk alongside it, because you find as much progress in sacred Scripture as you yourself have made in relation to it.

But if the winged living creature stretches itself upward in contemplation, the wheels are immediately raised from the earth, because you understand that the things which you previously believed were spoken in sacred Scripture according to an earthly manner are not earthly.

And it comes about that you perceive the words of sacred Scripture to be heavenly if, kindled by the grace of contemplation, you raise yourself toward heavenly things. The wondrous and ineffable power of sacred utterance is recognized when the reader’s mind is penetrated by love from above.

Because the living creature therefore raises itself to higher things, the wheel flies.

It follows:

**VERSE 20.** “Wherever the spirit went, there the wheels also were lifted up together with the spirit as it went, following it.”

9. For wherever the spirit of the reader tends, there the divine utterances also rise, because if you seek something lofty in them by seeing and understanding it, these same sacred utterances grow with you and ascend with you to higher things.

It is rightly said of these same wheels: “Following it.” If the reader’s spirit seeks something moral or historical in them, the moral or historical meaning follows it. If it seeks something typological, figurative speech is immediately recognized. If it seeks something contemplative, the wheels at once take on wings, as it were, and are suspended in the air [Col. 0844C], because heavenly understanding is opened within the words of sacred utterance.

Wherever, therefore, the spirit went, there the wheels also were lifted up together with the spirit as it went, following it. For the wheels follow the spirit because, as has often already been said, the words of sacred utterance grow in understanding according to the meaning sought by the readers.

10. In one and the same sentence of Scripture, one person is nourished by history alone; [Note: [Col. 0844D] So the German, Norman, and almost all the others. In the printed editions, however: “another [seeks] a typological [understanding], another indeed [seeks a contemplative understanding].”] another seeks a typological understanding, and another, through the type, a contemplative understanding. And it often happens, as was said, that all three are found together in one and the same sentence.

When Moses was called from the burning bush (Exod. 3:3), he drew nearer to see the sight; and behold, the bush was burning, yet was not consumed. This is a great miracle. If you seek in it history alone, there is something by which the reader’s mind may be nourished: you see that fire burns in wood without consuming it. But if you seek a typological understanding, what is the flame except the law, of which it is written, “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2)? And what did that bush signify except the Jewish people, covered with the thorns of their sins? Yet the burning bush could not be consumed, because the Jewish people received the fire of the law, but nevertheless did not abandon the thorns of their sins, nor did the flame of the divine word burn away their vices.

Perhaps another desires to contemplate greater things through the type in this event. Since its meaning expands, the wheels are likewise lifted up. The only Son of God became the one perfect man among human beings. He had no sins of his own, but took upon himself the thorns of our wickedness, and until his Passion deigned to humble himself for us, receiving in himself the fire of our tribulation. [Note: [Col. 0845D] German and Lyre: “according to humility.”] Yet he both burned and did not burn, because he died according to his humanity, while remaining immortal according to his divinity. He received from us that from which a sacrifice might be made for us, and yet in himself remained impassible and immutable, so that he might change us from our former state.

Perhaps another seeks, through history, moral meaning, and yet another, through allegorical understanding, contemplation. [Note: [Col. 0845D] Corbie, followed by the 1502 edition, reads: “another understands the morality of history through the allegory of the understanding.” The German, Norman, and the other better witnesses follow.] It is clear to everyone, according to the historical sense, what is written in the law: that the turtledove offered for sin should have its head twisted back toward its wings, so that it remains attached to its neck [Note: [Col. 0845D] Norman, Vallicelliana, Longpont: “the turtledove which.”] and is not completely severed (Lev. 1:15; 5:8). In these words there is no uncertain historical meaning for readers. But if you seek to understand them morally, the wheel is set in motion when the sentence of the sacred word is led toward moral understanding.

For we ourselves must be a turtledove in the sacrifice of almighty God, so that our head may be twisted back toward the wings—that is, so that the mind may be turned toward the virtues. [Note: [Col. 0845D] Longpont: “we twist [it] back toward the wings, that is, [our] minds.”] We rightly understand the mind by the head, because just as the head governs the body, so the mind governs actions. But the head is commanded to be twisted back toward the wings, so that you may do what you say and join the mouth to deeds. The head must not be cut off in such a way that it is separated from the body; rather, being cut through only in part, it is commanded to remain attached to its body. For our mind must be cut away from carnal pleasure, but it must not be cut off from the necessary care of the flesh. Hence it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). What is forbidden in the context of desires is plainly permitted in the context of necessity.

The turtledove’s head, therefore, is cut off in part and remains attached in part, so that, as was said, our mind may be cut away from the will of the flesh, yet not be severed from necessity. [Note: The 1502 edition, though erroneous, followed by later editions, reads “from the pleasure of the flesh.” The German, Corbie, Norman, and many others, not to mention them all, read “from the will.” What wonder, since in John 1 we read, “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh”?]

What if someone seeks to contemplate this kind of sacrifice under the typological understanding of our Redeemer? Let the mind rise to stronger things; let the living creatures be lifted up, so that the wheels likewise may be lifted up. For who is our head except the Redeemer of the human race? Of him it is written: “He gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body” (Eph. 1:22).

When the Jews persecuted him, they attempted to erase his name from the earth. And when they saw him crucified and buried, they believed that they had separated him from the love of everyone. But the turtledove’s head was both cut and yet not separated from its body, because by enduring death for us he more truly joined us all to himself in that very death; and by visibly withdrawing himself from our eyes, he invisibly rooted himself in our minds. The turtledove’s head, therefore, was cut and remained attached to the body, because our Redeemer suffered for us, yet was not separated from us by his Passion.

Since, therefore, the words of the sacred utterance grow together with the spirit of the readers, it is rightly said now: “Wherever the spirit went, there the wheels also were lifted up, going along with the spirit.” And it is added:

**IBID. — For the spirit of life was in the wheels.**

11. The spirit of life is in the wheels because through the sacred utterances we are made alive by the gift of the Spirit, so that we may drive away deadly works from ourselves. It may also be understood that the spirit goes wherever God touches the reader’s mind in different ways and arrangements: at one moment, by arousing it to zeal through the words of the sacred utterance, he raises it to vengeance; at another, he calms it toward patience; at another, he instructs it for preaching; at another, he pierces it with the laments of repentance.

But let us run briefly through these same words that we have mentioned, and see how the wheels follow the spirit, which is called the spirit of life and is said to dwell in the wheels.

Certainly, if the spirit of life touches the reader’s mind in the fervor of zeal, he immediately sees in the sacred utterances that Moses, returning to the camp and learning that the people had sinned through idols, struck them down with swords in the fervor of the spirit (Exod. 32:27); that Phinehas, pursuing sexual immorality, appeased the Lord’s anger with a sword (Num. 25:8); that Peter struck and killed with a word those who were lying to him (Acts 5:5, 10); and that Paul threatens negligent disciples with a rod (1 Cor. 4:21). [Note: Suessiones and Longpont: “strikes.”] [Note: Ebroicensis, Sagiensis, Vallicelliana, Longpont, Suessiones: “threatens with a rod.”]

12. If the spirit of life touches the reader’s mind so as to preserve patience, the wheels immediately follow as well, because in the sacred utterances he finds that Moses and Aaron, when they suffered persecution from the people while speaking what was right, ran to the tabernacle and prayed for the very people from whom they were fleeing (Num. 20:6). Their holy mind endured the swelling pride of the arrogant, yet did not erupt into hatred against them. True patience is that which loves even the one whom it bears. To endure while hating is not the virtue of gentleness, but a covering for anger.

In the same utterances he also finds that Samuel, having been removed from the leadership, confessed that he had prayed even for those who had removed him (1 Sam. 8:22); that none of the saints reached heavenly glory except by preserving patience; and that the very author of the human race endured spittle, blows, a crown of thorns, the cross, and the lance, yet prayed for his persecutors.

13. If the spirit of life excites the reader’s mind toward the discipline of preaching, the wheels immediately follow, because in the sacred utterances he finds Moses, at the Lord’s command, rising up against the king of Egypt with how many words of free preaching (Exod. 5:10); that Stephen said to the faithless Jews, “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51), and did not fear among the stones (ibid., 57); that Peter, beaten with rods so that he would not speak in the name of Jesus, replied with great freedom, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:28–29); and that Paul was bound with chains (Phil. 1:14), yet “the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). [Note: The reading *perfidian­tibus*, otherwise unusual, is found in the German manuscripts and most of the Norman ones. Suessiones and Longpont instead read “the Jews who were stoning him.”]

14. If the spirit of life pierces the reader’s mind with the laments of repentance, the wheels immediately follow, when the words of sacred Scripture present David in repentance: when, rebuked by the prophet because he had not submitted to the heavenly King, he was not ashamed to confess to the one rebuking him what he had done (2 Sam. 12:13); when the tax collector, who recognized the guilt of his wickedness, although he came to the temple unjust, returned from the temple justified (Luke 18:13–14); when Peter washed away the stains of his denial with tears (Matt. 26:75); and when the thief who acknowledged his guilt on the cross found forgiveness in that very death (Luke 23:43).

The prophet again repeats these matters concerning the wheels and adds:

**VERSE 21. — As they went, they went; and when they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted up from the earth, the wheels also were lifted up with them, following them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels.**

15. These things, as you know, dearest brothers, have for the most part already been said, but they are narrated again in a repeated description. Let us therefore not be reluctant to repeat briefly, by explaining them, what the Spirit deigned to narrate through the prophet by repeating it. The only new point added in these words is what is said: “When they stood, they stood.”

There are some who advance to the point of knowing how to distribute well the earthly goods they have received, who devote themselves to works of mercy and assist the oppressed. These people go, in that they direct themselves toward the benefit of their neighbor. With them, therefore, the wheels walk, because the sacred utterances arrange the steps of their words along their way. [Note: German, Bec, Rouen: “on his journey,” perhaps referring to the neighbor. The first two codices read “are arranged.”]

There are others who are so strong in holding fast to the faith they have received that they are able to resist every adversity. They are not only not dragged into the perversity of unbelief, but also oppose those who speak perversely and draw them toward uprightness. With these who stand, the wheels also stand, because the words of the sacred utterance confirm their uprightness when they hear: “Stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught” (2 Thess. 2:15). And again: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in faith” (1 Pet. 5:8–9). [Note: The printed editions read “because in them.” The word *in* is absent from the German, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

There are others who despise all earthly things, not deigning to possess any of the things that pass away, and, as was said above, suspend themselves in the contemplation of God. With these who are lifted up, the wheels are likewise lifted up, because the higher each person advances, the higher the sacred utterances speak to him.

The living creatures therefore go for the benefit of their neighbor, stand for the guarding of themselves, and are lifted up for the contemplation of God.

16. But the wheels likewise go, stand, and are lifted up, because sacred reading is found to be such as the one who seeks it himself becomes. If you have advanced to the active life, it walks with you. If you have advanced to steadfastness and constancy of spirit, it stands with you. If by God’s grace you have reached the contemplative life, it flies with you.

And again it adds: “Because the spirit of life was in the wheels.” This is said a second time—that the spirit of life is in the wheels—because there are two Testaments of sacred Scripture, and God’s Spirit willed both of them to be written in order to free us from the death of the soul.

Or certainly because there are two commandments of love, namely love of God and love of neighbor, through both of which the words of sacred Scripture give us life. It is therefore said a second time that the spirit of life was in the wheels, because we grasp love of God and neighbor in the divine utterances.

Through the commandments of sacred Scripture we come back to life, we who lay dead in guilt. Hence the Psalmist says to almighty God: “I will never forget your ordinances, because by them you have given me life” (Ps. 118:93). The Lord’s commandments are called ordinances, because by correcting us through them he justifies us. Of these the Psalmist says more plainly: “I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words” (ibid., 16).

In them, therefore, he gives us life, because through them he shows us spiritual life and pours it into our minds through the Spirit’s breathing. Since this occurs daily in the minds of the elect through the gift of grace, it is rightly said: “The spirit of life was in the wheels.”

17. This Scripture has become for us, in the darkness of the present life, the light of our journey. Hence Peter says: “You do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1:19). Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

Yet we know that our own lamp is itself obscure to us unless truth illumines it in our minds. Hence the Psalmist again says: “For you illumine my lamp, O Lord my God; illumine my darkness” (Ps. 17:29). What is a burning lamp except a light? But created light does not shine for us unless it is illumined by uncreated light.

Since almighty God himself both created and opened to our salvation the words of the holy Testaments, the spirit of life was in the wheels. It follows:

**VERSE 22. — And the likeness of a firmament over the heads of the living creatures, like the appearance of a terrifying crystal, [Note: Vallicelliana: “the likeness of a firmament over the heads of the living creatures.” “Of the living creatures” is absent from the German.] spread out [Note: Most Norman manuscripts: “spread out,” namely, the likeness.] above their heads from above.**

18. With the Lord’s generosity, we shall explain this in two ways, leaving it to the reader’s judgment to decide what should be chosen.

By the name “firmament,” the heavenly powers may be understood. This firmament is rightly called “like the appearance of crystal,” because crystal is indeed exceedingly hard, but is solidified from water. [Note: [Col. 0849D] Ebroicensis, Jumièges, Utica, and other Norman manuscripts read “strong crystal”; in the German and other witnesses followed by the printed editions, *crystallum* is neuter.] The angelic nature, when it was created, received free choice: whether it wished to remain in humility and continue in the sight of almighty God, or slip into pride and fall from blessedness. [Note: [Col. 0849D] In Gussanville the word “whether” (*an*) had dropped out, seriously impairing both sense and clarity; it has been restored from the printed editions and manuscripts.] In this respect it was like water.

But because, when others fell, the holy angels remained in their blessedness and received this as a gift—that they can no longer fall at all—their nature, since it can no longer be led into changeable descent, was hardened, as it were, into the magnitude of crystal. [Note: The printed editions, with excellent sense, read “cannot be cast down changeably.” But the German and all our manuscripts read “cannot be led.” Suessiones has “wonderfully” instead of “changeably.”]

This crystal is said to be terrifying and spread out over the heads of the living creatures because those angelic powers who stand before the sight of almighty God are still terrifying and fearsome to us, placed as we are in this corruption. Their joys are said to be above the heads of the living creatures because they exceed the capacity of our minds. For who, placed in corruptible flesh, could comprehend what that ineffable and endless joy of the angels is; what blessedness it is to see the face of the Creator without decline and to remain without change in his delight?

19. By the name “firmament,” however, our Redeemer himself may figuratively be understood: true God above all things and perfect man made among all things, in whom our nature was strengthened before the Father. Of him the Psalmist prophetically says: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself” (Ps. 79:18).

Before human nature was taken up by the Creator of all things, it was earth, for it was not yet a firmament. To sinful man it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3:19). But after it was assumed by the author of all things, raised into heaven, and led above the angels, that which had been earth became a firmament.

What appearance this visible firmament resembles is added when it is said: “Like the appearance of a terrifying crystal.” Crystal, as was said, freezes from water [Note: Gembloux, Utica, and other Norman manuscripts: “congeals.”] and becomes strong. We know how mobile water is. The body of our Redeemer, because it was subject to sufferings even unto death, was in a certain respect like water: by being born, growing, becoming weary, hungering, thirsting, and dying, it passed through the moments of time in changeable motion until his Passion. Observing this course, the Prophet says: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6).

But because through the glory of his resurrection he grew strong, emerging from corruption itself into the power of incorruption, he became hard like crystal from water, so that in him the same nature might remain, yet the mutability of corruption that had previously been in it might no longer remain. Water was therefore turned into crystal when the weakness of his corruption was changed through his resurrection into the firmness of incorruption.

20. But it should be noted that this crystal is called terrifying—that is, fearsome. Who does not know how beautiful crystal is? It is astonishing how beauty and terror meet in this crystal. Yet it is clear to all who know the truth that the Redeemer of the human race, when he appears as judge, will be beautiful to the just and terrifying to the unjust. The elect see him as gentle, while the reprobate behold this same one as fearsome and terrible.

But the elect will not then see him as terrifying because now they never cease to consider his terror. They carefully consider how terrifying he will come to judgment; they lament their past sins and avoid those that threaten; they place his fear daily before the eyes of their minds; and remain continually apprehensive of how dreadful he will appear; by fearing daily, they act so that they will not be terrified when he comes. [Note: The Vatican and Gussanville manuscripts read “they are suspended.” Our reading is found in all the manuscripts. The other reading was introduced by Gilot’s conjecture, who noted in the margin beside *suspecti*: “See whether it should be *suspensi*.”]

“The likeness of a firmament over the heads of the living creatures, like the appearance of a terrifying crystal.” And because the very fear of him, which they hold in their thoughts, protects their minds, it is rightly added: “Spread out above their heads from above.” This firmament, which appears like crystal over the heads of the living creatures, is both terrifying and spread out, because it protects good minds by the very thing through which it terrifies them. For if he were not fearsome in their hearts, he would not protect them now from sins and afterward from punishments. [Note: Suessiones: “and now would not rescue them from sins, nor afterward from punishments.” The German and others differ.]

Because they always consider what terror is impending from the judgment, they preserve the wings of their virtues in uprightness. Hence it is aptly added at once:

**VERSE 25. — Beneath the firmament their wings were straight, one toward another.**

21. The wings of virtues are straight beneath the firmament when one person applies to another the good that he possesses: the one who has received earthly wealth relieves the need of his needy neighbor; the one full of the grace of teaching illumines the darkness of an ignorant neighbor by the word of his preaching; the one supported by temporal power relieves those oppressed by violence; the one full of the spirit of prophecy turns away, by urging good, the evils threatening his neighbor’s life; the one who has received the grace of healing piously and humbly applies that grace, through his intercession, to the health of the sick; [Note: [Col. 0850D] All the manuscripts and the Paris 1518 edition read “in his intercession”; Gussanville altered this to “he may offer his intercession,” apparently because he did not perceive that “he may apply” refers most aptly to the grace of healing.] and the one freed from earthly activities and deemed worthy to devote himself to God alone prays for neighboring sinners.

It often happens that the one who is excessively occupied with earthly wealth does not attend to prayer as much as he should. And it often happens that the one who, stripped of all the world’s burdens, devotes himself to entreating the Lord has no means of sustaining his life.

But when the rich person extends food and clothing to the poor, and when the poor person offers his prayer for the soul of the rich, the wings of the living creatures are stretched straight, one toward another. For when he offers me the word of preaching and drives the darkness of ignorance from my heart with the light of truth, while I, because he is perhaps oppressed by a powerful person in this world, offer him the support of my defense and rescue him from violent hands, we in turn stretch our wings toward one another, so that by affection and mutual assistance we may touch one another with the good we have received. [Note: The printed editions read “I share.” We prefer the reading of the German, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

Hence the first shepherd rightly admonishes us, saying: “The end of all things is near. Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers; above all, maintain continual love for one another, because love covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without grumbling. As each has received a gift, administer it to one another” (1 Pet. 4:7–10 and following).

What is called a wing in Ezekiel is called received grace by the apostle Peter. And what he says, “Straight wings, one toward another,” the shepherd of the Church says thus: “As each has received a gift, administer it to one another” (ibid., 10).

Our wings are no longer straight if they are turned solely toward our own advantage. They become straight when we direct what we have toward the benefit of our neighbor. Since our good things do not come from ourselves, but we received them from the one by whom we were made to exist, the less we should retain them as private possessions, since we see that they were given to us by our Creator for common use.

Hence the apostle Peter rightly adds in exhortation concerning this matter: “As good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 4:10). And he adds further: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone serves, let him serve from the strength that God supplies” (ibid., 11).

It is as though he were plainly saying: Humbly apply your good things to your neighbors, because you know that what you have is not from yourselves. Every wing of virtue, when it is stretched out in giving to one’s neighbor, will not be straight if it lacks humility. It follows:

**IBID. — Each covered his own body with two wings, and the other was likewise covered.**

22. We have already said above that the body signifies action, while the wings signify virtues (Homily 4, no. 5). And since he says, “Beneath the firmament their wings were straight, one toward another,” it must be asked [Note: [Col. 0851D] Norman and most manuscripts: “what is likewise added afterward.” The received printed reading, retained here, is that of the German and older witnesses.] how he then adds: “Each covered his own body with two wings.” This clearly indicates that they both stretched their wings one toward another and nevertheless covered their own bodies with two wings. [Note: [Col. 0851D–0852D] Suessiones and the German manuscript, in an ancient second hand, read “wings”; the printed editions formerly read “toward the other.” Vallicelliana reads “wings and pinions.”]

What does this mean except that we ought to apply to others the virtues we have received in such a way that we do not cease carefully to consider the things in which we have sinned and daily to lament our guilt through fear and repentance? Above we said that the two wings by which the body is covered are fear and repentance.

Let us therefore grow in love so that we may stretch our wings toward our neighbors, and never cease to consider and lament ourselves. [Note: [Col. 0852D] Most Norman witnesses and Longpont repeat: “let us stretch our wings toward our neighbors”; the German and others lack this repetition.] Let the wings be stretched toward one another; let the wings cover the bodies, so that we may both provide examples of good deeds and have the evil we have done concealed by fear and repentance.

In the old translation these wings are described thus: “Two joined to each one, and covering their bodies.” From these words it is understood that the very wings which were joined one to another were also those that covered their bodies.

This is rightly understood figuratively, because the virtues that protect us before almighty God are those that we bestow upon and join to our neighbors out of love; while we live in harmony with them, we cover the evils we have committed.

These wings may therefore also signify the two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. By loving God, we pursue the evils within ourselves—that is, we cover the body. By loving our neighbor, we hasten toward the one in whom we can be useful—that is, we stretch our wings toward the other.

23. The phrase added here, “And the other was likewise covered,” is not found in the old translation. It may be asked why, after it has been said, “Each covered his own body with two wings,” it is added, “And the other was likewise covered.”

When we carefully examine the translations of the Seventy interpreters, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus, we find nothing of these words in them. But when we reread the writings of blessed Jerome, we learned that he found this sentence in the Hebrew truth in that form—not according to the word, but according to the sense.

It may indeed be asked why, after it has been said, “Each covered his own body,” it immediately adds, “And the other was likewise covered.” If it had said “one and the other,” the manner of speaking would stand. But after saying “each,” why is “the other” added, when all are included in “each”?

Yet if we distinguish the life of the perfect from the merits of those who are progressing, we see that “each” and “the other” have not been placed irrationally. Those who both lament their own sins and stretch the wings of their virtues toward their neighbors as an example are plainly perfect.

There are many little ones who see and imitate their tears. They might have been naked in their own wickedness, but they observe holy and watchful men; immediately, angered at their own wickedness, they are stirred to lament and inflamed toward repentance. And just as they see the saints covering their bodies, so they too are covered by the wings of their tears.

They strike themselves with great reproaches: Why do those who lack virtues not lament their sins at all, if even those who already stretch the wings of their virtues toward their neighbors by their example do not cease to lament?

24. In these words it is necessary that we, who are still little ones, always place both the virtues and the tears of the perfect before the eyes of our minds. Let us imitate what we see in them, so that, when we begin to grow through advancement, we may be able to cover the evils we have done from that strict examination.

In continual weeping and in our daily repentance, we have a priest in heaven who intercedes for us. Of him John also says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2). [Note: Suessiones: “Behold, the mind rejoices.”]

Behold, the mind rejoices when we hear of the power of our Advocate. [Note: Vallicelliana: “patience.”] Yet fear again wounds our rejoicing, because the one who is our Advocate is called righteous. We have unjust causes, but a righteous advocate in no way accepts unjust causes, nor does he consent to plead falsely on behalf of injustice.

What, then, shall we do, my dearest brothers? But behold, what we should do comes to mind. Let us both abandon the evils we have committed and accuse them. It is written: “The righteous man is the first to accuse himself” (Prov. 18:17). For any sinner who has been converted amid tears begins already to be righteous when he begins to accuse what he has done. Why should one not be righteous who already rages against his own unrighteousness through tears?

Our righteous Advocate, therefore, will defend us as righteous in the judgment, because we both recognize and accuse ourselves as unrighteous. Let us not trust in our tears or in our deeds, but in the pleading of our Advocate, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VIII

From verse 24 onward, the remaining part of the first chapter is explained together with the beginning of the second chapter; and much is discussed concerning the divinity of Christ, the Incarnation of the Word, preaching, and the gathering, increase, and unity of the Church.

1235 That many advance through the examples of the righteous was treated at the end of the preceding discourse. And the prophet opens this very matter to us more clearly when he adds to what he had said:

**VERSE 24. —** [Note: The German, Longpont, and others add: “and I heard.”] “And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters.”

**1.** In the sacred utterance, peoples are often signified by waters. Hence John says: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. 17:15). A people is signified by waters because in this life it has sound from the tumult of the flesh and flows away daily through the course of mortality.

As we have often said, the wings of the living creatures are the virtues of the saints. What, then, does it mean that the prophet hears the sound of wings as the sound of many waters, except that, by the mercy of almighty God, those wings of virtue that formerly sounded among a few saints now, through the spreading of preaching, resound in the manner of life of many peoples? [Note: Norman manuscripts: “in the conversion.”]

When the Lord had become incarnate, suffered, and risen again, there were few winged living creatures, because very few existed who desired heavenly things and lifted themselves on the wings of virtues to higher things. But after the preaching of his divinity had been spread throughout the world, how many little ones, how many mature persons, how many strong young men, how many weak people, how many converted female sinners, [Note: The same manuscripts: “how many converted sinners.”] how many old women and virgins now fly toward heavenly things through faith, hope, and love—who could say, who could estimate? [Note: [Col. 0854D] The printed editions read “how many aged virgins.” The German, Corbie, Suessiones, Vallicelliana, and Norman manuscripts read “how many old women [and] virgins.” It would perhaps be possible to read “how many old women and virgins,” but nothing has been added without manuscript authority.]

Behold, the sound of wings, which was formerly found among a few living creatures, now resounds among peoples; now the wings of virtues lift the multitude of the world toward heavenly desire. It is rightly said, therefore: “And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters,” because, as we have said, that sound of virtues which previously arose to God from a few saints was afterward multiplied through many waters—that is, through innumerable peoples.

Concerning this sound it is further rightly added:

**IBID. — Like the sound of the Most High God.**

**2.** What does it mean that the sound of the wings among the holy living creatures is called like the sound of the Most High God, except that almighty God himself both fills the minds of the saints with heavenly desire and hears those whom he has filled? He himself creates love in the hearts of the saints, and he himself receives prayer from loving hearts.

Peter wept bitterly over his offense, but it is nevertheless first stated there that “Jesus looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61–62). Mary Magdalene came, after many stains of guilt, with tears to the feet of our Redeemer (ibid., 7:38); but who infused her inwardly except the one who graciously received her outwardly? Who urged her to tears through the spirit of compunction except the one who, while reclining at table with the others, received her outwardly into forgiveness?

Our Redeemer therefore drew the sinful woman’s mind out of her guilt when he moved her to repentance, and received her in order to free her from guilt. [Note: Angers, Norman, and Vallicelliana: “he both drew and received the mind”; “he drew...” The Vatican reads “wiped away” instead of “drew out”; we follow the ancient German manuscript, with which Longpont agrees.]

The sound of the wings is therefore rightly called like the sound of the Most High God, because whatever is accomplished in the virtues of the saints belongs to the grace of him who bestows their merits. [Note: Vallicelliana: “in their minds.”]

### 3.

He is rightly remembered through the prophet as the exalted God. For in Holy Scripture God is sometimes spoken of nominally and sometimes essentially. He is spoken of nominally, as it is written: “Behold, I have appointed you god over Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). And as Moses says: “If anyone does this or that, bring him to the gods,” namely, to the priests (Exod. 22:8). He says again: “You shall not revile the gods” (ibid., 28), that is, the priests. And as the Psalmist says: “God has taken his stand in the assembly of gods; in the midst of the gods he judges” (Ps. 81:1).

[Note: The German C manuscript and most Norman manuscripts read “discerns”; the Vulgate editions read “judges.”]

God is spoken of essentially, however, as he himself says to Moses: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). Therefore the apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the nominal name of God from the essential, spoke of our Redeemer, saying: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

[Note: Longipontanus adds “amen, forever.”]

[Note: Here most old Paris editions (1502 and 1518) are corrupt, reading: “But he who is God essentially.” The Uticensis manuscript lacks “over all.” The Gussanville edition reads: “He who is called God nominally is God among all; he who is God essentially is by no means God over all.” The Vatican and Gilot editions, which reproduce the manuscripts exactly, should have been followed. Gregory employs his familiar antithesis concerning Christ: “among all,” “over all”; see *Moralia*, book XV, former ch. 10, now no. 20; book XVI, former ch. 14, now no. 37; and Homily 7, no. 19 above.]

He who is called God nominally is God “among all”; but he who is God essentially is God “over all.” Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, he remembered that Christ is not merely called God, but is God over all. For, as we said above, any chosen person may be called god, either because he excels in the example of righteousness or because he has been placed in a position of preeminence, but only “among all,” since he is god nominally. Christ, however, is God over all, because he is God by nature.

The one whom Paul calls God over all, the prophet Ezekiel calls the exalted God. After it has been said, “I heard the sound of the wings, like the sound of many waters,” and there is still added, “like the sound of the exalted God,” we can also understand this as referring to what we know will happen to all the elect. The sound of the wings, as we said, was found in the holy preachers; the sound of the waters, in the peoples who were converted and followed them. But this same sound will eventually become the sound of the exalted God, because the multitude now drawn to faith through holy teachers will one day be gathered into the heavenly homeland, so that there all the elect may praise without end when they behold without end the one whom they are to praise.

And because then the whole multitude of the saints becomes perfectly the body of the Redeemer, in accordance with Paul’s saying: “The creation itself will be set free from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21), and because they will then cling to him so closely that nothing of the corruption overcome through the resurrection will any longer oppose their holy love, but they will become united with the glory of their Redeemer, it is rightly said: “Like the sound of the exalted God.”

### 4.

[Note: The Norman manuscript says that the order must be examined.]

The order of the description should be noted: first there is the sound from the wings of the living creatures; afterward it is called like the sound of many waters; finally, like the sound of the exalted God. What the saints preached first, the peoples afterward converted to the faith believed and held; and finally, raised into heaven, they too will render praise to the liberator of all.

Thus the sound of the living creatures becomes like the sound of waters, and the sound of waters becomes like the sound of the exalted God, because the praise of the omnipotent Lord, which at first was proclaimed in the world by a few, was afterward proclaimed by many. And what many now proclaim, while their corruption still resists them within themselves, all the elect, already united to their Head in the heavenly homeland, will resound.

The works and virtues of the holy living creatures are still being described when it is added:

> **IBID. — When they walked, there was a sound like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of camps.**

### 5.

If the praise of our Creator in the heavenly homeland is signified by the sound of the exalted God, it is not surprising that the prophetic discourse turns again to the works of the saints who are still living in this present life. For the Holy Spirit shows within the hearts of the prophets all that he brings forth at once, but does not bring it all out simultaneously through the tongue.

The water of knowledge with which the prophet’s mind is filled overflows abundantly in contemplation. But because every human mouth—that is, the opening of the flesh—is too narrow to express the immensity perceived, the tongue varies as it brings forth now this thing and now that which it beholds.

[Note: Suessanus, Longipontanus, Valclusianus, Normanus, and Anglicus read: “What it sees is expressed in varying fashion by the tongue, which brings forth now this and now that which it beholds.” The German, Corbie, and older witnesses lack this gloss.]

After he has seen in heaven that the sound of the wings is like the sound of the exalted God, he returns again to earth and speaks of what the winged living creatures do here, so that they may deserve to attain that supreme state there. He says:

> **When they walked, there was a sound like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of camps.**

When the holy preachers travel throughout the world, preaching and drawing people to the faith, the living creatures walk. And because those whom they gather rise at once, as soon as they believe, to praise our Creator, there arises a sound like the sound of a multitude.

And because in their preaching they undertake the same warfare against the powers of the air, it is rightly added: “Like the sound of camps.” For when faithful peoples join themselves to the holy preachers, multitudes become camps in the battle-line of faith against evil spirits. And as the faithful are daily filled with heavenly desires, despise earthly things, and set before themselves hardships for the love of the heavenly homeland, they become camps against the powers of the air, because they advance armed with faith and fortified by good works.

[Note: The Sagiensis manuscript reads “they pitch [camp].”]

For the spiritual army is described by Paul as though it were a camp: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:11–12).

[Note: Suessanus reads “is led,” where he himself says.]

[Note: Rothomagensis and Beccensis add “the armor.”]

### 5.

[Note: Suessanus and Longipontanus read: “The multitudes of the saints are camps and the sound of camps.”]

The multitudes of the saints are therefore camps, having undertaken warfare against the powers of the air.

Hence the holy universal Church is also described under the figure of the beloved, when it is said: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle order” (Song 6:3).

Because Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” and by this name the heavenly homeland is signified, the holy Church is called sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, because her life and desire are already compared with the vision of inward peace. In loving her Creator and longing to see his form—for it is written, “Into which angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1:12)—she is said, through the very desires of her love, to be like the angels.

And the more she becomes beloved by God, the more she acts so as to become terrifying to evil spirits.

[Note: The printed editions read “the more she is acted upon.”]

How she is terrifying is shown by the comparison that follows: “As an army drawn up in battle order” (Song 6:5). Why should the holy Church be feared by her enemies like an army drawn up in battle? This comparison is not without profound meaning, and therefore it must be examined carefully.

We know, and it is certain, that an army is then displayed as terrifying to its enemies when it is so compact and densely arrayed that it appears broken at no point. For if it is arranged so that an empty space is left through which the enemy can enter, it is plainly no longer terrifying to its enemies.

Therefore, when we draw up the line of spiritual combat against evil spirits, it is supremely necessary that we be found always united and bound together by charity, never broken by discord.

[Note: The printed editions add “superfluously”: “because if any…”]

For however many good works may exist in us, if charity is absent, a place is opened in the battle line through the evil of discord, by which the enemy can enter to strike us.

### 7.

The ancient enemy does not fear chastity in us if it is without charity, because he himself is not weighed down by flesh and cannot be dissolved in its lust. He does not fear abstinence, because he does not use food and is not driven by bodily necessity. He does not fear the distribution of earthly goods if charity is absent from that work, because he himself has no need of the support of riches.

But he greatly fears true charity in us—that is, the humble love that we show to one another—and he is exceedingly envious of our concord, because we preserve on earth what he refused to preserve and therefore lost in heaven.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “our humble concord.”]

It is rightly said, then: “Terrible as an army drawn up in battle order” (Song 6:9), because evil spirits dread the multitude of the elect insofar as they see them united and gathered together against themselves through charity.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “fortified.” The printed reading is corrupt: “through the concord of charity.”]

### 8.

How great is the power of concord is shown when the other virtues are demonstrated not to be virtues without it. Abstinence is indeed a great virtue; but if someone abstains from food in such a way that he condemns others in the matter of eating, and even condemns the foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful (Rom. 14:3, 6), what has the virtue of abstinence become for him except a snare of guilt?

[Note: The editors thought it appropriate to add “in,” but this word is absent from all the manuscripts.]

Therefore the Psalmist too, indicating that there is no abstinence without concord, says: “Praise him with the tambourine and with the choir” (Ps. 150:4). In the tambourine, dry leather resounds; in the choir, voices sing together in harmony. What, then, is signified by the tambourine except abstinence, and what by the choir except the concord of charity?

Whoever therefore maintains abstinence while abandoning concord praises with the tambourine, but does not praise with the choir.

There are also some who, while striving to know more than is necessary, withdraw from peace with their neighbors, despising them as dull and foolish. Hence Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49), so that whoever strives to possess the salt of wisdom must take care never to depart from the peace of concord.

What we have said concerning these two virtues must also be understood of all the others. Hence Paul solemnly admonishes us, saying: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12:14).

[Note: The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read *pacem sectamini* (“seek peace”).]

### 9.

That nothing pleases God without concord Truth itself demonstrates when it says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first and be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

[Note: Longipontanus, together with many Norman witnesses, reads “before the altar.”]

[Note: The German and Valclusian manuscripts read: “that your brother has offended against you.” This reading conflicts with the Greek text and the versions.]

Behold: he does not wish to receive sacrifice from those who are at odds with one another; he refuses to accept the holocaust. From this, then, consider how great is the evil of discord, because of which even that is rejected by which guilt is forgiven.

Since the elect are always joined together in charity, and this same charity gives forth a sound of praise to its author, while it inflicts the punishment of fear upon evil spirits—that is, upon their ancient enemies—it is rightly now said of the winged living creatures:

> **When they walked, there was a sound like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of camps.**

### 10.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads *debet* erroneously. The reading is anticipated by the Paris editions of 1518 and 1571 and is corrected from the Anglic and our manuscripts.]

It is pleasing to extend the eye of faith from the origin of the holy Church to the end of the world and to see how these same camps walk.

[Note: The German, Longipontanus, and Valclusian manuscripts read: “For multitudes are called camps.”]

For armies are called camps when they proceed in battle array or remain encamped at some fixed place along the road. The road of these camps is therefore the life of the present age, in which all the saints live together in concord.

There are also the camps of preachers, who labor here and there in the battle array of holy work to gather souls. There are other camps of those who practice continence and withdraw from this world, preparing themselves daily in their hearts for battle against evil spirits.

There are other camps of good married people, who live together in love of the omnipotent God and pay to one another the debt of the flesh in such a way that they nevertheless never forget what they owe to God in good works. And if, as human beings, they commit any offenses, they continually redeem them through acts of piety.

Since, then, the distinct orders of the faithful, from the origin of the holy Church to the end of the world, live together in concord and fight against the powers of the air, they are camps that walk. And there arises something like the sound of camps, because in them the swords of virtues and the weapons of miracles resound to the praise of the omnipotent God.

The holy living creatures are further described:

> **And when they stood still, their wings were lowered.**

### 11.

The holy living creatures stand when they consider the things of God with intent contemplation. But their wings are lowered, because when they behold the lofty judgments of God, the virtues they possess become of little worth in their eyes.

This is plainly explained when it immediately adds:

> **VERSE 25. — For when a voice came from above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings.**

### 12.

Above, we judged that the firmament should be explained in a twofold sense. For, as has been said (Hom. 1, nos. 18–19), by the name “firmament” the heavenly powers can be understood. The name “firmament” can also signify the incarnate Only-Begotten, because in him our nature has been made firm for eternity.

Let us therefore first speak of what we understand concerning the angels, and afterward of the Lord of the angels.

Behold, it is said: “When a voice came from above the firmament, they stood and lowered their wings.” Here we must first understand that *lowering* does not mean extending from below toward above, but lowering the wings from above toward below, because it was previously said: “When they stood, their wings were lowered.”

We must therefore ask what voice it is that comes from above the firmament. We understand this voice better if, proceeding from the lowest things to the highest, we ascend as though by certain steps.

Just as bodily hearing is awakened by a voice, so the sense of the mind is awakened by understanding, which is produced from within. A voice in the mind is therefore a kind of sound of understanding.

But we should know that at times the voice of the flesh speaks to our senses, at times the voice of the soul, at times the voice of the firmament, and at times the voice that is above the firmament.

### 13.

Let us place before our eyes someone who has been injured by a neighbor and who, reasoning according to human judgment, thinks of returning the injury and repaying evil for evil. To him the voice of the flesh speaks in his mind. For since the divine commandments instruct us to do good to those who hate us (Matt. 5:44), whenever anyone considers doing evil to those who hate him, the voice of the flesh sounds in his soul.

We perform many earthly activities every day and afterward return to prayer. The soul is kindled to compunction, but the images of the things we have done move about in the mind and hinder the intention of compunction in prayer. What we willingly did outwardly, we suffer inwardly against our will, so that certain phantasms of thought scatter the mind through bodily images and prevent it from gathering itself wholly and strictly in prayer.

This too is the voice of the flesh.

### 14.

When we subdue these things as well and drive away all bodily images from the eyes of the mind, seeking within ourselves the nature of the soul itself—what sort of thing it is that can give life to the flesh but cannot restrain itself in good thoughts as it desires—we discover an intellectual spirit living through the power of the Creator and giving life to the body that it sustains, yet subject to forgetfulness and exposed to change, often afflicted by fear and lifted up by joy.

This intellect of the soul is its voice, because it sounds forth what it is. Yet this voice is still beneath the firmament.

### 15.

But transcending the soul, we seek the voice from the firmament when we investigate what the innumerable multitude of the holy angels is like in the sight of the omnipotent Lord: what their unending festival of beholding the Lord is, what joy without diminution, what ardor of love that does not torment but delights; how great in them is the desire for the vision of God together with satiety, and how great satiety together with desire.

In them desire produces no pain, and satiety produces no weariness. We consider how, by clinging to blessedness, they are blessed; how, by contemplating eternity always, they are eternal; how, joined to the true light, they have become light; how, always beholding the unchangeable, they have been changed into unchangeableness.

But when we think these things about the angels, the voice is still from the firmament, not above the firmament.

### 16.

Let the mind therefore pass beyond all created things, transcending even them. Let it fix the eyes of faith upon the light of its Creator alone: that God, who created all things, gives life to all; that he is everywhere and wholly everywhere; that he is unbounded and incomprehensible, capable of being apprehended but not seen; that he is absent nowhere and yet far from the thoughts of the wicked; that he is not absent even where he is far away, because where he is not present by grace, he is present by judgment.

He touches all things, yet he does not touch all things equally. He touches some so that they may exist, but not so that they may live and perceive, as with all insensible things. He touches others so that they may exist, live, and perceive, but not so that they may discern, as with brute animals. He touches others so that they may exist, live, perceive, and discern, as with human and angelic nature.

Although he himself is never unlike himself, he touches unlike things in unlike ways.

He is everywhere present and yet scarcely found; we follow him while he stands, but we cannot grasp him.

Let us therefore place before the eyes of our mind what that nature is which holds all things, fills all things, encompasses all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. It does not sustain from one side while surpassing from another; nor does it fill from one side while encompassing from another. Rather, by encompassing, it fills; by filling, it encompasses; by sustaining, it surpasses; by surpassing, it sustains.

When the mind, concentrated upon this nature, considers its power, the voice above the firmament comes to be, because the mind conceives an understanding that by its incomprehensibility transcends even the perception of the angels.

### 17.

When, therefore, the voice above the firmament comes, the living creatures stand and lower their wings, because when the minds of the saints consider the power of their Creator with attentive contemplation, the virtues they possess become of little worth in their own estimation. They become humble in themselves in proportion as that which sounds above the angels is exalted before them.

Perhaps they are teachers. But when they begin silently to consider what the ineffable wisdom of God is—wisdom that teaches human minds without the noise of words—and how, unless this same wisdom teaches the minds of their hearers, the voice of teachers labors in vain, their own teaching immediately becomes of little worth to them, because “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Perhaps they are prophets. But when they silently consider that the eye of their prophecy cannot penetrate all the mysteries of divinity at once, since, as the Apostle says, “we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9), they see within that immensity of secrets that everything they see is small. From that immense height of light they consider how little is what they saw with their intent eye, as though through cracks.

[Note: The Norman and Longipontanus manuscripts read “vastness” in place of “height.”]

Let them therefore lower their wings when the voice above the firmament comes—that is, let them humble themselves in what they grasp when they behold the higher things that cannot be comprehended by them.

### 18.

Often the good things that the saints possess themselves flatter their thoughts, so that their minds rise up in some confidence of themselves. But they immediately return to the hidden judgments of God and consider how some fall from virtues into hell through pride, while others, corrected from vices, are raised to heaven through humility.

Therefore the Prophet, calling us back to humility, terrifies and admonishes us, saying: “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 66:5).

Who can worthily consider how great is the terror of God’s counsels over us, when one person proceeds from virtues toward vices as his end, while another brings his end to completion in virtues after beginning from vices?

For, in the words of Solomon: “There are righteous and wise people, and their works are in the hand of God. Yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Eccl. 9:1).

And again: “There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end leads to death” (Prov. 14:12).

[Note: Suessanus reads: “There are fools and wise people.”]

To consider these depths of hidden judgment—what else is this than lowering the wings, that is, no longer trusting in any virtue but trembling under great fear? Whether they consider the nature of the omnipotent God or weigh his judgments, they tremble and are afraid.

For them, therefore, lowering their wings means humbling the virtues they possess.

### 19.

Thus Abraham lowered his wings. When he began to speak with God, he recognized that he was dust and ashes, saying: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27).

Thus Moses lowered his wings. Though “instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22), as soon as he heard the words of the Lord he discovered that he had no words, saying: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow and hesitant of tongue” (Exod. 4:10).

As though he were plainly saying: “After I hear from you the words of life, I recognize that I am confused in my former words.”

Thus Isaiah, whose life had pleased the Lord for preaching, when he contemplated that same Lord and a coal from the altar touched his mouth, said: “Woe is me, for I have been silent, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa. 6:3). Behold, raised to higher things, he was displeased with himself because of the uncleanness of his lips. For unless he had seen the heights of heavenly purity, he would not have discovered himself to be blameworthy.

Thus, while the Lord was speaking, Jeremiah cried out: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jer. 1:6). In view of the words he heard, he recognized that he had no words.

Thus Daniel, seeing a sublime vision, languished and was sick for many days (Dan. 8:27), because those who are strong in virtues become weak and feeble in their own estimation when they behold the higher things of God.

Thus blessed Job, of whom the Lord said to his friends, “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7), when he heard God speaking with him, replied: “I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge beyond measure” (ibid., 3). And shortly afterward: “Therefore I reproach myself and repent in dust and ashes” (ibid., 6).

Although he had spoken wisely insofar as human beings are concerned, when he heard God speaking to him he reproached himself for having spoken foolishly, because in the contemplation of true wisdom his own wisdom became worthless to him.

At the voice coming from above, therefore, the living creatures lower their wings, because whether we seek to contemplate the power of God in his nature or consider investigating it in his hidden judgments, since his lofty things are impenetrable to us, whatever good we thought existed in us becomes worthless.

And we who seemed to fly in however small a degree of knowledge stand humbly with lowered wings when we consider the invisible nature above us and its impenetrable judgments.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “seemed to see.”]

The text continues:

> **VERSE 26. — And above the firmament that was over their heads was something like the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne; and above the likeness of the throne was something like the appearance of a human figure above it.**

### 20.

What is signified by the throne except those angelic powers that surpass even the angels themselves by the dignity of their position? For although angels are called messengers, and angels often come to human beings to announce certain things, thrones are nowhere read to have been sent on a mission of announcement, because the Creator of all presides over them at a far higher level.

Hence the apostle Paul, describing the orders of the heavenly hosts that he had seen when he was caught up to the third heaven, says: “Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers; all things were created through him and in him” (Col. 1:16).

He therefore placed thrones before those orders of angels, recognizing that the thrones were set over them.

The throne is rightly compared with a sapphire stone, because sapphire has an airy or sky-blue color. The heavenly powers are therefore signified by the sapphire stone, because those spirits over whom omnipotent God presides at a higher level hold the dignity of a superior place in the heavens.

Above the throne, however, there is a likeness of a human being, because above those powers that precede even the angels stands the glory of our Redeemer.

[Note: The same codex reads: “the likeness of a human being is signified.”]

The order that is maintained should therefore be noted. Above the living creatures is the firmament; above the firmament is the throne; above the throne is the human being. For above holy human beings, who still live in this corruption of the body, are the angels; above the angels are the higher angelic powers nearest to God; and above the powers nearest to God is the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.

### 21.

But if, as we said earlier, by the name “firmament” the Mediator between God and human beings is to be understood with respect to the humanity he assumed—for through the spirit of prophecy many things are accustomed to be signified under a single name—then the voice above the firmament was the voice that sounded from heaven over the baptized Lord, saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22).

Or, as another Evangelist says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

Let us therefore ask how the living creatures hear this voice and lower their wings. Let the prophet Habakkuk answer when questioned: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Hab. 3:1).

What does the Father mean when he speaks of the Son, saying, “In whom I am well pleased”? Everyone who corrects something he has done through repentance indicates, by the very fact that he repents, that he was displeased with himself, because he amends what he did.

And because the omnipotent Father spoke of sinners in a human manner, insofar as human beings could understand it, saying, “I regret that I made the human being upon the earth” (Gen. 6:6), he seemed to be displeased with himself in the sinners he had created.

But in our one Only-Begotten Lord Jesus Christ he alone was well pleased, because he did not regret creating him as a human being among human beings. No sin was found in him at all, as the Psalmist says of him: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110:4).

The Father was therefore well pleased in our Redeemer alone, because in him alone he found no fault for which he might, as though through repentance, reproach himself.

### 22.

Let the holy living creatures therefore hear the voice above the firmament and be afraid, because if he alone is without sin, they see in his innocence how greatly they themselves sin every day—sins that they must continually lament.

Let them also consider that the author of life himself did not depart from this life without the pain of suffering. This too was the voice above the firmament, because the sentence of the omnipotent Father proceeded even concerning the death and resurrection of the Only-Begotten.

But when the voice above the firmament comes, the living creatures stand and lower their wings, because whenever the saints behold the Only-Begotten himself scourged in this world, they put aside whatever presumption they have concerning their own merits.

For if he who came without sin did not depart from here without scourging, how will those who came here with sin not be worthy of scourging?

The firmament itself, therefore, which is above the heads of the living creatures—that is, which transcends the minds of the saints—has a voice above it, because our Redeemer endured in the flesh the judgment that he had established with the Father in his divinity. When the righteous hear this, they are terrified and lay aside all presumption concerning their own strength.

[Note: Suessanus and Longipontanus read: “Whatever virtues they may possess, that is, the righteous.” The same honored witnesses read: “For what life is worthy?” Valclusianus reads: “Which life is worthy?”]

Whatever virtues someone may possess, what life of sinners is worthy, if even the life of him who was subject to no sin was scourged for us?

### 23.

But behold, a serious question arises when it is said that above the firmament, which was over their heads, there was something like the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne.

For if by the firmament the Lord is signified, and by the sapphire stone and the likeness of the throne those highest angelic powers are signified, how are they to be thought to be above the firmament, that is, above the Lord, when it is immediately added: “And above the likeness of the throne was something like the appearance of a human figure above it”?

For if, as has been said, the Lord is expressed by the firmament, and the Lord is again understood as the human being, how can he himself be understood to be both above the throne and beneath the throne?

But he himself resolves the tightly knotted difficulties of this question—the one of whom we are speaking, who opens through the breath of the Holy Spirit what is closed.

The incarnate Only-Begotten of the Father, insofar as he became human, was below the angels, as it is written of him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6). But rising again and ascending into heaven, he presides over all the angelic powers, as it is written of him there again: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (ibid., 7). And as he himself says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

The firmament is therefore beneath the throne, and the human being is above the throne, because through the assumption of human nature he was born beneath the angels and was exalted above the angels.

Even before he was exalted by the glory of the resurrection, he was above the angels in his divinity; yet, as has been said, in his humanity he was made lower than the angels, and in that humanity he was subject to death.

But after he trampled death by rising again, he placed his humanity above even the dignities of the archangels.

[Note: The printed editions read “above the majesties of the angels.” We follow the German, Norman, and Anglic manuscripts.]

First, therefore, the throne is described as seen above the firmament, and afterward the human being above the throne, because the Redeemer of the human race exalted by his ascent the humanity that he had assumed by descending beneath the angels.

We say that he was made beneath the angels in the same way that we have heard from the Apostle that he was made beneath the law (Phil. 2:9).

We understand, therefore, that the humanity he assumed was beneath the angels because of that lowering in which he deigned to appear.

### 24.

For as soon as the Word became flesh, God the human being was already, in power, above the angels. Of him it is written before the Passion: “Behold, angels came and ministered to him” (John 1:15; Matt. 4:11).

Yet, to show the weakness of his humanity, it is again written of him: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43).

[Note: All the manuscripts read this way; the printed editions depart considerably from them, reading “the garment of both natures.” It is not correct to say that divinity is the garment of the Word, as though he could put it off like clothing and as though it were accidental to him rather than essential. Here *documentum* means proof, testimony, or example.]

As proof, therefore, of both natures, he is described both as one to whom angels minister and as one whom an angel strengthens. He is one in both natures, because he who existed as God before the ages became human at the end of the ages.

Before his Passion, angels ministered to him, and an angel strengthened him. After his Passion and resurrection, angels can minister to him, but they can no longer strengthen him, because, as has been said, although the firmament previously appeared beneath the throne, the human being is now above the throne.

In his person, to show that he had seen the union of both natures, the holy prophet immediately added:
