> **VERSE 27. — And I saw something like the appearance of electrum.**
25. What is meant by the fact that the appearance of a man is seen on the throne as the appearance of electrum, except that in electrum, as we said much earlier (above, Homily 2, no. 14), gold and silver are mixed, so that one substance is made from two metals? In it, the brightness of gold is tempered by the silver, and through the brightness of the gold the appearance of the silver becomes radiant. In our Redeemer, however, [Note: [Col. 0865D] Here the manuscripts C. Germ. and Ebroic. diverge: “the two natures are united and joined to one another.” Longip. has: “the two natures, that is, divinity and humanity, are united to one another without confusion and inseparably” [Col. 0866D]. Gussanv. comes very close to this reading. In Norm. Anglic. and Suess., supported by Vatic. and Paris. 1502 and 1518: “the nature of divinity and humanity is united and joined to itself without confusion.”] the two natures—that is, divinity and humanity—are united and joined to one another without confusion and inseparably, so that through his humanity the brightness of his divinity might be tempered for our eyes, while through his divinity his human nature might shine forth in him and, exalted, possess a radiance beyond what it had when created. As he continues to describe the appearance of the man above the throne and the appearance of electrum that he saw, he adds:

**IBID.**—“Like the appearance of fire within, all around, from his loins upward; and from his loins downward I saw something like the appearance of shining fire all around.”

26. What does it mean that the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is described as having from his loins upward the appearance of fire within, all around, and from his loins downward the appearance of shining fire all around? We must investigate why from his loins upward he is said to have fire within, but not shining fire; whereas from his loins downward he is said to have the appearance of fire, but is not said to have it within, because he is described as having it shining and all around.

For what is expressed by the word “loins” except the succession of mortality? Hence it is also said of Levi that he was still in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met Abraham (Heb. 7:10). From Abraham’s loins the Virgin Mary came forth, and in her womb the Father’s Only-Begotten Son deigned to become incarnate through the Holy Spirit. Through this incarnation God became known to the whole world, as it is said through the Psalmist: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty” (Ps. 44:4). The Most Mighty took up a sword upon his thigh, because his word of preaching grew powerful through the incarnation.

What, then, does this fire signify except the ardor of the Holy Spirit, who sets alight the hearts that he fills? Concerning this the Truth himself says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). What, therefore, does it mean that in this appearance of the man who appeared to the prophet, fire burns within all around from the loins upward, while from the loins downward it is not fire within but shines around, except that before the incarnation of our Redeemer, the Only-Begotten, Judea alone possessed within itself the ardor of his love; but after his incarnation fire shone around him, because he poured forth the brightness of the Holy Spirit among the peoples throughout the whole world?

Previously, therefore, there was fire within, but there was no brightness, because the Holy Spirit indeed filled many fathers [Note: [Col. 0866D] So C. Germ., with Norm. and other manuscripts agreeing, as well as the old edition. In other copies, “parts” appears instead of “fathers.”] in Judea, but his light had not yet shone forth for the knowledge of the nations. From his loins downward, however, fire shines around, because after he took flesh from the Virgin, he spread the gifts of the Holy Spirit far and wide throughout the human race.

It should also be noted that this fire is described as being around him from the loins upward, not outwardly but inwardly, because, as has been said, the flame of love filled Judea throughout all its boundaries in its elect and spiritual men. Yet it did not go outward, because it did not spread among the multitude of the nations. This flame of ardor was afterwards seen shining around, because throughout the regions of the world the love of almighty God began to increase among all the nations.

27. There was therefore previously fire within, when Jacob said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49:18). What we call *salvation* in Latin is called *Jesus* in the Hebrew word. In this word the mind of blessed Jacob is revealed: how he burned with desire for Jesus, whom, as he was dying, he declared that he would await.

The fire burned when Moses said: “If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself, so that I may see you” (Exod. 33:13). The fire burned in David’s mind when he said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Ps. 41:3). Desiring the incarnation of the Word, he said: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Ps. 84:8). The fire burned when Simeon, desiring to depart from the corruption of the present life, heard that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord (Luke 2:26).

But behold, this fire now shines outwardly, as it were beneath the loins, because the whole Gentile world has been inflamed with love for the incarnate God.

28. Yet this may also be understood in another way, because our Redeemer, God the Lord Jesus Christ, became known to human beings through his humanity, whereas through his divinity he was known to the angels even before the incarnation. For us, therefore, he shines around from the loins downward, while his fire burns inwardly from the loins upward in heaven [Note: [Col. 0867D] In the printed editions the letter has been gratuitously inserted: *illic* appears instead of *illi*, contrary to the manuscripts.], because the heavenly spirits behold him in his divinity and are kindled by the fires of his love. We, however, who love him because of the humanity he assumed, still placed in this corruptible life, have the splendor of that fire outwardly.

Thus there is one who is above the throne: he has fire within above the loins in the angels, and fire around beneath the loins in human beings, because in everything loved by the angels and in everything desired by human beings, it is one and the same person who burns in the hearts of those who love.

Hence those great angelic powers are called *Seraphim*, that is, “burning.” Hence it is written of the Creator of all: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29; Deut. 4:24). God is called fire because he sets alight with the flames of his love the minds that he fills. And for this reason the Seraphim are called “burning,” because the powers nearest to him in heaven are inflamed by the immeasurable fire of his love.

Kindled by this fire, the hearts of the righteous burn on earth. Warmed by this fire, the hearts of sinners return to repentance; when set aflame, they turn fear into love with great intensity. For those hearts that had earlier begun to waste away in fear afterwards blaze with the fire of love.

And because the chosen angels in heaven are his members, and converted human beings on earth are his members, there is one man who burns inwardly above the loins and sends forth the brightness of his fire around below the loins, because through his divinity he held the angels in his love, and through his humanity he recalled human beings to desire his holy ardor.

It follows:

**VERSE 28.**—“Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day.”

29. Almighty God placed the bow as a sign between himself and human beings, so that he would not again destroy the world by a flood, saying: “I shall place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. And when I cover the sky with clouds, my bow will appear in the clouds, and I shall remember my covenant with you” (Gen. 9:13).

Thus in that same bow the color of water and fire is displayed together, because in part it is blue and in part red, so that it may be a witness to both judgments: one that is to come and the other that has already come. The world will indeed be burned by the fire of judgment; but because the other judgment is no longer to be carried out, it is no longer destroyed by the water of the flood (2 Pet. 3:7).

But what does it mean that the prophet saw the shining fire from the loins of the man presiding on the throne like the appearance of a bow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day? Since, as has been said, fire signifies the ardor of the Holy Spirit, what likeness is there between a bow and the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0867D] This passage is corrupt in Gussanv.; for it reads: “and the fire that appeared, so that it might appear as though . . .”], so that the fire that appeared might be said to have appeared like the appearance of a bow?

But if we attend to the vision of the bow that I mentioned earlier, we see how the bow signifies the Spirit. In the bow, as I said, water and fire appear. And after the Mediator’s coming, the power of the Holy Spirit shone forth in the human race to the degree that it both washed God’s chosen with the water of baptism and set them ablaze with the fire of divine love.

For when the Truth says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), a certain bow, as it were, composed of the mingled color of water and fire is placed in the cloud for propitiation [Note: [Col. 0868D] All printed editions have “for proof.” The wording differs in our manuscripts, Germ., Norm., and others, which Gussanv. examined and cites here.].

This bow is in the cloud on a rainy day because it is displayed in the Lord’s incarnation and in the outpouring of preaching, so that, while the Lord shows mercy, the hearts of believers may be recalled to forgiveness [Note: [Col. 0868D] Or, “by the Lord,” as the Norm. manuscripts present.].

We may appropriately understand the flesh of the Redeemer as the cloud of which the Psalmist says: “Who makes the cloud his ascent” (Ps. 103:3). He made the cloud his ascent because he who is everywhere in his divinity ascended to heavenly things in the flesh.

After completing the entire mystical vision, he adds:

**IBID., AND CHAPTER 2, VERSE 1.**—“This was the appearance of the brightness all around, and this was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.”

30. Observing what the grace of the Holy Spirit does throughout the world, he says: “This was the appearance of the brightness all around.” Wishing to consider what glory of that same Holy Spirit remains within, but unable to see it as it is, he adds: “And this was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.”

For he did not say, “The vision of the glory,” but “the vision of the likeness of the glory,” so that it might be shown that however intently the human mind strains itself—even if it already restrains from its thoughts the phantasms of bodily images, and removes from the eyes of the heart all bounded spirits—it still cannot, while placed in mortal flesh, see the glory of God as it is.

Whatever of it shines in the mind is a likeness, [Note: [Col. 0868D] Suess. adds: “even this itself is [a likeness].”] not the thing itself. Hence that preacher who had been caught up to the third heaven also said: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12).

31. In this matter a question arises that we should not disregard. When the evangelist John had described the unbelief of the Jews in relation to the miracles of our Redeemer, even from the prophetic words, he adds: “Isaiah said this when he saw his glory and spoke about him” (John 12:41). [Note: [Col. 0869D] Suess. has: “And if Isaiah saw his glory, what is it that this man saw—the likeness of the glory?”]

If Ezekiel saw not the glory but the likeness of the glory, why is the one described as having seen the likeness of the glory and the other as having seen his glory?

But when the evangelist John first narrated the miracles of our Redeemer and afterwards added the unbelief of the Jews, he makes clear that Isaiah saw the glory of that same Redeemer which appeared in the world. For everything wondrous that is divinely accomplished on earth is the glory of almighty God, and his glory is seen in all his works.

Isaiah therefore saw his glory on earth. Ezekiel, however, could not see his glory in heaven as it is, because his glory in created things is one thing, and his glory in himself is another. The glory that exists in created things can therefore be seen; but the glory that exists in him cannot now be seen except through a likeness.

Let us understand, then, that the prophet could not bear this likeness of the glory, even though he had been raised up to it. It follows:

**IBID.**—“And I saw, and I fell upon my face.”

32. What, then, would have happened to this man if he had seen his glory as it is, when he saw the likeness of that glory and, unable to bear it, fell? In this matter we must consider and weigh with great sorrow and tears into what misery and weakness we have fallen, since we cannot bear even the very good for the sight of which we were created.

There is, however, another matter for us to consider in the prophet’s action. As soon as the prophet saw the likeness of the Lord’s glory, he fell upon his face. Since we cannot see this likeness of the glory through the spirit of prophecy, we ought constantly to recognize and carefully contemplate it in sacred teaching, in heavenly admonitions, and in spiritual commandments.

When we perceive something of God, we fall upon our face, because we blush for the evils we remember having committed. A person falls there where he is put to shame. Hence Paul also said, as though to certain people lying upon their faces: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

33. Behold, by the gift of heavenly grace, we have examined the beginning of the book of the prophet Ezekiel, which is veiled in mysteries. In discussing its mystical statements in mortal language, we have brought the winged vision of prophecy down to earth [Note: [Col. 0869D] So the English manuscripts and most of our own. In the editions of Paris 1502 and 1518: “We have drawn the history of the prophet from the earth” [Col. 0870D]. In the others “also, the history” is read. In C. Germ.: “We have drawn the history of the prophecy from the earth.”], so that what formerly flew before the minds of children and people like me, but did not lift them up, may now be read and understood by them, and may both fly and raise them up.

Let us therefore give thanks to our Redeemer, who continually refreshes us with spiritual nourishment, who is the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33). He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY IX

The second chapter of Ezekiel is explained; in this exposition many matters are interpreted morally, and also a considerable amount is taught with great erudition concerning the necessity of prevenient grace, the consent and cooperation of free will, and the obscurity and interpretation of sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0870A]

1. By the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have examined in eight homilies the beginning of the book of the prophet Ezekiel, which is closed by great obscurities and bound by certain knots of mysteries. Now the passages that follow are clearer and less difficult.

We therefore address your Charity, giving thanks to the same almighty God [Note: [Col. 0870D] Gussanv. reads “giving thanks to God,” omitting “giving thanks,” perhaps through a typographical error; for in all copies, whether printed or handwritten, “giving thanks” is found.], because after so many shadowed forests we have at last come joyfully out into open fields, where we may place the fearless foot of our speech with free steps.

For behold, after the prophet had contemplated the likeness of the glory of the Lord and had fallen upon his face, he adds:

**EZEKIEL 2:1.**—“And I heard the voice of one speaking, and he said to me: Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I shall speak with you.”

Then it is further said:

**VERSE 2.**—“And the spirit entered into me after he spoke to me, and set me upon my feet.”

2. Behold, the divine voice commanded the prophet, who was lying down, to rise [Note: [Col. 0870D] The Vulgate copies have: “to rise again.”]. Yet he could not rise at all unless the spirit of almighty God entered into him, because through the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot accomplish them if he himself does not help who commands.

Thus Paul, when he admonished the disciples, saying, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12), immediately added who would work these very good things in them: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (ibid., 13).

Hence the Truth himself says to the disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

But in these matters we must consider: if our good works are so gifts of almighty God that nothing in them is ours, why do we seek eternal recompense as though it were due to our merits? If, however, they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of almighty God, why do we give thanks to almighty God for them?

We must understand that our evil deeds are ours alone; but our good deeds belong both to almighty God and to us. For by inspiring us he goes before us so that we may will, and by helping us he follows after us so that we may not will in vain but may be able to accomplish what we will.

Thus, when grace goes before and good will follows, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement: “I labored more than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). But lest he appear to have attributed what he had done to his own power, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

Because he had been preceded by a heavenly gift, he acknowledged himself as alien to his good work, saying: “Not I.” But because prevenient grace had made free will good in him, and through that free will he had followed the same grace in his work, he added: “But the grace of God with me.”

It was as though he said: “I labored in the good work—not I, but also I. Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone: not I; but insofar as I followed the gift by my will: also I.”

Having said these brief things against Pelagius and Coelestius, let us return to the order of exposition:

“Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I shall speak with you” (Ezek. 2:1).

3. We must note the order of speech and action: first the likeness of the Lord’s glory appears in order to cast him down; afterwards he addresses him in order to raise him up; then he sends the spirit of superabundant grace, raises him, and sets him upon his feet.

Unless we saw something of eternity in our minds, we would never fall upon our faces in repentance. But while we are lying down, the Lord’s voice consoles us so that we may rise to action, although we cannot do this by our own power.

His spirit therefore fills and raises us and sets us upon our feet, so that we who lay prostrate in repentance for our fault may afterwards stand upright in good works.

But what the standing prophet heard he adds, saying:

**VERSES 2–3.**—“And I heard him speaking to me and saying: Son of man, I am sending you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me.”

4. Thus the prophet describes his own circumstances in such a way as to signify ours. For what does this mean [I, dist. 30], that the one lying down is told: “Stand upon your feet, and I shall speak with you”? If he was speaking to one lying down, why does he promise that he will speak only to one standing?

We must understand that there are things we ought to hear while lying down, and other things while standing. The one lying down is told to rise; the one standing is commanded to go forth to preaching. Authority for preaching ought not yet to be given to those who are still lying in the confusion of weakness. But when we have risen in good works, when we have begun to stand upright, it is fitting that we should be sent to preaching in order to win others.

The standing prophet therefore saw a spiritual vision and fell; the fallen man then received a word of admonition so that he might rise; and once risen he heard the command to preach.

For when we still stand upon the summit of pride, but have begun to feel something of the fear of eternity, it is fitting that we should fall into repentance. And when, subtly recognizing our weakness, we lie humbly down, we are commanded through the consolation of the divine word to rise to courageous works. When we already persist firmly in good works, it is necessary that we should now raise others by preaching what has corrected us.

The one lying down is therefore not commanded to go on to preaching [Note: [Col. 0871D] Suess. has: “to rise.”], lest someone who is weak destroy by his conduct what he can build up by his speech.

Hence it is rightly said through the Psalmist: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of mud; he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps; and he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Ps. 39:3–4).

First he is brought out of the mire of wickedness, so that his feet may be made firm through faith upon the rock. But because right action must follow right faith, his steps were directed, so that after the direction of his steps—that is, after the perfection of good works—he might also receive a new song of preaching in his mouth.

Thus Saul, while he was proceeding proudly toward Damascus (Acts 9:6), was struck down and lay prostrate by the voice of the Redeemer. Though he was destined to become a preacher, he did not immediately hear that he should preach what he had seen. Rather, while he was lying down, he was told: “Enter the city, and it will be told you what you must do” (ibid., 7).

While lying down, therefore, he could hear only that, once risen, he would learn what he was to hear; once risen, he learned that he should preach what he had come to know [Note: [Col. 0871D] The printed editions incorrectly have “what he had heard.” Saul had not yet heard what he needed to do; rather, he was being sent to Ananias to hear it from him. Our reading is found in all the manuscripts.].

5. But we must ask why Ezekiel and Paul fall upon their faces, while it is said of the rider of the horse—that is, of one who has been exalted by the glory of this world—“May his rider fall backward” (Gen. 49:17). Again, it is written concerning the persecutors of the Lord: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18:6).

What does it mean that the chosen fall forward and the reprobate fall backward, except that everyone who falls behind himself undoubtedly falls where he cannot see, whereas whoever falls before himself falls where he can see?

The wicked, because they fall into invisible things, are said to fall backward, since they collapse where they cannot now see what will follow them then. The righteous, however, because they willingly cast themselves down in these visible things so that they may be raised up in invisible things, fall, as it were, upon their faces, because, pierced by fear, they humble themselves while seeing.

6. It should be noted that he says: “I am sending you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me.” Just as there are two ways of departing from God, so human beings become apostates from God in two ways.

Each person departs from his Creator either in faith or in conduct. Therefore, just as one who departs from the faith is an apostate, so one who returns to the wicked conduct from which he had departed is without any doubt counted an apostate from almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith.

One without the other can accomplish nothing, because neither faith without works nor works without faith are beneficial—unless perhaps the works are performed in order to receive faith, as in the case of Cornelius, who merited to be heard on account of his good works before he became a believer (Acts 10:4).

From this it follows that he performed good works in order to receive faith. For when the angel said to him, “Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial in the sight of God” (ibid.), and immediately, on account of that ascent, commanded him to send to Simon, who would come and preach to him, it is clear [Note: [Col. 0872D] C. Germ. has: “it is clear that he asked for this, from which he merited to be heard.”] that he had asked for that by which he merited to be heard.

It follows:

**VERSES 3–4.**—“Their fathers transgressed my covenant even to this day, and their sons are hard-faced and stubborn-hearted; to them I am sending you.”

[Col. 0873A]

7. Behold one fault of pride: they transgressed the covenant. Behold another, that of obstinacy: “even to this day.” Behold a grave fault of ignorance in the wickedness of the sons: they are “hard-faced,” because they are no longer ashamed of the evils they do, and they never return to repentance even after their sins, because they are “stubborn-hearted.”

When those to whom the prophet is sent are marked by such great wickedness and obstinacy, who would not see that the prophet’s person could be despised by such perverse people? But behold, authority is bestowed upon his person when it is added:

**VERSE 4.**—“And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God.”

It is as though he openly said: “Because you would be despised on your own account, you must speak from my voice. Do not let yourself, who are sent, be despised; uttering my words, show who sent you.”

It follows:

**VERSE 5.**—“If perhaps they at least will hear, and if perhaps they will cease, because they are an exasperating house.”

8. Since it is certain that almighty God knows all things, it is very surprising that he says: “If perhaps they will hear, and if perhaps they will cease.” We must therefore understand that this uncertainty in God’s speech does not arise from ignorance but from some signification.

For who does not know that he who made and sees all things knows all things? The Truth himself also says in the Gospel concerning the preachers of Antichrist: “They will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error” (Matt. 24:24).

Why is this stated with uncertainty, when the Lord foreknows what will happen? There is one of two possibilities: if they are elect, it cannot happen; but if it can happen, they are not elect. Yet it is said: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error.”

This uncertainty in the Lord’s words therefore signified the temptation of the hearts of the elect, because those chosen to persevere would be tempted by the signs of the preachers of Antichrist to fall [Note: [Col. 0873D] Suess. has: “They will be tempted before Christ’s strict judgment.”].

By the words “if it were possible,” then, what is expressed is that the elect will be tempted in their hearts. They waver, but do not fall. It is said “if it were possible” because they will tremble; yet they are called elect because they will not fall.

The uncertainty of the Lord’s speech thus expresses the trembling of the mind in the elect. He calls them elect because he sees that they persist in faith and good works.

Hence here too it is said: “If perhaps they will hear, and if perhaps they will cease.” By saying “if perhaps,” it is shown that only a few out of the great multitude will hear. What else, then, is signified by the uncertainty of God’s words except the small number of hearers?

9. It should be noted that after he had spoken of the evils of their deceased parents, he says, as he sends the prophet to the sons: “If perhaps they at least will hear, and if perhaps they will cease.”

What does “they at least” mean except that their fathers, who died in guilt, were unwilling to hear?

Consider, I beg you, what force there is in this shortcoming of the Lord’s speech, when he says: “If perhaps they at least will hear.” This is plainly said to us, who are afflicted, besieged, shut in, and have lost all the good things we possessed in this world.

We see cities torn down, camps overturned, fields laid waste, and churches dug up; yet we still follow our parents into iniquities and are not changed by the pride we saw in them. They sinned amid joys; we, what is more serious, sin even amid scourges.

But behold, almighty God, judging iniquities, has already taken away our predecessors and summoned them to judgment. He still awaits us for repentance; he holds back for us so that we may return. He who has already exercised judgment upon them grants us the long-suffering of his patience, lest he destroy us together with our predecessors, saying: “If perhaps they at least will hear, and if perhaps they will cease, because they are an exasperating house.”

10. Every soul, even after receiving the faith, if it either persists in or returns to its perversity, is called an exasperating house, because through wicked conduct it drives away from itself the God whom it had received as an inhabitant through faith.

A house is inhabited by its master. If, then, it is a house, why is it exasperating? But if it is exasperating, why is it a house, since it is certainly no longer inhabited?

It is a house because God had begun to dwell in it through faith; but it is exasperating because, driven out by wicked conduct, he departed from it, leaving empty what the heavenly inhabitant had previously filled.

Hence, as we have learned from the voice of the Truth, the most wicked spirit, returning with seven other spirits, finds a house swept clean (Matt. 12:45), because he fills the mind that has been alienated from virtues.

It follows:

**IBID.**—“And they shall know that a prophet has been in their midst.”

11. For the wicked, to know the good either tends toward the help of salvation or toward testimony for their condemnation [Note: [Col. 0873D] Suess. has: “to know the good. Val. Cl. reads: ‘the wicked know the good . . . either toward the help of salvation or toward the increase of condemnation they are accustomed [to know] . . .’ It is clear from the context that *bonos* should be read.”].

Let them therefore know that a prophet has been in their midst, so that, having heard the preaching, they may either be helped to rise [Note: [Col. 0874D] The Paris edition of 1502 and the other editions add: “or else may be condemned in their iniquities.” We have rejected this addition, overcome by the authority of all the manuscripts.] or be condemned in such a way that they have no excuse.

It follows:

**VERSE 6.**—“You therefore, son of man, do not fear them, nor fear their words, because they are unbelieving and subversive with you, and you dwell among scorpions.”

12. It is clear among how perverse people he is sent to preach, since he is admonished not to fear. And because all the wicked inflict other evils upon those who speak good things to them and threaten still other evils, he says, because of what they do: “Do not fear them”; and because of what they threaten, he adds: “Nor fear their words.”

Or, certainly, because the reprobate both inflict evils upon the good and always disparage their deeds [Note: [Col. 0874D] Norm. and Val. Cl. have: “their deeds . . . good acts.” “Good” is absent from Germ. and the others.], the prophet who is sent is admonished not to fear either their cruelty or their words.

Thus, in the words “Do not fear them,” authority for preaching is given to the prophet. And because all who live in God are instruments of the truth, so that he often speaks to me through another and often speaks to others through me, the authority of good speech ought to exist in us in such a way that the one who presides speaks what is right freely, and the one who is subject does not refuse humbly to bring forward what is good.

What a subordinate says to a superior is truly good if it is said humbly [Note: [Col. 0875D] Longip. has: “what is said by a lesser to a greater.”]. For if uprightness of thought loses humility of speech, it corrupts the root of its meaning in the branch of the tongue. This fault is no longer merely in the branch but in the root, because unless the heart became swollen, the tongue would not grow proud.

There ought therefore to be humble authority in the superior, and free humility in the subordinate. But often the very order of speaking becomes confused among human beings, as we said much earlier.

Sometimes one speaks through the swelling of pride and imagines that he is speaking by the authority of freedom. Sometimes another is silent through foolish fear and thinks that he is being silent through humility. The former, attending to the position of his rule, does not measure the meaning of his swelling; the latter, considering the position of his subjection, fears to say the good things he understands and does not realize how guilty he becomes toward charity by keeping silent.

13. Thus pride disguises itself under authority, and human fear under humility, so that often neither the one can consider what he owes to God nor the other what he owes to his neighbor.

The former, when he sees those subject to him but does not attend to the one to whom all are subject, is lifted up in exaltation and boasts of his pride as though it were authority.

The latter, sometimes fearing that he may lose the favor of a superior and thereby suffer some temporal loss, conceals the right things he understands and silently calls within himself the fear that binds him “humility.” Yet by remaining silent he judges in his thoughts the one to whom he is unwilling to say anything; and so, precisely in what he considers humility, he becomes more gravely proud.

Freedom and pride, humility and fear must therefore always be distinguished, lest either fear pretend to be humility or pride pretend to be freedom.

Ezekiel, then, because he was sent to speak not only to the people but also to the elders, is admonished not to mistake careless fear for humility, and is told that he must not fear: “Do not fear them.” And lest he perhaps fear their words of disparagement, it is added: “Nor fear their words.”

[Col. 0875D] **14.** The reason why he ought not to fear the tongues of those who disparage him is also added, when it immediately continues: “For they are unbelievers and subverters with you, and you dwell with scorpions.” Those to whom he was sent to speak would indeed have been worthy of fear if they had pleased almighty God in faith and conduct. But since they are unbelievers and subverters, disparaging him in their words, they are not to be feared; for it is utter folly to seek to please those whom we know do not please the Lord.

[Note: Longip. reads *habere* (“to hold”) instead of *haberi* (“to be held”).]

[Col. 0876A] The judgments of the righteous, however, ought to be held in fear and reverence, because they are members of almighty God, and on earth they condemn what the Lord rebukes from heaven. For the disparagement of the wicked is approval of our life, since it is already shown that we possess some measure of righteousness if we begin to displease those who do not please God. No one, after all, can be pleasing in one and the same matter both to the almighty Lord and to his enemies. He denies himself to be God’s friend who pleases God’s enemy. And he will oppose the enemies of truth who is inwardly subject to that same truth.

Therefore holy men, inflamed with the rebuke of an unrestricted voice, do not fear to provoke to hatred against themselves those whom they know do not love God. The Prophet, ardently displaying this, offered it almost as a gift to the Creator of all, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 138:21–22).

[Note: Lyran. and Longip. read *qui te oderant* (“those who hated you”).]

It is as though he said openly: “Consider how greatly I love you, since I do not fear to stir up against myself the hostility of your enemies.” Hence he says: “Those who repay evil for good were disparaging me, because I pursued righteousness” (Psalm 37:21).

[Note: C. Germ. and Longip. read “those who repaid.” Gussanv. has “I will pursue righteousness.” Beccens., instead of “righteousness,” has “goodness.”]

What the righteous person grants is supremely good when he freely opposes those who do evil. But the wicked repay evil for good when they disparage the righteous, because the righteous preserve the defense of justice against them. The righteous do not look to human judgments but to the examination of the eternal Judge, and therefore they disregard the words of those who disparage them.

Thus Paul said to the Corinthians who disparaged him: “But it is a very small thing for me to be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Corinthians 4:3). Since he could find nothing in his own heart for which he might be reproached, he added: “But neither do I judge myself.” Yet seeing that even his own judgment was insufficient for the perfection of holiness, he continued: “For I am not justified by this.” Why he did not trust even his own judgment about himself, he explained when he added: “But the Lord is the one who judges me” (ibid., 4).

It is as though he said openly: “I do not think that I should trust my own judgment about myself, because he judges me whose judgment I cannot comprehend.”

[Note: Norm. reads, “nor should I believe myself about myself.” Val. Cl. reads, “nor should I trust my own judgment about myself.”]

Hence blessed Job, when amid the pains of his wounds he suffered the darts of words through the disparaging tongues of his friends, immediately returned in thought to his conscience and looked to see whether his mind was steadfast, saying: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my confidant is on high” (Job 16:20). He also added: “My friends are full of words; my eye pours out tears to God” (ibid., 21).

**15.** In everything that is said about us, we must always return silently within ourselves, seeking the inward witness and judge. For what does it profit if everyone praises us while conscience accuses us? Or what can it harm if everyone disparages us while conscience alone defends us?

[Note: The same manuscripts read “if people praise,” and, below, “if people disparage us.”]

Blessed Job, therefore, standing with an unwavering mind amid disparaging tongues, saw that he was attacked on earth by false words and sought a witness in heaven.

[Note: Gemet. with other Norm. manuscripts reads *inflexus persistens* (“persisting, bent/resolute”).]

Hence Isaiah says: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your paths” (Isaiah 3:12). And lest that people attend to words of praise and perish more deeply in their faults, it is immediately said whom they should regard and whose judgment they should fear, when it continues: “The Lord stands to judge; he stands to judge the peoples” (ibid., 13).

It is as though it were said openly: “Why do you follow human judgments, when you know that the heavenly Judge stands over you?”

**16.** For this reason Truth denies that John the Baptist was a reed shaken by the wind, saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matthew 11:7ff.). That he said this by way of denial, not affirmation, is shown by the words that follow. For he says: “But what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses.”

[Note: C. German., Longip., Val. Cl., Norm., and others read *videre in deserto* (“to see in the wilderness”); the editors preferred *videre in desertum* (“to see into the wilderness”).]

A reed shaken by the wind is sometimes raised by the gusts and sometimes bent down by them. Every weak spirit, which is cast down by disparagement or exalted by praise, is a reed shaken by the wind. John was not such a reed, because amid human praise and disparagement he kept the summit of his mind unbent.

**17.** Yet the matter requires careful inquiry: when we hold to the way of a righteous work, should we always disregard the words of those who disparage us, or should we sometimes restrain them?

Concerning this we must know that, just as we ought not to stir up the tongues of slanderers by our own efforts, lest they perish, so we ought to endure patiently those tongues that have been stirred up by their own wickedness, so that our merit may increase. At times, however, we must also restrain them, lest, while they spread evil about us, they corrupt the hearts of innocent people who might have listened to us for their good.

Thus John rebuked the tongue of his detractor, saying: “Diotrephes, who loves to have first place among them, does not receive us. Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds, which he performs, chattering maliciously against us” (3 John 9).

[Note: The printed editions read “Diotrephes”; German. reads “Diotrepis.”]

Again Paul speaks of the Corinthians who disparaged him, saying: “For they say, ‘His letters are weighty and powerful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.’ Let such a person consider that what we are in word through letters when absent, such we also are in deed when present” (2 Corinthians 10:10).

[Note: The word *de* is absent from the manuscripts Norm. and many others; it has been retained here in adherence to other, more ancient manuscripts.]

**18.** Those whose life has been set forth as an example for imitation ought, if they can, to restrain the words of those who disparage them, lest those who could have listened to their preaching fail to hear it and, remaining in wicked conduct, disdain to live well.

[Note: Suess. reads, “but in this subtle inquiry.”]

But in this matter the mind must examine itself with subtle inquiry, lest perhaps it seek the glory of its own praise while our thought merely pretends to be seeking the gain of souls.

[Note: Suess. and Longip. read *lucra sequi nostra* (“to pursue our gains”).]

Often the mind is nourished by praise of its own name, and, as though under the pretext of spiritual gain, rejoices when it learns that good things are being said about it. Often also it becomes angry with those who disparage it in defense of its own glory, and fabricates for itself the idea that it is acting out of zeal for those whose hearts the detractor’s speech disturbs from the good path.

Therefore those should take the greatest care lest the words of their detractors prevail against their reputation who, carefully examining their conscience, find that they possess nothing in it arising from love of private glory.

**19.** This is why the righteous and perfect sometimes proclaim their virtues and recount the good things they have received from God—not so that they themselves may advance among people by displaying them, but so that by their example they may draw those to whom they preach toward life.

Accordingly, the apostle Paul tells the Corinthians how often he was beaten with rods, how often he was stoned, how often he suffered shipwreck, and how much he endured for the truth; he also tells them that he was caught up to the third heaven and led into paradise (2 Corinthians 11:25ff.), so that he might turn their minds away from false preachers. By making known what kind of man he was, he caused those whom he knew to be wrongly revered by them to become contemptible in their eyes.

[Note: The praised manuscripts read, “whom he had learned were received with wrongful veneration.”]

When the perfect do this—that is, when they speak of their own virtues—they are also imitators in this of almighty God, who speaks his praises to human beings so that he may be known by them.

[Note: Some witnesses read “so that he may be known by all.”] For although through his Scripture he commands: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth” (Proverbs 27:2), how does he himself do what he forbids?

[Note: Most Norm. manuscripts read *alienum* (“another’s [mouth]”), followed by “and not your own mouth.”]

But if almighty God were silent about his virtues, no one would know him; if no one knew him, no one would love him; and if no one loved him, no one would return to life. Hence the Psalmist says of him: “He will declare the power of his works to his people, so that he may give them the inheritance of the nations” (Psalm 110:6).

Therefore he declares his virtues, not so that he himself may advance through his praises, but so that those who have come to know him through his praise may attain the everlasting inheritance.

[Note: German., Longip., and Val. Cl. read, “may live.”]

Thus the righteous and perfect are not blameworthy, not only when they rebuke words of their own condemnation, but also when they speak of the virtues they possess to the weak, because through the life they recount they seek the life of others.

[Note: Suess. and Longip. read, “when they speak of their own condemnation.”]

**20.** Yet concerning them we must know that they never disclose their good deeds unless, as I have said, either the usefulness of their neighbors or some pressing necessity compels them. Hence, when the apostle Paul had enumerated his virtues to the Corinthians, he added: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12:11).

Sometimes, however, compelled by necessity, people seek in the good things they report about themselves not the benefit of others but their own. Thus blessed Job enumerates his deeds, saying: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and I diligently investigated a case that I did not know” (Job 29:15–16). He also recalls many other things that he had often done.

[Note: Longip. with Norm. reads, “which he said he had done piously”; Val. Cl. reads, “which he said he had accomplished.” We retain the reading of the printed editions, which is also found in German. and the more ancient manuscripts.]

But because, placed in the wound of his grief, he was being told by his reproaching friends that he himself had acted impiously and had been violent toward his neighbors and an oppressor of the poor, the holy man, caught between God’s blows and human words of reproach, saw his mind gravely shaken and driven toward the pit of despair. He could have fallen immediately unless he had recalled his good deeds, so that his spirit might be restored to hope and, crushed by words and wounds, he might not perish in despair.

Therefore, when he enumerates his good deeds, he does not desire to make himself known to others as though seeking praise; rather, he restores his spirit to hope.

Thus the righteous sometimes speak without arrogance of the good things they do, and likewise, without zeal for private glory, they rebuke the tongues of those who disparage them, because those tongues speak what is harmful. But when the tongues of detractors cannot be corrected, they must be endured patiently in every respect. Nor should the speech of slander be feared, lest, while the condemnation of the wicked is feared, the way of righteous action be abandoned.

Hence it is now said to the prophet Ezekiel: “Do not fear their words, because they are unbelievers and subverters with you.”

**21.** They would be less wicked if those who are unbelievers and subverters were not also subverters. Because they do not believe either in the rewards of the heavenly kingdom or in the punishments of Gehenna, they are abandoned to their perversions and subvert others in faith and conduct as well, so that no one else may attain the kingdom they themselves do not wish to seek.

[Note: Gilot. and Vatic. read *in suis gravitatibus* (“in their grievousnesses”); the English, with the other manuscripts, follows *pravitatis* (“perversions”).]

When they discover that certain more tender souls have begun to do good and already avoid evil, they turn their minds aside—sometimes by mocking what is promised in heaven, sometimes by disparaging what almighty God threatens concerning the punishments of hell, and sometimes by praising temporal goods and craftily promising the pleasures of the present age. Thus they pervert the paths of the innocent.

They rejoice if they can turn anyone back from life and draw him toward death; they delight in their own wickedness and exult in that of others. Their own punishment is plainly not enough for them, since they act so that they will not die alone.

But if they happen to find someone so just and so advanced in virtue that they do not dare to speak against him, then, since they cannot be subverters, they immediately become scorpions. A scorpion advances by touching gently, but strikes with its tail; it does not bite from the front but harms from behind.

All flattering and malicious people are therefore scorpions: they do not resist the good to their face, but as soon as they have departed, they disparage them, inflame others whom they can, and introduce whatever harm they are able to introduce; they never cease secretly to inflict deadly wounds.

[Note: Suess. and Longip. read, “whom they wish.”]

[Note: Longip. reads, “all are flattering, malicious, and harmless,” etc.]

Scorpions, then, are those who appear flattering and harmless to the face, but behind their backs carry the means by which to pour out venom. For those who strike in secret secretly drag death along with them.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “They surrounded me like bees, and they blazed like fire among thorns” (Psalm 118:12). Bees have honey in their mouths and a wound in the sting of their tails. All who flatter with their tongues but secretly strike out of malice are bees, because in speech they offer the sweetness of honey, but by striking secretly they inflict a wound.

In doing this they blaze like fire among thorns, because through the flames of detractors it is not the life of the righteous that is burned, but whatever thorns of sin might exist in them are consumed.

Let it therefore be said: “They are unbelievers and subverters with you, and you dwell with scorpions.” They are unbelievers with respect to God, subverters with respect to their weaker neighbors, and scorpions even with respect to the strong and steadfast. Although they do not dare contradict the latter openly, they nevertheless inflict the wound of disparagement in secret.

The unbelievers, subverters, and scorpions are the same people, because they do not believe what they hear concerning God, subvert those whom they can from good conduct, and strike with hidden schemes those whom they cannot bend.

**22.** In this connection we must also note that when it is said to the prophet, “They are unbelievers and subverters with you, and you dwell with scorpions,” a medicine of consolation is offered to us, who are often weary of living because we do not wish to dwell with the wicked.

We complain that not everyone who lives with us is good.

[Note: C. Germ. reads “we seek” (*quaerimus*) instead of “we complain” (*querimur*).] We do not wish to bear the evils of our neighbors; we decide that everyone ought already to be holy, while we ourselves do not wish to be what we must bear from our neighbors.

But in this matter it becomes clearer than daylight how far we ourselves still fall short of goodness, when we refuse to bear the wicked. For no one is perfectly good unless he is good even among the wicked.

Hence blessed Job declares concerning himself: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). Hence the apostle Paul says to his disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15).

Hence Peter, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, says that God “rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the injurious conduct of the lawless.” He was righteous in sight and hearing, living among those who day after day tormented the soul of the righteous man by wicked deeds (2 Peter 2:7).

Often, when we complain about the lives of our neighbors, we try to change our place and choose a secluded, more remote way of life, evidently ignorant that, if the spirit is absent, a place does not help. The same Lot of whom we speak was holy in Sodom but sinned on the mountain (Genesis 19:2, 30ff.).

Since places do not fortify the mind, the first parent of the human race himself bears witness to this: he fell even in paradise (Genesis 3:7). But all that we say from earthly examples is comparatively small. For if a place could save, Satan would not have fallen from heaven.

Therefore the Psalmist, seeing that temptations exist everywhere in this world, sought a place to which he might flee, but could not find a fortified place without God. For this reason he asked that God himself become a place for him, saying: “Be to me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me” (Psalm 30:3).

We must therefore endure our neighbors everywhere, because no one can become an Abel whom the wickedness of Cain does not exercise.

**23.** There is, however, one reason for which the company of the wicked must be avoided: lest, if they cannot be corrected, they draw us to imitation and, while they themselves are not changed from their wickedness, corrupt those who are joined to them.

Hence Paul says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). And as Solomon says: “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his paths and incur a snare for your soul” (Proverbs 22:24).

Therefore, just as perfect men ought not to flee their wicked neighbors, because they often draw them toward righteousness and are never themselves drawn toward wickedness, so all who are weak ought to avoid the company of the depraved, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils they frequently see but cannot correct.

By listening daily to the words of our neighbors, we take them into our minds just as, by blowing and breathing, we draw air into our bodies. And just as bad air, drawn in by continual breathing, infects the body, so perverse speech, constantly heard, infects the mind of the weak, so that it wastes away in delight in evil conduct and in the continual wickedness of speech.

It continues:

**IBID.**—“Do not fear their words, and do not be afraid of their faces, because they are an exasperating house.”

**24.** The good are to be feared lest they be offended, lest perhaps the One who always dwells in their hearts be provoked to anger through them. But, as was said above, if we offend the wicked, we need not fear, since our conduct displeases those who do not even approve the justice of the Creator.

What, then, is there to fear if those who are not pleasing to God are ungrateful to us? Hence it is rightly said now: “Do not fear their words, and do not be afraid of their faces, because they are an exasperating house.”

It is as though it were said openly: “They would be worthy of fear if they did not exasperate me by their actions.”

Of them it continues:

**VERSE 7.**—“Therefore you shall speak my words to them, if perhaps they will listen and be quiet, because they are provocateurs.”

**25.** What else does everyone who sins do except provoke within himself the anger of his Creator? We know that whenever we offend by deed, word, or thought, we provoke God against us.

Yet he bears with us and mercifully waits, exercising patience himself, while through his preachers he offers us a word of exhortation. Everyone who preaches what is right, if he is heard, appeases the anger of the Creator, who has been provoked against the transgressing people.

[Note: Suess. reads, “if he is not heard, he provokes the Creator’s anger against the transgressing people to a blow”; Norm. reads, “he appeases [that anger] over the transgression of the people.”]

Therefore he himself must not do the evil that customarily provokes the fury of his Creator against the people. For this reason it also continues:

**VERSE 8.**—“But you, son of man, hear whatever I speak to you, and do not be exasperating, as the exasperating house is.”

**26.** That is: do not yourself do the evils that you see being committed, lest you yourself commit what you have been sent to forbid.

[Note: The old and recent printed editions read *prohibere niteris* (“you strive to forbid”); all Norm., C. Germ., Corb., Longip., and Val. Cl. manuscripts read *prohibere mitteris* (“you are sent to forbid”).]

Every preacher must always consider this attentively in his mind: lest he who has been sent to raise up the fallen should himself fall with them into wicked conduct and be struck by Paul’s sentence: “In judging another, you condemn yourself” (Romans 2:1).

Hence Balaam, filled with the Spirit of God for speaking but nevertheless held back by his own spirit in carnal life, speaks of himself, saying: “The hearer of the words of God said, who knows the teaching of the Most High and sees the visions of the Almighty, who, falling, has his eyes open” (Numbers 24:14, 16).

He had open eyes while falling because he saw what he ought to say rightly but disdained to live rightly: falling, that is, in wicked conduct, yet having open eyes in holy preaching.

[Col. 0882B] **27.** There is another possible explanation for why blessed Ezekiel, who is sent to preach, is forbidden to be exasperating. Unless he obeyed when he was sent to speak the words, he would have exasperated almighty God by his silence just as the people did by their wicked conduct.

For just as the wicked sometimes exasperate God because they speak or do evil, so the good sometimes exasperate him because they remain silent about what is good. The fault of the former is to act perversely; the fault of the latter is to remain silent about what is right.

Thus the good exasperate God together with the wicked in this respect: by failing to rebuke what is perverse, they grant, through their silence, permission for the wicked to advance.

[Note: Val. Cl. reads, “permission to complete it.”]

It continues:

**IBID.**—“Open your mouth and eat whatever I give you.”

[Col. 0882C] **28.** We open our mouths when we speak what is right; and we eat what we receive from God because, when we begin to preach, the food of life is both given and increased within our understanding.

Hence another prophet says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Psalm 118:131). He would not have drawn in the spirit unless he had opened his mouth, because if he had not devoted himself to preaching to his neighbors, the grace of spiritual teaching would not have increased within him.

It continues:

**VERSE 9.**—“And I saw, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which a scroll was wrapped; and he unfolded it before me, and it was written within and without.”

**29.** Just as the order of preachers is signified through the prophet, so the pages of sacred Scripture are signified through the scroll he received.

The wrapped scroll is the obscure language of sacred Scripture, which is wrapped in the profundity of its meanings so that it cannot easily be penetrated by everyone’s understanding. But the scroll is unfolded before the prophet because the obscurity of sacred language is opened before preachers.

The hand of God had extended the wrapped scroll when he said to the apostles: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while the men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared” (Matthew 13:24ff.), along with the rest, which your Charity remembers even without my repeating it.

But he unfolded the scroll he had shown wrapped when he explained what he had spoken in riddles, saying: [Note: Val. Cl. with Norm. reads *qui seminavit* (“he who sowed”) instead of *qui seminat* (“he who sows”).]

“He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world. The good seed, these are the children of the kingdom; the weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age; the reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the consummation of the age” (Matthew 13:37ff.).

The wrapped scroll is therefore unfolded when what had been spoken obscurely is opened through the breadth of understanding. Truth unfolded this wrapped scroll when he brought about in his disciples what is written: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

**30.** Concerning this scroll it continues: “It was written within and without.”

The scroll of sacred language is written within through allegory and without through history; within through spiritual understanding, but without through the simple sense of the letter, which remains suitable for the weak.

Within, because it promises invisible things; without, because it orders visible things by the rectitude of its commandments. Within, because it promises heavenly things; without, because it teaches how contemptible earthly things are either to be used or fled from in desire.

For it speaks one set of matters about heavenly secrets, while in external actions it commands another. The things it commands outwardly are plain, but those that it relates about inward matters cannot be fully grasped.

Hence it is written: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters” (Psalm 103:2).

[Note: Recent printed editions read “who covers with waters”; C. Germ., Corb., Norm., and the other manuscripts add *eius* (“its”), here and below.]

What is signified by the name “heaven” except sacred Scripture? From it the sun of wisdom, the moon of knowledge, and the stars of examples and virtues from the ancient Fathers shine upon us.

It is stretched out like a skin because, formed by its writers through the language of flesh, it is spread before our eyes by the exposition of teachers’ words.

What is signified by the name “waters” except the most holy choirs of angels? Of them it is written: “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4).

The Lord covers the upper parts of this heaven with waters because the heights of sacred language—that is, what it relates about the nature of divinity or eternal joys—are, while we remain ignorant, known secretly to the angels alone.

This heaven is therefore stretched out before us, yet its upper parts are covered with waters, because some things in sacred language are already open to us through the disclosure of the Spirit, while other things, which can be manifest only to the angels, are still kept hidden from us.

Nevertheless, we already perceive a portion of these hidden things through spiritual understanding and have already received the pledge of the Holy Spirit. For although we do not yet know them fully, we nevertheless love them from the depths of our being, and in the many spiritual understandings that we have already come to know, we are nourished by the food of truth.

**31.** Let it therefore say: “It was written within and without,” because in sacred language the strong are filled by its more hidden and sublime sayings, while we who are little ones are nourished by its more openly stated commandments.

[Note: Corb. and Germ. read, “the little ones are not [fed] from the more hidden sayings,” omitting the remainder.]

Hence it is written: “The high mountains are for the stags; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Psalm 103:18).

[Note: Gemet. and other Norm. manuscripts read, “For the stags have the mountains.”]

Let those who already know how to leap through contemplation have the mountains of understanding. But let the rock be a refuge for hedgehogs, because we little ones, covered with the thorns of our sins, though we cannot understand lofty things, are saved in the refuge of our rock—that is, in faith in Christ.

Hence it is also said to certain people: “I judged myself to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).

It is as though he said: “Because I judged that you could not grasp the mysteries of his divinity, I spoke to you only of the weakness of his humanity.”

It continues:

**IBID.**—“And there were written upon it lamentations, a song, and woe.”

[Note: Most Norm. manuscripts read “and a song.”]

[Col. 0884C] **32.** There is no doubt that “song” can be spoken either in a good sense or in a bad one, since we can speak of a joyful song and a mournful song. But following the usage of sacred Scripture, which almost always places “song” among things prosperous, we understand the word in this passage in its good sense.

When almighty God had delivered his people from the Red Sea, it is written: “Then Moses and the children of Israel sang a song to the Lord” (Exodus 15:1). And when David had gained victory over his enemies, it is written: “David spoke to the Lord the words of this song” (2 Samuel 22:1).

Solomon likewise says: “Vinegar upon nitre, and one who sings songs to an evil heart” (Proverbs 25:20).

[Note: The printed editions read *corde pessimo* (“to a most wicked heart”); Lyran. reads *cordi pessimo* (“to a most wicked heart”).]

For if vinegar is poured upon nitre, the nitre immediately boils and bubbles up. So when a perverse mind is corrected by rebuke, or is urged toward good by the sweetness of preaching, it becomes worse through correction and is thereby inflamed in the wickedness of murmuring, through which it ought to have been restrained from iniquity.

[Note: Suess. and Lyran., with which almost all the printed editions agree, read, “good things are urged.” Gussanv. reads, “he is urged toward good.” We follow German., Norm., and other manuscripts.]

Through Elihu also it is said of the ungrateful person who despairs of himself: “And he did not say, ‘Where is God, my maker, who gives songs in the night?’” (Job 35:10).

A song in the night is joy in tribulation. We understand “song in the night” when, amid present afflictions, we are consoled by future joys.

The apostle showed us a song in the night when he said: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans 12:12).

David indicates that he has a song in the night when he says: “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounds me; my exultation, redeem me from those who surround me” (Psalm 31:7). For whoever says that he is surrounded by distress and nevertheless calls God his exultation is unquestionably singing a song in the night.

Therefore, since sacred Scripture almost always uses “song” in a good sense, it should also be understood in that sense by us here.

[Col. 0885A] **33.** In sacred Scripture, “woe” is more often understood of eternal grief than of present grief. Hence it is written: “Woe to the wicked in his evil; for the recompense of his hands will be made to him” (Isaiah 3:11).

Blessed Job also says: “If I am wicked, woe is me; but if I am righteous, I will not lift up my head, being filled with affliction and misery” (Job 10:15). The affliction of the righteous is temporal. Therefore, by saying “woe,” he distinguished it from temporal affliction, declaring that the righteous have affliction but the wicked have woe.

Truth itself also says: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18:7); and, “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6:25); and, “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (ibid. 21:23).

We must therefore consider how these three things are written in the sacred book: lamentations, a song, and woe.

**34.** Lamentations, because repentance for sinners is written in it. A song, because the joys of the righteous are foretold there. Woe, because the condemnation of the reprobate is expressed there.

Therefore, if you wish to punish your sins, read the lamentations written in this volume: “Tear your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13). And again: “Be miserable and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into grief” (James 4:9).

But if you wish to rejoice because of the promise of the joy to come, learn the songs of eternal praise written in this volume: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

And as a certain wise man says of the heavenly Jerusalem: “All its streets will be paved with precious and pure stone, and alleluia will be sung throughout all its lanes” (Tobit 13:22).

The citizens of the heavenly homeland came to announce this song to us, crying out together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

But if you are still attached in mind to the present age, if you still take pleasure in earthly delights, you cannot love the eternal joys you hear about. Therefore learn the woe written in this volume, and by fear drive from your heart what you love, so that you may be able, through judgment, to love the song you read.

There, under the figure of one condemned person, the whole multitude of the reprobate is expressed when Truth’s voice says: “Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:13).

Then the reprobate fall into the outer darkness because now, in their inner selves, they have voluntarily cast themselves down, refusing to follow the light of truth either by believing or by doing good.

They are commanded to be cast out with hands and feet bound because, while there is now time for working and running, they did not wish to have their hands and feet free for good action.

[Note: Rothomag. reads, “there the woe”; Ebroic. and Sag. read, “where the woe.”]

There the woe of the reprobate is written: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24). There it is said to the condemned and rejected: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

Thus this volume contains in writing everything that builds up and everything that instructs. You have sinned, and now repent that you have committed forbidden things; so that you may be taught to practice repentance, you find lamentations there.

[Note: Gussanv. corruptly reads “often.”]

You desire to raise your mind by hope of heavenly joys; for your consolation you find a song there. But if you have both committed evil and do not repent of having committed it, instead raising the neck of your mind and bowing to no lamentations of repentance, corrected by no expectation of heavenly joys, then, whether you wish it or not, you will hear woe written there.

Thus the one whom neither fear humbles toward repentance nor hope raises toward heavenly rewards may now foresee the punishment of his condemnation and fall without excuse into eternal punishment.

35. What, then, brothers, what must we wretched people do, except awaken to the words of this volume and punish with tears the evils we remember having committed, so that through the laments of repentance we may reach the song of life? Otherwise, if we are unwilling to be afflicted now by repentance, we shall afterward feel woe without end. Nor should the multitude of our wounds drive us into despair, because the physician’s power is greater than the magnitude of our sickness. For what can he not restore to health, who was able to create all things from nothing? For the Only-Begotten is coeternal with the omnipotent Father, God who lives and reigns with him in the unity [Note: [Col. 0886D] The word *God* is absent in the printed editions, but not in the manuscripts.] of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY X

In explanation of the earlier verses of the third chapter through verse fifteen, he especially commends Sacred Scripture, its constant reading, meditation, and preaching.

[Col. 0886C]

## 1

Certain people, when reading the writings of sacred eloquence and penetrating its loftier meanings, despise with swollen understanding the lesser commandments given to the weaker, and wish to transform them into another interpretation. If they rightly understood the lofty matters in it, they would not hold even the smallest commandments in contempt, because divine precepts speak of great things in some passages while nevertheless fitting the little ones in others, so that those who advance in understanding may grow, as it were, by certain steps of the mind and reach an understanding of greater things. Hence it is now said to the holy prophet:

**Ezekiel 3:1.**—“Son of man, whatever you find, eat.”

[Col. 0886D]

## 2

For whatever is found in Sacred Scripture must be eaten, because its lesser teachings shape a simple life, while its greater teachings build a subtle understanding. It continues:

**The same, verse 2.**—“Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the children of Israel. And I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that scroll.”

## 3

Sacred Scripture is our food and drink. Hence the Lord also threatens through another prophet: “I will send famine upon the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos 8:11). By saying that, when his eloquence is withdrawn, he wears us down with hunger and thirst, he demonstrates that his words are both our food and our drink.

But it must be noted that they are sometimes food and sometimes drink. In obscure matters, which cannot be understood unless they are explained, Sacred Scripture is food, because whatever is explained so that it may be understood is, as it were, chewed so that it may be swallowed. In clearer matters, however, it is drink. We swallow drink without chewing. Thus we drink the clearer commandments, because we are able to understand them even without explanation.

Because the prophet Ezekiel was going to hear many obscure and perplexing things, he is by no means told concerning the sacred scroll, “Drink,” but “Eat.” It is as though he were plainly told: “Examine and understand; that is, first chew, and then swallow.”

But in the words of sacred eloquence this order of our study must be preserved: that we learn these things in order that, pierced by compunction for our iniquity, we may recognize the evils we have done and avoid doing others.

## 4

And when, through long practice in tears, confidence in the remission of sins has begun to arise, let us also draw others to life through the words of God that we understand. They are to be understood for this purpose: that they may benefit us and, through spiritual purpose, be imparted to others. Hence it is rightly said here also: “Eat this scroll, [Note: [Col. 0887D] The Paris edition of 1518 and those following it add, “and go, speak.” The manuscripts C. Germ. and others likewise have this at the first occurrence of the passage, but not thereafter.] and go, speak to the children of Israel.”

It is as though he were told concerning the sacred food: “Eat and feed; be filled and pour forth; receive and scatter; be strengthened and labor.”

## 5

It should also be noted that the prophet adds: “And I opened my mouth, and he fed me with that scroll.” Another prophet testifies that the mouth is in the heart, saying: “Deceitful lips are in the heart, and with the heart [Note: [Col. 0887D] Norm. reads, “they spoke.”] they spoke evil” (Psalm 11:3). We open our mouth, therefore, when we prepare our understanding for the comprehension of the sacred word.

Thus, at the Lord’s voice, the prophet opens his mouth, because at the breath of the Lord’s command the desires of our heart gape open to receive something of the food of life. Yet it is not within our power to take this food unless he himself feeds us who commanded that it be eaten. For the one who cannot eat by himself is fed.

And because our weakness is not capable of receiving the heavenly words, he himself feeds us who at the proper time apportions to us our measure of wheat, so that, while in the sacred word we understand today what we did not know yesterday, tomorrow also we may grasp what we do not know today, being nourished by daily sustenance through the grace of divine dispensation.

For the omnipotent God stretches out his hand, as it were, to the mouth of our heart as often as he opens our understanding and places the food of sacred eloquence into our minds. He feeds us with the scroll when, by dispensing Sacred Scripture to us, he opens our understanding and fills our thoughts with its sweetness. Hence it is also added:

**Verse 3.**—“And he said to me: Son of man, your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled with this scroll that I give you.”

## 6

In the older translation it does not read, “Your belly shall eat,” but, “Your mouth shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled.” Our mouth eats when we read the word of God; our inward parts are filled when we understand and keep the things over which we labor in reading.

In the later translation, which we also believe to be more accurate, it is written: “Your belly shall eat, [Note: [Col. 0887D] Longip. and Val. Cl. add: “but your mouth also shall eat.” [Col. 0888D] And your inward parts.”] and your inward parts shall be filled.”

In sacred eloquence, the belly is sometimes customarily used for the mind. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “My belly, my belly, I grieve” (Jeremiah 4:19). Because he had said this of a spiritual, not a bodily, belly, he added: “The perceptions of my heart are troubled” (ibid.). For it would not have pertained to the salvation of the people if the prophet had proclaimed that he was grieving over a bodily belly. [Note: [Col. 0888D] Ebroic., Becc., Lyr. read, “but he grieved in his belly.”]

Rather, he grieved in his belly because he felt affliction of mind.

But why should we produce the example of the prophet when we have a clearer testimony from the Lord? And when Truth itself speaks, the prophet must be silent, because a lamp has no brightness in the sun. For he says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Because holy teachings flow forth from the minds of the faithful, rivers of living water stream, as it were, from the belly of believers.

And what else are the inward parts of the belly except the interior of the mind—that is, right intention, holy desire, humility toward God, and a loving will toward one’s neighbor? Hence it is rightly said now: “Your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled,” because when our mind has received the nourishment of truth, our interior is no longer left empty, but is satisfied with the food of life.

[Col. 0888C]

## 7

Let us consider, my dearest brothers, how loving is this promise: “Your belly shall eat, and your inward parts shall be filled with this scroll that I give you.”

Many people read, yet remain hungry from the reading itself. Many hear the voice of preaching, but depart empty after hearing it. Their belly eats, but their inward parts are not filled, because even if they receive an understanding of the sacred word in their minds, by forgetting and failing to keep what they have heard they do not store it in the inward parts of their hearts.
