Hence the Lord reproves certain people through another prophet, saying: “Set your hearts upon your ways. You have sown much and brought in little; you have eaten, and have not been satisfied; you have drunk, and have not been intoxicated” (Haggai 1:6).

[Note: [Col. 0888D] C. Germ. has this reading, with which all the printed editions agree. In the Norman manuscripts and most others, however, it reads *in corde* (“in the heart”).] He sows much in his heart but brings in little who, whether by reading or hearing, learns much from the heavenly commandments but, by acting negligently, produces little fruit. He eats and is not satisfied who, while hearing the words of God, desires the profits or glory of the world. He is rightly said not to be satisfied, because he chews one thing and hungers for another.

He drinks and is not intoxicated who inclines his ear to the voice of preaching but does not change his mind. For the understanding of drinkers is accustomed to change through drunkenness. Whoever, therefore, is devoted to learning the word of God but desires to acquire the things of this world drinks, [Col. 0889A] [Note: [Col. 0889D] The printed editions read, “and, having become intoxicated.” We adhere to the manuscripts C. Germ., Norman., Val. Cl., and others.] but is not intoxicated.

If he were intoxicated, he would undoubtedly have changed his mind, so that he would no longer seek earthly things and would no longer love the vain and transitory things he had loved.

Of the elect the Psalmist says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35:9). They are so filled with the love of the omnipotent God that, with their minds changed, they seem to themselves to have become strangers to themselves, fulfilling what is written: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24). He denies himself who is changed for the better, begins to be what he was not, and ceases to be what he was.

## 8

Often we see certain people who, at the voice of preaching, seem to be pierced as though by conversion, yet have changed their clothing, not their mind. They put on religious dress but do not trample upon their former vices; [Note: [Col. 0889D] The printed editions read *irae stimulis inaniter*; the manuscripts Anglic., Norman., Germ., and others correct this to *immaniter*, “violently.”] they are violently driven by the goads of anger; through the pain of malice they burn to injure their neighbor; they grow proud before human eyes over certain good deeds they have displayed; they eagerly seek the profits of the present world; and, merely because of the outward habit they have assumed, they place their confidence in holiness.

What else should be said to them except what [Note: [Col. 0889D] The printed editions read *doctor* (“teacher”); the manuscripts read *magister* (“master”).] the outstanding teacher says to certain people who observed the exterior aspects of the law: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any value, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Galatians 5:6)? It is not a matter of great merit if something is done outwardly to our body; what is done in the mind must be weighed with the greatest care.

## 9

For to despise the present world, not to love transitory things, to lay the mind’s very marrow low in humility before God and one’s neighbor, to preserve patience in the face of insults inflicted upon us, and, while preserving patience, to drive the pain of malice from the heart; to give one’s own possessions to the needy, not to covet what belongs to others; to love a friend in God; for God’s sake to love even those who are enemies; to mourn over a neighbor’s affliction; not to rejoice at the death of one who is an enemy—this is the new creation.

The same teacher of the nations [Note: [Col. 0889D] Longip. reads *apud illos*, “among them.”] seeks this among other disciples with vigilant attention, saying: “If, then, there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). [Note: [Col. 0889D] Germ. and several others add, “and they have become new.” We retain the other reading because it corresponds exactly both to the Vulgate and to the Greek text.]

## 10

It belongs to the old person to seek the present world, [Note: [Col. 0889D] Suess. and Longip. read *diligere* (“to love”) in place of *quaerere* (“to seek”).] to love transitory things out of desire, to raise the mind in pride, to lack patience, to think, out of the pain of malice, about injuring one’s neighbor, not to give one’s possessions to the needy, and to seek what belongs to others in order to multiply one’s own; to love no one purely for God’s sake; to return hostility to one’s enemies; [Note: [Col. 0889D] The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read, “to return hostilities to enemies.”] and to rejoice at a neighbor’s affliction.

All these are characteristics of the old person, which we plainly draw from the root of corruption. But the one who now surpasses these things and changes the mind toward kindness in accordance with the Lord’s commandments is rightly told: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.”

## 11

New things therefore come to be in our minds when the vices of the old person pass away from us; [Note: [Col. 0890D] Anglic., Norman., and most manuscripts, except C. Germ., read “then from us.” C. Germ. omits both “then” and the clause, “and then the vices of the old person pass away.”] and the vices of the old person pass away when the belly eats the commandment of sacred eloquence and the inward parts are filled to the marrow.

For often we have seen certain people devote themselves with their whole mind to the study of holy reading. Recognizing, amid the Lord’s words, how greatly they have sinned, they sacrifice themselves in tears, are continually afflicted with sorrow, and take no pleasure in any prosperity of this world, so that the present life becomes a burden to them and the very light a weariness. They scarcely admit ordinary conversation and reluctantly relax the strictness of discipline, rejoicing, for love of their Creator, only in mourning and silence. [Note: [Col. 0889D] Germ. reads, “rejoicing only in mourning and silence.”]

Their belly has eaten the sacred scroll, and their inward parts have been filled, because their memory has not lost the precepts of life that their understanding was able to grasp; rather, their mind, gathered into God, has preserved them by continually mourning and recalling them. [Note: [Col. 0890D] Longip. and Val. Cl. read *legendo*, “by reading.” Jamesius reports that this reading is also found in the Anglic. manuscripts, from which the Vatican edition emends the text. But the text itself should be emended from older codices such as Germ.]

## 12

It often happens that such people, through a gift of heavenly grace, also receive the word of teaching, and from the nourishment of truth—which they themselves inwardly ruminate with delight—they gently feed their neighbors.

Their preaching is certainly as sweet to their hearers as their conduct is not contrary to their preaching, because they draw from their own life what they impart to their neighbors through their tongue. Hence the prophet rightly adds here:

[Col. 0890C]

**The same.**—“And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey.”

## 13

The book that filled the inward parts became sweet as honey in the mouth, because those who have learned to love the almighty Lord truly in the inward parts of their heart know how to speak sweetly about him.

Sacred Scripture is sweet in the mouth of the one whose life is filled inwardly with his commandments, because it is sweet for him to speak to whom it has been inwardly impressed for living. [Note: [Col. 0890D] Suess. reads *ad videndum*, “for seeing,” in place of *ad vivendum*, “for living.”]

For speech has no sweetness when a wicked life gnaws at the conscience within. Hence it is necessary that the one who speaks the word of God first strive to live rightly, so that afterward, from his life, he may gather what he should say and how he should say it.

For preaching is built up more by the conscience of holy love than by practiced speech, because, by loving heavenly things within himself, the preacher learns how to persuade others that earthly things should be despised. The one who weighs his own life inwardly and, by admonishing others outwardly through his example, builds them up is like dipping the pen of his tongue in his heart when, with the hand of the word, he writes outwardly for his neighbors.

Hence the admirable preacher, after exhorting his disciples at length, because he bore within himself no contrary testimony of conscience, confidently added: “If there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline, think about these things; what you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me, do these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Philippians 4:8–9).

It continues:

**Verse 4.**—“And he said to me: Son of man, go to the house of Israel, and you shall speak my words to them.”

## 14

When the Lord says to the prophet, “You shall speak my words to them,” what else does he do than place upon his mouth a bridle of restraint, lest he presume to say outwardly what he had not first heard inwardly?

For false prophets spoke their own words, not God’s, concerning whom it is written: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you and deceive you; they speak the vision of their own heart, not from the mouth of the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:16). And again: “I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied” (ibid., 21).

From this it must also be understood that any interpreter who, in explaining sacred eloquence, composes something falsely in order perhaps to please his hearers speaks his own words and not the Lord’s, if he lies from a desire to please or mislead.

But if, seeking the power contained in the Lord’s words, he understands them differently from the one through whom they were spoken, and even if under another interpretation he seeks the building up of love, the words he recounts are the Lord’s, because God speaks to us through all of Sacred Scripture for this one purpose: to draw us to love of himself and of our neighbor.

It continues:

## 15

**Verses 5–7.**—“For you are not sent to a people of deep speech and an unknown tongue, to the house of Israel; nor to many peoples of deep speech and an unknown tongue, whose words you could not understand. And if you were sent to them, they would listen to you. But the house of Israel does not wish to listen to you, because it does not wish to listen to me.”

At the very beginning of the command [Note: [Col. 0891D] Val. Cl. reads *visionis* (“of the vision”) in place of *jussionis* (“of the command”).] by which the prophet is sent to preach, the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Israelites are clearly signified. For when it is said, “You are not sent to many peoples of deep speech and an unknown tongue, whose words you could not understand,” and it is immediately added, “And if you were sent to them, they would listen to you,” the obedience of the Gentiles is plainly declared: they would eventually follow the voices of preachers without delay.

When it is added, “But the house of Israel does not wish to listen to you, because it does not wish to listen to me,” the hardness of Judea is signified: it recognized the words of preachers but refused to follow them. The unknown tongue of the Gentiles did not delay in obeying, although it was foreign to the language of the law.

It is rightly said, “They do not wish to listen to you, because they do not wish to listen to me,” in accordance with what is written: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

The reason why they do not listen is also added:

**Verse 7.**—“For the whole house of Israel has a worn forehead and a hard heart.” [1269]

## 16

When the house of Israel is said to have a worn forehead, what else should be understood or considered except that frequent guilt wears away the forehead of the heart through shamelessness, so that the more often a sin is committed, the less the mind of the one committing it feels shame over it?

For this reason the sinner eventually reaches such hardness of heart that he is no longer sensitive to correction, because the one hardened by the habit of sinning in no way feels the word of the one correcting him—that is, the hand of the one touching him gently. Thus it is also said to Judea, which sinned with increasing frequency: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jeremiah 3:5).

Or certainly the forehead is worn through habituation to the activities of this world. For just as there are some who prefer rest to all the world’s rewards and honors, so there are others who sweat through earthly labors, attend to business, and become entangled in quarrels so that they may seem to be somebody in this world.

Although they feel their bodies failing amid their labors, conquered nevertheless by love of earthly things, they are delightfully wearied. To them it is said through the prophet: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hosea 10:11). A heifer accustomed to threshing on the threshing floor returns of its own accord even if it is released from labor. [Note: [Col. 0891D] Suess. and Val. Cl. read, “even if it is released, it returns of its own accord to labor.”]

So, for certain wicked minds, nothing is more burdensome than being commanded not to labor in the activities of this world. Often we see people who, having been removed from earthly activity, beg to return; they ask to be burdened and consider rest a grave danger to themselves. [Note: [Col. 0892D] Suess. reads, “they think they have incurred grave danger in rest.”]

Their forehead is therefore worn: they not only do not flee labor, but are not ashamed to appear importunate in the labors denied to them.

It continues:

**Verse 8.**—“Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads.”

## 17

Just as commendable shame exists in the presence of evil, so shame in the presence of good is blameworthy. To be ashamed of evil is wisdom; to be ashamed of good is foolishness. Hence it is written: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Sirach 4:25).

The one who is ashamed of the evils he has committed and repents reaches the freedom of life. But the one who is ashamed to do good falls from the state of uprightness and moves toward condemnation, as the Redeemer says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty” (Luke 9:26).

There are some who already conceive good things in their minds but do not yet openly oppose evil. These people, being good in mind but lacking authority in speech, are plainly not suited to defend the truth. The defender of truth must be one who neither fears nor is ashamed to speak what he rightly feels.

Hence it is now promised to the prophet as a great gift: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads.”

What is a sinner except one who is wounded? And what is a preacher except a physician? If the sinner who lies in a wound is not ashamed, why should the physician who provides healing through remedies be ashamed?

Often, however, it happens that a preacher is heard with reverence; at other times he is so despised by the perverse that it seems he is saying nothing beneficial to them. Hence it is rightly said now:

**Verse 9.**—“I have made your face like adamant and like flint.”

## 18

Adamant and flint are both hard, but one of them is precious while the other is worthless. Adamant is used for adornment; flint is trodden underfoot by travelers.

Often it happens that we are ashamed to say something to those whom we see listening very humbly to our correction. At other times, when we see people disregard our rebuke and hold it in contempt, we hesitate to bring them a word of preaching.

But if we are wise, we draw the authority to exhort or rebuke both from those by whom we see ourselves honored and from those by whom we see ourselves despised, so that we need neither be ashamed of the humility of the former nor fear the pride of the latter.

Let it therefore be said: “I have made your face like adamant”—that is, if you are honored by your hearers; “I have made your face like flint”—if you are trampled underfoot and despised by your hearers. Thus neither should the tongue be restrained by shame because of honor received, nor should it fall silent through weakness because of contempt.

It continues:

**The same.**—“Do not fear them, nor be afraid of their faces, because it is a house that provokes.”

## 19

This has already been said above. But we should note how harsh that house is, since its harshness is repeated so frequently. [Note: [Col. 0893D] C. Germ. reads, “since it is harsh.”]

The sinner must therefore be rebuked and never feared, because he is a house that provokes. A person ought to be feared if he himself, as a human being, feared the Author of all things. But one who possesses no rational sense of fear of God is to be feared in nothing, precisely because he is not what he ought to be.

It continues:

**Verses 10–11.**—“And he said to me: Son of man, receive in your heart all my words that I speak to you, and hear them with your ears; and go, enter among the exiles, the children of your people.”

## 20

We must observe attentively that the Lord’s voice tells the prophet first to hear his words and afterward to speak. We hear the words of God if we do them. And we speak them rightly to our neighbors when we have first done them ourselves.

The evangelist Mark confirms this well when, recounting the Lord’s miracle, he says: “They bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him” (Mark 7:32). He then indicates the order of the healing, adding: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him, ‘Ephphatha,’ which means ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke rightly” (ibid., 33ff.).

What does it mean that the God who created all things, wishing to heal the deaf and mute man, put his fingers into his ears and, spitting, touched his tongue? What are the fingers of the Redeemer except the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Hence, when he had cast out a demon in another place, he said: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20). For this reason another evangelist records him as saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). From both passages it is gathered that the finger of God is called the Spirit.

To put his fingers into the ears, therefore, is to open the deaf mind to obedience through the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But what does it mean that, spitting, he touched the man’s tongue? Saliva is the wisdom received from the mouth of the Redeemer in divine speech. Saliva flows from the head into the mouth. Thus, when that wisdom—which is he himself—touches our tongue, it is immediately shaped into words of preaching.

He groaned as he looked up to heaven—not because he himself needed to groan, since he was giving what was being requested, but because he taught us to groan toward the one who presides over heaven. Thus our ears should be opened through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the tongue should be released through the saliva of the mouth—that is, through knowledge of divine speech—for words of preaching.

Then he says to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened”; and immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was released. Here we must note that “Be opened” was said because his ears were closed. But when the ears of the heart have been opened to obedience, the bond of the tongue is undoubtedly also released, so that a person may speak to others of the good things he himself has done and of what they too should do.

The passage rightly adds: “And he spoke rightly.” For the one speaks rightly who has first done, by obeying, the things he urges others to do by speaking.

## 21

The fact that the prophet is sent to admonish the exiled people must be understood not only of the exile that had occurred bodily to that people, but also of the exile that had occurred in the mind.

He had come from Jerusalem to Babylon. And what is Jerusalem called except “vision of peace,” and what is Babylon called except “confusion”? Whoever falls from upright works into perverse deeds, because he slips from a good endeavor into vices, comes, as it were, from Jerusalem to the city of Babylon.

He has abandoned the summit of good contemplation and lies in the exile of confusion. [Note: [Col. 0893D] C. Germ. reads, “of good conduct.” Norm. reads, “of good action and contemplation.”]

This often happens to those who, while doing good, glory in their own virtue. Hence the Psalmist, praying to the Lord that he might not be carried captive from the vision of peace—that is, from good works—to Babylon, says: “My helper, I shall not emigrate” (Psalm 61:7). For if he had trusted in himself, he would have migrated by falling from works of righteousness.

## 22

Yet those who have fallen from the state of uprightness into perverse action are not to be despaired of [Note: [Col. 0894D] Ebroic. and some Norman manuscripts read *desperati sunt*, “are despaired of.”], because, behold, the prophet is sent to the exile of Babylon. And through another prophet the Lord says: “You shall come as far as Babylon, and there you shall be delivered” (Micah 4:10).

Often, after someone has fallen into the confusion of vices, he returns to repentance, ashamed of the evils he has committed, and raises himself from his falls by living well. What has such a person done except come as far as Babylon and be delivered there?

After committing perverse deeds in a confused state of mind, he becomes ashamed of the very evils he has done, rises up against himself, and returns to the state of uprightness by doing good. [Note: [Col. 0895D] The printed editions read, “coming therefore into Babylon.” Longip. reads, “delivered from Babylon.” No manuscripts have “coming.”]

He was therefore delivered in Babylon who is shown, through divine grace, to have been saved even from confusion. The prophet speaks to the exiled when he rebukes those who have fallen by migrating from the state of uprightness into the vices of error.

It continues:

**Verse 11.**—“And you shall speak to them, and say: Thus says the Lord God: If perhaps they will listen and cease.”

## 23

The difficulty of hearing is repeated so often in the divine words—“If perhaps they will listen”—that what else is signified except the hardness of the exiled people? [Note: [Col. 0895D] The printed editions read *quoties*, or *quod quotiens*—“whenever.”] There is great consolation for us in these words. If the omnipotent God, sending a prophet to a perverse people, declares that his words will be difficult to hear, why should we wretched people be saddened when we are often despised by our brothers in our admonitions?

We address those who repeatedly sin, rebuke them frequently, and often deal with them in gentle words; yet one listens while another refuses to listen; one accepts the word of exhortation in part, while another part he refuses to receive.

Thus we see daily fulfilled what the Lord, through another prophet, recounts as having done in anger, saying: “I rained upon one city [Note: [Col. 0895D] Gratian cites this at the assigned location with respect to its meaning, not its wording. The same passage is also read in the Ordinary Gloss on Amos 4.] and did not rain upon another. One part was rained upon, and the part that was not rained upon withered” (Amos 4:7).

When one mind accepts some words of holy exhortation while another refuses to accept them, the Lord rains upon one city and does not rain upon another. But when the very neighbor who listens corrects himself of some vices and scorns to amend himself of others, one and the same city is partly rained upon and partly remains dry, because it repels from itself the rain of preaching. [Note: [Col. 0896D] The manuscripts do not have a single reading here. Germ. reads *ipse qui proximus* (“he himself who is a neighbor”); Longip. reads *ipse qui proximum* [incomplete or uncertain as printed]; the printed editions read *ipse qui proximos* (“he himself who [the] neighbors”). We have preferred the Norman reading.]

There are some who do not listen at all to words of exhortation; these entirely refuse to receive the rain. And there are some who listen but nevertheless do not follow it inwardly, because they cut away some vices from themselves but allow others to persist gravely. [Note: [Col. 0896D] Longip. reads, “others from themselves.”]

Often we see some people who, through the word of preaching, drive the heat of avarice away from themselves. They no longer seize what belongs to others and even give their own possessions generously to the needy; yet they do not tame the goads of anger or preserve the restraints of patience through tranquility of mind.

Others, at the word of exhortation, overcome the uncleanness of the flesh within themselves and guard their bodies in chastity; yet they still do not incline their minds toward their neighbors as they ought, but raise themselves in thought through the harshness of pride.

In these people one part is rained upon, because it produces fruit, while the part that is not rained upon withers, because, not fully receiving the word of exhortation, it remains sterile in good works.

It continues:

**Verse 12.**—“And the spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great commotion: ‘Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.’”

## 24

What does it mean that, after the prophet is sent to the exile of the children of his people, he hears behind him a voice of great commotion saying, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place”?

He had turned toward the sinners of Babylon and heard behind him, as though at his back, the voice of the Lord’s glory from its place. The place of God is Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace—because those hearts see the things that belong to God and do not descend into the exile of Babylon, that is, into the vices of confusion.

God dwells where true peace is sought and the glory of inward contemplation is loved. Those who slide into perversity refuse to be God’s place. The place of God’s glory is therefore either every holy soul or each angelic spirit that remains in the heavenly realms.

The glory of the Lord is blessed from its place when eternal praise is sung to the Author of all things either by elect human beings or by holy angels.

When the righteous think about converting sinners, because by considering their vices they direct their gaze toward carnal actions, they turn their attention, as it were, toward Babylon. Yet, because of their state of uprightness, they never cease to consider the good deeds of the saints to the praise of God. Although their thought is directed elsewhere, they hear behind them, as it were, the voice of the Lord’s glory from Jerusalem—that is, from its place. [Note: [Col. 0896D] The printed editions read, “they direct their attention to something else.”]

[Col. 0896C]

## 25

But why linger over these matters, when, with the Lord’s help, we are able to understand these words of the prophet through another and subtler meaning and to express it more clearly?

He says: “And the spirit lifted me up.” The spirit lifts up the preacher when it raises his mind into love of the omnipotent God and makes it alien to earthly desires, so that he wishes to do nothing except those things by which he may gather spiritual profits and carry the fruit of his daily work to the heavenly kingdoms.

Hence we preachers are also commanded: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life” (John 6:27). [Note: [Col. 0896D] Val. Cl. reads, “and to new preachers.”]

## 26

It is rightly added: “And I heard behind me the voice of a great commotion.”

The prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, recounts as already completed what he foresees must be done, because in predestination those things that will later follow in action have already been accomplished. Hence in the older translation it is said through Isaiah: “He who made the things that are to come” (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

What, then, does it mean that the prophet heard behind him a voice of great commotion, except that after the word of preaching addressed to the hearts of sinners there follow the laments of penitents?

[Col. 0897A] **27.** For all the perverse, while they do evil and do not hear what is right from the righteous, do not know how grievous are the things they commit; and through this very ignorance they are secure in their stupor. Lying in their sins, they rest as though softly at ease, as it is said of a certain sinful and secure people: “He rested upon his dregs, because he lay secure in his sins” (Jer. 48:11).

**28.** But when the perverse begin to hear the word of preaching, and to learn what the eternal punishments are, what terror belongs to the judgment, and how searching the examination of each individual sin will be, immediately they tremble, are filled with groans, and are distressed by sighs that they cannot contain; shaken by great fear, they break forth into mourning and tears. Thus a voice of great commotion follows the prophet, because after the word of preaching the mourning of the converted and penitent is heard. Those who previously lay quietly in their wound, afterward touched by the hand of the physician, return to health with pain.

Of this commotion of the penitent another prophet says: “His feet stood, and the earth was shaken” (Zech. 14:4), because when the traces of truth are impressed upon the minds of hearers, the mind itself, disturbed by consideration of itself, is shaken. Hence the Psalmist prays for sinners, saying: “You who sit upon the cherubim, let the earth be moved” (Ps. 98:2). Hence, pleading for the afflicted and penitent, he says:

[Note: [Col. 0897D] The Paris manuscripts have *you have moved, Lord, the earth . . . because it has been moved*.]

“You have moved the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, because it has been moved” (Ps. 59:4). The earth moved and troubled is the sinner who, recognizing his guilt, is anxious and brought to the lamentation of repentance. [Col. 0897C] For it was said to sinful humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). Let him therefore pray that the fracture of the earth may be healed, because it has been moved, so that the sinner who is afflicted by his sins may be comforted by the joy of heavenly mercy. [1274] This, then, is the voice of great commotion: when each person judges his own deeds and is disturbed in the affliction of repentance.

**29.** But let us hear what the voice itself says: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” The hearts of sinners had been the place of the evil spirit; but when, in repentance, they become angry with themselves and return to life, they become a place for the Lord’s glory. Now they rise up against themselves; now, with the tears of repentance, they pursue the evils they have committed. Thus the blessing of glory is heard in praise of the Lord from the place where previously the insult to the Creator resounded through love of the present [Col. 0897D] world. The hearts of the penitent now become the Lord’s own place, whereas previously, situated in sins, they had been another’s place.

Those who turn from their sins to the Lord not only erase with tears the wrongs they have done, but also advance to higher things through wondrous works: they become holy creatures of almighty God; they fly upward through signs and virtues; they abandon the earth utterly; and, having received gifts, they lift themselves by desire toward heavenly things. Concerning these it is further added:

**VERSE 13.** — “And the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one another.”

[Note: [Col. 0897D] The printed editions incorrectly have *one against the other*. All the manuscripts have *one another*, and this is how it should be read, according to the Hebrew text and the Vulgate. The same expression occurs throughout below.]

**30.** The prophet hears behind him the sound of great commotion, because, as has been said, the word of preachers is followed by the mourning of penitents. He hears behind him the sound of the wings of the living creatures, because from the very mourning of penitents arise the virtues of the saints, so that they advance all the more in holy action the more they remember that before knowing life they acted wickedly.

Yet these words involve a serious ambiguity, because the prophet does not state plainly whether each living creature strikes its own wings against itself,

[Note: [Col. 0897D] Val. Cl.: “strikes its wings against itself.” We follow the reading of the German, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

or whether these same holy living creatures strike one another with their wings, so that one creature’s wing touches the other, and the other’s wing touches this creature.

**31.** But since sacred language often says something obscurely so that, by God’s wondrous dispensation, it may be expounded in several ways, we ought, with the Lord’s help, to explain both interpretations to your Charity. We have often already said that the wings of the living creatures signify the virtues of the saints (Hom. 4, no. 5; Hom. 7, no. 22; Hom. 8, no. 1).

How, then, does each living creature, shaking its wings, strike one wing against the other, unless it is plainly understood that, if we become holy living creatures, virtue arouses virtue within us, as one virtue urges another toward perfection? For behold, someone already possesses knowledge of the word of God.

[Note: [Col. 0898D] In Val. Cl., followed by Gussanv., there is added: “and through that same knowledge he learns.” This appendix is absent from the German, Norman, and other manuscripts. In some printed editions, instead of *he learns*, we find *let him learn*.]

Through knowledge of the word of God he learns: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41). When he has begun to be merciful in giving alms, he reads the words of sacred authority; and whatever is said in them about mercy, he now understands more deeply through experience. There it is written: “I was a father to the poor” (Job 29:16). Perhaps he had read this earlier and passed it by. But when mercy has begun to imitate nature in his heart, he reads and recognizes what it means to be a father to the poor, because, returning inwardly, he understands in himself what he hears outwardly.

For it is one thing to perform almsgiving by commandment, and another to do so from charity. To do good by commandment belongs to beginners; to do good from charity belongs to the perfect, who do not merely act because they are commanded, but also love, in doing, what they are commanded to do. Hence the Psalmist rightly says in praise of great virtue: “See that I have loved your commandments, Lord; in your mercy give me life” (Ps. 118:159). To perform God’s commandments as an order is the action of one who serves and obeys; to perform them out of love is the action of one who obeys and loves.

Since, therefore, mercy is learned through knowledge of charity,

[Note: [Col. 0898D] Longip., Val. Cl., and Norm.: “the charity of mercy.”]

and knowledge is multiplied in the contrite heart through the charity of mercy, one wing strikes another within us, because virtue arouses virtue. Thus the person who guards the good of chastity in his body is inflamed with zeal against those who live wantonly, so that they may be cleansed from the stains of impurity. Often, when he finds some people in falls, he subdues and afflicts them and restrains them toward the purity of chastity.

If his own mind should perhaps be tempted by the impurity of lust, then, through the very zeal with which he corrected others,

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Vaticanus and Gussanv.: “corrects himself,” while both printed and handwritten witnesses oppose this reading.]

he reproves himself and blushes to think impure thoughts, remembering that he corrected such thoughts in others. In this way one wing strikes another: virtue urges virtue and guards it from impurity.

**32.** But if, as we said above, the living creatures strike one another with their wings,

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Longip. and Val. Cl.: “and one wing strikes another”; below, Longip.: “they strike one another with their wings.”]

so that the wing of each strikes the other, the meaning of this description also becomes clear, with the Lord’s help. What does it mean that these winged creatures strike their wings against one another, unless that all the saints touch one another through their virtues and stir one another to advancement by contemplating another’s virtue?

Not everything is given to one person, lest he fall into pride. Rather, what is not given to you is given to this person, and what is denied to him is given to you, so that, when he considers the good that you possess and he himself does not, he may prefer you to himself in his thoughts; and, again, when you see that he possesses what you do not, you may place yourself beneath him in your own thoughts. Thus what is written may be fulfilled: “Considering one another superior to yourselves” (Phil. 2:3).

To mention only a few examples from many: this person is granted the virtue of remarkable abstinence, yet he does not possess the word of knowledge. To that person the word of knowledge is given, yet he strives to attain the virtue of perfect abstinence and cannot. To another is granted freedom of speech, so that, extending the solace of protection to the oppressed, he may speak freely in defense of justice; yet, while still possessing many things in this world, he wishes to abandon everything and cannot.

To another, however, it has already been granted to abandon all earthly things, so that he desires to possess nothing in this world; yet he still does not dare to exercise authority of speech against sinners.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] The recent edition is preferred: “does not presume to exercise it,” although the manuscripts and older printed editions disagree.]

The one who, because he no longer has anything binding him to the world, ought to speak more freely, refuses to speak freely against others, lest he lose the very quiet of his life. To another the virtue of prophecy has been given: he already foresees many things that are to come; yet, when he sees and sympathizes with the present affliction of his neighbor, he cannot heal it.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] Suess.: “considering and observing it”; below, “what will shortly happen to him,” instead of “what will shortly happen to himself.”]

To another the grace of healing has been given, and by prayers he removes from his neighbor’s body the present illness; yet he does not know what will happen to him shortly.

In wondrous dispensation, therefore, almighty God distributes his gifts among his elect in such a way that he gives to this person what he denies to that one, and grants one a greater measure of what he grants another in a lesser measure. Thus, when either this person sees that the other possesses what he himself does not, or the other considers that this person has received more while he himself has received less, all admire the gifts of God in one another—that is, reciprocally. Through this very admiration, each is humbled before the other, and whoever he sees possessing what he does not possess, he regards, by divine judgment, as preferred to himself.

The living creatures therefore strike one another with their wings when holy minds touch one another through their alternating virtues; by touching, they stir one another; and, once stirred, they fly toward advancement.

**33.** Let us see how Paul was touched by the wings of the apostles and stirred to repentance. Considering the evils of his former persecution and the innocent life of the apostles, he said: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

He considered the innocence of the apostles, and because of his former wickedness all the zeal he displayed in the Church became contemptible in his own eyes. He did not consider how many he surpassed through the understanding he had received, because, weighing their innocence, he grieved that he had once been a persecutor.

But let us see whether any of the apostles admired in Paul the understanding that had been given to him. We must first seek out the apostle who, admonishing his disciples, says: “As our most beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him, speaking of these things in all his letters, in which there are certain matters difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort” (2 Pet. 3:15–16).

Thus Paul admires the innocence of all the apostles, while the first of the apostles admires wisdom in Paul. They touch one another with their wings because from the very things by which they fly they mutually stir one another toward advancement.

**34.** Almighty God does in human hearts what he does in the regions of the earth. He could have given every fruit to any one region; but if one region had no need of the fruits of another, it would not have fellowship with it. Thus he grants this region an abundance of wine and another an abundance of oil; he makes one abound in flocks and another in the richness of crops. When one brings what the other does not have, and the other returns what the first did not bring, divided lands are joined together through their sharing in grace.

As, therefore, the regions of the earth are joined, so are the minds of the saints. By contributing to one another what they have received, they offer their fruits, as it were, from one region to another, so that all may be joined together in a single charity.

**35.** Yet amid these things we must understand that, just as all the elect always consider in others what they have received better from God than they themselves have received, so that they may prefer others to themselves in thought and submit themselves to them in humility, so the mind of the reprobate never considers what good another possesses more abundantly than itself, but what good it possesses more abundantly than another.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] Thus the German, Norman, and old Paris manuscripts, Gilot, and Vaticanus have *he himself*, instead of *itself*. Gussanv. has *they themselves . . . possess*.]

They do not weigh what spiritual goods another has received which they themselves lack, but what goods they themselves possess and what evils are present in the other. Although almighty God distributes virtues to individuals for the purpose of humbling one person before another in thought, the reprobate turn the good they have received toward this end: they are destroyed in pride, always considering the goods they possess and others do not, and never taking account of how many goods others possess that they themselves lack.

What divine mercy arranges for the increase of humility, reprobate minds turn toward the increase of pride;

[Note: [Col. 0901D] The German manuscript has “into an argument,” corrected by a later hand. The printed editions follow that reading. We have preferred the other reading, found in the Norman, Val. Cl., Longip., Suess., and other manuscripts.]

and through the diversity of gifts they fall away from the good by which they ought to have increased in humility.

**36.** For this reason, dearest brothers, it is necessary that you always look upon what you possess less of in yourselves, but in your neighbors upon what they have received more abundantly than you, so that, when you see them superior to yourselves because of the good they possess and you do not,

[Note: [Col. 0901D] Val. Cl.: “you consider them to be above yourselves because of the good you see that they possess and you do not.”]

you may also grow in humility in order to obtain that good. For if you take account of the goods received by them, and they consider the gifts you possess, you touch one another with your wings, so that, always stirred toward heavenly things, you may fly.

It follows:

**VERSE 13.** — “And the sound of the wheels following the living creatures, and the sound of great commotion.”

**37.** Above we said that the Testaments are signified by the wheels of sacred language (Hom. 6, no. 2 and following). The voice of the wheels, therefore, is the discourse of the Testaments. After the voice of the wings of the living creatures, the voice of the wheels is also heard, because, when the virtues of the saints, having received the preachers’ word, fly toward higher deeds and urge one another toward advancement, the condition of the holy Church is raised up, so that throughout the whole world the pages of the sacred Testaments may be read.

For now everywhere the holy Gospel resounds; everywhere the sayings of the apostles; everywhere the Law and the Prophets. The voice of the wheels follows the voice of the wings because, after the miracles of the saints, the words of sacred language are heard freely [Col. 0901D] within the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] Suess., together with Val. Cl.: “fittingly.”]

The wheels follow the living creatures because, as was said above, after the life of the saints has come to honor, the venerable words of the Testaments have likewise appeared to human beings.

**38.** Or certainly the wheels follow the living creatures,

[Note: [Col. 0901D] Gussanv. incorrectly has “the wheels of the living creatures.”]

because in the life of the holy Fathers we learn what we ought to understand in the volume of sacred Scripture. Their conduct opens to us what the pages of the Testaments say in their preaching.

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Val. Cl.: “in their preaching.”]

But we must ask why, after it was said above, “I heard behind me the sound of great commotion,” the voice of the wings and also of the wheels is followed by the words: “And the sound of great commotion.” If this is examined carefully, it can be discovered that the repetition is not pointless.

**39.** There are, in fact, two great commotions by which our hearts are moved. One commotion arises from fear, the other from charity; one is produced by the mourning of penitents, the other by the fervor of those who love.

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Alternatively: “from the fervor of those who burn with love,” as it stands in most of the Norman manuscripts.]

After the word of preaching, therefore, comes the first commotion, when we lament the evils we have committed. After the voice of the wings and the wheels comes the second commotion, when with great weeping we seek the heavenly goods we hear about.

For behold: within the holy Church we learn daily, as it were, the sound of wings, because from many Fathers we recognize examples of virtue; and, because the sacred words resound everywhere, we are stirred, as it were, by the voices of wheels. Since through those same sacred words we are inflamed with love for our Creator, we lament, burning with the fires of great fervor, that we are still far from the face of almighty God.

After the first voice of great commotion, therefore, there is finally another voice of great commotion, because those who began by knowing God to lament their sins now, by loving the one whom they have come to know, do not cease to desire him with tears. After the voice of the wheels, therefore, follows the voice of great commotion, because when the Testaments of God begin to sound in the ear of the heart, the spirit of the hearers, pierced by love,

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Suess.: “is moved by the love of compunction to lamentation.”]

is moved to lamentation.

Hence the words of sacred Scripture become savory in the hearts of readers; hence they are often read by those who love, in silence, as though secretly and furtively. Therefore another prophet says:

“You cut off the heads of the mighty in their alienation; nations shall be moved in it, and shall open their mouths as a poor man eating in secret” (Hab. 3:14).

Almighty God cuts off the heads of the mighty in their alienation because, by alienating the pride of the Jews from himself, he rejected it. In that alienation the nations were moved, because, while the Jews were falling away from the faith, the hearts of the Gentiles hastened toward knowledge of the faith. These nations open the mouth of their hearts to the nourishment of sacred reading and eat in secret like a poor man, because they receive the words of life with haste and silence as they read them.

**40.** But we must understand that the more hearers advance in charity and understanding,

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Suess.: “the more grace of the Spirit is given to the holy preachers, so that they may advance by meditation and speech. Hence . . .”]

the greater grace of the Spirit is given to holy preachers. Thus, after the prophet had first said, “The Spirit took me,” and “I heard behind me the sound of great commotion,” followed by the sound of the wings and wheels and then again of great commotion, he immediately adds:

**VERSE 14.** — “The Spirit also lifted me up and took me.”

**41.** Why does he who had already said that he was taken up by the Spirit now recount that he was again lifted up and taken?

The minds of preachers advance toward higher things when, through them, the understanding of hearers is moved toward desire for almighty God. These holy preachers advance for this reason: so that through their ministry the gifts of grace may be multiplied in the holy Church, as it is written of this same holy Church: “Watering its streams, multiply its generations; in its showers it shall rejoice when it rises” (Ps. 64:11).

The streams of the Church are the holy preachers, who pour water upon the soil of our hearts. But when the streams are watered, the generations of the Church multiply, because when preachers receive more abundant grace of the Spirit, the number of the faithful increases.

This holy Church rejoices in its showers. In a shower, water falls from the roof onto the earth, having first fallen from heaven onto the roof. The roof of the Church is the holy preachers, who protect us by interceding for us and fortifying us through their admonitions. But because their hearts are filled from God in preaching, water comes from heaven to the roof, as it were. Because we are watered by their words, water flows from the roof down upon the earth, as it were.

Thus the holy Church rejoices in its showers when it rises, because when it is born in faith and good works, it considers the gifts it has received and exults in the words of the preachers. Since, therefore, when hearers rise toward better things, grace is also multiplied in their preachers, the prophet says: “The Spirit also lifted me up and took me.” A preacher is lifted up and taken ever higher precisely where the hearer is changed into a better life.

**42.** But we must ask: since the Spirit does not lift up the mind unless he has taken it, why is it first said that he lifted it up and afterward that he took it? Here, however, “took” means that he held firmly. For there are some whom he lifts up but does not take: their understanding flashes toward spiritual things, but their life, remaining in carnal deeds, does not agree with their understanding.

Balaam, for example, had been lifted up by the spirit of prophecy, but he had not been taken up, because he was truly able to see from far off things that would happen long afterward, yet he was unwilling to separate his mind from earthly desires (Num. 24:4–5).

But because the holy prophet was lifted up in knowledge and was likewise taken up in life, let us now hear what sort of preaching he proceeds to undertake:

**IBID.** — “And I went away bitter, in the indignation of my spirit.”

**43.** Consider, dearest brothers: why did he go away bitter when the gifts of the Holy Spirit had increased in him? Does the same Spirit make every heart he takes bitter in the indignation of its spirit?

We must understand that the preacher whose present life is still sweet to him—even if he appears to speak the word of God—has not been lifted up and taken up. For the mind that the Holy Spirit fills, he moves toward bitterness at temporal things and delight in eternal things.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] Gussanv. alone has: “into bitterness at temporal things and delight in eternal things.”]

It is sweet to exist amid human affairs, but this is so for the person who has not yet tasted any joy of heavenly things; for the less he understands eternal things, the more delightfully he rests in temporal things. But if someone has already tasted with the mouth of his heart what the sweetness of heavenly rewards is, what those hymnic choirs of angels are, and what the incomprehensible vision of the Holy Trinity is, then, the sweeter that which he sees within becomes, the more everything he endures outside is turned into bitterness.

He quarrels with himself over the things he remembers having done wrongly, and he displeases himself once the one who created all things has begun to please him. He reproves himself for his thoughts, pursues himself over his words, and punishes himself for his deeds by weeping. He longs for things above and now tramples all earthly things underfoot through contempt in his mind.

As long as he does not yet possess in vision what he desires, it is sweet for him to weep and afflict himself with continual lamentation. Since he does not yet see himself in the homeland for which he was created, nothing pleases him more in the exile of this life than his own bitterness. He disdains to be subject to temporal things and ardently sighs for eternal things.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “Because in much wisdom there is much indignation, and he who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18).

[Note: [Col. 0904D] The German manuscript has “he who adds knowledge shall add sorrow.”]

For when we come to know heavenly things, we disdain to subject our minds to earthly things. As we begin to understand more about the things we have done wrongly, we grow angry with ourselves; thus in much wisdom there is much indignation, because the more we advance in knowledge, the more deeply we become indignant with ourselves over our perverse deeds.

As knowledge increases, so does sorrow, because the more we know eternal things, the more we grieve that we are in the misery of this exile. Or, as another translation has it: “He who adds knowledge adds labor.” For the more we begin to know what the joys of heaven are, the more we labor in weeping so that we may escape the snares of our errors.

Thus in much wisdom there is much indignation: if we now taste eternal things, we disdain to desire temporal things; if we now taste eternal things, we despise ourselves for having done what could separate us from the love of eternity. Conscience reproves itself, accuses what it has done, condemns through repentance what it accuses, and a quarrel arises within the soul, giving birth to peace with God.

**44.** Thus Ahab, the wicked king, rebuked by the prophet, was terrified when he heard the divine sentence against him and was weighed down by great sorrow,

[Note: [Col. 0904D] All the printed editions have “was exposed”; the German and other manuscripts disagree. Longip. has “through terror” instead of “through sorrow.”]

so that the Lord said to his prophet: “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days” (1 Kings 21:29).

In these words of the Lord we must consider how the sorrow of bitterness pleases him in his elect, who fear losing the Lord, if repentance pleased him even in a reprobate king who feared losing the present world. Or how pleasing spontaneous affliction for sins is to him in those whom he loves, if this was pleasing for a time even in one whom he rejected?

But we must understand that no one can undertake these things wholeheartedly for love of almighty God unless the Holy Spirit has taken possession of his mind. For when could anyone by his own strength suffice to despise earthly things, love heavenly things, seek peace with God, enter into conflict with himself, reprove himself in thought, and punish himself with groans? No one can do these things unless divine grace has strengthened him.

Hence it is added:

**IBID.** — “For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me.”

**45.** We cannot rise perfectly to good things unless the Spirit both lifts us up by going before us and strengthens us by following after us.

But we must ask: since it was written above concerning the scroll he had received, “It became in my mouth like sweet honey,” why is it later said, “I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit”? It would indeed be very strange if sweetness and bitterness could coexist.

According to the foregoing sense, however, we must understand that when the word of God begins to be sweet in the mouth of the heart,

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Longip.: “begins to delight.”]

the person’s spirit undoubtedly grows bitter against itself. For the more subtly he learns from it how he ought to reprove himself, the more harshly he chastises himself through the bitterness of repentance; and the more he sees in the sacred volume what he ought to love concerning almighty God, the more he displeases himself.

But because a human being cannot advance to these things by his own strength, it is rightly said now: “The hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me.” In sacred language the hand of the Lord is also sometimes called the only-begotten Son.

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Suess.: “sometimes the Holy Spirit, sometimes also the only-begotten Son.”]

For all things were made through him (John 1:3). Of his ascent Moses records the almighty Father saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven” (Deut. 32:40).

This hand, which strengthens the hearts of his elect, said to the disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

[Note: [Col. 0905D] The printed editions have “in everything.” The German and Norman manuscripts have “into everything,” in keeping with Gregory’s usage.]

In everything we think, therefore, and in everything we do, we must always pray that, with his inspiration, we may think, and with his help, may act—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY XI

Continuation of the explanation of Ezekiel, chapter 3, from verse 15 to verse 20, especially concerning pastoral office, the mutually connected sins of rulers and subjects, and the blindness of the mind.

[Col. 0905D] Among the other wonders of prophecy, the books of the prophets possess this further marvel: just as events are sometimes explained through their words, so words are sometimes explained through events, so that not only their utterances but also their deeds are prophecies.

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Suess.: “in their words.” The other witnesses do not support this reading.]

Thus it is now said:

**EZEKIEL 3:15.** — “I came to the exiles, to the heap of new grain, to those who dwelt beside the river Chebar.”

**1.** Since the circumstances required him to say that he had come to the exiles, what necessity of speech was there for him also to specify the place through the grain, saying, “to the heap of new grain,” unless causes are often signified through things and places?

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Suess.: “both things are signified through places, and causes through places.”]

For many years of captivity had already passed while Ezekiel was prophesying, and many of those who had been led into captivity had already died in the death of the flesh; the prophet was coming to speak to their sons. Hence it is said to him above: “Son of man, I am sending you to the sons of Israel, to apostate nations that have turned away from me. Their fathers transgressed my covenant up to this very day, and their sons are stiff-necked and hard of heart; to them I am sending you” (Ezek. 2:3ff.).

Since many of these would believe and, through obedience, attain the fruitfulness of good works, they are called a heap of grain.

For that good souls are called the grain of God another prophet testifies, saying: “Israel was holiness to the Lord, the firstfruits of his grain” (Jer. 2:3).

[Note: [Col. 0906D] The printed editions have “the Holy One of Israel.”]

The nations converted afterward to the faith also became the Lord’s grain. But because Israel first believed in the Lord, the prophet rightly called it his firstfruits of grain.

Since, therefore, the prophet was sent not to the earlier people but to the sons of that same people, he came to a heap of new grain. What is signified by the river Chebar we have already explained above (Hom. II, no. 6); we do not repeat it here, lest repetition produce weariness.

It follows:

[Col. 0906C] **VERSE 15.** — “And I sat where they were sitting, and I remained there seven days, mourning in their midst.”

**2.** Observe with what compassion the holy prophet joins himself to the captive people, uniting himself to their sorrow by sitting and mourning with them, because the root of the word is the power of action. A word is willingly received by the hearer when it proceeds from the preacher with compassion of heart.

Thus iron is joined to iron: it is first melted so that afterward each may hold fast to the other. If it does not first become soft, it cannot afterward hold firmly. So the prophet sat with the captive people and remained mourning in their midst, so that, by condescending to them through the grace of charity and making himself more gentle toward them, he might immediately hold them through the strength of the word.

[Note: [Col. 0906D] Val. Cl.: “but Israelite.” Our reading has some obscurity. Yet it is found in the German, Norman, and other manuscripts. The sense is: If it is said that Israel, which is called the “house of provocation,” was affected by no sorrow—for it did not recognize its sins even amid the scourges—the prophet nevertheless sat mourning among those who rejoiced.]

But if the Israelite people, called the house of provocation because they did not recognize their sins even amid the scourges, did not depress their spirit with any sorrow, the prophet took care to sit mourning among those who rejoiced, so that by keeping silent he might show what he had come to teach by speaking. Before he uttered words, he assumed the form of his words in the fact that he remained silent in mourning.

It follows:

[Col. 0907A] **VERSE 16.** — “When the seven days had passed, the word of the Lord came to me, saying.”

**3.** In the fact that he sat mourning for seven days and received the words of the Lord’s command after the seventh day, so that he should speak, he clearly indicates that during those same days he had kept silent in mourning.

He had been sent to preach, and yet, sitting for seven days, he remained silent. What does the holy prophet intimate to us through this silence, unless that the person who knows how to speak truthfully is the one who first learned to keep silence well? The discipline of silence is, as it were, a nourishment for the word. Rightly, too, one receives speech through an increasing grace when one has first kept silent in an orderly manner through humility.

Hence Solomon says: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:7). He does not say, “A time to speak, and a time to keep silence,” but places the time for silence first and afterward adds the time for speaking, because we must learn not to keep silent by speaking, but to speak by keeping silent.

If, therefore, the holy prophet who had been sent to speak first remained silent for a long time, so that afterward he might speak rightly, we must consider how great the guilt is of one who does not keep silent when no necessity compels him to speak.

It follows:

**VERSE 17.** — “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel.”

4. It should be noted that the one whom the Lord sends to preach he declares to be a watchman. For the person entrusted with the care of others is called a watchman, so that he may sit at the height of the mind and derive the title of his name from the virtue of his action. For one who is below is not a watchman. A watchman always stands in a high place, so that he may see from afar whatever is coming. And whoever is appointed watchman over the people ought to stand on high through his life, so that he may benefit them through foresight. Hence another prophet admonishes the watchman, saying: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40:9). That is, the one who has undertaken the office of preaching should ascend to the height of good action; he should pass over to lofty things and transcend the works of those entrusted to him, so that he may see the life of his subjects all the more clearly, the less he subjects his mind to the earthly things that he despises.

5. How harsh are these things that I am saying to myself, because by speaking I strike myself—one whose tongue neither sustains preaching as it ought, nor does his life follow his tongue insofar as it is able. I am often entangled in idle words, and, sluggish and negligent, I cease from exhorting and building up my neighbors. In the sight of God I have become both mute and talkative: mute in what is necessary, talkative in what is idle. But behold, the word of God compels me to speak about the life of a watchman. I cannot remain silent, and yet I fear to strike myself by speaking. I will speak, I will speak, so that the sword of God’s word may pass even through me to pierce the heart of my neighbor. I will speak, I will speak, so that the word of God may resound through me even against me. I do not deny that I am guilty; I see my sluggishness and negligence. Perhaps, before the merciful Judge, the very recognition of guilt will obtain pardon.

6. Certainly, while I was living in the monastery, I was able both to restrain my tongue from idle talk and to keep my mind almost continually intent upon prayer. But after I placed the burden of pastoral office upon the shoulders of my heart, the mind can no longer continually gather itself back into itself, because it is divided among many things. For I am compelled at one time to examine the affairs of churches, at another those of monasteries; often to weigh the lives and actions of individuals; at one time to bear the business of citizens; at another to groan over the swords of invading barbarians and fear the wolves lying in wait for the flock entrusted to me; at one time to take care of material matters, lest resources be lacking to those by whom the rule of discipline is maintained; at another to endure certain plunderers with equanimity, and at another to oppose them while striving to preserve charity.

*[Note: Norm., Anglic., Val. Cl. have “at one time,” instead of “often”; nevertheless, the reading found in C. Germ. agrees with the printed editions, and for that reason we have retained it.]*

When, therefore, the mind is driven, divided and torn apart, to think about so many and such great matters, when can it return to itself, so that it may gather itself wholly for preaching and not withdraw from the ministry of proclaiming the word? Since the necessities of my position often bring me into contact with secular men, I sometimes relax the discipline of my tongue. For if I keep myself under the continual severity of my own correction, I know that I will be avoided by the weaker, and will never draw them toward what I desire. Consequently, I often listen patiently even to their idle talk. But because I myself am also weak, having been drawn for a little while into idle conversation, I now willingly begin to say what I had begun to hear unwillingly; and where I was weary of falling, I take pleasure in lying there. What, then, or what kind of watchman am I, who do not stand upon the mountain of action, but still lie in the valley of weakness?

*[Note: Norm. reads “deliberately”; Sagiensis, however, has “I stand.”]*

Yet the Creator and Redeemer of the human race is able to grant to me, unworthy as I am, both height of life and effectiveness of speech. For love of him, I do not spare even myself in his proclamation.

7. The life of a watchman, therefore, ought always to be both elevated and watchful on every side. It ought to be elevated, lest it succumb to love of earthly things; watchful on every side, lest it be struck by the arrows of the hidden enemy. Nor is it enough for the watchman to live on high, unless by speaking he continually draws his hearers toward lofty things

*[Note: The printed editions read “that he live on high.” We are compelled to follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.]*

and, by speaking, sets their minds on fire with love for the heavenly homeland. and, by speaking, sets their minds on fire with love for the heavenly homeland. But he acts rightly in this only when his tongue has been set aflame by his life. For a lamp that does not burn within itself does not kindle the object beneath it. Hence the Truth says of John: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35)—burning, that is, through heavenly desire; shining, through the word. Therefore, if the truth of preaching is to be preserved, the height of living must necessarily be maintained.

Hence, too, the voice of the Bridegroom of the holy Church says rightly in the Song of Songs: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon” (Song 7:4).

*[Note: Some manuscripts of Norm. read “What praise, I ask, is this?”; we would have followed them if other manuscripts, especially C. Germ., did not stand against them.]*

What praise, then, my brothers, is it that the bride’s nose should be compared to a tower? But because through the nose we always distinguish smells and stinks, what is signified by the nose except the discernment of watchmen? This nose is said to be both like a tower and like Lebanon, because the discernment of those set over others ought always to be fortified with watchfulness and to stand at the height of life—that is, not to lie in the valley of weak action.

*[Note: We have removed “from,” which had crept into the printed editions, since it is absent at least from the ancient manuscripts.]*

*[Note: Another manuscript reads “of the lowly,” as it is found in Rothom. and Boce.; and this indeed better suits “valley.” Nevertheless, “of the weak” is read in C. Germ. and in the old manuscript.]*

For just as a tower is placed on a mountain for watching so that approaching enemies may be seen from farther away, so the life of a preacher ought always to remain fixed on high, so that, like the nose, it may distinguish the stinks of vices from the fragrances of virtues. It should foresee from afar the attacks of evil spirits and make the souls entrusted to it cautious through its vigilance.

It follows:

**IBID. — “And you shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me.”**

8. Behold, the prophet is again warned not to presume to speak what he has not heard, but first to open the ear of his heart to the Creator’s voice and afterward to open the mouth of his body to the ears of the people. Hence another prophet says: “I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my proposition on the psaltery” (Ps. 48:5). For the one who preaches rightly first inclines, as has been said, the ear of his heart to inward speech, so that afterward he may open the mouth of his body in proclaiming admonition.

It follows:

**VERSE 18. — “When I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you do not announce it, nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand.”**

9. What should we note in these words, what should we consider carefully, except that neither does the subject die through the fault of his superior, nor is the superior free from guilt when the subject, not hearing the words of life, dies through his own fault? Death is indeed due to the wicked person, but the way of life must be announced to him by the watchman, and his wickedness must be rebuked. But if the watchman remains silent, the wicked man will die in his iniquity, because the merit of his wickedness made him unworthy to receive the watchman’s word. Yet the Lord requires his blood from the watchman’s hand, because the watchman killed him: by remaining silent, he handed him over to death.

In both cases we must consider how closely the sins of subjects and superiors are joined, because where the subject dies through his own fault, the one who presides is held guilty of death because he was silent. Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, consider: the fact that we are not worthy pastors is also partly your fault, since we have been set over you as such.

*[Note: The printed editions wrongly read “and already”; Suess. has “our” instead of “your,” but this is erroneous.]*

And if at times you fall into iniquity, this too is partly our guilt, since you do not have us opposing and protesting against your evil desires.

*[Note: The Vulgate editions read “which”; the manuscripts reject this reading.]*

You therefore spare yourselves and us when you cease from evil works. You spare yourselves and us when we do not remain silent about what displeases us.

How free from the blood entrusted to him was that outstanding preacher who said: “I am clean from the blood of all; for I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27). For if he had not announced it, he would not have been clean from blood. But because he strove to announce to them the whole counsel of God, he was clean from their blood. By this saying we are summoned, constrained, and shown to be guilty—we who are called priests, who add the deaths of others to the evils that are our own, because we kill as many people as we see, each day, sluggish and silent, going toward death.

10. When it is said, “I will require his blood from your hand,” if in this passage the name “blood” signifies bodily death, our fear of silence is greatly increased. For if the one appointed watchman over his subjects is held so gravely guilty even for the bodily death of one who will at some time die, with what guilt is he bound concerning the death of the souls of his subjects, who could have lived forever if they had heard words of correction?

But it is better to understand sins as signified by the name “blood.” Hence someone, mourning the sins of the flesh, said: “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50:16). The blood, then, of the dying man is required from the watchman’s hand because, if the superior is silent, the sin of the subject is reckoned to his guilt. There is therefore something he can do so that, even when the subject dies, he may make himself free. Let him rise, keep watch, oppose evil actions, as it is written: “Run, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. 6:3–4).

Hence it is added here:

**VERSE 19. — “But if you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness and from his wicked way, he himself shall die in his wickedness, but you have delivered your soul.”**

11. The subject dies without you, then, when he has found you contradicting him in the cause of his death. For you are joined to the death to which you do not object. We should also note what things ought to be preached by the watchman—namely, faith and conduct. For he says: “If you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness and from his wicked way.” Wickedness pertains to unbelief, while the wicked way pertains to evil action. Every watchman ought therefore to strive first to draw people toward the piety of faith, and afterward toward the pious way—that is, toward good action.

12. But since the subject of exhortation has arisen, we ought briefly to make clear how great must be the order and consideration of speech in the mouth of a pastor. For a teacher must weigh what he says, to whom he says it, when he says it, how he says it, and how much he says. If any one of these is lacking, the speech will not be suitable.

For it is written: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4:7, according to the Septuagint).

We offer rightly when we perform a good work with good intention; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone discernment in the performance of good. We must therefore consider what we say, so that, in accordance with Paul’s words, “our speech may always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Col. 4:6).

13. We must also consider to whom we speak, because often one person admits a word of rebuke that another does not admit. And often the same person becomes different according to his conduct. Hence the prophet Nathan struck David with a powerful sentence of rebuke after his adultery. When he spoke about the man who had taken the sheep, saying, “The man who has done this is a son of death,” he immediately answered him: “You are that man” (2 Sam. 12:5, 7). Yet when he spoke to him about Solomon’s kingdom (ibid., 7), because there was no guilt in that matter, he humbly prostrated himself before him in worship.

*[Note: Val. Cl. reads “into prayer.”]*

Thus, in one and the same person, because the situation was different, the prophetic speech was also different.

14. We must also consider when we ought to speak, because often, even if rebuke is postponed, it is afterward received kindly.

*[Note: Most Norm. manuscripts read “if rebuke is postponed.” The word “and” appears superfluous and seems to produce a more obscure sense; nevertheless it is found in C. Germ. and other older parchment manuscripts.]*

And sometimes it loses its force if it has missed the time in which it ought previously to have been delivered.

*[Note: The printed editions, with C. Germ. agreeing, read “if that which before”; we are compelled to depart from them, since the Norm. manuscripts lead the way and the sequence of the context recommends it. For if “quod” is retained the sense is unclear; with “quo” admitted it is excellent.]*

For the wise woman, seeing Nabal drunk (1 Sam. 25:36–37), did not wish to rebuke him for his fault of obstinacy; but once the wine had passed, she usefully struck him with the words of her rebuke. And the Prophet announces that the tongues of flatterers should not be postponed to a later time, saying: “Let them be immediately confounded who say to me, ‘Well done, well done’” (Ps. 69:4).

*[Note: Longip. reads “to be deferred.”]*

For if flattery is patiently received even for a time, it increases, and for a little while soothes the mind, causing it to soften from the firmness of its rectitude in the pleasure of speech. But lest it grow, it must be struck immediately and without delay.

15. We must also consider how we speak. For often words that recall one person to salvation wound another. Hence the apostle Paul, who admonishes Titus, saying, “Rebuke with all authority” (Titus 2:15), exhorts Timothy, saying: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and doctrine” (2 Tim. 4:2).
