*[Note: This is the reading of C. Germ., Norm., Longip., and nearly all the manuscripts, whereas the printed editions have “with all patience.”]*

What does it mean that he commands authority for one and patience for another, except that he perceived one to be of a gentler spirit and the other of a more fervent one? Severity of speech had to be imposed upon the gentle person through the authority of command; but the one who burned in spirit had to be tempered through patience, lest, if he became more fervent than was right, he should not bring a wounded person back to salvation but wound one who was sound.

*[Note: C. Germ. reads “and for the other”; Norm. reads “and for the second.”]*

16. We must also take care how much we speak, lest, if we draw out the word of exhortation or rebuke too long for one who cannot bear much, we bring our hearer to weariness. Hence that outstanding preacher says to the Hebrews: “I beseech you, brothers, bear with the word of consolation, for I have written to you very briefly” (Heb. 13:22).

*[Note: Germ., followed by the printed editions—with the exception of Gussanv.—reads “through the word.”]*

This is especially suitable for the weak: they should hear only a few things, things they are able to grasp, but things that prick their minds toward the pain of repentance. For if the word of exhortation is spoken to them at one time in many forms, because they cannot retain much, they lose everything at once. Hence bodily physicians spread upon weak stomachs the coverings they apply with suitable medicine, but they apply them thinly, lest, if they are filled with too much medicine, they should not strengthen the stomach’s weakness but burden and overwhelm it.

17. Yet we should know that even if speech sometimes exceeds its proper measure in length, this is not dangerous for the hearers. But if care is not taken to observe how something should be said and to whom it should be said, that is exceedingly dangerous. For bashful minds, if perhaps they have committed some faults, should be rebuked gently, because if they are rebuked too harshly, they are broken rather than corrected. But harsh and shameless minds, if they are rebuked gently, are provoked by that very gentleness toward greater faults.

*[Note: Suess. reads “foolish.”]*

18. We learn this well from that same outstanding preacher. When he knew that the Corinthians had been divided into schism through partiality toward persons, he took care of their bashfulness and began his address

*[Note: Norm. manuscripts read “into schisms.” Paul’s epistle seems to support this, where 1 Cor. 1:10 reads, “that there be no schisms among you,” a verse cited below.]*

to them with thanksgiving and praise, saying: to them with thanksgiving and praise, saying: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been made rich in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you” (1 Cor. 1:4–6).

He adds further: “So that you lack nothing in any grace, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 7).

*[Note: Gussanv. corruptly reads “in one grace.”]*

I ask you, Paul: if nothing is lacking in them, why do you weary yourself by writing to them? Why do you speak while far away? Let us consider, therefore, dearest brothers, how greatly he praises them.

*[Note: Val. Cl. reads “how much he praises them”; “them” is absent from C. Germ. and from the other older manuscripts.]*

Behold, he asserts that the grace of God has been given to them; he says that they have been made rich in everything, in every word and in all knowledge; he declares that Christ’s testimony—that is, the testimony he gave concerning himself by dying and rising again—has been confirmed in their life; and he testifies that they lack nothing in any grace. Who, I ask, would believe that shortly afterward he would rebuke those whom he praises in this way?

For after the rest he adds: “I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you” (ibid., 10).

What schism could have crept in among people so perfect and so praiseworthy?

*[Note: Norm., Longip., Val. Cl. read “to steal upon” or “to creep in”; this reading is absent from Germ.]*

“For it has been reported to me about you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you. I mean this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ ‘I to Cephas,’ ‘I to Christ’” (ibid., 11–12).

Behold: those whom he had praised for being rich in every word and in all knowledge, of whom he had said that they lacked nothing in any grace—speaking for a little while, and coming gently to rebuke—he reproves as divided among themselves, and he reveals the wounds of those whose salvation he had first described.

For a skilled physician, seeing that a wound must be cut but perceiving that the patient is timid, strokes him for a long time and then suddenly strikes. First he laid upon them the soothing hand of praise, and afterward he fixed in them the sword of rebuke. For unless bashful minds are reproved by being gently touched, so that they hear in other matters something they can take as consolation, they immediately fall into despair through rebuke.

*[Note: The printed editions read “first with a gentle hand of praise.” We adhere to the manuscripts, whose agreement here is remarkable.]*

19. But did Paul lie when he first said that they lacked nothing in any grace, although afterward he would say that they lacked unity? Far be it from us to think so. Who, even in folly, would believe such things about him? Rather, because among the Corinthians there were some filled with every grace, while others had been cut off through favor toward particular persons, he began with praise of the perfect, in order to reach, through a restrained attack, the rebuke of the weak. In this too he drew an analogy for the medicine of the heart from the medicine of the body.

For when a physician sees a wound that must be struck, he first touches the healthy limbs around the wound, so that afterward he may reach the injured parts by gently touching them.

*[Note: Lyranus omits “limbs.”]*

*[Note: Gussanv. corruptly reads “the wounds.”]*

Thus, when Paul praised the perfect among the Corinthians, he touched the healthy limbs beside the wound; but when he rebuked the weak for their division, he struck the wound in the body.

20. Let us nevertheless observe how this same man, who approaches the rebuke of the Corinthians with such modesty and gentleness, deals with the Galatians, who had departed from the faith.

*[Note: This is the reading of C. Germ., Longip., Val. Cl., Ebroic., and many manuscripts of Norm. In Becc. and Rothomag., supported by the printed editions, the reading is “he raises himself” or “he should raise himself.”]*

No patience of modesty was first offered, and no sweetness of speech was placed beforehand. From the very beginning of his letter he attacks and rebukes those whom he knew to have departed from the faith. After the salutation, he began in this way: “I am astonished that you are transferring yourselves so quickly from him who called you in the grace of Christ” (Gal. 1:6). After other words, he addresses them in open rebuke: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (ibid. 3:1).

For hard minds, unless they are struck by open rebuke, would in no way recognize the evil they had committed. For often the shameless feel that they have sinned only as much as they are rebuked for their sins, so that they judge their lesser faults to be those which are chastised with lesser attack, and recognize as greater those for which they see themselves vehemently reproved.

*[Note: Suess. reads “foolish.”]*

*[Note: Sag. reads “when they are rebuked for their sins.”]*

Therefore the preacher’s speech must always be shaped according to the character of his hearers, lest he speak harshly to the bashful or gently to the shameless. But what is surprising if the dispenser of God’s word does this, when even the farmer who casts seed into the earth first considers the quality of the soil, judging which seeds it appears suited for, and after foreseeing its quality then scatters the seed?

*[Note: The printed editions read: “after he has observed the quality of the earth, he scatters it.”]*

But because we have prolonged our discussion of the quality of teaching, we ought to return to the order of exposition with which we began.

**VERSE 20. — “But if the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling block before him; he shall die, because you did not announce it to him. He shall die in his sin, and his righteousnesses that he performed shall not be remembered; but I will require his blood from your hand.”**

21. Because the preacher was silent when the righteous man fell into sin, he is held guilty of his blood. And the one who did not take care to be vigilant in preaching has become a participant in condemnation.

But when it says, “He shall die in his sin, and his righteousnesses that he performed shall not be remembered,” we must consider this above all: when we commit evil, we recall our past good deeds to memory without reason, because in the commission of evil there ought to be no confidence in past good works.

*[Note: On penitence, Distinction 4, chapter “Hoc nobis,” and Book IV of the Sentences, Distinction 5.]*

It may be asked whether the righteous man should be preached to after he has fallen, or even before he falls. The preacher ought certainly to keep watch so that he does not come to a fall, and therefore before he falls.

*[Note: Longip. reads “for the preacher ought to keep watch.”]*

For it follows:

**VERSE 21. — “But if you announce to the righteous man that the righteous man should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you announced it to him; but you have delivered your soul.”**

22. If, then, the preacher delivered his soul because he warned the righteous man not to sin, when the righteous man falls into sin while the preacher is silent, the preacher is held guilty because he was silent. But who among us, I ask, is sufficient for this—to rebuke sinners diligently and also to watch over the righteous so that they do not fall?

We, conscious of our weakness, when we see righteous men, do not presume to admonish them to remain on the way of righteousness, because we see that they are already walking in it. Yet it is the preacher’s duty also to admonish the righteous. Hence the outstanding preacher said: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1:14).

23. In all that has been said about the righteous man who turns to iniquity, there is one point that is difficult to discuss and greatly to be feared: the Lord says, “I will place a stumbling block before him.” For he says: “If the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling block before him.”

We say that if he commits iniquity, he stumbles, and what we say is altogether true. Why, then, does Almighty God still place a stumbling block before one whom he sees already to have stumbled and fallen through the iniquity he committed?

*[Note: C. Germ., Suess., and some Norm. manuscripts read, better than the printed editions, “already to have acted wickedly.” Certainly “to stumble” agrees with “to fall”; and below it is said, “that he may stumble more grievously.” We set aside here the question of the stumbling block against which one stumbles.]*

But the judgments of Almighty God are strict. The one who waits a long time for the sinner to return places before the one who does not return but despises him something over which he may stumble more grievously.

24. A sin that is not quickly removed through repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin, or simultaneously sin, the cause of sin, and the punishment of sin. Everything that is first committed is sin. But if it is not quickly cleansed through repentance, Almighty God, in just judgment, permits the sinner’s bound mind to fall into another fault, so that what it refused to correct by mourning and amending, it may begin to heap sin upon sin.

*[Note: The printed editions read “bound by sins,” but all the manuscripts reject this.]*

*[Note: Suess., followed by the printed editions, reads “to cleanse”; we follow the more authoritative codices.]*

The sin, therefore, that is not washed away by the lament of repentance is at once sin and the cause of sin, because from it arises that by which the sinner’s mind is bound still more deeply. But the sin that follows from sin is at once sin and the punishment of sin, because, as blindness increases, it is generated as a retribution for the earlier fault, so that the very growth of vices becomes, as it were, a punishment in the sinner.

Sometimes, however, one and the same sin is simultaneously sin, the punishment of sin, and the cause of sin. Let us place before our eyes someone who desired his neighbor’s property. Since he could not openly obtain it, he seized it by theft; but when accused of theft, he denied under oath that he had stolen it.

For this man, desire was sin and the cause of sin, because through it he came to robbery. The theft itself, by which he seized the object he desired, became for him both sin and the punishment of sin, because, as a retribution for desire that had not been restrained, he came to theft, and the fault of his heart grew into action as a punishment for his blindness.

*[Note: Gussanv., in a very serious error, reads “to the future.”]*

*[Note: Val. Cl. reads “from fault.”]*

But because he took care to cover the theft with perjury, from sin he generated sin once more. The theft, therefore, which proceeded from desire and produced perjury, became both sin and the punishment of sin in relation to the preceding fault, and sin and the cause of sin in relation to the subsequent fault, because, born from the former, it gave birth to the latter.

Paul expressed this well concerning certain people who understood God but did not honor him, saying: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21). Behold, there is sin and the cause of sin. He adds what followed from that cause: “And their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (ibid., 22–23).

*[Note: C. Germ. and the printed editions before Gussanv. read: “Behold, it is sin alone, and it would be the punishment of sin if another sin did not still follow from this sin.” This reading seems corrupt. For how can it be sin alone when it is also the punishment and cause of sin? We follow Cod. Norm., Anglic., and several others.]*

Behold, there is sin and the punishment of sin. But it would be only sin and the punishment of sin if another sin did not still follow from this sin. For after their unbelief it is added: “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonored their bodies among themselves” (ibid., 24).

Thus, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God; from that sin and cause of sin they were led also to fall into the worship of serpents and birds. But because through this blindness they also fell into impurity and the dishonoring of the flesh, the blindness of their unbelief was sin and the punishment of sin in relation to the understanding that preceded it, but became sin and the cause of sin in relation to the impurity that followed.

But because these matters have been treated at length in the Moral Books (Book 25 of the Moralia, sections 23–24), we must not dwell on them at greater length here.

25. We must consider with trembling how the just and almighty God, when he is angered by preceding sins, permits the blinded mind to fall into still other sins. Hence Moses says: “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed” (Gen. 15:16). David also says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Ps. 69:28). Another prophet says: “Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2).

For blood touches blood when sin is added to sin, so that, as iniquities are joined together before God’s eyes, the soul is stained with blood. The apostle Paul says: “That they may always complete their sins” (1 Thess. 2:16). It is also said to John through the angel: “Let the one who does harm do harm still; and let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Rev. 22:11).

Hence the Lord now also says: “If the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling block before him.” It is as though he openly said: Because he refused to see through repentance where he had already stumbled, I will justly abandon him and place before him something over which he may stumble elsewhere as well.

Yet the Lord’s “placing” does not mean pressing anyone to sin, but refusing to free him from sin, just as it is said concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exod. 7:3). The Lord does not harden the heart of the sinner; he is said to harden it when he does not free it from hardness.

For the merciful God grants us time for repentance. But when we turn the patience of his grace toward increasing our guilt, he turns the very time that he mercifully ordained for sparing us into a stricter means of striking us. Thus, when someone refuses to return even after receiving a period of time, he increases his evil and his guilt through the very means by which he could have washed it away, had he wished to turn back.

Hence it is written: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Rom. 2:4–5).

The reprobate, therefore, stores up wrath for himself from the kindness of Almighty God on the day of wrath, because while time is given for repentance, it is also made available for sinning, and he turns the remedy of grace itself into an increase of guilt. Thus Almighty God, seeing that the remedies he has granted are being drawn toward the increase of guilt, turns the very kindness he bestowed into the strictness of judgment, so that he may strike more severely from the place where he now waits more patiently.

And because a person does not wish to abandon evil in order to live, he increases that by which he will die. But whether the righteous falls into guilt or the sinner into death, the watchman must fear lest the guilt of those who sin involve him equally because of his silence.

26. Meanwhile, as I speak, I wish to turn my eyes away from myself, and behold, once again the divine word makes me stumble against myself, so that I may see my negligence and fear that these things I hear are being said to me.

For, as I said above (section 6), how can a heart that has scattered itself among countless cares gather itself back into itself?

*[Note: Longip. reads “spread out”; Val. Cl. reads “how can it gather itself back to itself when it has been scattered?”]*

When can I both care attentively for all the things around me and behold myself with an undivided mind? When can I correct the wicked by pursuing their evil deeds, and preserve the actions of the good by praising and admonishing them? When can I show terror to some and sweetness to others? When can I both think about what my brothers need and remain concerned for the city’s defenses against hostile swords, providing that the citizens do not perish in a sudden attack, and amid all these matters fully and effectively offer the word of exhortation for the protection of souls?

To speak about God belongs to a mind that is very peaceful and free. For the tongue is directed well in speech when the understanding has rested securely in tranquility. Even troubled water does not reflect the image of the one looking into it; the face of the person gazing into it is seen only when the water is still.

What exhortation, then, can your watchman, dearest brothers, give you, when he is disturbed by the confusion of so many matters?

Certainly, the prophet of whom we are speaking, seeing the temple in his final vision, recounts among other things what he saw in that temple, saying: “The ground reached up to the windows, and the windows were closed” (Ezek. 41:16). The apostle Paul also says: “For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17; 2 Cor. 6:16).

In this temple, the windows are the priests and watchmen, who pour out the light of holy preaching among the faithful. But when the ground reaches up to the windows, the windows are closed, because when earthly thought grows in the hearts of priests, the windows do not pour out light: the priests fall silent, withdrawing from the duty of preaching.

### 27

There is also another matter that is exceedingly burdensome in the order of priests: unlike those who lead a quiet and secluded life, they cannot remain fixed in one line of thought. For those who are far removed from the place of governance, as we said above, can wash away the stains of their sins with tears and, after their tears, continue in the same sorrow of heart—as is also written of the good woman who prayed at the tabernacle and did not change the intention of her heart after receiving the grace of compunction: “And her countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Sam. 1:18). [Note: All printed editions read “the faults of their sins,” although all the manuscripts read “the stains of their sins.”]

In her case we must consider this: if the woman who was seeking a son wept in such a way, how ought the soul that seeks God to weep?

A priest, however, even after compunction and tears, is compelled to learn whatever necessities concern his children, [Note: The printed editions read “necessary things also”; our reading is that of the German, Norman, Suess., Longip., and Val. Cl. manuscripts.] and patiently to hear those things from which his heart recoils; [Note: The printed editions read “which the mind recoils from,” against these same manuscripts.] after sighing for heavenly things, he must bear the burdens of all sorts of carnal people, and often, when people arrive, pour out his heart into different dispositions. [Col. 0918A–B] [Note: The German manuscript reads “into different qualities.”]

Sometimes he rejoices over spiritual gains, but when someone sorrowful arrives, unless he takes that person’s sorrow upon himself, he does not sympathize with the other’s tribulation. At other times he grieves over the losses of souls, and suddenly people arrive who rejoice over some of their own prosperity. If the priest does not rejoice with their joy, he is thought to love less the children whose happiness does not make him rejoice—especially since Paul says: “To rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15).

### 28

I therefore see nothing so burdensome for the priestly order as bending the mind’s rigidity through compassion and changing one’s disposition according to the people who arrive; [Note: Some read, “nothing so burdensome in the order,” as in the printed editions.] yet this is exceedingly necessary. For when, through his preaching, a sinner is brought back to the grace of good works, does the preacher himself appear ungrateful?

Hence, too, the same prophet says at the end:

> “And when the priests minister within, they shall not wear woolen garments” (Ezek. 44:17). [Note: The Norman manuscripts read, “when the priests minister within.”]

Concerning these it is added:

> “And when they go out to the outer court toward the people, they shall remove the garments in which they had ministered and shall put them in the treasury of the sanctuary” (Exod. 28:43; Ezek. 44:19). [Note: Becc. and some Norman manuscripts read “they shall take off their garments”; Val. Cl. reads “let them divest themselves of their garments.” We follow the German and older manuscripts.]

Woolen garments are, of course, the coarser garments. But when a priest approaches the holy ministry—when he enters inwardly through compunction— [Note: The printed editions read “approaches, that is, when”; “that is” is absent from the German, Norman, and other manuscripts.] he must, as it were, be clothed in a finer, linen garment. When he goes out among the people, however, he ought to put away the garments in which he had ministered within and appear before the people dressed in other garments. For if he remains in the severity of his compunction, if he persists in the sorrow he had during prayer, he does not permit himself to receive words concerning external matters. And what should the flock do about its necessities if the shepherd refuses to hear and consider even what the present moment requires?

Therefore, when he goes out before the people, let the priest put on the coarser garments, so that, for the benefit of his children, he may shape the disposition of his mind even to endure earthly matters. [Col. 0918C–D] [Note: The printed editions read “therefore”; the reading “I ask” is found elsewhere.]

Consider, I ask, most beloved brothers, how great is the labor of a watchman: to raise his heart to the heights and then suddenly bring it back down; to refine the mind amid the sublimity of inward knowledge and, because of the external circumstances of his neighbors, suddenly—as I may put it—become coarser in his thinking. [Col. 0919A] [Note: Some printed editions read “to advance”; others “to become gross,” and others “to become coarse.” We follow “to become coarse,” found in Gilot’s and the Vatican edition, because it agrees with the German and better manuscripts.]

### 29

It is not necessary for me merely to explain the prophet’s words; I must also bewail my own misery before you. Therefore I ask that your prayer make me such a person as may be able to benefit both myself and you. He is able, through your intercession, to grant these things to me, unworthy and weak as I am—the one who, in his own mercy, deigned to become weak for us. [Col. 0919B]

“For Jesus Christ our Lord is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24), who took upon himself our weakness in order to strengthen us by his own strength, and who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY XII

The remainder of chapter 3 is expounded, and the explanation is carried through to verse 4 of chapter 4; the discussion is turned toward various moral precepts and counsels for preachers and hearers.

### 1

While preserving the truth of the historical account, the divine utterances sometimes indicate causes by reference to time and sometimes by reference to place—causes that they do not disclose in explicit speech.

They indicate a cause by reference to time when, for example, the Evangelist says of the Lord as he preached to the Jews: “It was winter” (John 10:22). Among the mysteries that the Truth was proclaiming, what reason was there for adding the name of winter except to show the coldness of their hearts through the character of the season? For although they received the words of truth, the hearts of the Jews remained cold.

At other times Scripture indicates a cause by reference to place. Thus, when Moses came down from the mountain, the law was given to the carnal Israelite people in the plains (Exod. 20 ff.); whereas, seated on the mountain, the Lord spoke lofty and spiritual commandments to the holy apostles (Matt. 5:1). In this way the places showed that to the former, as carnal people, lesser commandments were given in the valley of the earth, while the latter, as spiritual and holy people, heard heavenly commandments on the mountain. It was thereby plainly shown that those who ascend in heart to heavenly things leave behind the lowest things of the world and stand upon the summit of the mind.

Thus the prophet Ezekiel now describes what he did in the places commanded by God, so that through the character of the places he might indicate what would subsequently follow from the mysteries of the prophecy. [Col. 0919C–D] [Note: C. Germ., Suess., Norm., and Val. Cl., with minor alterations in the printed editions, read: “describes, at God’s command, in what places he performed these things.”] For he says:

> **Verse 22.** “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he said to me: Arise, go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you.”

### 2

What does it mean that the Lord had first spoken to his prophet in the midst of the Israelites, and yet afterward says, “Go out into the plain, and there I will speak with you,” except that he first deigned to pour the grace of his prophecy into Judea and afterward to reveal it in the breadth of the nations?

For the plain is not without reason understood as the Gentiles, since they are spread far and wide—that is, throughout the whole world. And it is added:

> **Verse 23.** “And I arose and went out into the plain, and behold, there the glory of the Lord stood, like the glory that I had seen beside the river Chebar.” [Col. 0920A] [Note: The word “there” is absent from most Norman manuscripts.]

### 3

In the plain the prophet saw the glory of the Lord that he had seen beside the river Chebar in the midst of the Israelites, because that same majesty of his appeared to the Gentiles which, through the revelation of the Spirit, had previously declared itself to the chosen people in Judah. [Note: Suess. reads: “because through it his own majesty appeared.”]

The text continues:

> **The same passage.** “And I fell upon my face.” [Col. 0920B]

### 4

When the prophet sees the glory of the Lord, he falls upon his face, because although a human being is raised to understand sublime things, nevertheless, through contemplating God’s majesty, he recognizes the weakness of his own condition. He is, as it were, without a standing position when he sees himself to be ashes and dust before the eyes of God. [Note: Suess. reads: “in the presence of his majesty.”]

The text continues:

> **Verse 24.** “And the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet.”

### 5

When we humbly prostrate ourselves before God, when we recognize that we are dust and ashes, when, weighing the weakness of our own condition, we no longer possess the posture of rigidity and pride, almighty God raises us through his Spirit and sets us upon our feet. Thus we who have lain and lie humbly within ourselves through considering our weakness may stand upright in a good work, as though upon our feet. [Col. 0920C] [Note: Longip. reads: “we are prostrate.”] [Note: Suess. and Val. Cl. read: “through knowledge.”]

Why is this done to the prophet in the plain except to show specifically that the Holy Spirit would also be given to the chosen among the Gentiles? He would first cast down those whom he assumed from the position of their pride and afterward establish them upon their feet—that is, upon good works. As Paul says:

> “Lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12:12).

The text continues:

> **The same passage.** “And he spoke to me and said to me: Enter and shut yourself within the midst of your house.”

### 6

What does it mean that the prophet is led out from the midst of the Israelite people into the plain and afterward recalled from the plain to the house, except that the grace of preaching was taken away from the Jewish people and scattered across the breadth of the Gentiles?

Yet at the end of the world, when the Jews return to the faith, the prophet is, as it were, brought back to the house, so that preaching may again dwell among his own people—preaching that now shines like a light in the plain among the various nations. For it is written:

> “Until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

And another prophet says:

> “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. 10:22; Rom. 9:27).

[Note: The Sagiensis manuscript reads: “What does it mean that the prophet is led out from the midst of the Israelite people into the plain?”]

Let the prophet therefore go out from the midst of the people into the plain, and let him return from the plain to the house, so that the preaching given to Judea may go out to the Gentiles and, when the Gentiles have been filled with faith, spiritual teaching may return to Judea, which had lost its gifts. [Col. 0921A]

The prophet is commanded to be shut within the midst of his house because, in the time of Antichrist, the people of the Jews, having been converted, will be hemmed in by harsh persecutions from those Gentiles who have remained in unbelief. Hence it is written:

> “But the court that is outside the temple, cast out and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles, and they will trample upon the holy city for forty-two months” (Rev. 11:2).

> **Verses 25–26.** “And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you will not go out into their midst; and I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you will be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an embittering house.” [Col. 0921B]

### 7

If we follow these words according to the order of a typological interpretation, the prophet receives bonds and is bound in his house because, at the end of the age, when Judea has believed, he will experience the most severe persecutions in the time of Antichrist. The ministers of wickedness will not accept his preaching; rather, by resisting it, they will oppress it with bonds of suffering.

He does not go out into their midst because preaching does not reach the hearts of the wicked while the tongue of the good is silenced by tribulations. At that time there will be many unbelieving Jews who persecute those very people who have believed from among the Jews.

It should therefore be noted that the prophet is also said here to endure bonds in his own house, so that it may be shown that Judea, even when it has become faithful, will bear the tribulation of persecution from its own people. For as long as it is not believed that the Only-Begotten of the Most High Father, having become incarnate and died, rose again and ascended into heaven—as is proclaimed throughout the pages of Holy Scripture—prophecy will certainly be bound among the Jews. If it were to proceed into their understanding as it was spoken, it would, as it were, possess free steps for its preaching. [Col. 0921C]

### 8

At that time, therefore, the knowledge of preachers is compelled to be silent before the reprobate. Hence it is added here:

> “And I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you will be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an embittering house.”

But because, when Enoch and Elijah preach, many of those who will then have remained in unbelief among the Jews will return to knowledge of the truth—as it is said of Elijah himself, “Elijah will come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. 17:11; Mark 9:12; Mal. 4:5)—and because both are called “two olive trees” through Zechariah (Zech. 4:3) and “two lampstands” through John (Rev. 11:4), it is rightly added here:

> **Verse 27.** “But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God.” [Col. 0921D] [Note: Becc. and Rothomag. read: “you shall open your mouth.”]

### 9

Then, as it were, the prophet’s mouth is opened at the end, when, through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, it is recognized by the Jews who return to the faith that the prophecy of sacred speech concerned Christ. [Col. 0922A]

But since we have discussed these matters typologically, let us now interpret the same words morally for your charity.

### 10

What does it mean that the prophet is commanded to go out into the plain except that every preacher, because of those whom he corrects and restrains from iniquity—those placed outside himself—goes out into the plain by speaking?

There he sees the glory of the Lord, because he receives the grace of teaching more abundantly the more he extends himself in the labor of preaching out of love for his neighbors.

By going outside, he is led into a lofty vision, because from the very place where, through the ministry of his speech, he illuminates the blindness of ignorance in other people’s hearts, heavenly grace raises him to a higher understanding. [Note: Suess. and Norm. read: “in the height of vision”; Val. Cl. reads: “in the height of the vision.”] [Col. 0922B]

But because a preacher must always return to his own mind and preserve humility and purity within, after the plain he must return to the house, so that within his conscience he may recognize what sort of person he himself is in the matters he says.

For if he does not practice what he says, or if he seeks temporal glory from the things he preaches, he goes out into the plain by speaking, but, by failing to think of himself, he refuses to return to the house.

When we receive the Spirit, we are shut within the midst of the house, because through his grace we are recalled to examine the hidden places of our mind, so that the soul may rest in God within itself and no longer wander through external desires, driven by the shifting movement of thought toward the pursuit of praise and glory. [Col. 0922C]

### 11

Concerning this house of the heart, the Truth itself says to a man who had been healed:

> “Take up your bed and go to your house” (John 5:8; Mark 2:9). [Col. 0922D] [Note: Ebroic. and the other Norman manuscripts read: “concerning this movement of the heart.” The German and older manuscripts read: “concerning this house of the heart, to one who had been healed.”]

The bed on which the flesh rests signifies the flesh itself; the house signifies the conscience. And because, when dead in mind through vices, we lie in the pleasure of the flesh and rest in carnal delight, we are carried as sick people upon a bed.

But when we have been healed in mind, so that we now resist the vices of the flesh when they knock, we must also endure in our flesh the insults of temptations. Thus the sick man who has been restored to health is commanded: “Take up your bed”—that is, carry the bed on which you were carried—because once healed, a person must carry the reproach of the flesh in which he formerly lay sick.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Take up your bed and go to your house,” except: Carry the temptations of the flesh in which you have hitherto lain, and return to your conscience, so that you may see what you have done?

The prophet is therefore commanded to be shut in the house after the plain, so that every preacher, after ministering the grace of teaching to his neighbors, may return to his conscience and examine himself by a subtle scrutiny, lest he inwardly seek for himself some passing praise from the things he preaches outwardly. [Col. 0923A]

### 12

Hence Solomon also says:

> “Drink water from your own cistern and flowing water from your own well. Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5:15). [Note: Most Norman and Longip. manuscripts add “your.”]

He says, “Possess them alone, and let strangers not share in you” (ibid. 5:16).

Yet the statements “Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets” and “Possess them alone, and let strangers not share in you” seem entirely contrary. For how can he possess the water of knowledge alone if he divides it in the streets? How are others not participants in his water if his springs flow outward?

When we preach to the people, we certainly divide water in the streets, because we spread the words of knowledge among the multitude of hearers. But when, with the help of divine grace, we guard ourselves inwardly and carefully watch lest the evil spirits—who are rightly strangers to us because they have lost the portion of blessedness—steal upon us through pride, we possess alone the waters that we divide in the streets, so that strangers do not share in them with us. [Col. 0923B]

These are the ones concerning whom it is written:

> “Strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my soul” (Ps. 53:5).

Therefore, the person who divides water in the streets and possesses it alone is the one who, through preaching to many, does not exalt himself in his thoughts through the desire for temporal glory. A person possesses what he teaches when he rejoices not that he is known, but that he is useful.

The prophet is therefore brought back from the plain to the house, so that the one who speaks from God, after going out by speaking for the benefit of his neighbors, may always be recalled in humility to examine the secrets of his heart. Hence it is added: [Col. 0923C]

> **Verse 25.** “And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you will not go out into their midst.”

### 13

When every preacher is brought back to the house of his conscience, bonds are placed upon him and he is bound in them, because the more thoroughly he examines himself in thought, the more clearly he recognizes how many weaknesses of mortality bind the soul of the just.

If Paul had not seen himself as bound, he would certainly not have said:

> “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). [Note: Longip. reads: “I have the desire.”]

The Psalmist says:

> “To hear the groaning of the prisoners and to release the children of those who have been slain” (Ps. 102:21).

And again:

> “Let the groaning of the prisoners come before you” (Ps. 79:11).

Often, when the soul desires to go out in order to contemplate the appearance of its Redeemer, when it sighs to participate in heavenly joys, it sees and groans over the bonds of its mortality by which it is still held bound in the present world.

This is why Jeremiah, contemplating the subtle judgment of almighty God, says:

> “He has built against me so that I cannot go out; he has made my fetter heavy” (Lam. 3:7).

We have fetters: the weakness and corruption of our mortality itself. But when tribulation and groaning are added to us, our fetters become heavier. [Col. 0924A]

Indeed, as long as the just person remains in this life, he hastens, by speaking good things, to benefit others. But when he sees hard minds and observes them occupied with disputes, he restrains the word of preaching. He does not go out into their midst because he becomes silent about the good things he could have spoken, as Paul says:

> “Do nothing through contention” (Phil. 2:3).

And again:

> “If anyone wants to be contentious, we have no such custom” (1 Cor. 11:16).

Hence it is appropriately added here:

> **Verse 26.** “And I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you will be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an embittering house.”

### 14

At other times, however, the Lord kindles the hearts of preachers with zeal against the tongues of those who resist, so that they do not remain silent but press down the words of deceivers with the words of truth. [Col. 0924B] [Note: Val. Cl. reads: “press down the words of truth.”]

Hence it is added here:

> **Verse 27.** “But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God.”

### 15

Let us pass lightly over these matters, which we have briefly examined according to a twofold understanding, touching upon them in accordance with the literal sense. [Col. 0924C] [Note: Another reading has: “gently touching upon them,” as that manuscript has together with Norm.]

For what is commended to us through the very words of the historical account more than the virtue of obedience? The prophet is commanded at one moment to go to the settlement beside the river Chebar, at another to go out into the plain, and at another to return from the plain to the house. First he goes at a command, shortly afterward he goes out, then again he returns home and shuts himself in, always breaking the judgment of his own will against the command of the divine utterance, so that, suspended upon the heavenly command, he may fulfill not his own will but that of his Creator.

To him it is said:

> “And you, son of man, behold, bonds have been placed upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you will not go out into their midst.”

Here we must note that the prophet foreknows the adversities, so that he may be prepared for everything. Evils have less power against the mind when they do not come unexpectedly. Yet, when adversities are foreknown, the greatness of the virtue of obedience is displayed in the one who knows that he will suffer adversity and nevertheless does not disobey the Lord’s voice. [Col. 0924D]

The words that immediately follow require careful consideration:

> “And I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you will be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an embittering house.”

We must discern whether the word of preaching is withdrawn only because of wicked hearers, or sometimes also because of a fault in the preacher. [Note: The Paris edition of 1518 omits “of the preacher.” Gussanv. reads “because of the fault of preaching.”]

### 16

This matter is distinguished by four conditions. [Col. 0925A] [Note: The German manuscript reads, “Therefore, by four conditions.”]

Sometimes, because of wicked hearers, the word is taken away from good teachers. Sometimes, because of good hearers, the word is given even to wicked teachers. Sometimes, because of the justification of both teachers and hearers, the word is given to good teachers, so that they themselves may grow in merit and their hearers may progress in understanding and life. Sometimes, because neither those to whom the word of instruction is offered are worthy to receive it, nor those who occupy the place of teaching are worthy to offer it, the word of preaching is withdrawn, so that both parties may be judged strictly. [Note: The German manuscript reads: “because neither those to whom the word of instruction is spoken here are worthy to receive it, nor those who occupy the place of teaching there are worthy to offer the word of instruction.”]

Because of wicked hearers, the word is taken away from good teachers, as it is now said to Ezekiel:

> “I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you will be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is an embittering house.”

And as it is said to Paul:

> “Hurry and go quickly out of Jerusalem, because they will not receive your testimony about me” (Acts 22:18).

And when the apostles wished to preach in Asia, it is written that:

> “The Spirit of Jesus forbade them” (Acts 16:6).

Because of good hearers, the word is given even to wicked teachers, as the Lord says of the Pharisees:

> “Whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3).

Because of the merit of teachers and the justification of hearers, the word of instruction is granted, as it is said to the holy apostles:

> “Go and teach all nations” (ibid. 28:19).

But because of wicked hearers and the unworthy life of those who ought to have taught, the word of instruction is withdrawn. Thus Eli did not have a word of strict rebuke with which to correct his sons (1 Sam. 2:29; 3:13), [Note: Val. Cl. reads: “of instruction and rebuke.”] because both his negligence and the life of his sons demanded that, when the people fell with them, the ark of the Lord should pass to the Philistines (ibid. 4:11 ff.). [Col. 0925B]

Great indeed is the grace of almighty God when a harsh word of rebuke is spoken by teachers to those who act wickedly. In contrast, it is now said:

> “And you will be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes.”

He would have rebuked the delinquents if they had been worthy of the grace of rebuke.

### 17

But since there is such great diversity of merit in teaching and in silence that it cannot easily be known whether the word of teaching is withdrawn because of the fault of the hearer or because of the fault of the one who appears to occupy the place of teaching, what else are we commanded to preserve in doubtful matters except humility?

When we are able to speak, let us not become proud, lest perhaps this very grace of our speech has been granted not to us but to our hearers. And again, when we are unable to speak, let those entrusted to us not judge us too readily, lest perhaps we are unable to speak not because of our sin but because of the sin of those who hear.

All these things concerning our merits are therefore uncertain to us, so that we may hold fast to one certain grace: humility. Thus, when we speak, we may regard this as the gift of almighty God and as your merit. [Col. 0925C–D] [Note: Suess. reads, “that our merit comes from God’s gift.” The Paris edition of 1518 agrees. We follow the German, Norman, and English manuscripts, as well as the Gilot and Vatican editions. Gussanv. reads, “that this is God’s gift, not our merit”: sound in sense, but unknown in the manuscripts. Gussanv. also reads “that our merits are uncertain,” apparently through a printer’s error.]

And when we fall silent from the speech of teaching, although it may be our fault, you should nevertheless especially believe that it is your fault. Thus, when we assign evils to ourselves and good things to others, the grace of humility may cause the word of teaching that had been taken away to return. The text continues:

> **Verse 27.** “But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall speak to them: Thus says the Lord God: Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who rests rest, because it is an embittering house.”

### 18

Often some people desire to hear the word of God, but when they see others turning away their ear, they too turn aside from hearing what would bring salvation. [Note: Longip. and most Norman manuscripts read: “are led astray.”]

Very often many wish to remain quiet, to be free from all the activities of this world, and no longer to succumb to earthly desires. But when they see others prospering through restless activity and being exalted in this world by riches and honors, because they are not yet firm on the path of righteousness, they slide into evil deeds through the example of others. [Col. 0926A–B] [Note: The same manuscript as Val. Cl. reads: “they fall away.”]

This is why the Psalmist, speaking figuratively of the infirm, said:

> “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the prosperity of sinners” (Ps. 72:2–3).

Again he says:

> “When the wicked man is proud, the poor man is set ablaze” (Ps. 10:2).

And concerning Judah and Israel, the Lord’s voice says to the prophet Jeremiah:

> “Have you not seen what faithless Israel has done? She went up for herself upon every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there she committed fornication. And I said, after she had done all these things: Return to me—and she did not return” (Jer. 3:6–7). [Note: Longip. reads: “Have you not seen?”]

There it is immediately added how Judah also fell through rivalry with Israel, although she had seemed to stand. For he says:

> “And her treacherous sister Judah saw that, because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her and given her a bill of divorce; yet treacherous Judah, her sister, did not fear, but went and also committed fornication herself” (ibid. 3:8). [Note: Suess. reads: “the sinful woman.”] [Note: Vatic. and Gussanv. add: “and she went.”]

Behold, the merciful God is despised and yet calls; he opens the bosom of mercy to those who turn away, for he says to the sinner:

> “Return to me”—and yet she did not return (ibid. 3:7). [Note: Longip. reads: “and he calls her back.” This is not supported by the German or the other manuscripts.] [Note: Longip., Ebroic., and Sag. have a corrupted reading, followed by the Paris edition of 1518: “to those opposing.” Gussanv. is more corrupt, reading “sign” instead of “bosom,” and shortly afterward “of sinning” instead of “to the sinner.”]

But because the Israelite people abandoned almighty God and refused to return, they received a bill of divorce. They abandoned him through sinning, but received a bill of divorce by remaining in their iniquities without punishment.

The soul that sins departs. But if prosperity follows it after sin, and no discipline or rebuke of strictness recalls it to its heart, then, in the division it has made between itself and the Lord, it also receives a bill of divorce. Abandoned like a stranger, it does the evils it wishes and does not feel the scourges of God’s zeal, so that it may descend more deeply into eternal punishments. [Note: Longip. reads: “to discretion.”]

But her sister Judah, when she saw the Israelite people dismissed and indulging in their pleasures, likewise burned with the uncleanness of fornication. Because she saw the adulteress flourishing in her perversity, she too did not fear to sin more grievously and to depart from union with the Lord, as from the bed of a lawful husband.

It is therefore necessary for us to regard sinners as especially wretched when we see them abandoned in their guilt without punishment. Hence Solomon says:

> “The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32).

Whoever turns away from God and prospers becomes that much nearer to destruction, because he is found that much farther from the zeal of discipline.

Let it therefore be said:

> “Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who rests rest, because it is an embittering house.”

As though it were said openly: You who have already begun both to hear the words of truth and to rest from evil action, do not imitate those whose conduct you see provoking me. [Note: Val. Cl. reads: “to cease.”]

### 19

We can also understand this in another way.

Some hear the word without hearing it, because they place their ear beside sacred speech but do not tear their heart away from the desires of the world. There are also some who remain outwardly at rest but are not truly at rest, because although their bodies are free from evil deeds, they turn over the perversions of evil works in their minds through affection for them. [Col. 0927A–B] [Note: The printed editions read differently: “through delight.” Our reading is supported by the German, Suess., Longip., and Val. Cl. manuscripts. These two words are often confused in the manuscripts.]

Hence it is written concerning Judea when she was led into captivity:

> “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7).

Enemies mock the Sabbaths when evil spirits inject wicked thoughts into a mind at rest, so that, although the person rests from action, he does not rest from delight in evil actions.

It is therefore rightly said here:

> “Let the one who hears hear,”

so that the word may be in the ear of the body in such a way that it sounds in the ear of the heart.

And:

> “Let the one who rests rest,”

so that desires for wickedness may be driven from thought when they already appear to have been driven from action.

Lest we follow the examples of the wicked, as we have said, it is added:

> “Because it is an embittering house.” [Col. 0927C–D] [Note: The printed editions wrongly read “may they follow,” against the manuscripts.]

Although the wicked may be tolerated for a long time, they suddenly fall, and the weak see their punishments, so that those whose guilt they had considered unpunished may not imitate them.

Hence the desolation of the same Judea is also added here. She is called an embittering house when the Lord immediately says to his prophet:

> **Ezekiel 4:1–3.** “And you, son of man, take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem. Then arrange a siege against it, build fortifications, heap up a mound, set camps against it, and place battering rams around it. And you, take an iron griddle for yourself and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city; set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege, and you shall surround it. It is a sign of the house of Israel.” [Col. 0927D–0928A] [Note: Vaticanus and Gussanv. read: “and place it upon the wall.” Below they have “you shall place.”] [Note: Many printed editions read “to the house” here and below, against the manuscripts.]

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]

20. What else, then, is designated in these words according to the historical sense except the siege and destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and what else is expressed except the affliction of the sinful people? It is called an exasperating house when it is said plainly: “You shall arrange a siege against it, build siegeworks, heap up a ramp, establish camps against it, and set battering rams around it.” But because the words of prophecy generally narrate historical events in such a way that through them mystical realities also are described [Note: [Col. 0928D] C. German. reads, “all mystical realities as well.”], we ought to expound spiritually these same statements that we have quoted—especially since they contain something that does not seem capable of being understood literally, where it says: “Take an iron pan for yourself, place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city, set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege.” For unless mystical meanings were mingled with historical events, why would the prophet have needed an iron pan, to place it between himself and the city so that he might separate himself from its siege? When it says, “Take an iron pan for yourself and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city,” it is plainly declared that through that same iron pan the prophet makes himself free from the siege of the city. Hence what was foretold is immediately added: “And you shall set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege.” From this it is shown that the prophet will not be within that siege if he places an iron wall—the pan—between himself and the city. Yet whether in the captivity that occurred earlier or in that which later befell the Israelite people, no one was free from the danger of that captivity; rather, the same calamity enveloped everyone together. What, then, can be understood according to the literal sense, such that the prophet places an iron pan between himself and the city that is to be besieged? But although everything that is read in the description of the brick under the sign of the city of Jerusalem was literally done [Note: [Col. 0928D] Gussanville omits “was done.”], we must nevertheless recognize that something typological is signified by the pan, and that the siege of Jerusalem is truly being described.

21. From this we are instructed that, while we know that one thing has been fulfilled according to the historical sense [Note: [Col. 0928D] This reading is found unanimously in the English, Norman, C. German, Longipontanus, Suessionian, and other manuscripts. The editors changed “history” to “allegory”; thus they read, “and another according to allegory.” Perhaps the sense of these words was not evident to them; yet it is sufficiently clear. Indeed, if one read “according to allegory,” the passage would be deficient. For how is it contrary to reason, according to allegory, that something should be understood allegorically of a spiritual siege?], and recognize that another thing is lacking in rational coherence according to the historical sense, we should hold both meanings in the sacred word, so that we may believe both that the siege of Jerusalem, which literally took place afterward, was prefigured in the prophet’s words and actions, and that through this same siege another siege—that is, an interior one—is designated. In this siege we rightly ask what is signified by the iron pan, which is called an iron wall.

We already know that the siege by which the city of Jerusalem was destroyed has taken place; but let us now seek the other siege within, which occurs every day. By way of signification it is said of this: “And you, son of man, take a brick for yourself, place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem.”

22. But first we must inquire why the prophet Ezekiel, whenever he beholds sublime things or whenever he is commanded to perform some mystical action, is first called “son of man.” He is often lifted up to heavenly realities, and his mind is nourished by hidden and invisible things. It is therefore necessary that, amid the hidden things he penetrates, he should be called “son of man,” so that he may always recognize what he is and never become exalted because of the things to which he is led. For what does it mean that the prophet, lifted up to spiritual realities, is always addressed as “son of man,” except that he is made mindful of his own weakness? Thus, conscious of his frail condition, he ought not to become exalted in thought because of the greatness of his contemplation.

23. Since, as we have already said above, this same prophet represents the type of preachers or teachers, it is rightly said to him now: “Take a brick for yourself and place it before you.” For every teacher, when he receives some earthly hearer into the instruction of the heavenly word, takes up a brick. When he begins to tell him what the reward of the heavenly homeland is and what the vision of supernal peace is, he draws the city of Jerusalem upon the brick. He places it before himself because, with attentive mind, he considers the condition of the hearer—that is, he observes his progress or deficiency [Note: [Col. 0929D] The printed editions read “progress.” It is easy to change *v* into *f*, or vice versa. Thus, as Donatus observes in his commentary on Terence’s *Andria*, the ancients often wrote *Dafus* for *Davus*, *serfus* for *servus*, and *corfus* for *corvus*. By the same reasoning Fornerius, in Cassiodorus, *Variae* III.33, thinks that *Referendos curiae* should be *reverendos*, and that *provectae* should be read in the Etruscan Pandects instead of *profectae.]—and regulates the words of his preaching according to his understanding, so that the city of Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, may be drawn in the mind of the hearer.

Let it therefore be said: “Take a brick for yourself”—that is, the earthly heart of your neighbor. “And place it before you”—that is, so that you may guard his life and understanding with attentive mind. “And draw upon it the city of Jerusalem”—so that you may make known to him what the heavenly joys of the vision of peace are. Jerusalem is, as it were, already drawn upon the brick when an earthly mind begins truly to recognize the joys of that inner peace and to yearn to behold the glory of the heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 0929D] The English, Norman, German, and other manuscripts read this way; the editions have “as though the inner [peace].”]. The vision of peace is, as it were, drawn upon the earth when the mind that previously savored earthly things is already raised through love to contemplate the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

24. But as soon as the soul begins to love heavenly things, as soon as it has gathered itself with undivided attention toward the vision of inner peace, that ancient adversary who fell from heaven becomes envious, begins to lie in wait more intently, and applies sharper temptations than he was accustomed to do. Thus he often tests a resisting soul in a manner in which he had never tested it before, when he possessed it. Hence it is written: “My child, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1). Hence also the demoniac who is healed by the Lord is torn by the departing demon, as it is written: “Crying out and tearing him violently, he came out of him” (Mark 9:25). What does it mean that the ancient enemy, who had not torn the possessed man while possessing him, tore him as he departed, except that when he is expelled from the heart he often generates in it sharper temptations than he had previously aroused when he possessed it quietly?

Hence the Israelites also say to Moses and Aaron: “May the Lord see and judge, because you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and his servants, and you have given him a sword with which to kill us” (Exodus 5:21). In Moses and Aaron the Law and the Prophets are represented [Note: [Col. 0930D] The editions read *lex et prophetae figurati sunt*, against the manuscripts’ *lex et prophetae figuratae sunt*; the distinction is grammatical gender.]. And often the weak soul murmurs, as it were, against the sacred words, because after it has begun to hear and follow heavenly words, the adversity of the Egyptian king—that is, the temptation of the evil spirit—increases.

25. The teacher must therefore vigilantly make known to the progressing soul what temptations follow it, so that it may prepare itself cautiously against the snares of the evil spirit. Hence, after the city of Jerusalem has been drawn upon the brick, it is fittingly said now to the prophet: “And you shall arrange a siege against it, build siegeworks, and heap up a ramp.” For once the vision of peace has been drawn, it is necessary that the battles of temptations be announced to it. To reach those eternal joys of peace, it must undoubtedly endure here many struggles of tribulation. Of this it is rightly said: “You shall arrange a siege against it.”

The preacher arranges a siege against the soul to be instructed when, by forewarning it [Note: [Col. 0930D] Thus all our manuscripts, except C. German., which reads *cum praemonendum* (“when warning beforehand”), and Becc., which reads *cum praemuniendum* (“when fortifying beforehand”).], he indicates the ways in which vices oppose virtues: how lust strikes chastity; how anger disturbs the tranquility of the soul; how foolish joy weakens the mind’s strength; how excessive talk destroys the fortification of the heart; how envy kills charity; how pride undermines the citadel of humility; how deceit, after corrupting truth in speech, also corrupts it in understanding (*in cognitione*) [Note: [Col. 0930D] The reading *in cognitione* (“in understanding”) in some other editions seems better. But all the manuscripts we consulted resist it.], so that one who did not wish to say what he understood now does not even understand what he might say.

A siege is therefore arranged by the preacher when, through the words of holy admonition, he shows each virtue which vices lie in wait for and by what methods they do so. Against the Jerusalem that he draws upon the brick, the preacher builds siegeworks when he demonstrates how every evil approaches the mind in a fortified manner, so that vices may conceal themselves beneath the appearance of virtues. Thus, as we have often said, immoderate anger seeks to appear justice [Note: [Col. 0930D] Ebroicensis, Gemeticensis, Uticensis, and other Norman manuscripts read “immoderate.”]; the relaxation of discipline wishes to appear gentleness; stinginess calls itself thrift; and the disorderly squandering of possessions names itself benevolence. Siegeworks are, as it were, built against the mind when vices grow beneath the appearance of virtues and display themselves above in an image, though in action they always lie below.

26. It is further added: “And you shall heap up a ramp.” For to the extent that the mind begins to desire heavenly things, to that extent the evil spirits heap up earthly thoughts against it through their temptations. The prophet therefore heaps up a ramp when the holy preacher warns good minds how earthly desires usually creep in [Note: [Col. 0931D] Or, as the manuscripts have it, “steal in” or “secretly steal in.”].

And further it is added: “And you shall establish camps against it, and set battering rams around it.” The teacher, as it were, establishes camps against the soul when he reveals the gathered and united snares of evil spirits against it [Note: [Col. 0931D] Lyranensis reads “united ranks.”], so that they may sometimes tempt it not merely in one way, but through vices joined together [Note: [Col. 0931D] Longipontanus reads “not merely from one source.”].

27. For certain vices are close to one another, as though related by a kind of kinship: dissipation of spirit, appetite for food, and the uncleanness of lust; excessive talk, deceit, and perjury. From dissipation of spirit the mind is dragged toward gluttony, and when the belly is distended with food, the flesh is drawn toward lust, captured by pride. Again, deceit is generated from excessive talk, because it is very difficult for one who speaks much not also to lie; and often a lie is concealed by perjury, so that it may be covered before human judgments.

Pride likewise cannot exist at all without envy and empty glory. For every proud person envies others the honor that he himself desires. And when he has perhaps obtained it, he is lifted up into the exaltation of temporal glory, and rejoices that he possesses before others what he sees that they have been altogether unable to attain.

28. We must also know that often certain vices do not come to the mind all at once, but are substituted, so that one follows another in temptation. One comes directly before the face, while another presents itself from the side as a temptation, so that while the mind resists one, it is deceived and captured by the other. The very vices mentioned above often furtively substitute themselves for one another. Thus, sometimes, while we try to overcome anger within ourselves, gentleness occupies the mind more than is necessary, so that it fails to display the severity that ought to be shown toward sinners. Often, when we are displeased that heedless gentleness exists in us, zeal draws itself into fury and drags the mind captive beyond the bounds of patience.

Because, therefore, vices come against the mind mixed and united together, camps are rightly set forth in the preacher’s mouth against the Jerusalem that has been drawn. And because at times individual vices strike the understanding from different sides, battering rams are arranged around it. The preacher therefore sets battering rams around it when he carefully warns how gently lust strikes, how harshly impatience kills, how laboriously avarice inflames and destroys, and how arrogantly pride extinguishes. To place battering rams around it is therefore, by preaching, to show which swords of vice ordinarily strike the soul from every side.

29. It follows: “And you, take an iron pan for yourself [Note: [Col. 0931D] “For yourself” (*tibi*) was omitted in the earlier editions; we have restored it with the help of the manuscripts.], and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.” Since iron is a strong metal and food is fried in a pan, what is signified by the iron pan except the strong frying of spiritual zeal? Every spiritual zeal fries the teacher’s soul, because he is deeply distressed when he sees the weak abandoning eternal things and delighting in temporal ones. How well Paul had taken an iron pan when, tormented by zeal for souls, he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:20).

His own heart, which he had kindled with zeal for souls—what else had he made it than a pan, in which he burned with love of the virtues against vices? That which was burning was a pan. For it grew hot and cooked: it was set on fire with bitterness, yet from its afflicted thought it prepared nourishment for the virtues.

30. But what does it mean that the prophet places this same pan as a wall between himself and the city, except that the same strong zeal which is now active in the teacher’s mind will be a witness on the day of the final judgment between him and the soul for which he has shown zeal against vices [Note: [Col. 0931D] Gemeticensis and most Norman manuscripts read “for which he is zealous.”]? Thus, even if the one being taught has refused to listen, the teacher will nevertheless not be held guilty for the hearer’s negligence on account of the zeal he has shown.

He places an iron wall between himself and the city because, at the time of retribution, the teacher is protected from the danger of condemnation by that very thing through which he now suffers the frying of zeal for guarding the heart. For no sacrifice is so acceptable to almighty God as zeal for souls. Hence the Psalmist says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10).

How much the frying of the heart that is produced through spiritual zeal pleases the almighty Lord God is clearly shown when the Law commands fine flour to be offered in sacrifice. Of it is written: “It shall be fried in a pan sprinkled with oil, and the priest who lawfully succeeds his father shall offer it hot, for a most pleasing aroma to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned on the altar” (Leviticus 6:21–22). Fine flour is then fried in a pan when the pure mind of the righteous is burned by the ardor of holy zeal [Note: [Col. 0932D] C. German. reads “which has been sprinkled with oil”; Longipontanus, “which has been sprinkled.”].

It is commanded to be sprinkled with oil—that is, to be mingled with the brightness of mercy—which burns and shines in the sight of the almighty Lord. Let the mind, therefore, that is fried in the pan be sprinkled with oil [Note: [Col. 0932D] The editions read, against the manuscripts: “because in the strictness of holy zeal it is necessary that it should burn and shine.” The Sagiensis Codex reads: “because the holy discernment of zeal is necessary.”], because the strictness of holy zeal must both burn and shine through the virtue of mercy. For it loves the very one whom it appears to pursue.

Hence it is commanded to be offered hot as a most pleasing aroma to the Lord, because if zeal does not possess love, the fine flour offered from the pan has lost its warmth [Note: [Col. 0932D] Vallicellanus Cl. and several Norman manuscripts read “through spiritual zeal”; Longipontanus, “on account of spiritual zeal.”].

It should also be noted who is commanded to offer it: namely, the priest who lawfully succeeds his father. For that priest lawfully succeeds his father who shows by his conduct that he is a son of the almighty Lord, and who does not differ from his inner nobility by the ignobility of his works.

It is commanded to be wholly burned upon the altar, so that it may become a whole burnt offering. For we call a whole burnt offering something entirely consumed by fire. Hence, in another translation, this same fine flour fried in the pan is commanded in this passage to become a whole burnt offering.

There is, however, this difference between a whole burnt offering and a sacrifice: every whole burnt offering is indeed a sacrifice, but not every sacrifice is a whole burnt offering. Many good things are performed as sacrifices but are not whole burnt offerings, because they do not set the whole mind on fire with spiritual love [Note: [Col. 0933C] Gemeticensis, Uticensis, and several Norman manuscripts read “direct the whole mind toward spiritual love.”]. Those who do the things of God in such a way that they nevertheless do not abandon certain things of the world clearly offer a sacrifice and not a whole burnt offering. But those who abandon everything that belongs to the world and set their whole mind on fire with the fire of divine love [Note: [Col. 0933C] Suessionianus reads “are set on fire with the fire of divine love in their whole mind.”] become for almighty God both a sacrifice and a whole burnt offering.

The fine flour in the pan is therefore the pure mind of the righteous in the affliction of spiritual zeal: it is fried through concern for souls, and is judged to be not only a sacrifice but also a whole burnt offering for the Lord.

Let us therefore take an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between ourselves and the city—that is, let us take up strong zeal, so that we may afterward find this strong fortification between ourselves and the soul of our hearer. We shall then find this iron wall if we now hold it firmly: by teaching, guarding, persuading, rebuking, soothing, frightening, acting sometimes gently and sometimes even more severely [Note: [Col. 0933C] Longipontanus reads “by rebuking.”].

Concerning this severity it is rightly added: “And you shall set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege.”

31. What does it mean to set one’s face firmly against the Jerusalem drawn upon the brick except that, when the teacher announces the vision of heavenly peace to the soul and sees that it is still weak in its actions, he should not show himself more lenient or more indulgent toward it? Hence it is written: “Do you have daughters? Preserve their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face” (Sirach 7:26).

Weak souls and those devoted to worldly desire are sometimes better preserved by severity, so that a hardened face—that is, one withdrawn from every hope of frivolous leniency through the guardianship of severity [Note: [Col. 0934C] Longipontanus reads *obducta* (“covered over”), instead of *abducta* (“withdrawn”).]—may terrify the unstable soul and restrain it from the pleasure of vices by the force of discipline [Note: [Col. 0933C] The German, Norman, and other manuscripts read *atque ad appetitum* (“and to desire”); the editions have *atque appetitui* (“and to desire,” with a different inflection).].

When the teacher does this, it is always necessary that sweetness and humility be retained in the heart, so that he may love greatly and never, through arrogance, become proud against the one whom he nevertheless refuses to display his love and humility toward, for that person’s benefit.

32. It follows: “And you shall surround it.” The teacher surrounds the soul of his hearer when he warns that snares of temptation can be placed upon everything done in this life, so that, while the mind is made fearful everywhere, it may live everywhere watchful; and the more timid it is, the more vigilant it may be.

33. It follows: “It is a sign for the house of Israel.” If this refers to the historical siege that literally took place, the sign for the house of Israel is what the prophet did. If it refers to the mystery that the teacher enacts daily concerning each person’s soul, then both what he did and what he announced by doing it are a sign for the house of Israel. For just as the house of Israel endured a bodily siege, so every soul that has begun to serve almighty God feels the snares of evil spirits besieging it.

If it truly desires to be rescued from them, it must know that it cannot be rescued by its own strength. Rather, it must hope for the help of the one who, through the mystery of his redemption, can strengthen us—even while we live in corruptible flesh—against the spirits that are without flesh: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK TWO

[Note: [Col. 0933D] The manuscripts read: “Here begins the second book of the homilies of Saint Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, on the final part of the prophet Ezekiel, consisting of ten homilies.”]

[Col. 0933]

## Preface

[Col. 0933D]
