1307 Since, pressed by many cares, I was unable to examine the entire book of the prophet Ezekiel systematically before your Charity, it pleased your good desires to ask that at least its final vision—the vision shown to him of the building situated on the mountain, and the most obscure of all his visions—should be expounded. Indeed, I must comply with your wish; but two things disturb my mind in this matter.

First, this same vision is covered with such clouds of obscurity that scarcely anything in it seems to shine through to the understanding [Note: [Col. 0933D] Vallicellanus and Claramontanus read “to shine through.” For the rest, concerning the obscurity of Ezekiel’s prophecy, consult what we said in the preface.]. Second, we have learned that Agilulf, king of the Lombards, who was hastening with the greatest urgency to besiege us, has already crossed the Po [Note: [Col. 0934D] The Norman manuscripts read “to cross the Po.” See above, Homily 11, no. 26, and Book V, Letter 40.].

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, what the wretched mind, occupied by the disturbances of its fear, can accomplish in penetrating obscure and mystical meanings [Note: [Col. 0934D] The oldest manuscript of the Church of Laon and others read “in obscure [matters].” Ebroicensis and Lyranensis read “in mystical readings.”]. For the more it is distressed about earthly things [Note: [Col. 0935D] The printed editions read “strives the more.”], the less it sees in heavenly things; and because it is led outside itself by its cares, it is greatly diminished within, since, as it is written: “The earthly habitation presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

What, then, will a mind be able to accomplish when divided, if even when gathered together it is not sufficient to penetrate higher things? We know—indeed, we all know—that a river divided into many streams is dried out from its channel. Yet amid all this, heavenly grace is present. And if the burdens of my thoughts weigh down my mind, the wings of your desires lift it up.

The work we are undertaking is indeed very obscure, but let us bear in mind that we are making a journey by night. It remains, therefore, for us to grasp our way forward by touch.

## HOMILY ONE

[Note: [Col. 0935D] In the printed editions, against the manuscripts, “the thirteenth homily.”]

On the exposition of the first three verses of Ezekiel chapter 40 and the beginning of the fourth; chiefly concerning Christ and the Church, the elect, and God’s hidden judgments concerning them.

[Col. 0935B]

1307 **Ezekiel 40:1.**—“In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, fourteen years after the city was struck, on that very day the hand of the Lord was upon me, and he brought me there.”

1. Since I am about to speak of mystical matters, I first set forth the historical narrative [Note: [Col. 0935D] The editions, except Gussanville, read: “About to give a mystical account, he first sets forth a historical narrative.” The English manuscripts and others support the present reading.], so that I may establish in time what is to be believed as proceeding from revelation. It should be noted that at the beginning of this book he indicated in what year he began to prophesy; at the end he inserted when he saw the final vision, so that it may be known over how many years he extended the book of his prophecy [Note: [Col. 0935D] All the Norman manuscripts, together with the Paris editions of 1502, 1518, and 1571 and the Vatican manuscript, read “over how many years he spoke.” The Longipontanus reads “arranged.”].

For he placed the time when he began to prophesy at the beginning of his speech, saying: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of the Lord on the fifth [day] of the month; that was the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin” (Ezekiel 1:1). But now he says: “In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity.” The same prophet had been led into Babylonia in the first captivity with King Jehoiachin (4 Kings 24:25) [Note: [Col. 0935D] Vallicellanus and Claramontanus, together with the Norman manuscripts, read “into Babylon.” Here and everywhere thereafter both manuscripts and editions, except Gussanville, read *Joachim*. It should be written *Jehoiachin* or *Joiachin*, as it is found in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin copies of the prophet Ezekiel and of the Fourth Book of Kings; thus he is distinguished from his father, called Jehoiakim.].

For concerning the second captivity of Jerusalem he adds: “Fourteen years after the city was struck.” For eleven years Zedekiah had reigned in the city of Jerusalem after the first captivity, in which the prophet Ezekiel was led into Babylon with King Jehoiachin [Note: [Col. 0936D] The Norman manuscripts omit “into Babylon.”]. After the captivity of that same Zedekiah—which was already the second captivity of the city—the prophet saw the final vision in the fourteenth year [Note: [Col. 0935D] All the editions read “which was also.”].

Eleven and fourteen joined together therefore make twenty-five. If, then, he spoke of the first vision in the fifth year of the earlier captivity and describes this final vision as having occurred in the twenty-fifth year, it is plainly evident that he extended the course of his speech over twenty years, up to the words of his final vision [Note: [Col. 0936D] The older editions read “up to the final words of his vision”; the more recent ones, “up to the last.” The manuscripts of Norman and Vallicellanus support the latter reading. The Laon, Suessionian, and Longipontanus manuscripts, however, read “up to the final words of his vision.”].

Nor should anyone be disturbed by the fact that in the middle of his prophetic book, when he was speaking of the king of Babylon, he mentions the twenty-seventh year. Since in that passage he inserts nothing concerning the time of his own captivity, he plainly demonstrates that he is describing the times of that king, concerning whom he had received a prophecy to utter [Note: [Col. 0936D] Vallicellanus, with the Norman manuscripts, reads “concerning whom he had begun to prophesy.”].

When he says, “At the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month,” he simply expresses the time, so that from the time itself he may also fix in the hearts of his hearers the root of the word according to the literal sense [Col. 0936B], from which spiritual fruits may afterward emerge.

2. It should also be noted that he says: “In the fourteenth year after the city was struck, on that very day.” For what does it mean that almighty God, through this final vision, chose to bestow the mercy of his promise on that very day on which he fulfilled the anger of his justice against the stricken city, except that that power of divinity [Note: [Col. 0936D] Suessionianus, Laonensis, and other older witnesses read “that divine nature.”], which is not drawn into movement and mutability through diversity, gives life to the afflicted and penitent by that same light of justice by which it strikes the proud and obstinate? Having first stated the time of his vision, he adds:

**Verses 1–2.**—“The hand of the Lord was upon me, and he brought me there in visions of God. He brought me into the land of Israel and set me upon a very high mountain, on which there was something like a building of a city facing south.”

[Col. 0936C]

3. The building of this city cannot in any way be understood according to the literal sense. For shortly afterward he says that this same building was measured with a reed six cubits and a handbreadth long, while the gate of the building was measured at fourteen cubits, and he declares that the fronts of its gates were sixty cubits long [Note: [Col. 0936D] The printed texts add “of the same city,” without manuscript authority. The difficulty is readily resolved: the prophet says that a reed of six cubits and a handbreadth was used for measuring the city, not that the city itself equalled that measure except where this is repeatedly stated.]. None of these things can stand according to the literal sense. For how can the entire building be measured with a reed—that is, six cubits and a handbreadth—while the gate of the building extends fourteen cubits and the fronts of the gates extend sixty cubits? The gate is within the city, while the fronts are within the gates. No acceptable reasoning permits this, because the container is smaller than what it contains.

In sacred Scripture, however, even things that can be understood historically are often to be understood spiritually, so that faith may be maintained in the truth of the history and spiritual understanding may be derived from the mysteries of allegory. We know this also from what the Psalmist says: “For I shall see your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you founded” (Psalm 8:4).

Behold, in the outward description the statement stands as a rational one: the heavens are God’s works, and the moon and stars were created and founded by him. But if the Psalmist, according to outward works alone and not also according to mystical understanding, declares that the heavens are God’s works, why, when he is about to mention the moon and stars, did he not also enumerate the sun, which we know to be his work (Genesis 1:16)? If he were speaking according to the literal sense alone, when he was about to say “the lesser light,” he ought first to have mentioned “the greater light,” so that he might assert that the sun was founded before the moon and stars.

But because he was speaking according to mystical understanding [Note: [Col. 0937D] Gussanville corruptly reads “so that we must all understand one moon,” etc. The two German manuscripts and the other manuscripts read *ut lunam* (“so that [we might understand] the moon”), as the sequence of the sentence requires.], and so that we might understand the holy Church as the moon and all the saints as the stars, he did not wish to name the sun, because he was speaking to that eternal Sun of whom it is written: “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4:2). Of him the reprobate will say at the end: “The sun of righteousness has not risen for us.”

By saying, therefore, “the moon and the stars that you founded” (Wisdom 5:6), and yet remaining silent about the sun that was made, he indicated that he was speaking to that Sun who made not only the sun, moon, and stars bodily, but also spiritually made the moon—the Church—and the stars—all the saints.

If, then, when something is absent from the historical sense, we are led by clear reasoning to an allegorical understanding [Note: [Col. 0937D] Laonensis reads “when we speak of something according to the clear reasoning of history.”], how much more should those things be understood spiritually in which, according to the reasoning of the literal sense, nothing historical is expressed?

“The hand of the Lord was upon me, and he brought me there in visions of God; he brought me into the land of Israel.” What he had said, “He brought me there,” he repeated and then added: “He brought me into the land of Israel.” For he says: “The hand of the Lord was upon me, and he brought me there in visions of the Lord.” The hand signifies the power of authority, while the visions signify the revelation that he had received. The hand in a vision is therefore power in contemplation.

What do these words plainly indicate except that he is not speaking literally about the city he saw [Note: [Col. 0937D] Laonensis and Longipontanus read “according to the historical sense.”]? For he speaks spiritually about the city that he contemplates spiritually.

4. “And he set me upon a very high mountain.” Whom, then, does the high mountain signify except the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus? He is from the earth, yet beyond the earth, because the flesh of our Redeemer has its material from the depths, but by its power it excels in the heights.

It would have been insufficient to call him high unless he added “very,” because he was made not only human but, from the conception of that humanity assumed by him, God-man—not merely a human being above human beings, but also a human being above the angels [Note: [Col. 0938D] Longipontanus reads “above the angels.” We have removed the conjunction “and” inserted here by the editions and restored *ex* before *ejusdem*, as found in all the better manuscripts.]. Hence Isaiah says of him: “On that day the fruit of the earth shall be exalted” (Isaiah 4:2). Because our Creator was incarnate for us, he became for us the fruit of the earth. But now the fruit of the earth is exalted, because the human being born on earth reigns above the angels in heaven, since, according to the words of David and Paul, “He has placed all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8:8; Hebrews 2:8). For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.

This mountain is therefore both high and very high: although he is from the earth according to the substance of his humanity, he is nevertheless incomprehensible in the height of his divinity [Note: [Col. 0938D] Ebroicensis, Lyranensis, and Vallicellanus read “incomparable.”].

Hence, when the prophet Isaiah foresaw the same Lord who was to come in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0938D] Laonensis and Lyranensis read “would come to be incarnate.”], lifted up by the spirit of prophecy, he said: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isaiah 2:2). The house of the Lord was the Israelite people. The mountain of the house of the Lord, therefore, was called the one who deigned to become incarnate from the Israelite people.

There were holy men within that same people who rightly could be called mountains, because by the merit of their lives they drew near to heavenly things. But the only-begotten Son, when incarnate, was not equal to those mountains [Note: [Col. 0938D] Laonensis and Longipontanus read “because by nature, life”; Suessionianus, “because he transcended the nature and merits of all by his divinity.”], because by his divinity he transcended the nature, life, and merits of them all.

Hence he is rightly called the mountain above the summit of the mountains, because he was found exalted by his divinity even above the peaks of the saints, so that those who had made great progress in God could scarcely touch his footprints from the summit of their thought. He, therefore, who there is called the mountain above the summit of the mountains is here said to be a very high mountain.

It follows:

5. Upon it was something like a building of a city facing toward the South. It should be noted that it does not say, “Upon it was a building,” but “something like a building,” so that it might be shown that everything was being said not of a bodily but of a spiritual city’s building. [Note: [Col. 0938D] Laud. and Longip.: “not of a bodily, but of a spiritual, [building].”] For whoever declares that he saw not a building but something like a building directs the hearts of his hearers toward a spiritual structure, just as it is said through the Psalmist: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3). Since that vision of inward peace is constructed from the gathering of holy citizens, heavenly Jerusalem is built as a city.

Yet while it is struck with scourges and beaten by tribulations in this land of pilgrimage [Col. 0938D], its stones are squared every day. This city is the holy Church, which, although destined to reign in heaven, still labors on earth. To its citizens Peter says: “You also, like living stones, are being built up” (1 Pet. 2:5). And Paul says: “You are God’s cultivated field, God’s building” [Col. 0939A] (1 Cor. 3:9).

This city already has here, in the conduct of the saints, a great part of its building. In a building, one stone supports another, because one stone is placed upon another; and the one who supports another is himself supported by another. Thus, in the holy Church, each person both supports another and is supported by another. For those who are near to one another bear with one another, so that the building of charity may rise through them. Hence Paul exhorts us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). Declaring the power of this law, he says: “The fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. 13:10).

For if I neglect to bear with you in your conduct, and you disdain to tolerate me in mine, how does the building of charity arise between us, whom mutual love does not join through patience? In a building, as we have said, the stone that supports is itself supported, because just as I now tolerate the conduct of those who are still inexperienced in a good way of life, so I too have been tolerated by those who preceded and supported me in the fear of the Lord, so that, having been supported, I might learn to support others. But they too were supported by those who came before them.

The stones, however, that are placed at the top and outermost edge of the structure are indeed supported by others, but they do not support others at all. For those who will be born at the end of the Church, that is, at the end of the world, are indeed tolerated by their predecessors so that their conduct may be shaped toward good works [Note: [Col. 0939D] Laudun. and Longip.: “toward good merits.”]; but since they do not follow those who might advance through them, they bear no stones of the faithful structure above themselves.

Now, therefore, others are supported by us, while we have been supported by others. But the foundation supports the entire weight of the structure, because our one Redeemer alone bears the conduct of everyone together. Of him Paul says: [Note: [Col. 0939D] Plur. reads: “But no other foundation can anyone lay ... which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”] “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).

The foundation bears the stones, but is not borne by the stones, because our Redeemer bears all that is ours, while in him there was no evil that needed to be borne. Hence it is rightly said here: “He left me upon a very high mountain, upon which there was something like a city building,” because he alone supports our conduct and our faults who bears the entire structure of the holy Church. Through the prophet’s voice he says of those who are still living perversely: “I am weary of bearing” (Jer. 6:11). Yet the Lord does not become weary by bearing, since no fatigue touches the power of his divinity; but, speaking in human terms, he calls his patience toward us labor.

6. It should also be noted that the same city which the prophet saw facing toward the South was seen by him in that direction. Those who are diligent students of sacred expression recognize that the South wind is customarily understood as a type of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, the North often signifies the devil, because the former relaxes by its warmth, while the latter constricts by its cold. Truth says: [Note: [Col. 0939D] Longip. reads “will abound”; Laudun. reads “will grow cold.”] “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” [Col. 0940A] (Matt. 24:12). The prophet also declares concerning Judea, saying: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so she made her wickedness cold” (Jer. 6:7).

Hence, as the same prophet bears witness, the devil is said to have declared: “I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the North” (Isa. 14:13). But this city faces toward the southern region, because the grace of the Holy Spirit loosens the mind’s torpor. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn our captivity, Lord, like a stream in the South” (Ps. 125:4). Our captivity, which had remained sluggish in following God because of the cold of torpor, is loosened by the warmth of the Holy Spirit so that it may run toward the love of God.

Therefore it is now said that the city established upon the mountain faces toward the South, because the Church of the elect opens its thoughts [Note: [Col. 0939D] Laudun. reads: “in affection.”] through the breath of the Holy Spirit; and, descending from every summit of its pride, it conceives the warmth of love for God in whom it believes, so that it desires nothing except to submit to his grace, [Note: [Col. 0939D] Gussanville alone adds here: “to be elevated toward good works”; “of his ...,” etc. He does not indicate where this was taken from; therefore we judged that it should be removed. In the same place Laudun. and Suess. have “to be warmed by delight in him.”] to be warmed by love, and always to be filled by the gift of his inspiration.

Hence the contemplative, inflamed with powerful love, said: “My soul will rejoice in the Lord and will delight in his Savior” (Ps. 34:9). For what is called *salutaris* in Latin is called *Jesus* in Hebrew. Since, therefore, the prophet was contemplating through the spirit of prophecy his ways and miracles, as well as the mystery of our redemption, he declares that he rejoices in the Lord and delights in Jesus [Note: [Col. 0940D] Laud. and Longip.: “and delights”], because he had conceived joy in his mind from the very source through which he burned strongly with love.

Let us consider, then, what guilt is ours if the minds of the spiritual fathers delighted in him who had not yet come but was foreseen, while, after he has come and accomplished redemption, we do not love his ways, his examples, and his teachings.

This city, therefore, is said to face toward the South, as though it were plainly said that the earlier city, namely the Synagogue, stood toward the North in its unbelievers and endured in the cold of faithlessness [Note: [Col. 0940D] Longip. reads “grew hard”; Norm., with Val. Cl., “chose to remain.”]. But the holy Church, which has conceived the charity of faith, faces toward the South through warmth and leans, as it were, upon a warm wind, because it rejoices not in confidence in itself but in the gift of spiritual grace. This follows:

**VERSE 3.—“And he brought me in there.”**

7. He enters the building of the heavenly city who, by imitating the ways of the good, attentively considers them in the holy Church. To enter the building upon the mountain is to consider with love how the elect of the holy Church, established upon the heights of virtue, advance in the Lord.

One person leads a life bound by marriage, is content with his own possessions, does not seize what belongs to others, gives to the needy from what is his whatever he is able to give, and does not neglect to weep over the sins without which daily life cannot be lived by married people. Because the cares of the household disturb his spirit, he stirs himself to tears.

Another has already abandoned everything belonging to the world [Col. 0941A], desires to possess nothing of it, feeds upon the practice of contemplation alone [Note: [Col. 0941D] Laudun.: “is nourished by contemplation alone”], and rejoices amid tears in the hope of heavenly rewards. He rises above even those things that are permitted to be possessed, seeks to maintain a daily secret communion with the Lord, is troubled by no care of the passing world, and continually expands his mind in expectation of heavenly joys.

Another has already abandoned everything of this world, and his mind is lifted into contemplation of heavenly things; yet, holding a position of governance for the edification of many, he does not succumb to passing things through desire, but sometimes turns back toward them out of compassion for his neighbors, so that through care for them he may show mercy to the needy. He preaches the word of life to his hearers and supplies what is necessary both for their souls and their bodies. Although through contemplation he already soars toward heavenly desire for his own sake, he still labors amid temporal affairs for the progress and benefit of his neighbors. [Note: [Col. 0941D] Laud., Suess., Longipp., Val. Cl., and others read *pro* (“for”), which is necessary to complete the sense; the printed editions omit it.]

Whoever, therefore, diligently strives to consider how he may advance in the holy Church—whether in the life of the good married, or in the citadel of those who practice continence and abandon everything belonging to this world, or even at the summit of preachers—has entered the building of the city set upon the mountain. For whoever neglects to consider the life of those who are better in order to advance still stands outside the structure. And if he admires the honor that the holy Church already possesses in the world, he sees and marvels at something like a building from outside. Since he is intent only upon external things, he has not entered within. This follows:

**THE SAME PLACE.—“And behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze.”**

8. The one who is figured in the mountain is signified in the man. This man is said to measure the building. And rightly is the Lord signified both by the man and by the mountain, because he both orders everything within the holy Church by judgment and bears that same holy Church, lifting it toward heavenly things by bearing it.

Thus, in the holy Gospel, our same Redeemer speaks, saying: “He who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10:1). A little later: “I am the door” (ibid., 7). And again, shortly afterward, he adds: “I am the good shepherd” (ibid., 11). If, therefore, he is himself the shepherd, himself the door, and the shepherd enters through the door, why should he not also be understood here as both the mountain and the man who measures the building upon the mountain?

[Col. 0941D] 9. But we must ask why it is said of this man, “His appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” We all know, brothers, that bronze is a very durable metal and also entirely resonant. What, then, does it mean that the appearance of the Mediator of God and human beings is compared with the appearance of bronze, unless it is what we plainly know: that the only-begotten Son, taking the form of a servant, transformed the frailty of human flesh into immortality through the glory of his resurrection, because in him the flesh has become enduring without end? For, having risen from the dead, “he no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9).

What does it mean that his incarnation itself is compared with resonant metal, unless that through this same assumption of our humanity [Note: [Col. 0941D] Laud. and Longip.: “resounded to all with the glory”] the glory of his majesty resounded to everyone? And he has, as it were, the appearance of bronze [Note: [Col. 0942D] Another reading: “he has it from the body, which the commonly received copies display.”] in his body, because God became known to the world through flesh.

Hence it is also said through John: “He had written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16). For what is his garment except the body [Note: [Col. 0942D] Laud., Longip., Lyr.: “which he assumed”] that he assumed from the Virgin? Yet his garment is not one thing and he himself another. For our garment too is called flesh, but we ourselves are nevertheless the flesh with which we are clothed.

Long before, Isaiah, seeing this garment stained with blood through the passion of the cross, said: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. 63:2). He himself replied: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the peoples there was no man with me” (ibid., 3). For he alone trod the winepress in which he was trodden, who by his own power conquered the passion he endured. Although he suffered even to the death of the cross, he rose from death in glory.

It is rightly said: “And of the peoples there was no man with me” (ibid.), because those for whom he had come to suffer ought to have shared in his passion. Since at that time they did not yet believe, he complains in his passion about the very people whose life was being sought through that passion.

The thigh signifies the propagation of the flesh. Since, therefore, he came into this world from a virgin through the propagation of the human race—as the genealogical lines are described by Matthew (Matt. 1:1 ff.) and Luke (Luke 2:7; 3:23 ff.)—and through the mystery of his incarnation made known everywhere to all peoples that he was King and Lord, he had written on his garment and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16). For where he became known in the world, there he impressed upon it the knowledge of the reading concerning himself [Note: [Col. 0942D] Suess.: “the meaning of the reading.”]

His preaching, therefore, proceeding from the flesh, is like a sound from bronze. Let it rightly be said: “Whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” This follows:

**THE SAME PLACE.—“And a linen cord was in his hand.”**

10. In the Septuagint interpreters, “linen cord” is not found, but “mason’s cord.” [Note: [Col. 0942D] In Laud. “mason’s” is always written.] If we retain their translation in this verse for purposes of exposition, whom else do we understand by masons than the holy teachers, who, by speaking spiritual things, arrange living stones—that is, the souls of the elect—for the heavenly building?

Whatever the ancient fathers said, whatever the prophets said, whatever the apostles said, and whatever the successors of the apostles have said: what else has it been but the arrangement of stones in this structure of the saints that is built day by day?

With a mason’s cord, the usual purpose is to make it possible to determine the equality or straightness of a wall as it rises: if a stone is set inward, it is pushed outward; if it projects outward, it is drawn back inward. [Col. 0943A] And certainly the preaching of teachers does this every day: each soul for whom it perhaps is not suitable to undertake the burdens of governance is drawn back inward even if it desires to appear outwardly; while the soul that wishes to remain hidden and care only for itself, if it can be useful both to itself and to many, is brought out so that it may appear, even though it desires to remain concealed.

Thus the order of the holy stones is maintained: the one who willingly seeks honor is often rejected, while the one who flees honor is raised to the height of the sacred order.

But because, as we have learned through our interpreter, the Hebrew text does not have “mason’s cord” but “linen cord in his hand,” we ought to explain what is more certainly attested among us. We know that a linen cord is finer than cords made from other materials. What, then, should we understand in the linen cord except a finer preaching [Col. 0943B], that is, spiritual discipline? [Note: [Col. 0943D] Laud.: “that is, we ought to understand spiritual correction. For the law was a cord.”]

The discipline of the law was indeed a cord, but it was not linen, because it restrained a crude people not with subtle preaching. Through the sentence of punishment it cut away not sins of thought but sins of deed [Note: [Col. 0943D] Ebroic. and Lyr., supported by Suess. and Longip.: “through penance.”].

But after the Lord himself, by preaching, had also bound human thoughts and had made known that sin is complete even in the heart, he held a linen cord in his hand. For he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you that whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27; Exod. 20:14).

The linen cord, therefore, is subtle preaching, which binds the mind of the hearer so that it does not loosen itself even in a wretched thought. It should also be noted that it is said that the cord is in his hand, that is, that preaching is embodied in action. [Col. 0943C] For he showed in himself everything that he taught, as it is written: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). And because he also committed to writing the very things he said, so that they might be handed down to later generations, it is rightly added:

**THE SAME PLACE.—“And a measuring reed was in his hand.”**

11. Through another prophet, the Lord promises the holy Church, saying: “The greenness of the reed and the rush will arise in it” (Isa. 35:7). I remember having explained this elsewhere (Book 29 of the *Moralia*, no. 51), so that the writers should be understood through the reed, and the hearers through the rush.

But since both the rush and the reed ordinarily grow in water, and both are nourished by the same water, while the reed is taken up for writing but one cannot write with the rush, what should we understand by the rush and the reed except that there is one doctrine of truth, which waters many hearers?

Some, once watered, advance so far in the word of God that they even become writers, like reeds; others hear the word of life and retain the greenness of good hope and upright works, but are entirely unable to advance to writing. [Note: [Col. 0944D] Longip.: “What else, I say, are these ...?”] What else are these in the water of God, so to speak, except certain rushes? They indeed advance by becoming green, but they cannot express letters at all.

Our Redeemer, therefore, because he granted that the words he spoke should also be written through the diligence of teachers, held a reed in his hand. It is called a measuring reed because, through a certain dispensation of hidden judgment, the work of teachers is kept within a measure, so that it may benefit some readers but be unable to benefit others.

Hence, when the holy apostles sought a teacher of truth who would speak more openly to them and asked why he spoke to the crowds in parables, they heard: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not” (Matt. 13:11).

Or certainly the measuring reed is so called because, in his sacred speech that has been written for us, we recognize that his hidden dispensations are present. For by his incomprehensible judgment one person is brought within the measure of the elect, while another is left outside, so that he is in no way deemed worthy to belong to the number of the elect [Note: [Col. 0944D] Norm., with Val. Cl.: “to reach”; Suess.: “to attain.”]

Thus he has a cord; he has a measuring reed in his hand. For one who measures a place with a cord draws the cord in one place, pulls it back elsewhere, brings here the one whom he withdraws from another place. Thus, precisely thus, our Redeemer acts in the gathering of human beings: he leads some out of their iniquities and leaves others in their iniquity.

In those whom he has deemed worthy to gather, he has drawn the cord of hidden measure; from those whom he has judged should be abandoned, what else has he done but pull back the cord? Thus the good are kept within the measure of the heavenly structure, while the wicked, in whom the things considered good are not found, remain outside the structure as though without measure.

12. Our Redeemer held this cord and measuring reed in his hand when he deigned to admonish the apostle Paul through a man appearing as a Macedonian, so that the same Macedonian said: [Note: [Col. 0944D] Longip.: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.”] “Cross over and help us” (Acts 16:9). Yet, when the apostles wished to go to preach in Asia, the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.

What does it mean that the holy apostles are called to go where perhaps they were not thinking of going, while they are forbidden to go where they desired to go, except that the cord of hidden judgment and the measuring reed are held in his hand, so that some may hear the words of life while others are in no way deemed worthy to hear them?

The cord, therefore, is a measuring cord, drawn in one direction and pulled back from another.

13. We have also learned from the witness of the holy Gospel that one came saying: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. 8:19). He was answered: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (ibid., 20).

Another came saying: “Teacher, allow me first to go and bury my father.” He is told: [Note: [Col. 0944D] Laud., Norm., Longip.: “Allow the dead to bury ...,” etc. Val. Cl.: “Allow the dead to bury their dead.”] “Allow the dead to bury their dead; but you, follow me and announce the kingdom of God” (ibid., 21–22).

What does it mean that the former promises to go and is rejected, while the latter wishes to return home and is nevertheless commanded to follow? The former is not received, while the latter is not released from service even for an hour.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] The manuscripts vary here. Laud. reads: “Therefore, in the land of hidden judgment.” Suess.: “In anger.” Val. Cl.: “Therefore, within the hidden judgment of the judge.”] Within the hidden dispensation of judgment, therefore, the cord and measuring reed are drawn: one is pulled along, while the other is left behind, so that the heavenly structure may be built neither without a loving nor without a just examination.

14. The measuring reed may also be understood as sacred Scripture, because whoever reads it measures himself within it: how far he advances in spiritual virtue, or how far he remains separated from the good things that have been commanded; how far he has already risen toward doing good, and how far he still lies prostrate in wicked actions. This follows:

**THE SAME PLACE.—“But he was standing at the gate.”**

[Col. 0945B] 15. Whoever stands at a gate is in one respect inside and in another outside, because one aspect of him is seen outside while another is hidden within.

Our Redeemer, therefore, mercifully incarnated for us, stood before human eyes as though at a gate, because he appeared visible through his humanity while preserving himself invisible in his divinity.

For this reason the Jews, who had awaited him on the basis of the prophets’ promise, were thrown into confusion by the shame of their faithlessness, because they saw as mortal the one whom they had believed would come for their deliverance.

Whoever stands at a gate, as was said above, is seen partly outside and partly inside. Therefore even the faithlessness of the Jews was not abandoned without an indication of divine power. Seeing his miracles, they were drawn toward belief; but, considering his sufferings in turn, they disdained to believe him God, since they saw him mortal in the flesh. Thus it happened that they doubted their knowledge of him.

They saw him hungry, thirsty, eating, drinking, [Note: [Col. 0945D] Laud.: “growing weary.”] becoming weary, and sleeping, and they judged that he was merely a human being. They saw him raising the dead, cleansing lepers, giving sight to the blind, and driving out demons, and they understood that he was more than human. But his humanity, considered in their hearts, disturbed them in the face of his very miracles.

Therefore the holy Church, already openly desiring to see him in the voice of the bride, says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song 2:9). For he who displayed to human eyes what he had assumed from mortal nature, while remaining invisible in himself, stood as though behind a wall before those seeking to see him openly, because he did not offer himself to be seen in manifested majesty.

He stood, as it were, behind a wall because he displayed the nature of humanity that he had assumed and concealed from human eyes the nature of divinity. Hence it is added there: “Looking through the windows, looking through the latticework” (ibid.). Whoever looks through windows or latticework is neither wholly hidden nor wholly seen.

Thus, precisely thus, our Redeemer appeared before the eyes of those who doubted. If, while performing miracles, he had endured nothing as a human being, he would have appeared to them fully as God. Conversely, if, while suffering as a human being, he had done nothing as God, he would have been thought merely human. But because he both performed divine deeds and endured human sufferings, he looked upon human beings as though through windows or latticework: he appeared as God through his miracles and remained hidden through his sufferings; he was perceived as human through his sufferings, yet through his miracles was recognized as more than human.

But since this man is said to stand at the gate, we must ask whether he stood with his face inward and his back outward. [Note: [Col. 0946D] In the old edition, before Gussanville, the question reads: “whether he stood with his face inward ...” Gussanville’s question, after “and his back outward,” adds: “or with his back inward and his face outward.” “We stand” is supported by the manuscripts.]

If we consider what has been stated before and what follows, we quickly discover how he stood. First it is said: “There was something like a building of a city facing toward the South, and he brought me in there.” Shortly afterward, concerning the same man, it adds: “But he was standing at the gate.” Immediately it continues:

**VERSE 4.—“And the same man spoke to me.”**

[Col. 0946B] Since he who spoke while standing at the gate after the prophet had been brought into the building clearly stood with his face inward and his back outward, the prophet who had been brought in, to whom the man standing at the gate spoke, undoubtedly held his face toward the gate, from which he heard the speaker’s words.

What does it mean, then, that the man looks inward while the prophet looks outward? What does it mean that the face of the same man is turned toward the building, while the prophet’s eyes are turned toward the gate, except that the Only-Begotten of the Father was incarnated for this reason: to bring us into the spiritual building, that is, into the faith of the holy Church?

His eyes always look upon his building, because they continually attend to how far each person advances in virtues. The prophet, however, looks toward the gate, because whoever hears the words of God must always direct the eyes of his heart toward the exit and continually meditate on when he will leave the present life and reach eternal joys.

For this reason God became incarnate: to bring us into faith [Note: [Col. 0946D] Thus the manuscripts Norm., Val. Cl., etc. The editions read “and lead us out,” which completes the sense.], and to lead us back to the sight of his vision. Hence, in the holy Gospel, Truth speaks, saying: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10:9). He will enter, namely, into faith; he will go out into sight; and he will find pasture in eternal satiety.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit” (Ps. 120:8). For the Lord guards the entrance of each soul by which it enters into faith, and also the exit by which it goes out into sight, so that neither, when entering the Church, may it be overthrown by errors, nor, when going out from this temporal life into the eternal, may it be snatched away by the ancient enemy.

With reference to this exit of ours, which we ought daily to meditate upon, the Apostle speaks of our Redeemer, saying: “To sanctify the people through his own blood, he suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For here we have no enduring city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. 13:12–14).

The man, therefore, who appeared at the gate stood there and thus spoke, because Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and human beings, gave the precepts of life to his disciples even at the very time of his passion, so that those who believe in him might always look toward the gate and, carefully considering his passion, not turn the eyes of their hearts away from their own exit.

When we too begin to despise the barriers of the flesh, to pass beyond the narrow confines of our mortality through desire for immortality, to strive toward the freedom of heavenly light, and to long for the joys of our heavenly homeland, we keep our eyes fixed upon the gate. For while we desire to pass from temporal things to eternal ones [Note: [Col. 0947D] Suess.: “from temporal burdens”], we have, as it were, already turned our backs on the present life and keep the face of our heart directed toward our departure.

For it is written: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15). Thus, through contemplation, we already stretch in mind beyond the constraints of the flesh; yet, even in the sacraments that we have come to know, we are still held within the gate by that same carnal confinement.

17. Often the mind is so suspended in divine contemplation that it already rejoices, through a certain image, in perceiving something of that eternal freedom “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard” (1 Cor. 2:9). [Note: [Col. 0947D] Norm. and Val. Cl.: “yet, struck back by the weight of mortality ...,” with certain variants.] Yet, struck back by the weight of its mortality (Isa. 64:4), it falls back to lower things and is held bound by certain chains of punishment.

He therefore directs himself toward the gate who sees the joys of true freedom and already longs to go out, but is not yet able to do so.

Hence it is that the Hebrew people, freed from the servitude of Egypt, when they saw the pillar of cloud while God was speaking, stood each at the door of his tent and worshiped (Exod. 33:10). A little earlier it is said of them: “When Moses went out to the tabernacle, the whole people rose, and each person stood at the entrance of his tent” (ibid., 8). [Note: [Col. 0947D] Lyran.: “There, therefore ...”]

We stand there where we fix the eyes of our mind. Hence Elijah says: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1). He stood, certainly, where he had fixed his heart.

What does it mean for the people to look at the pillar of cloud, stand at the doors of their tents, and worship, except that when the human mind perceives, however obscurely, those higher and heavenly things in a riddle, it already goes beyond the barriers of its bodily dwelling through elevated thought and humbly worships the one whose substance it cannot see, yet whose power it already marvels at through the illumination of the Spirit?

And when Moses enters the tabernacle, the people look upon his back and remain at the entrances of their tents, because when a holy preacher speaks lofty things about God, he already enters, in some fashion, the tabernacle of the heavenly dwelling. Although the weak cannot fully weigh the power of his preaching, they nevertheless look, as it were, upon his back [Note: [Col. 0947D] Longip.: “or at least his back, that is ...”], because they follow in understanding those final things that they are able to grasp.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] With broad agreement Laud., Longip., Val. Cl., Ebroic., and other manuscripts read this way. Both old and recent printed editions, however, read: “but even in those things which they are less able to grasp ...”]

But even in those lesser things that they are able to grasp [Col. 0948A], they already go out from their tents, as it were, and stand at the entrances, because they strive both to leave behind the dwellings of the flesh and to advance toward the joys of eternal life that they hear about.

Hence also Elijah, when he heard the voice of the Lord speaking with him (1 Kings 19:9), is described as standing at the entrance of his cave and covering his face. For when, through the grace of contemplation, the voice of heavenly understanding arises in the mind, the whole person is no longer within the cave, because care for the flesh does not possess the soul; but he stands at the entrance because he is meditating on leaving the narrow confines of mortality.

18. But whoever stands at the entrance of the cave and perceives the words of God in the ear of his heart must cover his face. For while we are led by heavenly grace to understand higher things [Col. 0948B], the more subtly we are lifted up, the more we must always press ourselves down in humility within our understanding, lest we try to know more than we ought to know, but instead “know with sobriety” (Rom. 12:3); lest, while examining invisible things too deeply, we go astray; lest in that incorporeal nature we seek something belonging to bodily light.

To incline the ear and cover the face is to hear through the mind the voice of the inward substance and nevertheless turn the eyes of the heart away from every bodily appearance, lest the mind imagine anything bodily in that nature which is wholly everywhere and everywhere without limits. [Note: [Col. 0948D] Norm.: “the voice of the higher one.”]

We, therefore, dearest brothers, who have already learned eternal joys through the death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of our Redeemer, and who know that our fellow citizens, the angels, appeared outwardly as witnesses to his divinity, let us desire the King and long for the citizens whom we have come to know. Standing in this building of the holy Church, let us keep our eyes upon the gate; let us turn the backs of our minds upon this corruption of temporal life and direct the face of our hearts toward the freedom of our heavenly homeland.

But behold, many things still oppress us through care for corruptible life. Since, therefore, we cannot go out completely, let us at least stand at the entrance of our cave, destined one day to go out successfully through the grace of our Redeemer, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

**HOMILY II.** In explaining two verses of chapter XL, namely the fourth and fifth, the holy Doctor discusses at length the active and contemplative life and, in his customary manner, inserts many moral teachings.

[Col. 0948D]

1321

### 1

Perhaps some may reproach me in silent thought for presuming to discuss such profound mysteries of the prophet Ezekiel, untouched by great commentators. Let them recognize the spirit in which I do so. I do not undertake this rashly, but humbly. For I know that often, while standing before my brothers, I have understood many things in sacred eloquence that I could not understand by myself. From this understanding I have also tried to understand this: namely, that I might know on whose merit the understanding was granted to me. It is evident that this is given to me on behalf of those for whom it is granted while they are present with me. [Note: Ebroicensis: “who grant it to me.”] By this means, through God’s generosity, both understanding increases and self-exaltation diminishes, since for your sake I learn what I teach among you; for, to speak truthfully, I often hear with you what I say. [Col. 0949A]

Whatever, therefore, I understand less well in this prophet is due to my blindness; but if I am able to understand anything appropriately, it is, through God’s gift, due to your reverence. Often, moreover, by the grace of the almighty Lord, certain passages in his eloquence are understood better when the word of God is read more privately. Then the mind, conscious of its sins, while recognizing what it has heard, is struck by the dart of grief and pierced by the sword of compunction, so that it desires nothing but to weep and wash away tear-stains with flowing tears. [Col. 0949B] [Note: According to the manuscripts this should be read as “and wash away the stains of flowing tears.” The earlier editors corrupted the passage before Gussanville by writing “and the flowing spots of tears.” To remedy this corruption, Gussanville, without consulting the manuscripts, thought that *fons* (“spring”) should be read instead of *fluentes* (“flowing”), certainly with a better sense. Val. Cl. has “and with flowing tears.”]

Amid such experiences the mind is sometimes also carried away to contemplate higher things, and in longing for them is tormented by sweet weeping. The soul grieves that it is here, where it still lies prostrate through weakness, and is not yet there, where, illumined, it might flourish in strength and no longer draw the eye of the mind back to the darkness of mortality. Hence, from this, from this, ardor arises in the mind, and mourning springs from the ardor. And because it is not yet able to cling to heavenly things, it rests, wearied by its own fervor, in tears.

But one thing is at issue when the progress of one person is concerned, and another when the edification of many is concerned. Therefore, with God’s generosity, we must bring forth in our doctrinal discourse those things that shape the life and conduct of our hearers. [Col. 0949C] Let us now pursue, as we began, whatever in the prophet’s words may build us up toward the practice of goodness.

### Ezekiel 40:4

> “Son of man, see with your eyes and hear with your ears.”

### 2

Having been led to speak of spiritual realities, what does it mean that when he says, “See with your eyes,” he adds “your,” and when he says, “Hear with your ears,” he likewise adds “your”? We must understand that bodily eyes and ears are also present in carnal people, and are used for things that are perceived bodily. The eyes and ears of the heart, however, belong solely to spiritual realities: they see invisible things through understanding and hear the praise of God without sound.

The almighty Lord was seeking these ears when he said:

> “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

Who in that crowd at the time could have been without bodily ears? Yet when it is said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” it is plainly shown that he was seeking those ears which not everyone could possess. [Col. 0949D]

Let it therefore be said:

> “Son of man, see with your eyes and hear with your ears” (above, Homily 12, no. 21).

In the earlier part of our discourses [Note: That is, of the homilies, or sermons, which in Greek signify the same as *sermones* or *locutiones* in Latin.] we have already explained why, whenever the prophet is led to see spiritual things, he is called “son of man.” But lest this have slipped from the mind, I briefly repeat that by this designation he is always reminded of what he is through weakness, lest he become elated by the greatness of contemplation. [Col. 0950A]

It should also be noted that it is one thing for him to be told, “See with your eyes, hear with your ears,” and another that he is nevertheless called “son of man.” What else is plainly said to him through these words except: “Look upon spiritual things spiritually” [Note: Ebroicensis and Lyra: “receive them.”] and yet remember your carnal weaknesses?”

### 3

This is also why it often happens that the person who is more greatly carried away in contemplation is more heavily wearied in temptation. The same often happens to those who are making good progress: when their mind is either touched by compunction or carried beyond itself by contemplation, temptation immediately follows, lest they become proud of the things to which they have been carried. [Col. 0950B]

For through compunction or contemplation the mind is raised toward God, but by the weight of temptation it is thrown back upon itself. Thus temptation weighs it down, lest contemplation inflate it; and contemplation raises it up, lest temptation overwhelm it. If contemplation were to raise it so that temptation were entirely absent, the mind would fall into pride. And if temptation pressed it so that contemplation did not raise it, it would fall completely into sin. [Note: This is the reading of all the English, Norman, and other manuscripts, or simply *plane*, which fewer manuscripts have. Recent editions preferred *pene* (“almost”), which overturns the sense intended by Gregory.]

But by a wondrous dispensation the soul is balanced in a kind of middle position, so that it neither becomes proud in good things nor falls in evil ones. Hence it is said of the Lord through blessed Job:

> “He weighs the waters by measure” (Job 28:25; 19:25).

For God’s weighing the waters by measure means that he preserves the understanding of souls in humility amid prosperity and adversity, gifts and temptations, exalted things and lowly things. [Col. 0950C]

Thus Elijah had brought down fire from heaven and had bound the waters to heaven, yet, terrified by the fear of a single woman, he fled through the wilderness (1 Kings 18:38; 17:1; 19:3). An angel appeared to him as he fled and provided food; he foretold that a long journey remained, and yet he did not remove fear from his heart (1 Kings 19:7–8), because in the prophet’s mind there was both a great safeguard of strength and that weakness of fear.

The text continues.

## Verse 4

> “Set your heart upon all that I shall show you, because you have been brought here so that they may be shown to you. Announce everything that you see to the house of Israel.”

### 1

“Set your heart.” It is as though he were saying: “Consider.” “Because you have been brought here so that they may be shown to you, and announce everything that you see”—that is, you have been brought here in order to see, and you see in order to announce, because whoever advances by seeing spiritual things ought also to offer them to others through speech. [Col. 0950D]

He sees in order to announce who, in that by which he advances within himself, also takes care through preaching for the progress of his neighbor. Hence it is written elsewhere:

> “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17).

For whoever already hears the voice of the calling God in his heart must necessarily burst forth in voice toward his neighbors through the ministry of preaching; and for this reason he calls another, because he himself has already been called. [Col. 0951A]

Hence the bridegroom also speaks in the Song of Songs, saying:

> “You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening; make me hear your voice” (Song of Songs 8:13). [Note: All editions, disregarding the manuscripts—although our reading is found in all the Norman, Laudian, Vallicellian, and Longipontan manuscripts—have *amica ausculta*, “listen, beloved.” This reading is rejected by the Greek text and all its versions; indeed it is rejected by Gregory himself, since shortly afterward we read: “because friends are listening,” namely, all the elect.]

The holy Church dwells in gardens, and each soul dwells in gardens that is already filled with the greenness of hope and the love of good works. [Note: Suessensis: “which is already filled with the greenness and beauty of good works.”] The hope of this world is dry, because everything loved here withers quickly; and the apostle Peter urges us to hasten, saying:

> “Into an imperishable, undefiled, unfading inheritance” (1 Peter 1:4).

Therefore she who already dwells in gardens ought to make her bridegroom hear her voice—that is, to send forth the song of good preaching [Note: Laudian manuscript: “song.”], in which the one whom she desires may delight, because friends are listening, namely, all the elect, who desire to hear the words of life so that they may live again for their heavenly homeland. [Col. 0951B]

But now let the prophet disclose to us what he sees. [Note: Laudian and Longipontan manuscripts: “what he has learned.”]

The text continues.

## Verse 5

> “And behold, a wall outside, all around the house on every side.”

### 5

Often in sacred eloquence the incarnate Lord himself is accustomed to be called a wall, because of the protection he provides, as it is said of the holy Church through the prophet:

> “A wall and a rampart shall be set up in it” (Isaiah 26:1).

For he is our wall, enclosing and guarding us on every side. The prophets, however, were the rampart of our wall: before the Lord appeared in the flesh, they were sent to build up faith through prophecy.

Thus in the holy Church the Lord has been set as our wall and his prophets as the rampart, because the words of the prophets have come to us for the building of faith, to us whom he himself perfectly protects. Hence it is fitting that the wall is placed first and the rampart afterward, because we, who were called from the nations, would not have received the sayings of the prophets unless we had first come to know the Lord. [Col. 0951C]

It should also be noted that this wall of the spiritual building is said to be outside. A wall constructed for the fortification of a building is normally placed not inside but outside. Why, then, was it necessary to say “outside,” since a wall is never normally placed within? It was necessary because, being placed outside, it protects what is within.

But what is plainly demonstrated by this word except the Lord’s own incarnation? God is our wall within, but God-man is our wall outside. Hence it is said to him through a certain prophet:

> “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Habakkuk 3:13).

This incarnate wall—namely, the Lord—would not be a wall for us if he had not been outside, because he would not protect us within if he had not appeared outwardly. [Col. 0951D]

Nor should we carelessly pass over the fact that this same wall is said to be placed all around the house on every side. The house of God is not only the holy angels, of whom the Psalmist says:

> “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where the glory of your tabernacle dwells” (Psalm 25:8),

but we too are the house of God, since he deigns to dwell in our minds. [Col. 0952A]

This wall is all around the house on every side because the Father’s Only-Begotten, who above is the strength of the angels, became below the redemption of human beings: strength for them, so that they might not fall; help for us, so that we might rise after falling.

### 6

If, however, by the house of God the multitude of redeemed human beings alone is signified here, the Lord is our wall on every side and all around because, in order to guard us perfectly, he showed us everything that he taught, as it is written:

> “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

Because he came to call us to our heavenly homeland, he taught us to despise transitory goods and not to fear temporal evils. Therefore he did not despise insults, endured injuries, did not fear death, and did not shrink from the cross. When they wished to seize him and make him king, he immediately fled (John 6:15). By these examples what else did he suggest to us except that we should neither fear the adversities of this world nor pursue its prosperity? For its good things often occupy the mind more than its evils disturb it. [Col. 0952B]

Before his passion he heard insults and yet did not return insults. He endured his betrayer in silence for a long time and did not refuse to give a kiss to the one who greeted him deceitfully. He accepted death so that we would not fear dying; he showed the resurrection so that we might believe that we can rise again.

After his passion he also called those who had crucified him to the grace of faith and returned a gift for their wickedness. Thus, because he instructed us by his example in all things, he became our wall all around and on every side. [Col. 0952C]

The text continues.

## The same passage

> “And in the man’s hand was a measuring reed six cubits long and a palm.”

### 7

In the preceding reading (Homily above, no. 14) we already said that the sacred Scripture is signified by the reed. It is called a measuring reed because in it we measure all the activity of our life, so that we may see either how far we have progressed or how far we remain from progress.

For often, when we are doing something, we believe ourselves already to possess a certain merit. But when we return to the words of God and hear his sublime commandments, we recognize [Note: Val. Cl.: “how far we fall short of perfection.”] how far we fall short of perfection. The reed is therefore a measuring reed because the life of the hearers is measured through the hands of those who write. [Col. 0952D]

The reed is said to be in the hand of a man either because sacred eloquence is in the power of the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, or certainly because he completed by his deeds what he wished to be written.

This same reed is described as six cubits and a palm in length. There are two lives in which the almighty God instructs people through sacred eloquence: the active and the contemplative. What else is expressed by the six cubits than the active life? For on the sixth day God completed all his works (Genesis 2:1). [Col. 0953A]

The palm, however, which is said to be above the six cubits, already belongs to the seventh, yet is not a cubit. The active life is therefore signified by the six cubits, and the contemplative life by the palm, because we complete the former through works, whereas in the latter, even when we strive, we can scarcely touch a little of it. [Note: All printed editions have “when we direct the heart.” We follow the Norman, Vallicellian, and many other manuscripts.]

### 8

The active life is to give bread to the hungry, teach the word of wisdom to the ignorant, correct the one who errs, call back a proud neighbor to the way of humility, care for the sick, distribute to each person what is suitable, and provide for those entrusted to us so that they may be able to endure.

The contemplative life, on the other hand, is to retain the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, while resting from outward action, clinging solely to the desire for the Creator, so that one no longer wishes to do anything [Note: Longipontan manuscript: “wishes to possess.”], but, trampling down every concern, the mind burns to see the face of its Creator. It comes to know how to bear the burden of corruptible flesh with sorrow, and with all its desires longs to take part in the angelic choirs that sing hymns, to be mingled with the citizens of heaven, and to rejoice before God in eternal incorruption. [Col. 0953B]

Thus, in the palm, the hand and fingers are stretched out. Yet only a small amount of a cubit’s measure is reached through the palm, because however greatly the mind may burn with love, and however strongly it may stretch itself toward God in thought [Note: The word *cogitatione* (“in thought”) is absent in the Laudian, Ebroicensis, and Sées manuscripts.], it does not yet see perfectly what it loves; it is still only beginning to see what it loves. For, as the most powerful preacher says:

> “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

And:

> “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (ibid.).

We therefore touch the palm of the seventh cubit because, placed in this life, we taste only the beginnings of inward contemplation. Since the active life can be held perfectly, and human beings were created on the sixth day (Genesis 1:27) to do good works, the reed has six cubits.

### 9

Those two women, Martha and Mary, fittingly signified these two lives (Luke 10:40). One was busy with extensive service, while the other sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to words from his mouth.

When Martha complained against her sister because she neglected to help her, the Lord replied:

> “Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (ibid., 41–42).

Behold, Martha’s part is not condemned, but Mary’s is praised. He does not say that Mary chose a good part, but the best part, so that Martha’s part too might be shown to be good. [Col. 0953D]

Why Mary’s part is the best is added when it is said: “which shall not be taken away from her.” For the active life comes to an end with the body. Who in the eternal homeland will offer bread to the hungry, where no one hungers? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies? [Col. 0954A]

With the present world, therefore, the active life is taken away. The contemplative life, however, begins here in order to be perfected in the heavenly homeland, because the fire of love that begins to burn here will blaze more intensely in love for the one it loves when it sees him himself.

The contemplative life, therefore, is not taken away, because after the light of the present world has been withdrawn, it is perfected.

### 10

These two lives, as was also said before us (Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 22, chapters 54–55), were signified by the two women of blessed Jacob, Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:16). [Col. 0954B]

Leah is interpreted as “laborious,” while Rachel is interpreted as “sheep” or “the beginning of sight.” [Note: Val. Cl.: “Rachel, however, means rest or sheep.”]

The active life is laborious because it sweats in work. The contemplative life, however, in its simplicity, longs only to see the beginning—namely, the one who said:

> “I am the beginning, and therefore I speak to you” (John 8:25).

Blessed Jacob desired Rachel, but received Leah at night, because everyone who turns to the Lord desires the contemplative life and longs for the rest of the eternal homeland. Yet first it is necessary that, in the night of the present life, he perform whatever good he can, sweat in labor—that is, receive Leah—so that afterward he may rest in Rachel’s embrace, beholding the Beginning. [Note: Val. Cl.: “and in labor receive the active life, that is, Leah.”]

Rachel saw, but was barren; Leah was bleary-eyed, but fruitful. [Note: In the Vatican and Gussanville editions the following passage is inserted here: “For surely, when the mind seeks leisure in contemplation, it sees more but generates fewer children for God; but when it directs itself toward the labor of preaching, it sees less but bears more. Rachel …” This is unknown in our manuscripts and in the old editions and should certainly be regarded as an interpolation.]

Rachel was beautiful and barren because the contemplative life is beautiful in the mind, but while it desires to rest in silence it does not produce children through preaching. It sees and does not give birth, because while it loves the pursuit of its own rest, it is less inflamed with the gathering of others; and however much it sees inwardly, it is not sufficient to disclose it to others through preaching. [Note: Ebroicensis and Lyra: “to increase.”]

Leah, however, was bleary-eyed and fruitful because the active life, while occupied in work, sees less; but while it kindles neighbors to imitation, now through words and now through example, it begets many children in good works. Although it cannot stretch the mind into contemplation, nevertheless, from what it does outwardly it is able to beget followers. [Note: In the Vatican and Gussanville editions: “is able.”]

[Note: Vatican and Gussanville read “is able.” They then insert: “After Leah’s embrace Jacob comes to Rachel, because every perfect person is first joined to the active life for fruitfulness and afterward united to the contemplative life for rest.” Gussanville admits that this added material, through “Rightly,” is not contained in the manuscripts; we find it in none of them or in the old printed editions.] It is rightly said, then, in the measure of the reed that there are first six cubits and afterward a palm, because first the active life is practiced, so that afterward one may come to the contemplative life. [Col. 0954C–D]

### 11

But it must be understood that, just as the proper order of living is to advance from the active life to the contemplative, so the mind often usefully turns back from the contemplative to the active, so that, through what contemplation has inflamed in the mind, the active life may be held more perfectly. [Col. 0955A]

The active life ought therefore to lead us to the contemplative life; yet sometimes, because of what we have seen inwardly with the mind, the contemplative life ought to lead us back more effectively to the active life. [Note: Suessensis: “to lead contemplation back more effectively to the active life.” Ebroicensis and Lyra: “from the contemplative life.”]

Hence Jacob too returned to Leah after Rachel’s embrace, because after seeing the Beginning, the laborious life of good works is not to be abandoned altogether.

### 12

In the contemplative life there is a great struggle of the mind: when it raises itself toward heavenly things, when it stretches the soul toward spiritual realities, when it strives to pass beyond everything that is seen bodily, when it constricts itself in order to be enlarged.

Sometimes it conquers and overcomes the resisting darkness of its blindness, so that it may furtively and faintly touch something of the unbounded light. Yet immediately it is thrown back upon itself and returns; from that light, toward which it passed by breathing deeply, it returns with a sigh to the darkness of its own blindness. [Col. 0955B]

Sacred history aptly portrays this when it tells how blessed Jacob wrestled with an angel. [Note: After these words the Laudian and Suessian manuscripts add: “For this reason Jacob wrestles with the angel and limps on one foot, since …”]

When he was returning to his parents, he encountered an angel on the way and engaged in a great contest with him in wrestling (Genesis 32:24). The one who wrestles sometimes finds himself superior to his opponent and sometimes inferior to the one with whom he contends.

The angel therefore signifies the Lord, while Jacob, who contends with the angel, expresses the soul of every perfect man engaged in contemplation. When this soul strives to contemplate God, it is placed, as it were, in a contest. At one moment it seems to prevail, because by understanding and feeling it tastes something of the unbounded light; at another it succumbs, because even while tasting it, it again fails. [Col. 0955C]

The angel is therefore, as it were, defeated when God is grasped by intimate understanding.

### 13

But it should be noted that the same angel, once defeated, touched the sinew of Jacob’s thigh [Note: Many manuscripts: “held it.”] and immediately caused it to wither; from that time Jacob limped on one foot. For when the almighty God is already known through desire and understanding, he dries up in us every pleasure of the flesh. [Col. 0955D]

Previously, as though standing on two feet, we seemed both to seek God and to hold fast to the world. After recognizing God’s inner sweetness [Note: Laudian and Suessian manuscripts: “inner sweetness”], one foot remains sound in us while the other limps, because the love of the world must be weakened so that the love of God alone may grow strong in us.

If, therefore, we hold the angel, we limp on one foot, because as the strength of inward love grows in us [Note: Laudian manuscript: “the love of God.” Norman and Vallicellian manuscripts: “we are weakened … by the strength of the flesh.”], the strength of the flesh is undoubtedly weakened.

Everyone who limps on one foot relies only on the foot that remains sound. Thus, when earthly desire has already withered, a person supports himself with all his strength on the single foot of the love of God.

He stands upon it because he now carries suspended from the earth the foot of worldly love that he had been accustomed to place upon the earth. [Col. 0956A]

If, then, we return to our own parents—that is, to our spiritual fathers—let us hold the angel on the way, so that we may grasp God with inner sweetness.

The sweetness of the contemplative life is exceedingly lovable. It carries the soul beyond itself, opens heavenly things [Note: English manuscripts, with the Norman manuscripts: “seeks heavenly things.”], shows that earthly things ought to be despised, discloses spiritual realities to the eyes of the mind, and conceals bodily things.

Hence the Church rightly says in the Song of Songs:

> “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). [Note: Laudian manuscript: “I slept.”]

She sleeps with a watchful heart because, by advancing inwardly through contemplation, she rests from restless outward activity. [Note: Vatican and Gussanville editions: “from evil.”]

### 14

Amid these matters we must understand that, so long as one lives in mortal flesh, no one advances so far in the power of contemplation that he can fix the eyes of the mind upon the ray of the unbounded light itself. [Col. 0956B]

For the almighty God is not yet seen in his own glory; rather, the soul beholds something beneath him, from which it is refreshed [Note: Norman and Val. Cl.: “restored.”] and advances, afterward reaching the glory of his vision.

Thus Isaiah, when he confessed that he had seen the Lord, saying:

> “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and exalted” (Isaiah 6:1),

immediately added:

> “And the things beneath him filled the temple.”

When the proud and presumptuous King Uzziah dies, the Lord is seen, because when the pride of this world dies to the mind’s desire, then the mind itself contemplates the glory of God.

It should be noted that the Lord sits upon a high and exalted throne. What is his throne except the angelic or human creature, over which he presides through the understanding he has given it? [Col. 0956C]

This throne is called high and exalted because human nature, raised to heavenly glory, advances; and because the angelic creature, having been established in heaven through the many spirits who fell, has been exalted from the very place where it was confirmed so that it might not fall.

His temple is the same as his throne, because the eternal King dwells where he sits.

We are therefore his temple, since he deigns to dwell in our minds. But the things beneath him filled the temple because whatever of him is seen at present is not yet he himself, but is beneath him. [Col. 0956D]

Thus Jacob saw an angel and confessed that he had seen the Lord (Genesis 32:30), because when we behold his ministries, it is already a great thing that we are lifted above ourselves.

It should also be noted that it says, “They filled the temple,” because although an angel appears, he satisfies the desire of a weak mind, so that if it cannot yet see something greater, it may nevertheless admire the lesser thing that it sees.

The things beneath him therefore fill the temple because, as has been said, even when the mind has advanced in contemplation, it does not contemplate what he himself is, but what is beneath him.

In this contemplation a taste of inward rest is already touched. Since it is, as it were, a part of that rest and cannot yet be perfect, it is rightly written in the Apocalypse:

> “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Revelation 8:1).

Heaven is the soul of the righteous, as the Lord says through the prophet:

> “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 66:1).

And:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1).

When, therefore, the rest of the contemplative life takes place in the mind, there is silence in heaven, because the noise of earthly actions falls silent in thought, so that the mind may apply its ear to the innermost secret. [Note: Vatican and Gussanville editions: “may apply the mind to the ear.” This is refuted by our manuscripts and the English manuscripts.] [Col. 0957A]
