But because this rest of mind cannot be perfect in the present life, it is not said that silence was made in heaven for a full hour, but “about half an hour.” Even that half hour is not fully experienced, since “about” is prefixed: as soon as the mind begins to raise itself and to be suffused with the light of inward rest, the noise of thoughts quickly returns, and the mind, confused about itself, is blinded. [Col. 0957B]

The contemplative life, therefore, which there is called “about half an hour,” is called not a cubit but a palm by the prophet Ezekiel.

Behold, dearest brothers, while we wished to explain the reasons for each life, we have spoken somewhat more broadly than necessary by digression. But for good minds, to whom each of these lives is lovable in practice, this should not be burdensome to hear.

The text continues.

## The same passage

> “And he measured the breadth of the building with one reed, and its height also with one reed.”

### 15

The almighty God, who is neither stretched out by great things nor confined by small ones, speaks of the whole Church at once as though he were speaking of a single soul. Often, too, nothing prevents us from understanding as referring to the whole Church what he says of one soul. [Col. 0957C]

The breadth of the building pertains to charity, of which the Psalmist says:

> “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm 119:96).

For nothing is broader than to receive everyone into the embrace of love and to endure no narrowness of hatred. Charity is so broad that, in the vastness of its love, it can contain even enemies. Hence we are commanded:

> “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27).

We must also consider that breadth is extended in equality, while height is extended in sublimity. Breadth therefore pertains to love of neighbor, and height to understanding of the Creator. [Note: Val. Cl., with the Norman manuscript: “to the understanding of contemplation.”] [Col. 0957D]

But the breadth and height of the building are measured by one reed, because each soul will be as high in knowledge of God as it has been broad in love of neighbor. By enlarging itself beside itself through love, it raises itself upward through knowledge; and it becomes as exalted above itself as it stretches itself beside itself toward love of neighbor. [Note: Lyra: “by love of the righteous.”]

Since the building inhabited by God is completed from both angelic and human nature, the two creatures can be signified by the breadth and height of the building: the angelic creature is above, while the human creature is still below. [Col. 0958A]

Yet both are measured by one reed, because human humility will one day be brought to equality with the angels. Hence it is written:

> “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).

And hence it is said through John:

> “The measure of a human being, which is also the measure of an angel” (Revelation 21:17).

Humanity is led to that height of glory in which the angels rejoice that they have been established.

The breadth of the building is therefore as great as its height, because all the elect who now labor in lowly places will one day not be unequal to those blessed spirits.

Amid these matters, let us return to our own minds and love God and our neighbor with all the depths of our hearts. Let us be enlarged in the affection of charity, so that we may be exalted in the glory of sublimity. Let us share our neighbor’s suffering through love, so that we may be joined to God through knowledge. Let us stoop to our least brothers on earth, so that we may be made equal to the angels in heaven, because the man who signifies the Redeemer by his image measured the breadth of the building with one reed and its height also with one reed. [Col. 0958B]

Now he measures conduct, weighs deeds, and considers thoughts, so that afterward Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten of the Father, may render recompense without end—he who lives and reigns with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY III

In the explanation of three verses, the building of the Church, constructed from all the righteous under both Testaments, is principally described.

### 1

> “The man in whose hand a measuring reed is described as being.” [Note: This should be read according to the manuscripts, not as the printed editions have it: “the man whose measuring reed is described as being in his hand.”]

[Col. 0958C]

## Ezekiel 40:6

> “He came to the gate that faced toward the eastern road.”

Who else is signified by the name of this gate except the Lord himself and our Redeemer, who became for us the door of the heavenly kingdom? As he himself says:

> “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

But since we have said that the same man clothed in linen bears the figure of the Lord, we must ask how it is fitting that the same Lord can be signified both by the man and by the gate, when the man comes to the gate. Does he perhaps come to himself? [Note: Longipontan manuscript: “to himself through himself—is it not so?”]

Or is this indeed the case, since he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying:

> “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber. But whoever enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10:1–2). [Col. 0958D]

A little later he says:

> “I am the door” (ibid., 9).

And again he adds:

> “I am the good shepherd” (ibid., 14).

If, then, the shepherd enters through the door, and he himself is the door and the shepherd, then undoubtedly he enters through himself.

Behold, while we wish to unravel Ezekiel’s meaning, we have also raised a question from the Gospel. We must therefore ask how he both enters and enters through himself.

Our Lord and Redeemer, together with the holy Church which he redeemed, is one substance according to the flesh, as Paul testifies when he says:

> “I complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Colossians 1:24). [Col. 0959A]

The Church is the body of this head, and Christ is the head of this body (Ephesians 1:22). The body—that is, the holy Church—rejoices in this head of hers when it says through the Psalmist:

> “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Psalm 27:6).

Because she herself is also to be exalted one day, she now rejoices in heaven that her head has already been exalted above her enemies.

When, therefore, each of the elect comes to life, because they are his members and enter through him to him, he himself enters through himself to himself. For he himself is in his members who enter; he himself is the head to whom the entering members come. [Col. 0959B]

The prophet Ezekiel indicates this in many ways. He says that the man came to the gate and shows what that gate is, saying:

> “It faced toward the eastern road.”

For he himself is the way for us, who said:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

He is also the eastern way, of whom it is written:

> “Behold, a man; his name is Orient” (Zechariah 6:12).

The gate therefore faces toward the eastern road because it signifies him who made a path for us toward the rising of the light.

## 2

Each preacher may also be understood by the name “gate,” because whoever opens for us by his mouth the door of the heavenly kingdom is a gate. Hence twelve gates are described either in John’s Apocalypse (Rev. 21:21) or in the final vision of this prophet. By the name “gate” the knowledge of sacred Scripture may also quite appropriately be understood, since, when it opens understanding to us, it unfolds the door of the heavenly kingdom. By the name “gate” we may also understand faith, which we first touch in order to enter the structures of the virtues. Hence it is plainly added:

> **IBID. — And he ascended by its steps.**

## 3

For what are the steps of this gate except the merits of the virtues? Whether in the knowledge of the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, or in the knowledge of divine speech, or in the faith itself that we have received concerning him, we reach higher attainments by certain steps. No one suddenly becomes supreme; rather, in a good way of life, each person begins with small things in order to arrive at great ones.

The Psalmist says of these steps: “God will be known in her steps when he receives her” (Ps. 47:4). For when the Lord receives holy Church [the text is cited in *De poenitentia*, distinction 2, chapter *Cum sanctam*], he is known in her steps, because her glory is revealed through her growth. The more holy Church advances by ascending, the more God becomes known to human beings through her virtues.

Blessed Job also speaks of these steps, saying: “I shall declare him according to my individual steps” (Job 31:37). He declares the omnipotent Lord according to his individual steps who, through the increases of virtue that he receives, continually returns to him the praise of his goodness. If there were no steps in the ascent of the heart, the Psalmist would not say: “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. 84:8).

## 4

Nor is it surprising that there are steps from strength to strength, since each virtue is increased, as it were, by certain steps and is thus brought through growth in merit to the highest things. The beginnings of a virtue are one thing, its progress another, and its perfection another.

For if faith itself were not led to its perfection by certain steps, the holy apostles would certainly not have said: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5).

[Note: Several manuscripts read *auge* (“increase”).] And someone came to Jesus who wished his son to be healed; when asked whether he believed, he answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:24).

Consider, I beg you, what is being said. If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? Yet because faith grows through the hidden inspiration of grace by stages of merit, at one and the same time the man who did not yet believe perfectly both believed and was unbelieving.

## 5

The Lord describes these steps under the figure of the harvest, saying:

> “The kingdom of God is like this: as if a man should cast seed into the earth, and sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he does not know it. For the earth bears fruit of its own accord, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when it has produced the fruit, immediately he sends the sickle, because the harvest has come” (Mark 4:26–29).

[Note: Laudensis, Longipontanus, and most others read *si iaciat* (“if he casts”).]

[Note: The words “then the ear” are omitted in the Vatican and Gussanville editions; we have restored them from the manuscripts, the old edition, and the text of the Gospel.]

[Note: The manuscripts Laudensis, Longipontanus, Normannicus, and others read *cum se produxerit fructus* (“when it has produced the fruit”), whereas the printed editions read *Et cum ex se produxerit fructus* (“and when it has produced the fruit of itself”).]

A man casts seed into the earth when he implants a good intention in his heart.

[Note: Laudensis reads *miserit, sano sensu* (“has placed it, with sound understanding”).] After he has cast the seed, he sleeps, because he rests in the hope of good work. He rises night and day, because he advances amid adversity and prosperity.

[Note: Laudensis and Longipontanus read *quia in adversa* (“because amid adverse things”).]

The seed germinates and grows while he does not know it, because, even when he is not yet able to measure his growth, the virtue once conceived is led onward to progress. The earth bears fruit of its own accord because, with grace going before it, the human mind spontaneously rises toward the fruit of good work.

But this same earth produces first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. To produce the blade is still to possess the tender beginnings of goodness. The blade reaches the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward toward the progress of good work. The full grain in the ear bears fruit when the virtue has advanced so far that it can become the substance of a strong and perfect work.

But when it has produced the fruit, immediately he sends the sickle, because the harvest has come. For the omnipotent God sends the sickle when the fruit has been produced and cuts down his harvest, because when he has led each person to perfected works, he cuts short that person’s temporal life by a sentence he issues, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly storehouses.

When, therefore, we conceive good desires, we cast seed into the earth. When, however, we begin to do what is right, we are the blade. When we grow toward the progress of good work, we reach the ear. And when we are made firm in the perfection of that same good work, we bring forth the full grain in the ear.

[Note: The Roman correctors, citing this passage in *De poenitentia*, distinction 2, chapter 15, point out that the original lacks the words “But when we grow toward the progress of good work, we reach the ear.” Nevertheless, they occur in all our manuscripts.]

## 6

Peter had indeed been the blade. At the time of the Passion, following the Lord through love, he feared confessing him at the voice of a servant girl (Luke 22:57). There was already greenness in his mind, because he believed in the Redeemer of all; but he was still exceedingly pliable, and the foot of fear trampled him.

He had already risen into the ear when he saw alive in Galilee, at the angel’s announcement, the one whom he had feared confessing as destined to die.

[Note: Suessionensis reads “but he had reached the full grain in the ear.”]

But then he had reached the full grain in the ear when the Spirit came from above and strengthened his mind in love of Christ, so that he became so firm that, when beaten, he despised the strength of his persecutors and freely proclaimed his Redeemer amid the blows (Acts 5:29).

Therefore, no one who is still seen to be in the tender stage of the mind with regard to a good purpose should be despised, because God’s grain begins with the blade in order to become grain.

The man clothed in linen came to the gate because our Lord and Redeemer is brought to himself as his members enter. And he ascended by its steps because, as we make progress, he is exalted all the more to us, the higher and more incomprehensible he is recognized to be. He is said to ascend by the steps of our virtues because he is shown to be so much higher as our mind is separated from lowly things.

It follows:

> **IBID. — And he measured the threshold of the gate with one reed in width—that is, one threshold with one reed in width.**

## 7

Why, after “the threshold of the gate” has been said, is “one threshold” immediately added, unless it plainly indicates that another threshold farther below is still being mentioned?

[Note: Vallicellanus reads “the lowest threshold.”]

The gate rises from the threshold in order to be a gate. If, therefore, the Lord is the gate, who is the threshold of this gate except those ancient fathers from whose lineage the Lord was graciously pleased to become incarnate? As Paul says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

It should be noted in this statement of Paul that gods and other human beings have also been so called, as it is said to Moses: “I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). And through the Psalmist it is said: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. 82:6). Again: “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Ps. 82:1).

But it is one thing to be called God by designation, and another to be called God by nature.

[Note: Laudensis reads “essentially.”]

Although Moses was appointed as a god to Pharaoh, he is called a god within all things, not God above all things. But he who was incarnate within the Virgin’s womb is called God above all things.

Thus the threshold of the gate is the ancient fathers, from whom he was born who opened for us access to the kingdom of heaven. The threshold of the gate is measured with one reed because those ancient fathers, who were able to proclaim our Redeemer both by prophecy and by good living, possessed, as it were, six cubits in the perfection of work and a palm in the beginning of contemplation.

Because their life was made sublime by perfect action united in the unity of faith and by contemplation begun, the measure of the threshold was in one reed.

It follows:

> **VERSE — And the chamber, one reed in length and one reed in width.**

## 8

Let us consider what ordinarily takes place in a chamber, and from that let us gather what takes place in holy Church. In a chamber the bridegroom and bride are joined in covenant and united to one another in love.

What, then, are the chambers in holy Church except the hearts of those in whom the soul is joined to the invisible Bridegroom through love, so that it burns with desire for him, desires none of the things that are in the world, counts the length of the present life as punishment, hastens to depart, and rests in the embrace of love in the vision of the heavenly Bridegroom?

The mind that has already become such receives no consolation from the present life, but sighs, burns, pants, and is troubled from its inmost depths for the one whom it loves. Bodily health itself becomes worthless to it, because it has been pierced by the wound of love. Hence in the Song of Songs it says: “I am wounded with love” (Song 2:5, according to the Septuagint).

A heart’s health is evil when it does not know the pain of this wound. But when the soul begins to pant toward heavenly desire and to feel the wound of love, it becomes healthier through the wound by which it was previously sick.

## 9

For a mind that loves its Bridegroom ardently, there is ordinarily one consolation for the delay of the present life:

[Note: All printed editions before Gussanville, supported by the Norman manuscripts, read *de amore vitae* (“concerning love of life”); this is a manifest error.] that, while it is itself kept from his vision, other souls may advance through his word and burn with the flames of love for the heavenly Bridegroom.

It grieves because it sees itself delayed; everything it sees is sad to it because it does not yet see the one whom it desires to see. But, as I have said, there is no small consolation if, while the fervent soul is delayed, many are gathered through it, so that it may see him later with many whom it had wished to see sooner by itself.

Hence again the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Sustain me with flowers, and surround me with apples, because I am sick with love” (Song 2:5).

For what are the flowers except souls beginning good works and giving off the fragrance of heavenly desire? What are the apples among the flowers except minds already perfected in goodness, which reach the fruit of good work from the beginning of a holy purpose?

She who is sick with love therefore asks to be sustained with flowers and surrounded with apples, because, if she is not yet permitted to see the one whom she desires, it is a great consolation for her to rejoice in the progress of others. Thus the soul languishing in holy love is sustained by flowers and apples, so that, while it is not yet able to contemplate the face of God, it may rest in the good work of its neighbor.

## 10

Let us consider, I beg you, what kind of chamber Paul’s mind had been. He said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). To what extent had he joined himself to the omnipotent God in love, when he counted Christ alone as life for himself and death as gain?

For this reason he says again: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ is much better” (Phil. 1:23).

But since you desire to depart, let us see with what love you languish. Since you see that you are meanwhile delayed, do you not, I ask, seek to be sustained with flowers? Certainly you do, for he continues: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:24).

And to his advancing disciples he says: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ?” (1 Thess. 2:19).

## 11

This is why that same chamber is said to have been measured with one reed in length and one reed in width. Length pertains to the long-suffering of expectation, and width to the breadth of charity.

Each chamber therefore has as much length as it is able to have width, because the mind kindled by heavenly desire shows as much perseverance in waiting for God as it has love for gathering in its neighbor, and patiently bears the delays of its length because the breadth of charity expands itself in the progress of its neighbor.

[Note: Laudensis reads “joined to heavenly love.”]

[Note: Vallicellanus reads *portat de compassione primi moras longitudinis* (“bears, out of compassion for the first, the delays of length”); the reading is uncertain.]

The length itself may also signify the long-suffering patience shown toward one’s neighbor. And because width signifies charity, which opens the bosom of the mind and receives both friends and enemies into love, the chamber has as much length as width: to the degree that the mind is broad through love, it is also patient through long-suffering.

For each person bears his neighbor to the degree that he loves him. If you love, you bear; if you cease to love, you cease to endure. For the less we love someone, the less we tolerate him, because, when disgust rushes in, the deeds of our neighbor are more quickly brought upon us as a burdensome weight, which the feather of charity does not make light for us.

It follows:

> **IBID. — And between the chambers, five cubits.**

## 12

He had spoken above of one chamber, and afterward he says that there are five cubits between the chambers, for the reason, evidently, that many chambers make one, just as many churches are called one Church. Thus in John’s Apocalypse letters are written to seven churches, through which the one catholic Church is signified.

As we have said, those in holy Church who thirst to see God in fervent love and are already joined to him through desire are called chambers. Yet there are some in her who, unable to penetrate subtle things and still weighed down by the five bodily senses, love him who made all things less because they are more tightly bound to the things that have been made.

They already strive to exercise themselves in the fear of the Lord and to extend themselves toward love of neighbor; they perform good works bodily and redeem sins by almsgiving. But because they do not know how to burn with intimate love toward heavenly desire, they are still held, as it were, bound by bodily senses.

These, therefore, are not chambers, but they are contained among the chambers, because, under the guidance of those who love the vision of God perfectly, they too are directed toward the advancement of the mind.

There are therefore five cubits between the chambers, because those who have not yet risen from the external five senses to mystical understanding, while they are among those who burn with the spirit of love, progress in the construction of faith as though they were dwelling among chambers, and are not separated from the measure of the heavenly building.

For they withdraw themselves little by little from the appetite of bodily senses, and, enlarging the space of the mind, extend themselves here and there toward the chambers by imitating the charity that they behold.

The fact that they are described not by six cubits but by five signifies their remaining imperfection.

## 13

Nevertheless, through good desire they are remembered as being within the measure of the spiritual building, since the voice of holy Church says through the Psalmist: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. 139:16).

Again the same Psalmist says: “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small together with the great” (Ps. 115:13).

Although these people are imperfect and small, insofar as they are able to understand, they love both God and their neighbor, and therefore do not neglect to perform the good things they can. Although they have not yet advanced to spiritual gifts so as to raise the soul either to perfect action or to burning contemplation, they nevertheless do not withdraw from love of God and neighbor insofar as they are able to embrace it in mind.

[Note: Lyrensis reads: “so that they may raise the soul to contemplation; nevertheless, from the love of God and from the practice of good works, insofar as they are able to grasp them in mind, they do not withdraw.”]

Thus it happens that they too, although placed in a lower position, nevertheless belong to the building of holy Church. For although they may be lesser in teaching, prophecy, the grace of miracles, or the fuller practice of contempt for the world, they stand upon the foundation of fear and love, in which they are made firm.

Although they do not burn with the fire of heavenly desire, they are nevertheless animated in those outward matters that they are able to practice by the warmth of charity, and they are contained among the buildings of their more excellent neighbors.

Hence the bride rightly speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its recliner of gold, its ascent of purple; the midst he paved with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3:9–10).

We should not believe that Solomon, a king of such greatness, who abounded in immense riches so that the weight of his gold could not be reckoned and silver had no value in those days, made himself a wooden litter.

Rather, our Solomon, that is, our Peaceful One, made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. The cedars of Lebanon are exceedingly imperishable wood.

## 14

The litter of our King, therefore, is holy Church, constructed from strong fathers—that is, from imperishable minds.

[Note: Laudensis and Suessionensis read “as though from cedar woods, that is, from imperishable [minds].”]

It is rightly called a litter because it carries souls each day to the eternal banquet of its Creator. Its columns were made of silver because the preachers of the Church shine with the light of sacred eloquence.

[Note: Laudensis reads “with the light of holy speech.”]

With the silver columns there is also a golden recliner, because through what is spoken clearly by the holy preachers, the minds of their hearers find the radiance of an inner brightness on which they may recline.

[Note: The printed editions, against the English, Norman, and other manuscripts, read “the radiance of charity”; the words that follow strongly establish that *claritatis* (“brightness”) should be read.]

Through what they hear lucidly and openly, they rest in that which shines in the heart. Its columns, therefore, are silver and its recliner is made of gold, because through the light of speech the brightness of repose is found in the mind.

That inner radiance illumines the mind, so that through intention it may rest there where the grace of preaching is not sought.

Of this same holy Church it is written: “The wings of the dove are covered with silver, and the hinder parts of her back are in the appearance of gold” (Ps. 68:14).

[Note: Suessionensis reads “in pallor.”]

Here, because she is filled with the spirit of gentleness and has wings covered with silver like a dove, she contains the appearance of gold in the hinder parts of her back: here she clothes her preachers with the light of speech, but in the age to come she displays in herself the radiance of brightness.

But to what kind of ascent the clear thing shown within pertains, he adds when he immediately continues concerning the same litter: “Its ascent is purple” (Song 3:10).

True purple, because it is dyed from blood, is rightly seen in the color of blood. And because a very great multitude of the faithful reached the kingdom at the beginning of the Church’s birth through the blood of martyrdom, our King made the ascent in the litter purple, because one reaches what is seen clearly within through the tribulation of blood.

## 15

What, then, shall we wretched people do, deprived as we are of all strength? We cannot be columns in this litter, because in us neither strength of action nor the light of preaching shines forth.

We do not have a golden recliner, because we do not yet behold, as we ought, the repose of inner brightness through spiritual understanding. We are not a purple ascent, because we are unable to pour out our blood for our Redeemer.

What, then, is to be done with us? What hope will there be if no one reaches the kingdom except one endowed with the highest virtues?

Yet our consolation is also present. Let us love God as much as we can; let us also love our neighbor; and together we too belong to the litter of God, because, as it is written there: “He paved the midst with charity.”

[Note: Ebroicensis and Lyrensis read “we reach it.” Laudensis reads “we shall reach it.”]

Have charity, and without doubt you arrive there where both silver columns are raised and the purple ascent is held.

[Note: Laudensis, Suessionensis, Longipontanus, and Ebroicensis have this reading. In the Uticensis manuscript it was once read thus, but the word *pervenis* was struck through with an obelus; *pertines* (“you belong”) is now written above it, as in the printed editions.]

For that this is said on account of our weakness is plainly shown when he immediately adds there: “For the daughters of Jerusalem.”

For the word of God, which says not “sons” but “daughters,” what else did it signify by the female sex except the weakness of minds?

Thus what is there said to be present among the silver columns, the golden recliner, and the purple ascent—the midst being charity for the daughters of Jerusalem—is here designated between the chambers by five cubits. Those who are weak in virtues, if they do not neglect to do the good things they can with charity, are not alien from God’s building.

It follows:

> **IBID. — And the threshold of the gate beside the vestibule of the gate, within, one reed.**

## 16

When the threshold now being described is said to be within, beside the vestibule of the gate, it is plainly shown that the threshold described earlier was outside.

But if the Lord is the gate, let us ask what the threshold of the gate is within and what it is outside. Through a threshold, everyone enters the gate. What, then, are these two thresholds except the fathers of the Old Testament and the fathers of the New Testament?

Not only those from whom the Lord was graciously pleased to become incarnate, but all the fathers of the Old Testament were the threshold of this gate, because those who were worthy to foretell him and to hope in him opened the way of faith to all who came to him; and all who believed in the Lord through them entered, as it were, through the threshold of this gate.

But why is the outer threshold mentioned first and the inner threshold afterward, unless because the fathers of the Old Testament came first and the teachers of the New Testament afterward?

The outer threshold rightly designates the fathers of the Old Testament, because through their preaching wicked deeds were punished. But through the words of the new fathers each person’s mind is also restrained from unlawful thoughts, since guilt is shown to be complete even in the deliberation of the heart.

They took care to prohibit the souls of their hearers from crimes, acts of cruelty, and robbery. These, however, by cutting away not only wicked deeds but also unlawful thoughts, became for us nothing other than the inner threshold.

Hence Truth himself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother [without cause] shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:21–22).

[Note: “Without cause” is absent from the manuscripts Normannicus, Longipontanus, and Vallicellanus.]

The outer threshold also rightly designates those fathers who stood farther away in time from the incarnation of our Redeemer.

Certainly, with Abel’s blood, the Passion of the Church had already begun, and there is one Church of the elect who came before and those who came afterward. Yet because it is said to the disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke 10:24), it was as though the ancient fathers stood outside, since they did not see the presence of our Redeemer bodily.

They were therefore outside, but not divided from holy Church, because in mind, in deed, and in preaching they already held the mysteries of this faith and beheld the exalted state of this holy Church, which we behold not while still awaiting it, but already possessing it.

For just as we were saved by faith in the past Passion of our Redeemer, so they were saved by faith in the same Passion that was still to come. They were therefore outside, not outside the mystery, but outside the time.

## 17

Hence, too, in the construction of the tabernacle, in order that the silver columns might stand within, bronze pegs were commanded to be fixed all around on the outside, to which the tabernacle would be fastened and held.

The silver columns therefore are fixed within, while the bronze pegs are fixed outside, and ropes are tied to them so that the tabernacle may remain firm. In this way, so that the holy apostles might stand firm in the light of their preaching and the entire tabernacle—that is, holy Church—might stand in the integrity of faith, the fathers of the Old Testament and the prophets were fixed outside like bronze pegs.

With the ropes of their words they bound the minds of the preachers in firmness and fastened this dwelling of God in the stability of faith.

[Note: All the printed editions read “are fixed in a circle,” contrary to our manuscripts.]

The pegs are therefore outside because they belonged to the time before this holy Church. Yet they bind those who are within it, because, by proclaiming the heavenly mysteries that were to come, they made them believable to all after they had been revealed.

Thus, so that the columns within might stand immovable, the pegs outside hold the ropes. For the preaching of those who were able both to see and to foretell the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation before it happened obtained for the holy apostles a perfect belief in that mystery.

Hence the first of the apostles himself, clearly a great column of the true tabernacle, rightly says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1:19).

By these words he indicates that, although he had risen higher from the summit, he nevertheless remained bound there in faith.

[Note: Gussanville alone reads *ibi religatus* (“bound there”). “Bound” refers to the column. In the Vatican and Gussanville editions, after “in faith,” the following is added: “The writing of the prophetic word, however, was made for us a lamp in the darkness of the present life and a light for the journey; hence the Psalmist says: ‘Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths.’ Yet this, and so forth.” The editors do not indicate where this material was taken from. Gussanville admits that it is absent from the manuscripts and from certain printed editions. It appears to be a note that entered the text from the margin.]

Nevertheless, the lamp of prophetic speech now shines for those who understand, but remains covered for those who do not yet understand by the obscurities of allegories.

Hence the Psalmist also says of those same words of the prophets: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 18:12), because the knowledge in the prophets is hidden.

Nor is it without reason that the columns were made of silver but the pegs of bronze, because what the apostles now preach clearly, the prophets spoke obscurely under mystical understanding.

They were therefore rightly signified by the metal bronze, since they were not clear in their preaching. But the holy apostles, because they possessed the light of preaching concerning the mystery of our Redeemer, were represented by silver columns.

[Note: From these words, which had been badly read, the editors produced the reading “who, concerning the mystery of our Redeemer …”]

It should be noted that silver both sounds and shines, whereas bronze sounds but does not shine. The preachers of the New Testament spoke openly of things that they were also able to show. But the preachers of the Old Testament, because they uttered obscure sayings about the heavenly mystery beneath the shadows of allegories, produced sound as though without light.

Thus what is there designated by pegs and columns is here designated by the outer threshold and the inner threshold.

## 18

But if in this passage we understand the gate as sacred Scripture, it too has two thresholds, an outer and an inner, because it is divided into the letter and allegory.

The outer threshold of sacred Scripture is the letter; its inner threshold is allegory. Because we proceed through the letter toward allegory, we come, as it were, from the threshold that is outside to that which is within.

In Scripture there are very many things that build up the mind according to the letter, so that through what is done outwardly the mind of the hearer is drawn inward.

[Note: Laudensis reads “is said.”]

There we find commandments for action and examples of virtue. There it is commanded what we ought also to do bodily. There what is prescribed for action is displayed in the deeds of holy and courageous men, so that, after clearer commandments and the examples of the righteous have instructed us in good action, we may then direct the foot of the mind toward the inner threshold—that is, toward the mystical understanding of inner contemplation—if we are able.

Study, I beg you, dearly beloved brothers, to meditate on the words of God. Do not despise the writings of our Redeemer that have been sent to us. It is a very great thing that through them the mind is rekindled to warmth, lest it grow numb in the cold of its iniquity.

## 19

When we recognize that those righteous men who came before us acted courageously, we too gird ourselves for the courage of good action, and the mind of the reader is set ablaze by the flame of holy examples.

It sees what courageous deeds they performed and is greatly indignant with itself because it does not imitate such things. Hence the voice of the bridegroom rightly says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with its battlements. A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty” (Song 4:4).

For in the neck there is the throat, and in the throat there is the voice.

## 20

What, then, is signified by the neck of holy Church except her sacred utterances? When a thousand shields are said to hang from it, the universal number is shown by this perfect number, because all our defenses are contained in sacred speech.

There are God’s commandments there; there are the examples of the righteous.

If the mind grows sluggish in desire for its Creator, let it hear what is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your mind and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37).

[Note: Lyrensis reads “with all your heart.”]

Perhaps someone is slipping into hatred of his neighbor? Let him hear what is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39).

[Note: Longipontanus reads “hatred,” omitting “into.”]

Does he covet another’s property? Let him hear what is written there: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. 20:17).

Is the mind inflamed with anger over an injury inflicted by the mouth or deed of a neighbor? Let it hear what is said: “You shall not seek vengeance, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (Lev. 19:18).

Is the mind, badly wounded by the lust of the flesh, inflamed? So that the eye may not follow the mind, let it hear what was said a little earlier: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

[Note: This passage is not cited anywhere in the whole homily, unless we suppose that the same context is being combined from these words and from the preceding words already cited: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients,” Matt. 5:21 and following.]

Perhaps someone is preparing to release his heart against an enemy into hatred? Let him hear what is written there: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:35).

But perhaps one who no longer steals what belongs to others still retains his own possessions in a disordered way? Let him hear what is said there: “Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke 12:33).

[Note: Laudensis, Vallicellanus, and Longipontanus read “for the pleasure of desire.”]

Does the weakened mind desire to enjoy both God and the world? Let it hear what is written there: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24).

[Col. 0969B] Another person retains what he possesses not from the necessity of livelihood but according to the will of desire? Let him hear what is said there: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

For some abandon everything, while many renounce everything even while possessing it, because they retain possessions for use in such a way that they do not succumb to them through desire.

Does someone wish to remain sluggish and avoid undertaking labor for the Lord even when he is able? Let him hear what is written there: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23).

Thus, on the neck of the Church—that is, in the preaching of sacred speech, which is said to resemble the tower of David in its defense and height—a thousand shields hang, because there are as many defenses for our breast as there are commandments there.

[Col. 0969C] **21.** To preserve innocence, do we hasten to remain humble even when injured by our neighbor? Let Abel come before our eyes (Gen. IV, 8), of whom it is written that he was killed by his brother, yet we do not read that he resisted. Is purity of mind chosen even in the marital union?

[Note: Laud. reads “with conjugal [purity].”]

Enoch should be imitated, who, though living in marriage, walked with God and was no longer found, because God took him away (ibid., V, 22).

Do we hasten to place God’s commandments above our present advantage?

[Note: The same manuscript reads “our humility,” which is wholly unacceptable, however much authority its antiquity gives it.]

Let Noah come before our eyes. Setting aside the care of his household,

[Note: Beccensis and Lyr. read “who, attending to mysterious matters.”]

at the command of the almighty Lord he spent a hundred years occupied with the construction of the ark (ibid., VI, 14).

Do we strive to undertake the virtue of obedience? We must look to Abraham (ibid., XII, 5), who, leaving home, kindred, and country, obeyed by departing for the place that he was to receive as an inheritance, and went out not knowing where he was going (Heb. XI, 8). He was ready to kill, for the sake of an eternal inheritance, the beloved heir whom he had received. And because he did not delay to offer his only son to the Lord, he received in his offspring the whole multitude of the nations (Gen. XXII, 16–17).

Does simplicity of conduct please us? Let Isaac come to mind, whose tranquil way of life adorned him in the sight of almighty God (ibid., XXIV and following).

Are we seeking laborious courage, so that it may be attained? Let Jacob be recalled (ibid., XXIX, 20; XXX, 29), who, after learning to serve a man courageously, was brought to such virtue that he could not be overcome by the angel who wrestled with him (ibid., XXXII, 25).

Are we trying to overcome the allurements of the flesh? Let Joseph return to mind. When his mistress tempted him, he took care to preserve chastity even at the risk of his life (ibid., XXXIX, 12, 20). Hence it came about that, because he knew how to govern his own members well, he was also placed in charge of governing all Egypt.

[Note: Laud. reads “by governing.”]

[Col. 0970B] Are we seeking to attain gentleness and patience? Let us bring Moses before our eyes (Num. XII, 3). Ruling six hundred thousand armed men, apart from children and women, he is described as being gentler than all the people who lived upon the face of the earth.

Are we inflamed with zeal for uprightness against vices? Let Phinehas be brought before our eyes (ibid., XXV, 7, 8, 11). Piercing those who were coupling with the sword,

[Note: Rothomag. and Lyr. read “he restored chastity to the people.”]

he restored chastity to the people and, in his anger, appeased the anger of God.

Do we seek to rely upon the hope of almighty God amid uncertainties? Let Joshua be recalled (Josh. III, 5, 8). While he faced doubtful battles with a resolute mind,

[Note: Ebroic., Rothomag., and Lyr. read “he added battles to battle.”]

he reached victory without hesitation.

Do we now wish to set aside enmities in our minds and enlarge our spirit in kindness? Let Samuel be brought to mind (I Sam. VIII, 5). When the people had deposed him from leadership and that same people asked him to pour out prayers to the Lord on their behalf, he replied: “Far be it from me to commit this sin against the Lord, that I should cease to pray for you” (ibid., XII, 23).

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read “to punish enmities.” Although the error is gross, it was propagated from the first edition into all the others, no editor noticing that “to punish enmities” does not pertain to the kindness proposed here, nor is it taught by Samuel’s example. Laud. reads “to set aside enmities.”]

For the holy man believed that he would commit a fault if, in prayer, he did not return the kindness of grace to those whom he had endured as adversaries even to the point of his deposition.

Again, when he was sent by the Lord’s command to anoint David as king, he replied: “How shall I go? Saul will find me and kill me” (ibid., XVI, 2).

[Note: Pl. Norm. reads “How shall I go?”]

And yet, because he knew that God was angry with that same Saul, he had afflicted himself with such great grief that the Lord said to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him?” (ibid., 1). Let us therefore consider how great a flame of charity burned in his heart: he wept for the man from whom he feared death.

But do we wish to take precautions against someone whom we fear? We must carefully consider whether, if we should perhaps find an opportunity, we might return evil for evil to the very man from whom we flee.

Let David therefore return to our memory. He found the king who was pursuing him in a situation where he could have killed him, yet, placed in the very power to strike, he chose the good that he himself ought to do, rather than the evil that the other deserved to suffer, saying: “Far be it from me to lay my hand upon the Lord’s anointed” (ibid., XXIV, 7; XXVI, 11). And when that same Saul was later killed by his enemies, he mourned the man whom he had endured as his persecutor while he lived (II Sam. I, 17).

Do we resolve to speak freely to the rulers of this world when they go astray? Let the authority of John return to our minds. Rebuking Herod’s wickedness, he did not fear being killed for the sake of speaking rightly (Mark VI, 18, 27). And because Christ is the truth, he laid down his life for Christ precisely because he laid it down for the truth.

Are we now hastening to lay down our flesh for God in death? Let Peter come to mind (Acts V, 41), who rejoices amid scourging, who, after being beaten, resists the rulers, and who despises his own life for the sake of life.

When we are preparing, through desire for death, to despise adversities, let Paul be brought before our eyes. Ready not only to be bound but also to die for Christ, he does not make his life more precious than himself (Acts XX, 22, 24).

Do we seek to set our hearts ablaze with the fire of charity? Let us weigh the words of John, whose every utterance is heated by the fire of charity (I John I and following).

**22.** Since, then, whenever we seek a defense of virtue in the voice of sacred eloquence, we find one there, a thousand shields hang from it, “the whole armor of the strong” (Song IV, 4). If we wish to fight against spiritual wickedness, let us seek in the neck of the Church, which stands upright for us like the tower of David—that is, in divine eloquence—the weapons of protection, so that, through discernment of the commandment, the strength of assistance may be taken up against vices.

For behold, do we hasten to be strong against the powers of the air? In this tower we find the armor of our mind, taking from it the commandments of the Creator and from it the examples of those who came before us, by which we may be armed invincibly against our adversaries.

Whenever you desire to undertake any virtue and see that it has already been fulfilled there by the fathers, you find there the armor by which you may be fortified against spiritual battles. A thousand shields hang there: let anyone who desires to fight take one, fortify his breast with that virtue, and send forth the arrows of words.

**23.** It should also be noted that it is said to have been built with its battlements. The battlements perform the same function as the shields, because both protect the combatant. Yet there is this difference between them: we move a shield wherever we wish for our protection; with a battlement we can defend ourselves, but we cannot move it. A shield is in the hand, whereas a battlement is not held.

What, then, is the difference between battlements and shields, except that in sacred eloquence we read both the miracles of the fathers who came before us and hear of the virtues of their good works? There we learn that one man was able to divide the sea, another to halt the sun, another to raise the dead, another to raise up a paralytic by a word, another to cure the sick by his shadow, and another to ward off fevers by his waistcloths (Acts XIX).

[Note: All the manuscripts read “by his waistcloths.” Only Cod. Rothomag. gives in the margin, as an alternative reading, “by his presence,” which is adopted by the Paris editions of 1502, 1518, and 1571; Vatic. Gussanv. reads “by his personal presence.”]

Yet all of them were gentle through the long endurance of patience, fervent in their zeal for uprightness, rich in the preaching of the word, and at the same time generous in mercy. Their miracles testify how truly they spoke about God, for they would not have performed such things through him unless they had spoken truthfully about him. Their deeds testify how devout, how humble, and how kind they were.

If, therefore, we are tested concerning the faith that we have received through their preaching, let us contemplate the miracles of those who spoke, and we shall be strengthened in the faith that we received from them. What, then, are their miracles except our battlements? Through them we can indeed be fortified, yet we do not hold such things in the hand of our own will, for we are unable to perform them.

A shield, however, is in the hand and gives defense, because the virtue of patience and the virtue of mercy, with grace going before us, are both within the power of the will and protect us from the danger of adversity.

[Note: Longip. reads “from the adversity of danger.”]

Our tower, then, has been built with its battlements. A thousand shields hang in it, because in sacred Scripture we are hidden from the arrows of adversity beneath the miracles of the fathers, and we also hold in the hand of action the defenses of holy conduct.

It should be noted, however, that the threshold of the gate is measured by one reed. The reed extends to six cubits and a handbreadth, because in sacred Scripture we find both the teaching of perfect action and the beginning of heavenly contemplation.

But if by “gate” each preacher is understood in this passage, the outer threshold in the gate is the active life, while the inner threshold is the contemplative life. Through the former one walks in faith; through the latter one hastens toward sight.

[Note: “Sight,” as it is contrasted here with faith, signifies vision and apprehension, from the ancient verb *spicio*, whence *aspicio*, *conspicio*, and so forth.]

The former leads outward, so that each person ought to live well; the latter leads inward, so that from a good life one may attain eternal joys.

This is sufficient for us to have discussed today. Since, in passing on to other matters, we have spoken for a long time in ecstasy, let us reserve what follows for another reading, recovering through silence and hoping in the Word who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY IV

*Four verses, from the ninth through the twelfth, are explained allegorically or morally, and the homily is concluded.*

[Col. 0972D] 1341 **1.** “The man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze”—Ezek. XL, 9: “He measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits, and its front, two cubits.” And lest we suppose that the vestibule was outside the gate, the text adds:

**ibid.**—“The vestibule of the gate was on the inside.”

What is signified by the inner vestibule except the breadth of eternal life, which is now conceived in the mind through hope amid the narrow confines of the present life? Of this the Psalmist says: “Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns of confession” (Ps. XCIX, 4).

When we confess our sins through tears, we enter the gate of the narrow life.

[Note: Val. Cl. reads “of the narrow way.”]

But when afterward we are led into eternal life, we enter the courts of our gate with the praises of confession, because there will no longer be narrowness when the joy of perpetual festivity has welcomed us.

[Note: Ebroic. reads “of felicity.”]

Because of the narrowness of our confession, the Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII, 13). And when the Psalmist presumed that he had been received into the breadth of eternal joy, he said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. XXX, 9).

[Note: Vatic. with the earlier editions reads “to receive … eternal joys.” The Laud. manuscript supports this reading.]

One therefore reaches the court through the gate, because one arrives at the breadth of solemn joy from the narrowness of confession. Those joys that are called courts in David are called the inner vestibule in Ezekiel.

Hence this vestibule is also said to have been measured as eight cubits. There all are to be received who now labor in the practice of works and sigh for eternal joys through the grace of contemplation.

**2.** Nor is it without reason that the vestibule is set at eight cubits, because the whole of time unfolds through seven days. For the eternal day that follows when the succession of the seven days has been completed is the eighth.

Therefore, too, the Psalmist, considering the day of resurrection and about to speak of the severity of the final judgment, prefaced the title by saying: “For the end: a psalm of David for the eighth” (Ps. VI, 1). And to show which “eighth” he meant, namely that day of dreadful terror, he continued at the beginning of the psalm: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (ibid., 2).

Now, whenever anyone is corrected through scourges and amended by correction, he is corrected in gentleness, not in anger. But in that strict examination every rebuke and correction is fury and anger, because there is no forgiveness after the correction.

The reason for this number eight is that after the Sabbath the Lord wished to rise from the dead. The Lord’s Day, which is the third from the Lord’s death, is counted as the eighth from the creation of the days, because it follows the seventh.

Thus the true passion and true resurrection of our Redeemer also prefigured something concerning his body in the days of his passion. He suffered on the sixth day; on the Sabbath he rested in the tomb; but on the Lord’s Day he rose from the dead.

The present life is still a sixth day for us, because it is spent in pain and tormented by afflictions.

[Note: Rothomag. and Lyr. read “in labors.”]

But on the Sabbath, as though in a tomb, we rest, because after the body we find rest for the soul. On the Lord’s Day—that is, the third from the Passion and, as we have said, the eighth from the creation—we shall rise bodily from death and rejoice in the glory of the soul together with the flesh.

What our Savior wonderfully accomplished in himself, therefore, he truly signified in us, so that pain may receive us on the sixth day, rest on the seventh, and glory on the eighth.

Hence Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, because you do not know what evil will be upon the earth” (Eccl. XI, 2).

[Note: All the printed editions read “give portions”; below they read “for portions to seven.” We follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts, which is supported by the Vulgate, the other versions, and the Hebrew text itself. The sense is: “Give a part,” or portion, “to those seven.”]

We give a portion both to seven and to eight when we arrange the things that unfold during the seven days in such a way that through them we may come to eternal goods; when, by acting cautiously now, we avoid the anger of the terrible judgment that is to come.

The vestibule is therefore measured on the inside by eight cubits, because through the light that follows the seven days the breadth of eternity is opened to us.

**3.** But no one comes to it unless he has devotedly kept love of God and neighbor here. Hence the text adds: “And its front, two cubits.”

The front of the gate is the good merit of the present life. Just as the inner vestibule ought to be understood as eternal rest, so through the front of the gate the quality of visible life must necessarily be signified.

The front of the gate is therefore measured by two cubits, because whoever strives here to preserve love of God and neighbor will himself reach the court of eternity. Our life, then, in order to be measured by two cubits, must daily be stretched through charity toward love of both God and neighbor.

Charity is not true if it has less than two cubits. Hence, when Moses expressed the virtues of the elect through the colors of the garments, he commanded that scarlet twice-dyed be used in the priestly ornament (Exod. XXVIII, 5).

For what is signified by scarlet except charity, which is always kindled by the flame of love? Scarlet is dyed twice when our charity is inflamed not only by love of God but also by love of neighbor.

For whoever loves God in such a way that he abandons care for the neighbor entrusted to him still has scarlet dyed only once within him. And whoever loves his neighbor in such a way that he diminishes the desire with which he ought to burn toward God does not yet possess the color of a doubled dye.

We must therefore love those with whom we live and, together with those whom we love, hasten toward the one in whom we truly live.

For behold, we who appear to be clothed in religious garb have gathered from the various conditions of the world for faith and to hear the word of almighty God. Gathered from dissimilar iniquities, we have been brought together in the harmony of the holy Church, so that what is said through Isaiah concerning the Church’s promise already plainly seems to have been fulfilled: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid” (Isa. XI, 6).

For through the entrails of holy charity the wolf dwells with the lamb, because those who were predators in the world rest in peace with the gentle and the meek. And the leopard lies down with the kid, because the one who was marked with the varied spots of his sins consents to be humbled with the one who despises himself and confesses that he is a sinner.

The text also adds: “The calf and the lion and the sheep shall dwell together” (Isa. XI, 6), because the one who prepares himself through a contrite heart for a daily sacrifice to God, another who once raged fiercely like a lion in cruelty, and another who persists like a sheep in the simplicity of innocence have come together within the folds of the holy Church.

Behold what charity is like: it kindles, burns up, and fuses differences of mind, reshaping them, as it were, into a single form of gold.

But insofar as the elect love one another in this way, they must hasten toward the one whom they may deserve to see in eternal joy in heaven. For one is our Lord and Redeemer, who both binds the hearts of his elect here into unanimity and continually urges them toward heavenly love through inward desires.

Hence the text there also adds: “And a little child shall lead them” (ibid.).

Who is this little child except the one of whom it is written: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us” (ibid., IX, 6)? He leads those who dwell together because, lest our hearts cling to earthly things, he daily inflames them through inward desire.

And this is precisely what his leading means: to kindle us unceasingly toward his love, lest, while we love one another, we remain in mind in this exile; lest the rest of this life please us in such a way that it leads us to forget our homeland; lest a mind delighted by prosperity grow numb.

[Note: Ebroic. and Val. Cl. read “whence also the Lord [does this] to his own.”]

Therefore he mixes scourges with his gifts, so that everything that delighted us in the world may become bitter to us, and so that the fire may rise in the soul that continually disturbs us, awakens us, and, so to speak, bites us delightfully, torments us gently, and saddens us cheerfully, toward heavenly desire.

[Note: Laud. and Longip. read “may disturb and awaken, and so forth.” All the printed editions read “may awaken in quiet,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

The little child therefore leads us because he who was made a little lower than the angels does not permit us, through the charity he grants us, to fix our minds in this world.

Scarlet is thus twice-dyed in us if we love our neighbors as ourselves here and hasten with those whom we love toward the author of all things.

If, therefore, our life is twice-dyed with perfect charity, the front of the gate is measured in us by two cubits.

Whether, then, the doctor, sacred eloquence, or faith is signified by the name “gate,” charity is appropriately understood in the measure of the two cubits: the one truly preaches it who teaches love of God and neighbor; it is the sure knowledge that charity builds; and faith is strong when it exercises itself in love of God and neighbor.

The text continues:

**VERSE 10.** “The chambers of the gate toward the eastern way were three on this side and three on that side, and the measure of the three was one.”

**4.** We have already said above what the chambers and the eastern way signify (Hom. 3, no. 8 and following), and we do not think it necessary to repeat those matters at greater length.

But we must ask what is meant by the statement: “Three on this side and three on that side.” The chambers beside the eastern way are the hearts of those fervent in the love of God.

Whether these were the elect who lived under the Old Testament or those who followed under the New, it is certainly clear that all were inflamed by love of the Trinity. For they would not truly have loved God if they had not received the grace of that Trinity, which is God.

Thus, beside the eastern way, there are three chambers on this side and three on that side, because, when the Lord deigned to become incarnate among the ancient and the new fathers, the eastern way appeared, as it were, in the midst of the chambers. The chambers were adorned for the true appearance of virtues through knowledge of the Trinity.

But if we refer the same number to the virtues of the elect, there are three virtues without which one who is already capable of doing anything cannot be saved: faith, hope, and charity.

And because the same faith, hope, and charity existed in the ancient fathers as in the new teachers,

[Note: Laud. reads “and in the new teachers.”]

three chambers on this side and three on that side are described beside the eastern way.

**5.** Or certainly because there were three distinctions among the ancient fathers, three others among the new follow under grace.

The ancient people had fathers before the law, then fathers under the law, and afterward prophets. In the new people, first the firstfruits of the Hebrews believed; afterward the fullness of the nations followed in faith; and finally, at the end of the world, the remnant of the Hebrews will be saved (Rom. IX, 27).

Because, therefore, the incarnation of the Lord had on its earlier side fathers before the law, fathers under the law, and finally prophets, while on its later side it will gather believers from the Hebrews, believers from the nations, and afterward the remnant of the Hebrews, the eastern way is said to have three chambers on this side and three on that side.

We may also understand this appropriately if we say that there are three orders of the faithful. Whether in the Old Testament or the New, there is one order of preachers, another of those who practice continence, and another of good married people.

Hence the same prophet saw three men delivered in the earlier passage: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV, 14). In these three, preachers, those who practice continence, and married people are signified.

Noah guided the ark upon the waters and therefore represented rulers (Gen. VII, 1–2 and following). Daniel devoted himself to abstinence in the royal court and therefore signified the life of those who practice continence (Dan. I, 16). Job, living in marriage and exercising care for his household, pleased God; through him the order of good married people is fittingly represented (Job I, 8).

Because, therefore, even before the Mediator’s coming there were preachers, those who practiced continence, and good married people who awaited that same coming and longed with great thirst of desire to see him, and because afterward there are, as we see, preachers, those who practice continence, and good married people who no longer desire our Redeemer to become incarnate but to be contemplated in the glory of his majesty, the eastern way has three chambers on this side and three on that side.

This agrees with the Psalmist’s words concerning that same way, namely our Redeemer: “Around him were his tents” (Ps. XVII, 12).

[Note: The printed editions read “his tabernacle.”]

[Col. 0976D] **6.** But we must weigh carefully what is said: “The measure of the three was one.”

Although the excellence of preachers is far above that of those who practice continence and keep silence, and the eminence of those who practice continence is far above that of married people, what does it mean that the measure of the three is said to be one?

Married people, although they act well and desire to see almighty God, are nevertheless occupied with household cares and, compelled by necessity, divide their minds between both things.

Those who practice continence, however, are removed from the activity of this world and restrain the pleasure of the flesh even from licit marriage. They are entangled by no concern for a spouse, no concern for children, and no harmful or difficult thoughts about household affairs.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “occupation.”]

Preachers, moreover, not only restrain themselves from vices but also prevent others from sinning, lead them to the faith, and instruct them in the pursuit of good conduct.

How, then, is their measure one, when the equality of their lives is not one?

Yet the measure of the three is one because, although there is great diversity among their merits, there is no difference in the faith in which they are stretched out. For the same faith that makes these firm in great things contains the weakness of those others in small things.

Or certainly the measure of the three is one because, in the final recompense, although the same dignity will not belong to all, there will nevertheless be one blessed life for all.

Hence the Lord himself says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2). Yet those who were led into the vineyard, although they came at different hours, received one denarius (Matt. XX, 9).

How, then, can many dwelling places agree with one denarius, except that the dignities of the blessed citizens will indeed be different, but the rest of eternal recompense will nevertheless be one?

For although the merit of individuals will be unequal, there will not be a diversity of joys. Even if one rejoices less and another more, one joy nevertheless delights them all through the vision of their Creator.

**7.** This too must be understood, whether of the ancient or the new fathers: although the eastern way has three chambers on this side and three on that side, the measure of the three is one, because the same faith and the same merit that held the hearts of those who came before filled the hearts of those who followed under the New Testament.

As Paul also says: “Having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 1), “we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13).

Those spiritual fathers believed that almighty God is the Trinity in the same way that the new fathers openly proclaimed that same Trinity.

Isaiah heard the angelic hosts in heaven crying out: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI, 3). The word “holy” is said three times to reveal the Trinity of persons; but to show that the substance of the Trinity is one, it is not said “of the Lords of hosts,” but “the Lord God of hosts.”

David likewise, understanding this, says: “May God bless us, our God, may God bless us” (Ps. LXVI, 8). After naming God three times, he added, to show that this God is one: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him.”

Paul also says: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36): “from him,” namely from the Father; “through him,” through the Son; “in him,” in the Holy Spirit.

After saying “him” three times, he added: “To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (ibid.). For by not saying “to them” but “to him,” by saying “him” three times he distinguished the persons, and by adding “to him be glory” he did not divide the substance.

[Note: The printed editions read “he distinguished by the persons,” where “by” is superfluous.]

Because, therefore, the faith of the ancient and new fathers is one, the measure of the chambers is rightly described as one for the three. This is repeated in other words when the text adds:

**ibid.**—“And the measure of the fronts on both sides was one.”

**8.** On both sides there is one measure of the fronts, because our fathers, whether coming earlier from the Old Testament or now from the New, agree in the one faith of the Mediator.

Because they are full of charity, they tame their flesh through abstinence, illumine the hearts of their hearers with the light of preaching, perform signs, and accomplish works of power. Since their good deeds are made known to us outwardly, they are not improperly called the fronts of this heavenly building.

Everything that is now displayed openly is a front, just as the vestibule of the building is that which is reserved for us inwardly.

Hence it is said to the holy Church in the Song of Songs: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you” (Song VI, 6).

The cheeks are the spiritual fathers of the holy Church, who now shine within it through miracles and appear venerable, as it were, upon its face.

When we see many people performing wonders, prophesying what is to come, abandoning the world perfectly, and burning with heavenly desires, the cheeks of the holy Church blush like the rind of a pomegranate.

But what is all that which we admire when compared with the thing of which it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9; Isa. LXIV, 4)?

Well, therefore, when he admired the cheeks of the Church, he added: “Apart from what is hidden within you” (Song VI, 6). As though it were said openly: “The things in you that are not hidden are indeed great, but those that are hidden are altogether ineffable.”

[Note: Vatic. and Gussanv. read “inestimable.”]

The text continues:

**VERSE 11.** “And he measured the width of the threshold of the gate, ten cubits, and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits.”

**9.** We have already said much above about the meaning of the gate, but we must retain one point through which the reader’s understanding may penetrate the rest.

It has been said that the gate can signify sacred Scripture. But we must now examine carefully why the width of the threshold of the gate is measured at ten cubits, while the length of the gate is measured at thirteen cubits.

Here “length” means height, just as we call someone tall when we speak of his “long stature.” The length of a gate cannot mean its transverse dimension, since its width is shown by ten cubits.

[Note: Laud. reads “by ten cubits.”]

What, then, is the width of the threshold of the gate except the law of the Old Testament? And what is the length of the gate except the grace of the New Testament?

Sacred Scripture, while through the Old Testament it restrained crimes of action and commanded the giving of tithes (Deut. XII, 6), lay, as it were, through humble commandments in the width of the threshold.

But while through the New Testament it restrained evil thoughts and commanded that all things be abandoned and the life of the body be despised for God together with the present world (Matt. XV, 19; Mark VII, 21; Luke IX, 24), our gate rose, as it were, into the height of length.

The commandments given to the Israelite people through the law were smaller; hence Moses spoke to that same people on the plain (Exod. XIX, 7 and following). The Lord gave higher commandments to the holy apostles; hence he taught them the commandments of life on the mountain.

But when our Redeemer says through the Gospel: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matt. V, 17), he had come to fulfill the law by adding the grace of justice to the law, so that what the law commanded in lesser things he might help to perfect in higher things, and what it restrained from action he might cut away from the heart.

Thus the law, which lay in breadth, when understood rose into height.

The knowledge of God that existed among the spiritual fathers under the Old Testament was not known to the whole Hebrew people. For although the prophets preached almighty God, namely the holy Trinity, the people were ignorant of it; they held only the Decalogue in the law, without knowing the faith of the Trinity.

[Note: All the printed editions read “held in faith the law of the Trinity,” contrary to the manuscripts, including Anglic., Norm., and others, and indeed contrary to the sense itself.]

The width of the threshold of the gate is therefore measured by ten cubits because that hard people, ignorant of the subtlety of faith, served the commandments of the Decalogue.

[Note: Val. Cl., together with Norm., reads “sublimity.”]

But the length of the gate is measured by thirteen cubits because, through the New Testament, knowledge of the Trinity grew in the heart of the faithful people beyond the commandments of the Decalogue, which it observes more truly.

[Note: Ebroic. reads “believes in the knowledge of the Trinity.”]

And it fulfills the commandments of the law precisely insofar as it believes that the Trinity is the almighty Lord.

[Col. 0979C] **10.** Here it may reasonably be asked why, after saying above that this width of the threshold of the gate was measured by one reed, he later added that it was measured by ten cubits, and then added that the length of the gate was measured by thirteen cubits.

For, as has often been said, one reed has six cubits and a handbreadth; ten cubits already exceed the measure of the reed, and thirteen exceed ten.

What, then, does it mean that first the threshold of the gate is measured by one reed, afterward its width by ten cubits, and finally the length of the gate by thirteen, except that the holy fathers whom we know to have existed before the law through sacred Scripture knew that there is one almighty God, namely the holy Trinity, but did not openly preach the same Trinity that they knew?

Obeying his commands and preserving purity of life, they possessed, as it were, in the six cubits of the reed the perfection of action, and, often seeing angels, they possessed a handbreadth of contemplation.

When the law was given, that unformed Hebrew people tried to observe the commandments of the Decalogue, but was not instructed in knowledge of the holy Trinity.

And although the spiritual fathers had known it perfectly, the great multitude of the Synagogue could neither discover the mystery of the Trinity nor know how to seek it.

[Note: Val. Cl. reads “nor took care to seek it.”]

11. When grace came through the New Testament, every faithful people recognized that the one God is the Trinity, and fulfilled the power of the Decalogue in acknowledging him. First, therefore, the threshold of the gate is measured by one reed; afterward its breadth by ten cubits; and finally the length of the gate by thirteen cubits, because both active and contemplative life existed among the holy fathers before the Law, while under the Decalogue of the Law the people, unaware of the mystery of the divine substance [Note: Suess.: “of the knowledge of God.” Moreover, when this holy Doctor calls it “the mystery of the divine substance,” he means the Trinity, which, as he taught above, was revealed in this manner to the patriarchs [Col. 0980D], no. 7, yet remained unknown to the Jewish people. See above, no. 9, and below, no. 10. Hence, when he says in no. 4 that all the elect, even those of the Old Testament, were inflamed by love of the Trinity, this must be understood of the grace bestowed upon both groups of elect through the Trinity—although not explicitly known by all—so that they might burn with love. The holy Doctor’s meaning is clear from the immediately following words; for they would not truly love God if they had not received the grace of that same Trinity, which is God.], served within the breadth of the commandments. And now, under grace, when the precepts of the Decalogue are observed more truly, everyone who has come to the faith recognizes the mystery of the holy Trinity. [Col. 0979D] [Col. 0980B]

12. Here we must also understand that, as the ages advanced, the knowledge of the spiritual fathers increased. Moses was instructed in the knowledge of almighty God more than Abraham; the prophets more than Moses; the apostles more than the prophets. I would be mistaken if Scripture itself did not say this: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII, 4).
