But let us, if possible, demonstrate from the words of that same Scripture what we have said about Abraham, Moses, the prophets, and the apostles. Who does not know that Abraham spoke with God (Gen. XII and following)? Yet the Lord says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and I did not reveal my name Adonai to them” (Exod. VI, 3; likewise, III, 6). Behold, more had been made known to Moses than to Abraham, since God tells Moses about himself what he declared he had not made known to Abraham.

But let us see whether the prophets were able to grasp more of divine knowledge than Moses. Certainly the Psalmist says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day” (Ps. CXVIII, 97). And he added: “I have understood more than all my teachers, because your testimonies are my meditation” (ibid., 99). And again: “I have understood more than the elders” (ibid., 100). Thus, when he recalls that he meditates on the law and testifies that he has understood more than all his teachers and more than the elders, he shows that he had received more divine knowledge than Moses.

How shall we show, then, that the holy apostles were taught more than the prophets? Certainly the Truth says: “Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see, and to hear what you hear, but they did not see it” (Luke X, 24). They therefore knew more of divine knowledge than the prophets, because what the prophets saw only in spirit, the apostles also saw bodily. Thus was fulfilled the saying of Daniel mentioned above: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII, 4).

Let the measure of the reed, which is six cubits and a palm, therefore be extended to ten cubits; and let the measure of ten cubits finally rise to thirteen, because the farther the world is brought toward its end, the more generously the entrance to eternal knowledge is opened for us.

It follows:

**VERSE 12.—“And the border before the chambers was one cubit.”**

13. As we have often said, the chambers are the hearts of the elect, burning with love for almighty God. What, then, is expressed by the border before the chambers, if not faith? Unless faith is held first, one can in no way reach spiritual love. Charity does not precede faith; faith precedes charity. No one can love what he has not believed.

The border, therefore, is before the chambers: faith is before the ardor of charity. For, as has been said, unless you believe what you hear, you will in no way be inflamed with love for what you have heard. But the border before the chambers is one cubit, because faith joins the hearts of hearers to the love of God when it is not divided by errors and schisms but perseveres in unity. Thus the border of one cubit leads the mind of the hearer to the chamber, because the form of the heavenly Bridegroom whom he proclaims here he later displays in heaven.

Here he rightly adds:

**IBID.—“And one cubit was the end on both sides.”**

14. “On both sides” is said as though it meant “for both,” namely, for the threshold and for the gate. We have said that the breadth of the threshold and the length of the gate signify the Old and New Testaments. Finally, it is added that one cubit is the end on both sides, because the Old Testament announced to us one Mediator between God and human beings, and the New Testament likewise announces that he will come in eternal glory—the one whom we already know to have been incarnate for us.

One cubit, therefore, is the end of both [Note: In several manuscripts of Norm. and others, instead of *utrorumque* (“of both”) one finds *utrinque* (“on both sides”), here and below.], because the one whom the Law foretold appeared in the flesh, and he whom the New Testament now proclaims will appear in the glory of his majesty. He will be the end of both when, seen in the power of his divinity, he fulfills everything that has been foretold.

For it is written: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). [Col. 0981D] He is the end—not one who destroys, but one who perfects. He perfected the Law when, as the Law had foretold, he appeared incarnate. But the New Testament still speaks much about his judgment; it still tells much about his kingdom, and much of this has not yet been fulfilled. The Gospel is read daily; the life to come is proclaimed. The end of the New Testament, therefore, will come when the Lord fulfills what he promised concerning himself.

15. The New Testament will indeed be ended because it will be perfected. When the one of whom it speaks is seen, the words of that Testament will cease. Hence, to holy Church, awaiting the day of true light like the springtime season, it is said through the voice of the Bridegroom: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in the earth” (Song II, 10–11).

Whether it is holy Church or each individual elect soul, she is the beloved of the heavenly Bridegroom through love, a dove through the Spirit, and beautiful through the beauty of her conduct. When she is already being led out from the corruption of the flesh, winter undoubtedly passes for her, because the torpor of the present life departs. The rain also goes and departs, because when she is led to contemplate almighty God in his own substance, drops of words will no longer be necessary, as though the rain of preaching still had to be poured upon her. What she could hear only imperfectly, she will see more fully.

Then flowers appear upon the earth, because when the soul begins to taste beforehand something of the sweetness of eternal blessedness, it already smells, as it were among flowers, what after leaving this life it will possess more abundantly in fruit. Hence it is added there: “The time of pruning has come” (ibid., II, 12). In pruning, sterile branches are cut away so that those capable of bearing fruit may produce it more abundantly. The time of our pruning therefore comes when we abandon the fruitless and harmful corruption of the flesh, so that we may reach the fruit of the soul.

That fruit will be for us exceedingly abundant: the vision of the One. Thus one cubit is the end on both sides, because he is the one who said: “I am solitary until I pass over” (Ps. CXL, 10). [Col. 0982C] He alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, presides in heaven, like a solitary sparrow upon the building (Ps. CI, 8). Just as he fulfilled the Law through the mystery of his incarnation and perfect humanity, so he will fulfill the promises of the New Testament through the manifestation of the glory of his splendor.

16. The measure of the ark also spoke to us of this one cubit. The ark, which was commanded to be made three hundred cubits long, sixty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high (Gen. VI, 15), was completed in one cubit. What is signified by the ark if not holy Church, which is broad below and narrow above? It is gathered from three hundred, sixty, and thirty cubits into one cubit, because from the breadth that holy Church still possesses in her weaker members she is gradually narrowed and, advancing upward, tends toward the One.

Reason itself requires us to believe that in the breadth of the ark all the beasts, quadrupeds, and reptiles were below, while human beings and birds were above. For there was a window in the side near the upper part, through which the man sent out the raven and the dove, so that he might know whether the waters of the flood had already receded. And since the ark was completed in one cubit, human beings and birds were near the cubit.

Thus the ark rightly signifies the whole Church, which is still broad in her many carnal members and narrow in her few spiritual ones. And because she is gathered toward one human being who is without sin, she is completed, as it were, in one cubit.

17. We see many people within the bosom of that same holy Church rising up in pride, dissolving in carnal pleasure, yearning for earthly possessions, crossing seas at the command of greed, serving anger, devoting themselves to quarrels, and harming their neighbors whenever they can. But because holy Church still tolerates them so that they may be converted, the beasts remain below in the breadth of the ark, as it were.

We see others no longer seeking what belongs to others, bearing injuries inflicted upon them with equanimity, content with their own possessions, and living humbly. But because these are already few, the ark is narrowed.

We see still others abandoning even what they possess, showing no concern for earthly things, loving their enemies, subduing the flesh from every pleasure, restraining every impulse under the judgment of reason, and being lifted up on the wing of contemplation through heavenly desire. But because such people are extremely rare, the ark is now brought near the cubit, where human beings and birds are contained. [Note: All our manuscripts read this way, whereas the printed editions differ: “They are led in the ark near the cubit.”]

Yet let us ask whether any of them can be without sin, and none is found. Who, then, is a human being without sin, except he who was not conceived in sins? The ark is therefore completed in one cubit, because there is one author and Redeemer of holy Church who is without sin, toward whom and through whom all advance who know themselves to be sinners.

Let it therefore be said of the threshold and the gate: “And one cubit, the end on both sides,” because when the one Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, appears in his majesty, he will fulfill everything foretold and promised in both Testaments.

18. But if in this passage he mentions both the border and the chambers, this too does not conflict with the interpretation, because when the majesty of our Redeemer has been shown to us, faith comes to an end, since a human being then begins to see what he believed. The chambers also reach their end, because the hearts of the faithful are perfected in his love incomparably more than they are now.

One cubit, therefore, is the end on both sides, because the vision of the one Lord and Savior brings faith to an end in his elect and perfects charity.

19. It is worthwhile to consider who we are who discuss these things. Certainly we came from the nations; certainly our parents were worshipers of wood and stone. How has it come about, then, that we investigate such profound mysteries of the prophet Ezekiel, mysteries that the Hebrews themselves still do not understand? [Note: The Hebrews confess the obscurity of the prophet Ezekiel, especially in the vision explained here, as we touched upon in the preface, no. 2.]

Let us therefore give thanks to the One who fulfilled in deed everything written about him in the sacred word, so that what could not be understood when heard might be disclosed when seen. There his incarnation is contained; there his passion, his death, his resurrection, and his ascension. But who among us would have believed these things when heard, unless we had recognized them as accomplished?

Thus the sealed book, as we read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. V, 3, 5), which no one could open and read, was opened by the Lion from the tribe of Judah, because he disclosed all its mysteries to us in his passion and resurrection. And by enduring the evils of our weakness, he showed us the blessings of his power and glory.

20. He became flesh in order to make us spiritual; he graciously humbled himself in order to raise us up; he went forth in order to bring us in; he appeared visibly in order to show us invisible things; he endured scourges in order to heal us; he bore insults and mockery in order to free us from eternal disgrace; he died in order to give life.

Let us therefore give thanks to him who gives life and who died—and all the more to him who gives life because he died. Hence Isaiah, contemplating both our salvation and his passion, rightly says: “That he may do his work, his strange work; that he may perform his work, his work is alien to him” (Isa. XXVIII, 21).

For God’s work is to gather the souls he created and recall them to the joys of eternal light. But to be scourged and smeared with spittle, [Note: The manuscripts have this better than the printed editions, which read “to be smeared with it.”] to be crucified, to die, and to be buried—this is not God’s work in his own substance, but the work of sinful humanity, which deserved all these things through sin. [Note: Val. Cl., with Norm., reads “for sin.”]

Yet he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree (1 Pet. II, 24). And he who in his own nature remains forever incomprehensible deigned to be comprehended and scourged in our nature, because unless he assumed what belonged to our weakness, he would never have raised us to the power of his strength.

Thus, “that he may do his work, his strange work; and that he may perform his work, his work is alien to him,” because God, having become incarnate in order to gather us to his righteousness, deigned to be beaten for us like a sinful human being. He performed an alien work in order to perform his own, because by enduring the evils of our weakness he brought us, who are his creatures, to the glory of his strength, in which he lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY V

The fortieth chapter of Ezekiel is expounded from the latter part of verse 12 through verse 17, with particular discussion of contemplation.

1. After mentioning the chambers above, the prophet adds that the chambers were six cubits on this side and on that. Here a major question arises for us: why did he say above that the chamber was measured by one reed, which he declared to have six cubits and a palm, while below he says that the chambers were measured by six cubits alone? If they are measured not by a reed but by six cubits, the palm is missing, although above it was said to be present in the measure of the reed.

But if the chambers are the perceptions and thoughts of the faithful, in which chaste souls are joined to their Creator in love; if the six cubits signify perfect action and the palm the beginning of contemplation, then we ought to examine the members of the holy universal Church, and we quickly discover that some chambers in it are measured by one reed, while others are measured by six cubits alone.

For some faithful love almighty God in such a way that they are both perfect in action and lifted up in contemplation. These clearly possess the reed as their measure, because they have both the six cubits of action and the palm of contemplation.

Others indeed love almighty God and apply themselves perfectly to good works, but they do not know how to contemplate his greatness with a more refined understanding. They love him, but do not know how to investigate the joys of his glory. These have six cubits but do not have the palm, because they are already joined to him through love but are separated from him in contemplation.

Nevertheless, these chambers are said to be on this side and on that after the mention of one cubit, because faithful souls from both the Jewish people and the nations have come together in love of our Creator and Redeemer.

2. Hence our same Redeemer, when he was sitting upon the colt and heading toward Jerusalem, as the evangelist testifies, had many people spread their garments on the road; while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. Those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Mark XI, 7 and following).

Our Savior goes toward Jerusalem sitting upon a colt when, ruling the soul of each faithful person—that is, his own beast—he leads it to the vision of inward peace. [Note: In all the corrupt printed editions, “the faithful soul, ruling.” According to that reading, the soul is not ruled by Christ but itself rules, which overturns the comparison drawn from Christ sitting upon the ass. Moreover, this expression, “sitting upon the colt,” is familiar to Gregory. We have restored the passage from all our manuscripts and from the English manuscript.] He also sits upon the beast when he presides universally over holy Church and kindles her with desire for heavenly peace. [Note: We have already noted this Gregorian expression in note c (our col. 537, volume LXXV), book I of the *Moralia*, no. 23. How common it is with the holy Doctor is evident even from this passage, where it occurs three times; above we read, “when he was sitting upon the colt,” and shortly afterward, “Our Savior, sitting upon the colt.”]

Many spread their garments on the road because they subdue their bodies through abstinence, preparing a path for him to the mind or offering good examples to those who follow. Others cut branches or leafy boughs from the trees and spread them on the road, because from the discourse of the fathers they pluck words and teachings of truth and, coming along God’s road toward the mind of the hearer, lay them down through humble preaching.

Even we, unworthy though we are, do this now. For when we take up the teachings of the fathers in a sermon of exhortation, we cut branches from the trees in order to spread them on the road of almighty God.

But those who went before and those who followed cried out: “Hosanna.” The Jewish people went before; the Gentiles followed. And because all the elect—whether those who could be found in Judea or those who now exist in the Church—believed and believe in the Mediator between God and human beings, those who go before and those who follow cry out “Hosanna.”

“Hosanna” is said in Latin to mean “save us.” From him the former sought salvation, and the present seek it; and they confess him blessed who comes in the name of the Lord, because there is one hope and one faith of the peoples who go before and those who follow.

For just as they were healed by his awaited passion and resurrection, so we are saved by his past passion and his resurrection, which endures forever. The one whom our predecessors from the Jewish people believed in and loved as the one who would come, we believe and love as the one who has come, and we are inflamed by desire for him, so that we may contemplate him face to face.

His chambers, therefore, are on this side and on that, because the hearts of those who love him embrace the faith that is in him from the beginning of the world and from its end.

It follows:

**VERSE 13.—“And he measured the gate from the roof of one chamber to the roof of the other, a breadth of twenty-five cubits.”**

3. We have often said that the gate signifies faith, and through that same faith our Lord and Redeemer himself, the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, can be signified, because through the faith that is in him the entrance to life stands open.

But we may also appropriately understand the sacred Scripture as the gate, since it opens to us that same faith for understanding our Redeemer; when it is known as it ought to be, we enter into the understanding of invisible things.

If, therefore, as we said earlier, the gate is understood here as Scripture, we must ask what is signified by the roof of the chamber and by the roof of the gate. The chamber has a roof because the mind of those who love is covered, and the fervor of love is still hidden. The gate also has a roof because Scripture was indeed written entirely for our sake, but is not entirely understood by us.

4. Many things in it are written so openly that they nourish the little ones; others are veiled in more obscure sayings so that they may exercise the strong, so that, when understood with labor, they may be more pleasing. Some things are shut up in it in such a way that, while we do not understand them, recognizing the weakness of our blindness, we may advance more toward humility than toward understanding.

There are also things that speak of heavenly realities in such a way that they are disclosed only to those heavenly citizens who remain in their homeland, while they are not yet opened to us who are pilgrims. For if someone traveling to an unknown city hears many things about it on the road, he gathers some from reasoning, but others, because he does not yet see them, he cannot know at all. The citizens themselves, however, who are in that city, both see what is left unspoken about it and understand what is said about it.

We, then, are still on the road. We hear many things about that heavenly homeland; some we already understand through spirit and reason, while some, not understood, we reverence.

Hence it is written of that same sacred word: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its higher parts with waters” (Ps. CIII, 2). Heaven is stretched out like a skin because sacred Scripture is explained to us in expositions through the mouths of mortal human beings. But there are waters in heaven—namely, the higher multitudes, the ranks of angels—by which the higher parts of that heaven are covered, because the higher and more obscure things in the sacred word are disclosed only to angelic spirits and remain still unknown to us.

The chamber therefore has a roof, because a neighbor does not yet know how greatly he is loved by his neighbor. The gate also, that is, the sacred word, has a roof, because we cannot yet penetrate with our understanding everything we hear about heavenly things.

5. It remains, then, that in the things we understand we should walk daily in the progress of charity. And although even our neighbors do not see how much they are loved by us, and although in the sacred word we humbly revere what we do not yet understand, nevertheless, in those things to which we have attained through understanding, we ought to expand through good action.

Hence it is said: “And he measured the gate from the roof of the chamber to its roof, a breadth of twenty-five cubits.”

We possess five bodily senses: sight, taste, smell, hearing, and touch. The same number five, multiplied by itself, rises to twenty-five. But we cannot perform anything externally concerning the heavenly commandments without these five bodily senses. Within, the judging mind presides over these functions, and it recognizes what it can do justly or mercifully outwardly as though these functions were reporting and serving it.

When, therefore, the mind is filled with fear of almighty God, it is necessary that our five senses, like subordinate offices, serve us in good action. When through them we begin to act mercifully, mercy itself opens more widely each day and expands, as it were, into a kind of bosom of good work.

The five senses are therefore multiplied in themselves when what is done through them is multiplied daily by progress in good works. Hence the breadth is said to be twenty-five cubits, because fear, greed, and sluggishness are narrowness.

Whoever is afraid to give bread to the needy lest he himself lack it is still confined within the narrowness of fear. Whoever does not offer clothing to the freezing person because he desires to possess it alone is still constricted by the narrowness of his greed. Whoever does not do good because he grows sluggish through tepidity has his own torpor as his narrowness. [Note: Another reading has “grows numb,” as in the printed editions.]

To look upon the needy, to hear a prayer, to give alms, to offer defense, and, in defense of the poor person, not to fear the hostility of anyone who opposes him—this is great breadth of mind.

Let the breadth between the chamber and the gate therefore be measured at twenty-five cubits, because by the operation of the outward senses it is proved and recognized how much inward generosity of goodness one possesses. [Note: Norm. and others examined by Gussanv.: “For what shall I say about sacred Scripture? As much as you have learned.”] For how much you have learned from sacred Scripture and how silently you love your neighbor, you show in the breadth of good work.

6. Let the breadth between the chamber and the gate therefore be twenty-five cubits. [Note: Laud.: “in breadth.”] Good action is the witness between charity and knowledge. If it is lacking, it is certainly clear that you have neither known God nor loved your neighbor—that is, you possess neither the gate of the sacred word nor the chamber of love.

It should also be noted that the measure is said to extend from the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate. For our humility is tested by those things that are covered for us in sacred Scripture. Whatever we do not understand in it, we ought not proudly to criticize but humbly to revere.

Hence it is written of the Lord: “His eyelids question the children of human beings” (Ps. X, 5). His eyelids are his judgments, which close some things to us and open others. By opening, they question us whether we are not lifted up when we understand. By closing, they question us whether we do not despise what we cannot understand.

Through the things we do not say to our neighbors about our charity, we are more truly tested in the sight of God. In some people’s mouths charity is feigned; in others’ hearts it is genuine. Often love is displayed where it does not exist, and what does exist is not demonstrated. Our love for our neighbor is therefore expressed more by good action than by the tongue, so that in the good work itself our neighbor may see that he is loved.

And when we cannot do as much as we wish, let the hidden things of our love suffice for almighty God. [Note: Lyr.: “of our heart.”] From the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate, then, let there be great breadth, so that from the hidden things of our charity for our neighbor to the humility of knowledge for God’s sake, we may always perform good works as far as we understand and are able.

7. The gate can also be understood as the entrance itself to the heavenly kingdom. The chamber has a roof now, and the gate also has a roof, because neither the extent of our charity toward God and neighbor nor the time when we shall be brought from this world into the rest of eternal life is known.

Our Creator wished the day of our death to be unknown to us, so that, while it is always unknown, it might always be believed to be near; and so that each person might be more fervent in action the more uncertain he is about his summons.

Hence a breadth of twenty-five cubits extends from the chamber to the gate, because through the charity that we have once conceived toward God and our neighbor, we must multiply and ceaselessly perform everything we can until we enter the kingdom.

There is therefore great breadth from the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate, because from the grace by which we begin to love God until that very love which opens for us the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, we must expand ourselves in the abundant practice of good works: patiently endure adversities; willingly give good things; love even those by whom we suffer; give what we possess; not desire what we do not possess; love our neighbors as ourselves; regard their good as our own; and mourn their evils as though they were our own.

There is great breadth in such a mind, in which there is no narrowness of hatred. We conceive this breadth from love of God and neighbor, and we learn it through the sacred commandments.

We may also understand the twenty-five cubits of breadth appropriately according to the sacred word. He had said that the chambers were measured by six cubits, and the human being was created on the sixth day (Gen. I, 27); on that day the Lord is also described as having completed his works. Hence the number six is customarily used for perfection.

And because we have learned every good action through the four books of the holy Gospel, if we multiply six by four, we reach twenty-four. One is added to this, [Note: All our manuscripts read this way; in place of it, the printed editions have: “in the one God we all always act well.”] because there is one through whom all act well.

The breadth therefore had to be expressed by twenty-five cubits, because every good action is known through the four books of the holy Gospel, as we have said, and is completed in the knowledge and confession of the one God.

It follows:

**VERSE 13.—“And door opposite door.”**

8. Here “opposite” does not signify opposition but alignment. Door is opposite door when one reaches the inner entrance by a straight path from the outer one.

In the knowledge of almighty God, our first door is faith; the second is his appearance, to which we arrive by walking through faith. In this life we enter through the first, so that afterward we may be brought to the second.

Door is therefore opposite door, because through the entrance of faith the entrance to the vision of God is opened.

If someone wishes to understand both these doors as existing in this life, that too does not conflict with a sound interpretation. We often wish to consider the invisible nature of almighty God, but we are wholly unable to do so. Then the soul, wearied by these very difficulties, returns to itself [Note: Laud.: “falls back upon itself”] and makes for itself a ladder of ascent from itself, so that first it may consider itself, if it is able, and then investigate, as far as it can, that nature which is above it.

But if our mind has been scattered among bodily images, it is not sufficient to consider either itself or the nature of the soul, because by however many thoughts it is led, by so many obstacles it is blinded.

9. The first step, therefore, is to gather itself to itself; the second is to see what it is once gathered; the third is to rise above itself [Note: Several copies of Norm. and Val. Cl.: “and submit itself in contemplation,” or “to contemplation.”] and, by directing itself toward contemplation of the invisible Creator, subject itself to him.

But it does not gather itself to itself at all unless it has first learned to restrain from the eyes of the mind the phantasms of earthly and heavenly images; to reject and trample underfoot whatever concerning sight, hearing, smell, touch, and bodily taste occurs to its thought, so that it may seek within what it is without these things.

For when it thinks of these things, it turns certain shadows of bodies inward, as it were. [Note: The same manuscripts: “to be cast away.”] Everything must therefore be driven away from the eyes of the mind by the hand of discernment, so that the soul may consider itself as it was created under God and above the body, in order that, vivified by what is above, it may give life to what is below, which it governs.

It has been infused into the body in such a way that it is not divided according to the parts of the limbs. For if any part of the body is struck in any place, the whole soul suffers pain. Yet, in a wondrous manner, while presiding over the limbs through one and the same act of giving life, and while in its own nature it is not divided, through the body it performs different actions.

It is the soul itself that sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the mouth, touches through all the limbs, and by touching distinguishes the soft from the rough. Although it performs such different actions through the senses, it orders them—not as different things, but as one—in that reason in which it was created.

When, therefore, the soul thinks of itself without bodily images, it has already entered the first door. But from this door it proceeds toward another, so that it may contemplate something of the nature of almighty God.

The soul is the life of the flesh in the body; God, who gives life to all things, is the life of souls. If, then, life that has been given life is of such greatness that it cannot be comprehended, who can comprehend through understanding how great is the majesty of the life that gives life?

Yet even to consider and discern this is already, in some measure, to enter, because from its own estimation the soul gathers what it should think about the unbounded Spirit [Col. 0990C], who incomprehensibly governs those things he incomprehensibly created. [Note: All Norm. manuscripts, with Longip. and Val. Cl., read “who governs it,” namely, the soul; and below, “which he created.” Nevertheless, *ea* and *quae* seem preferable, since all the kinds of creatures are enumerated here.]

### 10

For our Creator presides over his creation in a manner incomparably far above it. He causes some things to exist, but not to live; others to exist and live, but not to possess the ability to discern anything concerning life; and still others to exist, live, and discern. One and the same being brings all things about, yet is not divided among them (1 Cor. 12:6). For he is truly supreme and is never unlike himself.

Although the soul is not diverse from itself by nature, it is nevertheless diverse through thought. At the very moment and instant when it thinks about sight, it forgets to think about hearing; and at the moment and instant when it thinks about hearing or taste, it cannot prevail upon itself to think about smell or touch. Through attention and forgetfulness, therefore, it is always unlike itself, so that now it holds one thing, now another, in thought.

[Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read “at the moment’s blow,” a phrase repeated below in Laudunensis.]

But almighty God, because he is not unlike himself, sees all things by the power by which he hears them all; by the power by which he creates, he judges what has been created. Thus, for him, seeing all things is at once to govern them, and governing them is to see them.

[Note: This reading, “and governing them is to see them,” is found with excellent sense in Laudunensis, Suessionensis, and Longipontanus, as well as in the Norman manuscripts. The printed editions read “and to behold what has been governed,” or, as Gussanville has it, “and in governing, to behold.” These readings accord less well with the holy Doctor’s meaning, for here he teaches that, in God, seeing and governing creatures are altogether the same: when he beholds, he governs; when he governs, he beholds.]

He does not assist the righteous with one thought and condemn the unrighteous with another; rather, by one and the same power of his singular nature, which is always unlike nothing in itself, he orders things unlike one another. Why, then, should we marvel at this concerning the Creator’s power, when we also see traces of his power in created things?

The nature of mud is different from that of wax. The sun’s ray, however, is not different, yet, though it is not different, what it does in mud and in wax is different: by the one and the same heat of its fire it hardens mud and melts wax. But perhaps this is due to the nature of mud or wax, not to the substance of the sun itself, which appears to act differently upon different natures.

Almighty God, however, possesses in himself the ability to order mutable things without changing, to do diverse things without any diversity in himself, and to form unlike things without any succession of thoughts. God, therefore, who is never unlike himself, acts in a manner far unlike upon things unlike one another; he is both everywhere and wholly everywhere.

For he says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). And it is written of him: “He measures heaven with his span and encloses the earth in his fist” (ibid. 40:12).

### 11

From this we must consider that he who presides over heaven as though over a throne is both above and within it. And he who measures heaven with his span and encloses the earth in his fist is outside, above, and below it.

Therefore, to indicate that he is within and above all things, almighty God declared heaven to be his throne. But to show that he surrounds all things, he says that he measures heaven with his span and encloses the earth in his fist. He is therefore both within and outside, both below and above: above by governing, below by bearing; within by filling, outside by surrounding. He is within in such a way that he is outside; he surrounds in such a way that he penetrates; he presides in such a way that he bears; he bears in such a way that he presides.

When, therefore, the soul, raised toward itself, understands its own measure and recognizes that it transcends all bodily things, and when from understanding itself it reaches toward understanding its author, what else does it now behold but the door that stands opposite the door? Hence the Prophet says to the author of all things: “Your knowledge has been made wondrous from me” (Ps. 138:6), because however intently the soul may apply itself, it is not fully able to penetrate itself—how much less the greatness of him who was able to create the soul?

And while it labored intellectually in the knowledge of God, growing weary and failing, it added: “It has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to reach it” (ibid.).

But when we who strive and reach out desire already to see something of the invisible nature, we grow weary, are struck back, and are repelled. Although we cannot penetrate the inner regions, we nevertheless now see the inner door from the outer door. The labor of contemplation itself is a door, because it displays something of what is within, even though the power to enter is not yet present.

It continues:

**Verse 14.** “And he made fronts sixty cubits long, and in front of the gate was a court all around.”

### 12

We have often said that the number six signifies the perfection of a good work (Hom. 2, Book II, no. 7 and following). We do not follow what the sages of this world attempted to establish when they said that the number six is perfect because, when counted in its proper order, it is completed—for when one, two, and three are named, the number six is fulfilled—or because it is divided into three parts, namely a sixth, a third, and a half, that is, one, two, and three. Rather, we say that the number six is perfect because, as was stated shortly before, on the sixth day God completed all his works (Gen. 1:21; 2:1).

Since he gave the sinful human being the law, which is written in ten commandments, and six multiplied tenfold rises to sixty, the perfection of good works is rightly signified by sixty cubits. The Lord also clearly indicates this in the Gospel. When he explained the parable of the sower, he said: “Another fell on good soil and produced fruit, rising and growing; it yielded one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold” (Matt. 13:8; Mark 4:8; Luke 8:8).

The good earth bears thirtyfold when the mind has conceived the perfection of faith, which is in the Trinity. It bears sixtyfold when it has brought forth perfect works of a good life. It bears one hundredfold when it has advanced to the contemplation of eternal life.

Our left hand is the present life; the right hand is the life to come. And contemplation of eternal life is rightly signified by the number one hundred, because when, after thirty and sixty, we reach the number one hundred by counting, that number passes over to the right hand.

[Note: This alludes to the ancient method of counting. Formerly, all numbers up to one hundred were represented on the fingers of the left hand, whether extended or bent in various ways. When one reached one hundred, the reckoning was transferred from the left hand to the right. On this matter, see Caelius Rhodiginus, *Antiquarum lectionum*, Book 23, chapters 11 and 12. Sidonius Apollinaris, Letter 9 to Faustus, Book 9: “Since your years have now been counted by the right hand,” a passage on which see the notes of J. Sirmond.]

Faith and action are still on the left, because while we are still placed here, we believe what we do not see and work so that we may see. But when the mind has raised itself into contemplation of eternal life, its reckoning has, as it were, reached the right hand.

[Note: Laudunensis reads “arranged.”]

He therefore made fronts sixty cubits long. Since perfection is signified by the number sixty, what is signified by the fronts of the building except those works that are seen outwardly? To give the word of preaching, to provide food for the hungry, to give clothing to the cold, and patiently to endure adversity for the sake of a good work—what are these other than the fronts of the heavenly building? The outward beauty of works adorns the dwelling of God, which is still hidden within.

[Note: Lyra and some others read “tabernacle.”]

But these fronts have a court all around them, because works are great when the breadth of charity expands them in the mind. Of charity it is written: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). Again the Psalmist says of it: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9).

### 13

But behold, while I speak, the question arises in my mind: How is charity broad? If one reaches God through charity, and Truth itself says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13); and again I hear the Psalmist saying: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16:4); and in the Gospel the Lord says: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30)—how, then, is charity broad if the gate is narrow? Or how is the yoke easy and the burden light if the ways that are kept in God’s commandments are hard?

Charity itself quickly resolves this question for us: the way of God is narrow for those who are beginning, but broad for those already living perfectly. The things we propose spiritually to our minds against their accustomed habits are hard, yet God’s burden is light once we have begun to bear it, so that, out of love for him, even persecution becomes pleasing, and every affliction endured for him comes with sweetness to the mind, just as the holy apostles rejoiced when they endured scourging for the Lord (Acts 5:41).

[Note: Laudunensis reads “may be pleasing.”]

[Note: This should be read on the authority of all the manuscripts: “every affliction,” not “every affection,” as all the printed editions have it. The preceding word, “persecution,” sufficiently indicates that affliction is meant here.]

Thus the narrow gate becomes broad for those who love; the hard ways become smooth and level for those who run spiritually. For when the mind knows that it will receive eternal joys in exchange for temporal sufferings, it begins to love what afflicts it.

[Note: By restoring the little word *enim* (“for”), we have given this sentence grace and clarity.]

The court before the fronts is therefore the breadth of love in the perfection of the work.

### 14

It should be noted that it says “all around,” so that in everything he does a person may always expand himself within the breadth of charity, lest fear or hatred constrict him.

If someone speaks the word of God but does not preserve in his mind the charity that he preaches, he has the front of the building but no court before the front. If someone gives alms generously to the needy but is perhaps lifted up in his heart by this act, and does not relieve his neighbor’s poverty out of charity but silently exalts himself through pride, he displays a front in the building but has not made a court beside the front.

If someone endures insults inflicted by his neighbor and silently bears the evils cast against him, the patience he displays is great. But only if he has no pain in his heart and seeks to win to the tranquility of gentleness even the person who had acted wrongly. For if, while practicing patience outwardly, he retains pain within and does not love the person whom he tolerates, he indeed has a front in the building but no court before the front, because the person who has subjected himself to the narrowness of hatred has plainly lost the breadth of charity.

For, as we have already said in the earlier part (Hom. 9, especially no. 22 and following), that patience is true which also loves the person whom it bears. To tolerate someone while hating him is not the virtue of gentleness, but a covering for rage.

It should also be noted that this court itself is called the court of the gate. Our gate is the entrance to the kingdom. To love God and one’s neighbor perfectly is already to reach toward entry into the kingdom. To the degree that each person loves, to that degree he approaches the entrance. To the degree that he neglects to love, to that degree he refuses to enter, because he does not strive to see what he desires.

We therefore have the court of the gate when, through the breadth of charity, we already enter by desire into the heavenly life that we are not yet at all able to attain.

When, therefore, a good work is done toward one’s neighbor, it remains that the intention of that good work be discerned: whether the mind seeks no recompense of present favor, but directs its hope toward the future promise, so that from temporal things it may hope for eternal things, and from earthly things for heavenly things. Hope in heavenly things makes the mind firm, so that it is not shaken by the waves of earthly disturbances.

Of this Paul also says: “Which we have as a sure and firm anchor of the soul, entering even within the veil” (Heb. 6:19).

[Note: The word “of the soul” is absent from the Norman manuscripts. It occurs in the Greek text and in the Vulgate.]

Concerning these inner regions, it is also added here:

**Verse 15.** “And before the face of the gate that reached as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.”

### 15

What is said here, “before the face of the gate,” describes not the outer space before the gate, but the inner space, since it is said to reach as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate. Hence this same place is said to have been measured at fifty cubits.

For the number fifty signifies eternal rest. The number seven possesses its own perfection, because by it the number of the days is completed. Through the law, the Sabbath was given for rest.

[Note: Laudunensis reads, “The Sabbath was given …”]

The number seven, multiplied by itself, reaches forty-nine; when one is added to it, it arrives at fifty, because all our perfection will consist in contemplation of that One in whose vision nothing less of salvation or joy will remain for us.

For this reason also the Jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year, was given for rest, because whoever reaches the eternal joys of almighty God will have no further labor or groaning.

### 16

It should be noted that the place described as extending fifty cubits is said to reach as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate. The prophet therefore does not describe here the vestibule itself of the inner gate, but the place within that extends toward the vestibule of the inner gate.

[Note: Longipontanus reads, “but the place outside.” The construction should be: “but the place that leads inward to the vestibule.” Transpositions are frequently observable in Gregory.]

Through this place, as we have said, our hope is signified. While it seeks eternal rest, it leads the mind toward the vestibule of the inner gate. The very fact that we desire heavenly things, sigh for promised joys, and seek the rest of eternal life means that we are already drawing near to the face of the inner vestibule.

Let faith, therefore, be signified by the gate; charity by the court; and hope by the place that approaches the face of the vestibule of the inner gate. Without these three virtues, no one who is already capable of using reason can enter the heavenly building.

Let faith, then, be held in the gate, which introduces to understanding; charity in the court, which expands the mind into love; and hope in the place described as fifty cubits, because through desires and sighs it introduces the mind to the secret joys of rest.

[Note: Vallicellianus, Longipontanus, and the Norman manuscripts read, “through desires one reaches the secret joys of rest.”]

Although we do not yet see the light of truth as it is in that rest,

[Note: Laudunensis, Suessionensis, and Longipontanus read, “as the light of truth is.”]

we nevertheless already see something through the cracks of understanding.

[Note: Ebroicensis and Lyra read, “through the senses.”]

Hence it is added here:

**Verse 16.** “And oblique windows in the chambers.”

### 17

In oblique windows, the part through which the light enters is narrow, but the interior part that receives the light is broad. So too, although the minds of contemplatives see something of the true light only faintly, they are nevertheless expanded within themselves with great breadth. Indeed, they can scarcely contain even the little that they see.

What contemplatives see of eternity is exceedingly small, but from that small portion the bosom of their minds is enlarged into an increase of fervor and love. They become broad within themselves precisely where they admit into themselves the light of truth, as it were, through narrow openings.

Because this greatness of contemplation can be granted only to those who love, the oblique windows are said to be in the chambers, or in those structures that are said to be beside the chambers—not already outside, but within. For concerning these same windows it is added:

**Ibid.** “And in the fronts of those that were within the gate, all around.”

### 18

They were in the chambers, and they were also in the fronts of those structures that had been built within the gate all around. For whoever has a heart broad within himself also receives the light of contemplation.

[Note: Longipontanus reads, “whoever has a heart broad within,” a phrase repeated below.]

Those who still think excessively about outward things do not know what cracks of contemplation there may be through which the eternal light enters.

[Note: The same codex reads, “cracks of thought.”]

The infusion of incorporeal light cannot be received through images of bodily things. While only visible things are being considered, invisible light is not admitted into the mind.

[Note: The Norman manuscripts omit “alone.”]

But whoever already directs his attention toward the light of contemplation must take great care to keep his mind always in humility, never exalt himself because of the grace poured into him, and consider what kind of oblique windows signify the minds of contemplatives.

Through oblique windows light enters, but a thief does not enter, because those who are truly watchmen always press their understanding down into humility.

[Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read, “through humility.”]

The understanding of contemplation enters their minds, but the boasting of self-exaltation does not. Thus the windows are both open and fortified: the grace by which they are filled is open within their minds, yet they do not permit the adversary to enter them through pride.

### 19

It should be noted that oblique windows are said to exist within the gate, all around. The grace of contemplation is not given to the greatest while withheld from the least. Often the greatest receive it; often the least; more frequently those who are remote from prominence; sometimes even married people.

If there is no office among the faithful from which the grace of contemplation can be excluded, then anyone who has a heart within can also be illuminated by the light of contemplation. Oblique windows have been constructed within the gate, all around, so that no one may boast of this grace as though it belonged to him alone.

No one should think that he possesses the gift of true light privately, because in the very matter in which he thinks himself to possess something exceptional, another may often be richer—someone whom he had not thought to possess any good thing.

Hence it is aptly added here:

**Ibid.** “Likewise, there were windows in the vestibules, in a circuit within.”

### 20

After saying that there were windows in the fronts, he adds that there were windows in the vestibules, in a circuit within. For not only do the exalted members of holy Church, who stand out above the others, possess the grace of contemplation; often this gift is also received by those members who, although they already soar toward the heights through desire, still lie below through the duties they perform.

If almighty God did not also pour the light of contemplation upon those who appear despised, there would not have been windows in the vestibules.

We see some people established in the highest places of holy Church speaking lofty things about heavenly realities and, with wondrous zeal, examining the secrets of the heavenly homeland to the extent that an enlightened mind is capable: these are windows in the fronts.

But others are held within the bosom of holy Church and appear despised in human eyes. Nevertheless, they devote themselves inwardly to the study of wisdom, yearn for heavenly things, and, as far as they can, contemplate what the eternal joys are: these too are oblique windows, but in the vestibules.

### 21

It is rightly said, “in a circuit,” because every investigation of hidden matters involves circling, when the mind says in its thought: “Could this be it? Could that be it?” It circles around in order to find what it seeks.

When the unbounded light begins to burst forth in knowledge,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts read; alternatively, “into recognition.” The printed editions read “into thought.”]

the ray of truth comes, as it were, through an oblique window. In contemplation, by circling around many things in our thoughts, we make progress,

[Note: Laudunensis and Suessionensis read “we seek.”]

just as we often seek examples of good people in order to advance in conduct.

When the mind is already thinking of passing over to better things, it seeks whatever better thing it may be able to hear about others. Now it examines the life of one person, now that of another saint.

Hence a certain chosen person, who had cast the eyes of his mind throughout the world in the open bosom of holy Church, seeking the lives of good people for imitation,

[Note: The printed editions read, “in the extended stream.” We do not know on what manuscript authority, since all our manuscripts read “in the bosom.”]

said: “I will go around and offer in the tabernacle of God the sacrifice of jubilation” (Ps. 26:6).

Behold, he went around in order to offer the sacrifice of jubilation, because unless he sent his mind here and there to seek out the lives of good people, he would not reach the sacrifice of jubilation.

When holy men are led within holy Church to positions of eminence, their life is placed, as it were, in a mirror, so that all may see the good things they ought to imitate. Hence it is aptly added:

**Ibid.** “And before the fronts was a painting of palms.”

### 22

What is signified by palms except the rewards of victory? They are customarily given to those who conquer. Hence it is written concerning those who had conquered the ancient enemy in the contest of martyrdom and were already rejoicing as victors in their homeland: “And palms were in their hands, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Rev. 7:9).

To have palms in one’s hands is to have held victories in one’s works. The palm of that work is repaid where one already rejoices without contest.

Hence it does not say here, “Palms before the fronts,” but “before the fronts was a painting of palms.” The palm of victory will be seen there, where joy will already be without end.

Here we often see holy men perform wonders, accomplish many works of power, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, and foretell future things through the spirit of prophecy. We see them drive away bodily diseases by touch.

[Note: The printed editions changed “drive away” to “heal,” a reading found in none of the manuscripts available to us. Diseases properly are not “healed,” since disease and health are contrary states.]

None of these things is yet a palm, but only a painting of palms, for such things are sometimes also given to the reprobate. Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” And then I will declare to them: “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23).

One sign of election, however, is the steadfastness of charity, as it is written: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

When the elect perform these miracles, they perform them in a manner far different from the reprobate.

[Note: The printed editions read “the reprobate perform them,” although all our manuscripts resist that reading.]

What the elect strive to do out of charity, the reprobate strive to do out of self-exaltation. Yet even for the elect, the very wonders they perform through charity are not yet palms, but still paintings of palms, because they reveal outwardly what they are held to be inwardly by almighty God. They will have the palm there, where the struggle with death will no longer exist.

The distinguished preacher recognized that the true palm would then be given to those who conquer, when he foresaw the resurrection of the dead. He says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. And when this mortal has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:53 and following).

Then victory will be perfect, when death has been completely swallowed up. In everything that we now see being done wondrously through signs, we see not victory itself but still images of victory.

Because powers and signs are often given even to saints placed in high positions, so that others may be drawn toward good works, a painting of palms is displayed before the fronts of the inner building.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “dictated.”]

Let what has been discussed today suffice, so that with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ we may come with greater strength to what follows. He lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily VI

Only three verses are explained, and it is shown how great the perfection that shone forth in Christians, especially in the apostles, was.

### 1

After the prophet had said many things while indicating the oblique windows of the grace of contemplation, he says that he was led outside and recalls that he saw storehouses. What else is signified by these storehouses except the knowledge of teachers?

Yet a question may rightly be raised here. Since holy teachers teach spiritual and inward things, why does the prophet say that he was led outside and saw the storehouses externally?

We must understand that one kind of contemplation sees what it is unable to express, whereas another kind of knowledge and teaching sees what it can express through the tongue.

[Note: Laudunensis and Suessionensis read: “For in contemplation of the true light …”]

Compared with that light which cannot be expressed in words, everything that can be expressed in words is, as it were, outside.

He therefore says:

**Ezek. 40:17.** “And he led me into the outer court, and behold, there were storehouses and a pavement laid with stones in the court all around.”

### 2

Since in Greek *φυλάττειν* means “to preserve” or “to guard,”

[Note: Ebroicensis and Sagien­sis read φυλάξαι.]

and *gaza* means “riches” in the Persian language, the place where riches are kept is commonly called a *gazophylacium*, a storehouse.

What, then, is signified by the storehouses except, as we said earlier, the hearts of teachers filled with the riches of wisdom and knowledge? For, in Paul’s words: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

There are some who, through the gift of grace, understand even those things they have not heard expounded by teachers; these have received the word of wisdom. And there are some who cannot understand by themselves what they have heard, but retain what they have read in commentators and present with understanding what they have learned by reading.

What, then, except the word of knowledge, fills these people? This may also be understood in another way, since wisdom pertains to life, while knowledge pertains to teaching.

Someone who lives well and preaches prudently is therefore rightly called a storehouse of the spiritual building, because heavenly riches are dispensed from his mouth.

The same teacher of the nations saw that his disciples abounded in these riches when he said: “You have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. 1:5).

Thus storehouses are constructed in the building of holy Church, because the tongue of teachers abounds in the riches of knowledge.

Truth itself declares that these are true riches when, speaking of transitory riches, it says: “The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word” (Matt. 13:22).

[Note: The printed editions read “the word of knowledge.” The final word is absent from all our manuscripts and is not found in the Greek text or the Vulgate.]

The wisdom and knowledge of spiritual teaching are true riches; in comparison with them, things that can pass away are called false riches. Of these riches Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21:20).

Apart from the fact that spiritual riches lead to the eternal homeland, they differ greatly from earthly riches. Spiritual riches increase when distributed; earthly riches either diminish when distributed or, when retained, are of no use.

Those who contain these true riches within themselves are therefore rightly called storehouses.

### 3

These storehouses themselves have a pavement all around, because the humility of their hearers adheres to them and lies beneath them.

This pavement is rightly said to be laid with stones in the court, because faithful souls are joined to one another in the breadth of charity.

[Note: Sagien­sis and Longipontanus read “are subjected.”]

They are called stones because of the strength of their faith, and they are laid upon the pavement in the structure of humility. The apostle Peter had perceived the minds of these faithful people as strong in faith when he said: “And you, like living stones, are being built up into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2:5).

[Note: The printed editions read “spiritual houses.” This reading is contrary to the sense and is not found in the Greek source or in the Vulgate.]

Concerning these stones of holy Church, the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates into carved stones, all your boundaries into desirable stones, all your sons taught by the Lord” (Isa. 54:12–13).

[Note: Laudunensis reads “carved.” We restored this passage, which is partially mutilated in Gussanville’s text, partly from German and other manuscripts and partly from the earlier printed editions.]

Almighty God placed jasper, a green-colored stone, as the battlements of holy Church, because he strengthened the minds of its preachers with love of inward verdure, so that they might despise all transitory things, desire nothing in this world enclosed by an end, and regard all its joys as dry and withered.

Hence the pastor of the Church himself, calling his hearers to the pastures of eternal verdure, speaks of God, saying: “According to his great mercy, he has regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven” (1 Pet. 1:3–4).

### 4

The gates of this holy Church are set in carved stones, because those through whose voice we enter into eternal life, by displaying within themselves the holy works commanded by God, have held those works as though carved into themselves.

The gates would not be carved but plain if they uttered the voice but did not display holy works in themselves. But when they show themselves living according to what they speak, they are both gates, because they lead within, and carved, because by living they preserve what they tell others.

We see all the boundaries of this holy Church set in desirable stones when we observe within it the faithful, strong in faith and charity. To show which people he meant by stones, Isaiah added: “All your sons taught by the Lord” (Isa. 54:13).

What Isaiah saw as all the boundaries of the Church being desirable stones, Ezekiel described as a pavement laid with stones all around. For he adds concerning the storehouses:

**Ibid.** “Thirty storehouses around the pavement.”

### 5

The number ten is always understood as signifying perfection, because the observance of the law is contained in the ten commandments.

The active and contemplative life are joined together in the commandments of the Decalogue, because in it we are commanded both to love God and to love our neighbor. Love of God pertains to the contemplative life; love of one’s neighbor pertains to the active life.

But for each teacher to expand himself fully into the active life and rise vigilantly into the contemplative life, he must be perfected in faith in the Holy Trinity. Hence the storehouses are said to be thirty in number: when ten is multiplied threefold, the life and speech of the teacher are made firm in the Trinity.

### 6

But in this matter we must observe carefully that the prophet, after describing the chambers, added: “The pavement all around.” And below he added: “The chambers around the pavement.” Thus the chambers appear to be around the pavement, and the pavement around the chambers. The pavement and the chambers were arranged in such a way that the chambers were laid between one pavement and another, and the pavement between the chambers.

This, brothers, is not said without a great mystery: the pavement is said to be around the chambers, and the chambers are reported to be around the pavement. The pavement has chambers around it because the life of those who listen is daily instructed and guarded by the speech of teachers. Good teachers, in the words of holy instruction, watch over the lives of their hearers, sometimes with the nourishment of gentleness, sometimes with the sharpness of reproof, so as to defend them from vices.

Yet the chambers themselves have pavement around them, because often the heart even of teachers is touched by the temptations of vices, so that it is sometimes lifted up by the pride of self-exaltation [Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read “by the boastfulness of pride” (*jactatione superbiae*)], sometimes inflamed by the goads of anger. But when they consider the life of good hearers and reflect that it has progressed through their exhortations, they are ashamed not to be such as, by God’s agency, they see others have become; and they establish themselves beforehand in their minds lest they fall fully into sin. [Note: We have emended the recent editions—Gussanville, Roman, Gilot, and others—from the manuscripts, especially Laudunensis and Suessionensis, and from old printed editions. The former reading was: “and they establish themselves in mind so much the more firmly as they were falling more fully into fault” (Gussanville: “almost”). Uticensis reads as Gussanville and the other recent editions, but in a later revision, though in an old hand and perhaps with the same ink. Laudunensis here reads: “the teachers’ words return to memory.”] For when their own words return to the teachers’ memory, they are ashamed not to keep what they say.

Hence Solomon also says: “The soul of the laborer labors for him, because his mouth has compelled him” (Prov. 16:26). Our mouth compels us to labor when, through what we say, we are restrained from vices, because it is exceedingly shameful for us to fall through negligence precisely where, by preaching, we have attempted to raise others.

The chambers therefore have pavement around them, because the venerable life of the hearers is a great safeguard for the teachers. Their own speech becomes a help to them, because they are ashamed not to resist the vices that assail them, when they have armed others against those vices.

### 7

For as long as we live in this life, what else are we doing against evil spirits than standing in battle array? As we said above, the teacher’s mind may perhaps be assailed by some form of elation. But whether to prevent his own destruction or to keep his example from drawing others to perdition, he carefully and quickly examines himself, reproves himself in his thoughts, and, recalling the life of his hearers, humbles himself. In whatever ways he can, he acts lest elation gain mastery in his mind or dominate his conduct.

For it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15). What fruit of a good work, then, will exist before God if it has rotted from the root of self-exaltation?

Often, as has been said, his mind is tempted by anger. But by examining himself he quickly gathers himself back to himself; and, pressing himself down beneath the weight of discipline, he acts lest the mind’s agitation pass into speech or burst forth in his voice. Thus the anger of a troubled mind, arising through negligence, is there suffocated and dies through judgment.

As a result, the mind gives birth to virtue from conceived guilt: although it did not firmly guard itself so as not to rise into agitation, it nevertheless firmly conquered itself in the midst of agitation. Hence Solomon rightly says: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities” (Prov. 16:32).

The patient man is rightly preferred to the conqueror of cities, because in that action of victory a man is victor over other men, whereas in this gentleness of patience the mind is victor over itself.

It follows:

### Verse 28

“And the pavement in front of the gates, along the length of the gates, was lower.”

### 8

If we refer the length of the gates to the place where the gates had been constructed, the pavement was lower along the length of the gates, because the lower pavement extended as far as the space occupied by the gates could contain. [Note: Nearly all printed editions read “was contained” (*tenebatur*); the reading is corrected from the English manuscripts and ours.] The length of the pavement therefore did not differ from that of the gates, but the pavement was nevertheless not equal in height to the gates.

What does it mean that the pavement was equally long with the gates but was not equal to them, except that the life of the people is far removed from the life of teachers? For although those striving toward the heavenly kingdom possess the same enduring hope, they do not possess the same commitment to living.

Let the pavement therefore extend equally in length, because the hearers retain within themselves the very faith and the very hope that preachers are certainly known to possess. But let the pavement lie lower, so that all hearers may recognize that their preachers far surpass them in merit.

If, however, by the length of the gates we should understand their height, as we said above, then—since a little later it is written that one ascended to the gates by steps—the pavement lies lower in proportion as each gate rises in height. For the holier the teacher’s life, the humbler the understanding of the hearer becomes. He despises himself when he perceives his preacher’s life rising to great height.

He may perhaps imitate some of the preacher’s good qualities, but not others. In those things in which he prevails, he makes progress; in those in which he does not prevail at all, he grows in humility. And this itself is therefore a form of progress for him: that something which he cannot imitate for the sake of advancement nevertheless advances him.

### 9

For consider: if we weigh the words and deeds of our preachers that we read about, we recognize to what height the gates have risen. [Note: The same manuscript has *portae* (“of the gate”), perhaps for *portae* in the singular.] To say nothing of the display of miracles, let us speak of the virtues of their hearts.

Certainly Paul, who says that he died to the law through the law, because the law itself preached this to him so that he might believe in Christ (Rom. 2:10), was kindled with great fervor of faith. He did not wish to observe the precepts of the law carnally and forbade circumcision to be performed among the Gentiles. [Note: Laudunensis reads *teneri* (“to be observed”), which better suits the Apostle as teaching what must be done; hence below also, “he forbade circumcision … to be performed.” Other manuscripts, however, prevent adoption of this reading.] And when the apostle Peter still wished the custom of observance of the law in circumcision to be maintained, Paul opposed him to his face and says that Peter was blameworthy in this matter (Gal. 2:11).

Speaking to the disciples, he calls this conduct not merely a fault but, what is more serious, hypocrisy—that is, pretense—saying: [Note: We have removed the particle *in* before *studium* (“conduct”), which the editions introduced against the manuscripts.] “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (ibid., 11). And shortly afterward: “The rest of the Jews joined him in his pretense” (ibid., 13).

Yet this same foremost of the apostles, while admonishing the disciples on many matters and learning that certain people disparaged Paul’s writings, says: [Note: The printed editions lack *de* (“concerning”), supplied by the manuscripts, especially Laudunensis. Some read *detrahi scripta* (“that writings were disparaged”).] “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, speaking in them about these matters, among which there are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable twist, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Pet. 3:1).

Behold: Paul wrote in his Epistles that Peter was blameworthy; and behold: Peter asserts in his Epistles that Paul was admirable in what he had written. For unless Peter had read Paul’s Epistles, he would not have praised them. But if he read them, he found that he himself was said to be blameworthy. [Note: Gussanville reads “he is found,” against the manuscripts and other editions.]

A friend of truth therefore praised even the fact that he had been reproved, and this very thing pleased him: that in those matters in which he had thought otherwise than he ought, he had not pleased Paul. Peter also yielded assent to his younger brother and, in the same matter, became a follower of his inferior, so that he might surpass him even in this: he who was first at the summit of the apostolate might also be first in humility. [Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read “called first in the apostolate.”]

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, upon what summit of mind stood the man who praised those Epistles in which he found himself written as blameworthy. What gentleness could have been so great? What tranquility of spirit, what firmness of mind, what undisturbedness of thought? [Note: Vallicellianus and the Norman manuscripts read “untroubledness” (*imperturbatae*).]

Behold, he is reproved by his inferior, and he does not disdain to be reproved. He does not recall that he was the first to be called to the apostolate, nor that he received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, nor that whatever sins he loosed on earth would be loosed also in heaven (Matt. 4:18; 16:19 and following), nor that he walked on the sea with his feet (Matt. 14:29), nor that by commanding in Jesus’ name he had raised paralytics (Acts 9:33), nor that he had healed the sick by the shadow of his body (ibid. 5:15), nor that he had slain liars by a word (ibid. 5:10), nor that he had raised the dead by prayer (ibid. 9:40).

Thus, so that he would not disdain to hear words of reproof, he drove from his memory, as it were, all the gifts he had received, in order to hold firmly to the one great gift of humility.

Which of us, I ask, if he had performed even some minor miracle and were reproved by a younger brother, would patiently hear the words of reproof? We have performed no miracle, and if someone perhaps reproves us for our conduct, we immediately swell with pride. We silently imagine ourselves to be great; we recall virtues to ourselves, even virtues that we do not possess.

But Peter, humble even amid his virtues, remained under reproof; and so the gate rose in height. We cannot imitate such great gentleness; but because we are the pavement, we lie far below.

### 10

There are, however, some who understand not Peter, the chief of the apostles, but another man named Peter, who was reproved by Paul. If they had read Paul’s words more carefully, they would not say this.

For when Paul was about to say, “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face” (Gal. 2:11), in order to show which Peter he meant, he prefaced his account with these words: “The Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of the circumcision was entrusted to Peter. For he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles” (ibid., 7–8).

It is therefore clear which Peter Paul is speaking about: the one whom he calls an apostle and whom he says presided over the Gospel of the circumcision.

### 11

There were also some who said that the Second Epistle of Peter, in which Paul’s Epistles are praised, was not written by Peter. But if they had carefully considered the words of that Epistle, they could have held a very different opinion.

For it is written there: “A voice of this kind came to him from the magnificent glory: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (2 Pet. 1:17). [Note: Most Norman manuscripts read “in whom I was well pleased.”] And it continues: “And we ourselves heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain” (ibid., 18).

Let them read the Gospel, and they will immediately recognize that when this voice came from heaven, the apostle Peter stood with the Lord on the mountain. [Note: The words “on the mountain,” omitted in the printed editions, have been supplied from the Laudunensis, Suessionensis, Longipontanus, Norman, and English manuscripts.] He therefore wrote this Epistle who heard this voice concerning the Lord on the mountain.

### 12

But since we have said a little about Peter, let us now, if you please, turn to Paul’s gentleness and consider whether we can understand how gentle he was in his devotion to patience—he whose zeal in preaching was so ardent that he did not spare even the foremost of the apostles.

Let us say nothing of the fact that he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, and spent a day and a night in the depths of the sea, or that from the Jews he received five times “forty less one” blows (2 Cor. 11:2–3 and following). The evils inflicted upon us by open adversaries move the mind to anger less; what usually hurts more is what we suffer from our own people. [Note: Longipontanus reads “more severely,” *melius, laedere*. On the authority of one manuscript, not otherwise very ancient, nothing is altered, especially since Gregory is known sometimes to have spoken imprecisely. All the Norman manuscripts read “what we suffer from those near to us.”]
