Hence Truth itself, through the Psalmist, speaks against its betrayer, saying: “For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have borne it. But you, my equal, my leader, and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food” (Ps. 54:15).

Let us therefore consider, if we can, how patient the apostle Paul was among persecutors and how gentle among disciples.

Certainly, when he came to Corinth, he drew the Corinthians away from the service of idols, [Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read “coming to Corinth.”] made known who the true God was, and preached to them the joys of eternal life. And when he had gathered a great multitude of the people into the faith, he endured such poverty there that he suffered under severe necessity for his sustenance.

He did not receive earthly bread from the disciples to whom he preached the bread of heaven. He devoted himself to speech for the life of his hearers; he devoted himself to the labor of his hands for the life of his body (1 Cor. 4:12; 1 Thess. 2:9; 2 Thess. 3:8). Support was also sent to him by disciples from other lands, so that he might be able to preach to the Corinthians.

For afterward he says to those same Corinthians in an Epistle: “When I was present with you and was in need, I was burdensome to no one; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked” (2 Cor. 11:9). He prefaced this with a serious reproach, saying: “I robbed other churches, receiving support for your ministry” (ibid., 8).

Let us consider, if we can, how great a gentleness this was: to preach the bread of the spirit and not receive the bread of the flesh; to instruct the hearts of hearers concerning eternal riches and, among those same faithful and prosperous disciples, to suffer hunger; to endure want among the well-fed and yet not speak of what he suffered; not to speak of what he suffered and yet not grieve; to see the hard hearts of miserly hearers toward him and nevertheless not abandon his preaching.

For, as the Acts of the Apostles testify, he preached continually in that same city for a year and six months (Acts 18:11). After he had departed from those same Corinthians, he later wrote to them about what he had endured while among them (2 Cor. 11:23 and following).

Why did he never say this to them while living among them? So that what they had not done toward him out of good will would not be done by command, and so that, once their mercy became known, their willingness would remain unknown. [Note: The printed editions read “their misery,” against the manuscripts.]

Why, then, does he write about it later, when he is far away? So that the disciples would not remain wholly uncorrected and, just as they had been toward their teacher in their stinginess, would not be the same toward other brothers.

In this Paul truly was the teacher of the Gentiles: neglecting his own interests and caring for those of others. He fulfilled what he had preached: “Let no one seek his own, but the good of the other” (1 Cor. 10:24); and, “Let each of you consider not his own interests, but those of others.”

How great, then, was this virtue of gentleness! How great the tranquility of spirit! Which of us, if he had converted one rich man of this world to the service of almighty God, then saw himself in need while that man did not provide him with the necessities of life, would not immediately have despaired of that man’s life? Who would not say that he had labored in vain? Who would not fall silent in exhorting someone whom he did not see first bearing the fruit of good works in himself?

### 13

But Paul, made firm at the summit of virtue through gentleness, persisted, preached, loved, and completed the good work he had begun. By enduring and persevering, he brought the hearts of the disciples to mercy (2 Cor. 9:3–4 and following).

Later, indicating that he knew of their progress, he writes in the same Epistle: “Concerning the ministry that is carried out for the saints, it is more than sufficient for me to write to you. [Note: The Norman manuscripts and Vallicellianus read “more than sufficiently” (*ex abundanti*). For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you to the Macedonians, saying that Achaia has been ready since the previous year, and your zeal has stirred up very many” (ibid., 1).

Again he says of them: “You began not only to do but also to desire, from the previous year” (2 Cor. 8:10). Since in these people he was seeking not so much works as pious intentions, he plainly praises their pious intentions more than their works.

It must nevertheless be noted that this very consolation contains a reproach when he says: “From the previous year.” They had indeed done well, but they had done so late; therefore the teacher praised them without omitting reproof. He is a physician: he applies medicine to the wound, which both soothes what has been cleansed and bites into what is found to be rotten.

By enduring and preaching, however, he completed what he had begun. Through the remarkable virtue of patience, he softened the disciples’ hardness into the bowels of mercy, because the length of the gate rose in height.

But we are weak and unfit to imitate such great gentleness and patience, because we are the pavement and lie despised in our conduct.

### 14

Behold, while I speak of two leaders of the heavenly army, the martyr Stephen also comes to mind. Seized for the name of his Creator and brought into the midst of his persecutors, he stood undaunted, taught boldly, and sharply rebuked his persecutors out of zeal for the truth, saying: “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

When they ran at him with stones and killed him with stones, he knelt and prayed for those same persecutors, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (ibid., 59).

What virtue, then, was this: to burn with zeal so as boldly to declare the reproach of their unbelief to those by whom he was being held, and yet to love them so that even in death he prayed for those by whom he was dying?

He burned with zeal as though he possessed no gentleness at all; yet he remained gentle in his love for them as though he possessed no fervor against them. Amid all this, let us consider where the guilt of our own conscience lies.

Which of us, if he received even a verbal insult from a neighbor, would not immediately return the insult, be deeply disturbed, burst into hatred, and forget the commandment of love?

But blessed Stephen was able to do this through the grace of almighty God, because, rising in height, he was a gate. [Note: The Roman edition inserts here: “who, being full of the Holy Spirit, looking into heaven saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand, and said: Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, because, rising …” This is merely the addition of an idle copyist.] We miserable people cannot imitate this by our own strength, because we lie far below like pavement.

### 15

What, then, do we say in our admiration of the lives of the saints, when even the ancient fathers, considering the life of the preachers of holy Church, were greatly amazed?

Did not the Psalmist admire their life when he said: “But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their rule has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. 138:17)?

Ask the Gospel concerning which of God’s friends he speaks; there Truth says to the preachers: “You are my friends” (John 15:14).

Isaiah too, gazing upon their life, says: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8).

The holy preachers are rightly called clouds, because they rain through their words and flash with miracles. They are also said to fly like clouds because, although living on earth, they were beyond the earth in all that they did.

Hence it is said through a certain cloud: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10:3).

The earlier fathers used marriage, fathered children, possessed property, and devoted themselves to the concerns of household affairs. Foreseeing these men already through the spirit of prophecy, Isaiah calls them not walking on earth like human beings but flying like clouds: [Note: Recent editions read “foreseeing,” in the singular, against all our manuscripts and the English manuscripts; perhaps they wished the statement here to refer not to the earlier fathers but to Isaiah alone. Vallicellianus, with the English manuscripts, reads “as human beings” (*velut homines*) for “among human beings.”] abandoning property, not seeking marriage, not fathering children, seeking nothing on earth, and possessing nothing.

For they fly because in mind they contemplate heavenly things. They scarcely touch the earth because they desire nothing in it. They are also like doves at their windows because, through the spirit of their gentleness, they desire nothing in this world with their eyes.

Let us therefore consider how lofty are the gates of this spiritual building, which even the spiritual fathers admire. How greatly, then, must we humble ourselves in our admiration of them, we who are the pavement?

But since we have understood height under the designation of the length of the gates, let us now learn something about their breadth.

It follows:

### Verse 29

“And he measured the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court, externally, one hundred cubits, toward the east and toward the north.”

### 16

If in these words we understand the gate as the entrance by which we enter into knowledge of the Lord, the lower gate is faith, while the inner court is contemplation.

The lower gate has breadth at its front because faith, through the amplitude of its love, possesses the visible activity that it displays toward its neighbors. When we see more perfect people carry this out vigorously, we, who are constrained in good works, receive from them examples of great activity. Each holy action becomes for us a kind of widening of the road that had previously been narrow with difficulty.

The inner court also has a front, because the contemplative life shows through certain signs of longing and sighing how much it sees within, since it loves so greatly.

The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Hence perfection is rightly signified by one hundred, just as Truth says concerning the elect: “Everyone who leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

No saint, however, abandons earthly things in order to possess more of them in this world. For whoever leaves the earth out of earthly desire does not leave the earth but desires it. Nor will the man who abandons one wife receive a hundred wives. Rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred, after which eternal life is also promised: whoever for the name of God despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind even in this life, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life.

He receives a hundredfold, therefore, who, receiving the spirit of perfection, has no need of earthly things, even when he does not possess them. For the poor man is the one who needs what he does not have. But the person who does not possess something and does not desire to possess it is rich. Poverty consists in the want of the mind, not in the quantity of possessions. For one to whom poverty is a suitable companion is not poor.

The man therefore measured the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court, externally, one hundred cubits, [Note: Laudunensis reads “to the front of the gate of the inner court.”] because our Redeemer daily measures the life of the faithful through teachers and instructors according to the measure of perfection: either in the manifestation of a good work through faith or in holy desires through contemplation. [Note: The same manuscript reads “or in the display” (*vel in exhibitione*).]

### 17

Many appear to be established in faith and to perform great works, but they are not measured by one hundred cubits because, through the very things they do, they seek earthly glory.

Some appear to be tormented by abstinence, devoted to sighing; but their measure is not brought to one hundred cubits, because in what they do they seek praise from human judgment. [Note: Longipontanus reads “is brought”; Vallicellianus reads “of those things which,” for “in those things which.”]

Who, then, is measured by one hundred cubits except the person whose good action proceeds from a right intention, so that in what he does he is not turned toward seeking earthly gain or passing praise?

### 18

Behold: to show mercy to one’s neighbors, to distribute one’s possessions, to give quickly to the needy—this is the breadth at the front of the lower gate.

But if, while giving what is yours, you do not desire what belongs to another, and if you do not seek earthly glory from the good work itself, you are rightly measured by the number one hundred, that is, by perfection.

For the person who appears to give his own possessions mercifully but perhaps violently seizes what belongs to another still does not know what the way of perfection is, nor has he understood from where one advances toward perfection, because he has not even found its beginning.

He ought first to have torn desire from his mind, and afterward to have given away what he rightly possessed. Hence it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:37). For what good can the person do who has not yet turned away from evil?

There are also some who, as has been said, abstain from food and chastise the flesh, but when they are tested, they are found to be panting after the glory of the world. These display the front of the inner court, but they are not measured by one hundred cubits.

### 19

These, then, belong to the number of perfection, concerning whom Paul says: “They have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

It must be noted that it is not said that these things are measured internally but externally, because our Redeemer, when he either approves or judges the deeds of human beings performed through us, measures them not internally but externally.

Hence he also says through the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16). For through what we see we recognize the mind of the one acting, which we do not see. Thus we measure externally either the breadth that is at the front of the lower gate or the front of the inner court.

When we see some people giving alms, hastening to the afflicted, helping the oppressed, [Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read “coming to the aid of” (*occurrere*).] seeking no glory in this world, and yearning for none of this world’s advantages; and when we see others subduing the flesh, devoting themselves to tears, occupied with heavenly words, and desiring none of the honor that passes away—what else should we do except believe them to be perfect and consider them holy?

Because we see them to be perfect through what we observe, we measure their life externally by one hundred cubits.

### 20

And because many among the Jews, but very many among the Gentiles, attained this summit of perfection, it is rightly added: “Toward the east and toward the north.”

The Jewish people is rightly called the East, because from its flesh was born he who is called the Sun of justice. Concerning him the prophet says: “But for you who fear the Lord, the Sun of justice will rise” (Mal. 4:2).

The Gentiles, however, are represented by the north, because for a long time they lay numb in the cold of their unbelief; and in their heart reigned the one who, as the prophet testifies, said of himself: “I will set my throne toward the north” (Isa. 14:13).

Since almighty God, having become incarnate, made some perfect from the Jews and others perfect from the Gentiles within holy Church, he measured one hundred cubits not only toward the east but also toward the north.

### 21

But since, under the name of the north, the discourse has turned to the Gentiles, it is worthwhile to consider how abundantly the compassion of our Creator has been poured out upon us.

For all of us come from the Gentiles. Our ancient parents served wood and stones, and, abandoning the God by whom they were made, worshiped gods whom they themselves had made.

But through the grace of almighty God we have been brought from darkness into light. Let us therefore recall from what darkness we came, so that we may give thanks for the light we have received. For the person who does not remember his own misery does not understand divine mercy.

Hence it is said to God through the Psalmist: “Make your mercies wondrous, Lord, for you save those who hope in you” (Ps. 16:7). The mercies of God become wondrous to us when the memory of our misery is recalled to us, because, remembering what we were, we understand to whom we owe what we are.

Let us therefore sing with joy to our Creator, because we have shaken the collars of our minds free from the service of created things. Let us rejoice that what was said through Isaiah has been fulfilled in us: “And the bridle of error that was on the jaws of the peoples will be for you a song, like the voice of a sanctified solemnity” (Isa. 30:23, 29).

The bridle of error had bound the jaws of the peoples when the Gentiles, fettered by the error of idols, did not know how to offer the true God the praise of confession. But this very bridle of error has now been turned for us into a song, as we rejoice, sing psalms, and chant:

“All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 96:5).

And again:

“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see; they have ears, but they will not hear; they have noses, but they will not smell; they have hands, but they will not feel; they have feet, but they will not walk” (Ps. 115:4 and following).

When we sing these things to almighty God, we have made the very bridle of our error—which had bound our mouths from the praise of God—into a song for the true Lord. [Note: Most Norman manuscripts, with Longipontanus, read “which [had bound our mouths] to praise,” rather than “from the praise of God.”]

It is rightly said: “Like the voice of a sanctified solemnity” (Isa. 30:29), because when we render to God the praise of confession, we rejoice in a sanctified solemnity.

Let us therefore respond in our conduct to the great mercy of our Redeemer; and, having recognized the light, let us shun the darkness of evil works.

### 22 [Cols. 1010A–1011A]

What, I ask, is there now in this world that can give pleasure? Everywhere we see mourning; on every side we hear groaning. Cities have been destroyed, camps overthrown, fields laid waste, and the land reduced to desolation. No inhabitant remains in the countryside, and scarcely any resident remains in the cities; yet even these few remnants of the human race are still struck daily and without respite. The scourges of heavenly justice have no end, because even amid the scourges the sinful action has not been corrected.

[Note: Laudunensis and Vallicellianus read “the actions of sin.”]

We see some led into captivity, others mutilated, others killed. What, then, is there to delight in during this life, my brothers? If we still love such a world, we love not joys but wounds. And Rome herself, which once seemed to be the mistress of the world—what she has become, we see.

[Note: The same witnesses, together with Longipontanus, read “you see” (*conspicitis*).] Worn down by immense sufferings in many forms, by the desolation of her citizens, the pressure of enemies, and the frequency of her ruins, so that we see fulfilled in her what is said much earlier through this same prophet against the city of Samaria:

“Set on the pot, set it on, I say, and pour water into it, and heap its pieces into it” (Ezek. 24:4).

And shortly afterward:

“Let its boiling boil fiercely, and let its bones be cooked through in its midst” (ibid., 5).

And again:

“Heap up the bones, which I shall set alight; the flesh shall be consumed, and the whole composition shall be cooked, and the bones shall waste away. Set it also empty upon the coals, so that it may grow hot and its bronze may melt” (ibid., 10–11).

The pot was then set before us when this city was established. Water was poured into it, and its pieces were heaped in it, when peoples flocked to it from every direction—peoples who, like boiling water, seethed with worldly pursuits and, like pieces of meat, melted in the midst of their own fervor.

[Note: Vallicellianus, with most Norman manuscripts, reads “in her herself, that is, Rome” (*in ipsa, id est Roma*).]

The statement is therefore appropriate: “Its boiling boiled fiercely, and its bones were cooked through in its midst,” because at first the activity of secular glory grew exceedingly hot in her, but afterward that glory, together with its followers, failed. By “bones” the powerful of the world are signified, and by “flesh” the peoples, because just as flesh is carried by bones, so the weakness of peoples is governed by the powerful of the world.

But behold, all the powerful of this world have now been taken away from her; therefore her bones have been cooked through. Behold, the peoples have failed; her flesh has melted. Let it therefore be said:

“Heap up the bones, which I shall set alight; the flesh shall be consumed, and the whole composition shall be cooked, and the bones shall waste away.”

[Note: The same manuscripts read “which shall be set alight” (*quae igne succendantur*); shortly afterward Longipontanus reads “shall be cooked” (*coquentur*): “its whole composition shall be cooked, and its bones shall waste away.” This is also the reading above where the same context is cited.]

For where is the senate? Where now is the people? The bones have wasted away, the flesh has been consumed, and all the pomp of secular dignities in her has been extinguished.

[Note: The printed editions read “the order of dignities.”]

Her whole composition has been cooked through. Yet even the few of us who remain are still oppressed daily by the sword and daily by countless tribulations. Let it therefore be said:

“Set it also empty upon the coals.”

Because the senate is absent, the people have perished, and yet pains and groans multiply daily among the few who remain, Rome now burns empty.

Why, however, should we speak of these things concerning human beings, when we see that the buildings themselves are also being destroyed as ruins grow more frequent? Accordingly, the following is aptly added concerning the city, now empty:

“Let it grow hot, and let its bronze melt.”

For the pot itself is now being consumed—the pot in which flesh and bones were previously consumed—because after the people have failed, even the walls are falling.

Where are those who once rejoiced in her glory? Where is their pageantry? Where their arrogance? Where the frequent and immoderate rejoicing?

### 23

What is said through the prophet against destroyed Nineveh has been fulfilled in her:

“Where is the dwelling place of the lions, and the pasture of the young lions?” (Nahum 2:11).

Were her leaders and princes not lions, who, ranging through the various provinces of the world, seized plunder by raging and killing? Here the young lions found pasture, because boys, adolescents, young men of the world, and the sons of worldly people flocked here from every direction whenever they wished to advance in this world.

But now, behold, she is desolate; behold, she is crushed; behold, she is oppressed by groans. No one now runs to her in order to advance in this world; no powerful and violent person remains who might seize plunder by oppression.

Let us therefore say:

“Where is the dwelling place of the lions, and the pasture of the young lions?”

What the prophet says concerning Judaea has happened to her:

“Widen your baldness like an eagle” (Micah 1:16).

A human being’s baldness ordinarily occurs only on the head, whereas an eagle’s baldness occurs over its whole body, because when it has grown very old, its feathers and wings fall from all its limbs. Thus she widens her baldness like an eagle, because she has lost her feathers by losing her people. The feathers of her wings have also fallen, with which she was accustomed to fly toward prey, because all her powerful men have been extinguished—those through whom she plundered what belonged to others (John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 66).

[Note: Longipontanus reads: “Rome widens her baldness like an eagle.”]

### 24 [Cols. 1011D–1012A]

We know that what we say about the crushing of the city of Rome has happened in all the cities of the world.

[Note: Laudunensis reads “has now happened almost in all”; this is truer than the unqualified “in all.”] Some places have been laid waste by calamity, others consumed by the sword, others tormented by famine, and others swallowed up by chasms in the earth.

Let us therefore despise this present age with all our heart, even though it is extinguished. Let us at least end our desires for the world together with the world’s end; let us imitate, as far as we can, the deeds of the good.

For in the East and the North there are many who, in the perfection of their life, are measured at one hundred cubits. From Judaea and from the Gentiles they have grown, as has been said, to the summit of holiness.

The East and the North may also be understood as the righteous and sinners. The righteous are not improperly called “the East,” because, born—as it were—in the light of faith, they have persevered in innocence. By “the North” we rightly understand sinners, who, having fallen away through the coldness of their minds, have grown numb beneath the shadow of their sin.

But because the mercy of almighty God also calls such people back to repentance, washes them through compunction and tears, enriches them with virtues, and raises them to the glory of perfection, they are led not only to the East, where there are one hundred cubits, but also to the North. For sinners, together with the righteous, come to perfection through gifts and repentance, by the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Vallicellianus and most Norman manuscripts lack this concluding clause.]

## HOMILY VII [in some copies XIX] [Cols. 1012A–1020B]

It comprises an exposition of seven verses, from 20 to 27, and at the same time presents numerous moral instructions: concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the stages leading to them, concerning true perfection, and concerning the necessity of good works.

### 1

Readers must exercise great discernment, so that when a single statement is made in sacred Scripture, it is not always thought to signify one and the same thing. Thus the sun is sometimes understood positively and sometimes negatively. Under the name “sun,” our Redeemer himself is sometimes signified, and sometimes persecution.

For, as the Book of Wisdom testifies, the ungodly will say in hell:

“We went astray from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness did not shine upon us” (Wis. 5:6).

And concerning the seed that was sown the Lord says:

“When the sun had risen, they were scorched” (Matt. 13:6),

because, when persecution has arisen, the words of preaching dry up in the hearts of the reprobate.

In the same way, the lion signifies the Lord. Thus it is written:

“The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5).

Again, the likeness of the devil is expressed under the name “lion,” as it is said through the chief shepherd:

“Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

[Note: Rothomagensis and Lyrensis read “our adversary” (*adversarius noster*).]

In the same way, a wise person is signified by the ox. Hence it is written:

“You shall not yoke an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22:10),

that is, you shall not join a wise person with a fool in preaching.

[Note: Laudunensis and Longipontanus read “you shall not yoke” (*non jungas*); Laudunensis shortly afterward reads “you shall not associate” (*non socias*).]

Again, the fool is represented by the ox, as is said of the one who has been captured by the love of shameful things:

[Note: Vallicellianus, with the Norman manuscripts, reads “in the love of shamefulness” (*in amore turpitudinis*).]

“Immediately he follows her, like an ox led to the slaughter” (Prov. 7:22),

that is, just as a fool is dragged to death.

I have said this, therefore, so that because I have explained “door” as signifying the Lord, or preachers, or sacred Scripture, or faith, no one should think that wherever “door” is now read in this prophet it signifies the same thing. When the prophet was speaking at length of one door, faith was rightly understood, because there is one faith of all the elect. But when other doors are named, the mouths of preachers may be understood, as was also said much earlier, through which true life is known and through which one ascends to knowledge of spiritual mysteries.

[Note: Suessionensis, Vallicellianus, and five Norman manuscripts read “while the prophet was speaking at length” (*propheta diutius loqueretur*). Laudunensis and Suessionensis read: “the mouths, etc., may be understood, as was said much earlier” (*intelligi … ora, etc.*).]

The door through which we said that faith is signified must be noted as being called “lower.” For while we are in this life, we are placed, as it were, at the bottom and are still held below. The lower door is rightly faith, because, for us who are placed on earth, it opens the knowledge of God.

Thus it is now said:

### Verses 20–22

“And he measured the door that faced the way of the North, belonging to the outer court, both in length and in width. Its chambers were three on this side and three on that side; and its fronts and its vestibule were according to the measure of the former door: its length was fifty cubits and its width twenty-five cubits. Its windows, its vestibule, and its sculptured work were according to the measure of the door that faced the East; and its ascent consisted of seven steps, with its vestibule before it.”

### 2

Concerning the door that faced the way of the North, belonging to the outer court, the same things are repeated that were already said above concerning another door; other things are then added that the prophet had left unsaid about that earlier door.

To discuss these matters more fully, then, which have not yet been examined, we must briefly repeat what has already been said. The door faces the way of the North when every preacher recognizes the life of a sinner and opens to him the inner things of life through the word of preaching.

It is called the door of the outer court. For the present life is the outer court, in which everything done bodily is also seen bodily. It is measured both in length and in width, because when a sinner is led to faith, his teacher must consider how far, through his admonition, he is progressing in the length of hope and in the breadth of charity.

One who is converted to God has no length if he still hopes in the good things of the present life, because the life in which he has placed his hope is short. If he is still constricted by desire for earthly things and by hatred of his neighbor, he has no breadth, because he does not know either how to despise transient things or how to expand himself in love of his neighbor.

But when a person who has been converted patiently hopes for the joys of eternal life, bears the troubles of his neighbors with charity, and despises the desire for what he does not possess, the door has both length and breadth, because the progress of the hearer is the glory of the preacher.

Hence it is said to certain people through the great preacher:

“My joy and my crown” (Phil. 4:1).

And again:

“For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8).

And again:

“What is our hope or joy? Are you not our hope before the Lord?” (ibid. 2:19).

The length and breadth of the door that faces the North therefore exist because, when a preacher has converted an unbeliever who is numb in the coldness of his sin, he makes the man’s glory his own by extending him in the length of hope and expanding him in the breadth of charity.

[Note: Suessionensis reads “holds” (*tenet*) for “extends.”]

And because, through the word of preaching, hearers advance in the knowledge of the Holy Trinity and in love of that same Trinity, this door has three chambers on this side and three on that side. For whatever the Creator says about the Trinity through the New Testament, he also demonstrates through the Old Testament.

[Note: Vallicellianus, with the Norman manuscripts, reads “concerning the Trinity of the Creator” (*de Trinitate Conditoris*). Gemeticensis, Uticensis, and other Norman manuscripts do not contain the words “this same door.”]

The heart of the hearers also advances in love of the heavenly homeland, so that the soul, clinging to God like a bride to her bridegroom, already sits in a certain chamber and turns itself wholly away from earthly desires.

[Note: The recent editions read “is perfected” (*perficit*) for “advances.”]

### 3

Or certainly, as was said much earlier (Homily 4, no. 5), there are three orders of those who live well: the good married, the continent, and preachers. Some, living in marriage, yearn for love of the heavenly homeland; others, through hope of eternal joy, mortify the flesh, flee all earthly actions, and disdain involvement in the concerns of this age; others despise earthly goods and preach the heavenly joys that they have come to know.

[Note: Ebroicensis reads “heavenly goods” (*bona*) for “joys.”]

What are these people except chambers in the spiritual building, in whose thought and meditation the soul is joined to its heavenly bridegroom?

Since the Church has these three orders of the good not only from the Gentiles but at times also from the Synagogue—when a great multitude of spiritual people ardently awaited the grace of the Redeemer—the door of the heavenly building has three chambers on this side and three on that side.

For every preacher, when, summoned to the higher homeland, he summons a hearer, shows that both the new fathers and the old yearned with heavenly desire.

[Note: Laudunensis reads “summoned to higher things” (*ad superna provocatus*).] Examples more often bring compunction than words of reasoning. When a preacher says what kinds of people there were in the New Testament in marriage, continence, or preaching with regard to the love of almighty God, and what kinds there were in the Old Testament, the door that speaks shows that it stretches forth three chambers on each side.

[Note: Laudunensis reads “stretches forth” (*tendit*) for “shows.”]

This door also has a front, because there are manifest works in the preacher’s life that can be seen. It has a vestibule before the front, because before he introduces good works, he preaches faith, through which the soul comes humbly and is raised to the height of good deeds.

All these things are according to the measure of the former door, as follows:

### Verse 21

“For he measured its length at fifty cubits and its width at twenty-five cubits.”

### 4

You remember that I discussed this more fully above (Homily 5, book II). Through the number fifty we said that rest is represented, because the fiftieth year was also given to the ancient people for rest, since it was called the Jubilee.

[Note: Laudunensis, Longipontanus, Gemeticensis, and other Norman manuscripts support this reading. The old editions read “was given for rest, which was called”; other copies, “given for rest, was called.”] The number seven, by which the whole of this time is completed, multiplied seven times, comes to forty-nine. One is added to it, because eternal rest is perfected in the contemplation of the One.

This number fifty is therefore length for us, because no one can reach that rest unless he can now stretch his hope toward it with perseverance. Since through the number fifty we are summoned to eternal rest, this also teaches us fully: in the tabernacle, ten curtains were commanded to be made, having fifty loops and fifty golden clasps on the side and at the top (Exod. 25:4ff.).

[Note: Saguntinus and Ebroicensis read, “for there were ten curtains.” Laudunensis everywhere has *curtinae* rather than *cortinae*.]

The curtains of the holy tabernacle are all those who, through the various colors of virtues, advance in the adornment of the holy Church. They veil the inner things and adorn the outer things entirely, because insofar as their life is visible, it is an ornament; and their understanding is hidden within, since the heavenly things they hold in their minds but cannot express are in some way veiled in them.

There are rightly ten curtains, because the hearts of the saints have advanced through observance of the Decalogue.

[Note: The printed editions changed “observance” to “zeal”; all manuscripts read “observance.”]

Fifty blue loops were commanded to be made for the curtains. Blue has the appearance of heaven. The loops of the curtains are therefore heavenly commandments, in which souls are bound so that, raised from lower things, they may hang above.

These loops also have golden clasps, signifying understanding shining with true wisdom. Because this understanding must be circumspect in every respect and fortified by vigilant, cautious concern, it is rightly represented by clasps.

### 5

It must also be noted that the loops or clasps are commanded to be made at the side and at the top of the curtains. For heavenly commandments and spiritual understanding ought not only to suspend us above in love of God, but also to unite us to our neighbor in charity.

Insofar as we love our Creator, we hang, as it were, in the air through the upper loops. But insofar as we love our neighbors as ourselves, we have loops and clasps at the side, so that the curtains of the tabernacle—that is, the souls of the faithful—may be joined by charity and not divided by discord.

Thus, after the length of fifty cubits, the width of twenty-five cubits is immediately added.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “in the mind” (*in mente*).] This width pertains to love of one’s neighbor. It expands itself in love of the brethren and exercises among them every good work of which it is capable.

All good works performed bodily are carried out through the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell. The number five, multiplied by itself, reaches twenty-five, because when good works begin to be performed, through fervor they stir the soul to increase, and through themselves they multiply.

Hence they also create breadth in the mind, so that it is not narrow through sluggishness, but expanded in good deeds through charity.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “through tepidity” (*per torporem*).] Every sluggishness is the narrowness of tepidity, while every kindness of charity is great breadth.

Even if the resources that might be offered to a needy neighbor are lacking, the substance of good will is abundant enough for the repayment of the kingdom, as it is written:

“Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

It follows:

### Verse 22

“Now its windows, its vestibule, and its sculptured work were according to the measure of the door that faced the East.”

### 6

All these things have already been discussed more fully above, and therefore the exposition should not be delayed by a lengthy treatment.

[Note: The printed editions read “be delayed” (*tardare*), against Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, Longipontanus, and the other manuscripts.]

It must nevertheless be noted carefully that the door to the North is said to have all the same things as the door to the East: namely, windows of contemplation, a vestibule of humility, and sculptured work of good action.

All who, through being born to God in their way of life, have persevered in innocence have a door to the East, because the entrance to the heavenly kingdom lies open to them through the light they have received.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “are joined” (*juncti sunt*); the Norman manuscripts read “to the light” (*ad lumen*), whereas the printed editions read “from the light” (*ex lumine*).]

All who afterward fell into sins and were weighed down by the coldness of their sluggishness, but who, when they return through repentance, grow warm again in love of the heavenly homeland, have a door to the North, because even after the coldness of their sin the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened to them through mercy.

The door to the North is therefore said to have what the door to the East has, because converted sinners are enriched with virtues just as those who avoided falling into sin are rich in them.

[Note: Vaticanus and the recent editions, except Gussanville, read “into repentance for sin” (*in peccati poenitentiam*); the English, French, and other manuscripts oppose this reading.]

Hence the Lord says through the voice of the Psalmist:

“I ate ashes like bread” (Ps. 101:10),

because he receives penitents as he receives the righteous. For it is written concerning sinners:

“Long ago they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11:21).

Ashes are eaten like bread when a sinner is recalled through repentance to the grace of his Creator as an innocent person.

The door to the North therefore has windows, a vestibule, and sculptured work, because when a sinner is restored to life after his offenses, he often receives the light of contemplation; and from the very memory of his iniquity he takes the grace of great humility and the efficacy of good action, so that everything commanded to be done appears in his life to have been sculpted there.

### The same passage

“Now its ascent consisted of seven steps, and its vestibule was before it.”

### 7

One ascends to the door by seven steps, because through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit the entrance to heavenly life is opened to us.

Isaiah enumerates this sevenfold grace in our Head himself—or in his body, which is us—when he says:

“The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him; the spirit of counsel and strength; the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2).

[Note: Laudunensis reads “shall rest … and shall fill” (*requiescit … et replevit*).]

Speaking of heavenly things, he counted these steps by descending rather than ascending: wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, and fear.

Yet since it is written:

“The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Prov. 9:10),

there is no doubt that one ascends from fear to wisdom; one does not return from wisdom to fear, because wisdom possesses perfect charity. And it is written:

“Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

The prophet, therefore, because he was speaking from heavenly things down to lower ones, began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, who are striving from earthly things toward heavenly ones, should enumerate the same steps by ascending, so that we may be able to reach wisdom from fear.

The first step of ascent in our mind is the fear of the Lord; the second is piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, strength; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; the seventh, wisdom.

The fear of the Lord is present in the mind. But what kind of fear is it if piety is not with it? One who does not know how to have mercy on his neighbor, who pretends not to notice his neighbor’s tribulations, has no fear before the eyes of almighty God, because he is not raised to piety.

Yet piety often errs through disordered mercy, if it perhaps spares what ought not to be spared. Sins that can be punished by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the rod of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares someone temporarily, drags that person toward eternal punishment.

Therefore, for piety to be true and well ordered, it must be raised to another step, namely knowledge, so that it may know what to punish in judgment and what to forgive in mercy.

But what if someone knows what ought to be done and lacks the strength to do it? Our knowledge must therefore grow into strength, so that when it sees what ought to be done, it can do it through strength of mind, lest it tremble through fear and, collapsing in panic, be unable to defend the good that it recognizes.

Yet strength often falls through its own presumption if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices. It must therefore ascend to counsel, so that by foreseeing it may fortify in advance everything that it can do courageously.

But counsel cannot exist if understanding is absent. For one who does not understand the evil that burdens the person acting—how can he make firm the good that helps him? We must therefore ascend from counsel to understanding.

But what if understanding is alert with great acuity and does not know how to govern itself with maturity? From understanding, then, one must ascend to wisdom, so that wisdom may arrange maturely what understanding has discovered sharply.

Since, therefore, through fear we rise to piety, through piety are led to knowledge, through knowledge are strengthened in fortitude, through fortitude advance to counsel, through counsel progress into understanding, and through understanding arrive at the maturity of wisdom, we ascend by seven steps to the door through which the entrance to spiritual life is opened to us.

It is rightly said that a vestibule was before it, because unless someone first possesses humility, he does not ascend to these steps of spiritual gifts, as it is written:

“Upon whom shall my spirit rest, unless upon the humble and peaceful person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

[Note: Laudunensis reads “rests” (*requiescit*).]

The Psalmist says of this:

“He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6).

A valley is a low place, and every sinner, while humbly afflicting himself in tears within his heart, progresses through an ascent of virtues.

[Note: Vallicellianus, with the Norman manuscripts, reads “through the ascent to virtue” (*per ascensum ad virtutem*).]

He says again:

“He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. 103:10),

because almighty God grants the gifts of spiritual grace to the humble.

### 9

The vestibule may also be understood as faith. It stands before the steps and the door, because we first come to faith and afterward enter the way to heavenly life through the steps of spiritual gifts.

We do not come to faith through virtues; rather, through faith we attain to virtues. The centurion Cornelius, whose almsgiving was praised before baptism according to the testimony of an angel, did not come to faith through works; he came through faith to works (Acts 10:1ff.).

For the angel says to him:

“Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended in the sight of God” (ibid., 4).

[Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts—Suessanus, Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, Longipontanus, and all the Norman copies—read: “For if he had not truly believed in God …, what was he praying for?” One German manuscript supports the printed editions; another has the common reading of the other manuscripts.]

For if he had not believed in the true God even before baptism, whom was he praying to? Or how would almighty God have heard him if he was not asking to be perfected in good things by him?

He therefore knew God, the Creator of all things, but did not know that his almighty Son had become incarnate. Nor could he have done good unless he had first believed. For it is written:

“Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

He therefore possessed faith, since his prayers and almsgiving were able to please God.

[Note: The printed editions read “works” (*operationes*) in place of “faith”; the English manuscripts and our manuscripts read otherwise.] Through good action he merited to know God perfectly and to believe the mystery of his incarnation, so that he might reach the sacraments of baptism.

Through faith, therefore, he came to works; but through works he was established firmly in faith. The vestibule is thus before the steps, because the one who first believed afterward ascends through the steps of virtues to the entrance of the door.

It follows:

### Verse 23

“And the door of the inner court was opposite the door of the North and the Eastern door.”

### 10

Here “opposite” does not signify opposition but alignment. The door of the inner court was placed in such a way that the doors of the North and the East led directly toward it.

What does it mean that the inner door is shown placed in a straight line opposite the doors of the East and the North, except that it is plainly understood that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened equally to the Jewish and Gentile peoples, or to the righteous and to sinners who have converted after their sins?

The mercy of our Creator is broad. The inner door faces not only the door of the East but also that of the North, because the joys of the inner court are opened not only to those who remain in innocence but also to sinners who condemn their sins through repentance, so that they may recognize the ineffable mysteries of the heavenly homeland; recognizing them, thirst for them; thirsting, run toward them; and running, arrive.

[Note: The printed editions read “these secrets of eternal joy.”]

He had recognized these secrets of inner joy when he said:

“My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3).

[Note: The printed editions read “these secrets of eternal joy” (*haec aeterni gaudii secreta*).]

The preacher to the Gentiles yearned for this entrance to the heavenly kingdom when he said:

“I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

The bride had recognized these secrets of hidden exultation when she said:

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” (Song 5:4).

The beloved puts his hand through the opening when the Lord strikes our mind by his power through subtle understanding. The belly trembles at his touch because our weakness, touched by understanding of heavenly joy, is disturbed by its very exultation. Fear with gladness arises in the mind, because it already senses what it loves in heavenly joy, yet still fears that it may not receive what it scarcely and faintly senses.

What therefore remains except that all who recognize those joys of the heavenly homeland should direct themselves toward the course of a perfect life?

Accordingly, the following is aptly added:

### The same passage

“And he measured from door to door one hundred cubits.”

### 11

We said above (Homily 6, no. 16) that the number one hundred, being produced by multiplying ten by ten, signifies perfection.

[Note: Ebroicensis, Gemetensis, and other Norman copies read: “The number one hundred, which is produced by multiplying ten by ten, is always understood as perfection.”]

Whoever therefore sees the entrance of the inner court must necessarily run through a life of perfection and proceed from the door of beginning to the entrance of completion.

Let the inner court, which extends from the outer doors to the inner door, therefore be measured at one hundred cubits, so that the one who has begun to enter through love may possess the breadth of perfection in his mind. Thus, in the one he loves, neither adversity may constrict him nor prosperity elevate him; instead, despising all transient things, he may run through the court of perfection until he reaches the secret joys.

There are many who have already entered through the seven steps to the entrance of the outer door, according to a certain order of heavenly dispensation: humble through fear of God, merciful through devotion to piety, discerning through knowledge, free through strength of mind, cautious through counsel, prudent through understanding, and mature through wisdom.

Yet, still bound by certain necessities, they serve the concerns of this world; in the very place from which they have already shaken off much of their mind, they are still held unwillingly. While they carry the burdens imposed by earthly occupation, they exercise themselves less in the heavenly commandments.

They have no leisure to yearn from the depths of their being for the eternal homeland; their very desires somehow grow weak within them, because one whose mind is obstructed by temporal cares cannot love the true joys he has recognized as much as he wishes.

[Note: The printed editions read “and while they yearn” (*et dum anhelare*), against the manuscripts. Most manuscripts read “which he has recognized” (*quae cognovit*); Laudunensis has “because, with the mind … impeded …, [he cannot love] what he has recognized,” and Gussanville agrees after changing *cognovit* to *cognoverunt*. Vaticanus and others read “impedes … which they have recognized” (*praepedit … quae cognoverunt*).]

Such people often shake the yoke of the world from the necks of their minds, abandon everything, lay down the burdens of earthly concern, and, in order to widen the heart’s capacity for heavenly desire, seek a secluded life. Devoted to holy prayers and sacred meditations, they afflict themselves with daily weeping, melt the oldness of their hearts in the fire of love, and renew themselves by setting themselves ablaze for heavenly joy.

Often, kindled by their very desire, they long already to depart from the flesh and do not wish to return to the present life after their weeping. Yet their departure is delayed, so that love delayed may advance through the very delay, and so that what is denied may grow, as it were, through ardent desire.

Thus, in the region of the Gerasenes, the man who had been freed from a legion of demons already wished to go with the Lord; yet he was told:

“Return to your house and tell how much the Lord has done for you” (Luke 8:39).

Thus the bride in the Song of Songs speaks anxiously in holy desire:

“On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I did not find him” (Song 3:1).

She seeks the beloved on her bed when, in the very rest and leisure she desires, her soul already longs to see the Lord, longs to depart to him, and yearns to be free from the darkness of the present life. But she seeks him and does not find him, because although she desires to see the one she loves with great love, she is not yet granted that vision.

12. What else, then, do the minds of such holy persons accomplish in this desire, except that they are already running from the outer gates, through the inner court, toward the gate? It often happens to them that, when they see themselves moved by the great gift of heavenly grace, they consider themselves already perfect and think themselves obedient. But since no one is ordering them to do hard things, they believe themselves patient; since no one is assailing them with insults and adversities, they think themselves patient. Often, too, they unwillingly undertake a spiritual ministry and are led into the governance of the faithful. When they have been struck from every side by great tribulations, they become troubled in mind and discover that they are imperfect, although, before being assailed, they had believed themselves perfect.

As a result, they are compelled to gather themselves together, to blush silently before themselves at the reproach of their weakness, and, strengthened by this very shame, to oppose patience to adversity and to advance through tribulation—although previously, at leisure and because of their very security, they had been sluggish. They truly begin to be what they had previously imagined themselves vainly to be.

When, therefore, such persons are delayed from the outer gates to the inner gate through the court of good endeavor, this court itself is measured in them by one hundred cubits, because through delay and holy exercise they advance daily toward perfection.

[Note: Suess., “recalled.”]

[Note: The printed editions, contrary to the testimony of all the English and French manuscripts, read *deseruntur* (“are abandoned”); below they read *dilectione* (“by love”) instead of *dilatione* (“by delay”), with great loss of meaning. For here it is signified that the faithful are delayed from the state of perfection so that, conscious of their weakness, they may be humbled; and through this delay they advance by their daily desires.]

[Note: Ebroic., “and while daily desires advance in the mind, the inner court is, as it were, measured by one hundred cubits.”]

For to advance in the mind through daily desires is, as it were, for the inner court to be measured by one hundred cubits. Therefore there are one hundred cubits from gate to gate, so that the very delay of living may be, as it were, a certain postponement of the journey, through which one grows daily in virtue and reaches the inner entrance more perfectly.

The text continues:

**VERSES 24–26.**—“And he led me to the way of the south, and behold, a gate that looked toward the south; and he measured its front and its vestibule according to the earlier measurements, and its windows and its vestibules all around, like the other windows: fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. And it was ascended by seven steps, and its vestibule was before its doors.”

13. All these things have already been said concerning the eastern and northern gate, and it is not appropriate for us repeatedly to repeat what we have explained once and twice. We must nevertheless note that, in the spiritual building, one entrance opens toward the east, another toward the north, and another toward the south.

For just as sinners are designated by the cold of the north, so those who are fervent in spirit are signified by the southern way. Set aflame by the heat of the Holy Spirit, they increase in virtues like plants beneath the southern light.

[Note: Longip., “are exercised.”]

Let the gate toward the east be open, so that those who have begun well in the mysteries of faith and afterward have not been submerged in any depth of vice may reach the hidden joys. Let the gate toward the north be open, so that those who, after beginning in heat and light, have fallen away into the cold and darkness of their sins may return to pardon through the compunction of repentance and learn what the true joy of inward recompense is.

Let the gate toward the south be open, so that those who are fervent in virtues through holy desires may enter daily, through spiritual understanding, into the mysteries of inward joy.

[Note: Laud., Sues., Longip., “who, after the beginning of the light they received, [are fervent] in holy things, etc.”]

In this connection one may ask: since there are four regions of this world, why are not four but three gates of the outer court mentioned in this building?

[Note: Suess., “these outer [gates] are not four but three.”]

This would rightly have been asked if the prophet had seen not a spiritual but a bodily building. Holy Church, however—that is, the spiritual building—has only three gates by which it reaches the hidden joys: faith, hope, and charity. One is toward the east, another toward the north, and the third toward the south.

The gate toward the east is faith, because through it the true light arises in the mind. The gate toward the north is hope, because anyone situated in sins, if he despairs of pardon, utterly loses mercy.

[Note: Thus read the English, Norman, and nearly all the better manuscripts. The printed editions read, “if he has despaired,” and he perishes completely.]

Therefore it is necessary that the one who has been extinguished by his own iniquity should come back to life through hope in mercy.

[Note: Laud. and Suess., “may come back to life unto mercy.”]

The gate toward the south is charity, because it burns with the fire of love. For in the southern region the sun is carried upward, because through charity the light of faith is lifted up in love of God and neighbor.

Thus one reaches the inner court through three gates, because through faith, hope, and charity one arrives at the hidden joys.

Another question also arises: why is the gate of the inner court said to be placed opposite the eastern and northern gate, while it is not said to open toward the southern gate? But since we have said that those beginning are signified by the east, and those who have fallen by the north, it was fitting that it should be expressly stated—whether concerning those beginning, for whom the sun is still in its warmth, or concerning those who have fallen but return through conversion—that the gate of the inner court is open to them, so that through these persons he might assure us concerning those about whom doubt might have arisen.

This did not need to be said concerning the southern gate, because no one is unaware that those who remain fervent in spirit in the virtues reach the inward joys.

[Note: We restore the passage in brackets from the Laudun and Longipontan manuscripts. It is absent from the Norman manuscripts.]

[The practice of sacred language is to state openly things about which doubt might arise and to leave unspoken things that are certain, as is said through the Psalmist: “They provoked Moses in the camp, Aaron, the holy one of the Lord” (Psalm 105:16). Aaron had made the idol at the people’s insistence, and there could rightly have been doubt concerning his life. Moses, therefore, is not called holy, because everyone knows that he was holy; but Aaron is called “the holy one of the Lord,” so that doubt concerning his life may be removed for us.]

The text continues:

**VERSE 26.**—“And there were sculpted palm trees, one on this side and another on that side, on its front.”

14. What does it mean that earlier a painting of palm trees was mentioned on the fronts, whereas now sculpted palm trees are said to be on the front? In the carving of stones, works appear externally. But, as we already said above, the painting of palm trees is the display of signs. Now, however, the carving of palm trees is said so that the demonstration of good works may be signified.

For to the chief preachers themselves it is said: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Those, therefore, who show that holy works are impressed upon their life have palm trees sculpted on their front, because they already display in their holy works how great a victory will follow them in the future.

Or certainly, since we said that faith is signified by the eastern gate, hope by the northern gate, and charity by the southern gate, we must note that the eastern gate is said to have a painting of palm trees, whereas the northern and southern gates have carvings.

[Note: That is, “on the gates.” The printed editions should be corrected, since they read, “but in the north and south.”]

For it often happens that those who are still beginning have not yet exercised themselves in solid and great works. Those, however, who return from iniquities to virtues are often exercised in great works, so that they may be able to cover their faults before the eyes of almighty God. Those who have already grown through the fervor of the spirit in virtues burn like the south in holy deeds.

[Note: Longip. and Val. Cl., “as in the south.”]

Therefore there is a painting on the eastern gate, but a carving on the northern and southern gates, because the sign of victory that is displayed in those who are beginning is held more solidly and more firmly in those who return and those who are fervent.

**15.** We must also note with the greatest care what is said: “on this side and on that side.” For all who are making their way toward the entrance of life ought to have a palm on both the right and the left side. What is said, “on this side and on that side,” signifies both sides.

The one who is not lifted up by prosperity has a palm on the right; the one who is not cast down by adversity has a palm on the left. Paul carried a palm, as it were, on both sides when he said: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Corinthians 6:7).

Adversity did not break him, nor did prosperity lift him into pride of mind. Thus he carried a palm on both sides, because he remained strong in adversity and humble in prosperity.

For whoever is lifted up by prosperity does not know how to have a palm on the right side. Whoever is broken by adversity does not know how to carry a palm on the left. Therefore, for a palm to be carried on the forehead on both sides, confidence in adversity and fear in prosperity must always be present in our minds, lest adversity drag us into despair or prosperity lift our spirit into self-confidence.

Hence the same outstanding preacher said: “I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed, both to be satisfied and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:12).

**16.** Is it really some sort of skill, brothers, to be humbled and to abound, to be satisfied and to hunger, to abound and to suffer want, so that such a great preacher should imply that he knows these things as something significant? It is indeed a skill, and a remarkable knowledge of discipline, which we must learn with the whole effort of our heart.

Whoever is not broken by his poverty, is not drawn away from thanksgiving by it, and is not set aflame by a desire for temporal goods knows how to be humbled. In this passage the Apostle calls “being humbled” suffering want. For immediately he adds the opposite: “I know how to abound.”

Whoever is not lifted up by the things he has received, does not twist them toward the use of vainglory, and does not possess alone what he has received but mercifully shares it with those in need knows how to abound.

Whoever uses the food he has received not for filling his belly but for restoring strength, and does not grant the flesh more than necessity demands, knows how to be satisfied. Whoever endures scarcity of food without complaining, and does nothing because of the need for nourishment by which his soul might fall into the snare of sin, knows how to hunger.

Therefore, whoever is not raised up by pride in abundance and is not provoked by greed in need knows how to abound and how to suffer want.

When he immediately added, “I can do all things,” lest we think these words expressed presumption, he added, “in him who strengthens me.”

[Note: The words “in whom” (*in quo*) are absent from all the printed editions. They are found in the Laudun, Vallicellan, Gembloux, and other manuscripts.]

Behold, a branch has grown upward; but because it remained attached to the root, it stayed green. Growing upward, it would wither if it had separated itself from the root. He attributes nothing to himself, because he confesses that he can do all things not in himself but in him who strengthens him.

Thus the outstanding preacher has a palm on both sides: abundance does not draw him into pride, nor poverty into greed.

**17.** Let us learn, therefore, brothers, to give thanks not only in prosperity but also in adversity. In his kindness the Father became our creator and nourishes us, his adopted children, for the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. He not only refreshes us with gifts but also instructs us with scourges.

Let us learn, then, how to abound, so that we may share with those in need everything we have received from him. Let abundance not lift up the mind, lest it perhaps rejoice because one possesses what another lacks and rejoice no longer in the common good but in what belongs to oneself.

Truth recalls the disciples from private joy to the common good when, as they returned from preaching and rejoiced in the subjection of demons, he warned them, saying:

[Note: Most Norman manuscripts, with the Vallicellan manuscript agreeing, read, “to the common good.”] “Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice and exult because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Not all the elect cast out demons, but the names of all the elect are nevertheless recorded in heaven. The disciples are therefore admonished to lay aside private joy and to rejoice in the common and everlasting happiness.

[Note: Longip., “the chosen disciples.”]

Whoever, then, rejoices in what another does not have possesses a private joy, made worse by his very abundance.

[Note: Ebroic. and Lyr., “through this private joy he possesses it.”]

Against this desire for abundance John admonishes us, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). He immediately added the reason why: “If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him” (ibid.).

No one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24), because one cannot love transitory and eternal things at the same time. If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not as objects of affection.

He immediately supplied the same reason, saying: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

**18.** People desire to have something and to desire more than is necessary for this reason: so that they may grow proud through possessing it and exalt themselves in their thoughts because another does not have it. Whoever is such has not yet learned how to carry abundance.

Often, what avarice suggests from desire, one considers a necessity; although less would suffice, one grieves that more is lacking, and the unwary soul suffers a kind of necessity that it itself has created. Although the things it desires are excessive, it somehow excuses its own greed.

Abundance, therefore, is close to pride.

[Note: Or, “it is nearby,” as many manuscripts read.]

If greed should also seize it, this is, so to speak, a foreign captivity invading it.

[Note: Ebroic., “the captivity of a foreigner.”]

If, then, we wish to know the art of abounding, we must flee not only the vices that are near but also those that come from far away. Let us learn to suffer want, so that we do not demand with guilt to possess what we do not have, and let us not consider those happy whom we see burdened with possessions.

The things they prepare for themselves, as though for the expenses of the present life, are exceedingly many. They carry much, but on the short road of this journey poverty is a great companion for us. It does not constrict the soul when earthly substance is lacking, since we will not have to render an account to the eternal Judge concerning it. We proceed more freely toward our homeland because, as on a journey, we are free from burdens.

**19.** Let us learn to be satisfied, so that in taking food we may serve necessity rather than the appetite of the belly. Desire asks for more than necessity. Often, while we are taking care to satisfy the weakness of the flesh, pleasure slips in and exceeds the proper measure of nourishment.

Thus guilt passes into guilt, because another temptation of the flesh often arises from this very thing: the flesh is served excessively in its refreshment. For, because of the sin of the first human being, nature having been weakened, we are born into this world with our temptations.

The flesh is sometimes our helper in good work, but sometimes our seducer into evil. If, therefore, we give it more than we ought, we nourish an enemy. If we do not give it what we owe to its necessity, we kill a fellow citizen.

The flesh must indeed be satisfied, but only to the point at which it is capable of serving us in good work. Whoever gives it so much that it grows proud does not know at all how to be satisfied.

It is therefore a great skill to be satisfied, lest anyone, through the satiety of the flesh, break out into the wickedness of shameful behavior.

Let us learn to hunger, so that, because of the abundance that follows, our present want may please us. Let not the need of the belly draw us into guilt; let not deprivation suggest sin to the mind itself; let not the spirit, while the flesh is afflicted by hunger, be provoked into greed and seek, with guilt, to provide something by which it may satisfy the flesh in its need; let not the heart leap into indignation and set the tongue aflame with the bitterness of complaint.

Whoever, therefore, looks around on every side in the poverty of his flesh and guards himself from the snare of sin knows how to hunger.

[Note: Lyran., “gluttony.”]

**20.** Therefore, dearest brothers, let us flee anger and avarice in adversity and avoid pride and immoderate joys in prosperity. Since we desire to enter the court of the inner life through the three gates of faith, hope, and charity, let us hold palms on both sides.

It is pleasant to call to mind another citizen of the heavenly homeland and to show how he held a palm on both sides.

[Note: Gemet. and four other Norman manuscripts read: “It is pleasant indeed to bring [lacuna] military service to mind.”]

For blessed Job, although he was richer than the men of the East and possessed every form of prosperity—his sons were flourishing, his household was growing, and his flocks were multiplying—remained in such great fear of almighty God that, amid the keeping of discipline, the practice of justice, and many acts of humility, he devoted himself to works of mercy and, dedicated to offering sacrifices, sacrificed burnt offerings to the Lord for each of his sons, lest any of them had sinned at least in his heart (Job 1:2 and following).

[Note: The printed editions read “he was flourishing with sons,” but this should be corrected in accordance with the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.]

Let us consider, then, how great was his vigilance in good works, since he expiated the sins of the heart in his sons through sacrifices.

But although his righteousness had become known in prosperity, it was entirely unknown whether he could remain righteous amid blows. He therefore had to be struck, so that this holy man might be tested through adversity in the midst of prosperity; so that the one known to almighty God might become known to us and to himself through scourges.

Thus, by the Lord’s disposition, the flocks were destroyed, the keepers killed, the house overturned, the sons slain, and his flesh struck from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. His wife alone remained unharmed, to increase his wounds with the arrows of her words.

But the holy man, sound in his trial and wise in his wound, instructs her and answers: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also accept evil things?” (Job 2:10).

Friends also came to console him, but broke out into insults and added wounds of words to the pain of his wounds. They called him merciless, named him a robber, declared him violent, and accused him of oppressing the poor.

What, then, was the soldier of God to do, caught amid painful wounds and bitter words?

[Note: Laud. and all our other manuscripts read “caught” (*deprehensus*); the printed editions prefer “cast down” (*depressus*).]

Behold, the scourges of God and the words of men together press his afflicted soul toward despair. But, full of spiritual strength, lying in the wounds of his flesh yet standing firm in the strength of his mind, he recalled to mind the good things he had done and resisted the assault of despair.

Because he had been merciful, he said: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). And again: “I was a father to the poor” (ibid., 16).

Because he had been both a guardian of discipline and kind, he said: “When I sat like a king, with the army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the mourners” (ibid., 25).

[Note: The printed editions read “with an army looking around me [lacuna]”; the manuscripts support “with an army surrounding me.”]

Because he had been humble, he said: “If I have scorned to enter into judgment with my servant and my maidservant when they contended against me” (Job 31:13).

Because he had been hospitable, he confessed: “If I have disregarded a passerby because he had no clothing” (ibid., 19).

Because he had been generous in gifts, he said: “If his loins have not blessed me, and he was not warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (ibid., 20).

Because he had not been violent, he testified, saying: “If I have raised my hand against the orphan when I saw myself superior in the gate” (ibid., 21).

Because he had never rejoiced at the danger of an enemy, he said: “If I have rejoiced at the ruin of the one who hated me” (ibid., 29).

Because he had been patient and had endured even the malice of his own people with equanimity, he said: “If the men of my tent have not said, ‘Who will give us some of his flesh, that we may be filled?’” (ibid., 31).

Why, then, did the holy man enumerate so many of his virtues amid the scourges? Why did he praise with his own mouth the works he had done? It was because, amid wounds and words that could have drawn him into despair, he restored his soul to hope by recalling them.

He had been humble in prosperity; by recalling his good deeds, he remained unbroken in adversity. Whose soul would not have been driven to despair by those words amid so many scourges, unless he had recalled to himself the good things he had done?

The holy man saw his mind shaken toward despair after hearing so many evils, and he wonderfully strove to make it firm in certain hope through his good deeds. Thus what is written was fulfilled: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils, and in the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclesiasticus 11:27).

If, when we possess good things, we remember the evils that we have either already suffered or may still suffer, the good things received do not lift up the mind, because fear of the remembered evils weighs down its joy. And if, when we possess evils, we remember the good things that we have either already received or still hope to receive, the weight of evils does not crush the soul into despair, because the memory of good things lifts it toward hope.

If, therefore, dearest brothers, we walk according to the Lord’s commands and the examples of the saints, so that neither prosperity lifts us up nor adversity breaks us, we show that we bear palms on both sides before the eyes of almighty God.

[Note: In Laud., Suess., and Longip. the following is added: “Let us therefore rejoice in the assistance of him who, in those who follow him, shows us all the things that he has commanded—our almighty Redeemer, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.”]

To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VIII [formerly XX]

Verses 27 and the following, through verse 38 inclusive, are expounded by most writers briefly and by others at greater length; the principal doctrine established is that of the resurrection.

**1.** The words of the prophet that, by the Lord’s favor, are to be spoken to your charity today require reading more than exposition.
