For they repeat in the three inner gates what has already been said a second or even a third time concerning the outer gates. A few things, however, are altered in their description.

Therefore we must pass quickly in reading over what has already been said, so that we may explain more freely what has not yet been said. Accordingly, the text now reads:

**VERSES 27–30.**—“And the gate of the inner court was toward the southern way, and he measured from gate to gate along the southern way one hundred cubits. And he brought me into the inner court by the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the earlier measurements, its chamber, its front, and its vestibule according to the same measurements, and its windows and its vestibule all around: fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width, and the vestibule all around.”

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “and its vestibule all around.”]

[Note: The printed editions read, “in the southern way.”]

You remember that all these things were said and explained above, especially in the preceding homily. But what is added concerning the same vestibule has not yet been said:

**VERSES 30–31.**—“Twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width, and its vestibule toward the outer court.”

Again what had already been said above is repeated when it says: “And its palm trees on the front” (ibid.). Immediately, however, what had not yet been said is added: “And there were eight steps by which it was ascended” (ibid.).

[Note: Laud., together with Longip., “by which it was ascended.”]

What is written concerning the southern gate is also narrated concerning the eastern gate in the same order. For it immediately continues:

**VERSES 32–34.**—“And he brought me into the inner court by the eastern gate, and he measured the gate according to the earlier measurements, its chamber, its front, and its vestibule as above, and its windows and its vestibules all around, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. And its vestibule—that is, of the inner court—and the sculpted palm trees on its front, on this side and on that side, and its ascent by eight steps.”

[Note: Longip., with Laud. and Suess., “of the outer court.” We think this should be corrected.]

Those things that were said concerning the southern and eastern gates are repeated in the same words concerning the gate that faces north. For it continues:

**VERSES 35–37.**—“And he brought me to the gate that faced north, and he measured it according to the earlier measurements, its chamber, its front, and its vestibule, and its windows all around, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width. And its vestibule faced the outer court, and the carving of palm trees was on its front, on this side and on that side, and its ascent was by eight steps.”

**2.** What is signified by the inner court, the chamber, the fronts, the vestibule, the windows, the length and width, and the carving of palm trees, we have already explained at length above (Homilies 6 and 7). We ought not to occupy ourselves with these things again, but only with what has not yet been said.

We must now ask what these three inner gates are; what it means that the vestibules of these gates are measured at twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width; and why they are ascended not by seven steps, as was said concerning the outer gates, but by eight.

For the gate of the inner court mentioned above is not one of these three inner gates.

[Note: Suess. reads “of the outer court,” but erroneously.] The former is said to face the eastern and northern gate, whereas these are individually said to be placed within, toward the south, the east, and the north.

Therefore the inner entrance is rightly signified by that gate, because, as was already said in the preceding discussion, it is open either to Jews and Gentiles, or to those beginning and persevering in good, or to those who fall from good but rise again through repentance after their sins.

[Note: Laud. reads, “through those [gates] … who, as [was said] …”; Gemet., other Norman manuscripts, and Longip. add “work” after “good.”]

Now, however, after the individual gates toward the east, north, and south have been described, why are individual gates of the inner court again described toward the south, east, and north?

With the Lord’s help, great attention is needed to investigate such a profound matter. If by the name of gates we understand holy preachers, we must know that there is one Church in the preachers of the Old and New Testaments.

The gates have seven or eight steps because they preach together the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Laud., Suess., Longip., Val. Cl., “but by the eighth step they announce the reward of eternal recompense.”]

By the eighth step, however, they announce the reward of eternal recompense. Hence it is written: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11:2).

[Note: The printed editions read, “Give portions”; the Laudun, Longipontan, Norman, and other manuscripts read, “Give a portion.”]

What, then, can we understand the outer gates to be except the ancient fathers, who through the precepts of the law knew how to guard the works of the people more than their hearts? The inner gates, therefore, must be understood as the preachers of holy Church, who guard the hearts of their disciples with spiritual admonitions, lest they take pleasure in thought even in evils they do not commit.

The outer gates are said to be ascended by seven steps, whereas these gates are said to have an ascent of eight steps, because under the veneration of the law there was a seventh day, while in the New Testament the eighth day has a sacramental meaning: the day called the Lord’s Day, which is third from the Passion but eighth from creation, because it follows the seventh.

**3.** But if by the name of gates we understand only the holy apostles, who were the first preachers of the holy Church and taught us above all to hold faith, hope, and charity, then they themselves are gates for us in these virtues, since through those same virtues they lead us to the inner understanding of eternal wisdom.

But if they are the outer gates, whom do we understand as the inner gates? If they are the inner gates, whom do we understand as the outer ones?

[Note: Laud., “whom we look upon.”]

In this matter it can usefully be understood that they are simultaneously outer and inner gates for us. When they preach to those who are still beginning not lofty and mystical things but matters that they are capable of grasping, they are outer gates. When they speak profound and mystical things to the perfect, they are inner gates.

[Note: Suess., “lofty and mystical.” Laud., “profound, lofty, and mystical.”]

Let us see how the outer gate is opened: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:1).

Let us see how the inner gate is opened: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (ibid., 2:6).

Let us see whether the same gate is both inner and outer: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1:14). Again he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5:13).

In that he is beside himself in contemplation and speech before the wise, he is an inner gate. In that he soberly restrains himself in preaching before the little ones and does not display how much spiritual intoxication is poured into the mind when he preaches, he shows himself to be an outer gate.

They are therefore both outer and inner gates for us: they instruct us at the first entrance of faith, hope, and charity, and, when they preach the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom to those who have already advanced, they lead us through a subtler sense into the interior.

**4.** Hence their ascent is first described by seven steps and afterward by eight. For the mysteries of that life are signified by the eighth step—a life that the perfect understand fully in its secrets, those who have learned to transcend all temporal things in mind, who fully despise the present life that unfolds in the course of seven days, and who are nourished by inward contemplation.

[Note: Ebroic. and Sagiens. read “fully.”]

The gates of the spiritual building therefore have seven steps because they preach to their hearers the fear of the Lord, piety and knowledge, fortitude and counsel, understanding and wisdom. But when they command that everything be abandoned, when they warn that nothing in this world is to be loved or held through affection, when they urge devotion to the contemplation of the heavenly homeland and advise delight in its mysteries, they add a step and lead people into the interior.

[Note: Ebroic. reads, “that nothing imperfect be retained.”]

Truth showed this step to a certain person. When the commandments of the law were recited to him, he replied: “I have kept all these things from my youth” (Matthew 19:20). He was standing, as it were, on seven steps when he said that he had kept everything from his youth.

But immediately he is told: “One thing is still lacking to you: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (ibid., 21).

In these words he saw the eighth step, but he did not wish to ascend it, because he went away sad.

Whoever, therefore, nourishes himself on the contemplation of eternity after despising temporal possessions, and searches out the joys of the heavenly kingdom, has entered through the eighth step into the entrance of the inner gate, after holding fast through fear and action, and growing through the understanding of wisdom, to the seven steps.

### 5.

The number eight also signifies both the day of the eternal judgment and the resurrection of the flesh. Hence the Psalm that is inscribed “for the eighth” begins with fear of the judgment, when it says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. 6:2).

[Note: [Col. 1030D] Many Psalms are inscribed “for the eighth”; this, however, is the first.] For now is the time of mercy, but in that judgment there will be a day of wrath. On that day, evidently, all this period that unfolds over seven days comes to an end. [Col. 1030C] Since it follows the seven days, it is rightly called the eighth. On it our flesh will also rise from the dust, so that it may receive from the Truth either the good or the evil that it has done.

Hence circumcision is also commanded by the Law to take place on the eighth day. For through the member that is circumcised mortal propagation is generated, and the number of those who depart and those who succeed them is increased. But because in the resurrection of the dead there will no longer be propagation of the flesh, nor any departure or succession—for, as it is written, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30)—the foreskin is commanded to be cut off on the eighth day. For the propagation of the flesh no longer has a place where the risen flesh possesses the permanence of eternity.

Through this member the virgin Mother came down, she who conceived God in her womb without a man's union; he first showed us, in his resurrection, the glory of the eternal homeland. Having risen from the dead, he no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9). He gave us an example, so that we might believe that on the last day the things will happen to our flesh that we have recognized as having happened to his flesh on the day of the resurrection.

[Note: Earlier printed editions, before Gussanville, read “through this word.” The reading is corrected from English manuscripts and our own.]

### 6.

But since our discourse has introduced the resurrection of the flesh, it is exceedingly sad and deeply grievous that we know some people to stand within the Church and doubt the resurrection of the flesh. The ancient fathers believed with the utmost certainty that it would come, even when they had not yet possessed any example of that same resurrection. By what condemnation, then, are those worthy who have both received the example of the Lord’s resurrection and yet still distrust their own resurrection? They hold the pledge, but do not have faith. They fill the Church, but because they doubt their resurrection, they stand there empty in mind.

Of this resurrection blessed Job says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God; whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (Job 19:25–27).

[Note: Lyra: “I shall see God, my Savior.” Moreover, what is said here to cast doubt upon the resurrection is also read in Book XIV of the *Moralia*, no. 70. See our preface to the books of the *Dialogues*, no. 10.]

Hence the Psalmist also says: “In his sight all who descend into the earth fall down” (Ps. 21:29).

[Note: Gemeticensis, Rothomagensis, and most Norman manuscripts, together with the Val-Cl., read *procedunt* (“go forth”). This reading is not inconsistent with Gregory’s purpose, but it is rejected by the Hebrew text, the Vulgate, and the other versions.]

For in the earth the dead descend not in spirit but in body. Therefore those who descend into the earth fall in the sight of the Lord, because those who now rot in the dust come to judgment by rising again.

Again he says: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly also did my flesh” (Ps. 62:2). The soul thirsts to see God; but what does the flesh thirst for except to rise again?

Again he says: “Take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29). Immediately he adds concerning the resurrection of the flesh: “Send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (ibid., 30).

Again he says: “Arise, Lord, to your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. 131:8). The Lord arose to his rest when he raised his flesh from the tomb. After him the ark also rises, because the Church rises.

Hence, through the same prophet of whom we are speaking, it is written: “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you will live. And I will lay sinews upon you, and I will cause flesh to grow over you, and I will stretch skin over you, and I will give you spirit, and you will live” (Ezek. 37:4–6).

Hence another prophet saw the human race raised up at the end through the Lord’s resurrection and said: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos. 6:2).

[Note: Another reading: “in the resurrection of the Lord,” as found in most Norman manuscripts and in the Val-Cl.]

[Note: Laudensis reads *vivificavit … suscitavit* (“he revived … he raised up”).]

Hence, when the Lord was speaking about himself, he added: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. And those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

[Note: Gemeticensis, Beccensis, Lyra, Uticensis, Rothomagensis, and others, in agreement with the Gospel text, read *audient* (“will hear”); the printed editions read “his voice.”]

Hence Paul says: “From there also we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21).

Again he says: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thess. 4:14). Again he says: “Christ, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. 15:20). For if we do not rise from the sleep of death, how do we have the Lord’s resurrection as firstfruits?

### 7.

Behold, the ancient and the new Fathers agree with one another, by one Spirit, concerning the resurrection of the flesh. Behold, the Truth itself first taught by its voice what it afterward demonstrated by its deed concerning the resurrection of the flesh; and yet the weakness of some still lacks faith, though it stands in the house of faith.

They are accustomed to wonder how flesh can revive from dust. Let them wonder, then, at the height of heaven, the mass of the earth, the abysses of the waters, all that exists in the world, and even the angels themselves, created from nothing.

[Note: The same manuscripts, supported by Ebroicensis, read “the vastness.”]

It is far less to make something from something than to have made everything from nothing. The elements themselves, the forms of things themselves, preach to us an image of the resurrection. Every day the sun dies before our eyes; every day it rises again. The stars set for us in the morning hours and rise again in the evening.

We see trees full of leaves, flowers, and fruits in summer; in winter they remain bare of leaves, flowers, and fruits, almost dry, but when the spring sun returns and moisture rises from the root, they are clothed again in their former beauty.

[Note: This is the reading that should be adopted from the Norman and English manuscripts. Laudensis does not have “with flowers.” It is also absent from the printed editions, where, instead of “fruits,” we read “crops.” Below, where the text reads “bare of leaves, flowers, and fruits,” Ebroicensis, Sag., and Lyra read simply “and they remain almost dry.”]

Why, then, is humanity distrusted when what appears to happen in trees is believed? Yet they often look upon the dust of decaying flesh and say: “From where will bones and marrow, flesh or hair, be restored in the resurrection?”

As they investigate these matters, let them look at the small seeds of enormous trees, and, if they can, let them say: “Where in them is hidden such a mass of strength, such diversity of branches, such abundance and greenness of leaves, such beauty of flowers, such abundance, taste, and fragrance of fruits?”

[Note: Suessionensis and Longipontanus read: “such abundance of flavors, and so forth.”]

Do tree seeds have the fragrance or taste that the trees themselves later produce in their fruits? If, therefore, what cannot be seen can be produced from the seed of trees, why is it doubted that from the dust of human flesh a form that cannot be seen can be restored?

### 8.

They often bring forward a foolish little question, saying: “A wolf ate a man’s flesh; a lion devoured the wolf; the lion died and returned to dust. When that dust is raised, how will the man’s flesh be separated from the flesh of the wolf and the lion?”

What else should we answer them except that they should first consider how they came into this world, and then they will discover how they will rise again?

Certainly, you who say this, at one time in your mother’s womb you were foam of blood; there you were a small, fluid globule formed from your father’s seed and your mother’s blood. Tell me, I beg you, if you know: how did that moisture of the seed harden into bones? How did it remain fluid in the marrow? How was it solidified into sinews? How did it grow into flesh? How was it extended into skin? How was it differentiated into hair and nails, so that the hair was softer than the flesh, and the nails more tender than the bones but harder than the flesh?

If, therefore, so many and such diverse things were differentiated from one seed and yet remained joined together in one form, what is astonishing if almighty God can, in the resurrection of the dead, distinguish human flesh from the flesh of beasts, so that one and the same dust does not rise insofar as it is the dust of a wolf and a lion, yet rises insofar as it is the dust of a human being?

See, then, human being, how you came to life, and do not doubt at all how you will return to life. Why do you wish to comprehend by reason how you will return, when you do not know how you came? Grant to the power of your Creator what you cannot comprehend about yourself.

Certainly, because you were made from earth, and earth from nothing, you were created from nothing. Do not, therefore, despair of the resurrection of your flesh; wisely consider that it is less for God to restore what existed than to make what did not exist.

### 9.

But if you cannot comprehend the effect of the resurrection by reason, consider how many things there are whose manner of existence you do not understand, yet whose existence you do not doubt.

Tell me, I beg you, if you know: where do the circuits of heaven, the hinges of the earth, and the abysses of the waters end? Where are they suspended?

[Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read: “the circuit of heaven … the abyss.”]

We know, however, that what was made from nothing hangs upon nothing. But if there is something called “nothing,” it is no longer nothing. If, however, nothing is nothing, nowhere does the mass of the world hang, nor is there any place where what was created to exist can be. How, then, is that nowhere which we know exists?

But perhaps these matters are too much for you. Human being, return to yourself. Certainly you were created from spirit and mud—from one invisible and the other visible, from one perceptible and the other imperceptible. How, then, could spirit and mud be mingled in you and produce from different things something not different, so that spirit and mud were mingled in such harmony that when the flesh is worn down the spirit withers, and when the spirit is afflicted the flesh wastes away?

But perhaps you are not yet strong enough to examine yourself. Consider, I beg you, if you can: how the Red Sea was divided by a rod (Exod. 14:21); how, when the rock’s hardness was struck by a rod, it poured forth waves (Num. 20:11); how Aaron’s dry rod blossomed (ibid., 17:8); how the Virgin, descended from his lineage, conceived; how she also remained a virgin in childbirth (Luke 1:27 and following; 3:23 and following); how a man dead for four days, raised at a command, came out of the tomb with his hands and feet bound—whom the Lord afterward commanded his disciples to unbind (John 11:44 and following);

[Note: The printed editions read “bound.”]

how our same Redeemer, rising in true flesh and bones, entered to his disciples through closed doors (John 20:26).

### 10.

Behold, you cannot investigate these things, and yet you believe them. Why, then, do you doubt the glory of the resurrection by arguing and examining it, when you have believed so many mysteries without examination?

[Note: Laudensis, in the margin: “on the resurrection of the flesh.”]

Yet if you do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh, you have believed everything without purpose, because in this spectacle of the angels you appear indeed to run swiftly, but after completing the race you turn away lest you receive the prize.

Hence Paul says: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24). Again he says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:19).

The mysteries of divine power, which cannot be comprehended, should not be examined by understanding but revered by faith. We must therefore know that whatever can be comprehended by human reason can no longer be marvelous; in miracles, the only explanation is the power of the one who performs them.

[Note: Suessionensis reads “while we are speaking of the glory of the resurrection.”]

Behold, while speaking about the resurrection of the flesh, we have digressed somewhat from the order of exposition. Let us therefore return to what we began.

### 11.

The inner gates also have vestibules, which measure twenty-five cubits in length. For if we multiply eight by three, we arrive at twenty-four. One is added to this, so that we have twenty-five.

[Col. 1034C] Good hearers, who are like certain vestibules of the gates, possess the long endurance of eternal hope; they sustain the eighth day in faith in the Trinity. This Trinity, because it is one God, multiplies eight by three, but they are made firm in confession of the one God.

[Note: The words “because it is one God” are absent from Longipontanus and Val-Cl.]

[Note: Laudensis, Longipontanus, and Suessionensis read “in the vision.”]

The vestibules are level because the hearts of good hearers are humble. They have length because they persevere with the long endurance of hope. Their length is measured by twenty-five cubits because they believe in the resurrection of the flesh on the eighth day through the Trinity, and confess that this same holy Trinity is one God.

They also have five cubits in width because, through the simple life that is conducted by the five senses, they are enlarged toward love of neighbor. It should be noted that after the vestibules of the gates were previously described as one thing, later the vestibule that has five cubits in width is said to look outward, because there are some hearers who penetrate more deeply into the understanding of the inner life by advancing in virtues, while some are simple and live well but according to the bodily senses.

Hence they are also said to look outward. They look outward, as it were, because they live according to the bodily senses. Yet, even while looking outward, they are within, because, although they do not know how to transcend the bodily senses through understanding, they nevertheless humbly hold faith and charity. Thus they are within the spiritual building through love, and seem to look outward through simplicity.

### 12.

The outward-looking vestibule can signify the faith of beginners, and the inner vestibule the faith of the perfect, who already shine through it in signs and virtues. The inner vestibule can also signify higher commandments, while the outward-looking vestibule can signify commandments that are still more elementary.

Through the vestibule one goes to the steps and the gate, because through the commandments of preaching one reaches virtues and access to heavenly grace.

When some are commanded to meditate on eternal things in their thoughts and to savor heavenly things, and are told to live in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (Col. 3:16), the inner vestibule is shown, which is measured by fifty cubits in length and twenty-five in width. We now remain silent about these numbers, because we have already said much about them above.

But when others are commanded, “Let the husband render to his wife her due, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:3), the vestibule that looks outward is signified. Although it looks outward, it is nevertheless within, because the inexperienced hearer still does what belongs to the flesh, yet is not excluded from the number of the good.

### 13.

The Lord can also be signified by the eastern gate, Judea by the southern gate, and converted Gentility by the northern gate.

[Note: We have restored within brackets the material found in the Laudensis, Suessionensis, and Longipontanus manuscripts.]

We call the Lord the gate because through him we enter to him. We appropriately call Judea and Gentility gates because we have recognized that access to the heavenly building was granted first to the Hebrews and afterward to the fathers who came from the Gentiles.

But in this matter a question strikes the mind: why, in the preceding account, did the prophet describe first the eastern gate, afterward the northern, and then the southern gate? Yet, when he described these same gates in the inner court, he described first the southern gate, then the eastern, and third the northern.

Why did he not keep the same order with which he had begun, but change it in his description of the gates, so that he first mentioned the eastern, northern, and southern gates, and afterward the southern, eastern, and northern?

But if Gentility is signified by the name “northern,” it is clear to all who read carefully that Gentility existed before the Synagogue. For Heber himself, from whom the Hebrews were named, was chosen from among the Gentiles (Gen. 10:21).

Let the eastern gate, then, be mentioned before the northern and southern gates, because the Lord, in his divinity, was born before Gentility and Judea—and indeed before all the ages.

In the subsequent account, however, let the southern, eastern, and northern gates be mentioned, because our Redeemer deigned to be born in human nature between Judea and Gentility, since he came both at the end of the Synagogue and before the beginning of the Church, which he gathered from the Gentiles.

[Note: This is the reading of Laudensis, Longipontanus, and the Norman manuscripts, together with the English and Val-Cl.; the printed editions agree in reading “in faith.” “At the end of the Synagogue” is preferable because of the contrast with “the beginning of the Church.”]

In the first description, therefore, let the eastern gate stand before the northern and southern gates; but in the second, let the eastern gate be named between the southern and northern gates, because by his divinity he preceded all things, while by his humanity he came among all things. He became both the end of departing Judea and the beginning of succeeding Gentility.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “of the one departing.”]

Since, therefore, we have examined, as far as the Lord granted us, the matters that had not yet been discussed, and have passed quickly over those that had often been repeated, let us now come to the matters that are presented in sequence in such a way that almost nothing in them is repeated from what has already been said.

### Verse 38

“And through each treasury, a doorway in the fronts of the gates.”

### 14.

Above (Homily 6, formerly 18, nos. 1 and following) we said that the treasuries are the hearts of teachers, which preserve the riches of knowledge. The fronts of the gates are the words and deeds of preachers, in which we recognize outwardly what sort of people they are inwardly.

There is a doorway through each treasury in the fronts of the gates because each teacher opens understanding in the heart of the hearer through the words and deeds of the fathers. When we examine the preaching of the apostle Peter, when we scrutinize the words of Paul, when we investigate the Gospel of John, and through their words draw our hearers toward inner understanding, what else are we doing but opening a doorway in the fronts of the gates?

Let it therefore be said: “Through each treasury, a doorway in the fronts of the gates,” because if a teacher does not confirm what he says by the words of the apostles, he has no doorway in the fronts of the gates. And if he has no doorway, he cannot be called a treasury of the spiritual building,

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “because if he does not open understanding of these things …”]

because if he does not open understanding, he is not a teacher.

But when good hearers learn the words and deeds of the apostles through the mouths of teachers, they silently reproach themselves for their faults and pursue with tears everything they remember having done wickedly.

[Note: Alternatively, “silently,” as in Laudensis and Longipontanus.]

Hence here too, concerning the doorway that is in the fronts of the gates, it is added:

### Ibid.

“There they washed the burnt offering.”

### 15.

Those who have devoted themselves to the Lord through faith in a holy way of life have become a burnt offering to the Lord. But because they still suffer many things from their corruptible flesh, because the purity of their heart is still stained by filthy thoughts, they return daily to tears and are afflicted by continual weeping.

They consider the words and deeds of the holy fathers, and when they judge themselves unworthy, they wash the burnt offering at the doorway of the gates.

For example, someone may have devoted himself, out of fear of almighty God, to being patient: to return no insult for an insult, to endure everything with equanimity.

[Note: Laudensis and Suessionensis read *qui se* (“one who has devoted himself”).] Yet when an insult suddenly strikes him from the mouth of his neighbor, he may become disturbed and say something he ought not to have said.

Certainly, this man is already a burnt offering, but one still defiled. Perhaps he displayed patience toward the insults inflicted upon him and remained silent; nevertheless, he is touched by grief at the same insults he bears, and his spirit is wounded in charity.

True patience is that which loves even the person whom it endures. For to endure while hating is not the virtue of gentleness but a covering for fury.

This man, then, often judges himself in his thoughts. He reproaches himself because he grieves, yet cannot prevail with himself not to grieve. Thus he is already a burnt offering through good devotion, but is still defiled by the grief that touches him.

Another person has determined within himself to give everything he possesses to the needy, to reserve nothing for himself, and to entrust his life solely to the governance of heaven. But while giving to the poor what he has, a thought may creep into his mind saying: “How will you live if you give everything away?”

[Note: Lyra reads “hesitation.”]

Yet he does not cease giving; rather, what he began to give joyfully he later offers sadly. What is this person’s mind but a burnt offering of mercy, still defiled by sadness of thought?

Either he ought not to have made so great a decision, or after making it he ought in no way to have doubted.

Another person, having despised the pride of the world, has resolved to avoid the honors and dignities of this age and seeks to hold the lowest place among human beings, so that he may be found all the higher in enduring glory the humbler he is seen to be in passing life.

Perhaps, when he suddenly realizes that he is despised by his neighbor, he disdains being despised. He wants to occupy a humble place, but does not want to be regarded as contemptible. Devotion already lifts him up, but weakness still weighs him down. Thus he is already a burnt offering through devotion, but is still defiled by weakness.

Those, therefore, who in the very things they have devoted themselves to do exceptionally well are touched by some fault of weakness, understand the words of the fathers through the words of teachers, recognize in what great guilt they lie, and afflict themselves with the lamentation of repentance: they wash the burnt offering at the doorway of the gates.

### 16.

We must understand the difference between a sacrifice and a burnt offering: every burnt offering is a sacrifice, but not every sacrifice is a burnt offering. In a sacrifice, part of the animal was accustomed to be offered; in a burnt offering, the whole animal. Hence *holocaustum* in Latin means “wholly burned.”

Let us therefore consider what a sacrifice is and what a burnt offering is. When someone vows something of his own to God but does not vow something else, it is a sacrifice. But when he vows to almighty God everything he has, everything that lives, and everything that understands, it is a burnt offering.

For there are some who are still held in mind by this world, yet provide assistance to the needy from their possessions and hasten to defend the oppressed. In the good things they do, these people offer a sacrifice, because they immolate part of their activity to God while reserving part for themselves.

There are others who reserve nothing for themselves but immolate to the almighty Lord their understanding, tongue, life, and substance that they have received. What do these people offer except a burnt offering? Indeed, they become a burnt offering.

The Israelite people first offered sacrifice in Egypt, and then a second time in the wilderness (Exod. 12–13). Whoever still has his mind in the world but is already doing some good has offered a sacrifice to God in Egypt.

But whoever abandons the present world and does the good he is able to do offers sacrifice in the wilderness, as though Egypt had already been left behind, because, having driven away the tumult of carnal desires, he immolates to God in the quiet and solitude of his mind whatever he does.

[Note: Ebroicensis, with the other Norman manuscripts, reads *tumultu* (“tumult”) for *strepitu* (“noise”).]

Although, as has been said, a sacrifice is also a burnt offering, a burnt offering is nevertheless greater than a sacrifice, because the mind that is not burdened by the world’s delight burns everything it has in the sacrifice of almighty God.

[Note: Laudensis and Val-Cl. read “by love.”]

### 17.

We must understand, however, that there are some who, even while abandoning the world, offer everything they have, yet are not at all pierced by the good things they do. The good they do is indeed a burnt offering, but because they do not know how to weep and judge themselves, and do not kindle themselves to tears out of love, their burnt offering is not perfect.

Hence the Psalmist says: “May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering be made rich” (Ps. 19:4). A dry burnt offering is a good work that the tears of prayer do not moisten. A rich burnt offering exists when what is done well is irrigated with tears by a humble heart.

Hence again it says: “I will offer you burnt offerings full of marrow” (Ps. 65:15). Whoever does a good work but does not know how to weep from love and desire for almighty God has a burnt offering, but has no marrow in the burnt offering.

But whoever does good works, longs already for the vision of his Creator, hastens to reach the joys of eternal contemplation, and slaughters himself in tears through the love by which he is inflamed, has offered to the Lord burnt offerings full of marrow.

We must therefore strive both to abandon evil completely and to do the good we are able to do, and in those good things we do to be pierced by love of the eternal light.

[Note: Laudensis reads: “and that in those good things which we do, we may be pierced [by compunction].”]

For love of the light itself dispels the darkness of the heart, so that we may see more subtly whether anything crooked is mixed into the good things we do. We must consider what our work is like, what thought is present in the work, and what intention is present in the thought.

When we recognize that some evil or perverse pleasure has been mixed into our good work, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

### 18.

There are some who devote themselves to the Lord in great actions and reach such perfection that they are never bent by any difficulty: through their resolve concerning chastity, the flesh does not lay the mind low in the pleasure of an evil thought. For even if temptation sometimes strikes by suggestion, it is not permitted to rise up, because it is crushed by the strength of judgment.

In their resolve concerning patience, neither does disordered speech issue from their mouth nor does silent grief weigh upon their spirit. In their generosity of almsgiving, no suspicion of poverty generates sadness. In their resolve concerning humility, no contempt wounds their spirit.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “grief” (*dolor*) for “contempt” (*despectus*).]

[Note: The printed editions read “insofar as from the decision …”]

But when they already show themselves steadfast in the things they have rightly devoted themselves to, they nevertheless recall their earlier sins—those they committed before their good resolve—and mourn whatever they remember having done unlawfully.

These people are a burnt offering through the life they now lead, but through the life they formerly led they are defiled. They therefore wash the burnt offering at the doorway of the gates, because, in the understanding they have received from the words of the fathers, they afflict themselves with daily lamentation and cleanse with tears the life they once defiled by wicked deeds.

Let us, then, amid these things, turn the eyes of our mind toward our past life and remember who we were when we followed the desires of this world. And if we now serve the Lord with our whole heart, let us weep because we remember that we sinned; let us wash the burnt offering in tears.

[Note: Alternatively, “what we were,” as read in Gemeticensis, Ebroicensis, and others.]

[Note: Suessionensis reads “let us dissolve in tears.”]

### 19.

Behold, we have devoted our chastity to almighty God. But if an impure thought still stains the mind, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

Behold, we have resolved to preserve patience. But if anger still disturbs us, if silent grief still torments the mind, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

Behold, we now know how to give away what we possess and to hold a humble place in this world. If any suspicion of poverty still depresses the spirit, if contempt from our neighbor confounds us with some indignation, let us return to tears and wash the burnt offering.

For the bosom of mercy is great with our Creator for receiving the tears of the humble.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “for receiving the tears of human beings.”]

Where the tears of countless human beings have been received, there our tears too will find their place.

Let us consider what is said through another prophet: “It shall be that whoever among them stumbles on that day shall be like David, and the house of David shall be like God, like the angel of the Lord in his sight” (Zech. 12:8).

This is the day of mercy that was promised to us through the coming of our Redeemer. Whoever has offended will be like David, because the sinner returns to repentance. But the house of David will be like God, because each person who returns to righteousness becomes the dwelling place of his Creator, so that he is like an angel in his sight, since he announces and offers to others the merciful compassion that he himself has experienced.

Hence it is also said there shortly afterward: “On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13:1).

### 20.

The hidden fountain is the invisible God, the Father’s only-begotten Son.

[Note: Val-Cl., with the agreement of the Norman manuscripts, reads “the only-begotten of the Father.”]

The open fountain is that same God incarnate. This open fountain is rightly called the house of David because our Redeemer came to us from David’s lineage.

“Jerusalem” is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Those inhabit Jerusalem who fix their minds upon the vision of inner peace.

The sinner and the menstruous woman signify either one who sins in action or a mind that slips into an evil thought. This pollution is like menstruation because it is not touched by another’s flesh and yet is defiled by its own flesh.

Such, then, such is every soul that, even if it does not commit an evil deed, nevertheless becomes polluted and filthy through thought.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “in thought.”]

Hence another prophet, under the figure of Judea, speaks of the soul occupied by unclean desires: “All who seek her will not fail; in her menstruation they will find her” (Jer. 2:24).

For malignant spirits do not cease seeking when they desire to bring about destruction, and they are not repelled by any uprightness of good thought.

[Note: Another reading: “of conduct,” as found in Gemeticensis and other Norman manuscripts.]

They find the soul in its menstruation when they easily draw it into perverse action because it is situated in polluted thoughts.

Let it therefore be said: “On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13:1), because the fountain of mercy is now open to us: our Redeemer, who deigned to become incarnate in the house of David in order to wash the sinner from perverse action and cleanse the menstruous mind from impure thought.

The fountain is therefore open. Let us run with tears; let us be washed in this fountain of mercy.

### 21.

David himself was washed in this fountain when, after the stains of grave sin, he returned to the lamentation of repentance. He was seeking to find this fountain when he said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (Ps. 50:14).

For *Jesus* is Hebrew; in Latin it is called *salutaris*, “Savior.” And what did he mean by asking that the joy of Jesus be restored to him, except that before his sin he had been accustomed to contemplate him, and had lost the joys of that contemplation through his sin?

Therefore, after repentance, he rightly sought that the joy of his vision be restored to him.

Mary Magdalene was washed in this fountain of mercy. Formerly a notorious sinner, she afterward washed away the stains with tears and wiped away the stains by reforming her conduct (Luke 7:37–38 and following).

[Note: Laudensis and Longipontanus read “the stains of her crime.” Here the holy Doctor assumes that Mary Magdalene and the sinful woman—whom many of the holy Fathers distinguish—are one and the same. On this controversy, see Tillemont and others, whether interpreters of the holy Gospel or writers of sacred history.]

In this fountain of mercy Peter washed, before everyone, what he had denied, because he wept bitterly (Matt. 26:75).

[Note: All our manuscripts have this reading, except that Suessionensis and Longipontanus read “before all the apostles.”]

In this fountain of mercy the thief was washed at the end of his life. Condemning himself in death, he was cleansed from his guilt by his confession of the truth (Luke 23:41).

[Note: Ebroicensis, Lyra, and Val-Cl. read: “that blessed thief rolled about.”]

22. Why, then, are we sluggish? Why do we remain numb and cold, when we know that so many have already washed themselves in this fountain of mercy [Col. 1040D]? Shall we despair of our cleansing, when we hold so many examples of mercy as a pledge? And shall we cease to seek forgiveness and to place our trust amid tears, when we have already received the cleansing of so many as a pledge of our hope? We ought to seek the fountain of mercy even if it were closed. Now it stands open, and we neglect it. Let us cast the eyes of faith upon the whole world; let us consider how many sinners, day and night, are washed in this fountain of mercy through lamentation; how many return from darkness to light, and how many from stains to purity. Let us therefore run with such people, after the darkness of death, to the water of life. Let us consider how greatly we have sinned, how greatly we sin each day, and, so that we may appear clean after our offenses, let us wash the holocaust. [Note: The remainder is missing in Norm. and in the Editions, except Gussanv. It survives in Laud. and Longip., where we read: “who lives and reigns with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.”] To accomplish these things, the grace of our Redeemer is present—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY IX [Alternatively XXI]

Five verses, from 39 to 43, are proposed for exposition. After scarcely attempting the literal sense, the spiritual and moral senses are brought forth, and the duties of the shepherd are discussed above all.

What are we going to say about the mystical meanings of the prophet Ezekiel, when we scarcely grasp the very words of his historical account? For he says:

**VERSES 39–41.**—“And in the vestibule of the gate were two tables on this side and two tables on that side, so that upon them the holocaust, the offering for sin, and the offering for guilt might be slaughtered. And on the outer side, which rises toward the entrance of the gate that leads toward the north, were two tables; and on the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, were two tables. Four tables on this side and four tables on that side, along the sides of the gate. There were eight tables on which they slaughtered.”

1. In these words, a great obscurity of uncertainty arises: are these things spoken of one particular gate, of two gates, or of each individual gate? But since four tables are described along the sides, and afterward the conclusion says, “There were eight tables on which they slaughtered” [Col. 1041C], it is clear that the Spirit does not speak here of each of the gates he described above. For if the six gates previously enumerated had four tables along their sides, all of them together would be said to have not eight but forty-eight tables.

Again, if this is said of one gate, our understanding is struck by a great obstacle. After the vestibule of the gate has been described, where two tables on this side and two on that side were said to be, two further tables are mentioned on the outer side that rises toward the entrance of the gate leading toward the north [Note: Thus Suess., Longip., Val. Cl., with Norm. and Anglic. The Becc. and Rothomag. manuscripts are mutilated here. The Editions read “reaches” (*pertingit*).], and then it is added: “And on the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, two tables.” For if within the vestibule of the gate there were two tables on each side, when it is added, “And on the outer side two tables, and on the other side before the vestibule two tables,” between which the gate facing the northern road is also said to stand, it is plainly evident that one vestibule was inside and another outside [Col. 1041D]. [Note: Laud., Suess., and Longip. read: “because here the interior northern gate is described, opposite which they do not doubt that the exterior gate stands before the vestibule.”] For earlier he had described three gates, and he also mentioned three others belonging to the inner court, of which he had identified the outermost as the northern gate—but, as has been said, as belonging to the inner court. [Note: In Laud., Suess., and Longip., here and below, many readings occur that are entirely discordant with the Vulgate reading. Since they cannot be reported here, we noted them in the preceding preface, no. 11.]

Now, therefore, when two tables on this side and two tables on that side are described in the vestibule of the gate, the discourse still concerns the same inner gate, since it immediately continues: “On the outer side, which rises toward the entrance of the gate that leads toward the north, two tables; and on the other side, before the vestibule of the gate, two tables.” Thus the inner gate is described as having two tables on each side in its vestibule, and the outer gate likewise has two on each side. Four on this side and four on that side are therefore obtained: two on each side in the vestibule of the inner gate, and two on each side outside at the northern gate. Together these make eight tables, on which they slaughter.

Having thus examined the exterior account, let the discourse return to the spiritual meaning. By the Lord’s generosity, it ought now to be all the easier, since our ignorance of the exterior description no longer constrains us.

2. As was said above, the name “gates” may signify holy preachers, so that the vestibule of the gate is the people. When the people receive the words of preaching with humble minds, tables for sacrifice are constructed within them from virtues. Again, there is nothing to prevent us from understanding the gate as that which is opened to us through the mouths of preachers—the understanding of sacred eloquence—so that the vestibule of this same gate consists of the words of preaching that we first receive humbly, in order afterward to arrive at an understanding of sacred eloquence. [Note: Laud., Longip., and Suess. read: “Let us therefore consider the holy Church and the Synagogue, and let it be.”]

Let the inner gate, then, be for us the New Testament, and the outer gate the Old Testament, because the former opens spiritual understanding, while the latter preserved for minds still inexperienced in the history of sacred eloquence the letter of the text. [Note: Laud. and Longip. read: “the vestibule of the inner gate.”] The inner gate, among the already great multitude of faithful peoples, has two sides: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. There are two tables on this side and two on that, because in the love of God faith [Note: Suess., Laud., and Longip. read: “purity of life.”] and life must necessarily be maintained, while in the love of neighbor patience and kindness must be preserved with the utmost care.

For faith and life are necessary in the love of God, since it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6). And again it is written: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20, 26). Patience and kindness must be preserved in our love of neighbor, because it is written of that same love: “Charity is patient, charity is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4). Patient, that is, so that it may bear calmly the injuries inflicted by neighbors; kind, so that it may generously devote its own goods to its neighbors.

The outer gate, namely the Law, also has two sides: the spiritual fathers and the carnal people. In each of these there are two tables, because among the spiritual fathers there are teaching and prophecy, while among the carnal people there are circumcision and sacrifice.

On these eight tables the sacrifice is slaughtered, because whatever faith believes, whatever life displays by the example of good works, whatever patience endures humbly, whatever kindness generously supplies, whatever teaching beneficially instructs, whatever prophecy foretells concerning the future, whatever circumcision bound by the external commandment, and whatever sacrifice the devotion of the one offering performed—all this shows itself to be a victim in the eyes of almighty God. For under the Law, through the carnal sacrifice, what else was the people offering except the devotion of its heart?

It should be noted, however, that only four tables are said to have been for the holocaust. We understand these as the tables of the inner gate’s vestibule, [Note: Longip. reads: “so that we may understand that the other four belonged to the outer vestibule.”] so that we may judge that the remaining four were constructed for sacrifice, not for the holocaust. For, as I have already stated in a preceding discourse (the preceding Homily), a holocaust is called something wholly burned.

The Law commands that God and neighbor be loved, that the divine commandments be observed, and that one be restrained from coveting another’s possessions; yet it does not command that everything be relinquished. In the New Testament, however, the Truth testifies to us, saying: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). And again he says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (ibid. 9:23).

The tables of the inner gate therefore have a holocaust, because in the virtues of the New Testament we burn everything as in a holocaust when we renounce all that belongs to this world. The tables of the outer gate have a sacrifice, but not a holocaust, because the legal commandments order tithes to be offered, but do not order everything to be relinquished. [Note: Laud. reads: “the sacrifice of the outer vestibule.”]

3. Of the four tables of the inner vestibule it is said: “So that upon them the holocaust, the offering for sin, and the offering for guilt might be slaughtered.” The difference between sin and guilt is this: sin is doing evil, while guilt is abandoning good things that ought above all to be held fast. [Note: The English manuscripts, agreeing with Lyr., read: “which must be avoided.”] Or certainly, sin lies in an act, while guilt lies in thought.

It is therefore rightly said that in the four tables of the inner gate the holocaust is slaughtered both for sin and for guilt, because whoever is able to despise the present age completely and, abandoning everything, to offer himself to the Lord as a holocaust already knows perfectly how to mourn both the sins of action and the [Note: Lyr. and the full Editions, especially that of 1502, read: “sins.”] faults of thought—both the evil he has done and the good he ought to have done but has not done.

For whoever has abandoned everything now sees his faults more freely in tears. And when earthly concern no longer impedes his mind, what else has he given to almighty God as a holocaust than his mind, mourning both action and thought?

4. Nor does it seem foreign to reason that, when the prophet spoke of the outer side and mentioned the entrance of the gate, he added: “Which leads toward the north.” In the outer keeping of the letter, the Law was held. The entrance of the gate is the historical understanding of the Law itself, which leads to fear of the Lord. This gate is said to lead toward the north because that same Law confined the cold hearts of the Jewish people under the fear of death. That people would have run, as it were, through warmth if they had kept the Lord’s commandments out of love. But because they preserved the letter under the fear of the threatened death, they remained, as it were, in the numbness of cold. [Note: Val. Cl. and Norm. read: “under the fear of threats.”]

Hence it is said to the new peoples, who love eternal rewards rather than fear temporal punishments and who are already warmed: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

Let it also be said: “Four tables on this side and four tables on that side, along the sides of the gate.” When faith and life, teaching and prophecy are preserved in the minds of the good, our gate—that is, the understanding of sacred eloquence—has four tables on one side. And when holy preaching preserves patience and kindness among peoples who are making progress, whereas previously it preserved circumcision and sacrifice among carnal people, four tables are likewise shown on the other side.

Together these make eight for slaughtering: four inner ones for the holocaust, and four outer ones for sacrifice. For those who in the holy Church preserve faith, [Note: Laud. and Longip. read: “purity of life.”] life, patience, and kindness are undoubtedly already endowed with the highest virtues; and those who in the Synagogue knew teaching and prophecy, circumcision and sacrifice, by offering some things and retaining others for themselves, gave the victim of their devotion to almighty God.

But because it was said above that the four tables of the inner vestibule were constructed so that upon them the holocaust might be slaughtered, both for sin and for guilt, it is explained below from what these tables were constructed, when it is added:

**VERSE 42.**—“But the four tables for the holocaust were constructed of squared stones.”

5. Whom do we understand by the squared stones mentioned here except certain saints, whose life has learned to stand firmly in prosperity and adversity? For a square stone stands evenly, whichever side is turned downward. Whoever, therefore, is not lifted up in prosperity, is not broken in adversity, is not drawn toward evil by persuasion, and is not called back from good works by reproach, is a squared stone. He stands, as it were, on every side, because he has no fall in any change of circumstance.

Certainly, when the prophet knew that the Jewish people were perishing from faith and foresaw the holy apostles rising in the Church, through whom many from the nations were to be strengthened in the firmness of faith and life, he spoke in great consolation, saying: [Note: Laud. and Longip. read “bricks.” Below they read “the fall of the bricks”; the Hebrew text, the Vulgate, and other versions agree. The sense intended by the prophet supports this. Nevertheless, in the other manuscripts, especially Norm., “stones” and “of stones” are read, and all the Editions follow them. Gregory could easily have written “stones” instead of “bricks.”] “The stones have fallen, but we will build with squared stones” (Isa. 9:10).

Seeing apostles, martyrs, and teachers arise in the holy Church, he grieved less over the fall of the stones—that is, over the destruction of the Jews—because he saw the building of almighty God, namely the holy Church, being constructed from squared stones.

The four tables, then, are constructed from squared stones, because faith and life, patience and kindness, were given from the lives of the saints as examples to succeeding peoples, so that the vestibule might now have tables—that is, so that the people might possess the virtues of life [Note: Suess., Laud., and Longip. read: “so that the faithful people may recognize those virtues through which …”] on which to kindle the sacrifice of prayer to almighty God upon the altar of their hearts.

For whatever good the faithful people of the holy Church have done or do, they have received as an example from the lives of their preachers. From where, indeed, would the vestibule have these tables if it had not found squared stones?

To bring one of the squared stones briefly into the discussion: Do you wish to see faith, dearly beloved brothers? “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). Do you wish to know life? “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Do you wish to hear patience? “Up to this very hour we are hungry [Note: Lyr. adds: “and thirsty”], and we are beaten, and we are homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands; when cursed, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when blasphemed, we entreat” (1 Cor. 4:11–13). Do you wish to know kindness? “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls” (2 Cor. 12:15).

And lest we perhaps think that he was indebted to the love of those for whom he desired to spend himself [Note: The word *amori* (“love”) is absent from almost all the manuscripts, but occurs in nearly all the manuscripts.], he immediately adds to those same disciples, saying: “Although loving you more, I am loved less” (ibid.). [Note: Laud. and Longip. read: “but let it be so. Therefore …”]

When the life of the holy preachers is known by the faithful people for the imitation of the saints’ virtues, tables are certainly constructed in the vestibule from squared stones.

The Synagogue also had spiritual fathers in teaching and prophecy, from whom it could draw an example of life in the virtues. But its inexperienced people served more through fear than followed through love. They did not wish to imitate the life of the fathers whom they had seen; and therefore [Note: The cited manuscripts read: “the outer vestibule of the gate.”] the outer gate that leads toward the north does not have tables for the holocaust.

But since we have spoken of these things in a moral sense, it remains for us to examine the same tables according to their typological meaning.

6. Our gate in the inner vestibule has four tables, because the holy Church has been instructed by the preaching of the four evangelists, through whose teaching it has learned to rise [Note: Gussanv. reads *accendere*, “to kindle.”] in its heart into love of almighty God and to sacrifice its thoughts to him as an offering. Two are reported to be on this side and two on that, because two evangelists testified to what they had seen [Note: Suess. reads *ea quae*, “those things which.”] concerning the Lord, while two narrated what they had learned by hearing from those who preceded them.

Or certainly, the four tables of the inner vestibule are what we plainly behold, because the holy Church receives, for the instruction of the faithful peoples, four governing orders, which Paul enumerates as gifts of almighty God, saying: “He gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers” (1 Cor. 12:28; Eph. 4:11). He names pastors and teachers as one governing order, because the one who teaches is truly the one who feeds God’s flock. [Note: The words in brackets are absent from all the Editions except Gussanv., which contains them here. They are also omitted in Sagiensis and Lyr., but are found in the others.]

The outer gate also had four tables, because the Synagogue maintained the observance of external service through the chief priests and elders of the people, through the scribes and Pharisees. Those Pharisees, moreover, were also called teachers of the Law. [Note: Laud. and Longip. read “the outer vestibule”; shortly below they read “whether in the outer or inner vestibule.” Everywhere they read “vestibule” instead of “gate.”]

Whether of the outer or inner gate, there are two tables on this side and two on that, because at its beginnings the holy Church had apostles and prophets. By prophets we mean not those who existed among the ancient people, but those who arose in the holy Church after the apostles. In the later period, which is the present, it has evangelists and teachers.

Because “Gospel” means “good news,” we call evangelists those who announce the good things of the heavenly homeland to inexperienced peoples. These evangelists and teachers existed in the earlier period as well, and by the Lord’s generosity they continue to exist to this day, because even now we see unbelieving peoples being drawn daily to the faith and the faithful being instructed in good morals through teachers.

The apostles and prophets, however, have been taken away from the present age. Therefore we say that these tables of our gate—that is, of the holy Church—were, as it were, on another side.

7. The gate that leads toward the north also has two tables on this side and two on that: the same chief priests and elders of the people whom we mentioned, in the greater authority of government, and the scribes and Pharisees, who presided over that inexperienced people in a lesser position.

[Note: Laud., Suess., and Longip. read: “But these tables are situated in the outer vestibule, because these orders of the Synagogue sought in the words of the almighty Lord no mystical meaning, but only the historical one. Therefore they were constructed outside, because they were not instructed in inward understanding. Yet they had a sacrifice, which they held firmly according to the letter. But the inner tables …”]

These tables are beside the gate that leads toward the north because, while these four orders ruled the people, the Synagogue, raging in persecution against our Redeemer, broke forth into the numbness of unbelief. Nevertheless, these tables had a sacrifice, which they held according to the letter alone; hence they also fell into the numbness of cold, because they were not kindled by the flame of the Spirit.

The inner tables, however, have a holocaust, because whether in the hearts of the apostles and prophets or in the minds of the evangelists and teachers, the fire of the Spirit both burned and burns. Since it consumes all their thoughts in good works, the flame of the love of God burns up everything it finds at once, like a complete holocaust. For those who are thoroughly kindled either in good works or in holy thought offer a holocaust. [Note: Laud. and Longip. read “of evangelizers.”]

8. These tables were made from squared stones because, as they meditate daily on the words of sacred eloquence in their hearts, they are constructed, as it were, from squared stones in order to offer the Lord the holocaust of prayer.

The words of sacred Scripture are squared stones because they stand everywhere, since they are found blameworthy on no side. In everything they narrate about the past, in everything they announce about the future, in everything they preach morally [Note: Gilot, Vatican, and Gussanv., through a gross error, read *quod mortaliter*; the reading is corrected from the English manuscripts and our own.], and in everything they proclaim spiritually, they have a standing, as it were, on different sides, because they have no grounds for reproach.

The hearts of the saints, therefore, are God’s tables, constructed for the holocaust from squared stones, because those who always think upon God’s words slay themselves to the Lord in thought, taking themselves away from carnal life. Hence it is written: “His God’s law is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted” (Ps. 36:31). And again it is said: “In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:11).

But since we have learned from what these tables are constructed, let us also hear what their measurements are. It follows:

**VERSE 42.**—“The length of one cubit and a half, the breadth of one cubit and a half, and the height of one cubit.”

9. Someone [Note: Namely Jerome, Book XII of his commentary on Ezekiel, at chapter 40. Gregory was compelled to correct his interpretation but spared him by name—an outstanding sign of Gregory’s modesty.] explained this passage by saying: “In length and breadth the tables have one cubit and a half, that is, they are square; taken together, these make three cubits. Those three cubits have a height of one cubit, so that they preserve the mysteries of the Trinity in the measure of one cubit—that is, of the divine majesty.”

This interpretation cannot stand, because in that Trinity which created and contains all things, a half is nothing, nor does anything one arise from two halves. That substance has no diminution or division, since, always remaining unchangeable, it receives neither loss nor increase.

We have often said that length pertains to the long-suffering of hope, while breadth pertains to the amplitude of charity. The tables constructed for the holocaust are therefore measured as one cubit and a half in length, because the holy fathers and teachers who extend themselves patiently toward the innermost secrets of hope are, insofar as human measure is concerned, very perfect through the fact that they live in the virtues. But insofar as those divine mysteries are concerned, which cannot be fully grasped by human beings, they are not perfect so long as they remain in this mortal flesh.

In themselves, therefore, they already have one cubit, but in God they do not yet have one cubit, because they already make complete progress in the virtues, yet still know God only partially.

Once again Paul comes forward as a testimony to the measure of the table. Let us see whether his life can be measured by a complete cubit. For he says: “Let as many of us as are perfect think this way” (Phil. 3:15). Let us see whether, in what he understands concerning God, he has already stretched himself out perfectly to receive the mysteries: “I do not consider that I have comprehended” (ibid., 13). Again he says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). And again: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (ibid., 12).

If, therefore, he is perfect and knows in part, he has a cubit with respect to himself, but still has a half above himself. Let the hearts of the saints therefore be stretched out in the long-suffering of hope; let them be stretched out to the perfection they possess, one cubit. But because they cannot yet see fully where they direct the eye of hope, let what they have beyond one cubit be cut down to a half-cubit, so that in this life they may always see themselves as imperfect and run more ardently toward perfection. [Note: Val. Cl., Rothomag., and other Norm. manuscripts read “are stretched out.”]

10. The tables also have a breadth of one cubit and a half, because the hearts of the saints, expanded in the amplitude of charity, possess a cubit with regard to the neighbor whom they love and see. For they can perfectly love those whom they are able perfectly to know in some respect.

They love almighty God from the depths, and follow him from the depths, yet cannot love him as much as they ought, because they are not yet able to see the one whom they love. The measure of love is smaller where the measure of knowledge is still smaller.

They therefore have one cubit and a half, because what is already complete in their mind—that is, charity toward the neighbor—is much less; while what is much greater in them—that is, love of God, whom they do not see—is not yet complete. [Note: Norm., Anglic., Val. Cl., and others read as Gussanv., whereas the Editions read “in love.”] [Note: Suess., agreeing with Norm., reads: “which is much less in charity with the neighbor”; below Suess. and Ebroic. read: “is greater in the love of God.” The other manuscripts, especially Anglic., support our reading.]

Isaiah rightly speaks of this love, which begins here so that it may be perfected through the vision of the Lord in the eternal homeland, saying: [Note: Laud. and Longip. read “the Lord said.”] “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9).

To be a furnace is more than to be a fire, because a fire can be small, whereas in a furnace a larger flame is kindled. Zion means “watchtower,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” Here, meanwhile, we contemplate our peace, so that afterward we may see it fully there.

Thus, from the love of the Lord there is fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem, because here we burn to some extent with the flames of his love, where we contemplate something concerning him; but there we shall burn fully, where we shall fully see the one whom we love.

11. The height of the tables is one cubit. For what is the height of the saints except faith in invisible things? Through faith one believes what is not seen, and therefore by faith the mind of the righteous is led upward, so that it despises all visible things on earth and follows in heaven what it hears is invisible. [Note: All the Editions, despite the manuscripts, read “the table of the righteous.”]

But the tables have a height of one cubit because the faith in the hearts of all the saints is one. Both the fathers of the Old Testament and the preachers of the New have confessed that God is one Trinity.

The height of the tables therefore has neither more nor less than one cubit, because the faith of all the fathers agrees with itself in great unity. But those who, already making progress through the highest virtues in the long-suffering of hope, have one and a half cubits, and who are measured by one and a half cubits in the breadth of charity, while they exceed one cubit in the height of faith—these are great and worthy of veneration with the highest admiration.

They ought therefore to receive the souls of little ones into the bosom of their manner of life and offer them before the Lord like a certain holocaust and sacrifice. Hence it plainly follows:

**THE SAME PASSAGE.**—“Upon which they place vessels in which the holocaust and the victim are slaughtered.”

12. For what are the souls of the faithful except holy vessels that receive words of piety, so that from their minds the holocaust of life and prayer may be sacrificed? Hence it is that Paul, while still inexperienced in his call to faith, because he had already received the Lord’s words and was full of heavenly grace, is called a vessel when it is said: “He is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9:15).

Hence the prophet admonishes pastors and teachers, saying: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). For those who instruct and sustain the lives of the faithful, so that they may eventually bring that life to the Lord as a holocaust and sacrifice, carry the Lord’s vessels like tables.

Nor should we overlook the fact that the holocaust and the victim are said to be slaughtered in these same vessels. For a holocaust, as we also said above [Note: “The preceding Homily.”], is a victim, but a victim is not always a holocaust. For when something is offered in part and retained in part, it is indeed a sacrifice, but it is not a holocaust.

Among the great multitude of the faithful, there are some who abandon all worldly things, give away all that they possess, reserve nothing for themselves, yearn from the depths for the eternal homeland, and slaughter themselves in tears with their whole heart. These are vessels upon the table in which a holocaust is sacrificed.

There are others who care for their own household, think of their children, and preserve an inheritance for them; yet, mindful of the eternal judgment, they show mercy to the poor and give them food and clothing according to the portion they have determined. These too are vessels upon the table, in which a victim has been sacrificed, but not a holocaust.

For through admonishing and enduring, persuading and frightening, the patience and teaching of the saints instruct some hearts to the point that they abandon everything and kindle themselves wholly in the love of the Lord. They instruct others to the point that, because they cannot abandon everything, they at least become merciful to the extent they are able and divide their care of the flesh with their care of the soul.

Thus the tables of the Lord, furnished from squared stones, carry vessels in which a holocaust and a victim are sacrificed: the perfect, as has been said, abandon everything and kindle their whole heart in the love of the Lord, while the imperfect offer a sacrifice that they have devoted in part.

It follows:

**VERSE 43.**—“And their lips were one palm in breadth, turned inward all around.”

13. What does it mean that the lips of the tables are measured by a palm, except that the hand is extended in the palm, and that the holy fathers and teachers preach those things in which the works of their hearers are extended? For we extend our hand, as it were, when we enlarge our works.

Let every teacher speak; let him exercise the heart of the hearer and shake off the torpor of the idle. When he stretches them toward good works, let him show that he has a palm in his lips. [Note: Laud. and Longip. read: “on the side.”]

It should also be considered that in the palm the largest and smallest fingers are extended. What is signified by the largest and smallest finger except a great and an ultimate action?

Let the table therefore have a palm in its lips, so that through the preaching of its teachers the hearer may perform great works [Note: Suess., with Ebroic. and other Norm. manuscripts, reads: “let the hearer awaken, and thus through their admonition perform great works.”], while not omitting even the smallest deeds. Let him be so attentive to small things that he is not sluggish in performing greater ones.

Hence the Truth says through the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the Law, judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to do, and not omit those” (Matt. 23:23).

Through judgment, mercy, and faith, the larger finger of action is shown. Through mint, dill, and cumin, without doubt the smallest finger is represented. “These you ought to do, and not omit those,” because if we wish to measure our work by a palm, the smallest finger must be extended in such a way that the larger finger is not drawn back. [Note: Laud. reads: “in the lip”; Laud., Longip., Val. Cl., and Norm. read “in the lip.”]

14. It is fitting that, when the lips of the tables are measured and the measure of a palm is mentioned, “one” is added, so that, just as unity is maintained in faith through the preaching of teachers, so unity of minds may also be preserved in action, lest, because of the good work one person performs, another break forth into the evil of discord.
