We ought to do good works in such a way that through them we preserve unanimity, insofar as we rightly can, with those with whom we live—not by abandoning what we are doing, but by forestalling through good persuasion the evil of discord that we fear.

Thus Paul, preserving the unity of the palm in his works, prevented discord from arising when he saw that the Corinthians wished to receive someone who had fallen and had already been expelled from the Church. He said: “If you have forgiven anyone anything, so have I. For whatever I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done it for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan” (2 Cor. 2:10).

For Satan is accustomed to produce evil from good and to draw into discord what is done in charity. Hence he immediately adds concerning him: “For we are not ignorant of his thoughts” (ibid., 11).

But if a teacher, through the good things he preaches, forms right action in his hearers without binding the minds of those who act to unanimity, he has a palm in his lips, but does not possess the unity of the palm that has been described.

15. We must carefully consider what is said: the rims of those same tables are bent inward. The rims of the tables are bent inward when teachers recall to their conscience, through silent reflection, what they say—when they examine themselves closely to see whether they do what they teach. When the rims of the tables are rightly said to be bent inward, the phrase “all around” is also added, so that they do not examine themselves in only one part and neglect to assess themselves in another, but inspect themselves everywhere and, insofar as they are able, strive to fulfill in action each thing they teach. Otherwise, if they preach good things while refusing to do them, they become their own destroyers while cultivating another’s field. [Note: Laud. and Lyr., and elsewhere, read atque alias in semetipsos (“and elsewhere [consider] themselves”); Ebroic. and the altered exemplar of Longip. have alia (“other [things]”).]

O teacher, behold: you are already a table; you already carry vessels; already, in faithful vessels, you bear the weight of burnt offerings and sacrifices. But bend the rim inward—recall your speech to your heart. Hear what you say; practice what you preach. For if you neglect to fulfill what you preach, you sow a harvest for others while yourself fasting from participation in the grain. Hence it is written: “The hungry shall eat his harvest” (Job 5:5). The hungry person eats the teacher’s harvest when he speaks good things but does not practice them, because the one who hungers for the bread of righteousness practices the commandments he hears, while the one who labored by sowing has no fruit himself.

Hence Solomon says: “The sluggard hides his hand beneath his armpit” [Note: Most printed editions read “under his arm.” We follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.] “and does not bring it back to his mouth” (Prov. 19:24). No one is so lazy that he would think it burdensome to bring his hand to his mouth even for eating. But the sluggard does not bring his hand to his mouth who is unwilling to practice what he says.

Again, concerning those who teach well but act badly, it is said: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. 77:9) [Note: Norm. reads “Ephrem.”]. They bend the bow and shoot arrows who set forth the sentences of Holy Scripture and strike the vices of their hearers with upright words; but they turn back on the day of battle because, in temptation by their vices, they return to themselves and refuse to present their breast in resistance, since they do not withstand the struggle of temptations.

Again it is said: “You have turned away the help of his sword, and you have not assisted him in battle” (Ps. 88:44). The teacher’s sword is the word of God. Hence Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). Therefore, when almighty God sees that a teacher is unwilling to practice what he says, on the day of battle he turns away the sword that was his help, because in the struggle of temptations he does not permit the words of the teaching he gave to serve him as an aid [Note: Longip., Ebroic., and Lyr. read “in the temptation of the struggle.”].

He has the sword, therefore, but it does not help him in battle, because when the adversity of temptation breaks out, he forgets the word he was teaching. Suppose, for example, that the teacher is speaking about patience and, compelled by the office of his teaching, must explain how patience is preserved in response to inflicted losses and insults that have been heard. But when he himself has been provoked by loss or insult, he forgets what he taught and goes beyond the proper measure either in injuring his neighbor or in returning the insult more harshly.

Amid all this, then, let him consider that he is God’s table; let him bend the rim inward and preserve what he preaches. For it is written: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). And again it is written: “The instruction of a man is known through patience” (Prov. 19:11). If patience is the test of instruction, each person is shown to be learned in proportion to his patience.

For this reason that good disciple who saw his master being taken up into the air cried out with the affection of great love: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” (2 Kings 2:12). What does it mean, dearest brothers, that Elijah is called the chariot of Israel and its charioteer, except that the charioteer drives and the chariot carries?

The teacher, therefore, who both bears the conduct of the people through patience and teaches by the words of sacred eloquence is called both chariot and charioteer. He is a chariot because he carries by enduring; a charioteer because he drives by exhorting. He is a chariot because he bears evils; a charioteer because he exercises the people through good admonitions.

16. Perhaps the teacher is speaking against vainglory and explaining admirably how it ought to be avoided, yet by those very speeches with which he argues against vainglory he seeks the vainglory itself. If he desires to obtain what he forbids, the table does not bend its rim inward. The table of the Lord, constructed from squared stones, will then have its rim bent inward if it strives to hear what it says.

For it is written: “Do nothing through contention or through empty glory” (Phil. 2:3). And again the excellent preacher says: “Nor seeking glory from human beings, neither from you nor from others” (1 Thess. 2:6). To seek passing praise from the labor of preaching: what else is this than to sell a great thing at a cheap price?

But there is grave danger in the words of teaching [Note: Another reading: “in the teaching of the word.”], because often the favor of hearers follows the speech of teachers. When teachers do not wish to appear lesser in their words than they have become known to be, they later labor for the praise of the teaching-word that they originally began, out of love for almighty God, in order to acquire the souls of their hearers [Note: Val. Cl., together with Norm., reads: “when they now wish to be greater in their words.”]. Those who first sought spiritual profit in the words of God later pursue temporal approval.

Thus it happens that both upright actions and the words of holy teaching perish before the judgment of almighty God when someone longs through them for passing approval. Hence the prophet says to Judea what an unwary mind discovers in itself if, at least after the fault, it carefully investigates its thoughts: “The Lord called your name: a fruitful, beautiful, productive, splendid olive tree. At the sound of a great utterance, fire has blazed in it, and its thickets have been burned” (Jer. 11:16) [Note: Laud., Longip., and Val. Cl. read “its thickets” here and below.].

The Lord calls fruitful and beautiful, productive and splendid, the olive tree whose effectiveness in action or holy zeal in words he approves. But “at the sound of a great utterance fire has blazed in it,” because when someone begins to be praised, he perhaps becomes ashamed to appear less than he is called and strives to become what he is said to be. The great sound of speech is the favor of the flatterer. Hence it is written: “Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, is like one who curses” (Prov. 27:14).

At the sound, therefore, of the great utterance, fire blazes in it, because amid the greatness of approval a flame of love for praise is kindled in the heart. But all the olive tree’s thickets are burned, because in the eyes of almighty God both what was done well and what was spoken with knowledge perish when they are no longer performed out of love for the Lord but with the intention of passing praise.

A sinister thought is often joined to a good thought in such a way that the mind itself, which generates both thoughts, scarcely recognizes them. Hence the excellent preacher, speaking with subtlety, says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4:12). Immediately he adds: “Of joints also and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (ibid.).

17. The word of God distinguishes joints and marrow because it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart [Note: Longip., following Laud., reads “will distinguish … will discern.”]. Bones are joined to bones through joints. Often, while we do something with a right thought, we suddenly turn aside into love of praise and do for the sake of praise what we had begun to do for the sake of truth [Note: Longip. reads “for God.”]. Thus thoughts are joined to thoughts, and a kind of joints are formed in the spirit.

But the bones joined in a joint also have marrow. The holy preacher made this clearer when he added: “A discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (ibid.). Our thoughts are the joints; our intentions are the marrow. Often we think one thing, while our thought intends another [Note: Lyran reads “toward which,” instead of “which.”].

If someone defends the case of an orphan or widow for the sake of a promised payment, and perhaps, entering a church, says to God in his prayers, “You see that I defend the case of the orphan and the widow,” he undoubtedly knows what he is thinking, but he does not know what his thought intends. He thinks one thing but intends another [Note: Laud., with Longip., reads “he intends something else.”]. He is not seeking the defense of the orphan or widow but the payment of money. Take away the temporal reward, and he will not defend the orphan or widow.

The word of God, therefore, is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart, because it does not look at what you think within yourself, but through the marrow of the joint—that is, through the intention of the thought—it sees what you seek to gain.

It remains, therefore, that when the teacher speaks, as God’s table he should always bend the rim inward, lest he either begin to speak with a wicked intention or, having begun well, be led astray by approval into another desire.

[Col. 1054B] 18. Perhaps the teacher is speaking about the preservation of discipline. It often happens that he knows how to state the rule of discipline but does not know how to keep it, either because, moved by excessive zeal, he restrains himself too little through gentleness, or because, placid through excessive gentleness, he is insufficiently inflamed against vices by the spur of zeal.

We must consider very carefully what is written: in the vessels of the temple, between the crowns and wreaths, oxen, lions, and cherubim were carved, and beneath the oxen and lions were hanging cords (1 Kings 7:29) [Note: Suess. and Longip., following Laud., read “on the bases of the temple.”].

The crowns signify the sign of victory; the wreaths signify the concord of unity; cherubim are said to represent the fullness of knowledge. Priests and teachers, represented by oxen, lions, and cherubim between the crowns and wreaths—that is, between the strength of good works by which they run toward victory and the concord of charity through which they do not disagree among themselves—must, in the fullness of knowledge they possess, preserve both the gentleness of oxen and the fierceness of lions, so that in the discipline they preach they may be inflamed by holy zeal and tranquil through paternal sweetness.

Let cords hang beneath them, so that they may diligently extend to their subjects the restraints of their discipline, by which they themselves are bound. For cords hanging beneath them means keeping the bonds of discipline for those subject to them. These are rightly preserved when neither the gentleness of oxen is lost in the fervor of zeal nor the terror of lions degenerates into gentleness.

There must be such great discernment that neither discipline is excessive nor mercy lax. Otherwise, if guilt is dismissed without order, the guilty person is bound more severely in his offense; and again, if guilt is retained without measure, the person being corrected becomes worse in proportion as he sees that no grace of kindness is being shown toward him.

Harshness must therefore be displayed toward the wicked, but charity must be held in the heart, so that the hard outward display may restrain the offender while the preservation of charity does not lose the reward of gentleness.

19. Behold, while I am speaking, Joseph comes to mind, so that he himself may appear as a witness to what I say. When he told his brothers the dream he had seen concerning his future advancement, the innocent report aroused against him the goads of malice (Gen. 37:5). He was sold by those same brothers to the Ishmaelites (ibid., 21), brought into Egypt, and, through the wondrous dispensation of almighty God, placed over that same Egypt (ibid., 41:41).

When famine arose in the land of Canaan, his brothers came to Egypt, found Joseph placed over Egypt, and worshiped him with their necks bowed to the ground (ibid., 42:7). Since they could not change God’s plan, they worshiped the one whom they had sold so that they would not worship him, because they had sold him.

Then the man of God, full of the spirit of discernment, recognized his brothers without being recognized by them [Note: Laud. and Longip. add “by them.” Val. Cl. and Norm. read “unrecognized by his brothers.”]. But mindful of their guilt and forgiving of the injury, he neither sought to repay his brothers’ evil nor to release them without purification.

For he immediately said in a suspicious tone: “You are spies. You have come to see the weaker parts of the land; now I shall test you. By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave here” (ibid., 9) [Note: Lyr. reads: “For you have come to inspect the weaker parts of the land.”].

O dart in the heart! They had come as foreigners; they were fleeing the danger of famine; they had not obtained the grain they sought, and moreover they saw themselves being struck by the imputation of a crime [Note: Ebroic., together with the other Norm. and Val. Cl. witnesses, and agreeing with the 1502 edition, reads: “and they saw that an accusation of crime was being brought against them.”].

Meanwhile they are led to prison, and after three days are brought out, yet are still terrified by the same harshness. Their heart now returns to itself; the memory of their guilt strikes their minds, and they say among themselves: “We rightly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother. We saw the anguish of his soul when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen; therefore this tribulation has come upon us” (ibid., 21).

At this, Joseph’s heart is overcome by love. He withdraws and, weeping, releases what he owed to compassion. He returns to his brothers sternly [Note: Longip. reads: “so that the anguish of their hearts might free them from guilt.”], so that the anguish of their hearts might free them from guilt.

After this, one brother is bound in fetters, while the others are sent away with grain, so that the one brother whom they had said was their youngest might come [Note: Anglic., Lyr., and Val. Cl. read “and he orders”; Sag. reads “and he asks”] (ibid., 34–35).

The brother later comes. Compassion overcame his mind when the brother appeared innocent, but harshness remained in outward display so that the guilty brothers might be purified. Grain is given; the cup is hidden in the younger brother’s sack; and an investigation for theft is instituted against them after they have departed (Gen. 44:2). They are sent for and brought back, and it is decreed that the one in whose possession the cup is found shall be sentenced to slavery. It is found in the sack of the youngest brother.

Then Benjamin is brought back, and all the afflicted brothers follow. O tortures of mercy! He torments, and he loves. They return and, prostrate on the ground with tears, ask pardon. Mindful of what they had promised their father concerning him, they were wasting away in intolerable grief.

Then compassion, no longer able to restrain itself, burst forth from its confinement into the open and shook the tears of charity from the face of severity (Gen. 45:1). The anger that appeared, but was not present, was wiped away; the mercy that was present, but did not appear, was revealed.

Thus the holy man both pardoned and punished his brothers’ crime. Thus he held clemency within firmness, so that toward his delinquent brothers he was neither compassionate without retribution nor strict without compassion.

20. Behold the teaching of discipline: to know both how to spare faults with discernment and how to cut them away with kindness [Note: Thus Laud., Val. Cl., Lyr., and Longip.; most printed editions read: “to know how to spare faults and correct them with discernment.”].

Those who do not possess the spirit of discernment either dismiss sins in such a way that they do not correct them, or strike as though correcting in such a way that they do not forgive. Therefore, the teacher who must speak about the moderation of discipline should know that he is God’s table and bend the rim inward, so that what he says in teaching he may vigilantly practice under the spirit of discernment.

Nor, if he recognizes that certain things are lacking in himself, ought he on that account to be silent about preaching them. His position requires him to speak. Let him therefore confront himself with his own words; and if he does not speak because he does not practice, let him practice because he is compelled to speak [Note: Printed editions, contrary to the mind of Saint Gregory, read “because he practices.”].

Wherever he sees himself fulfilling in action what he says, there let him admonish his hearers and kindle their minds toward the pursuit of good works [Note: All our manuscripts read thus; the edition reads “equip them.”]. But wherever he does not yet see himself fulfilling what he says, let him likewise inflame himself toward the good things about which he admonishes his hearers, so that he too may learn in action what truth speaks through him in preaching.

Often, what we do not know by living, we learn by speaking, compelled by the language of teaching [Note: This is how it is read in Val. Cl. and several manuscripts. Others, with Suess. and Longip., have “from knowledge,” etc.; Laud. has “from knowledge of our laziness.”]. And while the guilt of our laziness is born in our thoughts, a sudden compunction pierces that same mind, and, awakened by its own voice, it arouses itself to action—the mind that had previously lain sluggish in idleness without a voice.

But behold: when the rim of the table is extended by a palm—that is, when the teacher’s mouth argues against vices and the hearts of hearers are kindled toward good works—many who hear his words recognize how many and how great are the evils they have committed. They come to him confessing and ask with tears that he become their intercessor for their sins, so that by praying he may wipe away the faults he reveals by preaching. Hence it is added:

**VERSE 43. — “And upon the tables, the flesh of the offering.”**

21. When holy teachers pour out prayers to almighty God for repentant and confessing sinners, by asking pardon for their carnal life they carry the flesh of offerings upon the tables of the Lord.

In order that there may be people for whom they can pray after their conversion and tears, they must first preach to them while they remain in sin. Once they begin to abandon their sins and hasten toward innocence, the teacher’s preaching must increase toward them, and he must press the word of his teaching upon them with greater force in proportion as he sees that they have fallen more grievously. He knows that he will receive a greater reward in proportion as, through his words, he raises others from deeper sins.

22. At this point I wish to bring forward the words of the holy Gospel, whose sacred history, by narrating a miracle that happened, announces wondrous things that occur every day. When exhausted and hungry crowds had gathered to the Lord, the Lord said to the disciples: “I have compassion on the crowd, because behold, they have remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat; and if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way, for some of them have come from far away” (Mark 8:2–3).

The crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, converts to God in action, speech, and thought. The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their homes, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners faint on the road of the present life if they are sent away in their conscience without the nourishment of holy teaching.

Therefore, lest they grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed with holy admonition [Note: Laud. reads “lest they be relaxed.”]. We must carefully consider the pious statement that came from the mouth of Truth: “For some of them have come from far away” (ibid.).

One person, having experienced no fraud and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of almighty God. He did not come from far away, because through incorruption and innocence he was near. Another, stained by no impurity or crime but having experienced marriage alone, turned to spiritual service. He too did not come from far away, because, using the permitted union, he did not go astray through unlawful things.

Others return to repentance after carnal crimes, others after false testimonies, others after thefts, others after acts of violence, others after committing murders, and turn to the service of almighty God. These come to the Lord from far away. For the more each person has gone astray in wicked action, the farther he has withdrawn from almighty God.

The prodigal son, who abandoned his father, went away into a distant region, where he fed swine, because he nourished vices (Luke 15:16).

Let nourishment therefore also be given to those who come from far away, because converted sinners must be provided with the food of holy teaching, so that they may recover in God the strength they lost through their crimes. Often it is necessary for teachers to satisfy them with more abundant nourishment of teaching in proportion as they have come exhausted by greater vices.

When they have begun to confess the evils they committed, and by confessing to abandon them and punish them with tears, holy teachers must earnestly pray for their sins, so that they may carry the flesh of offerings upon the tables of the Lord.

Whenever they do this, insofar as they intercede for the sins of others, they wipe away their own sins more fully before God’s eyes, because they justify themselves through that very charity by which, with wondrous compassion, they sacrifice themselves in lamentation for the iniquities of others.

Nor should it be burdensome for teachers to shed tears for converted sinners, since he himself who created all things, having become human, shed his blood on the cross for our iniquities [Note: “The same—for us.”], who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY X [Another: XXII]

In explaining the four verses from 44 to 48, the holy Doctor ranges more freely over faith, hope, charity, and the good works to be offered to God upon the altar of the heart, and brings this work to completion.

1417 1. Prudently understanding the mystical meanings of sacred eloquence through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the Prophet says: “Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out” (Ps. 118:129) [Note: Val. Cl., Ebroic., and Lyr. read: “The mystical meanings of sacred eloquence are [understood] by the Prophet.”]. Again he says: “Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (ibid., 18).

The person who does not yet understand hidden things from what is manifest has veiled eyes. But the person who already understands considers the wonders of God’s law with unveiled eyes, examining the words of the letter spiritually and weighing what greatness lies hidden within.

Is it not wonderful when one thing sounds in the ears, while something else, which did not sound outwardly, emerges into the understanding? To what, then, should I compare the word of sacred eloquence except a stone in which fire lies hidden? It is held cold in the hand, but when struck with iron it flashes with sparks and emits the fire that will later burn—although earlier the hand held only something cold.

So, indeed, so are the words of sacred eloquence. Through the narrative of the letter they are held as something cold; but if someone, with the Lord’s inspiration, strikes them with attentive understanding, he draws fire from their mystical meanings, so that the mind may afterward burn spiritually in those words which earlier, through the letter, he too heard as cold.

Behold, the prophet says:

**VERSE 44. — “And outside the inner gate were the treasuries of the singers, in the inner court, which was at the side of the gate looking toward the north; and their fronts were toward the southern way, one at the side of the eastern gate that looked toward the northern way.”** [Note: Longip. and Val. Cl. read “the eastern way.”]

2. In these words of the letter, what mind would not be inflamed with love of God—or rather, would not grow cold from their very reading? But if the spiritual marrow hidden in the letter is examined, sparks of understanding emerge and kindle what previously sounded cold to the ears of the heart.

Nevertheless, in order that the interior understanding may open for us with the Lord’s inspiration, the narrative itself must first be made clear according to the letter. It says that there was an inner gate, and outside it a court called inner; then other gates—the northern, southern, and eastern—are described, so that the court which he had said was outside the inner gate might be shown to be inside the outer gates [Note: Longip., with Norm., reads “which he himself.”].

This court, therefore, is both outside and inside: outside because it is beyond the inner gate, but inside because it lies within the outer gates. The treasuries of the singers are also said to be in this same court, and are said to have been placed at the side of the gate looking toward the north. Yet these same treasuries look toward the southern way. And it is added: “At the side of the eastern gate that looked toward the northern way.”

From these words it is clearly understood that the treasuries of the singers had been placed between the side of the gate looking toward the north and the side of the eastern gate, which gate evidently looked toward the northern way. The fronts of the treasuries were therefore toward the southern way, but their position was between the eastern and northern gates [Note: Laud. and Longip. read “opposite the eastern way.”].

The inner gate therefore had the northern gate on one side and the southern gate on another. At the front of the vestibule stood the eastern gate, and thus the court that was outside the inner gate was also inside, surrounded by the gates that lay outside it [Note: Suess., Laud., and Longip. read: “and thus the court that was outside the inner gate was also inside, while the gates surrounding it lay outside.”].

3. We have passed briefly over these words of the letter, so that we may seek in them meanings that are not brief. [Note: Here Longip., Laud., and Suess. read: “In the upper section three gates are described, namely those of the east, north, and south. Three others are narrated, namely those of the south, east, and north. This inner gate, facing north, is said to be between two vestibules. Through each of these two vestibules we have said that the old people, outside, and the new people from the Gentiles, through that which is inside, are figured. But after these matters have been completed, etc.” This stands in place of the printed text.] In the upper section three gates are described: the eastern, northern, and southern. Immediately afterward three others belonging to the inner court are recounted: the southern, eastern, and northern. Then the gate of the inner court is mentioned, in which tables constructed from squared stones are remembered; and the gate looking toward the north, in which tables were for sacrifice, not for burnt offerings.

Hence we said that the inner part signifies the Church, and the outer part the Synagogue. But after this has been completed, the prophet again begins to describe the inner gate and three others—the northern, southern, and eastern—and says that in their inner court, which was outside the inner gate, there were treasuries, singers, priests, the temple, the altar, and sacrifices [Note: Norm. reads “there were treasuries of the singers.” A little later it reads: “let there be treasuries of the singers.”].

Since in these words he began to narrate matters concerning the establishment of the holy Church different from what he had said earlier, it is clear that he changed the meaning of the inner gate. For if he were saying everything under one meaning, he would not repeat the same things in a new arrangement and with different details.

How can we say that outside the inner gate there were a court, treasuries, singers, priests, a temple, an altar, and sacrifices, if in this passage the holy Church is signified by that same inner gate? Since all these things are within it, how are they outside the inner gate if they are not outside the Church? [Note: Lyr. reads “outside the outer gate.”]

The inner gate can therefore be understood as the one of which we spoke much earlier, said to be positioned opposite the northern and eastern gates. We said that it represents the entrance opened for us to the inner joys of our heavenly homeland; thus here also the gates narrated around the vestibule may represent the holy Church, while the inner gate represents the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.

But lest anyone think that I am forcibly bending the words of the Holy Spirit toward my own understanding and say that, after once assigning to the inner gate the meaning of the holy Church, I ought not to change it, let us, with the grace of almighty God shining upon us, retain what we began, so that the inner gate may signify the Church that leads us to inner joys, while the treasuries, singers, priests, temple, altar, and sacrifices may be in the court outside the gate and yet not be outside the Church [Note: Laud. and Suess. read: “Let us retain the same meaning that we assigned to the type of the holy Church, as we began.”].

If we investigate carefully, nothing prevents us from understanding the inner gate, as has been said, as the holy Church. Of it we now read: “And outside the inner gate were the treasuries of the singers, in the inner court.” For two things are being said: the inner gate, and outside it the inner court, so that this same court is both outer and inner—outer in relation to the gate, but inner, as we said earlier, in relation to the gates that are subsequently described.

4. The holy Church has two lives: one that it leads temporally, and another that it receives eternally; one in which it labors on earth, and another in which it is rewarded in heaven; one in which it gathers rewards, and another in which it already rejoices in the rewards it has received. In both lives it offers sacrifice.

Here it offers the sacrifice of compunction; there, the sacrifice of praise. Of the former sacrifice it is said: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit” (Ps. 50:19). Of the latter it is written: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings” (ibid., 21). Again he says: “That my glory may sing to you, and I may not be pierced with sorrow” (Ps. 29:13).

In both sacrifices flesh is offered. Here the offering of flesh is the mortification of the body; there the offering of flesh is the glory of resurrection in praise of God. There, then, flesh will be offered as a burnt offering when, transformed into eternal incorruption, it possesses nothing resistant and nothing mortal, because, wholly kindled together by the fires of love, it will remain in praise without end.

This inner gate, therefore—that is, the holy Church—should have its inner realities: that life, namely, which is still hidden from our eyes. It should have outside it an outer court—that is, the present life, in which every good thing is done so that one may arrive at the good without end.

5. Let there therefore be in the inner court, which is nevertheless outside the gate, the treasuries of the singers, because all the elect and perfect who still exist in mortal flesh are both within the bosom of the holy Church and still outside the secret joys of the inner life [Note: Suess. and Longip. read: “Let there therefore be the treasuries of the singers outside the inner gate and within the outer gates, inner and outer, because…”].

Let the treasuries of the singers be both inside and outside, because the hearts of the saints, who sing their desire to almighty God through the love of great ardor, are already inside and yet are not still fully inside. They have been placed in the bosom of the holy Church and already see spiritually what they ardently love within, yet they do not yet perfectly see what they love.

Let the treasuries therefore be in the inner court but outside the gate, so that they are already inside through desire but are not yet inside through complete realization. What are the treasuries of the singers except the holy desires of those who love? They preserve divine commandments in the mind as though they were treasures, and preserve them by singing, because they fulfill God’s commandments not out of fear but out of love [Note: The same witnesses, together with Laud., read “they preserve them.” “To sing” belongs to one who rejoices, and the precepts of sacred eloquence themselves become …].

The precepts of sacred eloquence become singable to them because they always act not from sadness but from desire.

Do you wish to hear the heart of the righteous as the treasury of a singer? “Your statutes were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118:54). We call God’s statutes the divine commandments, which make us righteous if they are fulfilled [Note: Laud. and Longip. add “by us.”]. They become songs for us in the place of our pilgrimage when, in this pilgrimage of the present life, we love those same commandments and fulfill them out of desire.

Hence the same Psalmist again reveals himself as coming from the treasury of the singers when he says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

### 6

The Lord’s mercy, by which sins are forgiven, ought also to be sung by the sinner—that is, it should be proclaimed and hoped for with joy. But who is so just that, when he recalls the Lord’s eternal judgment before the eyes of his mind, he does not tremble, **or rather** dares, hastens, and rejoices to come to the examination of so great a judge? Whoever he may be, he is great, because, by singing of the Lord’s mercy and judgment, he loves with the whole devotion of his mind the omnipotent God, who mercifully forgives his sins, and therefore does not fear His judgment. For perfect love, as the apostle John says, “casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). He sings of the judgment which he does not dread to enter.

Let that person’s mind, then, be a treasury of singers, so that through the riches of mercy which he receives he may proceed joyfully toward the judgment which he no longer fears. Let us see, if it pleases you, dearly beloved brothers, another treasury of a singer. Perhaps he too sings of judgment. For what does he say?

> “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:6–8).

Conscious of his labors, remembering the contest he endured and the faith he kept, he says that a crown has been laid up for him at the judgment, and hopes that it will be rendered to him on that day rather than simply bestowed as a gift. It is therefore plainly evident that he sings of the judgment which he desires to come. Hence he adds:

> “And not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing” (ibid., 8).

For no one loves the judge’s appearing except one who knows that he has a good case in the judgment. The hearts, therefore, of those who love the judge’s appearing are treasuries of singers, because through confidence in grace and life the righteous sing of the judgment which all the unrighteous fear.

**Notes:** All the English, Norman, and other manuscripts read *ac potius* (“and rather”); the printed editions read *an potius* (“or rather”), changing the sense. Norman manuscripts read *justi judicis* (“of the just judge”).

### 7

Your Charity remembers that in the preceding discussion we said that faith is signified by the eastern gate, hope by the northern gate, and charity by the southern gate. These treasuries, then, are said to be between the eastern and northern gates and to face the southern way, because the hearts of the saints, placed between faith and hope, face the southern way, since they burn with the fires of holy charity.

That eastern gate is also said to face the northern way, because through faith all our sins are forgiven in baptism; nevertheless, while we still live here, even after faith we often turn aside toward sins. The eastern gate, as it were, faces the northern way when our life, after receiving faith, still grows sluggish to some extent in the cold of guilt.

For who in this life can live without sin after faith, when John says:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

James agrees with these words, saying:

> “For we all offend in many things” (James 3:2).

If past sins have been forgiven upon receiving faith, while after faith we still turn toward sins, what confidence in righteousness or hope of enduring life can we have, except that now, while we are still between the eastern and northern gates, we should lift the eyes of our mind toward the southern way, so that, burning with holy charity, the warmth of love may free us from the guilt of sluggishness and coldness?

Let the treasuries, then, be between the eastern and northern gates; but, as has been said, let them turn their faces toward the southern way, so that, between the fact that we were born in faith and the fact that afterward, having fallen into sins, we presume upon the hope of mercy, we may exercise ourselves in the ardor of charity and direct the eyes of our hearts toward the place where we are kindled by the fires of love.

**Note:** The printed editions read “from the sluggishness of guilt,” against the English, Norman, Vallicellian, and other manuscripts.

### 8

The northern gate, however, may signify the Gentiles; the southern way, Judea; and the eastern gate, the Lord Himself. For the Gentiles are not inappropriately represented by the north, since they were held by the one who said:

**Note:** The printed editions wrongly read *possidet* (“holds”); the manuscripts and the sense require *possedit* (“held”).

> “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13).

The southern gate, likewise, is rightly understood as Judea, in which the spiritual fathers burned with heavenly love. One of them says:

> “Turn again our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south” (Psalm 125:4).

Although Judea possessed a carnal people in whom it bore, as it were, the cold of the north, nevertheless in its holy teachers and prophets it burned with the warmth of charity toward God and neighbor.

The eastern gate, however, appropriately signifies Him of whom it is written:

> “Behold, a man whose name is the East” (Zechariah 6:12),

and of whom Zechariah says:

> “The East from on high has visited us” (Luke 1:78).

Let the treasuries of singers therefore be on the side of the northern gate, because hearts of saints were not spiritually kindled only in Judea; even among the multitude of the Gentiles, hearts of saints converted to the mysteries of holy faith burn with love of the heavenly homeland, long for eternal joys, and sigh for fellowship with their fellow citizens in heaven. Yet they receive examples of this ardor, which they have received through the gift of the Holy Spirit, from the spiritual fathers of the Synagogue.

Hence these treasuries too, though placed on the northern side, turn their eyes toward the southern way. For behold, we have come from the Gentiles; but in that we are warmed by the love of the Holy Spirit, we look toward the fathers of Judea, who every day offer us examples of holy desire in their teachings.

### 9

Was he not burning, as it were, with the heat of the southern fervor, who cried out:

> “As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:2–3).

Again he says:

> “I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way, when you will come to me” (Psalm 100:2).

He too had been kindled by this ardor who said:

> “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

**Note:** Gemeticus, with the agreement of other Norman witnesses, reads “you dismiss,” which is supported by the Greek text.

Since, then, we have come from the Gentiles but set before ourselves the holy fathers of Judea as examples for imitation of divine love, we are, as it were, certain treasuries of singers on the side of the gate that faces the northern way, but we turn our faces toward the southern way.

### 10

It should also be noted that these same treasuries are said to be between the northern and eastern gates, because after the Lord’s incarnation a multitude of Gentiles came to the faith, and among the faithful peoples themselves, in the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, which they love from the depths of their hearts, the hearts of those who love rise upward.

**Notes:** Longipontanus reads *ex sacramentis* (“from the sacraments”). The printed editions read *sancti gazophylacia*; all our manuscripts have *sancta gazophylacia* (“holy treasuries”).

Let them therefore have holy treasuries, on one side the eastern gate and on the other the northern, because among the very mysteries of their redemption which they follow, and among certain carnal people whom they tolerate even within the holy Church, many advance toward God with a strong love, increase in virtues, seek the coming of the eternal Judge, and, between the things they love and those they endure, keep in their minds spiritual riches as certain treasuries.

Nor do they fail between the mysteries they love and certain contrary things they bear, because they turn their faces toward the southern way. For what do we endure that our fathers did not previously endure for the love of the Lord?

### 11

It should indeed be noted that the eastern gate is described as being between the southern and northern gates, because our Lord and Redeemer was born from Judea and immediately drew the Church from the Gentiles into His faith.

**Note:** The Vallicellian manuscript, with all Norman witnesses, reads *construxit* (“built [the Church]”) for *traxit* (“drew”). He appeared, as it were, between the southern gate and the northern one, because He came from the former and converted the latter to His service.

Hence it is also rightly said that this same eastern gate faces the northern way, because the Lord, having been born, abandoned the Synagogue and gathered the multitude of the Gentiles.

It should also be noted that when it was said of the treasuries, “And their faces toward the southern way,” the word “one” was added, so that we might clearly understand that there is not one way to the heavenly homeland for us who have come from the Gentiles and another for those fathers who were in Judea. Rather, this same one way belongs to us and to them, the way that leads us to eternal joys, the way that says to us through the Gospel:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Of this way the Psalmist says:

> “That we may know your way upon earth, your salvation among all nations” (Psalm 66:3).

What is called *Jesus* in Hebrew is called *salutaris*—“salvation” or “the saving one”—in Latin. The way is therefore known upon earth, because Jesus, God before the ages and made man at the end of the ages, has been manifested to the nations.

There is therefore one way both for those who are from the south and for those who face the northern side. **Note:** The manuscripts read *parte* (“side”); the printed editions read *porta* (“gate”). For the elect among Jews and Gentiles our Lord and Redeemer, having driven away the punishment of fear, has become for the Father a path of love and an aid to reaching Him.

What follows:

> **Verse 45.** “And he said to me: ‘This treasury which faces the southern way belongs to the priests who keep watch over the temple guard.’”

And immediately afterward:

> **Verse 46.** “Moreover, the treasury which faces the northern way shall belong to the priests who keep watch over the ministry of the altar.”

### 12

In these words of the prophet we must first inquire who the priests of the higher order are: whether those who keep watch over the temple guard, or those who serve at the altar. But because it is added shortly afterward, “The altar was before the face of the temple,” it is plainly shown that those who keep watch over the temple guard are the priests of the higher order, because they serve at the altar that is within. Those, however, who keep watch at the altar which is before the face of the temple are lower in rank, insofar as they serve in the outer places.

We must therefore inquire who the priests are who guard the temple, and who are said to keep watch over the ministry of the altar. The Teacher of the Gentiles, writing to the faithful, says:

> “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

Who, then, are the priests who guard the temple of God, except those who, by praying, preaching, and keeping watch through spiritual actions, defend the holy Church from the assaults of evil spirits, from the persuasions of the wicked, and from the errors of heretics?

Was he not a guardian of the temple who, recounting the labors of his suffering, says:

**Note:** Longipontanus reads *qui laboris sui passiones* (“who [recounts] the sufferings of his labor”).

> “In labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11:27)?

And immediately he adds:

> “Besides those external matters, there is my daily pressure, my concern for all the churches” (ibid., 28).

Consider, I ask, with how great a concern the guardian of the temple keeps watch. Behold, he endures immeasurable sufferings in himself and shares the concern of his heart with others. What virtue is this, I ask, to think more about the benefit of one’s neighbors than about one’s own affliction? Who could estimate it worthily? Who could weigh it adequately?

He labors, mourns, hungers, thirsts, suffers cold, fasts, and keeps watch; yet, while keeping watch, he thinks about the concern of all the churches. Behold, the most diligent guardian of the temple has been set before us as an example. Let whoever is able imitate him.

To suffer adversity for the truth, to devote good things to one’s neighbors, to keep watch over the care of souls, to investigate and restrain anyone from falling into unbelief, arrogance, plunder, or impurity: this is to guard the temple of God, that is, the holy Church.

### 13

There are also priests of the lower order who keep watch over the ministry of the altar.

**Note:** The Laudian manuscript reads *in auditorum malorum* (“of evil hearers”); Longipontanus reads *in auditorum suorum* (“of their hearers”). They carefully investigate the sins of offenders as an aid to their superiors, correct the lives of carnal people, and lead them so far that, through the lamentation of repentance, they burn the flesh in sacrifice which they had previously allowed to live in sin.

For those who preside over the holy churches cannot accomplish everything by themselves. While they are occupied with spiritual matters, if anything wicked or carnal is committed, they entrust it to others to examine and correct. Through these men, as the carnal life is corrected and those who are making progress advance to the practice of abstinence and prayer, the flesh is, as it were, already burned upon the altar, so that before the sight of the omnipotent Lord a sacrifice may give off its fragrance from the very place where guilt had previously been displeasing.

### 14

But a question arises in this matter. It was said above that the treasuries had their faces toward the southern way. How, then, is it now said that the treasury which faces the southern way belongs to the priests who keep watch over the temple guard, while the treasury which faces the northern way belongs to the priests who keep watch over the ministry of the altar?

If both faces extended toward the southern way, how is one now said to face the southern way and the other the northern way?

**Note:** Lauda, Longipontanus, and Rouen read *tenebant* (“held” or “turned”) for *tendebant* (“extended”).

From these words we understand that the treasury of the priests who keep watch over the temple guard had been placed so that it faced only the southern way. The treasury of the priests who keep watch over the ministry of the altar, however, was in the court in such a way that its face extended both toward the southern way and toward the northern way.

**Note:** Lyra and Longipontanus read: “so that the treasury of the priests…” Lauda reads: “and since the treasury…”

Thus it faced the southern way together with the treasury of the priests who keep watch over the temple guard; yet, apart from the treasury of those same priests, the treasury of the priests who keep watch over the ministry of the altar could see the northern way.

But what is this, dearly beloved brothers? What mystical meaning can we perceive in these words except what the spiritual hearer already understands from what was said earlier?

**Note:** Lyra reads *adjutor majoris ordinis queat intelligi* (“may be understood as an assistant of the higher order”); this was formerly also read at Rouen.

That meaning is: that the priests of the higher order, who keep watch over the temple guard, look only toward the southern way, because, occupied solely with spiritual pursuits, they always attend diligently to the things that belong to the love of God.

The priests of the lower order, however, who are responsible for examining the sins of offenders, also turn their eyes toward the northern way, so that they may see in the minds of sinners the coldness of sluggishness and, bringing it through words of correction to the groans of repentance, may burn it like flesh upon the Lord’s altar.

Let them also look with the great priests toward the southern way, because, insofar as it depends on themselves, they burn with the fire of charity and are kindled by the flames of love for God. But because they frequently correct the sins of offenders, they also turn their eyes back toward the northern way.

Of both orders of priests it is then added:

> **The same passage.** “These are the sons of Zadok, who approach from the sons of Levi to the Lord to minister to him.”

### 15

*Zadok* is rendered in Latin as “just.” But who is just except the one to whom it is said:

> “You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right” (Psalm 118:137)?

Who are the sons of the just one except those of whom it is written:

> “But to all who believed in him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12)?

**Note:** Lyra adds *vel receperunt eum* (“or received him”).

*Levi* is interpreted as “taken up.” But who has been taken up by the Lord except the faithful people, who through the mysteries of faith have been separated from the faithless?

All, therefore, who persistently devote themselves to spiritual actions are sons of the just one. And from the sons of the people who have been taken up they approach the Lord to minister to Him, because from among those faithful as well are chosen those who come to the service of the omnipotent God and devote themselves to heavenly pursuits for the instruction of the people.

### 16

But we must carefully inquire who those are who minister to the Lord. For not all who read, not all who preach, not all who give away their possessions, and not all who chastise the body through abstinence minister to the Lord.

Those who seek their own glory by reading and preaching, who desire to receive praise from people by giving away what they possess and by mortifying their bodies through abstinence, minister to themselves, not to the Lord.

Against this the Lord says through the Psalmist:

> “The one who walks in the blameless way was ministering to me” (Psalm 100:6).

For one who sets before himself the reward of earthly glory in the good work he performs has a blemish in his way. One who seeks to receive his reward in this world stains, before the sight of God, the appearance of his good work with the blemish of a corrupt intention.

Perhaps someone, devoted to the discipline of correction, burns with zeal and cuts away the faults of offenders; yet if he is led to do these things not by love of the omnipotent God but by his own zeal, he ministers in them to himself and not to the Lord.

Another, so as not to appear harsh, tolerates many things gently that are wickedly committed. Since he does not wish to appear strict for the Lord’s sake, through his zeal for gentleness he ministers to himself and not to the Lord.

It remains, therefore, that whether we labor in the ministry of the word, distribute our possessions to the needy, subdue the flesh through abstinence, are moved by zeal, or sometimes tolerate wrongdoing gently through patience, we must examine our intention with the utmost care, so that everything we do may be done out of zeal for the Lord and not for ourselves, lest in what we do we minister to ourselves rather than to the Lord.

For they ministered not to the Lord but to themselves of whom Paul said:

> “All seek the things that are their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21).

But Paul himself, together with the elect brothers, hastened not to minister to himself but to the Lord, both by living and by dying, saying:

> “None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we belong to the Lord” (Romans 14:7–8).

**Note:** Lauda and Longipontanus read: “whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we belong to the Lord.”

The saints neither live nor die for themselves. They do not live for themselves because in everything they do they long for spiritual gain, and by praying, preaching, and devoting themselves to holy works, they desire to multiply the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

They do not die for themselves because before the eyes of human beings they glorify God through their death, and by dying they hasten to reach Him.

Let us therefore consider in the death of the saints not how great their disgrace was among unbelievers, but how great the praise of the Lord increased in the hearts of the faithful. If they had sought their own praise, they would certainly have feared enduring so many insults in death.

**Note:** The printed editions read “none of them.” This differs from all the manuscripts.

But “none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself,” because they sought their own glory neither in living nor in dying.

Let us see whether that first shepherd of the Church, who did not live for himself, died for himself. Let John, his companion, be consulted, and let him speak from the Lord’s words concerning the death of that shepherd:

> “Now he said this to indicate by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:19).

He therefore did not die for himself who glorified God in his death.

Let us learn, then, my brothers, to examine our intention carefully in everything we do, and not to seek our own interests, if we wish to minister to the omnipotent God.

But because we have said that from the faithful people the sons of Zadok are taken up for the service of the omnipotent God—**the manuscripts read *assumi* (“to be taken up”), while the printed editions read *assumptos* (“taken up”)**— are there not many in that same people who are found to live perfectly according to the commandments of God? There certainly are, for it follows:

> **Verse 47.** “And he measured the court: one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in breadth, square.”

### 17

We have often said that length signifies the long-suffering of hope, while breadth signifies the expansiveness of charity. The meaning of the number one hundred, in which ten is multiplied by ten, as signifying the sum of perfection, has already been fully explained above (Homily 6, formerly 18, no. 16).

What, then, is the court of the spiritual building except the breadth of the faithful peoples? The long-suffering of hope and the breadth of charity are not empty in the hearts of the faithful, for faith works whatever it is able. Hence Paul says:

> “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

If, then, in the life of the faithful, according to a certain measure, the long-suffering of hope is perfect in each person, the breadth of charity is perfect, the certainty of faith is perfect, and the zeal for action is perfect, the court of the temple has one hundred cubits in a square.

In the measurement of a square, one side is not greater and another smaller; all four sides extend together over an equal space. So too, as long as we live in this life, we find these same virtues—faith, hope, charity, and action—to be equal in us.

Charity is therefore said to be greater than hope and faith because, **Note:** Longipontanus reads *major spei et fidei* (“greater than hope and faith”) for *major spe et fide*.

Because, after we arrive at the vision of our Creator, hope and faith pass away, but charity remains. For now, as much as we believe, so much we love; and as much as we love, so much we presume in hope.

The apostle John also testifies concerning faith and action, saying:

> “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

Knowledge of God belongs to faith; keeping the commandments belongs to action. When the time and opportunity for action are available, therefore, a person acts as much as he knows God. **Note:** The Évreux, Sées, Rouen, and Lyra witnesses read *tempus et locum operandi appetit* (“seeks the time and place for acting”) for *tempus et locus operandi suppetit* (“the time and place for acting are available”).

He and he shows that he knows God as much as he does good for God’s sake.

Let the virtues of the faithful peoples therefore be measured as a square. **Note:** Longipontanus reads *fideles populi* (“faithful peoples”) for *fidelis populi* (“of the faithful people”).

For everyone who is engaged in the practice of the active life believes as much as he hopes, loves, and acts; hopes as much as he believes, acts, and loves; loves as much as he believes, hopes, and acts; and acts as much as he believes, loves, and hopes.

**Note:** In Longipontanus: “as much as he hopes, loves, and acts; he hopes as much as he believes and loves.” The remainder is lacking. Before Gussanville, the printed editions read: “who is engaged in this exercise of life believes as much as he hopes and loves, and acts as much as he believes, loves, and hopes.” We have supplied what was lacking from the Norman and English manuscripts. The Laudian codex breaks off here.

Since, then, among the people of the holy Church there are many who are strong through faith, long-suffering through hope, expansive through charity, and effective through action, the court of the temple is measured as one hundred cubits in a square.

### 18

To speak somewhat about their virtues, we often see among them people prudent in understanding, strong in adversity, just in action, temperate in pleasures, and moderating themselves with measured judgment in every zeal.

While they possess prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—or, as some prefer to enumerate them, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—they have the measure of the spiritual court in a square.

For the very virtues which we said that good and faithful people possess are so squarely balanced that one does not exceed another.

Prudence is great; but if a person is less temperate from pleasures, less brave in dangers, and less just in actions, he is certainly less prudent.

Temperance is great; but if a person understands less clearly from what he should abstain, if he has less strength to endure adversity, and lowers his spirit in fear, or if through rashness he sometimes bursts into acts of injustice, he is less temperate.

Fortitude is great; but if a person understands less clearly which good things he should preserve and which evils he should resist, if he restrains himself less from the desire for pleasure and is overcome by delight, or if he holds less firmly to works of justice and is at times conquered by the domination of injustice, he is less brave.

Justice is great; but if a person distinguishes less carefully than he ought between just and unjust actions, if he restrains his heart less from the world’s delights, or if he strengthens himself less against adversity, he is less just.

**Note:** The Vallicellian and Norman manuscripts, with the older editions, read *si minus curam mundi delectatione temperat* (“if he tempers the care of the world less by pleasure”) for *si minus cor a mundi delectatione temperat* (“if he restrains his heart less from the world’s delight”).

Let the life of perfect believers therefore be measured as a square, and let one side of the spiritual court be as great as each of the others. Each person is prudent insofar as he is temperate, brave, and just; temperate insofar as he is prudent, brave, and just; brave insofar as he is prudent, temperate, and just; and just insofar as he is prudent, temperate, and brave.

Yet there are many among them who still live in a carnal manner. Even if they perhaps do not know letters and cannot read the commandments of God, certainly they see good things in the conduct of many faithful people that they can imitate.

Behold, the voices of the holy Gospel and of the apostles resound in the Church; behold, examples of those who live well are presented daily before the eyes of all. Nor will they be able to say in excuse, “We did not see what we ought to imitate.”

Hence it follows:

> **The same passage.** “And the altar before the face of the temple.”

### 19

What is the temple except the faithful people? As the apostle Paul says to the disciples:

> “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

And what is the altar of God except the mind of those who live well? They wash away the stains of their sins with tears, mortify the flesh through abstinence, do not entangle themselves in any activities of this world, give what they possess to those in need, and do not desire to possess what they do not have.

Their heart is therefore rightly called the altar of God, where the fire of remorse burns and the flesh is consumed.

And do we not, dearly beloved brothers, see such people every day in this holy faithful people, as though in the court of the temple?

**Note:** The Vallicellian manuscript reads *fieri populo* (“in the people that is becoming”) for *fideli populo* (“in the faithful people”). Do we not continually behold their life set before us as an example?

The altar is before the face of the temple when many are placed in the sight of the holy Church who, mindful of eternal judgment, daily slaughter themselves as a sacrifice to God in the grief of repentance.

As was said above, they chastise their bodies so that they may fulfill what is said through the Teacher of the Gentiles:

> “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).

A victim is killed so that it may be offered. But a living sacrifice is a body afflicted for the Lord. It is called both a sacrifice and living, because it lives in virtues and has been slain by vices.

It is a sacrifice because it has already died to this world by the death of its wicked actions; it is living because it performs every good work of which it is capable.

### 20

But because, under the name of the altar, the discussion has introduced the flame of remorse, I think it necessary to show what varieties of remorse there are.

One kind of remorse arises through fear, another through love, because it is one thing to flee punishments and another to desire rewards.

Hence the Law also commands that two altars be made in the tabernacle: one outside and another inside; one in the court and another before the ark; one covered with bronze and another clothed with gold. On the bronze altar, flesh is burned; on the golden altar, incense is kindled (Exodus 39:37–38; 40:5 and following).

What is this, dearly beloved brothers—that flesh is burned outside and incense within—except what we see every day: that there are two kinds of remorse?

**Note:** In Gemeticus and other Norman manuscripts, one member of the sentence is placed before the other. Some still weep through fear, while others already afflict themselves in lamentation through love.

For many, mindful of their sins, afflict themselves with daily tears while fearing eternal punishments. They mourn the evils they have committed and burn the vices with the fire of remorse whose suggestions they still endure in their hearts.

What are these people except a bronze altar on which flesh burns, because they still mourn carnal works committed by them?

### 21

Others, however, freed from carnal vices or made secure through long weeping, burn with the flame of love in the tears of remorse. They set before the eyes of their hearts the rewards of the heavenly homeland and already long to be among the citizens above.

Service appears harsh to them, as does the length of their pilgrimage. They desire to see the King in His beauty and do not cease to weep daily out of love for Him (Isaiah 33:17).

What are these people except a golden altar, in whose heart incense has been kindled, because virtues burn there?

It is rightly said of this same altar that it is placed before the veil of the ark in the Holy of Holies. The ark of the covenant has become for us the one of whom we know it is written:

> “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

The ark within the veil is our Redeemer in heaven. The golden altar in which incense is kindled before the veil is the hearts of the saints.

**Note:** This wording is restored on the authority and grounds of the manuscripts. The printed editions read *ante velum, quia sanctorum corda* (“before the veil, because [it is] the hearts of the saints”), a reading that appears to make Christ both ark and altar, contrary to Gregory’s meaning: Christ is the ark, whereas the hearts of the faithful burning with charity are the golden altar. When these hearts have been set ablaze with great virtues in the love of God, they burn through holy desire for the one whom they cannot yet see with unveiled face.

There is a veil between the ark and the altar, because the obstacle of our corruption, which still separates us from the vision of God, has not been removed. But as long as we are before the veil, we ought to burn like incense with the flame of love.

Through the tears of remorse we must seek nothing earthly, nothing transitory.

**Note:** The printed editions read, contrary to the evidence of all our manuscripts, “He alone fulfills our desire.” The following words are also printed as “so that we may be gathered together in mind.”

He alone should be sufficient for us who made all things. Let us transcend all things through desire, so that we may gather our mind into unity.

No longer kindled by fear of punishments or by the memory of vices, but set ablaze by the flame of love, let us burn in tears with the fragrance of virtues.

### 22

This prayer of the elect was already foreseen when it was said in praise of the bride:

> “Who is this who comes up through the desert like a slender column of smoke from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song of Songs 3:6).

The holy Church of the elect, when she rises from this world in holy prayers with ardent love, ascends through the desert which she abandons.

He adds how she ascends:

> “Like a slender column of smoke from the perfumes” (ibid.).

Smoke arises from incense, as the Psalmist says:

> “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140:2).

Smoke commonly brings tears. Thus smoke from perfumes is the remorse of prayer conceived from the virtues of love.

Yet this prayer is called a slender column of smoke because, while it asks only for heavenly things, it advances so directly that it does not turn back to seek earthly and temporal things.

**Note:** Longipontanus reads *appetendo, pro terreno studio minime reflectatur* (“by desiring, it is not turned aside for an earthly pursuit”) for *petenda minime reflectatur* (“it does not turn back to seek [such things]”).

It should also be noted that it is called not a column but a slender column, because sometimes, in the ardor of remorse, the power of love is so subtle that even the mind itself, which has deserved to possess it after being enlightened, cannot comprehend it.

### 23

It is rightly said, “of myrrh and frankincense.” By the Law, frankincense is burned in sacrifice to the Lord. With myrrh, dead bodies are embalmed so that they may not be corrupted by worms.

Those, therefore, offer a sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense who afflict the flesh so that the vices of corruption may not dominate them, and who kindle before the Lord the fragrant sacrifice of their love, presenting themselves to God in holy virtues.

Hence it is added there:

> “And every powder of the perfumer.”

The powder of the perfumer is the virtue of one who acts well. It should be noted that the virtues of those who act well are called not perfumes but powders.

When we perform any good deed, we offer perfumes. But when we reconsider even the good things we have done and, so that there may be nothing sinister in them, examine them through the judgment of reflection, we make, as it were, powder from perfumes, so that through discernment and love we may kindle our prayer to the Lord with greater subtlety.

**Note:** Longipontanus adds: “Myrrh, therefore, because they torment themselves and, by tormenting themselves, preserve themselves from vices. Frankincense, because they love the vision of God, toward which they burn inwardly to attain, and they themselves…” [the note is incomplete].

24. Behold, these matters, insofar as by God’s generosity we have been able, we have examined before you, dearest brothers. Let no one blame me if after this discourse I cease [Note: [Col. 1072D] Longipontanus: “if after this I cease from speaking.”], because, as you all see, our tribulations have increased: on every side we are surrounded by swords [Note: [Col. 1072D] Ebroicensis: “hemmed in on every side.”], and on every side we fear the imminent danger of death. Some return to us with their hands severed; others are reported captured, others killed (John the Deacon, bk. IV, ch. 67). Now I am compelled to restrain my tongue from exposition, because “my soul is weary of my life” (Job 10:1). Let no one now demand from me study of sacred eloquence, because “my harp is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep” (ibid., 30:31). The eye of my heart is no longer watchful in examining mysteries, because “my soul has slumbered from weariness” (Ps. 118:28). Reading is now less sweet to my spirit, because “I have forgotten to eat my bread because of the voice of my groaning” (Ps. 101:5). But for one who is not permitted to live, how can it be fitting to speak of the mystical meanings of Sacred Scripture? And when I am compelled daily to drink bitter things, when can I offer sweet ones?

What, then, remains except that amid the scourges we suffer because of our sins, we give thanks with tears? For he who created us has also become our father through the spirit of adoption that he gave us. At times he nourishes his children with bread; at times he corrects them with a scourge, because through pains and gifts [Note: [Col. 1072D] Normanus: “through countless pains.” Vallicellianus: “through countless pains and wounds.”] he trains them for the everlasting inheritance.

Therefore, glory be to our almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILIES ON THE GOSPELS

[Col. 1071]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK

1431 I. We are prevented from prefacing the following homilies at greater length by the letter of Saint Gregory placed before them in lieu of a preface; in it nearly everything worth knowing about them is explained. We have placed these homilies after the homilies on Ezekiel for the same reason that, in the sequence of the Sacred Scriptures, the Gospels and the books belonging to the New Testament are placed after the books of the Old Testament. Otherwise, that at least some of them were delivered before the holy Doctor began to expound the prophet Ezekiel to the people will immediately be clear to anyone who reads the first one. Indeed, as an excellent shepherd, wishing to benefit those entrusted to him both by word and by example, as soon as he ascended the apostolic chair he considered himself entitled to no respite from preaching the divine word, even though he was afflicted by continual illnesses and distracted by countless cares.

II. In his letter to Secundinus, which will shortly be placed below, our humble Ecclesiastes lamented with still more remarkable humility that these homilies had immediately been received with remarkable eagerness. How highly they have always been esteemed is clear from the fact that all of them—perhaps with one or two exceptions—were long ago incorporated into the divine offices, above the homilies of the other holy Fathers. And rightly so, since in them, after the literal sense has first been briefly explained, there flows an exceedingly rich abundance of observations bearing on morals, many of which are truly worthy of being written in letters of gold. Would that they might be engraved and carved into human hearts through continual reading and meditation! We once selected and discussed some of them in the French Life of the holy Doctor, bk. IV, final chapter, no. 13.

III. Nor are Christian morals the only things instructed by these homilies; the doctrines of the faith are also confirmed, and Christians are forearmed against future heretics. The mystery of the Incarnation is repeatedly defended against the mutually opposed and conflicting errors of the Nestorians and Eutychians, but especially in Homily 38, no. 3. Nearly everything customarily taught to Christians in schools concerning angels is drawn from Homily 38, nos. 7–15. The necessity of confession and priestly absolution is treated at length in Homily 26, nos. 5 and 6, and also in Homily 40, no. 2; but above all, Homily 21 cuts down the impious doctrine of Calvin, who asserted that Christ the Lord suffered the punishments of the damned.

These are Calvin’s words, *Institutes*, bk. II, ch. 16, § 10, where he proposes to prove that Jesus Christ was subjected in the place of criminals as their sponsor and surety, and therefore as though he himself were guilty: “so that we may know,” he says, “that not only was Christ’s body delivered as the price of redemption, but that there was another greater and more excellent price, namely, that he endured the dreadful torments in his soul of a condemned—and, I shudder to repeat it, lost—man.” This insulting assertion concerning Christ, the conqueror of hell and death, is most powerfully refuted by our Gregory, namely in Homily 21, no. 7, where, by presenting Samson as a type, he teaches that the Lord emerged from hell not only free and victorious but also destroyed the very gates of hell.

IV. Through these and many other matters, the cause of the Church is wonderfully aided against those who attack it as heterodox. It should not be omitted that the Gospel sections expounded here by Gregory are the same passages that were already being read on the prescribed days during the solemn celebration of Mass, according to established custom, and that are still recited on nearly those same days. Hence it is clear how tenacious the Roman Church is in preserving its rites. From this we may also establish the antiquity of processions and stations, as well as of public supplications in basilicas and the cemeteries of the martyrs. For, as John the Deacon observed, bk. II of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, ch. 18, and bk. IV, ch. 74, during those processions or stations the most vigilant shepherd either delivered homilies on the Gospels himself or dictated them to be delivered.

V. There is, moreover, some controversy among scholars concerning the assignment of these stations, and the manuscript codices do not agree everywhere. The Lateran Codex nowhere designates the basilica of Saint John the Baptist called Constantinian, although it occurs very frequently in other codices of the highest quality, especially in the Corbeiensis Germanensis and the Belvacensis-Bigotianus, but most particularly in the Codex of the Queen of Sweden. In that codex, whenever the Lateran Codex or others read “the basilica of the Holy Savior called Constantinian,” the name of Saint John the Baptist appears instead.
