John Fronto also maintains, in his preliminary notes to the Roman calendar, p. 80, that there was no Constantinian basilica other than the Church of the Holy Savior; but the learned man proves this least convincingly. For his assertion that Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Life of Pope Leo*, who occupied the see in the year 595, mentions the Church of Saint John the Baptist situated beside the Lateran patriarchate, but does not call it Constantinian, whereas he always calls the basilica of the Holy Savior Constantinian, is weak. 1432 What force, then, does this argument have when it denies the clear and indisputable testimony of so many manuscripts—those of Belvacensis, Bigotianus, Carnotensis, Gemeticensis, the Queen of Sweden, and above all Corbeiensis Germanensis, which is not later in date than Anastasius?

In this codex, Homily 16, on the Gospel passage “Jesus was led into the desert,” is said to have been delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint John called Constantinian. The same designation is prefixed to Homilies 22, 25, and 39.

VI. John Fronto adds that the basilica of Saint John the Baptist was a monastery. Now, in the oratories of monasteries, stations and gatherings of the people were not formerly held. The learned man is refuted by Gregory’s own authority, since Gregory assigns the church of Saint John the Baptist—not calling it an oratory—as the place to which the clergy were to assemble and from which the litany was to proceed for the sevenfold litany, or supplication and procession. This is also confirmed by the testimony of John the Deacon, bk. I, chs. 41 and 42.

Furthermore, the basilica of Saint Pancratius was a station in Saint Gregory’s time, as is clear from Homily 27, delivered there; and that the station continued there afterward is established by ancient records of the Church. The Church of Saint Pancratius, which had previously been held by priests, was transferred to monks after the priests had been expelled because of their carelessness and negligence, by command of the most holy pope, as is made clear by Letter 18 of book formerly III, now IV, indiction 12.

Finally, Homily 5 was delivered in the basilica of the Apostle Saint Andrew, on his feast day, namely in the church of the monastery that Gregory himself had founded. Therefore, that rule which, out of concern for the quiet of monks, forbade stations and gatherings of the people in their churches admitted many exceptions.

VII. In the Roman calendar published by John Fronto, the stations do not everywhere appear to be assigned in the same way as in the Gregorian homilies, and this is not surprising. First, according to John Fronto’s judgment, that calendar was written only in the eighth century, around the year 731—that is, a full century and almost a half after Gregory’s homilies on the Gospels had been delivered. During so long an interval, therefore, it was easy for something concerning the stations to have been changed.

Second, the collection of homilies indicates the place where each homily was delivered, while the calendar indicates the place of the station. Nothing, however, compels us to say that the sermon was always delivered at the place of the station. What prevents us from believing that the sermon was sometimes delivered before the procession, especially in summer?

VIII. Having resolved all the difficulties that could be raised either from the Roman calendar or from the observations of its editor, we must now append a few remarks concerning this latest edition of the praised homilies. Although in the ancient manuscripts and older printed editions the forty homilies are contained in one and the same book, we nevertheless decided to follow Gregory himself, who says in his letter to Secundinus:

“I also took care to place the same homilies, in the order in which they were delivered, in two codices, so that the first twenty, which were dictated, and the later twenty, which were spoken before my eyes, might be distinguished in separate volumes.”

Although their order is not the same in our manuscripts—for the three codices, namely the Lateran, Corbeiensis, and Queen of Sweden, differ both from the others and from one another—since all the others, and those of greater antiquity, agree, we had them printed in the same sequence in which they had always previously been printed.

We have placed shorter notes beneath the columns. They contain either variant readings, or the reasons for the restorations we have made—many of them substantial and not to be disregarded—or explanations of certain sentences of Saint Gregory; and whenever some difficulty arose, we have untangled it.

IX. To mention a few examples from the passages we have corrected: in Homily 2 there are four. In no. 1: “For the human race is blind,” instead of “blind” in the neuter form, and so forth. In no. 4: “but what of these things?” instead of “but who still?” In no. 5: “we fix Jesus in the mind,” instead of “we fix Jesus.” Finally, in no. 7: “saved in mind,” instead of “illumined in mind.”

In Homily 3, no. 3, we restored “obtained” instead of “endured”; and in no. 4, “we strike ourselves against the air of the curse,” instead of “we strike the injury of the curse against the air of the one who curses,” which the editors invented without any reason.

In Homily 5, no. 4, we now read “to desire nothing ever, and to possess nothing even without desire,” where previously we read “to desire nothing ever, and to possess nothing even with desire,” which produced a corrupt sense.

In Homily 6, no. 2, we restored “nor did anyone’s slander make him harsh in anger,” instead of “nor did the anger of anyone’s slander make him harsh.” In no. 3, “with expression,” instead of “with holiness.” In the same place, “clothed in woven hairs,” instead of “in woven garments of hair,” which is corruptly read in the Gussanvian edition.

In Homily 7, no. 3, “does not wash” instead of “does not heal”; and “was begotten by the Father outside time,” instead of “was begotten by the Father before the ages without a mother.” In no. 4, the Gussanvian edition reads “to possess the Israelite people by contradiction,” instead of “to possess them thereafter without any contradiction.”

In Homily 9, no. 3, at the end, we supplied a great lacuna in the Gussanvian, Vatican, and other more recent editions. We call “more recent editions” those prepared from the middle of the sixteenth century onward.

In Homily 11, no. 3, we restored “led” instead of “unconquered.” It would be excessive to pursue the rest. Of the many passages we have healed, it will therefore suffice to add a single one: namely, Homily 21, from whose corruption an error against the divinity of Christ appears to have arisen.

In no. 4, the printed editions formerly read: “He is not here”—that is, Christ—“it is said, through the presence of majesty.” But from the manuscripts we must read, according to the sound teaching of the Church: “He is not here,” it is said, “through the presence of the flesh, yet he will nowhere be absent through the presence of majesty.”

Hence, if I am not mistaken, it is clear that the editions already issued necessarily had to be reviewed again by us and corrected from the manuscript codices. Here, then, is a list of the codices we used.

X. A very ancient parchment codex of the archive of the Constantinian basilica of the Holy Savior at the Lateran, marked 1674.

The Corbeiensis Codex, now kept in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which we therefore call Corbeiensis Germanensis, marked 166. It is almost certain from the form of its script that it was written at least in the ninth century. In the same library we consulted two other ancient codices, which we shall call either Sangermanenses or simply Germani. We compared the codex of the Royal Library with the printed editions only at certain places, not throughout.

The Codex of the Church of Beauvais appears to have been written at the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century. At the end are poems copied in a more recent hand concerning Roger, the recently deceased bishop, who governed the Church of Beauvais at the end of the tenth and the beginning of the eleventh century.

The Corbeiensis Codex numbered 163 rivals all the foregoing in antiquity.

The Turonian Codex, a distinguished codex of the Church of Saint Martin and no later in age, contains only the first twenty homilies.

The Codex of the Queen of Sweden, marked 43.

Two codices of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, six hundred years old.

The Bigotian Codex is five hundred years old.

The Gemeticensis Codex appears to be no less ancient. Two other codices of that celebrated monastery are scarcely three hundred years old. The first often agrees with the older codex; the second does not.

The codex of the Cistercian monastery of Vallis Clara.

The codex of the monastery of Longpont, of the same order.

To these should be added four English copies, whose variant readings were supplied by Thomas James.

We also thought it appropriate to use the assistance of old editions: the Antwerp edition of 1509; the Rouen edition printed by François Regnaut—which is erroneously said to have been produced in 1421—the Paris editions of 1518 and 1571, and finally other more recent editions.

XI. At the end we thought it fitting to add a sermon delivered by Saint Gregory on mortality—as it is entitled in the old parchments—after he had been elected to the Roman see. It had already been published among the Gregorian letters, at the very beginning of the book formerly XI, now XIII, indiction 6; in the *Life of the same holy Doctor* by John the Deacon, bk. I, chs. 41 and 42; and among the works of Gregory of Tours, who records this discourse in bk. X of his *History*, ch. 1.

We have reviewed and compared it anew with two codices of the Bigotian Library at Rouen: one containing the forty homilies on the Gospels, and the other containing the *Life of Saint Gregory* written by John the Deacon; with one codex of Utica, or Saint-Evroult, of the same *Life*; and finally with Corbeiensis Germanensis of the forty homilies on the Gospels, at whose end this sermon has been placed.

It also exists in certain manuscript codices of the Register before all the letters, namely in two Tellerian codices, now in the Royal Library, and in the Colbertine Codex.

Make use now of our labor, devout reader, and remember gratefully to pray for us who have labored in this field.

[Col. 1075]

# THE TWO BOOKS OF THE FORTY HOMILIES ON THE GOSPELS OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Note: [Col. 1075A] The title varies in the manuscript codices. In most of them it reads: “Here begins the book of the homilies of the blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, on various Gospel readings.”] (C, S)

## Preface: TO SECUNDINUS, BISHOP OF TAUROMENIUM

[Col. 1075A] 1434 To the most reverend and holy brother Secundinus, bishop [Note: [Col. 1075A] This is a different Secundinus from the servant of God to whom Gregory sent two codices of homilies, according to the letter formerly 54 of book formerly VII, indiction 11, now book IX, letter 52. John the Deacon asserts that the homilies on the Gospels were sent to Secundus or Secundinus, bk. IV, ch. 74. In the Chartres Codex it reads “To Father Secundinus.” Numerous letters of Saint Gregory to this bishop of Sicily survive.], Gregory, servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 1076A] We shall discuss this title in the notes to the letters.]

During the solemn celebrations of Mass, I expounded forty readings from the holy Gospel, selected from those customarily read on appointed days in this Church. The exposition of some of them, having been dictated, was read aloud by a notary while the people were present; but I myself delivered the explanation of others before the people, and it was taken down just as I spoke.

Certain brothers, however, burning with zeal for the sacred word, transferred what I had said before I had brought it to the intended form by careful correction. I might rightly compare them to famished people who are eager to eat their food [Col. 1077A] [Note: [Col. 1077A] Corbeiensis Germanensis and most others: “before the food has been more fully digested.”] before it has been fully cooked.

Now, when the passage was written, “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil” (Matt. 4), I first expounded it as though under a certain ambiguity, but afterward corrected that same uncertainty by a definite explanation [Note: [Col. 1077A] The first Gemeticensis and the second Chartres Codex: “by a clarification.”]. 1435 I also took care to place these same homilies in the order in which they were delivered, in two codices, so that the first twenty, [Note: [Col. 1077A] Corbeiensis Germanensis, the third Gemeticensis, the old Antwerp edition of 1509, and the Paris edition of 1518: “which were dictated.”] which were dictated, and the later twenty, which were spoken before my eyes, might be distinguished in separate volumes.

The fact that some homilies have been placed first even though they occur later in the Gospel, while others have been placed later even though they are found earlier in the evangelist’s writing, should in no way trouble your Fraternity, because just as they were delivered by me at different times [Note: [Col. 1078A] Thus most manuscripts and old editions; not “dictated,” as it is read in another edition.], so they were also entered by the shorthand writers in the codices.

Therefore, if your Fraternity, always attentive to sacred readings, finds the aforementioned passage of the Gospel presented ambiguously, or discovers that these same homilies have not been arranged in the manner I described, know that they have remained uncorrected, and correct them according to the copies that I have taken pains to send through the present bearer. Do not permit them in any way to remain uncorrected.

The published copies are kept in the archive of our holy Church, so that any who happen to be far from your Fraternity may find here a source from which to become more certain about those matters that have been corrected.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1077]

## HOMILY ONE

[Col. 1077B]

Delivered to the people [Note: [Col. 1077D] Thus the Corbeiensis Germanensis, Bigotianus, the first two Gemeticenses, and all editions. In the Lateran Codex, marked 1674, it reads: “in the Basilica of Saint Mary at the Crib.” In the Codex of the Queen of Sweden and in many manuscripts, no place is assigned where this homily was delivered.] in the basilica of the Apostle Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1077D] This is found only in the second Gemeticensis; nevertheless we have retained it because it is also found in the editions, including the older ones.], on the Second Sunday of the Advent of the Lord.

### GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO LUKE 21:25–32

At that time [Note: [Col. 1077D] The first Gemeticensis: “The Lord Jesus said.” The Bigotianus: “The Lord Jesus Christ said.”], Jesus said to his disciples:

“There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves; people will wither from fear and expectation of what is about to come upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven [Note: [Col. 1077D] Belvacensis, Corbeiensis, Bigotianus, and Corbeiensis Germanensis: “will be shaken.”] will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds [Note: [Col. 1078D] Corbeiensis Germanensis and Bigotianus: “in the clouds of heaven.”] with great power and majesty.

“But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

And he told them a parable:

“Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they already put forth fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. Amen, I say to you: This generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

1436 1. Our Lord and Redeemer, dearest brothers, desiring to find us prepared, announces what evils will follow upon the aging world, so that he may restrain us from loving it. He makes known how many blows will precede its approaching end [Note: [Col. 1078D] The second Chartres Codex: “as its end approaches.”], so that if we do not wish to fear God in tranquillity, we may at least, worn down by the blows, fear his judgment when it is near.

For shortly before this reading from the holy Gospel, which your Fraternity has just heard, the Lord said: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences, and famines” (Luke 21:10). After inserting certain intervening words, he added what you have just heard:

“There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves.” [Note: [Col. 1078D] Corbeiensis Germanensis, Belvacensis, and many others: “and there will be.”]

Of all these things, some we already see accomplished, while we fear that others are shortly to come. For we see nation rising against nation, and their distress pressing upon the earth, more in our own times [Note: [Col. 1078D] Corbeiensis Germanensis, Corbeiensis, the first Gemeticensis, and the English copies: “in our tribulations.”] than we read in the books. How frequently we have heard from other parts of the world that earthquakes have overthrown innumerable cities [Note: [Col. 1078D] The editions: “overthrow,” against the manuscripts.]. We suffer pestilences without cessation.

As for signs in the sun, moon, and stars, we do not yet clearly see them, but because these too are not far off, we infer their approach from the very alteration of the air. Although, before Italy was handed over to be struck by the sword of the pagans, we saw fiery armies in the sky and the blood of the human race, which afterward was poured out, flashing [Note: [Col. 1078D] Thus Corbeiensis Germanensis and most others. Belvacensis and the second Chartres Codex: “flashing.” The editions: “flashing things.”].

But no new confusion of the sea and the waves has yet arisen. Since many of the things foretold have already been fulfilled, there is no doubt that the few remaining things will also follow, because the fulfillment of past events is the certainty of what is to come.

1437 2. We say these things, dearest brothers, so that your minds may awaken to the pursuit of vigilance, lest they grow sluggish through security or grow weak through ignorance; but so that fear may always trouble them and concern for good works strengthen them, weighing what follows in the voice of our Redeemer:

“People will wither from fear and expectation of what is about to come upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven will be shaken.”

What else does the Lord call the powers of heaven than angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers? At the coming of the strict Judge, these will then appear visibly to our eyes, so that they may then demand strictly from us what the invisible Creator now bears patiently in us.

Then it is added:

“And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds [Note: [Col. 1079D] The Gemeticensis and Vallicellianus: “in power.”] with great power and majesty.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “They will see in power and majesty the one whom, when he was placed in humility, they refused to hear, so that they may then feel his power all the more strictly because now they do not bend the neck of their hearts to his patience.”

3. But because these words were spoken against the reprobate, the discourse immediately turns to the consolation of the elect. For it continues:

“But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

It is as though the Truth plainly admonished his elect, saying: “When the wounds of the world multiply, when the terror of judgment is revealed through the shaking of the powers, lift up your heads—that is, gladden your hearts—because, while the world whose friends you are not is coming to an end, the redemption that you sought is drawing near.”

In Sacred Scripture, the head is often used for the mind, because just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind. [Note: [Col. 1079D] The two Chartres Codices and the first two Gemeticenses: “Therefore to lift up the head is to lift up the mind.”] To lift up our heads, therefore, is to raise our minds toward the joys of our heavenly homeland.

Those who love God are commanded to rejoice and be glad at the end of the world, because they will soon find the one whom they love, while the one whom they did not love is passing away. For far be it from us [Note: [Col. 1079D] Belvacensis and the third Gemeticensis: “lest the faithful person.” Shortly afterward the second Gemeticensis has “through persecutions” instead of “through blows.”] that any faithful person who desires to see God should mourn over the blows inflicted upon the world, since he knows that the world will be brought to an end by those very blows.

For it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James 4:4). Therefore, whoever does not rejoice when the end of the world approaches shows himself to be its friend, and by this is proved to be an enemy of God.

But far be this from the hearts of the faithful; far be it from those who both believe by faith that another life exists and love it through their works. To mourn at the destruction of the world belongs to those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of it, who do not seek the life to come, who do not even suspect that it exists.

But we, who have come to know the eternal joys of our heavenly homeland, ought to hasten toward them as quickly as possible. We should desire to depart sooner and reach it by the shorter road. For what evils does the world not endure? What sadness, what adversity, does not distress us? What is mortal life except a road?

And consider, my brothers, how strange it is to grow weary from the labor of the road and yet not wish that the same road should end.

That the world ought to be trampled underfoot and despised, our Redeemer demonstrates by a well-chosen comparison when he immediately adds:

“Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they already put forth fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Just as the nearness of summer is recognized from the fruit of the trees, so the nearness of the kingdom of God is recognized from the ruin of the world.”

These words plainly show that the fruit of the world is ruin. For it grows in order to fall. [Note: [Col. 1080D] Nearly all editions, supported by the third Gemeticensis, add: “It falls in order to sprout.”] It sprouts in order to consume in disasters whatever it has caused to sprout.

The kingdom of God is rightly compared to summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away, and the days of life shine with the brightness of the eternal sun.

4. All these things are confirmed with great certainty when the following sentence is added:

“Amen, I say to you: This generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

Nothing in the nature of bodily things is more enduring than heaven and earth; yet nothing in the nature of things passes more quickly than speech. For words, so long as they are incomplete, are not words; but when they have been completed, they no longer exist at all, since they can be completed only by passing away.

He therefore says:

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Everything that among you appears enduring does not endure unto eternity without change; and everything that is seen to pass away in my presence is held firm and without passing away, because my word, which passes away, expresses judgments that remain without change.”

5. Behold, my brothers, we now see what we used to hear. The world is pressed daily by new and increasing evils. You see how few remain from that countless multitude; and yet even now sudden disasters press upon us daily, and new and unforeseen calamities afflict us.

For just as in youth the body flourishes: the chest remains strong and sound, the neck muscular, the lungs full; but in the years of old age the stature bends, the dried-up neck droops, the chest is oppressed by frequent sighs, strength fails, and breath interrupts the words of the speaker [Note: [Col. 1080D] Turonianus: “the breath cuts off the speaker.”]. Even if sickness is absent, health itself is often an illness to the senses.

So the world, in its earlier years, flourished as though in youth. It was strong for multiplying the human race, vigorous in the health of its bodies, rich in the abundance of its possessions. But now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though approaching death, is pressed by troubles that are increasing [Note: [Col. 1080D] Corbeiensis Germanensis, Corbeiensis, Bigotianus, and the first two Gemeticenses: “with increasing troubles.” Longpontanus: “with troubles increasing more frequently.” The Antwerp edition agrees.].

Therefore, my brothers, do not love what you see cannot stand for long. Lay in your hearts the apostolic commandments by which he admonishes us, saying:

“Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15).

Just three days ago, brothers, you learned that ancient groves were uprooted by a sudden whirlwind, houses destroyed, and churches overturned from their foundations. How many people, healthy and unharmed at evening, thought they would carry out some task on the following day, and yet that same night died a sudden death, caught in the snare of the ruin?

6. But we must consider, beloved, that in order to bring these things about, the invisible Judge moved the breath of a very light wind, raised a storm from a single cloud, and overthrew the earth, shaking the foundations of so many buildings that were about to fall.

What, then, will this Judge do when he comes in person and his anger burns in punishment of sinners, if he cannot be endured when he strikes us through a very thin cloud? What flesh will stand in the presence of his anger if, merely by stirring the wind, he overthrew the earth, agitated the air, and toppled so many buildings?

Considering the severity of the coming Judge, Paul says: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). The Psalmist expresses the same thing, saying:

“God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him” (Ps. 49:3). [Note: [Col. 1081D] Corbeiensis and the two Gemeticenses: “Our God will come manifestly.”]

A storm and fire accompany the severity of so great a justice, because the storm examines those whom the fire consumes [Note: [Col. 1081D] Thus the Turonianus, together with ten other manuscripts. The editions have: “the severity of so great a judgment.”].

Place that day, therefore, dearest brothers, before your eyes, and whatever now seems grievous becomes light in comparison with it. For concerning that day the prophet says:

“The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and very swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the mighty man will be troubled. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and trumpet blast” (Zeph. 1:14ff.).

Concerning this day the Lord again says through the prophet:

“Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Hag. 2:22).

Behold, as we said, he shook the air, and the earth did not remain firm. Who, then, will endure when he shakes heaven?

What else should we call the terrors that we see but heralds of the anger that is to come? Hence we must consider that these tribulations differ from that final tribulation only as the person of a herald differs from the power of the Judge.

Think, therefore, dearest brothers, with complete attention upon that day; correct your life, [Note: [Col. 1081D] The first Chartres Codex: “change your minds.”] change your conduct, overcome temptations to evil by resisting them, and punish sins already committed with tears. You will one day see the coming of the eternal Judge with greater security in proportion as you now anticipate his severity by fearing it [Note: [Col. 1081D] In nearly all manuscripts the homily ends with these words: “by fearing it you anticipate it.” The old editions agree. Other copies add: “with the Lord’s help,” etc. The Belvacensis has: “with the help of him who lives and reigns, God.” The two first Gemeticenses have: “you reach it, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.”].

## HOMILY II

[Col. 1081D]

Delivered to the people [Note: [Col. 1082D] Thus the Lateran Codex and the Codex of the Queen of Sweden; the Corbeiensis Germanensis, Belvacensis, and nearly all the other manuscripts agree. In the Lateran Codex the order of the homilies is different, and the one that is second here is ninth there. The second Gemeticensis adds “Sunday in Quinquagesima,” which is absent from the others.] in the basilica of the Apostle Saint Peter, on Quinquagesima Sunday.

### HOLY GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO LUKE 18:31–44
In that time, Jesus took aside his twelve disciples and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon. And after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.” And they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said.

Now it happened that, as he was approaching Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road, begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. They told him that Jesus the Nazarene was passing by. And he cried out, saying: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” Those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” Then Jesus stood still and ordered him to be brought to him. When he had come near, he asked him, saying: “What do you want me to do for you?” He said: “Lord, that I may see.” [Col. 1082B] And Jesus said to him: “See; your faith has saved you.” And immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying God. And when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God.

### 1.

Our Redeemer, foreseeing that his disciples’ minds would be disturbed by his Passion, foretells to them long beforehand both the suffering of that Passion and the glory of his Resurrection, so that when they saw him dying, as had been foretold, they would not doubt that he would also rise again. [Note: Two manuscripts from Chartres add “also the Resurrection.”]

But because the disciples were still carnal and utterly unable to grasp the words of the mystery, a miracle follows. Before their eyes a blind man receives his sight, so that those who could not grasp the words of the heavenly mystery might be established in faith by heavenly deeds. Yet the miracles of our Lord and Savior, dearly beloved brothers, must be received in such a way that they are believed to have truly happened, while nevertheless conveying something to us through their symbolism. For his works reveal one thing through their power and speak of another through their mystery.

Behold, we do not know who this blind man was historically, but we do know whom he signifies mystically. [Note: Recent printed editions—Gilot, Vatican, Gussanville—read “for the blind man.”] The blind man is the human race, which, expelled from the joys of paradise in its first parent, suffers the darkness of its condemnation, ignorant of the brightness of the heavenly light. Yet through the presence of its Redeemer it is illumined, so that it already sees, through desire, the joys of the inner light and sets the steps of good works upon the way of life.

### 2.

It should be noted that when Jesus is said to be approaching Jericho, the blind man is illumined. Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” and in sacred language the moon signifies the failing of the flesh, because, diminishing at monthly intervals, it represents the decline of our mortality. Therefore, when our Creator approaches Jericho, the blind man returns to the light, because, when the Godhead assumed the failing of our flesh, the human race received again the light it had lost. For from the fact that God suffers human things, man is raised up to divine things.

This blind man is rightly described as sitting beside the road and as begging. The Truth itself says: “I am the way” (John 14:6). Whoever does not know the brightness of eternal light is blind; but if he already believes in the Redeemer, he sits beside the way. If he believes but pretends not to ask, and ceases from prayer, in order to receive eternal light, then the blind man indeed sits beside the way, [Note: Two manuscripts from Chartres and three from Jumièges read: “but disdains to beg.”] but does not beg at all. [Note: Beauvais, Corbie, one manuscript from Chartres: “But if he both believes and entreats, he sits beside the way and begs.” The German manuscript of Corbie, Longpont, and Val-Clos differ only slightly from these.]

But if he both believes, recognizes the blindness of his heart, and asks to receive the light of truth, the blind man sits beside the way and begs. Whoever recognizes the darkness of his blindness, whoever understands the light of eternity that he lacks, let him cry out from the depths of his heart; let him cry out also with the voice of his mind, saying: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me.” But let us hear what follows concerning the blind man who cries out: “Those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent.”

### 3.

What do these people who go before the approaching Jesus signify, if not the crowds of carnal desires and the tumults of vices which, before Jesus comes to our heart, scatter our thoughts through their temptations and disturb the voice of our heart in prayer? Often, when we wish to turn back to the Lord after committing sins, when we try to implore forgiveness for those very vices we have committed, the images of the sins we have done come before the heart, strike against the vision of our mind, confuse the spirit, and suppress the voice of our supplication.

Therefore, those who went before rebuked him, telling him to be silent, because, before Jesus comes to the heart, the evils we have committed, impressed upon our thoughts through their images, disturb us in the very act of our prayer. [Note: Two later Jumièges manuscripts and three older witnesses—the Antwerp, Rouen, and Paris editions—read “mocked/derided” (illusa).]

### 4.

But let us hear what this blind man, who was to be illumined, did in response. It follows: “But he cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me.” Behold, the crowd rebukes him and tells him to be silent, yet he cries out more and more, because the more severely we are pressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more fervently we ought to persist in prayer.

The crowd contradicts us so that we may not cry out, because in prayer also we often suffer the images of our sins. Yet it is certainly necessary that the voice of our heart, the more harshly it is repelled, should persist all the more forcefully, so that it may overcome the tumult of unlawful thoughts and, through the excess of its importunity, break through to the merciful ears of the Lord.

I suspect that each of us recognizes in himself what we are saying. When we turn our minds from this world to God, when we devote ourselves to prayer, the very things we previously did with delight afterward become intrusive and burdensome in our prayer. Scarcely can the thought of them be driven away from the eyes of our heart by the hand of holy desire; scarcely are their images overcome through the lamentations of repentance. [Note: In the printed editions: “is cast away.” We follow the manuscripts of Tours, Corbie, the German manuscript of Corbie, and others.]

### 5.

But when we persist vehemently in our prayer, we fix the passing Jesus in our mind. Hence it is added there: “Then Jesus stood still and ordered him to be brought to him.” Behold, he who had been passing by stands still, because while we still suffer crowds of images in prayer, we sense Jesus as passing by to some extent. But when we persist fervently in prayer, Jesus stands still in order to restore the light, because God is fixed in the heart and the lost light is restored. [Note: Gussanville omits “in the mind,” which is found both in other manuscripts and in the printed editions.]

### 6.

In this matter the Lord also indicates something else to us, which may usefully be understood concerning his humanity and divinity. Jesus, while passing by, heard the blind man crying out, but, standing still, performed the miracle of illumination. Passing by belongs to humanity; standing still belongs to divinity.

Through his humanity he had to be born, grow, die, rise again, and go from place to place. Since there is no mutability in the divinity—and to be changed is itself to pass by—that passing is plainly from the flesh, not from the divinity. Through his divinity, however, it is always his nature to stand, because, being present everywhere, he neither comes through movement nor departs through movement. The Lord therefore hears the blind man crying out while passing by, but illumines him while standing still, because through his humanity he pitied us, sympathizing with the voices of our blindness, while through the power of his divinity he poured the light of grace into us. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie reads “not sitting, but standing.”]

### 7.

We should also note what he says to the blind man who comes to him: “What do you want me to do for you?” Did the one who could restore light not know what the blind man wanted? But he wishes the man to ask for what he already knows both that we will ask and that he will grant. He urges us insistently to pray, and yet says: “For your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8). He asks, therefore, in order that the request may be made; he asks in order to stir the heart to prayer.

Hence the blind man immediately adds: “Lord, that I may see.” Behold, the blind man asks the Lord not for gold but for light. He considers it of little importance to seek anything outside the light, because, even if a blind man can possess anything whatsoever, without light he cannot see what he possesses.

Let us therefore imitate him, dearly beloved brothers, whom we have heard to have been saved both bodily and spiritually. [Note: The printed editions read “illumined,” although all the manuscripts read “saved.”] Let us ask the Lord not for false riches, not for earthly gifts, not for fleeting honors, but for light—not the light confined to a place, ended by time, altered by the interruption of night, and seen by us in common with the animals, but the light which we may see together with the angels, which no beginning initiates and no end confines.

Faith is plainly the way to this light. Hence the response to the blind man, who was immediately illumined, is rightly given: “See; your faith has saved you.”

But carnal thought says: “How can I seek spiritual light, which I cannot see? How can I know that it exists, since it does not shine upon bodily eyes?” To this thought anyone may briefly reply: even these very things that he experiences he thinks not through the body but through the soul. No one sees his own soul, yet no one doubts that he has a soul, which he does not see. For the visible body is governed by the invisible soul. If what is invisible were taken away, that which seemed visibly to stand would immediately collapse. We therefore live in this visible life through an invisible substance, yet doubt that invisible life exists?

### 8.

But let us hear what happened to the blind man once he had asked, and what he himself did. It follows: “Immediately he saw, and followed him.” He sees and follows who does the good that he understands. But he sees and does not follow who indeed understands the good but disdains to do good works.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, if we recognize the blindness of our pilgrimage; if, believing in the mystery of our Redeemer, we sit beside the way; if, by entreating, we ask our Creator daily for light; if, having been illumined after our blindness, we now see that same light through understanding, then let us follow in deed the Jesus whom we see in our minds. Let us look at where he walks and hold fast to his footsteps by imitating him. For whoever imitates Jesus follows him.

Hence he says: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22). “Follow” means “imitate.” Again he admonishes us, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26).

Let us therefore consider where he walks, so that we may deserve to follow him. Behold, although he is Lord and Creator of the angels, he came into the womb of the Virgin in order to assume our nature, which he had created. Yet he did not wish to be born into this world through the rich; he chose poor parents. Hence his mother found no lamb to offer for him, but brought the young of doves and a pair of turtledoves for the sacrifice (Luke 2:24).

He did not wish to prosper in the world; he endured reproaches and mockeries, spitting, scourges, blows, a crown of thorns, and the cross. And because we fell from the inner joy [Note: Longpont reads “from eternal joy”] through delight in bodily things, he showed with what bitterness one returns there. What, then, ought a human being to suffer for himself, if God endured so much for human beings?

Whoever has now believed in Christ but still pursues the profits of avarice, is lifted up in the pride of honor, burns with the torches of envy, defiles himself with the uncleanness of lust, and desires the prosperity that belongs to this world, refuses to follow the Jesus in whom he has believed. He walks by a different road if he seeks joys and pleasures while his guide has shown him the way of bitterness.

Let us therefore recall before our eyes the sins we have committed. Let us consider how terrible a judge will come to punish them. Let us form our minds for lamentation. Let our life become bitter for a time in repentance, lest it feel eternal bitterness in punishment. Through tears we are led to eternal joys, as the Truth promises when it says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

Yet one arrives at tears through joys, as the same Truth testifies when it says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25). If, then, we seek the joy of recompense upon arrival, let us hold fast to the bitterness of repentance along the way.

Thus it comes about that not only does our life advance toward God, but our very conduct also kindles others to the praise of God. Hence it is added there: “And when all the people saw it, they gave praise to God.” [Note: The word “eternal” is absent from the German manuscript of Corbie, Bigot, and the two earlier manuscripts of Jumièges. Tours, Val-Clos, and one manuscript of Jumièges read “conversion.”]

# HOMILY III

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Felicitas the martyr, on the day of her festival. [Note: Concerning Saint Felicitas, see the Acts of the Martyrs collected by our Theodore Ruinart, p. 20 and following.]

## LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 12:46–50

At that time, while Jesus was speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. Someone said to him: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.” But he answered the one who told him and said: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And extending his hands toward his disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, and sister, and mother.”

### 1.

The reading of the holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, is short, but pregnant with the great weight of mysteries. Jesus, our Creator and Redeemer, pretends not to know his mother, and indicates who his mother and relatives are—not through kinship of flesh but through union of spirit—saying: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, and sister, and mother.”

What else does he suggest to us by these words except that, gathering many from among the Gentiles who obey his commands, he does not recognize Judea, from whose flesh he was born? Hence his mother, when she is treated as though she were not recognized, is said to stand outside, because the Synagogue is not recognized by its Creator for this reason: holding fast to observance of the law, it lost spiritual understanding and fixed itself outside at the guardianship of the letter. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, the second manuscript of Jumièges, and four English manuscripts read “with his brothers, as though she were not recognized.”]

### 2.

But when the one who does the will of the Father is called the Lord’s sister and brother, there is nothing surprising in this, because both sexes are gathered into the faith. What is greatly astonishing is how such a person is also called a mother.

He deemed his faithful disciples worthy to call them brothers, saying: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matthew 28:10). Therefore, whoever can become the Lord’s brother by coming to faith—how can he also become a mother?

We must understand that whoever is Christ’s brother and sister through believing becomes his mother through preaching. For he gives birth, as it were, to the Lord when he pours him into the heart of a listener. He becomes his mother if, through his voice, the love of the Lord is generated in the mind of his neighbor.

### 3.

The blessed Felicitas, whose festival we celebrate today, provides a fitting confirmation of this. Through believing she became Christ’s servant, and through preaching she became Christ’s mother.

As is read in the more reliable accounts of her deeds, she feared to leave seven sons alive in the flesh after her in the same way that fleshly parents commonly fear sending the dead on before them. Caught in the labor of persecution, she strengthened the hearts of her sons through preaching in the love of the heavenly homeland. She gave birth in spirit to those whom she had borne in the flesh, so that through preaching she might give to God those whom she had borne in the flesh for the world.

Consider, dearly beloved brothers, a manly heart in a woman’s body. She stood before death without fear. She feared losing the light of truth in her sons if she were not bereaved of them. Shall I call this woman a martyr? Rather, more than a martyr.

Certainly, when the Lord spoke about John, he said: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Indeed, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matthew 11:7). And John himself, when questioned, replied: “I am not a prophet” (John 1:21). Because he knew himself to be more than a prophet, he denied that he was a prophet.

He is called more than a prophet because it is the prophet’s office to foretell what is to come, but not also to show it. John, however, is more than a prophet because he pointed out with his finger the one whom he foretold in words. [Note: One manuscript from Chartres and the third from Jumièges read “whom he foretold in words.”]

I would therefore call this woman not a martyr but more than a martyr. Having sent seven children ahead to the kingdom, she died as many times before herself; she came first to the punishments, but arrived as the eighth. [Note: Bigot, the two earlier manuscripts of Jumièges, and Val-Clos read “having died so many times before herself.” Val-Clos reads “she did not come.”]

The mother looked upon the death of her sons, both tortured and fearless, and applied the joy of hope to the grief of nature. [Note: This passage is read with remarkable variation in the manuscripts. Tours and the German manuscript of Corbie have “she applied the joy of hope to the grief of nature,” but corruptly. The two earlier manuscripts of Jumièges read “the joy of hope erased the grief of nature,” which is excellent. The first manuscript of Chartres has the corresponding reading: “the joy of hope restrained the grief of nature.”]

She feared for them while they lived and rejoiced when they died. She wished to leave no one behind her, lest, if she had any survivor, she could not have a companion. Let none of you, dearly beloved brothers, think that her heart, when her sons were dying, was not also touched by natural affection. She could not see dying without grief those whom she knew to be her own flesh. But there was an inner force of love that overcame the grief of the flesh.

Hence it is said to Peter, who was to suffer: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18). Peter could not have suffered for Christ if he had wholly refused to do so; rather, the martyrdom that he did not wish for through the weakness of the flesh he loved through the strength of the spirit. While he trembles at punishment through the flesh, he rejoices in glory through the spirit; and it came to pass that he willed, though unwilling, the suffering of martyrdom. [Note: Beauvais reads “by willing he would have been unwilling.”]

So too [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, the first manuscript of Chartres, and others read “as we too”], when we seek the joy of salvation, we drink the bitter cup of purification. The bitterness displeases in the cup, but the salvation restored through bitterness pleases. Felicitas therefore loved her sons according to the flesh, but for love of the heavenly homeland she also wished those whom she loved to die before her eyes. She received their wounds, yet she herself grew through them as they went before her to the kingdom.

Rightly, then, I would call this woman more than a martyr. Having been desirably extinguished so many times in her sons, while she obtained multiple martyrdoms, she even surpassed the martyr’s palm. [Note: All the manuscripts agree with the older printed editions. More recent editions read “she endured martyrdom.”]

It is said that among the ancients it was customary for anyone who became consul to hold the place of honor assigned to him according to the order of his tenure. But if someone who came to the consulship later became consul not once but perhaps twice or a third time, he would surpass in praise and honor even those who had been consuls no more than once.

Blessed Felicitas therefore surpassed the martyrs. Her sons died before her, and for Christ she fell repeatedly, because her own death alone was not enough for her love of him. [Note: One manuscript from Chartres reads “because not even for her lover.” There are several other variant readings, but they differ only slightly.]

### 4.

Let us consider this woman, brothers; let us consider ourselves, who are men in bodily members, and ask what we shall be judged by comparison with her. Often we propose to do some good, but if even the slightest word against us bursts from the mouth of someone mocking us, we immediately recoil, broken and confused, from our intended action. Behold, words often recall us from good work. But not even tortures could break Felicitas from her holy purpose.

We yield to the breath of cursing; she went forth to the kingdom even through iron and considered nothing an obstacle. [Note: All the English manuscripts and ours read “against the breath” or “in the air.” Both readings make excellent sense and are elegant: he contrasts breath with iron. We yield to breath, whereas Felicitas did not yield to iron. Not understanding this, the editors interpolated: “we hurl the insult of a curse into the ear of the curser.”]

We do not wish to give even our surplus in obedience to the divine commands; she not only gave her possessions to God, but also gave her own flesh for him. When we lose our children through the divine command, we mourn without consolation; she would have mourned them as dead had she not offered them.

When the strict Judge comes to that terrible examination, what shall we men say when we see this woman’s glory? What excuse will men then have for the weakness of their minds, when she is displayed who conquered both the world and her sex?

Let us therefore follow, dearly beloved brothers, the strict and difficult way of the Redeemer. Through the practice of virtues it has already become so level that women gladly walk along it. Let us despise all present things, for they are destined to pass away. It is shameful to love what is plainly destined to perish quickly.

Let not the love of earthly things overcome us; let pride not inflate us; let anger not tear us apart; let lust not defile us; let envy not consume us. Our Redeemer died out of love for us, and let us learn, out of love for him, to conquer ourselves.

If we do this perfectly, we shall not only escape the punishments that threaten us, but shall also be rewarded with glory together with the martyrs. For although the opportunity for persecution is absent, our peace too has its martyrdom, because, even if we do not submit the necks of our flesh to the sword, we nevertheless slaughter carnal desires in the mind with the spiritual sword, with his help, and so forth.

# HOMILY IV

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Stephen the martyr, concerning the apostles. [Note: The words “concerning the apostles” are not found in the manuscripts of the German manuscript of Corbie, Beauvais, Jumièges, Bigot, and the Swedish Royal manuscript.]

## LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 10:5–10

At that time, Jesus sent his twelve disciples, commanding them and saying: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel. As you go, preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You have received freely; give freely. [Note: In Beauvais and the German manuscript of Corbie, these words conclude the Gospel lesson; likewise, nothing that follows is explained in the homily.] Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff. For the laborer is worthy of his food.”

### 1.

Since it is clear to all, dearly beloved brothers, that our Redeemer came into the world for the redemption of the Gentiles, and since we see Samaritans called to the faith every day, what does it mean that, when sending his disciples to preach, he says: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel”?

It means what we infer from the outcome of the matter: he wished the Gospel to be preached first to Judea alone, and afterward to all the Gentiles, so that, when Judea refused the call to conversion, the holy preachers might proceed in due order to the calling of the Gentiles. Thus the preaching of our Redeemer, rejected by his own people, would seek foreign peoples as strangers, and what had happened to the Jews as a testimony would become an increase of grace for the Gentiles.

At that time there were people from Judea who were to be called, while there were people from the Gentiles who were not yet to be called. For in the Acts of the Apostles we read that, when Peter preached, first three thousand Hebrews believed, and afterward five thousand (Acts 2:41; 4:4).

And when the apostles wished to preach to the Gentiles in Asia, they are said to have been forbidden by the Spirit (Acts 16:6). Yet the same Spirit that first forbade the preaching afterward poured it into the hearts of the Asians. For it has long been the case that all Asia has believed.

He therefore first forbade what he later did because at that time there were in Asia people who were not to be saved. At that time there were people there who had not yet deserved to be restored to life, nor yet to be judged more severely for despising the preaching. [Note: The third manuscript of Jumièges reads: “because there were in it people who had not yet deserved to be called to life. Yet they did not…” Tours, one German manuscript of Corbie, the two earlier manuscripts of Jumièges, Bigot, and two manuscripts of Chartres read: “deserved to be restored. Yet the ministry of preaching is usefully withdrawn from them, lest they deserve to be judged more severely for despising the preaching. Thus, by a subtle…” We follow the German manuscript of Corbie, the other German manuscript, the Royal manuscript, and others.]

Therefore, by a subtle and hidden judgment, holy preaching is withdrawn from the ears of some because they do not deserve to be raised up by grace. Hence it is necessary, dearly beloved brothers, that in everything we do we fear the hidden counsels of almighty God concerning us, lest, while our mind is poured out externally and does not withdraw itself from its pleasure, the terrible Judge should inwardly arrange adverse things against it.

The Psalmist, observing this well, says: “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his counsels concerning the children of men” (Psalm 45:9; Psalm 65:5). He saw that one person is mercifully called while another is rejected as justice demands. And because the Lord arranges some things by sparing and others by anger, he was terrified by what he could not penetrate. Seeing him not only as unsearchable but also as inflexible in certain judgments, he declared him terrible in his counsels.

### 2.

But now that the preachers have been sent, let us hear what is commanded: “As you go, preach, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

Even if the Gospel were silent, dearly beloved brothers, the world itself now cries this out. Its voices are the signs of its ruin. For, battered by so many blows and fallen from its glory, it displays to us, as it were, from close at hand the other kingdom that follows. It has already become bitter even to those who love it. Its very ruins proclaim that it should not be loved.

If a house were threatening to collapse upon itself, anyone living in it would flee; and whoever had loved it while it stood would hasten to withdraw from it as quickly as possible when it began to fall. If, then, the world is falling and we embrace it while loving it, we wish to be crushed rather than dwell in it, because no reasoning separates us from its ruin when love binds us to its sufferings.

It is easy now, when we see everything destroyed, to detach our minds from love of the world. But this was extraordinarily difficult at the time when they were sent to preach the invisible kingdom of heaven, while far and wide they saw all the kingdoms of the earth flourishing. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, Beauvais, Bigot, and three manuscripts of Jumièges read “while they all saw.”]

### 3.

Hence miracles were also added to the holy preachers, so that displayed power might give credibility to their words, and those who preached new things might perform new deeds, as the same reading continues: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.”

While the world was flourishing, the human race increasing, flesh continuing for a long time in this life, and material wealth overflowing, who would believe, on hearing it, that there was another life? Who would prefer invisible things to visible things?

But when the sick returned to health, the dead rose to life, lepers received the purity of their flesh, and those possessed were rescued from the power of unclean spirits—when so many visible miracles had been performed—who would not believe what he heard concerning invisible things?

Visible miracles flash forth for this purpose: to draw the hearts of those who see them toward faith in invisible things, so that through what is wondrously done outwardly, they may perceive that what is inward is far more wondrous.

Therefore now also, although the number of the faithful has increased, there are many within the holy Church who possess the life of virtues but do not possess signs of virtues, because a miracle is displayed outwardly to no purpose if there is nothing within for it to accomplish. For, in the words of the Teacher of the Gentiles: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14:22).

Hence that same outstanding preacher, while preaching, raised by prayer in the presence of all the unbelievers Eutychus, who had been sleeping, had fallen from a window, and had been utterly deprived of life (Acts 20:9 and following). When he came to Melita (Malta), knowing the island to be full of unbelievers, he healed Publius’s father, who was afflicted with dysentery and fevers, by praying (Acts 28:8). [Note: Or “saved”; the second Jumièges manuscript reads “raised.” Several manuscripts corruptly read “Mitilene,” “Militene,” or “Militinae.”]

But Timothy, his companion in pilgrimage and helper in holy preaching, weakened by an ailment of the stomach, he did not cure by a word but restored by medical treatment, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5:23). [Note: The two earlier manuscripts of Chartres read “he prepares to heal,” as does Tours, except that it has “to heal” instead of “to prepare to heal.”]

Why, then, does he save an unbeliever who is sick by a single prayer, but not strengthen his sick companion by prayer? Clearly, the unbeliever had to be healed outwardly by a miracle because he was not inwardly alive, so that the inner power might bring him to life through what the outward power displayed. But outward signs were not to be shown to the sick faithful companion, who was living inwardly in a healthy manner. [Note: Recent editions add “and, as we believe, dead” to “the sick unbeliever.” We reject this addition, since it is absent from the manuscripts and older printed editions.]

### 4.

But after granting the power of preaching and granting the miracles of virtues, let us hear what our Redeemer adds: “You have received freely; give freely.”

For he knew that some would turn this very gift of the received Spirit into a means of commerce and bend the signs of miracles to the service of avarice. Hence Simon Magus, seeing miracles performed through the laying on of hands, wished to obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit with money (Acts 8:18 and following), so that he might sell more expensively what he had wrongly purchased. [Note: Tours, the German manuscript of Corbie, and many others read “desiring them.”]

Hence our Redeemer drove the crowds from the temple with a whip made of cords and overturned the seats of those selling doves (John 2:15). To sell doves means to give the laying on of hands by which the Holy Spirit is received—not for the merit of life but for a reward. [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “for the reward of worldly commerce.”]

There are some who indeed do not accept monetary rewards for ordination (1, q. 1, c. “Nonnulli”), yet confer sacred orders for human favor and seek from that very generosity only the reward of praise. Such people do not give freely what they received freely, because they demand a coin of favor for the office of holiness they have bestowed.

Therefore, when describing a righteous man, the prophet rightly says: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah 33:15). He does not say, “He who shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds “every,” because one kind of gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue.

A gift from service is an improperly rendered submission; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. [Note: Val-Clos reads “the submission of an improperly imposed servitude.”] Whoever confers sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.

5. But you, dearly beloved brothers, whom secular dress and manner of life hold fast, when you recognize what belongs to us, turn the eyes of your mind back to what belongs to you. Do everything toward one another freely. Do not seek a recompense for your work in this world, which you already see has failed with such great rapidity. Just as you wish your evil deeds to be concealed lest others see them, so take care that your good deeds not appear for human praise. Do not perform either evil or good deeds for a temporal reward. Seek as the witness of your work the one whom you await as judge. Let him now see your good deeds in secret, so that at the time of his recompense he may display them openly. [Col. 1092B]

Just as you provide food daily for your flesh so that it may not fail, so let good works be the daily nourishment of your mind. The body is fed with food; let the spirit be nourished by pious work. Do not deny to the soul that will live forever what you give to the flesh that will die. For whenever a sudden fire consumes a dwelling, whoever its possessor may have been, he snatches away whatever he can and flees; he counts it as gain if he carries anything away with him from the flames. Behold, the flame of tribulations is consuming the world, and the approaching end is already laying waste, like a fire, to all the things that seemed splendid in it. [Col. 1092C] Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, consider it the greatest gain if you carry something away with you from it, if, as you flee, you take something with you, if you preserve for an everlasting recompense, by giving it away, what could have perished by remaining here.

For by preserving earthly things we lose them, but by giving generously we preserve them. Time flees swiftly. Since, then, we are driven with great urgency to see our Judge sooner, let us prepare ourselves for him with good works in haste, with the Lord our God granting this, etc.

# HOMILY V

Delivered to the people in the basilica of the blessed apostle Andrew, on his feast day.

## THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 4:18–22

At that time, as Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and his brother Andrew, casting a net into the sea [Note: Three manuscripts of Gemeticum read “beside the sea”; Codex Germanensis agrees. Codex Germanensis, Bigotianus, and others read “their nets” (*retia sua*).] (for they were fishermen), and he said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” Immediately they left their nets and followed him. Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and his brother John, in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets, and he called them. At once they left their nets and their father and followed him. [Col. 1092D–1093A]

1450

1. You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, that at the voice of a single command Peter and Andrew left their nets and followed the Redeemer. They had not yet seen him perform any miracles, nor had they heard anything from him about the reward of eternal recompense; nevertheless, at the Lord’s single command they forgot what they seemed to possess [Note: This is a manner of speaking very familiar to our Gregory, and also to the other Gregory, of Tours. See Book IV of *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 11: “Let all these things remain under Saint Martin’s authority, which I seem to possess.”]. How many miracles of his do we see, by how many scourges are we afflicted, by how many harsh threats are we frightened, and yet we disdain to follow him when he calls? [Col. 1093B]

He now sits in heaven, he who admonishes us concerning conversion; he has already subjected the necks of the nations to the yoke of faith; he has already laid low the glory of the world; and, as its ruins multiply, he announces that the day of his strict judgment is drawing near. Yet our proud mind does not wish voluntarily to abandon what it daily loses against its will. What, then, dearly beloved, what will we say at his judgment, when we are moved neither by commands nor corrected by blows to withdraw our love from the present age?

2. But perhaps someone may say silently to himself: “At the Lord’s voice, what or how much did these two fishermen leave, since they possessed almost nothing?” But in this matter, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to weigh their devotion rather than their possessions. He left much who kept nothing for himself; he left much who, however little it was, abandoned it all [Note: Codex Germanensis, Bigotianus, and Longipontanus read: “who, however small [it might be].”]. [Col. 1093D]

Certainly, we possess even what we have with affection, and we seek in desire what we do not have at all. Peter and Andrew therefore left much when both of them also abandoned the desire to possess. He left much who, together with the thing possessed, renounced his desires. Thus those who follow Christ have left as much as those who do not follow him could have desired. [Col. 1093C]

Therefore, let no one, even when he sees certain people leaving many things behind, say to himself: “I want to imitate those who despise the world, but I have nothing to leave.” You leave much, brothers, if you renounce earthly desires [Note: Codex Germanensis and others read “desires of the flesh.”]. For the Lord is satisfied with our outward possessions, however small they may be. He weighs the heart, not the substance; he does not consider how much is offered in his sacrifice, but from how great an affection it is brought forth [Note: Three manuscripts of Gemeticum read “from how great an affection.”]. [Col. 1093D]

For if we weigh the outward substance, behold, our holy merchants purchased the perpetual life of the angels with nets and a boat. The price has no monetary valuation, yet the kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess. Half of his substance was of value to Zacchaeus, because he reserved the other half for restoring fourfold whatever he had unjustly taken (Luke 19:8). Nets and a boat were of value to Peter and Andrew when they left them (Matthew 4:20); two small coins were of value to the widow (Luke 21:2); a cup of cold water was of value to another (Matthew 10:42). [Col. 1094A] Thus, as we have said, the kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess.

3. Consider, then, brothers, what is cheapest when it is purchased and what is most precious when it is possessed. But perhaps not even a cup of cold water is available to give to someone in need. Even then the divine word promises us security. For when the Redeemer was born, the citizens of heaven appeared, crying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). [Col. 1094B]

Before God’s eyes, the hand is never empty of a gift if the treasury of the heart is filled with good will. Hence the Psalmist says: “In me are your vows, O God, which I shall fulfill, praises to you” (Psalm 56:12). It is as though he plainly said: “Although outward gifts to offer are not available to me, within myself I nevertheless find what I may place upon the altar of your praise, because you are not nourished by our gifts but are better pleased by the offering of the heart.”

For nothing is offered to God more richly than good will [Note: The two later manuscripts of Gemeticum read “more devoutly.”]. Good will is to fear another’s adversities as though they were our own; to rejoice over our neighbor’s prosperity as over our own progress [Note: Corbie reads “to fear another’s adversities in the same way as our own”; Bellovacensis reads “in the same way as our own,” and so forth.]; to regard another’s losses as our own and another’s gains as our own; to love a friend not for the world’s sake but for God’s sake; to endure even an enemy with love; to do to no one what you do not wish to suffer; to deny no one what you rightly desire to be done for you; not merely to assist your neighbor’s need according to your strength, but also to wish to benefit him beyond your strength. [Col. 1094C]

What, then, is richer than this holocaust, when through what the soul sacrifices to God on the altar of the heart, it slays itself?

4. But this sacrifice of good will is never fully offered unless the desire for this world is completely abandoned. For whatever we desire in it, we undoubtedly begrudge our neighbors. It seems, after all, that we lack what another attains. And because envy is always at odds with good will, as soon as the one has seized the mind, the other departs.

Therefore the holy preachers, so that they might love their neighbors perfectly, took care in this world to love nothing, desire nothing ever, and possess nothing even without desire [Note: So it should be read according to most manuscripts, and indeed with a fuller meaning than the reading in the printed editions, “to possess nothing even with desire,” which seems superfluous after “to desire nothing” has been said. In Codex Germanensis, after “to desire nothing ever,” there immediately follows “whom he rightly…,” etc.]. [Col. 1094D]

Isaiah rightly saw such men and said: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isaiah 60:8). He saw them despising earthly things, drawing near in mind to heavenly things, raining down words, and flashing with miracles. Because holy preaching and lofty living had lifted them away from earthly contamination, he calls them both flying creatures and clouds. [Col. 1094D–1095A]

Our windows are our eyes, because through them the soul looks upon what it desires outwardly. A dove is a simple animal, alien to the malice of gall. Thus those who desire nothing in this world, who look upon everything simply, and who are not drawn by predatory eagerness toward the things they see, are like doves at their windows. But the kite, not the dove, is at his windows who pants with a desire for plunder after the things he observes with his eyes.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, since we are celebrating the feast of the blessed apostle Andrew, we must imitate what we worship. Let the solemnity of our unchanging devotion display the service of our minds; let us despise earthly things and, leaving temporal things behind, purchase eternal ones. But if we are not yet able to leave our own possessions, at least let us not desire those of others. If our minds are not yet kindled with the fire of charity, let them at least restrain their ambition with the bridle of fear, so that, strengthened by the steps of their progress, while they are restrained from desiring what belongs to others, they may eventually be led to despise what belongs to themselves, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. [Col. 1095B]

# HOMILY VI

Delivered to the people in the basilica of the saints Marcellinus and Peter, on the third Sunday of the Lord’s Advent [Note: This is absent from the royal Swedish manuscript and from the others except the second manuscript of Gemeticum.].

## THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 11:2–10

At that time, when John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Go and report to John what you hear and see. The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.”

As they were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’” [Col. 1095C–D]

1452

1. We must ask, dearly beloved brothers, why John—a prophet, and more than a prophet—who pointed out the Lord coming to the baptism at the Jordan [Note: The phrase “of the Jordan” is absent from Codex Germanensis, Corbeiensis, and Bigotianus.], saying, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29, 36), and who, considering both his own humility and the power of his divinity, says, “He who is of the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth, but he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3:31)—why, when he is in prison, does he send his disciples and ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” It seems as though he does not know the one whom he had pointed out, and is uncertain whether it is he whom he had proclaimed by prophesying, baptizing, and pointing him out. [Col. 1095D]

But this question is quickly resolved if the time and order of the event are considered. Standing at the waters of the Jordan, he asserted that the Redeemer himself was the one who would come; but when sent into prison, he asks whether he is coming—not because he doubts that he is the Redeemer of the world, but so that he may know whether the one who had come into the world by himself would also descend by himself to the bars of hell [Note: The first manuscript of Carnutum and Bigotianus read “into prison, whether they should expect another or whether he himself would come.”]. [Col. 1096A]

For the one whom, as forerunner, he had announced to the world, he also preceded into the underworld by dying. Thus he says: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” It is as though he plainly said: “As you deemed it worthy to be born for human beings, indicate whether you will also deem it worthy to die for human beings, so that I, who became the forerunner of your birth, may also become the forerunner of your death, and announce to hell that you are coming—the one whom I have already announced to the world as having come.”

Therefore, when questioned, the Lord responded by listing the miracles of his power and immediately speaking of the humility of his death: “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.”

In view of so many signs and such great miracles [Note: The two earlier manuscripts of Gemeticum and Bigotianus read “miracles.”], no one could have been scandalized, but rather filled with wonder. Yet the mind of unbelievers suffered a grave scandal in him when it saw him dying after so many miracles. Hence Paul also says: “But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a scandal and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians 1:23). [Col. 1096B]
