It seemed foolish to human beings that the author of life should die for human beings; and from this a human being took scandal against him—from the very thing by which he ought to have become still more indebted. For God is to be honored more worthily by human beings precisely to the extent that he accepted unworthy things for human beings.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me,” except openly to signify the lowliness and humility of his death? It is as though he plainly said: “I indeed do marvelous things, but I do not disdain to endure what is lowly.” Since, then, I follow you by dying, human beings must take great care not to despise death in me while they venerate signs. [Col. 1096C]

2. But after John’s disciples have been dismissed, let us hear what he says to the crowds about that same John: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” He introduced this not by asserting it, but by denying it. As soon as a breeze touches a reed, it bends toward the other side. And what is signified by the reed except a carnal mind? As soon as it is touched by favor or criticism, it immediately inclines in whatever direction.

If a breeze of approval has blown from a human mouth, it becomes cheerful, is lifted up, and bends itself wholly as though toward favor. But if the wind of criticism bursts forth from the same place from which the breeze of praise came, it immediately bends him toward the other side, as though under the force of anger.

But John was not a reed shaken by the wind, because neither did favor make him yielding, nor did the anger of any detractor make him harsh [Note: Thus Codex Germanensis, Carnutensis, Corbeiensis, and others; the printed editions read “nor did the anger of any criticism make him harsh.”]. Prosperity did not know how to raise him up, nor adversity how to bend him. John, therefore, was not a reed shaken by the wind, for no change of circumstances bent him from the uprightness of his position. [Col. 1096D–1097A]

Let us learn, then, dearly beloved brothers, not to be reeds shaken by the wind. Let us fortify our minds, placed amid the breezes of human speech; let the posture of our minds remain unbending. Let no criticism provoke us to anger, and let no favor incline us toward an unprofitable leniency. Let prosperity not exalt us and adversity not disturb us, so that, fixed in the solidity of faith, we may not be moved at all by the mutability of passing things.

3. [Note: The printed editions read “of his holiness.” This would be excellent, were the manuscripts not opposed.] His description continues: “But what did you go out into the desert to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.” John is described as having been clothed in fabric woven from camel hair. What does it mean to say, “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses,” except to demonstrate plainly that those who avoid hardship for God’s sake, being devoted only to outward things, and seek the softness and pleasure of the present life, serve not a heavenly but an earthly king [Note: Bellovacensis, the first manuscript of Carnutum, Valcellensis, and Longipontanus read “kingdom.”]? [Col. 1097B]

Therefore no one should think that sin is absent from indulgence in and pursuit of flowing garments. If this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the harshness of his clothing. If this were not a fault, the apostle Peter would not have restrained women by his letter from desiring costly clothing, saying: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Peter 3:3; 1 Timothy 2:9). Consider, then, what a fault it is even for men to desire what the pastor of the Church took care to forbid women.

1455

4. Nevertheless, the statement that John was not dressed in soft clothing can also be understood figuratively. He was not dressed in soft clothing because he did not indulge the life of sinners with flattering words, but rebuked it with the vigor of harsh denunciation [Note: Some witnesses read “with severity,” as in Corbie, Codex Germanensis, Gemeticum, Bigotianus, and others.], saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3:7; Luke 3:7). [Col. 1097C]

Hence it is also said through Solomon: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly in” (Ecclesiastes 12:11). The words of the wise are compared to nails and goads because they do not know how to caress the faults of sinners, but to pierce them.

5. “But what did you go out into the desert to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” The ministry of a prophet is to foretell what is to come, but not also to point it out. John, therefore, is more than a prophet, because he both prophesied the one whose forerunner he was and pointed him out when he came.

But since it is denied that he was a reed shaken by the wind, since he is said not to have been dressed in soft clothing, and since the name “prophet” is declared insufficient for him, let us now hear what may properly be said of him. The text continues: “This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you’” (Malachi 3:1).

What is called *angel* in Greek is called *messenger* in Latin. Rightly, therefore, the one sent to announce the heavenly Judge is called an angel, so that his name may preserve the dignity which he fulfills in his work. It is a lofty name, but his life is not beneath the name. [Col. 1097D]

6. Would that, dearly beloved brothers, we not say this to our own condemnation: all who are accounted by the name of the priesthood are called angels, as the prophet testifies when he says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). [Col. 1098A]

But you also, if you wish, can merit the loftiness of this name. For each one of you, insofar as he is able and insofar as he has received the grace of heavenly inspiration, if he recalls his neighbor from wickedness, if he takes care to exhort him to good works, if he announces eternal kingdom or punishment to one who is wandering, is certainly an angel when he offers words of holy proclamation.

Let no one say: “I am not capable of admonishing; I am not fit to exhort.” Offer whatever you can, lest you be required to answer in torments for having badly preserved what you received [Note: Thus the manuscripts more simply than the printed editions, which read: “lest you be required in torments to pay for the talent you received.”].

For the one who took greater care to hide his talent than to distribute it had not received more than one talent. And we know that in God’s tabernacle not only bowls but, at the Lord’s command, also cups were made (Exodus 37). The bowls signify overflowing teaching; the cups signify limited and restricted knowledge. [Col. 1098B]

One person, full of the teaching of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers. By saying this, he surely offers a bowl. Another cannot fully express what he understands, but because he announces it somehow, he surely provides a taste through a cup.

Therefore, placed in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—if you cannot serve bowls through the wisdom of teaching, give your neighbors cups of good speech insofar as divine generosity enables you. To the extent that you judge yourselves to have advanced, strive to draw others along with you [Note: Turonensis and five other manuscripts add “strive also to draw others along with you.”]; desire to have companions on the way of God.

If one of you goes to the marketplace or perhaps to the bathhouse and notices someone idle, he invites him to come with him. Let your earthly activity itself address you: if you are journeying toward God, take care not to come to him alone. [Col. 1098C]

Hence it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17), so that whoever has already received in his heart the voice of heavenly love may also return outwardly to his neighbors the voice of exhortation.

Perhaps he does not have bread with which to offer alms to someone in need; but one who has a tongue has something greater that he can give. For it is more to refresh a mind that will live forever with the nourishment of the word than to satisfy the belly of dying flesh with earthly bread.

Do not, then, brothers, withhold from your neighbors the alms of the word. I admonish you together with myself to spare idle speech and avoid speaking uselessly. As far as we can restrain the tongue, let words not flow away into the wind, since the Judge says: “Every idle word that human beings have spoken, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). [Col. 1098D]

An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of righteousness or the reason of just necessity. Therefore turn idle conversations toward the pursuit of edification. Consider how swiftly the times of this life pass; attend to how strict the Judge will come. Place him before the eyes of your hearts; impress him upon the minds of your neighbors, so that, insofar as your strength permits, if you do not neglect to announce him [Note: Corbie reads “if you do not refuse to announce him,”], you may be worthy, with John, to be called angels by him. May he himself grant this, the God who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen. [Col. 1099A]

# HOMILY VII

Delivered to the people in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter, on the fourth Sunday of the Lord’s Advent [Note: In the second manuscript of Gemeticum alone this Sunday is indicated, and no other day is assigned in the manuscripts.].

## THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN 1:19–28

At that time, the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John to ask him: “Who are you?” He confessed and did not deny; he confessed: “I am not the Christ.” And they asked him: “What then? Are you Elijah?” And he said: “I am not.” “Are you the prophet?” And he answered: “No.” They therefore said to him: “Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?”

He said: “I am the voice of one crying in the desert: ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.” Those who had been sent were from the Pharisees. And they questioned him and said to him: “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”

John answered them, saying: “I baptize in water” [Note: Codex Germanensis and Bigotianus read “I indeed baptize.”]; “but one stood among you whom you do not know. He is the one who is to come after me, who was made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” [Note: Bellovacensis and Codex Germanensis read “whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen.” Bigotianus also has “to loosen.”]. These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. [Col. 1099B–C]

1456

1. From the words of this reading, dearly beloved brothers, John’s humility is commended. Although he possessed such great virtue that he could have been believed to be the Christ, he chose to stand firmly in himself, lest he be vainly carried above himself by human opinion.

For he confessed and did not deny; he confessed: “I am not the Christ.” Since he said, “I am not,” he plainly denied what he was not, but he did not deny what he was. Speaking the truth, he thus became a member of the one whose name he would not falsely claim for himself.

Because he did not wish to seek the name of Christ, he became a member of Christ. By humbly acknowledging his own weakness, he deserved truly to possess Christ’s greatness.

But when another saying of our Redeemer is recalled from another reading, a very perplexing question arises from the words of this reading. In another place, when the disciples questioned the Lord about the coming of Elijah, he answered: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished. And if you wish to know, he himself is Elijah” (Matthew 17:12). [Col. 1099D]

Yet when John is questioned, he says: “I am not Elijah.” What is this, dearly beloved brothers? What the Truth affirms, the prophet of the Truth denies. “He himself is” and “I am not” plainly sound very different from one another. How, then, is he a prophet of the Truth if he is not in agreement with the words of that same Truth?

But if the truth itself is sought carefully, it is found how what sounded contrary is not contrary. For the angel says to Zechariah concerning John: “He himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). He is said to come in the spirit and power of Elijah because, just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, so John preceded his first coming. As Elijah will be the forerunner of the Judge, so John was made the forerunner of the Redeemer. [Col. 1100A]

John, therefore, was Elijah in spirit, but he was not Elijah in person. What the Lord affirms concerning the spirit, John denies concerning the person. It was right, therefore, both for the Lord to give the disciples a spiritual judgment concerning John and for John to answer the carnal crowds not concerning his spirit but concerning his body.

What John said therefore seems contrary to the Truth, but nevertheless he did not depart from the path of the Truth. [Col. 1100B]

2. When he also denies that he is a prophet—because he was able not only to proclaim the Redeemer but also to point him out [Note: The manuscripts of Gemeticum and some others read “to foretell”]—he immediately declares who he is by adding: “I am the voice of one crying in the desert.”

You know, dearly beloved brothers, that the only-begotten Son is called the Word of the Father, as John testifies when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). And from your own speech you know that a voice sounds first, so that a word may afterward be heard.

John therefore asserts that he is the voice because he precedes the Word. Preceding the Lord’s coming, he is called the voice because through his ministry the Father’s Word is heard by human beings. He also cries in the desert because he announces the comfort of the Redeemer to Judea, abandoned and desolate [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the old edition. The recent editions read “the comfort of its redemption.”]. [Col. 1100C]

He indicates what he cries when he adds: “Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said” (Isaiah 40:3). The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when the word of truth is heard humbly. The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when life is prepared for obedience to the commandment.

Hence it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Whoever therefore raises his mind in pride, whoever pants with the fever of greed, whoever pollutes himself with the defilements of lust, closes the door of his heart against the Truth; and, lest the Lord come to him, he fastens the chambers of his soul with the bolts of vices. [Col. 1100D]

3. But those who were sent continue to ask: “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?” The Evangelist quietly made known that this was said not out of a desire to know the truth but out of malicious rivalry when he added: “Those who had been sent were from the Pharisees.”

It is as though he plainly said: They ask John about his actions who do not know how to seek teaching, but only how to envy it. Yet every holy person, even when questioned with a perverse intention, is not changed from his pursuit of goodness.

Thus John also answered words of envy with the proclamation of his life. For he immediately adds: “I baptize in water; but one stood among you whom you do not know.” [Col. 1101A]

John baptizes not in the Spirit but in water [Note: The recent editions read “in the Spirit … in water.”], because, being unable to release sins, he washes the bodies of those baptized through water, but nevertheless does not cleanse the mind through forgiveness [Note: The printed editions read “does not heal,” against the manuscripts.].

Why, then, does he baptize when he does not remit sins through baptism? It is so that, preserving the order of his forerunning, the one whom he had preceded by being born might also be preceded by him in baptism; and that he who became Christ’s forerunner by preaching might also become his forerunner in baptism, through an imitation of the sacrament.

Amid these things, announcing the mystery, he asserts that this one both stood among human beings and was unknown, because the Lord appeared through the flesh, visible in body but invisible in majesty.

Concerning him he also adds: “The one who comes after me was made before me.” For “was made before me” is said as though it were “was placed before me.” He came after John because he was born later; but he was made before John because he was preferred to him. [Col. 1101B]

Yet, saying this a little earlier, John also disclosed the reasons for Christ’s precedence when he added that he was before him. It is as though he plainly said: “He surpasses me even though he was born later, because the times of his birth do not confine him.” For the one who is born in time through his mother was generated timelessly by the Father [Note: The printed editions read “he is without a mother before the ages,” etc. We have restored this passage from the English manuscripts and all our own manuscripts.].

By adding, “whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen,” he reveals how much reverence he owes him. It was the custom among the ancients that if someone did not wish to accept the woman who was to be his wife, the man who came as bridegroom by right of kinship would loosen his sandal. [Col. 1101C]

What, then, did Christ appear among human beings to be, except the bridegroom of the holy Church? The same John also says of him: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29).

But because people thought that John was the Christ—a claim John himself denies—he rightly declares himself unworthy to loosen Christ’s sandal strap. It is as though he plainly said: “I am unable to uncover the footsteps of our Redeemer, because I do not wrongfully claim for myself the name of bridegroom.”

This can nevertheless be understood in another way as well. Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? When the incarnate Lord came, he appeared, as it were, shod, because in his divinity he assumed the deathliness of our corruption. Hence through the Prophet he also says: “Into Edom I will extend my sandal” (Psalm 60:10). By Edom is signified the Gentiles; by the sandal, the mortality that was assumed.

The Lord therefore asserts that he will extend his sandal into Edom, because when the Godhead became known to the Gentiles through the flesh, it came to us as though shod. [Col. 1101D]

But the mystery of this incarnation is beyond the capacity of the human eye to penetrate. It cannot be investigated at all how the Word becomes embodied, how the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the mother’s womb, how the one who has no beginning both exists and is conceived. [Col. 1102A]

The sandal strap, therefore, is the bond of the mystery [Note: The two earlier manuscripts of Gemeticum, Bigotianus, Longipontanus, and Valcellensis read: “the cause of this mystery, bound to our understanding.” One manuscript of Saint-Germain agrees. We follow Codex Germanensis, the royal manuscript, Corbie, Carnutum, and others.].

John cannot loosen the sandal strap of Christ because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, cannot sufficiently investigate its mystery. What, then, does it mean to say, “I am not worthy to loosen his sandal strap,” except openly and humbly to profess his ignorance? It is as though he plainly said: “What wonder is it that he is preferred to me, whom I consider to have been born after me, but whose birth-mystery I cannot comprehend?” [Col. 1102D]

Behold, John, filled with the spirit of prophecy, shines with marvelous knowledge, and yet indicates what he does not know.

## 4

In this matter, dearly beloved brothers, [Col. 1102B] we must reflect and think with our whole attention on how holy men, so that they may preserve the virtue of humility within themselves, when they know certain things miraculously, nevertheless strive to call before the eyes of their minds what they do not know, so that, while they consider their weakness on one side, their mind may not become proud on the side on which it is perfected.

[Note: The Vulgate reads “on which they are perfected”; all the manuscripts disagree.]

Knowledge is indeed a virtue, but humility is the guardian of virtue. Therefore the mind must humble itself in everything it knows, lest the wind of conceit carry away what the virtue of knowledge gathers together.

[Note: Turon., C. Germ., and others read “carry away”; the printed editions read “scatter.”]

When you do good, brothers, always recall your evil deeds, so that, while your fault is carefully observed, your mind may never rejoice carelessly over a good work. Look to one another’s superiors—especially those who have not been entrusted to you—as your neighbors, because, when you see some of them committing evil deeds, you do not know what good things may lie hidden within them. Let each person therefore strive to be great, but in some way remain unaware of being so, lest, while he arrogantly attributes greatness to himself, he lose it.

[Note: After “lose it,” the editions add “what it had within.”]

For this reason it is said through the prophet: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). Hence Paul says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Romans 12:16). Conversely, to the proud Saul it is said: “When you were little in your own eyes, you became head among the tribes of Israel” (1 Samuel 15:17). It is as though he were plainly told: “When you regarded yourself as little, I made you great above the others. But because you regard yourself as great, you are judged little by me.”

By contrast, when David despised the power of his kingdom by dancing before the ark of the Lord’s covenant, he said: “I will play, and I will make myself still lower than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Samuel 6:22).

What would not have exalted him: breaking the jaws of lions, crushing the arms of bears, being chosen over his older brothers, being anointed to the helm of the kingdom after the rejected king, striking down Goliath—feared by everyone—with a single stone, bringing back a great number of Philistine foreskins after slaughtering the foreign enemies at the king’s command, receiving the kingdom by promise, and afterward possessing the whole Israelite people without any further opposition? [Col. 1102D–1103A]

[Note: Some editions read “the tabernacles” instead of “the helm.”]

[Note: Gussanv. reads “possessing the people by opposition.”]

Yet in all these things he despises himself, confessing that he is humble in his own eyes.

If, then, holy men, even when they perform mighty deeds, think little of themselves, what will those say in their defense who swell with pride without any work of virtue? But even if any good works are present, they are nothing unless they are seasoned with humility.

[Note: Belvac. and others read “but any good works whatsoever.”]

A remarkable deed accompanied by pride does not exalt but burdens. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind; and from the very place where he is seen to bear something, he is blinded more grievously.

In everything you do, therefore, my brothers, hold humility as the root of the good work. Do not look at those over whom you are already superior, but at those to whom you are still inferior, so that, while you set before yourselves the examples of better people, you may always be able through humility to rise to greater things.

[Note: C. Germ. and Turon. add “with the Lord our Jesus Christ granting it.” Turon. further adds: “to whom are honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”]

## HOMILY VIII

Preached to the people in the basilica of the Blessed Virgin Mary, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

### Reading of the Holy Gospel according to Luke 2:1–14

At that time, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. This registration was the first, when Quirinius was governor of Syria. And everyone went to be registered, each to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant.

And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth.

[Note: Belv. has “Mary’s days were fulfilled, so that she might give birth.”]

And she gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for him in the lodging. [Col. 1103C]

And there were shepherds in that same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and the glory of God shone around them, and they were afraid with great fear. And the angel said to them: “Do not be afraid. For behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, a host praising God and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

[Note: The word “host” is absent from the manuscripts C. Germ., Belv., and Bigot. Shortly afterward, Corb. Germ. and Belv. read “in the highest places” instead of “in the highest.”]

Since, by the Lord’s generosity, we are going to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass three times today, we cannot speak at length about the Gospel reading. Yet the very nativity of our Redeemer compels us to say at least something briefly. [1460]

What does it mean that, when the Lord was about to be born, the world was registered, except that it openly shows that the one who would register his elect in eternity was coming in the flesh?

[Note: The printed editions read “because he appeared in the flesh.”]

Conversely, the prophet says of the reprobate: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Psalm 68:29).

He is also rightly born in Bethlehem. Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread.” For he himself is the one who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41, 52). The place, therefore, where the Lord is born was previously called “house of bread,” because it was certainly destined that there he should appear through the substance of flesh who would refresh the minds of the elect with inward nourishment.

He is born not in his parents’ house but on the road, clearly showing that, through the humanity he had assumed, he was born as though in a foreign place. I say “foreign” not according to his power but according to his nature. For of his power it is written: “He came to his own” (John 1:11). In his own nature he was born before time; in ours he came in time. Therefore, although remaining eternal, when he appeared as one subject to time, the place into which he descended was foreign. [Col. 1104B]

And because it is said through the prophet: “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6), having become human he turned our grass into grain—the one who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). Hence, too, once born, he is laid in a manger, so that he might refresh all the faithful, the holy animals, with the grain of his flesh, lest they remain hungry for the nourishment of eternal understanding.

[Note: Carnut. 1 and a few others read “lest they remain without the nourishment of inward understanding.”]

But what does it mean that an angel appears to the shepherds while they are keeping watch, and that the glory of God shines around them, except that those who know how to watch attentively over faithful flocks deserve, more than others, to see heavenly things?

[Note: Belvac. and C. Germ. read “are concerned.”]

While they themselves devoutly keep watch over the flock, divine grace shines more abundantly upon them. [Col. 1104C]

## 2

An angel announces that a king has been born, and choirs of angels sing in harmony with his voice, crying out together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

Before our Redeemer was born in the flesh, we were at odds with the angels. Because of the deserts of our first sin and our daily offenses, we were far removed from their brightness and purity. Since by sinning we had become strangers to God, the angels, citizens of God, regarded us as strangers to their fellowship. But once we acknowledged our King, the angels acknowledged us as their fellow citizens.

Because the King of heaven assumed the flesh of our earth, that angelic height no longer despises our weakness. The angels return to peace with us; they set aside their former hostility; and those whom they had previously despised as weak and rejected, they now honor as companions.

For this reason Lot (Genesis 19:1) and Joshua (Joshua 5:15) worship angels, and yet are not forbidden to worship. John, moreover, in his Apocalypse, wished to worship an angel, but the same angel restrained him from worshiping him, saying: “See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Revelation 22:9).

[Note: Turon., Corb. Germ., Belvac., Gemet., and others read “that Lot or Joshua,” where “or” is understood as the conjunctive particle “and.”]

[Note: The word “his” is absent from Turon. and several others.]

What does it mean that, before the Redeemer’s coming, angels allowed themselves to be worshiped by human beings and remained silent, but afterward refused to be worshiped, except that, once they saw our nature—which they had previously despised—assumed above them, they feared to see it subjected beneath them? They no longer dared to scorn as weak beneath themselves the nature that they revered above themselves in the King of heaven. Nor do they disdain to have a human being as their companion, since above themselves they worship a human being who is God.

Let us therefore take care, dearly beloved brothers, that no impurity defile us, since in God’s eternal foreknowledge we are both citizens of God and equal to his angels. Let us vindicate our dignity by our conduct. Let no lust stain us; let no shameful thought accuse us; let no malice gnaw at our minds; let not the rust of envy consume us; let not pride inflate us; let not ambition tear us apart through earthly pleasures.

[Note: This sentence is absent from Belv., Corb., and C. German.]

Let anger not set us ablaze. Human beings have indeed been called gods. Therefore, O human being, defend for yourself, against the vices, the honor of God, because for your sake God became human—the one who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY IX

Preached to the people in the basilica of Saint Silvester, on the day of his nativity.

[Note: This is how it is read in all our manuscripts, but nowhere is “Felix” found; Gussanv. recorded it as a variant reading. In two older Gemet. manuscripts, “of Pope Silvester” is read; in another, “of the bishop.” In the Roman calendar edited by John Fronton, which he thinks was written before the year 731, a different Gospel is assigned to the feast of Saint Silvester.]

### Reading of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew 25:14–30

At that time, Jesus told his disciples this parable:

“A certain man going abroad called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and immediately he went away. [Col. 1105C]

The one who had received five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five. Likewise, the one who had received two gained another two. But the one who had received one went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money.

After a long time the lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them. The one who had received five talents approached and offered another five talents, saying: ‘Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained another five besides them.’

His lord said to him: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

The one who had received two talents also approached and said: ‘Lord, you gave me two talents; behold, I have gained another two.’

[Note: Corb. Germ. and Norm. read simply, “I have gained.”]

His lord said to him: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

The one who had received the one talent also approached and said: ‘Lord, I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter. And, being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the ground. Behold, you have what is yours.’

But his lord answered and said to him: ‘Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter. Therefore you ought to have given my money to the money-changers, so that, when I came, I might at least have received what was mine with interest.’

[Note: C. Germ., Belv., and Bigot. read “to entrust.”]

‘Take therefore the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents. For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away. And cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’”

## 1

The reading of the Holy Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, warns us to consider carefully lest we who are seen to have received more than others in this world from the author of the world should therefore be judged more severely. For when gifts increase, the accounts of the gifts also increase. Therefore each person ought to be more humble and more ready to serve in proportion to the gift by which he sees himself more deeply obligated to render an account. [Col. 1106B]

Behold, the man who goes abroad calls his servants and distributes talents among them for business. After a long time he returns to settle accounts, rewards those who have worked well for the profit they have brought, but condemns the servant who has grown sluggish in good work.

Who, then, is this man who goes abroad, except our Redeemer, who, in the flesh he had assumed, went up into heaven? For the proper place of flesh is the earth, and it is led as though into a foreign place when, through our Redeemer, it is established in heaven.

[Note: Belvac. reads “as though a foreigner.”]

But this man going abroad entrusted his possessions to his servants because he granted spiritual gifts to his faithful people. To one he entrusted five talents, to another two, and to another one.

There are five bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. The gift of the five senses, that is, knowledge of outward things, is therefore expressed by the five talents. By the two, understanding and action are signified. By the name of the one talent, understanding alone is signified. [Col. 1106C]

But the one who had received five talents gained another five, because there are some who, although they do not know how to penetrate inward and mystical things, nevertheless, with a view to the heavenly homeland, teach those whom they can what is right from the outward things they have received. While they guard themselves from the wantonness of the flesh, from the pursuit of earthly things, and from delight in visible things, they also restrain others from these by admonishing them.

There are also some who, as though enriched with two talents, receive understanding and action: they understand subtle things concerning inward realities and perform marvelous works outwardly.

More recent editions add “they bear a double talent,” a phrase absent from both the older printed editions and the manuscripts.

And while they preach to others both by understanding and by action, they bring back, as it were, a doubled profit from their business.

It is rightly reported that another five or another two came as profit, because when preaching is given to both sexes, the talents received are, as it were, doubled.

[Note: Carnot. 1 reads “for both sexes.”]

But the one who had received one talent went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money. To hide a talent in the ground is to involve the received ability in earthly activities, not to seek spiritual profit, and never to lift the heart above earthly thoughts.

There are indeed some who have received the gift of understanding but nevertheless think only about the things of the flesh. Of them it is said through the prophet: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jeremiah 4:22).

But the Lord, who bestowed the talents, returns to settle accounts, because the one who now mercifully grants spiritual gifts will strictly demand an account of merits in judgment. He considers what each person has received and weighs what profit each has brought from what was received.

## 2

The servant who brings back doubled talents is praised by his lord and brought to eternal reward, when the lord’s voice says to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

[Note: The editions read “is introduced” instead of “is brought.”]

All the good things of the present life are little in comparison with eternal reward, however numerous they may appear.

[Note: This is absent from Belv., Corb., the two oldest Gemet., the two Carnut., and Longip. It is found in C. Germ., written by another hand, but an ancient one.]

But the faithful servant is set over much when, after every corruption has been overcome, he rejoices in eternal joys in that heavenly dwelling. He is perfectly admitted into his lord’s joy when, taken up into that eternal homeland and joined to the choirs of angels, he rejoices inwardly in the gift in such a way that there is nothing outwardly left for him to grieve over because of corruption. [1465]

## 3

But the servant who did not wish to work with the talent returns to his lord with words of excuse, saying: “Lord, I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter. And, being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the ground. Behold, you have what is yours.”

It should be noted that the useless servant calls his lord hard, although he evades serving him for profit. He says that he was afraid to expend the talent for profit, though he ought to have feared only that he might return it to his lord without profit.

There are many within the holy Church whom this servant represents. They fear to undertake the paths of a better life, yet do not fear to lie inert in the laziness of their own sluggishness. When they consider themselves sinners, they hesitate to seize the paths of holiness, but they do not fear to remain in their sins.

Peter, while he was still in weakness, aptly represents them when, having seen the miracle of the fish, he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8).

Indeed, if you consider yourself a sinner, you ought not to drive the Lord away from you.

[Note: Two Carnut. manuscripts add “in truth.”]

But those who refuse to seize the paths of a better state of life and the summit of a more upright life because they see themselves as weak both confess themselves sinners and drive the Lord away. They flee from the one whom they ought to have sanctified within themselves, and, as though in confusion they have no counsel, they die while fearing life.

[Note: C. Germ., Belv., and the better manuscripts read “whom they ought to have sanctified within themselves”; the printed editions read “in whom they ought to be sanctified.”]

Therefore the following is immediately said to this servant: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter. Therefore you ought to have given my money to the money-changers, so that, when I came, I might at least have received what was mine with interest.” [Col. 1108A]

The servant is trapped by his own words when the lord says: “I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter.” It is as though he plainly said: “If, according to your judgment, I demand even what I did not give, how much more do I demand from you what I gave for distribution! Therefore you ought to have given my money to the money-changers, so that, when I came, I might at least have received what was mine with interest.”

[Note: Here the lacuna of two lines has been filled from the manuscripts and ancient editions.]

To give money to the money-changers is to impart the knowledge of preaching to those who are able to exercise it.

## 4

But just as you see our danger if we retain the Lord’s money, so, dearly beloved brothers, consider carefully your own danger, because what you hear is demanded from you with interest. With interest, even money that was not given is received. For when what was received is returned, something additional is also paid that was not received.

Consider, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, that you will pay interest on this money of the word that you have received. Take care that, from what you hear, you also strive to understand other things that you do not hear, so that, gathering one thing from another, you may learn from yourselves to do even those things that you have not yet learned from the preacher’s mouth.

Let us hear by what sentence the lazy servant is struck: “Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.” [Col. 1108B]

## 5

It seemed very appropriate that, when the one talent is taken from the wicked servant, it should be given rather to the one who had received two talents than to the one who had received five. It ought to have been given to the one who had less rather than to the one who had more.

[Note: The editions have supplied “more,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]

But, as we said above, the five talents signify the five senses, that is, knowledge of outward things; the two signify understanding and action. Therefore the one who had received two talents had more than the one who had received five, because the one who earned the administration of outward things through the five talents was still lacking understanding of inward things.

The one talent, therefore, which we said signifies understanding, ought to have been given to the one who had faithfully administered the outward things he had received. We see this happening every day in the holy Church: many, while faithfully administering the outward things they receive, are led through the added grace to mystical understanding, so that those who faithfully administer outward matters also grow strong in inward understanding. [Col. 1108C]

## 6

A general sentence is immediately added: “For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.”

To the one who has, more will be given, and he will abound, because whoever has charity also receives other gifts. Whoever does not have charity loses even the gifts he seemed to have received.

Therefore, my brothers, it is necessary for you to watch over the preservation of charity in everything you do. True charity is to love a friend in God and to love an enemy for God’s sake.

Whoever does not have this loses every good thing he possesses, is deprived of the talent he had received, and, according to the Lord’s sentence, is cast into the outer darkness. He falls into the outer darkness as punishment who, through his fault, willingly fell into the inner darkness; and there he is compelled to suffer the darkness of retribution who here willingly endured the darkness of pleasure.

[Note: Corb. and Belv. read “the darkness of the will.”]

## 7

It must also be understood that no lazy person is secure from receiving a talent. No one can truthfully say: “I received no talent at all; there is nothing for which I can be compelled to render an account.”

For, under the name of a talent, even this will be reckoned to any poor person: that he received something, however little. One person has received understanding; from his talent he owes the ministry of preaching. Another has received earthly wealth; from his possessions he owes the distribution of his talent. Another has received neither inward understanding nor abundance of possessions, but has nevertheless learned a trade by which he makes his living; that very trade is reckoned to him as the reception of a talent.

Another has attained none of these things, but perhaps has earned a position of intimacy with a rich person; he has certainly received the talent of intimacy. If, then, he says nothing to him on behalf of the needy, he is condemned for retaining his talent.

Let the one who has understanding take great care not to remain silent. Let the one who has an abundance of possessions watch lest he grow sluggish in generosity toward mercy. Let the one who has a trade by which he supports himself earnestly strive to share its use and benefit with his neighbor. Let the one who has access to speak with a rich person fear condemnation for retaining his talent if, when he is able, he does not intercede with that person for the poor.

The coming Judge will demand from each of us as much as he has given. Therefore, so that each person may be secure concerning the account of his talent when the Lord returns, let him consider daily, with trembling, what he has received. [Col. 1109C]

For behold, it is already near that the one who went abroad will return. He went away, as it were, because he departed far from this earth in which he was born. But he certainly returns to settle accounts concerning the talents, because, if we grow sluggish in good action, he will judge us more strictly concerning the very gifts he bestowed.

[Note: Val. Cl. reads “concerning those very good things.”]

Let us therefore consider what we have received and remain watchful in distributing it. Let no earthly concern hinder us from spiritual work, lest, if the talent is hidden in the earth, the lord of the talent be provoked to anger.

For the lazy servant lifts the talent from the earth when the Judge is already examining sins. There are many who then withdraw themselves from earthly desires or works, when they are already being dragged by the Judge’s sentence to eternal punishment.

[Note: Corb. reads “from earthly obligations.” Turon. reads “from earthly desires, thoughts, or works.”]

Let us therefore be watchful beforehand concerning the account to be rendered for our talent, so that, when the Judge is already approaching to strike, the profit we have made may excuse us. May God grant this to us, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY X

[Note: It is the ninth in the Swedish Royal Manuscript.]

Preached to the people in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, on the feast of the Epiphany.

[Note: Belv. reads “of the Theophany.”]

### Reading of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew 2:1–12

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.”

When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. They said to him: “In Bethlehem of Judea. For so it is written through the prophet:

‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you will come a ruler who will govern my people Israel.’”

Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him.”

When they had heard the king, they went away. And behold, the star that they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above the place where the child was. Seeing the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they worshiped him. And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way.

## 1

As you heard in the Gospel reading, dearly beloved brothers, when the King of heaven was born, the king of earth was troubled, because earthly height is confounded when heavenly exaltation is revealed.

But we must ask why, when the Redeemer was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds in Judea, while the Magi from the East were led to worship him not by an angel but by a star.

The reason is that the Jews, as beings who used reason, ought to have been preached to by a rational creature, that is, an angel.

[Note: This refers to the outward human form which angels customarily assume, though Saint Gregory elsewhere declares them incorporeal. See *Dialogues* IV.29, where he asks his disciple: “Tell me, I pray, do you suppose apostate spirits . . . to be bodily or incorporeal?” Peter replies: “Who, being of sound mind, would call spirits bodily?”]

But the Gentiles, because they did not know how to use reason, were led to know the Lord not by a voice but by signs.

[Note: From “but by signs” to “to unbelievers,” this is absent from the manuscripts Belv., C. Germ., two Carnut., Big., and one Gemet.]

Hence Paul also says: “Prophecies are given to believers, not to unbelievers; but signs to unbelievers, not to believers” (1 Corinthians 14:22). Prophecies were given to the former as believers, not as unbelievers; signs were given to the latter as unbelievers, not as believers.

It should also be noted that, when our Redeemer had reached mature age, the apostles preached him to these same Gentiles; but while he was still a little child and not yet speaking through the functions of a human body, a star announced him to the Gentiles. The order of reason required that, once the Lord was speaking, speaking preachers should make him known to us, while mute elements should preach him when he was not yet speaking. [Col. 1110C–1111A]

## 2

But in all the signs that were displayed either at the Lord’s birth or at his death, we must consider how great was the hardness of heart in certain Jews, who recognized him neither through the gift of prophecy nor through miracles.

All the elements testified that their Creator had come. To speak of them in human terms, heaven recognized that he was God, because it immediately sent the star. The sea recognized him, because it offered itself to be trodden beneath his feet. The earth recognized him, because it trembled at his death. The sun recognized him, because it hid the rays of its light. Stones and walls recognized him, because they were split at the time of his death. The underworld recognized him, because it restored the dead whom it held.

And yet the hearts of unbelieving Jews do not recognize as God the one whom all the insensible elements perceived as Lord. Harder than stones, they do not wish to be split open for repentance, and they deny confessing him whom the elements, as we have said, proclaimed as God either by signs or by being split apart.

[Note: Corb. Germ., three Gemet., and Val. Cl. read “the one whom all the elements recognized as God.”]

To increase the burden of their condemnation, they had long before foreseen the one whose birth they despised. They knew not only that he would be born, but also where he would be born. When questioned by Herod, they specify the place of his birth, which they had learned from the authority of Scripture. They produce the testimony showing that Bethlehem would be honored by the birth of a new ruler, so that their very knowledge would become for them a testimony of condemnation and for us an aid to faith.

[Note: Belv. and C. Germ. read “their twofold knowledge.”]

Isaac aptly represented them when he blessed his son Jacob (Genesis 27:28 ff.). Though his eyes were dim and he was prophesying, he did not see his son in the present, although he foresaw so many things about him in the future. In the same way, the Jewish people, full of the spirit of prophecy yet blind, did not recognize in the present the one about whom they had foretold so many future things. [Col. 1111C]

## 3

When Herod learned of the birth of our King, he turned to crafty schemes lest he be deprived of his earthly kingdom. He asks to be informed where the child might be found and pretends that he wishes to worship him, so that, as though he might find him, he could destroy him.

[Note: We are compelled to read this on the strong consensus of the manuscripts. The printed editions have “so that, if he could find him, he might destroy him.”]

But how great is human wickedness against the purpose of God! For it is written: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30).

The star that had appeared leads the Magi onward. They find the newborn King and bring gifts, and they are warned in a dream not to return to Herod. Thus it happens that Herod cannot find Jesus, whom he seeks.

[Note: Corb. and Corb. Germ. read “whose character is represented by those who pursue some matter hypocritically.”]

And whom does Herod’s character represent except the hypocrite, who, while pretending to seek, never deserves to find the Lord?

## 4

But it must be known that the heretics called Priscillianists believe that every human being is born under the configurations of the stars. In support of their error they seize upon the fact that a new star appeared when the Lord appeared in the flesh; they think that the star that appeared was his fate.

But if we consider the words of the Gospel, which say of that star, “until it came and stood above where the child was,” then, since it was not the child who ran to the star but the star to the child, so to speak, the star was not the child’s fate; rather, the child who appeared was the star’s fate.

But may it be far from the hearts of the faithful to say that there is such a thing as fate. The Creator alone, who created human life, governs it. For human beings were not made for the sake of the stars; rather, the stars were made for the sake of human beings. And if a star is called a person’s fate, the person is said to be subject to his own servants.

Certainly, when Jacob, coming forth from the womb, held the heel of his older brother in his hand (Genesis 25:25), the elder could not have come forth completely unless the younger had also begun to emerge. Yet although the mother brought forth both at the same time and in the same moment, the quality of their lives was not the same.

[Note: Longip. and Val. Cl. read “the equality of their lives.”]

5. But to this mathematicians are accustomed to reply that the power of a constellation lies in the instant of the point of birth [Note: [Col. 1112D] All our manuscripts except Belv. read “at the stroke of the goad” (in ictu pungentis), and later “at the stroke of the point” (in ictu puncti)]. To them we answer, on the contrary, that there is a considerable delay in the process of birth. If, then, the constellation changes in the instant of the point, it will now be necessary for them to say that there are as many fates as there are limbs of those being born. Mathematicians also commonly admit that whoever [Note: [Col. 1112D] Absent in Belv., C. Germ., Gemet., etc.] is born under the sign of Aquarius is destined in this life for the occupation of a fisherman [Note: [Col. 1112D] Belv. and C. Germ., “service” (ministerio)]. But, as is reported, Getulia has no fishermen. Who, then, could say that no one there is born under the star of Aquarius, [Col. 1112C] where there is absolutely no fisherman? Again, those whom they assert to be born under the sign of Libra they say will become money-changers; yet the provinces of many nations know no money-changers. They must therefore admit either that this sign is absent among them or that its fatal effect has no force at all. In the lands of the Persians and the Franks, too, kings arise from a lineage. Who, when these kings are born, could reckon how many are born from servile condition at those same instants of hours and times? And yet the sons of kings, born under the same star as slaves, advance to kingship, while the slaves who were begotten with them [Note: [Col. 1112D] The first two Gemet. and Big. read nati, “born.”] die in servitude. We have said this briefly about the star, lest we seem to have passed over the folly of the mathematicians without examination.

[Col. 1112D] 6. The Magi, moreover, offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Gold is fitting for a king; frankincense was placed in sacrifice to God; and with myrrh the bodies of the dead are embalmed. Thus the Magi proclaim, by the mystical gifts they offer, the one whom they adore: a king by gold, God by frankincense, and mortal by myrrh. There are, however, certain heretics who believe that he is God, but by no means believe that he reigns everywhere. These certainly offer him frankincense, but refuse to offer gold as well. There are others who regard him as a king but deny that he is God. These, plainly, offer him gold, but refuse to offer frankincense. And there are others who confess that he is both God and king, but deny that he assumed mortal flesh. These indeed offer him gold and frankincense, but refuse to offer myrrh for his assumed mortality.

Let us therefore offer gold to the Lord at his birth, so that we may confess that he reigns everywhere; let us offer frankincense, so that we may believe that the one who appeared in time existed as God before time; let us offer myrrh, so that, while we believe him impassible in his divinity, we may also believe that in our flesh he was mortal. Yet gold, frankincense, and myrrh may also be understood in another way. Gold signifies wisdom, as Solomon testifies when he says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. XXI, 20, according to the Septuagint). By the frankincense burned for God the power of prayer is expressed, as the Psalmist bears witness when he says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). By myrrh the mortification of our flesh is represented; hence holy Church says of her workers who contend for God unto death: “My hands dripped with myrrh” (Song V, 5).

We therefore offer gold to the newborn King if we shine before him with the splendor of heavenly wisdom [Note: [Col. 1113D] Turon., “we shine with the light of the splendor of the heavenly homeland.” C. Germ., “we shine with the light of the splendor of heavenly wisdom.”]. We offer frankincense if, through the holy practice of prayer, we burn the thoughts of the flesh on the altar of our hearts, so that by heavenly desire we may be able to give off a fragrance pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 1113D] Secundus Carn., “if we burn the desires of the flesh.”]. We offer myrrh if through abstinence we mortify the vices of the flesh. For, as we have said, myrrh is used to prevent dead flesh from rotting. Dead flesh rotting means that this mortal body serves the corruption of lust, as the prophet says of certain people: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I, 17). For beasts to rot in their dung means that carnal people bring their lives to an end in the stench of lust. We therefore offer myrrh to God when, through the seasoning of continence, we preserve this mortal body from the corruption of lust.

7. The Magi also suggest something of great importance to us by returning to their own country by another way. In what they do after being warned, they plainly indicate what we ought to do. Our country is paradise; after coming to know Jesus, we are forbidden to return to it by the way on which we came. We departed from our country by growing proud, disobeying, pursuing visible things, and tasting the forbidden food [Note: [Col. 1113D] The first two Gemet., “by eating” (comedendo)]; but we must return to it by weeping, obeying, despising visible things, and restraining the appetite of the flesh. We therefore return to our country by another way, because we who departed from the joys of paradise through pleasures are recalled to them through lamentation.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must always be fearful and always wary, placing before the eyes of our hearts on one side the sins of our conduct and on the other the judgment of the final severity. Let us consider how strict the Judge will be when he comes: he threatens judgment and yet remains hidden; he threatens sinners with terrors and nevertheless still bears with them. For this reason he delays his coming, so that he may find fewer whom he must condemn. Let us punish our sins with tears, and with the Psalmist’s voice let us come before his presence in confession (Ps. XCIV, 2). Let no deception of pleasures mislead us; let no empty joy seduce us. The Judge is near, who said: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI, 25). Hence Solomon says: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning will take possession of the end of joy” (Prov. XIV, 13). Again he says: “I counted laughter as error, and to joy I said: Why are you deceived in vain?” [Col. 1114B] (Eccl. II, 2). Again he says: “The heart of the wise is where sadness is, and the heart of fools where joy is” (ibid., 75).

Let us therefore fear God’s commandments if we truly celebrate God’s solemn feast. Affliction directed against sin is a sacrifice pleasing to God, as the Psalmist testifies: “The sacrifice acceptable to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. L, 19). Our past sins were released at the reception of baptism [Note: [Col. 1113D] Corb., secundus Carn., Gemet., Bigot., “were forgiven.” C. Germ. and primus Carn., “were erased.”], yet after baptism we have committed many more sins, and we cannot again be washed with baptismal water. Since, therefore, after baptism we have defiled our life, let us baptize our conscience with tears, so that, returning to our country by another way, we who departed from it delighted by good things may return to it embittered by evil things, through the favor of our Lord, and so forth.

# HOMILY XI

[Note: [Col. 1114D] In Corb. it is the thirty-third; in the Swedish royal manuscript, the thirty-seventh. In all manuscripts it is said to have been delivered on the feast of Saint Agnes, or Agna.]

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Agnes, on the day of her nativity.

## LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW XIII, 44–52

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples [Note: [Col. 1114D] Bigot., “the Lord Jesus.” In Belvac. this parable is omitted.]: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and out of joy over it he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he has found one precious pearl, he goes and sells everything he has and buys it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out, and sitting beside the shore they selected the good fish into vessels, but threw the bad away. So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and throw them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Have you understood all these things?” [Note: [Col. 1114D] Belvac. and C. Germ., “They say to him: Yes.”] They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.” He said to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.”

1472 1. Dearest brothers, the kingdom of heaven is said to be like earthly things for this reason: so that from things the mind knows it may rise to things unknown [Note: [Col. 1115D] We have rejected “which it does not know” (quae non novit), found in other editions, for it is absent from Turon. and the better manuscripts; it occurs in C. Germ., but not in the first hand.]. Thus, through the example of visible things, it may be carried toward invisible things, and through what it has learned by experience it may, as though rubbed, grow warm, so that through loving what is known it may also learn to love things unknown.

For behold, the kingdom of heaven is compared to a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides, and out of joy over it goes and sells everything he has and buys that field. Here we must also note that the treasure found is hidden so that it may be preserved, because the person who does not hide the pursuit of heavenly desire from human praise is not sufficiently able to guard it from evil spirits.

In the present life we are, as it were, on a road [Note: [Col. 1115D] Corb. Germ., Longip., Val. Cl., “because we are journeying toward our homeland.”] by which we are traveling toward our homeland. Evil spirits lie in ambush along our road like bandits. Therefore the person who carries his treasure openly on the road desires to be robbed. I say this not so that our neighbors should fail to see our good works [Note: [Col. 1115D] This word is omitted in C. Germ., Turon., Belv., and the first two Gemet.], since it is written: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16), but so that through what we do we should not seek praise outwardly. Let the work therefore be public in such a way that the intention remains hidden: thus we may offer our neighbors an example through our good work, while through the intention by which we seek to please God alone we may always desire secrecy.

The treasure is heavenly desire; the field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of the pursuit of heaven. Whoever renounces the pleasures of the flesh and tramples all earthly desires beneath the guardianship of heavenly discipline buys this field by selling everything, so that nothing which flatters the flesh is now pleasing to him, and nothing which slays the life of the flesh is dreaded by his spirit.

2. Again, the kingdom of heaven is said to be like a merchant who seeks good pearls but finds one precious pearl. Once he has found it, he sells everything and buys it, because whoever has perfectly understood, insofar as human ability permits, the sweetness of heavenly life willingly abandons everything he had loved on earth. In comparison with it, everything becomes worthless: he abandons what he possesses, scatters what he has gathered, and his mind burns with desire for heavenly things. Nothing earthly pleases him; whatever had pleased him in the appearance of earthly possessions is seen as deformed, because only the splendor of the precious pearl shines in his mind.

Of the love of this pearl Solomon rightly says: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII, 6), because just as death destroys the body, so the love of eternal life kills the love of bodily things. For whoever it has perfectly absorbed, it renders outwardly indifferent to earthly desires [Note: [Col. 1116D] In secundus Carnot. the reading is desideria nequaquam sancto velut (“desires—not at all—as if holy”), an apparently disordered variant.].

3. Indeed, this holy woman whose nativity we celebrate today could not have died for God in the body if she had not first died in mind to earthly desires. Her mind, raised to the summit of virtue, scorned torments and trampled rewards beneath its feet. Led before armed kings and governors [Note: [Col. 1116D] Printed editions, “unconquered”; the manuscripts read “while they resisted.”], she stood there stronger than the one who struck her and higher than the one who judged her.

What do we bearded and feeble men say amid these things, when we see girls going through iron to the heavenly kingdoms—men whom anger overcomes, pride inflates, ambition disturbs, and lust defiles? If we cannot attain the kingdom of heaven through the battles of persecution, let it at least be shameful for us that we do not wish to follow God even through peace [Note: [Col. 1116D] C. Germ., “let this very thing be a fear to us.”]. Behold, at this time God says to none of us, “Die for me,” but only: “Kill in yourself unlawful desires.” If, therefore, we are unwilling to subdue the desires of the flesh in peace, when would we give that very flesh for the Lord in war?

4. Again, the kingdom of heaven is said to be like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it is full, it is drawn to the shore, and the good fish are selected into vessels, while the bad are thrown out. The holy Church is compared to a net [Note: [Col. 1116D] Belv., “which has been cast by fishermen.”], because it has been entrusted to fishermen and through it each person is drawn from the waves of the present age toward the eternal kingdom, lest he be submerged in the depths of eternal death.

It gathers fish of every kind because it calls the wise and foolish, free and enslaved, rich and poor, strong and weak to the forgiveness of sins. Hence the Psalmist says to God: “All flesh shall come to you” (Ps. LXIV, 3). The net is filled universally when the whole of the human race is brought to its conclusion at the end. They draw it out and sit beside the shore, because just as the sea signifies the world, so the shore of the sea signifies the end of the world.

At that end the good fish are selected into vessels, while the bad are thrown out, because each of the elect is received into eternal dwellings, whereas, deprived of the light of the inner kingdom, the rejected are dragged into outer darkness. Now the net of faith holds the good and the bad together as mixed fish; but the shore reveals what the net—that is, the holy Church—has drawn in. Fish that have been caught cannot be changed; we, however, are caught while bad and are changed into goodness. Let us therefore consider our capture, lest we be separated on the shore.

Behold how pleasing today’s solemnity is to you, so that it would be no small loss to anyone who happened to be absent from this gathering of yours. What, then, will the one do on that day who is torn away from the sight of the Judge, separated from the company of the elect, darkened by the loss of light, and tormented by eternal burning? Hence the Lord briefly explains this same comparison when he adds: “So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and throw them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Dearest brothers, this is now something to fear rather than explain. The torments of sinners have been declared in clear words, lest anyone resort to ignorance as an excuse if something concerning eternal punishment [Note: [Col. 1117D] Primus Carnot., “judgment” (judicio).] were said obscurely. Hence it is also added: “Have you understood all these things?” They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.”

4. In conclusion it is added: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.” If by “new and old” we understand both Testaments, we deny that Abraham was instructed, although he knew the deeds of both the New and Old Testaments, since he did not proclaim their words. Nor can we compare Moses to an instructed householder, for although he taught the Old Testament, he did not bring forth the sayings of the New Testament. [Note: [Col. 1117D] This passage, through “but in that,” is absent from Corb. Germ., the other Corb., the first two Gemet., and Bigot.]

Since we are therefore excluded from this interpretation, we are called to another. When the Truth says, “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder” [Note: [Col. 1117D] The first two Gemet., “like a householder.”], it can be understood that he was not speaking of those who had existed, but of those who could exist in the Church. They bring forth things new and old when they speak the teachings of both Testaments through their words and conduct.

Yet this may also be understood in another way. It was ancient for the human race to descend into the chambers of hell and endure eternal punishments for its sins. Through the coming of the Mediator something new was added: if a person strives to live rightly here, he can enter the kingdom of heaven; and a human being born on earth can die to corruptible life in order to be placed in heaven. It is therefore old that the human race should perish in eternal punishment on account of guilt; and it is new that, when converted, it should live in the kingdom.

What the Lord added at the conclusion of his speech is therefore precisely what he had said before. First he brought forth the treasure that had been found and the good pearl as comparisons for the kingdom; afterward he related the punishments of hell through the burning of the wicked; and in conclusion he added: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.” It is as though he had said plainly: “He is an instructed preacher in the holy Church who knows how to bring forth new things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom and to speak old things concerning the terror of punishment, so that those whom rewards do not invite may at least be terrified by punishment. Let each person hear about the kingdom what he may love, and about punishment what he may fear, so that if love does not draw the sluggish mind, which clings intensely to the earth, fear may threaten it.”

For behold, concerning the depiction of Gehenna it is said: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” But since present joys are followed by perpetual lamentation, flee empty joy here, dearest brothers, if you fear weeping there. No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord. Therefore restrain the fleetingness of temporal joy and tame the pleasures of the flesh. Whatever pleases the mind from the present world, let it become bitter through consideration of the eternal fire. Whatever laughs childishly in the mind, let the discipline of youthful judgment restrain it, so that, while you willingly flee temporal things, you may grasp eternal joys without labor, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] In Corb. it is the thirty-fourth; in the Swedish royal manuscript, the thirty-sixth.]

# HOMILY XII

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Agnes, on the day of her nativity [Note: [Col. 1118D] In the same manuscript, in C. Germ., and in the first Gemet., “Saint Agna.”].

## LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW XXV, 1–13

At that time Jesus said this parable to his disciples [Note: [Col. 1118D] C. Germ. and Belvac. do not have “this parable.”]: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish, and five wise. The five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them; but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. While the bridegroom was delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept. But at midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’ Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. The foolish said to the wise: ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ The wise answered, saying: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.’ While they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, and the door was shut. Finally the other virgins came, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ But he answered and said: ‘Amen I say to you, I do not know you.’ Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

1476 1. Dearest brothers, I often exhort you to flee evil deeds and avoid the pollutions of this world; but today’s reading from the holy Gospel compels me to say that you must also fear the good things you do with great caution, lest through what is rightly done by you human favor or approval be sought, lest the desire for praise creep in [Note: [Col. 1118D] Most manuscripts, “steal in.”], and lest what is displayed outwardly be emptied of its reward inwardly.

For behold, in the voice of the Redeemer ten virgins are mentioned, and all are called virgins, yet not all are received within the door of blessedness, because some of them, while seeking glory for their virginity outwardly, did not wish to have oil in their vessels. But we must first ask what the kingdom of heaven is, or why it is compared with ten virgins who are also called wise and foolish. Since it is certain that no reprobate enters the kingdom of heaven, why is it said to be like foolish virgins as well?

We must understand that in sacred speech the Church of the present time is often called the kingdom of heaven. Elsewhere the Lord says of it: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. XIII, 41). For in that kingdom of blessedness, where there is perfect peace, there can be no scandals to gather. Again it is said: “Therefore whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people so, he shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does and teaches them, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., V, 19).

A person loosens a commandment and teaches this when he proclaims in words what he does not fulfill in his life. But he cannot reach the kingdom of eternal blessedness if he refuses to fulfill in his conduct what he teaches. How, then, will he be called least in that kingdom which he is in no way permitted to enter? What, then, is meant by this saying except that the present Church is called the kingdom of heaven? In it, a teacher who has loosened a commandment is called least, because when his life is despised, his preaching likewise remains subject to contempt.

Each person subsists in the five senses of the body; when five is doubled, it completes the number ten. And because the multitude of the faithful is gathered from both sexes, the holy Church is declared to be like ten virgins. Since in it the wicked are mixed with the good and the rejected with the elect, it is rightly said to be like both wise and foolish virgins.
