There are many continent people who guard themselves from external appetite and are carried inwardly by hope; they mortify the flesh and yearn with their whole desire for the heavenly homeland; they seek eternal rewards and refuse to receive human praise for their labors. These certainly do not place their glory in the mouths of human beings but conceal it within their conscience.

There are also many who afflict their bodies through abstinence but seek human favor for that very abstinence; they devote themselves to teaching and give much to those in need. Yet they are plainly foolish virgins, because they seek only the reward of passing praise. Hence it is aptly added: “The five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them; but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.”

By oil the radiance of glory is signified; our vessels are our hearts, in which we carry everything we think. The wise therefore have oil in their vessels, because they retain the radiance of glory within their conscience, as Paul testifies when he says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12). The foolish virgins do not take oil with them, because they do not possess glory within their conscience, while they seek it from the mouths of their neighbors [Note: [Col. 1119D] In Corb. the words that follow, through “because they generally,” are absent.].

It must be noted, however, that all have lamps, but not all have oil, because often the wicked display good works together with the elect, but only those who seek glory inwardly for what they have done outwardly come to the bridegroom with oil. Hence the Psalmist also says of the holy Church of the elect: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV, 14).

2. “While the bridegroom was delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept,” because while the Judge delays coming for the final judgment, the elect and the rejected are lulled into the sleep of death. To sleep means to die. Before sleep, however, to grow drowsy means to weaken in salvation before death, because the sleep of death is reached through the burden of illness.

“At midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’”

3. A cry concerning the bridegroom’s coming is made at midnight because the day of judgment steals upon us in such a way that it cannot be foreseen when it will come. Hence it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thess. V, 2).

Then all the virgins arise, because both the elect and the rejected are awakened from the sleep of their death. They trim their lamps because they reckon up the works they bring with them, for which they expect to receive eternal blessedness. But the lamps of the foolish virgins go out because their works, which had appeared bright to human beings outwardly, are darkened inwardly at the Judge’s coming [Note: [Col. 1119D] Belvac., “and they do not come to receive recompense.”]. They do not receive recompense from God because for them they have already received from human beings the praise they loved.

What is it that they then ask from the wise for oil except that, when they find themselves inwardly empty at the Judge’s coming, they seek testimony outwardly? It is as though, deceived in their self-confidence, they say to their neighbors: “Since you see us rejected as though without works, tell us what you have seen of our works.”

But the wise virgins answer, saying: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” On that day—and here I speak of certain people resting in the peace of the Church—the testimony of each person for himself will scarcely be sufficient; how much less will it suffice both for himself and for his neighbor? Hence they immediately add by way of rebuke: “Go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.”

The sellers of oil are flatterers. Those who, having received some favor, offer the radiance of glory through their empty praises sell oil, as it were. Concerning this oil the Psalmist says: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Ps. CXL, 5). For our ruling faculty is our head. By the designation “head,” the mind that rules the body is meant. The oil of the sinner therefore fattens the head when the favor of the flatterer soothes the mind.

But while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, because while they are seeking testimony about their life from their neighbors, the Judge comes, who is the witness not only of works but also of hearts. “Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, and the door was shut.”

4. O, if the palate of the heart could taste it, what wonder is contained in the words, “The bridegroom came!” What sweetness in, “They entered with him into the wedding feast!” What bitterness in, “The door was shut!”

He came whose arrival shakes the elements, before whose sight heaven and earth tremble [Note: [Col. 1120D] C. Germ., the first two Gemet., and others, “heaven together with earth.” Shortly afterward primus Carnot. and ultimus Gemet., “who on that day.”]. Hence through the prophet he also says: “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Hag. II, 7; Heb. XII, 26). The whole human race is brought before his tribunal. To punish the wicked and reward the good, angels, archangels, thrones, principalities, and dominions attend upon him.

Consider, dearest brothers, what terror there will be on that day before the sight of so great a Judge, when there will no longer be a remedy in punishment; what confusion will seize the one whose guilt demands that he blush in the assembly of all angels and human beings; what fear will overwhelm the one who sees him angry whom the human mind cannot even fully comprehend when tranquil.

The prophet, gazing rightly upon that day, says: “A day of wrath is that day, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zeph. I, 15). Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, with what bitterness the prophet saw the day of the final judgment make the hearts of the rejected bitter; he cannot express it by so many names [Note: [Col. 1121D] C. Germ., Belvac., and the two Carn., “he is unable to exhaust it.”].

How great, however, will be the joy of the elect, who merit to rejoice in his vision, when they see all the elements tremble before his sight and enter the wedding feast together with him! They rejoice in the bridegroom’s wedding, and yet they themselves are the bride, because in the bridal chamber of the eternal kingdom God is joined to our vision [Note: [Col. 1121D] Belvac., Turon., Longip., “who rejoice in the wedding feast.”]. This vision will never thereafter be torn away from the embrace of its love.

Then the door of the kingdom will be closed to those who mourn, although now it is opened daily to those who repent. There will indeed be repentance then, but it will no longer be fruitful, because the one who now loses the time suitable for forgiveness will by no means find forgiveness then. Hence Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). Hence the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. LV, 6).

5. Therefore the Lord does not hear those same foolish virgins when they call, because once the door of the kingdom has been shut, the one who could have been near will no longer be near [Note: [Col. 1121D] Thus simply in Turon., Belvac., C. Germ., etc. In Corb. Germ., however, another hand has added the reading found in the printed editions: “he who now through being heard could be near.”].

For it follows: “Finally the other virgins came, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’” But he answered and said: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you.” There the person who refused here to hear what God commanded cannot merit from God what he asks; having lost the time for appropriate repentance, he comes uselessly with prayers before the door of the kingdom.

Hence the Lord says through Solomon: “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes. I also will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you. When sudden calamity falls upon you and destruction like a storm rushes upon you, when tribulation and distress come upon you, then they will call upon me, and I will not hear; they will rise early and will not find me” (Prov. I, 24 ff.).

Behold, they cry out for the door to be opened [Note: [Col. 1121D] The Gemeticenses, “Behold, they cry out, ‘Open!’”], and compelled by the pain of their rejection, they repeat the title of the one who rules them, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” They offer prayers, but they are not known, because then the Lord abandons as strangers those whom now he does not recognize as his own through the merit of their life.

6. An appropriate general exhortation to the disciples is also added when it is said: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” Since God accepts repentance after sins, if each person knew at what time he would leave the present age, he could assign one period to pleasures and another to repentance. But the one who promised forgiveness to the repentant did not promise tomorrow to the sinner.

We must therefore always fear the final day, which we can never foresee. Behold, we have received this very day on which we are speaking as a reprieve for conversion [Note: [Col. 1121D] Bellovac., “and as a postponement.”], yet we refuse to weep over the evils we have committed. We not only fail to mourn what we have done; we also increase the things that must be mourned. But if some illness attacks us, if signs of illness announce approaching death, we seek a reprieve for living so that we may mourn our sins, and we ask for these reprieves with great ardor of desire [Note: [Col. 1121D] Secundus Carn. and ultimus Gemet., “with a great longing of earnest desire.”], though, once received, we now regard them as nothing.

[Col. 1122B] **7.** I shall relate, dearest brothers, an event from which your charity will be greatly instructed if it wishes to hear it attentively, by reflecting upon it. [Note: [Col. 1122D] The Bellovacensis, German, Longipontanus, and Valerian-Clare manuscripts read, “which, if your charity wishes to attend to it.” The second Carnot manuscript reads, “with attentive ear,” etc.] There was a certain nobleman in the province of Valeria named Chrysaorius, whom the rustic tongue of the people called Chryserius: a man of very considerable means [Note: [Col. 1122D] The second Carnot manuscript, the two earlier Gemeticensis manuscripts, and Bigot read “rich.”], but as full of vices as of possessions; swollen with pride, subject to the pleasures of his flesh, and inflamed with the torches of greed in acquiring property. But when the Lord had determined to put an end to so many evils, he was struck by bodily illness, as I learned from a certain religious man, a relative of his who is still alive.

When he came to his final hour, at the very moment when he was about to depart from the body, he saw, with his eyes open, foul and exceedingly black spirits standing before him and pressing upon him violently [Note: [Col. 1122D] On this word, consult the notes on chapter 38 of Book IV of the Dialogues.], so that they might drag him away to the gates of hell [Col. 1122C]. He began to tremble, grow pale, and sweat, and to beg for a delay in loud cries. He called his son, Maximus by name—whom I myself, already a monk, saw as a monk—with frantic and disordered shouts, saying: “Maximus, hurry! I have never done you any harm. Take me under your protection.” Maximus soon arrived in confusion and mourning, and the household gathered with loud lamentation.

The people present could not see the evil spirits whom he was enduring as they pressed heavily upon him; but they saw their presence in the confusion, pallor, and trembling of the man who was being dragged away. Terrified by the horror of their appearance, he turned this way and that in his bed. He lay on his left side but could not endure their sight; he turned toward the wall, but they were there too. When, being bound with extreme force, he despaired of ever being released [Note: [Col. 1122D] The Corbie manuscript and the German manuscript read “to release.”], he began to cry out in a loud voice: “A delay, at least until morning! A delay, at least until morning!” But while he was crying this out, in the midst of his very cries he was torn from the dwelling of his flesh.

From this it is plainly evident that he saw these things not for himself but for us, so that his vision might benefit us, whom divine patience still awaits with long-suffering. For what benefit did it bring him to see the foul spirits before his death and to beg for a delay, when he did not receive the very delay he requested? Let us therefore, dearest brothers, now carefully consider these things, lest our time pass away uselessly, and lest we seek to live for good works only when we are already being compelled to depart from the body [Note: [Col. 1123D] The same manuscript, together with Bellovacensis and the first Carnot manuscript, reads “to come”].

Remember what the Truth says: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:20). For by the commandment of the Law it is not permitted to walk a long distance on the Sabbath (Exodus 6); and winter too is an impediment to walking [Note: [Col. 1123D] The Tours, German, and Bellovacensis manuscripts read “is an impediment.”], because the numbness of the cold constricts the steps of those who walk. He therefore says: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.” It is as though he openly said: “Take care not to seek to flee from your sins at the time when it is no longer permitted to walk.” That time, therefore, when flight is not permitted must now be considered, while it is still permitted. We must always keep the hour of our departure before our eyes, and always place before our minds this admonition of our Redeemer, in which he says: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

# HOMILY XIII

Preached to the people in the basilica of the blessed Felix the Confessor, on his feast day.

[Note: [Col. 1123D] This is how it is read in the royal Swedish manuscript, the Bellovacensis, the German manuscript, and two Carnot manuscripts. In the Lateran manuscript and the third Gemeticensis only “of blessed Felix” is read. In the printed editions: “of blessed Felix the martyr.” In the royal Swedish manuscript it is the thirty-fourth homily; in the Lateran, the thirty-eighth. Who this Felix was is not clear. In the Sacramentary, 29 July is recorded as the feast of Saint Felix, whom our Hugo Menard, in his notes, proves to have been Felix II, who was substituted for Pope Liberius. See the place cited.]

## Reading of the Holy Gospel according to Luke 12:35–40

At that time Jesus said to his disciples:

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands. And be like men waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding feast, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him. Blessed are those servants whom, when their master comes, he finds watching. Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them. And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants. But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into. Therefore you also be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.”

### 1.

The reading of the holy Gospel which you have just heard, dearest brothers, requires not exposition but admonition. For human frailty does not presume to examine what Truth itself has explained. Yet in this very exposition by the Lord there is something that you ought carefully to consider. If we were to tell you that the seed signifies the word, the field the world, the birds demons, and the thorns riches, perhaps your minds would hesitate to believe us. Therefore the Lord himself deigned to explain what he said, so that you might know to seek the meanings of things even in those matters which he did not himself choose to explain. Thus, by explaining what he had said figuratively, he made known that he was speaking figuratively, in order that he might make you confident when our frailty unfolds for you the figures in his words. For who would ever believe me if I wished to interpret thorns as riches, especially since the former prick and the latter delight? Yet they are thorns, because they tear the mind with the prickings of their thoughts and, when they draw it as far as sin, make it bleed as though by an inflicted wound. Another Evangelist testifies that in this passage the Lord rightly calls them not riches, but deceitful riches (Matthew 13:22). They are deceitful because they cannot remain with us long; they are deceitful because they do not drive away the poverty of our mind. The only true riches are those which make us rich in virtues. Therefore, dearest brothers, if you desire to be rich, love true riches. If you seek the height of true honor, strive toward the heavenly kingdom. If you love the glory of dignities, hasten to be enrolled in that heavenly court of angels.

# HOMILY XIV

[Note: [Col. 1127D] In the Corbie manuscript this is the eighteenth homily; in the royal Swedish manuscript, the tenth; in the Lateran manuscript, the twentieth.]

Preached to the people in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, on the second Sunday after Easter.

[Note: [Col. 1127D] The printed editions read, “of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Only the second Gemeticensis manuscript reads, “the first Sunday after the octave of Easter.”]

## Reading of the Holy Gospel according to John 10:11–16

At that time Jesus said to the Pharisees [Note: [Col. 1128D] The German and Bellovacensis manuscripts and three Gemeticensis manuscripts read “to his disciples.”]:

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep. But the hireling, who is not the shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf seizes and scatters the sheep. The hireling flees because he is a hireling and has no concern for the sheep. I am the good shepherd; I know my sheep, and my sheep know me. Just as the Father knows me and I know the Father, I lay down my life for my sheep. And I have other sheep that are not from this fold; I must bring them too, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd.”

### 1.

You have heard, dearest brothers, the instruction of your faith in the Gospel reading, and you have heard our danger as well. For behold, he who is good not by an accidental gift but essentially says: “I am the good shepherd.” And he adds the form of that goodness for us to imitate, saying: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.”

He did what he commanded; he displayed what he ordered. The good shepherd laid down his life for his sheep, so that in the mystery of our salvation he might transform his body and blood and satisfy the sheep whom he had redeemed with the nourishment of his flesh. The way of contempt for death that we should follow has been shown to us; the pattern to which we should be conformed has been set before us.

Our first duty is mercifully to expend our external possessions for his sheep; our final duty, if necessary, is even to offer our own death for those same sheep [Note: [Col. 1128D] The German manuscript reads “for the same sheep.”]. From the first, lesser duty one reaches the final, greater one. But since the soul by which we live is incomparably better than the earthly substance that we possess outwardly, whoever does not give his substance for the sheep—when will he give his soul for them?

There are some who, because they love earthly substance more than the sheep, rightly lose the name of shepherd. Concerning them it is immediately added: “But the hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.”

### 2.

He is called not a shepherd but a hireling who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of inward love but for temporal rewards. A hireling is one who indeed holds the place of a shepherd but does not seek the profit of souls; he longs for earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of authority, feeds upon temporal gains, and delights in the respect shown him by people [Note: [Col. 1128D] Bigot reads “by all.”].

These are the hireling’s rewards: in return for laboring in governance, he finds here what he seeks, while in the future he remains excluded from the inheritance of the flock.

Whether someone is a shepherd or a hireling cannot truly be known if no occasion of necessity arises. In a time of tranquility, a hireling often stands guard over the flock just as a true shepherd does; but the coming of the wolf reveals with what disposition each had been standing watch over the flock.

The wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and the humble. But the one who seemed to be a shepherd and was not leaves the sheep and flees, because, fearing danger to himself from that person, he does not dare resist his injustice. He flees not by changing his location but by withdrawing his support. He flees because he saw injustice and kept silent. He flees because he hid himself under silence.

To such men the prophet rightly says: “You have not gone up to confront them, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5). To go up to confront someone is to oppose, with the free voice of reason, any authorities who act wickedly. And we stand in battle for the house of Israel on the day of the Lord and set up a wall when, by the authority of justice, we defend faithful and innocent people against the injustice of the wicked. Because the hireling does not do this, when he sees the wolf coming, he flees.

### 3.

But there is another wolf that daily, without ceasing, tears apart not bodies but minds: namely, the evil spirit, which prowls around the folds of the faithful, lying in wait and seeking the deaths of souls. Concerning this wolf it is immediately added: “And the wolf seizes and scatters the sheep.”

The wolf comes and the hireling flees, because the evil spirit tears apart the minds of the faithful in temptation, while the one who holds the shepherd’s place has no care of vigilant concern. Souls perish, and he himself rejoices in earthly advantages.

The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep when he draws one person into lust, inflames another with greed, raises another up in pride, divides another through anger, goads one through envy, and trips another through deceit. Thus the devil scatters the flock when he destroys the people of the faithful through temptations.

But the hireling is stirred by no zeal against these things and awakened by no fervor of love. Since he seeks only external advantages, he carelessly endures the flock’s internal losses. Hence it is immediately added: “But the hireling flees, because he is a hireling, and the sheep are not his concern.”

The sole reason for the hireling’s flight is that he is a hireling. It is as though it were said openly: “He cannot stand in danger for the sheep who, in presiding over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit.” While he embraces honor and rejoices in temporal advantages, he is afraid to oppose himself to danger, lest he lose what he loves.

But because our Redeemer made known the faults of the false shepherd, he again showed the pattern to which we ought to be conformed, saying: “I am the good shepherd.” And he adds: “And I know my sheep” [Note: [Col. 1129D] The Corbie manuscript, Bellovacensis, and the two earlier Gemetic manuscripts read “and I know mine”], that is, “I love them”; “and my sheep know me.” It is as though he plainly said: “Those who love obey.” For whoever does not love the truth has not yet truly known it.

### 4.

Since you have heard, dearest brothers, of our danger, consider in the Lord’s words your own danger as well. See whether you are his sheep; see whether you know him; see whether you know the light of truth.

When I say “know,” I do not mean through faith alone but through love. When I say “know,” I do not mean through belief alone but through action. For the same John the Evangelist who says this testifies: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4) [Note: [Col. 1129D] Bellovacensis and the German manuscript read “that he knows him.”].

Hence the Lord immediately adds in this passage: “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep.” It is as though he openly said: “It is evident that I know the Father and am known by the Father because I lay down my life for my sheep”; that is, by the love with which I die for the sheep, I show how greatly I love the Father.

Since he had come to redeem not only Judea but also the Gentiles, he adds: “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd.”

The Lord was looking upon our redemption—we who have come from the Gentile people—when he said that he must bring in other sheep. You see this happening daily, brothers; today you see it accomplished in the reconciliation of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 1129D] The German manuscript, the two earlier Gemetic manuscripts, and Bigot read “in the reconciliation of the Gentiles.”]. For he makes one fold out of two flocks when he joins the Jewish and Gentile peoples in his faith, as Paul testifies when he says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). Choosing simple-hearted people from both nations for eternal life, he leads the sheep into his own fold.

### 3.

Concerning these sheep he says again: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27). Concerning them he says somewhat earlier: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (ibid., 9).

He will enter into faith; he will go out from faith into sight, from belief into contemplation; and he will find pasture in eternal refreshment. His sheep therefore find pasture, because whoever follows him with a simple heart is nourished by the food of eternal verdure.

And what are the pastures of these sheep except the interior joys of the ever-green paradise? The pasture of the elect is the present vision of God: while he is seen without decline, the mind is satisfied without end by the food of life.

In these pastures, those who have already escaped the snares of temporal pleasure rejoice in the fullness of eternity. There are the angelic choirs that sing hymns; there is the fellowship of the citizens above. There is the sweet solemnity of those returning from the sorrowful labor of this pilgrimage. There are the prudent choirs of the prophets; there is the distinguished company of the apostles; there is the victorious army of countless martyrs, all the happier there because they suffered more harshly here. There is the steadfastness of confessors, comforted by receiving their reward. There are the faithful men whom the pleasure of the world could not soften, despite the strength of their manhood [Note: [Col. 1130D] The German manuscript reads “from their verdure.”]. There are the holy women who conquered both the world and their sex. There are the children who here surpassed their years in character. There are the old, whom age here made weak but did not deprive of the strength of their works.

### 6.

Let us therefore seek, dearest brothers, these pastures in which we may rejoice amid the solemn assembly of so many citizens. Let the very festival of those who rejoice invite us.

Certainly, if a people were celebrating a fair somewhere, or if everyone were hurrying to the dedication of a church after a solemn celebration had been announced, we would all hasten to be present together, and each person would make every effort to attend [Note: [Col. 1130D] Bellovacensis and three Gemetic manuscripts read “to attend such a solemnity.”]. He would consider himself afflicted by a serious loss if he did not see the solemnity of the common joy.

Behold, in heaven the joy of the elect citizens is celebrated; they congratulate one another in their assembly. Yet we, lukewarm in our love of eternity, burn with no desire and do not seek to attend so great a solemnity; we are deprived of its joys, and yet we are happy.

Let us therefore kindle our spirit, brothers. Let faith grow warm in what it has believed; let our desires for things above catch fire. To love in this way is already to be on the journey.

Let no adversity call us back from the joy of the inward solemnity, because if someone desires to go to a proposed destination, no roughness of the road changes his desire. Let no flattering prosperity deceive us, because a foolish traveler is one who, seeing pleasant meadows along the road, forgets where he was heading [Note: [Col. 1130D] The German manuscript, three Gemetic manuscripts, and Bigot read “forgets to go where he was heading.”].

Let the soul therefore pant with its whole desire for the heavenly homeland. Let it desire nothing in this world, which it is certain to leave all the sooner, so that, if we truly are sheep of the heavenly Shepherd, because we do not become fixed in the delights of the journey [Note: [Col. 1130D] The Corbie manuscript reads “in love of the journey.”], we may be satisfied by the eternal pastures when we arrive [Note: [Col. 1130D] Bellovacensis adds: “through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”].

[Note: [Col. 1131D] This is the eighth homily in the Corbie and Lateran manuscripts, and the eleventh in the royal Swedish manuscript.]

# HOMILY XV

[Col. 1131A]

Preached to the people in the basilica of the holy apostle Paul, on Sexagesima Sunday.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] The Carnot manuscript reads “of Saint Peter.”]  
[Note: [Col. 1131D] This is entirely absent from the German manuscript, Bigot, and the two earlier Gemetic manuscripts.]

## Reading of the Holy Gospel according to Luke 8:4–15

[Note: [Col. 1131D] The Bellovacensis and German manuscripts read: “At that time Jesus spoke this parable to the crowds: ‘A sower went out,’ etc.”]

At that time, when a very large crowd had gathered and people were hurrying to Jesus from the cities, he spoke by way of a parable:

“A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell beside the road, was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it. Some fell upon the rock, and when it had grown, it withered because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns [Note: [Col. 1132D] The German manuscript reads “among thorns.”], and the thorns that sprang up with it choked it. Some fell on good soil, grew up, and produced fruit a hundredfold.”

Saying this, he cried out: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

His disciples asked him what this parable meant. He said to them:

“To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

“Now this is the parable: The seed is the word of God. The seed beside the road represents those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, so that, believing, they may not be saved.

“The seed upon the rock represents those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy. [Note: [Col. 1132D] The German manuscript and Bigot read: “For those upon the rock are those who, when they have heard …”] But they have no roots; they believe for a while, and in the time of temptation they fall away. The seed that fell among thorns represents those who have heard but, as they go on their way, are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of life, and do not produce fruit.

“The seed that fell on good soil represents those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, hold on to it and produce fruit with perseverance.”

### 1.

The reading of the holy Gospel that you have just heard, dearest brothers, requires not exposition but admonition. For human weakness does not presume to dissect what the Truth itself has explained. But there is something in this very exposition of the Lord that you ought carefully to consider.

If we were to tell you that the seed signifies the word, the field the world, the birds the demons, and the thorns riches, your minds might perhaps hesitate to believe us. Therefore the Lord himself deigned to explain what he was saying, so that you might learn to seek the meanings of things even in those matters that he did not himself choose to explain.

By explaining what he had said figuratively, he made known that he spoke in figures, in order to make you confident when our weakness of speech reveals the figures in his words. For who would ever believe me if I wished to interpret thorns as riches—especially since thorns wound, whereas riches delight? And yet riches are thorns, because they lacerate the mind with the prickings of its thoughts and, when they drag it as far as sin, make it bleed as though from an inflicted wound.

The Lord rightly calls them here—not, as another Evangelist testifies, simply “riches,” but “deceitful riches” (Matthew 13:22). They are deceitful because they cannot remain with us for long; they are deceitful because they do not drive away the poverty of our mind. Only those riches are true which make us rich in virtues.

If, therefore, dearest brothers, you wish to be rich, love true riches. If you seek the summit of true honor, strive toward the heavenly kingdom. If you love the glory of dignities, hasten to be enrolled in that heavenly court of angels.

## 2

[Col. 1132B] Retain in your minds the words of the Lord that you receive with your ears. For the word of God is food for the mind. And just as food that has been taken in is vomited up by a weak stomach, so the word that has been heard is rejected when it is not retained in the stomach of memory. But whoever does not retain nourishment is plainly beyond hope of life. Fear, therefore, the danger of eternal death, if you receive the food of holy exhortation but do not retain in your memory the words of life—that is, the nourishment of righteousness. Behold, everything you do is passing away, and each day, whether you wish it or not, you hasten toward the final judgment without any intervening moment. Why, then, love what must be left behind? Why neglect that destination to which you are going?

Remember what is said: “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” All who were present there had bodily ears. But when he says to all who possess ears, “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear,” he undoubtedly seeks the ears of the heart. Take care, therefore, that the word you have received remains in the ear of your heart. Take care lest the seed fall beside the road, lest the evil spirit come and remove the word from your memory. Take care lest the rocky soil receive the seed and send forth the fruit of good works without the roots of perseverance.

For many delight in what they hear and resolve to begin good works; but as soon as they begin to grow weary under adversities, they abandon what they have begun. [Col. 1132C] The rocky soil, therefore, had no moisture, since it did not bring what it had germinated to the fruit of perseverance. Many, when they hear a word against greed, detest that same greed and praise contempt for all possessions; but as soon as the mind sees something it desires, it forgets what it was praising. Many, when they hear a word against lust, not only do not desire to commit bodily impurities but are even ashamed of those already committed; but as soon as the appearance of the flesh presents itself to their eyes, the mind is swept away to desire, as though it had never resolved anything against those very desires. It does condemnable things, although it remembers that it had already condemned whatever it recalls having done [Note: C. Germ.: “and he himself condemned it”].

Often, too, we are pierced with compunction against our faults, yet after weeping we return to the same faults. Thus Balaam, contemplating the tents of the Israelite people, wept and asked that he might become like them in death, saying: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs” (Num. 23:10). But as soon as the hour of compunction had passed, he burned with the wickedness of greed. For the sake of the promised gifts, he gave counsel for the destruction of the people whose death he had wished to resemble; and he forgot what he had lamented when he refused to extinguish what was burning within him through greed. [Col. 1133A]

## 3

It should be noted that, in explaining the passage, the Lord says that anxieties, pleasures, and riches suffocate the word. They suffocate it because, through their unwelcome thoughts, they strangle the throat of the mind [Note: Belvacensis: “because anxieties are troublesome”]; and, by not allowing a good desire to enter the heart, they kill, as it were, the passage of vital breath.

It should also be noted that he joins two things to riches—namely, anxieties and pleasures—because riches both oppress the mind through care and dissolve it through abundance [Note: The first two Gemeticensis manuscripts and Bigot: “through curiosity”; the second Carnot manuscript: “through negligence”]. Indeed, by contrary effects they make their possessors both afflicted and sensual. But since pleasure cannot coexist with affliction, at one time they afflict them through anxious guardianship of their possessions, and at another they soften them into pleasures through abundance. [Col. 1133B]

## 4

But the good soil yields fruit through patience, because whatever good we do is worthless if we do not also bear patiently the evils of our neighbors. For the higher someone has advanced, the more severely he finds himself burdened in this world, because as our mind’s love for the present age declines, the adversity of that same age increases [Note: Bigot., the first two Gemeticensis manuscripts, Longipontanus, and Val. Clar.: “delight”].

This is why we see many people doing good and yet laboring beneath a heavy burden of tribulations. They have already fled earthly desires, yet they are wearied by harsher scourges. But, in accordance with the Lord’s word, they yield fruit through patience, because when they humbly receive the scourges, after the scourges they are exaltedly received into rest.

Thus grapes are beaten underfoot and dissolved into the taste of wine. Thus the olive, pressed by blows [Note: C. Germ., Corbie, and many others: “by crushing”], abandons its lees and grows rich as oil. [Col. 1133C] Thus, through the threshing of the threshing-floor, grains are separated from chaff and, purified, reach the granary.

Whoever, therefore, desires fully to overcome vices should strive humbly to endure the scourges of his purification, so that he may come to the Judge all the cleaner because the fire of tribulation is now cleansing away his rust. [p. 1491]

## 5

In the portico through which those going to the church of blessed Clement had access, there was a certain man named Servulus, whom many of you knew together with me: poor in possessions, rich in merits, and weakened by a long illness (*Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 14). From early youth until the end of his life he lay paralyzed. Why should I say that he could not stand? He was never able to rise in his bed even to sit, never able to bring his hand to his mouth, and never able to turn himself onto his other side. [Col. 1133D]

His mother and brother were present to serve him, and whatever he was able to receive in alms, he distributed to the poor through their hands. He knew no letters at all, but he bought copies of sacred Scripture for himself and, receiving religious people as guests, continually made them read them aloud in his presence. [Col. 1134A] Thus, to the extent proper to him, he learned the whole of sacred Scripture, although, as I have said, he was entirely ignorant of letters.

He always strove to give thanks amid his suffering and to devote himself day and night to hymns and praises of God. But when the time had come for such great patience to receive its reward, the pain of his limbs returned to his vital organs [Note: The second Carnot manuscript: “heat”]. When he recognized that he was already near death, he urged the traveling men who had been received as guests to rise and chant psalms with him in expectation of his departure.

As he himself was dying and singing psalms with them, he suddenly silenced the voices of those singing with a cry of great fear, saying: “Be silent! Do you not hear how great are the praises resounding in heaven?” [Col. 1134B] As he directed the ear of his heart toward those same praises that he heard within, that holy soul was released from the flesh.

When it departed, the whole place was filled with such a great fragrance that all who were present were filled with indescribable sweetness [Note: Turonensis and Longipontanus: “all who were there”]. By this they clearly recognized that those praises had received her in heaven. Our monk was present at this event; he is still alive and is accustomed to testify with great weeping that the fragrance of that odor did not leave their nostrils until his body had been committed to burial.

Behold the end by which he departed this life, who had patiently endured scourges in this life. In accordance, therefore, with the Lord’s word, the good soil yielded fruit through patience: plowed by the discipline’s plowshare, it reached the harvest of reward.

But I ask you, dearly beloved brothers, what argument of excuse will we have at that strict judgment—those of us who, sluggish in good works, have received both possessions and hands—if a poor man without hands has fulfilled the Lord’s commandments [Note: Printed editions: “was able to fulfill them”]? Let the Lord not then set the apostles before us, who by preaching drew crowds of the faithful with them into the kingdom; let him not display against us the martyrs, who reached the heavenly homeland by shedding their blood. What will we say then, when we see this Servulus of whom we have spoken, whose long illness held his arms but did not bind them from good works?

Do these things with one another, brothers. Stir yourselves to the pursuit of good works in such a way that, when you now set the good before yourselves for imitation, you may then be able to share in their company.

# HOMILY XVI

[Note: It is the tenth in the Lateran and Corbie manuscripts, and the twelfth in the royal Swedish manuscript.]

[Col. 1134D] Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint John, called Constantiniana [Note: Lateran manuscript: “in the basilica of Saint Saviour, which is called Constantiniana”; the first two Gemeticensis manuscripts: “of Saint Saviour in the Lateran”], on the first Sunday of Lent [Note: Royal Swedish manuscript: “On Sunday, the beginning of Lent.” The words “Sunday,” etc., are lacking in Belvacensis, C. Germ., and the first and third Gemeticensis manuscripts].

## Gospel Reading according to Matthew 4:1–11

[Col. 1135A] At that time Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. And the tempter approached and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, say that these stones should become loaves of bread.” He answered [Note: Belvacensis and Corbie German manuscript: “he said to him”] and said: “It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’”

Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will carry you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.’” [Note: The same manuscripts: “Jesus said to him again.”] [Col. 1135B]

Jesus said to him: “Again it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: “I will give you all these things, if you fall down and worship me.”

Then Jesus said to him: “Go away, Satan. For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

Then the devil left him, and behold, angels approached and ministered to him.

## 1

Some people are accustomed to wonder by what spirit Jesus was led into the desert, because the text goes on to say: “The devil took him into the holy city,” and again: “He took him to a very high mountain” [Note: “Very high” is absent from C. Germ. and three Gemeticensis manuscripts].

But it is truly and without any question appropriate to understand that he was led into the desert by the Holy Spirit, so that his own Spirit might lead him to the place where the evil spirit would later find him for temptation.

Yet when it is said that the God-man was taken by the devil either to a high mountain or into the holy city, the mind recoils and human ears are frightened to hear it. Nevertheless, we recognize that these things are not incredible if we consider other events in him. [Col. 1135C]

Certainly, the devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head. Was Pilate not a member of the devil? Were the Jews who persecuted Christ and the soldiers who crucified him not members of the devil? What, then, is surprising if he allowed himself to be led by him onto a mountain, when he even allowed himself to be crucified by members of that same one?

It was therefore not unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed. For it was right that he should conquer our temptations by his temptations, just as he had come to overcome our death by his death.

But we must know that temptation occurs in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. When we are tempted, we usually fall into pleasure, or even into consent, because, having been propagated from the sin of the flesh, we carry within ourselves the source of the struggles we must endure.

But God, who, having taken flesh in the Virgin’s womb, came into the world without sin, endured no internal contradiction within himself. He could therefore be tempted through suggestion, but the pleasure of sin did not wound his mind. Thus all that diabolical temptation was external, not internal. [Col. 1135D]

## 2

But if we examine the sequence of his temptation, let us consider how greatly we are freed from temptation. The ancient enemy rose against our first human parent with three temptations: he tempted him with gluttony, vainglory, and greed. By tempting him he overcame him, because through consent he subjected him to himself. [Col. 1136A]

He tempted him through gluttony when he showed him the forbidden fruit of the tree and persuaded him to eat. He tempted him through vainglory when he said: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). And he tempted him through the advancement of greed when he said: “Knowing good and evil.”

For greed concerns not only money but also height and status. It is rightly called greed when exaltation is sought beyond measure. If the seizure of honor did not belong to greed, Paul would never have said of the only-begotten Son of God: “He did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). In this, the devil drew our parent into pride: he stirred him to greed for exaltation. [Col. 1136B]

## 3

But by the same methods with which he laid the first man low, he himself fell when he tempted the second man [Note: Corbie German manuscript and the first Carnot manuscript: “he succumbed when he tempted the second man”].

He tempts through gluttony when he says: “Say that these stones should become loaves of bread.” He tempts through vainglory when he says: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” [Note: First Carnot manuscript: “through the exaltation of greed”]. He tempts through greed for exaltation when he shows him all the kingdoms of the world and says: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.”

But he is defeated by the second man through the same means by which he boasted that he had defeated the first, so that he might leave our hearts through the very entrance by which, once admitted, he had held us captive.

There is something else, dearly beloved brothers, that we must consider in this temptation of the Lord. When tempted by the devil, the Lord responded with the commands of sacred Scripture. Although by the word that he was he could have plunged his tempter into the abyss, he did not display the power of his might; he gave only the commands of divine Scripture, so as to offer us an example of his patience, teaching us that whenever we suffer something from wicked people, we should be stirred rather to instruction than to revenge. [Col. 1136C]

Consider how great is God’s patience and how great is our impatience. If we are provoked by insults or any injury, moved by fury we either avenge ourselves as far as we can or threaten to do what we cannot.

Behold, the Lord endured the devil’s hostility and answered him with nothing but words of gentleness. He bears with one whom he could punish, so that his glory might grow greater if, by enduring for a time rather than extinguishing him, he overcame his enemy [Note: The same manuscript: “to the praise of his glory”]. [p. 1494]

## 4

[Col. 1136D] It should be noted that the text continues: “When the devil had departed, angels ministered to him.” What else is shown by this than the two natures of one person? He is both man, whom the devil tempts, and that same one is God, whom angels serve.

Let us therefore recognize our nature in him, for unless the devil had seen him as a man, he would not have tempted him. Let us venerate his divinity in him, for unless he were God above all, angels would in no way minister to him.

## 5

[Col. 1137A] Since the reading appointed for these days is appropriate—for we have heard of the forty-day abstinence of our Redeemer, and we are beginning the season of Lent—we must examine why this abstinence is observed for the number forty.

Moses fasted for forty days a second time in order to receive the law (Exod. 34:28). Elijah abstained for forty days in the desert (3 Kgs. 19:8). The author of humanity himself, coming among human beings, took no food at all for forty days (Matt. 4:2). We too, insofar as we can, should strive during the annual season of Lent to afflict our flesh through abstinence.

Why, then, is the number forty observed in abstinence, unless because the power of the Decalogue is fulfilled through the four books of the holy Gospel? [Col. 1137B] Ten multiplied by four rises to forty, because we fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue when we keep the four books of the holy Gospel.

From this another meaning may also be discerned. In this mortal body we subsist from four elements, and through the pleasures of that same body we transgress the Lord’s commandments. The Lord’s commandments were given through the Decalogue. Since, therefore, through the desires of the flesh we have despised the commandments of the Decalogue, it is fitting that we afflict that same flesh four times ten.

There is, however, another interpretation that may be understood concerning this season of Lent. From the present day until the joys of the Paschal solemnity there are six weeks, which amount to forty-two days. When the six Sundays are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. [Col. 1137C]

Since the year consists of 365 days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we offer God, as it were, the tithes of our year: having lived for ourselves through the year we have received, we mortify ourselves through abstinence in the tithes belonging to our Creator [Note: Longipontanus: “to our Creator”; and below, “for the author indeed [is] death …”]. [p. 1495]

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, just as you are commanded in the law to offer tithes of your possessions (Lev. 27:30 ff.), so strive to offer him also tithes of your days. Let each person, insofar as his strength permits, discipline his flesh, afflict its desires, and put to death shameful lusts, so that, in Paul’s words, he may become a living sacrifice (Rom. 12:1).

A sacrifice is both slain and alive when a person does not cease to live in this life and yet puts to death within himself his carnal desires [Note: The first two German Gemeticensis manuscripts: “and yet kills carnal desires within himself”]. The flesh that led us joyfully into guilt should, when afflicted, lead us back to pardon.

For the author of our death transgressed the commandment of life through the fruit of the forbidden tree. Therefore, since we fell from the joys of paradise through food, let us rise again to them, insofar as we can, through abstinence.

## 6

[Col. 1138A] But let no one believe that this abstinence alone can suffice, since the Lord says through the prophet: “Is this not rather the fast that I have chosen?” He then adds: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:6–7).

God therefore approves that fast which raises the hands of almsgiving to his eyes, which is practiced with love of one’s neighbor, and which is prepared through compassion. Give to another what you take away from yourself, so that from the source where your flesh is afflicted, the flesh of your needy neighbor may be restored. [Col. 1138B]

For this reason the Lord says through the prophet: “When you fasted and mourned, did you really fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (Zech. 7:5–6).

The person eats and drinks for himself who receives bodily nourishment—which is the common gift of the Creator—without sharing with the needy. And a person fasts for himself if he does not give to the poor what he temporarily takes away from himself, but stores it up to offer later to his belly.

Hence Joel says: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel 1:14; 2:15). To sanctify a fast is, by joining other good works to it, to show a bodily abstinence worthy of God.

Let anger cease; let quarrels be put to sleep. The flesh is worn down in vain if the mind is not restrained from its wicked pleasures, since the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found. Behold, you fast for disputes and strife, and you strike wickedly with your fist, and you demand all your debts” (Isa. 58:3).

For the person who demands from his debtor what he gave does nothing unjust; but it is fitting that whoever afflicts himself in repentance should also forbid himself what he is justly entitled to. [Col. 1138C] Thus, when we are afflicted and repentant, God forgives what we have done unjustly if, for love of him, we relinquish even what is justly ours.

# HOMILY XVII

[Note: It is the thirty-sixth in Corbie, the thirty-fourth in the Lateran, and the thirteenth in the royal Swedish manuscript.]

[Note: We have restored the title from the Lateran, royal Swedish, Corbie German, Bigot, and other manuscripts. The first two Gemeticensis manuscripts have only “at the assembly of bishops.” The printed editions read: “Delivered to the people in the Lateran basilica, on the apostles.” But that this homily was delivered to assembled bishops is especially clear from sections 13 and following. In fact, much here is already said in the *Pastoral Rule*.]

Delivered to the bishops at the Lateran baptismal fonts.

## Gospel Reading according to Luke 10:1–9

[Col. 1138D] At that time the Lord appointed another seventy-two [Note: Belvacensis: “Jesus appointed”] and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. And he said to them:

“The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest. Go; behold, I send you like lambs among wolves. Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals, and greet no one along the way.

“Into whatever house you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you.

“Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have. For the laborer is worthy of his wage. [Note: The passage from here through “and into whatever city,” etc., is absent from Belvacensis and C. Germ.]

“Do not go from house to house. And into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you; cure the sick who are in it, and say to them: ‘The kingdom of God has drawn near to you.’” [Col. 1139A]

## 1

Our Lord and Savior, dearly beloved brothers, sometimes admonishes us through words and sometimes through deeds. For his deeds themselves are commandments, because when he silently does something, he makes known what we ought to do.

Behold, he sends his disciples to preach two by two, because there are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor; and charity cannot exist with fewer than two. No one is properly said to have charity toward himself, but love extends toward another so that it may be charity. [Col. 1139B]

The Lord sends disciples to preach two by two in order silently to indicate to us that one who does not have charity toward another should in no way undertake the office of preaching.

## 2

It is rightly said that he sent them before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. The Lord follows his preachers, because preaching goes before him; and the Lord then comes to dwell in the habitation of our mind when words of exhortation have gone before and, through them, truth is received into the mind.

For this reason Isaiah says to those same preachers: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:3). Hence the Psalmist says to them: “Make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Ps. 67:5). [Col. 1139C]

The Lord ascends above the setting, because from the place where he set in his passion, from that same place he revealed his greater glory by rising again. He ascends above the setting because, by rising, he trampled underfoot the death he endured.

We make a way for him who ascends above the setting when we preach his glory to your minds, so that, coming afterward, he too may illuminate them through the presence of his love.

## 3

After sending the preachers, let us hear what he says: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” [Note: C. Germ., Turonensis, Corbie, Belvacensis: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few”]. [Col. 1139D]

There are few laborers for the plentiful harvest—a statement we cannot make without deep sorrow—for although there are people who hear good things, there are few who speak them.

Behold, the world is full of priests, yet a laborer in God’s harvest is found to be exceedingly rare, because we have indeed undertaken the priestly office but do not fulfill the work of that office. [p. 1497]

Consider, dearly beloved brothers, consider what is said: “Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.” Ask him for us, so that we may be able to labor worthily for you, lest our tongue grow numb to exhortation, and lest, after we have accepted the place of preaching, our silence condemn us before the just Judge.

Often the tongue of preachers is restrained because of their own wickedness; often, however, the fault of those subject to them causes the word of preaching to be withdrawn from those who preside.

The tongue of preachers is restrained because of their own wickedness, as the Psalmist says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousness?” (Ps. 49:16). Again, because of the fault of those subject to them, the voice of preachers is silenced, as the Lord says to Ezekiel: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, unable to act as a man who rebukes, because it is a rebellious house” (Ezek. 3:26). [Col. 1140A]

It is as though he were saying plainly: “For this reason the word of preaching is taken from you, because while the people provoke me by their actions, they are not worthy to receive an exhortation of truth.”

Because of whose fault the word is withdrawn from a preacher is not easily known. But it is known with complete certainty that the silence of a pastor sometimes harms himself, but always harms those subject to him.

## 4

But if only we cannot attain the power of preaching, may we at least hold the office of our position in the innocence of our lives. For the text continues: “Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves.”

Many, when they assume the authority of governance [Note: Belvacensis, Turonensis, C. Germ.: “when they assume the care of governance”], burn to tear apart those subject to them. They display the terror of power and harm those whom they ought to benefit. Because they do not possess the inward organs of charity, they desire to appear as lords and do not recognize themselves as fathers. They change the place of humility into an elevation of domination, and, whenever they flatter outwardly, they rage inwardly. [Col. 1140C]

Of such people Truth says elsewhere: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15).

Against these things we must consider that we are sent like lambs among wolves, so that, preserving the disposition of innocence, we may not possess the bite of malice.

Whoever undertakes the place of preaching should not inflict evils but endure them, so that through his own gentleness he may calm the anger of those who rage and heal the wounds of sinners in others by himself being wounded through afflictions.

Even if zeal for righteousness sometimes requires him to be severe toward those subject to him, that anger should arise from love, not cruelty, so that he may display the rights of discipline outwardly while loving inwardly with paternal affection those whom outwardly he chastises as though pursuing them.

A ruler displays this properly when he does not know how to love himself through private affection [Note: Turonensis, C. Germ., Longipontanus: “when he does not love himself”], when he desires none of the things of the world, and when he does not in any way submit the neck of his mind to the burdens of earthly desire.

## 5

Hence the text continues: “Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals, and greet no one along the way.” [Col. 1140D]

A preacher ought to have such trust in God that, even if he does not provide for the expenses of the present life, he nevertheless knows with complete certainty that they will not be lacking to him, lest, while his mind is occupied with temporal matters, he provide less for eternal things.

He is also forbidden to greet anyone along the way, so that the great haste with which he must proceed on the journey of preaching may be shown [Note: C. Germ., the first Gemeticensis, and Bigot: “on the journey”; Longipontanus and Val. Clar.: “while traveling”; the first Carnot manuscript: “on the journey”].

If anyone wishes these words to be understood allegorically as well, money is enclosed in the purse; but enclosed money signifies hidden wisdom. Whoever therefore possesses the word of wisdom but neglects to distribute it to his neighbor is like someone keeping money tied up in a purse. [Col. 1141A]

Hence it is written: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what use are either of them?” (Ecclus. 41:17).

What is signified by the bag except the burdens of the world? And what is signified here by sandals except examples of dead works?

Whoever undertakes the office of preaching ought not to carry the burden of worldly affairs, lest, while this weighs down his neck, he fail to rise to preach heavenly things. Nor should he look upon examples of foolish works, lest he think to protect his own works, as it were, with skins taken from the dead.

For there are many who defend their wickedness by the wickedness of others. Because they observe others doing such things, they think they may do them freely. What else are these people doing except trying to cover their feet with the skins of dead animals? [Col. 1141B]

Everyone who greets along the way greets because of the opportunity presented by the journey, not from the purpose of desiring that very salvation. Whoever therefore preaches salvation to his hearers not out of love for the eternal homeland but from a desire for rewards greets along the way, because he wishes salvation for his hearers as an opportunity rather than as his intention.

## 6

The text continues: “Into whatever house you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you.” [Col. 1141C]

The peace offered from the preacher’s mouth either rests in the house, if a son of peace is there, or returns to that same preacher. For either a person will be predestined to life and will follow the heavenly word that he hears, or, if no one wishes to hear, the preacher will not be without fruit, because peace returns to him: the Lord repays him with a reward for the labor of his work [Note: Belvacensis, Longipontanus, Val. Clar.: “is repaid for the labor of his work”].

## 7

Behold, the one who forbade carrying a bag and a purse permits expenses and nourishment to be received from that same preaching. For the text continues: “Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have. For the laborer is worthy of his wage.” [p. 1499]

If our peace is received, it is fitting that we remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have, so that we may receive earthly support from those to whom we offer the rewards of the heavenly homeland.

Paul therefore, regarding these very things as insignificant, says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9:11) [Note: The two later Gemeticensis manuscripts: “Is it a great matter if…”].

It should also be noted that the text says: “The laborer is worthy of his wage,” because the very food that sustains us is already a wage for the work, so that here the wage begins from the labor of preaching, while there it is completed in the vision of truth.

In this matter we must consider that two wages are owed for one work of ours: one on the way, the other in the homeland; one that sustains us in labor, the other that rewards us in the resurrection. [Col. 1142A]

The wage received in the present ought to accomplish this in us: that we strive more vigorously toward the wage that follows. Therefore, a true preacher should not preach in order to receive a wage in this present time, but should receive a wage in order to continue preaching.

Whoever preaches for the purpose of receiving here either a reward of praise or a payment unquestionably deprives himself of the eternal reward.

But whoever desires what he says to please people for this reason—that, while what is said pleases, not he himself but the Lord may be loved through those words—or whoever receives earthly support in preaching so that poverty may not weary him from the voice of preaching, for such a person nothing at all prevents the reception of his reward in the homeland, because he has received support on the way.

8. But what are we doing—something I cannot say without grief—what are we doing, O Shepherds, [Note: We have restored *agimus* from manuscripts and old printed editions. It is absent in the recent edition.] who both receive a remuneration and yet are in no way laborers? For we receive the fruits of the holy Church in our daily stipend, but we do not labor in preaching for the eternal Church. Let us consider the nature of the condemnation involved in receiving here, without labor, the reward of labor. Behold, we live from the offerings of the faithful, [Note: The German manuscript and two later Gemet manuscripts read: “but do we labor for…,” etc.] but what labor do we undertake for the souls of the faithful? We take for our stipend what the faithful have offered for the redemption of their sins, yet we do not sweat as we ought against those same sins, either through the devotion of prayer or through preaching. We scarcely rebuke anyone openly for his fault. And further—and this is worse—if a person happens to be powerful in this world, his errors are sometimes praised lest, if he becomes hostile, he withdraw in anger the gift he had been providing.

But we must continually remember what is written concerning certain people: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hosea 4:8). Why are they said to eat the sins of the people, unless because they encourage the sins of sinners so that they may not lose their temporal stipends? But we too, who live from the offerings of the faithful—offerings which they made for their sins—if we eat and remain silent, undoubtedly eat their sins. Let us therefore consider what a crime it is before God to eat the price of sins and to do nothing against those sins by preaching.

Let us hear what is said in the words of blessed Job: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it; if I have eaten its fruits without payment” (Job 31:38–39). [Col. 1142D] 1500 For the land cries out against its possessor when the Church justly murmurs against its shepherd. Its furrows also weep when the hearts of the hearers—which earlier fathers have plowed by the voice of preaching and the force of exhortation—see something in the shepherd’s life that should make them grieve. The good possessor does not eat the fruits of this land without payment, because the discerning shepherd expends the talent of the word, lest he take the Church’s stipend as nourishment to his own condemnation. We eat the fruits of our land with payment when, while receiving ecclesiastical support, we labor in preaching.

For we are heralds of the Judge who is to come. Who, then, will announce the coming Judge if the herald is silent? [Note: The Chartres manuscript reads: “announces the Judge to the world.”]

9. Therefore we must take care that, as far as each person is able and capable, he strive to impress upon the Church entrusted to him both the terror of the coming judgment and the sweetness of the kingdom. And whoever is unable, with one and the same exhortation, to admonish everyone at once should instruct individuals as far as he can, edify them through private conversation, and seek fruit in the hearts of his children through simple exhortation.

For we must continually weigh what is said to the holy apostles, and through the apostles to us: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). If, then, we are salt, we must season the minds of the faithful. You, therefore, who are shepherds, consider that you feed God’s animals. Concerning these animals the Psalmist says to God: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Psalm 67:11). We often see a salt rock placed before brute animals, [Note: The German manuscript, the Beauvais manuscript, and two later Gemet manuscripts read: “so that they may lick from that same salt rock.”] so that they must lick the same salt rock and become better. Thus the priest ought to be like a salt rock among the brute animals of the peoples.

The priest must take care to say to each person whatever is necessary, and to admonish each one in the appropriate way, so that whoever joins himself to the priest may, as though touched by salt, be seasoned with the flavor of eternal life. We are not the salt of the earth if we do not season the hearts of our hearers. That seasoning is truly bestowed upon one’s neighbor by the person who does not withhold the word of preaching. [Note: The second Chartres manuscript, three Gemet manuscripts, and the German manuscript read: “For the priest must take care…”]

10. But we truly preach what is right to others only if we show our words by our deeds; if we ourselves are pierced by divine love; and if, through daily tears, we wash away the stains of human life, which cannot pass without sin. We are truly pierced with compunction for ourselves when we carefully consider the deeds of the fathers who came before us, so that, when we behold their glory, our own life may appear sordid in our eyes. We are truly pierced when we diligently search out the Lord’s commandments and strive ourselves to advance through those things by which we know that those whom we revere have already advanced.

Hence it is written of Moses: “He also made a bronze basin in which Aaron and his sons were to wash when they entered the Holy of Holies; he made it from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle” (Exodus 38:8). Moses placed a bronze basin in which the priests were to wash and then enter the Holy of Holies, because the law of God first commands us to be washed through compunction, so that our impurity may not be unworthy to penetrate the purity of God’s mysteries. The text rightly says that the basin was made from the mirrors of the women who continually kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. [Col. 1144A] 1501 The mirrors of the women are the commandments of God, in which holy souls always behold themselves and discover whatever stains of ugliness they possess. They correct the vices of their thoughts and, like faces resisting or recoiling, compose themselves as though from an image restored, because, while they diligently attend to the Lord’s commandments, they undoubtedly recognize in them what pleases or displeases the heavenly man within them. As long as these women remain in this life, they cannot enter the eternal tabernacle. Yet the women keep watch at the entrance of the tabernacle, because holy souls, even while still burdened by the weakness of the flesh, continually watch for entry into the eternal dwelling.

Moses therefore made the priests a basin from the mirrors of the women, because the law of God provides the cleansing of compunction for the stains of our sins, while it offers us the heavenly commandments to contemplate—those things by which holy souls have pleased the heavenly Bridegroom. [Note: The German manuscript, two Chartres manuscripts, and the third Gemet manuscript read: “provides.”] If we attend to these carefully, we see the stains of our inner image. When we see the stains, we are pierced with the grief of repentance; and once pierced, we are washed as though in the basin made from the mirrors of the women. [Note: The Tours manuscript reads *poenitentes* (“repentant”); the Chartres manuscript reads *remittentes* (“remitting” or “releasing”).]

11. It is very necessary, however, that when we are moved to compunction for ourselves, we should also zealously guard the lives entrusted to us. Let the bitterness of compunction affect us in such a way that it does not turn us away from the care of our neighbors. For what good does it do if, while loving ourselves, we abandon our neighbors? Or what good, again, does it do if, while loving or showing zeal for our neighbors, we abandon ourselves?

In the adornment of the tabernacle, scarlet cloth dyed twice is commanded to be offered (Exodus 25:4), so that before God’s eyes our charity may be colored by love of God and neighbor. The person truly loves himself who loves the Creator purely. The scarlet is dyed twice when the spirit is inflamed with the love of truth toward itself and toward its neighbor. [Note: The Longpont manuscript reads *actorem* (“maker”); the reading here is *auctorem* (“Creator”).] [Note: The second Chartres manuscript reads: “from the love of charity.”]

12. Amid all this, we must know that zeal for righteousness must be exercised against the wrong actions of our neighbors [Note: The same manuscript reads: “of the worst people.”] in such a way that the virtue of gentleness is in no way abandoned amid the fervor of strictness. For a priest’s anger must not be rash and disordered, but rather moderated by the gravity of deliberation. [Note: The recent edition, against the testimony of the English and our manuscripts, has *metuenda* (“to be feared”), which gives a different sense.] We must therefore bear with those whom we correct, and correct those whom we bear, lest, if one of the two is lacking, priestly action be found deficient either in fervor [Note: The German manuscript and three Gemet manuscripts read: “in anger.”] or in gentleness.

This is why, in the service of the temple, lions, oxen, and cherubim were represented by carved work on the bases of the temple. For cherubim signify the fullness of knowledge. But why are neither lions without oxen nor oxen without lions made on the bases? What else do the bases in the temple signify but priests in the Church? While they bear the burden of governance, they carry the load placed upon them like bases.

Cherubim are therefore represented on the bases because it is fitting that priests’ hearts be filled with the fullness of knowledge. The lions signify the terror of severity, while the oxen signify the patience of gentleness. Thus neither lions without oxen nor oxen without lions are represented on the bases, because in the priestly heart the virtue of gentleness must always be guarded together with the terror of severity, so that gentleness may season anger, [Col. 1145A] 1502 and zeal for strictness may inflame that same gentleness lest it become lax. [Note: The German manuscript, the Gemet manuscript, Bigot, Longpont, and Vallicelliana read: “the cherub is represented.”]

13. But why are we saying these things when we still see many people weighed down by even more atrocious deeds? I speak to you [Note: The Beauvais manuscript reads: “priests.”] priests in mourning, because we have recognized that some of you, by carrying out ordinations for rewards, sell spiritual grace and accumulate temporal profits from the iniquities of others, at the cost of sin.

Why, then, does what the Lord’s voice commands not return to your memory: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8)? Why do you not recall before the eyes of your mind that, when our Redeemer entered the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves and poured out the money-changers’ coins? (John 2:1–2.) Who are those in God’s temple today who sell doves, unless they are those who accept a price for the laying on of hands in the Church? [Note: The Beauvais manuscript reads: “who are in the Church.”] Through that laying on of hands, the Holy Spirit is given from heaven. A dove is therefore sold because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price.

But our Redeemer overturned the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such traders.
