Hence the sacred canons condemn the heresy of simony and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. [Note: The German manuscript, Bigot, and the first Chartres manuscript read: “accept payment.”] The seat of those selling doves is overturned when those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood, whether before human eyes or before the eyes of God.

There are indeed many other evils among those set over others which now escape human eyes. And often pastors present themselves as holy to human beings, while in their hidden lives they do not blush to appear shameful before the eyes of the inner Judge. The day will come—indeed, it will certainly come, and it is not far off—when the Pastor of pastors will appear, bring everyone’s deeds into the open, and condemn the evils of those set over others by his own action, he who now punishes the faults of subjects through their superiors.

Hence, when he entered the temple, he himself made a whip as though from cords and, driving the wicked traders from the house of God, overturned the seats of those selling doves (John 2:1–2), because he strikes the faults of subjects through pastors, but strikes the vices of pastors by himself. Now what is done secretly can be denied before human beings. But that Judge will certainly come; no one can hide himself from him by remaining silent, nor deceive him by denial. [Note: The first Chartres manuscript and many others read: “and most of them.”]

14. There is another matter, dearest brothers, that greatly afflicts me concerning the life of pastors. But lest anyone perhaps think what I assert insulting, I accuse myself along with you, although, compelled by the necessity of these barbarous times, I lie very deeply in these faults against my will. [Note: The Beauvais manuscript reads: “of barbarous fear.” The Tours manuscript preserves both readings.]

We have slipped into external affairs, accepting one responsibility because of our office while displaying another in the conduct of our actions. We have abandoned the ministry of preaching and, as I see it, to our own punishment are called bishops while possessing the name of honor but not its virtue.

Those entrusted to us abandon God, and we remain silent. They lie in wicked deeds, and we do not extend the hand of correction. Every day they perish through many forms of evil, and we negligently see them hastening toward hell. But when can we correct the lives of others, when we neglect our own? For, intent upon secular concerns, we become inwardly so much more insensitive as we appear more diligent about outward matters. Through habitual concern for earthly things, the mind grows hard against heavenly desire; and, becoming hardened through its very involvement in worldly activity, it cannot be softened toward what pertains to the love of God.

Hence the holy Church rightly says concerning its weakened members: “They made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I did not keep” (Song of Songs 1:5). Our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate through the habit of daily labor. But, placed as keepers in vineyards, we do not guard our own vineyard, because, while entangled in external activities, we neglect the ministry of our own work. [Note: The German manuscript reads *in nullum* (“in no one”); Bigot and the two earlier Gemet manuscripts read *in nullo* (“in nothing”).]

I think, dearest brothers, that God suffers no greater injury from others than from priests, when he sees those whom he placed for the correction of others giving examples of wickedness in themselves; when we ourselves sin, though we ought to restrain sins. Often—and this is worse—priests who ought to give what belongs to them even seize what belongs to others. Often, when they see people living humbly and chastely, they mock them.

Consider, then, what happens to the flocks when the shepherds become wolves. Those who take charge of guarding the flock do not fear plotting against the Lord’s flock, against whom God’s flocks ought to have been protected. [Note: This sentence is absent from the Beauvais and Corbie manuscripts; immediately after *metuunt* (“fear”), they continue with *nulla*, etc.] We seek no gain of souls; every day we devote ourselves to our own pursuits; we desire earthly things; we pursue human glory with our minds fixed upon it.

And because, by the very fact that we have been placed over others, we possess greater freedom to do whatever we wish, we turn the ministry of the blessing we received into an instrument of ambition. [Note: The second Chartres manuscript reads: “an increase.”] We abandon God’s cause and devote ourselves to earthly affairs; we receive a place of holiness [Note: The German manuscript reads: “the yoke of holiness.”] and become entangled in earthly actions. What is written has certainly been fulfilled in us: “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Hosea 4:9). A priest does not differ from the people when he surpasses the conduct of the common crowd by no merit of his own.

15. Let us call upon Jeremiah’s tears. Let him consider our death and, lamenting, say: “How the gold has grown dim! How the finest color has been changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4:1). The gold has grown dim because the life of priests, once bright with the glory of virtues, is now shown to be blameworthy through base actions. [Note: The Tours manuscript, the German manuscript, the Gemet manuscripts, and others read: “through weak actions”; the first Chartres manuscript reads: “through the lowest of actions.”]

The finest color has been changed because that habit of holiness has, through earthly and despicable works, come to the disgrace of contempt. The stones of the sanctuary were kept within and were not placed upon the body of the high priest except when, entering the Holy of Holies, he appeared in the secret presence of his Creator. [Note: The two earlier Gemet manuscripts and Bigot read: “on his breast.”]

We, therefore, dearest brothers—we are the stones of the sanctuary, and we ought always to appear in the secret presence of God. We should never need to be seen outside, that is, never to be seen in external activities. But the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street because those who ought always to remain within through life and prayer are occupied outside through a reprehensible life.

Behold, scarcely any activity of the world remains which priests do not administer. Therefore, while established in a holy habit, they display external things; they lie outside like stones of the sanctuary. Since in Greek the word for “street” derives from breadth, the stones of the sanctuary are “at the streets” when religious people pursue the broad roads of the world. They are scattered not only in the streets but also at the head of the streets, because they both carry out worldly works through desire for this world and seek the summit of honor from their religious habit. [Col. 1147C] They are scattered at the head of the streets because they lie low through the ministry of their work and yet wish to be honored for the appearance of holiness. [Note: Three Gemet manuscripts, Bigot, and the second Chartres manuscript read: “for the imitation [of holiness].” The old editions agree.]

16. You see how the world is struck by the sword; you see by what daily blows the people perish. Through whose fault does this happen if not chiefly through ours? Behold, cities have been depopulated, fortified camps overthrown, and churches and monasteries destroyed and reduced to the solitude of the countryside. [Note: We have rightly corrected this from the German, Tours, Bigot, and other manuscripts, replacing the earlier reading: “they have been reduced to the solitude of the countryside.” The reference is to monasteries being reduced to the desolation of rural lands.]

But we are the authors of death for the people who are perishing, though we ought to have been their guides to life. [Note: Longpont and Vallicelliana read: “to whom we ought to be [guides to life].”] The multitude of the people has been struck down because of our sin, since, through our negligence, it was not instructed for life.

What else shall we call human souls but the food of the Lord? They were created for this purpose: to be transferred into his body, that is, to advance the growth of the eternal Church. But we ought to have been the seasoning of this food. As we said a little earlier, it is said to the preachers who were sent: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). If, then, the people are God’s food, priests ought to be the seasoning of that food.

But because, while we cease from the practice of prayer and holy instruction, the salt has lost its savor, [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and old editions; other printed editions have: “God’s food cannot be seasoned,” a reading nevertheless supported by the Corbie manuscript.] it cannot season God’s food, and for that reason it is not accepted by its maker, since, because of our foolishness, it is in no way seasoned.

Let us therefore consider who has ever been converted through our tongue; who has repented after being corrected by our rebuke for his wicked deed; who has abandoned lust, avarice, or pride because of our instruction. Let us consider what profit we have made for God—we who, having received a talent, were sent by him to conduct his business. For he says: “Do business until I come” (Luke 19:13). Behold, he has already come; behold, he demands profit from our business. What profit of souls shall we show him from our trading? How many sheaves of souls shall we bring before his sight from the harvest of our preaching?

17. Let us place before our eyes that day of such strict judgment when the Judge will come and settle accounts with his servants to whom he entrusted talents (ibid.). Behold, he will appear in terrible majesty amid the choirs of angels and archangels. In that great examination the multitude of all the elect and the reprobate will be brought forward, and each person’s deeds will be displayed.

There Peter will appear with the converted Judea whom he drew after him. There Paul will appear leading, so to speak, the converted world. There Andrew will lead Achaea after him; John, Asia; Thomas, India—all converted into the presence of their King. There all the rams of the Lord’s flock will appear with the gains of souls, those who by their holy preaching draw the flock subject to God after them.

When, therefore, so many pastors with their flocks have come before the eyes of the eternal Pastor, what shall we wretches say, who return to our Lord empty after our business, who possessed the name of pastors but have no sheep nourished by us to display? Here we were called pastors, but there we do not lead the flock.

18. But if we neglect them, does almighty God abandon his sheep? By no means. For, as he promised through the prophet, he himself feeds them (Ezekiel 34), and all whom he foreordained for life he instructs through the goads of scourges and the spirit of compunction. [Note: The second Chartres manuscript reads: “rescues.”]

Indeed, through us the faithful come to holy baptism; through our prayers they are blessed; through the laying on of our hands they receive the Holy Spirit from God; and they themselves reach the kingdom of heaven, while behold, through our negligence we hasten downward. The elect, purified by the hands of priests, enter the heavenly homeland, while the priests themselves, through a reprehensible life, hasten toward the punishments of hell.

To what, then, shall I compare wicked priests, if not to baptismal water, which washes away the sins of the baptized and sends them to the heavenly kingdom, while afterward it descends itself into sewers? Let us fear these things, brothers, and let our ministry correspond to our conduct. Let us think daily about the release of our sins, lest our life remain bound by sin—the life through which almighty God daily releases others. Let us continually consider what we are; let us weigh our business and the burden we have undertaken. Let us settle each day the accounts we have with our Judge.

And we must care for ourselves in such a way that we do not neglect the care of our neighbor, so that whoever joins himself to us may be seasoned by the salt of our tongue. When we see someone unmarried and living loosely, he should be admonished to strive to restrain his wickedness through marriage, so that through what is permitted he may learn to overcome what is not permitted.

When we see a married person, he should be admonished to exercise such care for the world that he does not put the love of God second; to please the will of his spouse in such a way that he does not displease the Creator.

When we see a cleric, he should be admonished to live in such a way that he may provide an example of life to secular people, lest, if something is justly reproved in him, the reputation of our religion itself be burdened by his fault.

When we see a monk, he should be admonished always to watch over the reverence due to his habit in his conduct, speech, and thoughts; to abandon perfectly the things of the world; and to display before God’s eyes in his morals what he shows to human eyes by his habit.

Thus, whoever is already holy should be admonished to grow; whoever is still wicked should be admonished to correct himself, so that everyone who joins himself to a priest may depart seasoned by the salt of his speech.

Think carefully about these matters with one another, brothers; bestow these things also upon your neighbors; prepare yourselves to render fruit to almighty God from the business you have received. [Note: The second Chartres manuscript, the Gemet manuscript, and Bigot read: “hope.”] But what we say will be more effectively obtained from you by praying than by speaking.

LET US PRAY.

God, who have willed to call us as shepherds over peoples, grant, we beseech you, that we may be able to be in your eyes what we are called by the human mouth. Through our Lord, etc.

[Note: This is Homily 11 in Corbie, Homily 12 in the Lateran manuscript, and Homily 14 in the Royal and Swedish codices.]

HOMILY XVIII.

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle. [Note: These words are not found in the Lateran codex, the German manuscript, the Beauvais manuscript, the Swedish Royal codex, or Bigot.]

Sunday of the Passion.

GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO JOHN 8:45–69.

At that time Jesus was saying to the crowds [Note: The German and Beauvais manuscripts read: “to the crowds: Which of you…”] of the Jews and to the chief priests:

“Which of you will convict me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear them, because you are not of God.”

Then the Jews answered and said to him: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”

Jesus answered: “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges. Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

Therefore the Jews said: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets, and you say: ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’ Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died. Whom do you make yourself?”

Jesus answered: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God, and you have not known him. But I know him. And if I were to say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar. But I know him and keep his word. Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

Therefore the Jews said to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?”

Jesus said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

Therefore they took up stones to throw at him. [Col. 1150B] But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.

1506 1. Consider, dearest brothers, the gentleness of God. He came to release sins, and he said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” He does not disdain to prove by reason that he is not a sinner, though by the power of his divinity he could justify sinners. [Note: Longpont and Vallicelliana read: “he had come.”]

But what follows is exceedingly terrifying: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear them, because you are not of God.” For if the person who is of God hears the words of God, and no one who is not of him can hear his words, let each person question himself whether he perceives the words of God in the ear of his heart, and he will understand from whom he comes.

Truth commands us to desire the heavenly homeland, to crush the desires of the flesh, to turn away from worldly glory, [Note: The German manuscript and the first Chartres manuscript read: “to turn away from the glory of the world.”] to avoid seeking what belongs to others, and to give away what belongs to us. Let each person therefore consider within himself whether this voice of God has grown strong in the ear of his heart, and recognize that he is already of God.

For there are some who do not deign to receive God’s commandments either with the ear of the body or with the ear of the heart. [Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads: “neither with the ear of the heart nor with the ear of the body.”] There are some who indeed perceive them with the bodily ear, but embrace them with no desire of the mind. And there are some who willingly receive the words of God, so that they are even pierced with tears, but after the time of tears they return to iniquity. These certainly do not hear the words of God, because they disdain to put them into practice.

Recall your life, therefore, dearest brothers, before the eyes of your mind, and with deep reflection fear what sounds from the mouth of Truth: “Therefore you do not hear them, because you are not of God.” But what Truth says concerning the reprobate, the reprobate themselves demonstrate about themselves through their deeds. For it follows: “Then the Jews answered and said to him: ‘Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?’”

2. Let us hear what the Lord answered after receiving such an insult: “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.” Since *Samaritan* means “guardian,” and he is truly the guardian of whom the Psalmist says, “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Psalm 126:1), and to whom Isaiah says, “Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11), the Lord did not wish to answer, “I am not a Samaritan,” but, “I do not have a demon.”

Two things had been said against him: he denied one and silently accepted the other. He had come as the guardian of the human race; and if he had said that he was not a Samaritan, he would have denied that he was the guardian. But he kept silent about what he recognized and patiently rejected what he heard falsely said, declaring: “I do not have a demon.”

In these words, what else is confounded but our pride? When it is even slightly provoked, it returns insults more savage than those it received; it does whatever evil it can and threatens even what it cannot do. Behold, when the Lord receives an insult, he does not become angry or answer with abusive words. If he had wished to answer those saying these things, “You have a demon,” he would certainly have spoken the truth, since, unless they had been filled with a demon, they could not have spoken such perverse things about God.

But after receiving the insult, Truth did not wish even to say what was true, lest he appear not to have spoken the truth but to have returned an insult because he was provoked. What does this teach us, then, except that when we receive insults from our neighbors through falsehood, we should remain silent even about their true faults, lest we turn the ministry of rightful correction into weapons of rage?

But because whoever uses zeal for God is dishonored by wicked people, the Lord gave us in himself an example of patience, saying: “But I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.” But he teaches us by his example what we should do in these circumstances when he adds: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

We know, certainly, what is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son”; and yet behold, the same Son, receiving insults, does not seek his own glory. He reserves the insults inflicted upon him for the Father’s judgment, clearly showing us how patient we ought to be, since even he who judges does not yet wish to avenge himself.

But when the perversity of wicked people increases, preaching must not only remain unbroken but also increase. [Note: Recent printed editions read: “preaching must not be diminished”; this reading would be preferable were the former reading not that of nearly all manuscripts and the old editions.] The Lord admonishes us to this by his own example. After he had been called one who had a demon, he bestowed the benefits of his preaching even more generously, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

But just as it is necessary for the good to become better even through insults, so the reprobate always become worse through a benefit. For after receiving the preaching they say again: “Now we know that you have a demon.”

Because they had clung to eternal death, and did not see the same death to which they clung, looking only upon the death of the flesh, [Note: The Beauvais manuscript and the two earlier Gemet manuscripts read: “the flesh of death.”] they were blinded by the word of Truth, saying: “Abraham died, and the prophets died, and you say: ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death’?” [Note: Bigot and the second Gemet manuscript read: “will not see.”]

Thus they themselves set Abraham and the prophets before Truth himself, as though venerating them. But reason clearly shows us that those who do not know God also falsely venerate God’s servants. [Note: “The dead prophets” is omitted in the German and Beauvais manuscripts.]

3. It should be noted that the Lord saw them resisting him in open opposition, yet he did not cease to preach to them again and again, saying: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (Genesis 18:1 ff.).

Abraham saw the day of the Lord when, as a figure of the supreme Trinity, he received three angels as guests. After receiving them, he spoke to the three as though to one, because although there is a numerical distinction of persons in the Trinity, there is unity of divinity in nature.

But the carnal minds of the hearers do not lift their eyes above the flesh; they consider only the age of his flesh, saying: “You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?” Our Redeemer kindly draws them away from contemplating his flesh and leads them to the contemplation of his divinity, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

“Before” belongs to past time, whereas “I am” belongs to the present. And because the Divinity does not possess past or future time but possesses eternal being, he did not say, “Before Abraham, I was,” but, “Before Abraham, I am.” Hence it is also said to Moses: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the Israelites: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14).

Abraham, therefore, had a before and an after, since he could approach through the manifestation of his presence and depart through the course of life. But Truth possesses eternal being, because nothing begins for him in an earlier time, 1509 nor is anything brought to an end in a later time.

But because the minds of the unbelievers were unable to endure these words of eternity, they ran to the stones and sought to crush the one whom they could not understand.

4. What the Lord did in response to the fury of those who were throwing stones is shown when it immediately continues: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.” It is very astonishing, dearly beloved brothers, why the Lord avoided his persecutors by hiding himself, since, if he had wished to exercise the power of his divinity, by a silent inclination of his will he could have bound them in their own assault, or overwhelmed them with the punishment of sudden death. But because he had come to suffer, he did not wish to exercise judgment. Certainly, at the very time of his Passion, he both showed how much he could do and nevertheless endured that for which he had come. For when he said to his persecutors who were seeking him, “I am he” (John 18:6), by this one utterance he struck down their pride and laid them all prostrate on the ground. He who therefore could also in this place have escaped the hands of those throwing stones without hiding himself—why did he hide himself, unless because our Redeemer, having become human among humans, speaks one thing to us by word and another by example? What does he speak to us by this example except that, even when we are able to resist, we should humbly avoid the anger of the proud? Hence Paul also says: “Give place to anger” (Rom. 12:19). Let a person consider with what great humility one ought to flee the anger of one’s neighbor, if God avoided the fury of those who were angry by hiding himself. [Note: Thus in the English manuscripts, Tours, the German manuscript of Gembloux, and others. Longpont and Vallicelliana read: “ought to be endured.” The printed editions read: “ought to endure.”]

Let no one therefore rise up against insults received; let no one return insult for insult. For in imitation of God, it is more glorious to flee an injury by remaining silent than to overcome it by answering.

5. But pride says in the heart: “It is disgraceful that, after receiving an injury, you remain silent. Whoever sees that you receive an insult and remain silent does not think that you are showing patience, but that you acknowledge the charges.” But from where does this voice arise in our heart against patience, unless because we have fixed our thoughts in the depths below, and, while we seek glory on earth, do not care to please him who looks upon us from heaven?

After receiving an insult, therefore, let us meditate on the word of God: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:50). What is written about the Lord—“He hid himself”—can also be understood in another way. He had preached many things to the Jews, but they mocked the words of his preaching. Indeed, they became worse through that preaching, since they went so far as to throw stones. What does the Lord signify by hiding himself except that the very Truth is hidden from those who disdain to follow his words? For Truth flees the mind in which it does not find humility. And how many there are today who detest the hardness of the Jews because they refused to hear the Lord’s preaching, yet, while they accuse those people of having been such with respect to faith, are themselves such with respect to conduct. They hear the Lord’s commandments and recognize his miracles, but refuse to turn from their wickedness. Behold, he calls, and we do not wish to return. Behold, he endures, and we disregard his patience. While there is still time, therefore, brothers, let each person abandon his wickedness and fear the patience of God, lest he be unable later to escape him whom he now despises as tranquil when he has become angry. [Note: The third manuscript of Gembloux adds: “after death.”]

[Note: In the Lateran and Corbie manuscripts this is the seventh homily; in the Swedish Royal Codex, the fifteenth.]

## HOMILY XIX

Delivered to the people in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence, on Sunday in Septuagesima. [Note: The Lateran manuscript adds: “outside the walls.” In the second manuscript of Chartres and the first two manuscripts of Gembloux, instead of “of the blessed Lawrence,” it reads “of the blessed apostle Peter.” Moreover, neither in the Lateran manuscript, nor in the Swedish Royal Codex, nor in the German manuscript of Corbie or Beauvais, does the phrase “on Sunday in Septuagesima” occur.]

### GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 20:1–16

At that time Jesus said to his disciples this parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and he said to them: ‘Go you also into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you.’ So they went. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hours, and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and he said to them: ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ They said to him: ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them: ‘Go you also into my vineyard.’

“When evening came, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and ending with the first.’ Therefore, when those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, they received a denarius each. When the first also came, they thought that they would receive more. But they too received a denarius each. On receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: ‘These last worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.’ But he answered one of them and said: ‘Friend, I am not doing you an injustice. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give this last one as much as I give you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Is your eye evil because I am good?’ Thus the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

1510

1. In its exposition, this reading from the holy Gospel calls for much to be said, which I wish, if I can, to touch upon briefly, lest both the length of the discourse and the prolixity of the explanation seem burdensome to you.

The kingdom of heaven is said to be like a householder who hires laborers to cultivate his vineyard. Who more properly represents the householder than our Creator, who governs those whom he has created and possesses his elect in this world as a master possesses subjects in his household? He has a vineyard, namely the universal Church, which, from righteous Abel to the last elect who is to be born at the end of the world, has produced so many saints that it has sent out as many branches, so to speak.

This householder therefore hires laborers to cultivate his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, because from the beginning of this world to its end he has never ceased to gather preachers for the instruction of the faithful people. The morning of the world was from Adam until Noah; the third hour from Noah until Abraham; the sixth from Abraham until Moses; the ninth from Moses until the coming of the Lord; and the eleventh from the coming of the Lord until the end of the world. In this last period the holy apostles were sent as preachers, and those who came late received the full reward.

Therefore, in order to instruct his people, the Lord never ceased to send laborers, as it were, to cultivate his vineyard, because first through the fathers, then through the teachers of the Law and the prophets, and finally through the apostles, while he cultivated the conduct of his people, he labored in the cultivation of the vineyard through laborers. Yet, in whatever degree or measure, whoever has lived with right faith and good works has been a laborer in this vineyard.

The laborer of the morning, the third, the sixth, and the ninth hour designates that ancient Hebrew people which, in its elect, from the beginning of the world, while striving to worship God with right faith, did not cease, as it were, to labor in the cultivation of the vineyard. At the eleventh hour the Gentiles are called, to whom it is said: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” For those who had neglected to labor for their life after so long a period of the world stood idle, as it were, all day.

But consider, brothers, what they answer when questioned. They say: “Because no one has hired us.” No patriarch had come to them; no prophet had come to them. What does it mean to say, “No one hired us for work,” except that no one preached to us the ways of life?

What, then, will we say in our defense, who cease from good works, who came to the faith almost from our mother’s womb, who heard the words of life from our very cradles, who drank the nourishment of heavenly preaching from the breasts of holy Church together with the milk of the flesh? [Note: The printed editions read “we have drawn in,” which we would not at all reject if the manuscripts agreed.]

2. We can also distinguish these same differences of hours according to the stages of each person’s life. The morning is the childhood of our understanding. The third hour can be understood as adolescence, because the sun, as it were, is already rising high while the heat of youth increases. The sixth is youth, because the sun seems to stand at the center of the sky while the fullness of strength is consolidated in it. The ninth is understood as old age, in which the sun, as it were, descends from the high axis, because that age declines from the heat of youth. The eleventh hour is the age called decrepit or very old.

Hence the Greeks call the very elderly not γέροντες (*gerontes*, “old men”) but πρεσβύτεροι (*presbyteroi*, “older men”), to indicate that those whom they call more advanced in age are more than merely old. [Note: The printed editions say: “in Greek.”]

Therefore, because one person is brought to the good life in childhood, another in adolescence, another in youth, another in old age, and another in decrepitude, laborers are called to the vineyard at different hours.

Look, then, dearly beloved brothers, at your conduct, and see whether you are already God’s laborers. Let each person weigh what he is doing and consider whether he is laboring in the Lord’s vineyard. Whoever in this life seeks what belongs to himself has not yet come to the Lord’s vineyard. For those labor for the Lord who think not of their own gain but of the Lord’s, who serve with zeal for charity and devotion to piety, who keep watch to win souls, and hasten to bring others with them to life. But whoever lives for himself and feeds upon the pleasures of his flesh is rightly reproved as idle, because he does not pursue the fruit of divine work.

[Col. 1155D] 3. Whoever has neglected to live for God until the final stage of life has stood idle, as it were, until the eleventh hour. Hence it is rightly said to those who remain sluggish until the eleventh hour: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” As though it were plainly said: “Even if you did not wish to live for God in childhood and youth, at least come to your senses in your final age, and, since you will no longer have much time in which to labor, come at least late to the paths of life.”

The householder calls such people too, and often they are rewarded first, because they leave the body for the kingdom sooner than those who seemed to have been called from childhood. Did not the thief come at the eleventh hour? Though he did not come late in age, he did come late through repentance: he confessed God on the cross and almost with the words of his sentence breathed out his life.

The householder began to distribute the denarius from the last, because he brought the thief to the rest of paradise before Peter. [Note: Tours, the German manuscript of Corbie, Chartres, Gembloux, Bigot, and others read: “called.”] How many fathers lived before the Law, and how many under the Law; yet those who were called at the Lord’s coming reached the kingdom of heaven without any delay. Those who labored at the eleventh hour therefore receive the same denarius that they who labored at the first had awaited with the whole desire of their hearts, because those who came to the Lord at the end of the world received an equal reward of eternal life with those who had been called from the beginning of the world. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, Tours, and Beauvais read: “which they awaited.”]

Hence those who had gone before in labor murmur, saying: “These last worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.” [Note: We have restored this passage in accordance with the manuscripts and the old edition. In the recent editions it reads: “those who labored from the beginning of the world”; and, “because they had lived for a long time,” etc.]

Those bore the burden of the day and the heat who, because it happened that they lived here from the beginning of the world, necessarily had to endure the longer trials of the flesh. For to bear the burden of the day and the heat is to be wearied by the warmth of one’s flesh through the longer periods of life.

4. But it may be asked how those who are called to the kingdom even at the last hour are said to have murmured. No one who murmurs receives the kingdom of heaven; no one who receives it can murmur. But because the ancient fathers, however justly they may have lived, were not led into the kingdom until the Lord’s coming, unless he descended who would open the gates of paradise to human beings by the intervention of his death, their murmuring consisted precisely in this: they lived rightly in order to receive the kingdom, yet they were delayed for a long time before receiving it. Since, after having accomplished righteousness, the places of hell received them, although peaceful, their having labored in the vineyard also involved their having murmured.

Thus, as it were, after their murmuring they receive the denarius—those who, after a long period in hell, came to the joys of the kingdom. But we who have come at the eleventh hour do not murmur after our labor, and we receive the denarius, because, coming into this world after the advent of the Mediator, we are led to the kingdom as soon as we leave the body, and without delay receive what the ancient fathers merited only after a great delay. [Note: Gembloux and Bigot read “of the one who is coming,” that is, of the Mediator.]

Hence the same householder says: “I wish to give this last one as much as I give you.” And because the very reception of the kingdom is his goodness and free will, he rightly adds: “Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?” [Note: Beauvais, Gembloux, and the second manuscript of Chartres read: “Or is it not lawful?”]

It is a foolish question for a human being to raise against the kindness of God. [Note: This should be read according to the better manuscripts—the German manuscript of Corbie, the other manuscript of Corbie, and others. In the old edition the reading is corrupt; in the recent editions it is impeded and confused: “For the complaint ought to be not that he did not give what he ought not to give, but…”] The complaint should not be that he does not give what he ought not to give, but that he does not give what he ought to give. Hence it is aptly added: “Is your eye evil because I am good?”

Let no one exalt himself over his work; let no one exalt himself over the length of time, since, after this statement has been completed, the Truth cries out: “Thus the last will be first, and the first last.” For behold, even if we already know what good works we have done and how great they are, we still do not know with what subtlety the heavenly Judge examines them. And certainly everyone ought to rejoice exceedingly at being even the least in the kingdom of God.

5. But after these words, what follows is exceedingly terrifying: “For many are called, but few are chosen,” because many come to the faith, but few are brought to the kingdom of heaven. Behold how many of us have gathered for today’s festival and fill the walls of the Church; yet who knows how few there are who will be counted in that flock of God’s elect?

Behold, the voice of all cries out “Christ,” but the life of all does not cry out. Most people follow God with their voices but flee from him in their conduct. Hence Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but in their actions they deny him” (Tit. 1:16). Hence James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20, 26). [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, Corbie, Tours, Beauvais, Bigot, and Longpont read “is idle,” contrary to the Greek text and the testimony of the Vulgate, where it reads “is dead,” νεκρά ἐστι. In the *Maxima Bibliotheca*, this variant reading is noted as coming from Vatablus.]

Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). When the Lord calls, the faithful are multiplied beyond number, because sometimes even those come to the faith who do not attain to the number of the elect. [Note: The recent editions corruptly read “therefore,” as is clear from the contrast between “here” and “there,” and especially from the German manuscript of Corbie, Gembloux, and others.]

Here they are mingled with the faithful through confession, but because of their evil life they do not deserve to be numbered there among the lot of the faithful. This sheepfold of holy Church receives goats with the lambs; but, as the Gospel testifies, when the Judge comes, he separates the good from the evil, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (Matt. 25:32). For those who here serve the pleasures of their flesh cannot there be numbered among the flock of sheep. There the Judge separates them from the lot of the humble—those who here exalt themselves on the horns of pride. Those who, though placed in the heavenly faith, seek the earth with their whole desire cannot receive the kingdom of heaven.

6. You see many such people within the Church, dearly beloved brothers, but you must neither imitate them nor despair of them. [Note: The printed editions read, against the manuscripts: “nor despise them.”] We see what someone is today, but we do not know what each person will be tomorrow. Often the one whom we see coming after us surpasses us through the speed of his good work, and scarcely do we follow tomorrow the one whom we seemed to precede today. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, Tours, Chartres, and Beauvais add: “who will come after us.”]

Certainly, when Stephen was dying for the faith, Saul guarded the garments of those who were throwing stones. He himself threw stones with the hands of all those who were throwing them, for he made everyone eager to stone him. [Note: Corbie reads “whom he had urged on”; the printed editions read “whom he had set free.” We follow the German manuscript of Corbie, Tours, Chartres, and others.] Yet he surpassed in the labors of the holy Church that very man whom, by persecuting him, he made a martyr.

There are therefore two things that we must carefully consider. Since many are called but few are chosen, the first is that no one should presume on himself, because, even if he has already been called to the faith, he does not know whether he is worthy of the eternal kingdom. The second is that no one should dare despair of his neighbor, whom he perhaps sees lying in vices, because he does not know the riches of divine mercy.

7. I shall relate, brothers, something that happened recently, so that, if you recognize yourselves to be sinners from the heart, you may love the mercy of almighty God all the more. This present year, in my monastery, which is situated near the church of the blessed martyrs John and Paul, a certain brother came for conversion. He was devoutly received, but he himself conducted himself even more devoutly. (*Dialogues* IV.38.) His brother followed him to the monastery in body, but not in heart.

For he greatly detested the life and habit of conversion. He lived in the monastery as a guest, and, while fleeing the monks’ way of life in his conduct, he could not leave the monastery because he had neither anything to do nor any means by which to live. His wickedness was burdensome to everyone, but all patiently tolerated him out of love for his brother. Proud and dissolute, he did not know whether any life would follow after this world, and he mocked anyone who wished to preach such a life to him.

Thus he lived in the monastery in secular clothing: light in his words, unstable in his movements, swollen with pride in his mind, composed in his dress, and disorderly in his actions. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie, Gembloux, and the second manuscript of Chartres read “in his gestures.” The other manuscript of Chartres reads “in his conduct.”] [Note: The editors thought that *incompositus*, “disordered,” should be read, against the English manuscripts, the German manuscript of Corbie, Gembloux, and others.]

But in the July that has just passed, he was struck by the devastation of the pestilence you know. Coming to his end, he began to be pressed to give up his soul. Since the final extremity of his body was already dead, vital power remained only in his chest and tongue. The brothers were present and, insofar as God granted them the ability, guarded his passing with prayer.

Suddenly he saw a dragon coming to devour him, and began to cry out in a loud voice, saying: “Behold, I have been given to the dragon to be devoured, who cannot devour me because of your presence. Why are you delaying me? Give way, so that it may be permitted to devour me.” [Note: Another manuscript reads “but because of.”]

When the brothers urged him to make the sign of the cross upon himself, he answered with whatever strength he had, saying: “I wish to sign myself, but I cannot, because I am being pressed by the dragon. The foam from its mouth smears my face; my throat is being strangled by its mouth. Behold, my arms are being crushed by it, and it has already swallowed my head in its mouth.”

As he said this, pale, trembling, and dying, the brothers began to persevere more fervently in prayer and to aid by their prayers the man oppressed by the dragon’s presence. Then, suddenly freed, he began to cry out in a loud voice, saying: “Thanks be to God! Behold, it has departed; behold, it has gone out. Before your prayers, the dragon that had seized me has fled.” [Note: In the first manuscript of Chartres, after “had seized me,” the following is added: “Now intercede for my sins, because I am ready to be converted and to abandon secular life completely.”]

Immediately he vowed that he would serve God and become a monk. From that time until now he has been afflicted by fevers and wearied by pains. He has indeed been snatched from death, but he has not yet been fully restored to life. Because he has been oppressed by long-standing and prolonged iniquities, he is wearied by a prolonged sickness; and the fire of purification burns his hard heart with a still harsher flame, because by divine providence it is brought about that a prolonged illness should consume his more prolonged vices.

Who would ever have believed that he would be preserved for conversion? Who could sufficiently contemplate such great mercy from God? Behold, the wicked young man saw at death the dragon whom he had served in life. He did not see it so that he might utterly lose life, but so that he might know whom he had served, resist him through that knowledge, overcome him by resisting, and see him from whom he had previously been held without seeing him, so that afterward he might not be held by him.

What tongue could suffice to tell of the depths of divine mercy? What spirit would not be astonished at the riches of such piety? The Psalmist considered these riches of divine compassion when he said: “My helper, to you I will sing psalms, because you, God, are my sustainer; my God, my mercy” (Ps. 58:18).

Beholding the tribulations in which human life is established, he called God his helper. And because God receives us from present tribulation into eternal rest, he also calls him his sustainer. But considering that God looks upon and bears our evils, tolerates our faults, and nevertheless preserves us through repentance for rewards, he did not wish to call God merely merciful, but called him mercy itself, saying: “My God, my mercy.” [Note: The second manuscript of Chartres reads “through patience.”]

Let us therefore bring before our eyes the evils we have committed; let us weigh by how great a kindness of God we are tolerated; let us consider the depths of his compassion, so that he not only forgives sins but also promises the heavenly kingdom to the penitent after their sins. And from every marrow of the heart let each of us say—let us all say: “My God, my mercy”—who lives and reigns, threefold in unity and one in Trinity, through endless ages of ages. Amen. [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie adds: “who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit.” The first manuscript of Gembloux adds: “to whom, in unity and Trinity, be honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”]

## HOMILY XX

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, on the Saturday of the Ember Days before the Nativity of Christ. [Note: The Lateran manuscript reads: “in the basilica of Saint Saviour, which is called Constantiniana.” In the Roman calendar, the station is at Saint Peter’s.] [Note: These words are not found in the Lateran manuscript, the Swedish Royal Codex, the German manuscript of Corbie, or Bigot.]

### HOLY GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO LUKE 3:1–11

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.

And he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, as it is written in the book of the sayings of Isaiah the prophet:

“The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low. The crooked shall become straight, and the rough ways shall become smooth. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

Therefore he said to the crowds who were coming out to be baptized by him: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Produce fruits worthy of repentance, and do not begin to say: ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Indeed, the axe has already been laid at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

And the crowds asked him, saying: “What then shall we do?” He answered and said to them: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none, and let the one who has food do likewise.”

1516

1. At what time the precursor of our Redeemer received the word of preaching is indicated by the Roman ruler and the kings of Judaea being named, when it says: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the wilderness.” [Note: The German manuscript of Corbie and Gembloux read “of Ituraea.”]

Because John was coming to preach him who would redeem some from Judaea and many from the Gentiles, the times of his preaching are indicated through the king of the Gentiles and the rulers of the Jews. Since the Gentiles were to be gathered and Judaea scattered because of the guilt of its faithlessness, the very description of earthly rule also shows this: in the Roman state one ruler is described as presiding, whereas in the kingdom of Judaea many ruled over its fourfold division.

For by the voice of our Redeemer it is said: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste” (Luke 11:17). It is therefore clear that Judaea had reached the end of its kingdom, since it was subject to so many divided rulers. It is also fitting that not only the rulers but also the priests under whom these events occurred are identified, because John the Baptist was to preach him who would exist as both king and priest. Thus the evangelist Luke designated the time of John’s preaching through both kingdom and priesthood.

2. “And he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.”

It is clear to all who read that John not only preached a baptism of repentance but also gave it to some; nevertheless, he could not give his baptism for the forgiveness of sins. The forgiveness of sins is granted to us through the baptism of Christ alone. [Note: In Corbie this is the third homily; in the Swedish Royal Codex, the sixteenth; in the Lateran manuscript, the fourth.]

It must therefore be noted that it says: “Preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” Since he could not give a baptism that would release sins, he preached it, so that, just as he preceded the incarnate Word of the Father by the word of preaching, so he might precede with his own baptism—which cannot release sins—the baptism of repentance, by which sins are released. Since his discourse preceded the presence of the Redeemer, his baptism too, by preceding, would become a shadow of the truth. [Note: Bigot reads “by preceding.”]

It continues:

3. “As it is written in the book of the sayings of Isaiah the prophet: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (Isa. 40:3).

When John the Baptist was asked who he was, he answered, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23). As we said earlier, he was called “a voice” by the prophet because he preceded the Word. [Note: Beauvais, the German manuscript of Corbie, Longpont, and the two later manuscripts of Gembloux read: “as was said earlier by us.”]

What he was to cry out is revealed when it adds: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Everyone who preaches right faith and good works does what other than prepare a way for the coming Lord to the hearts of his hearers? He prepares a way so that the force of grace may enter, so that the light of truth may shine, and so that he may make straight paths for God by forming pure thoughts in the mind through the word of good preaching.

“Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low.” What is designated here by the name of valleys except the humble, and by mountains and hills except proud people? At the Redeemer’s coming, therefore, valleys were filled, while mountains and hills were brought low, because, according to his word: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14).

A valley, when filled, rises; a mountain or hill, when brought low, diminishes. For in the faith of the Mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus, the Gentiles received the fullness of grace, while Judaea, through the error of faithlessness, lost the very thing by which it had been swollen with pride.

“Every valley shall be filled,” because the hearts of the humble will be filled with the grace of the virtues through the speech of sacred doctrine, according to what is written: “He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. 103:10). And again: “The valleys will abound with grain” (Ps. 64:14).

Water flows down from the mountains, because the teaching of truth abandons proud minds. [Note: Beauvais and Corbie read: “the truth of doctrine abandons them.”] But springs rise in the valleys, because the minds of the humble receive the word of preaching. Already we see it; already we observe the valleys abounding with grain, because the mouths of those who seemed meek and simple and contemptible to this world have been filled with the nourishment of truth.

4. The people had seen John the Baptist himself endowed with wondrous holiness and thought that he was that uniquely lofty and solid mountain of which it is written: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Mic. 4:1). For the people thought that he was the Christ, as the Gospel says: “While the people were considering it and all were thinking in their hearts about John, whether perhaps he was the Christ, whom they were also asking about, saying: ‘Are you the Christ?’” (Luke 3:15).

But unless John himself had been a valley in his own eyes, he would not have been filled with the grace of the Spirit. To show what he was, he said: “One mightier than I is coming after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (Mark 1:7). And again he said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:29–30).

Behold, although, because of his wondrous working of virtues, he was such that he was thought to be the Christ, he not only answered that he was not the Christ but also declared himself unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal—that is, unworthy to examine the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “to conceal what he was.” Shortly afterward, Beauvais, Corbie, and Longpont read: “One mightier than I is coming, whose…”]

Those who thought John was the Christ believed that the Church was his bride. But he says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” He seems to say: “I am not the bridegroom, but I am the friend of the bridegroom.” He declared that he rejoiced not because of his own voice but in the bridegroom’s voice, because he was not happy in his heart on the grounds that the crowds listened humbly to him as he spoke; rather, he rejoiced because he heard the voice of truth within himself so that he might speak it outwardly.

He rightly says that this joy has been fulfilled, because whoever rejoices in his own voice does not possess complete joy. Hence he adds: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

[Col. 1162C] 5. In this matter we must ask in what way Christ increased and in what way John diminished. The people, seeing John’s abstinence and observing that he was withdrawn from human company, thought that he was the Christ. But when they saw Christ eating with tax collectors and walking among sinners, they thought that he was not the Christ but a prophet.

But as time passed, Christ—who had been thought to be a prophet—was recognized as the Christ, and John—who had been thought to be the Christ—was shown to be a prophet. Thus what Christ’s precursor had foretold was fulfilled: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

In the estimation of the people, Christ increased because he was recognized as what he was; and John decreased because people ceased to call him what he was not. Therefore, since John himself persevered in holiness because he remained steadfast in humility of heart, while many fell because they swelled with exalted thoughts in themselves, it is rightly said: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low,” because the humble receive the gift that proud hearts repel from themselves.

6. It follows: “And crooked things shall be made straight, and rough ways into level roads.” Crooked things are made straight when the hearts of the wicked, bent away through injustice, are directed toward the rule of justice [Col. 1163A] (Isa. 40:4). Rough ways are changed into level roads when harsh and angry minds, through the infusion of heavenly grace, return to the gentleness of meekness. For when the word of truth is not received by an angry mind, the roughness of the road—as it were—repels the step of the traveler. But when an angry mind receives the word of correction or exhortation through the grace of meekness, the preacher finds a level road where previously, because of the roughness of the way, he could not proceed—that is, could not set down the step of preaching.

7. It follows: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Since “all flesh” means every human being, not every human being in this life could see the salvation of God, namely Christ. Where, then, does the prophet direct the eye of prophecy in this statement, if not toward the day of the final judgment? [Note: Belvac., “to the end of the judge’s day.” Longip., “to the end of the day of judgment.”] On that day, when Christ appears with the heavens opened, the angels ministering, and the apostles seated upon the throne of his majesty, all shall see him together—the elect and the rejected alike—so that the righteous may rejoice without end in the gift of their reward, while the unrighteous may groan forever under the vengeance of punishment.

Since this statement is directed toward the fact that he will be seen by all flesh at the final judgment, it is rightly followed by: “And he said to the crowds who came out to be baptized by him: Broods of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” The coming wrath is the final execution of vengeance, which the sinner cannot then flee if he does not now turn to the lamentation of repentance. It should be noted that evil offspring, imitating the deeds of evil parents, are called “broods of vipers,” because in envying the good, persecuting them, repaying some with evil, and seeking injuries against their neighbors, they follow in all these things the ways of their carnal forebears; they are, as it were, poisonous children born from poisonous parents.

8. But because we have already sinned, because we are entangled in the practice of an evil habit, let him tell us what we must do so that we may be able to flee the coming wrath. It follows: “Therefore, produce fruits worthy of repentance.” In these words it should be noted that the Bridegroom’s friend admonishes us to produce not merely fruits of repentance, but fruits worthy of repentance. For it is one thing to produce the fruit of repentance and another to produce a fruit worthy of repentance.

To speak, then, of fruits worthy of repentance, we must understand that whoever has committed no unlawful acts may rightly make use of lawful things, and may perform works of piety without, if he does not wish to do so, abandoning the things of the world. But if someone has fallen into the guilt of fornication or, what is more serious, into adultery, he ought to cut away from himself lawful things in proportion to his remembrance that he has perpetrated unlawful acts. For the fruit of a good work ought not to be equal for one who has sinned less and one who has sinned more, or for one who has fallen into no crimes and one who has fallen into some crimes [Col. 1164A], [Note: In Belvac. and nine other ancient manuscripts this clause is absent: “and for one who has fallen into many.” [Col. 1164D] Yet it seems required for a complete division.] and one who has fallen into many.

Therefore, by the words “Produce fruits worthy of repentance,” each person’s conscience is confronted, so that through repentance he may seek profits of good works proportionate to the greater losses he has inflicted upon himself through sin. [Note: In two later Gemet. manuscripts, “may acquire.”]

9. But the Jews, boasting of the nobility of their lineage, did not wish to acknowledge themselves as sinners because they had descended from Abraham’s stock. To them it is rightly said: “And do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” [Note: Conversely, in Val. Cl. and the third Gemet., “for what are the hearts of the Gentiles except stones?”]

For what were stones except the hearts of the Gentiles, insensible to the understanding of almighty God? Thus it is also said to certain Jews: “I will take the heart of stone from your flesh” (Ezek. 11:19). Nor are the nations signified without reason by the name of stones, since they worshiped stones. Hence it is written: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:8).

From these stones, then, children were raised up for Abraham, because when the hard hearts of the Gentiles believed in Abraham’s offspring—that is, in Christ—they became his children, having been joined to his offspring. Hence the outstanding preacher also says to those same Gentiles: “But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. 3:29).

If, therefore, through faith in Christ we are already Abraham’s offspring, the Jews, because of their unbelief, have ceased to be Abraham’s children. But that good parents cannot help their evil children on the day of that dreadful judgment, the prophet testifies when he says: “Noah, Daniel, and Job, if they were in the midst of them” [Note: C. Germ. and several others, “in the midst of it.”] “as I live,” says the Lord God, “they shall deliver neither son nor daughter, but they themselves shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness” (Ezek. 14:14).

And again, because good children benefit evil parents nothing, but the goodness of children rather contributes to the condemnation of evil parents, Truth itself says to the unbelieving Jews: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges” (Luke 11:19).

10. It follows: “For now the axe is laid at the root of the tree. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire.” The tree of this world is the entire human race. The axe is our Redeemer, who is held, as it were, by its handle and iron in his humanity, but cuts through his divinity.

This axe is already laid at the root of the tree because, although he waits patiently, what he is about to do is nevertheless apparent. “Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire,” because every perverse person who scorns to produce the fruit of good works here finds the burning of Gehenna prepared for him all the sooner.

It should be noted that he says the axe is laid not beside the branches but at the root. When the children of the wicked are taken away, what else are they than the fruitless tree’s branches, which are cut off? But when the entire offspring is removed together with its parent, the fruitless tree has been cut off at the root [Col. 1165A] 1521, so that nothing remains from which a crooked offspring might grow again.

The words of John the Baptist show that the hearts of his hearers were shaken, since it immediately follows: “And the crowds questioned him, saying, ‘What then shall we do?’” Those who sought counsel had been struck with terror.

11. It follows: “And answering, he said to them: ‘Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none; and whoever has food, let him likewise do.’” Since a tunic is more necessary for our use than a cloak, it belongs to the worthy fruit of repentance that we should share with our neighbors not only outward possessions and things less necessary, but even the things that are very necessary for us—namely, either the food by which we live bodily or the tunic with which we are clothed.

For since it is written in the law, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39, from Lev. 19:18), the person who does not share with his neighbor, in that neighbor’s need, even the things necessary for himself is shown to love his neighbor less.

Therefore the command to share two tunics with one’s neighbor is given because this could not be said of one tunic: if one is divided, no one is clothed. For when a tunic is divided in half, both the one who receives and the one who gives remain naked.

Meanwhile, we should understand how greatly works of mercy are worth, since they are prescribed above all else as fruits worthy of repentance. Hence Truth itself says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Again it says: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:38). It is written here: “Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins” (Sir. 3:33). Again it is said: “Enclose almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will intercede for you” (ibid. 29:15). Hence the good father admonishes his innocent son, saying: “If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, willingly strive to share even a little” (Tob. 4:9).

12. To show how great a virtue there is in self-restraint and in receiving those in need, our Redeemer says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10:41).

In these words it should be noted that he does not say, “He shall receive a reward from the prophet,” or “a reward from the righteous person,” but, “He shall receive a prophet’s reward,” and “a righteous person’s reward.” For a reward from a prophet is one thing, and a prophet’s reward another; a reward from a righteous person is one thing, and a righteous person’s reward another.

What does “He shall receive a prophet’s reward” mean except that the person who supports a prophet by his generosity, although he himself does not possess prophecy, will nevertheless have the rewards of prophecy before almighty God?

Perhaps this person is righteous, and because he possesses nothing in this world, he has all the greater confidence to speak on behalf of righteousness. When someone who possesses something in this world supports him, while perhaps not yet daring to speak freely for righteousness, that supporter makes the righteous person’s freedom his own by participation, so that he may receive together with him the rewards of righteousness—he who, by supporting him, helped him to speak that same righteousness freely.

The prophet is full of the spirit of prophecy, but nevertheless needs bodily nourishment. If the body is not restored, it is certain that the voice itself will be taken away. Therefore, whoever supplies nourishment to a prophet because he is a prophet gives the strength of prophecy for speaking.

He will therefore receive a prophet’s reward together with the prophet [Col. 1166A] 1522, because even though he was not full of the spirit of prophecy, he nevertheless displayed before God what he had helped.

Hence John says to Gaius concerning certain traveling brothers: [Note: C. Germ., the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, and Longip., “Gaius.”] “For they have gone forth for the sake of the name of Christ, receiving nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such persons, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 7–8).

Whoever gives temporal assistance to those who possess spiritual gifts becomes a fellow worker in those spiritual gifts. For since there are few who receive spiritual gifts and many who abound in temporal possessions, through this means the rich join themselves to the virtues of the poor, by comforting these holy poor from their own wealth.

Hence, when through the voice of Isaiah the Lord promised the abandoned Gentile people—that is, the holy Church—the merits of spiritual virtues, like groves in a desert, he promised an elm as well, saying: “I will make the desert into pools of water, and the impassable land into streams of water; I will give in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, the myrtle and the olive tree; I will set in the desert the fir, the elm, and the box tree together, so that they may see and know, reflect, and understand together” (Isa. 41:18, 20).

13. The Lord made the desert into pools of water and the impassable land into streams of water because he gave the Gentiles, who previously bore no fruits of good works through the aridity of their minds, the streams of holy preaching. The same people, to whom the way had previously been closed to preachers because of the harshness of their dryness, later poured forth streams of doctrine.

To this people he further promises as a great gift: “I will give in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn” (ibid. 19). Since the cedar has a powerful fragrance and an incorruptible nature, we rightly understand it in the promise. But concerning the thorn, since it was said to sinful humanity, “Your land shall produce thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18), what wonder is it if that which is multiplied as punishment for sinful humanity is promised to the holy Church?

By the name of cedar, therefore, those who display virtues and signs in their works are signified; they can say with Paul: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15). Their hearts have been so firmly established in eternal love that no decay of earthly love can now corrupt them. [Note: The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, Longip., and Val. Cl., “within.”]

By the thorn, spiritual teachers are signified. As they discuss sins and virtues, now threatening eternal punishments, now promising the joys of the heavenly kingdom, they prick the hearts of their hearers. Thus they pierce the mind with the pain of compunction, so that tears flow from their eyes like a kind of blood of the soul.

The myrtle is a symbol of the virtue that moderates, so that by tempering it restrains relaxed limbs. [Col. 1167A] What, then, is signified by the myrtle except those who know how to sympathize with the afflictions of their neighbors and moderate their tribulation through compassion? In accordance with what is written: [Note: Longip., “I give thanks to God.”] “But thanks be to God, who comforts us in all our tribulation, so that we too may be able to comfort those who are in every distress” (2 Cor. 1:4).

When they bring to afflicted neighbors a word or assistance of consolation, they undoubtedly restore them to a state of uprightness, lest they be broken into despair by excessive tribulation.

Whom do we understand by the olive except the merciful? For in Greek, ἔλεος means “mercy,” and, like the oil of the olive, the fruit of mercy shines before the eyes of almighty God.

To this he further adds in the promise: “I will set in the desert the fir, the elm, and the box tree together” (Isa. 41:19).

By the fir, which rises very high as it grows and is lifted toward the heights of the air, who are signified except those who, although still placed within earthly bodies in the holy Church, already contemplate heavenly things? Although they came forth from the earth by birth, nevertheless through contemplation they already raise the summit of their mind near the ether.

And what is expressed by the elm except the minds of secular people? While they still serve earthly concerns, they produce no fruit of spiritual virtues. Yet although the elm has no fruit of its own, it usually supports a vine bearing fruit; for secular men within the holy Church, although they do not possess the gifts of spiritual virtues, nevertheless, while supporting by their generosity holy men full of spiritual gifts, do they not carry the vine with its clusters?

But whom else does the box tree signify? It does not grow tall, and although it bears no fruit, it nevertheless remains green. It signifies those who, within the holy Church, because of the weakness of their age are not yet able to produce good works, but who, following the faith of believing parents, retain the faith of perpetual greenness.

After all this, it is appropriately added: “So that they may see and know, reflect, and understand together.” The cedar is placed in the Church for this purpose: whoever draws from his neighbor the fragrance of spiritual virtues [Note: Here the manuscripts, both handwritten and printed, disagree among themselves. Gemet., followed by all the printed editions except Gussanv., reads ipse quoque in terrenae; the others, both English and our own, read ipse quoque internae, or ad internae, or ab internae.] should not himself grow cold in the love of eternal life [Note: Belvac. and four others, “in delight”], but should burn with desire for heavenly goods. [Note: This is the reading of Corb. Germ., with many later manuscripts and the old editions.]

The thorn is placed for this purpose: whoever has been pierced by the word of its preaching should also learn by its example to pierce the hearts of those who follow him with the word of preaching.

The myrtle is placed for this purpose: whoever has received the moderation of consolation from the mouth or work of a compassionate person in the heat of tribulation [Col. 1167D] should also learn how to offer the moderation of his own consolation to afflicted neighbors.

The olive is placed for this purpose: whoever recognizes the works of another’s mercy should learn how he too ought to show mercy to a needy neighbor.

The fir is placed for this purpose: whoever has recognized the power of its contemplation should himself also be kindled to contemplate eternal rewards.

The elm is placed for this purpose [Col. 1168A]: whoever has looked upon one who cannot possess the fruit of spiritual virtues but nevertheless supports those who are full of spiritual gifts should himself serve the life of the saints with as much generosity as he can, and should carry, by supporting them, the clusters of heavenly goods that he cannot produce by giving birth. [Note: C. Germ., “placed in weak age.”]

The box tree is placed for this purpose: whoever observes that many people, still placed in weakness, possess the greenness of true faith should be ashamed to be himself an unbeliever.

Thus, after the trees have first been described, it is rightly said: “So that they may see and know, reflect, and understand.” And “together” is appropriately added, because although diverse human dispositions and diverse orders exist within the holy Church, all must learn together, since spiritual people of differing qualities, ages, and ranks are seen together in it for imitation.

But behold: while we seek to point out the elm, we have wandered farther afield through many groves. Let us therefore return to the reason for which we brought forward the prophet’s testimony: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward.” Although the elm has no fruit, by carrying a vine with its fruits it makes these its own [Note: The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “which it supports as good things”]—the things that it rightly supports in another.

14. Since John urges us to great works, saying, “Therefore, produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:8; Luke 3:8), and again, “Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none; and whoever has food, let him likewise do” (Luke 3:11), it is now plainly understood what Truth means when he says: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

These words of the heavenly judgment must be examined by us with the greatest care. For we must ask how the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence. Who inflicts violence upon heaven? And again, if the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence, why has it suffered this violence from the days of John the Baptist and not also before?
