But when the law says, “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death,” it is clear to all who read that it struck sinners with the punishment of its severity, but did not restore them to life through repentance.

When John the Baptist, preceding the grace of the Redeemer, preaches repentance, so that the sinner who died through guilt may live through conversion, then surely from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.

What, moreover, is the kingdom of heaven except the place of the righteous? For the rewards of the heavenly homeland are owed only to the righteous, so that the humble, chaste, meek, and merciful may attain the joys above.

But when someone who is swollen with pride, polluted by carnal crime, inflamed by anger, or impious through cruelty returns to repentance after his sins and receives eternal life, the sinner enters, as it were, into another’s place.

Therefore, from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence [Col. 1169A] 1525, and the violent seize it, because the one who imposed repentance upon sinners taught nothing other than how violence might be done to the kingdom of heaven.

15. Let us therefore recall, dearest brothers, the evils we have committed, and let us wear ourselves down with continual lamentation. Let us seize through repentance the inheritance of the righteous, which we did not retain through our life. Almighty God wishes to suffer such violence from us. For he wishes the kingdom of heaven to be seized through our tears, although it is not owed to our merits.

Therefore, let no quality or quantity of our evils break the certainty of our hope. That venerable thief gives us great confidence in forgiveness—not venerable because he was a thief, but a thief because of his cruelty and venerable because of his confession.

Consider, then, consider how incomprehensible are the depths of mercy in almighty God. This thief, dragged away with bloodstained hands [Note: C. Germ. and the third Gemet., “from the face of the road”] from the throat of the road, was hung upon the gallows of the cross [Col. 1170A]. There he confessed; there he was healed; there he deserved to hear: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

What is this? Who is sufficient to speak of or estimate such great goodness of God? From the very punishment of his crime he reached the rewards of virtue.

Almighty God permitted his elect to fall into certain lapses so that, while others lay in guilt, he might restore hope of forgiveness to them if they rose to him with their whole heart, and through the lamentation of repentance might open for them the way of mercy. [Note: The printed editions read, “might already open the heavenly homeland.” We follow almost all the manuscripts. In two Gemet. manuscripts, “truth” is read instead of “mercy.”]

Let us therefore exercise ourselves in lamentation; let us extinguish through tears and fruits worthy of repentance the sins we have committed. [Note: Turon., together with Longip., Val. Cl., three Gemet. manuscripts, and Bigot., has this instead of “forgiveness,” which is read in the printed editions. The passage is absent from C. Germ., Belvac., and the first Carn., where only this is read: “Let us extinguish … the sins.” [Col. 1170B] “Let the time granted to us not pass away.”]

Let the time granted to us for forgiveness not pass away, because when we see many already healed from their iniquities, what else do we hold but a pledge of heavenly mercy? [Note: After “we hold,” the homily concludes in the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts as follows: “Therefore, let there be honor to Jesus Christ our Lord, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.” In the third Gemet.: “May he himself whom we love, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever, help us. Amen.”]

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1169]

[Note: It is the fourteenth in Lateran. In the royal Swedish manuscript, the seventeenth. In Corb., the twelfth.]

## HOMILY XXI

[Col. 1169B]

Delivered to the people in the basilica of the blessed virgin Mary, on the holy day of Easter.

### LESSON FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK, 16:1–7

At that time, Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome [Note: Belvac. and C. Germ., “going away, bought.”] bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus. And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen. And they said to one another: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” [Note: In the same manuscripts the following immediately appears: “for it was very large.” And, “And looking up, etc.” Thus the hyperbaton of the Vulgate, and indeed of the Greek text, is removed. In those manuscripts, this precedes.] And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away. For it was very large. And entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished. He said to them: “Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you.”

1526 1. For many Gospel readings, dearest brothers, I have been accustomed to speak to you by dictation. But because, as my stomach grows weak, I myself cannot read what I have dictated, I see some of you listening less willingly [Col. 1169D]. Therefore, I now wish to demand of myself, contrary to custom, that during the sacred solemnities of Mass I expound the reading of the holy Gospel not by dictating but by speaking.

Let it be received as we speak, because the voice of conversation awakens drowsy hearts more than the discourse of a reading and, as it were, knocks with a hand of solicitude so that they may awake. Indeed, I do not see that I am sufficient for this task; yet charity supplies the strength that incapacity denies. For I know who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11).

Let the good work therefore be present in our will, for its perfection will come from divine assistance. The great solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection itself also gives boldness for speaking, because it is utterly unworthy that the tongue of flesh should be silent about the praises owed on the day when the flesh of its Creator rose again.

2. You have heard, dearest brothers, that the holy women who had followed the Lord came to the tomb with spices, and that they ministered with human devotion even to him whom they had loved while living, though he was now dead.

But the event signifies something that must be done in the holy Church. We must hear what happened in such a way that we may also consider what we ought to do in imitation of it. If, then, believing in him who died, we seek the Lord filled with the fragrance of virtues and with the reputation of good works, we surely come with spices to his tomb.

Those women who came with spices see angels, because those minds behold the citizens above which, with the fragrances of virtues, proceed toward the Lord through holy desires. [Note: C. Germ. and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “toward God.”]

We should also note why the angel is seen sitting on the right. What is signified by the left except the present life, and what by the right except perpetual life? Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6).

Since our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the present life, the angel who came to announce his perpetual life rightly sat on the right. He appeared clothed in a white robe because he announced the joys of our solemnity. The whiteness of the garment signifies the splendor of our solemnity.

Shall we say “our,” or “his”? But, to speak more truly, let us say both “his” and “ours.” The resurrection of our Redeemer was our solemnity because it restored us to immortality; and it was the solemnity of the angels because, by restoring us to the heavenly places, it replenished their number. Thus, at his and our solemnity, the angel appeared in white garments, because when we are restored to the heights through the Lord’s resurrection, the losses of the heavenly homeland are repaired.

3. But let us hear what he says to the women who have arrived: “Do not be afraid.” As though he were openly saying: Let those be afraid who do not love the arrival of the citizens above; let those tremble who, weighed down by carnal desires, despair of being able to attain their fellowship. But why are you afraid, when you see your fellow citizens?

Matthew likewise, describing the angel’s appearance, says: “His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. 28:3). [Note: C. Germ., Belvac., Longip., and the third Gemet., “in brightness.”] In lightning there is the terror of fear, but in snow the soothing quality of whiteness.

Since almighty God is both terrible to sinners and gentle to the righteous, the angel who testified to his resurrection is rightly shown both with a face like lightning and with a garment of whiteness, so that by his very appearance he might terrify the reprobate and comfort the devout.

Hence it is also rightly said that a pillar of fire went before the people journeying through the desert by night, and a pillar of cloud by day (Exod. 13:21–22). There is terror in fire, but in cloud the gentle comfort of vision. Day signifies the life of the righteous, while night signifies the life of the sinner. Thus Paul says to converted sinners: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

Therefore, by day the pillar was shown through a cloud, and by night through fire, because almighty God will appear gentle to the righteous and terrible to the unrighteous. At the judgment, when he comes, he will soothe the former through the gentleness of mercy, but terrify the latter through the severity of justice.

4. But let us now hear what the angel adds: “You seek Jesus of Nazareth.” In Latin usage, Jesus is interpreted as “salutary,” that is, “savior.” At that time, however, many could be called Jesus, though not in substance but merely by name. Therefore the place is added, so that it may be made clear of which Jesus he speaks: “of Nazareth.”

And immediately he added the reason: “crucified.” Then he added: “He has risen; he is not here.” “He is not here” is said in respect of the presence of his flesh, although he is nowhere absent in respect of the presence of his majesty. [Note: Here we restore much that is absent from most editions; it is found in C. Germ., the two Carn. manuscripts, the third Gemet., and others, as well as in the Antwerp edition. The other reading, “he is not here through the presence of his majesty,” is corrupt and mutilated. But the point is clear.]

“But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you into Galilee.” We must ask why, after naming the disciples, Peter is designated by name. If the angel had not expressly named him, the one who had denied his master would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name so that he would not despair because of his denial.

In this matter we should consider (Dist. 50, ch. 53) why almighty God permitted the man whom he had decided to place above the entire Church to fear the voice of a servant girl and deny himself. We recognize that this was done through a dispensation of great mercy, so that the one who was to become the Church’s shepherd might learn through his own guilt how he ought to show mercy to others.

First, therefore, he displayed him to himself, and then placed him over the others, so that through his own weakness he might learn how mercifully to bear with the weaknesses of others.

5. It is rightly said of our Redeemer: “He is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you.” Galilee is interpreted as “made transmigration.”

Our Redeemer had already passed from suffering to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption 1528. After his resurrection he is first seen by the disciples in Galilee, because we shall see the glory of his resurrection afterward with joy if we now migrate from vices to the heights of virtues.

He who is announced in the tomb is shown in transmigration, because the one who is recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the transmigration of the mind.

These things, dearest brothers, we have briefly passed over concerning the exposition of the Gospel reading in honor of so great a day’s solemnity. But let us speak somewhat more subtly about this same solemnity.

6. There were two lives: one we knew, the other we did not know. One was mortal, the other immortal; one corruptible, the other incorruptible; [Note: The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “one mortal”] one a life of death, the other a life of resurrection.

But the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, came; he took upon himself one and displayed the other. He endured one by dying and displayed the other by rising again.

If, then, while we knew mortal life, he promised us the resurrection of the flesh but did not visibly exhibit it, who would believe his promises? Thus he appeared as a human being in the flesh, deigned to die by his will, rose by his power, and showed by his example what he promised us as a reward.

But perhaps someone will say: He rightly rose, since, being God, he could not be held by death. To instruct our ignorance and strengthen our weakness, he did not wish the example of his resurrection alone to suffice for us. He alone died at that time, yet he was by no means the only one to rise. For it is written: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose” (Matt. 27:52).

Thus every argument for unbelief has been removed. No one should say: “A human being ought not to hope for himself in what God the man displayed in his own flesh.” [Note: Belvac., “the God-man ought.”] Behold, we know that human beings rose together with God—and we do not doubt that they were pure human beings.

If, then, we are members of our Redeemer, let us presume for ourselves what is established as having occurred in the head. If we cast ourselves down greatly, we ought to hope for ourselves, his lowest members, what we have heard concerning his higher members.

### 7.

Behold, in truth, what the Jews, insulting the crucified Son of God, said returns to our memory: “If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (ibid. 42). If he had then come down from the cross, yielding, as it were, to those who insulted him, he would not have demonstrated to us the power of patience. But he waited a little, endured their insults, bore their mockery, preserved his patience, and postponed their astonishment; and he who did not wish to come down from the cross rose from the tomb. Therefore it was greater to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross. It was greater to destroy death by rising again than to preserve life by coming down.

But when the Jews did not see him come down from the cross in response to their insults, and saw him dying, they believed that they had conquered him and rejoiced as though they had extinguished his name. But behold, from his death his name grew throughout the world—from that death by which this faithless crowd believed it had extinguished him [Note: [Col. 1173D] The first Carn., “from which him.” Val. Cl. and Gemet., “from which this faithless [one].”]; and the one whose death they had rejoiced over, they mourned as dead, because they recognized that he had reached his glory through punishment [Note: [Col. 1173D] C. Germ. and Bigot., “and the one who had rejoiced.”].

This is well signified by the deeds of that Samson in the Book of Judges (Judg. XVI, 1–3). When he had entered Gaza, a city of the Philistines, the Philistines, immediately recognizing his entrance, suddenly surrounded the city with siegeworks, stationed guards [Note: [Col. 1173D] The second Carn., “carried away”], and rejoiced that they had already seized Samson, the strongest of men. But what Samson did, we know. At midnight he carried away the city gates and climbed to the summit of the mountain.

Whom, dearest brothers, does that Samson signify in this deed, if not our Redeemer? What does the city Gaza signify, if not hell? What is demonstrated by the Philistines, if not the faithlessness of the Jews? When they saw the Lord dead, and his body already placed in the tomb, they immediately appointed guards and rejoiced that they had caught him who had shone forth as the author of life, held fast in the prison of hell, as Samson in Gaza.

But Samson at midnight not only went out, but also carried away the gates, because our Redeemer, rising before the light, not only came forth free from hell but also destroyed hell’s very prison-bars. He carried away the gates and climbed to the summit of the mountain, because by rising again he removed the bars of hell, and by ascending he entered the kingdoms of heaven.

Let us therefore love with our whole mind this glory of his resurrection, which was first indicated by a sign and afterward made manifest in fact [Note: [Col. 1173D] In more recent editions, “appeared.”]; let us die for love of him. Behold, in the resurrection of our Author we have recognized his angels as our fellow citizens. Let us therefore hasten to that solemn assembly of these citizens. Since we cannot yet join them by sight, let us unite ourselves to them in desire and mind. Let us pass from vices to virtues, so that we may be worthy to see our Redeemer in Galilee.

May almighty God assist our desire for life—he who for us gave his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, to death—who with him lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1174D] In the Lateran manuscript it is the seventeenth. Where it is said to have been delivered in the Basilica of Saint Saviour, which in the Codex Regius of Sweden is called the eighteenth. In Corbie, the sixteenth.]

## HOMILY XXII

Delivered to the people in the basilica of blessed John, which is called Constantiniana, on the Saturday after Easter.

### LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN XX, 1–9

At that time, on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb. So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved [Note: [Col. 1174D] C. Germ., Belvac., Bigot., and the third Gemet., “whom he loved”], and said to them: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have put him” [Note: [Col. 1174D] Bigot., “I do not know.”].

Then Peter and the other disciple went out and came to the tomb. Now the two were running together, and the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came first to the tomb [Note: [Col. 1174D] C. Germ. and Bigot., “came earlier.”]. And when he bent down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.

Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded separately in one place.

Then the other disciple, who had come first to the tomb, also entered [Note: [Col. 1174D] Belvac. and C. Germ., “and the other disciple who had come first.”], and he saw and believed. For they did not yet know [Note: [Col. 1174D] Bigot. and C. Germ., “he did not know.”] the Scriptures, that he had to rise from the dead.

### 1.

My stomach, weakened by a prolonged illness, long prevented me from speaking to your charity about an exposition of the Gospel reading. For my very voice fails under the exertion of shouting; and because I cannot be heard by many, I confess that I am ashamed to speak among many. Yet I myself reprove this shame in myself. For what follows? If I cannot benefit many, should I not care even for a few? And if I cannot carry many sheaves from the harvest, ought I to return empty to the threshing floor? Although I cannot carry as many as I ought, I shall certainly carry at least a few, at least two, at least one. For the very intention amid infirmity has the assurance of its reward, because our heavenly Judge, although he considers the burden in recompense, nevertheless weighs one’s strength in assessing the burden.

### 2.

The Gospel reading that you have just heard, brothers, is very clear on the surface as history; but its mysteries must be sought briefly for our benefit.

Mary Magdalene came to the tomb while it was still dark. In the historical sense, the hour is noted; in the mystical sense, the understanding of the one seeking is indicated. For Mary was seeking in the tomb the Author of all things, whom she had seen dead in the flesh; and because she did not find him there, she believed that he had been stolen [Note: [Col. 1175D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “taken away secretly.”].

It was still dark, therefore, when she came to the tomb. She ran more quickly and announced it to the disciples. But those who ran ahead of the others were those who loved more than the others—namely, Peter and John.

The two were running together, but John ran ahead faster than Peter and came first to the tomb, yet he did not presume to enter. Peter came afterward and entered. What, brothers, what does this running signify? Should we believe that so subtle a description by the evangelist is empty of mysteries? Certainly not. For John would not have said that he both went ahead and did not enter if he had believed that his very hesitation contained no mystery.

What, then, is signified by John if not the Synagogue, and by Peter if not the Church? Nor should it seem surprising that the Synagogue is represented by the younger and the Church by the older, because although the Synagogue preceded the Church of the nations in the worship of God, in the order of the world the multitude of the nations preceded the Synagogue, as Paul testifies when he says: “It is not the spiritual that is first, but the natural” (I Cor. XV, 46).

Thus Peter, the elder, signifies the Church of the nations, while John, the younger, signifies the Synagogue of the Jews. Both ran together, because from the rising of the sun to its setting, the Gentile world and the Synagogue ran along an equal and common path, though not with equal and common understanding [Note: [Col. 1175D] Bigot., “life.”].

### 3.

The Synagogue came first to the tomb but did not enter, because it received the commandments of the Law and heard the prophecies concerning the Lord’s incarnation and passion, yet did not wish to believe in the dead man.

John saw the linen cloths lying there but did not enter, because the Synagogue recognized the mysteries of Sacred Scripture and yet delayed entering by belief into faith in the Lord’s passion. It saw him present whom it had long and extensively proclaimed in prophecy, yet rejected him [Note: [Col. 1175D] In the printed editions, “refused to receive him.”]; it despised him as a human being and refused to believe that God had become mortal in the flesh.

What does this mean, then, except that it ran more quickly and nevertheless stood empty before the tomb? But Simon Peter came after him and entered the tomb, because the Church of the nations followed later and recognized the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, as dead in the flesh, yet believed him to be the living God.

He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin that had been over his head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded separately in one place. What, brothers, do we believe this means—that the napkin of the Lord’s head is not found in the tomb with the linen cloths—except that, as Paul testifies (I Cor. XI, 3), God is the head of Christ, and the incomprehensible mysteries of divinity are separated from the knowledge of our weakness, while his power transcends the nature of creation?

It should also be noted that it is said to have been found not only separately [Note: [Col. 1175D] We have supplied here certain words omitted in the more recent printed editions.], but also folded in one place. For a linen cloth that is folded reveals neither its beginning nor its end. Rightly, therefore, the napkin of the head was found folded, because the height of divinity neither began to be nor ceases; it is neither born through a beginning nor confined by an end.

It is well added: “In one place,” because God is not found in the division of minds. God is in unity, and those deserve to possess his grace who do not divide themselves from one another through the scandals of sects.

But because the sweat of laborers is usually wiped away with a napkin, the name “napkin” may also express God’s labor. In himself he always remains at rest and unchangeable, yet he declares himself to labor when he bears the hard perversities of human beings. Hence through the prophet he says: “I have labored in enduring” (Jer. VI, 11).

God appeared in the flesh and labored because of our weakness. When unbelievers saw the labor of his passion, they did not wish to honor him. They saw him mortal in the flesh and disdained to believe him immortal in divinity.

Hence Jeremiah also says: “You will repay them, Lord, according to the works of their hands; you will give them the shield of their heart, your labor” (Lam. III, 64–65). Because they disdained the labor of his passion, lest the arrows of preaching pierce their hearts, they held that very labor as a shield, as it were, so that they would not allow his words to pass through to them, since they had seen him laboring even unto death [Note: [Col. 1175D] In C. Germ., the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, and Bigot., the words that appear here between “they saw” and “therefore the napkin” are absent [Col. 1176D].].

But what are we except members of our head, that is, of God? Through the linen cloths of the body, therefore, the bonds of labor are signified, which now bind all the elect, that is, his members.

The napkin that had been over his head is found separately, because the passion of our Redeemer is far removed from our passion: he endured without guilt what we endure with guilt. He willingly submitted to death, whereas we come to it unwillingly.

### 4.

It follows: “Then the other disciple also entered, who had come first to the tomb.” After Peter entered, John also went in. The one who had come first entered later. [Note: [Col. 1176D] Belvac. first, Carn. and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “It should be noted, brothers.”]

It should be noted, brothers, that at the end of the world Judea too will be gathered into faith in the Redeemer, as Paul testifies when he says: “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI, 25–26).

“And he saw and believed.” What, brothers, should we think that he believed? Did he believe that the Lord had risen, the one whom he was seeking [Note: [Col. 1176D] Corbie and Belvac., “whom they were seeking.”]? Certainly not, because it was still dark at the tomb [Note: [Col. 1177D] Bigot., “it was still dark when he came to the tomb.”], and the words that follow contradict this when it is said: “For they did not yet know [Note: [Col. 1177D] Corbie and Longip., “he did not know.”] the Scriptures, that he had to rise from the dead.”

What, then, did he see, and what did he believe? He saw the linen cloths lying there and believed what the woman had said: that the Lord had been taken from the tomb.

In this matter we should weigh the greatness of the divine dispensation: the hearts of the disciples are both kindled so that they seek and delayed so that they do not find, so that the weakness of the soul, tortured by its very grief, may become purer for finding and may hold all the more firmly what it finds, precisely because it found more slowly what it was seeking.

### 5.

These matters, dearest brothers, we have passed over briefly from the Gospel reading. Now it remains for us to say something about the nobility of so great a solemnity.

I shall rightly call this the nobility of a solemnity, because it surpasses all other solemnities. Just as in sacred language the “Holy of Holies” or the “Song of Songs” is named on account of its greatness, so this festival may rightly be called the “solemnity of solemnities.”

From this solemnity the example of resurrection has been given to us, the hope of the heavenly homeland has been opened, and the glory of the heavenly kingdom has already been made an object of confident expectation. Through it the elect—although they were in the bosom of tranquility, they were nevertheless held in the prisons of hell—were brought back to the delights of paradise.

What the Lord said before his passion he fulfilled in his resurrection: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32). For he drew all things, because he left none of his elect in hell [Note: [Col. 1177D] Belvac., “because from.”]. He took away all things—that is, all the elect. For the Lord did not restore to pardon by rising again all unbelievers, who had been given over to eternal punishments for their crimes; rather, he snatched from the prisons of hell those whom he recognized as his own in faith and deeds.

Hence he also rightly says through Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. XIII, 14). What we kill, we cause not to exist at all. From what we bite, we take away a part and leave a part. Therefore, because he utterly killed death in his elect, he became the death of death. But because he took away part of hell and left part, he did not kill it utterly but bit hell.

Thus he says: “I shall be your death, O death.” As if he plainly said: “Because I utterly destroy you in my elect, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell, because after taking them away I pierce you only in part.”

What, then, is this solemnity that destroyed the prisons of hell and opened for us the gates of the heavenly kingdom? Let its name be examined more closely. Let the outstanding preacher be consulted.

### 6.

Let us see what he declares concerning its meaning. For he says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V, 7). If Christ is the Passover, we must consider what the Law says about the Passover, so that we may investigate more closely whether those words appear to have been spoken about Christ.

For Moses says: “They shall take some of the blood of the lamb and put it on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which they eat it; and they shall eat the flesh that night, roasted in fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuce. You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted in fire. You shall consume its head with its feet and its entrails, and nothing of it shall remain until morning. If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. XII, 7ff.).

And it is added: “This is how you shall eat it” [Note: [Col. 1177D] C. Germ. and Bigot., “you shall eat it”]: “You shall gird your loins and have sandals on your feet, holding staffs in your hands, and you shall eat in haste” (ibid., 11).

All these things bring us great edification if they are examined through mystical interpretation. You have learned what the blood of the lamb is—not now by hearing, but by drinking [De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter 73]. The blood is put on both doorposts when it is received not only by the mouth of the body but also [Note: [Col. 1178D] The first Carnot. and Bigot., “by the love of the heart.”] by the mouth of the heart.

For the blood of the lamb is placed on both doorposts when the sacrament of his passion is received with the mouth for redemption and also contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation. Whoever receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he still does not wish to imitate his passion has placed the blood on one doorpost; it must also be placed on the lintels of the houses.

For what do we understand spiritually by houses except our minds, in which we dwell through thought? The lintel of the house is the very intention that stands above the action. Whoever therefore directs the intention of his thought toward imitation of the Lord’s passion places the blood of the lamb on the lintel of the house.

Or certainly our houses are our bodies themselves, in which we dwell as long as we live. We place the blood of the lamb on the lintel of our houses because we carry the cross of his passion on our foreheads.

Of this lamb it is further said: “And they shall eat the flesh that night, roasted in fire” (Exod. XII, 8). We eat the lamb at night because in the sacrament we now receive the Lord’s body, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences.

Yet this flesh must be roasted in fire, because fire dissolves flesh that has been boiled in water, whereas what fire cooks without water it strengthens. The flesh of our Lamb was cooked by fire because the very force of his passion made him stronger for the resurrection and strengthened him for incorruption. For he who recovered strength from death had his flesh hardened, as it were, by fire.

Hence he also says through the Psalmist: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). For what is a potsherd before fire except soft clay? But through fire it is made solid. Thus the strength of his humanity dried up like a potsherd, because through the fire of his passion it grew into the strength of incorruption.

### 7.

But the sacraments of our Redeemer, once received, are not sufficient for the true solemnity of the mind unless good works are joined to them as well. For what benefit is it to receive his body and blood with the mouth and contradict him through wicked conduct?

Hence it is further said concerning the eating: “And unleavened bread with wild lettuce” (Exod. XII, 8). He eats unleavened bread who performs righteous works without the corruption of vainglory, who carries out the commandments of mercy without an admixture of sin, lest he wickedly seize what he appears to administer rightly.

They too had mixed this leaven of sin into their good action, to whom the Lord said through the prophet in rebuke: “Come to Bethel and act impiously” (Amos IV, 4). And shortly afterward: “And sacrifice praise from what is leavened” (ibid., 5). He offers praise from what is leavened who prepares a sacrifice for God from robbery.

Wild lettuce is exceedingly bitter. The flesh of the Lamb must therefore be eaten with wild lettuce, so that when we receive the body of our Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves in tears for our sins, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe away from the stomach of the mind the unhealthy fluid of a perverse life.

It is then added: “You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water” (Exod. XII, 9). Behold, the very words of the historical account now repel us from a merely historical understanding. Did that Israelite people living in Egypt customarily eat the lamb raw, so that the Law had to say to them, “You shall not eat any of it raw”? It adds: “Nor boiled in water.”

But what does water signify except human knowledge, according to what is said through Solomon in the voice of heretics: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17)?

What does the raw flesh of the Lamb signify except his humanity left unconsidered and without reverent reflection? For everything that we consider carefully we, as it were, cook in the mind.

But the flesh of the lamb must be eaten neither raw nor boiled in water, because our Redeemer must neither be regarded as a mere human being nor be examined through human wisdom as to how God could become incarnate.

Whoever believes that our Redeemer is merely human—what else does he do but eat the flesh of the lamb raw, since he has refused to cook it through an understanding of his divinity? Whoever attempts to examine the mysteries of his incarnation according to human wisdom wants to cook the flesh of the lamb in water; that is, he wants to penetrate the mystery of his dispensation through undisciplined knowledge.

Whoever therefore desires to celebrate the solemnity of Paschal joy should neither cook the lamb in water nor eat it raw, so that he neither seeks to penetrate the depth of his incarnation through human wisdom nor believes in him as though he were merely a human being. Rather, he should eat the flesh roasted in fire [Note: [Col. 1179D] Belvac., “to administer”], so that he may know that all things are administered through the power of the Holy Spirit.

Of this it is further rightly said: “You shall consume its head with its feet and its entrails” (Exod. XII, 9) [Note: [Col. 1179D] These words, from “because our Redeemer” through “at the end of the ages,” are absent from Bigot. and the third Gemet.]. For our Redeemer is the alpha and the omega—God before the ages and human at the end of the ages.

And as we have already said, brothers, we have learned from Paul that God is the head of Christ (I Cor. XI, 3) [Note: [Col. 1179D] These words, through “therefore the head,” are not found in C. Germ., Belvac., or the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts.]. To consume the head of the lamb, therefore, is to receive his divinity by faith. To consume the feet of the lamb is to seek out the traces of his humanity by loving and imitating him.

What are the entrails except his hidden and mystical commandments? We consume them when we take in the words of life eagerly. In this word “consume,” what else is reproved except the sluggishness of our laziness? We neither seek out his words and mysteries by ourselves nor listen willingly when they are spoken by others.

“Nothing of it shall remain until morning” (Exod. XII, 10), because his words must be examined with great diligence, so that before the day of the resurrection appears, all his commandments may be penetrated through understanding and practice during the night of this present life [Note: [Col. 1179D] Belvac., “in the calling of life.”].

But because it is very difficult for all Sacred Scripture to be understood and all its mystery to be penetrated, it is rightly added: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (ibid.). We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand or penetrate concerning the mystery of his incarnation, so that no one presumptuously dares either to despise or to proclaim what he does not understand, but hands it over to the fire when he reserves it to the Holy Spirit.

### 8.

Since, therefore, we have learned how the Passover should be eaten, let us now recognize by what sort of people it should be eaten [Note: [Col. 1180D] Three Gemet. manuscripts, “by whom.”].

It follows: “This is how you shall eat it: You shall gird your loins” (ibid., 11). What is understood by the loins except the pleasure of the flesh? Hence the Psalmist also asks, saying: “Burn my loins” (Ps. XXV, 2). If he did not know that the pleasure of lust resides in the loins, he would certainly not have asked that they be burned.

Since the devil’s power has prevailed especially through lust over the human race, the divine voice says of him: “His power is in his loins” (Job XL, 11). Whoever therefore eats the Passover must have his loins girded, so that he who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through vices, may subdue his pleasures, and may restrain the flesh from lust.

For he has not understood what the solemnity of incorruption is who is still subject to corruption through lack of self-control.

These things are harsh for some, but “narrow is the gate that leads to life” (Matt. VII, 13). And we already have many examples of those who practiced self-control.

Hence it is further well added: “You shall have sandals on your feet” (Exod. XII, 11). For what are our feet except our works? And what are sandals except the skins of dead animals? Sandals protect the feet. What are the dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected except the ancient fathers who went before us to the eternal homeland? When we contemplate their examples, we protect the feet of our own work.

To have sandals on one’s feet, therefore, is to contemplate the life of the dead and to guard our steps from the wound of sin.

“Holding staffs in your hands” (ibid.). What does the Law signify by the staff except pastoral guardianship [Note: [Col. 1181D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “pastoral care”]? It should be noted that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to hold staffs, because those should undertake pastoral care who already know how to subdue the impulses of lust in their own bodies, so that when they preach what is strong to others, they themselves do not succumb weakly to soft desires.

It is well added: “And you shall eat in haste” (ibid.). Notice, dearest brothers, notice what is said: “in haste.” Learn the commandments of God, the mysteries of the Redeemer, and the joys of the heavenly homeland with haste, and take care to fulfill the commandments of life with haste.

For we know that today we are still permitted to act well, but we do not know whether we shall be permitted to do so tomorrow. Eat the Passover, therefore, in haste—that is, yearn for the solemnity of the heavenly homeland.

Let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland. Let no one weave delays in pursuing studies [Note: [Col. 1181D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “in pursuing good studies”], but let him complete what he has begun, lest he be unable to fulfill what he has begun [Note: [Col. 1181D] C. Germ., the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, and Bigot., “what he begins badly.”].

If we are not lazy in loving God, he whom we love himself assists us—Jesus Christ our Lord [Note: [Col. 1181D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, honor and imperial power belong throughout all ages, etc.”]—who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1181D] It is the fifteenth in the Lateran manuscript, the nineteenth in the Codex Regius of Sweden, and the thirteenth in Corbie.]

## HOMILY XXIII

Delivered to the people in the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1182D] This is absent from Belvac., Corbie, C. Germ., the three Gemet. manuscripts, the Lateran manuscript, and the Codex Regius of Sweden.], on the day after Easter.

### LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE XXIV, 13–35

At that time, two of Jesus’ disciples were going that same day to a village that was sixty stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus [Note: [Col. 1182D] Absent from C. Germ. and the three Gemet. manuscripts: “on that very day.”], and they were speaking with one another about all the things that had happened.

And it came to pass, while they were talking and questioning one another, that Jesus himself drew near and went along with them. But their eyes were prevented from recognizing him.

And he said to them: “What are these words that you are exchanging with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?” One of them, whose name was Cleopas, answered and said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?”

He said to them: “What things?” And they said: “About Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to condemnation of death and crucified him.

“But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And now, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened” [Note: [Col. 1182D] Belvac. and C. Germ., “on which these things happened.”].

“But certain women from among us terrified us. They were at the tomb before dawn, and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels who say that he is alive.

“And some of our number went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see” [Note: [Col. 1182D] The same manuscripts, “they did not see him.”].

And he said to them: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” [Note: [Col. 1182D] Belvac., “Was it not thus necessary?”]

And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

And they drew near to the village to which they were going. And he pretended that he was going farther. But they urged him, saying: “Stay with us, because it is toward evening and the day is now declining.” And he entered in with them.

And it came to pass, while he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and handed it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.

And they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?”

And rising at that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven gathered together, and those who were with them [Col. 1182B], saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.”

And they recounted what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread.

### 1.

Since you are laboring in the daily solemnity, only a few things should be said to you; and perhaps these will be more useful because food that is less sufficient is often consumed more eagerly.

I have therefore decided to discuss the meaning of the Gospel reading summarily, not examining each word, lest a more extended exposition burden your love.

Behold, dearest brothers, you have heard that while two disciples were walking along the road, the Lord appeared to them. They did not in fact believe, but nevertheless they were speaking about him; yet he did not show them an appearance by which they could recognize him.

Thus the Lord effected outwardly, in the eyes of the body, what was taking place within them, in the eyes of the heart. For within themselves they both loved and doubted; while outwardly the Lord was present with them, yet did not reveal who he was.

To them, therefore, as they spoke about him, he displayed his presence; but to them, as they doubted about him, he concealed the appearance by which they would know him. He exchanged words with them, rebuked the hardness of their understanding, and opened the mysteries of Sacred Scripture that concerned himself; yet, because he was still a stranger to faith in their hearts, he pretended that he was going farther.

For we call “pretending” the act of shaping or forming; hence we call those who shape clay “potters.” The Truth, therefore, did nothing simple through duplicity, but displayed himself to them in the body as he was in their minds.

They were to be tested, to see whether those who did not yet love him as God could at least love him as a stranger. But because those with whom the Truth walked could not be strangers to charity, they invited him to lodge with them as a stranger.

Why do we say that they invited him, when it is written there, “And they compelled him”? From this example it is plainly gathered that strangers should not only be invited to hospitality but also urged to accept it.

They set out a table, offer food, and recognize in the breaking of bread the God whom they had not recognized in the exposition of Sacred Scripture.

[Cols. 1183B–D; 1539] 2. They were not enlightened by hearing God’s commandments, but by doing them, because it is written: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” (Rom. 2:13). Whoever wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action what he has already been able to understand. [Textual note (Col. 1183D): The printed editions read “hear” (*audire*) for “understand.”] Behold, the Lord was not recognized while he was speaking, but deigned to be recognized while he was being fed.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, love hospitality; love works of charity. Hence Paul says: “Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality. For by this some, having received angels as guests, pleased God” (Heb. 13:1). Hence Peter says: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Pet. 4:9). [Textual note (Col. 1183D): C. Germ. and three Gemeticum manuscripts read “without grumblings” (*sine murmurationibus*).] Hence Truth itself says: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25:35).

A remarkable story, handed down to us through the report of our elders, is told. A certain householder, together with his entire household, devoted himself zealously to hospitality. Since he received strangers daily at his table, one day a certain stranger came among the others and was led to the table. While the householder, following his customary humility, wished to pour water over the man’s hands, he turned to take the pitcher; but suddenly he did not find the one over whose hands he had wished to pour the water. As he wondered at this within himself, that same night the Lord said to him in a vision: “On the other days you received me in my members; yesterday you received me in my own person.” Behold, when he comes to judgment, he will say: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40). Behold, before the judgment, when he is received through his members, he also seeks out those who receive him through his own person; and yet we are sluggish in the practice of hospitality.

Consider, brothers, how great is the virtue of hospitality. Receive Christ at your tables, so that you may be worthy to be received by him at the eternal banquets. [Textual note (Col. 1183D): Belvacensis reads “at the eternal banquet” (*in convivio aeterno*).] Offer hospitality now to Christ in the stranger, so that at the judgment he may not know you as strangers, but may receive you as his own into the kingdom. [Textual note (Col. 1183D): Bigotianus, Longipontanus, and Val. Cl. read “as his own servants” (*ut proprios servulos*).] May he himself help us, he who lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note (Col. 1183D): In the royal Swedish manuscript this is the twenty-first homily; in Corbie, the fourteenth.]

## HOMILY XXIV

[Note (Col. 1183D): These words occur only in recent manuscripts, such as the two later Gemeticum manuscripts.]

Delivered to the people in the basilica of blessed Lawrence the martyr, outside the walls of the City, on the Wednesday of Easter week.

### HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN 21:1–14

[Cols. 1183D–1184B]

At that time Jesus revealed himself again to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself in this way. Simon Peter, Thomas who is called Didymus, Nathanael who was from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them, “I am going fishing.” They said to him, “We are coming with you.” They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing. [Textual note (Col. 1184D): Belvacensis and C. Germ. read “they caught nothing” (*nihil ceperunt*); likewise, below, where the text reads “which you have caught,” they read “which you have now caught” (*quos nunc cepistis*).] When morning came, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, do you have anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.” And he said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were unable to haul it in because of the multitude of fish.

That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord.” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded his tunic around himself—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land, only about two hundred cubits, dragging the net full of fish. When they came ashore, they saw a charcoal fire laid, with a fish placed upon it, and bread. Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have caught now.” Simon Peter went up and dragged the net ashore, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.

Jesus said to them, “Come, eat.” None of those reclining at table dared ask him, “Who are you?” for they knew that it was the Lord. [Textual note (Col. 1184D): The same manuscripts read “because he was the Lord” (*quia Dominus esset*).] Jesus came, took the bread, and gave it to them, and likewise the fish. This was now the third time Jesus had revealed himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.

### 1

[Cols. 1184B–C; 1540]

The reading from the holy Gospel that has just been read in your hearing, my brothers, strikes the mind with a question; yet by striking it, it reveals the power of discernment. For one may ask why Peter, who had been a fisherman before his conversion, returned to fishing after his conversion. Since Truth says, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62), why did he resume what he had abandoned?

But if the power of discernment is considered, it quickly becomes clear that it was not a fault to resume after conversion an occupation that had existed without sin before conversion. We know that Peter was a fisherman and Matthew a tax collector. After his conversion Peter returned to fishing, but Matthew did not return to the business of the tax office (*De poenitentia*, distinction 5, chapter 7), because seeking one’s livelihood through fishing is one thing, while increasing one’s wealth through the profits of tax collection is another. There are many occupations that can scarcely, or not at all, be practiced without sin. Therefore, whatever involves sin must not be returned to by the soul after conversion.

### 2

It may also be asked why, while the disciples were laboring at sea, the Lord stood on the shore after his resurrection, although before his resurrection he had walked upon the waves of the sea in the presence of his disciples (Matt. 14:25). The reason is quickly understood if we consider the cause that was then present. For what does the sea signify except the present age, which is dashed against the tumult of worldly affairs and the waves of corruptible life? [Textual note (Col. 1184D): The printed editions add “of events” (*casuum*), absent from the manuscripts; Gregory commonly calls the tumult of affairs “causes” (*causae*).] And what is signified by the firmness of the shore except the perpetual rest of eternal peace?

Because the disciples were still amid the waves of mortal life, they labored at sea. But because our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh, after his resurrection he stood on the shore. It was as though, through the circumstances, he were speaking the mystery of his resurrection to his disciples, saying: “I no longer appear to you at sea, because I am no longer with you amid the waves of turmoil.”

For this reason, elsewhere after his resurrection he says to those same disciples: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you” (Luke 24:44). He was not absent from those to whom he was bodily present; yet he now denies that he is with them because, through the immortality of the flesh, he was separated from their mortal bodies. There, while placed with them, he declares that he is not with them; here also he indicates the same thing by the position of his body, showing that, while they were still sailing, he was already on the shore.

### 3

[Cols. 1185B–D; 1541–1542]

A great difficulty in fishing was imposed upon the disciples so that, when the Master came, a great sublimity of wonder might arise. He immediately said: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”

Twice in the holy Gospel we read that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: once before his Passion and once after his resurrection. Before our Redeemer suffered and rose again, he commanded that the net be cast for fishing, but he did not command whether it should be cast on the right or on the left. After his resurrection, however, appearing to the disciples, he commanded that the net be cast on the right.

In the former fishing so many were caught that the nets were torn; in this one many were caught, yet the nets were not torn. Who does not know that the good are represented by the right and the wicked by the left? That fishing, in which no particular side is designated for the casting of the net, signifies the present Church, which gathers good and wicked together and does not choose whom it will draw in, because it does not know whom it may choose. This fishing, however, which took place after the Lord’s resurrection, was cast only on the right, because only the Church of the elect reaches the vision of his radiant glory, and it will possess nothing belonging to the work of the left.

In the former fishing the net is torn because, now, together with the elect, so many of the reprobate enter the confession of faith that they even tear the Church itself through heresies. In this fishing, however, many fish, and large ones, are caught, and the net is not torn, because the holy Church of the elect, resting in the continual peace of its Creator, is no longer torn apart by any divisions.

### 4

After such large fish had been caught, “Simon Peter went up and dragged the net ashore.” I believe that your Charity already understands what it means that Peter drags the net to land. The holy Church was entrusted to him; to him in particular it is said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–16). What is later disclosed in words is now signified in action.

Since the preacher of the Church separates us from the waves of this world, it is necessary that Peter bring the net full of fish to land. He draws the fish to the firmness of the shore because, through the voice of holy preaching, he displays to the faithful the stability of the eternal homeland. He did this through words, through letters, and he does it daily through signs of miracles. Whenever we are converted through him to love of eternal rest, whenever we are separated from the tumult of earthly things, what else are we than fish caught in the net of faith and drawn to the shore?

But when the net is said to be full of large fish, their number is also added: one hundred and fifty-three. This number is not without a great mystery, and the profundity of so great a mystery awaits your attention. For the evangelist would not have carefully stated the total unless he had judged it to be full of sacramental meaning.

You know that in the Old Testament every work is prescribed through the commandments of the Decalogue, while in the New Testament the power of that same work is bestowed upon the faithful in multiplied form through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. The prophet, announcing this Spirit, says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety”; and he will be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11:2). [Textual note (Col. 1185D): The first Carnotensis manuscript reads “the grace of working” (*gratiam operationis*) for “the work of this Spirit.”]

But a person perceives the work of this Spirit only if he acknowledges faith in the Trinity, believing the Father, the Son, and the same Holy Spirit to possess one power and confessing them to be of one substance. Since the seven things mentioned above have been given more fully through the New Testament, while ten commandments were given through the Old, all our virtue and work can be fully comprehended in ten and seven.

Let us therefore take seventeen by the triangular number, and the result is fifty-one. [Textual note (Cols. 1185D–1186D): Belvacensis reads “the result is fifty”; the two earlier Gemeticum manuscripts read “they make fifty.”] This number too is not without a great mystery, because in the Old Testament we read that the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the Jubilee year (Lev. 25:11), in which the whole people was to rest from every work. But true rest is in unity. One cannot be divided; where there is the division of a schism, there is no true rest.

Let us therefore take fifty-one by the triangular number, so that the result is one hundred and fifty-three. Since all our work, performed in faith in the Trinity, tends toward rest, we multiply seventeen three times, so that we arrive at fifty-one. Our true rest is then present when we already recognize the very glory of the Trinity, which we firmly hold to exist in the unity of the Godhead. We multiply fifty-one three times, and thus we arrive at the number of the elect in the heavenly homeland, represented as one hundred and fifty-three fish.

After the Lord’s resurrection, therefore, it was fitting that the net cast should catch as many fish as would designate only the elect citizens of the heavenly homeland.

### 5

[Cols. 1186D–1187D; 1543]

In addition to these things, yesterday’s reading from the holy Gospel and today’s admonish us to examine carefully why our Lord and Redeemer is read to have eaten a roasted fish after his resurrection. The repetition of an action is not without mystery. In today’s reading he ate bread and a roasted fish; in the reading that was read yesterday (Luke 24:13 ff.), he ate, together with the roasted fish, a honeycomb.

What do we believe the roasted fish signifies except the suffering Mediator between God and human beings? He deigned to lie hidden in the waters of the human race; he wished to be caught in the snare of our death; and, as though roasted by affliction, he endured the time of his Passion. But he who deigned to become a roasted fish in his Passion became a honeycomb for us in his resurrection. [Textual note (Col. 1187D): Corbie, Germ., and the better manuscripts support this wording. Gussanville reads: “and he who wished to be figured in the roasted fish by the tribulation [of his Passion]” (*et qui in pisce asso figurari voluit tribulatione*).]

Or did he who wished the roasted fish to signify the tribulation of his Passion wish the honeycomb to express both natures in his person? A honeycomb contains honey in wax; and honey in wax is divinity in humanity. This also agrees with today’s reading, for he ate a fish and bread. He who could be roasted as a fish in his humanity refreshes us with bread in his divinity, saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41, 52).

He therefore ate a roasted fish and bread, to show us through his food that he endured suffering through our humanity and provided our refreshment through his divinity. [Textual note (Col. 1187D): The two earlier Gemeticum manuscripts and the earlier Carnotensis read “and our resurrection” (*et resurrectionem nostram*) for “our refreshment.”]

If we examine this attentively, we see how it also applies to us as something to imitate. The Redeemer reveals his own works in such a way as to prepare the way of imitation for those who follow him. Behold, in his food our Lord wished to join a honeycomb to a roasted fish, because he receives into his body for eternal rest those who, while experiencing tribulations for the Lord here, do not depart from the love of inward sweetness. The honeycomb is taken with the roasted fish because those who accept affliction for the sake of truth here are satisfied there with true sweetness.

### 6

[Cols. 1187C–1188D; 1544–1545]

It should also be noted that the Lord is described as having shared his final meal with seven disciples. Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples are remembered as having been present. Why does he celebrate his final meal with seven disciples, except to declare that only those who are full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit will be with him in the eternal refreshment? [Textual note (Col. 1187D): The first Carnotensis reads “in the eternal resurrection.”]

The whole of this age also unfolds through seven days, and perfection is often signified by the number seven. Those, therefore, feast at the final meal from the presence of Truth who now, out of a desire for perfection, transcend earthly things. The love of this world does not bind them; and although it disturbs them to some extent through temptations, it does not blunt their desires once begun.

Of this final meal John says elsewhere: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19:9). He says that they are invited not to a luncheon but to a supper because, at the end of the day, the banquet is a supper. Those who, when the time of the present life has ended, come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are invited [Textual note (Col. 1187D): Longipontanus reads “to the contemplation of the heavenly refreshment.”] not to the Lamb’s luncheon but to his supper.

This supper is expressed by the final meal at which the seven disciples are remembered as present, because, as we have said, inward refreshment then restores those who are now filled with the sevenfold grace and pant with love of the Spirit. [The printed *anbelant* is evidently *anhelant*, “pant.”]

Therefore, brothers, practice these things among yourselves; desire to be filled with the presence of this Spirit. Consider what may follow for you in the future from your present condition. Reflect whether you are filled with this Spirit; you know whether you will be able to reach that banquet.

For whoever he may be whom this Spirit does not now restore certainly fasts from the refreshment of that eternal banquet. Remember what Paul says about this same Spirit: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). This Spirit of love is, as it were, the title deed of divine possession. [Textual note (Col. 1187D): The first Carnotensis reads “of the divine Passion” (*divinae passionis*) for “of divine possession.”]

Does the person whose mind is scattered by hatred, [Textual note (Col. 1187D): The same manuscript reads “is overcome by hatreds” (*odia superant*).] inflated by pride, embittered by anger even to the point of division of mind, tormented by avarice, and weakened by lust have the Spirit of Christ? Consider what the Spirit of Christ is. Surely it is the Spirit that causes friends and enemies to be loved, earthly things to be despised, heavenly things to be longed for, the flesh to be chastened because of its vices, and the mind to be restrained from its desires.

If you wish to know the right of God’s possession, consider the character of your possessor. [Textual note (Col. 1187D): The manuscripts and old editions read “the right of God’s possession”; recent editions read “the possessions of God.”] For Paul proclaims in truthful words what we have said: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). It is as though he were saying plainly: Whoever is not now ruled by God dwelling within him will not later rejoice in the sight of the divine glory.

Yet we are weakened by these things that have been said; we have not yet reached the summit of perfection. Let us daily place the steps of holy desire on the road of God. Truth consoles us through the Psalmist, who says: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all will be written” (Ps. 138:16).

Our imperfection will not altogether harm us if, established on the road of God, we neither look back to what has passed nor delay in hastening toward what remains. For he who graciously inflames the desires of the imperfect will at some time strengthen them toward perfection. [Textual note (Cols. 1187D–1188D): Longipontanus, the two earlier Gemeticum manuscripts, and Bigotianus read “will one day” (*hic quandoque*). The two earlier Gemeticum manuscripts read: “Jesus Christ our Lord strengthens [them], to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honour and dominion through all [ages], etc.”] This is through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note (Col. 1188D): In Corbie this is the fifteenth homily; in the Lateran manuscript, the sixteenth; in the royal Swedish manuscript, the twentieth.]

## HOMILY XXV

[Cols. 1188D–1193D; 1544–1549]

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint John, called the Constantinian, on Thursday of Easter week. [Textual note (Col. 1188D): The latter words occur in no old manuscript, but only in the two later Gemeticum manuscripts and others of the same or a lower date. In Lateranensis the heading reads: “in the basilica of Saint Saviour, which is called …”]

### HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN 20:11–18

At that time, Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down and looked into the tomb; and she saw two angels in white, sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed. They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him.”

When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him, “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.”

Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni,” which means “Teacher.” Jesus said to her, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.’” Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had said these things to her.

### 1

Mary Magdalene, who had been a sinful woman in the city, washed away the stains of her crimes with tears by loving the Truth. The voice of Truth is fulfilled in her case, which says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). She who had previously remained cold through sinning afterward burned fiercely through love.

After she came to the tomb and did not find the Lord’s body there, she believed that it had been taken away and reported this to the disciples. They came, saw, and believed that it was as the woman had said. Immediately it is written of them: “Then the disciples went away again to their own homes.” Then it is added: “But Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping” (John 20:10–11).

In this matter we should consider how great was the force of love that kindled this woman’s mind. Even when the disciples departed, she did not leave the Lord’s tomb. She was seeking the one she had not found; she wept as she sought him; and, inflamed by the fire of her love, she burned with longing for the one whom she believed had been taken away.

Thus it happened that she alone saw him at that time, because she remained in order to seek him. For the power of a good work is perseverance, and Truth says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

[Note (Col. 1189D): This passage is used in the same sense in *Morals* I, no. 56 (formerly ch. 20). Alluding to it, Bernard, in Epistle 78 to Abbot Suger, writes: “Join the tail of the victim to its head; and then, with God’s grace, take care to make it embroidered and ankle-length” (*Hostiae caudam junge capiti, ac tum cum Dei gratia jam polymitam cura facere et talarem*).]

The command of the Law also requires the tail of the sacrificial victim to be offered in sacrifice (Lev. 3:9). The end of the body is in the tail; and one sacrifices well who brings the offering of a good work to the end of its proper performance.

For this reason Joseph is described as having a long tunic among his other brothers (Gen. 37:3). A tunic reaching to the ankles signifies a good work carried through to completion.

### 2

But Mary, as she wept, bent down and looked into the tomb. She had certainly already seen that the tomb was empty; she had already announced that the Lord had been taken away. [Textual note (Col. 1189D): Belvacensis reads “had announced the Lord to the disciples” (*Dominum discipulis nuntiaverat*).] Why does she bend down again and desire to see again?

For one who loves, looking once is not enough, because the force of love multiplies the intensity of searching. She sought at first and found nothing; she persevered in seeking, and thus it happened that she found him. Her postponed desires grew, and, having grown, they grasped what they had found.

Hence the Church says of the same Bridegroom in the Song of Songs:

> “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves;  
> I sought him, and did not find him.  
> I will rise and go around the city;  
> through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1).

She repeats the failure to find him, saying: “I sought him, and did not find him.” But because finding does not remain far away if searching does not cease, she adds:

> “The watchmen who guard the city found me.  
> Have you seen him whom my soul loves? [Textual note (Col. 1189D): Three Gemeticum manuscripts and Bigotianus read “whom my soul loved” (*dilexit*).]  
> A little while after I had passed them,  
> I found him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:3–4).

We seek the Beloved on the bed when, amid the slight rest of the present life, we sigh with longing for our Redeemer. We seek him at night because, although the mind is already awake in him, the eye is still dim.

But whoever does not find the Beloved must rise and go around the city—that is, must traverse the holy Church of the elect in mind and in search. He must seek him through the streets and squares, that is, observe those who walk along narrow and broad ways, searching whether he may find in them any trace of him; for there are some, even among those living a worldly life, who possess something in their conduct worthy of imitation.

As we seek, the watchmen who guard the city find us, because the holy fathers who guard the condition of the Church come to meet our good efforts, teaching us by word or writing. When we pass them a little way, we find the one we love, because our Redeemer, although human among human beings in his humility, was nevertheless above human beings in his divinity. [Textual note (Col. 1190D): The two earlier Gemeticum manuscripts and the second Carnotensis read “although [he was so] by humanity” (*etsi humanitate*). The editor judges this reading preferable because of the antithesis of humanity and divinity, were it not opposed by the more numerous and better manuscripts and by the editors’ consensus.]

When the watchmen have been passed, the Beloved is found, because when we see that the prophets and apostles are beneath him, we understand that he who is God by nature is above human beings. He is therefore sought without being found at first, so that afterward, when found, he may be held more closely.

As we said earlier, holy desires grow through delay. If they fail through delay, they were not desires. Whoever has been able to reach the truth has burned with this love.

Hence David says: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3). Hence he admonishes us, saying: “Seek his face continually” (Ps. 104:4). Hence the prophet says: “My soul desired you in the night; indeed, with my spirit within me I will watch for you in the morning” (Isa. 26:9). Again the Church says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded with love” (Song 4:9).

It is right that she who carries in her breast the wound of love from the heat of desire should reach healing through the vision of the physician. Again she says: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5:6).

The mind of one who does not seek the likeness of its Creator is badly hardened, because it remains cold within itself. But if it begins to burn with desire and to follow the one it loves, it runs, melted by the fire of love.

It becomes anxious with desire; [Textual note (Col. 1191D): The third Gemeticum reads “and when it is anxious with desire” (*et cum sit desiderio anxia*).] all the things that pleased it in the world become worthless. Nothing outside its Creator delights it, and the things that previously gave pleasure to the mind afterward become exceedingly burdensome. Nothing consoles its sorrow until it beholds the one it desires. The mind grieves; even light is distasteful to it. By such fire the rust of sin is boiled away in the mind, and the soul, kindled like gold—for through use it had lost its appearance—becomes bright through burning.

### 3

Let us therefore examine what fruit the power of love produces in this woman, who loves in such a way and bends again over the tomb she had already inspected. The account continues:

“She saw two angels in white, sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.”

What does it mean that two angels are seen at the place of the Lord’s body, one sitting at the head and the other at the feet, except that in Latin the word *angelus* means “messenger,” and the one who was to be proclaimed through his Passion is both God before the ages and human at the end of the ages?

The angel sits, as it were, at the head when the apostle John proclaims: [Textual note (Col. 1191D): Belvacensis, Germ., and two Carnotensis manuscripts read “when it is preached through the apostles”; three Gemeticum manuscripts read “when it is preached through the apostle.”] “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The angel sits, as it were, at the feet when he says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

We may also understand through the two angels the two Testaments, one preceding and the other following. These angels are joined to each other at the place of the Lord’s body because both Testaments, with the same meaning, proclaim that the Lord became incarnate, died, and rose again. Thus the earlier Testament sits, as it were, at the head, and the later Testament at the feet.

For this reason also the two cherubim who cover the mercy seat look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy seat (Exod. 25:20). *Cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge.” What are signified by the two cherubim except the two Testaments? And what is signified by the mercy seat except the incarnate Lord? Of him John says: “He himself is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2).

While the Old Testament announces that what the New Testament proclaims about the Lord will be accomplished, the two cherubim are like one another looking toward the mercy seat. Their faces are turned toward it because, seeing the incarnate Lord placed between them, they do not differ in their vision; they concordantly proclaim the mystery of his dispensation.

### 4

The angels ask Mary, saying: “Woman, why are you weeping?” And she says to them: “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have placed him.”
