The sacred Scriptures themselves, which stir tears of love within us, also console those tears when they promise us the likeness of our Redeemer. But historically it should be noted that the woman did not say, “They have taken away the body of my Lord,” but, “They have taken away my Lord.”

It is the practice of sacred language sometimes to signify the whole by a part and sometimes a part by the whole. It signifies the whole by a part, for example, when it is written concerning the sons of Jacob: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. 46:27). The souls did not descend into Egypt without their bodies; rather, the whole person is signified through the soul alone, so that the whole is expressed by a part.

Only the Lord’s body had lain in the tomb, yet Mary sought not the Lord’s body but the Lord who had been taken away, thereby signifying a part by the whole.

When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. It should be noted that Mary, who was still doubting the Lord’s resurrection, turned around to see Jesus, because through that very doubt she had, as it were, turned her back toward the Lord’s face, since she did not at all believe that he had risen.

But because she loved and doubted, she saw and did not recognize him. Love showed him to her, while doubt concealed him. [Textual note (Cols. 1191D–1192D): Val. Cl. and Longipontanus read “him whom love showed to her”; the partly erased letters in C. Germ. suggest that it once had the same reading.] Her continued ignorance is expressed when it follows: “And she did not know that it was Jesus.”

He said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” He asks the cause of her grief so that her desire may increase, and so that, when she named the one she was seeking, she might burn more ardently with love for him.

Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I will take him.”

Perhaps this woman did not err even when she seemed to err by believing Jesus to be the gardener. Was he not spiritually a gardener to her, who planted within her heart, through the seeds of his love, the living shoots of virtue?

### 5

But what does it mean that, having seen the one she believed to be the gardener, she said to him—although she had not yet told him whom she was seeking—“Lord, if you have taken him away”?

It is as though she had already said from whose loss she was weeping, since she names the one she had not named. But the force of love commonly does this in the mind: the one whom it continually thinks about, it believes that no one else can fail to know.

Rightly this woman does not say whom she is seeking, yet she says, “If you have taken him away,” because she does not think that the other person is unaware of the one for whom she herself continually laments in longing. [Textual note (Col. 1192D): Bigotianus reads “laments as desired” (*plangit desideratum*).]

Jesus said to her: “Mary.” After he had addressed her by the common designation of her sex and she was not recognized, he called her by name. It was as though he plainly said to her: “Recognize the one by whom you are recognized.”

To the perfect man also it is said: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33:12), because “human being” is a common designation for all of us, whereas “Moses” is a proper name. It is rightly said to him that he is known by name, as though the Lord were saying plainly: “I do not know you generally, as I know the others, but specifically.”

When Mary is therefore called by name, she recognizes her Creator and immediately calls him *Rabboni*, that is, “Teacher,” because he was both the one whom she was seeking outwardly and the one who was inwardly teaching her to seek him.

The evangelist does not now add what the woman did, but indicates it through what she heard. [Textual note (Col. 1193D): The first Carnotensis reads “is found” (*invenitur*) for “is indicated.”] He says to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

These words show that Mary wished to embrace the feet of the one she had recognized. But the Teacher says to her: “Do not touch me.” This was not because the Lord later refused to be touched by women, since it is written of the two who came to his tomb: “They approached and held his feet” (Matt. 28:9). [Textual note (Col. 1193D): Bigotianus reads “running” (*currentibus*); the third Gemeticum agrees.]

6. The reason why he ought not to be touched is also added when it follows: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.” For Jesus ascends to the Father in our heart when he is believed to be equal to the Father. For whoever does not believe him equal to the Father still does not have the Lord ascend to the Father in his heart. He therefore truly touches Jesus who believes the Son coeternal with the Father.

For Jesus had already ascended to the Father in Paul’s heart when Paul himself said: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). Hence John too touched our Redeemer with the hand of faith when he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” (John 1:1–2). He therefore touches the Lord who believes him equal to the Father in the eternity of his substance.

But perhaps someone is troubled by a silent question: how can the Son be equal to the Father? In this matter, what human nature cannot comprehend with wonder must recognize as credible to itself on the basis of another wonder. It has a brief answer to offer concerning this. For it is certain that he himself created the mother in whose virginal womb he was to be created in his humanity. What wonder, then, if he is equal to the Father who existed before his mother?

We have also learned from Paul’s testimony that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). Whoever therefore considers the Son lesser derogates especially from the Father, whose wisdom he declares to be unequal to him. For what powerful person would bear with composure someone saying to him: “You are indeed great, but your wisdom is nevertheless lesser than you”? The Lord himself also says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And again he says: “The Father is greater than I” (ibid., 14:28). Of him it is also written that “he was subject to his parents” (Luke 2:51). What wonder, then, if in his humanity he asserts himself lesser than the Father in heaven, since in that same humanity he was subject even to his parents on earth?

It is in reference to this humanity that Mary is now told: “Go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.”

[Note: In C. Germ., Belvac., and the third Gemet., “to my God.”]

Since he says “my” and “your,” why does he not say “our” in common? But by speaking distinctly he indicates that he possesses the same Father and God differently from us.

[Note: The second Carn., likewise.]

“I am ascending to my Father,” namely, by nature; “and your Father,”

[Note: Bigot., that is, by grace.]

by grace. “To my God,” because I descended; “to your God,”

[Note: The three Gemet. manuscripts and Bigot., “because you have ascended.”]

because you will ascend. Because I too am human, God is my God; because you have been freed from error, God is your God. Thus the Father and God are distinctly mine, because the one whom he begot as God before the ages he created as a human being with me at the end of the ages.

[Note: Corb. Germ. and the first two Gemet. manuscripts, “created me.”]

Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had said these things to her. Behold, the guilt of the human race is cut off at the point from which it arose. For because in paradise the woman offered death to the man (Gen. 3:7), from the tomb a woman announces life to men; and she recounts the words of her vivifier, who had recounted the words of the death-bearing serpent. It is as though the Lord were saying to the human race, not in words but in deeds: “From the hand from which the drink of death was brought to you, receive the cup of life.”

7. We have passed briefly over these matters concerning the exposition of the Gospel reading. Now, with the help of the same Lord of whom we speak, let us consider both the glory of his resurrection and the depths of his mercy.

He wished to rise from death quickly, so that our soul might not remain long in the death of unbelief. Hence the Psalmist aptly says: “He shall drink from the brook in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109:7).

[Note: Longip., Val. Cl., the three Gemet. manuscripts, and Bigot., “he drank . . . he lifted up.”]

For in the human race, from the very beginning of the world, a torrent of death had flowed forth. But the Lord drank from this torrent on the way, because in passing he tasted death. And therefore he lifted up his head, because what he had laid down in the tomb by dying, he raised above the angels by rising again; and from the place where he temporarily allowed the hands of his persecutors to rage against him, he struck down the ancient enemy forever.

The Lord plainly indicates this to blessed Job when he says: “Can you catch Leviathan with a hook?” (Job 40:19–20).

8. By Leviathan, whose name is said to mean “their addition,” that devouring monster of the human race is signified. When he promised to add divinity to the human being, he took away immortality. While multiplying through his most evil persuasion the guilt of transgression that he had offered to the first human being, he continually heaps punishments upon those who follow him.

In a hook, bait is displayed while the barb is concealed. The almighty Father therefore caught him with a hook, because he sent his incarnate only-begotten Son to his death, in whom the passible flesh could be seen, while the impassible divinity could not be seen. When this serpent bit the bait of the body in him through the hands of the persecutors, the barb of divinity pierced him.

Previously he had recognized him as God through his miracles, but he fell from that knowledge into doubt when he saw him capable of suffering. Thus the hook held the jaws of the devourer: the bait of flesh lay open in him, which the devourer desired to swallow; and the divinity, which was to destroy him, remained hidden during the passion.

He was caught on the hook of his incarnation, because, while desiring in him the bait of the body, he was pierced by the barb of divinity. There was humanity, drawing the devourer toward itself; there was divinity, piercing him; there was manifest weakness, provoking him; there was hidden power, transfixing the ravager’s throat. He was therefore caught on the hook because he died where he bit. And he lost the mortals whom he had held by right, because he presumed to attack with death the immortal one in whom he had no right.

9. This is also why this same Mary of whom we speak lives: because he who owed nothing to death died for the human race. This is why we return to life each day after our sins: because our Creator descended to our punishment without sin.

[Note: Val. Cl., Longip., and Bigot., “our Creator descended to our punishment.”]

Behold, the ancient enemy has lost the spoils he had begun to seize from the human race; he has lost the victory of his ambush. Each day sinners return to life.

[Note: The Rothomag edition, the Antwerp edition, and other older editions: “by coming to forgiveness they withdraw from his power.”]

Each day they are snatched from his jaws by the hand of the Redeemer.

Hence it is also rightly said again to blessed Job in the voice of the Lord: “Or will you pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” (Job 40:21).

A bracelet, wherever it is placed, constricts by encircling. What, then, is signified by the bracelet except the divine mercy that surrounds us? It pierces the jaw of this Leviathan when, after we have committed what he prohibited, it still shows us the remedy of repentance.

The Lord pierces Leviathan’s jaw with a bracelet, because by the power of his ineffable mercy he so confronts the malice of the ancient enemy that he sometimes causes him to lose even those whom he has already seized. And those who return to innocence after committing sins fall, as it were, from his mouth.

For who, once seized in his mouth, could escape his jaw if it had not been pierced? Did he not hold Peter in his mouth when Peter denied him (Matt. 26:76 ff.)? Did he not hold David in his mouth when David plunged himself into so great a chasm of lust (2 Sam. 12:4)? But when each returned to life through repentance, this Leviathan somehow lost them through the opening in his jaw. Through the opening in his jaw, therefore, those were snatched from his mouth who returned through repentance after committing such great wickedness.

Yet what human being can escape the mouth of this Leviathan so as to commit nothing unlawful? From this we recognize how greatly we are indebted to the Redeemer of the human race, who not only prevented us from entering Leviathan’s mouth but also granted us the possibility of returning from his mouth. He did not take away hope from the sinner: he pierced his jaw in order to provide a way of escape, so that at least after the bite the one who carelessly refused to take precautions against being bitten might flee.

Everywhere, therefore, heavenly medicine meets us: he gave human beings commandments so that they would not sin, yet he also gave the sinner remedies so that he would not despair. Hence we must take the greatest care lest anyone be seized through the delight of sin by the mouth of this Leviathan. Yet if someone is seized, he must not despair, because if he mourns his sin perfectly, he will still find an opening in Leviathan’s jaw through which to escape.

10. This same Mary of whom we speak is a witness to divine mercy. When the Pharisee wished to obstruct the fountain of mercy, he said: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39).

[Note: Throughout this homily Gregory has combined into one the accounts of three holy women: Mary, the sister of Lazarus; Mary Magdalene; and the sinful woman whose sins were forgiven because she loved greatly. Numerous dissertations on this question exist. See especially what the very learned Tillemont wrote on this subject in his commentaries on Ecclesiastical History, volume 1.]

But she washed away the stains of her heart and body with tears, and touched the feet of her Redeemer.

[Note: In the old Antwerp and Rothomag editions, etc., “wiped his feet.”]

She had abandoned her former sinful ways. She sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to the word from his mouth. She had clung to the living one; she sought the dead. She found alive the one whom she had sought as dead. And she found such a place of grace with him that she herself announced him to the apostles, who were his messengers.

What, then, brothers, what should we see in this except the boundless mercy of our Creator, who has set before us, as a sign and example of repentance, those whom he caused to live after their fall through repentance?

I consider Peter, I think of the thief, I look upon Zacchaeus, I contemplate Mary, and in them I see nothing except examples of hope and repentance placed before our eyes. Perhaps someone has fallen in faith: let him look upon Peter, who bitterly wept for what he had timidly denied (Matt. 26:75). Another has burned against his neighbor with the wickedness of cruelty: let him look upon the thief, who even at the very moment of death reached the rewards of life through repentance (Luke 23:43). Another, panting with the fever of avarice, has seized what belonged to others: let him look upon Zacchaeus, who, if he had taken anything from anyone, restored fourfold (Luke 19:8). Another, inflamed by the fire of lust, has lost bodily purity: let him look upon Mary, who burned out in herself the love of the flesh in the fire of divine love.

Behold, almighty God everywhere places before our eyes those whom we ought to imitate; everywhere he sets forth examples of his mercy. Let evils now displease us, even those we have experienced. Almighty God readily forgets that we were guilty; he is prepared to reckon our repentance as innocence. Though defiled after the waters of salvation, let us be reborn from tears.

Therefore, according to the voice of the first Shepherd, “like newborn infants, long for pure milk” (1 Pet. 2:2). Return, little children, to the breast of your mother, eternal Wisdom; suck the abundant breasts of God’s mercy; mourn what is past and avoid what threatens. Our Redeemer will console our momentary tears with eternal joy,

[Note: In the first two Gemet. manuscripts: “to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and imperishable glory,” etc.]

who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In Corb., this is the seventeenth homily; in Lateran., the eighteenth; in the Swedish Royal Codex, the twenty-first.]

## HOMILY XXVI

[Col. 1197A]

Preached to the people in the basilica of blessed John, called Constantinian,

[Note: In this codex, “of blessed John the Baptist.”]

on the octave of Easter.

[Note: These words are absent from the Lateran Codex, the Swedish Royal Codex, and the two Carn. manuscripts. In the Roman Calendar of John Frontus it reads: “On Saturday at the Lateran.” Moreover, a learned man, in his notes to that calendar, maintains that there was no Constantinian basilica apart from the basilica of the Savior, since no mention is ever made of St. John Lateran. We have discussed these matters in the preliminary notice.]

### HOLY GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO JOHN 20:19–31

At that time, when it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst

[Note: In many manuscripts and printed editions, “their” is absent.]

and said to them: “Peace be with you.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord.

Then he said to them again: “Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

But Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. The other disciples therefore said to him: “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them: “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came when the doors were shut, stood in their midst, and said: “Peace be with you.” Then he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.”

Thomas answered and said to him: “My Lord and my God.” Jesus said to him: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and so that, believing, you may have life in his name.

[Note: C. Germ. and Belvac., “eternal life.”]

1. The first question raised by this Gospel reading strikes the mind: how was the Lord’s body truly a body after the resurrection, when it could enter to the disciples through closed doors?

We must know that if a divine work can be comprehended by reason, it is not marvelous; nor does faith have merit when human reason supplies proof. But these very works of our Redeemer, which cannot at all be comprehended in themselves, should be measured against another of his works, so that more marvelous deeds may give faith to marvelous things.

For that body of the Lord entered to the disciples through closed doors which, through his birth, had emerged before human eyes from the closed womb of the Virgin. What wonder, then, if after his resurrection he entered through closed doors, now destined to live forever, when, coming to die, he emerged without opening the Virgin’s womb?

But because the faith of those who looked upon the body that could be seen was wavering, he immediately showed them his hands and side; he offered flesh to be touched, the very flesh that he had brought in through closed doors.

In this he displayed two wonders, highly opposed to each other according to human reason: after his resurrection he showed his body both incorruptible and yet palpable. For what is touched must necessarily be subject to corruption, and what is not subject to corruption cannot be touched.

But in a marvelous and immeasurable manner our Redeemer presented a body that was both incorruptible after the resurrection and palpable, so that by showing it incorruptible he might invite them to the reward, and by offering it palpable he might strengthen them in faith.

[Note: The two Carn. manuscripts and Longip., “might form them.”]

Thus he showed himself both incorruptible and palpable, plainly demonstrating that after the resurrection his body remained of the same nature but possessed another glory.

2. “He said to them: ‘Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, so I send you.’” That is: just as God the Father sent me, God, so I send you, human beings, as a human being.

The Father sent the Son, appointing him to become incarnate for the redemption of the human race. He wished him to come into the world for suffering, yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffering.

The Lord likewise sends the chosen apostles into the world not to worldly joys but, just as he himself was sent, to sufferings. Since the Son is loved by the Father and yet is sent to suffering, so the disciples are loved by the Lord and yet are sent into the world to suffer.

Therefore it is said: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” That is: I love you with the same love with which I am sending you amid the scandals of persecutors as the Father loves me, whom he caused to come to endure sufferings.

Yet being sent may also be understood according to the nature of his divinity. For the Son is said to be sent by the Father precisely in that he is begotten by the Father. The Son likewise declares that he sends the Holy Spirit, who, although coequal with the Father and the Son, was not incarnate, saying: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26).

If being sent were to be understood only as becoming incarnate, then surely the Holy Spirit, who was not incarnate at all, would in no way be said to be sent. But his sending is his very procession, by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Just as the Spirit is said to be sent because he proceeds, so the Son is not improperly said to be sent because he is begotten.

[Note: Theodulf of Orléans cites these words in his work On the Holy Spirit to Charles, as evidence that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son.]

3. “When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’”

We must ask what it means that our Lord gave the Holy Spirit once while remaining on earth and once while presiding in heaven. For the Holy Spirit is not plainly shown to have been given elsewhere

[Col. 1198D]

except now, when he is received through the breathing, and afterward, when he comes from heaven and is manifested in various tongues (Acts 2:1 ff.).

Why, then, is the Spirit first given to the disciples on earth and afterward sent from heaven? Is it not because there are two commandments of love, namely, love of God and love of neighbor? The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; the Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved.

Just as there is one love and two commandments, so there is one Spirit

[Note: Belvac. and Bigot., “and two given Testaments.”]

and he is given twice: first by the Lord while he remained on earth, afterward from heaven, because through love of neighbor one learns how one ought to attain to the love of God.

Hence the same John says: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

The same Holy Spirit was already present in the minds of the disciples for faith, but he was not given in a manifest gift until after the resurrection. Hence it is written: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

Hence it is also said through Moses: “They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the hard rock” (Deut. 32:13). For nothing of this sort is read according to the literal history if the whole sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed.

[Note: The second Carn. manuscript, “is reconstructed.”]

That people nowhere sucked honey from a rock, nowhere oil. But because, according to Paul’s saying, “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), they sucked honey from the rock who saw the deeds and miracles of the same Redeemer.

They sucked oil from the hard rock because after his resurrection they were worthy to be anointed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Thus the weak rock gave honey when the still mortal Lord showed his disciples the sweetness of his miracles. But the hard rock poured forth oil because, after his resurrection, having become incapable of suffering, he caused the gift of holy anointing to flow through the breathing of the Spirit.

4. Concerning this oil the prophet says: “The yoke shall rot before the oil” (Isa. 10:27).

[Note: Many manuscripts, “shall decay.”]

We were held beneath the yoke of demonic domination,

[Note: Bigot., “of demonic condemnation.”]

but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. And because the grace of freedom has anointed us, the yoke of demonic domination has rotted, as Paul testifies: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

It must be understood that those who previously possessed the Holy Spirit, so that they themselves might live innocently and benefit certain people through preaching, received him openly after the Lord’s resurrection so that they might benefit not a few but many.

Hence in this very gift of the Spirit it is said: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained.” It is worth observing to what a height of glory those disciples were raised who had been summoned to such great burdens of humility.

Behold, they are made secure not only concerning themselves, but they also receive the power to release others from their bonds; they receive a share in the authority of the heavenly judgment, so that in God’s place they retain the sins of some and release the sins of others.

Thus it was fitting that God should raise up those who had agreed to humble themselves so greatly for God. Behold, those who fear God’s strict judgment become judges of souls; they condemn or free others, though they had feared being condemned themselves.

5. In the Church, bishops now hold the place of these men. Those who receive the office of governance assume the authority to bind and loose. Great is the honor, but heavy is the burden of this honor.

For it is difficult that one who does not know how to govern his own life should become judge of another’s life. And it often happens that the place of judgment is held by someone whose life does not at all correspond to the office.

[Note: Belvac. and Bigot., “that this person should hold the place of judgment.” C. Germ. and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “that this person should hold the place of judgment.”]

It often happens that he condemns the undeserving or, himself bound, releases others. Often, in releasing and binding his subjects, he follows the impulses of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus he deprives himself of the very power of binding and loosing when he exercises it according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of his subjects.

[Note: Ibid., chapter 60.]

It often happens that a pastor is moved toward a particular neighbor by hatred or favor. But those who follow either their own hatred or their own favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly.

[Note: Ibid., chapter 61.]

Hence the prophet rightly says: “They put to death souls that should not die, and they gave life to souls that should not live” (Ezek. 13:19). He puts to death one who should not die when he condemns the righteous. And he tries to give life to one who will not live when he attempts to free the guilty from punishment.

6. The cases must therefore be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing must be exercised.

[Note: The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “must be exercised.”]

It must be seen what fault preceded,

[Note: Belvac., the three Gemet. manuscripts, and Bigot. omit “what fault preceded”; “what the cause was.”]

or what repentance followed the fault, so that those whom almighty God visits by the grace of compunction may be absolved by the pastor’s sentence.

Then the superior’s absolution is true

[Note: In the Vulgate editions, “when it follows the judgment of the eternal [Judge].”]

when it follows the decision of the inner Judge.

This is well signified by the raising of the four-day-dead man, which demonstrates that the Lord first called and brought the dead man to life, saying: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43); and afterward the one who had come out alive was released by the disciples, as it is written: “When the one who had been bound came out, then he said to the disciples: ‘Release him and let him go’” (John 11:45).

Behold, the disciples release the man who was already living, whom the Master had raised when he was dead. For if the disciples had released Lazarus while he was dead, they would have displayed stench rather than power.

From this consideration it must be understood that through pastoral authority we ought to release those whom we know our Creator has brought to life through his reviving grace.

[Note: We formerly cited this entire passage in our French treatise On Confession, part 1, chapter 12, and defended it against Dallaeus’s quibbles.]

This revivification is already recognized in confession itself, before the work of righteousness. Hence the dead Lazarus is not told, “Come back to life,” but “Come out.”

For every sinner, while hiding his guilt within his conscience, lies hidden inwardly and concealed in his own chambers. But the dead man comes out when the sinner freely confesses his wickedness.

Therefore Lazarus is told: “Come out.” It is as though any dead person in guilt were plainly being told: Why do you hide your guilt within your conscience? Come out now through confession, you who lie hidden inwardly before yourself through denial.

Let the dead man therefore come out; that is, let the sinner confess his guilt. Let the disciples release the one who comes out, so that the pastors of the Church may remove the punishment he deserved, since he was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

I have spoken briefly about the order of release,

[Note: The first Carn. manuscript, “I have briefly stated the order of this release.”]

so that the pastors of the Church may strive, with great moderation, either to release or to bind. But whether the pastor binds justly or unjustly, the flock must nevertheless fear the pastor’s sentence, lest the one who is subject, even if perhaps bound unjustly, deserve the very sentence of his bondage because of another fault.

Let the pastor therefore fear absolving indiscriminately, and fear binding. But the one who is under the pastor’s hand should fear being bound, even unjustly; nor should he rashly criticize his pastor’s judgment, lest, although unjustly bound, he turn a fault that did not exist into a fault through the pride of his swollen criticism.

But since we have said these things briefly by way of digression, let us return to the order of the exposition.

7. “Thomas, one of the twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.” This one disciple was absent; when he returned, he heard what had happened, but he refused to believe what he heard.

The Lord came again and offered his side to the unbelieving disciple to be touched; he showed his hands and, displaying the scars of his wounds, healed the wound of his unbelief.

What, dearly beloved brothers, what do you perceive in this? Do you think it happened by chance that this chosen disciple was absent at that time, then came and heard, hearing doubted, doubting touched, and touching believed?

This did not happen by chance but by divine dispensation. Heavenly mercy acted in a marvelous way so that, while that doubting disciple touched the wounds of the flesh in his Master, he might heal in us the wounds of unbelief.

Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more for faith than the faith of the believing disciples, because while he was brought back to faith by touching, our mind, setting aside every doubt, is made firm in faith.

Thus the Lord permitted the disciple to doubt after his resurrection, yet he did not abandon him in his doubt,

[Note: 27, question 2, chapter 45.]

just as before his birth he wished Mary to have a betrothed husband, yet that husband did not come to her wedding. For the doubting and touching disciple became a witness to the true resurrection, just as the bridegroom of Christ’s mother had been the guardian of her utterly pure virginity.

8. “He touched him and exclaimed: ‘My Lord and my God.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.’”

Since the apostle Paul says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1), it is plainly clear that faith is the evidence of things that cannot be seen. For things that are seen no longer have faith but recognition.

Since Thomas therefore saw and touched, why is he told: “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? But he saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen by mortal humanity. He saw a human being and confessed him as God, saying: “My Lord and my God.”

By seeing, therefore, he believed: in contemplating the true human being, he exclaimed that this was God, whom he could not see.

9. What follows brings great joy: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” In this sentence we are especially marked out, we who hold in our mind the one whom we have not seen in the flesh.

We are marked out—but only if we follow our faith with works. For the one truly believes who practices in action what he believes. In contrast, Paul says of those who retain faith in name only: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). Hence James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:26).

Hence the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the ancient enemy of the human race: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished,

[Note: C. Germ., Belvac., and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “and will have confidence.”]

and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18).

For what is signified by the river except the flowing course of the human race? This race flows from its beginning to its end and, like water, runs on until its appointed limit through the liquid substance of the flesh.

What is signified by the Jordan except the form of the baptized?

[Note: Thus Belv., C. Germ., and other manuscripts; the printed editions have “in the river of the Jordan.”]

Because the author of our redemption deigned to be baptized in the river Jordan, the multitude of those held within the sacrament of baptism is rightly expressed by the name Jordan.

The ancient enemy of the human race swallowed the river because, from the beginning of the world until the Redeemer’s coming, he drew the human race into the belly of his malice, with scarcely a few of the chosen escaping.

Of this it is rightly said: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished” (ibid.), because he does not consider it a great thing when he seizes unbelievers.

But what follows is exceedingly grave: “And he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (ibid.), because after seizing all the unbelievers from the beginning of the world, he still presumes that he can seize the faithful as well.

For every day he devours with the mouth of his poisonous persuasion those whose life disagrees with and rejects their confession of faith.

[Note: Bigot. and Longip., “those whom a reprehensible life rejects and separates from the confession of faith.”]

10. Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, fear this with your whole attention; consider it among yourselves with an anxious mind.

Behold, we are celebrating the solemnities of Easter. But we must live in such a way that we may deserve to reach the eternal festivals. All things celebrated as festivals in time pass away. Take care, you who attend these solemnities, lest you be separated from the eternal solemnity.

What does it profit to be present at the festivals of human beings if it should happen that one is absent from the festivals of angels? The present solemnity is the shadow of the solemnity to come. For this reason we celebrate it annually, so that we may be led to that which is not annual but perpetual.

When this celebration takes place at its appointed time, our memory is renewed toward the desire for that one.

[Note: C. Germ., the first Carn., and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts, “may be directed toward it.” In the third Gemet., followed by the Antwerp edition and other ancient editions, “may be fixed upon it.”]

Through the repeated experience of temporal joy, therefore, let the mind grow warm and burn with longing for eternal joys, so that it may enjoy in the homeland the reality of joy that it contemplates on the way in its shadow.

Therefore, brothers, order your lives and conduct. Consider beforehand how strict he who rose gentle from death will be when he comes in judgment. Certainly, on the day of the terrible examination, he will appear with his angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers,

[Note: Belvac., “with principalities.”]

while heaven and earth burn, and all the elements are shaken in terror at his service.

Place this Judge of such great terror before your eyes. Fear his coming, so that when he comes you may see him not in fear but in security. He must therefore be feared so that he may not be feared. Let his terror train us in the practice of good works; let fear of him restrain our lives from wickedness.

Believe me, brothers: we shall then be as secure concerning his presence as we now strive to be watchful concerning guilt.

11. Certainly, if one of you were to be brought before my court tomorrow to plead a case against his adversary, he might spend the entire night sleepless, anxiously and restlessly turning over in his mind what might be said to him and how he would answer the charges. He would greatly fear that he might find me harsh; he would dread appearing guilty before me.

And who am I? What am I? Surely, not long afterward I shall be a worm after humanity, and dust after the worm. If, then, the judgment of dust is feared with such care, with what attention must the judgment of such great majesty be considered, and with what fear must it be anticipated?

### 12.

But since there are some who are uncertain about the resurrection of the flesh—and we teach this more effectively when we also address the hidden questions of your hearts—we must say a few things about faith in that resurrection. For many doubt the resurrection, as we ourselves once did, when they see flesh reduced to corruption and bones to dust in the tombs; they distrust that flesh and bones can be restored from dust, and thus, reasoning with themselves, they say: “When is a human being brought back from dust? When is it brought about that ashes become living?” We answer them briefly: it is far less for God to restore what once existed than to create what did not exist. Or what is so astonishing if he restores a human being from dust, when he created all things together from nothing? For it is more astonishing to establish heaven and earth from things that did not exist than to restore a human being from earth.

[Note: This is so in the Corbie, Saint-Germain, and better manuscripts. In the printed editions, with some manuscripts agreeing, the reading is “doubting, as we also once did, while [we saw] the flesh …” Concerning this error, which was prevalent in Gregory’s time, see the preface to the books of the *Dialogues*.]

But ashes are observed, and the possibility of their returning to flesh is despaired of; the power of divine action is sought as though it could be grasped by reasoning. Those who say such things in their thoughts do so because God’s daily miracles have become cheap in their eyes through their constant repetition. For behold, within a single, very small seed lies hidden the entire mass of the tree that is to grow. Let us place before our eyes the extraordinary size of any tree; let us consider where it began in its origin, when it reached such a great mass by growing. Without doubt we find its origin in a very small seed.

Let us now consider where, in that little grain of seed, there lies the strength of the wood, the roughness of the bark, the greatness of its flavor and fragrance, the abundance of its fruits, and the greenness of its leaves. The seed-grain, when touched, is not strong; from where, then, did the hardness of the wood arise? It is not rough; from where did the roughness of the bark burst forth? It has no flavors; from where comes the flavor in the fruits? When smelled, it gives off no scent; from where does the fragrance in the fruits arise? It displays nothing green in itself; from where did the greenness of the leaves emerge?

Thus everything lies hidden together in the seed, although everything does not emerge from the seed together. From the seed the root is produced; from the root the shoot emerges; from the shoot the fruit arises; and in the fruit a seed is also produced. Let us add, then, that a seed also lies hidden within the seed. Why, therefore, is it astonishing if he restores bones, sinews, flesh, and hair from dust, when he daily restores wood, fruit, and leaves in the great mass of a tree from a small seed?

When a doubting mind seeks a rational account of the power of the resurrection, questions should be put before it concerning things that are continually happening and yet can in no way be comprehended by reason. Thus, when it is unable to penetrate through the sight of a thing into what it sees, it may believe, on the promise of divine power, what it hears.

Therefore, dearest brothers, contemplate with me those promises that endure; but regard with contempt those things that pass away with time, as though they had already been abandoned. Hasten with all your purpose toward the glory of this resurrection, which the Truth has manifested in himself. Flee earthly desires, which separate us from the Creator, because you reach the sight of almighty God all the more deeply the more uniquely you love the Mediator between God and human beings.

He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript this is the thirty-seventh; in the Lateran manuscript and in the Royal Swedish Codex it is the thirty-second.]

## HOMILY XXVII

[Col. 1204D]

Preached to the people in the basilica of Saint Pancratius the martyr, on his feast day.

[Note: This homily is lacking in three Gembloux manuscripts and in the Lateran manuscript. It is found in the Royal Swedish Codex, the Corbie Saint-Germain manuscript, and others.]

### LESSON FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN 15:12–16

At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends.”

[Note: In the Bigot and Corbie manuscripts: “that he lay down his life,” omitting “than.”]

“You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.”

### 1.

Since all the sacred writings are full of the Lord’s commandments, why does the Lord speak of love as though it were a singular commandment, saying, “This is my commandment: that you love one another,” unless it is because every commandment concerns love alone, and all the commandments are one, since whatever is commanded is established in love alone?

For just as many branches of a tree grow from one root, so many virtues arise from one love. A branch of good works has no greenness if it does not remain in the root of love. The Lord’s commandments are therefore both many and one: many in the diversity of their works, one in the root of love.

He himself indicates how this love is to be held. In many statements of his Scripture he commands that friends be loved in him and enemies be loved for his sake. The person who truly possesses love is the one who loves a friend in God and loves an enemy for God’s sake.

For there are some who love their neighbors through affection for kinship and the flesh, and yet the sacred writings do not oppose them in this love. But one thing is what is freely offered to nature, and another is what is owed in obedience to the Lord’s commands through love. Such people indeed love their neighbor, but they do not attain the lofty rewards of love, because they offer their affection not spiritually but carnally.

Therefore, when the Lord said, “This is my commandment: that you love one another,” he immediately added, “as I have loved you.” It is as though he said plainly: “Love for the purpose for which I loved you.”

### 2.

In this matter, dearest brothers, we must carefully observe that the ancient enemy, when he draws our minds toward the delight of temporal things, arouses against us a weaker neighbor who tries to take away the very things that we love.

[Note: Thus in the Belvac, Saint-Germain, Gembloux, Carn, and other manuscripts; the printed editions have “the love of temporal things.”]

When he does this, the ancient enemy is not concerned to remove earthly possessions, but to strike love within us. For suddenly we burn with hatred; and while we wish to be invincible outwardly, inwardly we are grievously wounded. While we defend small things outwardly, we lose great things within, because while we love a temporal possession, we lose true love.

Everyone who takes away what is ours is an enemy. But if we begin to hate the enemy, there is something within that we lose. Therefore, when we suffer something outwardly from our neighbor, let us watch against the hidden plunderer within, who is never defeated more effectively than when the outward plunderer is loved.

There is one supreme proof of love: whether the very person who opposes us is also loved. Hence the Truth himself both endured the gallows of the cross and nevertheless offered affection of love to his very persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

What is so astonishing, then, if the disciples love their enemies while they are alive, when the master loved his enemies even while he was being killed? He expresses the fullness of this love when he adds: “No one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life for his friends.”

The Lord had come to die even for his enemies, and yet he said that he would lay down his life for his friends, clearly showing us that, when by loving we can make gain even from our enemies, those who persecute us are themselves also friends.

### 3.

But behold, no one persecutes us even to death. How, then, can we prove whether we love our enemies? Yet there is something that ought to be done in the peace of the holy Church, by which it may become clear whether, in a time of persecution, we would be able to die for love.

The same John certainly says: “Whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17).

[Note: This clause is absent from three Gembloux manuscripts and the Saint-Germain manuscript.]

John the Baptist also says: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give to the one who has none” (Luke 3:11). Therefore, whoever does not give his tunic for God in a time of peace, when will he give his life in persecution?

The virtue of love, then, if it is to remain unconquered in turmoil, must be nourished by mercy in tranquility, so that it may first learn to offer its possessions to almighty God and afterward itself.

### 4.

It follows: “You are my friends.” O how great is the mercy of our Creator! We are not worthy to be servants, yet we are called friends. How great is the dignity of human beings: to be friends of God!

But you have heard the glory of this dignity; hear also the labor of the struggle: “If you do what I command you.” You are my friends if you do what I command you. It is as though he said plainly: “You rejoice at the summit; consider by what labors one reaches the summit.”

Certainly, when the sons of Zebedee, through the intervention of their mother, asked that one of them should sit at God’s right hand and the other at his left, they heard: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). They were already seeking a place of exaltation; the Truth calls them back to the way by which they would come to exaltation. It is as though he said: “Now the place of exaltation delights you, but first let the way of labor train you.”

Through the cup one reaches majesty. If your mind desires what delights, first drink what causes pain. Thus, through the bitter cup of affliction, one reaches the joy of salvation.

[Note: The Antwerp edition and other older and more recent editions have “of confession” instead of “of preparation,” which is the reading found in the English manuscripts and ours.]

“I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you.”

What are all the things he heard from his Father—things he wished to make known to his servants so as to make them his friends—except the joys of inward love, except those festivities of the heavenly homeland that he daily impresses upon our minds through the inspiration of his love?

[Note: The two earlier Gembloux manuscripts read “of inward brightness.”]

For while we love the heavenly things we have heard, we already know what we love, because love itself is knowledge.

[Note: The Corbie and two earlier Gembloux manuscripts read “the heavenly things above”; the third Gembloux manuscript reads “always heavenly things.”]

He had therefore made all things known to those who, transformed from earthly desires, were burning with the torches of supreme love.

[Note: The first Gembloux manuscript reads “the torches of his love.”]

The Prophet had seen these as friends of God when he said: “But to me, O God, your friends are exceedingly honorable” (Psalm 138:17).

A friend is so called as though he were a guardian of the mind. Since the Psalmist perceived that God’s elect, separated from love of this world, guarded God’s will in heavenly commandments, he marveled at the friends of God, saying: “But to me, O God, your friends are exceedingly honorable.”

And as though we might immediately ask him to disclose to us the reasons for such great honor, he added at once: “Their rule has been exceedingly strengthened” (ibid.).

Behold: God’s elect subdue the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, shine with virtues, despise present things, proclaim the eternal homeland with voice and conduct, love it even in dying, and reach it through torments. They can be killed, but they cannot be bent. “Their rule has therefore been exceedingly strengthened.”

In this very passion, through which they fell into the death of the flesh, see how great was the height of their mind. Whence did this come, except because their rule was strengthened?

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Belvac, Gembloux, Longpont, Val-Clos, and old printed editions. In recent editions: “lest you think that they are so great,” etc. Three English manuscripts appear to support this, except that the English manuscripts have “if” instead of “so.”]

But perhaps only a few are so great? He added: “I shall number them, and they will multiply beyond the sand” (ibid., 18). Look upon the whole world, brothers: it is full of martyrs.

[Note: The first Carn manuscript reads: “Now we can scarcely see so many.” The second: “Now we who see can scarcely see so many.”]

Now there are scarcely as many of us who see as we have witnesses of the truth. They have therefore multiplied for us beyond the sand and are countable to God, because their number cannot be comprehended by us.

### 5.

But whoever reaches this dignity, so as to be called a friend of God, should look upon himself within himself, but regard the gifts he receives as above himself. Let him attribute nothing to his own merits, lest he break out into hostility.

Hence it is added: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit.”

[Note: The first Carn manuscript reads: “I chose by grace; I appointed you to go.”]

“I appointed you to grace; I planted you so that you might go by willing and bear fruit by acting.” I said “go by willing,” because to will to do something is already to go there in the mind.

What kind of fruit they ought to bear is then added: “And that your fruit should remain.” Everything for which we labor according to the present age scarcely lasts until death. For death intervenes and cuts off the fruit of our labor. But what is done for eternal life is preserved even after death; and it begins to appear when the fruit of bodily labors has ceased to be seen.

There, then, the reward begins where this life ends. Therefore, whoever has already come to know eternal things should regard temporal fruits as worthless. Let us produce such fruits as remain; let us produce such fruits as, when death destroys everything, themselves take their beginning from death.

For the Prophet testifies that God’s fruit begins from death when he says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm 126:2–3).

Everyone who sleeps in death loses an inheritance; but “when he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord,” because God’s elect, after they have reached death, will then find their inheritance.

### 6.

It follows: “So that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.” Here he says: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.” Again, elsewhere, through the same Evangelist, he says: “If you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name” (John 16:23–24).

If the Father gives us everything we ask in the Son’s name, what then are we to make of the fact that Paul asked the Lord three times and did not deserve to be heard, but was told: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9)?

Did that eminent preacher not ask in the Son’s name? Why, then, did he not receive what he asked? How, then, is it true that whatever we ask the Father in the Son’s name the Father gives us, if the Apostle asked in the Son’s name that the angel of Satan be taken away from him, and yet did not receive what he asked?

But since the Son’s name is Jesus, and Jesus means “savior” or is also called “saving,” the person who asks in the Savior’s name is the one who asks for what pertains to true salvation. For if what is not beneficial is asked, the Father is not asked in Jesus’ name.

Hence the Lord says to those same apostles, while they were still weak: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name” (John 16:23). It is as though he said plainly: “You have not asked in the name of the Savior, because you do not know how to seek eternal salvation.”

[Note: The Belvac and Saint-Germain manuscripts read “in the name of the Saving One.” The two earlier Gembloux manuscripts add “because you did not know.”]

This is why Paul also is not heard: for if he had been freed from the temptation, it would not have benefited him for salvation (2 Corinthians 12:9).

### 7.

Behold, dearest brothers, how many of you have gathered for the martyr’s feast. You bend your knees, beat your breasts, utter words of prayer and confession, and moisten your faces with tears. But weigh your petitions, I ask you; see whether you ask in Jesus’ name—that is, whether you seek the joys of eternal salvation.

In the house of Jesus you are not seeking Jesus if, in the temple of eternity, you pray importunately for temporal things. Behold: one person asks in prayer for a wife, another asks for a farm, another requests clothing, another begs that food be given to him.

Certainly, when these things are lacking, they should be requested from almighty God. But we must immediately remember what we have received by the command of that same Redeemer of ours: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

To ask Jesus for these things, then, is not to err, provided they are not requested excessively. But, more seriously, another person asks for the death of an enemy, and persecutes in prayer the one whom he cannot persecute with a sword.

The person who is cursed is still alive, and yet the one who curses is already held guilty of that person’s death. God commands that an enemy be loved (Matthew 5:44), and yet God is asked to kill an enemy. Whoever prays in this way fights against the Creator in his very prayers.

Hence it is said under the figure of Judas: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108:7). Prayer becomes sin when one asks for what the one being petitioned himself forbids.

### 8.

Therefore the Truth says: “When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything in your hearts” (Mark 11:25).

We can show the virtue of forgiveness more clearly if we bring forward one testimony from the Old Testament. When Judah had offended the justice of its Creator through sins that demanded punishment, the Lord, forbidding his prophet to pray, said: “Do not raise up praise and prayer for them” (Jeremiah 7:16). “If Moses and Samuel should stand before me, my soul is not toward this people” (ibid., 15:1).

What does it mean that, with so many fathers passed over and left aside, Moses and Samuel alone are brought forward, and their remarkable power of obtaining a hearing is displayed, when it is said that not even they can intercede? It is as though the Lord plainly said: “I do not even hear those whom I do not disregard on account of the great merit of their petition.”

Why, then, are Moses and Samuel preferred to the other fathers in petition, unless it is because these two alone, throughout the entire series of the Old Testament, are read as having prayed even for their enemies?

One is attacked with stones by the people (Exodus 17:4), and yet he begs the Lord for the one who stones him; the other is deposed from leadership, and yet, when asked to intercede, he confesses, saying: “Far be it from me to commit this sin against the Lord, that I should cease to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23).

[Note: The printed editions read “for those who stone him.” But the manuscripts, with great agreement, read “for the one who stones him,” namely, the people of Israel. Gregory alludes to this passage of Exodus 17: “A little more, and he will stone me,” namely, the people. Nowhere else do we read that Moses himself was attacked with stones.]

“If Moses and Samuel should stand before me, my soul is not toward this people” (Jeremiah 15:1). It is as though he plainly said: “Even now I do not hear them merely on behalf of friends, for I know them to pray, by the merit of their great virtue, even for enemies.”

The virtue, therefore, of true prayer is the height of love. Each person then obtains what he rightly asks when his mind, in petition, is not darkened even by hatred of an enemy.

But often we overcome a reluctant mind by praying even for our enemies.

[Note: The Bigot, Longpont, and Val-Clos manuscripts add “even when we pray for enemies.” We follow the Saint-Germain manuscript and others of antiquity.]

The mouth pours out a prayer for adversaries—but would that the heart retained love! For often we offer prayer for our enemies, but we pour it out more from obedience to a command than from love. We even ask for the life of our enemies, and yet fear that we may be heard.

But since the inner judge considers the mind rather than the words, a person asks nothing for an enemy if he does not pray for him sincerely out of love.

[Note: The Bigot manuscript reads: “He asks nothing for a friend who does not truly pray for an enemy out of love.”]

### 9.

But behold, an enemy has grievously wronged us: he has inflicted losses, injured those who helped him, and persecuted those who loved him. These things would have to be retained if our sins did not have to be forgiven.

For our Advocate composed a prayer for us in our case; and he himself is the judge of that same case—the one who is the Advocate. He inserted a condition into the prayer he composed, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

Since the judge himself has come, who was our Advocate, he himself hears the prayer that he made. Either, then, we say, without doing what it requires, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” and by saying this we bind ourselves even more; or perhaps we omit this condition from the prayer, and our Advocate does not recognize the prayer he composed, immediately saying to himself: “I know what I taught; this is not the prayer I made.”

What, then, are we to do, brothers, except offer the affection of true love to our brothers? Let no malice remain in the heart. May almighty God observe our love toward our neighbor, so that he may extend his mercy to our iniquities.

[Note: The printed editions and our manuscripts read “our love.”]

Remember what we are instructed: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). Behold, something is owed to us, and we owe something. Let us therefore forgive what is owed to us, so that what is owed by us may be forgiven.

But the mind resists this. It wants to fulfill what it hears, and yet it struggles against it.

We stand at the martyr’s tomb, and we know by what death he reached the heavenly kingdom. If we do not lay down our bodies for Christ, let us at least conquer our spirit. God is appeased by this sacrifice; in the judgment of his mercy he approves the victory of our peace.

For he sees the struggle of our heart; and he who rewards those who have conquered now helps those who are fighting, through our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son,

[Note: The two earlier Gembloux manuscripts add: “to whom be praise and glory forever,” etc.]

who with him lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In the Royal Swedish Codex this is the twenty-third; there it is said to have been preached in the cemetery of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. In the Lateran Codex it is the twenty-ninth; in the Corbie manuscript, the twenty-sixth.]

## HOMILY XXVIII

Preached to the people in the basilica of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, on their feast day.

### LESSON FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN 4:46–53

At that time there was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum. When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea into Galilee, he went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, for he was beginning to die.

Jesus therefore said to him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

The royal official said to him: “Lord, come down before my son dies.”

Jesus said to him: “Go; your son lives.”

The man believed the word that Jesus had said to him, and he went away. But while he was going down, his servants met him and reported that his son was alive. He therefore asked them at what hour he had improved.

[Note: The Belvac and Corbie manuscripts have the better reading: “at what hour he had become better.”]

They told him: “Yesterday, at the seventh hour, the fever left him.”

The father therefore recognized that it was at the same hour when Jesus had said to him: “Your son lives.” And he himself believed, and his whole household.

### 1.

The lesson of the holy Gospel that you have just heard, brothers, needs no exposition. But lest we appear to have passed over it in silence, let us say something about it by way of exhortation rather than exposition.

There is only one matter concerning its meaning that seems to require investigation: why did the man who had come to ask for his son’s healing hear, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe”? For the person who sought healing for his son certainly believed. He would not have sought healing from one whom he did not believe to be a savior.

Why, then, is it said, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe,” when he believed before seeing the sign? But remember what he asked, and you will clearly recognize that he doubted in faith. For he asked Jesus to come down and heal his son. He was therefore seeking the Lord’s bodily presence, although the Lord was nowhere absent in spirit.

He believed less in the one whom he thought unable to grant healing unless he were bodily present. For if he had believed perfectly, he would certainly have known that there was no place where God was not present.

He therefore distrusted to a considerable extent, because he did not honor majesty but bodily presence.

[Note: Thus the Saint-Germain manuscript and nearly all the manuscripts. Hence I am surprised that the old edition and more recent editions preferred “because he did not ascribe power [to him].” The Longpont manuscript may have provided the occasion for this reading, since it has “who did not honor the power of his dignity.”]

He asked for healing for his son, and yet doubted in faith, because he believed that the one to whom he had come was powerful enough to heal, but nevertheless thought him absent from his dying son. But the Lord, who is asked to go, indicates that he is not absent where he is invited; by a single command he restored health, although by his will he created all things.

### 2.

In this matter we must carefully observe something that, as we learn from another Evangelist, the centurion came to the Lord saying: “Lord, my servant lies paralyzed in my house and is suffering terribly.” Jesus immediately answered him: “I will come and heal him” (Matthew 8:6–7).

What does it mean that the royal official asks him to come to his son, and yet Jesus refuses to go bodily, whereas the centurion does not invite him to his servant, and yet Jesus promises that he will go bodily?

He does not deign to be bodily present at the royal official’s son, but does not disdain to go to the centurion’s servant. What does this mean except that our pride is rebuked? We honor in human beings not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but honors and riches.

When we consider what surrounds them, we fail entirely to attend to what is within, because we consider what is apparent in their bodies and neglect to consider what they are.

Our Redeemer, however, to show that what is exalted among human beings is to be despised, while what is despised among human beings is not to be despised by the saints, did not wish to go to the royal official’s son but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant.

[Note: Two Carn manuscripts and the Corbie manuscript read “what is exalted among human beings is to be despised by the saints.”]

Our pride was therefore rebuked: it does not know how to consider human beings on account of their humanity. It considers only what surrounds people; it does not look at their nature or recognize the honor of God in them.

Behold, the Son of God does not wish to go to the royal official’s son, and yet he is ready to come for the servant’s salvation. Certainly, if one of someone’s servants asked us to go to him, our pride would immediately answer us in silent thought: “Do not go; you demean yourself, your honor is being disregarded, and the place is beneath you.”

Behold, the one who came from heaven does not disdain to meet a servant on earth; yet we, who are from earth, disdain to humble ourselves on earth.

What could be more worthless or despicable before God than preserving one’s honor before human beings while not fearing the eyes of the inward witness? Hence, in the holy Gospel, the Lord says to the Pharisees: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings, but God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God” (Luke 16:15).

Take note, brothers, take note of what is said. If what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God, then the thought of our heart is all the lower before God the higher it is before human beings; and the humility of our heart is all the higher before God the lower it is before human beings.

### 3.

Let us therefore despise whatever good we may do. Let none of our actions inflate us; let neither abundance of possessions nor glory exalt us. If we inwardly swell with pride over any abundance of good things, we are despised by God.

By contrast, the Psalmist says of the humble: “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Psalm 114:6).

Because he calls the humble “little ones,” after stating this judgment he adds an instruction. For as though we might ask what he himself should do in this matter, he added: “I was humbled, and he delivered me” (ibid.).

[Note: The second Carn manuscript reads “let us look upon [ourselves].”]

Consider these things, then, brothers; weigh them with your whole purpose. Do not honor the goods of this world in your neighbors. For God’s sake, honor this in human beings: that they have been made in the image of God, although you have not been entrusted with them.

You truly preserve this for your neighbors if you do not first swell with pride in your own hearts. For whoever still exalts himself over passing things does not know how to venerate in his neighbor what endures.

[Note: The two earlier Gembloux manuscripts read “over temporal things.”]

Do not therefore consider in yourselves what you possess, but what you are. Behold, the world that is loved is fleeing. These saints, at whose tomb we stand, trampled the flourishing world under the contempt of their minds.

There was long life, continual health, abundance of possessions, fruitfulness in offspring, and tranquility in lasting peace; yet while the world flourished in itself, it had already withered in their hearts.

Behold, now the world has withered in itself, and yet it flourishes in our hearts. Everywhere there is death, everywhere mourning, everywhere desolation; from every side we are struck, from every side we are filled with bitterness. Yet, with the blind mind of carnal desire, we love its very bitterness; we follow what is fleeing and cling to what is falling.

And because we cannot hold back what is falling, we fall together with it, holding on to what is collapsing.

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Belvac, Corbie Saint-Germain, and better manuscripts. In the second Carn manuscript: “the pleasure of the world drew us back from God”; all the printed editions follow this, except that the Gussanville edition omitted “by pleasure.”]

At one time the world held us through pleasure; now it is so full of blows that the world itself sends us to God. Consider, therefore, how worthless are all things that pass away in time.

[Note: The Belvac and other manuscripts read “how nothing they are.”]

The end of temporal things shows how insignificant what passed away was. The collapse of possessions indicates that a passing thing was almost nothing even when it seemed to stand.

Consider these things carefully, therefore, dearest brothers; fix your hearts upon the love of eternity, so that, while you disdain to attain earthly heights, you may reach the glory of him whom you hold by faith, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In the Lateran manuscript this is the twenty-first; in the Royal Swedish Codex, the twenty-second; in the Corbie manuscript, the nineteenth.]

## HOMILY XXIX

[Col. 1213B]

Preached to the people in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, on the Ascension of the Lord.

[Note: This is absent from the Lateran manuscript and the first Gembloux manuscript. It is found in the Saint-Germain manuscript, the Royal Swedish Codex, and others. In the sacramentaries edited by Pamel and Menard, and in the Roman calendar of J. Fronto, the reading is *Ascensa* (“Ascended”), not *Ascensio* (“Ascension”).]

### LESSON FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK 16:14–20

At that time, while the eleven disciples were reclining at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen.

[Note: The Saint-Germain manuscript reads “the Lord Jesus.”]

And he said to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. But they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.

### 1.

The fact that the disciples were slow to believe the Lord’s resurrection was not so much their weakness as, so to speak, the future strengthening of our own faith. For the resurrection itself was demonstrated to them, while they doubted, by many proofs. When we recognize these as we read, what else do we gain from their doubt except a firm foundation?

Mary Magdalene, who believed more quickly than Thomas, who doubted for a long time, benefited me less. For by doubting he touched the scars of the wounds and cut away the wound of doubt from our hearts.

[Note: The Gembloux and Saint-Germain manuscripts read “the wound of our doubt.”]

To make known the truth of the Lord’s resurrection, we should also note what Luke reports when he says: “While eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem” (Acts 1:4). And shortly afterward: “While they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (ibid., 9).

Mark the words; note the mysteries. “While eating, he was lifted up.” He ate and ascended, so that through the effect of eating the truth of his flesh might be revealed.

But before the Lord ascended into heaven, Mark records that he reproached the disciples for the hardness of their hearts and their unbelief. What should we consider in this except that the Lord reproached the disciples at the very time when he was leaving them bodily, so that the words he spoke as he departed might remain impressed more firmly in the hearts of those who heard them?

After their hardness has been reproached, let us hear what he says by way of admonition: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

## 2

Were the holy Gospel, my brothers, to be preached to senseless things or to brute animals, so that it should be said to the disciples: [Note: [Col. 1214D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.”] “Preach to every creature”? By the name “every creature,” however, the human being is signified. There are stones, but they neither live nor perceive. There are grasses and shrubs: they do live, but they do not perceive. I say that they live, not through a soul, but through greenness, since Paul too says: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (1 Cor. 15:36). Therefore what dies lives, so that it may be made alive. Stones, then, exist, but they do not live. Shrubs, on the other hand, exist and live, but do not perceive. Brute animals exist, live, and perceive, but do not discern. Angels, however, exist, live, perceive, and discern.

The human being possesses something of every creature. For he shares being with stones, living with trees, perceiving with animals, and understanding with angels. If, then, the human being shares something with every creature, in a certain respect the human being is every creature. Thus the Gospel is preached to every creature when it is preached to the human being alone, because he is taught for whose sake all things were created on earth, and from whom, by a certain likeness, nothing is wholly alien.

The name “every creature” can also signify every nation of the Gentiles. Earlier it had been said: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10:5). Now, however, it is said: “Preach to every creature,” so that the preaching rejected first by Judea might then become our aid, when she had proudly rejected it as a testimony to her own condemnation.

But when Truth sends the disciples to preach, what else does he do in the world than scatter grains of seed? He sends only a few grains in the sowing, so that from our faith he may receive the harvest of many crops. For such a harvest of believers would not arise throughout the whole world if those chosen grains of the preachers had not come from the Lord’s hand upon rational soil.

The text continues:

## 3

“He who believes and is baptized will be saved, but he who does not believe will be condemned.”

Perhaps each person says to himself: “I have already believed; I shall be saved.” He speaks truly if he holds the faith by his works. For true faith is that which does not contradict in conduct what it says in words. Hence Paul says of certain false believers: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. 1:16). Hence John says: “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

Since this is so, we ought to recognize the truth of our faith by examining our life. We are truly faithful only when we fulfill by our works what we promise in words. On the day of baptism we promised to renounce all the works of the ancient enemy and all his pomps. Therefore let each of you turn the eyes of his mind back upon himself; [Note: [Col. 1215D] The second Carn. manuscript: “let him consider whether he keeps it.”] and if, after baptism, he keeps what he pledged before baptism, let him rejoice, already certain that he is faithful.
