But suppose he has not kept what he promised at all, [Note: [Col. 1215D] Belvac. and the two Carn. manuscripts read: “has kept it, for the practice,” etc.] if he has fallen into the practice of evil works and the desire for the pomps of the world. Let us see whether he now knows how to mourn that he has gone astray. Before the merciful Judge, even he will not be regarded as deceitful who returns to the truth after having lied, because almighty God, when he gladly accepts our repentance, conceals by his judgment what we have done wrongly (32, q. 1, c. 10). [Note: [Col. 1215D] Bigot., after “conceals,” adds: “because God accepts repentance in place of sin, but the signs …”]

The text continues:

## 4

“These signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well.”

Surely, my brothers, because you do not perform these signs, you do not believe? But these signs were necessary at the beginning of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1215D] This is to be read thus on the authority of Corb., Belvac., C. Germ., Carnut., Gemet., and others, and of the old editions. The more recent editions have: “for in order that it might grow toward faith,” etc.] For in order that faith might grow, it had to be nourished by miracles, just as, when we plant shrubs, we pour water over them for as long as it takes us to see them [Col. 1215B] already strengthened in the earth; [Note: [Col. 1215D] The manuscripts and old printed editions read likewise, whereas the more recent editions preferred to write “until they have already grown together.”] and once they have taken root, [Note: [Col. 1216D] The Vulgate editions read “watering will cease.” We judged that the authority of the manuscripts Corb., Belvac., C. Germ., and others should be followed, since it supports our reading.] we stop watering them.

Hence Paul says: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. 14:22).

We have yet to consider these signs and wonders more subtly. For the holy Church performs spiritually every day what it then performed bodily through the apostles. When her priests (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter 67), by the grace of exorcism, lay a hand upon believers and forbid evil spirits to dwell in their minds, what else do they do but cast out demons?

And all the faithful who now abandon the worldly words of their former life and sound forth the holy mysteries, proclaiming, as far as they can, the praises and power of their Creator—what else do they do but speak in new tongues? When by their good exhortations they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they pick up serpents. When they hear poisonous suggestions but are not drawn into evil action, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it does not harm them.

Whenever they see their neighbors growing weak in good works, and come to their aid with all their strength, strengthening by the example of their conduct the lives of those who stumble in their own actions—what else do they do but lay hands upon the sick, so that they may be well?

These miracles are truly greater in proportion as they are spiritual; they are greater in proportion as through them not bodies but souls are raised up. Therefore, dearest brothers, if you wish, you perform these signs by God’s authority.

For life cannot be obtained from those outward signs by those who perform them. Bodily miracles sometimes display holiness, but they do not produce it. These spiritual miracles, however, which take place in the mind, do not display the virtue of life but produce it. The wicked too can possess the former; only the good can enjoy the latter.

Hence Truth says of certain people: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?’ And then I will confess to them, ‘I do not know you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22–23; Ps. 6:9). [Note: [Col. 1216D] Longip. and Val. Cl. read: “because I never knew you.”] [Note: [Col. 1216D] We have removed “all,” which had crept into the recent edition contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.]

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not love signs [Note: [Col. 1216D] The two Carnut. manuscripts: “which the good can possess in common with the reprobate.”] that can be shared with the reprobate; love instead those miracles of charity and devotion that we have just described. They are all the safer because they are hidden, and with regard to them the recompense is greater before God precisely as the glory is less before human beings.

The text continues:

## 5

“And indeed, after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.”

In the Old Testament we know that Elijah was carried up into heaven. But the atmospheric heaven is one thing, the ethereal heaven another. The atmospheric heaven is close to the earth; hence we speak of the birds of heaven, because we see them flying through the air.

Elijah, then, was lifted up into the atmospheric heaven, so that he might suddenly be led to a certain hidden region of the earth, where he would live in great repose of flesh and spirit until he should return at the end of the world and pay the debt of death. He postponed death; he did not escape it.

Our Redeemer, however, because he did not postpone death but overcame it, consumed it by rising again and proclaimed the glory of his resurrection by ascending.

It should also be noted that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might be plainly demonstrated that a mere human being needed the help of another. For those aids were made and displayed through angels, since the one weighed down by the weakness of his nature could not ascend even into the atmospheric heaven by himself.

Our Redeemer, however, is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was clearly borne above all things by his own power. He was returning to where he was, and from there he was returning while remaining there, because as he ascended into heaven through his humanity, through his divinity he continued to contain earth and heaven alike.

## 6

Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers, prefigured the selling of our Redeemer, so Enoch, translated, and Elijah, lifted up into the atmospheric heaven, signified the Lord’s Ascension.

The Lord therefore had heralds and witnesses of his Ascension: one before the Law, the other under the Law, so that at last he himself might come who could truly penetrate the heavens. Accordingly, their respective elevations are distinguished by a certain progression.

For Enoch is recorded as having been translated (Gen. 5:24), whereas Elijah is recorded as having been carried up into heaven (2 Kings 2:11), so that afterward there might come one who would penetrate the ethereal heaven by his own power, neither translated nor carried up.

Because he would also bestow purity of flesh upon us who believe in him, [Note: [Col. 1217D] Even the old printed editions, against the manuscripts and against the sense, read: “because [he would bestow] the purity of his flesh.”] and because under him the virtue of chastity would increase with the passage of time, he displayed this even in the translation of those servants who, as servants, signified the Lord’s Ascension, and in his own person, the Lord who ascended into heaven.

For Enoch had a wife and sons; Elijah, however, is not read to have had either a wife or sons. Consider, then, how the purity of holiness grew through successive stages, as is clearly shown both by the translated servants [Note: [Col. 1217D] The first Carnut. manuscript: “through the Lord’s Ascension.”] and by the person of the ascending Lord.

Enoch was translated, having been begotten through intercourse and himself begetting through intercourse. Elijah was snatched away, having been begotten through intercourse but no longer begetting through intercourse. The Lord, however, was taken up neither begetting through intercourse nor begotten through intercourse.

## 7

We must consider what Mark means when he says: “He sits at the right hand of God,” while Stephen says: “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55). What does it mean that Mark testifies to seeing him seated, while Stephen testifies to seeing him standing?

But you know, brothers, that sitting belongs to one who judges, while standing belongs to one who fights or gives help. Therefore, because our Redeemer, taken up into heaven, now judges all things and will come at the end as Judge of all, Mark describes him as sitting after his Ascension, [Note: [Col. 1217D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts and Bigot. read: “after the Ascension.”] because after the glory of his Ascension he will be seen as Judge at the end. Stephen, however, placed in the struggle of combat, saw him standing, because he had him as his helper: while Stephen overcame the unbelief of his persecutors on earth, the Redeemer fought for him from heaven by his grace.

## 8

The text continues: “But they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed.”

What should be considered in these words, what should be entrusted to memory, except that obedience followed the command, and signs followed obedience?

But because, with God as our author, we have passed briefly through the exposition of the Gospel reading, it remains for us to say something about the consideration of so great a solemnity. [Note: [Col. 1217D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts: “the nobility.”]

## 9

First, we must ask why, when the Lord was born, angels appeared, yet are not read to have appeared in white garments, whereas when the Lord ascended, angels are recorded as having been sent and as appearing in white garments.

For it is written: “While they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments” (Acts 1:9).

White garments indicate joy and solemnity of mind. What, then, does it mean that, when the Lord was born, angels appeared not in white garments, but when the Lord ascended they appeared in white garments, except that great solemnity came to be among the angels when God, having become human, penetrated heaven?

When the Lord was being born, divinity seemed to have been humbled; when the Lord was ascending, humanity was exalted. White garments are more fitting for exaltation than for humiliation. [Note: [Col. 1218D] C. Germ., Belvac., Gemet., Longip., and Bigot. read this way. The printed editions have “at the Ascension.”]

At his assumption, therefore, the angels ought to have been seen in white garments, because he who appeared humble God in his Nativity was shown to be exalted man in his Ascension.

## 10

But on this solemnity, dearest brothers, we must weigh with the greatest attention that on this day the document of our condemnation was erased and the sentence of our corruption was changed. For the nature to which it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19), has today gone into heaven.

On account of this very lifting up of our flesh, blessed Job calls the Lord a bird by way of figure. Because he saw that Judea did not understand the mystery of his Ascension, he pronounced judgment upon its unbelief, saying: “The path of the bird was unknown” (Job 28:7).

The Lord is rightly called a bird, because he lifted a body of flesh into the ether. Whoever has not believed that he ascended into heaven has not known the path of this bird.

Of this solemnity the Psalmist says: “Your majesty has been lifted above the heavens” (Ps. 8:2). Again he says: “God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet” (Ps. 46:6). Again he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67:19).

Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, because by the power of his incorruption he swallowed up our corruption. He gave gifts to men because, having sent the Spirit from above, he granted to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the grace of powers, to another the grace of healings, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of words (1 Cor. 12:8). Thus he gave gifts to men. [Note: [Col. 1218D] In the recent edition, after the words “to men,” there had crept in: “while through the grace of this Spirit their power grew in the world. Concerning this …” Since it is found neither in the manuscripts nor in the old printed editions, we judged that it should be removed.]

Of the glory of his Ascension Habakkuk also says: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 3:11, according to the Septuagint). For who is signified by the name “sun” except the Lord, and who by the name “moon” except the Church?

Until the Lord ascended into heaven, his holy Church was utterly afraid of the adversities of the world. But after she was strengthened by his Ascension, she openly preached what she had believed secretly. Therefore the sun was lifted up and the moon stood in its order, because when the Lord sought heaven, his holy Church increased in the authority of her preaching.

Hence, in the voice of the same Church, Solomon says: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills” (Song 2:8). He considered the heights of such great works and said: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains.”

In coming to redeem us, he made, so to speak, certain leaps. Do you wish, dearest brothers, to recognize his very leaps? From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb he came into the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross he came to the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven.

Behold, so that he might make us run after him, the Truth made manifest in the flesh took certain leaps for us, because “he rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6), so that we might say to him from the heart: [Note: [Col. 1219D] Corb. and C. Germ.: “Draw me after you.”] “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3).

## 11

Therefore, dearest brothers, we ought to follow him there in our hearts where we believe that he ascended in the body. Let us flee earthly desires; let nothing now delight us in the lowest places, since we have a Father in heaven.

We must weigh this carefully: he who ascended in gentleness will return in terror, and whatever he commanded us with meekness, this he will demand from us with severity. Let no one think lightly of the time granted for repentance; let no one neglect to care for himself while he has the ability, because our Redeemer will then come in judgment with severity all the greater as he has shown us great patience before the judgment.

Therefore, brothers, practice these things with one another; turn them over in your minds with diligent thought. Although your spirit may still waver amid the disturbances of worldly affairs, fix the anchor of your hope already in the eternal homeland; establish the purpose of your mind in the true light.

Behold, we have heard that the Lord has ascended into heaven. Let us therefore preserve in meditation what we believe. And although we are still held here by the weakness of the body, let us nevertheless follow him with the steps of love.

He does not abandon our desire—the same Jesus Christ our Lord who gave it—who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1219D] In Corb. it is the twentieth homily. In the Codex regius Suec. it is the twenty-fourth. In the Lateran manuscript it is the twenty-second.]

# HOMILY XXX

[Col. 1220A]

Preached to the people in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, [Note: [Col. 1219D] This is absent from the Lateran manuscript and from the first Gemet. manuscript.] on the holy day of Pentecost.

## HOLY GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO JOHN 14:23–31

At that time, [Note: [Col. 1219D] In Belvac. and several others: “the Lord Jesus was saying.” The printed editions have “Jesus said.”] Jesus was saying to his disciples: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you.

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you: ‘I am going away and I am coming to you.’ If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going [Note: [Col. 1219D] Belvac.: “to my Father.”] to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.

“And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe. I will no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me. But this is so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that just as the Father commanded me, so I do.”

## 1

Dearest brothers, I wish to pass briefly over the words of the Gospel reading, so that afterward we may have more time to linger in contemplation of so great a solemnity. Today the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples with a sudden sound (Acts 2:2 ff.), changed the minds of carnal people into love of himself, and, while tongues like fire appeared outwardly, made hearts inwardly aflame, because when they received God in the vision of fire, they burned sweetly with love.

For the Holy Spirit himself is love. Hence John says: “God is love” (1 John 4:8, 16). Whoever desires God with an undivided mind already possesses the one whom he loves. [Note: [Col. 1219D] The first Carn. manuscript reads: “what he loves.”] For no one could love God if he did not possess the one whom he loves. But suppose each of you is asked whether he loves God: with complete confidence and a secure mind he answers, “I love him.”

At the very beginning of the reading, however, you heard what Truth says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” The proof of love, therefore, is the presentation of works. Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 4:20). For we truly love God if we restrain ourselves from our pleasures in order to keep his commandments. [Note: [Col. 1219D–1220D] So C. Germ., Belvac., the second Gemet., the first Carn., Bigot., and the better witnesses, with which the old editions agree. Other witnesses read: “and we keep his commandments, if we [restrain ourselves] from our own …”; Longip., Val. Cl., and the first Gemet. read: “if we keep his commandments, we truly love him, if from our own …”] Whoever still flows away through illicit desires plainly does not love God, because he contradicts him by his own will.

## 2

“And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Consider, dearest brothers, how great is this solemnity: [Note: [Col. 1220D] The more recent editions preferred “dignity” to “solemnity”; the latter word, however, is found in the ancient manuscripts and printed editions.] to have God’s coming as a guest in the lodging of one’s heart. Certainly, if some rich and powerful friend entered your house, the entire house would be cleaned with every haste, lest there perhaps be anything that might offend the eyes of the entering friend. Therefore let the one who prepares a dwelling for God in his mind wipe away the filth of evil conduct.

But observe what Truth says: “We will come, and we will make our dwelling with him.” For he comes into the hearts of some but does not make his dwelling there, because through compunction they indeed perceive God’s regard, but in the time of temptation they forget the very things over which they had been moved to compunction; and so they return to committing sins as though they had never mourned them.

Whoever, therefore, truly loves God and keeps his commandments has the Lord both come into his heart and make his dwelling there, because the love of divinity penetrates him in such a way that he does not depart from this love in the time of temptation. He truly loves whose mind is not overcome by sinful pleasure through consent. For each person is separated from heavenly love in proportion as he delights in lower things.

Hence it is further said: “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” Return inwardly, therefore, to yourselves, dearest brothers. If you truly love God, examine yourselves; yet let no one believe whatever his mind answers him without the testimony of works. In the love of the Creator, let tongue, mind, and life be examined. The love of God is never idle. If it exists, it performs great things; if it refuses to act, it is not love.

“And the word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.”

You know, dearest brothers, that the only-begotten Son who speaks is the Word of the Father. Therefore the word spoken by the Son is not the Son’s but the Father’s, because the Son himself is the Word of the Father.

“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.”

When would he not remain with them, since, about to ascend into heaven, he promises, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20)? But the incarnate Word both remains and departs: he departs bodily, but remains divinely. He therefore says that he remained with them at that time because the one who was always present by invisible power [Note: [Col. 1221D] Belvac. and C. Germ.: “was in authority.”] was now departing from them in bodily appearance.

## 3

“But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you.”

Many of you know, my brothers, that in Greek usage *paraclete* is called in Latin *advocate*, or *consoler*. He is called an advocate because he intervenes before the Father’s justice on behalf of sinners’ wrongdoing. Although he is of one substance with the Father and the Son, he is said to intercede for sinners because he makes those whom he fills into intercessors.

Hence Paul says: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26). But one who pleads is inferior to the one for whom he pleads. How, then, is the Spirit said to plead when he is not inferior? The Spirit himself pleads because he inflames those whom he fills to plead.

The same Spirit is called the Consoler because, when he prepares hope of forgiveness for those grieving over the commission of sin, he lifts the mind from the affliction of sorrow. Of him it is rightly promised: “He will teach you everything.” For unless that Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless. Let no one therefore attribute to a human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless the one who teaches is within, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

Behold, you all hear one voice speaking, yet you do not all perceive the meaning of the voice you have heard in the same way. Since the voice itself is not different, why is the understanding of the voice different in your hearts, unless there is an inner teacher who, through what the speaker’s voice commonly urges, teaches some people in a particular way about the meaning of the voice?

Concerning this anointing of the Spirit, John says again: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27). A person is therefore not instructed by the voice when the mind is not anointed by the Spirit.

But why do we speak of this regarding human teaching, when the Creator himself does not speak for a person’s instruction unless he speaks to that same person through the anointing of the Spirit? Certainly Cain, before he committed fratricide in deed, heard: “You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:7, according to the Septuagint). But because, in accordance with the demands of his sins, he was admonished by a voice and not by the Spirit’s anointing, he could hear God’s words but scorned to keep them.

We must also ask why it is said of the same Spirit: “He will remind you of everything,” since “to remind” ordinarily belongs to one who is lesser. But because we sometimes use “to remind” to mean “to supply,” the invisible Spirit is said to remind us, not because he brings knowledge into us from below, but from what is hidden.

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you.” Here he leaves; there he gives. He leaves it to those who follow; he gives it to those who arrive.

## 4

Behold, dearest brothers, we have briefly examined the words of the sacred reading; now let us transfer our minds to contemplation of so great a festival. But since, together with the Gospel reading, the reading from the Acts of the Apostles was also recited to you (Acts 2), let us draw something from it for the use of our contemplation.

You heard that the Holy Spirit appeared upon the disciples in tongues of fire and gave them knowledge of all languages. What did this miracle signify except that the holy Church, filled with the same Spirit, would speak in the voice of all nations?

Those who attempted to build a tower against God lost the communion of one language (Gen. 11:8), but among those who humbly feared God all languages were united. Here, therefore, humility earned power; there, pride earned confusion.

## 5

But we must ask why the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, appeared in fire; why in fire and tongues together; why he is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire; why he appeared over the only-begotten Son in the form of a dove, but over the disciples in fire (Acts 2:2 ff.), so that he neither came upon the Lord in fire nor appeared over the disciples in a dove.

Let us return by resolving these four questions that we have proposed.

The Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, is shown in fire because God is incorporeal, ineffable, and invisible fire, as Paul testifies: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29). God is called fire because by him the rust of sins is consumed.

Truth says of this fire: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). Earth is the name given to earthly hearts, which, because they continually pile up low thoughts within themselves, are trampled by evil spirits. But the Lord casts fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, [Note: [Col. 1223D] Belvac.: “the minds of carnal people”; C. Germ. and Gemet.: “the heart of carnal people.”] he sets carnal hearts ablaze.

The earth burns when the carnal heart, previously cold in its wicked pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and is kindled to the love of God. The Spirit therefore rightly appeared in fire, because from every heart that he fills he drives away the torpor of coldness and kindles it with desire for his eternity.

He was shown in fiery tongues because the same Spirit is coeternal with the Son, and the tongue has the greatest kinship with the word. The Son is the Word of the Father. And because the substance of the Spirit and [Note: [Col. 1223D] Belvac.: “and of the Son’s Word.”] the Word is one, the same Spirit ought to be shown in a tongue.

Or certainly, because the word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in tongues because whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses the Word of God, that is, the only-begotten Son. He cannot deny the Word of God, because he already possesses the tongue of the Holy Spirit.

Or certainly, the Spirit appeared in fiery tongues because he makes all whom he fills both burning and speaking. Teachers possess fiery tongues because, while they preach that God must be loved, they inflame the hearts of their hearers. The speech of a teacher is idle if it cannot provide the fire of love.

They had received this fire of teaching from the very mouth of Truth who said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). From the word heard, the mind catches fire; the coldness of torpor departs; the mind becomes anxious in heavenly desire and alien from earthly cravings.

True love, when it has filled a person, torments him with tears; but while he is tormented by such ardor, he is nourished by the very torments he suffers. He takes pleasure in hearing heavenly commands; and as many commandments as instruct him, so many torches, as it were, inflame him. What previously grew sluggish through desire afterward burns through words.

Hence Moses rightly says: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2). The reprobate are called the left, and they are to be placed on the left; the elect, however, are called God’s right hand. The law is therefore fiery in God’s right hand because the elect do not hear heavenly commandments with a cold heart; rather, their inward loves burn toward them like torches. The word is brought to the ear, and their mind, angry with itself, is consumed by the flame of inward sweetness.

The Holy Spirit was shown both in a dove and in fire because he makes all whom he fills simple and ardent: simple in purity, ardent in zeal. For neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity can please God.

Hence Truth himself says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). In this matter it should be noted that the Lord wished to admonish his disciples neither about the dove without the serpent nor about the serpent without the dove, so that the serpent’s cunning might kindle the dove’s simplicity and the dove’s simplicity temper the serpent’s cunning.

Paul says: “Do not become children in your understanding” (1 Cor. 14:20). We have heard about the prudence of the serpent; now let us be instructed about the simplicity of the dove: “Be infants in wickedness” (ibid.). Of blessed Job it is said: “He was a simple and upright man” (Job 1:1). For what is uprightness without simplicity, or what is simplicity without uprightness?

Because, then, this Spirit teaches both uprightness and simplicity, he ought to be shown both in fire and in a dove, so that every heart touched by his grace might become tranquil through the gentleness of meekness [Col. 1224B] and kindled by zeal for justice.

### 6

Finally, we must ask why, in our own Redeemer, the Mediator of God and human beings, the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, but in the disciples in the form of fire. Certainly, the only-begotten Son of God is the judge of the human race. But who could have endured his justice if, before gathering us through gentleness, he had wished to examine our sins through the zeal of righteousness? Therefore, having become human for human beings, he showed himself gentle toward human beings. He did not wish to strike sinners, but to gather them. First he wished to correct them gently.

[Note: Bigotianus, Longipontanus, and Vallicellanus read “to correct.”]

so that he might have people whom he could later save in judgment. [Col. 1224D]

Thus the Spirit had to appear above him in the form of a dove, since he did not come to strike sins already through zeal, but still to tolerate them through gentleness. By contrast, the Holy Spirit had to be shown above the disciples [Col. 1224C] in fire, so that he might set those who were simply human—and therefore sinners—ablaze against themselves as spiritual servants, and so that they might punish in themselves through repentance the sins that God would spare through gentleness.

For neither could those who adhered to the heavenly Master be without sin.

[Note: The two earlier Gemeticensis manuscripts, Longipontanus, and Vallicellanus read “to the heavenly Master.”]

As John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Therefore, he came among human beings in fire, but appeared in the Lord in the form of a dove, because the sins that the Lord piously tolerates through gentleness, we must carefully observe in ourselves through the zeal of righteousness and continually burn away with the ardor of repentance.

Thus the Spirit was shown in the Redeemer through a dove, but in human beings through fire, because the more the severity of our judge has been tempered toward us, the more intensely our weakness ought to be set ablaze against itself. [Col. 1224D]

Having therefore completed the explanation of these four propositions, let us proceed to contemplate the gifts of this same Spirit.

### 7

Of this Spirit it is written: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job 26:13). For the adornments of the heavens are the virtues of preachers. Paul enumerates these adornments when he says:

“To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:8ff.). [Col. 1225A]

Therefore, as many as are the virtues of preachers, so many are the adornments of the heavens.

Again it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6). For the Word of the Lord is the Father’s Son. But, in order to show that the entire Holy Trinity acted together in fashioning these same heavens—that is, the holy apostles—the text immediately adds, concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit: “And by the breath of his mouth all their strength” (ibid.). [Col. 1225B]

The strength of the heavens, therefore, was taken from the Spirit, because they would not have dared to oppose the powers of this world unless the strength of the Holy Spirit had made them firm. We know what teachers of the holy Church were like before the coming of this Spirit, and we see what strength they acquired after his coming.

### 8

Certainly, let the maidservant who kept the door tell us how weak and fearful this very shepherd of the Church, beside whose most sacred body we are seated, was before the coming of the Spirit.

[Note: Secundus Carnotensis: “of how much uncertainty.”]

Struck by the voice of a single woman, he denied life because he feared death (John 18:17). [Col. 1225D]

And then Peter denied him on earth, while the robber confessed him on the cross (Luke 23:41–42).

[Note: We follow Belvacensis, C. Germanicus, Gemeticensis, Bigotianus, and others here rather than the printed editions, where it reads: “And one must consider that Peter denied on earth the one whom the robber confessed on the cross when he had been hung.” In Longipontanus and Vallicellanus: “whom the robber confessed when he had been hung.”]

But let us hear what sort of man this person, so fearful before, became after the coming of the Spirit. The magistrates and elders assembled; the apostles were beaten and warned that they must not speak in the name of Jesus. Peter replied with great authority: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29). And again: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge. For we cannot refrain from speaking about what we have seen and heard” (ibid. 4:9–10). [Col. 1225C]

And they went away from the council rejoicing, because they had been considered worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus (ibid. 5:41).

[Note: The printed editions read “insult” (*contumeliam*).]

Behold: Peter rejoices in beatings, though earlier he was afraid of words. The one who previously feared when questioned by a maidservant, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, though beaten, crushes the power of rulers. [Col. 1225D]

It is a pleasure to raise the eyes of faith toward the power of this craftsman and to consider, here and there, the Fathers of the New and Old Testaments. Behold, with these same eyes of faith opened, I look upon David, Amos, Daniel, Peter, Paul, and Matthew, and I wish to consider what sort of craftsman this Holy Spirit is; yet in the very act of considering him I am overwhelmed.

He fills a boy who plays the lyre and makes him a psalmist (1 Kings 16:18). He fills a shepherd tending cattle and pruning sycamores and makes him a prophet (Amos 7:14). He fills a boy who practices abstinence and makes him a judge of elders (Dan. 13:46ff.). He fills a fisherman and makes him a preacher (Matt. 4:19). He fills a persecutor and makes him a teacher of the nations (Acts 9:1ff.). [Col. 1226A] He fills a tax collector and makes him an evangelist (Luke 5:27–28).

O what a craftsman this Spirit is! No delay occurs in teaching whatever he wishes. As soon as he touches the mind, he teaches; indeed, for him to touch is already to teach. For as soon as he illumines the human soul, he changes it: he suddenly rejects it as what it was and suddenly displays it as what it was not.

[Note: Disregarding the manuscripts, the printed editions have *abnegat hoc* (“he denies this”). We adhere to Belvacensis, C. Germanicus, Gemeticensis, Carnotensis, and others.]

### 9

Let us consider what condition he found our holy preachers on this present day, and what he made them.

[Note: Longipontanus reads “the present day.”]

Certainly, they were sitting in one room out of fear of the Jews. Each knew the language in which he had been born, yet they did not even dare to speak openly of Christ in the language they knew.

The Spirit came and taught them in their mouths through the diversity of languages, while in their minds he strengthened them with authority (Acts 2:2ff.). [Col. 1226B] They began to proclaim Christ in foreign languages, although previously they had feared speaking of him even in their own language.

For their inflamed heart despised the tortures of the body, which previously it feared; love of the Creator conquered the force of bodily fear.

[Note: Bigotianus: “love of the Creator.”]

Those who had previously yielded to their adversaries through fear now stood above them through authority. What else, then, should I say raised them to such a height, except that he made the minds of earthly human beings into heavens?

Consider, dearest brothers, what this present solemnity concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit is like after the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God. For just as the former is honorable, so also is the latter. In the former, God, remaining what he was, assumed humanity; in the latter, human beings received God coming from above. In the former, God naturally became human; in the latter, human beings became gods by adoption. [Col. 1226C]

If, therefore, we do not wish to remain fleshly in death, let us love this life-giving Spirit, dearest brothers.

### 10

But because the flesh does not know the spirit, someone may perhaps say to himself in a carnal frame of mind: “How can I love one whom I do not know?” We concede this as well, because the mind, intent upon visible things, does not know how to see the invisible.

[Note: Bigotianus: “For nothing visible thinks except visible things.” Primus Carnotensis: “For no visible thing thinks except…”]

It thinks only of visible things, and even when it is not engaged with them, it draws their images inward. While it lies immersed in bodily images, it cannot rise to incorporeal realities. Hence it happens that the more familiarly it carries bodily creation in its thoughts, the more grievously it fails to know the Creator. [Col. 1226D]

But although we cannot see God, we have something we can do, by which a path may be made for the eye of our understanding to reach him. Certainly, although we are in no way able to see him in himself, we can already see him in his servants. When we behold them doing wondrous things, it becomes certain to us that God dwells in their minds.

In an incorporeal matter, let us draw an analogy from bodily things. None of us can clearly behold the rising sun by fixing our gaze upon its sphere, because eyes strained by its rays are dazzled; but we look upon mountains illuminated by the sun, and, because the sun has already risen, we see. [Col. 1227A]

Therefore, because we cannot see the Sun of Righteousness in himself, let us look upon the mountains illuminated by his brightness—that is, the holy apostles, who shine with virtues and flash with miracles. The brightness of the rising sun flooded over them, and although it is invisible in itself, through them, as through illuminated mountains, it made itself visible to us.

For the power of divinity in itself is like the sun in heaven; the power of divinity in human beings is like the sun on earth. Let us therefore behold the Sun of Righteousness on earth, whom we cannot see in heaven, so that, while we walk through him on earth with the unimpeded step of our works, we may at last raise our eyes to heaven to gaze upon him.

Our journey on earth proceeds with an unimpeded step if God and our neighbor are loved with an undivided mind. For neither is God truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor truly loved without God.

This is why, as we have already said in another homily (above, Homily 26, no. 3), the same Spirit is read as having been given to the disciples twice: first by the Lord dwelling on earth, and afterward by the Lord presiding in heaven. [Col. 1227B] On earth he is given so that the neighbor may be loved; from heaven he is given so that God may be loved.

But why first on earth and afterward from heaven? Clearly this is made known because, according to John’s saying, “If anyone does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

Let us therefore love our neighbor, brothers; let us love the one who is beside us, so that we may be able to reach the love of the one who is above us. Let the mind meditate on what it should offer God in its neighbor, so that it may perfectly deserve to rejoice in God together with its neighbor.

Then we shall reach the joy of the heavenly multitude, of which we have now received the pledge of the Holy Spirit. Let us strive toward this goal with all our love, in which we shall rejoice without end. There is the holy fellowship of the citizens above; there is a secure solemnity; there is safe rest; there is true peace, which is no longer left to us but given to us by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen. [Col. 1227C]

[Note: In the Codex Regius Suecicus it is the twenty-fifth; in the Lateranensis, the twenty-seventh; in Corbeiensis, the twenty-eighth.]

## HOMILY XXXI

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr,

[Note: Thus it is read in the Codex Regius Suecicus, in Corbeiensis Germanicus, and in several others. In the Lateranensis, however, this homily is said to have been delivered in the Basilica of Saint Peter.]

on the Saturday of the September Ember Days. [Col. 1227D]

### LESSON FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE 13:6–13

At that time Jesus told the crowds this parable:

“A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it but found none. He said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have been coming seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down, then. Why should it even occupy the ground?’ [Col. 1228A]

“But he answered him, ‘Lord, leave it this year also, until I dig around it and spread a basket of manure. And if it bears fruit; but if not, afterward you shall cut it down.’

“Now he was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths. And behold, there was a woman who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not look up at all. When Jesus saw her, he called her to himself and said to her, ‘Woman, you are released from your infirmity.’ And he laid his hands on her; and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God,” and so forth.

[Note: Here the Gospel reading ends in the manuscripts of Belvacensis, C. Germanicus, Bigotianus, and at least certain other older manuscripts. In the printed editions it continues through verse 17 inclusive, but without basis, since Gregory says nothing in the homily about verse 14 or the following verses.]

### 1

Our Lord and Redeemer sometimes speaks by words in the Gospel, sometimes by deeds, sometimes says one thing by words and another by deeds, and sometimes declares by words what he also does by deeds. You have heard of two things: the barren fig tree and the bent woman; mercy was shown to each. The fig tree signifies what the woman signifies, and the tree spared what the woman made straight signifies. The vineyard-owner came three times and found no fruit; the woman had been bent for eighteen years. This number signifies the threefold visitation. Having surveyed the whole briefly, let us explain each point in order. [Col. 1228B]

### 2

The fig tree is human nature; the bent woman signifies the same nature. It was well planted like the fig tree and [lacuna] like the woman; but, falling voluntarily into sin, it neither keeps the fruit of action nor the state of uprightness. It would not bear the fruit of obedience and lost its upright state. The Lord came before the Law, under the Law, and under grace: by waiting, warning, and visiting he sought the nature of humankind.

### 3

Before the Law he came through natural understanding, making known that each should treat a neighbor as he wishes to be treated; in the Law, by teaching; after the Law, by showing the presence of his grace. Yet he complains that in all three visits he finds no fruit, since some wicked minds are corrected neither by natural law, nor by commands, nor by the miracles of the Incarnation. The vinedresser signifies the order of rulers in the Church. Peter was the first cultivator; unworthy as we are, we follow him insofar as we labor for your instruction by teaching, praying, and rebuking. [Col. 1229A]

### 4

Hear with great fear: “Cut it down; why does it occupy the ground?” Whoever holds a place in this present life but bears no fruit of good action occupies the ground and denies others an opportunity to work. A powerful person without good fruit also impedes those beneath him: his evil example shades them from the light of truth. He occupies the ground by burdening other minds and by failing to work good in the place he holds. [Col. 1229C]

### 5

Yet we must pray for such persons. To dig around the fig tree is to rebuke fruitless minds; every ditch is low, and rebuke humbles the mind by showing it itself. The basket of manure is the remembrance of sins: sins of the flesh are called manure. When we recall past vices to a carnal mind, we pour manure at the tree’s root, so that the memory of evil may make it fertile for compunction. The heart’s root returns to fruitfulness when penitence makes it lament, hate what it was, and kindle itself toward better things. But whoever will not become fruitful through rebuke here will fall where repentance can no longer raise him. [Col. 1230B]

### 6

The eighteen years of the bent woman signify the same threefold visitation: humanity was made on the sixth day, and six multiplied by three makes eighteen. The sinner who thinks earthly thoughts and does not seek heavenly things cannot look upward; pursuing lower desires, the mind is bent from its uprightness. One thinks of honors, another money, another estates: all these are low things. When the mind is entangled in them, it cannot rise to heavenly desire. [Col. 1230D]

### 7

Jesus called and raised her: he enlightened and helped her. He calls but does not raise when grace enlightens us but our merits do not permit help. Often we see what should be done but fail to do it; the mind sees uprightness, but strength of action falls short. Habitual fault binds the mind, so that where it long stood willingly it falls even unwillingly. “I am bent and humbled utterly.” The evil spirits say, “Bend down, that we may pass”: a soul stands straight when it desires heavenly things; they cannot pass through it unless it bends itself to lower desires. [Col. 1231C]

### 8

Let us not give evil spirits a road in us by desiring earthly things. The bent person always looks at the ground and forgets the price of redemption. Thus one oppressed by a hump is excluded from the priesthood; yet all redeemed by Christ’s blood are members of the highest priest. Fish without fins are forbidden: finned fish leap above the water, signifying elect souls who, supported by virtues, leap by heavenly desire even though mortal flesh pulls them back. Let the bent woman and barren tree stand before our eyes; remember our evils and pour the basket of manure at the heart’s root, so that what stank here in penitence may be fertile in the fruit of recompense. If we cannot perform the highest virtues, God delights in our lament. Yet in this very consideration I fail. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever. Amen. [Note: The two earlier Gemeticensis manuscripts read the concluding doxology.] [Col. 1232B]

## HOMILY XXXII

[Note: Numbered thirty-third in Codex Regius Suecicus, thirty-fifth in Lateranensis, and thirty-sixth in Corbeiensis.]

Because our Lord and Redeemer came into the world as a new human being, he gave the world new commandments. To our old life, nourished in vices, he set the contrariety of his newness in opposition.

[Note: Belvacensis, C. Germanicus, Gemeticensis, and Carnotensis read *praedicamenta* (“prescriptions”), whereas the editors altered it to *medicamenta* (“remedies”). The former reading is clearly preferable from what follows: “that he might prescribe self-restraint to the lustful . . . humility to the proud.”]

For what did the old, carnal human being know except to retain what was his, seize what belonged to others if he could, and covet it if he could not? But the heavenly physician applies remedies opposed to each individual vice. For just as in the art of medicine hot things are cured by cold and cold things by hot, so our Lord set opposite prescriptions against sins: that he might prescribe self-restraint to the lustful, generosity to the greedy, gentleness to the angry, and humility to the proud. [Col. 1233A]

Certainly, when he proposed new commandments to those who followed him, he said: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). As if he were openly saying: “You who, through your old way of life, covet what belongs to others, through the practice of the new way of life give away even what belongs to you.”

[Note: Primus Carnotensis reads “by the practice [*studium*] of the new way of life, neither seize what belongs to others and give away what is yours.”]

Let us hear what he says in this reading: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” There he says that we should renounce what is ours; here he says that we should renounce ourselves.

And perhaps it is not difficult for a person to leave behind his possessions, but it is very difficult to leave himself. For it is a lesser thing to deny what one has, but a very great thing to deny what one is. [Col. 1233B]

### 2

As we come to him, the Lord commands us to renounce what is ours, because whoever comes to the contest of faith takes up the struggle against evil spirits. The evil spirits possess nothing of their own in this world. Therefore, naked, we must wrestle with the naked.

For if a clothed person wrestles with someone naked, he is more quickly thrown to the ground because the clothed person has something by which he can be held. For what are all earthly things except a kind of clothing for the body? Therefore, whoever rushes into battle against the devil should cast off his garments, lest he be overcome.

Let him possess nothing in this world by loving it; let him seek none of the pleasures of passing things, lest he be held fast by the very things with which he is covered to his satisfaction and through which he is brought down.

Yet it is not enough to leave what is ours unless we also leave ourselves. What does it mean when we say, “Let us leave ourselves as well”? If we leave ourselves, where shall we go outside ourselves? Or who is it that goes, if he has abandoned himself?

[Note: The same codex has: “Or what is the destination of one who has abandoned himself?”]

But we are one thing as fallen through sin and another as created by nature; one thing is what we have made ourselves, another what we have been made. Let us leave ourselves as we made ourselves through sin, and remain ourselves as we have been made by grace.

For behold, if someone who was proud, having turned to Christ, becomes humble, he leaves himself behind. If someone who was lustful changes his life to one of self-restraint, he has certainly denied what he was. If someone who was greedy has stopped coveting and has learned to give away his own possessions, although previously he seized what belonged to others, he has undoubtedly left himself behind. [Col. 1233C]

He is the same by nature, but he is not the same through wickedness. Hence it is written: “Turn the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12:7). For when the wicked are converted, they shall be no more—not because they shall cease altogether to exist, but because they shall no longer exist in the guilt of wickedness. [Col. 1233D]

We therefore leave ourselves and deny ourselves when we avoid what we were through oldness and strive toward what we are called to be through newness.

[Note: Recent editions read *mutamus* (“we change”) in place of *vitamus* (“we avoid”), the latter being the reading of C. Germanicus and other manuscripts and printed editions.]

[Note: Belvacensis and the first Gemeticensis: “toward what we are called through newness.”]

Let us consider how Paul had denied himself when he said: “It is no longer I who live” (Gal. 2:20). That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and the devout preacher had begun to live. For if he had remained himself, he certainly would not have been devout.

But let him who denies that he lives say from where it is that he cries out holy words through the teaching of truth. He immediately adds: “But Christ lives in me” (ibid.).

[Col. 1234A]

As if he were openly saying: “I have been extinguished as far as I am concerned, because I do not live carnally; yet I have not died essentially, because I live spiritually in Christ.”

Let Truth therefore speak; let it speak: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.” For unless someone departs from himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him; nor can he grasp what is beyond himself if he does not know how to put to death what he is.

Thus plants are transplanted so that they may flourish and, so to speak, are uprooted so that they may grow. Thus seeds of things perish in their mingling with the earth so that, in the restoration of their kind, they may rise more abundantly. From the place where they seem to have lost what they were, they begin to appear as what they were not. [Col. 1234B]

[Note: Primus Gemeticensis and Longipontanus begin this sentence with the words “From that point…”]

### 3

But once someone has denied himself with respect to vices, he must seek virtues in which he may grow. For when it is said, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” it immediately adds: “And let him take up his cross daily and follow me.”

The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor.

Let us consider how Paul had taken up his cross in both ways. He said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27).

[Note: Bigotianus reads “subject [it]” (*subjicio*).]

Behold, in the affliction of the body we have heard of the cross of the flesh; let us now hear of the cross of the mind in compassion for one’s neighbor. For he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

The perfect preacher, in order to provide an example of abstinence, carried the cross in his body. And because he drew into himself the injuries of another’s weakness, he carried the cross in his heart.

3. But because certain vices lie close beside the virtues themselves, we must say what vice besieges abstinence of the flesh and what vice besieges compassion of the mind. For vanity often besieges abstinence of the flesh from nearby, because when thinness is observed in the body and pallor in the face, the virtue is exposed and praised; and it pours itself outward all the more quickly, the more it emerges before human eyes through displayed pallor. It frequently happens that what is believed to be done for God’s sake is done only for human approval.

This is well signified by that Simon who, found on the road (Matt. XXVII, 32), carries the Lord’s cross under compulsion [Col. 1234D]. For alien burdens are carried under compulsion when something is done out of zeal for vanity. Who, then, are signified by Simon, except those who are abstinent and proud? Through abstinence they afflict the flesh, but inwardly they do not seek the fruit of abstinence. Simon therefore carries the Lord’s cross under compulsion, because when a person is not led to a good work by good will, a sinner performs the deed of the just without its fruit. Hence Simon carries the cross, but does not die [Col. 1235A], because the abstinent and proud afflict their bodies through abstinence, but through their desire for glory they live for the world.

False pity, however, often secretly besieges compassion of the mind, so that it sometimes drags compassion as far as indulgence toward vices, whereas one ought not to exercise compassion toward faults, but zeal. Compassion is owed to the human being, and righteousness to the vices, so that in one and the same person we may love the good for which he was made and pursue the evils that he has done. Otherwise, while we carelessly pardon faults, we may seem no longer to have compassion through charity, but to have fallen through negligence [Note: [Col. 1235D] Belvac., “not so much through charity.” At this point the manuscripts diverge. Corb. has *consensisse* (“to have consented”). Primus Carn., Bigot., Val. Cl., and Longip. have *conscendisse* (“to have ascended”). The first two Gemet. have *concessisse* (“to have yielded”). Secundus Carnot. has *descendisse* (“to have descended”).]

4. It follows: “For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; and whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it.” Thus it is said to the faithful: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; and whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it.” It is as though one said to a farmer: “If you preserve the grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it.” For who does not know that when grain is sown as seed, it vanishes from sight and perishes in the earth [Note: [Col. 1235D] Longip. and Val. Cl. add: “in renewal it grows, in the dust it dies”; but …]? Yet from where it rots in the dust, from there it grows green again in renewal.

Because holy Church has one period of persecution and another of peace, our Redeemer distinguishes these periods in his commands. In a time of persecution, one must lay down one’s life; in a time of peace, earthly desires that might gain greater dominion must be broken. Hence it is now said: “For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world, but loses himself [Col. 1235C] and suffers the loss of himself?”

When persecution by adversaries is absent, the heart must be guarded with much greater vigilance. For in a time of peace, because it is permitted to live, it is also permitted to covet [Note: [Col. 1235D] The editors incorrectly changed *libet* (“it is pleasing”) to *licet* (“it is permitted”). *Libet* is read in C. Germ., Gemet., Corb., and others.]. This greed is well restrained if the condition of the covetous person himself is carefully considered. For why should he persist in gathering when the one who gathers cannot himself remain standing? Let each person therefore consider his course, and he will recognize that the little he has can suffice for him.

But perhaps he fears that provisions will be lacking on the journey of this life. The shortness of the road reproves our lengthy desires [Note: [Col. 1236D] Tertius Gemet., “life is short.”]; much is carried uselessly when the destination is near. Often, moreover, we overcome greed, but are still hindered because we hold the paths of righteousness with too little vigilance toward perfection. Frequently we despise all passing things, yet we are still obstructed by the habit of human shame, so that we cannot yet express in speech the righteousness that we preserve in our mind. We neglect God’s face in defending justice all the more as we fear human faces in opposition to justice.

But an appropriate remedy is added to this wound when the Lord says: “Whoever is ashamed of me [Note: [Col. 1236D] Longip. and Val. Cl., “is ashamed of me before human beings.”] and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels” [Col. 1236A].

5. But now people say to themselves: “We are no longer ashamed of the Lord and his words, because we openly profess him.” To them I reply that in this Christian people there are some who confess Christ for this reason: they see that everyone is Christian. For if the name of Christ were not today held in such glory, holy Church would not have so many professors of Christ.

The spoken profession of faith is therefore not sufficient as proof, when general profession protects it from shame. Yet each person has a point at which he must examine himself, in order to prove himself truthful in confessing Christ: whether he is no longer ashamed of his name, and whether, with the full strength of his mind, he has subjected human shame [Note: [Col. 1236D] Bigot., “whether he has quickly … himself.” The first two Gemet. have “having fully subjected human shame to the virtue of the mind.”].

Certainly, in a time of persecution the faithful could have been ashamed, stripped of their possessions, cast down from their dignities, and afflicted with blows. But in a time of peace, since these things are absent from persecution by our own people, there is another sphere in which we are revealed to ourselves. We are often afraid of being despised by those close to us; we disdain enduring verbal insults; and, if a quarrel with a neighbor should occur, we are ashamed to be the first to make amends.

The carnal heart, while it seeks the glory of this life, rejects humility. Often the very person who is angry with someone at odds with him wishes to be reconciled, but is ashamed to go first to make amends. Let us consider the deeds of Truth, so that we may see where the actions of our perversity lie. For if we are members of the supreme Head, we ought to imitate the one to whom we are joined.

What does the outstanding preacher Paul say as an example for our instruction? “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. V, 20). Behold: by sinning, we created discord between ourselves and God, yet God first sent his ambassadors to us, so that we who sinned might be entreated to come to God’s peace [Note: [Col. 1236D] Primus Carn., “being asked to return to peace.”].

Let human pride therefore be ashamed and let each person be confounded if he does not first make amends to his neighbor, since after our fault God himself, who was offended, entreats us—through the intervention of ambassadors—to be reconciled to him.

6. It follows: “But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” Dearest brothers, in sacred Scripture the kingdom of God is not always called the kingdom that is to come; sometimes the present Church is called by that name. Hence it is written: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. XIII, 41). There will be no scandals in that kingdom, since the reprobate are certainly not admitted there. From this example it is gathered that in this passage the present Church is called the kingdom of God.

And because some of the disciples were destined to live in the body long enough to see the Church of God established [Note: [Col. 1236D] The first two Gemet., “constituted.”] and raised up against the glory of this world, it is now said by way of consoling promise: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God” [Col. 1237A].

But since the Lord had given so many commands concerning the death that had to be undergone [Note: [Col. 1237D] Bigot., “commands that had to be carried out”], why was it necessary for him suddenly to come to this promise? If we attend to it carefully, we recognize with what gracious dispensation this was done.

For the inexperienced disciples also had to be promised something concerning the present life, so that they might be strengthened more firmly for the future one. Thus, when the Israelite people were being liberated from the land of Egypt, the land of promise was promised to them; and when they were to be called to heavenly gifts, they were persuaded by earthly promises.

Why was this done? So that, while they received something close at hand, they might believe more faithfully what they could hear from afar [Note: [Col. 1237D] Gussanv., against all printed and manuscript witnesses: “Why this, unless so that he might already believe through faithful people?” And below, likewise corruptly, “from those faithful people,” instead of “more faithfully.”]. For if the carnal people did not receive small things, they would not believe great ones. Almighty God therefore, by bestowing earthly things, persuades them toward heavenly things, so that, receiving what they could see, they might learn to hope for what they could not see; and they might become more steadfast concerning invisible things, insofar as visible promises supported them toward certainty of hope.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “He gave them the territories of the nations, and they possessed the labor of the peoples, so that they might keep his statutes and seek his law” (Ps. CIV, 44–45). Thus, in this passage, Truth speaks to inexperienced disciples and promises that they will see the kingdom of God on earth, so that they may anticipate it more faithfully in heaven. From the kingdom that we already see exalted in the world, let us therefore hope for the kingdom that we believe will be received in heaven [Col. 1237C].

For there are some who are counted by the name of Christianity but do not possess the faith of Christianity. They think that only visible things exist and do not desire invisible things, because they do not even suspect that such things exist.

We are standing beside the bodies of the holy martyrs, my brothers. Would these men have given their flesh over to death unless it had been utterly certain to them that there was a life for which they ought to die? And behold, those who believed in this way shine with miracles. The sick who are living come to their extinguished bodies and are healed; the perjured come and are freed from the demon’s oppression; the possessed come and are liberated [Note: [Col. 1237D] Observe here the custom already then established of purging oneself and freeing oneself from suspicion of hidden crimes by taking an oath at the martyrs’ tombs. Hence the holy Doctor writes to Castorius: “If Maximus of Salona, after taking an oath, confirms that he is not held by the Simoniac heresy,” and concerning other matters, before the body of Saint Apollinaris, and elsewhere, Book VII, indiction 2, formerly Letter 82, now Book IX, Letter 81. The same things are read in the preceding letter to Marinianus, now Letter 79 of the same book.].

How, then, do they live there where they live, if they live amid so many miracles here, where they are dead?

7. Brothers, I shall tell you of an event brief in words but not small in merit, which I learned from the account of certain devout elders. In the time of the Goths there was a very devout married woman [Col. 1237D] who frequently came to the church of these martyrs.

One day, when she had come according to custom to pray, as she was leaving she found two monks standing there in pilgrims’ clothing. Believing them to be pilgrims, she ordered that some alms be given to them. But before her distributor had approached them to give the alms [Note: [Col. 1238D] Primus Carn., “before the servant who was to distribute the alms …”], they came nearer and said: “You are visiting us now; we shall seek you on the day of judgment, and we shall provide you with whatever we can.” When they had said this, they vanished from her sight.

Terrified, she returned to pray and poured herself out at greater length in tears. After this she became so much more earnest in prayer as she became more certain of the promise.

Now, if we follow Paul’s words—“Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebr. XI, 1)—we no longer merely say that you should believe in the life to come, because behold, those who live in it are visibly present to human eyes. For what can be seen is more properly said to be known than believed. The Lord therefore wished us to know the life to come rather than merely believe it, since he visibly shows us to be living with him those whom he receives invisibly [Col. 1238B].

8. Dearest brothers, make these men your advocates in the matter of your examination, which you will undergo before the strict Judge; call upon them as your defenders on that day of such great terror. Certainly, if one of your cases were to be argued tomorrow before some great judge, your entire day today would be spent in thought, and your brotherhood would seek an advocate, praying earnestly that a defender might come on your behalf before so great a judge.

Behold, the strict Judge, Jesus, is to come; the terror of that great assembly of angels and archangels is present. Our case will be examined in that gathering, yet we do not now seek advocates whom we may then have as defenders [Col. 1238C]. Our holy martyrs are present as our defenders. They wish to be asked and, so to speak, they seek to be sought.

Seek them, then, as helpers of your prayer; find them as protectors from your guilt. For he who judges himself wishes to be asked not to punish sinners. Hence he threatens anger for so long a time and yet mercifully waits.

May his mercy therefore refresh us in such a way that it does not make us negligent in any respect. May our sins trouble us in such a way that our minds do not collapse into despair [Col. 1238D], because, although we fear while presuming, and hope while fearing, we shall gain the eternal kingdom all the sooner [Note: [Col. 1238D] The first two Gemet. add the customary conclusion: “through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and dominion throughout all ages.”], through him who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1238D] This is number thirteen in the Lateran manuscript, number twenty-six in the Codex Regius Suecicus, and number twenty-seven in Corb.]

HOMILY XXXIII

[Col. 1238D] Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Clement, [Note: [Col. 1238D] These words are absent from Bigot., the two Gemet., Corb. Germ., and most others. In C. Germ. one reads: “in the basilica of Saint Clement on his feast day.”] on the Friday of the September Ember Days.

READING OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE VII, 36–50

At that time, a certain Pharisee invited Jesus to eat with him. And he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that Jesus was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house [Note: [Col. 1239D] Belvac., C. Germ., and some others: “that he had reclined at table.”], brought an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind him beside his feet, she began to bathe his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head; she kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment.

When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.”

And Jesus answered and said to him: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” He replied: “Teacher, say it.” [Note: [Col. 1239D] The same codices: “And Jesus answered and said: ‘Two.’” Bigot., “And Jesus answered: ‘Two.’”]

“There were two debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both of them. Which of them, then, loves him more?” [Note: [Col. 1239D] C. Germ., Belvac., and others: “which of them loved him more.”]

Simon answered: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” [Note: [Col. 1239D] Bigot., “Simon answered: ‘The one to whom more was forgiven.’”] And he said to him: “You have judged correctly.”

And turning toward the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she has bathed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not give me a kiss, but she, from the time she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.

“Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. But the one to whom little is forgiven loves little.”

Then he said to her: “Your sins are forgiven.” And those who were reclining at table with him began to say among themselves: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” But he said to the woman: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” [Note: [Col. 1239D] Belvac. and C. Germ.: “And Jesus said to her: ‘Your sins are forgiven.’ And some of those who were reclining with him began …”]

1. When I think about Mary’s repentance [Note: [Col. 1239D] In the printed editions: “of Mary Magdalene.” “Magdalene” is absent from at least the older manuscripts—Corb., C. Germ., Gemet., and others. Nevertheless, it is clear both from this homily and from the eighth homily on Ezekiel, section 2, that the holy Doctor did not distinguish the sinful woman from Mary Magdalene.], I would rather weep than say anything. Whose heart, even if made of stone, would those tears of this sinful woman not soften as an example of repentance?

She considered what she had done and did not wish to restrain what she was doing. She entered among the banqueters without being summoned; she came uninvited; amid the courses she offered her tears. Learn with what sorrow she burns, since she is not ashamed to weep even during a meal.

This woman whom Luke calls a sinful woman and John calls Mary, we believe to be that Mary of whom Mark testifies that seven demons had been cast out [Note: [Col. 1240D] Primus Carn., “Matthew.”]. And what are signified by the seven demons except all vices? Since the whole of time is comprised in seven days, the totality is rightly represented by the number seven. Mary therefore had seven demons, because she was full of every vice.

But behold: because she saw the stains of her shame, she ran to the fountain of mercy to be washed and was not ashamed to enter among the banqueters. Because inwardly she was deeply ashamed of herself, she thought there was nothing of which she should be ashamed outwardly.

Why, then, brothers, are we astonished: at Mary coming, or at the Lord receiving her? Shall I say, receiving her, or shall I say, drawing her? I shall say it better: drawing and receiving her, because he himself drew her inwardly through mercy, while through gentleness he received her outwardly.

But let us now run through the text of the holy Gospel and examine the very order in which she came to be healed.

2. “She brought an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing behind him beside the feet of Jesus, she began to bathe his feet with her tears; and she wiped them with the hair of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment.”

It is clear, brothers, that the woman, previously devoted to illicit acts, had used ointment for the fragrance of her flesh. What she had shamefully offered to herself, she now laudably offered to God. With her eyes she had coveted earthly things, but now, crushing them through repentance, she wept. She had used her hair to adorn her face [Col. 1240B], but now she wiped away her tears with her hair. With her mouth she had spoken proudly, but by kissing the Lord’s feet she fixed this in the footsteps of her Redeemer.

Thus, as many pleasures as she had possessed in herself, she found as many sacrifices from herself. She converted the number of her crimes into a number of virtues [Note: [Col. 1240D] Primus Carn., “she converted the number of crimes into virtue.” So formerly in C. Germ.], so that everything by which she had despised God in guilt might serve God entirely in repentance.

3. But when the Pharisee sees this, he despises it; and he reproves not only the sinful woman who is coming, but also the Lord who is receiving her, saying to himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.”

Behold the Pharisee, truly proud in himself and falsely righteous, reproves the sick woman for her sickness and the physician for his assistance, while he himself was also sick from a wound of pride and did not know it.

A physician was present among two sick people. One sick man retained sound judgment in his fever [Note: [Col. 1240D] The first two Gemet., “retained his judgment.”]; the other, in the fever of the flesh, had lost the judgment of his mind. She was weeping over what she had done; the Pharisee, elated by false righteousness, magnified the force of his own illness. In his sickness, therefore, he had also lost his judgment, since he did not know even that he was far from health.

Amid all this, we are compelled by groans to look upon certain men of our own order who, endowed with priestly office, immediately despise their subjects if they have perhaps done something outwardly just, however slightly. They disdain sinners among the people, refuse to have compassion on those who confess their guilt, and, like the Pharisee, despise being touched by a sinful woman.

If this woman had come to the Pharisee’s feet, she would surely have departed driven away by kicks. He would have believed that he was being defiled by another’s sin. But because true righteousness did not fill him, he was sick from another’s wound.

Hence, whenever we see sinners, it is always necessary that we first weep for ourselves in their calamity, because perhaps we have fallen into similar things, or may fall if we have not fallen already.
