And although the authority of teaching must always pursue vices with the force of discipline, we must nevertheless carefully distinguish that strictness is owed to vices, but compassion to human nature. For if the sinner is to be struck, the neighbor is to be nourished. But when, through repentance, he himself strikes what he has done, our neighbor is no longer a sinner [Note: [Col. 1241D] The printed editions have: “when he directs God’s justice against himself,” a reading we would approve if it were not rejected by the better manuscripts—C. Germ., Belvac., Gemet., and nearly all others.], because when he directs God’s justice against himself and punishes in himself what divine justice condemns.

4. But now let us hear by what sentence this proud and arrogant man is convicted. A parable is set before him concerning two debtors, one of whom owes less and the other more. After the debts of both have been forgiven, he is asked which of them will love the one who generously forgave the debt more [Col. 1241B].

At once he replied: “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more.” In this matter it must be noted that, when the Pharisee is convicted by his own judgment, he carries, like a madman, the rope by which he is to be bound.

The woman’s good deeds and the false righteous man’s evils are listed when it is said: “I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she bathed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not give me a kiss, but she, from the moment she entered [Note: [Col. 1241D] Gemet., “from the moment I entered”], has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.”

After this enumeration, the verdict is added: “Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.”

What do we believe love to be, my brothers, except fire? And what do we believe guilt to be, except rust? Hence it is now said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “She has completely burned away the rust of sin, because she burns intensely with the fire of love.” For the rust of sin is consumed all the more as the sinner’s heart is burned by the great fire of charity [Note: [Col. 1241D] Belvac. and Corb., “which burns.” Longip., Val. Cl., and Bigot. [Col. 1242D], “which burns.”].

Behold, the sick woman who had come to the physician has been healed, but others are still sick because of her healing. Those reclining together complained, saying among themselves: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?”

But the heavenly physician does not despise the sick whom he sees becoming worse even because of the medicine. He confirms the woman whom he had healed through his merciful verdict, saying: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

Faith saved her because she did not doubt that she could receive what she asked. But she had already received that very certainty of hope from the one from whom she sought salvation through hope.

She is commanded to go in peace so that she might not thereafter turn aside from the path of truth into the way of scandal. Hence it is also said through Zechariah: “To guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luke I, 79). We direct our steps into the way of peace when we travel along that course of action in which we do not depart from the grace of our Creator.

5. Dearest brothers, we have passed briefly through these matters in their historical exposition. Now, if you please, let us discuss what has been said according to its mystical meaning.

Whom does the Pharisee, presuming upon false righteousness, signify except the Jewish people? And whom does the sinful woman, coming to the Lord’s feet and weeping, signify except the converted Gentiles?

She came with an alabaster jar, poured out ointment, stood behind the Lord beside his feet, bathed his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and did not cease kissing the very feet that she was bathing and wiping.

We are represented by that woman—yes, we are—if after our sins we return to the Lord with our whole heart, if we imitate her mourning of repentance [Note: [Col. 1242D] Primus Carn., “the fruit of her repentance.”].

What is expressed by the ointment except the good fragrance of reputation? Hence Paul also says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God in every place” (II Cor. II, 15) [Note: [Col. 1242D] Gemet., Bigot., Val. Cl., and Longip., “except the good fragrance of reputation.”].

If, therefore, we perform upright deeds by which we sprinkle the Church with the fragrance of a good reputation, what do we pour upon the body of the Lord except ointment?

But the woman stood beside the feet of Jesus. We stood against the Lord’s feet when, placed in sins, we were hindered from following his paths. But if after our sins we turn to true repentance, we now stand behind him beside his feet, because we follow the footsteps of the one whom we had opposed.

The woman bathes his feet with tears. We too truly do this if we bow toward any of the least members of the Lord through the affection of compassion; if we suffer with his saints in tribulation; if we regard their sorrow as our own.

The woman wiped with her hair the feet she had bathed. Hair is something that grows in excess of the body. And what does abundant earthly substance resemble except hair? When it exceeds the use of necessity, even when cut off it is not missed [Note: [Col. 1242D] So Belvac., C. Germ., and many others. The printed editions have “it is not perceived.”].

We wipe the Lord’s feet with our hair when we show mercy to his saints, with whom we compassionately suffer, even from what is superfluous to us—so that the mind may grieve through compassion in such a way that the generous hand also displays the feeling of grief.

He bathes the Redeemer’s feet with tears but does not wipe them with his hair who, in some measure, sympathizes with the sorrow of his neighbors but does not show them mercy from what is superfluous to him. He weeps but does not wipe who offers words of sorrow but, by failing to provide what is lacking, does not diminish the force of their grief at all.

The woman kisses the feet that she wipes. We too do this fully if we diligently love those whom we sustain through generosity, so that our neighbor’s need is not burdensome to us, so that his very want—which is being supported—does not become oppressive to us, and so that, while our hands provide what is necessary, our mind does not grow dull in love [Col. 1242D].

6. The feet may also be understood as the mystery of his incarnation itself, by which divinity touched the earth because he assumed flesh. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

We therefore kiss the Redeemer’s feet when we love the mystery of his incarnation with our whole heart. We anoint his feet with ointment when we proclaim, with the good reputation of sacred eloquence, the power of his humanity.

But the Pharisee sees this and is envious, because when the Jewish people see the Gentiles preaching God, they waste away inwardly in their own wickedness. Our Redeemer therefore enumerates the deeds of this woman as the good deeds of the Gentiles, so that the Jewish people may recognize in what evil they lie.

Thus the Pharisee is rebuked, so that through him, as we have said, that faithless people may be revealed.

“I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she bathed my feet with her tears.” Water is outside us, whereas the moisture of tears is within us. The faithless people never gave the Lord even what was outside themselves; but the converted Gentiles poured out for him not only their material possessions, but also their blood [Col. 1243B].

“You did not give me a kiss, but she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet.” A kiss is a sign of love. That faithless people did not give God a kiss, because they did not wish to love him from charity, though they served him from fear.

But the Gentiles, once called, do not cease kissing the footsteps of their Redeemer, because they continually sigh in his love. Hence, in the voice of the bride, it is said of the same Redeemer in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 7) [Note: [Col. 1243D] Belvac., “with the kisses of his mouth.”]. She rightly desires the kiss of her Creator who prepares herself to serve him through love.

“You did not anoint my head with oil.” If we understand the Lord’s feet as the mystery of his incarnation, then his head appropriately signifies divinity itself. Hence Paul says: “The head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI, 3).

The Jewish people professed belief in God, but not in him as though in a human being [Col. 1243C]. Yet it is said to the Pharisee: “You did not anoint my head with oil,” because he neglected to proclaim with fitting praise even the power of his divinity, in which the Jewish people had professed that they believed.

“But she has anointed my feet with ointment,” because when the Gentiles believed the mystery of his incarnation, they also proclaimed his lowest aspect—the human nature he assumed—with the highest praise.

But our Redeemer now concludes his enumeration of the woman’s good deeds when he adds the verdict: “Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “Although what is being boiled is exceedingly hard, the fire of love by which even hard things are consumed is abundant.”

7. In the midst of these matters, it is pleasing to contemplate such great mercy. With what esteem does Truth hold the deeds of the sinful woman—though she was repentant—that he enumerates them before her adversary with such careful ordering?

The Lord reclined at the Pharisee’s meal, but in the repentant woman he delighted in the feast of her mind. Before the Pharisee, Truth was fed outwardly; before the sinful woman—but now converted—it was fed inwardly.

Hence holy Church says to him whom she seeks under the figure of the fawn of the deer, in the Song of Songs: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie at noon” (Song I, 6).

The Lord is called the fawn of the deer because, according to the flesh he assumed, he is the son of the ancient fathers. At noon the heat burns more intensely, and the fawn seeks a shady place where the fire of the heat cannot affect it.

The Lord therefore rests in those hearts that the love of the present age does not set on fire, that the desires of the flesh do not consume, and that, inflamed by their anxieties amid the desires of this world, do not wither.

Hence it is also said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35). The fawn seeks shady places at noon in which to feed, because the Lord feeds upon minds that, through awareness of grace, are temperate and are not burned by bodily desires.

The repentant woman therefore fed the Lord inwardly more than the Pharisee fed him outwardly, because our Redeemer, like a fawn fleeing the heat of carnal desires, had fled into the mind of the woman, where the shade of repentance tempered the fire of her former vices [Col. 1244B].

8. Let us consider how great was his compassion: not only to admit the sinful woman to himself, but also to offer his feet for her to touch. Let us contemplate the grace of the merciful God, and condemn the multitude of our guilt. Behold, he sees sinners and bears with them; he tolerates those who resist, and yet each day he mercifully calls them through the Gospel. He desires our confession from a pure heart, and has forgiven everything in which we offend. The mercy of our Redeemer has tempered the rigor of the law for us. For in it is written: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death”; “If anyone does these or those things, let him be overwhelmed with stones” (Exod. 19:12; Lev. 20 and following). Our Creator and Redeemer appeared in the flesh and promises sinners who confess, not punishment but life; he receives the woman confessing her wounds and sends her away healed. Thus he bent the harshness of the law toward mercy, because those whom it justly condemns he mercifully frees.

Hence it is also well written in the law that Moses’ hands were heavy; so they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it, while Aaron and Hur supported his hands (Exod. 17:12). Moses sat upon the stone when the law came to rest in the Church. Yet this same law had heavy hands, because it did not bear with sinners mercifully, but struck each one with severe rigor. Aaron, however, means “mountain of strength,” while Hur means “fire.” Whom, then, does this mountain of strength signify except our Redeemer, of whom the prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2)? Or who is signified by fire except the Holy Spirit, of whom the same Redeemer says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49)?

Aaron and Hur, therefore, support Moses’ heavy hands and make them lighter by supporting them, because the Mediator of God and human beings, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, shows us through spiritual understanding that the commands of the law—which, while held carnally, could not be borne—are tolerable. For he made Moses’ hands seem lighter, since he turned the burden of the law’s commands toward the power of confession.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] The second Carn. reads: “toward the assurance of conversion.”]

He hints to us at this following promise of mercy when he says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11).

[Note: [Col. 1244D–1245D] C. Germ., the two earlier Gemet., and the second Carn. read *nobis sequentis* (“to us, of the following”); the third Gemet. reads *nobis sequentem* (“to us, the following”).] Again, under the figure of Judea, it is said to every sinful soul: “If a man divorces his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3:1). Behold, he presented the example of a shameful woman. He showed that after disgrace she cannot be received. Yet he overcomes this very example that he brought forward through mercy: he says that a prostituted woman can in no way be received, and yet he himself awaits the prostituted soul in order to receive it.

Consider, brothers, the weight of such great compassion. He says that something cannot happen, and shows that he himself can do it even contrary to custom. Behold, he calls; and those whom he declares defiled he also seeks to embrace, those by whom he complains that he has been deserted. Therefore, let no one waste the time of such great mercy; let no one cast away the remedies offered by divine compassion. Behold, heavenly goodness calls us back when we have turned away, and prepares for us, when we return, the embrace of its mercy.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read “opens its bosom.” The first Carn. has, departing from the others, “prepares a sign.”]

Let each person, then, consider by what debt he is bound, since God awaits him and is not provoked even by being despised.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] Corb.: “when God does not spurn him even when despised.” Belvac. and the two earlier Gemet.: “when … not even contempt exasperates him.” We have followed C. Germ. and the others.]

Let the one who did not wish to remain return; let the one who scorned to stand rise at least after his fall. Our Creator indicates how greatly he awaits us when he says through the prophet: “I waited and listened; no one speaks what is good; there is no one who reflects in his heart and says, ‘What have I done?’” (Jer. 8:6). Certainly, we ought never to have thought evil things. But because we were unwilling to think what was right, behold, he still bears with us, so that we may reflect.

See the bosom of such great compassion; consider the womb of mercy opened for you. Those whom evil thinking destroyed, he seeks when they think rightly.

Therefore, dearest brothers, turn the eyes of your minds back to yourselves; set the repentant sinful woman before you as an example for imitation. Weep over whatever offenses you remember committing in adolescence and in youth; wipe away with tears the stains of your conduct and deeds. Let us now love the footsteps of our Redeemer, which we despised by sinning. Behold, as we have said, the bosom of heavenly compassion is opened to receive us, and our stained life is not despised. By shuddering at our defilement, we are already brought into harmony with inner purity. The Lord mercifully embraces us when we return, because the life of sinners can no longer be unworthy of him when it is washed by tears—in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1245D] In the Lateran manuscript this is the twenty-fourth homily. In the Codex regius Suecicus, the twenty-seventh. In Corb., the twenty-third.]

## HOMILY XXXIV

Delivered to the people

[Note: [Col. 1245D] The second Carn. reads: “in the basilica of blessed John the Apostle, on Sunday.” “The third Sunday after Pentecost” is absent from most manuscripts.]

in the basilica of the blessed John and Paul, on the third Sunday after Pentecost.

### HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE 15:1–10

At that time,

[Note: [Col. 1246D] C. Germ., Lateran., Belvac., and the three Gemet. manuscripts read: “were coming eagerly to Jesus.”]

tax collectors and sinners were approaching Jesus to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes were murmuring, saying: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” And he told them this parable, saying: “What man among you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he places it upon his shoulders, rejoicing; and when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.’

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Bigot. reads: “which I had lost.”]

I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents

[Note: [Col. 1246D] “More” is understood.]

than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Corb. Germ. reads: “who have not gone astray.”]

“Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.’ So I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

1600

1. The summer season, which is very harmful to my body, prevented me from speaking about the exposition of the Gospel after such a long interruption.

[Note: [Col. 1246D] Gussanv. reads: “but not because the tongue was silent,” and so forth. We do not know from what manuscript or other edition he transcribed this reading, which differs from the others.]

But did love cease to burn because the tongue was silent? For this is what I say: each one of you recognizes it within himself. Love is often hindered by various occupations and nevertheless burns intact inwardly in the heart, while it is not displayed in action; just as the sun, when covered by a cloud, is not seen upon the earth, yet it burns in heaven. So love is accustomed to be occupied: it exerts the force of its heat within, but does not display outwardly the flames of action. But since the time for speaking has now returned, your eagerness kindles me, so that I desire to speak all the more because your minds await this more desirously.

2. You heard in the Gospel reading, my brothers, that sinners and tax collectors approached our Redeemer; and they were received not only for conversation, but also for eating together. When the Pharisees saw this, they disdained it. From this, understand that true justice has compassion (Dist. 45, ch. 15), while false justice has disdain, although even the righteous sometimes rightly show indignation toward sinners.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] The printed editions read “to disdain.” The Corb., Carn., Germ., Gemet., and other manuscripts have “to be indignant,” although “disdain” occurs above.]

But one thing is done through the arrogance of pride, and another through zeal for discipline. They show indignation, but are not disdainful; they despair, but are not despairing; they stir up persecution, but while loving, because although outwardly they intensify their rebukes through discipline, inwardly they preserve sweetness through charity. In their hearts they often place those whom they correct before themselves and consider even those whom they judge to be better than themselves. By doing this, they guard their subordinates through discipline and themselves through humility.

But, on the other hand, those who are accustomed to pride themselves on false justice despise everyone else; they show no compassion by condescending to the weak; and the less they believe themselves to be sinners, the worse sinners they become. The Pharisees had certainly belonged to their number. Judging the Lord because he received sinners, they reproached the very fountain of mercy with withered hearts.

3. But because they were sick in such a way that they did not know themselves to be sick, the heavenly physician, so that they might recognize what they were, heals them with gentle remedies. He sets before them a kindly example and presses upon their hearts the swelling of the wound. For he says: “What man among you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost?”

Behold, through a wonderful dispensation of compassion, Truth offered a likeness that a human being might recognize in himself, yet which specially pertained to the author of humanity. Because a hundred is a perfect number, he himself had a hundred sheep when he created the substance of angels and human beings. But one sheep then perished when, by sinning, humanity abandoned the pastures of life. He left the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness because he left the highest choirs of angels in heaven.

But why is heaven called a wilderness, unless because a wilderness is called a deserted, abandoned place? Humanity deserted heaven when it sinned. The ninety-nine sheep remained in the wilderness while the Lord sought the one on earth, because the number of rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—which had been created to behold God, was diminished when humanity perished; and, so that the complete number of sheep might be restored in heaven, the lost human being was sought on earth.

For what this Evangelist says “in the wilderness,” another says “in the mountains,” signifying “in the heights” (Matt. 18:12), since the sheep that had not perished stood in lofty places. And when he has found the sheep, he places it upon his shoulders, rejoicing. He placed the sheep upon his shoulders because, taking human nature upon himself, he himself bore our sins.

“And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.’” Having found the sheep, he returns home because, after restoring humanity, our Shepherd returned to the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1248D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts read: “because our Redeemer.”]

There he finds his friends and neighbors, namely, those choirs of angels who are his friends because they continually preserve his will in their steadfastness. They are also his neighbors because they continually enjoy the radiance of his vision. And it should be noted that he does not say, “Rejoice over the sheep that has been found,” but “with me,” because our life is his joy, and when we are brought back to heaven, we fulfill the solemnity of his gladness.

4. “I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”

We must consider, my brothers, why the Lord confesses that there is more joy in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing, unless it is what we ourselves frequently know by daily experience of vision: those who know that they are burdened by no heavy mass of sins generally stand on the way of righteousness and commit nothing unlawful, but nevertheless do not anxiously yearn for their heavenly homeland. They give themselves so much freedom in lawful matters because they do not remember having committed anything unlawful. Often they remain sluggish in practicing outstanding good deeds because they feel very secure in having committed no serious evils.

On the other hand, sometimes those who remember having done certain unlawful things, pierced by the pain arising from that very fact, burn with love of God, exercise themselves in great virtues, seek every difficulty of holy struggle, abandon everything in the world, flee honors, rejoice when they receive insults, blaze with desire, and yearn for their heavenly homeland. Because they recognize that they have strayed from God, they repay their earlier losses with subsequent gains.

Thus there is more joy in heaven over a converted sinner than over a righteous person who remains standing, because even a commander in battle loves more the soldier who, after fleeing, returns and presses the enemy fiercely than the one who never turned his back and never performed any courageous deed. So a farmer loves more the land that produces abundant crops after thorns than land that never had thorns and never produced a fertile harvest.

5. Yet amid these things we must know that there are many righteous people whose life contains such great joy that no sinner’s repentance can in any way be preferred to it. For many are conscious of no evils in themselves, and yet exert themselves in such intense affliction as though they were constricted by every sin.

[Note: [Col. 1248D] The printed editions changed the word “exert themselves” to “exercise,” but “exert themselves” is found in all the old manuscripts, especially Corb. and Germ.]

They reject even all things that are lawful; they gird themselves sublimely for contempt of the world; they refuse to permit themselves anything whatsoever; they cut away from themselves even permitted goods; they scorn visible things and are inflamed by invisible ones; they rejoice in laments; they humble themselves in everything. Just as some lament sins of action, so they lament sins of thought.

What, then, should I call these people except both righteous and penitent—those who humble themselves in penitence for the sin of thought and nevertheless always persevere in right action? From this, then, we should understand how much joy a righteous person gives God when he weeps humbly, if an unrighteous person gives joy in heaven when he condemns through repentance what he has done wickedly.

6. It follows: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds the drachma that she had lost?”

The one signified by the shepherd is also signified by the woman. For he is God himself, and he is also the Wisdom of God. Because an image is impressed upon a drachma, the woman lost the drachma when humanity, created in the image of God, withdrew through sinning from the likeness of its Creator.

But the woman lights a lamp because the Wisdom of God appeared in human nature. A lamp is light in an earthen vessel; light in an earthen vessel is divinity in flesh. Concerning this earthen vessel of his body, Wisdom itself says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16). Because a potsherd is hardened in fire, his strength dried up like a potsherd, since through the tribulation of his passion he strengthened the flesh he had assumed for the glory of the resurrection.

After lighting the lamp, she overturns the house, because as soon as his divinity shone forth through the flesh, all our conscience was shaken. The house is overturned when the human conscience is disturbed by consideration of its guilt. This language of overturning does not differ from what is read in other codices, namely, “cleanses,” since the perverse mind, unless it is first overturned through fear, is not cleansed from its habitual vices.

When the house has been overturned, the drachma is found, because when a person’s conscience is disturbed, the likeness of the Creator is restored in the human being. And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost.”

Who are these friends and neighbors except those heavenly powers mentioned above? They are close to heavenly Wisdom in proportion as they approach it through the continual vision of grace.

Yet amid these things we must by no means carelessly neglect to ask why this woman, through whom the Wisdom of God is signified, is said to have had ten drachmas, of which she lost one and found it when she sought it. The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings to know him; and when he willed it to endure unto eternity, he undoubtedly created it in his likeness. The woman had ten drachmas because there are nine orders of angels. But so that the number of the elect might be completed, the human being was created as the tenth. He did not perish from his Creator even after guilt, because eternal Wisdom, flashing with miracles through the flesh, restored him by the light of the earthen vessel.

7. We have said that there are nine orders of angels because, as sacred Scripture testifies, we know that there are angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Almost all the pages of sacred Scripture testify that there are angels and archangels. The books of the prophets often speak, as is well known, of cherubim and seraphim.

The Apostle Paul also enumerates the names of four orders in his Letter to the Ephesians, saying: “Above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion” (Eph. 1:21). Again, writing to the Colossians, he says: “Whether thrones, or powers, or principalities, or dominations” (Col. 1:16). He had already described dominations, principalities, and powers when speaking to the Ephesians; but when he was also going to mention them to the Colossians, he prefaced them with thrones, about which he had not yet said anything to the Ephesians. Thus, when thrones are joined to the four he mentioned to the Ephesians—namely, principalities, powers, virtues, and dominations—five orders are specifically expressed. When angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim, are added to these, there are evidently found to be nine orders of angels.

Hence it is also said through the prophet to the first angel who was created: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12).

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Belvac., C. Germ., and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts add: “which should be noted.”]

Here it should be noted that he is not said to have been made in the likeness of God, but “the seal of likeness,” so that, the more subtle his nature is, the more similarly the image of God may be shown expressed in him.

[Note: [Col. 1250D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts and the second Carn. read: “the more subtly.”]

Immediately afterward the passage continues: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (ibid. 28:13). Behold, he named nine kinds of stones, because there are certainly nine orders of angels. That first angel was adorned and covered with these orders because, while he was set over all the angelic hosts, he was more splendid by comparison with them.

8. But why have we touched upon these choirs of the angels who remained steadfast, unless we also explain their ministries with careful subtlety? In the Greek language, angels are called *angeloi*—“messengers”—and archangels *archangeloi*—“chief messengers.” It should also be known that the word “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. For those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4). It is as though he plainly said: “He makes those whom he always possesses as spirits into angels also, whenever he wishes.”

Those who announce minor matters are called angels; those who announce great matters are called archangels. Hence it is that Gabriel the archangel, not just any angel, is sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:26). It was fitting that the highest angel should come for this ministry, since he was announcing the highest of all things.

They are also designated by individual names so that their names may indicate what they are capable of in their activity. For they do not receive proper names in that holy city, which perfect knowledge of the vision of almighty God completes, because their persons could not otherwise be known without names. Rather, when they come to us to carry out some ministry, among us they derive their names from their ministries.

9. Michael means “Who is like God?” Gabriel means “the strength of God,” and Raphael is called “the healing of God.” Whenever something of marvelous power is accomplished, Michael is said to be sent, so that from the action itself and from his name it may be understood that no one can do what God is able to do.

Hence that ancient enemy, who in his pride desired to be like God, saying, “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13), when at the end of the world he is abandoned in his own power to be destroyed by ultimate punishment, is said to battle with Michael the archangel, as John says: “There was a battle with Michael the archangel” (Rev. 12:7). Thus he who had proudly exalted himself toward the likeness of God may learn, when slain by Michael, that no one should rise toward the likeness of God through pride.

Gabriel, who is called the strength of God, is also sent to Mary (Luke 1:26). He came to announce the one who, in order to defeat the powers of the air, deigned to appear in humility. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:9–10). And again: “The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory” (ibid.).

Therefore, he who is Lord of virtues and mighty in battle, who was coming to war against the powers of the air, had to be announced through the strength of God.

[Note: [Col. 1251D] So C. Germ., Carn., Gemet., the old editions, and others. The recent printed editions instead read: “to defeat the powers of the air.”]

Raphael, as we said, is interpreted as “the healing of God,” because, when he touched Tobit’s eyes as though in the course of a healing ministry (Tobit 11:13 and following), he wiped away the darkness of his blindness. Since he was sent to heal, it was fitting that he should be called the healing of God.

But since we have briefly touched upon the interpretation of the angels’ names, it remains for us briefly to explain the names of their offices themselves.

10. Those spirits through whom signs and miracles are more frequently performed are called virtues. Those who have received this more powerfully than others within their order are also called powers, so that hostile virtues may be subject to their authority and may be restrained by their power from being able to tempt human hearts as much as they wish.

Those who preside even over the good angelic spirits are called principalities. While arranging what must be done for those subject to them, they exercise primacy over them in fulfilling divine ministries.

Those who transcend even the powers and principalities by lofty superiority are called dominations.

[Note: [Col. 1251D] The passage from here through “these angelic hosts” is absent from the manuscripts Corb., Belvac., and C. Germ. It is read in Gemet., Bigot., and others.]

For to exercise primacy is to be first among the others; to dominate is also to possess those who are subject. Those angelic hosts that excel through marvelous power are therefore called dominations because the other hosts are subject to them in obedience.

Those hosts that almighty God always presides over in order to exercise judgment are also called thrones. Since in Latin we call thrones “seats,” those who are filled with so great a grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and decrees his judgments through them are called the thrones of God. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “You sit upon the throne, judging equity” (Ps. 9:5).

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Bigot. reads: “judging justice.”]

Cherubim are also called “the fullness of knowledge.” Those loftier hosts are called cherubim because they are filled with more perfect knowledge in proportion as they contemplate the radiance of God more closely; according to the measure of a creature, they know all things fully in proportion as they approach by the merit of their dignity through the vision of their Creator.

Seraphim are also called those hosts of holy spirits that burn with incomparable love because of their singular nearness to their Creator. Seraphim means “burning” or “kindling.” Because they are so joined to God that no other spirits stand between them and God, they burn all the more intensely in proportion as they see him more closely. Their flame is love, because the more subtly they behold the radiance of his divinity, the more powerfully they blaze with love for him.

11. But what benefit is there in our briefly discussing these angelic spirits if we do not strive to apply them to our own progress through suitable reflection? Since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and since we believe that as many human beings will ascend there as elect angels remained, as it is written, “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32:8), we too ought to draw something from the distinctions among those heavenly citizens for the conduct of our own lives, and kindle ourselves through good practices toward an increase in virtue.

Since it is believed that as many human beings will ascend there as angels remained, it follows that human beings who return to their heavenly homeland should imitate something of those hosts as they return there. The distinct ways of life of individual human beings correspond to the orders of the various hosts, and through the likeness of their conduct they are assigned a place among them.

There are many who understand little, yet do not cease to announce even these small things piously to their brothers. Such people run among the number of the angels. There are some who, refreshed by the gift of divine generosity,

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Longip. and Val. Cl. read: “filled with it.”]

are able both to grasp and to announce the greatest of heavenly secrets. To what number, then, are such people assigned except that of the archangels?

There are others who perform marvelous deeds and powerfully work signs. To what lot and number, then, do such people correspond except that of the heavenly virtues?

There are some who even drive evil spirits from possessed bodies and cast them out through the power of prayer and the force of the authority they have received. To what merit, then, do such people belong except to the number of the heavenly powers?

There are some who, having received virtues, even surpass the merits of elect human beings; and while they are better than the good, they also preside over their elect brothers. To what lot, then, have such people received their place except among the numbers of the principalities?

There are some who so dominate all vices and every desire within themselves that, by the very right of their purity, they may be called gods among human beings. Hence it is said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1).

[Note: [Col. 1253D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts read: “Therefore, even if—by comparison with them—the other human beings are, so to speak, servants …”]

To what number, then, do such people belong except that of the dominations?

There are some who, while ruling themselves with vigilant care and examining themselves with attentive purpose, always cling to the fear of God. As a gift of virtue they receive the ability to judge rightly and to judge others as well. Since divine contemplation is present to their minds, the Lord, presiding in them as upon his throne, examines the deeds of others and marvelously dispenses everything from his seat.

What, then, are such people except thrones of their Creator? Or to what number do they belong except that of the heavenly seats? Through them the holy Church is governed, and often even the elect are judged with regard to certain of their weak actions.

There are some who are so filled with love of God and neighbor that they may rightly be called cherubim. For, as we said above, cherubim means “the fullness of knowledge,” and we have learned from Paul that “the fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13:10). All who are more abundantly filled than others with love of God and neighbor have received, according to the merit of their deeds, their lot among the numbers of the cherubim.

There are some who, kindled by the torches of heavenly contemplation,

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Gemet. and Bigot. read: “by the firebrands of contemplation.”]

yearn for nothing but the desire of their Creator; they now desire nothing in this world, but feed solely on the love of eternity. They cast away all earthly things, transcend all temporal matters in their minds, love and burn, and find rest in that very burning. They burn through loving; by speaking they kindle others also; and those whom they touch with their word they immediately make burn with the love of God.

What, then, should I call such people except seraphim, whose heart, transformed into fire, both shines and burns? They illuminate the eyes of their minds toward heavenly things

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Belvac. adds: “and by pricking them.”]

and, by piercing them with compunction, cleanse the rust of vices through tears. Since they are thus inflamed with love of their Creator, where but among the number of the seraphim have they received the lot of their vocation?

[Col. 1253D] 12. But while I speak of these things, dearest brothers, turn inward and lead yourselves back to yourselves; examine the merits and thoughts hidden within you. See whether you are already doing any good within yourselves; see whether, among the number of those hosts that we have briefly touched upon, you find the lot of your vocation.

Woe to the soul that recognizes nothing of the good things we have enumerated in itself; and a worse woe still threatens it if it understands that it has been deprived of gifts and nevertheless does not lament. Whoever is such, my brothers, is greatly to be mourned because he does not mourn.

Let us therefore consider the gifts received by the elect, and with whatever strength we possess let us yearn for the love of so great a lot. Let the one who recognizes no grace of gifts in himself lament. But let the one who recognizes lesser gifts in himself not envy greater gifts in others, because those heavenly distinctions among the blessed spirits were also so established that some are set above others.

It is said that Dionysius the Areopagite, that ancient and venerable Father, taught

[Note: [Col. 1253D] We do not investigate here whether these writings were composed by Dionysius the Areopagite, since this question has already so often been reconsidered and examined. On this subject one may consult Natalis Alexander, vol. II; Ludovicus Ellies du Pin, in the *Bibliotheca Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum*; our Nicolaus le Nourry, in the *Apparatus ad Bibliothecam Patrum*; Guilielmus Cave, in the *Historia Literaria Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum*; our Claudius David, in his French dissertation on the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite, published in 1702; and many others. Gregory does not assertively attribute these writings to Dionysius the Areopagite, but does so with some hesitation, as is clear from the words “Dionysius the Areopagite is said … to say.” The verb “is said” signifies some doubt and hesitation. This doubt does not seem to have concerned the teaching of the book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, which was in everyone’s hands and whose reading could easily have resolved the matter. Therefore, “is said” rather concerns the author of the book; and by speaking in this way the holy teacher seems to indicate that he is not following his own opinion, but the common view. Nevertheless, prudent reader, I leave this to your judgment.]

(*On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapters 7, 9, and 13), that those who are sent forth from the lesser angelic hosts to fulfill a ministry, whether visibly or invisibly, are sent because they come for human assistance as angels or archangels. For those higher hosts never depart from the inner presence, since those who are preeminent have no use for an external ministry.

What Isaiah says appears to contradict this: “And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth” (Isa. 6:6–7). But in this statement of the prophet it is to be understood that those spirits who are sent receive the designation of those whose office they perform. Because the angel carries a coal from the altar in order to burn away the sins of speech, he is called a seraphim, which means “burning.”

This interpretation is also not inappropriately supported by what is said through Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). To minister is one thing, and to stand before him is another, because those minister to God who go forth to us by announcing; but those stand before him who so enjoy intimate contemplation that they are not sent forth to perform external works.

13. But since in certain passages of Scripture we have learned that some things are accomplished through the cherubim and others through the seraphim, whether they do these things themselves or whether they are done through subordinate ranks—which, as is said, receive the names of the greater ones because they come from the greater ones [Note: [Col. 1254D] Bigot.: “greater names”]—we do not wish [Col. 1255A] to affirm what we do not establish by clear testimonies. Yet this we know with complete certainty: in order to fulfill a ministry from the heights, some spirits send others, as the prophet Zechariah testifies when he says: “Behold, the angel who was speaking with me was going out; and behold, another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: ‘Run and speak to that boy, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls’” (Zech. II, 3–4). For when one angel says to another, “Run and speak,” there is no doubt that one sends the other. The lesser are those who are sent; the greater are those who send.

But we also hold this with certainty concerning the very ranks that are sent: when they come to us, they fulfill their ministry outwardly in such a way that they nevertheless never cease to be present inwardly through contemplation. They are therefore both sent and present, because although an angelic spirit is circumscribed, the supreme Spirit himself, who is God, is not circumscribed. Thus the angels are both sent and before him, because however they may come when sent, they run within him.

14. It must also be known that very often the orders of blessed spirits take the names of the orders nearest to them. We have said that the Thrones—namely, the seats of God—are a distinct order of blessed spirits; yet the Psalmist says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear” (Ps. LXXIX, 3), because, while the cherubim are joined to the Thrones in the distinctions among the ranks, the Lord is also said to sit upon the cherubim by reason of the equality of the neighboring rank.

For in that supreme city certain things belong specially to individuals, and yet are common to all; and what each possesses in part within itself, another order possesses in its entirety. But for this reason they are not commonly designated by one and the same name: the order should be called by the particular name of that reality which it has received more fully as its gift. We have called the seraphim “burning,” and yet all alike burn with love of the Creator. We have called the cherubim the “fullness of knowledge” [Note: [Col. 1255D] Same manuscript: “of knowledge, they see God; and yet”]; yet who there can know anything in ignorance, where all together see God himself, the fountain of knowledge? The ranks over which the Creator presides are also called Thrones; but who can be blessed unless his Creator presides over his mind? Therefore, what is possessed in part by all has been given as a private name to those who have received it more fully as a gift. For even if some there possess things in such a way that others cannot possess them—just as the Dominions and Principalities are called by particular names—everything there belongs to each, because through the love of the Spirit what one has is possessed by others.

15. But behold: while we examine the secrets of the heavenly citizens, we have wandered far from the order of our exposition. Let us therefore sigh for those of whom we are speaking, but let us return to ourselves. We must remember that we are flesh. Let us meanwhile be silent about the secrets of heaven, and before the eyes of our Creator let us wipe away, with the hand of repentance, the stains of our dust.

Behold, divine mercy itself promises this, saying: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents”; yet through the prophet the Lord says: “On whatever day the righteous man sins, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten before me” (Ezek. XXXIII, 13). Let us consider, if we can, the dispensation of heavenly mercy [Note: Primus Carn.: “if we can recognize the dispensation of heavenly compassion.”]. To those who stand, he threatens punishment if they fall; but to those who have fallen, he promises mercy so that they may desire to rise. He terrifies the former, lest they presume upon their good works; he consoles the latter, lest they despair in their evils. You are righteous: fear wrath, lest you fall. You are a sinner: presume upon mercy, so that you may rise.

Behold, we have already fallen; we were wholly unable to stand, and we lie in our perverse desires. Yet he who struck us down when we were upright still waits for us and urges us to rise. He opens the bosom of his mercy and seeks to receive us back to himself through repentance (On Penance, Dist. 3, chapter “Penance”). But we cannot practice repentance worthily unless we also understand the nature of that repentance. To practice repentance is both to mourn the evils one has committed and not to commit again those that ought to be mourned. For whoever laments some evils while still committing others either pretends to practice repentance or does not understand it.

What good does it do if someone weeps over sins of lust while still panting with the fever of greed? Or what good does it do if he now mourns the faults of anger while still wasting away in the flames of envy? Yet what we have said is far from sufficient: the one who mourns sins must not commit sins that ought to be mourned, and the one who laments vices must fear committing vices.

[Col. 1256C] 16. For it must be considered with the greatest care that whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this he may make satisfaction to his Creator. The one who committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what is permitted, and should rebuke himself in small matters if he remembers having sinned in great ones. [Note: Here we follow the old manuscripts of Beauvais, C. Germ. and others. In the printed editions, supported also by some manuscripts, we read: “the small things are…”]

What I am saying is excessive if I do not confirm it by the testimonies of sacred speech. Certainly, the Law of the Old Testament forbids coveting another man’s wife (Exod. XX, 17), but it does not forbid the king, under penalty, to command brave deeds of his soldiers or to desire water. We all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, both coveted and took another man’s wife (II Kings XI, 4). Deserved blows followed his fault, and through the lamentations of repentance he corrected the evil he had committed.

Much later, when he was sitting opposite the enemy ranks, he desired to drink water from the cistern at Bethlehem (II Kings XXIII, 14ff.). His chosen soldiers broke through the midst of the opposing troops and brought back unharmed the water that the king had desired. But the man instructed by scourges immediately reproved himself for having desired the water at the risk of his soldiers, and, pouring it out to the Lord, offered it as a libation, just as it is written there: “He poured it out to the Lord” (II Kings XXIII, 17; I Chron. XI, 18). For the water, poured out, was made into a sacrifice to the Lord, because through the penitence of his self-reproach he had slain the fault of desire [Note: Bigot.: “cleansed” it].

Thus he who formerly had not feared coveting another man’s wife afterward feared even that he had coveted water. Because he remembered that he had committed unlawful acts, he was now strict toward himself and abstained even from lawful things. This is how we practice repentance, if we mourn perfectly the things we have committed.

Let us consider the heavenly riches of our Creator. He saw us sinning, and he bore with us.

17. He who before our fault forbade us to sin does not cease, even after our fault, to wait for our pardon. Behold, he himself, whom we despised, calls us. We have turned away from him, yet he does not turn away. Hence Isaiah rightly says: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing you behind your back” (Isa. XXX, 20–21).

A person is admonished face-to-face when, created for righteousness, he receives the commandments of uprightness. But when he despises these same commandments, he is as though he has turned the back of his mind toward his Creator’s face. Yet behold, he still follows behind and admonishes us, because we have already despised him, and nevertheless he does not cease to call us.

We have, as it were, given our back to his face when we despise his words and trample upon his commandments. But standing behind our back, he calls us back when we have turned away: he sees what is despised, and yet through his commandments he cries out and through patience he waits. Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, if a servant of any one of you suddenly grew proud while you were speaking to him and turned his back toward your face: would not his despised master strike his pride and inflict wounds of severe correction?

Behold, by sinning we have given our back to our Creator’s face, and yet we are spared. He kindly calls back those who have turned away in pride, and he who could have struck us for turning away promises gifts so that we may return. May such mercy from our Creator therefore soften the hardness of our guilt; and may the person who could have been made, by a blow, to experience the evil he committed at least blush because he has been waited for.

18. I shall briefly relate, brothers, an event that I learned from the venerable Maximianus, then abbot and presbyter of my monastery, but now bishop of Syracuse. If you listen to it attentively, I believe it will be no small help to your charity.

In our own times there was a certain Victorinus, also called by another name, Aemilianus, not poor in property according to the ordinary standards of life [Note: In the printed editions, with the support of later manuscripts: “not poor in substance.”]. But because the fault of the flesh often reigns amid an abundance of possessions, he fell into a certain crime which he ought greatly to have feared and ought to have considered the dreadful nature of his death.

Struck by reflection upon his guilt, he rose up against himself, abandoned everything in this world, and sought a monastery. In that monastery he displayed such humility and imposed such strictness upon himself that all the brothers who had grown there in the love of divinity were compelled to despise their own lives when they saw his repentance.

With all the effort of his mind he strove to torment his flesh, break his own desires, seek out secret prayers, wash himself daily with tears, desire contempt of himself, and fear the honor offered him by the brothers. He was accustomed to anticipate the brothers’ nighttime vigils. Since the mountain on which the monastery was situated rose on one side into a more secluded area, he had made it his custom to go there before the vigils, so that every day he might sacrifice himself in the tears of repentance, the more secretly and therefore the more freely.

He contemplated the strictness of his coming Judge and, already in agreement with that Judge, punished the guilt of his crime in tears. One night the abbot of the monastery, who was awake, secretly observed him going out and followed him slowly. When he saw him lying prostrate in prayer in a secluded part of the mountain [Note: Second Carn.: “lying in a secluded part of the mountain,” with no improper sense], he wished to wait until he rose, so that he might also test the long duration of his prayer.

Suddenly a light sent down from heaven was poured over him as he lay prostrate in prayer. So great a brightness spread through that place that the entire region shone from the light. When the abbot saw it, he trembled and fled.

After a long interval, the brother returned to the monastery. The abbot, wishing to discover whether he knew of the outpouring of such great light over him, asked him, saying: “Where were you, brother?” Believing that he could conceal the matter, he answered that he had been in the monastery.

When he denied this, the abbot was compelled to tell him what he had seen. Realizing that he had been discovered, the brother also disclosed what he had concealed from the abbot, adding: “When you saw the light descend upon me from heaven, a voice also came at the same time, saying: ‘Your sin has been forgiven.’”

Almighty God could indeed have released him from his sin in silence; but by speaking through a voice and shining through a light, he wished, by the example of his mercy, to shake our hearts toward repentance [Note: Thus Beauvais, C. Germ., Gemet. and others. The printed editions, however, read “to convert.”]

We marvel, dearest brothers, that the Lord cast down his persecutor Saul from heaven and spoke to him from heaven. Behold, in our own times a sinner and penitent also heard a voice from the heavenly places. To Saul it was said: “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4). But this man deserved to hear: “Your sin has been forgiven.”

This penitent sinner was far inferior to Paul in merits. Yet because we are still speaking here of Saul, who was breathing out the cruelty of murder, we may boldly say that Saul heard a voice of rebuke because of his pride, whereas this man heard a voice of consolation because of his humility. Humility had laid this man low, and divine mercy raised him up; pride had raised Saul up, and divine severity humbled him.

Have confidence, therefore, my brothers, in the mercy of our Creator. Consider what you are doing; reconsider what you have done. Look upon the generosity of heavenly compassion, and while the merciful Judge still waits, come to him with tears. In considering that he is just, do not neglect your sins; in considering that he is merciful, do not despair.

God made man provides man with confidence before God. Great is our hope when we repent, because our advocate has become our judge.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: It is the thirty-fifth in the Swedish Royal Codex, where it is attributed to Saint Mennas; the thirty-sixth in the Lateran manuscript and the thirty-ninth in Corbie.]  

## HOMILY XXXV

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Mennas the martyr, on his feast day.

## READING OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE XXI, 9–19

At that time, Jesus said to his disciples: “When you hear of wars and uprisings, do not be terrified; for these things must happen first, but the end will not come immediately.” Then he said to them: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines, and terrors from heaven, and there will be great signs.” But before all these things they will lay their hands upon you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons, dragging you before kings and governors because of my name. These things will happen to you as an opportunity for testimony. Therefore settle it in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will be unable to resist or contradict. You will be handed over by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death. You will be hated by everyone because of my name, yet not a hair from your head will perish. By your patience you will possess your souls.

[Note: C. Germ., Bigot. and the third Gemet. manuscript read “he was saying.” The first two Gemet. manuscripts read “the Lord Jesus said.” In the Gallican Sacramentary edited by D. J. Mabillon, *Musei Italici*, vol. I, part II, “Lord” always precedes the name “Jesus.”]

[Note: Gussanville: “Before all these things they will begin to lay their hands upon you.” Shortly afterward: “and they will hand you over,” with other manuscripts contradicting this, although later, in section 2, this Gospel passage is read in this form in the manuscripts. Finally, at the end, “and by relatives and friends” is omitted without reason.]

1612 1. Because we have gone some distance from the city, and the late hour may hinder us from returning, it is necessary for a shorter discourse to pass rapidly through the exposition of the holy Gospel.

Our Lord and Redeemer announces beforehand the evils that will precede the world’s destruction, so that the things to come may disturb us less because they have been foreseen. Missiles that are anticipated strike less forcefully; and we receive the evils of the world more tolerably if we arm ourselves against them with the shield of foreknowledge.

For behold, he says: “When you hear of wars and uprisings, do not be terrified; for these things must happen first, but the end will not come immediately.” We must weigh the words of our Redeemer, through which he announces that we will suffer one thing inwardly and another outwardly. Wars pertain to enemies, but uprisings to citizens. Thus, in order to show that we are disturbed both inwardly and outwardly, he acknowledges that we suffer one thing from enemies and another from brothers.

But because the end will not immediately follow these evils that precede it, he adds: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be great earthquakes in various places, and pestilences and famines, and terrors from heaven; and there will be great signs.” Or, as certain manuscripts read: “and terrors from heaven and storms.” Then it adds: “And there will be great signs.”

The final tribulation is preceded by many tribulations, and through the frequent evils that come beforehand the everlasting evils that will follow are indicated. Therefore the end does not come immediately after wars and uprisings, because many evils must precede it, so that they may announce the evil that will have no end.

But since so many signs of disturbance have been mentioned, we should briefly touch upon each of them, because it is necessary for us to suffer some things from heaven, others from the earth, others from the elements, and others from human beings.

He says: “Nation will rise against nation”—behold, the disturbance of human beings. “There will be great earthquakes in various places”—behold, the visitation of wrath from above. “There will be pestilences”—behold, the disorder of bodies. “There will be famine”—behold, the barrenness of the earth. “And terrors from heaven and storms”—behold, the disorder of the air.

Because everything is to be brought to completion, everything is disturbed before the completion. And because we have sinned in all things, we are struck in all things, so that what is said may be fulfilled: “The whole world will fight on behalf of him against the senseless” (Wis. V, 21).

For everything that we received for the use of life we turned to the use of sin; but everything that we bent toward the use of depravity is turned against us for the use of punishment. We turned the tranquility of human peace to the use of empty security. We loved our earthly pilgrimage as though it were our homeland. We reduced the health of our bodies to the service of vices. We twisted the abundance of fertility, not toward the needs of the flesh, but toward the perversion of pleasure. We compelled the very serene delights of the air to serve our love of earthly enjoyment.

It is therefore just that everything should strike us together, since everything together served us after being wickedly subdued by our vices, so that as many joys as we previously possessed unharmed in the world, so many torments we may afterward be compelled to experience from it.

It should be noted that he says: “Terrors from heaven and storms.” Since winter storms ordinarily come in the regular course of the seasons, why are storms in this passage foretold as coming as a sign of destruction, unless the Lord is announcing storms that do not at all observe the order of the seasons? Things that come in an orderly fashion are not signs; but storms are signs when they themselves confound the established order of the seasons. We too recently experienced this, when we saw the entire summer season transformed into winter rains.

2. Since all these things do not arise from the injustice of the one who strikes but from the merit of the world that suffers, the deeds of wicked people are mentioned beforehand when it says: “But before all these things they will begin to lay their hands upon you, and they will persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and leading you before kings and governors because of my name.”

It is as though he plainly says: First human hearts are disturbed, and afterward the elements, so that when the order of things is confounded it may be shown from what retribution it proceeds.

For although the end of the world depends upon its own order, nevertheless it becomes clear that it finds the more perverse people, who are worthy to be crushed by its ruins, when it adds: “Leading you before kings and governors because of my name.”

[Note: Corbie reads: “These things will happen to you.”]

“These things will happen to you as an opportunity for testimony.” Testimony, clearly, concerning whom, if not concerning those who either inflict death by persecuting or, by seeing, do not imitate? The death of the righteous is a help to the good but a testimony against the wicked, so that by the very means through which the perverse perish without excuse, the elect may receive an example of salvation and live [Note: Second Carn.: “receive the profit of their work, so that they may live.”]

3. But when they heard so many terrors, the hearts of the weak could be disturbed; therefore consolation is immediately added: “Settle it in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will be unable to resist or contradict.”

It is as though he plainly says to his weakened members: “Do not be terrified; do not fear. You approach the contest, but I do the fighting. You utter words, but I am the one who speaks.”

It follows: “You will be handed over by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death.” Evils inflicted by strangers cause less pain. The torments we suffer from those whose goodwill we trusted rage more fiercely within us, because, along with the injury to the body, the loss of affection torments us.

Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning Judas, his betrayer: “Indeed, if my enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it; and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would certainly have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food, we walked in the house of God in harmony” (Ps. LIV, 13ff.) [Note: The first two Gemet. manuscripts: “I would have endured it”; shortly afterward, “perhaps from him,” with Bigot agreeing].

And again: “The man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me” (Ps. XL, 10) [Note: Bigot.: “multiplied”]. It is as though he openly says concerning his betrayer: “I endured his transgression all the more grievously because I experienced it from one who seemed to be mine.”

Therefore all the elect, because they are members of the supreme Head, also follow their Head in sufferings, so that in their own death they experience those adversaries whose life they had trusted; and the reward of their work increases for them to the extent that their gain in virtue advances through the loss of another’s affection [Note: Beauvais: “the gain of their work.”]

4. But because the things foretold concerning the affliction of death are harsh, consolation concerning the joy of resurrection is immediately added: “Not a hair from your head will perish.”

We know, brothers, that cut flesh feels pain, but cut hair does not. Therefore he says to his martyrs: “Not a hair from your head will perish,” plainly saying: “Why do you fear that what hurts when cut may perish, when even that which does not hurt when cut cannot perish in you?”

It follows: “By your patience you will possess your souls.” Possession of the soul is placed in the power of patience because patience is the root and guardian of all virtues [Note: Second Carn.: “the root of all good things”]. By patience we possess our souls because, as we learn to rule ourselves, we begin to possess precisely what we are.

Patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be inwardly stung by pain even against the one who inflicts the evils. For whoever bears the evils of his neighbor in such a way that he nevertheless grieves silently and looks for an opportunity to make a fitting return does not display patience but only makes a show of it.

For it is written: “Charity is patient, charity is kind” (I Cor. XIII, 4). It is patient so that it may tolerate the evils of others; it is kind so that it may love even those whom it bears [Note: Bigot. adds: “and so that it may bestow its own good things more generously”]. Hence Truth himself says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V, 44; Luke VI, 27).

It is therefore a virtue before human beings to tolerate adversaries, but before God it is a virtue to love them, because God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes upon the altar of good works.

[Col. 1262B] 5. It must be known, however, that we often seem to be patient because we are unable to repay evil with evil. But whoever does not repay evil because he is wholly unable to do so is certainly not patient, as we said above, because patience is not sought in outward display but in the heart.

Through the vice of impatience, the very teaching that nourishes the virtues is scattered. For it is written: “The instruction of a man is known by patience” (Prov. XIX, 11). Thus the less patient someone is shown to be, the less learned he is proved to be. For he cannot truly impart good instruction by teaching if, in his life, he does not know how to endure the evils of others with equanimity.

Solomon again indicates the greatness of the virtue of patience when he says: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities” (Prov. XVI, 32). The victory of capturing cities is therefore lesser, because what is conquered lies outside oneself. Greater is what is conquered through patience, because the mind itself is overcome by itself and subjects itself to itself when patience lays it low in the humility of endurance.

It must also be known that it often happens to the patient that, at the very time when they suffer adversity or hear insults, they are touched by no pain and display patience in such a way that they also strive to preserve the innocence of their hearts. But when, after a little while, they recall to memory the very things they endured, they are provoked by the fire of vehement pain, seek arguments for retaliation, and, judging themselves in retrospect, lose the gentleness they possessed while enduring.

6. The crafty adversary wages war against two people: he inflames one so that he may first inflict insults, and provokes the other so that, having been injured, he may return the insults. But because he has already conquered the one whom he moved to utter insults, he grieves more fiercely against the one whom he could not move to return them. Thus he raises all his strength against the one whom he sees has endured the insults firmly.

Since he could not move him during the very assault of the insults [Note: Vallicelliana and Longipontanus: “during the insult of the injuries”], he withdraws for a time from open combat, seeks an opportunity for deception in secret thought, and, having lost the public battle [Note: Gregory often uses this word absolutely, as in the preface to *Moralia*, chapter 5, section 8: “What else does he accuse him of having lost except God, who had been set before him?”], burns to lay hidden ambushes.

When the time of rest has come, he returns to the mind of the victor and recalls to memory either the losses of property or the shafts of insults. Exaggerating intensely everything that was inflicted upon him, he shows that it was intolerable and disturbs the mind of the one who is at rest with such fury that often the patient man, even after victory, is ashamed, as though he had been taken captive, that he endured those things with equanimity. He grieves that he did not return the insults and seeks, if an opportunity is offered, to repay them with worse.

To whom, then, are such people similar except to those who are victors in the field through courage but are afterward captured within the city walls through negligence? To whom are they similar except to those whom the onset of a severe illness does not take from life, but whom a recurrent fever, arriving gently, kills? [Note: Beauvais, Longipontanus, and Vallicelliana: “but gently”; Second Carn. has “revived” instead of “recurrent.”]

Therefore he truly preserves patience who both endures the evils of others for the time being without pain and, recalling them afterward, rejoices that he endured such things, lest the good of patience perish during a time of rest—the good that is preserved amid disturbances.

7. But because today we celebrate the feast of a martyr, my brothers, we must not think ourselves strangers to his virtue of patience. For if, with the Lord’s help, we strive to preserve the virtue of patience and live in the peace of the Church, we nevertheless possess the palm of martyrdom.

There are two kinds of martyrdom [Note: In the Corbie manuscript: “one in public, the other in mind and action together.” In Bigot. and the second Carn. manuscript: “one in public, the other in secret; one in the mind, the other in the mind and action together”]. Thus we can be martyrs even if we are slain by no sword of our persecutors.

To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in an open deed; to endure insults and love the one who hates us is martyrdom in hidden thought. For since there are two kinds of martyrdom, one in secret action and the other in public, Truth testifies to this when he questions the sons of Zebedee, saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX, 22).

When they immediately answered him, “We can,” the Lord at once replied: “You will indeed drink my cup.” What do we understand by the cup except the pain of suffering? Concerning it he says elsewhere: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

And the sons of Zebedee—that is, James and John—did not both die by martyrdom, yet both heard that they would drink the cup. John did not end his life by martyrdom, but he was nevertheless a martyr because he preserved in his mind the suffering that he did not undergo in the body.

We too, therefore, may be martyrs without the sword by this example, if we truly preserve patience in our minds. I do not think it irrelevant, dearest brothers, if I tell you one example for the strengthening of patience.

8. In our own days there was a certain man named Stephen, abbot of a monastery situated near the walls of the city of Rieti, a very holy man and singular in the virtue of patience. Many are still alive who knew him and relate both his life and his death.

His speech was rustic, but his life was learned. For love of the heavenly homeland he had despised everything, avoided possessing anything in this world, shunned the turmoil of people, and devoted himself to frequent and prolonged prayers.

The virtue of patience had nevertheless grown exceedingly strong in him, so that he considered anyone who inflicted some annoyance upon him to be his friend. He returned thanks for insults; if any loss had been inflicted upon him in his very poverty, he considered it the greatest gain; and he regarded all his adversaries as nothing other than helpers.

When the day of his death pressed him to leave the body, many gathered to commend their souls to so holy a soul as it was departing from this world. While all those who had gathered stood around his bed, some saw angels entering with bodily eyes but were entirely unable to say anything; others saw nothing at all. Yet such a vehement fear struck everyone present that no one was able to remain there when that holy soul departed.

Both those who had seen and those who had seen nothing at all were struck and terrified by one fear, and all fled. No one could remain there while he was dying.
