Consider, therefore, brothers, how the Almighty God will terrify us when he comes as a strict judge, if he so terrified those standing nearby when he came as one who is gracious and rewarding; or how greatly he can be feared when he may be seen, if he prostrated the minds of those present even when he could not be seen.

Behold, dearest brothers, having preserved that patience amid the peace of the Church, to what height of reward did it raise this man? What did his Creator give him inwardly, of which he made so great a glory known to us outwardly on the day of his departure?

With whom should we believe him to have been joined except with the holy martyrs, since it is clear, with bodily eyes also bearing witness, that he was received by blessed spirits? He died without being struck by any sword, yet at his departure he received the crown of patience that he had held in his mind.

Every day we prove the truth of what was said before us: holy Church, full of the flowers of the elect, possesses lilies in peace and roses in war.

[Note: Saint Cyprian, Book II, Letter 6, to the Martyrs and Confessors, at the end. These are Cyprian’s words at the cited place: “Its flowers lack neither lilies nor roses.” In the latest edition it is now Letter 10, without any division of the books.]

### 9

It should also be known that the virtue of patience is usually exercised in three ways. Some things we endure from God, others from the ancient adversary, and still others from our neighbor. From our neighbor come persecutions, losses, and insults; from the ancient adversary, temptations; but from God we endure chastisements. Yet in all three of these circumstances the mind must watch over itself with vigilant attention: it must not be drawn by the evils inflicted by a neighbor into repaying evil with evil; it must not be led by the adversary’s temptations into the pleasure or consent of sin;

[Note: The two earlier Gemet and Bigot manuscripts read “pleasure and consent.”] and it must not rush, in response to the Maker’s chastisements, into excessive murmuring.

For the adversary is perfectly overcome when our mind, amid his temptations, is not dragged into pleasure or consent, amid our neighbor’s insults is guarded from hatred, and amid God’s chastisements is restrained from murmuring.

[Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads “is restrained.”] Nor, while doing these things, should we seek present goods in return; for the rewards of patience are to be hoped for in the life to come, so that the reward of our labor may begin precisely when all labor has entirely ceased. Hence the Psalmist says: “The poor man will not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor will not perish forever” (Psalm 9:19). Patience seems to have perished when nothing is repaid to the humble for it in this life. But the patience of the poor will not perish forever, because its glory is received when all hardships come to an end together.

Therefore, brothers, preserve patience in your minds and, when circumstances require, exercise it in action. Let none of you be stirred to hatred of your neighbor by insulting words; let no loss of perishable things disturb you. For if, with a steadfast mind, you fear losses that endure, you do not regard the losses of passing things as serious; if you behold the glory of eternal recompense, you do not grieve over a temporal injury.

[Note: The manuscripts and older editions read “you desire”; the recent editions read “you behold.”] Endure your adversaries, then, but love as brothers those whom you endure. Seek eternal rewards in exchange for temporal losses. And let none of you trust that he can fulfill this by his own strength; rather, obtain through prayers that the One who commands it may himself grant it.

[Note: Bigot reads “that he can fulfill these things.”]

And we know that he gladly hears those who ask, when what he commands is requested as a gift. When he is continually importuned in prayer, he swiftly comes to our aid in temptation: through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with him lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVI

[Note: In the Lateran manuscript it is the twenty-third homily; in the Swedish Royal Codex it is the twenty-eighth; in the Corbie manuscript the twenty-second.]

Preached to the people in the basilica of the blessed apostles Philip and James, on the Second Sunday after Pentecost.

[Note: The Lateran manuscript reads only “in the basilica of the holy apostles.” The Swedish Royal Codex also makes no mention of the Second Sunday, nor does the earlier Gemet manuscript.]

### LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE 14:16–24

At that time Jesus spoke this parable to the Pharisees:

“A certain man gave a great dinner and invited many. At the dinner hour he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ And they all began together to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to excuse me.’ Another said, ‘I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to excuse me.’ Another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’

“And the servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the household, becoming angry, said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.’ And the servant said, ‘Master, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled. For I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my dinner.’”

### 1

There is usually this difference, dearest brothers, between bodily pleasures and those of the heart: bodily pleasures kindle a painful desire when they are not possessed, but when they have been obtained and consumed, satiety immediately turns the eater toward disgust. Spiritual pleasures, on the contrary, are distasteful when they are not possessed, but when they are possessed they are desired; and the more greatly they are hungered for by the eater, the more greatly they are consumed by the hungry. In the former, appetite is pleasing but experience displeasing; in the latter, appetite is worthless, while experience is more pleasing. In the former, appetite produces satiety and satiety produces disgust; in the latter, appetite produces satiety and satiety produces appetite.

Spiritual pleasures increase desire in the mind even while satisfying it, because the more their flavor is perceived, the more it is recognized that they are to be loved with greater avidity. For this reason they cannot be loved before they are possessed, since their flavor is unknown. Who can love what he does not know? Accordingly, the Psalmist admonishes us, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). It is as though he plainly said: “You do not know his sweetness if you do not taste it at all. Touch the food of life with the palate of your heart, so that, having tested its sweetness, you may be able to love it.”

Now man lost these delights when he sinned in paradise (Genesis 3:6); he went out from it when he closed his mouth against the food of eternal sweetness.

[Note: Gemet and Bigot have “the inner sweetness.”]

Thus we too, born into the misery of this pilgrimage, arrive here already full of disgust, and we do not know what we ought to desire. The disease of our disgust grows worse in proportion as the mind withdraws farther from eating that sweetness; and it no longer craves inward delights because it has long and deeply fallen out of the habit of consuming them.

[Note: Bigot reads “has ceased.”] We waste away through our disgust and are wearied by the prolonged plague of famine. And because we do not wish to taste the sweetness prepared within, miserable as we are, we love our hunger outside. Yet heavenly mercy does not abandon us, even when we abandon it.

[Note: The second Chartres manuscript adds: “nor does it leave those who despise its good things.”]

### 2

For it recalls those despised delights before the eyes of our memory, sets them before us, shakes off our sluggishness by its promise, and invites us to repel our disgust.

[Note: Beauvais, the German manuscript, and Bigot read: “invites; for a certain man,” etc.]

It says:

“A certain man gave a great dinner and invited many.”

Who is this man except the one of whom it is said through the Prophet: “He is a man, and who has known him?” (Jeremiah 17:9.) He gave a great dinner because he prepared for us the satisfaction of inward sweetness. He invited many, but few come, because sometimes even those who by faith are subject to him contradict his eternal banquet by living badly.

It follows: “He sent his servant at the dinner hour to say to those who had been invited that they should come.” What is the dinner hour except the end of the world? We are certainly in that hour, as Paul testified long ago, saying: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). If it is already the dinner hour when we are called, then we should be all the less likely to excuse ourselves from God’s banquet, the nearer we see the end of the age to be. For the more we consider that nothing remains, the more we ought to fear that the time of grace now available may pass away.

This banquet of God is called not lunch but dinner because after lunch dinner remains, whereas after dinner no banquet remains. And because God’s eternal banquet will be prepared for us at the end, it was right that it be called not lunch but dinner.

But whom does this servant, sent by the master of the household to invite, signify, except the order of preachers? Although we are still unworthy of this office, although we are weighed down by the burden of our sins,

[Note: Beauvais reads “unworthy of this.”] we are nevertheless living in these days. And when I say something to you about your edification, this is what I am doing: I am a servant of the supreme master of the household. When I admonish you to despise the world, I come to invite you to God’s dinner.

Let no one despise me here because of who I am. Even if I appear wholly unworthy to invite you, nevertheless the delights I promise are great. Often, my brothers, what I am saying comes to pass: a powerful person may hold his servant in contempt, yet when through him he sends some message to his own people or to strangers, the person of the speaking servant is not despised, because reverence for the sending master is preserved in the heart. Those who hear do not consider through whom they hear, but what they hear and from whom.

Act in this way, then, brothers. Even if you perhaps rightly despise us, nevertheless preserve in your minds reverence for the Lord who calls you.

[Note: Bigot has “the Lord who sends.”]

Gladly obey, so that you may become guests of the supreme master of the household. Examine your hearts and drive mortal disgust from them. Everything is already prepared to repel your disgust. But if you are still carnal, perhaps you are seeking carnal food. Behold, the very carnal foods have been transformed for you into spiritual nourishment. To wipe away the disgust of your mind, that unique Lamb has been slain for you at the Lord’s dinner.

### 3

But what are we to do, when we still see many doing what follows? “And they all began together to make excuses.” God offers what ought to have been requested; unasked, he wishes to give what could scarcely have been hoped for, because he deigns to bestow it when requested—and yet he is despised. He announces that the delights of eternal refreshment are prepared, and yet all together make excuses.

[Note: We have restored this corrupted and interpolated passage from the German, Beauvais, and Chartres manuscripts. The printed editions read: “because he would deign to bestow it when requested, and yet he is despised; but for those who despise him, [the delights] are prepared,” and so forth.]

Let us place small matters before the eyes of our minds, so that we may be able to weigh great ones properly. If some powerful person sent someone to invite a poor man, what, I ask, would that poor man do except rejoice at the invitation, give a humble reply, change his clothing, hurry as quickly as possible, and take care that no one else arrived before him at the powerful man’s banquet? A rich man invites, and the poor man hastens to come; we are invited to God’s banquet, and we make excuses.

But in the midst of this I can imagine what your hearts are saying to themselves. Perhaps they say in secret thoughts: “We do not wish to make excuses; for we rejoice both to be called to and to reach that banquet of heavenly refreshment.”

### 4

Your minds speak the truth in saying such things, if they do not love earthly things more than heavenly ones, and if they are not more occupied with bodily matters than with spiritual ones. Hence the very reason for the excuses is added here, when it immediately continues:

“The first said: ‘I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to excuse me.’”

What is signified by the farm except earthly property? The one who goes out to see the farm is the person who thinks only about external matters for the sake of property.

Another said: “I have bought five yokes of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to excuse me.” What are we to understand by the five yokes of oxen except the five bodily senses? They are rightly called yokes because they are doubled in both sexes. Since these bodily senses cannot comprehend inward things, but know only what is external, and, abandoning what is within, touch what is outside, curiosity is rightly signified through them.

While curiosity seeks to examine another person’s life, it is always ignorant of its own inner life and strives to think about external matters. Curiosity is a grave vice: while it leads someone’s mind outward to investigate his neighbor’s life, it always conceals his own inner self from him, so that, knowing what belongs to another, he does not know himself. The more the curious person becomes knowledgeable about another’s merit, the more ignorant he becomes of his own.

For this reason it is also said of the same five yokes of oxen: “I am going to test them; I ask you to excuse me.” The very words of the one making the excuse correspond to the meaning of his vice when he says, “I am going to test them,” since testing sometimes belongs to curiosity.

But it should also be noted that both the one who excuses himself because of the farm and the one who excuses himself because of the yokes of oxen he intends to test mixes his words with humility, saying:

[Note: Beauvais reads “first said.”] “I ask you to excuse me.” When he says, “I ask you,” yet refuses to come, humility sounds in his voice but pride appears in his action. And behold, every wicked person judges these things when he hears them, yet does not cease doing what he judges.

For when we say to someone acting perversely, “Turn back, follow God, abandon the world,” what are we doing except inviting him to the Lord’s dinner? But when he replies, “Pray for me, because I am a sinner; I cannot do this,” what else is he doing but both asking and making excuses? By saying, “I am a sinner,” he suggests humility; by adding, “I cannot turn back,” he displays pride. In asking, therefore, he makes excuses: he overlays humility on his voice while practicing pride in his action.

### 5

Another said: “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.” What is signified by the wife except carnal pleasure? Although marriage is good and was established by divine providence for the propagation of offspring, nevertheless some people seek through it not the fruitfulness of children but the desires of pleasure. Thus a just matter can appropriately signify an unjust one.

The supreme master of the household invites you to the dinner of the eternal banquet. But while one person is devoted to greed, another to curiosity, and another to carnal pleasure, all the reprobate together make excuses. While one is occupied by concern for earthly things, another is devastated by the shrewd consideration of another’s conduct, and another’s mind is polluted by carnal pleasure, every person filled with disgust fails to hurry to the food of eternal life.

[Note: The same witnesses read “earthly things occupy [him].”]

### 6

It follows: “The servant returned and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the household, becoming angry, said to his servant: ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.’”

Behold: the person who clings to earthly property more than is right refuses to come to the Lord’s dinner; the person who labors at curiosity grows weary of the food prepared for life; the person who serves carnal desires rejects the food of the spiritual banquet.

Since the proud refuse to come, the poor are chosen. Why? Because, in Paul’s words, “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

[Note: Bigot, Vallicelliana, and Longpont have: “Why is this so, except because...”]

But we should observe how those who are called to the dinner and come are described: “the poor and the weak.”

[Note: In the Chartres, Bigot, and fourth English manuscripts, “the poor” is omitted.]

The poor and the weak are those who, in their own judgment, are weak in themselves. For there are poor people who are, as it were, strong: they are proud even in their poverty. The blind are those who have no light of understanding. The lame are those who do not have straight steps in their actions.

But when vices of character are represented by the weakness of bodily members, it is plainly evident that just as those who were called but refused to come were sinners, so those who are invited and come are also sinners. Yet proud sinners are rejected, so that humble sinners may be chosen.

### 7

God therefore chose those whom the world despises, because very often contempt itself recalls a person to himself. The one who left his father and squandered wastefully the portion of property he had received, after he began to hunger, came to himself and said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread?” (Luke 15:17.)

He had gone far away from himself when he was sinning. And if he had not hungered, he would never have returned to himself, because after he became needy in earthly things, he began to consider what he had lost in spiritual things.

The poor, therefore, the weak, the blind, and the lame are called and come, because those who are weak and despised in this world often hear God’s voice all the more quickly because they have nothing in this world in which to delight.

This is well represented by that Egyptian servant-boy of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30:11 and following). When the Amalekites were plundering and running about, he was left sick on the road and wasted away from hunger and thirst. David found him, however, and gave him food and drink; immediately recovering, he became David’s guide. David found the Amalekites feasting and, with great strength, struck down those who had abandoned him in his weakness.

The Amalekite people are called “the licking people.”

[Note: Beauvais and the German manuscript have “licking.” Shortly afterward they read “they lick” and “the one licking.”]

What is signified by a licking people except the minds of worldly persons? They lick, as it were, by coveting everything earthly, while delighting only in temporal things. A licking people makes plunder, as it were, when those who love earthly things increase their profits through the losses of others.

But the Egyptian servant-boy is left sick on the road because, when any sinner begins to grow weak in the condition of this world, he immediately becomes despised by worldly minds. David nevertheless finds him and gives him food and drink, because the Lord, strong of hand, does not despise the world’s rejected ones. Often he turns those who, unable to follow the world, remain as though on the road toward the grace of his love, and offers them the food and drink of his word. He chooses them as his guides on the road, as it were, when he also makes them his preachers.

For when they bring Christ into the hearts of sinners, they lead David, as it were, against his enemies. They strike the feasting Amalekites with David’s sword, as it were, because by the Lord’s power they overthrow the proud who had despised them in the world.

Thus the Egyptian servant-boy who had remained on the road kills the Amalekites, because often those who overcome worldly minds through preaching are precisely those who previously were unable to run through this world with worldly people.

### 8

But after the poor have been brought to the dinner, let us hear what the servant adds: “Master, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room.”

[Note: Beauvais has: “what you commanded.”]

Many such people were gathered from Judea to the Lord’s dinner, but the multitude of those who believed from the people of Israel did not fill the place at the heavenly banquet. A crowd of Jews has already entered, but room still remains in the kingdom where the multitude of the Gentiles may be received.

Hence the same servant is told: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled.”

When the Lord invites certain people to the dinner from the lanes and streets, he signifies that people who knew how to keep the law within an urban way of life. But when he commands his guests to be gathered from the roads and hedges, he plainly seeks to gather a rustic people—that is, the Gentiles. Their significance is expressed by the Psalmist: “Then all the trees of the forest will rejoice before the face of the Lord, for he has come” (Psalm 95:13).

The trees of the forest are called the nations because in their unbelief they were always twisted and fruitless. Those who have been converted from that rustic way of life have come to the Lord’s dinner, as it were, from the hedges.

### 9

It should be noted that in this third invitation he does not say, “Invite,” but “Compel them to enter.” Some are called and refuse to come; others are called and come; of others it is not said that they are called at all, but that they are compelled to enter.

Those are called and refuse to come who receive the gift of understanding but do not follow that same understanding in their actions. Those are called and come who perfect the grace of understanding they have received through their works. Some, however, are called in such a way that they are also compelled.

There are people who understand that good things ought to be done, but cease from doing them. They see what they ought to do, but do not follow it out of desire. As we said above, it often happens to such people that the adversity of this world strikes them amid their carnal desires. They attempt to grasp temporal glory but cannot; and while they plan to sail across the high sea, as it were, toward the greater concerns of this age, they are continually driven back by contrary winds to the shore of their humiliation.

When they see themselves broken in their desires by the opposition of the world, they are reminded of what they owe their Maker, so that they return in shame to him whom, in their pride and love of the world, they had abandoned.

[Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads “so that they may seize” at “they attempt to grasp temporal glory”; the Corbie and German manuscripts and nearly all the manuscripts read “they are reminded,” while the older editions read “they recall” and the recent editions “they are admonished.”]

[Note: The first Chartres manuscript has “so that they may seize.”]

Often people who wish to advance to temporal glory waste away through prolonged illness, collapse under injuries, or are afflicted by severe losses. In the pain of the world they see that they ought to have placed no confidence in its pleasures; and, reproaching themselves for their desires, they turn their hearts to God.

Concerning such people the Lord says through the Prophet:

“Behold, I will hedge your way with thorns, and I will enclose it with a wall, and she will not find her paths. She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; she will seek them and will not find them, and she will say: ‘I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now’” (Hosea 2:6–7).

God is the husband of every faithful soul, because the soul is joined to him through faith. But the soul that had been joined to God follows its lovers when the mind that has already believed through faith still submits itself in action to unclean spirits, seeks the glory of the world, feeds on carnal pleasure, and is nourished by refined delights.

Yet often almighty God mercifully regards such a soul and mingles bitterness with its pleasures. Hence he says: “Behold, I will hedge your ways with thorns.” Our ways are hedged with thorns when we find the pricks of pain in what we wrongly desire. “And I will enclose them with a wall, and she will not find her paths.” Our ways are enclosed with a wall when hard obstacles in this world resist our desires. We cannot find our paths because we are prevented from obtaining what we wrongly seek.

“She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; she will seek them and will not find them,” because the soul does not attain the fulfillment of its desires from the evil spirits to whom it has submitted itself through those desires.

But he adds how great a benefit arises from this salutary adversity: “And she will say: ‘I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now.’”

After she finds her paths enclosed with thorns, after she is unable to overtake her lovers, she returns to the love of her first husband. Often, after we cannot obtain in this world what we want, after we are wearied by the impossibility of earthly desires, then we bring God back to mind. Then the one who had been displeasing begins to please us; the one whose commands had been bitter to us suddenly becomes sweet in our memory; and the sinful soul that attempted to be adulterous, yet could not do so openly, determines to become a faithful wife.

Those who, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God and are corrected away from the desires of the present life—what are such people, my brothers, except those who are compelled to enter?

### 10

But the sentence that follows is exceedingly dreadful. Receive it attentively with the ear of your heart, brothers and masters of mine—as sinners, my brothers; as righteous, my masters.

[Note: Bigot reads: “Receive this with the ear of your heart.”] Receive it attentively with the ear of your heart, so that you may feel it less severely in the judgment in proportion as you now hear it more fearfully in preaching.

[Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads “at the final examination.”]

For he says: “I tell you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my dinner.”

Behold, he calls through himself; he calls through angels; he calls through the patriarchs; he calls through the prophets; he calls through the apostles; he calls through pastors; he calls even through us. Often he calls through miracles; often through chastisements; sometimes through the prosperity of this world; sometimes through adversity.

Let no one despise him, lest, while making excuses when called, he be unable to enter when he wishes to do so. Hear what Wisdom says through Solomon: “Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and they will not find me” (Proverbs 1:28). Hence the foolish virgins, coming late, cry out: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matthew 25:11). But then it is said to those seeking entrance: “Truly, truly, I say to you, I do not know you” (ibid.).

What else, dearest brothers, should we do in these circumstances except leave everything, set aside the concerns of the world, and yearn only for eternal desires? But these things have been given to few.

### 11

I want to admonish you to leave everything, but I do not presume to do so. If, then, you cannot leave everything in the world, hold what belongs to this world in such a way that you are not held by it in the world; let earthly property be possessed, but not possess you; let what you have be subject to the dominion of your mind, lest, if your mind is conquered by love of earthly things, it itself be more possessed by its possessions.

Let temporal property be used on the journey, and let the eternal be desired upon arrival. Let whatever is done in this world be viewed, as it were, from the side. Let the eyes of the mind look ahead while, with complete attention, they behold the things to which we are coming.

Let vices be uprooted completely—not only removed from outward action, but torn from the heart’s thoughts as well. Let neither carnal pleasure, nor the anxiety of curiosity, nor the heat of ambition hinder us from the Lord’s dinner. Let us touch even the honorable things we do in the world as though from some side of the mind, so that earthly things that please us may serve our body only insofar as they do not impede the heart.

[Note: The German manuscript, Beauvais, and three Gemet manuscripts read “in this world”; the printed editions read “in the world.”]

Therefore, brothers, we do not dare tell you to leave everything. Yet, if you wish, you can leave everything even while retaining everything, if you conduct yourselves in temporal matters in such a way that your whole mind nevertheless strives toward eternal things.

### 12

For this reason the apostle Paul says: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:29 and following).

A man has a wife, but is as though he had none, when he knows how to fulfill the obligations of the flesh in such a way that he is not compelled to cling to the world with his whole mind because of her. For when the same excellent preacher again says, “He who has a wife thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (ibid., 33), the man who has a wife is as though he did not have one when he strives to please his spouse without displeasing his Maker.

He also weeps, but as though he did not weep, when he is afflicted by temporal losses in such a way that he always consoles his mind with eternal gains. He rejoices, but as though he did not rejoice, when he exults in temporal goods in such a way that he always considers everlasting torments; and while lifting his mind with joy, he immediately presses it down with the weight of prudent fear.

He buys, but as though he did not possess, when he prepares earthly things for use while carefully foreseeing that he will soon leave them. He also uses the world, but as though he did not use it, when he reduces all necessary things externally to the service of his life, yet does not allow these same things to rule his mind, so that things subject to him serve externally and never break the intention of the soul striving toward higher things.

[Note: Bigot has “toward other things.”]

Whoever is such, then, has all earthly things present not for desire but for use. He uses what is necessary, but wishes to have nothing to do with sin. From the very possessions he holds, he acquires rewards daily, and rejoices more in good works than in good possessions.

[Note: Bigot, the two earlier Gemet manuscripts, Longpont, and Vallicelliana have “they seek rewards.”]

### 13

And lest these matters seem difficult to some people, I shall relate an event concerning a person whom many of you know. I learned this event from faithful persons in the city of Centumcellae three years ago.

Recently, in that same city, there was a count named Theophanius (Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 27), a man devoted to works of mercy and attentive to good deeds, especially devoted to hospitality. Occupied with the duties of governing his county, he conducted himself amid earthly and temporal affairs—but, as became clearer from the end of his life, more from obligation than from intention.

[Note: The printed editions have “but, as became clear afterward, more...” We have restored “more” before “afterward” in accordance with the German, Beauvais, Gemet, Chartres, and other manuscripts.]

When the time of his death was approaching, a very violent storm prevented him from being carried out for burial. His wife, weeping most bitterly, asked him, “What shall I do? How can I carry you out for burial, when I cannot leave the door of this house because of the excessive storm?”

He replied: “Do not weep, woman, for as soon as I have died, the weather will become clear.”

Immediately death followed his words, and clear weather followed his death.

His hands and feet, swollen with the fluid of gout, had been transformed into wounds, and they lay open with pus flowing from them.

[Note: This should likewise be read from the manuscripts as “they lay open with pus flowing,” not “they did not lie open,” as the printed editions have.]

But when his body had been uncovered, as usual, for washing, his hands and feet were found so healthy that they appeared never to have had any trace of a wound.

He was therefore carried away and buried. On the fourth day his wife thought that the marble placed over his tomb ought to be changed. When that marble had been removed from above his body, such a fragrance of scent flowed from the body that it seemed as though spices had boiled in place of worms from his decaying flesh.

I have related these things so that, by a nearby example, I might show that some people wear worldly clothing while not possessing a worldly spirit.

[Note: The German Corbie manuscript and Bigot have “so that I might show.”]

Those whom necessity binds in the world, so that they cannot be stripped of the world in every respect, must hold the things of the world in such a way that they do not know how to succumb to them through the breaking of their minds.

Think about this, then. When you cannot leave all that belongs to the world, conduct your external affairs well externally, but hasten inwardly and ardently toward eternal things. Let nothing delay the desire of your minds; let the delight of no thing in this world entangle you.

[Note: The two earlier Gemet manuscripts have “the love of no thing.”]

If something good is loved, let the mind delight in better goods—that is, in heavenly things. If something evil is feared, let eternal evils be set before the mind, so that, when it sees there both more to love and more to fear, it may cling here not at all.

For these things we have the mediator between God and human beings, our helper, through whom we shall obtain everything more quickly if we burn with true love for him: he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit as God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript this is the fortieth homily; in the Lateran manuscript and the Swedish Royal Codex, the thirty-fourth.]

## HOMILY XXXVII

Preached to the people in the basilica of the blessed martyr Sebastian, on his feast day.

### LESSON OF THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE 14:25–33

At that time Jesus said to the crowds:

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

“For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost required to complete it, to see whether he has enough to finish it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to complete it, all who see him will begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish.’

“Or what king, going to engage another king in battle, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

“So therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.”

[Note: Beauvais has “does he not first sit down?”]

1626

1. If we consider, dearest brothers, what and how great are the things promised to us in heaven, everything possessed on earth becomes worthless in our estimation. For earthly substance, compared with heavenly happiness, is a burden, not a support. Temporal life, compared with eternal life, should rather be called death than life. For what else is the daily decay of corruption but a certain prolongation of death?

What tongue could describe, or what understanding could grasp, how great are the joys of that heavenly city: to take one’s place among the choirs of angels, to stand with the blessed spirits before the glory of the Creator, to behold the face of God present, to see the boundless light, to be touched by no fear of death, and to rejoice in the perpetual gift of incorruption? At hearing of these things the soul catches fire, and already longs to stand there where it hopes to rejoice without end.

But one cannot arrive at great rewards except through great labors. Hence the outstanding preacher Paul says: [Note: Col. 1275D. Gemet. and Bigot.: “No one will be crowned unless he…”] “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). Let the greatness of the rewards, then, delight the mind, but let the contest of labors not frighten it. Hence Truth says to those coming to him: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.”

2. But one may ask how we are commanded to hate parents and relatives according to the flesh, when we are also commanded to love our enemies. Certainly Truth says concerning a wife: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). And Paul says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church” (Eph. 5:25). Behold, the disciple proclaims that a wife is to be loved, while the Master says: “Whoever does not hate his wife cannot be my disciple.” Does the Judge announce one thing while the herald proclaims another? [Col. 1275D] Or can we both hate and love at the same time?

But if we weigh the force of the command, we can do both through discernment: we should love those joined to us by kinship of the flesh, whom we recognize as close to us, and should hate—and not recognize as close—those whom we endure as adversaries on the way of God. [Note: Belvac.: “and by which [we know] neighbors . . . and by which [we know] adversaries.”] For one loves a person, as it were, through hatred when that person, thinking according to the flesh and imposing evil things upon us, is not obeyed.

To show that this hatred toward those close to us does not proceed from lack of affection but from charity, the Lord immediately added, saying: “And even his own life.” We are therefore commanded to hate those close to us, and to hate our own life as well. It is clear, then, that one who hates his neighbor as himself must hate him while loving him. We hate our own life rightly when we do not comply with its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its pleasures. Thus, when our life is despised and led toward what is better, it is loved, as it were, through hatred.

So, certainly, we must display toward those close to us such a discerning hatred that in them we love what they are, while hating what obstructs us in the way of God.

[Note: Some manuscripts—C. Germ., Belv., Corb., first Gemet., and others—suggest reading “not from affection,” whereas the editions have “not from lack of affection.”]

3. Certainly, when Paul was going to Jerusalem, the prophet Agabus seized his belt and bound his own feet with it, saying: “This is how the man whose belt this is will be bound in Jerusalem” (Acts 21:11). [Note: Bigot.: “and bound his own feet.”] But what did the man who had perfectly hated his own life say? “I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 13), and “I do not count my life more precious than myself” (Acts 20:24). [Note: The editions insert “the Jews” here, against the manuscripts C. Germ., Gemet., and others.]

Behold how he hated his own life while loving it—or rather, how by hating it he loved it—for he desired to hand it over to death for Jesus, so that he might raise it from the death of sin to life.

From this discerning hatred of our own life, then, let us derive the pattern for hatred of our neighbor. Let everyone in this world, even an adversary, be loved; but on the way of God, let one who opposes us not be loved, even if he is a relative. Whoever now longs for eternal things must become, in the cause of God he has undertaken, outside father, outside mother, outside wife, outside children, outside relatives, outside himself, so that he may know God more truly in proportion as he recognizes no one in God’s cause.

For it is a serious matter that carnal affections strike at the mind’s purpose and obscure its vision. Yet we do not suffer them to be harmful if we hold them down by restraining them. Those close to us must therefore be loved; charity must be shown to everyone, both relatives and strangers; nevertheless, because of that same charity we must not be turned away from the love of God.

4. We know that when the ark of the Lord returned from the land of the Philistines to the land of the Israelites, it was placed upon a cart, and cows were yoked to the cart. They are said to have been nursing cows, whose calves had been shut up at home. And it is written: “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh, traveling by one route, going and lowing, and they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (1 Sam. 6:12). [Note: Gemet., C. Germ., and many others: “Bethsamis.”]

What, then, do the cows signify if not the faithful within the Church, who, while considering the precepts of sacred speech, carry the Lord’s ark placed upon them, as it were? It should also be noted that they are said to have been nursing cows, because there are many who are inwardly established on the way of God but are bound outwardly by carnal affections. Yet they do not turn aside from the straight road, because they carry the ark of God in their minds.

Behold, the cows proceed toward Beth-shemesh. Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun,” and the Prophet says: “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. 4:2). [Note: Bigot.: “for you who fear the name of the Lord.”] If, then, we are heading toward the dwelling of the eternal sun, it is certainly fitting that we not turn aside from God’s path because of carnal affections.

We must consider with all our strength that the cows yoked to God’s cart proceed while lowing: they utter groans from their inmost parts, yet do not turn their steps from the road. In just this way the preachers of God, and all the faithful within the holy Church, must share the sufferings of those close to them through charity, yet not deviate from the way of God through compassion.

5. Truth makes clear how this hatred of one’s own life should be displayed by adding: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” [Note: The same manuscript adds: “and follows me.”] The cross takes its name from suffering. We carry the Lord’s cross in two ways: either by afflicting the flesh through abstinence, or by considering the need of our neighbor as our own through compassion. Whoever shows pain over another’s need carries the cross in his mind.

It must be understood, however, that some practice abstinence from the flesh not for God but for empty glory. And there are many who offer compassion to their neighbor not spiritually but carnally, so that, by pitying him, they support him not in virtue but in sin. [Note: First Carn.: “encourage” (*foveant*).] Such people appear indeed to carry the cross, but they do not follow the Lord.

Hence Truth rightly says again: “Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.” To carry the cross and follow the Lord is to practice abstinence from the flesh, or to show compassion toward one’s neighbor, for the sake of an eternal purpose. Whoever practices these things for a temporal purpose carries the cross, indeed, but refuses to follow the Lord.

6. Since sublime commands have been given, a comparison with the construction of a lofty building is immediately added: “For which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the expense required, to see whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish.’”

Everything we do must be preceded by careful consideration. Behold, according to Truth’s saying, the person building a tower first prepares the cost of construction. If, then, we wish to build the tower of humility, we must first prepare ourselves against the adversities of this age.

This is the difference between an earthly and a heavenly building: an earthly building is constructed by gathering expenses, whereas a heavenly building is constructed by scattering expenses. [Note: Bigot. adds “we gather.” Shortly afterward it reads *habere noluit* (“did not wish to meet it”) for *habere non potuit* (“could not meet it”).] We spend for the former if we gather what we do not possess; we spend for the latter if we also abandon what we possess.

That rich man could not meet this cost. Possessing many things, he sought out the Master and said: “Good Master, what must I do to possess eternal life?” (Matt. 19:16). When he heard the command to leave everything, he departed sorrowfully; and from the very place where he was outwardly broader in possessions, he became inwardly constricted. Because in this life he loved the expense required for exaltation, he did not wish to bear the expense of humility while journeying toward the eternal homeland.

We must also consider the words: “All who see it will begin to mock him.” For, in Paul’s words, “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9). In everything we do we must consider our hidden adversaries, who are always intent upon our deeds and always rejoice in our failure. The Prophet, looking upon them, says: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame, nor let my enemies mock me” (Ps. 24:2–3).

If, intent upon good works, we do not carefully keep watch against evil spirits, we suffer as mockers the very ones whom we have as persuaders to evil. [Note: In the first Carn. there is inserted: “and carefully against those very despisers,” and so forth.]

But since the comparison was given concerning the construction of a building, a likeness from the lesser to the greater is now added, so that greater things may be measured from the smallest. For it follows: “Or what king, going to wage war against another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he can meet with ten thousand the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.” [Note: Belvac.: “does he not first sit down?”]

One king comes against another on equal terms for battle, yet, if he judges himself unable to prevail, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. With what tears, then, ought we to hope for pardon, who in that terrible examination will not come to judgment on equal terms with our King—those whom our condition, weakness, and cause show to be inferior? [Note: Gemet. and first Carn.: “the condition of weakness.” Bigot., Longip., Val. Cl., and second Carn.: “the weakness of our condition.”]

7. But perhaps we have already cut away the sins of evil deeds and now avoid every outward wrong. Are we therefore sufficient to render an account of our thoughts? The one who comes against him with twenty thousand is said to be the one whom this man, coming with ten thousand, is entirely unable to meet. Ten thousand compared with twenty thousand are onefold compared with twofold.

But even if we make great progress, we scarcely keep our outward works in righteousness. For even if sexual indulgence has already been cut away, it has not yet been entirely cut away from the heart. He who comes to judge, however, judges outward and inward things together; he weighs deeds as well as thoughts.

He comes with a twofold army against a single army when he examines us, scarcely prepared in works alone, concerning both our works and our thoughts. What, then, should we do, brothers, except that, recognizing that we cannot suffice with a single army against his double army, while he is still far away we should send a delegation and ask for terms of peace?

He is said to be far away because he is not yet seen as present in judgment. Let us send our tears as a delegation to him; let us send works of mercy; let us slaughter upon his altar sacrifices of reconciliation; let us acknowledge that we cannot contend with him in judgment; let us consider the power of his strength and ask for terms of peace.

This is our delegation, which appeases the coming King. Consider, brothers, how gracious it is that he who by his coming is able to overwhelm us delays his arrival. Let us send our delegation to him, as we have said, by shedding tears, giving alms, and offering sacred sacrifices.

For the sacrifice of the sacred altar, offered with tears and kindness of heart, is uniquely effective for our absolution, because he who, having risen from the dead in himself, no longer dies, nevertheless suffers again through this sacrifice in his mystery on our behalf. For whenever we offer him the sacrifice of his Passion, we renew his Passion for our absolution.

8. Many of you, dearest brothers, I think, have happened to know the event that I wish to recall to your memory by relating it. It is said to have happened not long before our own times that a certain man was captured by enemies and taken far away (Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 57). When he had long been held in chains, his wife, since she did not receive him back from that captivity, thought he had died. For him, as though he were already dead, she regularly arranged for sacrifices to be offered every week.

His chains were loosened in captivity as many times as sacrifices had been offered by his wife for the absolution of his soul. After a long time he returned and, greatly amazed, told his wife that on certain days, every week, his chains had been loosened. When his wife examined those days and hours, she recognized that he had been released precisely when she remembered that a sacrifice had been offered for him.

From this, then, dearest brothers, draw a certain conclusion: if a sacrifice offered by another could loosen bodily chains in one person, consider how much the sacred sacrifice offered by us can loosen the bonds of the heart in ourselves. [Note: Bigot.: “it is inferred.”]

9. Many of you, dearest brothers, know Cassius, bishop of the city of Narni. His custom was to offer daily sacrifices to God, so that scarcely a day of his life passed on which he did not sacrifice a sacrifice of reconciliation to almighty God (Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 56).

His life was in profound harmony with his sacrifice. For he gave everything he possessed in alms, and when the hour of offering the sacrifice arrived, he seemed to pour himself out entirely in tears and sacrificed himself with great contrition of heart.

I learned of both his life and his death from the account of a venerable deacon who had been brought up by him. He said that one night the Lord appeared in a vision to the bishop’s presbyter and said: “Go and tell the bishop: Continue what you are doing; carry on the work you are performing. Let neither your foot nor your hand cease. On the feast of the apostles you will come to me, and I will repay you your reward.”

The presbyter arose. But because the feast of the apostles was approaching, he feared to announce to the bishop the day of so near an end. On another night the Lord returned and severely rebuked his disobedience, repeating the same words of his command.

Then the presbyter arose to go, but again weakness of heart became an obstacle to announcing the revelation. Even after the command had been repeated, he hardened himself against going and neglected to reveal what he had seen.

But because a greater anger of vengeance usually punishes the contempt of great gentleness, [Note: First Carn.: “in a third vision.”] the Lord appeared a third time and added blows to his words. He was beaten with such severe punishment that bodily wounds softened the hardness of his heart.

The presbyter therefore arose, instructed by the blows, went to the bishop, and found him already standing according to custom near the tomb of blessed Juvenal the martyr, preparing to offer the sacrifice. He asked for privacy and threw himself at the bishop’s feet.

When the bishop could scarcely raise him from the ground, weeping profusely, he sought to learn the cause of his tears. The presbyter, however, wishing to relate the sequence of the vision, first let his garment fall from his shoulders and exposed the wounds on his body—so to speak, witnesses of the truth and of his fault. He showed how severely the blows he had received had furrowed his limbs, leaving them marked with bruises. [Note: The first two Gemet. manuscripts: “the wounds he had received.”]

As soon as the bishop saw them, he was horrified and asked, with words of great astonishment, who had dared to do such things to him. The presbyter replied that he had suffered them on the bishop’s account.

His wonder increased with terror. The presbyter no longer delayed answering his questions but disclosed the secret of the revelation and reported to him, in the very words he had heard, the Lord’s command: “Continue what you are doing; carry on the work you are performing. Let neither your hand nor your foot cease. On the feast of the apostles you will come to me, and I will repay you your reward.”

When he heard this, the bishop prostrated himself in prayer with great contrition of heart. He had come at the third hour to offer the sacrifice, but because of the length of his prayer he prolonged it until the ninth hour.

From that day onward, the profits of his devotion increased more and more. He became as strong in his work as he was certain of his reward, since, by that promise, he had begun to regard as his debtor the one to whom he himself had been indebted.

It had been his custom to come to Rome every year on the feast of the apostles. Now, made fearful by this revelation, he did not wish to come according to custom. At the same time he remained anxious, suspended in expectation of his death: in the second year, and likewise in the third; then similarly in the fourth, fifth, and sixth. He might already have despaired of the truth of the revelation if the blows had not lent credibility to the words.

Then, behold, in the seventh year he remained unharmed until the sacred vigils of the expected feast arrived. But during the vigils he was touched by a mild fever, [Note: The two Carn. manuscripts and Bigot.: “pain touched him.”] and on the very feast day, while his sons were awaiting him, he refused to perform the solemn rites of Mass.

But they too were all apprehensive about his departure and came together to him, unanimously binding themselves not to allow the solemn celebration of the Mass to take place that day unless their own bishop, as their intercessor, approached the Lord on their behalf. [Note: First Carn.: “unless he celebrated the solemn rites.”]

Then, compelled, he celebrated Mass in the chapel of the episcopal residence and with his own hand distributed the Lord’s body and the peace to everyone. After completing the entire ministry of the sacrifice that had been offered, he returned to his little bed. As he lay there and saw his priests and ministers standing around him, he seemed to be saying his final farewell and exhorted them to preserve the bond of charity, teaching how greatly they ought to be united among themselves in harmony.

Suddenly, in the midst of this holy exhortation, he cried out in a terrible voice: “It is the hour.” At once he himself handed those standing nearby the linen cloth which, according to the custom for the dying, was to be stretched over his face. When it had been stretched out, he gave up his spirit; and thus that holy soul, reaching eternal joys, was released from the corruption of the flesh.

Whom, dearest brothers, whom did this man imitate in his death, if not the one whom he had contemplated in his life? Saying, “It is the hour,” he departed from the body, because Jesus too, after completing everything, said, “It is finished,” bowed his head, and gave up his spirit (John 19:30). What the Lord did by authority, therefore, the servant did by calling.

10. Behold how much peace with the coming King that delegation achieved—daily sacrifices sent with alms and tears. Let the person who can leave everything do so. But whoever cannot leave everything should, while the King is still far away, send a delegation and offer gifts of tears, alms, and sacrifices.

For he wishes to be appeased by prayers, since he knows that he cannot be borne when angry. The fact that he still delays his coming means that he is allowing the delegation of peace to continue. He would already have come, if he wished, and slaughtered all his adversaries. Yet he indicates how terrifying he will come, while still delaying his arrival because he does not wish to find anyone whom he must punish.

He declares our guilt in despising him, saying: “Therefore, none of you who does not renounce all that he possesses can be my disciple.” Yet he also provides the remedy of hoped-for salvation, because the one who cannot be endured in anger wishes to be appeased through the delegation of requested peace.

Wash away, therefore, dearest brothers, the stains of sins with tears; wipe them clean with alms; atone for them with sacred sacrifices. Do not possess through desire what you have not yet actually abandoned. Fix your hope on the Redeemer alone; pass over in mind to the eternal homeland.

For if you no longer possess anything in this world by loving it, then even while possessing everything you have abandoned it all. May he grant us the joys we desire, he who has given us the remedies of eternal peace, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: It is numbered twenty-fifth in Corb., twenty-eighth in Later., and twenty-ninth in the Swedish Royal Manuscript.]

## HOMILY XXXVIII

Delivered to the people in the basilica of blessed Clement the martyr.

[Note: In Corb. Germ., Lateran., the Swedish Royal Manuscript, the first Gemet., and several others, “martyr” is not read.]

### THE HOLY GOSPEL READING ACCORDING TO MATTHEW 22:1–13

[Note: Belv.: “Jesus was speaking to the crowds: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like …’”] At that time Jesus was speaking to the chief priests and Pharisees in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son and sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding, but they did not wish to come. Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those who have been invited: Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding.’ But they disregarded it and went away, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, treated them outrageously, and killed them.

“When the king heard this, he became angry; and, sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city. Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding is ready, but those who had been invited were not worthy. Go, therefore, to the crossroads, and invite to the wedding everyone you find.’ The servants went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, bad and good, and the wedding hall was filled with those reclining at table.

“But when the king entered to see those reclining at table, he saw there a man who was not dressed in a wedding garment. He said to him: ‘Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?’ But he was speechless. Then the king said to the attendants: ‘Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ For many are called, but few are chosen.”

1634

1. Dearest brothers, if I can, I wish to pass briefly through the text of the Gospel reading, so that at its conclusion I may have more room for speaking at length. But we must first ask whether this is the same reading in Matthew as the one described in Luke under the designation of a dinner (Luke 14:16ff.).

There are indeed certain things that appear discordant: here a dinner is mentioned, there a supper; here the person who entered the wedding without a worthy garment is rejected, while there no one who is said to have entered is reported to have been rejected. From this it is rightly inferred that here the present Church is signified by the wedding, whereas there the eternal and final banquet is signified by the supper, because some enter the former only to depart, while whoever once enters the latter will not depart again.

But if someone should insist that this is the same reading, I think it better, without compromising faith, to yield to another’s interpretation than to serve contentiousness. For it may perhaps reasonably be understood that Matthew said of the man who had been cast out because he did not come in a wedding garment what Luke left unsaid.

As for the fact that the one passage calls it a supper and the other a dinner, this in no way obstructs our understanding, since among the ancients dinner was held daily at the ninth hour, and that very dinner was also called supper.

2. I remember that I have often already said that in the holy Gospel the kingdom of heaven generally means the present Church. The assembly of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven. Since the Lord says through the prophet, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1), and Solomon says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7:27), while Paul also says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), we must clearly conclude that, if God is wisdom and the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, then, since heaven is said to be the seat of God, heaven is therefore the soul of the righteous. [Note: This passage has already been cited by the holy Doctor in *Moralia* 29.55, where some of our conjectures have already been set forth. The same sentence, as though belonging to sacred Scripture, is cited by Augustine on Psalm 46, verse 9, and more frequently by Bernard: namely, Sermon 1 on the Purification, Sermon 5 on the Words of Isaiah, and Sermon 27 on the *Song of Songs*. See the notes to the same Bernard, in the latest recension by our Mabillon, note 289, where the sentence in question is derived from the Book of Wisdom, chapter 7, verse 7. It may perhaps be found more felicitously in verse 27, where it is said of wisdom: “It passes into holy souls.” In many places one reads statements very close to this, such as Lev. 26:11–12; 2 Cor. 6:16; 1 Cor. 3. But here Gregory indicates Solomon, to whom the Book of Wisdom is commonly attributed, although Gregory does not explicitly ascribe it to him. If this conjecture seems less satisfactory to you, reader, you may perhaps prefer another, put forward in *Moralia* 29.55.]

Hence the Psalmist says of the holy preachers: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2). The kingdom of heaven, therefore, is the Church of the righteous, because, since their hearts desire nothing on earth, the Lord already reigns in them as in heavenly places, by the fact that they yearn for things above.

Let it therefore be said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.”

3. Your Charity already understands who this king is, the father of the king’s son: plainly the one to whom the Psalmist says, “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1).

“He made a wedding feast for his son.” God the Father made a wedding feast for God the Son when he joined him to human nature in the womb of the Virgin, when he willed that the God who existed before the ages should become human at the end of the ages.

But because this union is customarily said to be made from two persons, far be it from our understanding to believe that the person of our Redeemer, Jesus Christ, God and human, was united from two persons. We say that he exists from two natures and in two natures; but we reject as impious the belief that he was composed from two persons.

It can therefore be stated more clearly and safely that the Father made a wedding feast for the King, his Son, in that he joined the holy Church to him through the mystery of the Incarnation. The womb of the Virgin Mother was the bridal chamber of this Bridegroom.

Hence the Psalmist says: “He has set his tent in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming out of his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18:6). He came forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber because God, having become incarnate in order to join the Church to himself, came forth from the undefiled womb of the Virgin.

He therefore sent his servants to invite friends to this wedding. He sent them once, and he sent them again, because he made the preachers of the Lord’s Incarnation first prophets and afterward apostles. He sent servants twice to invite people because he foretold the future Incarnation of the Only-Begotten through the prophets and announced its accomplishment through the apostles.

But because those who had first been invited did not wish to come to the wedding feast, the second invitation now says: “Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready.”

4. What do we understand by the bulls and the fattened animals, dearest brothers, if not the fathers of the New and Old Testaments? Since I am speaking to ordinary people, I must also explain the very words of the Gospel reading.

We call fattened animals *altilia*, because the word derives from *alere*, “to nourish”; hence we call them, as it were, *alitilia*. When, however, the Law says, “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43; Lev. 19:18), permission had then been granted to the righteous to suppress God’s adversaries and their own with whatever strength they could muster and to strike them lawfully with the sword. [Note: Gratian reads: “by the edge of the sword.”]

This is undoubtedly restrained in the New Testament, when Truth himself proclaims: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). [Note: The two Carn. manuscripts and Bigot.: “What, then, is signified by…”]

Who, then, are signified by the bulls if not the fathers of the Old Testament? Since, by the permission of the Law, they had received authority to strike their adversaries in requital of hatred, what else were they, so to speak, but bulls, who gored their enemies with the horn of bodily strength?

What, on the other hand, are signified by the fattened animals if not the fathers of the New Testament? Having received the grace of inner richness, they rise away from earthly desires and are lifted by the wings of contemplation toward what is sublime. [Note: C. Germ., Corb., Belvac., and the other manuscripts read *a terrenis desideriis enitentes* (“rising away from earthly desires”); the editions print *aeternis desideriis innitentes* (“relying on eternal desires”).]

To place one’s thought in the lowest things—what else is this but a certain dryness of mind? But those who, through holy desires, are already nourished by the food of inward delight in heavenly things become fattened, as it were, by richer nourishment. The Prophet desired to be fattened by this richness when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6).

Because the preachers of the Lord’s Incarnation endured persecution from unbelievers—first the prophets, and afterward the holy apostles—it is said to those who were invited but did not wish to come: “My bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready.” It is as though he said more openly: “Look upon the deaths of the fathers who came before, and consider the remedies for your life.”

It should be noted that nothing is said of bulls and fattened animals in the first invitation, whereas in the second the bulls and fattened animals are already remembered as having been slaughtered. For when almighty God sees that we do not wish to hear his words, he adds examples, so that everything we believe impossible may become easier for us to hope for, the more we hear that others have already passed through it.

5. It follows: “But they disregarded it and went away, one to his farm, another to his business.” To go to one’s farm is to devote oneself excessively to earthly labor; to go to one’s business is to pursue the profits of worldly activities.

Because one person, intent upon earthly labor, and another, devoted to the activities of this world, pretends not to consider the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation or to live according to it, he refuses to come to the king’s wedding, as though going to his farm or his business.

Often, what is more serious, some not only reject the grace of the one who calls but also persecute it. Hence it follows: “The rest seized his servants, treated them outrageously, and killed them.”

But when the king learned this, he sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city. He destroys the murderers because he kills the persecutors. He burns their city with fire because not only their souls but also the flesh in which they had dwelt is tormented by the eternal flame of Gehenna.

He is said to have destroyed the murderers by sending his armies because all judgment among human beings is carried out through angels. For what are those hosts of angels if not the armies of our King? Hence this same King is called the Lord of Sabaoth. *Sabaoth* is interpreted as “of armies.” [Note: Recent editions preferred “armies,” against the manuscripts and the old edition.]

He therefore sends an army to destroy his adversaries, because the Lord exercises vengeance through angels. Our fathers then heard of the power of this vengeance; we now behold it.

Where are those proud persecutors of the martyrs? Where are those who raised the neck of their hearts against their Creator and swelled with the deadly glory of this world? [Note: Belvac. and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts: “deadly,” which was formerly read in C. Germ.]

Behold, the death of the martyrs now flourishes in the faith of the living, while those who gloried in their cruelty against them scarcely come to our memory, even among the number of the dead. By what has happened, therefore, we understand what we hear in the parables.

6. But the man who sees that he, though inviting, is being despised will not have the wedding feast of the king’s son empty. He sends to others, because even if he labors among some, nevertheless the word of God will eventually find where it may rest. Hence it is added:

> Then he said to his servants: “The wedding is indeed ready, but those who were invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the exits of the roads, and invite to the wedding whomever you find.” [Col. 1285C]

If in sacred Scripture we understand “roads” as actions, we understand the “exits of the roads” as failures of action, because those whom no prosperity accompanies in earthly activities generally come easily to God. It follows:

> And his servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good; and the wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table.

7. Behold, the very character of the guests plainly shows that by this wedding of the king the present Church is signified, in which the wicked meet together with the good. It is mixed in the diversity of its children, because it gives birth to all alike into the faith, yet it does not bring all, through a change of life and as their sins demand, to the freedom of spiritual grace. For as long as we live here, it is necessary that we proceed together, mingled along the road of the present age. [Note: [Col. 1285D] The printed editions read “the life of the present age,” whereas the manuscripts, in strong agreement, read “the road.”] We are separated only when we arrive. The good alone are nowhere except in heaven, and the wicked alone are nowhere except in hell. This life, situated between heaven and hell, just as it stands in the middle, likewise receives citizens of both realms together; yet the holy Church receives them indiscriminately now and separates them afterward at their departure. [23, q. 4, c. 15] If, therefore, you are good, tolerate the wicked patiently for as long as you remain in this life. For whoever does not tolerate the wicked is himself, by his intolerance, a witness to himself that he is not good. He refuses to be Abel whom the wickedness of Cain does not exercise.

Thus, on the threshing floor, grains are pressed beneath the chaff; thus flowers arise among thorns, and the fragrant rose grows together with the thorn that pricks. The first man had two sons, but one of them was chosen and the other rejected (Gen. I, 1 ff.). Noah’s ark contained three sons, but two of them were chosen and one rejected (ibid., VI, 7). Abraham had two sons, but one was chosen and the other rejected (ibid., XXI, 10 ff.). Isaac had two sons, but one was chosen and the other rejected (ibid., XXVII, 37). Jacob had twelve sons, but one of them was sold because of his innocence, while the others, through their wickedness, became sellers of their brother (ibid., XXXVII, 28). Twelve apostles were chosen, but among them one was mixed in who would test, and eleven who would be tested (John VI, 71). Seven deacons were ordained by the apostles (Acts VI, 5), but while six remained in the right faith, one became the author of error. [Note: [Col. 1286D] He means Nicolaus, whom many of the holy Fathers considered the father of the shameful Nicolaitans.] In this Church, therefore, neither can the wicked exist without the good, nor the good without the wicked.

Recall to mind, therefore, dearest brothers, the times that have gone before, and strengthen yourselves for tolerating the wicked. For if we are children of the elect, it necessarily remains for us to walk according to their examples. He was not good who refused to tolerate the wicked. Hence blessed Job says of himself:

> I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches (Job XXX, 29).

Hence, through Solomon, the voice of the Bridegroom says of the holy Church:

> As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters (Song II, 2).

Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel:

> Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions (Ezek. II, 6).

Hence Peter glorifies the life of blessed Lot, saying:

> And he rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the outrage of the wicked; for he was righteous in sight and hearing, dwelling among those who day after day tortured the righteous soul by wicked deeds (2 Pet. II, 7–8 ff.). [Note: [Col. 1286D] Here we follow the manuscripts rather than the printed editions, where “from the outrage of the ungodly” is read.] [Note: [Col. 1286D] Gemet. and Bigot. read “among them.”]

Hence Paul both praises and strengthens the life of the disciples, saying:

> In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life (Phil. II, 15).

Hence John bears witness to the Church of Pergamum, saying:

> I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith (Rev. II, 13).

Behold, dearest brothers, by reviewing nearly everything, we recognize that no one was good whom the perversity of the wicked did not test. To put it this way: the iron of our soul is never brought to the fineness of a sharp edge unless the file of another’s wickedness has worn it down.

8. You should not, however, be terrified because there are many wicked and few good in the Church. The ark upon the waters of the flood, which bore the figure of this Church, was broad below and narrow above, and at its summit it rose to the measure of a single cubit. Below, we must believe, it contained four-footed animals and reptiles; above, birds and human beings. It was broad where it contained beasts, and narrow where it preserved human beings, because the holy Church is broad among the carnal and narrow among the spiritual. Wherever it tolerates the beastly ways of human beings, there it spreads its bosom more widely. But wherever it has those who are supported by spiritual reason, there it is indeed raised to the summit, yet because they are few, it becomes narrow.

> Broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who go by it; and narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it (Matt. VII, 13). [Note: [Col. 1287D] Bigot. reads, “The gate is narrow.”]

The ark is narrowed at the top until it reaches the measure of one cubit, because in the holy Church the holier people are, the fewer they are. At the summit it reaches the one who alone was human among human beings and, without comparison with anyone else, was born holy. He, in the words of the Psalmist,

> Was made like a solitary sparrow on the building (Ps. CI, 1).

The wicked, therefore, must be tolerated all the more because they are more numerous; for on the threshing floor there are few grains kept for the granaries, while great heaps of chaff are burned in the fires.

9. But since, by the Lord’s gift, you have now entered the wedding house—that is, the holy Church—look carefully, brothers, lest the king who enters find something blameworthy in the disposition of your minds. We must consider with great fear of heart what immediately follows:

> The king entered to see those reclining at table, and he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment.

What, dearest brothers, do we think is expressed by the wedding garment? If we say that the wedding garment is baptism or faith, who has entered this wedding without baptism and faith? By that very fact he is outside, since he has not yet believed. What, then, should we understand the wedding garment to be except charity? He enters the wedding, but does not enter wearing the wedding garment, who, standing in the holy Church, possesses faith but does not possess charity. [Note: [Col. 1287D] The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts read “remaining.”]

Charity is rightly called the wedding garment, because our Creator possessed it in himself when he came to enter into marriage with the Church.
