[Note: [Col. 1288D] Belvac. reads “displayed it.”] It was solely through the love of God that his only-begotten Son united to himself the minds of his chosen human beings. Hence John says:

> For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for us (John III, 16).

He who came to human beings through charity made known that this same charity is the wedding garment. Therefore, everyone among you who, placed in the Church, has believed in God has already entered the wedding; but he does not come wearing the wedding garment if he does not preserve the grace of charity.

And certainly, brothers, if someone were invited to a human wedding, he would change his clothing and show by the beauty of his appearance that he rejoiced with the bridegroom and the bride; he would be ashamed to appear among those rejoicing and celebrating the feast in neglected clothing. We have come to God’s wedding, yet we pretend not to change the garment of our hearts. The angels rejoice when the elect are taken up to heaven. With what state of mind, then, do we behold these spiritual festivities, when we do not possess the wedding garment—that is, charity—which alone makes us beautiful?

10. It must be understood that just as a garment is woven on two pieces of wood, an upper and a lower, so charity consists in two commandments: namely, in love of God and of one’s neighbor. For it is written:

> You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself (Mark XII, 30, from Deut. VI, 5).

Here we must note that a measure of love is established in love of one’s neighbor when it is said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” whereas no measure restricts love of God when it is said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.” One is not commanded how much he should love, but from how much, when it says, “With all”; for he truly loves God who leaves nothing of himself for himself.

Whoever therefore wishes to have the wedding garment at the wedding must keep these two commandments of charity. Hence, in the prophet Ezekiel, the vestibule of the city’s gate, situated on the mountain, is measured at two cubits (Ezek. XL, 9), because the entrance to the heavenly city is not opened to us if, in this Church—which is called the vestibule because it is still outside—the love of God and of neighbor is not maintained.

Hence it is commanded that scarlet dyed twice be woven into the curtains of the tabernacle (Exod. XXVI, 1). You are the curtains of the tabernacle, brothers—you are, because through faith you veil the heavenly mysteries in your hearts. But scarlet dyed twice must be present in the curtains of the tabernacle. Scarlet has the appearance of fire. What, then, is charity except fire? But this charity must be dyed twice: dyed through love of God and dyed through love of neighbor.

Whoever loves God in such a way [Note: [Col. 1288D] Belvac. reads, “so that, because of contemplation of him...”] that through contemplation of him he neglects his neighbor is indeed scarlet, but not scarlet dyed twice. Again, whoever loves his neighbor in such a way that through love of his neighbor he abandons contemplation of God is scarlet, but not scarlet dyed twice.

Therefore, so that your charity may be scarlet dyed twice, let it kindle itself both to the love of God and to the love of neighbor, so that it neither abandons contemplation of God out of compassion for its neighbor nor, clinging more than it should to contemplation of God, casts aside compassion for its neighbor. Every person living among human beings should therefore yearn for the one he desires, yet not abandon the one with whom he was running; and he should offer help to the latter, yet not become sluggish toward the one to whom he was hastening.

11. It must also be understood that love of one’s neighbor is itself divided into two commandments, as a certain wise man says:

> Whatever you hate to have happen to you, take care not to do to another (Tob. IV, 16).

And Truth itself proclaims:

> Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do the same to them (Matt. VII, 12).

For if we impart to others what we rightly wish to be given to us, and avoid doing to others what we do not wish to be done to us, we preserve the laws of charity unharmed.

But when someone loves another, let no one immediately think that he possesses charity unless he first examines the force of his love. For if someone loves another but does not love him for God’s sake, he does not possess charity, although he thinks he possesses it. True charity exists when a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake. He loves those whom he loves for God’s sake who already knows how to love even those by whom he is not loved.

Charity is usually proved by the single test of hostility. Hence the Lord himself says:

> Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you (Luke VI, 27). [Col. 1289B]

He therefore loves securely who, for God’s sake, loves the one whom he understands does not love him.

These things are great and lofty, and difficult for many to carry out; yet this is the wedding garment. Whoever, reclining at the wedding, does not possess it should already fear anxiously lest, when the king enters, he be sent outside. For it is said:

> The king entered the wedding to see those reclining at table, and he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment.

We are the ones, dearest brothers, who recline at the wedding of the Word; we already possess faith in the Church; we are nourished by the banquets of sacred Scripture; we rejoice that the Church is joined to God. Consider, I ask, whether you have come to this wedding wearing the wedding garment; examine your thoughts with careful inquiry. Weigh your hearts concerning each matter: whether you now harbor hatred against anyone; whether you are kindled by any flame of envy against another’s happiness; whether, through hidden wickedness, you hasten to harm anyone.

12. Behold, the king enters the wedding and examines the disposition of our heart; and to the one whom he does not find clothed in charity he immediately says in anger:

> Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?

It is exceedingly astonishing, dearest brothers, that he both calls this man “friend” and reproves him, as though he were saying more plainly, “Friend—and not a friend”; a friend by faith, but not a friend by deeds.

But he was silent, because—what cannot be said without groaning—in that final severity of reproof every argument of excuse ceases, since the one who reproves outwardly is the witness of conscience who accuses the mind inwardly.

Meanwhile, it must be understood that whoever possesses this garment of virtue, but does not yet possess it perfectly, should not despair of forgiveness when the merciful king enters, because he too gives us hope through the Psalmist, saying:

> Your eyes saw my unfinished state, and in your book all will be written (Ps. CXXXVIII, 16).

But since we have said these few things for the consolation of one who possesses this garment but is weak, let us now turn our words to the one who has it not at all. It follows:

[Col. 1290A]

13. Then the king said to his attendants:

> Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Then the feet and hands are bound by the severity of the sentence—those which now refused to be bound from wicked works by improvement of life. Or certainly punishment then binds those whom guilt now bound from good works. The feet that neglect to visit the sick and the hands that give nothing to the needy have already been bound from good work by their own will. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Longip., Val. Cl., and the two earlier Gemet. manuscripts read, “which therefore are now,” referring to the hands.] Whoever, therefore, is now willingly bound in vice is then bound unwillingly in punishment.

It is rightly said that he is cast into the outer darkness. We call blindness of heart the inner darkness, and the eternal night of condemnation the outer darkness. Then, therefore, each condemned person is sent not into the inner but into the outer darkness, because there he is unwillingly thrown into the night of condemnation who here willingly fell into blindness of heart.

There, too, weeping and gnashing of teeth are said to exist, so that there the teeth may gnash which here rejoiced in gluttony; there the eyes may weep which here were occupied with unlawful desires; [Note: [Col. 1290D] “In the world” is added in three Gemet. manuscripts.] so that each particular member that here served subject to each particular vice may there be subjected to punishment.

14. But after the one man has been rejected—in whom, clearly, the whole body of the wicked is represented—a general sentence is immediately added:

> For many are called, but few are chosen.

What we have heard is exceedingly fearful, dearest brothers. Behold, we have all already been called through faith and have come to the wedding of the heavenly king; we both believe and confess the mystery of his incarnation; we partake of the banquets of the divine Word. But on the future day of judgment the king will enter.

We know that we have been called; whether we have been chosen, we do not know. Therefore, each of us must humble himself in humility all the more because he does not know whether he is chosen.

Some do not even begin to do good; others do not persist at all in the good things they have begun. One is seen to lead nearly his entire life in wickedness, but near the end of life is recalled from his wickedness by the lamentations of strict penance. [Note: [Col. 1290D] Bigot. reads, “by renewed lamentations.”] Another appears to lead a chosen life, yet near the end of life it happens that he turns aside into the wickedness of error. One begins well and completes better; another, from his earliest age, casts himself into wicked deeds and is brought to completion in those same works, always becoming worse than himself. [Note: [Col. 1290D] The printed editions read “exercises himself,” contrary to all the manuscripts.]

Each person, therefore, must fear for himself with the greater care because he does not know what remains, since—as must often be said and retained without forgetting—many are called, but few are chosen.

15. But because sometimes the minds of listeners are moved more by the examples of the faithful than by the words of teachers, I wish to tell you something concerning people close to us, which your hearts may hear with greater fear because it sounds to you from nearby. For we are not speaking of events that happened long ago, but recalling events of which witnesses still exist and which they report having personally witnessed.

My father had three sisters, all three of whom were sacred virgins. One was called Tharsilla, another Gordiana, and the third Aemiliana. [Note: [Col. 1291D] In Corb. “Gardiana” is always read, and in C. Germ. “Aemeliana.”] Converted with one zeal, consecrated at one and the same time, and living under strict discipline according to a rule, they led a common life in their own house (Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 16).

When they had remained for a long time in the same way of life, Tharsilla and Aemiliana began daily to grow in love of their Creator; although they were present here in body alone, each day they passed in spirit to eternal things. But Gordiana’s mind, by daily losses, began to grow lukewarm from the warmth of inward love and little by little to return to love of this age. [Note: [Col. 1291D] Recent editions read “decreases” (decrementa).] Tharsilla often used to say to her sister Aemiliana, with great groaning:

“I see that our sister Gordiana does not belong to our lot; for I perceive that she is slipping outward and is not guarding the heart to which she had resolved.”

They took care each day to correct her with gentle reproof and reform her from lightness of conduct to the seriousness of their way of life. During the words of correction she would suddenly reassume a serious expression, but when the hour of that correction had passed, the assumed gravity of propriety immediately passed as well, and she would quickly return to frivolous speech. She rejoiced in the company of lay girls, and any person not devoted to this world was extremely burdensome to her.

One night, however, my aunt Tharsilla—who among her sisters had risen to honor and the summit of holiness through her continual practice of prayer, her devotion to ascetic discipline, her singular abstinence, and the venerable gravity of her life—as she herself recounted, saw in a vision my great-grandfather Felix, bishop of this Roman Church. He appeared to her and showed her a dwelling of perpetual radiance, saying:

“Come, for in this dwelling of light I receive you.”

Immediately afterward [Note: [Col. 1291D] Bigot., Val. Cl., and Longip. read “on the following night.”] she was seized by a fever and reached the final day of her life.

Just as many people gather around noble women and men who are dying in order to console their relatives, at the hour of her death many men and women stood around her bed; my mother was also present. Suddenly, looking upward, she saw Jesus coming and began to cry out loudly to those standing around her:

“Go away, go away; Jesus is coming.”

As she fixed her attention upon the one she was seeing, that holy soul was released from the flesh. Suddenly the whole place was filled with such a fragrance of wondrous odor that the sweetness itself showed everyone that the author of sweetness had come.

When her body was stripped according to the custom for washing the dead, hardened skin was found to have grown on her elbows and knees from her long practice of prayer, like the knees of camels; and her dead flesh bore witness to what her living spirit had always done. [Col. 1291D]

These things happened before the day of the Lord’s Nativity. After it had passed, she soon appeared in a nocturnal vision to her sister Aemiliana, saying:

“Come, so that, because I celebrated the Lord’s Nativity without you, I may now celebrate the holy day of the Theophany with you.”

Concerned for the salvation of her sister Gordiana, she immediately answered:

“And if I come alone, whom shall I leave our sister Gordiana with?”

Then, as she reported, Tharsilla again said sadly:

“Come, for our sister Gordiana has been numbered among the laywomen.” [Note: [Col. 1291D; 1292D] By “laywomen” understand women serving the world; among virgins dedicated to God, this was considered a grave offense. In other respects, laypeople are often mentioned by Tertullian, Cyprian, and other earlier Fathers.]

A physical illness immediately followed this vision, and, just as had been said, before the day of the Lord’s manifestation, as the illness grew worse, Aemiliana died.

But as soon as Gordiana found that she had been left alone, her wickedness grew, and what had previously lain hidden in the desire of her thoughts she afterward carried out in wicked action. [Note: [Col. 1292D] Longip. and Val. Cl. read “through its fulfillment.”] For, forgetting fear of the Lord, forgetting modesty and reverence, and forgetting her consecration, she later took the steward of her estates as her husband.

Behold, all three had first been converted with one zeal, but they did not remain in one and the same devotion, because, according to the Lord’s word, many are called, but few are chosen.

I have said these things so that no one already engaged in a good work may attribute the strength of that good work to himself, and so that no one may place confidence in his own conduct. For although he knows what he is like today, he does not yet know what he will be tomorrow. Let no one therefore rejoice securely in his present works when, amid the uncertainty of this life, he does not know what end will follow him. [Note: [Col. 1292D] The same reading is found in Gemet. and Bigot.: “what end will follow him.”]

But since I have related a matter that has terrified your hearts through the severity of divine judgment, I shall still relate another nearby matter that may console your terrified hearts through divine mercy. I remember, however, that I have already mentioned it in another sermon, though you were not present.

16. Two years ago a certain brother came to my monastery, situated near the church of the blessed martyrs John and Paul, out of a desire for religious life; after being kept under examination for a long time, he was eventually received (Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 38). His brother followed him to the monastery not out of devotion to the religious life but out of carnal affection.

The man who had come for the religious life was greatly pleasing to the brothers; his brother, by contrast, differed greatly from his life and character. Nevertheless, he remained in the monastery more from necessity than from willingness. Although he was perverse in all his actions, everyone tolerated him patiently for the sake of his brother.

He was light in speech, wicked in action, elegant in clothing, and uncultivated in conduct. He could not bear anyone speaking to him about the way of life proper to the holy habit. His life had become burdensome to all the brothers to behold, yet, as has been said, it was tolerable to all for the sake of his brother. He was extremely indignant if anyone spoke to him about correcting his wickedness. He could neither do good nor even hear about it. He repeatedly testified, by swearing, becoming angry, and mocking, that he would never adopt the habit of the holy way of life.

During the pestilence that recently consumed a large part of the population of this city, he was struck in the groin and brought to the point of death. As he was breathing his last, the brothers gathered to protect his departure by prayer. His body had already died from its extremities upward; only in his chest did vital warmth still breathe. All the brothers began to pray for him with the greater earnestness because they saw that he was about to depart swiftly.

Suddenly, while those same brothers stood nearby, he began to cry out as loudly as he could and interrupt their prayers, saying:

“Go away, go away! Behold, I have been given to the dragon to be devoured, but because of your presence he cannot devour me. He has already swallowed my head in his mouth. Give way, so that he may torment me no longer but do what he is going to do. If I have been given to him to be devoured, why do I suffer delay because of you?”

Then the brothers began to say to him:

“What is this that you are saying, brother? Make the sign of the holy cross upon yourself.”

He answered as best he could:

“I want to make the sign, but I cannot, because I am held down by the dragon.”

When the brothers heard this, they prostrated themselves on the ground and began to pray with tears even more fervently for his rescue.

And behold, suddenly the sick man began to recover and to exclaim with whatever voice he possessed:

“Thanks be to God! Behold, the dragon that had seized me to devour me has fled; driven out by your prayers, he could not remain. Now intercede for my sins, because I am ready to repent and to abandon the secular life completely.”

The man, therefore, who, as has already been said, had been dying from the extremities of his body, was preserved for life and turned to God with his whole heart. Disciplined by long and continual scourges in that same religious life, he died a few days ago when his bodily illness grew worse. When he was dying, he no longer saw the dragon, because through the change of his heart he had conquered it.

Behold, my brothers: Gordiana, whom I mentioned above, fell from the excellence of the sanctimonious habit into punishment, while this brother, of whom I have told you, returned from the very moment of death to eternal life. [Note: [Col. 1293D] The first Carn. manuscript reads, “from the danger of death itself.”]

No one therefore knows what is being done concerning him in the hidden judgments of God, because many are called, but few are chosen. Since no one is certain about himself that he has been chosen, it remains that all should tremble, all should fear concerning their conduct, all should rejoice in divine mercy alone, and no one should presume upon his own strength.

There is one who perfects our confidence: the one who deigned to assume our nature in himself, Jesus Christ, who with the Father lives and reigns, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HOMILY XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1293D] It is the twenty-fourth in Corb.; in Lateran, the twenty-sixth; in the royal Swedish manuscript, the thirtieth.]

Delivered to the people in the basilica of the blessed John, which is called Constantiniana. [Note: [Col. 1293D] In Lateran: “in the basilica of Saint Saviour.”]

[Col. 1293D] READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE XIX, 42–47

> At that time, when Jesus drew near Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “If you had known—and indeed you, in this your day, the things that are for your peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side; they will throw you and your children who are within you to the ground; and they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” [Note: [Col. 1294D] Belvac. and C. Germ. read “they will lay you low.”] And entering the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in it, saying to them: “It is written: My house is a house of prayer. But you have made it a den of robbers.” And he was teaching daily in the temple.

1644 1. I wish, if I can, to run briefly through this brief Gospel reading in a brief discourse, so that those who know how to think much from little may give it more extended attention. [Note: [Col. 1294D] This is how it should be read from the manuscripts and old editions. The printed editions have “that by the weeping [Lord].”]

No one who has read the history of the destruction of Jerusalem is unaware that the overthrow of Jerusalem is here described by the weeping Lord—the destruction carried out by Vespasian and Titus, the Roman emperors. The Roman rulers are indicated when it is said:

> For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you and hem you in on every side; they will throw you and your children who are within you to the ground.

The further statement,

> They will not leave in you one stone upon another,

is also attested by the subsequent displacement of that same city. For since it is now built in the place where the Lord was crucified, outside the gate, that former Jerusalem, as is said, was utterly destroyed.

The fault for which the punishment of its destruction was inflicted is then added:

> Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.

The Creator of all deigned to visit it through the mystery of his incarnation, but it did not remember his fear and love. Hence, too, in a prophetic rebuke of the human heart, the birds of heaven are summoned as witnesses, when it is said:

> The kite in heaven knows its time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork observe the time of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord (Jer. VIII, 7).

But first we must ask what is meant by the words:

> Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “If you had known—and indeed you.”

The Redeemer first wept over the ruin of the faithless city, before the city itself knew that this ruin was coming upon it. The weeping Lord rightly says to it:

> If you had known—and indeed you—

with “you would have wept” understood, though now, because you do not know what threatens you, you rejoice. [Note: [Col. 1294D] In C. Germ., “you would have wept” is understood. The same is read in Corb. and Gemet.]

Hence it is added:

> And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace.

For since it gave itself over to the pleasures of the flesh and did not foresee the evils to come, it possessed in its own day those things that could be for its peace. Why it regarded present goods as peace is made clear when it is said:

> But now they are hidden from your eyes.

If the evils that threatened had not been hidden from the eyes of its heart, it would not have been joyful amid present prosperity. Its punishment, which, as I said, was impending from the Roman rulers, is immediately added.

2. After this has been described, what the Lord did is related: entering the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in it, saying to them:

> It is written: My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers (Isa. LVI, 7).

The one who announced the evils to come and immediately entered the temple to drive out from it those selling and buying clearly made known that the people’s ruin arose chiefly from the fault of the priests. In describing the destruction, yet striking those selling and buying in the temple, he showed by the very effect of his action from where the root of perdition sprang.

As we have learned from another evangelist, doves were sold in the temple (Mark XI, 15). What, then, are understood by doves except the gift of the Holy Spirit? But he drives the sellers and buyers out of the temple, because he condemns either those who for a payment confer the laying on of hands or those who attempt to purchase the gift of the Spirit. [1, q. 3, c. 10]

Of that temple it is immediately added:

> My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.

Those who remained in the temple in order to receive gifts would certainly seek to injure those who did not give them; there can be no doubt of this. The house of prayer, therefore, had been made a den of robbers, because they knew how to stand in the temple for this purpose: either to persecute bodily those who did not give gifts, or to kill spiritually those who did give them.

But because our Redeemer does not withhold the words of preaching even from the unworthy and ungrateful, after he had maintained the force of discipline by driving out the perverse, he immediately displayed the gift of grace. For it follows:

> And he was teaching daily in the temple.

We have briefly passed through these matters as they concern the historical sense.

### 3

But since we know that Jerusalem has already been overthrown and, through its overthrow, transformed for the better; since we know that the robbers have been expelled from the temple and that the temple itself has now been destroyed [Col. 1295C], we ought to draw some likeness inward from outward things and fear, from the ruin of the buildings, the collapse of morals.

“For when he saw the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you had known—even you.’” He did this once, when he announced that the city was destined to perish. Our Redeemer does not cease to do this daily through his elect, whenever he sees that some have passed from a good life to depraved conduct. He mourns those who do not know why they are being mourned, because, in the words of Solomon, “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II, 14). If they had recognized the condemnation threatening them, they would have mourned themselves with the tears of the elect.

The sentence that follows appropriately applies to the soul destined to perish: “And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes.” The perverse soul has its own day, in which it rejoices in what passes away. The things present are for its peace, because, while it rejoices in temporal possessions, while it is lifted up by honors, while it dissolves itself in bodily pleasure, and while it is frightened by no fear of the punishment to come, it has peace in its own day—though on another day it will have the grave stumbling-block of its condemnation.

There it will be afflicted where the just will rejoice [Col. 1296A]; and everything that is now for its peace will then be turned into the bitterness of strife, because it will begin to quarrel with itself: why did it not dread the condemnation it is suffering? Why did it close the eyes of its mind to the evils that were to follow? Hence it is said to it: “But now they are hidden from your eyes.” For the perverse soul, devoted to present things and dissolved in earthly pleasures, hides the evils to come from itself, because it refuses to foresee the future evils [Note: Longip., “to foresee future evils”]; these would disturb its present joy. And while it abandons itself to the delights of the present life, what else does it do but go toward the fire with closed eyes?

Hence it is rightly written: “In the day of good things, do not be unmindful of evils” (Eccli. XI, 27). And through Paul it is said: “Those who rejoice, as though they were not rejoicing” (I Cor. VII, 30), because even if there is some joy in the present time, it must be lived in such a way that the bitterness of the coming judgment never departs from memory. Thus, while the fearful mind is pierced by dread of the final vengeance, the subsequent wrath may later be tempered in proportion as present joy is now restrained.

Therefore it is written: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. XXVIII, 14). For the anger of the coming judgment will then be borne all the more severely in proportion as it is now scarcely feared, even amid sins.

### 4

It follows: “For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart” [Luke XIX, 43]. Who are ever greater enemies of the human soul than the evil spirits, who besiege it as it departs from the body and cherish it, when it is set upon love of the flesh, with deceptive pleasures?

They surround it with a rampart because, bringing before the eyes of its mind the sins it has committed, they hem it in as they draw it toward fellowship in their condemnation. Thus, caught at the very extremity of life, it sees by what enemies it is enclosed, yet cannot find a way of escape, because it is no longer permitted to perform the good works that it despised when it was permitted to do them.

Of these words what follows may also aptly be understood: “They will surround you and press you in on every side.” For evil spirits constrict the soul on every side when they bring back to its memory not only the sins of its deeds, but also those of its speech and, moreover, of its thoughts. Thus the soul, which previously spread itself widely through many crimes, is at the end constricted by all of them in retribution.

It follows: “And they will strike you down to the ground, and your children who are in you” [Col. 1296D]. The soul is cast down to the ground through knowledge of its guilt [Note: In most manuscripts, both in the Gospel reading and in the homily and exposition, the reading is “they will cast you down to the ground” (ad terram consternent te). This passage seems to indicate that Gregory read “is cast down to the ground” (ad terram consternitur).] when the flesh [Note: As in C. Germ., Corb., Gemet., and Longip.; the printed editions have, “when the flesh to which it believed its life”]—which it believed to be its life—is forced to return to dust.

Its children fall into death when the unlawful thoughts that now proceed from it are scattered in the vengeance at life’s end, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Ps. CXLV, 4). These hard thoughts may also be understood through the symbolism of stones. For it follows: “And they will not leave in you one stone upon another” [Col. 1297A]. When the perverse mind adds an even more perverse thought to a perverse thought, what else does it do but place one stone upon another? But in the destroyed city no stone is left upon stone, because, when the soul is led to its punishment, the entire structure of its thoughts is scattered.

Why it suffers this is then added: “Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.” [Note: Bigot., “for every perverse soul.”]

Almighty God is accustomed to visit every perverse soul in many ways. He visits it continually by commandment, sometimes by scourging, and sometimes by miracle, so that it may hear the truth it did not know and yet, while still growing proud and despising it, may either return, pierced by grief, or, overcome by benefits, blush at the evil it has done.

But because it does not recognize the time of its visitation, at the end of life it is handed over to those enemies with whom it will be joined in the eternal judgment by an everlasting fellowship of condemnation. As it is written: “When you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort to be freed from him, lest perhaps he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer cast you into prison” (Luke XII, 58). [Note: Belvac., C. Germ., and Longip. have, “hand you over to the judge.” Bigot. and the first Carn., “hand you over to the judge.” From the Greek text, “drag” or “drag forcibly” should be read.]

Our adversary on the way is the word of God, which in the present life is opposed to our carnal desires. The one who is freed from it is the person who humbly submits to its commandments. Otherwise, the adversary will hand the sinner over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, because, on account of his contempt for the Lord’s word, the sinner will be held guilty in the judgment of the judge.

The judge hands him over to the officer because he permits him to be dragged by the evil spirit to punishment, so that the spirit itself may lead the compelled soul out of the body to punishment, though the soul had voluntarily consented to the spirit for the commission of guilt. The officer casts it into prison because through the evil spirit it is thrust into hell, until the day of judgment arrives, after which the spirit itself will also be tormented together with it in the fires of hell.

### 6

When, therefore, the destruction of the city has been completed—we have applied it as a likeness of the soul that is perishing—the text immediately adds: “And he entered the temple and began to cast out those who sold and bought in it.”

Just as the temple of God is in a city, so the life of religious persons is in the faithful people. Often some assume the religious habit and, when they receive a place among the sacred orders, turn the office of holy religion into a commerce in earthly business.

Those who sell in the temple are those who grant as a reward what belongs by right to certain people [1, q. 3, c. 10] [Col. 1297D]. For to sell justice is to preserve it in exchange for receiving a reward. Those who buy in the temple are those who, while unwilling to pay their neighbor what is just, and while refusing to do what is owed by right, purchase sin by giving a reward to their patrons.

To them it is rightly said: “My house is a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers,” because when perverse people sometimes occupy a place of religion [Note: Bigot., “some perverse people”], there they kill with the swords of their wickedness [Col. 1298A], where they ought to give life to their neighbors through the intercession of their prayer. [Note: The first two Gemet. manuscripts have “a place of governance”; the others differ.]

### 7

The temple and house of God is also the mind itself and the conscience of the faithful. Whenever it brings forth perverse thoughts to the injury of its neighbor, robbers sit there as in a den and kill those who walk innocently [Note: Longip. and Val. Cl., “whenever they pierce them with the sword”], when it drives its swords into those who are guilty of no offense.

The mind of the faithful is no longer a house of prayer but a den of robbers when, abandoning the innocence and simplicity of holiness, it strives to do something by which it may harm its neighbors.

But because we are constantly instructed against all these perversities by the words of our Redeemer through the sacred pages, what is now being done is what is reported to have been done then, when it is said: “And he was teaching daily in the temple” [Col. 1298B]. For whenever Truth carefully teaches the minds of the faithful to avoid evils, it teaches daily in the temple.

We must know, however, that we are truly instructed by the words of truth if we gaze upon our final evils with fear and without ceasing, in accordance with what a certain wise man says: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Eccli. VII, 40).

We ought daily to weigh what we have heard from the voice of that same Redeemer: “And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes.” While the strict Judge delays and does not yet stretch out his hand to strike; while there appears to be some security of time before the final vengeance of retribution, we ought to weigh the evil that follows [Col. 1298C]: weighing it, to groan; groaning, to avoid it; and looking unceasingly upon the sins we have committed, looking, to weep; and weeping, to wipe them away.

Let no joy of transitory prosperity dissolve us [Note: C. Germ., “let no prosperity of transient praise and joy dissolve us”; Bigot. agrees], nor let transient things block the eyes of our mind [Note: Corb., “nor let the blind be led to the fire”], nor let them lead the blind to the fire.

For if the weight of the reproach is strictly considered, it is recognized from the mouth of Truth, when it is said to the negligent person who does not foresee the future: “And indeed in this your day, the things that are for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes.”

### 8

We must think very seriously how terrifying the hour of our departure will be: what fear of mind there will then be, how great the memory of all evils, what forgetfulness of past happiness, and what dread and consideration of the Judge.

What, then, ought there to be for us in present things that gives delight, when, while everything passes away together, what threatens cannot pass away? When what is loved is utterly ended, and that place begins where pain never ends?

Then evil spirits seek their works in the departing soul; then they bring back the evils they suggested, so that they may drag their companion to torments. But why do we speak of this only concerning a perverse soul, when they also come to the elect as they depart, and, if they prevail, seek something of their own in them?

There was one among human beings who, before his passion, said with a free voice: “I will not speak much more with you, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV, 30) [Col. 1299A]. Because he saw this man as mortal, the prince of the world believed that he could find something of his own in him. But he departed from the corruption of the world without any sin, just as he came into the world without sin.

Peter did not dare say this about himself against the prince of the world, although he was worthy to hear: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19). Nor did Paul dare say it, although, before paying the debt of death, he reached the secrets of the third heaven (II Cor. XII, 2). Nor did John dare say it, although, because of his exceptional love, he reclined at the breast of his Redeemer at supper (John XXI, 20).

For since the Prophet says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth” (Ps. L, 7), the one who came into the world with guilt could not be in the world without guilt. Hence the same Prophet says: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). Hence Solomon says: “There is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII, 21). Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8). Hence James says: “For we all offend in many things” (James III, 2).

It is therefore certain that all who have been conceived through the pleasure of the flesh have, without doubt, something belonging to the prince of this world in either their action, their speech, or their thought [Col. 1299C]. But for this reason he could neither seize them afterward nor hold them beforehand, because the one who rescued them from their debts paid on our behalf the debt he did not owe, so that our debts might not hold us under the power of our enemy: Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and human beings, freely paid on our behalf what he did not owe. [Note: Some manuscripts have, “Jesus, as though from a debt, freely repaid what he did not owe.”] [Note: The first two Gemet. manuscripts have “without doubt.”]

For he who paid on our behalf the debt of an undeserved bodily death freed us from the deserved death of the soul.

He therefore says: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Hence we must take care and think daily with great tears how furious and terrifying the prince of this world will come on the day of our departure, seeking his works in us, if he came even to God dying in the flesh and sought something in him in whom he could find nothing [Col. 1299D]. [Note: C. Germ. has “how swift”; Carnut. and many others, “how savage.”]

### 9

What, then, shall we wretches say, and what shall we do, who have committed innumerable evils? What shall we say when the adversary seeks and finds much of his own in us, except what is our one certain refuge and solid hope: that we have become one with him in whom the prince of this world both sought something of his own and could find nothing? For he alone is “free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5).

We are released from the service of sin by true freedom because we are joined to the one who is truly free. We cannot deny it; we acknowledge it truthfully: the prince of this world has much in us. Nevertheless, at the time of our death he is no longer able to seize us, because we have become members of the one in whom he has nothing.

But what good does it do that we are joined to our Redeemer by faith if we are separated from him in conduct? He himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Right works must therefore be joined to right faith. Let us wash away the evils we have committed through daily lamentation. Let the upright works that arise from love of God and neighbor overcome our past wickedness. Let us refuse no good that we are able to offer our brothers and sisters.

For we do not otherwise become members of our Redeemer except by clinging to God and showing compassion toward our neighbor.

### 10

But because examples generally rouse the hearts of hearers to love of God and neighbor more than words do, I wish to tell your charity what my son Epiphanius, the deacon who is present here and who came from the province of Isauria, regularly relates about a miracle that occurred in the neighboring land of Lycaonia.

He says that in that region there was a highly venerable monk named Martyrius, who was traveling from his own monastery to another monastery for the sake of a visit; a spiritual father presided over the latter.

As he traveled, he found on the road a leper whose limbs had been disfigured by elephantiasis and dense sores. The man wished to return to his lodging but was unable to do so because of exhaustion. He said that his lodging was along the very road to which the monk Martyrius was hastening.

Moved by compassion for the leper’s weariness, the man of God immediately threw his cloak onto the ground and spread it out. He placed the leper upon it, wrapped him all around in his cloak, lifted him onto his shoulder, and carried him back with him.

When he was already approaching the monastery gates, the spiritual father of that monastery began to shout loudly: “Run! Open the monastery gates quickly, because Brother Martyrius is coming, carrying the Lord.”

As soon as Martyrius reached the entrance of the monastery, the one who had appeared to be a leper leapt from his neck and appeared in the form in which the Redeemer of the human race, God and man, Christ Jesus, is accustomed to be recognized by human beings. In the sight of Martyrius he returned to heaven, and as he ascended he said to him: “Martyrius, you were not ashamed of me on earth; I will not be ashamed of you in heaven.”

As soon as the holy man entered the monastery, the father of the monastery said to him: “Brother Martyrius, where is the man you were carrying?” He replied: “If I had known who he was, I would have held his feet.”

Martyrius then related that, when he had carried him, he had felt none of his weight. And no wonder: how could he feel the weight of the one who was carrying the bearer?

In this we must consider how powerful fraternal compassion is, and how the bowels of mercy join us to almighty God [Col. 1301A]. We draw near to the one who is above all things precisely where, through compassion for our neighbor, we lower ourselves even beneath ourselves.

In bodily matters no one touches high places unless he is stretched upward; in spiritual matters, however, it is certain that the more we are drawn downward through compassion, the more truly we approach the heights.

Behold, the Redeemer of the human race did not consider it sufficient for our instruction to declare that at the final judgment he would say: “As long as you did it for one of these least of my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV, 40). Before the judgment he also wished to demonstrate in himself what he had said, so that he might show that whoever now performs good works for the needy renders them especially to the one for whose love he performs them.

And each person receives a greater reward in proportion as he does not despise even the one who appears more deserving of contempt.

For what is higher in human flesh than the flesh of Christ, which has been exalted above the angels? And what is lower in human flesh than the flesh of a leper, which is torn by swollen wounds and filled with exhaled stench?

Yet behold, he appeared in the form of a leper; and the one who is worthy of reverence above all did not disdain to be seen as despised below all. Why did he do this, except to warn us, whose understanding is slow, so that whoever hastens to serve him who is in heaven may not refuse to humble himself on earth and to show compassion even toward brothers who are lowly and contemptible?

I had resolved to speak briefly to your charity; but since “a person’s way is not in himself” (Jer. X, 23), the discourse cannot be restrained when the one about whom we speak directs it. He lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: In Corb. it is the twenty-first; in Lateran. the eleventh; in the Swedish royal manuscript, the thirty-first.]

# HOMILY XL

Delivered to the people in the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr [Note: This is absent from C. Germ. and many others. In the first two Gemet. manuscripts this homily is said to have been delivered in the basilica of Saint Savior; otherwise in the Lateran manuscript, the Swedish royal manuscript, Corb., Germ., and others.]

## LESSON FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE XVI, 19–31

At that time Jesus said to his disciples:

“There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen [Note: Belvac. and Corb. Germ., here and below, “and he clothed himself”], and he feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything. Moreover, the dogs came and licked his sores.

“Now it happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into the bosom of Abraham. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And lifting up his eyes when he was in torments, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom. And he cried out and said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water, so that he may cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.’

“And Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted here, while you are tormented. And in all these things a great chasm has been established between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to here.’

“And he said: ‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.’

“And Abraham said to him: ‘They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.’

“But he said: ‘No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’

“And he said to him: ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.’”

### 1

In the words of sacred Scripture, dearly beloved brothers, the truth of the history must first be preserved, and afterward the spiritual understanding of the allegory must be sought. The fruit of allegory is then tasted sweetly when it has first been made firm through history as upon the root of truth.

But because allegory sometimes builds up faith, and history builds moral character, we who, with God as author, now speak to the faithful do not think it inappropriate to reverse the order of speaking. Thus, since you already hold firm faith, you should first hear briefly something about the allegory; and what is especially necessary for you from the morality of the history should be reserved for the end of our exposition, because what is heard afterward is often remembered better.

### 2

We shall therefore pass briefly over the allegorical meanings, so that we may come more quickly to the breadth of moral instruction.

“There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day.” Whom, dearly beloved brothers, does this rich man signify—the one who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day—if not the Jewish people? It possessed an outward cultivation of life; it used the delights of the law it had received for splendor, not for usefulness.

Whom does Lazarus, full of sores, figuratively express if not the Gentile people? When he turned to God and was not ashamed to confess his sins, he had a wound in his skin. For in a wound of the skin, corruption is drawn from the inward parts and bursts outward. What, then, is the confession of sins except a kind of breaking open of wounds? In confession, the corruption of sin that lay hidden pestilently in the mind is healthfully opened.

Wounds of the skin draw putrid moisture to the surface. And when we confess our sins, what else do we do except open the evil that lay hidden within us?

But Lazarus, wounded, desired to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any, because that proud people despised admitting any Gentile to knowledge of the law. Since it possessed the teaching of the law not for charity but for exaltation, it swelled with pride as though from wealth it had received.

And because words flowed from its knowledge, they fell like crumbs from a table. But, on the other hand, dogs licked the wounds of the poor man who lay there.

In sacred Scripture, preachers are sometimes understood by dogs. The tongue of a dog, when it licks a wound, heals it; likewise holy teachers, when they instruct us in the confession of our sin, touch the wound of the mind, as it were, with their tongue. Because they rescue us from sins by speaking, they restore us to health as though by touching our wounds.

Since the tongue of preachers is signified by the name of dogs, the Lord says through the Psalmist: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him” (Ps. LXVII, 24). From the unbelieving Jews holy preachers were chosen; in their assertion of the truth against thieves and robbers who came, they gave, so to speak, great barking for the Lord.

By contrast, concerning the rejection of certain people it is said: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI, 10).

Therefore, because holy preachers condemn sins but approve the confession of sinners, saying, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James V, 16), the dogs lick Lazarus’s sores. For when holy teachers receive the confessions of the Gentiles, they restore the wounds of their minds to health.

Hence Lazarus is rightly interpreted as “helped,” because they help him toward deliverance, healing his wounds through the correction of the tongue.

The licking of dogs may also signify the broad tongue of flatterers. To flatteringly lick our wounds is what they often do when, through wicked favor, they praise even the evils that we ourselves condemn in ourselves. [Note: The first Carn. has, “for it is thus marked, while …”]

It happened that both died. The rich man, who had been clothed in purple and fine linen, was buried in hell; but Lazarus was led by angels into Abraham’s bosom.

What does Abraham’s bosom signify except the hidden rest of the fathers? [Note: C. Germ., Gemet., and Belvac. have, “signifies the bosom of the father.”] Concerning it Truth says: “Many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII, 11).

The one who is said to have been clothed in purple and fine linen is rightly called a child of the kingdom. He lifts his eyes from far away to see Lazarus because, while unbelievers are below in the punishments of their condemnation, before the day of the final judgment they observe the faithful resting above them; but they cannot in any way contemplate their joys afterward. What they see is far away because they cannot reach that place by merit.

He is shown to burn more intensely in his tongue when he says: “Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water, so that he may cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke XVI, 24) [Note: Belvac. has, “and cool it.”]

The unbelieving people held the words of the law in their mouth but refused to preserve them in practice. Therefore it will burn more intensely there, where it showed that it knew what it refused to do.

Hence Solomon rightly says of the learned and negligent: “All the labor of a person is in his mouth, but his soul will not be filled” (Eccl. VI, 7). Whoever labors only to know what he ought to say fasts with an empty mind from the very nourishment of his knowledge. [Note: The first two Gemet. manuscripts and Bigot. have, “from the knowledge of its very nourishment.”]

He desires to be touched by the tip of the finger because, given over to eternal punishments, he wishes to share even minimally in the works of the just. He is told that he received good things in this life [Col. 1304A], because he considered all his joy to consist in transitory happiness.

The just too can have good things here, yet not receive them as recompense, because, while they desire better things—that is, eternal things—whatever goods may be present appear to them, while they burn with holy desires, to be no goods at all.

Hence the prophet David, who was supported by the wealth of a kingdom and many attendants [Note: The second Carn. has, “and many honors.” “Attendants” means servants attending him, as in Book II of the Dialogues, chapter 4, where it says that other attendants and sword-bearers were provided for him], although he saw that these too were good for necessity, nevertheless yearned ardently for the one Good alone, saying: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28).

Meanwhile, we should notice that he is told: “Remember, son.” Behold, Abraham calls him son, yet does not free him from torment, because the faithful forefathers of this unbelieving people, seeing that many have strayed from their faith, do not rescue them from torments by any compassion, although they recognize them as sons according to the flesh.

The rich man, placed in torments, says that he has five brothers because that same proud Jewish people, already condemned in large part, knows that it left behind on earth followers devoted to the five bodily senses. [Note: There is disagreement among the manuscripts here. We follow the ancient Belvac., Corb., C. Germ., and Bigot.; in it, however—unlike the others—the word “knows” is added. The first Carn. has “left behind,” and says that the five books of Moses were understood carnally by those devoted to the five bodily senses.]

He expresses by the number five the brothers he had left behind, because, while placed in hell, he grieves that they do not rise to spiritual understanding, and asks that Lazarus be sent to them.

He is told that they have Moses and the prophets. But he says that they will not believe unless someone rises from the dead. He is immediately answered: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe him if someone rises from the dead.”

Certainly Truth says concerning Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John V, 46). What is said in Abraham’s answer is therefore fulfilled. The Lord rose from the dead; but because that Jewish people refused to believe Moses, it also refused to believe him who rose from the dead. And because it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not reach the one about whom Moses had spoken.

### 3

Let it suffice, dearly beloved brothers, that we have briefly passed over these matters in order to investigate the mysteries of the allegory [Note: The printed editions have “to indicate the mysteries of the allegory”]. Now let the mind return to contemplate more broadly the moral meaning of the event:

“There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay before the rich man’s gate, full of sores.”

Some think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New; but they are deceived by this inconsiderate judgment. In the former, it is not stinginess but robbery that is punished (II Kings XII, 6). There, a thing unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution (Matt. XIX, 8). Here, however, this rich man is not reproved for taking what belonged to another, but for failing to give what belonged to himself. He is not said to have oppressed anyone by force, but to have exalted himself in the possessions he had received.

From this we must conclude with the utmost care what punishment awaits one who seizes what belongs to another, if the condemnation of hell strikes the person who does not give what is his own. [Note: The first Carn. reads, “if he is struck in the depths of hell by condemnation.”]

Let no one therefore consider himself secure by saying: “Behold, I do not seize what belongs to another, but I enjoy possessions lawfully granted,” because this rich man was not punished on account of taking what belonged to another, but because he abandoned himself wickedly amid the possessions he had received. [Note: The first two Gemet. manuscripts have, “I use granted possessions.”]

This also was what handed him over to hell: he was not cautious amid his happiness; he bent the gifts he had received toward the use of arrogance; he ignored the bowels of compassion; and, although he had abundant means, he refused to redeem his sins.

There are also some who do not think that the cultivation of fine and costly clothing is a sin. But if this were not a fault, the word of God would never so carefully have expressed that the rich man who was tormented in hell had been clothed in fine linen and purple [Col. 1305B].

No one seeks especially distinguished clothing except for empty glory—that is, so that he may appear more honored than others. That more costly clothing is sought for empty glory alone is shown by the fact that no one wishes to wear expensive clothes where he cannot be seen by others. [Note: All our manuscripts agree on this reading, and the older editions agree with them. More recent editions, instead of “especially,” have “costly.”]

We can also gather the nature of this fault more clearly from the opposite case. If the rejection of cheap clothing were not a virtue, the Evangelist would not have carefully said of John: “He was clothed in camel’s hair” (Matt. III, 4).

But we must carefully note the order of narration in the mouth of Truth concerning the proud rich man and the humble poor man. Behold, it says: “There was a certain rich man,” and immediately it adds: “And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus.”

Certainly, among the people, the names of the rich are usually more widely known than those of the poor. What, then, does it mean that the Lord, speaking of the poor man and the rich man, gives the poor man’s name but does not give the rich man’s, except that God knows and approves the humble but does not know the proud?

Hence, at the end, he will say to certain people who are proud of the power of miracles: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23). [Note: Bigot. has, “who work iniquity.”] But to Moses he says: “I know you by name” (Exod. XXXIII, 12).

Thus he says of the rich man: “A certain man.” He says of the poor man: “A needy man named Lazarus.” It is as though he were openly saying: “I know the humble poor man; I do not know the proud rich man. I hold the former as known through approval; the latter I ignore through the judgment of rejection.”

[Col. 1305D] 4. We must also consider how thoughtfully our Creator orders all things. For one thing is done not merely for one purpose. For behold, the beggar Lazarus, covered with sores, lies at the rich man’s gate. By means of this one circumstance the Lord accomplished two judgments. For the rich man might perhaps have had some excuse if Lazarus, poor and covered with sores, had not lain at his gate; if he had been far away; if his poverty had not been an unwelcome sight before the rich man’s eyes. Conversely, if the rich man had been far from the eyes of the sore-covered poor man, the poor man would have endured a lesser trial in his heart. [Col. 1306A] But when He placed the needy and wounded man before the gate of the rich man, who abounded in luxuries, through one and the same circumstance He both imposed an accumulation of condemnation upon the rich man, who did not show mercy at the sight of the poor man, and, again, tested the poor man daily by the sight of the rich man. [1656] For how many temptations do you suppose this needy man, beset with wounds, endured in his thoughts, when he himself lacked bread and did not even have health [Note: [Col. 1306D] This should be read on the basis of the manuscripts of Beauvais, Corbie, Saint-Germain, Jumièges, and others. Here *salutem* signifies health, as the printed editions have it.], while he saw before him a rich man possessing health and [Note: [Col. 1306D] Beauvais: “wealth.”] luxuries with delight; when he saw himself afflicted by pain and cold, while the other rejoiced, clothed in fine linen and purple; when he was weighed down by wounds, while the other overflowed with possessions; when he was in need, while the other was unwilling to give? How great, my brothers, do we suppose the tumult of temptation then was in the poor man’s heart [Col. 1306B]—he for whom poverty alone might have been sufficient punishment, even had he been healthy, and illness alone might likewise have been sufficient, even had assistance been available? But so that the poor man might be tested more fully, both poverty and illness together consumed him.

[Col. 1306D] Moreover, he saw the rich man going out, supported and surrounded by throngs of attendants, while no one visited him in his sickness and want. Indeed, because no one came to visit him, the dogs bear witness: they freely licked his wounds. Thus, from one circumstance almighty God displayed two judgments, permitting Lazarus the poor man to lie before the rich man’s gate so that the wicked rich man might increase the punishment of his condemnation, while the tested poor man might grow toward his reward. The one saw daily the man toward whom he showed no mercy; the other saw the man by whom he was being tested. [Col. 1307A] [Col. 1306C] Two hearts below, but one observer above: He exercised the one through testing toward glory, and by tolerating the other awaited him for punishment. For the text continues:

5. “It came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell.” This rich man, who in this life had been unwilling to show mercy to the one now placed in his punishment, seeks him as a patron. For immediately it is added: “Lifting up his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham far off and Lazarus in his bosom. And crying out, he said, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.’”

O how subtle are the judgments of God! O how rigorously the recompense of good and evil deeds is administered! It was certainly said above that in this life Lazarus sought the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any; now, concerning the rich man’s punishment, it is said that he desires water to be dripped into his mouth from the tip of Lazarus’s finger. From this, brothers, from this, gather how rigorous is the severity of God. For this rich man, who had been unwilling to give even the smallest thing from his table to the wounded poor man, once placed in hell, came to seek even the smallest thing. He who denied crumbs of bread asked for a drop of water.

But we must carefully consider why the rich man, placed in the fire, asks that his tongue be cooled. It is the custom of sacred Scripture sometimes to say one thing while suggesting another through the same statement. Above, the Lord had said that this proud rich man was not devoted to loquacity but to extravagant feasting. Nor did He describe him as guilty of talkativeness, but as having sinned through gluttony, pride, and greed. [Note: [Col. 1307D] Thus it is read in the manuscripts. The editors chose to print *notavit* (“noted”) in place of *narravit* (“described”).] Yet because talkativeness commonly accompanies banquets, the man who is said here to have feasted wickedly is said to burn more grievously in hell upon his tongue. For the first fault that attends those who feast wickedly is loquacity; after loquacity comes the frivolity of play. [1657] That gluttony is followed by play is attested by Holy Scripture, which says: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” [Col. 1307B] (Exod. XXXII, 6). But before the body moves to play, the tongue is moved to jokes and empty words. What, then, is indicated by the fact that the rich man, placed in torment, asks for his tongue to be cooled, unless it is that the man who had sinned more grievously through loquacity while feasting was, by the justice of retribution, burning more fiercely in his tongue?

6. But we must consider with very great fear [*On Penance*, distinction 3, canon “Cavendum”; Note: [Col. 1307D] Gratian does not report the exact words at the cited place, but only the sense, and indeed only in part.] what is said to him in Abraham’s reply: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted, and you are tormented.” This statement, my brothers, requires fear rather than explanation. [Col. 1307D] For if any of you have received some outward good in this world, you ought, so to speak, to fear that outward gift itself [Col. 1307C], lest it have been given to you as recompense for some of your deeds; lest the Judge who here restores outward goods exclude you from the recompense of inward goodness; lest honor or wealth here be not an aid to virtue but payment for labor.

For when it is said, “You received good things during your life,” it is indicated that this rich man possessed some good for which he received good things in this life. Again, when it is said of Lazarus that he received evil things, it plainly shows that Lazarus too possessed some evil that needed to be purified. But the fire of poverty purified Lazarus’s evils, while the prosperity of passing life rewarded the rich man’s good things. Poverty afflicted and cleansed the one; abundance rewarded and rejected the other.

Therefore, all of you who possess good things in this world, when you recall that you have done good, fear greatly because of those very things, lest the prosperity granted to you be their recompense. And when you see certain poor people committing reprehensible acts, do not despise them and do not despair of them, because perhaps what the excess of the slightest perversity [Note: [Col. 1307D] The printed editions read “those whom excess...”] stains, the furnace of poverty purifies. Fear greatly concerning yourselves, because even some who have acted badly have been followed by a prosperous life. [Col. 1308A] But consider their condition with concern, because their teacher, poverty, torments their life until it leads them to uprightness.

7. It continues: “And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us.” Here we must ask carefully how it can be said, “Those who wish to cross from here to you cannot.” For there is no doubt that those who are in hell desire to cross over to the lot of the blessed. But in what way can it be said that those already received into the lot of blessedness wish to cross over to those who are tormented in hell?

Yet just as the rejected desire to cross over to the elect—that is, to depart from the affliction of their punishments—so it belongs to the righteous to cross over mentally to the afflicted and those placed in torment, through mercy [Col. 1308B], and to wish to set them free. But those who wish to cross from the seat of the blessed to the afflicted and those placed in torment cannot, because although the souls of the righteous possess mercy according to the goodness of their nature, they are then joined to the justice of their Creator and bound by such complete uprightness that they are moved by no compassion toward the rejected. [Note: [Col. 1307D] In the Longipont manuscript, after “are moved,” there is added: “even if they wished to show mercy, then they could no longer do so at all. For they...”]

They agree with the Judge to whom they cling, and they do not stoop even through mercy toward those whom they cannot rescue [1658], because they will then see them to be as alien from themselves as they see them rejected by their Creator, whom they love. [Note: [Col. 1308D] The first two manuscripts of Jumièges: “they perceive themselves to have been in no way rejected.”] Thus the unjust do not cross over to the lot of the blessed, because they are bound by everlasting condemnation; nor can the righteous cross over to the rejected, because, already raised up through the justice [Note: [Col. 1308D] Chartres: “of the Judge.”] of judgment, they have no compassion for them in any way. [Col. 1308C]

8. But after hope for himself has been removed from the burning rich man, his mind turns back to the relatives whom he had left behind, because punishment eventually teaches the minds of the rejected—though uselessly—to love, so that they then love spiritually even their own, whom here, while they loved sins, they did not love themselves. [Note: [Col. 1308D] The first manuscript of Chartres: “whom here, while they loved sins, they neither loved nor loved together with themselves.”]

Thus it is now added: “I beg you, therefore, Father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, [Note: [Col. 1308D] Beauvais, Saint-Germain, and the first two manuscripts of Jumièges: “so that Lazarus may testify to them.” Saint-Germain, however, has “so that he may testify” in the Gospel reading.] so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.”

Here we must note [Col. 1308D] how many things are heaped upon the burning rich man for his punishment. For knowledge and memory are preserved for his punishment. He recognizes Lazarus, whom he despised, and he remembers his brothers, whom he left behind. His vengeance against the poor man would not be complete if he did not recognize him in the recompense. Nor would his punishment in the fire be complete if he did not fear for his own relatives the very thing he himself suffers. [Note: [Col. 1308D] Beauvais: “what he suffers in himself.”]

Thus, in order that sinners may be punished more severely in their torment, they see the glory of those whom they despised, and they are tormented also by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly.

It should be believed that before the final judgment of retribution the unjust [Col. 1309A] behold certain righteous people in repose, so that, seeing them in joy, they may suffer not only because of their own punishment but also because of the blessedness of those others. The righteous, however, continually behold the unjust in torment, so that their joy may increase from seeing the evil which they mercifully escaped; and they give greater thanks to their Deliverer as they see in others what they themselves might have suffered had they been left behind.

Nor does the sight of the rejected’s punishment darken that great brightness of blessedness in the minds of the righteous, because where compassion for misery will no longer exist, it will certainly not be able to diminish the joy of the blessed. What wonder is it, then, if, while the righteous behold the torments of the unjust, this contributes to their joys, when even in a painting black is placed beneath another color so that white or red may appear more vivid? [Col. 1309B] For, as has been said, the joys of the good increase in proportion as the evils of the condemned, from which they escaped, lie beneath their eyes. And although their own joys fully suffice for their enjoyment, they nevertheless always behold the evils of the rejected, because those who see the glory of their Creator can see nothing that is done within creation which they cannot see.

9. When the rich man asks that Lazarus be sent, Abraham immediately replies: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” But the man who had despised the words of God supposed that his followers could not hear these things. Therefore the rich man replied: “No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will believe.” To him the truthful sentence is immediately spoken: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead,” because [Col. 1309C] those who despise the words of the Law will fulfill the commands of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, with all the greater difficulty the more profound those commands are.

For whatever is said through the Law is less [Deut. XII] [1659] than what is commanded through the Lord. The Law commands the giving of tithes, whereas our Redeemer commands those who pursue perfection to relinquish everything. The Law cuts away sins of the flesh, whereas our Redeemer also condemns illicit thoughts (Luke XIV). If, therefore, they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead, because when will those who neglect to fulfill the less demanding precepts of the Law grow strong enough to obey the higher commands of our Savior? And it is plainly evident that those who refuse to fulfill his words certainly refuse to believe in him. Let what we have said concerning the consideration of the event itself [Col. 1309D] suffice.

10. But you, brothers, knowing both Lazarus’s rest and the rich man’s punishment, act diligently: seek intercessors for your sins, and procure the poor as advocates for you on the day of judgment. For you now have many Lazaruses; they lie before your gates and need those things which, when you are already satisfied, fall daily from your table.

The words of sacred reading ought to instruct us to fulfill the commands of compassion. [Col. 1310A] Every day, if we seek Lazarus, we find him; every day, even if we do not seek Lazarus, we see him. Behold, the poor thrust themselves upon us uninvited and beg us—those who will then come as intercessors for us. Certainly we ought altogether to have been the ones begging, yet we are begged. Consider whether we ought to refuse what is requested when those who ask are our patrons.

Do not, therefore, lose the times of mercy; do not disregard the remedies granted to you. Before punishment, think about punishment. When you see people cast down in this world, even if some reprehensible things seem to characterize them, do not despise them, because perhaps those whom weakness of character wounds are healed by the medicine of poverty. If they possess faults that ought rightly to be reproved, turn them, if you wish, to the use of your reward, so that from their very vices an increase of compassion may be accumulated for you [Col. 1310B]; give them both bread and the word—bread for refreshment together with the word of correction—so that those who were seeking one nourishment may receive two from you, being filled outwardly with food and inwardly with instruction.

When a poor person is seen to be blameworthy, he should be admonished, not despised. But if he has nothing blameworthy, he should be honored with the greatest reverence as an intercessor. Yet behold, we see many people whose worth we do not know. All, therefore, must be honored, and you must humble yourself before everyone all the more necessarily [Col. 1310C] because you do not know which of them is Christ. [Note: [Col. 1310D] Corbie: “who among them is Christ.”]

11. I shall relate an event which my brother and fellow priest Speciosus, who is present here, knows well. [Col. 1310D] At the same time that I entered the monastery, a certain old woman named Redempta, living in the habit of a nun, dwelt in this city beside the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin [Note: [Col. 1310D] The adverb “ever” is omitted in the printed editions; we have restored it from the manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Jumièges, Bigot, and others.] (*Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 15). She had been a disciple of Herundina, who, renowned for great virtues, was said to have led an eremitical life in the mountains above Praeneste.

Two disciples in the same habit clung to her: one named Romula, and the other, who still survives, whom I know by sight but not by name. These three, living together in one dwelling, led a life rich in virtues but poor in possessions. The Romula whom I have mentioned surpassed the other fellow disciple whom I have described in the great merits of her life. [1660] She possessed extraordinary patience and the highest obedience; she guarded her mouth in silence and was exceedingly devoted to continual prayer.
