But because those whom people already consider perfect often still possess some imperfection in the eyes of the supreme Craftsman—just as inexperienced people often see seals not yet perfectly carved and already praise them as if they were finished, while the craftsman still examines and smooths them, hearing them praised but not ceasing to strike them in order to improve them—the Romula whom I have mentioned was afflicted by the bodily illness which physicians call, in Greek, *paralysis*. For many years she lay on a bed [Col. 1311A] almost deprived of the use of all her limbs [Note: [Col. 1311C] Another reading: “she lay almost entirely deprived of the use of her limbs.”], yet these scourges did not drive her mind to impatience. For the impairments of her limbs became increases in virtue, because she grew ever more diligently in the practice of prayer, precisely because she was entirely unable to do anything else.

One night she called the aforementioned Redempta, who nourished both her disciples as though they were daughters [Note: [Col. 1311C–D] Gussanville ridiculously prints *silvarum* (“of forests”) in place of *filiarum* (“of daughters”), doubtless through a gross typographical error; yet the expurgatory index denied it a place.], saying: “Mother, come; mother, come.” Redempta immediately rose with the other disciple, as both of them later related, and as the event became known to many; I also learned of it at the same time.

When, in the middle of the night, they stood beside the bed on which Romula lay, suddenly a light sent from heaven filled the entire space of her cell. The radiance of such brilliance flashed forth that it struck terror into the hearts of those standing by [Col. 1311B]; as they themselves later reported, their whole bodies stiffened and they remained in sudden stupor.

Then there began to be heard what seemed to be the sound of a great multitude entering. The door of the cell was shaken, as though a crowd of those entering were pressing against it. They said that they sensed the multitude coming in, but because of the excess of fear and light they could see nothing: terror had weighed down their eyes, and the brilliance of so great a light dazzled them. That light was immediately followed by a fragrance of wonderful sweetness, so that the pleasantness of the scent soothed their spirits, which the light sent from heaven had terrified.

But when they could no longer endure the force of that brilliance, Romula began to console Redempta, who stood beside her trembling—the teacher of her way of life—with a gentle voice [Col. 1311C], saying: “Do not be afraid, mother; I am not dying now.” When she had repeated this often, the light that had been sent gradually withdrew, but the fragrance that followed it remained. Thus the second and third days passed, while they remained enveloped in the fragrance.

On the fourth night she called her teacher again. When Redempta came, Romula asked for and received the viaticum [Note: [Col. 1311D] Although *viaticum* does not always signify the Eucharist, which according to Christian custom is given to those departing this life, here it must be understood in that sense. We discussed this subject in the notes to the *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 15.].

Redempta and the other disciple had not yet withdrawn from the bedside of the one who lay there when, suddenly, before the door of that cell in the street, two choirs of those singing took their places. As the women themselves said, they distinguished the sexes by their voices: the men sang the psalmody, and the women responded. While a heavenly funeral procession was being conducted before the door of the cell [Col. 1312A], that holy soul was released from the flesh. When she had been led to heaven, the higher the choirs of singers ascended, the more softly the psalmody began to be heard, until both the sound of the psalmody and the sweetness of the fragrance faded away in the distance.

12. While she lived in the body, who honored her? She seemed unworthy to everyone and despised by all. Who would deign to approach her, or even to see her? Yet God’s pearl lay hidden in a dunghill. [Note: [Col. 1312D] “Dunghill” is absent from Beauvais. Brothers, by this dunghill I mean the very corruption of the body. It is nevertheless read in another manuscript, especially in the very ancient Corbie-Saint-Germain manuscript.]

Brothers, by this dunghill I mean the very corruption of the body; I call the abjection of poverty a dunghill. The pearl, therefore, which lay in the dunghill was taken up and placed in the adornment of the heavenly King. Now it shines among the citizens above; now it flashes among those fiery stones of the eternal diadem. [Col. 1312B]

You who either believe yourselves to be rich in this world or actually are rich, compare, if you can, your false riches with Romula’s true riches. You possess everything on the road of this world only to lose it all; she sought nothing on the journey and found everything upon arrival. You lead a joyful life and fear a sorrowful death; she endured a sorrowful life and reached a joyful death. You seek the service of human beings for a time; she, despised by human beings, found the choirs of angels as her companions.

Learn, therefore, brothers, to despise all temporal things; learn to scorn passing honor and to love eternal glory. Honor those whom you see to be poor, and consider those whom you see outwardly despised by the world to be inwardly friends of God. Share with them what you possess, so that they may one day deign to share with you what they possess.

Consider what is said by the mouth of the teacher of the nations [Col. 1312C]: “At the present time, let your abundance supply their want, so that their abundance may also supply your want” (II Cor. VIII, 14). Consider what Truth itself says: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV, 45). Why are you slow to give, when what you extend to one lying on the earth you give to one seated in heaven?

But may almighty God, who speaks these things through me into your ears, speak them through Himself into your hearts—He who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1311]

## PRAYER OF SAINT GREGORY TO THE PEOPLE CONCERNING MORTALITY (C, S)

[Col. 1311D] 1660 Dearest brothers, we ought to fear the scourges of God that we should have dreaded were coming; at least let us fear those that are now present and experienced. Let sorrow open for us the way to conversion [Note: [Col. 1311D] Saint-Germain: “of conduct.”], and let the punishment we already suffer dissolve the hardness of our hearts. For, as the prophet testifies [Col. 1312D], it was foretold: “The sword has reached even to the soul” (Jer. IV, 10). [Note: [Col. 1312D] Bigot: “even to our souls.”]

[1661] Behold, the whole people are struck by the sword of heavenly anger, and individuals are laid waste by sudden death. Illness does not precede death; rather, as you see, death itself outruns even the delays of illness. [Col. 1313A] Each person who is struck is carried off before turning to the lamentation of repentance.

Consider, therefore, in what condition one reaches the presence of the strict Judge [1662] when he has no time to mourn what he has done. [Note: [Col. 1313B] The first two manuscripts of Bigot and Utica: “for whom it is not permitted...”] The inhabitants are not taken away only in part but fall together. Houses are left empty; parents look upon the funerals of their children, and their own heirs precede them to destruction.

Let each one of us, therefore, flee to the lamentation of repentance while there is time to weep before the blow falls. Let us recall before the eyes of our mind whatever we have committed through error, and punish by weeping what we have wickedly done. Let us go before His face in confession (Ps. XCII, 2), and, as the prophet exhorts: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God” (Lam. III, 41). To lift the heart to God together with the hands means to raise the devotion of our prayer together with the merit of good works. [Col. 1313B]

He certainly gives confidence to our trembling who cries through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). Let no one despair because of the enormity of his sins. A three-day repentance wiped away the long-standing offenses of the Ninevites (Jon. III), and the converted thief earned the rewards of life even while under sentence of death (Luke XXIII).

Let us therefore change our hearts and presume that we have already received what we ask. The Judge is more quickly bent toward prayer if the one asking is corrected from his wickedness. As the sword of so great a punishment hangs over us, let us persist in urgent prayers. For the importunity that is usually displeasing to human beings is pleasing to the judgment of truth, because the merciful and compassionate God [1663] wishes pardon to be demanded from Him through prayers—He who does not wish to grow angry in proportion to what we deserve. [Col. 1314A] [Note: [Col. 1313B] The printed editions read “to the true Judge,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts, without a single exception. Gregory of Tours also reads “to the judgment.”]

For this reason the Psalmist says: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. XLIX, 15). He is therefore His own witness that He desires to show mercy to those who call upon Him, since He urges them to call upon Him.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite hearts and corrected deeds, let us come tomorrow, from dawn on Wednesday itself, to the sevenfold litany designated below, with devoted minds and tears. [Note: [Col. 1313B] The first manuscript of Bigot reads: “let us come to the sevenfold litany... with a mind devoted to tears.” The sermon ends here in the Saint-Germain manuscript and in the first Bigot manuscript.]

Let none of you go out into the fields for earthly work; let no one presume to conduct any business, so that, gathering together at the church of the holy Mother of the Lord, we who have all sinned together [Col. 1314B] may all together lament the evils we have committed, and so that the strict Judge, seeing us punish our own sins, may Himself spare us the sentence of the condemnation He has announced.

[Note: [Col. 1313B] The order of persons and places differs in Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book X, chapter 1, and in Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 25. See what we have observed regarding Book I, chapter 42, of the *Life of Saint Gregory* by John the Deacon.]

The litany of the clergy shall go out from the church of blessed John the Baptist; the litany of the men from the church of blessed Marcellus the martyr; the litany of the monks from the church of the martyrs John and Paul; the litany of the handmaids of God from the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian; the litany of married women from the church of blessed Stephen, the first martyr; the litany of widows from the church of blessed Vitalis the martyr; and the litany of the poor and children from the church of blessed Cecilia the martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1314B] In the printed editions, after “Cecilia,” there follows: “These things were done in the basilica of Saint Sabina on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the sixth indiction.” Only one Corbie manuscript contains this. The sixth indiction is certainly an obvious error, for these events must necessarily be assigned to the eighth indiction. Note that the sixth indiction found in the Corbie manuscript, which contains part of the *Register of Letters*, should not be applied to this sermon but to the following letter, which is the first of all those belonging to the sixth indiction.]

[Col. 1311]

## INDEX TO THE THREEFOLD LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY

The numbers in this index correspond to the bold numbers inserted in the text of the threefold *Life* which you, reader, have at the beginning of the preceding volume, from column 41 to column 500. ### A
**Abbot.** Gregory is elected abbot, 24. At the request and under the compulsion of the brethren, 213. Saint Gregory’s concern in choosing worthy abbots, 208. An abbot devoted to personal interests should not be elected, ibid. In Gregory’s time many abbots were distinguished by priestly rank, 66, 247, 257. Whether abbots were formerly forbidden to go outside, 241. Monks could not be ordained without the abbot’s consent, 256. Nevertheless, they could be seized for the episcopate even against the abbot’s will, 257. Abbots who had fallen could never return to priestly office, but, after correcting their way of life, could return to the governance of monasteries, 257, 303. Very useful admonitions to abbots, 296. The first origin of commendatory abbots, 232. Abbesses are forbidden to receive the veil or blessing unless they are sixty years old, 247.

**Castorius,** subdeacon of the Roman Church, ordained bishop of Rimini, 86. Because of his illness, another is permitted to be ordained in his place, 276. Gregory’s charity toward Castorius when the latter resigned, 157.

**Castorius,** master of soldiers. He is accused before Maurice of negligence in gathering grain, 235.

**Castorius,** notary and chartularius of the Roman Church at Ravenna, 64, 69, 126, 130, 131.

**Castorius,** notary of the Histrian patrimony, 64, 149.

**Casula.** What it is, 61.

**Catellus,** monk, 206.

**Major and more difficult cases.** Gregory orders that they be referred to him, 236.

**Cases of clerics and bishops.** See *Clerics; Bishops*.

**Cellararii.** Who were so called, 238.

**Ceolfrid,** abbot and successor of Benedict Biscop, 268.

**Cerbonius,** bishop of Populonia, 201.

**Chagan,** king of the Avars, invades the province of Venetia, 291.

**The Council of Chalcedon** offered Saint Leo the title “ecumenical,” 248.

**The effects of charity.** Many, 236, 280.

**Gregory’s charity.** He grants freedom to the slaves of the Roman Church, 271. He provided for the support of those who abandoned schism or heresy, 271. He assisted three thousand nuns, 272. He wrote to Maurice on behalf of peoples oppressed by exactions, 235. When the revenues of bishops were insufficient to feed the poor, he himself supplied what was necessary, 271. See *Alms; Poor*. He devoted himself entirely to the salvation of souls, 7, 192. See *English; Jews; Peasants*. As far as lay within him, he wished to save everyone without exception, 105.

**Childebert,** son of Sigebert and Brunhilda, king of Austrasia, 222. Through Brunhilda’s efforts he is rescued from the hands of Fredegund and proclaimed king, 255. Through her help he is made heir by Guntram, ibid. In what year he succeeded after his father was killed, 212. He wages war successfully against the Lombards, 212. While still young he crosses the Alps and grants peace to the king of the Lombards when the latter requests it, 221. Many monasteries were founded by him, 286.

**Chlodesinda,** daughter of King Clothar. She brought Alboin to the Christian faith, 259.

**Chosroes,** a refugee. With Maurice’s help he regains his kingdom, 221, 240. Whether he embraced the Christian faith, 240. His generosity toward Christian churches, ibid.

**Chrismation of the forehead.** It is forbidden to priests in Sardinia and later permitted, 246.

**Christians.** Gregory did not permit Christians to be subjected to Jews, 153, 154. Those Christians whom he could not free by force from Jewish servitude he redeemed with money, 154.

**The coming of Christ.** It is to be loved and desired, 224, 225.

**Circumcision.** Gregory permitted no pagan to be circumcised, 155.

**Claudius,** a monk of the monastery of Gregory and afterward abbot of Classe, 207. He recorded Gregory’s homilies, 49, 169, 298. He is sent to the city of Fano to ransom captives, 241.

**Claudius.** Who was administrator of the Spanish kingdoms, 287.

**Cleph,** king of the Lombards, killed, 203.

**Clematius,** lector, 145.

**Clementina,** a patrician woman, 9.

**Clerics.** Gregory called them his most beloved sons, 160. He confirmed by his authority pledges made by bishops to clerics, 146. He did not wish the customary stipends of any clerics to be reduced because of bodily illness, 145, 146, 150. Clerics who had fallen were punished only by irrevocable deposition, 289, 298. He sometimes ordered them confined in very poor but especially observant monasteries, 229. He wished the cases of clerics to be brought before bishops, 273, 295. Gregory chose clerics as his familiar companions and table companions, dismissing laymen, 48. He sometimes incardinated clerics of another parish in his own church and sometimes in another church, 94 ff. He never preferred clerics ordained later to those ordained earlier, 95. He prohibited curials and men bound to secular business from becoming clerics, 240. Why many laymen aspired to the clerical state in Gregory’s time, 49, 224. How he wished them to be tested, 50, 224. He forbade men stained by crimes to attain the clerical state, 50. He did not wish to receive foreign clerics without letters from their bishop, 229, 272. Gregory did not excuse clerics from the watches and guard duties of the cities, 280. Whether Gregory prohibited clerics from embracing the monastic profession, 247. Whether he prohibited monks from the clerical state, 247. See *Monks*. He did not wish clerics who had become monks in a monastery to return to their own churches, 227, 247. Why he did not wish clerics to be appointed to govern monasteries, 65, 66 ff., 253.

**Clothar II,** son of Chilperic, king of Neustria, 222.

**Clotsinda,** sister of Childebert, marries Reccared, 222.

**The Council of Clovesho** praises the Rule of Saint Benedict under the name “monastic Rule,” 206, 267.

**Tenant farmers of the Church.** Gregory did not wish them to be harassed by evil customs, 232.

**The dove.** In the form of a dove, the Holy Spirit suggested to Gregory what he should write, 14, 15, 169.

**Saint Columbanus** is harassed in Gaul on account of the rites of the Scots, 290. He consults Gregory, ibid. He is received kindly by Agilulf, 229. He founded the monastery of Lobium in Agilulf’s territory, 290.

**Columbus,** bishop of Numidia. Whether he was primate and vicar of the apostolic see, 231.

**Gregory’s compassion toward the sick,** 157, 158.

**Eucharistic communion.** The formula for giving communion, 10. Another formula closer to the present one, ibid. Formerly laymen and women offered bread and wine for communion, 10.

**Two kinds of compunction,** 276.

**Como.** The clerics of the Church of Como complain to the Roman Church about an estate that had been usurped, 283. What Gregory replied, 284.

**Councils.** Gregory venerated the four general councils as the four Gospels, 46, 47, 218. He likewise venerated the Fifth Council, 46. Which councils are called ecumenical, 248. What an ecumenical council is, 248. He held a council of twenty-four bishops at Rome, 198. The Roman Council. See *Synod*.

**Concordius,** bishop of Cesena, 303.

**Tenants.** He arranged that what had been unjustly taken from the Church’s tenants be restored, 301.

**Confession of Saint Peter,** that is, the place of his burial, 218.

**Conon,** abbot of Lérins, 296.

**Marriage between blood relatives.** To what generation Gregory permitted the bond of consanguinity, 56, 57. See *Marriage*.

**Counselor.** One must abstain from wicked counselors, 105, 106.

**Gregory’s steadfastness,** unconquered, 244, 250.

**Constantia Augusta,** 109, 112, 129. At the urging of John of Constantinople, she requests from Gregory the head of Blessed Peter, or his relics, 116, 244.

**The ambition of the patriarchs of Constantinople.** By what stages it rose, 249.

**Constantine Copronymus,** emperor, 172.

**Constantine,** successor of Saint Benedict. In what year he died, 204.

**Constantius,** a monk unsuccessfully proposed for the abbacy, 298.

**Constantius** is designated bishop of Milan, 138. In what year he became bishop, 203. After his election he presented his confession of faith to the pope, 245. The people of Brescia demand from Constantius an oath that he had not condemned the Three Chapters, ibid. He exercises the pontificate with distinction, 138.

**New customs.** Gregory introduced new customs in the Church, 50, 51. He responds humbly to those who murmur about them, 51 ff. He permitted no one to violate ancient customs, 137. He tried to remove evil customs from the Church, 47.

**The full force of conversion,** 6, 37.

**Copiosus,** a monk of the monastery of Saint Gregory, 27, 28.

**To lift the heart to the Lord with the hands.** What it means, 5, 37.

**“Let us change our hearts and presume upon forgiveness,”** 6, 37.

**Gregory’s awareness of the weakness of his heart,** 173, 174.

**Pope Cornelius.** Why he made Novatian the archdeacon a priest, 210.

**Correction.** Gregory bore correction given to him by others with the greatest patience, 222.

**Cortis.** The word has several meanings, 185.

**Corsica.** The island belonged to the prefecture of Africa, 277. Gregory attends to Corsica, which had been devastated by oppression and enemy incursions, 235, 277. The conversion of the Corsican idolaters, 278.

**Cortona,** an ancient city of the Bruttians, 34.

**Cosmas,** made subdeacon from a monk and afterward a priest, 89. Gregory assists Cosmas, who was burdened by debt, 68, 69.

**Crementius,** primate of Byzacena, is accused by his fellow bishops, 288. His case is heard in the synod of the province of Byzacena, ibid.

**Manifest crimes.** Gregory never passed them over without punishment; but concerning doubtful matters he never pronounced a certain sentence, 104, 105. Once crimes had been heard, he did not leave them unexamined, 144, 145. He excluded criminals from the familiarity of bishops, 106.

**Fault.** Gregory never permitted one person to be punished for another’s fault, 106, 107.

**Care.** How heavily Saint Gregory was occupied with cares, 7.

**Curials and men bound to secular business** are barred from the clerical state, 240.

**Cyla,** patriarch of the Arian Vandals in Africa, 231.

**Cyprian,** deacon and administrator of the Sicilian patrimony, 62, 64, 68, 69, 89, 94.

**Cyriacus,** successor of John in the see of Constantinople, 120, 137, 220. Why he was elected late, 274. His encomium, ibid. He sends envoys to Gregory, 273. He claims for himself the title “ecumenical bishop,” 250. Nevertheless, Gregory receives his synodical letter, 222. The title “ecumenical” is forbidden him, 251. He is praised immoderately by certain people, 274.

**Cyriacus,** abbot, 80, 85, 99. Gregory sends him as legate to Gaul, 285. His journey through Gaul, 286. His legation to Spain succeeds happily, 287.

### D
- The deacons formerly did not use dalmatics indiscriminately, but tunics, 286. The use of dalmatics is permitted to the bishop of Gap and to the deacons of Arles, ibid.
- The bishops of Dalmatia are separated from communion with Maximus under excommunication, 129.
- Prayer by the righteous does not benefit the condemned, 60.
- What *dapsilis* and *dapsilitas* signify, 183.
- Decius, patrician, 33.
- The dedication of a basilica of the Arians, 54. Miracles performed at this dedication, ibid.
- Temples of idols are consecrated as churches according to the Christian rite, 56, 269.
- The custom of dedicating basilicas with the relics of holy martyrs, 54.
- What should be done concerning those churches whose dedication is uncertain, 304.
- **Defending.** Gregory never permitted anyone to be unjustly defended by the Church, 159, 160.
- The seven defenders are honored with the rank of *regionarius*, 51, 281.
- Those who usurp the office of defenders are punished, 289.
- Deira, a province of greater Britain, 8. An allusion to that name, 8, 30, 193.
- A false informer must be punished by the penalty of retaliation, 144.
- Demetrius, bishop of Naples, is deposed on account of crimes, 94.
- Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, 221. He is rebuked for teaching grammar, 100, 295. What Gregory replied to him when he requested privileges for his own Church, 286.
- Deusdedit, bishop of Canterbury, 270.
- Deusdedit, elected bishop of Milan, 138, 293.
- Formerly only seven deacons were ordained in the Roman Church, 3, 30, 187, 188, 210. They were called *regionarii*, ibid. They could also be called cardinals, 210.
- In Gregory’s time there were nineteen deacons in the Roman Church, 86.
- Gregory becomes the seventh deacon, 3, 30, 187, 196, 210. By which pope, 3, 30, 210. Whether he was a cardinal deacon, 210.
- After becoming a deacon, he is compared with an angel for his humility and skill in ministering, 30, 31.
- Which bishops Gregory ordained from among the deacons of the Roman Church, 86, 87.
- Rectors are appointed for each deaconry, 63, 64.
- What *diacoposis* is, 34.
- The devil, disturbing the monastery of St. Gregory with a tremendous crash, is driven away, 180. He harasses the Barbilian estate, 182. He pursues Ursellus, who is fleeing to Gregory’s monastery, but is forced to abandon him, 182, 183.

[Col. 1322]

- Gregory published four books of the *Dialogues* at Peter’s request, 7, 16, 172, 192, 197, 198. Also at the request of his friends, 171. With what intention, 172. In what year, 205, 215.
- He discussed these books with Peter, 169, 172, 196.
- He sent them to Queen Theodelinda, 16, 196, 197. In which year of his pontificate, 242.
- Pope Zacharias translated the books of the *Dialogues* into Greek, 172.
- They are cited by Pope Hadrian I, 194.
- The first book is cited by Hincmar, ibid.
- In the *Dialogues*, where Gregory speaks of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, the Greeks erased the word “Son,” 172.
- **Letters of dismissal.** Foreign clerics could not be received without letters from their own bishop, 229, 272. Those who were elected bishops likewise needed letters of dismissal, 272.
- Dinocrates, brother of St. Perpetua, is freed from the torments of purgatory through prayers, 275.
- **Ecclesiastical discipline.** Gregory’s concern for its preservation, 301. To prevent greater things from being presumed, he took care that even minor abuses not be committed, 128.
- **Dissension.** How St. Gregory conducted himself in settling dissensions, 236, 237, 277.
- Gregory earnestly requested the dissolution of his body, 165.
- It is not possession of riches but desire that makes one rich, 78.
- **Divorce.** A rich man is struck with anathema for rejecting his wife, 13, 59.
- Doclea, the city; to which metropolitan see it belonged, 297.
- Dominica, daughter of the patrician Narses, a nun, 276.
- Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, 123, 221. When the council of Carthage was convened, he decreed that heretics were to be restrained by the bishops, 231. He sends Gregory a congratulatory letter on his assumption of the pontificate, 236. Gregory consoles him, 292.
- The pitiful death of Dominicus, a priest and superior, because he abducted a nun, 185.
- Domitian, a relative of the emperor Maurice, bishop of Melitene, 213, 240. Metropolitan of Armenia, a most holy man, 220. Maurice appointed him tutor to his sons, 221. He preaches the faith to the Persians without success, 240.
- *Domnus*, a title of honor granted by Gregory to an elderly abbot, 236.
- *Domus praesidium*, an expression familiar to Gregory of Tours; what it signifies, 187.
- Donadeus, a deacon, complains that he was unjustly deposed, 298.
- Gregory expels the African Donatists from the Church, 79. His efforts against the Donatists, 231. That they repented under him is probable, 231, 232. At the Council of Carthage it was decreed that the Donatists were to be restrained by the bishops, 231. Those who rose from among the Donatists to the episcopate are forbidden to become primates, 231.
- Donatus, archdeacon, is sought for the episcopate of Ravenna; why he is not ordained, 253.
- Why the body of St. Donatus was transferred from the city of Euria to the island of Corcyra, 244.
- Donus, one of the cardinals of the Roman Church, ordained bishop of Messina, 86. He is criticized for demanding too high a price for burial, 280.
- Dorovern, a city and the metropolitan see of the kingdom of the Kentish people, 55. See *Canterbury*.
- A *dromo*, a very swift type of ship, 135, 136.
- In doubtful matters an absolute judgment must not be pronounced, 105.
- The notable testimony of the Second Council of Dusiacum in favor of the rule of St. Benedict, 207.
- *Dypticha*, tablets on which the names of the living were written, 138.

## E

- Eadbald, king of Kent, persecutes the English Christians and later converts to the faith, 270.
- Ecclesius, bishop of Chiusi, 97, 98.
- The wretched condition of the Church at the time of Gregory’s ordination, 219, 220. How he came to its aid, 79, 220. With what helpers, 220, 221.
- He recalls the Ligurians, Venetians, and Iberians to the unity of the Church, 79.
- In what frame of mind he assumed responsibility for all the Churches, 276, 277.
- He preserved the rights and privileges of the Churches inviolate, 273.
- How he provided for ruined churches, 226.
- Under Gregory the Roman Church was such as it had been under the apostles, 49.
- He devoted himself to building and adorning churches, 7.
- He restrains with words and reforms a certain tyrant who was invading the possessions of the Church, 13.
- How the revenues and goods of a Church were preserved intact after the death of its bishop, 233. Those to whom their care was entrusted, ibid., 234.
- What Gregory decreed concerning the revenues of the Church, 280.
- In former times churches were scarcely dedicated without the relics of the saints, 232.
- Formerly no churches in Sicily and Italy were consecrated without Gregory’s permission, 273.
- Under Gregory, ecclesiastical duties were performed only by ecclesiastics, 49.
- He did not wish two ecclesiastical offices to be entrusted to one person, 65, 66.
- Edilberthus. See *Ethelbertus*.
- Edilfrid, king of the Northumbrians, makes war upon the Britons, 269.
- What Gregory’s education was like, 201. How noble boys should be educated, ibid.
- The procedure for episcopal elections in Gregory’s time, 233. The consent of the supreme pontiff was sometimes required, ibid., 293.
- Episcopal elections were conducted by the clergy and the people, 138, 293. Sometimes they were entrusted to the bishops themselves, sometimes to judges and magistrates, 234.
- How Gregory conducted himself in elections, 245.
- He refused to claim for himself the election of the bishop of Syracuse, which had been entrusted to him, 252.
- To confirm the elections of the supreme pontiff and the metropolitans, Athalaric imposed a huge sum of money, 216.
- Election of the pope. See *Pope*.

### The Election of St. Gregory

- Although Gregory resisted with all his strength, he was elected pontiff, 5, 36, 187, 194.
- He wrote to the emperor Maurice, asking him not to give his assent to the people; but his letter was intercepted, 5, 36, 188, 216.
- He asked John of Constantinople to arrange for his election to be annulled, 216.
- His election was confirmed by the emperor, 5, 36, 188, 216.
- Whether money was paid to obtain the emperor’s consent, 216.
- Which of the nobles strengthened Gregory’s election with their votes, 216.
- While fleeing and hiding, Gregory is discovered by a column of light as a sign, 6, 38, 218.
- At that time he was only a deacon; he is not recorded as having been made a priest, 216.
- How sincerely he refused the pontificate, 38 and following pages.
- Other reasons, besides humility of spirit, for his avoiding the episcopate, 219, 220.
- Why he finally consented to undertake the pontificate, 42.

### Almsgiving

- Gregory’s devotion to giving alms, 301.
- After founding monasteries, he sold his possessions and distributed them to the poor, 2, 187, 194, 204.
- Four times a year he distributed alms from his patrimony to the poor, 53.
- On every Kalends he distributed from his revenues various provisions according to the season, ibid.
- Under him the Roman Church was regarded as a common granary, 53.
- He purchased grain for the distribution of alms, 77.
- He supported three thousand handmaids of God, ibid.
- He assisted not only those present but also those living far away, 7.
- He himself arranged almsgiving locally and personally, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70.
- See *Sick*, *Poor*.
- He willingly gave to everyone who asked, 70.
- Even to those who did not ask, he supplied what was necessary, ibid., 71.
- Having nothing from which to give alms, he ordered a silver dish to be given to a poor man, 25.
- Some people seize what belongs to others in order to give alms, 71.
- How far Gregory was from such a crime, 71, 72 and following pages.
- He is stirred by a conversation with angels to distribute greater alms, 52, 196.
- Nevertheless, he did not wish what had been granted as alms later to be demanded back as though it were a debt, 289.
- He hesitated to accept the distribution of another person’s alms, out of fear, 97.

- Eleutherius, a monk and companion of St. Gregory, a most holy man, 24, 209.
- Through the prayers of Eleutherius and his own prayers, Gregory obtains the power to fast, 24, 209. Nevertheless, he attributes the miracle to Eleutherius alone, ibid.
- Elias, priest and abbot in the province of Isauria, 70, 94.
- Gregory was eloquent through habitual practice, not through deliberate study, 172.
- Who praised his eloquence, 172, 173.
- **Council of Ephesus.** The false Council of Ephesus is repeatedly put forward by heretics in place of the true ecumenical council, 279.
- Epiphanius, a deacon of the Roman Church, consecrated bishop, 86.
- Epiphanius the subdeacon is appointed judge in the case of the bishop of Nepi, 226.
- Epiphanius, a cleric, whom Gregory made a deacon of the Roman Church from being a monk of Elias, 94.
- **Bishop.** Gregory ordained bishops whom he could find to be better than others, wherever they might come from, 86, 89, 90. What he required in bishops, 98.
- He strove to remove from the episcopate those unworthy of it, 292.
- Whom he selected as bishops from among the ministers of the Roman Church, 86, 87.
- The bishops of Italy were immediately subject to the Roman pontiff, 226.
- Which bishops Gregory calls “his own,” 245.
- How concerned he was to establish peace among the bishops, 303. His prudence in their cases, 304.
- Among bishops stained by crime Gregory showed himself superior; among the innocent, equal, 142.
- The devil incites certain bishops against Gregory, 110.
- He corrected negligent bishops with the utmost severity, 103, 104.
- He forbade bishops to use wicked counselors, 105, 106.
- Whom he excluded from the familiarity and companionship of bishops, 106.
- He restored bishops who had been unjustly deposed, 138, 139, 140.
- He restored communion to one who had been unjustly deprived of communion, 147.
- He supplied necessities to bishops in need, 97, 98.
- He ordered the bishops of Sicily to come to Rome only once every five years, 97.
- He considered all bishops, himself included, to be equal according to the rule of humility, 237.
- What he decreed concerning a bishop who omitted the sacrifice of the Mass, 303.
- Under Gregory, the bishops either built new churches or restored old ones, 98.
- The cases of bishops: by whom and where they were to be judged, 232, 273.
- The emperor entrusted episcopal cases to the metropolitans, 237, 303.
- Sometimes episcopal cases were permitted to be referred to the emperor, 280.
- Episcopal cases were entrusted to other bishops, 280, 297.
- Sometimes they were entrusted to a defender, 302.
- The judgment passed against Bishop Natalis is announced after prior admonitions, 233.
- Gregory preserved and energetically defended the rights and privileges of bishops, 144, 236, 273.
- He did not diminish them, 142.
- Fallen bishops are deposed, 94, 238, 277, and are confined in a monastery, 297.
- A bishop who strikes someone is excommunicated, 238.
- A bishop who unjustly rages against an innocent person must be severely punished, 298.
- So that the reputation of bishops might not suffer from suspicions, they were ordered to have stewards (*cellarii*), 238.
- The crimes of bishops must be examined with the greatest caution, 140, 141, 142.
- How the faults of bishops that were not crimes were punished, 140.
- What Gregory decreed concerning the property of fallen and deposed bishops, 232.
- **Residence of bishops.** See *Residence*.
- The transfer of bishops, 226. Gregory wished such transfers to be made only for a just reason, 93, 94.
- Bishops expelled from their sees by enemies were incorporated into other vacant churches, or placed over two churches, 91, 92, 93, 226.
- Sometimes he joined them to other bishops for their support, 93, 226.
- He did not wish to remove bishops on account of illness unless they themselves requested it by submitting a petition, 150, 151, 295, 301.
- But afterward he wished them to be supported from the revenues of the church they had left, 151, 152, 301.
- What he decreed concerning a demented bishop, 301.
- He entrusted bishops with visiting churches deprived of a pastor, 95, 96.
- A bishop cannot make a will concerning the property of his church or property acquired during his episcopate, 271.
- The Church stands through good bishops and falls through bad ones, 91.
- Bishops should not close the bowels of mercy to their needy relatives, 227.
- They should restrain heretics, 231.
- The faithful should beware of pursuing bishops with slander and calumny, 304.

- Gregory wrote as many books of letters as he lived years in the pontificate, 170, 197.
- Why he left the fourteenth book unfinished, 170.
- The collection of these letters is called the *Register*, 197.
- From Gregory’s letters, two volumes of decretals were excerpted in the time of Pope Hadrian I, 170.
- The epitaph of St. Gregory, 168, 169, 193.
- What *epitimium* is, 61, 62.
- Whether the institution of St. Equitius continued in the monastery of St. Gregory, 206. After his death he protected his disciples against the fury of the Lombards, ibid.
- The body of St. Erasmus rests in the church of Formiae, 91.
- A hermit’s dream concerning Blessed Gregory, 78.
- Ethelbert, king of Kent, converts to the faith, 9. He kindly receives Augustine and his companions, 55. He is praised as another Constantine, 261.
- Etherius, bishop of Lyons, 151, 221. Gregory confirms the faith in the Eucharist by a miracle, 10, 11, 58. The doctrine of transubstantiation did not then appear to be new, 11, 58. The custom of carrying the Eucharist during sea voyages, 34.
- *Eulogiae* are small gifts, 206.
- Eulogius, a former monk and patriarch of Alexandria, 220. A most vigorous enemy of heretics, ibid. Highly esteemed by Gregory for his virtues, ibid.
- Gregory warns him to resist the pride and ambition of John of Constantinople, 250. Gregory congratulates him on the subjugation of the heretics, 279.
- Why adolescents on the island of Eumorphiana are forbidden to be received into monasteries before their eighteenth year, 208, 227.
- Why women who had fled there out of fear of enemies are removed, 227.
- Euphemius, a cleric, 145.
- Euplus, a tenant, 74.
- Eupraxia, a nun abducted from the monastery of St. Andrew, 185.
- Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica, 175.
- Eusebius, abbot, 68. His dispute with Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, 236. Gregory gives him one hundred solidi for the needs of the monastery, 237.
- The error of Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning the resurrection of bodies, 4, 31, 191. Gregory attacks him, ibid., 32 and following pages, 33, 212.
- At the emperor’s command, Eutychius’s book on this doctrine was committed to the flames, 32, 33, 212.
- Eutychius repents of his error, 33.
- He was renowned for miracles, 4. He was driven into exile because of the faith, ibid. In what year he died, 212.
- Euthymius, superior, or head, of the monastery of St. Andrew, 182.
- **The Gospel.** Whether Gregory expounded the entire text of the Gospels, 197, 198.
- Evangelus, a deacon of Sipontum, 152.
- Who first obtained the name *exarch*, 203.
- *Exenia*. See *Xenia*.
- While Gregory was expounding the prophecy of Ezekiel, the Holy Spirit suggested what he should write under the appearance of a dove, 15.
- Weakened by hostile incursions and by bodily infirmity, he is forced to desist from expounding this prophecy, 165, 166, 234.
- How many homilies on Ezekiel he published, 7, 172, 192, 196, 197, 198.

- Forgers must be punished, 295.
- How Gregory assisted the people during a famine, 77. After his death famine prevailed, 169.
- Fantinus, a defender, 62, 64, 69. He is appointed heir by a monk, 232.

- Felix, a subdeacon, 64.
- Felix, a tenant, 76.
- Felix, the slave of Christianus the Samaritan, 155.

- Florentius, ordained bishop from being a deacon of the Roman Church, 86.

## J

The bishops of Jadera are separated from the communion of Maximus of Salona by excommunication, 129. Having abandoned Maximus, they ask pardon, 129, 130.

Januarius, bishop of Caralis, 154, 160. He is reproved for avenging injuries inflicted upon him, 99. He is rebuked because of the harvest he had ploughed, ibid. His negligence in calling the barbarians to the faith is censured, 216. He is despised by his clerics and ministers, ibid.

John the Evangelist sometimes simply called “the Apostle,” 268. Pieces of his garments were given as relics in Gregory’s time, 118. The efficacy of these pieces, 118. Gregory receives the tunic of Saint John from a bishop, 118, 119, 244.

Pope John III, 138, 202.

Pope John VIII proceeds against the Saracens, 185. At his urging, John the Deacon wrote Gregory’s life, 21, 210.

John, a monk of Constantinople, becomes patriarch, 111. Whether he was a monk, 249. He is substituted for Eutychius despite his resistance, 38, 111, 212, 249. Because of his extraordinary abstinence he is called “the Faster,” 212, 220, 249. Whether he gave the liturgy attributed to Chrysostom a better form, 249. After convening a synod, John assumes the title of “ecumenical patriarch,” 111, 220, 248, 249. Pope Pelagius invalidates the acts of this synod, 111, 112, 212, 249. To secure the title “universal bishop” more safely, John purchases the emperor’s consent with money, 112. Gregory forbids a deacon-responsalis to celebrate the solemn Masses with John, 111. Nevertheless, he never withdrew from John’s communion, 250, 251. John’s pride and hypocrisy are described, 112–116, 250. He is accused of indolence and negligence, 238. He allowed the presbyter Athanasius to be disgracefully struck in the Church of Constantinople, 238. While accusing others of error, he himself falls into error, 239. He attempted to alienate the mind of the Augusta Constantina from Gregory, 244. Saint Gregory’s efforts to make John relinquish the title of ecumenical patriarch were fruitless, 251. The year in which he died, 119, 220, 251. His virtues, 220. He is venerated by the Greeks, ibid.

John of Jerusalem, successor of Eustochius, 45, 220.

John, bishop of Callipolis, 140.

John, bishop of Corinth, 85, 145.

John, bishop of Eurya in Epirus, is compelled to abandon his church, 303. He attempts to remove the fortress of Cassiopa from the jurisdiction of another bishop, ibid. Condemned, he does not immediately submit to the sentence, 304.

John, bishop of First Justiniana, 150, 151. Gregory sends him the pallium and entrusts his own authority to him, 97. He unjustly deposes Bishop Hadrian, 139, 140. He is suspended from communion for thirty days, 237.

John, bishop of Larissa, unjustly deposes Bishop Hadrian, 237.

John, bishop of the city of Lisbon: why he is incardinated at Squillace, 92.

John, bishop of Palermo, 146.

When John wished to send alms to Severus, bishop of Grado, why he was forbidden, 234. He is censured for using the pallium in solemn litanies and permitting his presbyters and deacons to use *mappulae* [liturgical napkins], 124, 125, 239. He asks that the use of the pallium be restored to him, 125, 239. He disparages Gregory, 125. He is reproved for various vices, 125, 126, 239. Because John neglected to correct these matters, he died in the same year, 126, 252.

John, formerly archdeacon of the Church of Catania, is elected bishop of Syracuse, 89, 90, 94, 109, 155, 173, 252. His various virtues, ibid. He rejects the offerings of Venantius, the former monk and patrician, 109, 272. Gregory exhorts him to peace, 272.

John of Salisbury, 202. His story about the Palatine library being burned by Gregory, ibid.

Why Gregory did not wish the presbyter John to be promoted to the episcopate, 253.

The poem of John the Deacon to Pope John VIII, 19. He calls himself the last of the Levites, ibid. On what occasion he wrote the life of Saint Gregory, 19, 20, 21, 210. John, subdeacon of Ravenna and Gregory’s representative, 169, 173.

John, subdeacon and rector of the patrimony of Liguria, 138.

John, abbot of Saint Lucy at Syracuse, 118, 119, 277. Negligent in preserving monastic discipline, 241.

John, a Persian abbot, 161.

The conflict of John, presbyter and superior of the monastery of Saint Andrew, with the devil, and his terrible death, 177, 178, etc., 179.

Gregory foretells in an apparition the death of John, a monk of the same monastery, 180, 181.

John the notary, 64.

Job: why he was struck by God with a wound, 173. At Leander’s urging, Gregory undertakes a literal, allegorical, and moral exposition of the Book of Job, 4, 31, 170, 171, 189, 196–198. He was then a deacon and *apocrisiarius*, 170, 191. He revised this work in the monastery, 215. Having become pope, he completed it, 170, 191. He first sent it to the monasteries of Rome and afterward to Saint Leander, 171.

Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum, 233.

Jocundus, patriarch of the Arian Vandals in Africa, 231.

The manner in which the Jews were treated by the Roman pontiffs, 156. Gregory forbids the Jews to be unjustly harassed, 278. Nevertheless, he restrains them when they become insolent toward Christians, ibid. He orders that the place taken from the Jews where they assembled to celebrate their solemnities be restored to them, 229. Gregory was exceedingly concerned to secure the salvation of the Jews, 62. He gives clothing for baptism to Jews being baptized, 62, 63, 278. What dispositions he required in Jews who were to receive baptism, 63. He wished the Jews to be brought to the faith by preaching, not by violence, 153, 229. Later, however, he wished them to be burdened with taxes, 257. He ordered that the burdens of their payments be partly relaxed for Jews converted to the Church, 257. He considered it unlawful for Christians to be subjected to Jews, 153, 154, 242. The laws prohibited this, 242. The slaves of Jews who took refuge with the Church were granted freedom, 154. The slaves of Jews who preceded their masters in embracing the faith were forbidden to remain subject to them, even if the masters became Christians, 155. Gregory judged the gifts of Jews abominable, 155, 156. A Jew is compelled to restore church vessels that he had purchased for himself, 229. A Jew mocks Christians under the false guise of devotion to the prophet Elijah, 242. The leader or president of a synagogue of the Jews is called *nasi*, ibid. The conversion of the Jews of Agrigentum, 278.

Judge. How Gregory conducted himself toward corrupt and unjust judges, 107–110, 292. He freely defended everyone’s liberty against the insolence of judges, 107. He complains about the judges’ plundering, 235, and about their perversity and injustice, 280. The devil stirs up judges against Gregory, 110. The procedure of ecclesiastical judgments, 273, 289. An ecclesiastical and a secular judge jointly investigate the same matter, 226.

“I judge.” How cautious Gregory was in judging cases, 288.

Julianus Scribo, 159.

The emperor Justinian, 148, 160. By interfering excessively in ecclesiastical affairs, he became a leader of error, 202. To drive the Goths from Italy, he summoned the Lombards, ibid.

The emperor Justin drives Anastasius of Antioch into exile, 138.

Justinus, praetor of Sicily, 105, 153, 203. His avarice, 242.

Justus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gregory, is severely punished by Gregory at death for having kept money hidden, 27, 213. He is freed from his punishments through the offering of the sacrifice of the Mass for thirty continuous days, 27, 28, 214.

In his letters Gregory calls laymen “lords” and women “ladies,” 160.

*Lama* and *Lang* are Lombard words; what they mean, 202.

The origin of the Lombards, 202. Why they were so called, ibid. The clothing and customs of the Lombards, 291. At first they obeyed dukes, then kings, 202. Latin culture flourished again at Rome under Gregory, 49.

The power of the robber’s repentance, 6, 37.

How the praises should be heard, 295.

Why Gregory made princes the objects of praise, 137.

The manner he observed in praising friends, 273.

Laurence, bishop of Milan, 138, 147. How many years he held the episcopate, 203. He sent a caution concerning the Three Chapters to the apostolic see, ibid.

The couch on which Gregory reclined while singing, preserved in the Lateran patriarchium, 47.

Pope Leo I, 116, 149. Where he was buried, 168. He rejected the title “ecumenical” when it was offered to him, 248.

Pope Leo IV, 177.

Liberatus, a merchant, 76.

Gregory defended everyone’s liberty against unjust judges, 107.

How those who wished to burn Gregory’s books after his death were prevented, 169, 197.
