The schismatic Ligurians are recalled by Gregory to the unity of the Church, 79.

The clerics of the church of Lindisfarne followed a monastic way of life, 261, 262.

Disputes. What Gregory’s attitude was toward disputes, 232.

While still a deacon, Gregory instituted litanies during a time of plague, 6, 16, 37, 188, 189, 217. By what authority he instituted them, 217. Gregory of Tours and John the Deacon disagree about the basilicas to which the people assembled during the litanies, 188, 189. How their accounts can be reconciled, 217. The greater and lesser litanies seem to have originated from these supplications, ibid. In these litanies Gregory carried an image of the Mother of God, ibid. Gregory ordered litanies to avert the enemies from Sicily, 158, 159, 294. What the sevenfold litany is, 6, 16, 37.

Liuba II, successor of Reccared, king of Spain, 296.

*Locusta*, as though from *loco sta* [“stand in place”], 9.

What the locust sitting on the book Gregory was holding seemed to signify to him, 9, 30.

Longinus, successor of Count Narses, was the first to assume the title of exarch, 203.

Longinus Strator, 49.

Saint Luke. Gregory places the head of Saint Luke in his monastery, 213. Relics of the same saint are brought from Achaia to Constantinople, 244.

Gregory foretells in an apparition the death of Lucidus, bishop of Ficulina, 181. Struck by fever and plague, he puts on the monastic habit, 181. In an apparition he learns the hour of his death, ibid.

Lucillus, bishop of Malta, is deposed for crimes and confined in a monastery, 289.

Profit. How far Gregory was from sordid profit, 235.

Luidhard, bishop of Senlis, minister of sacred things at the court of Bertha, queen of Kent, 259.

Lights formerly used in churches, 50, 168, 296.

Lupus of Ferrières is summoned to suppress the Pelagian heresy in Britain, 258.

## M

Magistrianus brings the emperor Maurice the hermits’ response, or prophecy, 135.

Why it is sometimes difficult to assign Mangatum a homeland, 200.

Magnus, a presbyter of Milan, 147.

The magi who attack Gregory’s horse with their magic are struck blind and handed over to demons, 13, 59.

Malchus, bishop and, before his episcopate, administrator of ecclesiastical property in Dalmatia, 243. Through his faction Maximus invades the see of Salona, 128. He suddenly dies during the night, 243. Gregory is accused before the emperor Maurice concerning his death, 162.

Pagan slaves who wish to come to the faith ought not to be sold, 154, 155.

The slaves of Jews: see Jews.

Gregory separates the Manichaeans from the body of the Church, 79. He wished the Manichaeans who could not be brought to the faith to be burdened with taxes, 257.

Hands. What it means to raise one’s heart to the Lord with one’s hands, 5, 37.

Manuscripts. The suspicion that Vatican manuscript codices had been substituted is disproved, 279.

Gregory did not wish the presbyters and deacons of Ravenna to use *mappulae*, 124, 239.

Marcellinus, count, 202.

The death of the monk Marcellus is foretold, 28.

Gregory sends an alms to Marcellinus, a layman assigned to penance, 67.

Mareshamus. His opinion concerning the late propagation of the Benedictine Rule in the English monasteries is refuted, 268.

Marianus, or Marinianus, 141.

Marinianus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gregory and later bishop of Ravenna, 49, 66, 86, 126, 151, 158, 167, 178. The year in which he was elected bishop, 253. His faith, ibid. He allows monasteries to be harassed, 253, 254. He is reproved for harshness toward the poor, 78, 253. Gregory grants him the pallium under certain conditions, 126. Marinianus asks that the use of the pallium be restored to him, ibid., 127. The investigation of the case of Maximus, invader of the see of Salona, is entrusted to him, 130.

*Marpahis* or *Marhais*, a Lombard word; what it means, 202.

After usurping the office of defensor, Martianus refuses to submit to the judgment of the bishop and is deported into exile, 289.

Martinus, bishop of Corsica, 92.

Martinus, deacon and abbot, canonically cleared of the crimes alleged against him, is declared innocent, 277.

Gregory foretells in an apparition the death of Martinus, a monk, 180, 181.

Martinus, a *scholasticus*, 288.

The origin of martyrologies, 279.

The antiquity of the Roman Martyrology is asserted against Valesius, 279, 280.

Gregory restrains astrologers who announce future events, 202.

Marriage within prohibited degrees was permitted only temporarily and as a concession to the English, 56, 57, 269, 304.

A marriage is to be dissolved if one of the spouses is of servile status, 277.

Maurentius, master of soldiers, 241.

Maurentius, chartularius, 38.

In what year the emperor Maurice began to reign, 212. In what year he married Constantina, daughter of the emperor Tiberius, 213. Maurice was called Tiberius, 23. John the Deacon calls him exceedingly avaricious and rapacious, 111–113, 131, 135. He was hostile to God, 116, 150. He was hostile to Gregory, 131, 162. He despised the priests of Christ, 119, 120. Nevertheless, he burned with zeal for the Catholic faith, 221. At Gregory’s suggestion, Maurice restored Anastasius of Antioch, who had been expelled from his see, 139. He provided assistance to bishops driven out by the fury of the enemy, 226. The political condition of the Christian world under Maurice, 221, 222. He kindly received Chosroes, the fugitive king of the Persians, and restored him, 221. He placed the exarch Smaragdus in command of the war against the Lombards, 221. He stirred up the Franks against the Lombards, ibid. Deceived by the counsels of wicked men, he refused to make peace with the Lombards, 252. He forbade the schismatics to be compelled to return to the Church, 150. Why, 234. By a law he forbade soldiers to be received into monasteries, 49, 240. With what freedom Gregory condemned this law, 111, 240. On what occasion the law was enacted, 241. It is not wholly to be rejected, ibid. Whether Maurice, or Gregory himself, softened that law before it was published, 240, 241. Maurice demands an accounting from those accused of extortion, 291. He supports John of Constantinople in usurping the title “ecumenical,” 120.

Maurice’s hostility toward Gregory, 131, 132, 134. His death by the sword is foretold while he was raging against Gregory, 134. Coming to his senses, he asks for the prayers of Gregory, the bishops, and the monks, 134, 299. In a dream he sees himself, with his wife and children, handed over to the soldier Phocas by divine judgment, 134, 299. He summons Philippicus in order to ask his pardon for his rash judgment, 134, 135, 299. He hears the sentence of his death while glorifying God, 135. He orders the army to winter in the region of the Slavs, 135, 299. Taking advantage of this, the army acclaims Phocas as exarch, 135. When a sedition breaks out at Constantinople, the people call Maurice a Marcionist, 135. Whether he changed his clothing, 135, 299. At Phocas’s command, however, he is beheaded with his wife and children, 135, 300. With what fortitude he met death, ibid. Why Gregory spoke more harshly about Maurice, 300.

Maurice the monk flees from the monastery, 208.

The manner in which the episcopate of Maurienne was separated from the jurisdiction of Turin, 287. How this city was named, ibid.

Maurisius, a duke, defects from the Lombards, 234.

Maurus is appointed abbot of the monastery of Classe, 298.

Maurus is made abbot of the church of Saint Pancratius after monks have been introduced there, 246.

Maximianus, the abbot under whom Gregory served, 24, 34, 205. He accompanies Gregory when Gregory goes to Constantinople, 211. The year in which he returned, ibid., 213. He is saved from shipwreck through Gregory’s merits, 34, 35, 211. He is made bishop of Syracuse, 34, 49, 66, 86, 141, 146, 155, 159, 171, 209. He is appointed vicar of the apostolic see for Sicily, 49, 97, 236. He is rebuked for excommunicating the abbot Eusebius for too slight a cause, 236. Gregory mourns Maximianus after his death, 252.

Maximus invades the episcopate of Salona, 128, 242. How he wins over Maurice’s support, 128. He publicly tears up Gregory’s letters threatening excommunication, 243. Although excommunicated, he celebrates Mass, 129, 243. Gregory forbids his name to be recited at the altar, 129. He also suspends from office those who ordained him, 242. Maximus unjustly accuses Gregory of having murdered the bishop Malchus, 243. Maximus, as a penitent, asks pardon, 130. His case is entrusted to be examined at Ravenna, ibid., 243. He performs penance publicly at Ravenna, 130, 243. After this humble satisfaction, he is granted the grace of communion, and the pallium is promised to him, 131, 243. Why Gregory consented to ratify Maximus’s ordination, 243.

Maximus, subdeacon, 76.

Whether the Church of Milan was equal to the Roman Church, 293.

Megistus, bishop of Ostia, librarian of the apostolic see, and prefect of the monastery of Saint Andrew, 177.

Mellitus is sent to England as Augustine’s companion, 9, 16, 194. He was then an abbot, 261. He is made bishop of London, 86, 265, 270. Later he comes to Rome with Boniface to discuss matters necessary for the Church of the English, 266. During the persecution raging against the English Christians, he crosses into Gaul, 270. He succeeds Laurence as bishop of Canterbury, ibid.

Menas, bishop of the Roman diocese, 289.

The measure prescribed by Saint Gregory and kept in his monastery: what happens if anyone wishes to use it, 185, 186.

Why it is permissible to use either a single immersion or a triple immersion in baptism, 190.

The monk Merulus dreams that he is crowned with flowers and immediately dies, 29. In what year, 205, 209.

The Church of Metz restores Gaul to the former sweetness of Gregorian chant, 48.

What authority metropolitans had over the bishops of their province, 288, 289. Wandering bishops are referred to the metropolitan, ibid. It belongs to the metropolitan to pass judgment on the bishops subject to him, 303. See Primate.

Formerly soldiers were marked on the hand, 111, 241.

Soldiers are forbidden to be received into monasteries: see Maurice.

Minulfus, duke of the island of Saint Julian, defects from the Lombards to the Franks, 234.

Gregory obtains the grace of miracles for others, 10. With what attitude his miracles are related, 10, 58.

The Mass celebrated over the bodies of the holy apostles, 50, 193.

The origin of the thirty Masses for the dead, 27, 28.

What Gregory added to the canon of the Mass, 50, 193, 194, 223.

Gregory preached to the people during the solemn celebration of Mass, 12.

The illness of the minister does not harm the sacrifice of the Mass, 303.

Private Masses in private houses, 272.

What the *mitra* is, 200.

What the matron’s *mitra* and the virgins’ *mitra* are, 176.

The *modius* prescribed by Saint Gregory and kept in his monastery: what happens if anyone wishes to use it, 185, 186.

Monk. After building seven monasteries Gregory becomes a monk, 2, 23, 24, 187, 190, 194–196, 198, 204, 205. Why he delayed for so long to fulfill his purpose of monastic life, 204. Why he did not seek retirement anywhere other than in the City, 204. The year in which this occurred, 204. Baronio’s error concerning Gregory’s late adoption of monastic life, 212. He was not a monk of Saint Equitius but of Saint Benedict, 206–208. He persevered in the monastery for a long time, 209. His devout exercises as a monk, 2, 3, 24, 188, 190, 208, 209. How much others advanced through his example, ibid. How much the companionship and example of the monks benefited Saint Gregory, 3, 4, 31, 49, 191, 211. Monastic perfection flourished together with pontifical discipline in his palace, 49. After becoming pontiff, he wished to have monks as his associates and table companions, 48, 49, 264. How highly he regarded monks, 211. When a monk prostrated himself on the ground before him, Gregory prostrated himself, 161. Formerly, as now, monks were distinguished from laymen by clothing and tonsure, 205. Whether monks were forbidden to go outside, 241. It was not Gregory’s intention that monks should obtain their livelihood by their own labor, 204. Formerly food and clothing were at times supplied to monks from the resources of the Church, 204. Whether monks were unworthy of priestly office and unfit to perform ecclesiastical duties, 247, 253, 266. In Gregory’s time only a few monks were without priestly orders, 65. He either ordained some monks from his monastery as bishops or ordered them to be ordained, 86. At the synod, Boniface IV decreed that monks were not to be barred from sacred ministries, 207, 208. Of the monks whom Augustine brought with him to England, many were advanced to the episcopate, 265. Through the aid of monks the English were converted to the faith: see Augustine. Monks are admitted into the church of Saint Pancratius, 246. The basilicas of the monks were already accustomed to be frequented by the people, ibid. Whether a monk, once appointed to ecclesiastical care, ceased to be a monk, 262, 263. Monks were formerly commonly called clerics, 263. Monks, even recluses, were employed in ecclesiastical or political affairs, 241, 284. The monks of England were Benedictines from the beginning, 267, 268. Monks could not be raised to the presbyterate or placed in charge of churches against the will of the abbot, 256. The situation was different if they were sought for the episcopate, 257. Monks appointed to govern churches could no longer continue living in the monastery, ibid. Monks made presbyters for monasteries were subject to the jurisdiction of the abbots, 257. They could not be ordained without the consent of the abbot and the congregation, ibid. Communion was not to be restored by presbyters to monks excommunicated by their abbot, 290. Whether the marriages of monks or nuns are adulterous, 230. What Saint Augustine’s view was, ibid. If a monk puts on the monastic habit against his wife’s will, he must be returned to his wife, 295. Whether monks may make wills, 232. Why a monk was granted the power to make a will concerning property belonging to him before he assumed the monastic habit, 295, 296. Privileges granted to monks by Gregory, 254, 277, 281. For what purpose he granted these privileges, 254. He did not permit monks to be burdened by bishops or clerics, 226, 253, 254. Gregory assigns annual stipends to the monks living on Mount Sinai, 64. Monks are exempted from civil lawsuits, 232. Vigilance is necessary for monks, 284. Monks are not excused from watches and guard duties necessary for the defense of cities, 280. A monk severely punished by Gregory at death for having kept a private hoard, 27. Terrified by his example, the monks bring to Gregory every worthless object they possessed, ibid. Two monks fleeing from the monastery are miraculously discovered, 26. A monk is tormented by a demon because of theft, 25. Fugitive monks are miraculously corrected, 25, 26. A monk in the monastery of Saint Andrew is struck by a spear wielded by a demon, 180. When he lies gravely ill, under what condition health is restored to him, 180, 181. Gregory appears to a monk asking for his brother’s health and promises it to him by giving a sign, 181, 182. Monks accused of Manichaean heresy are acquitted after presenting a confession of faith, 238. How concerned Gregory was about monastic discipline, 241, 277, 298, 303. He restrains wandering and immoral monks, 226, 277. He orders women to be removed from the island of Eumorphiana, lest they provide monks with an occasion for falling, 227. Women are barred from entering monasteries, 246. Whether they are also barred from the monks’ churches, ibid. The visitation of a monastery is entrusted to a defensor, 303. Whether clerics are forbidden to embrace monastic life, 247. Why the discipline of monasteries should not be entrusted to clerics, 252, 253. Clerics who have become monks are forbidden to return to their own churches, 227. Monastic vows, 230. Why Gregory forbade adolescents under eighteen years of age to be received into monasteries, 208, 227. He did not absolutely define the time of profession, 227. A law forbids soldiers to be received into monasteries, 240. Gregory disapproves this law, ibid. Entry into a monastery must be denied neither to curiales nor to debtors, 240. Whether monastic profession sometimes took the place of the subdiaconate, 299. Monastic life was prescribed according to the pattern of life instituted by the apostles, 264, 266. It is sketched in the condition of the Church of Alexandria under Saint Mark and in Philo’s account of the Therapeutae, 264. To whom the institution of monastic life is to be attributed, 266.

Gregory built six monasteries in Sicily and a seventh, that of Saint Andrew, on the Scaurus slope in his ancestral house, 2, 23, 24, 187, 194, 204. He was placed in charge of this monastery, 195. He was thought to preside over it not alone but together with Saint Andrew the Apostle, 25. Baronio’s error in assigning the succession of abbots of this monastery, 105. That succession restored, 105. Saints Andrew and Gregory did not wish this monastery to become a lodging house, 183, 184. How concerned Gregory remained about this monastery even after his death, 179, 180 and through 186. In this monastery are preserved a measure and a pound established by Saint Gregory, and a *modius* prescribed by him, 185. What happens if anyone wishes to use these measures, 185, 186. Many illustrious men came forth from this monastery, 285. It passed from Latin monks to the Greeks, from whom it afterward returned to the Latins, 175, 176, 204. The atrium of this monastery is described, 176. No one in this monastery was permitted to possess private property, 27, 61. It is probable that there was another monastery at Rome of Saints Andrew and Lucy, or rather of Saint Luke, 204. Monasteries were formerly endowed, 240, 246. Gregory’s concern and generosity toward monasteries, 226, 246, 254, 289, 290, 292, 293. The monasteries of Gaul were granted privileges, 286. A privilege was granted to the monasteries of Saints Andrew and Thomas near Rimini, 237. Gregory did not permit monasteries to be governed or burdened by clerics, 65, 66. He orders new monasteries to be built, 227. The monastery of Saint Hermes near Palermo, one of the six Gregorian monasteries, 206. The monastery of Saint Theodore in the territory of Palermo, 226. The monastery of Saint Theodore near Messina, ibid. A monastery on the island of Corsica built by a woman named Sabina, 227.

*Monastriae*, that is, servants of God or nuns, 53.

Gregory takes care of the honor and tranquility of the nuns, 247. He makes certain decrees on behalf of nuns, 257. He assists three thousand nuns in the city of Rome, 53, 272. He professes that he and all the Romans are still indebted to them, ibid. Whether the marriages of nuns are adulterous, 230.

The Monophysites renounce their error, 297.

The books of the *Moralia*: see Job.

Gregory is afflicted by very serious illnesses, 7, 165–168. See Illness.

The dying must not be disparaged, nor judgment passed upon them, 178.

Death must not be feared, 224, 225.

Gregory regarded death as the entrance into life and the reward of his labor, 3, 190.

In what year Gregory died, 16, 18, 168, 190, 193, 201, 304.

After Gregory’s death famine prevailed at Rome, 169.

Why the world was oppressed by so many calamities after his death, 18, 198.

After his death Gregory was accused by his adversaries of being wasteful and of squandering the Church’s goods, 169. They wished to burn his books, ibid.

When Moses sorrowfully kept silent, he could have seemed to cry out, 60.

Foreign women are barred from the company of priests and clerics, 301.

Women are forbidden to enter monasteries, 246.

Gregory believed that the end of the world was near, 162, 163, 167.

Gregory rejects gifts, 227. See Gifts.

What *mutacismus* is, 172.

## N
Narses the Patrician, 40. A very close friend of Gregory, 213. Baronius wrongly confuses him with another Narses, ibid. He was a monk and abbot, 276. Narses the count, 148. Wishing to restrain the rioting schismatics, he is excommunicated by them, 202. He summons the Lombards into Italy, 202.

Nasas the Jew, a most wicked man, 153. He mocks Christians under the false pretense of Elijah’s worship, 242.

Natalis, bishop of Salona, 87, 88, 140. He is accused of devoting himself to banquets while neglecting pastoral care, 100. When he tries to excuse himself by his own explanations, he is refuted, ibid., 101. By his bad example bishops turn aside from the right path, 242. Why he tried to remove Honoratus the archdeacon from office, 233. Gregory threatens deprivation of the pallium and excommunication, 233. He repents, 233.

Naples belonged by jurisdiction to the Roman Church, 271. In that city artisans had been divided into different corporations, 293.

Neophytes are barred from the orders, 254.

Nepesina belonged by jurisdiction to the Roman Church, 271. The visitation of the Church of Nepesina is entrusted to John the bishop, 94, 226.

Which Nestorians returning to the Church are to be received, 295.

Pope Nicholas I, 156.

The power of the Ninevites’ repentance, 6, 37.

How Gregory used his nobility, 2, 190.

Nonnosus the abbot, 172.

Nordulfus, 110, 132.

Cardinal Noris’s *Chronology of the Abbots of the Monastery of Saint Gregory*, 205.

Formerly the notaries among the emperors possessed great dignity and power, 240.

Why Novatus, archdeacon of the Roman Church under Pope Cornelius, was made a presbyter, 210.

Why Gregory assigned two years to the probation of novices, 208. See *Monastic profession*.

Numidia, the second of the seven provinces of Africa, 231.

The words of those who nourish: “milk,” if they are good; “poison,” if they are bad, 201.

What the *Nymphaeum* or *Nymphium* was, 175, 176.

## O

The ancient use of offerings, 10, 58.

What *obnoxius* signifies, 186.

“Ecumenical” means the same as “universal,” 248. The word “ecumenical” has a broader meaning than the word “general,” 249. Gregory vigorously refuted the title “ecumenical bishop.” See *John of Constantinople*. When it was offered to him, he rejected it, 120. Saint Leo the Great had also rejected it, 248. What a monstrous thing an ecumenical bishop is in the Church, 248. Why this title ought to be rejected, ibid., 249. It was later tolerated, 251. In what sense it does not suit even the pope himself, 251.

Gregory decrees that two offices should not be entrusted to one person, 65, 66.

Saint Gregory acquires many olive groves for the lamps of the basilicas of the Apostles Peter and Paul, 50.

Gregory wishes a suitable man to be promoted to pastoral care, 90.

Optatus the defensor, 64.

[Col. 1336] Good works must be added to prayer, 294.

Gregory established that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited after the canon, 51.

*To ordain.* How cautious Gregory was in ordaining bishops, 86, 99, 91. He ordained no one by force, 87, 91. Those promoted by others through force he restored to their former rank, 87. Those driven from the orders by slander he restored, 88. Formerly no clerics were ordained except for a definite church, 88. Whether Gregory was made a presbyter before he was ordained bishop, 216. The ordination of laymen and neophytes is prohibited, 254. Repeated ordinations are prohibited, 236. It is forbidden to give or receive anything for receiving ecclesiastical orders, 85, 86.

Gregory gave the Roman Order published by Gelasius I a better form, 50, 223.

Gregory was never idle, 7.

## P

Gregory bought pagan children so that they might become Christians, 61. He did not wish pagan slaves who wanted to come to the faith to be sold, 154, 155. He did not wish pagan slaves who had preceded their masters into the faith to remain subject to those masters, even if the masters became Christians, 155. He permitted no pagan to be circumcised, 155. For the sake of recently converted pagans, he sometimes relaxed something of the rigor of discipline, 56, 269.

Palatina, the widow of Urbicus, 67.

The *palla corporalis* was formerly wrapped around and covered the body of Christ, 10.

Palladius, bishop of Saintes, requests relics, 272. Gregory consoles the presbyter Palladius, who had been attacked by accusations, 294, 295.

Palladius the abbot in Arabia, 64, 111.

The pallium was formerly granted neither to all metropolitans nor exclusively to metropolitans, 286. What the use of the pallium formerly was, 239. Augustine receives the pallium from the Apostolic See, 56. Leander of Seville also receives it, 287. The bishops of London and York also receive it, 56, 261. Why Gregory delayed giving the pallium to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, 80. It is prohibited to give or receive anything for the use of the pallium, 85, 86. Gregory’s pallium is found during the translation of his body, 174, 175.

Palmaria island. Why adolescents not yet of mature age are prohibited from being received into the monasteries on this island, 208, 227.

Gregory foretells in an apparition the death of Palumbus the monk, 180, 181.

Saint Pancratius. Monks are admitted to the church of Saint Pancratius at Rome, 246.

Pancratius, deacon of the Church of Vienne, 247. He becomes a monk, 299.

The miracle of the multiplication of bread, 186.

Pantaleon, prefect of Africa, is accused of excessive indulgence toward heretics, 231.

Pantaleon the notary, 64, 71.

What *paracoemomenus* means, 134.

The negligence of Paschasius, bishop of Naples, is censured, 103, 104, 144, 301. Gregory wishes him to resign the office of *vicedominus* (steward), 65.

The dalmatic of Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church, was kept beneath the altar together with the tunic of Saint John the Evangelist, 119. A demoniac is freed by touching it, 119. Some falsely say that this was the pontifical garment of Saint John the Evangelist, 119.

Pasivus the bishop, 90.

What *pastellus* is, 85.

[Col. 1337] On what occasion Gregory wrote the book *Pastoral Care*, 171, 196, 197, 198. What it contains, 7, 171, 189, 192. With what intention and in what year he composed it, 223. Gregory sent this book to the emperor, 171, and to John, bishop of Ravenna, 189. Anastasius the bishop translated this book into Greek, 171. The duty of a good shepherd, 171. Gregory was kind and dutiful toward good shepherds, 240.

Pateria, Gregory’s aunt—that is, his father’s or mother’s sister—67, 200, 201, 227.

Paterius the notary, made *secundicerius* by Gregory, 48.

It was the custom of the patriarchs not to have the name of any pontiff recited at the altar until they had received his synodal letter of faith, 137, 138.

The Roman Church formerly possessed many estates throughout the entire Christian world, 271. Gregory appointed separate administrators over each estate, 64, 65. Why he did not wish laymen to be placed over them, 224. He did not wish the Church’s estate to be increased by plunder, 235.

Ecclesiastical patronage should not be bestowed on wicked men, 289.

The acts of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, were formerly customarily read at vigils, 19.

Paulinus, the schismatic bishop of Aquileia, presides over the synod of Italy, 202. He is called patriarch, 203. He withdraws to the island of Grado, ibid.

Paulinus, bishop of the city of Tegesta in Numidia, is accused of many things, 297.

Paulinus the presbyter, 67.

Paulinus the monk is sent to England with Augustine, 261. He is ordained bishop, 86.

The Church of Naples is entrusted to Paul, bishop of Nepesina, for visitation, 94, 226. He is requested by the Neapolitans as their bishop, 94. He is mistreated near Naples, 226.

Paul, bishop in Numidia, after being harassed, appeals to the Roman See, 280. His case is entrusted to the bishops of Numidia, ibid.

Paul, bishop of Doclea, is deposed after a lapse, 297.

Paul the Deacon, 145.

Paul the scholasticus, 38.

The poor. Gregory ministers to the poor, 20, 194. How highly God valued his poverty, 78. Gregory’s generosity toward the poor is tested by an angel, 25, 52, 196. The same generosity is rewarded, 25, 52, 196. What care he took of the poor, 61, 77, 224. He gave the help of his generosity not only to those present but also to those living far away, 7. He supplied the poor with food together with the nourishment of the word, 50. Whatever money he possessed, he took care to distribute to the poor, 192. So that he might assist the poor more easily, he appointed administrators over the separate estates in the various provinces, 64, 65. If the administrators and agents of the estates were not present to assist the poor, he immediately rebuked them, 227. He wished the property of deceased bishops to be preserved for the poor, 271. If the revenues of bishops were insufficient to feed the poor, he supplied them with whatever was necessary, 271. From where he obtained enough for such great expenditures, ibid. Gregory mourns for a poor man who died from want as though he had killed him with his own hands, 53. When twelve poor men were invited to his table, he found a thirteenth—namely, an angel—among them, 195. What care he took of the poor even after death, 15, 179, 180. What true poverty consists in, 78.

No one was permitted to possess personal property in the monastery of Saint Gregory, 27, 61. [Col. 1337] A monk was severely punished at death for having kept personal property, 27, 213, 214. A monk was excommunicated for three coins, 61.

Pope Pelagius I succeeds Vigilius, 202. How many years he lived in the pontificate, ibid.

Pope Pelagius II. In what year he was created pontiff, 210. He sends Bishop Sebastian to Gregory, then serving as apocrisiarius at Constantinople, 33. His letter to Gregory, 33. Pelagius’s concern to drive out the Lombards, 212. He invalidates the acts of the synod convened by John of Constantinople, 111. He forbids his deacon residing at Constantinople to communicate in the celebration of the sacred rites with John of Constantinople, 111, 212. That deacon appears to have been someone other than Saint Gregory, 212. Pelagius employs Gregory as an assistant in writing letters, 214. What he did to recall schismatics to the bosom of the Church, 214. His reverence toward the four councils, ibid. He is the first of all to die of the plague, 5, 35, 187, 216.

Gregory took the greatest care of pilgrims, 224.

Whether the Persians were converted to the faith in Gregory’s time, 240.

The bubonic plague devastates Rome, 5, 6, 35, 37, 187, 216. In what year, 217. What the cause of this plague was, 4, 5, 35, 187, 216. It struck people like an arrow sent down from heaven, 35. Eighty people die within the space of one hour, 6, 38, 189, 217. As the disease rages, Gregory preaches repentance to the people, 5, 6, 36, 37, 188, 216. He orders litanies, 217. See *Litanies*. Whether an angel was seen putting a drawn sword back into its sheath, 217.

Among the ancients, the confession of the Apostle Saint Peter is used for the place of his burial, 218.

Peter, bishop of Corsica, 63.

Peter, bishop of Istria, 149.

Peter, bishop of Numidia, 273.

Peter, formerly one of the subdeacons of the Roman Church, bishop of Trecalita, 86.

Peter, subdeacon of Campania, 64, 67, 72, 77. He was later made a deacon, 7, 48. At his request Gregory published the books of the *Dialogues*, ibid. He discussed these books with Peter, 169, 196. How Peter prevented Gregory’s books from being burned, 169, 197. After giving testimony to Gregory’s holiness, he dies as a confessor of the truth, 169.

Peter the Roman presbyter, 61.

Peter the archdeacon, 177.

Peter, Augustine’s companion, is sent to England, 258. He is sent to Gregory to report the conversion of the English, 55, 260. The first abbot of the monastery at Canterbury, 261.

Peter, abbot of the Gregorian monastery, 29, 205.

Peter the praetor, 135.

Peter the tenant-farmer, 74.

Philippicus, son-in-law of Emperor Maurice, 134. Summoned by Maurice, and thinking that he was destined for destruction, he fortified himself with Holy Communion, 134.

Philippicus the presbyter, 70.

Philippus, count of the excubitors, 42. He strengthened Gregory’s election with his vote, 216.

The qualities of Phocas, 135. Raised on a shield by the army, he is acclaimed exarch, 135, 299. He enters Constantinople, 299. He orders Maurice to be beheaded with his wife and sons, 135. When he began to reign, 17. The images of Phocas and Leontia are brought to Rome and placed in the oratory of Saint Caesarius, 135, 136, 300. The clergy and senate acclaim Phocas and Leontia in the basilica of Julius, 136. Gregory congratulates Phocas, 136, 300. Phocas requests an apocrisiarius, 136, 137.

What Gregory’s *phylacteria* are, 174.

[Col. 1338] Pimenius, bishop of Amalfi, is censured because he did not reside in his church, 101, 102, 272.

In Gregory’s time the Pisans were independent, 301.

The power of repentance, 6, 36, 37. A trace of public repentance in Maximus of Salona, 130, 243. Gregory rejoiced at the repentance of those who had fallen and gone astray, 233.

What the Gelasian *Polypticum* is, 53. From that *polypticum* Gregory’s estates and revenues were distributed to the poor, 53.

Pompeius the bishop, 141.

Gregory is consecrated pontiff, 6, 38, 189, 218. In what year and on what day, 17, 198, 218. At his ordination he makes a profession of the faith, ibid. What gifts and virtues he brought to the pontificate, 222. Once made pontiff, he took care to turn his house into a monastery, 191. He humbly replies to those who congratulate him on having assumed the pontificate, 219. He appears to grow angry with John the former consul, who had supported his election, ibid. See *Election*.

Formerly the supreme pontiff was called “the Apostolic,” 11, 12. Formerly the emperor’s consent was required for the election of the supreme pontiff, 5, 36, 188, 216. Where this custom originated, 216. Charlemagne and his successors possessed this right, ibid. For the election of the supreme pontiff, Athalarius ordered three thousand solidi to be paid, 216. Whether Catholic rulers demanded money for the same election, 216. Why the people formerly paid money during elections, 216, note. Until the elected pontiff was consecrated, to whom the administration of the Roman Church was entrusted, 217.

As patriarch, the Roman pontiff was responsible for the ordination of many bishops, 243. In what sense the Roman pontiffs could have been called ecumenical, 248. In what sense they could not be called so, 251. From Gregory himself it is clear that the Roman pontiff enjoys jurisdiction throughout the whole Church, 251. The ancient authority of the supreme pontiffs in Gaul, 286, and in Africa, 298. Their power to confer or remove ecclesiastical honors, 255. The same power in approving or rejecting books, 20. Gregory and Bernard disapproved of admitting lay boys to the chamber of the supreme pontiff, 223. See *Apostolic See*.

Possession. The Roman Church enjoyed possession of its property by a hundred-year prescription, 226.

*To preach.* Whether formerly no one preached or taught in the Roman Church, 224. Gregory preaches to his people, 6, 50, 224, 226. See *Plague*. His method of preaching, 224, 225. He sends preachers to the barbarians, 225. He supported the preaching of others with his prayers and exhortations, 9, 194.

Praejectus, bishop of Narni, 64.

Gregory becomes praetor of the City, 23, 196. In what year, 203. How he conducted himself in the praetorship, 23, 203, 204. Who first held the praetorship of the City, 203.

The importunity of prayers is pleasing to God, 6.

The efficacy of prayers, 5, 6, 37.

Whether Gregory was a presbyter before he was consecrated pontiff, 216, 217. Who were formerly called presbyters and who priests, 15. Comparing himself with a presbyter, Gregory declares that the latter is superior and better, 161. Whether formerly monks could not be elevated to the presbyterate, 247. See *Monks*.

Pretiosus, superior—not abbot—of the monastery of Saint Andrew, 27, 28, 205. He is called *οἰκονόμος* (*oikonomos*, “steward”), 28. He celebrates the sacrifice of the Mass for thirty days for Justus the monk, 214.

Who the primate was among the Africans, 231. [Col. 1339] A primate should be chosen not according to the rank of his see but according to the merit of his life, 231. The primate ought to reside in the city, ibid. Those who had risen to the episcopate from the Donatists could not become primates, ibid. See *Metropolitan*.

To which Church the dignity of primacy in England was attached, 261.

Probinus, successor of Paulinus of Aquileia, 203.

Probinus the presbyter, 155.

Probus, abbot of the monasteries of Saints Andrew and Luke, 204. He did not preside over the monastery of Saint Andrew at the Clivus Scauri, 205. Probus the abbot is sent by Gregory to Jerusalem to assist the poor and construct a hospice, 49, 64. He is sent to Agilulf to negotiate peace, 282.

What *proceed* signifies in sacred authors, 13.

The procession of the Holy Spirit, 172. The deceit of the Greeks concerning that doctrine defended by Gregory, ibid.

Gregory possessed the spirit of prophecy, 159.

Those who enjoy prosperous circumstances should learn to despise temporal goods, 292.

Providentius, bishop of Istria, 149.

Gregory’s prudence in his various decrees, 289.

What ΠΤΥΚΙΣ (*ptykis*) signifies, 53.

Canonical purgation by sacrament or oath, 277.

Purgatory. Dinocrates is freed from purgatory by prayers, 275.

What a *pyctacium* is, 61, 62.

What *Pyrgibasis* or *Pyrgobasis* is, 169 and 170.

## R

Abduction is to be punished, 304.

Reccared, king of the Visigoths, 155. By whom he was brought to the faith, 221. He arranges for the Arian heresy to be condemned at the Council of Toledo, ibid. He obtains peace from the Franks and marries Clotsind, 222. He permits no heretic to serve in the army in his kingdom, ibid. His encomium, 287. He rejects money offered by Jews, 288. He always found the Arians extremely hostile, 296. He dies, ibid.

Recluses were sometimes compelled to leave their cells for public affairs, 284.

Who were called *regionarii*, 199. From where they were appointed, 281.

Abbot Claudius added certain things to the exposition of the Books of Kings made by Gregory, ibid.

How relics were formerly sent, 11, 12, 59. The source of their miraculous effects, 12, 59. How highly the relics of the saints should be esteemed, 12. The sacrilegious fraud of certain Greek monks concerning relics, 244. Until Gregory’s time, a *brandeum* was sent by the Roman pontiff in place of relics, 116, 117, 244. Throughout the West it was sacrilegious to touch the bodies of the saints, 213, 244. Later, however, pieces of the clothing of Saint John the Evangelist were given as relics, 116. The efficacy of these pieces, 117. In former times basilicas were scarcely dedicated without sacred relics, 54, 232, and neither were altars, 272. But where some body had previously been buried, no relics were deposited, 232. Gregory’s veneration for the relics of the saints, 285. Gregory regarded translations and destructions of relics with suspicion, 244. Nevertheless, some are recorded as having been carried out in antiquity, ibid. Gregory obtains relics from the emperor and brings them to Rome, 213. He sends relics to Gregory of Tours, 189, and to Reccared, 288.

The translation of Saint Gregory’s body, 174, 305.

Residence. Saint Gregory’s view concerning the residence of bishops and clerics, 101, 102, 272.

[Col. 1339] What a *reponsalis* is, 211.

Among the blessed Gregory and Benedict, *responsum* means the same as “business” or “matter,” 206.

Restitution. How concerned Gregory was that things which had been taken away should be restored, 284, 301.

Resurrection. What the Church’s faith concerning the resurrection is, 4, 31, 191. Eutychius’s error concerning the resurrection. See *Eutychius*.

Gregory thought of the day of retribution in all his words and deeds, 162.

Rhisina or Rhisinum, a city of Mesopotamia, 91.

Rome is afflicted by an inundation of the Tiber, 4, 35, 187, and by the plague, 5. See *Plague*. The sorrowful condition of Rome, 5. Rome’s miserable condition under the Lombards, 34, 163, 164, 165, 234. It suffers from famine, 235. Gregory’s concern that Rome not be captured, 7. His concern that it not lack grain, 226, 234, 235. How great a patron Rome lost when Gregory died, 169.

The Roman Church is the mother of all Churches, 255.

Whether formerly no bishop or anyone else preached in the Roman Church, 224.

Roman pontiff. See *Supreme pontiff*.

The generosity of the earlier Roman pontiffs in assisting the needy, 272.

Romanus, exarch of Italy, 107, 110. Why he refused to make peace with the Lombards, 234, 252. His wickedness, 235. He is censured because he assisted nuns who had returned to secular life, 257.

Romanus the defensor, 69, 101, 159.

Romanus the notary, 64.

Gregory foretells in an apparition the death of Romanus the layman, 180, 181.

What the rubrics are, 185.

Ruferius, count of Corsica, 277.

Rufinianus the monk, sent by Gregory to Augustine in England, 261.

Rusticiana, a patrician woman, 158, 160, 168.

Rusticianus, 76.

Rusticus, deacon of Ancona, 90.

Bishops must not neglect the rustic pagans, 62. Gregory wished rustic pagans who persisted in their unbelief to be burdened with the payment of a tax, 62. He recalled the peasants of Campania from pagan error, 79.

## S

The death of Saba the monk is foretold by Gregory in an apparition, 180, 181.

Those who observe the Sabbath too scrupulously are attacked, 156, 157, 302.

Sabinianus, Saint Gregory’s successor, 18.

Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, 129. Because he had adhered to Maximus the usurper, he renounces the episcopate and withdraws into a monastery, 243. He is recalled to the episcopate, ibid.

Sabinianus the deacon, Saint Gregory’s *responsalis*, 112, 115, 162.

Sabinus, formerly a monk, is consecrated bishop of Callipolis, 86.

The ancients did not usually designate a presbyter by the name “priest,” 15, 617. Why Gregory, while still a deacon, was called a priest, 617.

Gregory called priests “brothers and fellow ministers,” 160.

Fallen priests are confined in the poorest monasteries, 229. What Gregory decreed concerning their property, 232.

Among the Romans, priests were found in the provinces and flamines in the municipalities, 15.

Sagittarius, bishop of Gap, was deposed in many councils, 286.

Salpingus the Jew, 75.

Holy women. See *Nuns*.

The title “holiness,” now given only to the pope, was formerly common to many, 16.

[Col. 1340] The acts of the saints were formerly customarily read at vigils, 19.

The saints do not pray for the damned, 275.

Under Gregory’s pontificate, Wisdom had erected a temple for herself, supported as if by seven columns—that is, by the liberal arts, 49.

The pagans of Sardinia used to pay the praetor a price so that they might be permitted to sacrifice to their idols, 235. After their conversion Gregory forbade that price to be exacted, ibid. The faith is propagated in Sardinia, 294. What Gregory did to convert the Sardinians, 79, 246.

Saturninus the monk, 177.

Savinus the subdeacon, 160.

Saxulus, a tenant-farmer, is tormented by the devil, 182.

What the Lombard word *scala* means, 202.

We ought to remove scandal whenever we can, 295.

What the Lombard word *schilpor* means, 202.

The schismatics in the affair of the Three Chapters are invited to hold a conference for the extinction of the schism, 214. To defend their obstinacy in the schism, they write an apology, ibid. They order the supreme pontiff to withdraw from the condemnation of the Three Chapters, ibid. Who were regarded as schismatics, 245, 297, 228. In Gregory’s time only the bishops of Istria and Venice stood by the schism, 228. How Gregory conducted himself toward the schismatics, 229. He invited them to the unity of the Church, 79, 149, 245. Gregory’s charity toward the schismatics, 283, 284. The Capritan schismatics return to the Church, 283. What Gregory did to confirm them in the unity of the Church, 283. What the returning schismatics promised, 297. Maurice orders that they be treated more mildly, 150, 234.

Scholasticus, judge of Campania, 87.

The Slavs invade Italy, 291.

The misuse of Sacred Scripture in flattering speech is condemned, 274.

Sebastianus, bishop sent to Gregory by Pelagius, 33.

Sebastianus, bishop of Sirmium, 91, 110.

Secundinus, a servant of God and recluse, 98, 137, 284. Gregory employs the services of Secundinus to arrange peace with Agilulf, 241. Secundinus receives the son of Theodelinda from the sacred font, 284. He writes against the condemnation of the Three Chapters, yet is not a schismatic, ibid. His humble confession, 284.

Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium, 281.

Excessive security is dangerous, 275.

The Apostolic See is consulted in questions of faith and discipline, 228. It belongs to the authority of the Holy See to confirm the customs of Churches, 231.

Septimus, a place near Constantinople, 135.

Burial. It is forbidden to pay a price for burial, 51, 280. Where Gregory was buried, 168, 304.

Serenus, bishop of Marseille, is accused concerning the destruction of images, 98, 99. How his action may be excused, 284, 285. He is censured because he admits wicked men into his fellowship, 106. He regards Gregory’s letters presented to him as spurious, 285.

Sergius, master of soldiers, 184.

Sergius the defensor, 64. He is accused of negligence, 103.

Servus Dei, deacon, 74, 76.

Gregory was the first of all to call himself “servant of the servants of God,” 45.

[Col. 1341] Severus, bishop of Aquileia or Grado, the head of the schism, 149, 150. Compelled by both apostolic and imperial commands, he is taken to Ravenna, 150, 215. In what year, 229. He falsely renounces the schism, 150, 215, 229. The schism did not cease during Gregory’s lifetime, 150. Gregory invites Severus to peace, 229. He surreptitiously obtains the emperor’s order, which prohibited the schismatics from being compelled to return to the unity of the Church, 229. Why Gregory forbade alms to be given to Severus, 234.

The visitation of the Church of Ravenna is entrusted to Severus, bishop of Ficulina, 126.

Sicily, one of the suburban provinces in which there was no metropolitan, 225. Gregory orders a synod to be held annually in Sicily, ibid. He granted the bishops of Sicily permission to come to Rome only once every five years, 226, 272. He arranges for grain to be brought from Sicily to Rome, 226, 235. Sicily is afflicted by depopulation, 235. Litanies and prayers are ordered to avert enemies from Sicily, 158, 159, 294. Gregory foretells that Sicily, infected with simony, will perish, 159.

Sigobert the recluse is sent to Rome, 284.

Vigilius succeeds Pope Silverius after the latter has been deposed, 202.

Silvia, Saint Gregory’s mother, 1, 23, 195, 199. She used to send vegetables to Gregory the monk, 25, 195, 209. An image of Silvia in the atrium of the monastery of Saint Andrew, 176, 199. Silvia is honored by the Church, 199. An oratory formerly existed dedicated to her name, 176, 199, 200.

Simony, the first heresy to arise against the Church, 81. The threefold form of simony, 86. Simony is the granting of divine orders for human favor, 86. Simony is prohibited in a Roman synod, 297, 298. Gregory pursues it as it rages in Gaul, 79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84, 254, 287. He requests that a synod be convened against it, 85, 285. He did not obtain this, however, 287. Gregory foretells that Sicily, infected with simony, will perish, 159.

Where Pope Simplicius was buried, 168.

Simplicius, the third abbot of the monastery of Cassino after Saint Benedict, 204. In his time the Rule of Saint Benedict had already spread through many provinces of Italy, 207.

Smaragdus, exarch, 150. Successor of Longinus and *chartularius* of the sacred palace, 213. Sent by the emperor to free Italy from the Lombards, ibid., 221. He brings Severus of Aquileia to Ravenna, 150, 215.

*Solatium* is used for “assistance,” 206.

How the annual solemnity of Saint Gregory was celebrated, 174.

What “to build solitudes” means, 203.

The hermit’s dream concerning Blessed Gregory, 78.

Speciosus the presbyter, 108.

The Holy Spirit, under the appearance of a dove, dictates to Gregory what he should write, 14, 15, 169, 198. Hence he is depicted in the form of a dove above Gregory’s head, 169.

Gregory used his authority to confirm the agreements made by bishops with clerics, 146.

Stations are appointed in the basilicas or cemeteries of the martyrs, 50.

Pope Stephen III granted the monastery of Saint Dionysius to Greek monks, 175, 204. He is likewise believed to have granted the monastery of Saint Andrew to Greek monks, ibid.

Stephen the bishop, 141, 161. His zeal in bringing schismatics back into the bosom of the Church is praised, 277.

The customary stipends are to be distributed even to infirm clerics, 145, 146. See *Clerics*.

[Col. 1341] Gregory orders that a violated virgin either be taken by her violator or that the violator be assigned to a monastery, 152.

A subdeacon who slanders is removed from office, 144.

Gregory orders stripped subdeacons to proceed, 51.

Which bishops Gregory ordained from among the subdeacons of the Roman Church, 86.

Pelagius II orders the married subdeacons of Sicily to separate from their wives, 230. Gregory permitted them to retain their wives on what condition, ibid. No subdeacon is to be ordained unless he promises chastity, ibid. In the Roman Church subdeacons observed celibacy, 230.

The heterodox story about the killing of the children of clerics is rejected, 230.

Whether Gregory believed that monasticism could take the place of the subdiaconate, 299.

Gregory and his mother bestow estates and possessions on the monastery at Subiaco, 246.

ΣΥΓΚΟΠΙΣ (*synkopis*) is called by Celsus a fainting or collapse of the soul, 3.

Gregory was prudent toward the proud, 123.

Suppo, count of Picenum, 183. In a vision he is ordered to leave Gregory’s monastery, 184.

Syagrius, bishop of Autun, a man of great authority among the princes of Gaul, 221, 287. He receives the pallium from Gregory, 286. Under what conditions, 287. He is appointed vicar of the Apostolic See, 286. Why Gregory delayed sending him the pallium, 80.

Gregory published a creed by which he might fortify the faith and disperse all heresies, 45.

Where Pope Symmachus was buried, 168.

Symmachus the defensor of Sardinia, 64.

What a synodal letter is and why it is so called, 219.

Gregory sends a synodal letter to all the patriarchs, 45, 46, 137, 218, 219.

A synod is to be held annually in Sicily, 225. Gregory granted the bishops of Sicily permission to come to Rome for a synod only once every five years, 226.

A Roman synod was held under Gregory, 253. The presbyters and deacons subscribed to it, ibid.

## T

The prefects of military units were called *taxiarchs*, 135.

The wills of bishops. See *Bishops*.

The wills of monks. See *Monks*.

Tharsilla, Gregory’s aunt, 23. Consecrated to God, 102. As she is dying, she sees Christ coming to her, 23, 102.

Themistius the deacon, from whom the Agnoites were called Themistians, 290.

Theoctista, sister of Emperor Maurice, 39, 53, 213. Her piety, 276. The emperor entrusts his sons to her to be educated, 201, 276. Gregory consoles her when she is accused of heresy, 294. The points of her alleged heresy are refuted, 295.

Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, 160. Dedicated to Christ, 16. She marries Authari, king of the Lombards, 221. She brings the Lombards to the faith, ibid. After Authari’s death, she takes Agilulf as partner in the kingdom and marriage, 229. She urges him to embrace the faith, ibid. Through her suggestions Agilulf makes peace with the Romans, 17. She withdraws from communion with Constantius, bishop of Milan, because of the Three Chapters condemned by him, 241, 245. Gregory recalls her from her error by envoys and letters sent to her, 245. He sends her the books of the *Dialogues*, 16, 196, 197, and gifts, 304.

[Col. 1342] Theoderic, king of the Franks, sends an envoy to Gregory, 301.

Which writings of Theodoret were condemned at the Fifth Council, 215.

Theodorus, bishop of Gaul, 153.

Theodorus, bishop of the diocese of Milan, 289.

Theodorus, sent to England by Vitalian and consecrated bishop of Canterbury, brings the Britons to the unity of the Roman Church, 270. He is sent to reform the chant throughout Gaul, 48. He is called bishop of York, 48.

The writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia were rightly condemned, 215.

Theodorus the deacon, envoy to Cyriacus of Constantinople, 273.

What happened to Theodore the boy, a monk in Gregory’s monastery, 35, 36. When that Theodore was ill, Saint Gregory was absent from the monastery, 216.

Theodorus the lector, 175.

Theodorus the physician, 111.

The soldiers of the legion distinguished by the name of Theodosius, the son of the emperor, were called Theodosians, 234.

Theodosius, son of Emperor Maurice, refused the empire offered to him, 135. Whether he was slaughtered together with the other sons of that emperor, 300.

Philo’s Therapeutae sketched the way of life of monks, 264.

Theutgaudus, bishop of Trier, deposed by Pope Nicholas I, 183. Through the generosity of Pope Hadrian he resides in the monastery of Saint Gregory, 183. From where he is compelled in a vision to depart, ibid.

*Thia*, that is, a father’s or mother’s sister, 67.

The emperor Tiberius Constantine, 33. He assisted Gregory in overthrowing the heresy of Eutychius, 4, 33, 191. He orders Eutychius’s book to be destroyed by fire, 212. Distracted by wars and other concerns, he gives little thought to recovering Italy, 212. In what year he died, ibid.

When the body of Saint Timothy was brought to Constantinople, 244.

The tonsure of monks was formerly distinctive, as it is now, 205. The tonsure is the distinctive mark of coenobites, not hermits, ibid. In Gregory’s time many laymen wished to be tonsured, 49. See *Clerics*.

Totila, king of the Goths, 164. In what year he began to reign, 201. He besieged Rome twice, 201.

Whether the emperor Trajan was freed from the punishments of hell, 14, 59, 60, 274, 275. What John the Deacon thinks about him, 60, 275.

Trajan the presbyter, 89.

Trajan the abbot, appointed in place of Lucillus, bishop of Melitene, 289.

Translations of relics. See *Relics*.

Transubstantiation. See *Eucharist*.

Tullianus, master of soldiers, 103.

The most destructive inundation of the Tiber, 4, 5, 35, 187, 216. In what year, 215. The swelling of the Tiber had formerly also been fatal, 215.

## U

Ulric, bishop of Augsburg, in what period he lived, 230.

Ulfari, duke of Treviso, defects from the Lombards, 234.

Unions of Churches effected by Gregory, 91, 92, 93.

The title “universal honor.” See *Ecumenical*.

Whether Urban II believed that regular canons had been instituted by Gregory, 265, 266.

[Col. 1343] Urbicus the abbot, 152. A kind of general superior of Gregory’s monasteries in Sicily, 206, 302. Why Gregory did not wish him to be ordained bishop, 302.

Urbicus the defensor, 64.

Ursellus is freed by Gregory in an apparition from the blows of the devil, 182.

Ursicinus, bishop of Turin, 287.

## V
Valentinianus, provost of the Lateran monastery, 204. The death of the monk Valentinianus is foretold, 28. Valentinus is rebuked for having allowed women to enter his monastery, 246. Valentio, or Valentius, abbot of the monastery of St. Gregory, 205. Whether he was a disciple of St. Equitius, 206. Valeria. The Rule of St. Benedict was propagated in the province of Valeria, 207. Valerianus, monk, 69. Valerius, chartularius, 71. Venantius, bishop of Luni, 154. Venantius, bishop of Perugia, 97. Venantius Patricius, formerly a monk, 90, 105, 108, 166. He was not chancellor of Italy, 230. After leaving the monastery, he married a wife, 230. He complains to Gregory that his offerings were rejected by the bishop, 109, 230. He sends armed retainers into the episcopal see, 272. Gregory was exceedingly concerned about his salvation, 230, 294. Gregory recalled the Venetians from schism to the unity of the Church, 79. *Vestiarium* is used for a person or a place, 214. Veteranus, priest, 159.

[Col. 1343] With what authority the vicars of the Holy See were invested, 255. The bishops of the more distinguished cities were honored with this dignity, ibid. This authority was at times increased and at times diminished, ibid. Victor, bishop of Panormus, 153. He is accused of negligence, 104. Gregory undertakes the care of widows, 227. What Gregory’s vigilance was, 1, 23, 201. Vigils. In former times, the acts of the saints were read at vigils, 19. In what year Vigilius was made pope, 202. Because of his condemnation of the Three Chapters, many bishops of the West withdrew from his communion, ibid. Why he initially refused to condemn the Three Chapters, 214, 215. Vipera, a certain place in Rome, in the district of the Seven Ways, 185. Virgilius, bishop of Arles, 153. He was made, from a former monk of Lérins, abbot of the monastery of Autun, and afterward bishop of Arles, 221. Gregory entrusted his vicariate in Gaul to him and granted him the pallium, 254. What authority he exercised over the bishops subject to him, 255. Vision. What the vision of angels ascending and descending, granted to a hermit at the election of Blessed Gregory, signified, 6. Why and when Gregory entrusted the visitation of churches to bishops, 94, 95, 96, 126, 226. Both clergy and monks observed the common life in Gregory’s palace, 49. The common life implies no more a regular canon than a monk, 264.

[Col. 1344] Pope Vitalianus sent singers throughout Gaul to reform the chant, 48. Vitalianus, bishop of Sipontum, is accused of negligence, 103. Vitalis, defensor in Sardinia, 246. Viviana, widow, 67. Warnilfrida, counselor of Ariulfus, 282. St. Wilfrid, propagator of the Rule of St. Benedict in England, 267. The monarchy of the Visigoths included Spain and Narbonese Gaul, 221. The Visigoths were called to the faith through St. Leander, ibid. Witericus, king of Spain, 296.

## X

What *xenia* are, 11. Formerly called *exenia*, ibid. How averse St. Gregory was to receiving gifts of hospitality, 96, 97. Gregory appoints superintendents over guesthouses, 63, 64. He did not permit the guesthouses to be neglected, 303. He established a guesthouse in Jerusalem, 64.

## Z

Zabarda, duke of Sardinia: how he compelled the Barbaricini to accept the faith of Christ, 246. Pope Zacharias, 172. Zacharias, bishop of the city of Anagni: the period in which he lived, 182, 185. Zacharias, a physician, became an apostate and went over to the Saracens, 179. Gregory’s zeal in correcting vices, 137. St. Zeno, bishop and martyr, 35. During the flooding of the Athesis, its waters did not dare enter his church, 35. Zeno, bishop, 68.
