They question those whom they correct and deprive them of time to answer, 777. They say many foolish things, 817. They imitate the voices of the just, whose force they do not understand, 831. The arrogant person’s manner and style of speaking, 845, 881. It is arrogance in an inferior to extort a hearing from a superior, 881. The arrogant are rejected by God, 897. Every arrogant person either acknowledges his fault by repenting or learns his punishment by perishing, 1052. Arrogance arises from pride, ibid. The arrogant are poor, blind, and naked, 1118.

---

The arrogant imitate Lucifer, 737. They display knowledge they do not possess, 738. They pretend that the voices of the Church are not addressed to them, ibid. They do not know how to conceal their knowledge, 739. They falsely claim to be full of the Holy Spirit, 741. The arrogant person’s pride in teaching, 742. The arrogant person’s pretense in speaking, 743. The arrogant desire to rebuke more than to console, 745. They assume the appearance of teachers, 778, 845. They pretend humility, 778, 811. They do not know how to sympathize with the afflicted, 814. They rebuke others by lying, 818. They want to be heard, 830. They feed on human praises, 842. They despise what belongs to others and admire what is their own, 845. Under the pretext of religion they swell with pride, 846. They wish to appear more as judges than as comforters, 852. They say certain good things, but must be heard cautiously, 853. The arrogant are called monstrous, 863. Through their own words the arrogant condemn themselves, 887. God does not know the arrogant, 897.

Arrogance is the daughter of pride, 1052. Arrogance strengthens vices, 282. There are four kinds of arrogance, 736.

Arts that can scarcely be practiced without sin should be abandoned, 1540.

What the fat hanging from the sides of the wicked powerful man signifies, 411.

The various meanings of “reed” in Scripture, 1078. What a reed-bed signifies, 1079. What a reed shaken by the wind signifies, 1256, 1454.

Ascent occurs through labor; descent through pleasure, 224. What it means to ascend above the setting sun, 606. To rise from the earth is to grow proud of earthly glory, 1110. What the purple ascent of the litter signifies, 1334. What it means to ascend from the opposite side, 1486. How Christ’s Ascension took place, 1572. See Christ’s Ascension.

What is signified by the name “donkeys,” 24, 57, 65, 523, 1159, 1161. What it means for the Lord to come to Jerusalem seated on a donkey, 24, 1352. What the strong donkey lying between boundaries signifies, 25. Female donkeys signify lustful impulses or simple thoughts, 30, 65. What it means to exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep, 870. The donkey is a symbol of lust, 228, 870, 1161. What it means to possess female donkeys, 30. Balaam’s female donkey uttered rational words, 853.

The asp is a small snake, 475. What the gall of asps signifies, 474. What small asps signify, 475. What it means to break the eggs of asps, 476. The hole of an asp signifies the hearts of the wicked, 555.

What it means to stand before God, 39, 542, 1608. See Angel.

Assur, the proud king, signifies Lucifer, 335. To rise up is characteristic of one contending, 70.

What the morning stars are, 909. By whom the names of the stars were discovered, 293. Why Scripture uses the names of the stars, ibid. How it is to be understood that the stars are not clean, 256.

The cunning of our enemies is called a snare and trap, 441. How the wise are caught in their own cunning, 194. The scheme of the wicked is signified by the name “quiver,” 1025.

The court is the breadth of the present life, 900. What it signifies that the prophet did not measure the court of the temple, ibid. What the court before the fronts of the temple signifies, 1359, 1426. What the temple court, one hundred cubits square, signifies, 1426.

Boldness in the way of God produces weakness; in the way of the world, strength, 153. Vanity makes a person bold through sin, 349.

What the differences are between hearing and being heard, 136. What it means to “hear a hearing,” 868. What it means to hear God, 1145. The qualities of a good hearer, 1396. The danger of those who hear the word of God but do not advance through it, 1465, 1489, 1506. Whoever does not hear God now will not himself be heard in judgment, 1479. What it means to hear the word of God, 1506. Whoever wishes to understand what he has heard must fulfill in action what he has already heard, 1539. Unless the Holy Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless, 1577. Why those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not even hear the risen dead, 1658.

Auguries are to be detested, 262. What a gentle breeze is, 168. Why the voice of God is called a gentle breeze, ibid. Tribulation opens the ear, 843. What it means to stop one’s ears so as not to hear blood, 755. What piercing the servant’s ear with an awl signifies, 1197. How spiritual ears differ from carnal ones, 1320, 1489.

What the rising of the dawn denotes, 122. The rising of the dawn is the brightness of inward truth, ibid. Dawn signifies the mind of the just, 530. The Church of the elect, 113, 576, 918. As long as we live, it is dawn, not yet perfect day, ibid. What the place of dawn is, 919.

Gold denotes wisdom, 131, 573, 1470. What gold tested in a furnace signifies, 516. What darkened gold is, 580, 673, 886, 1128. Fine gold signifies the angels, 590. Likewise, the mind, 700. And the intellect, ibid. What fine gold is, 698. By gold faithful souls are signified, 886. The brightness of divinity, 1128. The splendor of the heavenly city, ibid. Likewise, charity, ibid. The shine of temporal glory, ibid. Likewise, the splendor of holiness is signified by gold, ibid.

---

What it means not to believe that gold is one’s strength, 700. What it means for gold to have come from the north, 887. What it signifies to spread gold like mud, 1129. What is signified by the gold offered to the Savior by the Magi, 1470.

The south wind denotes the Holy Spirit, 196, 266, 883, 1038, 1187, 1312. What the inner parts of the south signify, 196, 878, 1422. Who are said to dwell in the land of the south, 756. What it means to spread wings toward the south, 1038. What it means to turn one’s face toward the southern road, 1422. Judea is signified by the name “south,” 886.

Divine help is never lacking for afflicted people who are just, 661. A corruptible human being cannot attain a state of incorruption except by God’s help, 400.

Avarice is the head of all evils, 462, 646. Avarice is compared to fire, 478. Avarice arises from two causes, 480. Avarice is signified by the name “lead,” 460. It is signified by the name “jar,” 461. A talent of lead signifies the weight of the sin of avarice, 461. Impiety is held within avarice, ibid. Avarice is supported by pride and empty glory, 462. Avarice steals in either through fear or through elation, 480. It is called the root of the juniper, 646. It is the root of all sins, ibid. The kinship of avarice and pride, 1387. The first human being was tempted and overcome by the Devil through avarice, 1493. What the daughters of avarice are, 1036. What its temptations are like, 1037.

---

How avarice torments the greedy person, 128. The greedy person has within his soul a tumultuous crowd of passions, ibid. Those who burn here in the fire of avarice will also burn in the fires of Gehenna in the flesh, 416. The greedy person resembles both a dropsical man and fire, 441, 478. Some pursue avarice through flattery, others through open force, 649. The miseries of the greedy, 479. They are miserable both here and forever, 480. Let each person consider his own course and recognize that the little he has may be sufficient for him, 1589.

Why the birds of heaven are so called, 66. Christ is called a bird, 1573. See Bird.

What eating unleavened bread signifies, 1534.

[Col. 1357] B

Babylonia is the confused multitude of sinners, 97, 1271. All the reprobate together are called Babylonia, 157. The daughter of Babylon is called “my barren one” [*meus infecunda*; wording uncertain], 192. The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, possessor of inward confusion, 229. The tower of Babylon was built in the land of Shinar, 462. By the name of Babylon the glory of this world is signified, 1128. What Babylon’s golden cup is, ibid. What the migration of Babylon signifies, 1271. The staff signifies pastoral authority, 1536. How Balaam, lying down, had his eyes open, 881. Balaam rebuked by the she-ass, 853. Who taught Balaam at Pergamum, 923. While falling, he had his eyes open, 1260. Raised up by knowledge, but not taken up in life, 1279. Balaam, pierced with remorse for an hour, soon returns to the wickedness of avarice, 1490. Baldad is interpreted as “antiquity alone,” 15, 91, 731. Belshazzar’s vision was not a prophecy, 378. The girdle of kings, which God dissolves, 374.

Baptism removes original sin, 102, 313, 491. The guilt of the first parent is washed away through baptism; we pay its penalties throughout our whole life, ibid. We are immersed in baptism, 599. All sins are released in baptism, 1421, 1517. We are faithful if we fulfill in deed what we promised in baptism, 1570.

—Infants who die without baptism: what punishment they receive, 102. Unregenerate infants are condemned to eternal punishments on account of original sin, 303. See *Original Sin*. The baptism of John was given in water, not in the Spirit, 1458. Sins were not forgiven through John’s baptism, 1516.

Barachel is interpreted as “the blessing of God,” 735. What it means that the Redeemer shaved his beard and head, 61. Saint Gregory does not avoid the confusion of barbarisms in writing, 6. The bases of the Church are the holy teachers, 901. Likewise, the prophets, ibid. The bases of the soul are its intentions, 908. One must consider not what the bases support, but where they are supported, ibid. What the bases covered with silver, supporting the four columns of the tabernacle, signify, 901. What the bases of the temple sculpted with lions and oxen signify, 1501. *Basileus* in Greek is called in Latin *basis populi* (“the foundation of the people”), 300.

By receiving the blessedness of souls and bodies, the Church of the Elect will receive a twofold blessedness at the end of time, 16. There is one blessedness before the resurrection, but afterward a double blessedness, 17, 1153. How the memory of sins in heaven does not hinder blessedness, 138. The bodies of the blessed are represented as shining like gold and transparent like glass, 594. The blessed see God not only in his radiance but in his very nature, 601. The blessed who thirst are satisfied, and, though satisfied, thirst, 602. They do not see God as he sees himself, ibid. Everything that abounds without the vision of God is poverty, 672. The dawn hastens to its place when the saints long for eternal blessedness, 919. The vision of God alone is the true refreshment of our mind, 1041. Although the merits of the saints are diverse, their life of blessedness is nevertheless one, 1345, 1512. Blessedness is given to the saints as they depart from this world, 127, 296, 433, 1513. The delay of blessedness is a cause of lamentation for the faithful, 218. What the blessed in heaven enjoy, 296. The weak are called to blessedness by right of inheritance together with the strong, 1166. The state of eternal blessedness, 1240. See *The State of Glory*.

[Col. 1357] Behemoth is interpreted as “animal,” 1055, 1094. By the name of Behemoth the ancient enemy is signified, ibid. What it means that he was made together with man, 1056. What Behemoth’s tail signifies, 1058. Like a cedar, he strives toward high things, 1062. Behemoth’s head is grass, and his tail a cedar, 1064. He wounds with his tooth and binds with his tail, ibid. Behemoth is called the beginning of God’s ways, 1071. He is said to have been covered with nine stones, that is, adorned with the nine orders of angels, 1072. He was created capable of charity, ibid. Who is described as stretched out and protecting, 1073. What Behemoth’s sword is, ibid. Who are the mountains—that is, the exalted ones of the world—who bear Behemoth’s grasses, 1076. How the willows of the torrent surround him, 1082. He was caught by a hook in his own eyes—that is, he recognized and bit Christ, 1085. By exposing his most cunning ambushes, the saints, like a stake, pierce his nostrils, 1085. While investigating Christ’s divinity, he was impaled by Christ’s words in the nose and captured, 1086.

—Behemoth is compared to an ox, 1056. Behemoth’s tail is called the Antichrist, 1058. Who enlarges his own tail, 1059. What Behemoth’s testicular sinews are, 1065. What Behemoth’s bones are, 1067. What Behemoth’s plans are, 1068. Behemoth is permitted to strike many, 1074. The proud serve Behemoth, 1076. What Behemoth’s nostrils are, 1085. Behemoth strikes people with one vice so that they fall, and binds them with another so that they do not rise again, 1092. Behemoth’s temptations are deceitful, ibid. See *Devil*, *Leviathan*, *Satan*.

What it means mystically to suffer war, 12. What it means for God to rain war, 480. From where the just man’s inward war arises, 204. Those proceeding to war under Christ as leader should demonstrate by their deeds what they proclaim with their mouths, 991. What it means to smell war from afar, 1029, 1034, 1035. The war of the faithful against the powers of the air, 1237. War against vices attacking together with united forces, 1303. Against those attacking successively and in different divisions, ibid. Against other things stealthily taking the place of others, 1304. Who are converted on the day of battle, 1412.

“To bless” is sometimes taken in a bad sense, 27. Whoever conceals the benefits of God that he has received does not deserve to receive new ones, 829. Samuel is an example of kindness, 860. Why all Israel did not strike the tribe of Benjamin until it had first been struck twice by it, 449. Bersabee is called “the seventh well,” 94. Bersabee signifies the law of the letter, ibid.

What the beast of the earth is, 203. What it signifies that the beast was forbidden to touch the mountain, 209. What it means for a human being to end in a beast, 228. What the beasts of the forests are, 876. What the beast of the field denotes, 1003, 1076. Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread,” 1460. Why Christ was born in Bethlehem, ibid.

Who are called scorpions—the flattering and malicious, 1258. And bees, ibid. Why fire burns thorns, ibid. They are unbelieving toward God, overturners of the weak, and scorpions to the strong, ibid.

Good things mixed with evil are rejected, 18. How, even through the good things we do, we may approach what is worse, 32. When we lose good things, God receives what is his; he does not take away what is ours, 51. The empty labor of those who yearn for transitory goods, 230. The just do not love the earthly things they possess, 263. Our good things perish if they are disclosed too quickly, 280. The wicked rely on fleeting things, with which they perish, despising true goods, 662. Some goods are supreme, others intermediate, 888. Goods are called evils, or evils goods, comparatively, 913. Our good works are God’s [Col. 1358] works, 1212. What good is, and when it is imperfect, 1224. Let us in turn devote the good we possess to the benefit of our neighbor, 1232. We ought not to retain as private possessions what has been given to us for the common good, 1233. How fearful we should be of the goods we receive here, 1657.

—A good thing is not spoken of well, 732. A good thing is spoken of badly, ibid. Good things are to be cautiously extracted from evils, 287. Why God grants good things to the wicked, 507. The devil pursues our good things in three ways, 34. How our good things may please God, 36. Our good things must be referred to God, 64, 958. A good thing is easily lost, 82. Good works must proceed from a pure heart, 112. Lesser goods should be set aside for greater ones, 626. Lesser goods are not always to be neglected, 627. God rewards all good things, 683. Our good things are from God, 737. In good actions, the elevation of the heart must first be overcome, 741. Pride arises from knowledge of good works, 850. What it means to speak a good word well, 1168. What it means to do good well, 1286.

The memory of good things is great consolation in tribulation, 80. The just make good use of temporal goods, 263. The wicked grow proud from temporal goods, 367. Good things often befall the wicked, 438. What it means to possess good things, 490. Why God takes good things away from the just, 511. How much the goods of this world prick, 654. How many labors and troubles they produce, ibid., 1657.

—The good person uses this world in a stewardly manner so as to enjoy God, 45. Why the good are afflicted here, 77, 137. Why they sometimes prosper, 138. God purifies the good through the persecution of the wicked, 541. The good desire to have not a portion from the Lord but the Lord himself as their portion, 485. Those are truly good who are good among the wicked, 17, 673. The difference between the good and hypocrites, 273. The good become better through the insults they receive, 1508. The good are nowhere alone except in heaven, 1637. He is not good who does not patiently endure the wicked, 1638. No one is good before having been tested by the wicked, ibid. See *The Just*, *The Saints*. When the good will be separated from the wicked, 1638. The good cannot be without the wicked in this life, ibid. The good are few, and the wicked many, ibid. See *The Just and the Wicked Compared*.

Oxen signify various things in Scripture, 24, 25, 57, 65, 215, 218, 1160, 1376. The yokes of oxen signify harmonious virtues, 30. What plowing oxen signify, 65. What it means to plow with the firstborn of an ox, 280, 1184. What it means not to muzzle the ox treading out the grain, 1160. Five yokes of oxen signify the five bodily senses, 1621.

What the arm signifies, 694. Christ is called the arm of the Lord, 868. Britain, subjected to the faith, resounds with “Alleluia,” 862. The *bruchus* signifies a voracious appetite for eating, 1113. Christ has satisfied us with butter and honey, 477. What it means to wash the feet with butter, 615, 616. Boxwood signifies the children of faithful parents, 1523. What the boxwood color signifies, 1012. Buzites is interpreted as “contemptible,” 735. And “despised,” 1185. What fine linen signifies, 967.

C
Cadaver is so called from *cadere* (“to fall”), 1043. What it signifies, 1044. What it means to fall away from the Holy Spirit, 61. Who are said to fall upright, or on their face, 1016. Blindness of mind arises from desires for earthly things, 192. Whether blindness precedes or follows the habit of sinning, 229. The man blind from birth, 266, 1440. The blindness of man concerning spiritual things is to be lamented, [Col. 1359] 296. Punitive blindness of mind in the knowledge of oneself, 305, 428, 800. The man who refused to stand in the light by fleeing lost his eyes, 310. Blindness, although just, is nevertheless harsh to the mind, 311, 315. Man wishes to endure his blindness for a long time, 390. The astonishing hardening and blindness of certain wicked people, even while they are being struck, 493. The evil that we commit places a barrier before the eye of the mind, 653. How great is the blindness of the wicked, 653. God blinds by not freeing a person from blindness, 801. The blinding of the mind arising from sins, 1290. The blind man illumined by Christ signifies the human race, 1440. What is signified by the blind man sitting beside the road and begging, ibid. Christ hears the blind man crying out as he passes by, and, standing still, illumines him, 1442. Why Christ asks the blind man what he wants, ibid.

Cain: why, although admonished by the divine voice, he could not be changed, 370. Cain was a member of Antichrist, 923. He refuses to be Abel whom the malice of Cain does not exercise, 673, 1259, 1638.

The various meanings of reeds and rushes in Scripture, 1078, 1315, 1323. Reeds proceeding from a shaft signify preachers, 1216. What is signified by the reed six cubits and a handbreadth long, 1340. See *Arundo*.

Calamity compared with sand, 213. What it means to be in calamity, 650. Why Christ warned about the calamities preceding the end of the world, 1612.

The heel signifies the end of an action, 36. The devil watches the heel when he attempts to corrupt the end of a good action, ibid. The shoe signifies the protection of preaching, 1123. Among the ancients, the custom of removing the shoe belonged to the man who refused the woman legally owed to him as his bride, 1458. John denies that he is worthy to remove Christ’s shoe, 1459. The shoe signifies the mortality assumed by Christ, ibid. The strap of the shoe is the bond of the mystery, 1459, 1518. Shoes signify examples of dead works, 1498. To have shoes on one’s feet means to contemplate the life of the dead and to guard our footsteps from sin, 1536.

Gloom is the very confusion of our mind through repentance, 117. The cup is set before those striving toward the joys of exaltation, 538. Through the cup one reaches majesty, 1562. The cup signifies the sorrow of the Passion, 1616.

Slanderers are all the wicked, 821.

The camel: what is signified by the camel in Scripture, 23, 30, 66, 1159, 1169, 1161. He possesses camels who either subjects what is lofty and tortuous in himself to faith or bends it before charity, 30. What it means for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, 1160.

A Canaanite made tributary to the tribe of Ephraim: what this signifies, 121. Who is the Canaanite to whom the Church handed over the belt, 1097.

The candlestick: what it signifies, and what it means for a lamp to be placed upon it, 992, 1215.

The brightness of a garment: what it signifies, 1526, 1527, 1573.

What is meant by the tongue of dogs in the Church arising from enemies, 642. The teachers of the Church are called dogs, 642, 1652. Why the tongue of dogs heals a wound by licking it, 1653. The broad tongue of flatterers is signified by the tongue of the licking dog, 1653.

The differing custom concerning the time for growing or cutting the hair during affliction, 50. Hair signifies thoughts, 70, 1596. What it means to cut the hair, 61. What is signified by the Lord’s cut hair, ibid.

The goat signifies the contemplative life, 1048.

The first Babylonian captivity was that of King Jehoiachin, the second that of Zedekiah, 1308. He who is redeemed is freed from captivity, 585.

What it means to shave the head, 70, 71. The head signifies the mind, 70, 612, 1437, 1478. The head of man is divinity, 266. What it means to shake the head, 419, 1153, 1154. What it means to lift up the head, 1437. To place one’s head upon the stone means to cling to Christ, 163.

Coals that differ from lamps, 1208. By both are signified holy men, ibid. Coals signify hidden saints, ibid.

What kind of prison the devil’s prison is, 260. To be confined in prison means that one is unable to accomplish what one wishes, 250. What it means for saints to be in prison, 260. He who acts wickedly makes his conscience a prison for himself, 370.

What a song in the night signifies, 822, 1262. What “song” and “woe” mean in Holy Scripture, 823, 1262. A twofold song, ibid.

What “flesh and blood” denotes, 87. “Flesh” is taken in Scripture in two ways, 466. What it means not to be in the flesh, 483. Why the flesh is subject to so many evils, 763. We must care for the flesh, 1227. The offering of flesh is twofold, 1419.

—The movements of the flesh roar while tempting, but do not reach the point of biting, 204. Rather, they procure peace for us with God, ibid. The time of the flesh is compared with a web, 253. The law of the flesh makes a person detestable, 315. The troublesome usefulness of temptations of the flesh, 327, 609. Temptation of the flesh and contemplation together in one mind, 347. From where the flesh is refreshed, from there the spirit grows weak, 358. Weakness is signified in the flesh, strength in the bone, 457. What it means to bring flesh to eat, 459. Flesh is spoken of in one way according to nature, in another according to guilt, 466. It is asserted that after the resurrection the flesh will be tangible, 465. Not to be in the flesh means not to love carnal things, 483. Flesh is rottenness and worms, 533. A powerful thought for subduing the appetites of the flesh, 534. What flesh is called barren, 535. By abstinence, the vices of the flesh—not the flesh itself—are to be extinguished, 675, 984, 1388. We are scourged by that very flesh which we have placed before God’s commandments, 763. The flesh plunges down those whom proud knowledge elevates, 824. The mind rightly loses dominion over the flesh that refuses to serve God, 824. The desires of the flesh, not the flesh itself, must be put to death, 984. He who has chastised the incitements of the flesh is able to ascend toward understanding sublime things, 985. What the impulses of the flesh are, 1206. The carnal impulse often mocks us under the appearance of the spiritual, 1207. Care for the flesh is to be exercised in necessity, but not in accordance with desires, 1227. The flesh is signified by the word “bed,” 1296. By flesh the peoples are signified, just as by bones the rulers, 1374. He nourishes an enemy who grants the flesh more than is fitting, 1388. He kills a fellow citizen who does not satisfy its necessity, ibid. What it means for dead flesh to rot, 1471. “All flesh is grass”: what is green today dries up tomorrow, 1484.

The crowd of carnal people in the Church presses upon Christ, 88. Carnal people sometimes offer counsel through fear, sometimes through boldness, ibid. The labor of the carnal is heavy, that of the spiritual is none, 188. How burdensome the words and behavior of carnal people are to the elect, 218. The grace of the flesh, creeping in, should not impede the force of heavenly love, 232. The sea signifies the hearts of carnal people, 259. The hearts of carnal people are confined in prison when they are unable to accomplish what they wish, 260. Those who speak carnally must be recalled to silence, 381. Those devoted to the flesh experience greater tribulations from the flesh, 403. The wicked man burns with the torches of carnal desires together with those joined to him, 413. Carnal people either suspect that God does not exist or disdain serving him, [Col. 1360] 489. Carnal people delight in worldly cares, by which they are gnawed as by worms, 532. If the holier are not free from stains, how filthy are the carnal, 544. Carnal people do not know the desire for the heavenly homeland, 577. Scripture marks carnal people under the name “man,” or “humanity,” 602. What zeal carnal people show for earthly things, and what no ardor they have for heavenly things, 630. In the heart of carnal people Christ sits last; in the heart of the righteous, first, 639. Carnal people grieve at having no companions in their death, 650. A description of the life of carnal people, 653. Carnal people, despising true goods, rely upon transient things with which they perish, 662. Christ rescued and renewed us from the punishments of carnal life, 763. The carnal person is like a reed, 1454.

The persecutions of carnal people in the Church, 88. Carnal minds are called women, 90. Carnal people in the Church are the devil’s helpers, 181. The life of carnal people is designated by the names “hay” and “straw,” 1056.

The cartilage of the beast: what it signifies, 1063. Why it is compared with iron plates, 1064, 1069.

Cassia, the name of one of Job’s daughters: what it signifies, 1164. The custom of Bishop Cassius of offering sacrifice daily, 1631. His almsgiving and devout tears, ibid. He was divinely forewarned of the day of his death, 1632. He was accustomed to come every year to Rome on the feast of the holy apostles, ibid. He celebrated Masses in the episcopal residence and died, 1633. He had imitated Christ in life and likewise had a death resembling Christ’s death, ibid.

Chastity without love of neighbor is vain, 205. The devil attempts to corrupt chaste thoughts, 66. There is no chastity of the flesh that the sweetness of the mind does not commend, 205. Pride is the downfall of chastity, 374. Proud chastity profits nothing, 680, 697. Chastity and humility mutually protect one another, 823. How great a concern must be shown for chastity, 1480. Chastity is not acceptable to God without good works, 1482.

The spiritual camps: what they are, 1237. The various camps of the Church, 1239. The different ranks of the camps in the Church, ibid. Which are called camps, ibid. What it means to go out of the camp polluted, 325. The camps of the faithful against evil spirits, 1237. What it means to camp against the soul, 1303.

The fall is more serious when greater elation preceded it, 97. From the very virtues a more serious fall threatens, 245. The saints think themselves bound with chains as long as they dwell here, 839.

The chair is the authority of teaching, 617.

What it means to offer the tail of the victim, 38. The tail of the victim is perseverance in a good work, 1546. What the tail signifies, 453. What the tail of Behemoth is, 1058. Like a cedar, this tail has grown hard through the habit of sinning, 1064.

Let the downfall of the greater be a warning for the lesser, 1090.

What is signified in Holy Scripture by the name “cedar,” 207, 1058, 1522.

Speed, or haste, is commended, 1537.

What true, false, or participated exaltation is, 1134.

He who censures his own words judges those of others more correctly, 243.

A census is not a crime, but the intention is, 361.

The number one hundred designates contemplation of eternal life, 1358. What it means to bear fruit a hundredfold, ibid. The number one hundred signifies perfection, [Col. 1361] 1372, 1382, 1384, 1426, 1601.

The faith of the centurion Cornelius is explained, 1381. Why Christ went to heal the centurion’s servant, but healed the son of the official while absent, 1566.

What the horned serpent signifies, 1015.

A description of the contest in the arena, its conditions and customary practice, 19.

The speed of the stag is described, 821. The elect are like these, ibid. Hinds extinguish serpents, 972. Which stags cross rivers, ibid. What it means to watch hinds giving birth, 975. What are the shady places that the fawn of the stags seeks at midday, 1597.

The neck of the proud has been reduced to mud, 381. A fat neck signifies wealthy pride, 411.

The whale signifies Antichrist, 110. Why it signifies the devil, 260, 1185.

The Chaldeans are interpreted as “fierce,” 59. They are captors and, as it were, demons, 1185. Who are signified by the three companies of Chaldeans, 59, 67. What is signified by the Chaldeans called fierce, 192.

The Canaanite: what it signifies, 121. What is signified by the Canaanite made tributary to the tribe of Ephraim, ibid. Why, when Ham sinned, the sentence of vengeance was pronounced upon Canaan, 829.

Oil is a type of charity, 70. Oil on the head is charity in the mind, ibid. Charity is called the law of Christ, 340. Charity is compared with heat, 531. Charity is the bond of perfection, 916. Charity is the mother of the virtues, 1550. Charity is intimated under the name of gold, 1128. Charity is called the breadth of the spiritual building, 1327. Healing comes from the wound of charity, 1332. What is signified by the litter spread in the middle with charity, 1335. Charity is not true if it is less than two cubits wide, 1342. Scarlet dyed twice signifies the charity of God and neighbor, ibid., 1343, 1640. Charity is called fire, 1595. Why charity is signified by the wedding garment, 1639. See *Amor*, *Dilectio*.

—The two commandments of charity, which are joined to one another, 223, 1554. Charity begins from two commandments and extends to innumerable things, 340. The only charity commanded by Christ, 1560. What consummating charity is, 29. What is the breadth of charity, 1328, 1354, 1359, 1379. In what true charity consists, 1359. Charity is distinguished in three ways, 340. Charity in many forms is shown by the examples of the saints, 341. The strength of charity, 357. The fear that passes into charity, 722. The four dimensions of charity, 1222. The enemy fears no virtues if charity is absent, 1238. Why the enemy envies mutual charity, ibid. True charity is humble love, which we mutually show one another, ibid. Charity and long-suffering have the same measure, 1332. Charity fuses different minds into one, 1343. True charity is to love one’s friend in God and one’s enemy for God’s sake, 708, 1466, 1560. Charity is directed toward another, 1496. God is in unity, not in division of minds, 1532. Whatever is commanded is made firm in charity alone, 1560. The perfection of charity, 1561.

—There are two commandments of charity, 50, 340, 1496, 1560, 1639. The two commandments of charity are signified by the two cubits of the vestibule of the city gate, 1640. Scarlet dyed twice signifies charity toward God and neighbor, 1342, 1343, 1640. Charity is called manifold, 1560. The duties of charity are explained, 343. Charity is patient toward evils and kind, so that it may love those whom it bears, 1615. Charity toward one’s neighbor consists in two things, 768, 1560. All virtues arise from charity as from a root, 341, 342. Charity alone makes us disciples of God, [Col. 1361] 708. The proofs and signs of charity, ibid. By the strength of inspired charity, the Lord restrains the vices arising in the heart, 916. The effects of charity in the congregation of the faithful, 1343. A sure proof of charity is good action, 1354, 1575. May charity protect us in all our works, 1359. Without faith, hope, and charity no adult is saved, 1360. Placed between faith and hope, let us strive toward charity, 1421. Those pricked by charity are signified by the golden altar placed before the veil of the ark, 1428. The necessity of charity, 1466. He who does not have charity loses even what he seemed to possess, ibid. The power of charity in the loving soul, 1548. The rust of sin is consumed by the fire of charity, 1595. Charity often burns whole in the heart but is not displayed in action because it is hindered, 1600. Charity is usually tested solely by opposition from hatred, 1640. Charity is often weakened by scourging, 69. There is no charity outside the Church, 574. See *Amor*, *Dilectio*, *Charitas Christi*.

Charity in administering graces, 1232. The many works of charity, 1359. The two tables of charity are patience and kindness, 1404. Charity hindered outwardly burns inwardly, 1600. A person must begin charity with himself, 624.

What the cherub signifies, 1073. The cherubim signify the fullness of knowledge, 1414, 1501, 1547, 1605. What is signified by the two cherubim who look upon one another over the mercy seat, 1547. The cherubim are spirits more perfect in knowledge insofar as they contemplate God more closely, 1605. Why God is said to sit above the cherubim, 1608. All angels see the fountain of knowledge together, but the cherubim see it more fully, 1608.

What Chobar signifies, 1185.

The name “choirs” designates the harmony of charity, 1238.

Christ is called Advocate, 718, 1234; Equity, 515; Lamb, 986; Alpha and Omega, 1535; Angel of Great Counsel, 373, 759; Tree, 604; Rider of the horse, 1015; Bird, 580, 1573; Arm of the Lord, 1185; Camel, 23; Head of the Church, 14, 15, 83, etc.; Our Head, 1228; Guardian, 1507; Sublime God, 1236, 1331; Right Hand of God, 400; Horseman, 1015; End of the Law, 1349; Our End, ibid.; Firmament, 1231, 1240; Open Fountain of Mercy, 1041; Sublime Fruit of the Earth, 1310; Foundation of Foundations, 899; Foundation of all the stones of the building, 1311; Fawn of the stags, 1597; Man who went abroad, 1464; Infant at the breast, 555; Righteous One, 1234; Lamp, 364; Cornerstone, 902; Lawgiver, 853; Strongest Lion of the beasts, 959, 986; Green Wood, 395, 632; True Lucifer, 13, 952; Light, 132; Hand of the Lord, 1185; Our Physician, 760; Mountain at the summit of the mountains, 1075, 1310, 1313, 1598; Death of death, 398; Wall, 662, 1322, 1323; Wild ass, 985, 986; Dawn, 26, 660, 1421; Door, 1313, 1329; Bread, 755; Sparrow, 629, 1639; Shepherd, 1313, 1329; Master of the house, 1510; Rock, 985, 1040; Gate, 183, 1327, 1329, 1397, 1422; Little child, 1343; Root, 395; King, 1516; Priest, ibid.; Leaping over the mountains, 1574; Salvation of God, 1519; Wisdom of God, 370; Scarab, 986; Axe laid at the root, 1520; Serpent, 986; Mustard seed, 604; Sun, 279, 1126, 1310, 1573; Bridegroom of the soul and the Church, 1332; Scales, 212, 683; Morning Star, 952; Thunder, 938; Bar, 911, 914; Hidden Word, 160; Worm, 986; Eastern Way, 1329; Man, 1313, 1329, 1598; Vulture, [Col. 1362] 580.

—Job prefigured Christ not only by speaking but also by suffering, 14, 21, 717. The saints of the Old Testament prophetically promised Christ through things and words, 14. The Lord is represented by the camel, 23, 1160. What it means for the Lord to come to Jerusalem while seated upon an ass, 24. What it means for flesh to be placed upon a rock, 96. Christ is principally called good, 308. Why the ancient Fathers are said to have been ships carrying apples, 309. Why eagles are said to feed on Christ’s flesh, 309. Elisha raising the son of the Shunammite woman is a figure of Christ, 318. Jews and Gentiles came together in Christ, the cornerstone, 909. Human beings and angels, 902. Both the active and contemplative life, ibid. Samson is a figure of Christ, who killed more enemies in dying than while alive, 928. Why Christ is a free, released wild ass, 986. The bonds of this wild ass, which were loosened in the resurrection, 986. Christ is represented by the four living creatures, 1039, 1201. The finest gold is Christ’s head—that is, God is Christ’s head, 1128. Ezekiel beside the river Chobar is a figure of the incarnate Word, 1185. Why Christ is compared with electrum, 1188, 1245. How Christ is prefigured by the four living creatures of the Evangelists, 1201. Christ is signified by the candlestick, 1215; and by the mercy seat, 1219; and by the burning bush, 1227; and by the firmament stretched above the heads of the living creatures, 1231, 1240. Christ is far above the Thrones themselves, 1243. Among all human beings, God the Father was pleased with Christ alone, 1243. The cloud signifies Christ’s flesh, 1248. Christ, the hand of God, strengthens us, 1280. Signified by the foundation, Christ carries everyone and is carried by no one, 1311. In what sense he labors while sustaining, 1312. Christ is the man whose appearance is like bronze, 1313. Christ is our wall: inwardly God, outwardly God-man, 1322. He became a wall for us on every side by his example, 1323. Who is called the measuring reed in Christ’s hand, ibid. Christ is the eastern way, and the man coming by it, 1329. Christ is the gate whose light is the holy patriarchs, 1331, 1335. Christ is God above all, 1331. Christ is the end of both Testaments, 1348. The end—not one that destroys, but one that perfects, 1349. Christ under the figure of the eastern gate stands between Jews and Gentiles, 1422. There is one way to heaven for both, ibid. Christ is the ark of the covenant, 1428. Why Christ did not deny that he was a Samaritan, 1507. Samson’s departure from Gaza by night is a figure of Christ rising and ascending into heaven, 1529. The roasted fish signifies Christ the suffering mediator, 1543. Christ is a roasted fish in the Passion and a honeycomb in the resurrection, ibid. Christ was best believed by Mary as the gardener, 1548. The mountain of strength signifies Christ, 1548. Christ is prefigured by the one cubit with which the ark was completed, 1639. Christ is signified by the single sparrow in the building, ibid.

—Christ was prefigured by the ancient Fathers, 14. Christ is one person with the holy Church, ibid., 112, 615, 731, 1329. How Christ came naked from the womb of his mother, the Synagogue, 62. Who returns into the womb of his mother, ibid. Christ is designated in Scripture through all the elect, 181. Christ is the head of all the elect, 1200. All the faithful are Christ’s body, 1215. See *Ecclesia*. Christ was figured through many actions, 1218. Christ first called the foolish of the world, before the wise, 25. Those who die without knowledge of the Redeemer are consigned to eternal fires, 255. Job desires a mediator who may free us by his death, 306, 269. Christ, seated in us, consoles the sorrowful like a king, [Col. 1363] 640. Christ, God and man, intercedes with God for human beings, 718, 760. How he intercedes, 761. Christ joined the lowest with the highest by assuming our nature, 866. He joins the Pleiades and disperses the circle of Arcturus, 951. In Christ all things in heaven and on earth have been restored, 1041. Choosing the weak things of the world, he defeated the devil’s strength, 1095. Christ became for us a way of love to the Father and an aid for reaching him, 1423.

—Christ is the mediator between God and human beings, 84, 717. Job desires a mediator, asking freedom from sin, 269, 306. Christ the helper and mediator is to be sought, 718. Christ is the mediator between God and human beings, ibid., 760. The faith of the righteous in both Testaments is one faith in the mediator, 1345, 1352. The communication of idioms in Christ, 598. What it means for Christ to speak and intercede for us, 761, 718. Christ alone will free us and has propitiated God, 762. No human intercessor for human beings has appeared righteous before God, 763. Christ praying for us kindles us to pray, 764. Christ the mediator between God and human beings is signified by electrum, 894. Why he is in the middle of the fire, ibid. Christ displayed to the Jews the proofs of both his natures, 1317. Christ was afflicted in vain with respect to himself, but not in vain with respect to us, 84. Christ alone is pure, because conceived without the pleasure of the flesh, 392. Christ’s blood speaks better than Abel’s, 426. Christ’s blood is his cry, ibid. Christ is the witness of every faithful person, 427. Christ is the expectation of the righteous, 434. Christ was unknown in his own house and existed as though a stranger, 455. Christ became poor so that he might enrich us, 670. Christ became like us, 760. In what ways he is unlike us, 761. He assumed no punishment from necessity, ibid. He became an intercessor for us, 762. Christ still suffers in his members, 956.

Christ incarnate maintained simplicity together with uprightness, 22. God exposed the devil’s snares by the light of incarnate Wisdom, 54. In what sense the incarnate Lord is simple, upright, etc., 55. Christ, as God with the Father, gives everything; as man, he receives everything from the Father, 62. To have the Spirit permanently is Christ’s privilege, 72. If the first man had not sinned, the second would not have come to suffer, 84. Heretics sit with us on earth when they agree with us concerning the Incarnation, 93. Why human nature was restored rather than angelic nature, 108. Christ had to become what he redeemed, 109. The wicked, through the benefit of the Incarnation, were rescued from grievous labor, 433. Christ alone had nothing from an unclean conception, having been born from a Virgin, 392. Through the Incarnation the Son of God extended to man the right hand by which he raised him to the glory of incorruption, 400. The incarnate God satisfied us with honey and butter, 477. Through Christ’s weakness access to pardon is granted to human beings, 515. Through the Lord’s Incarnation the world was subdued after its swelling had been pressed down, 551. The economy of the Incarnation, 552, 760. What “overshadowing” signifies concerning the manner of the Incarnation of the Word, 571. The Incarnation of Christ is described under the figure of the vulture, 580. Eternal Wisdom alone was sufficient to heal the great sick one, that is, the human race, 591. Wisdom assumed human flesh together with a rational soul, 597. The manner of the Word’s Incarnation, 598. Christ’s devotion and compassion toward human beings in the Incarnation, 670. Christ became for human beings the way of returning to God, 718. Christ was born from a priestly tribe, 719. The Lord assumed neither guilt from defect nor punishment from necessity, 771. He differs from us in the magnitude of punishment but agrees with us in the truth of nature, ibid. The ways of divine Wisdom are open to all through the Incarnation, 804. Of the three Persons, only the Son is called an angel in Scripture because of the Incarnation, 896.

—A person is all the more indebted to God because God also assumed things unworthy of him for that person’s sake, 917. When God assumed the weakness of human nature, he gave human beings knowledge of the glory to come, 920.

—The incarnate Lord, in the form of a servant, is less than the Father and than himself, 986. The Word mounted the horse when he assumed animated flesh for himself, 1014. Divinity assumed flesh through the mediation of the soul, 1014, 1095. The devil was caught on the hook of the Incarnation of the Word, 1085. Christ’s body is the house of Wisdom, 1095. The Incarnation of the Word was revealed to Ezekiel, 1185. The obscurity of humanity tempered for us the splendor of divinity, 1188. Human nature before the assumption was earth; assumed by the Word, it became firmament, 1231. Christ is above the throne and, through the assumption of human nature, is himself beneath the throne, 1244. Proofs of both natures in Christ, 1245. Christ is one in both natures, 1245. The conjunction of both natures was made without confusion and without separation, ibid. He who was previously known by few became known through the Incarnation to a multitude of nations, ibid. The fire that had previously burned inwardly shone outwardly, 1246. Christ was known to the angels through the divine nature and became known to human beings through the assumed human nature, ibid. Why the Incarnation of the Word is compared with air, 1313. The flesh of the Word compared with a garment, 1314. Through the Incarnation Christ is King and Lord, ibid. What it means that Christ, by reason of the Incarnation, stands at the gate, 1316. What it means that he stood behind the wall, 1317. Doing divine things and enduring human things, he looked through windows and lattices, ibid. The Son of God became incarnate to introduce us to the faith of the Church, ibid. The incarnate Lord, under the name of the eastern way, stands between the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, 1344. The benefits conferred upon us through the Incarnation of the Word, 1351. The incarnate God performed an alien work by being scourged, and his own work by gathering us into his righteousness, 1352. Christ is the fountain of mercy, opened through the Incarnation, 1401. From the place where God suffers human things, man is raised to divine things, 1440. Through the Incarnation human blindness was healed, ibid. Christ became visible among human beings in body, invisible in majesty, 1458. In Christ there is one person but two natures, 1494, 1635. He who believes Christ to be a mere man eats the lamb’s flesh raw, 1535. He who investigates the mystery of the Incarnation with human wisdom eats the lamb’s flesh cooked in water, ibid. What is not understood concerning this mystery is handed over to the fire, since it is reserved for the Holy Spirit, 1535. Christ must be proclaimed in both natures, 1547. Christ is less than the Father according to his humanity, but equal to him according to his divinity, 1549.

—A comparison between the Incarnation of the Word and the mission of the Holy Spirit, 1580. The mystery of the Incarnation is understood through the Lord’s feet, 1596. He who loves this mystery kisses the Lord’s feet, ibid. Christ placed the lost sheep upon his shoulders by assuming human nature, 1682. The light in the clay vessel is divinity in the flesh, 1603. The wedding of the Son of God is his Incarnation, 1635. The incarnate God spoke through the prophets of the future Incarnation and through the apostles of the accomplished Incarnation of the Only-Begotten, 1636. Love was the sole cause of the Incarnation, [Col. 1364] 1639.

—Judea and the Gentile world desired Christ’s coming, 215. Many among the Gentiles awaited the coming of the Redeemer, ibid. The saint of the Old Testament longed for the bodily presence of his Creator, 386. Christ’s first coming was in humility, the second in terror, 555. See *Adventus*.

—Christ was born in another’s place, not according to power but according to nature, 1461. Christ is signified by gold, frankincense, and myrrh as God, king, and man, 1470. Christ is like others in humanity and unique in divinity, 26. At times Christ speaks as if doubting because of our doubt, 28. What it means that Christ fell to the ground through humility, 61. Why Christ, when born, was placed in a manger, 215. Divinity laid itself low before human beings through humanity, and, rising, raised them up, 515. Why Christ appeared in the flesh, 684. The Son of God, unknown to us in his eternal birth, wished to be born in time so that he might offer himself for imitation, 917. The birth of the flesh, despised by the world’s wise, is life, ibid. Christ was made lower than the angels, and as man was exalted above the angels, 1244. Christ passes through humanity and stands through divinity, 167, 1442. For him, his poor mother offered not a lamb but young pigeons, 1443. The outstanding testimonies of John the Baptist concerning Christ’s divinity, 1458.

—Christ, who feared God, 22. Christ became the model of preachers by acting during the day and spending the night in prayer, 207. Christ is the lamp despised here, 364. Christ was rejected by Herod, 364. Christ revealed hidden things and changed the shadow of death into light, 376. Christ made manifest the sins that lay hidden, 386. He alone among all offered pure prayers to God, 426. Christ alone spoke with authority, 742. Through Christ light shone upon all, 885. What he taught by speaking, he confirmed by acting, 914, 1496. Christ alone possessed within himself all the operations of the Holy Spirit, 72, 952. Christ, made man among human beings, found some things when he came and taught others by living, 987. He fled what everyone seeks and sought what everyone flees, ibid. What the author of life teaches, and what the author of death teaches, 1141. Before reaching mature age, Christ did not teach but asked questions, 1183. What Christ taught us by acting and suffering, 1323. Christ instructed us about everything by his example, ibid. Christ did not wish to prosper in the world, 1443. Christ assumed our temptations in order to overcome them, 1492. Those who saw Christ’s deeds and miracles sucked honey from the rock, 1554. Those who required Christ’s bodily presence in order to perform miracles did not think rightly about him, 166. Christ speaks not only in words but also through events, 1582. Christ does not withdraw the word of preaching from the ungrateful, 1646. What Christ teaches in the temple of God—that is, in the faithful mind, 1648. What use should be made of his teaching and admonitions, 1649. Whether Christ alone is the one in whom the devil had nothing, ibid.

—Christ is the Wisdom and Power of God, 370. Christ is to be compared with none of humanity or the angels, 592, 598, 1310. Certain heretics said that he was a mere man, 597. Those who say Christ is like the other saints are refuted, ibid. Nestorius taught that Christ had attained by merits that he might become God, 598. Christ is one thing from the Father and another from the Mother, but not another person, ibid. Christ is God not merely in name but essentially, 1256, 1551. Christ is God above all, [Col. 1365] ibid. Christ passes through humanity and stands through divinity, 1442. The outstanding testimonies of John the Baptist concerning Christ’s divinity, 1458. Divinity, like footwear, became known to human beings through the flesh, 1459. The strap of the shoe is the bond of the mystery, ibid. To believe in Christ’s divinity is to devour the head of the lamb, 1535. Christ is equal and coeternal with the Father, 1549. He touches Christ who believes him equal to the Father, ibid. Christ’s divinity is signified by the head, 1597. To anoint Christ’s head means to believe that he is God himself, ibid.

—Christ, as a clay vessel—that is, through his flesh—scraped away the pus of sin, 87. Christ’s flesh was handed over to the wicked devil, 307. He who does not cover Christ’s blood with earth, 426. The devil tempted Christ outwardly but did not touch his soul, 86. From the beginning of the world Christ was struck in his members, ibid. He suffered persecution from Jews and Gentiles, 878. Who the Spirit of Christ is, 1545. How great was Christ’s power, which he refused to use against his persecutors, 1509. Christ subjects us to obedience by his example, 1155. He preserves this obedience even when he comes as judge, ibid. Christ is the helper to be sought, who is lawgiver and judge, 719. No legislator resembles Christ, 853. Christ is sought at night, but is not found unless the prophets and patriarchs have been crossed, 854.

—When the devil saw the humble Christ, he, being proud, doubted that he was God, 56.

—Christ sat in the dungheap when he chose the weak things of the world, 87. What the terror of the law did not arouse, Christ recalled to life by his humility, 318. Christ’s path is humility; the world’s is pride, 505. The Jews, ignorant of the ways of Christ’s humility, lost the fruit of his death, 580. Christ is humble in weakness and exalted in strength, 853. By God’s humility the devil’s pride was crushed, 1187. The descent of truth became the ascent of our humility, 1212. Christ’s example of humility is necessary for us, 1509. Christ teaches humility by his example and restrains pride, 1566, 1567. See *Humilitas*. *Superbia*.

—Christ joined gentleness with the strictness of justice, 22. Christ corrected us by gentleness rather than terror, 317. He did not return the injury he received but responded by bearing it gently, 1507. Christ ruled us by gentleness, not severity, 317.

—Christ taught by his example to bless God amid scourging, 62. Christ voluntarily stirred himself and groaned, 86. In his Passion, like Job, Christ did not go out through the door by keeping silent, 717. Christ’s patience in the Passion, as he prayed for his persecutors, 1229.

—Christ taught us by his example to show patience in injuries received, 1508. A wondrous example of patience and humility in Christ, 1509.

—It is demonstrated that the devil could not overcome Christ’s soul, 86. Christ is the Wisdom and Power of God, 370. Why, at his first coming, Christ is Wisdom and Power, and at his second, Power and Wisdom, 373. Christ feared because of our weakness, so that he might strengthen us by his own strength, 399. The righteous, fearing God’s strength, desire weakness in the humanity he assumed, 515. The Son of God, strong above all, appeared weak among all, ibid. Which Christ is meant by the one who has put his hand into the den of the basilisk and the asp,
555.—Christ, innocent yet scourged, while blessing the Father, showed what the guilty should do under scourging, 63. Contemplating Christ innocent and scourged, the saints are terrified and humbled, 1244. In Christ alone the Father found no fault; therefore in him alone he was well pleased, 1243. In estimating Christ’s charity and patience: how Satan is deceived, 85. Christ did not wish to be feared as God, but wished to be loved by us as Father, 317. The law of God and the charity of Christ, 340. This law of God is manifold, 343. The highest praise of God’s charity is that he accepted for us what was unworthy of him, 404. Christ’s blood pleaded forgiveness for his persecutors, 426. Christ shed tears over Jerusalem, 1645.—Christ continually offers himself as a holocaust for us, 28. Because of what he suffered, Christ made his divinity doubtful to the devil, 55. “A violent wind from the region of the desert” is a strong temptation against the faithful in the Lord’s Passion, 59. Christ, equal to the Father, came for us to the scourging in the flesh, 84. How Satan moved the Father against Christ, his Son, ibid. God afflicted the innocent Christ with punishments, ibid. Christ was handed over by the Father into Satan’s hands in his Passion, 85. Christ still suffers much in his own members, 88. By one death Christ destroyed the twofold death of humanity, 117, 306. Christ was a tree cut down in the Passion and multiplied in the Resurrection, 395. From what Christ suffered we learn our misery and his mercy, 213. By suffering, Christ reproved human guilt and appeased God’s anger, 317. What it means that Christ tore his garment in his Passion, 60. The sacrament of the Lord’s Passion must not be fruitless in us, 426. Christ accepted the punishment of our guilt without guilt of his own, 429. Christ was in bitterness through the Passion and was freed through the Resurrection, ibid. While Christ suffered, the holy women clung to him like feet when the apostles fled, 457. Christ died so that we would not fear dying, 463. He who, when he was to be judged, felled his enemies with one word—what will he do when he comes to judge? 556. In his Passion Christ fulfilled the virtues that had preceded in Job, 717. The Lord’s passions are called gates against which the waves of the world break and scatter, 914. The world mocked them and afterward was terrified, ibid. From Christ’s death we learn what follows after death, 927, 928. By dying Christ overcame the gates of death, 928. Through Christ’s death the Church grew, ibid. Christ foreknew and ordained from eternity the beginning, end, and course of his human life, 933. Dying, Christ did not hear the cry of the devil the exactor, 988. Laban was a type of the devil the exactor; Jacob, of Christ; Rachel, of the Church, ibid.—We ought to be nourished by meditation on Christ’s Passion, 1043, 1318. The devil, wishing to swallow Christ, was caught as if by a hook, 1085. It was fitting that the death of him who died unjustly should dissolve the death of those who died justly, 1095. Christ alone trod the winepress, 1314. How much Christ did and suffered for us, 1323. Through faith in Christ’s Passion and death the ancient Fathers were saved, 1336. Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, opened the sealed book by his Passion and Resurrection, 1351. Why Christ foretold his death and Resurrection, 1440. What Christ endured for humanity, 1443. Humanity took scandal from Christ’s death, when it ought thereby to have become more indebted to him, 1454. Christ is to be honored more because he accepted what was unworthy of him for us, ibid. The power of Christ’s humanity grew from the fire of the Passion into incorruption, 1534. How Christ drank from the torrent on the way, 1550. The Father loved the Son whom he sent to the Passion, 1554. How Christ’s strength dried up like a potsherd, 1603. Without owing the debt, Christ paid the debt of death for us, 1619.—Christ gradually revealed his Resurrection to the disciples, 53. What it means for Christ to lie down and rise, 60. By rising, Christ overcame the tongues of the Jews and the sword of the Gentiles, 197. And he made firm the hope of his own, ibid. Whom Christ brought out of hell when he rose, 398. Job openly foretells Christ’s Resurrection, 463. Christ rose so that we might be confident that we too shall rise, ibid. When Christ ascended into heaven, the holy Church was strengthened on earth, 543. “To ascend above the setting” means to rise again, 606, 1180, 1496. Christ who intercedes for us with the Father, 718. How far Christ’s Resurrection differs from ours, 761. Christ alone ascended into heaven, which is open only to his members, 866. Christ, by rising, showed the life that we do not know, 928. Rising in the morning, Christ became for us the morning star, 952. By rising, Christ loosed the weaknesses of our mortality to which he had willingly bound himself, 986. The locust signifies Christ’s Resurrection, 1018. Christ’s Ascension is signified under the name of the eagle, 1039. Christ reigning in heaven gathers the elect to himself, 1044. What Christ’s rising on the eighth day signifies, 1150.—Christ’s body, like water until the Passion, became hard by rising, like crystal formed from water, 1231. Christ was born beneath the angels and, by rising, was himself exalted above the angels, 1244. By rising, Christ changed the frailty of the flesh into eternity, 1313. Christ’s Resurrection is the pattern of ours, 1393. Why Christ foretold his death and Resurrection, 1440. The Lord, ascending into heaven, went to the wedding feast, 1482. Why the angel announcing Christ’s Resurrection appeared on the right, 1526. The Lord’s Resurrection is a festival for us and for the angels, ibid. The repose of contemplation is signified by the silence that occurs in heaven, 1327. No repose of the mind is perfect or lasting here, ibid. Various stages in the contemplation of God, 1356. The mind’s expansion through contemplation, 1361. Those who think excessively about external things are unfit for contemplation, ibid. How necessary humility is for it, ibid. Contemplation is denied to no condition of the faithful, not even to those who lie in the lowest places, 1362. In contemplation we advance through inquiry, ibid. Through more perfect contemplation, things are seen that the tongue cannot express, 1363. The distinction between faith and contemplation, 1371. See Active and contemplative life.

Contempt for the world: the Pastor, urging this, invites us to God’s banquet, 1620. What it means to contend with God, 289, 378. The flood of the world is overcome only by ardent striving of mind, 391. The life of the continent is represented by Daniel, 23, 1344. How blessed is the life of the continent, 1344. The excellence of continence, ibid. Each continent person, as one chosen, scorns to go after the tracks of the flocks, 981. “Against” is not set in opposition to adversity, but in relation to uprightness, 1356, 1382. The wicked contradict the words of the righteous, 337, 338. What it means to be tested at the waters of contradiction, 822. What form contrition takes, 118. Contrition sometimes comes from God, sometimes from the adversary, 219. What the contrition of the wicked is, 797. The greatest contrition of the reprobate is to have sought the creature after abandoning the Creator, ibid. Two kinds of contrition, 1428. An insult received should not be repaid, following Christ’s example, 1507. Even to those who reproach us falsely, true accusations should not be thrown back, ibid. The good become better through insults received, 1508. To bear insults and love the one who inflicts them is a kind of martyrdom, 1616.

The conduct of the good is highly praiseworthy, 31. When one undertakes to turn one’s ways toward better things, the devil is stirred up against one, 121. The soul’s conversion as it returns to God, 200. A person, seeing what he loves, understands what he grieves over, 213, 249. The beginnings of a good life must be dedicated to God alone, 280. Why one should not keep silent sooner, ibid. Conversion begins with uprightness of action and proceeds toward uprightness of mind, 351. Conversion is impossible without God’s grace, 370. When grace breathes upon the heart that savors earthly things, it is overturned and changed, 371. The effect of conversion, 372, 376, 631. An example of true conversion in Saint Paul, 372. Conversion must be strengthened by the practice of good works, 414. We must turn to God by faith and come to him through works, [Col. 1373] 432. The manner of conversion, 631. God patiently awaits each person’s conversion, 484. Through the Church’s preaching, the powerful of the world are brought to knowledge and worship of God, 582. When the spirit calls us here and the flesh calls us back, this is the heavy sorrow of conversion, 771. When the bonds are broken with God’s help, joy succeeds the sorrow of converts, ibid. Three stages of conversion, 772. The pattern of conversion in the people of Israel, divinely liberated from Egypt, ibid. The beginnings of conversion are followed by severe temptations, ibid., 1306. Why the beginnings of conversion are sometimes peaceful, 773. Why temptations are sharper after conversion than they were before, ibid., 1302. The converted soul has the labor of struggle; hence it desires the joy of pleasure, 775. The more a person begins to live above, the more he begins to die below, 783. A person converted by grace remembers that he is dust, ibid. Holy preachers converted the ends of the world to faith by words and miracles, 862. Those recently converted are still clothed in cloud, 913. — Human conversion is completed gradually and by invisible grace, 936. Those converted from iniquity should be admonished by gentle words by the Pastor, 962. How we should conceive and then give birth to the resolve for a better life, 975. The Lord converts those whom he looks upon, 992. The Lord is nourished by the good works of converts, ibid. The beginnings of conversion are mixed with good and evil ways, 1030. At the beginning of conversion God raises us up like locusts, ibid. Those beginning are placed between hope and fear, ibid. Because of the struggles of the flesh, which they therefore tame vigorously, 1031. They investigate the enemy’s ambushes and deceits, ibid. A person makes a wound from a remedy; God makes a remedy from a wound, 1092. The order of conversion, 1153. The conversion of sinners consoles Christ and the Church, 1155. God first casts people down by terrifying them, then raises them up, and confirms those who have been raised by grace, 1259. Definition of true conversion, 1266. What the new creation in Christ is, 1266, 1274. In Babylon the person who is liberated is the one who, having been confounded by the confusion of vices, is converted, 1271. A description of conversion arising from terror, 1273. The progress of conversion from the mourning of repentance to tears of love for God, 1278. What order should be observed by those laboring for the conversion of souls, 1302. One who begins to serve God is besieged by the devil’s snares, 1306. From these he cannot be rescued by his own strength, ibid. Converts must be nourished with the food of sacred doctrine, 1416. A converted sinner ought to sing mercy and judgment to God, 1420. We have received the present time as a reprieve for conversion, 1479. Those whom God long endures so that they may be converted, if they are not converted, he condemns more harshly, 1483. The one whose patience he now despises will later experience him as angry, 1509. We will scarcely follow tomorrow the one converted whom today we seemed to see going before us as an evil person, 1514. A remarkable example of conversion in a young man at death, ibid. The conversion of the wicked and angry is promised, 1519. What the fruits of conversion are, 1584. Unless a person departs from himself, he does not draw near to God, 1588. After rejecting vices, virtues must be sought, ibid. An exhortation to return to God through conversion, 1599. Why there is greater joy in heaven over a converted sinner than over righteous people who remain standing, 1602. In how many ways God compels us to return to him, 1623. The usefulness of adversities for the conversion of a sinner, 1624. Through conversion the soul is said to return to its former husband, ibid. See Contrition; Repentance.

[Col. 1373] The righteous do not return insults, 418, 1507. One readily tolerates insults when, in the secrecy of one’s mind, one recalls the evils one has committed, 974. Those who insult deserve grace more than anger, ibid. Even to those who reproach us falsely, true accusations should not be thrown back, 1507.

Banquets are scarcely held without fault, 20. The devil finds a place even at restrained banquets, 49. Talkativeness accompanies banquets, 20, 1656. The banquet of the reprobate is delight in temporal pleasures, 1108. What the future banquet at the end of the world concerning the conversion of the Jews signifies, 1158. What Christ’s final banquet after the resurrection signifies, 1543. Those invited to God’s banquet should examine their hearts and drive away deadly weariness, 1620. The Lord himself is served at it, the slain Lamb, ibid. Woe to the one who comes to this banquet without a wedding garment, 1639. One enters through faith, ibid. Those approaching the sacred banquet should carefully examine themselves, 1641. Otherwise they will be scrutinized by Christ with care and punished severely, ibid. Talkativeness and games follow banquets, 1656. The basket of dung is the memory of sins, 1584. The chief of the cooks signifies the belly, 982.

The body’s function is the instrument of the heart, 6. One should not rashly judge another person’s heart, 21. The human heart is compared with air and stones, 222, 579. Waters stirred by the wind, 531. The source of security, 714. What a crooked heart is, 783. What the steps of the heart are, 790. What the place of the heart is, 867. Those who eagerly desire to protect earthly things lose the quiet of their heart, 230. God removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, 350. What it means to rebuke the heart in prayer, 352. What it means for a person’s heart to be destroyed or built by God, 370. What it means to raise the heart with the hands, 560. The human heart is called an abyss, 588. The necessity of guarding and watching over the heart, 621. The heart is the altar on which the fire is commanded always to burn, 794. One must return from external things to the heart, 795. What it means to dig through the wall of the heart, 814. Among human beings hearts are weighed by words; before God, words are weighed by the heart, 818. The heart is often far removed from a person, 841. Restlessness of the heart outside God, for whom it was made, 849. What the wantonness of the heart is, 897. What the cutting away of the foreskins of the heart signifies, 898. The human heart is a boiling sea that God alone can restrain, 915. This sea is wrapped in darkness, ibid. What boundaries God sets for this sea while it rages, 916. That raging sea scatters the virtues unless they are strengthened by charity, 916. Snow or hail signifies the cold and hard hearts of the wicked, 933. God alone opens hearts by grace, 939. Hearts are like a desert not made fertile by the rain of grace, 941. Even the hearts of the righteous grow dark before God’s hidden inspirations, 956. Christ abandons parched hearts and seeks those that live by faith and hope, 993. What the hardening of the heart by God is, 1008. When human hearts desire earthly things, they lay themselves down to be crushed by the devil, 1013. The hardness of the heart is signified by digging through a wall and penetrating a rock, 1021. There are two great kinds of disturbance of the heart, 1277. Any heart taken up by the divine Spirit becomes bitter, 1279. The heart’s frying—that is, God is appeased by spiritual zeal, 1304. The hand is never empty of a gift if the ark of the heart is filled with good will, 1451. The door of the heart is shut against the truth: what this means, 1458. God comes into the hearts of some, but does not remain, 1576. [Col. 1374] Why earthly hearts are called “earth,” 1577. See Soul; Mind; Will.

To walk before oneself means to attend to oneself, or to be present to oneself, 1204.

The centurion Cornelius deserved to be heard because of his good works, 1252. He did not come to faith through works, but came from faith to works, 1381. Through works he was established in faith, 1382. His conversion, 886.

What the horns of the beast indicate, 1061. The horn signifies the pride of the arrogant, 995, 996, 1105. What it means to carry a horn in the nostril, 1010. What is signified by the name *Cornustibium*, 1163. The song of those rejoicing is expressed by the name *Cornustibium*, 1165.

The crown is the reward of victory, 452. It is a sign of victory, 1414. The crown on the head is the heavenly recompense in the mind, 452. The crown is removed from the head of the Church when prelates neglect spiritual goods, 453. What it means for the saints to cast crowns before the Lord’s throne, 708. What the crown in recompense is which was borne in work, according to Sacred Scripture, 720. God protects and helps some, and crowns them by rewarding them, 1105.

Bodily infirmities weaken the spirit, 6. How much care the body requires, 135. How many and how great are the body’s needs in this life, ibid. The body weighs down the soul so that it cannot devote itself long to contemplation of heavenly things, 267. The body is the garment of the soul, 324. The devil and all the wicked are one body, 430. How the Lord’s body entered to the disciples through closed doors, 1552.

One who corrects others must himself be clean, 238. The wicked correct the good, not out of zeal for purification but out of envy, 459. What must be considered in correcting, 742. What the corrections of the saints are like, 814. Why they act in this way, 815. Anger must be avoided in correcting, 848, 1000. Those whom we cannot correct by admonishing, we must tolerate by enduring, 417. We escape the hand of the one who strikes only through amendment, 572. When we correct the faults of others, we must first measure our own, 848. The wicked, who could scarcely be corrected when divided, will be corrected when united, 1108. The righteous patiently endure their own correction, 338. The wicked are impatient of correction, ibid. Who is more ready to die than to be corrected, becoming worse through the very reproof, 274, 1262. When evils can be amended, to remain silent is to consent, 341. Those sin venially who, through the fervor of zeal, exceed the proper measure of correction, 343. When the righteous rage outwardly against the wicked, inwardly they sympathize with them, 380, 780. One who is mourning should not be rebuked, 418. Whether correction should be delayed or not, so that it may be useful, 419. Those who sin publicly must be corrected publicly, 420. The Church’s grief over the wicked corrected in vain, ibid. We must first rise up against ourselves, then against the wicked, 448. The wicked do not observe this order of correction, ibid. What measure should be observed in correction, 780, 781, 852. In correction, swelling places must be pressed down in such a way that wounded places are cared for, 814. Holy teachers are accustomed to exaggerate the vices of delinquents, ibid. What it means to dig through the wall of the heart, ibid. The pastor of souls’ devout severity in examining the heart’s hidden sins, 815. The pastor who ceases from correction should fear condemnation, ibid. The order for correcting and instructing delinquents toward repentance and piety, ibid. In administering correction, anger should be subordinate, not dominant, 848. The discretion of the saints in correcting, which the arrogant lack, 852. Nothing harms the soul more gravely than a virtue conscious of itself, unless it is exercised by corrections, 891. [Col. 1375] With what attitude those who offend in certain external matters should be corrected, 1008. The wicked raise the shield of excuse against those correcting them, 1105. Adam and Eve used this shield, 1106. Those corrected obliquely turn their guilt back upon the Creator, ibid. Covered with the scales of defense, they resist the darts of truth, ibid. The hedgehog is an image of the defense of malicious minds, 1107. The hedgehog has a burrow among the reprobate, 1108. The wicked protect one another through mutual defense, ibid. As vinegar poured on soda, the mind becomes worse after correction, 1262. Through the frequency of sin comes hardness of heart, by which the heart becomes insensitive during correction, 1269. One must not cease from correction because of either the humility or the pride of delinquents, 1270. Those who are not heard while correcting should not lose heart, 1271. Some do not listen; others listen to correction only in part, 1272. The weak should be corrected or taught with few words, 1287. Some should be reproved gently, others more harshly, ibid. A skilled physician probes a wound for a long time and afterward soothes it, 1287. Harder minds must be rebuked more sharply, 1288. It is a great grace of God when a harsh word of rebuke is directed at the wicked, 1298. Harshness should be displayed outwardly toward the wicked, charity held inwardly, 1414. Why the words of the wise are said to resemble keys and goads, 1455. How great is the danger of one who is corrected but not amended, 1584. Bread of refreshment should be given to sinful poor people together with the word of correction, 1659. See Reproof.

What the strap of a sandal signifies, 1459, 1518. In how many ways the soul approaches corruption and deadly things, 759. The person who judges himself far removed from corruption by his own strength descends into corruption, 762.

What the ten curtains of the tabernacle signify, 1379. What the fifty violet loops of the curtains signify, ibid. What the golden rings signify, ibid.

From a certain flash, the saints taste beforehand the inner sweetness of contemplation, 1210.

The young ravens are the sons of the Gentiles, 969. The raven signifies the Jewish people, 970. The raven is a learned preacher, 971. The diligence of ravens in raising their young, ibid.

God has not promised tomorrow to the sinner, 1479. Anxiety is forbidden for tomorrow but permitted for today, 336.

Ignorance of the Creator is the origin of all vices, 17. In what sense God is said to create evil, 79. The Creator holds all things through himself, 127. In order to make himself visible, the Creator assumed our humanity, 167. All things proclaim God as their Creator, 568. God created and preserves all things, 518. In what sense God is said to have created all things at once, 1055. At once in substance, not at once in appearance, ibid. In what sense angel and human being were created together, 1056. How creation took place over several days, 1055. The Creator is sometimes said to pass by, 167. Who are said to rise up against their Creator, 411. The traces of our Creator are the wondrous works of visible creation, 819. The Creator is immortal because he is not changeable in the manner of creatures, 1049. What has been made from nothing depends upon nothing, 1395. The Creator had a hundred sheep when he created the substance of angels and human beings, 1601. God created both natures, of angels and of human beings, capable of seeing him, 1603.

All creatures are subordinated to one another, 127. How the creature, unwillingly, has been subjected to vanity, 135. Who is delivered from the slavery of corruption, ibid. [Col. 1375] Through creatures, as through certain cracks, God offers himself to be admired, 161. Creation is in continual flux; only the Creator stands firm, 167. However good a creature may be, it must be rejected for love of the Creator, 172. The rational creature was made in the image of God, 167. The division of creatures, 190. A spiritual creature is not sufficient to contemplate God, 301. All creatures confess that God exists, 368. Compared with God, creatures are as though they did not exist, 518. They act only when moved by God, ibid. Rational creation is mutable of itself toward worse things, and through God’s grace toward better things, 791. Creatures are God’s traces, 819. They are roads to the Creator, ibid. We withdrew from God through visible things; through those same things we must return to God, ibid.
