Whatever in created things is compared with God becomes empty and nothing, 1143. In the presence of his Creator, a human being sees that he is dust, 1294. The word “creature” signifies every human being, 1569, and every nation of the Gentiles, 1570. What the new creation is, 1267. All created things are good, 308. All things created were made from nothing, 518. Everything created had a beginning, 857. Some created things had a beginning but will never have an end, ibid.

Every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime, 688. Sin pollutes the soul; crime extinguishes it, ibid. A greater crime arises from greater virtue, 579.

The firmament is said to have the appearance of crystal, 1230. What being solidified from water signifies, ibid.

Bearing the cross is not always fruitful, 277. What it means to carry the cross with the Cyrenaean, 277, 1588. The cross is signified by the name “wood,” 394. The wood of the cross is declared throughout all parts of Scripture, 1218. By the wood of the cross we are carried into our homeland, ibid. Christ’s cross appeared foolish to unbelievers, 1454. How Christ, when exalted, drew all things to himself, 1533. The cross must be borne in two ways, 1588, 1629. The cross is so called from suffering (*cruciatus*), ibid. It is not enough to carry the cross unless we follow Christ, 1629.

What the reed of six cubits and a span signifies, 980, 1323, 1340. What the gnat signifies in Scripture, 23.

The evil of guilt is sometimes prophecy in Scripture, 94. Guilt is committed in two ways, 198. Guilt continually grows when nourished by favor, 125. A single fault is often the occasion of many that follow, 227. Knowledge of our faults moderates the pain of scourging, 343. When faults have been wiped away in prayer by tears, the mind does not fall back into them, 352. The order of judgment increases according to the stages of guilt, 682. Guilt must be extinguished inwardly, where it arises, before it emerges into action, 685. From the point at which righteousness is recognized, the nature of guilt is seen, 1045. The more serious faults are those that imitate virtues, 1207. Guilt passes into guilt when one serves desire rather than necessity, 1387. No one in this life is free from guilt, 269. God justly permits the evil of guilt to occur, 367. God makes good use of evils, 1130. Evils are often hidden under the appearance of good, 1223. God leaves no evils unpunished, 683. The person who tramples worldly prosperity truly pursues his own guilt, 120. Guilt is easily forgiven when it is not committed deliberately out of malice, 344. See Sin.

Desire must be abandoned so that the sacrifice of good will may be offered to God, 1452. Desire is the root of all evils, 646.

[Col. 1376] Excessive concern for worldly affairs brings upon the agitated soul a throng of thoughts, 129. The saints put themselves to death because of these concerns by the sword of the sacred word, 142. What sort of people are affected by these concerns—the wicked in mind, 147, 287—and how devout minds should conduct themselves toward such concerns, ibid., 432. How greatly excessive concern for household affairs harms salvation, 230, 335. These concerns must not be cut away entirely but moderated, 336. Care of the flesh should serve, not rule, ibid. Freedom from earthly cares brings rest and work, 356. Excessive concern for affairs, because it occupies the mind, blinds it, 411. Concerns renounced through conversion must not be taken up again, 414. The saints prefer to suffer evils rather than be wearied by earthly cares, 433. Worldly cares are compared with worms, 532. Greater cares open an easier path to vices, 546. Those distracted by earthly concerns do not enjoy God’s wisdom, 588, 749. The crowd is cast outside so that the girl may be raised, 589. The good are entangled in earthly cares, but not with earthly zeal, ibid. Earthly concerns must be attended to in accordance with God’s will, while striving to devote oneself to God alone, 590. Let the person who desires to hear God’s voice rest from worldly cares, 749. The bondage of worldly cares is great, 979, 1269. As worldly cares increase, the windows do not pour forth light when priests cease from the office of preaching, 1292. A mind divided by earthly cares is less capable of seeing heavenly things, 1308, 1503, and is not prepared for perfection, 1383. The cares of the world are compared with waves and storms, 695.

Heretics who scrutinize divine things inquisitively suffer from poverty and sterility, 644. The curious person, who knows what belongs to others, does not know himself, 1621. Curiosity is signified by the five senses of the body, represented by the five yokes of oxen, ibid. How great the vice of curiosity is, ibid.

What the office of a runner is, 308. Why the elect who preceded the Redeemer’s coming are called runners, ibid.

The crooked person always looks at the earth, 1585. What it means for angels to be bent beneath God, 301. How the human heart is crooked, 783. Who is bent down completely, 1585.

How necessary the guarding of the soul is, 621. Human vigilance is useless against the enemy without God’s protection, 267. Guarding the heart is useless if even one entrance is left open to the enemy, 621. What the guarding of God’s Temple—that is, the Church—is, 1423. God is called the guardian of human beings, 267.

The skin signifies those in the Church who serve only external concerns, 252, 674. What it means for the skin to dry out and contract, 252. What the beauty of the skin is, 442. Those whose skin has clung to their bones, 1071.

What the cup signifies in the tabernacle, 636, 1455.

# D
Daemons wander in the air, 66. The unclean spirits whom they capture drive into despair, 57. Daemons are signified by the Sabaeans, ibid. A demon deceives through dreams, 262. Daemons are called robbers, 282, 453, 1472. Daemons do not see God’s wisdom, 605. Daemons possess nothing as their own in this world, 1587. Daemons always lie in wait for us, 1472. The game of demons is to roll human minds from one vice into another, 1076. See Devil, Satan.

The various punishments of the condemned, 202. The condemned are tortured inwardly and outwardly, ibid. For the condemned there is no return to forgiveness or to the things they loved, 256. No mercy remains for them to hope for, [Col. 1377] 331. Those whom the pain of burning torments are darkened by the punishment of blindness, 332. How just these punishments are, ibid. What it means for the condemned to be bound in bundles, 333. Angels and reprobate human beings are involved in one punishment, 335. The condemned are always dying, never consumed by death, 477. Those who invented many things for guilt are tormented with newly devised punishments, ibid. He who did not distribute what was his own, and still more he who seized what belonged to another, must be punished with eternal punishment, 478. The more the wicked shine here, the more harshly they will be punished in Gehenna, 481. The reprobate are bodily burned by bodily fire, 482. They are tormented by fire according to both body and soul, ibid. The wicked, who are now unwillingly led out of the body, will then be held unwillingly in the body, 483. The reprobate will be tormented for their sins, even the smallest, 484. Eternal condemnation is signified under the name of the sword, 1123. The condemned in their punishments will see those whom they here directed in a disorderly manner, 334. Those destined for condemnation are often tolerated for a long time, 496. Whether the condemned would wish to pass over to the saved, or the reverse, 1657. Knowledge and memory are preserved for the condemned in their punishment, 1658. The condemned see the condemned, to increase their punishment, ibid. See Hell, Gehenna.

Antichrist will arise from the tribe of Dan, 1015. Why Dan is called a serpent and a cerastes, ibid. Daniel is to be imitated by one who longs for contemplation, 974. The taste of the fleshly is to be restrained by his example, ibid. Daniel became weak after he had seen higher things belonging to God, 1242. Daniel is a figure of the continent, 23, 1344. Daniel’s moderation, 974.

What David’s history with Uriah and Bathsheba signifies, 94. What the history signifies of the Egyptian boy who was abandoned by an Amalekite because of illness and received by David, 173. Why David is forbidden to build God’s temple, 239. Why David appeased God when He raged against the people, but could not appease Him when He was angry with himself, 299. David was despised by his father and chosen by Samuel, 362. David, a high mountain, fell through a sudden collapse, 402. What the history of David’s beheading Goliath with his own sword signifies, 566. David affected by compunction in four ways, 751. How greatly David guarded against the pride close to powerful men, 835. David teaches us piety and humility, 860. David’s remarkable humility in high position, 888. David dancing before the ark is valued more highly than fighting against enemies, 889, 1460. By fighting enemies and pursuing humility, he conquered himself, ibid., 1460. He displayed himself outwardly as lowly and was humble inwardly, 889. David kept himself within his proper limits, 905. The humility and patience of King David, 973, 1135, 1460. He regarded insulting words not as abuses but as aids, ibid. God frightened us by the fall of our ancestors, but strengthened us by their restoration, 1091. From David’s example toward Saul, we learn that good should be repaid for evil, 1339. David, washed in the tears of repentance at the fountain of mercy, 1402. How greatly David was inflamed by the love of God, 1422. Leviathan held David in his mouth, from which he escaped through the opening made by repentance, 1551. With what repentance David washed away his adultery, 1609. He poured out to the Lord the water brought to him from the cistern of Bethlehem, ibid. He who remembered that he had committed unlawful acts abstained from lawful ones, 1610.

Why David cursed the mountains of Gilboa, 103. His love toward God, 130. Love of enemies, 1339. Humility of heart, 834, 1135, 1460. Looking ahead to the affliction of the Church, David composed a psalm about the winepresses, [Col. 1377] 526. David corrected by Nathan, 713. David often offered God the sacrifice of humility, 835. His gentleness and humility, 860.

We give tithes to God in Lent, 1495. What the devil’s snare laid across the path signifies, 441. God’s decrees are immutable and eternal, 393. To disdain sinners who call themselves just, as did the Pharisees, 1600. One thing is done from the pride of arrogance, another from zeal for discipline, ibid. Heretics are called defenders, 15, 380, 533. When it is permissible to defend one’s property, 1006. How sinners defend themselves, 1105. Fearing to fall into what is already flowing, let him flee, 698. What it means to sleep securely in a dug-out place, 356.

The beginning of pleasure must be chastened by the lamentations of repentance, 115. Healthy sorrow over wrongful pleasure, 117. What it means to delight in God, 564. The soul cannot exist without delight, ibid. What it means to abound in delights in God, 509. The joy of human pleasure is called bread, 756. The taste of fleshly pleasures, which must be restrained, 974. The soul overflowing in contemplation of truth with spiritual delights despises earthly things, 510. How fleshly and spiritual delights differ, 1618.

In what sense God does not pardon the offender, 313. What an offense is, 386. How offenses and crimes differ from one another, ibid. What distinguishes sin from offense, 1404. How our offenses are marked in the sack, 400. It is clear that the saints offend here in deed, speech, or thought, 1203.

The number ten signifies perfection, 24, 30, 1162, 1365. Everyone receives the same denarius in heaven, 137, 1162. The denarius is given to the laborers beginning with the last, 1512.

In Scripture, teeth signify holy preachers, 382; and wicked preachers, ibid., 1104; and inward senses, 382.

Our prayer is often repelled from the sight of the Judge, 302. What state the soul abandoned by God is in, 328. Why God sometimes abandons us, 323. God does not leave us even when we are rejected, 957. God does not abandon what He has made, 822. In what sense God is said to abandon the elect, 75, 95. God never abandons His own, 97.

What the region of the desert signifies, 59, 67. What the wind coming from the region of the desert is, 59. Human hearts, like deserted land, are watered and made fruitful by the rain of grace, 941. What it means for the desert to be made into pools of water, 1522.

God often delays fulfilling the pious desires of the saints so that they may grow, 141, 513, 827, 1546. The great cry of blessed souls is their great desire, 42, 718. The desires of the saints grow when the end is nearer, 141. The mind strives through desires for heavenly things so that it may not descend to lower things, 192. Good desires are useless when they do not attain their effect, 226. The punishments of the innocent are the desires of the just, 307. The wicked person, drawn by evil desires toward an evil action, becomes entangled through fear, 441. Punishments draw toward good desires those whom rewards do not attract, 839. God hears our desires, 718, 1235.

Sloth in good works arises from a lesser love of God, 312. The despair of a sinner is signified by the name of hell, 257. The hearts of those who despair are like clouds, ibid. What it means for the just to despair, 264. The most wretched state of a soul despairing of salvation, 409, 440. To avoid despair, God’s benefits must be recalled to memory, 828. Whoever considers past gifts should not despair of future ones, 829. The abyss of despair swallows the one whom the narrow pit of evil habit encloses, 844. Whoever despairs of the future relaxes himself in present evils, 997. One seized by Leviathan’s mouth should not despair, because there is an opening in his jaw through which he may escape, 1090, 1514.

God chose those who were despised, 173. Many fear being despised, 716. Being despised recalls a person to himself and to God, 1622.

Slanderers devour human beings like beasts, 459. What it means for the slanderer’s drowsiness to be clothed in rags, 460. The good use of tongues that slander, 706. When slanderers should be despised or restrained, 1256. Those whose lives are set before others as an example ought to restrain them, as should those who are untouched by love of private glory, ibid. When the tongues of slanderers cannot be corrected, they must be endured with equanimity, 1257.

God, the human being’s place, was deserted through disobedience, 257. The two extremes are the human being and the Creator, dust and God, 391. In God certain things are spoken because of the effect of His work, others because of the substance of His majesty, 1051. In what sense God is said to be clothed in splendid garments, 1051, and to be wrapped in light as in a garment, ibid. The brightness of divinity is signified by the name of gold, 1128. Why God is called a consuming fire, 1208, 1247, 1577. God is sometimes named in a titular sense, sometimes essentially, 1236, 1331. God is called the master of the household, 1510. God is called helper, protector, and the very mercy of the human being, 1515. God is signified by the shepherd of the lost sheep and the woman of the lost drachma, 1603. God is called the husband of the faithful soul, 1624. He is called the King of Sabaoth, 1637.

God’s speech is manifold, 41, 42, 43. What “to speak of God” means, 43. What the face of God means, 46, 385, 765. In what sense God is said to be moved, 75. God is said to blow, 155. What God’s answering means, 175, 1145. God descended in fire and smoke, 209. What God’s laughing means, 307, 637. How God’s wrath is said to pass and pass through, 398. What it means to forget and remember God, 534. How God flees from us, 549. What seeing God means, 583. What God’s standing means, 605. What God’s looking upon means, 535, 606, 992. Passions are improperly attributed to God, 666. What it means to say that God is jealous, ibid. God is said to be angry, ibid. He is called merciful, ibid. In what sense He is said to repent, ibid. God is called cruel, 667. God’s speaking is His begetting the Word, 748. What it means for God to enter into and penetrate the mind, 929. Nothing bodily is to be imagined in God, 1049. God often compares Himself with created things, 1050. Certain sensible expressions concerning God show the effect of His operation, ibid., and likewise the substance of His majesty, 1051. What it means for God to have an arm, ibid. What it means for God to thunder with His voice, ibid. What hearing God means, 1145. What is signified by the sound of the Most High God, 1235. God sometimes speaks under the form of doubt, 1252. God is the life of all things, 1356.

God’s simplicity in being and diversity in operation, 1357. In what sense God is said to have bodily limbs, 456, 1050. What is meant by the soul of God, 519. God is what He has, 521, 596. God’s being is the same as His wisdom and His being strong, 552.

We ought to enjoy God alone and use the world in a stewardly manner, 45. Conversely, some use God and enjoy temporal goods, ibid. God must be sought above all in prayer, 489, 1428. He remains unbroken who, after losing everything else, has not lost God, 494. We must go to God through rough and smooth ways, 821. No one should live or die for himself, but for God, 1425. We must not turn aside from God’s path because of carnal affections, 1628. See Blessedness.

Knowledge of God in this life is called a vision at night, 162, 750. The soul is raised from knowledge of itself to knowledge of God, 166, 856. God is not known by the soul joined to the body without images, 167. God reveals Himself here only in small measure, however holy people may be, 168, 549. We know God imperfectly and speak of Him as though stammering, 168, 887. Just as a blind person speaks of light, so a human being speaks of God, 885. God whispers to us because He does not reveal Himself fully, 161. Through creatures, as through certain cracks, God presents Himself to us as worthy of admiration, ibid. We know God imperfectly by recognizing that we know nothing perfectly about Him, 169, 856, 887. Few things, and those very imperfectly, do we know here about God, 169, 521, 1358. God’s judgments concerning human beings are incomprehensible, 339, 855. The height and depth of God are unsearchable, 436, 516. It is one thing to know something about God, another to have wisdom, 369. God is incomprehensible, 489, 516. The elect, knowing God by faith, long to see Him in vision, 513. What must be avoided by those attempting to know God, 516, 550. By fearing God, you already know what wisdom is in you, although you cannot yet know what it is in Him, 610. Knowledge of God is called the face of God, 765. We go to knowledge of God through creatures as through footprints, 819. God is seen only from afar, even by the elect, 856. We see God acting, but are in darkness concerning His action, ibid. By knowing God we recognize ourselves and judge ourselves more strictly, 875. God is known only by a tranquil heart, 1113. Unless God declared His virtues to human beings, no one would recognize Him or be saved by loving Him, 1257. Through the progress of time, the knowledge of spiritual fathers increased, 1347. All knowledge concerning divine things is imperfect, 1408; even in Paul himself, ibid. The measure of love of God is knowledge, 1409.

Knowledge of God is reached through creatures, 161. We know God through visible things, 489. Knowledge of God is twofold, 513. God must be investigated through the traces of His love, 344. God cannot be investigated by human or angelic subtlety, 345. In this life God can be seen through certain images, but not in His essence, 600. No one sees God spiritually while living carnally, 601. Whether God is seen by the blessed in His brightness or in His nature, ibid. How God will be seen in the homeland, 602. We must infer God’s existence from reason, 856. God is known from His works, ibid. God’s mysteries are not to be dissected by the intellect, 1396. God is visible in His servants, 1581.

No one in this life, however holy, can see God as He is, 121, 600, 1326. We do indeed know invisible things, but only fleetingly, 165. God is not plainly seen here, 345. Here God is seen through His footprints, 345. God’s invisibility is known through the rational soul, 489. The invisible and incomprehensible God must be sought everywhere, 515. Certain saints in the Old Testament saw God, 600, 601. In what sense God dwells in inaccessible light, 602. One is the vision by which the blessed see God, another that by which God sees Himself, 602. No one in this life can see God’s glory, but only His likeness, 1248. Isaiah saw the glory of Christ, ibid.

In this life we perceive of God rather what He is not than what He is, 167. God is incomprehensible even to the angels, beneath whom they bow, 301. The angelic or human mind does not fully behold God’s essence, 345. God alone exists in comparison with whose essence our being is nonbeing, 518, 596. In God there is not one thing called being and another called having, 521. Nothing separated from the solidity of the eternal essence can subsist, 538. The wicked do not believe that God exists, 489. What God’s being means, 518, 1192. God alone possesses being, 596. What God’s place is like, 605. Who have believed God to be corporeal, 1049.

God is immutable; what is understood when He is said to have been moved in Job, 75. God is tranquil in Himself but appears turbulent to those who perish, 155, 166, 1051. What God’s standing means, 167, 605. What God’s repentance means, 294, 666. God’s immutability is asserted from eternity, 321. What the immutable motion of God means, 381. God alone is free from mutability, 406, 791. God’s sentence seems to change outwardly, but His inward plan does not change, 519, 667. God is immutable by nature and by will, ibid., 1052. What it means to say that God forgets and remembers, 533, 1050. What it means to say that God is jealous, angry, merciful, and foreknows, 666. This change is not in the quality of the judge but in the mind of the one undergoing it, 667. What it means to say that God alone possesses immortality, 791. God is immortal because He is immutable, 1052. God’s being is to remain eternal and unchangeable, 1192. God’s labor in sustaining hard human minds, 1532.

God is within and outside, above and below, all things, 47. God’s immensity is described, ibid., 505, 515, 1241. How God transcends all things, 345. God is immense without spatial extension, eternal without beginning or end, 857. God is present and equal to all things and everywhere, 869. Where God is not present by grace, He is present by vengeance, 1241. God is within in such a way that He is also outside, 1357. There is no place where God is not, 1566. God is higher than heaven, longer than the earth, and broader than the sea, 345. God is everywhere, not in a part, 515. God is not everywhere locally, but through His preachers He walks locally through the regions of the world, 861. God is wholly everywhere, 1357.

God orders times without time, 52, 1357. The things that flow outward in the course of time remain fixed in God’s eternity, ibid., 667. God, ordering diverse things, is not diverse, 53. Compared with the Creator, the creature is narrow, 133. Standing belongs to God alone, 167. The difference between human days and eternity, 321, 521. With the Almighty, things that pass away stand firm, 392. God’s day is His eternity, 521, 857. In eternity there is nothing past or future, but all is now, 521, 666, 1508. Perfect knowledge of eternity is granted to no one in this life, 550. God’s eternity is ineffable to human beings, 885. The eternity of the Word is signified under the name of a reed, 1078. God alone is immortal and immutable by nature, 406. God alone exists principally and immovably, 519. God’s eternity cannot be known, 857. God orders mutable things without undergoing change, 1357.

God does not reveal His perfections to the human mind all at once but gradually, 52. We ought to follow God’s footprints, 517. Why God praises His own perfections to human beings, 562. We can neither say nor think anything worthy of God, 665. A human being can neither harm nor benefit God, 818. God is great in strength, judgment, and justice, 887. God is not properly called perfect, because He was not made, 917. Whatever in created things is compared with God becomes empty and nothing, 1143. The divine substance receives neither diminution nor increase, 1408. God alone is unchangeable, 166, 406, 519, 1357. God’s breadth, length, height, and depth, 346. His excellence is unsearchable, ibid. God does not need our goods, 501. In what sense God is said to change, 519, 667. God’s greatness and perfection are described, 1241. God is ineffable, 885.

God sees darkness in light, seeing mutable things immutably, 53. God penetrates all the hearts of the guilty and innocent, 306, 792. The difference between divine and human sight, 321. How God’s plan and understanding differ, 370. God knows the plots of the wicked in judgment, but does not know them in love, 373. What it means to say that God forgets and remembers, 533. Things are not seen by God because they exist; rather, they exist because they are seen, 667. God is said to know by making us know, 683, 898. Whoever does not believe that he is seen by God keeps his eyes closed in the sun, 792. God’s knowing is approving, 897.

What God’s not knowing means, 40, 373, 733, 897. God comprehends good and evil without distinction, 53. What God’s knowing means, 373, 610, 683, 897. God saw and decreed future things from eternity, 393. What God’s knowing means, 683. In Holy Scripture God comprehended whatever can happen to individuals, 748. Everything is open in God’s sight, 790. God is ignorant of nothing and forgets nothing, ibid. In God’s foreknowledge there is a first planting of the just and a second in their works, 395. In God’s foreknowledge the times of each person’s life are immovably fixed, 414. God sees the end of offenders and the repentance of those who are corrected, ibid.

We must devoutly obey God’s known will, 196. God’s face is the regard of grace, 45. Whoever resists God falls from peace, 289. What the wicked do unjustly, God justly permits to be done, 367. Against our own will we must obey God’s will, 399. God’s will is fulfilled in the just and in the unjust, 483. God’s will must be searched out in Scripture, 517. What appears to happen against God’s will does not oppose it, 519. God’s just and hidden plan is signified by the name of a quiver, 1025. God’s will is immutable, 505, 519.

The wicked who resist God’s plans serve those very plans, even unwillingly, 194. God, as wise, cannot be deceived or evaded, 289. Why God is called wise, ibid. What the public and hidden works of God’s wisdom are, 339. Few are able to inquire into these, but no one can discover them, 339. God’s wisdom orders even evils themselves, 367, 541, 576. God preferred to strike the devil through wisdom rather than through strength, 552. God’s wisdom has neither a place nor a price that can be assigned, 584. It is not due to the merit of any good work, 585. One who serves pleasures is excluded from wisdom, 586. God’s wisdom is essential and subsistent, 596. God’s wisdom is revealed from hidden things, 597. It has one kind of place and another kind of way, 605. Those who seem wise to themselves cannot contemplate God’s wisdom, 890. God’s wisdom in the distribution of His gifts, 903.

God is called strong because He strikes forcefully what He has known, 289. Why God is called great in strength, 887.

God alone is holy, 598. From consideration of God’s holiness, the saints fear their own good works, 256. They recognize the filth of their life, 315. God is the author of nature, not of guilt, 942.

God’s power is manifested in the temptations of the saints, 13. God’s wondrous works have become cheap through familiarity to the eyes, 188. God’s works are praised more eloquently by amazement than by speech, 297. How God overturns heaven, hell, earth, and sea within us, 347. He who granted being to what was not also provided the manner in which what now exists should be, 368. God creates nonexistent things by seeing them and sustains existing things by seeing them, 1050. God destroys the soul not by defeating it but by withdrawing from it, 370. We live in God’s sight in two ways, 383. When “who?” is placed in Scripture as a question, the Almighty is signified, 497. God alone is powerful and to be feared, 541. He who gives life also gives wisdom, 545. Considering God’s omnipotence, we are reminded of our weakness, 948, 950. The ring in the devil’s nostrils is God’s omnipotence, 1088. Through it He pulls many whom the devil has devoured from his jaws, 1089. God touches all things unequally through omnipotence, 1241. Everything is subject to God, 1101.

God’s providence, even when afflicting us, is always just and always to be loved, 51. Sometimes God abandons us in order to preserve us, 95, 1092. In a wondrous way, what is done against God’s will is subjected to His will, 196. Why God presses some down with scourges and supports others with successes, 154, 223. How necessary God’s protection is against the hidden enemy, 267. Nothing happens among human beings without God’s plan, although it is hidden, 393. God orders the devil’s evil wills, 1093. God disregards the complaints of the grieving in order to increase their benefit, 451. An excellent description of God’s providence, 505. God attends to all in such a way that He is present to each individual, ibid. The just causal reasons for things that appear disordered are with God, 514, 541, 550. Some, foolish in adversity, deny that God exists or that He cares for human affairs, 505, 869, 557. God does and orders good things; He does not do evil things, but orders them, 576. God Himself governs the world He created, 782. God provides for the smallest as for the greatest, and for individuals as for the whole, 806. In temptation we must rely on divine providence, 822, 828. Divine providence in the punishment of the wicked, 830. God’s providence toward the highest and lowest things, 869. His ordering lies in God’s hand, not in the human hand, 901. God does not abandon the human being, 926. The Creator alone administers human life, 1469.

God relates to human beings in various ways, 161, 574, 640. He raises His own in adversity, 193. He uses the plans of the wicked for good, 194. This is confirmed by the example of Joseph’s brothers, ibid., and of Saul and Jonah, 195. Why God created one whom He foreknew would perish, 511. God arranged everything from eternity, 393. His providence is not deceived, ibid. Why God permits the wicked to commit worse offenses, 496. God now comforts human beings and now terrifies them, 640, 1084. How God behaves toward the saints, 661; toward sinners, 868. Why God sometimes does not immediately hear the saints, 665. Now He raises up, now He casts down, 1321.

God’s patience and kindness toward sinful humanity, 318, 1259. The strict inflictor of punishment, who for a long time remained a silent witness of guilt, 304, 789. Foolishly and impiously, someone reasons from God’s patience either that his crimes are not seen by God or that they are approved, 789. God patiently holds back His anger, which at last He pours out irrevocably, 829. God tolerates here for a long time those whom He will condemn eternally, ibid. Why God is called a patient avenger, 1483. The power of divine anger is incomprehensible to human beings, 145. God’s breath may be called His punitive visitation, 155. We must fear lest, in mercy, God not become angry with our vices, 220. The elect forestall the anger of the Judge, 258. A human being is not sufficient to answer God when He judges or strikes, 298. In what way no one can resist God’s anger, 299. How great God’s severity is toward those whom His patience endured for a long time, 302. God wishes to be reproved by us, 316. We possess nothing with which we can appease God, 321. God’s fury, free from disturbance, is completed at the end of the world, 398. Those whom God strikes as enemies, 453, 571. It is a sign of greater anger when what is wrongly desired is granted, 478. No sin is hidden from divine anger, 547. Every divine striking is either a striking of the present life or the beginning of the punishment to come, 571. What it means for God to make a road for Himself from the path of His anger, 800. The crafty hypocrite not only deserves God’s anger but provokes it, 840. God grows angry tranquilly, 1051. What is called the anger of the dove as God’s fury, 1052. God shows mercy even when angry, 1181. He pursues faults and protects sinners, 1182. Future divine anger must be measured from the present ruins of the world, 1439. God threatens punishment to those standing if they should fall, and promises mercy to those who have fallen so that they may rise, 1609.

God grants some things when favorable and permits others when angry, 196. God wounds for salvation in two ways, 200. God mercifully corrects the one exalting himself over his virtues, 220. The one whom mercy alone does not rescue in this life, justice claims after death, 255. The saints expect their salvation from God’s mercy alone, 256, 265, 298, 314, 514, 544, 932. God’s mercy is necessary for fallen humanity, 267. God’s seeing means His unwillingness to show mercy to human affliction, 307. Through prevenient mercy God grants us life; through subsequent mercy He preserves it, 324. One thing God mercifully grants, another He permits to be possessed in anger, 367. How great God’s mercy toward sinners is, 527. Mercy shown to and neglected by the sinner is turned into punishment, 537. God’s hand appears hard to the weak person when He rages mercifully, 668. In this life God does not always repay each person according to his works, 782. Looking upon the power of God’s mercy, let him suppress the elevation of his own justice, 926. How the mercies of God become wondrous among us, 1055. After guilt, mercy is to be hoped for, 1090. God shows mercy even when angry, 1181. The mercy of our Creator is abundant, 1382. Let the sinner sing mercy and judgment to God, 1420. An example of divine mercy in a young man converted when death was pressing upon him, 1514. Because of His mercy toward us, God first asks us to be reconciled with Him, 1590. May God’s mercy comfort us in such a way that it makes us negligent in no respect, 1593. Let no one squander the time of divine mercy, 1599.

God’s justice must be considered in afflictions, 51. God permits the elect to be struck by the unjust in a just order, 527. God permits the just to be afflicted and the wicked to prosper, 826. How can God, being just, condemn one who ought not to be punished? 84. God sometimes swiftly cuts down the unjust, 154. God afflicts the human being in two ways, 200. God sometimes crushes us, 219. God judges us in two ways, 319. God sometimes brings counselors to a foolish end, 373. God sometimes abandons for a time those whom He loves eternally, 661. God cannot condemn in vain, 782. God’s justice, hidden from human beings, moves the just to fear and tears, 145. God is aptly said to blow when He repays vengeance, 155. God’s correction sometimes punishes and sometimes tests, 199. The just themselves know that they will perish if God judges them after removing His mercy, 256, 514, 932. God’s approach to or withdrawal from the soul is not known in this life, 298. No one is safe from God’s reproof, 385. What it means for God to open His eyes, 392. God does not consider how much evil someone is able to do, but how much he wishes to do, 408. God appears cruel when, although striking justly, He does not spare, 667. Just as no good exists without reward, so no evil exists without punishment, 683. Let us believe that what we suffer from God, who is better than we are, is just, 746. A person struck by God, considering the order of his condition, finds the justice of the blow, 747. God’s judgments are just, although hidden, 782, 806. What it means to say that God hardens, 945. God’s justice is to be feared before guilt and mercy hoped for after guilt, 1090. God simultaneously comforts the repentant and strikes the obstinate with justice, 1309.

Why God afflicts His elect here so severely, as though despising them, 77. God calls people from every class of humanity to knowledge of Himself, 190. God wounds in two ways those whom He prepares to restore to salvation, 200. God’s calling is His regarding us with love and choosing us, 386. God raises certain elect persons through inward gifts and outward honors, 652. God freely chooses whom He wishes, 1100. Election proceeds from mercy; reprobation from justice, ibid., 1448. God chooses those whom the world despises, 173, 1622. See Election, Elect.

God rejects those whom He says He does not know, 40, 733. What it means for God to destroy the reprobate, 370. What hardening means, 371, 945. See Reprobation.

At the beginning of life God raises some to the summit of virtue and abandons the others, 574. There is no true worship of God outside the true Church, 437. What the right hand of God is, 54. By the right hand the Jews are to be understood; by the left, the Gentiles, 659. The faithful people are understood under the name of the right hand, 660. What the right and left signify, 991, 1201, 1386. The right hand is the life to come, while the present life is the left, 1358, 1526. The right hand signifies the good, the left the wicked, 1542. The right hand signifies joy and prosperity, 1201. What the right-hand things signify, 966.

The devil is called day and night, 107. Why the devil is called the solitary night, 109. Why he is called Leviathan, 110. He is called a bar because he strikes for death, 111. Why he is called a serpent, ibid. The devil is called an exactor, whose voice is the temptation of wretched suggestion, 136, 981, 988, 1648. He is called a lion, a tiger, and a myrmecoleon, 156, 555, 1056. To some he is a lion, to others an ant, 158. He is called a whale, 260; destruction, 443; and a robber, 453. Malignant spirits are called dreadful, 481. The devil is signified under the name of the north, 266, 547, 570, 1186. He is called the twisted serpent, 554; a scorching wind, 570, 859, 1199. The birds of heaven are called devils, 603; and foxes, ibid. Perdition and death, 604. The beast, 876, 1003, 1076. The devil is called the gates of death, 928; dark entrances, ibid. The devil is called the ancient enemy, 1019. His instigation is signified under the name of the nostrils, ibid. Unclean spirits are called armed enemies, 1031. The devil is called Behemoth, 1055, 1094, 1056; a lurking lion, 1060. What it means for the lion to eat grass like an ox, 1057. A perpetual slave by covenant: why the devil is so called, 1093. The devil is called a four-footed animal because of the folly of unclean action, 1094; a dragon because of his harmful malice, ibid.; a bird because of his exaltation, ibid. Why the devil is compared to an anvil, 1121. The devil’s anger and evil persuasion are expressed under the name of the sword, [Col. 1383] 1123. He is called a hammer, 1125. He sits on the sides of the north when he possesses the cold minds of human beings, 1186. The devil is called wicked, 628; the seal of God’s likeness, 1072; a mountain, 1075; a beast of burden, 1094; a small king, 1112; a wolf, 1486; the prince of the world, 1650. See Behemoth, Satan.

Malignant spirits were created without the weakness of flesh, 235. The devil, or evil angel, was created first, 1071. How great was the beauty in which he was created, 1072, etc. The first angel was created in such a way that he might fear God chastely, 1134.

Why the devil’s sin is irremissible, 322. What the devil’s fall was like, 925. What the fall of the angel teaches human beings, 1073. The deserter angel lost the gifts of grace through sin, but not those of nature, 1056, 1059, 1134. See The Sin of the Evil Angels.

The source of the devil’s uncertainty concerning Christ’s divinity, 55, 85. The devil knew that the Redeemer of the human race had come into the world, 56. The devil does not grasp our thoughts, 96. The devil had heard reports about Christ but had not seen His wisdom, 605. In four ways God speaks to the devil, and in three ways the devil speaks to God, 43.

The devil does not see God, 40. He will suffer one punishment in the present and another in the future, 108. What it means for the devil to be in prison, 260. Why the devil is condemned without forgiveness, 1072. The apostate spirit is day, which is wished to perish in such a way that it may fare badly, 107. In the essence of life it continues to subsist even while dying, ibid. In what respect it is day and in what respect night, ibid. What is wished for it when it is wished to perish, ibid. In what storm the devil was carried away to eternal punishments, 109. The eternal condemnation of the devil and all the reprobate is to be publicly displayed before the elect, 1099. See Satan, Behemoth, Leviathan.

The devil’s speech, both in himself and through his own agents, 85. He spoke through the mouth of the serpent, 554. What the author of death teaches, 1141.

The devil can do nothing unless God permits it, 45, 454, 459, 558, 1073. His will is evil, but his power is just, 45, 454, 558. The devil goes out from the face of the Lord when he receives power to tempt, 47, 56. Satan’s hand is his power, 85. The devil is shown unable to overcome Christ’s soul, 86. His power will be extinguished at the end of the world, 110. He is restrained in prison when he is unable to accomplish what he wishes, 260. The devil often prevails while he remains hidden, 377. The devil rages sometimes through hidden, sometimes through open persecution by means of the wicked, 421. What the devil’s teeth and eyes are, 422. Those who do not resist the devil’s first suggestions allow themselves to suffer a giant by whom they are oppressed, 425. Those whom he deceives by flattering persuasions he drags to punishment with violent bonds, 443. The devil’s power over human beings was weakened by Christ’s death, 552. From…
from the hearts of sinners, as though from their caverns, the devil has been expelled by the hand of God, 554. The powers and deceits of our enemy are described, 1055. The devil, bound by divine power, will once be released, 1058. Through the Antichrist he will perform many signs, ibid. He will be released by deceit and power, 160, 1116. When their merits demand it, the devil is permitted to strike many, 1074. He is conquered all the more powerfully by the elect the more humbly they submit themselves to God, ibid. God’s omnipotence is set against his powers, 1143. The devil’s sending forth: why he is called a whirlwind, 1187. The ancient enemy of humanity, who swallowed up the river, 1557. He devours daily those whose wicked life is at variance with the faith, ibid.

—The devil proudly rules those subject to him, 120. Even unwillingly, a human being serves the devil, 126. The devil blinds human beings, 229. He examines each person’s character in order to tempt him, [Col. 1383] 441. The devil’s evil will is ordered by God, 519. The devil wages war only against human beings, 555. He possesses the hearts of the reprobate, 876.

—The devil stirs up inner temptations, while external ones are raised in vain, 12. How craftily the devil seeks grounds on which to accuse us, 44. Why the devil should not be feared, 45. The devil’s remarkable arts in tempting, 35, 44, 49. God exposed the devil’s snares by the light of incarnate Wisdom, 54. The devil traverses the earth, ibid. Christ restrained his power by his humility, 55, 1074. How God reveals the devil’s snares to us, 63. In the sequence of Job’s temptations, what the enemy’s arts were, 78. The devil habitually sends dreams by which he deceives, 262. How great the devil’s craft is in deceiving, 441. Which people the invading evil spirits besiege, 453. In temptation the devil first creeps in gently, then drags violently, 475. The devil’s arts in Christ’s temptations confounded, 553. The devil’s snares are called millstones, 629. Treacherous spirits are designated by the name “eagles,” 1038. How great a danger threatens from the devil’s crafty counsels, 1067. Christ mocked Satan with the flesh of his own body as bait, piercing him with the hook of divinity, 1086. Christ displayed the bait to Satan and concealed the snare, 1095. God reveals the devil’s cunning to the elect, 1103. Deceit in the devil’s hand is fraud in the exercise of power, 1116. Infinite divine wisdom is set against his machinations, 1143. The devil hides himself beneath the guise of virtue, 35. He watches for the time to tempt, 47. The devil’s deceits in removing thoughts, 65. The devil’s cunning in disguising virtues, 99. A remedy against the devil’s snares, 100. The devil’s suggestions become sweet, 499. The devil makes light of what God threatens, 765. Under the appearance of virtue the devil sets wickedness against us, 1031.

—The devil accuses us day and night before God, 44. Christ restrained the devil’s pride by his own virtues, 55. The devil envies the conversion of human beings through the apostles’ preaching, 56. God rebukes the weakness of the devil’s pride, 73. In envy the ancient serpent shakes and vomits out all his venom, 179. The immense pride of the devil and his members, 1135. The devil’s pride is the cause of humanity’s ruin, 1137.

—The devil’s will is evil, but his power is just, 45. From his malice he expects evil from one whom he has found to be good, 73. The blindness of error so overwhelms the devil that he cannot recover to the light of repentance, 108. Christ is already destroying his malice; at the end of the world his power will be extinguished, 110. Satan’s impenitence, 1120. The devil first accuses our deeds, then our words, and finally our thoughts, 44. When he finds no evil to accuse, he seeks to bend good things toward evil, ibid. The devil tries to affect the hearts of the righteous through dreams, 262. The devil sows evil among the righteous, 1085. The more swiftly the devil sees himself being conquered by the elect, the more savagely he will rage against them, 1125. The devil despises the torments of the judgment awaiting him above, 1126. The devil seduced Adam through Eve, 77. He seduced him craftily, 111. The devil shattered the uprightness of the first human being with four blows, 123. He falsely promised human beings impossible things, and truly took away possible ones, 111. He gently persuaded the standing human being, but drags the fallen one who resists, 476. Through pride the devil cast down the human being who followed him, 1137. The first Adam was overcome by three temptations, 1493.

—The devil goes out from the presence of the Lord when he receives power to tempt Job, 47. He chooses the times for tempting, [Col. 1384] ibid. “Satan’s hand” should be understood not as power but as temptation, 56. Once defeated, he renews the battles against Job, 73. Why Satan is commanded to spare Job’s life, 75. The order of Job’s temptations, 77. The devil’s purpose in afflicting Job, 320. Job, struck by Satan, does not attribute his affliction to Satan, 459. As many wounds as the devil inflicted on Job, so many victories he bestowed on the holy man, 729. The devil stirred up Job’s friends against him from their several places, 730. Job’s scourges inflicted by Behemoth, 1074.

—The devil tested Christ’s divinity by temptations, 56. Through his satellites the devil extinguished Christ’s flesh for three days, 308. Striking the Redeemer with three temptations, he could not presume to assault him, ibid. Having tempted Christ inwardly in vain, the devil attacked him outwardly, 552. The devil knew that the incarnate Son of God had come, but did not know the order of redemption, 1085. The divinity was hidden from the devil during the Passion, 1087. Christ took upon himself our temptations in order to overcome them, 1492. It is not unworthy of our Redeemer that he wished to be tempted, since he had come to be killed, ibid. Christ’s temptation remained at the level of suggestion and did not reach delectation, ibid. Christ was tempted by the devil with gluttony, vainglory, and avarice, and conquered him who had overcome the first human being by the same three vices, 1493. Christ patiently bears the one whom he could punish, 1494. By what weapons Christ conquered the devil, 1493. The devil perished, caught on a hook by the very thing he bit, 1550. By attacking Christ, who owed him nothing, the devil lost his right over sinners, ibid. In Christ alone the devil had nothing, 1649.

—The devil unjustly demands that the good be put to the test; God mercifully permits it, 10. The devil lies in wait for good works in three ways, 34. The devil observes not only what a person does, but also when he does it, in order to tempt him, 47. He rises up more fiercely when he recognizes that the guardians of discipline serve their belly, 49. He strikes as many saints with darts as he afflicts with temptations, 51. The devil often inserts himself into our thoughts, 63. He customarily tempts human beings in two ways, 77. He tempts us not only by himself but also through his own who are among us, 78. Why he sometimes ceases from temptation, 95. The devil is strong against those who consent and weak against those who resist, 158. Through every vice he pours venom into the human heart, 179. Sometimes he appears unarmed, sometimes armed, 186. He attacks us in many ways, 202. He does not tempt us as much as he wishes, 260. He assails the good with temptations from every side, 424. Beneath earthly advantages he conceals snares, 441. His suggestions are varied, 453, 1114. The devil’s snares serve the advantage of the good, 519. The devil cannot rest from temptations, 664. The more he sees the devout resisting him, the more he strives to conquer them, 772. The devil’s cunning in tempting, 984, 1033, 1066, 1067, 1082, 1085, 1102. He tempts more powerfully at the end, 1064. He tempts under the appearance of good, 1069, 1102. Once expelled, the devil attempts to inflict sharper goads, 1065. The devil’s various illusions, 1077, 1131. He tempts chiefly through three vices, 1094. He tempts the righteous differently from worldly people, 1102. He tempts the righteous in two ways, 1129. He gravely tempts the saints in their minds, 1187. He provokes them to impatience, 1615. See Temptation.

—The devil tempts us through prosperity and adversity, 44. God distributes temptations to the righteous with wondrous grace, 46. When the devil attacks us, he is pierced by our humility and patience, 51. In how many ways the devil attempts to circumvent the good, 63. How variously he lies in wait for our virtues, [Col. 1385] 65. He often permits knowledge in order to corrupt life, 186. The devil tries in vain to overthrow the saints at the end, 203. What it means for dreadful spirits to go to and fro over the wicked, 481. Evil spirits besiege the city of our mind, 509. He fights externally against those in whom he does not reign internally, 555. What it means for the devil to be brought up from the bottomless pit in which he is now held, 588, 611. The devil sometimes enters the minds of the good, but does not remain in them, 877. At the end of the world the devil will bind hearts with torpor, 1186.

—The devil neglects to tempt those whom he feels he possesses by an undisturbed right, 772. He tempts them craftily, 877. He often tempts them openly, 1102. The devil provokes them against the good, 1616. See Temptation.

—How one should resist the devil’s temptations, 51. The devil’s hand cannot be escaped unless one hastens to return to repentance, 35. With what vigilance we must meet the devil’s efforts, 65. The devil’s sharper snares compel us to implore the help of grace, 204. Whoever fights against the devil should cast off his garments, lest he succumb, 1587. By humbly submitting himself to God, a human being conquers the devil, 1076.

—All who live wickedly are members of the devil, 85, 924, 1492. The devil and the wicked are one body, 112, 308, 430. Imitation of the devil is called the shadow of death, 116. Through the wicked the devil rages against the Church, 421. The prince of the wicked has some as companions and others as sons, 430. The army of the devil is led by pride, whose offspring are the seven principal vices, 1035. The lustful are members of the devil, 1058. The eternal punishments of the devil and his members serve the glory of God and the elect, 1093. The devil’s members are cut off when sinners are separated from his body so that they may be joined to Christ, 1096. The devil’s members are called cast shields, 1105. As a culmination of iniquity, the devil and his members are allowed to do more wickedly what they wickedly desire, 1116. The devil’s members are the disciples who cling to him, 1119. What are called the members of his flesh, ibid. Those who submit themselves to the devil, even if they appear to be gold, are mud, 1129. The devil’s teeth are the persecutors of the good, 422. The devil’s companions are the apostate angels, 430. The devil’s sons are perverse human beings, ibid. The arrogant imitate the devil, 737. Those who imitate the devil’s malice have lost the entrails of charity, 944.

One of the deacons ordained by the apostles was the author of error, 1638.

What it means to say “of God,” 43. Whoever knows how to keep silence in an orderly way knows how to speak rightly, 968. Statements lacking gravity do not require an elaborate exposition, 817. See Speech, Silence, Keeping silent.

“Day” signifies understanding, 26, 31, 93; prosperity, 44, 114, 432; the devil, 107; the minds of the elect, 109; angelic spirits, ibid.; the Antichrist, 110; the Church, 113; the delight of sin, 114; the eternal homeland, 291; the life of the righteous, 1527. What it means to turn day into darkness, 107. What it means to halve one’s days, 172. Days are compared with shadows, 272. What the days of God are, 521. Why a day is called joyful, 683. When the day of the Church will come, 918. There will be a day when no darkness of sin remains, 919. What the name of Job’s one daughter, “Day,” signifies, 1163. Who is called empty of days and who full of days, 1166. What is the soul’s own day and what is another’s, 1646.

—The Lord’s Day: why it is called the eighth day, 20, 1341. What the sixth day of the Passion, the Sabbath of rest, and the Lord’s Day of resurrection signify, 1341, 1391. The Lord’s Day is the third after the Passion but the eighth from creation, 1391.

Why God delays the voices of those who ask, 665. The disciples were beneficially delayed, lest they should find Christ risen again, 1532.

The finger signifies discernment, 486. What it signifies to place a finger upon the mouth, ibid. The finger of God is the Holy Spirit, 1270. What it means to put one’s fingers into one’s ears, ibid. What the larger and smaller fingers signify in the palm, 1411.

Temporal dignity is understood under the name of a horse, 1015. Those established in dignities scarcely attend to their own frailty, 76. How great human dignity is: to be friends of God, 1561. The place of exaltation is pleasing, but first let the way of labor exercise one, 1562.

Divine love arises through fear, 223. Love of one’s neighbor is proved in the neighbor’s troubles, ibid. It is scarcely recognized in prosperity, ibid. Loss of happiness tests the power of love, ibid. The thing we love is the house of our thought, 277. Why the strength of love is compared with death, 357, 1473. The ardent affections of the soul that loves Christ the Bridegroom, 1332. In leisure one should seek the beloved, 1383. Everything else is referred to love, which is properly Christ’s commandment, 1560. Scripture does not contradict those who love their neighbors through affection of kinship and the flesh, 1560. The form of Christian love: “Love to this end, to which I have loved you,” ibid. See Love.

—Love of God requires three things, 340. Love of one’s neighbor requires two, ibid., 708, 1560, 1640. Love of enemies is necessary for salvation, 1560. What kind of proof love requires, 1575. What it means truly to love God, 1576. Love of God has no measure, 1639. See Charity.

What dawn means, 265.

The four dimensions attributed to God, 345, 346. Which dimensions pertain to God in relation to humanity in this life, 346. The allotments of the dimensions are marked by cords, 1087.

We must forgive others if we want God to forgive us, 353. We are bound to forgive the person who confesses his sin before sunset, 502. Forgiveness must be from the heart, 1564. It is owed to us, and we owe it; it will be forgiven us if we forgive, 1565.

Gregory praises the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite, 1607.

What “diplois” signifies morally, 319.

Those lacking discipline are not lifted from the lowest things to heavenly ones, 430. God makes the hearts of the wicked far from discipline by permitting it, 429, 1300. When the wall of discipline is destroyed, as though a wall had been breached, the enemy enters, 662. The remarkable knowledge of discipline by which we know how to be humbled and how to abound, to be filled and to hunger, 1386. The best instruction in discipline, 1415. The discipline of the study of heaven is like a field, 1472.

Only charity makes us disciples of God, 708. The modesty of disciples toward teachers, 971. Why Christ’s disciples were forbidden to preach to the Gentiles and Samaritans, 1446. The marvelous dignity of Christ’s disciples, 1555. How much the disciples’ unbelief benefited us, 1568.

How great the evil of discord is, 1239. When fighting against evil spirits, we must never be interrupted by discord, 1238. By sinning we created discord between ourselves and God, 1590.

Discernment avoids the danger of temptations, 66. How necessary discernment is in action, ibid., 961. Discernment grows through temptations, 70. We must consider not only what we do, [Col. 1386] but also with how much discernment we carry it out, 83. If a discerning person acts badly, he quickly restores himself to the rule of discernment, 389. Discernment is signified by the name of fingers, 486. Discernment is necessary in a preacher, 636, 1414. Discernment is especially necessary on the narrow way of salvation, 906. The works of the same virtue must be performed or omitted according to the line of discernment, 906. We must beware lest the name of discernment be used to serve our own advantages, 907. The discernment of a shepherd is signified by the understanding given from above to the cock, 961. The fruit of discernment in a teacher of truth, 972. Double discernment is needed in action, lest we be deceived, 1207, 1223, 1224. Discernment is necessary for a ruler, 1414. The tongue must be restrained by discernment, 486. Discernment in eating, 983.

Excessive or nonexistent examination of ourselves is dangerous to us, 305.

Our reclining in heaven means resting there, 1482.

The administration of earthly affairs is subject to how many dangers, 66. God’s hidden dispensations, 1315. God’s wondrous distribution of spiritual gifts and temptations toward human beings, 1321.

What it means to dispute with God, 378. See Contending.

When one restrains outward distractions, an inner retreat is opened, 974.

The administration of earthly riches is exceedingly dangerous, 66. How difficult the salvation of the rich is, 103. In former times the dead were buried with their riches, 143. By means of the tomb, whoever becomes rich, ibid. The righteous use their possessions for necessity, but do not love them, 263. Whoever displays his riches to his enemies provokes them to plunder, 282, 472. Possession of riches is not a crime, but desire for them is, 361. Those who lack wealth but swell with arrogance should be considered rich, ibid. Those who love riches despise the despisers of the world, ibid. How much audacity wealthy proud people display in wicked works, 411. Those who cling to an unjust powerful person swell with his power, ibid. The rich can scarcely avoid pride, 442. The rich person taken from this life goes naked to the Judge, 479. The anguish of the rich arising from satiety, 479. In acquiring and guarding riches, anxiety foreshadows eternal punishments, ibid. God’s darts rain down upon the avaricious rich person, 480. Whoever guards against temporal poverty is consigned to perpetual poverty, ibid. However great the happiness of the rich, it ends in eternal misery, 487. Wicked rich people are possessed by their own goods, 490, 1625. What it means to have one’s goods in one’s hand, ibid. From the source where the rich person rejoices vainly, the poor person is afflicted even more vainly, 495. The rich person possesses with fear the goods that the poor person desires with anxiety, ibid. The rich, like sleepers awakening in death, grieve that they are empty, 568. Everything that abounds without the vision of God is poverty, 672. One must trust not in fleeting riches but in God alone, 698. The saints who seek God count the abundance of the present life as poverty, ibid. Riches can be possessed with humility, 442. What the riches of the wise are, 700.

—How the devil urges one to toil at acquiring riches, 1068. Which riches are true and which false, 1364, 1488. Whoever does not desire what he needs is rich, 1372. Christ did not wish to be born from rich parents, 1443. Riches are thorns, 1488. Riches are deceptive, ibid. How the rich should join themselves to the poor, 1522. In a human being we should consider nature, not riches and honors, 1567. In material abundance the fault of the flesh generally reigns, 1610. Compared with heavenly happiness, earthly substance is a weight, not a support, [Col. 1387] 1626. It does no harm to possess goods in this world, provided that we cling to God, 1654. Let the rich fear lest the prosperity granted to them be the recompense for their good works, 1657.

—Who the truly rich are, 361, 490. The rich easily despise others, 361. The rich person is compared with one suffering from dropsy, 441. Preachers of error attach themselves to the rich, 536. The rich are compared with ears of grain, 540. The rich person is compared with a poor man who dreams that he is rich, 568. The rich who distribute their possessions badly, 1063. Why the rich man feasting in hell asked for water, 20, 569. Why he wished to help his brothers, 255. Why he is not named by Christ, 1655. The rich man feasting in hell knew what he had neglected to know in the world, 569. Why he was condemned, 1654.

Teachers are called angels, and however holy they may be, they are not without fault, 171. They are signified by the name of the Hyades, 294. The senators in the Church are true teachers, 525. Teachers are like the raven, 971. Teachers are represented by hinds and not by stags, 976. Teachers are the foundations of the Church, 901. They are disciples of the Church, 968. Why teachers are signified by ibexes and hinds, 972. The skill of teachers is designated by the name of a reed, 1078. A bad teacher who understands and speaks correctly has a harvest for others to eat, 180. His ignorance is grievous when he wishes to teach someone better than himself, 212. A censor of his own teachers judges more rightly about others, 243. Whoever loses the order of living well loses uprightness of speech, 374. The words of teachers are called the rains of the mountains, 524. Some are given over to judgment so that they know certain things correctly, 565. We must consider not what the teachers of the Church are in themselves but what they have become by grace, 575. The wicked pursue praise for their teaching, 271. Those who teach themselves as more learned are like squanderers of their own wealth, 358. Every teaching office is approved in the examination of charity, 686. What must be avoided because of the gift of understanding: vainglory, 701. Because the gift of understanding has been entrusted to them, the righteous fear more than they rejoice, ibid. Proud teachers are sharp-eyed outwardly but blind within, 745. Whoever hears a proud teacher should pluck the roses and beware of the thorns, 853. The knowledge of a teacher is perfect if he does not know himself to be learned, 882, 969. Proud teachers are ignorant, 897. Holy teachers imitate the apostles of the Church like lionesses their cubs, 968. He knows how to speak rightly who knows how to keep silence in an orderly way, ibid. Because of the disciples’ eager hunger for truth, the gift of understanding increases in the teacher, 972. Teachers may be understood by hinds and hearers by ibexes, 973. Often a word is either granted or withdrawn from a teacher according to the merit or fault of the hearer, 993. Sometimes a word is granted or denied to a teacher because of the merit of the teacher alone, or also of the hearers, 994. We are taught more truthfully the more we recognize that our teaching does not come from ourselves, ibid. The grace of God nourishes the sons of wicked and good teachers, 1002. Wicked teachers are not concerned for their offspring, unlike the good, 1003. The latter burn with charity toward their children, but not the former, 1004. Wicked teachers, wholly poured out into external things, do not know the entrails of charity toward their own, 1005. The teacher’s relief is the transformation of the one who is making progress, 1155.

—Let no one presume to teach before reaching mature age, 1183. When the devil holds the hearts of teachers, he presides over the mountain of the covenant, 1186. Their own teaching becomes worthless to teachers who contemplate the wisdom of God, 1241. Whoever has progressed to understanding spiritual things should offer them to others, 1321. What teacher must fight against elation and anger, [Col. 1387] 1366. How much teachers should excel their hearers, 1367. If he does not open the understanding, he is not a teacher, 1398. Whoever teaches rightly feeds God’s flock rightly, 1407. Great things must be done in such a way that they also teach that little things are not to be neglected, 1410. Teachers who do not do what they teach are destroyers of themselves and cultivators of others, 1411. Which teacher’s harvest the hungry person may eat, ibid. The teacher’s sword is the word of God, 1412. The teacher’s patience is the proof of his teaching, ibid. Every faithful person in the Church ought to teach his neighbor, 1455. Teachers should have tongues of fire, 1578. When holy teachers instruct us, they touch the wound of the mind with the tongue, 1653.

Heretics take away the teaching of the holy Fathers from the idle and unwary, 525. God revealed the depths of the Law and the Prophets to the sacred teachers, 583. Sacred teaching is called bread, 755. Teaching that tastes of filth is called mud, 1129. The strict teaching of living well is called a path, 882. The good or bad use of teaching, 888. Teaching overflowing is signified by the bowls of the tabernacle, but narrow teaching by cups, 1455. Teaching that is true flees elation, 742. What the proper order of teaching is, 743. Teaching is to be preferred to bodily nourishment, 1456. See the Church’s teaching; the teaching of heretics.

What it means to sow or reap sorrows, 154. Insensibility in sorrow is harmful, 50. The force of sorrow is a proof of salvation, 199. Sorrow flows from the conscience when it speaks peacefully; by keeping too silent it torments more, 240. The sorrowful despise the present and await the future, 250. Any fault pollutes the soul’s life; sorrow preserved for one’s neighbor kills, 352. God disregards the complaints of the sorrowful in order to increase their benefit, 451. The sorrow of the condemned is infinite, 478.

Among human beings deceit is considered prudence, but with God it is folly, 63. Whoever acts deceitfully never believes that others act toward him simply, 409. See Cunning.

Those who rule others should look to the one Lord of all, 689. To rule subjects through fear is evil, 785. All things are subject to God’s dominion, 1101. What it means to rule, 1605. How ruling and exercising sovereignty differ, ibid. “Dominions” are those spirits who transcend the Powers and Principalities, ibid. Unrestrained and harsh dominion is condemned, 785. Rulership must be avoided by prelates, 1497. Lords must attend to the equality of condition, 786.

Those who are said to inhabit houses of clay, 171. The house of the mind is that in which it dwells by loving, 257. “House” means the inhabitation of the heart, ibid., 1534. The hypocrite’s house is human favor, 277. “House” signifies the same as “dwelling,” 931. Our houses are our bodies, 1534. What the threshold of our houses is, ibid. Whoever works the field of the body builds the house of the mind, 1031. An exasperating house is a soul that repels God as its inhabitant, 1253. The house of God consists of angels and holy human beings, 1322. Which are called deserted houses, 412. What the woman overturning the house with a lighted lamp signifies, 1603. We must tolerate household members and those familiar to us who oppose us, 710.

What “until” signifies, 285.

The gift received from God in tranquility is manifested in tribulation, 10. God’s gifts are his footprints, by which we are summoned to heavenly things, 344. Some strengthen us, others adorn us, 375. A gift should be valued especially according to the promptness of giving, 691. God wisely distributes his gifts to individuals, 903, 1464. Why God mingles scourges with his gifts, 1343. Those who have received greater things from God should be more concerned to give an account, 1463. God’s various gifts, 1275. For what purpose God’s gifts are given, 1276. See the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

What it means to sleep on the journey, 163. To sleep is to lie in sins, 251. What it means to sleep with a watchful heart, 1326. To sleep is to die; to doze is to languish, 1478.

By sinning we turn our back on God, 1610.

What the lost drachma signifies, 1603. What it means for the drachma to be found after the house has been overturned, ibid. What the ten drachmas signify, ibid.

The dragon signifies malice, 228, 673, 1001. What it means for the dragon’s tail to cast down the stars of heaven, 1060. In death the dragon attempts to devour the young man who is freed through the prayers of the monks, 1514.

What the doubtful person chooses, 1067. How a mode of speaking marked by uncertainty in the word of God is to be understood, 1252.

What sweetness and bitterness together are, 1280.

The number twelve designates universality, 363.

What it means to receive double from God, 16, 1153. Whoever looks upon sublime things with true love does not know how to desire to walk with double desires, 134.

A skilled leader neither always brings an army against the enemy nor always withdraws it, 1024.

Who the wicked leaders are, 785.

E
Spiritual drunkenness, what it is, 1266. To be drunk with wormwood, what it signifies, 654. Those are drunk who, troubled by love of the world, do not feel the evils they suffer, 1113. Ivory, what it signifies, 1070. Who are “redder than ancient ivory,” ibid. What the ivory steps signify, 1164.

“Behold” denotes a present matter, 856.

The Church is called dawn, 113, 576. The daughter of kings, whose glory is within, 283. It is called Arcturus, 294, 949. Why the people of the holy Church are called orphans, 241, 522. The Church is called a widow, 523. It is called a field, 524; a vineyard, ibid., 1149. The Church is called a city, and cities are called Churches, 526, 798, 1311. The moon, 543, 1309. The earth, 547, 620, 921. The columns themselves are called Churches, 550. The Church is called a lioness, 581, 967. The place of those who see, 801. It is signified by the name Rachel, 988. It is called a threshing floor, 999. Heaven, 1060. A mountain, 1075. The kingdom of heaven, 1097, 1476, 1510. A dragnet, 1097, 1473. A sling, 1125. Noah’s ark, 1149, 1349. God’s garden, 1186.

The root of the Church is the incarnation of the Redeemer, 631. The beginnings of the Church are signified by the almond blossom, 1017. The Church is God’s beauty and adornment, 1051. The saints who preach are called the Church’s teeth, 1104. The Church is clothed as though with the sun and tramples the moon beneath her feet, 1126. The prerogatives of the Church, 1148. The house in which the lamb is eaten is a figure of the Church, 1149, as is also the vineyard in which the laborers work, ibid. The universality of the Church is signified by the number seven, 1151. Rebecca descending from the camel, etc., figures the Church coming from the Gentiles, 1160. The Church figured by the widow of Sarepta, 1194. With how many kinds of flowers the field of the Church is adorned, 1214. The Church figured by the shaft of the lampstand, 1216. The rulers of the Church are called princes, 131. What the Church’s inward parts are, 424. How the Church is compared to mud, 665. Likewise to ashes and cinders, [Col. 1389] ibid. The Church is called Christ’s garment, 664. Noah’s ark is a type of the Church, 1349. In it carnal people are contained below, as in an ark for beasts, 1350; spiritual people above, ibid.

The Church now contains many reprobates, 421. The Church forms one body with Christ, 14, 15, 83, 615, 731, 904, 1329. The Church consists in the unity of the faithful, as the body consists in the unity of its members, 627. The Church is gathered from evil and good alike, 1009, 1637, 1638. The stones of the Church are Christians, 1311, 1314. Christ is the foundation of the Church, 1311, 899. Why heretics do not acknowledge the Church, 92. The multitude of the nations converted to the Church, 103. The Church does not wish to hear truth about morals from those who assert false things about the faith, 235. The Church was established through the teaching of humility, 242. In its weak members the Church has empty months; in its strong members, laborious nights, 249. The Church groans over the fruitless labor of its wicked children, ibid. In this life the Church does not cease to mourn the losses caused by its mutability, 250. The flesh of the Church rots and becomes foul in its slippery members who seek earthly things, 252. In the Church the apostles shone, then the martyrs, afterward the teachers, 295. God divided the spoils of the Synagogue for the Church, 376. The Church, which now and afterward at the final judgment will judge the wicked, 379. The Church has Christ in heaven as witness to His resurrection, 427. Outside the Church there is no true worship of God, 437. The Church demands that its words be engraved on hard hearts, 462. The Church was founded upon the Gentiles who had been reduced to nothing by sin, 547. The Church was entrusted to Peter and is signified by his little boat, 548. The Church regards an evil Catholic as an unbeliever, 561; and he is struck by God as though impious, 801. Whoever does not agree with the Church in conduct also differs from it in faith, 561. Which stones the Lord laid in the Church, 579. The harvest of the Church is to be attributed to the dew of grace, 632. Reprobates are gathered into the Church outside the rule of measure, 798.

The Church’s final times, 611. The various ages of the Church, 613. In old age the Church remembers its fruitfulness, ibid. What it means that the Church receives double at the end, 1153. The duration of the holy Church, 1167. The Church does not lose its days, ibid. How the Church, full of days, dies, ibid. The Church has two lives, temporal and eternal, 1419. The Church began with righteous Abel, 1336, 1510.

The Church has three distinctions among the faithful, 23, 1065. There are two kinds of people in the Church, 252, 1349, 1477. The various orders of the Church, 966, 1425, 1606. Four orders of rulers in the Church, 1407. In the members of the Church there are orders resembling the orders of angels, 1606. Those who burn with love and kindle others by speaking may be called Seraphim, 1607. Whoever recognizes that he belongs to none of the angelic orders should mourn, ibid.

Why the Church is one throughout the whole world, 526. Whence its harmony comes, ibid. Heretics strive to dissolve the unity of the Church, ibid. Whatever is tolerated outside the Church torments rather than purifies, 573. With what zeal the unity of the Church must be preserved, 574. All the Churches together make one Catholic Church, under the name “young women,” 613, 1333. The foundations of the Church are the holy teachers, 901. They are made firm upon Christ the foundation, 902, 1311. There can be neither innocence nor obedience except in the one true Church, 1158. The Church of the Old and New Testaments is one, 1336, 1391, 1510. Outside the Church there is no salvation, 1148, nor any work that is fruitfully good, 1149. At the end of the world the Church will be one, from Jews and Gentiles, 1153, 1161, 1487, 1516.

The wicked are members of the Church by faith, 252. The Church’s grief when it sees the wicked corrected in vain, 420. The strong are signified by bones, the weak by joints, ibid. The wrinkles of the Church are wicked Christians, ibid., 1541. In its strong members the Church mourns together with repentant weak members, 425. The weak members of the Church are sometimes deprived of righteousness for a time, 452. What it means to take the crown from the head of the Church, 453. Who are called the children of the Church, 614. Who are called the feet of the Church, 616, 660. The superiors owe these members an infusion of fatness—that is, the voice of preaching—ibid. The imperfect fear the vigor and uprightness of the Church; the perfect love them, 618. The Church both feeds and protects its children, 620. The members of the Church are distinguished by office but joined by charity, 627, 904. The offices and fruits of each become the possession of all through charity, ibid., 905. The children of the Church must remain in its nest and bosom if they are to enjoy peace, 629. The Church mourns for children whom it recognizes as returning to their former life, 632. What the army of the Church is, 640, 1237. It consoles its mourning children, ibid. The wicked are in the Church only in outward appearance, 657. The feet of the Church are sometimes overturned by the ambushes of enemies, 660. The garment of the Church is the life of the faithful, 664, 883, 922. What it means for the Church’s inward parts to boil over, 671. In the Church the righteous are far fewer than the wicked, 847, 1638. The enemies of the Church unjustly confuse the righteous with the unrighteous and thereby despise the Church, 847. Those who cling to the Church grow warm through the breath of the Holy Spirit, 883. The various gifts of the Church’s members, 904. The harmonious diversity of the Church’s members, 905. Each member of the Church should devote himself to the duties assigned to him and not usurp those belonging to another, ibid. The various orders of the faithful offer their gifts to fulfill the worship of the Church, 966. The Church has enemies in its own bosom, against whom it seeks the aid of rulers, 999. The Church tolerates many hidden wicked people, 1009. Why the wicked are mingled with the good in the Church, ibid., 1638. How great the Church’s future joy will sometimes be over the conversion of the Jews, 1158. In Job’s doubled herds and flocks the gathered totality of the faithful is signified, 1159. The multiplication of the faithful and of the saints, who were few, 1235.
