What it means for the Church to rejoice in its own gutters, 1279. Christ, the foundation of the Church, carries everyone and is carried by no one, 1311. Who labors by bearing Christ, 1312. The stones of this building both carry and are carried, 1311. Christ arranges everything in the Church, ibid., 1343. What use the builders’ cord has in the construction of the Church, 1314. The breadth of the spiritual building is charity, 1327. Its height is the understanding of the builder, 1328. Why breadth and height are measured with one reed, ibid. The elect are members of Christ, their head, 1329. The condition of the less perfect in the Church, 1333. These are parts of the heavenly building, ibid. Provided that they are supported on the foundation of fear and love, 1334, 1335. The construction of the Church and its various parts, 1334. What place there is for us weak people in this building, ibid. The columns of the Church are the sacred utterances, 1337. Christ as a little child threatens those dwelling together in the Church, 1343. The cheeks are the righteous of the holy Church, shining with virtues, 1346. Among the faithful, some love and contemplate God; others do not rise to contemplation, 1351. The conditions of the faithful signified by the east, north, and south, 1384. People of every condition are gathered into the Church, 1474. Good and evil alike are separated on the shore in the Church’s dragnet, [Col. 1390] ibid. Who in the Church are like the prudent virgins and who like the foolish, 1477. How much the future Church of the elect will differ from the present one, 1541. The holy Church has lilies in peace and roses in war, 1617.

The Church has a twofold beauty, 266. How the Church has no wrinkle, 421. The various ranks of the saints in the Church, 1513. The holy Fathers of the Old Testament admired the foreknown holiness of the Church’s earlier leaders, 1371. The Church’s adornment from the various virtues of the saints, 1379. The holy Church has lilies in peace and roses in war, 1617. In the Church there are more wicked than good and holy people, 1638. See Holiness; Holy.

Sometimes the Church, as though sparing the wicked, does not spare them, and vice versa, 419. The Church illumines the blind and supports the lame, 625. It snatches prey from the devil when it recalls someone from error or sin, 628. In compassion for its repentant children, the Church joins tears to prayers, 670. The Church’s grief over the perversity of the wicked, 420. Through voluntary repentance the Church recalls sinners to itself, 425. The Church receives all who return to it from the heretics, 502. The Church mourns for those whom it cannot draw by exhortation, 676.

The holy Church confesses that God had true flesh and a true death, 404. Heretics say that this confession of the Church is an insult to God, ibid. The Church refutes falsehood before teaching truth, 243. The Church does not openly profess one thing while concealing another, as the heretics do, ibid. The Church is wise unto sobriety, 448, 503. We are watered by the opinions of the holy Fathers as by flowing streams, 524. Heretics take away the teaching of the holy Fathers from the idle and careless, 525. The Church’s doctrine is a broad and open river, 584. Good works and the chair of doctrine are the Church’s insignia, 617. Amid the opposing false opinions of heretics, the Church proceeds safely by the power of truth, 618. The Church always applies itself to spiritual knowledge, 631. The faithful listen to the Church when it teaches, following its words rather than judging them, 635. They add nothing to its doctrine, ibid. How the Church’s doctrine is received by the humble, 636. In preaching, it tempers the hope of its children with fear, 640. After the struggles with heretics, sharper understanding and more intricate investigation of words emerged, 736. Sacred doctrine was handed down successively through patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and the holy Fathers, 857. The Church teaches the necessity of faith and good works, 949. Those who grow fat on the food of sacred doctrine gently feed others, 1267. The Fathers of the Old Testament commanded the external works of the law; those of the New Testament, the guarding of the heart, 1391. He rightly feeds God’s flock who teaches, 1407. See Preaching; Good Preachers; Doctrine; Heretical Doctrine.

The Church advances through adversities, 92. Who receives double for the Church’s labors, 16. The corners of the house—that is, the Apostles—were shaken and dispersed while Judaea raged against the Lord, 60. How great are the labors of the pilgrim Church, 91. The Church’s progress through persecutions, 293, 658. The Church oppressed by false friends who pretend to be comforters, 417. The Church suffers persecutions from reprobate children, 421, 660, 816, 847. What it means for the wicked to strike the cheek of the Church, 423; what it means for the Church’s inward parts to be poured out upon the earth, 424. Those who persecute Christ sitting in heaven rage in vain upon the earth, 429. The Church’s days are prosperity, its nights adversity, 432. The Church’s enemies are restrained neither by fear of God nor by shame before human beings, 447. The Church suffers the persecutions of its enemies through words or swords, against which it sets wisdom and patience, 557, 611, 847. Only the Catholic Church has martyrs, 573. After obtaining peace from outsiders, the Church began to be tested by its own people, 597. What the Church will suffer at the end of time from carnal people and heretics, 611. Having already suffered great things, it will then suffer greater ones, 612. The Church is distressed when the weak fall, ibid. Persecution distinguishes the citizens from the Church’s enemies, 634. Outside, the Church is pressed by heretics; within, by evil Catholics, 648, 659, 846, 847. The reprobate trample the Church of the elect as mud, ashes, and cinders, 665. Why the prayer of the Church asking for deliverance is not immediately heard, ibid. The Church’s grief, even in a time of peace, as it endures persecution from its own, 671. The Church either converts the wicked ways of the evil or tolerates them, as well as the complaints of the arrogant, 846. The Church’s night is when the unlearned and weak occupy the places of teachers and strong men, 848. God restrained the malice of the persecutors by one wise in childish things, 911. What God holds and shakes at the ends of the Church, 921. Sometimes God shakes the Church, and sometimes He does not, ibid. In the Church’s persecutions false Christians are shaken out like chaff, 921. The Church is now adorned with many garments, but when persecution rages it will be stripped naked, 922. Those who were once persecutors of the faith afterward became its preachers and defenders, 998. He who formerly raged against the Church now promulgates laws on its behalf, 999. Those who, through fear of rulers, do not dare to harass the Church attack it by various frauds, 1000. There can be no Church without an enemy, ibid. The persecutions that will be inflicted on the Church by Antichrist and his members will be terrible, 1119, 1123, 1124, etc. In the final persecution the anger of the reprobate will boil over against the saints, 1130. Those who will fight against the saints on behalf of Antichrist will believe that they are rendering service to God, 1131. The Church will someday receive double in return for its persecutions, 1153, 1161.

Why God afflicts the Church with various adversities, 405. The Church suffers persecution from false speakers during its time of peace, 421. The Church is surrounded by spears by its own enemy, 424. What it means for the Church to be cut down by wound upon wound, 425. Why the Church suffers the adversities of the present life, 427. The Church’s persecutors tread it as a winepress, 526. In the time of affliction the Church becomes a proverb to the wicked, 657. The Church grows through sufferings, 658. The reprobate bind the holy Church tightly, as though by the neck of a tunic, 664. In the time of persecution the holy Church stands by faith and cries out through its desires, 665. The Church is beaten daily by blows, 1311. The Church’s passion began with the blood of Abel, 1336.

The Church’s temporal power in all parts of the world, 846. Its enemies reproach it for this unjustly, ibid. Although some in the Church grow proud of its glory, ibid. Whoever is exalted temporally in the Church falls, ibid. After the Lord’s Ascension the Church grew in the authority of preaching, 1574. When the rulers of the earth had been humbled, the Lord raised the Church through them above the summit of the world, 910. The Church’s condition was raised through preaching, 1277.

Whoever eats the Church’s goods ought to pay the debt of preaching, 725.

There is a twofold poverty in Scripture, 1117.

Pride must be avoided even in the good things we do, 32, 245, 323, 376. An elated mind bursts out into tyranny, 71. Who are the satellites of an elated mind, ibid. The pride of those who do little and think highly of themselves, [Col. 1391] 97. Human exaltation, how insignificant it is even when it shines, must be weighed, 184. Pride destroys virtue, 223. Pride is born from virtue, 228, and also from wickedness, ibid. The bull is a symbol of pride, ibid. The elect do not have pride here, 288. Elation of mind excludes the divine compunction of love, 328. Pride arising from prosperous management of one’s household must be avoided, 336. Elation of mind is usually punished by carnal sins, 374, 823. What the Lord removed from the hearts of His disciples—their pride, 737. The inflation of pride sometimes imitates zeal arising from the movement of the Holy Spirit, 740. In good actions the pride of the heart must first be conquered, 741. Pride is the vice proper to the arrogant, 742. For the righteous, the pride of the arrogant is an occasion of virtue, 830. How pride of heart is to be restrained, 832. Hidden pride of heart is inexcusable, but that expressed in words is more so, 831. Those devoted to God must beware of pride, 850, 903. See Arrogance; Pride; Proud.

Eleazar, oppressed by his victory, signifies those who are lifted up by conquered vices, 622.

Election and reprobation are just, 805. Election is not based on foreseen merits, 855, 1100. Election and reprobation are marked by lines and measures extended according to God’s will, 900, 1315.

What the sign of election is, 1142, 363. Human beings’ ignorance of their own election and reprobation, 932. The elect angels are called sons of God, 39. The elect may be called the soul of Christ, 86. The elect are compared to wheat, 211, 879. The day, month, and year signify the multitude of the elect, 109, 113. The Church of the elect is called dawn, 113. The elect shine like stars in the night of the present life, 122. Why the elect are called stones of the regions, 203. The elect person is a servant insofar as he remains subject to corruption, 247. The elect are compared to hired laborers, 246, 248. Why the elect of the Old Testament are called runners, 308. The elect are called orphans, 522, and soldiers of God, 543. The mind of the elect is called God’s soil, 544. The elect are called a pilgrim people, 577. They are called fawns of the roe deer, 767, and are compared with deer, 821. The minds of the elect are signified by heavens, as though cast from bronze, 884. Elect human beings are called evening stars, just as angels are called morning stars, 909. The Church of the elect is signified by the name heaven, 980. The elect are signified by the names of the herodius and the hawk, 1001. The elect are called members of Christ, 1200. Every elect person is figured by the four living creatures, 1201. The elect are stones of the heavenly building, 1314. Whose task it is to arrange these stones, ibid.

God chooses those whom this world despises, 173. The number of the elect is infinite, 543. The number of the elect is definite and certain, 798. Those who perish are counted outside the number of the elect, ibid. Some of the elect undergo judgment, others do not, 836. Some of the elect will not be judged but will become judges, 837. No one should investigate why one person is chosen and another rejected, 805, 943. The sole sign of election is the steadfastness of charity, 1363. The elect are few in number, 1513, 1638. Who the elect are, and why, is unknown, 1641, 1642. Some are dragged unwillingly, while others who are willing are rejected, 1316.

God grants perseverance to the elect, 64, 926. When He hands them over to the devil to be tested, God keeps them in His hand, 75. The elect always increase in the conversion they have begun, 631. Now the elect wither in themselves, but in God they flourish, 663. Pressed by the examples of the wicked and the threats of tyrants, the elect are strengthened, 821. It is impossible for the elect to be completely captured in error, 1112. When they see the miracles of Antichrist, the elect will stagger, [Col. 1392] 1111. How greatly they will then burn with zeal, 1112.

What God wipes away of the sins of the elect, 313. This life of the elect is mingled with the darkness of sin, 919. At the end God diligently purifies His elect, 926. Many appear to be elect but are not, 1057. Why God does not preserve the elect from carnal vices, 1091. From the place where the devil crushes God’s elect, he loses them, 1092. How it can happen that the elect are led into error, 1112. Why God permits His elect to fall into sins, 1525. God restrains the elect as they rush into wicked desires, 1116.

What the affection of the elect is toward earthly and eternal things, 28. The more the mind of the elect strives to live according to counsel, the more it is wearied by the pain of the narrow path, 29. God is the place of the elect, 134. The elect endure the grave labors of this life in continual struggle, 135. Through the elect, as through members, sacred Scripture signifies the Redeemer, 181. At death the elect often receive security of mind, 203. The time of the elect is not the present life but the future one, 211. The elect person, like a hired laborer, desires his days to pass quickly, 246. Who labors in another’s field while awaiting his own reward, ibid. The elect are now weighed down by the punishment of corruption, 247. Why the elect are said to have empty months and laborious nights, 248. Out of love for truth the elect complain that they are shut up in prison, 260. The path of the elect person going to heaven is described, 362. Who among the elect are without a wrinkle, 421. The elect are compared to stars, 543. All the elect in the world are pilgrims, 577. Why the elect are mingled among the reprobate, 673. What the first and second causes of the elect’s groaning are, 513. The ardor of the elect desiring to enjoy God, ibid. The elect venerate God’s hidden judgments, 514. By contemplating them they are inflamed to repentance, 514. God tempers the virtues of the elect so that they are not exalted by being mingled with weakness, 607. Three times the elect are accustomed first to be affected by sorrow and afterward by joy, 771. The offspring of the elect, produced in its proper season, is vigorous, 975. The Church of the elect is situated on a mountain, 980. Like an eagle, the elect despise all earthly things, 1040. They build their nest in the rocks—that is, in the loftiness and steadfastness of the holy Fathers, ibid. Here they are guests, but by desiring heavenly things they are already fixed in the heights, 1041. God reveals the devil’s cunning to the elect, 1103. The smoke issuing from Leviathan’s nostrils touches the eyes of the elect for a time, 1112. The poverty of the elect is to have lost heavenly riches, 1017. God tolerates the hidden evils of some so that the good things they do openly may benefit the elect, 1130. The falls of some benefit the progress of the elect, ibid. Humility is characteristic of the elect, 288, 1135. The beauty of the elect, 1165. Among the strong and perfect, the weak and humble obtain the inheritance of eternal life, ibid. What it means for the elect to extend their faces and wings upward, 1202. Some of the elect rise through contemplation; others grow fat through the works of the active life, 1215. The Holy Spirit first casts the elect down from pride so that afterward He may raise them up, 1294. The virtues of the elect are signified by the colors of the high priest’s garments, 1342. What the prayer of the elect is, 1429. How the authority of the elect has been greatly strengthened, 1562. The elect have been placed so that they may go willingly and bear fruit by acting, ibid. To will to do something is already to go there in the mind, ibid. The elect bear fruit that remains forever, 1563. When the elect reach death, they will find their inheritance, ibid. The elect burn with the torches of love toward God’s commandments, 1578. See Saints on earth.

The elect advance through the degrees of virtue, [Col. 1393] 199. Here the elect must be purified so that they may escape eternal punishments, ibid. The elect pursue sins with tears, 258. Christ, risen from the dead, drew all the elect to Himself, 398. The closer the elect approach judgment, the more they examine their consciences, 428. The elect are invited to heavenly things in two ways, 432. The elect will tremble during Antichrist’s persecution, 446. The elect sometimes sin through ignorance or weakness, 452. The elect strive to do more than has been commanded them, 477. The elect are supported by God’s help so that they can resist the enemy, 497. The elect are still bound by the chains of weakness, 544. When tempted by empty glory, the elect immediately return to their heart, 701. The elect do not delight in their own praises, 707. The examination of the elect in relation to the future judgment, 793. In what respects the elect resemble deer, 821. Even the life of the reprobate advances the life of the elect, 934. The elect take pride in no virtue, 1135. The elect become more humble the more gifts they receive from God, 1276. The life of the elect is varied, 1312. The elect are friends of God, 1561.

The distinction between the elect and the reprobate, 28, 29, 98. What the elect think of themselves because of another’s fault, and what the reprobate think, 98. The elect and the reprobate receive temptation differently, ibid., 877. If Adam had not sinned, only the elect—those who are now to be saved—would be born, 131. Here the elect and the reprobate are in bitterness; what is the distinction between them? 140. The reprobate and the elect die: the former in folly, the latter in wisdom, 174. At the final judgment the elect will see while the reprobate groan, 203, 1099, 1437. How grievous to the elect are the words and ways of the reprobate, 218. In what the reprobate is strong, the righteous person is sluggish, 221. At God’s striking, the reprobate are feebly strong, while the elect, though weak, are strongly weak, 223. The reprobate receive their soul in vain; the elect do otherwise, 230. The steadfastness of the elect brings shame upon the reprobate, 234. The elect think about death while sound; the reprobate do not even do so when death is imminent, 253. The difference between confessions of sins made by the elect and by the reprobate, 258. God punishes the sins of the elect differently from those of the reprobate, 319, 326. The reprobate hear the words of wisdom; the elect also taste them, 369. At the final judgment the reprobate will be condemned before the elect are endowed with glory, 372. The elect end their life in humility, the reprobate in pride, 408. The elect differ from the reprobate as they approach judgment, 428. The difference between the reprobate rich person and the elect poor person in this life and in the future life, 480.

The life of the elect and the reprobate is different, but the death of the flesh is the same, 494. The reprobate are dragged by the devil into the perpetual mourning of vices, whose sweetness the elect detest, 499. The reprobate dedicate themselves in this life; the elect await their dedication in the future, 506. The elect now see and groan over the sins of the reprobate; at their condemnation they will exultingly mock them, 507. God scourges the elect here in order to spare them, but the reprobate in order to begin punishing them, 571, 829. God looks upon the end of the elect and of the reprobate, 576. Thoughts of earthly things are first in the reprobate and last in the elect, 639. The elect touch truth by doing it; the reprobate press it down by knowing it, 657. Here the reprobate mock the elect, ibid. Even the power of the reprobate serves the benefit of the elect, 661. The elect travel by a harsh road toward the homeland of salvation; the reprobate travel by pleasant ways toward the pit, 681. The reprobate are converted to the examples of worse people, while the elect are converted to the virtues of better people, [Col. 1393] 769. No one should investigate why one person is called and drawn while another is rejected, 805. The anger of divine judgment begins here with the correction of the elect and comes to rest in the eternal condemnation of the reprobate, 829. The elect are within the measures established by Christ; the reprobate are outside them, 900. When the elect advance, the reprobate are stirred to fury, 910. The hidden Judge, looking upon some, redeems them; abandoning others, He destroys them, 920. Death restores the elect to their light, but takes away the reprobate’s light, 927. The word of God becomes a morning star for the elect, but, by God’s hidden judgment, evening for the reprobate, 952. Heavenly things are hidden from the reprobate and revealed to the elect, 964. Visible things detain the reprobate here but compel the elect toward better things, 965. The elect have few things here that weigh them down and many that lift them upward; the reprobate have the opposite, 1001. At the judgment the elect and the reprobate will see Christ’s humanity, but the elect will also see His divinity, 1043, 1519. At the judgment God will appear tranquil to the righteous and angry to the reprobate, 1052, 1478. At the judgment Christ will be beautiful to the elect but terrifying to the reprobate, 1231. The elect find in mercy something to praise, while the reprobate have nothing in justice to accuse, 1101. Neither is mercy shown to the elect without justice, nor justice to the reprobate without mercy, ibid. The smoke issuing from Leviathan’s nostrils disturbs the minds of the elect differently from how it blinds the eyes of the reprobate, 1113. It is a divine gift that the elect do not have the power to bring to completion whatever evil they may think, whereas the reprobate do, 1116. At the judgment the reprobate will be crushed by lightning, while the elect remain unharmed and rejoice, 1120. While the elect tremble, how great will be the shaking of the reprobate, 1122, 1478. The falling reprobate show the elect who follow them that the pit must be avoided, 1130. God knows how to use the evil of the reprobate for the salvation of the elect, ibid. Evils help the elect; good things harm the reprobate, 1136. Pride is the sign of the reprobate, humility of the elect, 1142. Among the elect there is the impulse of the spirit; among the reprobate, the impulse of the flesh, 1205. Why the elect fall on their face, while the reprobate fall backward, 1251. The elect prefer others to themselves; the reprobate prefer themselves to others, 1276. The signs preceding the final judgment will terrify the reprobate and comfort the elect, 1437. The elect become better through insults, the reprobate worse through benefits, 1508. The reprobate are signified by the left, the elect by the right, 1578. See The Righteous and the Wicked Compared.

Evil things are dispensed to the elect by the wondrous grace of the Creator, 46. The elect advance through temptation, 64. What the devil prepares for ruin, God turns into glory for the elect, ibid. The elect are in God’s hand and, through temptations, in the devil’s hand, 75. The elect are taken out of the devil’s power, 86. The reprobate persecute Christ in the elect, 88. Sometimes God abandons us in order to preserve us, 95. God consoles here those of the elect who suffer for Him, 191. By ridiculing the works of the good, the wicked persecute the elect with the scourge of the tongue, 201. The reprobate are put to shame by the steadfastness of the elect, 234. Through the afflictions of this life God wipes away the sins of the elect, 313. The spirit of the elect remains unbroken in adversity, 417. The elect are temporarily handed over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy, 423. God tests and proves the elect by the burning of tribulation, 516. He who is preserved for life must be reproved by strict justice, 891. The howling of the reprobate against the elect, 1029. The elect waver in severe temptation but do not fall, 1252.

The elect are in bitterness, 140. Here the elect must be purified so that they may escape eternal punishments, 199. God does not permit the elect to be tempted beyond their strength, [Col. 1394] 201. The light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, 251. God often binds the elect with the reins of adversities, 350. After temptations the elect burst forth from darkness like the sun, 354. The elect are everywhere pressed down by the reprobate, 361. The elect are often weighed down by continuous adversities, 362. How much the elect suffer from false brothers in the time of adversity, 420. Scourges recall the elect to life, 493. The elect endure two kinds of persecution, 611. The elect are threshed like grains, ibid. The elect do not promise themselves security here, 638. God permits the adversaries of the elect to grow temporarily, 661. In persecution the elect are more prepared to die than to remain silent, 665. The elect who die for the faith are judged unhappy by the reprobate, ibid. The elect know how to fight against the temptations of outward excellence, 672. Earthly goods are denied to the elect, 681. The elect do not rejoice in great abundance, 698. The elect sometimes become subject to the reprobate, 807. God subjects His elect to the devil for instruction, 1093. See Persecutions of the Church; Adversity; Scourges; Temptation, etc.

What electrum signifies, 894, 1188. Why it was seen in the midst of fire, 894. As electrum in fire, God made man in persecution, 1188.

Almsgiving: for what purpose and in what manner it is to be done, 341, 413. Almsgiving is beneficial when we mourn and renounce our sins, 413. By distributing temporal goods to the poor, we store them up for ourselves, 568, 1451. Whoever gives alms but does not cease sinning gives his property to God and himself to sin, 624. Almsgiving is judged chiefly by the disposition of the mind, 669. Those who ask beyond the limits of need do not deserve to obtain, 691. Those who give alms after uttering insults scarcely make satisfaction for the injury inflicted, 692. The poor are to be supported both with gentle speech and through the ministry of generosity, ibid. Whoever gives gifts to the needy gives presents to his patrons, ibid. Let us sow what we may afterward reap with great interest, 693. Alms should also be given to those unknown to us, ibid. The meritorious conditions of almsgiving, 711. What is given is received according to the giver’s heart, ibid. Alms must be given even from what is necessary, 1521, especially when given to preachers of the divine word, ibid. To wipe Christ’s feet with one’s hair means to minister to the poor from one’s surplus, 1596. We kiss the Lord’s feet when we give cheerfully to the poor, ibid. Those who seize what belongs to others, and those who do not distribute their own goods to the needy, deserve eternal punishment, 1655. The poor are to be sought as intercessors before God, 1659. We should ask as patrons those who ask alms of us, ibid. Vicious poor people are to be corrected and fed, ibid. An exhortation to honor and relieve the poor, 1661.

Almsgiving from stolen goods is evil, 413. Almsgiving is called the price of sins, ibid. The almsgiving of the proud is empty, ibid. Almsgiving performed from fear belongs to beginners, 626. What almsgiving is perfect, 669. Almsgiving must proceed from a pure mind, 711. How great is the virtue of almsgiving, 1521.

All the elements testified that God had come, 1458.

Elijah fearlessly rebuked Ahab, 236. Elijah will restore the hearts of the children to their fathers, 375. He will be killed by Antichrist together with Enoch, 446. He fled from Jezebel, 608. Elijah’s virtue tempered by weakness, ibid., 1321. Elijah is displayed in miracles and preserved in weaknesses, 608. Elijah postponed death but did not escape it, 669, 1572. Elijah stood where he had fixed his heart, 1318. What it signifies that Elijah stood at the entrance of the cave and veiled his face, 1319. Elijah’s weakness of fear was a great safeguard of his courage, 1121. Who is called the chariot of Israel, and who its charioteer, 1412. Elijah will precede the coming of Christ the Judge, 1457. Elijah was taken up into the aerial heaven, 1571. He was transferred to a hidden region of the earth, 1572. Why he was carried away in a chariot through the ministry of angels, ibid. Elijah practiced chastity, ibid. He was a type of Christ’s Ascension, ibid.

What Eliphaz signifies, 15, 91, 731. Eliphaz was rash in speech, 152.

Elisha fearlessly attacked Joram, 237. He did not raise the Shunammite woman’s son with a staff, but through the ministry of compassion, 317. The wood of the axe sinking, and the iron…
lifting it up again—what it signifies, 701, 1178. The seven breathings of Elisha over the dead child—what they signify, 1151. The Holy Spirit reveals the future to Elisha, but not the past, 1178. Elizabeth prophesied simultaneously concerning the past, present, and future, 1177. The divine utterances are compared with silver, 183, 509, 566, 573, 591, 901. They are called harvests and riches, 183. Sacred discourse is despised by most people, 634. The divine utterances contain a song and a woe, 823, 1262. The wondrous profundity of God’s utterances, 1205. The obscurity of God’s utterances is of great usefulness, 1213. The power of sacred discourse, 1226. It is exceedingly difficult to understand sacred discourse, 1535. See Word of God; Sacred Scripture.

“Buying as though not possessing”—who this is, 1625. Who those buying in the temple are, 1648. Enoch and Elijah will be killed by Antichrist, 446. The first Enoch, from the line of Cain, and the seventh Enoch from Adam, from the line of Seth—what they signify, 506. The preaching of Enoch and Elijah, 1295. They are called the two olive trees and the two lampstands, ibid. By his example Enoch urges us to conjugal chastity, 1338. Enoch’s translation and Elijah’s being lifted up were types of Christ’s ascension, 1572. The sword upon the thigh—what it signifies, 638.

Epiphanius the Deacon, born in the province of Isauria, 1650. The bishop is called the head of the faithful, 453. Bishops are called rams, 959. Bishops are teachers of the peoples who follow them, 960. Bishops are called the stones of the sanctuary, 1503. They receive the authority to bind and loose, 1555. Whoever abuses this authority deprives himself of it, ibid. When they ought to use the power of binding and loosing, ibid. With great moderation, the pastors of the Church should strive either to loose or to bind, 1556. Bishops occupy the place of the apostles, 1555. Great is the honor, but heavy the burden of honor, ibid.—Bishops are stirred by Job’s example to care for the salvation of their household dependents, 616. Christ strikes the faults of subjects through their superiors, and through himself strikes the faults of pastors, 1502. God tolerates no greater injury than that inflicted by priests, 1503. It is a hard thing that one who does not know how to govern his own life should become judge of another’s life, 1555. Whoever condemns the righteous puts to death one who is not dying, ibid. The absolution given by the presiding bishop is genuine when it follows the judgment of the inner judge, ibid.—Bishops must not neglect the works of their subjects, 21. The nobles are overthrown when they pursue temporal gains rather than eternal ones, 374. Bishops ought to preach, 616. The simony of bishops is severely reproved, 1502. Bishops are accused of many other things, ibid. Bishops must avoid external business, ibid. [Col. 1395] The heedlessness of bishops who carelessly look upon souls perishing everywhere, ibid. The stones of the sanctuary are scattered when bishops are occupied with the world’s external business, 1503. Bishops must be moved neither by hatred nor by favor toward anyone, 1555.

The rich man at the banquet is a type of the Jewish people, 1652. He was buried in hell, 1653. What the rich man’s five brothers signify, 1654. For what faults he was condemned, 1655. By tolerating the rich man, God was waiting to punish him, ibid. The man who denied Lazarus the crumbs of bread asked in vain for a drop of water, 1656. Why he burned more fiercely in his tongue, 1657. God rewarded him with abundance and rejected him, ibid.

By the name “horseman” the soul of a holy man is signified, 1009. A holy soul’s horse is its own body, 1009. Many things are signified by the name “horse” in Sacred Scripture, 1015. What the rider of a horse signifies, 1016. The nourishment of horses and oxen is different, 1057.

Let us first rise up against ourselves, and then against the wicked, 448. Certain errors should be passed over, which cannot be corrected without fault on the part of the corrector, 710. An error is more difficult to correct when it is believed to be a virtue, 1070.

The caterpillar—what it is, 1113. What the caterpillar signifies, ibid. Esau represents worldly people, 147. Why Esau, having been rejected, did not find a place for repentance, 371. Esau was rejected because of his excessive appetite for cheap food, 983. Esau signifies the Jewish people, and Jacob the Gentiles, 1213. The food of the righteous is the conversion of the perverse, 1044.

Ethan is interpreted as “strong,” 1088. Which Lord dried up the rivers of Ethan, ibid.

The sacrifice of the Eucharist contains the real presence of Christ’s body, 710. The flesh and blood of Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist, 1484, 1533. The blood of the lamb is placed on both doorposts when it is received simultaneously by the mouth of the body and of the heart, 1533. We receive Christ’s body in the sacrament, 1534. To receive the Lord’s body and blood with the mouth while opposing him by contrary conduct is of no benefit, 1534. The Lord’s body must be received with the bitterness of repentance, ibid. What it signifies to eat the flesh of the lamb neither raw nor cooked in water, 1535.

Eutychius’s error concerning the resurrection of tangible bodies, 465. It is refuted, 466. Whether his little book was condemned to the flames by the emperor, ibid. Eutychius recovered from his error, 467.

The comparison of Eve with Job’s wife, 79. Eve intoxicated by the golden cup, 1128. What Eve’s being produced from the side of the sleeping Adam signifies, 1218.

That is said to vanish which is suddenly removed from the eyes of those looking at it, 348. The Gospel, rejected by the Jews, was spread among all the nations, 292, 1570. The counsels of the Gospel are above the commandments, 836. The preaching of the Gospel was granted not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles, 880. What the sacrament of the Gospel is, 1178. How the Gospel is to be preached to every creature, 1569. What the stature, height, and appearance of the Gospel signify, 1221. “Gospel” means “good news,” 1407. The Lord scattered grains of seed throughout the world by sending disciples to preach the Gospel, 1570. The evangelists are represented under the form of the four living creatures, 1039, 1189, 1190, 1200. The evangelists were formed from the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 1396] and made firm in the fire of persecution, 1189. The evangelists, who together represent the perfect, 1190. The wondrous agreement of the evangelists, 1191. All reached Christ’s divinity by flight, 1193. There was one faith among them all concerning the incarnation of the Word, and an equal contemplation of his divinity, ibid. Their feet were straight, ibid. Who are called evangelists, 1407. After the apostles and prophets were taken away, the evangelists remained, through whom the faith is defended, ibid.

The devil is called the exactor, 136, 981, 1648. The exactor’s voice is heard when we are struck by temptation, 136. When we resist his temptation, the exactor’s voice is not heeded, ibid., 982. By persuasion the devil introduces guilt; by savagery he exacts punishment, 988. How Christ overcame the exactor’s scepter, 989.

Each person ought to examine his life daily, 1204, 1505. It is a lesser fault not to know the truth than not to remain in a truth once known, 380.

“On high.” What it means to dwell on high, 1042.

The excuse for sin, passed from the first human being to his descendants, doubles the sin, 119. The first parents wrongly used the shield of excuse, 1106. The vice of making excuses is signified by the name “hedgehog,” 1108. The futile excuses of those invited to the dinner are explained, 1620. The proud reply of those making excuses feigns humility, 1621. The first reply belongs to the greedy, the second to the curious, and the third to those devoted to pleasures, ibid.

The value of the examples of the fathers and of superiors, 49. Examples of piety are effective in rousing a sluggish soul, 328, 973. God recalls us to himself through the examples of the good, 329, 768. What movements of the soul the good things we see in others ought to arouse in us, 329, 767, 1427, 1523. The virtues of the saints are diverse, so that each person may imitate one virtue in another, 768, 1523. What it means for them to strike one another with their wings, 769. Peter and Paul stir one another through reciprocal examples, 769. Aided by divine commandments and the examples of the saints, we are lifted from the old way of life, 795. Only those things that are firm should be displayed as examples, 1184. Certain unusual things should not be held up as examples, ibid. Those whose lives serve as an example to others may sometimes proclaim their own virtues, 1256. They kindle one another to progress by their examples, 1275. What the examples of the holy fathers of the Old Testament provide for us, 1337. Examples arouse compunction more than words do, 1378. The example of Chrysaorius’s most dreadful death should move us to repentance, 1481. Someone wrongly defends his own depravity by the depravity of others, 1498. How much harm is done by the bad examples of those appointed for our correction, 1503. We should neither imitate those who act wrongly nor despair of them, 1514. God everywhere sets before us examples of repentance and of divine mercy, 1551. How useful the examples of the good are to us, 329, 704, 766, 768. The wicked pay attention to the examples of those who are worse, 769. The examples of the fathers strengthen us, 794, 859, 905, 1235, 1338, 1372. The examples of the fathers are an armory against the devil, 1339. We have examples of those who live well every day, 1427. God sets the examples of the fathers before us, 1636.

The army of heaven—of whom it consists, 54. What the army of Christ the King, seated in the mind of the righteous, is, 640. The howling army of vices, 1037. The multitude of the faithful is an army, 1237. The armies of our King are ranks of angels, 1637. See Warfare.

By exorcism through the laying on of hands, priests cast out demons, 1571.

An exhortation to humility, 1140. We love the punishments of exile in preference to love of the heavenly homeland, 219, 1613. Ignorance of itself causes the soul to groan over exile, 305. For a wise person in this exile there are many reasons for groaning and none for rejoicing, 587. See Homeland.

What it means to expect temptation, 251. Sacred interpreters succeed the apostles, 858. The speech of sacred interpreters is compared with torrents, ibid. The righteous shun concern for external things, 147. See Care.

Some await the end of life in order to return to God, 870. See Repentance.

What was added to the life of Hezekiah, 393, 414, 506. Hezekiah justified himself in thought, 406. Why Ezekiel, carried away to behold sublime things, is called “son of man,” 690, 1301, 1321. Beginning to prophesy in his thirtieth year, he is a type of Christ, 1184. Ezekiel is interpreted as “fortitude of God,” 1185. What Ezekiel, son of Buzi, signifies, ibid. The incarnation of the Word revealed to Ezekiel, ibid. When and in what years he prophesied, 1307. He was carried captive to Babylon with King Jehoiachin, ibid. The obscurity of Ezekiel’s prophecies with respect to the literal sense, 1249, 1402. Through Ezekiel the person of superiors is signified, 814. Ezekiel represents the teachers, 815, 1302. Why Ezekiel began with a conjunction, etc., 1183. Why Ezekiel and Paul fall upon their faces, 1251.

## F

God’s making: what it is, 810. God’s face: what it is, 45, 385, 765. The inner face of a human being is the mind, 351. What it means to receive God’s face, 380. God’s face is understood in two ways, ibid. The face signifies the mind’s intention, 411. In what sense everyone who acts wickedly covers his face, 529. The face denotes knowledge, 1117, 1191—and faith, ibid. What it means to walk before his face, 1198. What it means to walk in the presence of the face, 1204. What it means to fall on one’s face, 1249. Why the righteous are read as falling on their face, and the wicked backward, 1251. What it means to go out from God’s face, 47. What lifting one’s face to God signifies, 351, 510.

A sharp sickle signifies divine judgment, 1089. Reputation is not to be hunted down through good works, 704. The mind’s famine is the silence of divine speech, 201. The flesh’s famine is the withdrawal of bodily support, ibid. The impious wastes away with hunger, 442. The senses of the mind fail because they are refreshed by no inward nourishment, ibid. Who knows how to hunger, 1386, 1388. The carnal person loves his own hunger, 1619.

A large household must be restrained under the rule of the mind, 31. Stupidity is signified by the nostrils, 1019. A fool is signified under the name of an ox, 1376. See Stupidity.

Christians do not admit fate, 1469.

**Throat.** What it means to speak in the throat, 743.

Fauns, called *Panes* in Greek, are incubi, 228. What they signify, ibid. [Col. 1397]

Human approval is called the hypocrite’s house, 277.

By believing, the holy Felicitas became Christ’s handmaid; by preaching, Christ’s mother, 1444. Through preaching she gave birth to those whom she had borne in the flesh for the world, ibid. The encomium of this holy martyr, ibid. She was more than a martyr: she first came to the punishments and reached the eighth, 1445. Through inward love she overcame the pain of the flesh, ibid. One death is not sufficient for Felicitas, 1446. Let men be ashamed not to imitate this courageous woman, ibid.

The prosperity of this life is weighed, 486. The prosperity of this world does not belong to the righteous, 960. In this life, not everything that is done well is prosperous, nor is everything prosperous good, ibid. Prosperity makes people more negligent, 1034. See Prosperity; Blessedness.

Felix, the ancestor of Saint Gregory, appeared as a holy pope to the virgin Saint Tharsilla, 1642.

In former times women were deprived of inheritance, 1165. The thigh signifies the propagation of the flesh, 1314. What Jacob’s thigh, with its sinew withered by the angel’s touch, represents, 1326.

The body’s windows are called the five senses, 678. What the slanting windows in chambers signify, 1361. They are both open and fortified, ibid.

The glory of the world is compared to the flower of hay, 538. Hay is the life of carnal people, 1050, 1057. Likewise, the flesh is hay, 1461, 1484.

What Solomon’s litter signifies, 1334. What its golden reclining-place and silver columns signify, ibid.

Leaven, and what it means to offer praise to God from what has been leavened, 1534.

Iron signifies present necessities, 480. What the iron that fell from the axe-head into the depths signifies, 701.

Excessive fervor, unless restrained, is exposed to the danger of pride, 946. Through the fervor of charity, the torpor of sin is shaken off, 1421. How pleasing to God is the fervor of a righteous and innocent man, 1602.

We worthily celebrate festivals by imitating those whom we honor, 1453, 1557. Present festivals are figures of eternal festivals, ibid. It is of no benefit to attend human festivals if one happens to be absent from the festivals of the angels, 1558. Haste is commended on the way of salvation, 1537.

Some fetuses are miscarried because they are premature, 975. What the unfruitful yet spared fig tree signifies, 1582. What it means for God’s fig tree to be stripped of its bark, 282.

Faith is expressed through a seal, 922; through a gate, 1329, 1360, 1377. Who the shields of faith are, 1340. Faith is signified by a rope, 1087, and by the face, 1191. Earth and sea together signify the certainty of faith accompanied by a small degree of doubt, 347. Faith is the proof of things not seen, 1557. Faith is the first of all the virtues, 64. Under the scourges, the faith, hope, and charity of the righteous often waver, 69. When faith falters, how it is to be strengthened, 189. By God’s hidden judgments, some nations come to faith and others depart from it, 377. In former times, faith alone was effective among the Gentiles for wiping away original sin in infants, 102. What the mind believes, let the tongue not keep silent about, 426. Faith is not given to everyone, 863. Right action should follow right faith, 1251. The uselessness of faith without works and of works without faith, ibid. Faith precedes charity, 1348. The breadth of the lower gate signifies faith active through charity, 1371.

—Faith is the beginning of every good, 64. Through faith one reaches the virtues, and not conversely, 1381. Through faith all our sins are released in baptism, 1421. Faith derived from the testing of reason has no merit, 1552. There is one faith among beginners and another among the perfect, 1396. Placed between faith and hope, let us strive toward charity, 1421. Faith, hope, charity, and the practice of goodness should stand at the same level, 1426. What faith, and of what kind, is necessary for salvation, 1570. What can be seen is said to be better known than believed, 1591. Faith together with hope is the cause of salvation, 1595.

—Faith concerning Christ’s resurrection is to be regulated by the faith of the apostles, 465, etc. The beginnings of faith and its growth by stages, 722, 1330. Faith is the foundation of the earth—that is, of the righteous person’s soul, 903. Before all else God provides his soldiers with the strength of faith, 1030. Good works are useful for attaining faith, 1252. Many come to faith, but few are brought to the kingdom, 1513. What the ancient Fathers contribute to the solidity of faith, 1336. Without faith in the true God there are no good works, 1382. Through good works we make progress in faith, ibid. By faith are believed things that cannot be grasped by reason, 1395.

—Faith is sometimes shaken, 69. The faith of Christ was transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles, 216. Some lose faith through excessive inquiry, 532. Every sinner is guilty of unbelief, 536. As the wicked increase, faith will become a reproach, 657. The faithful who live wickedly often lose their faith, 802, 923, 1591. They are sexually defiled even to the crown of the head, ibid. Many die in the house of faith without faith, ibid. How received faith is to be preserved, 903. What it means to lose faith, 802. The light of faith does not illuminate those who cloak their wickedness under the name of faith, 923.

—Faith without works is rejected, 536, 802, 923, 1082, 1251, 1570, 1650. True faith is that exercised through action, 1557, 1570. Very many hold the faith but do not hold the life of faith, 863, 1082. The faith of those who preceded us was the same as that of those living now and of those yet to come, 1345, 1353. The height of the saints is faith in invisible things, 1409. True faith does not contradict in conduct the words that it believes, 1570. True faith is the foundation of works, 802. Once the heart has been marked with faith, the adversary does not dare to break in by temptation, 922. Faith is the way to the light, 1442. The one who does what he understands to be good both sees and follows, 1443. The merit of true faith, 1557. What signs ought to accompany true faith, 1570.

The multitudes of the faithful are signified by Job’s daughters, 23. The three orders of the faithful, ibid. All the faithful are members of Christ, 457. Why the faithful tolerate heretics, 241. The more they see the wicked being indulged, the more the faithful lament, 513. A faithful person declares that he is suffering when he sees those whom he loves suffering, 663. What states of the faithful are designated by the East, North, and South, 1384. The souls of the faithful are vessels, whether of a whole burnt offering or of a sacrifice, 1409. Who offer a whole burnt offering and who a sacrifice, 1410. The twofold life and sacrifice of the faithful, 1419. All the faithful ought to discharge the office of angels, 1455. Who are truly faithful, 1570. If someone returns to the truth, the Lord will judge him not at all deceitful, ibid. The diversity of the faithful in the Church, 1410. The order of the faithful of the Church, 640. The people of the faithful are exalted, 735. The end of false believers, 923. Most of the faithful are insensitive to the words of God, 941.

Self-confidence, how harmful it is, [Col. 1399] 223. The saints are so uncertain that they trust, and they trust in such a way that they do not grow sluggish, 314. From where we derive confidence in God’s mercy, 324, 1611. The greatest confidence is to be placed in God, ibid.

A multitude of children provokes parents to avarice, 19. Who the children of fools are, 656. Why holy souls are called daughters of kings, 1164. Job’s daughters signify three states of the human person, 1165. The daughters of Jerusalem are called weak souls, 1335. Why Ezekiel is called “son of man,” 1301. Good parents will not benefit wicked children, nor wicked parents good children, at the final judgment, 1520. The axe laid at the root signifies that offspring together with its parent will be removed, ibid.

—The Son of God is called a servant on account of the form assumed, 55. He is not called adopted, because he is God by nature, ibid., 853. The Son of God is called the hidden Word, 160. He is the image of the Father, 167. He is called the hand of God, 564, 1051. God’s speaking is the begetting of the Word, 748. We ought to marvel at this generation, not investigate it, ibid. The Father begot the one Word without time, 748, 918. The only-begotten Son of God is called the mouth of God, 868; also the arm of God, ibid., 1051; and the voice of God, ibid. Why the speech that the Son speaks is said to be not his but the Father’s, 1576. As the Son of God is the Word, so the Holy Spirit is the tongue, 1578. The Lord’s Word is the Son of the Father, 1579. Why he is said to be lesser than the Father, 1549. See Christ; Word of God.

The sons of God are called angels, 39.

To fashion means the same as to compose, 1538. A potter is called one who composes clay, 1538.

Why we always desire an end, 248. While the end of things is considered, everything that passes away is reckoned as though it had already existed, 136. What is enclosed by an end is not long, 225, 233, 254, 469. God willed that our end should be hidden from us, 408, 1645. The end of wicked people, 540. Why Christ is called the end of the law, 1349.

—The final end of the human being is God, 45. We ought to enjoy God alone and use the world in a ministerial way, ibid. No one should live or die for himself, but for God, 1425. We must not turn aside from God’s path on account of carnal affections, 1628.

The firmament signifies two things, 1230, 1231, 1240.

What the scourges of God, called evils, are, 79. Through scourges we return to God when we are recalled to peace, ibid. The punishment of the scourge, remembrance of the gift; joy is to be tempered by fear of the scourge, 80. The minds of the elect are fortified against the scourge of a mocking tongue, 201. The scourge of the tongue is the sentence of the final punishment, 202. Scourges are to be weighed in quality and quantity, 76. The scourge of the tongue is the reproach of an inflicted insult, 201. The saints desire God’s scourges, 220. Those who murmur when scourged contradict God’s words, ibid. The distress of the righteous person who does not know why he is scourged, 220, 451. Divine scourges should sometimes be desired by the wicked, 418. What it means to be girded with scourges and to be struck with scourges, 451. What allays the distress of the righteous person scourged by God, 747.

—Not to feel God’s scourges, or to feel them excessively, is a fault, 49. Why the righteous continually suffer scourges, 147. From the hidden merits of minds, the manifest scourges of punishments proceed, 187. By considering our countless faults, we endure God’s scourges with equanimity, 343. When a human being advances into illicit freedom, God mercifully restrains him with scourges, 350. Scourges are grievous to one who does not consider eternal rewards, 354. How great is the usefulness of God’s scourges, 384, 757, 828, 1098. What it means to have God write bitter things, 387. God spares the reprobate for a time, though they are to be scourged eternally, 403, 782. We painfully do not know for what sin we are being scourged, 428. The foolish opinion of the common people concerning the scourges of the elect, 430, 449, 469, 496, 529, 745. When the weak are astonished and blinded by the scourges, they sometimes fall, 431, 438. How complaints about God’s scourges among human beings are to be restrained, 170, 746, 1098. Whoever tastes heavenly things endures lower things with equanimity, 170. The humble prayer of one who has been scourged, 321. The method of consoling those who have been scourged, 419, 747. With God permitting it, though by a hidden judgment, the elect know that they suffer evils, 658. It belongs to the elect to be crushed here by scourges so that they may be prepared for eternal rewards, 829. The judgment of God who scourges is just but hidden, 1046, 1049. God’s scourges do not seem grievous if we weigh the wars of the hidden enemy, which are more grievous, 1098. Let us fear not the father’s scourge but the enemy’s sword, 1099. Why God mixes scourges with his gifts, 1343. God scourges some as sons and others as enemies, 453, 571. God does not persecute us by raging, 450, 500. One scourged by God needs not reproof but consolation, 459. The opinion of those who measure faults by scourges is false, 496, 529, 745. When creatures rage, the scourged person ought to look to God, who inwardly directs them, 518. From what we suffer, we learn to fear what we have not yet suffered, 519. God’s power to scourge is incomprehensible, ibid. The impious are scourged by the very things in which they take pride, 654. God is always just when he scourges, 746, 828. Scourges are, for carnal people, increases of virtues for spiritual people, 1181. God pursues faults and protects sinners, 1182. It is most grievous to sin amid scourges, 1253. Whoever is scourged here is corrected in gentleness, 1341. At the final judgment correction will occur in fury and anger, ibid. An example of a Christian soul devoutly lamenting amid scourges, 1430.

—God’s scourges have different effects in the good and in the wicked, 145, 187, 214, 571, 696, 745. To the extent that the flesh is afflicted by scourges, the mind is lifted to higher things, 187. The elect must be worn down here by continual scourges, 199. At God’s striking, some are stones without sound, others resounding bronze without understanding, 222. If they do not wipe away sins, God’s scourges increase the merits of the righteous, 385, 782, 1044. Through the striking of the righteous, they are kindled to love of the heavenly homeland, 394. The weak members of the Church are disturbed by continual scourges, 451. From the blows suffered by the righteous, we must learn what we ought to fear, 486. The scourges of the righteous either cleanse sins already committed or avert future ones, 520, 828. God scourges the elect here in order to spare them, but the reprobate in order to begin punishing them, 571. The scourge will wash away guilt when it changes the life, ibid. Some are struck by God for instruction, not destruction, 669, 681. Paternal compassion scourges those whom it preserves for an inheritance, 681. When is scourging the discipline of a father rather than the anger of a judge? One scourged by God, mindful of his condition, must not accuse the Creator’s justice, 747, 782. Let him acknowledge that he has been struck less than he deserves, 770. Punishment questions us whether we truly acknowledge our guilt, ibid. The stupidity of those who become worse after being scourged, 840. The righteous are scourged so that they may be trained to greater vigilance, 845. With what joy the conscience of the saints expands while they are scourged outwardly, 930, 1022. Whoever, scourged by God, unites his own will to the divine will has already been corrected of his injustice, [Col. 1400] 1049. In a profound dispensation God presses his servants either with threats or even with scourges, 1098. By scourging us, God calls us to repentance, 1253. See Affliction; Adversity; Tribulation; Temptation; The Saints in Adversity.

What the flame of the fire of the impious is, 438. How the flame of the fire of the righteous differs from the flame of the impious, 439.

What breath mystically signifies, 155.

Who is unable to weep over his own sorrow, 330. Through weeping one reaches eternal joys, 1443. Through joys one reaches weeping, ibid. Who can weep in such a way as to be “as though not weeping,” 1625.

A human being is called a flower, 390. The world is filled with as many flowers destined soon to wither as there are human beings, ibid. What the various fragrances of flowers signify, 1214. With how many kinds of flowers the field of the Church is adorned, ibid.

Swelling waves express the cares of this life, 695. Sacred writers are compared to a river, 4, 584. What a river signifies, 1082, 1557. Why holy preachers are called rivers, 1212.

Stench signifies sin, 462. Whoever loosens what is dead displays not virtue but stench, 1556.

The hidden fountain is the invisible God, the Father’s only-begotten Son, 1401. The open fountain is the same God incarnate, ibid.

The formation of a human being in the mother’s womb, 1395. To fornicate inwardly is to delight outwardly in forbidden things, 797.

Who are truly strong, 134. The strong sometimes take upon themselves words of weakness, 399. Those who sympathize with the weak become stronger, 219. Job is strong not through madness but through a state of salvation, 222. Let the strength of the flesh grow sluggish while the virtue of the mind increases, 134. Strength is shown in adversity, 153. What the strength of the righteous is, 221. What constitutes the strength of the reprobate, ibid. The strength of the righteous is assumed from the weakness of the Divinity, 515. What it means to change one’s strength, 576, 631. Strength needs the gift of counsel, 1381.

How we are hidden in a pit of earth, 1021.

The kings of the Franks proceed from a lineage, 1470.

Brothers who preserve harmony while a father’s substantial estate is being divided: this is praise of paternal instruction, 20.

How fraud insinuates itself into good works, 312. Fraud is committed in three ways, ibid.

What it means to put a bridle on the mouth, 658. What the bridle of error constraining the jaws of peoples is, 1374. This bridle turned into a song, ibid.

What cold denotes morally, 38. Iniquity is compared to cold, 532, 934.

What a worn brow signifies, 1269.

Why all fruits were not granted by God to every region, 1276. The various fruits of the righteous, 1358. When one considers eternal things, the temporal fruits of works become worthless, 1563. God comes to us seeking fruit, 1583.

God’s crops are those from Jews and Gentiles who have believed, 1281. The elect are God’s grain, 879. What it means for a thistle to grow instead of wheat and a thorn instead of barley, 726. What full grain in the ear signifies, 1330. God’s grain begins from the blade so that it may become a kernel, 1331. Grain becomes green again in renewal from the place where it decays in the dust, 1589.

What it means to afflict Job without cause, [Col. 1401] 74, 782. God does not condemn without cause, 782. What it means to meet someone fleeing with loaves, 756. Whoever remains silent when he ought to speak flees when the wolf comes, 924, 1486. When it is or is not permissible for an apostolic man to flee dangers in God’s cause, 1023, 1024. The person who always throws himself into adversity is reckless; the one who always hides himself is fearful, 1024. Our flight must not take place in winter or on the Sabbath, 1481.

Who is called the midday brightness, 354. Lightning signifies miracles, 862. Saints returning from contemplation bear the likeness of flashing lightning, 1211. The holy preachers are lightning, ibid. The sentence of the final judgment is signified by a thunderbolt, 1120.

What the smoke proceeding from Leviathan’s nostrils signifies, 1111, 1112. By this smoke the light of inward repose is lost, 1113. This smoke disturbs the minds of the elect in one way and blinds the eyes of the reprobate in another, ibid. What is signified by smoke from aromatic substances, 1429.

The Church is signified under the name of a sling, 1125. What it means to lay a foundation in the earth, 506. Christ is the foundation of the Church, 899, 1311. The apostles are the foundations of the Church, 899, and so are the preachers, ibid.

What ropes signify in Scripture, 374, 1087. Whose loins God girds with a rope, 374. What ropes fall in pleasant places, 1087. What the cords of masons signify, 1314. Their use in the construction of a spiritual building, ibid. What a linen cord signifies, 1315. The cord in the hand is preaching put into action, 1315. What cord of measurement Christ uses, ibid. What it means to draw and draw back, lead and withdraw, the cord, 1316.

Like a thief, the heretic hides himself by night, 528. What the thief breaking into a house while its master sleeps signifies, 1483.

Why the future is always desired, 250. The certainty of subsequent events is the presentation of past events, 1436. The present is to be ordered in view of the future, 1649.

## G
Gabriel the archangel was sent for the highest ministry of all, 1604. Gabriel is called “the strength of God,” ibid. Why Gabriel is sent to announce Christ’s coming, 1605.

The Gadites and Reubenites signify those who claim the heavenly homeland, although they do not love it, 864. Galilee signifies transmigration, 1527. Those who pass from vices to virtue will see Christ, 1528.

The cock designates preachers, 959. Why its loins are girded, ibid. What is signified by its having received understanding so that it first examines the hours of the night, 961.

We bring joy to God through our punishment, 307. The joy of the wicked quickly fails, 439. The joy of the wicked is above them, while that of the just is below, ibid. The just regard the joys of the present life as dung; the wicked make much of them, 470. The saints regard the joys of this life as losses of sorrow, 538. Every joy of the mind is excluded by temptation, 757. An ineffable joy arises from a certain compunction, 764. One does not reach it unless the mind has first been purified by the fire of tribulation, ibid. Through joys one comes to weeping, 1443. No one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord, [Col. 1401] 1475. A fervent penitent gives God greater joy than a languid just person, 1602. God rejoices more over certain just people than over any penitent, 1603. Who rejoices and is, as it were, not rejoicing, 1625. The deadly joy of the wicked, 530. The joys of the world must be avoided, 1475.

Gaza the city signifies hell, 1529. Samson’s carrying its gates onto a mountain figures Christ rising and ascending, ibid.

By treasuries (*gazophylacia*) the knowledge of teachers is signified, 1363, 1397. From where *gazophylacium* is derived, ibid. What the pavement of the sacred treasury signifies, 1365. What the thirty treasuries around the pavement signify, ibid. The treasuries of the singers are the holy desires of those who love, 1420. And the hearts of those who love the Judge’s coming, 1421. What the treasuries between the northern and eastern gates signify, 1422. What the treasuries of the Church are, 1364.

What Gideon fighting against the Midianites denotes, 989. The name Gideon signifies the Lord’s incarnation, 990. What Gideon’s soldiers, who drank kneeling and were rejected, represent, ibid. What Gideon’s trumpets, lamps, and jars signify, 991. What it means to hold the trumpet in the right hand and the jar in the left, ibid.

The punishment of Gehenna’s fire is twofold, 334. Gehenna is one for all, but tortures individuals in different ways, 333. The fire of Gehenna is corporeal, 482. The fire of Gehenna is wondrously nourished, ibid. It was kindled from the beginning of the world, ibid. See *Hell*.

Gilboa is interpreted as “a descent” or “a flowing down,” 103. The mountains of Gilboa signify the proud hearts of the Jews, ibid. They signify those who curse, ibid. The hearts of the Jews are compared with ice, 942. What it means for waters to flow from ice, 878. Satan is called ice, 943. Ice signifies adversity, 947.

The saints groan because of the hardships of this exile, and more grievously amid prosperity, 139. Whoever knows himself to be an exile does not cease groaning here, 213. The just groan, and why, 214. Why Christ groaned when opening the ears of the deaf man, 1271. One who does not take care to groan as he ought is to be lamented, 1607.

The four generations signify the four seasons, 1167. Offspring (*genimina*) signify the soul’s good works, 688.

The nations are the firstfruits of the Church, 103. The calling of the nations, hidden from ancient times in God’s plan, 324. The calling of the nations proceeded from the rejection of the apostles by the synagogue of the Jews, 581. The calling of the nations, 613, 659, 939, 970, 1373, 1446. The Church softened the hardness of the nations and overthrew their pride, 582. The Gentile world preceded Judea in receiving the faith, 597. The Gentile world is called the place of God’s mercy, 880. Through the breadth of the plain the nations to be called to the faith are prefigured, 1293. The life of the Gentiles is set before Christians as an example, 9. Why the Gentiles are called blind, 625. The peoples of the Gentiles who were called are signified by the five hundred asses, 25, 1159. The Gentile world consumed the harvest of the Jews, that is, the divine utterances, 183. The nations are foretold as seeking the food of the Law, 216. The Gentiles were raised from their fall on account of faith, 375. The Christian religion was propagated chiefly by the Gentiles, 886. The Gentile world is designated by the north, ibid., 1373, 1397, 1421. Concerning the conversion of the nations, the apostles and other believers from the circumcision praised God [the text reads “lau laverunt”; likely *laudaverunt*, “praised,” but the reading is uncertain], ibid. The Gentile world is a desert watered, as by rain, with heavenly grace, 939. The Gentile world, impassable to prophecy, was opened to grace, ibid. The Gentile world produced works and teaching of eternal life, [Col. 1402] 940. The Gentiles, hard in unbelief, are called stones, 943, 1520. From stones the Gentiles became children of Abraham, ibid., 1520. The converted Gentile world is a raven, whose young are the holy preachers, 969. Before the Lord’s coming the Gentile world is called a wilderness and a land of salt, 987. In that land Christ received a house from the Father, ibid. After Judea was abandoned, Christ possessed the hearts of the Gentile world, ibid., 1017, 1188. The Gentile world, under the names of dragons and ostriches, is destined to glorify God, 1001. The Gentile world is marked by the name of wild honey, 1017. And by the name of locusts, ibid. The Gentile world renewed is designated by the renewal of the hawk, 1038. The foolishness of the Gentiles is signified by the name of asses, 1161. The simple who come to the faith from the Gentile world are signified by Job’s camels, ibid. The calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jews foretold by Ezekiel, 1268. When the Jews fell, the nations were substituted in their place, 1278. God’s glory, previously known to the Jews, was revealed to the nations, 1293. Judea is designated by the east, and the Gentile world by the north, 1373, 1397, 1421. God’s mercy poured out upon the Gentiles, 1373. Why the Gentile world is called a gate, 1397. The Jews are called first, so that, when they refused to come, the Gospel might be preached to the Gentiles, 1446. Why the apostles were forbidden to preach in Asia, 1447. Before the eleventh hour the Gentiles did not labor in God’s vineyard, 1511. The Gentile world destined to be gathered into the Church is prefigured, 1516. The valleys filled signify the Gentile world, filled by the grace of faith in the Mediator, 1518. The sinful woman coming to Christ signifies the converted Gentile world, 1595. The Gentiles are called to the banquet from the roads and hedges, 1623. The nations are called by the prophet “trees of the forest,” ibid.

Getulia has no fishermen, 1469.

Why a hunchback was forbidden by the Law to be advanced to the priesthood, 1585.

Giants are called apostate angels and proud human beings, 546. What it means for giants to groan beneath the waters, ibid.

What it means for ice to come forth from God’s womb, 942, 944.

Spiritually, the sword is the word of God, 634. What it means merely to have a sword, and what it means also to hold it, ibid. What it means to pass from corruption to the sword, 753. By the name of the sword a nearby striking is signified, 1105. The sword signifies many things in Scripture, 1122. What the benevolent and the evil swords are, 1123. Whom the sword is said to seize, ibid. What the sword around the thigh of the Most Powerful signifies, 1246.

Gravel consists of the small stones of rivers, 498, 647. What it mystically signifies, 499, 647, 653. What it means to dwell upon gravel, ibid.

What golden clods signify, 580. What clods compacted in the earth are, 966, 998, 999.

The saints shun the glory of the world, 140, 141. How fragile human glory is, 184. The glory of the world is compared with spiders’ webs, 476. The glory of the world is nothing, 496. How brief human glory is, 538. It is compared with hay, ibid. It is made firm by no stability, 539.

To seek the glory of God through a publicly displayed work belongs to the perfect, 283. In this life God’s glory is known only in part, 549. Through love of heavenly glory, sins that have been committed are felt as more grievous, 839. God promises heavenly glory to people who are almost despairing, 865. Heavenly glory is signified by the name of the cedar, 1058. Ezekiel saw not glory itself but the likeness of God’s glory, 1248. So too what Isaiah saw was God’s glory, ibid. God’s glory is seen in all his works, [Col. 1403] ibid. The place of God’s glory is a holy soul or an angel, 1272.

The glory of the heavenly homeland, 266. God’s glory must be sought through his ways, 538.

Vain glory sometimes arises from wickedness that has been committed, 228. Good works should be hidden, but revealed for God’s glory, 283. Vain glory belongs to a weak mind, 359. Empty glory and pride are two principal vices, 461. They are joined to impiety, ibid. A way to solid and eternal glory is shown to those who seek glory, 538. One lifted up by empty glory soon falls, ibid. And by swelling up is scattered, 539. Vain glory must be avoided when the gift of knowledge is distributed among the people, 701. Those who pursue empty glory in the Church are designated by Elihu, 897. The fruits of the Egyptians ravaged by locusts signify the works of those who seek empty glory, 1018. The splendor of temporal glory is signified by the name of the reed, 1079. And by the name of gold, 1128. Who are more exposed than others to the weapon of empty glory, 1084. Empty glory is signified by the name of the locust, 1113. And by the name of Babylon, 1128. And by the golden cup, ibid. Without zeal for private glory, the just sometimes rebuke the tongues of those who disparage them, 1257. Adam was tempted by the devil through vain glory and overcome, 1493. The daughters of empty glory, 1035. What their temptations are like, 1036.

What is denoted by Goliath’s being beheaded by David with his own sword, 566. What is signified by his being struck with the stone from the sling, 1125.

Gordiana, Saint Gregory’s aunt, 1642. She began well but did not persevere, ibid. She married, having forgotten her consecration, and fell from the state of holiness, 1643.

What a bed signifies in Scripture, 753. Why the healed man is commanded to rise and carry his bed, ibid.

The degrees of the virtues in the saints, 720. What the fifteen steps of the Temple signify, 1151. What the ivory steps signify, 1164. One must not remain at the seventh degree of virtue but must reach the eighth, 1392. What the eighth degree is, ibid. The steps at the gate of the Church are the merits of the virtues, 1329.

What hail is morally, 933. Why hail is called the free rebuke of the saints, 934.

Grace is often thought to be anger, 297. The concurrence of grace and free will, 585. The necessity of grace, which free will must accompany and follow, 511. The harmony of prevenient grace and subsequent free will, 770. The necessity of prevenient grace and the consent of our will for good works, 1101, 1249, 1340. See *Free will*.

Grace is not given for merits, 737. All human beings are born without grace, 598. By God’s grace a person puts off the old man, 1038. No one merits the first grace, 1100. The face of God is the regard of grace, 45. Grace is sometimes usefully withdrawn from the just, 68, 266. By the waters of grace God waters all things, 190. Job ascribes his strength to God, not to himself, 223. The grace of Christ does not free after death the one whom it does not reform now, 255. A blind person thinks that what is grace is anger, 297. Why grace is infused into souls, 323. One must consider what the holy teachers escaped through grace, not what they are through themselves, 575. Infused grace softens the heart toward love and strengthens it for action, ibid. The harvest must be attributed to grace’s dew, 632. We must always consider what we have been from ourselves, 902.

Prevenient grace is called the light of God, 543. In good works God precedes us, 324, 512, 737, 770, 1100. Grace makes us work well, 632, 912. Grace calls the soul of the just; temptation questions it, 661. God’s grace is necessary in all things, 912. God does not abandon one striving toward righteousness, since by his grace he forestalls the sinner, 324. From the inspiration of grace and free will follows meritorious action, 585. Grace is the beginning of merit, ibid., 1100. God does not abandon us even when he is rejected by us, 957. God’s grace is freely given, 1100.

The necessity of actual grace for right living, 324, 543, 708. Grace does not abandon the just person in temptation, 354. The mind that God, in response to guilt, has abandoned cannot be converted, 370. No one resists God when he calls; no one confronts him when he abandons, 371. When grace is withdrawn, the heart withers, ibid. When grace breathes upon it, the earthly-minded heart is overturned and changed, ibid. Having attained purity, one should not attribute it to oneself but to him who alone is pure, 392. God enlightens us by his visitation, not on account of our merit, 639. When he wills, God directs the crooked hearts of human beings toward himself by raising them up through his grace, 783. Then the flesh fails, and the human being returns to ashes through humility, ibid. The one whom grace rescues it fills with the delight of inward satisfaction, 844. God sounds forth wondrously because he does so with silent and hidden power, 872. He refreshes the soul with heavenly food at the same time, ibid. How great is the necessity of grace for overcoming every temptation, 916. God alone opens hearts through grace, 939. Divine grace is necessary so that we may both will and accomplish what is good, 1249. Grace precedes; the will follows, 1249, 1340. Grace is necessary for repentance, 1280. We cannot rise perfectly to good things unless the Holy Spirit precedes and strengthens us, ibid., 1585.

The usefulness of withdrawn grace, 68, 72, 74. The withdrawal of grace is a teacher of humility, ibid. When grace is withdrawn, a human being, who is clay, becomes dust, 323. By disciplining the elect, grace preserves them, while in a sense abandoning them by striking them, 760.

The necessity of cooperating grace, 512. Grace that may quell the heart’s upheavals is necessary, 915. It precedes by inspiring and follows by assisting, 1249. Unless God supplies mercy, the life he grants cannot be preserved, 324. Subsequent grace is the ability to do the good that we will, 708. Those whom God had cast down by frightening them, grace confirms when they have been raised up, 1250. We cannot rise perfectly to good things unless the Holy Spirit both raises us by preceding us and strengthens us by following us, 1280. We must ask for this grace for every work, both for thinking and for doing, 1281.

The walls of the freely given graces are not fortifications of the mind, 376. What the freely given graces are, 554, 888. They will be withdrawn from the Church before the coming of Antichrist, 1118. Or only a few will remain, 1119. Hence mercy is lavished more generously upon the good, while just anger is heaped up against the wicked, ibid. Grace is not given for merits, 737. Rain is called voluntary because it signifies the infusion of grace, 941. Why there are divisions of graces, 1275. Humility is fostered by this division of graces, ibid. Charity is nourished, 1276. Freely given graces are bestowed for the benefit of others, 73. Why they are sometimes withdrawn, 74. God distributes the gifts of graces in different ways, 768, 772, 903. Freely given graces are sometimes bestowed upon the reprobate, 1363.

Human grace. See *Favor*.

There is one kind of gravity through steadfastness and another through guilt, 607.

The conversion of Gregory the Great from the world to the monastic life, 1. Why he delayed his conversion, 2. He changed his mind before his clothing, ibid. He mourns the loss of the quiet of the monastery, ibid. Resistance was overcome by imposing upon him the ministry of the altar and thereafter the burden of pastoral care, 3. Why he had monkish companions in his retinue, ibid. How holily he lived in the monastery, 1283. Lowliness of spirit and trust in God, 3.

Gregory’s low opinion of himself and his very high opinion of Ambrose and Augustine, 1174. With what humility he approached the exposition of the word of God, 1200.
