The humble confession of Saint Gregory, 1283. Gregory’s humility in mourning his own misery, 1293. With humility as his guide, he investigated the higher things of Sacred Scripture, 1319. Saint Gregory’s modesty toward Saint Jerome, 1408. What caused Gregory to interrupt his preaching ministry, 1430. He provides an example of modesty and humility, 993, 1168.

With what diligence Gregory discharged his pastoral care, 1283, 1291. During the solemn celebrations of the Masses he recited—or dictated for recitation—homilies on the Gospels, 1434, 1526. When he could not benefit many by speaking, he at least strove to benefit a few, 1530. Though Gregory’s tongue was silent, his charity burned, 1600.

Gregory carefully compares the Vulgate with the Old Translation and with the translations of the Septuagint, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus, 1233. On what occasion he undertook the exposition of the Book of Job, 3. After completing the exposition, what he thought about himself, 1168.

Gregory once received Christ as a guest, 1600.

How God numbers our steps, 400, 790. What God’s steps are, 517. Steps signify the movements of minds, 682. What the steps of the heart are, 790.

The flock signifies unlearned peoples, 522. What the flock of the holy Church is, 642. One flock from Jews and Gentiles, 1487. Woe to flocks when shepherds become wolves, 1503.

The evils of gluttony, 982. Those who do not take care to subdue the appetite rise heedlessly to spiritual battles, ibid. Gluttony overwhelms all the virtues, ibid. In five ways gluttony tempts us, 983. It is not the food but the appetite that is at fault, ibid. What the daughters of gluttony are, 1036. The temptations of gluttony, 1037. Gluttony is signified by the name of the caterpillar, 1113. Gluttony often carries to excess the refreshment begun for the sake of health, 1168. Adam was tempted and overcome by the devil through gluttony, 1493.

What a hovel signifies, 1097.

- Women were deprived of inheritance according to the law among the Hebrews, 1165. Under the new law the Father also granted women rights to the heavenly inheritance, 1166.
- Heresy is the younger Church, 642, 735.
- Heresiarchs are teachers of heretics; through them the wise are foolishly vaunted, 407.
- The teachers of heresies are the bones of Antichrist, 1063.
- The teachers of heresies are compared with moths, 567.
- They are signified by the gates of Leviathan, 1103, and by his teeth, 1104.
- The Church rejected the ancient heresiarchs from the number of its teachers, 643.
- The inventors of perverse doctrines are called torrents, 647.
- The parents of heretics are foolish and ignoble, 648.
- The powers of the world fortify them, 1104.
- Some rage with words, others with savage swords, ibid.
- Heretics are signified by Job’s friends, 15, 90, 181, 731, 1148.
- How much the Church suffers from heretics, 91.
- The names and actions of Job’s friends signify heretics, ibid.
- While attempting to defend God, heretics offend him, 366, 1148.
- Heretics call their teachers rocks, 438.
- Heretics are like wild asses, 523, and like the ten lepers, 567.
- They are called lamias, 619.
- By the mountain the heretic is understood, 1075.
- Heretics are called rams, 1149.

- Heretics are called defenders, 15.
- Who are called heretics, the friends of the Church, [Col. 1405] 92.
- Those who are wrapped in the errors of heretics are called the heretics’ garments, ibid.
- Lepers represent heretics, 151.
- Why they are called adulterers, 529.
- Why they are called bulls, 1149.
- Heretics are called ungodly and violent, 565.
- Which heretics receive a portion from God and an inheritance from God, ibid.
- Who the widows of heretics are, 566.
- Who are their descendants, 565.
- The curiosity, loquacity, and hypocrisy of heretics are signified by the places associated with Job’s friends, 91.
- By feigned humility they attempt to persuade people of proud things, 93.
- While apparently concerned for God’s honor, they detract from his goodness, 404.
- While appearing to defend divine glory, they look after their own, ibid.
- The works of heretics, which appear great, are rejected by the Church, 643, because they have abandoned love of God and neighbor, ibid.
- Under Christ’s name they wage war against Christ, 644.
- The sacrifices of heretics do not please God, but those offered for them by the Church do, 733.
- Heretics desire to appear learned, not to be learned, 92.
- Heretics pretend to accommodate themselves to the weakened Church, 93.
- Heretics are friendly to those who are silent and oppose those who speak, 94.
- Heretics begin by speaking gently, 151.
- Heretics are as though secure concerning their holiness, 157.
- They pretend to have heard the Lord’s voice, 160.
- They praise the ancient Fathers together with us, 273.
- They despise the present Fathers while claiming that the ancient ones agreed with them, 403.

- Heretics, like Job’s friends, deceive people when they wish to appear to be giving advice, 14.
- Discord among heretics exposes their deceptions, 93.
- At one moment they exalt themselves on account of their unique wisdom, 159; at another they pretend to be afraid, ibid.; at another they pretend to know things incomprehensible to themselves, ibid.
- They say some things openly and keep others hidden, 243.
- What heretics promise their followers, 272.
- Some among the heretics possess purity of heart, 503.
- Heretics hunt the weak and unlearned, both by force and by flattery, 525.
- Heretics cover their faces like adulterers, 529.
- Under the pretext of giving advice, heretics conduct the business of seduction, 731.

- Under the appearance of flattery, heretics prepare deceptions, 93, 94, 151, 158.
- By various devices they persecute the faithful, 94.
- They mix good things with evil, 151.
- The praises of heretics are deceitful, ibid., 273, 380.
- Heretics speak even of holy things fraudulently, 357.
- Heretics protect themselves with the weapons of the powerful, 1022.
- They often mix truth with falsehood, 406, 567.
- They frequently bring forward things not contained in the sacred books, 573.

- Heretics seek only the antiquity of their doctrine, 91.
- They agree against the Church, 92, but are divided into many factions by quarrelling among themselves, ibid., 618.
- They derive earthly meanings from heavenly words, 93.
- While softening their words, they infuse poison, ibid.
- Sometimes they are forced to remain silent, 94.
- The statements of Job’s friends, in which some things are right and others perverse, correspond to heretics, 150, 366, 406.
- Heretics mix right things with perverse ones, 151.
- Heretics are like lepers, ibid.
- Why they seek a new and hidden doctrine, 158.
- To show that what they teach is lofty, they declare that they scarcely understand it themselves, 159.
- They speak certain true and sublime things, 160.
- The Church does not wish to hear from those who bring false teaching about the faith, even when they teach true things about morals, 235.
- The Church refutes the false doctrine of heretics before teaching the truth, 243.
- Heretics abuse the authority of the ancient Fathers, 272.
- They sometimes bring forward good things, but not rightly, 273.
- They then strike themselves with their own sword, ibid.
- The presumption of heretics who consider themselves more learned than others, 358, 407, 448, 505.
- Heretics are fabricators of falsehood, [Col. 1405] 379.
- While pretending to defend God, heretics offend him, 380.
- They falsely flatter themselves concerning the teaching and agreement of the ancient Fathers, 405.
- Heretics boldly define what they do not know, 448, 503, 644.
- Heretics accuse the Church of ignorance when they speak about things unknown, 503.
- Some favor virginity to such an extent that they condemn marriage, 504.
- They presume to teach Catholics, promising peace to those who yield, 508.
- Heretics shift the boundaries of knowledge established by the Fathers, 522.
- What it signifies that the cow of the widow is taken by heretics as a pledge, 523.
- The knowledge of heretics puffs them up, ibid.
- In teaching they carry out not God’s work but their own, ibid.
- They watch for prey, twisting the words of the righteous to suit their own meaning, ibid.
- They devastate a field that is not theirs and a vineyard that is another’s—that is, sacred Scripture, 524.
- By destroying good works, they leave people naked, ibid.
- Heretics are adulterers, corrupting the word of God and perverting the faithful, 529.
- Catholics defeat heretics by the very scriptural testimonies that heretics produce, 566.
- What heretics have said beneficially must be distinguished, 567.
- The teachers of heresies corrupt the minds they occupy, ibid.
- Heretics must be challenged by the sacred pages and the books of the ancient Fathers, 573.
- Heretics were forced into silence in the time of Saint Gregory, 618.

- What is lofty among human beings is abominable before God, 1567.
- An exhortation to humility, ibid.
- Humility is man’s true wisdom, 897.
- Humility repaired man’s fall, 995.
- The lesson of humility is the withdrawal of grace, 68.
- Humility is strengthened by the danger of impending temptation, ibid.
- When someone has subdued grave sins, God leaves him subject to some very slight fault, in order to humble him, 121.
- The rebellious movements of the flesh are useful for humility, 327.
- Man should consider from where he has come and what he is, lest he become proud, 543.
- God tempers the virtues of the elect with temptations so that they may not be exalted, 607.
- The debtor is not acquitted who repays much, but the one who repays everything, 703.
- Humility arises from temptation, 851.
- By a wise distribution of gifts, God takes care of both humility and love, 904.
- When the good consider God’s hidden judgments, they are not exalted and the wicked do not despair, 935.
- Humility is commended by the example set forth by David, 1135.
- When God’s holiness is considered, every saint is called to humility, 1049.
- Humility is fostered by the distribution of graces among the saints, 1275.
- God’s marvelous dispensation in guarding the soul in humility amid prosperity and adversity, 1321.

- God is truly worshiped through humility, 71.
- Let the victor over temptation preserve humility, 97.
- Humility generates love in the one reproved by the reprover; pride generates hatred, 237.
- The saints are troubled by slippery thoughts so that they may know what they are from themselves and what they are from God, 265.
- The saints attribute their good things not to themselves but to God, 691.
- Mercy toward the poor should be accompanied by humility, 692, 697.
- Our strength depends upon humility, 762.
- Humility is the guardian of chastity,
and of the other virtues, 888. The greater the humility, the greater the hope of increase, 972. To the extent that our good works diminish in our own estimation through humility, they increase all the more before God, 973. Humility is a sign of predestination, 1142. Humility exalts, 1294.

—The judgment of humility is to attribute nothing to oneself, but everything to God, 71. At times the righteous may humbly speak of their good works, 405, 450. This is asserted by the examples of Paul and Job, ibid., 450, 623. However humble the righteous may be, they do not fail to recognize their good works, 516. Those who attribute nothing to their own merits are truly humble and holy, 599. When the saints recount their good works under compulsion, they do not serve self-exaltation but the benefit of their hearers, 624. To confess one’s guilt is an indication of humility; to excuse oneself, of pride, 712. The signs of feigned and genuine humility, 811. The mask of humility is quickly cast off, ibid. The more someone knows himself, the more displeasing he becomes to himself, 1145. Let each person strive to be great, but remain unaware that he is great, 1459. One must weigh not what we have, but what we are, 1568. The proud reply of those who excuse themselves feigns humility, 1621.

—It belongs to humility to choose the active life when one’s strength is not suited to the contemplative life, 208. The saints preserve humility at the summit of honor, [Col. 1411] 671. What thoughts of a humble mind are to be maintained amid human praises, 706. When necessity compels one to speak truthfully of the good in oneself, this does not conflict with humility, because it accords with truth, 813. Some, by thinking humbly of themselves, fear being despised; others, by desiring to be despised, become proud of their humility, 889. The humble perform splendid deeds in order to suppress swelling pride, 1045, 1459. Exhortation to humility, 1148, 1461, 1567. One should attend to that in which one’s neighbor surpasses oneself, 1277, 1459. The saints’ devotion to humility, 1459. Humility must be preserved amid scourges, 220. Humility must be retained in knowledge, 503. Humility must be shown in living and speaking, 742. Discernment must be preserved in humility, 846. The rule of humility, 1141, 1567. Humility must be maintained in doubtful matters, 1298.

—Seeing Christ as humble, the proud devil doubted that he was God, 56. The wound inflicted on humanity by the proud devil was healed by God’s humility, 995. The humble God teaches that a human being must not be proud, 1140. What Christ’s teaching concerning humility is, and what opposing teaching belongs to the devil and his members, 1141. Christ commends humility by his example, 1567.

—Humility and power are rarely joined, 835. Superiors should consider the equality of their condition, not the authority of their rank, 689. Unless the necessity of correcting a vice compels them, superiors should avoid being feared or esteemed above others, 690. Understanding does not puff up the heart when consideration of the duty that must be carried out keeps it down, 702. When correcting by right of authority, a superior should consider himself equal to those being corrected: this is the safeguard of humility, 834. Humility must be preserved in the heart, and discipline in action, ibid. God condemns pride in the exercise of power, not eminence itself, 835. Superiors are led toward humility, 1140. The proper relation of humility between superiors and subjects, 1299.

—Humility and pride are compared with one another, 562. Hypocrites strive to appear what they are not; the saints, on the contrary, strive not to appear what they have merited to become, ibid. Some of the saints’ distinguished statements about themselves arise from charity; those of hypocrites from a desire for empty glory, 562. The saints attribute their wisdom to God; the proud attribute it to themselves, 564. The hidden things of Holy Scripture are opened to the humble, while even what is almost openly stated is closed to the proud, 645. Humility opens the light of understanding; pride closes it, 804. Saul was preferred through humility and rejected through pride, 833. In his own eyes Saul was little, but before God he was great—and the reverse, ibid., 1135. The humble esteem even the small works of others and despise their own, even when great; the proud do the opposite, 845. The proud, exalting themselves, bring themselves low; the humble, humbling themselves, are exalted, 1054. Thus pride deserved to be cast down, and thus humility deserved to be exalted, 1074. A discussion of the rule of humility and of pride, 1135. God’s humility against the devil’s pride, 1141. Pride is the clearest sign of rejection; humility, of election, 1142. Truth abandons the proud; it shines upon the humble, 1518. The humble receive the gift that the proud reject from themselves, 1519. Pride earned the confusion of languages; humility earned unity, 1577. When the proud are rejected from the banquet, the humble and poor are chosen, 1621. The Lord knows the humble poor person but does not know the proud rich person, 1655.

Hur is interpreted as “fire,” 1598. Hus is the land of the Gentiles, 17. Hus is interpreted as “conciliator,” 21. Hyacinth signifies hope of heavenly things, 967. The Hyades signify teachers, 294. From where they are so called, 295. [Col. 1412] The dropsical man signifies the avaricious person, 440. The water-filled jars, later changed into wine, signify [something], 1215. Why the present life is signified by winter, 874. How winter may pass, 1349. What it means that our flight should not take place in winter, 1481.

Hypocrisy is designated by the name of the ostrich, 228, 1000. Hypocrisy is signified by a garment woven of wool and linen, 285. Hypocrites cloak their vices under the appearance of virtues, 99, 100. In Scripture hypocrites are sometimes called stars, 111. They are called tigresses, 156. The praise of hypocrites is called plunder, ibid. Those who are like Simon the Cyrenaean: hypocrites, 277, 1588. Why they are called wicked, 285. They are compared to a dungheap, 471. The hypocrite’s place is the heart of flatterers, 472. Hypocrites are called both rich and poor, ibid. The youth of the hypocrite, ibid. The hypocrite is called a thief, 475, 561. In Greek, *hypocrite*; in Latin, *simulator*—a pretender, 561. Hypocrites are like whitewashed tombs, 562. Who is truly a hypocrite, ibid. Hypocrites are designated under the person of Herod, 1469, and by the lamia, 1107.

—The hypocrite feeds wicked spirits with his fruits, 276. He feeds himself for the present, but not after death, ibid. The hypocrite, having assumed the appearance of holiness, is worse, 279. The boastfulness of hypocrites, 282. What it means to prepare the hypocrite’s womb for deceit, 418. Who is innocently stirred up against the hypocrite, 431. The hypocrite’s life is like an apparition, 471. Hypocrites, pretending to possess many things they do not have, lose even what they do possess, 473. They confess things they have never committed, 474. All vices are joined together in the hypocrite’s mind, 482. The shoot of the hypocrite’s house is his intention, 484. Hypocrites are members of Antichrist, 807.

—The virtues of hypocrites are false and disfigured by concealed vices, 156, 278. As the tigress seizes its prey, so the hypocrite seizes the glory of human approval, 156. The hypocrite has the appearance of good works, but not their fruit, 273, 651. The hypocrite is impatient of correction, 274. The abstinence of hypocrites is empty, 277. The hypocrite imposes the cross upon the flesh but lives for the world, ibid. As soon as he acts rightly, he wants to be praised, 279, 281. He considers the work lost if it is done without witnesses, 281. The hypocrite who displays his riches to enemies provokes them to plunder, 282, 1472. The hypocrite flees God’s sight while wishing to please human eyes, 383. Why the hypocrites’ good works wither, 414. Hypocrites rebuke the sins of others more harshly but leave their own untouched, 449. The conduct of hypocrites is described, 470. The life of hypocrites is exposed at the end, 471. Vices never leave them, 472. The hypocrite is without faith, hope, and charity, 476. The hypocrite is avaricious and rapacious, 561. The ambition of hypocrites, ibid. Hypocrites consider themselves holy because they are called holy, 841. Whoever attempts to deceive others is also deceived about himself, ibid. They display the appearance of virtue while lacking true virtue, 945. The appearance of a feather seems to lift hypocrites, but the weight of their life brings them down, 1001. Why hypocrites do not know the compassion of charity toward their own, 1005. Neglecting the guardianship of their children, they ward off even minor temporal losses with quarrels, 1006. How certain people differ from hypocrites by defending temporal goods more fiercely, 1007. The hypocrite mocks not only the saints but God himself, 1008. The devices of hypocrites, who conceal what they are inwardly, 1102.

—Hypocrites desire to imitate the works of the righteous, 113. They desire daily to appear loftier, 281. The various deceptions of hypocrites, 156. Hypocrites feign all virtues through vices, 156. Those who conceal their craftiness, 285. The characteristics of hypocrites, 286, 1006, 1202. In the hypocrite’s mouth evil is sweet, 473. The fabrications of hypocrites, 649, 1000. Hypocrites wish to appear imitators of the holy Fathers, ibid. Under the appearance of serving God, they yearn for earthly things, 1096.

—It belongs to hypocrites to put forward sweet words while plotting perverse things in their thoughts, 473. The hypocrite desires to be instructed in the holy mysteries of Scripture, not in order to live by them but in order to exalt himself, 474. He understands a word of Holy Scripture perversely, because he seeks it wrongly, ibid. The hypocrite loses the knowledge that he refused to put into practice when he knew it, ibid. In the words of his teaching he holds opinions by which he will be condemned, 475. Hypocrites neglect to support and nourish by good examples those whom they beget through their word, 1002.

—The life of hypocrites is compared to a reed, 273, 278, 281, 284. Hypocrites receive the greenness of good action from a divine gift, 274. Why the speech of hypocrites does not set others aflame, 276. The vanity of hypocrites’ abstinence, 277. The hypocrite’s mind is never free from thoughts of wickedness, 416. What the hypocrite’s way of life is like, 470. The hypocrite’s life is compared to a dream, ibid. Hypocrites say one thing and do another, 473. The hypocrite will be condemned more severely because of his teaching, 475. Hypocrites are without mercy, 1601.

—The hope of hypocrites is vain, and they have no reward from God, 112, 275. Hypocrites cannot long enjoy their hope, 275. The hypocrite is like a fruitful but neglected vine, 276. The hypocrite’s confidence is vain, ibid. The hypocrite’s good works are nothing before God, ibid. The hypocrite’s vain reward is scattered in the presence of the inner Judge, 277. He procures the admiration of human beings for himself with all his intention, 281. God grants the hypocrite the gifts needed for works but denies him a share in the inheritance, 284. Why the hypocrite’s good works are sterile, 416. Here the hypocrite occupies another’s place, only to be thrust later into his own, 446. The hypocrite will pay eternal punishment as though it were a debt, 472. The hypocrite’s hope is intent upon present things, and none upon future things, 562. Deceived by eternal hope, hypocrites do not flee to the remedy of confession even at the point of death, 841. The labors of hypocrites are fruitless, 1372. The works of hypocrites fail before the end of life, 274. They are compared to spiders’ webs, 276.

—The light of hypocrites is darkened by manifest error, 112. They will not see the glory of the Church at the final judgment, 113. They do not persevere in good works, 274. The hypocrite’s house cannot stand when praise passes away with life, 278. Nor will the hypocrite’s confidence in holiness stand at the judgment, ibid. The hypocrite’s house is supported in vain and falls at the judgment, ibid. Now the hypocrite is believed holy, but when Christ comes he will appear wicked, 279. At the end the hypocrite is rejected, 284. The hypocrite’s end is like the awakening of one who is asleep, 472. What portion the hypocrite has from God, 484. Hypocrites die in a sudden storm, 842.

—Hypocrites, seeing the works of the righteous but not their intention, desire their praises, 113, 651. Hypocrites, having overcome even one vice, consider themselves perfect, 158. They misuse God’s gifts to their own condemnation, 273. They do not desire to be holy, but to be called holy, 274, 470, 561. The hypocrite sells a thing of great value for a cheap price, 275. The blindness of the hypocrite who believes that he has pleased God as he has pleased human beings, 384, 471. Outwardly the hypocrite abounds; inwardly he is empty, 472, 614. The hypocrite does not call upon God except when placed in distress, 564. Hypocrites do not possess religion but pretend to it, 614. What they are like, they refuse to be seen by human beings as being, [Col. 1413] 652, 841. The torpor of hypocrites toward heavenly things and their ardor for earthly things, 1005. Hypocrites place the usefulness of temporal things before the usefulness of souls, 1006. The hypocrite neglects the correction of his subjects, ibid.

—Hypocrites are darkened by the fog of their error, 112. For the sake of empty favor they receive eternal torments, 276. Their punishment is manifold, both for themselves and for those whom they deceived, 284; also because of good works performed without a good intention and because of their deceits, 285. The hypocrite is tormented by the goods of others, 416. The joy in which the hypocrite delights passes quickly; his punishment remains eternal, 470. The glory in which he delights is turned into the venom of asps, 474. The more quickly the hypocrite grows, the more swiftly he is carried off to eternal punishments, 479. The hypocrite who has neglected the days of patience will be dragged away on the day of wrath, 484. Since he did not hear God speaking in the Law, when he prays at the end God will not hear him, 563. Even when struck, hypocrites are ashamed to confess their sins, 840. A description of the punishments inflicted at the end upon the minds of hypocrites, 841. God gave hypocrites over to a reprobate mind, 1008. In hypocrites the scales of their defenses are harder, 1107. Exalted by their arrogant claim to holiness, they are poor, blind, and naked, 1118.

Hyssop: what it denotes, 207.

# I

- **Ibexes:** what they are and what they signify, 972.
- **The idol of jealousy:** what it is, 1005.
- What it means that Rachel covered the idols while sitting, 989.
- **Idumea** signifies the Gentile condition, 1459.
- **Fire** signifies zeal, 18.
- **The fire of God:** what it is, 66, 1247.
- The double punishment of hellfire, 335.
- How light and darkness can simultaneously exist in fire, 334.
- Fire, for restraining or exercising action, is subject to the Creator, 335.
- It acts equally upon reprobate angels and upon human beings, ibid.
- The fire of hell is corporeal, 482. See **Hell; Gehenna**.
- Fire signifies the Holy Spirit, 1187, 1246; and also the wickedness of the mind, 1187.
- What the fire burning the thorns signifies, 1258.
- The wicked man is cast into the furnace of fire, 1474.

- **Ignorance:** the human mind suffers from ignorance of itself, 269, 305, 929, 1045.
- The usefulness and disadvantage of this ignorance, 304.
- How serious it is for a righteous person to be ignorant of where he goes astray, 316, 803.
- Many are ignorant of the weight of the sins by which they are burdened, 330.
- The punishment of those who are ignorant of God, 446.
- Ignorance of God’s hidden matters is useful to us, 448.
- Ignorance of what ought to be done is the punishment of sin, 452.
- It is one thing not to know God’s ways, another to be unwilling to know them, 488, 804.
- Not knowing is ignorance; having been unwilling to know is pride, 804.
- The former deserve; the latter provoke God’s anger, 840.
- If anyone knows what he now is, he utterly ignores what he will be, 933.
- No human being knows his own beginning or end, ibid.
- Christ is exempt from this law, ibid.
- Ignorance of judgment is called night, 1478.

- He commits nothing unlawful who abstains from what is lawful, 146.

- **Image:** Created according to the image of his Maker, man disdains to imitate the multitude of the common people, 981.

- **Rain:** what the late rain signifies, 636.
- What “seasonal” and “late” rain mean, ibid.
- What the rain of God’s strength and the rain of God’s weakness signify, 874.
- The course of rain is the fervor of preaching, 938. See **Rain**.

- We ought to imitate the life of the saints who preceded us, 204.
- We ought to follow God’s footsteps by imitating his piety and patience [Col. 1414], 517.

- The proud are called savage, 863.
- A description of the savage who exists in a place of humility, 864.

- He cannot stand immovably who loves mutable things, 275.

- Impurity destroys all virtues, 688.
- Impurity is signified by the ass, 870.

- Impatience is almost always allied with power, 672.
- Impatience must be avoided in temptations, 852.
- Against the impatient, 1370.
- Human beings are for the most part impatient, 1494.
- The impatient disclose certain things about themselves that were unknown, 716.

- It is the vice of inexperience to understand what is right incorrectly, 897.

- **The impulses of spirit and flesh:** what they are, 1205.
- We must attend to what impulse leads us—of the flesh or of the spirit, 1206.
- What the contrary effects of each are, ibid.

- Human impiety harms the one whom it defiles by corrupting him, 820.
- Impiety does not differ from pride, 1053.
- Impiety belongs to unbelief, 1285.
- The wicked are compared with a fruitless tree, 535.
- How the wicked differ from the unrighteous, 561.
- Likewise, how they differ from the sinner, 801.
- Who is properly called wicked, ibid., 835.
- The wicked way pertains to perverse action, 1285.

- The wicked praise and defend their evil works, 119.
- The eyes of the wicked fail: they desire earthly things and neglect eternal ones, 357.
- The one concern of the wicked is to satisfy their own desires, 358.
- Having despaired of salvation, the wicked continually increase in wrongdoing, 409.
- Each wicked person rushes headlong by his own counsel, 439.
- What the counsels of the wicked are, ibid.
- The wicked care not to be good, but only to be called good, 470.
- The wicked despise the ways of the Lord, 488.
- The wicked always desire to sin with impunity, 530.
- The wicked will be carried away by a burning wind—that is, by the devil, 570.
- The wicked strive to reproach the good for the exaltation of their deeds, 350.
- The wicked presume to teach others, 358.
- They consider themselves alone to be wise, ibid.
- They thrust their evils upon the good by reproach, 417.
- What the counsel of the wicked is, 320, 439.
- The wicked reject God by their conduct, 488.
- They are unwilling to know the ways of God, ibid.
- They lay their foundation in the earth, 506.
- The heart of the wicked is compared with a stone, 1120.

- The weak are disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked, 184.
- The prudent despise their glory, ibid.
- For the wicked there is some escape from misery here; after death there is none, 357, 439.
- From the prosperity of the wicked their sins multiply, 440.
- Thus they rejoice in the night of sin as though the light of righteousness surrounded them, 530.
- The exaltation of the wicked is ruin, 508.
- The wicked are nourished by human praise, 112.
- The goods of the wicked are transitory, 663.
- Why God permits the wicked to prosper, 154, 660.
- The wicked are fattened here like calves destined for slaughter, 681.
- Everything is granted to the wicked as to hopelessly ill persons, ibid.
- In prosperity they are fixed with a firm root, 184.
- In this life they pitch their tent, 286.
- In grievous circumstances the wicked seek escape, 357.
- They trust only in earthly matters, 408.
- The end of the wicked’s complete prosperity comes in an instant, 487.
- Emerging groans often interrupt the joys of the wicked, 490.
- The prosperous wicked are reserved for the day of destruction, 496.

- The wicked does not escape God’s vengeance through his own cunning, 306.
- The wicked mind is always in distress, 409.
- When the wicked person finds himself bound by desire, he burns more fiercely, 440.
- Guilt closes the eyes of the wicked; punishment opens them, 492.
- Those who have hardened themselves in iniquity, 493.
- In what sense God is said both to behold and to forget the life of the wicked, 535.
- One must grieve over the misery of the perishing wicked person and rejoice with the Judge’s justice [Col. 1415], 709.
- The wicked are always trembling, 409.
- The wicked will be tormented without end, 477.
- They will be punished in soul and body, 482, 508.
- In an instant the wicked descend to hell, 487.
- At the judgment the wicked will be scattered like chaff and ashes, 491.
- How the wicked are taken away before their time, 505.
- In Gehenna the wicked will be crushed, 535.
- God does not hear the cry of the wicked in distress, 563. See **Unrighteous; Evil; Sinner**.

- Frequent guilt generates shamelessness, signified by a worn forehead, 1259.

- The earring is a symbol of obedience, 1155.

- The benefits of Christ’s incarnation, 212.
- The order of Christ’s incarnation, 552.
- When the Lord was incarnate, discordant hearts were joined together, 551.
- The wonders of God’s incarnation, 598.
- The manner of the Word’s incarnation, ibid.
- The incarnation of the Word is the root of the Church, 631.
- The incarnation is signified by the name “shadow,” 1077. See **Christ’s incarnation**.

- The incestuous Corinthian was unwillingly handed over to the one to whom he had voluntarily submitted himself as punishment, 1086.

- For God to enclose a sinner is for God not to open what has been shut, 371.

- The extent and source of the instability of the human mind, 849. See **Mind**.

- **Reproof:** that affliction should be abandoned, 418.
- How great the freedom of the saints is in reproving rulers, 236.
- The powerful generally ought to be reproved, 419.
- How great is the danger of the person who is not made better by reproofs, 1584.

- **India and Indian-dyed colors:** what they signify, 592.

- We are needy all the more truly the more inwardly we are so, 693.

- The periods granted for repentance must not be neglected, 1479, 1481. See **Repentance**.

- **Indulgence** is the remission of some fault, 1067.
- Whoever now indulges himself in sin will not later be indulged in punishment, 383.

- Infants are condemned to eternal punishments on account of original sin unless it is removed by baptism, 303. See **Baptism; Original sin**.

- **Hell:** why it is called the dark earth, 331.
- It is called a lake, ibid.
- It is the land of misery and darkness, ibid.
- Whoever neglects to mourn his sins goes there, 331.
- Hell contains vengeance, not light, 332.
- What it means to descend into hell with one’s weapons, ibid.
- A description of the punishments of hell, 333.
- The reprobate are tormented by the sight of their companions in crimes, 334.
- Hell is twofold, interior and superior, 397.
- The superior is the place where the righteous rested until Christ’s coming, 397, 433. See **Bosom**.
- Why Christ is said, by rising again, to have bitten hell, 398, 1533.
- The hell of the devil is called the expanse of the air, 435.
- What it means for the living to descend into hell, 565.
- Hell is believed to have no bottom, 844.
- The Lord descended for us not only into the world but also into hell, 927.
- The Lord walked about in hell, coming free to those who were bound, ibid.
- By rising again Christ did not restore those condemned to eternal punishments to forgiveness, 1533.
- Each bodily member will be tormented by punishments appropriate to it, 1641.
- There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, ibid.
- Why the chief heat of hellfire is in the tongue of the rich banqueter, 1653.
- Hell cannot be penetrated by any sense of ours, 927.

- The punishments of hell are neither temporary nor imaginary, 331.
- How great the pain in hell is, 261.
- The fire of hell has no light, but only burning, 332.
- Those whom hell holds are tortured outwardly and blinded inwardly, 331.
- The punishments of the damned are proportioned by the just Judge to their crimes [Col. 1415], 332, 1132.
- They are not ordered within the heart of the damned, 333.
- There fire denies light for consolation but preserves it for torment, 334.
- It is not useful to know the punishments of hell beforehand, but to escape them, 335.
- The reprobate do not believe in the eternity of punishments, 1132.
- The eternity of this fire is affirmed, ibid.
- It is just that sinners be assigned to eternal punishments, ibid.
- In hell, knowledge and memory are preserved for the reprobate’s punishment, 1658.
- To increase their punishment, the reprobate see the glory of those whom they despised, ibid.
- One must think about punishment itself before the punishment, 1659. See **Gehenna**.

- The virtues of unbelievers are nonexistent, 65.
- The life of those placed under the Law is reproved by the life of unbelievers, 9.
- Unbelievers will not rise in order to be judged, but in order to be tormented, 836.
- The savagery of unbelievers toward preachers of the Word of God, 955. See **Nations; Gentiles**.

- The weak are disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked, 184.
- When they suddenly see the wicked cast down, they then condemn their prosperity, ibid.
- When the weak and undiscerning person has sometimes acted well, he is raised up more dangerously, 389.
- The weak should not reproach the deeds of the strong, 148.
- When the weak see the wicked flourishing and the righteous being tormented, they often desist from good work, 431.
- Why the weak envy the successes of the wicked, ibid.
- The weak measure sins by the scourges of others, 496.
- The weak consider someone as righteous in proportion to his prosperity, 511.
- Lowly teachings ought to be preached to the weak, 548.
- The spirit of the weak trembles at hearing the truth, 572.
- Many of the weak, compelled by persecution, will fall at the end, 612.
- The losses of the weak pass over to the hearts of the strong, ibid.
- The weak, struck by severe tribulation, fail through faintheartedness, 822.
- Fear restrained the weak people from sin, 913.
- Whoever considers his hidden weaknesses presses himself down in humility, 1008.
- God chose the weak and ignoble things of the world to destroy the devil’s strength, 1095.
- The ruin of the strong supplies increase to the perdition of the weak, 1127.
- The weak ought to flee the company of the wicked, 1259.

- Bodily weaknesses weaken the mind, 6.
- Our weakness is strengthened by God’s strength, 134.
- Consideration of one’s own weakness calms anger, 177.
- How many weaknesses the human body is subject to, 268.
- Bodily health itself is a kind of illness, ibid.
- How many weaknesses the soul itself is also subject to, ibid.
- Weakness is the guardian of virtue, 608, 609.
- What the weakness of human nature is like, 649.
- Consideration of our weakness is necessary when correcting others, 743.
- How great human weakness is when God abandons it, 760.
- How useful it is to consider one’s weakness, 762.
- The weakness of a person unable to sustain the good for which he was created, 1248.

- Why a slow disposition is given to the diligent and a keen one to the negligent, 187.

- The ungrateful mind recalls by how many gifts of God it has been pricked, 259.
- We ought to be ashamed to fight against God by means of his benefits, 974.

- He pursues with desire an enemy who is standing, though he rejoices when that enemy has fallen, 708.
- How one may rejoice at an enemy’s ruin without injury to charity, or grieve over his glory, 709.
- It is one thing to be wicked and another to endure an enemy, ibid.
- What must be avoided in sadness or joy concerning an enemy’s ruin or glory, ibid.
- Evil must not be wished upon an enemy, 710.

Job confesses that he received piety from God, from whom he received existence, 691. Job’s humility was as great as is scarcely found in a few people, 705. He attributed his good works to God their author, not to himself, 708. Job’s humility in confessing sin, 714. Job was more exalted in confessing sins than in performing virtues, ibid. In recounting his virtues he was moved neither by pride nor impatience, 717. Job was greatest because he was inferior to God alone, 892. Job humbly confessed to God, who reproved him, that he had sinned, 1047. After contemplating God’s wisdom, Job’s own wisdom seemed worthless to him, 1242. Why Job said that he had spoken foolishly, 1143. Job believed that he was scourged for guilt and not for grace, 1147.

Job was strong not through madness but through a state of salvation, 222. Job’s steadfastness in the loss of his substance and children, 19, and against all the devil’s devices, 729, 730. He was afflicted inwardly and outwardly, 304. Job’s courage, by which he was not overcome by the successive changes of his adversaries, 337. How great a contempt for riches shone forth in Job, 366. Job remained unbroken: after losing everything else, he had not lost God, 494. How greatly Job feared God’s judgment, 303.

Job devoted himself to works of mercy, 619, 625. Job’s generosity in giving truly to the poor according to their requests, 691. Job’s generosity must be assessed not only by the gift but also by the speed of giving, ibid.

Job’s curses cannot be understood literally without absurdity, 101. Neither David’s nor Jeremiah’s imprecations are to be taken literally, 103. Job’s curse proceeds not from the malice of the offender but from the rectitude of the judge, 106. He curses the day of mutability from the perspective of eternity, ibid.

Job’s wife signifies those who give evil counsel through mental arrogance, 89, and the carnal thought that assails the mind, 98. Job’s wife is a figure of the carnal people in the Church who assist the devil, 181.

Whether Job’s friends sat with him for seven days and nights continuously is uncertain, 82. They approached Job with the right intention of consoling him, but abandoned uprightness in speech, 83. Job’s friends had a pious intention but incautious speech, 148, 273, 406, 446. What they ought to have done in order to fulfill their pious intention, 148. In what way God censures, and Paul commends, the statements of Job’s friends, 150, 406. Their statements are [Col. 1421] valid in many cases but are wrongly applied to Job, 150, 182, 337, 438, 469, 784, 818, 830, 844, 852. Eliphaz’s harsh words against Job, 155. Provoked by the words of his friends, Job answered rightly, 211. Job’s friends, ashamed because of his trust in God, 234. Bildad’s harsh words against Job, 446. Job’s friends ought to have mourned for themselves, not harshly reproved their afflicted friend, 448. The error of those who think that everyone afflicted by God has been condemned by him, 449, 469, 485, 496. What the bulls and rams sacrificed for Job’s friends signify, 733, 1151. Elihu, thinking rightly but speaking arrogantly, is rejected, 897. God’s judgment concerning Job and his friends, 1146. Why Job is acquitted while they are condemned, ibid. God reproved Job’s friends through justice and converted them through mercy, 1148. What the seven sacrifices they are commanded to offer signify, 1151. The order of the forgiveness granted by God to Job’s friends, 1152. Provoked by the disparaging words of his friends, Job returned to his conscience, 1255. Driven by false speeches onto the earth, he sought a witness in heaven, ibid.

Job stood between God and the devil, who were contending in him, 11, 44. The order observed by the devil in tempting Job, 11, 49, 77, 104. God permits the tempter some things and denies others, 46. The devil tries to overthrow Job’s steadfastness through sudden calamities, 48. He multiplies the wounds and provokes Job to hatred of God, ibid. Job’s blows were sudden and numerous, 49. Why the devil struck Job’s children in the house of the firstborn, ibid. Job struck down the proud enemy by humility and crushed the cruel one by patience, 52. Job inflicted harsher wounds on the enemy than he endured, ibid. Tested, Job lost earthly goods but multiplied heavenly ones, ibid. The devil’s envy toward Job, 73. Job, handed over to the adversary, was preserved under the guardianship of his helper, 75. Why Satan was commanded to spare Job’s life, 76. By marvelous arts the devil tested Job in an attempt to overthrow him, 77, 78. He stirred up Job’s wife against him, 78. The devil’s intention in afflicting blessed Job, 320. Struck by Satan, Job did not attribute his affliction to Satan, 459. As many wounds as the devil inflicted on Job, so many victories did he confer on the holy man, 729. The devil stirred Job’s friends against him from their several places, 730. The scourges inflicted on Job by Behemoth, 1074.

The devil brought inward poisons of counsel against Job through his wife, 12. Using the woman as a kind of ladder into Job’s heart, the devil tried in vain to climb, 78. The devil moved Job’s wife’s tongue, ibid. Job’s wife insulted him, 88, 1388. Job’s wife is a figure of the carnal in the Church, 88, 181, 731. Job regarded the woman as subject to him, not set over him, 78. Job’s wife represented those who succumb through the pride of the wicked, 89. What Job’s wife’s provoking him to curse signifies, 98, 731.

Job’s friends led him toward despair, 11. They went beyond bounds more from ignorance than malice, 12, 13. They are figures of heretics, 15, 90, 271, 379, 403, 731, 1148. The interpretations of their names, 15. Blessed Job was tested through his friends, 80. Their right intention was darkened by indiscretion, 81. In order to lift up afflicted Job, his friends first tried, through mourning, to harmonize with his grief, 81. Job’s friends grieved in consolation more than was necessary, 82. His friends sinned in speech, though they had first earned merit by silence, ibid., 83. The circumstances of Job’s friends correspond to the actions of heretics, 91. What it means that Job’s friends are said to have sat with him in the dust for seven days, 93. What it means for Job to sit on the ground, ibid. Through the things [Col. 1422] rightly done by Job’s friends, the things wrongly to be done by heretics are signified, 95. Job’s friends sinned by rising up against him, 149. Job’s friends preached many good things to him, 152. Job answered his friends in three ways, 236. In the three names of Job’s friends, three falls into destruction among heretics are expressed, 732.

Afflicted by God, Job refrained from murmuring with mouth and heart, 52. The God who afflicted Job both fruitlessly and not fruitlessly, 74, 429, 450, 516, 729, 782, 844, 1049. God afflicted Job, his friend, with pains as far as the dung heap, just as he willed his prophet John to be punished by beheading, 77. Struck by blows, Job gave thanks, 211. Job judged himself to have been struck by God as an enemy, 454. Job questioned by God through the scourges, 898. Whether Job was afflicted by God’s just judgment, 450. Why God testifies that he afflicted blessed Job without cause, ibid. Amid the scourges Job believed that he had displeased God, 486. Why Job was permitted to be scourged, 516, 1049. Job was scourged for grace, 745. Job differed from God in no fault, 1049. Why he was reproved by the Lord’s words, ibid. Why Job was humbled by God, 1388.

Job receiving double, what he represents, 16, 1153. Job preserved his innocence more gloriously under the blow, 74. The epilogue of Job’s sufferings, 891. First he is praised by God’s voice, then he grew through the blow, ibid. How God answered Job from the whirlwind, 896. God’s pious and measured reproof of Job, 1044. Job was justly corrected so that, even unknowingly, he might submit to God’s hidden judgments, 1049. How greatly Job profited from the scourging, 1145. Whether Job sinned after the scourges, ibid. After the scourges, Job represents Christ at the end of the world, 1155. Why the Lord did not double Job’s children as he did his other substance, 1159. What is signified by the animals restored to blessed Job after the scourges, ibid. The reason for the number of animals restored to blessed Job, 1162. What Job’s daughters’ names signify, 1163. Job, restored to his former condition and also increased in possessions, is a type of the Church, 1166.

Who was the author of the Book of Job, 7. Job himself wrote it after the contests had been completed, ibid. The mode of speech in Job is parabolic and mystical, 557. The Book of Job was first written in Arabic, 665. Comparison of passages in Job and Isaiah, 1042. Some believe that Job was Jobab, 7.

Jonah vainly tries to resist God, who is sending him to Nineveh, 195. God’s marvelous providence toward Jonah, ibid. Why Jonathan deserved the sentence of death, 983. What is signified by the name Jordan, 1082, 1083, 1557.

Joseph the patriarch fleeing after abandoning his cloak, what he signifies, 62. His history is described, 194, 1414. From it it is evident that those who resist God’s plans, or do so unwillingly, nevertheless serve them, ibid. Joseph teaches us continence, 860, 974, 1338. By what means he conquered lust, 974. Joseph teaches discretion as the mean between excessive severity and overly lax mercy, 1414. He acts harshly toward his brothers out of charity, 1415. Mercy lay hidden under the appearance of anger, ibid. The Lord willed Joseph to have as his spouse the mother of the one who did not come to her wedding, 1557. Joseph was the unimpeachable guardian of Mary’s virginity, ibid.

Joshua teaches us steadfastness, 860, and hope in doubtful circumstances, 1339. Jovinianus condemned virginity, 618. The Jubilee year signifies complete rest, 22, 1360, 1378. The lips [Col. 1423] are filled with jubilation when the voice sounds what speech cannot explain, 285. What jubilation is, 764, 910. Why jubilation is fitting for human beings but not for angels, ibid. Why the Jubilee year was instituted, 1150.

The penance of Judas the betrayer was condemnable, 370. He repented of his sin worse than he had sinned, 371. Comparison of Judas and the Thief: God mercifully established the latter at the end, but justly crushed the former, 797. Judas, who succumbed to the cruelty of Antichrist, 923. Judas harmed the Lord more grievously than if he had not belonged to his household, 1614.

God gave Judea to Christ and took it away, 62. Judea did not recognize the Redeemer who was coming, 113. It saw neither the light of the coming Christ nor that of the rising Church, ibid. Judea is signified by the south, 886, and by the gate, 1397. At Christ’s advent Judea was divided into four kingdoms, 1516. Judea will be converted at the end of the world, 1532.

The preachers of the Jews are called oxen, pressed by the yoke of the law, 25. Jews adhering only to the letter of the law are like camels, 59. The Jews are Christ’s brothers, known and related to him, 454. The priests of the Jews are called tenants of God’s house, ibid. The Jewish people are called the stone of darkness, 576. The Jewish people were the shadow of death, ibid. Why the Jews are called inaccessible, 578. The Jews are called wild asses and dragons among the rocks, 940. Why the Jewish kingdom is represented under the name of a shaken reed, 1079. Why the Jews are called broods of vipers, 1519.

The Jews suffered darkness in the daytime, 196. The Jews, believing Christ to be merely human, were deprived of knowledge of his divinity, 62, 377. The Jews are crushed in Christ, who is the gate, 183. The Jews, who unwillingly cared to join the faithful to Christ their head through death, 195. The Jews repelled the light of the Gospel from themselves by casting out the apostles, 290, 291, 967. The Jews were deprived of the gift of prophecy, which they had abused, 309. The Jews’ blindness toward Christ suffering humanly and displaying divinely, 377. The hearts of the Jews are called the cave of the beast, that is, of the devil, 876. Blinded by the glory of their knowledge, 921. Through pride they lost the light of understanding, 1014. The Jews boast of their blindness, 290. The Jews were blinded because they refused to believe the truth, 921, and because they clung to the letter, 955. The Jews, wrapped in a great cloud and blinded after rejecting Christ, 1187. The blindness of the Jews who deny Christ, whom all things confess, 1468. The Jews had foreknown that Christ would be born and where, to their condemnation as a testimony, but to our assistance in believing, ibid. The Jews are like Isaac in his blindness, ibid. The Jews were blinded by the pride of unbelief, 1518. Christ gave the Jews, who are a shield, the labor of the heart, 1532.

The Jews rejected spiritual understanding in carnal sacrifices, 95. At Christ’s coming they refused to follow faith, 103. They denied Christ present whom they had foretold as coming, 375. Few of the Jews were converted by Christ, 455. The Jews resisted while the apostles preached, 290, 578, 1268. How the heart of the Jewish leaders was changed, 377. The Jews refused to be subject to their author; therefore they were scattered and subjected to the nations, 291. The fall of the Jews was so much more grievous as they had been adorned with more gifts, 579. The fire consuming Job’s sheep and boys signifies the priests’ envy against Christ, 58. God gave them the shield of hardness of heart, 1106. The Jews are compared to stones because of their insensibility, 943. The hearts of the Jews [Col. 1423] hardened against God through the frost of envy, 878. The Jews were cast out, as it were, from the womb of divine mercy because of their hardness, 942. The Jews’ hardening was foretold, 1268. The hardness of the Jewish heart at the Lord’s birth, 1468. The terrible hardening of the Jews, 113, 378, 659, 955. Christ hides himself from the Jews, who became worse through his preaching, 1509. Many Christians who condemn the Jews imitate their hardness, ibid.

The Jews were subjected to the nations because they refused to be subject to God, 291. They were destroyed by the Romans because they rejected the Gospel, 290.

The Jews are foolish and subject to the curse of heretics because they rejected Christ, 182. All the unbelieving are the children of these Jews, ibid. They believed that Christ would come but denied him when present, 375, 377, 454, 457, 1154, 1468. The Jews were despised because of their unbelief, 375. Christ appeared as a stranger in the eyes of the Jews, 455. Christ was despised by his servant, that is, by the Jewish people, ibid. When Christ ceased performing miracles, the Jews disparaged him, 456. The teachers of the law abominated Christ, 457. The Jews raged against Christ with the anxiety of cruelty, 877. The Jews swelled with malicious pride like dragons drawing in the wind, 940. The Jews despised the labor, that is, the humanity, of the Lord, 1106. Blinded even to the madness of persecution, the Jews broke out against Christ, 1187. He manifested his divinity to them, 1508. Through Christ’s preaching the Jews became worse, 1509. They ceased to be children of Abraham because of unbelief, 1520. The Jews rejoice that he was killed, but grieve that he is dead, 1529. By what devices the Jews sought to kill Christ, 877. They persecuted Christ because of his miracles, 878. They refused to believe in him because of his humility, 1106. The Jews’ pride preferred to despise Christ’s incarnation rather than follow it, 378. The Jews held the law in their mouths but persecuted the author of the law, 579. After so many benefits had been conferred upon them by God, the Jews arranged his death, 921. The Jews’ unbelief and rejection, 310. Once the Jews were rejected, the Gentiles were chosen without merits of their own, 547, 805. The Jews were stripped of the sacred utterances, 567. The gold by which the Jews shone was darkened by the shadows of unbelief, 580. The Jews refused to receive the words of life, raging against its preachers, 581. The Gentiles were substituted for the Jews in faith, 659, 942, 943, 967. Why no one should investigate this, 805, 854. The apostles and other faithful feared the rejection of the Jews, 887. Serving the letter, they refused to cling to God through charity, 921. They lost knowledge of the law because they refused to believe the truth, ibid. The Jews’ proud observance of the law was rejected, ibid. The Jews, from being children of Abraham, became stones through obstinacy, 943. Judea, caught in the snare of its error, awaits Antichrist instead of Christ, 1016. The devil shakes the Jews with the wind of a whirlwind when the Lord is incarnate, 1187. From the fire in which the Jews burned, light shone upon the Gentiles, 1188. The Jews first raged against the Lord and then against the apostles, ibid. The Jews’ rejection because of unbelief is prefigured, 1516. The Jews’ impenitence arose from pride, 1520. The Jews’ unbelief in guarding Christ in the tomb is figured by the Philistines’ guarding Samson in Gaza, 1529.

The Synagogue of the Jews is an overturned house, its four corners shaken, 60, 290. Christ’s garment, that is, the Synagogue, was torn, since some believed from it and others did not, 60. From Judea Christ chose a few rejected and humble people and shook out the ungodly, 920. [Col. 1424] It is foretold that the preaching of the Gospel would be transferred from the Synagogue to the Gentiles, 290. Light failed the Synagogue after its preachers were expelled, 291. Whoever has understood the Church as above the Synagogue, 375. By the priests and Levites Christ was regarded as an outsider, 454. Christ appeared as a stranger in his own house, 455. The bride, the Synagogue, shuddered at Christ, ibid. The Synagogue is called the stone of darkness and the shadow of death, 576. After abandoning the Synagogue, the Church devoted itself to gathering the nations, 581. The Synagogue was shaken by Christ, 920. The Synagogue is like an ostrich: possessing wings, it crawls along the ground, 1013. It abandoned the apostles whom it had begotten according to the flesh, to be given life by Christ’s grace, ibid. The Synagogue’s cruelty toward its own children, 1014. Raging in this way, it believed that it was rendering service to God, 1014. The Synagogue first rose secretly against God and afterward openly, ibid. What the Synagogue derides in the horseman and his rider, 1015. What it means that the Synagogue stood toward the north while the Church inclines toward the south, 1312. There were four orders of rulers in the Synagogue, 1407. After persecuting the Redeemer, the Synagogue plunged into the torpor of unbelief, ibid. By holding to the literal observance of the law, the Synagogue lost its spiritual understanding, 1444. The Synagogue, signified by John, came first to the tomb but did not enter, 1531. It saw the linen cloths, that is, the mysteries of Holy Scripture, but did not enter through faith in the resurrection, ibid. Because the Jews did not fill the place at the banquet, the Gentiles entered, 1623. The Jews are gathered from the streets and lanes, ibid.

The Jews will be converted at the end of the world, 103, 1153, 1294, 1532. They will come with gifts to worship the Lord, 1158. At the end of the world Christ will return to the Jews from whom he came, 62, 103, 1154, 1294. The Jews will eventually cease from insults against Christ, 197. Judea must be recalled to the faith, 291, 659, 865, 920, 1153. A brand snatched from the fire indicates the future conversion of the Jews, 660. God melts the hearts of some Jews through the inspiration of his love, 878. The conversion of the Jews at the end of the world was foretold, 1154, and figured by Esau returning late from the field, 1215. How great the Church’s consolation will be from their conversion, 1155, 1158. What the converted Jews ought to offer to Christ, 1155. The Jews converted in the time of Antichrist will suffer severe persecutions, 1295, both from their own Gentiles and from foreigners, ibid.

The Jewish people are the elder son of the Lord, 56, 59. The Jewish populace was corrupted and perverted by corrupt Pharisees, 59. The Jewish people boast of their knowledge of the law, 95. The ancient enemy carried off the Jewish people, 183. It is foretold that the Jews will not disdain association with the nations, 217. How great is the impiety of the Jewish people, 308. Who destroyed the walls of the Jews and afterward their fortifications, 376. Christ pleaded for the servant resisting commands, but was not heard, 455. Why the Jewish people is called a servant, ibid. The people, signified by the name “fools,” followed the unbelief of the teachers of the law, 456, 457. It is called the stone of darkness and the shadow of death, 576. Why the Jewish people is called lame, 625. It envied the nations the preaching and faith of the Gospel, 886. The Jewish people is compared to frost and ice, 942. The Jewish populace is signified under the name of ravens, 970. Once it sees the conversion of the Gentiles, it will come to its senses and blush for its foolishness, 971. The Jewish people is understood under the name of the rhinoceros or unicorn, 1010, and under the name of locusts, 1017. It made certain [Col. 1425] leaps and fell to the ground, ibid. The same people is signified by the burning thornbush, 1227. That people, full of the spirit of prophecy yet blind, is like Isaac blessing Jacob, 1469. Simon the Pharisee signifies the Jewish people, 1595. He did not give Christ a kiss, serving him from fear rather than love, 1596. The rich glutton is a type of the Jewish people, 1652. He who did not believe Moses did not believe Christ rising from the dead, 1654.

God is judge and witness of sinners, 304. In the presence of a merciful judge, guilt is not left without forgiveness, 343. Who the judges will be with the supreme Judge, 363. The supreme Judge can be appeased by prayers before judgment, but not during judgment, 468. The Judge now observes and awaits sinners, 484. The just judge puts himself in the place of his neighbor, 622. The duty of a just judge, ibid. The just always think of the coming Judge, 689. A judge must not be rash in pronouncing sentence, 628. When Christ appears as judge, he will be beautiful to the just and terrifying to the unjust, 1231. The inward Judge considers the mind rather than words, 1565. The equity of the Judge who gives more to one possessing more, 1465. The Judge is the examiner of works and witness of hearts, 1478. The Judge’s coming: what wonder, sweetness, and bitterness it contains, ibid. He does not wish to open to the Judge who knocks, remembering that he had despised him, 1482. Who can joyfully endure the Judge, ibid. The Judge will appear to all in the form of a servant, 1483. No flesh will see Christ except on the day of judgment, 1519. In recompense the Judge considers the weight and assesses strength according to the weight, 1530. The coming Judge must not be feared: he must be feared now, 1558. If the judgment of a human being’s dust is feared with such care, with what dread must the judgment of majesty be anticipated? 1558. The more patience Christ previously displayed, the more severe he will come in judgment, 1575. He who judges also wishes to be asked not to punish sinners, 1593. Christ delays coming as Judge because he does not wish to find people whom he must punish, 1633. Here we must approach the merciful Judge with tears, 1611. The Judge will judge inward and outward things, 1630. While the strict Judge delays, we must consider what awaits us, 1649.

To judge inward matters is forbidden, 21. What God judges, he illuminates with light, 116. Inferiors ought not lightly to judge the deeds of superiors, 149. The habit of the human mind in judging the affairs of others, 184. God judges a person in two ways, 319. Christ judges the deeds of mortals every day, 373. Whoever fears being judged at the end should judge himself here as much as he can, 386. Whoever does not first judge himself does not know what he should judge rightly in others, 448. The saints judge God’s deeds piously, 514. What it means to judge twice, 572. God judges justly, showing no partiality, 787. What it means to be judged before God and by God, 792. The two orders of those to be judged, 835. No one judges well what he does not know, 855. We must judge ourselves before we judge others, 1205. Whoever judges his own things and those of his neighbor differently has unequal weights, ibid. What it means to judge on God’s behalf, 380. God’s judgments are to be feared, 83. God’s judgments concerning good and evil in this life are a great abyss, 137, 145, 339, 348, 493, 551.

797, 901, 931, 943, 953, 1315. What the divine judgment concerning oneself is, no one knows, 144. How greatly God’s judgments are to be feared, 145, 148, 261, 265, 298, 373, 1242. Those weighed down by the burden of corruption cannot debate God’s judgments [Col. 1425], 301. The equity of divine judgment, 304, 855. God’s lips are his judgments, 339. By not discovering God’s hidden judgments, a person discovers them, 339, 953. A person anticipates God’s judgment by examining himself, 115, 792. God’s hidden judgments are in some respects darkness, 116, 805. By a just judgment God allows the deceiver to fall into worse things, and knows the deceived, allowing him to fall into evils of which he is unaware, 373. In his hidden judgments God sees everything and is himself unseen, 377. By God’s hidden judgments some fall and others rise, ibid., 797, 805. The severity of divine judgment in punishing even evil thoughts, 388. God’s judgment is compared with a bronze bow, 480. God’s hidden judgments, which nevertheless must not be scrutinized with excessive curiosity, 493, 855, 1049, 1447. The just are never secure from God’s strictness, either inwardly or in the future, 520. The most minute thoughts and the thinnest words will be examined in God’s judgment, 682. The saints endure being unjustly burdened by human judgments, so that they may be examined more gently in the divine judgment, 694. No one is hidden from God’s judgment, which forgets or knows nothing, 790. Some wicked people do not fear appealing to God’s judgment as though they were saints, 812. God’s judgments must neither be scrutinized nor criticized, 855. Angels and teachers praise them, although they do not understand them, ibid. Examples of God’s hidden judgments in infants who die without baptism or after baptism, ibid. God’s hidden judgments in the conversion of the wicked are to be feared, 887, 1447. The clouds of God’s judgments are impenetrable to the rays of our mind, 931, 954. God’s judgment is signified by the names “circle” and “sickle,” 1089. There is no way of escape on any side, because the one who judges is everywhere, ibid. Some judgments are God’s, others human, 1147. The strict judgments of God, who places a stumbling block before the sinner, 1289. God sometimes draws the unwilling, and by a hidden judgment repels the willing, 1316. God’s purposes concerning human beings are terrifying, 1448. The equity and severity of God’s judgments, 256, 1656. Nothing happens to human beings without God’s hidden judgment, 393. God’s hidden judgments are not known by the prelates of the Church, 425. How God’s judgments are incomprehensible, 854, 900. The marvelous judgments of God in rejection and election, 796, 931. How divine judgments are directed toward one soul, one city, or one nation, 806. Divine judgments hear our words as they are spoken from our inmost selves, 818. Similes for God’s judgments, 855. We ought to venerate God’s judgments with as much humility as their obscurity prevents them from being seen, ibid. The hidden measure of divine judgment, 912. When divine judgments are unknown, they must not be investigated, 1046. God’s judgments are called abysses, 1132. To ponder God’s profound judgments and lay aside one’s wings, 1242. God displayed two judgments from one thing, 1656.

— The uprightness of human judgment: on what it depends, 254. What it means to set judgment before God, 514. Our judgments must be weighed before the supreme Judge, 540. Why the judgment of the just is called a diadem, 622. The order of judgment by which we ought to strike ourselves in this life, 792. Conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, and grief torments, 793. This judgment, which the wicked avoid, the just always exercise; how beneficially we should undergo it, 793. Everyone is blind in his own judgment, 304. To dispute belongs to judgment, 379. How false human judgments are, 511. Our judgments must not be hasty, 628. A good man exercises judgment upon himself every day, 792.

— In ancient times elders sat at the gates to judge cases [Col. 1426], 617. Who are the contemptible persons who should be appointed to judge, 626. Let us not be hasty in judgments, 628.

— Hypocrites confidently await God’s final judgment, trusting in human judgment, 112. The just anticipate God’s judgment by examining themselves, 115, 792. In judgment God will not punish what he finds already corrected by repentance, 115, 116. God must be asked that our evils not be brought against us in judgment, 119. The day of judgment is the gate of the Kingdom, 185. Then the one who refused correction here will not be able to escape, ibid. How great is the fear of the wicked as God’s judgment approaches, 225, 1436. The just come to judgment with their sheaves, 230. The trembling of the reprobate at judgment, 234. Then Christ will see the reprobate in order to strike those whom here he did not see in order to have mercy, 256. God will not acknowledge in judgment those who despised him here, 257, 1093. A person is shaken by present punishments through fear of the more severe judgment, 269. How great and of what kind the confusion of the reprobate will then be, 286. The severity of the final judgment, 302. Especially against those whom God’s patience has long endured, ibid. Christ, now despised as a lamp, will shine forth on the last day, 364. Why he does not burn now for pardon but will then burn for punishment, 365. Only the one who, by the omnipotence of his nature, does not know how to sin can examine sins without compassion, 380. Here the just examine and punish themselves, so that they may become incapable of judgment, 386. How devout minds approaching the final judgment should prepare themselves, 428. The wicked are urged to repentance by the final judgment, 468, 514. With how much terror we ought to be affected by continual reflection upon it, 469. At the final judgment the wicked will experience the just and the unjust as accusers, 483. Then the evils hidden within will be revealed, 484. Even the smallest sins will be condemned in judgment, ibid. A terrifying description of God’s judgment, 556, 1099, 1558. The greater the present mercy, the greater the severity will then be, 563. The whirlwind of divine judgment will overwhelm the wicked when he does not expect it, 569. Fire will divide the good and the wicked at the final judgment, 176. Why the final judgment is signified by the name “bow,” 633. Preliminary signs of the final judgment, 696, 1436. If the saints fear the final judgment, how much more should the unjust fear it, 696. Christ, who is now the author of the book, will then be the author of judgment, 719. What it means to offer the book to Christ when he comes to judgment, 724. What is now carried out in secret judgment will then be demonstrated publicly, 796. Who at the final judgment will be not judged but judges, 837, 815, 1190. What it means for the saints to sit on thrones with Christ, 838. The sinner’s conversion begins with fear of the final judgment, 868. Reflection on the final judgment shakes the sinner’s heart with fear, ibid. The disordered movements of the soul are restrained by remembrance of the divine judgments, 929. The just awaits and desires the final judgment; the sinner dreads it, 1020. Saint Gregory’s statement concerning the imminent day of final judgment, 1021. What it means for judgment to be called to the fire, 1084. The part of the Lord’s house that is consumed by fire, ibid. After judgment the beauty of the universe will follow, 1094. The proclamation of the sentence of eternal damnation against the devil and the reprobate, 1099. The eternal separation of chaff from grain by the winnowing-fan of the final judgment, 1120. The final judgment is called a whirlwind, 1189. Why it is said to come from the north, ibid. It is also called a cloud, because of the gloom of blindness, ibid. Why it is called enveloping fire, ibid. At the final judgment Christ will be beautiful to the just and terrifying to the unjust [Col. 1427], 1052, 1231. The bow is the sign of both judgments: of the one already carried out through water, and of the one still to be carried out through fire, 1247. The final judgment and the resurrection are signified by the number eight, 1392. Who sings mercy and judgment to God, 1420. Who loves the coming of the Judge, 1421, 1438. The expectation of judgment compels us to fear and vigilance, 1437. The reprobate will see Christ in majesty, whom they refused to hear in humility, ibid. From the calamities of the world growing old, one should understand the harshness of the final judgment, 1439. The storm tests those whom the fire will consume, 1439. For one who considers the final judgment, whatever is troublesome in the present seems light, ibid. Morals must be changed for the better through reflection on the final judgment, ibid. Who can await God the Judge securely, ibid. Because of fear of the final judgment, the tongue must be restrained from idle words, 1457. The final judgment must always be considered and feared, 1471, 1558. Why God delays the day of the final judgment, 1471. While it is delayed, the elect and the reprobate are lulled by the sleep of death, 1477. The day of the Lord will overwhelm the unwary like a thief in the night, 1478. What terror and confusion it will be for the guilty to appear before the angry Judge, ibid. All, both good and wicked, will be brought to judgment to be judged, 1504. There all the rams of the Lord’s flock will appear with the gains of souls, ibid. How great will be the confusion of useless shepherds appearing without the gain of sheep, 1504. Those purified by the hands of priests are received into heaven, while the priests themselves are thrust into punishments, 1505. The coming wrath is called the final vengeance, 1519. Let us now provide ourselves with the saints who will be our advocates at the final judgment, 1592. With what tears the final judgment must be anticipated, 1630. In the strictness of the final rebuke every argument of excuse ceases, 1641. We hasten without interruption toward judgment, 1489.

— The final judgment is called the day of the Lord’s wrath, 484. Its various names, 569, 1479. It is called lightning, 1120. It will take place in fire, 1189. To flee God’s judgment means to hide oneself in repentance, 116. Those who act wickedly deny the final judgment, 468. The saints always stand before God’s judgment, 520. God’s judgment against those who neglect his commandments, 563. The final judgment must always be meditated upon, 1575.

— Christ’s second coming, and how it differs from the first, 364, 555. Why it is called night, 569. God anticipated the judgment of the Sodomites by the fire of judgment before the judgment, 628. Every convert never ceases to attend to how strict the eternal Judge will be when he comes, 775. The future judgment must be set before oneself, 792. What the examination of conscience should be like in considering the future judgment, ibid. Some are not judged at the judgment, yet perish, 835. At the judgment those hear the Judge’s words who have kept the words of his faith, 836. Some are judged and perish, ibid. Some are judged and reign, ibid. In judgment God will punish the unjust with gentleness, 1052. On the day of the final judgment the repentance of the wicked will be useless, 1093. Each person will give an account in judgment of the talents he has received, 1504.

The yoke of Christ: why it is gentle, 25, 133. The exceedingly heavy yoke of worldly servitude, 654, 979. Having shaken off the heavy yoke of servitude to temporal things, one enjoys the sweetness of freedom, 979. Beasts and birds of heaven: what they signify, 368, 825. For beasts to rot in their dung: what it means, 766, [Col. 1427] 1471, 1584. Human beings are called beasts, 824. Reed: what it signifies, 941, 1315. The juniper signifies sins, 646. Avarice is signified by the root of the juniper, ibid., 651. To utter an oath: what it means, 1048. Quarrel. Those who answer harshly when challenged wrongly consider themselves innocent, 813.

“Justifications” are called the Lord’s commandments, 1230, 1420. To defend justice out of love of reward is unjust, 305. Justice is compared with a garment, 452, 621. Justice is the root of the virtues, 625. Our justice: when it should be concealed or displayed, 1472. What justice is, 1427. To sell justice: what it means, 1648. Justice is the cause of the good, 845. Those who possess false justice despise others, 1600. To be clothed with justice: what it means, 621.

— Justice must be joined to gentleness, 21. Justice comes before mercy, 624. True justice possesses compassion, 1600. Human justice is injustice when compared with divine justice, 169, 301, 306, 543, 694. With God there is no human justice if arrogance of mind exalts it, 511. For the defense of justice we ought to expose ourselves, 1023. How our justice is sometimes perverted, 68, 452. Lost justice is restored through repentance, ibid.

— Our justice requires the pleading of forgiveness, 301, 697. The glory of each person is justice, 452. Whoever abandons justice through fear of punishments often does not escape them, 453. God does not need our justice, 501. Let us please God even by the mere beginning of justice, 1587. Let human shame not hinder us from defending justice, 1589. True justice shows compassion; false justice disdains and despises, 1600. The wicked praise God’s justice when things go well for them, but condemn it when things go badly, 271. What it means to make someone just justly or unjustly, 305. In what way the justice that belongs to God is called ours, 765. How justice is turned into judgment, 838. Justice is designated by the name of light, 931. It is scattered only gradually, 936.

The just person is represented by a tree, 394. The just are represented by light, 550. No one is born just, 598. See Original Sin. The life of the just is compared with palm trees, 630, 631. The offspring of the just is compared with the grass of the earth, 206. The meditations of the just, 139. The mind of the just is the ark of the covenant, 149. The contemplation of the just concerning divine judgment, 261. The life of the just is compared with Lucifer, 355. The just: in what sense they are coals, and who are called lamps, 1208. A person is not just if he abandons justice in suffering, 449. The just person is just through God’s illumination, not through comparison, 543.

— The just are dead to the world, 362. The just person recognizes himself as a sinner by himself and as having been made just by a gift, 384. The first planting of the just is in God’s foreknowledge, the second in their works, 395. In this life the souls of the just are called stars, 543. The just person inwardly pleads his case with his neighbor and justly condemns himself as guilty, 622. Christ first sits in the heart of the just, 639. The just fly like clouds, 678. The just always stand before God like servants before their master, 517. The just always behold God as present to them, 614. The days of the just are days of affliction, 663. What is proper to the just, 90, 458. The just person is weary of living, 305. It is proper to the just to seek not only their own edification but also that of their neighbor in words and deeds, 383. The just regard the glory of the world as dung, 471. The more the just labor here, the more they consider and contemplate God [Col. 1428], 514. It is the concern of the just to examine their deeds daily according to the way of truth, 517. The just always return to the secret chamber of the heart, 520. There are two kinds of just persons, 857.

— The simplicity and uprightness of the just, 29. The seed of the just is manifold, 206. Some of the just possess earthly things, while others renounce them, 263.
