To the carnal eyes the just are without light, but before God they burn and shine, 362. The just are higher than temporal glory, ibid. It is the concern of the just to observe the ways of truth, 517. The remarkable insight of the just gathered within themselves, 1005. The courage of the just in battle, 90. The just are corrected by rebuke, 338. The prudence of the just is considered folly by the wise of the world, 360. The simplicity of the just is despised by the reprobate, ibid. Although the just may rebuke the deeds of others with severity, they do so with compassion, 380. The just person who suffers unjust things is moved not so much to anger as to prayers, 458. The just cannot rejoice at the error of those who perish, 507. The just are constant in good works, 631. The abundance of the just consists in doing good and enduring evil, 674. The just are sometimes gentle and sometimes severe in corrections, 780. The confidence of the just is compared with a lion, 1022. The just endure divine scourges with equanimity, 1099. The virtues of the sons of the just: what they are, 1425. The mind of the just longs for torments, 219. The courage of the just: in what it consists, 221.

— The just begin with fear and are perfected in love, 29. The fear and tears of the just arising from contemplation of God’s judgment concerning themselves, 145, 316. The just themselves know that they would perish if they were judged by God without mercy, 256, 261, 265, 270, 288, 298, 301, 314, 406, 544, 776, 1147, 1168. The just person, when subjected to God, preserves justice; when self-reliant, he loses it, 288. Why the just person is not crushed in the whirlwind, 303. The just fear God when tranquil, lest they experience him when stirred, 391. The just are troubled by fear of death and of the final judgment, 775. When the just see the faults of others, they attend to their own and judge them, 98. The just are bound by continual hardship in life, 135. They fear God’s judgment because of their sins, 137, 269. They fear even their good deeds, 143, 145, 164. The just are always afraid, 158, 164, 302, 312, 514, 519, 638, 683. The fear of the just, 220, 256. How they judge themselves, 622.

— The just do good deeds so as to please God alone, 139. The intention of the just is signified by the eyes, 357, 907, 1224. See Intention.

— The words of the just are burdensome to the unjust, 270. The good deeds of the just increase until the end of life, 274. The moderation of the just in rebuking, 380. The words and works of the just and unjust are often similar, but their intention is different, 405. The just sometimes confess their good deeds out of necessity, 406, 813. What the judgments of the just concerning themselves are like, 622. From where the inward war in the just arises, 204. Why the just grieve that they are shut up in prison, 260. The just person commits no fraud in God’s work, 313. The just person recognizes himself as detestable in many respects because of the rebellion of the flesh, 315. The memory of the just is eternal, 381. God searches out the ways of the just and tests them, 516. The just carefully attend to what they owe God and what they owe their neighbor, 622. The just themselves make progress through consideration of other saints, 768. The various virtues of the saints, which each person should imitate in another, ibid. The just person meets adversaries fearlessly, 1023. The just, placed in the distress of their own tribulation, do not abandon concern for another’s welfare, 90. The just are sometimes afflicted inwardly and outwardly, 98. No movement of carnal desires holds the just, 134. The just are troubled in prosperity [Col. 1429], 138. In this life the just fear prosperity more than adversity, 139. Why the just continually suffer scourges, 147. While the just grieve over present punishments, they fear future ones, 214. The good are pierced by scourges and the terror of judgment, 217. What the spirit of the just poor, oppressed, and foolish for God’s sake is like, 235. The just person returns from outward things to the heart, yet finds no rest there, 261. What disposition the just have concerning earthly goods, 287. The anxiety of the just person who does not know why he is scourged, 320. The just suffer hard things here, but it will be well with them at the end, 355. The just praise God even in adversity, 383. No adversity comes suddenly upon steadfast minds, 423. The just who are unjustly afflicted are regarded more by God, 837. The just are strongly armed against their attackers, 202. The just consider affliction a rest, 219. The just completely despise the joys of this life, 236. The just are patient in adversity and fearful in prosperity, 287. The just care neither for present goods nor fear future evils, ibid. For the just, the exercise of virtue consists in enduring outward adversity alone, 303. The just do not grow angry in persecutions, 458. The just, afflicted by sorrow, are consoled by contemplation of heavenly things, 587. The just are steadfast in prosperity and adversity, 658. The just receive heavenly consolation temporarily in tribulation, though they do not ask for it as a temporal thing, 826. The just endure divine scourges with equanimity, 1099. The souls of the just are tested like gold through fire, 516. See Scourges, Adversity, Prosperity, Saints, etc.

— The just always consider their sins, 97. The just always detest their sins in confession, 258. The just lament their smallest defects in themselves, 382. If the just do not slip in deed, they slip in thought, 385. Thoughts often pollute the hearts of the just, 521. The just cannot be entirely without sin, 561. The falls of the just: how useful they are to them, 1092. The just are corrected by the punishments they endure, 214. The just person does not know how to spare his own faults, so that God may spare him, 383. See Sin, Fault.

— Why God permits the just to be scourged, 10, 77, 148. The devil tempts the just in two ways, 77. The just are sometimes cut off, 154. What the despair of the just is, 264. The just person does not despair of the abundance of divine mercy, ibid. Grace is often withdrawn from the just, lest they be exalted, 323. Why the just are sometimes permitted to fall, 328. Grace does not abandon the just person placed in grave temptation, 354. Those whom God loves eternally he sometimes usefully abandons for a time, 661. Why the lamp of the just is widely despised, 364. The just are afflicted by the reprobate in this life, 820. The progress of the just’s desire through delay, 826. Why God allows the adversaries of the just to prosper, 661. See Prosperity.

— If the just endure so many scourges, what punishments await the wicked? 148. The better persons’ words or deeds often displease the worse, 148. The perverse attack the life of the good in two ways, 152. The just will feel no mercy toward the condemned, 203. Singularity must be avoided by those who live justly, ibid. What the courage of the just and of the wicked is, 221. The words of the just are burdensome to the unjust, 270. The just use temporal goods, and the unjust enjoy the same goods, 288. The labor of the just indicates what punishment awaits the reprobate, 329. The just person is hidden from the scourge of the tongue condemning the wicked, 202. How the just and the wicked differ in correction, 338. For the wicked, present security produces labor; for the just, present labor produces security, 356. What is pleasure for the wicked is punishment for the just, 358. The just make good use of the riches they possess; the wicked make bad use of them [Col. 1429], 361. The just and the wicked agree in their understanding of God’s power, but do not live in agreement, 368. How far the just and unjust differ in adversity, 383. The words of the just and the wicked are often similar, but their hearts are different, 405. God, who grants temporal goods to the wicked, does not deny eternal goods to the just, 431. The joy of the just is beneath them; that of the wicked is above them, 439, 470. The false judgments of the reprobate concerning the scourges of the good, 449. See Scourges. The just possess their goods; they are not possessed by them, whereas the wicked are, 490. The elect foresee sin so as not to commit it; after the fall, punishment opens the eyes of the wicked in vain, 492. The foundation of the wicked is in earthly things, that of the just in heavenly things, 506. The just now waste away over the sins of the wicked, but will one day rejoice at their destruction, 507. The wicked are troubled by the prosperity of the just, 530. If the just offend, they are not to be rebuked by the wicked, 540. The just speak from the root of humility; the wicked do otherwise, 778. The sinner forgets his mortality; the just person does not, 783. Why the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust, 820, 826. The just, oppressed by the wicked, ask to be delivered for the salvation of their oppressors, but are not heard, ibid. From what the just person glories and the sinner is terrified, 1020. The just are rescued from the hands of unjust people who are at odds among themselves, 1120. Why the just person is said to fall forward and the unjust backward, 1251. God is terrifying to the wicked but gentle to the just, 1527. Therefore the pillar of fire appeared by night and the pillar of cloud by day to the people of Israel, ibid.

— Where the just were before the Lord’s ascension, after death, 127, 668. The just person, despised here, will shine with great power in the future life, 363. Even now, while falling outwardly, the just person is renewed inwardly, 355. The just produce abundant fruits in us through their death, 395. The death of the just is accompanied by joy, 776. The rewards of the heavenly kingdom are due to the just alone, 1524. The death of the just is a help to the good, 1614. See Saints.

Young men in Sacred Scripture: who are called young men, 618. The vigor of young men is described, 1438. Youth is signified by the sixth hour, 1511.

## L

Laban was a type of the devil as exactor, 988; and of one attempting to oppress the elect of the world, ibid. What Laban’s daughter, who is taken away from her father’s house, signifies, ibid. Laban’s idols signify avarice, ibid.

Not to sin with the lips: what this means, 80. We offend in two ways with the lips, ibid. What the lips left only around Christ’s teeth signify, 458.

The saints labor more strenuously the nearer they approach their rewards, 142. The vision of the one laboring is a relief from labor, ibid. The labor of a journey is lightened by the companionship of a fellow traveler, ibid. What human labor consists in, 188. The labor of the carnal is burdensome, ibid., and vain, 230. Through transitory labor we are rescued from everlasting pain, 201. Labor is lightened by consideration of the reward, 248. What it means to spend laborious nights, ibid. Labor undertaken for the sake of the world is recognized as vain by its end, 249. The just endure hard labors here, but eternal rewards await them, 355. The labor of the just, that they may find themselves and mourn once found, 386. What it means for the just to labor in adversity, 531. The labors of heretics are sterile, 536. The wicked take more delight in the harshness of labor than in the sweetness of rest, 655.

What the bronze basin in which the priests must wash signifies, 1500.

The tears of the saints because they do not know God’s judgment concerning themselves, [Col. 1430] 144. Joy of contemplation often follows tears, ibid. The soul is nourished by mourning and raised through weeping to heavenly joys, ibid., 1279. Tears cleanse when they flow with humility, ibid. Which tears are fruitless, 314, 1202. In what manner God leaves us to mourn our grief, 331. Tears extinguish the flame of the devil’s suggestions, 1116. The tears of prayer are the sacrificial offerings of our oblation, 1202. How great is the necessity and usefulness of penitential tears, 1234; some tears are poured out from fear, others from love, 1428. Through the compunction of tears, nothing transitory should be sought, ibid. Through weeping we are led to eternal joys, 1443. The mind tortured by the ardor of love is nourished by its own tears, 1578. What it signifies to bathe the Lord’s feet with tears, 1596.

What is signified by the name “milk,” 1070. Who are whiter than milk, ibid. Wild lettuces signify the bitterness of repentance, 1534.

A lake is sometimes called hell, 331.

The true joy of God’s servants, and the madness of the wicked, 193. How great is the joy of the saints in heaven, 285. The Creator is the true joy of the mind, 403. The just do not rejoice in the errors of the wicked, 507. Private joy must be deferred to common and perpetual happiness, 1387. Joy should be practiced in such a way that the bitterness of the coming judgment does not depart from memory, 1647.

What little jars that do not contain new wine signify, 741.

Laments without humility are of no benefit, 314. Laments of humility are signified by waters of snow, ibid. Lamentations indicate the repentance of sinners, 1262.

What lamiae signify mystically, 619, 1107.

The lead plate signifies Judea, 460.

The despised lamp is called the just man, 362. Likewise Christ, 364. What the lamps proceeding from the mouth of Antichrist signify, 1110. Holy men are compared with lamps and coals, 1208. They are lamps who burn and shine, ibid. What it means to adorn lamps, 1478. What it means for the lamps of the foolish virgins to be extinguished, ibid.

### Wool

What a garment woven from wool and linen signifies, 285.

What it means to place a stone beneath the head of one sleeping, 163. What it means for stones to be hollowed out by waters, 401. What it means to embrace stones, 525. What the transformation of a stone dissolved by heat into bronze signifies, 575. The stone of darkness signifies the Jewish people, hardened by perfidy, 576. In Sacred Scripture a stone is sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense, 579. What the hewn stones are into which the Lord placed the gates of the Church, ibid. What the twelve stones signify that the priest carries on his breast, 899. Christ is the cornerstone, 902. What a stone signifies according to its hardness, 943. Nine kinds of precious stones, 1072, 1604. They are compared with the nine orders of angels, ibid. What it means to walk amid burning stones, 1073. The hearts of the wicked are compared with stones, 1120. The stones of the Church are the elect, 1311, 1314. Christ is the stone placed in the foundation, 1311. Faithful souls are called stones, 1365. What is signified by square stones, 1405. The words of Sacred Scripture are called square stones, 1407. The comparison of a stone emitting fire with Sacred Scripture, 1417. What it means to place stone upon stone, 1647. [Col. 1431] What it signifies not to leave stone upon stone, ibid.

What it means to take a brick and write upon it, etc., 1302.

What is the breadth of charity, 1327, 1354. The breadth of charity is expansive, whereas stinginess, sluggishness, and fear are constricting, ibid., 1426. What breadth of mind is, 1354.

A robber is said to give life if he does not take it, 114. Robbers are demons who lie in wait for our works, 282, 1472. Why demons are called God’s robbers, 453. The robber’s conversion on the cross by God, 586. The different deaths of the robbers on the cross, 872. In the fountain of mercy the robber was washed clean through confession of the truth, 1402. The robber, called at the eleventh hour, came into the vineyard, 1512. What the robber did not have because of his age, he had because of his punishment, ibid. Seized from the jaws of the way and carried to the cross, he confessed there and was healed there, 1525. God gave us the robber as an example of repentance, 1551.

The just are said to wash their hands in the blood of sinners, 572.

To praise God is to give good things and preserve what has been given, 64. Those who pursue human praise will have no reward at the final judgment, 112, 275. False praise: how harmful it is, 125. The praise of enemies: how powerful it is, 152. The desire for human praise is a little robber, 304, 1472. What benefit it is to the soul of one acting rightly not to be praised by people but to be mocked, 360, 706. The weak, occupied with outward actions, are easily and dangerously captured by human praise, 415. To praise the evil deeds of people is to increase them, 559. The saints sometimes praise themselves harmlessly, 562, 1256. Why God speaks of his own praises, ibid., 1257. It is forbidden even silently to rejoice in one’s own praises, 706. It is one thing to seek people’s favor, another to exult in the progress of those who praise, ibid. The saints are tormented by their own praises, 707, 842. While praise torments the just, it purifies them; while it delights the wicked, it shows them to be reprobate, ibid. Those are effeminate who are corrupted by human praises, ibid. Human praise extinguishes tender good things, 975. The intention of human praise overtakes the intention begun for God’s sake, 1168. The good things we do should not be disclosed unless the neighbor’s benefit or a great necessity compels it, 1257. The just speak of their own good deeds without arrogance, ibid. Human praises: how greatly they must be feared, 1472. Care must be taken lest good works be corrupted by the desire for praise, 1476. What fearful praise is, 886.

The raising of Lazarus is a pattern of the resurrection of a soul dead through sin, 713, 1555. The raising of Lazarus blinded some through envy and enlightened others through faith, 872. The raising of Lazarus signifies the order of priestly absolution, 1556. The dead man comes out when the sinner voluntarily confesses his wickedness, ibid. Lazarus—“beggar”—is interpreted as “helped,” 805, 1653. Lazarus signifies the Gentile people, 805, 1652. What Lazarus’ desire to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table signifies, 1652. What the dogs licking Lazarus’s wounds signify, 1653. Lazarus, dead, is led by angels into Abraham’s bosom, 1653. Why the poor man’s name, rather than the rich man’s, is reported in the Gospel, 1655. By testing the poor man God trained him for glory; by tolerating the rich man, he awaited him for punishment, ibid. How many temptations Lazarus suffered from the rich man’s sight, 1656. Poverty afflicted and cleansed him, 1657. Many Lazaruses lie before the gates and must not be neglected, 1659.

The living reading is the life of the just, 767. To read the word of God is to eat, 1265. In sacred reading we are fasting unless God fills the inward parts of the mind, [Col. 1431] 1266. The fruit of sacred reading is the old man, 1267. The sacred writer is the measuring reed, whose writings benefit some readers but not others, 1315.

A bed signifies the secret place of the heart, 261. What it means for holy men to sleep in a bed, 750. A bed signifies three things in Scripture, 753. What it means to seek the beloved in bed, 854, 1383, 1546.

What embassy we ought to send to God, 1631. This embassy is the offering of tears, almsgiving, and sacrifices, 1633.

The lion signifies Christ by its strength and the devil by its savageness, 157. The devil too is signified by the name of lion, 1375, 1376. What lion cubs are called, 157. By the name of lioness the holy Church is sometimes designated, and sometimes Babylon, 157, 967. By what art a lioness is captured, 327. What is signified by a captured lioness, 327. What the master of the lioness captures as prey, 968.

Heretics are like lepers, 151.

What it means to lift one’s face to God, 510. What it means to lift one’s heart with one’s hands to God, 560. What raising the head signifies, 1437.

Leviathan is called Antichrist, 110, and the devil, ibid., 1086, 1094. How he was caught with a hook, 1550.

Leviathan is interpreted as “human addition,” 110, 1086, 1550. Leviathan designates the devil, 1086, 1094, 1550. What the head of Leviathan signifies, 1097. Likewise, what the skin of Leviathan signifies, ibid. What are the gates of Leviathan’s face, 1103. What Leviathan’s sneezing is, 1109. Why Leviathan is called a little king, 1112. What the flesh of Leviathan is, 1119. Leviathan is compared with an anvil, 1121. What the teeth of Leviathan are, 1104. Who are those from whose mouth his lamps go forth, 1110. What Leviathan’s mouth is, ibid. What it means for smoke to go out from Leviathan’s nostrils, 1111. Leviathan’s neck designates the extension of his pride, 1116. What the opening of Leviathan’s jaw is, 1551. What it means to enter into the midst of Leviathan’s mouth, 1103. Why Leviathan is signified by a corporeal animal, 1137. How the Lord has bound Leviathan’s tongue, 1087. The ring in Leviathan’s nostrils is the power of divine omnipotence, 1088. Why Leviathan’s body is compared with cast shields, 1105. What his body covered with scales signifies, 1106. What the scales adhering to scales are, 1108. Why Leviathan’s eyes—that is, his counselors—are compared with the eyelids of dawn, 1109. The flame proceeding from his mouth is the instigation of hidden speech, 1115. It burns only wood, hay, and straw, 1116. Tears extinguish his flame, ibid. Whom poverty precedes before Leviathan’s face, 1118. What Leviathan will do with straw, if the strong are considered by him to be like straw, 1124. What are the rays of the sun beneath Leviathan, 1127. Leviathan now secretly tramples gold as if it were mud, and later openly, 1129. What it means for Leviathan to conceal counsel without knowledge, 1143. No one escapes Leviathan’s mouth without committing unlawful acts, 1151. By the Redeemer’s benefit, the one who did not take care not to be bitten escapes his bite, ibid.

Leviathan placed the torch of pride in Eve’s mind, 1114. The smoke issuing from Leviathan’s nostrils darkens the eyes of the elect’s hearts, 1111. Leviathan kindled Cain’s mind with the flame of envy, 1114. Leviathan burned Solomon’s heart with the torches of lust, ibid. Leviathan consumed Ahab’s mind with the fire of avarice, ibid. What it means for burning coals to glow through Leviathan’s breath, 1115. Why Leviathan is permitted to have the unity of the wicked in the reprobate, [Col. 1432] 1120. Leviathan despises the words of preachers, 1124. Leviathan is not moved by the power of preaching among the reprobate, ibid. At the end the wiser will be subjected to Leviathan’s power, 1127. How Leviathan makes the hearts of the reprobate foolish, 1132. Leviathan is king over the proud, 1142. How God has bound Leviathan’s strength for his handmaids, 1095. What it means to be withdrawn from Leviathan’s mouth, 1551.

Levi is interpreted as “assumed,” 1424. The souls of the Levites are called handmaids, 454. What the age of the Levites signifies, whether for serving at the tabernacle or for guarding the vessels, 741. Who are called the sons of Zadok and Levi, 1424.

For what purpose the law was given to human beings by God, 9. The law of Christ is charity, 340. Why the law of Christ is called manifold, 341. The ancient law is the law of death, 385. The severity of the ancient law, 950. The saints before the law was given were saved through faith in the Mediator and mortification of pleasures, 132. There were far more saints before the law was given than Moses mentions, ibid. The world was then clothed in cloud, 913.

The old law, with its sacred rites, was abandoned by Christ, 61. The saints under the law are said to have been conceived and not to have seen the light, 122. The law, tasted carnally, was insipid; Christ seasons it with salt, 215. The law, tasted carnally, was deadly, 216. How great was the desire of the just under the old law for the incarnation of the Word, 307. The old law did not fulfill righteousness through fear, 385. The just dying under the old law did not attain blessedness before Christ’s death, 397, 433. Under the old law certain things were permitted to the weak which the truth under the new law pursues with punishment, 559, 913. Under the darkness of the letter of the old law, the world was wrapped, as in the swaddling clothes of infancy, 913. The old law was imperfect and weak, ibid. It is perfected through the new law, 914. Through the old law the world is instructed for the new, ibid. What is signified by the old law through Arcturus, 950. What part of the old law Christ fulfilled, 1346. Christ fulfilled the law when he appeared incarnate, 1349. In the old law outward works were commanded; in the new, the guarding of the heart, 1391. The old law bound the cold hearts of the Jews through fear of death, 1405. The old law commands lesser things; the new law commands greater things, 1659. Why the grace of the new law is signified by the Pleiades, 950. What the fiery law in God’s right hand signifies, 1578. Before the law, under the law, and under grace, the Lord awaits, admonishes, and visits the human being, 1582. The mercy of the Redeemer tempered for us the strictness of the law, 1597.

Who the lawgivers were, and how greatly Christ differs from all of them, 853.

Leah is called “laborious,” 210. She is a figure of the active life, ibid., 1324. What Leah’s substitution for Rachel during the night signifies, 1324. What Leah, bleary-eyed and fruitful, signifies, 1325. See Active and contemplative life.

The sacred books are veins of silver, 573. Noncanonical books were published for the edification of the Church, 622. The book of life is the very vision of the judge who is coming, 767. What the rolled-up book is, 1260. How it was written inside and outside, 1261. What was written in it, 1262. The lion from the tribe of Judah opened the sealed book, 1351. See Sacred Scripture.

What free will possessed in the first man’s state of innocence for meriting, 126. What it possessed in an angel, 170. We sin through free will, with the devil suggesting it, 424. What is meant by one drawn toward sin by the devil and following by free will being called free, 979? See Free will.

[Col. 1433] What freedom from sin is, and where it is found, 137. The freedom of the saints amid oppressions, with their attention directed toward heavenly things, 236. The freedom of the children of God is reserved for the saints in heaven, 247, 269, 1197. There is no freedom in guilt, 479. The distinction between freedom and pride, 1254.

Lust consumes the flesh, and through it all good works, 688. If the flame of lust is not extinguished through purity of heart, virtues of every kind arise in vain, ibid. The poison of lust is born from the root of pride, 824. See Lust.

Many things are signified by the name “wood” in Sacred Scripture, 394. What it means for a cut-down trunk to put forth foliage, 395.

The just are called lilies, among which we must feed, 767. What the lilies of the lampstand signify, 1216.

The threshold of the gate signifies the ancient Fathers from whom Christ arose, 1331. What the inner and outer thresholds signify, 1335.

By what stages the tongue falls into the pit of its own ruin, 239. To let water go is to release the tongue into excessive speech, 152, 239. The tongue should be restrained by discipline and released when necessity requires it, 241. Because the reins of the tongue have been loosened, the proud man must be tortured most severely, 413. What it means to have sweetness beneath the tongue, 473. The uncontrolled tongue rushes toward worse things, 501. The saints take care to cover the faults of the tongue with the merits of their lives, 1047. The tongue of the sea is secular doctrinal knowledge, 1088. The tongue must be restrained from idle words and released for words of exhortation, 1457. In what new tongues each of the faithful speaks, 1571. What fiery tongues signify, 893, 1577.

The tongue sins in two ways, 80. The lack of restraint of the tongue gives birth to discord, 152, 239. How harmful the tongue of the wicked is to the good, 201. What the scourge of the tongue is, ibid. The two evils of the tongue, 239. See Speech; Word.

What the linen cloths of Christ’s buried body signify, 1532. What linen signifies, 285.

In this life people often quarrel with great shouting over a worthless stipend, 651. Pastors are forbidden to devote themselves to the care of the people entrusted to them while setting quarrels first, 1006. With what disposition one should quarrel when necessity and charity compel it, 1007. One should quarrel out of love for one’s neighbor who is taking away our possessions, not from a desire for revenge, ibid. With what moderation, ibid. How those who defend temporal goods more fiercely differ from hypocrites, ibid. With what caution these people should be rebuked, 1008. From the anxiousness of those who quarrel, let us learn anxiousness in the work of salvation, 1558.

How harmful the effects of envy are, 179. Envy blinds the eyes of the mind, so that it does not see the good things of others but attends only to whatever evils they may have, 198. See Envy.

The dwelling place of the good is humility, 91. The dwelling place of the wicked is pride, ibid. God is the dwelling place of the elect, 134. God is a dwelling place, not a localized one, ibid. God, the human being’s dwelling place, was abandoned through disobedience, 257. The hypocrite’s dwelling place is the heart of flatterers, 472. What the dwelling place of the mind is, 849. The dwelling place of the human heart is delight in the present life, 867. What dry places are, 1079. Moist places are places of pleasure, 1080. Places do not make one holy, 1259. If the Spirit is absent, a place does not help, ibid. Adam fell in paradise, Satan in heaven, ibid. God alone is our fortified dwelling place, 1259. Neighbors must be endured everywhere, ibid. The devil’s dwelling place is the hearts of sinners, 1274. The hearts of penitents become the Lord’s dwelling place, ibid.

What the locust signifies mystically, 1017, [Col. 1433] 1018, 1030. The locust, fattened with the richness of heavenly grace, signifies the Gentiles infused with that richness, 1017. The name “locust” expresses empty glory, 1113.

The speech of God is manifold, 41. What the speech of angels is, 42. What the devil’s speech to God is, 43. Three kinds of speech, 151. The wicked are rash in speech, 152. The hunger of the mind is the silence of divine speech, 201. Two kinds of speech harmful to human beings, 239. Speech consisting in an abundance of words with a lack of meaning is wicked, 270. The simplicity of speech is the praise of great virtue, 743. How human speech comes about, 744. The speech of God is twofold, 893. God’s inward speech raises the soul by filling it, ibid. How the sins of speech are covered, 1203. Perverse speech heard continually is to the soul what unhealthy air, drawn in by constant breathing, is to the body, 1250. The five conditions of speech that a pastor must observe, 1286.

The long-suffering and piety of God are to be imitated by us, 517. Long-suffering is signified by length, 1426. Why God is called both long-suffering and just, 1483.

Talkativeness is the companion of banquets, 20. What it means to speak foolishly against God, 52. We offend by speaking in two ways, 80. God, often silent, speaks through deeds, 221. The power of speech is fourfold, 270, 732. When God speaks to a human being, and when a human being speaks to himself, 339. What is rightly said is often corrupted by the indiscretion of the speaker, 358, 784, 830. How a human being speaks to God and God answers the human being, 386. When we speak evil things well and good things badly, 732, 830, 897. What it means to speak from God and before God, 717. What it means for God to speak once, 748. In how many ways, and by what means, God speaks to human beings, 892, 894. God sometimes speaks through an angel or through himself, 893, 894. What it means to speak one thing and another illicitly, 1047. Our speaking to God is to yearn toward him with our desires, 1145. What order of speaking should be preserved or confused, 1254. The one who has first learned to be silent well knows how to speak well, 1282. One must learn to be silent not by speaking, but to speak by being silent, ibid. It is a fault to speak unless necessity compels it, ibid. What is more dangerous in speaking, 1287. To speak about God belongs to a very peaceful and free mind, 1291. By what manner God either grants or withdraws the gift of speech from preachers, 1298. By this preachers are urged toward humility, ibid.

The reins of the Church are the precepts of discipline, 997.

Lot is praised by Saint Peter because he was good among the wicked, 17. Lot was just in the perverse city but sinned on the mountain, 1259.

Luke the Evangelist was one of the two disciples going to Emmaus, 8. Why he is noted under the appearance of a calf, 1200.

A lamp placed in a ray of sunlight is human righteousness compared with divine righteousness, 169. What the light in a jar signifies, 439. The lamp of the wicked is extinguished sooner, ibid., 490. What this lamp of the wicked is, 490. The lamp is the word of God, 612, 1230. What burning lamps in the hands signify, 897, 1481. What the lamp that the woman lights signifies, 1603. What it means to put a lamp under a bushel, 992.

The life of the just is compared with Lucifer, 355. What it means to bring forth Lucifer as father, 952. By the hidden judgment of God, the one who is Lucifer for the elect becomes Vesper for reprobate hearers, ibid. Lucifer will fight with Michael at the end, 1605.

The holiness of many is tested by the profit of the present life, 652. What it means to play with the beasts of the field, 1076. What it means to play with unclean spirits, 1077.

What it means to gird up the loins of flesh and mind, 679, 897, 959, 1058, 1481, 1535. What it means to be struck in the loins by the enemy, 424. Lust is signified by the loins, 897, 1480. What the loins signify, 1245.

The human race lost the light of the Creator through sin, 387. The punishment of those who reject divine light is blindness, 527. The light of God is prevenient grace, 543. God is the light that illuminates; the saints are lights that have been illuminated, 596. As he wills, God either hides or reveals the light, 865. What the true light is, 1442. Whoever has received the light follows Christ, ibid.

What the moon, receiving light from the sun, signifies, 704. The moon signifies fame, ibid. The moon signifies the mutability of temporal things, 1126, and the weakening of the flesh, 1440.

The wolf dwells with the lamb in the Church, 1342. What it means for the wolf to come upon the sheep, 1485.

Human bodies are called houses of clay, 170. The human being was formed from clay, 322. In Scripture clay is taken for iniquity, 922. It signifies earthly contagions, ibid. Clay signifies several other things in Sacred Scripture, 1128.

Light signifies prosperity, 139, 438. What it means to rise before daylight, 281. Light signifies joy, 439, and also the just, 550. The present light of the dying is the eternal light of the living, 776. Light signifies righteousness, 931, 936. Light progressively increases in the minds of the just, 936. In what ways light is introduced into the human heart, we do not know, ibid. As this light increases, temptations also increase, ibid. The light by which God himself may be seen is to be sought from God, 1442. Faith is the way to this light, ibid. What inaccessible light is, 602. Light is hidden in the hands, 863. What it means for light to come, 865. What scattered light is, 935. How light is given to the wretched, 139. Our light is our eternal homeland, 530. The more unchangeably the eternal light, which is God, shines, the more penetratingly it sees, 791. The light of the proud is the glory of the present life, 927. Light should be sought from the Lord, not earthly gifts, 1442.

Lust is called the fire of God, 66. Lust is designated by moist places, 1080. Lust is signified by the name “caterpillar,” 1113. The sins of the flesh are rightly compared with foul and burning sulfur, 444. Lust is a fire devouring even unto destruction, 688. Lust arises from the frequent movement of shameful thoughts, 128. Lust arises from pride, 823, 1058, 1091. The seedbed of lust is in the loins in men and in the navel in women, 959, 1058, 1480. Lust arises from gluttony of the belly, 1036.

Through the temptation of lust, the devil disturbs chaste movements of the soul, 66. What the habit of lust is, 226. Whoever is a citizen of heaven should abandon lust, not from fear but from charity, 580. It does no good to flee lust if one pursues avarice, 1609.

Mental lust is condemned, 679. Lust is perpetrated by thought or by deed, ibid. Through Moses lust perpetrated in deed is condemned, but through Christ even lust conceived in thought is condemned, 679. The serpent crawls through the breast and belly when it pollutes some by thought and others by deed as well, 680. What lust of the flesh is, and what lust of the heart is, 897.

Lust extinguishes all good works, 688. What the daughters of lust are, 1036. What kinds of temptations belong to lust, [Col. 1435] 1037. Through lust the devil usually rules both sexes, 1058. He rules human beings through pride or through lust, 1080. Pride is a greater sin than lust, 1091. People are more ashamed of lust, ibid.

When lust has been conquered, a person unwillingly remembers what he willingly did, 244. Let the lustful person consider what a dead thing is that he loves as though it were alive, 534. Lust must be restrained—not only of the flesh but also of the proud heart, 897. By what art the patriarch Joseph conquered lust, 974. How lust must be restrained, 679. The remedy against the goads of lust, 974.

How great is the blindness of the lustful, 533. The lustful person carries within himself a tumultuous crowd of shameful thoughts, 128. The mind of the lustful is corrupted if it delights in transitory things, 842. The lustful person is signified by the name of a horse, 1015. The lustful person is a member of the devil, 1058. He is designated by the name of an ox, 1160. The lustful are signified by the names of male and female asses, 1161.

## M
Mac. **Whether the books of the Maccabees were canonical in the time of Saint Gregory**, 622.

The **Midianites** signify the enemies of the Lord, destined to be justly destroyed by his judgment, 990. **Mary Magdalene** represents the contemplative life, 210, 1195, 1324. Mary Magdalene was a sinner, 1235, 1544, 1551, 1593. How great was her love for Christ, 1545. The Evangelists speak of her in various ways, 1593. What inwardly afflicted her through compunction, Christ received outwardly, 1235, 1594. Washed with tears in the fountain of piety, she wiped away stains by correcting her conduct, 1402, 1551, 1594. The love and tears of Mary Magdalene, 1544. Her perseverance in seeking Christ, 1546. The force of love multiplies the intensity of the search, 1546. She had clung to the living Christ and was seeking him dead, 1551. See **Mary**.

The **Magi** come to Christ under the guidance of the star, 1468, etc. Through mystical gifts the Magi proclaim the one whom they adore, 1470.

One who desires eternal things is great, 180. Whoever does great things knows that what he does is great, 850.

To **curse God**, what it means, 34. Why God is said to curse, 105. God curses, while man is forbidden to curse, ibid. To curse the saints, to what extent it may be done, ibid. To curse the day of one’s birth, what it means, 106. To curse the beauty of a fool, what it means, 184. Why the Jews received the curse, 103. What the curses of Sacred Scripture signify, 104. Sacred Scripture forbids cursing, 105. The twofold curse, 105. One curse is approved, another condemned, ibid. One must abstain from curses, 709.

What is signified in Scripture by the name **hammer**, 1125.

**Malice** is signified by the dragon, 228. Sinners provoke God’s anger through malice, 840. Malice is represented by cold, 933, and by the name of fire, 1187.

How God is said to create evil, 79. One must beware of doing evil in any way, and of doing good carelessly, 83. Things that are good by nature become evil for those who transgress, 79. Those whom present evils do not correct are led on to subsequent ones, 319. Evils that cannot be amended must be endured, 341. The evils of this life are not grievous to one who contemplates eternal goods, 354. Evil without substance and without foundation, 844. See **Punishment, Adversity, Tribulation**.

The **wicked** enjoy this age and use God only transitorily, [Col. 1435] 45. The evil one whom God calls is invited to repentance, 40. The thoughts of the wicked are often futile, yet their conscience is no less guilty, 194. The wicked person is the devil’s tomb, 335. The separated souls of the wicked do not know what is done here, 403. The wicked fear that people may see them as they are, 652.

—The wicked love the exile they suffer in place of their homeland, 28. The wicked consider themselves righteous because of the fall of others, into which they themselves do not fall, 97. The wicked are always occupied with the turmoil of temporal things, 147. The wicked hunt after praise for their teaching, 271. The malignity of the wicked against one who rebukes them, 338. The dissimulation of the wicked, ibid. Whatever the wicked devise against others, they fear that others may devise against them, 409. God sometimes mercifully resists the will of the perverse, which in anger he sometimes allows to be fulfilled, 410. When reproved, the wicked often become worse, 659. See **Wicked, Unjust, Reprobate**.

—The wicked oppress the good in the Church, 14, 88, 181, 218, 820. Let the wicked not criticize the deeds of the better, 148. The wicked are accustomed to disparage the good, 199. What the wicked do unjustly, God permits to be done justly, 367. What the righteous suffer from the wicked, 447. Whether the righteous remain silent or speak, they always experience the wicked as adversaries, ibid. Who are rebuked by the righteous as wicked, 497. The wicked gather to oppress the righteous, though separated from one another by their desires, 510. When the wall is broken, the wicked rush upon the good, 662. The life of the perverse serves the advantage of the innocent, 661, 933. Why the wicked are mixed with the good here, 673, 933, 1000. The wicked purify the good by oppressing them, 820. The wicked, devoted to visible things, are held by no desire for invisible goods, 965. The disparagement of the wicked is an approval of our life, 1254.

—Why the wicked are sometimes afflicted and sometimes prosper, 138. What it signifies that the reprobate are cut down from morning until evening, 172. Those who pursue earthly things appear to be raised up on a firm root in prosperity, 184. The wicked are often cast down from prosperity, 497. Why God often heaps prosperity upon the wicked, 507, 511. The prosperity of the wicked is a more grievous punishment, 827. How severely those must be punished who are not restrained from corrupt morals even by scourges, 839. See **Prosperity, Adversity**.

—To tolerate the wicked patiently is to lie prostrate like Christ; to rise is to take action against them, 60. Why God sometimes tolerates the wicked and sometimes strikes them immediately, 154. The wicked must be tolerated in this life, 673, 1259, 1638. God tolerates the hidden evils of some so that the good they openly do may benefit the elect, 1130. What it benefits the wicked to know about the good, 1253. The wicked are not to be feared, 1254. It is useful to live among the wicked, 1258. One who does not tolerate the wicked lacks much that is good, ibid. The company of the wicked is no reason for changing one’s place, 1259. No one can become Abel if Cain’s malice does not exercise him, ibid. Neighbors must be tolerated everywhere, ibid. Nevertheless, the weak must flee the society of the wicked, ibid. The wicked, long tolerated, suddenly fall, 1300. When the company of the wicked is harmful, 1259. The more abundant the wicked are, the more they must be tolerated, 1638.

—The fire now torments the wicked through envy, and later through vengeance, 58. God punishes the wicked by the very things they preferred to the Creator through sinning, 79. By the very act of sinning, the wicked strike themselves, 408. With how many and what kinds of punishments the wicked are afflicted, 490. The wicked are like willows: they are green, but bear no fruit, 1081. The wicked become worse through benefits received, 1508. We must neither despair of the wicked nor imitate them, 1514. Some of them may perhaps be elect, ibid. The wicked are nowhere alone except in hell, 1637. See **Ungodly, Unjust, Wicked**, [Col. 1436].

What it means for the bride to be surrounded by the wicked, 1332.

**Morning** signifies prosperity, 172; the beginning of life, ibid.; the day of judgment, 269, 528; the advent of the Lord’s incarnation, 528; the prosperity of the present life, ibid. Morning signifies the first age of the world, 1510, and the childhood of man, 511.

What **manhu** signifies, 872.

The **Manichaeans** establish two principles, 321, 1056. The Manichaean rages against Moses, 575. The Manichaean condemned marriage, 618.

**Manna** signifies the divine word, which is wise for each person according to his disposition, 191, 1010. What is represented by the Israelite people, who grew tired of manna and desired the pots of Egypt, 655. Manna signifies the soul’s inward refreshment through the voice of compunction, 872.

The various **mansions** in heaven, 136, 1166, 1345. What it means for God to make a dwelling in the soul, 1576.

Gentleness must be joined to justice, 21. False gentleness, 1207.

When **Manoah** sees the angel, he trembles, 164. Manoah’s wife, having seen the Lord, becomes bold, ibid.

What the **hand of Satan** means, 56, 75, 85. What it means to be in the hand of God and in the hand of the devil, 75. The hand is Satan’s strength, 235. What is meant by the hand of the strong, ibid. Hands signify works or action, 210, 314, 350, 572, 790, 1046. What it means to stretch out one’s hand against God, 411. What the hand of plague means, 513. The hand of God signifies power, 368, 1310. Christ is called the hand of God, 564. What it means to clench the hand, 572. What is called the hard hand of God, 668. What hand in hand signifies, 790. What it means to place the hand over the mouth, 1046. In a vision, the hand is power in contemplation, 1310. What it means to place the hand upon Leviathan, 1098. What it means for the beloved to put his hand through the opening, 1382.

Why the Evangelist **Mark** is represented under the name of the lion, 1200.

The **sea** signifies the world, 293; the hearts of the carnal, 259, 588. God walks upon the waves of the sea, 293. The sea signifies the mind, 396, 929; human life, 396; the present age, 551, 912, 927, 1474, 1540; the life of worldly people, 588, 1130; the human heart, 915. What it means that the sea retains living bodies but casts out the dead, 141. How God surrounds the sea with its boundaries, 911. What the broken wave of the sea, beaten back upon itself, signifies, 912. God enters the depth of the sea when he visits the sinner’s mind, 929. The deep sea signifies the hidden thoughts of worldly people, 1130. The shore of the sea signifies the end of the world, 1474. Let us beware, as captives in the dragnet, lest we be separated on the shore, ibid. The shore of the sea signifies the stability of blessed eternity, 1541.

The **precious pearl** is the sweetness of heavenly life, 1473. Having found it, the merchant purchases it after selling everything, ibid.

To the **Virgin Mary, Mother of God**, refreshment of mind was granted, 570. The Virgin conceived the Son of God, 598. Thus Mary conceived and bore the Word of God, so that she was at once Virgin and Mother of God, ibid. Christ is one thing from the Father and another from his mother, but not another person, ibid. Mary, the Mother of God, came forth from the loins of Abraham, 1245. What Christ signified by not acknowledging his mother, 1444. He himself created the mother from whom Christ was born, 1549.

—**Mary**, Martha’s sister, is a figure of the contemplative life, 210, 1324. Mary’s portion is the better one, just as Martha’s is good, 1324. Mary seeks the author of life among the dead, but she was in darkness, 1530. What it means for Mary to turn backward, 1548. In Mary’s conversation [Col. 1437] with the Lord, mutual love is proved, ibid. She is called by name by the Lord, ibid. Mary Magdalene is a witness of divine mercy, 1551, and an example of repentance, ibid. The repentance of sinful Mary calls us to tears, 1592. There is one sinful woman, and Mary Magdalene is Martha’s sister, 1235, 1593. She was full of every vice, ibid. Drawn by grace, she came to Christ, 1594. As many pleasures as she had, so many holocausts did she offer, ibid. The tears of the penitent are sweet food for Christ, 1597. May the repentance of the sinful woman move us also to repentance, 1599. See **Magdalene**.

**Martha** is a figure of the active life, 210, 1324. Martha’s portion is good, ibid. See **Contemplative and active life**.

The intercession of the **martyrs** must be implored, 525. Not everyone is able to gird himself to undergo bodily torments for God, 218. The Catholic Church alone has martyrs, 573. Under Christ as their leader, the martyrs conquered their enemies armed with trumpets, jars, and lamps, 991. What is signified by the trumpets, jars, and lamps, ibid. The holy preachers benefited more by their death than by their speech, ibid. The bodies of the martyrs in heaven are represented by white horses, 1009. Various punishments of the martyrs are recounted, 1059. The blood of the martyrs is compared to the flower of the rose, 1214. The saints neither die for themselves nor live for themselves, 1425. The world is full of martyrs, 1562. If we do not offer our bodies for Christ, let us at least conquer our spirit; God is appeased by this sacrifice, 1565. The contests of the martyrs are proofs of the future life, 1591. The tombs of the martyrs are glorified by miracles, ibid. They are present to those who ask their help, ibid. In the peace of the Church we can obtain the rewards of the martyrs, 1616. The death of the martyrs flowers in the faith of the living, 1637. The peace of the Church has its own martyrdom, 1447. There are two kinds of martyrdom: one in the mind, the other also in action, 1616.

The monk **Martyrius** placed Christ, under the appearance of a leper, upon his shoulders to carry him, 1650. Appearing to Martyrius in his own form, Christ was seen returning to heaven, 1651. Christ showed him how much Martyrius’s brotherly compassion pleased him, ibid.

What is signified by the mother who, while asleep, crushed her own son and seeks another’s, 686. The false mother does not fear killing one whom she did not bear, ibid. Whoever becomes Christ’s brother or sister by believing becomes his mother by preaching, 1444.

The superstition of the **astrologers** is condemned, 1088. Their opinion concerning the birth of infants is refuted, 1469.

The vision of a religious **matron**, 1591.

How much the Evangelist **Matthew**, called from the tax office, advanced, 575. Matthew prepared a great banquet for Christ—indeed, he himself became one, 993. After his conversion Matthew did not return to the tax office, 1540. Why Matthew is represented under the figure of a man, 1200.

Why **Matthias** received the twelfth place among the apostles by lot, 1061.

What is signified by the **jawbone of an ass** with which Samson killed his enemies, 423. The perverse strike the jaw of the Church when they persecute good preachers, ibid. What the pierced jaw of the devil signifies, 1090, 1092.

Job desires a **mediator** who might free us by his own death, 306. All the saints must be passed through in order to reach the mediator, 595, 644. The intercession of our mediator is absolutely necessary for us, 718. What this intercession of the mediator is, ibid. Christ is the mediator between God and human beings, [Col. 1437] 854. Christ the mediator is represented by electrum, 894. Through the coming of the mediator, light was spread, 935. Why Christ the mediator is compared to the appearance of bronze, 1313. Christ the mediator alone frees us from sins: he repaid what he did not owe, 1650. See **Christ, God and human being, mediator**.

What the office of a skilled **physician** is, 780. A skilled physician probes a wound for a long time and then cuts it, ibid., 1287. Medicine cures opposites with opposites, 760, 1586.

What Christians should meditate on daily, 794, etc.

Excessive eating of **honey** is harmful, 448. What the sweetness of honey tasted too abundantly signifies, ibid. What it means for us to be filled by God incarnate with honey and butter, 477. What it means to eat enough of the honey that has been found, 503. What wild honey signifies, 1017. What the honeycomb signifies, 1543. What it means to suck honey from the rock, 1554.

Who are the **members of the devil**, 85. Who have been members of Christ from the beginning of the world, 86. We become members of Christ in two ways, 1650. A member signifies the weak, 420. The functions of the bodily members, 627. How the members of the Church should conduct themselves, ibid. We do not perceive that the members in us increase or change, 793. Joined together, corrupt habits make one body, 923. While one member is improperly nourished, another is stirred up to insult, 1036. What one member of another member means, 1119.

The memory of our sins, which forgiveness has removed, often defiles and disturbs the mind, 326. The memory of God’s gifts is great consolation in adversities, 51, 80. Vain people strive to leave a memory of their name, 381. The memory of fools is compared to ashes, ibid. The memory of the righteous, who desire eternal things, ibid.

The **mind** sometimes signifies the head, 70, 93, 612, 1227, 1437, 1478. The mind of the righteous is called the ark of the covenant, 149. The mechanism of the mind is the force of love, 209. The blindness of the mind is called night, 114. Forgetfulness of the mind is called the shadow of death, 116. The mind is called a tabernacle, 351. The mind is called the inner face of the human being, ibid. What is the place of the mind, 401, 849. Why the mind is called the belly and womb, 417. Earthly minds are like shrubs, 631. The sea is the human mind, 929. The human mind is called an abyss, ibid. The incomprehensible minds of human beings are a great abyss, 1084. The food of the mind is the word of God, 1489. The faithful mind is a house of prayer, 1648. How the mind of the faithful becomes a den of thieves, ibid.

—From where the senses of the mind fail, 442. The wisdom of God rests in the human mind, which it makes holy, 600. When the law of the mind strikes the law of the flesh, and conversely, light and shadow struggle, 919. The mind, contemplating sublime things, recognizes in itself many things that had lain hidden and that deserve condemnation, 1045.

—The entrances of the mind must be fortified with every strength, 33. The mind is preserved from deception more by praying than by investigating, ibid. At the door of the mind one must place not a female doorkeeper but a male doorkeeper who does not sleep, ibid. What it means to purge wheat at the door of the mind, ibid. By what steps the sluggish mind falls into the pit of ruin, 239. The mind never contemplates perfectly unless it is first quieted from the tumult of earthly desire, 164. The mind must first be cleansed of the appetite for earthly things before it is raised to the citadel of contemplation, 209. The mind must be restrained from carnal senses, 679.

—Through the first sin the human mind lost the light of invisible things, [Col. 1438] 166. The mind lacking counsel within is anxious outwardly, 192. The instability of the human mind is compared to a millstone, 193. When the mind ceases to yearn for what is above it, it continually rushes inward upon itself, ibid. The mind blinded by the habit of sin does not know where it is going, 229. The agitation of the mind: its origin, 347. Various disturbances of the mind, ibid. In what the confidence of the mind consists, 510. The cause of the mind’s instability, 849. The mind that is not wholly present to itself cannot think about itself, 1005. The inconsistency of the mind is signified by a reed, 1078, 1256, 1454. Places do not fortify the mind, 1259. Perfect rest of mind cannot exist in this life, 1327. The perfect minds of the good are signified by apple trees, and those beginning by flowers, 1332.

—How the minds of the elect conduct themselves toward temporal things, 28. How the upright mind receives the cares of administering earthly things, 67. The mind of the righteous, once illuminated, fears more, 162. The mind raised to heavenly secrets trembles, 161. The faithful mind is sometimes moved by doubt, 347. The place of the holy mind is justice, 401. The mind of the righteous is compared to the dawn, 530. The higher one reaches toward God, the more truly the mind humbles itself within, 551. The mind that strives always to begin anew through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness, 700. The mind of the righteous is designated by the name of gold, 886. The mind must be emptied and dug out without ceasing, 1021. Satan cannot sleep in it, 1078. The daily nourishment of a good mind is good works, 1449. The mind of the righteous is called the house of God, 1576. Whoever prepares a house of the mind for God must wipe away the filth of evil works, ibid.

—The tranquil mind is disturbed in temptation, 302, 850. A strong mind is swallowed up by a vice that steals in lightly, 401. One must beware lest the mind, while it is lifted up, fall, 798. The breadth or expansion of the mind in adversities, 930. Sometimes through a sudden dullness of mind the heart is humbled, and wisdom is established in it, 68.

—Why carnal minds love the world, 253. The mind occupied with outward desires does not grow warm with the fire of divine love, 277. The mind excluded from the light of truth finds nothing in itself but darkness, 386. The disturbed minds of worldly people are alien from wisdom, 590. Our mind, cast down by love of the present age, dozes, 868. God terrifies hard minds in many ways, 926. The slower the mind abandons a vice, the less it is ashamed of what it commits, 1070. The minds of the carnal, devoted to temporal glory, are like reeds, 1079, and like damp places, 1080. In the carnal mind, some globes of the smoke of desire dissipate above, while others rise below, 1113. Vices succeed vices in the carnal mind, ibid. The carnal mind is signified by the name of a pot, 1114. The carnal mind is like a coal kindled by the devil’s breath, ibid.

—The mind of the ungodly is always in troubles, 409. The mind of the ungodly is compared to water, 531. The mind expanded by perverse thoughts is compared to a full belly, 751. The perverse mind glories in defending what is right, 1069. In cold minds Satan lies secure, 1078. The devil inhabits a mind alien from the virtues, 1253. The mind of the ungodly is called an exasperating house, ibid. Nothing is more burdensome to perverse minds than not to labor in the affairs of the world, 1269. Why God permits a blinded mind to slip into other sins, 1290.

What it means to adorn a **table while passing by**, 1057. What the table set out by Wisdom signifies, 1096. The two tables of the vestibule of the gates are faith and life, 1403. What is designated by the four outer tables, [Col. 1439] 1405. What is designated by the inner ones, ibid.

The gathering of days is signified by the name of **months**, 249. What our number is before God, 392. What a month spiritually signifies, 612, 1221. What “month from month” means, ibid. What is designated by months, 976. What it means that Christ measured the dimensions of the earth with lines, 900. In accordance with the measure of each sin, blindness of understanding is generated in the senses, 382. A right measure must be preserved in spiritual matters, 905.

Who is called a truthful man who does not know how to lie, 40. Whoever lies to secure another’s welfare slaughters his own mind, 245, 558. A lie is constructed out of words just as a building is constructed out of stones, 379. The way of truth is level; the path of lying is rough, 410. How hateful lying is to the saints, 500, 559. It is not for a liar to accuse another of lying, 540. Why lying is called iniquity, and conversely, 558. How speaking a lie and meditating a lie differ, ibid. A lie is sometimes venial, ibid. How the lie of the Egyptian midwives is to be interpreted, 559. In the Old Testament a lie was judged a lighter fault than in the New, ibid. Even in the Old Testament it is scarcely found to have been committed by perfect men, ibid. Which prophet truly said that every human being is a liar, 715. It is not permissible to lie for the sake of humility, 813.

The life of the elect is compared to the days of a **hireling**, 246, 248, 393. A hireling aims at three things, 248. Like a hireling, one who has understanding of eternal things labors in another’s work and desires his days to pass more quickly, 246. Just as a hireling does, so the elect take care that no day pass empty of work, ibid. He desires shade after the heat of labor and temptation, 247. The labor of the elect is lightened by the thought of the reward, 248. What the day of the hireling is, 394. The marks of a hireling shepherd, 1485. What it means for the hireling to flee when the wolf comes, 1486. He flees for this reason: because he is a hireling, ibid. The hope of the hireling, 248. The closer the hireling is to the end of his work, the closer he is to the payment of his reward, 393.

The reward of the saints is certain, 279. What it means to receive the reward of a prophet or righteous person, but not from a prophet or righteous person, 1521. Our judge considers weight in repayment, but weighs strength in the weight, 1530. A single work of ours is owed a double reward, 1499.

At **noon**, the heat of vices is expressed, 992. What it means for the Lord to lie down at noon, ibid., 1597. What place the young stag of the deer seeks at noon, ibid. Who those are who have taken their midday rest, 526.

Human beings deserved one thing through justice and received another through grace, 585. By natural reason God intimates to a human being what he should do and what he deserves, 875. No one can deserve from God what he asks if here he was unwilling to hear what God commanded, 1479. Our merits are God’s gifts, 512, 585, 1249. Here there is a distinction of works; in heaven there will be a distinction of dignities, 136. As the work increases, confidence in the reward advances, 246. How merits will be rewarded at the final judgment, 585. From the inspiration of grace and free will there follows an action to which eternal recompense corresponds, ibid. The beginning of merit is not subject to merit, ibid. God does not act according to our merit, 639. Let no one rely on his own merits, 618. God questions human life solely according to the quality of its merits, 787. No one precedes God by merits, 1100. In the election or reprobation of little ones who die before or after baptism, God takes no account of future merits on the condition that they might have had them, [Col. 1439] 855. In election God is merciful; in reprobation, just, 1100.

What the **harvest of the Church** is, 632. The harvest of the Church is to be attributed to the dew of grace, ibid.

What **metacism** is. Saint Gregory neglected metacism in the *Moralia*, 6.

Most people do not usually fear God because they do not see him, 505.

What the **crumbs** falling from the rich man’s table signify, 1652.

**Michael** is interpreted as “Who is like God?”, 1604. Michael is the prince of Judea, 541. To whom Michael is sent, 1604. He will fight at the end of the world and break the pride of the apostate angel, 1605.

**Michal** mocked David as he danced, 889.

With what arms the **soldier of God** ought to be equipped, 242. The soldiers of God are strong not by their own powers but by the gift of grace, 543. Every faithful person is a soldier of God, 1030. Faith must first arm the soldier of God, ibid. The soldier of God despises the threats of the enemy, 1032. By rightly subordinating his own concerns, the soldier of God prevents the enemy from approaching the mind of his neighbor, ibid. He despises fear and does not yield to the sword, ibid. The enemy attacks him now by open force, now by fraud and deceit, 1033. Sometimes he is attacked by force and deceit together, ibid. Against one whom the enemy cannot conquer with bow or spear, he sets up a shield, ibid. Through holy fervor and concern for progress, the soldier of God resists all the enemy’s forces, 1034. No unforeseen attacks tempt him; therefore they do not overcome him, ibid. Those who flee hardships and pursue softness do not serve God as soldiers, 1454.

Our life is warfare, 244, 399. Temptation itself is warfare, ibid. Our life, like warfare, decreases as it grows and comes to an end, 246. What the warfare of heaven is, 699.

The number **one thousand** signifies totality, 289, 588, 1059, 1162, 1337; and the perfection of a good life, 289, 723, 1162. It signifies the time of the holy Church, 1069. One thousand is a perfect number, 1162. It signifies the fullness of God’s gifts, 723.

The **kite** at its windows pants after what it sees, driven by a desire for plunder, 1453. What the nature of the kite is, 461.

Ministers of the Church who care for earthly things are called its feet, 616. Who those are who minister to the Lord, 1425.

The **wonders of God** are inscrutable, 188. God’s wonders in producing trees, 189. Miracles were necessary at the beginning of the nascent Church, 869, 1571. At the end of the world miracles will be withdrawn from the Church, 1118. The Antichrist will perform many things, ibid. Miracles are necessary for holy preachers, 862, 1211. Signs were given not to the faithful but to unbelievers, 870, 1448, 1571. Human hearts are disturbed by miracles, 957, 995, 1211. The miracles of the saints are our defenses, 1340. They are not certain proofs of holiness, 1363, 1571. In what the miracles of the elect and of the reprobate differ, ibid. In miracles the only relevant consideration is the power of the one who performs them, 1396. Miracles are granted for the weak, 1440. The miracles of Christ show one thing through power and speak of another through mystery, ibid. How miracles accompanying true faith are to be understood, 1571. Miracles sometimes prove holiness but do not produce it, ibid. Why the tombs of the martyrs are glorified by miracles, 1591.

—The miracles of the saints illuminate the darkness of our insensibility, 862. Miracles have become cheap through their frequency, [Col. 1440] 1559. Spiritual miracles occur daily in the Church, 1571. Miracles ought not to be examined by the intellect, 189. Why we marvel at miracles, while God’s marvelous works have become cheap to us through constant use, 188. What it means to consider God’s miracles while standing and while lying down, 881. The gleam of weapons is the brightness of miracles, 957. Why miracles are joined to preaching, 1448. Miracles of charity and compassion are proper to the saints, 1571. Why Christ performed miracles by day and devoted himself to prayer by night, 207. Those who despise invisible things can be moved by visible miracles, 826. Miracles do not produce the same effects in everyone, 872. The violence of tyrants was broken by the miracles of the saints, 910. God broke the rigid powers of this world not by words but by miracles, 996. The effects of miracles are various, 1448.

—The greater miracle is the creation of a human being than the resurrection, 188. The production of seeds is greater than the multiplication of loaves, 189. The production of wine from the vine is greater than the changing of water into wine, ibid.

The **misery of human beings** exists both in soul and in body, 135. Human misery is compared to passing waters, 354. How many and how great are the miseries of mortal life, 390. In what human misery consists, ibid. Who can endure in miseries, 419. Miseries themselves are scourges of sin, 429. See **Scourges, Adversity, Tribulation**.

What **mercy** is, 666. Mercy is learned through knowledge of charity, 1274. Mercy surpasses every law, 1598. A person should show mercy to himself by living well before showing it to his neighbor through action, 624. Whoever purely mourns the sins of others completely washes away his own offenses, 671. Let mercy in sparing be followed by mercy in giving, 711. Let the mind of the righteous, burned by the heat of zeal, be sprinkled with mercy, 1305.

—God’s mercy is the greatest consolation of the sorrowful, 71. Without God’s mercy no one can resist the temptations of demons, 320. Life cannot be preserved without God’s mercy, 324. We continually need God’s mercy, ibid. The generosity of divine mercy, by which God grants a human being such great glory after sin, 400. God’s mercy forgets the person who has forgotten his justice, 532. God’s mercy toward sinners, 926, 1182, 1609. How great God’s mercy is, 1059. One must never despair of God’s mercy, 1090. Whoever does not remember his own misery does not understand God’s mercy, 1373. David, Mary Magdalene, Peter, and the Thief were washed in the open fountain of God’s mercy, 1402. The mercy of our Creator is immeasurable, 1551. Christ’s compassion and mercy toward sinners, 1597. See **God’s mercy**.

—There is no mercy after death, 255. Let no one lose the time of mercy, 1599, 1659.

The works of mercy, both bodily and spiritual, are provided by the Church, 620. Works of justice are to be preferred to works of mercy, 624. By what art the devil recalls a righteous person from spiritual works of mercy, 1069. Works of mercy are compared to the flower of the olive, 1214. Mercy opens its lap to one who practices mercy, 1354. It is more important to nourish a soul that will live forever with the word of God than a body that will die with bread, 1456. Whoever lacks bread has a tongue, ibid. Works of mercy belong to the worthy fruits of repentance, 1521. For charity to be unconquered in persecution, it must be nourished by mercy in peace, 1561. How pleasing works of mercy are to Christ is proved by an example, 1650.

—The great works of mercy are to have compassion on the poor, orphans, and widows, 619. Two things are required for showing mercy, 624. Works of mercy must be done with cheerfulness and kindness, 692. Humility should accompany works of mercy, ibid. Works of mercy must be shown even to those who are unknown, 693. What works of mercy consist in, 693, 1354. See **Almsgiving**.

One is called **merciful** who is moved toward his neighbor by compassion, 666.

The three **Masses** customarily celebrated at the Nativity of the Lord, 1460. How powerful the sacrifice of the Mass is with God, 1631. See **Sacrifice**.

The sending of the **Son** by the Father into the world through the incarnation, 1553. The sending of the Son by the Father according to divinity is his eternal generation, ibid. The sending of the Holy Spirit is his procession from the Father and the Son, 1554. A comparison of the incarnation of the Word and the sending of the Holy Spirit, 1580.

David is an example of **modesty**, 1339.

What the **bushel** signifies, 992. What it means to place a lamp under a bushel, ibid.

The **walls of Christians** are faith, hope, and charity, 376.

Excessive grief removes the sensation of pain, 330. The three alternations of grief and joy, 771.

What a **mill** spiritually signifies, 193. What an ass’s millstone signifies, 208. What the millstones and teeth of the wicked are, 629. The upper and lower millstones are hope and fear, 1091.

The troubles both of soul and body in this life are innumerable, 135. Why God sometimes permits us to be exercised by troubles, 947.

A **monk** ought to live in a monastery as in a safe harbor, 2. Excessive love of relatives recalls a monk to the nets of the world that he had broken, 231. The definition of true conversion, 1266. A monk takes religious clothing in vain unless he abandons his vices, ibid. Monks devoted to exercises of repentance, 1292. By leaving everything they offer a holocaust, 1399, 1410. Rather, they themselves become a holocaust, ibid. A holocaust is greater than a sacrifice, ibid. A certain person converted at the point of death in a monastery through the monks’ prayer, 1514, 1643. Monks ought not to break into tribunals or occupy themselves with the quarrels of the world, 231. Let monks not occupy themselves with lawsuits through love of relatives, ibid.

**Mountains** are preachers, 290. They also signify the powerful and exalted of the world, 582, 992. Who are the mountains overturned from their roots, 582. What the mountains of pasture are, 985, 992. The various meanings of the mountain in Scripture, 992, 1075, 1517. What the mountain signifies in the singular, 1075. What it means to raise a sign upon the dark mountain, 1075. What Mount Testament signifies, 1186.

**Moralia on Job.** See the preface placed before it.

Good **morals** are related to certain vices, 441. Different kinds of morals, 961. Not everyone is bound by an equal quality of morals, ibid.

What it means to die perfectly to the world, 142. The human being was created mortal in such a way that he could have not died if he had not sinned, 126. The **shadow of death** is called the separation of the soul from the body, 117, 332. Death is in the desire of one who is touched by longing for heavenly life, 219. Death attacks everyone, 306, 669. What exterior and interior death are, 270, 332. Bodily death is the shadow of the soul’s death, 376. At every moment of life a human being hastens toward death, [Col. 1441] 390. Why death is called sleep, 397, 1477. Death must be feared because it cannot be foreseen, 408, 1439. Whoever considers what he will be like in death always becomes cautious in his conduct, 428. What things belonging to him all follow the dying person, 436. The inextricable bonds of the ungodly person’s sins at death, 440. Death opens the sinner’s eyes so that he sees temporal goods fleeing from him and punishment taking their place, 568. What it means for death to climb through the windows, 678. What must be feared when death is imminent, 776. By this fear the souls of the righteous are cleansed from slight faults, ibid. The soul of the righteous, having overcome fear of death and judgment, finds security, ibid. The death of all the ungodly is sudden because it was not foreseen, 787. Death restores the elect to their own light but removes their light from the reprobate, 927. Death is signified by the name of blood, 1285. Death must always be contemplated, 1317, 1439. The Lord guards each soul’s entrance into faith and exit into vision, 1318. Looking toward death, we turn our backs on the present life, ibid. Ignorance of the time of death admonishes us to hasten to work well, 1355, 1485. Sudden death must be feared, 1439. Why the hour of death ought to be hidden from us, 408, 1355, 1484. Christ killed death by rising again, 1533. The death of the righteous is assistance to the good and testimony against the evil, 1614. The hour of death must be carefully placed before the eyes of the mind, 1481, 1649.

—The present death is the punishment of sin, 269. Human beings are bound by the punishment of a twofold death, 306. Exterior death divides the soul from the flesh; interior death divides the soul from God, 332. For the miserable there is death without dying, 334. Sin kills the soul, 442. Who desire death, 142, 246, 1482. Holy men live as though dying daily, 233, 253. How useful meditation on death is, 428. As death approaches, every soul is rightly terrified, 775. The variety of our life ought to impel us to contemplate death, 1115. After death there is no further possibility of absolution, 532. What…

Let him consider, and how greatly the dying man is terrified as he approaches the strict judgment of his entire life, 775. The temptations of the devil are more severe at the end of life, 1065. Those who mortify themselves, as though digging, seek a treasure, 142. The effect of mortifying oneself, ibid. To place flesh upon a rock means to chastise our body by imitating Christ, 96. They are kings who keep the mortified movements of the soul subject to themselves, 128. No one falls into illicit things who does not also at times restrain himself from things permitted, 146. No one here is so perfect that there does not continually arise something requiring removal, 165. The three dead whom Christ raised: what they signify, 125. What it means for the dead to be buried by the dead, ibid. In former times the dead were buried with their riches, 143. The dead do not know what is done here, 403. Consideration of the dead: how profitable it is, 533. The movements of the flesh make peace for us with God, 204. The movements of the heart are strong when they perceive nothing except what belongs to virtue, 950. How the movements of the flesh are to be restrained, 382. See *Flesh*.

Moses resisted the wrath of God when, by offering his own death, he checked the force of the blow from above, 299. Why Moses, who by his prayers had turned God’s wrath away from others, was unable to turn it away from himself, ibid. Moses, with the staff—that is, with the terror of the law—did not raise the dead, 318. Through patience Moses washed away the guilt of homicide, 575. What Moses speaking with veiled face signifies, 584. Moses endured as though seeing the Invisible One, 614. In the breast of Moses, mercy was joined to severity, 641. Moses teaches us gentleness, 860, 1338. Who Moses was as the cloud and the tent of God, 861, 862. By his own example Moses teaches us perfect obedience, 1157. His humility, 1242. What it signifies that, as Moses entered the tabernacle, his back was looked upon by the people, 1319. Moses, who was the god of Pharaoh, 1331. What it means for Moses to be known by God by name, 1548. Why Moses and Samuel alone, if they pray for the people, are not to be heard, 300, 1564. These two alone in the Old Testament are read to have pleaded for their own enemies, ibid. Moses sat upon a stone: the law rested in the Church, 1598. What Moses’ heavy hands signify, ibid. Why those who listen neither to Moses nor to the Prophets will not even listen to the dead when they rise again, 1658. Moses attacks Pharaoh with authority, 236. Moses saw God in an image, 600. Moses’ goodness toward the people of Israel, 641. Moses did not hear the voice of the Lord in Egypt, but in the desert, 749. When Pharaoh came, Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt even against their will, 820. Moses’ gentleness is described, 860. Moses’ zeal and patience, 1228, 1338. Moses prayed for his enemies, 300, 1564.

In Scripture, “woman” is sometimes used with reference to sex, sometimes with reference to weakness, 389. The woman who administered iniquity, 406. A woman offered death to a man; a woman announces life to men, 1549. The woman bent over for eighteen years: what she signifies, 1582, 1585. The steadfastness of the women during Christ’s Passion, 457.

Loquacity: how many evils it causes, 239. By loquacity the mind, scattered outwardly, is dissipated, 240. No one becomes perfectly clean in this age, whether by life or by tears, 314. For the mind to be clean, the iniquity of one’s actions and then of one’s heart must first be cut away, 351. This purity grants confidence in prayer; the opposite occurs if it is lacking, 351.
