A person striving for purity attempts to overcome what he is, 392. No one is clean before God, 406. Those who wish to cleanse others must first be cleansed themselves, 449. The purity of our hands comes from God, 511. Whoever does not desire purity of heart drives away from himself the author of purity, 680.

Who is dead to the world, and to whom is the world dead? 140. What it means for the world to be crucified and for one to be crucified to the world, ibid. Those dead to the world hide themselves within from earthly things, 142. Those whom the heart draws toward the world, and whom the world repels from the heart, 173. Some flee the world’s activities, but exercise themselves in no virtues, 163. Love of the world overturns the seat of judgment in the soul, 192. Some are ensnared in the nets of the age under the name of propriety, 230. The wicked love the very world from which they are driven away, 536. The world is worthless to God, 583. The wisdom of the world is foolish, 656. The origin of the world, 899. When the world was still near its origin, laws were established by God, 913. Those who love the world as it collapses no longer love its joys but its wounds, 1374. The world must be despised at least in its downfall, 1376, 1438, 1448, 1569. May Christ deter us from love of the aging world, 1436, 1489. He is a friend of the world who mourns when it collapses; an enemy who rejoices, 1438. From the world’s ruin it is known that the kingdom of God is near, ibid., 1448. The fruit of the world is its ruin, ibid. The world grows so that it may fall, ibid. By what disasters the world is afflicted daily, ibid. The youth and old age of the world, 1439. Love of the world is condemned, ibid. The end of the world is announced, 1448. How dangerous it is to cling to what is falling, ibid., 1569. By love of the world, we are neither bent by commandments nor corrected by blows, 1450. The various ages of the world, 1510. The world that is loved flees, 1568. Those who cling to the falling world fall with it in a grievous collapse, 1569. He is invited to God’s banquet who is admonished to despise the age, 1620. Who uses this world as though he did not use it? 1625. All worldly people try to leave behind a memory of what they do, 381.

Fortifications built against the mind: what they signify, 1303. What fortifications are to be set against hostile weapons, ibid.

A gift from the heart, from the mouth, and from the hand, 312, 416. A gift from service, from the hand, and from the tongue, 1449. The righteous man shakes his hands free from every gift, 313, 1449. The hypocrite seeks a gift from the mouth, 416. Fire will devour those who take delight in these gifts, ibid. God does not look at gifts but at the heart, 1451. Before God’s eyes the hand is never empty of a gift if the chest of the heart is filled with good will, ibid.

Let the tempted beware of murmuring, 72. The murmuring of subjects against their superiors rebounds upon God, 728. Those who murmur in afflictions accuse God’s justice, 170. One must not murmur in afflictions, 232. Who are said to have murmured, although afterward they attained blessedness, 1512.

What it means for the wall of faith to be broken, 662. What it means to cross the wall, 822. What the iron wall placed by the prophet between himself and the city signifies, 1304. Christ is a wall for us, 1322. What it means to set up a wall for the house of Israel, 1486.

What the flies with which Egypt was struck signify, 589. Whence mutability proceeds in the creature, 170, 791, 849. Mutability is a kind of death, 406, 791. Rational creation is mutable of itself toward what is worse, but through God’s grace toward what is better, 791. All creatures are subject to mutability, 791. What it means to change the mind, 1266. Who are called mute, 497.

What the *myrmicoleon*—the ant-lion—is, 156. It signifies those who are timid toward the stronger but bold toward the weak, ibid. Why the devil is called an ant-lion, 157.

Who offers the sacrifice of myrrh and incense, 1429, 1470. Myrrh is a symbol of mortification, 1470. What it means for the myrtle to grow in place of the nettle, 570. The myrtle signifies men who sympathize with the afflictions of others, 1522.

The mysteries of divine power are to be venerated by faith, not examined by reason, 1396.

# N

Naamah signifies beauty, 92. A Naamathite is one who desires not to be learned but to appear learned; such are heretics, ibid. Naaman the Syrian healed in the Jordan, 237. Why Nebuchadnezzar was changed into an irrational animal, 146. He is designated by the name of the great eagle, 1039. He who, coming to Lebanon, carried away the cedar’s marrow, ibid. His pride was swiftly followed by his downfall, 1138. By the name Natium, folly is designated, 1019. Also the devil’s snares, ibid. Also foreknowledge, ibid. Also the thoughts of our hope, 1030. Why the spirit of our Redeemer is said to be in the nostrils, 1019. The nostrils of Behemoth signify his cunning snares, 1085. What it means for a ring to be placed in Leviathan’s nostrils, 1089. The nose signifies the prudent discernment of the saints, 1034. Why the nose of the Church is said to be like a tower in Lebanon, ibid., 1284. Nathan’s and other saints’ restrained freedom in rebuking the powerful, 236. Not from the fault of arrogance, but from zeal for truth, 237. His discernment toward David, 1286. Why Nathanael was not an apostle, 1096. The ineffable birth of the Only-Begotten, 748. Birth and conception are sometimes the same thing, 933. The superstition of astrological nativities, 1088, 1469. On the Lord’s Nativity, three Masses are customarily celebrated, 1760. Why the world is enrolled at the Lord’s Nativity, ibid. By being born, Christ changed our hay into grain, 1461. Through Christ’s Nativity, peace was given to humankind, 1462. Why Herod was troubled when he heard of the Lord’s Nativity, 1468. Christ’s body came forth into the light while the Virgin’s womb remained closed, 1552. See Birth of Christ.

The divine nature is perceived by an intent mind without sight, heard without sound, and received without movement, 167. The divine nature is present everywhere, 166. The divine nature alone is immutable, ibid., 170. Our nature was made to exist outside nature, 252. How cares arise from corrupted nature and bad habit, 434. Danger concerning the necessities of nature, 649. Those who serve the necessities of nature beyond measure increase its weaknesses, ibid. Human nature, through its own fault, fell into calamities, 649. Nature created all human beings equal, 689. Those things must be taken up which the necessity of nature requires, 983. Study of human nature, 987. See the state of integral, fallen, and restored nature.

Ships carrying fruit: what they signify, 309, 310. By Peter’s ship, the Church entrusted to Peter is signified, 548. Why the Nazaraeans let their hair grow, 71. What they signified, ibid. By the name of Nazaraeans, the life of those practicing abstinence and continence is signified, 1070. What mist is morally, 955, 956. Every necessity is called iron, 480. Why the necessities of this life are called iron weapons, ibid. Under the pretext of necessity, we serve pleasure, 650, 984. Negligence often turns virtue into sin, 82. The double weight and measure of merchants, 1205. The Savior drove the crowds of merchants from the Temple with a whip, 1449. Certain commercial activities can scarcely be conducted without sin, 1540. What it means to go about one’s business, 1637. A neophyte, recently converted, should not be promoted to external offices, 279. Our good things perish if they are revealed too soon, 280. What the tangled sinews of Behemoth’s testicles signify, 1062, 1065. Whom God placed in the sinew of a man’s thigh, 388. What it means for God not to know, 40, 535, 733, 810, 897. Those who do not know inward things despair over outward evils, 419. It is one thing not to have known, another to have been unwilling to know, 488. Not to know belongs to ignorance; to have been unwilling to know belongs to pride, 804. The error and impiety of Nestorius raging against Christ, 598. What the nest signifies mystically, 629. Those who become black after being white: having lost God’s justice, they fall into sins previously unknown, 1071. The waters of snow are the laments of humility, 314. Snow signifies the white hearts of the saints, 873. Snow, through its coldness, denotes the hearts of the wicked, [Col. 1444] 934. The whiteness of snow signifies heavenly life, 1070. Who are whiter than snow, ibid.

What true or false nobility is, 656. Those whom God professes not to know are foolish and ignoble, ibid. The proud desire to harm the good, from whom they hope for comfort, 260. It is one thing when our enemy harms the good, and another when he harms himself and others, 709. Noah signifies the life of shepherds, 23, 1344. Noah survived the devastation of the Flood, 132. Noah had three sons of different dispositions, 673, 1638. What it means that Noah’s sons, turning away, covered their father’s nakedness, 808. Leaving domestic concerns behind, Noah obeyed God, 1338. The ark contained Noah’s three sons, one of whom was rejected, 1638.

**Name.** The hidden mysteries in the names of Job’s three daughters, 1163. What it means to be known by name by God, 1548. What it means to ask in prayer in Jesus’ name, 1563. Recognition of the face is signified by the name, 1117. What the newness of life is, 1266.

Night signifies ignorance, 26, 93, 249, 569; adversity, 44, 114, 139, 432; the devil, 107, 110; the present life, 291; oppression, 822; grief, 851. The night in which an act is performed foretells its disastrous end, 39. What is meant by a solitary night, 109. What it means to possess the night and to be possessed by the night, 118. What it means to pass laborious nights, 248. How night is turned into light, 265. Night is called ignorance of the coming end, 569. What it means to pass through the middle of the night, 788. What it means to prolong the night, 848. Some things are harmful in themselves, others because of circumstances, 832. People devoted to vanity are compared with clouds, 256. The hearts of the despairing are like clouds, 257. The just fly like clouds, 678. Clouds signify various things in Scripture, 859, 1199, 1248. Like clouds stretched above us, we are sheltered by the life of the ancient Fathers, 861. What it means for a cloud to scatter light, 879. Clouds signify preachers, 547, 879, 957, 1371. How being naked differs from walking naked, 525. Naked, we must wrestle with naked malignant spirits, 1587. Numbers possess various hidden mysteries in Scripture, 1162, 1542. What the testing of a coin signifies, 1111. What it means to give money to money-changers, 1465. The words of messengers are not despised because of reverence for the Lord who sends them, 1620. The people gladly frequent markets; what this implies for morals, 1487.

Certain heretics condemn marriage so that they may seem to favor virginity, 504. When the Lord went to a wedding, 1482. When Christ’s wedding took place, 1635. The present Church is signified by a wedding, 1634. The house of the wedding is the holy Church, 1639. What the wedding garment is, ibid. One enters the wedding feast through faith, ibid. The wedding garment is love of a friend in God and of an enemy for God’s sake, 1640.

# O

The hardening of the mind abandoned by God and the compunction of the mind visited by him, 328. The insensibility of a hardened soul, 350, 493. In what sense God is said to harden, 371, 945, 1008, 1291. Hardening proceeds from preceding sins, 799. Hardening is called blindness of heart and night, ibid. We offer obedience in order to receive wisdom, and then we buy gold, 131. The perplexing temptations of the obedient, [Col. 1445] 1066. Obedience signified by the name of the ear, 1155. The commendation of obedience, ibid., 1297. Obedience is rightly preferred to sacrifices, ibid. Obedience must be maintained unto death, 1156. Evil must never be done through obedience, but good may sometimes be omitted, ibid. Prosperity is to be undertaken solely at command, adversity also out of devotion, 1157. Obedience should be the ornament of innocence, 1158. The will must be broken according to God’s pleasure, 1297. Signs and miracles follow obedience, 1573. Obedience is the cause of all virtues, 1155. How great the virtue of obedience is, 1156. Abraham as an example of obedience, 1338. Obedience sacrifices the personal will, 1156. When obedience has no merit and when it has little merit, 1556. An obedient man speaks of victories, 1156. In adversity obedience should have something of its own; in prosperity, nothing, 1157. Obedience must be preserved not through fear of punishment but through love of justice, 1158. Obedience alone possesses the merit of faith, 1156. Obedience is imperfect when we obey according to our own desire, 1157. Those who strive to obey heavenly commands complete their days in goodness and their years in glory, 839. No one obeys God unless he is innocent, and conversely, 1158.

What it means to divide offerings correctly, 82. An offering is right before God when it proceeds from the root of justice, 625. An offering cannot appease the judge’s anger unless it pleases him through the purity of the one offering it, 711. Without concord no offering is acceptable to God, 1239. What it means to carry the flesh of an offering upon tables, 1416. Forgetfulness is called the shadow of death, 116. Of whom God is said to be forgetful, 534. How harmful forgetfulness of one’s own weakness and former iniquity is to a converted sinner, 903. Why obscure things are mingled with things that are evident, 899. What *obrizum* signifies, 700. What it means to render true service to God, 318. What it means for a siege to be organized by a preacher, 1303. The Egyptian midwives lied out of love for the present life, not with the intention of receiving payment, 559. Why God built houses for them, ibid. The speech of a slanderer is not to be feared, 1257. The destruction caused by slanderers, ibid. What is signified by the term “overshadowing,” 571. Overshadowing is sometimes the mind’s relief from the heat of carnal thoughts, 1077. Overshadowing sometimes signifies Christ’s incarnation, ibid.

What the west toward which we go signifies, 516. Why the eighth day is called the Lord’s Day, 20, 1341. What the eighth day signifies, 1341, 1391. What the psalm for the eighth signifies, ibid. What the eighth step of the Temple signifies, 1392. The reason and meaning of the number eight, 1341. The perfection of the number eight, 1150, 1341, 1392.

The eye of the mind is disturbed by vicious anger and is disposed to see more clearly by good anger, 177. What the right eye signifies, and what the left, 208. The eye denotes intention, 357, 907, 1224. Eyes that snatch toward guilt, 679. The eye must not serve a heart desiring illicit things, 684. Whoever uses his outward eye negligently is justly blinded in his inward eye, 685. Bad Christians have their eyes open in faith and closed in works, 801. The eye of the heart is blinded by self-love, 1204. How much spiritual eyes differ from carnal eyes, [Col. 1445] 1320. Why eyes are called windows, 1453. The eyes of the elect are opened before the Fall, those of the perverse after the Fall, 492. Guilt closes the eyes; punishment opens them, ibid., 796. What it means to incline the eyes, 511. How far the eyes of fools and the eyes of the wise differ, 537, 538. How the eyes are to be moderated, 678, 684. What it means to have eyes all around and within, 614. Through the eyes, evil thoughts pass into the mind, ibid. Which are the devil’s eyes, 1109. We do not have an eye when we neglect certain things, 1225.

What it means to hate ourselves and our relatives, 231, 1628. Hatred bores through the conscience, 179. Hatred of one’s neighbor hinders the fruit of prayer, 353. The devil’s arts for stirring us to hatred, 1560. Which relatives are to be loved through hatred, 1628. When a person who is despised is led to something better, the soul is loved, as it were, through hatred, ibid. Paul provided an example of hatred toward himself, ibid. From where the pattern for hatred of one’s neighbor should be taken, 1628.

Good odor comes from virtue, just as stench comes from vice, 462. Odor signifies the fragrance of virtues, 1163. The odor of a fertile field signifies the virtues of the elect in the world, 1214. The odor of a good reputation is expressed by the alabaster of ointment, 1596.

By offering a sacrifice for us every day, the Son never ceases, 28. To offer a holocaust one by one is the watchful and pure intention of individual virtues, 33. A blameless man ought to be offered for us, 552. What it means to offer correctly and not divide correctly, 1286. What it means to ask oil from one’s neighbors, 278, 1477, 1478. What the streams of oil poured out in the Church signify, 616. The anointing of the Holy Spirit is signified by oil, 617. What the “son of oil” is, ibid. What it means not to have oil in one’s vessel, 739, 1477. Oil signifies the splendor of glory, ibid. The sellers of oil are flatterers, 1478. What it means to suck oil from a firm rock, 1554. Who it is whose yoke has rotted away because of oil, 1555. What is signified by the luxuriant and beautiful olive, 1413. The olive is a type of mercy, 1522.

The heated pot is the human heart inflamed by the devil’s suggestions, 570, 1114. The pot boils when the human mind is kindled through consent, ibid. By the name of the pot, carnal conscience is signified, ibid. The heated pot is the mind of the Jews raging against Christ, 1188.

The wild ass signifies the Gentile people, 215; also the faithful, 217; solitaries, 979; Christ, 985. God mercifully restrains a man like a young wild ass with a bridle, 350. What the wild ass is, 523. The wild ass signifies heretics, ibid. What it means for God to loose the bonds of the wild ass, 980. What the house of the wild ass in the wilderness is, 981. What it means for the wild ass to search out green things, 985. The onocentaur signifies the lustful and the proud, 228. Its etymology, ibid.

Christ does not impose a heavy burden upon his own, 133. How God’s burden is light when it appears hard and heavy, 1359. Human praise often changes the mind of the one who acts, 34. Action must be supported by prayer, 560. Whoever attributes to himself what he does denies the grace of his author, 708. We do not forestall God by acting, 1100. The laborer who refuses to endure the evils of others loses his own good things, 695. The diversity of administration among workers of righteousness, 780. Who are the idle laborers in the Lord’s vineyard, 1512.

The works of God are inscrutable, 188, and wondrous, 189. Works are signified by hands, [Col. 1446] 314, 350. By the name “noble sons,” good works are signified; by “ignoble,” perverse works, 403. Works are signified by the name “arms,” 442. Works are denoted by the name “harvest,” 444; likewise by the name “feet,” 1536. Nearly all good works arise from thought, 351. No one should be lifted up by his good works, and no one should despair over his evil works, 935, 1514. Works of eternal life are called green grasses, 940. The good works we perform belong both to God and to us, 1101, 1212, 1249. Works are superior to signs, 1385. What God’s work is, 1351. What the sinner’s work is, 1352.

We labor in vain at a good work if we do not persevere to the end, 38. The discernment of works in this life, 136. A work is often the cause of condemnation when we think it is virtue, 143. Two vices often accompany good works, 312. In a good work fraud is committed in three ways, ibid. A person is uncertain here about his own works, 403. Greater works must be preferred to lesser ones, but none must be neglected, 626, 1410. Those who cannot act by themselves are obliged to exercise works of charity through others, 627. Works are built upon faith, 802. Many contradict by their works the faith they profess, 923. We must take care first not to do evil, and second not to do good carelessly, 1035. Some think that, because of the small good things they do, more serious evils are permitted them, 1205. When good works should be done and when omitted, 1224. Neither faith without works nor works without faith is beneficial, 1251. One must first turn away from evil before doing good, 1372. If the work is in our will, its perfection will come from divine assistance, 1526.

As for our good works, care must be taken that they are neither few nor unexamined, 36. Teaching without works is empty, 206. When a good work is despised, knowledge too is often lost, 474. It is one thing not to do good, another not to love it, another to hate it, 803. Faith without good works is useless for salvation, 1083. Whoever does the good he understands sees and follows Christ, 1443. Good works commend chastity, 1481. We recognize what we are by our works, not our words, 1590. Right works must be joined to right faith, 1650. See Action.

Good works are examined better through prayer than through discussion, 33, 1400. The enemy’s various snares for corrupting good works, 34. How great the dangers within good works themselves are, 313, 702. Good works may perish through the thief’s fraud or fail through negligence, 313. In good works, attention should be paid not to the beginning but to the end, 415. One is clothed in the cold who does good works at one time and evil works at another, 524, 621. No works are good if they are stained by evil, 621. It is better to do good works from charity than from fear, 626. The just take care to be in good works what the unjust were in evil works, 630. A debtor is not acquitted who repays much, but he who repays everything, 703. Pride must be avoided in good works, 711. Our evils are purely evil, but our good works cannot be pure, 1168. Through every good thing we do, let us return to the source of true light, 1212. Without faith, works are useless, 1251. Most good works are defiled, 1398. They must be supported by the laments of repentance, 1399. Unity of minds must be preserved in good works, 1411. Good works must be examined and washed away with tears in prayer, 1400. Faith, hope, charity, and the practice of goodness should be on the same level, 1426. We must bring a pure intention to good works, 1449, 1482 [Col. 1447]. Let us seek as witness of the good work the one whom we will endure as judge, 1449. The reprobate often display good works together with the elect, but they differ in intention, 1477. Good works must proceed from a pure heart, 112. Just as clothing protects the body, so good works protect the soul, 524. It is one thing to perform a work from command, another from affection, 626.

Through the practice of good works the mind expands, 1379. Those who do good works for earthly things are fools, 1477. In all our works we help ourselves, not God, 501. Good works assist in receiving faith, 1252. The reward sought from a good work is lost through an evil one, 1206. The thirtieth fruit of works, etc., 1358.

A work which the devil could not corrupt he tries in many ways to pervert as it progresses, 34. Good works should be concealed so that they may be preserved more safely, 623. They should be deliberately hidden; necessity may make good works public, ibid. The elect scarcely see their own good works, which they offer for all to see as an example, 703. When it is permissible to recall or recount good things done by oneself, ibid. Good things scarcely become known without danger, 734. Whoever publicly carries a treasure along the road wishes to be robbed, 282, 1472. With what precaution good works should be done publicly, ibid., 1476. Things revealed at the wrong time perish, 280.

In cutting away outward works that are evil, one must discern oneself inwardly, 351. Our inward works are visible only to God’s eyes, 613. No one should be lifted up by his own works, 935. Works of justice must precede works of mercy, 624. Those who do good works must not forget their iniquities, 702. Outward gifts are prepared from the inward purity of the heart, 711. One must return from outward things to the heart, 795. How our work must be done so that it does not appear, and yet is commanded to appear, 1472.

Evil works must be attributed to us, but good works to God and to us, 1249. As long as we perpetrate evils, there must be no confidence in former good deeds, 1288. With what care one must abstain from an evil work, 34.

The manner of wishing in Scripture is not that of one cursing but of one declaring, 442. The riches of the heart are described first, then those of the body, 19.

How useful it is to pray for enemies, 300. The manner of praying, 352. In what state the one praying should be, ibid. Whoever prays without attention, crying out, is silent, 718. What it means to pray truly, 1102. That the saints pray for their enemies, 1133. Whoever prays for an enemy’s harm fights against God, 1564. What it means to call upon God, and what it means for God to answer, 175. How effective the Church’s prayer is, 1148. The good force of persistent prayer, ibid. An unclean mind is unfit for prayer, 351. Whose prayer is execrable, 352, 510. In prayer the mind must wipe away the memory of its sins with tears, 352. What it is that we are forbidden to repeat in prayer, ibid. Before prayer, unclean and earthly thoughts must be driven away, ibid. Prayer accomplishes nothing unless wrongs have been forgiven, 352. The order of things to be requested in prayer, 489. Prayer in which God is not sought becomes tedious more quickly, ibid. Action must be supported by prayer, and prayer by action, 560, 563. What should be asked of God, 1442. Temporal things, if lacking, are to be requested from God, but not excessively, 1563. What prayer becomes a sin, and whose prayer it is, 1564. One must pray for enemies from the heart, ibid. Even if they have inflicted serious losses, 1565. The virtue of true prayer is the height of charity, 1564. The one who became our advocate himself hears the prayer—the one who made us, 1565. God gladly hears when he is asked to bestow what he commands, 619. The minds of the faithful ought to be houses of prayer, 1648. What makes them dens of thieves, ibid. The prayer of the elect is never fruitless, 1429. Why the prayers of Moses and Samuel are preferred to the prayers of the holy Fathers, 300, 1564. Prayer prevents many unlawful things, 352. What the usefulness of prayer is, 560. What the powers of prayer are, 1429, 1564. What things are to be requested from God in prayer, 489.

The effectiveness of our prayer and why it is suspect to us, 302. If we do what God commands, we shall obtain what we ask, 560. Why the Church’s prayer asking for deliverance is not immediately heard, 665. God hears not words but the desires of the heart, 718. Prayers are fruitless when a devout life does not follow them, 1102. For some people prayer is turned into a business, ibid. What the prayer of the elect is, 1429. Why prayer is called a little column of smoke, ibid. Through persistence in prayer, God is fixed in the heart and the lost light of the mind is restored, 1442. Christ wishes us to ask for what he foreknows both that we will ask and that he will grant, ibid. The power of the monks’ prayer by which the young Theodore, oppressed by a demon at the point of death, was delivered, 1515, 1643. The one who asks in Jesus’ name is he who asks for what pertains to true salvation, 1563.

What true prayer is, 71, 1447. When prayer is said to be pleasing to God, 351. Before prayer one must consider what may be rejected in prayer, 352. How much attention in prayer benefits us, 718. Prayer must be joined with good action, ibid. God wishes to be asked persistently, 1442. The Lord imposed the condition of piety upon the constitution of petition, 353. True prayer is produced by bitter groans, not composed words, 1102. Prayer is heard more quickly when it is seasoned with love of one’s neighbor, especially one’s enemy, 1152. The tears of prayer are the victims of our offering, 1202. The compunction of prayer conceived from love of God is compared with smoke from spices, 1429. How few pray as they ought, 1563. Before prayer, debts must be forgiven, 1564.

The phantasms of earthly things hinder prayer, 245, as do those of sins, 1441. The mind’s alternating movements during prayer, 302. Whoever constantly and willingly thinks about earthly things suffers these thoughts in prayer even against his will, 352, 911. The more harshly the heart’s cry is rejected, the more vigorously we must cry out and persist in prayer, 1442. In this way we make Jesus, who was passing by, stand still, ibid. Two things hinder the fruit of prayer, 353. Why prayer is often not heard, 489, 510. During prayer demons attack us more fiercely, 509. During prayer unclean thoughts are often thrust upon us, 521. Prayers of the heart are heard slowly, 827. What it means for a cloud to be set against prayer so that it cannot pass through, 911. The prayers of many are useless, 1102, 1564.

Through the Lord’s Prayer we bind ourselves more tightly if we do not forgive, 1565. Those who remove the condition from the Lord’s Prayer make it impossible for the advocate to recognize it as his own, ibid.

What it means to carry the orb, and who are said to do so, 300. Those initiated into sacred orders sometimes turn religion into a commercial enterprise, 1648. The three orders in the Church, 1065, 1344, 1378. The various orders of angels, 1072, 1603. The three orders of those being saved, 1344, 1350.

The organ signifies preaching, [Col. 1448] 675, 1081. What it means to hang organs upon willows, ibid. Christ is called the East; Christians, however, are called Easterners, 26, 660. Angels are called Easterners, 31. What it means to go toward the East, 516. Judea is signified by the East, 1373; also the just, 1376; and those making a beginning, 1385. The error of the Origenists concerning the eternity of punishments is refuted, 1133, etc. The Orions rise in winter and stir up storms, 294. They signify martyrs, ibid.

The mouth of the heart, 636. The mouth is the door of the heart, 716. Speech is signified by the mouth, 1046. What it means to place one’s hand over one’s mouth, 1203. What it means to be compelled to labor by the mouth, 1366. What it means to open the mouth, 104. What it means to contract the mouth, 197, 199. What the mouth of the Lord signifies, 868. What it means to kiss one’s own hand, 699, 707. What kissing the Lord’s feet signifies, 1596. A kiss is a sign of love, ibid. What it means to desire God’s kiss, 1597.

Bones signify mighty deeds, 164, and the strength of the flesh, 263; also strong people, 420, 663, 674; also virtues, 754, 758; also the powerful of the age, 1374.

The gates are the holy teachers of the Church, 911. These gates are open to the humble and closed to the proud, 912. The gates opposed to the sea—that is, to the world—are the precepts of the Law and the Gospel, 912. The gates of the Church are also virtues, 916. What the dark gates are, 928, 930. The Lord sees these gates and makes them visible to us by his light, ibid. What it means for one door to be opposite another, 1356.

Idle words must be avoided, 102. What it means to utter idle—that is, vain—words, 239. Demons tempt idle minds, 163. What an idle word is, 240, 1457. Not even the saints can be excused from an idle word, 1046. In leisure the beloved is to be sought, 1383. One must beware of an idle word, 1457. Who stand idle in the vineyard, 1512. Having been idle for the entire day of life, let us at least work late, ibid.

The eggs abandoned in the dust, which God warms, 1003. The egg signifies offspring still tender in the spiritual life, 1002. What the one sheepfold is, 1487. One sheepfold was made from Jews and Gentiles, ibid. The sheepfold of the holy Church receives goats together with lambs, 1513. The sheep signifies innocence, 23, 66, 870, 1155, 1159. What it means to shear the firstborn of sheep, 280. By sheep, the faithful peoples from Judea are signified, 1161, 1487. What it means for the sheep to recognize the shepherd, 1486. Those who do not cling to Christ through faith and love are not his sheep, ibid. What the pastures of Christ’s sheep are, 1487. In them the minds of the elect are endlessly nourished with the food of life, ibid. Christ does not abandon his sheep when they are neglected by shepherds, 1505. Those who serve the flesh are not Christ’s sheep, 1513. Who is the one who has a hundred sheep, 1601. What the hundredth sheep that was lost signifies, ibid. What it means that the Lord placed the hundredth sheep upon his shoulders, 1602. Concerning the sheep that was found, the Lord commands us to rejoice not for the sheep but for ourselves, ibid. What it means to possess sheep, 30. Sheep signify the innocence of thoughts, 66, and the purity of good hearts, ibid. Uzzah, struck by God because of his presumption: what he signifies, 149.

# P
Large heaps of straw on the threshing floor, to be consumed by fire, 1639. Heavy things are pressed beneath the straw on the threshing floor, 1638. What the buckthorn signifies, 1081. [Col. 1449] What the cloak with which Rebecca covered herself when she saw Isaac signifies, 1160. What the palm signifies, 630. The nature of the palm, 629. The palm differs in some respect from every kind of tree, 630. The life of the righteous is compared with the palm, ibid. Palms signify victory, 1362. What it means to carry palms on the forehead, 1385. What the depiction of palms signifies, ibid., 1363. What it means to carry a palm on either side, 1386. The span expresses the beginning of contemplation, 1351. What it means for the lips to be measured by a span as a unit of measurement, 1410. What the unity of the span signifies, 1411. What the eyelids of God signify, 898, 1355. What it means for us to be questioned by God through eyelids, 898. The eyes are compared with the eyelids of dawn—that is, with the counselors of Leviathan, 1109. The eyelids of dawn signify the final hours of the night, ibid. Which people question the Lord’s eyelids, 1355. What the ash-baked bread signifies, 372, 1053. What it means to put wood into bread, 394. Bread is the provision of the present life, 409. Bread signifies understanding of Sacred Scripture, 474. Christ’s miracle of the multiplication of the loaves, 526. Many things are signified by bread in Sacred Scripture, 755. Bread signifies support for the present life, 756. What it means to turn over ash-baked bread, 1053. Who are said to eat unleavened loaves, 1534. What papyrus vessels are, and what they signify, 422. A parabola is a certain musical instrument, 557. The Paraclete is the same as the advocate, or comforter, 1576. What the four rivers of Paradise signify, 68. Paradise was the womb of the human race, whose entrance the serpent opened, 114. Our region is Paradise, 1471. We departed from it through illicit pleasures; we return to it through repentance, ibid. A description of the heavenly Paradise, 1627. Why God granted all the trees of Paradise for food, while prohibiting one, 1156. Many things must now be supplied that were not necessary in Paradise, 1164. Paradise is opened daily to those who repent, 1424. To spare. How it is understood that God does not spare the delinquent, 313. The leopard reclining with the kid in the Church, 1343. If the first parents had remained in their original state, they could have been transferred to heaven without death, 126. What first happened in the first parents happens daily in us through sin, 123. When the love of parents is harmful, 230, 231, etc. Parents must be left for God’s sake, 231. Unjust parents are punished through the punishments of their little children, 490. Why adult children are struck because of their parents’ fault, 492. The first parents, desiring the likeness of divinity, lost the gifts of immortality, 604. The first parents were required to confess when questioned about their fault, 712. While the first parents tried to defend their sin, they added to it so that their guilt might become more atrocious, ibid. The first parents turned their sin back upon God, ibid. See Adam, Eve. With what discernment we ought to love and hate parents and relatives, 1628. What a freshly built wall, which is easily destroyed, signifies, 280. What it means to plaster a built wall, 560. What it means to dig through a wall, 1021. What the portion of the wicked is, 484. What the portion of the saints is, 485. What it means to receive a portion from the Lord, or to have the Lord himself as one’s portion, ibid. Who are the portion of the house of the Lord, 1084. What giving a portion to seven, and also to eight, signifies, 1342, 1391. Small things are not to be neglected, 349. Who are called little ones in Scripture, 26. One is little who is killed by envy, 179. And one who loves earthly things, 180. Why little ones are often seized by demons, 492. Truth is revealed to little ones, 863, 1136. Who is little in his own eyes, 1135. Let little ones imitate the tears and virtues of the perfect, 1234. Easter is called the solemnity of solemnities, 1533. From this solemnity an example of the future resurrection was given, ibid. Christ is our Passover, ibid. Whoever celebrates the Paschal solemnity worthily should not eat the lamb’s flesh either raw or boiled in water in a carnal manner, 1535. By what sort of people Passover should be eaten, ibid. To eat Passover with one’s loins girded means that the pleasures of the flesh have been subdued, 1536. To hasten to eat Passover means to yearn for the solemnity of the heavenly homeland, 1537. The present Paschal solemnity is the shadow of the solemnity to come, 1558. Pastures denote eternal life, 978. What the pastures of Christ’s sheep are, 1487. With what and by what means Christ’s sheep are refreshed there, ibid. We must hasten to these pastures, ibid. To love them ardently is to go there, 1487. Those who have not subdued their passions carry within themselves a turbulent crowd, 128. While shepherds were keeping watch, why an angel announced Christ’s birth, 1461. Shepherds are called the sons of shopkeepers—that is, of the Apostles, 581. Let the elect examine whether his life corresponds to the position before accepting the honor of rule offered to him, 810. Shepherds are called the vessels of the Lord’s table, that is, those who carry the souls of the faithful, 1410. By interceding for the sins of the faithful, they cleanse their own, 1418. Shepherds are represented by the cultivator of the vineyard, 1583. The duty of good shepherds, 620, 1283, etc. A faithful shepherd wishes to be helped by everyone, 726. In good shepherds, kindness and authority, mercy and discipline are joined, 641, 779. It is the labor of shepherds to see wrongdoing and not correct it, 741. Good shepherds, like skilled physicians, first touch and examine, then strike, 780. It is one thing to strike when justice urges it, another when pride inflates, ibid. What measure should be observed in correction, 781. The proud do not observe it, ibid. Good shepherds know how at one time to correct severely, at another to plead humbly, 781. Good shepherds should shine before their subjects through the splendor of their virtues, 786. Sometimes a good shepherd is corrupted because of the flock’s offenses, 807. The differences between a good shepherd and a hireling, 1485. They cannot be distinguished in time of peace, ibid. When the wolf comes, who is a good shepherd and who is a hireling becomes known, ibid. What it means to set oneself as a wall for the house of Israel, 1486. The pattern of a good shepherd, ibid. Good shepherds ought to plead for the tree, 1584. And labor continually to obtain fruits, ibid. What the discernment of a good shepherd should be like, 1291. Watchful shepherds deserve to see lofty things, 1461. Wicked shepherds draw their subjects toward impiety, 785. Those who preside not to benefit but to dominate are apostates, ibid. Wicked leaders, by the example of their pride, drag their subjects headlong, ibid. The shepherd is fictitious who occupies the place of a teacher but does not perform the office, 805. So too the one who, neglecting preaching, is occupied with secular concerns, ibid. Those subject to bad shepherds should attribute this to their own fault, 806. Bad shepherds are to be honored, but not imitated, 808. Subjects, while turning away, should cover the shameful things of a bad shepherd with his cloak, ibid. God orders the evil examples of shepherds as punishment for proud subjects, 810. In what sense God makes a hypocrite reign, ibid. The Church patiently tolerates the vices of shepherds that it cannot correct, 846. Bad shepherds reap with exultation what their fathers sowed by dying, 847. It is night for the Church when the places of learned and strong men are occupied by the ignorant and weak, 848. He who remained silent when he ought to have reproved is a hireling shepherd who has fled, 924. Those who love earthly substance more than the sheep lose the name of shepherd, 1485. Shepherds kill as many as they negligently see going daily to death, 1285. A bad shepherd is called a hireling, 1485. The description of the hireling, ibid. The hireling flees when the wolf comes, ibid. He flees not by changing his place but by withdrawing consolation, 1486. What it means for the shepherd not to climb up from the opposite side, ibid. Inactive shepherds are reproved: they receive the reward of labor without laboring, 1499. Those who devote themselves neither to prayer nor to preaching, ibid. Those who flatter and court the powerful, ibid. Shepherds sometimes become wolves, 1503. The stones of the sanctuary scattered at the head of the streets are shepherds who lie fallen through the ministry of their work, 1504. The elect, cleansed by the hands of wicked priests, will be received into heaven, while those same priests are thrust down to the punishments of hell, 1505. Wicked priests are like baptismal water which, washing away the sins of the baptized, descends into sewers, ibid. What it means for a shepherd, under the figure of a barren tree, to occupy the soil, 1584.

The life of shepherds is signified by Noah, 23, 1344. Those who are still subject to vices should not presume to rule others, 741. The merits of shepherds and peoples are mutually connected, 807. To despise shepherds occupied with temporal matters is to accuse God, 808. To how many different thoughts and emotions shepherds occupied with temporal matters are liable, 1292. Shepherds ought to mourn with those who mourn and rejoice with those who rejoice, ibid. They are commanded to change their garments, that is, to put on various dispositions of mind, ibid. How fearful it is for shepherds if they are compared with Christ, 1484. What it means to lament the furrows of the earth concerning the shepherd’s life, 1500. A priest ought to be like a rock of salt among brute animals in the peoples, ibid. How great the shepherds’ concern must be regarding the account they will one day have to render for themselves to the supreme Shepherd, 1505. The shepherd’s life should be such that whoever approaches him departs from him better, ibid.

The concern of shepherds for the peoples subject to them, 21, 725. What the rod and staff in the shepherd signify, 641. The shepherd must speak more by his conduct than by his words, 742. The shepherd’s devout severity in examining the sins of the heart, 815. When the strong Apostles and members of the Church are called to rewards, God calls the weak to contests and strengthens them, 847. Following Peter’s example, let the shepherd be strong against hostile powers while possessing the humility of gentleness toward inferiors, 906. Shepherds should harmonize the pursuit of contemplation with care for their neighbors within themselves, 909. How much discernment rulers of souls need, 960, 971, 977. Different admonitions should be given according to each person’s character, 961. The wicked should be rebuked more harshly; those already converted from wickedness should be admonished more gently, 962. Skilled teachers withdraw the food of more exalted teaching from disciples who do not think humbly enough about themselves, 971. It is otherwise if they humble themselves in confession of sins, ibid. What qualities shepherds should possess in order to bring forth souls in faith and virtue, 975. Those who are fathers through the rigor of discipline should be mothers through the depths of compassion, 976. Offspring conceived at the proper time should be carried in the womb of the heart so that it may live, ibid. The shepherd’s discernment should be watchful and elevated, 1284. The sins of shepherds and subjects are interconnected, ibid. How great the order and consideration of speech should be in the shepherd’s mouth, 1286. The shepherd should open his ear to God before opening his mouth to the people, 1284. Zeal is necessary for the shepherd, even if it causes pain, 1304. Armed with this, he will escape divine judgment, ibid. How great the shepherd’s discernment must be between discipline and mercy, 1414. He should exhort people to virtues even those he himself does not possess, so that he may practice them, because he is compelled to speak about them, 1415. By praying, the shepherd himself should erase the faults that he exposes by preaching, 1416. The shepherd should generously provide external goods for the sheep, 1484. His soul too must be exposed for them if necessary, ibid. Shepherds are sent as lambs among wolves, 1498. At times severity must be employed out of love, ibid. The shepherds’ life should season the hearts of the peoples, 1500, 1505. Shepherds should be examples to others in contrition, 1500. Shepherds should join gentleness to zeal, 1501. Exhortation to shepherds, 1499, etc. The prayer of shepherds to God, 1505.

Shepherds must avoid concern for temporal matters, 2. To how many disturbances of mind and dangers this concern is liable, 67. Shepherds ought to seek not their own glory but that of the author, 702. The ruler of a church should not begrudge those who cooperate with him in preaching, 726. The various defects of shepherds, 727. Domination must be avoided by the shepherd, 742. Proud rulers rejoice in their position by despising their subjects, 785. It is disgraceful for shepherds to devote themselves to quarrels while neglecting care of the people entrusted to them, 1006. Excessive gentleness in a shepherd is hostile both to himself and to his subjects, 1207. Shepherds who present themselves to their subjects more as masters than as fathers are rebuked, 1497. Some flatter outwardly but rage inwardly, ibid. The grave error of shepherds, 1499. In binding or loosing, let the shepherd beware lest he be moved by hatred or favor, 1555.

Pastoral concern: how great the shepherds’ concern for their subjects should be, 725, 1283. Those who serve in external ministries should diligently withdraw to the secrets of the heart, 749. Pastoral care should be embraced not from desire but retained with fear, 787. Shepherds should know that they live under as great a responsibility as the number of those over whom they preside, 786. Why one who does not perform the office occupies the place of a teacher, 805. The power of government cannot be administered without devotion to temporal care, 809. What it means for a shepherd to take a brick for himself and arrange a siege around it, etc., 816. Through how many sorrows shepherds bring forth people into life, 975. Unless our shepherds descended to our weakness, they would not beget children in the faith, 977. The stability of shepherds in one place is asserted, 1209. How greatly even the most watchful shepherds must fear, 1291. What it signifies for a priest to change garments and be clothed in linen, 1292. How diligently shepherds should inspect and know their sheep, 1377. Subjects should be roused to great things in such a way that they know small things are not to be neglected, 1410. What pastoral care belongs to the Church, 1423. What it means for a shepherd to eat the sins of the people, 1199. Shepherds are heralds of the coming Judge, [Col. 1451] 1500. What it means for the earth to cry out against its possessor, ibid. The principal duties of shepherds are enumerated, ibid. Shepherds should watch over themselves in such a way that they do not neglect the keeping of their subjects, 1501, 1505. People of every condition should grow better through the shepherd’s speech and devotion, 1505. The shepherd should fear absolving anyone unjustly or binding anyone unjustly, 1556. Shepherds ought to show strictness toward vices and compassion toward nature, 1594. What pasture signifies, 978.

God the Father: how he is understood to have been moved against Christ the Son, 84. Whatever we perceive concerning the Father, we see through the Son, 167. In heaven the Father is witness and knower of the Son, 426. The place of wisdom is the Father, and the place of the Father is wisdom, 605. Wisdom is the image and Word of the Father, 610. The Father begot the Word outside of time, 748. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not called angels, 896. God the Father adopts us as sons, nourishes us with gifts, and educates us through scourges for the inheritance, 1387. See Son of God.

The father’s fault ought not to burden the son, 492. The fathers of the old law prefigured Christ, 14. How the fathers before Christ were abortive, 132. The ancient fathers are called ships carrying fruits, 309. They are compared with eagles, ibid. The ancient fathers desired to pass from fear of the law to the freedom of the Gospel, 317. How profitable it is to turn the sayings of the fathers over in one’s heart, 525. The ancient fathers are called lofty vessels of gold, 595. The ancient fathers were like fruitful trees, 730. The miracles of the fathers are read in Sacred Scripture, 1340. The ancient fathers and those of the New Testament are divided into three classes, 1343. A comparison of the ancient fathers with the Apostles, 1371. The holy fathers preserve the state of the Church, 1546. The fathers of the Old and New Testaments are called fattened cattle, 1636. A banquet prepared for us from the fathers of the Old and New Testaments, ibid. Why the holy fathers are marked by the name “rock,” 972. The perfection of the ancient fathers from whom Christ came, 1331. See Patriarchs.

We must endure unwillingly what we did deliberately and willingly, 123. Everything we suffer is just, 51. Whatever we suffer, our sins have deserved, 187. It is not granted to everyone to suffer punishments for God, 218. Some things we suffer from God, others from our neighbor, others from the devil, 1617. How each of these should be endured patiently, ibid. Who is truly called patient, 383. No one is perfect who is not patient amid the evils of his neighbors, 673, 1638. One who does not repay evil because he is unable to do so is not patient, 1615. Against the one who inflicts evil, the patient person is not gnawed by any pain, ibid. The less patient a person is, the less learned he is, ibid.

How we should preserve patience, 51. Patience must be practiced in action, ibid. The reward of patience is not to be sought here, 52. The mind of the patient is well known through the condescension of suffering, 10. Whoever holds to patience possesses his soul, 153. The method of preserving patience in unjust injuries inflicted upon us, 177. By tolerating the weaknesses of our neighbors, we are strengthened to undergo sufferings, 219. Patience grows through love of eternal things, ibid. How necessary patience is amid the evils of this life, 311. Concord in society cannot persevere without patience, 694. Without patience joined to charity, good works perish, 695. The saints are strengthened to patience by the example of suffering Christ, 956. Patience is signified by the name “breastplate,” 1123. It is likewise signified by the name “bronze,” ibid. What false patience is, 1207. Sacred Scripture teaches patience, 1228. True patience loves the very one whom it bears, 1228, 1359, 1398. Without patience no one of the saints reaches eternal glory, 1229. Who is better: the patient man or the strong man, 1367. Through patience the good earth yields fruit, 1490. The necessity of patience in doing good and enduring evil, ibid. Injuries are not to be avenged but patiently borne, 1494. Patience is the guardian of all virtues, 1614. Virtue consists, before human beings, in tolerating adversaries; before God, even in loving them, 1615. The signs of true and false patience, ibid. It is a lesser victory to conquer cities than to conquer oneself through patience, ibid. Patience often displayed immediately is later lost, ibid. The devil’s arts by which he inflames us to anger and impatience, ibid. An example of patience in Abbot Stephen, 1616. In how many ways patience is practiced, 1617. In return for the labor of patience, good things of the next life should be hoped for, ibid. Job, scourged, became through patience an example to all, 74, 729. See Job: patience.

The measure of patience, 80. We owe patience to the Creator, ibid. Patience is the shield of the saints against their attackers, 89, 242, 417. Perfection arises from patience, 153. Patience must be joined to kindness, 242. The measure of patience in enduring scourges, 354. Patience shines not in prosperity but in adversity, 383. The patience of the saints, 417. The purpose of God’s patience toward sinners, 537. Through patience the Church is exercised when it is tested by swords, 557. The patience of the righteous when they are burdened by inferiors, 694. Patience is preserved through charity, 695. Sinners think that God’s patience should be neglected, 789. Why patience is necessary, 954. The definition of patience, 1614. The conditions of patience, 1615.

Man willingly lost his homeland and is unwillingly expelled from the pilgrimage that he loves, 396. Those who regard this life as their homeland foolishly despise the mourning of the elect, 496. Some claim the heavenly homeland, yet do not love it, like the Gadites and Reubenites, 864. How useful remembrance of the heavenly homeland is to sinners, 865. When the light of the heavenly homeland is contemplated, the mind is carried into ecstasy, 867. Having despised earthly things, the heart sighs for heavenly things alone, ibid., 919. The heart burning with desire for the heavenly homeland is compared with the golden altar on which the spices of virtues are kindled, 1428. To it the slavery and length of its pilgrimage appear harsh, ibid.

The patriarchs who lived before the written law are called abortive, 132. The patriarchs grieved that they did not reach the times of Christ, 308, 434. We are satisfied by the sight and fruit of the one for whom they longed and whom they sensed by his fragrance, 309. Those who died did not attain blessedness before Christ’s death, 397, 433. None of them received the grace of adoption except through knowledge of the Only-Begotten, 730. Their fruit was also to signify his Church, 731. The holy patriarchs and prophets were stars producing rain, 857. Why they are called clouds, 859. They proclaimed Christ, 948. The holy patriarchs lived under the natural law, before the written law, 1217. The fire of the Holy Spirit that burned inwardly in the patriarchs shone outwardly after the Incarnation, 1246. The patriarchs are marked by the name “mountains,” 1310. The perfection of the patriarchs from whom Christ came, 1331. What it means that the patriarchs murmured because they were called to the kingdom later, 1513. See Fathers. [Col. 1453]

Let us now secure the saints as patrons who will be present at the final judgment, 1592. Why few come to Christ, 1620. Few good people in the Church, 638. The humility, charity, and firmness of faith of the faithful are signified by the pavement of the treasury, 1365. The Apostle Paul was snatched up to the third heaven, 266, 347. Paul was not Peter’s equal, 342, 1368. Paul bore hell together with heaven: contemplation of heavenly things and the temptation of the flesh, 347. Paul was a lamp despised by the carnal Corinthians, 363. Paul, from the tribe of Benjamin, is called a ravening wolf, 567. Paul was God’s tent, 861. Paul is signified by water changed into snow, 873. Paul was called to the apostolate from the ferocity of persecution, 932. Paul became snow and hail against the breasts of his adversaries, 935. He preceded Stephen in his labors, ibid., 1514. Paul is compared with a rhinoceros, 1010. Paul was one of the squared stones, 1406. Paul stoned Stephen with the hands of all those who were throwing stones, 1514.

Paul’s conversion was miraculous, 372, 608, 935, 1011, 1106. An example of the soul’s salutary transformation through grace in Paul’s conversion, 342. How God healed Paul’s offenses by marking them, 401. The ice returned to water when Paul, who had breathed threats, was converted, 879. Paul was questioned in his rapture and afterward answered the Lord, 898. The fierce Saul, from the Jews, was subdued by Christ, 1010. Saul was like a rhinoceros, 1011, 1012. This rhinoceros was bound to plow the Lord’s field, 1011. He broke the clods—that is, the hardness of minds, ibid. How much confidence God placed in his strength, 1012. He first winnowed God’s threshing floor—that is, the Church—by devastating it, and afterward gathered it by preaching, 1012. Before his conversion, Paul had been an assistant to the stoners from his youth, ibid. When the scales that had hardened Saul’s heart were divinely removed, it opened to the arrows of grace, 1106. The wolf turned into a sheep seeks the shepherd’s path when it follows him, 1107. Before his conversion, Paul despised Christ incarnate, ibid.

Paul sinned through ignorance, 803. Why Paul healed the father of Publius by a miracle but Timothy by nourishment, 870, 1449. Paul circumcised Timothy, 907. What Paul’s wanderings were, 969, 1044. Paul’s preaching after his conversion, 1012. Why Paul wanted to enter the theater at Ephesus and was let down from Damascus in a basket, 1023. Why Paul sometimes fled, ibid. Forty men conspired to kill Paul, 1025. Why Paul handed over the Corinthian man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, 1086. Paul knew the Gospel from what had occurred previously, but did not know who would suffer for it, 1178. Paul mourns what he had committed before baptism, 1203. Why Paul rebuked the Corinthians with moderation but the Galatians without moderation, 1288. Paul preached among the Corinthians for a full year and six months, 1369. Paul rebuked the Corinthians for impiety, 1370. Paul’s miracles are reported, 1448.

Paul’s virtues are enumerated, 89, 1406. His patience and courage amid adversities and persecutions, 89, 248, 363. His charity toward his neighbor, 89, 205, 969, 970. How great his humility was, 149, 781, 873, 898. How he condescended to the weakness of his neighbors, 630. He speaks fearlessly to the high priest, 237. His restraint in praising himself, 562. Why he sometimes commends himself, 623, 813, 1256. His prudence in reproving, [Col. 1453] 780, 1287. His discernment in the exercise of authority, 834. He always travels about in order to win someone, 969, 1044. His zeal and anxiety for the salvation of his people, 977, 1004, 1423. His zeal for Christ, 1022, 1339. Paul, having been stoned and driven outside the city, did not fear returning to it, 1027. His fervor in preaching, ibid. Paul remains strong in labors and rejoices in adversities, 1028. How Paul desired to die and feared to be stripped of the flesh, ibid. Paul’s zeal and patience, 1228, 1229; his gentleness and long-suffering, 1369, 1370, etc. Paul did not receive preaching wages from the Corinthians, ibid. Paul fulfilled what he preached, 1370.

Paul presents the shield of patience against those who strike him and hurls the darts of teaching against those who give bad advice, 89. Paul’s immense depths of charity, 90. Paul was born for flight, like a bird, 188. Paul was humble and at the same time placed on high, 191, 393. Paul became all things to all people by condescending, not by falling, 205. Paul suspended his soul, 263. By speaking certain excellent things about himself, he instructs the life of his hearers; by keeping certain things silent, he guards his own, 562, 704. The world was crucified to Paul, and Paul to the world, 601. Paul’s sublimity of virtues was tempered by the weakness of temptations for the preservation of humility, 608. Although already snatched up to the third heaven, he was not yet free from fear, 638. Paul was affected in contrition in four ways, 751. Paul placed the other Apostles before himself because of their innocence, 769, 1276. Paul provides superiors with a model for correcting subjects, 780. Paul maintained discipline toward the Corinthians and preserved humility for himself, 781. Paul showed himself superior toward sinners and equal toward those who stand upright, 834. Questioned by God’s open or closed eyelids, Paul answered rightly, 898. Paul restrained himself within the measures assigned to him by God, 905. Following the line of discernment, Paul changed his manner of acting in the same matter, 907. Paul confesses himself a child for grasping heavenly things, 915. Paul was pressed by the ice of discipline when he could not find how to accomplish the good he had conceived, 946. Charity, which unites what is divided, divided Paul’s heart among many, 970. Paul was like a hind groaning in childbirth, 977. Paul’s discernment was bent down so that he might bring forth children, 978. Paul did not forget his children like an ostrich but was supremely concerned for their salvation, 1004. Paul chastised his body through abstinence and strikes those devoted to the belly, 1012. Paul rejoiced amid scourges, 1022. By his example Paul teaches us perfect obedience, 1157. Paul flies upward on two wings—that is, virtues—and covers his body with two, 1203. Paul’s watchful concern and foresight, 1224. Before rising to preach, Paul lay down, 1251. Paul praises the Corinthians whom he later rebukes, 1287. In praising the Corinthians, Paul is free from falsehood and flattery, 1288. How vehemently Paul attacks the Galatians, ibid. Paul was tormented by zeal for souls, 1304. The consolation of Paul, who groaned over the delay of this life, 1332. Christ was Paul’s life, ibid. He desires to be supported by flowers and surrounded by apples, ibid. From Paul’s example we learn to despise adversities while longing for death, 1339. Paul’s excellence in words and deeds, 1367. Like a physician, Paul cherishes what has been cleansed and cuts away what is putrid, 1370. Through the long-suffering of gentleness he softened the hardness of his disciples, ibid. Paul was strong in adversity and humble in prosperity, 1386. One attributes nothing to himself who affirms that he can do all things in God, ibid. Paul was a devoted cultivator of unity of minds, 1411. Paul, the treasury of the singer, sings judgment to God, 1420. Paul was the most diligent guardian of God’s temple, 1423. The Holy Spirit fills the persecutor and makes him a teacher of the nations, 1580. In bodily affliction Paul carried the cross of the flesh; in compassion for his neighbor he carried the cross of the mind, 1588. Paul hated his soul by loving it, and loved it by hating it, 1628.

How great Paul’s labors were, and from what source he considered them light, 248. Paul girded with scourges, 451. Paul’s journeys and preachings were subject to divine commands, 879. Paul’s concern for nearly all the churches, 969, 1012. How great Paul’s courage was amid dangers rushing upon him, 1023. At times he wisely avoids danger, ibid. If the fruit gained from danger is smaller, otherwise not at all, 1024. It was not virtue that lacked a place, but a place that lacked virtue, ibid. Paul despised every fear and every hostile attack, 1025. When, and who, sounded the quiver over Paul, God’s horse, ibid. The blast of the trumpet does not terrify Paul: he can be killed, but cannot be overcome, 1027. Paul’s weakness was strong, and patience was his mistress, ibid. Paul loves what he appears to flee, and appears to flee what he loves, 1028. In difficult places Paul has a nest like an eagle, 1040, 1043. Paul, bound in chains, sits with Christ in the heavenly places, ibid. Paul, snatched up to the third heaven, saw the least and the farthest things of God, 1043. Teaching his disciples Christ crucified, Paul provides blood for the young like an eagle, ibid. The salvation of sinners was the reason for Paul’s flight as he traversed the world, 1044. Paul’s temptation was not an abyss of vices but a safeguard of merits, 1092, 1093. Why Paul was not heard when he asked the Lord three times, 1563. How great Paul’s adversities and hardships were, 89. Paul fears because of his good works, 362, 639. Paul, snatched up to the third heaven, suffered the contest of the flesh, 266, 347. Paul’s various labors, 608, 1032.

In his writings Paul sometimes uses the words of Job’s friends, 150, 182. How many letters Paul wrote, 1166. What the letter to the Laodiceans is, ibid. Paul wrote in his letters that Peter had been blameworthy, 1367. Peter read these letters and commended them to the faithful for reading, 1368.

What fear is, 867. The poor person signifies the humble, 198, 523, 691, 835. Some of the righteous possess earthly things, others renounce them, 263. The poor will judge the world on the day of judgment, 363. The wondrous security of heart belonging to the poor righteous person, 480. From the very thing in which the rich person rejoices vainly, the poor person is afflicted even more vainly, 495. The poor person anxiously desires the goods that the rich person possesses with fear, ibid. Humility should accompany mercy toward the poor, 692. What the cry of the poor is, and when it reaches God, 805. Whoever does not desire what he needs is rich, 1372. Christ chose poor parents, 1443. To wipe the Lord’s feet with one’s hair means to minister to the poor from one’s surplus, 1596. We kiss the Lord’s feet when the poverty of the needy is not burdensome to us, ibid. The poor and the weak are invited to the banquet, but not the poor and the proud, 1622. How the faithful person leaves everything while possessing everything, 1625. The poor should be sought as intercessors before God, 1659. The poor are the patrons whom we ought to entreat, ibid. Vicious poor people are to be corrected and fed, ibid. The honor due to the poor is demonstrated by example, ibid. Exhortation to honor and support the poor, 1661. The poor person, rejected and despised, is a pearl in a dung heap, 1661. Who the truly poor are, 691. One who does not have clothing is less needy than one who lacks humility, 693. The poor cry out against mute shepherds, 805. How the poor person is rescued from his distress, 842. The poor person is one who needs what he does not have, 1372. God knows the humble poor but does not know the proud rich, 1655. Poverty signifies humility, 523. Poverty is a certain emaciation, 411. What it means to be bound by the cords of poverty, 839. How the devil turns one away from a vow of poverty when he is considering making the vow, 1068. The poverty of the elect is the loss of heavenly riches, 1117. What virtue is weakened in poverty, ibid. The reprobate do not know this poverty, being empty of the riches of virtues, 1118. Whoever is not broken by want knows how to be humbled, 1386. On the road to the homeland, poverty is a faithful companion, 1387. By renouncing everything that belongs to this world, we offer a holocaust, 1404. By administering household goods out of charity, we offer a sacrifice, 1410. In abandoning earthly things, affection, not wealth, must be weighed, 1450. What the superfluity of the most tenuous depravity stains, the strong furnace of poverty purifies.

Peace with God becomes stronger the harsher the struggle with the devil, 204. In Sacred Scripture peace is called partly complete and partly begun, 205. It begins from desire for the Creator and is perfected through his vision, ibid. Whoever resists God falls from peace, 289. There is peace in the heights, although the angels contend among themselves, 541. Christ established peace between angels and human beings, 866. Those who are wiser than they ought to be recoil from the peace of their neighbors, 1239. Where true peace is, God dwells, 1272. Through Christ’s birth peace was given to human beings, 1462. Peace offered by a preacher never lacks effect, 1498. Christ leaves peace to those who follow and gives it to those who arrive, 1577. In time of peace, since it is permitted to live, it is also permitted to strive, 1588. What it means to go in peace, 1595. What the peg that a Jew must always carry on his belt signifies, 1021. What the bronze pegs in the construction of the tabernacle signify, 1336.

To sin secretly, deny the offense, and multiply it by defending it when convicted is a common vice of the human race, 712. If man had not sinned, he would have reached Paradise without redemption, 128. Whoever sins is a slave of sin, 986. It is one thing to sin through weakness, another through malice, 1007. No one is so perfect that he does not sin amid the very vows he makes, 1048. Everyone who sins provokes the anger of his Creator against himself, 1259. The womb of the sinner is called hidden guilt, 124. The instability of fallen man, 250. Foolishly the sinner tries to resist the divine order, 290. The weapons of sinners are their limbs, 332. The sinful person dies in guilt, is stripped of righteousness, and is consumed in punishment, 396. Which sinner drinks iniquity like water, 407. Every sinner is guilty of unbelief, 536. Why God tolerates sinners for so long, 537. The sinner discovers himself to be wicked by looking upon the examples of the saints, 766. Many sinners hide beneath the peace of the Church, 802. The sinner must be rebuked and never feared, 1270. Sinners are without excuse, 1427. When we look upon sinners, let us mourn for ourselves, 1594. God sees sinners and bears with them, 1597. The sinner is called dust and earth, 371, 394, 483, 1002, 1273. Sinners are called
The dead and the giants who even boast of their sin, 546. Not every sinner is impious, but every impious person is a sinner, 801. The sinner’s mind is called the depth of the sea, 929. Sinners, like dust, are carried away by every breath of temptation, 966. The sinner is called a corpse, 1044. Sinners are the devil’s shadows, protecting one another, 1080. The sinner is signified by the name “cloud,” 1199. Likewise by the names “night” and “darkness,” 1527. The sinner is compared to a wheel, 531.

Sinners are shaken by the tumult of desires, 133. The sinner neither fears God nor ceases to live; he blasphemes and prospers, 256. The sinner is so bound by the chains of sins that he does not recognize the burden he bears, 330. The sinner’s light is during the day, but darkness in the evening, 355. The wretched hope of sinners, 358. Sinners shut up in the prison of evil habit cannot escape by their own efforts, 370. The sinner recognizes that he is in sins but does not know for which sins he is scourged, 427. When the sinner strives to free himself from the snares of sin, he learns by what harsh bonds he is held, 440. The sinners’ fearful security, 1273. Likewise, their destructive prosperity, 1299. Human weakness and sterility after sin, 1584. The sinner, thinking about earthly things, cannot look upward, 1585.

Sinners deceive the simple by flattery and praise, 125. The sinner becomes daily more secure in proportion as he becomes worse, 328. What are the ways of sinners? 537. Sinners look not upon the ways of the Lord but upon their own, ibid. Sinners do not think God is present because they do not see him, 614. Those who falsely say that they are sinners, 770. Those who truly say that they are sinners, ibid. The pride, shamelessness, and obstinacy of sinners, 1252. By sinning they provoke God, yet God sustains them and patiently awaits them, 1259. Sinners secure through ignorance, 1273. Some sinners are proud, others humble, 1622.

Sinners of every condition are to be admonished by priests, 1605. Four sinners converted in the New Testament, 1551. In whatever sin someone is conscious, in that he defends other sinners, 1080. Sinners cling obstinately to one another, 1108. Whoever is fed on carnal things has his inner senses so dulled that he cannot chew—that is, understand—spiritual things, 382. The ways of sinners are darkness and slippery ground, 625. One thing is not to do good; another, not even to love it; another, to hate it, 803. Let the sinner fear being dragged from one sin into another, 1092.

How great the future punishments of sinners will be, 148. When God does not strike sinners, he is said to have his hand bound, 220. No sin is without punishment, 313. The sinner who was foolish in guilt will be wise in punishment, 493. The punishment of the wicked is to be erased from God’s memory, 534. Through the judge’s clemency the sinner’s punishment increases, 537. A wrongful act that delights in guilt pricks in punishment, 651. God sometimes punishes the sinner by blinding him, 799. God struck by abandonment the one whom he did not wish to save, ibid. What are the torments of sinners? 1474.

The sinner’s conversion is hindered either by presumption or by despair concerning God’s mercy, 124. Three kinds of sinners are easily corrected; the fourth with greater difficulty, 125. God gives place and time for repentance, unwilling that the sinner should perish, 256, 829. The converted sinner is troubled by intrusive thoughts of his sins, 325. Touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, the sinner recognizes his danger, 328. When visited by God, the sinner is afflicted more severely by him, ibid. Whoever returns to God after sins is cleansed in thought [Col. 1456] and deed, 508. The weak, when God heals them, become strong and shine before others through their teaching, 509. Those who boast of their sin cannot be converted, 546. The conversion of every sinner is easy for God, 547. The sinner is confounded when he looks upon God’s commandments, which he despised, 560. How great a merit it is to care for a sinner’s conversion, 621. The devil’s prey is snatched away when someone is recalled from error or sin, 628. God never abandons a mind that truly recognizes itself to be in sins, 701. The beginning of sinners’ illumination is the humility of confession, 712. By looking upon righteous people, the sinner makes a beginning of his conversion, 766. Whoever understands that he is a sinner has already begun, in part, to be righteous, ibid. God mercifully awaits sinners, 829. Great consolation for sinners in conversion, 867. The sinner who hears God’s voice in terror, 868. The miracle of divine grace in the conversion of a sinner placed at the point of death, 870. When grace breathes upon them, the groans and cries of repentance are heard, 871. The sinner’s true conversion, ibid., 1273. The voice of God that awakens the sluggish sinner is like thunder, 871. In what ways this voice insinuates itself into the ears of the heart is unknown, ibid. God works marvelous and astonishing things in the sinner’s conversion, 872. In praising God for the conversion of the wicked, we fear that those considered good may be abandoned, 887. The converted sinner should always consider what he has been, 903. Truth finds all whom it would convert in crimes or excesses, ibid. In how many ways God brings about the conversion of sinners, 926. God also receives sinners converted at a late hour, ibid. By visiting the sinner’s mind, God enters the depth of the sea, 929. In the conversion of the most wicked, God walks in the deepest abyss, ibid. Sinners, like dust, are solidified by the grace of the Holy Spirit and bound together by love, 966. The food of the righteous is the conversion of the perverse, 1044. How converted sinners cover their sins, 1047. Sinners ought to groan for two reasons, 1048. In two ways the sinner is regarded by the Lord, 1032. Excuses for sin, 1107. Those who recover from sin through repentance are drawn back from the devil’s mouth, 1090. In the sinner’s breast, hope and fear must continually be joined, 1091. What hinders sinners’ conversion to the Lord, 1441. The sinner must be told, like Lazarus: “Come out,” 1556. Why there is greater joy over converted sinners than over those who remain standing, 1602. Sinners who remember that they once did unlawful things sometimes become the best people, ibid.

The delight of sin is called day, and the night is blindness of mind, 114. What distinguishes sin from iniquity, 386. Sin is called an unripe grape, 382. It is called blood, 425, 755, 1285, 1290. Sins are compared with nets, 440. Likewise with a fire of sulfur, 444. Sin is called death, 442, 443. Sins are called debts, 502. Likewise thorns, 616. Sin is signified by the juniper, ibid. The difference between sin and crime, 688. Sin is called a well into which the sinner is immersed, 843. A pool into which he slips, ibid. Sins are signified by a rope, 1087. Sin is called a talent weighing down the soul, 1185. Sin is called rust, 1595. What it means to cover sins, 1047, 1203. Every sin is elevenfold, 1061. The distinction between sin and transgression, 1404. What it means to eat the sins of the people, 1499.

Sin is committed in thought, word, and deed, [Col. 1457] 145. Every sin is committed either by thought alone or by thought together with deed, 351. Who is the slave of sin, and who is free from it? 137. One sin is the cause of others that follow, 227, 1289. No one in this life is clean from every sin, 314, 543, 544, 681, 918, 1350, 1421, 1649. How greatly we sin daily against the law of love, 343. The devil does not lead us into sin unless we are willing, 424. When drawn by the devil into sin, we consent by our own will, 481. What is both sin and the punishment of sin, 128, 510, 544. Some sins arise from ignorance, others from weakness, 625. In corruptible flesh sin can fail to reign, but it cannot fail to exist, 681. One thing is to be unwillingly touched by the pleasure of sin; another is for the consenting mind to be destroyed, 684. The same sin is sometimes both the punishment and the cause of sin, 800, 1289, 1290. Sin is perpetrated either through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate purpose, 803. One thing is to sin through rashness, another through deliberation, ibid. Sin is admitted in three ways, 1064. The various kinds of sins, 1289. A blinded mind is both the punishment and the cause of sin, 1290. God does not impel anyone to sin, ibid. Sin arises from sin, 226, 425, 1303. The difference between sin in deed and sin in thought, 386. Every sin that is not quickly wiped away by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin, 799, 800, 1289.

Whoever is not regenerated by baptism remains bound by the guilt of original sin, 102. Whoever dies in original sin does not escape the punishment of guilt, ibid., 303. Remedies for original sin among the ancient Jews and Gentiles, and among Christians, 102. Man was created in the day of righteousness but born in the time of guilt, 106. Job confesses that he sinned in the first man and mourns the miseries of that sin, 126. We are born with the due of our death, 122, 306. Along with guilt, punishment is propagated from the beginning, 244. The punishments of the first sin, 269. God condemns infants solely as guilty of original sin, 303. See Infants.
