They are like a twisted bow, 888. They are destroyers of themselves and cultivators of others, 1411. Those who submit themselves to earthly powers for advantage or empty glory are already laying themselves down in the footsteps of Antichrist, 1127. Wicked preachers are called the gates of the devil, 1103. They arrogate to themselves an appearance of holiness, 1110. The perversity of bad preachers is explained, 1127. Why bad preachers are raised by the spirit but are not taken up, 1279. For the sake of good hearers, speech is granted even to bad preachers, 1298. Because of the bad conduct of both groups, speech is withdrawn, ibid. Those who say but do not act bend the bow, shoot arrows, and turn back on the day of battle, 1412. When a person’s life is despised, his preaching too must be disregarded, 1476. Bad preachers seek their own glory, 1485. Those who hear should not consider through whom they hear, but what they hear or from whom they hear it, 1620.

—The labors of preachers of error are sterile, 536. They do not benefit the widow—that is, the Church—ibid. They do not believe in their own life, ibid. The tangled arguments of the devil’s preachers, 1062. Hypocrites are false preachers, ibid. They are witnesses of Antichrist, ibid. The gates of Leviathan are called pseudo-preachers, 1103. The Lord opens these gates by revealing the teachers of error, ibid. The teeth of Leviathan are the same false teachers, 1104. The powers of the world fortify them, ibid. Some rage with words, others with swords, ibid. They are compared with horses whose power is in their mouth and in their tail, ibid. Knowledge is represented in the mouth, and the power of secular persons in the tail, ibid. The mouth of Antichrist consists of false preachers, 1110. The multitude of Antichrist’s preachers is signified by the beast resembling a lamb but speaking like a dragon, ibid. Many preachers of Antichrist already exist, ibid. Some now preach Antichrist with their voices, many by their conduct, 1111. Their life must be examined like a coin, ibid. Whether it agrees with the institutions of the ancient Fathers, ibid. The discernment of the elect distinguishes the quality, form, and weight of their life, ibid. The pseudo-preachers of Antichrist will perform miracles, 1252.

Predators are those who grow proud of the gifts bestowed on them by God, 367. Desired positions of authority cannot be administered without sin, 546. How dangerously those preside who are weak in virtue, 415, 786. Those who seek glory from people for their position of authority are without glory before God, 785. By nature a human being is set over not humans but animals, 690. A human being should not be a terror to humans but to beasts and beastlike people—that is, perverse subjects, ibid. To preside usefully is exceedingly difficult, 786. The power received in a position of authority must be regarded not as an honor but as a burden, ibid. Necessity, not ambition, should impose it, 787. How God causes a hypocrite to reign, 810. Superiors are substituted for the ancient Fathers, 847. The misery of usurped authority, 1066. Superiors of the Church are called princes, 131. A superior is called a judge, 374. Superiors are called the eyelids of their subjects, 425. When superiors fall, the weak collapse, 453. One is mentally placed beneath the people over whom one is set in dignity, 546. In a superior there should be neither rigid severity nor lax gentleness, 620, 637. A superior must not be occupied with earthly cares, 627. Whence cheerfulness tempered by severity arises in a superior, 637, 641. Those who preside over others should always recognize that they are subject to God, 689. A superior should consider the equality of condition, not the authority of rank, ibid. What it means for the earth to cry out against the superiors of the Church, 724. A superior holds the earth only to cultivate it, ibid. What is the office of superiors, 725. A superior should not love power out of desire but endure it through long-suffering, 788. Superiors who care for temporal things are not always to be rebuked, 808. The tangled temptations of superiors, 1066. The Lord will punish superiors himself, 1502.

—Superiors must interrupt their temporal occupations so that they may devote themselves to God, 146, 749. Whoever protects his own interests while neglecting the things that belong to God thereby proves that he loves himself more than God, 1006. The Lord created earthly things for our use and human souls for his own, ibid. The right-minded superior attends to what he owes himself and what he owes his neighbors, 67. A superior ought to be adorned with humility, 834. A superior must preserve humility both in his heart and discipline in his conduct, ibid. Often those who preside over others are exercised by more grievous temptations from the devil, 1032. Through discipline they guard their subjects, and through humility they guard themselves, 1601.

—A superior should know that he presides in order to benefit, not to exalt himself, 146. Acts carried out by superiors as stewards are not accidents but inclinations, 149. If anything in these matters is displeasing, it must not be concealed but expressed with great humility, ibid. Those who rebuke others must not flatter themselves, 238. Whoever wishes to correct others must be clean, ibid. What superior is brought to stupefaction, 374. How great must be a superior’s concern both for his own progress and for the edification of his subjects, 383, 725. Superiors grieve over the faults of others as over their own, 425. They should direct the paths of their subjects in place of eyes, ibid. Ministers who care for the Church’s earthly goods must watch over the salvation of their subjects, 616, 627. At times they should accommodate themselves to their subjects in caring for earthly necessities, 627. What kind of gravity a superior should have toward his subjects, 637. Unless restrained by the bridle of the Holy Spirit, superiors often rage against their subjects, 672. The superior’s patience toward delinquent subjects, ibid. In correcting subjects, a superior is angry and loving; he is fierce and calm, 673. Whoever does not live as he speaks crushes through negligence in action those whom he has begotten by his word, 686. A superior should attend to the common nature he shares with his subjects, 689, 834. He should strive more to benefit than to preside, ibid., 835. When there is no vice among their subjects to correct, superiors should rejoice not in the excellence of their power but in the equality of their condition, 690. If faithful subjects bear no fruit through the word or example of superiors, the superiors will give an account, 725. The one who is subject serves in obedience; the one who presides should serve through the word, 726. A silent superior demands what is owed to his body but does not provide what is owed to the hearts of his subjects, 725. Superiors must beware of bad examples, and subjects of rash judgments, 728. Many superiors, because of their swelling pride, despise all their subjects, 785. They should correct their faults prudently and humbly, 786. A superior who judges others should continually present himself before the heavenly Judge, ibid. Whoever occupies the place of a teacher should perform the office, 805. Superior and subjects should be contained in their respective orders through mutual humility, 808. Superiors suppose that all their subjects are less wise than they are, ibid. A superior sometimes rages against his subjects unwillingly but out of the zeal of charity, 815. A superior should rule vices rather than brothers, 834. A person is placed over subjects not by nature but because of fault, ibid. The sins of subjects and superiors are linked, 1284. Superiors who see the lukewarm and silent going to death and do nothing kill them, 1285. Superiors should be fathers, not lords, 1497. A superior must not be cruel toward his subjects, 1498. How greatly the unfruitful life of a superior harms his subjects, 1583. The perverse examples of superiors corrupt their subjects, 1585. See Pastor, Superior, Preacher, Ruler.

—When superiors serve pleasure, the reins are loosened for their subjects, 49. The bad life of superiors greatly harms weak subjects, 58. What those placed in authority commonly sin by thinking, speaking, and acting, 145. The stupor of a superior who does not watch over the conduct of his subjects, 374. Those who desire to preside over others are placed beneath those same people, 546. Regarding the injustice and errors of superiors: the less perfect cry out but do not grieve; the perfect remain silent and mourn, 724. How greatly superiors sin when they silently consume ecclesiastical goods, 725. How harmful the wicked examples of superiors are, 727, 1585. When superiors misuse their authority, a thistle arises in place of wheat and a thorn in place of barley, 726. The injustice of superiors defiles the few good things they do, 727. Many superiors wish to be venerated not so much for the Lord as in the Lord’s place, 785. Superiors rejoice in the distinction of their summit, not in the equality of their condition, ibid. Those subject to bad superiors should attribute this to their own fault, 806. Subjects should tolerate even bad superiors if they can do so without endangering the faith, 807. Superiors are guilty of unfaithfulness when, although bound to correct, they neglect to do so, 924. Excessive attention to temporal things and negligence concerning the salvation of souls, 1006. What pride suggests to a superior, 1139. A superior must beware of pride concealed under authority, 1254. The negligence of superiors is censured, 1502. How much God tolerates the injury caused by bad superiors, 1503. Pastors who become wolves, ibid. Superiors who are the stones of the sanctuary, scattered at the head of all the streets, ibid.

Spiritual battles, 204, 991. See War.

Those who neglect the rewards of the heavenly homeland fall here into their own pleasures, 374. The tasting of heavenly rewards, 1279. One reaches great rewards through great labors, 1627.

The dissolution of those set over others is the ruin of their inferiors, 49. While superiors seek their own glory, they overturn the hearts of their subjects, 58. How those set over others ought to conduct themselves toward their subjects, 690.

What it means to remove the foreskins of trees, 280. Foreknowledge is designated by the name of the nostrils, 1019. Our Redeemer possessed foreknowledge of future evils, which he foretold, ibid., 1612. What it means to foreknow, 666.

Present security brings labor to the wicked; present labor brings perpetual security to the good, 356. The manger signifies Holy Scripture, 997. Why Christ was laid in a manger, 1461.

Heretics who presume on their own merits live in security, 157. It is difficult to perform great deeds and not to place confidence in what has been done, 70. How harmful presumption on one’s own virtue is, 708, 941. Whoever presumes on his own strength denies God, 708. We must never presume on our own strength, 760. Whoever presumes on what belongs to another loses what is his own, 905. No one should presume on his vocation, because he is not certain of his election, 1514.

To pass over what one could have done was a small matter, 538. Rulers should not rejoice in presiding but in benefiting, 689. Those who preside over unbelievers or heretics persuade them of their perverse commands as though by reason, 1029. Foreseen darts strike less, 1612.

Why the midday meal was once called supper, 1634. We have been called not to a midday meal but to supper, 1544. Why the heavenly banquet is called not a midday meal but supper, 1620.

We must rely on prayers when we act rightly, 301. Our prayers are imperfect, 302. What is earthly or impure that an idle person previously considered commonly turns over in the mind of one praying, 352. Other people’s offenses must be forgiven toward us before prayer, ibid. Whoever is now familiar with God in prayer will later judge with him, 378. Those who despise God’s commands ask him in vain, 510. The saints are heard more effectively for merit the more quickly they are not heard according to their request, 665. Human prayers can be heard only through an advocate, 718. Blessed Job forbids oppressors to hear the prayers of the righteous whom they oppress, 826. Prayers are fruitless when a pious life does not follow them, 1102. Whoever offers prayers for others makes his prayers more effective for himself, 1152. See Prayer.

Presbyters are called in Greek *presbyteroi*, which in Latin means “very old men,” that is, old men of decrepit age, 1512. See Priest.

In Greek, a prince is called the foundation of the people, 300. Those who rule carry the world, ibid. Those who govern their own thoughts and movements are called princes, 376. The princes of the world are signified by the rhinoceros, 995. They are bound to Christ’s manger, 997. They proclaim the divine commands and take care that they are observed, ibid. With their horn raised, they threaten, but, bound by the reins of the fear of God, they lower their threats, 998. A prince offers help to the Church against her rebellious children, 999. God has entrusted the Church to earthly princes, ibid. The princes of the world promulgate laws on behalf of the Church, 1000. What is signified by princes walking as servants, 1015. The peoples are signified by flesh and the princes of the world by bones, 1374. What it means to exercise princely rule, 1605. How exercising princely rule and dominating differ from one another, ibid. The office of the heavenly principalities, ibid.

The brief work is enclosed at the beginning and the end, 470. We must keep watch over beginnings, 1058. The error of the Priscillianists concerning the birth of infants, 1469.

Testing tries less than recompense consoles, 1152. How God tests a human being, 265. The insolent utter a boastful remark so that by speaking they may seem learned [Col. 1474], 271. The insolent always answer rightly spoken words with the opposite, 337.

The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, 1554. What the prodigal son’s departure into a distant region signifies, 1417. God sets a limit to spiritual progress, 393. The zeal and measure of advancement are described in the just, 517. In the elect, the age of virtue increases as bodily age increases, 692. To advance toward God, we must decline from ourselves, 720. The various degrees of advancement expressed through Daniel, 721. One advances from fear to love, 722. No one knows how far he has advanced except amid adversities, 758. The greater the humility, the greater the hope of progress, 972. Something had to be promised even concerning the present life to disciples who were still unformed, 1591. If carnal people did not receive small things now, they would not believe the great things to come, ibid.

Prophets are called merchants, 581. They are also called clouds, 859; foundations of the Church, 901; mountains, 1075; and a bulwark, 662, 1322.

—The saints of the Old Testament promised Christ both by deeds and by words, 14. Through Peter’s mouth the Church professes Christ to be not one of the prophets but the Lord of the prophets, 595. What it means that, when the sons of the prophets were cutting wood, Elisha restored the iron that had fallen from the handle, 701, 1178. Not only the words but also the actions of the prophets are prophecies, 721, 1281. What it means for a prophet to be sent through water as far as the ankles, the knees, and the loins, 723. Prophets say many things out of the zeal of one who foretells, not out of a wish to curse, 810. Not all prophets attain the merit of holiness, 853. The prophets watered the earth by word, writing, and example, 857. Prophets speak as though reading, 893. At times prophets are inspired through angels, 895. What will happen in action has already happened inwardly in predestination, 900, 928. The apostles rely on the prophets, whom they illuminate, 901. In how many ways the prophets are touched by the spirit of prophecy, 1176. Certain prophets, speaking from their own spirit, are rebuked by the Holy Spirit and reproach themselves, 1180. The distinction between true and false prophets, 1181. Which prophets customarily write down their prophecies, 1183. Prophets join the word they utter outwardly to the word they hear inwardly, ibid. Why prophets sometimes speak about themselves as though about others, 1186. Then the sublimity of the presiding spirit is shown, ibid. Prophets see many things at once that they are forced to narrate successively, 1217, 1237. It is familiar to them to pass suddenly from one subject to another, 1223. How narrow the human heart is for narrating divine things, 1237. Prophets speak in God’s person, 1252. A true prophet speaks God’s words, not his own; a false one speaks his own words, not God’s, 1268. Even prophets cannot stand before God, 1294. Prophets explain things through words and words through things, 1281. Why the prophet went out from the midst of Israel into the field, from which he returns home, 1294. The prophets grasped divine knowledge more fully than Moses, 1348. The apostles were instructed in the knowledge of God more fully than the prophets, ibid. The prophets of the Old Testament marveled at the foreknown knowledge of the Church’s earlier leaders, 1371. What it means to receive a reward from the prophet but not on account of the prophet, 1521.

Prophecy, while other things perish, remains forever [Col. 1475], 57. The spirit of prophecy is not always present to the prophets, 72, 246, 1180; nor is it present in the same way, 1176. Prophecy speaks not only of future things but also of past things, 132. Certain prophetic gifts are walls of the mind, 375. There is no prophecy without understanding of what is foreseen, 378. The proud are sometimes filled with the spirit of prophecy, 853. The truth of what has happened must be held in such a way that the truth of what is to happen is not emptied, 1167. Time in its threefold form is the subject of prophecy, 1173. Prophecies concern hidden things of the past and present, 1175. Whence the word “prophecy” is derived, ibid. Past things are proved from the prediction of future things, and future things from past things, ibid., 1436. The order of prophecy, 1176. The modes of prophecy, ibid. Among the Jews, the sayings of the prophets are called deserts, 1200. Every prophecy, compared with the divine light, is swallowed up, 1241. Prophetic speech is firmer but more obscure, 1336. Prophecies are given to the faithful, and signs to the unfaithful, 1468. In prophetic speech, one person presides and another obeys, 1186.

The propitiatory signifies the incarnate Lord, 1547. What the two cherubim signify when they turn their faces toward the propitiatory, ibid.

To propose what is right is of no benefit unless we remain steadfast in what we have proposed, 226. What allegorical difference there is between a bulwark and a shield, 1340. What both signify, ibid.

Prosperity is signified by day and light, 44, 139. How many dangers spiritual prosperity is subject to, 70. Whoever is not supported by the memory of prosperity is worn down by adversities, 80. Day turns into darkness when the prosperous things promised by the devil are understood to be adversities, 107. Day signifies prosperity and night tribulation, 114, 432. Whoever tramples worldly prosperity pursues his own fault, 120. Prosperity burdens the saints more than adversity, 139. Temporal prosperity is dangerous, ibid. Those who look toward eternal things flee earthly prosperity, ibid., 147, 220, 287. Through morning and evening, the prosperity and adversity of this world are signified, 172. Whoever did not listen to God in prosperity will not be heard by God in adversity, 175. The prosperity of the wicked is immediately condemned by the prudent, 184. Those who desire the prosperity of the wicked are far from salvation, 185. Pride commonly arises from prosperity, 220. Why God depresses some with scourges and supports others with success, 223. God must also be feared in prosperity, 235. The wicked attribute prosperity to their own merits, 271. The voice of confession shaped by the delight of prosperity is despised, ibid. The dangerous prosperity of household possessions arising from one’s own provision, 336. It has been determined how much prosperity or adversity each person will have, 393. Prosperity often draws one away from good works, 415. Why the just despise prosperity, 431. Prosperity and adversity alternate in this life, 433. In this life, bad things often happen to the good and good things to the wicked, 438. The prosperity of the wicked is brief, ibid., 488. The prosperity of the world hinders the return to good works, 439. Prosperity joined with wickedness is bait in a trap, 441. Prosperity is not an argument for innocence, nor adversity for wickedness, 488. Human judgments concerning adversity and prosperity are false, 511. The wicked are disturbed by the prosperity of the just, 530. The mind of the saints flees prosperity and prepares itself for adversities, 538. The just attribute no prosperity to themselves, 672. Whoever desires no prosperity fears no adversity, 714. A person established in prosperity scarcely guards himself from pride and lust, 823. Prosperity closes…
ear of the heart, 843. Through prosperity alone we are loosened, and through adversity we are made firm in the virtues, 947. Evil is corrected with greater difficulty when it is supported by prosperity, 1117. One must neither exult in prosperity nor lose heart in adversity, 1386. How earnestly this art must be learned, ibid. How one should use both joyful and adverse circumstances, ibid. Elation and immoderate joy in prosperity must be avoided, 1388. In prosperity, God’s judgments must be remembered, 1646. God’s protection: if it deserts us, we are nothing, 759. By “shade” is signified the refreshment that comes from heavenly protection, 1077. Divine protection is signified by the name “shield,” 1105. To provoke God is to become proud among one’s neighbors because of his gifts, 367. To provoke God’s anger is knowingly to oppose his commandments, 840. Our kind is called “neighbor,” 205. Love of one’s neighbor is necessary for salvation, ibid. In what this consists, ibid. Each person bears his neighbor only insofar as he loves him, 1333. One’s neighbor must be loved if we wish to reach God, 1581. See *Love*, *Love of neighbor*.

Prudence without simplicity is empty, 18. How prudence grows cold in us, 68. The prudent despise the prosperity of the wicked, 184. How perverse the prudence of the world is, 360. Much prudence is not right, 545. Excess of prudence is blameworthy, ibid. The saints take care not to rely on their own prudence, 700. The prudence of the wise is their wealth, ibid. The prudent of the world incline their hearts to serve Satan, 1126. What prudence is, 1427. God mocks the prudence of the world, 1469.

By the name “embers” (*prunae*) are signified the minds of human beings set ablaze by desires, 1114. What the psalm “for the eighth” signifies, 21, 1341. The devout voice of psalmody prepares a way to the heart for God, 1180. Through compunction poured forth in psalmody, one reaches Jesus, ibid. The three Hebrew boys unharmed in the fiery furnace, 334. The games of the children of the rich, 487. Who are called the children of the Church, 614. Morning signifies childhood, 1511. The beauty of the skin is temporal glory, 442. In what the beauty of the universe will consist after the final judgment, 1094. When the Lord is said to knock, 1482. What it means to place a cushion beneath the head or elbow of one lying down, 560. What it means to gather dust on one’s feet, 27. What scattering dust above the head toward heaven signifies, 93. What it means to sleep in the dust, 495. Dust denotes sinners, 902, 966, 1002. The life of the wicked is hidden beneath the dust, 1053. The dyer’s powder is the virtue of one who acts well, 1429.

A citizen is punished one way, an enemy another, 984. The Church’s people are called orphans, 241, 620. The elect are called orphans, 522. Weak Christians are called orphans, 525. Who is the orphan without a helper, 620. To defend the case of orphans for money is to seek an earthly, not an eternal, reward, 1413. What the purple offered for the tabernacle signifies, 967. The fainthearted are compared with shrubs, 631. When the time of our pruning has come, 1349. What digging wells mystically signifies, 509. A narrow well signifies a bad habit, 844. There would be a bottom to the well, if sin had a measure, ibid. What Isaac’s digging wells among a foreign people signifies, 1021.

## Q

Lent, why one fasts, 1494. Moses and Elijah, and Christ himself, abstained from all food for forty consecutive days, ibid. The manifold, allegorical significance of these days of fasting, ibid. Sundays excepted from the Lenten fast, 1494. Lent is offered to God as the tithe of the days of the whole year, 1495. The joyful flesh drew us into guilt; when afflicted, let it lead us back to forgiveness, ibid. Let fasting be lifted up to God by almsgiving, ibid. What it means to fast for oneself, ibid. What sanctifies the fast, ibid. While the flesh is worn down by fasts, let the spirit be restrained from vices, ibid. See *Fasting*.

Everything that is said can be distinguished according to a fourfold quality, 732. What it means to seek God, 269. God must be sought while we have time, 335, 563. Some seek external gifts from God, not the author of the gifts himself, 489. How and where God is to be sought, 574. When those who first seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness do so, the Lord comes and sits first in their heart, 639. How diligently Christ must be sought, 1546. What it means to seek Christ during the night, ibid. What it means to go around seeking the city, ibid. What it means to seek through the lanes and streets, ibid. When we are seeking, the watchmen who guard the city find us, ibid.

“As if” (*quasi*) sometimes signifies a likeness, sometimes the truth, 561, 801. What is the force of this word, 1311. “A certain one” is said of someone whom we either do not wish, or are unable, to identify, 166.

True rest consists in despising the things of the world, 129. What it means for the heart to rest, 146. Rest in labor, and weariness in rest, 532, 1269. What harmful rest is, 1300. In this life there is no rest of the mind that is either perfect or lasting, 1327.

The significance of the number five, 1354. What the number five signifies when multiplied by itself, 1379. The number fifty signifies eternal rest, 22, 24, 741, 1360, 1378. The five external senses draw their power and discernment from the brain, 369.

## R

“Rabboni” signifies “teacher,” 1548. *Racha* in Hebrew is the word of one who is indignant, 682. Rachel is interpreted as “ewe” and “beginning of sight,” 210, 1324. Rachel represents the contemplative life, ibid. Rachel’s theft of her father’s idols was a figure of the Church, 988. Rachel sees but does not give birth: beautiful but barren, 1325.

What it means to scrape pus with a potsherd, 87. A root is called a hidden thought, 281, 412, 631. What it signifies to send down a root, 281, 412. The root of the righteous can be understood as human nature, 395. Likewise, the root of the righteous is holy preaching, 394. What it means for a root to be opened beside the waters, 631.

Ram—that is, “exalted,” 735. Raphael is interpreted as “medicine of God,” [Col. 1477] 1604. He was sent to heal Tobit’s blindness, 1605.

There are two kinds of robbers, 649. If one who does not give what is his is punished with so great a penalty, how much more severely must one be punished who has stolen what belongs to another, 478. The man who was stealing visibly is seized invisibly, 789. Robbers will suddenly be overtaken by eternal punishment, 790. Not only those who seize what belongs to others, but also those who do not give what is theirs, are worthy of eternal punishment, 1655.

Reason in the mind is like the mistress of a household, 31. Just as maidservants wander when the mistress is absent, so thoughts wander when reason is absent, ibid. Some are held to God more by reason than by faith, 532. A rational human being could not be redeemed through the victim of irrational creatures, 552. By the natural light of reason, as of the mind, what is wrong and what is right become known, 875. What it means to place the reason of heaven upon earth, 953. God is the reason of rational creatures, 964.

The guilt of the first sin prevented everyone from entering the kingdom before Christ’s coming, 128. See *Original sin*, *Abraham’s bosom*.

Rebecca designates the Gentile world, 23, 1160. What Rebecca’s presenting her younger son to his father for blessing signifies, 1213.

The wicked are rebels against the light, 527. The person who ought to submit to God’s commands has subjected himself to his own necessities, 268. The more he sees himself rebelling against himself, the more our enemy strives to conquer us, 772.

*Reblata* is interpreted as “many of these things,” 229.

There are two ways of departing from God, 1251. What the golden reclining couch of the litter signifies, 1334.

Who are called upright, 154. Care must be taken that what we begin with upright zeal we complete with an upright end, 82. We do not know whether what we consider our deeds to be upright are such in God’s judgment, 143. Those are not upright who fear enduring evils here in exchange for eternal goods, 154. The higher we contemplate God’s uprightness, the more we fear concerning our own, 164. Human uprightness, compared with divine uprightness, is crooked, 165, 169, 170. It belongs to an upright mind to test whatever is good in the words of an adversary and reject whatever is bad, 287. A person is not upright if he is not free from the desire for wickedness, 318. God gives us uprightness for living well, 324. The upright do not seek to appear as intercessors for others, 357. What praise from people harms an upright person who acts, and what mockery benefits him, 359. It is difficult to maintain uprightness in deed and thought, 389. Those who lack uprightness of foot, 1193. Uprightness signifies justice, 21. A person wrongly considers himself upright when he does not know the rule of supreme uprightness, 170.

The care of rulers for those subject to them, 21. There were three orders of rulers in the synagogue, 60. Discernment is necessary for a ruler, 620. The qualities of a good ruler, 637, 641. What the moderation of rulers ought to be, 637. A ruler must use justice and mercy, 641. Proud rulers suffer from the vice of apostasy, 785. The form of seeing a good ruler is described, 786. Rulers of the Church ought to pursue humility, ibid. Rulers of the Church will render an account in judgment for the souls entrusted to them, ibid. How they should conduct themselves in governance, 787. At times God gives perverse rulers, 807. Peoples are punished for the sins of their rulers, ibid. Peoples often follow the life of their rulers, ibid. Rulers endure stronger struggles with temptations, 1032. Everyone openly bears the sign under which ruler he serves, 1142. See *Shepherd*, *Prelate*.

How we ought to be reconciled with our neighbor, 1590.

All redemption arises from a preceding captivity, 585. If a human being had not wished to sin, he would have reached heaven without redemption, 128. Whether God could have redeemed the human race in a nature alien to humanity, 552. The condition of our Redeemer, 760. Above, the Son of God established the angels; below, he redeemed human beings, 1322. In order to accomplish his own work—that is, the salvation of human beings—God made it something alien to himself, namely, by enduring scourges and death in the likeness of a human being, 1352. We owe much to our Redeemer, 1551.

Redempta, a nun of great virtues, 1659. The Roman virgin Romula, a disciple of Herundina, ibid.

Those are called kings who govern the movements of their members, 374. Why the saints are called kings, 128. Those are kings who rule over their passions, 837. There are four orders of rulers in the Church, 1407. What the gifts offered to Christ by the kings signify, 1470. What a king about to wage war against another king signifies, 1630.

The highest place is governed well when the one who presides rules over vices rather than over his brothers, 834. The diversity of the governance of our body, 135. Those placed in governance should conceal the glory of their dignity, 146. What the governance of prelates ought to be, 786. The power of governance cannot be administered without devoted attention to temporal care, 809. What the person to whom governance is offered must examine, 810.

Our region is paradise, 1471. That God reigns everywhere, even though some deny it by their wandering, 1470.

The kingdom of heaven is called the Church, 1060, 1097, 1476, 1510, 1634. In the kingdom of God the robe of the saints is still single, 16, 1153. The heavenly kingdom is opened equally to Jews and Gentiles, and to the just and unjust who are converted to the faith, 1382. Why the kingdom of God is compared with summer, 1438. The ruins of the world proclaim that the kingdom of heaven is near, 1448. The kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess, 1451. Nothing is cheaper than heaven when it is purchased; nothing is more precious when it is possessed, ibid. One must advance from visible things to invisible things, 1478. The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, ibid. The one who strives to live rightly here will be able to enter the kingdom of heaven, 1475. If love does not draw one to the kingdom, let fear drive one there, ibid. The kingdom of heaven is compared with ten virgins, 476. How great is the joy of the citizens of this kingdom, 1487. Let us hasten there when invited, ibid. To love ardently is to hasten, ibid. Whether the kingdom of heaven can be given to those who murmur, 1512. Everyone ought to rejoice exceedingly at being in the kingdom of God, even if only last, 1513. To whom the kingdom of heaven will be denied, ibid. What it means for the kingdom of heaven to suffer violence, 1524. The kingdom of heaven is the place of the righteous, ibid. Hope should be placed in the future heavenly kingdom arising from the present kingdom of the Church, 1591. The Church of the righteous is understood above all as the kingdom of heaven, 1634.

The kingdom of the devil, the glory of this world, and the desire of the flesh have been crushed in the servants of God, 157.

The official [*princeps*] asked for his son’s health, yet doubted in faith, 1566. Why Christ did not wish to go to his son, ibid. The *regulus*, king of serpents, signifies Antichrist, the head of the reprobate, 476, 1112. The *regulus* kills not by its bite but by its breath, ibid. [Col. 1478]

The activity of religious persons is put to shame by the activity of secular people, 9. The person who approaches the service of God prepares himself for temptations, 121. Religious persons cast away earthly things in order to grasp the summit of perfection, 263. A religious person offers himself to God by professing the sacrifice, 326. Those who care only for external things do not possess religion but merely pretend to it, 614. Some seek glory through their profession of the Christian religion, 802. Under the pretext of religion some swell up through the vice of pride, 841. The Christian religion was propagated chiefly by the Gentiles, 888. With what devotion kings ought to serve God, 1000. By what art the devil dissuades one who is considering embracing the summit of monastic perfection, 1068. The life of religious persons among the common people is like a temple in a city, 1648.

God sometimes abandons his own for a short time, 661. The person who keeps nothing for himself leaves much for God’s sake, 1450. How we can leave ourselves, 1586. We can leave everything even while retaining it, 1625. Those who possess nothing in this world by loving anything have left everything even while possessing it all, 1633.

Remedies against the devil’s attacks, 202. For the health of the body, even what is unpleasant is willingly endured in a bitter remedy, 1028. What remedies Christ brought for our diseases, 1586. The removal of the devil’s authority and power, 555.

The kidneys signify carnal pleasure, 1535. Whoever eats the Passover must have his kidneys girded, ibid. What it means to be reproved by the heart, 560. Let us always be girded for reproving ourselves, 1021.

Christ reproved the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests, 920. God is not unjust in choosing some and rejecting others, 799, 1100. Rejection is first carried out inwardly and afterward shown outwardly, 797. The Church’s teaching concerning predestination and rejection nourishes the hope of the humble and restrains the pride of the arrogant, 798. Rejection and election are just, 806, 1101. They are also hidden, 855, 1447. The rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles are not to be investigated, 547, 805, 854. The rejection of those who do not obey God when he calls, 1624. The judgments of God in rejecting are just and hidden, as shown by the example of little ones dying without baptism, 855.

The reprobate are called lion cubs, 157. Why the reprobate are called brothers and passers-by by the righteous, 224. The reprobate are compared with a torrent, ibid. They are called tombs, 498; the gravel of Cocytus, 499; the devil’s cave, 876; the shadow of death, 1078; and the flesh of Leviathan, 1119. The devil is one person with the reprobate, 112.

From whom the reprobate are generated, 157. The Jews became reprobate because they refused to listen to the apostles, 578, 581, 921. The life of the reprobate is compared with embers and chaff, 491. The reprobate are innumerable, 798. They are in the Church beyond the number, ibid. Who are called both reprobate and elect at the same time, 1057. Examples of certain reprobate, 1638. In the blindness of their mind the reprobate exult as though in the brightness of light, 28. Whoever has often fallen willingly into guilt is sometimes seized unwillingly for punishment, 54. The characteristics of the reprobate, 112, 271, 796. The reprobate do not change their perverse mind even at the final hour, 172. The minds of the reprobate are always vigilant over perverse thoughts, 193. The thoughts of the reprobate are often futile, yet their conscience is no less guilty, 194. Wherein the strength of the reprobate consists, [Col. 1479] 221. The reprobate look only to present things, 224, 253. The paths of the reprobate are tangled, 226, 229. The reprobate often desire good things, but never withdraw from evil things, 227. The reprobate always desire to live here, 253. The reprobate remain attached solely to transitory things even when death presses upon them, 254, 286, 357. The reprobate often confess their sins but disdain to mourn them, 358. How great is the misery of the reprobate in death, 358. Through the good things received from God, the reprobate become worse, 367. In the hearts of the reprobate, fear does not produce rest; punishment produces fear, 381. The life and end of the reprobate, 408. Although the reprobate fears being struck by the heavenly Judge, he always increases that for which he will be struck, 409. The minds of the reprobate are hardened by scourges, 429. Those who proudly reject the light of truth from themselves are handed over to a reprobate mind, 527. The reprobate are now raised up like the tips of ears of grain, whereas the elect lie hidden like grains, 540. What it means for the reprobate to eat herbs and the bark of trees, 651. The reprobate rejoice in things subject to mourning for their crimes, 653. As with desperately ill people, the reprobate are not denied what they desire, 681. The daily failings of the reprobate, 784. While they carelessly neglect lesser things, they rush disastrously into worse things, ibid. It is characteristic of the reprobate always to do wrong and never to reconsider what they have done, 793. The reprobate never recognize their guilt except in punishment, 796. Being rejected into external things is a sign of rejection, just as being drawn toward interior things is a sign of predestination, ibid. The prosperity of the wicked in opposition to the good is a clear indication of rejection, 827. The light of the reprobate is the glory of the present life, 927. Covered with scales of defense, the reprobate resist the arrows of truth, 1106. The hedgehog has a lair among the reprobate, 1108. The wicked protect one another by mutual defense, ibid. The banquet of the reprobate is the delight of temporal pleasures, ibid. Empty of the riches of virtues, they do not know the poverty of heavenly joy, 1118. The poverty of the reprobate is the deprivation of merits, ibid. The reprobate do not understand their poverty, ibid. The harmful concord of the reprobate with Satan and among themselves, 1119. This concord of the reprobate is most evil, 1120. It is possible to dissolve this concord, as in the example of Paul, ibid. Holy preaching does not drive Satan from the hearts of the reprobate, 1124. The reprobate often show others the way of holiness, 1130. Deceived by the devil, the reprobate do not believe in the eternity of punishments, 1132. Their false arguments are answered, ibid. The reprobate do not maintain the pattern of mutual humility but despise it, 1136. Pride is the clearest sign of rejection, 1142. The reprobate turn the proof of humility into an occasion for pride, 1277. Negligence of and contempt for the word of God is an indication of rejection, 1506. The avaricious, the curious, and those devoted to the pleasures of the flesh are rejected from the banquet, 1621.

The state of the reprobate in this life, 28. The place of the reprobate is pride, 91. The number of the reprobate is infinite, 798. The final judgment of the reprobate, 234. The reprobate will be tortured inwardly and outwardly at the final judgment, 202, 286. The trembling of the reprobate at the final judgment, 234, 1478. For the reprobate there are empty months and laborious nights, 249. The punishments of the reprobate will never end, 285. The reprobate, having neglected the truth, are afterward justly blinded, 527. The barren tree that is the reprobate is cut down and crushed in Gehenna, 535. Some of the reprobate are judged, others are not judged, 835. At the judgment the reprobate will not see Christ in the form of his divinity, 856. What it means for the reprobate to be sanctified on the day of slaughter, 874. The punishment of the reprobate serves the glory of God and of the elect, 1093. The reprobate will be crushed by lightning at the judgment, while the righteous remain unharmed and rejoice, 1120. Why the reprobate fall into the outer darkness, 1263. The reprobate are in bitterness, 140. The destruction of the reprobate, 172. The unexpected end of the reprobate, 254. Eternal damnation follows the reprobate, 326. God did not draw the reprobate back from hell, 398.

What the strength of the reprobate is, 221. For the reprobate, the greatness of the gift becomes an increase of damnation, 273. The false and fruitless repentance of the reprobate at the judgment, 1479. Then their prayers are ineffectual, ibid. The imitators of the reprobate are called their children, 648.

The person who bears the burden of the day in this life desires eternal rest, 247. When God departs from a human being, no rest remains for him, 393. What true rest is, 480. What perfect rest is, 603. In the present life there is no rest from temptations, 754.

What it means to seek God, 40. Insensible things lead us to knowledge of sensible and intelligible things, 127. Sometimes events are evil in their action yet contain the power of prophecy in their meaning. A matter once stated is repeated for confirmation, 912. Desires increase along with possessions, 1075.

What it means to resist God, 290. No one can resist God, ibid., 299. The saints sometimes resist God, 299.

What it means for God to look upon, 535, 606, 992. By looking upon us, God reforms us through grace, 606. God looks upon the sinner in two ways, 1052.

What it means for God to answer blessed souls when they pray, 43, 1145. What it means to answer God with one for a thousand, 289. What it means to answer God, 318, 399, 1145. What an answer is, 1.

Job’s offering a sacrifice on the eighth day signifies the Lord’s resurrection, 20. The rising of dawn is the new birth of the resurrection, 122. By rising again Christ strengthened the hope of his own, 197. Christ’s resurrection prefigured our resurrection, 463. Our Redeemer showed the resurrection so that we might hope to rise again, ibid. Following Job’s example, we believe that resurrection has occurred; he knew that it would occur, 465. Christ’s resurrection is the festival of human beings and angels, 1526. See *The resurrection of Christ*.

Whence the resurrection of the flesh can be believed, 189. The resurrection of bodies can be grasped through examples but not through reason, ibid., 1396. The resurrection of the flesh is signified by the expression “a tree making *eomam*” [reading uncertain], 395. Job denies that the resurrection will occur before the end of the world, 397. We shall answer God when we rise incorruptible, 399. Incorruptibility surpasses the powers of human nature, 400. The world imitates our resurrection in its elements, 464, 1394. Christ’s resurrection was delayed for three days, ours until the end of the world, 463. The resurrection of the dead, with Christ rising, strengthens the confidence of many, 464, 1528. The faith of the resurrection is established, ibid. The quality of bodies after the resurrection, 455. What the error of Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, was concerning the palpability of bodies after the resurrection, ibid. Job believed that our flesh would be restored to its complete condition, 467. After the resurrection our flesh will be the same by nature and different by glory, ibid. Job was completely certain of his resurrection, [Col. 1480] 468. Who will rise for torment rather than for judgment, 836. The time of the resurrection was foreseen and foretold by Job, 961. Christ’s resurrection is the pattern of ours, 1393. In Gregory’s time some doubted concerning the resurrection, ibid. They are refuted and the resurrection is demonstrated, ibid., 1558. The soul thirsts to see God; the flesh thirsts to rise again, 1393. Both Testaments proclaim the future resurrection, 1394. The generation of a human being is a greater miracle than the resurrection, 1395. Many things in the nature of things are no less hidden from us than the resurrection, ibid. Apart from faith in the resurrection, the other things are believed in vain, 1396. The only explanation in miracles is the power of the one who performs them, ibid. Christ showed by example what he promised us as a reward, 1528. It is easier for God to restore what once existed than to create what did not exist, ibid. What follows from hope of the resurrection with respect to conduct, 1559. Hope of the future resurrection alleviates all evils, 1614.

Sins are compared with nets, 440. Why Christ commanded that the net be cast on the right side after, but not before, the resurrection, 1541. Why the nets are sometimes said to break and sometimes not to break, 1542. What it means for Peter to draw the net to land, ibid. Fish, 153. What the fish caught in the nets after the resurrection signify, 1543.

The harmonious diversity of rewards in heaven, 136. The glory of reward always follows the labor of the work, 191. Whoever awaits an eternal reward should devote himself to every cause that will bring about the future recompense, 626. The final reward of many shepherds, 726. Why we seek reward on the basis of merit and yet give thanks to God, 1101.

What it means to look back after the plow, 1198. We can turn back by deed or by thought, 1199. In the active life it is not permitted to turn back, 1210. Why the wicked are said to fall backward, 1251.

How God’s revelations take place, 893. Revelation is signified by the name “vision,” 1310. See *Utterance*, *Prophecy*.

The nature of the rhinoceros, 995, 1010. It is also called the unicorn, ibid. Whom the rhinoceros represents, 995. What the rhinoceros tied to the manger of Christ signifies, 997, 1010. By what means it is tamed, ibid.

What it means for God to laugh, 307, 637. The laughter of the saints after mourning, 285. Laughter of the heart arises from the joy of security, ibid.

The streams of the river are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 476. Who the strong are in the Church, 847.

The devastation of the Roman fields and of Italy in Gregory’s time, 1253. The miserable condition of Rome and Italy, 1374. The Senate was removed from Rome, ibid. The Roman people were carried off by plague or sword, 1375. Buildings collapsed, ibid. The Romans, who had previously plundered the world, were given over as plunder to all nations, ibid. Rome spread its baldness like an eagle, 1375.

Why the revolving sword was placed at the entrance to paradise, 397.

The holy virgin Romula, 1659. Her virtues, 1660. She bore with the paralysis by which she was afflicted with the greatest patience, ibid. The losses of Romula’s limbs became an increase of virtues, ibid. Strengthened with the Eucharistic provision (*viaticum*), Romula died happily, 1661. Her heavenly funeral rites, ibid. A pearl in a dunghill: Romula in the degradation of poverty, ibid. In poverty Romula was heaped with true honors and riches, ibid. [Col. 1481]

Dew coming from above is the grace of God, 632. The rose that gives off fragrance grows together with the thorn that pricks, 1638.

The prosperity of the wicked is compared with a wheel, 531. The wheel signifies sacred Scripture, 1213, 1277. What a wheel dragged upon the earth signifies, 1215. The wheel within the wheel signifies the New Testament contained in the Old, 1217. What the four faces of the wheels signify, ibid. The wheels have faces and paths, and move toward the four regions, 1219. What it means that the wheels go and do not turn back, ibid. The structure, height, and appearance of the inner and outer wheel, 1220, 1221. What it means for the wheels to walk with the living creatures as they walk and to be lifted up when they are lifted up, 1226. For the wheels to follow the spirit means that the divine words are raised up toward whatever the spirit of the reader is directed, ibid. What the spirit of life in the wheels signifies, 1228, 1230. What it means for the wheels to go, stand, and be lifted up with the living creatures, ibid.

The rust of vice could not be cleansed except by the fire of torment, 85. Rust signifies anger, 1113. What the burning bush in which God appeared to Moses signifies, 895, 1227.

The wrinkles of the Church are bad Christians, 420. Wrinkles signify duplicity, ibid. How a spot and a wrinkle differ, 664.

Let the ruin of the great be a warning for the lesser, 1090. The ruin of the strong increases the destruction of the weak, 1127. The ruin that condemns some humbles others, 1130.

## S
Saba is interpreted as “net,” 230. The Sabaeans are called “those who take captive,” 57. What it means that the Sabbaths are mocked by enemies, 163, 1300. What the Sabbath of God’s people is, 589. What “Sabbath from Sabbath” means, 1221. “Let our flight not be on the Sabbath,” 1481. Sabellius admitted one person in the Trinity, 618.

Every faithful person is a priest, who is commanded daily to feed the fire on the altar with wood placed beneath it, 794. These pieces of wood are the examples of the holy Fathers and the divine commandments, ibid. Set ablaze by the fire of charity, we are a holocaust to God, ibid. Priests of the greater and lesser orders, 1423. Souls are the Lord’s food; priests are the seasoning of souls, 1504. A priest is a rock of salt among the peoples, 1500.

The glory of a priest is the uprightness of his subjects, 374. Priests are the first part of the Lord’s members, 453. Priests are called the windows of the temple and watchmen, 1291. These windows are closed off by earth, ibid. They are chosen from among the faithful to minister to God and devote themselves to heavenly studies, 1425. Priests are called angels, 1455. Who fulfill the dignity of this name, ibid. The bases in the temple signify priests in the Church, 1501. The lions and oxen represented on the bases signify, in a priest, severity tempered by gentleness, ibid. How great must be a priest’s concern regarding the account he must render to God, 1505.

A priest rightly succeeds his father when he shows himself to be God’s son by his conduct, 1305. Nothing is so burdensome for priests as bending the rigor of the mind through compassion, 1292. The fullness of knowledge in a priest is signified by the cherubim represented on the bases, 1501. The priest’s anger seasoned with gentleness, 1502. A priest does not differ from the people when by the merit of his life he does not rise above the morals of the common people, 1503. The life of priests should correspond to their office and dignity, 1505. Scarcely any activity of the world now exists which priests do not administer, [Col. 1481] 1503.

Priests who neglect the care of their subjects are without glory, 374. The order and office of priests, 1292. Whose task it is for priests to guard the temple, 1423. What it means for the temple of God to be guarded by priests, ibid. Priests of the lesser order keep watch for the service of the altar, ibid. Priests of the greater order are occupied with spiritual studies, 1424. The world is full of priests, but laborers in the Lord’s harvest are rare, 1496. All undertake the priestly office, but few fulfill the work of the office, 1497. Let a priest consider how many sinners have been converted by his works, or how many good people have been moved to become better, 1504. With great moderation, let a priest strive either to loose or to bind, 1656. The priest’s sentence, even when unjustly pronounced, is to be feared, ibid. Priests can still cast out demons today, 1571. How priests ought to conduct themselves toward sinners, 1594.

Bad priests wrong God more than the others, 1503. With what tears the sins of bad priests must be mourned, ibid. “The gold has grown dim”: the life of priests changed for the worse, ibid. “The best color has been changed” when the habit of holiness, through disgraceful works, has fallen into dishonor, ibid. Bad priests are the cause of public calamities, 1504. Bad priests are the cause of the death of their subjects, ibid. The tasteless salt by which the Lord’s food is badly seasoned signifies bad priests, ibid. How severely bad and useless priests are to be punished at the judgment, ibid. Certain priests imitate the pride of the Pharisee who despised the sinful woman, 1594. The ruin of the people arises chiefly from the fault of priests, 1646. Priests lead others to the way of salvation through their office, but themselves hurry toward hell, 1505. Bad priests are like the baptismal water which, after washing away sins, sends the baptized to heaven while itself descends into the sewers, ibid. Prayer made to God for the priests themselves, ibid. See Pastor, Prelate, Preacher, Rector.

The priesthood of the Old Law is called smoking wood, 1079. What it means to sew a sackcloth garment over the skin, 425. What it signifies that the sun became like a sack of haircloth, 291. What it means to put one’s wages into a pierced bag, 1206. The heart of man is called God’s purse, 401. Our sins are marked in the purse, destined at some time to come out for public judgment, ibid.

The sacraments are of no benefit without good works, 1534. The sacrifices of heretics are useless, 15. Among the Gentiles, sacrifice was effective on behalf of ancestors for the wiping away of original sin, and faith alone on behalf of little children, 102. What it means to wash and burn the feet and entrails of the victim, 326. What the sacrifices of the Old Law signified, 914. What the perpetual sacrifice to be removed by Antichrist means, 1060. Who offer sacrifice in Egypt and who in the wilderness, 1399. In the carnal sacrifice, devotion of the heart was offered, 1404. A sacrifice pleasing to God, 1631. What the sacred sacrifice of the Mass accomplishes for the remission of sin, ibid. The sacrifice of the altar offered for the dead, 1631. The custom of Bishop Cassius of offering sacrifice daily, ibid.

Sadoch is called “just” in Latin, 1424. Who the sons of Sadoch and Levi are, ministering to God, ibid. Those desiring to die to the world are often compelled to serve in human ministries, 141. The world is signified by the sea, 910. The world raging against the saints is shut up by God, ibid. By the name of a horse the present world is signified, whose extremity the serpent Antichrist presses down, 1015. The temptations of those serving in the world, 1065. When love of the world has grown weak, it is necessary that the love of God alone grow strong within us, 1346. Some deal with worldly matters without a worldly mind, 1626.

Superiors ought not to rage against their subjects, 1498. The Church is figured by a dragnet, 1473. In the Church’s dragnet, fishermen were first caught, and afterward rhetoricians and philosophers through them, 1097. Let us think, when we are caught, lest we be divided on the shore, 1474.

What arrows signify, 213, 1124. What it means to pass through God’s arrows, 938. What the arrows of little children are, 1124. Who are those drawing the bow and shooting arrows, 1412. The salt of the Law is the power of hidden understanding, 215. Whoever possesses the salt of wisdom should not withdraw from harmony with the brethren, 1239. Why salt is applied to priests, 1504. What the salty land signifies, 981. By the name of saliva the flavor of innermost contemplation is understood, 266. Saliva signifies wisdom, 1270. The wicked resemble willow trees, green but without fruit, 1081. The just resemble willow trees in their greenness, ibid.

Why Solomon received wisdom at night, 39. Solomon fell little by little through sin’s stealthy enticement, 402. Having fallen, he built temples to idols, ibid. Solomon’s judgment concerning the two women, 686. Solomon’s downfall through excessive association with women, 402.

Who will be saved at the final examination, 511. No one can be saved by his own strength without God’s help, 1054. Some boast that they are saved by their own powers, 585. The one who understands less the danger from which he escaped loves his rescuer less, 1054. In order to recover salvation, we drink bitter things, 1445. No one here possesses complete salvation, 251. Bodily health itself is a kind of sickness, 268. Excessive concern for the present life harms eternal salvation, 335. Job trembling over his salvation: let no one be secure, 436. Outside the holy and universal Church there is no salvation, 437. The beginning of salvation comes from God’s prevenient grace, not from preceding merits, 585. The error of those who assert that a person can be saved by his own powers, 586. The foolishness of those who honor either Moses or some saint as the author of their salvation, 591. The foolish vine, full of thorns, signifies neglect of salvation, 662. The salvation of the wicked passes away like a cloud, 663. Fear of faith is built upon the construction of salvation, 903. Without faith, hope, and charity no adult is saved, 1360. Human salvation depends on God’s will, 1513. How great our concern for salvation ought to be may be learned from the concern of litigants, 1558.

“Salvation” in Latin is *Jesus* in Hebrew, 1180, 1246, 1312, 1402, 1423, 1527, 1563. Who is said to greet on the journey, 1498. The Samaritans resemble camels, 24, 59. What the Samaritan’s wine and oil signify, 641. Samaritan is interpreted as “guardian,” 1507. Christ did not deny that he was a Samaritan, ibid.

What Samson, blinded and assigned to the mill, signifies, 229. Samson, while living, killed few; when dying, he destroyed innumerable enemies, thereby prefiguring Christ, 928. Samson is a figure of Christ rising and ascending into heaven, 1529.

Why Samuel and Moses are commended by God above others, 300, 1564. Samuel’s kindness is revealed, 860, 1339. His patience toward those who rejected him, [Col. 1483] 1228, 1339. He prayed for his enemies, 300, 1564.

What the signs of holiness are, 644. No true holiness is not tested among the wicked, 673. By the name of gold the splendor of holiness is understood, 1128. Holiness before human beings is not always holiness before God, 1129. From Christ, or from the fountain, holiness flows into the holy, 1402.

The saints are compared with physicians, 90. The saints are called stars, 13, 111, 1309, and also the heavens, 406; likewise kings, 128, 837. The saints are called vessels of gold, 595, and birds, 604. A saint cleansed from sins is fit to intercede for the sins of others, 11. All the saints, like stars, illumine the night of the present life through their virtues, 13. The saints who lived under the Law before the Incarnation are said, when conceived, not to have seen the light, 132. Why the devil is permitted to affect the hearts of the saints through dreams, 262. The saints always consider their own lowliness, God’s gifts, and his judgments, 265. The saints receive from God what enables them to oppose his anger, 299.

The virtues of the saints become more clearly known through tribulations, 9. The virtues of the saints are our instruction, 37. In persecutions the saints are insulting neither toward God nor toward their adversaries, 90. The saints, not seeking human praise, are not recalled from good works by human mockery, 202. However brightly the saints shine in virtue, they do not understand the glory of the resurrection which they await, 123. The saints are strong and humble, 238; patient in evil and kind in good, 242. However pure the saints may be, they consider themselves impure, 315. Amid reproaches and insults the saints cling to God alone, 359. The saints patiently hear the evils charged against them by the wicked, 417. Amid adversity the saints remain unbroken and calm, ibid. The life of the saints is to be judged especially from their later deeds, 575. Through humility the saints conceal their virtues, 562, 623; sometimes they recount them while preserving humility, ibid. Those are truly saints who can live innocently among the wicked, 673. The saints are silent in a time of agitation; others act otherwise, 716. How and why the saints themselves can and ought to regard one another as superior, 768. In correcting, the saints preserve humility together with discipline, 780. The saints attribute all their good works to God, 958. The saints rejoice in suffering, 1027. What the discernment of the saints is like, 1035. The saints are humble in lofty contemplation, 1144. Love and hope lift the minds of the saints; fear and penitence cover their bodies, 1203. Holy men, while doing courageous things, think little of themselves, 1461.

The life of the saints is our instruction, 37. In the saints certain minor vices remain for the sake of exercise, 121. The saints unwillingly drag along some remnants of sin, ibid. However brightly the saints shine in virtue, they are always weak, 122. The saints rejoice with fear over vices brought under control, 158. Every saint is not free from fault, 256. The more perfectly the saints know God, the more stains of their own life they discover, 315. Before God’s judgment the saints cannot be perfectly clean, 406. Although the saints sometimes sin, they do not persist in pride, 408. The saints can exist without the reign of sin, but not without sin, 443. The saints regard their lesser sins as serious, 1045. Saints who fall away from their purpose of holiness become colder in mind, 1078, 1084.

The saints hurl the darts of doctrine against those giving evil advice, 89. Holy men who desire to mortify themselves to the world are compelled to preside in government, 141. The more prosperous holy men become, the more ruined they consider themselves, ibid. They exult in hope and tremble with fear, 158. Holy men confidently await the eternal reward from a good conscience of life, 247. The saints always return to the secrets of the heart, 261. The saints know with complete certainty that they cannot have rest in this life, 263. The saints’ “despair” is their renunciation of earthly pleasures, 264. The more truly the saints know the highest things, the more sublimely they despise earthly things, ibid. Holy men, freed from the concerns of others, devote themselves entirely to cleansing their conscience, 356. Holy men, mocked by the wicked, turn to God as the witness of their conscience, 360. In knowledge the saints humbly restrain their own judgment, 448. The minds of the saints are tormented by the guilt of another’s deceit, 500. The saints abhor the company of the worst people, 561. The saints do not seek the glory of their works, but shrink from appearing to be what they have deserved to be seen as, 562. Holy men rejoice not in ruling over people but in benefiting them, 689. When they preside, they attend not to the power of their rank but to the equality of their condition, ibid. They seek not their own glory but the justice of their subjects, 690. Holy men sometimes desire to be feared by their subjects, ibid. If they possess anything good, they attribute it not to themselves but to God, 691. When holy men contend with their inferiors, they prefer to be burdened rather than to burden, 694. They do not grow proud of their good works but fear because of them, 701. They glory neither in a good work nor in reputation, whether before people or in conscience, 702. They are not inflated by knowledge or by the greatness of their works, 704. Holy men sometimes rejoice in their good reputation, 706. The manner in which holy men should correct others, 852. The saints refer all their works to the praise of the Creator, 1212. They take care lest vices deceive them by pretending to be virtues, 1224.

The saints oppose a shield of patience to those who strike, 89. Amid tribulations they are concerned for the salvation of the weak, 90. Thus does a saint bear the burden of grief without exceeding the measure of humility, ibid. Here the saints appear to perish, 154. Glory and joy will receive the servants of God who are now despised and afflicted, 191. The saints find the words and ways of carnal people hard to bear, 218. The source of the patience of the saints outwardly oppressed, 236. He refuses to be Abel whom Cain’s wickedness does not exercise, 673, 1259, 1638. No saint reaches heavenly glory except by preserving patience, 1229.

Those who know how to sympathize with the afflicted understand the mind of the suffering saint, 10. From the scourges of the saints it is to be understood what reward is reserved for them and what punishment for the wicked, 77. The saints desire evils here, 92, 251. They fear prosperity more than adversity, 137, 490. How the saints use prosperity and adversity, 139, 638. Holy men, hastening to their homeland, despise the prosperity of this exile, 139. Holy men shrink from shining amid prosperity, ibid. In prosperity the saints conceal themselves, 146; they are silent and at rest, ibid. What the thoughts of the saints are in prosperity, 147. Often the innocent appear to perish here and the upright to be destroyed, 154. Holy men exult in hope and tremble with fear, 158. Who make good use of prosperity or adversity, 172. The saints make good use of the scourges of this life, 188. This is God’s gift, ibid. Holy men are despised outwardly, 191. The saints oppressed by evils are superior to all temporal things and secure in the hope of eternal things, 192. Why the saints fear in prosperity and desire adversity, 221, 247, 287, 490. The sublimity of the saints outwardly oppressed, 236, 826. Holy men are neither independent through self-exaltation nor submissive through fear, 238. For the saints, months are empty and nights laborious as they endure poverty and adversity, 248. The saints desire to be fortified by adversity lest they be exalted, 251. What it means for the saints to be scourged without cause, 303. The saints are afflicted by the misery of temptations, 327. When God abandons them, holy men do not perceive the damage of their ruin, 328. In the labors of this world the saints groan like hired laborers, 393. In adversity the minds of the saints are moved to prayer, not to anger, 458. For good minds even those things which appear adverse become prosperous, ibid. The minds of the faithful are never without bitterness even amid prosperity, 513. In the heights of honor the saints preserve humility, and in joyful circumstances they preserve sorrow, 671. They fight inwardly against prosperity, 672. In the temptation of agitation the saints shrink from displaying themselves, 716. While the saints are pressed outwardly by distress, they are enlarged inwardly, 930. Adversity makes the saints stronger, 947, and more cautious in guarding their inner gifts, ibid. Here even prosperity is burdensome to the saints, 965. Neither adversity casts down a holy man nor prosperity corrupts him, 1022. Holy men are terrified neither by snares, threats, arguments, nor punishments, 1025. The greater the persecution pressing upon a holy man, the more fiercely he is urged to preach, 1026. How adversity overcomes the one whom punishment encourages, 1027. Holy men scent war from afar during the Church’s peace, 1029. They neither exult in prosperity nor fail in adversity, 1386. In prosperity and adversity the saints are compared with squared stones, 1405. The groans of the Christian soul afflicted by God’s scourges, 1430. The persecutions of demons purify the saints, 519.

Holy men do not sin when they curse, 105. When the saints curse, they do so not for revenge but for justice, ibid. How holy men meet sins, 145. The difference between saints and hypocrites, 279. The saints fear not human judgment but divine judgment, 812.

The saints themselves serve the corruptibility of the body in this life, 135. Those desiring to die to the world are often compelled to serve in human ministries, 141. God’s marvelous providence toward the saints detained in the ministries of this life for their own and others’ progress, ibid. What causes the saints to mourn and tremble, 144, 798. Like hired laborers, the saints take care that no day pass empty of work, 246. The saints who perish in this world are preserved through perishing for eternal glory, 154. The life of the saints in this world is full of labors, 248, 973. The saints are always anxious about eternal recompense, 436. The wicked do not believe that the saints are afflicted here, 469, 512. Holy men are calm amid the waves of earthly cares, 590. The more they know God, the more worthless they seem to themselves, 596. They examine themselves outwardly and inwardly in the sight of God and human beings, 614. While the saints are inwardly free for God, the wicked seek only outward things, ibid. The saints are never secure in this life, 637. The saints examine their consciences incessantly, yet are not secure in their own judgment, 683. Compared with Christ, the saints recognize how far they fall short of holiness, 684. The saints take care not to exact too strictly what is owed to them, 693. The saints restrain their senses and continually gather themselves within their mind, 699. They do not exult in the splendor of their good works, 702. They consider not how much of the journey has already been completed but what remains to be done, 703. The saints are tormented by their own praises, 707. They attribute their good works to God, not to themselves, ibid. However great the saints’ virtue, it does not exclude bodily weaknesses and disturbances, [Col. 1485] 715. By God’s gift they are unshaken, but by their own weakness they are disturbed, ibid. These things do not hinder inner peace and contemplation, ibid. In this life God sometimes grants consolations to the saints without any loss to eternal life, 738. The saints are books from which we shall be judged, 767. As long as we are in this life, we need the examples of the saints, ibid. A saint is the temple of God, and from the sight of him we are put to shame over our iniquities, 768. Holy men are like sparks among a thicket amid the wicked, 783. While submitting themselves to God, they overcome and despise transient things, 825. The desires of the saints are heard all the more abundantly the later they are heard, 827. Here is the place of humility for the saints; in heaven, the place of exaltation, 838. The saints consider themselves bound in chains as long as they live here, 839. Clinging to God, the saints heal the anxiety of the heart, 849. The saints are God’s tents, in which he dwells and walks among us, 861. God shines through the saints when he performs miracles, 862. The rule of life must be taken from the saints, 905. The world raging against the saints is shut up by God, 910. In the darkness of this life the saints are compared with the Pleiades, 948. All the saints are joined by unanimity of faith and virtues, 949. The present is burdensome to the saints as they pant for eternal things, 965. As long as they live, the saints burn with desire for their heavenly homeland, 981. They disdain to follow the multitude of earthly people, ibid. They close their ears to the violent temptations of the devil, 982. What it means for the saints to be raised by a lock of hair between heaven and earth, 1005. God is the rider, possessing the soul of a just man who governs his body well, 1009. The desires of the saints and their expectation of the last things are signified by the nostrils, 1020. The saints meet their opponents fearlessly, 1023. Sometimes the saints prudently avoid dangers, ibid. Care must be taken lest we flee through fear rather than through prudent administration, 1024. A skilled leader neither always brings his army against the enemy nor always withdraws it, ibid. The understanding of the saints is signified by the voice of the eagle, 1039. The nesting eagle expresses the life and conduct of the saints, ibid. The life of the saints is signified by the name of the Kenite, who places his nest in the rock, ibid. The saints are lifted above the heights of the earth, 1040. The saints see the earth from afar, 1043. From the very thing by which the saints become more worthy, they seem to themselves more unworthy, 1045. With what lofty dispensation God presses his servants either by threats or even by scourges, 1098. No one is a saint except one who bears the likeness of Christ, 1190. What the four wings of the saints are, 1203. The saints need the covering of sins, ibid. The saints are always present to themselves, 1204. The saints are coals by which we are kindled and lamps by which we are enlightened, 1207. Some burn but do not give light, 1208. The saints possess the power to burn and shine only from the Holy Spirit, ibid. The vigilance of the saints, lest they be deceived by vices pretending to be virtues, 1223. Because of their vigilance the saints are said to be full of eyes, 1224, 1225. Why the saints are said to have eyes on their back, 1225. The saints not only walk but are lifted from the earth through contemplation, 1226. The saints go for the benefit of their neighbor; they stand for their own guardianship; they are lifted up for the contemplation of God, 1229. God fills the minds of the saints with heavenly love and hears those who are filled, 1235. How the saints lower their wings at the voice that comes above the firmament, 1241, 1242. The saints tremble when considering God’s hidden judgments, [Col. 1485] ibid. The saints kindle one another for progress, 1275. In the life of the saints, Holy Scripture is understood, 1277. The structure of the saints is built daily by masons, 1314. God’s marvelous dispensation of gifts and temptations toward the saints, 1321. We are fortified by the miracles, or defenses, of the saints, 1340. The saints have differing merit but one faith, 1344. Why the saints of both Testaments are called the fronts of the heavenly building, 1346. The examples of the saints must be investigated, 1362. The hearts of the saints are tables for a holocaust, made of squared stones, 1408, 1410. The height of the saints is faith in invisible things, 1409. Those who excel in faith, hope, and charity are to be admired, ibid. Now the saints are inwardly present through desire, but not through complete attainment, 1420. In this life the saints have some things to endure and others to love, 1422. The saints live neither for themselves nor die for themselves, 1425. The hearts of the saints burning with desire for their heavenly homeland are signified by the altar placed before the veil, 1428. Who offer the sacrifice of myrrh and incense, 1429. What reason the saints have for rejoicing as the end of the world approaches, 1438. The saints are enlightened by Christ as mountains are by the sun, 1581. The various orders of the saints resemble the orders of angels, 1606. See Just.

Before Christ’s resurrection the saints were detained in hell; now after death they are immediately received into heaven, 127. The saints born before Christ are called miscarriages, 132. The nearer the saints are to death, the more fervent they are, 142. The security of the just in death is the beginning of their recompense, 203. The laughter of the saints after mourning, 285. How greatly the saints fear the final judgment, which they approach closely, 775. What will the tablets do if the columns tremble? 776. The saints desire death, 399. Before Christ’s coming the saints were detained in hell without torments, 433. Those who trust in the resurrection understand that present death is not their destruction, 668.

The souls of the saints speak one way to God and God another way to them, 42. Whose prayers the saints do not hear, 175. Why in heaven the saints do not pity the reprobate in hell, 203, 285, 1094, 1658. The saints enjoy blessedness immediately after leaving this world, 296, 433, 1153. The first and second robe of the saints, 396, 1153. The beauty of the saints is partly that of their conduct and partly that of their rewards, 296. The saints in heaven see what takes place on earth, 403. The saints will shine in heaven like gold and will transmit light like glass, 593. In their faces the innermost feelings of the mind are seen, ibid. Who are the saints who are like and unlike God, 594. The just and the saints participate in divine wisdom, not by comparison with it, 596. The saints will never be satisfied with the vision of God, 602. The seat of the saints on the throne is eternal, 838. The Word, by the nature of his divinity, illumines the saints, 978. Seeing in the torments of the wicked the punishments they escaped, they are stirred to praise God, 1133, 1658. The saints no longer pray for their enemies condemned to Gehenna, ibid. The saints who have perfectly left the world will sit as judges with Christ, 1190. How the saints will be like Christ, ibid. In the glory of immutability the saints will participate in God, 1192. The body also will share in this, ibid. How great is the joy of the saints with whom God is joined in the bridal chamber of the eternal kingdom, 1479. Whatever is done in creation, the blessed can see in the Creator, 1658. See Blessedness; the state of glory.

The invocation of the holy martyrs is commended, 525, 1591. Catholics do not equate the saints with Christ, for they know that the saints are pure human beings, 595.
