Let us take care to have them as patrons, 1592. The saints wish to be asked by us, 1593. Those who do not know God falsely venerate God’s servants, 1508.

The death of the saints bears fruit in us through example, 395. The examples of the saints greatly assist us in renewal, 797. See Examples.

What it means to sanctify, 27. What it signifies to mix blood with a garment, 315. What it means that blood touches blood, 425, 1290. What is signified by blood being poured out upon a most limpid rock, 483. What it means to lick blood, 1043. What is understood by the name “blood” in Holy Scripture, 425, 755, 1285, 1290. The blood of Christ speaks better than the blood of Abel, 426.

What pus signifies, 96. What it means to scrape pus with a potsherd, ibid.

**Health.** Our hearts are badly healed, wounded by no love of God, 200.

What it means to be wise unto sobriety, 91, 503, 532, 545, 567, 644, 905, 1320. God catches the wise in their craftiness, 194, 196. The wise of this world rush headlong into their own judgment, 439. Who the truly wise are, 432. It is difficult to restore to humility the mind of one who considers himself wise, 532. How many of the ancient Fathers were wise and why they occupied themselves with temporal concerns, 589. The words of the wise of the world and the wisdom of God differ, 592. Old age of heart is required in the wise, 618. For the wise person there are many reasons to groan in and over his own exile, but none for rejoicing, 587. What it means that the eyes of the wise are in his head, 538, 637, 1191. Whoever is wise should strive to be wise, but not to appear wise, 734. Whoever sees that he can do more than others easily believes that he knows more, 832. The apostate presents himself as like an angel and superior to others, 833. By the name of the sun the understanding of the wise is signified, 1127. Those who seemed wise in the Church often incline the sharpness of their wisdom toward the devil’s footprints, ibid. He to whom God is sweet becomes bitter to himself, 1280. By the name of the ox the wise person is designated, 1376. The wise of the world will cling to Antichrist, 1109.

Wisdom, antecedent to the good things that follow, is born in the heart of the elect, 64. In whom the wisdom of the saints is placed, 360. Why it is mocked by the world, ibid. Though wisdom is one, its gifts and modes of indwelling are diverse, 369. The reprobate merely hear the words of wisdom; the elect also taste them, ibid. Wisdom is confirmed through the practice and experience of living, 370. Those deceived by confidence in their false wisdom cannot come to true wisdom, 432, 890. The wisdom of the Church is exercised when it is tested by words, 557. What it means not to know the price of divine wisdom, 584. Divine wisdom is not found in the land of those living comfortably, 586, 587. Those who are wise according to the flesh and the world are strangers to wisdom, 588. Wisdom is not in a restless heart, ibid. Why wisdom is not compared with the sardonyx or sapphire stone, 592. The distinction between wisdom and the servants of wisdom, 596. Wisdom does not have one kind of being and another kind of knowing, ibid. Wisdom is hidden from the eyes of all the living, 600. Wisdom, filling the human soul, makes it holy, ibid. The place of wisdom is the Father, just as the place of the Father is wisdom, 605. Wisdom is the teacher of good works, 723. Those who seem wise to themselves cannot contemplate God’s wisdom, 890. What is required for contemplating God’s wisdom, ibid. The wisdom of the saints comes from God, 960. Wisdom is placed not in words but in the inward parts, [Col. 1487] ibid. Whoever does not yet despise himself does not grasp God’s humble wisdom, 1136. What the ineffable wisdom of God is, 1241.

Our wisdom is faith, 64. Wisdom is often strengthened by the loss of folly, 68. Immoderate wisdom is harmful, 91, 532. Wisdom is called gold, by which eternal goods are purchased, 131. Through invisible wisdom we die to the world, 142. Secular wisdom is not to be rejected, 293. The folly of one who is proudly wise, 359, 545. What human wisdom consists in, 360. What the wisdom of the just is, ibid. What false wisdom is, 432. Carnal wisdom is to be despised by those who possess the light of truth, 498. Sober wisdom is difficult, 531, 545, 644. Wisdom can neither be held in one place nor bought with wealth, 585. The words of worldly wisdom often lie through arrangements of words, 592. The wisdom that teaches good works is given through growth, 723. The degrees of wisdom are various, ibid. Humility is necessary for wisdom, 888. The true wisdom of a human being is humility itself, 897. The wisdom of the world is unbelieving, 1042. Human wisdom compared with divine wisdom is foolishness, 1143. Saliva is a sign of wisdom, 1270. In much wisdom there is much indignation, 1279. The distinction between wisdom and knowledge, 1363. Wisdom pertains to life, knowledge to doctrine, 1364. One ascends from fear to wisdom, 1380.

Christ is called the Wisdom of God, 370. Incarnate Wisdom is signified by the name of wood, 394. How much incarnate Wisdom surpasses philosophy adorned with the polish of speech, 592. Why the Wisdom of God came into the world, 591. The Wisdom of God, made visible through assumed flesh, was recognized by the world, 597. The Wisdom of God is born from the Father, coeternal with him, 599. What God has made wisdom to be seen and recounted, prepared and investigated, 610. The incarnate Wisdom of God made the wisdom of the world foolish, 917, 1088. The body of Christ is called the house of wisdom, 1095. Whoever does not yet despise himself does not grasp God’s humble wisdom, 1136. The woman who has the lost drachma signifies the Wisdom of God, 1603. See Christ, the Wisdom of God.

What the sapphires on which the Church is founded signify, 579, 592. Who are said to be more beautiful than sapphire, 1071. What Sarah’s being reproved and then made fruitful signifies, 336. Sarah expresses trust in God, ibid. What the sardonyx stone signifies, 592. What the iron frying pan signifies, 1304.

Satan was present among the angels because he did not lose his nature, 40. Satan is present to God, and is present even when absent, ibid. Satan’s going to and fro is an indication of his anxiety, 41. He is clothed in no carnal nature, ibid. Satan’s will is always wicked, but his power is never unjust, 45. What it means for Satan to go out from the presence of the Lord, 47. From Adam until Christ’s coming Satan found no one who resisted him completely, 54. What Satan’s hand signifies, 56, 85. Satan customarily inserts evil thoughts among our good thoughts, 63. Satan is said to preserve what he is not permitted to break into, 76. All living wicked people are members of Satan, 85. By handing himself over to Satan’s hands, Christ compelled him to serve himself, ibid. Who are counted under the name of Satan, 89. Satan is held bound in the abyss until the end of the world, 114. Satan is called a lion and a tiger, 157. The variety of Satan’s deceit, ibid. Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, 107, 944, 988, 1103. He is said not to exist who has lost the good of existence, 444. Amid a multitude of sinners, as in a heap of dead bodies and in tombs, Satan keeps watch, [Col. 1487] 498. Satan is bitter to the elect but sweet to the reprobate, suggesting vices, 499. Through Antichrist at the end of the world Satan will draw all the carnal to himself; now he draws innumerable people, ibid. God preferred to strike Satan by wisdom rather than by strength, 551. What Satan standing at Jesus’ right hand and being rebuked signifies, 659. Statements concerning the hardness and rejection of the Jews can be understood of Satan, 943. Among those whom Satan makes cold, he easily rests as if in the shade, 1078. In them he lies secure, ibid. Satan nearly swallowed all people before the Redeemer’s coming, and afterward devours not a few, 1082. Satan, whether through himself or through his members, presented petitions to Christ, 1093—or is about to present them, 1101. Satan is like a ravenous wolf, 1486. How Satan, the wolf, may seize and scatter the sheep, ibid. See Devil; Demon; Leviathan; Behemoth.

The saints will never be satisfied in blessedness, 602. Why people cannot be satisfied here, 849. Who knows how to be satisfied, 1386, 1387. It is a great art to be satisfied, 1388.

God alone could make satisfaction for the human race, 763. Saul in vain …
pursues David, 195. Saul was good before receiving the kingdom, 583, 807, 833, 1135, 1460. Saul was advanced because of humility and rejected because of pride, 833, 1135, 1460. Saul was numbered among the prophets, 853. Saul, elected and rejected—how this was so, 1057. Why Saul was rejected, 1135. The origin of Saul’s pride, ibid., 1460. Fortifications of rocks: what they signify, 1042. The fortifications of rocks are our loftiness, ibid. Giving scandal to the brethren is dangerous, 388. The weak are drawn on by the examples of the wicked, 420. Whoever gives scandal to others by his words will be guilty of their sin, 548. The wicked try to corrupt the weak and those making progress, 650. The state of the soul is to be mourned when enemies rush into it after the wall of faith has been breached, 662. Those who strip us of virtues by wicked examples are worse than those who strip us of external goods, 821. It is one thing to advise vices by one’s manner of living, another to command them by frightening others, 821. Evil is administered more harmfully by the example of an action than by speech, 1062. When the scandal of one’s neighbor must be avoided and when it must be disregarded, 1224. Scandal is more usefully permitted than truth abandoned, 1225. The mind of unbelievers endured a grave scandal when it saw Christ dying after so many miracles, 1454.

Crimes: how they differ from offenses, 386. Gnawing the schismatics in the wilderness: what this means, 645. There are no martyrs outside the unity of the Church, 573. In schism there is no charity, 574. The schism of the Corinthians, and how prudently it was dealt with by Paul, 1287. God is in unity, not in division of minds, 1532.

Knowledge without piety is harmful, 32. The devil often permits knowledge in order to corrupt life, 186. Why sluggishness of intellect is attributed to the diligent and keenness to the negligent, 187. Human knowledge is useful, 293. Those who display their knowledge are vain, 358. The foolish boasting of knowing what no one is ignorant of, 359. Those who are proud of their knowledge are called plunderers, 367. The Church more usefully strives not to know what it cannot investigate, 448. Our knowledge, compared with divine knowledge, is ignorance, 501. Knowledge is signified by water, 547. Higher knowledge must be concealed from weak minds, 548. Some, because of their knowledge, become more liable to punishment, 565. Sacred knowledge is indicated by water, [Col. 1488] 607. Moderation must be observed in knowledge, 644. Knowledge of the sacred pages makes us more obligated to act, 701. Regarding the gift of understanding entrusted to them, the righteous fear more than they rejoice, ibid. The effects of true knowledge, 746. We must not imitate the arrogant in knowledge, 853. What knowledge is perfect, 882. How obscure our knowledge is, ibid. Knowledge adds labor, 1280. The difference between wisdom and knowledge, 1363. Wisdom pertains to life, knowledge to doctrine, 1364. The gift of knowledge without the gift of fortitude is useless, 1381. Knowledge is a virtue, 1459. Humility is the guardian of knowledge, ibid. Whoever labors to know, not to practice what he knows, remains fasting from his own knowledge, 1654.

For God to know is to approve, 373, 810, 897. For God to know is to make us know, 610, 683, 898. Rush signifies the life of a hypocrite, 273, 278, 281, 284. Who are called scorpions in the moral sense, 1258.

The sacred writers compared with a river, 4. The Holy Spirit speaks through the sacred writer of what belongs to the Spirit; and the writer himself writes what belongs to God within himself as though about another, 8. The sacred writer is the pen with which the sacred books were written by the Holy Spirit, 7. The writers’ custom in describing brave men, 19. Christ held the pen in his hand, moving the sacred writers, 13, 15. Why the pen is called a measure, ibid., 1316, 1323. Sacred Scripture is called a river in which the lamb may walk and the elephant swim, 6, 1213. It is called sometimes food and sometimes drink, 26, 1263. It is also called a mirror, 37. Harvest and riches, 183. The understanding of sacred Scripture is called bread, 474. Sacred Scripture is called a flying scroll, twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide, 475. It is also called a field and a vineyard, 524. The table set by the Lord, 551. Also a lamp, 612, 1230. Sacred Scripture is the bow of the Church, 633. Also the refreshment of bread, 756. The lofty meanings of sacred Scripture are called mountains of pasture, 985. Sacred Scripture is called a manger, 997. It is the rule of conduct, 1323. Knowledge of Scripture is signified by the name of a gate, 1329, 1353. The neck of the Church is the sacred utterances, 1337. Scripture is called a tower from which a thousand shields hang, 1339.

The apostolic see uses the new and the old translation of Scripture without distinction, 6. The Holy Spirit is the author of sacred Scripture, and the sacred writer is the pen, 7. The inspiration of sacred Scripture, 8. The Vulgate translation derived from the Hebrew and Arabic languages, 110. The use of the ancient translation, 239, 244. Saint Gregory does not seem to have counted the First Book of Maccabees among the canonical books, 622. The new translation of Scripture, made from Hebrew and Arabic, is preferred to the old, 665. How many letters of Saint Paul there are, 1166. The Old Testament was given to the Jews, the New—more excellent—to Christians, 1216. There are two translations of Scripture; the second is more truthful, 1265. The authority of both Testaments established, 1277. Sacred Scripture divided into four parts, 1217. The Old Testament is distinguished into the Law and the Prophets; the New into the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the sayings, ibid.

The meaning of sacred Scripture is manifold, 4. It is obscure and difficult, 5, 1205, 1260. In expounding sacred Scriptures, the art of speaking is to be disregarded, 6. Sacred Scripture describes things accurately, 37. Whoever investigates the spiritual meaning of Scripture must not depart from the historical meaning, 38. It expresses the qualities of causes in four ways, ibid. Sacred Scripture gradually leads us, accustomed as we are to temporal things, toward eternal things, 52. In sacred Scripture, using the whole for the part or the part for the whole is frequent, 82, 1548. In sacred Scripture, things rightly done sometimes signify things wrongly to be done, and conversely, 94. The letter of Scripture sometimes contradicts itself, 101. At such a time not the text but the meaning must be considered, ibid. Understanding sacred Scripture is acquired through humility and constant reading, ibid. It is the custom of sacred Scripture that, whenever it inserts something foreign, it soon returns to the subject under discussion, 173. Often a dull person understands through diligent study of Scripture what an ingenious person fails to understand through negligence, 186. By what way one reaches an understanding of Scripture, ibid. Why sacred Scripture uses the words of the world’s wise men, 293. Certain words of sacred Scripture seem wrong because their inner meaning is not understood, 449. We dig wells when we penetrate the depths of sacred Scripture, 509. Those who discern the multiple meanings in Scripture overflow with delights, ibid. God’s words must be hidden in the bosom, 518. What it means to adulterate the word of God, 529. The obscurity of sacred Scripture moves us to investigate its higher meaning, 557. Heretics who do violence to the force of sacred Scripture are to be struck by God, 565. Those who read Scripture for questioning rather than nourishment fast from knowledge of the truth, ibid. The books of Scripture are for us certain veins of silver, 573. The sayings of the Old Testament are obscure, 583. Sacred Scripture is to be preferred by far to other books, 635. Its excellence, ibid. Heretics do not eat the marrow of sacred Scripture but gnaw its bark, 645. Those who, when reading sacred Scripture, do not seek the love of God and neighbor feed on grass and bark, ibid. To understand much in the sacred writings is dangerous unless what is understood is guarded, 700. Sacred Scripture must be carried on the shoulder through action, 720. In sacred Scripture God teaches whatever it is proper for us to know, 747. In sacred Scripture we find the causes of our affairs, ibid. Sacred Scripture is a book in which lamentation, song, and woe are written, 823. How heresies arise from reading sacred Scripture, 945. Sacred Scripture tempers its threats so that we are neither found terrified into despair nor carelessly secure, 1084. Sacred Scripture sometimes uses the past for the future, and conversely, 1121. Repetition of a statement in the sacred writings is an argument for its unchangeability, 1151. The letter of sacred Scripture reports past things and foretells future things, 1161. With how much discernment sacred Scripture should be read, 1193. In it we must seek sometimes the letter, sometimes the spirit, ibid. The commendation of sacred Scripture, 1205. The usefulness of the obscurity of sacred Scripture, 1213, 1274. Sacred Scripture is like a wheel: it rises and descends, 1213. For little ones it is enough to believe the Gospel, whose mysteries the perfect humbly investigate, 1215. Scripture builds up in every respect, ibid. Especially in what it teaches about Christ, his members, the apostles, and the martyrs, 1216. The four faces of the wheel signify sacred Scripture, distinguished into four parts through the two Testaments, 1217. The divine utterances, although divided by times, are united in meaning, 1218. Scripture is straight in its commandments, lofty in its promises, terrible in its threats, 1220, 1223. Sacred Scripture is obscure unless it is illumined by supreme truth, 1230. How obscure the beginning of Ezekiel’s prophecy is, 1249. The book of sacred Scripture is closed and wrapped up, 1260. It is opened and unrolled by God’s hand, ibid. Everything that builds up and instructs is contained in this volume, 1264. We must awaken to the words of sacred Scripture, ibid. Sacred Scripture speaks to great and small, 1263. Whatever is found in it must be eaten, ibid. Sacred Scripture is food in obscure passages and drink in clearer ones, 1264. In Scripture, causes are often signified by things and places, 1281. From the circumstances of times and places, sacred Scripture designates things, 1293. The letter is the root of the spiritual fruits of sacred Scripture, 1309. The usefulness of sacred reading, 1319. We ought to flee for refuge to the defenses of sacred Scripture, 1338. Why sacred Scripture is called a tower built with fortifications, 1340. Heaven is stretched out like a skin when sacred Scripture is explained, 1353. From what we understand, let us take care to progress in charity, 1354. The use of sacred speech is to keep silent about what is certain and express what might be doubted, 1385. The obscurity of Ezekiel’s prophecy with respect to its literal meaning, 1402. The literal meaning of Scripture must precede the spiritual, 1417. Evangelical history contains many mysteries, 1530. Holy Scripture both moves us to tears and consoles us, 1547. In sacred Scripture, the truth of the history must first be established; afterward the allegorical meaning is to be sought, 1652.

Sacred Scripture: with what profit it should be read, 28. It promises the Redeemer of the world in its entirety, 181. Spiritual meanings proceeding from the root of history, 182. How the utterances of God are said to be eaten and drunk, 183. The words of sacred speech are the riches of the mind, 186. The sacred utterances are for condemnation to those who do not wish to know them or who, knowing them, despise them, 475. When God has driven away evil spirits, he enriches us with the silver of the divine utterance, 509. God’s will must be sought in the Scriptures, 517. The streams of oil poured out in the Church are the books of the evangelists, 616. The bow in the hand is sacred Scripture in action, 634. In explaining sacred Scriptures, neither the historical meaning alone nor the allegorical meaning must always be followed, 675. The more the divine word is worn down, the more its power increases, 926. Christ feeds tamed rhinoceroses with the nourishment of sacred Scripture, 997. Sacred Scripture is like the sea, 1218. Through the wood of the cross we are carried across this sea to our heavenly homeland, ibid. The ways of sacred Scripture to human hearts, 1219. What the stature, height, and aspect of sacred Scripture are, 1220. Unless we advance to higher things by reading Scripture, it lies for us as though in the depths below, 1226. The divine utterances are raised to whatever height the spirit of the reader tends, ibid. A manifold meaning lies hidden in the same Scripture, 1227. Holy Scripture sows in us spiritual life and the seeds of various virtues, 1228. Sacred reading is such for us as we are toward it, 1230. Sacred Scripture teaches love of God and neighbor, ibid., 1268. Sacred Scripture is a lamp for our feet, ibid. Sacred Scripture is a book written within and without, 1260. It is written within through allegory, without through history and moral precepts, 1261. Sacred Scripture is compared with heaven, ibid. The strong are satisfied with loftier statements, the little ones with clearer ones, ibid. Sacred Scripture should be read in such a way that it benefits both us and others, 1264. God feeds us with it, 1265. It is not within our strength to take this food, ibid. In sacred reading we are fasting unless God fills the inward parts of our mind, 1266. He eats and is not satisfied who, while hearing the words of God, desires worldly things, ibid. Those who grow fat on the food of sacred doctrine feed others gently, 1267. God speaks throughout all Scripture in order to draw us to love of himself and of our neighbor, [Col. 1490] 1268. Sacred Scripture is understood in the lives of the saints, 1277. In the Scriptures, things that lack truth according to the letter are to be understood allegorically, 1309. A spiritual meaning must be added to sacred history, ibid. Sacred Scripture is the measuring pen by which we should measure ourselves, 1316, 1323. Sacred Scripture has a twofold threshold: outwardly, the letter; inwardly, allegory, 1337. By what it presents—commands and examples—it arms us, ibid. Sacred Scripture is difficult to understand, 1353. It is open so as to feed little ones; so as to exercise the strong, it is veiled, ibid. Certain things in it are open only to the citizens of heaven, ibid., 1354. For the testing of humility, 1355. What discernment is needed in reading the sacred Scriptures, 1375. Sacred Scripture is like squared stones, 1407. The wonderful meanings of sacred Scripture, 1417. Sacred Scripture is like flint, from which fire is struck even though it is cold, ibid. Saint Gregory passes quickly over the literal meaning of Scripture in order to linger over the mystical meanings, 1418. Christ himself taught us to interpret sacred Scripture figuratively, 1488.

What the cups of the lampstand signify, 1216. What is signified in Scripture by the name of shields, 1105. That the Lord burns the shields with fire, ibid. Why cast shields signify the wicked, ibid. The retreat of the mind is opened to one who restrains outward wandering, 974. The senses of the flesh are not sufficient to penetrate the secrets of majesty, 298. The secrets of God must not be scrutinized, 311, 953. Our good works perish if they are disclosed too quickly, 280.

The ax placed at the root of the tree: how it signifies our Redeemer, 1520. Why it is said to be placed not at the branches but at the root, ibid. Security must be avoided in good works, 32, 68. There is no security from sin in this life, 137, 252, 638. The mind of the righteous trembles in order to be secure, 319, 520. The hardened soul is more secure the worse it is, 328. The difference between the security of the good and that of the wicked, 409. The remarkable security of hearts free from desire for earthly things, 714. Careless security is a grave danger, 638. Security of heart never exempts one from the discipline of watchfulness, 715. Security is the mother of negligence, 772. There is no security of salvation in this life, 932. The security of sinners is to be feared, 1273.

Zedekiah, deprived of his eyes after seeing the slaughter of his sons: what this signifies, 229. Sitting belongs to one who rests, 70. Sitting in dust: what it means, 192. Sitting on the ground: what it means, ibid. Sitting signifies the humility of repentance, 988. Sitting belongs to one who judges, 1572. Who Christ is that sits in heaven and at the same time stands, ibid. The fruit of Christ’s sitting in our heart, 639.

Seed signifies the word of God, 744, 999, 1488. The word of preaching is seed in the heart of the hearer, 1194. The production of seeds compared with the generation of virtues, 945. How great a harvest the seed of preaching produces, 1194. Seed signifies a good intention, 1330. What and how much lies hidden in a tiny seed is afterward to be explained, 1559. To sow upon all waters: what this means, 607, 685, 999, 1161. Those who sow much and bring in little, 1266.

A path: how it differs from a way, and what both signify, 388, 1015. A path is taken for an action, 931. To consider the paths of one’s house: what this means, 1167. What it means that we do not find our paths, 1624.

What the number six signifies, 201, 1196, 1355, 1358. Six is the first perfect number, 1162, 1355, 1358. Why six is a perfect number, [Col. 1491] 1162. What the number eighteen, formed from six, signifies, 1584. Sacred Scripture counts the old by their conduct, not by their years, 618. To grow old into the abyss: what this means, 1152. What the weakness of old age is, 1439. The very health of the old is sickness, ibid. The ninth hour signifies old age, 1512. In Greek, the very old are called presbyters, ibid.

Shinar: what it signifies, 462. Confusion is built in its valley, ibid.

The meaning of Scripture is manifold, 4. See Sacred Scripture.

It is the senses, not sex, that are at fault, 80. The outward senses must be restrained lest the mind unlawfully desire, 678. The senses are the windows of the mind, ibid. One ought not to look upon what one is not permitted to desire, 679. Whoever uses the outward eye negligently is justly blinded in the inward eye, 685. The internal senses are signified in Scripture by the name of teeth, 382. The common sense is the sense of the brain, the judge of the five senses and the discerner of sensations, 369. “Judgment” is derived from “sense,” 746. The Shepherd’s judgment, even when unjust, is to be feared, 1556.

To separate the precious from the vile: what this means, 1097. The grave signifies divine contemplation, in which the mind, dead to the world, rests, 142. The grave signifies sometimes the contemplative life, sometimes the active life, 206. It also signifies eternal rest, 210. The hearts of the reprobate are signified by graves, 498. The dead formerly buried with riches, 143. We find the riches of the mind among the dead, ibid.

The whole of time unfolds in seven days, 1341. Those who give a portion to seven and also to eight, 1150, 1151, 1342, 1391. The number seven signifies totality, 15, 93, 733, 1150, 1593. It is a perfect number, 22, 1149, 1162, 1543. What the number seven signifies in sacred Scripture, 1150, 1196, 1360. The number seven signifies eternal rest, 201, 1150. It also signifies the form of perfection, 22, 1162, 1543. It also signifies the contemplative life, 1196. The seventh day was given to human beings for rest, 22. Why, 1150.

“Seraphim” is interpreted as “burning,” 1247. It signifies “burning” or “setting on fire,” 1606. They burn more intensely the nearer they see God, ibid. Those in the Church who burn with love and kindle others by speaking may rightly be called Seraphim, 1607. “Seraphim” is sometimes said not from nature or rank but from office, 1608. Seraphim are so called because of their greater ardor of love; others also burn, ibid.

To sow signifies to preach, 685. Speech should be neither hasty nor indiscreet after the proper silence, 82. Some conceive wicked words and utter them; others restrain what they have conceived; others conceive nothing, 151. Multiplicity of speech reveals poverty of heart, 271. The circumstances of speech must be considered, 784. The word of God is distributed for various ends, 993. The word of doctrine is sometimes withheld, sometimes given by God, 1298. The passing word of God expresses abiding judgments, 1438. See Preaching; Word of God.

To watch the serpent’s head: what this means, 36. The serpent is not questioned about guilt when repentance was not sought, 1106. Who take up the faithful serpents, 1571. The dove’s simplicity should temper the serpent’s cunning, 1578. [Col. 1491]

To preserve: how the devil is said to do this, 76. To serve God: what this means, 1196. How the elect are called servants, 247. Christians are servants to one another, 725. Servants on horses: what they signify, 1015. How servants were made among the Hebrews, 1196. A servant who freely obtained liberty, and his garment: what they signify, ibid. The wife of a departing servant: what she signifies, ibid. What it means to give one’s servant a wife, 1197. The servant who loves his master and therefore does not wish to go out free: what he signifies, ibid. The useless servant calls his master harsh, 1465. Whom the wicked servant signifies in the Church, ibid. The vain excuse and punishment of the idle servant, ibid. Whoever hastens to gird himself for God’s service should prepare himself for temptation, 120, 772, 1302. Free service exalted the first angel; enslaved freedom cast him down, 1134.

Servolus, or Servulus, gave an example of patience, 1491. He took care that the alms he received should be distributed to the poor, ibid. He ordered the sacred Scriptures to be read to him, ibid. He prepared himself for death by the chanting of psalms, ibid. He gave his soul back to God amid the choirs of psalm-singing angels, ibid. With this blessed end he departed from life, having patiently endured the Lord’s chastisements throughout his life, ibid.

Severity must be mixed with kindness, 641. When severity is necessary, 1306. The ruler’s severity must inwardly be seasoned with charity and humility, ibid.

The meaning of the number sixty, 1358. Sixty cubits signify the perfection of good works, 1358. What it means to bring forth fruit sixtyfold, ibid. Solomon’s sixty mighty men signify all the perfect, 221.

Hissing: what it signifies, 572. “As” is sometimes taken in Scripture for likeness, sometimes for the truth of a thing, 561. Sidon: of what it is a figure, 9. Signs are given to unbelievers, prophecies to the faithful, 1468. See Miracles.

To seal God, or to heal offenses: what this means, 400. A seal signifies faith in sacred Scripture, 922. To have the seal restored as clay: what this means, ibid.

To be silent in heart: what this means, 146. One must remain silent unless one can benefit others by speaking, 716. How we know that we will benefit our hearers, ibid. Silence is often wisdom, 736. Some are silent proudly; they listen not to learn but to judge, 737. One must learn silence not by speaking but learn to speak by keeping silent, 1282. If the discipline of silence is absent, the whole mind lies open to the enemy, 240. The disadvantages of excessive silence, ibid. Silence of the mouth is harmful when accompanied by loquacity of the heart, ibid. The talkative person cannot be justified, 337. The usefulness of silence, ibid., 379, 1282. The half-hour of silence that occurred in heaven: what it signifies, 980. The discipline of silence is a kind of nourishment for the word, 1282. Something must be relaxed from the discipline of silence for the sake of the weaker, 1283. Silence is sometimes evil, sometimes good, 924, 980, 1254, 1260.

Flint signifies the hearts of the Gentiles, just as a sheet of lead signifies the hearts of the Jews, 460. What it means to give flint instead of earth, and golden streams instead of flint, 509. Flint: what it signifies, 1270.

The old Simeon, together with many Israelites, desired the time of the Incarnation, 215. With what love this old man was inflamed, 1422. Fine flour fried in a pan and sprinkled with oil: what it signifies, 1304. We shall be like God in heaven, 594, [Col. 1492] 1192. Who are like Christ, 1190, 1192.

Simon of Cyrene, carrying the Lord’s cross under compulsion, signifies hypocrites who fast, 277. Also arrogant abstainers, 1589. Simon carries the cross but does not die; those abstaining from the world live for it while afflicting the body, ibid. How dangerously Simon the Pharisee fell ill when he despised the sick Mary and her physician, 1594. He is condemned by his own mouth, 1595. That Simon signifies the Jewish people, ibid., 1596. Simon Magus joined himself to the pride of the Antichrist through his wicked desire for miracles, 923. Simon wished to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit, 1449. So that he might sell more wickedly what he had acquired wickedly, ibid.

The vice of simony: what it is, 1449. What is received freely must be given freely, ibid., 1502. The Holy Spirit, through the laying on of hands, is to be given for the merit of life, not for a reward, ibid. Various forms of simony, ibid. A grave rebuke of bishops concerning simony, 1502. Today there are those who sell doves in the temple of God, ibid., 1646. Simony is a heresy condemned by the sacred canons, 1502. Those who seek payment for the laying on of hands are deprived of the priesthood, ibid. Christ condemns those who sell and those who buy the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 1646.

Who should be called simple, 29. Simple in works, upright in faith, ibid. The simple, cleaving to the more perfect, are nourished by their understanding, 57. The gentleness of the simple is signified by the name of asses, 1161. What harmful simplicity is, 18. Simplicity is signified by the dove, ibid., 1578. For simplicity to be good, it must be joined to uprightness—that is, to prudence, ibid. Among hypocrites, simplicity is a crime, 284. The simplicity of the righteous is called foolishness by the hypocrite, ibid. Human simplicity vanishes when compared with divine purity, 306. The simplicity of the righteous is described, 360. Simplicity of heart is a most strongly fortified citadel, 409. Simplicity of conduct is to be learned from Isaac, 1338.

The image of a clever impostor, 840. He merits and provokes God’s anger, ibid. Having been struck, he is ashamed to confess his sins, ibid. No one but a person of subtler intelligence can pursue the falsity of pretense, ibid.

The sindon signifies the subtle interweaving of holy preaching, 1097. What sindon the Church made and sold, ibid.

Singularity must be avoided by those living piously, 203, 1045. The left hand of God: what it is, 54. The left signifies sadness and adversity, 1201. It also signifies the Gentiles, 659, and the present life, 1358, 1526. See Right hand.

The bosom in Scripture is often taken for the mind, 713. Abraham’s bosom is the place of hell in which the souls of the Fathers rested before Christ’s resurrection, 128, 397, 433, 668, 927, 1653. What is called the deepest hell, 435, 927. Rising again, the Lord made a way out of the prison, 927. Abraham’s bosom signifies the hidden rest of the Fathers, 1653.

Zion as a whole is the Church; and the sons of Zion are each and every one of the saints, 157, 1075. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” ibid., 1103, 1409. The holy preachers are called the gates of Zion, 1103.

To thirst: what this means for the wicked, 440. For the rich and powerful who lack offspring, their very power is a punishment, 486. The saints are joined by a division of graces, just as peoples are joined by a division of fruits, 1276.

God consumed Sodom with a rain of fire and sulfur, [Col. 1493] 444. Why God did not wish to judge Sodom before testing it on the basis of the crimes reported, 628. The Sodomites groping in vain for the door of Lot’s house signify the envious, 198. From the character of the vengeance God marked the stain of the Sodomites’ crime, 444.

The sun signifies preachers, 291. It also signifies the Lord, 1126, 1375; persecution, 1126; the manifestation of open vision, ibid.; and the understanding of the wise, 1127. The sun is sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one, 1375.

To build a solitude for oneself: what this means, 129. Who are the true solitary ones called “consuls,” 130. What the thoughts of solitary persons ought to be, 131. Those are solitary who, having come to know the truth, flee the laborious desires of the world, 133. Solitude signifies the abandonment of the good, 648. Solitary persons are signified by the name of free wild asses, 979. Solitude of heart and body: the latter is of no benefit without the former, 980. The remarkable insight of the righteous gathered within themselves, 1005.

The throne of God: what it is, 53, 513, 1326. Excessive anxiety over earthly matters overwhelms the mind through the weight of its thoughts, 67. How wicked minds are disposed toward temporal occupations, 147. How pious minds are disposed, ibid. Anxiety concerning temporal things is forbidden, 336. See Care.

Sleep is taken in Scripture in three ways, 162. The righteous too must rise from sleep—that is, from sin, 251. Six causes of dreams, 262. Dreams are not easily to be believed, ibid. Why the devil is permitted to affect the hearts of the saints through dreams, ibid. What a nocturnal dream in which someone is polluted signifies, 325. The sound of wings, of waters, and the lofty sound of God: what they signify, 1236. The sound of armies: what it signifies, 1239. The sound proceeding from the mouth of God: what it is, 868.

Zophar: what he signifies, 15, 91, 732.

A person is said to visit his own appearance by doing to another what he would wish another to do to him, 205. A handsome presbyter, 1659. A watchman is called one to whom the care of others is entrusted, 1282. The watchman should stand on high and look far ahead, 1283. Discernment is signified by the watchman’s nose, 1284. The watchman kills the one whom, by keeping silent, he has betrayed to death, 1285. To establish a watchtower for oneself: what this means, 1034.

Sacred Scripture is called the mirror of the mind, 37. What the mirrors of the women signify, from which Moses made the bronze basin, 1500.

When the mind ceases to hope for what is above it, it continually falls beneath itself, 192. What we see in uncertainty is what we hope for with certainty, 355. The righteous hopes in God all the more certainly the harsher the things he suffers for him, ibid. To despair of the Creator is to place hope in a creature, 698. Whoever does not fear justice hopes for mercy in vain, 1091, 1099. God gave commandments to human beings so that they would not sin, and remedies to those who sin so that they would not despair, 1551. Hope is sometimes weakened by fear, 69. Hope rises to dare greater things, 164. Hope raises the mind toward eternity, 197. Hope of delayed blessedness is the cause of groaning for the faithful, 218. Those who lose endurance, 233. Hope of reward lightens the burden of labor, 248. All the hope of the righteous is fixed on the author, 359, 698. The Church’s hope in adversity, strengthened by the resurrection of Christ, its head, 427. In adversity Christ alone is the hope of the righteous, 434. The righteous, pressed by fear, are lifted up by hope, 520. The hope of the saints tempered by fear, 638, 640, 798. To wish to solidify hope in passing things is to lay a foundation in flowing waters, 698. How weak hope is strengthened, 828. The hope of the righteous, which must be strengthened in tribulations, ibid. How great the hope of the penitent is, 867. Let fear accompany our hope rather than security, 932, 994, 1090. The hope of those who are perishing is the recovery of the lost, 1090. The hope of the world is dry, 1322. Hope of heavenly things makes the mind firm, 1360. The length of hope and the breadth of charity must be observed, 1377. We must strive toward eternal rest through the long endurance of hope, 1378. Hope of attaining heavenly glory is not without dread, 1382. How necessary hope is for sinners to repent, 1385.

The little sphere signifies preaching by its revolving motion, 1216. The little spheres pertain to labor, ibid.

To take away ears of grain from the hungry: what this means, 525. The ears of grain signify the judgments of the Fathers, ibid. To reach the ear of grain from the grass: what this means, 1330.

The thorn signifies sin, 646. Thorns signify the pricks of vices, 1081. What it means for the roads to be enclosed with thorns, 1117, 1624. Riches are thorns, 1488. Thorns signify men of spiritual doctrine, 1522. Flowers growing among thorns: what they signify, 1638.

The human spirit is understood in two ways, 368. Rational spirits were created first, 909. The body is nourished by food; the spirit by pious work, 1449. The Holy Spirit is signified by the dove, 18, 1578, 1579, 1646; by fire, 18, 1187, 1208, 1246, 1578; and by water, 395, 607. The Holy Spirit is called the mighty spirit, 168. The sound of God’s mouth, 869. The spirit of wisdom is mobile, 928. The finger of God, 1270. The Paraclete—that is, advocate and comforter, 1576.

Why the Holy Spirit wished to be seen in the form of a dove and of fire, 18, 893, 1187, 1208, 1246, 1578, 1598, 1646. How the Holy Spirit intercedes for the saints, 62, 1574. The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, 27. From the Father and the Son, 964, 1209, 1554. The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Son, always remains with him, 73. The speech of the Holy Spirit is called the hidden word, 160. It is perceived by few, ibid. This speech can be felt but not expressed, 161, 871. In how many ways the Holy Spirit addresses the mind, 161, 868. The irrigation of the Holy Spirit is signified by the name of water, 395, 607. The voice of the Holy Spirit, the gentle breeze, and the mighty spirit, 168, 869. The Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Son, comes to us through him, 869. Why he descended upon the disciples in tongues of fire, 893, 1577, 1578. Why the inward speech of the Holy Spirit is seen rather than heard, ibid. The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son and is coeternal with both, 964, 1209. The Holy Spirit is God, 1209. How the Holy Spirit is called stable and at the same time mobile, ibid. The Holy Spirit is signified by the bow, 1247. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, 1554. Why the Holy Spirit was first given by the Lord on earth and afterward sent from heaven, 1554, 1581. Those whom the outpouring of the Holy Spirit has anointed have sucked oil from the solid rock, 1554. What the effects of the infusion of the Holy Spirit are, 1555. The Holy Spirit is love, 1574. The Holy Spirit makes those whom he fills pray, ibid. How the Holy Spirit teaches us inwardly, 1576. One whose mind is not anointed by the spirit is not instructed by the voice, 1377. In what sense the Holy Spirit is said to suggest everything to us, ibid. As the Son is the Word, so the Holy Spirit is the tongue, [Col. 1494] 1578. Why the Holy Spirit sat upon Christ as a dove and upon the apostles as fire, 1579. How skilled an artisan the Holy Spirit is, 1580. To touch the mind alone is to teach it, ibid. The gift of the Holy Spirit is signified by the dove, 1646.

The Holy Spirit speaks through the sacred writers, 7. The Holy Spirit cleansed the apostles, 27. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by Job’s seven sons, 29. What it means to make a banquet of the gifts of the Holy Spirit on their day, 31. The connection of these gifts, 32. Faith, hope, and charity must be invited to this banquet, ibid. The virtues of the Holy Spirit must be purified by the holocaust of prayer, 33. The gifts of God are sometimes usefully withdrawn, 72, 1209. Why the Holy Spirit is said always to remain in the disciples, 73, 1209. The Holy Spirit is almost fixed in the soul through mortification, yet is not held for long, 166. It is a gift of God to use God’s chastisements well, 188. Those who abuse God’s gifts to the destruction of their own salvation, 273, 297. Whoever is lifted up by God’s gifts loses them, 289. Why the Fathers of the Old Testament brought forth for us the fruit of the Spirit while it was covered, 309. What a human being can do with the help of the Holy Spirit, 323. How diverse are the gifts of one wisdom, 369. Diverse gifts of wisdom are signified by waters, 371. They are called streams of a river, 476. When the grace of the Holy Spirit pours into us, it fills us with honey and butter, 477. The gift of the Holy Spirit is signified by the name of a pledge, 502. Streams of oil are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 617. The wise distribution of gifts, 903. Each gift belongs to all, so that through the bond of charity all belong to each, 904, 935.

What are called the splendor of fire and the lightning proceeding from fire
Holy Spirit, 1209. The Holy Spirit always remains with respect to certain virtues, but not with respect to others, ibid. In accordance with the gratuitously given graces, the Holy Spirit is sometimes present to the elect and sometimes not, ibid. Why the Holy Spirit is said to move among the perfect, 1210. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified by the fingers of God, 1270. By the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or by as many degrees, one must ascend to the spiritual life, 1380. The order and interconnection of the gifts, ibid. One ascends to these gifts through humility, 1381. And through faith, ibid. The gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated, 1579.

—The gifts of the Holy Spirit instruct our mind against temptations, 68. Certain gifts of the Holy Spirit are necessary for salvation, 73. Certain others are for the benefit of others, ibid. The Holy Spirit kindles heavenly desires, 161. What the Holy Spirit does in us, 168, 1576. The grace of the Holy Spirit, illuminating minds, moderates the temptations of the devil, 937. The sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit supplies the operation not only of the three theological virtues but also of the four cardinal virtues, 1150. The Spirit of life touches the mind of the reader in diverse ways and orders, 1228. Some are raised up by the spirit of prophecy, though they are nevertheless taken up, 1279. Through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, access to heavenly life is opened to us, 1380. All whom the Holy Spirit fills, he makes simple and ardent, 1578. The Holy Spirit is present to the prophets at one time and absent at another, 72, 246, 1180. Nor is he always present in the same way, 1176. The effects of the Holy Spirit’s presence, 869. The coming of the Holy Spirit, 893. The Spirit of Christ: in whom he is not present, 1545.

—The spirit of man is the spirit of exaltation, 214. The spirit of man is understood in two ways, 368. The more the power of the Spirit of God grows in us, the more our own spirit declines, 720. What are the impulses of the spirit against the flesh, 1206. The impulse of the flesh disguises itself under the appearance of a spiritual impulse, 1207.

—The good spirit. See Angel.

—The evil spirit of the Lord: what it is, 45, 558. The day is turned into darkness when the prosperity promised by the evil spirit is understood as adversity, 107. Evil spirits are called terrifying, 481. We suffer no enemies more than evil spirits, 509. See Devil, Demon, Satan.

Spiritual nature is not composed of soul and body, 41. The labor of the carnal is heavy, that of the spiritual is none, 188. Those who furnish earthly support to spiritual persons are called “the asses of the fatherless,” 523. The reprobate, covered with scales, resist the arrows of truth, 1106. Hardness of heart is signified by scales, ibid. What “scale joined to scale” signifies, 1108.

To stand: what it is, 38. To stand is to act rightly, 881, 1220, 1294. To stand is to persist in sin, 922. Not even a prophet is able to stand before God, 1294. Unless God raises him up, ibid. We stand where we fix our eyes, 1318. To stand belongs to one who is fighting, 1572. Christ was seen by Stephen standing, ibid. What God’s standing signifies, 167, 605. By the name “Stator” the Mediator between God and human beings is designated, 683. We cannot have a fixed state here, 391.

Stars signify the righteous, 13, 111. And hypocrites, ibid. And preachers, 291. What it means to shut up the stars under a seal, 291. What the stars of rain are, 857. What it means for stars to fall from heaven to earth, 1060. What the stellio, which holds the royal building by clinging with its hands, signifies, 186.

The steadfastness of the martyr Stephen in reproving, 237, 1229, 1370. Stephen’s humility generates love for those whom, out of zeal for truth, he rebukes, 237. Those whom he had not drawn by preaching, Stephen mourned for by loving, 676. While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed for his persecutors, ibid. How greatly he loved those whom he rebuked harshly, 1370. The remarkable union of zeal and gentleness in Saint Stephen, 1371. The remarkable patience of Abbot Stephen, 1616. Stephen’s blessed death, 1617.

The basket of dung: what it signifies, 1584. What it means for beasts to rot in their own dung, ibid. What it means to feed the sterile one, 535.

Sneezing: where it comes from, 1109. The sneezing of Leviathan signifies the final persecution of Antichrist, ibid.

The dung-heap: what it signifies, 76. What Job thought about himself on his dung-heap, ibid. What Job signifies on the dung-heap, 87. What it means to sit on a dung-heap, 97. Hypocrites are compared to a dung-heap, 471.

Drops of dew: what they are, 942. A human being is compared to dry straw and a leaf, 387. The Stoics’ apatheia, or freedom from passion, is rejected, 49.

The first robe is innocence, 396. What the single and double robes of the saints signify, 1153.

The ostrich signifies hypocrisy, 228, 673, 1000. And the synagogue, 1013. What it means for the ostrich to leave its eggs on the earth, 1002, 1013. Description of the ostrich, ibid. What the wings of the ostrich signify, 1008, 1013. What it means for the ostrich to mock the horseman and his mount, 1008, 1014.

The wisdom of the righteous is called folly and is mocked by the world, 360. Silence is useful for concealing folly, 379. What the folly of the word of God is, 456, 656, 952. How great is the folly of a human being who prefers his own wisdom to divine wisdom, 545. The folly of those who rejoice in small things and lose greater ones, 587. Folly is of two kinds: one noble, the other ignoble, 655. A praiseworthy foolishness is to be pursued, 890. Through the folly of the flesh, Christ corrects the folly of the world, 952. The first folly of the angel was exaltation of heart, 897. What the mind of fools is like when they are fools for God’s sake and oppressed, 235. What sort of end belongs to fools, 373. Correction is necessary for fools, 379. Fools judge others’ matters the more severely the more deeply they are ignorant of their own, 380. The memory of fools is compared to ash scattered by the breeze, 381. Two kinds of fools, 655. Those are fools and ignoble whom God declares that he does not know, 656. What it means for a fool to serve the wise, 661.

Style is often changed in a lengthy work, 365. An iron stylus signifies the strong sentence of God, 460.

Subjects should beware of condemning actions undertaken by prelates in the administration of their office, 149, 1556. At least through human fear, subjects should fear to sin when they do not fear divine judgments, 690. Subjects ought not to murmur against their superiors, 728. Rulers are given according to the character of their subjects, 807. David’s subjects, when he sinned, underwent vengeance on his behalf, ibid. Subjects should not rashly judge the life of their rulers, ibid. The vices of subjects that teachers either conceal from judgment or are unable to judge are reserved for divine judgment, 808. Subjects should tolerate prelates, even bad ones, if they can do so without endangering the faith, ibid. Subjects think they could act better if it happened that they were placed in authority, ibid. Subjects should hold to the way of uprightness and humility toward prelates, ibid. How much we owe to those who free us from the care of temporal matters by devoting themselves to those matters, 809. Subjects, generally following the example of wicked prelates, go astray in unbelief, 810. What is suggested to subjects through pride, 1139. Often, while subjects grow proud against their ruler, they also swell up against the judgments of God, ibid. Some, though accustomed to speaking wrongly, when corrected keep silence still more badly, ibid. Subjects are led to humility, 1140. Subjects should flee human fear disguised as humility, 1254. The sin of a subject is reckoned as the fault of the superior if the superior remains silent, 1285. Subjects should fear the sentence of the pastor, even when unjustly pronounced, 1556.

The oppressed, subjected to proud masters, cry out to God against them, 804. Whoever is disgusted with being subject to superiors imitates the devil, 924. Whatever could pass away was sudden, 488. For a human being, whatever he could not previously have imagined is sudden, 787. What it means to drink mockery as water, 779.

What things are said to be overturned in us by God, 347. The mind, overturned beneficially through the operation of grace, 372. Subverters act so that they alone may not perish, 1257. Subverters rejoice in their own depravity and exult in that of others, 1258. Why subverters are called scorpions, 1258. They are unbelieving toward God, subverters to the weak, and scorpions to the strong, 1258.

What the piercing of a servant’s ear with an awl by his master signifies, 1197. What the sudarium, separated from the linen cloths in the Lord’s tomb, signifies, 1532. Why it was found rolled up, ibid. Why it was in one place, ibid. The sudarium expresses the labor of God, who labors from our infirmity, 1532.

The stakes, or pales, by which the pointed counsels of the saints are signified, 1085. And the pointed words of the incarnate Wisdom himself, 1086.

What it means to suggest, 1577. How suggestion takes place, 123. The devil’s first suggestion is tender and easily crushed; afterward, however, its strength becomes intolerable, 1064. How the devil’s suggestion differs from his counsels, 1067.

Suhi is interpreted as “speaking,” 92. “Suhites” is said to derive from heat and loquacity; such are heretics, ibid.

What the furrows signify, 725. What it means to mourn over furrows, ibid. Sulfur signifies the sin of the flesh, 444.

No one reaches the summit suddenly, 1329.

Pride is the beginning of heresy, 91. How pride torments a human being, 129. The devil lays waste and crushes one who exalts himself over his virtues, 220. Pride generates hatred, 237. It is great pride to seek an explanation for divine judgments, 298. Thus a person lifted up by virtue is allowed to fall, so that he may be healed of pride, 327, 348. Pride is commonly signified by the neck, 372. The pride of human beings ends in corruption, 381. A fat neck is wealthy pride, 411. Pride is the firstborn of death, which the rich can scarcely avoid, 442. Pride and vainglory are two principal vices, 461. What belongs properly to pride and vainglory, ibid. Avarice is strengthened by these, 462. Pride arises from an abundance of possessions, 494. Pride of heart is like a certain fatness of thickness, ibid. Pride destroys every virtue, 511. Pride’s first manifestation is usually in the eyes, 511, 1137. Pride must be avoided above all, 622. Four kinds of pride, 736. The Lord restrains the movement of exaltation in the disciples, 737. Whoever claims the good for himself alone comes closer to the likeness of the devil, ibid. Wherever the vice of pride is understood to have arisen, it must be uprooted, 784. The more we suffer from the vice of pride, the less we see it, ibid. A remedy against pride, ibid., 1140, 1141. Pride is the seedbed of lust, 823, 1138. The mind must be guarded from pride with every care, 824. Pride is close to the powerful, 835. Pride is restrained by contemplation of divine judgments, 935. The punishment of pride is hardening, 944. Pride is the leader of the devil’s army, 1035. Pride is the queen of vices, ibid. The seven principal vices are the offspring of pride, ibid., 1077. Pride is the root of every evil, ibid., 1137. The place of the wicked is pride, 1053. Corruption of the flesh commonly follows the spirit of pride, 1058. Many fall into pride through works and gifts of virtue, 1092. Pride is a greater vice than lust, ibid. Pride is signified by the neck, 1116. Pride displays itself through the eyes, as through certain windows, 1137. Pride cast down the apostate angel, ibid. The devil is called king over all the sons of pride, 551, 833, 924, 1137. Pride attacks not merely one virtue and the other vices, but all virtues, 1138. How many are the devastations of pride in the soul, ibid. Ruin follows pride, ibid. One kind of pride arises from secular things, another from spiritual things, ibid. Pride arises from spiritual things, ibid. Pride tempts prelates in one way and subjects in another, 1139. The effects of pride, ibid. Pride is the clearest sign of rejection, 1142. Pride often oversteps itself in words and desires to appear as the freedom of purity, 1223. Freedom and pride must always be distinguished, 1254. Pride disguises itself under authority, ibid. Pride cannot exist without envy and vainglory, 1303. Pride says: “It is shameful to remain silent after receiving an injury,” 1509. Our pride is rebuked by the story of the Centurion, 1567. Our pride, which weighs the circumstances surrounding people but not the people themselves, ibid.

He is proud who does not abandon sin if he is permitted not to be punished, 124. The elect sometimes grow proud of their actions, 408. To grow proud against nature is wrong, 690. To grow proud against the Creator is to transgress his commandments by sinning, 753. Let no one grow proud of his learning or mock one less learned, 994. While they seek higher things in pride, they are thrust back to lower things, 1053.

The condition of the proud, 97, 226, 227. The proud are likened to Lucifer, 97. The proud glory in good actions, 157. The life and end of the proud, 381. The glory of the proud is compared to mud and ash, ibid. The proud are not enriched by virtues, 413. The proud have no root in this world, ibid. The tongue of the proud is accursed, 413. The proud person will perish before his days are fulfilled, 414. For proud minds, the burden of the teaching of humility is heavy, 485. The diversity among the proud, 495. The labor of the proud, 546. The proud attribute to themselves whatever they know, 564. When corrected, the proud do not listen or pretend not to hear, 738. The proud assert that they are full of the Holy Spirit, 740. The proud cannot properly express what they rightly think, 742. By frequently rebuking others, the proud often lie, 746, 781. The proud grow dim through seeing too much and become blind, 784. The proud despise the deeds of the Lord’s humility, 804. The proud do not wish to understand the ways of God, ibid. Humility is lofty to proud minds, 811. The proud do not know how to sympathize with the afflicted, 814, 852. Immense loquacity belongs to the proud, 817. The proud either speak falsely or, if they speak truth, speak what is inappropriate, 818. The exaltation of the proud commonly becomes an occasion of virtue for righteous men, 830. The vices of the proud are loquacity and impatience in listening, ibid. The proud measure their doctrine by their abundance of speech, ibid. While displaying themselves, the proud pretend to speak for God, ibid.

—The proud person is tormented by a crowd of tumultuous fantasies in the soul, 129. What it means for a proud person to stretch out his hands to God, 350. The higher the proud rise through understanding, the more heavily they fall through exaltation, 407. Every proud person exercises tyranny, 408. The proud stand without a root and are immediately laid low by a light breeze, 412. Because the reins of his tongue have been loosened, the proud person is to be tormented most severely, 413. Angels and human beings who are proud are enveloped in an abyss of ignorance, 546. Each person is as much more contemptible to God as he is more precious to himself, 583. For the proud, feigned humility is an unbearable burden, 811. Seeing the wicked strictly corrected by the Church while the innocent are unjustly afflicted, the proud complain, 845. The proud do not know how to observe measure in reproving, 852. The light of truth is hidden from the proud, 863. The vices of the proud are indicated, 864. While persecuting the light of truth, the proud have lost it, 865. Those who think rightly but speak proudly are rejected, 897. The heights of the mountains are the exaltations of the proud, 992. Let no one become exalted over what he has received, 994. The guilt of the proud is turned into punishment for them, 1033. By what he is raised up, by that he is cast down, ibid. God permits the hearts of the proud to be oppressed by earthly affairs and desires, ibid. The proud serve the devil more familiarly, 1075. The proud are called mountains, 1076. By doing evil, the exalted nourish demons, ibid. The proud person despises God’s vengeance, 1125. The proud set the life and merit of everyone else below themselves, 1135. Why the proud despise the works of others and always marvel at their own, 1138. What the proud build grows only toward ruin, 1140. The image of the proud person, ibid. The humble God teaches that a human being should not be proud, ibid. Many authorities against the proud, 1141. The proud are signified by the names of mountains and hills, 1517.

Surplus possessions should be distributed to the poor, 1596. Surplus is signified by hair, ibid.

God removes the deafness of the soul through an inner voice, 872. What Christ’s rising signifies, 60. To rise belongs to one who is fighting, 70. What it means to rise before the light, 281. We cannot rise without God, 1249.

What it means for an afflicted soul to choose hanging, 263. The deceitful person suspects deceit in everyone, 441. A robber suspects another of being a thief, 479. The whispering of a hidden word is the utterance of an inner breathing, 161. The veins of whispering are the origin of that utterance, ibid. What it means for God to whisper to us, ibid.

Sycamore is interpreted as “foolish fig tree,” 890. What it means to climb a sycamore, ibid. The Lord is seen passing by the sycamore, ibid. The synagogue is signified by the ostrich, 1013. See Jewish synagogue.

T

The Tabernacle: the wicked pitch it in this life, 286. What the tabernacles of the wicked are, 446, 482. One tabernacle is of the body, another of the heart, 508. The tabernacle signifies the dwelling-place of the mind, 613. Who are the tabernacle of God, 614. The house is for dwelling, the tabernacle for traveling, 987. In the construction of the tabernacle: what the bronze pegs and the columns signify, 1336. The tabernacle constructed by Moses is a figure of the Church, ibid. The women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle: what they signify, 1501.

To be silent is sometimes a sin, 80, 1254, 1499. How useful it is to be silent, 379. The saints sometimes keep silence beneficially, 716. What it means to deny Christ by keeping silent, 924. To be silent before speaking, 1282. See *Silere*, *Silentium*.

The torch: what it mystically signifies, 1110. The ankle-length tunic is a completed action, 38. The talent of lead: what it signifies, 461. A talent badly preserved is demanded under punishment, 1455. Talents are distributed to servants and are to be increased through profit, 1464. What the five, two, and one talents signify, ibid. Who knows the use of each person’s talent, ibid. What it means to hide a talent, ibid. A strict account will be demanded of the talents received, ibid. The justice of the Judge, who gives more to the one who has more, 465. The one who received two talents had more than the one who received five, 1466. To the one who ministers well, inner understanding is granted, ibid. No one is exempt from rendering an account for the talent received, 1466. How each person may progress by using his own talent, 1467. The Judge will soon return to demand an account from each person of the talents distributed to him, ibid.

The letter tau: what it signifies, 990. The bull is a symbol of pride, 16, 228. What offering bulls and rams in sacrifice signifies, 1149. Why bulls signify the Fathers of the Old Testament, 1636. Who the slaughtered bulls and fattened animals are, ibid.

The web represents human life, 253. How temperance withers in us, 68. What temperance is, 1427.

By the name of storm the whirlwind of divine judgment is designated, 569, 696. The cares of this life are compared with storms, 695. What it means to be heard in the hiding-place of the storm, 822.

He builds the temple of God who devotes himself to forming the minds of his neighbors, 239. The faithful people are the temple of God, 1427. What it means to measure the structure of the temple, 768. The building of the temple—that is, the house of God—is explained as existing either on earth or in heaven, 1126. The temple of God is the same as his throne: he dwells where he sits, 1326. The priests who guard the temple of God, 1423. Christ casts the sellers and buyers out of the temple, 1646. How the house of prayer becomes a den of thieves, ibid., 1648. The minds of the faithful ought to be houses of prayer, ibid. What Christ teaches in these temples, ibid.

The condition of time is that it has no fixed permanence, 101. The time of our mutability will one day wholly perish, 106. What it means to redeem the time, 172. The moments of time follow as they flee, 225, 234, 253. From past things we learn how quickly future things will pass, 272. For one who considers eternal things, everything that passes—whether evil or good—is nothing, 254, 1649. Whatever passes with such speed is as though it were not, 392. Time seems short to the one who orders it, but long to the one who loves it, 435. Whatever comes to an end is short, 469, 538. Scripture often uses the future for the past and the past for the future, 1121. Time flees with speed, 1451. What is the acceptable time, 1479.

The wicked seek temporal goods, but the good do not do so in the same way, 28. Temporal goods are to be considered of little value because we either have not had them or will not have them forever, 50. When God strips us, he does not take away our possessions but his own, 51. One who presses toward eternal goods bears the loss of temporal things lightly, 94, 985. One who serves the love of temporal things is tormented by countless cares, 129. Temporal goods are to be despised in comparison with eternal ones, 172, 254, 1320. The labor of those who hunger after transitory goods is empty, 230. The righteous despise temporal things, 263. Tears shed because of earthly goods are vicious, 314. Desire for temporal things increases as the end of life approaches, 357. Temporal goods, which God grants even to the perverse, are to be despised, 432. Those who cling lovingly to temporal things prosper along with things that are passing, 539. To flee from the God who stands firm is to cling to passing things, 698. The less a person usually possesses of eternal things, the more he rejoices that temporal things are present, ibid. The saints endure the burden of temporal goods either by giving them away or by laying it all down through contempt, ibid. To serve temporal things is exceedingly hard, 979. With what caution those who defend temporal goods too vigorously should be reproved, 1008. It is shameful to love what plainly perishes quickly, 1447, 1489, 1569. In comparison with the reward of eternity, the goods of the servant who has faithfully dispensed them are called few, 1464. To the one who dispenses temporal goods well, understanding of spiritual things is granted, 1466. Temporal things become worthless to the one who loves eternal things, 1569, 1626. Temporal things should be used, while eternal things should be desired, 1625. Who should use temporal things, ibid.

Man is surrounded by darkness, 144. How great are the inner darknesses of man in this life, ibid. What it means to suffer darkness in the daytime, 196. The wretched man voluptuously endures the darkness of his own condemnation, 213, 653. What it means to say in the light what has been heard in darkness, 376. Whoever does not seek the light of righteousness does not depart from darkness, 413. What it means to make one’s bed in darkness, 433. Darkness signifies sadness, 439. Darkness also signifies sinners, 550; ignorance, 790. What it means that the Lord places darkness and makes it night, 876. Darkness signifies iniquity, 931. When the darknesses of the mind have been shaken off, the mind itself is lifted above itself, 1045. Love of the light dispels the darknesses of the heart, 1400. The one who fell into inner darkness through sin is cast out into outer darkness as punishment, 1466, 1644. Inner darkness signifies blindness of heart; outer darkness signifies the night of condemnation, ibid.

Why God permits man to be tempted, 64, 757. The devil tempts Job through his wife, just as he tempted Adam through Eve, 78. The devil tempts us through those who cling to us, ibid. The saints desire to be tempted, 251. In how many ways we are tempted, 244. God does not permit us to be tempted beyond measure, 320, 324, 937. God permits temptation only justly, 558. Why beginners are not often tempted, 773. God’s testing is to question us by great commands, 898. A strong temptation is called a violent wind, 59, 68. How variously the devil lies in wait for our virtues, 65. The gift of discernment in temptation, 66. Temptation takes place, while the soul remains safe, when consent is refused, 96. Temptation is a struggle against evil spirits, 244. Temptation is warfare, ibid. Why human life itself is called temptation, ibid. No one in this life is free from the temptation of sin, 251, 266. Man is moved like a leaf by the wind of temptation, 387. Unclean temptation consumes human flesh like a moth consumes clothing, 389. Violent temptation is called the cry of the exactor, 982, 988.

There are two kinds of temptation, 77, 401, 557. The kinds of the devil’s temptations against rebels, 120. The difference between the temptations of the righteous and the unrighteous, 326. The multitude of temptations sometimes overwhelms, 354. The various temptations of man, 387. What human temptation is, 580. What demonic temptation is, 681. The three stages of temptation, 771.

Man is tested by temptations, 265. What it means that God is said to lead, or not to lead, us into temptation, 76, 429. God sometimes abandons us in order to protect us, 95. Those whom God has enriched with gifts he tests by temptations, 265. As the light of righteousness increases in the soul, temptations increase, 936. The devil arouses harsher temptations when he hides snares under the appearance of virtue, 1069.

The cause of temptation is presumption, whether it exists or lest it exist, 71. Human life, fallen from the condition of its creation, became for itself the source from which it is tempted, 244. Why God permits the mind rising toward what is right to be attacked, 348, 850. Unclean temptation arises in man not from elsewhere but from himself, 389. The devil’s various temptations, 454, 944. Why temptation follows conversion, 772.

The devil’s arts of temptation, 34. The devil tempts us in three ways, ibid. Times suitable for temptations, 47. Why the devil sometimes rests from temptations, 95. Temptation sometimes knocks from outside and inside, 98. The diversity of temptations, 226, 773, 1102. How one temptation follows another, 244. The condition of the soul oppressed by the force of an urgent temptation, 354. Some are overthrown by sudden temptations, others by slow and flattering ones, 401. The enemy attacks us on every side with the arrows of temptation, 424. The demon tempts according to each person’s character, 441, 937. Sudden temptation kills some, slow and prolonged temptation kills others, 476. At the end of time many weak people will succumb to temptations, while the strong grieve over their fall, 612. Temptation is sometimes drawn in through the eyes and sometimes conceived inwardly, 684. Why temptations are harsher after conversion than before it, 772, 773. What the measure of consolation and temptation is for converts, 773. Temptations often do not appear, 774. Temptations are dangerous when despised through their persistence, ibid. Joy follows temptation when it has been conquered with God’s help, ibid. The violence of temptation, 915. How great the devil’s temptation is, 937. God moderates temptations so that they are neither too many nor too great, ibid. How greatly capital vices stir the mind by temptation, 1036. When the end of life draws near, temptations become heavier, 1064. The devil tempts men through three vices: lust, malice, and pride, 1094. Why the devil is called a beast of burden, a dragon, and a bird, ibid. Against one whom the beast could not reach, the dragon came, 1095. He tempts religious minds in one way and those devoted to the world in another, 1102. The devil attempts to corrupt the minds of the faithful now by action, now by persuasion, 1103. He mocks some under the appearance of holiness and baits others with filthy vices, 1129. Why the devil’s temptation is called a whirlwind, 1187. Temptation is conducted in three ways, 1492.

God would not have permitted Job to be tested if he had foreseen that he would perish, 44. The pious mind amid adversities suffered from men rests in the consolation of divine grace, 48. The devil does not wound the hearts of the good unto destruction; rather, they become more cautious through it, 64, 69, 71, 298. We grow through being instructed by temptation, 71. Temptation instructs us, ibid., 757. Temptations give others an example of virtue, 74. Temptations prove what sort of person someone is, ibid. The elect become richer in virtues insofar as the crafty enemy tempts them more frequently, 202. Temptation often extinguishes good impulses, 226. Temptation assists salvation, 251. The elect do not fear temptation but prepare themselves against it, ibid. In temptation it is uncertain whether God is testing or killing, 298. In temptation man is somewhat abandoned by grace so that he may be humbled, 323. God strengthens the righteous person in temptation, 324. After temptation the mind is more vigorous, 354. Temptation cannot be absent from man in this life, 443. The wondrous effects of temptation, 609. Without temptations man cannot live at all, 754. Through temptation we learn what we can do by our own strength and what by divine gift, ibid. How much temptation contributes to progress, 755. Temptation knocks at us but does not overthrow us, ibid. Whatever is sweet becomes bitter through the force of temptation, 757. The usefulness of temptation, ibid., 758. Temptation gives self-knowledge, ibid. In temptation the strength of the soul is revealed, ibid. In temptation we are freed from impending corruption, 759. After harsh temptations the light of truth breaks forth upon our mind, 764. God tests by temptations; he does not reject, 774. God permits us to be struck by temptation so that we may not presume upon ourselves, 850. The violence of temptation casts down thoughts of virtue, ibid. One caught in temptation falls into the darkness of sorrow, 851. Beginners are pressed by temptations so that they may not become exalted and may afterward progress more securely, 946. Through temptations the saints become more solicitous to preserve their gifts, 947. Temptation is sometimes the guardianship of merits, 1092. Christ took our temptations upon himself in order to overcome them, 1492.

When the devil attacks us through temptation, he is pierced by our humility and patience, 51, 1074. Precautions for avoiding temptations, 68, 70. Those struck by temptations should flee to the grief of repentance and to humility, 70, 96. What the tempted person should do, 72. How to resist harsh or flattering temptations, 98. The beginnings of temptations must be resisted, 115, 685. The exactor’s voice is not heard when the tempter is resisted, 136. A soul nourished by the food of God’s word becomes stronger in temptation, 201. When guilt tempts the mind, it should consider how brief its pleasure is, 330. How God comes to the aid of the soul almost succumbing to the gravest temptation, 354. Whoever sets aside the sword of God’s word cannot resist temptations, 634. The hidden root of temptations must be completely uprooted, 774. God helps us in temptation, ibid. He whom God created in kindness he does not permit to be tortured or tempted unjustly, 822. What the person pressed by temptations should do, 851, 910, 937. Love of neighbor breaks unjust suggestions, 916. Our enemy should die from the place from which he arises, 974. The soldier of God, being strong, despises temptations, 1032. The repulsion of temptations, ibid. Remedies against temptations, 1116. In temptations one must pray more fervently, 1441.

Why God rarely permits beginners to be tempted, 773. Whatever was flattering in the world becomes temptation to the mind returning to God, 200. Temptations arising from the recollection of shameful things are dangerous, 326. How severely the newly converted are tempted, 772. Whoever is broken by temptation does not seriously consider God’s providence, 822. Satan subjects converts to harsher temptations, 1302. Of what things the Teacher and Pastor should take care to remind them, ibid.

What the temptation of religious people is like, 1068.

Some temptations belong to the righteous, others to the wicked, 98. The temptations of the righteous are useful, ibid. God allows the devil to renew war against the saints so that, being defeated more often, he may fall silent, 75. The devil tempts those who stand either by breaking them through tribulations or softening them through persuasions, 77. Those who despise his tyranny stir up the devil against themselves, 120. The saints fear temptations, 157. Why the saints desire to be tempted and scourged, 220. Those whom God has enriched with gifts he tests by temptations, 265. The saints are struck by temptations so that they may learn what they are from God and what they are from themselves, ibid., 1074. God moderates scourges according to the strength of the saints, 320. The saints are tempted lest they fall into pride, 327, 607, 850, 1098. Temptation sometimes inclines the righteous almost to despair, 354. Temptations cleanse vices and increase merits, 516. When the wisdom and patience of the saints are made manifest in temptations, 557. Temptations of vices are not absent even from the perfect, 609.
