We cannot live without temptations in any retreat, 754. All the elect are subject to temptations, 759. In the exercise of temptations, joy succeeds sorrow, 772. Temptations are harsher after divine illumination, 937. The saints do not consent to the violent temptations of the devil, 982. Because long-lasting peace makes many idle, the saints rejoice to be tempted, 1034. No unforeseen temptations assail the saints, and therefore do not overcome them, ibid. Those who seek the way of holiness, having sometimes fallen into error, are corrected more slowly, 1070. It is fitting that the devil be conquered by dust, since he thought himself strong after abandoning his Creator, 1074. The devil especially lies in wait for the saints, 1083. By tempting the saints, the devil unwillingly preserves them for the kingdom, 1092. In tempting the saints, the devil serves their advantage and God’s will, 1093. Those carried up to contemplation are wearied by temptations lest they forget their own weakness, 1321. Temptation weighs them down lest contemplation puff them up, ibid. The temptations of the wicked are useless, 98. Wicked people who murmur in temptation come to nothing, 72. The devil’s temptations are sweet to the wicked, 499. The devil’s temptation kindles the reprobate to various vices, 1114. God permits some things to the tempter and denies others, 46, 76. The tempter’s cunning, 47. The devil does not tempt those whom he has obedient to himself, 120. While fighting against the many-formed adversary, we must prepare ourselves in many ways, 202. If the first suggestion is not resisted, the tempter suddenly slips wholly into the inner chambers of the heart, 554, 1064. The speech and cry of the exactor are an incipient and violent temptation, 982. What is meant by the pact constituted by the permission granted the devil to tempt, 1093. The tempter rages more fiercely the nearer he is to the completion of his punishment, 1115.

The tempted person learns not only from whom he receives strength but also with what vigilance he must preserve it, 69. Those who are tempted approach death unless they are delivered by God, 759.

What a tent signifies, 861. The losses caused by lukewarmness, when seen in others, usually move us more deeply, 233.

Who the boundaries of the earth are, 869, 870. Why earth is called the mother of all things, 51. By the name of earth into which Job fell, sinful pagan humanity is designated, 61. The Incarnation of the Mediator may be signified by earth, 93. By the name of earth, flesh is expressed, 307. What the dark earth is, 331. Why this earth is called one of miseries but not of darkness, 332. Earth signifies the sinner, 368, 371, 483, 1273. What it means that God overturns the earth, 371. By the name of earth the Church is signified, 547; likewise the soul of the righteous, 903. Earth always remains in its essence, although in its image it continually passes away, 539. What it means to make the earth cry out and lament its furrows, 724. Earth designates a person who thinks of lowly things, 926. The face of the earth is renewed when infused with grace, 941. Earth signifies the word of God, 1010. What the lower parts of the earth are, 1040. What the heights of the earth are, ibid. The shaking of the earth signifies the sinner’s repentance, 1273. Whoever leaves the earth through earthly preoccupation does not leave it but desires the earth, 1372. What it means for the earth to burn, 1577. Thorny earth is sometimes loved more than earth that has never had thorns, 1602.

Concern for earthly things is not free from disturbance, 30, 67. When it is properly governed, ibid. Those attached to earthly rewards are not upright, 154. The multiplicity of earthly concerns blinds, 411. Concern for earthly things is burdensome to the righteous, 432. The righteous despise earthly things out of love for heavenly things, for which they sigh, 510. The carnal desire earthly things even when they cannot possess them, 536. Earthly things are compared with sleep, 568. Earthly business must not be entrusted to spiritual men, 627. Our light falls to earth when we desire earthly things, 637. What the saints despise, the wicked desire, 652. Those who rejoice in transitory things are afflicted by heavy cares, 653. The multiplicity of earthly things is signified by the name of mud, 1128. Contempt for earthly things is a sign of unbroken virtue, 1023. The eternal reward of one who faithfully dispenses earthly goods, 1464. The vanity of earthly things, 1568. The bent woman signifies one thinking about earthly things, 1585. By giving earthly things, God urges us toward heavenly things, 1591.

What Job scraping the bodily pus with a potsherd teaches us, 76, 87, 96. A potsherd before the fire is clay; it is hardened by fire, 1534. The potsherd signifies Christ’s humanity, hardened by the fire of his Passion, ibid.

The saints of the Old Testament desired the law of love by which they might serve God, 385. With ardent desires the saints of the Old Testament longed for Christ, 434. Not everything we read in the Old Testament is to be imitated, 559.

The Old Testament is called a shady mountain, 1075. What it means for the devil to preside over the mountain of the Testament, 1186. The Old Testament is signified by the wheel that appeared above the earth to Ezekiel, 1216. The New Testament lay hidden in the letter of the Old, 1217. The agreement of both Testaments, 1218. The Old Testament, spiritually understood, and the New Testament remain unchangeable, 1220. The Old Testament punishes evil deeds; the New also punishes illicit thoughts, 1335. What the Fathers of the Old Testament contribute to the firmness of faith, 1336. In the Old Testament we find the precepts of action and examples of virtue, 1337. The death of the righteous is a help to the good but a testimony against the wicked, 1614. They are witnesses of God who bear witness to eternal truth by the example of good works, 328.

What the chambers are in the Church, 1332, 1378. The chambers have one measure in length and breadth, 1332. Many chambers make one, 1333. What the three chambers on this side and three on that side signify, 1344, 1353, 1378. What the margin before the chambers signifies, 1348. What the one-cubit margin signifies, ibid. What the roof of the chamber signifies, 1353. What the great breadth from the roof of the chamber to the roof of the gate signifies, 1355. How Christ the Bridegroom proceeded from his chamber, 1636.

Tharsilla, the aunt of Saint Gregory, a virgin devoted to good works, 1642. Called to glory by Saint Felix, pope and great-great-grandfather of Saint Gregory, she died most holy, ibid. After her death she appeared to her sister Aemiliana, whom she called to glory, 1643.

Thema. Whence “Themanite,” that is, “one coming from the heat of immoderate wisdom,” as heretics do, 91. *Thema* is interpreted as “south wind,” ibid. *Theman* signifies the same, 230.

Theodore is snatched from the very jaws of the devil, 1515, 1643. After a life wasted in vices, he was converted at the end of his life, 1644.

Theophanius dealt with temporal things more from duty than from intention, 1626. He was a man devoted to works of mercy, ibid. He rested in a most holy end, ibid. By his example we learn that neither the good nor the evils of this life should hold us back from love of eternal things, 1627.

The treasure in the field is hope in repentance, 35. The saints are compared with those digging out treasure, 142. Why it is called treasure, 934. The treasure hidden in the field is heavenly desire, 1472.

By the name of breastplate the strength of patience is designated, 1123. The twelve thrones signify the universal judgment, 838. For the Lord to sit on a throne with the Father means that he is equal to the Father in power, ibid. For the saints to sit on thrones with Christ means that they judge by his authority, ibid. Why the throne is compared with a sapphire stone, ibid. Christ is above the throne and himself beneath the throne, 1244. Thrones are called the spirits in which the Lord sits and through which he decrees his judgments, 1605. God presides over all the angels, but more fully over the thrones, 1608.

The virtue of prayer is expressed by incense, 1470.

The hypocrite is called a tiger, 156. The tiger signifies the devil, 157.

What it means to fear God, 18. What should be feared, 45. God’s judgment must be feared not only because of the evils we have done but also because of the good things we have done, 83, 143, 145, 256, 312, 314. In prosperity the saints should fear divine judgments concerning themselves, 139, 255. Surrounded by darkness, we must fear God’s judgments concerning us, 144, 932. The mind trembles more deeply over its deeds the more highly it is raised toward God, 162. We must fear lest God keep his hand bound against striking our vices, 220. Death must always be feared because its hour is uncertain, 233. Some do not know how to fear God unless they are terrified by adversity, whether their own or another’s, 235. Exaltation arising from virtues themselves must be feared, 245, 251. Why the saints always fear, 302, 312, 514, 518, 683, 776, 1231. In their good works the righteous fear idleness and deceit, 312. The righteous fear lest present punishments be the beginnings of future ones, 319. The righteous fear God before experiencing him as angry, 381. The righteous escape God’s judgments by fearing them, 514. The invisible God, who sees all things, is to be feared by us all the more, 515. While the wicked display security, the righteous always fear, 520. Whoever does not fear God as just will not find him merciful, 532, 1091. God alone is powerful and to be feared, 541. Those who now tremble will not fear Christ at the final judgment, 1231. From the point by which he terrifies the minds of the good, he also protects them, 1232. The wicked are not to be feared, but the judgments of the righteous are to be feared, 1254. One who does not fear God should not be feared, ibid. Why the good, not the wicked, should be feared, 1259, 1270.

Whoever does good out of fear has not wholly departed from evil, 29. What good fear is, 124. What the fear of the saints is like, 137, 139, 1030. The way of God begins with fear, 153. Fear of God drives out every other fear, ibid. The saints rejoice with fear over conquered vices, 158. Fear of God in life excludes fear of the devil in death, 203. The weight of fear is the anchor of the heart, 208. Those who abandon righteousness through fear of temporal losses fall into eternal evils, 225. How useful fear of the final judgment is for salvation, 270. Fear could not rouse us from sin, 317. Fear does not render God worthy service for his gifts, 318. Fear arising from consideration of divine strictness penetrates the soul, 350. Who is free from fear, 353. Whoever serves God through fear cannot be righteous, 386. Fear of God is his gift, 520. Fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, 610. What the night terrors are, 638. How powerful the fear of God is in persuading us to despise everything, 695. One progresses from fear to love, 722. The saints’ fear arises from uncertainty about perseverance, 798. God first chastises us through fear of judgment and afterward refreshes us with the consolation of heavenly sweetness, 868. The sound from God’s mouth is the force of fear rushing upon us through heavenly inspiration, ibid. Divine fear is the foundation of faith, 903. God sets the barriers of inspired fear against the wicked movements of the heart, 915. Whoever God shakes with fear, he holds fast, 920. Fear must be joined to hope, 932, 994, 1030, 1091. Our hope should bear the bite of fear against presumption, 1090. One fear is chaste, another servile, 1134. Fear and repentance conceal the past evils of the saints, 1203, 1233. We are armed with fear and vigilance, 1306. The usefulness and effect of fear of God, 1354. One ascends from fear to wisdom, 1380. Fear of the Lord without piety is worthless before God, ibid. The distinction between fear and humility, 1254. What fear of the Lord is like, 1380.

Why Timothy was not healed by Saint Paul, 870, 1449. What the purest tinctures are, 599.

What thunder signifies, 938. Where topaz gets its name and what it signifies, 597.

Torments afflict many but do not correct them, 214. Torments do not restrain some from their abandoned ways, 839.

What it means to tread the winepress of the Church, 526. What was hidden from the sluggish becomes more subtly known to those who mourn, 259. Confidence in the saints drives out sluggishness, 314. Tranquility of mind comes from a single desire for the heavenly homeland, 129. The source of the love of tranquility, 133. Whatever cannot persist in tranquility brings confusion upon itself, 289.

Why the garments of the transfigured Christ became white as snow, 1051. How the good and the wicked regard transitory things, 28. To those passing through the world, temporal prosperity seems worthless, 496. People pass through life and pass completely through death, 789. What it means for one passing in mind from this world to desire to serve God, 1196. What it means that the Lord, “passing by,” ministers to his servants, 1482. What the Lord’s passing means, ibid.

What Gideon’s three hundred soldiers signify, 990.

The various kinds of tribulations, whether of the good or of the wicked, 12. Joy arising from satiety is a forewarning of tribulation, 47. The perfection of the number thirty, 1365. The number thirty pertains to the active and contemplative life, ibid. What it means to bear thirtyfold fruit, 1358.

The unity of the Trinity demonstrated in Scripture, 948, 949, 1345. After the Resurrection the blessed recognize the Trinity distinctly, 964. Sadness leads to avarice, ibid. What the daughters of sadness are, 1035. What the temptations of sadness are like, 1036.

What the two silver trumpets made by Moses signify, 962. What their cut-off blast signifies, 963. What it means to blow the trumpet, 1026. What it means not to fear the sound of the trumpet, ibid. What it means to sound the blast of the trumpet, 1034.

Pride must be avoided when doing good to one’s neighbors, 341. The swelling of one who boasts modestly of singular wisdom must be restrained, 359. The first form of swelling is believing that one possesses goodness from oneself, 736. The second is believing that it has been given to oneself for one’s merits, 737. The third is falsely attributing some good to oneself, ibid. The fourth is claiming it for oneself alone while despising others, ibid. The swelling of the mind is an obstacle to truth, 745. The tumult of the heart is the force of a great cry, 146. External tumults never reach the inner beings of the righteous, 590.

The tunic reaching to the ankle is a good work continued to completion, 1546. What the command to divide two tunics with one’s neighbor implies, 1521.

When turtledoves and a pigeon were offered in sacrifice, the throat was cut but not completely severed, 195. What the nest of the turtledove is, 629. What is signified by the two turtledoves, 1048. The tambourine signifies mortification of the body, 1097, and abstinence, 1238.

conceal [them] under the guise of virtue, 99. Some vices feign virtues, ibid., 740, 1069, 1223, 1303. The vice of defending error, inherited from Adam, persists to the present day, 119. Vices tinged with the color of virtues are all the more wicked because they are not recognized as vices, 1014. Pride disguises itself under the authority [of office], and human fear under humility, 1254. A fruitful but neglected vine is a figure of the hypocrite, 276. Glass reveals whatever it contains within, 593. What glass signifies, ibid. What the heifer of threshing signifies, 654. How the calf, lion, and sheep dwell together in the Church, 1343. In Scripture, “living” is used for “knowing,” 565. What God’s calling is, 40. The incarnate Wisdom calls the elect to their eternal homeland, 54. God calls people from every class of humanity to knowledge of him, 190. God calls when he chooses us by loving us; we respond to him by obeying, 386. He calls when he goes before us with gifts, to which we respond by using them well, 455. Those whose hearts were lairs of lions were called to the faith, 555. Let the one who has been called call another, 1322. In the various stages of life, people are called by God into the vineyard, 1511, 1512. When the Lord calls, the faithful multiply beyond measure, 1513. Who are called but not chosen, 1585. What it means for a person to be called by God “before his face” or “behind his back,” 1610. The poor and the weak, the blind and the lame, are called and come, 1622. The condemnation of those who do not obey God when he calls, 1624. In how many ways God calls us and calls us back from errors, ibid. Others are called in place of those who reject the call, 1637. “Many are called, but few are chosen”: a profoundly fearful saying, 1641. Those assured of their calling to the faith should not presume upon their calling to the eternal kingdom, 1514. The various callings, 1624. Some not only reject the grace of the call offered to them but also persecute it, 1637.

[Col. 1512] The birds of heaven signify the wise who pursue lofty things, 368. The flight of animals signifies the sublimity of evangelists and teachers, 1144. Holy Scripture sometimes understands the birds of heaven in a bad sense, sometimes in a good one, 603. Ambitious people are called the birds of heaven, 823, 825. Why Scripture is called a flying scroll, 475. People fulfill God’s will even when unwilling, 194, 195. One must serve a known will, 196. One must subject one’s own will and the pursuits of one’s life to God, 350. God considers the will of the wicked rather than the outcome, 408. By our own will we fulfill what the devil wrongly suggests to us, 424. Evil wills are ordered by God, 519. How people conform themselves to the divine will, 590. Will is required for everything desired in this life, 810. In what ways God makes his will known, 894. How harmful it is to follow one’s own wills, 906. Nothing is more difficult for a person than to break his own wills, 1071. Those whom a perverse will corrupt are generally corrected by adversity, 1117. The will must be broken in accordance with God’s pleasure, 1297. How great is the substance of a good will, 1379, 1451. Before God’s eyes, the hand is never empty of a gift if the chest of the heart is filled with good will, ibid. Nothing richer than good will is offered to God, ibid. What constitutes good will, ibid. To will to do something is already to do it in the mind, 1562.

When elders serve pleasure, the restraints of wantonness are loosened in their juniors, 49. The perfection of pleasure is sought in vain, 128. Every descent is into pleasure, 224. Whoever now expands himself wickedly in pleasures will later be constricted by punishment in torments, 439. Pleasure often arises from necessity, 649. The wicked consider delights to consist in remaining beneath the senses, 654. Few escape the pit and destruction of pleasures, 669. God teaches us to avoid the pleasures of the flesh, 823. How people fall into the pleasure of beasts, 824. Under the appearance of necessity, pleasure disguises itself in eating, 984. Desire for filthy pleasure is designated by the name “mud,” 1129. Against the pleasures of the world, 1471. Let former pleasures return to the memory so that they may be mourned, ibid.

The sooner a bad vow is permitted to be fulfilled, the sooner it is punished, 479. As punishment for sin, it happens that a vow made to God is not fulfilled because of weakness; 510. To utter an oath is to bind oneself by a vow to divine service, 1048. How satisfaction is made for sins committed against vows, ibid. Whenever good vows attain their fulfillment, they multiply, 1145. Those consecrated to God by a vow are a burnt offering to be washed by tears, 1398.

The voice of angels. See “Locution.” The voice of the saints—what it is, 42. The voice of the head is often transferred to the voice of the body, and often the voice of the body to the voice of the head, 637. The voice of God is said to be heard not in joy but in terror, 868. How the voice of the Lord is heard, 871. The voice of God, awakening the sluggish sinner, is like thunder, ibid. How powerful the voice of God is, 872. How many voices address us, 1239. A voice in the mind is, as it were, a sound of understanding, 1240. How many voices address our senses, ibid. What the voices of the flesh sound like in the soul, ibid. The intellect is the voice of the soul, but beneath the firmament, ibid. What the voice of the firmament is, ibid. What the voice above the firmament is, and how it also speaks to God, 1241.

Who constitute the common poor, 525.

[Col. 1513] Whoever is not struck down by a single wound is struck two or three times, so that he may be wounded to his inmost parts, 48. Closed wounds cause greater torment, 240. How wounds are multiplied without cause, 303. A human being makes a wound from a remedy; God makes a remedy from a wound, 1092. What foxes signify, 603. In what manner the wicked cover their face, 529. What is designated by the name “vulva,” 910. What it means to come forth from the womb, 913. Who the Visigoths are, and how they differ from the Ostrogoths, 2.

# Z

Zacchaeus climbing a sycamore tree in order to see the Lord: whom he signifies, 890. For Zacchaeus, the kingdom of God was worth half his possessions, 1451. God has set Zacchaeus before us as an example of repentance, 1551. [Col. 1513] Zeal is signified by fire, 18. How it comes about that the people perish in the fire of zeal, 58. When zeal for righteousness is aroused, it must not stray from righteousness but obey reason, 178. The zeal of saints rebuking rulers proceeds from humility, not arrogance, 237. Zeal must be restrained within its limits, 341, 1195, 1207. Zeal must be joined to gentleness and justice, 341. Excess of zeal in correction is venial, 344. Heretics call the Church’s zeal fury and madness, 437. What it means to be zealous, 666. Because of the fall of the weak, the strong are burned by the fire of their zeal, 674. What kind and how great a zeal a pastor needs against wrongdoers, 816. Zeal is an iron frying pan, ibid., 1304. With what discretion it must be exercised, 817. It must not proceed from hidden hatred, ibid. Zeal must rage on behalf of righteousness in such a way that it does not satisfy the madness of fury, 848, 1501. The zeal of the saints [Col. 1514] for the Church, 1005. What the idol of zeal is, ibid. By what tricks the devil tries to extinguish the zeal of charity toward one’s neighbor, 1069. Through reading Sacred Scripture, the fervor of zeal is aroused, 1228. How necessary zeal is for a preacher, even when it causes pain, 1304. Zeal for souls is a sacrifice more pleasing to God, ibid. Strong zeal is a frying of the heart, ibid. The mind of the righteous, burned by the ardor of zeal, is signified by fine flour mixed with oil and fried in a pan, ibid., 1305. If zeal has no love, the flour lacks heat, ibid. The soul of the righteous, burned by zeal, becomes a sacrifice and holocaust to the Lord, ibid. The strong action of zeal, ibid. Neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity pleases God, 1578. What it means to have a golden belt around the breasts, 1128.

[Col. 1513]

## TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

[Col. 1513] CONTINUATION OF THE MORAL BOOKS OF ST. GREGORY.

**BOOK XVII.**—Explains what remains of chapter 24 of the Book of Job, beginning halfway through verse 20, together with chapters 25 and 26 in their entirety, chiefly in the moral sense. 9

**BOOK XVIII.**—Contains an exposition of chapters 27 and 28 of the Book of Job, up to the middle of verse 21, according to their manifold senses. 37

**BOOK XIX.**—The exposition having been carried from the final part of verse 21 of chapter 28 up to, but excluding, verse 21 of the following chapter, various senses are opened up no less learnedly than piously, especially concerning Christ and the Church. 95

**BOOK XX.**—The five final verses of chapter 29 of the Book of Job, together with the whole of chapter 30, are explained at greater length, especially concerning heretics and carnal people who vex the Church. 135

**BOOK XXI.**—Chapter 31 of the Book of Job is expounded through verse 24 exclusively; after first praising chastity, humility, and mercy, it teaches chiefly many things about avoiding occasions of sin. 187

**BOOK XXII.**—What remains of chapter 31 of the Book of Job is explained, with particular commendation of lowliness and moderation of spirit, patience, charity, and solicitude toward subjects. 211

**BOOK XXIII.**—Chapters 32 and 33 are expounded through verse 22, where, while Job is silent, the younger Elihu sets forth many things that are right and sound, though not with a right or sound intention. 249

**BOOK XXIV.**—The eleven verses following in chapter 33 and the first eighteen verses of chapter 34 are expounded; excellent instruction is given concerning Christ the mediator, contemplation, the order of conversion, and the pastoral office. 287

**BOOK XXV.**—In the explanation of chapter 34, from verse 19 to verse 30, the punishment of the reprobate and God’s hidden judgments are discussed. 319

**BOOK XXVI.**—The holy Doctor expounds the seven final verses of chapter 34 and chapter 35 in its entirety, together with the first twenty-one verses of chapter 36. Here he ranges very widely through both allegorical and moral senses. 347

**BOOK XXVII.**—The twelve final verses of chapter 36 are expounded, together with the whole of chapter 37, with ingenious interpretations sought to establish both Christian doctrine and Christian ethics. 399

**BOOK XXVIII.**—The first eleven verses of chapter 38 are explained in their manifold senses, especially the moral sense. 445

**BOOK XXIX.**—Twenty-two verses of chapter 38, from verse 12 through verse 33 inclusive, are explained; many things are taught, especially concerning Satan’s arts and snares, grace, predestination, reprobation, and God’s hidden judgments. 477

**BOOK XXX.**—Contains an exposition of the eight final verses of chapter 38 and an equal number of verses from chapter 39. Here the holy Doctor speaks at great length, piously and learnedly, especially concerning the preaching of the Gospel. 521

**BOOK XXXI.**—Verse 9 and the remaining verses of chapter 39 are explained, with only the final three omitted; the efficacy of divine grace, especially in the preaching of the Gospel and the conversion of sinners, is demonstrated. 571

[Col. 1514] **BOOK XXXII.**—After the final two verses of chapter 39 have been explained, the first fourteen verses of chapter 40 are expounded; many things are taught both about God’s infinite power and about Satan’s harmful designs against human beings. 631

**BOOK XXXIII.**—Presents an exposition of verse 15 and the remaining verses of chapter 40, as well as the first twelve verses of chapter 41, where various arts of the devil are exposed, and gratuitous predestination is taught and reconciled with free will. 667

**BOOK XXXIV.**—Verse 13 of chapter 41 and the remaining verses are expounded, especially concerning the devil’s pride and the fiercest persecutions of the saints by Antichrist. 717

**BOOK XXXV AND LAST.**—In this book, many matters already stated are recalled by way of recapitulation, and this immense work is brought to a close with the most humble confession of human weakness. 749

Admonition concerning the following books of homilies. 781

## THE FIRST BOOK OF HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 785

**HOMILY I.**—About to expound the prophet, the holy Doctor first speaks concerning the times and modes of prophecy. 786

**HOMILY II.**—The first five verses of Ezekiel’s prophecy are expounded according to their manifold senses, especially the allegorical and moral senses. 795

**HOMILY III.**—Four verses, from the sixth through the tenth, are expounded concerning holy preachers and their twofold life, active and contemplative. 806

**HOMILY IV.**—In explaining the tenth, eleventh, and beginning of the twelfth verses, many moral precepts are proposed, especially concerning continual attention directed toward God and attentiveness to oneself. 814

**HOMILY V.**—In the exposition of three verses, from the twelfth through the fifteenth, a learned discussion is given concerning the Holy Spirit and his impulse, movement, and indwelling in the saints. 821

**HOMILY VI.**—Verses 15, 16, and 17, together with the middle part of verse 18, are explained, with the meaning of the prophetic discourse turned chiefly toward commendation of Sacred Scripture and the Gospel. 828

**HOMILY VII.**—Verse 18 and the five following verses are expounded, chiefly concerning the usefulness of sacred reading and the performance of charitable duties with such caution that we may direct our attention above all to ourselves through repentance. 840

**HOMILY VIII.**—Beginning with verse 24, what remains of the first chapter is explained, together with the beginning of the second chapter; many matters are discussed concerning Christ’s divinity, the Incarnation of the Word, preaching, and the gathering, growth, and unity of the Church. 853

**HOMILY IX.**—The second chapter of Ezekiel is explained; in this exposition many things are interpreted morally, and also much is discussed with great learning concerning the necessity of prevenient grace, the consent and cooperation of free will, and the obscurity and interpretation of Sacred Scripture. 870

**HOMILY X.**—In explaining the opening verses of the third chapter through the fifteenth verse, he commends above all Sacred Scripture, its constant reading, meditation, [Col. 1515] and preaching. 886

**HOMILY XI.**—He continues the explanation of Ezekiel chapter 3, from verse 15 through verse 20, discussing especially the pastoral office, the mutual connection between the sins of prelates and subjects, and the blinding of the mind. 905

**HOMILY XII.**—He proceeds through what remains of the third chapter and carries his explanation through verse 4 of the fourth chapter, turning it toward various moral precepts and counsels for preachers and hearers. 919

## THE SECOND BOOK OF HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 933

**HOMILY I.**—In explaining the first three verses of Ezekiel chapter 40 and the beginning of the fourth, he discusses especially Christ and the Church, the elect, and God’s hidden judgments concerning them. 935

**HOMILY II.**—In explaining two verses of chapter 40, namely the fourth and fifth, the holy Doctor discusses at length the active and contemplative life and, in his customary manner, intersperses many moral teachings. 948

**HOMILY III.**—In the explanation of three verses, the building of the Church, constructed from all the righteous under both Testaments, is chiefly described. 958

**HOMILY IV.**—After four verses, from the ninth through the twelfth, have been explained allegorically or morally, the work is brought to completion. 972

**HOMILY V.**—From the final part of verse 12 through verse 17 of Ezekiel chapter 40 is expounded, and contemplation is discussed especially. 984

**HOMILY VI.**—Only three verses are explained, and it is shown how great a perfection has shone forth in Christians, and especially in the apostles. 998

**HOMILY VII [Elsewhere XIX].**—Contains an explanation of seven verses, from 20 through 27, and at the same time presents many moral precepts concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the stages leading to them, true perfection, and the necessity of good works. 1012

**HOMILY VIII [Elsewhere XX].**—Verse 27 and the remaining verses, through verse 38 inclusive, are explained—most briefly in some cases, more fully in others—and the doctrine of the resurrection is chiefly established. 1027

**HOMILY IX [Elsewhere XXI].**—Five verses, from 39 through 43, are proposed for explanation; with scarcely any attempt at the literal sense, the spiritual and moral senses are brought forth, and the pastoral office is discussed above all. 1041

**HOMILY X [Elsewhere XXII].**—In explaining four verses, from 44 through 48, the holy Doctor ranges more freely over faith, hope, charity, and the good works to be offered to God upon the altar of the heart, and brings this work to completion. 1058

Admonition concerning the following work. 1071
